### Series Title Page

*The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscripts, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continually illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with separate analytical indexes following each volume and each author of importance; embellished with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance, and the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily learn which Fathers commented on the individual books of Scripture and in what places of their works they did so. An extremely accurate edition, easily to be preferred to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and the number of the works reprinted, the very convenient format of the volumes, consistently alike throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this collection itself—single, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but gathered for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.*

## [Appendix to the Works of Saint Leo the Great]

### [Col. 0009]

## To the Reader

Why we add this volume, which contains an excellent and most ancient collection of canons and other documents of ancient canon law, to the edition of the works of Saint Leo the pope under the name of an appendix must be explained briefly. Quesnell included the aforementioned collection of canons after the works of Saint Leo in his edition because he thought it was a code of the Roman Church, which had been used under the pontificates of Innocent, Zosimus, and Leo and had received many additions from Leo himself. Although we shall prove in this same volume, in our observations on Quesnell’s twelfth dissertation, that this is entirely false, nevertheless, so that nothing might be lacking from our edition—for we promised to reproduce the whole Quesnellian edition—the same code of canons had to be reprinted.

Since his edition, however, did not present the code itself in a wholly complete form, nor consistently with the better and more genuine readings, what we have accomplished in restoring and illustrating it will become clear from the preface attached to it, and still more clearly from the annotations placed after it. On this occasion, since it was necessary to work through manuscript codices and documents of the most ancient canon law, we discovered many things by which ancient canon law could be illuminated. We perceived that publishing these materials would be useful and welcome. Hence we have added the old Latin edition of the canons, which, because it appeared in the very rare *Bibliotheca juris canonici* prepared by Guillaume Voellus and Henri Justel, is scarcely known, collated against the manuscripts, complete, and more accurately corrected.

Moreover, we decided to insert several other extremely ancient and previously unpublished translations of the Greek canons, and to append certain selected documents of ancient canon law that had not yet been printed or had not been sufficiently circulated.

Since, for these reasons, we had examined very many manuscript copies of ancient collections, both published and unpublished, on which ancient canon law depends, we judged that a treatise should be prepared and prefixed on the ancient collections and collectors of canons, both published and unpublished, down to Gratian. From the table of chapters, which we shall append shortly, you will readily see how extensive this treatise is and how much it contains that is useful for illuminating or restoring the canons and for understanding ancient canon law. (As is customary, we have relegated this table to the end of the volume.) Thus this volume is, as it were, a body of ancient canon law, and the ancient sources of that law will be disclosed by the treatise prefixed to it.

Finally, Quesnell’s dissertations on the aforementioned collection of canons had to be added at the end and subjected to critical review through notes and observations. This preliminary explanation should suffice.

### [Col. 0009]

# Preface to His Eminence Fortunatus Tamburini, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church

All who are thoroughly versed in canon law know how greatly the ancient collections of canons preserved in manuscript copies contribute to knowledge of ancient and modern canon law; and you know this especially well, most eminent Cardinal, since among the sacred studies in which you have passed your entire life with the highest distinction, you take particular delight in canon law.

You understand perfectly well that these collections are the sources from which the ancient documents of the canons and papal constitutions arose. You also understand that what several different collections contain, even if each contains little, is to be valued more highly than what the many copies of a single collection contain. For if someone were to discover and examine, for example, one hundred ancient codices of the Dionysian collection, he would find no other canonical monuments than those which Dionysius received. And in those very materials—apart from scribal errors—he would detect an almost astonishing agreement of readings and would learn nothing other than that Dionysius read them in this way.

But whoever consults copies of different collections will repeatedly find different documents; and when, in documents common to several collections, he encounters different readings, he will recognize that he has been greatly assisted, both in correcting scribal mistakes with greater security and in selecting and preferring the best readings from among all of them.

Only two collections were formerly published: the Dionysio-Hadriana and the Isidoriana. Since many ancient documents of canons and decretals were first published by Merlin from the latter—which, besides many spurious materials, had admitted into its genuine documents not a few freer readings and arbitrary corrections, as we shall explain in its proper place—those documents subsequently passed into editions of the councils, and consequently less accurate readings of the same documents became more widely established.

The publication of the Dionysio-Hadriana collection, which was printed after Merlin, was of no small assistance. Yet, apart from the fact that this edition does not present a pure Dionysius, it is of very great importance to know what Dionysius published and what was added to Dionysius. There are also several other collections in manuscript codices that are either older than Dionysius himself or at least derive from a source different from Dionysius.

Quesnell published one of these [Col. 0011]; and when we reprint it in this volume in a more complete and corrected form, the notes to that collection will make clear how much support was supplied by the manuscript copies of the other ancient collections that we discovered.

Knowledge of later collections will also be useful, since their authors took some materials from Dionysius and derived others from elsewhere. Indeed, anyone versed in the matter will readily see how useful it is to describe also those collections that contain abbreviations of earlier ones, or that represent the decrees of the Roman pontiffs and the canons of councils distributed into books and titles, and, if possible, to uncover their origin.

From the whole of this material it will be possible to learn what beginnings and developments the study of canon law had; what was transferred from one collection into others; what the beginnings of the apocryphal materials were; what interpolated, corrupted, or mutilated material crept in; and when documents in the ancient collections began to be divided into parts and distributed according to subjects—a practice long since accepted as more convenient for use.

Therefore, although we owe much to those who have discussed the published collections, we are still greatly indebted to those who, examining ancient archives, have given us some knowledge of the old manuscript collections. Peter Lambecius was planning to publish a description of very many such codices, which abound in the Imperial Library at Vienna, as he himself testifies in Book I, chapter 8, page 932 of his *Commentaries on that Library*. After identifying an exceedingly ancient codex of the Spanish collection in that same library, he adds:

> I shall deal with this matter elsewhere, with God’s will, at much greater length and with greater accuracy, in a special dissertation on more than two hundred ancient and well-regarded manuscript codices of the most august Imperial Library, partly Greek and partly Latin. Through their help and benefit, the history of both general and provincial councils can be enriched to no small degree.

The same idea concerning Roman copies had occurred to Emanuel Schelestratus, keeper of the Vatican Library. In the third volume of his *Antiquities* he intended to publish a *Synodical Work* on the canons of councils, on collections of canons, and on papal decrees. In the appendix to that work he had intended to publish various collections, for the most part extracted from manuscripts, as he recorded in a memorandum left after his death and inserted into the preface to the second volume of the same *Antiquities*.

But no one worked harder than the glory of the Benedictine Order, Father Peter Coustant, in this matter. His preface to the first volume of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs* provides a most ample description of the ancient manuscript collections that he was able to discover.

While we were searching more carefully, with the same purpose, for copies of such collections hidden in libraries, we encountered extremely ancient codices in which partly unknown collections were discovered and partly special information about already published collections came to light. Thus we saw that a fuller treatise could be prepared on collections of canons, both published and unpublished, and that it could appropriately be prefixed to this third volume, which contains an excellent collection and other documents of ancient canon law.

This entire treatise will be divided into four parts. The first will deal with the Greek code of canons and with certain passages, or canons, that present some difficulty in it. The second will concern the older Latin collections, whether older than Dionysius or not derived from Dionysius; among other matters, it will provide an exact examination and distinction of the African canons, which are entangled in many difficulties. The third will explain the Dionysian collection and the others that received certain documents from Dionysius, such as the Hadriana, the Spanish, and the Isidoriana. The fourth will discuss ancient abbreviations of the canons and other Latin collections that arranged canon law into books and titles.

When, on this subject, one of us was speaking with you in Rome, most eminent Cardinal, and was opening to you our entire plan, which had then scarcely been conceived, you added sharper encouragement that it should be completed. After he had returned to his homeland, you most kindly supplied to the work the assistance you had promised whenever it should be needed.

Therefore, confident that you will not find this treatise, whatever its quality, unwelcome, we have thought that it should be addressed to you, so that it may provide a perpetual testimony both to your outstanding interest and favor in this matter and to our grateful spirit and devotion toward you.

### [Col. 0011]

# Disquisitions of the Ballerini  
## On Ancient Collections and Collectors of Canons

# Part One  
## On Greek Collections of Canons

### [V] Chapter One

On the most ancient of all Greek collections of the canons of the apostles. What the collection of Sabinus, the Macedonian bishop of Heraclea, was. The first explicit mention of a Greek code of canons at the Council of Chalcedon. The Code of the Canons of the Universal Church published by Christopher Justel was neither an ancient Greek code nor a code of the universal Church. On the Greek collection attributed to Stephen, bishop of Ephesus.

### [Col. 0011A]

### [Col. 0012A] 1

Although our purpose is chiefly to discuss ancient Latin collections of canons [Col. 0013A], since the most ancient canons of the Greek synods were translated into Latin and transferred into Latin collections, we must first discuss the Greek collection from which the Latin translators derived them.

Moreover, since those canons that circulate under the name of the apostles also reached the Latins in addition to the canons of the Greek councils, we must briefly touch upon the oldest collection of these, about which several writers have discussed at length—not everything that might be said, but what must not be omitted, lest anything appear to be lacking from this treatise.

It is certain that no body can ever be governed or maintained without established laws. Hence there can be no doubt that the apostles laid down definite rules, or canons, for governing the Church. It is sufficiently credible that these rules, which they transmitted orally to the churches, were subsequently collected in writing and headed with the title *Canons of the Apostles*.

Nor do we therefore believe that everything contained in those canons should be attributed to the apostles. For such works commonly retain in their title the name of the person under whose authorship they were first begun or established, even though they are enlarged by various additions, as Father Coustant wisely observed [Col. 0013B] (*In the Preface to Volume I of the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, no. 51).

Since, however, some canons inserted into them contain manifest errors that cannot be attributed to the rules handed down by the apostles, many people readily withheld their assent from them, as Dionysius testifies (*Letter to Stephen*); and they were rightly counted among the apocrypha in the celebrated decree concerning books to be received or not received. Thus the preface to the Spanish collection states:

> As for the canons called apostolic, since neither the Apostolic See receives them nor the holy Fathers have granted them their approval, because they are recognized as having been composed by heretics under the name of the apostles, although some useful things are found in them, it is nevertheless clear that their proceedings have been removed from apostolic authority and assigned to the apocrypha. Whatever is useful in them may be consistent with the apostles.

### [Col. 0013C] 2

The name of the month Hyperberetaeus, which is read in canon 38, shows that these canons were collected and written not by the European Greeks or by the Egyptians, who gave different names to the months, but by Eastern peoples who used the Syro-Macedonian names of the months.

Peter de Marca, in Book III, chapter 2 of his *Concordia*, not implausibly maintains that this collection was assembled before the Council of Nicaea in those regions of the East where the error of rebaptism prevailed. [VI] Most of the regulations laid down in these canons certainly agree with the ecclesiastical discipline of the second and third centuries, and some rules cited by Easterners of the fourth century can be found only in these canons.

### 3

No one disputes the ancient use of these canons, or of this most ancient collection, among the Greeks. See Peter de Marca in the place cited shortly above, and William Beveridge in his *Illustrated Code of the Church of the Primitive Age*.

There is dispute, however, concerning their use among the Latins before Dionysius Exiguus. Some believe that Latin Fathers, and even Roman pontiffs earlier than Dionysius, frequently cited the apostolic canons under the name of ecclesiastical rules, by which they are also designated by Dionysius himself. Quesnell openly asserted this in Dissertation 16, § 6.

But they were not used by the Latins until after the Dionysian translation, which was the first, indeed the only, translation. (See Part II, chapter 10, § 2, no. 12, and our observations on Quesnell’s Dissertation 16.) There is certainly no indication anywhere of an earlier translation by which those canons could have been used by the Latins.

If certain rules mentioned by ancient Latin writers agree with the apostolic canons, that makes no difference. For many such rules had been transmitted orally by the apostles themselves before they were published in Greek under the title *Canons of the Apostles*, and, as orally transmitted rules, they could have been cited by earlier Latin writers before the Greeks’ canons—which were unknown to the Latins before Dionysius [Col. 0014A]—were known to them.

Quesnell made an excellent observation on this point in note 8 on Letter 10 (Vol. II, col. 1324):

> Just as the apostolic canons themselves had been formed by the Easterners from customs and rules transmitted and received, as it were, hand to hand from the apostles and apostolic men, so it is certain that many ecclesiastical rules prevailed in the Roman Church from the earliest times, derived from no other source than ancient custom and the tradition of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. Since these agree with certain apostolic canons, who could be surprised, when the faith of all the apostles was one and their discipline generally one, descending from the school of one teacher? Hence it happened that certain papal enactments appear to have been taken from those canons, as Dionysius Exiguus says in the preface to the canons, whereas in fact those enactments flowed from the source of the common tradition just as much as did the apostolic canons.

He further says that he readily admits that Saint Leo, in the same Letter 10, had one apostolic canon in view, but nevertheless did not wish to call it an apostolic canon, lest authority thereby be lent to doubtful and not-yet-received canons. This conjecture is entirely weak, indeed incredible, unless it is proved that some translation existed before Dionysius by which those same canons were known to the Latins. That, however, has not yet been proved, nor, as we believe, can it ever be proved.

Nor should the decree of Gelasius concerning books to be received or not received be brought forward. Although it was published before Dionysius’s translation and places the apostolic canons among the apocrypha, it nevertheless establishes that Gelasius knew of them in some fashion.

First, Gelasius could have assigned these canons to the apocrypha even though they had not yet been circulated among the Latins, just as he included in the same catalogue certain other Greek works that had not yet been translated into Latin.

Moreover, it seems sufficiently probable to us that this section of Gelasius’s decree concerning the apostolic canons was omitted from most and more authoritative copies of the Gelasian decree and belongs among the additions that have Hormisdas as their author, as we shall conjecture in Part II, chapter 11, § 5. The very words of Dionysius in his *Letter to Stephen, Bishop of Salona*—“because very many did not readily grant their assent to them [the canons], we did not wish Your Holiness to be unaware of this”—indicate that the matter was unknown to the Latins.

Consequently, what follows—“although afterward certain enactments of the pontiffs appear to have been taken from those canons”—must be understood not of Roman pontiffs or Latin bishops, but of the Greeks, certain of whose enactments, issued in episcopal assemblies, as he says there, agree with the apostolic canons.

### 4

This Greek collection of the same canons appears to have been distinct from the code of synodal canons that was compiled later. Hence, in certain manuscript copies, the canons of the Greek synods were marked with a continuous numerical series beginning with the Nicene canons, because the apostolic canons, which ought to have preceded the Nicene canons, were absent from those copies.

For this reason Dionysius Exiguus, who used a Greek code of this kind [Col. 0014D], took the apostolic canons from another code when he prefixed them in Latin to his translation. He found only fifty apostolic canons in his code and translated them into Latin.

In other Greek copies, however, used by John Scholasticus and other later authors of Greek collections, there were eighty-five. We know that this larger number was already ancient from the Council of Constantinople of the year 394. There it was decreed that henceforth no one under examination should be deposed by three bishops, much less by two, but only by the judgment of a larger synod and of the bishops of the province, “as the apostolic canons have defined.” This decree is contained in apostolic canon 74 (Vol. II of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 1380).

But enough concerning this original Greek collection. Anyone wishing to know more should consult Beveridge in the place cited, where he discusses these canons clearly in three books.

### [Col. 0015A] 5

More must be said about another Greek collection, namely, the collection of those canons enacted by synods. These, in particular, flowed into the Latin collections and constitute the principal portion of ancient canon law.

Peter Pithoeus, in his historical synopsis of those who collected the canons, presents Sabinus, bishop of Heraclea in Thrace, as the first compiler of the Greek collection. Socrates, in Book I, chapter 8, testifies that Sabinus composed a compilation of what had been produced in writing by priests through various councils.

But this bishop of the Macedonian sect did not collect the documents of the Catholic councils. Rather, he collected those documents that pleased his own judgment and inserted into his collection especially synods held by heretics. Accordingly, the same Socrates writes of him in Book II, chapter 17:

> Sabinus, a bishop of the Macedonian sect, in his collection of synods—or, better, as Valesius observed, of synodal acts—for instead of *τῶν συνόδων* one should read *συνοδικῶν*, as it appears in Book III, chapters 10 and 25, and Book IV, chapter 12—did not at all include the letters of Julius, although he did not entirely omit the letter that the bishops assembled at Antioch wrote to Julius. Sabinus, however, was always accustomed to act in this way. If any synodal letters happened either to conceal or entirely reject the doctrine of consubstantiality, he diligently inserted them into his work; but those that were contrary to it he knowingly and deliberately passed over in silence.

Thus he dealt at greater length with the Council of Seleucia of the year 359, with the Macedonian synods, with the Council of Antioch of the year 363, and with other similar councils, as the same Socrates relates (Book II, chapters 15 and 39; Book III, chapters 10 and 25).

By contrast, he disparaged the Nicene Fathers so greatly that he portrayed them as crude and uneducated men (the same author, Book I, chapter 9). Therefore this work of Sabinus must not be reckoned among the codes of sacred canons that we are presently discussing.

### 6

As for the Greek collection of canons, some believe that it was already indicated in the time of the Council of Ephesus by the Greek expression *ἀκολουθία τῶν κανόνων*—“the succession of the canons”—which frequently occurs in that synod, because in such a collection all the canons of the various councils were written out in a continuous and consecutive numerical series. John Scholasticus called this *τάξιν καὶ ἀκολουθίαν ἀριθμῶν*—“the order and succession of numbers”—as it was displayed in the code of canons.

We shall show in chapter 6, no. 3, however, that this expression was used at the same Council of Ephesus with an entirely different meaning.

More certain and manifest evidence of this Greek collection is available from the Council of Chalcedon. In several of its sessions, not only is explicit mention made of a code of canons, but several canons are also recited from such a code, some distinguished by numbers that demonstrate a continuous numerical series appropriate only to a collection of canons.

In the fourth session, Aetius, archdeacon of the holy and Catholic Church of Constantinople, said:

> This is the rule placed among others by the holy Fathers . . . .

And he read the following from the code:

> Concerning clerics and monks who suspend themselves from communion. If a presbyter or deacon, despising his bishop, etc.

All the most reverend bishops cried out:

> This accords with the rule; this is the rule of the Fathers.

(Vol. IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 1418, d.)

This is canon 5 of the Council of Antioch.

In the session concerning Carosus and Dorotheus, the numbers of the canons are designated. The holy synod said:

> Let the sacred canons of the Fathers be read and inserted into the records.

Aetius, archdeacon and chief secretary of the Great Church, took up the book and read:

> Canon 83: If any bishop, etc.  
> Canon 84: If any presbyter or deacon, etc.

(Ibid., col. 1427, e.)

These are the fourth and fifth canons of Antioch. In the code they were written after the 20 Nicene canons, the 25 Ancyrene canons, the 14 Neocaesarean canons [VIII], and the 20 Gangran canons; in the continuous numerical series beginning with the Nicene canons, they were canons 83 and 84.

Likewise, in the eleventh session, two other Antiochene canons, 16 and 17, were recited with the numbers 95 and 96, which belonged to the same code.

Stephen, the most reverend bishop of Ephesus, said:

> I ask that the canons be read . . . .

The most glorious judges said:

> Let these canons be read.

Leontius, the most reverend bishop of Magnesia, read from the code:

> Rule 95: If any bishop is without a see, etc.

(Ibid., col. 1610, d.), as in Antiochene canon 16.

Immediately afterward the same most reverend Bishop Leontius read from the same code:

> Rule 96: If any bishop [undertakes] an ordination, etc.

This is Antiochene canon 17.

It should be noted that these canons are not called Antiochene, but are distinguished only by the number in the code. This shows that this code, and this method of citation, had long been established and was familiar to everyone.

Likewise, the bishops of the province of Pisidia, in their synodal letter to the emperor Leo, which is inserted in the *Encyclical Code*, cited the aforementioned fourth Antiochene canon by the similar number 83 from such a code:

> We judge them to be strangers to the Church of God, according to the regular succession, with no pardon or hope of restoration remaining to them in any way, as the eighty-third rule clearly decrees concerning such persons. It begins: If any bishop, deposed by a synod, etc.

(Vol. IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 1877, c.)

Dionysius Exiguus had a somewhat different Greek code of canons. When he translated it into Latin, he described it more precisely in the letter prefixed to his translation, addressed to Stephen of Salona, in these words:

> We have arranged the rules of the Council of Nicaea and, thereafter, those of all the councils, whether held before it or afterward, down to the synod of the one hundred and fifty bishops who assembled at Constantinople, under the order of numbers—that is, from the first chapter all the way to the one hundred and sixty-fifth—as it is found in the Greek authority.

The Greek code translated by Dionysius therefore contained the canons of Nicaea, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea, and Constantinople. Since it presented all these canons marked by a continuous numerical series, it extended the numbering to 165.

We have said that this code was somewhat different from the one read at Chalcedon with its continuous numerical numbering, for Dionysius’s numbers are lower by one [Col. 0016C].

Dionysius himself, in his first Paschal Letter, cited the first canon of the Council of Antioch according to the sequence of his code in this manner:

> In the holy canons, under title 79—which is the first canon of the Council of Antioch—the following is expressly found: “All who have dared to dissolve,” etc.

This first Antiochene canon, which was number 79 in Dionysius’s code, was canon 80 according to the calculation of the numbers by which the Antiochene canons are cited at the Council of Chalcedon, in the copy used by the Chalcedonian Fathers.

Whether all the ancient Greek codes were marked by this continuous numerical series, as most people believe, we shall discuss in chapter 6, no. 3 and following.

### 7

Christopher Justel preferred to regard the Code of the Canons of the Universal Church, which he published at Paris in 1610, as the ancient Greek code that was read at the Council of Chalcedon and that had authority throughout the universal Church, both Eastern and Western, before the Council of Chalcedon.

This code contains the canons of the Councils of Nicaea, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon, distributed in a continuous numerical series up to number 207.

He did indeed assign these numbers to the canons in such a way that they corresponded to the numbers cited at Chalcedon. But he did not possess any ancient code that contained this collection in the form in which he published it.

He took the Greek text from the books of later Greek collections, both published and manuscript. Hence the following words appear in the title of his work:

> Christopher Justel first restored it; he collected and corrected it from published and manuscript Greek codices.

But the entire collection, as well as the distribution of the numbers, was assembled by his own judgment and rested on no ancient code.

He admits this quite openly in the letter prefixed to the edition and addressed to Jacques Leschaser. After writing:

> Having collated and compared with one another all the published and handwritten Greek and Latin collections of canons that I was able to find, I discovered none older than the Latin one that we still possess from the translation of Dionysius Exiguus, which from the beginning bore the title “Code” or “Corpus of Canons,”

he adds that, in order to restore it to its original light, both in Latin and in Greek, he had first thought of producing the Greek text from the edition of Tilius and correcting it against manuscript codices.

When he discovered, however, that Tilius’s edition contained many things that were not in the older Greek collection used by Dionysius Exiguus, he ultimately adopted a method of restoration that had previously been unknown to him and that the aforementioned Leschaser had indicated in a *Consultation* of the year 1607, a fragment of which Justel himself inserted.

The method proposed there may be summarized briefly as follows: the code should contain the canons of those synods whose canons Dionysius found in his Greek code, and they should be presented in the same order, in a continuous and uninterrupted numerical series, so that the numbers designated at Chalcedon correspond exactly to those same canons.

But the person who followed this method in assembling his code certainly found no copy corresponding to his collection. Instead, calling both published and manuscript Greek collections to his aid, he composed and corrected, on his own authority, what he believed to be the ancient and original code of the universal Church.

Hence, in his notes, he cited only the codices of Zonaras and Balsamon, as well as the edition of Tilius, for the sake of their readings.

### 8

Nor should you reply that Justellus himself writes in the preface: “There exists an as-yet unpublished collection of canons by Stephen, bishop of Ephesus, which agrees in every respect with the ancient codex of the universal Church and presents, in the same series and order, the canons of the Councils of Nicaea, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea, and Constantinople, to which he himself added those of Ephesus.” This Stephen, bishop of the Ephesians, is believed to have been the man who lived at the time of the pseudo-Ephesian and Chalcedonian Councils.

Justellus’s codex, therefore, rests upon this most ancient exemplar. Before answering this argument, however, the error of Guillaume Voel and [Col. 0017C] Henricus Justellus in the preface to the *Bibliotheca juris canonici*, printed at Paris in 1661, must be exposed. There, concerning the codex of the universal Church, they write:

> It was collected shortly after the First Council of Constantinople, under Theodosius the Great, by a certain Stephen, bishop of Ephesus, as the old Palatine codex formerly indicated—a codex seen by Justellus, as reported by Petrus de Marca, archbishop of Toulouse.

This archbishop, in Book III, chapter 3, no. 4 of his *Concordia*, stated that the canons of the ancient councils—165 in number—had been collected into one body through the industry of some bishop, “perhaps Stephen of Ephesus,” as was indicated by an old manuscript codex in the Palatine Library, “as I received from a man of the highest trustworthiness and integrity”; and in the margin Christophorus Justellus is named.

He does not speak categorically but conjecturally, as the word “perhaps” indicates; nor does he carry such a collection back to the age of Theodosius the Great. The words of Christophorus Justellus, which we quoted shortly before, establish most clearly both the manifest error of Voel and Henricus Justellus and a certain misapprehension on the part of Petrus de Marca in understanding and reporting Christophorus’s testimony. For [Col. 0017D] Christophorus did not identify Stephen of Ephesus as the author of the entire collection under the reign of Theodosius the Great; he attributed to him only the addition of the canons of Ephesus, made, of course, after the Ephesian Synod—and even that he expressed by the word “perhaps,” as a qualification of what preceded.

“Afterward,” he says, “eight canons of the Third, Ecumenical Council of Ephesus were added to this ancient codex, perhaps by Stephen of Ephesus, whose collection of canons, not yet published, exists,” and so he continues as above. In his first edition, that of 1610, he did not disclose where this unpublished collection was located. But in the second edition, of 1661, when these words of his were inserted into the preface, he states:

> This collection, however, is kept in the Palatine Library, in Hamburg, among the heirs of Gelhart Ermenhorst; from them we have so far been unable to obtain it.

If he was unable to obtain this codex, then he certainly did not use it in his edition. Perhaps he had once seen the codex; and when he later recalled it from memory, it may have seemed to him similar to his own collection.

To remove all remaining doubt concerning this Palatine codex [Col. 0018A], the words of Johann Albert Fabricius should be appended here, from volume XI of the *Bibliotheca Graeca*, no. 10, p. 26:

> In the Imperial Library there are several collections of canons not yet published, such as the *canonical synopsis* (*κανονικὴ σύνοψις*) of Stephen of Ephesus mentioned by Lambecius, III, p. 66, which was also in the Palatine codex 33 and contains the canons of the apostles and of the Councils of Nicaea and Ancyra. See Friedrich Sylburg’s catalogue of the manuscripts of the Palatine Library, p. 14, where that Stephen of Ephesus is called a bishop.

Friedrich Sylburg, who published the catalogue of the Palatine codices, did not identify another collection in them as bearing the name of Stephen of Ephesus, except one which contained not the complete canons of the councils but a synopsis of the canons. These canonical synopses belonged to a later period. Even if the Ephesian canons were added to the synopsis in question, this occurred—as we shall say later—much later than the Council of Chalcedon. Consequently, [Col. 0018B] if Stephen of Ephesus is believed to have been the author of this collection or synopsis, he was not the Stephen who is mentioned in the age of the Council of Chalcedon, but another, later Stephen, who in the manuscript of the Imperial Library lacks the title of bishop.

### 9

But to return to the codex of canons published by Christophorus Justellus: several arguments clearly demonstrate that it is not that ancient collection cited at Chalcedon, and which Dionysius Exiguus is believed to have used.

The more ancient Greek codices of the canons, from which the two older interpretations—the Isidorian and the *Prisca*—were derived, included, along with the Nicene canons, a creed and also the subscriptions, or catalogue, of the Nicene Fathers. The same versions testify to this. Moreover, it is clear not only from the versions just mentioned but also from the Greek text itself that, in those manuscripts, the letter of the Council was written together with the Gangran canons; that the Antiochene canons were likewise transmitted with synodical letters and with the names of the bishops; and that the Constantinopolitan [Col. 0018C] canons were not without episcopal subscriptions.

Justellus’s edition passes over all these matters. Although the Dionysian interpretation likewise lacks all of them, this is nevertheless a weak defense of Justellus’s Greek codex. While he presents it as the codex of the universal Church, it corresponds to Dionysius’s version and is absent from those older Greek codices from which the earlier versions were taken. What is more, it does not fully agree with the Dionysian version. In Dionysius’s interpretation, no less than in the Isidorian and *Prisca* versions, and in the Greek text itself, certain annotations precede the canons of Ancyra, Neocaesarea, and Gangra. By these annotations the first two councils are presented as earlier than Nicaea, while the third is presented as later. You will look for these in vain in Justellus’s codex.

### 10

Moreover, Justellus adds other material that did not exist in the ancient Greek codex. To the four canons of the Council of Constantinople of 381, he added three others. [Col. 0018D] These certainly were not in the ancient Greek codex, since they are found neither in the Dionysian version nor in the other ancient versions. Certainly the seventh canon does not belong in any way to that Council of Constantinople. For this reason it is not found in John Scholasticus either, although he did receive the fifth and sixth canons, despite their being additions. This seventh canon was composed much later, let alone added at that time.

The fifth and sixth canons may perhaps have been enacted at another Council of Constantinople, in the following year, 382. Because this second council was confused with the earlier one through the identity of the city’s name and the proximity of the dates, the canons of one were easily confused and combined with those of the other.

No version presents the Ephesian canons, just as they were not presented by the Greek codex of Dionysius Exiguus. Nor did this synod properly enact together those eight canons which Justellus’s edition displays; rather, they were excerpted here and there from different acts of the council. This was done only at a later period.

The oldest Greek collection known to us in which these Ephesian canons were listed with the others [Col. 0019A] was the codex used by John Scholasticus after the middle of the sixth century. From that codex they passed into later Greek collections. Justellus himself, in his notes on these canons, p. 91, when indicating the later sources from which he drew them, says:

> These eight canons of the Council of Ephesus are found in Tilius’s codex and in the manuscript codices of Balsamon and Zonaras, as well as in the Acts of the Council of Ephesus, vol. I of the *Ecumenical Councils*, published at Rome in 1608: namely, the first six on p. 499, and the final two on pp. 492 and 497.

To the Chalcedonian canons—which number only 27 in the ancient Greek codex, in its ancient versions, and also in the Dionysian version—Justellus added two others, which were received only by later Greek codices. John Scholasticus, although he lived in the sixth century, reports only 27 canons.

Who, then, can regard this codex of Justellus as the genuine ancient [XI] codex of the canons [Col. 0019B], when it omits some things from the ancient codex and adds others?

### 11

Still less should it have been entitled *Codex of the Universal Church*, as though it had possessed authority before the Council of Chalcedon not only among the Eastern but also among the Western Church.

During this period the Roman and Western Church had received no other canons except those of Nicaea and those of Sardica, which were received under the name of the Nicene canons, as we shall prove in Part II, chapter 1. Everyone knows how strongly Innocent I rejected the Antiochene canons in Letter 7 to the clergy of Constantinople, and likewise how firmly Leo the Great resisted the Constantinopolitan canons inserted into the Greek codex—canons which St. Gregory testifies were not accepted even in his own age, in Book VII, Letter 34, to Eulogius.

How, then, could that codex published by Justellus be affirmed to belong to the universal Church, and consequently also to the Western and Roman Church, when it contains canons then rejected by that Church and lacks the Sardican canons which it chiefly accepted?

Justellus vainly attempts to support himself by Leo’s own authority when, on p. 16, he cites Leo’s words from Letter 44 [Col. 0019C], written in his own name and that of the Roman Synod to the emperor Theodosius. In that letter Leo requested that the emperor order a general council to be held, which, he says, was necessarily demanded after Flavian’s appeal had been lodged, as “the decrees of the canons enacted at Nicaea testify . . . . . which are appended below.” Justellus reasonably maintains that by the words “appended below” we should understand the canons of the councils which, from Nicaea to Constantinople, had been collected into one body in continuous numerical order and were found in the ancient codex of the canons.

He is mistaken—and mistaken so obviously that by these words Leo refers only to the Sardican canons, which are absent from Justellus’s codex. Accordingly, the Sardican canon concerning appeals is appended to this letter in the published Greek text. Compare what we have said on this matter in the admonition prefixed to Letter 43, no. 8, and in annotation 18, column 831, note c, on Letter 44.

[Col. 0019D] P. Coustant, who likewise rejects the title of Justellus’s codex, writes in the preface to volume I of the *Epistles of the Roman Pontiffs*, no. 58:

> It therefore seems that Justellus’s collection could be more suitably and accurately entitled: “A Codex of Canons such as existed in the Greek Church in the middle of the sixth century.”

He conceded too much to his opponent. For from John Scholasticus, who indeed flourished in the middle of the sixth century, we learn that the Greek codex contained the Sardican canons, as well as the canons of the apostles, which Justellus excludes. Conversely, the seventh canon of Constantinople and the final two Chalcedonian canons, which are read in Justellus, had not yet been introduced into it.

## CHAPTER II  
### What the Ancient Codex of Canons among the Greeks Was at the Beginning, and How It Was Subsequently Enlarged

### 1

Since the numbers assigned to the Antiochene canons in the codex of canons read at the Council of Chalcedon [Col. 0020A] generally correspond to the numbers found by Dionysius Exiguus in his Greek codex—“generally,” because the numbers mentioned at Chalcedon exceed the Dionysian numbers by one—a common supposition has prevailed that the Greek codex of canons used at that synod resembled the codex of Dionysius. In that codex, under 165 numbers or titles, there were contained 20 Nicene canons, 24 Ancyran, 14 Neocaesarean, 20 Gangran, 25 Antiochene, 59 Laodicean, and 3 Constantinopolitan canons.

It is also thought that this was the first Greek collection of canons, compiled after the Council of Constantinople in this order and with this number of canons. This, however, does not seem to us as certain as it does to most people. To shed some light on a matter belonging to such an ancient period, since Greek exemplars from this age are lacking, we must have recourse to the older Latin interpretations preceding Dionysius, which were translated from the most ancient Greek codices of the canons, and also to other very ancient Latin collections which derived the canons of the Greek synods from interpretations earlier than Dionysius’s.

### 2

We possess two versions of these canons that are earlier than Dionysius [Col. 0020B]: the *Prisca*, which Justellus published and which we shall reprint in a fuller and more accurate form in this volume; and the version which, having been received by Isidore from the Hispanic collection, is commonly called the Isidorian—not because Isidore was its author, but because it was first published together with Isidore’s collection.

The *Prisca* version, as it was printed by Justellus, follows this order. It presents 24 Ancyran canons, 14 Neocaesarean, and 21 Nicene canons. From our manuscripts we shall add an equal number of Sardican canons, which are mutilated in Justellus; then 20 Gangran, 24 Antiochene, 27 Chalcedonian, and four Constantinopolitan canons. To these is added, without a number, another Chalcedonian canon concerning the primacy of the Church of Constantinople. These make 165 canons—or, if the Chalcedonian canon appended to the Constantinopolitan canons is also counted, 166 canons.

The Isidorian version presents all the canons, including the 27 Chalcedonian canons, which are read in Dionysius. The ancient Latin collections, which we shall describe individually below, did not receive the Greek canons from only one version; some came from the Isidorian version and others from the *Prisca*.

### 3

With these preliminary remarks [Col. 0020C], two matters in particular deserve notice in the *Prisca* version.

First, the Laodicean canons are absent from it. Nor should this be attributed to a peculiar defect in the codex found by Justellus. They are likewise absent from two very ancient collections which, from other ancient manuscripts of the *Prisca* interpretation, received several other canons of the Greek councils—namely, the collection of Vatican, Regina 1997, and another preserved in two manuscripts, Lucan 88 and Colbert 784.

The author of another very ancient collection contained in Barberini 2888 and Vatican 1342, who drew upon the same *Prisca* version, took the Laodicean canons from the Isidorian version because he did not find them in the *Prisca*. These facts make it clear to us that the canons were absent from the beginning, no less from the *Prisca* version than from the Greek codex from which the author of this version produced his Latin translation of the Greek canons. Otherwise he would have given the Laodicean canons Latin form just as he did the others.

The Laodicean canons, therefore, were not inserted into the Greek collection at the very beginning but were added later.

Second, [Col. 0020D] in this same *Prisca* version the Constantinopolitan canons are listed after the Chalcedonian canons. They are described in the same order in three other distinct and very ancient manuscript collections mentioned shortly before: Vatican, Regina 1997; the Lucan-Colbertine collection; and Vatican, Barberini. These collections received the canons of those councils from the *Prisca* version.

Thus, in this reversed order, the Constantinopolitan canons were also placed after the Chalcedonian canons in the Greek codex used by the author of that version. The canons of the Council of Constantinople, therefore, were added after Chalcedon in the *Prisca*. This is so evident that the Chalcedonian canon concerning the primacy of the Church of Constantinople is counted among the canons of that same Constantinopolitan synod, and the subscriptions of the three legates of the Roman pontiff are appended to those same canons. These subscriptions belong not to the Council of Constantinople but to the Council of Chalcedon, as will become clear from the edition of the *Prisca* version inserted in this volume. See below, column 555.

Whether one attributes this addition of the Constantinopolitan canons [Col. 0021A] to the author of the version—who, not finding these canons in his Greek collection, translated them from elsewhere—or to the Greek collection of canons which he used (the latter seems more probable to us, for the reasons that will be given in note 5 on the same canons of this version), it will always remain true that they were absent from the Greek collection at the beginning. Otherwise they would not have been absent from any exemplar of this collection, nor would they have had to be added after the Chalcedonian canons in any Greek manuscript or in the *Prisca* version.

For this reason perhaps Lucentius, the legate of the Apostolic See, said at the Council of Chalcedon, in action 16, concerning the Constantinopolitan canons: “They are not found in the synodical canons” (*Tome IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils*, column 1747), namely because they were absent from the published collection and codex of canons.

Thus the primordial [Col. 0021B] Greek codex of canons lacked both the Laodicean and the Constantinopolitan canons. This is considerably confirmed by the most ancient *Breviatio canonum*, found in two manuscripts, Veronese 59 and Lucan 88.

For its author, who presented in abridged form certain excerpts from various older codices of canons, gives, at no. 2, an abbreviation of the Greek canons, distributing them in continuous numerical order up to number 91. After reporting the Nicene, Sardican, Ancyran, Neocaesarean, and Gangran canons, he ends with the Antiochene canons.

Is this not evidence that the Latin codex from which the abbreviations of this second number were excerpted derived from a Greek exemplar of the canons which did not proceed beyond the Antiochene canons and therefore contained neither the Laodicean nor the Constantinopolitan canons? If the Laodicean and Constantinopolitan canons were absent at the origin of the first Greek collection, then this collection was not originally the one which Dionysius Exiguus found in his codex with those canons and rendered into Latin.

### 4

Although the Isidorian version—perhaps older than the *Prisca* interpretation—now contains [Col. 0021C] both the Laodicean and Constantinopolitan canons, it does not follow that they always existed in the first exemplar of that version. We suspect that this exemplar originally lacked both sets of canons and that they should be regarded as later additions.

This version certainly once lacked the Chalcedonian canons, as may be inferred from Ferrandus. When he transferred the Greek canons from the Isidorian version into his *Breviarium*, he omitted the Chalcedonian canons for no other reason, as we shall show in its proper place, than that he did not find them in his exemplar of that version.

The same is discovered in the very ancient Corbie collection, which likewise lacks the Chalcedonian canons, because the author of that collection did not find them in the codex of the Isidorian version from which he received the canons of the other Greek synods.

For the same reason [Col. 0021D], the author of the Quesnellian collection reprinted in this volume, who derived all the other Greek canons from the Isidorian source, took the Chalcedonian canons alone from the *Prisca*.

Just as the Chalcedonian canons were later added to the Isidorian interpretation, so we consider it credible that the Laodicean and Constantinopolitan canons were also added to it at a later time.

Another substantial indication of this is supplied by an ancient Latin collection preserved in the Lucan and Colbertine manuscripts mentioned above. Its author took the canons of the earlier councils from the Isidorian version, but added the Constantinopolitan and Chalcedonian canons from the *Prisca*, evidently because the exemplar of the Isidorian version which he used did not contain them. He completely omitted the Laodicean canons because he found them neither in the *Prisca* nor in his exemplar of the Isidorian version.

### 5

Since, moreover, the Antiochene canons are also transmitted [Col. 0022A] in this Latin collection of the Lucan and Colbertine manuscripts from the *Prisca* version, and not from the Isidorian version, from which the canons of the four preceding synods were copied, the suspicion arises that the Antiochene canons too were absent from the original exemplar of the Isidorian interpretation. Consequently, because the author of the collection just mentioned did not find them in his exemplar of the Isidorian version, he was compelled to copy them from the *Prisca*.

If this is judged probable, it will have to be said that the Greek collection originally contained only the canons of Nicaea, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, and Gangra. From this first exemplar of the Greek codex, the first author of the Isidorian version rendered into Latin only those same canons, which also passed into the Lucan-Colbertine collection mentioned above.

Indeed, only the canons of these four councils are distinguished by special chronological annotations in all the Latin interpretations of different origin, and also in John Scholasticus himself and in Tilius’s Greek manuscripts. By these annotations, the Ancyran and Neocaesarean canons are presented as earlier than the Nicene canons, although they are written after them, while the Gangran canons are presented as later than the Nicene canons.

These special annotations [Col. 0022B] seem to indicate a distinct ancient collector of these synods and canons. If he had collected the canons of other councils as well, he does not seem likely to have omitted a similar annotation.

On this view, the canons of the other synods, which are read in the Greek codex after the Gangran canons, must be said to have been added later. This will become still clearer if the Gangran canons were issued between the years 362 and 370, which we shall prove to be much more probable in chapter 4, § 1.

For if the first author of the Greek collection had collected the Antiochene canons together with the others, he would certainly have placed them before the Gangran canons, since they were earlier. They are therefore found after the Gangran canons for this one reason: they were not copied into the codex of canons by the first author but were added later.

### 6

Here we may also offer a conjecture concerning the first author of this collection.

We observe that the three synods of Ancyra, Neocaesarea, and Gangra [Col. 0022C] belonged to the diocese of Pontus. For Galatia, in which Ancyra was situated, no less than Pontus, in which Neocaesarea lay, and Paphlagonia, in which Gangra was located, is assigned to the diocese of Pontus—not only in the *Notitia* published by Scipio Maffei, which was written under Theodosius I, but also in the *Notitia dignitatum*.

Hence the law of Theodosius cited by Sozomen assigns to Helladius, bishop of Caesarea in Pontus, the entire region extending from Bithynia all the way to Armenia.

It therefore seems probable to us that the first author of the Greek codex was some learned man from the diocese of Pontus. Accordingly, besides the universally celebrated general Synod of Nicaea, he had at hand and entered into his codex only the canons of the three more celebrated particular councils of his own diocese.

Since he believed that the general Council of Nicaea ought to be given the first place out of reverence, he prefixed to the others those annotations by which readers could understand that the Councils of Ancyra and Neocaesarea were earlier than Nicaea, while Gangra was later, lest a chronological error should perhaps thereby creep into their minds.

When several copies had subsequently been made from this original collection [Col. 0022D]—one of which, we have suspected, lay before the first author of the Isidorian version—someone else, perhaps from the diocese of the East, added the Antiochene canons. Although these were earlier than the Gangran canons, he wrote them after Gangra, either so as not to disturb the order of the original codex or so as not to have to copy the entire codex.

These canons were certainly contained in the Greek codex of canons before the fifth century, since they seem to have been brought forward from that same codex by the enemies of St. John Chrysostom against him, and later were likewise thrust forward by the Easterners against St. Cyril.

The erroneous heading prefixed to these canons—“at the dedication,” concerning which we shall speak in chapter 4, § 2—if it was attached when they were inserted into the Greek codex, indicates that the addition of these canons took place later, since the time and occasion of this synod could easily have been forgotten. Compare what will be discussed in the cited chapter.

### 7

[Col. 0023A] What should be thought concerning the Sardican canons as regards the Greek collection, we shall explain in chapter 6.

Moreover, in a certain codex which had received the addition of the Antiochene canons, the Chalcedonian and Constantinopolitan canons were added. The codex from which the *Prisca* version was taken was of this kind.

In other codices, the Laodicean canons were first added after the Antiochene canons in their proper order, and then the Constantinopolitan canons. Such was the Greek codex from which the interpretation of Dionysius Exiguus proceeded; Dionysius himself appended his version of the Chalcedonian canons from another source.

In other manuscript exemplars, the Laodicean, Constantinopolitan, and Chalcedonian canons were subsequently annexed together, and the Isidorian interpretation was at some point added to them.

Around the middle of the sixth century, the Ephesian canons were added in their proper place only in Greek exemplars; they were never inserted into the ancient Latin interpretations. They were found together with the other canons in the Greek codices available to John Scholasticus and to certain others before him. Their collections were distributed into sixty titles, which he mentions in his preface, although they are no longer extant.

For the canons inserted in these collections are said [Col. 0023B] to have been taken from ten synods, among which the Council of Ephesus is certainly included. John himself inserted the canons of that council into his collection, which was divided into fifty titles.

Dionysius seems to have found only fifty Apostolic Canons in his Greek codex, since he prefixed only that number to his Latin version. But in other Greek exemplars mentioned by John Scholasticus, a larger number of them was found, namely as many as 85.

### 8

Moreover, canons from the letters of St. Basil to Amphilochius were added to the Greek codex. John Scholasticus himself bears witness to this, since in his preface he describes the order of the canons presented, at least in his own codex, as follows:

[Col. 0023C]

## ORDER OF THE CANONS

The holy disciples and apostles of the Lord issued 85 canons through the work of Clement. After these come the canons which follow, as set out below.

The 20 canons of the 318 holy Fathers assembled at Nicaea, during the consulship of the illustrious Paulinus and Julian, in the 606th year from Alexander, on the nineteenth day of the month Desius, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July.

The 25 canons of the holy Fathers assembled at Ancyra. These were earlier in time than the Nicene canons, but later in authority—or, rather, by reason of the freedom belonging to a general council.

The 14 canons of the holy Fathers assembled at Neocaesarea. That synod too was earlier than Nicaea and later than Ancyra; but Nicaea was placed before it out of respect.

The 21 canons of the Fathers assembled at Sardica, after the Nicene Fathers.

The 20 canons of the Fathers assembled at Gangra, by whom they were set forth.

[Col. 0023D] The 59 canons of the Fathers assembled at Laodicea in Phrygia, by whom they were set forth.

The 6 canons of the Fathers assembled at Constantinople, by whom they were set forth.

The 7 canons of the Fathers assembled at Ephesus, by whom they were set forth. In the body of the work, however, title 1 also cites an eighth.

The 27 canons of the Fathers assembled at Chalcedon, by whom they were set forth.

There also exist 68 canons of St. Basil, contained, that is, in the second and third of his canonical letters, as we have learned from the canons quoted by John himself in his collection.

This collection was once attributed to Theodore of Cyrrhus, bishop, because of an erroneous inscription in a codex of the Royal Library of Paris. But Christophorus Justellus restored it to its proper author on the basis of three manuscripts of good reputation. Those codices bear the name of John Scholasticus, not Theodore; to them may be added other Imperial codices mentioned by Lambecius in Book VI of his *Commentaries on the Imperial Library*, pp. 55, 56, and 61, and in Book VIII, p. 458.

[Col. 0024A] Accordingly, the additions to the Greek collection just indicated belong not to the age of Theodore but to that of John Scholasticus.

### 9

Further additions were made to the Greek codex at the time of the Council in Trullo. In its second canon, that council approved as already received into the codex the canons of Carthage rendered into Greek from the collection of Dionysius Exiguus, as we shall prove in its proper place. It also approved the Council of Constantinople of the year 394, and the canonical letters of Dionysius, Peter, Athanasius, Timothy, Theophilus, and Cyril, bishops of Alexandria; likewise those of Gregory Thaumaturgus, Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nyssa, Gregory the Theologian, or Nazianzen, and Amphilochius of Iconium; the letter of Gennadius of Constantinople; and the Council of Carthage of St. Cyprian.

Later were added the canons of the Councils in Trullo and of Nicaea II, together with the letter of Tarasius of Constantinople to Hadrian I, Roman pontiff.

From a codex in the library of the canons of St. Hilary of Poitiers, Joannes Tilius [Col. 0024B] published the canons of the councils mentioned above in Greek at Paris in 1540. He was also planning to publish a second volume in which the canonical letters of the Greek Fathers would be presented.

This complete Greek collection can be read in the celebrated Oxford edition of Guillaume Beveregius, published in 1672, in which he also inserted the scholia of Zonaras and Balsamon.

Among the Greek manuscript exemplars preserved in the library of the monks of St. Basil in Rome, two—numbered 19 and 20—contain a Greek collection written in the tenth century. For the catalogue of Byzantine bishops and Constantinopolitan patriarchs ends with Tryphon, who, while those codices were being written, died at the end of that same century.

In this collection, which is divided into 40 chapters, the most recent council is Nicaea II. The canonical letters of Gregory the Theologian and Amphilochius are absent, as are the letters of Gennadius and Tarasius.

But appended to the canons of the Council of Chalcedon [Col. 0024C] are two letters: one of St. Flavian to Leo, and the other of St. Leo to Flavian. In our edition these are Letters 26 and 28. The same Letter 28 of Leo is found in the Imperial manuscript of the Greek collection at Vienna, mentioned by Lambecius in Book VI of his *Commentaries*, p. 51, and Book VIII, p. 431.

In another manuscript collection of the same monks of St. Basil, divided into 26 titles or chapters, another letter of Gennadius of Constantinople is added after his letter to the metropolitans concerning simoniacs. This second letter is addressed to Martyrius, bishop of Antioch, concerning the reception of heretics. It is also read in a Greek manuscript of the Imperial Library.

These seemed to be the more important and ancient additions that needed to be listed. We omit the later additions presented in other codices.

[Col. 0024D]

## [XVI] CHAPTER III  
### On the Catalogues of the Nicene, Ancyran, Neocaesarean, and Gangran Fathers; Whether They Derive from the Primordial Greek Codex

### § 1

The catalogue of the Nicene Fathers appended to the Creed was contained not only in the primordial Greek codex of the canons but is also older than the Greek collection itself. The provinces designated in it correspond to the civil administrative arrangement in force at the time of the Council of Nicaea.

The division of certain civil provinces into two is shown to have occurred after the Council of Nicaea. Phrygia had not yet been divided into two provinces at the time of the Council of Sardica. A passage of St. Hilary is corrected. The heading of the synodical letter of Sardica in Theodoret is corrupt. The date of the Council of Laodicea is established.

1. Having described the Greek manuscript of the canons, I would like to set forth some observations that occurred to my mind while examining it and that did not seem useless. First [Col. 0025A], something must be said [Note: [Col. 0025D] This catalogue, collated with manuscripts of various versions, will be found twice in this volume: first in the collection to be presented in chapter 1, col. 30, and then in the old edition, col. 503.] about the catalogue of the Nicene Fathers, which some regard as a work of a later age and of little authority. Four versions of different origin transmit this catalogue: the old version, which in this volume we shall provide in a supplemented and corrected form; another more ancient version, namely the one received by Isidore and commonly called the Isidorian version; a third, extremely ancient version, which is read in the manuscripts of the collections of Vat. Regina 1997 and the Quesnelliana, to be reprinted in this volume; and finally the version inserted in the manuscripts of the Hadriana collection, which is entirely different from the three preceding versions.

Since, moreover, the first three versions derived the Greek canons from different Greek sources, this catalogue of the Nicene Fathers likewise derives its origin from the Greek. For this is why the same catalogue is read in these different versions, none of which depends upon another: it was found by the authors of these translations in a Greek exemplar, or in a Greek collection of canons, together with the Nicene canons.

This Greek origin is especially evident from the fourth version of the same catalogue, which was appended to the Nicene canons of the Dionysian version in the manuscripts of the Hadriana collection. In these manuscripts (as in Vallicellianus A. 5), certain Greek expressions are reproduced which, while showing that the translator was not very skilled at rendering them into Latin, reveal the Greek origin of the catalogue. Examples are *Alexandrias micreas* for “of lesser Alexandria,” and the name of the province *Nesson* for “of the Islands.”

Just as the Greek collection from which such versions were derived is extremely ancient, so this catalogue is of the greatest antiquity and must consequently be recognized as having proceeded from genuine Greek exemplars no less than the canons themselves. Hence another very ancient translator of the Nicene canons, whose version from the manuscript of the chapter of Verona we shall publish in this volume, although he omits the catalogue of bishops, reveals that it nevertheless existed in the Greek exemplar he used, in these words: “Their names, together with their provinces and cities, are contained in the exemplars.”

Nor does it matter that the version of Dionysius, as it is contained in his uncontaminated manuscripts [Col. 0025C], lacks this catalogue. For it also lacks the Creed, which is certainly Nicene, and it further lacks certain passages from other synods which, although absent from Dionysius’s Greek exemplar, were nevertheless found in other Greek manuscripts and rendered into Latin by other translators.

2. Besides the four versions mentioned above, other ancient writers also confirm this catalogue. It is clear that Gelasius of Cyzicus, who wrote his history of the Nicene Council before Dionysius, found in his Greek exemplars a catalogue of the Nicene Fathers plainly similar to the one that will be published with the old version. For after the annotation prefixed to the catalogue in that same version, [XVII] when listing the Nicene Fathers (*Hist. conc. Nic.*, Book II, chapter 27), he first names Hosius and the Roman presbyters, just as they are listed first in that and all the other versions mentioned above. He then names the principal bishops among the remaining Fathers, together with each one’s province, in such a way that he evidently had the catalogue itself before his eyes.

Saint Jerome also indicates this same catalogue, not obscurely, in his *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, written in the East around the year 378. “Let us read,” he says in section 20, “the Acts and THE NAMES OF THE BISHOPS” (this is the very title of the aforementioned catalogue in the collection to be published in this volume, as well as in certain others), “at Nicaea; and we shall find that those whom, as we said above, we know to have been received signed *homoousion* among the rest” (below, col. 30). He plainly refers here to our catalogue, in which those men are indeed listed whom he had established from the names, or catalogue, of the bishops as having been received by the Nicene Council.

We shall add another testimony of the greatest importance from Socrates. In Book I, chapter 13, after saying that it would be useful to record the NAMES OF THE BISHOPS who assembled at Nicaea, together with the province and [Col. 0026A] city of which each was bishop, he begins with Hosius and the Roman presbyters, as follows:

“Hosius, bishop of Corduba in Spain, as I believe, just as it has been written above. Vitto and Vincentius, presbyters of the city of Rome.”

He continues:

“Alexander, bishop of Egypt; Eustathius of great Antioch; Macarius of Jerusalem; Arpocration of Cynopolis; and the rest, whose names are set out in full in the book of Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, entitled *The Synodical*.”

Several points must be observed here. First, the title “names of the bishops,” and their distribution by provinces, with the name of each one’s city added, correspond exactly to our catalogue. Next, the first two subscriptions are found in the same words in that catalogue. After these, Socrates begins by designating the province of Egypt, just as it is listed first in the catalogue.

As for the names of the bishops, apart from the three bishops of the principal sees—the Alexandrian, the Antiochene, and the Jerusalemite—whom he thought worthy of being named individually as a mark of honor, he mentions only Bishop Arpocration of Cynopolis among the others whom he indicates indistinctly by the formula “and the rest.” Since Arpocration would not have required such mention either in himself or because of the special prominence of his see, he can be said to have been named for no other reason than that, when Socrates wished to name one among the other bishops, he found him first in his catalogue. Indeed, he is listed first after Alexander of Alexandria in the catalogues of the old and Isidorian versions.

But if Arpocration is nowhere called bishop of Cynopolis in any version of the aforementioned catalogue, although he is so called by Socrates, while in those versions Adamantius is called bishop of Cynopolis—or Cynensis, or Cyni—and is placed immediately after Arpocration, Socrates’s easy error becomes apparent: in a glance of the eye he took Arpocration’s city from the bishop who followed him.

This observation confirms all the more strongly that, in describing the Nicene Fathers, he used a catalogue entirely similar to those of the old and Isidorian versions. In these, after Alexander, Arpocration—called there *Alphocratensis*—is listed, and after him Adamantius *Cynensis*, that is, of Cynopolis. If Socrates found this same catalogue, with the same names of bishops, provinces, and cities, in Athanasius’s *Synodical* book, which has perished, who would not see how greatly the authority of this catalogue is confirmed by the testimony of so important a bishop who had attended the Nicene Council?

3. That it was not unusual in that ancient period to collect the names of bishops who had sat in synods and arrange them by provinces is also evident from the First Council of Arles. From it we possess not the subscriptions themselves but a catalogue of the bishops arranged by provinces, plainly similar to the Nicene catalogue. We have convincingly defended its antiquity in the observations on Quesnell’s fifth dissertation, part II, chapter 3, no. 14.

Something similar occurred also with the Council of Chalcedon, except that we possess not only a catalogue of the Fathers of that council, likewise divided by provinces, as may be seen in the manuscripts of the Hadriana collection and consequently in volume IV of the councils in the latest Venetian edition, col. 1710, but also the actual subscriptions of those Fathers, with which the same catalogue, taken from the Greek original, agrees most closely.

Just as these two catalogues of the Arlesian and Chalcedonian Fathers are known to have been excerpted from the actual documents, or Acts, of the First Council of Arles and the Council of Chalcedon, so the catalogue of the Nicene Fathers must likewise be said to have been taken from the records of that council, or certainly from a reliable knowledge of those Fathers preserved by Athanasius or another contemporary author.

4. Another observation will establish much more firmly the antiquity and authority of this catalogue. For when we examine the provinces designated in it and compare them with the provinces listed in the subscription of the Philippopolitan, or pseudo-Sardican, synod, we find that both the catalogue and this subscription indicate a similar arrangement of provinces, so that in both places the names of those provinces that were established at a later time are absent.

In both, for example, Euphratesia and Osroene are omitted; and in the Nicene catalogue the bishops of these provinces are assigned to the provinces to which they belonged before the division. We would likewise read the same thing in the subscriptions of the pseudo-Sardican council if the provinces listed in the synodical inscription were named there.

That this reflects the ancient civil arrangement of the provinces which prevailed in the time of the Nicene Council becomes clear from the Antiochene synod, which consisted almost entirely of the same Nicene Fathers and was held in the year 332, as we shall prove in the following chapter, § 2. Bishops from all the provinces of the East subject to the Church of Antioch assembled at this synod.

Although bishops who, after the later division, belonged to Osroene and Euphratesia were present, neither Osroene nor Euphratesia appears in the Greek synodical inscription among the provinces individually listed. Why? Because these provinces had not yet been established and divided in the civil arrangement; one was still included in Mesopotamia and the other in Syria.

Just as the catalogue of the Nicene Fathers, by omitting these two provinces, Osroene and Euphratesia, reflects the ancient division of the East that prevailed in the age of Constantine, so it displays the same arrangement in the other provinces as well, corresponding to the time of the Nicene Council. This is the clearest possible proof of its antiquity.

5. If, however, you object that among the provinces named in the subscription of the pseudo-Sardican synod are counted both Phrygias and Hellespont, which the aforementioned catalogue does not mention, we shall make two replies.

First, it is not proper to cast suspicion upon an earlier document because a document of a later age indicates a provincial arrangement in which the earlier document does not share. In the course of time, especially during the fourth century, new provinces were repeatedly carved out and a new arrangement introduced.

In the very inscription of the pseudo-synod mentioned above, the province of Osroene is not read, although Bassus of Car, that is, the bishop of Cara, signed the proceedings of that assembly; the *Description of the Whole World and Its Peoples* places him in Osroene. The *Description of the Whole World and Its Peoples*, published in Greek and Latin by Jacobus Gothofredus and reprinted by Schelestratius in volume II of *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, p. 625, reveals that Osroene had already been divided; it was written during the reign of the sons of Constantine.

Would anyone therefore reject the entirely certain document of the pseudo-Sardican council in which Osroene is omitted? Or would he rather infer from this that the celebrated *Description of the Whole World* was composed after this pseudo-synod, and that Osroene was divided from Mesopotamia—which had previously contained Osroene—after the time of this assembly?

The same must therefore be said of Hellespont. If it is known from the inscription of the pseudo-Sardican council that this province had already been divided at the time of that assembly, our catalogue proves that at the time of the Nicene Council it was included within Asia. Its division from Asia must consequently be placed after Nicaea and before the pseudo-Sardican synod.

Second, as regards Phrygia, the commonly transmitted inscription of the faith of this same pseudo-Sardican synod, preserved by Saint Hilary in his book *On Synods*, does indeed name two Phrygias. But we are certain that an error lies hidden in the commonly transmitted text. For in the extremely ancient manuscript of the chapter of Verona, no. 55, the same inscription and the same creed that are read in Saint Hilary are presented from another very ancient version, and in it only one Phrygia is named.

Indeed, Hilary himself, in the third fragment, where he transcribes the entire letter of the same pseudo-synod together with the creed, or formula of faith, likewise records only one Phrygia in the synodical inscription. It follows, therefore, that the text of the book *On Synods* has been interpolated. Since Father Coustant, in his notes to the same book, observes that several good manuscripts read *Asiae, Phrygiis*, without the word *duabus*, *Phrygiis* should be corrected to *Phrygia*.

[XIX] Only one Phrygia is likewise named in the aforementioned *Description of the Whole World*, which we have shown to have been composed after the Council of Sardica.
