From this we see that this Phrygia was divided into two after that work and before the Council of Constantinople in the year 381, in which two Phrygias are mentioned.

It is therefore clear that an error also entered the inscription of the letter of the true Sardican synod inserted by Theodoret in Book II, chapter 6 of his *History*, where two Phrygias are distinguished although there was only one.

Nor is the error limited to the two Phrygias. The inscription in the same Theodoret incorrectly counts as well several other provinces—Asia, Caria, Bithynia, Hellespont, Pisidia, Cappadocia, Pontus, Cilicia, Pamphylia, Lydia, the Cyclades, and Galatia—which are rightly omitted in the aforementioned manuscript of Verona [Col. 0028B], just as they are absent from the heading of the other Sardican letter to the Church of Alexandria preserved by Saint Athanasius in *Apology* 2.

I say that they are rightly omitted in that manuscript. For the bishops of these provinces, together with those of Phrygia, belonged not to the Sardican assembly but to the pseudo-Sardican gathering, and may consequently have slipped into the inscription of the Sardican letter preserved by Theodoret.

Indeed, when Saint Athanasius, at the beginning of *Apology* 2, names thirty-six provinces whose bishops supported him at the councils of Alexandria, Rome, and Sardica, he names none of the provinces just mentioned as belonging to the pseudo-Sardican council.

6. If, then, from what has been argued thus far, the catalogue of the Nicene Fathers is seen to preserve that ancient arrangement of the provinces which prevailed at the time of Nicaea, who could fail to recognize that it was excerpted with the utmost accuracy from the actual records of that council, or from reliable information about it?

For if it had been compiled later without some ancient document, it would have followed the divisions of later times, or at least could not accurately have reproduced an ancient arrangement unknown to its compiler.

Just as the catalogue of the Fathers of the Council of Constantinople of the year 381—which distinguishes Osroene, the two Phrygias, Lycaonia, Euphratesia, and other new provinces—is rightly believed to have been composed at that time, or to have been drawn from the actual subscriptions of those Fathers, with which it agrees, because it represents the arrangement of provinces then prevailing, so the same must be thought of the catalogue of the Nicene Fathers, which reflects the arrangement of the provinces in force in the age of the Nicene Council.

7. We must now answer certain difficulties that troubled Tillemont. The principal ones may be reduced to two points: first, because our catalogue does not list 318 Fathers, the number of Nicene bishops reported by several ancient witnesses; and certainly some bishops who, according to other documents, unquestionably attended the Nicene Council are absent from it; second, because, on the contrary, it designates certain men who appear to have to be excluded from the Nicene Fathers.

He adds two lesser objections: namely, that Narcissus of Neroniadis and Narcissus of Irenopolis are named as distinct bishops of Cilicia, although Neroniadis and Irenopolis were one and the same city; and that the bishop of Ancyra is called Pancratius in the commonly transmitted texts, although all writers call him Marcellus.

8. So that none of these points may prejudice the antiquity of our catalogue, already sufficiently established, we shall first present another example. No one can doubt the antiquity and authority of the subscriptions of the pseudo-Sardican council produced by Saint Hilary. Nevertheless, almost the same difficulties are indicated in them by Tillemont himself, note 52 on Athanasius.

Some bishops are certainly omitted there, just as we shall see that several are omitted by the same Hilary in the subscriptions of the true Sardican council. Moreover, two bishops of Troas are listed there, although all geographers know only one Troas. The bishop of Chalcedon is written as Thelaphus, although he was called Maris.

If these points may indeed lead us to believe that such subscriptions are incomplete and erroneous in places, but not to deny their antiquity, which Saint Hilary sufficiently safeguards, or their origin in the Acts of the pseudo-synod itself, why should similar difficulties not produce the same judgment concerning the catalogue of the Nicene Fathers, which we have shown to have been compiled at the very time of that council?

9. Some defects must be attributed to the carelessness of scribes. Since the city of Narcissus was first called Neroniadis and later Irenopolis, it was easy for the latter name to be added subsequently in the margin and then transferred from the margin into the text, so that one bishop came to be regarded as two. Compare what we shall observe on this subject in the notes to chapter 1 of the following collection, col. 35.

The manuscripts of the collections of Vat. Regina 1997 and the Quesnelliana to be published in this volume, which derive from one source, assign the name Pancratius, or Pancarius, to the bishop of Ancyra [Col. 0029B]. They are corrected by the other versions, the old and Isidorian, which derive from another source and in which Marcellus is recorded. See the notes in the same place, col. 37.

Here too, in the reading “Pancratius,” an ancient copyist’s error, which passed into other manuscripts, is plainly evident. Nothing is more common in old books; this fact cannot therefore give rise to suspicion that the work is a forgery.

10. A smaller number of Fathers, and the omission of some Fathers, could more easily have occurred in the Nicene catalogue than in the subscriptions of the Sardican or pseudo-Sardican councils.

Although it is highly probable to us that all 318 Nicene Fathers subscribed the Creed, the number of their subscriptions would nevertheless have been excessive. It therefore appears that several copies were excerpted from the original of the Creed, which contained the individual autograph subscriptions, with only the two subscriptions of Hosius and the legates of the Roman Church preserved for us after the Creed [Col. 0029C]. For the sake of brevity, the names of the other bishops were omitted.

Someone compiled only their catalogue, either at the council itself or shortly afterward. He did not have before his eyes the autograph of the council containing the 318 subscriptions, and could not recognize all the Fathers from the subscriptions of that autograph.

Thus even Eusebius, although he was one of the Nicene Fathers, did not know their number as 318. In the *Life of Constantine*, Book III, chapter 8, he reports that there were more than 250. Likewise Saint Eustathius of Antioch, who attended the Nicene Council, says in a fragment preserved by Theodoret, Book I, chapter 8:

“When the great council had assembled at Nicaea on account of these matters, with about 270 bishops gathered together, I cannot state the number exactly because of the immense size of that assembly; for I was not inquisitive about determining it.”

If several copies of the Creed had been issued with all 318 subscriptions, and each one individually, the number of the Nicene bishops could not have escaped these Fathers, nor would it have been necessary to investigate it.

What Saint Eustathius did not wish to undertake with greater curiosity, the author of the catalogue undertook. But since he compiled it neither from the complete subscriptions of the Creed nor from fuller Acts of the council—which, as John Albert Fabricius sufficiently proved after Valesius and Pagi, were not written down—*Bibliotheca Graeca*, volume II, Book VI, chapter 4, p. 356—but from a recent recollection of events and from other documents of the council, which would not always necessarily have displayed all the names in the form in which we believe they were recorded in the subscriptions of the Creed, it is not surprising that he passed over the names of some Fathers.

Perhaps the author used a document of the Nicene Council to which fewer bishops had subscribed than to the Creed, as we see happened in the Sardican synodical letter to the Churches of Mareotis printed in this volume (below, col. 607). It does not report all the bishops who signed, because, as Athanasius testifies in his letter to those same Churches, not all the bishops were present to sign (ibid., col. 610).

11. Once the deficiency in the number of bishops has been cleared away, the catalogue would be more difficult to defend if it listed men who had not been among the Nicene Fathers. Tillemont noted two: Zeno of Tyre and Theodore of Tarsus.

He believes that Zeno must be excluded from the episcopate of Tyre at the time of the Nicene Council and that Paulinus should be substituted for him. But Epiphanius, *Against Heresy* 69, chapter 4, listing six bishops to whom Saint Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, wrote shortly before the Nicene Council, names among them Zeno of Tyre. It is most improbable that he alone was not a bishop, especially since the context itself shows that the letter was addressed to bishops.

Although this Zeno is named last among the six bishops, he is commended by the special title ἀρχαῖος, that is, “principal,” because he surpassed all the others. For the bishop of Tyre was the *protothronos*, or first bishop after the bishop of Antioch in the entire diocese of the East [Col. 0030B].

Therefore, just as the other five bishops named by Epiphanius, contemporaries of the Nicene Council, are rightly recorded in our catalogue, so too is Zeno of Tyre.

If the two Paulini of Tyre are distinguished, one earlier than Zeno and the other later, the entire difficulty introduced by Tillemont into the *Life of Saint Eustathius* disappears.

As for Theodore of Tarsus, Tillemont, relying on the authority of Suidas—or rather of Philostorgius—objects that he was ordained bishop much later. But apart from the fact that he relies on a writer who is mistaken in several other matters and who is certainly later than our catalogue, if the Theodore mentioned by Philostorgius was bishop of Tarsus at a later date, it would be necessary to posit another, earlier Theodore, contemporary with the Nicene Council, as the more ancient testimony of our catalogue requires.

It should nevertheless be noted that this Theodore of Tarsus is omitted from the same catalogue appended to the Isidorian version in the extremely ancient manuscript of the chapter of Verona, no. 58.

Tillemont also adds Macedonius of Mopsuestia, the famous supporter of the Eusebians [Col. 0030C], whom none of those who named other Nicene Fathers favorable to Arius listed among the Nicene Fathers. But this is merely a negative argument and can establish nothing.

Macedonius, called “the confessor of Mopsus” in the synodical letter of the pseudo-Sardican council, appears to have been an ancient bishop who had confessed the faith during the persecution and could therefore have attended the Nicene Council. Perhaps he had not yet joined the Eusebian party at that council, or supported it so mildly that he was not to be counted among its prominent leaders.

Secundus of Ptolemais presents a greater difficulty. Since he was condemned and driven into exile together with Theonas of Marmarica because he refused to sign the Creed, he ought not to be counted among those Fathers who subscribed the Creed.

But we have observed that our catalogue was taken not from the subscriptions of the Creed but from another source. It is uncertain whether the title THE NAMES OF THE BISHOPS prefixed to the catalogue was intended, in the mind of its author, to present the names of those who attended Nicaea or those who subscribed.

Since Secundus of Ptolemais certainly attended the Nicene Council, he could be included in the catalogue in the former sense. But if, because it was placed beneath the first two subscriptions, the catalogue was intended to include only those who signed the Creed, Secundus of Ptolemais was inserted through some confusion similar to that recorded by us in the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon: in the Fathers of Act 15, as well as in Act 16, published by us, Stephen of Ephesus is listed even though he had been deposed in the preceding Act 12 and certainly did not obtain a place among the Fathers in the later acts.

We have noted other errors in the names at this council in the notes to the same Act 16 (our col. 1251, no. 2), and then in notes 4, 5, 6, and 7 (ibid., no. 3 ff.). If such errors can enter the very Acts of councils, who would be surprised if Secundus of Ptolemais was inserted into our catalogue?

Even if, therefore, some mistakes and omissions can be noted in this catalogue, none of them contributes anything toward excluding the antiquity [Col. 0031A] that we seem to have demonstrated above, an antiquity that similar difficulties do not take away from other catalogues or from the subscriptions of the Sardican or pseudo-Sardican council preserved by Saint Hilary.

12. Since in this paragraph we have defended the arrangement of the Eastern provinces recorded in the catalogue of the Nicene Fathers, we may append, as it were, a corollary from what has been established, by which the date of the Council of Laodicea—much disputed among scholars—may be determined with greater certainty than before.

This council is transmitted as having been held at Laodicea of Phrygia Pacatiana, both in Greek and in all the ancient versions. But since, in the civil arrangement that prevailed at the time of the Sardican Council, only one Phrygia is named, as we proved earlier, the name “Phrygia Pacatiana,” which was introduced after that Phrygia was divided into two—namely, Salutaris and Pacatiana—must be placed after the Council of Sardica.

Some have therefore wrongly thought the Council of Laodicea to have preceded Sardica. Since, moreover, in the Greek exemplars and in the Isidorian and Dionysian versions the Laodicean canons are set down before the Constantinopolitan canons, there can be no doubt that the Council of Laodicea was held between the Councils of Sardica and Constantinople, that is, between the years 347 and 381, the period to which it most appropriately belongs.

[XXII] § 2. The catalogues of the Fathers of Ancyra and Neocaesarea, which are presented in the commonly transmitted texts of the councils together with the names of cities and provinces, are shown to be foreign to the Greek manuscript of the canons and spurious.

13. We defended the catalogue of the Nicene bishops arranged with the names of cities and provinces because it was inserted in the Greek text by the first author of the manuscript from some older exemplar composed around the time of the council itself, and because it agrees with the arrangement of the provinces at that time.

The situation is different with the catalogues of bishops that are presented, together with the names of cities [Col. 0031C] and provinces, after the Ancyrene and Neocaesarean canons in the commonly transmitted texts of the councils (volume I of the Venetian edition, cols. 1505 and 1518).

We believe these catalogues should be considered worthless, both because they are found neither in the original Greek manuscript nor in the ancient versions, and because they in no way reflect the civil arrangement of the provinces that prevailed at the time of each council.

Of the three ancient Latin translations, only two—the Isidorian and the old version—have transmitted to us in the Ancyrene canons merely the names of the bishops and cities, and in the Neocaesarean canons merely the names of the bishops.

In both groups Dionysius knows none of these names of bishops, as we learned from two manuscripts, Vaticanus 5845 and Vaticanus Palatinus 577, which contain the uncontaminated Dionysian text.

The copies of the Hadriana collection, however, which received the Dionysian version of these canons, added to that version the names of the bishops and cities in the Ancyrene canons, but only the names of the bishops in the Neocaesarean canons [Col. 0031D], from another translation. This arrangement agrees neither with the Isidorian nor with the old version, as may be seen in volume I of the Venetian edition of the councils, col. 1499, note 1, and col. 1515, note 1, where these two series of bishops are wrongly attributed to Dionysius.

Therefore the designation of the provinces found in the commonly transmitted catalogues of these synods, col. 1505 d and col. 1518 c, since it is supported by no ancient version or original Greek text, must be referred to a later addition.

14. The names of the provinces themselves demonstrate the later forgery much more clearly. They do not express the arrangement corresponding to the time of those councils, but another arrangement introduced later.

For not only is Phrygia Pacatiana named, which we have proved to have been established after the Council of Sardica, but Cilicia I and II, Galatia I, and Cappadocia I are also presented, although these divisions were made much later. Nothing more decisive for establishing a later interpolation could be desired.

# CHAPTER IV. On the chronological notices by which the Ancyrene and Neocaesarean canons are said to have preceded the Council of Nicaea, while the Gangran canons are said to have followed it; and on the true date of the Antiochene canons and the council at which they were composed

[Col. 0032A]

## § 1. The chronological notices prefixed in the collections to the Ancyrene, Neocaesarean, and Gangran canons derive from the original Greek manuscript. The statement that the Gangran synod preceded Nicaea is removed, and its date is established. Whether the canons of the earlier synods were read and confirmed at Nicaea.

1. The chronological notices prefixed to the Ancyrene, Neocaesarean, and Gangran canons have come under suspicion in some quarters because of the Gangran council. For although the Gangran rules are stated in the notice to have been issued after the Nicene Council [Col. 0032B] (*Preface to volume I of the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, no. 61), Father Coustant nevertheless considered this notice inferior to a certain preface or address of Hosius, recorded in a very ancient manuscript of Corbie written around the time of Vigilius. In it [XXIII] these same canons, no less than the Ancyrene and Neocaesarean canons, are said to have been read and confirmed at the Nicene Council and consequently to have preceded Nicaea.

For after the title “The Constitutions of the Canons of Ancyra Begin,” the following address of Hosius is recorded:

“Hosius the bishop said: Since many things have been omitted (perhaps ‘prefaced’) that pertain to the strengthening of the Church, which have already been established by the previous synod of Ancyra, Caesarea, and Granius (that is, Gangra), and are now before us, let Your Blessedness order that they be unfolded by being read aloud, so that all may thus come to know the acts (or ‘know them’), and that what was done by our predecessors may be recited.”

“And they were read.”

The Ancyrene, Neocaesarean, and Gangran canons are then appended, followed finally by the Nicene canons. Father Coustant therefore thinks that the preceding address of Hosius, although placed under the title of the Ancyrene canons, belongs to the Nicene Council, whose Fathers wished the decrees of the earlier synods mentioned above to be reread and confirmed before they composed their own canons [Col. 0032C].

This opinion, then, which asserts that the Gangran synod preceded Nicaea, rests solely upon this address of Hosius, which he excerpted from a single Corbie manuscript.

## 2.

This passage, however, presents several clear indications of being an interpolation. We possess several distinct and very ancient versions of the Nicene canons, found in the manuscripts Vat. Regina 1997 and of the Veronese chapter-house 55. We also possess three other versions of all the Greek canons—the Isidorian, the ancient, and the Dionysian—which were translated from old Greek exemplars. We likewise possess Greek codices of these same canons, some already published and others still unpublished. Yet nowhere does this passage appear.

Moreover, the Corbie codex presents the Nicene canons from the translation of Dionysius Exiguus, as Coustant himself clearly demonstrated by transcribing the version of the eighth Nicene canon in his admonition to Innocent’s Epistle 17, p. 826. But it presents the Ancyran, Caesarean, and Gangran canons from the ancient Isidorian version. Now this passage of Hosius is found neither in the Dionysian translation, nor in the Isidorian, nor in any of those collections that derived these same canons from either version. Indeed, those collections contain an entirely contrary annotation, which we shall discuss shortly. It is therefore evident that this passage, foreign to those versions, was inserted into the Corbie exemplar.

It is also inserted after the heading, “The constitutions of the canons of Ancyra begin,” as though it pertained not to the Council of Nicaea but to the synod of Ancyra. P. Coustant suspects that *Anquirit.* should be corrected to *Nicaen.*, on the hypothesis that this passage must pertain to the Council of Nicaea, in which Hosius participated, and not to Ancyra, in which he did not participate. But this very error in the heading makes the passage much more suspect and shows that the hypothesis rests on an exceedingly weak foundation.

Before P. Coustant, Stephanus Baluzius found this passage in the same Corbie manuscript, but suspected nothing concerning the Council of Nicaea. He judged that it belonged to the Council of Elvira, at which Hosius was present; yet he likewise established this conjecture with no probability.

Nor do the words of Andrew of Rhodes, recorded at the Council of Florence in the second session held at Ferrara, support Coustant’s view; rather, they oppose it. “Before the first [general] synod,” he says, “many other synods were celebrated: at Antioch against Paul of Samosata; at Ancyra against those who did not receive those approaching the faith because they had denied Christ under torture; and a third at Neocaesarea. The Nicene synod received all these synods.” Although this much later bishop—who is not a competent witness in an ancient matter—believed that the synods preceding Nicaea had been [Col. 0033B] received by the Nicene Fathers, he did not present Gangra as earlier than Nicaea, but three others that had genuinely preceded it.

## 3.

Once this passage of Hosius has therefore been set aside, greater credence must be given to the chronological annotation by which the Gangran synod is recognized as later than Nicaea. Nor should this annotation be attributed to a later addition by some Latin copyist. Since it is found, no less than the other two annotations prefixed to the Ancyran and Neocaesarean canons, in Latin with the same meaning, although in different words, in three ancient translations of diverse origin—the Isidorian, the ancient, and the Dionysian—it cannot be doubted that it derived from the original Greek codex of the canons and was found there by all three translators.

Indeed, in the surviving Greek codices of the canons this annotation is still read. It is plainly known not to have been translated from Latin exemplars into Greek, but to have been taken from more ancient Greek manuscripts. Who, in the face of all these Latin and Greek exemplars, would judge that a single Latin Corbie codex, and the passage of Hosius transcribed in it—which is weakened by several indications of interpolation—should be preferred?

Nor should one, with P. Coustant, insist upon the antiquity of the Corbie collection. Since, as we noted shortly before, it presents the Nicene canons from the Dionysian version, this Corbie collection is certainly later than Dionysius’s version itself, not to mention the Isidorian and ancient versions, and still more so than the original Greek codex from which that annotation passed into those versions. There can be no reason why this later Corbie collection should be preferred to all those earlier witnesses that support the annotation.

Indeed, the passage of Hosius, supported only by this collection, is shown even more clearly to be an interpolation by the many earlier witnesses that report the Gangran synod as later than Nicaea, if—as P. Coustant interpreted it—it indicates that the Gangran canons were read at Nicaea and were earlier than it.

## 4.

What is more, the same chronological annotation is confirmed by two Greek writers, Socrates and Sozomen, who sufficiently declare that the date of the Gangran synod was later not merely than Nicaea but also than the Council of Sardica.

The entire question depends upon identifying the Eustathius who is mentioned in the synodical letter prefixed to the Gangran canons and addressed to the bishops of Armenia. All ancient writers, together with Socrates (*Book II, chapter 43*) and Sozomen (*Book III, chapter 14*), agree in identifying him as Eustathius, bishop of Sebaste, who lived in Armenia around the middle of the fourth century.

Sozomen seems to excuse Eustathius, as though it were not he himself but his disciples, who had gone over to various factions, who were proponents of the heresies condemned at that synod. The wording of the synodical letter favors this interpretation, insofar as it principally attacks the Eustathians. Among these, St. Epiphanius, *Heresy* 75, names Aerius, and he certainly attributes to him several of the errors condemned in that synodical letter.

If he adds other errors of which the synodical letter says not a word, these may be believed to have been added later by Aerius himself. On this subject, see the fuller discussion in the *Life of St. Basil*, which the Benedictine Fathers prefixed to volume three of his works, chapter 5, nos. 4, 5, and 6.

The objection raised from the fact that Eustathius, mentioned in the synodical letter, is not called a bishop is of little importance. It is clearly outweighed by the agreement between the errors noted there and those which Epiphanius attributes to the disciples of Eustathius of Sebaste.

## 5.

Further substantial confirmation of this view can be drawn from the heading, or the names of the bishops prefixed to the synodical letter. This heading, not only in Greek but also in the Latin exemplars of various collections and versions that preserve the synodical letter, gives Eusebius first place.

In the synodical pamphlet, where the Gangran council is discussed, we read: “It had Dion, Δίον, as its president.” Since no bishop of this name is ever recorded in the aforementioned heading, some have suspected that we should read [Col. 0034B] Hosius, whom the commonly circulated councils, from some codex, place among the Gangran Fathers in the following manner: “Hosius of Cordova” (vol. II of the Venetian edition, col. 423).

But we possess the Greek text of this synodical letter, as well as two further versions, the Isidorian and the ancient. Dionysius omitted the synodical letter; but in the Hadriana collection, which received the canons from Dionysius, the synodical letter was added from the Isidorian translation.

Now the name of Hosius is absent not only from the original Greek, but also from the oldest and best manuscripts of both the Isidorian and ancient versions, and even from the Hadrian manuscripts that we were able to collate. The names of the bishops are transcribed from these in vol. II of the *Councils*, col. 428a. Compare note 9 on chapter 4 of the *Code of Canons*, which we shall publish in this volume, col. 121.

Even if the name of Hosius is found in some later manuscript of the Isidorian or Hadrian collection, one not mentioned in the commonly circulated editions of the councils, there can nevertheless be no doubt that it was inserted, contrary to the testimony of the Greek text and the other Latin codices, at the discretion of some copyist.

Another indication of this addition may be that, whereas the other bishops are presented in the heading without the name of a city, only in the case of Hosius is the patronymic designation “of Cordova” recorded.

Since Hosius therefore should not be counted among the Gangran Fathers, we believe that the synodical pamphlet did not read *Dion*, δίον, but the mutilated form *bion*, βίον, [XXV] written for *Eusebion*, Εὐσέβιον, “Eusebius.” Since this name is certainly listed first by all the Greek and Latin catalogues, or rather by all the headings, we rightly judge him to have been president of the Gangran synod.

He appears to have been none other than Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. Since, by virtue of the prerogative of his see, he held primacy throughout the diocese of Pontus, and consequently in Paphlagonia and Armenia, he presided over the Gangran council of that diocese.

His period agrees with the time of Eustathius of Sebaste and his disciples. Moreover, since this same Eusebius, the celebrated predecessor of St. Basil the Great, held the see of Caesarea from A.D. 362 to A.D. 370, we may reasonably conclude that the Gangran synod was held within this period.

Thus the testimonies of Socrates and Sozomen, the dates of Eustathius and Eusebius, and the order of the synodical pamphlet and of the heading or catalogue of bishops agree well with one another; and the chronological annotation stating that the Gangran canons were composed after the Nicene canons is proved to be entirely true.

## 6.

This view, by which we placed the Gangran synod between the years 362 and 370, would have been accepted by more people had it not been opposed by the order of the canons in the Greek codex, in which the Gangran canons precede the Antiochene. From this they appear to have been earlier than the Antiochene council, a conclusion wholly inconsistent with the period of Eusebius of Caesarea in Cappadocia and Eustathius of Sebaste.

This objection, which greatly influenced Tillemont (*Notes 27 and 28 on St. Basil*, vol. IX) and other men of great reputation, can easily be dissolved on the basis of what was established in chapter 2, no. 5: namely, that the original Greek collection ended with the Gangran canons, while the Antiochene canons, together with the others, were appended to the Gangran canons in a later addition, without disturbing the original order of the codex.

## § 2. The Renown of the Antiochene Canons. Various Opinions Concerning Their Authors and Date. It Is Shown That, Contrary to the Prevailing View, They Do Not Belong to the Antiochene Synod Convened by the Eusebian Heretics at the Dedication in 341, but to Another Earlier Synod, Held in 332 and Composed Almost Entirely of Nicene Fathers. The Catalogue of the Fathers of This Synod, Published in the Councils after the Synodical Letter, Is Proved to Be an Interpolation. On the Number of the Fathers Who Issued These Canons.

## 7.

The source of the Antiochene canons is a Greek collection from which they passed into the Latin collections after being translated into Latin in three versions—the Isidorian, the ancient, and the Dionysian.

When the Fathers of Chalcedon cited several of these canons, they used a Greek codex of the canons that displayed a continuous sequence of numbers, as we observed in chapter 1.

This general council conferred great renown and authority upon the canons themselves, since it treated them as regulations of the Fathers. For in the fourth session, after the fifth Antiochene canon had been read, all the most reverend bishops cried out: “This is the just rule of the Fathers.”

John II transcribed the fourth and fifteenth Antiochene canons among the canons addressed to Caesarius of Arles. Pope Zacharias calls these same canons “the sanctions of the blessed Fathers” in Epistle 7, addressed to Pippin. Nicholas I, in Epistle 9 to the emperor Michael, calls them “the venerable Antiochene canons” and “sacred canons.”

Leo IV, at the Roman council, makes the most honorable mention of these canons in the following words: “What else can we think or declare except that the holy Fathers who, while seated in the Antiochene council, promulgated in the third chapter and established inviolably…” (vol. IX of the Venetian edition of the *Councils*, col. 1137).

## 8.

It is of great importance to know the authors of these canons, for they have been wrongly understood by some. We find four opinions on this matter.

The first is that of Cardinal Bellarmine, *On Councils*, book I, chapter 6. After listing four Antiochene councils, he says:

“The fifth is a Catholic provincial council of thirty bishops, whose twenty-five canons are found in volume I of the *Councils*. It seems to have been held in the time of Jovinian and Liberius. See Sozomen, book VI, chapter 4.”

But in this passage Sozomen mentions a council convened at Antioch in the year 363 under Meletius. He attributes to it only a synodical letter to Jovinian concerning the faith and says nothing of any canon issued by it.

Since the bishops who subscribed that synodical letter differ from the bishops placed beneath the Antiochene canons, who would fail to see that these canons belong to another Antiochene synod?

## 9.

The second opinion is that of the most eminent Baronius and many others, who think that these canons were composed at the Antiochene council held by the Eusebians against St. Athanasius in the year 341, on the occasion of the dedication of the famous Antiochene church which Constantine the Great had begun to build and his son Constantius had completed.

This opinion rests on two foundations. The first is the heading “At the dedication,” or “At the consecration,” prefixed to these canons in the ancient versions of Dionysius, the Hadriana collection, and the ancient version. These headings indicate that the same inscription had once been found in the Greek text by the translators as well.

The second is the testimony of Palladius and other defenders of St. John Chrysostom. When the fourth Antiochene canon was brought against him, they replied that this canon had been issued by forty Arians against St. Athanasius. The Arians who arranged for St. Athanasius to be condemned at Antioch belonged to the Antiochene synod held at the dedication in the year 341.

## 10.

Schelestratius, however, regarded Baronius’s opinion as improbable, since he considered it incredible that canons composed by Arians should have been received by the Church, both Greek and Latin.

Accordingly, in his work on the Antiochene council, printed at Antwerp in 1681, he endeavors to prove that the twenty-five canons do indeed belong to the Antiochene council convened at the dedication in 341, but that they are wrongly attributed to the Arians.

Although forty Arians had assembled there, he maintains that a greater number of Catholic bishops nevertheless gave authority to those same canons. He considers the canon brought against John Chrysostom, which Palladius attributes to the forty Arians, different from the fourth canon: the latter, he says, was enacted together with the other canons at the aforementioned synod by approximately ninety-five bishops, most of them Catholics, rather than by forty.

Accordingly, he argues that the words of the canon brought against Chrysostom, which Palladius quotes, differ from the fourth Antiochene canon. He therefore thinks that the canon described by Palladius was composed after the dedication synod by the Eusebians alone against St. Athanasius, whom he endeavors to show was condemned by those same men after that synod.

Those who have investigated the history of events more carefully have demonstrated with reliable evidence that, although at the larger synod convened on the occasion of the dedication the Eusebians, though fewer in number, prevailed and at the beginning of the synod drew other bishops into the condemnation of Athanasius, they nevertheless do not doubt that the canon brought against St. John Chrysostom and said to have been issued against St. Athanasius was composed at the beginning of that same synod by all the Fathers, and that it is itself the fourth Antiochene canon.

If the wording of this fourth canon and that produced by Palladius does not entirely agree, what difference does that make, since the meaning is the same in both places? Palladius did not recite the canon itself in the same words, but expressed a summary of it in the sense required by the circumstances of John Chrysostom.

The entire difference consists in the fact that Palladius has the words “justly or unjustly,” which the fourth canon does not contain. But when the enemies of Chrysostom saw that the charges brought against him could not be proved, they said that not another crime but this one alone should be brought to judgment: namely, that after his deposition he had placed himself upon the episcopal throne without a conciliar sentence (Socrates, book VI, chapter 16).

When they pressed upon him the fourth Antiochene canon, which prohibited this, it was as though they were saying that the canon had equal force whether someone had been deposed justly or unjustly. Palladius explained it in this sense, which suited the case, in order to neutralize the force and perverse interpretation of the canon being brought against him.

Certainly Palladius knew this canon from no other source than the Greek collection. Because his Greek codex of that collection bore the heading “At the dedication,” he attributed it to the Arians, whom he had learned from history to have condemned St. Athanasius at the dedication.

Therefore Socrates, who took from Palladius and from other defenders of St. John Chrysostom what relates to John’s case, attributed not only the fourth canon but all the Antiochene canons to the same council held at the dedication.

## 11.

Although Tillemont has no doubt that this fourth canon was composed by the Eusebians at the synod of the year 341, he nevertheless noticed that several matters found in the edition of these canons do not suit that council or those same Eusebians.

The letter prefixed to the canons, indicating a time of peace, is wholly inconsistent with the great disturbance of affairs stirred up by the Arians at that time, especially at that synod.

Some of the canons also seem impossible to attribute to Eusebian authors. The ordination of Gregory of Alexandria is rejected in canon 19, and the translations of Eusebius of Nicomedia are rejected in canon 21. Nor is it plausible that, under Constantius, when the Arians were prevailing, the Nicene synod would have been praised with solemn honor in the first canon, which also speaks of Constantine as still living rather than dead.

The very small number of thirty bishops prefixed or appended to the canons likewise does not suit the much larger synod of the year 341, especially since among them are not found the leading Eusebians who conducted everything at that synod, and Flacillus is absent, although he should not have been away in that year while governing the Church of Antioch.

Moreover, the bishops who were the authors of the canons are said to have been summoned from the provinces of the Eastern diocese subject to the bishop of Antioch, whereas the synod held at the dedication was composed also of bishops from the dioceses of Pontus and Thrace.

For this reason the eminent Tillemont suspected (*Note 26 on Arian History*) that two Antiochene councils had been confused into one by the Greek compiler: namely, the very large council held at the dedication in 341, to which he attributes the fourth canon against Athanasius, composed by the Eusebians, and perhaps also the twelfth, which he considers to have been issued against the same man; and another council convened from the provinces subject to the bishop of Antioch before the year 335, to which he thinks the letter, subscriptions, and remaining canons should be attributed.

## 12.

Although Tillemont’s opinion seems more probable than the others, it does not entirely satisfy us. We regard this confusion by the ancient Greek compiler as unlikely.

If the compiler had found the fourth and twelfth canons, which are thought to have been composed by the Eusebians at the dedication, issued by and distinct from different synods, he would not have intermingled them with the canons of another synod, but would have added them at the end.

When the Nicene and Sardican canons were joined together, the Nicene canons were transcribed first and the Sardican afterward. Likewise, when the canons of the Council of Constantinople of the year 381 were joined in the Greek codex with two others belonging to another synod, those two are found appended after them.

Therefore either all the Antiochene canons must be attributed to the synod of the year 341, if the fourth—or even the twelfth—had Eusebians as its authors; or all were enacted at an earlier synod, and the fourth canon was assigned to the council of the year 341, in the time of Chrysostom, only through hallucination and error.

What then? Judging Tillemont’s observations to be extremely serious, and investigating the matter more carefully to determine whether an earlier Antiochene council could be found to which all the canons would apply, we finally and successfully discovered that they correspond precisely to the Antiochene synod of the year 332.

## 13.

Since the names of the bishops to whom the Antiochene canons are attributed provided us with an indication of this matter, something must first be said about them more precisely.

The Greek collection, as it has come down to us from Greek codices written around the time of Photius—codices that omitted some material from the ancient manuscripts—lacks the names of the bishops and mentions only the provinces from which they assembled, in these words:

“Holy and peaceful synod, gathered by God at Antioch from the provinces of Coele Syria, Phoenicia, Palestine, Arabia, Mesopotamia, Cilicia, and Isauria, to the holy fellow priests in the Lord who are present throughout the provinces: greetings.”

The names of the bishops, however, have been preserved for us in the most ancient Latin versions, which formerly received these canons from older Greek exemplars.

In the Isidorian version thirty bishops are listed; in the ancient version only twenty-two bishops’ names are given, although they agree with the names in the Isidorian version.

The translation of Dionysius omits the names of the bishops, as we conclude from two manuscripts containing pure Dionysius, Vat. 5845 and Palat. 577. In the manuscripts of the Hadriana collection, however, which received the Dionysian version, the names of the bishops were added from another source.

In these Hadrian manuscripts, each of the first seven bishops is assigned a province. These seven provinces agree with those mentioned shortly before in the Greek codex. Thus the text reads:

“Eusebius of Palestine; Theodotus of Mesopotamia; Theodore of Isauria; Antiochus of Phoenicia; Agapius of Arabia; Alphius of Cilicia”—so it should be read from the Pithoean codex, cited by Hardouin; otherwise, corruptly, [Col. 0038A] “of Vilicia,” [XXVIII] or “of Syria”—“Narcissus of Coele Syria.”

The remaining bishops are appended without the name of their provinces.

In the commonly circulated editions of the councils, however, after the synodical letter prefixed to the Antiochene canons, the catalogue of bishops is presented in such a way that each province is given with its bishops and each bishop with the name of his city:

“Of the province of Palestine, Eusebius of Gadara; of the province of Phoenicia, Anatolius of Emesa; Aeneas of Ptolemais,” and so forth (vol. II of the Venetian edition of the *Councils*, col. 585).

As Hardouin noted, no codices display this method of cataloguing.

This catalogue was therefore compiled later by some diligent scholar. Understanding that the Fathers of the Antiochene synod belonged to the seven Eastern provinces named in the manuscripts of the Isidorian version (see this volume, col. 424), and comparing them with the catalogue of the Nicene Fathers—for most of them attended both councils—he extracted and transcribed from that catalogue the cities and provinces of each man.

Since he did not find the names of two bishops, Patricius and Alexander, among the bishops of those seven provinces in the Nicene catalogue, he relegated them to the end without any designation of city or province, adding Eustathius, because he recognized that he was different from Eustathius of Antioch, who had already been deposed.

This diligent scholar, however, while making Eusebius—who had been bishop of Caesarea in Palestine—a bishop of Gadara, absorbed an error from the catalogue of the Nicene Fathers preserved in the Hadrian manuscripts.

The Isidorian and ancient versions list two bishops of Sebaste among the bishops of Palestine, as follows: “Marinus of Sebaste, Gaianus of Sebaste,” and then continue: “Eusebius of Caesarea, Sabinus of Gadara, Longinus of Ascalon,” and so forth (see below, col. 32).

In the Hadrian manuscripts, however, so that two bishops of the same Sebaste would not be listed, after “Marinus of Sebaste” the city names were transferred from the following bishops to the preceding ones, as follows: “Gaianus of Caesarea, Eusebius of Gadara, Sabinus of Ascalon,” and so forth.

Apart from this error of that diligent man, the designation of cities and provinces in the case of the other bishops may seem not implausible when derived from the Nicene catalogue, since most of the Antiochene Fathers were also Nicene.

We therefore recognize that the catalogue transcribed in the Hadrian exemplars is rather erroneous, assigning each of the first seven bishops his own province. Only the province of the first bishop, Eusebius of Palestine, agrees with the Nicene catalogue; the others do not.

It consequently becomes clear that the names of the seven provinces, which in the Greek text and in the Isidorian version are given separately, so that each refers indeterminately to only some of the bishops, were attached and adapted in the Hadrian manuscripts to the first seven bishops at the discretion of some copyist, without any prior examination of whether the province affixed to each actually suited him.

In the Greek original, as we recognize it from the ancient versions, only the names of the bishops were expressed, without any indication of province. Moreover, whenever anything is added to the names of bishops, it is usually the name of the city in particular, not merely that of the province, that is given.

## 14.

With these facts established, in the year 332, while the see of Antioch was vacant before the election of Euphronius, a synod was convened at Antioch to appoint a new bishop.

For this purpose only the bishops of the Antiochene diocese ought to have assembled. Since Constantine’s letter to the Antiochene synod convened for this reason is addressed to Theodotus, Theodore, Narcissus, Aetius, Alphius, and the other bishops who are at Antioch (*Eusebius, Life of Constantine*, book III, chapter 62), there can be no doubt that these were the principal bishops of that synod from the provinces of his diocese.

The same emperor also wrote a separate letter on this matter to Eusebius of Caesarea. Since Eusebius had come there from the province of Palestine, which was subject to Antioch, and since there was no bishop of Antioch, it is known that he played the leading role in that council on account of his eminence.

He had written separately to Constantine rather than together with the other bishops because all the votes had converged upon his election. But he himself recoiled from it and did not wish to place his name in the synodical letter of the other bishops, by which his confirmation was being requested; instead, he earnestly asked in another letter that this not be done.

Here, then, you have the principal names of the bishops who assembled at this Antiochene synod from the provinces of the Antiochene diocese in the year 332: Eusebius, Theodotus, [XXIX] Theodore, Narcissus, Aetius, and Alphius.

Among these six, do you not see five of the names that we listed shortly before in first place from the Hadrian codices? One, Aetius, who is identified among the Nicene Fathers as bishop of Lydda in Palestine, is absent from the catalogue of those same codices. Yet, through a very slight alteration caused either by copyist error or by the author of the Greek collection, he seems to have been wrongly transformed into “Enius,” or “Aenius,” as the same Hadrian manuscripts read. The author of the Isidorian version rendered this as “Aeneas.”

There should therefore be no doubt that the aforementioned canons were composed at this Antiochene synod of the year 332, and not at that of the year 341.

## 15.

This is confirmed above all by the fact that, on this interpretation, all the difficulties proposed by Tillemont are resolved and everything is properly reconciled.

The peace which Constantine celebrates in his letter to the people of Antioch as having been happily restored after the gravest dissension of the Antiochene Church agrees remarkably with the words of the Antiochene synodical letter:

“Holy and peaceful synod, etc.; the grace and truth of Jesus Christ, our Lord and Savior, visiting the holy Church of Antioch and joining it together in concord and agreement through the most peaceful spirit,” and so forth (*Eusebius, Life of Constantine*, book III, chapter 60).

Eusebius of Caesarea, through whose intervention peace was made among the Antiochenes (ibid., chapter 59), played the leading role in that synod, as we noted. Consequently, he is named first both in the catalogue prefixed to the canons and in the subscriptions, according to all witnesses.

The name of the bishop of Antioch is absent because this synod was held while the see of Antioch was vacant.

Since Eusebius had refused a translation or transfer of his see, canon 21, which prohibits such transfers, is especially appropriate to this synod. This is particularly so because the emperor, declaring in his letters to the synod that such transfers were contrary to ecclesiastical discipline, wrote that he wanted them to determine, before the election of the new bishop, what accords with the tradition of the apostles.

“Once these matters have been established,” he says, “your prudence will be able, according to the rule of the Church and apostolic tradition, to direct this election in the manner required by the order of ecclesiastical discipline” (ibid., chapter 62).

From this the precise time at which the canons were composed in this synod is clear: namely, after the emperor’s letter and before the election of Euphronius.

Since Euphronius was ordained by the bishops of his own diocese, canon 19 presents no difficulty.

The Nicene synod was held in the highest honor while Constantine the Great was still living. Consequently, the first canon agrees perfectly with this synod and period, especially since Eusebius took particular care to confirm in that canon the Nicene ruling concerning Easter and extolled it with the highest praise (ibid., chapter 18).

The number of thirty bishops and the seven provinces of the Antiochene diocese alone, listed both in the Greek text and in the Latin versions, agree well with this synod; they do not in any way agree with the larger synod of the year 341.

If Theodore, Jacobus, and Anatolius, listed in the Antiochene catalogue, are—as they appear to be—Theodore of Laodicea, Jacobus of Nisibis, and Anatolius of Emesa, who are found in the Nicene catalogue, this would provide a new and more evident confirmation for establishing the synod of the year 332 and excluding that of the year 341.

For in the year 335 Theodore no longer held the see of Laodicea; George held it instead, and he sat at the council of Tyre in that same year, as is clear from Athanasius’s *Second Apology*.

St. Jacobus of Nisibis had died in the year 649 of the Greek era—that is, A.D. 338—as is recorded in the Edessene Chronicle and also in another chronicle of Dionysius, patriarch of the Jacobites, preserved by Joseph Simon Assemani, vol. I of the *Bibliotheca Orientalis*, pp. 18 and 395.

Finally, Anatolius of Emesa could not have attended the council of the year 341, since at the beginning of that council Eusebius was appointed bishop of the Church of Emesa.

In view of such complete agreement among all the circumstances with the synod of the year 332 alone, who could still doubt whether the Antiochene canons should be assigned to that synod?

16. Nor should Canon 4 cause any scruple, which the defenders of St. John Chrysostom reported as having been issued against St. Athanasius in the Arian synod of the year 341. For, apart from the fact that the Theophilians—enemies of that same Chrysostom, who had brought this canon against him—denied it, we believe that Chrysostom’s defenders were mistaken in this matter and led others, both ancient and recent, into the same error. All the crimes alleged against St. Athanasius by the Eusebians are accurately reported in Pope Julius’s letter and in the works of [XXX] St. Athanasius himself. Yet in these [Col. 0040B] there is nowhere any indication of the crime addressed by the fourth canon—namely, that after his deposition he returned to his see without any new judgment—although this above all would have been the charge they ought to have brought against Athanasius if they had issued that canon against him.

The defenders of St. John Chrysostom presumed only this much because, having found among the Antiochene canons the canon which the Theophilians had brought against that holy bishop, they knew of only the Antiochene synod held *in encaeniis* in 341, and it was already well known from other documents that this synod had condemned St. Athanasius. Hence, again through error, they assigned these canons to that more numerous and fuller synod, reducing the number of bishops to forty, as we learned from Palladius. Yet in his text, instead of τεσσαράκοντα, “forty,” one should read τριάκοντα, “thirty”; for the Greek collection contained that number, as can be gathered from the ancient Isidorian and Hadrianic versions.

They evidently took this number of bishops not from the Acts of the synod of 341 [Col. 0040C] themselves, but from the Greek collection. For if they had consulted the Acts of that synod and found the canons there, they would have learned that approximately ninety-five bishops, not thirty or forty, had assembled at that council. Thus, because of the prejudice by which they knew only the Antiochene synod of 341, they attributed to that synod the canons found in the Greek collection, together with the same number of thirty or forty bishops. Indeed, they seem to have imbibed this error from the very inscription of the Greek codex, which in certain copies stated that these same canons had been established at Antioch *in encaeniis*.

We said “in certain Greek copies,” not in all. For since the words *in encaeniis* are omitted by the pure version of Dionysius in the codices mentioned earlier, the Greek exemplar of Dionysius plainly lacked them as well. Furthermore, if Innocent I, in Letter 7, no. 3, attributes the Antiochene canons to heretical authors, since he wrote this not from his own knowledge but on the report of Chrysostom’s defenders, to whom he was replying—and indeed admits there that the Roman Church recognized only the [Col. 0040D] Nicene canons—this should cause no difficulty. Nor should the authority of later writers, who transmitted the same account from those same defenders of Chrysostom, cause any difficulty.

17. Meanwhile, even if one does not believe that the fourth canon was issued against St. Athanasius at the synod of 341, it contains nothing in itself that is not entirely consonant with ecclesiastical discipline. It is therefore unsurprising that both the Greek and the Latin Church included it among the rules of the Fathers, together with the other Antiochene canons, which likewise, when their perverse interpretation is set aside, are in themselves most equitable.

For although Canons 2 and 5 appear to have been issued at the council of 332 against those Catholics who, in communion with St. Eustathius of Antioch—who had been unjustly deposed somewhat earlier through the machinations of the Arians—refused communion with the bishops who had been substituted for him, nevertheless those same heretics, while secretly operating under Constantine’s rule, had not [Col. 0041A] brought forward the true reason for which they took care to depose him as an ardent defender of the Nicene faith. Instead, they produced fictitious charges through a deception that misled even many who were not Arians. He could therefore rightly have been considered deposed, and consequently those canons were rightly regarded as having been enacted at this council against the Eustathians who avoided communion with his successors.

Once this deception is set aside, the same canons, issued against schism, are so just that they could have won the assent even of St. James of Nisibis and St. Paul of Neocaesarea, provided that these are the James and Paul listed in the catalogue of this synod. No doubt therefore remains that all these canons should be assigned to the Antiochene synod of 332.

# CHAPTER V  
## On the Sardican Canons

They were issued by the synod itself in two forms, Greek and Latin. The difference between these forms. What should be thought of the notable variant readings of the Latin copies, on account of which some have supposed that different Latin interpretations should be preferred.

[Col. 0041B]

1. When the Sardican synod, in its letter to Pope Julius preserved by St. Hilary (*Fragment* 1, no. 10), mentions what was “done,” “carried out,” and “established,” no one doubts that by the word “established” it indicates the canons composed by that synod. [XXXI] Yet some question whether these same canons were issued in Greek or in Latin. Since most of the Sardican Fathers used Greek speech and fewer used Latin, the opinion became prevalent that the canons had been written in Greek rather than Latin.

Consequently, before the publication of Dionysius Exiguus’s letter to Stephen, many believed that the Latin text of these canons, published by Dionysius, was a translation from the Greek. This seemed all the more credible because the Latin text received by Isidore appeared to be another interpretation. This opinion was current even in ancient times. For in the old manuscript 55 of the Veronese Chapter, [Col. 0041C] after the Sardican canons had been rendered into Latin from the Greek, the same canons are appended by a later but ancient hand as they were issued by Dionysius, with this title prefixed to them: “The same canons according to another translation.”

The edition of these same canons inserted in the ancient version, which we shall reprint in this volume, differs so greatly from the Dionysian and Isidorian readings that such variety appears to have arisen not from the same Latin original but from a different interpretation. Moreover, when it was observed that Dionysius testifies in the aforementioned letter that he had transmitted the decrees of the Sardican and African councils, which were issued in Latin, people began to think that, just as the African decrees originated in Latin, so the Sardican decrees too had been issued in Latin by the synod itself.

2. To prevent anyone from thinking that the Greek text we possess is a translation from a Latin original, it is necessary to believe that the Sardican canons were written at the council in two original forms: a Greek form for the Greek Fathers and a Latin form for the Latin Fathers.

We possess several [Col. 0041D] letters of this council that were either sent to all the bishops, with particular reference to the Greeks, or written to Greek Churches. Their Greek text survives, or else a Latin translation from the Greek, because they were issued in Greek. But we possess the letter to Pope Julius only in Latin, both in St. Hilary and in several Latin collections that do not appear to have received it from Hilary, since they differ somewhat in their subscriptions.

Nevertheless, the Latin text is the same in all of them, because both Hilary and the authors of those collections derived the letter from the same Latin original, from which several copies had formerly been published. The Sardican Fathers—among whom there were not a few Latins—thought that they should write to Pope Julius, who used the Latin language, not in Greek but in Latin.

In the other Greek councils—the Ancyran, Neocaesarean, Nicene, Gangran, Antiochene, Laodicean, and Constantinopolitan—[Col. 0042A] from which we have received canons rendered into Latin, either no Latin bishops or very few were present. It is therefore unsurprising that those canons were written only in Greek. But although there were more Greeks at the Sardican council, quite a few Latin Fathers nevertheless assembled from Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, and Pannonia. It will be clear from the catalogue of the Sardican Fathers, to be supplied shortly below, that at least twenty-seven bishops belonged to these provinces.

The canons, however, had been established not for the Greeks alone but also for the Latins, and some were enacted especially for the benefit of the Latins. They therefore had to be written not so much in Greek for the Greek Fathers as in Latin for the Latin Fathers. If the general synodical letter of that council, sent to Greeks no less than to Latins, appears to have been issued not only in Greek but also in Latin—as is shown by the formulas of the Latin exemplar in Hilary, which are entirely different from the Greek text and do not correspond to a translation—how much more must the same be judged concerning the canons? (See vol. II of the *Councils*, fifth edition, cols. 700 and [Col. 0042B] 711.)

3. Several, and by no means insignificant, differences between the Greek and Latin texts provide clear evidence of this twofold original form of the canons; because of these differences, one text cannot be said to have arisen from the other by translation.

In the commonly transmitted Greek text, three canons are absent that are read in every Latin text, namely Isidore’s Canons 10, 12, and 18. Conversely, two canons are absent from every Latin text that are found in the Greek, namely Canons 18 and 19.

If one of the three canons missing from the commonly transmitted Greek text—namely Isidore’s Canon 18, which begins “January”—did exist in the Greek exemplar from which the most ancient translation of these canons was taken, the translation that we shall publish in this volume and that has been preserved for us in the aforementioned manuscript 55 of the Veronese Chapter, nowhere nevertheless have we been able to find in Greek the other two canons that occur in the Latin exemplar. Likewise, among the many Latin copies of different origin, nowhere have we been able to find those two canons [XXXII] that all the [Col. 0042C] Greek copies consistently display.

If one text had been a translation of the other, the same canons would unquestionably have been read in both the Latin and Greek texts; one text would not have omitted some canons and added others. In addition, the order of the canons is entirely different in the two texts. For although the order of the canons in the Greek text agrees in all manuscripts, and the order of the canons in the Latin text is likewise found to be the same in Latin collections of different origins, the order of the Greek canons differs most substantially from the order of the canons in the Latin text. Such a difference is utterly foreign to the idea that one text is a translation of the other.

4. We shall present a clearer account of the twofold Greek and Latin original. Two canons in the Greek text mention a metropolitan, whom one searches for in vain in the Latin text.

The sixth Greek canon is rendered into Latin as follows:

> If it should happen in a province in which there are many bishops that one bishop does not attend the assembly, and through some negligence does not wish to assemble or to assent to the institution and election of bishops, [Col. 0042D] while the assembled multitude of the people insists that the bishop whom they request be appointed, that bishop who was not present must first be admonished by letter from the exarch of the province, namely, the metropolitan bishop, that the people are asking for a shepherd to be given to them; and I think it right that he too should be awaited, so that he may be present. But if, having been summoned by letter, he does not appear, and does not even reply, the will of the people is to be satisfied. Bishops must also be summoned from the neighboring province for the institution of the metropolitan bishop.

The most ancient translation from the Greek, found in the aforementioned Veronese manuscript, has “for the ordination of bishops” instead of “for the institution of the metropolitan bishop.” Since this rendering agrees with the context—for the matter concerns not the metropolitan but the ordination of a bishop by the metropolitan in the performance of his duties—it indicates that the translator had before him another and better reading than that found in the commonly transmitted Greek text.

In Dionysius’s Latin text, however, this same canon is given as Canon 5:

[Col. 0043A]

> If it should happen in a province in which there are many bishops that one bishop should happen to remain alone, and he through negligence should be unwilling to ordain a bishop, while the people have assembled, the bishops of the neighboring province must first approach the bishop who resides in that province and point out that the people are asking that a ruler be given to them, and that it is just that they too should come—or, according to another reading, that he himself should come—and ordain the bishop together with him. But if, having been summoned by letter, he remains silent, dissimulates, and gives no reply, the people must be satisfied: bishops should come from the neighboring province and ordain the bishop.

What in the Greek is attributed to the primate, or metropolitan, of the province is asserted in Dionysius’s Latin text—and likewise in the other Latin collections—with an entirely different meaning: it is attributed to the bishops of the neighboring province.

Similarly, in Canon 14 of the Greek text, concerning a deposed presbyter or deacon, we read:

> The one who has been expelled shall have the power of taking refuge with the bishop of the metropolis of the same province. But if the metropolitan is absent, he may go to the neighboring bishop and ask that his case be carefully examined. For [Col. 0043B] ears must not be denied to those who ask. The bishop who expelled him, whether justly or unjustly, must also bear calmly that the case be examined, so that his judgment may either be confirmed or corrected.

In Dionysius’s Latin text, however, it appears as Canon 17:

> Let the one who has been rejected have the power to appeal to the neighboring bishops, and let his case be heard and treated with greater care, because a hearing ought not to be denied to one who asks for it. Let that bishop who rejected him, whether justly or unjustly, patiently endure the matter being examined, so that his judgment may either be approved by the majority or amended.

In the Greek, the matter and judgment are entrusted to the metropolitan of the same province or, if he is absent, to the metropolitan of a neighboring province; in the Latin, they are entrusted to neighboring bishops.

Why is this so? These matters, which have caused difficulty to many, will easily be understood if one distinguishes two originals of the canon: one Greek for the Greeks, and the other Latin for the Latins. Since among the Greeks metropolitans had long been established in considerable numbers, the appeal of clergy of the lower orders to metropolitans [Col. 0043C] was prescribed in the Greek text.

But among the Latins—especially in Italy, Gaul, and Spain—at this time metropolitans had not yet been instituted as they were among the Greeks, as we have shown in the observations to Quesnell’s Dissertation 5, part II, chapter 5. For this reason, the Latin text decreed that clerical appeals should be brought not to metropolitans but to neighboring bishops [XXXIII]; and for the same reason, what in the Greek canon cited above is attributed to the exarch of the province, or metropolitan, is attributed in the Latin to neighboring bishops.

Here too a certain necessity becomes evident for publishing these canons in both a Greek and a Latin form, so that they might be adapted to the differing discipline and ecclesiastical organization of the Latins and Greeks.

Nor should you argue, in support of establishing metropolitans among the Latins as well, from Canon 9, which decrees that letters of recommendation be received from the bishop who is in the larger city, as the Greek text has it, or, as Dionysius’s Latin text reads, from the bishop who resides in the metropolis. We believe that a civil or geographical metropolis, [Col. 0043D] not an ecclesiastical one, is indicated here. Hence in other Latin manuscript copies—Vatican Regina 1997 and the Isidorian copy—we read: “who resides in the largest city, that is, the metropolis.” Here “largest city” explains a geographical or civil metropolis.

Among the Africans, to be sure, the bishop of a civil or geographical metropolis was not thereby a metropolitan. Nevertheless, at the synod of Hippo in 393, when the Mauritani Sitifenses requested their own primate, who according to African custom was the senior bishop, they simultaneously asked that, if anything had to be announced by the primate of Carthage to the Mauritanian bishops for the sake of discipline, it should be communicated to the bishop of Sitifis—that is, to the bishop of the civil or geographical metropolis.

Similarly, it was established at the council of Milevis in 402 that the register and archive of Numidia should be located both at the primary see and in the metropolis, that is, Constantina. Why, then, could something similar not have been established at Sardica, so that those traveling to the imperial court [Col. 0044A] might be given letters of recommendation by the bishop of the civil or geographical metropolis, even though among the Latins he did not possess metropolitan jurisdiction?

Since metropolitan bishops had not yet been instituted among them, it seemed appropriate that the bishop of the metropolis should be preferred over others in issuing letters of recommendation, because their metropolises and bishops were better known and more distinguished. This does not imply that ecclesiastical metropolises had already been instituted among the Latins; we have proved elsewhere from other documents that they were established only later. We have also seen that their absence at this time is substantially confirmed by the two Sardican canons in the Latin form.

Meanwhile, the fact that the sense of these canons is presented differently in the Greek and Latin texts, so that it might be adapted to the differing arrangements of the Latins and Greeks, wonderfully confirms the existence of distinct Greek and Latin originals. Perhaps for the same reason two canons issued in the Greek text were omitted from the Latin exemplar: since they concerned the Church of Thessalonica, they established nothing that could contribute to the [Col. 0044B] rule of the Latin Churches.

5. Nor should those variant readings found in Latin collections of different origin, which are so conspicuous that they have seemed to some to exhibit one and another form—or virtually one and another translation—of these same canons, lead anyone to reject a Latin original. For apart from the fact that their number and order, and also several of their statements, differ too greatly from the Greek to admit of a translation theory, anyone who weighs and compares the individual readings in the Latin copies more precisely will see that the entire variation consists in certain words scattered here and there, while complete lines and whole clauses agree word for word. Since this is not found in genuinely different translations, the original Latin text can be recognized as having been altered in places by the freer variants of copyists, while remaining identical at its root.

[Col. 0044C]

Nor should such great license among ancient copyists, and such extensive variation in a text originally written in Latin, seem incredible. A completely similar and unquestionable example is available from the African canons of the famous Carthaginian synod of 419, which Dionysius likewise affirms that he transmitted as being of Latin origin and as having been issued in Latin.

The canons of this synod, which in the aforementioned Dionysius are the first thirty-three African canons, we shall publish in this volume from the manuscript collections Vatican Regina 1997, Vatican 1342, and the Lucan-Colbertine collection. They are not only divided differently into forty canons but also contain notable variant readings of the kind we have found in the Sardican canons.

If no one can doubt their Latin original on account of such variants, neither should the Sardican canons be suspected for having received similar variants, since Dionysius testifies to the same Latin origin of both.

Anyone who wishes to recognize more clearly the Latin original of the Sardican canons preserved in the Latin collections should compare two translations of these same canons from the Greek [XXXIV]: the more recent one printed in the councils, [Col. 0044D] and the ancient one that we shall publish in this volume from the manuscript of the Veronese Chapter. When he perceives the enormous difference in both subject matter and order, as well as in wording, he will recognize that the Latin text, which coheres throughout the various collections, was not rendered from the Greek but proceeded from a Latin original.

# CHAPTER VI  
## Whether the Sardican Canons Were Inserted into the Greek Codex of Canons

Not all Greek codices of canons were alike, nor were the canons in all of them marked by a continuous numerical series. On the authority of the Sardican canons among the Greeks, including the Eastern Greeks.

1. It should be clear from the discussion in the preceding chapter that the Sardican canons were issued from the beginning not only in Latin but also in Greek, so that the Greek original text preserved for us by the Greeks themselves differs from the Latin original in the order and number of the canons and also in certain provisions [Col. 0045A] adapted to the discipline of the Greek Churches.

The whole controversy now concerns whether and when these same canons, written in Greek, were transferred into the Greek codex of synods and canons, and whether they always possessed authority among the Greeks, especially among the Eastern Greeks.

Christopher Justellus believed that the same canons were entered into the Greek codex only at a later date and had not been received by the ancient Easterners. He therefore judged that they should be excluded from the primitive Greek codex of canons, which he called the codex of the universal Church and constructed according to his own judgment, as we showed in Chapter 1.

The principal—or rather the sole—foundation of this opinion is drawn from Dionysius Exiguus. For the continuous series of 165 titles or canons, which he noted as having been set out from the Nicene canons through the Constantinopolitan canons in his Greek authority, or Greek codex of canons, leaves no proper intervening place for the Sardican canons. Hence he did not translate them from the Greek, as he did the others that he found in that codex [Col. 0045B], but added them in Latin, as they had been issued.

To prevent this from being thought peculiar to Dionysius’s one Greek codex, Justellus presents it as common to all Greek copies. In his preface he says:

> Hence it appears that the Fathers of the primitive Church, when compiling that ancient codex of canons according to which judgments concerning sacred matters were conducted, arranged the successive councils in a definite order and numbered their canons in a definite and continuous sequence, without interruption, so that nothing could be taken away from or added to this codex. For this reason the Ephesian and Chalcedonian Fathers and other ecclesiastical writers commonly call it τάξις and ἀκολουθία τῶν κανόνων, ἀκολουθία ἐκκλησιαστική, and ἀριθμῶν ἀκολουθία—“the order and succession of the canons,” “the ecclesiastical succession,” and “the succession of numbers” (vol. I, *Bibliotheca Juris Canonici*, p. 16).

Thus, from the very origin of the Greek codex of canons—which Justellus supposes to have been compiled and established by the authority of the Fathers and the Greek Church—it presents all the canons marked by a continuous [Col. 0045C] numerical series and succession, just as they were found in Dionysius’s exemplar and likewise in the similar one used by the Chalcedonian Fathers.

The whole purpose of this argument is to exclude the Sardican canons from the Greek codex of Dionysius on the ground that they had been removed from this numerical series, and thereby to show that they had not been received but rejected by the ancient Greek Church.

2. This argument, however, is unstable on many grounds. First, it is false that Justellus’s initial assumption is correct: namely, that the primitive codex had been compiled and approved by the authority of the Fathers and the Greek Church. We believe instead that the Greek collection of canons was assembled through private effort and for a long time lacked any public authority.

This is made plainly evident by what occurred in the case of St. John Chrysostom. His enemies brought against him the fourth Antiochene canon. The canons of the Antiochene synod had already been entered into the codex. What did Chrysostom and [Col. 0045D] the bishops of his party do in response? They protested that those canons had been composed not by Catholics but by Arians, and possessed no authority.

Let Palladius be read, who in his dialogue on the life of that same saint reports the discussion held on this matter by both sides. They were indeed deceived by the inscription “in encaeniis,” which those canons bore in the Greek codex, as we explained in Chapter 4, [XXXV] § 2.

But those who thus rejected these canons, even though they had been entered into the codex of canons, plainly did not know that this codex had been composed and approved by the Fathers of the Greek Church. If John Chrysostom and the other Eastern bishops of his party did not know of an approved codex, we do not understand how it can be established that the Greek Church had approved it before this time.

3. Second, we likewise judge it no less false that Justellus asserts that in the primitive Greek codex of canons, and consequently in the other ancient Greek copies, the canons of all the synods had been [Col. 0046A] marked by a continuous numerical series, just as they stood in the Greek authority, or exemplar of Dionysius Exiguus, in which the number of all the canons reached 165.

The argument he produces from the testimonies of the Ephesian and Chalcedonian councils, set out before his preface, is utterly empty. He plays upon and relies upon the Greek expressions τάξις and ἀκολουθία τῶν κανόνων, which he translates as “the series of the canons” and “the succession of the canons,” as though these formulas indicated a codex in which the canons were contained in a consecutive numerical series.
