But the words τάξις and ἀκολουθία signify neither a series nor a numerical succession. They signify the canonical order, method, and procedure, as it is called, which must be followed by those who wish to act properly according to the prescriptions of ecclesiastical rules and canons.

Thus, in Act 1 of the Ephesian synod, judgment is decreed to be conducted κατὰ τὴν τῶν κανόνων τάξιν, “according to the order of the canons” (Justellus translates it “series”) (vol. III of the *Councils*, fifth edition, col. 1005, e).

Elsewhere, unlawful and irregular proceedings against St. Cyril [Col. 0046B] and Memnon are described in the report of that same synod to the emperor as having been conducted ἔξω πάσης ἀκολουθίας ἐκκλησιαστικῆς καὶ κανόνων, “contrary to every ecclesiastical order and contrary to the canons” (ibid., col. 1185, a). Again, shortly afterward, they are said to have been conducted παρὰ θεσμούς, καὶ κανόνας καὶ πᾶσαν ἀκολουθίαν ἐκκλησιαστικήν, “against laws and canons and every ecclesiastical order”; and again παρὰ πᾶσαν τὴν τῶν κανόνων ἀκολουθίαν, “against the whole order of the canons.”

A little later the same meaning is expressed more clearly:

> For this reason, since he himself—John of Antioch—and the others whom he has with him have acted so ἀκανονίστως καὶ ἀτάκτως καὶ ἔξω πάσης ἀκολουθίας ἐκκλησιαστικῆς, “illegitimately, disorderly, and contrary to every ecclesiastical order” (col. 1188, a).

Nor are these same words understood in another sense at the Council of Chalcedon, as could be confirmed, if necessary, by many testimonies of that council.

4. The expression ἀριθμῶν ἀκολουθία, “the succession of numbers,” which Justellus introduced into the text quoted above, [Col. 0046C] occurs in only one testimony of John Scholasticus (in the preface, p. 500), which Justellus himself also cited on p. 8.

But John uses that expression in an entirely different sense, one that does not support Justellus. In explaining the arrangement of his own work, not of the codex of canons, he says:

> Since we have earnestly endeavored to collect into one body the things that had been determined at various times by them—the ten synods—and have distributed them among fifty titles, οὐ τάξιν τινὰ καὶ ἀκολουθίαν ἀριθμῶν, “we have not preserved a certain order and succession of numbers,” joining together, so to speak, the first, second, third, fourth, and fifth canons in succession, but have connected like things with like, and attached each corresponding matter to its appropriate heading, and so forth (vol. II, *Bibliotheca Juris Canonici*).

In his work, then, John did not set out the Nicene canons one after another together, nor the Ancyrean canons together, nor those of other synods in a continuous numerical and canonical series belonging to each synod. Instead, he distributed among fifty titles the canons of different councils, taking from here and there [Col. 0046D] those belonging to each title.

Whether the codex from which he transferred the canons into his work contained a numerical order and continuous series extending from the canons of the first council to those of the last, there is no evidence. Indeed, from his method of citing the canons of each synod by that synod’s distinct and proper number—for example, “the first, second, or third canon of the Antiochene council,” rather than “Canon 80, 81, or 82,” as they would have been numbered in a codex presenting a continuous series of numbers and canons—it appears plainly that John used a codex of canons that lacked such a continuous numerical series.

5. The two ancient versions, the Prisca and the Isidorian, exclude this continuous numerical series from certain Greek copies even more clearly. In the Nicene synod, in addition to the canons, these versions display the Creed and the catalogue of the Fathers. These two sections are likewise found in two other ancient translations, one of which is contained in the manuscript Vatican Regina, while from the other [Col. 0047A] the Creed and catalogue of the Fathers were inserted into the Hadrianic collection.

The Greek copies from which these versions were taken therefore contained both the Creed and the catalogue of the Nicene Fathers. Certainly, when the Africans in 419 requested from Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, information about the Nicene canons, he sent them not so much the canons as the Creed translated into Latin from his Greek copies. See Part II, Chapter 2, no. 3.

In the same way, the Greek copies used by the authors of the Prisca and Isidorian versions contained, in addition to the canons, synodical letters among the Gangran and Antiochene materials. Their Greek text has indeed been found and published.

All these materials are absent from Dionysius’s pure version, as could be gathered from his two pure manuscripts, Vatican 5845 and Vatican Palat. 577. The Greek exemplar of Dionysius, which he rendered accurately from beginning to end, therefore certainly lacked them.

The Greek codices of canons used by the other ancient translators just mentioned were consequently different from Dionysius’s, and so different [Col. 0047B] that they did not at all bear the numerical series possessed by Dionysius’s codex. For the additions of at least the Creed among the Nicene materials, and of the synodical letters among the Gangran and Antiochene materials, would have increased the numbers and introduced a different and fuller computation. This alone would suffice to reject from those codices the numerical series of Dionysius’s codex and to refute the opinion that there was a public codex marked by this established numerical sequence.

Since there is no indication of such a continuous numerical notation in these versions, we believe it more probable that the Greek codices from which they derived lacked numbers marked by such a continuous succession.

6. We do not for that reason deny that some codices of canons existed which were marked by this numerical series. Indeed, it seems probable to us that the person who introduced this continuous numerical series into a Greek codex, intending to count only the canons, passed over the other materials that are not canons—[Col. 0047C] namely, the Creed, subscriptions or catalogue of the Fathers, and synodical letters—as happened in Dionysius’s Greek codex.

What we maintain for our present purpose is simply that not all Greek codices of canons were of this kind, that this numerical series was not introduced into the codices that possessed it by public authority, and that the Greek Church did not receive only those canons contained in codices distinguished by such a numerical series.

The fourth Antiochene canon brought against St. John Chrysostom is not distinguished by any number in Palladius. The same canon was also brought against St. Cyril without any number, in the letter of the legates of the pseudo-synod of Ephesus to Rufus.

Socrates, drawing on the ancient version of Epiphanius Scholasticus in the *Tripartite History*, book XI, chapter 8, cites Antiochene Rule 18 by the proper canon number of that synod—the number 18 having dropped out of the commonly transmitted Greek text of Socrates. If he had been using a codex in which there was a continuous numerical series, he would have cited the canon or rule as number 97.

[Col. 0047D] 7. Texts that indicate a codex with a continuous numerical series are exceedingly few. In the Chalcedonian proceedings concerning Carosus and Dorotheus, two Antiochene canons are quoted from a codex with numbers in continuous succession, and likewise two in Action 11. The bishops of Pisidia, too, in the letter inserted into the encyclical codex and addressed to the emperor Leo, cite an Antiochene canon in the same manner, as Rule 83. Apart from these two or three earlier testimonies dating from before Dionysius, no other evidence has so far been found indicating a similar numerical series.

In the same Council of Chalcedon, Action 4, the fifth Antiochene canon was read by Aetius of Constantinople from a codex without any indication of either synod or number:

> Aetius, archdeacon of Constantinople of the holy and universal Church, said: “This is a rule placed among others by the holy Fathers; observing it, the most holy bishop-Fathers instruct clergy, monks, and all who worship Christ. If they find persons resisting, or unwilling to acquiesce, they apply this rule.” And he reread the following from the codex: “Concerning clergy and monks who suspend themselves from communion. If a presbyter or deacon, despising his bishop, etc.”

(*Tom. IV Conc.*, col. 1418, d).

The distinctive title, “Concerning clergy and monks, etc.,” recorded in Aetius’s codex—one found neither in any ancient version, nor in the Dionysian version, nor in the common Greek text—clearly reveals a different codex, in which no number, not even a distinctive one, had been attached to the canons; it was also different from the Dionysian codex, which contained a continuous numerical series.

In the proceedings concerning Photius of Tyre, Atticus, bishop of Nicopolis [XXXVII], read the fourth Nicene canon from a codex under this title:

> “The fourth canon of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers who had assembled at Nicaea.”

(*Ibid.*, col. 1438).

The same canon was read again in Action 13, without any title, from another codex produced by Eunomius, bishop of Nicomedia:

> “The most illustrious judges said: Let the canons be read.” Veronicianus, a devout man, an officer of the master of offices (*magistrianus*) and secretary of the divine consistory, read from the codex given by the most reverend bishop Eunomius the sixth chapter: “A bishop ought, above all, to be ordained by all the provincial bishops, etc.”

(*Ibid.*, col. 1634, d).

A noteworthy difference appears in the citation of this canon: in the proceedings concerning Photius it is called a canon—κανὼν δʹ, “the fourth canon”—whereas in Action 13 it is called a chapter—κεφάλ ϛʹ. Here the latter should be corrected to δʹ, “the fourth chapter.” We further observe that in those testimonies which cite canons from a continuous numerical series, the word *canon* (κανών) is consistently preferred, as may be seen in the cited proceedings concerning Carosus and Dorotheus and in Action 11. The codex produced by Eunomius, therefore, seems to have differed from those containing a continuous numerical series.

If the reading κεφάλ ϛʹ, “the sixth chapter,” which is uniformly found both in Greek manuscripts and in the ancient version of the Council of Chalcedon, as well as in the codices of Rusticus in Action 13, is not to be attributed to an ancient scribal error, as Baluzius indicated, it should rather be attributed to a different division of the Nicene canons. In some Greek codex that division may have made this canon the sixth, just as in the manuscript of the collection to be published in this volume it was numbered sixth; in the Vatican Codex Reginae 1997, under another division, it becomes the seventh. This would provide a new basis for demonstrating more clearly the distinct character of Eunomius’s codex.

8. An even clearer testimony to a Greek exemplar different from that in which the canons were cited with a continuous numerical series is supplied by Action 16. Before establishing this, however, two faults contaminating the received text must be exposed.

In the same action, after Paschasinus had recited the sixth Nicene canon in the form presented by the Italian codices, the editions of the councils introduce Constantine the secretary, who read that same sixth Nicene canon and another canon of the Constantinopolitan synod from the Greek codex of Aetius the archdeacon. A strong suspicion first arises that this repeated recitation of the sixth Nicene canon has been interpolated—not only because this Nicene canon, presented as though by Aetius of Constantinople, would contribute nothing to the question then under discussion concerning the see of Constantinople, and would rather oppose it, while the Constantinopolitan canon alone would be introduced by the Constantinopolitans for that purpose; but much more because in the ancient version, which is preserved in pure form in the codex formerly belonging to Jolius and now to the Paris chapter, this repeated sixth canon is omitted, as Baluzius noted. Hence it was not found by the first translator in his Greek codex.

Perhaps, because the reading of the same canon produced by Paschasinus differed somewhat in its opening words from the reading of the Greek codices, some learned Greek once wrote the reading of those codices in the margin, and it subsequently slipped from the margin into the text. Since this insertion is read in the manuscripts of Rusticus’s edition, it is known to be ancient.

Rusticus’s own edition, moreover, although it accepted this addition, reveals a later corruption of the common Greek text. In it, besides the inserted Nicene canon, the Constantinopolitan canon is introduced with different words as follows:

> Ὁ αὐτὸς σηκρητάριος ἀνέγνω ἀπὸ τοῦ αὐτοῦ βιβλίου συνοδικὸν τῆς δευτέρας συνόδου. Τάδε ὥρισαν οἱ ἐν Κωνσταντινουπόλει χάριτι Θεοῦ συνελθόντες ἑκατὸν πεντήκοντα ἐπίσκοποι ἐκ διαφόρων ἐπαρχιῶν, etc.

> The same secretary reread from the same codex the synodical document of the second synod: “These things were decreed by the 150 bishops who, by the grace of God, assembled at Constantinople from various provinces, etc.”

(*Tom. IV Conc.*, col. 1749, a).

The opening words, “The same secretary reread from the same codex,” are superfluous once the Nicene canon has been deleted; they are also omitted in the ancient version, which knows nothing of that canon, and they are absent from Rusticus. Consequently, Rusticus did not find them in his Greek codices either.

Furthermore, while retaining the reading of the ancient version in what follows, Rusticus does not have “the synodical document of the second synod.” The designation “second synod” applied to the Constantinopolitan council belongs to a later period, when in Greek canon collections general councils began to be separated from local councils, and Constantinople began to be placed after the Council of Nicaea.

[XXXVIII] 9. Let us now produce, for our purposes, the genuine text, which, with the repetition of the Nicene canon excluded, gives the true reading, from the ancient version.

> Constantine, a devout man and secretary of the divine consistory, read from the codex given by Aetius of the most holy Church of the Constantinopolitans: “The synodical document of the first council under Nectarius, bishop of Constantinople, of the 150 bishops. These things were decreed by the bishops who, by the grace of God, assembled at Constantinople from various provinces, in accordance with the summons of the most religious emperor Theodosius, under Nectarius, bishop of Constantinople. The faith and the rules of the 318 Fathers who assembled at Nicaea in Bithynia are not to be rejected; rather, let that faith remain in its proper form, and let every heresy be anathematized, etc.”

(*Tom. IV Conc.*, col. 1747, d).

Here the canons of the Constantinopolitan synod—two, or perhaps three—are recited in one continuous passage, without any distinction of canons or numbers.

Two points must be noted. First, attention must be paid to the title prefixed to the Constantinopolitan canons in Aetius’s Greek codex itself: “The synodical document of the first council under Nectarius, bishop,” together with what follows. Since these words are found neither in the Greek text of the canon codex nor in any of the versions, they indicate a different collection of canons. This is all the more so because the words “of the first council” signify that at least another council under the same Nectarius was included later in the same canon codex—either the council of 382, to which the two canons appended to that first council seem to belong, or another council of 394, whose acts are found in several Greek manuscript collections. See above, chapter 1, no. 10.

Second, since only the third canon—or, according to another division, the second—concerning the privilege of the see of Constantinople was relevant to the matter at hand, only that canon should have been recited if it had been distinguished from the first or even the second canon in Aetius’s codex. All these canons, however, were recited in one continuous passage because Aetius’s codex lacked the distinction of canons and numbers found not only in the Greek manuscript of Dionysius but also in other codices used by the authors of the Isidorian and Prisca versions.

Aetius’s Greek codex, therefore, differed from all whose indications have reached us. If, then, different kinds of codices were read in the Council of Chalcedon—some with a continuous numerical series, others without such numbers, and still others fuller than those—Justellus’s hypothesis is plainly empty: he presumed that only the canon codex displaying a continuous numerical series had been received by the Fathers of the Church and read and approved at Chalcedon.

Add to this that the explicit approval of the canons issued by that same synod in its first canon is not restricted to this or that codex of canons that was read, but extends to the canons of all the Fathers and of every preceding synod:

> “We have decreed that the rules of the holy Fathers established in each council down to the present time shall retain their proper force.”

[Col. 0050A] 10. To return now to the Sardicene canons: whether they were actually absent from the codex read at the Council of Chalcedon with a continuous numerical series, as they were absent from the Greek codex of Dionysius, cannot be determined with certainty.

For the numbers cited at that council do not go beyond the Antiochene canons. Who, then, could affirm that the Sardicene canons were not written in that codex after the Antiochene canons, since they were composed after the Antiochene council? Indeed, since the Greek canon codex was not composed all at once at the beginning but was gradually enlarged without preserving chronological order, as we noted in chapter 2, no one can assert that these canons were not added at least after the Laodicean or Constantinopolitan canons in the celebrated Chalcedonian codex.

The similarity of Dionysius’s Greek codex, which, although distinguished by a numerical series, did not contain the Sardicene canons, is not conclusive. Since Dionysius’s Greek codex differs by one number in the Antiochene canons from the numbers of the codex read at the Council of Chalcedon, that codex is recognized as somewhat different from the latter.

Just as the codex from which he translated the fifty Apostolic Canons into Latin was incomplete—for many more of those canons had already long been received before Dionysius, as we established in chapter 1, no. 4—so he may likewise have used an incomplete exemplar of the synodal canons. Thus it cannot be said that all codices displaying a similar numerical series lacked the Sardicene canons.

11. But even if these canons had been omitted from such codices, were they also absent from every other exemplar lacking that continuous numerical series?

Certainly, it cannot be denied that they were written in at least some of the codices of those very numerous [XXXIX] Greek Fathers who assembled at the Council of Chalcedon, especially in the Churches of Illyricum, for which some of the Sardicene canons had been established.

Moreover, the Council of Sardica is included among those councils whose rules were confirmed by the first canon of Chalcedon. The faith of the Sardicene Fathers is praised in the address of the Council of Chalcedon to the emperor Marcian:

> “Those who assembled at Sardica against the remnants of Arius sent to the Easterners the decisions of their judgment.”

(*Tom. IV Conc.*, col. 1766).

These decisions are shortly before called a decree concerning the faith. The reference is evidently to the decree of faith read at the end of the Sardicene synodical letter in Theodoretus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 6.

Everyone now admits that this decree, or this additional exposition of faith, was an addition appended to the celebrated synodical letter. Yet this addition existed before Chalcedon and had been inserted in codices from which, even before Theodoretus, Socrates, book II, chapter 20, and Sozomenus, book III, chapter 12, cited the same exposition of faith as having been issued by the Council of Sardica.

Certainly, this addition to the synodical letter, in which an exposition of the Nicene faith composed by the Sardicene Fathers is presented, had already been written in the year 362. It may also be gathered from the Alexandrian council of that same year that it had been proposed at Sardica by some Fathers but rejected by many others and by the synod. In the common interpretation of the record of that synod, the added exposition of faith is referred to under the name of a “tablet”:

> “Do not even permit the tablet which certain people boast of, as though it had been written at the Council of Sardica concerning the faith, to be read or presented once. For the synod defined nothing of the kind. Although certain men wished to append certain things as though they were lacking from the Council of Nicaea, and pressed the matter vigorously, the holy synod assembled at Sardica nevertheless endured this indignantly and decreed that nothing further should be written concerning the faith. They declared themselves satisfied with the Nicene faith, since nothing was lacking from it and it was full of piety; nor was another profession of faith to be issued, lest the one written at Nicaea be considered imperfect, or an opportunity be supplied to those who repeatedly wish to define and write concerning the faith.”

(*Tom. II Conc.*, col. 944, a).

Similarly, in the subscription of the same Alexandrian council by Saint Eusebius of Vercelli, the tablet of the Council of Sardica is said to have been excluded, lest anything other than the Nicene faith be thought to have been decreed.

(*Ibid.*, col. 949, c).

Since this tablet, or exposition of faith, was objectionable for this reason alone, it is not surprising that copies containing this addition were circulated, and that later writers consequently believed the exposition to have been composed by the Council of Sardica.

The Fathers of Chalcedon, therefore, who held the Council of Sardica in the highest regard, possessed the celebrated synodical letter with this appended exposition of faith in some Greek codex, just as Socrates, Sozomenus, and Theodoretus possessed it.

Which codices contained this Sardicene synodical letter with the celebrated addition can be learned from a very ancient and notable codex, written in large letters and belonging to section 55 of the chapter of Verona, in which we find a translation of that synodical letter. Since this translation differs from the version translated by Epiphanius from Theodoretus and inserted into the *Tripartite History*, book IV, chapter 24, it derives from another, more ancient Greek exemplar. In it, moreover, other exceedingly rare and valuable documents concerning the Council of Sardica were presented; all these documents have been translated into Latin and are contained in the same Veronese codex. See below, part II, chapter 9.

Among the other documents preserved for us in this single codex and to be inserted in this volume, before the aforementioned synodical letter and after the title “Decrees at Sardica,” there is a letter of Hosius and Protogenes to Pope Julius. Although this letter is regarded as apocryphal, it is nevertheless contemporary with the supposed addition to the synodical letter, whose rationale is explained in it.

Perhaps Hosius and Protogenes were among those by whom this exposition of faith was proposed to the Council of Sardica together with the letter. Both, however, were rejected there and must therefore be counted among the apocrypha.

Since Sozomenus, book III, chapter 12, cites this letter together with the synodical letter and its addition, both were found in his Greek codex.

Furthermore, in the aforementioned Veronese manuscript, after the synodical letter just mentioned and without another title, the Sardicene canons are appended in the same order as in the common Greek text, but translated from a Greek exemplar of different origin, previously unknown. Among these canons there is one which, although it exists in all exemplars of the original Latin text beginning with “Januarius,” is entirely absent from the common Greek text.

The translator of these and of the other Sardicene documents that we shall publish had a Greek exemplar containing all these materials. That they had already been collected long before the Council of Chalcedon is confirmed by Socrates, Sozomenus, and Theodoretus, who, writing before that synod, transmitted two of these documents.

This collection is recognized as even older because it contains three other genuine Sardicene monuments which are not otherwise available and therefore seem to have been collected around the time of the Council of Sardica or not long afterward.

If Socrates, Sozomenus, and Theodoretus, as is entirely probable, cited the Sardicene exposition of faith, or even the letter of Hosius and Protogenes, from some Greek codex of this collection, just as the Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon did, then here is the Greek codex used by those Fathers, in which the Sardicene canons, together with the other Sardicene documents, had already been written long before.

12. Further arguments are available showing that these canons existed in Greek codices.

The author of the Prisca version, who preceded Dionysius Exiguus, found a Greek codex in which the Sardicene canons appear to have been placed after the Nicene canons. If he did not translate them from the Greek but preferred the Latin original, this happened because it was customary among Latin translators, whenever they found a Latin original, to insert it into their collections and refrain from translating it from the Greek.

Thus the ancient translator of the Council of Chalcedon inserted the Latin original of Leo’s Letter 28 to Flavian into Action 2 instead of translating it from the Greek. Similarly, Epiphanius Scholasticus, the translator of the encyclical codex, appended to his translation the Latin original of Letter 156 of the same pontiff to the emperor Leo.

Accordingly, if the author of the Prisca version copied the Sardicene canons from the Latin original, it does not follow that he did not find them in his Greek codex. Indeed, since he did not add them at the end after the Greek canons but placed them among the canons of the Greek synods immediately after the Nicene canons, it is most probable that he found them in this order in the Greek codex.

Otherwise, if the Greek exemplar he used had lacked them, after translating the Greek canons that he found in that manuscript he would have appended the Sardicene canons from the Latin original at the end, as Dionysius Exiguus did, or at least would have transferred them to another place appropriate to the chronology of that synod, after the Antiochene canons.

13. That Greek exemplars of the canons once existed in which the Sardicene canons were placed immediately after the Nicene canons is confirmed by the order of the canons found by John Scholasticus in his Greek codex. We gave this order in chapter 2.

Christophorus Justellus, who was unfavorably disposed toward the Sardicene canons, asserts in his preface to the *Synagoge* of the canons of that same John Scholasticus that John was the first to add the Sardicene canons to the Greek codex.

(*Tom. II Biblioth. Jur. can. vet.*, p. 495).

But he is plainly mistaken.

First, John himself testifies that he was not the first to compose a collection of canons containing the Sardicene canons. Others before him had undertaken the same task, arranging it under sixty titles from the canons of the same ten synods, whereas he reduced it to fifty titles, adding only the canons of Saint Basil, which they had omitted:

> “Since we were not the only ones, nor the FIRST among others, to be moved to undertake this task, but found that others had divided those things—the statutes of the ten synods—into sixty titles and had not joined the canons of Saint Basil with the others, etc.”

Second, neither John nor those who labored at this work before him were the authors of the Greek collection. From a Greek collection whose exemplar they had before their eyes, they reduced the canons of the ten synods contained in it—without preserving the order and sequence of the canons—to definite sections and titles: they arranged them under sixty, whereas John arranged them under fifty.

Among these ten synods was also the Council of Sardica, whose canons both collections incorporated into their *synagoge*. There were therefore Greek collections which, before John Scholasticus—and even before others earlier than John—presented the Sardicene canons together with the rest.

The order of the canons which John placed first from the ten synods, putting the Sardicene canons after the Nicene and before the Gangrene canons, as is likewise found in the Prisca version, is not a chronological order, according to which the Sardicene canons ought to have been placed after the Antiochene canons. It can only be the order that existed in John’s Greek codex.

If this observation confirms that a similar Greek codex was available to the author of the Prisca translation, who could have followed this order for no other reason, it will be demonstrated more clearly that the Sardicene canons existed in certain Greek exemplars not merely before John Scholasticus but long before Dionysius Exiguus, whom the Prisca version preceded.

If older Greek exemplars of the canons had survived to us, we could establish this more decisively. But to deny, merely because such older codices are lacking, that these canons possessed authority among the ancient Greeks—canons which we have certainly seen issued in Greek by the synod itself for the Greeks, and whose original Greek exemplar has been preserved for us in the later Greek collections that alone survive—is excessively audacious.

If older Greek exemplars than those of the Council of Chalcedon are lacking, they are supplemented by the collections, though more recent, of the Eutychians, which have an origin older than Chalcedon. Separated from the Church in the fifth century, they accepted from the ancient canons only those that were already present in the Greek codex before their separation. Their collections are therefore so many testimonies to that ancient Greek codex which possessed authority in the Greek Church before the Eutychian heresy.

For this reason, those collections do not contain the Chalcedonian canons. But they do contain the Sardicene canons together with the others, as may be seen in P. Echard (*T. II de Script. ord. Praedic.*, p. 193) and Job Ludolf (*Letter to Hottinger*, in the latter’s *Bibliotheca Orientalis*, p. 325).

The Sardicene canons, therefore, were in the Greek codex before the Eutychians separated from the Church.

14. We can certainly demonstrate the authority of these canons among the more ancient Greeks of the East from a very ancient Eastern council.

The Fathers of the Council of Constantinople of the year 382, in their letter to Damasus and the other Westerners, recorded by Theodoretus, book V of the *History*, chapter 9, cited a Sardicene canon under the name of the Council of Nicaea in these words:

> “Concerning the administration of the individual Churches, both the ancient law, as you know, has prevailed, and the decision of the holy Fathers at the Council of Nicaea: namely, that the bishops of each province, together with neighboring bishops, should conduct the ordinations for the good of the Churches, whenever they deem it appropriate.”

This is the fifth Sardicene canon, as Father Harduinus noted in this passage and in his annotation on that Sardicene canon.

Father Coustantius likewise says, in volume I of *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, col. 566, no. c:

> “The fourth canon of the Council of Nicaea decrees: ‘A bishop ought especially to be ordained by all the bishops who are in the province’; but it says nothing about summoning neighboring bishops whenever this is considered appropriate. The fifth Sardicene canon, or the sixth according to the Greeks, explains when someone ought to be ordained by the bishops of neighboring provinces.”

If the Easterners now had this canon in view, it must be said that the Sardicene canons were regarded not only in the West but also in the East as Nicene canons. It must also be added that in the codex used by these Fathers they were placed after the Nicene canons.

More will be said in part II, chapter 1, concerning this conjunction of the Nicene and Sardicene canons, by which the latter were treated as Nicene. For now, it is sufficient to observe that this very ancient testimony of the Easterners provides certain evidence that the Sardicene canons were received by the Greek Easterners as well, inserted into their codices, and that the Churches of the East were governed by their authority. Immediately after the words quoted, the same letter continues:

> “From the prescription of this law and decision, know that not only are the other Churches among us administered, but that the priests of the most illustrious Churches are chosen.”

Nothing more distinguished or more evident could be desired for overturning Justellus’s theory.

For at this council the Illyrian Greeks belonging to the Western Church—who are thought to have received the Sardicene canons for that reason—did not assemble. Rather, the bishops of the entire East assembled, almost all of them being those who had gathered there at the synod of the preceding year, 381.

Theodoretus, book V of the *History*, chapter 8, after listing the bishops of the preceding synod, gives the following account of the present synod:

> “In the following period, when MOST of them had come to the same city—for ecclesiastical affairs had summoned them there again, etc.”

The Eastern bishops, therefore, even at this ancient time administered their Churches according to the prescriptions of the Sardicene canons and carried out the ordinations of priests. They approved the ordinations of Nectarius of Constantinople and Flavian of Antioch as canonically performed according to the norm of that celebrated synod.

The canons that provided the Easterners with the rule for governing Churches and ordaining bishops must therefore be said to have been received by them and held in great authority, whether they had then been inserted into the Greek codex or not. For the authority of the canons depended upon the authority of the councils themselves, not upon the Greek codex, which we have seen to have been composed by private rather than public authority.

From this we may incidentally gather how wrongly some maintain that the Council of Sardica—whose canons were issued in Greek for the Greeks and were treated in the fullest Eastern synod with the same place and title as the Nicene canons—was a Western council and therefore should not be counted among the ecumenical councils.

# CHAPTER VII  
## The Subscriptions and Number of the Sardicene Fathers. An Accurate Catalogue Compiled from More Reliable Monuments. Whether the Sardicene Synod Was Ecumenical

[Col. 0054A]

1. Just as the three or four Sardicene documents that we are about to cite display several subscriptions of the Fathers, so we have no doubt that the canons of the Fathers were also confirmed by subscriptions.

The subscriptions properly belonging to those canons have disappeared. In their place, in certain manuscripts and consequently in the common books of the councils, the names of the Sardicene Fathers that are read after the Sardicene letter to Pope Julius in Hilary are appended to the canons.

In these very subscriptions, however, the same manuscripts and printed books, through an obvious error, present Vincent of Capua, Januarius of Benevento, and Calepodius of Naples as legates of the Apostolic See. This error is not found in Hilary; other men served as legates of the Apostolic See at the Sardicene embassy.

Since the Sardicene canons were joined to the Nicene canons in the older Latin exemplars and were regarded as Nicene, as we shall establish in part II, chapter 1, not a catalogue of the Sardicene Fathers but a catalogue of the Nicene Fathers was attached to them, as we have found in several very ancient codices that join these canons together. Consequently, the subscriptions of the Sardicene Fathers—which unquestionably seem to have been marked in the original—dropped out.

When these Sardicene canons later began to be separated from the Nicene canons, they were written in some codices without any subscription. In others, only the initial formula of the first Nicene subscription was retained, as we have observed in the pure Dionysian exemplars and in Justellus’s edition.

In still others, in order to restore the subscriptions of the Sardicene Fathers to those same canons, the subscriptions appended in Hilary’s fragments after the letter of the Sardicene synod to Pope Julius were transferred from that letter to the canons. Consequently, certain Latin manuscript collections, after recording these subscriptions following the canons, present the letter without subscriptions.

An ignorant copyist, however, finding no names of apostolic legates among the subscriptions of the synodical letter and transferring those same subscriptions to the canons, arbitrarily declared the three aforementioned suburban bishops to be legates of the Apostolic See.

But these very subscriptions—or rather, these names of the Sardicene Fathers—are fewer than the Fathers actually were. Hence a major dispute has arisen among scholars concerning the number of those Fathers.

Since we believe that, through more diligent study and with the assistance of the documents to be published from the Veronese codex, we can contribute something more certain on this matter, we trust that a fuller discussion here will not be unwelcome to readers.

2. Many have believed, on the basis of Saint Athanasius, that there were approximately three hundred Sardicene Fathers. At the beginning of his *Second Apology*, he states that three hundred supported him; and then, after reproducing the letter of the Sardicene synod, he appends the names of approximately two hundred and eighty bishops who subscribed to it.

But in the first passage he did not identify only the bishops of the Council of Sardica. After mentioning three councils—the Alexandrian council, at which one hundred bishops were present; the Roman council, at which fifty bishops sat; and finally the Sardicene council—he adds:

> “More than three hundred bishops from the provinces supported the decisions made on our behalf.”

He gives the names of thirty-six provinces.

It is clear from these words that Athanasius did not intend to indicate three hundred bishops of the Sardicene council alone, but included all those who either supported him in the three councils previously named or, although absent, subscribed to the Sardicene decree.

This is evident from another passage [XLIII] of the same *Apology*, in which, after reproducing the Sardicene synodical letter and about to list the names of 282 bishops, he introduces them as follows:

> “The holy Council of Sardica sent these matters, committed to writing, to those who could not be present; they too approved the decrees of the synod by their own votes. The names of those who subscribed in the synod, and of the other men”—

these words concerning “the other men” must be noted, since they refer to the absent—

> “are as follows.”

It should also be added that Athanasius, in his *History of the Arians to the Monks*, concerning the bishops who initially assembled at the Council of Sardica, writes:

> “Bishops from both East and West assembled in the city of Sardica, somewhat more than 170.”

(*Tom. I Athan.*, p. 352).

The Eusebians then separated from them and formed the pseudo-synod of Philippopolis. According to Sabinus, as reported by Socrates (*Book II*, chapter 16), these Eastern Eusebians numbered seventy-six; but in the subscriptions of the Philippopolitan pseudo-synod only seventy-three are listed.

Thus the Catholic bishops who stood for Athanasius at Sardica and constituted the Sardicene synod must be said to have numbered approximately ninety-four or ninety-seven.

Who these bishops were, and of what cities and provinces, has until now been more difficult to determine.

Saint Hilary, in the subscriptions of the Sardicene letter to Pope Julius, names only fifty-nine bishops, omitting several whose presence is otherwise known. The names of the fifty-nine Fathers appended to the Sardicene canons in the common editions of the councils and in manuscript collections agree with Hilary.

Some codices, however, list above these bishops one additional Alexander, “from Acia,” or alternatively “from Acha, of Ceporisma”—which should be read “from Achaia, of Cyparissa”—as, for example, the Vatican Codex 1342 and Vallicellian Codex A 5. This yields sixty bishops.

Yet it is sufficiently indicated that not all are included by the clause added after the final bishop in those same codices:

> “And the others subscribed.”

Among the 282 names of bishops presented by Athanasius, however, since he mentioned both the absent and the present, it has not been easy to identify the names of the Sardicene bishops.

3. Most recently, two outstanding documents relating to the Council of Sardica, together with their subscriptions, were published by the Marquis Maffei from manuscript 55 of the Chapter Library of Verona [Col. 0055C]. They will appear in this volume, illustrated with other documents. The first is a letter of the Sardican synod itself to the Churches of Mareotis, in which only the names of twenty-six or twenty-seven bishops are read as subscribed. The second is a letter of Saint Athanasius to the same Churches, subscribed by sixty-one bishops. The first eighteen appended only their names; the others added the name of their city and sometimes also that of their province.

In the first letter, special attention must be paid to the final subscription:

> Vincentius, bishop: I wish you health in the Lord, most beloved brothers. Ordered by my brothers and fellow bishops, I wrote and subscribed on behalf of the others.

Hence it is not surprising that few subscribed, since not all subscribed personally, but all instructed Vincentius to subscribe on behalf of the others. For this reason Saint Athanasius, in the other letter—by which he sent the preceding synodal letter from Sardica to Mareotis—says:

> Although not all the bishops were able to be present to write, nevertheless it was written by all, and they subscribed on behalf of all.

If the Vincentius who subscribed at the end on behalf of the others is the same person as the bishop who had earlier subscribed personally under that name, there are twenty-six subscriptions. If he is another Vincentius, there are twenty-seven.

When we compare the subscriptions of these documents with those appended to the Sardican letter to Julius—the same applies to similar names attached to the canons from that letter—we find that some episcopal names are missing from the subscriptions of the documents just mentioned, although they occur in the subscriptions of the letter to Julius. Other names, however, appear in those documents that are absent from the letter to Julius. From these documents, therefore, thirty subscriptions, or bishops, are supplied. If to these we add the fifty-nine bishops who subscribed the letter to Julius, we obtain eighty-nine Sardican Fathers.

4. Having established this number of Fathers, we compared Athanasius’s catalogue of two hundred and eighty-two bishops, preserved in the Second Apology [Col. 0056A], with the eighty-nine bishops just mentioned. Since we found nearly all the names of the latter among the seventy-eight bishops whom Athanasius first designates separately from the others, we discovered that these seventy-eight bishops had attended the Sardican synod. Accordingly, after the name of Hosius, they are listed together, without any distinction of provinces [XLIV]. The others, whom Athanasius subsequently distributes among the provinces, are those who, although absent, approved the Sardican decree.

This corresponds precisely to the order in which Athanasius, in the testimony quoted above, stated that he would produce the names: first, those who had subscribed at the synod; and then the other bishops who, although unable to attend, nevertheless approved the synod’s decrees by their own votes after the synodal letter had been sent to them.

Moreover, six further bishops are added to Athanasius’s first series, although they are not found either in the subscriptions of the letter to Julius or in the two other documents. If these are added to the eighty-nine whom we know from the subscriptions, the Sardican bishops number ninety-five [Col. 0056B]. In addition, two other bishops—Euphratas of Agrippina and Gratus of Carthage—were certainly omitted both by Athanasius in his first series and from the subscriptions, although we shall prove elsewhere that they must be counted among the Fathers of the same synod. Thus, in the catalogue which we present here, ninety-seven Sardican bishops will be listed. This agrees well with the calculation proposed shortly before from Athanasius: approximately ninety-four or ninety-seven bishops.

### Alphabetical catalogue of the Sardican Fathers, compiled and confirmed from the documents

**I. Adolius.** He is mentioned only in Saint Athanasius’s catalogue.

**II. Aetius of Macedonia, from Thessalonica.** Only the name of Aetius is found in Athanasius and in the synodal letter to the Churches of Mareotis. In the subscriptions preserved by Saint Hilary, however, the names of the province and city are added. Nor is there any difficulty from the letter of the pseudo-synod of Sardica [Col. 0056C]—more properly, of Philippopolis—in which John, bishop of Thessalonica, is mentioned by Labbe. Father Coustant proves that John’s name must be removed from that same letter, in volume II of his edition of Hilary’s works, Verona edition, column 658, note 6. That Aetius, not John, was bishop of Thessalonica is also confirmed by Sardican canon 20 in Dionysius, where he himself speaks of the metropolitan see of Thessalonica.

**III. Alexander Gyparensis of Achaia.** Thus in Athanasius’s letter to the Churches of Mareotis. Perhaps *Cyparissensis* should be read, since Cyparissa is found in Achaia. He is the same person as the one added after the canons in certain manuscripts mentioned earlier, as follows: “Alexander from Acia,” or “from Achaia, from Ceporisma.”

**IV. Alexander of Achaia, from Montemni.** Thus in Hilary’s subscriptions. In the printed editions of the councils, *de Moreniis*; in manuscript Vatican 1342, *de Moromis*. Vallicellian manuscript A 5 omits the name of the city.

**V. Alexander of Thessaly, from Larissa.** So Hilary and the editions of the councils. Saint Athanasius names only two Alexanders. One appears in the subscriptions of the synodal letter to Mareotis, and one in the subscriptions of Saint Athanasius’s letter. Whether the same person subscribed in both places, or whether they were two different men, is unknown.

**VI. Alypius of Achaia, from Megara.** He is listed in all the subscriptions. Only in the synodal letter is he called Alysius. Alypius is mentioned by Athanasius and also occurs in the canons.

**VII. Amasitius of Viminacium, through the presbyter Maximus.** In the subscriptions of Athanasius’s letter and likewise in Athanasius’s catalogue.

**VIII. Ammonius.** In the subscription of the same letter.

**IX. Anianus of Castulon, or Castolona, from Spain.** In Hilary and in the Councils. In the subscriptions of Athanasius’s letter he is incorrectly written “Ammianus of Castello in Pannonia.” Anianus’s name appears in Athanasius’s catalogue.

**X. Antigonus Pallenensis of Macedonia; correct to *Pellensis*.** In Athanasius’s letter, and praised in Athanasius’s catalogue.

**XI. Appianus.** In the same letter, where the following two are also listed.

**XII. Aprianus of Petabio in Pannonia.** In the same place and in Athanasius’s catalogue.

**XIII. Aprianus.** Another, in the subscription of Athanasius’s letter.

**XIV. Arius of Palestine.** In Hilary, in the Councils, in the synodal letter to Mareotis, and in Athanasius’s catalogue. In his letter to the Solitaries, Athanasius calls him Arius of Petra in Palestine.

**[XLV] XV. Asclepius of Palestine, from Gaza.** In Hilary, in the Councils, in Athanasius’s letter, and in his catalogue.

**XVI. Asterius of Arabia.** Thus in the Councils, in the synodal letter, and in Athanasius. In Hilary and in some manuscripts he is called Asturius. In his letter to the Solitaries, Athanasius calls him bishop of Petra in Arabia.

**XVII. Athanasius of Alexandria in Egypt.** In all the documents.

**XVIII. Athenodorus of Achaia, from Blatea; correct to *Platea*.** In Hilary. In the Councils, erroneously, “Athenodorus from Dacia, from Blacena.” He is mentioned in the subscriptions of the synodal letter and of Athanasius’s letter, as well as in Athanasius’s catalogue.

**XIX. Bassus of Macedonia, from Diocletianopolis.** In Hilary and in the Councils. Saint Athanasius, in his catalogue and in the synodal letter to Mareotis, praises this Bassus. He is also mentioned in the pseudo-Sardican letter, no. 20. Since no Diocletianopolis in Macedonia is found, although other cities of that name occur in other provinces, there appears to be an error in the words “of Macedonia,” just as “of Macedonia” was mistakenly inserted into the subscription of Marcellus, who was bishop of Ancyra in Galatia. Perhaps Bassus was bishop of Diocletianopolis in Thrace.

**XX. Calepodius of Campania.** In Hilary. In the Councils he is called Neapolitanus. This Calepodius is mentioned in the synodal letter to Mareotis and also in Athanasius’s catalogue.

**XXI. Calvus of Dacia Ripensis, from Castrum Martis.** In Hilary and in the Councils. In the subscriptions of Athanasius’s letter he is called Caloes of Castrum Martis.

**XXII. Caloes.** Another, in the same letter of Athanasius. Perhaps he is the one called Galba in Athanasius’s catalogue.

**XXIII. Castus of Spain, from Caesaraugusta.** In Hilary, in the Councils, and in Athanasius’s letter and catalogue.

**XXIV. Cocras of Achaia, from Asapofebiis.** In Hilary and in the Councils. In Achaia, Hierocles places Asopolis, while Strabo and Ptolemy have Asopus. Is this the city meant? Athanasius names Socrates. Was Cocras written in place of Socrates?

**XXV. Cydonius of Cydonia in Crete.** He subscribed Athanasius’s letter.

**XXVI. Diodorus of Asia, from Tenedos.** In Hilary and in the Councils. He is listed in Athanasius’s catalogue. In the subscriptions of Athanasius’s letter he is incorrectly called Liodorus.

**XXVII. Dionysius of Achaia, from Elis.** In Hilary, in the Councils, and in the synodal letter. He is listed in Athanasius’s catalogue and in the pseudo-Sardican letter, no. 20. Elis is a metropolis of Aetolia in Achaia.

**XXVIII. Dioscorus of Thrace.** In the same documents.

**XXIX. Domecius of Acaria, from Constantia.** Thus corruptly in the subscriptions of Athanasius’s letter. Is he one of the two Domitians listed in Athanasius’s catalogue?

**XXX. Domitianus of Spain, from Asturica.** Thus in Hilary and the Councils. Only his name occurs in the subscriptions of the synodal letter to Mareotis, as also in Athanasius’s catalogue.

**XXXI. Eliodorus, or Heliodorus, of Nicopolis.** In Hilary, in the Councils, in the synodal letter, and also in Athanasius’s catalogue.

**XXXII. Eucarpus Oponsius of Achaia.** In Athanasius’s letter and catalogue. It should be read *Opuntius*, from Opus, a city of Achaia.

**XXXIII. Eucarpus.** Another, in the same letter.

**XXXIV. Eucissus Chisamensus.** In the same place. Cissamus is a city of Crete, from which other bishops also attended the Sardican council.

**XXXV. Eugenius of Hecleal Cychnis.** In the same letter of Athanasius. In Hilary, “Evagrius of Macedonia, from Heraclea Lyncestis”; in the Councils, “from Heracleopolis.” There is a Heraclea in Macedonia, and Hierocles has Heraclea Laoci.

**XXXVI. Eugenius.** Another, in the subscriptions of the aforementioned letter. Athanasius lists one Eugenius in his catalogue.

**XXXVII. Eulogius.** In the same letter and in the same catalogue.

**XXXVIII. Euterius of Pannonia.** In the Councils. In Hilary, Eutasius.

**XXXIX. Euterius of Procia, from Caindus or Candos.** In Hilary and [XLVI] in the Councils. The passage is corrupt. One Euterius is found in Athanasius’s catalogue.

**XL. Eutychius of Methone.** In Athanasius’s letter. In the Councils he is written “Tychius of Asia”—read “of Achaia”—from Methone; in Hilary, “Thitius of Asia, from Montonus.” This Eutychius was bishop of Methone in Achaia and is listed in Athanasius’s catalogue.

**XLI. Eutychius of Achaia.** Hilary and the Councils list another, distinct from the preceding. Athanasius’s catalogue likewise mentions two Eutychii.

**XLII. Florentius of Spain, from Emerita.** In Hilary and the Councils. He appears in the aforementioned catalogue. In Athanasius’s letter he is corruptly written “Florentius of Meria in Pannonia,” in place of “of Emerita in Spain.”

**XLIII. Fortunatianus of Italy, from Aquileia.** In Hilary and the Councils. In Athanasius’s catalogue he is called Fortunatus.

**XLIV. Gaudentius of Achaia—correct to Dacia—from Naissus.** In Hilary and the Councils. In Athanasius’s letter, “Gaudentius of Naissus.” He is mentioned in Athanasius’s catalogue and in the Sardican canons themselves.

**XLV. Gerontius of Macedonia, from Brevi.** In the Councils and in Hilary. Only his name is given in the three other documents.

**XLVI. Helianus of Tyrtanis.** In the subscriptions of Athanasius’s letter. His catalogue names this same bishop.

**XLVII. Hermogenes of Syceon—perhaps of Sicyon in Achaia.** Thus in both places.

**XLVIII. Himenaeus of Hypata in Thessaly.** Hilary, the Councils, and Athanasius’s catalogue preserve the correct name of the bishop. The subscriptions of Athanasius’s letter give the name of the city, but incorrectly write Hypeneris for Himenaeus. In the Councils and in Hilary the city’s name is badly rendered as Pearata or Pharata.

**XLIX. Januarius of Campania, from Beneventum.** In Hilary, in the Councils, and in Athanasius’s letter and catalogue.

**L. John.** In the subscriptions of the synodal letter.

**LI. Jonas of Macedonia, from Particopolis.** In Hilary and in the Councils. He also appears in the synodal letter and in Athanasius’s catalogue.

**LII. Irenaeus of Sicyon.** In Athanasius’s letter. Elsewhere, “Irenaeus of Achaia, from Secorus,” in the Councils and in Hilary, where the name is incorrectly given simply as Lerenius. In Vatican manuscript 1342, “from Scorus,” perhaps “from Scyrus in Achaia.” Irenaeus is also listed in Athanasius’s catalogue.

**LIII. Julianus of Theris in the Heptapolis.** In the subscriptions of Athanasius’s letter. In Hilary, “Julius of Achaia, from Thebes of the Heptapylos”; in the Councils, “Julius of Achaia, from Thebessa”; in Vatican manuscript 1342, “from Theepus”; in Vallicellian manuscript A 5, “from Teressa.” This Julianus, also listed in Athanasius’s catalogue, was bishop of Thebes in Achaia, called in Greek Ἑπτάπυλοι (*Heptapyloi*), “the Seven-Gated,” because of its seven gates [Col. 0059A], to distinguish it from Thebes in Thessaly, whose bishop Moysius likewise attended Sardica.

**LIV. Julianus.** Another, who subscribed Athanasius’s letter. Athanasius’s catalogue lists two Julians.

**LV. Lucius of Thrace, from Caenopolis.** In Hilary and in the Councils. In the other three documents only his name is given. All agree that it should be corrected to “of Hadrianopolis,” since Hadrianopolis is known to be in Thrace and Lucius of Hadrianopolis attended the Sardican council, as Socrates testifies in book II, chapters 20 and 23.

**LVI. Lucius of Italy, from Verona.** In Hilary, in the Councils, and in Athanasius’s letter. Saint Athanasius always calls him Lucillus, not only in his catalogue but also in the First Apology. By this name the three older Veronese documents call our sixth bishop.

**LVII. Macedonius of Dardania, from Ulpiana.** In Hilary and in the Councils. In Athanasius’s letter, “Lypianensis” is incorrectly written for “Ulpianensis” [Col. 0059B]. He is listed in Athanasius’s catalogue. Hierocles places Ulpiana among the cities of Dardania.

**LVIII. Marcellus of Ancyra in Galatia.** In Hilary and in the Councils, where another province, Macedonia, has been erroneously inserted. In the subscriptions of Athanasius’s letter [XLVII] only the name Marcellus is read. Athanasius’s catalogue mentions a Marcellianus; if he is not someone different from Marcellus of Ancyra, the name Marcellianus is erroneous.

**LIX. Marcus of Siscia in Savia.** In Athanasius’s letter. In Hilary, however, “Marcus of Asia, from Fischia”; in the Councils, “of Asia, from Scisia.” Correct to “of Savia, from Siscia.” Athanasius’s catalogue lists Marcus. At the beginning of the Second Apology, Athanasius also includes Siscia among the thirty-six provinces whose bishops had supported him. Since there was no province of Siscia, but Siscia was a city situated on the Sava and belonged to the province of Savia, an obvious error entered Athanasius’s Apology. It seems to have arisen because, in the subscription of this same Marcus, the name of the city was taken for the name of the province.

**LX. Martyrius of Naupactus.** In Athanasius’s letter. In Hilary and in the Councils, “Martyrius of Achaia, from Neapolis”; Vallicellian manuscript A 5 has “from Neapot.” Correct to “of Naupactus,” for Naupactus was a city of Achaia.

**LXI. Martyrius.** Another, in the same letter of Athanasius, who recalls one Martyrius in his catalogue.

**LXII. Maximus of Tuscia, from Luca.** In Hilary, in the Councils, and in Athanasius’s catalogue.

**LXIII. Maximus, likewise through letters, from Gaul.** Thus in the subscriptions of Athanasius’s letter, but corruptly. With the Marquis Maffei, it seems that we should read “Maximus,” or “Maximinus,” bishop of Trier from Gaul, whom the enemies of Athanasius attack in the pseudo-Sardican letter. Athanasius places him in the first series, but in the second series, where those who supported him in his absence are mentioned. In this series, however, he mentions him first and joins him with Verissimus, bishop of Lyon, whom we shall see was present at Sardica.

**LXIV. Mosinius of Heraclea.** Subscribed Athanasius’s letter among the bishops of Crete. There were many Heracleas. Strabo and Ptolemy mention Heraclea in Crete. In Athanasius’s catalogue he is called Musonius.

**LXV. Moysius of Thessaly, from Thebes.** In Hilary. In the Councils, however, Moschus; in Vatican manuscript 1342, Moestus; in Vallicellian manuscript A 5, Moystus. He appears to be the one called Musaeus in Athanasius’s catalogue.

**LXVI. Olympius of Aenus in Rhodope.** He subscribed Athanasius’s letter. He is named in the Sardican canons. Aenus, or Aenos, is a city in Thrace, in the province of Rhodope. From this subscription it can be recognized how rightly Tillemont suspected that the Olympius mentioned in the Sardican canons was the bishop of Aenus whom Athanasius praises in the Second Apology as having been harassed by the Eusebians.

**LXVII. Hosius of Spain, from Córdoba.** In all the documents.

**LXVIII. Palladius of Macedonia, from Dium.** In Hilary and in the Councils; more correctly in Vallicellian manuscript A 5 and in Athanasius’s letter, “from Diu.” Dium is in Macedonia. Athanasius’s catalogue names this bishop.

**LXIX. Paregorius of Dardania, from Scupi.** In Hilary and in the Councils. In the subscriptions of Athanasius’s letter, “Caspinus” is incorrectly written for “Scupinus.” He is mentioned in the synodal letter and in Athanasius’s catalogue.

**LXX. Patricius.** Only the names of these men are read in the same catalogue.

**LXXI. Peter.** Only the names of these men are read in the same catalogue.

**LXXII. Philologius.** Only the names of these men are read in the same catalogue.

**LXXIII. Plutarchus of Achaia, from Patras.** In Hilary and in the Councils. He is listed in the synodal letter and in the aforementioned catalogue.

**LXXIV. Porphyrius of Macedonia, from Philippi.** Thus in Hilary and in the Councils. He is also mentioned in the three other documents.

**LXXV. Praetextatus of Spain, from Barcelona.** In Hilary and in the Councils. In the subscriptions of Athanasius’s letter, however, it is corruptly written, “Praetextatus of Narcidona in Pannonia.” He is also named in Athanasius’s catalogue.

**LXXVI. Protasius of Italy, from Milan.** In Hilary, in the Councils, in Athanasius’s letter, and also in his catalogue.

**LXXVII. Protogenus of Dacia, from Serdica.** In Hilary, in the Councils, and in Athanasius’s catalogue. He also subscribed Athanasius’s letter.

**[XLVIII] LXXVIII. Restitutus.** He subscribed the synodal letter. He is listed in the same catalogue.

**LXXIX. Sapritius.** He is named in the aforementioned catalogue.

**LXXX. Severus of Calciso in Thessaly.** He subscribed Athanasius’s letter. Chalcis in Euboea was a celebrated city, assigned to Thessaly at the time of the Sardican council and later to Achaia.

**LXXXI. Severus of Italy, from Ravenna.** In Hilary and in the Councils. Athanasius’s catalogue names one Severus, and one is likewise read among the subscribers to the synodal letter.

**LXXXII. Spudasius.** Listed only in Athanasius’s catalogue.

**LXXXIII. Stercorius of Apulia, from Canusium.** In Hilary and in the Councils. In Athanasius’s letter, where two subscriptions have coalesced into one and the bishop’s name has been omitted, “Sunosio of Apulia” is corruptly written for “Canusio.” This bishop is listed in Athanasius’s catalogue.

**LXXXIV. Symphorus of Hierapythnis in Crete.** He subscribed Athanasius’s letter and is listed in his catalogue.

**LXXXV. Tryphon of Achaia, from Marciarce.** In Hilary. Vatican manuscript 1342 has “from Macarcens”; in the Councils, “from Macarce,” or “from Marathon”; in the subscriptions of Athanasius’s letter, “Tryphon of Magara.” Amid so many corrupt variants, it is difficult to establish the true city of this Tryphon, whom Athanasius’s catalogue also mentions. Megara would be preferable, unless Alypius of Achaia, from Megara, had already been listed above.

**LXXXVI. Valens of Dacia Ripensis, from Scytopolis.** Thus in the Councils. Vatican manuscript 1342 has “from Sciopolitanus”; Vallicellian manuscript A 5, “from Sciapt.” In Hilary, incorrectly, “of Ripensian Achaia, from Scio.” This bishop is named in the synodal letter and in Athanasius’s catalogue. The true name of the city cannot be established, since most of the cities of Dacia Ripensis are unknown.

**LXXXVII. Verissimus of Gaul, from Lyon.** In Hilary and in the Councils. In Athanasius’s letter, corruptly, “Broseus of Lyon in Gaul.” These three testimonies show that Verissimus attended the Sardican council. Nevertheless, Athanasius omits him from the first series of his catalogue and places him at the beginning of the second.

**LXXXVIII. Vincentius of Campania, from Capua.** In Hilary and in the Councils. He subscribes the synodal letter on behalf of the others. Since Athanasius’s catalogue names one Vincentius, it may be uncertain whether the man who subscribed at the end on behalf of the others is the same as, or different from, the one who had shortly before subscribed the same synodal letter under the name Vincentius.

**LXXXIX. Vitalis of Dacia Ripensis, from Aquae.** In Hilary and in the Councils. A place called Aquae in Dacia is mentioned in the *Itinerary of Antoninus*.

**XC. Vitalis Vertarensis of Africa.** He subscribed Athanasius’s letter. Athanasius’s catalogue lists two Vitales, and one is found among the subscribers to the synodal letter.

**XCI. Ursatius of Italy, from Brescia.** In Hilary, in the Councils, in Athanasius’s letter, and also in his catalogue.

**XCII. Zosimus of Macedonia, from Lignedus.** In the Councils. Vallicellian manuscript A 5 has “Zosimus of Dacia, from Lygmedon.” In Hilary he is called “Dionysius of Achaia, from Lignedum.” Pope Gelasius wrote a letter to Laurentius concerning Lignidus, which was subject to the metropolitan of Thessalonica. In Athanasius’s letter this same Zosimus is subscribed as follows: “Zosimus of Lychnis, Sunosio of Apulia.” The latter words, belonging to the subscription of Stercorius, bishop of Canusium [Col. 0061B], were wrongly attached to Zosimus. The city is called Lychnis by Livy, *Lychnidus*, Λυχνίδος by Stephanus. In Hierocles’s *Notitia* it is corruptly called Aulinidos and placed in New Epirus. Antoninus, bishop of Lychnidus, subscribed the letter of the bishops of New Epirus to the Emperor Leo.

**XCIII. Zosimus Oreomargensis.** He subscribed Athanasius’s letter. Correct to *Horreomargensis*. Horrea Margi is located in the *Itinerary of Antoninus* between Viminacium and Serdica. In Hierocles, Ortemarcus is placed in First Moesia together with Viminacium; it should be corrected there to Horreomargus.

**XCIV. Zosimus.** A third bishop, whose place is unknown, is read as a subscriber in the same letter of Athanasius. Athanasius’s catalogue does indeed list three Zosimi.

**XCV.** In addition to these, legates of Julius, the Roman pontiff, attended the Sardican synod and subscribed Athanasius’s letter to the Churches of Mareotis as follows:

> Archidamus and Philoxenus, presbyters, and Leo, deacon, from Rome: we wish you health.

In his catalogue, however, immediately after Hosius of Spain, Athanasius names only the presbyters in these words: “Julius of Rome, through the presbyters Archidamus and Philoxenus.” He omits Leo the deacon. But in the text of the Sardican synodal letter to Pope Julius preserved by Saint Hilary, both the two presbyters and Leo the deacon are mentioned as present at the synod.

We have extracted these names from five documents. Two others, omitted from those documents, must be added: Gratus of Carthage and Euphratas of Agrippina.

**XCVI.** That Gratus, bishop of Carthage, attended the Sardican council can be inferred clearly enough from the Greek text of canon 7, and even more clearly from canon 5 of the Council of Carthage held under the same Gratus. Athanasius does indeed list this Gratus in the second series, among the African bishops who, while absent, approved the Sardican decrees. But just as Athanasius omitted from the first series Verissimus of Lyon—who, as the subscriptions themselves show [Col. 0061D], was at Sardica—and Maximinus of Trier, placing them in the second series before those Gauls who had been absent, so he may have done the same with Gratus.

If he listed these three bishops in the second series because, after returning to their provinces, they approved the Sardican decrees together with the bishops of those provinces who had not attended the council, then they could have been placed by him in both series. The same appears to have happened for this reason with Arius of Palestine, who is found in both series of Athanasius’s catalogue: in the first, because he attended the council; in the second, because he later approved the aforementioned decrees together with the other Palestinian bishops.

**XCVII.** Euphratas of Agrippina, as a legate of the Sardican council together with Vincentius of Capua, went to the East and, undoubtedly together with Vincentius, attended the council itself. See Athanasius, *History of the Arians to the Monks*.

### V

Since most of these bishops, both Latin and Greek, came from the Western provinces, many consider the Sardican council not ecumenical but Western. Although they admit that the council was summoned with the intention that a general synod should be held from all the provinces of both East and West, nevertheless, since nearly all the Eastern bishops withdrew from Sardica and convened another council at Philippopolis, they think that the decrees enacted at Sardica without those Eastern bishops were and should be regarded as the decrees of a Western synod.

Peter de Marca, who supports this opinion, brings forward the testimonies of Saint Hilary and Epiphanius, since, as he says, they call that council “the council of the Westerners” (*Lib. VII Concord.*, ch. 3, no. 5). For this reason, even the Romans and other Latin bishops, while repeatedly emphasizing four general councils—Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon—never mention Sardica.

### VI

Since it is universally certain that this council was summoned as a general synod, just as no prejudice results if, after all the bishops have been summoned to an ecumenical council, many do not attend it, so there is no obstacle if some of those who have gathered at the place of the synod withdraw—especially if they go elsewhere for a perverse and schismatic purpose, to set up altar against altar and establish a schism.

Those who assemble at the summoned synod with the supreme pontiff, the head of the entire Church, present either personally or through legates, and who make decisions there, adequately represent the whole Church and the body of its pastors. They decide, judge, and establish laws and rules as an ecumenical council. The other body of bishops, separating itself from a synod lawfully assembled as the synod of the whole Church and from its head, must be regarded not as a legitimate synod but as a gathering and conventicle.

If that body could diminish the authority and right of the legitimate synod, perfidious men would have the power—by persuading bishops who belonged to their party and withdrawing them from the assembly of the others—to invalidate any general synod, and a privilege and right would be granted to a schismatic conventicle such as the Church has never recognized.

Thus, although approximately forty bishops, including nearly all those of the East, withdrew from the First Council of Ephesus, that synod nevertheless suffered no prejudice preventing it from being regarded as general. The same, therefore, must be thought concerning the Sardican council, from which the conventicle of the Eusebians, transferred by a perverse and unjust proceeding to Philippopolis, could not detract anything.

For this reason Saint Athanasius called Sardica “the great council” in the Second Apology. Pope Liberius, in Athanasius’s *History of the Arians to the Monks*, no. 37, called it “a synod convoked from the whole world,” that is, a general synod. Its decrees were once added by the Roman Church and by many Westerners—and, as we saw in the preceding chapter, also by the Eastern bishops of the Council of Constantinople of the year 382—to the Nicene decrees and cited as Nicene decrees. This sufficiently indicates that the council was regarded as ecumenical, just as Nicaea was.

If, in a later age, it was not counted among the four ecumenical councils even by the Romans themselves, this happened either because they included the Sardican council as annexed to the Nicene council, or rather because, when listing the councils that were to be received like the Gospels, they thought it necessary to mention only those councils that, in order to preserve the Catholic faith intact, condemned some particular heresy.

Thus the Council of Nicaea was praised because it proscribed the error of Arius; the Council of Constantinople, because it proscribed that of Macedonius; the Council of Ephesus, because it proscribed that of Nestorius; and the Council of Chalcedon, because it proscribed the error of Eutyches. Since the Sardican synod, while striking at the remnants of Arius, did not crush any distinct heresy, it was treated as an appendix to Nicaea and did not need to be listed separately. Nevertheless, this should not lead anyone to believe that it was therefore not regarded as ecumenical.

### VII

Indeed, although the Emperor Justinian frequently mentions the four general councils, he nevertheless called Sardica an ecumenical synod in his edict of faith (*T. VI of the Councils*, col. 393b). The more frequent commendation of the four general councils among later Greeks, who began to separate general synods from particular or local synods in their canonical collections, seems to have occasioned the listing of Sardica among the local synods. The older Greek canonical books, however, placed it immediately after Nicaea, as we observed in the preceding chapter from John Scholasticus.

I therefore establish it as ecumenical not only for the Western Churches but also for the Eastern Churches. Just as the restoration of Saint Athanasius of Alexandria, Marcellus of Ancyra, and Asclepius of Gaza was decreed and carried out by that synod, and concerned the Churches of the East, so also the canons which we saw cited under the name of the Nicene canons at the Eastern Council of Constantinople in the year 382 concerned Western as well as Eastern Churches.

Hence, in the manuscripts of the ancient edition and of the Hadrianic collection, immediately after the final canon, this clause is found, declaring legislative force throughout the entire world:

> The whole synod said: The Catholic Church, spread throughout the whole world, shall preserve all that has been established.

And they subscribed, etc.

The testimonies of Hilary and Epiphanius, which Peter de Marca adduces, do not undermine this conclusion. For Hilary, in his book *Against Constantius Augustus*, no. 25, writes:

> You also condemn the term “substance,” by which you pretended to the Westerners that you were pious both at the Sardican and at the Sirmian synod.

He is speaking not of the Sardican council but of the pseudo-Sardican council, just as he is speaking of the Sirmian council, which was not a gathering of Westerners but a conventicle of Easterners. His only intention was to signify that Constantius, condemning the term “substance” by the example of these pseudo-synods, had pretended to the Westerners that he was pious.

Saint Epiphanius, *Heresy* 71, chapter 1, must likewise be understood in another sense and offers no support to de Marca’s opinion. He calls the Sardican synod “Western,” or “of the Westerners,” in order to distinguish it from the Eastern assembly of the Eusebians: the former had assembled at Sardica, a city of the West, while the latter had assembled at Philippopolis, in the East.

Moreover, does Saint Epiphanius not seem in this passage to have taken the Sardican synod for the Sirmian or Milanese synod, as Tillemont conjectures in note 40 of volume VI of the *History of the Arians*?

### VIII

Some doubt whether the Sardican synod was regarded as ecumenical even in the West itself. They are influenced by the resistance of the Africans, who opposed the Sardican canons produced from the memorandum of Zosimus in the case of Apiarius.

Those who raise this objection must doubt not only whether the Sardican synod was ecumenical, but also whether it was a general synod of the whole West. Yet the latter cannot be questioned, so much so that even those most hostile to this synod admit that it was a general synod of the West.

We have explained at length what the African dispute concerned, so that no argument against the authority of the Sardican canons can be drawn from it, in the observations to Quesnell’s fifth dissertation, part I, chapter 6 (col. 000).

## PART TWO

On the more ancient Latin collections, whether they are earlier than Dionysius Exiguus or derive their origin from sources earlier than Dionysius.

[Col. 0063]

## CHAPTER ONE

On the primitive canonical collection among the Latins, especially the Romans, which contained only the Nicene canons together with the Sardican canons.

[Col. 0063C]

### § 1

The only canons that once possessed authority among the Latins, especially the Romans, were the Nicene and Sardican canons. The opinion is rejected according to which other Greek canons are said to have been cited under the name of the Nicene canons or to have been confirmed at the Council of Nicaea.

1. Although the canons of all the Greek synods contained in the Greek codex had once been rendered into Latin in the two ancient versions commonly circulated before the Dionysian version—the Isidorian and the Prisca, as will be said in the following chapter—nevertheless, since these versions had been produced and published through private scholarly effort, only the Nicene canons, together with the Sardican canons placed immediately after them without any distinction and inscribed under the same name of the Nicene canons, possessed public authority among the Latins, especially among the Romans. That the Roman Church received only the Nicene canons [Col. 0063D]—under which title, as we shall show in § 3, the Sardican canons were included—is expressly stated by Innocent I in his letter to Theophilus of Alexandria, where, after mentioning the Nicene canons, he adds: “For the Roman Church admits no other canon.” And in another letter to the clergy and people of Constantinople, no. 3:

> “But as regards the observance of the canons, we say that obedience is owed ONLY to those defined at Nicaea, which the Catholic Church ought to follow and acknowledge ALONE.”

That this was likewise true throughout the Latin Church may be inferred from the fact that before the sixth century no canons of any other Greek synods are found cited by Latin writers except the Nicene canons, and, under the name of the Nicene canons, the Sardican canons as well. It seems impossible that other canons could also have been received and yet that none should ever have been cited by anyone.

2. Some believe that by the name of “the Nicene canons” Innocent I meant all the canons of the Greek synods, on the grounds that all of them, being written in the canonical codices after the Nicene canons, could have been called Nicene from the title of the First Council of Nicaea. Thus Saint Gregory of Tours cited the fourteenth canon of the Council of Gangra as though it were Nicene. “I,” he says, “approaching the monastery, reread the decrees of the Nicene canons, in which it is contained that if a woman leaves her husband and rejects the marriage-bed in which she has lived well, etc.” (Book IX, chapter 33).

But this particular error of an author from a much later age cannot be transferred to Innocent I, especially since Innocent did not cite some canon of an individual synod, but established a general proposition: that the Roman Church received only the Nicene canons, and that the Catholic Church ought to follow and acknowledge only those. Perhaps Gregory of Tours took the Gangran canon from some later collection or abridgment of the canons, in which the decrees of different councils had been written without their own intervening titles, as in Codex 59 of the Verona Chapter, whose beginning bears this general heading: “From the Council of Nicaea, or from other councils” (see Part IV, chapter 4, no. 11).

[Col. 0064D] 3. Others, adopting another line of reasoning, maintain that the canons of other synods were regarded and cited by Innocent as Nicene because they had been confirmed at the Council of Nicaea. They say that this is evident concerning the canons of the three older synods—Ancyra, Neocaesarea, and Gangra—which were read and confirmed at the Council of Nicaea.
