Father Coustant drew this conclusion from a speech of Hosius inserted into the ancient Corbie collection, in the preface to volume I of the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, p. 61. Later, speaking of the passages quoted from Innocent I, he adds on p. 66:

> “What prevents those canons from being called defined at Nicaea which were read and confirmed at Nicaea and listed in the synodal Acts? Why should one not think that the person who follows the Nicene canons, and those alone, is following only those canons which the Nicene Fathers made their own by their own approval?”

We have shown in Part I, chapter 4, § 1, that the speech of Hosius on which Coustant’s opinion rests is spurious and of no authority; there [Col. 0065A] we also proved that the Synod of Gangra was later not only than Nicaea but even than the Council of Sardica.

That the Roman Church did not receive the Ancyrene canons is evident from the fact that they contain several provisions contrary to its discipline. Nor should it be claimed that these were revised by Hosius and adapted to Western discipline. Not all the canons found to conflict with Western discipline have been corrected; those that were corrected are found only in the Corbie and Quesnellian collections, printed in this volume. As we shall see, these were Gallican, not Roman. In the other Italian collections, however, which could have been used by the Romans, they are found without any correction.

Moreover, these corrections were not introduced into the Greek text—which, on this view, would have been read at the Council of Nicaea—but into the ancient version called the Isidorian version, which is received in the Quesnellian and Corbie collections mentioned above. Since older and purer copies of the same translation lack such corrections, it is clear that these emendations cannot be attributed to Hosius as having been introduced at that time.

Unless, therefore, it is demonstrated by other documents—not yet produced and, as we believe, never likely to be produced—that some Ancyrene, Neocaesarean, or Gangran canon was cited by supreme pontiffs or other Latin Fathers before the sixth century, it cannot be established that these canons were included by Innocent I under the name of the Nicene canons or that they possessed authority among the Latins.

§ 2. Neither the Antiochene nor the Constantinopolitan canons were formerly received by the Roman Church. The Constantinopolitan synod and its creed were celebrated by the Latins after the Council of Chalcedon; nevertheless, that synod was not regarded as ecumenical until somewhat later, nor were its canons received until Saint Gregory the Great; only its creed was received. Before Chalcedon this synod was not listed among the ecumenical councils even by the Greeks themselves. The words of Siricius and Celestine adduced in support of the use of the Greek canons among the Latins are explained. Their use among the Latins was introduced in the sixth century.

[Col. 0065C]

4. Much less, then, can the Antiochene and Constantinopolitan canons be said to have been included among, or received by, the Latins. Innocent I rejected the Antiochene canons when they were brought forward by Saint John Chrysostom’s enemies against him, and maintained that they should be rejected, in the cited letter to the clergy and people of Constantinople.

If one Antiochene canon is read in the Synod of Riez of the year 439 (volume IV of the Councils, col. 537), having been added from a Hispanic codex of the Church of Urgell by Stephen Baluze, there can be no doubt that it was inserted by a later addition. First, in that codex the Antiochene canon was substituted, together with another unknown canon, in place of the eighth canon, which, although it properly belongs to that synod—as is clear from other Gallican manuscripts—is nevertheless omitted there. Second, this addition is shown much more clearly to be foreign to the same synod if the codices containing the synod itself are considered.

The synod is presented by the codices of the Hispanic collection, from which it passed into the Isidorian collection, and by several copies of various Gallican collections. The codices of the Hispanic collection vary in fullness, as we shall explain in Part III, chapter 4. The Urgell copy belongs to the fuller Hispanic collection, such as we find in the manuscript of Cardinal Passionei and in another Vatican Palatine manuscript, no. 575.

After examining the different manuscripts of the Hispanic collection, both fuller and shorter, as well as the Isidorian manuscripts, which derive from the shorter Hispanic copies, we observed that all of them, in the Synod of Riez, present only seven canons, omitting the eighth. The latter, like an unnecessary concluding clause, may have seemed dispensable to the first author of the Hispanic collection. They also omit the Antiochene canon and the other unknown canon. Since these are found only in the Urgell manuscript, they can readily be recognized as additions. [Col. 0066A]

The eighth canon, however, emerged from Gallican collections of diverse origin. Yet these, just as much as the Hispanic and Isidorian copies, know nothing of the two canons found in the Urgell codex. Since, whenever councils of Gaul are concerned—as is the case with Riez—the Gallican collections ought to be preferred to the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, the eighth canon cannot be taken away from that council on the authority of the Gallican collections; the two added canons, however, must with much greater certainty be excluded from it, since all the Gallican, Hispanic (with the single exception of Urgell), and Isidorian copies omit them.

5. The Constantinopolitan canons were unknown to the Latins before Chalcedon; and even after that council, although they had been translated into Latin collections, they were not immediately received. Thus Saint Gregory, even in his own time, wrote in Letter 34 of Book VII:

> “The Roman Church does not yet possess or receive those canons or the Acts of that synod [the Constantinopolitan synod].”

Yet he says that it accepted that synod in this respect: that it accepted what had been defined there against Macedonius, namely, the Constantinopolitan creed.

Since some writers—including Quesnellus, in note 4 on Letter 106—maintain that the Constantinopolitan synod had always been counted among the principal and ecumenical councils, even by the Roman pontiffs, something must be added to make the whole matter clearer.

Certainly, the Roman synod of the year 385, under Felix III, in its letter to the orthodox residing at Constantinople and in Bithynia, when listing the ecumenical synods, mentioned only three: Nicaea, Ephesus, and Chalcedon; concerning Constantinople it said not a word.

“And so,” it says, “your Charity may recognize that we hold the venerable synods of Nicaea, the First of Ephesus, and Chalcedon against Nestorius and the most impious Eutyches, etc.” See volume V of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 248.

In the passage cited above, Quesnellus opposes this the decree of Gelasius concerning books to be received or not received, and Gregory’s Letter 24, now Letter 25 of Book I, in which the same synod is held in equal honor with the other three ecumenical councils. But the genuine decree of Gelasius lacks the Constantinopolitan synod, as it also lacks the words “and if there are any councils,” etc., as we shall prove in chapter 11, § 5, from older and also more numerous manuscript copies. Consequently, this very decree rather establishes the contrary view: that in Gelasius’s time that synod had not yet been received by the Roman Church among the ecumenical councils—not even with respect to the creed, which alone is discussed in the commonly circulated addition to the Gelasian decree.

If Saint Gregory, in the letter mentioned above, lists the same synod among the ecumenical councils, he does so under that name only because the error of Eunomius and Macedonius was condemned there. He is referring to one definition of faith, not to the canons, which in Letter 34 of Book VII he states had not yet been received by the Roman Church.

That he assigns an ecumenical place to the same council because of its definition and creed, although it did not possess that status in the age of Gelasius, proves that this recognition was introduced after Gelasius’s time. Formerly, the Constantinopolitan creed, together with the document to which the Easterners had subscribed in 378 or 379 at the Synod of Antioch—an exposition issued against the definition of the Roman council concerning the Macedonians—was sent to Damasus in the year 382. This is clear from the synodal letter of the other Constantinopolitan council held in that year, addressed to the same pontiff and to the other Fathers of the Roman synod, which is read in Theodoret, Book V, chapter 9.

Although both that creed and the document of the Antiochene synod were found to agree with the preceding Roman definition and were approved by the Westerners, it cannot therefore be said that the Constantinopolitan council of the year 381, at which the creed itself was composed, was regarded as ecumenical; nor was the Antiochene council, which issued the document. Nor does it matter that the same Constantinopolitan synod is called ecumenical in the synodal letter cited above. Saint Leo, in Letter 106, chapter 5, calls this synod “the assembly of a few bishops”; it could have been called ecumenical only in the sense in which Augustine and the other Africans customarily called a council assembled from all Africa plenary or universal, as Father Coustant aptly observed in note 6 on Letter 13 among the letters of Damasus, col. 566.

Only when the same Constantinopolitan creed was inserted into the Council of Chalcedon and approved with the highest praise did the Roman Church, while receiving the Council of Chalcedon as genuinely ecumenical, likewise receive that creed as a portion of Chalcedon’s Acts.

6. Indeed, it seems to us quite probable that the Constantinopolitan council began to be celebrated among the Greeks themselves at the Synod of Chalcedon, since it contributed greatly both against the Eutychian heresy and in favor of the prerogative of the Constantinopolitan see.

Before Chalcedon, mention is found nowhere of the Constantinopolitan council, but only of the Nicene council, whether in the Synod of Ephesus or among other Greek Fathers. Indeed, at the general Council of Ephesus the Fathers praised the Nicene creed in such a way that they refused to allow any other faith to be presented. The holy synod decreed:

> “No one is permitted to present, write, or compose another faith besides that defined by the holy Fathers who assembled at Nicaea with the Holy Spirit” (volume III of the Councils, col. 1219).

In the first session only the Nicene creed, not the Constantinopolitan creed, was recited; only at Chalcedon are both said to have been inserted.

At the time of the Ephesian synod, therefore, the Constantinopolitan council was not as famous as it later became at Chalcedon, nor does it appear to have been counted among the general councils. Otherwise, the Nicene creed alone would not have been approved by an explicit decree, with all others rejected—whatever might be put forward besides the Nicene creed.

Moreover, in the false Synod of Ephesus there is a profession of faith by Eutyches in which, with reference to the Council of Nicaea, the First General Council, the council held at Ephesus is called the Second General Council:

> “As the holy Fathers who assembled at Nicaea handed down the faith to us, so the holy Fathers confirmed it ἐν Ἐφέσῳ ἐν τῇ δευτέρᾳ συνόδῳ—at Ephesus, in the second synod” (volume IV of the Councils, col. 923).

He therefore did not count the Constantinopolitan synod as the second general council.

At Chalcedon, Eutyches himself was reproached for not receiving the Constantinopolitan creed and synod (ibid., col. 212, 914); nevertheless, he was never reproached for assigning second place among the general synods to Ephesus. Nor, if the Constantinopolitan synod had then universally been regarded by the Greeks as one of the ecumenical councils, would the Eutychians have dared oppose it.

And lest it be thought peculiar to the Eutychians not to count the Constantinopolitan council among the general councils, let us hear Eusebius of Dorylaeum, the accuser of Eutyches. At the Constantinopolitan synod of the year 448, assembled against that same heretic, he mentioned only the councils of Nicaea and Ephesus and affirmed that he remained steadfast in “the faith of the holy Fathers, the 318 assembled at Nicaea, and in all that was done at Ephesus by the holy and great synod” (ibid., col. 931).

Likewise, at the second session of the same Constantinopolitan synod of the year 448, when praising the general synods, the Fathers mentioned only Nicaea and Ephesus (ibid., col. 935e, 966, and 967a, c, d, etc.).

These facts indicate that the Constantinopolitan council of the year 381, although it fought most vigorously against Eutyches, was not regarded as possessing equal authority and had not yet been counted among the general councils. It is therefore not improbable that this council began to be celebrated among the Greeks themselves only after Chalcedon and began then to be counted among the general councils.

[LV] 7. If this is true of the Greeks, it is not surprising that the Latins, even after Chalcedon, did not yet count the Constantinopolitan council among the ecumenical councils, nor approve its creed as the creed of an ecumenical council, except insofar as it had been read and approved at the general Council of Chalcedon.

Thus, in his decree concerning books, Gelasius was satisfied to list the Council of Chalcedon among the general councils. He did not think it necessary to list Constantinople as a distinct ecumenical synod, since its creed had acquired the force of a general decree only through the Council of Chalcedon.

Later, however, after the disturbances arising from the affair of Acacius had been settled, when the Eastern bishops returned to unity and issued professions of faith in which the Constantinopolitan synod was distinctly listed with the other three ecumenical synods because of its condemnation of the error of Macedonius, the Roman pontiffs too began to mention that synod distinctly among the ecumenical councils. From that time Vigilius, Pelagius, and Saint Gregory began to praise four ecumenical councils, including Constantinople because of its definition and creed of faith.

8. What has been said about this creed must not be transferred to the canons of the same synod, which Saint Gregory himself testifies had not yet been received.

Nor does anything establish the reception of those canons that Baluze adduces in his additions to Book V of Peter de Marca’s Concordia, chapter 21, no. 14. He says that the names of Macedonius and Eunomius, which Saint Gregory himself mentions when commending the Constantinopolitan synod, are not cited from the creed but from the canons. Therefore, if the Romans derived the names of those heretics from the canons, one may conclude that the canons were known and approved by them no less than the creed.

But it is evident from Gregory himself that the Roman pontiffs attributed no authority to the catalogue of heretics inserted in the Constantinopolitan canons. Although Eudoxius and the Eudoxians were condemned in those same canons, Gregory wrote to Eulogius in Letter 34 of Book VII that he did not know them, because he had found nothing about them either in Philaster, Augustine, or other Fathers. The Roman see had not yet received the canons or Acts of the Constantinopolitan synod; therefore, not trusting them, he asked Eulogius to inform him by letter if any approved Greek Father had said anything about Eudoxius.

When Eulogius replied by producing testimonies against him from Saints Basil, Gregory, and Epiphanius, the holy pontiff responded in Letter 30 of Book VIII that he was satisfied by the authority of these very well-known Fathers.

The Romans, however, had learned of the heretics Macedonius and Eunomius from Augustine and especially from the profession of faith sent by Damasus to Paulinus. Consequently, they inserted their names into their letters not from the Constantinopolitan canons but from those sources.

Moreover, from the cited Letter 34 of Book VII of Gregory it is clear that copies of the Constantinopolitan canons did exist among the Romans at that time, and that Gregory had certainly read them when he wrote:

> “The canons of the Constantinopolitan council indeed condemn the Eudoxians.”

Yet the Roman Church had attributed no authority to them. In this sense he added:

> “But the Roman Church does not yet possess or receive those canons or the Acts of that synod.”

They were known, to be sure, from Latin collections and translations, of which many copies were in circulation; but these collections and translations were not a public codex. They had been arranged and published through private effort and had received no approval from the Roman Church.

9. Nor do the testimonies of Siricius and Celestine, in which they state that no one is permitted to be ignorant of the canons, contribute anything toward establishing a public codex received and used in the ancient Latin Church that contained the canons of several synods.

Siricius’s words, which are brought forward from his letter to Himerius—“Let no priest be free to be ignorant of the provisions of the venerable canons”—have a reasonable meaning if they are understood of the Nicene canons alone, including the Sardican canons. Innocent I expressly stated that the Roman Church received these alone.

Celestine, however, when he wrote in his letter to the bishops of Apulia and Sicily, “No priest is permitted to be ignorant of his canons, nor to do anything that could conflict with the rules of the Fathers,” used the name “canons” somewhat more broadly, including also the decrees of the pontiffs. Apart from the Nicene and Sardican canons, these decrees possessed the greatest authority.

Nor is it unusual for the term “canons” to include not only the canons of councils but also the letters of the Roman pontiffs. John II, writing in his letter to Caesarius of Arles, says: “What the canons prescribe concerning these matters, we have appended below.” He plainly names only canons, yet in the testimonies that follow he includes not only the canons of councils but also a chapter from Siricius’s letter to Himerius, which we recognize as being included under the term “canons.”

But why seek proof from John II when Celestine himself, in the very letter that is brought forward, makes clear that he was referring chiefly to pontifical decretals under the name of canons? After commanding, “No priest should be permitted to be ignorant of his canons,” he immediately gives a reason that expressly concerns the decretals:

> “For what matter will be properly preserved by us if the norm of the DECRETAL regulations is broken according to someone’s whim . . . ?”

Afterward, censuring ignorance, he adds:

> “Thus nothing that has been decreed so frequently is of any benefit, since it is ignored as though nothing had EVER BEEN WRITTEN ON THIS MATTER—that is, by the Roman see.”

And again, somewhat later:

> “We who guard the helm of OUR JURISDICTION—that is, of the CANONS.”

Here he calls our jurisdiction, or pontifical jurisdiction, “canons.” Accordingly, explaining immediately which canons these are, he warns that no one should admit a layman to the clerical order and allow something to be done from which he might generate causes against himself, “by which he may become liable under the DECRETAL REGULATIONS.”

Therefore, when Siricius or Celestine reject ignorance of the canons, no one should imagine that they had in mind a public codex of canons containing, in the Latin Church and especially in the Roman Church, other canons besides the Nicene and Sardican canons that had by that time been received and approved.

10. Although the canons of other Greek synods had been transmitted to the Latins in the ancient Isidorian and Prisca translations, the Latins began to cite them only later, namely in the sixth century.

Some bring forward the Sixth Synod under Symmachus, in which that pontiff is introduced as saying:

> “Therefore it is also written in the canons established by apostolic authority in the Church of Gangra . . .”

He then recites two canons of that synod, the seventh and eighth, from the translation of Dionysius.

It is especially surprising that highly learned men failed to detect that this Sixth Synod under Symmachus is spurious and was fabricated by Isidore Mercator in the ninth century. Consequently, nothing authoritative for the present question can be extracted from it. See what we discuss on this matter in Part III, chapter 6, no. 7.

Its falsity is also confirmed by the fact that these canons are said not merely to have been received but to have been established by apostolic authority, although no one sat at the Synod of Gangra who exercised apostolic authority. If in some codices of a later age Hosius is inserted among the Fathers of Gangra, on the assumption that he held a legation from the Roman see, we have shown in Part I, chapter 4, § 1, that this must be attributed to error.

Although Isidore may have had this erroneous addition in mind when fabricating the words cited above, nothing of weight for establishing the use of the Greek canons among the Latins at the beginning of the sixth century can be drawn from this fictitious council.

The earliest clear testimony that has come to our attention concerning the use of these canons among the Latins is that of the Synod of Epaon in the year 517. In its canon 31, it prescribed penance for homicide, as the Ancyrene canons had decreed.

In the year 534, Pope John II, in the headings appended to his letter to Caesarius, transcribed two Apostolic canons, one Neocaesarean—which, as we shall prove, must be supplied in the commonly circulated copies in chapter 10, § 2, no. 12—and two Antiochene canons, from the translation of Dionysius.

Nor should the First Council of Orléans, held in the year 510, be omitted, although the evidence is not entirely clear. Its canon 15 commands that the provisions of the ancient canons be observed, so that everything should remain in the bishop’s power. This appears to refer to the last two Antiochene canons.

Perhaps this observance and use of the Greek canons among the Latins were gradually introduced through the translation of the canons of the Council of Chalcedon, whose first canon decrees:

> “We have decreed that the rules established by the holy Fathers in each council down to the present time shall retain their proper force.”

They may also have been introduced through the complete Acts of that same synod, translated into Latin in the sixth century, in which the Antiochene canons, besides the Nicene canons, are found cited from the Greek codex of the canons.

§ 3. The conjunction of the Nicene and Sardican canons, by which the latter, placed after the Nicene canons without their proper Sardican name, were regarded as Nicene. Latin collections of different origins prove that this conjunction and designation of the same canons was widespread among the Latins. Hence the Roman pontiffs who cited the Sardican canons under the name of the Nicene canons are seen to have been entirely free of deceit and fraud. A similar union of the canons of the two synods seems to have existed in some ancient Greek codex.

11. Numerous testimonies prove that the Sardican canons, which were published in Latin for the use of the Latins and were received by the Latin, especially the Roman, Church, were formerly included under the name of the Nicene canons.

Indeed, in several documents of the Roman pontiffs certain canons are insistently presented as Nicene although they are found not among the Nicene canons but among the Sardican canons.

Two famous Sardican canons are attributed to the Nicene synod in the Commonitorium of Zosimus in these words:

> “We have inserted the words of the canons into this Commonitorium for greater firmness. For thus the brethren said in the Council of Nicaea when they were deciding about the appeal of bishops: ‘It was decreed that if a bishop should be accused,’ etc.” (volume II of the Councils, col. 1253c),

as in Sardican canon 7.

Later it says:

> “Concerning the appeal of clerics—that is, of those of a lower rank—there is a definite response of that synod. We have thought it right to insert what you should do in this matter, which was stated as follows: ‘Bishop Hosius said: What still moves me is . . .’” (ibid., col. 1256c),

as in Sardican canon 17.

Likewise Saint Leo, Letter 44, chapter 3:

> “What must necessarily be demanded after the appeal has been lodged by Flavian is attested by the decrees of the canons held at Nicaea, which were established by the priests of the whole world and are appended below.”

He is referring to the Sardican canons concerning appeals, as we observed at greater length in the preliminary admonition to Letter 43, no. 8.

Nor does Galla Placidia, when she writes in Letter 56 among the Leonine letters to the emperor Theodosius concerning the legates of the Roman pontiff sent to the council, use any other expression:

> “Those who are accustomed to act according to the definitions of the Council of Nicaea.”

She appears to indicate Sardican canon 7, which concerns the legates of the pontiff, who exercise their authority in councils.

Before these examples, the Sardican canons had been cited as Nicene in the canons of the Synod of the Roman bishops to the Gauls, which some attribute to Innocent I, while others, with Father Coustant, attribute them to Pope Siricius.

There we read in chapter 5, no. 13:

> “When the Council of Nicaea”—read: “in the Council of Nicaea”—with the assent of the divine Spirit had firmly established the confession of faith according to law, the bishops, assembled together, also wished to bring the apostolic traditions to the knowledge of all. Among other things, they decreed that a mutilated cleric should not be made, since the mutilated and the eunuch shall not enter the sanctuary of God. Then, after the grace of baptism and the remission of sins, when someone has gloried in the warfare of the world or taken delight in purple and official insignia, they ordered that he should by no means be admitted to the priesthood through any irregular intrusion. For they approach the summit of such dignity through merit and observance of the law; no one can reach it through Simon’s money, or through favor, or through popular support” (Coustant, volume I of the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, cols. 695–696).

The first part, by which mutilated men are excluded from the clergy, is found in the first Nicene canon. The second, which provides that no one should be admitted to the priesthood through any irregular intrusion from military or civil service—provisions similar to which Siricius attributes to the Council of Nicaea in Letter 6, in Coustant, no. 3—agrees with a Sardican canon.

Coustant himself admits this, adding the following note (same work, col. 695, note c):

> “If ‘through any irregular intrusion’ means an excessive haste, we shall not hesitate to recognize here Sardican canon 13, which we have also observed inscribed as Nicene in the ancient codex of the monastery of Morbach.”

In this canon, which is the tenth among the Greeks, we read:

> “If perhaps a rich man, or a lawyer from the forum, or someone from an administrative office, has been requested to become a bishop, he should not be ordained beforehand unless his life has been examined for a long period of time and his merits have been proved.”

The same Sardican council likewise notes the corruption of simoniacal stain in canon 2, where it says:

> “Since it is clear that a few men could be corrupted by payment and reward . . . so that they might shout in the Church and appear to be asking for the bishop himself.”

[LVIII] Moreover, since in the same canons of the Synod of the Roman bishops, no. 16, it is said that the same Nicene Fathers prohibited bishops from transferring from one Church to another, and imposed this penalty upon transgressors:

> “They ordered that such a bishop . . . be deprived of his bishopric,”

Coustant likewise noted that the Sardican canon was indicated here [Col. 0071B] under the name of the Nicene canon (ibid., col. 697, note a):

> “For although Nicene canon 15 forbids anyone to transfer from one city to another, that synod by no means commands that a transferred bishop be deprived of his episcopate, but that he be restored to his OWN CHURCH, IN WHICH HE WAS ORDAINED. ‘NOR SHALL HE WHO IS SUCH HAVE LAY COMMUNION,’ the Sardican canon commands.”

He then adds in the same note that this Sardican canon likewise appears to have been indicated under the name of the Nicene canon by Saint Jerome in Letter 83 to Oceanus, where he writes:

> “This was decreed by the Fathers at the Council of Nicaea: that a bishop should not transfer from one Church to another, lest, despising the companionship of a poor little virgin, he seek the embrace of a richer adulteress.”

This certainly agrees with the words of the cited Sardican canon:

> “Since no bishop has been found in this matter who transfers from a larger city to a smaller one.”

In Letter 3 to the Synod of Toledo, no. 9, Innocent I lists the Nicene rules to be observed in ordinations and then appends decrees found partly among the Nicene and partly among the Sardican canons.

In Letter 7 to the clergy and people of Constantinople, no. 2, when reproaching the opponents of Saint John Chrysostom—who, after expelling him from his see and appealing to a synod, substituted another bishop in his place—he says that this had never been done by the Fathers but had rather been prohibited. This may refer to Sardican canon 4, which decreed that no other bishop should be ordained in the see of one who appeared to have been deposed after his appeal, unless his case had been decided in the judgment of the Roman bishop.

Although in this passage he does not call the Nicene Fathers or canons to witness, since in the same letter he testifies that only the Nicene canons are to be followed, he plainly regarded this Sardican canon as Nicene.

12. We are not unaware that P. Constant opposes us in this matter (ibid., col. 799). While attacking Quesnellus in note 6 on the aforementioned letter 7 of Innocent, where Quesnellus writes that the Sardican canons were regarded by that pontiff as Nicene, and were honored and clothed with the name of the Nicene canons, Constant establishes two points. First, Innocent, in the same letter [Col. 0071D], praised under the proper name of the Sardican synod the proceedings of Sardica, which were believed to have condemned the canons of Antioch; and therefore, he says, it is no less evident that Innocent accepted the Sardican canons as distinct from the Nicene canons, not as regarded as Nicene or clothed with their name. Second, he says that the same pontiff commanded that only the Nicene canons be followed in this sense: not that those agreeing with them should be rejected or despised, but only those disagreeing with them; just as if, besides the Sardican canons, there had been other canons accepted by Innocent that did not contradict the Nicene canons, and as if he had stated that only the Nicene canons were accepted merely because of their agreement with them.

In both respects, however, this very learned man is mistaken. As regards the first point, when Innocent praised the Sardican proceedings, which were thought to have condemned the canons of Antioch, under the proper name of the Sardican synod, he was referring to the Sardican synodal letter to Pope Julius, in which Saint Athanasius and other bishops condemned by the Eusebians are said to have been restored, against whom certain canons of Antioch [Col. 0072A] promulgated by those same men were alleged to have been directed, as we explained in part I, chapter 4, § 2. What is true of the synodal letter sent to Julius under the proper name of the Sardican synod, and never inscribed with the title of the Nicene synod, is not equally true of the Sardican canons. We have seen that these canons were cited by other pontiffs and by Innocent himself, in letter 3 to the Council of Toledo, not under the proper name of that synod but under the name of the Nicene canons; and shortly we shall prove that they were inscribed under the same name in the most ancient copies.

As for the second point, Innocent’s own formula—“We have said that obedience must be given only to those [canons] which were defined at Nicaea”—and a similar statement in his letter to Theophilus—“The Roman Church admits no other canon besides the Nicene one”—refer so plainly to the Nicene canons that, although they can conveniently include other canons inscribed under the name of the Council of Nicaea, they can be twisted to refer to other canons called by another proper name, even if they agree with the Nicene canons, only by the greatest force and contrary to the obvious sense of the words. [Col. 0072B] Unless it is first proved that Innocent cited and praised some other canons under their own proper name [LIX]—which has not yet been proved—no one can be persuaded of this interpretation and extension, since it is excessively forced. It must therefore be concluded that, when Innocent used the Sardican canons, he included them no less than Zosimus and Leo did under the name of the Nicene canons and truly regarded them as Nicene, just as in his letter to the Council of Toledo he included them among the praised Nicene regulations. Hence P. Constant himself had admitted as much in note k on the fifth letter of Damasus: “Innocent regarded the Sardican canons as Nicene” (ibid., col. 510).

13. Among some people, this practice of citing the Sardican canons under the name of the Nicene canons aroused suspicion of fraud—as though the Roman pontiffs sought, for the Sardican canons, which expressly assert the prerogative of the Roman See in appeals, an authority under the venerable name of the Council of Nicaea, revered by everyone. The Magdeburg Centuriators developed this accusation with particular vehemence against Zosimus, as though, through an enormous crime, impiety, and frenzied ambition, he had passed off these same canons as Nicene in the case of Apiarius. They say that Boniface stubbornly persisted in a wicked falsification of the Nicene decrees, and that Celestine persisted no less obstinately, although he knew perfectly well that the African council had received more accurate copies of the Nicene canons from Constantinople and Alexandria, and that the criminal fraud of the falsifiers of the canons had been exposed.

Some have tried to avert this suspicion of fraud by conjecturing that perhaps the Sardican canons, composed by nearly the same Fathers under the leadership of Hosius who had established the Nicene canons, were appended to the Nicene canons in the codices used by the Roman pontiffs as though they were an appendix to the Nicene canons, and were joined to them without any distinction, so that they were genuinely regarded as Nicene. Thus Cardinal Bellarmine, *De Romano Pontifice*, book II, chapter 25; Baronius, under the year 347; and others. Peter de Marca considered this explanation sufficiently reasonable [Col. 0072D], provided that it could be proved by some codex. Accordingly, he wrote in book VII of the *Concordia*, chapter 16, no. 1:

“Our writers say that this arose from the fact that at that time the Nicene and Sardican canons were written in the same volume, without distinction, under the title of the Nicene canons. A plausible conjecture, if it rested upon the authority of an ancient codex, which has not yet emerged from the darkness.”

Baluzius added the following note in the margin:

“Here it should be noted that, when this seventh book was written, the codex of Christopher Justellus was still unknown to de Marca.”

By these words Baluzius refers to what Peter de Marca later wrote in dissertation 2, *On the Ancient Collections of Canons*, included in his *Opuscula*. There, speaking in chapter 1, no. 3, about the very ancient manuscript collection of canons belonging to Christopher Justellus, de Marca says:

“In that collection the heading was: ‘Nicene Canons.’ Then followed a series of forty canons, distinguished by their respective numbers. The first twenty were the true and genuine canons of the Council of Nicaea; the remaining twenty [Col. 0073A] contained the canons of the Council of Sardica, twenty-one in number, compressed into two chapters, with no mention whatever of this Council of Sardica. There can be no doubt that those Sardican canons were added immediately after the edition to the earlier collection of the Nicene canons, with consecutive numbering, under the ancient title.”

And shortly afterward, in no. 4, he adds:

“Therefore Innocent, Zosimus, and Leo are free from every deceit in producing the Sardican canons as though they belonged to the Council of Nicaea, since they relied upon the authority of their archives and of the ancient collection.”

14. Nor are there lacking many other ancient codices, in fact very ancient ones, belonging to different collections and regions, which demonstrate both that the same conjunction and inscription of the Sardican canons with the Nicene canons was widely disseminated in the West, and that the good faith of those Roman pontiffs is much more clearly established. Long ago Alan Cope, in the first dialogue against the innovators, published in 1573, cited the Atrebatian codex, in which forty-seven Nicene canons were listed; he also quoted the titles of canons 30 and 34, from which it could be recognized that Sardican canons had been added to the Nicene canons. But he spoke so obscurely on this matter that no one noticed what the actual situation was.

The first person to discover and bring such a collection to light was Paschasius Quesnellus. He found Sardican canons joined to the Nicene canons in two manuscripts, the Thuaneus and the Oxford manuscript, and prefixed to the most ancient collection, which he believed to be a codex of the Roman Church. Subsequently, other copies were discovered, belonging not so much to that collection as to other collections, in which both sets of canons were joined in a continuous [LX] numerical series and bore the title of the Nicene canons.

Besides the Thuaneus and Oxford copies, the collection edited by Quesnellus and reprinted by us in this volume includes two Bellovacian copies and the Pithoean, cited by Pierre Pithou in his *Historical Synopsis of the Collectors of Canons*; the Atrebatian codex of Saint Vedastus, used by Alan Cope; the Ubertine, mentioned by P. Constant; and two codices of the Imperial Library at Vienna, numbers 39 and 41 [Col. 0073C], which were useful to us.

P. Constant, in note d on the fifteenth letter of Zosimus, also mentions a very ancient codex of another collection, formerly Fossatensis and now Colbertinus, in which the same Sardican canons are joined to the Nicene canons and inscribed under the name of the Nicene canons.

In the preface, no. 77, page 71, he praises another collection contained in another very ancient Colbertine manuscript, number 1868. This manuscript has Sardican canons bearing the inscription “Nicene Canon”—to which a later scribe added, in a second revision, “or Sardican”—“which is not found in the Greek”; and the canons end with the following clause:

“Here end the statutes of the Nicene faith, at the metropolis of Bithynia, when Paulinus and Julian were consuls (that is, in the year 325), on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July.”

He testifies that this codex was used by the Gallican Church.

15. We have found three other outstanding collections that present the canons of both synods under the same designation, as Nicene. The first is in manuscript Vat. Reginae 1997 [Col. 0073D]. We shall show in chapter 4 that this collection is the oldest of all and Italian. It presents the Nicene canons in an ancient and hitherto unknown Latin translation, to be published in this volume, and places the Sardican canons after them without any distinction. It distributes both sets into forty-six chapters, omitting from the Nicene canons the canon concerning the prohibition against kneeling on Sundays and during the Paschal season.

The following title is prefixed:

“Here begin the chapters of the Council of Nicaea.”

After canon forty-six, which is the final Sardican canon, the following clause is read:

“Here end the decrees of the council.”

Immediately afterward follow the subscriptions and the catalogue of the Nicene Fathers.

A second collection exists in manuscript 58 of the chapter of Verona. It contains the Isidorian version of the Greek canons. It joins the Nicene canons of that version to the Sardican canons under the title:

“Here begin the canons of the Church, or the statutes of the Council of Nicaea.”

The Sardican canons, which are placed after the Nicene canons without any distinction, are followed by this clause:

“Here end the decrees of the Council of Nicaea” [Col. 0074A].

Then the Nicene Creed is copied, together with the catalogue of the Nicene Fathers.

A third collection is found in manuscript Palat. 574, which we discovered to be entirely similar to the Morbacian manuscript cited by P. Constant in the preface to the letters of the Roman pontiffs, no. 77. It contains a purely Gallican collection of canons; for, besides the joined Nicene and Sardican canons and a few apostolic constitutions, only Gallican synods are copied in these manuscripts.

It presents the Nicene canons from Rufinus’s abridgment, and then the complete Sardican canon 13, with the following inscription, which indicates that it was excerpted from an older collection in which the Sardican canons, placed after the Nicene canons, were regarded as Nicene:

“Here begins the chapter concerning the above-written canons, that is, the Nicene canons of the 318 bishops. Hosius the bishop said: ‘I also consider it necessary that you examine with the greatest care whether perhaps a rich man or a legal scholar from the forum …’”

—and the remaining words of that canon. See also what we shall note concerning another codex, number 59 of the chapter of Verona, in part IV, chapter 4, no. 11.

16. In the Sangermanian manuscript mentioned by P. Constant in the place cited, there is a compilation composed from the decrees of councils, Roman pontiffs, and Fathers, and produced among the Irish. Since the Sardican canons consistently bear the name of the Nicene canons, this compilation derives from some collection used among the Irish that joined the Nicene and Sardican canons.

Jacques Petit published, after Theodore of Canterbury’s *Penitential*, a considerable portion of the Herovallian collection, about which we shall say more in part IV, chapter 7. This collection, which is Gallican and was compiled in the eighth century, cites the Sardican canons under the name of the Nicene canons. Therefore the older codex from which this compiler copied the same canons must have prefixed the same inscription to the Sardican canons.

Moreover, several annotations are found in certain collections that identify the Sardican canons as Nicene. P. Hardouin mentions a codex of what he calls the Dionysian collection, more than eight hundred years old, preserved in the library of the Paris College of the Society of Jesus [Col. 0074C]. This codex places the following heading before the Sardican canons [LXI]:

“Nicene or Sardican Canon, which is not found in the Greek.”

(*Councils*, vol. II, col. 671, note i). It is entirely the same as the heading in Colbertine codex 1868, which we cited shortly before from P. Constant.

He also cites another codex of the Isidorian collection preserved in the same library of the Society of Jesus, in which the same canons bear this title:

“Here begin the twenty headings of the Council of Nicaea of bishops, which are not found in the Greek but are found only in the Latin.”

(Ibid., col. 679, note i.)

Those who prefixed such a title to the Sardican canons certainly attributed these canons to the Council of Nicaea because they had found them in other, older copies placed after the Nicene canons and inscribed under the same name of the Nicene canons.

In the table of councils prefixed to the Herovallian codex cited above, in Petit, page 265, we read:

“Nicene Canons of twenty bishops. This canon is not found among the Greeks, and by some is called Sardican.”

By this title, the author of the table and of the Herovallian collection calls the Sardican canons Nicene, because, seeing them joined to the Nicene canons and marked with the same heading in the Gallican codices that he used, he believed them genuinely to be Nicene. But when, in other codices presenting the version of the Greek synods—such as the codices of Dionysius—he found them separated from the Nicene canons and prefixed with the title “Sardican,” he affirmed that among the Greeks, that is, in the versions of the Nicene canons from the Greek, they were not found, and that by some they were called Sardican.

17. The edition of Dionysius published by Justellus appends the following subscription formula after the Sardican canons:

“And all the bishops subscribed as follows: I, that bishop of that city and of that province, BELIEVE THUS, just as it is written above.”

A similar formula is also read in the edition of the Councils, vol. II, col. 680.

Nor should it be thought that this formula, which is absent from the manuscripts of the Dionysio-Hadriana collection [Col. 0075A], was not added by Dionysius himself. It is described in exactly the same words in two manuscript codices that represent the pure collection of Dionysius, namely Vat. 5845 and Vat. Palat. 577. The latter, as will be said in part III, chapter 1, represents the first work of Dionysius with respect to the collection of canons alone.

In the manuscripts of the Dionysio-Hadriana collection, this formula was removed because the subscriptions of the Sardican Fathers, taken from another source, were substituted for it; these subscriptions should not be attributed to Dionysius, as will be clear from what is said in part I, chapter 7, no. 1.

Now the formula “I, that bishop of that city and of that province” indicates a person who, after the Sardican canons, found bishops listed with the names of their cities and provinces, as occurs in the subscriptions and catalogue of the Nicene Fathers. To avoid having to copy all their names, he composed one general subscription formula.

The word “believe,” however, inserted into the same formula, belongs properly to the Nicene [Col. 0075B] canons, which have the Creed appended to them. It cannot apply to the Sardican canons alone, since they establish nothing concerning the faith, unless they are placed after and attached to the Nicene canons and Creed, as could be seen in manuscript Vat. Reginae 1997. In that manuscript the Sardican canons are joined together with the Nicene canons and Creed, and the subscriptions and catalogue of the Nicene Fathers are placed after the final Sardican canon as follows:

“Hosius, bishop of the city of Corduba: I BELIEVE THUS. Victor and Vincentius, priests of the city of Rome, have subscribed on behalf of the venerable man, our pope and bishop: BELIEVING THUS, JUST AS IT IS WRITTEN ABOVE,” and so forth.

Thus the annotator of Dionysius’s formula, who did not render the Sardican canons from the Greek but inserted them from Latin copies circulated at Rome, used some copy in which either the Sardican canons were joined to the Nicene canons and received the proper subscriptions of the Nicene Fathers, or—if, as seems more probable, they were separated from the Nicene canons—they had already been excerpted from some older codex in which they had been joined to those same Nicene canons in the Roman manner [Col. 0075C].

18. The author of the poems that we shall place after this paragraph from codex 55 of the chapter of Verona also seems to have seen some similar copy. For when this author wrote that the Council of Nicaea was held under Pope Julius, he could not have taken such an opinion from Sozomen, who had not yet been translated into Latin, and from whom Bede (*On the Times*, book II, p. 116) and Freculphus (*Chronicle*, final chapter, *Library of the Fathers*, vol. XIV) later received it. It can therefore be understood that he wrote this on his own for no other reason than that he found the Sardican canons joined to the Nicene canons and inscribed under the name of the Nicene canons in some codex of canons, in which Pope Julius is mentioned [LXII].

We do not press the same argument from Sozomen, since the Roman editors of the Councils reasonably judge that his text has been corrupted by a faulty reading of a single Greek word (*Councils*, vol. II, col. 114, e).

Nor should a special observation concerning Ferrandus the deacon be omitted. In the *Breviary* he cites the final Nicene canon, concerning the prohibition against kneeling, as the first Sardican canon (*Breviary*, no. 214). He then cites the first Sardican canon as the second, the second as the third, and so on. Why is this so? Is it not clearly indicated that the Nicene and Sardican canons had been collected together in some ancient codex, perhaps containing the Isidorian version—for Ferrandus used the Isidorian version—and that when they were later separated, either by Ferrandus himself or by someone else, the final Nicene canon was mistakenly attributed to the Sardican canons? This erroneous division by Ferrandus therefore confirms the older conjunction of these same canons.

19. These copies from such different collections and regions prove that the union of the Sardican canons with the Nicene canons was ancient among the Latins and widely disseminated, so that it was not peculiar to the Roman Church alone. None of the versions of the Nicene canons in which we find the Sardican canons appended is the version used by the ancient Roman pontiffs, as will plainly appear in the following chapter. Consequently, the true Roman collection, which joined the Nicene and Sardican canons in the same manner, has not come down to us; and all the collections mentioned above that join the Nicene and Sardican canons belong to other Latin Churches.

The codex Vat. Reginae 1997 belonged to the Church of Theate. Codex 58 of the chapter of Verona, which joins the Isidorian version of the Nicene canons to the Sardican canons, proves that this conjunction was accepted at least in certain places where the Isidorian version had been received. Indeed, this very ancient copy seems to indicate that, at an earlier time, the Isidorian version received the Sardican canons joined to the Nicene canons, together with the subscriptions and catalogue of the Nicene Fathers; and that only later, when the Sardican canons were separated from that version, the subscriptions of the Sardican Fathers were substituted for the Nicene subscriptions. These had been taken from the Sardican synodal letter [Col. 0076B] to Julius, which are read in the commonly circulated Isidorian text.

The Quesnellian collection, which represents a version of the Nicene canons that is Isidorian at its root, but with the division of the aforementioned codex Vat. Reginae and with nearly all its titles, as well as with the same reading of the Nicene canon concerning the primacy of the Roman Church, was compiled in Gaul, as we shall prove in its proper place. Therefore the author of that collection found the Nicene canons joined to the Sardican canons in Gallican codices.

The codex Vat. Palat. 574 and the similar Morbacian codex belonged to the Gallican Church, as did the Fossatensian and Herovallian collections, from which we confirmed the same union. The collection cited by Constant from the Sangermanian codex proves that the same arrangement was accepted among the Irish.

If the codices of other ancient Churches still existed, the same conclusion, as we believe, would be apparent with respect to other Latin Churches as well. In the meantime, these many ancient testimonies both declare that the conjunction of the aforementioned canons was extremely ancient and received almost everywhere among the Latins, and they also remove every suspicion of fraud from the ancient Roman pontiffs, since, on the basis of manuscripts widely circulated in the Latin Church, they cited the Sardican canons as Nicene [Col. 0076C].

20. Moreover, it can sufficiently be gathered from the testimony of the Council of Constantinople of the year 382, which we quoted in part I, chapter 6, no. 14, and explained in the words of P. Hardouin and P. Constant, that certain Greek codices also existed within the Eastern Church itself that presented the Sardican canons in the same manner as Nicene. See what we wrote there; there is no need to repeat what has already been said.

This Eastern example contributes considerably both to demonstrating the antiquity of the conjunction of these canons and to defending the practice of the Roman pontiffs and removing every suspicion of deceit.

We shall add here another testimony from the elder Theodore Prodromus, who preceded Photius and was the most ancient of all the Greek interpreters of the canons. Nicetas of Paphlagonia, Aristenus, Balsamon, Harmenopulus, Blastares, Nicephorus [Col. 0076D] Blemmydes, and other eminent Greeks commend him in the highest terms. If desired, compare Fabricius, *Greek Library*, vol. XI, book VI, chapter 1, no. 16.

Nicholas Comnenus Papadopoulos examined this Theodore’s unpublished work, *περὶ Ἑρμηνείας*—“On the Interpretation of the Canons”—written more than nine hundred years ago, and repeatedly cites more extensive testimonies from it [LXIII] in his *Mystagogical Preliminary Instructions*. He also gives the following testimony concerning him in *Responses*, 6, § 6, no. 14, page 364:

“Prodromus lists the Sardican canons under the title of the Nicene canons, as though the Nicene and Sardican synods were one and the same.”

These words seem to indicate that Theodore Prodromus cited the Sardican canons as Nicene, just as the Fathers of the Council of Constantinople once did. If this is so, then in the time of Theodore—that is, before the schism of Photius—there existed among the Greeks some Greek codex in which the Sardican canons were appended to the Nicene canons and prefixed with the title of the Nicene canons, as we have found in several Latin codices.

21. To some people it seems surprising that, after the dispute between Zosimus and the Africans, through which it ought to have been discovered that the Sardican canons were not Nicene, Saint Leo should still have cited the same canons under the title of the Nicene canons and inserted them into letter 44 to the Emperor Theodosius, in the final chapter.

But the Africans seem to have established only that the canons cited in Zosimus’s memorandum had not been found among the Nicene canons in those Latin and Greek copies that, on this occasion, had been consulted in Africa, Alexandria, Antioch, and Constantinople. Indeed, they had not been found in any other synod of the Fathers either, since they had also compared the codices of other synods, as they wrote in the letter to Celestine.

Just as, in excluding these same canons from every other synod, including one that might be called Sardican, it is clear that the Africans either suffered from a shortage of codices or were less careful in examining the synodal codices, so it should not be surprising if the Romans, supported by the ancient copies of their own and other Churches in which these same canons were presented as Nicene, did not think they should abandon their established practice of citing these canons as Nicene [Col. 0077B].

Thus, since in Saint Leo’s age an ancient formula and practice, confirmed by so many codices, remained in force, he used it without any suspicion of falsehood when writing to that emperor. He had no interest in deceiving the emperor by a fabricated citation, particularly not at considerable risk to himself.

Indeed, the good faith of the Latins of this and earlier periods in citing the Sardican canons under the name of the Nicene canons seems to us so fully established that we believe they were then entirely unaware that these canons had been enacted at the Council of Sardica, and believed them to have been established at Nicaea.

For when so serious a dispute had been raised by the Africans against the Romans over these same canons, which the Romans had produced as Nicene in the affair of Apiarius, if the Romans had known from some codex that the canons had been enacted at Sardica, an easy way of settling the dispute would have been available: they could have pointed out to the Africans the true council that had established those canons. Nor could there have been any doubt that the Africans would accept that council, to which their ancestors had granted authority, especially since they had declared themselves ready to accept the same canons if they found them enacted in a council of Catholic Fathers.

See on this subject the *Observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 5*, part I, chapter 6, no. 20, vol. II, col. 955.

For this reason, then, the Roman pontiffs did not pursue this readily available course: they knew these canons from manuscript copies solely under the name of the Nicene canons and were completely unaware that they had been published at Sardica.

22. A few preliminary remarks must now be made concerning the verses that we have decided to place after this paragraph. They have been preserved for us in the very ancient manuscript Verona 55 and present a kind of dedicatory letter by which the book—perhaps belonging to some ancient collection of canons—was offered by an anonymous author to a Caesar named Dalmatianus.

Since the script of these verses differs from the script of the entire codex, this dedication does not belong to the collection contained in the codex but was transferred here from another unknown copy.

The Marquis Scipio Maffei, who published only the first four verses in the appendix to his *Theological History*, page 77, judged that the Caesar Dalmatianus was Dalmatianus, son of another Dalmatianus and grandson of Constantine, who was proclaimed Caesar in the year 335. But since the Council of Chalcedon is mentioned in the subsequent verses, another Caesar, much later, must be sought.

We have found no one named Dalmatianus. We therefore merely suspect that this name refers to the emperor Julius Nepos, who may have been called Dalmatianus because he was Dalmatian by birth. In the year 475, when he left Ravenna, he withdrew to Dalmatia, where he died in 480. His period indeed fits the time after the Council of Chalcedon.

Other Caesars of approximately this period, who soon afterward disappeared entirely, have nothing that corresponds to the designation Dalmatianus. [LXIV] Nor should a later period be considered, since the author praises only three ecumenical synods—Nicaea, Ephesus, and Chalcedon—which had been received by the Latins in the fifth century, as is clear from what we established more fully in the preceding paragraph.

Here, then, are the verses themselves. Although very inelegant and rough, they nevertheless contain certain useful information.

Dalmatianus, Caesar, whom the earth honors with enduring triumph,  
while all things fear your rule.

With sacred ears hear this man,  
and with blessed eyes behold him  
bearing a book containing  
the gravest deeds.

Let this be your vow: perpetual praise,  
sacred authority,  
while you uphold  
the sacred rights of the holy Church.

By plowing its furrows  
with the plowshare of Augustus,  
you will be a greater Constantine  
in the empire.

But whether or when you chose  
to embrace the sacred synods  
lay within your own discretion.

The times that have flowed backward  
from days now past  
testify that only those holy men  
held these synods.

The Roman pope himself hastened to them  
and sent his own representatives, observing their sacred commands.

This is proclaimed by Nicaea,  
at which Constantine shone forth,  
together with the holy Pope Julius.

[Col. 0078B]

Here Arius fell,  
while so great a teacher held the scales;  
from this council  
the holy faith drew its origin in love.

Marcian, its founder, likewise bears witness to Chalcedon,  
which follows this,  
as he struck Eutyches’ lips.

Nor does Ephesus, shining with the trophy  
of the holy Theodosius, keep silent:  
it tramples upon  
the doctrines of Nestorius.

[The surviving text contains a lacuna.]

Thereafter the Roman laws  
spread this throughout the world,  
extended everywhere,  
sacred under both bodies of law.

[The surviving text contains a lacuna.]

All the holy synods proclaim this  
through their doctrines:  
it is fitting that you preserve  
their rite.

You are no lesser Augustus;  
your authority is not less,  
nor is your imperial crown  
unlike his.

Twice six talents are not absent from you,  
balanced for you;  
whether to will or to be able  
is proper to another.

From this, may the rejoicing people of God  
feel increase,  
and may the holy faith  
flourish in your time.

Strengthened by these blessings  
under your governance, Caesar,  
may all the ages grant you  
perpetual song.

§ 4. Whether the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs were once brought together and published in a single codex together with the Nicene and Sardican canons

[Col. 0078C]

23. Quesnellus maintains, in dissertation 12, chapter 2, that in ancient times a codex was published with public authority that contained, besides the Nicene and Sardican canons, the decrees of the Roman pontiffs as well.

To prove this, he quotes Leo’s words from letter 4 to the bishops of Campania, Picenum, and Tuscia, chapter 5. In that letter Leo commands them to observe not only the decrees of Innocent but also those of all his predecessors.

“Lest anything,” says the holy pontiff, “be thought to have been perhaps omitted by us, we command that all the decretal constitutions both of blessed memory Innocent and of all our predecessors, which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the discipline of the canons, be so carefully observed by your affection that, if anyone should transgress them, he may know that forgiveness will henceforth be denied him.”

(*Tom.* I, col. 616.)

Quesnellus then adds:

“When Leo wrote this, he was turning the eyes of his mind toward those decrees of Innocent that are contained in the letter to Victricius of Rouen and in the other letter to the bishops of Macedonia [LXV], in which the ordination of digamists is condemned. But how could such decretal constitutions have been so well known in Italy, although they had been sent to the more remote parts of Gaul and to Macedonia, that they could be said to have been promulgated there, and that the people there were required to obey them, unless they had been inserted into a public and accepted codex?”

On this reasoning, since Leo commands that all the decretal constitutions both of Innocent and of all his predecessors be observed, a codex would have to be posited that contained all of them. But no such codex existed. For the codex published by Quesnellus himself and presented by him as a codex of the Roman Church does not contain everything; it lacks many pontifical decrees, including some of the more celebrated ones, as will be said elsewhere.

24. Yet all the decretal letters of Innocent and his predecessors could sufficiently be called promulgated because, although at first addressed to the bishops of certain provinces, [Note: [Col. 0079D] See note 11 below in dissertation 12.] they were subsequently communicated to other bishops and dispersed throughout the world. When pontiffs sent decrees to a particular bishop that they wanted to be useful to everyone, they ordinarily instructed him to communicate them by letter to one bishop after another.

Thus, when Siricius sent the book of *Rules* to Himerius of Tarragona, he ordered him to send these matters, which had been established by us in a salutary ordinance, not only to the bishops of his own province but also, he says,

“to all the Carthaginians and Baeticans, Lusitanians and Galicians, and even to those who border you on every side in neighboring provinces, under the transmission of your letters.”

Similarly, Zosimus wrote in his letter to Hesychius of Salona:

“Lest we diminish anything from the merits of your affection, we have directed the written decisions especially to you, so that they may come to the knowledge of all our brothers and fellow bishops—not only those who are in that province, but also those who are joined to the neighboring provinces of your affection.”

There are many similar testimonies from Leo in which he gives the same instructions. Among others, in letter 159 to Nicetas of Aquileia, chapter 7, he says:

“You shall cause this letter of ours, which we have sent in response to the consultation of your fraternity, to reach all your brother bishops and fellow provincials, so that the authority delivered may be beneficial through the observance of all.”

We believe that this was done with most of the decretal letters of the Apostolic See, just as Innocent reported concerning the letter of Siricius in his letter to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, no. 4:

“That form of ecclesiastical life and discipline traveled through the provinces from Bishop Siricius.”

This also explains why certain pontifical letters, initially delivered to particular bishops or provinces, were later communicated to bishops of other provinces and thus sent throughout all the provinces. In some manuscripts, this process gave rise to an additional phrase in their headings: “and to all the provinces.”

Thus Leo’s fourth letter is inscribed not only “to all the bishops throughout Campania, Picenum, and Tuscia,” to whom it seems initially to have been given, but also “and to all the provinces” [Col. 0079C].

Similarly, Siricius’s letter read at the Teleptine—or, more accurately, Zellensian—synod seems originally to have been directed only to the suburbicarian bishops. But it gradually came to the knowledge of the bishops of other provinces and was transmitted to the Africans with the substituted inscription found in the collection published in this volume, chapter 62:

“To the dearest brothers and fellow bishops throughout Africa, Siricius.”

See what we shall note concerning this same letter.

The same is true of Gelasius’s letter to the bishops throughout Lucania, Bruttium, and Sicily, which in this collection and in other ancient copies bears the inscription:

“To all the dearest brothers, the bishops, Gelasius.”

Is this promulgation throughout the provinces not sufficient?

There is therefore no need to posit a collection that, in addition to the Nicene and Sardican canons joined together, also contained all the pontifical constitutions and promulgated them with the authority of the Roman See. When Roman pontiffs occasionally cited these constitutions, they did not bring them forth from some public codex—of which no mention is found anywhere—but from the apostolic archives, or they appealed to the authority of those archives, as P. Constant proves at length in the preface to volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, no. 44.

Let it therefore stand that no codex of decretals was once published by the Roman Church, and that there was no need for such a codex in order for these constitutions to be promulgated and to possess authority among the Churches.

[LXVI] **CHAPTER II. On the ancient versions of the canons of the Greek synods composed before Dionysius’s work**

### § 1. The special Latin versions of the Nicene canons formerly used by the Latin Churches and distinct from the interpretations of the complete Greek book of canons. Which portions of the Council of Nicaea survive from the ancient version received by the Roman and African Churches. The complete version of the canons of that council preserved for us in the Vatican Regina manuscript. Abbreviations of the same canons composed by Rufinus and used by the Gallicans.

[Col. 0079D]

[Col. 0080A] **1.** For a long time in the Latin Church only the Nicene and Sardican canons possessed authority, as we showed in the preceding chapter. Since the Latin original of the Sardican canons had already been published in that Church, only an interpretation of the Nicene canons was necessary from the beginning. The particular versions of these canons, therefore, which were received among the Latins, must first be recalled; afterward we shall deal more fully with those ancient interpretations which, together with the Greek canons of the other synods, rendered the Nicene canons into Latin.

**2.** The Roman Church, which always followed the Council of Nicaea and its constitutions with the greatest reverence, possessed a very ancient version of these canons. This, however, has not come down to us. [Col. 0080B] We shall prove in our observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 12, chapter 1, no. 2, that the version inserted in the Quesnellian collection is not Roman. At first, however, we suspected that the interpretation of the Nicene canons joined to the Sardican canons—the version that we shall publish in this volume from Vatican Regina 1997, formerly belonging to the Church of Theate—was the one received by the Roman Church and thereafter transferred for the use of the other neighboring Churches as well.

But we possess two portions of the Council of Nicaea from that very ancient version which the Roman Church used: namely, the Creed, which is read in St. Leo, inserted into Letter 165, and the canon concerning the Cathari, which Innocent I quotes in his letter to Rufus and the other Macedonians, chapter 5, no. 10. Both, however, differ most plainly from the version of the aforesaid Vatican Regina manuscript.

Furthermore, when Felix III, in Letter 7 to the bishops established throughout various provinces, cites three Nicene canons for his own purpose, their wording—taken, as is plausible, from the Roman interpretation—[Col. 0080C] differs very greatly from the version of the aforesaid manuscript. Among other things, he quotes the following from canon 11:

> “If, however, they sincerely repent, let them be among the hearers for three years, and for seven years let them submit among the penitents to the hands of the priests; but for two years let them in no way be permitted to offer the oblations, but only join the people (or, according to another reading, the secular persons) in prayer.”

This canon is read in another division in the Vatican Regina version, as chapter 18, and is expressed in such different words that it plainly represents another interpretation.

**3.** We find the Nicene Creed from that same version received at Rome, which is read in Leo, also in St. Hilary’s *On the Synods*, no. 84, and in the Second Fragment; in Lucifer of Cagliari’s *On Not Pardoning Those Who Sin against God*; and also among the Africans, in the *Breviary of Hippo*, inserted in the collection to be published in this volume, chapter 2, col. 88; and in the Council of Carthage of 419, as is evident from the codex of the African Church (*T. II Conc.*, col. 1260b), and from the Hispanic and Isidorian collections in the Sixth Council of Carthage [Col. 0080D] (*T. III Conc.*, col. 448a).

At the Synod of Carthage in 525, this same version of the Creed is presented in volume V of the Councils, col. 778; but owing to an evidently corrupt reading of the manuscript, it is wrongly said to be the version that Bishop Atticus of the Church of Constantinople sent to Africa through the presbyter Innocent. For this version had already been inserted into the canons of the earlier Council of Hippo in 393, repeated at the Council of Carthage in 397, and finally repeated in another Council of Carthage in 419, before Innocent the presbyter—or rather Marcellus the subdeacon, sent as the African legate—was sent to Atticus of Constantinople.

Another interpretation of the Creed, written beneath the name of Atticus in the codex of the African Church, canon 137 (*T. II Conc.*, col. 1364), is indeed different. This version, composed by the Constantinopolitan interpreters together with [Col. 0081A] the version of the Nicene canons preserved in the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, was sent by Atticus to Africa.

Moreover, the version of the Nicene Creed received by the Roman Church, common to several ancient writers, seems to indicate that the same version was likewise their interpretation of the Nicene canons—especially among the Africans, who possessed copies of the faith and statutes of the Council of Nicaea which, as the Fathers of the Council of Carthage in 419 say, “were brought to our council by the bishop of blessed memory . . . Caecilianus” (*T. III Conc.*, col. 447).

Thus a substantial suspicion arises that, in the Creed no less than in the Nicene canons, the ancient Roman and African versions were the same: namely, that which both the papal legate brought to Rome from the Council of Nicaea and Caecilianus brought to Africa.

**4.** This conjecture seems to be opposed by Ferrandus, deacon of the Church of Carthage. For although in the other Greek canons he used the Isidorian interpretation, in the Nicene canons alone he seems to have abandoned it [Col. 0081B] in order to follow the ancient version of those canons preserved in African codices and famous in Africa.

Ferrandus, in his *Abbreviation*, presents the Nicene canon concerning the Cathari in such a way as to disclose a version different from the one used by Innocent I. For that pontiff, in his letter to Rufus and the Macedonians, no. 13, quotes the canon as follows:

> “Concerning those who call themselves Cathari, that is, pure, and who sometimes come to the Catholic Church, it has pleased the holy and great synod that, after receiving the laying on of hands, they should remain in the clergy.”

With Ferrandus, however, the same canon is expressed from the African version as follows, no. 172:

> “That those who are called Cathari, when they approach the Church, if they have been ordained, should remain in the clergy.”

These are not Ferrandus’s actual words of the version, but its summary. Nevertheless, the difference between the versions is sufficiently indicated by the sense: in Innocent, the laying on of hands is meant, whereas in Ferrandus the ordination previously received is declared.

Although, therefore, the interpretation of the Nicene Creed [Col. 0081C] among the Romans and Africans was the same, the same conclusion cannot apparently be drawn concerning the canons. Yet since the African codices of the canons did not contain only one ancient interpretation of the Nicene canons—the version brought by Caecilianus—but after the Council of Carthage in 419 another version of Philo and Evaristus was inserted, which the Fathers of that council had requested from Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, and which he sent to Africa, Ferrandus may be thought to have used this version. Both its abbreviation and that version express the canon concerning the Cathari in the same sense.

For the version of Philo and Evaristus reads:

> “If the Cathari should ever come to the Catholic Church, it has pleased the holy and great synod that, being already ordained, they should remain in the clergy,”

just as Ferrandus has, “if they have been ordained.”

The difficulty, therefore, which might have been raised from Ferrandus having been removed, the presumption returns that the ancient version of the Council of Nicaea brought by Caecilianus to Africa was the same in the canons as in the Creed, and the same as that which the Roman Church had received from the beginning. [Col. 0081D]

**5.** As for this ancient Roman version, apart from the Creed and the canon concerning the Cathari, Boniface I, in his letter to Hilary of Narbonne, professes to quote the wording of another Nicene canon:

> “No one,” he says, “can be unaware of the constitution of the Council of Nicaea, which commands as follows, so that we may set down the very words: In each province each metropolitan must have his own jurisdiction, and no one must have two provinces subject to him.”

Yet among the Nicene canons, neither in the Greek nor in any version, can one find the very words described by Boniface, or anything close to them. Indeed, we believe that we sufficiently proved in our observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 5, part II, chapter 6, no. 6 (*T. II*, col. 1043), that none of the ancient pontiffs possessed an interpretation which represented this as having been commanded by the Nicene Fathers. There we explained what may be conjectured on the matter.

Another fragment of the old Roman version may be seen in the sixth Nicene canon, which Paschasinus, legate of the Apostolic See, recited in the sixteenth session of the Council of Chalcedon. This canon not only has the distinctive opening, “The Roman Church has always [Col. 0082A] held the primacy,” and mentions Egypt alone, not Libya and Pentapolis, [LXVIII] but also contains two canons—the sixth and seventh—joined together.

Whether Paschasinus read this canon from a Roman codex or rather from that of his own Church of Lilybaeum is not clear from the context, since he went to the council not from the city of Rome but from his own see. If what we conjectured earlier is true—that the ancient version of the Roman Church was the same as the African version—then, since this same sixth canon, inserted from the ancient interpretation received by the Africans in the Council of Carthage in 525, differs from the version that Paschasinus produced at Chalcedon, Paschasinus’s version cannot be believed or asserted to be Roman. He may therefore have recited that canon from a codex of Lilybaeum.

The opening, “The Roman Church has always [Col. 0082B] held the primacy,” is indeed found in the same form in Vatican Regina 1997, formerly belonging to the Church of Theate, as well as in the codices of the Quesnellian collection and in other codices of other collections, which we shall mention in note 32 on chapter 1 of the book of canons to be published in this volume.

The mention of Egypt alone, with Libya and Pentapolis omitted, appears in the aforesaid Vatican Regina manuscript as it is presented by Paschasinus, but does not at all agree with the other collections mentioned. Yet, apart from the first part of the canon, the words quoted by Paschasinus differ in the rest from the version of the aforesaid codex, as does the number of the canon: in Paschasinus it is the sixth, whereas in that codex it is the eleventh. Consequently, the version of the two codices cannot be regarded as altogether identical.

**6.** It has now become clear from what has been discussed which portions or remains of the Nicene canons survive from the ancient Roman or African version. A few words must now be said about complete and older interpretations of those canons.

The first [Col. 0082C] place belongs to the version contained in the aforesaid Vatican Regina codex, to which the Sardican canons are attached in continuous numerical sequence. Since this version differs both in wording and in the division of the canons from all other known ancient interpretations, there seems to be no doubt that its origin must be assigned to a much earlier period.
