Since it was inserted into a very ancient Italian collection which belonged to the suburbicarian Church of Theate, it may be called Italian. We shall bring it to light in this volume, hitherto unpublished, after the Prisca version; more will be said about it there.

**7.** Another somewhat later interpretation of the same canons, composed by Philo and Evaristus of Constantinople and received by the African bishops from Atticus of Constantinople, has been preserved for us as regards the Creed in Dionysius, canon 137 of the African codex, and as regards the canons in the Hispanic collection and thereafter in the Isidorian collection, as we noted earlier. [Col. 0082D]

We find the Creed together with the canons of this version only in Vatican Palatine 577.

**8.** We have also encountered an ancient and unknown version of the same canons in manuscript codex 55 of the chapter of Verona, written in majuscule letters. It likewise offers an unpublished interpretation of the Sardican canons from a fuller Greek original than the one that has been edited, as well as another version of the Chalcedonian canons. Since these versions appeared worthy of publication, they will be inserted in this volume.

**9.** A particular practice of the Gallican Church deserves special mention. In place of the Nicene canons, it sometimes used the abbreviations of those canons presented by Rufinus in Book X of his *Ecclesiastical History*. This is clear from what is called the Second Council of Arles, as well as from the excerpts of the canons collected by Caesarius of Arles in the case of Contumeliosus of Riez, as Quesnellus correctly observed in Dissertation 16, to be inserted in this volume, no. 15. [Col. 0083A]

Two codices also, the Morbacensis and Vatican Palatine 754, which contain a pure and very ancient Gallican collection, present the same Nicene canons taken from Rufinus and joined to the Sardican canons.

Since, however, in the Gallican Council of Valence in 374 the Nicene constitutions are cited in canon 3, at a time when Rufinus’s abbreviations had not yet appeared, an older version of the Nicene canons existed among the Gauls. What that version was cannot be inferred from the wording of that council.

[LXIX] ### § 2. On the version of the entire Greek book of canons commonly called Isidorian

**10.** Since we are about to discuss the ancient Latin interpretations of all the canons of the synods contained in the Greek [Col. 0083B] codices, we think it should first be stated that these interpretations were composed for private study and use. None of them was received by any Latin Church before the sixth century, except perhaps in the case of the Nicene canons, which alone among the Greek canons we have shown to have retained authority for a longer period among the Latin Churches. We say “perhaps,” because although particular versions of the Nicene canons were in use, as we explained in the preceding section, it is uncertain, for lack of evidence, whether any of the versions mentioned, arranged before the sixth century, was used in the Nicene canons by any Latin Church.

**11.** There are three ancient versions of the entire Greek book of canons: the Isidorian, the Prisca, and the Dionysian. We must now discuss the first two, which were written before the sixth century; we shall treat the third in Part III, chapter 1, where the collection of Dionysius Exiguus will be explained.

Let us begin with the Isidorian, which appears to be older than the Prisca. It was circulated through the collection of Isidore, from whom it received its name; Isidore himself transcribed it from the older Hispanic collection. Nor should the compiler of the Hispanic collection be regarded as the author of this version. For it is much earlier, as will become clear from what [Col. 0083C] follows.

It presents in Latin the canons of Nicaea, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, and Gangra, to which the Latin original of the Sardican canons is appended in the manuscript collections of the Hispanic and Isidorian traditions; then the canons of Antioch, Laodicea, Constantinople, and Chalcedon.

**12.** Until now, only the codices of the aforementioned collections containing this version were known. We, however, discovered a very ancient one in the library of the chapter of Verona, marked number 58. It belongs to neither collection and also presents an older collection composed around the middle of the sixth century.

This codex itself may perhaps be older than the Hispanic collection. It contains the pure Isidorian version—we shall use this more familiar and widespread name for purposes of distinction—but since it is mutilated at the end, its final surviving folio ends at canon 16 of Laodicea.

In this pure Isidorian version, whose more reliable readings we supplied in the notes to the book of canons, two features especially deserve attention: [Col. 0083D]

1. The Sardican canons are joined to the Nicene canons.

2. Although the canons of all the synods are sufficiently distinct, they lack titles and numbers—signs of greater antiquity.

**13.** This interpretation of the Greek canons is so ancient that it may be questioned whether it was all assembled at one time, or whether at first only the canons of the earlier Greek synods—which seem to have been the first ones brought into the Greek book—were translated into Latin (see Part I, chapter 2), and afterward, as the Greek collection was enlarged with the canons of other synods, different interpreters successively added other canons rendered into Latin to the same version.

Among other things, the old Lucano-Colbertine collection, which we shall discuss in chapter 6, gave rise to this doubt. Since it supplies from the Isidorian version only the Nicene, Ancyrean, Neocaesarean, and Gangran canons, while it takes the remaining canons from the Prisca, [Col. 0084A] the compiler seems to have found only those canons in his copy of the Isidorian version—because those alone had been translated into Latin by the first interpreter.

We leave the value of this conjecture to the judgment of others. Certainly, since the Laodicean canons are not included in that collection, they were plainly not found by its author either in the codices of the Isidorian or in those of the Prisca version that he used. Just as they are thus lacking in the Prisca, because they were neither translated by its first author nor added to it later, so they are not lacking in the Isidorian, because—although absent at first—they were added to it by later efforts.

Since the deacon Ferrandus, whom we shall see using the Isidorian version, omits the Chalcedonian canons, his Isidorian codex evidently lacked them. The author of the Quesnellian collection appears to have possessed a similar codex. Although he received all the canons of the other Greek synods from the Isidorian version, [LXX] he did not find the Chalcedonian canons there and copied them from the Prisca. These canons, therefore, just as they were added later to the Greek body of canons, were also subsequently appended to the Isidorian version, which had given the Greek book to the Latins before the Council of Chalcedon.

**14.** The fact that this interpretation was received in Spain is clearly demonstrated by the Hispanic collection, which presents the canons of the Greek councils from this same version.

When the Fathers of the Council of Toledo in 400 decreed in their preface that the constitutions of the Council of Nicaea were to be observed perpetually (*T. II Conc.*, col. 1471a), the Nicene canons were perhaps already circulated among them in this version.

The same version, at least as regards the Nicene canons, also appears to have been received in Gaul in the fifth century, as may be gathered from the Council of Riez in 439, canon 3. Since that council decrees that the indulgence established by the Council of Nicaea should be observed toward Armentarius, improperly ordained in the Church of Embrun—namely, “that if charitable counsels should dictate such a course to any of the brethren, he may cede one of his parish [Col. 0084C] churches, in which he may be supported either under the name of chorepiscopus, as the same canon says, or, as they call it, by peregrine communion” (*T. IV Conc.*, col. 534d)—the words *parish* and *chorepiscopus* occur together only in the Isidorian version of Nicene canon 8, or canon 14 of the collection to be published in this volume, which received the Isidorian version.

This collection too, which we shall prove to have been compiled in Gaul, confirms the use of the same interpretation among the Gauls, no less than does the collection of the Corbie manuscript, which is likewise Gallican.

In canon 31 of the Council of Epaon in 517, concerning the penance of homicides, it is ordered that what the Ancyrean canons decreed should be observed (*T. V Conc.*, col. 715e). This is the first document in which Greek canons other than the Nicene are cited in a Gallican council. The form *Ancyritani* (“Ancyritan”) is peculiar to the Isidorian version; the Prisca has *Ancyrenses* (“Ancyreans”), while Dionysius has *Ancyranos* (“Ancyrenes”).

The Council of Valence in 374, canon 3, praises the Council of Nicaea and indicates its canon 11 [Col. 0084D] (*T. II Conc.*, col. 1068). At that time Rufinus’s abbreviations had not yet been written, and indeed neither had the Prisca version.

Since the Isidorian interpretation, when it was circulated in Gaul at its original stage, belongs to an earlier period, as we conjectured above, the Fathers of the Council of Valence may perhaps have received the Nicene canons from it. Unless one considers it more probable that they used that older version which prevailed among the Gauls, Romans, and Africans, from which shortly before St. Hilary of Poitiers had excerpted the Nicene Creed.

That the same Isidorian interpretation perhaps passed from Spain into Africa and was in use there in the sixth century is made clear by the deacon Ferrandus. Except for the Nicene canons, he abridged the other Greek canons from the Isidorian version. See Part IV, chapter 1.

In Italy as well, the very ancient collections composed in Italy and preserved in the codices of the chapter of Verona—[Col. 0085A] 55 and 58—together with Lucano 88, the similar Colbertinus 784, Barberinus 2888, and Vatican 1342, prove that this version was circulated in some places. For a considerable amount was translated from the Isidorian version into all these collections.

Let us conclude this section with Martin of Braga. In the preface to his collection of Eastern canons, he notes two defects in the canons previously rendered into Latin: namely, things expressed more obscurely by the translators, and things altered by the scribes.

He appears to have had the Isidorian version in view, the version that prevailed in Spain. In it, we found some passages that seemed to him to have been rendered more obscurely, and others altered or added in places by copyists in the manuscripts of the Hispanic collection, and much more freely in the copies of the Quesnellian collection inserted in this volume, as comparison with other codices containing a purer Isidorian version has shown.

We shall place the readings of these copies in the notes to the book of canons. From them both the alterations introduced will become evident and the pure text of the Isidorian version can be restored.

[LXXI] ### § 3. On another version called the Prisca

[Col. 0085B]

**15.** The Latin interpretation of the Greek canons is usually called the Prisca when it is found in a manuscript codex of venerable antiquity, written in majuscule square letters, formerly kept by Christopher Justellus and prepared for printing. It was published in Paris in 1671 by Henry, his son, and William Voellus, in volume I of the *Bibliotheca of Ancient Canon Law*.

The same editors affirm in their general preface that James Sirmond praised another Vatican codex exactly like the Justellian one. They quote his words from the censure of the Anonymous concerning the suburbicarian regions and Churches:

> “So far am I from rejecting the word ‘suburbicarian’ in this passage that I shall confirm it for you with new authority from the most ancient edition of the Nicene canons in the Vatican Library, where I remember this sixth Nicene canon [Col. 0085C] to have been formulated with the following title and beginning: ‘On the primacy of the Roman Church and the bishops of the other cities. It is the ancient custom that the bishop of the city of Rome should hold the primacy, so that he may govern the suburbicarian regions and his entire province with vigilant care.’”

The canon, the aforesaid editors add, is formulated in exactly the same words in Justellus’s codex, which clearly shows that one is extremely similar to the other. They also add the testimony of Peter de Marca, who in Book III of his *On Concord*, chapter 4, no. 6, mentions both the Justellian and Vatican codices, praised by learned men, as containing the same version.

But after carefully examining all the Vatican codices relating to the collections of canons, we were unable to find any manuscript example exactly like the Justellian codex that presented the pure Prisca version gathered into a single body.

We found only Vatican 1342, to which another codex of the Barberini Library, 2888, is similar. In it the Nicene canons are presented from the same Prisca interpretation, with the reading transcribed by Sirmond. We have no doubt that Sirmond praised this codex, and that Peter de Marca praised it from Sirmond.

We also found Vatican Regina 1997. In it, except for the Nicene [Col. 0085D] canons, which are drawn from a particular and very ancient version, the other Greek canons are presented from the Prisca. Thus, from the two codices it has been possible to obtain and usefully compare the entire Prisca version in the Vatican Library.

**16.** The Justellian edition of this version is defective and incomplete. We have judged that it should be reprinted in this volume, supplemented and completed with the aid of the codices just mentioned.

It is important to know why Justellus’s edition was mutilated and incomplete. Stephen Baluzius recounts the matter in his preface to the *Works of Peter de Marca*, published in Paris in 1681, nos. 10–13, in the following words:

> “When the most distinguished men William Voellus and Henry Justellus, the son of Christopher—the former a theologian of Paris, the latter a follower of Calvinist doctrine—had decided to gather into one body various codices of ecclesiastical canons formerly edited by Christopher, and also to add [Col. 0086A] some not yet published, especially a certain Latin collection which they possessed in Christopher Justellus’s very ancient manuscript codex; and when de Marca, then living at Toulouse, learned that the edition was being prepared, he believed—and rightly—that the Sardican canons might perhaps be suppressed. Since these immediately followed the Nicene canons, Christopher, still young and clever [perhaps *calidus*, ‘ardent,’ should be read], had cut them out with a knife and thrown them to the end of the book. De Marca therefore wrote about this to the most illustrious man Pierre Séguier, chancellor of France, asking him to defer publication of these books until he himself was in Paris.

> “When de Marca arrived there on the ninth day before the Kalends of October in the year 1660, and the printer was pressing for the release of the work, which was already complete, Voellus and Justellus could obtain this from the chancellor only if they gave de Marca an account of their work. Not long afterward, therefore, they came to him, together with Louis Henry Faye d’Espessaes, recently deceased, abbot of St. Peter of Vienne, in whose house Voellus was staying.

> “At first the matter was conducted with great contention, Voellus and Justellus raging and arguing that two old parchment leaves, which had been thrown to the end of the codex and contained some fragments of the Sardican canons, did not belong to this codex—especially since it was clear that five leaves were missing after the Nicene canons, whereas only two were found there. [Col. 0086B]

[LXXII]

> “At length, when the disturbance had subsided, it was established that these two leaves were of the same size as the others, of the same antiquity, with the same margins and writing; and when their lines and, so to speak, their words were counted and compared with the Binian edition of 1638, the material necessary to supply the five missing leaves from the subscriptions of the Council of Nicaea and the Sardican canons had become clearer than daylight; it was evident that those two remaining leaves ought to be restored after the Council of Nicaea in place of the five that had been cut away.

> “This was especially clear because de Marca gave assurance that Christopher had once told him so: Christopher had confessed that, while still young, he had cut them out more from impulse than from judgment. They therefore agreed that these fragments should be published and that the following [Col. 0086C] preface, written by de Marca in his own hand, should be placed at the front of the volume:

> “‘The reader should be informed that, through the carelessness of the copyist from whose transcript, made according to the manuscript codex, this edition was prepared, it happened that the canons of the Council of Sardica were not placed in their proper position, namely, after the Nicene canons. This required the editors to revise the edition and compare it again with the manuscript. In order to restore that omission, the Sardican canons surviving in the codex are added here at the front of the collection. After the subscriptions of the Nicene Council and before the Gangran canons, several leaves are missing, destroyed by age; nevertheless, two survive. They begin with Sardican canon 14 and continue through canon 19. The editors have wished to reproduce them here in good faith.’”

It happened otherwise, however. For after they had escaped that storm, they took, without de Marca’s knowledge, another way of settling the controversy. They placed those fragments of the Sardican canons after the Nicene canons, adding a preface in which they testified that they had done so by reasoning rather than on the basis of any [Col. 0086D] evidence or necessity drawn from the old book.

They therefore stated that the greater part of the Sardican canons had perished through the ravages of time, together with the final part of the subscriptions of the Council of Nicaea. They immediately added:

> “Nevertheless, we have placed the surviving fragments of the Council of Sardica after the Nicene Synod. For it is plausible that the author of this edition followed in his collection not the dignity of the councils but the order of time.”

They refer the entire matter to probability, although it had been both told and shown to them that the leaves containing the final part of the subscriptions of the Council of Nicaea and several Sardican canons had formerly been placed after the Nicene Synod in the manuscript codex, and had then been torn out by Christopher while still young, lest Catholics use that very ancient book to argue against heretics on the dignity and authority of these canons.

They ought, in accordance with their agreements, to have said that those canons had been omitted from their proper places and were now being restored.

So that no one may think [Col. 0087A] that I am inventing this entire story without basis, and that no trace of it exists, I want everyone first to know that I took part in this whole dispute and examination, that I have in my possession the brief preface described above, and that de Marca mentioned the matter in letters which he wrote on another occasion to Pope Alexander VII and to Lucas Holstenius.

I shall quote his words from the letter to Alexander:

> “The elder Justellus, also a follower of the Calvinist heresy, had once published the book of canons of the universal Church, deliberately omitting the canons of the Council of Sardica, which explicitly assert the power of the Roman pontiff, as though they had been cut away from the body of the canons by the judgment of the universal Church.

> “By the same fraud, his son had sent to the press, before my arrival in this city of Paris, a collection of Latin canons from a very ancient codex that had not been written for nine hundred years [read: ‘had been composed nine hundred years earlier’]. As soon as I discovered that the Sardican canons were absent—canons which I knew had indeed been cut out of the codex itself by Justellus the elder, but whose leaves had been thrown to the end of the same [Col. 0087B] volume—I did not cease, whether by threats from royal authority or by the most gracious pleas, until their proper place after the Nicene canons was restored in the edition according to the evidence of the manuscript codex. Otherwise, if this diligence had been neglected, the heretics would have triumphed, since the authority of those canons had been despised not only by the Greeks but also by the Latins, and [LXXIII] especially by the Gallican Church.”

Thus far Baluzius.

**17.** The Justellian codex formerly contained, if the editors are to be believed, the canons of the Councils of Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Nicaea, Sardica, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea, Constantinople I, and Chalcedon.

But in the brief preface to the reader they assert that the complete canons of the Synod of Laodicea and the greater part of the Sardican canons, together with the final part of the subscriptions of the Council of Nicaea, had perished through the ravages of time (*T. I, Bibliotheca of Canon Law*, p. 276).

From Baluzius we have learned the true reason why the greater part of the Sardican canons, together with the final part of the Nicene subscriptions, disappeared. [Col. 0087C] As for the Laodicean canons, we have established that they were absent from the Greek codex of the author of the Prisca version and were not rendered into Latin in the Prisca interpretation.

For when we found the canons of all the other Greek synods from the Prisca version in several Latin collections, we could find the Laodicean canons of that version in no collection. We found them either inserted from the Isidorian version or entirely omitted.

This last fact deserves particular attention in Vatican Regina 1997. Although, apart from the Nicene canons, it contains the whole and only the Prisca edition for the remaining material, it nevertheless lacks the Laodicean canons.

In the Justellian codex, Baluzius noted that only five leaves had been cut out. These contained part of the Nicene subscriptions and only the Sardican canons.

The editors asserted that the Laodicean canons had once been inserted in that codex solely because of the prejudice that they believed those canons had always existed in the Greek book of canons and in all copies of that codex, included in the continuous [Col. 0087D] numerical sequence which they thought common to every codex of this kind.

We removed this prejudice in Part I, chapter 2, no. 3, and showed that the Greek book of canons had at some time lacked the Laodicean canons. No loss in the Justellian codex is noted after the Antiochene canons, to which the Laodicean canons would have been appended if the author of the Prisca had rendered them into Latin.

**18.** In the same codex, the Constantinopolitan [Col. 0088A] canons are transcribed after the Chalcedonian canons, and a canon concerning the primacy of the see of Constantinople, which belongs to the Council of Chalcedon, is attached to them.

The editors attributed this rather to the hallucination or carelessness of the copyist who transcribed the codex than to an error or lack of expertise on the part of the author. But the matter should be attributed neither to the copyist nor to the author of the version.

We believe the true reason is that in the Greek codex used by the translator, the Constantinopolitan canons had been added after the Chalcedonian canons; consequently, the Chalcedonian canon established for the see of Constantinople had been attached to them. Compare what we observed on this matter in Part I, chapter 2, no. 3, and the note on the Constantinopolitan canons of the same version, which will be published complete in this volume.

### 19

This version of Prisca must be held to have been produced after the Council of Chalcedon, since all the Greek canons, including those of Chalcedon, were rendered into Latin by the same author from a Greek manuscript that had received the additions concerning Chalcedon and Constantinople. Certainly, however, the canons of the earlier synods were translated at a time when, after several ecclesiastical metropolises had already been established in Italy toward the end of the fourth century, a kind of distinct province of the Roman bishop, as metropolitan, was confined within the suburban districts. This is proved by the version of the sixth Nicene canon, which we cited shortly before from Sirmond. Hence this version too was composed by some Italian, or by someone well versed in Italian discipline. The Italian collections confirm the same point, for it is commonly found received in them, such as those preserved in the manuscript codices Vat. Reginae 1997, Vat. 1342, Lucano 88, and Colbertino 784. The fact that some codex of this version was brought into Gaul is suggested by the Quesnellian collection, which we shall prove to be Gallican; for the Chalcedonian canons were extracted from the interpretation of Prisca.

### 20

Dionysius Exiguus seems to indicate this version, which is sufficiently obscure and involved, when he wrote in a letter to Stephen, bishop of Salona, that Laurentius, apparently a Roman presbyter, offended by the confusion of the PRISCA TRANSLATION, had given him the stimulus to prepare a new version. Indeed, an Italian presbyter complained about the interpretation that was current in Italy. That Prisca’s version was in use there much more than the Isidorian version is learned from the aforementioned Italian collections. Nor should the name *Prisca* be an obstacle, since it may seem unable, in the time of Dionysius, to apply to an interpretation that had been produced after the Council of Chalcedon. For it is well known that the ancients repeatedly called something *priscum*—“old” or “former”—when it exceeded approximately fifty years in age, and sometimes even used this word of something that had happened not long before. Just as in Festus earlier colonies are called “old Latin colonies” in order to distinguish them from new ones, so Dionysius could call Prisca an earlier version in order to distinguish it from his own new version.

## CHAPTER III  
### On the Canons of the African Church, Which Were Inserted in Nearly All the Ancient Latin Collections, and on Their Ancient Codices

#### § 1. The necessity of discussing the African canons. The codices and collections in which the African canons are contained. The antiquity of the collection of the synods of Africa that was received into the Hispanic and Isidorian collections. Two codices of African canons produced at the Council of Carthage in 525. The canons of the Councils of Carthage under Gratus and Genethlius, which were contained in one of those codices.

### 1

Besides the canons of the Greek synods, rendered into Latin from a Greek codex and transferred into Latin collections, the canons of the African Church are found inserted in almost the same collections. They became so famous that, having been translated from Latin codices into Greek, they also passed into Greek collections.

Since among the Africans the canons of earlier synods were repeated in later synods and inserted into their acts, the same canons that had previously been established were often repeated without any mention of the earlier synods. Thus the same canons are found in different councils and are assigned now to one synod, now to another, to such an extent that it is often not easy to determine in which synod a particular canon was enacted. There is also the varying division of the synods, or their varying titles, recorded in different collections, as well as the fact that the number of canons belonging to the same synod is smaller in one place and larger in another. Some certain canons are omitted in one place, while others are certainly interpolated.

From this arises a great mixture, confusion, and uncertainty among the canons of the African councils, and many difficulties and controversies have consequently been stirred up, leading scholars to differing opinions. Among many other examples are the disputes concerning the Breviary of Hippo: Schelestratius, on the one hand, argued in order to accuse it of being a forgery, while Quesnellus, on the other, defended it. Not only did the one who supported the false position fall into many errors, but the one who defended the true position also did so; in attempting to clarify the history of the Hipponian canons, the Breviary, and the Third Council of Carthage, he greatly entangled it.

To bring some light into such great darkness, after P. Hardouin, who rendered valuable service concerning the African canons, we attempted something in the second part, chapter 19, of the *History of the Donatists*. Now, after consulting several further copies of the Latin collections and examining and studying those collections more carefully, we believe that we can contribute something new, from which a more exact and fuller knowledge of the African canons and councils may be produced.

### 2

After Christopher Justellus published a collection of the African canons in Greek and Latin under the title *Codex of the Canons of the African Church*, an opinion became widespread among many people that it contained absolutely all the canons enacted by the African Fathers and used by the ancient African Church. But it truly contains no other canons than those which Dionysius Exiguus excerpted from the Council of Carthage of 419, whose acts alone he had before his eyes.

Although the same acts contained canons enacted both at that synod itself and in the earlier councils of Aurelius, Dionysius did not give the whole of these acts, nor all the canons of each council in the order and number in which they had been inserted in the said acts. Rather, since the same canons had been repeated in most of the synods, he established the arrangement that seemed to him best suited to avoiding repetition. Consequently, his work does not provide a completely full account of the synods held under Aurelius before the year 419. This will become clearer from what is said in § 8, when we discuss the Council of Carthage of 419 at greater length.

### 3

Besides the Dionysian collection, another collection of the African synods exists in the manuscript codices of the Hispanic and Isidorian collections. Eight synods are described in it:

- Carthaginian I, namely the synod under Gratus;
- Carthaginian II, namely the synod under Genethlius;
- Carthaginian III, namely the synod of 397 under Aurelius;
- Carthaginian IV of 398;
- Carthaginian V of 401;
- Carthaginian VI of 419, on the seventh day before the Kalends of June;
- Carthaginian VII of the same year, on the third day before the Kalends of June;
- and the Council of Milevis of 402.

In these records, however, certain things that ought to have been distinguished were wrongly joined and confused, some things were omitted, and some were even inserted from elsewhere and subsequently attributed to the Africans, as we shall see.

Nor should this be attributed to the author of the Hispanic collection, and still less to Isidore. This collection of African synods was older than the Hispanic collection. This is established by the Second Council of Tours of 567, which preceded the Hispanic collection. For in its canon 20 we read:

> Since this too had been established in the ancient canons of Milevis: It was likewise resolved that, whenever any of the bishops is endangered by the necessity arising from threatened violation of virginal chastity, whether a powerful suitor or some abductor is feared, etc.

These are the words of canon 26, which in the aforementioned collection of the synods of Africa is wrongly attributed to the Council of Milevis, although it is truly a canon of the Council of Carthage of 418, as will be evident from what is said in § 7.

Therefore, long before the Hispanic collection, that collection of the African synods had been compiled which attached the canons of the Council of Carthage of 418 to the Council of Milevis. Accordingly, the author of the Hispanic collection did not arrange it himself, but transferred into his own corpus a collection that had already been arranged and circulated.

### 4

Other collections, older than the Hispanic and Dionysian collections, also received certain African documents. The collection contained in the manuscripts Vat. 1342 and Barberino 2888 gives the Council of Carthage under Genethlius. The Breviary of Hippo is transmitted in the same codices and also in manuscript 55 of the Chapter of Verona, in the Corbie codex, and in copies of the Quesnellian collection.

The collections Vat. Reginae 1997, Vat. 1342, Barb. 2888, and the Lucano-Colbertine collection present the Council of Carthage of 419, divided into forty canons, which we shall publish in this volume among the documents of ancient canon law. The two collections, Corbie and Quesnellian, give the Council of Carthage of 418 against the Pelagians.

### 5

Nor should Ferrandus, a deacon of the Church of Carthage, be passed over. In his *Breviatio* he presented the canons chiefly in abbreviated form and used very ancient African copies. Since, however, he cites the Councils of Carthage without any distinction, it will not be easy to determine to which council, among several from the same place, a particular canon should be assigned.

Nevertheless, after comparing and weighing all these materials with more careful attention, we hope to be able to present a clearer account of the African councils and their canons.

### 6

Two African codices of canons will serve as a torch for this work. They were produced from the archive of the Church of Carthage at the Council of Carthage in 525 under Boniface (*Councils*, vol. V, col. 778e), and contained a complete collection of the ancient African canons distributed in two volumes.

One is the codex from which several Nicene canons and one canon of the Council of Carthage under Gratus were read. The other is called *The Book of Canons from the Time of Aurelius*. The first seems to have contained, besides the Nicene canons, the canons of the African synods preceding Aurelius. The second contained the canons of the synods convened under Aurelius, which are enumerated in the aforementioned council of Boniface up to the twentieth.

To begin with the first codex of the ancient canons, we observed in the preceding chapter, § 1, that the Council of Nicaea had been received and entered among the Africans from that very ancient interpretation which Caecilianus had brought into Africa. There too we indicated that only the version of the Nicene Creed and of the sixth canon survived from that same interpretation, and we exposed the error made when, at the Council of Boniface, the version of the Nicene Creed belonging to the ancient African interpretation was attributed to the version transmitted by Atticus of Constantinople.

### 7

From the African councils preceding Aurelius, we have received only the canons enacted under Gratus and Genethlius, bishops of Carthage, and transferred into the Latin collections.

The Synod of Carthage under Gratus, with fourteen canons, was first published from Isidore’s collection, which had transcribed it from the Hispanic collection. In both collections it bears the title: “First Council of Carthage.” It was subsequently reprinted in a more corrected form by P. Labbe from a Vatican codex, whose copy, written in Holstenius’s hand, he received from P. Possinus.

In his *Breviatio*, Ferrandus generally cites these canons with Gratus’s name expressly given, as follows: “Council of Carthage under Saint Gratus.” In two places, however, he omits the name of Gratus, namely in no. 119, *Council of Carthage*, title 8, and no. 183, *Council of Carthage*, title 2. The canons designated by these numbers correspond to the numbers of the canons of the synod under Gratus alone—unless one should perhaps prefer to believe that these passages indicate another Council of Carthage, among those now lost, in which the same canons were repeated and listed under the same numbers.

Canon 11 of the Synod of Gratus is quoted in full at the Council of Boniface in 525. When Saint Augustine, at the beginning of 402, writes in Letter 65 to Xantippus, no. 2, “It was established by the council that the case of a presbyter should be settled by six bishops,” the Benedictine editors attached the following note to the word *council* in the margin: “The Council of Carthage under Gratus, in the year 348 or 349, canon 11.”

But it is clear that Saint Augustine was still unaware of the Council of Gratus when, in 406, he attacked the Donatist Cresconius, as appears from Book III against him, no. 38, and Book IV, no. 52. From these passages it is evident that he knew only the pseudo-synod of Sardica, which had sent a letter to Donatus. If he had known the legitimate Council of Sardica, in which Gratus took part, he would have learned enough from the fifth canon of the Council of Carthage under Gratus; and by distinguishing the legitimate Council of Sardica from the heretical one that had written to Donatus, he would have refuted the Donatists more clearly and forcefully.

We therefore believe it more probable that in the aforementioned Letter 65 this holy teacher was referring to a later Council of Carthage under Genethlius, in which the same regulation was repeated as canon 10.

Moreover, this Synod of Gratus was known in 419, since at the Council of Carthage of that year, which Saint Augustine attended, Bishop Aurelius established in canon 5 the provisions that are expressed in exactly the same words as canons 10 and 13 of the Council under Gratus.

### 8

The second Council of Carthage under Genethlius, in the year 390, emerged from the same sources as the council under Gratus. It contains thirteen canons and is called the Second Council of Carthage in the Hispanic and Isidorian collections.

Because of the corrupt Isidorian codex, the first edition accumulated so many errors that some people, together with Justellus, transmitted it as though it were spurious. After those errors were removed in the later edition from a Vatican codex, no one can doubt its authenticity. Ferrandus, who repeatedly cites its canons, confirms its *authentia* (αὐθέντια), its genuine character.

He expressly gives the name of the Council of Carthage under Saint Genethlius in numbers 24, 55, 96, and 194. Since in numbers 55 and 96, under title 8, he designates Genethlius’s canon that is the tenth in the printed editions, and in number 24, under title 9, he indicates the canon that is the eleventh in the printed editions, it is clear that in Ferrandus’s codex four canons of the same synod had been combined into two.

Since, moreover, in number 194 he cites title 6, which corresponds to the customary sixth canon, that union of canons did not occur before the sixth canon. Rather, the seventh canon must have been joined to the sixth, and the ninth to the eighth, in that same codex, so that the sixth and seventh canons together constituted canon 6, while the eighth and ninth constituted canon 7.

Accordingly, when Ferrandus, in numbers 90 and 101, cites “Council of Carthage, title 7,” while suppressing the name of Genethlius, we believe that he is indicating the eighth and ninth canons of that same Genethlius, which, joined together in Ferrandus, constituted canon 7.

Furthermore, when Ferrandus, in number 16, discussing the commandment concerning continence for bishops, presbyters, and deacons, cites “Council of Carthage, title 1,” although no canon 1 of any Council of Carthage decrees this, an error has entered the number. We think that canon 2 of the Council under Genethlius is meant, since it contains such a commandment.

### 9

At the Council of Carthage in 419, after the reading of the Nicene Council, thirty-three canons were established according to Dionysius’s division. Of the first thirteen, with the exception of the first and fourth, the remaining eleven were taken from the Council of Genethlius.

They retain nearly the same wording; only the names of the bishops speaking and proposing the measures are changed, so that Aurelius is substituted for Genethlius, and similarly other bishops who were living under Genethlius are replaced by bishops who were present at the council of 419. Only two names, Numidius of Massula and Felix, are found in both places.

Did these men live from the year 390, when the synod under Genethlius was held, until the year 419? In the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, this Synod of Genethlius is transmitted with certain names belonging to the bishops of the Council of 419. Hence there arose a stronger reason for doubting the genuineness of this synod.

But just as the other defects that we shall subsequently note in these collections concerning the African canons must be corrected from other sources, so the errors in this synod have rightly been corrected from the Vatican copy.

## § 2. On the African synods celebrated under Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, which were described in another codex produced at the council of 525. Their catalogue. On the Council of Hippo of 393 and on the First and Second Councils of Carthage under Aurelius

### 10

Let us now turn to the second codex, which at the Council of Boniface is called *The Book of Canons from the Time of Saint Aurelius* (*Councils*, vol. V, col. 780). At that same council, Councils III, VI, VII, IX, X, XI, XVI, XIX, and XX are mentioned. Their entire sequence must first be set out here.

The first synod of Aurelius is the celebrated Council of Hippo of 393. But since at the aforementioned Council of Boniface, where two complete Hipponian canons are quoted, it is not called the first synod of Aurelius, whereas the others are each designated by their own number—Council III, VI, and so on—this Council of Hippo does not seem to have been included among the twenty.

Other later synods of Aurelius besides the Council of Hippo are indeed found, and they correspond to the numbers indicated at the Council of Boniface. The collection of Dionysius Exiguus was helpful to us, since it lists those synods that were cited at the Council of Carthage in 419, during the time of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage (*ibid.*, col. 1277c). We therefore place below, in chronological order, those synods mentioned there after the Council of Hippo.

**I.** Council of Carthage of 394, on the sixth or sixteenth day before the Kalends of July (*ibid.*, d).

**II.** Council of Carthage of 397, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July (*ibid.*, col. 1296a).

**III.** Another Council of Carthage in the same year, 397, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September (*ibid.*, col. 1277e). At the Council of Boniface in 525 it is twice called Council III, *Councils*, vol. V, columns 779 and 781.

Before this third synod under Aurelius, another council had indeed been held at Carthage in the same year, on the Ides of August. In it, Mizonius, together with several bishops of Byzacena, while Aurelius was present, undertook to compose the Breviary of the Hipponian canons. This August synod ought therefore to have been regarded as the third under Aurelius.

But since what was done there was repeated and inserted at the beginning of the acts of the fuller synod convened shortly afterward, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, and since the Breviary of the Hipponian canons itself is usually cited by the ancient Africans from these acts, it happened, we believe, for this reason: the earlier synod of that year was passed over, and the later one received the name of the third synod in the codex read at the Council of Boniface.

**IV.** Council of Carthage of 399, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May (*ibid.*, col. 1296b).

**V.** Council of Carthage of 401, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July (*ibid.*, d).

**VI.** Another Council of Carthage in the same year, on the Ides of September (*ibid.*, col. 1304b). It is likewise called the Sixth Council at the Council of Boniface, vol. V of the *Councils*, columns 779e and 780e.

**VII.** Council of Milevis of 402, on the sixth day before the Kalends of September (*ibid.*, col. 1313c). It is called the seventh at the same Council of Boniface (*ibid.*, col. 780b).

**VIII.** Council of Carthage of 403, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September (*ibid.*, col. 1317d).

**IX.** Council of Carthage of 404, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July (*ibid.*, col. 1324b). This agrees with the Council of Boniface, where it is titled the ninth council of Aurelius (*ibid.*, col. 781a).

**X.** Council of Carthage of 405, on the tenth day before the Kalends of September (*ibid.*, col. 1328b). It is likewise called the tenth at the Council of Boniface (*ibid.*, col. 780b).

**XI.** Council of Carthage of 407, on the Ides of June (*ibid.*, e). It is likewise the eleventh at Boniface, in the place cited.

**XII.** Council of Carthage of 408, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July (*ibid.*, col. 1336e).

**XIII.** Another Council of Carthage in the same year, on the Ides of October (*ibid.*, col. 1337a).

**XIV.** Council of Carthage of 409, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July (*ibid.*, b).

**XV.** Council of Carthage of 410, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July (*ibid.*, b–c).

**XVI.** Council of Carthage of 418, on the Kalends of May (*ibid.*, c). It is called the sixteenth at the Council of Boniface (*Councils*, vol. V, col. 780c).

**XVII.** Two sessions of the Council of Carthage of 419: one on the eighth day before the Kalends of June (*ibid.*, col. 1252b), and the other on the third day before the Kalends of the same month (*ibid.*, col. 1349c). These two sessions are presented in the Hispanic and Isidorian collections as two distinct councils. Dionysius ends here.

**XVIII.** Council of Carthage of 421, on the Ides of June. We have brought this synod to light from a manuscript of the Chapter of Verona, and it will be published in this volume among the documents of ancient canon law. Nor can this be called Council XIX, which is cited at the Council of Boniface; for the canon said at that council to have been excerpted from Council XIX is not found in our council. Moreover, this council is said to have been held after the solemn observance instituted by the council had ceased for two years, namely after the last synod of 419, which, according to Boniface’s sequence, is Council XVII.

What Councils XIX and XX were has not been established; for no collections have transmitted to us any other African synod under Aurelius. At the frequently cited Council of Boniface, only one canon is quoted from Council XIX; Ferrandus likewise cites it in his *Breviatio*, no. 84 (*Council of Carthage*, title 3), and another canon from Council XX. The date of these councils is not certain.

It can only be conjectured that Council XX was the same council that sent a letter to Celestine sometime between 425 and 426, since the canon that the Council of Boniface assigns to this council speaks of appeals across the sea no less than that letter does. Council XIX, however, seems to have to be placed after 421 and before 425.

### 11

Nor are all the African synods convened under Aurelius—who held the see of Carthage from approximately 392 until 429—included in this number of twenty synods.

At the Council of Hippo in 393, a canon was issued providing that every year a plenary council should be convened, now in one province, now in another, to which all the provinces that had primatial sees should send delegates from their own councils.

In 394, a synod of the proconsular province is recorded as having been held at Carthage on the sixth or sixteenth day before the Kalends of July (*Code of the African Church*, vol. II of the *Councils*, Venetian edition, col. 1277d). From it, bishops of that province were sent as delegates to the Council of Hadrumetum, which is not included among those twenty.

This procedure was observed until 407, when it was decreed that a plenary synod should be summoned not every year, but whenever a common cause required it. See *African Code*, canon 55.

Thus, besides the provincial synods, fifteen plenary councils were convened up to the year 407. Of these, several are missing, perhaps because, apart from certain common causes that were settled in them, they established no particular canon but merely repeated and confirmed earlier decrees, especially those of the Council of Hippo of 393.

### 12

Ferrandus cites another Council of Hippo Regius, which must be distinguished from the Council of Hippo of 393; we shall prove from the codices of P. Hardouin in § 9 that it was held in 427.

The same Ferrandus also cites other particular synods of the province of Byzacena, namely those of Zella, Suffetula, Thusdritum, Macrianum, Septimunicum, Thenita, and Maracana or Maradiana. We shall conjecture in the same ninth section that these were held during the lifetime of Aurelius.

Only a fragment of the Council of Zella survives. It is otherwise called Telepte or Telle, and is found in the collection printed in this volume as chapter 62.

### 13

We must now investigate more exactly the canons of those synods that we have listed as having been convened under Aurelius.

The most famous of all is the Council of Hippo of 393, whose canons were generally repeated in abbreviated form at other synods. Hence the frequent mention of that synod. Its complete acts and complete canons, however, are missing.

For, apart from two canons fully described and preserved at the Council of Carthage under Boniface in 525—which were divided in the *Breviary* into three canons, 3, 6, and 7—only an abbreviation of the remainder survives. Since this abbreviation was inserted into the Council of Carthage of 397, it will become clear from the fuller discussion of that council how many Hipponian canons there were and which they were.

### 14

No canons are attributed to the First Council of Carthage of 394, held on the sixth or sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, from which delegates were sent to the Council of Hadrumetum. See the *Code of the African Church*, vol. II of the *Councils*, Venetian edition, col. 1277d.

### 15

From the Second Council of Carthage of 397, held on the Kalends of July, Dionysius Exiguus transmits this one canon in the same *Code of the African Church*, col. 1296b:

> It was resolved that no bishop should sail without a letter of authorization from the primate.

This is a repetition of the Hipponian canon that appears as canon 27 in the *Breviary*.

In number 64, Ferrandus attributes to the Council of Carthage, title 3, a canon that, repeating another Hipponian decree, prohibits an appeal from elected judges. He likewise assigns it to the Council of Carthage, title 15, where “title 19” must be corrected.

Since this second citation indicates the Council of Carthage of 397 held on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, where title 19 contains this canon, the first citation must clearly refer to an earlier Council of Carthage. Since the same canon is not found among the canons enacted by the Councils of Carthage under Gratus and Genethlius, all of which survive, it seems more correctly assigned to this Second Council under Aurelius, held on the Kalends of July in the same year, 397, than to the First Council of Carthage.

For Dionysius attributes no canons to the first council; from the second he did not transmit all the decrees, but referred his readers to its acts: “Whoever seeks the acts,” he says, “will find them in the authentic records.”

## § 3. The Council of Carthage of 397, the third under Aurelius, held on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, is restored; at it the Breviary of the Hipponian canons was read, confirmed, and inserted into the acts. The respect shown by the Africans toward the authority of the Roman see. The subscriptions of the bishops of the said synod recovered from an excellent codex

### 16

This Third Council of Carthage under Aurelius contains both the Hipponian canons, abridged into the *Breviary*, and other canons enacted at the council itself.

Two sources for this synod are available: the Isidorian collection, which derived this synod from the Hispanic collection, and the *Code of the African Church*, which proceeds from Dionysius Exiguus. In both, however, the canons differ in number and order, and the abbreviated Hipponian canons cannot be distinguished from the Carthaginian canons by any certain indication. Moreover, in both sources some things are missing that had certainly been inserted into the acts of that synod.

Hence the restoration of this synod is especially necessary. Three resources will assist in the restoration:

1. The Breviary of Hippo, which will be found in chapter 2 of the collection of canons to be published in this volume, collated against the manuscript codices of other collections as well. From it the number and identity of the Hipponian canons will become clear.

2. Ferrandus. Since he designates almost all the canons of this Third Council of Carthage by their respective numbers, he will supply the order both of the Hipponian and of the Carthaginian canons. For this purpose, more careful collation and observation were necessary, so that among the very many canons cited by him under the general formula “Council of Carthage,” those belonging to the Third Council of Carthage of 397, or to other councils of the same place, could be distinguished.

3. The Council of Boniface of 525, where, from the *Book of Canons from the Time of Saint Aurelius*, twenty-three titles of canons of the Third Council are presented in the same order as in Ferrandus.

When we have made this agreement and reconciliation clear through the restoration of the Third Council of Carthage, which follows shortly, many difficulties raised by several writers will disappear. Not understanding these documents properly, they not only cast suspicion on the Breviary of Hippo but also abandoned hope of distinguishing the canons of the Third Council of Carthage.

From what follows it will become clear that at this synod the Breviary, which had shortly before been compiled at Carthage by the bishops of Byzacena, was read and inserted first. Other canons were then enacted, but in such a way that both the canons of the Breviary that had been read and inserted and the canons enacted afterward were assigned to the same Third Council of Carthage in a continuous numerical sequence.

Here is the very sequence of canons on which the restoration of this council depends.

**I.** “When Caesarius and Atticus, most illustrious men, were consuls, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September,” etc., as in the *Code of the African Church*, before canon 34, vol. II of the Venetian edition of the *Councils*, col. 1277e, through the words “let each matter be considered by your Charity.”

This preface was omitted in the Hispanic and Isidorian collections when this Third Council of Carthage is presented. In place of the preface, the collector inserted these words: “These are the provisions determined in the present council.”

You will understand from Ferrandus’s reckoning, which begins with title 5, why we have assigned this and the following three numbers to the first four titles or chapters of the Third Council of Carthage.

**II.** After the aforementioned preface, the title of the synod in which the Breviary of the Hipponian canons was compiled must be supplied:

> Council of Carthage, on the day of the Ides of August, in the consulship of Caesar and Atticus.

We recovered this title from manuscript 59 of the Chapter of Verona, from which the other codices differ only slightly. See note 1 on chapter 2 of the codex to be published, col. 85.

Next should be placed the letter of Aurelius and Mizonius that precedes the *Breviary*:

> To our most beloved brothers and fellow bishops of the various provinces, etc.,

as in the same chapter, col. 87.

Some, believing that this letter was sent not from Carthage but from the synod of Byzacena, think that the name of Aurelius should be removed. They suppose that the letter was written to the Byzacenian bishops, who had not attended the synod, rather than to the bishops from the other African provinces who were to gather at the plenary Council of Carthage III.

But the fact that this synod was celebrated at Carthage on the Ides of August in 397 by Mizonius and several other bishops of Byzacena is attested not only by the title extracted from different codices, but also by Aurelius himself in the preface preserved by Dionysius, in these words:

> When the letter of our priests from Byzacena had been read, or when those same men who anticipated the time and day of the council had discussed with me—obviously at Carthage—etc.

The day appointed for the plenary council by the Council of Hippo of 393 was the tenth day before the Kalends of September, according to the *African Code*, canon 73. Anticipating this day, Mizonius and several bishops of Byzacena went to Carthage, where the plenary synod was to be held, and, together with Aurelius—for he says “with me”—held discussions on the Ides of August, composed the *Breviary*, and wrote the letter explaining its purpose.

Accordingly, Aurelius is rightly also named in the letter of the Byzacenian bishops, and in every manuscript codex he is found subscribed to the same *Breviary*. Just as Aurelius states in the cited passage that the *Breviary* was gathered for this assembly, that is, for the plenary synod, so too the letter was written for the purpose of gathering the *Breviary* for that same assembly.

Compare what we have discussed more fully on this matter in the second part, chapter 9, of the *History of the Donatists*, vol. IV of the works of Cardinal Norisius, col. 425, and the admonition on chapter 2 of the collection to be published in this volume, col. 79.

This letter is followed by the title of the *Breviary*:

> Abbreviated Statutes of the Council of Hippo, etc.,

below in this volume, col. 88.

**III.** The profession and faith of the Council of Nicaea were recited and confirmed, as follows:

> We believe, etc.

In the same place.

This Nicene Creed must not be removed from the *Breviary*, as some have thought. This is proved by the statement of Honoratus and Urbanus reported in the *Code of the African Church*, canon 47. After the *Breviary* had been inserted, they said:

> For we have heard the discussion of the faith of Nicaea, and also concerning the prohibition of sacrifices after the meal, etc.

These words refer to the same *Breviary* read at this Council of Carthage.

**IV.** “It was also resolved, because of the error,” etc., as in the *Breviary* in the same place, col. 89.

Here it must be noted that the following canons through chapter 47 should likewise be taken from the *Breviary* rather than from the *Code of the African Church* or from the manuscript codices of the Hispanic and Isidorian collections. In those collections, some canons that were repeated at the Council of 419 received different wording and different readings at that synod.

In Isidore this canon is canon 1; in the *Code of the African Church* it is omitted, but Epigonius cites it as a canon of the *Breviary* in the same *Code*, canon 34. It is given in full from the Council of Hippo at the Council of Carthage under Boniface in 525, vol. V of the *Councils*, col. 781.

**V.** “Cresconius, bishop of Villaregis,” etc., as in the *Breviary*, col. 89.

It is clear from the aforementioned statement of Honoratus and Urbanus in the *Code of the African Church*, canon 48, that the first part, concerning Cresconius, belongs to the *Breviary*. There they testify that they had heard confirmed what had been enacted against Cresconius of Villaregis.

Ferrandus cites the final part in number 24 as follows: “Council of Carthage, title 5.” The fifth title cited by Ferrandus indicates that four other canons preceded it in his codex.

This second part appears in Isidore as canon 20, but with an addition that is not found in the *Breviary*.

**VI.** “The proper primate,” etc., as in the *Breviary*, col. 89.

Ferrandus, no. 82, *Council of Carthage*, title 6. This canon, together with the following one, is quoted in full at the Council of Boniface from the Council of Hippo, vol. V of the *Councils*, col. 782. In the *Code of the African Church*, canon 17, it was adopted by the Fathers of the Council of Carthage of 419 and expressed in different words.

**VII.** “The other bishops of the first see also,” etc., as in the *Breviary*, the same col. 89.

Ferrandus, no. 83, *Council of Carthage*, title 7.

**VIII.** “That the readers should not greet the people.”

From Ferrandus’s sequence it appears that this first part of the first canon constitutes title 8 in the *Breviary* of our edition, col. 90, distinct from the second part, which in Ferrandus is title 9.

Likewise, the same first canon of our edition is divided into two canons in codex 55 of the Chapter of Verona. In Isidore, canon 4, this first part is placed after the second part, as it is also placed after it in the *Code of the African Church*, canon 16.

Compare what is said in the following canon, which presents the second part separately.

IX. “That before the age of twenty-five years,” etc., as in our edition of the Breviary, chapter 1, col. 90. Ferrandus, no. 121, [Col. 0096C] *Council of Carthage*, title 9. This canon is cited in the synod of Boniface of the year 525 from the third council, § 1. Isidore, chapter 4, and the African Codex, chapter 16, transmit this canon, but mutilated; for the passage beginning “so that first in the divine Scriptures,” etc., through the end is missing. This seems to have happened because both Dionysius Exiguus, from whom the published African Codex of the Church was taken, and the ancient author of the collection of African synods received by Isidore copied this canon joined to the preceding one—not from the Breviary, which in all our manuscripts presents the same canon with the same wording, nor from the true Council of Carthage of the year 397, into which the complete Breviary was inserted, but from the Council of Carthage of the year 419, in which the same canon is read among the first thirty-three canons without the words cited above. We shall later see that another passage from this same synod was wrongly attributed by Isidore to the Third Council of Carthage.

X. “That once bishops have been ordained,” etc., as in the Breviary, chapter 2, col. 90. It is cited in the Council of Boniface, § 2. In Isidore it is chapter 3; in the African Codex, chapter 18.

[Col. 0096D] XI. “That even during the most solemn Paschal days,” etc., as in the Breviary, chapter 3, col. 91. In Ferrandus, no. 226, title 11. In the Council of Boniface, § 3. Isidore, chapter 5.

XII. “That concerning the bodies of the dead,” etc., as in the Breviary, chapter 4, col. 91, through the words “nor eat.” Ferrandus, no. 227, title 12. Although in the edition of the Breviary this canon is joined to the following one, we nevertheless believe that the two must be separated when restoring the Council of Carthage of the year 397, because they are presented as distinct not only by Ferrandus but also in the synod of Boniface, which cited these two distinct canons from the Third Council of Carthage, one in § 4 and the other in § 5. Codex Barberinus 2888 separates these canons when presenting the Breviary itself. Isidore, chapter 6, and the African Codex, chapter 18, present both joined together.

XIII. “Next, care must be taken,” etc. In the edition of the Breviary this is the second part of canon 4, col. 91. From the sequence of numbers in Ferrandus’s manuscript, however, it was title 13. In Boniface it is described in § 5, and in Isidore, chapter 6. In the African Codex it is cited with different wording around the middle of canon 18; in adopting three, or rather four, joined canons of the Hipponensian Breviary, the Council of Carthage of the year 419 also altered certain words.

XIV. “That on account of causes,” etc., as in the Breviary, chapter 5, col. 91. From the sequence of titles in Ferrandus, however, it was title 14 in his manuscript. In Isidore, chapter 2. In the African Codex, the first part, with some alteration of wording, is read as canon 18; the second as canon 14.

XV. “That whoever among the bishops,” etc., as in the Breviary, chapter 6, col. 92. Ferrandus, no. 58, *Council of Carthage*, title 15. Isidore, chapter 7, and the African Codex, chapter 19, combine this canon with the following one into a single canon. Moreover, both have certain readings altered by the Council of Carthage of the year 419, by which it becomes clear that this canon was taken by the author of the collection of African synods transmitted through Isidore [LXXXII] from the Council of the year 419, to which the first thirty-three canons described in the African Codex belong; it was not excerpted from the Hipponensian Breviary or from the Council of Carthage of the year 397, where the two canons are distinguished and the name of Aurelius is not prefixed to the canon, just as all the other canons of that council are presented without any bishop proposing them. In the published Isidore, however, certain readings from the Breviary were inserted; but, as Father Hardouin notes, the manuscripts agree with the readings of the Council of the year 419.

XVI. “But if not even with regard to the council,” etc., as in the Breviary, chapter 7, col. 93. From Ferrandus’s sequence, it was title 16 in his manuscript. As for Isidore and the African Codex, recall what we observed concerning the preceding canon.

XVII. “But if presbyters,” etc., in the Breviary, chapter 8, col. 93. Ferrandus, no. 51, title 17. Isidore, chapter 8. The African Codex, with slight variation in reading, chapter 20.

XVIII. “Certainly, whoever among the bishops,” etc., as in the Breviary, chapter 9, col. 94. In Ferrandus, no. 67, it is title 18. In the synod of Boniface of the year 525: “From the Third Council of Aurelius,” § 6. Isidore, chapter 9. In the African Codex, chapter 15, the final sentence is omitted, [Col. 0097C] and the two following canons are joined to it.

XIX. “This also was resolved,” etc., in the Breviary, chapter 10, col. 94. Ferrandus, no. 62, cites the first part as title 19; in no. 64 he cites the second, where “title 19” must be corrected to “title 15.” In Isidore it is chapter 10; in the African Codex, chapter 15.

XX. “That the sons of bishops,” etc., as in the Breviary, chapter 11, col. 94. In Ferrandus, no. 40, it is title 20. The African Codex, chapter 15, and Isidore, chapter 11, express the same sentence partly in the same and partly in different words, and they also differ from one another in several words.

XXI. “That to pagans or even to heretics,” etc., as in the Breviary, chapter 12, col. 95. In Ferrandus, no. 39, it is title 21. In the synod of Boniface it is read in § 7; in Isidore, chapter 12. The African Codex, chapter 21, expresses it in entirely different wording.

XXII. “That bishops or clerics [concerning] their sons,” etc., chapter 13 of the Breviary, col. 95. In Ferrandus, no. 41, title 22. Isidore, chapter 14. The African Codex, chapter 35.

[Col. 0097D] XXIII. “That bishops or clerics [concerning] them,” etc., in the Breviary, chapter 14, col. 95. In Ferrandus, no. 33, title 23. It is cited in the synod of Boniface, § 8. Isidore, chapter 13—as it is read in the manuscripts—and the African Codex, chapter 22, prefer another reading proper to the synod of the year 419.

XXIV. “That bishops, presbyters, and deacons shall not be contractors,” etc., chapter 15 of the Breviary, col. 95. In the synod of Boniface it is read in § 9. In Ferrandus, no. 70, title 24. Isidore, chapter 15, and the African Codex, chapter 16, represent another reading peculiar to the synod of the year 419.

XXV. “That with all clerics without exception,” etc., as in the Breviary, chapter 16. Ferrandus, no. 122, cites this canon from the *Council of Carthage*, but the title is omitted; it must be supplied as title 25. In Isidore it is chapter 17.

XXVI. “That bishops, presbyters, and deacons shall not be ordained,” etc., in the Breviary, chapter 17, col. 95. In Ferrandus, no. 15, *Council of Carthage*, title 3, where an error has entered into the number, as is evident either from the synod of Boniface, in which [Col. 0098A] this canon is recited after the preceding one in § 10, or from the sequence of the remaining numbers in Ferrandus. It must therefore be corrected in Ferrandus to title 26. In Isidore it is chapter 18; in the African Codex, chapter 36.

XXVII. “That readers up to the years of puberty,” etc., chapter 18 of the Breviary, col. 95. In Ferrandus, no. 129, title 27; there, however, this canon is presented in different wording, as also in Isidore, chapter 18, and the African Codex, chapter 16.

XXVIII. “That an outsider cleric,” etc., chapter 19 of the Breviary, col. 96. In Ferrandus, no. 27, title 28. Isidore, chapter 21.

XXIX. “That no one shall be ordained,” etc., in the Breviary, chapter 20, col. 96. Ferrandus, no. 232, title 29. Isidore, chapter 22. It is read in the synod of Boniface, § 11.

XXX. “That no one in prayers,” etc., chapter 21 of the Breviary, col. 96. In Ferrandus, no. 219, *Council of Carthage*, title 31; from his sequence this must be corrected to title 30, especially since it is also cited in the Synod of Boniface, § 12, after the preceding canon, and the two following canons are appended to it as distinct canons; the last of these is marked title 32 in Ferrandus. In Isidore it is chapter 23.

[Col. 0098B] XXXI. “That no cleric [shall have] more,” etc., chapter 22 of the Breviary, col. 96. It is absent from Ferrandus, but is read in the synod of Boniface, § 13. In Isidore it is chapter 16, partly with the same and partly with a different reading. In the African Codex, chapter 16, it is expressed in entirely different words.

[LXXXIII] XXXII. “That in the sacraments,” etc., chapter 23 of the Breviary, col. 96. In Ferrandus, no. 213, title 32. It is cited in the synod of Boniface, § 14. It is the same in the African Codex, chapter 37. Isidore, chapter 24, omits some material and expresses other material in different words because of such omission.

XXXIII. “That clerics or those practicing continence,” etc., in the Breviary, chapter 24, col. 96. In Ferrandus, no. 132, title 33. The African Codex, chapter 38. Isidore, chapter 25.

XXXIV. “That the bishop of the chief see,” etc., chapter 25 of the Breviary, col. 97. Ferrandus, no. 81, title 34. It is read in the synod of Boniface, § 15. The African Codex, chapter 39. Isidore, chapter 26.

XXXV. “That clerics [shall abstain from] eating,” etc., chapter 26 of the Breviary, col. 97. In Ferrandus, no. 134, title 35. In Isidore, chapter 27. The African Codex, chapter 40.

[Col. 0098C] XXXVI. “That bishops shall not depart,” etc., chapter 27 of the Breviary, col. 97. Ferrandus, no. 86, title 36. In the manuscripts of Isidore, chapter 28, and in the African Codex, chapter 23, the final clause is missing.

XXXVII. “The sacraments of the altar,” etc., chapter 28 of the Breviary. From Ferrandus’s sequence it is title 37. It appears in the synod of Boniface, § 16; in Isidore, chapter 29; and in the African Codex, chapter 41. This canon, as a canon of the Hipponensian Breviary, is cited by the bishops Honoratus and Urbanus in chapter 47 of the African Codex.

XXXVIII. “That no bishops or clerics,” etc., chapter 29 of the Breviary, col. 97. In Ferrandus, no. 71, title 38. Isidore, chapter 30. The African Codex, chapter 42.

XXXIX. “That penitents,” etc., chapter 30 of the Breviary. Ferrandus, no. 49, title 39. The African Codex, chapter 43. Isidore, however, divides it into two canons, 31 and 32.

XL. “That consecrated virgins,” etc., chapter 31 of the Breviary, col. 98. In Ferrandus, no. 48, title 40. Isidore, chapter 33. The African Codex, chapter 44.

XLI. “That the sick, if they are able to answer on their own behalf,” etc., in the Breviary, chapter 32, col. 98. In Ferrandus, no. 202, [Col. 0098D] title 41. It appears in the synod of Boniface, § 17; in Isidore, chapter 34; and in the African Codex, chapter 45.

XLII. “That actors,” etc., chapter 33 of the Breviary. Ferrandus, no. 170, title 42. Isidore, chapter 35. In the African Codex it is added to the preceding canon, chapter 45.

XLIII. “That a presbyter, without consultation,” etc., chapter 34 of the Breviary, col. 98. In Ferrandus, no. 91, title 43. It is read in the synod of Boniface, § 18, and in Isidore, chapter 36.

XLIV. “That clerics in another [church],” etc., chapter 35 of the Breviary. In Ferrandus, no. 135, title 44. It appears in the synod of Boniface, § 19, and in Isidore, chapter 37.

XLV. “That apart from the Scriptures,” etc., in the Breviary, chapter 36, through the words “the Church should be consulted.” In Ferrandus, no. 228, title 45. The African Codex, chapter 24, where, because this canon was repeated at the time of the Council of the year 419, the name of Pope Boniface, together with other words, was inserted at the end. In the Breviary this canon is joined to the following one as chapter 36, as also in the synod of Boniface, § 20. In Isidore, chapter 47, both canons are likewise joined, but in such a way that it was copied from the synod of the year 419 and agrees completely with canon 24 of the African Codex. We have followed Ferrandus in the division, because it was possible to derive the division and order of all the canons of the Third Council under Aurelius solely from him.

XLVI. “Let it also be permitted to read the passions of the martyrs,” etc., as at the end of canon 36 of the Breviary, col. 100. Ferrandus, no. 229, title 46. The African Codex, chapter 46. In the synod of Boniface, § 20, and in Isidore, chapter 4, at the end.

XLVII. “It was also resolved that, since,” etc., chapter 37 of the Breviary, col. 101; and after the final words “the transmarine Church should be consulted,” the following must be added: “Concerning the Donatists, it was resolved that we should consult,” etc., as in the African Codex, chapter 47, through the words “that ministers of the sacred altar should not be promoted”; then the subscriptions should be appended: “Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage: these resolutions having been confirmed by us all,” etc., together with the remainder appended at the end of the Breviary, col. 104.

Since Ferrandus’s sequence allows only one final canon, canon 47 of the Breviary, to be inserted, we have no doubt that the two canons which establish provisions concerning the Donatists belonged to a single canon 47. One, taken from canon 37 of the Breviary, speaks of clerics of the Donatists being received into their rank with a certain restriction; the other, drawn from canon 47 of the African Codex, establishes provisions for admitting the children of Donatists into the clergy. In both, it is decreed that the transmarine Church should be consulted. In *The History of the Donatists*, part II, chapter 9, while accepting the second part concerning the children, we brought the first part, concerning the clerics and taken from the edition of the Breviary, under suspicion of being spurious. At that time the Quesnellian collection of canons was the only one known to us, and the Breviary had emerged from it; since that collection had wrongly accepted two other canons, 38 and 39, as additions to the Breviary, it was not surprising that canon 37 also seemed to have entered it from elsewhere.

But we have since found two other collections of different origin and of great antiquity in manuscript, both of which present the Breviary together with the same canon concerning the clerics: one in manuscript Barberinus 2888, the other in manuscript 55 of the chapter of Verona. The latter has the distinctive feature that it knows nothing of the other two canons, 38 and 39, which are certainly additions. From the agreement of these three very ancient collections, therefore, we recognized that this canon concerning the clerics should not be removed from the Breviary unless something wholly compelling required it. On examining more precisely the considerations which formerly pressed us so strongly, we found that they compelled nothing.

The words of this same canon—“It was established in the preceding councils that no Donatist should be received by us with his rank”—created the principal difficulty, both because no such prohibition is found in the earlier African synods whose memory survives, and especially because a contrary discipline rather prevailed in Africa from the beginning of the schism, as is reported in the Carthaginian Conference, first day, no. 16 (*Council*, vol. III, col. 158 d). But after reconsidering the matter more carefully, we believe that this establishment, or prohibition, must be referred to a transmarine council, and that the Africans, in order to obey it, seem to have repeated the same prohibition in their own synods. To prevent this from seeming an unsupported assertion, the matter must be explained more fully, especially since what follows will make clear how much the Africans deferred to the authority of the Roman Church.

The custom of the African Church from the beginning of the schism had indeed been that Donatist clerics returning to unity were received in their own rank. But the aforesaid prohibition of the transmarine council intervened; it is expressly asserted in the Council of Carthage of the year 401, on the Ides of September, canon 68 of the African Codex, in these words: “It was established in the transmarine council that those ordained in the party of Donatus, if they should wish, after correction, to pass over to the Catholic Church, should not be received in their offices.”

Another prohibition of the transmarine synod, in which the bishop of Milan took part together with the Roman bishop, is indicated in another Council of Carthage of the same year 401, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July: namely, that the children of Donatists returning to the Church should not be promoted to orders. [Col. 0100A] For there a legation to Pope Anastasius and to Venerius of Milan was decreed, so that, because of the scarcity of clerics and the need of the Church, a dispensation might be sought from them to ordain those same children, since this had been prohibited by those sees. See the African Codex, chapter 57, and its preface.

The African bishops obeyed these prohibitions so carefully that, when there were few Catholics to be ordained, there was an extreme scarcity of clerics, many Churches were deserted, and not even a single deacon could be found anywhere, as is related more fully in the preface just mentioned. In this crisis of the Churches, the African Fathers judged that those transmarine prohibitions should be partly abrogated and partly restricted.
