Yet, out of reverence for the authority of the transmarine Church, they would not themselves establish anything absolutely contrary to it, nor depart from the prohibitions by their own action, even though necessity pressed, or restore the former custom. Rather, whatever seemed expedient was to be set out in a canon, but not established or put into effect unless the transmarine Church had first been consulted. [Col. 0100B]

This was first expressly stated, so far as we know, in the synod of Hippo in the year 393, and then in our canon 47 of the Council of Carthage of the year 397, which was excerpted from the Hipponensian council. It was repeated again in another Council of Carthage of the year 401, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, canon 57 of the African Codex, and finally in another synod of the same year, on the Ides of September, canon 68 of the African Codex. In the latter, since the consent and, as it were, dispensation of the Roman pontiff is especially to be sought, it is recognized that the authority of this see in the transmarine council prevailed above all among the Africans.

This consultation of the transmarine, or Roman, Church, decreed so many times, declares that the aforesaid prohibitions were observed up to this time. This is particularly clear because in the last synod, on the Ides of September in the year 401, the Fathers testify that they were seeking this dispensation for the peace and benefit of the Church, not in order to dissolve the council held in the transmarine regions concerning this matter. Those who, even in the greatest necessity and scarcity of clerics, wished to interpret and establish nothing more leniently on their own, lest they dissolve the transmarine prohibition, unless they had first consulted the Roman pontiff and obtained a dispensation—everyone can see how much obedience and respect they accorded to the authority of this see.

The matter was delayed for so long because, although the decree that the transmarine Church should be consulted had been issued in the year 393 and repeated in the Breviary in the year 397, it had nevertheless not yet been put into effect in the year 401. Therefore, in that year, at the synod held on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, so that the consultation would not be delayed any longer, a legation was sent to the transmarine Church, through which the African bishops consulted concerning the children alone. Then, in another synod of the same year, on the Ides of September, they intervened by letter concerning the reception of Donatist clerics.

This history does not so much resolve the objection proposed against canon 47—by which, because it speaks of Donatist clerics, it seemed that the canon should be excluded from the Breviary—as it strongly confirms that the African Fathers were concerned about this matter, which had been prohibited by the transmarine Church, and had decreed that the transmarine Church should be consulted, although execution was delayed until the year 401.

A second difficulty remains, arising from Dionysius Exiguus, or from canon 47 of the African Codex. There, after the preceding canon of the Breviary, canon 46, concerning the passions of the martyrs, the canon concerning Donatist clerics is omitted, and it is decreed that only their children should be referred to Siricius and Simplicianus for consultation. The same is also read in Isidore’s collection, canon 48; moreover, in the synod of the year 401, canon 57 of the African Codex, this canon concerning the children is said to have been enacted by the preceding council.

That this was the final canon of the Hipponensian Breviary is clear from what immediately follows both in the African Codex and in Isidore: “When these matters had been inserted, Honoratus and Urbanus, legates of the province of Mauretania Sitifensis, said . . . For we have heard the treatise on the faith of Nicaea.” Here the Hipponensian Breviary is plainly indicated as having been read and inserted into the acts; consequently, the canon concerning the children, which [Col. 0101A] precedes the words “when these matters had been inserted,” belongs to the Breviary that was inserted into the acts. Hence this same canon is described without any bishop proposing it, just as the other canons of the same Breviary were likewise recorded without any bishop proposing them. By contrast, all the canons enacted after its reading in the Council of Carthage of the year 397 are presented with some bishop speaking and proposing them.

We have found that these matters are easily reconciled if neither the canon concerning the clerics nor the other concerning the children is excluded from the Breviary, but one canon is formed from both. First, the matter of the clerics was dealt with, but in such a way that the transmarine Church was to be consulted before the decision was finally confirmed. Since this seemed more difficult to obtain, it was meanwhile resolved to consult Siricius and Simplicianus concerning the children alone.

Likewise, although Aurelius, in the Council of Carthage of the year 401, canon 57 of the African Codex, after presenting the scarcity of Catholic clerics, strongly desired that Donatist clerics be received together with their congregations and offices, and judged that this should be left to the consideration of the transmarine [Col. 0101B] bishops, nevertheless, with this consultation postponed to another time, he thought that they should meanwhile be consulted only concerning the children. He says:

“Although some clerics of the same sect desire to pass over to us with their congregations and offices—men who, through love of office, either persuade others toward life or retain them for salvation—I judge that this should be left to the greater consideration of the aforesaid brothers [the Roman and Milanese bishops], so that, after they have weighed the words of our suggestion with their wiser counsel, they may deign to inform us what they think should be done in this matter. ONLY CONCERNING THOSE CHILDREN WHO HAVE BEEN BAPTIZED, we are taking care that, if it pleases them, they may AGREE with our will concerning their ordination” (*Council*, vol. II, col. 1297 e).

Do you see here how both decrees, concerning the clerics and concerning the children of the Donatists, are expressed in a similar manner and so joined together that we think they should be combined in our canon?

One objection may be raised: the two decrees of our canon are not joined together in any manuscript; rather, one is absent from the three cited collections that preserve the Breviary separately, while in Dionysius, or the African Codex, and in Isidore the other is missing. But we have already seen that Dionysius and Isidore’s collection omitted other canons of the Breviary. Why, however, the other part of our canon—which these witnesses show to belong to the Breviary—is absent from all the manuscripts of this Breviary, we do not know.

From all this, however, canon 47 of the Council of Carthage of the year 397 consists of two parts: namely, of canon 37 of the Breviary and of canon 47 of the African Codex. [LXXXVI] We have therefore judged it appropriate to append to this complete final canon of the Hipponensian Breviary the subscriptions of the Breviary itself, because it is most probable that the entire Breviary, together with these subscriptions, was inserted into the council just mentioned.

Thus what constitutes the true and complete Hipponensian Breviary, and which are the celebrated canons of the Council of Hippo of the year 393, has been plainly established. In the published edition of the Breviary and in certain manuscripts, two other canons are added at the end, but incorrectly. The first added canon belongs to the Council of Carthage of the year 397 and is composed from two canons of that same council, 49 and 50, which will shortly be indicated; the other is a canon of the Council of Carthage held on the Ides of September in the year 401. For this reason these canons are rightly omitted in the excellent manuscript 55 of the chapter of Verona.

There remain to be indicated the canons enacted in the plenary synod of the year 397 itself. These were proposed by bishops speaking in the assembly and can easily be distinguished from those contracted by the men of Hippo in the Breviary.

XLVIII. “When these matters had been inserted, Honoratus and Urbanus, bishops and legates of the province of Mauretania Sitifensis, said: Some time ago, before your holiness,” etc., as in the African Codex, chapter 47, somewhat before the middle of volume II of the Venetian edition of the *Councils*, col. 1284 d. Canon 48 must also be joined to it in a continuous text: “But we report this,” etc., through the end, there at col. 1285. The legation of these bishops of Sitifis is said to have been read immediately after the Breviary in the preceding assembly held at Carthage on the tenth day before the Kalends of September, in canon 1, or in the preface of Aurelius, which is prefixed in the African Codex to canon 34. Likewise, in this almost second session of the same council, held on the fifth day before the Kalends of the same month, in which the proceedings of the earlier assembly were repeated, it is rightly placed immediately after the reading of the Breviary.

We join canon 48 of the African Codex, which continues the same speech of Honoratus and Urbanus, to the final part of canon 47, because we have shown that the first part of this canon, concerning the children of the Donatists, through the speech of the Sitifensian delegation, belongs to canon 47 of this synod. Ferrandus, no. 175, cites this canon as follows: *Council of Carthage*, title 48. In Isidore it is chapter 38.

XLIX. “The bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said: We have also been charged with this,” etc., as in chapter 49 of the African Codex, col. 1285 c. In Ferrandus, no. 4, title 49. Isidore, chapter 39.

L. “But this too must be established,” etc., as in chapter 50 of the African Codex, col. 1288 a. In Ferrandus, no. 5, [Col. 0102B] title 50. Isidore, chapter 40.

LI. “The bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said: Since concerning our memorandum,” etc., as in chapter 51 of the African Codex, with which canon 52 of the same Codex must be joined, since Ferrandus found them joined together in his copy. For he cites chapter 53 of the African Codex in no. 13 as title 52, while he cites the first part of this canon 51 in no. 231 as title 5, where it must be corrected to title 51. Only this first part is read in Isidore, chapter 41.

LII. “The bishop Epigonius said: In this Breviary,” etc., as in chapter 34 of the African Codex, col. 1280 d, with which canon 53 of the same African Codex must be joined, col. 1289 a: “The bishop Epigonius said: In many councils this was established by the priestly assembly,” etc., through the end.

After the delegation of the bishops of Sitifis had been fully dealt with in the preceding canons, Epigonius proposed his own opinion. His first speech, which presupposes that the Breviary had been read, is reported in the African Codex outside what seems to be its proper place, as chapter 34, before the canons of the Breviary are enumerated. Formerly we believed that Dionysius could rightly have placed this speech after the preface of Aurelius, which is recorded in the same African Codex before canon 34. But since this preface of Aurelius orders the reading of the Breviary, it is more probable that the reading immediately followed it, and that Epigonius spoke these words after the Breviary had been read, once the delegation of the Sitifenses—presented first according to what has been said—had been completed and the opportunity for Epigonius to speak had arisen. This is especially likely because Epigonius thought that nothing in the Breviary needed to be corrected or added, except that the date of holy Easter should be made known at the time of the council. This seems to have been stated because the Sitifenses had requested it in the preceding canon 51 and Aurelius had granted it.

We join the two speeches of Epigonius because canon 53 of the African Codex, in which his second speech is presented, is cited by Ferrandus in no. 13 as title 52. In Isidore, the first speech of Epigonius is absent [LXXXVII]; the second is divided into two canons, chapters 42 and 43. The final part of the second speech is cited in the synod of Boniface, § 21.

LIII. “The bishop Epigonius said: In many councils this was established; even now it must be confirmed,” etc., as in canon 54 of the African Codex, col. 1292 a. In Ferrandus, no. 27, title 53. Isidore, chapter 44. In the synod of Boniface, § 22.

LIV. “The bishop Aurelius said: Accept my speech,” etc., as in chapters 55 and 56 of the African Codex, which must be joined here. We follow Ferrandus, who in no. 230 cites the first canon, canon 55 of the African Codex, as title 54, and in nos. 13 and 14 likewise cites the second, canon 56, as title 54. Isidore makes three canons and separates them from one another as chapters 45, 46, and 55. In the synod of Boniface, the first part is presented in full in volume V of the *Councils*, col. 781; the second is indicated in summary at col. 779, § 23.

This is the final canon of the Third Council of Carthage of the year 397. After it must be appended the subscriptions of the bishops who took part in that Third Council. [Col. 0103A] Only the subscription of Aurelius is read in the African Codex, chapter 56, col. 1296 a. Isidore adds two others, those of Epigonius and Augustine, while the remaining bishops are recorded with this formula: “Likewise all the bishops, forty-four in number, subscribed.” Other manuscripts have forty-seven or forty-eight.

Some raise a difficulty concerning Augustine’s subscription. Augustine, bishop of Numidia, does not seem to have been present at this synod, since the Numidians, delaying too long in coming to the council, were not awaited, as is clear from the preface of Aurelius recorded before chapter 34 of the African Codex, and also from canon 47. But in these passages only the legates of Numidia, who were awaited for some time, are under discussion. Augustine must be regarded as having come to the synod, even though he was not acting as the representative of his province, just as Augustine came to the Council of Carthage of the year 403 with Alypius and Possidius, although the legates of Numidia had not yet arrived. See the preface of that council, volume II of the *Councils*, col. 1320 d.

That Augustine was present among the others at the Third Council of Carthage is proved not only by the three published subscriptions that emerged from the manuscripts of the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, but is also confirmed by the manuscript of different origin, Vatican, Palatine 574. From it we append more extensive subscriptions to the restored council.

“Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, have consented to this decree, reread it, and subscribed; and the remaining bishops subscribed, namely: Victor, bishop; Felix, bishop; Numidius, bishop; Epigonius, bishop; Honoratus, bishop; Donatus, bishop; Elesius, bishop; Reginus, bishop; Palatinus, bishop; Honoratus, bishop; Victorianus, bishop; Posthumianus, bishop; Victor, bishop; Boniface, bishop; Felix, bishop; Restitutianus, bishop; Boniface, bishop; Donatus, bishop; Ferox, bishop; Antonius, bishop; Basilius, bishop; Restitutus, bishop; Paschasius, bishop; Victor, bishop; Augustine, bishop; and the remaining bishops, forty-three in number.”

[Col. 0103C] In the Isidorian edition, besides the defects noted above, another canon, canon 49, is incorrectly added, since it belongs to the Council of Carthage of the year 419 and is reported in the African Codex, chapter 32. The author of the collection received by Isidore, although he includes the Council of the year 419 among the Councils of Carthage and divides it into two, nevertheless did not wish to copy its first thirty-three canons, perhaps because he had noticed that nearly all of them were contained in the other earlier synods that he transmitted, with the exception of the five final canons. Of these, he judged only canon 32 not to be neglected and thought it should be added to the synod of the year 397.

[LXXVIII] § 4. Concerning the Council of Carthage of the year 398, on the sixth day before the Ides of November, published from Isidore’s collection. The antiquity and renown of the statutes contained in it are confirmed by other manuscript collections. In some manuscripts they are entitled *Ancient Statutes of the Church*; in others, *Ancient Statutes of the East*. In most manuscripts a different order of the statutes from that of the published text is noted. They do not belong to any African synod. They are a collection, or abridgment, of ancient canons, partly Eastern and partly Western. Formulas for the ordination of the officials of the Church are added at the end.

[Col. 0103D]

17. After the Council of Carthage of the year 397, we must discuss the 104 canons which, having been published from the Isidorian collection, are attributed to the Fourth Council of Carthage in Africa of the year 398. Christophorus Justellus, in his preface to the *Codex of the African Church*, argues that this council—of which there is no indication in the same collection of African canons—is fictitious and utterly to be rejected (*Bibliotheca of Canon Law*, vol. I, p. 317), and that no credence should be given to those 104 canons which are attributed to the cited council without authority.

Following his example, many either rejected this council entirely together with the canons attributed to it, or disseminated considerable doubts and difficulties. Others, however, undertook to defend the same synod, which is confirmed not so much by the Isidorian collection as by the Hispanic collection. Emmanuel Schelestratius, in dissertation 3 *On the African Church*, does not doubt that the earlier canons dealing with the rite of ordinations were enacted in the Council of Carthage of the year 398, because the published preface reads: “It was resolved . . . in this same holy synod to establish those matters which are necessary for ecclesiastical orders according to canonical disciplines”; and because in another manuscript this title is prefixed to the first canon: “Preface of the chapters concerning the sacred rites of ordinations.”

He thinks, however, that the remaining canons were not enacted in that synod, but were carefully gathered and stitched together by some private individual, partly from Eastern and partly from Western canons. Tillemont, in article 123 and note 29 on the *Life of Augustine*, attempts to defend this synod to some extent and to dismiss the objections raised against it. He thinks that Aurelius’s words, which are read in the preface to the Council of the year 402 prefixed to canon 86 of the African Codex, should be referred rather to the canons of this synod than to those of the synod of the preceding year, 397.

18. In this controversy, in order to state what seems more probable to us [Col. 0104B], several observations concerning the manuscript books in which those canons are found must first be set forth. It is not only the codices of the Isidorian and Hispanic collections, which have the same origin in the African synods, but also copies belonging to various other collections and regions that present these same canons, though in different ways. In the manuscripts of the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, these canons are prefixed with the title: “The Fourth Council of Carthage in Africa, attended by 214 bishops, in the consulship of Augustus Honorius IV and Eutychianus,” that is, in the year 398. Another collection, contained in two manuscripts, Verona 59 and Lucano 88, which we shall show in Part IV, chapter 4, to have been derived from another, more ancient source than the Hispanic collection, describes the same canons thus: “From the Council of Carthage in Africa, in the consulship of Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII,” that is, in the year 418. The Vatican Palatine Codex 574, similar to the Morbacensis, which represents a purely Gallican collection compiled before the middle of the sixth century, prefixes this double title: “African Synod of 214 bishops” [Col. 0104C], “The Ancient Statutes of the Church.” The very ancient Corbie collection, likewise Gallican—the codex of the library of the college of the Society of Jesus in Paris, cited by P. Hardouin (Tom. II of the Councils, col. 1433, note 1); Colbertinus Codex 3368, cited by P. Coustant (in the preface to volume I of the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, no. 102); the manuscript copies of Gembloux and of St. Bavo at Ghent, seen by P. Crabbus (Tom. II of the Councils, cols. 1435, e; 1441, c; and 1446, d); and other Gallican copies, identified without names by P. Sirmond (Tom. V of the Councils, col. 14, b)—display only this inscription: “The Ancient Statutes of the Church.” The Barberini Codices 2888 and Vatican 1342, belonging to one Italian collection; Vatican 5845, Vallicellian A 5, together with others belonging to a second collection; and Vatican 1343, belonging to a different collection—all Italian—are entitled: “The Ancient Statutes of the East.” Bishop Atto of Vercelli, in a letter to Ambrose, a priest of Milan, calls them “The Ancient Statutes of the Easterners,” on the basis of Italian manuscripts (Tom. I of the Spicilegium of Acher, p. 438). You see in these many Hispanic, Gallican [Col. 0104D], and Italian collections [LXXXIX], all of them ancient, which, although they contain the same canons, nevertheless differ in their presentation.

19. Two differences in particular must be carefully observed. First, not all the codices entitle them “The Council of Carthage.” The Italian collections have “The Ancient Statutes of the East”; the Gallican collections, “The Ancient Statutes of the Church.” The codices of the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, which give prominence to an African synod, have one and the same origin. If the Palatine and Veronese codices, which confirm the same title, nevertheless have different origins, the Veronese assigns the council to Carthage not in the year 398, to which the Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts attach it, but in the year 418. The Palatine, however, after the title of the Council of Carthage, which lacks a chronological designation, adds another title, “The Ancient Statutes of the Church,” which seems to conflict with the former title; for canons enacted in some synod cannot be called “ancient statutes.”

Second, the customary order of the canons [Col. 0105A] that derives from the Hispanic and Isidorian collections is entirely different from the order presented by all the other codices and collections. Labbe, using Barberini manuscript 2888, noted the numbers of the different order in his edition, but these are easily overlooked and cannot provide sufficient guidance. We have therefore judged that the same canons should be reprinted in this volume according to the order found in that and our other codices; and comparison of them with the editions will make it clear that the order attested by so many different collections—and preferred even in the very manuscripts of Verona and the Palatine, which title the synod as Carthaginian—is the original order. The order previously published from the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, on the other hand, was introduced by the compiler of the collection of African synods received in those collections, so that he might arrange the canons by a more suitable method and unite those belonging to particular subjects, which had been separated from their original contexts and scattered here and there.

It will further become clear from this that the canons concerning the ordination of the Church’s officials, which are placed at the beginning in the common editions, belong at the end; indeed, they are distinguished from the rest by the title prefixed to them [Col. 0105B]: “Recapitulation of the Ordinations of the Church’s Officials.” Here “recapitulation” seems to mean “chapter”; hence the Herovallian manuscript reads: “Chapter on the Ordination of the Church’s Official Ministers.”

20. Now, in order to determine what we believe to be more probable, let us first consider that so many codices and so many extremely ancient collections of different origins and regions, which contain the cited canons under various prefixed inscriptions, demonstrate their antiquity and renown. Among these, two—the Palatine and the Corbie—were compiled around the middle of the sixth century. The Hispanic collection itself, which places these canons under the name of the Fourth Council of Carthage, confirms the same antiquity. For we proved in § 1, no. 3, that the collection of African canons that passed into the Hispanic collection is older than the Second Council of Tours, held in the year 567.

We shall add another point of no little weight. In the collection of canons circulated under the name of the Second Council of Arles, when canon 49 commands, according to the statutes of the elders [Col. 0105C], that excommunicated persons be avoided not only by clerics but also by laypeople, our Statutes seem to be indicated. For although in other canons clerics are forbidden to communicate with the excommunicated, we do not read that this was forbidden to laypeople except in canon 40 of our Statutes. Since, moreover, the collection given the name of the Second Council of Arles was compiled under St. Caesarius, as we shall prove in chapter 10, § 2, no. 19, our Statutes are therefore known to be older than the sixth century and to have been cited as authoritative. Accordingly, whatever may be said about their various titles or inscriptions, these same canons cannot be regarded as spurious and worthless.

21. The entire difficulty concerns their author: namely, whether those Statutes should be attributed to the Council of Carthage. In fact, it is most evident to us, on many grounds, that this inscription—which most of the older codices and collections do not know—contains a falsification. The most serious point is this: if the synod were African, then, because of the number of its Fathers and the abundance [Col. 0105D] and excellence of its canons, it would have been the most celebrated of all; yet no trace of it is found either in Dionysius Exiguus or in Ferrandus, nor in the Council of Carthage under Boniface in the year 525, although it would above all have deserved mention among the African councils.

While Dionysius was listing the synods celebrated under Aurelius down to the year 419, he could indeed have passed over some canons of a synod, or even synods that enacted no special canons; but he could not have omitted a plenary council [XC] that established so many canons sought in vain among other councils. Ferrandus could even less have overlooked this synod, since he cited elsewhere particular and provincial synods of Africa unknown from other sources. In the synod under Boniface, moreover, when several canons are reported from the more celebrated councils held under Aurelius, Councils III, VI, and VII, through the twentieth, are distinguished by these numbers and canons. Since these correspond to the number and order of the synods reported by Dionysius, they leave no place for this Council of Carthage of the year 398 [Col. 0106A]. This is indeed a negative argument, but one that, if properly understood, supplies in this matter a clear and manifest proof.

22. But let us now produce positive and compelling evidence. The very preface that appears in the common editions from the Isidorian and Hispanic collections differs most markedly in style and wording from the other synods of Africa. The consulship should have been expressed in African fashion, not as “Augustus Honorius IV,” but as “the most glorious emperor Honorius Augustus IV, and Eutychianus being consuls.” The phrase “in the secretary’s office” is added without further specification, whereas in all the genuine councils the name of the basilica is always added: “in the secretary’s office of the Basilica of Faustus,” or “of Restituta,” and so forth.

Above all, the year 398 designated by that consulship conflicts with the first canon. In the profession of faith required of a bishop against heresies, it is reported, among other things, that he must also be asked whether in baptism all sins are forgiven—that is, both original sin contracted and those sins voluntarily committed. This openly attacks the Pelagian heresy, which, however, did not become known in Africa until the year 411 [Col. 0106B]. Nor is it credible that, before this error was known, so explicit a profession was required concerning a doctrine that no one before the Pelagians had called into question; nor will it be found inserted in earlier forms of faith.

Add that among the subscriptions found in Isidore, Donatianus of Talabrica is reported—correctly, Telepte—as the bishop of the first see. Yet in the year 398 he was neither senior nor bishop of the first see. Moreover, those subscriptions are the same as those appended by the same Isidore to the Council of Milevis; in reality, however, they belong to the Council of Carthage of the year 418, as do the 214 Fathers to whom these Statutes are attributed. Hence the consuls of the year 418 are less incorrectly noted in the Veronese Codex 59.

We shall demonstrate in the observations on Quesnell’s dissertation 13 that two African synods were convened in that year, one provincial and one plenary, against the Pelagians; there too we shall prove that the number of 214 Fathers reported by Prosper must be referred to the African synod. More actions against the Pelagians took place in both synods. Only the canons enacted in the plenary synod, however, are extensively reported by Dionysius, from canon 108 through canon 127, and among them you will find none of the Statutes.

Furthermore, in the first of these Statutes, not only the Pelagian heresy but also those of Nestorius and Eutyches are openly attacked; these arose much later. To omit other matters in the other Statutes that are altogether inconsistent with the African discipline of that age, this seems plainly decisive: in the first chapter, the authority or presence of the metropolitan is required in the ordination of bishops. The term “metropolitan” is not found in the African synods, in which “bishop of the first see,” “primate,” or “elder” were the customary designations.

Tillemont suspects that the word “metropolitan” was inserted by Isidore so as to conform it to the discipline and terminology of his own region. But in vain: it is not only the copies of the Isidorian collection that preserve the word “metropolitan,” but all the other collections and all the codices that [Col. 0106D] have a different origin. This agreement of all the codices shows both that the word “metropolitan” must be attributed to the author or authors of the canon itself and that such Statutes were composed in places where the title and authority of metropolitans prevailed.

23. To these Statutes, which number 104 in the Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts, Baluze added one canon from the Urgellensis Codex, belonging to the fuller Hispanic collection (Councils, col. 1446, a). If this canon is regarded as genuine in itself, it certainly belongs to some African synod, as is clear even from these words: “It pleased all the Fathers residing throughout the province of Carthage.” But this ought not to move anyone to attribute the remaining Statutes also to an African council.

For since this same canon, found in a single Urgellensis manuscript, is absent not only from the codices of the other Gallican and Italian collections, but also from the other Hispanic codices and from all the Isidorian ones [XCI], and since it displays a form plainly different from that of the other Statutes, it is more properly recognized as an addition; nor can it in fact remove the difficulties explained from the preface and the first chapter [Col. 0107A]. Add that, since from the words quoted it seems to refer to a synod of the single proconsular province whose capital was Carthage—unless someone would rather understand the Carthaginian province of Spain—it was certainly wrongly attached to a universal council of 214 bishops, to which two other provinces are also represented as subscribing in the same Urgellensis Codex: Donatianus of Telepte, primate of Byzacena, and Augustine, bishop of Hippo in Numidia.

24. Once the heading of the African council has been removed, two other inscriptions remain to be considered: “The Ancient Statutes of the Church” and “The Ancient Statutes of the East.” These formulas suggest that the same Statutes contain nothing newly enacted by any synod, but rather ancient decrees collected by someone through private initiative.

When Atto, bishop of Vercelli, found these Statutes in a manuscript copy of Dionysius’s Additions, still preserved in the library of the chapter of that cathedral church, together with a canonical letter—which we shall likewise insert in this volume among the documents of ancient canon law—he asked Ambrose, a priest of Milan, in a letter about the date and author of both works:

“We humbly ask your sincere charity concerning the letter found among the canons, which is also called the Canonical Letter, whose chapters are known to number eleven and which seem to us most useful. Its beginning is: ‘First of all, let all presbyters and deacons or subdeacons hold the Catholic faith in memory, etc.’ We also ask concerning the Ancient Statutes of the Easterners, whose chapters number one hundred. Among these, the first is inquired into among us at every consecration of bishops; its beginning is: ‘He who is to be a bishop must first be examined, etc.’ We ask that you kindly inform us concerning all these matters: at what time and place they were established, under which ruler, by which Fathers, how they are to be regarded, and whether they should be wholly received or rejected in some respect.”

The date of the Statutes can easily be inferred from what has been said [Col. 0107C], namely, shortly after the Eutychian heresy, since the preface demands a profession of Catholic doctrine opposed to it, and before the following sixth century, by which time these Statutes were already famous and had passed into collections.

The collector of these Statutes is unknown. He took not a few of them in abbreviated form from the synods of the Easterners. This may have been his first plan, and from it the title “The Ancient Statutes of the East” was initially prefixed. Since other material was added from the canons of Western synods and from certain ancient formulas or Latin rites, the title “The Ancient Statutes of the Church” seems to have been substituted. Some excerpts from African canons are also detected, and from these perhaps arose the inscription “African Synod,” or “Council of Carthage.”

The chapters added at the end concerning the ordinations of the Church’s officials, which are described in all the most ancient collections, prove the antiquity of the present rites. Since these are set forth not in abbreviated form but in exactly the same words in which they are read in the Gelasian Sacramentary (Gelasian Sacramentary, book I, chapter 95) [Col. 0107D], they are presented under a separate title. If time permits, we shall make further observations on the Statutes themselves when they are published in this volume according to the testimony and order of the oldest codices.

25. Finally, one observation may be made. In the original order of the Statutes that we shall present, the Statutes themselves precede the chapters concerning the ordination of the Church’s officials, but follow a preface in which the prerogatives of the man who is to be ordained bishop are set forth. They follow, in particular, the words concerning the bishop to be ordained: “Let him acquiesce in these definitions of the Fathers.” The Statutes therefore seem to have been collected by their author with the purpose of presenting, in abbreviated form, the whole—or nearly the whole—of ecclesiastical discipline to bishops about to be ordained, so that they might either observe it themselves or ensure that it was observed in every other rank of the Church.

[XCII] § 5. On the Council of Carthage of the year 399 and on two others of the year 401, namely Councils IV, V, and VI under Aurelius. The second council of the year 401 is restored.

[Col. 0108A]

26. Of the Council of Carthage of the year 399, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, which is the fourth under Aurelius according to Dionysius’s sequence, the aforementioned Dionysius preserved only this in his account after canon 56 of the African Code: a legation was appointed to the emperor to obtain a law on behalf of those fleeing to the Church, so that no one would dare to drag them away.

27. Dionysius distinguishes two Councils of Carthage, V and VI, under the same Aurelius: one held on the sixteenth or seventeenth day before the Kalends of July, from canon 57 through canon 65 of the African Code; the other on the Ides of September, from canon 66 through canon 85. In Isidore’s edition the two are joined together under the inscription “The Fifth Council of Carthage.” Since the customary preface lacked the consular designation by which its year could be identified, the year was unknown.

Moreover, the day noted in the common Isidorian text—six days before the Kalends of June—differed from both dates marked in Dionysius and indicated another council [Col. 0108B]. But after Hardouin, when the chronological designation had been supplied and corrected from the manuscripts, the wording reads: “After the consulship of Flavius Stilicho, vir clarissimus, on the sixteenth, or alternatively seventeenth, day before the Kalends of July.” This plainly indicates the first council of the year 401.

Among the fifteen canons that the same Isidorian edition assigns to this council, only the first two belong to the first council, held on the sixteenth or seventeenth day before the Kalends of July in the year 401, and they correspond to canons 59 and 62 of the African Code. In this matter it must especially be noted that Isidore presents these canons with the formulas: canon 1, “It must be established,” and canon 2, “This too must be established.” In Dionysius, however, canon 59 of the African Code reads in an entirely different form: “It should also be requested of the emperors that they deign to establish”; and canon 62: “This too should be requested, that they deign to establish.”

The remaining thirteen canons of the Isidorian edition belong to the second council held in the same year on the Ides of September. Thus Isidore’s edition omits seven canons of the first council [Col. 0108C]. For in Dionysius, or in the African Code, nine canons of that council are enumerated, so that the council may appear complete in this Code. When Ferrandus, at no. 193, cites “Council of Carthage, title 1,” he gives the first canon of the earlier synod, which is read as canon 57 in the African Code; he cites no other canon of this synod.

28. Dionysius recites twenty canons of the other council held on the Ides of September. Although this council too might appear complete in his work, since it is defective in Isidore, who, as we noted, reports only thirteen canons of this synod, a certain omission is nevertheless also detected in Dionysius. To avoid repetition, he omitted two canons that he had previously described among the earlier thirty-three canons of the synod of the year 419. This will become evident from Ferrandus’s sequence and from the Council of Carthage under Boniface. Consequently, this sixth synod under Aurelius, which is found complete neither in Dionysius nor in Isidore, must be restored.

29. Ferrandus, at no. 189, calls the third canon of this synod in Dionysius [Col. 0108D]—canon 68 of the African Code—the second in his own copy: “Council of Carthage, title 2.” Hence the first two canons in Dionysius constituted the first canon in Ferrandus’s copy; and since both concerned Donatists returning to unity, they had not improperly been combined into one.

Therefore, after the introduction to this synod (Tom. II of the Councils, col. 304, b), which is read in Dionysius before canon 66 of the African Code and begins, “Vincentius and Fravita, viri clarissimi, being consuls, etc.,” the first canon consists of canons 66 and 67, which we have said should be joined together. The second canon is canon 68 of the same African Code, which Ferrandus cites at no. 189 as title 2. The third is canon 69. These first three canons are absent from Isidore.

The fourth canon is canon 70, which Isidore gives as canon 3 of that Council of Carthage which he titles the fifth. The fifth canon, omitted by Dionysius—since he had reported a similar canon among those of the synod of the year 419 [Col. 0109A], canon 26 of the African Code—must be supplied from Isidore as canon 4. We infer this from the synod of Boniface in the year 525.

In that synod, nine canons are indicated from the sixth council under Aurelius. The first two are as follows: “That no one sell the property of the Church”; and “That no one, abandoning the principal see, betake himself to a diocese or remain for a long time in his own properties” (Tom. V of the Councils, col. 779, e). This second canon is cited by Ferrandus at no. 17 as title 6. Therefore the canon that preceded it in Boniface’s codex, corresponding to the fourth canon in Isidore, was title 5 in Ferrandus’s codex.

This canon, fifth in Ferrandus’s sequence, is also assigned to this synod in the manuscript codex of the college of the Society of Jesus in Paris, which contains an epitome of the canons. According to P. Hardouin’s note, the consular designation is prefixed to this canon as follows: “Vincentius and Fravita, viri clarissimi, being consuls; on the Ides of September, at Carthage, in the secretary’s office of the Basilica of St. Restituta, where the letters of Anastasius, bishop of Rome, against the Donatists were read.” Then follows the passage: “It also pleased [the council] that the property of the Church, etc.”

These are characteristics of the sixth council, and this is the canon that, fifth in Ferrandus’s sequence, is read in Isidore as canon 4, but is absent from Dionysius among the canons of this sixth council. The excellence of this Parisian codex must here be noted. Since the author of this epitome could not have derived both the chronological designation and this canon from Dionysius, who omits the canon in this synod; nor from Isidore, who lacks the chronological designation; nor from any other collection known to us, since no other collection containing this synod had yet been discovered, it is clear that he drew from the original African source.

This is confirmed much more strongly if one considers that in this codex two canons of the Synod of Hippo of the year 427 are cited—canons known to us from Ferrandus alone, as will be evident from § 9, no. 4. The author of this epitome therefore seems to have had before him a Code of African canons similar to Ferrandus’s.

30. To return to the order of the canons of the sixth council: the sixth canon is canon 5 in Isidore and is listed by Dionysius in the African Code as canon 71: “Again it pleased [the council] that no one, etc.” [Col. 0109C] As we noted shortly before, this canon is cited both by Ferrandus and by Boniface.

The seventh, indicated by Ferrandus at no. 203 with the references “Council of Carthage, title 7,” and described in § 3 of Boniface’s Synod as belonging to the sixth council, is given by Dionysius as canon 72 of the African Code and by Isidore as canon 6. It was wrongly added as the final canon of the published Breviary of Hippo.

The eighth is canon 73 in Dionysius and canon 7 in Isidore. The ninth, which is canon 74 in Dionysius’s African Code and canon 8 in Isidore, is cited by Ferrandus at no. 22 as title 9 and is divided into two parts in Boniface’s Synod, §§ 4 and 5. In the edition of this canon, “intercessor” must be written as “interventor,” a reading approved both by Ferrandus and by Boniface’s Synod.

The tenth canon, recited as canon 75 in the African Code and canon 9 in Isidore, was, according to the sequence in Ferrandus, title 10 in his copy. The same Ferrandus cites the eleventh at no. 75 as title 11. It is read as canon 76 of the African Code in Dionysius and as canon 10 in Isidore.

The twelfth, cited by Ferrandus at no. 118 as title 12, is absent from Dionysius, who had reported it among the canons of the synod of the year 419, canon 27 of the African Code. It is found, however, in Isidore as canon 11, and its final part is cited from the sixth council in Boniface’s Synod, § 6.

Two other canons, reported by Dionysius as canons 77 and 78 of the African Code, are indicated neither by Ferrandus nor in Boniface’s Synod, nor are they read in Isidore. Since they were found in Dionysius’s codex among the canons of this synod, they cannot be excluded. Consequently, either they were omitted from Ferrandus’s manuscript, from which we reconstruct the sequence of these canons, because they concerned the particular cases of Cresconius of Villarregia and the Church of the Hipponian Diaretenses, or else, joined with the eleventh, twelfth, or thirteenth canon, they formed a single canon. In restoring this synod, if Ferrandus’s sequence and numbers are retained, these two canons must be joined with one of those three canons; otherwise the number of canons must be increased by two.

[Col. 0110A] 31. The thirteenth canon, cited by Ferrandus at no. 136 as title 13, is canon 79 in the African Code and canon 12 in Isidore. It is cited by St. Augustine in Letter 65, written at the beginning of the year 402, no. 2.

The fourteenth, cited by Ferrandus at no. 28 as title 14, is canon 80 of the African Code and canon 13 in Isidore. The fifteenth, cited by Ferrandus at no. 32 as title 15 and in Boniface’s Synod, § 7, is canon 81 of the African Code, but is absent from Isidore.

The sixteenth canon is found only in Dionysius, as canon 82 of the African Code. The seventeenth is found both in Dionysius, as canon 83 of the African Code, and in Isidore, as canon 14. Ferrandus cites it at no. 171 as title 17, as does Boniface’s Synod, § 8.

The eighteenth is canon 84 of the African Code in Dionysius [XCIV] and canon 15 in Isidore. The nineteenth and final canon, whose first part is separately described in Boniface’s Synod (Tom. V of the Councils, col. 780, e), is recited in full by Dionysius as canon 85 of the African Code; the bishops’ subscriptions are appended to it. It is absent, however, from the Isidorian collection.

Thus the sixth Council of Carthage, held under Aurelius in the year 401 on the Ides of September, has been restored [Col. 0110B].

§ 6. The Synod of Milevis of the year 402, in Isidore compiled from the canons of several synods. It is read in genuine and complete form in Dionysius. On the other synods under Aurelius, from the eighth through the fifteenth.

32. We now come to the Synod of Milevis of the year 402, which the Council of Carthage under Boniface calls the seventh under Aurelius and which both Isidore’s collection and Dionysius Exiguus present. Although Isidore’s collection designates the consulship of the year 402 in its preface, it nevertheless displays only three canons of this synod.

Since it does not present any other later African synods except the one held in the year 419—which, although a single synod, it divides into two, namely the sixth and seventh Councils of Carthage—it assigns to the Council of Milevis the canons of the other synods held between the years 402 and 419. Consequently, this council in Isidore, and likewise in the Hispanic collection from which Isidore took the African synods, is more accurately a collection of the canons of four synods: the Synod of Milevis of the year 402 and three Councils of Carthage of the years 405, 407, and 418. Below we shall assign these canons to their respective synods [Col. 0110C].

In order to adapt the preface of the Synod of Milevis of the year 402 to this collection, the compiler added certain material at the end of the same preface that belongs to no African synod. Since Pelagians are mentioned in this addition to the preface, and since the first canons also establish provisions against those heretics, the ancient editors of the Councils, believing that an error had entered the chronological designation of the year 402, were misled by the name of the Synod of Milevis and supposed this to be another Synod of Milevis, held in the year 416, from which the Fathers of Numidia wrote to Innocent I concerning the Pelagians. In fact, the canons inserted against the Pelagians were enacted not in the provincial Synod of Milevis in Numidia, but in the plenary Council of Carthage of the year 418.

33. The true and complete Synod of Milevis of the year 402 [Col. 0110D] is read in Dionysius and is found in the common Code of the African Church, which was taken from Dionysius. We present here the order of the canons as Ferrandus and Boniface’s Synod found it in their Codes of African canons.

Ferrandus, at no. 78, “Council of Milevis, title 2,” cites canon 86 of the African Code; and at no. 10, “Council of Milevis, title 4,” refers to canon 89 of the same African Code. The preface of this synod, therefore, which is prefixed to canon 86 in the African Code, was title 1 in Ferrandus’s copy, while canon 86 was title 2. Likewise, in Boniface’s Synod, these two canons are distinguished as belonging to the seventh council, so that in his codex too the preface occupied the place of the first canon.

If canon 8 [lacuna] of the African Code was title 4 in Ferrandus, then canons 87 and 88 of the same African Code, joined into a single canon, constituted title 3. Finally, canon 90 of the African Code, the last canon of this synod, was title 5 in the cited copy of Ferrandus. Only three canons, corresponding to Ferrandus’s titles 2, 4, and 5, are found in Isidore as canons 13, 14, and 15.

34. The eighth synod under Aurelius is the Council of Carthage of the year 403. It concerns entirely the case of the Donatists. It was preserved by Dionysius alone. Its preface is read in the African Code, together with only the two canons enacted in it, which are there described as canons 91 and 92.

35. The ninth synod is the Council of Carthage of the year 404. It likewise concerns the controversy with the Donatists. It is found in the same African Code as canon 93. It seems to be cited in Boniface’s Synod, where certain words are produced from the ninth council. Since the same meaning is also expressed in the eleventh Council of Carthage of the year 407, and since the words produced in Boniface’s Synod (see the African Code) agree exactly with the words of that council, but not with those of the ninth council, it is sufficiently credible that an error entered Boniface’s Synod in the word “ninth” [XCV]. Perhaps the numeral letters XI, written at the beginning, were changed into IX through the copyist’s carelessness.

36. The tenth Council of Carthage, of the year 405, was summarized by Dionysius alone [Col. 0111B] in canon 4 of the African Code. “For,” he says, “things necessary for the moment rather than any general matters were established.”

One disciplinary canon is cited in Boniface’s Synod from the tenth council; in Dionysius’s abridgment it is indicated in the penultimate place: “That bishops should not readily travel overseas.” Since Dionysius’s summary makes it clear that during this period the Donatists began to return to unity and that something had been established by the same synod for this purpose, we suspect that the canon indicated by Ferrandus at no. 50, “Council of Carthage, title 2,” should be assigned to this synod. It corresponds to canon 23 in Isidore’s collection, where it was wrongly attributed to the Council of Milevis; it belongs to some African synod earlier than the year 419.

After the imperial laws were issued in February and March of the year 405, the Donatists began returning everywhere to the embrace of the Church. It therefore seems more probable that this canon was enacted at this synod, held on the tenth day before the Kalends of September, to regulate the reception of Donatists who were doing penance [Col. 0111C]. Since Dionysius sometimes omitted other canons, it is not surprising that he passed over this one in his summary of the synod.

One further point must be noted. In the Isidorian canon 23 just mentioned, heretics are called by that general name, whereas in Ferrandus’s abridgment the Donatists are named. It will become clear that this alteration of the reading is attributable to the author of the collection received by Isidore, from a similar alteration that we shall note in the other canons of the synod of the year 407 in the following section.

37. The eleventh Council of Carthage, of the year 407, held on the Ides of June, is found complete in Dionysius from canon 95 of the African Code through canon 106.

In the first part of no. 144, Ferrandus gives in abbreviated form the canon of this synod described as canon 95 in the African Code. Since this first part is not read in the Council of Antioch cited there, to which the second part belongs, it is necessary to supply the designation of the Council of Carthage and its title, omitted either through the carelessness of the author or, more probably, of copyists, as follows: “Council of Carthage, title 1.”

The same Ferrandus, at no. 13, when he cites “Council of Carthage in the basilica, title 5,” undoubtedly refers to canon 98 of the African Code, which in his copy was title 5 of the cited synod. For the words by which the establishment of a new bishopric and the authority of the primate are required can be found only in this council and in the canon indicated.

The same Ferrandus mentions two other canons of this synod: at no. 163, title 7, corresponding to canon 102 of the African Code; and at no. 43, title 9, corresponding to canon 104 in the same African Code. From Ferrandus’s sequence of numbers, in which canon 98 of the African Code is title 5 and canon 102 is title 7, it appears that canons 100 and 101 of the cited African Code were either omitted from Ferrandus’s copies because they concerned particular cases, or were joined with the preceding or following canon. We have seen something similar happen in the synod of the year 401 held on the Ides of September.

Boniface’s Council cites three canons of this synod—namely, canons 103, 104, and 105 of the African Code—in the same order from the eleventh council [Col. 0112A]. It also recites the final part of canon 106 in exactly the same words, although in the common editions it is assigned, through some error, to the ninth council. Compare what we said above at no. 4.

In Isidore’s collection, nine canons attributed to the Synod of Milevis belong to this council, but they are presented in a confused order and with a different division. Thus canon 95 of the African Code is included among the Milevitan canons in Isidore as canon 9. Isidore’s canon 16 contains the second part of canon 96 and the whole of canon 97 of the African Code. Canon 102 of this Code is presented in Isidore as canon 17, and canon 103 is read in Isidore as canon 12, with a more fully developed statement. Canon 104 is found as Isidore’s canon 19, while canon 105 is recited as canon 18.

Finally, Isidore divides canon 106 into three canons, 10, 11, and 20, but in such a way that canon 20 contains the first part of canon 106, canon 11 the second part, and canon 10 the final part. In Isidore’s canon 11, the text reads “against heretics,” whereas canon 106 of the African Code has “against the Donatists.” Thus it is recognized that the compiler of the collection received by Isidore altered or expanded something according to his own judgment.

38. To the Council of Carthage of the year 408, held on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, and to another of the same year, held on the third day before the Ides of October—the twelfth and thirteenth synods under Aurelius according to the sequence of the other councils [XCVI]—Dionysius assigns only two legations to the emperor, after canon 106 of the African Code.

39. In the African Code, canon 107 mentions the fourteenth Council of Carthage of the year 409, held on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July. According to Dionysius, it was not a plenary council but a provincial one. A single canon is quoted there, which Ferrandus cites in no. 52 in these words:

> “But so that one bishop might not claim the matter for his own adjudication, this was dealt with in another Council of Carthage.”

Since he does not, contrary to his usual practice, prefix the number of the title, this seems to have occurred because this Council of Carthage [Col. 0112C] was not plenary but provincial. Similarly, he gives neither title nor number when citing several councils of the province of Byzacena, which he repeatedly mentions. This canon, therefore, should rightly be assigned by Ferrandus to the council of the year 409.

40. Dionysius Exiguus reports, after canon 107 of the African Code, that at the fifteenth Council of Carthage, in the year 410, a mere embassy to the emperor was decreed.

## § 7. The sixteenth Council of Carthage of the year 416. The vindication of its canon issued against the Pelagian opinion that infants dying without baptism were assigned a place of salvation and rest outside the kingdom of heaven

41. The sixteenth Council of Carthage, held on the Kalends of May in the year 418 and convened chiefly against the Pelagian heresy, is famous. Although several of its canons concern that same heresy, more of them concern ecclesiastical discipline. Dionysius assigns twenty canons to it, from canon 108 of the African Code through canon 127, in which, contrary to Dionysius’s usual practice, a preface is assigned to the first canon. Ferrandus cites four of these canons. In the *Breviatio*, no. 190, he cites title 10, which corresponds to canon 117 of the African Code. Moreover, in no. 191 he cites title 11, which in the African Code is canon 118. Since in no. 25 he cites title 12, which in the same African Code is canon 120, it is understood that he found the two canons of that Code, 118 and 119, which deal with the same matter, joined together as one. This union of the two canons is also confirmed in Ferrandus’s codex by no. 30, where he notes title 18, which is recorded as canon 126 in the African Code but, according to the Dionysian reckoning, is canon 19. In the Council of Boniface, canons 108 and 127 of the African Code—that is, the preface and the final canon of this council—are quoted in full in volume V of the Councils, column 777; then canon 125 is reported in summary from the sixteenth council.

42. The first eight canons of this council, concerning the Pelagians, [Col. 0113A] are indicated neither by Ferrandus nor in the Council of Boniface. Yet they are found separately published, with one canon added, and inserted in the oldest collection of canons to be published in this volume, chapter 13, under this title:

> “Plenary Council held at Carthage against Pelagius and Coelestius.”

The special preface found in this collection is recognizable as an excerpt from the acts of this council. Difficulty is caused by the canon concerning infants dying without baptism, which is counted as the third in that collection. Many have cast suspicion upon it because it is absent both from Isidore and from Dionysius, who present all the other canons issued against the Pelagians.

A further and more important consideration is added by the *Chapters on Grace* appended to the letter of Celestine, whose author seems more probably to have been Saint Prosper. While three chapters of this council against the Pelagians are cited there, the third chapter is called what would have to be the fourth if the chapter against the natural blessedness of infants dying without baptism had occupied a place in the example of this council. Those, however, who defend this canon observe that the author of the oldest collection mentioned above, having published from chapter 6 through chapter 20 very rare documents relating to the Pelagian cause, found an older collection of these documents, apparently compiled during the time of the Pelagian controversy. Everyone can see how much authority this antiquity lends to the disputed canon.

It is further significant that not only one author of the collection to be published found an example of this council containing the said canon, but Photius did also. For, while citing another similar example of the same council in codex 53 of his *Bibliotheca*, he likewise reports the same canon in third place. He says:

> “I read the book, or council, against Pelagius and Coelestius at Carthage, in the great church of Faustus, etc.”

After reproducing the characteristics of the council of the year 418, he adds:

> “This council condemns those who assert that Adam was created mortal and was not punished with death because of transgression.” [Col. 0113C]

“This is the first canon.”

He continues:

> “Likewise, it condemns those who would say that newborn infants have no need of baptism, because they do not believe them subject to original sin from Adam.”

“This is the second canon.”

Indicating the third, he adds:

> “It also condemns those who would affirm that unbaptized infants live blessedly in some intermediate place between paradise and hell.”

He then testifies that six other chapters against the Pelagians followed, so that the example of this council which he possessed comprised nine chapters or canons, just as nine are read in the example inserted into the collection mentioned above. Moreover, Photius subsequently mentions imperial laws which are likewise found in the same collection, so that it is clear that he had before his eyes the same older collection of documents relating to the Pelagian cause.

Thus two distinct examples of this council and of the other documents relating to the Pelagians—one of which Photius read in Greek translation, while the other, in Latin, was available to the author of our collection—remove every suspicion of fraud. [Col. 0113D] Ferrandus provides no small additional weight in defense of the canon. Since he certainly used African codices, his testimony carries great authority. Although it was not his practice to cite the canons against the Pelagians, when in no. 190 he assigns title 10 to the canon which follows first among the chapters issued against the Pelagian heresy, we learn that his codex contained not eight but nine canons relating to that heresy.

It is true that he sometimes counted prefaces as the first title. But this never happened unless the prefaces contained some speech or decree. Since the very brief preface of this council presents only an indication of place and time, it could not occupy the place of the first title or canon. Ferrandus’s African codex, therefore, placed among the nine canons relating to the Pelagians the canon concerning infants dying without baptism, no less than did the two examples mentioned above. [Col. 0114A] These three testimonies certainly seem more weighty than the arguments advanced for the omission of the same canon, which are subject to several objections.

43. There is no need to be greatly troubled by Isidore’s collection, which did not publish this council in its entirety and assigned its canons, though not all of them, to the councils of Milevis. As for Dionysius, since he never counted the prefaces of African synods among canons distinguished by numbers, even when they were set forth with lengthy interventions, as Quesnellus observes at greater length in Dissertation 13, § 31, no. 5, and yet in the published copies a canon number is attached to the very brief preface of this synod, which contains nothing worthy of a canon, there arises no slight suspicion that the canon under discussion had a place in his collection from the beginning and was subsequently expunged or dropped out; and that, to fill its vacant number, it was attached to the preface. To the author of the *Chapters on Grace* one may reply that, in his codex, the third canon was not distinguished from the second because of their close connection in subject matter. [Col. 0114B] Compare Quesnellus’s other conjectures at the cited place.

44. At least no one can deny that copies of this synod formerly differed: some had this canon, as certainly did the two used by Photius and by the author of the collection inserted in this volume; others lacked it, which, if one prefers, were available to Dionysius and to the author of the *Chapters on Grace*. On this hypothesis, only one point can be doubted: whether the cited canon was inserted into the former copies or fell out of the latter. Besides the observations drawn from Ferrandus’s African Code, Augustine seems to settle the dispute. In book II, chapter 11, of *On the Origin of the Soul*, he writes:

> “The authority of the Catholic councils and of the Apostolic See most justly condemned the new Pelagian heretics, because they dared to assign to unbaptized infants a place of rest and salvation even outside the kingdom of heaven.”

Although in other preceding synods the Pelagian teaching that asserted eternal life for unbaptized infants [Col. 0114C] had been proscribed, the opinion that a place of salvation and rest was assigned to them outside the kingdom of heaven is found expressly proscribed in no other council of Catholics than the plenary council of the Kalends of May in the year 418. Perhaps the same Fathers had also suggested that it should be proscribed to Zosimus in the preceding African synod; and, since it was approved by that pope in his *tractoria*, Augustine praised the condemnation both of the Catholic councils and of the Apostolic See. But enough on this matter.

45. Isidore’s collection assigns sixteen canons of this council to the Milevitan councils. From canon 1 through canon 8, it presents canon 109 of the African Code and the following canons through canon 116. Then, in chapters 21 and 22, it reports canons 120 and 125 of the same Code. In canon 24 it joins canons 121 and 122, and in canon 25 two other canons of that Code, 123 and 124. Finally, in canons 26 and 27 it describes canons 126 and 127.

Apart from the canon concerning infants dying without baptism, however, it omits three canons of the African Code—117, 118, and 119—which concern the Donatist cause. Although the introduction prefixed to it gives the consuls of the year 402, it nevertheless indicates a number of 214 bishops, which belongs to the African council of the year 418. The subscriptions of three bishops also belong to the plenary council of that same year 418; among them Donatian of Telepte, of the first see, is named second. For Donatian reached the primacy of the province of Byzacena only around this period.

Aurelius and Donatian are indeed found named in the preface of this council, which is to be included in the collection published in this volume, and also in Photius’s *Bibliotheca*, codex 53. Donatian’s name is likewise inserted into the final canon, which is canon 127 in the African Code (volume II of the Councils, column 1349, b).

## § 8. The celebrated seventeenth Council of Carthage of the year 419, at which earlier councils were read and inserted. The deficiencies of the Isidorian and Dionysian collections. The two sessions of this council and what was done in each. The proceedings after this council concerning copies of the Nicene canons, and the copy of the version sent to Africa by Atticus of Constantinople. Its authentic subscription recovered from manuscripts

[Col. 0115A]

46. The seventeenth council under Aurelius is the Council of Carthage of the year 419, by far the most fully attended of all. Two hundred and seventeen Fathers and three legates of the Apostolic See took part: Faustinus, bishop of Potentia, and Philippus and Asellus, presbyters of the Roman Church.

The occasion for convening it was the case of Apiarius, presbyter of Sicca, on account of which a written admonition of Pope Zosimus was produced by the legates. Yet, besides the dispute arising from the reading of this admonition, several canons were issued at this council, and the statutes of earlier councils were also repeated, confirmed, and inserted into the proceedings, so that most of them have reached us only through the acts of this council. [Col. 0115B]

Two sources of different origin are commonly known for this council: Dionysius, or the published Code of the Canons of the African Church, which was taken from Dionysius’s collection; and the ancient collection of African councils, which was adopted by the author of the Hispanic collection and subsequently by Isidore, and printed from that collection under Isidore’s name.

We have found another source in three very ancient Italian collections. One is preserved in manuscript Vatican, Regina 1997; another in manuscripts Lucano 88 and Colbertino 784; and the third in manuscripts Vatican 1342 and Barberino 2888. These three collections divide the first thirty-three canons of this council, as they are read in the African Code, into forty canons in the same manner, and supply variants different from those of the published text. These two peculiar differences establish a different origin for this council.

Christophorus Justellus, in his notes on the Code of the African Church, mentions two other manuscript examples, the Thuaneus and the Bochardianus. Although he does not describe them, the indications he gives show that they belong to one or another of the Italian collections mentioned above. Indeed, the codex which was then called Thuaneus is now Colbertinus 784.

The information concerning this council is complicated because the two principal sources differ greatly. Isidore’s collection, which divides the two sessions of this same council into two councils—namely, the sixth and seventh Councils of Carthage—not only gives fewer materials than Dionysius, but sometimes presents even those materials in a different order and manner. Numerous questions have therefore arisen on both sides, causing the greatest difficulty for learned men. We, having established the canons of the earlier councils from the preceding discussions and having moreover found a third source in the Italian collections mentioned above, shall contribute something by which knowledge of this council too may be made more certain.

47. After the day appointed for the council, while the legates of several provinces were being awaited, certain matters were meanwhile conducted and prepared. Perhaps the case of Apiarius was settled at that time, concerning which the Africans, after the death of Zosimus, wrote to Boniface, his successor. The controversy concerning the Sardican canons remained; in Zosimus’s admonition they had been cited under the name of the Nicene canons.

When everyone had assembled, the first session was held on the eighth day before the Kalends of June in the secretarium of the basilica of Faustus. At the beginning, Aurelius requested that the statutes of the Council of Nicaea and of his predecessors be read. When the council approved this, the notary Daniel read:

> “The profession of faith, or statutes, of the Council of Nicaea are as follows.”

He then read the Nicene Creed and canons, and immediately the following words are added:

> “And when he said…”

The Italian collections mentioned above, which display another origin, have a somewhat better reading:

> “And when he was reciting…”

The ancient collector of African canons in Isidore has:

> “And when he had read…”

Although these formulas seem to differ, in reality they do not. For *and when he said*, or *was reciting*, has the same sense as *and when he had read*, or *had recited*, as anyone can see from the other formulas that follow in the same council.

Thus, after a canon from Zosimus’s admonition had been read, the following is added:

> “And when Bishop Alypius had recited it … he said.”

Likewise, shortly afterward, after another canon had been read, it says:

> “And when it was being recited, Bishop Augustine … said.”

It is therefore clear that the Council of Nicaea was recited at this point. Soon afterward, Faustinus, legate of the Apostolic See, produced from Zosimus’s admonition two Sardican canons inscribed under the title of the Nicene canons, which had not been read among the Nicene canons recited from the African codex.

A dispute concerning the Nicene canons therefore arose and is set out in several interventions.

[Note: On this question, see the *Observations* in Quesnellus’s Dissertation 5, part I, chapter 6, nos. 20 and following, volume II, p. 957.]

Aurelius then ordered that the Council of Nicaea be recited again from the copies which Caecilianus had brought to Africa, and that the statutes of his predecessors, as well as the matters which had now—that is, in the preceding common discussion—been arranged, be read and inserted into the proceedings. From this we understand that the thirty-three canons mentioned below had been prepared by the bishops in a common discussion before this session.

48. Dionysius and Isidore’s collection immediately add:

> “The notary Daniel recited in the African council the profession of faith of the Council of Nicaea, or its statutes.”

Then, after transcribing only the Nicene Creed from the ancient African version, Dionysius gives this note:

> “The statutes of the Council of Nicaea, in twenty chapters, were likewise recited, as they are found recorded above. Then the matters promulgated in the African councils are known to have been inserted into the present proceedings.”

He immediately adds the first thirty-three canons. This note is not read in Isidore, nor are the thirty-three canons, a matter to which we shall return later. The same note is also absent from manuscript Vatican Palatine 577, which exhibits the first form of the Dionysian collection, as we shall explain in part III, chapter 1, § 3; and it is likewise absent from the other Italian manuscript collections containing this first session.

All these collectors had before their eyes the complete acts of this council. In those acts, together with the Nicene Creed, all its canons from the ancient African version had been inserted at this second point, as Aurelius and the other Fathers had ordered. But, avoiding their transcription, the collectors each added different notes of their own choosing, though all amounting to the same thing. These are not words from the acts of the council itself but from the collectors.

The better note seems to be the one written in the oldest of all the collections, manuscript Vatican Regina 1997, which gives the paragraph concerning the notary Daniel in these words:

> “The notary Daniel recited: ‘The profession of faith, or statutes, of the Council of Nicaea are as they were read above’” [C, title 21, where the Creed is counted as the first title], “and he recited them in order. And when he was reciting them, Bishop Aurelius said: ‘These are the copies of the statutes which our Fathers then brought with them from the Council of Nicaea,’ etc.”

This is the first canon of this plenary council (volume II of the Councils, column 1260, d).

This note indicates that the reading of the Council of Nicaea, which had previously been read, was repeated, and that immediately after this repeated reading Aurelius began the canons with his intervention. Dionysius’s note, moreover, in which he adds that the matters promulgated in the African councils were inserted, presents no contradiction. It means only that most of the thirty-three canons immediately added were taken from and repeated from earlier councils.

Aurelius’s intervention, set out in the first canon, does demonstrate that the reading of the Nicene statutes immediately preceded it, as is clear from the words:

> “These are the copies which we have among us,” etc.

Thus, more suitably and clearly, the Vatican Regina codex, omitting Dionysius’s note, reads:

> “And he recited them in order [the Nicene statutes]; and when he was reciting them, Bishop Aurelius said: ‘These are the copies which we have among us,’ etc.”

49. Besides the Nicene statutes, Aurelius had requested that there be recited and inserted into the proceedings both “what our predecessors had here profitably established” and “what has now been ordained by us”—that is, in the common discussion held before this session (ibid., column 1257, d).

Two kinds of canons are here named: some belonging to Aurelius’s predecessors, which were to be repeated and confirmed; and others proper to this council, which had been prepared in the preceding discussion. These latter are contained in the first thirty-three canons according to Dionysius.

For canon 5, although proposed by Aurelius in some words, is recognized as having been formed from canons 10 and 13 of the Council of Carthage under Gratus. Canons 2, 3, 4, and 6 through 13 were taken from the council under Genethlius, although in that council the names of the proposing bishops are for the most part changed. Canons 14 through 24 were derived from the council of Aurelius in the year 397, with some wording changed. The next three canons were likewise excerpted from the council of the year 401. Canon 28 was repeated from the council of the year 418, with a small addition at the end, about which we have spoken more fully in the *Observations* on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 5, part I, chapter 6, no. 27.

The five final canons, since they are found in no previously known council, are proper to this council; they were established here—that is, in this very council—in the common discussion.

50. In reporting this first session under the title of the Sixth Council of Carthage, Isidore’s collection describes only the interventions of the Fathers prefixed to the canons and distributes them into ten chapters (volume III of the Councils, column 443). According to the edition of Merlin and our manuscripts, it adds three further chapters.

In chapter 11 it describes the letter of the Africans to Boniface. In chapter 12 it reports two letters of Atticus of Constantinople and Cyril of Alexandria to the Africans, together with the Nicene canons, which Atticus had sent to Africa after they had been translated into Latin by Philo and Evaristus. In chapter 13 [Col. 0117C] the letters of the Africans to Pope Celestine are read.

Although these three chapters do not in reality belong to the first session, they were appended to the chapters proper to that session because the controversies discussed in the session itself concerning the Sardican, or Nicene, canons point toward them as their continuation.

51. Since Isidore’s collection omits the thirty-three canons mentioned above, and since they are also absent from the African council which, published separately from Dionysius’s collection, appears to contain all the African councils under Aurelius, those canons came under suspicion among some writers (ibid., column 498).

Yet it is clear from the matters discussed earlier that the author of the collection received by Isidore possessed and used these canons. For he inserted several canons from this council of the year 419 into the Second Council of Carthage under Genethlius so clearly that he retained the names of Aurelius, Alypius, and other bishops proper to this council, although they are absent from the genuine council under Genethlius.
