Similarly, in the Third Council of Carthage of the year 397, he reported several canons not with the readings proper to that council but with those which he found in the council of the year 419, as is clear, among other instances, from canon 47 concerning the canonical Scriptures. See above, § 3, no. 45. Finally, he described canon 31, proper to this council, among the canons of the council of the year 397, chapter 49.

Isidore’s collection therefore does receive these canons; it merely detached them improperly from the council of the year 419 and transferred them elsewhere. Since the published African council is nothing other than a segment of Dionysius’s collection, it cannot prejudice the integrity of Dionysius’s complete collection.

Here it should be observed that Dionysius did indeed write all the African canons in one continuous numerical series through canon 138. This series is confirmed by the pure Dionysian codex Vatican 5845, and is likewise confirmed by the Greek translation from the same Dionysius which is commonly called the Code of the Canons of the African Church.

In later codices, however, which are designated by the name of the Hadrianic collection, the same African canons are found divided into two numerical series. The first series lists thirty-three canons; the second, the remaining 105. Cresconius, who used one Dionysian collection, found this bipartite numerical series in his own codex as well; from this it is clear that the division predates Hadrian.

Those who published the African council, omitting the first series, displayed only the second from the Mainz edition of 1525, in which the Dionysian-Hadrianic collection had been printed less accurately and, in some places, even disorderly with respect to this second series.

No prejudice, therefore, can be created against the thirty-three canons which Cresconius distinctly cites. Besides Dionysius, they are most clearly vindicated by the three oldest Italian collections mentioned above. Since these collections, both by their different division of the same canons into forty canons and by their better readings, display a different and more excellent origin, we have judged that these canons should be printed from the collections themselves among the documents of the ancient canon law.

But let us now continue the description of the council.

52. After the thirty-three canons had been established, the proceedings and canons of the earlier councils under Aurelius were read—namely, those held from the year 393 through the year 418. All these materials had been inserted into the acts.

Dionysius, however, omitted some canons in their proper place because they had been repeated elsewhere; other canons, although he had not produced them anywhere else, he passed over carelessly, as can be gathered from what we noted earlier concerning the canons of the individual councils. Moreover, he did not always report certain matters in the same words in which they had been written in the acts of this council; instead, he reported them in summary and referred readers to the acts themselves.

53. The second session was held on the third day before the Kalends of June in the secretarium of the basilica of Restituta. In Dionysius it begins after canon 127 of the African Code. It contains six canons (volume II of the Councils, column 1349, c).

Isidore’s collection assigns these to the Seventh Council of Carthage. Since it combines the fifth and sixth of them—that is, canons 132 and 133 of the African Code—into one, Isidore has five canons of this council.

Ferrandus, who nowhere cites the canons of the first session, does not neglect those of the second. He designates them by their own numbers, as though this session were a separate council in his codex.

The preface of this session was counted in his codex as the first title or canon, as is clear from his *Breviatio*, no. 199. There title 2 designates the first canon, which is canon 128 in the African Code; in no. 196, title 3 cites the second canon, recorded as canon 129 in the same African Code; and similarly, in no. 197, title 4 corresponds to canon 130 of the African Code.

When, however, in no. 73 he cites under title 2 canon 132 of the African Code, the error is clear from the preceding sequence of the others under number 2, and title 6 should be restored.

54. To canon 134 of the African Code, Dionysius adds the letter of the African Fathers to Boniface, which was written on the day after the second session (volume II of the Councils, column 1356, b).

Since in this letter the same Fathers dealt with the search for genuine copies of the Nicene canons, and for this purpose sent the presbyter Innocentius to Cyril of Alexandria and the subdeacon Marcellus to Atticus of Constantinople, Dionysius adds, as canons 135 and 136, the letters of these bishops. Through the same legates they sent the Africans copies of the Nicene canons drawn from the archives of their respective churches and translated into Latin.

These copies were sent to the aforementioned Boniface on the sixth day before the Kalends of December of the same year, 419. Only the version prepared by Philo and Evaristus of Constantinople survives.

In the first form of Dionysius’s work, which we have found in manuscript Vatican Palatine 577, both the Nicene Creed and the canons of this version are described. In the second recension of Dionysius, however, preserved in manuscript Vatican 5845 and in the published Code of the Church of Africa, he omitted the canons and supplied only the Nicene [CII] Creed of the same translation as canon 137.

In Isidore, only the canons are read, which he reports after Atticus’s letter in what he calls the Sixth Council of Carthage. The Nicene profession of faith which he had supplied shortly before is not from this version but from the ancient African version; concerning it, see what we said in chapter 2, § 1.

55. The three oldest Italian collections mentioned earlier, after the letter of the Africans to Boniface and before the letters of Atticus and Cyril to the Africans, give this note:

> “Here begins the letter of Atticus, bishop of the Church of Constantinople, to Boniface, bishop of the city of Rome, sent together with copies of the Council of Nicaea translated from Greek into Latin by the most blessed bishops Cyril and Atticus of the Churches of Alexandria and Constantinople, and sent through their presbyter Innocentius and Asellus—read Marcellus—the subdeacon of the Church of Carthage, as was recited above. The faith of the Council of Nicaea is in title 20.”

The letter itself is as follows:

> “Atticus, bishop of the Church of Constantinople, sends greetings to the holy brother Boniface, bishop of the city of Rome. I have issued the canons of the holy Fathers, written in my own hand and subscribed by me. Amen.”

A formula for writing the *formata* is then appended; it is described in chapter 63 of the collection to be published in this volume.

Atticus did not write to Boniface but to the Africans. Since they had requested copies of the Nicene canons from Cyril and Atticus under the attestation of their letters, we should not regard this note as wholly false. Since it is read in so many very ancient collections, it clearly claims an ancient origin. We suspect that the words of Atticus which are transmitted immediately after the Nicene canons—

> “I have issued the canons of the holy Fathers, written in my own hand and subscribed by me”

—were a formula appended by Atticus himself to the canons, in order to confirm the *authentia* (αὐθεντία, authenticity) of the copy of those same canons sent to the Africans. Some ancient collector then gave them the form of a letter.

In the manuscripts of Dionysius’s Additions, which Baronius calls the Cresconian collection, and also in the very ancient collection preserved in manuscripts Barberino 2888 and Vatican 1342, these words of Atticus, after the Council of Carthage of the year 419, are presented in the form of a letter, as we have just seen. The same words are also reported after the Nicene canons in another form, one that introduces an intervention, as follows:

> “What was done at Nicaea, the metropolis of Bithynia, from the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, continued until the eighth day before the Kalends of September, in the consulship of Paulinus and Julianus, which among the Greeks is the nineteenth day of their second month, Desius, in the year [read: according to the years] 636 of Alexander.”

And in another hand:

> “Atticus, bishop of the Church of Constantinople, said: ‘I have issued the canons of the holy Fathers, written in my own hand and subscribed by me.’ Amen.”

Then the *formata* follows, which will be presented in chapter 63 of the collection to be published.

In this different form, in which Atticus’s words are introduced as an intervention, if the word *said* is deleted, his autograph subscription is displayed—the subscription by which he confirmed the Nicene canons transmitted by him:

> “I, Atticus, bishop of the Church of Constantinople, have issued the canons of the holy Fathers, written in my own hand and subscribed by me. Amen.”

Similarly, in manuscript 55 of the Veronese chapter, the subscription of Aurelius appended to the *Breviary of the Canons of Hippo* is introduced as an intervention:

> “Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, said: ‘These decisions having been confirmed by us … I have subscribed, and the others likewise.’”

Here the word *said* was wrongly inserted.

The words *olographa manu* (“in an autograph hand,” literally “by a handwritten hand”) used by Atticus are an ancient formula signifying that something was written or subscribed in one’s own hand and was authentic.

Saint Hilary, in fragment 2, says:

> “He wrote in his own hand the copy of the letter which Valens sent after the announcement by the Easterners that Athanasius was not guilty in the city of Rome, and Ursacius subscribed it.”

An ancient author of the commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians among the works of Saint Ambrose, chapter 6, says:

> “For where there is an autograph hand, it cannot be called false.”

Pope Julius I, against the Arians, in a letter to the Easterners preserved by Saint Athanasius, mentions Ischyras’s *cheira holographon authentiken* (χεῖρα ὁλόγραφον αὐθεντικήν), that is, “an authentic writing in his own hand” (Athanasius, *Apology* 2).

Atticus’s original subscription is therefore expressed by those words of his, to which the *formata* was appended. More will be said about this in chapter 63 of the collection to be published. There we shall also see that after the *formata* the clause “The canons are completed” (*Expliciunt canones*) was added. These words confirm that both Atticus’s subscription and the *formata* were appended to the version of the Nicene canons sent by Atticus to the Africans, in order to prove the *authentia* of that version. [CIII]

Since a copy of this version, apparently fortified by Atticus’s subscription and the *formata*, was sent by the Africans to Boniface through the presbyter Innocentius and the subdeacon Marcellus, together with the letters of Atticus and Saint Cyril, the ancient author of the note mentioned above omitted the letters of Atticus and Cyril and, indicating only the canons, composed a letter from Atticus’s subscription according to his own judgment. He prefixed to it a rubric in which, wishing to adapt to his own letter the title found in African manuscripts before the genuine letters of Atticus and Cyril, he transferred many things incorrectly.

The genuine title is expressed in the Hispanic and Isidorian collections in these words:

> “Here begin the rescripts to the African council of Cyril, bishop of Alexandria”—the Escorial codex properly adds, “and of Atticus, bishop of Constantinople”—“in which they sent an authentic copy of the Council of Nicaea, translated from Greek through the presbyter Innocentius. These letters, together with the same Council of Nicaea, were sent through the aforementioned presbyter Innocentius and Marcellus, subdeacon of the Church of Carthage, to Saint Boniface, bishop of the Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of December” (volume II of the Councils, column 1362, note 2).

Dionysius likewise reports this in canon 135 of the African Code.

Just as the old author undoubtedly found this title in the manuscripts of the council and, in the note mentioned above, handled it in his own way, so there can be no doubt that he found in the same codices Atticus’s subscription, to which he improperly gave the form of a letter.

[Col. 0120C]

56. After the letters of Cyril and Atticus, and after the Nicene Creed of the aforementioned version by Philo and Evaristus, Dionysius, in canon 138 of the African Code, reports another letter of the Africans to Celestine, since it belongs to the same controversy debated at the council of the year 419.

For the same reason this letter is likewise read in Isidore at the end of the Sixth Council of Carthage. Since, however, this letter concerns another later council—namely, as we shall see, the twentieth council—the discussion of it will return in the following paragraph.

## § 9. On the Eighteenth, Nineteenth, and Twentieth Councils of Carthage under Aurelius; on the Council of Hippo Regius of the Year 427; on Other Councils of the Province of Byzacena Cited by Ferrandus; on What a Complete Code of the Canons of the African Church Ought to Have Contained; and Observations on the Commonly Published Code of the Canons of the African Church

**57.** The eighteenth council of Carthage under Aurelius was held in the year 421, on the Ides of June. We found it in manuscript 55 of the Chapter of Verona, from which it will be published among the documents of ancient canon law. From its preface we learn that, because of some necessity—although its nature is not explained—the solemn celebration of the council had ceased for two years, and that the statutes of the preceding councils had been reread and were to be inserted in the pages of the present council. This also confirms the custom of the African Church of repeating earlier decrees. In the manuscript, however, none of the earlier decrees is inserted. Only ten canons established in the same council are appended; these, nevertheless, were repeated from the council of the preceding year, 419, except for the fourth canon alone, which appears to belong specifically to this council. Compare the annotations that we shall append to that council.

**58.** The nineteenth council under Aurelius is cited by the Council of Carthage of the year 525, which quotes one of its canons. Ferrandus (vol. V of the Councils, col. 781) cites the same canon in no. 34, title 3. We have no other information about this council. As to its date, it seems to have been held after the year 421, when the eighteenth council took place, and before the year 425, when the twentieth council was held.

In no. 47 Ferrandus recalls a canon prescribing that bishops should not sell Church property without the advice of the primate, and he cites the Council of Carthage, title 5, and the Council of Hippo, title 9. Since this canon is not found among the canons of Hippo of 393, and since title 9 of the Breviary of Hippo contains another canon, the latter citation indicates—as we shall note shortly—the Council of Hippo of the year 427.

The earlier citation, “Council of Carthage, title 5,” indicating an earlier Council of Carthage, would indeed fit the eighteenth council, in which the same canon is plainly found with the primate expressly named. But since Ferrandus cites title 5, whereas in the eighteenth council this canon appears under title 9, unless a scribal error is concealed in the number 5, another Council of Carthage [CIV] is indicated, in which the same canon was repeated under title 5. It must therefore be assigned to the nineteenth or twentieth Council of Carthage.

Again, in no. 53 Ferrandus gives another canon, by which it was decreed that no excommunicated bishop, priest, or deacon should communicate. He cites the Council of Carthage, title 8—or, as the Corbie manuscript has it, title 9. This canon does indeed occur in the seventeenth Council of Carthage of 419 and in the eighteenth of 421, but not under title 8 or 9: in the former it is under title 29, and in the latter under title 1. It must therefore be believed to have been repeated under title 8 or 9 in one or the other of the nineteenth and twentieth councils, from one of which Ferrandus cited it.

**59.** The council under Boniface gives a brief account of one canon of the twentieth Council of Carthage: “That no one should dare to appeal overseas.” Since, in no. 143, Ferrandus cites another canon—“That councils be held twice a year in each province”—as belonging to the Council of Carthage, title 3, we believe that he is referring to this twentieth council. For this decree is altogether absent from the earlier councils down to the eighteenth. Another canon, however, is assigned by the same Ferrandus in no. 84, title 3, to the nineteenth council. Therefore only the missing twentieth council could have contained this canon under title 3.

Moreover, since the council of Boniface, in the canon that it reports in abbreviated form, dealt with appeals overseas, it is sufficiently likely that the same council also wrote the letter to Pope Celestine in which an appeal overseas is indeed discussed. For this reason, this twentieth Council of Carthage was held in the year 425 or 426, when learned scholars show that the letter to Celestine was sent. See, among others, Father Constantius, volume I of the *Epistles of the Roman Pontiffs*, col. 1058, note 6.

**60.** In numbers 34, 35, 38, 47, 54, 95, and 198, Ferrandus assigns several titles or canons to the Council of Hippo Regius which are found neither among the canons of the Council of Hippo of 393 nor in its Breviary. Another Council of Hippo, therefore, which is otherwise missing, must be admitted.

That this later council took place after 421 is sufficiently indicated by Ferrandus himself: in no. 47 he first cites the Council of Carthage, title 5—a title which, as we have seen in no. 2, belongs to the nineteenth council, held after 421—and then adds the Council of Hippo, title 9, which by the very order of the citations must be later than the nineteenth Council of Carthage.

Father Hardouin, in fact, mentions two manuscripts, one belonging to Pierre Pithou, the other to the College of the Society of Jesus at Paris. The latter manuscript, containing an epitome of the canons, is especially important, since it derives neither from Dionysius nor from any other collection known to us, but from the same African sources from which Ferrandus obtained his information about the African councils, as is clear from the annotations in § 5, no. 4.

In these two manuscripts the Council of Hippo is said to have been held in the year 427. For they read as follows:

> “In the consulship of Pierius and Ardabures, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, in the Basilica Leonina, it pleased the whole council, etc.”

(Vol. II of the Councils, col. 1275, note 4.) The Basilica of Hippo, which was called Leonina, is designated here. Since Aurelius was still alive in the year 427, when Pierius and Ardabures held the consulship, this council must certainly be counted among those celebrated under Aurelius, and it may be designated the twenty-first.

Two canons of this council, cited by Ferrandus in numbers 54 and 198, are identified by Hardouin from the manuscripts just mentioned; he notes that they were repeated from the Council of Carthage of 419, canons 29 and 30 of the African Code.

We, however, found all the canons of this same council cited by Ferrandus in another Council of Carthage of the year 421, which will appear in print in this volume. For the canon cited by Ferrandus in no. 54, title 3, which is also assigned to the Council of Hippo in Hardouin’s manuscripts, is canon 1 in the council of 421.

Ferrandus assigns two canons to title 5: one in no. 34 and the other in no. 198. An error has entered the number of one of them. We believe that in no. 198 the title should be corrected to title 4. For the canon indicated by that number properly follows the preceding canon marked title 3, and it is indeed placed after it both in the African Code, chapter 30, and in the council of 421, canon 2.

Furthermore, the title 5 cited by Ferrandus in no. 34 is found only in the council of 421, as its canon 4. Another canon, which Ferrandus assigns to the Council of Hippo Regius in no. 35, title 8, is found in the African Code, chapter 32, and in the Council of 421, canon 5.

Ferrandus divides the ninth canon of Hippo Regius, which is found in the African Code, chapter 33, into three numbers: in no. 95 he cites its first part; in no. 47 [CV], its second; and in no. 38, its third. In the council of 421 this canon forms two canons, 9 and 10.

It should be observed here that the passage cited by Ferrandus in no. 47—“That bishops should not sell Church property without the advice of the primate”—is expressed in the Council of 419, chapter 33 of the African Code, in these words:

> “Bishops are not permitted to sell Church estates without the knowledge of the council or of their own priests,”

in which the name of the primate does not appear. In the repetition of the same canon in the year 421, however, this name was substituted for the words “their own priests,” as will be clear from the council of that year, which we are about to publish, chapter 9.

The same decree was likewise renewed in another Council of Carthage, the nineteenth or twentieth, title 5, and in the Council of Hippo Regius, title 9; for Ferrandus cites both councils under the same number, 47.

**[Col. 0122C] 61.** The same Ferrandus cites eight other councils of the province of Byzacena: the Council of Suffetula in no. 2; the Council of Thusdrus in numbers 76 and 77; the Council of Junca in no. 26; the Council of Macriana in numbers 11 and 23; the Council of Septiminus in numbers 11, 56, 76, 139, 212, and 215; the Council of Thenita in numbers 61, 76, and 194; the Council of Marazana, or Maradiana, in numbers 44, 76, 127, and 220; and the Council of Zella, or Tiella, in numbers 3, 4, 6, 16, 65, 68, 130, 138, 174, and 218.

All appear to have been provincial councils. This is certainly clear in the case of the Council of Marazana, for the canon cited in no. 220 concerns a single province of Byzacena.

It is especially worthy of observation that, when identifying these councils, Ferrandus never designates the number of their titles or canons. This seems to have been his practice whenever the African councils were not plenary but provincial, as we also observed to have occurred with the provincial Council of Carthage of the year 409. This observation plainly confirms that the other African councils, including the Councils of Milevis and Hippo Regius of the year 427, which Ferrandus cites with the numbers of their titles, were plenary.

These councils of Byzacena repeatedly reproduce the same canon in accordance with African usage, as is especially clear from Ferrandus’s no. 76, where he assigns the same decree to four Byzacene councils.

Whenever Ferrandus cites the Council of Zella or Tiella, which others call the Council of Tellis or Telepte, he generally adds that it derives from a letter of Siricius, because the canons concern two letters of that pontiff which were read at the same council and inserted into its acts. The portion of this Council of Zella preserved for us in the Gallican collections contains only one letter of Siricius. What Ferrandus mentions in addition from the same council or from another letter of Siricius we shall list in the observations on Quesnel’s Dissertation 15, concerning the Council of Telepte.

The date of this council is clear from the preface prefixed to it: namely, the year 418. Whether the other Byzacene councils mentioned also belong to approximately the same period, or whether, as others think, they should be assigned to a later age, cannot be determined, since nothing of them survives except certain canons mentioned by Ferrandus (vol. III of the Councils, col. 461), which Baluzius carefully collected.

Since Africa was excessively afflicted after the invasion of the Vandals, such a frequency of Byzacene councils—as presupposes a time of peace—seems to belong to an earlier age. If, nevertheless, the Council of Carthage of the year 525 was celebrated under the Vandals, its preface sufficiently indicates that the ancient custom of holding councils had returned when liberty was restored. Victor of Tunnuna in his *Chronicle*, and the author of the *Life of Saint Fulgentius*, chapter 28, attribute this restoration to Hilderic.

In the same preface, a certain bishop whose name is lost addresses Boniface, the bishop of Carthage, in these words:

> “Fulfill, we beseech you, diligently the duties of your ministry, so that the general welfare of the African Church and the vigor of the holy canons may flourish again; and may your blessedness now restore what Aurelius, of blessed memory, the bishop of this city, established. For the Lord has appointed you his successor in honor, liberty, and peace.”

These words plainly suggest that, from the death of Aurelius onward, the ability to convene councils had ceased; and therefore the Byzacene councils mentioned above appear to have been held during the lifetime of Aurelius.

That the Council of Thusdrus was convened shortly before the Council of Zella of 418 is indicated by the words of Vincentius and Fortunatianus in the preface of the Council of Zella:

> “Even when we were at Thusdrus, as your recollection, which remembers with me, recalls, and we had given letters of the bishop of the apostolic see, Siricius of holy memory, to be read, etc.”

These words indicate that the Council of Thusdrus had been held shortly beforehand.

It may seem surprising that Ferrandus cites so many councils of the province of Byzacena, yet says nothing about the councils which, in the other provinces of Africa—and especially in Numidia—there is no doubt were convened through the zeal of Augustine, Alypius, and Possidius [CVI]. We believe that this should be attributed to the fact that, amid the Vandal disturbances by which the whole of Africa was devastated, the records of the councils of the other provinces perished or were scattered, and that the councils of the province of Byzacena alone came into Ferrandus’s hands.

**62.** From what has been discussed thus far it is clear which canons and which councils were contained in the Code—or in those Codes of the canons of the African Church—which were used in the sixth century by Ferrandus, deacon of the Church of Carthage, and at the Council of Boniface in 525.

Besides the twofold version of the Council of Nicaea—one, namely, the most ancient version received from Caecilianus, and the more recent one received from Atticus of Constantinople—they also contained the councils of Gratus and Genethlius; the complete Council of Hippo of 393, from which two complete canons are quoted in the Council of Boniface; in addition, twenty other councils under Aurelius; another Council of Hippo of 427; and several councils of the province of Byzacena.

A complete Code of the canons of the African Church ought to have contained all these councils.

The material that Dionysius Exiguus drew from the African canons was taken from the seventeenth council, held under Aurelius in 419. In that council the earlier councils, together with their acts, from the Council of Hippo of 393 through the sixteenth council of 418, were repeated and inserted.

But apart from the fact that councils earlier than Aurelius were omitted, while those held later could not yet be included, Dionysius, in listing those very councils whose acts had been inserted into the acts of the Council of 419, although he transcribed many of them in full, nevertheless—so as to avoid the repetition of canons characteristic of the Africans—passed over certain canons once stated when they were repeated elsewhere, sometimes skipped others inadvertently, reported some in abbreviated form, and in other cases referred readers to the acts. This is clear from the foregoing annotations, and Father Coustantius also discussed it at length in the preface to volume I of the *Epistles of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. XCIV and following.

This work of Dionysius was translated into Greek and transferred into Greek collections somewhat before the Council in Trullo, held in the year 692, which in chapter 2 lists the Carthaginian canons among the canons of the Greek Code.

**[Col. 0124A] 63.** We have considered these matters worth noting in order to make clear how improperly Christopher Justellus prefixed to this Greek interpretation of the African canons the general title *Code of the Canons of the African Church*, since it does not even contain exactly all the acts inserted into the Council of Carthage of 419.

He extracted the Greek version from the Greek collection of the canons published by Tilius, and added variant readings from the Royal and Palatine manuscripts, as he states in the notes on p. 418. He took the Latin text from the collection of Dionysius itself, which was contained in the manuscript of Nicolas Faber, and added variants from two other manuscripts, the Thuaneus and the Bochardianus, which presented the first thirty-three canons of the Council of Carthage of 419 distributed among forty titles.

But neither the Greek version nor those two Latin manuscripts, nor any other Latin manuscripts, bore the title *Code of the Canons of the African Church*. For in the Greek collection the following inscription is found:

> **Κανόνες τῶν ἐν Καρθαγένῃ συνελθόντων διακοσίων δέκα καὶ ἑπτὰ ἁγίων καὶ μακαρίων Πατέρων**  
> *Canons of the two hundred and seventeen holy and blessed Fathers who assembled at Carthage.*

In the Latin text of Dionysius as printed by Justellus:

> *Council of the Africans at Carthage, which established 138 canons.*

Moreover, in his dedicatory letter to Stephen, bishop of Salona, Dionysius undertook to provide not a *Code of the Canons* but the *Statutes of the African Council*.

These matters had to be discussed more fully in order to elucidate the canons and councils of Africa.

---

## [CVII] CHAPTER IV

### On the Oldest Collection of Canons Yet Discovered, in Vatican manuscript Regina 1997; on the Councils Celebrated under Symmachus; on Establishing the Date of the Palmarian Synod; and on Two *Epistolae Formatae* Published from the Same Manuscript

**1.** We are now going to discuss collections that are either older than the collection of Dionysius or derive from sources different from those used by Dionysius. We first point out that certain passages of Dionysius are indeed found in some of the collections to be presented in this second part. Since, however, the whole body of those collections and of the documents contained in them derives from other, non-Dionysian sources, we believe that these passages of Dionysius were generally inserted later by another hand, rather than being supplied by the authors of the collections themselves.

For later scribes, when copying an ancient manuscript, did not hesitate at times to alter, add, and insert certain things at their discretion—things that should not be attributed to the compiler. There is no lack of evidence of additions in our collections. Some are found affixed at the beginning, others at the end. Certain readings in the versions of the Greek canons, taken from the Dionysian version, have also been intruded into the interpretation of the *Prisca*, which the author of the collection had transcribed from the beginning.

The origin of collections must be judged not from these inserted and supplementary passages, but from the nature, order, and whole body of their documents. Nor can there be doubt that collections which, in their very composition, do not agree with the Dionysian collection have an origin different from Dionysius.

Clear evidence of this different origin is supplied by the collections to be reviewed in this second part. Their versions of the Greek canons differ from the Dionysian version. Quite a number of documents are found in them that are absent from Dionysius. The very documents that they share with the Dionysian collection are presented not only in a different order, with a different division and different titles and annotations, but also with different and sometimes better readings.

Certain passages omitted by Dionysius have been preserved for us in these collections, and many other matters will be pointed out in their description which will commend not merely their difference from the Dionysian collection but also their superiority.

We divide these collections into two classes. Some are general and contain together the canons of councils and the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs; others contain only decretal letters relating to a fairly definite matter.

**[Col. 0125A] 2.** Among the collections of the first type, we have discovered the oldest of all in the manuscript Vatican Regina 1997; for its more recent documents are the three councils held under Symmachus.

Since a catalogue of the Roman bishops follows the first council of that pontiff, held in the year 499, the original collection seems to have ended at that council. It may perhaps have been arranged before the two other councils of the same pontiff took place; these were added later, after the catalogue of the Roman bishops, which ends with Hormisdas, the successor of Symmachus.

The codex is almost square in format, and each page is divided into two columns. Its script is an ancient rapid hand, commonly called Lombardic. The same codex subsequently received certain additions, some few of which were written in the same ancient script, while others were written in a more recent but still old script, as will become clear from what follows.

The excellence of this collection is demonstrated by the monuments themselves. For nothing spurious is detected in the original collection. Moreover, certain documents otherwise unknown were preserved in this one collection alone.

Its Greek councils are in the ancient version. Only the Nicene council has a distinct translation, which we shall publish in this volume among the unpublished versions. The Sardican canons are joined to the Nicene canons in a continuous numerical series and are presented under the title of the Nicene canons. Other distinctive features will be noted in their proper places.

We infer that this collection is Italian because, from as early as the tenth century, this codex—which later passed into the library of Saint Sylvester at Nonantola—belonged to the Church of Chieti, as is indicated by the *epistola formata* (letter of communion) of the bishop of Chieti, copied in a more recent script on the first page of the codex and to be appended at the end of this chapter.

**3.** This collection begins with the canons of Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, and Antioch in the *Prisca* version; a table of chapters is prefixed to each of them. That nothing is missing at the beginning is made clear by the fact that the original script begins on the verso of page 1 with this title:

> “In the name of the Lord. Here begin the titles of the canons of Ancyra.”

We have made useful use of this outstanding collection in editing the *Prisca* version.

After the Antiochene canons, *Responses and Constitutions enacted at Carthage* are transcribed. This is the Council of Carthage of 419, held on the eighth day before the Kalends of June and divided into forty canons, which we shall give among the documents of the ancient canon law, no. 1.

The Africans’ letter to Boniface follows, with this heading:

> “Here begins the letter written by the whole council mentioned above to Boniface, bishop of the city of Rome”—read, “written by the whole council mentioned above to Boniface, bishop of the city of Rome”—“and with the acts which, having been drawn up there at Carthage, were sent through Faustinus the bishop and Philippus and Asellus the priests.”

(Vol. II of the Councils, col. 1356, c.)

The letter itself begins, “Since it has pleased the Lord,” etc., as it is found in the African Code, chapter 134.

Next follows the letter of Atticus, bishop of the Church of Constantinople, to Boniface, etc., together with the formula for the *formatae* (letters of communion); we have said more about these in chapter 3, § 8, no. 9.

Then comes the letter of Aurelius and the other Africans to Celestine:

> “We would wish, if indeed your holiness were greatly concerned about the arrival of Apiarius,” etc.

See the African Code, chapter 138.

The Chalcedonian canons follow, and then the Constantinopolitan canons in the *Prisca* version; on these, compare our edition of that same version.

The canons of the councils conclude with the Nicene and Sardican canons, joined to the Nicene canons and inscribed under the same Nicene title. All of them are divided into forty-six canons.

The translation of the Nicene canons is not the *Prisca*, as it is in the other Greek canons, but another most ancient version hitherto unknown, which we shall publish from this codex after the *Prisca*. See the admonition prefixed to it, where we shall note the matters that especially require attention in this version.

Since our compiler, apart from the Nicene canons—which he received from a special, most ancient, and apparently Italian translation—used the *Prisca* version for the other Greek canons, he omitted the Laodicean canons because he did not find them at all in that version. See above, chapter 2, § 3, no. 17.

**4.** As for the enactments of the Roman pontiffs, which follow the canons, the letter of Siricius to Himerius of Tarragona is transcribed first; it is printed in the collection in this volume, chapter 29.

Then follows the letter of Leo to Rusticus of Narbonne, together with Rusticus’s questions, which are absent from Dionysius. In our edition it is letter 167.

Another letter of the same pontiff to the Africans, in the abridged edition, is our letter 12, volume I, col. 669.

Another is addressed to Flavianus, our letter 28. Likewise, one to Torribius, letter 15; one to the Sicilians, letter 16; and one to Nicetas, letter 159.

Next comes the letter of Innocent I to Victor of Rouen, chapter 24 of our collection; the letter of Celestine to the bishops established throughout the provinces of Vienna and Narbonne, chapter 35 in the same collection; and the *Statutes of Saint Gelasius the Bishop to the Bishops Established throughout All the Provinces*, chapter 58 in the same collection.

Then follow the *Acts concerning Acacius*, beginning:

> “In the case of the Christian faith, whose enemies are proved never to have been absent from its very beginning,” etc.

This is the fuller history that Sirmond published from the Verdun manuscript; it is also found from that source in volume V of the Councils, Venetian edition, col. 173. A shorter version is found in our collection, chapter 43; see note 1 there.

The letter of Jerome to the priest Evangelus is inserted:

> “We read in Isaiah,” etc.,

as it appears in volume I of Saint Jerome’s works, Veronese edition, letter 146, formerly 85.

The letters of Innocent to Exsuperius, bishop of Toulouse, follow in chapter 21 of our collection; and another of the same pontiff to Rufus and the other Macedonian bishops, in chapter 22.

Next come the letter of Zosimus to Hesychius, bishop of Salona, chapter 32; that of Celestine to the bishops of Apulia and Calabria, chapter 36; and that of Boniface to the Emperor Honorius:

> “My Church, which our God,” etc.,

as in volume III of the Councils, col. 434.

The rescript of Honorius to the same pontiff follows:

> “The writing of your blessedness,” etc.,

in the same place, col. 436.

The law of the Emperor Glycerius, to be added to the *Novels*, and the edict of Himelco, the prefect of the praetorium, against simoniacs, will be made public among the documents of the ancient canon law, no. 6.

Then comes the letter of Pope Leo to the bishop of Aquileia, our letter 1; and another of the same pontiff to Bishop Septimus [CIX], in our edition, letter 2.

The First Roman Council under Symmachus, of the year 499, begins:

> “After the consulship of Paulinus, a man of clarissimus rank, on the day of the Kalends of March, in the Basilica of the Blessed Apostle Peter.”

The names of the bishops are prefixed, and the rest follows, together with the booklet of John the deacon to Symmachus, as Baluzius published it from the manuscript formerly belonging to Nicolas Faber and now numbered Colbert 1863. See volume V of the Councils, col. 446 and following.

The original collection appears to end here.

**5.** A catalogue of the Roman pontiffs follows, extending to Hormisdas, to whom nine years and eighteen days are assigned. After the death of Hormisdas, the following additions were made.

The *Constitutum* of Symmachus concerning the preservation of Church property. This is another council of the year 502, which appears in the same volume V, col. 471.

The king’s third order, sent to the council. It begins:

> “The order which was sent through the bishops Germanus and Carosus,” etc.,

dated on the sixth day before the Ides of August, in the consulship of Rufius Magnus Faustus Avienus, a man of clarissimus rank; ibid., col. 463. The commonly published texts, however, omit the title with the numeral III.

The king’s fourth order, sent to the council—read, “the fourth order”—begins:

> “King Theodoricus to all the bishops summoned to the council,” etc.,

dated on the sixth day before the Kalends of September, in the consulship of Rufius Avienus Fausius, a man of clarissimus rank; ibid., col. 464. It was not “Rufinus,” as is incorrectly read in the commonly published editions of the councils.

The third and fourth orders presuppose two other earlier ones. These may perhaps have been omitted because only those relating to the subsequent famous council were found together with the acts of that council.

The bishops’ report to the king follows:

> “We give thanks to God,” etc.,

ibid., col. 465.

Then comes a royal order:

> “King Theodoricus to all the bishops summoned to the council. It was indeed fitting,” etc.,

dated under the day of the Kalends of October; ibid., col. 466.

In the commonly published texts, from the aforementioned manuscript Colbert 1863, the following is appended:

> “To the ecclesiastical council, the king’s distinguished reader: The bishops are first to be greeted,” etc.;

and at the end:

> “Either let them themselves exact punishment, or let those whom we appoint pursue the offenses according to the laws.”

A very corrupt passage is noted here. Our codex, however, indicates the correction and reads as follows:

> “Reg. Ind. Ecl. qs Agnostic. Regis. First, the bishops are to be greeted,” etc.;

and at the end:

> “Either let them themselves exact punishment, or let those whom we appoint pursue the offenses according to the laws.”

The first abbreviated words of the title, *Reg. Ind.*, denote a *regium indiculum*, that is, an instruction issued by the king. Thus, too, the instruction given to the legates by Hormisdas is called an *indiculus* in volume V of the Councils, col. 612. See another example there, col. 655. Let more expert scholars interpret the remainder of the same title.

All these documents, which have been published in the same order from the single Colbert manuscript, may be corrected in other places from our codex.

Afterward follow the *Constitutions of the Bishops* in the council held at Rome by order of Theodoricus, in the consulship of Rufius Magnus Faustus Avienus, on the tenth day before the Kalends of November:

> “A council at the city of Rome,” etc.,

ibid., col. 457.

This consulship, which assigns the council itself to the year 501, cannot be called into question. For it is read not only in most manuscript copies of the Hadrianic collection, in all the Isidorian copies, and in the aforementioned Colbert manuscript, but also in Vatican 5845 among the Additions to Dionysius, and in our collection, Vatican Regina, the oldest of all and nearly contemporary with Symmachus, which gives it the greatest authority.

Add to this that the same consulship is also noted and confirmed in the two aforementioned orders of Theodoricus, which were written in the same year and refer to the same council.

6. P. Antonius Pagius, under the year 503, no. 2 and following, considers this consular notation an addition inserted by some ignorant person. No one will deny that this could have happened in a single document, and in the manuscripts of a single collection. But that the same thing should have occurred in three documents and in collections of different origins, and those of the greatest antiquity, with the authors of all these collections conspiring in the same insertion, is plainly incredible. Four codices—or rather five—belonging to collections of different origins, which we indicated shortly before [Col. 0127C], give the synod together with this consulship. The two edicts of Theodoric that concern this very synod likewise give the same consulship in the two manuscript collections in which they have so far been found: namely, in our Vatican Regina collection and in another, that of the aforementioned Colbertinus.

This consulship is indeed absent from the Sangermanensis codex of the Hadriana collection, which Pagius sets against it, and likewise from the Vallicellanus A. 5, among the documents of the same collection. But Isidore, who used an older copy of the Hadriana, found the consulship in it. Moreover, codex Vat. 5845, which represents the synods under Symmachus among the additions to the Dionysiana before they were inserted into the Hadriana collection, also gives the same consulship. From this it is clear that the absence of the consulship in certain Hadrianic codices must be attributed to omission. Thus the agreement of so many codices and collections in recording this consulship does not permit us to doubt the year of that synod.

In the place cited, Pagius brings forward codices in which this synod is called the Palmary Synod, is called the fourth, and is placed after the synod celebrated in the year 502. But the word “fourth,” marked in only certain codices, does not appear at all in our Vatican Regina codex, in Vat. 5845, or in other Hadrianic codices. Certainly, the codices that present the genuine synods under Symmachus report only three; none reports four.

If someone should regard as two distinct synods the two proceedings held in the same year, 501, at the king’s command before the Palmary proceeding—proceedings in which nothing could be concluded—one of which was held [Note: Vol. V of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 458, c.] in the basilica of Julius after the Paschal feast, and the other [Note: Vol. V of the Councils, col. 459, b.] in the Sessorian basilica at the beginning of September [Note: This synod was summoned for the Kalends of September; ibid., col. 463, c.], just as the proceeding held in the Sessorian basilica [Col. 0128A] is called the second synod in the bishops’ report to the king [Note: Ibid., col. 465, c.], then the third proceeding, or Palmary Synod, convened on the tenth day before the Kalends of November, could be called the third synod of the year 501; and, in relation to the earlier synod of the year 499, it could have been entitled the fourth synod.

As for the order, although most manuscripts present this synod in the last place, it is different in Vatican codex 5845. For there the same synod is described first. In other codices, however, the two synods of the years 499 and 502 could have been placed before this council because, in these collections of canons, the synods that establish disciplinary canons seemed preferable and were joined together; then the synod concerning Symmachus’s absolution was added, even though it had been celebrated in the intervening period.

Pagius presses into service the testimony of Theodorus the Reader from Book II of his History, where the following is read:

> “When this kind of disturbance had continued in the city of Rome for three years—not, as in the common version, for three consecutive years—after the ordination of Saint Symmachus and Laurence, Theodoric the African, who was then reigning at Rome, although he was an Arian by sect, nevertheless, after convening a synod, confirmed Symmachus in the episcopate of the City, while he appointed Laurence bishop of a certain city called Nuceria. Laurence, however, did not rest at all; rather, he continued to seek the episcopate of the city of Rome. For this reason Symmachus arranged for him to be deposed and sent into exile; and in this way the sedition was quelled.”

Pagius, however, on the hypothesis of four synods under Symmachus, thinks that this passage refers to a second synod of the year 500, which had perished, and which, after confirming Symmachus’s episcopate, placed Laurence over the Church of Nuceria. He assigns the Palmary Synod, which he regards as the fourth, to the year 503, believing that after three years a second schism was formed against Symmachus.

Once this supposed second synod is rejected—for there is no indication of it anywhere—the passage of Theodorus must be understood of the Palmary Synod held, as we have seen, in the year 501, at which Symmachus was confirmed [Col. 0128C] as Roman bishop. The fact that the same Theodorus, a Greek writer, reports Laurence as having been appointed bishop of the Church of Nuceria at approximately the same time must be attributed to his confusion. For Anastasius the Librarian states quite clearly that this happened immediately after King Theodoric’s judgment at the beginning of the year 499. After describing Theodoric’s judgment, by which Symmachus was made bishop, he adds:

> “At the same time Pope Symmachus convened a synod and appointed Laurence bishop in the city of Nuceria, out of consideration for mercy.”

The same point is stated even more clearly by the Anonymous author favorable to Laurence, whose fragment was published by Franciscus Blanchinius and subsequently reprinted more accurately by P. Joseph, his brother’s son, in the *Enarratio pseudo-Athanasiana*, p. 104. From this contemporary writer, although hostile to Pope Symmachus, the whole question can be settled. We learn from him that Symmachus and Laurence were ordained after the death of Anastasius II; that a schism arose for this reason; that both proceeded to Theodoric, by whose judgment Symmachus obtained the episcopate, while Laurence was sent to govern the Church of Nuceria, a city of Campania, [Col. 0128D] …

If this was done at a synod, as Anastasius relates, it must be attributed to the synod of the Kalends of March in the year 499. The Anonymous writer then continues by describing another schism, which was renewed after several years. He reports that many charges were brought against Symmachus, because of which, when a new synod had been convened by Theodoric’s edicts, the same pontiff was confirmed.

These details agree with the Palmary Synod of the year 501. He adds that Laurence’s supporters did not cease their activity—indeed, that they attacked the Palmary Synod in a pamphlet entitled *Against the Synod of Incongruous Absolution* is clear from Ennodius’s apology—[Col. 0129A] and that, when Laurence entered Rome, the schism continued for approximately four years. It was finally extinguished when, at the king’s command, Laurence withdrew to the estates of the patrician Festus—Theodorus says, “sent into exile.”

You see how well everything agrees, so that there is no need to multiply the councils, to dismiss as spurious and intrusive the consulship of Rufius Magnus Faustus Avienus, attested in so many very ancient collections, or to push the Palmary Synod back from the year 501 to the year 503.

One point remains to be mentioned. It is incredible to us that Caelius Laurence, archpresbyter of the title of Saint Praxedes, who subscribed to the synod of the year 499, was the same Laurence the presbyter who was consecrated bishop against Symmachus. These matters had to be discussed at greater length in order to clarify a controversy that is by no means simple and to vindicate our codex, which gives this consulship. We shall now continue the description of the same codex.

7. After the documents concerning Symmachus described above, the following comes next:

> “Here begins the Nicene faith.”

It is an unpublished little work of several pages, which we have had copied out and which, if God wills, we shall publish among our miscellanies at some future time. The ancient script of the codex concludes with certain statutes attributed to Pope Saint Sylvester:

> “Here begins the chapter published by Pope Sylvester when he was sitting in synod with the emperor Constantine, together with the 178 bishops and, sitting with them, 270 presbyters and 40 deacons, etc. It was decided that no layman should dare to bring a charge against a cleric except before suitable witnesses.”

There are also a few other apocryphal but ancient statutes. We believe that these were once added at the end by a later hand to this collection, which contains genuine documents, and that they were copied by our scribe in a single script.

8. The following items are added in a more recent script. A letter of Pope Gregory to Secundinus the recluse:

> “I have received the letter of your affection,” etc.

Another letter of Isidore to Bishop Masso:

> “When your religious servant Nicetius came to us,” etc.

Then follows an *Order for the Blessing of the Sacred Orders*:

> “These are the periods to be observed for each rank,” etc.

There are prefaces and formulas for each order. Finally, in still smaller script, prayers or litanies written in the ninth century, during the lifetime of Louis II and his wife Angelberga, are read. Among other things, the following appears there:

> “Hear, O Christ. R[espond]: For our lord Louis, crowned by God, the great and peaceful emperor: life and victory.”

And after a number of other petitions:

> “Hear, O Christ. R[espond]: For the empress Angelberga: health and life.”

Since Louis II was ruling in Italy, this collection is thereby confirmed as Italian.

We now present two *formatae*—formal letters—written on the first page of the codex in a more recent script. Since one of them is dated by a bishop of the Church of Teano, it indicates that the codex belonged to that same Church. See what we shall observe concerning such *formatae*, whose model is attributed to the Council of Nicaea, in annotation 1 on chapter 63 of the collection to be published.

### A Formal Letter

**IN NOM. ΠΑΤΡΗΣ ET ΦΙΛΙΗ ET ϹΡϹ ϹΚΗ** (*In the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit*). To the most holy and venerable lord, whom we name with the greatest affection, the illustrious bishop of that province, our brother in Christ the Lord.

I, the illustrious bishop, servant of Christ, humble bishop of your holy and illustrious Church, your fellow brother and devoted peacemaker, offer you in the Lord peaceful greetings for this transitory life and the future one. Finally, let your [.....]ship know that this cleric, named N., our tonsured cleric, has requested from our humility a letter of dismissal, or *formata*, so that he may be promoted by you to the sacred order. Therefore, yielding to his prayers, in accordance with the statutes of the holy Fathers of the Council of Nicaea, we send this letter of dismissal—or, as we have said, *formata*—to your fraternity and holiness, so that you may not hesitate to consecrate him to the burden of the priesthood [Col. 0130A] and return him to us.

And so that you may believe and recognize this more certainly, we have ordered it to be authenticated beneath by Greek letters together with their numerical values, according to the aforesaid council.

Fare well in the Lord, dearest and most beloved brother.

**ΠΟϹΑ**: 80, 70, 201.  
**ΠΔΜΟΛΛΩ**: indiction 15, question (?) Θ, 99.  
**ΑΜΗΝ**: 1, 48, 50.

### Another

To Celerimus (perhaps “most renowned”), a seer and most holy brother, ready in wisdom and worthy of commemoration with every honor, adorned in all things, faithful in the Lord and most learned, or adorned by all the orthodox with the grace of manifold knowledge, beloved in Christ, John. M., bishop and overseer of the holy see of the Church of Teano, …

We, the bishop of the holy see of the Church of N., in the Lord Jesus Christ, wish you great health and honor here and forever. Because of the difficulty of the journey, since I have been compelled to travel into the regions of Benevento, as the lady empress has made known by her letters, so that we may serve her—though we are already continually worn out by the affliction of our body—we consider ourselves unable to elevate the clerics of our diocese through the sacred orders.

Therefore, by this letter of our mediocrity, we entreat you to promote this present cleric of ours, Lupon, to the rank of deacons, and we send him especially to your fraternity. And so that this may be believed with greater certainty and probability, we order Greek letters to be inserted into this page according to the statutes of the holy and great Synod of Nicaea, namely, “of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.”

The first letters, **ΠΟϹΑ**, signify the numbers 80, 70, 200, and 1. The first letter of Peter, prince of the apostles, **Π**, likewise signifies 80. The first letter of our mediocrity is **Μ**; the second of your eminence, **Ο**; the third of the one who receives the order, **Π**; the fourth of our city, …; and the indiction of the present year is 15. His name is Lupon, a cleric who is to become a deacon. We have also added 98, represented by **Θ**. Through these Greek letters, **ΑΜΗΝ**, “Amen,” is indicated.

In this second *formata*, which is extremely corrupt and full of errors, we have omitted certain words indicated by dots because they yielded no sense. We have corrected a few other points ourselves, such as **M. speculator**, where the manuscript reads **inspeculator**. The bishop’s name indicated here begins with the letter M, as is stated toward the end of the *formata*; and through the easy carelessness of copyists, *in* is sometimes written for *m*. Although Ughellus’s catalogue of the bishops of the Church of Teano is [Col. 0130D] incomplete, it does not suggest the name of this bishop beginning with M.

Since an empress is mentioned who was staying in the regions of Benevento, and since the indiction is noted as 15, it appears that either Adelais, wife of Otto I, or Theophania, wife of Otto II, is meant; both were present in those regions on several occasions. For although Agilberga, wife of Louis II, was there, the fifteenth indiction does not correspond to her. Hence this bishop of Teano, M., lived under the rule of Otto I or Otto II and should be added to the catalogue of the bishops of Teano.

## CHAPTER V. On the Collection Transcribed in a Very Ancient Corbie Manuscript

1. We place this collection, transcribed in the venerably ancient Corbie manuscript codex 26, preserved in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés belonging to the Benedictine Fathers of Paris, after the Vatican-Regina collection, which we discussed in the preceding chapter. Both collections, in fact, provide a reliable witness to antiquity in the form of a catalogue of the Roman pontiffs. The Vatican-Regina collection ends with Hormisdas; the Corbie collection continues as far as Vigilius.

P. Sirmondus mentions this collection in several places and repeatedly made use of it. P. Mabillonius, in his celebrated work *De re diplomatica*, p. 356, supplied a specimen of its script, from which we learn that the codex was written in what are called uncial letters, without any spacing between words, apart from several annotations written in a rapid hand. P. Montfauconius gave us fuller information about it in *Bibliotheca Bibliothecarum*, vol. II, p. 1124, and especially P. Coustantius in the preface to volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, no. 61 and following. Since we were unable to inspect the codex itself, we shall append here what we have been able to learn from these writers.

2. After the provincial, or division of the provinces, mentioned by Montfauconius, the following note by the scribe is read at the beginning of the collection:

> “You who read, pray for me; and beware lest you transgress these rules and incur the judgment of this severity or censure.”

The title of the Ancyrean canons follows. Beneath it is the statement of Hosius that we gave in Part I, chapter 4, § 1, where we showed it to be spurious. After this statement come the Ancyrean, Neocaesarean—or, as they are called there, Caesarean—and Gangran canons, according to the ancient interpretation called Isidorian.

Between Gangran canon 20 and canon 21—or rather, before the conclusion of that synod—several items are inserted through an obvious scribal error: the letters of Innocent to Decentius; of Zosimus to Hesychius; likewise of Innocent to Victricius, to Exsuperius, and to the Macedonians; one letter of Celestine to the bishops established throughout the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne, and another to the bishops established throughout Apulia and Calabria; five letters of Leo to various bishops, which we discussed in the preface to volume I of his letters, § 3, p. 513.

Prayers of the bishops to the emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius are added. Then comes the *Brief of Statutes Pertaining to Africa*, or *Breviary of the Canons of the Council of Hippo*, which is found in the collection to be published in this volume, chapter 2; and the Council of Teles in the year 418, which you will find there in chapter 62. The conclusion of the Council of Gangra is relegated to the end of this material.

3. Next the canons of the Council of Nicaea are transcribed. The following point deserves particular notice. P. Coustantius writes in his admonition to Innocent’s Letter 17, no. 4, col. 826:

> “The Corbie codex, written in the middle of the sixth century—the date that plainly identifies the Corbie collection of which we are speaking—also agrees, and reports the Nicene canon as follows: ‘Concerning those who call themselves Cathars, that is, the Pure: if they should ever come to the Catholic Church, it has pleased the holy and great council that, after receiving the laying-on of hands, they should remain in the clergy.’”

This is the version of Dionysius Exiguus. We therefore recognize the Nicene canons as having been taken from it [Col. 0131D], not from the Isidorian version, from which the other canons of the Greek synods were received.

The names of the bishops who assembled at Nicaea follow. This catalogue of bishops is followed by the canons of the synods of Antioch, Laodicea, Constantinople, the African council of the year 418, Valence in the year 374, and Turin. These are followed by Innocent’s letter to the Council of Toulouse—or Toledo—Leo’s letter to the bishops of Vienne, our Letter 10, and Hilary’s letter to Leontius.

The canons of the Councils of Arles and Epaon are also inserted. Then come Innocent’s letters to Rufus and Eusebius and the other Macedonians; Symmachus’s letter to Caesarius of Arles; Damasus’s letter to Paulinus of Antioch; and Augustine’s address to the candidates for baptism.

Next follow the names of the bishops who assembled under Marinus at the Council of Arles; Paulinus’s letter to Faustus; the definition of the Council of Chalcedon; Flavian’s letter to Pope Leo; and Leo’s reply, our Letters 22 and 28.

[Col. 0132A] 4. Other documents of the same kind are subsequently added, together with the canons of mostly Gallican synods. No one has reported an exact knowledge of these synods or of the order in which they are listed in the codex. P. Sirmondus alone noted in the preface to the *Councils of Gaul* that ten Gallican synods are presented in this collection, the last of which is the Fifth Council of Orléans, held in the year 549.

“From this,” says Coustantius, “it is not obscure that this collection was the work of some diligent man living in Gaul. It seems that this person did not intend to copy out some particular codex of canons, but to gather as many writings of that kind as he could find that pertained to the rules of discipline.”

Among these documents [CXIV] is the celebrated *Breviary of the Canons* by Fulgentius Ferrandus, which has so far been found only in this copy and in another at Troyes. Montfauconius further mentions a single addition distinguished by a later script, namely the Fourth Council of Paris, held in the year 573. This Gallican document, later than the age of Vigilius, confirms that the collection was enlarged in Gaul and made Gallican.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Collection Contained in the Two Manuscripts Lucanus 88 and Colbertinus 784

1. This collection, which P. Coustantius used in publishing the letters of the Roman pontiffs and P. Mansius in the *Supplement to the Councils*, was also useful to us in reprinting the *Code of Canons* and the *Prisca* edition.

The Colbertinus codex, consulted by P. Coustantius, is described by him in the frequently cited preface to those letters, volume I, p. 79. P. Mansius, in his commentary on the celebrated codex of the age of Charlemagne, gave as accurate an account as possible of the codex belonging to the chapter library of Lucca; this commentary is printed in volume XLV of P. Calogera’s *Opuscula*, p. 76.

This codex contains many works that are found separately in other manuscripts. Here, however, we need consider only the collection of canons and decretals, which is found separately in the aforementioned Colbertinus manuscript. The two codices agree in this collection, except for the order of some documents, which was incorrectly altered in certain places in the Luccan manuscript.

The antiquity of the collection is shown by the documents in which nothing occurs or is indicated later than Gelasius, unless one regards as exceptions the four apocryphal monuments listed below, which, P. Coustantius believes, were fabricated under Symmachus.

P. Coustantius also plausibly suspected that this collection was of Italian origin, p. 87. For those spurious documents, fabricated in Italy, are found inserted in other Italian collections or in foreign collections that developed from Italian collections, as we shall explain later.

2. This collection begins with the Nicene canons in the version commonly called Isidorian, together with a catalogue of the bishops divided by provinces. These canons are preceded by a preface arranged in verse:

> “The holy council,” etc.,

and by a historical annotation:

> “When the holy and great council had assembled,” etc.,

just as we find these in other collections and shall publish them in the *Prisca* version.

P. Mansius notes that in the Luccan codex, after the canon concerning deaconesses and before the canon concerning the omission of kneeling on Sundays and during the Paschal period, the following addition is read:

> “Therefore, when the bishops had decreed all these matters as the reverence due to divine things required, and had also handed down to the Churches the ancient canon concerning the observance of Easter, by which no further diversity would arise, once everything had been duly arranged, the peace and faith of the Churches were preserved as one and the same in the regions of East and West.”

We believe that this passage concerning ecclesiastical history must necessarily be inserted. This addition, which mentions the Nicene decree concerning Easter and is expressed in the words of Rufinus from Book II of his *History*, chapter 6, is also found in other codices, especially in the Hispanic and Isidorian collections [Col. 0133A], at the end of the version of the Nicene canons by Philo and Evaristus, as can be seen in volume III of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 454, notes 1 and 2.

In our collection, however, it is appended to the canon concerning deaconesses because Rufinus appends it to that canon and omits the final canon concerning kneeling.

3. The canons of the synods of Ancyra, Neocaesarea, and Gangra follow, in the same Isidorian interpretation. Then the canons of the Council of Carthage of the year 419 are transcribed, divided into forty titles, precisely in the same manner and with the same African documents that we listed in chapter 4, no. 3, in the Vatican-Regina collection.

The Chalcedonian and Constantinopolitan canons follow, not in the Isidorian but in the *Prisca* version. We observed one special feature in the Luccan manuscript: in two of the Chalcedonian canons, because the *Prisca* version seemed obscure, the Dionysian version was substituted.

See our annotations 30 [CXV] and 33 in chapter 25 of that collection, which we shall publish in this volume, where the Chalcedonian canons are inserted from the *Prisca* interpretation.

Another especially notable point is to be observed in the Constantinopolitan canons: the canon concerning the primacy of the holy Church of Constantinople is counted among them, although it belongs not to the Constantinopolitan but to the Council of Chalcedon.

What P. Coustantius asserts on this matter in no. 96—that this is found in no other collection—does not stand. We have found it to be a characteristic of the *Prisca* version both in the Justellian codex, from which the *Prisca* was published, and in two other collections which, like the present collection, derived these canons from the *Prisca* interpretation: namely, the manuscript collection Vat. Reginae 1997 and another preserved in the two codices Vat. 1342 and Barb. 2888.

We explained how this happened in Part I, chapter 2, no. 3, and in annotation 5 on the Constantinopolitan canons of the same *Prisca* version.

4. The Sardican canons are then given, as we shall publish them in the *Prisca* edition; next come the Antiochene canons from the *Prisca* version.

Then four documents are inserted whose apocryphal character no one now doubts:

1. A decree of Pope Sylvester, with the title:

   > “The established canon: how rank or religious status is to be observed, by Sylvester, bishop of the city of Rome, to the lord Constantine Augustus.”

   It begins, “At that same time,” etc., as in P. Coustantius’s *Appendix* to volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, col. 43, and in Labbe’s volume I of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 1579.

2. The *Acts of Pope Liberius*, beginning:

   > “In the year of the reign of Constantine the king,” etc.,

   as in the same *Appendix*, col. 89.

3. The *Acts concerning the Exoneration of Xystus and the Accusation of Plychronius, Bishop of Jerusalem*, etc., in the same *Appendix*, col. 117, and in volume IV of the Councils, cols. 507 and 515.

4. The Council of Sinuessa concerning Pope Marcellinus, which is appended to the aforementioned acts without any title and begins:

   > “When the Augusti Diocletian and Maximian, while many during their lifetime,” etc.,

   in the aforementioned *Appendix*, col. 29, and in Labbe, volume I, col. 957.

Coustantius believes that these four documents were assembled not long after the age of Symmachus by an incompetent architect, in order to defend the Palmary Synod, which had been marked by many censures. See the cited preface, no. 99.

We have presented the order of the Colbertinus codex. In the Luccan manuscript, however, a somewhat disordered arrangement is found, apparently through the scribe’s carelessness, although the codex itself contains the same materials. These apocryphal documents are inserted after the Council of Chalcedon. They are followed by the canons of the Council of Sardica together with its synodical letter to Pope Julius; in the Colbertinus copy these are described, together with other booklets concerning the faith, shortly before the end.

Then come the canons of the Antiochene synod held at the Dedication, followed by the Constantinopolitan canons. After this the codex returns to the order that is parallel to that of the Colbertinus.

5. In both codices are produced the letters of Siricius to Himerius, or Hierius, bishop of Tarragona; Boniface’s letter to the emperor Honorius, beginning *My Church*, together with the emperor’s rescript; Zosimus’s letter to Hesychius; Celestine’s letter to the bishops established throughout the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne, and likewise to the bishops of Apulia and Calabria; Innocent’s letter to Victor of Rouen, another to Exsuperius of Toulouse, and another to Rufus and the other bishops of Macedonia. We listed these in chapter 4 of the Vatican-Regina collection, and they will be found in the collection to be published in this volume.

Four of Leo’s letters are read in this collection: the first to Rusticus of Narbonne, together with Rusticus’s inquiries; the second to the Africans, in an abridged edition; the third to the bishop of Aquileia; and the fourth to Septimus of Altinum. See volume I of our edition, cols. 1416, 669, 589, and 594.

At this point the definition of the faith against Eutyches is inserted in the Colbertinus manuscript; the Luccan codex presented it earlier. It has the following heading:

> “The episcopal synod of Chalcedon, held by five hundred and twenty bishops against Eutyches.”

At the end:

> “Here ends the universal synod, that is, the universal council at Chalcedon.”

It is taken from the ancient version presented in the collection to be published in chapter 25, whose beginning is:

> “The venerable assembly of the whole world,” etc.

According to Coustantius, the same Colbertinus codex contains beneath this definition [Col. 0134B] the portion of the Athanasian Creed that expounds the Catholic doctrine concerning the incarnation of the Word. It is preceded by a little annotation written in red:

> “I found this written at Trier in a book beginning in this manner: ‘Our Lord Jesus Christ’ and the rest: ‘Let him faithfully believe in our Lord Jesus Christ.’”

Then, in black ink, comes:

> “Therefore the right faith is,” etc.,

up to the end of the Creed, as these words appeared in the latest edition of Athanasius.

This annotation and portion of the Creed do not belong properly to the collection, for they are not found in the Luccan copy. They merely show that the Colbertinus codex was written in Gaul, where this Italian collection had already arrived.

6. In both codices the Nicene Creed is read, together with part of Damasus’s letter to Paulinus under the title:

> “Here begins the writing of Damasus to Paulinus, bishop of the city of Antioch, concerning the Council of Nicaea. We believe in one God,” etc.

It is taken from an ancient version up to the final words of the anathema:

> “The Catholic and Apostolic Church anathematizes them.”

Then, in the same sequence of discourse, a confession of faith sent by Damasus to Paulinus is added:

> “After this Council of Nicaea, a council was convened in the city of Rome by the Catholic bishops; they added concerning the Holy Spirit,” etc.,

as in the collection to be published in chapter 55, col. 400. From this we recognize that the Nicene Creed itself was inserted into this confession of faith within Damasus’s letter. See annotation 11 on the same chapter.

Then follows:

> “Here begins the exposition of the faith: We believe,” etc.,

as in chapter 39 of the same collection.

After that:

> “Here begins the Catholic faith: We confess the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit,” etc.,

in the same work, chapter 37.

Then, in the Colbertinus manuscript, comes the letter of the Council of Sardica to Julius, bishop of the city of Rome, which in the Luccan codex was appended to the Sardican canons.

Finally, in both codices:

> “Here begin the statutes of Pope Saint Gelasius. Gelasius, bishop, to all bishops established throughout each province.”

In the printed editions of the Councils it is entitled *To the Bishops Established throughout Lucania, Bruttium, and Sicily*. It begins:

> “The necessities of affairs,” etc.,

as in the collection to be published in chapter 58.

In the Colbertinus manuscript, Gelasius’s decretal concerning books to be received or not received is inserted after these statutes; in the Luccan codex it is more properly separated from those statutes. A distinctive and brief prologue is prefixed to this decretal, which does not appear in Labbe’s printed editions:

> “For the purpose of examining,” etc.,

as it can be read in P. Mansius, volume I of the *Supplement to the Councils*, col. 357. It contains the very brief form of the same decree, which we shall discuss in chapter 11, § 5.

Between these statutes and this decree, the Luccan codex also presents another decree of Gelasius:

> “Here begin the decrees of Pope Saint Gelasius, which the bishops receive at their ordination. Pope N. to the clergy and the order,” etc.,

as in volume V of the Councils, col. 383, where the words *at the middle of Saturday evening* are, on the evidence of the same codex, to be corrected to *and on the Saturday evening of mid-Lent*—that is, of the fourth Sunday of Lent.

After Gelasius’s decretal, only the Luccan codex contains two further additions:

> “Here begin the sayings of Pope Gelasius. Catechumens in Latin,” etc.

They were published by P. Mansius in the place cited.

And:

> “Here begin the chapters of Saint Augustine sent from the city of Rome. If anyone is right in all things,” etc.

These are the chapters published by Labbe from the manuscript of Saint Maximinus of Trier in the *Appendix to the Second Council of Orange*, volume V of the Councils, col. 818.

## CHAPTER VII. On Another Collection Preserved in the Manuscripts Barberinus 2888 and Vaticanus 1342

1. We can provide a more exact description of this collection because we were permitted to consult the codices in which it is contained. The codex of the Barberini Library, numbered 2888, is square in format and written partly in capital letters and partly in a rapid hand. It formerly belonged, apparently, to the monastery of Saint Savior on Mount Amiata in the territory of Chiusi in Etruria.

On an otherwise blank page of the codex, folio 133, a later ancient hand transcribed a report of the consecration of the church of that monastery in the year 1036, of the kind that Ughellus published from the complete original document of the monastery among the bishops of Chiusi (*Italia sacra*, vol. III, col. 623). We say “from the complete document” because in our copy the catalogue of the relics deposited in the individual altars is missing.

Perhaps this codex was one of those with which Theobald, bishop of Chiusi, enriched the Amiatine monastery under Louis the Pious—that is, shortly after the beginning of the ninth century—as the same Ughellus reports.

2. The Vatican codex 1342, which Montfaucon calls “most elegant and ancient” (*Bibl. Bibl.*, p. 131), is believed to be one of those belonging to the old Lateran Library [CXVII]. From this codex—or from another quite similar to it—we shall see that Cardinal Deusdedit, in the eleventh century, excerpted especially the canons of the Greek synods; see Part 4, chapter 14. It is written in letters of both larger and smaller form. It contains the same collection as the Barberine codex, but less completely; for several pages are missing both at the beginning and in the body [Col. 0135C], and in their place others, written in a more recent but ancient-looking script, were substituted.
