These contain several documents excerpted from the Dionysio-Hadriana collection.

Examples are found on p. 39: the constitution of Pope Hilary, issued under the consuls Basiliscus and Hermenericus, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December; on p. 42: three councils under Symmachus; on p. 51: the letter of Pope Anastasius to Anastasius Augustus; and so forth. Some writers have reported that the collection contained in this codex was called “Cresconian” by Cardinal Baronius, because the documents which he wrote that he had published from the Cresconian collection are found transcribed in this same codex. But they are mistaken. For this codex contains nothing from Cresconius that could have led to the collection being called Cresconian. By that name Baronius designated the Vallicellian codex A 5, at the beginning of which the *Breviarium* of Cresconius is placed, while the Hadriana collection with Dionysian Additions follows it. From those additions Baronius published the documents, most of which, as we shall see in Part 3, chapter 3, had been transferred from our collection into those same Dionysian Additions [Col. 0135D]. This collection also, like the preceding one, ends with Gelasius, and contains nothing from Dionysius except certain additions, of which we shall speak. From this its antiquity can be inferred clearly enough. Certainly, since its author had not seen the Dionysian collection, he drew upon sources different from and earlier than Dionysius himself.

3. At the beginning this collection presents a table of ninety titles. Since, in the earlier pages of the Vatican manuscript, additional canons of Chalcedon, Gangra, and Neocaesarea are written in a rapid and more recent script, the table of titles of the entire collection occurs on p. 10. It is prefaced by these words:

> In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Here begin the constitutions established by the three hundred and eighteen Fathers.

The ninety titles indicated in the table are set out as follows.

**I. Canons of the Apostles.**

**II. Nicene Canons.** In the body of the manuscript, however, immediately after [Col. 0136A] the table, there is first presented, without the author’s name, a letter of Dionysius Exiguus to Stephen, under this title:

> Here begins the preface to the Canons of the Apostles.

Then fifty canons are appended from the version of Dionysius himself. These apostolic canons, together with the letter mentioned, are wrongly known to have been inserted here. For the heading prefixed to the table clearly indicates that this collection began with the Nicene Canons, which are presented not from Dionysius but from the more ancient *Prisca* translation. The same is true of the other canons of the Greek synods: they derive either from the *Prisca* or from the Isidorian version, and none from the Dionysian version. From Vatican codex 1342, Sirmond published the Nicene canon concerning the primacy of the Roman Church in the *Prisca* version, which no other Vatican codex contains among the Nicene canons.

**III. Here begins how the *formata* is to be made.** In the body of the manuscript the text reads:

> It was enacted at Nicaea, the metropolis of Bithynia, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, etc.,

together with the *formata* letter, as we explained more fully in chapter 3, § 8, no. [Col. 0136B] 9. This annotation, “It was enacted at Nicaea,” etc., together with the same formula of the *formatae*, was repeated from this source in the Dionysian Additions. Baronius published it from Vallicellian codex A 5, which contains those same Additions and which he was accustomed to call the Cresconian collection.

**IV. Letter directed to the synod at Rome.** This is an apocryphal letter of the Council of Nicaea to Pope Saint Sylvester.

**V. Letter of Bishop Sylvester to the synod.** This is likewise an apocryphal reply to the same Nicene synod. These two letters are found in volume II of the Venetian edition of the Councils, cols. 79 and 80, and in the Appendix to volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, cols. 52 and 54, in the edition of P. Coustant. Coustant proves very well that their author appears to have been the same person who, in the age of Symmachus, fabricated the Synod of Sinvessa and other inept documents, which we found in the preceding Lucano-Colbertine collection and shall likewise see transcribed shortly afterward in this one [Col. 0136C].

**VI. Canons of Pope Sylvester.** Under this title there is presented not only the spurious [CXVIII] document which, with twenty canons, is produced in the preceding collection under the title “The Constituted Canon . . . . . by Bishop Sylvester,” but also another likewise apocryphal constitution of the same pontiff, with six canons. It is found in P. Coustant’s aforementioned Appendix, col. 55, and in volume II of the Councils, col. 417.

**VII. Canons of Ancyra. VIII. Canons of Neocaesarea. IX. Canons of Gangra.** All are from the ancient version called Isidorian.

**X, XI, XII, and XIII. Canons of the Council of Carthage of the year 419**, divided into forty titles with the same African documents, as they are read in the two collections, the Vatican Regina and the Lucano-Colbertine.

**XIV. Likewise, the Council of Carthage, title 40.** This is another council held at Carthage on the Ides of August [Col. 0136D] in the year 397, at which the *Breviarium* of the Hipponian canons was composed. Accordingly, under this number the *Breviarium* itself is transcribed, and it will be presented in the collection to be edited, chapter 2.

**XV. Letter of the Council of Carthage to Pope Innocent of the City.** It is read in the same collection, chapter 6.

**XVI. Rescript of Saint Pope Innocent to Bishop Aurelius.** It is found there, chapter 7.

**XVII. The universal council held at Chalcedon by six hundred and thirty bishops.** First the definition of faith is transcribed; then twenty-seven canons from the *Prisca* version are appended, as they are presented in the collection mentioned above, [chapter] 25.

**XVIII. Constantinopolitan Canons, title 5**, from the same *Prisca* translation.

**XIX. Sardican Canons, title 21**, as we shall insert them in the *Prisca* edition.

[Col. 0137A] **XX. Antiochene Canons**, of the same *Prisca* translation, title 25. It should be noted here that the author of this collection drew the Nicene, Chalcedonian, Constantinopolitan, and Antiochene canons from the *Prisca* version; but the Ancyrene, Neocaesarean, Gangran, and shortly afterward the Laodicean canons from the Isidorian version.

**XXI. Excerpts from the bishops’ statements recited against Nestorius at the Council of Ephesus, title 19.**

**XXII. Chapters of Nestorius’s blasphemies, and twelve chapters opposed by Cyril, Bishop of Alexandria.** These two numbered sections, which passed from this collection into the Dionysian Additions, contain material relating to the Council of Ephesus, most of which Baluze published from two manuscripts, the Vatican Palatine 234 and the Bellovacensis, under the title “The Sixth Session of the Council of Ephesus.” See volume IV of the Councils, Venetian edition, col. 197. Since these same codices contain the minor works of Marius Mercator, who flourished at the time of that council, Baluze considers that Mercator rendered them into Latin [Col. 0137B].

Several points, however, because they differ from the commonly published versions in our collection and in Dionysius’s Additions, must be carefully noted here. The heading of number XXI is distinctive:

> Here begin the excerpts from the bishops’ statements that were recited against Nestorius at the Council of Ephesus.

A table of nineteen titles follows:

1. On observing the decrees of the Council of Nicaea.  
2. On the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ.  
3. On Christ’s birth against the Arians.  
4. On Christ as perfect man.  
5. On the Lord’s Incarnation, addressed to the clergy of Alexandria.  
6. On Christ’s birth, and the comparison with the potter.  
7. On the benefits of the Lord and Savior.  
8. On the humanity of Christ’s body.  
9. On the fact that God became man.  
10. On all creatures, which do not know how to comprehend the Lord.  
11. On Christ clothed in the form of a servant.  
12. On Christ’s birth.  
13. On gold, frankincense, and myrrh.  
14. On Mary’s virginity and Christ’s passion and resurrection.  
15. On the petition of the presbyter Charisius and the other presbyters who had been deceived by Nestorius.  
16. On the creed of the Nestorians.  
17. On those anathematizing Nestorius and the entire heresy of the Tessarescaedecatites, and those who do not celebrate Holy Easter, and the Cathari.  
18. On Nestorius’s perverse replies.  
19. On those who preach contrary to the Nicene faith, all of whom are to be rejected.

After this table there is a preface of the following kind:

> After the consulship of our lords Flavius Theodosius, for the thirteenth time, and Flavius Valentinianus, for the third time, perpetual Augusti, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, which day is, according to the Egyptians, the twenty-eighth of Epiphi, by order of the most august and most pious princes, a synod was assembled in the metropolis of Ephesus. All having taken their seats in the episcopal residence of the most reverend and most religious bishop Memnon, the most holy and God-beloved bishops Cyril of Alexandria, also acting in the place of the most holy and most religious bishop of the Roman Church, Celestine; Juvenal of Jerusalem; Memnon of Ephesus; and Flavian of Philippi, also acting in the place of Rufus, the most holy bishop of Thessalonica, were present, together with Philip, presbyter and legate of the Apostolic See of the Roman Church.

This preface lacks the catalogue of bishops inserted in Baluze’s edition and also in the first session of the Council of Chalcedon, where the sixth session of the Ephesian synod was read (volume IV of the Councils, col. 1133). In Vatican manuscript 5845, among the Dionysian Additions, this same preface is read as it is in this collection. Only after the name of Celestine and before Juvenal are inserted the words “and Bishop Arcadius, legate, and Bishop Projectus and legate, Juvenal,” etc. The names of these two bishops representing the Apostolic See are more appropriately placed before Juvenal and the others than, as in Baluze’s manuscripts, relegated to the end of the catalogue, a placement inconsistent with the other Ephesian sessions as well.

After the preface just cited, the following is appended:

> And when these had taken their seats, Peter, presbyter of Alexandria, and Dionysius, chief of the notaries, said.

The same reading is found in two other very ancient codices, one belonging to Justellus and the other to the College of Paris of the Society of Jesus; they are mentioned in volume III of the Councils, col. 1200. The manuscripts of the Dionysian Additions, however, as well as Baluze’s codices, more correctly omit the word “Dionysius” and have, as in the rest of the Ephesian proceedings:

> Peter, presbyter of Alexandria and chief of the notaries, said.

[Col. 0138A] Peter’s speech follows:

> Your holy and great synod, exercising every care, etc.,

as in Baluze, volume IV of the Councils, col. 198, section d, through col. 206, section b, ending with the words “and for the forgiveness of the dead and eternal life.”

The following differs somewhat in our codices:

> I, Charisius, presented the petition as written above; anathematizing Nestorius and his followers, I subscribed with my own hand.

Then, with the earlier part of the Nestorian creed omitted—the part read in Baluze—only the latter part is appended, beginning:

> But we Catholics say that there is one Son and Lord, Jesus Christ, etc.,

from col. 207, section b, through col. 212, section b, ending:

> Flavius Palladius supplied this hand for him, because he did not know how to write.

All this is contained under number XXI, distributed among nineteen titles.

Under number XXII:

> Here begin the chapters of Nestorius’s blasphemies, by which, in letters sent to him by the holy bishops Celestine of the city of Rome and Cyril of Alexandria, he contradicted them, and, resolving in a very brief disputation the twelve chapters of the faith that had been sent to him, refuted them.

We have placed first the chapters of Bishop Cyril, which the Roman Church approved, and afterward those of Nestorius, translated from Greek into Latin. Cyril said:

> If anyone does not confess, etc.

Nestorius replied:

> If anyone does not confess him who is Emmanuel, etc.

And so the twelve celebrated anathemas of Cyril against Nestorius are presented one after another, each with its corresponding reply, or blasphemy, of Nestorius. These anathemas in the form in which each reply is appended to its corresponding statement do not exist in the Councils. Indeed, although Cyril’s anathemas have been published in both Greek and Latin from different sources, Nestorius’s replies, or blasphemies, have appeared separately only in the version preserved in this collection and in the Dionysian Additions, in volume III of the Councils, col. 971.

After these anathemas with their replies had been transcribed—even though they do not properly belong to the sixth session of Ephesus—the codices of this collection, together with those of Dionysius’s Additions, continue as follows:

> After these things had been recited, the holy synod decreed, etc.,

as in volume IV of the Councils, col. 212, section b. This is the decree of the Council of Ephesus, which is more correctly placed there after the recitation of the false Nestorian creed.

On the other hand, in the same edition many testimonies excerpted from Nestorius’s works are wrongly appended to this decree, and finally, without any suitable transition, the subscriptions of the Ephesian Fathers are introduced. In our codices, however, after the final words of the aforementioned decree—“but if he is a layman, let him be anathema, as was said above”—the appropriate addition is made:

> And they subscribed. I, Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, have subscribed;

and the remaining subscriptions are listed as in the edition mentioned, col. 216, section e, through the end, with the same closing formula:

> Here end the names of the bishops who were present at the synod against Nestorius, one hundred and ninety-three in number.

These are the points that seemed especially worth noting. Otherwise, many variant readings occur in the text, which may prove useful to future editors of these documents. Most of the ancient Latin canonical collections provide nothing from the Council of Ephesus [CXX]. The Spanish and Isidorian collections, and several Hadrianic codices, present under the title of that council two letters of Cyril to Nestorius that preceded the synod itself. In this collection, however, and consequently in the Dionysian Additions, the sixth session of that synod was received as the more important material, in the form we have described.

**XXIII. Imperial letter to Aurelius, Bishop of Carthage.** This is the law of Honorius against the Pelagians, which will be reproduced in the collection to be edited, chapter 16.

**XXIV. Letter of Bishop Aurelius to all the bishops established throughout the province of Byzacena.** It is found there, chapter 17.

**XXV. Excerpts from the proceedings held against Pelagius the heretic.** It is found there, chapter 18.

[Col. 0139A] **XXVI. Sacred letter of the emperor Constantine (read: Constantius), and of the younger Augustus Valentinian (supply: “the Father”), concerning the exile of Caelestius, the Pelagian heretic.** It is found there, chapter 19.

**XXVII. Ancient statutes of the East, title 102.** These will appear among the documents of the ancient Canon Law, no. 3, below, col. 653.

**XXVIII. Decretal letter to Anastasius, Bishop of Thessalonica.** This is Letter 14 of Leo, which is placed outside its proper location both in this table and in the body of the collection. Under this number the letter of Siricius sent to all the bishops ought to have been described; it is incorrectly presented as number XXXVIII, and Saint Ambrose and the other bishops respond to it in the following letter.

**XXIX. Rescript of the bishops and brethren.** This is the letter of Saint Ambrose and the other bishops to Siricius, which is read in the collection to be edited, chapter 31.

**XXX. Canonical letter which presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons must fulfill.** It will be published among the documents [Col. 0139B] of Canon Law, no. 4, below, col. 669.

**XXXI. Council of Laodicea**, in the Isidorian version.

**XXXII. Council of Carthage.** This is the council held under Genethlius in the year 390. Holstenius, using Vatican manuscript 1342 of this collection, restored this previously corrupted council to its integrity; from the same manuscript it was inserted in volume II of the Councils, col. 1243.

**XXXIII. Letter of Blessed Clement, Bishop of the City, to James, brother of the Lord, of Jerusalem.** It is indeed spurious, but was fabricated among the Greeks in antiquity and rendered into Latin by Rufinus. It is also inserted in the ancient collection to be edited, chapter 64.

**XXXIV. Precepts of Saint Peter concerning the preservation of the sacraments.** They will be presented among the documents as no. 5. See the admonition prefixed to those same documents, no. 5, below, col. 631.

**XXXV. Apocryphal proceedings concerning Liberius**, discussed in the preceding chapter, no. 4.

**XXXVI. Confession of the Catholic faith which Pope Damasus sent to Paulinus, Bishop of Antioch.**

**XXXVII. “To Paulinus, his most beloved brother: Damasus.”** These two documents are read in the collection to be edited, chapter 55, where only the letter of Damasus is placed before the confession of faith. See the first annotation to that chapter, where we shall observe that Pope Celestine read in his codex first the confession of faith and then the letter of Damasus, as they are transcribed in our collection. At the end of this letter is added:

> Confession of the presbyters or deacons of the Church of Constantinople. It begins: “I, that-and-that, deacon or presbyter of the Church of Constantinople,” etc.,

as at the end of the aforementioned chapter 55, below, col. 405. See also note 35 there.

**XXXVIII. Letter of Pope Siricius sent to all the bishops**, which will be found in the collection to be edited, chapter 30.

**XXXIX. Letter of Pope Siricius to Himerius, Bishop of Tarragona.** It is found there, chapter 29.

**XL. Innocent, Bishop of the City, to Exsuperius, Bishop of Toulouse.** It is found there, chapter 29.

**XLI. Likewise, his letter to the bishops of Macedonia.** It is found there, chapter 22.

**XLII. Innocent to Victricius, Bishop of Rouen.** It is found there, chapter 24.

[CXXI] **XLIII. Letter of Pope Innocent to Decentius, Bishop of Gubbio.** There, chapter 23.

**XLIV. Letter of Pope Zosimus to Hesychius, Bishop of Solina—read: Salona.** There, chapter 32.

**XLV. Petition of Pope Boniface to Honorius, beginning “My Church,” and Honorius’s rescript to Boniface.** They are found in volume III of the Councils, cols. 434 and 436.

**XLVI. Letter of Pope Celestine to all the bishops.** It is found in the collection to be edited, chapter 36.

**XLVII. Likewise, a letter of Pope Celestine, issued by the Roman Church, to the synod convened at Ephesus.** It was published in volume III of the Councils, col. 1143, and volume IV, col. 88, as well as by P. Coustant in volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, col. 1155.

**XLVIII. Likewise, another letter of Pope Celestine to Nestorius.** Volume III of the Councils, col. 903; also Coustant, col. 1114.

**XLIX. Likewise, another exhortatory letter of the same pontiff, sent to the clergy and people of Constantinople.** In the same volume III, col. 914, and in Coustant, col. 1131. These three documents were first printed by the Roman editors of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs* from the Cresconian collection—that is, from the manuscripts of Dionysius’s Additions—and were afterward reprinted by Cardinal Baronius in the *Annals*. From our collection they were subsequently transferred into the Dionysian Additions, as we shall see. They are also found in manuscripts of the ancient version of the Council of Ephesus, which Baluze and Coustant used.

**L. Celestine, Bishop, to all the bishops established throughout the province of Vienne.** It is found in the collection to be edited, chapter 35.

**LI. Accusation of Pope Xystus.**

**LII. Concerning Polychronius, Bishop of Jerusalem.**

[Col. 0140B] **LIII. Deposition of Pope Marcellinus.** These three spurious documents are also read in the preceding Lucano-Colbertine collection, in which the first two are joined into one. See what we said there, no. 4.

**LIV. Letter of Pope Leo to Rusticus.**

**LV. Rusticus’s inquiries and Leo’s replies.** In our edition, Letter 167.

**LVI. Letter of Leo to the Sicilians.** Letter 16 of our edition.  
**LVII. To the Bishop of Aquileia.** There, Letter 1.  
**LVIII. To the Africans.** Letter 12 of the abridged edition.  
**LIX. To Nicetas of Aquileia.** Letter 159.  
**LX. To Dioscorus of Alexandria.** Letter 9.  
**LXI. To Juvenal of Jerusalem.** Letter 139.  
**LXII. To Leo Augustus.** Letter 145.  
**LXIII. To Maximus of Antioch.** Letter 119.

In the body, Letter 80, to Anatolius of Constantinople, is added, although it was omitted from the table.

**LXIV. To Flavian of Constantinople.** Letter 23.  
**LXV. Letter 22 of Flavian to Leo.**  
**LXVI. Leo’s Letter 20 to Eutyches.**  
**LXVII. To Flavian of Constantinople.** Letter 28.  
**LXVIII. To Leo Augustus.** Letter 165.

[Col. 0140C] **LXIX. Copies of the proceedings in which the heretic Eutyches was condemned at the Constantinopolitan synod.**

**LXX. Subscriptions of Bishop Flavian, or of all the bishops who sat in that council.** The documents presented under these two numbers are found in the collection to be edited, chapter 42.

**LXXI. Murder of Proterius, Bishop of Alexandria.** Under this title a historical narrative is presented, which will be published in the collection mentioned, chapter 43, below, col. 308.

**LXXII. Letter of Bishop Simplicius to Acacius.** It is found there, chapter 44.

**LXXIII. Copy of the letter that Acacius sent to Bishop Simplicius.** There, chapter 45.

**LXXIV. Letter of Pope Felix to Zeno Augustus.** It is found in volume V of the Councils, col. 147.

In the table of the codices of this collection, three further numbers are given as follows:

**LXXV. Likewise, a letter of the same Pope Felix to Bishop Acacius.**  
**LXXVI. Copy of the letter that Acacius sent to Bishop Simplicianus.**

[Col. 0140D] **LXXVII. Here begins a copy of the letters of the most blessed Pope Felix of the city of Rome.** Since nothing corresponds to these numbers in the body of the collection itself, it is clear that this is an erroneous repetition of the two preceding numbers and of the following number.

**LXXVIII. Likewise, a letter of the same Felix to Acacius.** Volume V of the Councils, col. 143.

[CXXII] **LXXIX. Likewise, Emperor Zeno—read: “to the Emperor Zeno”—concerning the petition of John, Bishop of the Church of Alexandria.** This is a letter of the same pontiff, which is read in the same volume, col. 218.

**LXXX. Likewise, a letter of Bishop Felix to the aforementioned Acacius.** There, col. 217. The documents presented under numbers LXXIV, LXXVIII, LXXIX, and LXXX were transferred from this collection into the Dionysian Additions and were printed from those same Additions.

**LXXXI. Likewise, another letter of the same pope to Acacius.** It is read in the collection to be edited, chapter 46.

**LXXXII through LXXXIX. Testimonies of the Fathers**, omitted above under number LXVIII. They will be found appended to Leo’s Letter 165 to Leo Augustus, volume I, col. 1383. See there our first annotation, and also annotation 88, col. 1400.

**XC. Likewise, the faith of the Catholic Roman Church.** This is the little book of faith transcribed in the collection to follow, chapter 39; see annotation 1 there.

The table of both the Vatican and Barberine codices ends with this number, or title XC, from which we learn that the original collection ended there. At the end of both codices, however, after the same title XC, the *Institutes of Saint Bishop Gelasius* are presented in an ancient script; these are found in the collection to be edited, chapter 58.

Further additions occur in the Barberine manuscript, and others in the Vatican. On the reverse of p. 293 of the Barberine manuscript:

> Constitutions of Saint Pope Gelasius, which bishops receive at their ordination. Pope Illustrius to the clergy and people residing in the city of Illustrius, his most beloved sons in the Lord, greetings. “In response to your worthy desires,” etc.,

as found in volume V of the Councils, col. 383.

Then, in a more recent script:

- Letter of Pope Gregory to Castorius, Bishop of Rimini, found in Book II of Saint Gregory’s *Register*, Letter 41.
- Letter of Gregory to Vitalianus, the religious abbot of Benevento.
- Several fragments of Pope Gelasius.
- A statement of Felicianus, Bishop of Ruspe, found in volume V of the Councils, col. 931.
- Three statements of the emperor Charles, found in the *Capitularies*.

In the Vatican manuscript the following are appended in a later script:

- Decrees of Saint Gregory to the clergy in the basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle. This is the council of Saint Gregory I, volume VI of the Councils, col. 915.
- Other decrees of Gregory II at the Roman synod of the year 721, volume VIII of the Councils, col. 185.
- The council of Pope Eugenius, published by Holstenius in the *Roman Collection* and consequently in volume IX of the Councils, col. 1117.
- Finally, after several fragments from the Carthaginian synods, the council of Leo IV, printed by the same Holstenius and reprinted in the same volume IX, col. 1127.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the collection published by Quesnel and reprinted in this volume; and on another Colbertine collection, 3368

[Col. 0141C]

1. We shall demonstrate at length in the Observations to be appended to Quesnel’s Dissertation XII that the earlier collection, which we shall present in this volume in its entirety and in a more accurate form after Quesnel, was not a code of canons arranged or published with the public authority of the Roman See, nor received into use by the Roman Church under the pontificates of Innocent, Zosimus, and Leo. Rather, it was a collection composed by a private individual in Gaul. We have explained the antiquity and excellence of the collection in the preface that will be placed before it.

Quesnel accumulated several arguments in its praise in § 6 of the general preface to his edition, and we have reserved them for examination here. He says:

> It presents that ancient version of the Eastern canons which was in use among several Western Churches before the Dionysian version.

We possess part of this version in the Isidorian collection. Yet no one would dare confidently pronounce that version to be ancient before its comparison with ours made this clear; nor is it found entirely uncorrupted in Isidore, but is impaired by errors, interpolations, and other corruptions. The antiquity of this version is also confirmed by other very ancient collections that preserve the same translation. From these collections, the errors occurring in Isidore can be more safely recognized and corrected. The readings of the collection published by Quesnel are not always better, especially since some result from the freer license of the compiler, as we shall note in their proper places.

Quesnel continues:

> Furthermore, the ancient discipline of the Roman Church becomes known from this version, since it shows that some Eastern canons were rejected by that Church, others altered and adapted to its own use; a fact that remains obscure in Dionysius’s version, since he translated the canons according to the Greek text without considering the discipline received by the Roman Church.

And shortly afterward:

> It makes the relationship between Roman and African discipline more evident.

Then:

> The value of this codex is discerned in showing which Eastern synods, and at what time, were received for use in the Roman Church—namely, the Antiochene, Constantinopolitan, African, and any other canons that are called into question.

These three claims rest on the prejudice by which he wrongly believed this to be a code of the Roman Church. See more on these matters in the Observations to Dissertation XII.

He adds, most truthfully:

> I pass over the fact that it contains ancient and primary translations of works by several holy Fathers who were famous at the beginning of the fifth century, translations sanctioned by the use of the Roman pontiffs and councils; that it contains several little books of faith, some published and some not previously published; and that it restores certain African decrees omitted from the published editions.

What he adds—that it restores several letters of the Roman pontiffs and other documents to their integrity after they had been seriously interpolated—is entirely true, since a considerable number of excellent readings have been restored through this collection. If he is referring to the letter of Gelasius to the Dardani, which is longer in the published editions of the Councils but shorter in this collection, we shall remove the charge of interpolation from the published versions in chapter 11, § 4, where we shall demonstrate that Gelasius himself published two forms of that letter.

He continues:

> It presents not only what pertains to ecclesiastical discipline, but also nearly everything that was done or written in defense of the faith, either by the Apostolic See or by other bishops in those times. In this respect it surpasses both the Dionysian collection and the other codes of canons and constitutions, which touch upon nothing concerning matters of faith, except for the Chapters on grace and free will appended to Celestine’s letter, which are found in Dionysius and lacking in ours, and the anathemas of Gangra.

When he stated that the other codes of canons and constitutions touched on nothing concerning matters of faith, he did not sufficiently consider Isidore’s edition, and still less the other very ancient manuscript collections in which we find comparable decrees concerning the faith.

Finally, he especially extols the joining of the Sardican and Nicene canons, by which all the canons in this collection, though bearing the title “Nicene,” vindicate the supreme pontiffs from every deceit and fraud when they cited Sardican canons as Nicene. Although this same conjunction is also found in other ancient collections, which we mentioned in chapter 1, § 3, those collections were previously unknown; hence this type of vindication first became publicly known through the edition of this collection.

2. Some particular matters remain to be noted concerning the sources from which the author of the collection drew chiefly. He derived the Nicene canons joined with the Sardican canons from an ancient translation called Isidorian. At the same time, he had before his eyes another copy of the same canons, similar to that contained in Vatican Regina manuscript 1997. From it he took three things: the division and almost all the titles of the canons, the whole of canon 6, and the catalogue of the Fathers, as will be clear from the annotations.

For this reason he also passed over the final Nicene canon concerning the omission of kneeling on Sundays and during the Easter season. That canon is transcribed in the Isidorian version but is absent from the aforementioned Vatican royal copy.

In the other Greek canons that he received from the same ancient translation—namely, the Ancyrene, Neocaesarean, Gangran, Antiochene, Laodicean, and Constantinopolitan canons—he preferred a freer method of translation. As a result, certain canons differ from the pure ancient Isidorian version through the addition or alteration of words. Only the Chalcedonian canons were transcribed not from the Isidorian version but from the version called *Prisca*.

The compiler obtained a particular source for the African canons, from which he derived not only the Hipponian *Breviarium*, which was necessary for restoring the full Council of Carthage of the year 397, but also the letter of Mizo and the other Byzacene bishops, which until now has been found in no other collection. He also discovered a unique collection of documents relating to the Pelagian controversy, whose Greek version Photius reported in codex 53. From this source certain documents have been preserved for us that would otherwise have perished; moreover, among the canons promulgated at Carthage in the year 418 against the Pelagian heresy, we have received in restored form one decree omitted from other collections. See the annotations appended to the collection itself, in which we have uncovered several other matters.

3. We add here a few observations concerning another collection preserved in the ancient Colbertine manuscript 3368. P. Coustant discusses it in the preface to volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, pp. LXXXVII and following. The same codex contains two parts—or rather, two collections—which are distinguished by two tables or indexes of titles.

Here we shall discuss only the first part or collection, which received a considerable number of items from the Quesnel collection. We shall speak of the second in chapter 10, § 5, where the Gallican collections will be discussed; this second collection is more closely related to them.

The first collection, if one considers its table—which is evidence of its original form—consists of fifty-seven chapters. The remaining items not indicated in that table must be counted among later additions.

The table first lists all the chapters of the Lucano-Colbertine collection. Seven letters of Leo are added. Then, from the Quesnel collection, which we shall publish, the following chapters were excerpted: chapters 6, 13, and 42 through 50. These comprise the letter of the Council of Carthage to Innocent; the full council held at Carthage in the year 418 against Pelagius and Caelestius; the proceedings of the Constantinopolitan synod at which Eutyches was condemned by Flavian; the proceedings concerning the name of Acacius; the letters of Simplicius to Acacius and of Acacius to Simplicius; the letter of Pope Felix to Acacius; the tome of Gelasius concerning the bond of anathema; his *Commonitorium* to Faustus; the letter to the emperor Anastasius; and another document concerning the condemnation of Acacius.

Three additional letters of Leo and the letter of Saint Clement to James concerning the sacraments of the Lord were also added. In the body [Col. 0143C], however, the two final chapters, 56 and 57, which are indicated in the table—namely, Leo’s letter to the emperor and another letter of Saint Clement to James—are not presented in their proper places. Instead, they were inserted later among the documents subsequently added.

### 4.

The appended documents that are not listed in the preceding table are three other letters of Leo, together with a passage or clause from other letters of the same pontiff. Likewise included are all the documents concerning the Pelagians, which in the collection to be published are given from chapter 6 through chapter 20, whereas in the preceding table only two are indicated, the sixth and the thirteenth. These are followed by six other chapters taken from the same collection, chapters 30, 31, and 52 through 55. In addition, there are the Council of Telese and the rule concerning *formatæ*. From the Colbertino-Lucanian collection there is also added the decree of Gelasius concerning books.

Finally, at the end is copied the *Constitutum* of the lord Emperor Constantine, signed at Rome for the benefit of the Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of our lord Flavius Constantine Augustus for the fourth time and of Gallicanus, most illustrious men. This information I was able to gather from Father Coustant. If we had been able to examine the codex, we would have described this collection more distinctly.

One point, however, we clearly recognize: this collection had two sources, namely the Lucano-Colbertina collection, which was transferred in its entirety into this one, and another collection to be published in this volume, in which are found the remaining documents lacking from the Colbertino-Lucanian collection. The spurious *Constitutum* of Constantine, copied at the end and found in neither of these collections, appears to belong to a later addition.

## CHAPTER IX  
### On the collection contained in manuscript 55 of the chapter-house of the cathedral church of Verona

### On the synod held at Antioch around the year 379

The Western Tome is read and subscribed in it. The excellence of this collection lies in its very ancient translation and in the documents preserved in it.

[Col. 0144A]

### 1.

This codex is written on parchment, in a square format and in majuscule letters; its characters sufficiently indicate its antiquity. Two different codices are now found joined together in it. The first lacks its beginning, [CXXV] whereas the second is complete. The difference between these codices is clearly demonstrated by the pages: in the first, they consistently contain twenty-nine lines, while in the second they consistently display twenty-seven lines.

The first codex, defective at its beginning, contains part of the titles of the Council of Carthage of the year 419. These begin with title 49 and proceed to title 108. The canons themselves are then produced, with the same numbering, beginning with the record of the Council of Hippo of the year 393:

> Concerning the council held at Hippo Regius. In the consulship of the most glorious Emperor Theodosius Augustus for the third time and of Habundantius, most illustrious man, on the eighth day before the Ides of October, etc.,

[Col. 0144B]

as in Dionysius. If in that author (vol. III of the Councils, col. 501) the excerpts commonly printed from the Hadriana collection contain only 105 canons, this should cause no concern. In our codex the numbers are increased for the following reason: three numbers are attached at places that lack numbers in those same printed editions.

The African letter marked with number 108 is not given in full, but only up to the words:

> or could not be brought to this by many other obstacles;

nevertheless, this clause is appended:

> Here end the canons of various councils of the province of Africa, numbered 108.

Then follow two leaves that were formerly blank, on which something was written by a later hand and in a different ancient script. These include the verses addressed to Dalmatius, which we published at the end of chapter 1, § 3.

### 2.

The second complete codex then begins. Its quires are marked with the alphabetical letters A, B, and C. It contains a distinctive collection, which must be described more precisely.

#### I.

There is a hitherto unknown translation of the canons of Nicaea, [Col. 0144C] which we shall publish in this volume (below, col. 581). In this document and in the others, the titles are written in red, thicker majuscule letters; the text, however, is written in smaller black majuscule letters.

#### II.

The Council of Neocaesarea, in the Isidorian version, whose readings we used in correcting chapter 4 of the collection to be presented below.

#### III.

A specimen of the synod held at Rome, consisting of ninety-three bishops, from an imperial rescript:

> Damasus and Valerianus, etc., to the Catholic bishops established throughout the East, greetings in the Lord. We are indeed confident in your holiness, etc.

This is the synodal letter of Damasus and the other bishops of Italy and Gaul, first published by Holstenius and subsequently inserted in volume II of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 1043. Several excerpts from decrees are appended to it, and finally the subscriptions of the bishops of the Antiochene synod, with the clause:

> The Roman and Antiochene synod ends.

Since the letter placed first in this document was addressed to the Illyrians—for [Col. 0144D] Theodoretus, book II, chapter 22, and Sozomenus, book VI, chapter 27, quote it as inscribed to the Illyrians—Henricus Valesius, in his notes on Sozomenus, judged the inscription *To the Easterners*, found in the Holstenian codex, to be erroneous.

Our codex, however, sufficiently vindicates the same inscription. Nothing prevents us—as Father Coustant observes in his note to Damasus’s third letter, no. 3, p. 479—from believing that, although the letter had been written to the bishops of Illyricum, a copy of it was later sent also to the Easterners.

Indeed, since at the end of the letter both the Holstenian codex and our own read:

> I, Sabinus, deacon of Milan, the legate, have delivered this from the authentic copy,

it is evident that the original itself was not handed over to the Easterners. Rather, when it had been left in Illyricum, a copy of it, with the title to the Easterners inserted, was carried by Sabinus to the East.

Moreover, Saint Basil has a letter 69, bearing the names of thirty-two Eastern bishops and entrusted to the deacon Sabinus, so that it might be delivered to the bishops of Italy [Col. 0145A] and Gaul. At its conclusion these same Italians and Gauls praise and approve their synodal letter.

Since Sabinus proceeded to the East in the year 372, while the excerpts from the decrees appended in our codex and in that of Holstenius to the aforementioned synodal letter clearly belong to a later period, when the errors of Apollinaris had already appeared and were being attacked, Father Coustant therefore believed that the letter had been improperly joined to those decrees and that the two should accordingly be separated, as he argues in the place cited, no. 4.

It will cause no difficulty, however, if we believe that this document presents the proceedings of the Antiochene synod. The Easterners, wishing to demonstrate their faith to the Westerners, subscribed at the synod held at Antioch both to the synodal letter of Rome, previously sent to the East, and to those excerpts from the decrees which in both codices are appended to the synodal letter without any division. [CXXVI]

From letter 321 of Saint Basil we learn that Dorotheus, who had been sent by the Easterners to Rome [Col. 0145B] in the year 377, heard that Meletius of Antioch and Eusebius of Samosata had been branded as adherents of the Arian heresy. It may have been for this reason that a council was held at Rome and that the decrees—or the aforementioned excerpts from the decrees—were sent to the East.

After receiving them, a synod was subsequently convened at Antioch around the year 379. Saint Gregory of Nyssa appears to mention it in his letter to Olympius concerning the life of Saint Macrina. At that synod, so that every suspicion of Arian heresy might be removed, the bishops Meletius and Eusebius, together with the other Fathers of the synod, joined the letter of Damasus to those decrees and confirmed everything by their subscriptions.

The Fathers of the Council of Constantinople appear to have had this in mind when, in the canon that is fifth among the Greek canons—issued, as we believe, at the synod of the year 382—they decreed:

> We also receive from the Western Tome those who at Antioch confess one Godhead of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

Here the Western Tome corresponds to the synodal letter of Damasus together with the decrees, joined together and subscribed by those bishops at Antioch. In them they confessed the one Godhead of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy [Col. 0145C] Spirit.

(See volume II of the Councils, col. 1126, note e.)

The same document was surely indicated by the Constantinopolitan Fathers when they wrote in their letter to Damasus and the other bishops of the West:

> If you desire anything further concerning this matter, you will be sufficiently satisfied if you are judged worthy to read the TOME (Greek: τόμον) composed at Antioch by the synod that was held there . . . .

They called it the Western Tome in the aforementioned canon because both Damasus’s letter and those decrees had been sent from the West. Here they appropriately call it the Tome composed at Antioch by the synod, since that synod joined the same synodal letter of Damasus, previously received, to the aforementioned decrees and subscribed it.

It is pleasing to supply or correct several passages of this document, which has hitherto been printed from a single codex, by means of our manuscript.

In the first fragment of the decree, printed in volume II of the Councils, col. 1046, note b, after the words “the divine Spirit who made me,” the following should be added:

> for he who in operation, etc., must not be separated from the Godhead,

[Col. 0145D] and shortly afterward, in the same place, note c, the reading should be corrected as follows:

> or should communion easily be granted to transgressions (better, in the common edition, “to transgressors”), so that incentives to sin may be given to the rest.

In the third fragment, col. 1047, note a, after the words “or with corrupted understanding,” the following should be added:

> believing in the Trinity of coeternal essence.

Finally, it should be noted that our codex, like the common edition of Holstenius, states that 146 bishops subscribed. We mention this because in Hardouin’s notes it is written:

> In the Vatican codex there are said to be 163 subscriptions,

where the number should be corrected to 153.

The person who supplied this information to Father Hardouin counted the subscriptions of seven bishops, which are presented in full in this document, together with the other 146. Those latter subscriptions were omitted by the antiquary for the sake of brevity and are indicated by the formula:

> Likewise the other 146 Eastern bishops subscribed, whose subscription is today preserved in the authentic document in the archives of the Roman Church.

#### IV. The canons of Gangra.

#### V. The canons of Laodicea.

#### VI. The canons of Constantinople.

[Col. 0146A]

#### VII. The canons of Ancyra,

all from the Isidorian version.

#### VIII.

The Chalcedonian canons, in an interpretation different from the common editions and notes, which we shall insert below in this volume, col. 617.

#### IX.

The Letter to the Church of Alexandria. This is a letter of the Nicene Fathers in a version hitherto unpublished, which we shall likewise publish at col. 587.

#### X.

The following note is appended; it concerns the Council of Sardica:

> At that time the emperors were being harassed into convening a council, so that they might plot against Paul, bishop of Constantinople, at the instigation of Eusebius, Acacius, Theodore, Valens, Stephen, and their associates. And a council was assembled at Sardica in the consulship of Constantine and Constantine. It ends. Thanks be to God. Amen.

This note is erroneous with regard to Eusebius. Eusebius of Nicomedia had died before the Council of Sardica. Moreover, “the consulship of Constantine and Constantine” is corrupt; it should have been written [Col. 0146B] “the fourth consulship of Constantius and the third of Constans.”

Nevertheless, this consular notice agrees with what is transmitted in this same codex concerning the acts of Saint Athanasius. There it is said that this holy bishop, who returned to his see immediately after the Council of Sardica, came back during the consulships of Constantine IV and Constans III, where, through a similar error, “Constantine” is written [CXXVII] in place of “Constantius.”

This note was translated from the Greek, as were the other materials concerning the Council of Sardica. Whether these errors should be attributed to the Greek author, to the Latin translator, or to the copyist is not something that needs to be investigated more carefully here.

#### XI.

The series of Sardican documents being interrupted—for they will be presented later—the apostolic canons are inserted, in the version of Dionysius Exiguus.

#### XII.

Likewise the Antiochene canons, in the same translation.

#### XIII.

The Sardican documents follow:

> The Sardican canon begins. The holy synod was assembled at Sardica from various provinces, etc.

This is the creed of the pseudo-Sardican synod, with the same beginning as that found in Saint Hilary’s *Book on the Synods*, volume II, col. [Col. 0146C] 482 of the Verona edition, but in another unknown version, which we shall present in this volume at col. 615.

#### XIV.

A brief paschal cycle is inserted.

#### XV.

Then the following title is read:

> Definitions at Sardica. To the most beloved brother Julius, etc.

This is a translation of the letter of Hosius and Protogenes to Pope Julius, which Sozomenus mentions in book III, chapter 12. These materials, likewise previously unpublished, are printed in this edition at col. 597. See what we said above, part I, chapter 6, no. 11.

#### XVI.

An unpublished version of the Sardican synodal letter, with an appended exposition of the faith, which Theodoretus reports in book II, chapter 6. We shall also publish this version at col. 598.

#### XVII.

Then, without a new title, the Sardican canons are appended. They are not translated from the original Latin, but rendered into Latin from the Greek in an ancient interpretation, and include one canon beyond those found in the Greek text. We shall likewise publish this interpretation at col. 589.

[Col. 0146D]

#### XVIII.

In another script there is also inserted what appears to be another translation of the same canons: a Latin copy which Dionysius Exiguus received. Afterward, in the older hand, the series of Sardican documents continues.

#### XIX.

The Letter of Athanasius to the presbyters and deacons of the holy Church at Alexandria and Parembola, published by Marquis Maffei in the Appendix to the *Theological History*, p. 261, and to be reprinted in this volume at col. 611.

#### XX.

Another letter of the Sardican synod to the presbyters and deacons of Mareotis. It was published in the same Appendix, p. 258, and will likewise be reproduced by us at col. 607.

#### XXI.

A letter of Athanasius to the same persons, which several Sardican Fathers confirmed with their subscriptions. It was published in the same place, p. 259, and will again be printed in this volume at col. 609.

#### XXII.

Without any title, certain acts of Saint Athanasius are appended. Maffei published them in the same place, p. [Col. 0147A] 265. Since they mention Athanasius’s successors at the end and conclude with Theophilus, they seem to indicate the period in which they were written.

Perhaps no document has appeared in which chronological markers occur more frequently. In a brief narrative, twenty consulships are specified, and whenever more important events are reported, the month and day are also given. The names of the Alexandrian, or Egyptian, months show that the Greek original was composed in the city of Alexandria itself or in Egypt.

Nothing more distinguished could be found, were it not that manifest errors are detected here and there, on account of which this otherwise remarkable document has acquired a bad reputation among some scholars. Since, however, these acts themselves say that certain matters have been omitted, we do not believe that the errors can be attributed to the Greek author of the acts, who seems to have been a contemporary of Theophilus of Alexandria. Rather, they are due partly to the Greek compiler of these documents, who in some places excerpted less accurately from fuller acts; partly to the Latin translator; and partly also to the ignorance or negligence of the copyist.

[Col. 0147B]

Most of the errors lie in numbers and names, areas in which no experienced person is unaware how easily mistakes can occur. Others may have arisen from omissions in manuscripts—by no means uncommon—which break off the sense or divert it elsewhere. Still others may be due to the other hallucinations familiar to less skilled or less careful compilers, translators, and scribes.

These errors prove that one cannot always, or without qualification, rely on this document, so perversely corrupted, especially where other and more certain testimonies contradict it. Nevertheless, they do not prevent us from believing that these acts were originally written by a Greek Egyptian author under Theophilus. [CXXVIII] If his original had come down to us, or an accurate translation of it, so many faults or mistakes would certainly not be found.

#### XXIII.

After this, the following title is read:

> Likewise, the creed of the holy synod of Sardica.

Immediately afterward are appended the renunciations used in baptism and the Constantinopolitan Creed in an unknown version.

#### XXIV.

The Letter of Constantine concerning the Council of Nicaea:

> Constantine the Pious to the Catholic Orthodox Church throughout Alexandria: Rejoice, most beloved brothers. We have received perfect grace from divine providence, etc.

This is an unpublished version of the letter reported by Socrates, book I, chapter 9, and by Gelasius of Cyzicus, book II, chapter 36.

#### XXV.

The Law of Constantine against Arius, in an unpublished translation:

> Victor Constantine the Great and Pious to the bishops throughout every place and to the peoples. Arius, malicious and impious, imitating the devil, justly deserves, etc.

See this letter in Socrates and Gelasius of Cyzicus at the places cited.

#### XXVI.

Two letters: the first from four holy Egyptian bishops, at that time confessors and later martyrs, to Meletius, with a certain historical fragment appended; the second from Saint Peter, bishop and martyr of Alexandria. They concern the beginnings of the Meletian schism. These valuable documents were published from this codex by the aforementioned Marquis Maffei in the Appendix cited, pp. 254–255.

[Col. 0147D]

#### XXVII.

The codex is closed by the *Definition of Ecclesiastical Dogmas* of Gennadius, presbyter of Marseilles. This title was written in red by the first hand. But a line was drawn over it, and in the upper space a later hand, in black ink, wrote “of the most blessed Augustine, bishop,” in place of “of Gennadius, presbyter of Marseilles,” because this little work is wrongly attributed to Augustine in other codices. For that reason it was published in the Appendix to his works, volume VIII, col. 78.

### 3.

The following note, written in alternating black and red lines and in majuscule letters, is found on the final page:

> At last I transcribed these from faulty copies; and certain things indeed which . . . he corrected, not as he wished but as he could (supply: “and to correct, although not as I wished, yet as I could”). But I silently passed over certain things, leav[ing the rest] to the judgment of the Lord. You who read, pr[ay] . . . [for me, a] sin[ner]. [Uncertain surviving fragment:] “may you have re . . . the humblest of all dea . . . Theodosius, unworthy . . . deacon, made [this].”

[Col. 0148A]

The final words should be completed as follows:

> Theodosius, the least of all deacons, an unworthy deacon, made this.

The words “I have transcribed these from corrupt copies” indicate that Theodosius was merely a copyist, not the author of the translation found only in this codex.

Indeed, the same Theodosius, who is recognized from this very note as extremely unskilled in the Latin language, was so ignorant of Greek that, when copying canon 17 of Ancyra in the Isidorian version, he omitted the Greek words necessary for understanding the sense—words that are found in other manuscripts and in the common editions of the same version.

He was, however, the compiler of the present collection, in assembling which he used several codices. One particular codex contained Greek documents in an unpublished Latin translation. The ancient author of this translation used a Greek exemplar which, since it contained many documents peculiar to the Church of Alexandria, and since the Council of Nicaea itself begins with a notice concerning the sedition that occurred under Alexander, bishop of Alexandria—a notice not found in other Greek exemplars—appears to have been written in that Church [Col. 0148B] at least originally, after the Council of Chalcedon. It is, in fact, a more recent document rendered into Latin in a new version.

Theodosius, however, separated the documents of this unpublished translation according to his own judgment and inserted among them other documents from elsewhere: some from the Isidorian interpretation, some from Dionysius, and others from different sources. From these he derived especially the third and the twenty-sixth documents.

Moreover, in the same exemplar that contained the unpublished version, the only councils represented were Nicaea, Sardica, and Chalcedon. If it had included the canons of other Greek synods, all of them would have been rendered into Latin by the same translator; Theodosius would not have derived the remaining canons from the Isidorian or Dionysian versions.

Certainly, as far as [Col. 0148C] the Sardican documents are concerned, the Greek exemplar appears similar to those used by Socrates, Sozomenus, Theodoretus, and the Fathers of Chalcedon, as we have shown more fully in part I, chapter 6, no. 11. Thus, with regard to those documents, it was not peculiar to the Church of Alexandria; rather, several exemplars of this kind had been more widely disseminated throughout the East and throughout Greece and could readily have come into the hands of the writers and Fathers mentioned above. [CXXIX]

See what will be said concerning these documents in the Note to be prefixed to them, col. 378.

# CHAPTER X  
## On the Gallican collections

### § 1. Several ancient codices of canons among the Gauls, compiled through private effort; none arranged and published by public authority. On the more celebrated codices of this kind, especially Vatican Palatine 574

### 1.

There is no doubt that the Gallican Church possessed collections of canons for the bishops to use in governing it. Quesnellus appears to demand that some collection be published by public authority in order for the canons to have been promulgated. [Col. 0148D]

We shall refute this opinion of his in note II to Dissertation XII, chapter 2.

Up to now, it has not been proved by any certain or probable argument that such a collection was ever arranged, published, or approved among the Gauls by public authority. When canons or constitutions of the Roman pontiffs were cited by Gallican synods or bishops, even if they had been excerpted from some collection, the collection itself should not for that reason be called public or published by public authority. Nor did the cited constitutions or canons derive their authority from that collection, but from the councils or pontiffs by whom they had been issued. Compare chapter I, § 4.

Several collections compiled in Gaul in former times are found. If one collection had been public, why would so many collections have needed to be written? At the very least, the authors of these collections would have taken care not to omit any document belonging to the public collection. Yet in one collection several items are missing that are read in another.

Moreover, in certain codices, as we shall presently say, [Col. 0149A] the Nicene canons are found in Rufinus’s abridgment; in others, which Sirmond cites, they are found in the translation of Dionysius or in another, more ancient translation called Isidorian. Did the Gallican Church publish different collections officially? This can easily be asserted, but it cannot be proved.

It is evident that certain collections belonged to particular churches, among others from the collection of the Church of Arles, which we shall explain in chapter 13. Should all such collections be believed to have been written and published by public authority?

But why delay over this at greater length? Father Sirmond, who labored greatly in publishing the Gallican synods and carefully examined many Gallican codices throughout Gaul, removes every suspicion—arising from the very variety of the collections—of a public collection that would necessarily have been uniform. He says in the preface to the *Councils of Gaul*:

> The variety of the copies itself shows that the Gauls had no certain body or fixed collection of their synods and canons. For there are almost as many different collections as there are ancient codices. In some, there are usually more synods, or fewer; rarely are the same synods, or even a few of them, found in all.

He notes the difference among the most ancient codices of the councils of Gaul, a point that served his purpose. Shortly beforehand he had also noted differences in the versions of the Greek canons. A similar variety could have been pointed out in other canonical documents and in the constitutions of the Roman pontiffs. Add also the disordered sequence that he observed in certain collections. Since these features do not agree with a collection published by public authority, they demonstrate that all these collections were compiled privately in Gaul.

### 2.

Besides the Corbie, Quesnellian, and one Colbertine collection, which we reviewed in chapters 5 and 8 as having been assembled in Gaul, several others are mentioned by Gallican writers: the Fossatensis, Tiliana, Pithoeana, Aniciensis, Lugdunensis, Reinensis, and others. Since they were useful for the edition of the Councils of Gaul, they are known to have been particular to Gaul. But those who used such codices did not provide a distinct [Col. 0149C] account of them.

Concerning the Fossatensis, we have learned only that the Nicene canons in it are joined to the Sardican canons in the interpretation called Isidorian (Coustant, preface, vol. I, *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*), and that, in addition, thirteen Gallican synods are presented without order together with [CXXX] quite a few apostolic constitutions. Whether it also includes the canons of other Greek synods is unknown.

When Father Coustant, in his distinct survey of the Gallican manuscript collections containing Greek canons, describes the Corbie, Quesnellian, and Colbertine collections, but omits the Fossatensis, which he frequently cites in his edition of the letters of the Roman pontiffs (Coustant, preface to the *Councils of Gaul), this indicates to us that the Fossatensis likewise lacks the canons of the Greek synods. It is simply a codex which, besides the Nicene and Sardican canons inscribed under the name of Nicaea, contains only Gallican synods and apostolic constitutions.

[Col. 0149D]

If Father Sirmond, in his preface to the *Councils of Gaul*, also lists the Fossatensis among the Gallican codices that preserve the ancient Isidorian version (Sirmond, in the same preface), he could have done so because of the Nicene canons.

We leave it to those who will be able to examine the codices themselves to say more fully about this or about the other Gallican codices.

### 3.

Although we lack many other manuscript copies of this kind preserved in Gallican libraries, we can nevertheless provide here sufficient information for recognizing the ancient collections proper to the churches of Gaul, based on two Gallican codices that we found in the Vatican library.

The first is Vatican Palatine codex 574, which we discovered to be similar to the Morbacensis codex, written nine hundred years ago. Father Martène mentions it in volume IV of the *Anecdota*, p. 58, and Father Coustant in volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. LXXI, and elsewhere.

On the final folio, this Palatine copy is called the “Codex of Saint Nazarius at Lorsch.” From this we understand that it belonged to the celebrated monastery of Saint Nazarius at Lorsch, in the diocese of Worms, which Chrodegang, bishop of Metz, built around the middle of the eighth century.

The excellence of this codex is sufficiently commended by the celebrated [Col. 0150A] Council of Carthage of the year 525, which derives from it. Holstenius always calls it extremely ancient, and the antiquity is confirmed by the very form of the codex and the shape of its characters.

For the most part it does not present complete documents, but only excerpts, and sometimes abridged excerpts. Nevertheless, since these were taken from an older Gallican collection furnished with complete documents, the same codex very clearly indicates what that collection contained.

Two parts must be distinguished in this codex. One consists of those materials which, since they are designated in the preceding table of chapters, must be referred to the original collection. The other consists of those materials which, beyond the chapters indicated in the table, were added later.

Another formerly Gallican codex is Vatican codex 3827, about which more will be said below. We must now describe the collection contained in the aforementioned Vatican Palatine codex.

## § 2. Explanation and annotation of the collection in manuscript Vatican Palatine 574

### The Nicene canons received by the Gauls from Rufinus’s abridgment. The Sardican canons inscribed under the name of Nicaea and joined among the same Gauls to the Nicene canons, sometimes in abridged and sometimes in complete form. The Neocaesarean canon, among the titles sent by John II to Caesarius of Arles, to be supplied from the same codex in the common editions. The Second Synod of Arles appears rather to be an ancient collection of canons than a synod, and its date is established.

[Col. 0150B]

The following title, or preface, is placed at the front of the codex:

> In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Nicene canon concerning the sacred canons begins, abridged through careful effort so that what is needed may be found more quickly. We have omitted certain chapters that seemed by no means necessary at the present time. Nevertheless, we have transferred into this little book everything that we knew to be useful and necessary for all the churches.

A table of thirty-two chapters follows, [Col. 0150C] indicating the documents of the entire collection.

### 1. The Nicene Synod of 318 bishops

Only sixteen canons are presented, from Rufinus’s abridgment. Later, canon 13 of Sardica is described under the title of Nicaea as follows:

> The chapter concerning the canons written above, that is, of the 318 Nicene bishops, begins. Bishop Hosius said: “I also consider it necessary that you deal with this most diligently,” etc.

Father Coustant testifies in the aforementioned preface, p. LXXI, that the same reading is found in the manuscript of the diocese of Basel at Morbac.

Two points of the greatest importance should be noted here.

First, Rufinus’s abridgments were in use among the Gauls, as Quesnellus, Dissertation XVI, and several others have observed. This is evident from two other Gallican documents:

1. From the titles in the case of Contumeliosus, excerpted by Caesarius of Arles and appended to John II’s sixth letter to the same Caesarius, where the ninth Nicene canon is presented in Rufinus’s abridgment.

2. From the Second Council of Arles, which, as we shall shortly show, is more properly a collection of canons, where several canons composed from the same Rufinian abridgment are presented.

It would otherwise be unknown where this custom among the Gauls originated. From our codex, however, we learn that there were once Gallican collections of canons which received the Nicene canons in this abridged form from Rufinus. Consequently, the antiquity among the Gauls of the complete collection from which these excerpts were transferred can be recognized.

The same custom continued at a later time. For the Herouvallian collection, which we shall see was assembled in Gaul in the eighth century, presents Rufinus’s abridgments copied from an older Gallican codex of canons.

Second, we noted in § 1, no. 2, that the Gallican Fossatensis collection, which contains the complete Nicene canons in the Isidorian version, presented the Sardican canons joined to them and inscribed under the title of Nicaea. Our codex and the Morbacensis testify that the two groups were likewise joined and inscribed in another Gallican collection that had received the Nicene canons [Col. 0150D] in Rufinus’s abridgment.

[Col. 0151A]

This twofold arrangement of the Gallican collections—in which the Sardican canons are joined to the Nicene canons, whether complete or abridged—demonstrates that the Gallican Church itself regarded the same canons as Nicene. If Rufinus’s abridgments were received in place of the Nicene canons only in Gallican collections and codices of canons, then the Gallican Church, when it accepted those abridgments, appears to have added the Sardican canons to them because, in the more ancient period, the testimony of other codices joined them to the Nicene canons and regarded them as Nicene.

### II. The Synod of Arles of six hundred bishops

> To the most holy brother Sylvester, the assembly of six hundred bishops who were gathered in the town of Arles has reported to your charity what we decreed by common agreement.

Twenty canons follow. This is the First Council of Arles, held in the year 314. Father Coustant published the same heading from a similar codex of Morbac at col. 341, note a.

[Col. 0151B]

### III. The authority of Pope Innocent to Exsuperius, bishop of Toulouse

The body of the collection itself reads:

> The authority, or urban canon, of Innocent to Exsuperius, bishop of Toulouse, begins. Concerning the passage of the aforesaid authority, what he ought to observe regarding these matters, etc.

The first chapter of the same letter is abridged.

### IV. Likewise, the authority of Pope Innocent

The body reads:

> Concerning the aforesaid authority.

Two other chapters of the same letter are presented in abbreviated form. Here also two points deserve notice.

First, the constitutions of the Roman pontiffs are called “authorities.” This is shown to have been customary among the Gauls both by the petitions sent to Saint Leo, which we gave in volume I, Letter 65, where in chapter 2 the letter of Zosimus concerning the see of Arles is called an authority; and by Caesarius of Arles, who twice calls the letter of John II written to him in the case of Bishop Contumeliosus an authority; and by the Council of Agde, which in canon 9 calls the letter of Siricius to Himerius the authority of Bishop Siricius.

Second, the title “urban canon” [Col. 0151C] agrees with another Parisian codex of the college of the Society of Jesus. According to Hardouin’s testimony in volume III of the Councils, col. 13, note 1, the following inscription is placed before the aforementioned letter of Innocent:

> The urban canons begin. Innocent to Exsuperius, bishop of Toulouse.

### V. The authority of Pope Zosimus to Isicius, bishop of Toulouse, more accurately called Salonitanus in the body

> Your affection requires, etc.

The first two chapters of the same letter are recited.

### VI. The authority of Pope Celestine

In the body, almost the entire letter to the bishops throughout Apulia and Calabria is presented, up to the words:

> let us vindicate what accords with the rules.

Then, without any distinction or title, a fragment from chapter 3 of the same pontiff’s letter to the bishops of the provinces of Narbonne and Vienne is appended in the same continuous text:

> For he must first be a disciple, etc.,

together with another fragment from chapter 6.

[CXXXII] **VII. The authority of the decretal letter of Pope Saint Siricius.** In the main body, a fragment is quoted from chapters 5 and 6 of the letter to Himerius [Col. 0151D]. Then another fragment of the same letter is added under the heading, “Likewise, concerning the place about that synod”: “For very many priests of Christ …,” as it appears in chapter 7. Other excerpts from further chapters follow. The words “concerning that synod” should be noted, since they suggest that this letter was written from a Roman synod. Thus, too, Siricius’s letter appended to the Zella synod is reported as having been written at a council: “Given at Rome, in a council of eighty bishops.” Likewise, the letter either of the same Siricius or of Innocent, which in editions of the Councils is entitled “The canons of the Roman synod,” has the following heading in the Fossatensis manuscript: “Here begin the chapters of the Roman synod. The letter of the synod.” After the table of six chapters, it adds: “The canons of the Romans” (Coustant, vol. I, *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, col. 685, note a).

**VIII. Likewise, the authority of Pope Innocent.** Fragments from chapter 16 of the letter to Victricius.

**IX. The authority of Saint Damasus addressed to Paulinus.** A single brief fragment is given: “Those also who pass from their own churches to another church …” [Col. 0152A]. See this volume, col. 402, note 18.

**X. Saint Augustine, addressed to the Candidates for Baptism.** In the main body it is called a *Tractatus*. It begins: “Hear, dearest ones, members of Christ and children of Mother Church …,” as in Augustine’s Sermon 392, chapter 2, up to the words near the end of that same chapter, “whose end leads to destruction.” In the printed editions and in most manuscript lectionaries, this sermon is entitled “To Married People.” The Benedictine Fathers note that in some manuscripts it begins, as in our manuscript, with the words “Hear, dearest ones.” One defective passage in the printed editions is to be supplied from this same manuscript as follows: “What I say to the faithful and to the candidates for baptism, and to the penitents, let the catechumens hear.”

**XI. The authority of Pope Saint Symmachus addressed to Bishop Caesarius.** “Equity urges us …” This is the complete fifth letter to Caesarius in volume V of the Councils, col. 424.

**XII. The headings written below were sent by Pope Saint John from the Apostolic See.** The headings—or canons—are indicated that John II appended to his letter to Caesarius of Arles [Col. 0152B], which is found in volume V of the Councils, col. 902. Our abbreviator, however, omitted the letter itself. Of the headings or canons sent by Pope John to Caesarius, he passed over only the first, from Siricius’s letter to Himerius; the others he presents as follows:

“From the twenty-fifth canon of the Apostles: If a bishop, presbyter, or deacon has been condemned for crimes, he is not at all to be deprived of communion.”

This is the heading of Apostolic Canon 25 in the Dionysian version; it is absent from the printed editions of the Councils among the headings sent by John. Then the canon itself from that same version is appended. Another heading is added, together with Apostolic Canon 29.

Afterward follows: “From the ninety-fifth canon of Neocaesarea.” Heading: “Concerning presbyters who have committed fornication.” The canon itself reads: “If a presbyter has committed fornication or adultery …,” as in Neocaesarea, canon 1, in Dionysius’s translation. This Neocaesarean canon, omitted from the printed headings appended to the aforementioned letter, must be supplied from our manuscript.

The number of the canon—95—prefixed to this first Neocaesarean canon should also be noted. It indicates that the Dionysian manuscript from which Pope John II copied this canon preserved a continuous sequence of numbers, so that the numbering began with the fifty Apostolic Canons; after these, twenty Nicene canons and twenty-four Ancyran canons were added in continuous numerical sequence, making the first Neocaesarean canon number 95.

Since, however, Dionysius, in his letter to Stephen, gives another numerical sequence extending from the first chapter to the one hundred and sixty-fifth, this sequence began not with the Apostolic Canons but with the Nicene Canons. Thus the first Neocaesarean canon should have been numbered 45, and it seems that through an easy scribal error 95 was written instead of 45. However this is understood, it is clear that some older copies of Dionysius preserved a numerical sequence that we vainly seek in the Dionysian or Hadrianic manuscripts that have come down to us.

Next, two Antiochene canons are produced. They are not marked with a continuous numerical sequence, however, but with the proper numbers of those canons: “From the Antiochene canons, chapter 4,” and afterward, “From the canons written above, chapter 15,” together with the same headings and canons of the Dionysian version that appear in the printed editions. Did the Dionysian manuscript used by Pope John II, besides a continuous numerical sequence, also give the proper numbers of each synod? [CXXXIII]

**XIII. The African Synod of 214 Bishops. Ancient Statutes of the Church.** “Whoever is to be ordained bishop must first be examined …,” as in the ancient statutes among the documents of the old canon law to be published in this volume. They are divided into 95 chapters, with a few items omitted near the end. The African Synod of 214 bishops indicates the Council of Carthage of the year 418, at which the same number of bishops took part; these statutes are indeed attributed to that council in manuscript Veronensis 59, which we shall discuss in part 4, chapter 4. See what we discussed more fully above, chapter 3, section 4, concerning these statutes and this heading.

[Col. 0153A] **XIV. The Statutes of the Synod held at the Church of Valence, on the fourth day before the Ides of July, during the consulship of Gratian IV and Equitius.** Only three canons of this synod are produced. The erroneous chronological notation “Gratian IV” was likewise found by Hardouin in two manuscripts of the Paris College of the Society of Jesus, volume II of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 1068, note 2. It should read “Gratian III.”

**XV. The Synod of Fréjus.** “Although our blessed brother Concordius …,” as P. Martène published it from a similar Morbacensis manuscript as an unpublished document in volume IV of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, and thereafter in volume IV of the Councils, col. 2073. The heading is erroneous. For it is the letter of the preceding Synod of Valence to the clergy and people of Fréjus, published in volume II of the Councils, col. 1069.

**XVI. The Synod of Riez.** “When, by the will of the Lord, we had assembled at the Church of Riez …,” as in the printed editions, volume IV of the Councils, col. 533, up to the final words “had sought through contentiousness,” without the addition that Baluze published from the Urgellensis manuscript. See above [Col. 0153B], chapter 1, section 2, no. 4. The subscriptions of the same council follow, with the same chronological notation found in the printed editions.

**XVII. The Synod of Orange.** Only twenty canons are excerpted from the First Council of Orange. At the end appears this notation: “On the sixth day before the Ides of November, Ciro [supply: Cos.] being consul, in the Church of Justiana.” In the headings appended to John II’s letter to Caesarius, this is called the Synod of Justiana, after Justiana, a village in the territory of Orange in whose church this council was held.

**XVIII. The Synod of Vaison, on the Ides of November, Dioscorus being consul [supply: Cos.].** Six canons are produced.
