**XIX. The Synod of Arles, with 31 canons.** In the printed editions of the Councils after Sirmond, volume V, col. 1, it is given with 56 canons. This synod presents difficulties in several respects. The number and order of the canons differ astonishingly among the manuscripts.

The copies of the ancient Hispanic collection, and consequently also the Isidorian copies [Col. 0153C], contain only the first 25 canons, as we observed in two purely Hispanic manuscripts: one, Vatican Palatine 575, and the other belonging to Cardinal Passionei; also in another Hispanic manuscript of Gallican origin, Vatican 1341; in Vatican Isidorian 630; and in Vatican 1338, into which certain items were transferred from the Hispanic collection.

The Gallican manuscript collections of Corbie, Lyons, Fossat, and Til, omitting the three printed canons 10, 11, and 12, add eleven others to the remaining twenty-two—namely, the printed canon 46 and the others through 56—and thus present 33 canons. The manuscript of the Paris College of the Society of Jesus, cited by Hardouin in volume V of the Councils, col. 5, note γ, contains 36 canons: the first 25 and the final 11.

The printed editions of the Councils after Merlin and before Sirmond contain 37 canons: the first 25 and the final 12, from canon 45 through 56. Finally, Sirmond published from a Remensis manuscript 56 canons, inserting twenty canons after canon 25. Before these, in the same manuscript, a new heading is interwoven: “Chapters from the synod celebrated in the territory of Orange” [Col. 0153D].

All these canons, unlike those of the other synods of Gaul, are partly drawn from the Nicene Canons, sometimes from Rufinus’s abridgements; partly from the First Council of Arles; partly from the Council of Vaison; and partly from the First Council of Orange and similar synods, as Father Sirmond observed in his notes. No canons, apart from a very few Orange excerpts, are found copied word for word from those same synods. Their statements, however, agree completely.

Indeed, besides the identical statements, certain peculiar expressions in the Nicene Canons show that Rufinus’s abridgements were before the author’s eyes. Since, however, in those same Nicene Canons that preserve Rufinian abridgements, certain particles are inserted that are not found in Rufinus, it is entirely clear that, besides Rufinus’s abridgements, the writer had another version of those same canons at his disposal.

This variation among the manuscripts in the number and order of the canons shows that they were not all written at one time [Col. 0154A], but received additions at different times. The first exemplar may have been that which presents the smaller number of 25 canons in the Hispanic collection. Yet the older Gallican collections, which ought to be more genuine and authoritative in matters concerning the synods of Gaul, omit three of those same 25 canons and substitute twelve others in their place.

There can be no doubt about the addition of the twenty canons appended from a single Remensis manuscript, with the new heading placed before them: “Chapters from the synod celebrated in the territory of Orange.” The differing wording by which the statements of several canons are expressed indicates not merely a copyist who transcribed canons from different synods, but a writer who set forth the canons of different councils in his own words.

Whether this was done at the Synod of Arles or not, we strongly doubt. We believe it more probable that such a work belongs to no Gallican synod, but is a private collection to which several additions were made. Hence this document contains neither a preface [Col. 0154B], or proper introduction to the synods, nor a chronological note, nor a suitable conclusion, nor any subscriptions. No other Gallican synod can be found lacking all these features.

The catalogue of bishops, which in certain manuscript copies deriving from the Hispanic collection is placed after the epigraph and the headings of the canons of this synod or collection, has been transferred here improperly. It should have been placed before the same epigraph and appended to the First Synod of Arles, which immediately precedes it in those manuscripts; for it is clearly to that synod that the catalogue belongs.

The author of this collection, which is entitled “The Second Synod of Arles,” was apparently an Arlesian or someone devoted to the See of Arles. This is shown by canon 18, in which the prerogative of that see is established.

The collection is later than the Synod of Vaison of the year 442, which is mentioned in canon 47; but it is earlier than the Third Council of Arles of the year 524, before which these canons are prefixed in most manuscript collections under the name “of the Second Synod of Arles.”

That this collection was compiled under Saint Caesarius is indicated by canon 4, which reads: “Let no deacon, presbyter, or bishop admit a girl, whether freeborn or a slave, to the cellarer’s private quarters (*ad cellarii secretum*).” The words *ad cellarii secretum* provide a distinctive formula, which is similarly used in the Council of Agde of the year 506, presided over by the same Caesarius, canon 2: “It has been decided that female slaves or freedwomen are to be removed from service to the cellarer, or from confidential service, and from the same residence in which the cleric lives.” Who would not, from this agreement not merely of the meaning but of the distinctive formula, suspect approximately the same period?

**XX. The authority of Pope Saint Boniface, by which the following synod—that is, the Second Synod of Orange—was confirmed.** In the table, the title of this letter is placed before the title of the synod, just as the letter itself is placed before the same synod in the other Gallican manuscript collections, those of Fossat, Laon, and Hardy, with this note of an ancient Gallican compiler:

“Although the Synod of Orange was held before this authority, nevertheless, out of reverence for the Apostolic See, it seemed right to me that the authority of the lord pope should be written first” [Col. 0154D].

See the notes of Sirmond and Labbe, volume V of the Councils, cols. 814e and 815a.

In the main body of our manuscript, however, the same letter is placed after the synod. It begins: “Through our son Armenius …,” as it is read in the same place, col. 830, where the readings of this distinguished manuscript are recorded in the margin from Holstenius. The same chronological notation is marked there as in Sirmond’s other manuscripts: “The eighth day before the Kalends of February, Lampadius and Orestes being consuls.”

**XXI. The Synod of Orange concerning grace and free will.** “When, at the dedication of the basilica …,” as in volume V of the Councils, col. 808.

**XXII. The Synod of Agde.** This is the synod of the year 506, which is given in the same place, col. 521. Only 27 abbreviated canons are read.

**XXIII. The Synod of Orléans of the year 511.** It was published complete in the same place, col. 543; in our manuscript, however, only 22 abbreviated canons are presented.

[Col. 0155A] **XXIV. The Synod of Epaon of the year 517.** It is found in the same volume, col. 712, with 40 canons; in our manuscript, however, 31 canons are excerpted.

[CXXXV] **XXV. The Synod of Arles of the year 524.** It begins: “When, by the will of God …” The same is found in col. 763. Caesarius’s subscription is produced, in which the date is given as the seventh—not the eighth—day before the Ides of July, Opilio being consul. The subscriptions of the other bishops are also appended.

**XXVI. The Synod of Carpentras of the year 527.** The first period is omitted, and it begins: “When we had assembled at Carpentras, a complaint of the following kind came to us …,” with the subscriptions of the bishops, as in volume V of the Councils, col. 805.

**XXVII. The Synod of Vaison of the year 529.** Only an excerpt from the first canon is given.

**XXVIII. Concerning the synodal decree of the Apostolic See, that no bishop should presume to sell Church property.** In the main body, only canon 4 of the Roman Council held under Symmachus in the year 502 is cited: “Having therefore weighed these matters …,” as it appears in the same place, col. 475. After the cited canon, only in the main body it adds: “Here begins the ordinance—or rather, the law—of the most glorious King Theoderic,” which was published from our manuscript by Holstenius and thereafter in volume V of the Councils, col. 539.

**XXIX. Headings against the Manichaeans.** In the main body they read as follows: “Here begin the chapters of Saint Augustine, which they ought to read aloud publicly …” Twenty-one chapters are cited with Prosper’s subscription, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of the younger Olibrius, as they were printed from two other Gallican manuscripts in the same place, col. 800.

**XXX. The Synod of Clermont of the year 535.** It is divided into 17 canons.

**XXXI. The Synod of Orléans of the year 538.** It contains 36 canons. One canon in the printed editions is divided into two, and another into three. The first subscription reads: “In the fourth year after the consulship of Paulinus the Younger”—which should be supplied—“in the second indiction,” without mention of the regnal years of Childebert, as other manuscripts and the printed editions give it.

The second indiction is likewise recorded by the Lyons copy cited by Father Sirmond. This is thought to be an error, because other manuscripts mark the day of the Nones of the third month, during which the first indiction was running in the year 538 (volume V of the Councils, col. 1233, note 12). But neither our manuscript nor the Lyons manuscript gives the day or the month.

**XXXII. The Synod of Orléans of the year 541.** It is complete, as it appears in volume V of the Councils, col. 1363.

With these 32 chapters the table ends; this is an indication of the first collection. The material that follows, although it is added in the same handwriting in the manuscript, consists of later additions, and the preceding table makes no mention of it. Consequently, in the main body it is not written with any continuation of the numbering.

The first collection was therefore originally made before the middle of the sixth century—namely, after the Fourth Synod of Orléans of the year 541 and before the Fifth Synod of Orléans of the year 549, which is mentioned among the additions. Since the Gallican collections of Corbie and Fossat, believed to be the oldest of all, include the Fifth Council of Orléans in the first hand, as Father Sirmond testifies in his preface to the Councils of Gaul [Col. 0155D], it is clear that the original collection from which our manuscript was excerpted was somewhat older, since it does not know the Fifth Council of Orléans and received it among the later additions.

**§ 3. The additions to the same manuscript are listed.**

**Constitution of the Apostolic See.** “Silvester, bishop, to all the bishops throughout Gaul and the seven provinces. It pleased the Apostolic See that if anyone from any ecclesiastical rank …,” as in the whole of chapter 1 of Zosimus’s fifth letter, except that “the metropolitan of Autun” appears instead of “the metropolitan of Arles,” and Retitius has been substituted for Patroclus, as is noted from our manuscript in volume III of the Councils, col. 409.

The similar Morbacensis manuscript also has the same reading, as Father Coustant testifies in the Appendix to volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, col. 35. This is a spurious heading and interpolation by which Zosimus’s privilege for the See of Arles was transferred to Autun and wrongly attributed to Pope Silvester. Through a similar deception, this same letter of Zosimus, inscribed to Silvester, is transferred to the Church of Vienne in the Floriacensis manuscript, as may be seen in the cited passage of Father Coustant, col. 37.

[CXXXVI] **Zosimus to all the bishops established in the province of Vienne, in Narbonensis, and in the seven provinces:** “The metropolitan bishop of the city of Arles has always possessed a distinguished position …,” as in chapters 2 and 3 of the aforementioned letter of Zosimus. This letter is genuine, but its first chapter is missing; that chapter was attributed to the preceding letter falsely ascribed to Silvester.

**Avitus, bishop, to Bishop Victor, concerning the non-reception of heretical churches.** “You asked, or rather commanded …,” as in letter 6 of Avitus in Sirmond’s edition.

**The Canons of Orléans, enacted in the thirteenth indiction.** “The matter must be referred to divine grace …” This is the complete Fifth Synod of Orléans of the year 549, with 24 canons and subscriptions, as found in volume V of the Councils, col. 1375. The Morbacensis manuscript likewise presents all these materials. In our manuscript the following items are added.

**The letter of Dionysius Exiguus to Stephen, with distinctive readings**, an account of which we shall give in part 3, chapter 1, section 3. Only the Apostolic Canons from his version are appended.

**In the second year of the most glorious King Childeric, on the Nones of February, at Carthage, in the secretariat of the basilica of Saint Martyr Agileus.** “When Bishop Boniface …” This is the Council of Carthage of the year 525. It is particularly useful for many matters, especially for arranging and elucidating the African canons. It was published from this sole manuscript through the work of Holstenius and reprinted in volume V of the Councils, cols. 772–792.

This synod has no ending, but concludes with documents concerning the freedom of monasteries. From this one may infer that the synod was once copied by a monk in order to defend the liberty of monasteries [Col. 0156C]. The same synod was current in Gallican manuscripts and, with the same purpose, was cited in three Gallican monuments around the middle of the seventh century: first, in the *Life of Saint Babolenus*, under the year 647; second, in the privilege of the monastery of Saint-Denis in Paris, in the year 658; and third, in another privilege of the monastery of Corbie, in the year 664. See the same volume of the Councils, col. 771.

This synod is divided into two sessions. Two documents are improperly inserted into the second session: namely, Session 15 of the Council of Chalcedon, with the headings and 27 canons of that council from Dionysius’s version.

**Likewise, from the Council of Carthage under Bishop Lord Aurelius.** Brief excerpts are produced from the canons of the Council of Carthage of the year 397, with fuller subscriptions, which we gave in chapter 3, section 3.

Then follows:

**Here begins the Catholic faith of Blessed Athanasius, bishop.** “Whoever wishes to be saved …,” as in the Athanasian Creed.

**Concerning incest.** “If a man has committed incest, concerning these matters …” The ending is “for his own cause he committed it,” as in the printed editions of the Councils, volume VIII, col. 409, and in the *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*, volume I of Baluze’s edition, col. 177, where this decree is divided into ten canons.

Father Martène published a fragment of this decree from the Morbacensis manuscript in volume IV of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, p. 58, up to the words “so that the others may be corrected.” In the printed editions of the Councils, the canons of this document are attributed to the council or capitulary of Metz; a marginal note at col. 410 states that in one Vatican Palatine manuscript the first three canons are attributed to the Synod of Compiègne, while the remainder are attributed to the Council of Verneuil of the year 753.

But in this Palatine manuscript of ours, as also in the Morbacensis and in the other manuscripts cited by Sirmond and Baluze, neither the place of the synod or capitulary nor its date is specified. Baluze, however, at volume II, col. 1030, in connection with the words “Capitulary of Metz,” notes that the place is uncertain but assigns the date to the year 756.

There follow two questions of Augustine, bishop of the English, and the responses of Pope Saint Gregory. They are found in book XI of the *Register* in the Maurist edition, letter 64, questions 3 and 11.

**A Brief Order of the Ecclesiastical Life.** It begins: “How those who faithfully serve the Lord in monasteries are to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass, both according to the authority of the Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church and according to the arrangement of the rule of Saint Benedict …” It is a monastic order.

Since the most recent document in this appendix is the capitulary of the year 756, these additions seem to belong to the eighth century.

[CXXXVII] **§ 4. Concerning the Gallican collection contained in Vatican manuscript 3827. Verses published from this manuscript at the funeral of Lothair I.**

There is another Gallican collection, which we saw in the Vatican Library, contained in Vatican manuscript 3827. The manuscript is square in format and was written approximately eight hundred years ago. It belonged to the Church of Beauvais, as is clear from the note written beneath page 92: “This book belongs to Saint Peter of Beauvais” [Col. 0157B].

We describe this manuscript all the more willingly because, besides containing several Gallican synods included in the preceding manuscript, it continues the sequence of the later synods of Gaul. In this manuscript the synods are given complete, not in excerpts.

It begins with the Synod of Carpentras of the year 527. It then gives the Synod of Orange of the year 529; the Synod of Riez of the year 439; the First Synod of Orléans of the year 511; the Third Synod of Orléans of the year 538; the Fourth Synod of Orléans of the year 541; the Fifth Synod of Orléans of the year 549; and the Second Synod of Orléans of the year 533, which we mentioned in the preceding manuscript. In this same disordered sequence, the five Orléans synods are also described in the very old Colbertine copy, which we shall explain in the following section.

Afterward follows the Council of Vannes, believed to have been held around the year 465, published in volume V of the Councils, col. 79; the Second Synod of Vaison of the year 529; and the Synod of Epaon of the year 517.

**The First Synod of Tours**, of the year 461, volume V of the Councils, col. 73.

[Col. 0157C] **The Second Synod of Tours**, of the year 567, volume VI, col. 533.

**The First Synod of Mâcon**, of the year 581, in the same volume, col. 657.

**The Second Synod of Mâcon**, of the year 585, in the same volume, col. 671.

**The Council of Telenus, through the treatises of Siricius, bishop and pope of the city of Rome, concerning Africa.** This is the Council of Zella, also called the Council of Telepte in the province of Byzacena, which may be seen in this volume, col. 446. The Colbertine collection, which we shall explain in the following section, likewise places this same council among the same Gallican synods and with the same readings.

**The Council of Paris**, believed to have been held around the year 557, volume VI of the Councils, col. 491.

**Another Council of Paris**, of the year 555, in the same volume, col. 487.

**The Council of Auxerre**, of the year 578, in the same volume, col. 641.

**The Council of Chalon**, of the year 650, volume VII of the Councils, col. 395.

**The Synod held at Verneuil in the palace**, in the year 755, volume VIII of the Councils, col. 415.

**The Council of Soissons**, of the year 744, in the same volume, col. 290.

**The letter of Paulinus of Aquileia to King Charles, and the Synod of Fréjus**, in which the same Paulinus took part, of the year 791 or 796, volume IX of the Councils, col. 31.

**The letter of Pope Hadrian to the same Charles concerning images**, volume VIII of the Councils, col. 1553.

**The Capitulary of Theodulf of Orléans**, printed by Baronius and reprinted in volume IX of the Councils, col. 183.

**The Council of Paris of the year 829**, in the same volume, col. 702.

**The letter of Leo IV to Prudentius, bishop of Tri[lacuna]assus, and another to the bishops of Britain**, both of which were printed from this manuscript and are found in the same place, cols. 1625 and following.

**The Council of Toul held at Savonnières in the year 859**, published from this manuscript by Sirmond in volume III of the Councils of Gaul and thereafter inserted in volume X of the Councils in Father Labbe’s Venetian edition, col. 113.

Here the Gallican documents end. In the same manuscript there follow sixteen letters of Nicholas I, supreme pontiff. In the printed editions they are the first sixteen letters of the same Nicholas, volume IX of the Councils, from col. 1289 through col. 1407. The responses of the same pontiff to the inquiries of the Bulgarians are added; they are found in the same volume, col. 1534.

At the end, in an ancient hand, the following verses are copied. They were written at the funeral of the Emperor Lothair I, who died shortly after Pope Leo IV, in the year 855.

[CXXXVIII]

You were as great as the world itself, Caesar.

But now you are confined in a small cavern.

After you, let everyone know that he will serve,

And that no glory removes the necessity of dying.

Once the flourishing glory of the empire,

Now desolate at the death of its Caesar, languishes.

It will possess no appearance beyond this,

Which, dying with you, you have concealed.

O how Rome is oppressed by grief,

Suddenly deprived of her illustrious Fathers!

Weakened first by the death of Leo,

Now, Augustus, she languishes at your funeral.

The laws enacted by the elder Fathers,

Which the passage of time had long effaced,

You yourself restored in their entirety.

You strove to return them to Roman affairs.

What distant kingdoms and places,

Which no Caesar had been able to bend,

Did you not cultivate for Roman honor,

Strengthening the Roman bows with power?

What homeland did not grieve that you had died, Caesar,

Or what homeland did not fear you while alive?

But the homeland that feared you while alive,

Did not grieve that you had died.

For you were so gentle once they had been overcome,

And so harsh toward nations subdued by force,

That whoever did not grieve had rightly feared,

And whoever did not fear would rightly grieve.

Mourn, Rome, your name among the shades,

And mourn, in death, your two lights.

Break your bows, and thus take away from your enemies

The triumph over you, Rome.

[Col. 0158C] The remaining verses are missing.

**§ 5. Concerning another Gallican collection, contained in Colbertine manuscript 3368.**

We noted in chapter 8 that this manuscript contains two parts, or rather two collections, and there described the first. The second remains, and we have reserved it for this place because it contains chiefly Gallican synods. We owe our knowledge of it to Father Coustant, in his preface to volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, no. 102.

A table precedes it, listing the names of the synods that follow and the headings of their canons. At the beginning, the Gallican synods are given in this order: the First, Fourth, and Second Synods of Arles; the Synod of Carpentras; the Second and First Synods of Orange; the Synod of Turin; the Synod of Riez; the First, Third, Fourth, Fifth, and Second Synods of Orléans; the Synod of Epaon; the First Synod of Tours; the First and Second Synods of Mâcon; the Council of Telenus; the Third Council of Paris; the First Council of Auxerre; and the First Council of Chalon, the last of which was held in the year 650.

This collection of Gallican synods agrees closely with the preceding Vatican 3827, as we observed in the preceding section; accordingly, both derive from the same Gallican sources. The only difference is that the Colbertine manuscript places at the beginning three Synods of Arles, the First Synod of Orange, and the Synod of Turin, which are absent from the cited Vatican manuscript. The Vatican manuscript, on the other hand, contains four councils—the Council of Vannes, the Second Synod of Vaison, the Second Synod of Tours, and the Second Council of Paris—and adds several later documents after the Council of Chalon, none of which are found in the Colbertine manuscript.

After the Gallican monuments, the Hispanic synods are added: Elvira; Tarragona; Gerona; Zaragoza; Lérida; the First Synod of Toledo; [CXXXIX] Valencia; the Second, Third, Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, and Seventh or Eighth Synods of Toledo—the last is marked as having been celebrated on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, in the era 691, that is, on 16 December of the year 653; and the First and Second Synods of Braga.

Then follow the *Sentences*, which are not found in the old copies of the Councils but have been inserted into them by some persons. These are the 23 canons that we read appended to the canons of Agde in the printed editions, from canon 48 through canon 70, volume V of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 529.

The *Chapters of Martin of Braga* follow. Finally come the *Ancient Statutes of the Church*, which will be published in this volume. The table ends here.

In the body of the collection itself, however, three other Synods of Toledo follow: the Eleventh, Twelfth, and Thirteenth. There are also certain fragments excerpted from Theodore’s *Penitential*, from the writings of Saint Gregory the Great, and from Gregory III’s letter to Boniface.

The Hispanic synods were copied from some Hispanic manuscript. “Ancient Statutes of the Church” is a title that we find only in Gallican collections. Since these statutes, under this title and in this order, are not found in the Hispanic manuscripts that will be published below, they are an addition derived from another Gallican source. It is therefore beyond doubt that this type of collection was written in Gaul.

Even if the additions that were made later, apart from the documents listed in the table, are not counted, this collection is known to have been originally compiled in the seventh century: it is later than the Eighth Synod of Toledo, of the year 653.

**CHAPTER XI. Concerning the collections relating to the cases of Nestorius, Eutyches, and especially Acacius.**

**§ 1. Concerning two collections relating to the case of Nestorius and two others relating to the case of Eutyches. The earliest Ephesian collection, copied and supplemented from the Veronese manuscript.**

**1.** In the case of Nestorius, two collections above all are well known. The first is the one that, together with the ancient translation of the Council of Ephesus, presents numerous documents relating to events before and after that synod.

When publishing it, Baluze had decided to rely on the oldest Bellovacensis exemplar because he had determined that the Fifth Council had used a precisely similar exemplar—or, more accurately, that the ancient translator of the Fifth Council had used one [Note: [Col. 0159] Baluze, in the preface to the translation of the council, volume V, inserted in volume IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils, p. 1]. Since that manuscript was very mutilated and incomplete, however, he was forced to follow two others that were sound and complete, although they sometimes differed from the Bellovacensis manuscript both in the number and order of the documents and in the readings themselves. He also had to supply from elsewhere some items that were missing.

See his edition in volume IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils, cols. 1 and following; since various materials were excerpted here and there in it, the form of the original collection is not displayed.

We have found in Veronese Chapter manuscript 56 one very old manuscript exactly like the Bellovacensis manuscript but complete, from which many passages can be corrected and supplied. Here we append the title and table of contents, which display the original collection and the number and order of its documents.

Its epigraph is:

**“The Synod of Ephesus with its letters. The following are contained in this collection.”**

**I.** The first letter of Pope Celestine to Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, before the collection of the synod at Ephesus against Nestorius: “The sorrow of our heart …” Volume IV of the Councils, col. 38.

**II.** The same Pope Celestine’s letter before the synod to Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople: “For some days …” In the same place.

**III.** Nestorius’s letter to Celestine: “We have a fraternal relationship …” In the same place.

**IV.** Nestorius’s second letter to Celestine: “I have often written …” In the same place.

**V.** Celestine’s letter to the people of Constantinople: “To them …” In the same place.

**VI.** His letter to John, Juvenal, Rufus, and the others: “We would wish …” In the same place, col. 40.

[CXL] **VII.** Celestine’s letter to the Synod of Ephesus: “The presence of the Holy Spirit bears witness …” In the same place, col. 88.

**VIII.** Pope Celestine’s memorandum to the bishops and presbyters going to the East: “With our God …” Volume III of the Councils, col. 560.

**IX.** His letter to the Emperor Theodosius [Col. 0160A] concerning the convocation of the synod: “Although it is sufficient …” Volume IV, col. 90.

**X.** His letter to Cyril of Alexandria: “I understand the judgment …” In the same place.

**XI.** Copies of the acts conducted in the holy Synod of Ephesus, in the metropolis, concerning the true faith. “After the consulship …,” with the date the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, as it is cited in the Council of Chalcedon, session 1—not the tenth day before the Kalends of July, as it appears in the printed edition, volume IV of the Councils, col. 51.

**XII.** The letter of the Emperor Theodosius to Cyril of Alexandria: “The emperors Caesar Theodosius …” In the same place, col. 53, up to the words at col. 58d: “It follows that this also”—Cyril’s letter—“should be read”; and “it was read” are missing, as are the words “and placed among the preceding documents.” For Cyril’s letter itself is read inserted at this point in our manuscript, as will be clear from the following number.

**XIII.** “Here begins the first letter of Saint Cyril to Nestorius.” “Men of moderation …” In the same place, col. 15. In our manuscript an annotation is added: “This first letter …,” which Baluze appended from the Bellovacensis manuscript at col. 16.

**XIV.** The second letter to the same recipient: “Certain people object …” In the same place, col. 19. Our manuscript preserves the readings found in the Council of Chalcedon, in the Fifth Council, and in the Bellovacensis manuscript.

Afterward the acts of Ephesus follow, into which these two letters had been inserted: “And after the letter had been read …,” as in col. 58d, up to the words at col. 60c: “which had been expounded at Nicaea by the holy Fathers.”

XV. Nestorius to Cyril. “Indeed, the injuries …,” inserted in its proper place among the acts. It appears in the same volume IV, col. 23. There follow the interlocutions: “And after the letter had been read …,” ibid., col. 60d, through the interlocution of Juvenal, col. 62d, after the following letter had been read.

XVI. Celestine to Nestorius. “For some time …,” ibid., col. 37. The interlocutions of Peter and Flavian are appended, col. 62d and 63a, after which the following letter is inserted.

XVII. Cyril to Nestorius. “When our Savior said …,” ibid., col. 27. There follow the interlocutions and other material printed there from col. 63a through col. 76c.

XVIII. Letter of Capreolus of Carthage to the synod. “I was praying …,” the same volume, col. 76c. It then continues through col. 78c, at the words “from episcopal dignity and every priestly assembly.” After the rest has been omitted, the manuscript immediately adds:

“Peter, presbyter of Alexandria and chief of the notaries, said: A certain presbyter named Charisius, administrator of the holy Church of Philadelphia …,” with the readings of the Beauvais manuscript. Ibid., col. 122d, through Charisius’s subscription, col. 124d.

XIX. Copy of the exposition of the altered creed. “Whoever, now or henceforth …,” col. 125, through the words “let him be anathema,” as stated above, col. 128c. After the remaining material has been omitted, since it has been improperly inserted here in the common editions, the subscriptions of Cyril and the other Fathers immediately follow, from col. 129 through col. 134c.

XX. Acts concerning the excommunication of John, bishop of Antioch, and of the bishops who were with him. “After the consulship of our lords …,” ibid., col. 94d, through the words in col. 104c, “let them acknowledge what followed”; and in place of the subscriptions one reads, as in the Beauvais manuscript: “And the synod subscribed through 198 bishops.”

XXI. Report of the holy synod, “etc.,” as in the aforementioned Beauvais manuscript, ibid., col. 111a through col. 113b, with the same closing formula: “And the synod subscribed through 198 bishops.”

XXII. Copy of the letter written by the holy synod to the Roman archbishop Celestine, reporting everything that was done in the Council of Ephesus itself, “etc.” Ibid., col. 159.

XXIII. Celestine to the younger Theodosius. “For his own reasons …,” volume III of the Councils, col. 1591.

[Col. 0161A] [CXLI] XXIV. The same to Maximian of Constantinople. “We have seen and embraced …,” ibid., col. 1593.

XXV. The same to the clergy and people residing in Constantinople. “The mother’s exultation …,” ibid., col. 1594.

XXVI. The same to the Council of Ephesus. “At last, with the end of evils …,” ibid., col. 1588.

XXVII. Copy of the sacred letter sent by Aristolaus, tribune and notary, to John, bishop of Antioch, concerning the peace and union of the Churches. “Our intention …,” from the defective version published from the Beauvais manuscript in volume IV of the Councils, col. 176. From our manuscript, however, we supply the following two lacunae.

The first lacuna, col. 177, line 1:

“We have observed that, when all were coming to us—both the most holy bishop of this glorious city, and all the most reverend bishops found here, together with their entire clergy, who had previously been united for this purpose, while bitter suffering was proceeding—to fit together the members that had been torn apart from the true faith; so that, after meeting you and the most reverend and most holy Cyril, bishop of the Alexandrians, you may mutually remove among yourselves the difficulty and ambiguity that has arisen, while the most reverend men whom we have mentioned promise that, if you subscribe to the deposition of Nestorius and anathematize his teaching, no occasion for dispute will remain. Rather, immediately the most holy bishop Cyril, your Reverence, those who are with you, and the most holy bishop of glorious Rome, Celestine, together with all priests everywhere who hold the true faith, will enter into communion with your Reverence, etc.”

The second lacuna, ibid., letter d:

“Let no innovation be introduced from any episcopal constitutions, depositions, or any ordination whatever; but if anything should meanwhile have occurred, let it remain undisturbed and preserve the status of the catholic Church in tranquility. For the religious clergy who are present are sufficient to perform the divine ministries until complete union is achieved.

“Receive these things from us. We do not doubt that, seeing our intention to be sincere and immutable in all its strength and power, and worthy of Christian steadfastness, you too will act accordingly and will refuse to undertake no labor or fatigue, nor to disregard an injury, nor to forget anger, so that you may bring to completion the commands issued by our piety for the sake of the true faith and the unity of the holy Churches. But if—which we do not believe—you should attempt, through some personal purpose or under the pressure of human passion, to disregard this judgment and secret intention of ours, and neglect the other things commanded by us, you will have yourself to blame, because your holiness will receive fitting recompense for having spurned the effort toward the unity of God’s Churches.””

XXVIII. Letter of John, bishop of Antioch, to Cyril concerning peace. “Before this …,” as in the same place, col. 180, from the same Beauvais manuscript, whose lacunae we supply from our manuscript.

The same, col. 180, letter d:

“We did this for the sake of greater security because, since we could not meet and carry into effect in person the decrees made by our most pious emperors, we charged him to arrange, in our place and on our behalf and in our person, those matters that pertain to peace, which is the principal concern; but to communicate to your Reverence the exposition concerning the incarnation of our God Jesus Christ that we have formulated in agreement and sent to your Reverence through the aforementioned religious man. It is as follows:

“Concerning the Virgin who is the Mother of God, as we both understand and confess her, and concerning the manner of the incarnation of the only-begotten Son of God, we have necessarily drawn, not for the sake of adding anything, but for the sake of clarification, from both the divine Scriptures and the tradition of the holy Fathers; and we say briefly that we add absolutely nothing to the faith of the holy Fathers expounded at Nicaea. For, as we have already said, it is sufficient for all pious understanding and for every rejection of heretical unbelief.

“We speak without presuming upon forbidden matters, but as a confession of our own weakness, excluding those who wish to rise up against matters that we discuss beyond human capacity. We therefore confess our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man, etc.”

Then, col. 181, letter c:

“But we also consent to the ordination of the most holy and most reverend bishop Maximian of the holy Church of God at Constantinople, and we enter into communion with all the bishops beloved of God throughout the whole world, namely, all who possess and preserve the right and undefiled faith.”

And the subscription:

“May you remain safe, praying for us, most God-loving and most holy lord, and dearest of all brothers.”

XXIX. Letter of the holy Cyril to John of Antioch. “Let the heavens rejoice …,” ibid., col. 181.

XXX. Letter of the holy Xystus, bishop, to Cyril of Alexandria after peace had been made between Cyril and John. “We are filled with great joy …,” found in volume III of the Councils, col. 1689.

XXXI. Xystus to John of Antioch. “If the ecclesiastical body …,” ibid., col. 1695. Finally, this closing formula is appended:

“The holy Council of Ephesus, with the letters pertaining to it, is concluded.”

At the end of the same manuscript, in a later hand, there is also the Lateran Council under Stephen III. It was carefully transcribed by Father Joseph Blanchinus and most recently published by the distinguished Cajetan Cennius; Father Dominic Mansi reprinted it in volume I of the Supplement to the Councils, col. 641.

2. The second collection is the one published by Father Christian Lupus from two Cassinese manuscripts. It is a version of several documents concerning the case of Nestorius, whose author wrote under Justinian and revealed himself as a defender of the Three Chapters. Baluzius, intending to reprint it, regretted that Father Lupus had not even indicated what title the collection bears in the Cassinese books, what order is preserved there, and what he had omitted or altered. Learned readers can readily understand that he omitted and altered very much. But when he could obtain nothing through friends or letters, Baluzius was compelled to copy the collection from Lupus, prefixing only a conjectural title: *Synodicon against the Tragedy of Irenaeus*. See volume IV of the Councils, col. 235 and following.

Another copy of the same collection was indicated to us in Vatican manuscript 1319, from which others may benefit if they have the leisure. It bears this inscription:

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Here begins the translation of the First Council of Ephesus against the wicked doctrines of Nestorius of the august Church of Constantinople. Read with good fortune.”

3. There are likewise two collections relating to the case of Eutyches. Since they are sufficiently well known, it will be enough to indicate a few points. One is the Chalcedonian collection of Rusticus’s edition, furnished with numerous documents both before and after the acts; Baluzius described it accurately in volume IV of the Councils, Venetian edition, col. 1980 and following. Compare what we have discussed at greater length concerning the Greek origin and date of this collection, as well as the manner in which it was assembled in Latin, in the preface to the Letters of Saint Leo, § 18, volume I, p. 537. See likewise our remarks on Rusticus’s edition and manuscripts in volume II, in the note appended to cols. 1518 and 1519.

We also described, in the Observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 9, volume II, col. 1218 and following, a particular and very ancient little collection of certain documents relating to the Eutychian case, which we found in the single Vatican manuscript 1322.

4. Another collection relating to the same case is the *Codex encyclicus*, containing several synodical letters to Leo Augustus, in which the doctrine of the Council of Chalcedon was defended against the Eutychians. Baluzius presents the order of this collection in volume V of the Councils, col. 33 and following. But enough on these matters.

§ 2. On the Collections in the Acacian Case. Description of Two Manuscripts, the Verdun and the Veronese

1. More must be said about the particular collections relating to the case of Acacius. They display great variety and have not yet been sufficiently investigated. We have already listed, or shall later mention in their proper places, those collections that contain several documents from this case inserted into other collections as well. At present, two collections that contain only documents belonging to this case require special mention.

First must be cited the Verdun manuscript. From it Father Sirmond published several previously unedited documents.

I. Edict of the sentence of Pope Felix on account of the condemnation of Bishop Acacius, which he found appended to the *Brief History of the Eutychianists*, or, as the manuscript’s inscription has it, *Acts concerning Acacius*. It appears in volume V of the Councils, Venetian edition, col. 177.

II. Letter of Pope Felix, the ninth in the common editions, to Zeno Augustus. Ibid.

III. His letter 10, to the clergy and people of Constantinople. Ibid., col. 178.

IV. His letter 11, to Rufinus and Thalassius and the other monks residing around Constantinople and in Bithynia. Ibid., col. 179.

V. His letter 12, to the emperor Zeno. Ibid., col. 208.

[Col. 0163B] VI. His letter 13, to Flavitas, bishop of Constantinople. Although the manuscript attributes it to Gelasius, Sirmondus nevertheless thought it should be assigned to Felix. Ibid., col. 210.

VII. His letter 14, to Thalassius the archimandrite. Ibid., col. 213.

VIII. His letter 15, to Bishop Vetranio. Ibid.

IX. Fragment of a letter of the same pontiff to Andrew, bishop of Thessalonica. Ibid., col. 216.

X. An acephalous treatise of Gelasius, which is copied among the letters of that pontiff as no. 14. Ibid., col. 338.

The same manuscript also contains other material printed earlier, in whose editions it is repeatedly cited. But since neither Sirmondus nor anyone else has disclosed the series of items presented in that manuscript, we cannot say more about it.

2. Manuscript 46 of the Chapter of Verona, which contains a most important collection of Acacian documents, is square in format. Father Joseph Blanchinus supplied a specimen of its script in volume IV of the Venetian edition of Sirmond’s Works, after p. 579.

At the beginning it lacks only one page, which contained the catalogue of popes through Anastasius II. The other page, now the first, continues the same catalogue through Vigilius. A fragment of it was published by the distinguished Francesco Blanchinus in volume III of Anastasius, p. 209, by Muratori in volume III of *Italian Historical Sources*, and, more accurately, by Father Joseph Blanchinus in his *Exposition of the Pseudo-Athanasian Creed*, p. 104. From this it is possible to infer the age of the manuscript, namely, shortly after the death of Vigilius.

To this catalogue of popes are appended, in a single numerical sequence, the books of Jerome and Gennadius *On Illustrious Men*. Finally, the following Acacian documents are produced.

I. Narrative account concerning the wickedness of Dioscorus of Alexandria. It is in the collection printed in this volume, chapter 43.

II. “To the most beloved brother Achacius: Simplicius.” It is in the same collection, chapter 44.

III. Copy of the letter that Achacius sent to Pope Simplicius of holy memory, bishop of the Roman city, in which he reported that Peter of Alexandria had been condemned. Ibid., chapter 45.

IV. “Felix, bishop of the holy catholic Church, to the most reverend Achacius.” Ibid., chapter 46.

V. *Treatise on the Bond of Anathema* of Pope Gelasius. Ibid., chapter 47.

VI. *Memorandum* of Saint Gelasius to Faustus, master carrying out a mission to Constantinople. Ibid., chapter 48.

VII. Letter of Saint Gelasius, bishop, to the emperor Anastasius. At the end: “The letter of Pope Gelasius to Anastasius the prince is concluded.” Ibid., chapter 49.

VIII. “Here begins the account demonstrating that Achacius was duly condemned by the apostolic see.” Gelasius to all the beloved brothers, bishops established throughout Dardania.

The following closing formula is added at the end:

“The account demonstrating that Achacius was duly condemned by the apostolic see is concluded; nor can anyone, without endangering his soul, become a participant in his communion.” Ibid., chapter 50.

IX. “Here begins the account concerning the same matter, addressed to the bishops of the East.” Ibid., chapter 51.

X. Copy of the account of Blessed Pope Gelasius concerning the avoidance of communion with Achacius, sent to the eastern bishops. At the end: “The treatise of Blessed Gelasius concerning the avoidance of communion with Achacius is concluded.”

This lengthy treatise was edited from this single manuscript [CXLIV] by the marquis Maffei under the name of Felix III, volume V of the Councils, Venetian edition, col. 185; at the same time, under the name of Gelasius, by Joseph Blanchinus in volume IV of the Venetian edition of Sirmond’s Works, p. 553; and finally it was reprinted in the Appendix to the marquis Maffei’s *Theological History*, Tridentine edition, p. 220.

XI. “Here begins the letter of Saint Gelasius to Ephimius”—read *Euphemius*—“of Constantinople. To his most beloved brother Euphemius, Gelasius.”

It had been published by Merlinus from the manuscript of the Additions to Isidore. It is the first letter of that pontiff in volume V of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 284.

XII. Letter of Pope Gelasius to Succonius, an African bishop residing at Constantinople, who, fleeing the persecution of the Arians in Africa and imprudently entering into communion, is accused of having fallen into betrayal of the Council of Chalcedon; he is urged to correct himself.

This letter first appeared from the same manuscript, edited by Francesco Blanchinus in volume III of Anastasius, col. 50; it was then reprinted by the marquis Maffei in volume V of the Councils, col. 205, by Joseph Blanchinus in volume IV of Sirmond’s Works, p. 572, and finally in the Appendix to the *Theological History*, p. 234.

XIII. “Here begins the letter of Blessed Pope Gelasius to Natalis the abbot. To his most beloved son Natalis the abbot, Gelasius the bishop.”

It likewise appeared from the same manuscript in the same editions, after the preceding letter. The ancient hand of the manuscript ends with this letter.

There are four documents in this collection that are lacking in the manuscript collections to be published in this volume. Of these, three have been preserved for us in a single Veronese manuscript.

§ 3. On the Complete Collection of All Documents So Far Published in the Acacian Case. Some Are Marked as Spurious and Shown to Have Been Fabricated from Greek before the Fifth Synod. Two Letters Improperly Superscribed. On Three Fragments Published by Baluzius

1. If anyone wished to assemble a complete collection of everything relating to the Acacian case, seventeen documents under Simplicius would have to be placed first, namely, from letter 4 of that pontiff through letter 19. Then, under Felix III, twelve documents: letters 1, 2, and 6 of Felix himself, together with letters 10 through 15.

In addition, there is the petition of citation to Acacius sent by Vitalis and Misenus, which is read in volume V of the Councils, col. 217. There is also another petition sent by Pope Felix, by decree of the council, to the emperor Leo, ibid., col. 218.

In the manuscripts of the two Barberini collections, no. 2888 and the Additions of Dionysius, from which they were published, these petitions are inscribed as follows:

“Also, a letter of Pope Felix to the aforementioned Acacius, bishop of the city of Constantinople.”

“Also, to the emperor Zeno, concerning the petition of John, bishop of the Church of Alexandria.”

Next should be appended the letter of the Roman synod to the presbyters and archimandrites of Constantinople and Bithynia, ibid., col. 247.

In the Appendix, if desired, eleven other letters should be added, which we shall prove to be spurious: namely, letters 3 and 4 of Felix III to Peter of Antioch, and letter 5 to the emperor Zeno. Then the letter of Quintianus, bishop of Asculum, to Peter of Antioch, ibid., col. 219; another of Justin, bishop of Sicily, to the same, ibid., col. 225; another of Flavian, or Flaccian, bishop of Rhodope, to the same, ibid., col. 227; likewise, the letter of Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, to the same Peter, col. 230; of Antheas, bishop of Arsinoe, to the same, col. 233; of Faustus, or Faustinus, bishop of Apollonias, to the same, col. 235; of Pamphilus, bishop of Abydos, to the same, col. 239; and of Asclepiades, bishop of Tralles, to the same, col. 241.

After these, fifteen documents under Gelasius should be copied: namely, his first letter in volume V of the Venetian edition of the Councils; letters 2, 3, 4, 8, 11, 13, 14, and 15; the *Treatise on the Bond of Anathema*; another letter from the papers of Father Jerome Vignerius, ibid., col. 384; three documents from the Veronese manuscript, published after the letters of Felix III, ibid., cols. 185 and 205—which, although attributed to Gelasius in the manuscript, were assigned to Felix, the first and second respectively—and finally the Roman synod at which Misenus was absolved, ibid., col. 397.

Nor should the letter of Anastasius II to Anastasius Augustus be omitted, ibid., col. 406; and there should be added the petition of the Alexandrian *apocrisiarii* residing at Constantinople, delivered to the legates of the Roman see, col. 412.

Afterward should be joined letters 6 and 8 of Symmachus, together with another letter of the eastern bishops to Symmachus, col. 433.

The collection should be closed by several letters of Hormisdas, through which peace was achieved, along with the other documents placed before or inserted among the letters of that pontiff. These begin with the letter of Anastasius to Hormisdas, col. 561, and continue through the report of Epiphanius of Constantinople to Hormisdas, col. 685.

2. Among the letters under Felix III, we noted that eleven should be rejected into the Appendix as spurious. We possess ten of these in editions both Greek and Latin; the letter of Flavian, or Flaccian, appeared only in Latin.

The Latin text of the letters of Felix III is not original either, but an ancient translation from Greek. Two distinct versions must be distinguished. One, printed by Merlinus, used as its original the Greek text discovered by Binius and Fronto Ducaeus in manuscript copies containing the Constantinopolitan synod under Menas, and printed in 1618.

This ancient but highly barbarous version lacks the letter of Flavian, or Flaccian, just as it was not found in the common Greek text either. That letter is read from another, more ancient translation, preserved by the manuscripts of the Avellana collection. This version omits three of the same letters: two of Pope Felix, the third and fifth, and also the letter of Acacius.

After the translation of Felix’s fourth letter to Peter of Antioch, the following note is appended in the same collection, confirming that the version was made from Greek:

“Since we found, in the Greek volume, together with the letters of others addressed to the same Peter, certain letters translated from Latin, which we have now been compelled by necessity to translate again from Greek into Latin and copy because of the plots of the heretics, we have connected them with the letters of the aforementioned pope.”

Anastasius evidently saw and took account of this note when he wrote in the *Collectanea* cited above:

“From this it should be noted that, unless some things that had been published in Latin had been drawn up again from the fountain of Greek books, the Latin language would have lamented that they had been utterly buried beneath the weight of oblivion; just as it recovered, by drinking from that source, the letter of Blessed Pope Felix pronouncing sentence against Peter of Antioch in condemnation.”

Thus the very ancient author of the Avellana collection, who drew so many rare letters of the Roman pontiffs, apparently from the Roman archives, shortly after Pope Vigilius, did not find this fourth letter of Felix III written in Latin. He was therefore compelled to derive it, together with the other letters mentioned, addressed to Peter the Fuller of Antioch, from the Greek.

This is no slight indication that the letter is spurious.

3. Henry Valesius clearly proved that all these letters are spurious in chapter 4 of his *Dissertation on Peter of Antioch and the Synods Convened against Him*.

As regards the three letters attributed to Felix III, the evident argument for forgery is that, since Felix deprived Acacius of communion and episcopal rank in 484, it could not have happened that in letters written later—letters 3 and 5—he called him “the most God-loving and most religious bishop,” and that in letter 4 he presented him as the legitimate bishop of the see of Constantinople.

Father Antonius Pagius vainly attempts to eliminate this argument in his discussion of the year 478, no. 4, where he substitutes Simplicius for Felix III. For, apart from the fact that both the Greek text and both ancient Latin versions consistently display the name Felix, the letters to Peter the Fuller themselves, in the letters of Quintianus and Justin, are attributed not to Simplicius but to Felix.

“Although many bishops gave warning,” says Quintianus, “especially the most holy archbishop Felix”—words that imply that Felix’s third letter had already been written.

And Justin says: “May Felix, who presides over us, not issue against you a sentence according to the canons”—which indicates that Felix’s fourth letter was about to be written. Cyril of Scythopolis also read the name Felix prefixed to that letter in chapter 32 of the *Life of Saint Sabas*, when he reports that Peter was struck down by Pope Felix because of the addition to the *Trisagion*, which all these spurious letters discuss.

Moreover, Simplicius never communicated with Peter the Fuller, and when Peter invaded the see of Antioch for the second time during Simplicius’s pontificate, Simplicius opposed him so strongly that he would not have sent him friendly letters.

See also the many further arguments in Father Michael Le Quien’s fourth *Damascenic Dissertation*. He rightly conjectured that all these letters were composed in Greek by some Acoemete monk, at a time before the Fifth Synod when controversy was raging over the proposition “One of the Trinity suffered”—*Unus de Trinitate passus*. Since the Acoemetes vehemently opposed this proposition, they sought to fortify themselves with these letters, which rejected the addition to the *Trisagion*.

Several considerations confirm that the author of these letters was Greek, not Latin. First, the third letter attributed to Pope Felix mentions the pledge by which people promised, at the time of holy baptism, to believe “in one almighty God … in one Lord Jesus Christ,” etc. (volume V of the Councils, col. 158).

These words clearly indicate the Nicene Creed. Although the Greeks recited it at baptism, this rite was so unfamiliar to the Latins that Saint Leo once believed, according to the Latin rite, that the Apostles’ Creed was recited throughout the whole world by the voice of all who were to be regenerated. See letter 28 to Flavian, chapter 1.

Does this not reveal a Greek author familiar with the Greek rite?

Moreover, in Felix’s fifth letter to Zeno Augustus we read: “and Eustathius the confessor and presiding one (προέδρου) of the 318 Fathers who assembled at Nicaea” (ibid., col. 166a).

Who would suppose that a Roman pontiff granted Eustathius of Antioch the prerogative of presiding at a general synod?

The expressions used in the letter of Quintianus, who is presented as an Asculan—that is, Latin—bishop, are wholly inappropriate to him. They depend on the Greek words *Euthychis* and *Atychïs* and on their Greek meanings, and thus point to a Greek writer (ibid., col. 222a–b).

Furthermore, Cyril of Scythopolis, the disciple of Saint Sabas, whose mention of Felix’s letters we have noted, makes it sufficiently clear that these letters were fabricated before the Fifth Synod. We mention this so that no one will be surprised if Felix’s fourth letter, praised by Cyril himself, came into the hands of the author of the Avellana collection, who shortly after the Fifth Council translated it into Latin, together with other documents relating to the same case, and inserted it into his outstanding collection.

4. A few words about improperly superscribed letters. The fourth letter of Simplicius, which the manuscripts of the aforementioned Avellana collection present as addressed to Zeno Augustus, is addressed to Basiliscus in the Verdun manuscript. Father Antonius Pagius, in his discussion of the year 466, no. 11, and Tillemont in note 2 on the Life of Acacius, have extensively proved that this second superscription is the correct one.

Letter 13 of Felix to Flavitas of Constantinople is wrongly attributed to Gelasius in the Verdun manuscript from which it was published, as Father Sirmondus clearly proved (volume V of the Councils, col. 411); for that reason he substituted Felix for Gelasius.

Baluzius published three fragments of a letter of Anastasius II to Ursicinus from two manuscripts, the Beauvais and the Corbie. This Ursicinus appears to have been a bishop of Dardania or of some Illyrian province; for Gelasius mentions him in letter 3 to the Dardanians, saying:

“Moved, therefore, by our brother and fellow bishop Ursicinus, we have taken care to send writings concerning the present situation.”

The same three fragments are also found inserted into the second letter of the same pontiff to Laurentius of Lignidus. In that letter, however, the second fragment comes first, followed by the other two, the first and the third.

Since Lignidus, a city located on the borders of Macedonia or in New Epirus near Illyricum, belongs to the Illyrian region, we believe that this letter of Gelasius was an encyclical addressed to the Illyrians. It therefore reached both Ursicinus and Laurentius of Lignidus; consequently, those three fragments were wrongly attributed to Anastasius II.

§ 4. On Gelasian Letters, Additions, and Treatises Called into Question by Some

I. Several things must be said about the documents published in the Acacian case which, although genuine, are nevertheless viewed with suspicion by some.

There is no need to spend time refuting Dupinius, who, with extraordinary confidence, dared to describe as spurious three letters: one of Felix III to Acacius, which in the common editions of the Councils is entitled “the petition of citation,” etc. (volume V of the Councils, col. 217); another of the same pontiff to the emperor Zeno, published there under the title “the petition,” etc. (ibid., col. 218); and finally the letter to all the presbyters and archimandrites residing in Constantinople and Bithynia, written by the Roman synod of 485 against Acacius (ibid., col. 247). He likewise declares that this synod is spurious.

The first two documents are sufficiently and abundantly vindicated by two ancient collections in which they are contained, namely, the Vatican-Barberini collection and the Additions of Dionysius. The third is defended by the outstanding Avellana collection.

Father Bernard de Rubeis thoroughly dismantles Dupinius’s cavils in his dissertation *On the Single Sentence of Condemnation against Acacius*, §§ 12 and 19.

Nor need we labor over the letter of Gelasius to Succonius, printed from the Veronese manuscript. If it is said to have been written before the African bishops were recalled from exile, nothing prevents its assignment to the same pontiff, as the manuscript indicates. Gelasius was raised to the pontificate in 492, whereas the African bishops were recalled in August 494.

2. Gelasius’s letter to the Dardanians, which is copied in a shorter form in chapter 50 of the collection to be published in this volume, as also in the Veronese manuscript and in Isidore—where it was transferred from the aforementioned collection—received considerable additions in more recent editions of the Councils.

Quesnellus accused these additions of interpolation in the note that he appended to the aforementioned chapter 50 and that we insert here:

“I strongly suspect that the half-page and the preceding pages, which I previously noted as making the other editions longer, do not belong to Gelasius. As for this material, it contains nothing other than various examples of pontiffs who, with Christian liberty, either approached secular rulers themselves or exhorted them by letter—material that could easily have been added by another hand.

“Furthermore, the statement that Saint Ambrose suspended Theodosius from communion seems to me to belong to a more recent style. What he asserts about Pope Leo—that he freely rebuked Theodosius for supporting the Ephesine Robber Synod—is entirely false. Finally, his statement that he himself did not obey Odoacer when Odoacer issued unjust commands cannot be reconciled with the chronology.

“For in 490, that is, two years before Gelasius occupied the apostolic see, Odoacer was so defeated by Theoderic and confined at Ravenna until his death that he could have issued to Pope Gelasius no command, whether just or unjust.”

The marquis Maffei, adopting this same opinion in the *Acacian Supplement*, added another objection based on the following interpolated words:

“Behold, recently, against Huneric, king of the Vandal nation, the great and distinguished priest Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, and many catholic priests with him, steadfastly resisted while he raged … and even today they do not cease to resist their persecutors.”

Since the letter to the Dardanians is dated 495, the distinguished scholar cannot see how it could be said that something had “recently” happened when it had occurred at least eleven years earlier—for Huneric died in 484. Nor does he think that the words “even today they do not cease to resist” can apply to the year 495, since in the preceding year, 494, Guntamund, Huneric’s successor, had recalled the bishops from exile.

Moreover, since the passages inserted in defense of the sentence against Acacius agree with another treatise or letter from the Veronese manuscript, published by the same scholar and attributed to Felix, Maffei suspects that they were taken from Felix’s letter and inserted into Gelasius’s letter.

3. These considerations once troubled us as well, as long as we were unaware of the source of this expanded letter. But at Rome we were able to inspect and examine the manuscripts of the outstanding Avellana collection, from which it was published.

The antiquity of the collection, and still more the exceptionally rare and genuine documents gathered by its author—documents whose authenticity no one calls into question—adequately defend this expanded letter as likewise drawn from a genuine source.

An earlier testimony is also supplied by Facundus of Hermiane, who, before this collection, cited the same letter from an expanded copy in book V, chapter 4. He says that Gelasius, writing to all the bishops established throughout Dardania, “speaks as follows: ‘Let that city be renowned for the power of the present empire,’” and then continues by transcribing the lengthy text of the addition that is read in the common editions of the Councils, volume V, col. 333b–c.

Thus, before the Avellana collection, this letter had already appeared with its additions.

4. Nor is it unusual for two copies of one and the same letter to be found, one of which later received additions from the author’s own hand. See what we said in the note on Leo’s letter 12, nos. 10 and 14.

[CXLVIII] This expanded copy, since it bears both a closing formula and a chronological note, appears to have been sent to the Dardanians. The shorter copy, however, seems to have been the first, which Gelasius prepared in his initial work but did not complete.

The author’s hand is quite clearly exposed in the completion of the letter: in the expanded letter certain passages are reworked in different words; others are enlarged, sometimes briefly and sometimes at greater length; still others are omitted or expressed differently; and, because of the inserted additions, the wording of the earlier copy no longer agrees with it. We observed this especially in notes 14, 33, and 35 to chapter 50 of the collection to be published.

Interpolators do not ordinarily act with such care and freedom.

5. The objections that are brought forward are not weighty enough to establish that the interpolation is foreign to Gelasius. Quesnellus’ observation that the formula “suspends communion” is of a more recent style is of very little significance. We are also surprised that it should be falsely stated that Pope Leo freely rebuked the younger Theodosius for supporting the Ephesian Robber Synod, since a correction that was indeed moderate but nevertheless forthright is plainly evident in his letters to that same Theodosius. In them, opposing the Ephesian Robber Synod with the utmost clarity, he sought to remove the emperor himself from supporting that pseudo-synod.

More difficult seems to be what Gelasius writes about Odoacer: “It is also manifest that we, by God’s favor, in no way obeyed Odoacer, the barbarian heretic then ruling the kingdom of Italy, when he issued orders concerning things that ought not to be done.” The pronoun *we* may be understood of the pontifical dignity, which is one and the same in all Roman pontiffs. See the admonition to St. Leo’s first letter, no. 25. Thus, when Boniface I says in his fifteenth letter to Rufus: “Theodosius, not thinking that Nectarius’s ordination possessed validity because it was not within OUR jurisdiction, regularly requested that a *formata* be sent from the Roman See, which would strengthen his priesthood, after he had dispatched court officials from his side together with bishops,” the words “within our jurisdiction,” which refer to his predecessor Damasus, were understood not of himself but of the apostolic dignity shared by him and Damasus.

Similarly, Leo II, writing to the Spanish bishops, says: “From the various councils subject to this holy apostolic See, whose ministry we perform, archbishops were sent BY US” (*Concilia*, vol. 7, col. 1456 c), so that they might attend the Sixth Ecumenical Council, although they had been sent by his predecessor Agatho. He plainly used the pronoun *us* for the apostolic See, whose ministry he was exercising.

To omit examples from other pontiffs and come to Gelasius: when, in his letter to the Easterners inserted in chapter 51 of the collection to be published, no. 2, he says, “Nor was Peter in any way absolved by US, whom WE know WE condemned”; and in no. 12, “They complain that Acacius was condemned BY US” (events that had occurred under Felix III), he certainly understood the pronouns *we* and *us* of the apostolic and pontifical dignity; for it was not he, but Felix III, who had condemned both men.

If anyone should think that this raises doubt as to whether this letter too is Gelasius’s, another example may be produced from the *Commonitorium* to Faustus, which no one can doubt belongs to Gelasius, since it mentions his predecessor Felix. In chapter 4, we read: “But this is exceedingly shameless: they pretend that Acacius asked for pardon, while WE proved difficult”; and shortly afterward, speaking of Andromachus, whom Felix had sent to the East, he says: “He was abundantly instructed BY US to urge Acacius, having abandoned his obstinacy, to come to his senses,” and so forth. It is extremely weak to attribute these sentences to an interpolation.

We shall offer a still clearer example from another treatise, or letter, to the Easterners, published from the Veronese manuscript. Although the manuscript bears the name of Gelasius, the work was attributed to Felix in the customary editions of the Councils. The following words, expressing an objection of the Easterners, are relevant to the present matter:

“But even then,” he says (read: “you say”), “Acacius was in communion WITH YOU, when the heretic Timothy, or that Peter, was occupying the Alexandrian Church under the tyrant Basiliscus.”

The pontiff replies:

“You speak truly, but at that time Acacius was by no means in communion, and he remained in MY communion.”

The words “with you” and “in my” plainly refer not to the person of the writer but to the apostolic See and pontifical dignity. Whether Gelasius or Felix is believed to be the author of this letter, the events recounted concerning Timothy Aelurus and Peter Mongus belong to the time of Simplicius.

Felix, of course, succeeded Simplicius in 483. Basiliscus, having seized the empire in 476, installed Timothy in the Alexandrian See in that same year. After Basiliscus was expelled in 477, Timothy was driven into exile, where he later died by poison. After his deposition, Peter Mongus seized the same See; but he too was shortly afterward expelled by the emperor Zeno, and Timothy Solofaciolus, the Catholic bishop, was restored. On this matter Acacius wrote to Pope Simplicius in 478. After Solofaciolus died in 481, John Talaia was appointed by the Catholics in his place. Acacius then dealt with the emperor Zeno so that he might recall Peter Mongus, and this became the origin of the great disagreement between the Roman Church and Acacius.

From these facts it is evident that the words “with you” and “in my”—namely, that Acacius, under the tyrant Basiliscus, that is, between 476 and 477, had been “with you in communion” and had “remained in my communion”—belong to the time of Simplicius alone. They cannot be referred either to Gelasius or even to Felix. And if, nevertheless, this letter should be attributed to Simplicius, it would be clear that the pronoun *my* was taken not personally but with reference to the dignity common to all pontiffs.

Since, moreover, the expression “with you” was used in this sense by the Easterners in letters written under Felix or Gelasius, there is nothing surprising if Gelasius, responding to the objections of those same Easterners, thought that he should use a similar formulation, so that they would understand the words “we” and “my” as referring to the pontifical dignity.

6. Since, in the additions to the letter to the Dardani, which we are now discussing, Gelasius mentions certain actions belonging to his predecessors Leo, Hilary, Simplicius, and Felix, the words “we” likewise, when referred to the time of Odoacer, seem to suggest something peculiar to Gelasius himself. Although Odoacer had suffered the siege of Ravenna before Gelasius’s pontificate, he had not yet been defeated, nor had all his forces been overcome. Nor is it established that, before his death—which occurred in 493—Theodoric had obtained the kingdom within Italy properly so called and at Rome.

It could therefore have happened that, after Gelasius had been raised to the pontificate at the beginning of 492, Odoacer’s officials, to whom Rome was subject, enforced some order to which Gelasius resisted. Perhaps the reference is even to an order that concerned not only the pontiff but also the Roman clergy, to which Gelasius himself, before his pontificate, may have refused obedience while he was among the more distinguished clerics.

7. Moreover, the statement that something had recently occurred may indicate an event that had taken place eleven years earlier, just as in another letter of Gelasius to Anastasius, chapter 7, the words “with Nestorius recently expelled” express an event that had occurred sixty years before. The words “even today”—that is, in the year 495—“they do not cease to resist their persecutors” should not be understood of Huneric but of the Arian bishops. There can be no doubt that these men, designated by the term “persecutors,” and powerful under Gunthamund, attempted many things against the Catholic bishops after being recalled from exile.

Procopius, indeed, in *The Vandalic War*, chapter 8, reports that the persecution under Gunthamund had not entirely ceased. Nothing therefore remains by which these additions to Gelasius’s letter, supported by the authority of the ancient Avellan collection and of Facundus of Hermiane, could be brought under suspicion of forgery or interpolation.

8. Once this letter to the Dardani has been securely established as genuine in its entirety, it will be easier to pronounce judgment on the remaining works. In the same letter, chapter 10, Gelasius promises that “we shall strive to explain the same matters more fully, if the Lord grants the opportunity”; he therefore promises a more extensive treatment of the same subject. We believe this to be the work inserted in chapter 51 of the collection to be included in this volume, immediately after that letter.

Although it is not so lengthy as the word “more fully” seems to imply, it should be noted that it is acephalous, so that much is missing at the beginning. Perhaps Gelasius neither completed nor published it, but it came to light as it was found among his papers.

Three other acephalous works, ascribed to Gelasius and found in very ancient manuscript copies, present a greater difficulty:

1. The treatise *On the Bond of Anathema*, which will be presented in the collection to be published as chapter 47;

2. A copy of the account given by Blessed Pope Gelasius to the Eastern bishops concerning the avoidance of communion with Acacius, which was published from the Veronese manuscript;

3. A lengthy fragment of the same Gelasius, recovered by Sirmond from a manuscript at Verdun.

Tillemont casts doubt on the treatise *On the Bond of Anathema* in article 6 of his *Life of Euphemius of Constantinople*. It cannot indeed be denied that this little work, besides having an abrupt beginning, contains certain matters that seem connected neither with the title *On the Bond of Anathema* nor with the remainder of the discourse.

In the first and second chapters, the decrees of Chalcedon are discussed. It was said that they must either all be approved, or, if they were to be rejected in part, could not remain sound in their entirety. Then, in the third chapter, the subject of the bond of excommunication is introduced without any suitable connection and without an adequate introduction. At the end of the sixth chapter, however, the words “that the apostolic See …” return to the argument of the first and second chapters, and at this point have been inserted improperly. The matters supplied in the following chapters do pertain to the subject of the bond of anathema.

If it is observed that this work is incomplete, it will readily be understood why an account cannot be given of everything. A conjecture may nevertheless be offered. Since in the most ancient collections and manuscripts—not far removed in time from the age of Gelasius—the same work is attributed to this pontiff, and since both its subject matter and its opinions and style agree with him, there can rightly be no doubt that it was taken from his papers. Perhaps, however, because it was not complete in those papers, but had been prepared in a first draft and, as often happens with early compositions, written on several separate leaves without being fully assembled or connected, the compiler did not obtain all its parts and arranged those he found less suitably.

The first two chapters may belong to the subject of the bond of anathema if the Easterners are understood to have objected that the anathema issued against Acacius by decree of the Council of Chalcedon could be lifted by the pontiff in the same way that the canon of that council concerning the prerogatives of the See of Constantinople had been set aside by the Roman pontiffs.

Gelasius answers this objection by saying that one matter concerns the decree of faith issued at Chalcedon, which the Roman See confirmed because it accords with Scripture and tradition and which therefore acquired unshakable authority; another concerns the canon, which the same See rejected as defective on many grounds. Since the sentence against Acacius concerns the decree of faith, he argues that it cannot be lifted unless the error for which it was issued is abandoned.

If the beginning of the work had not been lost, these matters, as we believe, would be clearer. The statements at the end of the sixth chapter—“that the apostolic See did not consent,” and so forth—which have been inserted outside their proper place, seem to belong after the second chapter.

The statements in the third chapter—“Death was inflicted upon the sinful man,” and so forth—also require some connecting argument in order to be linked with what precedes and follows, and in order that a transition may be made to the sentence issued against Acacius and directed against the error condemned at the Council of Chalcedon.

The work is therefore incomplete and has been ill arranged by the compiler; but it should not for that reason be taken away from Gelasius.

9. Another little work published from the Veronese manuscript, since it presents Acacius, Peter Mongus, and the emperor Zeno as still living, seems more properly to be assigned to Felix III than to Gelasius, as the Marquis Maffei and P. Bernardo de Rubeis held.

Yet not only does the Veronese manuscript, written after the death of Vigilius, attribute it to Gelasius; so too does Nicholas I in Letter 42 to the archbishops and bishops of Gaul, when he recites the beginning of the same commonly published work under the title “To the Eastern Bishops.” Cardinal Deusdedit, part I, St. Anselm, book IV, chapter 27, and Gratian, *Decretum*, cause XVI, question 3, chapter 9, do likewise.
