Similarly, Ivo, part XIV, chapter 8, when citing another testimony from the same work—printed in volume V of the *Councils*, column 200 b—attributes the work itself to Gelasius under this heading: “Gelasius to the Eastern Bishops concerning the avoidance of communion with Acacius.” Gratian likewise repeats a testimony attributed to Gelasius in cause XI, question 3, chapter 46. From these sources it is clear that other manuscripts too presented Gelasius as the author.

There are also manuscripts belonging to another collection compiled in the eighth century, which we call the Dionysian Additions. In these, a fragment of this work is produced under the title: “From the letter of Blessed Pope Gelasius to the Easterners concerning the avoidance of communion with Acacius,” where it is implied that no bond is indissoluble except with regard to those who persist in error.

The fragment begins: “We did not therefore pronounce sentence against Acacius …,” as it appears in volume V of the *Councils*, column 195 a. Its style and opinions also agree with those contained in Gelasius’s letter to the Dardani and in the treatise *On the Bond of Anathema*.

The objections raised can be reconciled if we say that Gelasius composed this work in order to refute a petition written by the Easterners in the time of Felix, when Acacius, Peter Mongus, and the emperor Zeno were still alive; and that Gelasius thought the petition should be answered as though the response itself had been composed while those persons were still living.

Since this work explains more briefly and appropriately the matters concerning the sentence passed against Acacius and his never being released from the bonds of anathema—matters expounded more fully and intricately in Gelasius’s incomplete treatise *On the Bond of Anathema*—and since in both works the same testimonies from Scripture and the same opinions are brought forward concerning the same matter, if the treatise *On the Bond of Anathema* is to be attributed to Gelasius, this work too must be claimed for him. Otherwise Gelasius would seem to have labored so extensively and confusedly over a matter that Felix had already defined more narrowly and clearly.

To assign these two documents to Felix III without the authority of any manuscript or ancient witness, merely in order to take them away from Gelasius, to whom both manuscripts and ancient witnesses attribute them, is excessive confidence.

We believe that Gelasius did not publish the treatise that he left incomplete. In this later work, however, he inserted much from that same treatise in order to explain the cited words concerning the sentence. Since this work, now acephalous but formerly complete, was to be published—as it is indeed reported to have been sent to the Easterners—he applied care and diligence to arranging the matter more briefly and clearly, as he would undoubtedly have done in the treatise itself had he thought it should be completed and circulated.

10. As for the work printed from the manuscript at Verdun, it seems necessary to admit, with Tillemont in the passage cited, that it contains certain statements more appropriate to a private individual than to the Roman pontiff, such as these:

“It is not indeed proper to our humility to pronounce judgment on the discord of the whole world; yet it is our duty to be concerned for our own salvation.”

And also:

“We desire, whatever dangers and however great the dangers that the enemy may bring upon us, to endure them in the present age.”

And likewise at the end:

“For I believe, hope, and trust in Christ that neither tribulation, nor distress, nor the sword, nor persecution, nor life, nor death will ever be able to separate me from his love.”

“Let persecution press upon us; let the laws rage: for Christ’s soldier it is more glorious to die than to be conquered; it is better to be deprived of present advantages than to be without future ones.”

These statements, I say, present a man who was subject to violence in the East, not a Roman who, secure under Theodoric, had nothing to fear from the emperor of the East.

Moreover, this work—or, more accurately, this fragment of a work—very clearly presents not a translation from Greek but an original Latin composition.

What, then, are we to conclude? If the name of Gelasius stood at the head of the manuscript, as Sirmond does not report with complete clarity; or if the work was found among the works of Gelasius and originally taken from his papers, then what Tillemont conjectured is probable: the work was indeed written by Gelasius, whose style it does not contradict, but it was written not in his own name, rather in the name of those Easterners who were being harassed in the East, in order to strengthen them in their resolve to remain separate from profane communion.

§ 5. Whether and to what extent the decree concerning books to be received or rejected is to be attributed to Gelasius. Three forms of the same decree are presented, and the variation among the manuscripts is noted. The same decree is divided in some places into two. Manuscripts attributing the decree to Damasus, Gelasius, or Hormisdas. What seems proper to assert concerning each.

[Col. 0172C]

1. Since in this chapter we have discussed the works of Gelasius that several collections produce in connection with the case of Acacius, it is permissible, by way of an appendix, to add a few remarks concerning that famous decree on books to be received or rejected. In several collections it is presented in different forms and under different headings, and it has provoked no small controversy among scholars.

We have written at some length about this controversy in book II of the *Observations* on the works of Cardinal Noris, chapter 12. But, since in examining many manuscripts and collections we have found additional information about this decree that will contribute greatly to clarifying the matter, we trust that it will not be useless to return to the same subject.

This decree is reproduced differently in different collections. We have found three forms of the decree.

We found the fuller decree attributed to Pope Damasus in Codex Casanatensis D IV 23, dating from approximately the eleventh century, which contains excerpts from the canons of councils and the constitutions of Roman pontiffs. It reads there, on page 46:

“Here begins the council of the city of Rome under Pope Damasus concerning the explanation of the faith.”

At the beginning, a decree concerning the Holy Spirit is produced, which other manuscripts also attribute to Damasus, as we shall say later. It states that one must first discuss the sevenfold Spirit who rests in Christ, and so forth, as it was published from Holstenius in volume II of the Councils, Venetian edition, column 1047 e; except that, in place of the words “the manifold dispensation of the names of Christ,” this manuscript has: “Also concerning the manifold dispensation of the names of Christ.”

After the final words of this decree, “and he will announce them to you,” the same manuscript adds a canon of the sacred Scriptures as follows:

“Also it was said: Now we must discuss the divine Scriptures, what the universal Catholic Church receives and what it ought to avoid. Here begins the order of the Old Testament.”

After the books of the Old Testament have been listed, the books of the New Testament are added, as in the commonly published Gelasian decree, volume V of the Councils, column 385 a.

It continues:

“Also it was said: After all these prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic Scriptures that we have set forth above, by which the Catholic Church was founded through the grace of God,”

and so forth. After a brief encomium of the three principal sees—Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch—the general councils are listed, together with the decree concerning books to be received or rejected, as in the same Gelasian decree, columns 386 and following.

Among the councils alone, the following passage is omitted, which is found in the commonly published text:

“The holy Council of Constantinople, held under the emperor Theodosius the Elder Augustus, at which the heretic Macedonius received the condemnation due to him.”

Also omitted is the passage appended after the mention of the Council of Chalcedon:

“And if there are any councils instituted up to the present by the holy Fathers, after the authority of these general councils, we decree and command that they are both to be preserved and to be received.”

The same form of the decree, likewise attributed to Damasus, is also found in an ancient royal manuscript, according to P. Coustant in his note to Damasus’s fifth letter, no. 5, column 503.

Codex 61 of the Veronese Chapter, dating from the ninth or tenth century and containing a summary of the canons, the books of Halitgarius, and several other works, presents only that portion of this decree, likewise inscribed to Damasus, which begins with the words:

“After all these prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic Scriptures,”

and so forth. The demonstrative word “these” shows that the canon of the Scriptures preceded it in the complete decree from which this portion was taken.

The remainder is identical with the cited Casanatensis manuscript to the end, with the same omissions that we noted in the Casanatensis manuscript. The title there is:

“Concerning the council held in the city of Rome under Pope Damasus.”

At the end:

“The council under Pope Damasus is completed.”

2. The second form of the decree is somewhat shorter. It is the form published in the Councils at the place cited. It not only lacks the portion concerning the Holy Spirit edited by Holstenius, but also attributes the same decree to Gelasius.

It begins with the canon of the Scriptures. Among the approved councils it includes two passages: one concerning the Council of Constantinople and another concerning the councils of the holy Fathers to be received. These are entirely absent from the fuller form described above.

We were able to find this commonly published form only in copies of later collections, namely in Vatican Palatine manuscript 584, which contains a collection of a later period divided into twelve books, and also in Burchard, book III, chapters 117 through 121.

We were unable to find in any manuscript the chronological notice attached to the title in the printed editions.

Hincmar of Reims used a manuscript that contained this same form, with the sole exception that it did not add the Canons of the Apostles to the apocryphal books. Thus he writes in his *Opusculum of 55 Chapters* to Hincmar of Laon, chapter 24:

“Blessed Gelasius, in the catalogue in which he described which books should be received by the Catholic Church, after listing distinctly the authentic Scriptures, the Councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon, as well as other councils instituted by the holy Fathers, the works of orthodox writers, the decretal letters of the pontiffs of the apostolic See, and other writings, remained entirely silent about these Canons of the Apostles; nor did he place them among the apocrypha.”

See also chapter 25 of the same work.

In the manuscripts of the Isidorian additions, such as Vatican 1340 and Venice, St. Mark’s 169, the same commonly published form is found under the name of Gelasius, with two differences. The Council of Constantinople is absent, while the Canons of the Apostles are not listed among the apocrypha.

A double title also deserves notice. One is prefixed to the catalogue of the Scriptures:

“An order of the sacred books arranged by Pope Gelasius with seventy bishops.”

The other precedes the decree concerning the other books:

“Here begin the decrees of Pope Gelasius. The decree concerning apocryphal writings, held with seventy bishops.”

The same is found in the manuscript used by Merlin for his edition.

Vatican 1339, which presents a collection of canons divided into five books, describes the same commonly published decree under the name of Gelasius in the final chapter of book IV. In the first part, concerning books to be received, it omits the two passages concerning the Council of Constantinople and the other councils; in the second part, concerning apocryphal books, it does not list the Canons of the Apostles at all.

This same second form was printed from an old Florentine manuscript of St. Mark’s by P. Joseph Blanchini in volume IV of Anastasius, page 61, and there too it is attributed to Pope Gelasius.

Since, however, the author of the *Italian Literary History*, volume VII, describing the same manuscript, supplies on page 529 a heading attributing the decree not to Gelasius but to Damasus, we questioned a friend at the Florentine convent of St. Mark by letter. He replied that the following inscription could first be read:

“Here begins the council of the city of Rome under Pope Damasus concerning copies of the faith and concerning books to be received and not received.”

This title encompasses the entire decree according to the first form. Immediately afterward, however, only that portion of the decree concerning the Holy Spirit is supplied:

“One must first discuss the Holy Spirit,”

with the remainder through the words “and he will announce them to you,” as it was published by Holstenius.

Then another title follows, published by Blanchini:

“Here begins the decree concerning books to be rejected and received, written by Pope Gelasius with seventy most learned bishops in the apostolic See in the city of Rome.”

The canon of the Scriptures is then appended, with the remainder according to the second form. Here too the two passages mentioned above, concerning the Council of Constantinople and the other councils of the Fathers, are omitted, while the Canons of the Apostles are counted among the apocrypha.

3. The third form, the shortest of all, omits the catalogue of the Scriptures. After prefatory commendations of the three sees and of the councils, it presents the decree concerning books to be received or rejected. This third form is attributed to Gelasius.

Thus, in Vatican manuscript 3832, dating from approximately the twelfth century, we read:

“Here begin the decrees concerning books to be received and not received, written by Pope Gelasius with seventy most learned bishops in the apostolic See of the city of Rome.”

“After the prophetic and evangelical [books],” and so forth, as in the commonly published text, except that the Council of Constantinople is not inserted, as in the printed editions after Nicaea, but after Chalcedon, in these words:

“The Council of Constantinople also, at which the error of Eunomius and Macedonius was refuted.”

Immediately afterward the passage concerning the remaining councils is added:

“And if there are any councils established by the holy Fathers, after the authority of these four, we have decreed that they are both to be preserved and to be received.”

The Canons of the Apostles are not included among the apocrypha.

In the older copies containing this shorter form, not only are these canons omitted, but also the two passages concerning the Council of Constantinople and the other councils. Such is Vatican 630, belonging to the pure Isidorian collection. From it it is evident that the commonly published decree, which received several additions, did not originate with Isidore.

The same is true of other manuscripts that derived this decree from the pure Isidore. Other manuscripts older than Isidore also present this form.

Justus Fontaninius published precisely this same form in his *Appendix on the Antiquities of Horta*, page 317, from the exceedingly ancient and excellent Vatican Palatine manuscript 493, which preserved for us the old Gallican missal published by the venerable Cardinal Tommasi. There the following inscription is read:

“Here begins the decretal of Saint Pope Gelasius.”

Then: “After the prophetic …,” and so forth.

The same is found in the very old Lucano-Colbertine manuscript collection, from which P. Mansi printed this decree in volume I of his *Supplement to the Councils*, column 357, under the title:

“Here begins the decretal issued from the city of Rome concerning books to be received or not received, produced by the synod held under Gelasius, Pope of the city of Rome, with seventy bishops.”

4. The ancient collection of the Dionysian Additions requires particular attention. For it divides the fuller decree that we described in no. 1 into two, presenting the two parts separately, with other documents and titles interposed, and attributing one to Damasus and the other to Gelasius.

First, after the letter that Damasus sent to Paulinus, a decree concerning the Holy Spirit and the Scriptures is written under the name of Damasus with this title:

“The council of the city of Rome under Damasus concerning the explanation of the faith.”

“It was said: One must first discuss the sevenfold Spirit,” and so forth, as Holstenius printed this decree from the most ancient collection of canons in the Vatican Library, namely Vatican manuscript 5845, which contains the Dionysian additions.

After the final words printed by Holstenius, “he will announce them to you,” the same number adds:

“It was also said: Now we must discuss the divine Scriptures, what the universal Catholic Church receives and what it ought to avoid.”

After the catalogue of the Scriptures has been supplied, as we noted above in no. 1, the same number adds:

“It was also said: After all these prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic Scriptures that we have set forth above,”

and so forth, through the words of the commonly published Gelasian decree:

“The first name of the Christians, a new people, arose.”

These words conclude the mention of the three principal sees (*Councils*, vol. V, col. 387 a).

The most eminent Baronius had already published this final fragment from another Vatican manuscript, 1353, and from Vallicellana A 5 of this collection, which he called the Cresconian collection, under the year 382, no. 19.

Since this fragment, which is inscribed to Damasus, ends with the words just cited and lacks the remainder concerning the general councils, those who maintain that the decree must be removed from Damasus on the ground that it mentions the Councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon, Popes Celestine and Leo, and Eutyches and Nestorius—whose names are later than Damasus—are laboring under a false hypothesis.

Under that same false hypothesis, namely, that this decree includes a list of the general councils, P. Coustant, column 601, expressed wonder that the father of the *Annals*, a man of such keen sight, could so easily have been deceived by a title whose falsity is so obvious.

The portion concerning the councils, however, which mentions those names later than Damasus, begins in the same manuscript copies after several intervening titles and constitutes another decree concerning books to be received or rejected. It is attributed to Gelasius under this heading:

“Here begins the decretal concerning books to be received and not received, written by Pope Gelasius with seventy most learned bishops in the apostolic See of the city of Rome.”

“After the prophetic and evangelical [books],” and so forth, with the remainder concerning the general councils, books to be received, and apocryphal books, as in the third form described above.

It should be observed that here it is not written, as in the preceding decree inscribed with the name of Damasus, “After all these prophetic and evangelical [Scriptures],” because the catalogue of the Scriptures had not been placed before this text.

In these copies, moreover, the passages concerning the Council of Constantinople and the other councils of the Fathers are absent; the Canons of the Apostles, however, are listed among the apocrypha.

Atto of Vercelli inserted this decree in chapter 100 of his capitulary. There is no doubt that he copied it from the very ancient manuscript of the Chapter of the Church of Vercelli, which contains the Dionysian Additions.

5. Finally, the manuscripts of the fuller Spanish collection must be mentioned. They alone attribute this decree to Hormisdas.

In the table of titles of Vatican manuscript 1341, belonging to the Spanish collection, no. 102 reads:

“Decrees of the Roman See concerning books to be received and not received.”

Since this title, the last in the table, is placed not among the titles of Gelasius but after those of St. Gregory, it is recognized as an addition.

Although the decree is indicated in the table, we nowhere found it in the body of the manuscript, which is certainly not mutilated. Indeed, the table of the same collection that P. Coustant reproduces from other manuscripts in the preface to volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, page 109, does not include the title of this decree.

Moreover, in Vatican manuscript 4587, through which John Baptist Pérez supplied information about the manuscripts of the fuller Spanish collection, he reproduced a table from the same sources in which, under no. 103, this title is found:

“Decrees of the Roman See concerning books to be received and not received, issued by Pope Hormisdas.”

He added the following note:

“So in all the manuscripts, although in the printed editions and in Gratian they are attributed to Gelasius.”

Baluzius, in his notes to letter 132 of Lupus of Ferrières to Charles the Bald and to the *Dialogues of Antonio Agostino on the Correction of Gratian*, page 444, mentions a copy belonging to the Spanish Church of Urgell in which the same decree is attributed to Hormisdas.

P. Francis Chiffletius published this decree, inscribed to the same pontiff, from the Jurensian manuscript in his notes to Vigilius of Tapsus, page 149, under the following title:

“Here begins the decretal issued in the city of Rome by Pope Hormisdas.”

At the end:

“The decretal issued by Hormisdas, Pope of the city of Rome, is completed.”

P. Hardouin found the same decree attributed to Hormisdas in another similar manuscript of the Paris College of the Society of Jesus, from which he produced only the closing section in volume V of the Councils, Venetian edition, column 391, note 1.

These two manuscripts seem to have descended from Spanish manuscripts, which alone among the additions to the fuller Spanish collection received this decree under the inscription of Hormisdas.

As the decree was printed by Chiffletius from the Jurensian manuscript, it reproduces the second form explained above and agrees entirely with the commonly published Gelasian text. For it includes both passages concerning the Council of Constantinople and the other councils, and it inserts the Canons of the Apostles among the apocryphal books.

Whether the other Spanish manuscripts contain the same text we leave to be determined by those who have access to such books.

6. In such great diversity of manuscripts, what seems certain or more probable to us must be explained. First, it must certainly be acknowledged that the first form of the decree, attributed to Damasus in the Casanatense manuscript, cannot be ascribed to him, at least in that part which determines which books are to be received or rejected; for, besides the Synods of Ephesus and Chalcedon, among those books are listed several authors who flourished long after Damasus. Whether, however, that portion which concerns the Holy Spirit, the canonical Scriptures, and the three sees is his—since this alone is attributed to him in the manuscripts of the Additions to Dionysius—is no minor question.

The first section, which discusses the Holy Spirit, may indeed belong to him. Damasus, certainly, established the divinity of the Holy Spirit against the errors of Macedonius. Two fragments on this subject survive, which Holstenius found attached to the Roman synod’s letter under Damasus to the Easterners, with the title “Also from the section of the decree” prefixed to each fragment; we likewise found them in the very ancient manuscript 55 of the chapter of Verona. See above, chapter 9, no. 3. Perhaps, therefore, this section too is part of the same decree attributed to Damasus, in which a ruling is issued concerning that same Holy Spirit.

P. Coustantius promised to demonstrate, by a preliminary notice in this very decree of Gelasius, that this section should instead be restored to Gelasius and belongs to that Roman synod in which this pope issued the decree concerning the books, in volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 495. But the second volume, in which this notice was to be inserted together with the letters of Gelasius, has not yet appeared. Since, however, all the manuscripts that we have so far been able to obtain attribute this section of the decree to Damasus [Col. 0176D], while none attributes it to Gelasius, and since, so far as we know, Gelasius had no particular reason for issuing a ruling concerning the Holy Spirit such as Damasus had, we do not understand by what arguments or evidence he could have demonstrated this.

7. Doubt may be raised concerning the catalogue of the Scriptures which, in the cited manuscripts that place Damasus before the decree concerning the Holy Spirit, follows that decree—except in the Florentine manuscript of Saint Mark, which assigns to him only the section concerning the Holy Spirit. But the introductory words prefixed to that catalogue in the same manuscripts plainly prove that Damasus should not be regarded as its author:

“It has also been said. Now, however, we must discuss the divine Scriptures: what the universal Catholic Church receives, and WHAT IT OUGHT TO AVOID.”

These final words clearly indicate a decree concerning books not to be received, that is, concerning the apocrypha, which was to follow the catalogue of the Scriptures. This preface signifies that one and the same author composed both the catalogue of the Scriptures and the decree concerning the apocrypha. But just as the decree concerning the apocrypha cannot, as we have seen, be attributed to Damasus [Col. 0177A], so neither can the catalogue of the Scriptures, nor this preface, which presupposes both the catalogue and the decree.

Three consequences follow from this:

1. In the manuscripts of the Additions to Dionysius, the chapter in which the catalogue of the Scriptures follows the cited preface, without the decree concerning the apocrypha, is mutilated and incomplete.

2. If it is considered more probable that the preceding decree concerning the Holy Spirit belongs to Damasus, then the same catalogue, together with its preface, is an addition to that decree. The manuscript of Saint Mark in Florence presents this single decree, attributed to Damasus, more correctly.

3. Still more clearly an addition in those manuscripts—and wrongly attributed to Damasus—is the section appended to the catalogue of the Scriptures that briefly discusses the three principal sees, Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch. We shall soon see that this section must certainly be attributed to Gelasius.

8. Concerning Gelasius, therefore, there can be no doubt that the decree concerning the books must be attributed to him and to the Fathers of the synod which he held for this purpose, and not to Hormisdas. For Hormisdas clearly indicates that this decree had already been composed by the Fathers, in Letter 70 to Possessor.

Writing about the works of Faustus of Riez, which are rejected in that decree, Hormisdas states that he does not affirm that Faustus should be received, nor [does he affirm] the reception of any works which the examination of the Catholic faith does not receive on the authority of the Fathers. Here the authority of the Fathers suggests the decree concerning the apocrypha. Shortly afterward, referring to the same decree more explicitly, he says:

“Not rashly did the venerable wisdom of the Fathers define for faithful authority what the Catholic doctrines were; and, instructed by the Holy Spirit, prescribed a fixed selection of books, even ancient ones, to be received as authoritative.”

By these words he certainly indicates that the decree was not his own, but had been established by his predecessors in some synod of the Fathers. Since, according to what has been said, it cannot be attributed to Damasus, it remains that it must be claimed for Gelasius, to whom most collections and manuscripts indeed ascribe it.

The mention of the principal sees, which is briefly touched upon at the beginning of the decree concerning the books, must therefore also be assigned to Gelasius [Col. 0177C].

9. The only uncertainty is whether the second form of this decree, which places the catalogue of the Scriptures first, or only the third form, which lacks that catalogue, should be attributed to Gelasius.

The older manuscripts and collections prefer the third form. Among them, the origin of the Lucano-Colbertine Collection is not far removed from the time of Gelasius. The Collection of the Additions to Dionysius, compiled in the eighth century, derives from older collections. Vatican Palatine manuscript 493, of Gallican origin, bears every mark of great antiquity. Isidore Mercator himself, who arranged his collection at the beginning of the ninth century, found no other exemplar of Gelasius.

These manuscripts and collections should not be compared with those which attribute the second form of the decree—that is, the catalogue of the Scriptures as well—to Gelasius. Among them is one from the Paris College cited by Hardouin in volume V of the *Councils*, col. 385. It gives the heading:

“Notice of the Sacred Scriptures, or of the canonical books, with a description or annotation of Pope Gelasius.”

This appears to signify that only the annotation—understood as the decree concerning the books—was written by Gelasius.

Another collection, the Additions to Isidore, whose manuscripts place the catalogue of the Scriptures under the name of Gelasius, likewise removes it from him by several indications. For, after describing the catalogue of the Scriptures in a single chapter under the title “The order of the Old Testament … arranged by Pope Gelasius with seventy bishops,” the manuscripts of this collection do not immediately append, in the same chapter, the decree concerning the books with the opening that refers back to the catalogue:

“After all these prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic Scriptures …”

This is how it appears in the other books that join the two sections into one decree. Instead, in another chapter they place the following heading:

“Here begin the decrees of Pope Gelasius: the decree concerning the apocryphal Scriptures, held with seventy bishops, which begins: ‘After the prophetic and evangelical Scriptures,’ etc.”

Let the word “begin” be noted, as well as the opening “After the prophetic,” just as in the copies that do not place the canonical Scriptures first [Col. 0178A].

The difficulty that led some people to remove the decree concerning the books from Gelasius depends upon its chronological note—namely, the consulship of Asterius and Praesidius in the year 494, although certain books listed in the same decree are later than that year. Since, however, we have found this consular note in no collection and no manuscript, we have no doubt that it was improperly attached. For this reason P. Coustantius rightly proposed to himself, as his fifth point of demonstration—according to P. Mopinot in a letter published in 1724—that the chronological note, which has given rise to so many disputes, should be removed, since it rests upon no sufficiently firm authority and was even rashly imported from another letter of Gelasius.

10. We shall briefly indicate what should be said about the manuscripts of the Spanish Collection that attribute this decree to Hormisdas.

As we noted above, the decree belongs not to the original Spanish Collection, but to its enlarged form and later additions. Since, however, the material added to this enlarged collection is genuine, it seems that this decree was repeated for the sake of the Spaniards by Hormisdas and sent to Spain. Hence the name of Hormisdas is prefixed to this decree only in Spanish manuscripts, or in those that have taken something from Spanish manuscripts.

Perhaps this pope also placed the catalogue of the Scriptures first, if it is believed that it was absent from the decree of Gelasius. Since the two frequently mentioned sections concerning the Council of Constantinople and the other councils of the Fathers are not found in many and older manuscripts of the decree of Gelasius belonging to the various collections cited above, we think that these sections were inserted into the Gelasian decree in certain inferior copies.

The addition is particularly clear in Vatican manuscript 3832. There, the mention of the Council of Constantinople was inserted outside its proper place, after the Council of Chalcedon, and soon afterward another section concerning the other councils was added, as we noted in its proper place.

These additions, when suitably placed in Hormisdas’s decree, may perhaps have Hormisdas himself as their author; and later, from his decree, some people added them either outside their proper place or, when copying the decree of Gelasius, in their proper place.

Since peace with the Easterners had been established under Pope Hormisdas, and since they counted the Council of Constantinople among the general councils in the professions of faith that they sent to Hormisdas—as is evident from the report of Epiphanius, bishop of Constantinople, in volume V of the *Councils*, col. 666—perhaps that pope was the first to add this council to the general councils insofar as concerns its creed and definition of faith. From that time, under Vigilius, Pelagius, and Gregory, the Latins began to speak of four ecumenical councils.

We have spoken of the creed and of the definition of faith by which the heretic Macedonius received his due condemnation; that alone is presented in the addition to the decree, so that it is unnecessary to transfer this same reference to the canons of that council. Saint Gregory testifies that those canons had not yet been received by the Roman Church in his time, in Book VII, Letter 34. Compare what we wrote above, chapter 1, § 2.

As for the other addition—“And if there are any councils established up to this time by the holy Fathers,” etc.—it should be observed that these words do not indicate any definite and particular synod as though it had been received by the Roman Church as part of a code of canons. Rather, they approve conditionally and without specification any councils that may have been established by the holy Fathers.

Perhaps Hormisdas added this for the benefit of the Spaniards, so that he would not appear to reject the Spanish councils, or the African councils, or others that carried authority among them.

Although this decree, as we noted at the beginning, was not present in the original Spanish Collection, it may nevertheless be inferred that copies of it existed among the Spaniards when that original collection was compiled. This follows from the preface that the author of the collection placed at its beginning and that Saint Isidore of Seville copied almost in its entirety in his books of the *Etymologies*. In that preface, after mentioning the four councils, the author states that other councils of Catholic Fathers are likewise to be received, in such a way that he appears to have had this decree before his eyes and to have copied nearly the same words.

The section concerning the canons of the apostles, which is absent from most and best manuscripts containing the Gelasian decree but is absent from none that present Hormisdas, may also be counted among the additions of this pope.

Before Dionysius’s translation, these canons were not known to the Latins. Perhaps, therefore, after the decree of Gelasius they were first rendered into Latin and published among the Latins, and were then counted by Hormisdas among the apocrypha. For this reason the author of the aforementioned Spanish Collection—who transferred into his codex all the documents of Dionysius except the canons of the councils, which he obtained elsewhere—passed over the apostolic canons, which he knew only from Dionysius, because he found them listed among the apocrypha by apostolic authority, that is, by the decree of Hormisdas, as he indicates rather clearly at the end of the aforementioned preface.

Indeed, if those canons had been rejected as apocryphal by Pope Gelasius, Dionysius, who compiled his collection at Rome after that pope, would either not have allowed those same canons, which the pope had rejected as apocryphal, to stand at the head of his codex, or at least, when he thought it necessary to insert this warning in his preface—“because many had not readily given their assent to them, we did not wish your holiness to remain unaware of this”—he would have noted all the more clearly that Gelasius, whom he praises highly in his letter to the presbyter Julian, had judged them apocryphal.

Therefore, after Dionysius’s codex had been published, Hormisdas, instructed by Dionysius’s words that many among the Greeks themselves did not agree with those canons, judged that they should be added to the apocrypha.

From this it appears that only the third form of the decree should be claimed for Pope Gelasius: the form which, in the oldest manuscript collections, omits the two sections concerning the Council of Constantinople and the other synods of the Fathers, and does not list the apostolic canons among the apocrypha.

[CLVIII] CHAPTER XII. On the Avellana Manuscript Collection. Two previously unpublished letters of Hormisdas and certain fragments taken from this collection.

[Col. 0179C]

1. This especially remarkable and insufficiently known collection requires a more accurate description, since from it many important papal and ecclesiastical documents have emerged.

From this collection, as P. Constantius noted, numerous records concerning the election of Boniface I and the schism of Ursinus were published. From it also came certain unusual letters of Innocent and Zosimus concerning the case of Pelagius and Caelestius; the booklet of the deacon Paulinus against Caelestius; and five letters of Saint Leo written after Timothy the Cat had been expelled from the see of Alexandria and Timothy Solofaciolus had been raised to it.

From it came also several letters of Simplicius and Felix, and a great many letters which Hormisdas either himself issued or received from others concerning the settlement of the Acacian schism. There are likewise some letters of John I, Agapetus, and Vigilius. Those who are skilled in good literature know the value of all these writings.

In brief, the collection contains 246 documents. We would lack more than two hundred of them if this collection had not preserved them for us. Those documents that were published elsewhere, or could have been published elsewhere, sometimes contain in this collection genuine and notable additions that are not found in the other manuscripts; sometimes they are not found in books formerly published, but only in certain extremely rare copies, either later than the others or unknown to our compiler.

For the compiler seems to have adopted the policy of copying those materials that he found nowhere in the other collections known to him. No document in this collection that is of Latin origin is apocryphal. Only eight spurious letters to Peter the Fuller, translated from Greek, are included; in the preceding chapter, § 3, we showed that they were fabricated by some Greek writer before the Fifth Synod.

2. The documents in this collection are not arranged chronologically in the manner followed by Dionysius and the author of the Spanish Collection. The disordered sequence—in which quite a few older documents are placed after more recent ones, and letters of one and the same pope are found scattered here and there—plainly shows that the compiler copied the documents as they came into his hands. The same is true of the authors of other ancient collections.

It is clear, however, that this compiler used excellent sources. The documents of Hormisdas, especially, or those relating to Hormisdas—which are numerous—appear to have been drawn from the Roman archives.

For this reason, after the letter of that pope to the Council of Constantinople, the following note may perhaps be read:

“We have in the archives the acts in the case of Abundantius, bishop of Trajanopolis.”

Since this note has no connection either with the preceding or with the following letter of Hormisdas, neither of which discusses Abundantius, it appears to have been added by the compiler to indicate that he had found in the Roman archives those acts which he nevertheless did not think should be inserted into his collection.

The most recent letters in this collection are those of Vigilius. Accordingly, the collection must be said to have been compiled around the middle of the sixth century [Col. 0180B].

3. Several manuscript copies of this outstanding collection exist in Italy; so far as we know, none are found outside Italy. It should therefore be called an Italian collection, and indeed one compiled at Rome, especially if the compiler drew at least the letters of Hormisdas from the Roman archives.

We found four copies in the Vatican Library. The two older ones are numbered 3787 and 4961; the other two, copies of these, are numbered 3786 and 4903.

Two other recent copies are also preserved at Rome: one in the Angelica Library of the Hermits of Saint Augustine, distinguished by the marks 5 III 9; the other in the Corsiniana, no. 817.

We also found two copies in the Venetian Library of Saint Mark, nos. 171 and 172. One of these was copied at Rome in 1469 at the order of Cardinal Bessarion, perhaps from Vatican manuscript 3787, of the twelfth century. The other codex, 4961, as will soon be clear, was brought to Rome much later than Bessarion and then transferred to the Vatican Library [Col. 0180C].

Since this codex, Vatican 4961, is by far the most celebrated and the oldest, and formerly belonged to the monastery of Santa Croce at Fonte Avellana, we have called this collection the Avellana, so that it might be distinguished from the others by some proper name.

On the final page of the same codex the following note is written:

“This book belongs to the monastery of Santa Croce at Fonte Avellana, in the diocese of Gubbio. The lord Damianus acquired this book. S. +.”

From this we recognize the codex as having been acquired by Saint Peter Damian, celebrated for the holiness of his life and for his writings. He entered monastic life in that monastery and governed it around the middle of the eleventh century. The age of the codex is therefore certainly at least seven hundred years.

The codex later passed from the monastery of Avellana into the hands of Cardinal Marcello Cervini, bishop of Gubbio, who later became Pope Marcellus II. We infer this from a note written in his own hand on the second page of the codex. In smaller letters the following was added there:

“Those words were added by Marcellus II when he was still a Roman cardinal-presbyter.”

The codex subsequently belonged to Cardinal Sirletus. It was purchased from his manuscripts and eventually reached the Vatican Library, as we are informed by this note on the first page:

“Purchased from the books of Cardinal Sirletus.”

When the eminent Baronius published document 48 under the year 417, no. 16, and cited the codex of Sirletus, he cited this codex before it had passed into the Vatican. Elsewhere, however, when he cites the Vatican codex, he appears to be citing copy Vatican 3787.

4. The sequence and order of the documents must now be set out exactly, so that what has hitherto been obscure concerning this collection may become clear to everyone.

Since the previously unpublished documents were published partly by the Roman editors of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs* in 1591, partly by P. Sirmondus in his works, and partly by Cardinal Baronius in the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, while one document that still appeared to await publication has most recently been issued through the efforts of Pietro Francesco Foggini—only two shorter documents, which escaped everyone’s diligence, will be produced below in their proper place—we shall cite sometimes one edition and sometimes another.

Since most of the documents have been translated into editions of the *Councils*, we shall more frequently cite the latest Venetian edition, which is more readily available.

In the cited Vatican codex 4961, after the table of chapters, the following appears in place of a title:

“This codex contains 243 letters” [correct to 246].

I. The acts between the bishops Liberius and Felix, and a certain letter of the schismatics. “In the time of Constantine,” etc. Volume I of Sirmondus, latest Venetian edition, p. 133. This document and the next are also found in two other manuscripts, the Colbertine and the Remigian, cited by the editors of the works of Sirmondus. Whether Sirmondus printed them from these manuscripts or from some copy of the present collection that he saw at Rome is uncertain.

II. The petitions of the presbyters Marcellinus and Faustinus, submitted to Valentinian and Theodosius. “We beseech,” etc. Ibid., p. 137.

III. Letter of the emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius to Salustius, prefect of the City, concerning the construction of the basilica of Saint Paul. “Since we desired,” etc. Baronius, under the year 386, no. 30.

IV. Their congratulatory letter to Pinianus, prefect of the City, on the ordination of Pope Siricius. “Hail, dearest Pinianus,” etc. The same, under the year 385, no. 6.

V. Their letter to Praetextatus, prefect of the City, in which Ursinus and those with him are released from exile. “Hail, dearest Praetextatus,” etc. The same, under the year 368, no. 4.

VI. Valentinian, Valens, and Gratian to Praetextatus, concerning the return of the basilica of Sicin(i)us. “Since dissensions have arisen,” etc. Ibid., no. 2.

VII. The same to the same, concerning the expulsion of the associates of Ursinus from Rome. “It is innate in us,” etc. Ibid., no. 3.

VIII. The same to Olibrius, the praetor. “You indeed, as recently,” etc. The same, under the year 369, no. 3. In Vatican manuscript 4961, the title “Concerning those who were rebaptized” is prefixed to this letter. We have transferred it, more correctly, with the Venetian manuscripts and Vatican 3787, to number XIII. Likewise, the title of the following number had to be transferred with those manuscripts to number XIV.

IX. The same to Aginarius, the vicar. “All the more amid these dissensions,” etc. Ibid., no. 4.

X. The same to Olibrius, prefect. “Since nothing can be more pleasing,” etc. Ibid., no. 5.

[CLX] XI. To Ampelius, prefect. “By right of our gentleness,” etc. Baronius, under the year 371, no. 1.

XII. To Maximinus, vicar of the City of Rome. “This has been divinely established,” etc. Ibid., no. 3.

XIII. Concerning those who were rebaptized. Gratian and Valentinian to Aquilinus, vicar. “The judgment of the ordinary judges,” etc. Baronius, under the year 381, no. 2, and volume II of the *Councils*, col. 1190.

XIV. Concerning the proceedings between Boniface and Eulalius, when both seized the episcopate of the city of Rome through contentious ambition [Col. 0181D]. Copy of the report of Symmachus, prefect of the City, to Honorius. “Whatever is done in the city of Rome,” etc. Baronius, under the year 418, no. 79.

XV. Imperial letter in that case to Symmachus. “After all the proceedings had been reviewed,” etc. The same, under the year 419, no. 2.

XVI. Another report of Symmachus to the emperor. “As soon as the sacred speech,” etc. Ibid., no. 5.

XVII. Petition of the presbyters on behalf of Boniface to Honorius and Theodosius. “After the departure of Saint Zosimus, the pope,” etc. Ibid., no. 8.

XVIII. Imperial rescript on behalf of the presbyters to Symmachus. “After the report of your highness,” etc. Ibid., no. 11.

XIX. Another report of Symmachus. “When the most illustrious man Aphtonius,” etc. Ibid., no. 12.

XX. Copy of an imperial letter to the synod. “Although our clemency,” etc. Ibid., no. 14. The following note is added:

“This synod, disagreeing among itself, was unable to settle the present case. Therefore the venerable emperor Honorius thought that the matter should be referred to a larger council; and, in the meantime, because the days of holy Easter were approaching, he ordered both Boniface and Eulalius to depart from this city and ordered the bishop of Spoletium, named Achilleus, to celebrate the sacred mysteries. He conveyed the same instruction in writing to Symmachus, prefect of the City.”

Baronius also gave this note under the year 419, no. 15, where he reads “for the May Kalends” instead of “to a larger council.” Our reading, however, is confirmed by the edict to the people, discussed below at number 24.

XXI. Imperial letter to Symmachus, in which the emperor ordered Boniface and Eulalius to leave the City and, in the meantime, ordered the bishop of Spoletium to celebrate the sacred mysteries. We have taken this title, which was omitted from the body of the collection because of the preceding note, from the table prefixed to the collection. The letter begins: “After great deliberations,” etc. Baronius, under the year 419, no. 15.

XXII. Copy of the imperial letter to Achilleus. “Since the Roman priesthood,” etc. Ibid., no. 16.

[Col. 0182B] XXIII. The emperor’s speech to the Senate. “We know, illustrious Fathers,” etc. Ibid., no. 17.

XXIV. Edict of the same emperor to the people. “Guardianship of the faith, excellent Quirites,” etc. Ibid., no. 48.

XXV. Letter of the same emperor to Paulinus, bishop of Nola. “Our judgment among us was so firmly settled,” etc. Ibid., no. 20.

XXVI. Likewise, letter of the same emperor to the African bishops. “Our serenity, in all cases,” etc. Ibid., no. 21.

XXVII. Letter of the same emperor to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, concerning the same matter. “Another reason for seeing your veneration,” etc. Ibid., no. 22.

XXVIII. Letter of the same emperor, in identical form, to Augustine, Alypius, Evodius, Donatianus, Silvanus, Novatus, and Deutherius. “That it has reached your veneration,” etc. Ibid., no. 23. We have written “Deutherius” in accordance with our manuscripts, with which the Carthaginian conference of 411 also agrees, where Deutherius is named as bishop of Caesarea in Mauretania.

[Col. 0182C] XXIX. Report of Symmachus to Constantius. “Whatever suddenly,” etc. The same, under the year 419, no. 26.

XXX. Letter of Constantius the count to Symmachus. “So that we may be certain,” etc. Ibid., no. 29.

XXXI. Copy of an imperial letter to Symmachus. “For the purpose of healing,” etc. Ibid., no. 30.

XXXII. Letter of Symmachus to Constantius. “As soon as,” etc. Ibid., no. 32.

[CLXI] XXXIII. Copy of an imperial letter to Symmachus. “With exceptional moderation,” etc. Ibid., no. 33.

XXXIV. Report of Symmachus concerning Boniface’s entry. “Whatever is done with God as author,” etc. Ibid., no. 84.

XXXV. Imperial letter to Largus, proconsul of Africa. “Among all our concerns,” etc. Ibid., no. 36.

XXXVI. Letter of Largus the proconsul to Aurelius of Carthage. “Concerning the merit of the priest,” etc. Ibid., no. 37.

XXXVII. Imperial letter to Boniface establishing that henceforth, if two men contend for the Roman episcopate through ambition, neither of them shall be priest; rather, only he shall remain in the apostolic see whom divine judgment and the consent of the whole body, through a new election from among the clergy, shall choose. “The letter of your blessedness,” etc. Ibid., no. 41. This imperial letter, together with Boniface’s own letters to the emperor, by which he requested this enactment, is also found in other collections.

XXXVIII. Letter of Honorius to Arcadius concerning the person of Saint John, bishop of Constantinople. “Although concerning the image,” etc. Baronius, under the year 404, no. 80.

XXXIX. Letter of the tyrant Maximus to the younger Valentinian against the Arians and Manichaeans. “Unless our clemency,” etc. Volume II of the *Councils*, col. 1228.

XL. Victor Magnus Maximus to Siricius, his father. “We have received your letter,” etc. Ibid., col. 1227.

XLI. Letter of Innocent to Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, etc. “The letter of your fraternity,” etc. It is found in the collection to be published in this volume, chapter 11, and was formerly published from Isidore.

XLII. Innocent to the presbyter Jerome. “Never has anything good,” etc. Volume III of the *Councils*, col. 75.

[Col. 0183A] XLIII. The same to John, his brother. “Plunderings, massacres, and fires,” etc. Ibid.

XLIV. The same to Aurelius. “Most devoutly also,” etc. Ibid., col. 76.

XLV. Zosimus to Aurelius and the other Africans in defense of Caelestius. “A great weight,” etc. Ibid., col. 401.

XLVI. The same Zosimus to Aurelius and the others. “After Caelestius had been with us,” etc. Ibid., col. 803.

XLVII. The booklet of the deacon Paulinus against Caelestius, presented to Zosimus, bishop. “The justice of your blessedness,” etc. Ibid., col. 429.

XLVIII. Letter of Augustine replying to the foregoing, sent through Albinus the acolyte and Firmus the presbyter, to the presbyter Xystus. “From the time I came to Hippo,” etc. From other manuscripts it was printed among Augustine’s letters as Letter 191, formerly 104.

XLIX. Letter of Eusebius to Cyril, bishop. “In Christ I gave thanks,” etc. Baronius, under the year 417, no. 15.

L. Zosimus to Aurelius and the others in the Council of Carthage. [Col. 0183B] “Although the tradition of the Fathers,” etc. Volume III of the *Councils*, col. 416.

LI. Leo to the emperor Leo. This is Letter 169 in volume I of our edition, col. 1431.

LII. The same to Gennadius of Constantinople. Ibid., Letter 170, col. 1433.

LIII. The same to Timothy, bishop of Alexandria. Ibid., Letter 171, col. 1435.

LIV. The same to the presbyters and deacons of Alexandria. Ibid., Letter 172, col. 1436.

LV. The same to Theophilus and the other bishops of Egypt. Ibid., Letter 173, col. 1437.

LVI. Letter of Pope Simplicius to the emperor Zeno. “I would indeed wish,” etc. Volume V of the *Councils*, col. 96, where it is noted that this letter is also found in the Verdun manuscript under the name Basiliscus. See the preceding chapter, § 3, no. 4.

LVII. The same to Acacius. “Since our sons,” etc. Ibid., col. 101.

LVIII. Another letter to the same. “How great is the power of the presbyters,” etc. Ibid., col. 99.

LIX. To the people of Constantinople. “Through our son, the praiseworthy man Epiphanius,” etc. Ibid., col. 101.

LX. To the emperor Zeno. “Among the works,” etc. Ibid., col. 103.

LXI. To Acacius. “How effective it is,” etc. Ibid., col. 105.

LXII. To the emperor Zeno. “Through Peter, the distinguished man,” etc. Ibid., col. 106.

LXIII. To Acacius. “How many and how abundant,” etc. Ibid., col. 107.

[CLXII] LXIV. To the emperor Zeno. “Recently, when we were coming to the City,” etc. Ibid., col. 108.

LXV. To Acacius. “Recently, to your affection,” etc. Ibid.

LXVI. To the emperor Zeno. “Concerning the Church of Antioch,” etc. Ibid., col. 109.

LXVII. To Acacius, after he had appointed Calendion bishop of Antioch. “The letters of the most merciful emperor,” etc. Ibid., col. 110.

[Col. 0183D] LXVIII. To the same. “We are equally amazed,” etc. Ibid., col. 113.

LXIX. To the same. “The beginning of the Antiochene priesthood,” etc. Ibid., col. 112.

LXX. Roman synod at Saint Peter’s to the people of Constantinople and Bithynia. “Formerly and from the beginning,” etc. Ibid., col. 247.

LXXI. Letter of Pope Felix to Peter of Antioch. “Since by pestilential doctrines,” etc. After this letter the following note is appended:

“Here ends the letter of Pope Felix to Peter of Antioch, condemning him. As its text indicates, this letter appears to have been written before the condemnation of Acacius. But because, together with other letters addressed to the same Peter, we found them in a Greek volume translated from Latin, we have now, compelled by necessity on account of the plots of the heretics, translated them again from Greek into Latin and copied them, joining them to the aforementioned letters of the same pope.”

Anastasius saw this note, as we observed in the preceding chapter, § 3, no. 2, where we showed that this letter and the seven following ones were formerly fabricated by a Greek writer. In the edition of the *Councils*, the Greek text of the seven letters was published in volume V, cols. 159, 219, 226, 234, 235, 239, and 241; nevertheless, another translation of six letters was printed there. From the translation in our collection, this letter of Felix alone is found in volume I of the Roman edition of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs* of 1591.

LXXII. Quintianus, bishop of Asculum, to Peter of Antioch. “In many ways and by many means,” etc. Volume V of the *Councils*, col. 219.

LXXIII. Justinus, bishop of Sicily, to the same Peter of Antioch. “A soldier must be armed against the enemy,” etc. Another translation appears there, col. 226.

LXXIV. Antheon, bishop of Arsinoe, to the same. “I have earnestly protested against you,” etc. There, from another translation, col. 234.

LXXV. Faustinus, bishop of Apolloniadis, to the same. “Since the last may summon the first,” etc. Another translation appears there, col. 235, where *Fausti* is printed instead of *Faustini*.

LXXVI. Pamphilus, bishop of the Accidians—called Abydorum in the printed edition—to the same. “Great is the grief of my beloved children,” etc. There, from another translation, col. 239.

LXXVII. Flactianus—elsewhere Falcini in the text of the Venetian manuscripts, Flaviani or Flacciani in the printed editions—bishop of Rhodope, to the same Peter. “Hunters of wild beasts are not frightened by anger,” etc. The Greek text of this letter is lacking, and only this version from our collection was published after Baronius, in volume V of the *Councils*, col. 227.

LXXVIII. Asclepiades, bishop of Citralis—called Trallianus in the printed editions—to the same. “Behold, dearest, the world has been filled with the scandal of your exposition,” etc. There, from another translation, col. 241.

Thus far extend the spurious letters translated into Latin from a Greek text that had been fabricated before our compiler.

LXXIX. Letter of Gelasius sent to the bishops of Dardania and likewise to all the brothers throughout Dalmatia. “As soon as it is lawful to breathe again,” etc. Volume V of the *Councils*, col. 292.

LXXX. Dardanus, bishop, to Gelasius. “The most salutary commands of your apostolate,” etc. Ibid., col. 291.

LXXXI. Gelasius to Laurentius of Lignidus. “In the length of the letter,” etc. Ibid., col. 289.

LXXXII. Agapetus to the emperor Justinian. “We congratulate you, venerable emperor, because so great …,” etc. Ibid., col. 937.

LXXXIII. Vigilius to Justinian. “Amid innumerable anxieties,” etc. Ibid., col. 1317.

LXXXIV. John, bishop, to the emperor Justinian. “Among the illustrious works of wisdom,” etc. Ibid., col. 890. It is also found in the *Justinian Code*, Book VIII, “Concerning the Supreme Trinity.”

LXXXV. Reparatus and the other 217 bishops at Justinian Carthage in council, to Pope John. “The excellent custom,” etc. [CLXIII] Ibid., col. 900.

LXXXVI. Agapetus to Reparatus and the other Africans. “For a long time, dearest brothers,” etc. Ibid., col. 939.

[Col. 0184D] LXXXVII. The same to Reparatus of Carthage. “The letter of your fraternity,” etc. Ibid., col. 940.

LXXXVIII. The same to the emperor Justinian. “Although concerning the first fruits of my priesthood,” etc. Ibid., col. 941.

LXXXIX. The booklet of the emperor Justinian, which he delivered to Agapetus at Constantinople. “In the name of the Lord,” etc. “The first salvation is to preserve the rule of right faith,” etc. Ibid., col. 947. There, the chronological note should be corrected from our manuscripts as follows:

“Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, after the consulship of Belisarius, a man of illustrious rank.”

XC. A booklet of Menas, presbyter and director of a hospice, who was made bishop of Constantinople on 13 March, again after the consulship of Paulinus the Younger, vir clarissimus. “The first safeguard is right faith,” etc., as in the preceding volume V, col. 947, through the words “we proclaim what has been established by it.” It concludes with Menas’s own subscription: “Menas, by the mercy of God presbyter and director of a hospice, I accept,” etc.

XCI. Agapitus to Justinian. “We rejoice, venerable [Col. 0185A] emperor,” etc. In this letter, published in volume V of the Councils, col. 937, there is inserted a letter of Justinian to Agapitus beginning “Before the time,” etc., which is read in the same place, col. 936; and inserted within it are other letters of the same emperor to Pope John, beginning “Rendering honor,” as in the same col. 936. After these insertions, the earlier letter of Justinian to Agapitus continues: “For this reason we ask,” as in the same volume, col. 937, at the end; and finally Agapitus’s letter concludes: “Therefore, as was stated above,” etc., in the same place, col. 938. The chronological notices of the two letters—Agapitus’s to Justinian and Justinian’s to Agapitus—which had been corrupted in the same printed editions, were emended after Cardinal Noris from a Vatican manuscript of this collection by P. Antonio Pagi, as is noted in the Venetian edition of the Councils, the same col. 938, nos. 2 and 3.

XCII. Vigilius to Justinian. “The letters of Your Clemency,” etc. Same place, col. 1295.

XCIII. Vigilius to Menas. “Although all things,” etc. Same place, col. 1298.

[Col. 0185B] XCIV. Gelasius to the bishops of Picenum against the Pelagian heresy. “Until now, amid barbarian affairs,” etc. Same place, col. 301.

XCV. The same to Dardanus. “We were greatly astonished,” etc. Same place, col. 324. This letter is fuller than in the other collections; and we have shown in the preceding chapter, § 4, that these additions should be attributed to Gelasius’s own second revision.

XCVI. The same to Bishop Honorius. “We marvel at your affection,” etc. Same place, col. 300.

XCVII. Statements of the same Gelasius against the Pelagian heresy. It begins: “As for the views of the Pelagians,” etc. Same place, col. 365.

XCVIII. The same to Bishop Honorius. “Although amid the various difficulties of the times,” etc. Same place, col. 298.

XCIX. “It begins: In the cause of the Christian faith, whose enemies are shown never to have been absent from its beginning,” etc. This is the little work published in volume V of the Councils, col. 173, under the title *A Brief Account of the History of the Eutychianists*. From our collection it was first printed [Col. 0185C] before the letters of St. Leo in the Roman edition of the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs of 1591, volume I, p. 142. Later Sirmond published it as though it were unpublished, from another collection, and it was inserted into the Councils from that edition. In Sirmond’s copy, however, the final sentence and a fragment of the letter of Felix III are missing; both are read only in our collection and consequently in the aforementioned Roman edition.

We conjectured in note 1 to chapter 43 of the collection published in this volume, col. 308, that this work, having been published in three forms, received two additions from the author himself. We have also judged it probable that the author was Gelasius himself, among whose letters it is transmitted, as we argued in note 4 on Quesnell’s Observations on letter 28 of St. Leo, volume II, col. 1414.

We now believe that the final sentence and the fragment of Felix III’s letters, which are absent from the printed editions of the Councils, should be appended here. Therefore, after the editors’ final words, “he sent to the Church of Antioch,” the following should be added:

“After Bishop John arrived, whom the Roman Church received, St. Pope Felix, as stated, arranged the legation as was proper; among all those mentioned above it encountered every form of hostility. For, thrust into custody, with his documents lost, it scarcely returned amid great disgrace, bringing back confirmed the episcopate of Peter, to expel whom it had been sent—an episcopate which the Roman Church would anathematize.

Thus Pope Felix, after other matters, to the bishops established throughout Egypt, the Thebaid, Libya, and Pentapolis:

‘As for Peter, who separated himself from the unity of the Church under Proterius of blessed memory, and, at the latter’s death, joined himself to the parricide Timothy in persecuting the orthodox, we do not permit him to rejoice in any communion of so great a name or dignity, since he is found no different from his own progenitors; and from its very beginning what he considers [enduring] is found to be transitory. Therefore the aforesaid man is anathema to all, and let him never be believed received by the Catholic Church. For after the most frequent coercion [the Roman editors read: “the most frequent exhortation”], and after persevering for so many years in his own perversity, he has forfeited the place of satisfaction.’”

C. It begins: “Of the same Pope Gelasius against the senator Andromachus and the other Romans, who were resolving that the Lupercalia should be celebrated according to the ancient custom: Certain men sit in their houses,” etc. Volume V of the Councils, col. 359.

CI. Gelasius to the Dardanians and those throughout Illyricum. “When we heard the orthodox,” etc. Same place, col. 322.

CII. The booklet that the representatives of the Church of Alexandria gave to the envoys sent from the city of Rome to Constantinople. “To the most glorious and excellent patrician Festus,” etc. Same place, col. 412. After this booklet, written under Pope Anastasius, the following note, written in capital letters, is read in Vatican Codex 4961, p. 63:

“I, Dionysius Exiguus, translated [it] from Greek at Rome.”

Binius, in the cited volume V, col. 403, note a, incorrectly refers this note to the following document, which, since it was written in Latin, did not need to be translated from Greek by Dionysius.

[Col. 0186B] CIII. Copy of the proceedings concerning the absolution of Misenus. “In the consulship of Flavius Viator, vir clarissimus, on 13 May, in the basilica of Blessed Peter. With the venerable Pope Gelasius presiding in synod,” etc. Same place, col. 397. From this collection this synod was first published by the Roman editors of the letters of the Roman Pontiffs, and subsequently by Cardinal Baronius under the year 395, no. 6, with emendations from the manuscript of Verdun, whose readings he had received from P. Fronto Ducaeus.

CIV. Symmachus to all those throughout Illyricum and Dardania, etc. “That this should plainly be done,” etc. Same place, col. 431.

CV. Dorotheus to Hormisdas. “He says in a certain passage,” etc. Same place, col. 563.

CVI. Hormisdas to Dorotheus. “Where the concern of charity lies,” etc. Same place, col. 564.

CVII. The emperor Anastasius to Hormisdas. “We do not think that it is unknown to Your Beatitude,” etc. Same place, col. 561.

CVIII. Hormisdas to Anastasius. “We give thanks to the power above,” etc. Same place, col. 562.

[Col. 0186C] CIX. Anastasius to Hormisdas. “In all matters,” etc. Same place, col. 565.

CX. Hormisdas to Anastasius. “Your Clemency does well,” etc. Same place.

CXI. Anastasius to Hormisdas. “All that your kindness,” etc. Same place, col. 573.

CXII. Hormisdas to Anastasius. “To trouble your mind,” etc. Same place, col. 574.

CXIII. Anastasius to the senate of the city of Rome. “If you and your children are well,” etc. Same place, col. 575.

CXIV. The senate’s rescript to the same. “If the first thing is always,” etc. Same place, col. 576.

CXV. Hormisdas to Anastasius. “Properly and usefully,” etc. Same place, col. 570.

[CLXV] CXXII. Hormisdas to John of Nicopolis. “The letter that you sent,” etc. Same place, col. 582.

CXXIII. Memorandum through the subdeacon Pullio. “With God’s help,” etc. Same place, col. 583.

CXXIV. Hormisdas to the same John and the synod. “We would wish, beloved,” etc. Same place, col. 595.

CXXV. To the same John. “When Pullio returns,” etc. Same place.

CXXVI. The imperial letter of Anastasius to Hormisdas. “We give thanks to almighty God,” etc. Same place, col. 572.

[Col. 0187A] CXXVII. Hormisdas to Anastasius. “To the envoys some time ago,” etc. Same place, col. 586.

CXXVIII. Another letter to the same. “While Your Wisdom,” etc. Col. 594.

CXXIX. To Timothy of Constantinople. “He will not be surprised,” etc. Same place, col. 58[lacuna].

CXXX. Hormisdas to the bishops of the East. “Although my admonition,” etc. Same place, col. 589.

CXXXI. The same to the orthodox bishops. “It is indeed characteristic of the faithful,” etc. Same place, col. 590.

CXXXII. To Bishop Possessor. “The excellent [letter] of your charity,” etc. Same place, col. 592.

CXXXIII. To the Constantinopolitans. “If he who the cup,” etc. Same place.

CXXXVI. To the same. “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, with the intercession of,” etc. Same place, col. 594.

[Col. 0187B] CXXXVII. Copy of the report of Avitus, a Gallic bishop, to Hormisdas. “While I was considering the state of religion,” etc. Same place, col. 583.

CXXXIX. Anastasius to Hormisdas. “Although it is something great,” etc. Same place, col. 597.

CXL. Copy of the report of the least-ranking archimandrites and the other monks of Second Syria to the most holy and most blessed patriarch of the whole world, Hormisdas, who occupies the seat of the chief of the apostles, Peter, etc. Same place, col. 598.

CXLII. The emperor Justinus to Hormisdas. “The benefits of God,” [Col. 0187C] etc. Same place, col. 606.

CXLIII. Hormisdas to Justinus. “At the beginnings of your venerable reign,” etc. Same place.

CXLIV. Justinus to Hormisdas. “John, the most blessed man, bishop of this royal city,” etc. Same place, col. 607.

CXLV. Hormisdas to Justinus. “Having taken its origin from the beginning of your empire,” etc. Same place.

CXLVI. Hormisdas to John of Constantinople. “Spiritual joy,” etc. Same place, col. 609.

CXLVII. Copy of the report of John, bishop of Constantinople, to Hormisdas. “I salute Your Holiness,” etc. Same place, col. 608.

CXLIX. Hormisdas to Justinian. “From the sequence of your letters,” etc. Same place, col. 612.

CL. Hormisdas to the emperor Justinus. “So much by the grace of the Divinity,” etc. Same place, col. 614.

CLI. The same to John of Constantinople. “We have indeed returned,” etc. Same place, col. 616.

CLII. The same to the same. “Those things that your charity,” etc. Col. 617.

[CLXVI] CLX. Copy of the booklet of John of Constantinople to Hormisdas. “When your letter was delivered to me,” etc. Same place, col. 621. It is also in the Hispanic collection.

[Col. 0188B] CLXX. The same to John of Constantinople. “As I consider,” etc. Same place, col. 632.

CLXXI. To Bishops Germanus and John. “Concerning the matters reported by your charity,” etc. Same place, col. 636.

CLXXII. To Bishop John and the deacon Dioscorus. “We have discovered that Thomas and Nicostratus,” etc. Same place, col. 638.

CLXXIV. Another letter, whose heading is missing, but which begins: “Of your labor, which,” etc. Same place, col. 637, letter A.

In this little work the collection ends, and all the manuscripts, including the Venetian ones, which likewise present it mutilated, end at the same words.

[CLXIX] **CHAPTER XIII. On the Thessalonican and Arelatan Collections**

1. Although it is not part of our undertaking to explain collections that were not general but belonged to a particular Church, two among them are nevertheless so distinguished, and have supplied so many ancient, authentic, and otherwise almost unknown documents of the highest importance, that they cannot be omitted.

The first is the collection of the Church of Thessalonica, which was inserted in its entirety into the proceedings of the Roman synod of the year 531 under Boniface II. It contains chiefly several letters of Roman bishops, by which the jurisdiction of the apostolic see in Illyricum was entrusted or confirmed to the bishop of Thessalonica. This collection originated in the case of Stephen, bishop of Larissa and metropolitan of Thessaly in the same Illyricum. After he had been deposed by Epiphanius of Constantinople and the other bishops sitting with him, he fled to Rome. There, when a Roman synod had been convened, Theodosius, bishop of Echinum, who had been sent by Stephen to show that Epiphanius’s judgment was incompetent, demonstrated, by producing several documents, that the Roman pontiffs had expressly claimed for their own governance the Churches of Illyricum—and consequently also of Thessaly.

When Theodosius insisted that these documents should be read and that their authenticity should be established from the apostolic archive, Pope Boniface ordered: “Let the letters brought forward be read, and let the authenticity of the writings be sought in the archive of the apostolic see” (volume V of the Councils, col. 843). This contributes greatly to confirming their authenticity.

Twenty-six letters are found inserted in the proceedings of that synod, in the following order: two by Damasus, one by Siricius, two by Innocent, five by Boniface I; one by the emperor Honorius [Col. 0191B] to the emperor Theodosius, and the latter’s rescript to the same Honorius; one by Celestine; four by Xystus III; one by the emperor Marcian to Pope Leo; three by that pontiff; then one by Anatolius of Constantinople to the same; and four other letters by Leo, as may be seen in volume V of the Councils, Venetian edition, col. 843 and following.

Thus far the Barberini Codex 3386, from which Luca Holstenius published this notable collection—or, rather, this Roman synod containing such precious documents inserted in its proceedings. Although this Barberini codex is more recent, Holstenius nevertheless carefully copied it from two older Vatican manuscripts, then numbered 5751, fol. 55, and 6339, fol. 12; Holstenius’s own hand identifies these on the first page of the Barberini copy.

Leo Allatius had previously used one of them when, in *The Harmony of the Eastern and Western Church*, pp. 1370–1371, he cited from the oldest Vatican copy certain fragments of those letters that are not available elsewhere. Yet, despite all our diligence, we were unable to find either of these manuscripts among the Vatican codices [Col. 0191C]; consequently, we were able to collate only the Barberini codex in the letters of Leo.

It is indeed filled with numerous errors, which Holstenius corrected in his edition; it is also affected by several lacunae, which he suitably supplied. But Leo Allatius testifies that the Vatican copy from which the Barberini codex was transcribed was likewise defective and corrupt; and by several certain indications we have detected that the errors of the Barberini codex derive from errors in the Vatican copy. See the preface to the letters of St. Leo, § 17, volume I, p. 535.

2. Moreover, the complete Roman synod was not found in these manuscripts, and it ends with a letter incorrectly inscribed under Leo’s name to Anastasius of Thessalonica. Holstenius rightly restored this letter, from its context and consular notice, to Boniface I, addressed to Rufus, bishop of Thessalonica.

Since the collection of Thessalonican documents that had been inserted into the proceedings of the same synod breaks off after the aforementioned letter [Col. 0191D]—as is also shown by the words appended to that letter, “Likewise, the following was read,” which clearly point to another subsequent letter absent from the manuscripts—it is uncertain how many other documents belonging to the same collection followed.

That several were lost is indicated not obscurely by the words of Nicholas I in letter 2 to the emperor Michael. He says:

“The jurisdiction that our see exercised through the bishops established in your regions, namely the bishop of Thessalonica [the passage is corrupt or defective], who exercises the jurisdiction of the Roman see throughout Old Epirus, New Epirus, Illyricum, Macedonia, Thessaly, [CLXX] Achaea, Riparian Dacia and Mediterranean Dacia, Moesia, Dardania, Praevalitana, let no one presume to oppose Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; this jurisdiction was enlarged in the times of our predecessors, the holy pontiffs Damasus, Siricius, Innocent, Boniface, Celestine, Xystus, Leo, Hilary, Simplicius, Felix, and Hormisdas.

“Finally, we have taken care to send to Your August Power, through our envoys, the constitutions of those predecessors of ours that were sent to those regions, so that you may learn the truth of the matter.”

In the surviving proceedings of the Roman synod, documents from Damasus through Leo have been preserved for us, but we do not know whether any others by Leo also followed and are missing. Certainly the letters of Hilary, Simplicius, Felix, and Hormisdas are absent; there can be no doubt that, having been written before the synod of Boniface II, they were inserted into the same proceedings.

When Leo Allatius, in the cited work *The Harmony*, p. 1371, quotes from the Vatican copy that he used certain words of Leo’s letter to Anastasius of Thessalonica not found in the printed Leonine editions, no one should suppose that this is a fragment of Leo’s letter preserved by the Vatican codex but omitted by the copyist of the Barberini transcript. Those words are in fact from the aforementioned letter of Boniface to Rufus, which in the Vatican codex was incorrectly inscribed to Leo addressed to Anastasius, just as it is inscribed in the Barberini codex.

3. The testimony of Nicholas I just cited, even if nothing else were available, should be sufficient to prevent anyone from suspecting that such rare documents, printed from the Barberini codex, were unknown to antiquity.

Other testimonies older than Nicholas are also not lacking. For Gelasius cites the letter of Anatolius to Leo, which emerged from this collection alone, in his letter to the Dardanians, as we showed in note 9 on letter 132. Facundus of Hermiane also cites the same letter in book V.

Hadrian I transcribed the entire opening of Boniface’s letter beginning *Institutio*, which was published only from this collection, in letter 97 of the Carolingian Codex, p. 322 of Gretser’s edition.

Moreover, some letters of this collection have been found in other manuscripts of good standing. Thus, of the nine letters of the same collection under Leo, three had been published from other manuscripts before Holstenius’s edition. We found another in the excellent Regensburg manuscript, and Quesnell found one in the Grimani manuscript. Arnold found letter 100, Marcian’s letter to St. Leo, written in Greek, in the Bodleian copy; we found it in Vatican Greek Codex 1455. Compare the preface to Leo’s letters at the place cited.

Since all these facts repeatedly confirm the authenticity of the documents in this collection, Quesnell’s criticism will be judged excessively bold by everyone: in a note on chapter 1 of the collection to be published in this volume, he accused Boniface I’s letter to the bishops of Thessaly, published from this collection, of being an invention or interpolation. See our note 32 on the cited first chapter, col. 51, where Quesnell’s words are quoted and refuted.

4. The second collection is that of the Church of Arles, containing documents by which the privileges and rights of that Church are demonstrated.
