The Fathers of the synod of Frankfurt in the year 794 appear to have had this collection before their eyes when they report that certain papal letters were read which are contained in the same collection, and some of which have so far been found nowhere except there. For in canon 8 they say:

“Concerning the dispute of Ursio, bishop of Vienne, and the advocate of Eliphandus, bishop of Arles, the letters of Blessed Gregory, Zosimus, Leo, and Symmachus were read. They determined that the Church of Vienne ought to have four suffragan sees, over which that Church should preside as the fifth; and that the Church of Arles ought to have nine suffragan sees, over which it should preside” (volume IX of the Councils, col. 103).

Certainly three letters of Leo—nos. 40, 42, and 66 in our edition—have reached us with the assistance of this collection alone. The same is true of Zosimus’s letters and several others. Those found also in other collections, such as Gregory’s letter to Virgilius of Arles, which is extant in that pontiff’s *Register*, lend credibility to the others, especially since later letters mention earlier ones and the various letters provide testimony for one another.

5. Three ancient codices of this collection are cited: [Col. 0193A] two in the Colbert Library and one in the Royal Library. The latter is said to have been written in the ninth century by P. Coustant in the preface to volume I of the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, no. 165.

At Rome we saw a more recent copy in the Vallicellana Library, marked G 99. It had nevertheless been accurately copied from an ancient manuscript that had then belonged to the Church of Arles and later to the Colbert Library, and was sent by Nicolas Fabri to Cardinal Baronius.

To avoid any confusion, the two Colbert copies of this collection must be distinguished. For convenience, P. Coustant calls one the Arelatan and the other the Colbertine in his note on Zosimus’s letter 1, col. 933. There he indicates that the Vallicellana copy sent to Baronius had been taken from the Arelatan Colbert manuscript; but we have detected by several indications that it was copied from the other Colbert manuscript.

For not only do some readings of the Vallicellana differ from those of the Arelatan manuscript, as may be gathered from note 6 on Leo’s letter 66, volume I, col. 998, but the Vallicellana also lacks several documents [Col. 0193B] that are found in the Arelatan manuscript, as will become clear from what follows.

The Royal Codex 3989, older than the two Colbert manuscripts, supplies documents through Pelagius, according to the testimony of Coustant himself. How far the Arelatan Colbert manuscript, marked no. 1951, extends, we do not know. From the indications supplied by P. Coustant, it seems certain that it proceeds at least as far as St. Gregory the Great.

The Vallicellana codex, copied from the other Colbert manuscript, is fuller, since it incorporated several later monuments. The contents it presents are as follows:

I. Zosimus’s letter to the bishops established throughout Gaul and the seven provinces. It is found in volume III of the Councils, Venetian edition, letter 5, col. 409.

II. The same author’s letter to Aurelius and the bishops of Africa, to the bishops of Gaul and the seven provinces, and to the bishops of Spain, of equal rank. Same place, letter 6, col. 411.

III. The same author’s letter to the bishops of Vienne and of Second Narbonensis. Same place, letter 7, col. 413.

[Col. 0193C] IV. The same author’s letter to Hilary of Narbonne. Same place, letter 8, col. 414.

V. The same author’s letter to Patroclus of Arles. Same place, letter 9, col. 415.

VI. The same author’s letter to the same. Same place, letter 11, col. 417.

VII. The same author’s letter to the clergy, the order, and the people established at Massilia. Same place, letter 12.

VIII. Leo’s letter to Constantius and the other bishops of Gaul. In our edition it is letter 4.

IX. To Ravennus of Arles. Same place, letter 42.

X. The petition of the bishops of Gaul to Leo. Same place, letter 65.

XI. Leo’s rescript. Same place, letter 66.

XII. Pope Hilary’s precept concerning the Church of Die, where a bishop was improperly ordained by the bishop of Vienne. Letter 11 of the same pontiff, volume V of the Councils, col. 69.

XIII. Gelasius’s letter to Aeonius of Arles. It is Gelasius’s letter 12, same volume, col. 324.

[Col. 0193D] XIV. Symmachus’s letter to the same Aeonius. It is letter 1 of that pontiff, same volume, col. 421.

XV. The same author’s letter to the bishops of Gaul. Letter 9, same volume, col. 438.

XVI. The same author’s letter to Caesarius of Arles. Letter 5, same volume, col. 424. This letter is also extant in the Hispanic, Isidorian, and several other collections.

XVII. Hormisdas’s letter to Caesarius. Letter 30, same volume, col. 610.

XVIII. John II’s letter to the bishops of Gaul. Letter 4, same volume, col. 899.

XIX. The same author’s letter to the presbyters, deacons, and entire clergy of the Church in which Bishop Contumeliosus served. Letter 5, same volume, col. 900.

XX. Agapitus’s letter to Caesarius. Letter 6, same volume, col. 945.

XXI. The same author’s letter to the same. Letter 7, col. 946.

XXII. Vigilius’s letter to the same Caesarius. Letter 3, same volume, col. 1294.

[Col. 0194A] XXIII. The same author’s letter to Auxanius of Arles. Letter 6, same volume, col. 1299.

XXIV. The same author’s letter to the same. Letter 7, col. 1300.

XXV. Another letter of the same author to the same. Letter 8, col. 1301.

XXVI. The same to the bishops of Gaul. Epistle 9, col. 1302.

XXVII. The same to those same bishops. Epistle 11, col. 1306.

XXVIII. The same to Aurelianus of Arles. Epistle 10, col. 1305.

XXIX. The same to that same bishop. Epistle 13, col. 1308. It also appears in the seventh session of the Fifth Synod.

XXX. Pope Pelagius I to Sapaudus of Arles. Epistle 8, vol. VI of the *Councils*, col. 472.

[CLXXII] XXXI. The same to that same bishop. Epistle 9, col. 473.

XXXII. The same to King Childebert. Epistle 10, ibid.

XXXIII. The same to Sapaudus. Epistle 11, col. 476.

XXXIV. The same to that same bishop. Epistle 12, ibid.

XXXV. The same to King Childebert. Epistle 13, col. 477.

[Col. 0194B] XXXVI. The same to that same king. Epistle 14, col. 478.

XXXVII. The same to Sapaudus. Epistle 15, ibid.

XXXVIII. The same to King Childebert, to which Pope Pelagius’s statement of faith is appended. Epistle 16, col. 479.

XXXIX. The same to the bishops of Annonarian Tuscany. Epistle 6, col. 470.

XL. The same to the entire people of God. Epistle 7, col. 471. These three letters do not concern the Church of Arles. Since, however, they all treat the same matter of faith as the preceding Epistle 15 to Sapaudus of Arles, the compiler thought that they too should be appended to it.

XLI. Gregory to Manasses of Reims. This letter, prefixed to the letters of Gregory the Great, is not his; rather, it is by Gregory VII, and is read in the latter’s *Register*, Book VI, Epistle 2, dated the eleventh day before the Kalends of September in the year 1077. It was inserted in this collection because it commemorates the letters of St. Gregory and other earlier pontiffs written on behalf of the see of Arles.

[Col. 0194C] XLII. St. Gregory’s statements to Augustine, bishop of England. This is a fragment of a letter of that same pontiff in response to St. Augustine’s ninth question, in which the metropolitan of Arles is praised.

XLIII. The same to Virgilius of Arles. Epistle 53, Book V of the Maurist edition.

XLIV. The same to the bishops of Gaul. Ibid., Epistle 54.

XLV. The same to King Childebert. Ibid., Epistle 55.

XLVI. Letter of Nicholas I to Rotlandus, archbishop of Arles. It begins: “Having received the letters of Your Holiness,” etc. See vol. IX of the *Councils*, col. 1510e.

There follow the First, Second, and Third Synods of Arles, excerpted from the collection of Isidore, or from the Hispanic collection; afterward there follows a fragment of the Council of Turin up to canon 2, in which the controversy between the Churches of Vienne and Arles is discussed. Then are added the oaths sworn by bishops to the Church of Arles while Anno, Pontius, and Raimbald held that see: Anno from the year 981 to 994; Pontius, Anno’s successor, until the year 1030; and Raimbald from 1031 to 1065. These oaths, therefore, were given toward the end of the tenth century and in the eleventh century, when these additions, together with the aforementioned letter of Gregory VII, are known to have been inserted into this collection. Although some of these oaths have been published here and there, we nevertheless trust that it will prove useful in many respects to append each one here as it is written in our manuscript.

I, Pontius, now about to be ordained bishop of the see of Saint Mary of Aix, promise that I shall perpetually display toward the holy see of the Church of Arles and its rulers the due subjection, reverence, and obedience established by the Holy Fathers according to the prescriptions of the canons, in the presence of Lord Archbishop Raimbald; and I confirm this with my own hand upon the holy altar.

I, Brother Rostagnus, about to be ordained bishop of the Holy Church of Aix, [promise] the due [subjection, reverence, and obedience], etc., as above.

[Col. 0195A] I, Stephanus, called bishop of the Church of Vence, promise before God and his saints complete canonical submission and obedience and fidelity to the Church of Saint Stephen, the see of Arles, where the body of blessed Trophimus the confessor rests, and to Anno, the present archbishop, and to his successors, if I outlive him.

I, Arnulphus, called bishop of the Church of Vincennes, etc., as in the preceding oath. It has “to Pontius, the present archbishop” in place of “to Anno, the present archbishop.”

I, Bertrandus, now about to be ordained bishop of the Church of Fréjus, etc., as above in the oath of Pontius of Aix.

I, Bertrandus, called bishop of the Church of Riez, declare that henceforth I shall remain under the jurisdiction of the metropolitan of Arles and obey his commands.

I, Agelricus, now about to be ordained bishop of the holy Church of Riez, etc., as in the oath of Pontius of Aix.

[Col. 0195B] I, Adilricus, called bishop of the Church of Orange, etc., as in the oath of Stephanus of Vence.

I, Adilricus, called bishop of Orange and Tricastin, [Col. 0196A] etc., as in the oath of that same Stephanus. It has “to Raimbald” in place of “to Anno.”

I, Petrus, called bishop of the Church of Avignon, declare that I [shall remain under the jurisdiction of the metropolitan of Arles], etc., as in the oath of Bertrand of Riez.

I, Benedictus, called bishop of the Church of Avignon, swear before God and his saints complete canonical submission and obedience and fidelity to the Church of Saint Stephen, the see of Arles, where the body of the holy apostolic Trophimus rests, and to Raimbald, the present archbishop, and to his successors, if I outlive him.

Two documents are missing from the Vallicellian copy and the Colbertine exemplar; they were found in two other manuscripts of the same Arles collection. First, the *Factum* (or edict) addressed to the illustrious Agricola, prefect of Gaul under the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, published by P. Coustant, vol. I of *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, col. 977; it is preserved in manuscripts Colbertine Arles 1951 and Royal 3989. Second, the letter of the Synod of Arles to Pope Sylvester, preserved in one Colbertine Arles manuscript, 1951, and printed by the aforementioned Coustant, col. 345. See his notice at col. 341, at the end.

# PART THREE

On the Dionysian Collection and the Other Collections That Derive from Dionysius

[Col. 0195]

## CHAPTER ONE

On the Collection of Dionysius Exiguus

[Col. 0195B]

### § 1. Cassiodorus’s Testimony Concerning Dionysius

The Two Parts of the Dionysian Collection, and Their Description. The Continuous Numerical Series in the Greek Canons. Justellus’s Edition Included Two Additions Unconnected with Dionysius in Its Second Part. Pure Dionysian Manuscripts Are Rare and Must Not Be Confused with the Hadrianic Manuscripts.

1. Who Dionysius Exiguus was, how great was his proficiency in Greek and Latin literature, and how renowned he was in the study of all sacred learning, Cassiodorus sufficiently explained. Having been on familiar terms with him, Cassiodorus inserted the following distinguished testimony about him, after Dionysius’s death, around the year 556, in chapter 23 of *On Divine Readings*:

> Even today the Catholic Church continues to produce illustrious men, radiant with the splendor of approved doctrine. In our own time there was Dionysius, a monk, Scythian by nationality but entirely Roman in character, exceedingly learned in both languages. By his actions he rendered the justice which he had read in the Lord’s books. He had examined and understood the Scriptures with such divine diligence that, whenever he was questioned on any matter whatever, he had a suitable answer ready without any delay. He studied dialectic with me and, by the Lord’s favor, spent many years of his life in the example of glorious instruction.
>
> I am ashamed to say of a companion what I cannot find in myself. For in him great wisdom was joined with simplicity, learning with humility, and eloquence with restraint in speech; so that he did not place himself before even the lowliest servants, although without doubt he was worthy of the conversation of kings. May he intercede for us—the man who was accustomed to pray with us—so that, just as we are supported here by his prayers, we may now be aided by his merits.
>
> When Bishop Stephen of Salona asked him, Dionysius composed from Greek exemplars the ecclesiastical canons, in accordance with his own character, as he was straightforward and eloquent, and with the radiance of great eloquence. These are embraced today by the Roman Church in its most celebrated usage. You ought also to read them continually, lest you appear culpably ignorant of such salutary ecclesiastical rules.
>
> He also translated many other works from Greek into Latin, which can contribute to the benefit of the Church. He possessed such mastery of Latin and Greek that, whenever he took Greek books into his hands, he passed through them in Latin without difficulty; and again he read Latin books in Attic speech, so that one would believe that what his mouth poured forth with unhindered speed had been written in that language.

It would be too long to unfold everything about this man; Cassiodorus continues by discussing his other virtues.

2. The work of Dionysius most celebrated for our purpose is the *Collection of the Canons and Constitutions of the Apostolic See*, which is called Dionysian after its author. [CLXXV] It is divided into two parts: one contains the canons of synods, the other the letters of the Roman pontiffs. They were arranged and published separately, not at one and the same time; consequently, in pure Dionysian manuscripts they are distinguished by separate dedicatory letters.

He first devoted himself to the collection of the canons. After he had come to Rome following the death of Gelasius—whom he states that he had not seen in person—and had there given several demonstrations of his proficiency in Greek and Latin literature, Laurentius, offended by the inelegance of the earlier translation, repeatedly and familiarly urged him to render the canons of the Greek synods into Latin in a more accurate and polished translation. We have elsewhere conjectured with greater probability that the earlier translation which offended Laurentius is the one we shall publish in this volume.

Laurentius, whom Dionysius calls “our brother,” may perhaps have been a presbyter of the Roman Church. Two men bearing that name are found subscribed to the Roman Council under Symmachus in the year 499. Dionysius did not undertake the labor imposed by Laurentius, however, until the prayers of Stephen, bishop of Salona, had been added, as we infer partly from his letter to Stephen and partly from Cassiodorus’s testimony.

3. “At the beginning,” he says in his letter to Stephen, “we translated from Greek the canons that are called Apostolic. Since very many have not readily assented to them, we did not wish Your Holiness to be unaware of this fact. Then we arranged, in numerical order, the rules of the Council of Nicaea and thereafter those of all the councils, whether held before it or afterward, up to the synod of the 150 bishops who assembled at Constantinople: that is, from the first chapter through the 165th, exactly as they are found in the Greek authority.”

“Greek authority” indicates the Greek manuscript that he used. In it the numerical sequence was continuous, as it was in the manuscript which, in certain acts of the Council of Chalcedon, presented the Antiochene canons marked with nearly the same numerical sequence. See what we observed on this matter in Part I, chapter 6.

That Greek manuscript of Dionysius contained only 20 Nicene canons, 24 Ancyrean, 14 Neocaesarean, 20 Gangran, 25 Antiochene, 59 Laodicean, and 3 Constantinopolitan canons; together these make 165 canons. Since that manuscript lacked the 27 Chalcedonian canons, Dionysius added them, translated into Latin from another Greek exemplar; they closed the statutes of the Greek synods.

He then appended, from Latin exemplars, the statutes of the Council of Sardica and of the African Council, which had been published in Latin. For he did not translate the Sardican canons—which we have proved were published in both Greek and Latin from a twofold original exemplar in Part I, chapter 5—from Greek, but took them from a Latin original exemplar, just as he took the African canons. See what we noted concerning this particular Sardican exemplar in Part II, chapter 1, no. 17.

Dionysius concludes the dedicatory letter with the following admonition:

> After this preface, arranging the titles of all the decrees more concisely, we have placed in one view what was promulgated piecemeal in the individual councils, so that we may seem to have supplied some sort of compendium for the investigation of each matter.

He indicates that the titles of the canons had been worked out more exactly and described in the preliminary table; afterward he prefixed them again to their respective canons.

Thus the sequence of the first part is as follows. The place of a preface is occupied by the letter to Stephen. Then follows the table of titles. Next come the 50 Apostolic Canons. After these, in one numerical series, come the Nicene, Ancyrean, Neocaesarean, Gangran, Antiochene, Laodicean, and Constantinopolitan canons. Then come the Chalcedonian canons, all of which he translated into Latin from Greek in a new version.

These are followed by the 21 Sardican canons from the original Latin, and finally by the African canons, divided into 138 numbers. The first 33 numbers are the canons of the Council of Carthage of the year 419. Since the decrees of the preceding African synods under Aurelius were later read and inserted in that council, these begin at no. 34 and continue through no. 127. Then follow six other canons of the same council of 419, from no. 128 through no. 133.

Next come the letter of that synod to Pope Boniface, another letter of Cyril of Alexandria to the Africans, another of Atticus of Constantinople to the same, together with the Nicene Creed, and finally a letter of the later African synod to Celestine. All these begin at no. 134 and end at no. 138.

The continuous numerical series which Dionysius testified that he had preserved in the Greek canons [CLXXVI] is found in no manuscripts, not even in those which we shall mention below as pure Dionysian manuscripts. Nor did the manuscript used by Cresconius present that series. Nevertheless, that some manuscripts originally existed with such a series is clear from the titles appended to the letter of John II to Caesarius of Arles. In those titles, a Neocaesarean canon is cited according to that numerical series. See what we noted on this matter from manuscript Vatican, Palatine 574, Part II, chapter 10, § 2, no. 12.

Since, however, in the same titles of John II two other Antiochene canons are cited not according to the aforementioned series but by their own numbers, it is clear that the Dionysian exemplar of that pontiff was distinguished by a twofold numerical order: namely, both by the continuous series received by Dionysius from the Greek manuscript and by the particular number assigned to each synod’s canons.

P. Coustantius suspected from this very letter of John II that, if not by Dionysius, then certainly by certain scribes, the latter numbering had once been added. In the preface to vol. I of *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, no. 109, he further conjectured, not implausibly, that the continuous numerical series is nowhere found in the manuscripts that have come down to us because later scribes omitted Dionysius’s numbers and retained others, as being more commonly used and more suitable for distinguishing the subjects.

The numerical series in which the Dionysian edition appeared in the *Bibliotheca of Canon Law*, under the direction of Voellus and Justellus, derives not from some purer Dionysian manuscript—for it will become clear below from defects peculiar to that edition and alien to a pure Dionysian manuscript that the Justellian manuscript was not such a manuscript—but from Dionysius’s own letter, in which he testifies that he preserved the same series.

4. This first part of the Dionysian collection was received with universal approval, and especially by Julianus, presbyter of the title of Saint Anastasia. This approval encouraged Dionysius himself to collect, with equal diligence, the constitutions of the apostolic see that pertain to ecclesiastical discipline.

“Promptly complying with his wishes,” he says in his letter to that same Julianus, “I collected, with all the care and diligence I could, what I found among the instructions of the individual pontiffs, reducing it to a certain order and distinguishing it by composed titles. My arrangement was such that I brought to an end, under one numerical series, as many instructions as I found belonging to each pontiff, and appended all the titles to this preface, in the same manner in which I had earlier arranged the canons when translating the Fathers from the Greek language.”

In this part, one numerical series is found in the decrees of each individual pontiff, but not throughout the entire corpus from the first pontiff to the last. Dionysius followed the chronological order of the pontiffs exactly, whereas in other earlier collections that order is found to be confused.

The letter to Julianus, which serves as a preface, is placed first. The table of titles follows.

Then comes the letter of Siricius to Himerius of Tarragona, divided into 15 numbers; in the commonly used editions of the *Councils* it is Epistle 1 of volume II.

There follow 22 letters of Innocent, divided into 57 numbers, as follows:

I. To Decentius of Gubbio, from which the first eight numbers are taken. It is Epistle 1 of volume III of the *Councils*.

II. To Victricius of Rouen, from which the next 12 numbers are taken. It is Epistle 2.

III. To Exsuperius of Toulouse, represented by seven other numbers, 21 through 27. It is Epistle 3.

IV. To Felix of Nocera, divided into five numbers, 28 through 32. It is Epistle 4.

V. To Maximus and Severus, bishops among the Bruttii, under the single number 33. It is Epistle 5.

VI. To Agapitus, Macedonius, and Marianus, bishops of Apulia, under the single number 34. It is Epistle 6.

VII. To Rufus, Gerontius, and the other Macedonians, likewise under the single number 35. It is Epistle 7.

VIII. To Florentius of Tivoli, under number 36. [Col. 0198C] It is Epistle 8.

IX. To Probus, under number 37. It is Epistle 9.

X. To Aurelius and Augustine, under no. 38. It is Epistle 10.

XI. To Julianus, under no. 39. It is Epistle 13.

XII. To Aurelius, under no. 40. It is Epistle 11.

XIII. To the presbyter Boniface, under no. 41. It is Epistle 14.

[CLXXVII] XIV. To Alexander of Antioch, under no. 42. It is Epistle 15.

XV. To Maximinus, bishop, under no. 43. It is Epistle 16.

XVI. Likewise to Alexander of Antioch, under no. 44. It is Epistle 17.

XVII. Likewise to that same bishop, under three numbers, 45, 46, and 47. It is Epistle 18.

XVIII. To Acacius, bishop of Beroea, under no. 48. It is Epistle 19.

XIX. To Laurentius of Siena, under no. 49. It is Epistle 20.

[Col. 0198D] XX. To Marcianus, bishop of Naissus, under no. 50. It is Epistle 21.

XXI. To Rufus, Eusebius, and the other Macedonian bishops, under the remaining seven numbers, 51 through 57. It is Epistle 22.

The letter of Zosimus to Hesychius of Salona is divided into three numbers. In the edition of the *Councils* it is Epistle 1 of that pontiff.

The decrees of Pope Boniface I are contained in four numbers. No. 1 is his letter to the Emperor Honorius; no. 2 is the rescript of Honorius; no. 3 is that same pontiff’s letter to Patroclus, Remigius, and the other bishops of Gaul; no. 4 is another letter to Hilary of Narbonne. In the *Councils* these are Letters 1, 2, and 3, with the rescript of Honorius following Letter 1.

The three letters of Celestine are divided into 22 numbers.

I. A letter to Venerius, Marinus, and the other bishops of Gaul, with the authorities of earlier bishops of the apostolic see concerning the grace of God and free choice added. It is divided into 13 numbers. In the *Councils* it is Epistle 1.

II. To the bishops established throughout the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne, numbers 14 through 19. It is Epistle 2.

III. To the bishops throughout Apulia and Calabria, under the remaining three numbers, 20, 21, and 22. It is Epistle 3.

The seven letters of Leo are divided into 48 numbers.

I. To the bishops of Campania, etc., in five numbers. In our edition it is Epistle 4.

II. To the Italians, under the single number 6. It is Epistle 7.

III. To the Sicilians, numbers 7 through 13. It is Epistle 15.

IV. To Januarius of Aquileia, under no. 14. It is Epistle 18.

V. To Rusticus of Narbonne, numbers 15 through 30. It is Epistle 167.

VI. To Anastasius of Thessalonica, numbers 31 through 41. It is Epistle 14.

VII. To Nicetas of Aquileia, numbers 42 through [Col. 0199B] 48.

The decrees of Gelasius concerning ecclesiastical constitutions comprise 28 numbers. They appear in the collection published in this volume, chapter 58.

Finally, the letter of Anastasius II to the Emperor Anastasius is divided into eight numbers. It is Epistle 1 of volume V of the *Councils*.

5. This is the complete description of the pure Dionysian collection. No one should object by citing the edition of Christophorus Justellus, inserted by Guillaume Voellus and Henri Justellus, his son, in volume I of the *Bibliotheca of Canon Law*. Among the documents there listed as belonging to the second part, that edition presents two additional items: namely, appended to the decrees of Zosimus is his letter to the presbyter-legates at Ravenna, which constitutes number 4; and appended to the decrees of Leo is his letter to the Africans, which adds number 49.

These two letters are unknown to the pure Dionysian manuscripts so far discovered, of which there are two: the Royal Parisian manuscript 3887 and the Vatican manuscript 5845. The other manuscripts that contain these letters, as they were issued by Justellus and inserted into the body of the collection itself, are not pure Dionysian manuscripts but Hadrianic ones. They received these and other additions beyond Dionysius, as we shall explain more fully in the following chapter.

If, however, the titles of these same letters are listed in the preliminary table of titles of Vatican manuscript 5845, while the letters themselves are absent from the body of the collection and are written separately only after the body of the collection, together with the other additions, it is evident that these titles improperly entered the table itself.

Indeed, at the beginning of Leo’s titles the table reads: “Here begin the titles of the decrees of Pope Leo, no. 48,” not 49. Consequently, title 49 can be seen appended to the table itself at the end of Leo’s titles.

Furthermore, the titles of the aforementioned letters of Zosimus and Leo differ markedly from the other Dionysian titles, as Quesnellus observed in his notes on Epistle 12 of that pontiff, vol. II, col. 1338.

Moreover, those same two titles are not found in the Royal manuscript, either in the body of the collection or in the table of titles, as may be inferred from P. Coustant, note c on Zosimus’s Epistle 14, col. 969:

> Nor does even the genuine Royal exemplar of the Dionysian collection mention it in the general table of titles or exhibit it in the body of the work.

Finally, these two letters are cited neither in the collection of Cresconius nor in the Hispanic collection. Since all the documents of the Dionysian collection were received in those collections, these letters too would have been transcribed there if Cresconius and the author of the Hispanic collection had found them in their respective Dionysian manuscripts.

Therefore, in order that the Justellian edition may represent a pure Dionysian manuscript, these two letters must be removed both from the table of titles and from the body of the canons and rejected among the other additions to that edition.

Here we shall also add that the words *in encaeniis* in the heading of the Antiochene canons must be deleted. We observed that they are absent from the pure Dionysian manuscripts in Part I, chapter 4, § 2, where we praised the two pure Dionysian manuscripts that we were able to inspect: Vatican 5845, which contains Dionysius’s entire collection, and Vatican Palatine 577, which presents only the canons of the councils.

We shall provide a description of the first manuscript—which, in addition to the complete Dionysian collection as we have so far described it, contains several additions—in chapter 3, where we shall discuss the Dionysian additions. We shall discuss the other manuscript, Vatican Palatine 577, more fully in this same chapter, § 3.

## § 2. The Excellence of the Dionysian Collection

Whether Dionysius Was the First to Collect the Decretal Letters of the Roman Pontiffs. Observations on the Same Collection. How Widely It Was Disseminated. The Time at Which It Was Composed.

6. There can be no doubt that Dionysius’s collection surpasses the other earlier collections to a considerable degree: in its distinction between the canons and the decrees of the pontiffs, in the clarity of its translation of the Greek canons, in the order of its documents, and in the more suitable titles. It also surpasses them in the very integrity of all its decrees, since it admitted nothing apocryphal, except the Apostolic Canons—which Dionysius nevertheless thought should be distinguished from the other genuine canons by a specific warning.

Nor should one agree with certain writers that Dionysius was the first to collect the decrees of the apostolic see. He was indeed the first to separate them systematically into a volume distinct from the canons of the councils and to review them in order. In earlier collections they were mixed together with the decrees of synods, or confusedly intermingled among themselves, as can be seen in the collections that we described in the preceding part.

Those who use this distinction of the Dionysian manuscript as though before Dionysius only the canons, and not the constitutions of the apostolic see, possessed authority are greatly mistaken. Even if it were true—which we do not concede—that the manuscripts older than Dionysius which have not come down to us contained only the Greek canons of the councils rendered into Latin, what would follow from that?

Those manuscripts were private, and there was no public one, as we have shown elsewhere. Moreover, among the canons of the Greek synods, only the Nicene canons together with the Sardican canons had once been received among the Latins, as we proved in Part II, chapter 1. Nothing, therefore, can be drawn from these manuscripts either to establish or to remove the authority of the decrees of the Roman prelates.

The apostolic constitutions certainly retained their authority by themselves, whether or not they had been inserted into those private manuscripts. The testimonies of Celestine I in his letter to the bishops of Apulia and Calabria, and of Leo in Epistle 4 to the bishops of Campania, are clear. In them the authority not only of the canons but also of the decretal letters is commended.

The author of the *Life of St. Hilary of Arles*, chapter 16, reports that Bishop Chelidonius was accused as though he had formerly taken a widow as his wife, “which the authority of the apostolic see and the statutes of the canons prohibit.” Here it is evident that both the canons and the apostolic constitutions were in force among the Gauls. Compare what we shall observe in note 11 on chapter 2 of Dissertation 12 of Quesnellus, to be inserted in this volume, col. 697.

From Dionysius’s own letter prefixed to the collection of decretals, it is manifest that Julianus prompted him to collect, besides the canons, the decrees of the apostolic see precisely because not only the canons but also these decrees pertained to the regulation of ecclesiastical discipline. This is sufficiently indicated by the following words of that same letter:

> Stimulated by the pious zeal of Your Holiness, which omits absolutely nothing that pertains to ecclesiastical discipline in its inquiries, I collected, with all the care and diligence I could, the constitutions of the former prelates of the apostolic see.

Hence both the canons and these decrees were transcribed together in other earlier collections. Since Dionysius had provided only the canons in the first part, however, he collected and published the apostolic letters in the second part at Julianus’s urging, so that nothing might be lacking to those devoted to ecclesiastical discipline.

[Col. 0201A] 7. Although Dionysius’s collection surpasses the others, it is not perfect in every respect. The first part, which concerns the canons of the councils, suffers from several deficiencies.

In the Nicene material, the creed and the catalogue of bishops are missing. The subscriptions, or names of the bishops, are also absent from the Ancyrean, Neocaesarean, Gangran, Antiochene, and Constantinopolitan canons; likewise absent are the two synodical letters, one of the Council of Gangra and one of the Council of Antioch. All these materials are available from other ancient collections.

The only possible excuse for Dionysius is that the Greek manuscript he used lacked all these items. He took the African canons from a manuscript that contained the complete acts of the Council of Carthage of the year 419. Since all the earlier synods under Aurelius had been inserted into that manuscript, it contained more than Dionysius transcribed.

For, concerned with brevity, he testifies that in reporting certain councils he omitted some things which he found repeated, according to African practice, in an earlier or later synod; and in several other cases he preferred to use a summary rather than copy the actual words or acts. In doing so, he also inadvertently passed over certain canons that had not been repeated, which had to be sought out from other sources. See what we observed on this matter in Part II, chapter 3.

As for the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs, some have been persuaded that Dionysius, who prepared his collection at Rome, drew the letters he collected from the apostolic archives. We consider this wholly improbable, indeed even false.

Many highly celebrated pontifical constitutions are missing from his collection, although they are widely read in other, older collections; and he would have provided many more besides these if he had consulted the apostolic archives.

Were there not, even in the case of Leo alone, several letters of the greatest importance for discipline that he omitted—namely, Epistle 1 to the bishop of Aquileia; Epistle 9 to Dioscorus; Epistle 10 to the bishops of Vienne; Epistle 12 to the Africans; Epistle 15 to Turibius; Epistle 19 to Dorus of Benevento; Epistle 108 to Theodore of Fréjus; Epistle 119 to Maximus of Antioch; Epistle 166 to Neon of Ravenna; and Epistle 168 to the bishops of Campania?

Moreover, in Epistle 167 to Rusticus of Narbonne, which he did transcribe, the inquiries of Rusticus were omitted because of the titles that Dionysius prefixed to each chapter, although those inquiries are necessary for properly understanding Leo’s responses. See the preface to Leo’s letters, no. 13, vol. I, col. 517.

Finally, in publishing Leo’s letters and the *Code of Canons*, we clearly discovered that Dionysius’s readings are not always better. For this reason we repeatedly judged the text of other collections preferable.

Although Dionysius therefore indicates in his letter to Julianus that he had applied all the care and diligence he could to collecting the apostolic letters, it is nevertheless evident that he lacked knowledge of other earlier collections which preserve much that he omitted.

The same is indicated in his preface to his translation of St. Cyril’s letter to Nestorius, where he presents himself as the first translator to have given that letter to the Latins, in these words:

> Considering it entirely opportune at this time that the apostolic faith of so great a teacher, long well known to the Greeks but HITHERTO UNKNOWN TO THE LATINS, should become known ...

(*Councils*, vol. III, col. 959.)

There were, however, two earlier translations: one by Marius Mercator, and another inserted in the translation of the ancient Synod of Ephesus. Dionysius must be judged to have been unaware of them.

Let them therefore consider how weak is the argument advanced by certain persons, who do not hesitate to call into question, on the basis of Dionysius’s silence or omission, certain pontifical documents which, having been brought to light from other sources, are sufficiently secure unless something more serious is raised against them from elsewhere.

### 8.

Those notable virtues of the Dionysian collection which we reviewed shortly before so impressed and captivated everyone’s attention that copies of it immediately began to be sought everywhere [CLXXX], and it soon began to be put into use in Rome itself, especially because of its translation of the Greek canons, which rendered obsolete the inelegant earlier translation previously known there. Hence, within the space of a few years it was being used so generally that, around the middle of the sixth century, Cassiodorus wrote: “Those [Greek canons translated into Latin by Dionysius] the Roman Church today embraces with the most celebrated usage.” He speaks only of usage, for he claimed no public authority for that collection and did not make it an official codex of the Roman Church.

This use of it by the Roman Church is demonstrated, among others, by two pontiffs of the same century, John II and Vigilius. In the headings of the canons which John II sent to Caesarius of Arles, two Apostolic canons, one Neocaesarean canon, and two Antiochene canons were transcribed from Dionysius’s translation, together with the Dionysian headings, as we proved from Vatican manuscript Pal. 574, part II, chapter 10, § 2, no. 12. Pope Vigilius, in the sentence of condemnation against Rusticus and Sebastianus, which is read inserted in the seventh session of the Fifth Council, volume VI of the Venetian edition of the Councils, column 187c, quotes canon 29 of the Council of Carthage with the heading that is peculiar to the Dionysian collection [Col. 0202B].

So much concerning that part of Dionysius which presents the canons of the councils. As for the decretal letters, we have found a single example in the aforesaid John II, who, in the aforementioned headings of the canons sent to Caesarius of Arles, cited the text of Siricius’s letter to Himerius under the heading: “From the letter of Siricius, pope of the city of Rome, to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, among other matters, at chapter 7.” Since the division of decretal letters into chapters is not proper to the originals but to collections, and since different divisions are found in different collections, the text cited by John II seems to have been taken from that same Dionysian collection from which the other canons were taken; for in it the text is indeed found under chapter seven.

This, however, is the only such example among the Roman pontiffs. Other pontiffs were accustomed to cite apostolic constitutions from the Roman archives, and no one besides John II is found to have cited them from Dionysius before the seventh century, as we shall soon see. From Rome, however, examples of this collection were disseminated at an early date into other regions. The author of the Hispanic collection received from it all the apostolic constitutions, with the same headings as those of Dionysius. In Africa, Cresconius arranged his collection, divided into commonplaces, solely from Dionysius. Among the Greeks, since knowledge of the African canons held under Aurelius was lacking, those same canons were rendered into Greek from Dionysius before the Trullan Council; at that council the canons themselves are cited as already inserted into the Greek codex from the Greek version, chapter 2, volume VII of the Councils, column 1346.

We shall also prove in the Observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 16, chapter 1, that the same collection had circulated in Gaul and Britain before the age of Charlemagne. This Dionysian collection, and especially its translation of the Greek canons, pleased everyone so much that copyists sometimes, when transcribing other collections, altered certain readings so as to bring them into conformity with the Dionysian version.

In Lucan manuscript 88, where the Chalcedonian canons are transcribed from the old translation, canons 6 and 7 are corrected from the Dionysian version, and the final clause of canon 16 is taken from Dionysius. Likewise, in Vatican manuscript 1342, which presents the same old translation in those canons, canon 18 is entirely Dionysian. The Barb. 2888 codex sometimes gives the Neocaesarean and Gangran canons of the Isidorian version with Dionysian readings; and the Thuaneus-Colbertinus codex 932, in canon 10 of the Chalcedonian canons of the old translation, has incorporated several passages taken from Dionysius. Similar examples may be observed in other codices and collections.

From these examples it is clear how freely certain scribes acted, so that some readings which differ from most manuscripts and originated in the decisions of particular copyists should not readily be attributed to the ancient translator. Finally, this Dionysian collection became more famous after it had been enlarged by a few additions and delivered by Pope Hadrian to Charlemagne for the use of the Gallican Churches. At that time it was received almost everywhere and began to be called the Codex of Canons.

### 9.

It remains for us to say something about the time when Dionysius compiled this collection. In his first Paschal Letter, written to Petronius in the year 525, he quotes an Antiochene canon:

> In the holy canons, under heading 79—which is the first canon of the Council of Antioch—it is expressed in these words: “All who have dared to …,” and so forth.

This canon was taken from a copy of the Dionysian version. From this same copy Peter the deacon and the other Scythian monks quoted the chapters concerning grace and free will appended to the letters of Celestine, in the letter which they wrote at Rome to the African bishops exiled in Sardinia in the year 520, as we proved in the Observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 3, volume II, column 719. Therefore, the collection had been published before that time.

Moreover, Dionysius, who had not seen Gelasius, came to Rome during the pontificate of Anastasius II. Under that pontiff, it seems, he translated into Latin the booklet of the apocrisiaries of the Alexandrian Church, to be presented to Anastasius. The following note is appended to it in Vatican manuscript 4961 of the Avellana Collection: “Dionysius the Little translated it from Greek into Latin at Rome.” See part II, chapter 12, no. 102.

Perhaps Dionysius was also the author of the Latin translation of several other documents of Greek origin which were inserted into the same collection and belong to the pontificate of Hormisdas. Quesnellus, Dissertation 16, no. 13, argues that Dionysius’s collection was prepared after the Council of Agde in the year 506. He establishes only one point with sufficient probability: that the second part of the collection, containing the letters of the Roman pontiffs, was not compiled while Anastasius II was alive.

“For,” he says, “since Dionysius himself writes that he collected only the constitutions of former bishops of the Apostolic See—that is, of those who had already ceased to live—and yet includes a letter of Anastasius II, it follows that he did not begin this work before 16 November 498, the day on which Anastasius died. Therefore, he compiled this second part either under Symmachus or under Hormisdas.”

If Ennodius, in his Defense of the Roman Council of the year 501, which was written not long afterward, is believed to have had Dionysius’s collection before his eyes when he opposed his adversaries with the Council of Carthage, which the authority of the Apostolic See approved through the bishop Faustinus, who had been sent by that See and was present there—although, in his customary manner, he quotes the words of canons 129, 130, and 131 somewhat freely, volume V of the Councils, columns 483d–484—then it would become certain that at least the earlier part, concerning the canons, had been published under Symmachus, and perhaps even under Anastasius II.

Since the second part, containing the letters, ends with Anastasius and contains nothing from Symmachus, we more probably believe that it was compiled under Symmachus, especially since the presbyter Julian, of the title of Saint Anastasia, at whose request Dionysius composed this part, is found subscribed to the Roman synod of the year 499 under that same pontiff.

### § 3. Description of Vatican Palatine Codex 577, which contains only the first part of the Dionysian collection—or rather, its first form—and its considerable difference from the version which Dionysius compiled in a second recension

### 10.

Vatican Palatine Codex 577 is especially notable and well known for the Gallican documents which were either published or emended from it; but its contents relating to the first part of the Dionysian collection have been unknown. It is square in format. After Lucas Holstenius had copied some material from it, P. Possinus sent certain extracts from his papers to P. Labbe. From those same papers Labbe gave the following testimony concerning the codex in volume VIII of the Councils, column 269, in the margin beside the German Council of the year 742:

> The canons of this council and of the following Council of Liptina are found transcribed in the ancient Palatine Codex of the Vatican Library, written in an old Frankish script, from which Holstenius made some notes.

The Gallican character of the codex is indeed demonstrated by the documents which are described partly at its beginning, before Dionysius’s collection, and partly after the collection itself [Col. 0204A]. At the beginning one reads the aforementioned German Council, followed by the Liptine canons. Then the names of the bishops who were sent from Rome to preach in Gaul are given. The names which follow are the same as those listed by Gregory of Tours. Next comes:

> The names of the bishops or abbots who were at the public estate of Attigny, etc.,

as published from this codex in volume VIII of the Councils, column 861. This is the synod of the year 765.

Afterward appears:

> The renunciation of the devil, his works, and his superstitions,

which was later published from this same codex in the old Theotisc language in the cited volume, column 278, where the codex number is mistakenly given as 542.

Then comes:

> From Clement to James: the instructions of Saint Peter,

which we published in this volume among the documents of ancient canon law. These materials precede the Dionysian collection.

At the end, in another script, the following document is found:

> The rules of the ancient Fathers would indeed be sufficient, etc.

This is the Council of Verneuil, celebrated under Pippin in the year 755, for which variants from our codex were added in the margin of volume VIII of the Councils, column 417.

All these documents both prove that the codex is Gallican and demonstrate that it was written before the age of Charlemagne. Thus this codex also confirms that Dionysius’s collection had been brought into Gaul before Charlemagne.

### 11.

Only the first part of the Dionysian collection is contained in this codex. It begins on page 11 with Dionysius’s own letter, which must be inserted here in full, since it differs from the common version in more than one respect. First, it is addressed not to Stephen but to the bishop Petronius. It is also much shorter and presents considerable variation at the end.

> To my venerable lord and father, Petronius the bishop: Dionysius the Little sends greetings in the Lord.
>
> Although our dearest brother Laurence, offended, I believe, by the incompetence of the old translation, compelled our humility by constant and familiar exhortation to translate the ecclesiastical rules from Greek, nevertheless I undertook the labor imposed upon me out of consideration for Your Blessedness. Almighty God Christ, who in his customary mercy watches over the peoples, has bestowed upon you the dignity of the supreme priesthood.
>
> Thus, among the many ornaments of virtue with which you adorn the Church of the Lord by the holiness of your conduct, you may also preserve inviolate the most sacred laws arranged through the grace of God in episcopal councils, and govern clergy and people with perfect administration. You should not be content with the custom of our age, in which we more readily desire to know what is right than to do it; rather, joined to divine assistance, you should first accomplish what you command to be done, so that you may benefit the faithful by the most effective example.
>
> For great is the authority of one who commands, and likewise of one who first fulfills what has been commanded, so that, when the discipline of the ecclesiastical order is preserved unshaken, all may be enlightened by the duties which go before them in attaining everlasting blessedness, and the people may be enriched by spiritual growth.
>
> May divine grace preserve Your Blessedness unharmed and praying for us.
>
> The prologue ends.

Everything in this letter by which Dionysius describes the method of his collection and the series of its documents is absent [Col. 0204D]. This same shorter letter, with the same readings and conclusion, is also found in another ancient manuscript, Vatican Palatine Codex 574, which is likewise Gallican. Only the heading of Dionysius to Petronius is omitted there; in its place the scribe prefixed the title:

> Preface of Dionysius the Little to Stephen.

### 12.

This codex also differs from the other pure Dionysian codices in the canon collection itself, both in the number and in the order of the canons. A double table of chapters is distinguished. The first presents the chapters of the Apostolic Canons, to which the canons themselves are appended. The second is a general table of the remaining councils; yet in several headings it differs considerably in wording from the text of the other codices.

The Nicene, Ancyran, and Neocaesarean canons follow. The following note is appended to the last of these:

> These canons are judged to be those established at Ancyra—“and Caesarea” is added incorrectly—but they are earlier than the Nicene rules.

Then come the Gangran canons, with this note:

> These Gangran rules are judged to have been promulgated after the Nicene Council.

Next come the Antiochene, Laodicean, and Constantinopolitan canons.

The Chalcedonian canons do not follow these, as they do in the other Dionysian manuscripts. Instead, the Sardican canons follow, numbering twenty rather than twenty-one: canon four, beginning “Gaudentius,” is omitted, together with the latter part of the preceding canon, which ends with the words “let us honor the memory of Saint Peter.” Thus canon five of the other codices becomes canon four in this manuscript, and the remaining canons are likewise reduced by one in their numbering.

This loss of the fourth canon and mutilation of the third perhaps originated in a leap made by some scribe. All these canons preserve readings found in the pure Dionysian codices and do not include the additions which entered the Hadrianic manuscripts.

The acts of the Council of Carthage of the year 419 follow. They are placed before the canons, as in the other manuscripts of Dionysius and in the printed editions, and continue up to the words:

> We shall discuss this in the following treatise.

Then follows:

> Daniel, the notary of the Council of Nicaea, recited the profession of faith—or its decrees—in the African Council; these we have written together with the replies of the bishops of Alexandria and Constantinople.

After all the other material found in the common version has been omitted, only the first thirty-three canons of that council follow. Although they likewise number thirty-three in the preceding table, in the body of the text they amount to thirty-five because of a different division, and they end with the words:

> Nor should a presbyter usurp anything belonging to his own title.

Everything which was read from other synods in the same council is omitted, as are the canons of the second session—that is, everything after the commonly numbered canon 33 up to canon 133.

Next follows:

> The bishop Aurelius said: In accordance with the decrees of the entire council, etc.,

together with the subscriptions of the Fathers, as in the common version after canon 133. Then comes the letter of that council to Boniface, followed by the letters of Cyril and Atticus to the Africans.

Next is appended the Nicene profession of faith together with the Nicene canons, prefaced by this title:

> Here begin the decrees of the Fathers at the great and holy synod in the city of Nicaea in Bithynia, translated from Greek by Philo Evares for the Constantinopolitans.

Read “by Evaristus, for the Constantinopolitans,” or, as others prefer, “and by Evaristus, for the Constantinopolitans.”

Since in the manuscripts and printed editions of Dionysius only the creed from this translation is presented, a note indicating the omission itself is substituted in place of this title and the omitted canons. The Nicene canons are followed by the letter of the Africans to Pope Celestine.

Finally, the collection concludes with the Chalcedonian canons, which Dionysius rendered into Latin. The ending is indicated by the words:

> Thanks be to God; let it be done, let it be done.

### 13.

The difference between this part and the pure Dionysian codices and printed editions is sufficient to leave no doubt that it represents the first form of the collection. The order in which Dionysius first rendered into Latin the canons of his Greek codex, then the Sardican and African canons from the original Latin, and finally the translation of the Chalcedonian canons, seems to indicate that he initially intended a chronological sequence.

In his second recension, however, he judged that the Chalcedonian canons should be attached to the other Greek synods. In the African canons, apart from the acts of the first session of the Council of Carthage of the year 419, he initially presented only thirty-three canons, without mentioning the other synods whose canons had been recited and inserted at that council.

Since he had decided to transcribe the complete version of the creed and Nicene canons which Philo and Evaristus had prepared, he therefore added the following words to the note prefixed to the thirty-three canons, after “Daniel, the notary of the Council of Nicaea, recited the profession of faith, or its decrees, in the African Council”:

> These we have written together with the replies of the bishops of Alexandria and Constantinople.

This addition was omitted in the second recension, in which, after changing his plan, he passed over the canons of that version.

In this matter we suspect that Dionysius initially had before his eyes a codex of that African synod containing only the acts of the first session together with the thirty-three canons, and only the replies of the bishops together with Philo’s and Evaristus’s complete version. Other collectors seem likewise to have used such a codex, for they present those acts and the same thirty-three canons, divided differently into forty canons, as well as the replies of the bishops. Compare the note on the documents below, column 629, no. 1.

When Dionysius prepared his collection in the second recension, he seems to have acquired another codex containing the entire Council of the year 419. Since he judged that the canons of the other African synods recited and inserted there ought to be transcribed, he suppressed the aforementioned translation of the Nicene canons and substituted other notes which did not belong to the first form.

Hence, in his letter to Stephen, he added material appropriate to the second recension. The shorter letter of the first form, addressed to Petronius, may indicate that Dionysius had in mind the bishop Petronius to whom he gave one of his Paschal Letters in the year 525 [Col. 0206B]. Since, however, the same shorter letter is said to be addressed to Stephen in another codex, Vatican Palatine 574, some error on the part of a scribe in the name Petronius should be suspected.

[CLXXXIV] ## CHAPTER II. Concerning the collection which Pope Hadrian I delivered to Charlemagne

### 1.

The collection which Pope Hadrian I delivered at Rome to Charlemagne, king of the Franks, is commonly called the Hadrianic Collection. Since Charlemagne came to Rome three times during the pontificate of Hadrian I—namely, as Sirmond noted, in the year 774, when he was besieging Pavia; again in the year 781, when his sons Pippin, king of Lombardy, and Louis, king of Aquitaine, were anointed by that same pontiff; and finally in the year 787, when he proceeded from there to Capua and Benevento against the duke Grimoald—P. Constantius rightly conjectured that this codex belonged rather to the first expedition, on the basis of these words prefixed to the codex in the letter by which Hadrian addresses Charlemagne:

> Unharmed, you shall remain victorious with your men, namely through those very ones—Peter and Paul—who ask to enter the city of Pavia with you as victor, so that you may trample upon the necks of the wicked and perfidious King Desiderius.

This collection contains the Dionysian collection together with several additions, and differs from it on account of those additions. Nor should Hadrian I be thought to have been the author of this collection, as though he himself had inserted those additions into the Dionysian collection.

For in a letter written in the year 745 to Pippin and to the bishops and abbots of the Frankish kingdom, Pope Zacharias quotes certain canons from the African Council and others from the Council of Carthage. As we shall see, this distinction and inscription of the African canons is peculiar to the Hadrianic collection.

Although Cresconius distinguishes the first thirty-three canons from the later hundred by means of a numbering system derived from some Dionysian codex in which that distinction had begun to be introduced, he nevertheless presents all of them as inscribed to the Council of Carthage. Thus it is peculiar to the Hadrianic collection alone to attribute the later hundred canons to the African Council rather than to the Council of Carthage. We therefore clearly recognize that this arrangement was introduced under Pope Zacharias.

Moreover, it is clear from Vatican manuscript 5845, which we shall discuss shortly, that the additions of documents now read in their proper places within this collection had already been attached to the Dionysian collection at two different times, long before Hadrian and Zacharias. At what time these additions—of which the more recent belong to Gregory II—were inserted in their proper places according to chronological order cannot be known because of the lack of evidence.

### 2.

Since the difference between the Hadrianic and Dionysian collections depends chiefly upon the additions, these must be treated individually and distinctly. Some scholars have noticed only the additions of documents relating to the second part of the collection, namely the letters of the Roman pontiffs. We have nevertheless found other substantial additions in the first part, concerning the canons, and these must be discussed first.

At the Council of Nicaea, the creed was added together with a chronological note and a special catalogue of bishops, about which we spoke in part I, chapter 3, § 1. The Ancyran and Neocaesarean canons display the names of the bishops.

In the Gangran canons there is a synodical letter to the Armenians, in the translation commonly called Isidorian, together with the names of the bishops. The Antiochene canons received in their heading the added words “at the dedication” (*in encaeniis*); and in the pure copies of this collection they present only the names of the bishops added in a distinctive manner, about which see part I, chapter 4, § 2. The synodical letter of the same council, transcribed in the editions of Wendelstinus and Pithoeus from the Isidorian translation, was also added.

In the Constantinopolitan canons, the creed and a catalogue of bishops were added. In the Chalcedonian canons, a definition of faith was added together with a catalogue of bishops, which we have observed to be the same catalogue that was copied by Sirmond from the most ancient Maffeian codex and published by Labbe in volume IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils, columns 1710 and following.

The Sardican canons have an ending different from that of the Dionysian collection:

> The entire synod said: The Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world shall preserve all that has been established.

They also include a catalogue of bishops transcribed from the more ancient Italian collection Barb. 2888 or from some similar collection.

The African canons, which in Dionysius are arranged in a continuous numerical series numbering 138, bear only this heading:

> The African Synod at Carthage, which established 138 canons.

In the Hadrianic collection, however, they present two series with two headings [CLXXXV]. The first thirty-three canons bear this title:

> Here begin the canons of the Council of Carthage,

and conclude with:

> Here end the canons of the Council of Carthage.

Then another 105 canons are described in a new numerical series under this heading:

> Here begin the canons of the various councils of the African province, numbering 105,

and they receive the conclusion:

> Here ends the African Council.

We shall add another difference in this part. In the earliest copy of the Hadrianic collection, another preface by the pontiff himself to Charlemagne, arranged in verse, was substituted for Dionysius’s preface to Stephen of Salona. The initial letters of its verses give the following inscription:

> To Charles, the lordly son of the Church: Hadrian, pope.

This preface was preserved for us in the most ancient Sangermanian manuscript copy, published in volume VIII of the Councils, column 583. It was written in the year 805 while Charlemagne was emperor, but it is absent from the other codices of the same collection which we have seen.

If Dionysius’s letter to Stephen appears in some manuscripts of this kind, it may be suspected that they were copied from those older exemplars which, as we conjectured, contained the collection compiled before Hadrian. For genuine Hadrianic codices did not contain that letter of Dionysius but rather the other preface of Hadrian.

### 3.

Before the additions of the second part, containing the constitutions of the Apostolic See, were inserted into this collection, they had been attached to the pure Dionysian collection as an appendix [Col. 0207D]. We learned this from the most ancient Vatican Codex 5845, which contains the pure Dionysius.

After Dionysius’s collection has been transcribed, an appendix is added in the same script. It disregards chronological order and first reports three councils held under Symmachus: one of the year 501, another of the year 502, and, in third place, the one of the year 499.

Next come the headings of six decrees of Pope Hilary, two of Simplicius, and one of Felix; then the decrees themselves are recited under those headings.

Afterward Leo’s letter to the bishops of Mauretania is transcribed under the heading:

> In the case of Bishop Lupicinus: Leo to all the bishops established throughout Caesarean Mauretania.

The letter itself lacks chapters 6, 7, and 8, which we presented in the complete edition of that same letter. For this form, see the fuller discussion in the note on letter 12, volume I, column 645, no. 3.

Next is appended the letter of Zosimus addressed to the presbyters of Ravenna:

> Zosimus’s memorandum to the presbyters and deacons who are at Ravenna: From the report, etc.

These two letters, which should be counted among the additions to the Dionysian collection, were incorrectly inserted into Dionysius’s collection in the *Bibliotheca juris canonici*.

Finally, after all this, a new appendix is added in the same codex, containing a table of seventy-nine chapters, followed by the same number of documents. The first five of these are relevant to our subject:

**I. Justin Augustus to Hormisdas.** “As we have always been …” This letter appears in volume V, column 672.

**II. A copy of a petition from the Antiochene and Jerusalem clergy and monks, etc., to Justin.** “Draw water with joy, etc.” Same volume, column 473.

**III. Hormisdas to Justin.** “Among the matters which concern unity, etc.” Same volume, column 682.

**IV. Hormisdas to the presbyters, deacons, and archimandrites of Second Syria.** “Having read the letter, etc.” This letter is truncated through most of its length in the same place, retaining scarcely its beginning and ending with the words printed in volume V of the Councils, column 1114a: “and considering the labors of the prophet.”

**V. The decrees of Pope Gregory the Younger begin.** “In the name of the Lord, etc.” This is the council of the year 721, volume VIII of the Councils, column 185.

We conjectured in the aforementioned note on letter 12 of Saint Leo, no. 11, that the earlier documents, those preceding the table of seventy-nine chapters, were added to the Dionysian codex shortly after the death of Symmachus, while the later documents, namely these five chapters, were added during the age of Gregory II or shortly afterward.

All these documents—both the earlier ones and these five—are found inserted into the Hadrianic collection in their proper place in chronological order, neither more nor fewer. They were taken and inserted from some codex like the aforementioned Vatican Codex 5845, so closely that the Hadrianic copies display not only the same headings and the same readings as that codex, but also lack the three indicated chapters in Leo’s letter to the Moors, while the letter of Hormisdas to the presbyters, deacons, and archimandrites of Second Syria is likewise truncated and retains only its beginning.

As for why the other chapters which are transcribed in the Vatican manuscript after those five were not added to the Hadrianic collection, no other probable explanation occurs to us except that they were added later to the appendix of the Dionysian collection.

These documents are inserted into the Hadrianic collection in the following order. Another letter to the presbyters of Ravenna, numbered 4, follows Zosimus’s letter to Hesychius. At the end of Leo’s letters, numbered 49, his letter to the Moors is included.

Then six decrees of Pope Hilary are added, namely the council of the year 465 together with two letters of that pontiff read there; two decrees of Simplicius, or two letters of his—one to John of Ravenna, the other to Florentius, Equitius, and Severus; and one of Felix, namely the council of the year 487.

Then come the council held under Symmachus in the year 499, another of the year 501, and another of the year 502. Finally there are the five other documents mentioned above: four under Hormisdas and one under Gregory the Younger.

### 4.

From the time when this collection was delivered by Pope Hadrian to Charlemagne, it acquired a certain apostolic authority and began to be commonly called the Codex of Canons [Col. 0208D]. For this reason, some people later judged the forged letters of Isidore to be rejected because they were not recorded in the Codex of Canons, as is clear from letter 42 of Nicholas I, no. 5.

That the name Codex of Canons refers to the Hadrianic collection is evident from Hincmar of Reims. Rejecting the Isidorian productions, he asserts that only those canons should be used which the Apostolic See “and the whole Catholic Church call canons,” and which, he says, “are contained in our codices, which our ancestors received from the Apostolic See as books to be followed.”

From this it is clear, as P. Coustantius observed in the preface to volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, no. 131, that the book which we call the Hadrianic Codex was called by Hincmar and the Gallican bishops the Codex of Canons, in accordance with the usage and customary language received among Romans and Gauls.

### 5.

There are many manuscript codices of this collection which are commonly believed to be Dionysian [Col. 0209A]. We examined many of them at Rome. Among the older and more noteworthy are Vatican 4969, Vatican Palatine 578, Vatican Reginae 1021 and 1043, and the two Vallicellian codices A, 5 and 18.

Among these, Vatican Reginae 1021 bears at the beginning a special index, or rather an unpublished summary, of the contents of the same collection.

That some codices existed which presented the Hadrianic collection enlarged by two further additions is clear from the Codex of Canons which Leo IV describes and approves in his letter to the Britons, in these words quoted by Gratian, Distinction 20, chapter 1:

> It is not appropriate for anyone to judge from the booklets and commentaries of others while abandoning the canons of the holy councils or the rules of the decretals—that is, those which are held among us together with the canons.
>
> Those which we use in all ecclesiastical judgments are the canons of the Apostles, of Nicaea, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea, Constantinople, Ephesus, Chalcedon, Sardica, Africa, and Carthage; and together with them the rules of the Roman bishops Sylvester, Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Celestine, Leo, Gelasius, Hilary, Symmachus, Hormisdas, Simplicius, and Gregory the Younger.
>
> These indeed are those by which bishops judge and by which bishops, together with clergy, are themselves judged.

From this description it is clear that by the time of this pontiff two additions had already been made to the Roman codex containing the Hadrianic collection.

One addition concerned the councils, namely the Ephesian canons. By this title are meant the two letters of Cyril to Nestorius together with the twelve anathemas. They were transferred here from the Hispanic collection, in which they are likewise inscribed under the title of the Council of Ephesus and present the same version.

The other addition concerned the decretals, namely the apocryphal council of Sylvester. We learn that it entered the Hadrianic collection from older collections also through the *Annotation on the Apostolic Decretals*, which is found in Vatican manuscript 3833, prefixed to the collection of Cardinal Deusdedit, and in two codices of the older Sorbonico-Mutinensis collection. From that collection Franciscus Salmon published the annotation in his French work entitled *Treatise on the Study of the Councils*, page 258 of the Leipzig edition of 1726.

For this annotation, while presenting the sequence of the Hadrianic collection—which entirely agrees with the codex of Leo IV—mentions the council of Saint Sylvester before the decrees of Siricius.

[CLXXXVII] ### 6.

The example of Vatican Codex 1337 must not now be passed over. Although it is Hadrianic, it nevertheless contains certain peculiarities in the first part of the canons.

This codex was especially useful to the Roman correctors in the edition of Gratian, who call it the Codex of Canons. This is shown by note c on chapter 8 of Distinction 19, where they testify that a certain chapter of Anastasius II’s letter to the emperor Anastasius is found in the Codex of Canons, folio 156. On that folio of the Vatican manuscript just mentioned, the same letter of Anastasius is indeed transcribed.

In this codex the Apostolic Canons are omitted. The canons of the four general councils, however, precede the others in this order: Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon.

After the Nicene Creed there follows, without any heading:

> After the Council of Nicaea, a council was convened in the city of Rome, etc.,

as in the collection to be published in this volume, chapter 55. On this, see note 1, column 396, and note 11, column 400.

Under the name of the Council of Ephesus, the two letters of Cyril to Nestorius are presented, as we observed in the preceding discussion of Leo IV’s codex.

After the Chalcedonian canons follow the Ancyran, Neocaesarean, Gangran, Antiochene, Laodicean, the thirty-three Carthaginian canons, the Sardican canons, and the remaining 105 African canons.

In the second part, which contains the constitutions of the pontiffs, this codex differs in nothing from the pure Hadrianic copies. After that part, a brief annotation concerning the six general councils is transcribed, followed by a few other items.

Finally, in a more recent but still ancient script, approximately of the eleventh century, two annotations are found relating to the Latin, Sardican, and African canons inserted into the first part. Something similar does occur in the *Epitome*, as it is called, of the Hadrianic collection, printed in volume VIII of the Councils, column 574. Since, however, these annotations are fuller in our codex, they should be appended here.

The first concerns the canons of the Council of Carthage of the year 419.

There are also ecclesiastical rules composed in the African regions by a very numerous synodical council. Since these are found in many forms and in different arrangements—that is, differently in Dionysius and in the Hadrianic manuscripts, differently in the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, and differently in other codices—if any Catholic should come upon them, then, while preserving and keeping intact the Catholic faith expounded at Nicaea in Bithynia by the 318 Fathers and subsequently, in the city of Rome, beneficially supplemented by Catholic bishops concerning the Holy Spirit, he ought to follow whatever he finds in them that is reasonable, provided that it does not differ from the holy and Catholic Roman Church.

The second annotation, concerning the Sardican canons, is expressed in these words:

> Moreover, there are another forty rules attributed to Hosius, bishop of Córdoba, which are entitled as belonging to the twenty bishops at Sardica. They are found, however, not among the Greeks but chiefly among the Latins.

(The author of this annotation, ignorant of the Greek collections that contained the Sardican canons, wrote this for the following reason: being acquainted only with the Latin collections, and especially with the Dionysian collection, he had learned from Dionysius’s letter to Stephen that the Sardican canons had been added by him from the original Latin; he therefore mistakenly believed that they were absent among the Greeks.) Since, however, mention has been made of the aforesaid Hosius, it is necessary to make known to all Catholics that this same man was among the most holy 318 Fathers at Nicaea in Bithynia and was sent by the Apostolic See together with the priests Vincent and Victor, and that he remained in the flesh in Spain until the time of the emperor Constantius. For the aforementioned Constantius—as the highly learned Sulpicius Severus reports in his *Chronicles*, carefully embracing the matter and handing it down to our memory—assembled at Rimini in Italy a large episcopal synod from both parts of the world and, wishing to revive the poisons of Arius against the Catholic faith, or against the definition of the 318 Fathers, disturbed the Church of God by tyrannical usurpation.

Finally, compelled either by fear of the emperor or by the presence of Taurus, to whom the execution of the matter had been entrusted in such a way that, if the greater part of the council consented to the perfidy of the Arians, he himself would receive the insignia of the consulship, almost all the bishops who were there subscribed. But afterward, with divine assistance inspiring them once more, very many of them, doing penance and also submitting written statements, returned to the holy Catholic Church, from which they had departed more from necessity than from willingness. Hence the Council of Rimini is rightly called anathema by all Catholics forever [CLXXXVIII]; and whoever neglects to say this is not a Catholic.

Accordingly, concerning this Hosius, as the aforementioned Sulpicius reports, during the lengthy debate of the synod, since—as was stated above—he was still alive in the time of Constantius, it was decided that an episcopal delegation should be sent to inquire whether, in the holy and venerable assembly of Nicaea, at which he had been present, the Fathers had confessed *homoousion*, as we Catholics rightly confess—that is, the Son of one substance with the Father—or rather *homoiousion*, as the Arians contend—that is, the Son of a substance similar to the Father—which our 318 Fathers had decreed should be confessed. He is reported to have given the following answer, whether because he had become senile through extreme old age or because he was currying favor with the emperor: both parties were arguing correctly, whether *homoousion* or *homoiousion*. Since this opinion had been foolishly expressed, it was ridiculed and rejected with one voice by all Catholics and even by the Arians. Finally, in the city of Córdoba, where he had held the episcopate, his name was not afterward read among the Catholic bishops, whether his predecessors or successors, after this consultation or response.

> **Note [Col. 0209D]:** Sulpicius, in Book II of his *Sacred History*, reported only the following about Hosius: “It was also the opinion that Hosius had yielded from Spain to the same perfidy—the Arian one.
