This seems astonishing and incredible, because for almost the whole of his lifetime he was the most steadfast champion of our party, and the Council of Nicaea was regarded as having been completed under his direction—unless, as his age was failing (for he was more than one hundred years old), he had become delirious, as Saint Hilary relates in his letters.” See the note of P. Hieronymus de Prato on this passage of Sulpicius, vol. II of the Verona edition of Sulpicius’s works, p. 218.

These, then, are the rules attributed to the aforesaid Hosius and the twenty bishops, while preserving and keeping intact the Catholic faith expounded at that same Nicaea in Bithynia by the 318 Fathers, and afterward in the city of Rome, etc., as in the first annotation. Twenty abbreviated Sardican canons are then appended, followed once more by the same canons set out in full.

### 7.

Joannes Wendelstinus was the first to publish an edition of the Hadrianic collection, at Mainz in 1525, under the following title:

> *Canons of the Apostles, Constitutions of the Ancient Councils, Earlier Decrees of the Popes; Concerning the Primacy of the Roman Church, Transcribed from Three Most Ancient Exemplars.*

Two of these codices were entirely identical and purely Hadrianic. From the third, however, Wendelstinus added three items that are not Hadrianic: first, the two aforementioned letters of Saint Cyril to Nestorius under the name of the Council of Ephesus; second, the special annotation prefixed to the Sardican canons, which we previously presented from Vatican manuscript 1337; and third, the treatise on the primacy of the Roman Church, which was reprinted in vol. I of the Councils, col. 65.

The second edition was prepared by Franciscus Pithoeus at Paris in 1609, with the following title:

> *The Ancient Code of Canons of the Roman Church.*

It is a reprint of the first Mainz edition with three additional supplements, namely the *Abridgment of Ferrandus*, the *Breviary of Cresconius*, and the letter of Dionysius to Stephen.

A third, much superior edition, prepared through further efforts of the same Pithoeus, was published after his death under the title:

> *The Ancient Code of Canons of the Roman Church, Restored by Franciscus Pithoeus from Ancient Manuscript Codices and Illustrated with Notes.* Paris, 1687, folio.

Besides the additions of the earlier edition, other short works enlarge this appendix.

### 8.

We shall conclude this chapter with a brief observation concerning that epitome of the canons which was published at Ingolstadt in vol. VI of the *Ancient Readings* and subsequently transferred into editions of the Councils, where it was attributed to Hadrian. Sirmondus aptly observed (*Councils of Gaul*, vol. II, p. 117):

> Yet it is certain that what was offered to Charles was not an epitome, but the complete collection both of the canons from which that epitome was subsequently compiled and of the papal decrees from Siricius to Gregory the Younger.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the Collection of Dionysian Additions

### 1.

We call “Dionysian Additions” the documents that were added to the Dionysian collection. Two kinds of such additions are clearly distinguished in the pure Dionysian manuscript Vatican 5845. First, after the letter of Anastasius II, at which the Dionysian collection ends, three synods under Symmachus are presented as an appendix, together with six decrees of Pope Hilary, two of Simplicius, one of Felix, Leo’s letter to the Moors, and another of Zosimus to the presbyters of Ravenna. Then follows a table of seventy-nine chapters, to which an equal number of documents are appended.

We indicated the first five of these documents in the preceding chapter. For, together with those appended to the letter of Anastasius II, they passed into the Hadrianic collection, as we demonstrated there at greater length. We must now discuss the remaining seventy-four documents, which, since they are not read in the Hadrianic collection, we have thought should be distinguished by the name “Dionysian Additions.”

### 2.

Besides the Vatican manuscript 5845 of the pure Dionysian collection, from which we called them Dionysian, we also found these Additions appended to the Hadrianic collection in three codices: namely, in Vallicellian A 5; in Vatican 1353, which was copied in 1441 from an older Bergomate manuscript and presented to Cardinal Pietro Barbo, afterward Pope Paul II; and finally in a very ancient manuscript of the chapter-house of Vercelli, which we discovered had been used by Bishop Atto around the middle of the tenth century.

All these Italian codices attest to this Italian collection of the Additions. Hence we also believe that the pure Dionysian manuscript Vatican 5845 was Italian. Holstenius calls this very ancient Lombard codex, in Labbe, vol. V of the Councils, col. 792 A, a “Lombard” codex, since it is written in the script commonly called Lombard.

At the beginning, mutilated, it places before Dionysius part of the *Breviary of Cresconius*, beginning with chapter 245. Later, some leaves are again missing, and the table of titles of the first part of the Dionysian collection begins with title 16 of the Nicene material. Because of this loss of leaves, title 15 and the letter of Dionysius to Stephen are also absent. We believe that this letter was prefixed to the first part just as his letter to Julian is prefixed to the second part.

The canons of the councils do not bear the continuous numerical sequence that Dionysius says he received from the Greek codex; instead, they display only the numbers proper to each council. Only among the African canons is the sequence of 138 preserved, though not the division introduced by the Hadrianic codices.

Besides the Dionysian Additions, which are common to other manuscripts, three items are added at the end, one of which seems to indicate the age of the codex in the time of Charlemagne. The codex reached the Vatican Library only later, for the following note is read in the lower margin of the first page:

> To our most holy lord Paul V, D. Constantinus Abbas Cajetanus, D. D. In the year of Our Lord 1649, in the month of October.

### 3.

More must be said about Vallicellian A 5, to which the other two codices, Vercelli and Vatican 1353, are entirely similar. The catalogue of the Roman pontiffs indicates that this parchment codex, of very large leaves divided into two columns, was written in the ninth century, while Nicholas I was still alive. The catalogue, carried down to his pontificate, displays his name written in the original script; the years, months, and days of his pontificate, however, are visibly added and recorded by a later hand.

Our friend, the distinguished Count Joseph Garampi, inserted this catalogue in his learned dissertation *On the Silver Coin of Benedict III*, p. 161. The same catalogue is also found transcribed in Vatican manuscript 1353, from which Emmanuel Schelestratius published it in *Illustrated Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, vol. I, p. 626, and Franciscus Blanchinius in the prolegomena to vol. II of Anastasius, work 6, p. 18. They nevertheless end it, after Nicholas I, with Hadrian II and John VIII. These two later pontiffs are known to have been added in the Bergomate exemplar from which the same Vatican codex was copied, for they lack the indications of years, months, and days that are marked in the case of Nicholas I.

The Vallicellian book has at its beginning an index written in the hand of the most eminent Baronius, demonstrating that this collection had been useful to him. The ancient script begins with a table of 141 chapters. Since this is mutilated at the beginning, it starts with number 34. An inscription in large ancient red letters follows:

> *Breviary of Cresconius.*

Then come twelve sacred images holding a book in their hands, followed by Cresconius’s preface to Liberinus *On the Harmony of the Canons*. This is followed by the 300 chapters of the *Breviary of Cresconius*.

It must be observed here that this Vallicellian codex, beginning with the *Breviary of Cresconius*, is the one that Cardinal Baronius called the “Cresconian Collection.” We learned this with certainty from the page numbers noted by that father of the *Annals*, which agree entirely with the pages of this codex. Under the same title, “Cresconian Collection,” the Roman editors of the letters of the Roman pontiffs cited a similar codex, Vatican 1353.

Since P. Coustantius lacked this information, although he consulted friends living in Rome about this Cresconian collection and nevertheless received no suitable answers from them, he became entangled in various difficulties, as may be seen among other places in his preface to vol. I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, nos. 125 and 127.

After the *Breviary of Cresconius*, the aforementioned catalogue of the Roman bishops is copied in the Vallicellian manuscript. Then follows a table of the canons of the councils and of the decrees of the Roman pontiffs. These are followed by the canons and decrees themselves, with the same additions contained in the Hadrianic collection, inserted in the same places as in that collection.

After these, another seventy-four chapters are added. These are peculiar to this collection and have been distinguished by us under the name “Dionysian Additions.” These seventy-four chapters are connected with the preceding ones by a continuous numerical sequence, so that the earlier documents of the Hadrianic collection are distributed under numbers 1–68, while these Additions begin with number 69 and end with number 141.

### 4.

Since in Vatican manuscript 5845 the same Additions are appended separately to Dionysius and, together with five other chapters transferred into the Hadrianic collection, make up seventy-nine chapters, they begin with number 6. To avoid confusion, we shall describe these Additions with the numbers of the Vallicellian codex prefixed, since it is the more complete one—for we shall state in its proper place that two chapters are missing from the Vatican manuscript—while not omitting to record the numbers of the Vatican exemplar.

We observed that the author of these Additions had before his eyes the Vatican-Barberini collection, about which we spoke in Part II, chapter 7, and the Fragments of Saint Hilary, or the complete work of Hilary from which the Fragments were excerpted. Six chapters of these Additions are found in those same Fragments. Whatever is described in the Vatican-Barberini collection, the compiler transferred into these Additions, except only what is already contained in the earlier chapters of the Hadrianic collection. He received another nine chapters from an unknown source.

### 5.

Here is the order of these Additions, with the numbers found in the aforementioned Vallicellian manuscript A 5.

**LXIX.** In Vatican Dionysius 5845, number 6: *Instructions of Saint Peter concerning the preservation of the sacraments.* In the Vatican-Barberini collection, number 34. It will be published in this volume among the documents of ancient canon law, no. 5, col. 674.

**LXX.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 7: *Ancient Statutes of the East.*

**LXXI.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 8: *Recapitulation of the official ordinances of the Church.* These two numbers are joined as one in the Vatican-Barberini collection, number 27. They will be published among the aforementioned documents, no. 3, col. 653.

**LXXII.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 9: *Canonical Letter concerning what presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons ought to be.* It is in the Vatican-Barberini collection, number 30. This too will be found among the documents, no. 4, col. 669.

**LXXIII.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 10: *The deposition of Pope Marcellinus.* It is found in Vatican-Barberini, number 53.

**LXXIV.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 11: *Here begins how a formal document is to be made.* “Done at Nicaea, the metropolis of Bithynia,” etc., as in the Vatican-Barberini collection, number 3, to which we refer readers.

**LXXV.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 12: *Letter sent from the synod at Rome*—read *Romam*, “to Rome.” It is the spurious letter of the Nicene synod to Pope Sylvester, which is presented in the Vatican-Barberini collection, number 4.

**LXXVI.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 13: *Letter of Sylvester to the synod.* It is likewise spurious; concerning it, see Vatican-Barberini, number 5.

**LXXVII.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 14: *Canons of Saint Sylvester, bishop.* These are three apocryphal documents. The first and third, published by P. Coustant and Labbe, are those about which we spoke under number 6 of the same Vatican-Barberini collection. The second, however, which is included there as well, although it bears the marks of fabrication more than all the others, we append here because it was not found by the aforementioned scholars and confirms the fabrication of the others ever more strongly. Its errors should be corrected by whoever is able, since they must be attributed partly to the impostor and partly to the scribe.

> **Here begins the letter of Sylvester, bishop, sent to the Council of Nicaea through Abundantius the presbyter and Abundius the deacon, in the consulship of Paulinus and Julian, twelve days before the Kalends of October.**
>
> To the most blessed holy brothers and fellow bishops, or fellow presbyters, who are gathered in the Council of Nicaea: Sylvester, bishop and prelate of the apostolic and Catholic city of Rome, sends greetings in the Lord.
>
> When our most glorious and most devout son, Constantine Augustus, had learned through his own ears the enactments of your holiness that had been communicated to him, we receive them with affection at the command of our Lord Jesus Christ, and he makes known to the whole world the entrance to the right and declared faith. We have thought that this should be made known to your Charity: a council was convened by us in our diocese against Victorinus the bishop and Hippolytus the deacon, who were notorious associates of the Manichaeans, and against Jobianus and Calixtus, who in their arrogance said that Easter was not to be celebrated on its proper day or in its proper month, but was to be observed on the tenth day before the Kalends of May.
>
> Let the whole world know that they were condemned, expelled from the Church, and excommunicated. At the council of the Apostolic See, once the judicial inquiry had been made public, they, with minds polluted, kept silent and failed to understand aright; condemned for perpetrating wicked things by the abominable pollution of innocent compunctions.
>
> And because, during their disastrous secession, having been forestalled by death, they dared on the last day to leave behind the pollution of the priesthood through their own ordination, we command that this be condemned through our preaching and apostolic teachings and be refuted by holy men and fellow priests. Against Photinus, especially Sabellius and Arius, we condemn them as struck by an anathema [perhaps *struck*, plural, or *struck*, singular], confirming the matter as though with your voice. Whatever you established in the Council of Nicaea in the city of Bithynia, we likewise preserve in equal form for the governance of the universal Church [perhaps *for the governance of the truth*]: you judge with balanced weighing.
>
> Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of January.
>
> **In another hand:** May our Lord Jesus Christ deem it worthy to preserve you, holy brothers and fellow bishops.

**LXXVIII.** Missing in Vatican Dionysius. *The rules of the Council of Nicaea of twenty bishops, which are not found in Greek but are found in Latin, as follows:* “There are also ecclesiastical rules which, in the African regions,” etc., as in Vatican manuscript 1337. We presented this entire chapter in the preceding chapter, chapter 2, no. 6.

**LXXIX.** This chapter too is absent from Vatican Dionysius. *The law issued by Constantine Augustus concerning the condemnation of Arius and the handing over of every writing of his to the fire.* “The emperor Constantine Augustus to the bishops and peoples. Arius, who imitated wicked and impious men,” etc. This is an unpublished ancient version of that law, which in the printed editions is found both in Greek and in Latin, in Socrates, Book I, chapter 9, and in Gelasius of Cyzicus, Book II, chapter 36. Another ancient translation is also found in Epiphanius Scholasticus, *Tripartite History*, Book II, chapter 15.

**LXXX.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 15: *The Acts concerning Liberius.* They are in the Vatican-Barberini collection, number 35, and were published in the Appendix to vol. I of P. Coustant’s *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, col. 89.

**LXXXI.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 16: *Letter of Bishop Liberius, uniform in character, before he was exiled.* He wrote to the confessors, namely Eusebius, Dionysius, and Lucifer, who were established in exile. “Although under an image,” etc., as in Saint Hilary, Fragment 6, nos. 1 and 2.

**LXXXII.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 17: *Likewise, before going into exile, Liberius spoke to Vincent of Capua concerning Helianus of Spoleto.* “I do not want you to become Vincent,” etc., as in the same Fragment 6 of Hilary, nos. 3 and 4.

**LXXXIII.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 18: *His letter to the Eastern bishops.* “To the most beloved brothers and fellow bishops in the East, Liberius sends greetings. Because of reverence for God,” etc. In the same place, nos. 5, 6, and 7.

**LXXXIV.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 19: *Liberius likewise writes from exile to Ursacius, Valens, and Germinius.* “Since I know that you are sons of peace,” etc. In the same Fragment, no. 10.

**LXXXV.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 20: *Liberius likewise writes to Vincent concerning exile.* “I do not teach, but I admonish,” etc. In the same place, no. 10.

In Vatican Dionysius, number 21, the following is inserted:

> *Copy of the letter of the Sardican synod to Julius, bishop of the city of Rome.* “What we have always believed,” etc., as in Hilary, Fragment 6, no. 9, and vol. II of the Councils, col. 690.

In the Vallicellian codex it is missing at this place, and only the title is given without the letter itself under number 102, as will be noted below.

**[CXCII] LXXXVI.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 22: *Confession of the Catholic faith, which Pope Damasus wrote to Paulinus, bishop of Antioch.* “After the Council of Nicaea, which [was held] in the city of Rome,” etc. It is found in Vatican-Barberini II, 36, and also in the collection to be published in this volume, chapter 55; see note 1 below, col. 396.

**LXXXVII.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 23: *Explanation by the blessed presbyter Jerome to Pope Damasus concerning the three hypostases.* “When the ancient East was inflamed by the fury of its peoples against one another,” etc. This is Saint Jerome’s letter 15 in the Verona edition, and in Coustant, vol. I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, col. 545.

**LXXXVIII.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 24: *Reply of Pope Damasus to Jerome’s request, addressed to Paulinus.* “To his beloved brother Paulinus, Damasus.” It begins: “And through my son Vitalis,” etc. It is found in the Vatican-Barberini collection, number 37, and in the collection inserted in this volume, chapter 55.

**LXXXIX.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 25: *Council of the city of Rome under Pope Damasus concerning the explanation of the faith.* It first says: “We must deal with the sevenfold Spirit,” etc., as it is read from Holstenius in vol. II of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 1047.

After the final words published by Holstenius, “he will announce to you,” this collection adds the canon of Scripture as follows:

> “It was also said: Now we must deal with the divine Scriptures, what the universal Catholic Church receives and what it ought to avoid. Here begins the order of the Old Testament.”

After the books of the Old Testament, the books of the New Testament are also appended, as in the published Gelasian decree, vol. V of the Councils, col. 385.

It further adds:

> “It was also said: After all these prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic Scriptures that we have set forth above,” etc., continuing to the words of the aforementioned Gelasian decree: “the first name of Christians arose, a new people.” These words conclude with mention of the three principal sees.

Baronius published this final fragment under the year 382, no. 19. Compare what we discussed at length concerning these fragments in Part II, chapter 11, § 5.

**XC.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 26: *Letter of Pope Siricius sent to all the bishops.* “I would always wish,” etc. It is found in Vatican-Barberini, number 38, and in the collection inserted in this volume, chapter 30.

**XCI.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 27: *Reply of the bishops.* “We have recognized,” etc. It is read in Vatican-Barberini, number 29, and in the collection to be appended, chapter 31.

**XCII.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 28: *Letter of the Council of Carthage to Innocent.* “Since, according to custom,” etc. It is in Vatican-Barberini, number 15, and in the collection to be published, chapter 6.

**XCIII.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 29: *Reply of Saint Pope Innocent.* “In investigating the matters of God,” etc. It is found in Vatican-Barberini, number 16, and in the collection to be published, chapter 7.

**XCIV.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 30: *Imperial letter to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage.* “Some time ago,” etc., as in Vatican-Barberini, number 23, and in the collection to be published, chapter 16.

**XCV.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 31: *Letter of Bishop Aurelius to all the bishops established throughout the provinces of Byzacena and Arduzitania concerning the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius.* “Concerning the condemnation of Coelestius and Pelagius,” etc., as in Vatican-Barberini, number 24.

**XCVI.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 32: *Chapters excerpted from the proceedings held against Pelagius the heretic, together with other material concerning his written statements, which, when brought against him in the Palestinian synod, he was compelled to condemn.* “When [the matter was brought] from Jerusalem,” etc., as in Vatican-Barberini, number 25.

**XCVII.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 33: *Letter of Pope Coelestine of the Roman Church sent to the synod assembled at Ephesus.* “The presence of the Holy Spirit bears witness,” etc.

**[Col. 0216A] XCVIII.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 34: *Another letter of Pope Coelestine to Nestorius.* “For several days,” etc.

**XCIX.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 35: *Exhortatory letter of the same holy bishop Coelestine, sent to the clergy and peoples of Constantinople.* “To them I,” etc. The Roman editors of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs* printed these three letters of Coelestine from this collection, which they call Cresconian; they were subsequently published in the Councils, vol. III, cols. 1143, 903, and 914. See Vatican-Barberini, numbers 47, 48, and 49.

**C.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 36: *Extracts from the bishops that were read against Nestorius in the Council of Ephesus.* “After the thirteenth consulship of our lord Theodosius,” etc. See what we said concerning this and the following chapter under numbers 21 and 22 of the Vatican-Barberini collection, Part II, chapter 7.

**[CXCIII] CI.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 37: *Chapters of Nestorius’s blasphemies, in which he contradicts the letters sent to him by Saint Coelestine of the city of Rome and by Bishop Cyril, and in a very brief disputation rejects the twelve chapters of the faith that had been sent to him.* “Now of Bishop Cyril,” etc.

**CII.** *Copy of the letter of the Sardican synod to Julius, bishop of the city of Rome.* In the Vallicellian manuscript only this title is found; the letter itself is presented in Vatican Dionysius under number 21, as we noted above after number 84.

**CIII.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 38: *The accusation of Pope Xystus.*

**CIV.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 39: *Concerning Polycronius.* These two apocryphal documents are read in Vatican-Barberini, numbers 51 and 52.

**CV.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 40: *Saint Leo’s letter to Dioscorus*, letter 9 of our edition.

**CVI.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 41: *His letter to Turibius*, letter 15.

**CVII.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 42: *Another letter to Januarius*, letter 18.

**CVIII.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 43: *His letter to Septimus*, letter 2.

**CIX.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 44: *His letter to Theodorus*, letter 108.

**CX.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 45: *Another letter to the Sicilians*, letter 17.

**CXI.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 46: *His letter to Eutyches*, letter 20.

**CXII.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 47: *Copies of the proceedings in which, at the synod in Constantinople, the heretic Eutyches was heard and condemned by Saint Flavian the confessor.* “When the holy and great synod had again been assembled,” etc., as in Vatican-Barberini, numbers 69 and 70.

**CXIII.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 48: *Leo’s letter to Flavian*, letter 23 of our edition.

**CXIV.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 49: *Flavian’s letter to Leo*, letter 22 of our edition.

**CXV.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 50: *Leo’s letter to Flavian*, letter 28.

**CXVI.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 51: *His letter to Juvenal*, letter 139.

**CXVII.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 52: *Another letter to Maximus*, letter 119.

**CXVIII.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 53: *Another letter to Anatolius*, letter 80.

**CXIX.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 54: *Another letter to Leo Augustus*, letter 145.

**CXX.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 55: *To the same Augustus*, letter 165.

**CXXI.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 56: *Here begin the chapters sent at the synod of the 318 Fathers together with Pope Leo’s letter to Leo Augustus.* These are the testimonies of the Fathers appended to the aforementioned letter 165 of Leo. See also note 1 there, vol. I, col. 1383.

**CXXII.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 57: *Also, the faith of Saint Hilary of Poitiers.* “For we, adhering,” etc.

**CXXIII.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 58: *Also, the faith of Saint Augustine.* “We believe in the Father,” etc. We published these two additional testimonies in vol. I, note 88, col. 1400.

**CXXIV.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 59: *Here begins the faith of the Catholic Church of Rome.* “We believe in one God the Father,” etc. It is in Vatican-Barberini, number 90.

**[Col. 0217A] CXXV.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 60: *Confession of the presbyters or deacons of the Church of Constantinople.* “I, that deacon or presbyter of the Church of Constantinople,” etc., as in the same Vatican-Barberini collection, number 37.

**CXXVI.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 61: *Letter of Simplicius to Acacius.* “Set aside the concerns,” etc., as in Vatican-Barberini, number 72.

**CXXVII.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 62: *Copy of the letter that Acacius sent to Simplicius, in which he reported that Peter of Alexandria had been condemned.* “The concern of all the Churches,” etc., as in Vatican-Barberini, number 73.

**CXXVIII.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 63: *Copy of the letters of the most blessed Pope Felix of the city of Rome to the emperor Zeno through the bishops Vitalis and Misenus.* “It was certainly fitting,” etc., as in Vatican-Barberini, number 74.

**CXXIX.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 64: *Likewise, another letter of the same Felix to Bishop Acacius through the bishops Vitalis and Misenus.* “After the one of holy memory,” etc. In the same place, number 78.

**CXXX.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 65: *Likewise, to the emperor Zeno, in response to the petition of John, bishop of the Church of Alexandria.* “When peace had been restored to him,” etc., as in Vatican-Barberini, number 79.

**CXXXI.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 66: *Likewise, a copy of Felix’s letter to the aforementioned Acacius, bishop of the city of Constantinople.* “Episcopal diligence admonishing,” etc., as in the same collection, number 80.

**CXXXII.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 67: *Likewise, another letter of the same pope to Acacius.* “Of all transgressions,” etc., as in Vatican-Barberini, number 81.

**CXXXIII.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 68: *Here begins the decretal concerning books to be received and not received, written by Pope Gelasius together with seventy most learned bishops at the Apostolic See of the city of Rome.* “After the prophetic and evangelical [books],” etc. See what we said concerning this form of the Gelasian decree in Part II, chapter 11, § 5, no. 4.

**CXXXIV.** In Vatican Dionysius, numbers 69 and 70: *Here begins the judgment of Pope Gelasius, that the Apostolic See can loose all that has been bound, addressed to the bishops throughout Dardania.* “Nor do we altogether keep silent,” etc. This is a fragment of the letter to the Dardani, which you will find in the collection to be published in this volume, chapter 50, no. 4, col. 351.

**CXXXV.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 71: *From the letter of the blessed Pope Gelasius to the Easterners concerning avoidance of communion with Acacius, where it is made clear that there is no bond except with those who persist in error.* “We did not therefore pronounce sentence against Acacius,” etc. This too is a fragment of a longer treatise, published from a Veronese manuscript by Marquis Maffei, vol. V of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 195 a.

**CXXXVI.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 72: *The constitutions of Saint Pope Gelasius, which bishops receive at their ordination.* “The pope to the clergy, order, and people residing in that city. In response to commendable requests,” etc. This letter was added in Barberini manuscript 2888 after the final chapter of that collection, chapter 90. See vol. V of the Councils, col. 383.

**CXXXVII.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 73: *Decree of Saint Pope Gregory.* “Our Lord Jesus Christ reigning forever, in the times of the most devout and serene lord Mauritius,” etc. This addition too belongs to the aforementioned collection only in Vatican manuscript 1342. See vol. VI of the Councils, col. 915.

**[Col. 0217D] CXXXVIII.** In the Vallicellian manuscript this number is omitted by a jump. The documents, however, correspond with Vatican Dionysius.

**CXXXIX.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 74: *Gregory to Serenus, bishop of Marseilles, concerning images.* This is letter 13 of Saint Gregory, Book XI of the latest Maurist edition of the *Register*.

**CXL.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 75: *Synod of Pope Zacharias of the city of Rome.* This is the Roman council of the year 743, vol. VIII of the Councils, col. 283.

**CXLI.** In Vatican Dionysius, number 76: *Here begins Saint Augustine’s book on Ecclesiastical Rules, divided into fifty-five chapters.* It is a book by Gennadius wrongly attributed to Augustine, published in the Augustinian Appendix, vol. VIII, col. 78.

Here the collection ends in Vallicellian A 5. A second quire of another codex has been added to it, containing a fragment of the Roman council under John IX together with the canons of the Council of Ravenna. It begins:

> “A certain brief record was read,” etc.

P. Mabillonius published it from this codex in vol. I of the *Museum Italicum*, p. 86; and from Mabillon it is read in vol. XI of the Councils, col. 699. In the printed editions, the Council of Ravenna is assigned to the year 904. P. Antonius Pagius, however, established convincingly that both this council and the Roman council were held in the year 898.

Three other numbers, or three continuous chapters, are appended in Vatican Dionysius 5845.

**Number 77.** Here begins the preface concerning the creed held in the sacristy of Blessed Peter the Apostle between Lord Leo, most holy and angelic pope of the city of Rome, and the bishops Bernarius and Jesse, or Abbot Adalard, sent by Lord Charles, during the second indiction. See vol. IX of the Councils, col. 278.

**Number 78.** Letter of Saint Augustine to Bishop Auxilius concerning the case of unjust excommunication. “The most distinguished son of ours, Count Classianus,” etc. This is Letter 250, to which other testimonies of the same Augustine concerning unjust excommunication are appended in the manuscript. This letter, together with the same testimonies, is also found added at the end of the most ancient codex 60 of the chapter-house of Verona, after the Cresconian collection.

**Number 79.** *The Rule of the Definitions of Blessed Pope Gregory the Great.* A table of twenty-four titles precedes it, but in the body the titles continue up to thirty-two. It is a topical collection drawn from the sententiae of the letters of Saint Gregory, beginning on p. 306 and continuing to p. 327.

At the end of the codex, in a later hand, a brief fragment of the Council of Carthage under Boniface is copied; it is printed from Holstenius in vol. V of the Councils, col. 792.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning the Hispanic Collection

### § 1. The principal authors who discussed this collection. How it was compiled. Concerning its codices.

### 1.

It will become clear from what follows in Part IV, chapter 4, where discussion will be given of the very ancient abbreviation of the canons contained in manuscript 59 of the Veronese Chapter, that several very ancient collections, now lost and different from the one usually called the Hispanic Collection, once existed among the Hispanics [Col. 0218C]. The same is also demonstrated by two synods earlier than the Hispanic Collection, in which codices of the canons are reported to have been produced and read. The First Council of Braga, held in 563, states:

> “The canons both of the general synods and of the local synods were reread from a codex before the council.”

And the Second Council of Seville, held in 619, chapter 2:

> “When the canons had been produced, the synodal decrees were read through.”

Now, however, we must discuss the Hispanic Collection, of which several manuscript copies survive. After the Dionysian Collection, it is the most orderly and comprehensive of the others. The first person to provide a brief but sufficiently distinct account of this collection was Antonius Augustinus, archbishop of Tarragona, in his little work *On Certain Ancient Collectors of Canons*, chapter 17. Petrus de Marca reported a good deal about it in his *Opuscula*, although he had less certain knowledge of its origin and use. Stephanus Baluzius and others after him made use of copies of the same collection [Col. 0218D]; but they indicated so little about them that scarcely anything distinct can be extracted from their statements. Since the works of Antonius Augustinus were extremely rare and had gone unnoticed by most people, this distinguished collection remained little known until P. Coustantius discussed it at greater length in the preface to volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, § 10, from no. 132 through no. 152. Although he gave an accurate description of it, since we have been able to find and compare more manuscripts, we trust that we can offer something further by which the collection may be more fully elucidated.

### 2.

This collection, like the Dionysian, is divided into two parts, one of which presents the canons of councils and the other the letters of the Roman pontiffs. In the second part, the compiler drew upon Dionysius: for he copied from him all the letters that he found there, with the same titles, and inserted them into his own collection. Other pontifical letters, however, which he found elsewhere, he added in their proper places according to the same arrangement as Dionysius, with titles composed by himself [Col. 0219A].

As for the canons contained in the first part, he took nothing from Dionysius. Since, in regard to the Greek canons, another and older translation was current in Spain—a translation that was adopted from this collection by Isidore the Merchant and published from Isidore’s manuscripts, and that is therefore usually called the Isidorian translation—he did not wish to accept the new Dionysian translation, even though it was better and more carefully corrected, fearing that this novelty would offend the Spanish, who were accustomed to that ancient version.

The established use of his old version among the Spanish churches is sufficiently demonstrated by the Third Council of Toledo of 589, in which three passages from that same version are cited. For a similar reason, it must be said that he did not wish to borrow from Dionysius the African canons, although they are more accurately set out there: for another distinctive collection of African canons was becoming prevalent in the Spanish regions. This collection appears to have passed from Spain into Gaul, and is therefore praised at the Second Council of Tours in 567, as we proved in Part II, chapter 3, § 2, no. 4. From this we also concluded that certain errors which we carefully noted in the same paragraph in the recension of the African canons in this collection are to be attributed not to the Hispanic compiler but to the earlier author of that same African collection.

The Hispanic compiler did, however, provide at least this benefit in the Greek canons: following Dionysius’ method, he added titles to the individual decrees, whereas it is clear from manuscript 58 of the Veronese Chapter that these titles had been absent from the beginning of the ancient version. Nor did the Hispanic compiler produce only those canons of the councils of Greece and Africa that are read exclusively in Dionysius; he also added Gallican and Hispanic canons [CXCVI].

The authority of the Gallican synods was great among the Hispanics. Hence such synods were widely known among them, and they often framed their own canons from their words and judgments, even where they did not name them; indeed, they often openly and expressly proposed their example and authority as something to be followed. Sirmondus observed this in the preface to the *Councils of Gaul* and confirms it by the testimonies he cites. The Hispanic compiler therefore enriched his codex with these widely circulated examples of the Gallican synods.

We detected two errors in the same compiler in the First Council of Toledo, volume II, columns 1379 and 1380, note 5. We shall explain one of them, insofar as it slipped into the compiler’s work, on more appropriate grounds in the *Observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 14*, § 2, no. 3. We identified another error in the catalogue of bishops wrongly attributed to the Second Council of Arles, although it belongs to the First Council of Arles, in the *Observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 5*, volume II, columns 1018 and 1019, note 14. It was very easy to gather the Hispanic councils from the codices of the churches of Spain.

### 3.

Before describing the collection itself, a brief account must be prefixed of the codices on which its description depends. Copies of this collection are rare in Italy. We found one in the Vatican Library, marked no. 1341. That it was transferred from the Gallican church of Autun, or Augustodunum, is shown by the following profession of Theotardus, abbot of Saint Martin’s, which is written in a later script shortly after the beginning:

> “I, Theotardus, presently to be ordained abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin, promise that I shall perpetually show and confirm with my own hand the submission and reverence established by the holy Fathers, and obedience according to the precept of Saint Benedict, to the holy Church of God of Autun, in the presence of the lord bishop Agano”—

who flourished around the middle of the eleventh century—

> “And then: ‘Let this be read upon the altar.’”

We were permitted to see two other codices: one, Vatican Palatine 575, confused and mutilated, which once belonged to the monastery of Saint Martin at Mainz; the other in the library of the eminent Cardinal Passionei, likewise mutilated and apparently written in the tenth, and perhaps even the ninth, century.

The finest and oldest example of all, which we had collated for the letters of Leo, is the Caesarean Vindobonensis, marked no. [Col. 0220A] 41. Lambecius, in book II, chapter 8, page 932, no. 281, calls it “a parchment volume of astonishing antiquity, in folio, written throughout in ancient Gothic or Toledan letters in the year 736.”

There are many manuscripts of this kind in Gaul and Spain. Joannes Baptista Perezius describes four in particular among the many Spanish copies: the Lucense, Hispalense, Alveldense, and that of Saint Aemilianus, about which more will be said below. Garsias Loaisa, in the preface to the *Councils of Spain*, praises two other Toledan codices. He calls the one which Perez calls Alveldense the Vigilanus, because it was written by the presbyter Vigila. We have determined from the notation of the year 962 and from the documents contained in it that the manuscript he calls Hispalense is the same as the one Perez called the codex of Saint Aemilianus.

Petrus de Marca and Stephanus Baluzius mention two Rivipullensian manuscript books and one Urgellensian, as well as Colbertine manuscripts and one from Lyons, which agree with the same Hispanic copies. P. Coustantius praises a Hispanic copy from Gerona, and four Gallican ones: those of Laon, Noyon, Beauvais, and Soissons. He also indicates the Coislinian manuscript and one Colbertine manuscript, which seem to approach more closely the codices of Hispanic than of Gallican origin. Their differences will be discussed in § 5.

## § 2. On the original edition of this collection. Table of its contents. The letter of Innocent I to Aurelius is exempted from the suspicion of Isidorian forgery.

### 4.

Although some codices are more comprehensive than others, no codex represents an example of the original collection free from later additions. The original collection is usually established from the index, or table, of chapters, so that if chapters are found written in the body beyond those contained in the same table, they are recognized as later additions. If, among the tables of different codices [Col. 0220C] of the same collection, some present fewer chapters and others more, the table consisting of fewer chapters provides evidence of the original collection.

Among the codices of the Hispanic Collection mentioned above, fewer chapters are found in the tables of the Vindobonensis, Perez’s Hispalensis, the Rivipullensian manuscripts, Vatican 1341, and certain other Gallican copies. Although some chapters are inserted in their bodies, they received no additions in the prefixed table of chapters, as happened in certain other Hispanic copies. Their untouched indexes, or tables, are therefore rightly believed to belong to the original edition of this collection.

Accordingly, since we intend first of all to describe the first edition of the collection itself, we shall use the evidence of these shorter tables. The additions introduced later will be discussed afterward.

### 5.

The table of the first part is divided into forty-five chapters. We prefix the complete preface to this part.

> The canons of the general councils began in the time of Constantine [Col. 0220D]. For in the preceding years, while persecution was raging, no opportunity at all was given for instructing the peoples. Consequently, Christianity was divided into various heresies, because the bishops were not permitted to assemble in one place except in the time of the emperor mentioned above. For he gave Christians the freedom to meet together.
>
> Under him also the holy Fathers assembled at the Council of Nicaea from every part of the world and, in accordance with evangelical and apostolic faith, handed down the creed that follows the Apostles. There are four principal councils from which the Church possesses the fullest teaching of the faith, both concerning the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and concerning the incarnation of the aforesaid Son and our Savior.
>
> The first of these is the Nicene Synod, held under the emperor Constantine Augustus by 318 bishops. There the blasphemy of the Arian perfidy was condemned—the blasphemy by which that same Arius asserted inequality [variant: “concerning the inequality”] within the holy Trinity. Thus the same holy synod defined through the creed that the Son is God, consubstantial with God the Father [Col. 0221A].
>
> The second is the council of 150 Fathers assembled at Constantinople under the elder Theodosius. Condemning Macedonius, who denied that the Holy Spirit is God, it demonstrated that the same Paraclete is consubstantial with the Father and the Son. All Greece and the Latin world proclaim this in their churches.
>
> The third is the Ephesian Synod, composed of 200 bishops and held under the younger emperor Theodosius. It condemned Nestorius, who asserted two persons in Christ, with a just anathema, showing that one person of the Lord Jesus Christ remains in two natures.
>
> The fourth is the Council of Chalcedon, held under the emperor Marcian by 630 priests. It condemned Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople, who declared that the Word of God and the flesh had one nature, together with his defender Dioscorus, formerly bishop of Alexandria, and again Nestorius himself, along with the other heretics, by the united judgment of the Fathers. The same synod proclaimed that Christ God was born of the Virgin in such a way that we confess one person of the divine and human nature.
>
> These, as we have said, are the four principal and venerable synods embracing the entire Catholic faith [Col. 0221B]. But whatever councils the holy Fathers, filled with the Spirit of God, have established remain firmly confirmed after the authority of these four; their proceedings too are contained in this volume.
>
> At the beginning of this volume we have placed the Nicene Synod because of the authority of that great council. Next, we have arranged and placed within this volume, under their numerical and chronological order, the chapters of the various Greek and Latin councils, whether held earlier or later. We have also appended the decrees of the Roman bishops, in which, because of the eminence of the apostolic see, there is an authority no less than that of the councils. This has been done so that the discipline of ecclesiastical order, gathered and arranged by us into one body, may bind the holy bishops with their paternal rules [variant: “instruct them”], and so that the obedient ministers or peoples of the Church may be imbued with spiritual examples.
>
> As for the canons called Apostolic, since neither the apostolic see receives them nor did the holy Fathers grant them their approval [Col. 0221C], because they are recognized as having been composed by heretics under the name of the Apostles, their proceedings are nevertheless clearly removed from canonical and apostolic authority and assigned among the apocrypha, even though some useful provisions are found in them.

After this the following is appended:

> “The word *canon* is called in Greek and *regula* in Latin. Now *regula* is so called …”

as in Gratian, distinction 3, chapters 1 and 2; and after those words, at the end of the second chapter, “and correct what is wrong,” the following continues:

> “Now *synod* is translated from the Greek …”

as in the same Gratian, distinction 15, chapter 1, at the end. After the final words, “from the fellowship of many into one,” the following is appended:

> “The preface ends.”

The table of chapters of this first part is as follows.

### THE CHAPTERS OF THE COUNCILS OF GREECE BEGIN

**I.** Canons of the Council of Nicaea, of 318 bishops. In the body, after the canons, the creed, and the catalogue of the Nicene bishops in the ancient version—or, as it is called, the Isidorian version [Col. 0221D]—the compiler added the Faith of Saint Gregory the Great, which begins, “One God, the beginning.” It is an ancient translation of the faith written by Saint Gregory of Neocaesarea, published after the Greek text in volume I of the *Councils*, column 863.

**II.** Canons of the Council of Ancyra, of 12 bishops.

**III.** Canons of the Council of Neocaesarea, of 19 bishops.

**IV.** Canons of the Council of Gangra, of 14 [variant: 15] bishops.

**V.** Canons of the Council of Sardica.

**VI.** Canons of the Council of Antioch, of 31 bishops.

**VII.** Canons of Laodicea in Phrygia.

**VIII.** Canons of the Council of Constantinople, of 150 bishops.

**IX.** First Synod of Ephesus, of 200 bishops. In the body [Col. 0222A], under this title, two celebrated letters of Saint Cyril to Nestorius are presented. They were written before the Council of Ephesus but read and inserted there; one of them concludes with twelve anathemas.

The annotation of the Hispanic compiler prefixed to these letters is printed in P. Labbe’s *Observations*, volume III of the *Councils*, column 959. The first letter appears in column 960. Since it is a version separately published by Dionysius Exiguus, it is clear that the compiler took it from him.

The second letter—or rather, a fragment of a letter—begins with the words:

> “Thus the holy and great synod says: He who is naturally begotten from God the Father …”

It was taken from an older translation, from which Saint Leo appended a lengthy testimony beginning with the same words in Letter 165, volume I of our edition, column 1397, and in this volume, column 291.

This is the earliest collection in which these two letters of Cyril are inscribed under the name of the Council of Ephesus. Yet that usage is clearly older than the Hispanic Collection from manuscript 59 of the Veronese Chapter. This manuscript contains excerpts from older Hispanic copies, in which those letters were described among the councils of Greece under the same title of the Council of Ephesus. See what we shall note in Part IV, chapter 4.

**X.** The Council of Chalcedon, of 630 bishops. In the body, besides the canons, a version of Act 6 is added, from which the address of the emperor Marcian and the definition of faith are produced, as in volume IV of the *Councils*, column 2051. The subscriptions of the Fathers are also appended, together with three imperial laws:

1. To all peoples, beginning, “At long last,” and also found in the collection published in this volume, chapter 26.
2. To Palladius, prefect of the praetorium, beginning, “The divine power always …” See volume IV of the *Councils*, column 1811, note e.
3. To the same Palladius, beginning, “Although we have already issued the most sacred constitution …,” as in our collection, chapter 28.

**XI.** The formal letter of Atticus, bishop of Constantinople. It is the one that will be found in our collection, chapter 63. See note 1, column 451.

### COUNCILS OF AFRICA

**XII.** First Council of Carthage in Africa. It is the council held under Gratus, published in volume II of the *Councils*, column 745. See Part II, chapter 3, § 1, no. 7.

**XIII.** Second Council of Carthage in Africa. It is the council held under Genethlius, in the same volume II of the *Councils*, column 1389. See the same place, no. 8.

**XIV.** Third Council of Carthage in Africa, of 48 bishops. It is the council held under Aurelius in 397, in the same volume II, column 1397. See the same place, § 3, no. 1.

**XV.** Fourth Council of Carthage in Africa, of 210 bishops. The same volume II, column 1433 [CXCIX]. Under this title the ancient statutes are presented. Compare what we said in the same Part II, chapter 3, § 4.

**XVI.** Fifth Council of Carthage in Africa, of 33 bishops. Volume II of the *Councils*, column 1453. See Part II, chapter 3, § 5, no. 2.

**XVII.** Sixth Council of Carthage in Africa, of 217 bishops. Volume III of the *Councils*, column 441. Compare the same council in Part II, chapter 3, § 8, no. 4.

**XVIII.** Seventh Council of Carthage in Africa, of 19 bishops [Col. 0222D]. Volume III of the *Councils*, column 459. Consult the cited chapter 3, § 8, no. 7.

**XIX.** Council of Africa held in the city of Milevis, of 214 bishops. Volume III of the *Councils*, column 379. See Part II, chapter 3, § 6.

### COUNCILS OF GAUL

**XX.** First Council of Arles.

**XXI.** Second Council of Arles, of 113 bishops. Two points must be noted here:

1. After the table of chapters, a catalogue of bishops is described, and this belongs to the First Council of Arles. The number of 113 bishops also noted in the title must be referred to the same First Council of Arles, as we infer from the very ancient manuscript 54 of the Church of Novara, in which this title is prefixed to the First Council of Arles:

   > “The Council of Arles begins, held in the time of Marinus by 123 bishops, who also wrote to Pope Sylvester.”

2. Only twenty-five canons are presented, not thirty-seven, as in the commonly circulated Councils before Sirmondus, nor fifty-six, as Sirmondus published. See Part II, chapter 10, § 2, no. 19 [Col. 0223A].

**XXII.** Third Council of Arles, of 14 bishops.

**XXIII.** Council of Valence, of 20 bishops.

**XXIV.** Council of Turin.

**XXV.** Council of Riez, of 13 bishops.

**XXVI.** Council of Orange, of 16 bishops.

**XXVII.** Council of Vaison.

**XXVIII.** Council of Agde, of 25 bishops.

**XXIX.** Council of Orléans, of 20 bishops.

### COUNCILS OF SPAIN

**XXX.** Council of Elvira, of 18 bishops.

**XXXI.** Council of Tarragona, of 10 bishops.

**XXXII.** Council of Girona, of 7 bishops.

**XXXIII.** Council of Zaragoza, of 12 bishops.

**XXXIV.** Council of Lleida, of 9 bishops [Col. 0223B].

**XXXV.** Council of Valence, of 6 bishops.

**XXXVI.** First Synod of Toledo, of 18 bishops.

**XXXVII.** Second Synod of Toledo, of 9 bishops.

**XXXVIII.** Third Synod of Toledo, of 62 bishops.

**XXXIX.** Fourth Synod of Toledo, of 46 bishops.

**XL.** First Synod of Braga, of 9 [variant: 8] bishops.

**XLI.** Second Synod of Braga, of 12 bishops, in the Spanish Era 610.

**XLII.** Chapters from the synods of the Eastern Fathers, arranged and collected by Martin, bishop of Galicia.

**XLIII.** First Synod of Seville, of 8 bishops.

**XLIV.** Second Synod of Seville, of 8 bishops.

**XLV.** Judgments not found in the ancient copies of the councils but inserted by certain persons. These judgments are the twenty-three canons appended in the commonly circulated editions to the Council of Agde, from canon 48 through canon 70.

Here it must be observed that these judgments are omitted from the body of the Vindobonensis, Vatican 1341, and other similar codices, although they are noted under number 45 in the prefixed table of chapters [Col. 0223C]. Because of this omission, the chapters of this first part ought to number only forty-four. Since, however, the same judgments are appended in those manuscripts to canon 47 of Agde—perhaps so that they would not have to be repeated unnecessarily in chapter 44—they were omitted from the body of the collection.

But since, in the index of the table of the original collection, these judgments are attached to chapter 45 [CC], we have no doubt that they were described in this place in the original copies in the form in which we find them separately described in the manuscript of the more extensive Hispanic Collection belonging to Cardinal Passionei, and also in Vatican manuscript 4587 of Joannes Baptista Perezius. Perez notes that they are read at the end of all the councils in the Lucense codex. From other Hispanic codices Garsias Loaisa also printed them after the Seventeenth Council of Toledo; they were reprinted from his edition in volume VIII of the Venetian edition of the *Councils*, column 91. Compare what we shall say about the number of the canons of Agde in Part IV, chapter 4, no. 21.

After the table of the first part has been prefixed, the documents themselves are appended [Col. 0223D].

### 6.

Next the table of the second part is produced, with 102 chapters, and the following shorter preface is read in it:

> The councils of the holy Fathers having thus been arranged, the decrees of the Roman bishops will follow. The constitutions of the bishops of the aforesaid apostolic see that concern the rule of faith or ecclesiastical discipline have been collected in this book with diligent care, so that the decrees of each pontiff, insofar as we have found them, might be prefixed with their proper titles under the sequence of each pontiff’s letters, in the same manner in which the canons of the ancient Fathers were arranged above through our labor. Thus the diligence of the reader may more easily understand them as he attends to the chapters distinguished by their proper titles.

**LXXV.** To the bishops established throughout Campania, Samnium, and Picenum: Letter 168.

**LXXVI.** The synodal decree of Pope Hilary: Letter 1 in the edition of the *Councils*.

**[CCII] LXXVII.** The same pope’s letter mentioned above to Ascanios and to all the bishops of the province of Tarragona: Letter 2.

**LXXVIII.** The same pope’s letter mentioned above to the same Ascanios, bishop of Tarragona [Col. 0225D]: Letter 3.

**LXXIX.** Letter of Pope Simplicius to Zeno, bishop of Seville: Letter 1 in the *Councils*.

**LXXX.** Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, to the aforesaid Simplicius, bishop of the city of Rome: in the same place, after Letter 8 of Simplicius.

**LXXXI.** Letter of Pope Felix to the bishops throughout Sicily. It is Letter 7 of Felix III.

**LXXXII.** The same pope’s letter mentioned above to Acacius, bishop of Constantinople: Letter 6.

**LXXXIII.** To Zeno, bishop of Seville: Letter 8.

**LXXXIV.** The general decrees of Pope Gelasius: Letter 7 in the edition of the *Councils*.

**LXXXV.** To the Sicilian bishops: Letter 10.

**LXXXVI.** Letter of Pope Anastasius addressed to the emperor Anastasius. It is Letter 1 of Anastasius II.

**LXXXVII.** Letter of Pope Symmachus to Caesarius: Letter 5 in the edition of the *Councils* [Col. 0226A].

**LXXXVIII.** Letter of Pope Hormisdas to the emperor Justin: in the same place, Letter 79 of that pontiff.

**LXXXIX.** The imperial letter of Justin to Pope Hormisdas: in the same place, after Letter 40.

**XC.** Letter, or little book, of John, bishop of Constantinople, addressed to Pope Hormisdas: after the same Letter 40, volume V of the Venetian edition, column 621.

**XCI.** Pope Hormisdas to John, bishop of the Church of Ilici [variant: Milici]: Letter 24.

**XCII.** Another letter of Pope Hormisdas to the same bishop John: Letter 64.

**XCIII.** To the bishops established throughout Spain: Letter 25.

**XCIV.** Another letter of Pope Hormisdas to the same bishops of Spain, with copies of the little book of John, bishop of Constantinople, appended: Letter 51.

**XCV.** Another letter of Pope Hormisdas to Salustius, bishop of Seville: Letter 26.

**XCVI.** To Epiphanius, bishop of Constantinople: Letter 80.

**XCVII.** Another letter of Pope Hormisdas to all the bishops of the province of Baetica [Col. 0226B]: Letter 65.

**XCVIII.** Pope Vigilius to Bishop Profuturus: Letter 2 in the edition of the *Councils*.

**XCIX.** Letter of Pope Gregory to Leander, bishop of Seville: in the Maurist edition, book I of the *Register*, Letter 43.

**C.** The same pope’s letter mentioned above to the same Leander: book V, Letter 49.

**CI.** The same pope’s letter mentioned above to the aforesaid bishop: book IX, Letter 121.

**CII.** The same pope’s letter mentioned above to Reccared, king of the Goths: in the same place, Letter 122.

It must be noted that this table of chapters of the second part, in the manuscripts from which P. Coustantius published it, and likewise in another similar codex, Vatican 1341, suffers from two defects.

First, at number 17 it leaps over one of the same pontiff’s letters to the same bishop Aurelius after the two letters of Innocent to Aurelius. That letter is read in the body of those codices [Col. 0226C]. In the edition of the *Councils* it is Letter 12. The aforementioned P. Coustantius, in his account of Innocent’s letters, no. 41, column 932, lists it among those forged by Isidore the Merchant.

We are absolutely certain, however, that it is found in the genuine Hispanic Collection, which is earlier than Isidore and contains no spurious document. It exists not only in codices of Gallican origin belonging to this collection, which, as we shall note in no. 16, received a few spurious documents from Isidore, but also in copies of Hispanic origin that represent this collection without any Isidorian spurious addition. Such are the Vindobonensis manuscript and others used by Joannes Baptista Perezius. From these, indeed, he described it in the table of the same collection as number 17, as we learned from Vatican manuscript 4587.

This is especially confirmed by the ancient abbreviation of the Hispanic Collection published by Cardinal de Aguirre, which was excerpted from genuine copies of Hispanic origin. In it the same letter is cited in book I, title 34, in these words:

> “That no one may be made a bishop contrary to the order of the canons.”

It says “the sixteenth letter of Innocent in full,” but this must be corrected to “the seventeenth”; for the letter to Juliana, the noblewoman, which follows the letter to Aurelius in the same abbreviation, book X, title 6, is marked as number 18. This is precisely the title of Letter 12 to Aurelius.

Moreover, the same letter is similarly cited in another older abbreviation contained in manuscript 59 of the Veronese Chapter, which we shall see in Part IV, chapter 4, was excerpted from the older codices of the Hispanic Collection. For it reads there:

> “Also, Innocent’s letter to Bishop Aurelius: ‘Let not a hand be laid lightly [in ordination]. Let no one be ordained bishop from the laity.’”

These statements occur only in that Letter 12 to Aurelius.

Nor should the suspicion of forgery be aroused by the erroneous consular notation expressed in the commonly circulated copies as:

> “In the consulship of Julius the Fourth and Palladius, men of illustrious rank.”

It must instead be corrected to:

> “In the consulship of Junius the Fourth and Palladius, a man of illustrious rank,”

who was the Western consul of the year 416.

On the other hand [Col. 0227A], in his table P. Coustantius adds among Leo’s letters to Marcian one that is absent from the collection. For from numbers 58 through 61 he lists four letters of that pontiff to Marcian, whereas the body contains only three, and he omits one to Anatolius, which should be assigned number 58.

By correcting these errors in the table given above, we have restored the chapter numbers to the sequence of the letters that are actually read in the collection. These documents, then, neither more nor fewer, were described in the original collection.

## § 3. On the time, place, and author of this collection

### 7.

Since the Council of Toledo IV, celebrated in the year 633, is the latest document copied in the original Hispanic Collection, it is evident that this collection was arranged after that year.

Since, moreover, almost the whole preface of the first part is found in book VI of the *Origins* of Saint Isidore of Seville, chapter 16, it might be doubtful whether the author of the preface borrowed from Saint Isidore, or whether Saint Isidore instead made use of the preface, just as he habitually derived one thing and another from other authors while repeatedly suppressing their names.

The latter conclusion is strongly suggested by these words, found both in the preface and in Isidore’s excerpt:

> “The proceedings of these councils are also contained in this work.”

For, as P. Coustantius correctly observed after Antonius Augustinus, these words suit a preface prefixed to a collection of the proceedings of councils, but not the books of the *Origins*, which reproduce the proceedings of no synods. It must therefore be certain that Saint Isidore transferred that fragment of the preface into his books of the *Origins* and, while copying it, inadvertently included those words that ought to have been omitted in the work of the *Origins*.

This preface, then, together with the collection attached to it, was composed somewhat before Saint Isidore wrote the books of the *Origins*. Saint Braulio testifies in his prefatory notice to those same books that the books of the *Origins*, or *Etymologies*, were Saint Isidore’s final work, which he left unfinished when he died. Saint Isidore died in the year 636.

The date of the collection can therefore be clearly deduced: namely, between the year 633, in which the Fourth Council of Toledo was held, and the year 636.

8. It cannot be doubted that this collection, from whose preface St. Isidore, bishop of Seville, extracted the fragment mentioned above, was compiled in Spain. The older manuscripts of this collection, which come closer to its origin, are Spanish and written in the ancient Gothic script proper to the Spaniards. The distinctive Spanish notation of the Era, which is appended even in several non-Spanish documents after the consular datings, plainly declares its Spanish origin. What need is there to say about the Spanish synods with which this collection abounds? Or about the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs included in it, which were addressed to Spaniards? In this connection, the distinguished observation of P. Coustant in the preface to volume I of *Epistolae Romanorum pontificum*, no. 147, must not be omitted. [Col. 0227D] The fact that he omitted none of those ancient letters which we know to have been addressed to Spaniards proves, even if he himself were silent about it, that he was a Spaniard.

He was the first of all to publish Hilary’s letters to Ascanus of Tarragona; those of Simplicius and Felix to Zeno of Seville; two of Hormisdas to John of Elche; one of the same pope to Salustius of Seville and another to the bishops of Baetica; likewise two others to the bishops of Spain, sent together with John of Constantinople’s *libellus*; and finally Vigilius’s letter to Profuturus of Braga. Does he not also reveal himself as a Spaniard when, from Gregory’s letters—which we possess in almost [CCIV] countless numbers—he includes only four: three to Leander of Seville and one to the Gothic king Reccared, while leaving aside the others because they were not addressed to Spaniards? [Col. 0228A] Finally, the statement in the preface that the faith of the Constantinopolitan Creed was proclaimed by all Greece and Latinity in the churches [the printed word is *ECCLESUS*] plainly shows that the author of the preface and of the collection appended to it was a Spaniard. Seeing that what the Third Council of Toledo had ordered in its first canon to be done throughout all the churches of Spain was already received among them in his own time, he believed it to be equally customary among all the Latin churches. Certainly, since this practice was not admitted by the other Westerners until a later period, as P. Coustant proved in the same work, no one but a Spaniard could have inserted that statement into the preface. From this, the opinion of Peter de Marca collapses: in his *Opuscula*, p. 201, he had supposed that this collection was published after Chalcedon under Leo’s authority and was common to the Western churches.

9. We may now venture a conjecture concerning its Spanish author. Antonius Augustinus, in his judgment and critique of certain ancient collectors of ecclesiastical canons, testifies that some people in Spain attributed this book of canons to St. Isidore of Seville. Two matters, however, may cause difficulty here: first, that St. Braulio, in his prefatory notice to the books of the *Origins*, and St. Ildefonsus, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 9—both of whom compiled catalogues of St. Isidore’s works—make no mention of this collection [Col. 0228B]; second, that since a considerable part of the preface prefixed to this collection was transferred into the books of the *Origins*, it seems incredible that St. Isidore, who excerpted no small amount from other writers, should also have transcribed certain passages from his own preface.

Since, however, the more recent documents of this collection correspond especially well to St. Isidore’s lifetime—namely, the Second Council of Seville of 619 and the Fourth Council of Toledo of 633, over which he presided—it was not improperly long believed that its author was St. Isidore himself. This is also suggested by Gratian, who attributes a fragment of the preface, in the first part of the collection, specifically to Isidore (*Decretum*, distinction 16, chapter 1). Yet, even if it was not Isidore himself, at least someone appears to have arranged the collection at his command. For this reason it happened that Pseudo-Isidore, who incorporated this collection into his own, used the name of Isidore and prefixed to his own preface the title “of St. Isidore, bishop,” because tradition had reported that the collection had either been compiled by St. Isidore, bishop of Seville, or arranged under his direction.

[Col. 0228C] That there were older books of canons, and that they were read in the earlier Spanish councils, is clear from § 1, no. 1. Since some material was lacking in them, and perhaps what they contained was not entirely organized but confused, the idea occurred to St. Isidore of reviewing, enlarging, and reducing the ancient books to a better form. The Fourth Council of Toledo may perhaps have provided him with the occasion and impetus: in its fourth canon it prescribed the following general rule for the celebration of councils—that, while everyone sat silently in his proper place, a deacon dressed in a white garment, bringing the Book of Canons into the midst, should announce the chapters concerning the business of the councils.

§ 4. Concerning the additions that were subsequently made to the original Spanish collection. The documents appended in the enlarged Spanish collection to the Second Council of Constantinople, otherwise the Sixth Ecumenical Council, are vindicated.

10. [Col. 0228D] Having written these things concerning the original Spanish collection, we must now explain the additions that were subsequently inserted into it. The earlier additions are found in the very old Vindobonensis manuscript 41 and in other similar manuscripts. After the beginning of the First Council of Braga, which is marked as no. 40 in the preceding table, they insert, without any number and outside their proper place, nine Councils of Toledo—namely, the Fifth and the subsequent councils through the Thirteenth of 683. They then repeat the First Council of Braga and give it in full; after Martin of Braga’s chapters they add another Council of Braga, from the year 675; and they append the remaining material indicated in the aforementioned table of the primitive collection. Since manuscripts of this kind, which contain the Councils of Toledo collected with greater care, include the later Thirteenth Council of Toledo of 683 but lack the Fourteenth Council of Toledo, celebrated in the following year, 684, it seems established that these additions entered the earliest such example shortly after the Thirteenth Council of Toledo itself, before the Fourteenth had taken place.

[Col. 0229A] 11. The collection subsequently received new additions, which are found in the manuscripts consulted by Antonius Augustinus, in the Lucan exemplar praised by Perez, in the manuscript of the church of Urgell, and in several others. In these, however, all the councils of each city are described together in order, in a continuous series of numbers.

Among the Greek councils, after the First Council of Constantinople there is added the Second Council of Constantinople, dated to the Era 720, together with five letters relating to it: one of Leo II to the bishops of Spain; another of the same pope to Quiricus; a third of the same to the count Simplicius; a fourth of Benedict, the presbyter elected after Leo, to Peter, the regional notary; and a fifth of the aforementioned Leo II to King Ervig.

Among the Gallican councils, the Second Council of Vaison of 529 is appended to the First Council of Vaison; after the First Council of Orléans there is described another of 533; and five other Gallican documents are included: the Council of Epaon of 517, the Council of Carpentras of 527, the First Council of Clermont of 535, a letter of that same Council of Clermont to King Theudebert, and the Second Council of Clermont of 549. [Col. 0229B] Since this last has the same preface and the same canons as the Fifth Council of Orléans, Perez rightly observed that it should rather be called the Fifth Council of Orléans.

Among the Spanish councils, after the Fourth Council of Toledo there are placed, in order and with their own distinct numbers, thirteen other councils of the same city, from the Fifth through the Seventeenth, which was convened in 694. After the two Councils of Seville, the Council of Mérida of 666 is added. Nor are the *Sententiae* omitted, although they are absent from the older copies of the councils. Thus the chapters in this part amount to sixty-eight; for their sequence, see part IV, chapter 5, no. 3.

The Vatican Palatine manuscript 575 agrees with these manuscripts, although it is incomplete and its order is disturbed. So does the manuscript exemplar of Cardinal Passionei, though, since it is mutilated, it lacks the councils of Greece and Africa and, among the Gallican councils, breaks off after the two Councils of Vaison and the Council of Agde.

[Col. 0229C] These manuscripts also append to the Second Council of Toledo two letters of Montanus, bishop of Toledo: one to the brothers and sons of the territory of Palencia, and the other to Turibius. To the Third Council of Toledo they add a homily of St. Leander, bishop, delivered after the canons had been established on the conversion of the people, along with several other items. In the second part, after the letters of St. Gregory—which close the primitive collection—there are added, as no. 103, decrees of the Roman See concerning books to be received and not to be received, issued by Pope Hormisdas. One is a decree concerning apocryphal books, attributed to Gelasius in the printed editions of the Councils; concerning it, see part II, chapter 11, § 5.

12. [Col. 0229D] 12. This enlarged collection, whose latest document is the Seventeenth Council of Toledo of 694, was used by the author of the abridgment, or index, of the canons of the Spanish collection; we shall say more about him in part IV, chapter 5. For the numbers of the chapters under which the documents of that collection are cited there agree exactly with the numbers found in this enlarged collection.

This is the *Corpus of Canons* which Alexander III called authentic, as is clear from these words of Innocent III in letter 121 to Peter of Compostela, book II:

> “He proved by many arguments that the Council of Mérida was authentic: first, because it is contained together with other councils in the book called the *Corpus of Canons*, which Pope Alexander, by an interlocutory judgment, called authentic; and so forth.”

The Council of Mérida is described only in the enlarged collection mentioned above. All its documents are genuine, and the collection is free from every spurious addition.

Someone may raise a difficulty concerning the Second Council of Constantinople, which, as it is presented there, led some people—especially after the great Baronius—to suspect it, chiefly because of the letters appended to it. The Constantinopolitan council that is designated as the second in this collection is the Sixth Ecumenical Council, celebrated at Constantinople against the Monothelites. It is called the Second Council of Constantinople according to the order of the collection itself, in which it is placed immediately after the First Council of Constantinople; or perhaps because the Fifth Council was unknown to the Spaniards. For this reason, at the Fourteenth Council of Toledo [Col. 0230A], it was decreed that this Constantinopolitan council—the Sixth Ecumenical Council—should be received after Chalcedon and inserted into the book in its proper order.

Not all the acts of this council were sent to the Spaniards. Only the definition of faith, the acclamations of the bishops—also called the *prosphoneticus*—and the imperial edict of faith were transmitted. At the beginning, the complete acts were not translated and sent, but only the principal sections, as we have likewise seen in the case of Chalcedon, volume II, column 1218; Leo II states this in his letter to the Spanish bishops. In the council of Toledo just mentioned, those bishops declare that from this letter—not from a translation of the entire council—they learned the whole order of the proceedings and the proceedings of the individual sessions. Only the definition belonging to action 17 of the Sixth Ecumenical Council was inserted into the enlarged Book of Canons.

If this Constantinopolitan council, held in 680 and 681, is assigned in the same book the Era 720, corresponding to the year 682, this must be attributed to an error of the compiler, who, from the transmitted definition of that council, which lacked chronological indications, was entirely unable to determine the true [Col. 0230B] year.

It is objected that Leo II’s letters state that the council was celebrated in the ninth indiction, although the acts of the latest sessions, 17 and 18, bear the tenth indiction. Yet, although among the Greeks the tenth indiction began in September of the year 681, Leo chose to use the ninth indiction, which was still running among the Romans.

Nor should one be troubled by the fact that, in the letter of the same pontiff to King Ervig—appended in the manuscripts to Benedict’s letter, though Loaisa wrongly believed, contrary to the evidence of our manuscripts, that it should be attributed to Benedict—it is written that the emperor had sent letters concerning the convening of a council to Agatho, although he had sent them to Domnus. Since the same letters, written to Domnus, were brought to Rome after his death and delivered to Agatho, his successor, Leo could describe them as directed to Agatho.

[Col. 0230C] Therefore, nothing serious stands in the way of believing these documents—addressed to the Spaniards in the seventh century and added by Spaniards to this most ancient Spanish collection toward the end of that century or at the beginning of the eighth—to be genuine. Thus Alexander III was right to affirm that this body of canons, enlarged by these and other additions, was authentic.

13. The manuscript of St. Aemilianus, mentioned by Perez, supplied several distinctive documents concerning the Spanish councils: namely, the Second Council of Zaragoza of 592 and the Third of 691; two Councils of Barcelona, one around the year 540 and the other of 599; the Council of Huesca of 598; the Council of Égara of 614; two Councils of Toledo distinct from the seventeen already mentioned, one held in the twelfth year of King Reccared, that is, in 597, and the other under Gundemar in 610; and the law of King Chintila, which confirmed the Fifth Council of Toledo. It also supplied the Council of Narbonne of 589, which was inserted among the Spanish councils because at that time the province of Narbonne was subject to the Gothic princes ruling in Spain and was one of the six provinces of Spain; moreover, the metropolitan of Narbonne attended and subscribed the Spanish councils together with his suffragans.

[Col. 0230D] Stephen Baluzius writes in the preface to his new collection of councils, no. 13:
