> “Joannes Baptista Perez raises suspicion concerning the falsity of two Councils of Toledo: namely, that which is said to have been celebrated under King Gundemar, and the other under Reccared, as is clear from his second preface to the councils sent to Rome.”

But Perez’s words raise no suspicion of falsity. He merely expresses his surprise that these councils were not recorded with the others under their proper number and place, and he endeavors to conjecture why this happened. “What is more doubtful to me,” he says in the aforementioned second preface, published in the *Apparatus I* to the Venetian edition of the Councils, column 50, “is why this council under Gundemar, and the other Council of Toledo in the twelfth year of Reccared, also described here by us, were not included in the number of the Councils of Toledo, since in chronological order they ought to have been designated the Fourth and Fifth; that number is regularly assigned to the councils that follow.”

[Col. 0231A] Nor can anyone claim that the numbering was added to the Councils of Toledo in our own time, since we learn from chapter 9 of the Thirteenth Council of Toledo that the Goths used the same numbering: the council that for us is the Twelfth is plainly also called the Twelfth there. Nor, again, is it plausible that these two councils were unknown to later Goths while their memory was still so recent. Thus the reason remains unclear to me, unless perhaps the brevity and insignificance of these two councils prevented their being included in the number of the greater councils.

The authenticity of the documents in the aforementioned manuscript of St. Aemilianus is further supported by another, much older collection—or rather an older abridgment of the earlier collection—contained in the Veronese manuscript. We shall discuss it in part IV, chapter 4. Four of the councils mentioned are recorded there: the Second Council of Zaragoza, the First Council of Barcelona, the Council of Huesca, and the Council of Narbonne.

Likewise, the Second Council of Zaragoza was found in another manuscript, the Alveldensis, written by the presbyter Vigila. The Council of Toledo under King Gundemar was also found both in that same Alveldensis manuscript and in another from Soria, as Perez testifies in his second preface.

[Col. 0231B] Finally, in the same example of St. Aemilianus there are found a letter of Turibius, later bishop of Astorga, to Idacius and Ceponius; the renunciation of the Priscillianist heresy made by the bishops Dictinius and Symphosius; and the judgment of the First Council of Toledo concerning whether communion should be restored to or withheld from certain bishops. These documents, which Ambrosius Morales had published from the same manuscript of St. Aemilianus and which Baluzius and others called into question, we defended in volume I, column 1475, and more fully in volume II, column 1376 and following.

§ 5. A notable distinction between manuscripts of Spanish origin and those of Gallican origin

13. It is very important to distinguish two classes of manuscripts of this collection: some are of Spanish origin, others of Gallican origin. We call those manuscripts of Spanish origin which are more common in Spain, or which were carried from Spain into other regions, and which represent the pure Spanish collection.

[Col. 0231C] There are certain other manuscripts which, although they contain the same collection, differ considerably from the form presented by the pure manuscripts. They differ both because of numerous readings corrected according to individual judgment, which depart very far from the true reading, and because of certain added chapters or even complete documents that are not found in the pure copies of the collection.

We call these manuscripts of Gallican origin because all those we have found to belong to this class are more common in Gaul, while those existing elsewhere came from Gaul. Their origin therefore appears to be assignable to Gaul. Such are Vatican manuscript 1341, which we have seen belonged to the Church of Autun, and the three Gallican manuscripts mentioned by P. Coustant—Laon, Beauvais, and Noyon—which, from what Coustant himself noted, we have clearly seen to agree entirely with the aforementioned Vatican manuscript.

These manuscripts contain neither the original shorter collection nor the enlarged Spanish collection that we explained in no. 11. Rather, they contain the collection bearing the additions listed in no. 10, as we find it in the Vindobonensis manuscript of Spanish origin.

[Col. 0231D] 14. As for the arbitrary corrections by which the manuscripts of Gallican origin differ chiefly from those of Spanish origin, when preparing our edition of the letters of St. Leo we took care to compare both the Vindobonensis manuscript of Spanish origin and Vatican 1341 of Gallican origin. We discovered in the Vindobonensis several erroneous and corrupt readings that were corrected in the aforementioned Vatican manuscript and yielded a suitable sense.

Had nothing else been available to us, we would have believed these corrected readings to be the genuine readings of St. Leo. But when other copies of the same letters from different and even older collections became available to us, and we learned that they had preserved the true Leonine readings consistently [Col. 0232A], we found that the erroneous readings of the Vindobonensis manuscript of Spanish origin more frequently approached those true readings, while the corrections presented in the Vatican copy departed from them considerably.

It therefore becomes clear that some ancient Gallican scholar, who had undertaken to copy the Spanish collection from a Spanish manuscript as defective as the Vindobonensis, corrected those erroneous readings with excessive freedom and according to his own judgment, introducing new readings that differ from all the other manuscripts.

We could cite many more such examples from the letters of Leo. But since we have noted them in their proper places in volume I, and they are also listed in that volume’s index under the word “Spanish Collection,” we refer readers there.

There is no doubt that, just as that scholar acted in Leo’s letters, so he also acted in the other documents found in the manuscripts of Spanish origin, which commonly exhibit numerous errors. This is clear from the edition of the Councils by Severinus Binius, in which the Spanish councils are presented in two editions: one from the previously published edition, and the other from the edition of García Loaysa.

[Col. 0232B] The published edition derives from Isidore, who transferred the Spanish collection into his own work from manuscripts of Gallican origin. Loaysa’s edition, however, was established against manuscripts of Spanish origin. The remarkable variety of readings visible in that published edition must be attributed to arbitrary corrections by its old copyist, who, while transcribing a defective Spanish exemplar, believed he should correct it on his own authority.

Loaysa, on the other hand, happened to find purer and more accurate Spanish copies, and his edition is therefore free from the errors found in the Vindobonensis and similar manuscripts.

The exemplar used by that first Gallican copyist who corrected the Spanish collection was either the Vindobonensis itself [Col. 0232C] [Note: [Col. 0231D] Hence, just as in the Vindobonensis, so also in the aforementioned manuscripts of Gallican origin, when the First Council of Braga has scarcely begun and is immediately interrupted, nine [Col. 0232D] Councils of Toledo, from the Fifth through the Thirteenth, are attached; then the First Council of Braga is appended again, but in full] or another manuscript similar to the Vindobonensis, whose frequent errors provided the occasion for so many arbitrary corrections.

Two facts indicate to us that these freer corrections were introduced by the scholar into some manuscript before the publication of Isidore’s collection: first, that we find them already received in the Herovallian collection, which we shall show in part IV, chapter 7, to be earlier than the Isidorian collection; second, that when Isidore transferred the Spanish collection into his own, he copied its documents with the same corrections.

15. In this connection, it is worth observing that Isidore Mercator is accused of corrupting the heading of Pope Vigilius’s letter to Profuturus. In his work and in the aforementioned Gallican examples of the Spanish collection, the letter is addressed to Eutherius, although in the preceding table of those same manuscripts it is said to have been addressed to Profuturus.

In fact, the reading “to Eutherius” was introduced by that earlier copyist who corrected the erroneous readings of the Spanish manuscript. In the Vindobonensis, this defective title is found in the body of the text as follows: “Letter of Pope Vigilius to Futurus, bishop”; and in the heading: “To his most beloved brother Futurus, Vigilius.”

It was easy to read *Euturo* for *Futuro* [Col. 0232D], a name that seemed unfamiliar, and then to correct it to *Eutherio*. Thus Isidore, when he copied a manuscript of Gallican origin, did not change the name of Profuturus; rather, he transferred into his own collection the reading that he found corrected in that manuscript.

16. After Isidore, further hands were again applied to the same Spanish collection of Gallican origin. For, in addition to the readings arbitrarily corrected—which we have seen preceded the Isidorian collection—the aforementioned manuscripts received certain additions, partly genuine and partly apocryphal, which can be recognized as having been taken from Isidore’s collection.

First, before the preface there are placed not only notes concerning councils, a booklet concerning the provinces, and a description of Gaul, all of which likewise precede the work in Isidore; but there is also transcribed an [Col. 0233A] *Order for Celebrating a Council*, which Isidore testifies in his preface to have inserted into his own manuscript.

Then, after the table of the first part, the Apostolic Canons were intruded. The author of the Spanish collection rejected these as apocryphal in his preface. In Vatican manuscript 1341 these same canons are listed at the beginning of the preceding table, but without a number—for the numbering of the chapters begins with the Nicene canons. This confirms that these canons were added to these manuscripts.

They appear to have been added from the manuscripts of Isidore Mercator, who was the first to join these canons with the other documents of the Spanish collection.

In the second part, which begins with two letters of Damasus, three letters drawn from the spurious wares of Isidore Mercator are intermingled with another letter of that pontiff: one from Stephen, archbishop, and three councils to Pope Damasus; another from Damasus to the same Stephen and to the councils of Africa; and a third from the same pope to the bishops of Numidia. These letters are so intermingled with the genuine letters of Damasus [Col. 0233B], divided into sections, that we shall discuss them more distinctly in the Isidorian collection, chapter 6, § 5.

It is remarkable that the person who added these three spurious letters to the letters of Damasus abstained from several others that were available from the same source of Isidore under the following pontiffs. Only in the letters of Vigilius to Profuturus did he append from Isidore two chapters, the sixth and seventh, which are absent from the pure Spanish manuscripts.

Finally, from the genuine documents he appended one at the end, contrary to the evidence of the table and of all the manuscripts of Spanish origin: namely, the decree—or Roman council—of Gregory the Younger, with seventeen anathemas and the subscriptions of the bishops, which appears to have been taken from Isidore himself.

With the exception of these few additions, partly spurious and partly genuine, the aforementioned manuscripts of Gallican origin present, in the rest of their contents, that enlarged form of the Spanish collection which receives into the primitive collection the nine Councils of Toledo and the Council of Braga of 575 added in the Vindobonensis manuscript of Spanish origin.

[CCIX] Hence the copyist of the first exemplar [Col. 0233C] from which the four aforementioned manuscripts of Gallican origin—Vatican 1341, Laon, Beauvais, and Noyon—derive had two exemplars before him: one was a more freely corrected Spanish collection, from which he copied the same collection with its corrections; the other was Isidore’s collection, from which he extracted those additions.

If, of the three letters of St. Gregory the Great to Leander that are listed in the preceding table, the aforementioned manuscripts of Gallican origin present only two—for they lack the second—this must be attributed either to an omission by the first copyist from whom such manuscripts derive, or at least to the fact that that copyist used a Spanish manuscript in which a similar scribal omission had occurred.

This defect of the manuscripts of Gallican origin must be kept in mind because of what we shall say about Isidore in chapter 6.

17. We believe that one point should be noted here. [Col. 0233D] If all the manuscripts of Gallican origin belonging to the Spanish collection were of the same character as Vatican 1341 and the other three listed and cited by P. Coustant—so that, besides the freer corrections, they all also exhibited the additions extracted from Isidore, and not a single one could be found free from those additions and distinguished only by the freer corrections, a matter that we leave to those who are able to discover and compare more examples of this kind in Gaul—then a strong suspicion would arise that Isidore Mercator himself, whom we shall show to have been a Gallican, was perhaps the author of these manuscripts of Gallican origin.

That is, while copying a manuscript of Spanish origin, he corrected it according to his own judgment and at the same time enlarged it with the additions mentioned above, both genuine and spurious, before arranging his own collection, filled with many fabrications, into which he inserted the Spanish collection after he had already corrected it himself.

Nevertheless, this matter must be considered cautiously, especially if certain collections earlier than the Isidorian collection, such as the Herovallian, received some arbitrary corrections from Spanish manuscripts of Gallican origin [Col. 0234A] but none of the additions just mentioned.

§ 6. Concerning those who published or corrected documents from manuscripts of the Spanish collection, and especially concerning Joannes Baptista Perez

18. The first edition of the documents of the Spanish collection is Merlini’s. Since it derives from a manuscript of Isidore, it presents the same documents received by Isidore, with the readings of the manuscripts of Gallican origin that Isidore used. The readings of this edition, which were repeated in the printed editions of the Councils, must therefore be regarded with suspicion, since they contain the freer corrections indicated in no. 14.

To distinguish and restore the genuine readings of the Spanish collection, it would be necessary to compare manuscripts that preserve Spanish origin. The first person to render very useful service in this matter was Joannes Baptista Perez.

[Col. 0234B] When Gregory XIII was seeking everywhere old copies of the canons and decretals to be transcribed or compared for the edition and correction of Gratian’s books, and learned that excellent manuscripts of this kind were found in Spain, he entrusted the task to Gaspar Quiroga, then bishop of Cuenca, later archbishop of Toledo and cardinal. Quiroga was to arrange for these manuscripts to be compared with the printed editions, especially as regards the Spanish councils, and for unpublished material to be transcribed from them.

He entrusted this responsibility to his very learned associate, Joannes Baptista Perez, who later became a canon and head of the library of the Church of Toledo, and afterward bishop of Segorbe. Because of the pressure of time, Perez used one manuscript from Lugo, which seemed to be the oldest and richest of all, and occasionally two others. In the councils mentioned above he corrected five hundred notable passages, transcribed six unpublished synods, and likewise many fragments from other sources. He also transcribed the abridgment, or index, of the canons of the Spanish collection, which we shall discuss in part IV, chapter 5.

All this was written and sent to the pontiff in 1575 [CCX] in a book preserved among the Vatican manuscripts as no. 4887. From this manuscript of Quiroga we shall append at the end of this chapter his letter to Gregory XIII, Perez’s preface, and another special note by Perez himself, which will be useful for several matters.

Since this first work pleased the Roman bishop, and Perez was most generously rewarded for this outstanding labor and encouraged to undertake the other tasks he had promised, in the following year, 1576, he transcribed other Spanish synods that had not yet been printed, chiefly from the manuscript of St. Aemilianus. He also prepared with the greatest accuracy a chronology of the councils of Spain, later printed by Cardinal de Aguirre in volume I of the *Councils of Spain*, p. 13, in another book. From this book there will be found both another letter of Quiroga to the pontiff and Perez’s preface to the reader, published after Stephen Baluzius’s preface to the new edition of the Councils, and subsequently in the *Apparatus I* to the Councils in the Venetian edition of Labbe, columns 48 and 49.

Perez had also sent a copy of one of these two books to Antonius Augustinus, then bishop of Lleida and archbishop-elect of Tarragona [Col. 0234D], as we learn from two letters of that same Augustinus to Perez, published by Cardinal de Aguirre in volume IV of the *Councils of Spain*, pages 650 and 651 of the Roman edition of 1692.

These books later passed into the library of the distinguished Gaspar Mendoza Ibáñez, Marquis of Mondéjar and Count of Tendilla, who subsequently communicated them to Stephen Baluzius and then gave them as a gift to the aforementioned Cardinal de Aguirre.

19. The Roman correctors of Gratian made use of these distinguished labors of Perez when they corrected several passages on the authority of the Lucan manuscript. Cardinal Baronius, and Binius after him, published the Council of Narbonne of 589 as it had been transcribed from the manuscript of St. Aemilianus in Perez’s second volume.

In 1593 García Loaysa, of the Order of Preachers, at that time tutor to Philip III, king of Spain, and later archbishop of Toledo, used in his edition of the Spanish Councils almost the same manuscripts that Perez had used.

[Col. 0235A] Some suspect that Loaysa profited from Perez’s books. But several indications plainly show us that he had not seen these books. If he had examined them, he would not have asserted in his preface that the Lucan manuscript had been transcribed and sent to Rome, since Perez sent to Rome in his books not the entire manuscript but only its variant readings and the unpublished material from the Councils of Spain.

Moreover, of the four principal manuscripts cited by Perez, Loaysa recognized only three. Among these he calls one “the Sevillian,” whereas he would more correctly have called it “that of St. Aemilianus” had he read Perez.

We omit other observations, since these two points sufficiently clear Loaysa of the charge of plagiarism. If his edition agrees with Perez’s books in many respects, this is not surprising, since both used the same Spanish manuscripts.

[Col. 0235B] Accordingly, only the Spanish councils can be said to have been corrected or published against manuscripts of Spanish origin. The remaining councils—those of Greece, Africa, and Gaul—were published from Isidore, or from manuscripts of Gallican origin, and lack the readings of manuscripts of Spanish origin. In addition, most of the decretal letters of the pontiffs contained in the second part of the Spanish collection still await the same assistance.

We applied this diligence to the letters of Leo. Others have published genuine readings both in the remaining councils and in the letters of the pontiffs from other collections and manuscripts of the highest quality. But what readings belong to the manuscripts of Spanish origin, by which the authentic text of this collection may be established, remains in large part still to be determined.

20. We must now append from Vatican manuscript 4887 the material that we received earlier.

### Letter of Gaspar Quiroga, bishop of Cuenca, to Gregory XIII

> “To our most holy lord, Gregory XIII, supreme pontiff: Gaspar Quiroga, bishop of Cuenca, after the humblest kisses of the feet, presents his dutiful greetings.”

“Although the Catholic Church daily receives many benefits from the solicitude of Your Holiness [Col. 0235C], benefits that will consecrate the name of Your Beatitude to immortality, I believe that nothing will be more illustrious in the eyes of all posterity than your undertaking to cleanse the sources of canon law—that is, Gratian’s collection and the letters of the Roman pontiffs. Since nearly the entire discipline of ecclesiastical government rests upon the authority of these books; since no books are more constantly in everyone’s hands or more frequently cited in the schools; we heard, not without great embarrassment on our part, that they were filled with innumerable errors, contracted either through the defects of an unlearned age or through the negligence of printers. How earnestly Your Holiness is arranging for the correction of these books is sufficiently demonstrated by the fact that you have established at Rome a congregation of the most learned men for this very purpose, and that you are seeking out ancient copies everywhere, or ordering copies made from them to be brought to you. When Your Holiness learned that several ancient codices of the councils were preserved in the library of Saint Lawrence, which King Philip [Col. 0235D] the Catholic is furnishing day by day with books of every kind with no less zeal than that Ptolemy Philadelphus, you immediately instructed me, by an apostolic brief sent concerning the matter, to arrange for a certain book of canons to be transcribed from those codices, to compare the councils with the printed editions, and to send them to Your Beatitude. I immediately began to carry this out, in accordance with my devotion to Your Holiness and to the Apostolic See, and now, with God’s help, have brought it to completion. Because of my very substantial obligations, I made considerable use of the work of my household assistant, Juan Bautista Pérez, a learned young man highly practiced in this branch of scholarship. He has, if I am not mistaken, displayed outstanding fidelity and diligence in this work. I now humbly ask Your Holiness kindly to accept this evidence of my devotion and my greatest eagerness to serve you, and to command me frequently, as is your right, to undertake whatever you see that I am able to perform. May God Almighty preserve Your Beatitude, safe and sound, for his Church for as long as possible.

“Madrid, 18 March 1575.”

## Preface of Juan Bautista Pérez to Volume I of the Collations that he sent to Rome, transcribed in the aforementioned Vatican manuscript 4887

“**The Transcriber of These Collations to the Reader**

“My most reverend lord, Gaspar Quiroga, bishop of Cuenca and general inquisitor throughout Spain, having been ordered by our Most Holy Lord Gregory XIII to arrange for collations of the Spanish councils, selected me from among his other servants to entrust this work to me. Although I know that I have not fulfilled this duty adequately for its importance, nevertheless, whoever you may be who reads this, you will not entirely disapprove of my fidelity and diligence in it. So that you may understand what is contained in this volume and what work I have performed, it is necessary for me to offer a brief preface here. I shall not now labor to explain how much usefulness ancient manuscript codices bring to the preservation of the pure sources of all disciplines [Col. 0236B], since so many books of correction published by the learned men of our age have demonstrated this with great benefit to scholarship. Nor will anyone deny the immense usefulness of such labor unless he is either so blind that he does not see that every later copy, often transcribed from a single exemplar, continually deteriorates, or so senseless that he loves light no more than darkness and thinks it makes no difference whether something is affirmed or denied. If this diligence is praised in restoring Cicero, Galen, or Aristotle, it will be all the more praiseworthy when applied to ecclesiastical books and to the canonical decrees of councils and Roman pontiffs, whose authority is second only to that of the books of Sacred Scripture. There are many extremely ancient codices of the councils throughout Spain, all written in Gothic letters, which could provide especially great assistance in correcting these councils. [Col. 0236C] For, besides the four ancient codices preserved in the royal library of Saint Lawrence, built through the zeal of the Catholic King Philip (I shall speak of these before the Council of Eliberitanum), and two in the Church of Toledo, many others still exist in ancient churches, such as those of Oviedo and Urgell, and in the monasteries of Saint Facundus, Saint Zoilus, Saint Peter of Montes, Oña, and perhaps others of which I am not yet aware. If someone were to consult all these codices, it is astonishing how much light would be brought to the councils. In these collations of the councils I used almost exclusively a single codex from Lugo, both because the urgency of the work demanded haste [CCXII] and because this codex appeared to my lord bishop to be the oldest and fullest. I did occasionally use two others, but only in a few places, as I testify in the corrections themselves. If from a single book I corrected five hundred notable passages in the Spanish councils, what might one expect would have happened if I had used the remaining codices, and had collated not only the Spanish councils but also the Greek, African, and Gallic ones? [Col. 0236D] Moreover, if from this codex I added six councils that had not yet been printed—namely, the five later Councils of Toledo and one of Mérida—as well as many fragments elsewhere, how great would the addition have been if I had added from the codex of Saint Aemilianus the material it contains: three Councils of Toledo, one under Gundemar, another in the twelfth year of Reccared, and another in the first year of Chintila; as well as the Second and Third Councils of Zaragoza, two of Barcelona, and those of Huesca and Egara, all Spanish councils? I pass over those that are later than the destruction of Spain, though still ancient—the Councils of Compostela, León, Valladolid, Coyanza, and many similar ones that we possess. But since all these matters are reserved for another time and volume, let us now deal with this volume of ours, which is at hand and in which the following materials have been transcribed by us.

“First of all, we transcribed from the codex of Lugo the book entitled *Excerpta canonum* (for this title appeared at the head of every page), although the same work is also found in other ancient codices of the councils [Col. 0237A], such as those of Vigila and Oviedo. It is a certain collection, or index, of all the canons contained in councils or in the letters of the Roman pontiffs up to that time. It is arranged not in alphabetical order but by commonplaces, with the subjects distributed according to their kinds; and, so far as I know, nothing has yet been established concerning its author. It is certainly older than Burchard, Ivo, and Gratian, who arranged canon law by commonplaces. That it is not the work of Isidore is also shown by the fact that it repeatedly cites the Councils of Toledo down to the Twelfth, although it is established that Isidore died before the Sixth Council of Toledo. But, if it is permissible for me to speak conjecturally, I think it should rather be attributed to Julian, archbishop of Toledo, who flourished in those times and presided over four Councils of Toledo with great renown for his learning. This is indicated by the three works of his already committed to print—namely, *Prognostica*, *Against the Jews*, and *Antikimena*—besides others enumerated by his successor Felix [Col. 0237B]. Felix also reports that Julian amused himself with writing verse, so that one may even suspect that the poems placed before some books of this work were composed by him. As for the fact that these poems are empty and composed only of bombast, that defect may reasonably be excused in that unlearned age.

“In that book the reader should be warned that whenever it says ‘from chapter XX’ or ‘XXX,’ this means that the council, part of which is then being cited, is the twentieth or thirtieth council from the beginning, in the order of those contained in the codex of Lugo. The same applies to the letters of the pontiffs, which it likewise enumerates in order. You will understand this from the index of the councils and pontifical letters, which we shall place before the work itself.

“The Spanish councils follow, which we collated from the codex of Lugo with the printed edition of 1567. In these, for the sake of brevity, we used certain abbreviations, such as L., H., A., and AE., about which we shall speak shortly before the Council of Eliberitanum. Although we noted all the passages in which the printed editions differed from the manuscripts [Col. 0237C], we marked in the margin with an asterisk only those that we judged plainly and altogether in need of correction in the printed editions, so that a reader in haste might, if he wished, pass over the rest. No one should be surprised that we transcribed not only passages better preserved in the manuscripts but also those that we saw to be plainly corrupted in them. For who would deny that manuscripts too are erroneous in many places, and that the true reading must be recovered by collating many of them with one another? Nevertheless, we preferred to apply the greatest possible fidelity in this matter and to err on the safer side. Taught by experience, we hope that there will be no shortage of those who, by searching carefully, may discover traces of some true reading even in corrupted writing.

“Thus, in the other Councils of Toledo and in the Council of Mérida, which we have transcribed here in full, we often left corrupted writing in the text itself, as it stood in the codex, applying only the labor of correct punctuation, of which there was none at all in the codex; and we added our conjectures in the margin. In many of the most hopeless passages [CCXIII], perhaps, we have provided a remedy [Col. 0237D]. It remains only to say that, if we have erred anywhere in setting forth our judgment, we submit the whole matter to the correction of the Catholic Roman Church, which we do with the most obedient spirit.”

## A note by the same Pérez before the variants of the Council of Eliberitanum, where he discusses the four principal codices of the Spanish collection

“Among several excellent notes that Pérez wrote in the aforementioned Vatican codex, we append here especially the one in which he promised in the preceding preface to explain the sigla L., H., A., and AE. Since the siglum L. indicates the codex of Lugo, H. that of Seville, A. that of Albelda, and AE. the exemplar of Saint Aemilianus, he says the following about each:

[Col. 0238A] “These four codices are manuscript parchment books written in Gothic letters, and they are preserved in the royal monastery of Saint Lawrence near the Escorial, recently built by Philip II, the Catholic king of Spain.

“The codex of Lugo was brought from the Church of Lugo. It does not state the year in which it was written, but it is certainly six or seven hundred years old. Besides the councils already printed, it contains the following councils that have not yet appeared: the Council of Mérida and five Councils of Toledo [Note: [Col. 0237] The Thirteenth Council of Toledo, in Merlini’s edition, was so mutilated in Pérez’s time that it could be considered not yet published], from the Thirteenth through the Seventeenth.

“The codex of Seville began to be called by our people by that name because it is conjectured to have been written at Seville. It belonged to Martín de Ayala, archbishop of Valencia, and was written in the era 949, as it says in the codex—that is, in the year of Christ 911. It contains the councils commonly found also in the older printed editions, according to that division found in all the manuscripts, apparently first employed by Isidore [he means Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville]: namely, into Eastern, African, Gallic, and Spanish councils. In this [Col. 0238B] codex, however, the only council that is not extant is the Thirteenth Council of Toledo.

“The Albelda codex was written by the priest Vigila in the monastery of Saint Martin of Albelda in the era 1014, as it says in the codex—that is, in the year of Christ 976. Besides the printed councils, it contains the Fifteenth and Sixteenth Councils of Toledo and the Second Council of Zaragoza.

“The codex of Saint Aemilianus was brought from the monastery of Saint Aemilianus of La Cogolla near Nájera and was written in the year of the Lord 962, as it says there. It is by far the fullest of all. For besides the common material, it contains the following councils not yet printed: the Second and Third Councils of Zaragoza, two Councils of Barcelona, and those of Huesca and Egara; a Council of Toledo under Gundemar; another Council of Toledo in the twelfth year of Reccared; and yet another Council of Toledo in the first year of Chintila.”

Other materials read in this same manuscript, not yet printed and relating to the case of the Priscillianists, are indicated not only in another note, from which we gave an excerpt in volume II, col. 1376, but [Col. 0238C] are also transcribed in that same volume.

## CHAPTER V. On the Hadrianic-Spanish Collection Preserved in Vatican Manuscript 1338

1. Since the author of the ancient collection published by Luc d’Achery, and Rabanus Maurus—of whom there will be discussion in Part IV—cite the canons of the Greek synods, the African canons, and the Apostolic Constitutions with the same titles and numbers as those of the Hadrianic collection; and since, moreover, they cite among the canons of the councils a considerable number of African, Gallic, and Spanish canons that are contained not in the Hadrianic collection but in the Spanish collection, it is clear either that they used both of those collections or, at least, another collection that included the canons of the Spanish collection mentioned above in addition to those of the Hadrianic collection. The latter view seems more probable to us. For if they had used a complete and separate Spanish collection, they would have cited not only the canons of the councils found in it but also, at least occasionally, its decretal letters, which are absent from the Hadrianic collection. Lest this seem like a dream, we have obtained Vatican manuscript 1338, in which such a Hadrianic-Spanish collection is displayed.

2. It is a parchment folio codex, written in the eleventh or twelfth century, whose individual pages are laid out in two columns. A table of contents precedes the first part, which concerns the canons of the councils. The fourfold division of the councils is taken from the Spanish collection. First, the chapters of the councils of Greece are listed; then those of Africa; afterward those of Gaul; and finally those of Spain. The following note follows the table:

“This codex was written from that authentic exemplar which the lord Hadrian the apostolic gave to the most glorious Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans.”

[Col. 0239A] In the first series, which concerns the councils of Greece, there are presented not only the canons of the Greek synods in the Dionysian translation but also the Latin African canons that Dionysius transmitted, so that this first series contains the whole first part of the Hadrianic collection, with a few insertions, chiefly from the Spanish collection, as will become clear from the order that follows. This first series is divided into twelve chapters.

I. Fifty Apostolic Canons.

II. Twenty Nicene Canons, preceded by a chronological notice and the creed, and followed by a catalogue of the bishops, as we saw in the Hadrianic collection. What is peculiar, however, is that after the Nicene Creed and before the canons, without any title, the following is added: “After the Council of Nicaea, a council was assembled in the city of Rome by Catholic bishops, and they added concerning the Holy Spirit, etc.” We likewise saw this inserted in another Hadrianic collection, Vatican manuscript 1337, chapter 2, no. 6.

III. Twenty-four Canons of Ancyra.

IV. Under the name of the Council of Ephesus, two letters of Saint Cyril to Nestorius inserted from the Spanish collection. [Col. 0239B]

V. Fourteen Canons of Neocaesarea.

VI. Twenty Canons of Gangra, together with the letter to the bishops of Armenia and the catalogue of bishops, as in the Hadrianic collection.

VII. Twenty-five Canons of Antioch, with the names of the bishops transcribed from the Hadrianic collection.

VIII. Fifty-nine Canons of Laodicea.

IX. Three Canons of Constantinople, with the creed and subscriptions.

X. Twenty-seven Canons of Chalcedon, with the definition of faith and the catalogue of bishops.

XI. Twenty-one Canons of Sardica, with the same clause that we noted in the Hadrianic manuscripts.

XII. Finally, the Carthaginian canons, divided into two parts—a feature we observed to be peculiar to the Hadrianic collection. First, thirty-three canons are presented, preceded by the Dionysian material likewise received in the Hadrianic collection; after the thirty-third and final canon, the subscriptions follow. [Col. 0239C] Then, from the Spanish collection, the *Formata of Atticus of Constantinople* is inserted. Afterward, the remaining 105 canons from various councils of Africa are added, and these conclude the first part of the Hadrianic collection.

3. The materials presented under the headings of the councils of Africa, Gaul, and Spain were entirely excerpted from that Spanish collection which included the Councils of Toledo through the Thirteenth and the Council of Braga of the year 675. Although the African canons had already been transcribed above under the heading of the councils of Greece from the Hadrianic collection, because in the Spanish collection they are presented with a different division and numbering, they are here likewise displayed under the heading of the councils of Africa from that same Spanish collection. See what we noted in the preceding chapter, no. 10; from this you will learn the sequence of all the synods of Africa, Gaul, and Spain received here. The readings decisively show that these synods were transcribed not from the Isidorian collection but from the Spanish collection. It will suffice to give one especially important and evident example. All the Isidorian codices that we have carefully examined present an interpolated seventh canon of the Second Council of Seville. They contain the inserted word *chorepiscopos* twice and, at the end of the same canon, an additional passage—features all known to have been prohibited by the Apostolic See. This material concerns the spurious Pseudo-Isidorian letter of Damasus to the bishops of Numidia. These interpolations are absent from the manuscript books of the Spanish collection, as is clear from Loaysa’s edition, which was taken from pure Spanish exemplars. On this matter, see volume II of this edition, col. 1270, and our note 5 there. Since these interpolations are not found in the present Vatican collection 1338, it is clear that it received the canons of the councils of Africa, Gaul, and Spain from Spanish, not Isidorian, codices.

4. In the second part [Col. 0240A], which contains the Apostolic Constitutions, these were transcribed from the Hadrianic collection alone. Since the codex is mutilated at the end, it ends with Leo’s letter to Anastasius of Thessalonica.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Collection of Isidore Mercator

### § 1. On the spurious documents in this collection; how late the forgery was detected; whether Nicholas I approved such a collection; the principal arguments for its fabrication are presented

1. The collection of Isidore Mercator is distinguished from the preceding collections, especially by the fact that it is filled with numerous spurious documents. It presents several letters of the most ancient Roman pontiffs, from Saint Clement down to Saint Sylvester, although none of their decrees survives; it likewise attributes certain letters to later pontiffs down to Gregory the Great and inserts them among genuine documents. It is astonishing that so notable a forgery—one that did not emerge gradually or in parts but appeared all at once, in its entirety, in a single book—was not immediately detected [Col. 0240B]. It is believed that Hincmar of Reims and other Gallic bishops who wrote to Nicholas I sensed something suspicious. Yet they do not seem to have entertained any doubt about the letters’ falsity; rather, they thought that the letters should be deprived of authority only because, as they said, they were not recorded in the canonical book—that is, because they were not found in the Hadrianic collection, which at that time they called the Book of Canons, as it had become accepted for the use of the churches. In replying to those same bishops, Nicholas rightly considered this sole argument worthless (Nicholas I, Letter 42 to the Gallic Bishops), since not all of the otherwise thoroughly genuine constitutions of the Roman pontiffs, but only a very few, are found in that collection; and since those same Gallic bishops, whenever they see that these documents—the decretals of the earlier pontiffs—support their purpose, use them indiscriminately. Since they transmitted those same decretal letters, although they were not written in the canonical book and were less widely accepted, not as spurious but as genuine [Col. 0240C], using them whenever they wished, the same pontiff, who knew them only through the report of the Gallicans, could not reject them, suspecting nothing of the forgery so long as no evidence from elsewhere came to light. Nor can his words, by which he seems in some manner to have approved them, be taken as a true and legitimate approval resting upon that presumption, since the Gallic bishops had implanted it in him; such approval could not have been given without reading the letters themselves, which he did not possess. That Nicholas lacked them is evident from the fact that, in his own letters, when he had many opportunities to cite them, he more diligently commends other documents not found in the canonical book; he also commends certain apocryphal works that had formerly been fabricated and circulated and had found their way into older collections, such as the synod of Saint Sylvester, the other Synod of Sinvessa, the proceedings concerning the purgation of Sixtus III, and those concerning Polychronius. Yet he never used the Pseudo-Isidorian decretals. It is clear that these were not known to Leo IV, his immediate predecessor [Col. 0240D], from Leo’s letter to the Britons. In that letter, when reviewing the decretals contained in the canonical book, he begins with Sylvester and mentions the rest of the Hadrianic collection in such a way that, if any matter should arise that could not be resolved by them, recourse should be had to the writings of the holy Fathers Jerome, Augustine, and others; he gives no indication of the other circulated decretals.

2. These decretals and other Isidorian wares contain many marks of forgery that would easily have led attentive and skilled persons to detect their falsity at the very moment of their appearance. But the condition of those times and of the periods that followed was such that few people possessed a pure knowledge of the more remote antiquity or wished or were able to exercise sound criticism. The first person who sensed and indicated their fabrication was Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa, in Book III, chapter 2, of his work *Catholic Concordance*. Wycliffe, who had earlier blurted out, “The decretal letters are apocryphal, and they lead people away from the faith of Christ, and the clerics who study them are fools” [Col. 0241A], was not merely casting suspicion on the decretals fabricated by Isidore but was attempting to overthrow the authority of all decretals. After Cusanus, however, many others gradually became alert to the matter and brought forward so much substantial and convincing evidence for the fabrication that no one can now reasonably doubt such forgeries.

3. It is enough here to touch upon some of the arguments for the forgery. One of no small importance emerges from the preface itself. In its title it is assigned to Saint Isidore, and that same formula inserted into the preface also declares him a bishop, since it addresses the bishops as “our brothers.” The preface also presents him as a Spaniard, in the words: “At the beginning of this volume we have set down how a council is celebrated among us.” After the preface, there follows an order for celebrating a council taken from chapter 4 of the Fourth Council of Toledo. What other Isidore could there be who was Spanish, a bishop, and a saint [Col. 0241B], except that famous Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville? That this collection was commonly attributed to him soon after it appeared—that is, in the ninth century—is sufficiently known from the same preface and from Hincmar of Reims, Letter 7, chapter 12. But what greater forgery could there be than to attribute to Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, a collection containing eight Councils of Toledo, from the Fifth through the Thirteenth, and one Council of Braga, all of which were held after his death; and, with the same anachronism, to mention in the preface itself the Sixth Ecumenical Council, which had not yet been held while Saint Isidore was alive? Moreover, in the letters attributed to the pontiffs of the first three centuries, there are many testimonies from Sacred Scripture taken from Saint Jerome’s version, which was published later. Moreover, most of the consular notices attached to these same letters either name consuls who never existed in the consular fasti or, if they are found in the fasti, do not at all agree chronologically with the time of the pontiff who supposedly authored the letter. Add the invented names of magistracies—*archiflamines*, *first flamines*, and so forth—and the terms *primates*, *archbishops*, and *apocrisiarii* [Col. 0241C], which anyone even slightly acquainted with ancient history and ecclesiastical discipline will easily recognize as wholly foreign to the period and usage of those ancient pontiffs. Add also the fact that these letters contain no indication of ancient customs but much evidence of later discipline. Others have noted many additional arguments more fully; there is neither time nor need to report them here.

4. We do not think that two matters may be omitted. Although each might separately receive some answer, when joined together they provide an evident demonstration of the forgery. First, some of these letters are said to have been addressed to all bishops, others to all the orthodox, to all the churches, to the bishops of Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, Germany, and so forth. Many copies of them, therefore, must have been disseminated throughout the world. How could it have happened that, out of so many letters circulated throughout the entire world, not one was found and cited by anyone before the ninth century? Second, these same letters reproduce not merely the opinions but also the expressions and many fairly lengthy complete periods of authors from the later fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and even eighth centuries, as Father Philippe Labbe accurately noted in the margins of these letters after Blondel. The first argument may be answered by saying that the letters remained hidden until the ninth century and therefore were cited by no one. To the second, however, someone has replied that those later authors who present the indicated opinions in the same words copied them verbatim from the letters themselves. Neither answer is probable; indeed, each conflicts with the other. For if the letters remained concealed from their origin until the ninth century, so that no one could cite them, then they were not available to later writers either, who therefore could not have copied periods from them. But if complete periods were excerpted from them by several people separated by considerable differences of time and place, then they cannot be said to have remained buried in darkness [CCXVII] for so long. Whichever alternative one chooses [Col. 0242A], the forgery is always proved, and the conflict between the two answers makes this much clearer. If several ancient writers had taken opinions, words, and periods from the letters themselves, then the letters would have been known, worn smooth by frequent use, and useful for many purposes, so that many people could have cited them—especially those who had benefited from them. Among these would surely have been the supreme pontiffs, synods, and Fathers who present the same words and periods; they would have cited these letters of the most ancient pontiffs just as they are found to have cited other genuine letters of other authors. If, on the other hand, among so many men before the ninth century—men both most holy and renowned for learning—there was not one who mentioned these letters, because they truly took nothing from them, then the corresponding opinions and periods found also in the letters were undoubtedly derived by the maker of the letters from those very writers. This clearly demonstrates the spurious origin of the letters. Thus they were also cited by no other author before the ninth century [Col. 0242B], not because they were hidden or because there was no material or occasion for citing them, but because the person who would fabricate them had not yet been born. Otherwise, just as we find them widely cited after the time when they were fabricated and circulated, and find not a few passages from them transferred into collections, so we would discover that the same thing had happened in earlier times if they had truly been written and published by the ancient pontiffs to whom they were attributed.

### § 2. Other genuine documents inserted into the same collection, and the sources from which they were drawn; the importance of detecting these sources in distinguishing what Pseudo-Isidore fabricated; certain genuine documents interpolated by him; the final two synods attributed to Symmachus and the chapters ascribed to Hadrian I, which many believe genuine, are shown to have been fabricated by the same Pseudo-Isidore

5. Pseudo-Isidore did not construct his collection solely from the spurious documents [Col. 0242C] that he himself cobbled together. He mixed many entirely genuine monuments, known from elsewhere, among the false ones. The sources from which he derived these genuine documents must be detected, for this will be of considerable assistance in separating those very things that he invented out of his own mind. His principal source is the Spanish collection, which he inserted in its entirety into his own collection. Since the opinion had become widespread that Saint Isidore of Seville was the author of the Spanish collection, he willingly seized upon the name of Isidore, which was held in universal veneration, and inscribed it in the preface. He took the Spanish collection not in the form in which it first appeared and which extended no farther than the Fourth Council of Toledo, but in the slightly expanded form that included nine Councils of Toledo and the Council of Braga of the year 675. Nor did he use copies of this collection that were of Spanish origin, but those of Gallic origin, as we shall establish more fully in no. 14. A second source is the Hadrianic collection [Col. 0242D], from which Pseudo-Isidore excerpted certain items absent from the Spanish collection. A third source is the old collection published by Quesnel and reprinted by us in this volume. For not a few documents found in the Isidorian collection but read neither in the Hadrianic nor in the Spanish collection were derived from that source, sometimes in the same order. The author took a few other items from the *Tripartite History* and from other sources, which we shall identify below, each in its proper place in the catalogue.

6. It is so useful to have identified these sources that whatever is not found in them must with complete certainty be declared to have been fabricated by Pseudo-Isidore. If documents that are genuine in themselves are shorter in those sources but fuller in Pseudo-Isidore, then whatever addition appears that is not found in those sources may be affirmed to have been fabricated by that same impostor. Thus the sixth and seventh chapters, the two final chapters of Vigilius’s letter to Profuturus [Col. 0243A], are spurious: they are absent from the genuine codices of the Spanish collection but are read in the Isidorian collection. Moreover, since in this same collection certain otherwise apocryphal ancient documents, which had been received in some older collections but are shorter there, are likewise expanded, these additions too must be attributed to the impostor. Thus no one can now doubt that several more extensive chapters of two letters of Saint Clement to James were fabricated by him. These letters, once fabricated among the Greeks and translated into Latin by Rufinus, found their way into some old collections, but are much shorter in them; among Pseudo-Isidore’s materials they are found only in an expanded form containing those additions. Nor should we omit here the brief interpolation by which he inserted into the genuine seventh canon of the Second Council of Seville certain material about which we spoke in the preceding chapter, no. 3. Here, moreover, please observe the character of the impostor [Col. 0243B]: he was so inclined to fabricate that he spared neither genuine nor apocryphal documents, even though his inventions could easily be detected by collating older codices. With how much greater boldness, then, would he fabricate entire letters that need fear no comparison with older exemplars by which the fraud might be exposed?”

7. By the general rule that we have proposed, the two spurious synods—the fifth, as it is called, and the sixth under Symmachus—are exposed, as are also the chapters attributed to Pope Hadrian in the printed editions and in most manuscripts, which are found only in the Isidorian collection. It is astonishing to us that even many otherwise exceptionally keen critics, who have subjected the individual documents of that collection to close scrutiny, have raised no doubt whatever about the two aforementioned synods and the chapters. Indeed, Blondel, who attacked Isidorian fabrications more vigorously than anyone, was so far from doubting them that, among the older monuments from which Pseudo-Isidore fabricated his spurious letters, he repeatedly cites the synods just mentioned and Hadrian’s chapters, [Col. 0243C] as though these were genuine and more ancient, and did not have Pseudo-Isidore himself as their author.

First, with regard to the two synods under Symmachus: not only does the Hadrianic collection know nothing of them, but neither does the oldest of all the collections, preserved in Vatican manuscript Regina 1997, which, composed shortly after the time of that pontiff, presents with the greatest accuracy all his genuine synods and the other documents pertaining to them. If only three synods are reported there, rather than four, no one should suppose that the fourth genuine synod was omitted from that manuscript: for the opinion that there were four synods derives from a certain note that is absent from the older and better manuscripts, as we observed in part II, chapter 4, no. 5.

Moreover, if the three synods that alone are published as genuine are compared with the two described only in Isidore, everyone will detect the obvious difference in their introduction, style, and entire mode of expression; this sufficiently demonstrates that they had different authors. Add that in the sixth synod, as it is called, the canons of Gangra are said to have been enacted with apostolic authority; this is entirely false. Two such canons are cited from the version of Dionysius, although at that time the Roman pontiffs had received no canons of Greek synods apart from those of Nicaea and Sardica. See part II, chapter 1.

Finally, in the synod called the fifth, certain decrees are read which Symmachus declares to have been established by his predecessors: “For,” he says, “it was synodally decreed and confirmed by many of our predecessors.” The decrees produced, however, are quoted word for word in the spurious letters of Zephyrinus, Stephen, Eusebius, and Julius. The same person must therefore be recognized as the fabricator both of these letters and of that synod. Symmachus could not have praised letters that were fabricated so much later.

Nor should anyone find it incredible that Pseudo-Isidore, when assembling that synod, copied words from letters fabricated by himself and invoked the authority of the pontiffs to whom he attributed them. This was his customary practice in the letters that he assigned to later pontiffs: from fictitious writings issued in the name of their predecessors, he sometimes repeated decrees in the very same words and invoked the authority of those predecessors. Once the fabrication of such synods has been exposed by these arguments, there can be no doubt that the subscriptions attached to the pseudo-synods themselves—taken partly from Symmachus’s genuine councils and partly from the Council of Chalcedon, which makes the fraud especially clear—came from the same impostor.

8. We now turn to the chapters that are ascribed to Pope Hadrian I in the printed editions (T. VIII of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 597). We have seen in the Vatican Library a manuscript numbered 631 in which these chapters [CCXIX] are attributed not to Pope Hadrian but to Ingelram, or Angilramn, bishop of Metz. They begin as follows:

> Chapters collected from various councils and from the decrees of the Roman pontiffs by Angilramn, bishop of Metz, and presented to Pope Hadrian.

Another manuscript of the library [Col. 0244B] of Saint Victor in Paris bears precisely the same heading, as Baluze testifies in his preface to the books of Antonius Augustinus *On the Correction of Gratian*. Later, in his notes on the same books, p. 492, he cites another manuscript from the monastery of Laetium, where a similar title is expressed in these words:

> Book of chapters collected from various councils or decrees of the Roman pontiffs by Anilramn, bishop of Metz.

Most manuscripts, however, and the better ones—Vat. 630, 1340, 1344, 3791, and others—preserve the common reading:

> From Greek and Latin canons, Roman synods, and the decrees of Roman prelates and princes, these chapters were collected from various places and delivered at Rome by Blessed Pope Hadrian to Agilramn, bishop of the city of the Mediomatrici, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the ninth indiction, when proceedings were being conducted on account of his case.

That this title is altogether preferable is demonstrated by Hincmar of Reims, a contemporary of Pseudo-Isidore, who likewise read it in his manuscript. For in his short work against Hincmar of Laon, chapter 24, he writes:

> As for the judgments said to have been collected from the Greek and Latin canons and from the decrees of Roman prelates and dukes, and given by Pope Hadrian to Engelramn, bishop of Metz, when proceedings were being conducted on account of his case, etc.

The fuller heading, which specifies the time and occasion of the chapters and states that they were collected not only from the decrees of pontiffs and the canons of councils but also from the laws of Roman princes, is recognized as more authentic. Therefore there can be no doubt that this collection of chapters was attributed to Hadrian.

Pope Hadrian, moreover, gave his name to no other collection except the one that he himself delivered to Charlemagne and that is called the Hadrianic Collection. Hence Leo IV, in his letter to the bishops of Britain, when citing ecclesiastical canons—especially those by which bishops both judge and are judged—lists the canons contained in the Hadrianic Collection. But concerning these chapters attributed to Hadrian—which, since they contain scarcely anything other than material relating to episcopal trials, ought especially to have been mentioned—not even a word is said.

Furthermore, the chapters themselves contain certain provisions that a Roman pontiff would never have proposed. One is chapter 6, which states that cases of appeal are to be brought to Constantinople rather than to the apostolic see. Another is chapter 49, taken from book X of the Theodosian Code, title 10, no. 2, or from the *Breviary of Anianus*:

> Let the informer’s tongue be cut out, or, once convicted, let his head be cut off.

Everyone can see how foreign this is to ecclesiastical gentleness. Angilramn, bishop of Metz—called by his contemporary, Paul the Deacon, in book IV, chapter 6 of *The History of the Lombards*, a very gentle man and eminent in piety—would have been especially opposed to inserting such a sanction into a collection of canons.

We shall add, as fuller proof of the fabrication, that the pontifical decrees from which these chapters are said principally to have been collected are scarcely anything other than the spurious Isidorian decretals. In them the same judgments and the same words are repeatedly recited, as can be gathered from the notes of Antonius Augustinus on these chapters. Anyone who carefully considers the agreement between those letters and these chapters will easily perceive that they had the same architect.

Most people have hitherto failed to grasp the force of this argument because they believed that the author of the pseudo-letters had proceeded from the chapters, which appeared to be genuine. We, on the contrary, can demonstrate that the chapters were composed after the pseudo-letters and that, wherever they agree with those letters in identical judgments or words, they were plainly derived from them.

Many further examples could be brought forward. For the sake of brevity, one especially clear example will suffice. The same lengthy decree of a Roman synod that is read in chapter 5 of the chapters is also contained, word for word, in the spurious letter of Felix I to the bishops of Gaul. That this decree was transferred from the letter into the chapters, rather than from the chapters into the letter, is clear from the fact that the Roman synod to which the decree is attributed in the chapters is none other than the spurious synod described under Felix I in the same letter, which contains the account of that synod.

This is made clear by the following words of that letter (T. I of the Councils, col. 924):

> “We,” says Pseudo-Felix, “summoned more than seventy of our brothers and fellow bishops to assist you. With them we resolved to examine canonically the matters inserted below. For, after your letters had been read aloud before everyone—letters which, as you know, contained many complaints and accounts of your oppression—and after the decrees concerning the accusations of bishops had been read, the holy synod said: ‘These are the measures that henceforth, because of the snares of wicked men, etc.’”

After reporting this decree, Pseudo-Felix concludes his account of the synod held with these words:

> “These matters, brothers, were unanimously decreed in the synod for your assistance and that of all your fellow bishops, so that, if perhaps some fools should accuse you, etc.”

Therefore this Roman synod and its decree, recited in the chapters, could have been taken nowhere else than from this pseudo-letter of Felix I, through which alone it first came to light. If the author of the chapters took the same decree from this pseudo-letter, then the chapters are later than that letter and likewise later than the other spurious decretals, from which many other passages were similarly excerpted.

The chapters therefore cannot be attributed to Hadrian I, nor to Angilramn, bishop of Metz. During their lifetimes, neither those pseudo-decretals nor the chapters derived from them had yet appeared. Hence no one will be able to agree with Stephen Baluze, who, in the aforementioned preface to the books of Antonius Augustinus *On the Correction of Gratian*, attributed these chapters to Angilramn of Metz and wrote:

> He collected them for the most part from the recently produced letters of the ancient pontiffs and presented them to Hadrian, in order to seek support for his case.

Their author is that same Pseudo-Isidore who fabricated the letters themselves; consequently, they are found only in his collection.

In fact, in the oldest of all manuscripts, Vat. 630, they are indeed found in an appendix to the Isidorian collection, [Col. 0245D] because they were composed from the spurious documents contained in the first form of the collection and were produced through Pseudo-Isidore’s later efforts, being added as an appendix to the earlier copies, as will become clear from the notes in § 5. In the first form of the collection, which the same impostor testifies in his preface to have carried down to Saint Gregory, these chapters attributed to Hadrian I could not have had a place. They are therefore confirmed as having been fabricated and added only later.

9. For a clearer understanding of the impostor’s character, we believe that this point must be noted here: when copying from the pseudo-letter of Felix the Roman synod’s decree that we mentioned shortly before, he altered some words of the same decree with excessive freedom.

For whereas the pseudo-letter reads:

> At a suitable time, that is, in autumn or summer, they shall regularly convoke a council according to the canons,

the chapters state in chapter 5:

> At the time prescribed by the canons of Nicaea, they shall canonically convoke a council.

The impostor had noticed [Col. 0246A] that a Nicene synod could not be invoked in the letter and synod of Felix I, who preceded the Council of Nicaea. But since he had actually taken from the Council of Nicaea the provision attributed to that synod in the passage prescribing the convocation of councils, he did not hesitate to indicate that council in the chapters attributed to Hadrian, who lived later.

Thus he reveals a double fabrication: one, when he attached to the Roman synod a provision that belongs to the Council of Nicaea; the other, when he interpolated the decree taken from that Roman pseudo-synod by altering several details.

§ 3. The purpose for which Pseudo-Isidore fabricated so many spurious documents. Whether ecclesiastical discipline was altered by these spurious documents.

10. It must not be omitted in what spirit and with what purpose Pseudo-Isidore fabricated so many documents. Some maintain that he was led and prompted to produce them by a desire to enlarge or defend the authority of the Roman pontiffs. But they are plainly mistaken. Although the greatness and authority of the apostolic see are commended in many passages of these documents, that was not the impostor’s purpose. Nor did that see, whose privileges and rights rest upon very many genuine and ancient documents, need these apocryphal writings, as Cardinal Baronius noted under the year 865, no. 8.

Pseudo-Isidore’s purpose was quite different, as can be sufficiently discerned from the preface to the collection itself. After listing the documents that were to be inserted into his collection, he gives the following reason for assembling them:

> So that the discipline of the ecclesiastical order, gathered and arranged by us into one body, may instruct holy prelates in their paternal rules; so that ministers obedient to the Church, and the peoples, may be instructed by spiritual examples; and so that they may not be deceived by the perversity of wicked men. For many, crushed by perversity and greed, have oppressed priests by ACCUSING THEM.

He continues at length, vehemently attacking those who dare to accuse bishops in order to excuse themselves through them or enrich themselves from their goods. He reports many disadvantages arising from such judicial proceedings and insists that bishops cannot be compelled to answer a case if they have been accused, stripped of their property, deprived of their rank, or expelled from their see, unless they have first been restored. He adds several points concerning the rejection of accusers and accusations. Through all this he clearly indicates that he composed the collection chiefly with the intention of protecting bishops who were being accused.

This is much more clearly evident in the spurious documents that he fabricated. He consistently displays the same care and concern for accused bishops. Whenever he praises the authority of the apostolic see, he always directs everything toward this end: that bishops who have been attacked by accusations and condemned, if they feel themselves wronged, may flee to that see, which can reconsider the judgments of synods and, if it deems it just, invalidate them.

The same purpose is especially apparent in the chapters attributed to Hadrian. Since these were excerpted chiefly from the apocryphal letters, they may be called a kind of abridgment and compilation of the spurious documents. Most of those chapters are directed toward ensuring that bishops cannot be accused by just anyone; that, if accused, they are not readily surrendered to their accusers; that, for many reasons, both accusers may be rejected and judges refused; that the judgments of synods may be reconsidered; and that other measures of the same kind, likewise inserted into the apocryphal documents, may be applied. If all these provisions are believed to have been collected and fabricated for the protection, defense, and safeguard of bishops who are accused, stripped of their possessions, or deposed, no one can justly disprove it.

11. Quite a few people complain harshly about Pseudo-Isidore, as though his fabrications had abolished the ancient discipline and introduced a new one, with the result, they claim, that the ancient canons were abandoned, the sinews of discipline broken, the rights of bishops and provincial councils disturbed, the laws governing trials removed, and various other injuries inflicted upon ecclesiastical affairs.

Everyone will readily understand how unfair this criticism of a new and altered discipline is if he observes two things. First, most of Isidore’s pseudo-letters are excerpts from the opinions of the holy Fathers, from genuine constitutions of the Roman pontiffs after Siricius, from the canons of councils, and from Roman laws. These are certainly not a new law or a new discipline. The remaining material, for the most part, presents a discipline that had either already long been established or had begun to be introduced somewhat earlier.

The fabrication lies in this: Pseudo-Isidore attributed those judgments to authors to whom they do not belong and attached the discipline of a later age to earlier pontiffs, as though it had flourished equally in the earlier centuries of the Church.

In any case, as for the claim that a new discipline was introduced, the impostor would have been utterly foolish if he had hoped that his collection would be accepted by people while containing a completely new discipline, one that was even contrary to the practices and customs of his own age. If whatever is introduced contrary to custom—even when good and useful—usually causes disturbance by its novelty, then this would be all the more true of someone attempting to overthrow and alter a discipline that was in itself excellent, supported by more sacred laws, and accepted by everyone through long usage.

No disturbances or outcries were heard over the introduction of the apocryphal decretals except in the area concerning the cases and trials of bishops. Some matters relating to these are found in Hincmar and in the letters of Nicholas I. Yet even in these cases and trials, what is transmitted in the pseudo-letters and Isidorian synods was not entirely new.

Were not the more serious cases involving accusations against bishops reserved to the apostolic see by definite decrees of ancient pontiffs, so that they could not be decided without its consent? See, among others, Leo’s letters 6, 13, and 14, and Gregory IV’s first letter to all the bishops.

Have we not proved in the Observations on Quesnel’s Dissertation 5, part I, chapters 5, 6, and 7, that episcopal appeals to that same see rested upon the ancient canons and custom, as well as upon the right of primacy?

It had been provided in canons 128, 129, 130, and 131 of the African Code that not everyone indiscriminately should be admitted to accuse a bishop; and likewise in canon 6 of the Council of Constantinople, which Nicholas I cites from a Greek manuscript in his eighth letter.

That bishops who had been expelled and stripped of their property were not to be compelled to trial unless they were first restored to their rank and everything taken from them was returned can be inferred from chapter 87 of the Code of the African Church.

These and other provisions of the same kind, which are attributed to the Pseudo-Isidorian decretals as innovations in discipline, may be read in letters 8, 9, and 38 of Nicholas I. Yet he confirms them not from those apocryphal writings, which he did not possess, but from more ancient documents. Gregory IV had done the same before him in his first letter to all the bishops, in which he reserved the trial of Bishop Wenilo to himself.

It may indeed have happened that this discipline, although established by ancient rights and decrees, did not prevail widely—or prevailed only rarely—in certain places that followed other customs and canons. It may also have happened that the same discipline, established in favor of the upright to prevent fraud, was drawn by some into abuse and served the impunity of the wicked.

We have learned from Pseudo-Isidore’s preface, however, that his purpose was entirely removed from such wickedness: it was simply to assist bishops who had been unjustly oppressed.

Perhaps also, in that part of Gaul where Mainz is situated, where these wares of Pseudo-Isidore were fabricated, as we shall soon explain, the discipline proposed in them had long before become established through the work of Saint Boniface, bishop of Mainz. Since he served as an apostolic legate, his letters show how much deference he paid to apostolic authority and how earnestly he sought to introduce the same observance in those regions.

See, among others, his letter 105 to Cuthbert, archbishop of Canterbury, in which several principal elements of the discipline established in those regions by that holy martyr and apostle of Germany are presented and later repeated in the Isidorian pseudo-letters. The same spirit also passed to his successors Lull, Riculf, and Autgar, as is evident from other monuments.

If the Pseudo-Isidorian decretals promote a discipline that was supported both by older decrees and canons and had already long prevailed, at least in those regions where Pseudo-Isidore composed them, everyone will understand whether the criticism attributing the introduction of a new discipline to those decretals is fair.

Nevertheless, it seems impossible to deny that this same discipline spread more widely and took much deeper root after the decretals had been published and circulated, and soon praised in certain councils, and later inserted into the collections of Regino, Burchard, and others, which were highly useful because of their brevity and method.

§ 4. On the author and date of this collection.

12. We indicated in no. 3 that the name of Isidore was inscribed in the preface by the impostor so that the work might be attributed to Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville; there we also proved that this collection cannot be ascribed to that saint.

Most people assign it to Riculf, bishop of Mainz. Hincmar of Reims reported in his work against Hincmar of Laon, chapter 24, that Riculf had published at Mainz the collection brought from Spain, as it was thought, by Isidore of Seville, and had disseminated it through the neighboring regions of Gaul. He writes:

> If you collected such material as seemed appropriate to you from the aforementioned judgments of Angilramn and the frequently mentioned letters, by cutting them up, putting them out of order, and disarranging them, because perhaps you thought that no one besides you possessed those judgments or the letters themselves, and therefore believed that you could freely collect such things, this is astonishing, since this land is full of those very judgments, just as it is full of the book of letters collected by Isidore, which Riculf, bishop of Mainz, brought from Spain and obtained—being as industrious in such matters as he was in royal chapters—and from which he caused these regions to be filled.

But since Riculf of Mainz, who succeeded Lull in 786 or 787, died in 814, while the Isidorian collection contains, for example, certain letters of Urban I and John III into which the impostor inserted verbatim several judgments from the Council of Paris held in [CCXXIII] 829, it is clear that these fabrications cannot be attributed to Riculf.

[Note: [Col. 0247D] Blondel infers from book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 205, now 281, that Riculf introduced something new, since he is said to have produced at the assembly of Worms a letter of Pope Gregory, of which there is no record either before or after that time. But this is not a spurious letter; it is the genuine letter of Gregory II to Boniface of Mainz, which is read in vol. VIII of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 178.]

Hincmar should be excused, since we believe that he accepted this information in good faith from Benedict the Levite. In the preface to books V, VI, and VII of the Capitularies, which he himself arranged and published around the year 845, Benedict had written:

> We found these chapters, which we have endeavored to gather together in the following three books, scattered in various places and on various sheets, just as they had been published in various synods and general assemblies; especially we found them stored in the archive of the holy metropolitan Church of Mainz by Riculf, metropolitan of that holy see, and finally discovered by Autgar, his second successor and kinsman. We have preferred to insert them into this work in the form written above.

Among the chapters inserted by him in these books are several taken from the apocryphal letters of the ancient pontiffs, some from the pseudo-synods of Symmachus, and almost all the chapters attributed to Angilramn and Pope Hadrian. Yet they are quoted without any author’s name.
