Nor should you suppose that Benedict the Levite took these materials from some capitulary of the Frankish kings, from which Pseudo-Isidore likewise excerpted them and attributed them to those ancient pontiffs, the synods of Symmachus, and Hadrian I. For if those decrees had been contained in genuine capitularies, some such capitularies would certainly have been found—if not all, at least some—in which they were read.

Thus, when Ansegisus compiled his four books from genuine capitularies, diligent scholars found those same capitularies, containing nearly all of Ansegisus’s chapters, as well as the chapters omitted by Ansegisus but added by Benedict the Levite from genuine capitularies in his own books.

What reason is there, then, why not a single chapter from those apocryphal documents is found in any older capitulary, unless Benedict derived them not from genuine capitularies but from the Pseudo-Isidorian wares in which alone they are found?

These chapters of the Pseudo-Isidorian collection therefore appear to be among those that Riculf is said to have stored in the archive of the Church of Mainz. Since Benedict himself attributes this collection to Riculf, or at least associates it with Riculf’s time, although we have already seen that Riculf died before it was composed and published, he seems to have done so for no other reason than to create authority for the same documents and remove suspicion from a fabrication of which he was not unaware.

Hence, since Benedict himself was the first, or almost the first, to use such fabrications, and since he was a Levite of the Church of Mainz, from which that collection emerged, some people, together with Blondel, suspect that he may himself have been the architect of those fabrications.

13. This much is certain: the collection was composed at this time and in Germany—Germany being counted under the old arrangement among the lands of Gaul and subject to the Frankish kings—not in Spain. It therefore had a Germanic-Frankish author.

Since the most recent document from which the impostor excerpted entire judgments in constructing the apocrypha is the Council of Paris of 829, the publication of the collection cannot be placed before that year. Moreover, the Council of Aachen of 836, chapter 2, no. 8, decrees that holy oil is to be prepared by the bishops each year on Maundy Thursday, according to apostolic tradition and the provisions of the decretals, in which the same matter is prescribed; this is believed to indicate Fabian’s second pseudo-letter.

The publication must therefore apparently be placed after 829 and before 836.

It is astonishing, however, that Rabanus, who shortly after the year 841 dedicated a *Penitential* to Otgar, or Autgar, bishop of Mainz, produced nothing from the Isidorian apocrypha. Whether he did so because he placed no reliance on them, or because they had not yet appeared, so that the decree of the Council of Aachen is incorrectly referred to Fabian’s pseudo-letter, others may judge.

If the latter view is considered more probable—and still more if, with Blondel, one believes that the impostor excerpted certain formulas and phrases from the letter of Jonas of Orléans to Charles the Bald, who obtained the kingdom in 839—the Isidorian collection must be said to have been published around the time when Benedict the Levite issued his books of the Capitularies, namely around 845. The first explicit mention of the apocrypha is then found in a letter of Charles the Bald to the bishops, written at the assembly of Quierzy in 857.

Nor should one be influenced by the collection attributed to Remedius of Chur and published by Goldast under this heading:

> Ancient canons of the Alamannic Church excerpted from the letters of pontiffs by Remedius, bishop of Chur, at the command of Charles the Great, king of the Franks and Alamanni.

(Vol. II of *Alamannic Matters*, part II, p. 134, 1730 edition.)

Since this king died in 814, Goldast thinks that the collection itself was composed around 813. It was a larger collection, and additions were made to it by Noting, bishop of Constance, who died in 934. Goldast nevertheless reports that these additions by Noting, together with a considerable portion of the canons collected by Remedius, were cut out and removed from his manuscript.

The chapters published by Goldast that survive number only forty-nine. They present, in order, excerpts solely from the pseudo-letters of the ancient pontiffs, from Saint Clement through Saint Urban. These very excerpts, which the author derived from Pseudo-Isidore’s collection after Charlemagne, as we have seen, plainly show that there is an error either in the title or in the explanation of the title concerning Charlemagne. Remedius, who is said to have been the author of these excerpts, must be assigned to a later age.

Perhaps Charles the Great should be understood as Charles the Fat, who was called Charles the Great in the same way that the emperor Louis II is found called Louis the Great. Charles the Fat was king of the Alamanni when the Pseudo-Isidorian collection was already in circulation, and later became emperor.

14. Many things prove that Pseudo-Isidore was not a Spaniard but a Germanic Frank. We have learned from Hincmar that the collection emerged from Mainz and that copies were disseminated throughout Gaul. Although Hincmar is mistaken in assuming that the author was Saint Isidore of Seville and reporting that the collection was brought from Spain, his statement that the collection was disseminated from Mainz is strongly confirmed by the testimony of Benedict the Levite.

For this reason, those who first cited these apocrypha in the ninth century were Germanic Gauls; no Spanish writer, nor any writer from another region, cited them. That the Spaniards were for a long time unaware of this collection, or did not accept it, may be inferred from book II of Innocent III’s letter 121.

From that letter we learn that, in a certain case, the Spaniards presented Alexander III with their book of canons, in which the Council of Mérida was described together with other councils. Since this council, along with the others, is not described in the Isidorian collection but in the fuller Spanish collection, it follows that, at that time as well, the body of canons received among the Spaniards was the Spanish collection.

The oldest Isidorian manuscripts are Germanic-Frankish. Even those that were transferred to other regions and reach the ninth century came from Gaul, as will become clear in the following section concerning two Vatican manuscripts written in the ninth century.

Add that the pseudo-letters contain many Germanic-Frankish idioms and the same barbarity of style found in other Gallic and German writers of the same age. Yet they contain none of the idioms peculiar to the Spaniards, which can be observed in Etherius and Eulogius.

The case is even clearer because the impostor transcribed a considerable amount from the letters of Saint Boniface, bishop of Mainz, and from the letter of the abbess Cangith to that same Boniface. These materials could have been found not in Spain but in Mainz and Germany, where those persons lived.

Finally, an argument that seems to us the most compelling of all must be added. When the impostor inserted the Spanish collection into his own, he did not use manuscripts of Spanish origin but manuscripts of Gallic origin.

This became known to us when we compared the letters of Saint Leo. We used two manuscripts of the Spanish collection: Vienna 41, of Spanish origin, and Vatican 1341, of Gallic origin. We have already noted the remarkable variation between these manuscripts in their readings, in chapter 4, no. 13. In the Vienna manuscript the readings are indeed corrupt, but its errors approach the true reading; in the Vatican manuscript there are evident arbitrary emendations that depart from the original text.

We recognized that three other Gallic manuscripts cited by Father Coustant have readings and emendations exactly like those of this Vatican manuscript, which came from Gaul to the Vatican Library. No one can doubt that such manuscripts, found and disseminated in Gaul, derived from some diligent Gallic antiquarian who once copied and emended a corrupt Spanish manuscript. See what we noted on this matter in the place cited.

We also compared the same [CCXXV] letters of Leo with Merlini’s edition, which was produced from an Isidorian manuscript, and with other Isidorian manuscripts, especially Vat. 630. Among the Isidorian manuscripts, this is the oldest of all and contemporary with Pseudo-Isidore; it preserves a purer form of his collection.

The readings of these manuscripts not only differ greatly from those of the Vienna copy of Spanish origin; they represent exactly the same readings and emendations found in Vatican 1341, which is of Gallic origin. This was so evident that, when we compared Isidorian manuscript Vat. 630 with Spanish manuscript Vat. 1341 in the same Leonine letters, the one appeared to have been copied word for word from the other.

There can therefore be no doubt that, when inserting documents from the Spanish collection into his own collection, Pseudo-Isidore used a manuscript not of Spanish but of Gallic origin. Why? Because he composed his collection in Gaul, where such manuscripts existed, and not in Spain.

Who, then, after so many clear indications of a Gallic, or Germanic-Frankish, author, could still think that the matter is uncertain?

§ 5. On the Isidorian manuscripts. The order and catalogue of the documents of this collection, taken from the oldest manuscript of all, Vat. 630. Spurious, genuine, and interpolated materials are carefully distinguished.

### 15.

Although manuscript codices of the Isidorian collection are more common in libraries, most of them differ from one another so greatly that many doubt what the primitive collection contained. For many codices contain only decretal letters and lack the canons of councils, although it is clear from his preface that Pseudo-Isidore inserted these into his collection. Among the former, some contain more letters and others fewer; some also occasionally differ in their order. Those that present the canons together with the letters likewise do not always agree. Some are fuller in their letters, which they either insert among the Isidorian materials or add at the end.

We were able to find thirteen copies. Of these, five lack the canons of councils and generally differ both in the number and in the order of the letters. They are the codices Vat. 629, 3788, 3791, 4873, and the Vallicellianus D 38.

The following eight codices containing both letters and canons—none of which P. Coustant was able to find—were available to us: Vat. 630, 631, and 1340; the Vatican Ottobonianus 93; Casanatensis A 11, 14; Florentinus, PP. Praedicatorum S. Marci 182; Patavinus 100 of the Lateran Canons of S. John in the Green Cloister; and the Venetian codex of the ducal library of S. Mark, divided into two volumes, one designated no. 168 and the other 169. Some of these, however, are mutilated and lack certain letters at the beginning or end.

### 16.

In order that, amid such great manuscript variety, it may be discerned [Col. 0251C] which collection was truly Pseudo-Isidore’s, or which documents were inserted in his original work, the following words of his preface will shed light. In them he describes the character of his collection and states the number and order of its documents:

> “At the beginning of this volume we have set down how a council is to be celebrated among us, so that those who wish to follow our order may know how they ought to conduct it. Those, however, who choose to conduct it better should do what they judge by a just, canonical, and most prudent deliberation. Finally, because of their authority, we have placed before the other councils the canons called Apostolic, although some call them apocryphal, since many accept them, and the holy Fathers strengthened their judgments by synodal authority and placed them among the canonical constitutions. Next we inserted the decretal letters of certain apostolic men—that is, of Clement, Anacletus, Evaristus, and the other apostolic men—which we have so far been able to find, up to Pope Silvester. Afterwards we established the Nicene Synod because of the authority of that great council. Thereafter we placed within this volume, under their numbered and chronological order and in their respective chapters, the various councils of the Greeks and Latins, whether held earlier or later; and we added the remaining decrees of the Roman bishops up to S. Gregory, together with certain letters of his, in which, because of the eminence of the apostolic see, there is an authority not inferior to that of councils.”

Therefore those codices which first, after the preface, present the order for celebrating a council; then give the canons of the Apostles; afterwards the letters of the apostles, or ancient pontiffs, from S. Clement to S. Silvester; then Nicaea together with the other Greek and Latin councils; and finally the other letters of succeeding pontiffs up to S. Gregory—these codices, I say, must be held to contain the true and complete Isidorian collection.

We found two codices that are altogether of this kind: Vat. 630 and 631, which are plainly complete. Three others—Vat. Ottobon. 93, the Florentine S. Marci, and the Casanatensis—although they contain both decretal letters and the canons of councils, cannot provide knowledge of the complete collection because they are mutilated.

Another codex, Vat. 1340, and the two Venetian codices of S. Mark add several documents after S. Gregory. Since these cannot be attributed to Pseudo-Isidore, they must be assigned to the additions discussed in the following chapter. We did not have sufficient time to examine closely the Patavine codex 100 of S. John in the Green Cloister, although it is complete and belongs to a later period.

Accordingly, from the two complete and pure Isidorian codices, Vat. 630 and 631, which we examined more carefully, we shall give below a description of the entire Isidorian collection; concerning the others we shall add some remarks later. Between these two complete Vatican codices, however, we shall chiefly follow codex 630 in its series and order.

It is altogether preferable to all the others, since it is not only Gallican—that is, from the region in which this collection was compiled—but [Col. 0252B] is also praised by Montfaucon and Cardinal de Aguirre as the oldest of all. Two things prove its Gallican origin:

1. A notation written at the beginning in a more recent hand: “This book belongs to the use of John, bishop of Arras.”
2. The letter of Luitard, bishop of Vence, to Wenilo, bishop of Rouen.

Its great antiquity, and the fact that it is nearly contemporary with Pseudo-Isidore, are shown by the catalogue of Roman pontiffs, which ends with Leo IV, Benedict III, and Nicholas I. From this it is recognized that the codex was written under Nicholas I—that is, between the years 858 and 867—at a time when the documents of this collection began to be cited by Hincmar and other Gallican bishops.

This codex must therefore be regarded as one of the earliest copies of the collection. The fact is further and repeatedly confirmed by two appendices of certain documents. Since Pseudo-Isidore added these in later revisions, they were appended at the end in this example of the original collection, whereas in other codices they are found inserted in their proper places.

Everyone can therefore see how much greater weight must be given to this codex than to the others in establishing and describing the same collection.

### 17.

Before the collection, besides the catalogue of Roman pontiffs—which, as we noted, ends with Nicholas I—there is an annotation concerning the four general councils. It is found in Gratian, *Decretum*, distinction 15, chapter 1, and is taken from S. Isidore of Seville, *Etymologies*, book VI, chapter 16.

Next follows an annotation concerning six councils, as in the same Gratian, distinction 16, chapter 10. Then comes another annotation concerning twenty-one other councils. The first eight of these are Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Sardica, Antioch, Laodicea, Carthage, and Africa, which reproduce the sequence of the Hadrianic collection. The remaining thirteen are Gallican, with no Spanish council among them. This indicates that the annotation was composed in Gaul.

The same material appears in Gratian, distinction 16, chapter 11, where three additional Gallican councils are added, thereby bringing the number to twenty-four. Then, in the codex, after the mention of the Council of Mâcon under number 21, eight further numbers, from 22 through 29, are supplied but left blank. After these come eighteen more numbers, from 30 to 47, under which the Spanish councils and the remaining councils are indicated; they are later listed under the same numbers in the table of councils.

A notice concerning the provinces is added, which Andreas Scotus, Petrus Bertius, and Emmanuel Schelestratius published; afterwards comes a notice concerning Gaul, which has been published by several scholars. All these annotations and notices occur not only in the same form in ms. Vat. 631 and in the other copies containing the complete Isidorian collection, but also in codex Vat. 1341, which contains the Spanish collection of Gallican origin. There can therefore be no doubt that they were either transferred into Isidore’s manuscripts from some such copy of the Spanish collection, or passed into those codices of the Spanish collection from Isidorian manuscripts.

All these materials that precede [CCXXVII] and do not belong to Isidore’s collection [Col. 0253A] are closed by the aforementioned letter of Luitard, bishop of Vence, to Wenilo, bishop of Rouen, written in the year 868. It is peculiar to manuscript Vat. 630 and was published from it in volume X of the *Councils*, Venetian edition, column 1403.

### 18.

After these materials the Isidorian collection begins with a preface bearing the title:

> “Here begins the preface of S. Isidore the bishop. Isidore Mercator, servant of Christ, sends greeting in the faith to his fellow servant and father in the Lord, the reader. I am urged by many…” (*Incipit praefatio S. Isidori episcopi. Isidorus Mercator servus Christi lectori conservo suo et parenti in Domino fidei salutem. Compellor a multis, etc.*)

It was published from codex Vat. 630 by Cardinal de Aguirre. See volume I of the *Councils*, p. 4. Merlin omits *Mercator* and reads *fideli* instead of *fidei*. The published editions of the *Councils* replace *Mercator* with *peccator*, but none of our codices has that reading. *Mercator* is also found in the Parisian codex seen by Harduin, as well as in Ivo’s *Decree*; only in the margin of the latter does *peccator* appear.

Attached to the preface is the spurious letter of Aurelius to Damasus, beginning, “The glory of the apostolic see” (*Gloriam apostolicae sedis*), together with the apocryphal reply of Damasus, beginning, “The writings of your holiness” (*Scripta sanctitatis tuae*). See volume II of the *Councils*, columns 1011–1012.

In ms. Vat. 631 these are copied before the preface, but incorrectly; for Hincmar of Reims, in his treatise against Hincmar of Laon, chapter 24, praising Damasus’s reply to Aurelius, says that “Isidore attached it to his preface and placed it before the collection.”

Next follows the *Order for Celebrating a Council* (*Ordo de celebrando concilio*), beginning, “At the first hour of the day” (*Hora diei prima*), as in volume I of the *Councils*, from column 8 through column 12. The author had accepted this order, which was taken from the Fourth Council of Toledo, as something to be placed at the beginning of the collection, and had prefixed it there in the preface.

Then comes a table of councils with forty-seven titles. The first forty-five are those that we presented in the Spanish collection, chapter 4, no. 5. The other two are:

> XLVI. Decrees established by certain Roman bishops concerning the rule of faith and ecclesiastical discipline.  
> XLVII. The Council of Toledo of sixty-eight bishops.

This same table, with the same forty-seven titles, is also found in the Casanatensis codex A 11 and in Vat. 1341, which contains the Spanish collection of Gallican origin. It therefore passed from one source into the other. Certainly the two titles 46 and 47, which agree neither with the body of the Spanish nor with that of the Isidorian collection, are additions.

There is an error in title 46, which does not designate any council. It is the very title prefixed in the Spanish collection to its second part, which contains the decretal letters of the apostolic see.

Two other spurious letters follow: one from S. Jerome to Damasus, beginning, “The glory of your holiness” (*Gloriam sanctitatis tuae*); the other from Damasus to Jerome, beginning, “The Church rejoices in your fountain” (*Gaudet Ecclesia tuo fonte*). They were published by Henschenius, Schelestratius, and others; most recently they were inserted into the Appendix to the works of S. Jerome, volume XI of the Veronese edition, p. 275.

Since these letters are also found in certain manuscripts of the Roman *Pontifical* attributed to Damasus, which Pseudo-Isidore used, it is impossible to determine whether their fabrication belongs to Pseudo-Isidore himself or to some earlier author from whom he received them.

Immediately afterwards fifty Apostolic canons of the Dionysian version are copied from the Hadrianic collection.

Then follow the letters of the ancient pontiffs, from S. Clement through Melchiades. All are spurious and were fabricated by Pseudo-Isidore, except for two letters attributed to S. Clement, which he nevertheless interpolated. Here is their sequence, as may be found in the published editions of the *Councils*:

Five letters of S. Clement: two to James; the third to all bishops, presbyters, and others; the fourth to Julius and Julian; the fifth to those dwelling in Jerusalem with James the bishop.

The first two had already been fabricated by some Greek author and, after being translated into Latin by Rufinus, had passed into older Italian and Gallican collections. Only the second letter is entitled in the Italian collections, “The Precepts of S. Peter.” Under this title we shall publish it from those same collections in this volume among the documents of ancient canon law. In the Gallican codices identified by Harduin and Coustant, however, it is entitled “The Letter of the Precepts of S. Clement, pope, sent to James, the brother of the Lord,” or “The Letter of S. Clement of Rome to James concerning the sacraments of the Church.”

Pseudo-Isidore excerpted these two letters from Gallican collections, which is why he retained the inscription of the second letter. He himself fabricated the other three letters [CCXXVIII]. To the two spurious letters that he received from elsewhere, he added new deceptions by enlarging them with extensive interpolations.

Anyone can recognize these interpolations by comparing the same letters as published from the Isidorian collection in the *Councils* with the much shorter versions presented in this volume from the Rufinian translation and the older collections: the first is to be placed in the collection at chapter 64, column 454; the second among the documents mentioned shortly above, no. 5, column 674.

Three letters of S. Anacletus: the first to all the Orientals; the second to the bishops of Italy; the third to all bishops.

Two of S. Evaristus: one to the African bishops; the other to the Egyptians.

Three letters of Alexander I: the first to all the orthodox; the other two to all bishops.

Two letters of S. Xystus I: the first to all Christians; the other to all bishops.

One of Telesphorus, to all Christians.

Two of Hyginus: one to all Christians; the other to the Athenians.

Likewise two of Pius I: the first to all Christians; the other to the Italians.

One of Anicetus—written *Anitius*—to the bishops of Gaul.

Two of Soter: the first to the bishops of Campania; the second to the bishops of Italy.

One of Eleutherius, to the provinces of Gaul.

Two of Victor I: one to Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria; the other to the Africans.

Two of Zephyrinus: the first to the bishops of Sicily; the other to the bishops of Egypt.

Two of Callistus I: one to Bishop Benedict; the other to the Gallic bishops.

One of Urban I, to all Christians.

Two of Pontian: the first to Felix Succribonus; the other to all Christians.

One of Anterus, to the bishops of the provinces of Baetica and Toledo.

Three of Fabian: the first to all bishops; the second to the Orientals; the third to Bishop Hilary.

Two of Cornelius: one to all bishops; the other to Bishop Rusticus.

One of Lucius I, to the bishops of Gaul and Spain.

Two of Stephen I: the first to Bishop Hilary; the second to all bishops.

Two of Xystus II: the first to Bishop Gratus; the second to the bishops of Spain.

Two of Dionysius: one to the prefect Urban; the other to Bishop Severus.

[Col. 0254D] Three letters of Felix I: the first to Bishop Paternus; the second to the bishops of Gaul; the third to Bishop Benignus.

Two of Eutychian: the first to the bishops of Baetica; the second to the bishops of Sicily.

One of Gaius, to Bishop Felix.

Two of Marcellinus: one to Bishop Solomon; the other to the bishops of the East.

Two of Marcellus: the first to the bishops of the province of Antioch; the second to the tyrant Maxentius.

Three of Eusebius: the first to the bishops of Gaul; the second to the bishops of Egypt; the third to the bishops of Tuscany and Campania.

One of Melchiades, to the bishops of Spain.

In this first part, which concerns the ancient pontiffs from S. Clement through Melchiades inclusively—or, exclusively, up to S. Silvester—Pseudo-Isidore fabricated fifty-nine letters and reproduced and interpolated two letters formerly attributed to S. Clement.

### 19.

The section containing the councils follows. It is prefaced by a short work entitled *On the Primitive Church and the Nicene Synod*. Since this work is placed after the letters of Melchiades, it is cited by Gratian and others under that pontiff’s name. In the codices, however, it bears no name. It is, as it were, Pseudo-Isidore’s prologue to the constitution that follows. It begins, “No one who reads the divine Scriptures…” (*Nemo qui divinas Scripturas legit*), as in volume I of the *Councils*, Venetian edition, column 1562.

This is followed by the *Constitution of Constantine to Silvester*, beginning, “In the name…” (*In nomine*), and “Those things which our Savior and Redeemer…” (*Ea quae Salvator et Redemptor noster*), ibid., column 1564.

This document is apocryphal. [CCXXIX] Some attribute it to Pseudo-Isidore. Balsamon quotes certain Greek fragments of it. P. Possinus found the complete document written in Greek in the Vatican Greek codices 614, fol. 76; 789, fol. 185; 973, fol. 39; and 1416, fol. 127, as P. Labbe noted.

For this reason Baronius and Binius not implausibly suspected that this constitution had been fabricated by the Greeks, subsequently rendered into Latin, and excerpted by Pseudo-Isidore. It is indeed read in Latin in the Gallican collection presented first in the ancient Colbertinus codex 3368. See what we said in part II, chapter 8, no. 3.

Although this document appears there to be an addition, since the Colbertine collection is older than Pseudo-Isidore and received nothing Isidorian, it is sufficiently credible that he drew this monument from it, or perhaps from another still older Gallican collection.

Next follows: “At what time the Nicene Council was held. The canons of the general councils began in the time of Constantine…” (*Quo tempore Nicaenum concilium habitum sit. Canones generalium conciliorum a temporibus Constantini coeperunt*), ending with the words, “they handed down the creed second after the Apostles” (*secundum post apostolos symbolum tradiderunt*). This is the beginning of the preface to the Spanish collection, which we gave in full in chapter 4, no. 5.

Then begins the letter or preface of the Council of Nicaea: “To the most blessed Silvester, bishop of the apostolic see in the city of Rome…” (*Beatissimo Silvestro in urbe Roma apostolicae sedis antistite*). It is a preface taken by Pseudo-Isidore from the collection published in this volume. See column 22.

[Col. 0255C] The canons of the Greek councils are then copied: Nicaea, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Sardica, Antioch, Laodicea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon, together with the formula of Atticus. There follow the canons of eight councils of Africa, seven Carthaginian councils, and the Council of Milevis.

Next come the canons of the councils of Gaul: the three Councils of Arles, and those of Valence, Tauriana, Riez, Orange, Vaison, Agde, and Orléans.

Finally come the canons of the councils of Spain: Elvira, Tarragona, Gerona, Zaragoza, Lérida, Valencia, and the First, Second, Third, and Fourth Councils of Toledo; the beginning of the First Council of Braga; then, interrupting it, nine other Toledan synods, from the Fifth through the Thirteenth. The last of these is mutilated at the end in Merlin, but is read complete in Vat. 630 and in the other Isidorian codices.

Afterwards the First Council of Braga is again added, this time complete, followed shortly by the Second Council of Braga. Then come the chapters of Martin of Braga and the Council of Braga of the year 675; finally, two synods of Seville.

Pseudo-Isidore took all these materials [Col. 0255D] from the fuller Spanish collection of Gallican origin, such as that found in ms. Vat. 1341, with the same repetition of the First Council of Braga and the same more freely corrected readings, as we noted earlier. Only in the Nicene material is the catalogue of bishops omitted; it is read in the corresponding codex of the Spanish collection.

### 20.

The third section follows, presenting the letters of the remaining Roman bishops from S. Silvester through S. Gregory. The same preface is placed before them, beginning, “The councils having thus far been arranged…” (*Hactenus digestis conciliis*), which we presented in the Spanish collection, chapter 4, no. 6.

The first document produced is spurious. It begins: “Certain excerpts from the synodal acts of Pope S. Silvester. In the time of Pope S. Silvester and the most pious Augustus Constantine, a great council was held at Nicaea…” (*Incipiunt excerpta quaedam ex synodalibus gestis S. Silvestri papae. Temporibus S. Silvestri papae et Constantini piissimi Augusti, factum est magnum concilium in Nicaea*), as in volume I of the *Councils*, from column 1575 through the words in column 1578, “the written instrument may be designated” (*designatus sit chirographus*).

Since the edition of the *Councils* places after these excerpts the synodal acts of S. Silvester themselves, under the title “Canon, or Constitution of Silvester” (*Canon, sive Constitutum Silvestri*), from which Pseudo-Isidore extracted these excerpts, those acts—which are equally spurious—are likewise transmitted there as embedded in the Isidorian collection.

Although they are read in one Isidorian codex, they are absent from our codex and from the others that we consulted. He would have undertaken a pointless labor by arranging excerpts from those same acts if he had intended to insert the acts themselves into his collection.

Hincmar of Reims mentions finding only these excerpts in his own codex, in the frequently cited treatise against Hincmar of Laon, chapter 24, where he also rejects such acts as apocryphal. Since they were composed under the age of Symmachus together with other apocryphal documents and were inserted into certain Italian collections, and since they also passed into Gaul—as they are read in the ancient Colbertine manuscript 784, concerning which see part II, chapter 6, nos. 4 and 5—Pseudo-Isidore must be said to have derived these excerpts from some such Gallican copy [Col. 0256B].

It is also certain that he had before his eyes the Roman *Pontifical* attributed to Damasus, whose author presents the same synodal acts of S. Silvester in abridged form. For some passages of Pseudo-Isidore’s excerpts agree more closely with the abbreviation in the *Pontifical* than with the acts themselves.

The spurious letter of Athanasius and the other Egyptians to Pope Mark follows. In it they request a copy of the Nicene canons; Mark’s reply to them is likewise spurious. See volume II of the *Councils*, columns 488 and 490.

“The Faith Discussed in the Holy Roman Council by the Most Blessed Pope Julius and the Other Bishops of the True Faith. In the name of the Lord God and Savior…” (*Fides in sacro Romano tractata concilio a beatissimo Julio papa et reliquis verae fidei episcopis. In nomine Domini Dei et Salvatoris*), ibid., column 549. This too is a Pseudo-Isidorian fabrication.

The letter of the same Pope Julius to the Orientals on behalf of S. Athanasius: “You ought, brothers, to instruct others in ecclesiastical disciplines…” (*Decuerat vos, fratres, alios ecclesiasticis instruere disciplinis*), ibid., column 497. It is apocryphal.

[Col. 0256C] The reply of the Orientals is likewise apocryphal: “Although concerning all…” (*Licet circa omnes*), ibid., column 502.

The reply of Julius to those same Orientals: “You ought, against the holy Roman and apostolic Church…” (*Decuerat vos adversus sanctam Romanam et apostolicam Ecclesiam*), ibid., column 506. It is apocryphal.

The synodal letter of Athanasius and the Egyptians to Pope Liberius is apocryphal: “The rights of your most blessed fatherhood…” (*Vestrae beatissimae paternitatis jura*), volume II of the *Councils*, column 817.

Liberius’s reply to them is likewise spurious: “Formerly and from the beginning…” (*Olim et ab initio*), ibid., column 819.

The apocryphal letter of Athanasius and the Egyptians to Pope Felix: “We bring to the attention of your holy apostolate…” (*Vestro sancto suggerimus apostolatui*), ibid., column 993.

The reply of Felix: “Your sacred synodal letter…” (*Sacram vestram synodicam*), ibid., column 999. Another letter of the same pope to the same recipients: “Grace to you…” (*Gratia vobis*), ibid., column 1005. Both are spurious.

The letter of Liberius to all the bishops: “There is nothing that can stand…” (*Nihil est quod stare*), ibid., column 815. It is apocryphal.

Damasus to Paulinus: “Through my son Vitalis…” (*Per filium meum Vitalem*), [Col. 0256D] ibid., column 1014. This genuine letter of Damasus was taken from the Spanish collection.

Afterwards Pseudo-Isidore divided another genuine letter of the same Damasus to the same Paulinus, taken from the Spanish collection and elsewhere entitled *Confession of Faith*, into three parts. He inserted three apocryphal letters among them, preceded by a table of six chapters. The three genuine parts of the letter and the three spurious letters that follow the table correspond in this manner:

**I. The same Damasus to Paulinus.** “After the Council of Nicaea, another council was subsequently assembled in the city of Rome…” (*Post Nicaenum concilium, aliud in urbe Romana postea congregatum est*), as in volume II of the *Councils*, column 1061, through the words, “If anyone thinks correctly concerning the Father and the Son but does not hold a right belief concerning the Holy Spirit, he is a heretic” (*Si quis de Patre et Filio bene senserit, de Spiritu sancto autem non recte habuerit, haereticus est*).

This is the first part of the aforementioned letter, or confession of faith, to Paulinus, except that the decree against those who migrate from their own churches to others is omitted here; it is supplied below under title 6.

[Col. 0257A] **II. The letter of Stephen and the three councils of Africa to Damasus.** “We make known to your blessedness…” (*Notum vestrae facimus beatitudini*), ibid., column 1018. It is spurious.

**III. That all heretics who hold evil opinions concerning the Son of God and the Holy Spirit are found in the unbelief of the Jews and Gentiles.** “But if anyone allows God the Father, God the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be called gods…” (*Quod si quis patiatur Deum Patrem, et Deum Filium, et Spiritum sanctum deos dici*), etc.

This is the final part of the aforementioned genuine letter to Paulinus, ibid., column 1063. But after the final words, “let us believe without doubt” (*sine dubio credamus*), the Isidorian codex adds several other passages that are not read in the pure copies of the Spanish collection.

**IV. The letter of Damasus to Prosper of Numidia and the other Africans.** “Although, dearest brothers, they are known to us…” (*Licet, fratres charissimi, nobis sint nota*), ibid., column 1025. It is apocryphal.

**V. On priests who migrate from their own churches to others.** “Those priests, however, who move from churches to churches…” (*Eos autem sacerdotes qui de Ecclesiis ad Ecclesias*), ibid., column 1062, through the words “let him rest in the Lord” (*quiescat in Domino*). This is a decree from the aforementioned genuine letter of Damasus to Paulinus, which had earlier been omitted.

The synodal letter of Damasus to the Illyrian bishops—“We believe your holy faith…” (*Credimus sanctam fidem vestram*)—was taken from Epiphanius’s version in the *Tripartite History*, book V, chapter 29. Pseudo-Isidore added a spurious chronological note: “Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of the illustrious men Siricius and Ardabur” (*Dat. XVII kal. Nov. Siricio et Ardabure VV. CC. consulibus*). See volume II of the *Councils*, column 1031.

The apocryphal letter of Damasus to the bishops of Italy: “I had wished, beloved…” (*Optaveram, dilectissimi*), ibid., column 1033.

Three letters of Siricius, all genuine and taken from the Spanish collection: one to Himerius; [CCXXXI] another to various recipients against Jovinian; the third to the orthodox throughout the various provinces. They are found there in columns 1212, 1218, and 1223.

Two spurious letters of Anastasius: the first to the bishops of Germany and Burgundy; the second to the most noble man Nerianus. They are found there in columns 1428 and 1430.

Twenty-three letters of Innocent, all genuine and excerpted from the Spanish collection. They are read in volume III of the *Councils*, from letter 1 of that pontiff [Col. 0257C] through letter 23, columns 13 and following.

The letter of the Council of Carthage to Innocent and Innocent’s reply; then the letter of the Council of Milevis to the same pontiff together with his reply; likewise the private letter of five African bishops to Innocent and his response; finally, the private letter of Innocent to Aurelius. These seven letters are read in the Gallican collection printed in this volume, from which Pseudo-Isidore drew them. See below, from column 128 through column 164.

Two letters of Zosimus excerpted from the Spanish collection: one to Esychius; the other to the clergy of Ravenna. They are found among the letters of Zosimus in volume III of the *Councils*, letters 1 and 2.

The letter of Pope Boniface to Augustus Honorius together with the latter’s reply, and another letter of the same pontiff to the bishops of Gaul. These are genuine and were taken from the Spanish collection. They are found among the letters of Boniface in the same volume III of the *Councils*.

Three letters of Celestine, likewise from the Spanish collection: one to Venerius and the other Gallic bishops; another to the bishops established throughout the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne; the third to the bishops of Apulia. In the *Councils* they are letters 1, 2, and 3 of this pontiff.

One apocryphal letter of Xystus III to the Oriental bishops. It is in volume IV of the *Councils*, letter 3.

From the Spanish collection there follow, in precisely the same order, thirty-nine letters of S. Leo and others, which we listed in the description of the Spanish collection, chapter 4, no. 6.

Three documents of Pope Hilary from that same Spanish collection: a synodal decree and two letters to Ascan ius of Tarragona. In the *Councils* they are letters 1, 2, and 3.

The letter of Pope Simplicius to Zeno of Spalatum and the letter of Acacius to Simplicius, from the same collection. The former is letter 1 of that pontiff in the *Councils*; the latter follows letter 8.

[Col. 0258A] Three letters of Felix II—Felix III in Pseudo-Isidore—from the same Spanish collection: one to the Sicilians, another to Acacius, and the third to Zeno of Spalatum. In the *Councils* they are letters 7, 6, and 8.

The decree of Pope Gelasius concerning books to be received or not received, beginning, “After the prophetic and evangelical Scriptures…” (*Post propheticas et evangelicas Scripturas*), as in volume V of the *Councils*, column 386. This genuine decree was copied from some older Gallican collection or codex, such as Colbertinus 784, discussed in part II, chapter 6, and Colbertinus 3368, discussed there in chapter 8.

Another general decree of the same pope, elsewhere entitled “Letter to the bishops of Lucania and Sicily.” Also another letter of the same pope to the Sicilians. These two, excerpted from the Spanish collection, are found in volume V of the *Councils*, letters 7 and 10.

Four letters of the same Gelasius: the first to the master Faustus; the second to the emperor Anastasius; the third to the bishops of Dardania; the fourth to the Orientals. These were taken from the Gallican collection printed in this volume, chapters 48, [Col. 0258B] 49, 50, and 51.

The letter of Pope Anastasius to Augustus Anastasius from the Spanish collection. It is found in volume V of the *Councils*, letter 1 among the letters of that pontiff.

The letter of Pope Symmachus to Caesarius of Arles, likewise from the Spanish collection. It is found there as letter 5 among the letters of Symmachus.

Three genuine councils under the same Symmachus follow, from the Hadrianic collection. In volume V of the *Councils* they are designated Synods I, III, and IV.

In most Isidorian codices, two other synods under the same pontiff are inserted here. We have proved these to be fictitious, together with another genuine document taken from Ennodius. In ms. Vat. 630, however, these are relegated to the end of the collection; they will be discussed below.

Eight letters of Hormisdas and two letters to Hormisdas, in the same order in which we listed them in the Spanish collection, from which Pseudo-Isidore derived them.

[CCXXXII] Two letters of Pope John I: one to Zacharias, [Col. 0258C] archbishop; the other to the Italian bishops. They are spurious.

Two other letters of Felix III—Felix IV in Pseudo-Isidore—likewise spurious: the first to all bishops; the second to Sabina.

The apocryphal letter of Boniface II to Eulalius.

The apocryphal letter of John II to Bishop Valerius.

The apocryphal letter of Agapetus I to Anthemius, bishop of Constantinople.

The letter of Bishop Amator to Pope Silverius and the latter’s reply: both are spurious.

The genuine letter of Vigilius to Profuturus, taken from the Spanish collection; but in Pseudo-Isidore it is entitled “to Eutherius” because of a corrupt reading, concerning which see chapter 4, no. 15. To this letter he added two chapters of his own, the sixth and seventh.

The spurious letter of Pope Pelagius I to Bishop Vigilius; in Vat. 631, to Julius.

The spurious decrees of Pope John III to the Germans and Gauls.

The apocryphal letter of Pope Benedict to Bishop David.

Three letters of Pelagius II, all apocryphal: one to the bishops of the Council of Constantinople; the second to Archbishop Benignus; the third to all bishops, especially those of Campania and Italy.

Six letters of S. Gregory the Great. The first three are genuine and were taken from the Spanish collection: the first and second to Leander, bishop of Seville; the third to King Reccared. They are read in book I of the *Register*, letter 43 of the Maurist edition, and in book IX, letters 121 and 122.

Afterwards three other letters of Gregory follow, which may have been taken either from his *Register* or from other Gallican collections. One is to Secundinus, found in book IX, letter 52, but interpolated by Pseudo-Isidore with a long addition that, as we shall see in part IV, chapter 8, was fabricated by another earlier impostor [Col. 0259A]. The second is to the patrician Theoctista, found in book XI, letter 45. The third is to Augustine, containing Augustine’s questions and Gregory’s answers, as they are read in the same book XI, letter 64.

A synod under the same Gregory the Great, with six canons, through the words “desires to undergo servitude” (*subire appetit servitutem*), as found in volume VI of the *Councils*, column 1310.

The decrees of Pope Gregory the Younger. This is the Roman synod printed in volume VIII of the *Councils*, column 185. The primitive collection of Pseudo-Isidore ends with this synod.

Moreover, in ms. Vat. 630, from which we have reproduced the description of this collection, a blank leaf follows. This confirms that the same collection ended with the aforementioned synod, so that the materials added after that leaf in the same codex must be counted as a later addition.

The following documents, written in the same hand throughout the codex, are then added; they concern the case of Pope Symmachus.

The apologetic booklet of Ennodius on behalf of the Palmary Synod of Rome and on behalf of Symmachus [Col. 0259B]. See volume V of the *Councils*, column 479.

Synods V and VI under the same Symmachus, which we proved spurious in no. 7. They are found there in columns 501 and 509.

Two letters of Ennodius attributed to Symmachus: one to Laurentius of Milan, beginning, “The movement of a religious conscience betrays itself” (*Prodit religiosae motum conscientiae*). It is found in the works of Ennodius, but with the title “The Third Speech of Ennodius, given to Stephen, a *vir spectabilis* and vicar, to be delivered to Bishop Maximus” (*Dictio tertia Ennodii data Stephano V. S. vicario dicenda Maximo episcopo*). The other is to the patrician Liberius and is found in Ennodius as letter 1 of book V.

Since these documents, especially the two spurious synods, are attributed to Pseudo-Isidore and are found inserted in other copies of the Isidorian collection after the three genuine synods of Symmachus, they appear to have been added in Pseudo-Isidore’s later revisions. For this reason they are copied at the end of the aforementioned codex Vat. 630, which in its preceding leaves contains the primitive collection [Col. 0259C] without these documents.

After such additions, another page is left blank and empty in the same codex; then the following materials are added in the same hand.

The chapters attributed to Pope Hadrian and delivered to Angilram, bishop of Metz. There are fifty-two chapters, to the last of which another nineteen chapters are immediately attached. [CCXXXIII] We demonstrated in no. 8 that these, published in volume VIII of the *Councils*, column 599, are spurious and were arranged by an impostor after the first work.

The disputation of the emperor Constantius and Liberius, Roman pontiff: “The emperor Constantius said…” (*Constantius imperator dixit*), as in the *Tripartite History*, book V, chapter 17.

Certain sanctions collected piecemeal from the proceedings of the Council of Chalcedon, which we have also found in other collections.

On the transfer of bishops, from book XII of the *Tripartite History*, chapters 8 and 11.

Also from a letter of Pope Pelagius: “That a bishop ought not to move from one city to another.”

[Col. 0259D] Here is the end of the codex. The chapters attributed to Hadrian I, which in other Isidorian codices that insert the pseudo-synods of Symmachus in their proper place are placed after the decrees of Gregory the Younger, are believed to belong to the Isidorian collection (for they are found only in it and in those derived from it). Certainly, the fabrication of these chapters reflects the character of Pseudo-Isidore, and we have observed that they were excerpted from the spurious letters composed by him, so that the same author of all of them is apparent. But since Pseudo-Isidore wrote in his preface that he would set out the decrees of the Roman bishops not up to Hadrian, but only up to St. Gregory, it must be said that these chapters did not belong to his original work, but were fabricated by the same author later; and for that reason they are rightly listed separately among the additions in our codex.

21. Codex Vat. 631, formerly belonging to Cardinal Peter, bishop of Rouen, written in the twelfth century, [Col. 0260A] contains everything found in Vat. 630, except the two final additions concerning the transfer of bishops and the letter from Pope Pelagius. Only the order is altered in some places: the additions relating to Symmachus are copied in their proper place after the three genuine synods of that pontiff, whereas the chapters of Hadrian, together with the rest, are appended after the decrees of Gregory the Younger without any indication that they are additions. This codex has the special feature that, after the Isidorian collection, it adds the entire Hadrianic collection and the version of the Sixth Council under Pope Agatho.

§ 6. Concerning certain manuscript codices that contain the Isidorian collection neither wholly pure nor complete. Certain apocryphal letters wrongly attributed to Pseudo-Isidore.

22. We have explained above what the pure and complete Isidorian collection is. We must now discuss certain codices that present it with additions foreign to it, or even not entirely complete. The first to appear is Codex Vat. Ottobonianus 93, a parchment in-folio, written in a very ancient, small script and divided into two columns, displaying the age of the ninth or tenth century. That it was formerly Gallican is shown by a piece of parchment attached at the end to reinforce the codex, containing the act of Gallicanus, bishop of Paris, and of Thomas de Corcellis, professor of sacred Scripture and dean of the Church of Paris, under Pope Pius II. The same codex presents at the beginning the letters of the ancient pontiffs, then the canons of the councils, and afterward the decrees of the subsequent rulers of the Apostolic See—that is, the Isidorian collection itself. But since it lacks its beginning and end, it does not preserve that collection in its entirety. Two other codices supply this defect: Casanatensis, belonging to the Friars Preachers of the Minerva, marked A 11, 14, and Vat. 3791. The former, wholly complete, contains the letters of the ancient pontiffs and the canons of the councils; the latter [Col. 0260C] contains the decrees of the subsequent pontiffs through to the end. Thus these codices agree with the cited Vat. Ottobonianus manuscript in their respective portions, as though it had been divided into two parts and incorporated into those two codices; consequently, whatever is missing from it at either beginning or end can safely be supplied from them.

23. P. Coustant saw similar Isidorian codices that lacked only the canons of the councils. For he notes (Preface to the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, no. 155) that in them a double table of chapters had been prefixed: one at the beginning, before the letters of the ancient pontiffs, which also indicates the canons of the councils, although omitted from those codices; and another before the letters of the later pontiffs. We have found these tables only in the copies mentioned: the first in the Casanatensis—for Vat. Ottob. is mutilated at the beginning—and the second in Vat. Ottob. and in another Vat. 3791. Moreover, in his codices he found certain pseudo-letters attributed to Damasus, Jerome, and Leo, which we were able to find inserted together only in the codices just mentioned. Accordingly, we have recognized with much greater certainty that the codices seen by P. Coustant are exactly like ours. He attributed those pseudo-letters, as well as the other spurious documents, to Pseudo-Isidore, because the only Isidorian codices he had encountered seemed to him to contain the pure Isidorian collection. We, however, having had the opportunity to examine manuscript Vat. 630, the oldest and complete of all, and other similar manuscripts that preserve the pure Isidorian collection, have perceived by comparison that the copies just mentioned contain the same collection not in a wholly pure form.

24. As regards the first part, which comprises the letters of the ancient pontiffs and the canons of the councils, those codices may indeed be called purely Isidorian, since they present the documents belonging to that part in the same order that we noted in Vat. 630. Only this part, as we learned from the complete Casanatensis, [Col. 0261A] begins with Isidore’s preface, omitting the annotations and notices that precede the preface in Vat. 630 but are relegated, in the codices under discussion, to after the end of the second part, as we discovered from manuscript Vat. 3791. It is followed by an index of 77 chapters. Although this index is absent from the pure copies of Isidore, it corresponds exactly to the Isidorian documents. The first 30 numbers are assigned to the same number of pontiffs, from St. Clement to Melchiades, whose letters are copied in this part; the remaining 47 numbers belong to the councils, distributed into the same number of chapters, as we have seen elsewhere.

25. In the second part, however, which concerns the letters of the later pontiffs, the difference between these codices and the pure Isidorian copies is considerable. Two facts show that the index of chapters prefixed to this part, found only in these manuscripts, cannot be attributed to Isidore:

1. It lists fewer letters than are contained in the Isidorian collection. For example, of the seven letters of Gelasius it indicates only two, and of the four documents of [Col. 0261B] Symmachus only one. Moreover, the table of the Casanatensis manuscript ends with Anastasius, while that of the Vat. Ottobonianus codex concludes with Hormisdas; yet, as the author himself testifies, the Isidorian collection extends to Gregory.

2. The order of the letters found in this index agrees neither with the order of the other Isidorian codices nor with that of Vat. Ottobonianus itself or of the other Vat. 3791.

In the body of these codices, the letters not only fail to correspond to the prefixed index, but also differ from the Isidorian collection; and it is chiefly on account of this difference that we cannot believe this to be the true collection of Isidore. First, for example, the order of the letters of St. Leo is not Isidorian. Pseudo-Isidore transferred Leo’s 39 letters from the Hispanic collection into his own in precisely the order in which they appear in the Hispanic collection, as the codices Vat. 630, 631, and others demonstrate. Accordingly, the author of the enlarged Isidorian collection, which we shall describe in the following chapter, likewise retained that order. Although he inserted several additions, he nevertheless reproduced the letters copied from Isidore in the same order in which he found them in the Isidorian codices. In the manuscripts now under discussion, however, an entirely different order of Leo’s letters is introduced, and the same disorder of sequence occurs in the letters of Innocent and others.

Next, in Damasus, no. 15 and no. 22, the confession of faith that he sent to Paulinus, beginning “After the Council of Nicaea,” is presented twice. It is read only once in the pure Isidorian copies. Furthermore, Leo’s letter to the Africans is presented in the fuller form to which the Hadrianic edition appends certain chapters omitted in that shortened form, whereas Isidore, drawing from the Hispanic collection, gave a shortened form. See our admonition on letter 12 itself.

Finally, several letters are added, partly genuine and partly spurious, which are absent from the pure Isidorian manuscripts. Thus, among the letters of Damasus, three are inserted (Vol. II of the Councils, col. 1017): two are apocryphal—one of his to Jerome, beginning “Although many bodies of books”; the other, Jerome’s reply, beginning “I have humbly read the letters of your Apostolate.” The third is a letter of Damasus without a title, beginning “Since due reverence is owed to the Apostolic See” [CCXXXV]. It is genuine, translated from Greek into Latin, and inserted by Epiphanius Scholasticus in the Ecclesiastical History in Three Parts, book IX, chapter 15, where it is said to have been sent to the Easterners.

Among Leo’s letters there are eighteen additions. Among them, letter 28 to Flavian is copied twice from different sources. There is also an apocryphal letter that we rejected into the appendix to the first volume, concerning the privilege of chorepiscopi or presbyters, addressed to all the bishops of the Churches of Germany and Gaul. We nevertheless learn that it was fabricated earlier from the letters of John III, themselves falsely attributed by Pseudo-Isidore, in which the same letter of Leo is cited.

Moreover, after the letters of St. Gregory, excerpts of letters from various places are added—namely, passages excerpted from various letters of St. Gregory the Great. [Col. 0262A] After the chapters of Hadrian, three items are appended:

1. A letter of the pope and bishop of Spalato—that is, St. Isidore of Seville—to Laudefridus of Córdoba, published by Loaisa from a Spanish manuscript and reproduced from Loaisa in Vol. VII of the Councils, col. 434.

2. Another letter of Isidore to Bishop Masona concerning the restoration of priests, considered spurious by Joannes Morinus, On Penance, book IV, chapter 15, no. 6.

3. A catalogue of the names of the heretics who disturbed the unity of the Church. It begins: “Certain heretics also,” etc., as in Gratian, Cause 24, question 3, chapter 39. It is taken from book VIII, chapter 5, of the Etymologies of St. Isidore of Seville.

These final additions, absent from Vat. Ottob. 93 because the codex is mutilated at the end, became known to us from manuscript Vat. 3791, in which this second part is preserved complete.

Does not this manifold difference between such codices and the other, older and purer, Isidorian copies demonstrate that the pure collection of Isidore is not found in them? Nor should anyone suppose that the added documents, especially the three apocryphal ones we mentioned, were appended in Pseudo-Isidore’s later activity. This is decisively disproved above all by codex Vat. 630. Since that codex contains the later additions of the same Pseudo-Isidore in a double appendix at the end, there can be no doubt that the added documents of the codices mentioned would likewise have been appended there with the others if they had been introduced by Pseudo-Isidore himself. Hence the three spurious letters are wrongly attributed to Pseudo-Isidore: one from Damasus to Jerome, another from Jerome to Damasus, and another from Leo to the bishops of Germany and Gaul. They are absent from the pure Isidorian codices and are found only in those that differ from the pure Isidorian collection in several respects and have received certain additions from elsewhere.

Pseudo-Isidore was not the only fabricator of apocryphal documents; several others of the same character have been discovered. To omit certain older forgeries, the letter of Pope Deusdedit to Gordianus, bishop of Seville, together with the three others cited in it—those of Julius, Innocent, and Celestine to the bishops of Isauria, Ephesus, and Jerusalem—plainly reveals its fabrication; yet, since it is found in no Isidorian codex, it cannot be attributed to this forger. The same is true of certain other fictitious writings, which will be discussed in the following chapter under the Additions to Isidore.

26. Codex Florentinus of St. Mark, numbered 182, written around the twelfth century and containing both letters and canons, differs somewhat in its final part from the pure Isidorian collection. For after the letters of Innocent it adds the law of the emperor Constantius to Volusianus and the edict of Volusianus himself in the case of the Pelagians; these are read in the collection of canons to be published in this volume as chapters 19 and 20. Then, in Leo, besides an order different from that of the Isidorian codices, it presents several letters absent from those codices. It also gives letter 12 to the African Moors not in the shortened form found there, but complete and accurately copied, in a form that we have been unable to find in any other collection. See [Col. 0262D] the preface to Leo’s letters, § 14, where we listed the twenty-four letters copied in that codex. Since letter 24 lacks its ending because the codex is mutilated, we do not know whether other letters of Leo followed, or whether anything else differing from Isidore’s collection was inserted among the other pontiffs.

27. More should be said about manuscript codex Vat. 1340 and about the two similar Venetian codices of St. Mark, 168 and 169, which likewise contain, in their final part, many documents from the Isidorian collection, some inserted within it and others added at the end. But since these materials are more extensive, they must be treated separately in the following chapter.

28. Codex Vat. 629, of the twelfth century and in-folio, places before the Isidorian collection certain minor works of St. Isidore of Seville and Rufinus’s Ecclesiastical History. [CCXXXVI] Pseudo-Isidore’s preface follows. Then comes an index of chapters with this title:

“Here begins the abridgment of the canons of the Apostles and of the first apostolic bishops, from St. Clement to St. Damasus, following their own order; their acts also, contained in this work, are set out under their respective chapters.”

It says “up to Damasus” because, after the canons of the Apostles, all the letters of the Isidorian collection from St. Clement through Damasus are copied in continuous sequence, with the intervening canons of the councils omitted, together with the treatise on the primitive Church and the Council of Nicaea.

With the remaining pontiffs, however, the copyist, exhausted, omitted much and added little. He gave only one letter of Siricius, to Himerius; one spurious letter of Anastasius to the bishops of Germany and Burgundy; one of Innocent to Decentius; one of Zosimus to Hesychius; Boniface’s letter to the emperor Honorius and the latter’s reply; one of Celestine to the bishops of Gaul, beginning “The words of the apostolic command”; one apocryphal letter of Sixtus III to the Easterners; only three of Leo’s letters—to Rusticus, Anastasius, and Nicetas—all excerpted from Isidore; and one of Hilary to Ascanus of Tarragona, which in the Councils is letter 2 of that pontiff.

He added two letters of Simplicius absent from Isidore: one to John, bishop of Ravenna, and another to Bishops Florentius, Equitius, and Severus, which in the Councils are letters 2 and 3 of that pontiff and appear to have been excerpted from the Hadrianic collection. Immediately afterward, the decrees of Felix at the synod held under the consulship of Flavius Boethius, vir clarissimus, are appended from the same collection, etc., as in Vol. V of the Councils, col. 275. In Isidore, only the letter addressed to the Sicilians and inserted into that synod is read.

Afterward, from Isidore, only another letter of the same Felix is produced, his sixth, to Acacius; one of Gelasius to the bishops of Lucania; the first council of Symmachus; only one letter of Hormisdas, no. 25, to the bishops of Spain; one spurious letter of John I to Archbishop Zacharias; and, finally, one letter of Felix III, or IV, to the bishops of various provinces. In Isidore this letter is complete, but here it is shortened at the preface, for it begins with the final period of that preface: “The writings of your Holiness, which [were sent] to the Apostolic See,” etc.

Moreover, before the letters of each pontiff, an encomium of that pontiff is prefixed, taken from the Roman Pontifical attributed to Anastasius the Librarian. Although no constitutions of the subsequent pontiffs are copied in the same codex after the cited Felix, encomia of all of them are nevertheless supplied through Hadrian.

The ten chapters of Gregory VII follow, beginning: “Whoever, whether a soldier or a person of any order or profession, [holds] ecclesiastical estates,” etc., as in the Roman council held in the year 1078. Then follows the order concerning the discernment of penitents, established by Pope Gregory. It assigns three years of penance to those guilty of certain sins, one of them on bread and water; five years for certain others; and so forth. It ends: “that we may attain eternal life.” We have so far found this order nowhere else.

The final document is the synod of Pope Urban II held at Piacenza in the year 1095, which appears in Vol. X of the Councils, col. 824.

29. Codex Vallicellanus D 38, dating approximately from the tenth century, contains, with the canons of the councils omitted, the letters of the Isidorian collection from St. Clement through Damasus, as in the preceding codex. Besides Pseudo-Isidore’s preface, it also contains a treatise on the primitive Church. It appends the letters of Nicholas I concerning the case of Rothadus, bishop of Soissons, which are found in the edition of the Councils. The codex closes with a letter of Pope Vitalian to Paul, archbishop of Crete, which in the Councils is letter 1 of that pontiff.

30. Two codices, Vat. 3788 of the eleventh century and 4873 of a later period, present the same Isidorian letters from St. Clement to Damasus. They then append certain writings of St. Gregory the Great not found in Isidore.

Two Isidorian codices preserved at Padua in the library of St. John in the Garden, numbered 100 and 159, have received various materials foreign to Isidore, which we have not had time to record in our notes. Nor do we doubt that other codices exist elsewhere, differing through various omissions or additions. From the careful description of the pure Isidorian collection that we provided in § 5, however, anyone can readily understand what belongs to Isidore and what has been added or omitted.

[Col. 0264A]

[CCXXXVII] CHAPTER VII. On the additions to the Isidorian collection published by Merlin, which are contained in manuscript Vat. 1340 and in two other manuscripts of the Venetian library of St. Mark.

1. The first edition of the Isidorian collection received by subsequent editors of the Councils was published at Paris in 1523 through the work of Jacques Merlin; it was reprinted at Cologne in 1530 and again at Paris in 1535. In its final part, however, which follows the canons of the councils, it was enlarged by numerous additions, mostly genuine, which are absent from the pure Isidorian collection.

These added documents were not inserted by Merlin. Rather, we find them carefully collected and copied here and there before his time by some learned person in manuscript Vat. 1340, and we have discovered that a similar copy was before his eyes in preparing his edition. Since Merlin also omitted several documents and, apparently because his copy was defective, carried the collection only as far as Zacharias, whereas the cited codex contains more materials extending to the Council of Rheims in the year 1148 under Eugene III, we consider it necessary to set out here separately the information concerning these additions derived from that codex.

We have recognized from several reliable indications that copies exactly similar are found in Gaul. Quesnell cites one of them, the Herovallianus; both Quesnell and P. Coustant mention another, the Rheims manuscript of St. Remigius. We found another divided into two parts in the ducal library of Venice, St. Mark’s. The first part, ending with the letters of Celestine, is found in manuscript no. 168; the second, beginning with the letters of Sixtus III and proceeding to the aforementioned Council of Rheims, contains more numerous and more important additions and is copied [Col. 0264C] in manuscript 169.

These additions could not be distinguished unless an accurate, complete description of the whole pure Isidorian collection had preceded it; we supplied such a description from the pure codices of Pseudo-Isidore in the preceding chapter, § 5. Once it is clear what Pseudo-Isidore placed in his collection in his earlier activity and what he added later, the other materials found copied in this or that codex must rightly be assigned to foreign additions.

From this distinction between the additions and the documents of the pure Isidorian collection, one benefit will follow: everyone will see how wrongly certain persons have attributed to Pseudo-Isidore materials that do not belong to him but to the aforementioned additions of others.

2. Codex Vat. 1340, from which we shall draw chiefly our description of these additions, is a parchment in-folio of the twelfth century. At the end it contains a double catalogue of the Roman pontiffs: one, giving a brief notice of them, ends with Eugene III and Hadrian IV; the other ends with Clement III, who died in 1191.

At the beginning, before Pseudo-Isidore’s preface, all the materials are prefixed that we noted in describing codex Vat. 630, except for the catalogue of the Roman bishops and the notice of the provinces, which are relegated to the end of the codex. After the preface, everything proceeds exactly as in the same Vatican manuscript 630 through Siricius.

After Siricius’s letters, two items are inserted:

1. The Council of Telese, together with a letter of the same pontiff to the Africans.

2. A letter of Ambrose, Sabinus, Bassianus, and others to Siricius, which will be found in the collection printed in this volume as chapters 31 and 62.

Everything else through Leo is as in the same Vatican codex. Only after the letters of Celestine I is this closing note recorded:

“Here ends the first part of the canons.”

This entire part is found in Venetian manuscript St. Mark 168. Then follows the second part, which comes afterward in codex Vat. 1340 and is contained in the other Venetian codex, 169. It is prefixed by a table of chapters with the title:

“Here begin the chapters of the following work.”

It begins with the letters of Sixtus III.

3. In Leo’s letters, which follow those of Sixtus III, the author of the additions exercised particular care. For whereas Isidore has only 39 letters, he added another sixty, which we listed in the preface to the letters of St. Leo, § 13, Vol. I, p. 350. Among them is Leo’s pseudo-letter concerning chorepiscopi.

Since the collector of the additions had given Leo’s letter 12 to the Africans in the shortened edition that he found in Isidore, he appended to the aforementioned pseudo-letter concerning chorepiscopi, without any title, those chapters of the same letter to the Africans that are missing from the shortened edition.

Among Leo’s letters he inserted two letters belonging elsewhere. One is a letter of Leo, Victorius, and Eustochius to the bishops established in the third province. We restored it to Leo of Bourges and the other Gallican bishops in the appendix to the letters of St. Leo, Vol. I, [Col. 0265B] p. 1471. Hincmar of Rheims cited it twice as though it were a letter written by St. Leo the pope together with the Roman synod: first in the booklet addressed to King Charles, short work 1, Vol. I of the Councils, Venetian edition, col. 1253; and again at the beginning of short work 2, in the same place, col. 1268. It is therefore not surprising that our collector, under the same delusion, counted it among the letters of that pontiff.

The other is a letter of St. Cyril to Nestorius, from the ancient version published in the collection printed in this volume as chapter 66.

In these letters Merlin not only altered the order of our codices in some places, but also omitted three letters: one from Peter of Ravenna to Eutyches, which is read in Isidore himself; another from Ceretius, Salonius, and Veranius to St. Leo; and a third from St. Cyril to Nestorius.

4. After Leo’s letters, the following materials are presented in both our Vatican and Venetian codices, likewise omitted by Merlin:

I. An abridgment of the case of the Nestorians, divided into 24 chapters, compiled by Liberatus.

II. A letter of John of Constantinople to Theodore of Mopsuestia, beginning: “If indeed it were possible to come,” etc.

III. A letter of Gregory of Nazianzus to the same man: “It is time for me to say that passage of Scripture,” etc.

IV. Another letter to Theodore: “We are delighted by the signs of affection,” etc.

V. Part of another letter of the same Gregory to the same man: “He who assumed David,” etc.

VI. Another letter of the same author to the same man: “Indeed, envy existed even among us,” etc.

VII. A letter of Isidore of Pelusium to Cyril: “The examples of the divine Scriptures terrify me,” etc.

VIII. Another to the same: “Compassion does not see acutely,” etc.

IX. Another: “There are indeed many testimonies,” etc.

X. Another: “The admirable must always be unchangeable,” etc.

These four letters of St. Isidore of Pelusium are letters 370, 310, 323, and 324. These nine documents, numbered 2 through 10, were taken from an ancient version produced during the period of the celebrated controversy over the Three Chapters. The defenders of those chapters also used them, as may be inferred especially from the works of Facundus of Hermiane.

XI. A defense of the faith made by Cyril: “With equally unconquerable truth we defend the homoousion,” etc.

XII. “Of Blessed Cyril, and testimonies of the Holy Fathers.” “It is certain that the divine nature, as one thing dwelling in another, [is present] in humanity,” etc. “Here begin the testimonies of various authors.” Of St. Cyril, from book XXII of the Treasury: “For there is not one natural operation,” etc.; and other passages are added from St. Athanasius and Gregory of Nyssa, from Gelasius’s letter to the Dardanians, and from Theodoret.

XIII. A letter of St. Quintianus, bishop of Asculum, to Peter of Antioch: “Therefore, whoever says the nature of God,” etc. Twenty-one anathematisms are appended to his spurious letter. See Vol. V of the Councils, col. 223, and the note of Severinus Binius. Compare also what we said concerning this and five other apocryphal documents of the same kind in part II, chapter 11, § 3. Hardouin found this pseudo-letter in the Gallican manuscripts of Beauvais and Victorinus.

XIV. A letter of Athanasius to Epictitius (read Epictetus), and another of Cyril to John of Antioch, from the version that you will find in the collection published in this volume as chapters 52 and 53.

XV. Augustine’s booklet Against All Heresies: “We believe in one true God,” etc. It was published in the appendix to Vol. VIII of the Works of St. Augustine, col. 78.

5. The collection returns to the Isidorian form. After the three documents of Pope Hilary copied from Isidore, which Merlin also published, it adds, together with Merlin, a letter of the same pontiff to Leontius, Veranius, and Victurius, and two letters from Ascanus and other bishops of the province of Tarragona to that pontiff. See Vol. V of the Councils, under Hilary, letters 4, 1, and 2.

Then, among the letters of Simplicius copied from Isidore in our codices and in Merlin, three other letters of the same pontiff are inserted: one to John of Ravenna; another to Florentius, Equitius, and Severus, excerpted from the Hadrianic collection; and a third to Acacius, which the codex of canons to be published in this volume gives as chapter 44.

In Isidore, as also in the Hispanic collection, only one letter of Felix III to the Sicilians is produced. In our manuscripts and in Merlin, however, the complete Roman synod of that pontiff is copied from the Hadrianic collection; at that synod the same letter was read, addressed not to the Sicilians but to the bishops established in the various provinces.

Besides the letters of Gelasius found in Isidore, a volume On the Bond of Anathema is added, taken from the cited codex of canons, chapter 47. His first letter to Euphemius of Constantinople is also appended.

The Decree of Gelasius on Books, which Isidore places before his letters, is not only moved to the end; it is also preceded by an order of the Old and New [Col. 0266C] Testament, inscribed with the name of the same pontiff and not found in Isidore. In the decree itself, after the mention of the Council of Chalcedon, a sentence is added: “And if there are any councils,” etc., which is absent from Isidore.

6. As in Isidore, all the documents of Anastasius and Symmachus follow, together with the latter’s apocryphal synods and the other documents transcribed from Ennodius, as well as the letters of Hormisdas. Two further documents taken from the Hadrianic collection are appended to these:

1. A letter of the Emperor Justin to the same Hormisdas, beginning: “What we have always been.”

2. A copy of the petition sent to Justin by the Jerusalemites and Antiochenes and the clergy of Second Syria, beginning: “Draw water with joy.”

From the subsequent pontiffs, from John I through Silverius, nothing beyond Isidore’s collection is produced. The letter of Silverius to Vigilius, beginning “Entangled in many transgressions,” published by Merlin, is wrongly counted among Pseudo-Isidore’s forgeries because it is found in these enlarged codices but not in the pure Isidorian manuscripts.

In our codices, this letter is followed by St. Prosper’s book Against Cassian, which Merlin omitted. From Vigilius through St. Gregory the Great, everything agrees with Isidore.

After the synod of the same St. Gregory, two letters are appended: one from Felix, bishop of Sicily, to Gregory, and the pontiff’s reply. In the edition of the Benedictine Fathers of St. Maur, these are letters 16 and 17 of book XIV.

Thus everyone can see how wrongly these letters, which are absent from the pure Isidorian manuscripts, have been accused by some of being spurious and attributed to Pseudo-Isidore’s fabrications. If they are spurious, this forgery is nevertheless older than our additions, since Deacon John quoted one fragment in The Life of St. Gregory, book II, chapter 3, and Hincmar of Rheims quoted it in letters 37 and 59, as well as in the treatise On the Divorce of Lothair and Theutberga, questions 5 and 7 and question 12 near the end.

[Col. 0267A]

7. At the decrees of Gregory the Younger, where the Isidorian collection ends, our codices, together with Merlin, append the following additions.

Four letters of Pope Vitalian: one to Paul of Crete; another to Vaanus, the chamberlain; a third to the aforementioned Paul of Crete; and a fourth to Gregory of Syracuse. In the edition of the Councils these are letters 1, 2, 3, and 4 of that pontiff.

Also a letter of Martin I to Amandus, bishop of Utrecht, which is read in Vol. VII of the Councils, col. 391.

Several documents concerning St. Boniface, bishop of Mainz, follow: namely, his profession and oath made to Gregory II, found in Vol. VIII of the Councils, col. 167; then Gregory’s first letter to Boniface; also letter 3 to all the bishops, etc.; then letter 4 to the clergy and people of Thuringia; letter 5 to the nobles of Thuringia; letter 7 to the Saxons; letter 8 to Boniface; and another to the same, which in the common editions is letter 1 of Gregory III.
