Under the name of Gregory the Younger, letter 2 of the same Gregory III to all bishops, priests, and abbots is presented; also letter 3 to the nobles and people of the provinces of Germany; letter 4 to the bishops of Bavaria and Alamannia; and another to Boniface, which is letter 13 of Gregory II.

Then comes letter 7 of Gregory III to Boniface; followed by a letter of Boniface to Pope Zacharias, which is found in Vol. VIII of the Councils, col. 227. Also letter 2 of Zacharias to Wito, bishop of Barbarana, [CCXL] which in the Councils is addressed to Burchard, bishop of Würzburg. See Pagi’s observation there. Also letter 11 of the same pontiff to Ruginfrid and the other bishops of Gaul and Germany. Also three letters of the same pontiff to Boniface, namely letters 9, 12, and 1.

Thus far Merlin follows them; afterward his codex leaves them. In our copies, however, two letters of Boniface to Pope Stephen II are appended. The first was published in Vol. VIII of the Councils, col. 403; the second is letter 97 among the works, or letters, of St. Boniface himself.

Then comes Daniel’s letter to all kings, dukes, etc., likewise letter 33; followed by the letter of Charles the Mayor of the Palace to the bishops, dukes, etc., Vol. VIII of the Councils, col. 175.

Afterward comes the council of the year 742, called “Germanic” in the common editions, in the same place, col. 269. Also another synod held on the Kalends of March at a place called Liptinas, ibid., col. 273.

Then follows letter 19 of Boniface of Mainz to King Æthelbald of Mercia, and finally another letter of the same, letter 20, to Bugga, an abbess.

8. After the chapters transmitted by Pope Hadrian I to Angilram, copied from Isidore’s collection, and the excerpts from the proceedings of the Council of Chalcedon together with the dispute between Liberius and Constantius, the following documents are added:

Two letters of Innocent II: one to Samson of Rheims and Ervicus of Sens with their suffragans; the other to Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux. They are inserted in the Council of Sens of the year 1140, Vol. XII of the Councils, col. 1531.

The Council of Rheims of the year 1148, under Eugene III, in the same place, col. 1652.

The collection closes with the notice of the provinces, which is also copied in other Isidorian manuscripts. At the end, shorter lives and a catalogue of the Roman pontiffs are added, concerning which we spoke in no. 2.

9. Since after the documents relating to St. Boniface of Mainz there is nothing there from the three succeeding centuries until Innocent II and the Council of Reims, a considerable suspicion arises that these latter documents are more recent additions of the twelfth century; whereas the collector of the other additions was some earlier learned man, who stopped with the letters and councils relating to St. Boniface. Whatever one may believe on this matter, the additions of documents certainly show that this collection was arranged in Gaul, since they are either Gallican or were excerpted from older Gallican collections. Those relating to St. Boniface of Mainz—the letter of Leo of Bourges, Victor of Le Mans, and Eustochius of Tours to the bishops established in the third province [Col. 0268A], the Council of Beme, and others of the same kind—are so specifically Gallican that they could scarcely have been so readily found and gathered by anyone other than a Gallican. The Council of Thelese has been found only in Gallican collections. The collector took much from the collection of canons that we are reprinting, which we shall show to be not a Roman but a Gallican codex in the Observations on Quesnel’s Dissertation 12. The remaining additions are found in other Gallican collections, or in the Hadriana, which, having been sent to Charlemagne, had been disseminated throughout Gaul. The importance of these additions is apparent from the fact that they contain much that we would lack had it not proceeded from them. See, among other things, what we have observed concerning Leo’s letters in this connection, vol. I, p. 529, no. 26. Almost all the documents in these additions are genuine; the few that are apocryphal, however, have an older origin and were therefore found in other, more ancient manuscripts. Indeed, the collector of these additions, who searched out such precious records with the greatest diligence [Col. 0268B], does not display the kind of inventiveness that would have led him, as Pseudo-Isidore did, to insert many more fabricated materials.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Cambridge codex praised by Fabricius and Larroquanus; on the two Vatican manuscripts 1343 and 1344; and on the letter of St. Gregory the Great in which he responds to Augustine’s questions, produced from these same manuscripts with a preface not previously printed and in a form different from the common versions

1. It is clear from what has been discussed thus far that Merlin did not publish the pure Isidorian collection, but the one enlarged by many additions. Hence several learned men have greatly desired that the pure collection of Isidore should be published and reviewed separately, according to the authority of more reliable manuscripts [CCXLI]. But care must be taken lest those copies be regarded as genuine Isidorian exemplars which [Col. 0268C] differ from manuscripts Vatican 630 and 631, from which we transcribed it in Chapter Six. John Albert Fabricius, in vol. XI of the *Bibliotheca Graeca*, book VI, chapter 1, p. 17, while presenting the same desire of scholars, lists among the more distinguished exemplars of the Isidorian collection against which that edition ought to be measured a Cambridge codex that had been purchased in the eleventh century by Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, and is highly praised by Matthew Larroquanus in a letter published by Basnage of Beauvais, which Fabricius thought should be reprinted. Larroquanus notes that the preface and the order for celebrating the synod are absent from this codex; that it contains only three letters of St. Clement; and that the others generally differ greatly from the common versions, which are repeatedly a third or even half again as extensive as in that codex. He also mentions a different order, which he says is found in another, more recent Cambridge manuscript and differs not so much from the common versions as from Lanfranc’s codex. He states that a letter of Aurelius and Mizonius to the Council of Carthage [Col. 0268D] was prefixed to the First Council of Carthage; this letter is not read in Merlin. From these facts Larroquanus concluded that the pure collection of Isidore was contained not in Merlin’s edition but in this codex. He attributed the fuller documents in Merlin to the scribes, who, in copying them, had added whatever pleased them. But since we have obtained Vatican codex 630, contemporary with Pseudo-Isidore, with which other Isidorian codices, both ancient and more recent, likewise agree, there can be no doubt that these should be preferred to the Cambridge exemplar just mentioned. The very absence both of the preface and of the order for celebrating the council sufficiently demonstrates that this exemplar is foreign to the complete Isidorian collection. Apart from the older codices mentioned above, Hincmar, who lived close to the age of Pseudo-Isidore, also cites these two items from the primitive copies of the collection. The other features of this codex noted by Larroquanus, which do not agree with the older and more reliable codices, should be explained by the fact that it contains not Isidore’s pure and complete collection but an imperfect and mixed one, in which, according to the particular judgment of the scribe, some materials were omitted here and there, others abridged, and still others added from elsewhere [Col. 0269A]. Among these additions must be counted the letter of Aurelius and Mizonius. Since it is found only in the ancient collection published by Quesnel and to be reprinted by us in this volume, it is evident that the scribe of that codex added it from there. We have described several other codices of the Isidorian collection in Chapter Six, no. 28 and following, which omit some things and add others beyond the authority of the more reliable and older exemplars of Isidore. Anyone who supposed that he had found Isidore’s pure and complete collection in them would therefore be greatly mistaken. We have also found several other codices in the Vatican Library in which only certain documents excerpted from Isidore at the scribes’ discretion are copied together with documents from other collections. No one will be able to recognize the Isidorian collection in these either, but only a mere excerpt from several collections [Col. 0269B]. We shall briefly explain two of these in this chapter.

2. One is found in Vatican manuscript 1343, dating from approximately the tenth century, which formerly belonged to the Church of Pavia, as can be recognized from two documents copied at its beginning and end. This codex had three principal sources, namely the Hadriana, the Additions to Dionysius, and the Isidorian collection. First, the canons of the councils from Nicaea through the African councils were taken from the Hadriana. The use of the Hadriana is demonstrated not only by the distinction between the thirty-three Carthaginian canons and the other African canons, but also by the indication of the subscriptions, or catalogue of the Nicene bishops, which is appended in the Hadriana but not in the pure Dionysius. Not all the canons of each synod are copied; rather, some are repeatedly omitted by skips. From the Council of Constantinople only the Creed is presented. In the papal decrees excerpted from the same collection, many more items were omitted in the same way. Indeed, nothing is brought forward from the decrees of Boniface; nor anything [Col. 0269C] from Hilary, Simplicius, Felix, Symmachus, or the younger Gregory.

3. From the Additions to Dionysius are produced the Precepts of St. Peter concerning the preservation of the sacraments, listed in those Additions as no. 69; the Ancient Statutes of the East, there nos. 70 and 71; and the Canonical Letter, no. 72. From another unknown source is inserted a Decree of Pope Sylvester, beginning: “If any bishop, without any necessity imposed by ecclesiastical reason …,” which is chapter 14 in the Capitula of Martin of Braga [CCXLII]. The documents then return to the Additions to Dionysius: St. Leo’s letter to Theodore of Fréjus, there no. 109; his letter to the Sicilians, no. 110; another to Eutyches, no. 111; examples from the proceedings in which, at the council in Constantinople, the heretic Eutyches was heard and condemned by Bishop Flavian, no. 112; and the judgment of Pope Gelasius, addressed to the bishops throughout Dardania, that the Apostolic See can loose the bonds of all. Also from his letter to the same persons comes the statement that the Apostolic See has the authority, without a synod, both to absolve and to condemn: these two passages are found in the Additions as no. 134. Gelasius’s letter to the Easterners concerning avoidance of communion with Acacius, no. 135; the Decrees of Pope Gelasius, no. 136; and the Decrees of Pope Gregory, no. 137, follow. There is added a letter of the same Gregory to Augustine, whom he sent to Saxony and Britain, with a beginning absent from the common versions and in a form different from them, which we shall provide at the end of this chapter. A fragment of Jerome’s letter to Evangelus follows: “For at Alexandria, etc.” It is found in the Verona edition of the works of the same holy teacher, vol. I, col. 1076.

4. Next, from the Isidorian collection, several apocryphal letters of the ancient pontiffs, or fragments of them, are appended down to Damasus. Then come Nicholas’s letters in the case of Rothadus. In these the scribe seems to have had before his eyes an Isidorian codex like Vallicellian D 38, about which we spoke in chapter 6, no. 29.

5. Next is given Leo’s letter to Dioscorus, which [Col. 0270A], together with what follows, was derived from other collections. Then come a letter of St. Gregory to Serenus, bishop of Marseille; a synod of Pope Zacharias; and Gennadius’s book on Ecclesiastical Rules, inscribed under Augustine’s name. These three are read in the same order in the Additions to Dionysius, nos. 139, 140, and 141. Next comes a fragment of St. Gregory’s letter to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari, and two letters of Innocent I: one to Marcianus, bishop of Naissus, and another to Rufus and the other bishops of Macedonia, beginning, “Great rejoicing has come to me.” Also a letter of Hormisdas to the bishops throughout all the provinces concerning the lapsed: “It is most manifestly clear, etc.,” as it is read at the end of the headings appended to the sixth letter of John II to Caesarius of Arles, vol. V of the Councils, col. 903. This fragment, wrongly inscribed under the name of Hormisdas, is quoted by Gratian, *Decree*, Distinction 50, chapter 29, and also by some others of greater antiquity. See what we shall say in Part IV, chapter 7, § 2, no. 7. There is also St. Gregory’s letter to Etherius, bishop of Lyons, which in the Maurist edition is letter 106 of book IX [Col. 0270B]. Finally come the words of Pope Zacharias: “That no one ought to be joined in marriage with one related by blood, etc.” At the end of the codex was copied a formal letter of the bishop of Pavia to the archbishop of Milan, whose beginning we give here:

“In the name of the Father Π, and of the Son Φ, and of the Holy Spirit Ϲ. A., to the most sacred A., archbishop of the holy Church of Milan, by divine regard, A., bishop of Pavia, offers devoted service in Christ with due reverence. Let your Prudence be held by no uncertainty, because we are daily prepared to obey you in all matters that our ability supplies and ecclesiastical discipline confirms by admonition. Therefore we grant to your Church the `ill.` whom you requested as a minister of your bishopric, so that he may be subject to your bishopric by the same law by which he was subject to ours; and thus you may remove him as though he bore the tonsure of your Church. By this grant, which the sacred canons call a *formata*, etc.”

At the end he notes that the indiction of the present year is the ninth. There are several archbishops of Milan [Col. 0270C] whose names begin with the letter A and whose episcopates coincide with the ninth indiction. The published tables of the bishops of Pavia, however, contain many lacunae. Those who have at hand other documents from Pavia of this period may perhaps find a bishop of Pavia whose name began with A, from which something more certain may be established.

6. Vatican codex 1344, a parchment manuscript in folio from the twelfth century, contains part of a larger collection beginning with number 132, which indicates that the missing portion comprised numbers or chapters 1–131. This portion presents the entire Isidorian collection from Silverius to St. Gregory, the chapters of Hadrian I, and excerpts from the Council of Chalcedon. It also includes more material received from elsewhere and intermingled here and there, which must be noted in this place. It should first be stated that, since the leaves became confused when the codex was rebound, the order is disturbed in many places, so that some items have been placed after those that ought to precede them, while others that should be joined have been separated. To avoid appearing to introduce anything according to our own judgment, we shall follow the order of the codex [Col. 0270D].

At the beginning of the codex, before the documents of Pope Simplicius relating to the case of Acacius, is prefixed the order of the Narrative concerning the wickedness of Dioscorus of Alexandria, which is read in the collection to be published in this volume as chapter 43. Three letters of Simplicius are inserted that are absent from the pure Isidore: one to Zeno Augustus, another to John of Ravenna, and a third to Florentius, Equitius, and Severus. In the Councils these are letters 8, 2, and 3 of the same pontiff. The beginning of the Roman synod under Felix is prefixed to Felix’s letter to the Sicilians; that same letter had been inserted in it. In the section on Silverius, his letter to Vigilius is added; it is contained in the Isidorian Additions. Four items are added in the section on St. Gregory: namely, his letter to Augustine, with the preface to be appended at the end of this chapter; another to Etherius, bishop of Lyons, which we also saw copied in the preceding codex; another to Brunhild, queen, which in the Maurist edition [Col. 0271A] is letter 109 of book IX; and finally several excerpts from letters of the same pontiff. A synodical letter of Pope Martin I against Theodore and Cyrus is also included. Twenty canons taken from Martin’s Lateran Council are given; they are read in vol. VII of the Councils, col. 358 and following.

After Hadrian’s chapters to Angilramnus, this heading is appended: “On the freedom of monks and monasteries.” Then St. Gregory’s letter to all the bishops is produced, as in vol. VI of the Councils, col. 1341, with the subscriptions printed there from a Vatican codex at col. 1343D. Other subscriptions are appended in the same volume from a manuscript of Flavigny. Since the first subscriptions, excerpted by Cardinal Baronius from this codex of ours, as we believe, record the day before the Nones of April and the fourth indiction, this synodical letter of Gregory the Great is assigned to the year 601. It is surprising, however, that no one has observed that these subscriptions were wrongly attached to this synodical letter of Gregory: they were taken from the subscriptions of the bishops of another synod, that of Gregory II in the year 721. The genuine subscriptions of the bishops, corresponding to the period of St. Gregory I, are those supplied by the Flavigny codex; yet no certain year can be deduced from them [Col. 0271B].

After this, fragments of other letters of the same St. Gregory the Great, concerning monks and monasteries, are placed below. Then follow Nicholas I’s letters in the case of Rothadus, bishop of Soissons, which we have also found in other collections. Next come letters 1, 2, 3, and 4 of Pope Vitalian; two letters of St. Isidore of Seville, one to Laudefredus of Córdoba and the other to Masonius; a letter of Justin Augustus to Hormisdas; and a copy of a petition to the same Justin, which appear to have been taken from the Hadriana collection.

There follow the chapters of the Fifth Holy Council held at Constantinople under Justinian. These are the thirteen canons of the same council that were recited and inserted in the Lateran Synod of Martin I. See vol. VII of the Councils, col. 254. Several fragments from the Sixth Ecumenical Council follow under this heading: “The following items are taken from the Sixth Council at Constantinople.” There are also several excerpts from St. Ambrose, from Sacred [Col. 0271C] Scripture, from Saints Jerome and Augustine, and from other Fathers, together with two excerpts from the pseudo-letters of Fabian and Clement.

Then, from the fuller Spanish collection, in addition to the Council of Nicaea and the Council of Constantinople under Theodosius in the era 419, another synod of 163 bishops in the time of Constantine, in the era 720, was transcribed, together with the appended letters of Leo II to the Spaniards, to Quiricus, to Simplicius the count, and of Benedict the presbyter to Peter the regional notary, as well as another letter of the aforementioned Leo II to King Ervig. These are found in precisely this form and order only in the fuller Spanish collection. See chapter 4, no. 11. Then follow the Ephesian Synod, the Council of Chalcedon, the *formata* of Atticus of Constantinople, and the First Council of Carthage under Gratus, as they are presented in the same collection. The remaining councils are absent, and the codex breaks off at the Carthaginian council just mentioned.

We have no doubt that similar collections will be found in other libraries, in which learned men copied documents excerpted here and there from older collections, sometimes complete and sometimes mutilated. These two, however, which we have explained in this chapter, are sufficient for understanding the freer and more variable form of the others [Col. 0271D].

7. We shall conclude with Gregory the Great’s letter to Augustine, which we have included here as an appendix.

[CCXLIV] **Preface to the following letter**

This letter exists in two forms in the common editions. One, which is read in the edition of St. Gregory’s works, contains eleven questions of Augustine and an equal number of Gregory’s answers; in addition, after the ninth answer it appends Augustine’s entreaty and Gregory’s concession. The other, inserted by Bede in book I, chapter 27, of the *History of the English*, joins the first and second answers while omitting the second question; it also suppresses the [Col. 0272A] seventh question and joins the sixth and seventh answers, and it knows nothing of Augustine’s entreaty or Gregory’s concession.

In Vatican codex 1343, however, we have found a third form. It contains a preface to the letter, which all the common books lack, and presents the body of the letter itself in an entirely different arrangement and order. The preface does not appear open to doubt. For not only have we found the same preface in two other manuscripts—namely, Vatican 1344 and Patavine 159 of the Lateran Canons of St. John in the Green Garden—but what it says about the presbyter Laurence and the monk Peter agrees with Bede’s account in the passage cited, where he says that Augustine sent them to Rome, and that they submitted several questions to the holy pontiff and brought back his answers:

“Therefore, the man of God Augustine,” he says, “. . . having returned to Britain, immediately sent to Rome the presbyter Laurence and the monk Peter, who were to report to the blessed pontiff Gregory that the English people had received the faith of Christ and that he himself had been made a bishop; at the same time he received answers to those questions that seemed necessary [Col. 0272B], and these answers we have also thought it useful to insert in this history of ours.”

The gout mentioned in the same opening also agrees with other statements of Gregory himself, in which he disclosed that he had suffered from the pains of gout repeatedly and for many months. See book IX, letters 52 and 124; book X, letter 36; book XI, letter 30; and elsewhere.

There is also a significant difference in the letter itself as found in the aforementioned Vatican codex 1343. Whereas in the common versions and in the two other codices mentioned everything is presented through Augustine’s questions and Gregory’s answers, in this manuscript the questions proposed by Augustine are inserted into the text of the letter itself under such a formula as: “In the first chapter you asked, etc.” This seems to have been the more authentic form of the letter, from which the questions in the common version, perhaps through Bede, were excerpted. In most other copies of letters of this kind the questions are expressed in a not dissimilar manner.

Furthermore, the first chapter comprises the first and second answers [Col. 0272C]; the second contains the third answer; the third, the fourth; the fourth, the tenth; the fifth, the eleventh; and the sixth, the fifth. The other four answers—the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth—together with Augustine’s entreaty and Gregory’s concession, are absent. Since the conclusion and chronological note that occur in Bede’s complete copies of Gregory’s letters are also lacking from this codex, we suspect that this exemplar is mutilated at the end. Nothing can therefore be inferred from it that would lead one to believe that the portions absent from this codex should be rejected as not belonging to St. Gregory. Whatever the truth may be, here now is the letter itself as it is presented in the codex mentioned.

### Letter of Gregory the Great to Augustine

“Also Gregory to Augustine, bishop, whom he had sent to Saxony and Britain [Note: [Col. 0271D] Vatican codex 1344 and Patavine 159 of St. John in the Green Garden add an inscription that agrees completely with the other headings of Gregory’s letters quoted by Bede: ‘To his most reverend brother Augustine, bishop, Gregory, servant of the servants of God.’ [Col. 0272D]]

“Through my beloved sons, Laurence the presbyter and Peter the monk, I received the letters of your Fraternity, in which you wished to ask me about many matters [Col. 0272D]. But since my aforementioned sons found me afflicted with the pains of gout, and, when they pressed to be dismissed more quickly, were released in such a way that they left me amid that same affliction of pain, I was unable to respond at greater length to each matter, as I ought.

“For in the first chapter you asked that a book be sent in which it might be explained how a bishop should conduct himself with his clergy; what portions ought to be made of those things that come to the altar from the offerings of the faithful; and how a bishop ought to act in the Church. Sacred Scripture testifies how well, etc.,” as in the Maurist edition, book XI, letter 64, through the end of the first answer, col. 1151. “Everything was common to them”; after this, the codex joins the second answer, as it is also joined in Bede, as follows:

“But if there are any clerics outside the sacred orders, etc.,” through the end of the same answer.

“In the second chapter you ask why, although the faith is one, the customs of the Churches are different, and why the custom of celebrating Mass is observed one way in the holy Roman Church and another way in the Churches of Gaul. Your Fraternity also adds that you greatly cherish the custom of the Roman Church in which you remember having been nurtured. But it pleases me that whether in the Roman Church, etc.,” as in the common fourth answer, col. 1152.

“In the third chapter you ask what punishment should be imposed if someone has stolen something from the church. But your Fraternity can weigh this according to the person involved, etc.,” as in the common fourth answer.

“In the fourth chapter you asked whether a pregnant woman ought to be baptized, or, after she has given birth, after how much time she may enter the church, or even be baptized; or, lest death overtake what she has borne, after how many days it is permitted to receive the sacrament of holy baptism, or after how much time her husband may join with her in carnal intercourse; or, if she is subject to her monthly period, whether she may enter the church or receive the sacraments of holy Communion [Col. 0273B]; [Col. 0274A] or whether a man who has had intercourse with his wife may enter the church before washing with water, or even approach the ministry of holy Communion. I think that your Fraternity was asked all these things by the unlearned people of the English, to whom I do not doubt that you have already given an answer. But what you yourself have been able to say and think, etc.,” as in the common tenth answer, col. 1157.

“In the fifth chapter you asked whether, after the illusion that ordinarily occurs in a dream, anyone may receive the Lord’s Body, or, if he is a priest, dare to celebrate the sacred ministries. Indeed, the law of the Old Testament calls such a person unclean, as we said in the preceding chapter, etc.,” as in the common eleventh answer, col. 1161.

“In the sixth chapter you asked whether two brothers of the same parents may each marry sisters descended from that distant lineage. But this is permitted in every way; nor is anything found in the sacred writings that appears to contradict this chapter.”

At this point Vatican codex 1343 ends. Two other codices, Vatican 1344 and Patavine 159, after the preface, append nine questions of Augustine and an equal number of answers by St. Gregory, exactly as in Bede.

## PART FOUR. On ancient abridgements of the canons and other Latin collections arranged under headings and commonplaces, down to Gratian

[Col. 0273]

[CCXLVI] ## CHAPTER ONE. On the abridgement of the canons by Ferrandus, deacon of Carthage; several obscure citations explained, others supplemented or corrected, which will be useful for a new edition

[Col. 0273C] 1. Having explained the collections that present canonical documents either in full or nearly in full, we must now discuss those collections that represent abridgements of the canons or distribute the same canons under headings and commonplaces. Among the abridgements, the first place belongs to that of Fulgentius Ferrandus, deacon of the Church of Carthage. He flourished in the time of Justin and Justinian. For in the *Chronicle* of Victor of Tunnuna he is said to have become distinguished in the sixth year after the consulship of Basilius, that is, in the year 547. He used St. Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, as his teacher, as is clear from his writings. Facundus of Hermiane, in book IV of *In Defense of the Three Chapters*, chapter 3, calling Ferrandus “a man worthy of honorable remembrance,” indicates that he had already died. Facundus wrote his books in the year 551, as can be gathered from Victor’s *Chronicle*; consequently, Ferrandus had died before that year. In the preface to his collection, Cresconius calls him [Col. 0273D] “the most reverend deacon of the Church of Carthage” and “a most wise man.” It is unnecessary to list his writings, which are included in volume IX of the *Library of the Fathers*. Several things, however, must be said about the Abridgement of the Canons, which is the subject of our present work.

2. Only two codices of this Abridgement have so far been found: the Troyes codex and the Corbie codex. Francis Pithaeus first published it at Paris in the year 1588 from a codex of the Church of Troyes. Later, Pierre-François Chifflet, S.J., in the Dijon edition of 1649, using the Corbie manuscript, corrected several passages and illuminated them with notes. From these two editions the same little work was reprinted several times and inserted into volume I of the *Bibliotheca canonica*, p. 418, as well as volume IX of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, and elsewhere.

3. In citing the Nicene canons, Ferrandus appears to have followed the version of Philo and Evaristus that had been copied in the African codices of the canons, as we observed in Part II, chapter 2, § 1, no. 4. The numbers of the Nicene canons or headings that he cites agree with the other versions up to canon six [Col. 0274B] [see vol. III of the Councils, col. 449], with which he joins canon seven: for in no. 172 he calls it the seventh heading, although in the common versions it is canon 8. The common canons 9 and 10 are joined together in his no. 87, heading 8. In the published editions he designates canon 11 as heading 9, no. 146. He cites canons 12, 13, and 14 nowhere [Col. 0274C]. Since in no. 18 he assigns the common fifteenth canon to heading 11, the three omitted canons in Ferrandus’s codex were partly joined to the ninth and partly formed the tenth heading. The canon that is canon 16 in the common versions is heading 12 in Ferrandus, no. 27; but canon 17, no. 123, is mistakenly called heading 14, whereas from the series mentioned it ought to be heading 13 [CCXLVII]. For in no. 106 heading 14 is assigned to the common canon 18, and in no. 173 heading 15 is assigned to canon 19. The final Nicene canon, canon 20, is called the first Sardican canon in no. 214; we shall discuss this later.

Two points must be observed here. First, not only the division but also the order of the canons differs from the Isidorian version. The canon concerning deacons, designated as heading 14 after the canon concerning usurers, is placed in the Isidorian version before several other canons. Thus it is confirmed that Ferrandus followed a version different from the Isidorian in these canons. Second, when we conjectured that Ferrandus used the version of Philo and Evaristus [Col. 0274D], the division of the common edition into twenty canons should cause no difficulty. His codex could have presented the same version under a more compressed number of headings, just as the canons of other synods, although identical, receive various divisions in different copies.

4. In the remaining canons of the Greek synods, Ferrandus had before him the interpretation commonly called Isidorian. For, besides the names of the councils of Ancyra and Neocaesarea, which are peculiar to the Isidorian interpretation alone, when in no. 149 he cites heading 17 of the Council of Ancyra, the words “let them pray among the possessed” derive from the Isidorian version alone. Likewise, when in no. 80 he cites heading 8 of the Council of Antioch, the words “vicars of the bishops” agree with that version; and in no. 144 words of the same Isidorian version are repeated from canon 16.

There are more indications in the Laodicean canons. For when in no. 115 he cites heading 5 of Laodicea, the words “usury and profits,” that is, “one-and-a-half-fold,” belong to the Isidorian version. The cited canon 11 [Col. 0275A] in no. 221, the canon designated as 15 in no. 131, the canon indicated as 17 in no. 225, and likewise the canons 25 and 27 cited in nos. 142 and 216—which in the common editions are canons 26 and 28—are either found to have been transcribed entirely in the same words from that version or to preserve its distinctive expressions, as will be clear to anyone who compares them. The same is true of canons 35 and 47, cited in nos. 185 and 200, which in the common Isidore are canons 37 and 47.

Since these examples are sufficient, we omit the rest of the same kind for the sake of brevity. There is no need to discuss the numbers of the canons of each synod when two common canons of the Isidorian interpretation are sometimes combined into one in Ferrandus: anyone can easily understand from comparison which ones have been joined. Concerning the Sardican canons, which Ferrandus cites from the original Latin together with Isidorian readings, only one point deserves notice [Col. 0275B]: in no. 214 the last Nicene canon, concerning the omission of kneeling on Sundays and during the Paschal season, is cited as heading 1 of the Council of Sardica; elsewhere the first canon of that council is cited as heading 2, the second as heading 3, and so forth, so that all the remaining Sardican canons are increased by one number. This arose, as we indicated in Part II, chapter 1, no. 18, because these canons were once joined to the Nicene canons, including those of the Isidorian version. We found both sets joined in this way in the very ancient codex 58 of the chapter of Verona; later, however, in separating them, someone began less accurately with the final Nicene canon and assigned it to the Sardican canons as though it were the first. See Part II, chapter 1, no. 15.

5. More must be said about the African canons, which Ferrandus cites more frequently. Since several councils were held in the same place—for example, at Carthage—and Ferrandus generally uses the formula “the Council of Carthage” when citing the canons of those councils, it is unknown to which Carthaginian council a given canon belongs. In some places the number of a heading or canon is also either missing or corrupt. Since we have devoted considerable labor to distinguishing these synods and supplying or correcting the numbers of the headings [Col. 0275C], we believe it will be useful to explain here, omitting those citations of Ferrandus that are clear in themselves, the obscure citations, following the sequence of the Ferrandian Abridgement, and to identify the council to which each canon belonged.

**No. 4.** The Council of Carthage, heading 49, is cited in Ferrandus’s Abridgement. This is the synod of the year 397; the canon itself is read in the African Church codex, chapter 49, which codex is published in vol. II of the Councils, Venetian edition, col. 1252 and following.

[CCXLVIII] **No. 5.** Council of Carthage, heading 50. This is the same synod of the year 397, canon 50 of the African Codex.

**No. 9.** Council of Carthage, heading 10. This is the same synod. The canon, however, is read as chapter 18 of the African Codex.

**No. 13.** Council of Carthage, heading 52; also heading 54, “Council of Carthage in the basilica,” heading 5. The first is the same council of the year 397, chapters 34 and 56 of the African Codex. The second, however, is another council, from the year 407, chapter 98 of the African Codex.

**No. 14.** Council of Carthage, heading 54. This is the synod of the year 397, chapter 56 of the African Codex [Col. 0275D].

**No. 15.** Council of Carthage, heading 3; heading 26 should be read instead. This is the synod of the year 397, chapter 36 of the African Codex.

**No. 16.** Council of Carthage, heading 1. We believe that the council under Genethlius in the year 390, chapter 2, is indicated; consequently, heading 2 should be read in Ferrandus instead of heading 1. This canon is found repeated in the Council of Carthage of the year 419, chapter 3 of the African Codex.

**No. 17.** Council of Carthage, heading 6. This is the synod of the year 401, on the Ides of September, chapter 71 of the African Codex.

The canon itself is read in full in the Abridgement of the Council of Hippo of the year 393, which was repeated and inserted into the Council of Carthage of the year 397. See the Abridgement in the collection printed in this volume, col. 89, and compare what we noted in this [Col. 0276A] connection in Part II, chapter 3, § 3, concerning the fifth canon of the synod of the year 397.

**No. 25.** Council of Carthage, heading 12. This is the council of the year 418, chapter 120 of the African Codex. Although it is canon 13 there, we have shown in Part II, chapter 3, § 7, no. 1, that in Ferrandus’s codex this canon had been joined with the twelfth.

**No. 27.** Council of Carthage, heading 28; also heading 53. This is the synod of the year 397. The heading, or canon 28, omitted from the African Codex, is contained in the Abridgement of Hippo, chapter 19. Heading 53, however, is found in chapter 54 of the African Codex.

**No. 28.** Council of Carthage, heading 14. It belongs to the council of the year 401, chapter 80 of the African Codex.

**No. 30.** Council of Carthage, heading 18. This is the synod of the year 418, chapter 126 of the African Codex.

**No. 32.** Council of Carthage, heading 15. This is the synod of the year 401, on the Ides of September, chapter 81 of the African Codex.
