From these materials it is clear that Ferrandus possessed, besides the code of Greek canons of the Isidorian version—in which the canons of Chalcedon, never cited by him, appear to have been lacking—codes of African canons containing the two Councils under Gratus and Genethlius and all the synods under Aurelius through the Council of Hippo of 427. It should not seem strange, however, that he never mentioned the Council of Hippo held under the same Aurelius in 393, nor the canons of the first session of the Council of Carthage of 419. For he judged it preferable to cite the canons of that Council of Hippo from the Council of Carthage of 397, into which their Breviary had been inserted. The thirty-three canons of the first session of the Council of Carthage of 419 he cited partly from earlier and partly from later synods, in which they had either been enacted or repeated. He also used a special code of the canons of the province of Byzacena, from which he cites several synods of that same province. See what we noted on this subject in Part II, chapter 3, § 9, no. 5, where we also touched on the Council of Zella and the two letters of Siricius inserted into that synod, which he cites repeatedly.

## CHAPTER II  
### On the Collection, or Chapters, of St. Martin, Bishop of Braga

1. After Ferrandus’s Breviary, the Collection of Chapters of St. Martin, bishop of Braga, deserves mention. He flourished in the same century. St. Gregory of Tours testifies in his *History of the Franks*, book V, chapter 38, that he was born in Pannonia [Col. 0279B]; consequently Garsias Loaisa was mistaken in believing him to have been Greek. From Pannonia he migrated eastward to visit the holy places, where he cultivated Greek literature and the best branches of learning. He progressed so far in them that he was inferior to none of the most learned men of his time. From the East he crossed into Galicia, where he converted the Suevic peoples from Arian impiety, established for them the rule of faith and the precepts of religion, instructed the churches, and founded monasteries, as St. Isidore of Seville has recorded (*On Illustrious Men*, chapter 22, or 35).

He is said to have built the monastery of Dumium at the Tenth Council of Toledo, canon 3, of which he was also the first abbot. The same St. Isidore calls him bishop of the monastery of Dumium in his *History of the Goths*. This episcopal dignity, first conferred upon the Church of Dumium in recognition of Martin’s merits, passed to several of his successors. For this reason, some have not implausibly interpreted the bishop Martin who is recorded as a signatory at the First Council of Braga in 563—or, as Loaisa believes, in 561—as our Martin, bishop of Dumium. Indeed, since at the Second Council of Braga the same Martin declared that the decrees of the First Council of Braga had already been confirmed by him, while at that time Lucretius held the see of Braga, he could certainly have confirmed those decrees at the First Council under no other title than that of bishop of Dumium.

To this period, when he was bishop of Dumium, that Latin translation mentioned by Sigebert in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 117, appears to belong: “Bishop Martin, through the agency of the deacon Paschasius, translated in the monastery of Dumium many questions and answers of the holy Egyptian Fathers.” This translation was published in the appendix to the *Lives of the Fathers*, printed by the Plantin press in 1628. Rosweyde notes, however, that in two manuscripts only Martin’s name is given. Among these, an old book of St. Florian, written in the ninth century, bears this title: “Questions and Answers of the Egyptian Fathers, which Bishop Martin translated from Greek into Latin [Col. 0279D] in the monastery of Dumium.”

Paschasius’s translation may instead be assigned to another similar work printed in the same edition as book seven, which the manuscripts attribute to Paschasius as translator. Martin was subsequently promoted to the see of Braga and presided over the Second Council of Braga in 572, to which he subscribed: “Martin, bishop of the metropolitan Church of Braga.” The statement of St. Gregory of Tours, which assigns approximately thirty years to his priestly office, concerns not only the bishopric of Braga but also that of Dumium.

2. Among his works, the one relevant to our undertaking is a collection of eighty-four canons or chapters divided into two parts. The first sets out matters relating to bishops and the clergy as a whole; the second encompasses matters concerning the laity. He compiled this collection chiefly from Greek canons translated into Latin. In the prefatory letter he explained the reason for composing it in these words:

“The canons established in the regions of the East by the ancient Fathers were first formulated in the Greek language; afterward, as time passed, they were translated into Latin. Since it is difficult to transfer something from one language into another in a simpler form, and since it also happens that, over so long a period, writers—whether because they did not understand or because they were asleep—omit many things, some matters in the canons themselves consequently appear obscure to simpler readers. Therefore I decided, with all diligence, to restore in a simpler and more accurate form both what the translators had expressed obscurely and what the copyists had altered.”

The Latin translation of the Greek canons that was current in Spain, and that was consequently incorporated into the Hispanic Collection, is the translation later received by Isidore and commonly called the Isidorian version. In this version Martin found certain passages rendered obscurely. In some copies he also found certain matters altered or omitted by scribes who either understood too little or were inattentive. In the notes to the same version contained in the code of canons soon to be published, we shall point out several passages translated and modified with greater freedom, as well as certain shorter portions that were omitted.

3. Paschasius Quesnel, *Dissertation* 12, no. 10, believes that Martin composed his collection from the ancient translation contained in the *Code of Canons* published by Quesnel, and not from the Greek; he declares that those who proclaim Martin the author of a new translation of the canons were deluded. We shall refute in our Observations on that same Dissertation 12, chapter 2, no. 10, the arguments he brings to prove that Martin used the cited *Code of Canons*.

That Martin composed his collection from a Greek code, and not from any ancient version, is indicated not only by the words quoted above, in which he demonstrates that he compared the Greek text with the commonly used translations, but is also evident from the Chapters themselves, which agree with no Latin translation. It is true, however, that Martin did not propose to labor over a new translation of the Greek synods. Rather, by a new and easier method, he wished to compose a new and concise collection from those chapters that seemed more useful to clergy and laity:

“While also observing this,” he says, “that the matters relating to bishops or the clergy as a whole should be written together in one section; and similarly that the matters relating to the laity should be gathered together, so that anyone who wishes to know about a particular chapter may find it more quickly.”

To promote the readers’ understanding and convenience in this matter, he examined the canons of the Greek synods chiefly in the Greek source itself; but he did not always translate into Latin those that he judged useful and worthy of excerpting. For the most part, he reported them in such a way that he explained at greater length certain matters that seemed obscure to simpler readers, omitted others, and even inserted some material as he judged more useful for the discipline of his people. It was, we believe, on account of this freedom that he never indicated from where this or that chapter had been taken.

With the same purpose, he corrected chapter 39, the tenth canon—or, in another enumeration, the ninth—of the Synod of Ancyra, which he had before his eyes, and adapted it to Western discipline. That canon permits deacons who, at their ordination, had declared that they wished to marry, but nevertheless received ordination, to remain in the ministry if they later entered marriage. Martin, however, forbids the ordination of those who have made such a declaration.

Since no chapter is produced that in any respect agrees with the canons of Chalcedon, Martin appears to have used a Greek code that lacked those canons.

[CCLIII] 4. Although readers of the preface might think that everything excerpted from the Eastern synods came from those synods, some material was also drawn from Latin sources. It is certain that certain passages were taken in almost the same words from the First Council of Toledo; some others, though more rarely, appear to have been derived from the First Council of Braga and from the African councils. We believe, however, that not a few passages—which until now have not been found in any Greek or Latin canons earlier than Martin—should be attributed to Martin himself.

In the edition included in the *Bibliotheca of Canon Law* by Gulielmus Voellus and Henricus Justellus, the canons of the councils from which Martin’s individual chapters are believed to have been extracted are annotated opposite each chapter as though they were its sources. This diligence is useful and commendable, and the editors ascribe it to Joannes Doujatius. Yet the Eighth Nicene Canon and the Thirty-ninth Laodicean Canon agree so little with Chapters 36 and 73, to which they are attached, that it is not easy to believe that Martin had those canons in mind in these chapters.

The case is the same, indeed much stronger, with respect to the Second Council of Tours, whose Canon 22, or 23, is placed together with the Laodicean canon alongside the cited Chapter 73, and with respect to the Council of Agde, whose Canon 64 is assigned to Chapter 64 as well. For, apart from the fact that the cited canons agree poorly with those chapters, it is incredible that these Gallic synods were before St. Martin’s eyes, since he is not found to have excerpted anything from the Gallic councils.

Moreover, since the Second Council of Tours was held at approximately the same time as Martin composed the Chapters, and since it is not found inserted even in the later and fuller Hispanic Collection, it appears to have been unknown to the Spaniards. Why a canon of some council from book VI of the *Capitularies*, no. 198, is attached to Chapter 68, we do not understand. For not only does that canon fail to agree with Martin’s chapter, but no council earlier than Martin is cited there from which the chapter could have been excerpted.

Some, deceived by this annotation, have made the much worse claim that Martin also took canons from the *Capitularies*, which were compiled long after his time. For a similar reason, the citation of the Third Council of Arles, Canon 5, drawn from no. 194 of the same book of the *Capitularies* and attached to Chapter 69, is not convincing, especially since nothing of the sort is found in the canons of the Third Council of Arles.

The materials attributed by Ivo of Chartres to the Councils of Carthage and Braga in connection with Chapters 65, 74, and 75 are nothing other than the actual words of these chapters of Martin, which cannot be found in any Council of Carthage or Braga. Perhaps Ivo called the Council of Braga the very chapters of Martin that some people designate under the name of the Council of Braga.

These canons, therefore, together with the others mentioned shortly before, appear to be attributable to Martin himself. Some think that certain Apostolic Canons have been wrongly assigned to Chapters 26 and 27, especially because they believe that Martin was unaware of them, or even that they had not yet been composed while he was in the East. We have shown in Part I, chapter 1, that they are much older. Certainly Dionysius Exiguus, who composed his collection before St. Martin, had already translated them from Greek into Latin.

Whether Martin took anything from the cited Apostolic Canons and, in his usual manner, explained it more fully, or whether these Chapters 26 and 27 should likewise be counted among those of which he himself was the author, we do not dare to determine.

5. Martin addressed this collection of Chapters to Nitigius and the entire Council of Lugo. Nitigius, with his suffragan bishops, took part in the Second Council of Braga, over which Martin presided. These same chapters are believed to have been read and confirmed at that council. What is reported to have been read and confirmed there, however, was not these chapters but the acts of the First Council of Braga, as is clear from Martin’s own intervention.

These chapters were preserved for us by the Hispanic Collection, from which they passed into the Isidorian Collection. They were first published from the Isidorian manuscript used by Merlin; later Loaisa reprinted them on the authority of manuscripts of the pure Hispanic Collection. Justellus and Voellus recorded the readings of both editions and the manuscript variants with the utmost diligence in the appendix to volume I of the *Bibliotheca of Canon Law*.

In the very extensive manuscript collection of canons belonging to the Paris College of the Society of Jesus, these chapters are entitled “The Council of Pope Martin,” as P. Hardouin noted. Hence it is not surprising that some later collectors of canons occasionally cite them as decrees, or as a council, of Pope Martin. Led by this error, some people, thinking that these same chapters had been sanctioned by St. Martin I, supreme pontiff, at a Roman council, attributed to that pontiff the relaxation of discipline by which these chapters permit bigamists to remain in the lower grades of orders. Consequently, they also maintained that, by virtue of these same chapters—which they attributed to Pope Martin—a bishop could even at that time dispense with a bigamist in the lower orders. Sixtus V eventually rejected this opinion as resting on a false foundation, as may be seen in Fagnanus’s Commentary on the second chapter *De bigamis*.

## CHAPTER III  
### On the Breviary and Collection of Cresconius

1. Two works by Cresconius—or, as others prefer, Crisconius—an African bishop, are mentioned: one, the *Concordance of Canons*; the other, a poem on the Libyan Wars. We have seen both works identified in the Vallicellian manuscript 18, page 136, where a table of the contents of that same codex is given.

Under the first item in that table are these words: “The *Concordance of Canons*, compiled by Cresconius, African bishop, under three hundred chapters.” This Cresconius, it says, described in hexameter verse the wars and victories that Johannes the patrician waged in Africa against the Saracens, in books . . .

Only the first work survives. The second, which has thus far been lost, was contained under the title *On the Libyan Wars* in a manuscript of the monastery of Monte Cassino among the books said to have been added to the library of that monastery by Desiderius, abbot and later Roman pontiff Victor III, according to the contemporary author Leo of Ostia in the *Cassinese Chronicle*, book III, chapter 63.

The knowledge of this work has nevertheless yielded the useful information that Cresconius’s date can be determined from it. Since the victory of the aforementioned Johannes the patrician is dated both by Anastasius the Librarian in his *Ecclesiastical History* and by Cedrenus to the third year of the emperor Leontius—that is, [Col. 0282C] the year of Christ 697—Cresconius, who described it in verse, flourished at that time.

2. We now turn to the other work, entitled the *Concordance of Canons*. This work, which he compiled at the request of Bishop Liberinus, contains the entire collection of Dionysius divided into three hundred titles. It does not present entire councils or the complete letters of the Roman pontiffs, as they are read in Dionysius, in continuous sequence; rather, it gathers together all the decrees of councils and pontiffs that relate to a single subject, excerpted from various places, and places them under definite titles.

Since this work was not published all at once but in separate portions, its nature has not been sufficiently understood. In 1588, under the direction of Franciscus Pithoeus, only that portion of the work of Cresconius was published together with Ferrandus’s Breviary which, after Cresconius’s preface to Liberinus, does not present complete canons or complete decrees but merely gives a brief indication, under each title, of the chapters of canons and decrees corresponding to it, as we observed in the case of Ferrandus’s Breviary.

The edition bore this title at its beginning: “The Canonical Breviary of Crisconius, African Bishop. Here is contained the *Concordance of the Canons of the Councils and of the Roman Prelates*—namely, of the Apostolic Canons, the Nicene, Ancyran, Neocaesarean, Gangrian, Antiochene, Laodicean, Chalcedonian, Sardican, and Carthaginian canons; likewise of the prelates Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Celestine, Leo, and Gelasius.”

We found the opening words of this title, “The Canonical Breviary of Crisconius, African Bishop,” in no manuscript; in all of them the title begins with the words, “Here is contained the Concordance,” and so forth. Yet it is not inappropriate that this first part should be called a Breviary, since it presents not the complete work of the *Concordance* but only a summary of it.

This same Cresconian Breviary was later reprinted by many and inserted, together with Ferrandus’s Breviary, in volume I of the *Bibliotheca of Canon Law*, page 456. When, after that volume had been completed, Gulielmus Voellus [Col. 0283A] and Henricus Justellus, the editors of the cited *Bibliotheca*, obtained from a manuscript of the library of the Clermont College of the Society of Jesus the complete work of the *Concordance of Canons*, in which the entire canons were transcribed and distributed under titles, they printed it separately in the appendix to that volume, page 33, as a second work distinct from the Breviary, with this title:

“Book of Canons of Crisconius, African Bishop, in which he transcribed the complete canons of the councils and the decrees of the pontiffs in the same order in which they are cited in the Breviary.”

3. This method of publication led several learned men, who had been unable to inspect manuscripts of the complete work, to divergent opinions. Some regarded the Breviary and the Book of Canons as two works by Cresconius. Others preferred to believe that Cresconius wrote only the later work, in which the complete canons are set out, and suspected that the Breviary had been excerpted by someone else who thought Cresconius’s work too lengthy and wished to provide a bare summary of the canons to aid the memory.

P. Coustant was initially uncertain whether Cresconius had composed a Book of Canons in addition to the Breviary. To decide the matter on the authority of the more celebrated manuscripts, he wrote from Rome to his colleagues and friends, asking them to examine the Vallicellian and Vatican manuscripts cited by Cardinal Baronius. When they replied that in both places there was no manuscript except one containing the mere Breviary, he finally concluded that Cresconius had composed only the Breviary.

As for the fuller Book of Canons, he conjectured that some diligent scholar had been found who clothed the Canonical Breviary with flesh over its skeletal framework—that is, who, following the form of the *Concordance* outlined by Cresconius, transcribed the complete canons in place of their summaries, while preserving the original order of subjects and the number of titles (*Preface to volume I of the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, nos. 125–126).

He was confirmed in this opinion by the Clermont manuscript from which the same Book of Canons had been published. For after the Breviary, which is preceded by Cresconius’s preface, there follows in that manuscript a sort of preface placed before the Book of Canons. In the judgment even of the editors themselves, many considerations show that this preface is not by Cresconius. The Book of Canons itself, which follows immediately, bears the name of Cresconius neither at the beginning nor anywhere else.

4. We, however, who have fortunately succeeded in finding and examining several copies of Cresconius’s work, will be able to establish the matter with greater certainty. We have indeed acquired four codices in which only what is called the Breviary is read, without the fuller Book of Canons: namely, Vatican manuscripts 1353 and 5845, Vallicellian A 5, and the Vercelli manuscript. All of them contain the Dionysian, or Dionysio-Hadrian, Collection together with the Dionysian Additions.

In these manuscripts Cresconius’s Breviary is placed before the collection of Dionysius from which it was excerpted. The Book of Canons is absent from them because the collection of Dionysius itself, which follows immediately, contains in full the documents indicated in the same Breviary. The Book of Canons, in which those same documents are repeated by another method and distributed under titles, therefore appeared superfluous. Anyone can easily find the canons and pontifical decrees in that collection from the numbers of the titles marked in the Breviary, which correspond exactly to the Dionysian Collection.

Those colleagues and friends of P. Coustant inspected only these manuscripts and reported to him that only the Breviary could be found in the Vatican and Vallicellian cases. A similar manuscript must have come into the hands of Franciscus Pithoeus, since he published the mere Breviary. But since the purpose of these manuscripts was not to present Cresconius’s complete work, but to excerpt from Cresconius the portion that seemed useful to the Dionysian Collection, nothing can be inferred from them in favor of assigning only the Breviary to Cresconius—especially since all the other manuscripts that present Cresconius without the Dionysian Collection never exhibit the Breviary alone, but always both the Breviary and the fuller Book of Canons.

[Col. 0284A] 5. We found six manuscripts of this kind: namely, Verona 60; Vatican Palatine 579; Vatican Regina 849; Vatican 1347 and 5748; and Vallicellian XVIII. Of these, the oldest and closest to Cresconius’s time is the copy of the chapter of Verona marked with the number 60, believed to have been written in the eighth century. The Vatican Palatine codex 579 is somewhat later.

In all these manuscripts the Breviary is joined to the Book of Canons in such a way that it is clear that both are the work of the same Cresconius. It is also evident that the Breviary functions as an index or table of the chapters of the fuller work, or Book of Canons, which in the Clermont manuscript follows immediately, without the intervening preface improperly inserted there.

For this reason, what is called the Breviary in the printed editions is more properly entitled *Chapters* in the manuscripts, both at the beginning and at the end. At the beginning, after Cresconius’s preface to Liberinus—as it is also read in the Pithoean edition—the following words appear: “Next follow the Chapters.” At the end: “The Chapters are finished,” or “The Chapter-book of the Canons is finished.”

[CCLVI] This name, *Chapters*, ordinarily indicates an index of the work that follows, as we learn from certain other collections. Cresconius evidently wished to imitate Dionysius, from whom he excerpted his own collection. Just as Dionysius prefixed to his collection an index or table entitled “Titles of the Canons,” so Cresconius prefixed an index of the chapters.

Therefore, these Chapters—or this Breviary—which is prefixed under the name of Cresconius in all the manuscripts, both of the first and of the second type, cannot be assigned to anyone other than Cresconius himself.

6. The more extensive book, which immediately follows the same chapters in so many and such ancient codices, is attributed to Cresconius himself in the preface in such a way that there can be no doubt about its author. For he relates that he was urged by Bishop Liberinus to gather into one work all the canonical enactments which, from the very beginnings of the Christian warfare, both the holy apostles and apostolic men had promulgated through the succession of the ages, and, by establishing their **CONCORD**, inserting also a **LIST OF THE TITLES**, [Col. 0284C] to explain them more clearly. The distinction between the Concord, which indicates the book of the canons itself, and the preliminary listing of the titles, which corresponds to the Breviary or Chapters, is noteworthy.

But while seeking to avoid this labor, Cresconius had proposed that this Breviary of the canons had already been arranged by the most reverend Ferrandus, deacon of the Church of Carthage, and that it ought to suffice for our instruction. Liberinus replied that this work of Ferrandus—which indicates only the titles of the canons and does not set out the canons themselves—was insufficient for the unlearned, who constitute the great majority, since Ferrandus had placed it before them “for investigating matters which are neither found by everyone nor, when found, read through without boredom.” No one, indeed, is unaware how burdensome it is for a reader when, eagerly awaiting knowledge of a particular matter, he is directed to a book which he perhaps has not read or does not know where to find.

[Col. 0284D] Liberinus therefore requested not a mere Breviary like Ferrandus’s, which would list only the titles of the canons, but that the canons themselves be transcribed in full; this required the more extensive work. Cresconius declares that he yielded to this request:

> “I have deemed it necessary,” he says, “to list beforehand, as has been said, in this work, under a series of titles, all the ecclesiastical enactments that have come to our knowledge, and to remove the labyrinth of uncertainty for those able and willing to learn them, so that their complete instruction may henceforth depend not upon the difficulty of the writer but upon the reader’s negligence.”

The words “to list beforehand under a series of titles” signify the Breviary placed first, in which, following Ferrandus’s example, the titles or chapters of the canons are listed in advance. The “complete instruction” by which the labyrinth of uncertainty is removed for those able and willing to learn refers to the more extensive work. From it, indeed, it will follow that if anyone lacks full instruction in the canons, this will depend not upon the difficulty of the writer, who avoided transcribing the longer canons, but upon the reader’s negligence.

Both works, therefore, must be attributed to Cresconius—or rather, both parts belong to one and the same work, entitled the *Concord of the Canons*.

[Col. 0285A] 7. A complete edition of this work, based on the evidence of the codices that preserve it in its entirety, should be arranged as follows. First, this heading should be placed at the beginning:

> “Here is contained the Concord of the Canons of the Councils listed below,” etc., as we have already given it in no. 2.

There should follow the preface or letter of Cresconius to Liberinus, with the heading:

> “Here begins the preface of Cresconius concerning the Concord of the Canons, addressed to Liberinus.”

Then the Breviary should be transcribed, with the heading:

> “The chapters follow,”

as the published text has it in Codex Vat. Palat. 579; or:

> “Here begin the chapters,”

as it is read in the Veronese codex. At the end of the Breviary should appear:

> “The chapters are completed,”

or, as we have observed in other manuscripts:

> “The chapters of the Concord of the Canons have been completed.”

Next should be placed the Book of Canons itself. In both the Claromontane codex and the aforementioned Palatine codex it bears the heading:

> “Here begins the Book of Canons”;

in Vallicellian manuscript 18, however:

> “Likewise, the Concord of the Canons.”

The passages read in the appendix to volume I of the *Bibliotheca Juris Canonici*, p. 33—“The bishop who is to be ordained,” etc.—were inserted into the Claromontane manuscript and taken from canon 1 of the published Fourth Council of Carthage. They should therefore be omitted, and Cresconius’s book should begin with no. 1:

> “On the ordination of a bishop. In the canons of the apostles,”

as in the same appendix, pp. 34 and following. At the end there should be the closing formula:

> “The Concord of the Canons is completed.”

The Vatican Palatine codex adds:

> “Written by Cresconius for Blessed Liberinus, the pontiff.”

As for the number of chapters, the published division into three hundred chapters should be retained, since it is confirmed by most of the older codices. If, however, Vatican Codex 1347 and Vat. Palat. 579 divide the work into 301 chapters, while another Helmstedt codex cited by Fabricius divides it into 303, this is because they split one or another chapter into two. Conversely, in Vat. Reginae 849 the number 297 chapters is given, since some have been joined into one. This is Cresconius’s pure and complete collection.

8. At this point we must not omit the Cresconian collection frequently cited by the eminent Baronius, by the Roman editors of the letters of the Roman pontiffs, [Col. 0285C] and, after them, by Binius and others—a collection contained in the Vallicellian manuscript and in another Vatican codex. Since certain documents cited or excerpted from it are found neither in Cresconius nor in Dionysius, considerable difficulty has arisen for many.

From the codices mentioned above we discovered that the name “Cresconian collection” had been applied to Vallicellian Codex A 5 and Vatican Codex 1353, which begin with Cresconius’s preface and Breviary. Since the Dionysio-Hadriana collection follows the Breviary, together with several other documents that we listed and described among the Dionysian Additions in part III, chapter 3, all these materials were carelessly cited under the same name, “Cresconian collection.”

Since Cresconius’s date was not yet certain and his complete work was not known from other manuscripts, it was easy to attribute to Cresconius, whose preface is transcribed at the beginning, the entire collection contained in the codices mentioned above. This was so even though most of its documents are nowhere indicated in the Breviary, and some are in fact later than Cresconius’s lifetime.

[Col. 0285D] 9. Another error concerning the work of Cresconius is also revealed—namely, the error of those who formerly thought that Burchard, bishop of Worms, and Ivo, bishop of Chartres, were the first to depart from the practice of the ancients in their collections, who had published synods and letters of the Roman pontiffs in full and in chronological order, by dividing them into sections and distributing them under titles.

Nor should it seem surprising that otherwise very learned men held this view, since no collection older than those bishops had yet appeared in which the same method could be detected. The first example of this method among Latin writers is supplied by Cresconius. He alone excerpted decrees from the documents of a single Dionysian collection. Later writers, taking more material from other sources as well, divided it into books and titles; in addition, they introduced the sentences of the holy Fathers and sometimes even testimonies from the laws of emperors, [Col. 0286A] as will become clear from what will be said about certain collections and collectors who preceded Burchard and Ivo.

# CHAPTER IV. On the abbreviation of the canons contained in manuscript 59 of the chapter-house of Verona and in another, 88, of the chapter-house of the Church of Lucca

1. The Veronese parchment codex, filthy from the many vicissitudes of time, is of a smaller square format. Its letters are large, but they have been written so awkwardly and distortedly that it is extremely difficult to read. It appears to belong to the eighth century.

It contains an abbreviation of the canons and enactments of the Apostolic See, divided, as it were, into two parts. One presents in abridged form the canons of the councils; the other, the apostolic enactments. The author was very inexperienced and sometimes failed to grasp correctly the meaning of the same canons and enactments, [Col. 0286B] explaining them incorrectly—so much so that nothing useful can be extracted from his abridgements for explaining or correcting the original texts.

Sometimes he does not summarize all the decrees of a synod or enactment, but only those he happened to choose. He also repeatedly joins two canons into one, thereby reducing the number of canons, although in reality he omits no canon. Occasionally, but more rarely, he carelessly repeats the same canon in abbreviated form with different wording.

To this are added the errors and barbarisms of a thoroughly incompetent copyist, which will be sufficiently apparent from the notice he placed at the end of the codex; as a result, the entire codex became still more corrupted. [CCLVIII] Nevertheless, since this very ancient abbreviation was taken from codices and collections of canons much older than itself, it retains certain indications of a more remote antiquity and supplies us with quite a few useful things. For that reason, this abbreviation is by no means to be considered insignificant.

[Col. 0286C] P. Joannes Dominicus Mansi discovered the same abbreviation in another very ancient codex of the chapter-house of the cathedral church of Lucca. He described it in his *Commentary on a Celebrated Codex Written in the Age of Charlemagne*, as may be seen in volume XLV of the *Opuscula* of P. Angelo Maria Calogera, p. 114. He also frequently mentions the same abbreviation in volumes I and II of P. Labbe’s *Supplement to the Councils*, in which he printed certain portions of it.

Although the marquis Scipio Maffei had discussed some matters concerning this same abbreviation, contained in the Veronese manuscript, before Mansi, in his *Notice of Chapter-House Codices*, inserted in the appendix to the *Theological History*, p. 78, it will nevertheless be quite useful to present here a more accurate description of it, together with appropriate observations.

2. This title is found in our Veronese codex:

> “Here begin the chapters of all the holy councils established by the blessed Fathers, or of the decretal letters decreed by pontiffs or apostolic men, collected and written down in brief.”

[Col. 0286D] There follows a table or index of the chapters of the first part, which concerns the canons of the councils.

**I. Excerpts from the councils by St. Martin, bishop of Galicia.** In the body of the work this title is more accurately expressed as follows:

> “Sentences excerpted from the canons alone, from the book of Martin, bishop of Galicia, concerning various councils.”

Eighty-four canons are presented in abridged form, exactly as many as the chapters of the same Martin are listed as having in the published editions.

**II. Chapters of the Council of Nicaea and of the Council of Sardica, where Hosius was present, as the 214 African bishops of the council testify.** In the body of the work, preceded by the notation “From the Complutensian book,” it is more accurately written:

> “From the Council of Nicaea, or from other councils.”

Ninety-one abbreviated canons are presented, without any indication of the synod to which each belongs. Their sentences had to be compared with the published texts in order to discover which council they belonged to.

The first seventeen canons are Nicene. The following twenty-one, [Col. 0287A] numbers 18 through 38, are Sardican. Canon 39, however, is the final Nicene canon concerning the omission of kneeling on Sundays and during the Paschal season. Then, from no. 40 through no. 55, come the canons of Ancyra. After that, the Neocaesarean canons are mixed with additional Ancyrene canons through no. 72. The Gangran canons follow from no. 73 through no. 83, and the section concludes with the Antiochene canons, from no. 84 through no. 91.

Three points here deserve notice. First, in that earlier collection from which these ninety-one canons were excerpted in abridged form, not only the Constantinopolitan and Chalcedonian canons, it seems, but also the Laodicean canons were absent, since the abbreviator presented not even one of them.

Second, since the canons reported here lack the notation of their respective councils, while the title prefixed to them in the body of the work expressly mentions only Nicaea, an inattentive reader might have had occasion to cite the following canons also as Nicene, although they are not Nicene. Perhaps St. Gregory of Tours used a similar collection when he cited a Gangran canon under the name of Nicaea.

Third, since the Sardican [Col. 0287B] canons, placed after the Nicene canons, are concluded by the final Nicene canon, there is substantial evidence that the author of this abbreviation copied them from a codex in which they were joined to and inserted among the Nicene canons and were entitled under the name of the Nicene canons. If, in the heading of the table prefixed at the beginning of the codex, the Sardican rather than the Nicene canons are mentioned, this may have been done by the author of the abbreviation, who had found the two groups distinguished in other manuscripts.

**III. Chapters of the Council of Nicaea given by Pope Innocent.** In the title inserted in the body of the work:

> “From the letter of Pope Innocent concerning the Council of Nicaea.”

These are twenty-two Nicene canons from the abbreviation of Rufinus. We have seen that this abbreviation was received in Gallican codices in place of the canons themselves and was sometimes used by Gallicans; see part II, chapter 10, § 2. The abbreviator may have attributed these chapters to Pope Innocent [Col. 0287C] because the cited Rufinian abbreviation followed Innocent’s letters in his codex. P. Mansi published these chapters from the Lucan codex in volume I of the *Supplement to the Councils*, p. 277.

**IV. From the Council of Arles.** Twenty canons of the First Council of Arles of the year 314.

[CCLIX] **V. From the Council of Ancyra, 18 canons.**

**VI. From the Council of Neocaesarea, 12 canons.**

**VII. From the Council of Gangra, 19 canons.**

**VIII. From the Council of Laodicea in Phrygia, 53 canons.**

**IX. From the Council of Constantinople, 5 canons.**

**X. From the Council of Ephesus, 12 canons.** These are the twelve anathemas from the letter of St. Cyril to Nestorius.

**XI. From the Council of Chalcedon, 27 canons.**

**XII. From the Council of Antioch, 24 canons.**

Although all these canons of the councils of Greece are abbreviated, they clearly indicate the so-called Isidorian translation. The author of this abbreviation therefore found an older codex containing all these councils of Greece, collected into one body in the same version; among them, the letter of St. Cyril to Nestorius [Col. 0287D] was inscribed under the name of the Council of Ephesus, as it was later received in the Hispanic and Isidorian collections.

**XIII. From the Council of Valence, on the fourth day before the Ides of July, in the consulship of Gratian and Equitius, in the year 374, 4 canons.**

**XIV. From the Council of Riez, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the seventeenth year of Theodosius Augustus, in the consulship of Messala, a man of consular rank, in the year 439, 6 canons.**

**XV. From the Council of Orange, on the sixth day before the Ides of November, in the year 441, 27 canons.**

**XVI. From the Council of Vaison, on the Ides of November, in the consulship of Dioscorus—the other consul being omitted—in the year 442, 8 canons.**

**XVII. From the Council of Orléans, in the year 511, 27 canons.**

**XVIII. From the Council of Arles, usually called the Second, 36 canons.**

**XIX. From the Synod of Carthage in Africa, in the consulship of Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII, chapter 103.** This is the collection which in other manuscripts is entitled *Ancient Statutes* [Col. 0288A] and which will be published in this volume among the documents of ancient canon law, no. 3. See part II, chapter 3, § 4, where we discussed the different titles of these same statutes.

**XX. From the Synod of Carthage, on the Ides of August, in the consulship of Ceranius—read Caesarius—that is, in the year 397, chapter 71.** These seventy-one chapters were published from the Lucan manuscript by P. Mansi in volume I of the *Supplement to the Councils*, p. 255. It is the Hipponian Breviary, marked by the same chronological notation, and it will be printed in chapter 2 of the collection to be included in this volume. The canons of this Breviary are considerably fewer. But just as the aforementioned collection accepted two additional African canons, so in this abbreviation many more were added from the Third Council of Carthage and other African synods.

**XXI. From the Council of Agde, on the Ides of September, in the twenty-second year of our lord King Alaric, in the consulship of Messala, a man of consular rank—that is, in the year 506.** Forty-six canons are presented. Since two canons have been joined into one, these comprise the forty-seven published canons of the same council, the number assigned to that Gallican [Col. 0288B] synod in the ancient Gallican copies. The remaining twenty canons, inserted before the conclusion in the published texts from codices of the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, are absent; they are rightly believed to be additions based on the evidence of those older Gallican codices.

**XXII. From the Council of Arles, in the year 524, 2 canons.**

**XXIII. From the Synod of Tarragona, in the year 516, 11 canons.** In both the preceding table and the body of the codex, numbers XXIV and XXV are omitted.

**XXVI. From the Council of Gerona, in the year 517, 9 canons.**

**XXVII. From the Council of Toledo under Thiudis**—*Thiudi* in both the table and the body of the work. This is the Second Council of Toledo, in the year 531, with three canons. In that year, 531, King Theudis succeeded Amalaric in December, whereas the Second Council of Toledo was held in May; therefore other codices correctly designate the fifth year of King Amalaric.

**XXVIII. From the Synod of Lérida, in the year 524, or more accurately 546, as learned men have established from Hispanic manuscripts, which record not the fifteenth year of Theodoric [Col. 0288C] but the fifteenth year of King Theudis. See Pagius on the year 546, nos. 10 and 11.** Fifteen canons are reported.

**XXIX. From the Council of Vallis.** This is the Hispanic Council of Valence of the year 546, chapter 5.

The following note is added:

> “From the book of Agabrinus,”

which should be read:

> “From the book of Agabrensis.”

[CCLX] In the Lucan manuscript it is mutilated:

> “From the book of Gabrensis,”

where the letter *A* has fallen out through the copyist’s error.

**XXX. From the Council of Elvira, 69 canons.**

**XXXI. From the Synod of Toledo, era 438, in the year 400, 23 canons.**

**XXXII. From the Council of Braga, in the year 563, 22 canons.**

**XXXIII. Likewise, from the Synod of Braga, in the year 572, 10 canons.**

**XXXIV. From the Council of Toledo.** This is the Third Council of Toledo, in the year 589, with twenty-three canons.

**XXXV. From the Council of Zaragoza, 7 canons.** This is the First Council of Zaragoza, believed to have been held in the year 381.

**XXXVI. From the Council of Auvergne in Gaul, in the year 549, chapter 22.** In the published *Councils*, volume V of the Venetian edition, [Col. 0288D] column 1389, only sixteen canons are presented from the Fuxian codex, from which Sirmond published this synod under the title “of Auvergne.” But since the preface to this synod, added from the Urgell manuscript, names not the city of Auvergne but that of Orléans, and since the canons are the same as those of the Fifth Council of Orléans, it is rather the Fifth Council of Orléans. That council, in the same published volume, column 1377, and in the Gallican manuscripts from which it was edited, presents thirty-four canons.

Thus the Fuxian codex is deficient not so much in its preface as in the number of canons. Our abbreviator, however, used a codex in which the number of canons was complete, as in the manuscripts of the more extensive Hispanic collection—namely, the Urgell manuscript of Peter of Marca and the Lucan manuscript cited by Pérez. The name “Council of Auvergne” in place of “Council of Orléans,” found only in Hispanic manuscripts, confirms that the codex from which this abbreviation was derived was Hispanic.

**XXXVIII. From the Synod of Turin, on the tenth day before the Kalends of October, around the year 401, 1 canon.**

**XLII. From the Synod of Huesca, in the year 598, 1 canon.**

> “Likewise, a capitulation of the decretal letters, sentences alone.”

A new series of numbers then begins.

**I. From the letter of Blessed Clement to James, chapter 4.**

From the instruction of the person mentioned above, chapter 5.** These two documents, falsely attributed to St. Clement, had been published from the common version of Rufinus and are therefore found inserted in ancient Latin collections. See note 1 to chapter 64 of the collection to be placed later in this volume, column 454, where the first document is read; compare also the preface to the documents of ancient canon law, no. 5, column 631, where the second document is presented in column 674.

**XXIX. From the letter of Pope Felix to the Sicilian bishops.** [Col. 0290A] By comparing the material asserted under this title, and from the numbers and abbreviated sentences, we discovered that it indicates the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, published in the appendix to volume VIII of the works of St. Augustine, p. 78.

This book is also found in certain manuscript collections of canons, sometimes under the name of Augustine, sometimes under that of Gennadius, who is the true author of the work, and sometimes without any author’s name. Perhaps our abbreviator prefixed Pope Felix’s name to it because he found this little work in some collection after Felix’s letter to the Sicilian bishops.

**XXX. From the letter of Pope Siricius to Himerius.** Eight sentences from this letter are presented; they differ from those which the abbreviator produced from the same letter under no. 111.

**XXXI. From the letter of Pope Leo to Balconius.** This is a lost letter, from which the abbreviator nevertheless presents no sentence in abridged form, although he gives its title both in the table and in the body of the work. See the dissertation on the lost letters of St. Leo, volume I, [Col. 0290B] column 1444, no. 19.

**XXXII. From the letter of Jerome to Bishop Patroclus concerning the ranks of the clergy.** Seven ranks are presented. This letter, addressed to Rusticus, is read in the appendix to volume XI of the works of St. Jerome, p. 114 of the Verona edition.

Many infer that this letter was falsely attributed to St. Jerome not only from the difference in style but also from the age of Rusticus, who held the episcopate after St. Jerome’s death. They think it was written long after St. Isidore of Seville, from whose *Book VII of the Etymologies*, chapter 12 and following, they believe it was excerpted.

Our codex removes the difficulty posed by Rusticus the bishop, however, since it gives the letter as written not to Rusticus, as in the published texts, but to Patroclus, who governed the Church of Arles in Jerome’s time. As for St. Isidore, since everyone agrees that it was his customary practice to transfer into the books of the *Etymologies* many passages relevant to his purpose without naming their authors, why should it not be believed that he copied the aforementioned seven [Col. 0290C] ranks of the clergy from this letter? If the style is judged alien to Jerome, one may at least infer from the author of our abbreviation—who, as we shall see, used codices older than St. Isidore—that this letter preceded St. Isidore, and that he derived the same ranks from it.

The ancient Abbreviation ends with this letter. A fragment is then added in the same script, but without a number, from a decree of Gregory the Younger against illicit marriages; it belongs to the Roman synod of the year 721. Finally, the following notice by an incompetent copyist is read:

> “Thanks be to God. You who read, pray for me, a sinner: may he thus have God as his helper.”

The Lucan codex lacks the aforementioned fragment of Gregory the Younger, which confirms that it is an addition in the Veronese manuscript. It has, however, other additions—for example, the letter of Leo III to Alcuin, placed before the aforementioned letter attributed to Jerome. Since this letter is absent from the otherwise complete Veronese manuscript, it is recognized as wrongly inserted and foreign to the original collection of this kind.

[Col. 0290D] [CCLXII] 3. Something remains to be said about the antiquity of the codices and collections from which the author derived this abbreviation. The collection from which he arranged the canons of the Greek synods in no. 11 into chapter 91 lacked the Laodicean and Constantinopolitan canons; this is an indication of remote antiquity.

In the following numbers he reports the councils of Greece, Africa, Gaul, and Spain, just as they are also described in the Hispanic collection. But it is evident that he drew from other, older sources as well. For he does not include the two Councils of Seville or the Fourth Council of Toledo, which are found in the original Hispanic collection.

Conversely, he presents certain councils [Col. 0291A] absent from that original Hispanic collection—namely, the Council of Auvergne, or rather the Fifth Council of Orléans, which was later added to the Hispanic collection, and four other extremely rare synods: the Second Council of Zaragoza, the Council of Narbonne, the Council of Huesca, and the Council of Barcelona, which were published from a unique codex of St. Emilianus.

Of all the synods presented by the abbreviator, the most recent is the Synod of Huesca of the year 598, somewhat earlier than the Hispanic collection in which the later Second Council of Seville, of the year 629, and the Fourth Council of Toledo, of the year 633, are presented. The abbreviator therefore used codices not only different from those of the Hispanic collection but also older than it.

He mentions only three codices: “from the Bracarensian book,” “from the Complutensian book,” and “from the Agabrensian book”; these cities belong to Spain. Braga is still a celebrated archiepiscopal see. Complutum was formerly an episcopal city in the province of Carthage, subject to the metropolitan of Toledo. Agabra was likewise an episcopal city in the province of Baetica, subject to the metropolitan of Seville. See the references to it in the Second Council of Seville, chapters 1, 5, and 8, and in the *Hispanic Notices* published by Loaisa, volume VI of the Venetian edition of the *Councils*, column 558 and following.

These Hispanic codices therefore seem to contain collections older than the one called Hispanic. In our own time we have also learned of a fragment of a very ancient codex of the chapter-house of Novara, which preserves indications of an older Hispanic collection.

4. It also seems that the abbreviator used not only Hispanic but Gallican codices. This can be inferred from the African synods he cites.

He praises only three African councils. First, in no. 19, he presents the ancient statutes [Col. 0291B] of the African synod of the year 418, assigning them the title:

> “From the Synod of Carthage in Africa, in the consulship of Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII.”

He did not take these statutes from the source from which they passed into the Hispanic collection, both because in that collection the statutes are prefixed with the consuls of the year 398 and because the order of the statutes differs substantially. We found the order of our codex, under the same title of the African synod of 418, in Vat. Palat. 574, which contains a very ancient Gallican collection. See part II, chapter 10, § 2, no. 13.

Second, in no. 20, he presents the Hipponian Breviary [Col. 0291C] from the Synod of Carthage, on the Ides of August, in the consulship of Ceranius—read Caesarius—which is found not in Hispanic but in Gallican collections.

Third, in no. 40, he presents in abridged form the Council of Telepte, which to date has been found only in Gallican collections.

Moreover, the Nicene canons in no. 3 are presented from Rufinian abbreviations, which we know to have been used at times only by the Gallicans. See part II, chapter 10, § 2, no. 1.

Nor should it be omitted that among the letters of the Roman pontiffs two documents attributed to St. Clement are reported under nos. 1 and 2. These are absent from the Hispanic collection, while both are found in Gallican collections; moreover, in those collections alone the second is entitled “instructions” or “precepts of St. Clement,” as in our codex. See part III, chapter 6, § 5, and note 1 to document 5 in this volume, column 673.

The author of this abbreviation, therefore—whether he was Hispanic or Gallican—did not see the Hispanic collection but used both Hispanic and Gallican codices that preceded it.

[CCLXIII] # CHAPTER V. On the abbreviation of the Hispanic collection published by Cardinal de Aguirre

[Col. 0291D]

1. There is a notable ancient abbreviation, arranged by common topics, of the material contained in the more extensive Hispanic collection. John Baptista Pérez found this valuable document in a Hispanic Lucan manuscript and sent it to Gregory XIII in Rome, together with other documents accurately transcribed in a book now among the Vatican codices, no. 4887.

Another copy of this book came into the hands of Cardinal de Aguirre, who published the same monument at Rome in 1693, at the beginning of volume III of the *Councils of Spain*, with the following heading:

> “Index of the sacred canons and councils by which the Church, especially the Hispanic Church, was governed from the beginning of the sixth century to the beginning of the eighth, now published for the first time from the ancient manuscript of the most distinguished Marquis of Mondéjar, formerly belonging to the illustrious John Pérez, canon and librarian of the Church of Toledo, and afterward bishop of Segorbe.”

Finally, Gaetano Cenni, having ably elucidated this same work from Aguirre’s copy, reprinted it at Rome in 1739 under the title:

> “Codex of the Ancient Canons of the Hispanic Church.”

2. Besides the Lucan codex, Pérez mentions two other manuscript copies in which the same document is transcribed: the *Vigilian* and the *Ovetan*. P. Coustant lists two others in two libraries, the Colbertine and the Coislinian.

All these codices belong to the more extensive Hispanic collection that we described in part III, chapter 4, § 3, no. 11. This abbreviation cites not only the documents of the original Hispanic collection but sometimes also those inserted among the additions to the same expanded collection; and it cites all of them by the numbers corresponding not to the original collection but to the expanded one.

For example, the Council of Elvira, which appears as chapter 30 [Col. 0292B] in the original collection, is cited in this abbreviation as chapter 38, corresponding to the expanded collection, in which eight other synods had previously been inserted and had increased the chapter numbers.

Similarly, the First Council of Braga, listed as chapter 40 in the original collection, is cited in book II of this abbreviation, title 20, as chapter 61. Synods absent from the original collection are also cited by the numbers of the expanded collection. These include not only the Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, Eighth, Ninth, Tenth, and Twelfth Councils of Toledo, which had been added in earlier supplements, but also, in book V, title 13, the Sixteenth Council of Toledo, cited as chapter 59, which was added in later accretions.

Since the Sixteenth Council of Toledo is cited as chapter 59 of the Hispanic collection, while the First Council of Braga is cited as chapter 61, it is clear that chapter 60 of the same collection contained the Seventeenth Council of Toledo, although it is nowhere cited in this abbreviation, just as the author similarly passed over many other items.

Add to this that book IX, title 9, cites a homily of the Third Council of Toledo, delivered by Leander [Col. 0292C] in praise of the Church on the conversion of the Gothic people, which was added in the more extensive supplements.

3. To make this clearer, and at the same time to show the sequence and order of the documents of the expanded collection cited in the abbreviation by its numbers, we give the complete table here.

In this table, the chapters displayed in italic type, as it is called, are those cited in the abbreviation under the same number. Those displayed in roman type, although never cited in the abbreviation, nevertheless correspond within the collection to the number or chapter to which they are attached.

We present only the table of the first part, since the second part, having no documents added to it, is the same in the expanded collection as in the original collection.

### 4

The work, or abridgment, of which we are speaking is arranged by commonplaces and subjects and divided into ten books [Col. 0293B], each of which is subdivided into several titles. Since it has already been published, it will be sufficient here to give the headings of the books together with the numbers of their titles. The heading of the entire Lucensian volume—which contains not so much this abridgment as the fuller Spanish collection—is as follows:

> In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Here begins the book of the canons of the holy Fathers in general.

This heading appears to refer to the entire volume, not merely to the abridgment, which, according to Pérez, is prefixed on each page by the words: *Excerpts of the canons*.

**Book I.** On the institutions of the clergy. Divided into 60 titles.

**Book II.** On the institutions of monasteries and monks, and on the orders of penitents. In 23 titles.

**Book III.** On the institutions of judgments and the administration of affairs. In 44 titles.

**Book IV.** On the institutions of offices and the order of baptism. In 40 titles.

[Col. 0293C]

**Book V.** On the diversity of marriages and the crime of disgraceful acts. In 18 titles.

**Book VI.** On the general rules of the clergy and of other Christians, and on princely government. In 6 titles.

**Book VII.** On the honor and affairs of princes. In 11 titles.

**Book VIII.** On God and on the things that are to be believed concerning him. In 9 titles.

**Book IX.** On the renunciation of heretics. In 9 titles.

**Book X.** On idolatry and its worshipers, and on the writings of peace and the gifts sent. In 7 titles.

### 5

Although Cajetanus Cennius considers this work to be attributable to Saint Isidore of Seville, he judges the titles in which additions belonging to the Spanish collection later than Saint Isidore are cited to be interpolations. This seems to us wholly incredible. For not merely a few titles described in this or that book, but almost the entire seventh book would have to be called interpolated, since it cites, almost throughout, the Toledan synods held after Saint Isidore. Moreover, if this original abridgment [Col. 0293D] had been composed by [CCLXV] Saint Isidore for the much shorter original Spanish collection, rather than for the fuller one, why would it have been found only in manuscript copies of the fuller collection, and nowhere in the shorter collection, in so many other codices that represent the same collection without its numerous additions?

Furthermore, the numbers of the chapters in this abridgment agree exactly not with the numbers of the original collection but with those of the expanded collection. This sufficiently demonstrates that the author of the abridgment took them not from the original collection but from the fuller one. Otherwise it would have to be said that a later author, to whom certain additions are thought to belong, altered all the other numbers of the original abridgment for the sake of those additions, though they are fewer in number, and adjusted them to the sequence of the fuller collection—a supposition that may not even be entertained without clear evidence.

Finally, add the verses composed by the author of the abridgment himself [Col. 0294A], which, having been omitted by Cardinal de Aguirre, we shall reproduce below from Pérez. They are so inelegant, tasteless, barbarous, and foreign to the laws of poetic meter that they cannot be attributed to Saint Isidore of Seville. Although they may properly be disregarded in themselves, we shall present them so that everyone may see how unworthy they are of Saint Isidore. The aforementioned cardinal omitted them because he believed them to be foreign to the author of the abridgment and to be the mistaken insertion of some *βαρβαρώτατος*—“most barbarous”—little poet. But he formed this opinion without grounds. Their relation to the abridgment is so evident that they serve as a kind of preface and seem to reduce to a compendium whatever is contained in the books themselves. Among other things, the same author of both the verses and the compendium is revealed by the following lines near the end of the first general preface:

> And thus, filling a new body with its original limbs,  
> I shape brief compendia for sluggish minds.

Antonius Augustinus, therefore, who had no doubt that these verses were composed by the author of the abridgment, rightly wrote in chapter 17 of his *Judgment concerning Certain Ancient Collectors of Ecclesiastical Canons*:

> I have seen indexes that attributed it to the same Isidore, bishop of Seville; but they are gravely mistaken. For the writer himself betrays who he is by using these inept verses, which reveal him to have been a young man then first withdrawing his hand from the schoolmaster’s rod.

### 6

In the preface to the first volume, which we gave in Part III, chapter 4, section 6, Joannes Baptista Pérez conjectured that this abridgment should be attributed to Julian, archbishop of Toledo. “He flourished in those times,” Pérez says, “and is said—on the report of Felix, his successor—to have played with verses; so that one may even suspect that the poems prefixed to some books of this work were written by him. For although they are empty and consist only of bombast, this defect may reasonably be pardoned in that unrefined age.”

He, however, had in mind the Toledan councils cited throughout the abridgment up to the twelfth, and failed to notice that the sixteenth Council of Toledo is also cited once, and that from the sequence of the numbers it can be known that the seventeenth Council of Toledo was likewise described in the collection used by the abridger, as we observed above. Although Julian presided over four Toledan synods, from the twelfth through the fifteenth, the two following ones, the sixteenth and seventeenth, were held after his death. Therefore the author of the abridgment and of the poems must be placed after the year 694, in which the seventeenth Toledan synod was held—namely, toward the end of the seventh century or the beginning of the eighth.

Perhaps the person—whoever he was—who added several documents to the Spanish collection, revising the chapter numbers, was also the author of the abridgment itself. Hence the abridgment is found prefixed to the codices of that same collection by its compilers.

### 7

Here, finally, are the poems that we found prefixed only to the first five books and transcribed by Pérez in Vatican manuscript 4887. Before the first book—indeed, before the heading of the first book itself, as though it were the preface to the entire abridgment—the following verses are read under the title:

#### A Versification Begins: A Question

> Lofty and fearsome book, who are placed upon a throne,  
> because you are the living order:  
> what name is in you?  
>

>
