## CHAPTER VI

### On the Older Collections of Penitential Canons Composed by Theodore, Bede, and Egbert; the Published Book *On Remedies for Sins* Attributed to Bede and Asserted to Belong to Egbert; Egbert’s Work *On Priestly Law* and Its Fragments; Excerpts of Canons from This Work to Be Attributed to Hucarius the Levite; the Penitential Divided into Four Books Not to Be Attributed to Egbert; and the Collection of Canons Contained in Book Four, from Which Regino Is Shown to Have Benefited

[Col. 0296D]

### 1

Since the use of canons had become more frequent in governing penitents, the decrees and sayings of pontiffs and the statements of the Fathers that served this purpose began to be collected into one body. Hence arose penitential books composed from the judgments of canons, pontiffs, and Fathers. Some of these present their regulations collected together so distinctly that they may rightly be counted among collections of canons.

The older and more celebrated penitential books, apart from the Roman one that Halitgar drew from the Roman archives, are those of Theodore, bishop of Canterbury; Bede, the priest; and Egbert, bishop of York. These are especially mentioned by Gregory III—or by whoever was the author of the *Excerpt from the Sayings of the Fathers and the Judgments of the Canons concerning Various Crimes and Their Remedies*.

The Penitential of Theodore of Canterbury, who died in the year 690, was published in Paris by Jacques Petit from two manuscripts of the House of Thou. It is not complete. For this reason Petit was compelled to add several fragments of Theodore’s Penitential, which he diligently collected from other authors.

Since many passages are found repeated in another order and sometimes in different words in the *Chapters of Theodore* edited by Luc d’Achery from a Corbie manuscript, there is strong suspicion that neither this codex nor the two manuscripts of Thou, nor other manuscripts of the same kind, contain Theodore’s Penitential itself or a fragment of it. Rather, various learned men collected in these codices, from here and there, Theodore’s *Chapters* that were later cited from Theodore in subsequent penitentials.

Indeed, in the chapters published from the manuscripts of Thou and from the Corbie manuscript, Theodore himself is cited. This cannot agree with an authentic copy of his work. Thus, in chapter 12, in Petit, page 11, from the manuscripts of Thou:

> Therefore Theodore granted one permission.

And in chapter 21, in d’Achery, page 487, from the Corbie manuscript:

> Penitents, according to the canons, ought not to communicate before the completion of their penance. Theodore says: But we, out of mercy, etc.

Henry Spelman reports in the first volume of his *Councils of Britain* that he found in the celebrated library of Saint Benedict at Cambridge a longer penitential book of Theodore, from which he published only the titles of the chapters. There are seventy-eight titles, which Jacques Petit reprinted in volume I, page 85.

Since the work itself is not available to us, it is impossible to determine whether this too has Theodore as its author. Certainly, its final title, expressed in these words—“Augustine, bishop of Orléans, said”—does not seem capable of being attributed to Theodore. For the text attributed in the same excerpts to Augustine of Orléans consists of three parts [CCLXIX]: the first reports the words of Pope Celestine, the second those of Leo I, and the third those of Aurelius Augustine of Hippo.

### 2

Bede’s Penitential is praised by many. He is believed to have enlarged Theodore’s Penitential. At least, he transferred almost the whole of that Penitential into his own work. Hence Regino, in book I, chapter 297, cites a text from the Penitential of Theodore the archbishop or Bede the priest; and in book II, chapter 246, he gives another text from the Penitential of Theodore the bishop and Bede the priest, because the same texts of Theodore had been received into Bede’s Penitential.

Egbert testifies that this Penitential of Bede was enlarged not long afterward by additions from others. We shall see him to be the author of the testimony quoted by Burchard in chapter 8 of book XIX. “In Bede’s Penitential,” he says, “many useful things are found, but many others have been inserted by others that agree neither with the canons nor with other penitentials.”

This Penitential of Bede has reached us neither in a pure nor in an expanded form. A book *On Remedies for Sins* is attributed to him, and it is also commonly called a Penitential. But we believe its author to have been Egbert of York. That it cannot properly be attributed to Bede is made clear by chapter 1 of the same work, in which Bede is praised three times.

Burchard gives this entire chapter in book XIX, chapter 8, where, among other things, the following is read concerning a Penitential book:

> It is to be arranged both according to the authority of the canons and according to the judgments of the three penitentials: that of Theodore the bishop, that of the Roman pontiffs, and that of Bede. But in Bede’s Penitential, etc.

And shortly afterward:

> All these things we have gathered truthfully from the canons, from the judgments of the holy Fathers, from Jerome, Augustine, Gregory, Theodore, Bede, and from the Roman Penitential.

Those who attached this book *On Remedies for Sins* to Bede seem to have removed from the text the words bearing Bede’s name, lest the little book become suspect because Bede would thereby be citing Bede. But every suspicion will disappear if the book is taken away from Bede and assigned to its proper author.

The true author is sufficiently revealed by the heading prefixed in the manuscripts themselves and in the printed copies to chapter 1 [Col. 0298A]:

> Excerpt from the canons of the catholic Fathers, or Penance [perhaps: “Penitentials”], for the remedy of souls, of Lord Egbert, archbishop.

Understand this as Egbert of York. The same is confirmed by Rabanus Maurus, archbishop of Mainz, who flourished shortly after Egbert. In his letter to Heribald, chapter 18, while discussing perjury, he writes:

> Likewise Ecbert, bishop of the English, defines as follows: Whoever has sworn an oath in a church, or on the Gospel, or on the relics of the saints, shall do penance for seven years, etc., as in chapter 9 of the book *On Remedies for Sins*.

This ancient writer, therefore, strongly confirms that Ecbert, or Egbert, was the author of that book.

If other collectors of canons later than Rabanus—such as Regino and Burchard—attribute some testimonies from this little book now to the Roman Penitential, now to Theodore, and now to Bede, this happened because, just as later authors of penitentials derived most of their material from earlier ones, so Egbert also—as is indicated in the text that we quoted from Burchard in an authentic and unabridged form—excerpted much from the three penitentials of Theodore, the Roman Penitential, and Bede.

This is confirmed still more strongly by Vatican Palatine manuscript 485, which presents the same work under Egbert’s name and without additions. It differs considerably from the published book *On Remedies for Sins*, both in order and in the substance and number of its chapters. Some chapters are shorter than those in the printed copies, while others are entirely absent, as will become clear from the following table of chapters.

#### Chapters Begin: On the Canons of the Fathers

I. On the preface.  
II. On capital offenses.  
III. On greed and other disgraceful acts.  
IV. On the penance of the clergy.  
V. On the oath.  
VI. On women’s contrivance.  
VII. On auguries and divinations.  
VIII. On minor sins.  
IX. On theft.  
X. On drunkenness.  
XI. On the Eucharist.  
XII. On various causes.  
XIII. On the person who cannot fulfill what is written in the Penitential.

Then this title is read, together with the author’s name:

> Here begins the Penitential book taken from the canons of the catholic Fathers for the remedy of souls, of Lord Egbert, archbishop.

The published preface, to which the name of Bede is prefixed in other manuscripts and printed editions, gave rise to the common opinion. Chapters 2, 3, 4, and 15—which are shown by the very reading of the context to have been inserted—are absent from this same codex. In place of the preface stands the first published chapter, beginning:

> That holy institution …

This chapter is read without mutilation in Burchard, book XIX, chapter 8.

As for the variants occurring in the individual chapters, we note only this: chapter 8 of the codex differs especially from chapter 6 of the published version, whose title is *On Minor Sins*. This little book of Egbert *On Remedies for Sins* is part of a larger work, of which we shall speak shortly.

### 3

In volume IV of the *Anecdotes* of P. P. Martène and Durand, column 31, an ancient collection of penitential canons is presented, which P. Dominicus Mansi believes should be attributed to Bede in volume I of his *Supplement to the Councils*.

We do not agree. Several decrees are missing there that had been inserted in Bede’s Penitential. See, among others, those that Burchard cites from Bede in book XIX, chapters 29, 84, 102, and 146.

This brief collection of canons was composed in the time of Gregory II, as the title at column 37 proves:

> Likewise from the decree of Pope Gregory the Younger, who NOW governs the Roman mother Church.

We shall conjecture in the Observations on Quesnel’s dissertation 16, section 1, no. 4, that it was compiled in Gaul rather than in England.

It presents the sense, but not the wording, of a single Nicene canon; for that reason it agrees with no translation. A few other canons of Greek synods are cited either from the Isidorian or from the Dionysian version. There are no Spanish canons, but only Gallican and Irish ones, ancient statutes of the Church, and one canon from the Council of Hippo Regius concerning penitents—the thirtieth canon of the *Breviary of Hippo*, which is read inserted into the Council of Carthage of the year 397, in Dionysius, chapter 43.

Among Roman pontiffs, Innocent, Celestine, Leo, Gregory the Great, and Gregory the Younger are cited; among the Fathers, Basil, Augustine, Cassian, and Isidore. Among the penitentials, that of Theodore alone is cited explicitly by name.

### 4

Two works are mentioned under the name of Egbert of York by Henry Spelman in volume I of the *Councils of Britain*. From them he published several pieces, which were taken up by P. Labbe and inserted into volume VIII of the Venetian edition of the *Councils*.

The first work is entitled:

> Excerpts of Ecbert, archbishop of York, compiled from the sayings and canons of the holy Fathers and useful for the establishment of ecclesiastical order.

Although these excerpts were taken from a fuller work by Egbert himself, they have not Egbert but Hucarius as their author. This was established for us with sufficient certainty by the Anglican writer James Ware, a man thoroughly versed in British manuscripts. In his annotations on the synod of Saint Patrick, while discussing canon 25 of that synod, he writes:

> Canon 25, concerning the bed of a deceased brother, is also found in manuscript excerpts from *Priestly Law* of Ecberht, archbishop of York, by Hucarius the levite, under the title, etc.

The canon cited there by Ware is found in the excerpts published by Spelman as number 128:

> Likewise, the synod concerning the bed of a deceased brother, which is canon 25 of the second synod of Saint Patrick, volume IV of the *Councils*, column 760.

Since Ware cites these excerpts not from Spelman’s edition but from manuscripts, he must therefore have seen British manuscripts that presented Hucarius as the author of these excerpts. Hence Bale also, as we believe, indicates these excerpts when he asserts that Ecbert’s constitutions were abridged by Hucarius the levite.

Spelman, however, may perhaps have been misled by a marginal note in the Cotton manuscript. In the catalogue of the manuscripts of Britain, volume II, page 47, the following is said concerning Cotton manuscript Nero A 1:

> In the margin: Excerpts of D. Egbert, archbishop of the city of York, from *Priestly Law*.

But here too Egbert’s genuine work has been improperly confused with Hucarius’s excerpts. The two must be distinguished, as Ware distinguishes them. [Col. 0299C]

Egbert’s work was entitled *On Priestly Law*. From it Hucarius the levite excerpted certain material that is contained in the published excerpts.

### 5

Egbert’s extensive work *On Priestly Law* has not yet been published in its entirety. Only certain portions of it have appeared. We believe that the book *On Remedies for Sins*, which we previously attributed to Egbert, as it is contained in Vatican Palatine manuscript, is a portion of the same work.

Another portion of the same work may be seen in Egbert’s Penitential, which Joannes Morinus published from a Roman manuscript of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme in the appendix to his books *On Penance*. Its title is:

> Excerpt from the canons of the catholic Fathers, or from the penitentials, for the remedy of souls, of Lord Egbert, archbishop of the city of York.

But this title does not correspond to the body of the little work itself, in which nothing is taken from the canons; rather, ritual prayers and the order of the reconciliation of penitents are described.

Since two chapters taken from chapters 1 and 5 of the published book *On Remedies for Sins* are prefixed to these prayers and this order [Col. 0299D], and since in the Vatican Palatine codex they are chapters 1 and 2 of a book bearing the same title, the title belongs not to the body of the little work edited by Morinus but to the book *On Remedies for Sins*, from which those two chapters were copied immediately after the title.

Therefore only these two chapters belong to Egbert’s work.

The excerpts arranged by Hucarius more certainly belong to the work *On Priestly Law*. Hence in the Oxford codex they are inserted with the following heading:

> These are the RIGHTS OF PRIESTS, which they ought to observe, as is noted in the margin of the Councils.

Since Egbert’s complete work is lacking, what remains to be said concerns the chapters excerpted from it.

Spelman found only twenty-one excerpts in the Oxford codex. He added the rest, up to number 145, from another codex, which was nevertheless damaged and mutilated. David Wilkins, in volume I of the newest London edition of the *Councils of Great Britain*, published in 1737, supplemented the same excerpts from the Cotton manuscript mentioned by Spelman, though he had not used it, bringing their number up to 163. [Col. 0300A]

Nothing in these excerpts—apart from one or two exceptions—is later than Gregory the Younger. This agrees perfectly with Egbert’s period, since he was elevated to the see of York around the year 734 and held it for more than thirty years.

One point that may cause difficulty is canon 7, in which prayer is prescribed for the life and reign of the lord emperor and for the safety of his sons and daughters. In chapter 30 of the synod of Cuthbert, archbishop of Canterbury and Egbert’s contemporary, a prayer is expressly recorded for the safety of kings and rulers and of the entire Christian people. An emperor and the emperor’s sons and daughters do not fit Egbert’s period, especially in Britain, which was subject to its own kings.

Another point that creates greater difficulty is canon 131, copied word for word from chapter 38 of book II of the *Life of Saint Gregory*, whose author, John the Deacon, lived later than Egbert. From this it is recognized that certain canons excerpted from Egbert were inserted from elsewhere.

Add to this certain errors that certainly do not seem capable of being attributed to Egbert himself. In the preface prefixed to the excerpts, three testimonies have been mistakenly joined into one: one from Celestine, another from Leo, and a third from Aurelius Augustine, and all three are attributed to Augustine of Orléans. These three are properly distinguished in the work wrongly attributed to Egbert, as we shall soon show. They are distinguished, I say, in book IV, chapters 232, 233, and 234, and each is assigned to its own author.

Several other matters are found confused and corrupted, both in the titles of the canons and in the canons themselves. In number 39, a certain decree is cited under the name of an African canon; it is recited among the chapters of Theodore’s Penitential by d’Achery, chapter 21, with the words “Theodore says” inserted.

In number 68, it is cited as an Agathensian canon, although it is not read among the Agathensian canons. It is likewise cited by Regino in book II, chapter 271, and by Burchard in book XI, chapter 64. More correctly, in the collection of which we shall speak shortly, book IV, chapter 127, it is attributed to Saint Ferreolus.

Since, however, the preceding number 126 in this collection cites a canon from the Council of Agde, if something similar was also found in Egbert’s work from which the excerpts were taken, it could easily have happened that, through the excerptor’s confusion, the title of the preceding canon was transferred to the following one. The same happened to Ivo, who, in letter 80 to William of Fécamp, cited from Burchard’s book III, chapter 11, with a similar error, a canon from a letter of Hyginus as coming from the Council of Meaux, chapter 5, after transferring the heading from the preceding chapter 10 of Burchard’s same book.

Moreover, in number 139 of the excerpts, a decree of Vigilius is recited, which later writers attribute to Pope Hyginus on the basis of Burchard. Yet it is read neither in the spurious letters of Hyginus nor in Vigilius’s letter to Profuturus in the same form and sense.

Certain unusual citations are also noteworthy. In number 53, under the title “Canon of the Saints,” canon 23 of the third Council of Carthage in the Isidorian—or rather, Spanish—collection is produced.

In number 94, the laws of the Roman emperors and Frankish kings seem to be designated under the name of Roman and Frankish canons—laws that prescribe the punishment of crimes and the coercion of criminals.

For the rest, from number 30 of these excerpts, which Hucarius took, at least for the most part, from Egbert’s fuller work, it becomes certain that abridgments of Rufinus’s version of the Nicene canons existed in England. The Dionysian version is likewise revealed in numbers 31, 33, 43, and 59.

Irish canons and the synod of Saint Patrick, the rules of Fructuosus, Aurelian, and Isidore, and several canons of the synods of Gaul are cited. Among the latter are the canons of Epaon, which are found neither in the original Spanish collection nor in its earliest additions.

6. The second work that Spelmann attributes to Egbert is the Penitential, from which he published several canons under the heading: “From the second book of Egbert’s Penitential in the public library at Oxford, under the title: ‘From this point onward, various judgments concerning various offenses’” (vol. VIII of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 350). [Col. 0301A] Having transcribed only thirty-five canons from it, Spelmann added the following note in volume I of the Councils of Britain, p. 278:

“Thus far extend the canons near the end of the second book of the Penitential; and in the fourth book there are many others, drawn from the letters and sayings of the Fathers, the decrees of the popes, and the enactments of various councils, occupying forty-two folios of that book in the Oxford manuscript.”

He himself had not seen this codex; for on p. 275 he stated that he had obtained these canons, excerpted from the second book, through the eyes and efforts of others. He adds that the Penitential in the same codex comprises four complete books.

We, however, have succeeded in finding this work, divided into four books, in manuscript Vat. 1352. Its second book contains the thirty-five canons edited by Spelmann, while its fourth book presents the fuller collection of canons mentioned above; we found this latter collection separately transcribed in another Vatican codex, Vat. 1347.

In neither of these two codices, however, is Egbert’s name found. Indeed, the prefaces—which Spelmann did not see—make it clear that this work was written by some private author at the instruction of someone, either an abbot or a bishop, as may be inferred, among other things, from these words in the preface to the fourth book:

“You earnestly requested and commanded, most dear rector, that, for correcting or instructing the conduct of your subjects, certain passages from the divine constitutions …”

These words do not suit Archbishop Egbert. Certainly this is not his work On Priestly Law, which may be called his Penitential. For certain chapters found in the excerpts taken from Egbert’s work do not occur in these books; nor is the chapter that Rhabanus cites from Egbert found here. Moreover, the same excerpts cite a canon of the Synod of Agde which, in the fourth book of this work, chapter 127, is attributed to its author Ferreolus.

We therefore believe that Spelmann, who did not examine the Oxford codex, was misled by the fact that in the same manuscript, before these books—which bear no name of Egbert—there stood twenty-one chapters of excerpts. Although these lacked the title of Egbert, another Cottonian codex, mentioned by us in no. 4, at least presented Egbert as their author (albeit erroneously); and so Spelmann believed that this same Egbert was also the author of the work in four books that followed those chapters. [Col. 0301C]

The first three books are composed almost entirely of sayings of the Fathers. In them the books On the Contemplative Life are frequently cited under the name of Prosper, as was customary among writers of the eighth and ninth centuries. The fourth book, however, contains a collection of canons divided into 381 titles or chapters.

No testimony occurs later than Gregory II and Bede, who died before the middle of the eighth century. Nothing apocryphal is quoted. In transcribing the testimonies, the author is generally exact; yet at times, like others of his period, he is found to have used a freer pen or abridgment.

The Roman Penitential and Bede’s Penitential are cited, as are the monastic rules of Saint Benedict and of the holy Fathers Basil, Aurelian, Caesarius, Fructuosus, Ferreolus, Isidore, Columbanus, and others of the same kind. The collection of Dionysius was used; from it the Greek synodical canons and the African canons were chiefly taken. [Col. 0301D]

In the African canons the compiler sometimes followed the Hispanic collection, from which he assigned to the Council of Carthage canons that are incorrectly attributed in that collection to the fourth Council of Carthage. Nothing from the canons of the synods of Spain is reported that is not found in the same Hispanic collection.

Besides the Hispanic collection, he had another exemplar of the Gallican canons before him. For he cites the Councils of Tours, Vannes, and Epaon, as well as several Councils of Orléans, which are absent from the Hispanic collection. He also seems to have benefited from the collection to be published in this volume. [CCLXXIII] For in chapter 213 he reports a canon of Chalcedon from the Prisca translation; in chapter 238, a Nicene canon; in chapter 247, an Antiochene canon; and in chapter 312, a Laodicean canon from the ancient version, with readings found only in the collection mentioned above.

Most noteworthy, moreover, is that Regino used the fourth book of this work. He plainly copied many canons from it, often in the same order and under the same titles. [Col. 0302A]

The extremely diligent edition of Regino prepared by Stephanus Baluzius was therefore highly useful; for it is chiefly through this edition that the collections of Burchard and Ivo, who drew from Regino, are illuminated. How much more useful will an edition of the work from which Regino derived so much prove to be? If God grants it, we shall one day publish this edition, which is nearly ready.

# CHAPTER VII. On three ancient collections that distribute the canons under common topics

## § 1. On the Hibernian Collection

1. The ancient collections of Hibernensis, Herovalliana, Andegavensis, Divionensis, Pithoeana, and others of this kind prefer the method of distributing canons under titles and common topics. Since these collections, praised by P. Sirmond, Jacques Petit, and others, are not defiled by the fabrications of Pseudo-Isidore and contain nothing later than the eighth century, they seem to have been composed around this period and before the Isidorian collection.

Let us speak first of the Hibernensis. From it P. Lucas Acherius, using the Corbie codex, first published the Hibernian canons (vol. I of the new edition of the Spicilegium, p. 492). Later, from the Bigot manuscript, P. Edmund Martene added other Hibernian canons, which had either escaped Acherius’s diligence or, more probably, were absent from his codex.

This ancient compilation, formed chiefly from fairly abbreviated decrees of Roman councils, bishops, and Fathers, consists of sixty-five books, each divided into several chapters. The copyist seems to indicate the name of the compiler at the end of the oldest Corbie codex in these words:

“I, Arbedoc the cleric, have written these collections, with Haelhucar as abbot directing the piecemeal compilation, which has here been gathered together in this codex from the holy Scriptures and divine sources, as well as the decrees that the holy Fathers and synods established among various peoples and in various languages.”

[Col. 0302C] In his notice, Acherius conjectures that Hucarius the levite, who arranged the excerpts from Egbert, may perhaps be the person called Hael Hucar. But Haelhucar appears to be a single name, and he is moreover called an abbot.

The Corbie codex itself, written in the eighth century, as Mabillon attests in On Diplomatics, p. 360, demonstrates the antiquity both of the collection and of its compiler. That it was certainly composed among the Irish is proved both by the sayings of Saint Patrick and Gildas the Wise and by the decrees of the Hibernian synod, which is generally called the holy synod or simply the synod.

“This collection,” says Acherius, “teaches and establishes what concerns sacred ordinations, the various duties of the Church’s ministers, the manner of administering the sacraments, the proper observance of ecclesiastical discipline, and the religious instruction of laypeople in Christian conduct. Finally, it prescribes remedies and the imposition of penances upon the fallen.”

In this collection, the Sardican canons are consistently cited under the name of the Nicene canons, as P. Coustantius establishes in the preface to volume I of the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, no. 77, p. 72. From the few portions published by Acherius, it is clear that African and Gallican canons were inserted in these books and that the collection of Dionysius was used in Ireland. For the Gangran canons are cited from the Dionysian interpretation, as is evident from book XLIII, chapter 2, where the tenth Dionysian canon is transcribed word for word.

The compiler explains in the prologue the freer method of presenting canons in abridged form that had arisen in this period and become common in other collections of the kind. “Seeing,” he says, “the countless number of synodical exemplars … I arranged a brief, clear, and harmonious exposition from the immense forest of writings into the text of a single volume, adding much, reducing much, arranging much along the same path [read: organizing], and asserting much according to the sense while disregarding the path of the words.”

2. We had already written this when, while reviewing our annotations in Vallicellian manuscript 18 of the tenth century, which contains various collections, we suspected that no. 3 might present the same Hibernian collection. Nor was the suspicion unfounded. For P. Franciscus a Puteo, a priest of the Roman Oratory, whom we have found to be a collaborator in our studies on account of his kindness, was asked to transcribe and send us the index of titles and certain chapters of this little work from that codex. From these materials we discovered that everything agrees with the collection mentioned above.

Only the sections are called “titles” there, whereas Acherius calls them “books.” There is also some difference in the division. For this reason, in the Vallicellian exemplar there are sixty-eight titles, whereas the Corbie codex has sixty-five books.

Thus, for example, the third book of the Corbie manuscript, entitled by Acherius “On the Deacon,” includes subdeacons. In the Vallicellian manuscript, however, it is more properly divided into two titles, the third and fourth, one entitled “On the Deacon,” the other “On the Subdeacon.” Conversely, the Vallicellian manuscript lacks the title “On Regions of the Census,” which is book XLVI in the Corbie manuscript.

We now append the heading of the collection itself, as it is read in the Vallicellian manuscript, together with the index of titles and the number of chapters. From these, everyone will more clearly recognize its agreement with the Hibernian collection published by Acherius.

“Here begins the most welcome collation of the canons, strengthened by testimonies from Scripture and sayings of the saints, which delights the reader; and if anything appears to disagree, that is to be chosen which is judged to possess the greater authority.”

The Preface to the same collation follows: “Seeing the countless number of synodical exemplars,” etc., as in Acherius, volume I of the Spicilegium, p. 492, where the reading “synodorum examplariorum” is less correct.

Then follows a brief account of the four councils, taken from Saint Isidore’s book of Etymologies or from the preface to the Hispanic collection. Soon afterward comes the item: “Preface of Dionysius to Stephen on the various synods.” Instead of Dionysius’s preface, however, the compiler excerpted only the titles and the number of canons that he found in the Dionysian codex. [Col. 0303C]

He seems to have had before him only that part of Dionysius which contains the canons. From it he indicates the Carthaginian canons as written in a continuous numerical series, as in the Vatican exemplar of the pure Dionysian text. The number assigned to these canons is 138, a number corresponding not to the Hadrianic codices but to the pure Dionysian codices. Thus it reads:

“The rules at Carthage in Africa, one hundred twenty-eight [correct: one hundred thirty-eight].”

The twentieth Antiochene canon from Dionysius’s version follows. Then this table of titles is transcribed; to each title we have thought it appropriate to add the number of chapters excerpted from the body of the collection.

I. On the bishop, ch. 24.  
II. On the presbyter, ch. 30.

## § 2. On the Herovallian Collection

1. The Herovallian codex is said by P. Coustantius to be seven hundred years old, volume I of the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, col. 709. It belonged to Antonius de Heroval, then to Jacques Petit, and finally, by the latter’s will, passed into the library of the Benedictine Fathers of the Congregation of Saint Maur at Saint-Germain.

The aforementioned Jacques Petit published several excerpts from this collection in volume I, following Theodore’s Penitential, pp. 102 and following. John Morinus had previously cited the same collection in the appendix to his books On Penance.

“It is divided,” says Petit, “into ninety-two titles. The canons of councils, the decrees of pontiffs, and the sayings of the Fathers from which it was compiled are all ancient.” Several features especially worthy of notice occur in this collection.

2. An index is prefixed of the synods cited in the collection itself. Apart from the Greek and African synods and the Roman canons, there are more than twenty other Gallican synods, extending to the Council of Autun of Saint Leodegarius, bishop. Of the Spanish councils, only Toledan canons are cited. This number of Gallican councils shows that the collection was composed in Gaul. [Col. 0304C]

3. The author of this collection drew not from a single codex or collection but from several. Thus, for example, the Nicene canons are sometimes presented from Rufinus’s abbreviation, which we have seen received in certain ancient Gallican collections, part II, chapter 10, § 2; and sometimes from the ancient version called Isidorian, which is found in other Gallican manuscripts.

It is remarkable that the same sixth Nicene canon, under the same sixth title, is first cited on p. 120 from an interpretation approaching the Isidorian version and then presented again on p. 122 from Rufinus’s abbreviation.

The Dionysian translation was also used by the compiler, whatever Petit may argue to the contrary. For this reason, in our Observations on Quesnel’s Dissertation 16, we shall draw from this an important argument confirming that the codex of Dionysius reached Gaul before the time of Hadrian I and Charlemagne.

Seven Chalcedonian canons cited on pp. 127, 192, 196, 197, 249, and 261 clearly display Dionysius’s version. The same version is also found in one Nicene canon on p. 163, one Ancyran canon on p. 245, another Antiochene canon on p. 132, and two Laodicean canons on pp. 122 and 208.

The canons of the apostles were disseminated among Latins solely through Dionysius’s interpretation, so that the author writes the following about them in the table prefixed to the collection:

“Canons of the apostles, which Dionysius the bishop [correct: Dionysius Exiguus] translated from Greek into Latin at the request of Bishop Stephen.”

Four such canons, on pp. 182, 201, 205, and 211, represent that version. If other apostolic canons differ from it, we believe that this should not be attributed to another interpretation—for there is no indication of any such version anywhere—but to some codex or collection in which the same canons, taken from Dionysius, were expressed more freely.

This is confirmed by Gregory of Tours, book V of the History, chapter 19. “He himself,” he says, “King Chilperic, departed, sending a book of canons in which a new quire was attached, containing what were called apostolic canons, as follows: ‘A bishop discovered in homicide, adultery, or perjury is to be removed from the priesthood.’”

This is the twenty-fifth apostolic canon. Since it lacks the word “theft,” which is found in Dionysius, and has the word “homicide,” which is absent there, it plainly reveals the freer license of some copyist. Compare what we shall say on this matter in note 14 to Quesnel’s Dissertation 16.

Other canons of the Greek synods likewise often exhibit the same freedom in the Herovallian codex. Sometimes they are abridged rather than translated from Greek; at other times they are expressed in various words that are found in no version or that reveal some interpolation.

Therefore Jacques Petit’s view cannot be accepted, according to which a unique and extremely ancient interpretation is introduced in such canons. Errors in citations occasionally occur. Thus, in title 5, p. 109, a Chalcedonian canon is cited as “canon 20,” although it is an abridgment of Antiochene canon 20.

4. The use of the Dionysian codex in the present collection is especially confirmed by the African canons. None are cited from the Hispanic collection. Their being presented from Dionysius is demonstrated by the very numbers assigned to them. [Col. 0305B]

They are called “Hipponian canons,” although they are read in Dionysius after canon 33. Since the first synod praised by Dionysius after that canon 33 is the Council of Hippo, our compiler carelessly assigned the following canons to it, although they concern other African synods.

The numbers by which these Hipponian canons are cited do not follow the series by which, in the Hadrianic collection, the later canons are distinguished from the first thirty-three. Rather, they are the numbers by which, in the pure Dionysian codices, the same canons are designated in a continuous series from first to last.

Allow for some error in the numbers; nevertheless, the numbering comes closer to that of the pure Dionysian text than to that of Hadrian. The compiler therefore excerpted the African canons not from the Hadrianic collection but from the pure collection of Dionysius. This proves that the compilation predates Hadrian. It also shows that a pure Dionysian codex reached Gaul before it was transmitted by Hadrian I to Charlemagne. [Col. 0305C]

5. The Sardican canons are cited under the name of the Nicene canons because they were taken from collections in which they were joined to the Nicene canons without a distinct Sardican title, as in the Gallican codices mentioned by us in part II, chapter 10, § 2.

See in Petit, pp. 133, 135, 149, 188, and 202, the Nicene heading assigned to Sardican canons in the Herovallian manuscript. The compiler cites one canon under the name of Sardica on p. 194; it is not Sardican, however, but Nicene, or rather an abridgment of Nicene canon 18.

He attributes the same canon to the Council of Nicaea on p. 143, where he quotes it under the Nicene title in the same words; and on p. 193 he likewise cites it under the name of Nicaea from Rufinus’s abbreviation.

6. The ancient Statutes of the Church, which we shall publish among the documents of canon law, are generally cited in the Herovallian codex under the title “African Canon” or “Canons of the Africans”; sometimes under “Carthaginian Canon”; and once, on p. 255, under the title “Ancient Statutes of the Church.”

We have found the same statutes under these various titles in Gallican manuscript exemplars, such as Vat. Palat. 574 and Verona 59. The former presents two titles together, “African Synod” and “Ancient Statutes of the Church”; the latter has “From the Synod of Carthage in Africa.”

The numbers by which the same statutes are designated correspond to those found in these Gallican exemplars, not to the numbers by which the statutes are arranged differently in codices of the Hispanic collection under the title “Fourth Council of Carthage.”

Not all the canons called Carthaginian in the Herovallian collection belong to the ancient statutes. Some are taken from the first thirty-three canons of the Council of Carthage of 419; three others come from the later canons, although their numbers have been so corrupted that they agree neither with the series of the Hispanic collection, nor with the Hadrianic series, nor with that of the pure Dionysian text. [Col. 0306A]

7. In title 26, p. 163, an Arelatan canon, “canon 1,” is expressed in these words:

“We have therefore decreed that the Lord’s Pascha be observed throughout the whole world on one day.”

These words are not found in the first canon but in the letter of the First Council of Arles, published from a very rare Gallican codex. See the letter itself in P. Coustantius, p. 346, volume I of the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, no. 3.

The Roman canons are also cited no less than in the Pithoean and Andegavian manuscript collections and in the second little work in Vallicellian manuscript 18, all of which are ancient collections of Gaul.

These canons, likewise published by Sirmond from the Gallican Fossatensis collection, were attributed to Innocent I, but Coustantius places them among the letters of Siricius, p. 686.

In addition, certain excerpts are cited from Siricius’s letter to Genesiu[s], which is likewise cited under this title in two other Gallican collections, the Pithoean and the Vallicellian 18, second little work. Coustantius collected and printed these in columns 709 and 710. There he aptly noted that they are nothing other than the material published by Sirmond and Labbe from the Saint-Marie of Laon codex: responses 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, and 14 of Pope Stephen II, which were either truncated or altered with the utmost freedom by the person who excerpted them.

He reasonably supposes that they were attributed to Siricius in our collection and in other similar Gallican collections, of which we shall speak in the following section, because in Sirmond’s edition, according to the Laon codex, the eighth response from Siricius’s letter to Himerius immediately precedes these responses. An unskilled ancient compiler, however, thought that the following chapters and responses, which are presented without a cited author, also belonged to the same letter of Siricius. From corruption of the word “Himerius,” a careless copyist could easily have written “Genesius.”

Thus far P. Coustantius. See also col. 637, note 6, where he discusses another fragment of Siricius, which is found at greater length in the Corbie codex but much more briefly in the Herovallian codex. [Col. 0306C]

The “constitution of Silvester,” from which our compiler transcribes the text on p. 192, is an apocryphal document attributed to that pontiff, which other, more ancient collections also received. See part II, chapter 6, no. 4.

A text from a letter of Pope Hormisdas “to all the provinces” may cause some difficulty. It is found under a similarly corrupt heading in Vat. 1343, after the books of Halitgar in the Saint Gall manuscript cited by Heinrich Canisius (Thesaurus Monumentorum, vol. II, part II, p. 143), and also in Gratian, Distinction 50, chapters 29 and 58.

In the Herovallian manuscript, however, according to Petit, the name of Hormisdas appears to have been added later. The text in fact belongs to the excerpts from the titles appended to the letter of John II to Caesarius of Arles, volume V of the Councils, col. 903. With Sirmond, we believe Caesarius himself to be their author.

8. We now present from Petit the ninety-two titles of this collection.

III. Pope Leo’s judgment concerning apocryphal Scripture.

LXVII. On reading at table.

LXXI. Canons of Pope Saint Gregory, ch. 12.

LXXVI. On women who practice witchcraft.  
LXXVII. On those who inflict death upon themselves through any negligence.  
LXXVIII. On those who bind themselves by an oath not to return to peace.  
LXXIX. That the offerings of disputing brothers not be accepted.  
LXXX. On those who, upon entering the church, abstain from receiving the sacrament because of their excessive luxury.  
LXXXI. On not allowing laypeople to command religious persons.  
LXXXII. On penitents who transgress.  
LXXXIII. That penitents not be received by other bishops or presbyters, nor communicate elsewhere, except in the places from which they were excluded.  
LXXXIV. That no bishop, nor anyone below him, presume to hear cases on Sunday.  
LXXXV. That a bishop hear no one’s case without the presence of his clerics.  
LXXXVI. That a bishop not personally appoint anyone for promotion to the episcopate.  
LXXXVII. If a powerful person despoils anyone and, when admonished by the bishop, does not restore the property, let him be excommunicated.  
LXXXVIII. On the thirty-year prescription: after thirty years no one may bring a claim concerning what the lapse of time established by law has excluded.  
LXXXIX. That a bishop travel through his diocese.  
XC. That a bishop receive only two solidi and not demand a third part of the offerings; and that clerics not be subjected to exactions in the manner of slaves.  
XCI. That *vallematia* [an uncertain term] and obscene songs be prohibited.  
XCII. That the ordinations of presbyters and deacons be celebrated at fixed times.

## § 3. On the Collection Contained in Vallicellian Manuscript 18

1. Three other collections, likewise Gallican—the Andegavian, Divionian, and Pithoean—are of approximately the same character and period. P. Sirmond praises them, and we would gladly describe them if we had been able to see them.

In their place, however, we shall discuss another collection that is altogether similar and is contained in the second little work of Vallicellian manuscript 18. We infer that it is of Gallican origin because it cites the Roman canons, Siricius’s letter to Genesius, and other materials of the kind that we have found only in Gallican collections.

It agrees in many respects with the preceding Herovallian collection. Yet it differs from it in other respects, and also differs from the Andegavian and Divionian collections; for we were unable to find in it certain items cited from those collections by P. Sirmond.

Whether it is the same as the Pithoean collection is suggested by the fact that the materials quoted from the latter were likewise found by us in the Vallicellian collection. But since we have not been able to compare the whole collection, we dare not affirm this.

In the Vallicellian collection, the canons of the Greek synods are cited from the ancient interpretation, as it is called, the Isidorian interpretation, and sometimes from Dionysius’s version. The councils of Africa, Gaul, and Spain are cited. The most recent pontiff mentioned is Gregory the Younger.

No forged works of Isidore occur. Testimonies of the Fathers are interspersed among the canons, as we have also seen in the preceding collections described both in this and in the earlier chapter. From this it is evident that this practice, later adopted by collectors of canons, began in the eighth century.

2. It will be sufficient to present the title and chapters of this collection.

[Col. 0308C] HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTERS OF THE SACRED CANONS, NUMBER 72.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the collections of Acherius, Halitgarius, and Rabanus

1. We call the collection “Acherian” the one published by Lucas Acherius from three manuscripts—the Thuaneus, Baluzianus, and Agobardinus—in volume I of the latest edition of the *Spicilegium*, p. 510. Blessed Beatus Rhenanus had seen the preface of this collection and had published a fragment of it in his admonition on Tertullian’s doctrines; yet he could not find the entire collection, as he desired. We found the same collection in three other very ancient manuscripts, namely Vat. 1347 and the two Vatican Regina manuscripts 446 and 849. In Acherius’s edition the following title is prefixed: *An Ancient Collection of Penitential Canons*. Acherius notes that it would more properly be called simply *Collection of Canons*, unless the author himself had added the word “penitential.” Our manuscripts, however, do not know this title; they bear only the following heading, which in that edition is placed after the title just mentioned: “Here begins [the discussion] of the usefulness of penance, and how one ought to believe concerning the remission of sins through penance, with the preface of the work that follows.”

Certainly, the preface shows that the author’s intention was to transmit the manner of penance prescribed by the sacred canons. The first book, indeed, is almost entirely concerned with penance, but the remaining two are not. This collection is divided into three books, whose subject the author sets out in the preface itself in these words:

> “The first little book,” he says, “contains matters concerning penance and penitents, crimes, and judgments. The second deals chiefly with the accused and their accusers, judges and witnesses, together with the other ecclesiastical rules pertaining to these matters. The third concerns the sacred orders, those who are to be promoted to the clergy and those who are to be removed from the clergy, and the rules and privileges of all clerics and prelates.”

Peter Pithoeus, in his *Historical Synopsis of Distinguished Men Who, Besides Gratian, Collected and Arranged Canons and Ecclesiastical Decrees*, writes of this collection: “There are found here and there three penitential books by an uncertain compiler, drawn from synods, letters, and the judgments of the holy Fathers.” Unless by “holy Fathers” the supreme pontiffs are meant, this final phrase must be deleted; for no holy Fathers are cited in these books, but only the canons of councils and the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs.

2. The author recites the canons and decretals of the Greek synods from the Hadriana collection, with the same numbers and titles. He also extracted the African material from that collection in such a way that he cites it in two separate and distinct series of numbers: the earlier thirty-three canons under the name of the Council of Carthage, and the later 105 canons under the title of the African Council, just as they are set out in the Hadriana. From this it is beyond doubt that the Hadriana collection was available to him.

Besides the Hadriana collection, he also used the Hispanic collection, from which he copied quite a few additional African, Gallican, and Hispanic canons absent from the Hadriana. Thus the author drew from these two collections, the Hadriana and the Hispanic—or rather, from some similar collection contained in Vatican manuscript 1338, in which the councils of Africa, Gaul, and Spain had been inserted into the Hadriana collection from the Hispanic collection, as we explained more fully in Part III, chapter 5.

Indeed, nothing occurs throughout all those books that is not found in the same collection of Vatican manuscript 1338, nor is anything cited from those documents that are additionally found in the complete Hispanic collection. Hence these books also lack apocryphal writings, which indicates that this collection is earlier than the Isidorian collection. Acherius believes it was arranged before the ninth century.

Certainly, Halitgarius, who died in 831, seems to have borrowed his preface from that of this collection, as the following words demonstrate:

> “Let no one suppose that this letter is mine, lest it become worthless to him because of the insignificance of my name. Rather, let him know that it was collected by our predecessors from the judgments of the saints, and that I have excerpted it, so that its excessive length might not produce weariness in negligent readers.”

By “our predecessors,” who collected a fuller preface from the judgments of the saints, he indicates, as we believe, the author of the preface placed before the present collection, in which the same judgments of Augustine and Gregory are found that Halitgarius abridged more briefly. If, however, by “our predecessors” Halitgarius meant our compiler, then this compiler preceded Halitgarius by at least approximately fifty years. This collection is therefore commended above all by the authenticity of its documents and the antiquity of its author.

3. A few words will suffice concerning Halitgarius, bishop of Cambrai, who drew upon this same collection. At the request of Ebbo of Reims, around the year 825, as Basnage supposes, he wrote six books on penance. Henricus Canisius published the first five books from the St Gall manuscripts; they were reprinted in volume II, part II, of the *Thesaurus Monumentorum*, p. 91, together with a sixth book that Stevartius had printed from another manuscript. This book was absent from Canisius’s manuscripts, just as it is also absent from the ancient manuscript 61 of the Verona Chapter. In that manuscript, however, Halitgarius’s preface also mentions the sixth book, as may be seen in the Appendix to Maffei’s *Theological History*, p. 79. Father Menard, having found all these books in a Corbie manuscript with the complete preface, inserted the sixth book in his annotations on St Gregory’s *Sacramentary*, note 679. See volume III of that saint’s works, col. 461.

The first book, on the eight principal vices, and the second, on the active and contemplative life, are for the most part excerpted from the works of St Gregory and from the books of Prosper—or, more accurately, of Julianus Pomerius—on the contemplative life. The third, on the order of penitents; the fourth, on the judgments of laymen; and the fifth, on the orders of clerics, were taken from the canons of councils and the constitutions of the Roman pontiffs.

Just as Halitgarius derived his preface from the one prefixed to the Acherian collection mentioned above, so he drew almost all the canons and constitutions from the three books of that collection and distributed them in another order. Thus nothing from the impostures of Pseudo-Isidore occurs in Halitgarius, which is confirmed by the fact that these impostures were published after Halitgarius. Finally, the sixth book is the *Roman Penitential*, which the author testifies that he took from the archives of the Church itself.

4. The two collections of Rabanus Maurus should not seem to be separated from these, since they present penitential canons without any Isidorian apocrypha. The first is the *Book of Penitents*, which he wrote while he was abbot of Fulda, shortly after 841 and certainly before 847, when he was elevated to the see of Mainz and succeeded Otgar; for he dedicated the same book to that bishop at that time.

This book appears among the works of Rabanus and was later reprinted and supplied with notes by Antonius Augustinus in a work entitled *Penitential Canons*. In the preface, Augustinus noted the sources from which the author had drawn the canons in these words:

> “Rabanus appears to have used the body of canons and the first edition of Isidore Mercator, insofar as provincial councils alone are concerned. For he cites no letters of the Roman pontiffs except those written after Damasus and found in the body of canons.”

By “the body of canons” he means the Hadriana collection. Instead of “the first edition of Isidore Mercator,” he should more properly have written “the Hispanic collection.” Rabanus, indeed—with the exception of the testimony of St Gregory in his letter to Secundinus, which we shall discuss shortly—cites no pontifical constitution that is not found in the Hadriana collection; nor does he cite any conciliar canon that is not found either in the Hadriana or in the Hispanic collection, as we observed when discussing the Acherian collection.

It is moreover remarkable that this writer, who lived at that time and in those places where the Pseudo-Isidorian collection was compiled and published, received nothing from it. Nor should one object with the testimony concerning fallen clerics from St Gregory’s letter to the servant of God Secundinus, which is found in Isidore as an appended addition to that letter and is spurious. Since Rabanus excerpted nothing from so many other spurious wares of Isidore, it seems more probable to us that this addition to the letter was fabricated by another earlier forger, and that Rabanus derived it not from Isidore but from another source.

Indeed, the letter to Secundinus, copied with the same addition, is found [Note: See volume II of the works of St Gregory, Maurist edition, col. 965, note a, on Letter 62, Book IX, and col. 967, note l.] in the very ancient original Corbie manuscript of Paul the Deacon, preserved in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. This codex, sent by Paul himself to St Adelard, abbot of Corbie—as is clear from Paul’s own letter prefixed to the collection of St Gregory’s letters in the same codex—contains fifty-four letters of that pontiff. According to the Benedictine editors (*Preface* to volume II of St Gregory’s works, p. 433), thirty-four of these were corrected in Paul’s own hand.

Since Paul the Deacon died in 801, that addition is recognized as predating the Isidorian collection. Consequently, Rabanus, who copied nothing from Isidore’s certain fabrications, must be said to have drawn that testimony from a different and earlier source.

This can also be confirmed by another observation. When Rabanus quotes pontifical constitutions from the collection of canons, he consistently uses the formula “From the decretals of Siricius,” “From the decretals of Innocent,” “From the decretals of Celestine,” and so forth, indicating the chapter in which the collection reports the decree itself. But when he cites St Gregory’s letter to Secundinus, he does so without mentioning either a decree or a chapter, praising it in the same manner as he praises other Fathers. This indicates that he received that letter, like the texts of the Fathers, not from the collection of canons but from elsewhere.

Similarly, from another source he evidently reported a long fragment of a letter of St Isidore of Seville to Mason, which deals with the same discipline concerning fallen clerics and is likewise believed to be spurious. For it is not found at all in Pseudo-Isidore, or in his pure manuscripts.

5. Rabanus’s other collection, contained in a lengthy letter that he wrote to Heribald in 853 while he was bishop of Mainz, is entirely of the same character as the preceding collection. Indeed, a considerable amount is found there copied word for word from the same *Book of Penitents*, including the same addition to St Gregory’s letter to Secundinus and the fragment of St Isidore of Seville’s letter to Mason.

Here too, insofar as the canons of councils and the decrees of pontiffs are concerned, there is nothing that is not found in the Hadriana and Hispanic collections, except for certain canons of the councils of Reims, the Third Council of Tours, and Mainz, which were held in Rabanus’s own time. This letter, divided into thirty-four chapters, was first published by Peter Stevartius in volume VI of Henricus Canisius’s *Ancient Readings*, and later by Étienne Baluze in the Appendix to Regino, p. 467.

## CHAPTER IX. On the collections of the capitularies of Ansegisus and Benedict the Levite, and on their additions. Excerpts from the same capitularies by Isaac, bishop of Langres. On the chapters of Herard, archbishop of Tours; Theodulf of Orléans; Ahyto of Basel; and others of the same kind

1. The capitularies of the Frankish kings contain many provisions pertaining to the governance of the external organization of the Church. They were for the most part enacted in assemblies attended by several bishops and were also collected here and there by the bishops themselves at the command of the kings. Many were excerpted from the judgments of the holy Fathers and the canons of councils, as Baluze noted (*Preface to the Capitularies*, no. 9).

Hence a broad agreement between these capitularies and the ecclesiastical canons emerged. For this reason, the bishops assembled at Trosly in the diocese of Soissons in 909, after praising the institutions of the canons, called the capitularies their “attendants” (*Council of Trosly*, ch. 3). Since they were confirmed both in synods and by pontiffs, they sometimes even acquired the name of canons, as the aforementioned Baluze proved (*Preface*, no. 18).

The collections of these capitularies, compiled by Abbot Ansegisus and Benedict the Levite, therefore seemed not improperly to be included among the collections of canons, especially since the capitularies inserted into later collections of canons were for the most part derived from the same canonical sources.

2. Before the year 827 these capitularies had been written separately, as they had been enacted separately, and had not yet been collected into a single body. Abbot Ansegisus—not of Lobbes but of Fontenelle, as Baluze demonstrates (*Preface*, no. 40)—was the first to collect certain capitularies of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, so that they would not be consigned to oblivion. He arranged them into four books, whose order Ansegisus himself gives in the preface:

> “Those things that Lord Charles enacted concerning ecclesiastical order I gathered together in the first little book. Those ecclesiastical matters that Lord and most devout Emperor Louis added I set down in the second. Those things that Lord Charles enacted at various times concerning secular law I gathered together in the third. Those things that the illustrious Emperor Lord Louis enacted for the strengthening of secular law I collected in the fourth.”

Baluze observes that although Ansegisus’s plan was to set down in the first book only the chapters of Charlemagne, he nevertheless mixed in by mistake certain chapters of Louis the Pious, from chapter 79 through chapter 104. These were taken from Louis’s capitulary of 816. He derives a not implausible explanation for the error from the fact that when Ansegisus found two chapters of Charlemagne at the beginning of the capitulary enacted by Louis, he assumed that the remaining chapters of the same edict also belonged to Charles.

The capitularies from which Ansegisus fashioned those books were found and published through the diligence of learned men in ancient archives.

3. Since Ansegisus had omitted many chapters of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, Benedict the Levite of Mainz, at the command of Otgar, archbishop of the Church of Mainz, undertook around the year 845 to collect their omitted constitutions, which were frequently used. He also thought that the provisions previously established by Pippin and Carloman should be added.

He did not excerpt material solely from the capitularies of kings and emperors. He also took much from the books of sacred Scripture; from the sayings of the holy Fathers; from the Theodosian Code, or from the interpretations of Anianus; from the opinions of Paulus the jurist; from the Novels of Julianus the antecessor; from the code of Visigothic laws; and from documents that, as he himself says, “we found scattered in various places and on various sheets, as well as in various synods and general assemblies, and especially stored by Riculfus in the archive of the holy metropolitan Church of Mainz, and which we eventually found after they had been discovered by Autcarius II, his successor and kinsman.”

This final clause chiefly indicates the spurious Pseudo-Isidorian wares wrongly attributed to the age of Riculfus, portions of which are found incorporated into Benedict’s books. On this matter, see what we observed in Part III, chapter 6, § 4.

Benedict’s collection is divided into three longer books. Added after Ansegisus’s books, these constitute the fifth, sixth, and seventh books of the capitularies.

4. In addition to these seven books of capitularies, four additions have been found. They contain many chapters that are found neither in Ansegisus nor in Benedict.

The first addition, which in certain manuscript copies is joined to the third book of Benedict the Levite in a continuous series of numbers, so as to form part of it, consists of the Capitularly of Aachen of 817, in which eighty chapters were enacted for keeping monks in their proper observance.

The second addition contains twenty-eight chapters comprising matters that were to be announced generally to the people throughout the parishes.

The 124 chapters of the third addition properly concern bishops or the various orders. They must not only observe these provisions themselves but also teach those subject or entrusted to them to carry them out.

The fourth and longer addition, which concerns various matters of discipline, consists of 171 chapters. Among these, most are taken from the Pseudo-Isidorian impostures.

Since Benedict the Levite mentions no document from which he excerpted the chapters, distinguishing what was spurious from what was genuine required no small amount of study and comparison. In the fourth addition, however, the spurious sources themselves are cited under the titles found in Isidore. This indicates not only that the author of this addition was different from Benedict the Levite, who refrained from citing his sources, but also that by the time this addition was made the Isidorian collection had become famous and widely disseminated, so that its documents could be identified by titles already familiar.

The date of this addition can be deduced from the brief preface attached to it, in which the following is read:

> “We have taken care to collect certain following chapters from the decrees of the holy Fathers and the edicts of the emperors, and, after general consultation, we have ordered our chancellor Erchembald to insert them among our chapters, to be held by the strictest force of law.”

Two chancellors named Erchembald are mentioned: one under Charlemagne and the other under Lothair I. Since this addition accepted the spurious wares of Isidore, which appeared long after Charlemagne, the Erchembald named in the heading must be recognized as the one who flourished under Lothair I. Thus it was during this period that the fourth addition was attached to the capitularies.

5. This entire body of capitularies, together with its appendices, was formerly published. The most outstanding edition, however, is that of Étienne Baluze, published at Paris in 1677 in two folio volumes. In them he illustrated the same capitularies with many documents and notes. Among other things, he prefixed all the original capitularies that he was able to find, some published and some unpublished, from which the aforementioned compilers—Ansegisus, Benedict the Levite, and the authors of the additions—derived their chapters as from sources.

6. The chapters of Isaac, bishop of Langres, should not be separated from the books of the capitularies of the Frankish kings, since they were excerpted from those same capitularies. According to the author of the *Chronicle of Saint Benignus*, this bishop composed, beginning in 859, a book called the *Canons of Isaac*. By selecting the more useful material from the books of canons, he condensed it into a single volume.

He took everything from the three last books of the capitularies, which had been issued after Ansegisus by Benedict the Levite and were contained in a separate volume. In his preface, the same bishop states that he excerpted those chapters that the venerable Boniface, legate of the holy Roman and apostolic Church and archbishop of Mainz, acting in the place of Pope Zacharias together with the orthodox Frankish prince Carloman, had drawn up in two councils of bishops for the honor and advancement of the Church of God, and that Pope Zacharias himself had confirmed them by apostolic authority in the year 742 of the Lord’s Incarnation and established them as irrefragably binding upon all the faithful of the Church of God.

By making this preliminary statement in order to give authority to his collection, Isaac reveals how great the authority of the Apostolic See was among the Gauls. It must, however, be observed that Isaac made these claims on the authority of Benedict the Levite himself, who inserted the same account in his preface.

This delegation of St Boniface and the confirmation of Pope Zacharias concern only the opening chapters of Benedict’s first book, which is the fifth among the capitularies. Chapter 1 contains a letter of Pope Zacharias addressed to the Franks and Gauls; chapters 2 and 3 present two synods celebrated by St Boniface, the apostolic legate, in the presence of Carloman—one in 742 and the other at Liptinae in 743 (*Baluze*, vol. I, p. 1233).

Isaac’s collection is divided into eleven titles, and each title comprises several chapters.

7. Étienne Baluze (*vol. I, p. 1283*) also adds the chapters of Herard, archbishop of Tours, which are believed to have been collected from the capitularies of the Frankish kings. They are 140 chapters, which he ordered to be read at a diocesan synod in 858, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June.

The same Baluze places notes from the books of the capitularies in the margin, from which he believes each chapter to have been excerpted in summary. Yet there is no evidence that these chapters were taken from the capitularies rather than from other sources of canon law. The same judgments are found in several other canons.

Herard’s chapters seem to be of the same kind as those of Theodulf of Orléans. Since Theodulf flourished before the books of the capitularies, he certainly derived nothing from them. The chapters of Ahyto of Basel, Walter or Gualter of Orléans, Hincmar of Reims, Rodulf of Bourges, Riculfus of Soissons, Atto of Vercelli, and others of the same kind are likewise of this character. They could have been derived no more from the capitularies than from synods.

We add here only that the aforementioned chapters of Herard are also found in Vatican Regina manuscript 612, where several chapters are joined together and constitute forty-six sections.

## CHAPTER X. On the manuscript collection of Sorbonico-Mutinensis, divided into twelve parts. It is shown to have been composed in Italy at the end of the ninth century. On the use of Roman laws in collections

[Col. 0315A]

1. The collection preserved in the elegant manuscript 841 of the Sorbonne Library, surpassed by none either in extent or antiquity, is commended by P. Coustant in the preface to volume I of the letters of the Roman pontiffs, no. 169, and by François Salmon, prefect of the same library, in a treatise in French entitled *On the Study of Councils and Their Collections*, Part II, chapter 1.

The Roman correctors, moreover, in their edition of Gratian, mention a collection of canons from the library of the church of Modena. Since they cite from it nothing except certain readings, what it was remained unknown. We, however, found in the Vatican Library a manuscript numbered 4899, copied from the Modena exemplar and used by those same Roman correctors.

When we compared the titles reported from the Sorbonne manuscript by the writers mentioned above with the titles we found in this Vatican exemplar, we discovered that exactly the same collection was contained in both. For this reason, as a matter of distinction, we have called it the Sorbonico-Mutinensis collection.

We also found in the Vatican Library two other very ancient manuscripts, Pal. 580 and 581. One of them contains only the first four parts of the same collection, while the other contains only the first three parts. Both, however, lack the preface that is found in the Sorbonne, Modena, and Vatican exemplars.

From these manuscripts, which we were able conveniently to examine, it will be possible to provide a more accurate description of this distinguished collection.

2. This collection is divided into twelve parts. In the Vatican manuscript the following preface is placed before it:

> “To the magnificent lord, most vigilant shepherd, and most excellent archbishop Anselm: we, the smallest little sheep of his flock and, in a certain sense, his own household slaves, earnestly pray that you may receive the inexpressible reward of pontifical dignity.
>
> “Illustrious shepherd, your keenness, which looks ahead carefully and wisely to ecclesiastical interests and continually strives inwardly and outwardly for the common advancement of the flock entrusted to you, is to be preferred above all praise of your providence. You do not refuse frequently to admonish our littleness also among the rest of your servants and to incite us to better studies, commanding and enjoining in every way that we should take whatever care our little intellect permits to gather together and fit into a single form the institutions of the sacred canons—whatever the teachers of the holy and catholic Church, namely the apostles and apostolic men, have set down in their writings for the instruction of posterity from the very beginnings of the Christian faith.
>
> “We, however, being thoroughly conscious of our ignorance, smallness, and weakness, would have judged that a work so arduous ought not to be undertaken with any rashness or presumed upon with any audacity, unless the authority of your command compelled us—especially since it is certain that stronger and more discerning men, both Greek and Latin, have labored at this very task. For on the one hand Ferrandus, a deacon of the Church of Carthage, and on the other a certain Cresconius, an imitator of the same work, seem to have produced a kind of harmony of ecclesiastical sanctions. We must take great care lest, by patching together the same work, we incur the disgrace either of being compilers or of diminishing what has been handed down.
>
> “Therefore, so that we may be able to satisfy your command, which presses us beyond measure, and your most ardent love, after the divine assistance we ask above all for the aid of your fatherly blessing. May it enable us, among the other pupils of your lordship, even if not from our own labor, at least from the labor of others, not to appear wholly free from obligation in the judgment of your most provident wisdom.
>
> “To carry out, then, the little work of our smallness, insofar as the Lord, the maker of good works, shall deign to grant increase, we have judged that all the pages of the canons of the Fathers, of councils, and of decretal letters should be divided into twelve parts, in the likeness of an apostolic genealogy. This is to be done in such a way that suitable chapters are prefaced to each part, presenting clear testimony to the matter at issue like truthful witnesses, and opening to the eager reader an accessible path to find what he desires.
>
> “Let no one whom we ask take offense if, concerning each matter, we carefully add what each of the teachers has thought. For the judgment supported by the authority of a greater number of judges appears more settled and unshaken.”

3. The index with the titles of the individual parts is then added as follows:

The first part of this work, which with God’s help we undertake, contains material concerning the primacy and dignity of the Roman See and of the other primates, patriarchs, archbishops, and metropolitans. **133 chapters.**

The second part contains material concerning the appropriate honor and dignity, and the various affairs, of bishops and chorepiscopi. **300 chapters.**

The third part contains material concerning the celebration of a synod and the summons to a synod; accusers and accusations; witnesses and testimony; those unjustly despoiled; and judges and ecclesiastical or secular judgments. **186 chapters.**

The fourth part contains material concerning the appropriate dignity and various affairs of presbyters and deacons, as well as of the remaining ecclesiastical orders. **182 chapters.**

The fifth part contains material concerning the instruction of clerics, their support, and the quality of their life. **199 chapters.**

The sixth part contains material concerning the way of life of monks and the profession of consecrated women and widows. **142 chapters.**

The seventh part contains material concerning laypeople—namely emperors, princes, and the other orders of the secular world. **141 chapters.**

The eighth part contains material concerning the rule of the Christian faith, the grace of Christ, and the carrying out of the divine commandments. **89 chapters.**

The ninth part contains material concerning the sacrament of baptism, those to be baptized, and those who have been baptized. **66 chapters.**

The tenth part contains material concerning the establishment and worship of the temples of God, and their lands; and concerning sacrifices, offerings, and tithes. **169 chapters.**

The eleventh part contains material concerning the solemnity of Easter and the other feasts and weekdays. **47 chapters.**

The twelfth part contains material concerning heretics, schismatics, Jews, and pagans. **26 chapters.**
4. The preface itself, which we have reproduced from an apograph of the Vatican manuscript preserved at Modena, suggests that more than one person worked simultaneously on the preparation of this collection. “We,” they say, “the little lambs of that smallest flock, and in a certain sense its own household servants”; and throughout the entire composition they consistently speak in the plural. Yet since these words appear in the singular in the Sorbonic manuscript used by P. Coustant and Franciscus Salmon, and since in one or the other exemplar the copyist’s intervention must be assumed, it seems more probable that the scribe who thought there was a single author altered the text arbitrarily by introducing the singular, rather than that someone changed the singular into the plural.

The chapters are excerpted from four sources—the Hadrianic and Isidorian collections, the Register of St. Gregory, and the Roman laws contained in the Code, the Novels, and Justinian’s Institutes—according to this consistent method: first, the largest number of chapters is transcribed, partly from the Hadrianic collection, [Col. 0316D] from which, among other things, the canons of the Greek synods in Dionysius’s version were taken, and partly from the collection of Isidore, which supplied spurious documents; next, some material from the Register of St. Gregory follows; and finally, certain passages from the Roman laws are appended.

Thus, for example, the first part presents the canons of councils and the decrees of popes from the collections just mentioned down to chapter 119. Thereafter, certain passages from the Register of Blessed Gregory are given from chapter 120 through chapter 128. Finally, some passages from the Roman laws are supplied from chapter 129 through chapter 133. We observe that in the third part the canons of councils and the decrees of popes are numbered down to chapter 186. After that, several chapters from Gregory’s Register and from the Roman laws are appended without numbers. [CCLXXXVII]

5. Most people believe that Ivo was the first to introduce Roman laws from Justinian’s Code and Novels into a collection of canons. But this collection [Col. 0317A] is earlier than Ivo and, as we shall soon see, earlier even than Burchard and Regino.

Moreover, it should not be omitted here that in the Vatican, Modenese apograph, and in the Sorbonic manuscript, certain documents were added that do not belong to the original collection. For each part ends, according to the compilers’ plan, with the Roman laws. After the Roman laws in the third part, however, the following are added:

I. “On the disturbance of the council. The definition of the Fathers,” and so forth.

II. “Here begins the account of the four principal synods. The canon in Greek,” and so forth.

III. “Likewise, an account of the canons of the apostles and of the six principal synods.”

IV. “Likewise, a brief note on the remaining synods,” derived from the foregoing material of the Isidorian collection.

V. “Likewise, a note on the decretals of the Apostles”—one should read “apostolic decretals”—which was published from the Sorbonic manuscript by Franciscus Salmon in the cited book, part II, chapter 1, p. 258 of the Leipzig edition of 1726.

VI. “On formal letters.” There is presented a formal letter from Regembert of Vercelli to Andrew of Milan, which had previously been printed from another ancient manuscript of the present collection by Franciscus Bernardinus Ferrarius of Milan [Col. 0317B] in book I, chapter 5, of *On the Ancient Kind of Ecclesiastical Letters*, and from Ferrarius it was inserted by Baluze into the appendix to the *Capitularies*, vol. II, col. 1575, where the following date is found: “Given at Vercelli in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 904, indiction VII.”

In the Vallicellian manuscript B 58 we found this same formal letter without its chronological notation; it was printed from that manuscript by Mabillon, vol. I of the *Museum Italicum*, p. 240. Accordingly, Bishop Regembert should be added to Ughellus’s catalogue of the bishops of Vercelli, and his episcopate at Vercelli during this period is confirmed by a privilege of Pope Anastasius III addressed to the same Ragimpertus, which exists in manuscript 62 of the chapter of Verona. For Anastasius III held the pontificate from 910 to 912.

VII. “The order for celebrating a council,” as it is found in Isidore.
