At the end of the fifth part, chapters of Pope Nicholas, collected and confirmed at a council in 861 against John of Ravenna, are added with their subscriptions. [Col. 0317C] They were published from the Modenese manuscript of this collection by P. Abbot Bacchini in the appendix to *Agnellus of Ravenna*, and are reprinted in vol. X of the Venetian edition of the *Councils*, col. 189.

The additions to the third part are absent from the Vatican Palatine manuscripts, which present that same part.

6. In investigating the date of this collection, P. Coustant declares that it was certainly compiled before the year 1009. For, he says, this is clearly shown by the person who copied the Sorbonic exemplar, at whose end the following note is found:

“By order of the lord Heimo, venerable bishop of the Church of Verdun, I, Rodulphus, obediently and gladly received this book for copying, and finished it in the year 1009 of the Lord’s Incarnation, indiction VII, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, while Henry was reigning in the kingdom of Lothar. I beg you, whoever you are who read here, to remember me, the aforementioned Rodulphus, an unworthy sinful monk, so that I may not receive punishment for my offenses, but through your prayer, or through that of all who here examine the laws, may receive some share of eternal refreshment. Farewell, blessed lord Bishop Heimo, and kindly remember your little servant.”

Thus far P. Coustant, who was able to conjecture nothing further about the date. Since, however, the two aforementioned Vatican Palatine codices, 580 and 581, square in format and divided into two columns, are believed to have been written at least at the beginning of the tenth century, the collection itself seems assignable to that century. Yet that it is older, and was composed in the ninth century, will be plainly demonstrated by what is presented under number eight.

7. The Roman laws cited here from Justinian’s Code, Institutes, and Novels suggest that this collection was composed in Italy. In Gaul, Salic law and the Capitularies of the Frankish kings were in force; in Germany, besides those same Capitularies, the ancient laws of the Ripuarians, Alemanni, and Bavarians, as well as other native laws, were in force. A Gallic or German compiler would have cited these.

In Italy, however, from the time of Justinian, who ruled there, the Roman laws of his Code, Institutes, and Novels were in use. Hence St. Gregory the Great repeatedly cites them in his letters. See *Epistles* I.9 [CCLXXXVIII], III.38, IV.25, VI.36, VII.23 and 39, IX.6 and 7, and XIII.3, 4, 11, and especially 45.

For this reason Leo IV wrote in a letter to the Emperor Lothar, who ruled in Italy:

“We beseech your clemency that, just as hitherto Roman law has prevailed . . . so now it may retain its proper strength and its own vigor.”

This fragment appears in Ivo, part IV, chapter 131, and in Gratian, Distinction 10, chapter 13.

The Roman correctors note:

“It seems that Lothar granted to the Roman people what Leo requested here; for in the Lombard laws, book XI, title 57, we read: ‘Emperor Lothar. We wish that the entire Roman people be asked according to which law they wish to live, so that they may live under the law under which they have professed that they wish to live,’ and so forth.”

But this law of Lothar was enacted in 824, under Pope Eugenius II, who preceded Leo IV, as Stephanus Baluzius correctly demonstrated in the preface to the *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*, no. 24. Therefore this had already been granted before Leo IV.

Since Lothar also sought to have the Capitularies of the Frankish kings accepted by the Romans, as we infer from the ancient poems that we published from a manuscript, part II, chapter 10, § 4, at the end, Leo IV insisted that what had long been established by custom should not be disturbed by any innovation.

The clergy of Italy universally professed that they wished to live according to Roman law, as Ludovicus the Emperor had decreed concerning them in book III of the Lombard laws, title 1, no. 37. By the term “Roman law” were understood those laws written in Justinian’s Code, Institutes, and Novels.

Thus the authors of the present collection—who were certainly members of the clergy—by adding Roman laws from these sources at the end of each part, but never Salic laws or those of other nations, show themselves to be Italians. Regino, a German, did cite certain laws from the Theodosian Code through Annianus, since these had long been in use among foreigners; [Col. 0318C] but he also presented the Capitularies and the laws of the Ripuarians and Burgundians, and never Justinian’s laws, which were peculiar to the Italians.

If certain foreigners excerpted some passages from Justinian’s Novels, they are known to have used the epitome of Julian the Antecessor; almost the Italians alone reproduced the actual text of the Novels themselves. Ivo of Chartres, although a Gaul, later cited laws from the same Justinian sources because the public study of those laws, instituted in his age, had begun to spread more widely.

The Italian origin of the collection is also confirmed both by the formal letter of Regembert of Vercelli to Andrew of Milan, which was added near the end of the third part, and by the Roman synod under Nicholas I against John of Ravenna, added to the fifth part. These are two Italian documents. Formal letters, in particular, are usually copied in manuscripts from the region in which they were issued or received.

8. If we knew who the archbishop Anselm was to whom the preface is addressed, the place [Col. 0318D] and date of the collection would become clearer. Since P. Coustant, perhaps assuming that the collection was Gallican, sought him among the archbishops of Gaul, he admits that he could discover nothing.

We, however, having no doubt that the collection is Italian and searching among the Italian archbishops, discovered that he was Anselm II of Milan, who flourished in the ninth century, from the year 883 until 897. There was indeed another Anselm, archbishop of Milan, who lived at the beginning of the ninth century, and yet another who governed the same Church around the middle of the eleventh century.

But this collection cannot belong to the first, since several chapters were transferred into it from the Isidorian compilation, which circulated after his time. Nor does it fit the third Anselm, before whom the Sorbonic exemplar and the two Vatican-Palatine manuscripts had already been written. Therefore this Italian collection must be placed under Anselm II, archbishop of Milan, at the end of the ninth century.

[CCLXXXIX] CHAPTER XI. On the Collections of Regino and Abbo

[Col. 0319A]

1. The collection of Regino, abbot of Prüm, is famous; later collectors, Burchard and Ivo, took many things from it. Regino compiled it at the beginning of the tenth century at the command of Rathbod, archbishop of Trier, in whose diocese the monastery of Prüm was located.

This is clear from the title itself, which Baluze, in his excellent Paris edition of 1671, reproduced from manuscript codices as follows:

“Here begins the little book on ecclesiastical discipline and the Christian religion, collected by order of the lord Rathbod, metropolitan bishop of the city of Trier, by Regino, formerly abbot of the monastery of Prüm, from various councils of the holy Fathers and decrees of the Roman pontiffs, successfully, in the name of God. Amen.”

Regino relates in his *Chronicle* that Richarius succeeded him in the governance of the monastery of Prüm in the year 899. That the collection, which he composed after relinquishing the abbacy, was certainly not published before the year 906 is evident from chapters 448 and 449 of the first book, in which two formal letters are presented: one from Rathbod himself to Robert, bishop of Metz, and the other from Dado, bishop of Verdun, to the aforementioned Rathbod, both dated 906. [Col. 0319B]

2. This collection is divided into two books. The first treats of ecclesiastical persons and matters, the second of the laity. Regino seems to have borrowed this division from Martin of Braga.

The first book begins with an inquiry into what the bishop or his ministers ought to investigate in their district or territory concerning ecclesiastical matters and persons. As Baluze astutely observed, this same inquiry appears among the *Capitula* of Hincmar, title 2. Therefore Regino must either be said to have taken it from Hincmar’s *Capitula*, or this formula must have been older and copied first by Hincmar and afterward by Regino; the latter seems more probable.

Similarly, in book II, chapter 5, an inquiry is proposed concerning the bishop’s treatment of the laity. In both places, after the inquiry, [Col. 0319C] canonical authorities are appended to prove each of the matters previously set out in the inquiry.

Thus, after the inquiry in the first book, we read:

“These matters, which we have expressed above as items to be investigated, ought to be strengthened by canonical authority.”

And after the inquiry in the second book:

“These chapters, which we have noted in order, ought to be strengthened by canonical decrees.”

The first book consists of 443 chapters, while the second comprises 446 chapters.

3. The authorities cited to prove the chapters are taken not only from the canons of councils, the decrees of Roman pontiffs, and the sayings or judgments of the holy Fathers, but sometimes also from the laws of the Theodosian Code—or rather, from the words of its interpreter Annianus—from the Capitularies of the Frankish kings, and likewise from the laws of the Burgundians and Ripuarians.

Since the spurious letters of pseudo-Isidore are rarely cited, some infer that Regino did not think highly of them. For, says Baluze (*In the preface*, no. 8), “it cannot be said that they were unknown to him, since he makes use of their authority several times; and since it is also certain that he received very many things from Isidore’s collection.”

We, however, believe that he took more from collections older than pseudo-Isidore, which, having been arranged under common topics, could supply nothing from the latter’s spurious wares. That he excerpted much from a manuscript collection of this kind, which we discussed in chapter 6, no. 6, is so certain that we have found entire chapters belonging specifically to that collection transcribed in Regino in the same order and under the same titles.

It is sufficiently credible that he likewise derived other material from collections of this sort that had circulated in Gaul and Germany before the Isidorian collection, just as Baluze reports that he took material from Halitgar and Rabanus (*ibid.*, no. 12).

At any rate, he used a collection in which the canons of councils and the decrees of pontiffs, gathered from various places, were described in a long sequence of numbers. For this reason, in book I, chapter 61, he cites the first canon of the Council of Nantes under the title: “From the Council of Nantes, 419,” that is, chapter 419. Similarly, in the same book, chapter 117, when he presents a decree of Innocent, he says that he received it from “the letter of Pope Innocent, chapter 387.”

These numbers of chapters or canons, 419 and 387, can correspond not to any collection that presents complete documents, [CCXC] but only to those codices of canons that describe several canons of councils and decrees of pontiffs indiscriminately, intermingled under one sequence of numbers.

Indeed, the aforementioned decree of Innocent is transmitted in the manuscript collection mentioned shortly before, from which we observed that Regino took many other things, in the same words. There it is numbered 377, not 387, as it is read in Regino; this seems attributable to a copyist’s error.

Therefore, although most of the material quoted by Regino is found in the Dionysian, Hadrianic, Hispanic, and Isidorian collections, it does not follow that he extracted the decrees from those collections. [Col. 0320B] He generally used collections that had excerpted the canons from them before his time.

Consequently, since in collections of this kind the canons of the Greek synods are not always presented according to the ancient—or, as it is called, Isidorian—translation, but frequently according to the Dionysian version, Regino could derive from these sources sometimes the ancient version and sometimes the Dionysian.

He added through his own diligence the authorities of the Capitularies and the laws of the Burgundians and Ripuarians, as well as certain other more recent materials absent from the collections mentioned above. By the same method, we believe that he excerpted a few items from the wares of pseudo-Isidore that he thought might serve his purpose, so that it cannot on that account be inferred that he regarded them as suspect.

4. Near the end of the same tenth century in which Regino flourished, Abbo, abbot of the monastery of Fleury, published a collection with a preface addressed to the Frankish king Hugh and his son Robert. Since King Hugh died in the year 997, this collection was compiled before that year.

Its title is as follows:

“Here begin the canons of the lord Abbo, abbot . . . excerpted from other canons.”

It is divided into fifty-two chapters and is composed from the canons of councils, the decrees of pontiffs, the Capitularies of the Frankish kings, and the Novel constitutions, arranged in such a way that Abbo’s own words are repeatedly inserted and provide continuity to the work.

It was published through the efforts of Mabillon in vol. II of the *Analecta*, p. 248; the folio edition is on p. 133.

CHAPTER XII. On the Collection of Burchard, Bishop of Worms; His Practice of Attributing to Synods, Pontiffs, or Fathers the Sayings of Certain Later Writers; the Penitential of the Churches of Germany, Received and Enlarged by Him

1. Burchard, a Hessian by birth, was not a monk, as many have believed, but a canon and royal chaplain. He was afterward promoted to the see of Worms before the year 1002 and held it until the year 1025, when he died, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September.

While he was bishop, he compiled a collection of canons at the urging of Brunicho, provost of the Church of Worms. Stephanus Baluzius, in the preface to the books of Antonius Augustinus *On the Emendation of Gratian*, § 18, observed that the true author of this collection ought rather to be called Olbert, a monk of Lobbes and afterward abbot of Gembloux. Under Olbert’s direction and instruction, Burchard supposedly assembled that great volume of canons into a patchwork, if what is read in the book *On the Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux* is true.

But Bartholomaeus Fisen relates the matter differently from the Gembloux and Liège manuscripts in *The Flowers of the Church of Liège*, p. 328. Since Burchard used Olbert, his teacher and intimate associate, as an assistant, it cannot be denied that he employed him as a collaborator in the work.

Thus Sigebert, in his *Chronicle* under the year 1008, writes that Burchard, “with the collaboration of his teacher Olbert, a man learned in every respect,” produced a great volume of canons. The anonymous author who composed Burchard’s life after his death, included in the Cologne edition, mentions another assistant in the same work:

“At the same time, he labored not a little on the Collection of Canons . . . For, with the assistance of Walter, bishop of Speyer, and at the urging and prompting of Brunicho, the provost, he gathered the canons into a single body.”

The title *Collection of Canons* deserves notice, for the manuscript codices have no title at all. It agrees, however, with Burchard’s own preface, which is appended shortly afterward and at whose end he calls his collection a *Collection*.

2. In the same preface Burchard testifies that he prepared the work for the use of his Church of Worms. It is inferred that the work was not begun before the year 1012 from book II, chapter 227, where he presents his formal letter written to Walter of Speyer in that same year, on the Ides of March.

We learn that the work had already been completed before Burchard attended the synod of Seligenstadt in 1023 because, since he could not insert the canons of that synod into the collection, he appended them all at the end.

Joannes Molinaeus, in the preface to Ivo’s *Decree*, states that much is lacking from the editions of Burchard’s books which he himself saw in fuller form in ancient manuscripts, but that the material was divided into only twelve books, of which the sixth part is the published book.

For this reason, as we believe, Joannes Albertus Fabricius states in vol. XI of the *Greek Library*, p. 8, that Burchard collected twelve volumes of decrees, and adds:

“This work itself has not yet seen the light in its entirety, but only excerpts from it, divided into twenty books.”

Yet not only does the codex from which the edition was produced assign twenty books to Burchard, but so also do those very ancient exemplars mentioned by Petrus Pithoeus.

We likewise saw four complete codices: two in the Vatican Library, marked nos. 1350 and 1355; one among the Benedictine Fathers in the monastery of Padolirone; and another at Padua in the library of St. Justina. All of them present the same number of books, inscribed to Burchard. We may add two other ancient Vatican exemplars, nos. 1356 and 4980, one of which begins with book VII and the other with book IX; each continues through book XIX, which lacks its ending because the codices are mutilated.

Since the sequence of books and their contents are the same in other complete exemplars, these two exemplars also confirm the same total of twenty books.

Moreover, since no codices known to date contain a collection distributed into twelve parts and bearing Burchard’s name, we fear that Joannes Molinaeus, misled by some ambiguity, inadvertently took another anonymous collection divided into the same number of parts for Burchard’s work because of the agreement between them in several respects.

Perhaps he had before his eyes the Sorbonic-Modenese collection, divided into twelve parts, which we described in chapter ten. He may have been deceived because there is complete agreement between the titles of Burchard’s books I, II, and the following books and the titles prefixed to parts I, II, III, IV, V, and X of that collection.

Certainly, the preface found only in manuscripts presenting twenty books has Burchard as its author and confirms those same books. This becomes much clearer from three Burchard codices—the Vatican 1355, the Padua manuscript of St. Justina, and the Padolirone manuscript—in which the preface itself, differing from the printed editions and, as we shall soon see, more genuine than the commonly circulated version, not only explicitly approves the same number of twenty books, but, presenting their titles within it, testifies that these, and no others, were compiled by Burchard.

An anonymous author contemporary with Burchard likewise agrees with him; in Burchard’s life he writes:

“He divided this body, or Collection, and distributed it into twenty books.”

Do not these two testimonies—the one from a contemporary writer and the other from Burchard himself—eliminate the theory of twelve books?

3. In the works of Georgius Cassander, pp. 1091 and 1098, Fabricius reports that the following is written:

“We also came upon a manuscript work of Burchard, which we compared only cursorily with the printed edition published at Paris in 1549, and we discovered that the wording of the letter had been entirely altered.”

We too observed the same thing in the three aforementioned codices, in which we found only the preface. In these manuscripts, the preface differs from the commonly circulated version not only in wording but also in order. For the material that in the printed editions appears to have been added by others at the end of the preface is inserted into the preface itself in these manuscripts, so that it is manifestly clear that it was written by Burchard as its author.

The agreement of these ancient exemplars—which, we do not doubt, is shared by other codices that contain the preface—suggests that this is the genuine preface, or letter, of Burchard to Brunicho. The same conclusion is confirmed by the very awkwardness of its style and syntax, which are especially appropriate to that age.

Since the commonly circulated preface differs so openly from the ancient manuscripts just mentioned, we believe that it was altered at the discretion of some learned person who preferred a more elegant style. In the meantime, we present it here as it is found in the codices.

[Col. 0322B] [CCXCII] 4.

“Burchard, bishop of Worms in name only, to his faithful Brunicho, namely the provost of that same see: greetings in the Lord Christ.

“For many days now, your familiarity, dearest brother, being present among us, has repeatedly urged and suggested that I gather into one body, for the benefit of our fellow priests, a little book drawn from various useful sources—both from the sayings of the holy Fathers and from the canons, as well as from various penitentials—with vigilant attention.

“This was especially necessary because the laws of the canons and the judgments concerning penitents in our diocese are so confused, diverse, and uncultivated; so entirely neglected; so greatly at variance with one another; and supported by the authority of almost no one, that because of their disagreement they can scarcely be distinguished even by persons of limited learning.

“Consequently, those who flee to the remedy of penance often cannot be helped at all, both because of the confusion of the books and because of the ignorance of the priests. Why is this? I think it happens chiefly because the canons do not define with sufficient care, clarity, and completeness the measure of time and the manner of the offense in the performance of penance for each crime, so as to state for each one how it ought to be corrected; rather, they establish that the matter should be left to the judgment of an understanding priest.

“Therefore, since this cannot be done except by the wise and those learned in divine law, your affection asked me to offer this book, briefly collected, for the boys to learn at last, so that what our fellow workers, occupied with mature age, had neglected in our own days through the tardiness of our predecessors might now be handed on to the young and to others who wished to learn.

“Thus they might first become good students, then teachers and masters of the people, and might receive in school what they would one day have to teach those entrusted to them.

“Your desire and request, brother, seem just to me, and I give thanks for such a wish. I also return manifold thanks to the one who made you such a person for me, because I knew that you had labored continually for the condition of our Church.

“But do not attribute the fact that I delayed for so long to carry out your repeated exhortation to my laziness, for two reasons had made it least of all possible for me to undertake this: namely, the various and unavoidable ecclesiastical necessities that arise daily like waves; and, in addition, the care of worldly affairs belonging to imperial commands, which greatly dulls the mind of one who is studying and striving toward higher things, because when anyone’s mind is divided among many matters, it becomes less capable of attending to each one.

“Nevertheless, obeying your holy requests, with God’s gift I collected the synodal precepts and sacred statutes both from the sayings of the holy Fathers and from the canons, and, as I was able, joined them together into one body. I divided that same body into twenty books. And if any diligent reader carefully examines them, he will find in them many benefits for our ministry.

[Col. 0323A] Index [Note: [Col. 0323D] This title, or at least Burchard’s name, appears to have been inserted at the discretion of the scribes.] of the individual books of D. Burchard, bishop of Worms, briefly showing what each book contains.

“Book One contains material on the power and primacy of the apostolic see, the patriarchs, the other primates, and the metropolitans; on the celebration of a synod and the summons to a synod; on the accused, accusers, and witnesses; on those unjustly despoiled; on judges and every appropriate honor and dignity; and on the various business and ministry of bishops.

“Book Two contains material on the fitting dignity, the various formation, nourishment, or quality of life, and the various business and ministry of priests, deacons, and the other ecclesiastical orders.

“Book Three contains material on the establishment, worship, and honor of divine houses; on tithes, offerings, and the rights of individuals; and on which books are to be received into the sacred Catalogue, which are apocryphal, and when they are to be added.

“Book Four contains the sacrament of baptism and the ministry of those who are to be baptized, those who have been baptized, those who are to be signed, and those who have been signed.

“Book Five contains the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood and their reception and observance.

[CCXCIII] “Book Six contains material on homicides committed voluntarily and involuntarily; on parricides and fratricides; on those who kill their legitimate wives and their elders; on the killing of members of the clergy; and on the observance and penance appropriate to each person.

“Book Seven contains material on incestuous intercourse within the degrees of kinship, on the degree at which the faithful ought either to marry or to separate, and on the restoration and penance of each person.

“Book Eight contains material on men and women dedicated to God who transgress their sacred commitment, and [Col. 0323C] on their restoration and penance.

“Book Nine contains material on un veiled virgins and widows, on those who abduct them and on their separation, on the joining of legitimate marriages, on concubines, and on the transgression and penance of each person.

“Book Ten contains material on enchanters, augurs, diviners, and sorcerers; on various illusions of the devil; on slanderers, contentious persons, and conspirators; and on the penance of each person.

“Book Eleven contains material on those who are to be excommunicated and those who have been excommunicated; on thieves and plunderers; on presumption, contempt, and negligence; and on their reconciliation and penance.

“Book Twelve contains material on perjury and its penance.

“Book Thirteen contains material on the veneration and observance of the sacred fast.

“Book Fourteen contains material on gluttony and drunkenness and on the penance appropriate to them.

[Col. 0323D] “Book Fifteen contains material on emperors, princes, and the other laity, and on their ministry.

“Book Sixteen contains material on accusers, judges, defenders, false witnesses, and the penance of each person.

“Book Seventeen contains material on fornication and incest of various kinds, and on the penance of both sexes and of different ages.

“Book Eighteen contains material on the visitation, penance, and reconciliation of the sick.

“Book Nineteen, called the Corrector and Physician, contains corrections for bodies and medicines for souls, and teaches every priest, even a simple one, how and in what manner he may aid each person—ordained or unordained, poor or [Col. 0324A] rich, child, young man, old man, or very old man, healthy or sick, of every age and of either sex.

“Book Twenty is called the Speculations. For it speculates on divine providence and predestination; on the coming of Antichrist and his works; on the resurrection; on the day of judgment; on punishments in hell; and on the happiness of everlasting life.

“Therefore, brother, if those who govern their peoples should lack any one of all these things, how will they be able to instruct and teach them? Indeed, the title of priest will scarcely remain established among them, because the Gospel threats are very dangerous, in which it is said: ‘If the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit.’

“But if there is some jealous person who, after seeing this, envies me and says that I gather food for myself from other people’s altars and make an empty name for myself from the labor of others, so be it.

“I confess that I gathered it from the labor of others, because I am not permitted to create canons by myself, but I am permitted to collect them—and that is what I did. God knows that I did this not out of any arrogance, but for the needs of our Church.

“To silence the murmuring of the detractor, however this book may be, let it belong to our people. I do not ask that it cross the threshold of our bishopric, but that it remain for our people to learn from.

“But I want you to hear how and from where I collected it; and if there is any sin in it, I leave it to your judgment to decide.

“I added nothing of my own except the labor; rather, I gathered with great effort from divine testimonies the things you will find in it. And I worked with the utmost diligence to make the things I had brought together authoritative.

“For from that very kernel of the canons, which some call the Body of Canons, I excerpted what was necessary for our time; some things from the canon of the Apostles, some from councils overseas, some from German councils, some from Gallican and Hispanic councils, some from the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, some from the teaching of Truth itself, some from the Old Testament, [CCXCIV] some from the Apostles, some from the sayings of St. Gregory, some from the sayings of St. Jerome, some from the sayings of St. Augustine, some from the sayings of St. Ambrose, [Col. 0324C] some from the sayings of St. Benedict, some from the sayings of St. Isidore, and some from the sayings of St. Basil.

“Some things are from the Roman Penitential, some from the Penitential of Theodore, and some from the Penitential of Bede.

“In this Collection, therefore, if you find anything useful, attribute it to the gifts of God. But if you find anything superfluous, ascribe it to my foolishness.

“Farewell, and in your sacred prayers I beg you to remember me, a sinner.

“Here ends the prologue.”

5. In this preface, or letter, of Burchard himself, the words “I have divided the same work into twenty books” should be noted. It should also be recalled, as we mentioned earlier, that Burchard inserted into this same preface the order and titles of the individual books, so that there can be no doubt that the published work which agrees exactly with this number of books, and with these same titles and arrangement, has Burchard as its author. In the commonly circulated preface, although it differs in several respects, the same number of books is indicated. The order, however, is different; and certain portions have been detached from that preface and relegated to the end in such a way that they may appear to have been written and added not by Burchard but by someone else. For not only has the list of the titles of each book been separated from the preface in the commonly circulated versions, but a list of the authors from whom Burchard derived the canons is also placed before it. This catalogue, likewise torn away from the same preface, bears a heading that cannot have come from Burchard: “From which authors’ written works he collected these ecclesiastical decrees.”

The nucleus of the canons, which Burchard praises at the beginning of the catalogue at the end of the preface, and which he says is called by some “the body of the canons,” is the collection of Pseudo-Isidore, from which he transcribed many apocryphal decrees. Stephanus Baluzius demonstrates at length in his preface to Regino that Burchard excerpted many more chapters from Regino, and also some from the two appendices appended in manuscripts to Regino’s collection. Yet he altered much in the titles, arbitrarily prefacing other titles; these titles, adopted from him by later collectors of canons, caused great confusion. Since many items in Burchard are inscribed with the names of councils or pontiffs in whose separately published decrees nothing of the sort is found, many believed that Burchard or his copyists had discovered them in lost documents of those councils or pontiffs. Consequently, they were added to editions of the Councils as precious fragments preserved by those authorities, each in its appropriate place.

Those who undertook a more careful examination of the matter discovered that Burchard attributed to synods, Roman pontiffs, or the holy Fathers chapters that Regino had recited either from the Capitularies of the kings, from Rabanus, from Ferrandus the deacon, or without mentioning any author.

Stephanus Baluzius noted the following about the books of the Capitularies in the preface cited above, §22:

> When Burchard compiled Regino, he preferred to attribute the chapters he took from that work to certain councils or ancient Fathers rather than to our kings, because the designation “Frankish”—with which the kings of Germany still gloried in the age of Regino and Witichind—had ceased to be used in Burchard’s time, and therefore all reverence for those Capitularies had been stripped from the Saxons. For Burchard cites the Capitularies of Charlemagne only once, in chapters 218 and 219 of his first book, adding that they had been highly commended by the bishops at Aachen; otherwise, perhaps, he would not have used them. It seems, however, that Burchard made it his practice to cite chapters taken from authors who were neither supreme pontiffs, nor synods, nor sufficiently well-known and celebrated Fathers under the name not of their respective author but of some more famous person. This observation will be very useful in reading the collections later than Burchard’s, for example those of Ivo and Gratian, who received many items of the same kind from Burchard.

All likewise attribute this merit to the collection: that it follows a sufficiently suitable method and, in addition, contains several canons of councils of later-period Germany which are found either only in very rare codices or even preserve excellent readings by which the commonly circulated texts can be corrected.

6. Finally, we do not wish to omit two matters. First, in the Vatican Library there is an old codex, no. 4227, entitled *Corrector and Physician*, without the author’s name. Jacobus Petit also saw a similar one in the Paris library of Saint Victor and published an excerpt from it in volume I of the *Penitential of Theodore*, p. 358. This work belongs to Burchard’s collection, in which the nineteenth book bears the same title, as is clear even from the titles previously listed in Burchard’s preface.

Second, manuscript Vat. 3830, from the eleventh century, contains a penitential in which are found questions to be put by confessors, together with the assigned penance. All these questions are copied verbatim in the same nineteenth book of Burchard, chapter 5. Only in Burchard’s chapter are there more of them than in the codex mentioned. The paragraphs of questions, which we have counted and distinguished by numbers to avoid confusion, total 194 in Burchard.

In that codex the questions are the same as those in Burchard’s fifth chapter, from no. 1 through no. 59, which begins: “Have you violated a tomb?” Then, in Burchard, the following numbers from 60 through 103 inclusive are added. They are headed: “On magic,” “On sacrilege,” “On gluttony and drunkenness,” “On irreligion,” again “On magic,” “On superstition,” and again “On magic.” All these numbers are absent from the aforementioned codex. After no. 59, “Have you violated a tomb?” and so forth, that codex continues: “Have you lain with your wife’s sister?” and so forth, as in Burchard no. 104; and it continues through no. 152, “Have you believed what some people are accustomed to believe, namely, that there are wild women?” It omits, however, what is added at the end of this number in Burchard: “In all these matters mentioned above, priests ought …” It also lacks the following number, 153, which begins: “Have you caused certain women, at certain times, to …”

The same codex then gives Burchard’s numbers 154, 155, and 156, but skips the next six numbers, from no. 157, “Have you done what certain women are accustomed to do, namely, with your little son …,” through no. 162. It gives no. 163, “Have you killed a son or daughter?” together with the following two numbers. It lacks no. 166, “Have you tasted semen?” Then, after copying no. 167, “Have you drunk chrism?” it omits the remaining fourteen numbers, from 168 through 181, and concludes with Burchard’s numbers 182, “Have you suffocated an infant?” and 183, “Have you found an infant?” Burchard adds eleven numbers at the end that are not found in the codex.

That this penitential was used among the German churches is indicated, among other things, by two numbers in which a German expression is mentioned: in no. 30, “what is called *carina* in German”; and what is stated as no. 151 in Burchard, “what common stupidity calls *Wervvolff*,” is expressed in the codex as follows: “what is called *Werevulf* in German.” From these facts it can easily be conjectured that Burchard inserted into his collection this penitential, which was in use among his people, and added from other penitentials what was lacking in it.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the collection of Saint Anselm, bishop of Lucca

1. It is of considerable importance to explain the collection of Saint Anselm, bishop of Lucca, almost the whole of which passed into Gratian, especially since it lies hidden in manuscripts and has not been sufficiently examined. Lucas Vadingus and Acherius had undertaken to publish it, but the former was overtaken by death and the latter distracted by other concerns, so they left the work unfinished. Since all knowledge of it depends upon the codices, those that we were able to examine must first be mentioned.

We found four manuscript codices in the Vatican Library, numbered 1364, 3531, 4983, and 6361. Of these, two are more recent paper manuscripts, namely 3531 and 4983. Since Gratian’s distinctions—or cases and questions—in which the same chapters were incorporated are noted in their margins, we believe these to be the codices used by Gratian’s correctors.

Codex 3531 places before the work a table of thirteen books, but ends in the seventh book, which is not complete. Another codex, 4983, contains all thirteen books. It derives from an ancient exemplar written under Innocent II, for at the end it gives a catalogue of the Roman pontiffs and records their years of pontificate through Calixtus II; without giving the number of years, it adds two other pontiffs, Honorius II and Innocent II.

The other two Vatican codices, 1364 and 6361, are older parchments. The first ends its catalogue of Roman pontiffs with Gregory VII, after whose death Anselm died while the see was still vacant. The other carries the catalogue through Paschal II; since the codex was written while he was still alive, it does not record the years of his pontificate.

In these two older manuscripts only twelve books are found, the eleventh, on penance, being omitted. Anselm’s name is absent from the two older codices, which have no title at all, and also from the more recent Vatican codex 4983. Only codex Vat. 3531 gives Anselm’s name, with this title on p. 12:

> Here begins the table of contents of the books which Blessed Anselm, bishop of Lucca, composed in this volume as individual books from corresponding cases.

Again, after the table of the books, on p. 16, it reads:

> Here begins the authentic and concise collection of the rules and sayings of the holy Fathers and authoritative councils, made in the time of Gregory, most holy pope, by Blessed Anselm, bishop of Lucca, his diligent imitator and disciple, who eagerly completed this work at his command and instruction.

In another, more recent Vatican manuscript, 4983, this latter inscription is found only as far as the word “councils.”

Two Barberini exemplars are cited. One of them is numbered 1881 and contains only the first seven books. At the beginning it presents the author’s name inserted into an old rhythmic poem:

> In the name of the Trinity,  
> Holy and undivided,  
> Here begins auspiciously  
> The series of this book,  
> Which Anselm, from Italy,  
> And a pontiff who was  
> Of the Lucan Church,  
> A prudent and catholic man,  
> Fervent in the faith of Christ,  
> Gathered from the whole body  
> Of the canons and holy Fathers, etc.

Two codices, numbers 765 and 766, of the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés are also mentioned. One is a copy of the Barberini exemplar, distinguished by the rhythmic verses just recited. The other, without an author’s name or any title, is called excellent and ancient by Baluzius in the preface to Antonius Augustinus’s books *On the Correction of Gratian*, §19. There he also attests that this codex contains nothing later than the year 1086, in which Saint Anselm died.

A more recent royal codex of Paris, from the sixteenth century, is also cited. It is entirely similar to Vatican 3531 and contains only seven books, with the same inscriptions bearing the author’s name.

Antonius Augustinus saw three codices. One of them, which he calls Roman, is manuscript Vat. 4983. Another, which he calls “my old one,” and which contains only twelve books, we have determined from various indications to be the codex later transferred to the Vatican Library and numbered 6361. He frequently used these two codices in his *Epitome of the Canons*. We have been unable to learn anything about his third codex.

Finally, an unidentified but ancient exemplar was communicated to us from the monastery of Saint Benedict at Padilirone. It is believed to have been written in the twelfth century and contains thirteen books without the author’s name.

2. Antonius Augustinus, who had three codices without the author’s name at his disposal, cast doubt upon Anselm’s authorship; several others subsequently adopted the same view. Two matters chiefly create difficulty.

First, no mention of this collection was made by those who reviewed the works of Saint Anselm. Among them, the chief difficulty is posed by the contemporary author of his life, who was also his penitentiary. Since he mentions other minor works, he does not seem likely to have passed over this one if he had known it to have been written by Anselm.

Second, some codices contain material belonging to the collection from Urban II and Paschal II, who were elevated to the apostolic see after Saint Anselm. Augustinus also notes considerable variation among the codices of the work itself. Apart from those codices that lack the eleventh book, there is great variation in the numbers of chapters in the individual books: some codices contain more chapters in almost every book, others fewer.

3. Since a clearer presentation of this matter contributes no less to understanding the collection than to forming a judgment about its author, the titles of the individual books should be set out together with the principal variations in the chapters.

**Book I.** On the primacy and excellence of the Roman Church. Alternatively, *On the power and primacy of the apostolic see*. Chapters 90, alternatively 91 or 94.

**Book II.** On the freedom of appeal. Alternatively, *On the primacy of the Roman Church and the freedom of appeal*. Chapters 78, alternatively 81 or 82.

**Book III.** On the procedure for accusing, giving evidence, and judging. Chapters 117, alternatively 124, 127, or 131.

**Book IV.** On the authority of privileges. Chapters 55, or 56 or 57.

**Book V.** On the ordinations of the churches, and on all their law and status. Alternatively, *On the ordination, law, and status of the churches*. Chapters 71, alternatively 83 or 93.

**Book VI.** On the election and ordination, and on all the power or status, of bishops. Chapters 201, alternatively 203 or 207.

**Book VII.** On the life and ordination of clerics. Alternatively, *On the life and ordination of priests, deacons, and the remaining orders*. Chapters 201, alternatively 207, 209, or 213.

**Book VIII.** On the lapsed. Chapter 39.

**Book IX.** On the sacraments. Chapters 64, alternatively 69.

**Book X.** On marriages. Chapters 63, alternatively 68, 70, or 76.

**Book XI.** On penance. Chapters 174, alternatively 179.

**Book XII.** On excommunication. Chapter 75.

**Book XIII.** On just vengeance and persecution. Chapters 28, alternatively 29 or 34.

4. It should be noted that this variation in the numbers arises from two causes: sometimes from dividing one number into two, or conversely; but more often from additions, which, being later, are generally found written at the end of the books and are not indicated in the preliminary table of chapters. Indeed, some additions are appended without a number and sometimes in a different script.

Thus, for example, the old codex Vat. 1364 contains two additional chapters, 56 and 57, in Book IV, which are not presented in the table of chapters. At the end of Book VI it adds, without any number, a letter of Urban II to L., provost of the Church of Saint Iventius at Pavia. In Book VII it adds the canons of the synod of Piacenza under the same Urban in the year 1095. In Book VIII it adds a letter of Alexander II to Landulf in Corsica. All these items are without numbers and occur at the ends of the books, which is clear evidence that they are additions.

Moreover, in Book XI another hand adds a letter of Innocent II to the archbishop of Milan and to the bishops of Como and Lodi.

The paper codex Vat. 4983 adds at the end of Book IV, in a different script, a decree of Calixtus II at the Lateran Council. Among other additions shared with the preceding codex, it appends to Book III the letter of Urban II to the provost of the Church of Saint Iventius, which is added at the end of Book VI in the earlier codex.

Some chapters are inserted not only at the end but also within the body of manuscript 4983, in Books V and VI. Since they are not found in the other codices, they are recognized as additions. Although this codex received more additions than Vatican 3531, it lacks two decrees of Urban II that are inserted in codex 3531 as chapters 150 and 175.

At the end of each book, the Padilirone codex displays several blank leaves that had formerly been left unused. On these leaves several later pontifical decrees were generally written in a smaller script; other such additions are also found from time to time in the margins.

5. Having made these preliminary observations, let us say briefly what should be thought about this collection. Its origin in Italy is shown not only by the codices more common in Italy or brought from Italy into other provinces, but especially by Italian and Roman records that are not found in the collections of other peoples.

Such materials include fragments from the *Roman Ordinal*, several chapters from letters and acts under more recent pontiffs, especially under Gregory VII, and some passages from the very rare letters of Gelasius I and Pelagius I. These seem to have been drawn from the apostolic archives and were received by Gratian from this collection; they became known through Gratian’s edition.

It is worth noting that this Italian author excerpted material not only from Roman laws but also from the Capitularies. If the additions are separated, it will become clear that this collection was composed under Gregory VII. For it contains nothing later than that pontiff. Whatever material was taken from Urban II, Calixtus II, and Innocent II, we have discovered to belong to the additions, as Antonius Augustinus also perceived when he wrote: “Those chapters could have been added after Anselm’s death by some diligent man.”

Indeed, the two codices in particular, Vat. 6361 and the old Saint-Germain manuscript praised by Baluzius, entirely lack all additions of this kind later than 1086. There is therefore no obstacle to attributing this collection to Saint Anselm, bishop of Lucca. Two distinct sources testify that he was its author: first, those codices that bear Anselm’s name in a double heading; and above all, the Barberini codex, which records the same fact in rhythmic verses. These verses provide testimony to an earlier period.

The rhythmic verses already quoted in the Barberini manuscript conclude with these other four lines:

> And these are the names of the saints,  
> Venerable in every respect,  
> The pontiffs of the Roman see,  
> Descending from Peter.

A catalogue of the Roman pontiffs from Saint Peter through Honorius II is then appended. Therefore, the person who composed those verses lived under Honorius II, that is, not long after Anselm’s death.

6. At first, this collection seems to have been issued without the author’s name; for that reason most codices lack Anselm’s name. The copies that bear his name either display merely the name “Blessed Anselm, bishop,” or add a eulogy of the kind appropriate to men distinguished by holiness who have died.

The collection does not appear to have been published during Anselm’s lifetime. Rather, it was found among his papers after his death and then circulated, though it was not entirely complete; consequently, it lacks a preface or dedicatory letter. This may explain why the author of his life and the other writers who list Anselm’s remaining works made no mention of this collection: it had not been published and completed by him.

After several copies without the author’s name had been transcribed and widely circulated, others who knew the author prefixed Anselm’s name in copies subsequently made from them.

As for the fact that in certain—and indeed ancient—codices the eleventh book, on Penance, is missing, although such a book is usually a principal part of collections of this kind, perhaps the first scribe from whom these manuscripts derive obtained only twelve books among the papers of Saint Anselm and copied them. The book on penance was later discovered by others with greater diligence and inserted in its proper place, just as it is in fact found in its proper place in the two ancient manuscripts, the Padilirone and Saint-Germain codices, as well as in Vat. 4983. Although the latter is more recent, we have observed that it derives from an older exemplar written under Innocent II.

7. The most eminent Cardinal Baronius, under the year 1086, §14, quotes a passage that he attributes to the anonymous penitentiary of Anselm who wrote his life:

> Anselm compiled from many and various volumes of the most holy Fathers a considerable body of canonical sayings.

These words seem to indicate a collection of canons. But in the complete and genuine *Life of Saint Anselm* that his penitentiary composed—as Baronius later adds—the passage is written differently, as follows:

> He compiled an *Apologetic* from various volumes of the holy Fathers, by which he might defend with canonical arguments the judgment of the lord pope, together with all his deeds and commands.

These words clearly indicate not a collection of canons but the *Apologetic* published by Canisius on behalf of Gregory VII against Guibert.

Oudinus (*Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. II, p. 721) says that certain learned men believe that the work printed by Canisius is nothing other than certain excerpts from Anselm’s collection of canons, obtained elsewhere by Canisius. Those who possess some manuscript copies of the collection of canons of Anselm of Lucca can easily test whether this conjecture is true by comparing them with the printed work.

We, who have seen several copies, found this conjecture groundless. The *Apologetic* is composed of numerous testimonies gathered and arranged for a particular purpose, and it is entirely unlike the manuscripts containing the collection of canons. In that *Apologetic*, which is certainly Anselm’s work, among the many testimonies presented in Book II are rarer fragments of Gelasius I and Pelagius I, as well as texts from Roman laws and the Capitularies, just as we observed in the collection of canons.

This agreement of citations and testimonies confirms that Saint Anselm was the author of the collection no less than of the *Apologetic*.

8. Some people include among the manuscript copies of Anselm’s collection codex Basilica Vaticana 118 C, from the eleventh century, in which Anselm’s name was written in a much more recent script. Although it contains a fair amount of material found in the other manuscripts of Anselm, it differs from them in many respects.

First, it differs in the number of books: it contains only nine, which generally lack titles and chapters. The pontifical decrees common to this collection and to Anselm’s are found in different books in Anselm and in this collection. Moreover, this collection lacks several pontifical decrees copied in Anselm and contains other decrees absent from Anselm.

Among the latter is a letter of Pope John to Isaac of Syracuse, which is found in Gratian, case 16, question 2, chapter 1. There the Roman correctors, who had carefully examined Anselm’s codices, praise a codex of Populeti—that is, the Tarragonese collection—because they had found that letter neither in Anselm’s manuscripts nor in any other collection.

In addition, several leaves were repeatedly left blank in this Basilica codex, so that it appears to be the first, incomplete offspring of the collection, lacking the author’s final revision.

In the upper margin of this codex, on p. 73, a libellus of accusation is copied under Eugenius III; we insert it here.

### Libellus of accusation

**Pope Eugenius.** On Tuesday, before the aforementioned lord Pope Eugenius, John the priest declared that he was formally bringing a canonical charge of simony against Lanfranc, bishop of Pavia. He said that Lanfranc had committed simony with the deacon Albert in the city of Novara, in the house of Peter Ruffus, in April, in the first year of Pope Lucius. I, John the priest, declare that I am the author of this libellus.

Among the bishops of Pavia, none named Lanfranc is listed in Ughelli’s catalogue during the time of Lucius II and Eugenius III. During this period Ughelli lists Alphonsus, Conrad, and Peter; Peter’s successor is identified as Saint Lanfranc. Since Lanfranc was ordained by Alexander III in the year 1178, he is different from the man who already occupied the see of Pavia under Lucius II and Eugenius III.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Vatican manuscript collection of Cardinal Deusdedit. Several previously unpublished documents are presented from it

1. Deusdedit, a cardinal-priest created by Gregory VII with the title of the Apostles in Eudoxia, wrote two works. Since each is divided into four books or parts and both contain much material from the sacred canons, some have confused them with one another; they must therefore be carefully distinguished.

One, compiled under Victor III, is a collection of canons. The other was written in the time of Urban II against invaders, simoniacs, and the other schismatics.

The Roman correctors of Gratian gave the following indication of one collection of canons in their catalogue of the books they used:

> The collection of canons of Cardinal Deusdedit, and the four books *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, from the Vatican.

That the four books *On Ecclesiastical Matters* are the same as the collection of canons cited in their notes is made clear by their note on Distinction 40, chapter 6, where they write:

> Deusdedit, cardinal-priest, title of the Apostles in Eudoxia, composed four books *On Ecclesiastical Matters* in the time of Pope Victor III; they are preserved in the Vatican Library. In Book I, chapter 201, from the acts of Boniface, martyr and archbishop of Mainz, legate of the apostolic see, he reports the following words of that most holy man concerning the Roman pontiff and the apostolic see, etc.

These same words are found in Book I, chapter 231, of the Vatican collection of canons belonging to the same cardinal.

Antonius Augustinus later mentioned both works of this cardinal separately in chapter 28 of his *Judgment on Certain Ancient Collectors of Ecclesiastical Canons*. From the preface to the collection of canons—which he testifies that he alone had read—he reported a few passages in which the division of the work is set out.

Since he had two manuscript copies of the other work, against the invaders, simoniacs, and other schismatics, transcribed from a codex of the Vatican Basilica, he frequently used it in his *Epitome of the Canons*.

Although this second work contains many canons and testimonies, it is not a collection of canons. Rather, it is a connected work composed by the cardinal himself, in which, while refuting the invaders, simoniacs, and schismatics of his time, he inserted several authorities in support of his case.

Accordingly, Antonius Augustinus rightly wrote of this work:

> He does not use the same method as Burchard, Ivo, Anselm, and Gratian, who merely gather sayings of the Fathers or councils. Rather, he himself employs many arguments; he confirms his arguments by the authority of the Fathers, refutes those of others, and deals more forcefully with the issue that was disturbing the Church of God in those times.

The cardinal himself expresses the division of this work in the following words:

> There are therefore four matters about which, with God as our author, we propose to write. First, that a king may not appoint bishops for the holy churches. Second, concerning simoniacs, schismatics, and their priesthood and sacrifice, etc. Third, that the clergy ought to be nourished and honored by secular persons, not defamed, etc. Fourth, that secular power may not introduce or expel clerics from the Church, nor govern ecclesiastical property or transfer it into its own jurisdiction.

The anonymous author of Melk, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 113, refers to this work when he says:

> Cardinal Deusdedit … wrote against the Guibertines.

For several lengthy fragments of this same work, which demonstrate that it is a connected composition, see the most eminent Baronius under the year 1059, §30 and following; under the year 1080, §31; and under the year 1081, §22 and following.

2. The collection of canons, however, is the proper subject of our undertaking. From it Cardinal Baronius published an excerpt of the preface alone, under the year 1080, §30, and under the year 1087, §22.

In former times Pandulfus of Pisa briefly praised it in his *Life of Victor III*, from which Platina and the other writers who composed the lives of the Roman pontiffs drew their material. He says:

> For Victor III, Deusdedit, priest of the title of the Apostles in Eudoxia, composed and arranged a book of canons.

The Vatican codex of this collection, cited by some authors, is numbered 3833. Peter Pithoeus indicates another codex in his historical synopsis of distinguished men who collected canons and ecclesiastical decrees. Speaking of the aforementioned collection of the same cardinal *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, he says:

> We once saw a copy of this collection in the library of the Dominicans of Valencia. It was divided into four books and contained much material from the archives of the Roman Church. We shall see several documents of this kind transcribed in the same collection.

The Vatican exemplar, which we were conveniently able to examine, is nearly contemporary with the author, as is clear not so much from the script of its period as from the catalogue of Roman pontiffs placed at its beginning, which ends with Paschal II, the successor of Urban II.

3. At the beginning of the codex are copied two annotations, one concerning general synods and the other concerning particular synods, which we have found in Isidorian manuscripts. This is followed by an annotation concerning apostolic decretals, which we mentioned in Part III, chapter 2, §5.

Next follows the aforementioned catalogue of the Roman pontiffs from Saint Peter through Paschal II. The collection then begins with a letter of Deusdedit to Victor III, from which the date of the collection can be determined. Victor III was elected in May of the year 1086 and died the following year, in September.

From this letter one can recognize not so much the plan and division of the work as the sources from which the cardinal drew. Since it has not yet been published, it should be inserted here.

> To the most blessed and apostolic man, the pontiff, our lord Pope Victor III, and to all the clergy of the holy Roman Church, Deusdedit, an insignificant priest of the title of the Apostles in Eudoxia.
>
> Your Blessedness knows that the holy Roman Church is called and believed to be the mother of all churches because Blessed Peter, its founder, first provided shepherds for the patriarchal sees in the East and afterward, from his own side, gave the first pastors to all the cities that are in the West.
>
> This arrangement was especially fitting for that apostle, whom Christ, the Son of God, having entrusted him with the keys of the heavenly kingdom, had commanded principally to feed his sheep, and whom he had ordered to strengthen his brethren in the same faith.
>
> Carefully considering the insignia and benefits of so excellent a privilege, the 318 Fathers who sat in the Council of Nicaea decreed—as Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, writes to Pope Felix—that councils ought not to be celebrated without the judgment of the Roman pontiff, that bishops ought not to be condemned, and that all greater matters ought to be referred to his judgment.
>
> The Council of Sardica, which had 300 bishops, as the universal synod testifies—the synod that is called the eighth by its founders—also established the same in chapters 3 and 4, and, in Corollaries VII and X, in chapters 6 and 9. Thus, among other things, it wrote to Blessed Pope Julius:
>
> “It will seem best and most entirely fitting if, from each province, the priests refer every matter to the head—that is, to the see of Blessed Peter the apostle—of the Lord.”
>
> Even before that synod, the ancient Fathers are read to have shown such reverence to this see that the distinguished martyr Cyprian, primate of the African province, is reported in his letters to have humbly obeyed the ordinances of the priests and deacons governing the Roman Church after the martyrdom of Fabian. He also rendered an account to them, by letters sent to them, of what was being done in his province.
>
> Indeed, the same clergy are read to have sent letters to Cyprian himself, to Sicily, and to various regions. While Cornelius had not yet taken his seat, they also summoned bishops to celebrate a synod at Rome because of the urgent matters then at hand.
>
> Since these things are so, it seems sufficiently impious for anyone who boasts of the Christian name not to heed the admonitions of the Roman Church in Christian times, when pontiffs worthy of God obeyed so devotedly under the cruelty of persecution, even while the see was without a pontiff.
>
> For the Fathers, filled with the Spirit of God, believed that the blessed apostles Peter and Paul lived and presided there through their magnificent merits, and that the faith which it had received from them—and which, as Blessed Paul himself bears witness, was proclaimed and praised throughout the whole world—would endure in that same Church forever. They believed that, as had been commanded to Blessed Peter, it would everywhere strengthen the brethren placed in the same faith.
>
> Although this faith is sometimes oppressed by the adverse winds of the world, it is not overwhelmed, because of the merits of the chief apostles, who live and preside in it. For although at times, for the sake of testing it, the gates of hell may prevail against it, they can never prevail absolutely, since the Lord Jesus prays that Peter’s faith may not fail.
>
> Therefore, wishing to make known to those who are ignorant of it the privilege of that authority by which the Roman Church stands above the entire Christian world, with the Lord’s help I have gathered into this little work, from various authorities of the holy Fathers and Christian rulers, the more important materials brought together into one. I have divided the work into four parts.
>
> The first book contains the privilege of the authority of that same Roman Church. Since the Church cannot exist without its clergy, nor the clergy without property by which they may be sustained in temporal matters, I have appended a second and a third book concerning the clergy and the property of that Church.
>
> Since secular power strives to subject the Church of God to itself, the freedom of the Church, its clergy, and its property is clearly demonstrated in the third and, above all, the fourth book.
>
> I have not arranged each excerpt inserted into this work according to the order of the chapters, because almost all of them contain either two or several matters within themselves. If they were assigned sections according to the number of matters they address, they would impose very great labor upon me and detract from the authority of the sources. Therefore, I warn the scribe, so that the reader may not be seriously offended, to exercise care not only in correcting the codex but also in keeping and correcting with the greatest caution both sets of numbers: namely, the number assigned to each chapter and the number placed throughout the entire codex before each excerpt.

«Moreover, if anything inserted here should seem contrary to something else—as also frequently happens in the Gospels—careful discrimination will readily show that they conflict neither with one another nor with the passages placed elsewhere. But if they should plainly prove to be contradictory, the lesser authority must yield to the greater. Accordingly, I first excerpted the best material from certain ecumenical synods, namely Nicaea, the First Council of Ephesus, Chalcedon, and the Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Councils, which are known to have been celebrated universally, partly by four or five patriarchs and partly by their vicars, at different times. No one but a madman doubts their authority.

Nor did I think it inappropriate to borrow from the other Eastern councils whatever seemed suitable, since I saw that the Roman pontiffs had received authority from them in their constitutions—a fact that the inquisitive reader will also be able to detect. In addition, I included certain material from the Council of Carthage, which was conducted under Pope Zosimus by 217 bishops, with his legates present—Faustinus the bishop, and the presbyters Philippus and Asellus. In the presence of these same men, the African councils were confirmed and incorporated into that synod under various headings; from them Coelestine, Symmachus, and Hadrian appear to have inserted certain passages into their decrees.

And since an adversary, when overcome by reason, attacks authority, it should be known that all councils, whether ecumenical or provincial, which had been held before the Council of Chalcedon, were afterward confirmed and strengthened in that council, chapter 1, which reads as follows: “We have decreed that the regulations of the holy Fathers established in each council up to the present shall retain their proper force.” For the Council of Chalcedon, held by 630 Fathers under Pope Leo, possesses such authority and firmness that, as Blessed Gregory says, whoever does not hold fast to its solidity, whatever sort of life and conduct he may have, even if he seems to be a stone, lies outside God’s building.

I have also collected material concerning the authority of the canons of the Apostles, which are said to have been translated from Greek into Latin by Clement, the Roman pontiff. The Seventh Ecumenical Council of 350 Fathers, and Gregory himself in his Register, also appear to have used these canons as authorities. Concerning their authority, then, and that of any other canons, Anastasius, librarian of the Roman Church, writes as follows to Pope John VIII in the preface to that same Seventh Ecumenical Council, which he translated from Greek into Latin:

“By the decree of your predecessor, Pope Stephen, and by the authority of your apostolate, the Church receives not only the fifty canons of the Apostles, as the trumpets of the Holy Spirit, but also accepts the regulations and institutions of all genuinely approved Fathers and sacred councils—provided only that they oppose neither right faith nor good morals, and do not in any significant respect conflict with the decrees of the Roman See; indeed, they powerfully attack its adversaries.”

The letters of Clement to James, against which some appear to chatter, are shown to be authentic by his successors Anacletus and Alexander, as well as by certain other pontiffs, and by Blessed Benedict, the father of monks, who inserted many statements from them into his writings.

I have also gathered here very much concerning the authority of the Apostolic See. I included some material from the works of Blessed Jerome, whose eloquence, as Augustine says of him against Julian, shines from East to West like the sun. I included some from the works of the blessed Cyprian, Ambrose, Augustine, and other Fathers. In every respect I took care that what I gathered here should possess the fullest authority. For I knew that just as there would be some to whom these things pleased, so there would certainly be others who begrudged them.

Moreover, I wished to insert into this work the ancient order for the election or consecration of the Roman pontiff and his clergy. For some men once wrote, in contempt of the sanctions of God and the holy Fathers, to display themselves and to claim for themselves a vainglorious authority that cannot stand upon any canonical laws, a new ordination of the Roman pontiff. I shudder to write what abominable and God-defying provisions they established in it. Let whoever reads understand.

As for the manner of instructing subjects, only a few things have been inserted here, since I judged it laborious and belonging to another work to excerpt the sacred Scripture for this purpose. The principal sources for this seemed to me to be the Gospel, the Epistles of the Apostles, Clement, Gregory’s Pastoral Rule, his forty homilies on the Gospels, and his homilies 8, 9, and 10 on Ezekiel.

And because, while striving for brevity, I regret passing over many useful things, I advise the inquisitive reader, whenever he has leisure, to study the works from which these excerpts were taken—not in order to add anything to the excerpts, but to satisfy his own desire.

I have therefore dedicated this work to Your Paternity, believing that it would benefit not only the holy Apostolic See but the whole Church and all the clergy. I beseech the reader in the Lord to intercede with the Lord for my offenses.»

From this letter the division of the collection into four books is clear. The first consists of 251 titles or chapters concerning the primacy and power of the Church; the second, of 131 chapters concerning the Roman clergy; the third, of 159 chapters concerning the property of the Church; and the fourth, of 162 chapters concerning the freedom of the Church and of its property and clergy.

[CCCIII] 3. What matters are contained in these books, and how weighty they are, is demonstrated by the table of titles itself, which follows immediately after the dedicatory letter. Serving as an index of subjects, or a summary of the entire work, it seems similar to the collection of Ferrandus, since, when listing the titles of the individual books, it likewise indicates from the other books whatever belongs to the same title—for example, the title of the first book.

In the body of the collection itself, the texts are presented in the following order. First, passages of sacred Scripture are quoted wherever appropriate; then come the canons of councils. The canons of the Greek synods are sometimes taken from the Dionysian translation, sometimes from the Prisca, and sometimes from both. Thus, in book I, no. 1, the sixth Nicene canon is first recited from the Prisca and then from the Dionysian version, with the notation: “Another translation reads as follows.” Occasionally, though more rarely, the Isidorian translation is also used.

Since whatever is cited from the Prisca or the Isidorian version is found in Vatican manuscript 1342, which is said to have belonged to the ancient Lateran library, it is highly credible that Cardinal Deusdedit used this manuscript. From the Prisca he cites several Nicene, Antiochene, and Chalcedonian canons; from the Isidorian version, one canon of Ancyra and another of Gangra. In that manuscript, of course, the former are written according to the Prisca translation and the latter according to the Isidorian.

The decrees of the Roman pontiffs follow the canons, including several passages from the apocryphal Pseudo-Isidorian documents. More material is supplied from the Register of Gregory VII, who preceded Victor III. Where appropriate, testimonies of the Fathers follow, together with several passages from the laws of Justinian; some from the History of Anastasius the Librarian; from the Roman Pontifical, in which the lives of the pontiffs are recorded; from the book of the Roman pontiffs called the *Diurnus*; from the History of Paul the Deacon; from the Chronicle of Victor of Tunnuna; and from the Acts of Saint Boniface, bishop of Mainz.

An ancient Roman Order is inserted, beginning: “In whatever school boys are found who have been well taught in letters, let them be taken up and nourished in the singing school,” and so forth. It is the ninth Roman Order published by Mabillon in volume II of the *Museum Italicum*, page 89; nevertheless, our manuscript preserves noteworthy variant readings and reflects an older age.

4. The cardinal adds much material from the volumes of the Lateran basilica relating to the patrimony of Saint Peter. He sometimes cites one volume and sometimes another, saying that they were kept in the archive of the sacred Lateran palace.

The celebrated book on censuses by Cencius the Chamberlain, who afterward became the Roman pontiff Honorius III, is well known. This book was printed by Muratori in volume V of the *Italian Antiquities*. We discovered that the material found in this book from page 827 of that edition—beginning “Pope Hadrian obtained,” and continuing to page 842—was transcribed by Cardinal Deusdedit from the Lateran volumes, word for word except for certain variants, in book III, chapter 149 and following, from page 85 of his manuscript through page 92.

From this it is evident that both authors drew from the same sources; Deusdedit, however, inserted the same material into his collection more than a century before Cencius. Deusdedit also added other documents from the aforementioned Lateran archive on page 92 and following, which are not found in Cencius’s published book—namely, complete privileges granted to the Roman Church by Louis the Pious, Otto I, and Henry I.

There are also oaths of Robert, duke of Apulia and Calabria, and of Jordan and Richard, princes of Capua, together with many other documents of the same kind, some published and some unpublished.

Besides the already printed registers of Gregory I, Gregory VII, and John VIII, the same cardinal supplies several fragments from the letters of Gelasius I, Pelagius I, Honorius I, and Gregory II, in which not a few passages survive only in this collection. Lucas Holstenius printed some of these, and they were later transferred into editions of the Councils.

We present here other passages which Holstenius omitted from the same manuscript. Although some of them are found in Gratian, since they were not published in editions of the Councils together with the other fragments excerpted from Gratian, they seemed worth indicating here so that they may not be omitted from a new edition of the Councils.

We shall indicate only those that we found in the collection of Deusdedit. We leave the other fragments found in Gratian, transcribed from elsewhere and not yet printed in the Councils, to be investigated and collected more carefully by those who will undertake a new edition of the Councils.

[CCCIV] FRAGMENTS OF THE LETTERS OF GELASIUS I, from the collection of Cardinal Deusdedit, contained in Vatican manuscript 3833.

“Gelasius to Bishop Helpidius of Volaterra, among other matters.

“‘With what audacity, with what recklessness, etc.,’” as in Gratian, *Cause* 23, question 8, chapter 26, where the Roman correctors, in their notes, supplied from the collection of Polycarp the passage omitted by Deusdedit. This fragment, omitted from the Councils, should be restored with the others.

“Gelasius to Bishops Majoricus and John.

“‘Thus the repeated slaughter of the bishops of Squillace, etc.,’” as in the same Gratian, *Cause* 25, question 2, chapter 25.

“Gelasius to Bishops Cresconius, John, and Messala.

“‘The statutes of our predecessors, etc.,’” as in Gratian, at the same place, chapter 19, where the text incorrectly reads “to the bishops of Messalia.”

“Gelasius to John, bishop of Sora.

“‘It is indeed certain, etc.,’” as in Gratian, *On Consecration*, distinction 1, chapter 7. Our manuscript adds at the end: “Given on the Ides of April.”

Gelasius to Bishop Senecio.

“‘The devotion of a pious mind is to be embraced, by which Julius, the honorable man—that is, *vir honorabilis*—in the matter of Juviana, etc.,’” as in Gratian, *Cause* 16, question 7, chapter 26. The manuscript adds at the end: “Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August.”

“Gelasius to Agilulf, after the other matters.

“‘I ask that you deign to defend the small estate of the blessed Apostle Peter situated among the Dalmatians, and that you order whatever my brother and fellow bishop Honorius may have suggested to you for its benefit, or whatever the tenants may have thought should be reported, to be provided as fully as possible.’”

[Note: Here Honorius was bishop of Salona; to him two other letters of Gelasius have been published.]

“Gelasius to Januarius, after the other matters.

“‘I confidently entrust to you the causes for which you eagerly desire the benefits of the blessed Apostle Peter to be continued. Let your nobility therefore provide that his properties receive the aid and protection of the poor, and let it support their tenants with benevolent favor, so that it may receive in return a corresponding recompense from him to whose merits and honor it devoutly pays these dues.’”

“Gelasius to Firmina, an illustrious woman, after the other matters.

“‘It certainly contributes to the increase of your reward if estates that have been improperly seized either by barbarians or by Romans are restored through your arrangements to the sustenance of the needy. Such a multitude of people from various provinces devastated by the calamity of war has flowed into Rome that, God as my witness, we can scarcely provide enough for them. You therefore perceive how much good work you acquire if the estates that each person has bestowed upon the blessed Apostle Peter for the sake of his own soul are restored, after God, through your protection. I ask that you deign to receive with a grateful mind the eulogies of this blessing which, out of affection, I have sent.’”

[Col. 0336B] “Gelasius to the urban agents.
