“‘It is clear that you have entered into the Church’s accounts, from the payment of the estate of Claculas, which you hold by lease, thirty gold solidi from the produce of the year of the consulship of Asterius and Praesidius, illustrious men, in the third indiction. I have noted it. On the fifth day before the Kalends of August, Flavius, an illustrious man, being consul.’”

[Note: That is, Flavius Viator, who was consul in the year 495.]

Another security document of the same day and in the same words follows, issued by the same Gelasius to Vincomalus; only the name of the estate is missing.

“Gelasius to Queen Hereleuva.

[Note: An anonymous author published by Valesius in *On the Deeds of King Theodoric* identifies this queen as the mother of that same Theodoric. His mother was called Ereliva in Gothic; she was a Catholic and was called Eusebia at baptism.]

“‘Because Peter, the defender of the Church, was pleading with letters from me to my most excellent son, the lord king, on behalf of the sustenance of the poor, I hastened to send him. When he arrived, I did not cease to greet Your Sublimity also, earnestly begging that you deign to assist the causes of the needy for the increase of your health and prosperity. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of March.’”

[CCCV] FRAGMENTS OF THE LETTERS OF PELAGIUS I, from the same collection of Deusdedit.

[Col. 0336C]

“Pelagius to the subdeacon Melleus, among other matters.

“‘We have learned through the report of the notaries of our See that, from the time when the patrimony of the Church was first entrusted to you until now, the accounts for no indiction have been settled [read: “are settled”]; and these accounts must necessarily be checked off, so that by faithful examination we may learn what is owed for ecclesiastical purposes and what has been usurped by anyone. Thus you, or your heirs, being fully secured for the future, may be able to endure no disturbances.’”

“Pelagius to Maurus, bishop of Praeneste, among other matters.

“‘We have learned that, concerning the patrimony of Hilviade, you faithfully paid over what you collected for the first, second, and third indictions to Ampliatus, formerly a presbyter, and Stephen, a deacon, who were acting as the pope’s representatives in the city of Rome. For the fourth indiction, according to the direction of our son Narses, a religious man of the sacred palace, you delivered what had been collected to our sons Dulcitius, Felix, and John, presbyters. But when we arrived and were ordained by God’s grace, you paid over to us from that same fourth indiction.’ And below: ‘Therefore, at the request of Your Affection, we have judged that your Fraternity should be secured by this discharge in respect of all the aforesaid six past indictions, so that no accusation may hereafter be brought against Your Charity by anyone.’”

“Pelagius to Narses, the patrician Anagnosticon, among other matters.

“‘Let Your Excellency know well that we presume in no way to give the property of the poor to men who already possess means and suffer no need, because we know that this would not please you, nor do we judge it consistent with our duty.’”

“Pelagius to Boethius, prefect of the praetorium of Africa, among other matters.

“‘The Roman Church, over which by God’s authority we preside, after fifteen and more continuous years of devastation caused by war in the regions of Italy, a devastation which has scarcely yet ceased, receives for the clergy and poor no support, however inadequate or slight, except from overseas islands or places.’”

“Pelagius to Julian, bishop of Cingulum.

“‘It is clear that Your Affection has entered into the Church’s accounts, from the payments of the estates, or farms, situated beyond the eleventh milestone in Picenum and entrusted to your care, five hundred gold solidi for the seventh indiction, paid to our son Anastasius, banker and treasurer of our Church. I have noted it on the third day before the Kalends of August [Note: ‘The eighteenth year after the consulship of Basil, that is, the year 559, should be supplied; in that year the seventh indiction was drawing to a close on the third day before the Kalends of August. Pelagius I died the following year, on the third of March, during the eighth indiction. Julian, bishop of Cingulum, is read as having signed the decree of Vigilius in the year 553. Another fragment of a letter of Pelagius I to the same man was published by Baluze in volume V of the *Miscellanies*, page 466, and reprinted by P. Mansi in volume I of the *Supplement to the Councils*, page 432.] after the consulship of Basil, the illustrious man.’”

“Pelagius to Dulcitius, defender, after certain other matters.

“‘Moreover, you sent us certain accounts disguised in the Greek manner concerning the payments of the sixth indiction, suggesting that you had collected estates for fifty solidi, and for another sixty, from the deacon Varinus and from I know not whom else. Although your estates increase daily on every side, you create difficulties for us over the payments. Is it not enough that, from notaries and various other offices, we were scarcely able to free you from … [lacuna] …, etc.’”

“Pelagius to Vito, defender, among other matters.

“‘Therefore, by the present order we command you not to neglect managing the affairs of that estate; knowing that we shall now exact from you both the remainder of the sixth indiction and thereafter all the payments of the individual indictions beginning with the seventh, so that, according to custom, you may issue the security in the scrinium and be able to receive the inventory of that patrimony.’”

TWO LETTERS OF HONORIUS I, transcribed from his Register in the collection of Deusdedit.

[Col. 0337C]

Honorius to Gratiosus, subdeacon.

“‘So that no one’s labor and diligence in the affairs of the Church may prove harmful to him, arrangements must be made in such a way that his labor is useful to him and that ecclesiastical property suffers no loss. Therefore, we grant you possession, for a period of twenty-nine years, of a house with its garden situated in this city of Rome near the Baths of Diocletian, in Region A, with everything belonging to it, at an annual payment of one gold solidus into the ecclesiastical accounts as rent. You are not thereafter to be expelled, nor are we to impose an increase of rent there. You must, however, diligently attend to the repair of the house in all respects, like a careful head of a household. After the completion of twenty-nine years, the same house with its garden must without doubt return to the right of the Holy Roman Church, whose property it is; and neither you nor your heirs shall have permission to reclaim anything spent on its improvement, because the order of reason does not allow one who received no increase in rent to reclaim expenses incurred for the improvement of the property. Given on the Ides of December, in the fourteenth indiction.’” (That is, in the year 625.)

“Honorius to Servodeus, notary.

“‘Whenever something is requested from us that is known to accord with reason, it is fitting for us to grant it willingly. Therefore, because you asked us to grant you for a fixed period the estate called Aurelianum, situated in its entirety together with its vineyards on the Portuensis Road near Saints Abdon and Sennen, yielding two and a half gold solidi and belonging to the jurisdiction of the Holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, we have accordingly issued this decree. From the present fourteenth indiction, we grant you the aforesaid estate with everything belonging to it for the days of your life, provided that each year you pay into the ecclesiastical accounts, without delay, two gold solidi and five tremisses as rent, so that you may thereby have some relief and the usefulness of our Church may not diminish. After your death, the aforesaid estate must without doubt return to the right of our Holy Church, whose property it is. Given on the fourth day before the Ides of May, in the fourteenth indiction.’” (That is, in the year 626.)

From the Register of Gregory the Younger.

[Col. 0338B]

“Gregory to Stephen the presbyter and two other successive holders.

“‘Whenever it is hoped that we will grant things that unquestionably accord with reason, it is fitting for us to grant them willingly and to provide appropriate assistance to the wishes of those who petition us. Therefore, because you asked us to grant you for possession, by an issued decree, the estate of Campanus, with its house and vineyard, situated on the Flaminian Road approximately fourteen miles from this city of Rome, which was held by Sergius, our presbyter and treasurer, by right of lease, and which estate belonged to the body of the Tuscan patrimony of the Holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, we have been inclined by your prayers.

“Accordingly, by the terms of this decree, we grant you possession of the aforesaid estate, with its house, vineyard, and everything belonging to it, in its entirety, for the days of your lives, beginning with the present eighth indiction. You must, however, pay three gold solidi into the ecclesiastical accounts at every indiction as rent, without difficulty or delay; and you must undoubtedly ensure, without distinction, every improvement and protection that the aforesaid estate, vineyard, and house require. There must afterward be no delay on your part in paying the annual rent; rather, it must be paid voluntarily from that time onward to the agents of our Holy Church.

“For if anything contrary to this should happen through you—God forbid—with respect to the aforesaid improvement, protection, or annual rent, we decree that this grant of ours shall be invalid. After your death, the aforesaid estate must return in its entirety to the right of our holy Church, whose property it is. Given on the Ides of April, in the eighth indiction.’” (That is, in the year 725.)

Two fragments from letters of Pope John VIII to the empress Angelberga and to the emperor Louis, together with a letter of the same pontiff to Anno, bishop of Freising, which Baluze published from Colbert manuscript 2576 in book V of the *Miscellanies*, pages 489 and 490, appear to have been excerpted long ago from our collection, where they are found in book III, chapters 121, 122, and 123.

CHAPTER XV. On the manuscript collection of Bonizo, bishop of Sutri.

1. Bonizo was formerly bishop of Sutri, distinguished for his outstanding learning and his zeal for ecclesiastical liberty. But after being expelled from the see of Sutri in defense of the Roman Church, following many captivities, tribulations, and exiles, he was received as bishop by the Catholic people of Piacenza, as Berthold of Constance says. But after his eyes were gouged out by the schismatics of that place, and almost all his limbs were mutilated, he was crowned with martyrdom.

So Berthold writes in his continuation of the *Chronicle of Hermann the Lame* under the year 1089; for that reason, this date is believed to be the year of Bonizo’s death. Muratori, however, published Bonizo’s booklet *On the Sacraments*, addressed to Gualterus, prior of the monastery of Leon, from a manuscript in the Ambrosian Library, in dissertation 37 of volume III of the *Italian Antiquities*. On page 602 Bonizo mentions a work he wrote against the schismatic Hugo.

He also mentions this work in book four of the collection soon to be described, in these words: “But if anyone wishes to know about the acts of Pope Urban II and about his victory, let him read the book I wrote against the schismatic Hugo; there he will find fully clarified whatever he wishes to know.”

The victory of Urban II mentioned here is the victory by which the antipope Guibert was expelled from Rome. This occurred in the year 1089. Bonizo therefore wrote his work against Hugo no later than that year. Later he labored over both his booklet *On the Sacraments* and his collection of canons, in which he praises that work as having already been written by him.

Therefore Bonizo’s death cannot be assigned to the year 1089; it must be said to have occurred later. If Berthold mentioned Bonizo in that year because he believed that Bonizo had already died, he was mistaken. He was likewise mistaken when he reported the death of Berengar of Anjou under the year 1083, since everyone agrees that Berengar died in 1088.

The anonymous author of Melk, a contemporary of Berthold, is even more clearly wrong when, in chapter 113 of his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, he stated that Bonizo’s collection was written under Gregory VII: “Bonizo, presbyter of Sutri” (it should read “bishop”) “wrote excerpts from the canons in the time of Gregory VII.”

2. This collection, composed somewhat after the year 1089, remained unknown for a long time. Lambecius was the first to describe, in volume II, chapter 8, of his *Commentary on the Imperial Library at Vienna*, the manuscript of this collection preserved in that library, in addition to Bonizo’s *Epitome of the Sentences of Saint Augustine*, entitled *The Augustinian Paradise*, divided into eight books and accompanied by a dedicatory letter to John the abbot. He described it as follows:

“‘It is a parchment volume in a small folio, or larger quarto, which, so far as one may judge from the writing and other circumstances, was copied not long after Bonizo’s death … The manuscript contains the hitherto unpublished Decretal of Bonizo, or *Syntagma of Ecclesiastical Decrees*, collected from sacred Scripture and approved councils, as well as from the records of the Roman pontiffs, the holy Fathers, and other orthodox authors, and divided according to commonplaces into seven books. In place of a preface there is prefixed to it an Epitome of the History of the Roman Pontiffs, from Saint Peter, prince of the Apostles, to Pope Urban II. The title of the aforementioned Epitome is: *Chronicle of the Roman Pontiffs, published by Bonitho, bishop of Sutri, a man most learned in every respect*.’”

Lambecius made a long fragment of this Epitome public. It begins: “Writing about the excellence of the Roman Church, etc.”

This Vienna manuscript, however, containing only seven books and beginning with the fragment just mentioned, presents not the complete collection of Bonizo but one lacking the first three books. This was made clear to us by the manuscript of the chapter of the church of Brescia, whose description the learned priest Charles Doneda of that city kindly communicated. We may therefore provide a fuller description of this collection.

3. This Brescian manuscript, a parchment quarto in an oblong format, nearly contemporary with Bonizo, was written at the end of the eleventh century or at least the beginning of the twelfth. On the last folio, in a later hand, there is recorded a statement of the rental income of the cathedral church of Brescia, dated to the year 1210, in the thirteenth indiction.

In this manuscript ten books are presented. Only one page of the first book is missing. In the upper margin of the other page, which is now the first, this title is written in a second hand: “A booklet of Bonizo, bishop, addressed to Gregory the presbyter, concerning the authentic canons of the holy Fathers.”

No title is prefixed to the books themselves. Instead, in place of titles, brief prefaces designate the subject proper to each book. To become acquainted with this collection, it will therefore suffice to quote a few passages from these prefaces.

Although, because of the loss of the first page, the preface of the first book has disappeared, its subject can be inferred not only from the book itself, which discusses baptism at length, but also from the beginning of the second book, where both a summary of the preceding book and the subject of the second are presented.

“Here begins the second book. In the preceding book we briefly explained, as best we could, that everyone must first be instructed before being baptized; what baptism is; in how many ways it is performed; from whom it took its beginning; when it should be performed; and how it ought to be performed. Then, after the catechumen had been cleansed at the appointed times through the exorcistic insufflation and the anointing with exorcised oil, we led him as far as the font. There, after being immersed or submerged three times, he testified, by his own confession of the mouth or through the faith of those receiving him, that he believed in God the almighty Father, in the Lord Christ, the crucified Son of God and man, and in the Holy Spirit, in the presence of the angels.

“After he had ascended or been lifted out, he was anointed with the principal oil and admitted to the banquet of the heavenly table. But since, according to the testimony of the Apostle James, faith without works is dead, it remains now to enumerate works worthy of faith, so that, like a wise architect, I may build a house upon the foundation that is Christ, which neither winds, nor rivers, nor rains can tear down.

“Now, trusting in God’s mercy, let us begin our discourse. The first and principal virtue of Christians is obedience, the daughter of humility, etc.”

After some further material, he declares that he wishes to provide an instruction from which all may learn how to live as Christians in their respective conditions. He proposes the following division of Christians:

“Some are clerics, others laymen; and among both groups some are subjects and others prelates. Among the prelates placed in the clerical order, some are bishops, others priests of the second order, and others judges.”

In this second book he deals with bishops and their functions, especially ordinations.

“Here begins the third book.” This is the only book that lacks a preface. It deals with metropolitans, the pallium, their duties toward their suffragans and, conversely, the duties of bishops; simoniacal ordinations; episcopal judgments; synods; the purgative oath; the transfer of bishops; and their duties. These three books are missing from the Vienna imperial manuscript.

“Here begins the fourth book. As I write about the excellence of the Roman Church, the privileges belonging to the bishop of that same Church, and its constitutions, I earnestly ask the diligent reader not to burst too quickly into reproach against me when he sees that, in so extensive a work, I have said little about great matters.”

This introduction is longer. Inserted into it is the Epitome of the Roman pontiffs from Saint Peter to Urban II, praised by Lambecius. It would not be useless to transcribe here one fragment of this Epitome.

“Moreover, if anyone wishes to know how Theophylact of Tusculum sold the papacy to John; how, at one and the same time, Theophylact, Gregory, and Sylvester did not govern the Roman pontificate but laid it waste; and how King Henry, son of Conrad, freed the Roman Church from such plagues, let him read the book I composed entitled *To a Friend*. There he will find these matters arranged in due order.

“He will also find there how Pope Clement was elected; how King Henry was ordained emperor by that same man; and concerning Damasus, his successor, how many days he spent in the papacy; and concerning the illustrious Leo, what he did in the papacy and how he ended his life; and concerning Victor, his successor, what he did and what new event occurred in his time; and concerning Stephen, the brother of Duke Godefrey, and how in his time the Pataria [variant: Patarea] arose at Milan; and concerning Pope Nicholas, the conflict he had with Benedict the usurper, and what he did in the papacy; and concerning Pope Alexander II, the conflict he had with Cadolus of Parma, his victory, what he did in the papacy, and his death; and concerning Gregory VII, his election, his life and morals; how he was captured at the altar of the Lord by Cencio, a cruel man, and liberated by God’s grace on that same day; concerning the war he endured against the emperor Henry; concerning the controversy he had with Wibert; concerning the hardships he suffered and the siege of the city and of himself; how he was freed by Robert, duke of the Normans; and how he came to rest in a blessed death—all these matters are most aptly explained.

“If anyone wishes to know the acts of Pope Urban and his victory, let him read the book I wrote against the schismatic Hugo; there he will find fully clarified whatever he wishes to know.

“Up to this point, beginning with Blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, and continuing to our own times, we have arranged in summary form the deeds of the Roman pontiffs. It remains now for us to discuss, with God’s help, the privileges belonging to the Roman pontiff and the prerogative of that See—not at length, but concisely.

“Here begins the fifth book. In the preceding three little books we briefly explained, as best we could, what sort of man a bishop ought to be, by whom, where, and when he ought to be consecrated, and how he ought to live properly after his consecration. We then treated concisely of the dignity of the metropolitan, the use of the pallium and its significance, episcopal excellence, delays, and the rejection of accusations brought by enemies and infamous persons, as well as of their judgment.

“Afterward, concerning the excellence of the Roman Church, the prerogative of the Roman pontiff, and the constitutions and customs of the aforesaid Church, we arranged, not at length but concisely, by selecting a very few things from many. It remains now to explain, as God grants, the priests of the second order, the deacons, and the other orders; and let us begin with ordination.

“Here begins the sixth book. We have learned from Blessed Benedict that there are four kinds of monks. The first is that of the anchorites, who, tested in monasteries and now like veterans, flee the sight of men, are surrounded by the protection of angels, and are refreshed by their speech.

“The second is that of the coenobites, who live under the rule of an abbot. Imitating our Lord Jesus Christ, they do not do their own will but the will of another.

“The third is the most dreadful kind, that of the sarabaites, who live according to their own inclination, without an abbot, three or two together in cells, seeking their food by the work of their hands.

“The fourth is that of the gyrovagues, so called because, wandering about in circles, they have no fixed dwellings.”

He then treats of monks at length.»
«The seventh book begins. Having written about kings, judges, and those established in the lay order, it seemed worthwhile for us briefly to clarify whence royal power derives, or from whom it first took its beginning, etc.

[Col. 0341D] «The eighth book begins. Since in the preceding book we briefly related, as best we could, matters concerning prelates placed in the lay order, it remains now, in a further book, to investigate briefly how their subjects ought to order their lives. Let us begin by dividing the common people. For among the common people some are artisans, while others are farmers, etc.» He subsequently treats of tithes, betrothals, marriage, fasting, and feast days.

«The ninth book begins. This book is entitled “Medicinal,” because it contains various medicines for the souls of the sick. And just as it belongs to skilled physicians to recognize the illnesses of individuals by feeling their pulses and examining their urine, so it belongs to prudent priests, after considering the penitent’s repentance, to apportion judicially what is appropriate, to whom, and in what measure. And in order that they may be competent to do this, they must not be ignorant of the canons of the holy Fathers, so that judgment may proceed from the authority of the holy canons, [Col. 0342A] and mercy, always following, may exalt judgment, etc.» After much else, he treats of penitents who have been excommunicated and of various kinds of sins.

«The tenth book begins. I remember saying in the preceding book that it lies within the discretion of prudent priests, after considering the humility and repentance of penitents according to the measure of their fault, to temper the severity of the canons. But since the authority of our predecessors has great force in the holy Church, it seemed worthwhile to me to insert the authorities and examples of the holy Fathers. Let us begin with the clergy.» What follows consists of many canons concerning penance.

4. Although no title of the books is present, and the prefaces serve in place of titles, the canons that are cited generally have their own titles prefixed. We trust that this collection will be published by Father Abbot John Chrysostom Trombellius, who obtained a copy of the Brescia manuscript.

CHAPTER XVI. On the Two Collections of Ivo of Chartres

[Col. 0342B]

1. Ivo was born in the Beauvais region in the middle of the eleventh century. In 1078 he was appointed abbot of the monastery of Saint-Quentin at Beauvais, belonging to the order of Canons Regular; finally, he was elected bishop of Chartres in 1092 and consecrated by Urban II. He died in 1115, or, as others prefer, in 1117. He was a man distinguished not only by outstanding learning but also by zeal, prudent steadfastness, faith, and holiness. For this reason Pius V, by a constitution issued in 1570, granted the canons of the Lateran congregation permission to celebrate Ivo’s memory on 20 May.

Two collections of canons bearing Ivo’s name have appeared. One, divided into eight parts, is called Ivo’s *Pannormia*; the other is Ivo’s *Decree*, which is divided into seventeen parts. The *Pannormia* was printed at Basel in 1499 under the supervision of Sebastian Brandt, and Melchior a [Col. 0342C] Vosmedian later arranged for it to be reprinted at Leuven in 1557, corrected of its errors. The *Decree* first appeared at Leuven in 1561 through the work and scholarship of Jean Molinaeus of Ghent, and was later printed at Paris in 1647 together with Ivo’s other works, corrected against the most ancient Victorine manuscript. In the commonly circulated editions, both works have prefixed to them exactly the same preface; its style, entirely consistent with that of Ivo’s other letters, demonstrates that it is Ivo’s.

2. Let us first list the titles of both works. The first part of the longer work, commonly called Ivo’s *Decree*, treats of baptism and confirmation. The second treats of the sacrament of Christ’s body, the sacrifice of the Mass, and the other sacraments, as well as simony. The third treats of the Church and ecclesiastical matters, and of the reverence and observance owed to them. The fourth treats of feasts, fasts, the canonical Scriptures, customs, and councils. The fifth treats of the primacy of the Roman Church, and of the order and rights of primates, metropolitans, and bishops. The sixth treats of the life, order, and discipline of the clergy. [Col. 0342D] The seventh treats of monks. The eighth treats of marriage and virginity, abduction, concubinage, and adultery. The ninth treats of incest and prohibited degrees. The tenth treats of voluntary and involuntary homicide. The eleventh treats of magicians, sorceresses, and actors. The twelfth treats of lying, perjury, etc. The thirteenth treats of theft, usury, hunters, drunkards, the insane, and Jews. The fifteenth treats of penance. The sixteenth treats of the office and judgments of laypeople. The seventeenth part contains the opinions of the holy Fathers, especially Gregory the Great, concerning faith, hope, and charity.

3. Here, moreover, are the titles of the other collection, entitled Ivo’s *Pannormia*, as the author himself set them forth.

«The first part of this book contains material concerning faith and various heresies; concerning the sacrament—that is, baptism—and the ministry of those who baptize, consecrate, sign, and are signed, as well as the observance of each of these matters; [CCCXI] and what baptism effects, [Col. 0343A] and what confirmation effects. It treats of the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood; of the Mass; and of the holiness of the other sacraments.

«The second part contains material concerning the constitution of the Church and the offerings of the faithful; the dedication and consecration of churches and altars; burial; priests and their churches; tithes and lawful possession; those who flee for refuge to a church; sacrilege; guardianship of children; the alienation and exchange of ecclesiastical property; the Scriptures; and authentic councils.

«The third part contains material concerning the election and consecration of the pope and archbishops; orders; clergy and laypeople who are, or are not, to be ordained; the transfer of bishops; those who have been ordained and are not to be reordained; the continence of the ordained; those ordained or ordaining simoniacally, who are to be deposed altogether, and who are to be reconciled mercifully; the profession of heretics; those who have fallen while in holy orders, who are not to minister, and who may be restored to ministry mercifully; clerics who have committed homicide, who are not to minister; usurers; slaves ordained through ignorance, specifying who are to remain in their ordination and who are not; drunken and buffoonish clerics; monks; the age at which parents may oppose their children’s entry into religion, and the age at which they may not; widows and veiled virgins; and abbesses.

«The fourth part contains material concerning the primacy and dignity of the Roman Church; councils to be convened; how a province is to be constituted; the power of primates and metropolitan bishops; the affairs and cases of clerics, and where they are to be handled; the restoration of those who have been dispossessed; accusation—how, in what order, by which persons, and against which persons it is or is not to be made; witnesses—who they are, how many there should be, how they should testify, and in what cases; judges—what sort they should be, and when they should deliver a judicial sentence; appeal—when and by what procedure it is to be made; and the penalty [Col. 0343C] for those who appeal improperly.

«The fifth part contains material concerning clerics accused solely on the basis of infamy, without witnesses, and the number of hands by which they must purge themselves; the cases and affairs of laypeople; the summons of those who are to be excommunicated; lawful and unlawful excommunication; absolution; those bound by fidelity or an oath to excommunicated persons, and whether they can be absolved from that oath without perjury; heretics to be excommunicated after death; and the rule that communion is not to be denied merely on account of the name of “excommunicated.”

«The sixth part contains material concerning weddings: at what time, between which persons, and for what reason they are to take place; the three things that make a marriage complete; complete and incomplete marriage; concubines; spouses one of whom has vowed continence without the other, or has taken the religious habit; wives who have married others while their husbands were held captive; and the question of what constitutes marriage between persons of the same religion or faith. Marriage cannot take place between Jews; nor can it take place between persons who do not share the same religion or faith. It also treats of the reasons for which a marriage ought not to be dissolved, what kind of union does not constitute marriage, and separation from marriage for reasons other than fornication.

«The seventh part contains material concerning separation from marriage on account of carnal fornication; the man who fornicates with another man’s wife, and the rule that he cannot take her as his wife after her husband’s death; those who kill their spouses; spiritual fornication, on account of which a wife may lawfully be dismissed; reconciliation between spouses; the sacraments that husbands must give to wives and wives to their husbands when they are reconciled; the subjection by which wives must be subject to their husbands; the reason why marriage must not take place between relatives; the rule that one man cannot marry two women who are his co-mothers-in-law, one after the other; and the case of a man who has had intercourse with his goddaughter or with his co-mother-in-law, or who baptized his son, or whose wife baptized her son, or who lifted his stepson from the sacred font, or held him at confirmation, and therefore wished to separate. It treats of the branch of consanguinity within which marriages may be contracted; accusation of consanguinity, including by which persons it is to be made; investigation of kinship; incestuous marriage; and divisions of the degrees of consanguinity arranged in the direct and collateral lines.

[CCCXII] «The eighth part contains material concerning voluntary and involuntary homicide, and what may be done without sin; the person who kills any cleric, and what he must make satisfaction for; the person who strikes a pregnant woman and causes a miscarriage, and whether or not he has committed homicide; incantations, divinations, and various kinds of magical art; the nature of demons; lots; observance of days and months; oaths—whether they must be kept and what companions they have; and every kind of lie.»

4. No one doubts that Ivo was the author of the earlier collection called the *Decree*. But a major controversy has arisen among critics concerning the *Pannormia*. Vincent of Beauvais, *Speculum historiale*, book XXV, chapter 84, after mentioning Ivo’s *Decree*, which he says is a volume of considerable size and not easily portable, adds:

“Hugh of Châlons is said to have composed from the same volume, in abbreviated form, a portable little book, which is also in my possession and is called Ivo’s *Summary of the Decrees*.”

From this Sebastian Brandt, who edited the *Pannormia*, was the first to suspect that it was rather Hugh of Châlons’s *Summary of Ivo’s Decrees*, excerpted from Ivo’s *Decree*, than a work of Ivo himself. Jean Molinaeus adopted and defended the same view in his edition of the *Decree*. The Roman correctors and P. Antonio Pagius subsequently followed them. Others, however, with Stefano Baluzius in his preface to the dialogues of Antonio Agustín on the emendation of Gratian, attributed the *Pannormia* to Ivo no less than the *Decree*. They judge that he first composed the *Pannormia*, and then, after seeing that it was well received by readers, applied himself to preparing a more extensive collection, adapting the same prologue to both works.

5. We shall explain briefly which of these opinions seems more probable to us. First, it is certain that some collection of canons must be attributed to Ivo. For this is affirmed not only by Sigebert, who was his contemporary, writing in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 168: “Ivo, bishop of Chartres, composed a distinguished volume of canons”; and likewise by the Anonymous of Melk, who lived shortly after Ivo, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 95: “Ivo, bishop of Chartres, wrote, among other things, *Extracts from the Canons*”; but Ivo himself also testifies in letter 262 to Pontius, abbot of the monastery of Cluny:

“I have sent you the collections of canons that you requested from me, together with the little works of mine that you wished to be added to them.”

By these words he appears to indicate a collection arranged by himself. Perhaps some will infer from this testimony that both collections—that is, both the *Pannormia* and Ivo’s *Decree*—must be attributed to him, since he wrote “collections” in the plural, not “collection.” Yet Ivo himself likewise says in letter 80, using the plural:

“In the collections of Burchard, bishop of Worms,”

although Burchard has only one collection. Nor are the passages of Sigebert, Robert of Torigni, and other writers, who mention a single volume, sufficiently effective to exclude two collections by Ivo. They may have seen one collection, entitled *Pannormia*, whose copies are more numerous, but not the other, namely the *Decree*, whose manuscripts are indeed rarer.

6. Second, it is certain that the *Pannormia* is not the *Summary of Ivo’s Decrees* said to have been composed by Hugh of Châlons. The reasons are that, because its division and arrangement differ from those of the *Decree*, the *Pannormia* is as far as possible from being an abridged form of that *Decree*; that it contains certain matters which one searches for in vain in the *Decree*; and that in ancient manuscripts it is nowhere entitled *Summary of the Decrees*, but *Pannormia* or *Ivo’s Extracts*. Hence the *Summary* arranged by Hugh and mentioned by Vincent of Beauvais was a different work, which perished through the ravages of time.

Certain decrees copied at the end of the final part from Innocent II, who was pope after Ivo, might seem to create difficulty for attributing the *Pannormia* to Ivo. But this difficulty is removed by ancient manuscripts of the *Pannormia*, in which those decrees of Innocent II are not found with the work; it is clear that they were added later in certain copies.

7. The matter seems therefore to be decided by the manuscripts. There are few manuscripts of the *Decree*. So far we have learned of only three: one from which the first edition was produced; the Victorine manuscript, praised by many, against which the second Paris edition was prepared; and the Vatican manuscript 1357, from the twelfth century, which we ourselves have seen. All of them contain the preface. But the Vatican manuscript, without the author’s name, bears this title:

“Here begins the book of extracts, or excerpts, from ecclesiastical matters, partly from the letters of the Roman pontiffs, partly from the acts of councils, Catholic bishops, and kings”;  

and it contains seventeen parts.

The Victorine manuscript, however, presents that preface not at the beginning but added at the end of the codex, in a more recent hand, under this inscription:

“The above-written book of canons, the decrees of Jovinian, which Ivo, formerly bishop of Chartres, composed; and it contains seventeen principal parts.”

So we learn from Baluzius in his preface to Augustine’s dialogues, no. 21.

There are more copies of the *Pannormia*. One, praised only by Antonio Agustín under the title “Book of the Sacred Canons,” lacks both the preface and Ivo’s name. The others bear either the preface or a title with Ivo’s name. Baluzius praises the very ancient Victorine manuscript and three manuscripts of Saint-Albin of Angers. François Salmon, in his treatise in French on the study of councils, part II, chapter 1, p. 269 of the 1726 edition, mentions a manuscript copy of the Paris church, F 4.

Besides one mutilated copy of Saint Benedict of Padilirone, we have found three others with the preface: one of the Vatican Basilica, 19 G; another, Vat. 1358, with a distinctive heading to the same preface addressed to an abbot—namely, as we believe, to Pontius, the abbot to whom Ivo professed in letter 262 that he had sent the collection; and finally a manuscript of the monks of Saint Justina at Padua, marked YY. V. no. 86, in which the following title is found:

“*Ivo, bishop of Chartres: Extracts from Ecclesiastical Canons*.”

The preface follows, together with the titles of the eight parts into which the *Pannormia* is divided.

This manuscript seems to resolve the controversy concerning the author of the work. Although it is believed to be from the fourteenth century, it was copied from an older exemplar that had been written immediately after Ivo’s death. For it appends a catalogue of the Roman pontiffs that ends with Gelasius II, omitting his years of pontificate, although those years are individually recorded for the preceding pontiffs. This occurred because the catalogue was written under Gelasius himself, when the years of his pontificate could not yet be recorded.

Gelasius II began his pontificate in 1118 and died in January [Col. 0345D] 1119. Ivo, however, had died, as we said at the beginning, in 1115 or 1117. The exemplar from which the Paduan manuscript was copied was therefore contemporary with Ivo. This testimony, so ancient and so clearly asserting the *Pannormia* to be Ivo’s, is of such weight to us that if one of the two works had to be regarded as doubtful, we would question the *Decree* rather than the *Pannormia*.

8. We do not therefore think that the *Decree* should be taken away from Ivo. Since the same preface of the *Pannormia* is also added to this work in ancient books, we believe that this was done because those ancient copyists had received this work also as having been composed by Ivo. It appears that Ivo first wrote and published the *Pannormia* together with its preface. Hence several copies of the same *Pannormia* were immediately written and circulated.

Later he arranged a longer collection, but perhaps did not himself publish it. Thus, after his death, it was found without its own prologue; in the rarer copies that were written, a prologue from the *Pannormia* was added to it. Consequently, in the most ancient Victorine exemplar the prologue is written not at the beginning but at the end of the *Decree*, as an addition.

9. The principal source from which Ivo derived his canons was the Isidorian collection. He also occasionally used Regino’s compilation. From it, among other things, he transferred word for word into the *Decree*, part VI, chapters 433, 434, and 435, the examples of formal letters reproduced by Regino in book I, numbers 437, 438, and 439. He took most of his material from Burchard. He himself also inserted quite a few other things, such as, for example, the material in the second part of the *Decree* against the errors of Berengar, and the material in part XVI drawn from Roman law and from the capitularies of the Frankish kings.

CHAPTER XVII. On the Manuscript Collection of the Priest Gregory, Entitled *Polycarpus*

1. The collection commonly cited under the title *Polycarpus* became known after the Roman correctors of Gratian praised it in their preface and notes. It is contained in Vat. 1354. Its author is identified from the dedicatory letter as Gregory, a priest, who entitled it *Polycarpus*.

Oudinus (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. II, col. 764) judged that its author was the celebrated Gregory who later became cardinal bishop of Sabina in the holy Roman Church. He is mistaken. That cardinal flourished under Pope Gregory VII and died under Urban II. But the author of the collection, since in book III, title 9, he praises a decree of Calixtus II, who began his pontificate in 1119, is different from the Gregory of Sabina mentioned above.

That this priest was Roman is inferred less from the heading of the Colbert manuscript reported by Oudinus than from documents that we sometimes find in this collection in fuller or more complete form than in Anselm and Deusdedit, so that he evidently derived them from the Roman archives.

2. The date can be established from the dedicatory letter. It is addressed to “D., worthily adorned with the pontifical mitre of the Church of Saint James.” We must investigate which bishop of the Church of Saint James—that is, Compostela—this was, whose name begins with the letter D.

At the beginning of the eleventh century two bishops of that church are found: Dalmachius and Didacus. The dedication cannot belong to the first, since he had already died in 1103 or 1104, in which year Didacus, his successor, received a letter from Paschal II that is found in volume XII of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 987.

Gregory’s collection cannot be placed before 1119, since it uses the aforementioned decree of Calixtus II. The dedication therefore belongs only to Didacus, Dalmachius’s successor.

Cardinal de Aguirre published two documents in which this Didacus is mentioned (vol. XII of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 1402). One is a privilege of Alfonso, king of Spain, appended to the Council of Palencia of 1129. In it the same king granted to Didacus, archbishop of the see of Compostela by the grace of God, all the royal rights formerly belonging to the archiepiscopal church of Mérida. Mérida was then occupied by the Saracens, and Calixtus II had transferred the archbishopric of Mérida to the Church of Compostela in recognition of the merits and reverence owed to the most blessed apostle James.

The other document is the Synod of Oviedo, to which Didacus, archbishop of James—that is, of Compostela—is recorded as having subscribed. In the commonly circulated editions this synod is assigned to the year 1115. But since the archbishopric of Mérida, if Alfonso’s privilege is genuine, was transferred to Compostela by Calixtus II, who became pope in 1119, the synod at which Didacus is called archbishop of James, or of Compostela, must have been held after 1119. Perhaps the year 1115 was written by a copyist’s error for 1125.

Moreover, we have discovered from a twelfth-century manuscript that two Didacuses, I and II, ruled the Church of Compostela. A copy of this manuscript is preserved by Count Giuseppe Garampi, canon of the Basilica of Saint Peter and prefect of the Vatican archives, who communicated to us the following information about these same Didacuses.

The manuscript in question contains a description of the Church of Saint James at Compostela. In it the church is said to have been begun under Bishop Didacus I and “the most valiant and noble man” in the era 1116, that is, in the year of Christ 1078.

When it describes a silver tablet decorated in repoussé work, it gives the following verses inscribed upon it, in which Didacus II is praised:

> This tablet Didacus, the second bishop of the Jacobean church,  
> made during his five-year episcopate.  
> Alfonso was king, and his son-in-law Raimund was duke,  
> when the aforementioned bishop completed the work.

The collection of Gregory belongs to this second Didacus. After obtaining the archiepiscopal dignity through the Church of Saint James, he was called archbishop of Compostela at the Council of Oviedo, “the Jacobean bishop” in these verses, and in the dedication of the present collection he is described as adorned with the pontifical mitre of the Church of Saint James.

Perhaps after this accession to dignity, under Calixtus II, Gregory, a Roman priest, composed the collection at Didacus’s urging and dedicated it to him.

3. The aforementioned Oudinus praises two Colbert manuscripts, numbered 696 and 4047, and mentions only four books. But the Vatican manuscript presents a collection divided into eight books. Each book is divided into several titles, which in turn contain many decrees and testimonies. The work is therefore not so small as many, after Antonio Agustín, have suspected. We reproduce here the dedicatory letter and the titles of the books from the Vatican manuscript.

[CCCXV] «To D., D., worthily adorned with the pontifical mitre of the Church of Saint James, Gregory, the humblest of priests, sends greetings.

[Note: [Col. 0347D] At the place cited, Oudinus, from the Colbert manuscripts that he cites, supplies the title absent from the Vatican manuscript and gives the beginning of the dedication in these words: “Prologue of Gregory of the Holy Roman Church concerning an excerpt from the authorities of the Roman pontiffs and other saints: To the beloved Lord D. of the Church of Saint James, etc.”]

«You have long requested, and often urged, that I undertake a difficult work beyond my abilities—namely, that I compose in orderly fashion a book of canons, selecting the more useful material from the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, the authorities of the other holy Fathers, and various authentic councils.

You did not ask this of me in my ignorance because either your wisdom was unequal to this labor, or because you lacked many others more suitable and wiser who would willingly obey your command. Rather, you asked it so that, having long exercised myself in this great task, I might become more instructed and prepared for the work of other, greater men . . .; or so that, if my limited intellect should fail in some respect, your prudence might extend to me its guiding and helping hand.

Although this investigation required a keen intellect and was entirely unsuited to my powers, and although I feared that some might judge it rash, nevertheless, lest I offend so great and distinguished a man by refusing, I consented. Finally, I obeyed your command chiefly in the confidence that, with your authority interposed, I would be defended from the attacks of detractors.

For just as formerly in the Church, and daily in public affairs, one matter follows another in various ways, and the proceedings of many cases increase according to the course of time, so I have connected under titles many chapters appropriate to each matter, after considering the time of their authors, and have briefly brought the volume to an end in eight books.

In accordance with the manner of its composition, and on the authority I received from you, I appropriately gave it the name *Polycarpus*. I earnestly beg your diligence to examine the composition and, by examining it, to complete with careful consideration whatever you discover to be lacking or to be present in greater measure than is proper, adding what is fitting and removing what is unfitting. With due moderation, may I be approved and commended to your praise and to the strengthening of obedience to your command.

Moreover, lest the absence of distinction in the sequence of the book confuse the reader, I thought it appropriate to place the titles of the work before it, so that the reader may gather in their proper places whatever he recognizes to have been set forth under the appropriate number.»

4. The first book treats of the primacy of the Roman Church and its privileges, title 27.

The second book treats of the election and ordination of prelates, the pallium, and the orders of the other clergy, title 38.

The third book treats of churches, monasteries, tithes, offerings, the celebration of offices, the rights of churches and monasteries; the body of Christ and its custody; baptism and the laying on of hands; rites; the divine Scriptures; the celebration of Easter; preaching; customs; fasts; etc., title 30.

The fourth book treats of how the law of God is to be read, and of the offices of bishops; chorepiscopi; abbots; monks; nuns; deaconesses; widows; and the offenses of clerics, title 40.

The fifth book treats of judgments, title 8.

The sixth book treats of emperors, princes, and other [Col. 0348B] laypeople; marriage and matrimony; various offenses; penance and penitents; rightful mercy; the good of obedience; and the rule that Christians should not rashly expose themselves to dangers, title 23.

The seventh book treats of excommunication, the power of binding, the unity of the Church, schism, heretics and schismatics, vengeance, etc., title 16.

The eighth book treats of the sick, death and purgatory, burial and offerings for the dead, the immortality of the soul, the torments of the wicked, and the reception of the souls of the righteous into heaven before the resurrection of their bodies, title 10.

CHAPTER XVIII. On Other Manuscript Collections Not Yet Published

1. We shall conclude this treatise with a brief survey of several collections that lie hidden in libraries and have either been discovered by us or indicated by others. Most of them were arranged in the eleventh century, when the study of the sacred [CCCXVI] canons began to flourish and spread more widely.

Although they derive from the same sources, and although most of them also agree in substance because they are more or less stuffed with apocryphal material, they differ greatly in the division of their books or parts. A brief account of them will therefore not be useless.

2. First, mention must be made of a distinctive collection found in Vat. Reginae 973. It appears to possess this particular feature: whereas other collections, divided into titles according to common topics, indiscriminately place under each title the texts appropriate to it from decretal letters and councils, or also from the Fathers, capitularies, and Roman laws, this collection separately presents the texts of pontiffs, councils, Fathers, and laws under their respective titles.

After a brief preface beginning “Since the decrees of certain Roman pontiffs ...,” it first describes selected decrees of the pontiffs, beginning with the apocryphal decrees of Clement, Anacletus, Evaristus, and others, and then presents the decrees of the remaining pontiffs in chronological order down to Nicholas I, John VIII, Alexander II, and Urban II. From this it is known that the collection was arranged in the eleventh century.

All the decrees of each pontiff are gathered together under titles and are not mixed with the decrees of other pontiffs. Thus, after Clement’s decrees have been divided into titles, the decrees of Anacletus follow under another distribution of titles, and the same is done for the other pontiffs.

After the decrees of the pontiffs, the canons of each council are likewise placed under titles. The collection begins with the canons of Nicaea and ends with those of the Second Council of Seville, in which the author followed the order of the Isidorian collection.

Next it presents testimonies from the sayings of the Fathers, into which certain canons of councils are occasionally inserted, as well as material from capitularies, the Novels, and the Theodosian Code.

3. The manuscript copy Vat. 3832, from the eleventh or twelfth century, after several complete or divided documents excerpted from Pseudo-Isidore, presents a collection divided into two books. The first contains 360 chapters or titles; the second contains nearly as many, although they are numbered only up to title 54.

The first chapter of the first book is entitled “On the Primacy of the Roman Church” and begins, “If something difficult and ambiguous ...” This chapter was perhaps copied from this collection, since it was found separately by Johann Wendelstinus, just as we too obtained it separately in Vat. 4977 and in another manuscript belonging to the eminent Passioneus. Wendelstinus published it together with the Hadriana collection at Mainz in 1525, and it has consequently been inserted in volume I of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 65.

Other chapters treat of monasteries, judgments, [Col. 0349B] marriage, perjuries, clerics, orders, etc. The collection is everywhere full of spurious documents. It produces an interpolated decree attributed to Gelasius concerning books to be received or rejected; this was discussed in part II, chapter 11, §5.

It presents an order for administering penance beginning, “Priests must admonish the people subject to them, etc.,” as it is found in Burchard, book XIX, chapter 2 and following. At the end is added a letter of Pope Urban to Gibeard, bishop of Constance, dated 18 April 1089, which was published in volume XII of the Councils, col. 737. From this the date of the collection can be inferred.

4. The manuscript Vat. 1339, from the eleventh century, contains a collection of canons divided into five books. On page 15, the following title is prefixed in capital letters:

“In the name of Christ, here begins a book of canons culled from many sayings of the Fathers, in which remedies for souls, gathered from various teachers, are contained for all who have fallen into innumerable cases. Beloved brothers, you will be able to find in this volume everything that pertains to the benefit of souls. This book, which shines divided into parts—[the reading seems to be: ‘which shines divided into five parts’]—has been collected here not out of temerity but as a remedy of charity for the sick. Therefore, if a prudent reader takes care to search it, he will find in it an appropriate remedy for every vice.”

In the short preface that follows, this collection is called the *Manual*, and it is said to have been compiled out of love for a certain priest Lupus, who was very dear.

The first book, divided into 164 chapters, is entitled: “On degrees and names, on ministries and merits, and on the character and ordination of clerics.”

The second, divided into 178 chapters, treats of “the primates of the Church; the times of councils; the life and chastity of clerics, especially the prohibition of association with women; and women discovered in fornication with clerics.”

The third, divided into 271 chapters, is entitled: “On baptism, chrism, the Lord’s Day, and the feasts of the saints.” These matters appear in the title of the third book. From the table of chapters, however, the following must be added: tithes and the revenues of the Church and their division; offerings of the living and the dead; the three kinds of eunuchs; the tonsure; the ministry of the altar; the canonical hours; excommunication; burial; the Eucharist, and how it is to be received and venerated; lots and auguries; the leadership of barbarians; savage beasts; and the origin of slaves.

The fourth book, divided into 444 chapters, bears this title: “On the usefulness of penance and the grace of communion, even for those at the point of death, and on other matters pertaining to Christianity.” It discusses at length various crimes and works of satisfaction.

The fifth book, containing 240 chapters, treats of “lawful marriages, abductors, multiple marriages, and concubines.”

A table of chapters precedes each book under the heading “Here begin the chapters.” The table of the fifth book, however, is entitled “Here begins the abridgment.” From this it is clear that *abridgment* and *chapters* are used interchangeably.

Testimonies are drawn from Scripture, councils, and the letters of the Roman pontiffs, both genuine and apocryphal; from the holy Fathers, especially Saint Isidore of Seville; and also, in certain cases, from capitularies and the laws of Justinian. The Hadriana and Isidorian collections supplied most of the decrees of councils and pontiffs. Some excerpts also appear to have been taken from the Irish collection.

### 5

Another collection, divided into seven books, is preserved in Codex Vat. 1346. Its date is established by the preceding catalogue of supreme pontiffs, which, in the first hand, ends with Paschal II in such a way that the day of his death, omitted by that same hand, was supplied by a later hand; afterward, in another script, the succeeding pontiffs were added down to Alexander III. This collection, therefore, was compiled at the beginning of the twelfth century, under Paschal II, whose Letter 88 to the soldiers and townspeople of San Gimignano is copied before the collection itself (vol. XII of the Councils, col. 1038). Here are the titles of the individual books:

Book I: On matters pertaining to the Roman pontiffs and the Roman Church.

Book II: On bishops.

Book III: On clerics.

Book IV: On various matters pertaining to clerics.

Book V: On the sacrament of baptism and matters pertaining to baptism, as well as on monks and monasteries.

Book VI: Various matters concerning laypeople.

Book VII: On sins and penance, etc.

### 6

Codex Vat. 1349, of the ninth or tenth century, contains a collection divided into nine books. It is written in an extremely difficult script, and because of lack of time we were able to copy only the titles of the books, which we present here.

Book I: On the order of clerics, or ordination.

Book II: On the celebration of councils, or synods.

Book III: On ecclesiastical ministries.

Book IV: On monks or nuns.

Book V: On the grace of those to be baptized, or on Christianity.

Book VI: On the most excellent collection of canons. This title refers to the heading of the Hibernian Collection; from that collection the following passage too has been copied:

> These matters, being confirmed by testimonies from the Scriptures and by the sayings of the saints: if anything here should appear to disagree, that is to be chosen from among them which is judged to possess greater authority.

See above, chapter 7, § 1, no. 2.

Book VII: On homicides and crimes, and their punishments; on lawful and unlawful unions; on adulteries and fornication; on theft; and on fasts and prayers.

Book VIII: On the usefulness of penance.

Book IX: On the judgment of penitents.

Texts are drawn not only from councils and decrees of pontiffs, but also from the Scriptures and the Fathers, and from Justinian. We leave the examination of further matters in this very ancient collection to others who will be better able to undertake it.

### 7

A collection divided into twelve books is found in MS Vat. Palat. 584.

**Book I.** On the pontiff, primates, metropolitans, etc., chapter 187.

**II.** On the sacred orders, chapter 188.

**III.** On the life of clerics, and on monks and laypeople, chapter 220.

**IV.** On churches and the celebration of Masses; on offerings and tithes; on burials; and on books to be read in church, chapter 241.

**V.** On the sacraments, and their reception and observance, chapter 198.

**VI.** On feasts and fasts at various seasons, chapter 82.

**[CCCXVIII] VII.** On homicides, chapter 99.

**VIII.** On marriages, and on various crimes involving the flesh, chapter 183.

**IX.** On the synod and ecclesiastical judgments, chapter 184.

**X.** On kings and princes; on counts, judges, witnesses, and various offenses; and on criminal persons, chapter 179.

**XI.** On the principal vices and their remedies; on penance and the reconciliation of the sick, chapter 177.

**XII.** On the virtues and condition of the created human being; on predestination; on the origin of death; on souls after death; on purgatorial fire; on eternal fire; on Antichrist; on the day of judgment; on the punishment of the wicked and the glory of the righteous, chapter 116.

[Col. 0351A] It includes quite a few apocryphal materials.

### 8

Rarer testimonies drawn from spurious documents occur in a manuscript collection preserved by Cardinal Passionei, which was arranged in thirteen books. Book I is missing. Book II, mutilated at the beginning, ends with chapter 56. Book III is entitled *On Various Kinds of Causes*, chapter 61. Book IV: *On Baptism and Chrism; on Sunday and the Feasts of the Saints; and on the Sick, or on Tithes and the Offerings of the Faithful*, chapter 38. Book V: *On Silence, and on Clerics Who Conduct Business, Carry Weapons, or Practice Hunting*, chapter 13. Book VI: *On Homicides*, chapter 58. Book VII: *On Truth and Falsehood, that is, on False Witnesses*, chapter 47. Book VIII: *On Oaths and Perjuries*, chapter 15. Book IX: *That All Christians Ought to Forgive Their Enemies from the Heart*, chapter 18. Book X: *On Abstinence from Meat and Wine; on Animals That Have Died a Natural Death and on Strangled Animals; on Those Who Eat Unclean Things; and on Negligence Regarding Sacrifices*, chapter 27. Book XI: *On the Canonical Hours, and on the Eucharist, and on Excommunication, on Burial, and on Lots, Divinations, and Sorcery*, chapter 51. Book XII: *On the Usefulness of Penance*, chapter 75. Book XIII: *On Bishops to Be Ordained, and on Abbots, Priests, and Other Ecclesiastical Orders; and on the Slaves of Ecclesiastics*, chapter 135.

These are the manuscript collections that we ourselves discovered.

### 9

We now turn to those mentioned by others. Gerhard von Mastricht, in his *History of Ecclesiastical Law*, no. 413, praises a collection preserved in a parchment codex of his library and divided into three books. The first book contains 45 titles, the second 56, and the third 46; he, however, reported only the titles of the first book.

He further notes that, besides several fragments from spurious letters of ancient bishops of the Roman See, among the materials drawn from the genuine letters of other pontiffs are several decrees of Agatho, Nicholas, and Hadrian II, whose enactments are inserted in uninterrupted sequence in Book II. If the most recent decrees in this collection are those of Hadrian II, the collection could have been compiled toward the end of the ninth century, or at least before the eleventh.

The same author quotes the following note written at the end of Book III:

> If anyone finds in these books, which we have excerpted from the body of the canons, anything which (so the codex reads) he judges to be contemptible, let him pardon the poverty of our understanding. We nevertheless consider the judgment of many preferable to the assumptions of individuals, etc.

We have detected that these words were improperly excerpted by an unskilled compiler from the concluding sentences of the preface to the Acherian Collection, which we discussed in chapter 8. There they read more appropriately and correctly:

> If anyone finds in these books anything concerning such councils as he judges either contemptible or unacceptable, let him pardon the poverty of our understanding. We nevertheless consider that the opinion of many ought to be preferred to the suspicions of individuals; and in all matters for which we do not possess the authority of general councils, we ought to follow the decisions of those synods held in the individual provinces rather than our own judgment.

[Col. 0351D]

### 10

Antonius Augustinus frequently mentions two collections in his works, calling one Tarraconensis and the other Caesaraugustana. The Tarraconensis is divided into six books. Antonius Augustinus of the Society of Jesus reports the following about it in the appendix to *The Judgment of Antonius Augustinus, Archbishop of Tarragona, Concerning Certain Ancient Collectors of Ecclesiastical Canons*, chapter 33:

> The Tarraconensis Collection—which the archbishop elsewhere calls Populeti—was presented to him as a gift from the distinguished monastery of Cistercian monks, situated in the region twelve miles from Tarragona, commonly called Populeti or Poblete. Since it lacked the name of its author, he named it after the diocese of Tarragona.

He further notes that the more recent documents in this collection are decrees of Gregory VII. The Roman correctors used it on occasion, and in their catalogue of books they call it “the collection of decrees of the Roman pontiffs by Augustine, Archbishop of Tarragona”; in their notes, however, they sometimes call it “the ancient codex of the monastery of Populeti.”

### 11

Concerning the Caesaraugustana Collection, the archbishop himself, Antonius Augustinus, states in Dialogue 5 *On the Emendation of Gratian* that it was sent to him from the Carthusian monastery of Zaragoza, to which it had come after the death of the royal historian Jerónimo Zurita. It is divided into fifteen books; and because it mentions no pontiffs after Urban II, it is believed to have been written at that time.

We obtained a copy of it in MS Barber. 2864, whose title reads on the front:

> The Caesaraugustan Book of the House of God, of Jerónimo Zurita.

We also found another paper codex of this collection, Vat. 4976, but it is mutilated at the end: it contains only the first nine books complete and breaks off in Book X at chapter 47. It will suffice to indicate the titles and chapters of the individual books.

**Book I.** On reason and authority, and which ought to be preferred to which, chapter 64.

**II.** On the privileges of the Roman Church, chapter 74, elsewhere 79.

**III.** On metropolitans and bishops, chapter 72, elsewhere 74.

**IV.** On various offenses and the duties of bishops and clerics, chapter 103, elsewhere 122.

**V.** On ecclesiastical judgments, chapter 94, elsewhere 97.

**VI.** On oaths and perjury, chapter 30.

**VII.** On sacrileges and the privileges of churches, etc., chapter 111, elsewhere 115.

**VIII.** On the life of clerics and the interpretation of the name, chapter 106, elsewhere 119.

**IX.** On the life and office of monks, chapter 69.

**X.** On marriages and virgins, chapter 141, elsewhere 143.

Thus far we have presented the book titles from the Vatican codex, which supplies them. In the following books, which are absent from that codex, we shall give only the title of the first chapter of each book, from the Barberini copy, which lacks general book titles.

**XI.** That the sacrifice of the altar is the true body of Christ, chapter 28. This attacks the error of Berengar, which arose in the middle of the eleventh century.

**XII.** How the uneducated ought to be preached to, chapter 96.

**XIII.** That in the one Catholic Church the true victim of Christ is offered, chapter 55.

**XIV.** On heretics and schismatics, and the difference between heresy and schism, chapter 49.

**XV.** On the condemnation of Constantine, and the reordination of those who had been ordained by him, chapter 81.

### 12

The editors of the Councils frequently praise two other manuscript collections and cite from them certain canons and decrees of pontiffs. They designate one by the formula “from the codex of five books,” because it was divided into that many books. The other they call “from the codex of sixteen books,” because it comprised sixteen books.

The same editors cite from those codices fragments which, since they did not find them in the published Councils and letters of the Roman pontiffs, they considered unpublished. More careful investigation, however, has shown that nearly all of them are cited in similar form in the collection of Burchard, who assigned the names of ancient pontiffs and councils to opinions drawn from capitularies and other writers of a later age, as we noted in chapter 12, no. 3.

Hence some have suspected that these collections are portions of Burchard’s work. Yet not only do the number and titles of the books fail to agree with Burchard’s collection; the order of the canons themselves and the chapters cited are also entirely inconsistent with it. It may safely be inferred, however, that the compilers of those collections took several materials from Burchard, or from another later collection that had received a great many items from Burchard.

### 13

The Roman correctors of Gratian, in their catalogue of the books they used, praise a manuscript collection of penitential canons by an unknown author, from the library of Michael Thomasius, Bishop of Ilerda (Lleida). Antonius Augustinus printed it from the same library at Tarragona in 1582, although he had found it without the name of either its writer or its book-title. Nevertheless, he called it the *Roman Penitential*, because it had come into his hands from the city of Rome.

This collection contains nine titles, each divided into several chapters. Since it cites decrees not so much of Gregory VII and Urban II as of Calixtus and Innocent II, it is evidently a twelfth-century work. It is of the same character as the preceding collections and was drawn from the same sources.

### 14

One matter must not be omitted at the end of this chapter. Hildebert of Le Mans, later bishop of Tours, speaks as follows in a letter to the bishop of Nîmes, written at the end of 1118 or the beginning of 1119, concerning a collection of canons on which he was working (*Book II, Letter 27*, Paris edition of 1708, p. 124):

> The excerpts from the decrees that we have decided to arrange in one volume have not yet been brought to completion. This work requires a mind free from cares, from which the episcopal office has not made us exempt. Nevertheless, we have already completed part of it, and, in order to accomplish what remains, we shall lay aside the episcopate. Once completed, it will come into your hands, and there will be no need for your messenger to tire himself by coming all the way to us to carry it. It will be our duty to have it sent to you through our own agent.

It is not known whether this collection was completed and published, as he had promised. The title *Excerpts from the Decrees*, by which he designates it, led some to attribute to Hildebert the *Decretum* of Ivo, which is prefaced by Ivo’s preface beginning with the word *Excerpts*. The Benedictine editors printed that preface at the end of Hildebert’s letters, just as it had previously been published under the title:

> Hildebert, Bishop of Tours, on his *Excerpts from Ecclesiastical Rules Concerning the Various Kinds of Divine Precepts*.

The editors themselves, however, believe that it should be attributed not to Hildebert but to Ivo; and the manuscript copies mentioned above in chapter 16 likewise assign it to Ivo. There we also attributed both the *Panormia* and the *Decretum* to the same Ivo.

Others, however, have suspected that what belonged to Hildebert was rather the Tarraconensis or the Caesaraugustana Collection—or perhaps some other collection among those mentioned above, which were compiled around the same time and whose authors are unknown. Unless something more certain comes to light, nothing can be affirmed.

### 15

These are the collections that we have considered it necessary to explain as having been compiled before Gratian. Gratian’s collection is sufficiently well known and has been elucidated by many; it requires no explanation. For that reason, we conclude our work with the collections earlier than Gratian, from which he derived almost everything.

One observation concerning Gratian himself, however, will not be useless. He drew most of his material not from ancient and original sources containing complete documents, but from collections of later periods, in which those same documents had been divided into sections and distributed under common topics. Since these collections, arranged under titles, offered considerable convenience because of their easier method, they were widely adopted; and as their copies multiplied through frequent use, love of and interest in the ancient and purer sources gradually declined.

The authors of these collections were not always accurate, nor did they always transcribe the canons and decrees from those ancient codices. We have seen above (Supplement, chapter 7, § 1, no. 1, and § 2, no. 3) that some did not always excerpt complete texts, but, with freer license, presented some in abbreviated form, others expressed in different words, others curtailed, and others interpolated. We have repeatedly noted that many spurious materials were inserted indiscriminately, and that some otherwise genuine materials were attributed to the wrong authors.

We have also seen (chapter 12, no. 5) that certain collectors of this kind drew almost all their material from corrupted collections of this sort and, while attempting to correct their errors, added new errors of their own in the process of excerpting.

Once the sources from which nearly all Gratian’s errors arose have thus been identified, anyone engaged in the study of Gratian will readily understand how useful our present work, in which we have discussed those sources or collections, may be.

---

[Col. 0353]

# Appendix to the Works of Saint Leo the Great, or

[Note: [Col. 0359B] This title is derived from two manuscripts of Quesnellus, three cited by Peter Pithoeus, and four others mentioned by P. Coustant in the preface to volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, no. 72, as well as from Caesarean Vindobonensis 42. All of them bear this inscription: “This codex contains ecclesiastical canons and constitutions of the Apostolic See.”]

# The Code of Ecclesiastical Canons and Constitutions of the Holy Apostolic See

The oldest of all those published to the present.

[Note: [Col. 0359B] “The oldest,” because, as we noted in the preface, it ends with Gelasius, whereas Dionysius Exiguus cites certain materials from Anastasius II, who succeeded Gelasius. Quesnellus further added to the title: “and the most extensive,” and indeed it was used in the Roman Church under the pontificates of Innocent I, Zosimus, and others, as well as Leo I. [Col. 0360B] We deleted this, because Isidore’s collection is more extensive among the published collections and includes the entire Hispanic collection, which is much richer than this one. We shall demonstrate most clearly in the Observations on Dissertation 12 that this was not, as he thinks, the codex of the Roman Church.]

First published by Quesnellus from the Thuaneus and Oxford manuscripts, but now revised against the outstanding Caesarean Vindobonensis 39 and corrected in numerous places, with variant readings added from manuscript copies of other collections, including unpublished ones.

[Note: [Col. 0360D] As we noted in note 1, this title is found in both of Quesnellus’s codices, in the four examined by P. Coustant, and in our Vindobonensis 42. Another Vindobonensis, however, older and purer, numbered 39, lacks both a table of chapters and a preface; accordingly, it also lacks the title prefixed to the table.]

This codex contains **ECCLESIASTICAL CANONS** and **CONSTITUTIONS OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE**. (C)

## Preface

[Col. 0353]

### 1

Although Petrus Crabbus, Jacobus Pamelius, Alanus Copus, and others made use of manuscript copies of this outstanding collection, no one before Peter Pithoeus published it as distinct from the Dionysian Collection. Indeed, Jacobus Pamelius, and Alanus Copus following him, assigned it to Dionysius Exiguus because a letter of the latter to the presbyter Julian is copied at the end of the Arras codex containing this collection.

Peter Pithoeus, however, in the *Historical Synopsis of Distinguished Men Who Collected Ecclesiastical Canons and Decrees Besides Gratian*, prefixed to the editions of the *Corpus of Canon Law* published at Paris in 1687 and Leipzig in 1705, having obtained three manuscript books of this collection, carefully distinguished it from the Dionysian Collection and attributed it to an unknown author:

> The author is unknown. Two copies of this collection are in the library of the Church of Beauvais. A third was possessed by François Pithou in Paris under this title: “This codex contains ecclesiastical canons and constitutions of the Apostolic See.” It begins with the canons of the Council of Nicaea, to which certain chapters of the Sardican Synod are added, together with a preface and a statement of faith. These are followed by the canons of the synods of Carthage, Ancyra, Caesarea, Gangra, and several others, with letters of the Roman pontiffs inserted from the time of Innocent up to Saint Leo. The collection concludes with Leo’s Letter 98 to Dorus, bishop of Benevento. It does not use exactly the same translations of the Greek canons as the earlier collection—namely, the one he had just described as called the *Corpus of Canons*—but rather those of Dionysius Exiguus, though not always.

This brief indication of the contents of the cited codices, and especially the number of chapters—98, the last of which ends with the letter to Dorus, bishop of Benevento—clearly identifies our collection. Since the third of those codices belonged to François Pithou and was later transferred to the college at Troyes, where it came to be called the Trecopithoean, there can be no doubt that the same codex belongs to our collection and is therefore distinct from the Corbie Codex, which contains another celebrated collection described by us in the preceding *Treatise*, part II, chapter 5.

It was necessary to mention this here so that no one might be misled by Quesnellus’s note in the *Catalogue of Manuscripts*, volume I, published on page 40, where he declares this Trecopithoean codex similar to the Corbie Codex. In the notes to Leo’s letters, published at the end of volume XI, however, he discovered that it resembles the Thuaneus copy of our collection. His note 7 on Letter 15 to Turibius reads:

> Thus, of the Thuaneus codices, there is one that agrees throughout with the Trecopithoean, so that one might say it was copied from the other.
