And note 7 on chapter 7 of Letter 16 states:

> These words are absent from the codices except for one Thuaneus codex and the Trecopithoean, one of which was copied from the other.

He had received only the variant readings of Leo’s letters from the Trecopithoean manuscript. If he had collated the entire codex, he would have found it agreeing with the Thuaneus not only in the other materials but throughout the entire collection.

### 2

Quesnellus was the first to make this same collection publicly available in an edition of Saint Leo’s works, in volume II, with the following title prefixed to it:

> Appendix to the Works of Saint Leo the Great, or the Code of Ecclesiastical Canons and Constitutions of the Holy Apostolic See, the oldest and most extensive of all those published to the present, which was used in the Roman Church under the pontificates of Innocent I, Zosimus, and others, as well as Leo I; now published for the first time from the Thuaneus and Oxford manuscript codices.

More briefly, at the head of each page it was entitled:

> Code of Canons, or of the Constitutions of the Roman Church,

which is the title by which it has more frequently been cited.

The reason why he assigned this collection to the Roman Church and appended it to Leo’s works must be explained. While seeking manuscripts from every quarter in order to correct or enlarge an edition of those works, he happened to learn from his close friend Edward Bernard that a manuscript copy, no. 7, existed in the Oxford Library containing this collection in addition to the sermons and letters of Saint Leo.

From the conjunction of Saint Leo’s works and this collection in the same codex, Quesnellus, an easy conjecturer, suspected that the collection was Roman and had been used especially under Leo. He therefore decided to establish it as such through an extensive discussion and publish it in Leo’s *Appendix*.

### 3

That this collection cannot be regarded as a code of the canons of the Roman Church compiled, published, and accepted for use by public authority under Saint Leo—or under the earlier or later pontiffs of that Church—will become clear from the Observations that we shall append to Dissertation 12, in which he strives at length to confirm and support his opinion.

It will also become clear that its author was a private and learned man unknown to us, as the Peter Pithoeus cited above had already perceived. We shall indicate, through plausible conjectures, as it seems to us, that it was composed in Gaul and therefore is not an Italian but a Gallican collection.

### 4

In the cited title Quesnellus made two assertions about this code of canons and constitutions: namely, that it was the oldest and the most extensive of all those published up to that time.

The second claim cannot be defended. Isidore’s collection is much more extensive among the others; even with its adulterated materials omitted, it contains far more documents.

It may be called the oldest of the codices so far edited that contain both canons and constitutions of the Apostolic See, insofar as it contains no documents later than Gelasius. Other collections previously printed include materials from later pontiffs, as can be learned even from the Dionysian Collection.

P. Coustant rightly concluded in the preface to volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs* that this codex was compiled in the age of Gelasius. He writes in no. 74:

> Since the first and substantial part of the preface was formed entirely from the very words of a letter of Gelasius—his letter concerning apocryphal books—and since the codex contains nothing extending beyond the age of Gelasius, this is surely evidence that the person who under the pontificate of Gelasius, or not long afterward, first set his hand to the codex also placed the final hand upon it; and that, while compiling various decrees of councils and pontiffs, he intermingled with them the statutes of Gelasius that were known and familiar to him.

Quesnellus believes that the part of the codex containing the Constantinopolitan canons was added after the age of Gregory the Great. He makes this conjecture, however, on the assumption that the codex was an official Roman Church codex from which, most certainly up to Gregory I, the cited canons would have been absent.

Since that assumption is entirely false, nothing prevents those same canons from having been inserted into this private codex under Gelasius, just as they are found inserted in other private collections compiled before or shortly after Gelasius. See our Observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 12, chapter 2, no. 8.

### 5

The excellence of this collection is established above all by two considerations.

First, it contains several notable documents that have reached us through this collection alone. Thus Petrus Crabbus published from an ancient copy of this collection the letter of Mizo and the other bishops of the province of Byzacena, prefixed to the *Breviary of the Hipponian Canons* in chapter 2, as well as several other materials unavailable elsewhere. Cardinal Baronius likewise inserted in his *Annals* certain imperial laws against the Pelagians, taken from a manuscript at Arras belonging to this collection and supplied to him by Henri Gravius; one would search for them in vain in the other collections.

Second, although most of the other documents are found in other Dionysian, Hispanic, and Isidorian codices, the author of our collection did not draw them from those sources but derived them from other, more ancient copies. He therefore transmitted to us repeatedly different readings, often more authentic ones, and sometimes even more complete documents.

Perhaps some people will be troubled by the fact that the spurious letter of Saint Clement to James was accepted into this collection. But since it had been disseminated in the translation of Rufinus and had been cited on his authority at the Gallican Synod of Vaison in 442, canon 6—at least as most codices report it—it is not surprising that it was transferred into this Gallican collection.

### 6

More must now be said about the need for and usefulness of a new edition, and about the materials used in preparing it.

Quesnellus did not publish this collection in a completely integral form, nor did he consistently print its better and more authentic readings. This arose from his having followed the more recent Oxford codex, in which some materials were omitted and others emended according to the discretion of some learned person, contrary to the authority of the ancient copies.

[Col. 0357]

When preparing his edition of this collection, he did obtain the older and reputable Thuaneus codex. Yet he neither supplied from it everything missing in the Oxford copy—he added only one letter of Gelasius and the rule concerning *formatae*—nor did he adopt its readings except in a very few places. He either relegated the others to the margin or omitted them altogether.

Hence P. Coustant, rightly, in the preface mentioned above, no. 88, after writing:

> Before we conclude, there is one matter about which we wish to warn our readers: several copies of the codex from which Quesnellus transcribed the Oxford exemplar are preserved in the Gallican libraries, each of them much older than the Oxford copy,

added, after listing the five best manuscripts:

> We add that, with the help of these copies, many errors that entered the published codex—that of Quesnellus—can be purged.

He could have added that certain omissions could also be supplied.

Therefore, in order to reprint this collection complete and more accurately, some materials had to be inserted and many others corrected.

Despite diligent investigation in the Italian libraries, we were unable to find anywhere a manuscript copy of the collection that could assist us. We did, however, obtain two codices in the Caesarean Library at Vienna, one numbered 39 and the other 42.

The first, nearly a thousand years old, is a parchment folio codex. Although it lacks the table of titles or chapters published from the Thuaneus manuscript, it nevertheless contains the same 98 chapters in the same order. Since Peter Pithoeus also found the same number of chapters in three other manuscripts, the last of which ends with Saint Leo’s letter to Dorus, as is likewise found in other copies, there can be no doubt—see what will be said in note 11 on chapter 67—that these 98 chapters belong to this collection. Quesnellus therefore ought not to be heard when, on the testimony of a single, more recent Oxford manuscript, he thought that Leo’s letters should be rejected as foreign to this collection.

In the Oxford copy these letters were not inserted into the collection itself because they had already been copied among Leo’s letters, which preceded the collection; the scribe did not think that the same material should be repeated.

In any event, the agreement of all the other ancient copies must rightly be preferred to that of the single Oxford manuscript. The table preserved in most codices, which indicates the same number of 98 chapters, confirms this as well.

A table is ordinarily evidence of the original work, so that if anything is missing somewhere from the body of the text, it ought to be regarded as having been improperly cut away; if anything is found inserted beyond the contents of the table, it should be said to have been added later.

For this reason we observed, in note 9 on Quesnellus’s preface, volume I, page 33, and in note 1 on Letter 120 of the same pontiff, column 1218, that certain documents read after Leo’s letters in the Thuaneus codex were additions, since they stood contrary to the testimony of the table and the purer codices.

It is therefore easy to judge the other Vienna manuscript, no. 42. After the prefixed table of the 98 chapters and the preface to the Council of Nicaea, it inserts a letter of Dionysius Exiguus to Stephen; then, in the body of the codex itself, it receives several added chapters.

Before the letters of Innocent appears a letter of that same pontiff to the people of Toulouse—read “Toledo”—beginning, “Often and exceedingly.” Then, before Siricius’s letter to Himerius, another letter of the same pontiff to various bishops is copied, beginning, “When we were considering.”

Next, among Leo’s letters, other letters of his are inserted; in our edition these are Letters 9, 20, 22, 23, 25, 60, 61, 69, 70, 71, 79, 80, 82, 83, 85, 90, 115, 130, 134, 166, and 168.

Finally, three other letters are added at the end: one from Pope Hilary to Ascanias, another from Simplicius to Zeno of Split, and a third from Innocent to Aurelius.

This codex is of a later age, and, with the exception of the letter of Dionysius Exiguus, the additions were transferred by the scribe from the Isidorian or Hispanic Collection.

Since the first Caesarean codex, Vindobonensis 39, is older and purer, we procured, at considerable expense, a most exact collation of it in particular; nevertheless, we did not neglect the other in places where we believed it especially important.

Nor did we omit other codices of the same collection wherever we discovered in them documents published or corrected by others. Accordingly, we carefully reviewed what Crabbus, Baronius, Sirmondus, Baluzius, Coustant, and other painstaking investigators of ancient copies had produced from some such codex.

With these aids we shall present this most ancient collection complete, corrected of many errors, and restored to its original form.

7. In order that something more useful might be added, we likewise judged that other, older, and generally unknown manuscripts and collections should be collated. In these, if not all, certainly nearly all the documents of our codex could profitably be found scattered here and there. Of this kind are three outstanding collections preserved in Roman libraries: the first is found in manuscript Vat. Reginae 1997, the second in Vat. 1342 and Barberino 2888, and the third in several other codices of the Additions to Dionysius. The copies of Isidore also contributed something, since he incorporated no small number of items from our collection.

Three other particular manuscript collections were added. Two of them are contained in two codices of the Veronese chapter, nos. 55 and 58, which were used for the canons of the Greek synods; the third was copied in another codex of the same chapter, Veron. 46, in which we found all the documents of our collection relating to the Acacian affair. Nor were the codices of the Corbie collection and of the Colbertine Lombard collection lacking; of the latter we found another copy in the library of the cathedral chapter of Lucca. We were able to learn their readings from P. Coustant’s first volume of *The Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, and the variant readings of the Lucca copy from P. Domenico Mansi in the *Supplement to the Councils*, or through correspondence.

Although editors ought to insert into the text the readings proper to a given collection, even if some of them may in places be less correct, the examination of the other collections, especially the most ancient ones, was nevertheless exceedingly useful. For wherever their readings agree with those of our collection, the readings of our collection acquire much authority from that agreement. Wherever they were found to differ, it was particularly useful to insert them in the annotations and submit them to the judgment of scholars. Until now, indeed, the readings of only two collections—the Dionysian and the Isidorian—have generally been known. Through our diligence, however, the readings of so many older collections of different origins will be brought to light. Since these readings generally agree both with one another and with the readings of our codex, everyone will recognize that the latter are more genuine and should be preferred to those commonly published.

The Roman editors of *The Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, Sirmond, Coustant, and others, using the same diligence in several manuscript collections, likewise published those letters and certain documents. We, however, revisiting all the collections mentioned above, compared all the documents of our collection with them and accurately recorded their readings. Since most of the records of those collections, though in a different order, are found transcribed in our codex, you will rightly understand that, through this edition of our collection, other older and unpublished collections have also been edited, so to speak, for the most part.

XCV. To Bishop Anatolius, concerning the presbyter Atticus: that the presbyter be compelled to renounce his acceptance of the Eutychian error.

XCVI. Rescript to Bishop Anatolius concerning the reception of the archdeacon Andrew and Euphratas, and concerning the rejection of the honor sought for the see of Constantinople.

22 XCVII. To the Council of Chalcedon, concerning the restoration to their own sees of bishops who had formerly been expelled on account of the Catholic faith, and concerning the firmness of the earlier Council of Ephesus.

[Col. 0367A] XCVIII. Letter of rebuke to Dorus, bishop of Beneventum.

[Note: Quesnel appended the following note to this table:

“You have above, learned reader, an index such as is exhibited, down to chapter LVI, by the Thuanus and Oxford codices, which agree completely thus far. From this chapter onward there is a threefold difference between them. First, the Oxford codex adds only five chapters to those above, completing the number sixty; the Thuanus, as you see, contains far more. Second, those five chapters are arranged in a different order in the Thuanus. The order of the Thuanus is visible in the index; that of the Oxford codex is as follows:

Chapter LVI: Cyril to Nestorius.

LVII: The Antiochene canons.

LVIII: The rules according to Laodicea.

LIX: The Constantinopolitan canons.

LX: The canons of the Council of Thelensis in Africa, according to the decretal letter of Pope Siricius.

Finally, the Thuanus contains some items that are not in the Oxford codex, namely the constitution of Pope Gelasius and the rule of the *formatae*, chapters LVIII and LXIII. We shall insert both into the codex, while omitting the letters of Leo, which have already been published above, and Clement’s letter to James, which does not seem to belong to the codex. For in the Thuanus codex itself, after the rule of the *formatae*, we read this clause: ‘In the name of the Lord, the canons are concluded.’ Nevertheless, we thought the complete Thuanus index should be reproduced, so that nothing which may have been inserted into the codex later, or appended to it from antiquity, might be withheld from the reader devoted to the study of ecclesiastical antiquity.”

Thus far Quesnel. Why Clement’s letter to James should not be omitted from this collection may be seen in note 1 on chapter 64. To what the formula incorrectly explained by Quesnel refers—the formula that follows the rule of the *formatae* in chapter 63, “In the name of the Lord, the canons are concluded”—we shall show in the annotations on that formula or clause, note 8 on chapter 63.]

[Note: [Col. 0367C] Isidore Mercator took this preface from our collection. In manuscript Vat. 630, which contains Isidore’s pure collection, the following title is placed before it: “Here begins the letter, or preface, of the Council of Nicaea.” A considerable part of it is also quoted by Aeneas of Paris in chapter 187 of his work *Against the Greeks*, vol. I of Acher’s *Spicilegium*, where he incorrectly attributes it to that pontiff under the name of Silvester. The author of our collection composed it and prefixed it to the Council of Nicaea. The beginning, which establishes the date of the Nicene synod, was assembled from certain annotations prefixed to the synod itself in the manuscripts. The rest the compiler excerpted partly from Gelasius’s decree concerning books to be received or rejected, and partly from the tenth book of Rufinus’s *History*, in almost the same words, as will be clear from the notes.]

## Preface

[Col. 0367]

[Col. 0367B] While the most blessed Sylvester was bishop of the apostolic see in the city of Rome, Constantine Augustus and Licinius Caesar were rulers, and the most illustrious men Paulinus and Julian were consuls, in the 1036th year from Alexander, in the month of June, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July: because of the heresies that had arisen, the Catholic faith was set forth at Nicaea in Bithynia, which the holy and most reverend Roman Church embraces and venerates. For 318 Fathers, through Victor and Vincentius, the most religious presbyters of the Roman see, inspired by God, set it forth in order to destroy the poisons of Arius. Certain rules were also appended, which the aforesaid Church accepted and confirmed.

[Note: The Thuanus codex reads “in the year 1034.” Quesnel adds the following note in a postscript: “Isidore has ‘from Alexander 336.’ But our codex Vat. 630, a pure Isidorian manuscript, has the reading given in the text, and Hardouin likewise published it from Isidore, from the Mertinian manuscript, and from the Colbertine copy, which is the same as the Thuanus of this collection. The same reading is also found in manuscript Caesareus Vindobonensis 42. There is an error in this chronological note: it ought to read 636, as is evident from the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, both in the Greek and Latin text, vol. IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils, pp. 1208 and 1210, from the ancient version of the canons of the Council of Nicaea, from Socrates, and from Gelasius of Cyzicus in book II, chapter 26, of his history of that council. In manuscript 58 of the Veronese chapter, the same consulship is also prefixed to the Nicene Creed, together with the year 636 from Alexander. That the consulship of Paulinus and Julian fell in the year 636 from Alexander, corresponding to the year 325 of the common era, in which the Nicene synod was held, may be seen in Cardinal Noris, *On the Epochs of the Syro-Macedonians*, dissertation 2, chapter 1, vol. II, p. 74. The error of our collection and of the ancient translator, however, derives from some faulty Greek exemplar; for the same reading is found in another very ancient Latin translation of the Nicene canons, which we shall present in this volume from Veronese manuscript 55. Since we are going to publish the collection as it exists in the manuscripts, we ought not to alter the text or correct the errors from other sources, since the errors themselves may sometimes be useful.”]

All Catholics should know, certainly, that [Col. 0368B] the holy Roman Church was not set above the other churches by synodal decrees, but obtained primacy through the evangelical word of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, when he said to the blessed apostle Peter:

“You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16:18–19).

[Note: From this word onward, the opening of Pope Gelasius’s decree concerning apocryphal Scriptures is read, with certain interpolations added.]

[Note: Gelasius adds “above the other churches.” Quesnel.]

The fellowship of the most blessed apostle Paul, the chosen vessel, was also joined to that same city of Rome. [Note: Gelasius reads: “who, contrary to what the heretics babble, was crowned by a glorious death with Peter in the city of Rome under the emperor Nero, suffering at the same time and on the same day”; and then “likewise.” Quesnel. Vindobonensis 42 reads “who, on one day and by one glorious death.” Shortly afterward, the Vatican Isidorian manuscript, together with Merlin, reads “and both alike.”]

He was crowned, suffering together with Peter under the ruler Nero, by a glorious death on one day and at one time. Therefore both of them together consecrated the holy Roman Church to the Lord Christ and, by their presence and venerable triumph, placed it above all other cities throughout the world.

[Note: The following passage down to the asterisk is absent from Gelasius.]

And although the prayer of all the saints is continually offered to the Lord on behalf of all, nevertheless the most blessed apostle Paul promises the Romans in his own handwriting, saying: “For God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit in the gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I always make remembrance of you in my prayers” (Romans 1:9).

[Note: This follows Gelasius.]

* Therefore the first see, by heavenly favor, is the Roman Church, which the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul dedicated by their martyrdom.

[Note: In Gelasius it reads: “Thus the first see is the Roman Church of the apostle Peter, having neither stain nor wrinkle nor anything of that kind. The second see, however, …” Since the author of the collection inserted a sentence into Gelasius’s text, he interpreted these words differently.]

The second see is at Alexandria, consecrated in the name of blessed Peter by Mark, his disciple and evangelist,

[Note: Gelasius reads: “He himself, sent by the apostle Peter into Egypt, preached the word of truth and completed his glorious martyrdom. The third, however, …” Quesnel. The Vatican Isidorian manuscript and Merlin read “because he too, in Egypt,” etc.]

because he himself, sent by Peter, first preached the word of truth in Egypt and underwent a glorious martyrdom; Abilius, a venerable man, succeeded him.

The third see is held at Antioch as venerable in the name of that same blessed apostle Peter,

[Note: Thus the Thuanus manuscript with Isidore and Gelasius. Isidore alone omits “in the name.” The Vindobonensis manuscript reads: “The third see is at Antioch, likewise venerable in the name of blessed Peter.” Quesnel retained the reading of the inferior Oxford codex: “The see is at Antioch, likewise venerable through the dwelling of blessed Peter, because …” Shortly afterward the Oxford codex reads “instituted” instead of “appointed.” The words “and appointed Ignatius bishop,” like the preceding words “to whom the venerable Abilius succeeded,” were added by the author of the collection and are not found in Gelasius.]

because he lived there before coming to Rome and appointed Ignatius bishop; and there the name “Christians” first arose for the new people.

[Note: Thus far follows Gelasius.]

The bishop of Jerusalem, too, is regarded by all as venerable because of the dignity of so great a place, especially because there the most blessed James, called the Just and also named, according to the flesh, the brother of the Lord, was ordained bishop by the apostles Peter, James, and John. Therefore, according to the definition of the ancient Fathers, Jerusalem is by no means called the first see,

[Note: Isidore adds “to be.”]

lest perhaps unbelievers or simpletons should think that the see of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is in heaven, is on earth. For his throne is heaven, while the earth is the footstool of his feet. Since all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made; since from him, through him, and in him are all things, to him be glory for ever and ever (Romans 11:36).

At Ephesus, however, the most blessed apostle and evangelist John lived for a long time after the resurrection [Col. 0370A] and ascension into heaven of our Lord Jesus Christ. There, too, by divine inspiration, he composed the Gospel called according to John and came to rest. For this reason the bishop of Ephesus, in memory of so great an apostle and evangelist, holds a more honored see in synods than the other metropolitan bishops.

[Note: The Vatican Isidorian manuscript reads: “After the Lord’s resurrection and ascension into heaven, he composed the Gospel by divine inspiration and came to rest.” Quesnel notes that the Oxford codex reads “he composed the Gospel and the Apocalypse,” but this is incorrect, since he wrote the latter on the island of Patmos.]

[Note: [Col. 0370C] So read the Codex of Thou, Colbert, Vindobonensis, and Vaticanus Isidorianus [Col. 0370D] with Merlinus. Quesnellus, from the Oxford manuscript: “But since the canons of the Council of Nicaea must be placed first of all, for what reason he did this.” The latter wording seems defective. In the same Oxford manuscript, after “some things,” it has “so many” instead of “so great.”]

But since it is necessary to discuss the Council of Nicaea 25, what was the reason for doing this, so that, after that most glorious preaching of the apostles, which had wondrously spread throughout the whole earth, so many bishops should be assembled under the emperor Constantine Augustus? Rufinus’s tenth book, which is joined to the nine books of the Ecclesiastical History published by the most learned man Eusebius of Caesarea, must necessarily be brought forward here, so that a few of the things he wrote at the beginning concerning the perversity of Arius may be recalled; for there is no doubt that the three hundred and eighteen most holy Fathers were assembled at Nicaea in Bithynia from the whole Eastern [Note: [Col. 0370D] Vaticanus Isidorianus and Merlinus delete “and Western.”] and Western world for this reason: so that, with Christ’s assistance, the impious doctrine of Arius might be utterly condemned, and so that, by salutary providence, they might determine what ought to be observed in the holy Catholic Church.

[Note: [Col. 0370D] The following passage is absent from the Oxford manuscript and is found in Thou and in Isidore, from Rufinus, book I, chapter 1.]

Likewise, a passage from the tenth book of Rufinus.

Accordingly, when Alexander had assumed the priesthood at Alexandria after Achillas, who had succeeded the martyr Peter [Note: [Col. 0370D] Elsewhere, “Achilles.” Immediately afterward Isidore, Vaticanus, and Merlinus read: “who succeeded Peter the martyr.”], because peace and relief from persecutions had come to us and the glory of the Churches rejoiced in the merits of the confessors, the prosperity of our affairs was disturbed by domestic conflict. For a certain presbyter at Alexandria, named Arius, a man religious more in appearance and outward form [Col. 0370C] than in virtue, but disgracefully desirous of glory, praise, and novelty, began to advance certain perverse ideas about the faith of Christ and matters that had previously never come under investigation [Note: [Col. 0370D] Rufinus, from whom this passage was taken, reads: “which had never before come under discussion.” Elsewhere: “he began to sever.”]. He attempted to cut off and separate the Son from the eternal and ineffable substance or nature of God the Father. This affair disturbed very many people in the Church.

But when Bishop Alexander, naturally gentle and peaceable, wished by continual admonitions to recall Arius from his wicked undertaking and impious assertions, and yet the matter did not proceed according to his wishes [Note: [Col. 0371B] The Vulgate reads “and whom.” The correction was suggested not so much by the context as by Rufinus’s edition and the Vindobonensis manuscript. Shortly afterward, “had dispersed” is read instead of Rufinus’s “had dispersed them.”], and when Arius had infected many people with the contagion of his pestilential assertion—not only at Alexandria but also throughout other cities and provinces—he, believing that it would be dangerous to remain silent about such things, reported the matter to many of his fellow priests. The question became more widely known. The report reached the ears of the religious ruler Constantine, who took care of our affairs 26 with every zeal and diligence.

Then, at the urging of the priests, he summoned an episcopal council at the city of Nicaea. There he ordered Arius to appear while three hundred and eighteen bishops were seated, and commanded them to judge his propositions and questions [Note: [Col. 0371B] Elsewhere, “to be judged.” After this word, the Vaticanus Isidorianus manuscript 630 and several other Isidorian manuscripts, as well as Merlinus, add a longer passage consisting of the same words as Rufinus. The text continues as follows: “But in that council I do not think the emperor’s remarkable action should be passed over in silence,” as in Rufinus, chapters 2–4, up to the passage after the middle of chapter 5: “was sought with the greatest deliberation.” Then follows “But after a long interval,” and the rest, by which our compiler concluded his preface.]

[Col. 0372A] [Note: [Col. 0372B] This is taken from Rufinus, chapter 5, after the middle.]

But after a long and extensive deliberation, it pleased everyone, and as though by the one mouth and heart of all it was decreed, that ὁμοούσιον should be written—that is, that the Son should be confessed to be of the same substance as the Father—and this was proclaimed as the firmest judgment of all.

At that time, only seventeen are said to have been those who preferred the faith of Arius, affirming that the Son of God had been created externally from things that had no subsistence and had not been begotten from the very divinity of the Father [Note: [Col. 0372B] Vaticanus Isidorianus, together with Merlinus and Rufinus, reads “subsisting things.” Shortly afterward, we have corrected “confirming” on the basis of Rufinus, Merlinus, and the Vindobonensis and Vaticanus Isidorianus manuscripts, especially since the context and meaning require it; the printed editions incorrectly have “those who confirm.”]

The judgment of the priestly council was conveyed to Constantine. He venerated it as something issued by God; and he declared that, if anyone attempted to oppose it, as though coming against divine decrees, he would send that person into exile.

### TITLE ONE

[Note: [Col. 0371D] Quesnellus gives: “The exposition of the Nicaean faith, the time at which the assembly was held, and the names of the bishops.” The words “the time at which the assembly was held” seem inappropriate here, since the time of the synod is specified in the preceding preface. We have therefore preferred the reading of our Vindobonensis manuscript. In manuscript 58 of the Verona chapter, which contains the version commonly called Isidorian, this title is given with an exact chronological notice, as follows: “The exposition of the faith of the council held at Nicaea, the metropolis of Bithynia, in the consulship of Paulinus and Julianus, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, which among the Greeks is the nineteenth day of their month ΔΕΣΙΕΙ, Desius, in the six hundred and thirty-sixth year of Alexander.” This agrees precisely with the chronological markers recorded at the Council of Chalcedon, session 2, concerning which Socrates also bears witness in book I, chapter 13, in these words: “The time when the synod was assembled, as I found in the chronological notices prefixed to the synod itself, was during the consulship of Paulinus and Julianus, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June” (an error has entered regarding the day and month), “in the six hundred and thirty-sixth year from the reign of Alexander of Macedon.” Gelasius of Cyzicus, chapter 26, likewise indicates that this chronological notice was prefixed to the creed; and we have found the same notice in another unpublished version, which we shall likewise print before the creed from another very ancient Verona manuscript, 55.]

The exposition of the Nicaean faith, or of synodical discipline, and the names of the three hundred and eighteen bishops, begins.

[Col. 0371C] [Note: [Col. 0372D] The ancient translators rendered not only the Nicaean canons but also the creed in various versions, as we have discovered from manuscripts of different collections, including the Dionysian-Hadrianic, Vatican Reginensis, Isidorian, and others. Since these versions differ in only minor words, most editors omitted this creed. Here we shall record the variants of one Vindobonensis manuscript of our collection.]

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who was born from the Father as the only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God; 28 begotten, not made, ὁμοούσιον—that is, of the same substance as the Father; through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth; who for us human beings and for our salvation descended, was incarnate, and became human; suffered, [Col. 0372C] rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, and will come from there to judge the living and the dead. And in the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0372D] The Codex of Thou adds “we believe.”]

But those who say, “There was a time when he was not,” and “before he was born he did not exist,” and that he was made from things that had no subsistence [Note: [Col. 0372D] Thus in the manuscripts of Thou and Vindobonensis. Quesnellus retained “existing things” in the text, following the Oxford manuscript. Shortly afterward, Vindobonensis omits “who” and reads “changeable” a little later.]; or who say that the Son of God is from another substance or essence and is τρέπτον—that is, changeable or alterable—the Catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes them.

[Note: [Col. 0373A] Father Jean Hardouin suspected that this annotation, appended to the Nicaean creed and placed before the subscriptions of the Nicaean Fathers, should be attributed to Dionysius Exiguus. Yet, apart from the fact that it does not appear in the two purely Dionysian manuscripts Vaticanus 5845 and Vaticanus Palatinus 577, nor in the Dionysian-Hadrianic manuscripts, there can be no doubt that it originated not with Dionysius but from a Greek source. For it is found not only in the manuscripts of this collection, which is not dependent on Dionysius, and in Vaticanus 1342 and Barberinianus 2888, which present the Nicaean canons from the ancient translation; we have also found it almost complete in Gelasius of Cyzicus, book II, chapter 26, who certainly did not extract it from Latin copies. Moreover, in the very ancient manuscript 55 of the Verona chapter there is a hitherto unknown translation of the Nicaean canons from Greek, which we shall print in this volume; and in it the same annotation, found in the Greek source, is presented immediately after the creed. Furthermore, in another manuscript of the same chapter, 58, which contains the purer interpretation commonly called Isidorian, this same annotation is copied, but it lists more heretical names than our collection does. These names, which are recorded by the Greek writer Gelasius in the same form and order, were drawn from a Greek source.]

This is the faith which the Fathers set forth, first against Arius, who blasphemed and said [Note: [Col. 0373C] The Vindobonensis manuscript reads “that the Son of God was a creature,” and “against every heresy.” Gelasius of Cyzicus inserts the authors of other heresies; likewise, in several of our manuscripts, from the ancient version called Isidorian, it reads: “And against every heresy of Sabellius, Photinus, Paul of Samosata, Mani, Valentinus, Marcion, and against every heresy whatsoever, if any should rise up against the Catholic and apostolic Church.” The same appears in Vaticanus 1342, which received the Nicaean canons from the Prisca version, as will be seen in note 1 on the Nicaean canons of that version.] that the Son of God had been created; and afterward against every heresy 29 that exalted and raised itself against the Catholic [Note: [Col. 0373C] Quesnellus’s edition inserts “faith”; we have deleted it on the authority of the Vindobonensis manuscript and another Verona manuscript, 55, which presents a new version of the Nicaean canons to be published in this volume. This heresy, together with its authors, was condemned at the aforesaid city of Nicaea by the three hundred and eighteen bishops assembled together; their names, together with their provinces [Note: [Col. 0373C] The Vindobonensis and Verona manuscripts delete “their.”] and cities, are appended below.

But the devoted servants of God took greater care to record the names of the Eastern bishops, because the Westerners had not had the same controversy concerning heresies [Note: [Col. 0373C] Quesnellus, following the Oxford manuscript, added: “This is why the number of names, three hundred and eighteen, does not correspond at all,” and noted that this material was absent from the Thou manuscript. ## 30 NAMES OF THE BISHOPS

[Col. 0374A] [Note: [Col. 0373D] We have added this title from the same Vindobonensis manuscript. In Verona manuscript 58 of the version commonly called Isidorian, it reads: “The names of the bishops and provinces begin.” Only the names of Hosius and the legates of the Apostolic See retain the form of subscriptions. The other bishops are distributed by provinces. We defended the antiquity and authority of this catalogue in the Treatise on Ancient Collections, part I, chapter 3, section 1. Here Hosius, bishop of Corduba, is first; then the Roman presbyters are subscribed before all the bishops, just as it is clear from Athanasius’s Second Apology that the same Hosius and two other Roman presbyters first subscribed the synodical letter of Sardica to all the bishops. He begins the catalogue of those who subscribed as follows: “Hosius from Spain; Julius of Rome, through the presbyters Archidamus and Philoxenus.” If these two Roman presbyters, together with Leo the deacon, likewise a Roman, subscribed Athanasius’s letter to the Mareotic Churches— which will be reprinted in this volume from Verona manuscript 55—after several bishops, this should trouble no one, since the subscriptions of the bishops were added spontaneously to this private letter of Athanasius, which was not a public synodical document, without any order being observed. Gelasius of Cyzicus reports in book II of the History of the Council of Nicaea, chapters 5 and 12, that Hosius, who precedes the Roman legates, together with the two aforementioned presbyters of the Roman Church, exercised the place and legation of Pope Sylvester. Yet there is no indication of a legation in his subscription. Perhaps, because Hosius had been employed by the emperor Constantine in very important matters and had already performed distinguished service in the case of Arius before the Council of Nicaea, the Roman legates had been instructed to show the eminent Western bishop the greatest deference; hence the opinion arose that he held some sort of legation. Among the manuscripts with which we compared the catalogue of bishops, we found that all derived from two Greek sources, both because of the double order of certain bishops and because of variant readings. We also observed that the manuscripts of Quesnellus’s collection agree in the catalogue of bishops with Vaticanus Reginensis 1997, while the manuscripts of the Prisca version agree with the catalogue of its older interpretation, which was received by Isidore and published from Isidore’s manuscripts and is commonly called Isidorian. The catalogue found in the manuscripts of the Hadrianic collection approaches this latter source, although it preserves a Latin version different from both the Prisca and Isidorian versions. Quesnellus printed the catalogue from the Oxford manuscript and noted variants in some places from the excellent Thou manuscript, as well as from the commonly circulated Isidore and Justellus. We used the Vindobonensis manuscript, which contains Quesnellus’s collection, and the recently mentioned Vaticanus Reginensis. Since the author of our collection derived, among other things, the catalogue of the Nicaean Fathers from the particular version preserved in Vaticanus Reginensis, we have sometimes followed its readings in the catalogue below as though they had come from the manuscript of our collection. For the Prisca version we collated Vaticanus 1342; for the Isidorian version, the very ancient Verona manuscript 58, which presents only the interpretation of the Greek canons. Among the Hadrianic manuscripts we used Vallicellianus A 5.]

Since the Prisca and Isidorian versions likewise list these two bishops as Sebasteni, an ancient error entered one of the places in the Greek manuscript itself. In the subscriptions of the false synod of Sardica in Saint Hilary, two bishops of Troas, Pison and Noconius, are similarly listed, although only one Troas is recognized. We believe that the city of Hypaepa in proconsular Asia is intended. The Vallicellian manuscript has *Mitre of Ypapton*.] Mitres of Popana. [Note: [Col. 0381B] So the manuscripts of this collection. Quesnellus divided the word *Iliaelesponti* into two, so that, after the name *Ilio Macrino* had been left, he prefixed a new provincial heading, *HELLESPONTI*, to the following bishops. Yet the other collections list Paul, who follows immediately, under the single heading of Asia. That the heading of the Hellespont was omitted by the compiler of this catalogue is clear from the fact that the bishop of Cyzicus, who was metropolitan of the Hellespont, is placed first under the heading of Asia. The Regina manuscript has *Marinus of Ilyolipontus*; Veronensis Isidore, *Ilivellespontanus*; Vallicellianus, *Ilivellespontenus*; Justellus, with Vatican 1342, *Liolypontianus*. Gelasius of Cyzicus, book II, chapter 27, calls Marinus “of the Troad.”] Macrinus of Hioelespontus. Paul [Note: [Col. 0381C] The Regina manuscript has *of Phanaea*; Vatican 1342, with Justellus, *of Andus*; Veronensis Isidore, more correctly, *of Aenea*, from Aenea in proconsular Asia; Vallicellianus agrees with *Aeneas*. After this Paul, Quesnellus inserts *Anaseus of Lydia*. The Vindobonensis likewise has this. But *of Lydia* is the heading of the province, as is shown not only by the other collections and by the Prisca, Isidore, and Vallicellian versions, but also by the Regina manuscript [Col. 0381D] of this version; all of these omit the word *Anaseus*. Perhaps this word was mistakenly introduced from a variant reading of *Aneadensis*.] of Panea.

Lydia.

Azana, however, is regarded as being in Phrygia.] Pisticus of Azanus. [Note: [Col. 0382C] Quesnellus, *Artemidorus*. The Vindobonensis, *Antiriodorus*. We preferred the Regina manuscript, with which the others agree. *Doriensis* is the same as *Doryleitanus*, or, as in Vallicellianus, *Dorilen*. Quesnellus adds *Leo of Dores*, as if he were another bishop. Our Vindobonensis, which has *Docti Leo*, sufficiently indicates that this corrupt word is a variant of the preceding *Doriensis*. The manuscript copies of the Prisca, Isidore, and Vallicellian versions insert after Athenodorus of Doryleum *Paul of Apamea* or *Apamene*. He is omitted from the manuscripts of our collection, as also from the Regina manuscript. Apamea does not belong to Phrygia but to Pisidia, where another bishop of Apamea is indeed noted below. Is *Apamenus* an error, and should *Apienus* be read instead, from the city of Apia, which is listed in Phrygia?] Athenodorus of Doryeum. Eugenius of Eucarpia. Flaccus of Hierapolis.

Pisidia [Note: [Col. 0382C] The Vindobonensis manuscript adds Caria.].

Eulalius of Iconium. Thelemachus [Note: [Col. 0382D] More correctly, in the Veronensis Isidore manuscript, *of Adrianopolis*, and in Vallicellianus, *Hadrianopolitan*. Immediately afterward the Vindobonensis and Regina manuscripts have *Esicius*.] of Adrianopolis. Esichius of Neapolis. Eutychius of Seleucia.
