46 [Note: [Col. 0387B] Quesnellus omitted this preface placed before the canons. It is found not only in our Caesarean Vindobonensis manuscript but also in the Hubertine and other manuscripts of this collection cited by Father Coustant in the preface to volume I of *Epistolae Romanorum Pontificum*, no. 88, p. LXXIX. Since it is also found in the Prisca version, as well as in the pure Isidorian version contained in the very ancient Veronensis manuscript 58; and since in the manuscripts of the Hadrian collection it is expressed in various other words, it may be suspected of deriving from a Greek source. What seems especially noteworthy here is that the Nicene synod is said to have sent the canons to St. Sylvester in the same way that the Council of Arles had previously sent its decrees to that same Sylvester, and the Council of Sardica later reported its acts to Pope Julius. The Roman synod of 485, in its letter to the Catholic presbyters and archimandrites residing at Constantinople and in Bithynia, records that this confirmation by the Roman see was sought from the Nicene Fathers; see volume V of the *Councils*, col. 248, published from the excellent Avellana collection: “The three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers assembled at Nicaea brought the confirmation of their acts and the authority of the holy Roman [Col. 0387D] Church.” Following this example, the Fathers of Chalcedon reserved the full force and confirmation of their acts for Pope Leo, as Anatolius of Constantinople wrote in letter 132 among the Leonine letters, chapter 4. See volume I, col. 1263.

It is surprising that in all the collections containing this preface an erroneous consulship is recorded, under the consuls Constantine Augustus and Licinius, although in the year 325 Paulinus and Julian held the consulship, as is clear from the very preface placed by the compiler before this first chapter; see note 1 there. This error was certainly present in the Greek exemplar, since this preface was translated into Latin from Greek. Perhaps its Greek author had before his eyes a chronological note in which, after mention of Constantine Augustus and Licinius Caesar, the actual consuls were listed; and, through some confusion or omission in passing over the consuls’ names, incorrectly attached the words “under the consuls Constantine and Licinius.” I will only point out that two chronological datings of the Nicene synod are found. One precedes the creed, as it appears in two manuscripts of the Veronensis chapter, from which we gave it in note 2 on chapter 1; this one gives the genuine consulship of Paulinus and Julian. The other is inserted in this preface, beginning *Cum convenisset*; expressed in other words in the Hadrian manuscripts before the creed, it was published in volume II of the Venetian edition of the *Councils*, cols. 30–31, and in all manuscripts it preserves the erroneous consulship [Col. 0388B].] When the holy and great council had assembled at Nicaea in Bithynia, the decrees written below were enacted; and it was agreed that all these matters should be sent to Sylvester, bishop of the city of Rome. The synod took place under the consuls Constantine Augustus and Licinius, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July.

47 [Note: [Col. 0388B] The author of this collection—or whoever it was who presents the Nicene canons joined to the Sardican canons in the form in which they appear in this collection—used two Latin sources: namely, the most ancient Italian version found in the Italian collection, Vatican-Regina manuscript 1997, and the equally ancient version that, first published with Isidore, is commonly called Isidorian. In interpreting the Nicene canons he generally followed the Isidorian version, though in several places the compiler altered it more freely, as will be evident from the annotations.

From the Italian version just mentioned he took the preceding catalogue of the Fathers, as well as the joining of the Nicene and Sardican canons, their division and numbering, and almost all their headings; moreover, he took from it the whole of canon 10, the only canon in which he entirely abandoned the Isidorian interpretation. He adopted the division and numbering of the canons of the Vatican-Regina manuscript—or rather of another older Italian manuscript similar to it—so closely that he omits the final Nicene canon concerning not kneeling, which is likewise omitted in the Vatican-Regina manuscript but is found in the Isidorian version.

In the order of the canons he followed neither the Isidorian version nor the Vatican-Regina manuscript exactly. The canon concerning deacons, which is placed before the canon concerning catechumens in the Veronensis Isidorian manuscript and in the Vatican-Regina manuscript, but follows the canon concerning catechumens in the common Isidore, is placed in this collection after the canon concerning usurers, as it is found in the Greek order adopted by the other versions.

It should be noted that the Nicene canons joined to the Sardican canons and accompanied by the same version of this collection are also found in the Fossatensis manuscript, which does not belong to this collection, as Father Coustant noted in the preface to volume I of *Epistolae Romanorum Pontificum*, no. 80. That manuscript, however, presents the common division of the twenty Nicene canons and does not omit the canon concerning not kneeling. The Pithoean and Hardy manuscripts likewise contain twenty canons with the same reading as the present collection, including the canon concerning not kneeling. Although Labbe published from the Hardy manuscript the headings and division of twenty canons—whereby the canon concerning deacons is recognized as following the canon concerning catechumens—he nevertheless noted in the margin that in the manuscript itself they are subdivided and prefixed with the headings found in our collection. See volume II of the *Councils*, pp. 48, 50–52. Father Coustant indicates that something similar is observed in the Fossatensis manuscript, p. 1033, note h: the canon that is tenth in our collection is sixth there, but subdivided, with the heading as in the Quesnellian collection.

Since the Fossatensis manuscript proves to resemble the Hardy manuscript in numbering the canons, lest it seem that contradictory statements have been written, we conjecture that those manuscripts preserve a total of twenty canons while at the same time subdividing the canons themselves into two paragraphs, so that the number of canons is not actually multiplied. Whoever examines those manuscripts will determine whether the matter is as we conjecture. In the meantime, in our collection this subdivision produced twenty-seven Nicene canons, with the canon concerning not kneeling omitted, as it is in the Vatican-Regina manuscript.

In comparing these canons we used the Vindobonensis manuscript 39, belonging specifically to this collection, and occasionally also the Thuan manuscript, whose variants Quesnellus recorded in places. We shall also cite the Pithoean and Claudian Hardy manuscripts: from the former the Nicene canons divided into twenty canons were published, and from the latter only the headings of the canons were published in the common editions of the *Councils*, volume II, Venetian edition, cols. 48 and 244. The Vatican-Regina manuscript 1997 will also be cited in places, as will the Fossatensis manuscript and others wherever we find them cited by Coustant or others.

Since, as we said, the reading of these canons derives for the most part from the Isidorian version, besides the common copy of Isidore we also collated the very ancient manuscript 58 of the Veronensis chapter, which contains a purer reading of that Isidorian version. In the annotations we rejected Quesnellus’s headings, which we believe were taken from the Oxford manuscript, because all the manuscripts cited that contain this Quesnellian version supply different headings, which we therefore judged preferable.] TITLE II. Concerning those who have been excised. (Canon 1 of Dionysius Exiguus, Isidore, and others.)

If anyone [Note: [Col. 0388D] The Thuan and Pithoean manuscripts have *per aegritudinem vel*; the common Isidore, *in aegritudine*.] has been cut by physicians because of illness, or [Col. 0389A] has been castrated by barbarians, [Note: [Col. 0389D] Veronensis manuscript 58, with the common Isidore, adds *placuit ut* (“it was decided that”).] let him remain in the clergy. But if anyone, while in sound health, has cut himself off, even if he is in the clergy, he must cease; and from that time no such person ought to be ordained. Just as, therefore, the provisions stated above have been enacted concerning those who have desired or dared to cut themselves off, so, if there are men who have been made eunuchs either by barbarians or by their masters, and who lead a reputable life, the ecclesiastical rule admits them [Note: [Col. 0389D] Quesnellus has *will receive*. We preferred the manuscripts of the Vindobonensis and Pithoean, together with the Veronensis and common Isidore, the last two of which have *the rule into the clergy* at the end.].

TITLE III. Concerning [Note: [Col. 0389D] So the Vindobonensis and Pithoean manuscripts, with a slight variation in the Hardy manuscript: “Concerning neophytes, neither bishops nor presbyters to be made.” The Regina manuscript agrees: “Concerning neophytes, neither bishops nor presbyters to be ordained.” Quesnellus has: “That neophytes may not become bishops or presbyters.”] neophytes, neither to be made presbyters nor bishops. (Canon 2 of Dionysius and Isidore.)

Since many things have been done either under compulsion or because people were driven by other circumstances, contrary to ecclesiastical discipline [Note: [Col. 0389D] The common Isidore, with the Veronensis manuscript, has “or for any reason contrary to the rule.”], so that people newly coming from pagan life [Note: [Col. 0389D] The Pithoean manuscript has: “still recently coming to the faith, and having been catechized or instructed for only a short time, immediately, when they came to spiritual baptism and had at once been baptized, also …” The common Isidore and the Veronensis manuscript have: “still recently catechized or instructed, they had immediately come to spiritual baptism, and when they were at once baptized, also …”] to the faith, and who had been catechized or instructed for only a short time, came immediately to spiritual [Col. 0389B] baptism; and as soon as they had been baptized, were also advanced to the episcopate or [Note: [Col. 0390B] So all our manuscripts and the common Isidore. Quesnellus has *the presbyterate*. Since immediately afterward the Veronensis manuscript, with the common Isidore, has “they have been advanced,” this reading was rightly judged preferable.] presbyterate: it has seemed right that nothing of this kind should henceforth occur. For time is needed [Note: [Col. 0390B] Quesnellus, from the Oxford manuscript, has: “so that a catechumen may be baptized, and after baptism”; he rejected the reading of the Thuan manuscript in the margin, but we have inserted it into the text with all our manuscripts and the common Isidore.] for a person to remain a catechumen; and after baptism he requires much testing. For the apostolic command is clear, saying: “Not a neophyte, lest, being puffed up, he fall into judgment [Note: [Col. 0390C] We have adopted the words “and the snare” from our manuscripts and the common Isidore.] and the snare of the devil.” But if, as time goes on, [Col. 0390A] [Note: [Col. 0390C] The common Isidore has: “if he has committed some mortal sin and has been convicted by two …” The Veronensis manuscript has: “if some mortal sin has been found in that person and he has been convicted …”] a sin harmful to the soul is found in that person, and he is convicted by two or three witnesses, whoever is such shall cease from the clergy.

TITLE IV. Concerning [Note: [Col. 0390C] So the Vindobonensis, Hardy, and Regina manuscripts. Quesnellus has: “Concerning transgressors of the canons.”] the punishment of those who act contrary to the canons.

But if anyone acts contrary to these provisions, as one acting against the statutes of this holy council, he too [Note: [Col. 0390C] Quesnellus has in the text: “from the rank of his status.” We corrected it from the Pithoean and Vindobonensis manuscripts, supported also by the Thuan manuscript, which Quesnellus himself cites in the margin. The Veronensis manuscript, with the common Isidore, has: “from the status of his clergy.”] will imperil his rank.

TITLE V. Concerning [Note: [Col. 0390C] So the Pithoean manuscript, with the Vindobonensis agreeing. The Hardy manuscript has: “Concerning *synecoitae*, or *synesactae*.” The Regina manuscript: “Concerning women whom they call *synectae* [read *synesactae*].” Veronensis Isidore: “Concerning introduced women, whom the Greeks call *synesactae*.”] *synesactae* (women companions). (Canon 3 of Dionysius and Isidore.)

The holy synod absolutely forbids and does not permit a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or any cleric whatsoever [Note: [Col. 0390C] The Veronensis Isidore adds “to be permitted.”] to have an unrelated woman living with him, unless she is perhaps his mother, sister, [Note: [Col. 0390C] The same Veronensis manuscript adds: “or his aunt, that is, his paternal or maternal aunt.” The common Isidore has: “or grandmother, or paternal or maternal aunt.” Immediately afterward both these Isidore manuscripts have: “for only in these persons … [Col. 0390D] every suspicion arising from women.”] or paternal aunt. For in these persons, 50 and in those similar to them, every suspicion is avoided. Whoever acts otherwise, contrary to these provisions [Note: [Col. 0390D] The Pithoean manuscripts and the Veronensis manuscript, with the common Isidore, have “acts.”], will imperil his clerical standing.

TITLE VI. Concerning [Note: [Col. 0390D] So the three manuscripts—Vindobonensis, Hardy, and Pithoean—with the Regina manuscript agreeing. Quesnellus has: “Concerning the ordination of bishops.”] bishops to be ordained by bishops of the same province. (Canon 4 of Dionysius and Isidore.)

The bishop ought to be ordained [Note: [Col. 0390D] The Verona manuscript and the Isidorian Vulgate delete *maxime*, “above all,” and then read: “by all, if possible, who …”] above all by all the bishops who are in the province. But if this should be difficult, whether because of pressing necessity or because of the length of the journey, certainly at least three bishops [Note: [Col. 0390D] We have added *in unum*, “in one [place],” from the Vindobonensis and Pithoean manuscripts, supported by the Verona manuscript and the Isidorian Vulgate. The latter delete the preceding adverb *omnino*, “certainly”; in its place the Pithoean manuscript has *omnimodo*, “in every way.”] must be gathered together in one place, so that they may also [Note: [Col. 0390D] The Verona manuscript with the Isidorian Vulgate reads: “hold in writing the agreement of the others who are absent.”] hold, in writing, the agreement and decisions of the others who are absent, and thus carry out the ordination.

## TITLE VII. On the authority of the metropolitan

The authority, or confirmation, shall belong in each province to the metropolitan [Note: [Col. 0391B] The Vulgate of Isidore adds “bishop.”].

## TITLE VIII. On those who are excommunicated by their bishops (Canon 5 of Dionysius and Isidore)

[Note: [Col. 0391B] Thus the Vindobonensis manuscript with the Vatican Regina and Pithoean manuscripts: “Concerning those who are excommunicated, whether clergy or laypeople.” Quesnellus: “Concerning the excommunicated.”]

[Note: [Col. 0391B] The words of the title are understood here. Thus the Pithoean manuscript, after the title cited, begins the canon as follows: “Concerning those who are excommunicated by their bishops.” Similarly the Isidorian Verona manuscript reads: “Concerning those who are excommunicated, whether clergy or laypeople, by their bishops throughout their respective provinces, let this be observed,” and so forth. The Vulgate of Isidore incorrectly begins with the words “Let this be observed,” omitting what precedes; it also does not recognize the second canon.]

Whether clergy or laypeople, if they are excommunicated by their bishops throughout their respective provinces, this judgment shall be observed according to the canon: those who are excommunicated by some [Note: [Col. 0391B] Quesnellus reads *ut si qui*, “so that if any.” We have followed all our manuscripts and the Isidorian Vulgate.] shall not be received by others [Note: [Col. 0391B] The Verona manuscript with the Isidorian Vulgate adds “to communion.” Quesnellus then reads: “lest anyone perhaps, because of some resentment … or any such [cause], has been excluded from communion.” We have corrected from the Pithoean manuscript, with which the Vindobonensis and Thuane manuscripts agree. The Verona Isidore reads: “lest anyone perhaps because of some … [Col. 0391C] or any such disturbance of his bishop’s anger has been excluded” [read: “may have been excluded”].]. It must, however, be investigated lest someone have been expelled because of some resentment of mind, contention, or any other agitation of an irascible bishop.

## TITLE IX. On a synod to be held twice each year in every province

[Note: [Col. 0391C] Thus the Vindebonensis, Hardy, and Vatican Regina manuscripts. Quesnellus: “On councils to be held.”]

[Col. 0391B]

In order, therefore, that these matters may be examined with appropriate care, it seemed right that twice each year councils of the bishops should be held in each of the several provinces, so that the bishops, assembling together from all the provinces [Note: [Col. 0391C] The Verona Isidore reads “from the entire province.” The Vulgate of Isidore incorrectly has “from the common [assembly].”], may examine questions of this kind; and finally, those who have deservedly incurred the offense of their bishops because of their faults may also be excommunicated by the other bishops [Note: [Col. 0391C] This is the better reading of the Vindebonensis and Pithoean manuscripts. Quesnellus: “may be excommunicated.” The Pithoean manuscript continues: “until it seems right to all in common, or to the bishop himself.” The Verona manuscript, differing slightly from the Isidorian Vulgate, reads: “Those who have been excommunicated shall likewise remain so until either all in common, or their own bishop, shall have judged it more humane … Let the council be held once”; and later: “The second shall be conducted concerning …”], until they are received into communion by everyone, or until their own bishop sees fit to pass a more merciful judgment concerning them. Let councils be held once before the days of Lent, so that, after all quarrels, if there are any, have been removed, a pure and solemn offering may be presented to God [Note: [Col. 0391C] Thus all our manuscripts and the Isidorian Vulgate. Quesnellus: “may be able to offer it.” The Vindebonensis adds *fiat*—“let it be made”—after the word *autumni*; in the Pithoean, “the second shall be held.”]; and a second time around the season of autumn.

## TITLE X. On the primacy of the Roman Church (Canon 6 of Dionysius and Isidore)

[Col. 0392B]

The Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0391D] Quesnellus preferred in the text, on the authority of a single defective and later Oxford manuscript, *semper habeat primatum*, “should always hold the primacy.” He appended the following lengthy note:

“*Semper habuit*, ‘has always held it,’ is read in the Thuane and Atrebatensis manuscripts, in Alanus Copus and Severinus Binius. The Greek version of the canon in the acts of the sixteenth session of the Council of Chalcedon agrees: Ἡ Ἐκκλησία Ῥώμης πάντοτε ἔσχε τὰ πρωτεῖα, ‘The Church of Rome has always held the primacy.’ This corresponds to the Latin canon itself as recited by Paschasinus, except that the conjunction *quod* is superfluous at the beginning of the canon: ‘That the Roman Church …’ This word appears neither in the Atrebatensis, Thuane, or Oxford manuscript, nor in the Greek of the Council of Chalcedon.

Boniface I, pope, also seems to have read *non habeat* but *habuit*, in his letter to the bishops established throughout Thessaly, cited by Nicholas I in Letter 42 and preserved complete in the Roman Council recently published by Lucas Holstenius in the *Collectio Romana* and in the Barberini Library. Speaking about the authority of the Roman pontiff, he says that the Council of Nicaea did not dare to establish anything above him. A canon would contradict him if he had read *habeat*, ‘should hold’; but it favors him if *habuit*, ‘has held,’ is read—although, to state frankly what I think, this letter is not free from suspicion of forgery or at least interpolation.

Even if the canon reads *habeat*, in a form expressing a determination, as the sequence of the canon seems to require, nothing is thereby taken away from the dignity of the apostolic primacy, which Christ himself established in Peter and which the sacred councils subsequently confirmed by their decrees.

Whether these words—‘The Roman Church has always held the primacy,’ whether read as *habuit* or *habeat*—form part of the canon or constitute its title has been questioned by some. The manuscripts, I believe, settle the matter: in them the title is distinct from these words and assigned to the canon, while these words begin the canon itself as part of it—but, I say, as an added part. For they appear neither in the Greek text, nor in any other version, nor in the later Roman manuscript of Dionysius himself. It is therefore beyond doubt either that they slipped from the margin into the text, or that they were added by clergy of the Roman Church or by others, lest the holy Fathers should appear to have forgotten the dignity of Rome.

Valentinian Augustus refers to this canon when, in the constitution issued against Saint Hilary of Arles at the urging of Saint Leo, he says: ‘Since, therefore, the authority of the sacred synod has also confirmed the primacy of the apostolic see, the merit of Saint Peter, who is the prince of the episcopal crown, and the dignity of the Roman city.’

To the Thuane and Atrebatensis manuscripts, which support the reading *habuit*, must be added the two Vindobonenses, numbers 39 and 12, as well as the Hardy and Fossatensis manuscripts cited by Labbe, the Pithoean, and another nine-hundred-year-old Parisian manuscript of the Society of Jesus, cited by Hardouin; finally, the Vatican Regina manuscript 1997, in which this canon is expressed in exactly the words used by Paschasinus in the sixteenth session of the Council of Chalcedon.

There is also the testimony of Father Coustant, who consulted several ancient copies of this collection. He writes in volume I of *Epistolae Romanorum pontificum*, column 1037, note 6: ‘In the ancient manuscripts one reads *Ecclesia Romana semper habuit*—not, as Quesnellus preferred, *habeat*—*primatum*, “the Roman Church has always held the primacy.” Since the reading *habuit* is established by the very consistent agreement of so many manuscripts and by the other testimonies produced by Quesnellus, we are greatly surprised that he nevertheless inserted *habeat* into the text and relegated the true reading to a note.

Moreover, Quesnellus’s claim that these words occur in no other version is sufficiently refuted by the ancient translation published by Justellus, which we shall reprint in this volume accurately according to the manuscript copies. In it, although not the same words, a similar meaning is contained in canon 6, prefaced by the title: ‘On the primacy of the Roman Church and the bishops of the other cities.’ The canon then begins: ‘It is an ancient custom that the bishop of the city of Rome should hold the primacy.’ These words are plainly equivalent to *semper habuit primatum*. It is therefore clear that two ancient translators understood the Nicene canon in this sense.

It is also clear from this how wrongly Quesnellus asserted, without hesitation, that this statement had either slipped from the margin into the text or been added by clergy of the Roman Church or others so that the holy Fathers would not seem to have forgotten the dignity of Rome. There is even less reason to suspect the clergy of the Roman Church, since the ancient Roman version was the same as the African version brought to Africa by Caecilian, which presented this canon differently, as we conjectured in the treatise *On Collections*, part II, chapter 2, section 1, number 4.

As for the letter of Boniface I to the bishops of Thessaly, which Quesnellus likewise brings under suspicion of forgery or interpolation, it is not only cited by Nicholas I in Letter 42 but also by the earlier Hadrian I in Letter 95 of the Carolingian manuscript; moreover, it was read in the Roman synod of Boniface II. These testimonies vindicate it so thoroughly that only rashly could anyone cast even the slightest suspicion upon it.

There is an important fragment of Gelasius, published by Sirmond and inserted in volume V of the Venetian edition of the Councils, column 341. When he says that ‘by the unassailable and singular judgment of the 318 Fathers, the most ancient honor was adjudged to the See of Saint Peter,’ he appears to have referred to this version or to the ancient one.

This canon, adopted in our collection from the most ancient Italian version, differs entirely from the Isidorian translation, which reads as follows: ‘Let the ancient custom continue in Egypt, Libya, and Pentapolis, so that the bishop of Alexandria may have authority over all these places, since a similar custom also belongs to the Roman bishop’—the Verona Isidore reads, ‘since the same custom exists there.’ ‘Likewise, in Antioch and the other provinces, let each Church retain its proper honor.’”]

has always held the primacy. Let Egypt, Libya, and Pentapolis also retain it [Col. 0393A], so that the bishop of Alexandria may have authority over all these places; for this is also the custom of the Roman bishop. Likewise, the one established in Antioch shall have it. Thus, in the other provinces also, let the privileges of the Churches remain intact.

## TITLE XI. On invalidating an ordination performed without the metropolitan’s consent

[Note: [Col. 0393D] Quesnellus: “That no one may be ordained bishop without the metropolitan’s consent.” We follow the Vindebonensis and Pithoean manuscripts and the Fossatensis, whose complete version of this canon was published by Father Coustant in volume I of *Epistolae Romanorum pontificum*, column 1033, note h. The same title is also found in Vatican Regina manuscript 1997.]

It must in every respect be clear [Note: [Col. 0394B] We have added this from the Vindebonensis, Pithoean, and Fossatensis manuscripts. The Verona manuscript, together with the Isidorian Vulgate, adds *et conscientiam*, “and knowledge,” after *voluntatem*, and shortly afterward both have “of the metropolitan bishop.”] that if anyone has been ordained bishop against the will of the metropolitan, the holy synod has decreed that he must not be a bishop [Note: [Col. 0394B] The Verona Isidore reads: “This great and holy council judged that this man ought not to be [a bishop].” The Isidorian Vulgate omits *hoc*, “this.” The Pithoean and Fossatensis manuscripts read: “This holy council decreed.”].

## TITLE XII. On following the greater number when there is disagreement concerning an ordination

[Note: [Col. 0394B] Thus the manuscripts cited above, as well as Vatican Regina. Quesnellus alone has “only in an election.”]

If, after a common and reasonable consensus of all has been reached and a decree has been made according to ecclesiastical rule, two or three persons should oppose it through their contentiousness, the decision of the greater number shall prevail.

## TITLE XIII. On the honor of the bishop of Jerusalem (Canon 7 of Dionysius and Isidore)

[Note: [Col. 0394B] Thus the Vindobonensis, Hardy, and Pithoean manuscripts with Vatican Regina. Quesnellus: “On [the bishop] of Jerusalem.”]

[Col. 0394A]

Since ancient custom and an old tradition have established that honor be paid to the bishop of Aelia, that is, Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0394C] The Pithoean manuscript reads “of Jerusalem,” more correctly. The Isidorian Vulgate: “Honor shall be paid to the bishop of Jerusalem, while the proper dignity of the metropolitan city nevertheless remains.” The Verona Isidore: “That the bishop who is in Aelia, that is, in Jerusalem, be honored and receive his honor, while the proper dignity of the metropolitan city remains.”], he shall consequently have his proper honor; but the metropolitan’s dignity shall remain intact.

## TITLE XIV. On those who are called Pure, and how they are to be received (Canon 8 of Dionysius and Isidore)

[Note: [Col. 0394C] Thus the Vindebonensis and Pithoean manuscripts, together with Vatican Regina. Quesnellus: “How the Cathari are to be received.”]

Concerning those who call themselves Cathari, that is, Pure, [Note: [Col. 0394C] The Verona Isidore adds “who are called Novatians,” and continues: “if any should wish to come to the Church.” The Isidorian Vulgate begins the canon differently: “If any from the Novatians should wish to come to the Catholic Church, it has been decreed,” and so forth.] if any of them come to the Catholic Church, the holy council has decreed [Note: [Col. 0394C] This version derives from the Isidorian version, which the author of this collection followed in most matters concerning the Nicene canons, and especially in the rendering of this passage and its meaning. But it does so incorrectly. It should not be translated “so that they may be ordained,” as though the ordination received by the Cathari outside the Church had been null, but “so that, having been ordained”—or, as is said below, “those who are found to have been ordained”—they should remain in the clergy. See the fuller discussion by which we established this interpretation and meaning in note 13 to Quesnellus’s observations on Letter 167 to Rusticus, volume II.] that they are to be ordained and thus remain in the clergy.

Before all else, however, [Note: [Col. 0394D] The Verona Isidore reads: “this confession must indeed be required of them in writing, so that they may profess that they will observe by common agreement.” The Isidorian Vulgate: “they must indeed have this confession, which [must be made] in writing,” and so forth, as in the reading described from the Verona manuscript.] it is fitting that they profess this in writing, so that they may declare that they will unanimously observe the statutes of the Catholic and Apostolic Church: that is, that they will communicate with those who [Note: [Col. 0394D] We have added the particle *forte*, “perhaps,” from our manuscripts, including the Verona Isidore, which reads: “that they will communicate also with those who perhaps …”] have entered a second marriage, or with those who fell during the time of persecution. A measure and period of penance has nevertheless been assigned to such persons [Note: [Col. 0394D] The Verona manuscript and the Isidorian Vulgate add “to those who have fallen”; afterward both omit *et*, “and,” in *in apostolica*.], so that in all things they may follow what is observed in the Catholic and Apostolic Church.

Thus, if anywhere, whether in villages or in cities, they alone are found to have been ordained, those who are found among the clergy shall remain in the same rank. But if a bishop or presbyter of the Catholic Church is the person to whom some of these come, it is certain that the bishop of the Church shall retain his dignity; likewise, the presbyter and deacon shall retain theirs [Note: [Col. 0395C] Quesnellus adds *habere*, “to have,” against all our manuscripts and the Pithoean. Quesnellus alone then reads “but from these.” The Isidorian Vulgate has *sacerdotii*, “of the priesthood,” instead of *presbyterii*.].

But those who come from them, if one of them happens to be a bishop, shall have the dignity of a presbyter—unless the Catholic bishop should choose to grant him also the honor of the episcopal title. If he does not choose to do so, let him find a place for him so that he may be a chorepiscopus in the parish, or a presbyter; provided that he is seen to remain in the clergy and that there are not two bishops in one city [Note: [Col. 0395C] The Isidorian Vulgate adds: “or a presbyter in the clergy, so that two bishops may not appear to be in one city and so that he may in every way be seen to remain in the clergy.” The Verona Isidore reads: “or a presbyter, provided that they may not appear to be in the city,” and continues as in the Isidorian Vulgate.].

## TITLE XV. On those ordained without examination (Canon 9 of Dionysius and Isidore)

[Note: [Col. 0395D] Quesnellus: “On those who are promoted without examination.” The Hardy manuscript has “ordained.” We have preferred the reading of the Vindobonensis, Pithoean, and Vatican Regina manuscripts.]

[Col. 0395B]

If any persons have been advanced as presbyters without examination and afterward, upon examination, have confessed their sins; and when they had confessed, men rashly imposed hands upon them, contrary to the rule, the ecclesiastical order does not receive them. For in all things the Catholic Church defends what is irreproachable.

## TITLE XVI. On those who have fallen and have been ordained (Canon 10 of Dionysius and Isidore)

Whoever among those who have fallen has been ordained through the ignorance or contempt of those who ordained him [Note: [Col. 0395D] Thus the Vindebonensis and Isidore, with the Pithoean, in which only *et*, “and,” is omitted. Quesnellus: “through ignorance or contempt … have been ordained; this does not prejudice [the rule].” The Thuane manuscript, as Quesnellus notes, likewise reads “this does not prejudice.”], this does not prejudice the ecclesiastical rule. For when the matter has been discovered, they shall be deposed.

## TITLE XVII. On receiving transgressors through penance (Canon 11 of Dionysius and Isidore)

[Note: [Col. 0395D] The words *per poenitentiam*, “through penance,” have been added from our Vindobonensis, Pithoean, Hardy, and Vatican Regina manuscripts.]

[Col. 0395C]

[Note: [Col. 0395D] The Verona Isidore reads: “Concerning those who have transgressed against the faith of the Lord … or have endured no danger, as happened under the renewed persecution of the tyrant Licinius.” The Isidorian Vulgate: “Concerning those who denied [the faith] without necessity, [Col. 0396C] or without the confiscation of their property, or without danger, or anything of this kind, which occurred under the tyranny of Licinius.” The Vindebonensis and Pithoean manuscripts delete *facta*, “which occurred.”]

Concerning those who transgressed without any necessity, without the confiscation of their property, or without danger, or any such circumstance as occurred in the final tyranny of Licinius, the holy council has decreed that, although they are unworthy of mercy, some humanity should nevertheless be shown toward them. If, therefore, they sincerely repent, let them be placed for three years among the hearers, if they are faithful, and for seven years among the penitents; for two further years they shall be outside communion, participating with the people only in prayer [Note: [Col. 0396C] The Verona Isidore reads: “Let them be counted among the penitents, provided that they are faithful, and for seven other years let them be among the penitents; but for two years they shall likewise participate with the people …” The Isidorian Vulgate is similar and differs only in the final words: “for two years, moreover, let these same persons remain in prayer alone, without the offering,” and so forth.].

## TITLE XVIII. On the penance of those who, after baptism, return to secular military service (Canon 12 of Dionysius)

[Note: [Col. 0396C] We have followed the Vindobonensis, Pithoean, and Hardy manuscripts, from which Vatican Regina differs only slightly. Quesnellus: “On those who return to military service after baptism.”]

[Col. 0396C]

If some who were called by the grace of God first demonstrated their faith by laying aside the military belt, but afterward returned to their own vomit, so that they gave money and sought to return again to military service, let them remain among the penitents for ten years, after the three years during which they were among the hearers [Note: [Col. 0396C] The Pithoean inserts *primum*, “first”; in the Vindebonensis it is also added by a second hand. It is read in the Verona Isidore and the Isidorian Vulgate, which in the latter two have *audientes*, “hearers,” and shortly afterward: “But above all let this be observed by everyone, that their disposition and the fruit of their penance …” In the Vindebonensis, for *species*, “form,” a second ancient hand has written *fructus*, “fruit.”].

In all cases, however, let this especially be observed: their disposition and purpose, or the character of their penance, must be investigated. For whoever, with all fear and persevering tears and good works, demonstrates his conversion at all times [Note: [Col. 0396D] We have added the words “with all fear” from the Pithoean and Verona manuscripts and the Isidorian Vulgate; in the Vindebonensis the reading is corrupt: “at every time and …”] not merely by outward appearance but by deed and truth, such persons, when they have completed the appointed periods, shall rightly share in prayers. The bishop may also decide to treat them somewhat more mercifully.

But if some have treated their fall with indifference and have thought that it was enough for their conversion merely to appear to enter the Church, they must in every way complete the appointed periods [Note: [Col. 0396D] The Verona manuscript and the Isidorian Vulgate read: “They demonstrate it not by words alone but by deed and truth; and when even these have completed the appointed period and have already begun to share in prayers, it shall be permitted to the bishop …” Shortly afterward: “But those who have fallen and think that it is enough that they have entered the Church shall in every way complete the appointed periods.” In the final words Quesnellus has “shall have to complete,” which our manuscripts do not have.].

## TITLE XIX. On granting reconciliation to the dying (Canon 13 of Dionysius, 12 of Isidore)

[Note: [Col. 0396D] Quesnellus alone adds “to penitents,” incorrectly.]

[Col. 0396C]

Concerning those who depart from the body, the ancient rule shall even now be observed [Note: [Col. 0396D] Thus the Vindebonensis, with the Pithoean and Isidore differing only slightly. Only the Pithoean, together with the Isidorian Vulgate, has *vitae suae*, “of their life,” instead of *viae suae*, “of their journey.” Quesnellus reads “shall be observed,” and at the end “of their journey,” and notes in the margin that this is read in the Thuane manuscript, which also has “not thus, as they depart from the body.” The Verona manuscript and the Isidorian Vulgate delete *donec statutum tempus compleatur*, “until the appointed period is completed.”], so that those departing from the body are not deprived of the final and necessary provision for their journey. But if a desperate person, after receiving communion, should survive, let him remain among those who communicate in prayer alone until the appointed period is completed.

In the case of all those who are departing from the body and request the Eucharist, the bishop must exercise care and discernment in giving them communion [Note: [Col. 0397C] The Thuane and Pithoean manuscripts read: “who depart from the naked body or from the body.” The Verona manuscript and the Isidorian Vulgate: “who depart from the body, in giving communion to them,” and so forth.].

## TITLE XX. On catechumens who have fallen (Canon 14 of Dionysius, 13 of Isidore)

[Note: [Col. 0397C] The Vindobonensis and Hardy manuscripts delete *lapsis*, “who have fallen”; it is nevertheless read with Quesnellus in the Pithoean and Vatican Regina manuscripts.]

Concerning catechumens who have fallen [Note: [Col. 0397C] We have supplied *lapsis*, “who have fallen,” from the Thuane and Pithoean manuscripts, with which the Verona Isidore agrees. Since this word is absent from Quesnellus’s manuscript, as also from the Vindebonensis, Quesnellus afterward wrote: “if they have fallen, for three years,” and so forth. But the words *si lapsi sunt*, “if they have fallen,” are absent from all our manuscripts and also from the Vindebonensis, although it lacks *lapsis*. The Isidorian Vulgate reads: “The holy and great council decreed concerning catechumens who have fallen that they should be among those hearing the word for three years only,” and so forth.], the holy council has decreed that they shall be among the hearers for three years only; after that they shall pray with the catechumens.

## TITLE XXI. On those who abandon their Churches and transfer to others (Canon 15 of Dionysius and Isidore)

[Note: [Col. 0397D] Thus all our manuscripts, two of which prefix *suas*, “their own,” to *Ecclesias*, “Churches.” Quesnellus: “That no one may transfer from one Church to another.”]

[Col. 0397B]

Because of the many disturbances and seditions that commonly arise [Note: [Col. 0397D] The Isidorian Vulgate adds “and frequent riots of factions, which commonly occur.” The Verona Isidore adds “among the people.”], it has been decided that this custom must be abolished entirely: if a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or cleric is found anywhere transferring, contrary to the rule, from one city to another [Note: [Col. 0397D] The Verona and Isidorian Vulgates read: “which is contrary to the rule, wherever it may occur—that is, so that neither a bishop … may transfer from one city to another.” Both delete “or a cleric.”], then, after the statutes of this holy council, if anyone should dare to attempt such a thing [Note: [Col. 0397D] The Isidorian Vulgate reads “to do”; the Verona Isidore: “should attempt anything, they shall be broken.” Both omit “in which he was ordained” from what follows.], every such attempt shall be annulled, and he shall be restored to his own Church, in which he was ordained bishop, deacon, or presbyter.

## TITLE XXII. On not receiving clerics of another Church (Canon 16 of Dionysius and Isidore)

[Note: [Col. 0398C] Thus our four manuscripts. Quesnellus: “That one who has transferred should not be received.”]

If any persons, acting without restraint and not having the fear of the Lord before their eyes, should depart from their own Church without knowing or observing the ecclesiastical statutes [Note: [Col. 0398C] The Verona and Isidorian Vulgates read “and observing.”], whether they are presbyters, deacons, or placed in any ecclesiastical order [Note: [Col. 0398C] The Thuane and Pithoean manuscripts read: “Such persons are nowhere [to be received].” The Verona and Isidorian Vulgates: “They ought not to be received in another Church.”], they must never be received in a Church; rather, they must be compelled by every necessity to return to their own Churches. If they remain, they must be regarded as excommunicated.

## TITLE XXIII. On not ordaining clerics belonging to another bishop without their bishop’s consent (Canon 17 of Isidore)

[Note: [Col. 0398C] Thus the Vindobonensis and Hardy manuscripts. Quesnellus: “That a bishop may not ordain another’s cleric.”]

[Col. 0398A]

But if anyone should dare to ordain in his own Church someone who belongs to another [bishop], without having the consent of the bishop from whom that cleric departed, such ordination shall be invalid [Note: [Col. 0398C] Quesnellus: “If anyone should dare to receive someone who belongs to another’s jurisdiction and ordain him in his own Church, although he does not have …” We have preferred the reading of the Pithoean manuscript, with which the Vindebonensis, Verona Isidore, and Isidorian Vulgate agree.].

## TITLE XXIV. On clerics who lend at interest (Canon 18 of Dionysius and Isidore)

Since many clerics pursue shameful profits out of greed and have forgotten the divine commandment that says, “Who has not given his money at interest” (Psalm 14:7), and, by lending at interest, demand hundredfold returns [Note: [Col. 0398D] The Thuane manuscript reads “hundredfold fruits.”], this holy council has decreed that if anyone is found, after this definition, to be receiving interest, or to be pursuing shameful profits from any such transaction, or even to charge among Greeks half-centesimal interest, or to give kinds of grain at one and a half times [their value] [Note: [Col. 0398D] Thus the Vindebonensis, Pithoean, and Thuane manuscripts, as Quesnellus notes. In his manuscript, together with the Oxford manuscript, the reading is “in quantities, half [of the hundredfold],” and so forth. The Verona and Isidorian Vulgates delete “in Greek, half-hundredfold kinds” and read “forms of grain.” Shortly afterward, instead of *sescu­plum*, “one-and-a-half times,” the Vindebonensis prefers *sesquiplum*. After *omnis*, “everyone,” Quesnellus inserts *ergo*, “therefore,” a word absent from all our manuscripts. Finally, instead of *abscindatur*, “let him be cut off,” the Pithoean reads *excidetur*, “he shall be cut off”; the Verona Isidore, *dejicietur*, “he shall be cast down”; and the Isidorian Vulgate, *dejiciatur*, “let him be cast down.”], everyone who has contrived such a thing for profit shall be cut off from the clergy and regarded as excluded from the ecclesiastical order.

## TITLE XXV. On deacons not being above presbyters (Canon 18 of Dionysius, 14 of Isidore)

[Note: [Col. 0398D] Quesnellus: “That deacons may not be above presbyters.” We have preferred our manuscripts.]

It has come to the attention of the holy council that in certain places and cities the sacraments are given to presbyters by deacons [Note: [Col. 0398D] The Verona manuscript, together with the Isidorian Vulgate, reads “that deacons offer [them]”; this is contrary to the rule. Shortly afterward the Isidorian Vulgate has “take” instead of *contingant*, “touch”; and then, in “Therefore let all these things,” we have deleted the particle *ergo*, “therefore,” on the authority of the Vindebonensis, Pithoean, and Verona Isidore.], although neither rule nor custom has handed down that those who do not have the authority to offer the sacrifice should present the body of Christ to those who do offer it. It has also become known that certain deacons touch the sacraments even before the bishop. Let all these practices be abolished, and let deacons remain within their proper measure, knowing that they are indeed ministers of the bishops but inferior to the presbyters. Therefore, after the presbyters, let them receive the Eucharist from the bishop or from a presbyter [Note: [Col. 0398D] The Vindebonensis adds, in a later hand: [Col. 0399A] “Nor shall they distribute the Eucharist to those presbyters; but while those presbyters are officiating, let them serve only. If neither the bishop nor the presbyter is present, then let the deacons themselves bring it forth [Col. 0399B] and give it.” This final sentence is also added in the text of the Pithoean and in the Verona and Isidorian Vulgates, which begin it: “But if he is not present.” The Isidorian Vulgate alone reads *edant*, “let them eat,” instead of *dent*, “let them give.” The entire sentence is absent from the Greek.].

Nor may deacons sit among the presbyters. For it is outside the rule and outside [Note: [Col. 0399B] The Verona Isidore reads “the order.” The Pithoean manuscript then has “does not wish this to be sufficient for them.”] the proper order for this to happen. If anyone is unwilling to be subject even after this decree, let him cease to be a deacon.

## TITLE XXVI. On the Paulianists, whom they call Homuncionites (Canon 19 of Dionysius and Isidore)

[Note: [Col. 0399B] The Isidorian Vulgate reads: “If anyone from the Paulianists and Cataphrygians takes refuge in the Catholic Church, it has been decreed that they must be rebaptized entirely.” The name “Cataphrygians,” which occurs in no other version or in the Greek, is clearly a later addition to this Isidorian version, as is evident from our Verona manuscript, which contains the pure ancient version adopted by Isidore. It reads: “Concerning the Paulianists: if anyone takes refuge in the Church, let it be decreed that they be rebaptized,” and so forth. The Thuane manuscript reads: “to the Church, it is immediately proper to baptize them entirely.” For the title, we have followed the Pithoean and Hardy manuscripts, as well as the Vindobonensis and Thuane manuscripts; the latter two add *homines*, “people,” before *Homuncionitas*. We have followed the reading of the Vindebonensis and Pithoean manuscripts. Only the Pithoean has *rebaptizari*, “to be rebaptized.” Quesnellus: “it has been decreed.” Quesnellus added the following note: “The Homuncionites were heretics who blasphemously asserted that Christ was not God and man but man alone. Among them are counted the Paulianists, so called from Paul of Samosata. Anyone wishing to learn more about this designation should consult the learned notes of Jean-Baptiste Cotelier on Book VI of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, page 271.”]

If any of them take refuge in the Church, let it be decreed that they are to be baptized in every respect. But if any of them were clerics, and are found to be blameless and irreproachable, after being baptized they shall also be ordained by the bishops of the Catholic Church [Note: [Col. 0399C] The Pithoean reads “rebaptized”; in the Vindebonensis a second hand adds “again.” The Isidorian Vulgate reads “baptized again”; the Verona Isidore, “rebaptized again.”]. But if, upon examination, they are found less suitable [Note: [Col. 0399C] Thus the Vindebonensis and Pithoean manuscripts, together with Isidore. Quesnellus: “if they are found less fit.” The Verona Isidore adds after “it is necessary”: “and they shall be in the order of laypeople.”], they must be deposed.

## TITLE XXVII. On deaconesses

[Note: [Col. 0399C] Quesnellus adds *eorum*, “of them,” a word absent from the Thuane, Vindebonensis, and Vatican Regina manuscripts.]

[Col. 0400A]

[Note: [Col. 0399D] Canon 20 of Nicaea is missing; concerning it, see the dissertation on this codex.]

Likewise, concerning the deaconesses and all who are found among their clergy, the same procedure shall be observed. [Note: [Col. 0399D] The Pithou codex has “concerning deacons,” as in the Vulgate Isidore; other Isidorian codices have “deacons.” But the Veronese Isidore and the Vatican Regina, with other codices of this collection, have “deaconesses.” Immediately afterward, the Thuaneus and Pithou manuscripts, with the Veronese Isidore, delete “their”; then Quesnellus alone has “shall be observed.”] We have also spoken concerning those deaconesses who have been found in this order: [Note: [Col. 0399D] In the Vindobonensis manuscript, *quia* is written by a second hand in place of *quae*. Then Pithou and the Veronese Isidore have *inter laicas* (“among laywomen”); the Vulgate Isidore has *ut et omnino inter laicas* (“so that they may altogether be among laywomen”).] since they have received no laying on of hands whatsoever, so that in every respect they are to be regarded among the laity. [Note: [Col. 0399D] The Vulgate Isidore adds: “Likewise, deaconesses, who are not found in the Catholic canon, are to be assigned in the same manner, that is, as laywomen and as though they had not been consecrated.” The Veronese Isidorian manuscript has the same, except that at the end it reads: “in a similar place, that is, as laywomen, they are to be regarded as though they had not been consecrated.” Canon 20 of Nicaea is absent from the manuscripts of this collection, as also from the Vatican Regina manuscript and Rufinus’s abbreviation. But in the Fossat., Pith., and Hardy manuscripts, although they contain this same version, the same canon is read as it appears in Isidore. We insert it here:

“Concerning Sundays and Pentecost, that on those days we should pray standing. Since on Sunday certain people kneel in prayer, and likewise during the days of Pentecost, therefore it has been established by the holy synod—because it is a uniform and fitting custom to be observed throughout all the churches—that we should offer our vows to the Lord while standing in prayer.”

The Hardy codex gives the title as: “That the knee should not be bent on Sunday.” The Veronese Isidorian manuscript, which places the Sardican canons after the Nicene canons as though they were Nicene, likewise places this same canon first, with the single difference that instead of “Pentecost” it has “the Fiftieth Day.” Concerning the absence of this canon, compare our Observations in Quesnell’s Dissertation 12, chapter 1, no. 9.]

## TITLE XXVIII. Concerning bishops who are also to be deprived of lay communion when they have changed cities (Sardican Canon 1 in Dionysius and Isidore)

[Note: [Col. 0400B–0400D] We explained in the treatise included in this volume, part II, chapter 1, section 3, to what extent this and the following canons—although truly Sardican—were attached to the Nicene canons and treated as Nicene. We preferred the title of the following canon from our Vindobonensis manuscript all the more readily because it is found not only in Dionysius Exiguus but also in other very ancient collections older than Dionysius, such as the Vatican Regina and Vatican 1342 manuscripts. We have found Quesnellus’s title, expressed in these words—“That a bishop transferring from one city to another should also be deprived of lay communion”—in none of our codices or in any other collection. Dionysius declares in his letter to Stephen that he did not interpret these canons from the Greek, but gave them as they had been published in Latin. In the treatise mentioned above, part I, chapter 5, we showed that these canons were issued by the Sardican synod itself not so much in Greek as in Latin. Hence the two Sardican canons produced in Zosimus’s Commonitorium under the name of the Nicene canons display the same reading received by Dionysius; and all the ancient Latin collections that do not derive from Dionysius likewise have the same wording at their foundation. Besides Dionysius, we find these canons in the Latin manuscript collections Vatican Regina 1997, Lucensis 88, Vatican 1342 (or Barb. 2888), the Quesnelliana, Justellus’s Prisca, and the very ancient collection commonly called Isidoriana. Quite a few variant readings introduced from time to time have seemed to some to present these canons in one form and then another, almost as though they were interpretations. But for those who examine and compare the individual readings more carefully, it will be clear that the entire variation is contained in certain words scattered here and there, while complete lines and entire clauses agree in the same words. Since this is incompatible with genuinely different interpretations, the primitive Latin original will be recognized as having been altered in places by freer variants, but as remaining the same at its foundation. Here we shall note, besides the variants of the manuscripts in this collection, only the readings of Dionysius. When these same canons are later published in the reissued Prisca collection, we shall then append the variants of the other unpublished collections—Vatican Regina, Vatican 1342, and Lucensis—and in some places also those of the Isidoriana, which anyone may compare with the common versions elsewhere.]

### 63

[Note: [Col. 0400D–0401C] Quesnellus appended this note: “The Oxford codex presents Canon 28, the first of the Sardican canons, in this manner; the Thuaneus manuscript and Isidore divide it into two, but in different ways; Dionysius Exiguus finally makes three canons of it. I had intended to follow the Thuaneus manuscript, because in the Oxford codex itself the title of chapter 1 indicates that the Nicene canons are comprised under forty-eight titles, while the Atrebatensis manuscript cited by Alanus Copus counts the same number less one, as will be stated in the dissertation on this codex. But when I observed that the Thuaneus manuscript, in which the individual Sardican canons are adorned with two headings, one Dionysian and the other taken from elsewhere, nevertheless has, in this latter part of the canon which it treats as a second canon, the single heading of Dionysius, I concluded that the division of the canon, together with its title, had come from a manuscript of Dionysius; the other division, as older and proper to this codex, should be retained. Not only the Atrebatensis codex but also our Vindobonensis 39, agreeing with the Oxford manuscript, support the division into chapters here printed.”]

Bishop Hosius said: “A custom no less evil than a pernicious corruption must be utterly eradicated: no bishop should be permitted to transfer from his own city to another city; for the reason why he attempts to do this is obvious, since no bishop has been found in this respect who wished to transfer from a larger city to a smaller one. [Note: [Col. 0401C] The Thuaneus codex has “made manifest.” The words “in this respect” are added from our Vindobonensis codex, proper to this collection; Dionysius Exiguus and the other Isidorian and Prisca collections add them as well. The Vindobonensis codex has “would wish to transfer.”] Hence it is apparent that they are inflamed by the ardor of avarice and serve ambition, so that they may exercise domination. [Note: [Col. 0401C] The Thuaneus codex, with the Vatican Regina, has “may have”; the Vindobonensis manuscripts and Dionysius then delete “therefore.”] If, therefore, this pleases everyone, let such a pernicious practice be punished more severely and more strictly, so that such a man may not even have lay communion.”

All replied: “It pleases us.”

(Canon 2 in Dionysius and in the Thuaneus codex.)

Bishop Hosius said: “Even if some such rash man should arise and perhaps, bringing forward an excuse, insist that he received letters from the people—although it is obvious that a few people without sincere faith could have been corrupted by reward and payment, so that they would shout in the church and appear to be requesting him as bishop—I judge that these frauds must be condemned entirely, in such a way that such a man may not receive lay communion even at the end.” [Note: [Col. 0401C–D] The Vindobonensis codex deletes “at the end.” Dionysius reads: “I judge that it should be so, that such a man may not receive lay communion at the end”; the Vindobonensis manuscripts and Dionysius then omit “therefore.”]

### 64

“If this therefore pleases all of you, enact it.”

The synod replied: “It pleases us.” [Note: [Col. 0401D] The Thuaneus codex adds this clause, which is found in no other collection: “at the end they may at least obtain lay communion.”]

Bishop Hosius said: “This also must be added: that bishops should not pass from their own province into another province in which there are bishops, unless perhaps they have been invited by their brethren, so that they may not appear to be excluded from the door of charity.” [Note: [Col. 0401D–0402A] Dionysius has: “so that we may not appear to close the door of charity.”]

## TITLE XXIX. That they should be heard among bishops of the same province

(Canon 3 in Isidore.)

[Note: [Col. 0402B] The Thuaneus codex and Dionysius omit “This also must be provided for” and have: “But if in some province…”]

This also must be provided for: if in some province a bishop has a dispute against another bishop, one of the two should not summon a bishop from another province as judge. [Note: [Col. 0402B] With our Vindobonensis codex, the other collections have “has”; Quesnellus has “may have.” Dionysius’s Mainz and Justellus editions, against the manuscripts consulted by Labbe, wrongly delete “not”; the Thuaneus codex has “nor.” Dionysius, with the Thuaneus codex, adds “as judge.”]

### 65

## TITLE XXX. Concerning appeals to the Roman bishop

(Canon 4 in Isidore.)

[Note: [Col. 0402B–C] Quesnellus has “Concerning appeal.” We have followed the reading of our Vindobonensis codex, which is also supported by another codex of this collection, the Atrebatensis cited by Alanus Copus. The same wording appears in the title of the Vatican Regina manuscript, whose titles are adopted in this collection.]

But if a bishop has been adjudged in some case and thinks that he has a good case, so that the council may be renewed: if it pleases you, let us honor the memory of the holy apostle Peter, so that it may be written either by those who examined the case or by the bishops who reside in the neighboring province, to the Roman bishop. If he judges that the judgment should be renewed, let it be renewed, and let him appoint judges; but if he determines that the case is such that what has been done should not be reopened, whatever he decrees shall stand confirmed. If this pleases everyone?”

The synod replied: “It pleases us.”

[Note: [Col. 0402C–D] Quesnellus, with the Oxford manuscript, has: “let it be written by those who examined the case to Silvester, the Roman bishop, so that, if he judges…” Dionysius has “Julius” instead of “Silvester,” and “and if he” instead of “so that, if he.” The Thuaneus codex reads: “let it be written either by those who examined the case or by Julius, the Roman bishop. If he judges…” The Vindobonensis manuscript reads: “let it be written either by those who examined the case or by the bishop, if he judges…” These last two codices, by repeating the particle “either,” which is absent in the Oxford manuscript and in Dionysius, leave the sense incomplete and indicate that the words “by the bishops who reside in the neighboring province” were omitted by a leap. We have thought it necessary to supply them from the manuscripts of the Prisca and Isidoriana and from the very ancient Vatican Regina 1997 collection. The leap is even more evident in Vindobonensis: the ancient copyist passed from the word “bishops” to “bishop.” The name Silvester was substituted for Julius, who flourished at the time of Sardica, in the Oxford codex, so that it would agree with the period of the Council of Nicaea, whose canons are joined to the Sardican canons in this collection. The name Julius is indeed also found in the Greek text; nevertheless, we omitted it, following those Latin exemplars of different origin that preserve the complete text.]

## TITLE XXXI. That no one who has appealed is to have another bishop superimposed upon him

(Canon 4 in Dionysius, 5 in Isidore.)

[Note: [Col. 0403C] We have taken the title from the Vindobonensis codex. Quesnellus has: “That a bishop should not be superimposed upon one who has appealed.”]

Bishop Gaudentius said: “Let this also be added, if it pleases you, to the sentence you have delivered, full of holiness: when a bishop has been deposed by the judgment of those bishops who reside in neighboring places, and he has declared that his case should be conducted in the city of Rome, another bishop must absolutely not be ordained in his place, after the appeal of the one who appears to have been deposed, unless the case has been determined in the judgment of the Roman bishop.” [Note: [Col. 0403C] The words “in his place” are absent from the other collections of Dionysius, the Prisca, and the Isidoriana.]

## TITLE XXXII. When a bishop is to be ordained in another province by neighboring bishops

(Canon 5 in Dionysius, 6 in Isidore.)

[Note: [Col. 0403C] Quesnellus has: “That a bishop from another province is to be ordained.” We preferred our Vindobonensis codex, which agrees with the Vatican Regina manuscript.]

Bishop Hosius said: “If it happens that in a province in which there are very many bishops, perhaps only one bishop remains, and he through negligence is unwilling to ordain a bishop, and the people gather the bishops of a neighboring province, I judge that the bishop who resides in that province must first be summoned, and it must be shown to him that the people are requesting a ruler for themselves; and it is just that they themselves should also come and ordain the bishop together with him. But if, after being summoned by letter, he remains silent and dissimulates, and sends no reply, the people must be satisfied, so that bishops may come from the neighboring province and ordain a bishop.”

[Note: [Col. 0403C–D] Only the Thuaneus has “not many.” Quesnellus adds: “Very properly, if I am not mistaken; for this is the reason why only one bishop remains. But there is no need to abandon the reading approved also by the other Latin collections together with the common Greek text. Perhaps, however, so that the difficulty and contradiction introduced at this point may be removed entirely, the participle ‘to be ordained’ should be supplied: ‘in which there are many bishops to be ordained.’ We found this reading in the ancient version of these canons, to be published in this volume from manuscript 55 of the Veronese chapter. Compare what we shall observe concerning it in annotation 7. Shortly afterward, the codices of our collection, together with the Vatican Regina manuscript, which our author is known to have used, pass over through negligence the words ‘but he, unwilling to ordain a bishop.’ We have judged that these words, necessary to the context and omitted by a mere leap because of the repeated word ‘bishop,’ should be inserted from all the other Latin collections—Dionysius, the Prisca, and the Isidoriana—as well as from the Greek. A little later, Justellus’s Dionysius reads: ‘when the people have assembled, the bishops of the neighboring province ought first to summon that bishop … and show that the people…’ The same is read in Dionysius’s edition of the Councils, except that instead of ‘the bishops … ought’ it has ‘the bishops … must,’ which is better.]

[Note: [Col. 0403D] Quesnellus, following the Oxford codex, inserted “him”; we have deleted it, with the Thuaneus and Vindobonensis manuscripts and the other collections agreeing.]

## TITLE XXXIII. That bishops are not to be appointed in villages and small cities

(Canon 6 in Dionysius.)

[Note: [Col. 0403D] So the Vindobonensis manuscript, together with the Vatican Regina. Quesnellus has: “That a bishop should not be ordained in a village or a small city.”]

Permission is not to be given to ordain a bishop either in some village or in a small city for which one presbyter is sufficient, because there is no need for a bishop to be appointed there, lest the name and authority of the bishop be cheapened. Those invited from another province must not appoint such a bishop, except either in cities that have had bishops or in any city that is so large and so populous that it deserves to have a bishop. If this pleases everyone?”

The synod replied: “It pleases us.”

[Note: [Col. 0403D–0404C] Only Quesnellus has “however” instead of “those,” which is supported by our codices.]

## TITLE XXXIV. Concerning the reopening of a provincial synod through the representatives of the bishop of the city of Rome, if an appeal has been made

(Canon 7 in Dionysius and Isidore.)

[Note: [Col. 0404C] Thus the Vindobonensis manuscript, together with the Atrebatensis cited by Alanus Copus and the Vatican Regina. The Thuaneus codex lacks a title. Quesnellus, apparently from the Oxford codex, has: “Concerning the reopening, in a provincial synod, of the case of one who has appealed.”]

Bishop Hosius said: “It has been decided that if a bishop has been accused, and the assembled bishops of his region have judged him and deposed him from his rank; if the one who has been deposed appeals and takes refuge with the bishop of the Roman Church, and wishes to be heard; if he thinks it just that the examination be renewed, let him write to those bishops who are in the neighboring and adjoining province, so that they may investigate the matter with complete diligence and determine it according to the faith of truth. But if the one who asks for his case to be heard again moves the Roman bishop by his petition to send a presbyter from his side, it shall be within the bishop’s power what he wishes and what he judges. And if he decrees that those who are to judge in person together with the bishops should be sent, having the authority of the one by whom they were appointed, it shall be at his discretion. But if the bishop believes that the bishops are sufficient, then let him bring the case to an end and do what he judges by his most prudent counsel.”

[Note: [Col. 0404C–D] Thus the manuscripts of this collection and Dionysius. Isidore’s edition reads: “If the one who appears to have been deposed appeals and takes refuge with the most blessed bishop of the Roman Church.” The Prisca edition, which will appear in this volume from Vatican 1342, reads: “If the one who has been deposed appears to have appealed and takes refuge with the most blessed bishop of the City.” The Vatican Regina 1997 and the Commonitorium of Pope Zosimus read: “and appears to have appealed and takes refuge with the most blessed bishop of the Roman Church, and wishes him to be heard” (the latter word is absent from the Commonitorium), “and he judges it just,” and so forth. After “to be heard,” Quesnellus, from the Oxford codex alone, inserts “the Roman bishop.” These words are absent from the Thuaneus and Vindobonensis manuscripts and from the other collections. Isidore places these words after “deign.” The other collections and Zosimus’s Commonitorium have “everything.” Quesnellus, with the Oxford codex alone, has “by whom they were sent.” A little later the Vatican Regina, with Zosimus’s Commonitorium, reads: “But if he believes that the bishops suffice to put an end to the business, he shall do what he judges by his most prudent counsel.” Dionysius and the Prisca and Isidorian editions have the same, though after “bishops” they add “of the same province” or “provincial.” We retained the reading printed by Quesnellus from the Oxford manuscript, since it is also found in the Vindobonensis codex. In a marginal note Quesnellus prefers the Isidorian reading, as though it were the same in the African Codex and the Thuaneus manuscript. But since *comprovinciales* is absent from the African Codex—that is, from Zosimus’s Commonitorium inserted in that codex—we do not know whether it is read in the Thuaneus manuscript.]

## TITLE XXXV. When bishops and in what cases they should go to the imperial court

(Canon 8 in Dionysius and Isidore.)

[Note: [Col. 0405C] Quesnellus, with the Oxford codex, prefixed this title: “For what cases bishops should go to the imperial court.” We have restored the title of the Vindobonensis codex, which agrees with the Vatican Regina.]

Bishop Hosius said: “Insistent demands, excessive frequency, and unjust petitions have caused us not to have as much confidence or favor, since certain bishops do not cease going to the imperial court, especially the Africans. For, as we have learned, they reject and disdain the salutary counsels of our most holy brother and fellow bishop Gratus, so that they bring to the imperial court not merely many and various cases that are of no benefit to the Church, [Note: [Col. 0405C] Another reading has “bring.” Immediately afterward, the Vindobonensis deletes “nor” and, with Dionysius, has “or it is necessary.”] nor, as is customary and necessary, seek assistance for the poor, widows, or orphans, but even ask for secular dignities and administrative offices for certain persons. This perversity has long aroused not only murmuring but also scandals.

“It is honorable, however, for bishops to offer their intercession to those who are being oppressed by unjust force, or when a widow is afflicted or an orphan stripped of his goods, provided that these persons have a just case or petition. If therefore this pleases you, dearest brothers, decree that bishops should not approach the imperial court, except perhaps those who have been either invited or summoned by letters from the religious emperor. But since it often happens that those who suffer injury take refuge in the mercy of the Church, or those who have been condemned for their offenses to exile or to the islands, or who have received any other sentence whatsoever, assistance must be given to them and pardon requested without hesitation. If this therefore pleases you?”

All said: “It pleases us, and let it be enacted.” [Note: [Col. 0405C–D] Quesnellus, with the Oxford codex, adds “let it be established”; the Vulgate Isidore has “let it be enacted,” and Dionysius “decree it.” We followed the Thuaneus and Vindobonensis codices, which have neither. The Vatican Regina and Veronese 58 similarly read, “If therefore this pleases you.” “All,” etc. After the second “pleases” we deleted the particle “so that,” adopted by Quesnellus, on the authority of our codices and Dionysius.]

## TITLE XXXVI. Concerning sending deacons to the imperial court under the sponsorship of the metropolitan

(Canon 9 in Dionysius and Isidore.)

[Note: [Col. 0405D] Thus the Vindobonensis and Vatican Regina manuscripts. Quesnellus has: “That deacons should be sent to the imperial court by the metropolitans.”]

Bishop Hosius said: “This also must be considered by your prudence, you who have decreed that the arrogance of bishops should not strive to make them go to the imperial court. Therefore, whoever has or receives petitions of the kind we mentioned above should send them through his deacon, because the person of a minister is not odious, and he will be able to report more quickly what he has obtained. It also seems fitting that the bishops of each province should send petitions to that brother and fellow bishop of ours who resides in the metropolis, so that he may send both his deacon and the petitions, providing letters of recommendation in the same manner to our brothers and fellow bishops who at that time reside in those regions and cities in which the fortunate and cheerful Augustus governs the state. If a bishop has friends in the palace who wish to obtain something that is nevertheless honorable, he is not forbidden to ask through his deacon and to inform those whom he knows can offer a gracious intercession on behalf of an absent person.”

[Note: [Col. 0405D–0406C] The Vatican Regina 1997 reads: “who resides in the largest city, that is, the metropolis.” Isidore, together with Veronese 58, has the same, except that it uses the plural: “to the brothers and fellow bishops who reside in the largest city, that is, in the metropolis.” Here the name “largest city,” explaining the word “metropolis,” indicates the civil or geographical metropolis of the province; for ecclesiastical metropolises had not yet been established in the West at the time of the Sardican synod. See our remarks in the aforementioned treatise, part I, chapter 5, no. 4. We prefixed the particle “and” before “deacon” from the Vindobonensis codex.
