## TITLE XXXVII. That the Roman pope should examine the reasons for which he sends a deacon to the imperial court, if circumstances permit

(Canon 10 in Dionysius.)

[Note: [Col. 0406C–D] Quesnellus has: “That the causes of one going to the imperial court should be examined.” We retained the title of the Vindobonensis codex, supported by the Vatican Regina manuscript, which reads more clearly: “the cases for which a deacon is sent to the imperial court,” and so forth.]

Those who have come to Rome, as was said, should hand over the petitions they have to our most holy brother and fellow bishop, the bishop of the Roman Church, so that he may first examine them; and if they are honorable and just, let him take care and show diligence that they be carried to the imperial court.

All said that this pleased them and was an honorable policy.

(Isidore, Canon 10.)

Bishop Alipius said: “If bishops undertake the hardships of travel for orphans and widows, or for those who suffer and have just cases, they will have some reasonable justification. But now, since they chiefly seek things that cannot be obtained without the envy and reproach of everyone, it is not necessary for them themselves to go to the imperial court.” [Note: [Col. 0406D] The particle “not” is rightly omitted in Dionysius of Justellus. Shortly afterward, “of the bishops” is absent from the Vindobonensis codex, Dionysius, and the Isidorian and Prisca editions. We supplied “themselves” from the Vindobonensis and the Prisca edition. Dionysius and the Vulgate Isidore have “them.” The Vatican Regina and Veronese 58 have “those.”]

## TITLE XXXVIII. That bishops who are stationed along the route should diligently examine bishops going to the imperial court

(Canon 11 in Dionysius and Isidore.)

[Note: [Col. 0406D] Quesnellus has: “That bishops stationed along the route should examine the cases of one going to the imperial court.” We followed the Vindobonensis codex, which agrees with the Vatican Regina.]

Bishop Gaudentius said: “The measures which you have wisely provided, agreeable to the judgment and esteem of all, and pleasing to God and to human beings, can retain their force only if fear is joined to this decision. For we ourselves know that, very often, because of the imprudence of a few, the respected priestly name has been reproached. If therefore anyone, resisting the judgment of all, should wish to please ambition more than God, he must know that, after giving an account, he will lose his honor and dignity.

“This can be carried out only if each one of us who is stationed along the route, when he sees a bishop proceeding, investigates his journey, examines his reasons, and learns where he is going. And if he finds that he is going to the imperial court, let him inquire whether the matter mentioned above has been fulfilled, lest perhaps he has been invited, so that permission may be granted for him to go. [Note: [Col. 0407C–D] Because of the repetition of the words “to the imperial court,” the following passage was omitted in this collection up to the second occurrence of “to the imperial court.” It was supplied by an ancient hand in the Thuaneus and Vindobonensis codices, and we have inserted it on their authority, especially since all the other collections present the same sentence. The Vindobonensis codex clearly reveals the leap: its text reads “to go to the imperial court, let him proceed,” where the verb “let him proceed,” without the inserted words, hangs suspended and indicates that something has been omitted. Quesnellus, following the Oxford codex, transcribed the quoted words in the margin.] But if, as your holiness stated above, he goes to the imperial court because of desires and ambitions, neither let his letters be signed nor let him be received into communion. If this pleases you, it ought to be confirmed by the judgment of all.”

All said that this constitution was honorable and pleased them.

(Canon 12 in Dionysius and Isidore.)

Bishop Hosius said: “But moderation is also necessary, dearest brothers, lest suddenly some people, unaware of what has been decreed in the synod, come to those cities that lie along the route. [Note: [Col. 0407D] Quesnellus omits “some” and “suddenly”; we added them from the Vindobonensis and from Dionysius’s edition of the Councils. Other collections have “certain,” while all have “suddenly.” Dionysius of Justellus does not have this final word.] Therefore the bishop of that city must admonish and instruct him, so that, once admonished, he may send his deacon from that place and himself return to his own parish.” [Note: [Col. 0407D] Quesnellus published “the one coming” instead of “him,” which we inserted from the Thuaneus and Vindobonensis manuscripts and Dionysius. Shortly afterward the Vindobonensis reads: “though he himself, having been admonished, should return.” Dionysius, Isidore, and the Prisca edition have the better reading: “though he himself, having been admonished, should return.”]

## TITLE XXXIX. That laymen are not to be made bishops

(Canon 13 in Dionysius and Isidore.)

[Note: [Col. 0407D] Thus the Vindobonensis codex. The Vatican Regina manuscript has “not to be made quickly.” Quesnellus has: “That laymen should not become bishops.”]

Bishop Hosius said: “I also consider it necessary that you examine this most carefully: if perhaps a wealthy man, a scholar from the forum, or someone from an administrative office is requested as bishop, he is not to be ordained beforehand unless he has first served in the ministry of lector and in the office of deacon or presbyter, and then, if he is worthy, has ascended through each rank to the summit of the episcopate. For through these promotions, which will necessarily require a considerable length of time, it can be tested with what faith, modesty, seriousness, and reverence he acts. And if he has been found worthy, let him be honored with the divine priesthood.

“For it is not fitting, nor do reason or discipline permit, that a person who is a recent convert should be rashly or lightly ordained either bishop, presbyter, or deacon, especially since the Apostle, the teacher of the nations, appears to have warned and forbidden that this should happen (2 Timothy 3:6). Rather, those whose life has been tested over a long period and whose merits have been proved…” [Note: [Col. 0407D–0408C] The Vindobonensis codex, together with Dionysius of Justellus, does not have “before,” and shortly afterward reads “having completed his service,” followed by “through each.” After some material, Dionysius of Justellus alone omits “who is a recent convert.” Dionysius adds: “All said that this pleased them.” The other collections differ somewhat.]

### 72

## TITLE XL. How long a bishop should remain abroad in another city, except in a serious emergency

(Canon 14 in Dionysius and Isidore.)

[Note: [Col. 0408C] Thus our Vindobonensis codex together with the Vatican Regina. Quesnellus has: “That a bishop should not be in another Church for more than three Sundays.”]

Bishop Hosius said: “You must also enact this: if a bishop wishes to pass from one city or from his own province into another province, and, serving ambition more than devotion, wishes to remain for a long time in another city—for perhaps it happens that the bishop of the place is neither so well equipped nor so learned, and the one who has arrived begins to despise him and frequently preach in order to dishonor and weaken his standing, so that on this pretext he does not hesitate to leave the Church assigned to him and transfer to another—then determine a period. For it is inhumane not to receive a bishop, but if he remains too long, it is harmful. This therefore must be provided against.

“I remember that our predecessors established that if a layman in the city where he lives does not hold an assembly for three Sundays, that is, for three weeks, he should be deprived of communion. If this has been established concerning laymen, much more is it neither permitted nor proper for a bishop, if there is no such serious necessity as compels him to remain absent from his Church longer than the period stated above.”

All said that this pleased them.

[Note: [Col. 0408C–D] Dionysius and the Thuaneus codex have: “from another city has come to another city, or from his own province to another province; and serving ambition…” We retained Quesnellus’s reading because it agrees with the Vindobonensis manuscript; from it alone, together with the other codices, we wrote “from his own province,” where Quesnellus omitted “from” and “his.” Quesnellus adds: “how long he should remain there.” We deleted this on the authority of all our codices, especially the Vindobonensis. Thus the Thuaneus and Vindobonensis codices, together with Dionysius, Isidore, and the Prisca edition. Quesnellus, with the Oxford manuscript, has: “should not hesitate to leave his own Church.” Dionysius and the Vulgate Isidore have “in the preceding council.” Veronese 58, which contains the collection received by Isidore, the Vatican Regina, and the Prisca edition of Vatican 1342, agreeing with the Greek text, have “in an earlier period.” This decree is found in canon 21 of the Council of Eliberis. Quesnellus has: “A bishop is neither permitted nor is it proper for him.” We preferred the Vindobonensis codex and Dionysius’s edition of the Councils.]

## TITLE XLI. That a bishop may not be absent for more than three weeks

(Canon 15 in Dionysius and Isidore.)

[Note: [Col. 0409C] Thus our Vindobonensis and Vatican Regina codices. Quesnellus has: “That a bishop should not remain in another’s estates for more than three weeks.”]

[The supplied source ends here.]

Osius the bishop said: Since nothing ought to be omitted, there are certain of our brothers and fellow bishops who do not possess property in the city in which they appear to have been established as bishops, or at least possess only a small amount there, while elsewhere they are known to have suitable estates, or [73] affection for relatives toward whom they may show indulgence.

[Note: [Col. 0409C] Quesnellus reads: “who have a small holding in the city in which they appear to have been established as bishops.” The reading of the Vindobonensis manuscript, with which Dionysius Justellus wholly agrees [Col. 0409D], was preferred. Vatican 1342 and Isidore agree, adding only “possess” after “in the city.” Vatican Regina and Veronensis 58 read “have” for “possess.”]

These men should be permitted, for the time being, to go to their estates and arrange or administer the produce of their labor, so that, if it is necessary for them to remain there for three Sundays—that is, for three weeks—they may stay on their own farms rather than elsewhere.

[Note: [Col. 0409D] The Vindobonensis manuscript, with Dionysius, Isidore, and the old edition, reads: “after three Sundays, that is, after three weeks.” Vatican Regina and the Greek text approve the reading published by Quesnellus from his manuscripts.]

Or, if there is a nearby city in which there is a presbyter, let them go there, so that they may not appear to spend the Lord’s Day without the Church. In this way, their domestic affairs will not suffer loss through their [Col. 0409B] absence, and by not coming frequently to the city in which the bishop resides, they will avoid the suspicion of ostentation and ambition. All said that this pleased them.

## TITLE XLII. On clerics who have been removed and are not to be received by others (Canon 16 of Dionysius and Isidore)

[Note: [Col. 0409D] Quesnellus: “Those excommunicated by another are not to be received.” We have restored the reading of the Vindobonensis and Vatican Regina manuscripts.]

Osius the bishop said: This also pleases us all [Note: [Col. 0409D] Another reading is “may it please”; Vatican Regina, “it will please.” The Thuanus manuscript then reads “or any of the clerics”; later, the Vindobonensis reads “to whom he has fled.”]: whether it be a deacon, a presbyter, or any cleric, if he has been deprived of communion by his own bishop and has gone to another bishop, and the bishop to whom he has fled knows that he was cast out by his own bishop, he ought not to grant him communion. If he does so, he should know that he will have to give an account before the bishops who have been summoned.

[Note: [Col. 0409D] The Vindobonensis and Oxford manuscripts, together with Dionysius, read “causes”; thereafter, the Thuanus manuscript has “agreement” instead of “peace.” Dionysius, however, reads: “and he will preserve peace and maintain concord.”]

All said: This statute will preserve peace and maintain concord.

## TITLE XLIII. On those excommunicated, to be heard by neighboring bishops (Canon 17 of Dionysius and Isidore)

[Note: [Col. 0409D] Thus read the Vindobonensis and Vatican Regina manuscripts. Quesnellus: “That an excommunicated cleric may appeal.”]

[Col. 0409C]

Osius the bishop said:

[Note: [Col. 0410C] The Vatican Regina and Veronensis 58 manuscripts, and the memorandum of Zosimus inserted into the Sixth Council of Carthage in Isidore, read: “What still troubles me.” A little later, instead of *commovetur*, some read *commoveatur*.]

I must not keep silent about what still troubles me. If some bishop, perhaps hot-tempered—which ought not to be—quickly and harshly becomes provoked against his presbyter or deacon and wishes to expel him from the Church, care must be taken that an innocent man is not condemned or deprived of communion. Therefore,

[Note: [Col. 0410C] The memorandum of Zosimus, together with the Vatican Regina manuscript, reads: “Let the one who has been expelled have the power …”]

the man who has been cast out must have the power to appeal to neighboring bishops, so that his case may be heard and [Col. 0410A] examined more carefully, for an audience ought not to be denied to one who requests it.

And that bishop, whether he expelled him justly or unjustly, should patiently accept that the matter be examined, and that his judgment either be approved by the [74] greater number or corrected.

[Note: [Col. 0410D] Other collections read “be treated.” A little later, Dionysius and Isidore read “be examined,” so that his judgment may either be proved.]

Nevertheless, before everything has been carefully and faithfully investigated, no one should presume to admit to communion a person who has been separated from communion, before the inquiry has been completed.

But if those who assemble to hear the case perceive in the clerics zeal and arrogance—for it is not fitting that a bishop should suffer insult or abuse—they should rebuke them in more severe language, so that they may obey a bishop who gives honorable commands. For just as a bishop ought to display toward clerics sincere love and charity, so likewise ministers ought to display toward their bishop unfeigned obedience.

[Note: [Col. 0410D] Dionysius Justellus likewise reads *fastidium* (“disdain”); another edition of Dionysius, together with Vatican Regina, Veronensis 58, and the old edition of Justellus, reads *fastigium* (“haughtiness” or “presumption”).]

## TITLE XLIV. On not soliciting the clerics of another bishop (Canon 18 of Dionysius and Isidore)

[Col. 0410B]

Januarius the bishop said: Let your holiness also decree that no bishop may solicit the ecclesiastical minister of the bishop of another city and ordain him in his own parishes.

All said: It pleases us, because disputes commonly arise from such conflicts. Therefore, the judgment of all forbids anyone to dare to do this.

## TITLE XLV. On not making another bishop’s clerics clerics without their own bishop’s consent (Canon 19 of Dionysius and Isidore)

[Note: [Col. 0410D] The Vindobonensis and Vatican Regina manuscripts agree also in this title. Quesnellus: “That the ordination of another’s cleric should not be valid.”]

Osius the bishop said: We all establish this also: if anyone from another parish wishes to ordain another’s minister without the consent and will of that minister’s bishop, his ordination shall not be valid. Whoever [Col. 0410C] among our brothers and fellow bishops usurps this authority must be admonished and corrected.

(Canon 20 of Dionysius and Isidore.)

Aetius the bishop said: You are not unaware of how great and important the city of the Thessalonians is. Presbyters and deacons often come to it from other regions, and they are not content to remain there for a short time; rather, they remain there, or at least are only with difficulty compelled to return to their own places after long intervals.

[Note: [Col. 0410D] The Vindobonensis reads *sed aut essent ibi* (“but either they were there”); it seems that, together with Dionysius and the Vatican Regina manuscript, one should read *sed aut resident ibi* (“but either they reside there”). Shortly afterward, instead of “intervals for their own places,” we have emended the text from the Vindobonensis, in agreement with Dionysius and other manuscripts. Quesnellus reads “periods.”]

All said: The periods that have been established concerning bishops and concerning their persons must be observed.

## 75 TITLE XLVI. On receiving those who suffer danger and persecution in defense of the truth (Canon 21)

[Note: [Col. 0411A] Quesnellus: “On receiving those who have been expelled for the Catholic faith.” The Vindobonensis manuscript always presents the same titles as the Vatican Regina manuscript.]

[Col. 0411A]

Osius the bishop said: At the suggestion of our brother and fellow bishop Olympius, this also pleased us: if anyone has suffered violence and has been unjustly expelled for the sake of discipline and the Catholic confession, or for the defense of the truth, and, fleeing danger, an innocent [76] and devoted man has come to another [Col. 0411B] city, he should not be prevented from remaining [Col. 0412A] there as long as he can either return or obtain a remedy for his injury.

[Note: [Col. 0411A] Quesnellus reads: “for the defense and confession of the Catholic faith and of the truth.” We have followed the Vindobonensis and Thuanus manuscripts, which agree with Dionysius and the old edition. Shortly afterward, for “from another city,” the Oxford and Vindobonensis manuscripts read “from another city.”]

For it is harsh not to receive one who is suffering persecution; rather, generous goodwill and kindness should be shown to him.

[Note: [Col. 0411B] Other collections read: “may have received or may receive a remedy.”]

[Note: [Col. 0411B] The Thuanus manuscript adds: “The entire synod said: The whole Catholic Church, spread throughout the entire world, shall observe all that has been established.” Those who had assembled also subscribed. These words are found likewise in Dionysius, inserted among the Councils, volume II, column 680—or rather, in the manuscripts of the Dionysius-Hadrian collection, from which the printed editions were taken—as well as in the old edition, which we shall publish in this volume. Quesnellus noted that, apart from Dionysius and the Thuanus manuscript, these words are found neither in the Greek text nor in other printed editions. Whatever may be the case concerning the Greek text—which we have elsewhere shown to be not a translation but an original text, just as is the Latin text—certainly, apart from Dionysius, or more accurately the Dionysius-Hadrian copies, the old edition also presents the cited words, drawn from two very ancient collections that we shall publish.]

[Note: [Col. 0411B] The following words conclude this first chapter in the Vindobonensis manuscript. The Oxford manuscript differs slightly: “These are the canons or decrees of the Council of Nicaea. All the bishops subscribed as follows: ‘I, that bishop of that city and province, believe thus, as written above.’” Only the scribe who copied this manuscript from an older exemplar in the eleventh or twelfth century added the following note: “It should be known, however, that in recent copies”—by “copies” he means the Dionysian and Isidorian copies, which in his time were more common and presented the Sardican canons as distinct from the Nicene canons—“twenty-six chapters are lacking. But this manuscript was transcribed from a very ancient exemplar; therefore no one should doubt the authenticity of the writings, either in this first chapter of the Nicene canons or in all those that follow, even though they are found differently in recent copies.”

Two other collections of different origin that were available to us, and which join the Nicene and Sardican canons, append a concluding formula after the last canon attributing all the canons transcribed to the Council of Nicaea.

In Vatican Regina manuscript 1997 the text reads: “Here end the decrees of the council,” followed by a catalogue of the Nicene Fathers: “Osius, bishop of the city of Corduba, thus believes. Victor and Vincentius, etc.” At the end: “The Nicene Council ends.”

In Veronensis manuscript 58: “Here end the decrees of the Council of Nicaea.” Then the Nicene Creed and a catalogue of the bishops of that synod are appended.

In the manuscript of Dionysius Justellus, and in the two pure Dionysian copies, Vatican 5845 and Vatican Palat. 577, in which the Sardican canons are presented separately from the Nicene, the following is appended after the last Sardican canon: “All the bishops subscribed as follows: ‘I, that bishop of that city and province, believe thus, as it is written above.’” We have explained the rationale of this formula in the *Treatise on Collections*, part II, chapter 1, section 3.]

The canons or decrees of the Council of Nicaea end here; all the bishops subscribed as follows: “I, that bishop of that city and that province, believe thus, as written above.”

## 77 ADMONITION TO THE SECOND CHAPTER

### On the Epitome of the Canons of Hippo; the need and excellence of this edition; where and when it was composed, and its vindication

[Col. 0411]

### 1

The following epitome of the canons of Hippo, which has come to light from the manuscripts of the present collection, shows its importance by the fact that without it we would lack not only knowledge of the canons of the celebrated Synod of Hippo of the year 393, which laid the foundations of African discipline, but also the complete plenary Council of Carthage of the year 397, in which this same epitome was inserted.

Although both Dionysius Exiguus and the ancient author of the collection of African canons received by Isidore present the Synod of Carthage of 397, neither of them accurately represents, as he ought, the epitome of the canons of Hippo. Compare our epitome with them: you will find neither all the canons among them, nor even those which they present described in the same order and repeatedly in the same words.

After canon 33 of the Council of Carthage of 419, Dionysius, speaking of the Council of Hippo of 393, writes: “The acts of this council have not been transcribed because the things established there have been inserted above.” One might suppose that the thirty-three preceding canons contain the Hipponian canons. Yet, first, not all thirty-three are Hipponian, nor are those that are identified by any notation.

Moreover, those among them that belong to the canons of Hippo, or to our epitome, having been repeated and adopted by the Fathers of the Council of Carthage of 419, are presented in another order and often in other words. Thus some things are found added, others removed, and others altered, as will be clear to anyone who compares them. See the preceding *Treatise*, part II, chapter 3, section 3.

We shall not conceal the fact that Dionysius recites other canons of the epitome—which are not found among the first thirty-three canons—among those of the Council of Carthage of 397, from chapter 35 through chapter 47 of the African Code. What is distinctive about these canons is that, although they were excerpted from the acts of that same synod, or from the epitome inserted into that synod, they are expressed in the same words.

But if these canons too are joined with those which were recited from the Hipponian canons among the first thirty-three, you will still recognize that some canons of our epitome are missing from Dionysius. For, apart from the letter of the Byzaceni, the Nicene Creed, and certain passages prefixed to the canons—which together constituted the canons in the Synod of 397—you will search in vain for canons 16, 19, 20, 21, 34, 35, and 37 of our epitome.

### 2

In Isidore’s collection, under the title of the Third Council of Carthage of 397, several canons of the epitome are found, but not all. Moreover, the order is greatly disturbed.

Finally, almost all the canons of the epitome that the author of this collection found transcribed among the thirty-three canons of the Synod of 419 were reproduced by him with the distinctive readings of that synod, not with those that appeared in the Council of 397 or in the epitome itself.

Dionysius, who had given these canons with those readings in the Council of 419, omitted them when reporting the [Col. 0413] Synod of 397. But the author of the collection attributed to Isidore, since he decided to omit the first thirty-three canons when reporting the Synod of 419, transferred them with those same readings to the Synod of 397.

From these editions, so different and responsible for so many difficulties, who could have safely recovered the true canons of Hippo, unless the epitome itself had come to light?

### 3

The first evidence of it was published [79] by Father Crabbus from an ancient manuscript of the monastery of Saint Bavo in Flanders. Besides the table of titles and the letter of the Byzaceni peculiar to our collection, which demonstrate that the cited codex belongs to the same collection, he transcribed the Nicene Creed and one canon at the beginning and another at the end, adding the following note (volume II of the Venetian edition of the Councils, column 1411):

“Here only the canons of the titles are written, with the chapters omitted, for the sake of avoiding length, because nearly everything is set out at length in the Third Council of Carthage held immediately above; here, however, reference is made to those passages.”

Crabbus did not follow his manuscript with complete accuracy in the few passages he presented, as we have discovered from our copies. First, he prefixed to the titles a complete canon that does not concern the titles. As a result, some have regarded the titles, increased by one in number, as the abbreviated canons themselves.

Other passages that he recorded more freely or altered, and which cannot be attributed to the manuscript exemplar, will readily be seen by anyone who compares them with our epitome.

Just as Crabbus printed here what was lacking in the Third Council of Carthage in Isidore, so in his edition of that same council he inserted five of its canons—4, 15, 19, 24, and 47—from ancient manuscripts, using a distinct typeface because of variation in the readings. It is believed that by “ancient manuscripts” he meant Isidorian copies that differed in their readings. Yet only one codex of Saint Bavo is indicated; for this reason Crabbus uses the singular in his note on chapter 47: “A certain ancient codex reads as follows.” The readings are those of our epitome, which he found in the same codex.

### 4

Quesnellus brought forth the complete epitome from the manuscripts of this collection, but not entirely complete, for he omitted both the titles and the Nicene Creed.

Only the codices of this collection are usually cited. Yet Father Coustantius testifies in the preface to volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, section 113, that the same epitome is also contained in a very ancient collection which he calls the Corbeiensis.

Moreover, we have found two other manuscript collections no less ancient containing the same epitome: one in Barberinus 2888, and the other in the manuscript of the chapter of Verona 55. Thus four ancient collections of different origin preserve this abridgment of the Hipponian canons.

### 5

There have been learned men who suspected this epitome of being fabricated, or at least interpolated. Four considerations chiefly moved them:

1. They contend that the synod in which this epitome was composed was not Carthaginian but Byzacene, and that it was held solely for the Byzaceni. They think this is suggested by the context of the letter prefixed to it, and therefore believe that the letter was addressed to the Byzacene bishops who had not attended the synod, rather than to the bishops of the other provinces of Africa, as the inscription states.

2. When cited by Ferrandus, a deacon of the Church of Carthage, several canons of the epitome are not called Hipponian but Carthaginian, and are numbered in a way that does not agree with the epitome.

3. Possidius testifies in chapter 8 of his *Life* that Augustine the bishop had arranged that a decree should be established that the statutes of councils, or of the council, should be read to ordinands, so that they might never plead ignorance of them. This canon cannot be Hipponian, since Augustine had not yet attained the episcopate at the time of the Council of Hippo.

4. Several matters that certainly had been decreed at the Council of Hippo, as is clear from the interventions of the Synod of 397, are not found in this epitome.

### 6

As to the first point, the opinion that this was a Byzacene synod ought to be sufficiently excluded by those very ancient collections of different origin which agree in asserting that it was a Carthaginian council, as well as by the words of the letter itself, which state that the Byzacene bishops met in the city of Carthage.

To establish this more clearly, it is certain, first, that Mizo, primate of the province of Byzacena, before the day appointed for the plenary synod—which, according to the decree of Hippo, was the tenth day before the Kalends of September—came to Carthage with several bishops from his province and held a discussion there together with Aurelius. Aurelius himself testified to this in the intervention prefixed to canon 34 of the African Code.

Second, it is certain that the same Byzaceni, unable to await the day of the synod before returning to their sees, gave Aurelius an epitome of the canons addressed to the plenary synod, together with the letter that is clearly prefixed to our epitome.

Hence Aurelius, in the same intervention, mentions “the letter of our brothers the Byzaceni,” as well as “the epitome which they appended to that letter and summoned to this gathering.”

Mizo also gave Aurelius another private letter, asking that the same epitome be examined in the plenary synod and, if anything should be noticed more carefully, reformed for the better.

After the Byzaceni had departed, the appointed day, the tenth before the Kalends of September, arrived. Aurelius explained in the same intervention what had been done, in these words:

“When the letter of our Byzacene priests had been read, and when what they themselves, having anticipated the time and day of the council, had discussed with me was read to your Charity,” and so forth.

You see that Aurelius affirms that the Byzaceni, who had anticipated the time and day of the council, had previously discussed matters with him; and that on the very day appointed for the council both their letter and whatever they had discussed with him were read.

Since the Numidians were absent on that tenth day before the Kalends of September, the council was postponed until the fifth day before the Kalends of the same month. At that session the cited letter and the epitome were again read:

“Let the letter of our brothers the Byzaceni, and also the epitome, summoned to this gathering, be read.”

Therefore, the discussion between the Byzaceni and Aurelius, which had been read in the earlier session together with their letter, is understood to have been the epitome. Consequently, this epitome was composed not at a Byzacene gathering but at the Carthaginian assembly in the presence of Aurelius.

It is therefore not surprising that the name of Aurelius is found not only in the inscription but also in the subscriptions of this epitome.

If, in the salutation that closes the letter, only the name of Mizo is written, it should be observed that another salutation without a name precedes Mizo’s salutation. We believe that this belongs to Aurelius, precisely as the salutation without a name placed first in the synodical letter of the bishops of Gaul to Saint Leo belongs to Ravennius of Arles, and is prefixed to the others, which are marked with the proper names of the other bishops. See volume I, letter 99, column 1110, note 24.

Although this epitome was arranged for the Byzaceni, since its review and confirmation were requested from the plenary synod, it was addressed to the bishops of the other provinces of Africa, who were to assemble in the same plenary synod after the departure of the Byzaceni—“summoned to this gathering,” as Aurelius says. Therefore, the inscription gives the names of the other provinces.

If the letter to which Aurelius testified that this epitome had been attached is believed to have been addressed only to the Byzaceni who had not taken part in the discussion or in the synod at which the epitome was written—although this is not clear—then the inscription prefixed to it should not be regarded as belonging to the letter alone, but as common to both the letter and the epitome, signifying that both were addressed to the Fathers of the plenary council.

### 7

The objection drawn from Ferrandus can easily be answered if one considers that he cited the canons of our epitome not as Hipponian but as those of the Carthaginian council because this epitome was inserted into the plenary Council of Carthage of 397.

Likewise, the Synod of Boniface in 525 cited several canons of the epitome from the Third Council under Aurelius, which is the same as the plenary council of the year 397. [The supplied text reads “597”; the context indicates the evident numeral error 397.]

If Ferrandus’s numbers do not agree with the numbers assigned in our collection or in the simple and separate epitome, [Col. 0415] they nevertheless agree with the numbers assigned to it in the plenary council, as will become clear from the *Treatise*, part II, chapter 3, section 3.

It follows, therefore, that our epitome was summoned to the same synod and was composed, above all, by the Byzaceni together with Aurelius in the city of Carthage.

### 8

When Possidius states in chapter 8 that Saint Augustine took care that it should be established by councils that the statutes of all the priests should be made known by the ordainers to those being ordained or already ordained, because Augustine himself had been ordained in the same see of Hippo while Valerius was still alive, contrary to the Nicene prohibition, which he did not then know, many explain this as referring to the plenary synod of 397, in which we have shown from the subscriptions of the synod itself that Augustine already participated as a bishop. See the *Treatise*, part II, chapter 3, section 3.

But the canon that issued that decree does not properly belong to this synod; it belongs to the Hipponian epitome. Therefore, it was established at the earlier Council of Hippo, when Augustine had not yet ascended to the episcopate.

What, then, follows? The Council of Nicaea was known to the Africans through the very ancient version brought into Africa by Caecilianus, from which the Creed had been inserted among the Hipponian canons. It is incredible that Augustine, when he was ordained bishop, could have been ignorant of it.

The prohibition just mentioned is not clearly expressed in any Nicene canon. Only in chapter 8, concerning the Cathari, it is decreed that, when their bishops come over to Catholic unity, if they are in places where Catholic bishops are found, they should be granted the honor of the presbyterate or merely the name of bishop, so that two bishops should not be found existing in one city.

This particular decree does indeed contain a general prohibition, but it can easily escape [83] the attention of readers. It therefore seems more likely that Augustine once failed to notice these words when he read the council.

This observation was prompted by Rufinus’s abridgment, which presents a distinct and general prohibition in canon 10, in these words: “There shall not be two bishops in one city.”

Therefore, when this abridgment of the Nicene canons, inserted into Rufinus’s history and known to Augustine, had disclosed such a prohibition, Augustine should be understood to have taken care that the councils of Africa should establish that the statutes of all the priests be read to those ordained or about to be ordained.

But this cannot refer to the Synod of 397, since Rufinus’s abridgment and history had not yet appeared. It must refer to the later provincial synods of Numidia, and especially to the general synod of 419. In that synod, where the canon of the epitome was repeated, as was customary, the word *council*, which is found in the purer manuscripts of the epitome in chapter 2, was replaced by *councils*, so that the statutes of all the priests might be included; other expressions more clearly explaining Augustine’s meaning were also substituted.

### 9

Finally, two details are attributed to the Council of Hippo that do not appear in our epitome: first, that the day appointed for the plenary synod was the tenth day before the Kalends of September; second, that the provinces were to be visited during the time of the council.

But since abridgments do not ordinarily set out every detail individually, this small omission has no force for rejecting as fabricated an epitome that is proved genuine by so many documents. Add to this that we think there were certain reasons why these details were omitted when the abridgment was composed. See what will be said in note 42.

Thus this epitome appears to have been sufficiently and abundantly vindicated.

### 10

A few words should be added concerning the manuscripts.

The exemplar of the chapter of Verona, like the codices of the present collection, begins the sequence of numbers with the canon “That readers.” But the Barberini manuscript collection assigns numbers also to the material prefixed to that canon.

Both codices differ in the division of the canons, and the difference will be noted in its proper places.

Only the codices of this collection have preserved Mizo’s letter for us.

A distinctive feature of the excellent Veronese manuscript is that it presents the epitome without the additions found in the other copies.

Besides these Veronese and Barberini codices, which we were able to collate, we used manuscript 39 of the Caesarean Library at Vienna, which properly belongs to this collection.

We shall also use the notable copy Vatican Palat. 574, which excerpted several canons of the epitome from the Council of Carthage of 397.

Quesnellus appended numerous marginal notes from the African Code—or more accurately, from Dionysius Exiguus—and from the Third Council of Carthage as found in Isidore, to indicate the number under which the canons of this epitome occur in those documents.

We shall omit these notes here, because we have indicated them more carefully in the *Treatise*, part II, chapter 3, section 3, where, in restoring the Council of Carthage of 397, we reviewed the canons of the epitome inserted into it. There we also cited the titles and canons of the epitome given by Ferrandus, which are mentioned in the Synod of Boniface of Carthage.

## 85 CHAPTER II

[Note: [Col. 0415A] The Vindobonensis codex reads: “Here begin the chapters and canons held at Carthage,” and so forth. The Hubertine manuscript, cited by Father Coustantius in the preface to volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, page XCVII, reads: “Here begin the chapters of the Council of Carthage held,” and so forth. The same wording is found in Barberinus 2888.

Quesnellus notes regarding this inscription that the Ides of August are indeed prefixed in the Thuanus manuscript. But in the Oxford manuscript, he says, it seems to be read as the day before the Nones of August.

Yet the Ides of August are consistently found also in the manuscripts cited above, in the Hubertine manuscript of Coustantius, which belong to different and very ancient collections. Another example is provided by manuscript 59 of the chapter of Verona, which contains a very ancient abridgment of the canons. In it, number 20 reads: “From the Synod of Carthage, on the Ides of August, in the consulship of Ceranius; read Caesarius.”

Father Dominicus Mansi also printed this abridgment of the Council of Carthage from a similar manuscript at Lucca, in volume I of the *Supplement to the Councils*, page 255, under the title: “From the Council of Carthage in Africa, on the Ides of August, in the consulship of Ceranius.”]

### CANONS HELD AT CARTHAGE ON THE IDES OF AUGUST, UNDER THE CONSULS ATTICUS AND CAESARIUS

[Col. 0415A]

[Note: [Col. 0416A] We have inserted these titles of the canons, which Quesnellus omitted. Although they are absent from the less accurate Oxford manuscript, they are nevertheless read not only in our Vindobonensis manuscript but also in the Hubertine manuscript, as Father Coustantius testifies at the place cited, and in the Thuanus manuscript itself, as Quesnellus testifies in dissertation 13, section 2.

Crabbus, who possessed a similar manuscript of this collection from the library of the monastery of Saint Bavo in Flanders, also published these same titles of the canons; they can be read in volume II of the *Councils*, column 1411.]

### Titles of the canons

I. That readers should not greet the people.

II. That instructed clerics should be promoted.

[Col. 0416A]

III. That the sacrament should not be given to catechumens.

IV. The Eucharist should not be given to the bodies of the dead.

V. That a council should be summoned every year.

VI. If a bishop is accused, let him refer his case to the primate of the province.

VII. If a bishop who has been accused does not come to the annual council, he shall be judged to have incurred the sentence of condemnation.

[Note: [Col. 0416B] Crabbus’s codex reads: “He shall be judged to have received the sentence of his condemnation.”]

[Col. 0417A]

VIII. If a presbyter has been accused, let the bishop hear his case with five colleagues from neighboring bishops; if he is a deacon, with two.

[Note: [Col. 0417C] Crabbus reads: “Let his case be examined; a deacon with two.”]

IX. If a charge has been brought against a bishop or cleric.

X. That ecclesiastical judges should not appeal a case to other judges.

XI. That the sons of clerics should not put on spectacles.

XII. That the sons of bishops should not be joined with heretics.

XIII. That bishops and clerics should not cast out their sons.

XIV. That bishops and clerics should not give any of their property except to Catholics.

[Note: [Col. 0417C] The Vindobonensis reads “should not confer.” The context persuaded us that Crabbus’s reading is preferable.]

XV. [Note: [Col. 0417C] The Vindobonensis manuscript reads: “Let neither bishop nor presbyter … not be.” Crabbus’s reading, which we have followed, is better.] A bishop, presbyter, or deacon shall not be a tenant or leaseholder.

## 86

XVI. That a cleric should not live with foreign women.

XVII. Concerning sacred orders.

XVIII. Concerning readers.

XIX. That no one should retain another’s cleric.

XX. That no one should be ordained before he has been tested.

XXI. That in prayers neither the Son should be named for the Father nor the Father for the Son.

XXII. That no cleric should receive more than he has given.

XXIII. In the sacraments nothing else should be offered except bread and wine mixed with water.

XXIV. [Note: [Col. 0417D] Thus in the same Crabbus manuscript. In the Vindobonensis, less correctly: “That neither bishops nor presbyters … should not approach.”] That bishops, presbyters, or clerics should not approach widows or virgins alone.

XXV. The bishop of the principal see should not be called the chief of the priests.

[Col. 0417C]

XXVI. Clerics should neither eat nor drink in a tavern.

XXVII. That a bishop should not travel overseas.

XXVIII. That the sacraments of the altar should be celebrated by those who are fasting.

XXIX. That neither bishops nor clerics should feast in the Church.

XXX. That a presbyter should not reconcile a penitent without consulting the bishop.

XXXI. That virgins should be entrusted to older women.

XXXII. That the sick should be baptized.

XXXIII. That reconciliation should not be denied to those who return.

[Col. 0418A]

XXXIV. That a presbyter should not prepare chrism.

XXXV. Clerics should not remain in another city.

XXXVI. [Note: [Col. 0417D] Crabbus: “What the canonical Scriptures are that are to be read in the Church, and that no others besides them should be read.”] These are the canonical Scriptures that are read in the Church; nothing else should be read besides them.

XXXVII. That Donatists should be received among the number of the laity.

XXXVIII. That a bishop should not be ordained by fewer than three bishops.

## 87

XXXIX. [Note: [Col. 0417D] Crabbus’s manuscript: “Concerning those who know that they were baptized according to no testimony, that they should be baptized.”] Infants whose baptism is uncertain should be baptized without hesitation.

To our most beloved brothers and fellow bishops of the various provinces of Numidia, of both Mauritanias, Tripolitania, and the proconsular province:

[Note: [Col. 0417D] Quesnellus reads “the consular province.” The reading in Crabbus’s codex is better. The council at which this abridgment was composed, celebrated by the Byzaceni together with Aurelius on the Ides of August, sent the epitome of the canons of Hippo to the bishops of the other provinces of Africa, who were to assemble in the plenary synod so that it might be confirmed by them, as we noted from Aurelius’s words in the preceding admonition.

Among such provinces, the proconsular province, which held the first place, certainly ought not to have been omitted. Nor should “consular province” be understood with Harduinus as the province of Byzacena, for Byzacena is never designated by the general name “consular province.”]

Aurelius, Mizo, and the other bishops.

For the sake of ecclesiastical usefulness, when we had assembled together in the city of Carthage [Col. 0418B] [Note: [Col. 0418C] Thus from the Vindobonensis manuscript and Crabbe’s copy, *conveniremus* (“we should assemble”). The Thuanus manuscript has *in Carthaginensem urbem convenimus* (“we assembled in the city of Carthage”). Quesnellus has *convenissemus* (“we had assembled”).] it was reported by many that certain persons, with reckless defiance, were refusing to observe those measures which had long before been formulated at the Council of Hippo and which are known to have been beneficially enacted and established according to law for the correction of discipline. As an excuse for such excesses, some alleged that they had omitted these measures because they were unaware of what had already been established by legal enactment.

For this reason, by common agreement [Note: From these words some have thought that this letter was addressed to the bishops of Byzacena and consequently that the heading presenting it as a letter addressed to the bishops of the other provinces of Africa is false. See what we discussed in the preliminary notice, no. 6.] we judged that these matters should be brought to the notice of everyone throughout the whole province of Byzacena [Note: [Col. 0418D] The Vindobonensis manuscript has *ab his* (“by these”). Crabbe has *in his quisquis* (“among these, whoever”), incorrectly.], so that from now on whoever proves to be a reckless violator of the decrees may know that he has incurred the loss of his own status. We have appended to this letter a brief summary of the enactments, in which everything appears to have been included and certain matters established more carefully [Note: Crabbe has *custodita* (“preserved”), incorrectly; and after a little further on, instead of *subdi fecimus* (“we appended”), Hardouin noted *subdidimus* (“we added”).], so that, by reviewing in summary what has been decreed [Col. 0418C], we may take greater care to observe it.

[Note: [Col. 0418D] This first greeting appears to belong to Aurelius. See the preceding preliminary notice, no. 6.]

We wish you, brothers, always to prosper in God and to remember us. And in the hand of the aged Mizonius [Note: Up to this point the Oxonian manuscript; what follows was supplied by Quesnellus from the Thuanus and Crabbe manuscripts. It is also read in the Vindobonensis manuscript.]: We wish you, brothers, always to rejoice blessedly in the Lord and to remember us.

## Abbreviated Statutes of the Council of Hippo, with certain of them compared with and more carefully examined at the Council of Carthage together with the bishops of Byzacena

These are as follows.

The profession and faith of the Council of Nicaea was recited and confirmed [Note: We supplied what follows from the Crabbe, Vindobonensis, and Hubertinus manuscripts preserved by P. Coustant. Following the Oxonian manuscript, Quesnellus omitted the creed [Col. 0419B], although he noted that it is found in the Thuanus manuscript. Thus the four better manuscripts of this collection transmit this creed, which we have proved truly to belong to the summary in our *Treatise on Collections*, part II, chapter 3, § 3, no. 3. It is absent from the Veronensis manuscript 55 of the different collection; but it is copied in another collection, manuscript Barberinus 2888, where it forms the first chapter. It is important to present this creed, since it belongs to the ancient translation which Caecilianus brought back to Africa from the Council of Nicaea. See what we said in the *Treatise*, part I, chapter 2, no. 3. We have also read this creed with Dionysius, that is, in the *Code of the Canons of the African Church*, vol. II of the Councils, col. 1260; with Isidore’s collection, vol. III, col. 448; and with the Carthaginian synod of Boniface in the year 525, vol. V, col. 778, where it is wrongly attributed to Atticus, as we observed in the same *Treatise*.] and it runs as follows:

We believe in one [Col. 0419A] God, the Father almighty, maker of things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, born only-begotten from the Father, that is, from the substance of the Father; God from God, light from light, true God from true God; begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father, which the Greeks call *omousion*; through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth; who for us human beings and for our salvation came down, was incarnate, and became human through the Virgin Mary [Note: The African Code, Isidore, and the Synod of Boniface omit *per Virginem Mariam* (“through the Virgin Mary”) [Col. 0419C]. Crabbe has only *per Virginem* (“through the Virgin”). The reading of the text is supported by the Vindobonensis and Barberinus manuscripts. A little later, the first three copies have *in coelos* (“into the heavens”) instead of *in coelum* (“into heaven”); in the Barberinus manuscript, *in coelis* (“in the heavens”) is a scribal error.]; he suffered and rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven [Note: The African Code and Isidore add: “he sits at the right hand of the Father; from there—or, in some copies, from where—he will come.”], coming to judge the living and the dead; and in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was a time when he was not,” and, “Before he was born, he was not,” and, “That he was made from things that did not exist,” or from another substance [Col. 0419B], saying that the Son of God is changeable and transformable—the catholic Church and apostolic discipline anathematize them [Note: The African Code, Isidore, and Boniface’s Synod have only “the catholic and apostolic Church.”].

[Note: In the Barberinus manuscript this is chapter 2. Quesnellus next printed *propter controversiam quae* (“because of the controversy which”). It was also decided, because of the error which often arises [Col. 0420A], that all the provinces of Africa should take care to receive from the Church of Carthage the determination of the date of Easter.

And from this it was decided that no one should usurp the people of another.

Mauretania Sitifensis was permitted, when it requested this, to have its own primate [Note: Quesnellus, together with the Oxonian manuscript, has *in longinquioribus* (“in the more distant regions”). In the Carthaginian synod of the year 419, this canon is explained in chapter 17 of the African Code as permitting Mauretania Sitifensis to separate from Numidia and to have its own primate because of its distance. But it could not for that reason speak of “the more distant Moors” in reference to it, since the more distant Moors were the Caesareans and the Tingitanians, not the Sitifenses. The Thuanus manuscript has *in coagentibus* (“in those being compelled”). Three of our manuscripts—the Vindobonensis, Veronensis, and Barberinus—begin *inchoantibus* (“when the Moors were beginning”).
