for the Moors who were making a beginning.

The remaining bishops of the first sees also declared, on the advice of the bishop of the Church of Carthage [Note: The Thuanus manuscript has *primatum esse constituendum* (“that a primate should be appointed”). The Barberinus has *primates suos constituendos esse professi sunt* (“they declared that their own primates should be appointed”); it lacks the remainder.], that the primates of their respective provinces should be appointed [Col. 0420B] if any dispute should arise [Note: Quesnellus, from the Thuanus manuscript, added: “What was promulgated in the African Council is confirmed in this Council of Carthage.” These are not words of the summary but of some annotator; consequently, since they are found in only one Thuanus manuscript, they are absent from our three manuscripts—the Vindobonensis, Veronensis, and Barberinus—and we judged that they should be removed from the text of the summary. The heading “Here begins the brief summary of the statutes,” inserted immediately afterward, is more correctly omitted in the Barberinus manuscript, since the preceding chapters are also abbreviated and belong to the Hipponian summary. In the Corbeiensis manuscript, according to P. Coustant, the heading “Brief summary of the statutes” is placed before the first chapter.].

## Here begins the brief summary of the statutes

### I

[Note: The Vindobonensis manuscript places before each canon its own title, which is listed in the preceding table of titles. P. Coustant reports the same concerning the Hubertinus manuscript. The other collections, Veronensis and Barberinus, have no titles. We do not repeat them here, since they can sufficiently be gathered from the preceding table. In the Veronensis manuscript this canon is divided into three chapters: chapter 1, “That readers”; chapter 2, “That before twenty-five”; chapter 3, “That first.” The Barberinus divides it into two: “That readers,” which is chapter 5 there, and “That first,” which it marks as chapter 6. Quesnellus notes that this canon is cited in the African Code, chapter 16, and in the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 4, that is, in Isidore, but with a different reading. Nevertheless, our reading is also found there in the oldest manuscripts used by the ancient editors of the Councils, such as the Venetian edition of 1581, where the different reading noted by Crabbe and preserved in editions of the Councils is understood. Crabbe, together with several other variants, appended it from his copy of Saint Bavo’s manuscript to the Third Council of Carthage in Isidore’s edition.]

Readers are not to greet the people. And before the age of twenty-five, neither clerics are to be ordained [Col. 0421A] [Note: The words “nor virgins consecrated,” omitted by Quesnellus, were absent from the manuscripts of this collection; hence they were added in an ancient hand in the Vindobonensis manuscript. They are read in the Veronensis and Barberinus manuscripts and in Vatican Palatinus 574. They ought to be inserted on the basis of Ferrandus, no. 121, and the Synod of Boniface in the year 525, where this canon is read with these words from the Third Council—that is, from the Hipponian summary—which had been inserted into this plenary council of the year 397.] nor virgins consecrated.

Let clerics first be advanced who are instructed in the divine Scriptures or educated from childhood, for the sake of the profession and affirmation of the faith [Note: The Thuanus manuscript has *promissionem* (“promise”).].

### II

[Note: In the Barberinus manuscript this is chapter 7. In the Veronensis manuscript the canon was omitted by the first hand and added in the margin by a second hand, without a number.]

Let the enactments of the council first be impressed upon ordained bishops or clerics by those who ordain them [Note: Thus from our manuscripts. Quesnellus has *statuta concilii* (“the statutes of the council”) and notes that in the Thuanus manuscript it is read: “Let the decisions of the councils be impressed upon their ears,” which is also read in the African Code, chapter 18, and in Isidore, chapter 3 of the Third Council of Carthage. From these sources this reading, like several others (see below, notes 44 and 63), was transferred into the Thuanus manuscript [Col. 0421C]; likewise, a little later, *poeniteant* (“let them repent”) was written from the same sources instead of *asserant* (“let them assert”). *Conciliorum* (“of the councils”) instead of *concilii* (“of the council”) is found here first in Ferrandus, no. 9, and in Boniface’s Synod. Since they derived this canon from the summary inserted into the Council of Carthage of the year 397, we would readily have written this if any of our manuscripts supported it, and if all the manuscripts—including Isidore and Dionysius—did not have *concilii* in the second place. At the end Quesnellus preferred *poeniteant*; we restored *asserant* from our manuscripts and the Oxonian manuscript. In the African Code this canon is not reported among the canons of the summary, or of the Carthaginian synod of the year 397, but among those of the synod of the year 419, where certain canons of the summary were repeated and renewed with some wording freely altered.] so that they may not assert that they have done anything contrary to the statutes of the council.

## 91

[Note: In the Barberinus manuscript this is chapter 8; in the Veronensis, chapter 4.]

### III

Even on the most solemn Easter days, the sacrament is not to be given to catechumens except the customary salt [Note: The Bodleian Veronensis manuscript has “the sacrament is not to be changed, because …”; above the line, in another hand, “the customary salt alone is not to be given.” Boniface’s Synod likewise has “is not to be changed”; but Ferrandus, no. 226, and Isidore in the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 5, read as in the text. A little later, from the Veronensis manuscript and Isidore, we added the particle *si* (“if”), for which Quesnellus had *enim* (“for”). Then, “the sacraments are not changed” is found in the Veronensis and Barberinus manuscripts.] because if the faithful do not change the sacrament during those days, neither ought the catechumens to change it.

[Note: In the Veronensis manuscript this is chapter 5. The Barberinus divides this chapter into two: “That to bodies,” chapter 9, and “Then,” chapter 10; it is divided in the same way in Ferrandus and in Boniface’s Synod.]

### IV

The Eucharist is not to be given to the bodies of the dead; for the Lord said: “Take and eat,” but corpses can neither take nor eat. [Col. 0422A] [Note: Quesnellus has *inde* (“hence”) and a little later *ne mortuum* (“lest the dead”). We wrote *deinde* (“then”) with all our manuscripts—the Vindobonensis, Veronensis, and Barberinus—supported by Isidore, chapter 6, and Boniface’s Synod.]

Then care must be taken lest the weakness of the brethren believe that the dead can also be baptized, since it has observed that the Eucharist is not given to the dead [Note: Since Quesnellus had printed the sentence without the negation, “since it has observed that the Eucharist is given to the dead,” he appended this note: “Thus the Oxonian manuscript together with the printed edition. But in the Third Council of Carthage and in the Thuanus manuscript it is read, ‘is not given.’ Both readings have a meaning that is not absurd. For the less instructed Christians, observing that the Eucharist was not given to unbaptized dead persons, could have thought that this happened because of the lack of baptism, and consequently that they could be baptized so that after baptism they might also be granted the gift of the Eucharist. And those who saw that the Eucharist was given to the dead could likewise fall into the error that those who had died without the grace of baptism could also be baptized. I prefer the latter interpretation and the reading corresponding to it. The former assumes that the Eucharist was denied only to the unbaptized dead; otherwise those simple believers could not have attributed the reason for the Eucharist’s not being given to the lack of baptism. But it is certain that, according to the custom of the universal Church, the Eucharist was given to no dead persons; nor did this error ever become established and receive canonical notice in such a way that it was generally granted indiscriminately after death.” This lengthy note rests upon the faulty reading of a single Oxonian manuscript, which lacks the particle *non* (“not”): all the other manuscripts, both of this collection—including the Thuanus and Vindobonensis—and of the other collections—the Veronensis and Barberinus—have *non dari* (“is not given”). He also praises the printed editions agreeing with the Oxonian manuscript [Col. 0422C]. But Isidore, who alone has the complete canon, preserves the negation. A little later, *animadvertit* (“observed”) is found in the Barberinus and Veronensis manuscripts and in some copies of Isidore.].

[Note: The Barberinus manuscript marks this as chapter 11; it joins the entire following canon and almost the whole of canon 7 to it. In the Veronensis manuscript it is chapter 6.]

### V

Because ecclesiastical cases often grow old to the detriment of the people [Note: In the complete canon, of which an abbreviated form is presented here, the date of the council was set as the tenth day before the Kalends of September, as transmitted in the African Code, chapter 73. This date seems to have been omitted from the summary because afterward the Fathers understood that synods could not be tied to that same date. In the cited African Code, canon 52, it is written: “It was established in the Council of Hippo that each province should be visited at the time of the council”; this is explained in the preceding canon 95: “It had been established in the Council of Hippo that every year a plenary council of Africa should be convened, not only here at Carthage, but also in the various provinces in their turn.” This appears to have been expressed in the present complete canon. Since it could not generally be observed because of the distance of the province of Tripoli and of Mauretania, it may for this reason have been omitted from the summary.] often arise, a council is to be convened every year [Col. 0422D]; to it all the provinces possessing principal sees are to send three delegates from their councils, so that the assembly may possess full authority and be less subject to jealousy and less burdensome in expense to its guests. And from Tripoli, because of the poverty of its bishops, one bishop is to come [Note: The Veronensis and Barberinus manuscripts have: “But from Tripoli, because of poverty.”].

[Note: In the Veronensis manuscript this is chapter 7, and after the words “nor is he marked off from communion” it is chapter 8. The Thuanus manuscript has: “Bishop Aurelius said: Whoever …”; this form of speech belongs not to the summary but was taken from the Carthaginian synod of the year 419, as can be read in the African Code, chapter 19, and was likewise transferred into the Third Council of Carthage in Isidore, chapter 7. It is absent from all our manuscripts and from Quesnellus’s Oxonian manuscript, in which *episcopus* (“a bishop”) alone is read instead of *episcoporum* (“of the bishops”).]

### VI

If any bishop is accused, the accuser is to bring the case before the primate of that province; and the person against whom the charge is brought is not to be suspended from communion, unless, summoned by a letter of the primate to state his case [Note: Vatican Palatinus 574 and the Soriensis manuscript cited by Hardouin have “by a letter of the principal see.” Then, in the Veronensis and Vatican Palatinus, “from the day on which.”], he fails to appear—namely, within the space of a month from the day on which it is established that he received the letter. But if he proves genuine reasons of necessity that clearly prevented him from appearing [Note: Quesnellus has *aliquis* (“some”). We preferred the reading of the Veronensis, Barberinus, and Vatican Palatinus manuscripts, with which Dionysius in the African Code and Isidore in the cited passages agree.], he is to have full opportunity to state his case within another month. But after the second month he is not to communicate until he has been cleared [Note: Alternatively, “until he has been purged.”].

### VII

But if he does not wish to appear before the annual universal council [Note: Some manuscripts omit *anniversarium* (“annual”), and the Barberinus manuscript has *occurrerit* (“has appeared”).], so that his case may be settled there, he is to be judged to have pronounced the sentence of condemnation against himself. During the time when he does not communicate, he is not to communicate among his own people either.

But if his accuser has never been absent during the days appointed for stating the case [Note: The Barberinus and Veronensis manuscripts omit “for stating the case.”], he is not to be removed from communion; but if he has at any time been absent, once the bishop has been restored to communion [Note: Alternatively, “restored into communion.”], the accuser himself is to be removed. Nevertheless, he is not to be deprived of the opportunity to complete the case if he proves that he did not refuse to appear on the appointed day, but was unable to do so.

It was also decided that when he begins to act before the judgment of the bishops, if the person of the accuser is culpable [Note: Quesnellus inserted *probata* (“having been proved”) from the Oxonian manuscript. We removed it because it is absent from our manuscripts, from the Thuanus manuscript itself, and from Isidore and Dionysius. A little later, the Vindobonensis, Barberinus, and Veronensis manuscripts have *non tamen si ecclesiasticas* (“but not if ecclesiastical matters”), and the last has *adserere* (“to assert”) instead of *dicere* (“to state”).], he is not to be admitted to accuse or conduct the case unless he wishes to state his own cases, but not ecclesiastical ones.

[Note: The Barberinus manuscript begins chapter 12 here. In the Veronensis manuscript: “It was also decided.”]

### VIII

But if presbyters or deacons have been accused, a lawful number of colleagues from neighboring places having been associated with them—that is, five in the case of a presbyter and two in the case of a deacon—their bishop is to examine their case [Note: “That is, in the case of a presbyter,” in which sense Saint Augustine speaks in Letter 142: “A letter of commendation was sent concerning their name throughout the whole world,” and so forth. Among the Councils there is also a booklet or letter of Pope Gelasius entitled “The Acts concerning the name of Acacius,” that is, concerning the case. In the Council of Carthage under Boniface in the year 525, in Labbe’s edition, p. 1646: “He seems to have raised a complaint concerning our name”; and p. 1647: “They seem to create jealousy concerning our name.” Likewise our Leo, Letter 12, now 14, to Anastasius of Thessalonica, chapter 6, concerning one elected bishop: “Concerning whose name,” he says, “the provincial priests should report to your notice.” Quesnellus’s note. A little later, the Barberinus manuscript and the second hand of the Veronensis have: “Let their bishop examine their cases.”] with the same observance of days [Note: The Veronensis and Vatican Palatinus manuscripts, together with Dionysius and Isidore, have *et dilationum* (“and of delays”) and *et a communione* (“and of suspension from communion”). Quesnellus appended the following note to *discussionis* (“of examination”): “So all [manuscripts]. See whether *discussionis* should not be read.”], or of delays, or of suspension from communion, and with the proper procedure for examining the persons of the accusers and the accused.

But the cases of the others [Note: The Barberinus manuscript and the second hand of the Veronensis add “or of clerics.”] the local bishop alone is to hear and settle.

[Note: The Barberinus manuscript, chapter 13; the Veronensis, chapter 9.]

### IX

Certainly, if any bishop or cleric, when a charge has been brought against him in the Church [Note: This is the reading of all our manuscripts. Quesnellus has *institutum* (“instituted” or “brought forward”). Then, instead of *et is relicto* (“and he, abandoning”), the Vatican Palatinus, Dionysius, chapter 15, and Isidore have *si relicto* (“if, abandoning”). A little later, the Veronensis manuscript has “wishes to be cleared in a public court.”], or when a civil case has been initiated, should abandon ecclesiastical judgment and wish to clear himself in the public courts, even if a judgment has been rendered in his favor [Note: The Barberinus and Veronensis manuscripts have: “he is not to be restored to his position,” and then, together with the Vatican Palatinus, omit *judicio* (“by judgment”).], he is to lose his position—and this in a criminal case. In a civil case, he is to lose what he has won, if he wishes to retain his position.

For since the authority of the Church is open on every side to him for choosing judges, he judges himself unworthy of fellowship with his brothers when, by thinking ill of the whole Church, he seeks help from secular judgment [Note: The Thuanus, Veronensis, and Palatinus manuscripts have: “he seeks secular help from the judgment.” A little later Quesnellus printed *ad Ecclesias* (“to the Churches”); the better reading, with the Barberinus, Veronensis, and Vatican Palatinus manuscripts, is *ad Ecclesiam* (“to the Church”).], whereas the Apostle commands that the cases of private Christians be brought before the Church and decided there.

[Note: The Barberinus manuscript, chapter 14.]

### X

This also was decided: if anyone appeals from any ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges, where there is greater authority, this is not to harm those whose judgment has been set aside if they cannot be convicted either of having judged with hostile intent or of having been corrupted by some desire or favor.

[Note: The same manuscript marks this as chapter 15. Then *provocare* (“to appeal”) is read in the Vatican Palatinus manuscript.]

But if judges have been chosen by agreement of the parties, even if by a smaller number than has been established, no appeal is permitted.

[Note: The Barberinus manuscript, chapter 16. A little later, *aut clericorum* (“or of clerics”) is found in the same manuscript and in Ferrandus, no. 40; *vel clericorum* (“or of clerics”) is found in the Veronensis.]

### XI

The sons of bishops and clerics are not to stage secular spectacles [Note: The following words are absent from the Veronensis and Barberinus manuscripts. Ferrandus reads *nec spectent* (“nor are they to watch”). After the word *spectent*, Quesnellus inserted, in parentheses, the following from the Thuanus manuscript: “although this has always been forbidden to all Christians, so that they do not go where there are blasphemies.” Since these words are absent from all our manuscripts, especially the Vindobonensis and Oxonian, we removed them from this collection. The Thuanus manuscript, like several other passages, received them from the distinctive reading of the Carthaginian synod of the year 419, in which certain words were added or altered. See the African Code, chapter 15. Similarly, in Isidore, this canon was attached to the Third Council of Carthage with this addition as chapter 2.] nor are they to watch them, since they are kept away from spectacles.

## 95

[Note: This canon is joined to the preceding one in the Barberinus manuscript. Then *etiam* (“also”) is deleted in that manuscript and in the Veronensis, which additionally has *vel*, that is, *aut schismaticis* (“or schismatics”).]

### XII

The sons of bishops or of any clerics are not to be joined in marriage to pagans, or even to heretics and schismatics.

[Col. 0425A] [Note: The Barberinus manuscript, chapter 17.]

### XIII

Bishops and clerics are not to permit their sons to leave their authority through emancipation unless they are confident concerning their character and age, so that their own offenses may now properly belong to them.

[Note: The Barberinus manuscript, chapter 18. A little later, instead of *in eos* (“upon them”), the Veronensis and Barberinus manuscripts have *eis* (“to them”).]

### XIV

Bishops and clerics are not to confer any of their property, either by gifts or by testament, upon those who are not catholic Christians, even if they are relatives.

[Note: The Barberinus manuscript, chapter 19.]

### XV

Bishops, presbyters, and deacons are not to be tenants or agents of private persons, nor are they to seek a livelihood through any such business as would make it necessary for them to travel about or be diverted from ecclesiastical duties.

[Note: The Vatican Palatinus has: “nor seek their livelihood through a shameful or dishonorable business.” Boniface’s Synod in the year 525 agrees: “nor seek their livelihood through shameful profit.”]

[Note: The Barberinus manuscript, chapter 20. — Edition: chapter 18 of the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 21; Ferrandus, chapter 122.]

### XVI

No women from outside the family are to live with any clerics whatsoever, but only mothers, grandmothers, maternal aunts, paternal aunts, and sisters, and the daughters of brothers or sisters, and any women who, because of domestic necessity, were already living with them as members of the household before they were ordained. Or, if their sons, after their parents had already been ordained, have taken wives, or if, since they have no servants in the household, necessity has led them to bring women from elsewhere [Note: The same manuscript, together with the Veronensis, has *suaserit* (“has advised them”).].

[Note: The Barberinus manuscript, chapter 21. We have written *omnes* (“all”), following our manuscripts, in agreement with the African Code, chapter 36, and Isidore, chapter 18 [Col. 0425D]. Quesnellus alone has *eos qui* (“those who”). — Edition: chapter 19 of the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 18, where *omnes* (“all”) is read instead of *eos* (“those”), as in the African Code, chapter 36.]

### XVII

Bishops, presbyters, and deacons are not to be ordained until they have made all those who are in their household catholic Christians.

[Note: In the Barberinus manuscript this is chapter 22. The Vatican Palatinus, together with Ferrandus, Dionysius, and Isidore, has: “Let readers, when they reach the years of puberty, be compelled either to take wives or to profess continence.”]

### XVIII

Readers are to read until the years of puberty; thereafter they are not to be permitted to read unless they have taken wives while preserving chastity, or have professed continence.

[Note: The Barberinus manuscript, chapter 23.]

### XIX

No one is to dare either to retain or to promote in the Church entrusted to him a cleric belonging to another bishop, unless that bishop grants permission. But readers are also to retain the designation “cleric” [Note: The Veronensis, Barberinus, and Vatican Palatinus manuscripts, together with Isidore, omit *sibi* (“to himself”), and then have *retinebunt* or *retinent* (“will retain” or “retain”). After the word *lectores* (“readers”), Isidore adds “and psalmists and doorkeepers.”].

[Note: The Barberinus manuscript, chapter 24. The Veronensis manuscript gives a longer form of this canon: “No one is to be ordained unless approved, if he has not had two wives—that is, is not a bigamist—or if, having had one, she was not a widow but a virgin; nor is one to be ordained who has had one woman as a concubine, not a married woman; nor one who has taken a widow, a repudiated woman, or a prostitute in marriage. Rather, the man is to be chosen whose life and reputation the bishop has examined, or who has been elected by the testimony of the people.” The other manuscripts, together with Ferrandus, Isidore, and Boniface’s Synod, support the reading of the text.]

### XX

No one is to be ordained unless approved either by examination of the bishops or by the testimony of the people.

[Note: The Barberinus manuscript, chapter 25.]

### XXI

No one is to name the Father in prayers in place of the Son, or the Son in place of the Father; and whenever one assists at the altar, the prayer is always to be directed to the Father. Whoever copies prayers for himself from elsewhere is not to use them unless he has first compared them with more instructed brothers.

[Note: In the Barberinus manuscript this is chapter 26.]

### XXII

No cleric is to receive more from anyone than he has lent [Note: Quesnellus remarks: “Note that no one is excepted.” A little later the Vatican Palatinus has: “If he gives money, money; if an object, an object; and only as much as he has given.”], whether he gives money or any kind of object.

[Note: The Barberinus manuscript, chapter 27. We inserted *ipse* (“he himself”) from our manuscripts. The words in parentheses are absent from Isidore, chapter 24, but are read in our manuscripts and in Quesnellus’s, as well as in Crabbe’s manuscript and the African Code, chapter 37 [Col. 0426D]. Boniface’s Synod likewise found the same sentence in its copy.]

### XXIII

In the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood, nothing is to be offered beyond what the Lord himself handed down, namely bread and wine mixed with water.

(The first fruits—that is, honey and milk, which on one most solemn day is customarily offered for the mystery of infants [Note: The Veronensis and Barberinus manuscripts, together with the African Code, have “for infants.” A little later Quesnellus, following the Oxonian manuscript, has “are customarily offered on the altar.” We preferred our copies, together with the Thuanus manuscript and the African Code. Later, the Veronensis, Barberinus, and African Code have “among the first fruits.” In the first hand of the Vindobonensis: “concerning the first fruits”; in the second hand: “among the first fruits.”]—although they are offered on the altar, nevertheless have their own proper blessing, so that they may be distinguished from the sacrament of the Lord’s blood and body.) Nor is more to be offered of the first fruits than grapes and grain.

[Note: The Barberinus manuscript, chapter 28. Quesnellus has: “or continent persons to widows or virgins, unless …” We deleted *vel* (“or”) and restored the reading preferred by all our manuscripts together with Dionysius and Isidore.]

### XXIV

Clerics or continent persons are not to visit widows or virgins unless by order or permission of the bishops or presbyters; and they are not to do this alone, but with clerics or with those whom the bishop or presbyter has directed. The bishops or presbyters themselves are likewise not to visit such women alone, but either where clerics are present or where some respected Christians are present.

[Note: The Barberinus manuscript, chapter 29.]

### XXV

The bishop of the principal see is not to be called “prince of priests,” “high priest,” or anything of that sort, but only “bishop of the principal see.”

[Note: The same manuscript, chapter 30. Then Quesnellus has *peregrinandi necessitate* (“because of the necessity of traveling”). We followed our manuscripts. Isidore, chapter 27, together with the African Code, chapter 40, has “compelled by the necessity of a journey.”]

### XXVI

Clerics are not to enter taverns for the sake of eating or drinking, unless compelled by the necessity of a journey.

[Col. 0426C] [Note: The Barberinus manuscript, chapter 31.]

### XXVII

Bishops are not to travel overseas unless they have consulted the bishop of the principal see of their respective province, so that they may especially receive from him the *formatae*—the canonical letters of identification. The council’s letters to overseas bishops are also to be sent from there.

[Col. 0427A] [Note: The same manuscript, chapter 32. The manuscripts of the other collections, together with Dionysius and Isidore, have: “That the sacraments …”]

### XXVIII

The sacraments of the altar are to be celebrated only by fasting persons, except on the anniversary day on which the Lord’s Supper is celebrated. For if a commemoration is to be made in the afternoon of certain deceased persons, whether bishops, clerics, or others [Note: We inserted the words *sive caeterorum* (“or others”) from our manuscripts; they are also read in Dionysius and Isidore. At the end, the Veronensis manuscript and Dionysius have *inveniuntur* (“are found”).], it is to be done with prayers alone if those who perform it are found already to have eaten.

[Note: The Barberinus manuscript, chapter 33. A little later the Veronensis, Dionysius, and Isidore have “because of the necessity of lodging, let them refresh themselves there.” Then Quesnellus has “from these banquets”; all the other manuscripts, together with Dionysius and Isidore, read as in the text.]

### XXIX

No bishops or clerics are to feast in a church, unless perhaps, while passing through, they refresh themselves there because of the necessity of lodging; the people, too, are to be kept away from such banquets as far as this can be done.

[Note: The Barberinus manuscript, chapter 34. In the Veronensis manuscript, as also in Isidore, this canon is divided into two.]

### XXX

For penitents, the bishops are to determine the periods of penance according to the difference of their sins. Presbyters are not to reconcile penitents without consulting the bishop [Note: The African Code, chapter 43, and the Isidore manuscripts, chapter 32, add: “unless the necessity of the bishop’s absence compels it.” The same is found in the Barberinus manuscript.], except when the bishop’s absence and pressing necessity compel it. But whenever a penitent’s crime is public and notorious, so that the whole Church knows it [Note: The African Code has: “which has disturbed the whole Church.” The Barberinus has: “which disturbs the whole Church.”], hands are to be laid upon him before the apse.

[Note: The Barberinus manuscript, chapter 35.]

### XXXI

When sacred virgins have been deprived of the parents by whom they were guarded, they are to be entrusted, through the care of the bishops or presbyters [Note: The African Code, chapter 44, together with the Veronensis manuscript, adds: “where the bishop is absent.” The Barberinus has: “where there is no bishop.” Isidore, chapter 33, has: “through the oversight of the bishop, or of the presbyter, where the bishop is absent, in a monastery of virgins or with more serious women,” and so forth.], to more respected women, so that, living together, they may guard one another, lest by wandering about indiscriminately they damage the reputation of the Church.

[Note: The Barberinus manuscript, chapter 36. A little later, *hi qui sui sunt* (“those who belong to them”) is found in the manuscripts of this collection and in Isidore, chapter 34. In the other manuscripts, together with the African Code, chapter 45, and Boniface’s Synod, only *sui* (“their own”) is found.]

### XXXII

The sick are to be baptized if, when they cannot answer on their own behalf, those who belong to them have, at their own risk, given testimony to their desire.

[Note: [Col. 0427C] Codex Barberinianus, chapter 37; shortly afterward, together with the Verona manuscript, it reads “converted to the Lord,” omitting the words “or turned back.” [Col. 0427D] Isidore, chapter 35, and Dionysius Justel, chapter 45: “Let grace or reconciliation not be denied to actors, mimes, and other persons of this kind, or to apostates who have converted,” etc. In the commonly published Codex Africanus, chapter 45, the words “or to apostates who have converted, or turned back to God” are absent; yet, since they are read in the Greek version, they were omitted through the carelessness of copyists. The word “mimes” is found in Ferrandus, no. 170.]

### XXXIII

That grace or reconciliation not be denied to actors or to apostates who have converted or turned back to God.

[Note: [Col. 0427D] Barberinianus, chapter 38. Shortly afterward, most manuscripts have *inconsiderately* instead of *without consultation*. In the Synod of Boniface, through a scribal error, they read *consignet* instead of *consecret*.]

### XXXIV

That a presbyter may not consecrate virgins without consulting the bishop; and that he may never prepare chrism.

[Note: [Col. 0427D] Barberinianus manuscript, chapter 39.]

### XXXV

That clerics may not remain in another city unless the bishop of the place, or the presbyters of the places concerned, have examined the justice of their reasons.

[Note: [Col. 0427D] The same codex, chapter 40.]

### XXXVI

That nothing be read in the church under the title of divine Scripture except the canonical Scriptures. The canonical Scriptures are: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, the four books of Kingdoms, the two books of Chronicles, Job, the Davidic Psalter, the five books of Solomon, the twelve books of the Prophets, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, Ezekiel, Tobit, Judith, Esther, the two books of Ezra,

[Note: [Col. 0427D] Quesnell omits “the two books of Maccabees,” and subsequently also omits in the text “the two letters of Peter, the three of John, one of James, and one of Jude”; in the margin he notes that these letters were added at the Third Council of Carthage, in Isidore, chapter 46, and in the African Codex, chapter 24. This led some to think that these sacred books had not been listed among the canonical Scriptures at the Council of Hippo in 393 or at Carthage in 397, but had been inserted only at the Council of Carthage in 419, during the pontificate of Boniface, whose name is found both in the African Codex and in Isidore at the passages cited.

Yet that these books too were included in the catalogue of Hippo, and in its *breviary*, is proved by three very ancient collections of different origin: the Corbie collection, in P. Coustant, volume I of *Epistolae Romanorum pontificum*, [Col. 0428C] page 101; the Barberinian collection; and the Vatican Palatine collection. The first two present the *breviary* itself, whereas the last places before it the canons from the plenary Council of Carthage of 397, into which the *breviary* was inserted. Hence it gives the reading proper to the *breviary*: “that the overseas Church be consulted for confirmation of this canon,” not the reading of the synod of 419, which introduces Pope Boniface.

The only manuscripts of this collection so far known omit the words in the text, an omission which P. Coustant rightly attributes to the carelessness of copyists. “We believe,” he says, “that this happened through the error of copyists, to whom it often happens, without their noticing it, that whenever they see the words they have just written repeated, they immediately omit the intervening words as though they had already been written. Thus the scribe who copied the statute of Hippo, after writing the words ‘the two books of Ezra,’ immediately passed, as if by a leap, to the books of the New Testament, omitting the intervening words ‘the two books of Maccabees’; he was surely deceived by the similarity of the words ‘two books,’ which are attached both to Ezra and to Maccabees.

“The same error occurred in the words ‘thirteen letters of the apostle Paul, one of the same apostle to the Hebrews, the Apocalypse’: before the word ‘Apocalypse,’ the two letters of the apostle Peter, the three of the apostle John, and one of James are missing, though they are listed in the Carthaginian statute. The error was produced by the word ‘one,’ which closes the two clauses ‘one to the Hebrews’ and ‘one of Jude.’ Once the first had been written, the copyist attached the word ‘Apocalypse’ in continuous writing, as though the other intervening letters up to ‘one of Jude’ had already preceded it.

“This conjecture is also supported by the fact—which no one will deny—that the First Letter of Peter and the First Letter of John were always received in all the churches, and therefore in the African Church. Since the canon of Hippo does not display either of them, they must have been omitted through the fault of a hurried and careless scribe.

“Moreover, the codex of Vienna gives an indication that the words we restore had been written in another, apparently older, exemplar of our collection. The ancient scribe who collated that codex with another older exemplar—for the notation ‘I have collated’ repeatedly occurs—undoubtedly found the same words in the other manuscript, where they had been omitted by the first hand, and added them in a second recension.

“Furthermore, the first hand of the Vienna text reads ‘fourteen letters of the apostle Paul,’ a number that includes the Letter to the Hebrews. The Corbie and Barberinian codices, as well as Dionysius, likewise give fourteen letters and, like the other letters of the apostle, do not list the Letter to the Hebrews separately. The Vatican Palatine codex, which gives thirteen letters, adds ‘one of the same to the Hebrews,’ as it is read in Isidore and in other manuscripts of our collection. Therefore, in the Vienna codex, either ‘thirteen’ must be corrected to ‘fourteen,’ or, if ‘fourteen’ is retained, the words ‘one of the same to the Hebrews’ must be deleted, since that letter is included among the fourteen.

“It should also be noted that in the same Vienna manuscript, somewhat earlier, we read ‘the book of the twelve minor prophets.’ Likewise, in Isaiah, the words ‘of the minor prophets’ and ‘likewise’ were added by a second hand. The same reading is supported by the Barberinian manuscript. Theodosius, the scribe of the Verona codex, chapter 55, who declares in a note that he silently omitted certain material—just as at the beginning of the *breviary* he omitted the Nicene Creed—also omitted the catalogue of the Scriptures at the end.”]

the two books of Maccabees; [Col. 0429A] and of the New Testament: the four books of the Gospels, one book of the Acts of the Apostles, thirteen letters of the apostle Paul, one of the same to the Hebrews, two of Peter, three of John, one of James, one of Jude, and the Apocalypse of John.

[Note: [Col. 0429B] Quesnell appends the following note: “After the enumeration of the canonical Scriptures, the following words are added in the Third Council of Carthage and in the African Codex, chapter 24: ‘Let this also be made known to our brother and fellow priest Boniface, and to the other bishops of those regions, for the confirmation of this canon: because we have received from the Fathers that these are to be read in the Church.’ In place of these words, the shorter statement which is also found in the ancient manuscripts is read; the editors of the Venetian edition of 1581 attest that it is found in the Oxford and Thuane manuscripts. It is as follows: ‘For the confirmation of this canon, let the overseas Church be consulted.’

“It is certain to me that this last statement was spoken at the Council of Hippo itself, whereas the former belongs to the Carthaginian council held in the time of Pope Boniface, where the canons of Hippo and of other African councils were reread and confirmed. How inappropriately the former statement is attributed to the Third Council of Carthage, held in 397, is sufficiently indicated by the single mention of Pope Boniface; this also proves, along with many other considerations, that the collection called the Third Council of Carthage in the volumes of the Councils is not a genuine collection of that council’s canons, but a forged compilation assembled from genuine canons gathered elsewhere: from the canons of Hippo; from the genuine Council of Carthage, which was assembled in 397 and was not absolutely the third, but the third under the primate Aurelius; and from the Council of Carthage held in 419 before the legates of the Roman pontiff.

“Two observations should be made concerning this. First, when he says that the editors of the Venetian edition of 1581 attest that the reading of our collection is found in ancient manuscripts, he refers to Crabbe’s note repeated in the Venetian edition, where, in canon 47 of the Third Council of Carthage, he writes: ‘An old codex reads as follows: “For the confirmation,” etc.’ The manuscript exemplar of Saint Bavo’s, proper to our collection, is indicated there.

“Second, what should be thought of the Third Council of Carthage as commonly published in Isidore will become clear from what we said in note 2 of the admonition, and more fully in the *Treatise*, part II, chapter 3, section 3, where we examine each of its canons.” In the Vallicellian manuscript B. 98, page 76, this canon on the Scriptures is given with the title: “That nothing except the Catholic Scriptures be read in the church. Chapter 24 of the Nicene Council.” The canon itself then follows, with the reading of the Carthaginian synod of 419, which decrees that confirmation of this canon is to be sought from Pope Boniface and the other overseas bishops.

“Some have therefore thought that the canon of the divine Scriptures had previously been established at the Council of Nicaea, and that the Africans merely inserted it in their councils as something received from the Nicene Fathers. But this entire opinion rests on the single heading of that codex, which belongs not, as some have written, to the eighth century, but at least to the eleventh; for on page 37 it contains letters of Regembert of Vercelli to Andrew, archbishop of Milan, and others edited by Mabillon in volume I of the *Museum Italicum*, which were written in that same tenth century.

“Just as the same codex, on page 79, gives a Sentence of Saint Leo on apocryphal Scriptures, which we have rejected as spurious, so we have no doubt that in the title of the canon on the canonical Scriptures—copied in its entirety from chapter 24 of the Carthaginian synod of 419 in Dionysius’s edition—the words ‘of the Nicene Council’ were written by mistake for ‘of the Carthaginian Council.’

“Certainly the African Fathers were so unaware that this canon had been established by the Nicene synod that at the Council of Hippo in 393 they thought that the overseas Church should be consulted about it, and at the synod of Carthage in 419 they decreed that it should be brought to the attention of Pope Boniface for confirmation. If they had known that the canon had been issued at the universal Council of Nicaea and received by the whole Church, would they still have thought that the overseas Church should be consulted and its confirmation sought?

“Add that, when the Council of Nicaea was read at the synod of 419 from the most ancient translation brought into Africa by Caecilian, only twenty canons besides the Creed were found, as is clear from the notes in the *Treatise*, part II, chapter 3, section 8, no. 2. The African Fathers therefore never counted the canon on the canonical Scriptures among the Nicene canons.”]

so that the overseas Church may be consulted for confirmation of this canon. It is also permitted to read the passions of the martyrs when their anniversaries are celebrated.

[Col. 0430A] 101

[Note: [Col. 0430C] When we undertook to complete the *History of the Donatists*, begun by Cardinal Noris, as far as we were able, we did not possess sufficiently certain knowledge of the collections that contained the *breviary*, and therefore brought this canon under suspicion of being spurious in part II, chapter 9, columns 429 and following. The suspicion was strengthened by the fact that Dionysius Exiguus, in the African Codex, chapter 47, attributes to the *breviary* another canon, not concerning clerics already ordained among the Donatists, but decreeing something concerning the children of Donatists; the same canon is also found in Isidore, in the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 48.

“But when, in addition to the present collection, we discovered two other very ancient collections which, while presenting the *breviary*, likewise contain this canon—and among them the collection preserved in the Verona manuscript 55, which lacks the two following interpolated chapters—we saw that there could rightly be no doubt about this canon. See the defense of this canon in the *Treatise*, part II, chapter 3, section 3, no. 47.”]

### XXXVII

It was also decided that, since it had been established by preceding councils that no Donatist should be received by us with his rank, but only among the laity, for the sake of salvation, which must be denied to no one ([Note: [Col. 0430D] The Verona codex adds “of clerics.”] [Note: [Col. 0430D] “For the churches in Africa suffer such a shortage of clerics to be ordained”]; [Note: [Col. 0430D] another reading is “such great … poverty.” Then, in the Verona manuscript, “throughout Africa.”] indeed the churches in Africa suffer such a shortage of clerics to be ordained that some places are entirely deserted), what was previously decreed should indeed be preserved in these matters, but with the exception of those who are shown not to have rebaptized, or who wish to pass over with their congregations to Catholic communion.

[Note: [Col. 0430D] In the Vienna codex, the first hand omits the words “in these”; a second hand added “instituted,” as it is also read in the Barberinian manuscript. Other codices, instead of this erroneous reading, have “in these matters.” The Verona codex perhaps has the better reading, “in them.” Shortly afterward, we printed “it was decreed” from all our manuscripts, Vienna, Verona, and Barberinian. Quesnell reads “it was handed down”; Crabbe, “it was believed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0431C] So from the Barberinian manuscript, as the following correction appears to require. Another reading is: “For thus.”] For if it is written, “If two Christians agree, whatever they ask, they will obtain,” it should not be doubted

[Note: [Col. 0431C] Thus the Verona and Barberinian codices. Another reading is “there should be no doubt.”]

that, when the scandal of disagreement has been removed and the whole people has been restored to unity,

[Note: [Col. 0431C] Quesnell reads: “in the unity of the whole people, through the compensation of peace and the sacrifice of charity, the sins which, following the authority of their ancestors, they committed by repeating baptism may be abolished.” The Vienna codex and Crabbe likewise have this reading, merely deleting *in* before “the whole people” and reading *of the invited* instead of *of unity*. We supplied from the Verona codex everything up to “the sins may be abolished,” except for the three words “of peace,” at the first occurrence, and “of charity,” which are retained in the other codices. From this complete reading it is clear that the defect in the other exemplars arose from an older codex in which the copyist skipped from the first occurrence of the word “peace” to the second. The continuation, “which, following the authority of their ancestors,” through “they committed,” is found in Crabbe’s exemplar. Verona omits “which” or “who” and adds “of those set over them.” Vienna has “which.” Barberinian and Verona support “they committed.”]

in a concord restored to the unity of peace, it is fit that they obtain from the mercy of the Lord that, through the compensation of that peace and the sacrifice of charity, the sins which they committed by repeating baptism, following the authority of their ancestors, may be abolished. But it was decided that this matter should not first be confirmed until the overseas Church had been consulted.

[Note: [Col. 0431D] The Verona codex reads “thereafter, the overseas Church”; the Barberinian, “from the overseas Church,” where *from* was written for *thereafter*.]

[Note: [Col. 0431D] The words enclosed in parentheses and printed in italics have been taken from the collection of Dionysius and that of Isidore. We proved in the *Treatise*, part II, chapter 3, section 3, no. 47, from Dionysius and the Isidorian collection, that they belong to the canon of the *breviary* in which the Donatists are treated, and constitute the final canon of that *breviary*. Compare what we discussed there.

“To join these words, which seem to have formed one canon with the preceding material, appropriately, the particle ‘Meanwhile,’ or something similar, should apparently be supplied at the beginning. The name of Simplicianus fits the period when the *breviary* was written and inserted into the plenary Council of Carthage in 397. At Hippo in 393, however, there is no doubt that, in place of Simplicianus, who had not yet attained the episcopate, the name of Ambrose was read.”]

(Concerning the Donatists, it was decided that we should consult our brothers and fellow priests, Siricius and Simplicianus, concerning only the infants who are baptized among them, so that the error of their parents may not prevent them from becoming ministers of the sacred altar when, with a salutary purpose, they have been converted to the Church of God, for something they did not do by their own judgment.)

[Note: [Col. 0432C] The two following canons do not belong to the *breviary* and therefore are rightly absent from the Verona codex. In the Barberinian manuscript they are not numbered. This canon, however, was enacted by the plenary council of 397; Dionysius gives it in the African Codex, chapters 49 and 50, and Isidore in the Third Council of Carthage, chapters 39 and 40.]

### XXXVIII

The bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said: “This also has been commanded to us: since our brothers, the two bishops of Numidia, recently presumed to ordain a bishop,

[Note: [Col. 0432C] Dionysius reads “our neighboring brothers.” The Barberinian manuscript omits this.]

you decree that ordinations be celebrated only by twelve bishops.”

[Note: [Col. 0432C] So Dionysius, Isidore, and the Barberinian codex, in agreement with the Greek version. Quesnell reads “the ordination.”]

Bishop Aurelius said: “The ancient practice shall be preserved, so that no fewer than three should suffice for ordaining a bishop. For perhaps barbarian peoples lie between Tripoli and Arzuges; for, as is reported, there are only five bishops in Tripoli, and perhaps two of that number may be occupied by some necessity. It is difficult for all of any number to be able to attend. Surely this ought not itself to be an impediment to the usefulness of the Church?

[Note: [Col. 0432C] Dionysius and Isidore read “ecclesiastical usefulness.” We supplied the following words from those same copies and from the Barberinian codex.]

“For in this Church, to which your holiness has deigned to assemble, we frequently have men to be ordained, almost on every Sunday.

[Note: [Col. 0432C] Quesnell inserts “bishops.” We have removed it, following the Vienna and Barberinian manuscripts, Dionysius, and Isidore. Shortly afterward, instead of “I can,” the three latter codices read “I shall be able.”]

Can I often summon twelve bishops, or ten, or not many fewer? But it is easy for me to add two neighboring bishops to my small number.

[Note: [Col. 0432C] The verb “to add” had to be inserted, following those same three exemplars.]

Therefore your charity sees with me that this cannot be observed. But this must be established: when we assemble to choose a bishop, if any opposition should arise—since such matters have been discussed among us—they must not presume to clear the man who is to be ordained with only three present;

[Note: [Col. 0432D] The African Codex reads “three bishops already”; but Dionysius’s edition in Justellus omits the word “bishops.”]

rather, one or two additional bishops must be summoned to reach the number stated above, and in the very congregation over which he is to be ordained the persons making the accusations must first be examined, and afterward the charges themselves must be fully investigated. When he has been cleared in the public presence, only then shall he be ordained. If this agrees with the mind of your holiness, let it be strengthened by the response of your dignity.”

And all the bishops said: “It is entirely satisfactory.”

[Note: [Col. 0432D] This canon belongs to the Council of Carthage of 401, held on the Ides of September. It is read in the African Codex, chapter 72, and in Isidore, in the Fifth Council of Carthage, chapter 6.]

### XXXIX

It was also decided concerning infants that, whenever no absolutely reliable witnesses can be found who testify without doubt that they have been baptized, and when they themselves are not of an age to answer concerning the sacraments entrusted to them,

[Note: [Col. 0432D] The Oxford manuscript omits the words “concerning the sacraments entrusted to them.”]

they are to be baptized without any scruple, lest this hesitation deprive them of the cleansing of the sacraments. For this reason our brothers, the envoys of the Moors, consulted us, since they redeem many such children from the barbarians. And in another hand.

Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage,

[Note: [Col. 0432D] The Verona codex erroneously inserts the word “said”; from that manuscript and from the Barberinian we added “these.” Shortly afterward, instead of “we judged,” the Verona codex has “we established.”]

having reread and acknowledged these decisions, confirmed by all of us, except for the matters of emancipation, concerning which we judged that consultation was necessary, have subscribed.

[Note: [Col. 0432D] The Verona codex adds: “and the others likewise.” Explicit: the Council of Hippo. The Barberinian reads: “and the others subscribed.” [Col. 0433C] The following subscriptions are preserved only by the present collection. Our Vienna exemplar confirms the reading edited by Quesnell.]

[Col. 0433A] Mizonius, bishop, having deferred the matter of emancipation for further consideration, have subscribed to the decisions set forth above; bishop of the chief see of the province of Byzacena.

Victorianus, bishop of the congregation of Massila, have subscribed.

[Note: [Col. 0433C] In the Vienna manuscript Nilus is placed before this Lupianus.]

Lupianus, bishop of the congregation of Tambita, have subscribed. Ninus, bishop of the congregation of Jubaltiana, have subscribed.

[Note: [Col. 0433C] The Oxford manuscript has “Philoligius,” incorrectly; for “Philologius” is also written in the Council of Carthage of 403 before canon 91 of the African Codex.]

Philologius, bishop of the congregation of Hadrumetum, have subscribed.

Ferox, bishop of the congregation of Macriana, have subscribed.

In this manner all who were present at this council also subscribed.

The canons of the Council of Carthage are concluded.

## CHAPTER III. HERE BEGIN THE CANONS

[Note: [Col. 0433C] These canons, which were taken from the version commonly called Isidorian, are elsewhere called Ancyretan or Ancyretan canons in the manuscripts of the same translation. Besides the exemplars of this collection, this same version is found in the Lucan manuscript 88, Vatican 1342, Barberinian 2888, the Verona manuscripts 55 and 58, and the Corbie manuscript. All these collections, of different origins, are earlier than the Hispanic collection from which Isidore received the canons.

The annotation “which was earlier than the Council of Nicaea,” etc., prefixed by Quesnell from the Oxford manuscript, is absent from the Thuane and our Vienna codices. Nevertheless, that it existed in this version from the beginning in substance no less than in the Dionysian and Prisca versions, just as it also exists in the original Greek, is proved by our Lucan, Vatican, and Verona 58 codices.

The Vatican reads: “These canons were indeed set forth before the Nicene canons; nevertheless, the Nicene canons were received [another reading: written] first because of the authority of the holy and great council held at Nicaea.” The Lucan codex is similar. The Verona 55 manuscript reads: “These canons or rules are indeed earlier than the Nicene canons; but for this reason they are written as earlier canons, because of the authority of the great and holy council held at Nicaea.”

After this annotation, the preface follows in these codices, though the author of the present collection omitted it. Since it lists the bishops who attended the council, it is important to append it here from those same codices. It will thereby become clear that, in the catalogue placed in the published Councils after the canons of the Isidorian translation (see the *Treatise on Collections*, part I, chapter 3, section 2), the names of provinces attached to the bishops are not to be attributed to the original translator.

We first give the preface from Vatican manuscript 1342, with the variants of the Lucan manuscript and of the Corbie codex as reported by P. Coustant in the preface to volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, page 62:

“When Marcellus of Ancyra, Vitalis of Antioch, Philadelphus of Heliopolis [better in Lucan and Corbie: of Juliopolis], Heraclius of Zela [incorrectly in Corbie: of Geliala], Munitus [Corbie: Ministius; both are incorrect: read Nunechius] of Laodicea, Narcissus of Neronia [read: of Neroniad; incorrectly in Corbie: Marcessus of Meragis], Lupus of Tarsus, Basil of Amasia, Eutholius [Lucan: Eutolus; Corbie: Eustolus] of Nicomedia, Peter of Iconium, Agricolaus of Caesarea, Epidaurus of Pergamum [Lucan: of Pergamus; it seems that, with the Prisca version, it should be read ‘of Perge’; these two are absent from Corbie], and Sergianus of Pisidian Antioch had come to the city of Ancyra, the following statutes were established by them.”

The Verona codex reads: “The following came together in the aforesaid synod of the city of Ancyra: Marcellus of Ancyra, Agricolaus of Caesarea, Lupus of Tarsus, Vitalis of Antioch, Basil of Amasia, Philadelphus of Juliopolis, Eustolus of Nicomedia, Heraclius of Zela, Peter of Iconium, Nunechius of Laodicea, Sergianus of Pisidian Antioch, Narcissus of Neronia.” Epidaurus of Perge is omitted.

The author of the *Synodicon* used a similar Greek codex; in no. 37 he likewise lists twelve bishops and reports that Marcellus of Ancyra and Agricolaus of Caesarea in Cappadocia presided, as they are naturally listed first in the Verona codex.]

### OF THE COUNCIL OF ANCYRA,

Which was earlier than the Council of Nicaea, but was placed before it because of its authority.

[Col. 0433B] 105

[Note: [Col. 0434D] We added these titles of the canons from the Caesarean Vienna manuscripts 59 and 42; there each canon is also prefixed with its own title, repeated from here. Quesnell, in dissertation 13, no. 2, testifies that these titles, omitted in the Oxford manuscript, are found in the Thuane codex.]

### Titles of the Canons

I. If a presbyter has sacrificed to idols.

II. That deacons who sacrificed and afterward returned be removed from the sacred ministry.

III. Those who, during the persecution, declared themselves to be Christians.

IV. Concerning laymen who sacrificed unwillingly.

V. Those who sacrificed in the temples of idols.

VI. Concerning those who ate in the temple wearing mourning dress.

[Col. 0434A] VII. Those who strayed from the faith: how they are to be received.

VIII. Concerning those who attended the banquets of pagans on their festival days.

IX. Those who sacrificed a second and a third time.

X. Concerning those who departed from the Lord’s faith.

XI. If deacons take wives, that they cease from the ministry or clergy.

XII. If a betrothed girl has been taken [another reading: abducted] by another man, it is decided that she be restored.

XIII. Those who sacrificed before baptism.

XIV. It is not permitted for episcopal vicars to perform ordinations.

XV. If presbyters or deacons wish to abstain from meat, they must not judge meat unclean, nor say that the vegetables in which it is cooked are polluted.

[Col. 0434B] XVI. If a presbyter has sold Church property, let it be restored.

106

XVII. Those who have been joined, like beasts, with a close blood-relative: how they are to do penance.

XVIII. If a bishop wishes to seize another church or cause a revolt.

XIX. Those who have promised virginity and afterward violate their pledge.

XX. Whoever has committed adultery shall do penance for seven years.

XXI. A woman who commits fornication and kills her child.

XXII. Whoever commits voluntary homicide.

XXIII. Whoever does so not voluntarily but by accident.

[Col. 0435A] XXIV. Those who observe omens and dreams.

XXV. Whoever has a betrothed woman and uses violence against her sister.

## CANON I

[Note: [Col. 0435C] The Vienna codex reads “Presbyters.” The Vatican manuscript 1342 has, instead of a title: “Concerning presbyters who sacrificed and afterward entered the contest again.” It attributes the following words, “If they did this,” etc., to the canon.]

If presbyters who sacrificed afterward entered the contest again, and did this in good faith, without preparing some pretext for themselves by which they might appear to have been seized again;

[Note: [Col. 0435C] The Verona manuscripts 55 and 58, together with the commonly published Isidore, add: “and thought that they would be subjected to torments as unwilling men.” In Verona 55 these words, which are read in the text, were deleted by a second hand. Shortly afterward, instead of “by agreement,” the Vatican codex has “with consent.”]

if, then, they struggled in good faith and did not themselves arrange matters by agreement for show, so that they might be captured,

[Note: [Col. 0435C] Both Verona codices read “so that they might be offered.” The Vatican reads “so that they might act.”]

it was decided that they should retain the honor of their own rank,

[Note: [Col. 0435C] Our Verona and Vatican codices, together with the commonly published Isidore, read “retain.”]

but that they may not offer, address the people, or perform any priestly functions.

[Note: [Col. 0435C] The commonly published Isidore and the two Verona manuscripts add “priestly.”]

## II

Likewise, deacons who sacrificed but afterward resisted should indeed retain that honor,

[Note: [Col. 0435D] Verona 55, together with the commonly published Isidore, adds “again.” Shortly afterward, instead of “that,” Verona 58 has “another,” and Verona 55 has “otherwise.” The commonly published Isidore then omits “honor.”]

but they must cease from every sacred ministry, so that they neither offer bread nor the chalice nor make proclamations;

[Col. 0435B] unless perhaps some bishops are aware of their labor, humility, and gentleness, and wish to grant them something more or take something away from them. The authority over these matters, therefore, shall rest with those bishops.

## III

Concerning those who, while fleeing during the persecution, were arrested or handed over by friends or members of their household,

[Note: [Col. 0435D] The commonly published Isidore reads “through fear.”]

or those who lost their own possessions, endured tortures, or were even shut up in prisons, and nevertheless declared themselves to be Christians; indeed, while the violence continued,

[Note: [Col. 0435D] The two Verona manuscripts, together with the commonly published Isidore, read “to that point.”]

they were driven to the point that their seized and forcibly dragged hands were placed upon sacrifices,

[Note: [Col. 0435D] Quesnell inserted “of the pagan.” We deleted it on the authority of our Vienna codex, the two Verona manuscripts, and the commonly published Isidore. Shortly after the word “placed,” the Vatican manuscript adds: “or were compelled by extreme necessity to receive some contaminated food.”]

while they continued to maintain their faith and cry out that they were Christians,

[Col. 0435C] [Note: [Col. 0435D] So the Thuane, Vienna, and two Verona manuscripts, together with the commonly published Isidore. Quesnell, following the Oxford manuscript, reads: “proclaiming; concerning these, therefore, it was decided that what happened to them,” etc.]

then, if they show by their grief and bitter sorrow of spirit that they endured this unwillingly, and if, walking in a humble manner through a good way of life, they demonstrate that they grieve over what they were compelled to do against their will,

[Note: [Col. 0435D] Thus our Vienna manuscript, together with the two Verona manuscripts and the commonly published Isidore. Quesnell reads: “that they humbly grieve over it through a good manner of life.” In Verona 55, where our reading appears in the first hand, Quesnell’s reading was introduced by a second hand.]

they are not to be barred from communion as though guilty. If, however, some have already excluded them from communion, whether for the sake of greater diligence and investigation or through the ignorance of certain persons, they ought to be received immediately. This is also to be observed concerning clerics

[Note: [Col. 0436C] The Vatican codex reads: “and it was investigated that this should be observed concerning all the laity; but also this, if they are able,” etc.]

and concerning all laymen.

## IV

[Note: [Col. 0436C] Only the codices of this collection separate this chapter from the preceding one. Shortly afterward, the commonly published Isidore reads “into similar necessities and circumstances.”]

Laymen, then, who have fallen into similar necessities and circumstances, as those who have committed no sin,

[Note: [Col. 0436C] The Thuane adds “showing this.” Shortly afterward, the word “especially” is found only in the manuscripts of this collection; the other collections, together with the commonly published Isidore, have “especially if,” which is better.]

especially because their respectable way of life commends them, were judged admissible to ordination.

## V

Concerning those who were not only compelled to sacrifice, but also those who dined in the temples of idols: if any of them were led to the temples in more elegant attire and there, after changing into costly clothing,

[Note: [Col. 0436C] Verona 58 and the commonly published Isidore read “more expensive.”]

became participants in the banquet of the idols, indiscriminately taking everything that had been set before them,

[Col. 0436B] it was decided that they should remain among the hearers for one year; for three further years they should do penance; but during those three years they should participate only in prayer for two years,

[Note: [Col. 0436C] So the Vienna manuscript, Verona 58, and the commonly published Isidore. Quesnell has “for two years.” This canon is absent from the other two codices, Vatican and Verona 55.]

and in the third year be reconciled to the sacraments.

## VI

But all those who went up into the temples in mourning dress and, reclining, ate,

[Note: [Col. 0436D] Our other collection’s codices, together with the commonly published Isidore, add “among others.”]

if they complete three years of penance, are to be received without offering.

[Note: [Col. 0436D] The commonly published Isidore and the Verona 58 codex add “to communion, that is, so that they themselves do not offer the oblation.”]

But if, after being led to the temples, they did not eat, they shall remain in penance for two years; in the third year they shall communicate, but without offering, as has been said.

[Note: [Col. 0436D] We supplied the wholly necessary word “year” from our manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0436D] The commonly published Isidore adds: “But in the fourth year they shall receive their full restoration.” Verona 58 reads somewhat differently: “so that in the fourth year they may already receive their full restoration.” The Vatican codex has: “they shall attain full restoration at the time of the fourth year.”]

The bishop, however, ought to have the authority, after examining the conduct of each person, to assign the standard and rule of his conduct:

[Note: [Col. 0436D] Thus from the Thuane, Vienna, and Verona 58 manuscripts and the commonly published Isidore. Quesnell has “the rule of penance.”]

that is, by acting more humanely according to the manner of life, he may shorten the time of penance for someone, or, if he sees that correction requires it, may also lengthen it.

[Note: [Col. 0436D] Vienna and Verona 58 delete “may”; in its place the commonly published Isidore has “add.”]

The former life and the later life of all these persons are to be examined, and thus priestly humanity is to regulate its conduct toward them.

### VII. On Those Who Yielded Only to Threats, or Were Deterred by the Confiscation of Their Property or the Penalty of Deportation

[Note: [Column 0437C] Manuscript Verona 58, together with the Isidorian Vulgate, reads: “sacrificed, and now.” The following words through “adopting” inclusive are absent in the Oxford manuscript.]

They strayed from the faith and have not yet repented or turned back, but now—that is, at the time of this synod—have presented themselves, adopting the resolve to return. It was decided that they should be received among the hearers until the great day, should perform penance for three years, then communicate for two further years without offering, and finally, after six years had been completed,

[Note: [Column 0437C] Thus our manuscripts and the manuscript of Thuane, together with the Isidorian Vulgate. Quesnellus, following only the Oxford manuscript, reads: “to perfection.”]

attain perfection. If some had been admitted to penance before this council, the beginning of the prescribed six-year period shall be reckoned from that time. If any danger of death should threaten one of them,

[Column 0437B]

whether through illness or for any other reason,

[Note: [Column 0437C] Other copies read “should occur.” In the Vatican manuscript: “should happen; under the fixed determination, communion shall not be denied him as viaticum, so that, if he recovers, he may complete the six-year period of penance.”]

communion shall not be denied them as their viaticum.

### VIII. On Those Who Attended the Banquets of Pagans on Their Festivals in Remote Places and Nevertheless Prepared and Ate Their Own Meals There

[Note: [Column 0437C] The Isidorian Vulgate reads: “carried.”]

It was decided that after two years of penance they should be received; yet each bishop shall examine whether they are to be received with the offering or admitted only to communion, taking into consideration their former and present manner of life.

### IX

Those who sacrificed a second and a third time after being compelled by force shall submit themselves to penance for four years; for two further years they shall communicate without offering; but in the seventh year they shall receive communion through satisfaction.

[Note: [Column 0437C] Two manuscripts of Verona, together with the Vatican manuscript and the Isidorian Vulgate, read: “to receive the perfection of communion in the seventh year.”]

### X

All those who not only deviated from the Lord’s faith

[Column 0438A]

but also rose up against others, persuaded their brothers, and became guilty of persuasion shall indeed be kept among the catechumens for three years; for another six years they shall be assigned a place among the penitents; but in the other year—that is, the tenth—

[Note: [Column 0437C] Thus the Vindobonensis and two manuscripts of Verona, together with the Isidorian Vulgate. Quesnellus deletes “communion” and reads: “let them be received without offering.” The Vatican manuscript reads: “let them be received without communion”; this was likewise corrected by a second hand in Verona 55.]

they shall receive communion without offering, so that, when the decade has been completed, they may enjoy perfection.

[Column 0438A]

During this period their life and conduct must be taken into consideration.

When deacons are ordained,
