### XII

It was decided that betrothed girls who were afterward abducted by others should be rescued and returned to those to whom they had previously been betrothed, even if it is established that they had lost the flower of their chastity at the hands of their abductors.

### XIII

It was decided that those who sacrificed before baptism and afterward received baptism could be advanced to ordination,

[Note: [Column 0438C] Verona 58 and the Isidorian Vulgate read “to the order.”]

as though cleansed from every crime by the sanctification of the saving bath.

### XIV

The deputies of bishops, whom the Greeks call *chorepiscopi*, may not ordain presbyters or deacons. Nor may they command the presbyters of a city to do anything beyond their authority without the bishop’s instruction, or act in any province without his written authorization.

[Note: [Column 0438C] The manuscripts of the other collections and the Isidorian Vulgate more correctly read “parish.”

[Column 0438D]]

### XV

[Note: [Column 0438D] This canon, which the author of the Isidorian version expresses in a fuller paraphrase, is transmitted with different readings in different collections. In Quesnellus: “Presbyters or deacons who are in the clergy and abstain from meat, so that they touch it but do not eat it, if they so wish.” In the Isidorian Vulgate: “Concerning those who are in the clergy, presbyters or deacons, and abstain from meat: it was decided that this should be established, that they should not despise it as unclean, but should touch it. If they wish to abstain from it …” The sentence beginning “But if only” is postponed after “from their order.” The Vindobonensis gives the purer and original reading of this version; three other Italian manuscripts of our collection, a Vatican manuscript and two manuscripts of Verona, likewise prefer it. From these we have inserted only the words “it was decided that this should be established,” which are omitted in the Vindobonensis but are necessary to the sense. The Lucensis agrees with the Vindobonensis.]

Concerning those who are in the clergy, presbyters or deacons, and abstain from meat, it was decided that this should be established: they may indeed touch it; and, if they so wish, they may abstain from eating it. But if they judge it so abominable that they consider even vegetables cooked with meat inedible, as though they did not conform to this rule, they ought to cease both from the ministry and from their order.

[Note: [Column 0439C] Quesnellus inserts “and let them be admonished”; we have deleted this with the Vindobonensis and our other manuscripts. Only manuscript Verona 58, which presents this very pure version, concludes the canon with the words “from the ministry and from their order”; it lacks what follows, which is found neither in the Greek nor in the other versions and must therefore be regarded as a later addition to this interpretation. The manuscripts of Verona 55, Lucca, and the Vatican, which received this addition, have: “so that they should not despise it as unclean, but nevertheless touch it.”]

They must not despise it, but nevertheless touch it. If they wish to abstain from it, they may do so,

[Note: [Column 0439C] Quesnellus adds “as has been said,” but the Vindobonensis, Lucensis, and Verona 55 do not. The same manuscript of Verona adds after a little: “and if he should regard them as abominable.”]

provided that, whenever vegetables are cooked with it, they do not judge those same vegetables polluted by the meat, but take them as food, even while abstaining from meat. If anyone, after being admonished of this rule, does not obey but, as has been said, regards meat as unclean and abominable, he must cease from his order.

[Column 0439B]

### XVI

If presbyters sell anything belonging to the Church while the bishop is absent,

[Note: [Column 0439C] Thus the Vindobonensis, two manuscripts of Verona, and the Isidorian Vulgate. Quesnellus reads: “when the bishop was not there, the presbyter sold it.” The Vatican manuscript has: “when the bishop was not there, the presbyter shall have sold it.” The Oxford manuscript: “to whom the bishop is not present.”]

it was decided that, after the contract has been annulled, the property should be restored to ecclesiastical ownership. It shall belong to the bishop’s judgment

[Note: [Column 0439D] The Isidorian Vulgate reads: “if a price had been fixed.”]

whether the price should be recovered or not, since it often happens that the revenues of things sold have returned a larger sum than the price paid for them.

[Note: [Column 0439D] Thus the Vindobonensis and the Isidorian Vulgate. The Thuane manuscript reads “for the price agreed upon.” Two manuscripts of Verona and another Vatican manuscript read “for the price received.” Quesnellus has “for the agreed price.”]

### XVII

The Greek words in this title are:

**Περὶ τῶν ἀλογευσαμένων, ἢ καὶ ἀλογευομένων**

which we can render as: “Concerning those who have behaved irrationally, or who are behaving irrationally.”

[Note: [Column 0439D] The Vindobonensis manuscript, writing the Greek words in Latin letters, adds *con*; Verona 58, in Greek letters, adds ΣΟΙΟΝΑΕ.]

The meaning of this sentence must be twofold, as is inferred from what follows, so that we may say: if any have, like animals,

[Column 0440A]

[Note: [Column 0439D] Two manuscripts of Verona read: “committed incest with blood relatives. Therefore, all those who, before the twentieth year of their age …” The Isidorian Vulgate: “have been joined incestuously to a blood relative. Therefore, all those …” The Vatican manuscript: “have been joined incestuously with blood relatives. All those …” The Vindobonensis and Thuane manuscripts add only “incestuously.”]

been joined to a blood relative and committed such a crime before the twentieth year of their age,

[Note: [Column 0440C] Thus the manuscripts of this collection, incorrectly; for the other manuscripts of other collections that prefer the Isidorian interpretation, together with the Greek text and the other versions, have fifteen years.]

after completing ten years in penance,

[Note: [Column 0440C] Vatican 1342 reads: “let them obtain only communion in prayers, and, remaining in this communion of prayers for another five-year period, let them then receive the sacraments of the offering.” “But let their conduct be examined …” Two manuscripts of Verona, together with the Isidorian Vulgate, read: “let them begin to communicate only in prayer, and, remaining for another five years in communion of prayer alone, let them be received into communion with the offering after the twentieth year.”]

let them begin to communicate only in prayer. But after the twentieth year let them be received into communion with the offering. Their life during the period of penance must also be examined, and thus they shall receive this indulgence.

But if some have persisted longer in abusing this crime,

[Note: [Column 0440C] Thus the Thuane and Vindobonensis manuscripts. The Isidorian Vulgate adds “having completed.” Quesnellus has “after reaching the age of twenty years.” The two manuscripts of Verona more correctly read: “that is, if, at the age of twenty years, while having wives, they fell into this crime, after completing twenty-five years of penance they should be admitted to communion in prayers; remaining for another five years in the communion of prayers, they should receive full communion with the offering. But if some, while having wives …” The Vatican manuscript: “But if some have persisted more stubbornly in this crime, let them submit to penance for a longer period. That is, if at the age of twenty years, while having wives, they fell into this crime, after twenty-five years of penance let them be admitted to communion in prayers, and the rest as in the text.”]

if, at the age of twenty years, while having wives, they fell into this crime, they shall be admitted to communion in prayers in the twenty-fifth year of their penance; remaining in that communion of prayers for another five years, they shall then be received into full communion with the offering. But if some, while having wives and being over fifty years of age,

[Column 0440B]

have fallen into this, let them deserve only communion until the end of life.

(Canon 17, Isidorian)

It was also decided that these people, not only made leprous by this kind of crime but also filling others with their own disease,

[Note: [Column 0440D] Two manuscripts of Verona, together with the Isidorian Vulgate, add “and,” which is better.]

should pray among those tossed by the storm,

[Note: [Column 0440D] The Vatican manuscript adds: “that is, those who are tormented by an unclean spirit.” Shortly afterward, in place of “are called,” two manuscripts of Verona and the margin of the Isidorian Vulgate read “are understood.”]

those whom we call energumens (the possessed).

### XVIII

If certain bishops have not been received by their own diocese, in which they had been designated, and wish to seize other Churches and do violence to the bishops whom they find there by stirring up seditions against them, they ought to be separated

[Note: [Column 0440D] The words “and recalled to the rank of presbytery” are additions belonging to this collection; they are incorrectly expressed in the Thuane manuscript as: “and let them be recalled from the rank of presbytery.” They are absent from our other manuscripts and from the Isidorian Vulgate, and likewise do not occur in the Greek or the other versions.]

and recalled to the rank of presbytery. If they wish to remain in the honor of the presbytery, they should not be deprived of their own dignity.

[Note: [Column 0440D] The manuscripts of Verona read “in the presbytery”; the Vatican manuscript, “in the order of presbytery”; and shortly afterward all have: “to remain in the Church where they had previously been, as presbyters.” The Isidorian Vulgate likewise has this, but alone omits the words “as presbyters.”]

But if they are proved to stir up seditions there also against the bishops established in that place,

[Column 0441A]

[Note: [Column 0441B] Verona 55 reads more correctly “shall be proved.” We have written “dignity” on the authority of all our manuscripts, which also agree with the Isidorian Vulgate and the Thuane manuscript. Quesnellus reads “honor.”]

they must be separated and nevertheless deprived of the dignity of the presbytery.

### XIX

All who, having promised virginity, have violated their pledge,

[Note: [Column 0441B] The Thuane manuscript omits the words “having despised the profession.” Manuscript Verona 55 adds to these words: “and entered into marriage.”]

having despised their profession, shall be counted among bigamists, who have entered into a second marriage. We forbid virgin girls who wish to live with those men as sisters

[Note: [Column 0441C] The Isidorian Vulgate, together with two manuscripts of Verona, reads “with certain men.”]

to associate with them.

### XX

If anyone has committed adultery, after completing seven years in penance

[Note: [Column 0441C] Thus all our manuscripts and the Isidorian Vulgate. Quesnellus reads “after completing.”]

let him be restored to perfection according to his former rank.

### XXI

[Note: [Column 0441C] Two manuscripts of Verona, another Vatican manuscript, and the Isidorian Vulgate have: “Concerning women”; and afterward: “but also concerning those … remove them from the Church.”]

As for women who fornicate and kill their offspring, and also those who act so as to expel what has been conceived in the womb, the ancient determination indeed removed them from the Church until the end of life,

[Column 0441B]

[Note: [Column 0441C] The Thuane manuscript reads “removes.” The second hand in the Vindobonensis ordered that they be removed. Shortly afterward Quesnellus has: “but more humanely now.” We have followed our manuscripts and the Isidorian Vulgate. Then we preferred “of penance” on the authority of those same manuscripts, with which the Thuane also agrees. Quesnellus, together with the Oxford manuscript, reads “in penance.”]

but now we determine more humanely that a period of ten years of penance be assigned to them.

### XXII

Those who have voluntarily committed homicide shall indeed continually submit themselves to penance; but toward the end of life they shall be considered worthy of communion.

[Note: [Column 0441C] In Isidore this canon is part of the preceding one.]

### XXIII

[Column 0441C]

But those who have committed homicide not voluntarily but by accident,

[Note: [Column 0441C] The manuscripts of Verona, together with the Isidorian Vulgate, read “committed,” and afterward “associated.” The Thuane reads “associates.”]

the earlier rule indeed associated with communion after seven years of penance,

[Column 0442A]

according to the prescribed ranks; but this more humane determination assigns a period of five years.

### XXIV

Those who observe omens, auspices, dreams, or any forms of divination according to the custom of the nations, or who introduce such people into their houses

[Note: [Column 0441C] The same manuscripts of Verona and the Isidorian Vulgate read: “in seeking something by the art of magic”; and in the second hand of Verona 55 this was corrected to: “to seek something by the art of magic.” Afterward, two manuscripts of Verona have: “according to the ancient rules established.”]

to seek something by magical arts, or to purify their houses, shall, after confessing, perform penance for five years according to the rules established in ancient times.

### XXV

If someone, having a fiancée, should perhaps commit violence against her sister

[Note: [Column 0441D] The manuscripts of Verona and the Isidorian Vulgate read “inflicted an offense”; in Verona 55 this was corrected by a second hand to “violence.”]

and attach himself to her as though she were his own; then, having abandoned the latter, he afterward marries the betrothed woman, while the woman who suffered the offense

if she should perhaps kill herself,

[Note: [Column 0441D] We supplied “if” from the Vindobonensis manuscript and our other manuscripts, together with the Isidorian Vulgate.]

[Column 0442B]

according to the established canons.

[Note: [Column 0441D] Quesnellus added this annotation from the Oxford manuscript in a different typeface: “And seventeen bishops who attended this council signed. Here end the canons of the Council of Ancyra, with the same meaning as in the newer copies, but generally with different spelling. All this is absent from the other manuscripts. The names of the bishops are written only in the preface. In the printed editions of the Councils a list of bishops is appended, with the names of their provinces; we noted that this cannot be attributed to the author of this interpretation in annotation 1. The names of the bishops were indeed taken from the preface of this synod, but the names of the provinces—in which certain provinces are listed that were established and divided later—were added by the author of the catalogue. In manuscript Verona 55, two canons are appended in another hand; they will be found among the ancient statutes, chapters 20 and 21. They are likewise appended to the Ancyran canons, in the same first hand, in Vatican manuscript 1342.]

## CHAPTER IV. HERE BEGIN THE CANONS OF THE COUNCIL OF NEocaesarea

[Note: [Column 0442C] Thus Quesnellus, following the Oxford manuscript. The other manuscripts of this collection, according to P. Coustant in the preface to volume I of *Epistolae Romanorum Pontificum*, p. 63, have “Caesarean”; this also appears in the first hand of the Vindobonensis, while “Neo” was added by a second hand. We have retained this reading, which is the correct one. These canons belong to what is called the Isidorian version, and in other collections that we have examined in annotation 1 to chapter 3 they are transcribed from this version. We compared them with the Vindobonensis manuscript of this collection, with the two manuscripts of Verona 55 and 58, and with Barberinus 2888, which belong to different collections. They are absent from the body of Vatican manuscript 1342, but the same canons are written in another hand on its preliminary leaves, from the version of Dionysius.]

NEOCAESARIAN,

[Note: [Column 0442C] This annotation, received by Quesnellus from the Oxford manuscript, is absent from the Thuane and Vindobonensis. Yet that it exists, at least in substance, not only in the Greek text and in the Prisca and Dionysian versions but also in Latin in our interpretation, is demonstrated by our manuscripts Lucensis 88, Barberinus 2888, and the two manuscripts of Verona. In Barberinus it reads: “These canons are second to those of Ancyra, which were promulgated at Neocaesarea; and they are earlier than those of Nicaea.” The Lucensis agrees. In both manuscripts of Verona it reads: “These canons are indeed second to those promulgated at Ancyra and Caesarea; but they are found before the Nicene canons.” Verona 55 adds: “And because they were promulgated when faith was failing, by the disciples of the disciples of our Lord Jesus Christ, they ought to be observed by everyone just as the Nicene canons are.”]

which was later than the Ancyran council but earlier than the Nicene.

[Note: [Column 0442D] We added these titles of the canons from Vindobonensis manuscripts 39 and 42; in them, moreover, each canon is preceded by its own title, repeated here. The same titles are found in the Thuane manuscript and other ancient manuscripts.]

## Titles of the Canons

I. If a presbyter marries, let him be degraded.

II. If a woman marries two brothers.

III. Concerning those who marry repeatedly.

IV. Concerning a desired woman.

[Column 0443A]

V. Concerning catechumens.

VI. Concerning pregnant women.

VII. A presbyter ought not to be present at a banquet celebrating a second marriage.

VIII. The husband of a woman who committed adultery while he was a layman ought not to be admitted to ecclesiastical ministry.

IX. If a presbyter committed a carnal sin before his ordination and afterward confessed it, let him be deprived of the altar office.

X. Likewise a deacon.

XI. Although of proven character, no one should be ordained presbyter before the age of thirty.

[Column 0443A]

XII. A person baptized during illness ought not to be ordained presbyter.

XIII. Foreign presbyters may not offer in the presence of the bishop or the city’s presbyters, nor [read: and] give bread.

XIV. Concerning the deputies of bishops.

XV. There ought to be seven deacons.

[Note: [Column 0443C] Two manuscripts of Verona omit the following ten words and the final words, and place before the canons only the simple names of the bishops, which in the printed editions of the Councils were appended to the canons of this version by a later hand, with the addition of the cities and provinces (see *Treatise on Collections*, part I, chapter 3, § 2). In the Corbeiensis, Barberinus, and Vindobonensis they are preceded by a similar preface. The order of the names differs in some places.]

When the holy and venerable bishops had assembled together in the city of Caesarea—Vitalis,

[Note: [Column 0443C] Thus the Thuane manuscript, two manuscripts of Verona, the Corbeiensis, and other versions. Quesnellus, following the Vindobonensis and Oxford manuscripts, reads “Germanicus.”]

Germanus, Gregorius, Alfius, Basilius, Salaminus,

[Note: [Column 0443C] Two manuscripts of Verona and Barberinus read “Sedus.” The Corbeiensis reads “Redus.” The Isidorian Vulgate has “Rudus,” with “Rodus” in the margin, and “Rodon.”]

Redux, Dicasius, Heraclius,

[Note: [Column 0443C] The Vindobonensis manuscript has “Eontius”; Quesnellus has “Contius.” We have corrected this to “Leontius” on the authority of the other manuscripts, supported by the other versions.]

Leontius, Amphion, Stephanus,

[Note: [Column 0443C] The Thuane has “Siricius”; Barberinus, “Eritius”; the Corbeiensis, “Eticlus”; two manuscripts of Verona, “Erythrius”; the Isidorian Vulgate, “Eretius,” with “Erytrius” in the margin. Shortly afterward, in place of “Valentinus,” it reads “Valentinianus.”]

Seritius, Lupus, Valentinus, Gerontius, Narcissus,

[Note: [Column 0443D] Verona 58 reads “Longinianus.” Later, “Sanctus” is absent from the Isidorian Vulgate. Conversely, another Leontius is added, who is likewise found in two manuscripts of Verona.]

Longinus, and Sanctus, and the rest—established the following provisions.

### I

[Note: [Column 0443D] The Isidorian Vulgate reads: “If a presbyter marries, he ought to be deposed from his order.” The Vindobonensis likewise reads “presbyter,” and adds “him.” Verona 55 has: “Whether a presbyter or a deacon has married, they ought to be removed from their order and deposed from their rank. But if they have fornicated … committed …”]

A presbyter who has married ought to be deposed from his order. But if he has fornicated or committed adultery,

[Note: [Column 0443D] Two manuscripts of Verona read: “he ought to be driven outside the Church and reduced to penance among laypeople.”]

let him be expelled from the Church and perform penance after being reduced to the status of a layman.

[Column 0444A]

### II

[Note: [Column 0443D] The Vindobonensis reads “If a woman”; afterward it deletes “and let her be expelled,” and also deletes “her” before “be reconciled.”]

A woman who has married two brothers ought to be expelled until the day of her death. But, out of mercy, at the end of her life

[Note: [Column 0443D] Two manuscripts of Verona and Barberinus, together with the Isidorian Vulgate, read “in the sacraments.”]

she ought to be reconciled through the sacrament, provided that, if she should recover her health, she be admitted to penance once the marriage has been dissolved. But if a woman dies while living in such a union, the penance of the surviving party will be difficult.

[Note: [Column 0443D] Two manuscripts of Verona read: “This sentence must bind both men and women.”]

By this judgment both men and women shall be bound.

### III

[Note: [Column 0444C] Quesnellus, following the Oxford manuscript, reads: “Those women who marry frequently, and those men who frequently take wives, shall observe the period established for them, etc.” We preferred the Vindobonensis manuscript, with which the Thuane copy cited by Quesnellus and the Isidorian Vulgate agree. Two manuscripts of Verona and Barberinus also agree, except that in second place they incorrectly read “who” for “who [feminine].”]

Concerning those who frequently take wives, and those women who marry repeatedly, they shall indeed observe the period established for them; but their conversion and faith shall shorten the period.

[Note: [Column 0444C] It should be read, with two manuscripts of Verona and Barberinus and the Isidorian Vulgate, “conduct.”]

### IV

[Note: [Column 0444C] The Thuane manuscript, as Quesnellus notes, joins this canon to the third. Nevertheless, it counts the same number of canons, dividing the fourteenth into two. Shortly afterward our two manuscripts delete “but.”]

If anyone desires a woman and also has a desire for intercourse with her, but the act does not follow, it is clear that he has been freed by divine grace.

[Column 0444B]

### V

A catechumen—that is, a hearer—who enters the church and stands with the catechumens, if he is seen to sin, shall hear the word while kneeling,

[Note: [Column 0444C] The true reading is found in two manuscripts of Verona: “But let him abstain from that sin which he committed; and if …” In the first hand of the Vindobonensis is the reading of the text, recognized as peculiar to this collection; the second hand added the words “that” and “which he committed,” but with the corrupt reading “from that idol’s sin: if he did it, which in him.” Barberinus has “from the sin of an idol,” from which erroneous reading our text “from the sin of an idol” seems to have arisen through an improper correction, whereas it should have been corrected to “from that sin.” The Isidorian Vulgate reads: “so that he may abstain from that sin which he committed,” deleting the particle “but.”]

but let him abstain from the sin of an idol; if he persists in it, he must be completely expelled.

### VI

[Note: [Column 0444D] Thus the Vindobonensis and two manuscripts of Verona. The Thuane agrees: “Concerning pregnant women, because they should be baptized when they wish.” The Isidorian Vulgate: “Concerning pregnant women, that …” Quesnellus, following the Oxford manuscript, has “Pregnant women ought …”]

Concerning pregnant women: they ought to be baptized when they wish, for there is nothing in this sacrament that is shared by the woman who is about to give birth and by that which is born from her womb;

[Note: [Column 0444D] Quesnellus adds “to the mother”; we have deleted this with our manuscripts and the Isidorian Vulgate. Shortly afterward, in the same Isidorian Vulgate, “which has been born” is printed in place of “that which has been born.”]

because the freedom of each person’s will is revealed in that confession.

### VII

A presbyter ought not to attend a banquet celebrating a second marriage, especially when he is asked to assign penance for a second marriage.

[Note: [Column 0444D] Thus the Oxford and Thuane manuscripts used by Quesnellus. It also appears in the first hand of the Vindobonensis, but the second hand corrected it to “ought.” The Isidorian Vulgate reads “is commanded.” Verona 55 reads “when penance is requested for a second marriage,” omitting “to assign”; in a second correction the reading of the text was introduced.]

What presbyter, then, would consent to that marriage on account of the banquet?

[Column 0445A]

### VIII

If it has been established that someone’s wife committed adultery while he was a layman, he must absolutely not be admitted to ecclesiastical ministry.

[Note: [Column 0445C] Two manuscripts of Verona read: “must not be admitted, and afterward, while in the clerical state …”]

But if, after he had already been established in the clergy, she committed adultery, he must dismiss her after granting a bill of divorce. If he wishes to retain her companionship, he cannot enjoy the ministry he has received.

### IX

If someone has committed a carnal sin and afterward has been ordained presbyter, and has confessed that he sinned before his ordination, he shall not offer;

[Note: [Column 0445C] Thus our manuscripts. Quesnellus reads “he shall offer.” Shortly afterward the two manuscripts of Verona have “but” in place of “nevertheless.”]

nevertheless, he shall remain in the other offices because of the usefulness of his diligence. For many judged that other sins also warranted deprivation of ordination.

[Note: [Column 0445C] Quesnellus inserts “in addition”; the Vindobonensis and two manuscripts of Verona more correctly delete it. After “to be deprived,” the Barberinus manuscript adds: “they said that he could be dismissed through the laying on of hands.” This was taken from the Dionysian version and entered the text from the margin.]

But if he has not confessed these matters and cannot be openly convicted by anyone,

[Column 0445B]

[Note: [Column 0445C] The Oxford manuscript reads “from this point.” Shortly afterward we have written “must be entrusted” from our manuscripts, also supported by the Thuane. Quesnellus, following the Oxford manuscript, has “must be committed.”]

authority over himself must be entrusted to this man himself.

### X

Likewise, if a deacon has been involved in the same fault,

[Note: [Column 0445C] Two manuscripts of Verona read “in that very kind of fault.” The Isidorian Vulgate agrees, deleting only “very.” Shortly afterward the same manuscripts of Verona read “shall restrain himself.”]

he shall restrain himself from the ministry.

### XI

A presbyter shall not be ordained before the age of thirty,

[Note: [Column 0445C] The Isidorian Vulgate, together with two manuscripts of Verona, has “not before the age of thirty.” Shortly afterward the words “our Lord Jesus Christ” are omitted in the same manuscripts of Verona.]

even if his life is of proven character; but he shall wait until the appointed time. For our Lord Jesus Christ was baptized in his thirtieth year, and then preached.

### XII

If anyone has been baptized while suffering from illness,

[Note: [Column 0445C] Verona 55 reads: “it is not permitted to ordain him presbyter.”]

he ought not to be ordained presbyter; for his faith is not voluntary but arises from necessity—unless afterward his zeal and faith should prove worthy,

[Note: [Column 0445D] Thus the Thuane, Vindobonensis, both manuscripts of Verona, and Barberinus, together with the Isidorian Vulgate. Quesnellus reads “or the scarcity of people.”]

or unless a shortage of people should compel it.

[Column 0446A]

### XIII

Presbyters who are from another region,

[Note: [Column 0445D] The Isidorian Vulgate deletes “not”; all our manuscripts and those used by Quesnellus retain it, as does Merlinus—and rightly, since Ferrandus, who used this version, has in no. 103: “So that presbyters of another region …” Rural presbyters are meant, as is clear from the Greek.]

may not offer in a church when bishops or the city’s presbyters are present, nor give bread;

[Note: [Column 0445D] The Isidorian Vulgate adds “consecrated.” The Vindobonensis, in a second hand, has “sacred.” Barberinus reads: “nor give bread for the prayer, nor the chalice,” which agrees with the Greek and the other versions. Verona 55: “but they shall give the chalice.”]

but in the prayer they shall give the chalice. If the priests of the city are absent and have been invited

[Note: [Column 0445D] The Isidorian Vulgate reads “to give the prayer.” Verona 55 lacks these words but has: “and they have been invited; then it is permitted for them to give bread.” Verona 58 and Barberinus: “and if he has been invited alone to the prayer, he may give it.”]

to the prayer, they alone may give it.

### XIV

[Note: [Column 0445D] The Isidorian Vulgate and the Barberinus and Verona 55 manuscripts, together with Ferrandus, combine canons 13 and 14 into one. Verona 58, together with the manuscripts of this collection, distinguishes them. Barberinus expresses it as follows: “The bishops [read: chorepiscopi] also seem to exist as an example and model of those seventy, but they are honored as fellow ministers because of the zeal they show toward the poor.”]

The deputies of bishops, whom the Greeks call *chorepiscopi*, have indeed been established as an example of the seventy elders; but, as fellow priests, they shall offer because of their concern and zeal for the poor and shall be held in honor.

### XV

There ought to be seven deacons according to the rule, even if the city is large;

[Note: [Column 0446C] Two manuscripts of Verona and Barberinus, together with the Isidorian Vulgate, read “of which rule.”]

the authority for this rule shall be the Book of the Acts of the Apostles.

[Note: [Column 0446C] This closing clause is not found in the Vindobonensis manuscript.]

Here end the canons of the Council of Neocaesarea.

# CHAPTER V. THE CANONS OF THE COUNCIL OF GANGRA BEGIN

[Note: [Col. 0446C] This version of these canons, commonly called Isidorian because it was received by Isidore from the Hispanic collection, is contained, besides the manuscripts of our collection, also in the Lucensis 88, Corbeiensis, Verona 55 and 58, and Barberini 2888 collections. From this same version alone the synodal letter of this interpretation was copied in Vatican 1342, which received its canons from the Dionysian collection. Dionysius omitted the synodal letter, and therefore it is not found in purely Dionysian manuscripts. Consequently, just as in the aforesaid Vatican manuscript 1342, so also in the manuscript exemplars of the Hadrianic collection, which derived their canons from Dionysius, it was supplied from other manuscripts that preserve the Isidorian version.]

[Note: [Col. 0446C] Although this annotation is absent from the manuscripts of this collection used by Quesnellus and from our Vindobonensis, since it is nevertheless found in the Hubertinus manuscript of the same collection, which Coustantius cites in the preface to volume I of *Epistolae Romanorum Pontificum*, p. 66, we have therefore thought it should be added, just as Quesnellus prefixed other similar annotations from a single Oxford manuscript to the Ancyran and Neocaesarean canons. For the author of this version certainly rendered this notice, which is found in the Greek original and in other versions, as is clear from the Lucensis, Barberini, and two Veronese collections that preserve the same interpretation. In the manuscripts Verona 55 and 58 it is expressed in these words: “And these canons written below were set forth after the Nicene canons.” For the time at which the Gangran synod was held, see the preceding Treatise, part I, chapter 4, § 1, where we defended the authenticity of this annotation.]

These Gangran regulations are shown to have been set forth after the Nicene synod.

[Col. 0446B]

[Note: [Col. 0446D] We have added these titles from the Vindobonensian manuscripts 39 and 42.]

## Titles of the Canons

Here begin the headings of the Gangran canons: that Eustasius wrongly condemns marriage, that no one placed in the married state should have hope before God, and concerning the prohibition against eating meat.

I. Whoever says that marriage or a woman is to be abhorred, let him be anathema.

120. II. Whoever forbids eating meat as a religious obligation.

[Col. 0447A]

III. That a slave should not despise his master under the pretext of religious observance.

IV. That the house of God should not be held in contempt.

V. Concerning private assemblies.

VI. That the firstfruits of crops be offered to the Church.

VII. Concerning giving and receiving produce without the bishop’s permission.

VIII. Whoever has professed virginity should not condemn marriage.

IX. That those who practice continence should not criticize those living in marriage.

X. That those who give alms should not be despised.

XI. Concerning the use of the cloak.

XII. That a woman should not wear male clothing.

XIII. That a woman should not leave her husband without permission.

XIV. That each person should nourish his own children.

[Col. 0447B]

XV. That children should obey their parents [read: “obey their parents,” dative].

XVI. That a woman should not cut her hair.

XVII. That one should not fast on Sunday.

XVIII. Concerning continence and fasting.

XIX. That assemblies held at the places of holy martyrs should not be despised.

121. To the honorable lords and fellow priests established in Armenia, Eusebius, Eulalius, Eugenius, [Note: [Col. 0447C] These names are transmitted in different orders in the various collections and in the Greek text. The order in this collection, however, is confirmed by the manuscript Verona 58, which contains the purer version. Verona 55 has “Bitanicus”; Verona 58 more correctly has “Bithynicus,” agreeing with the Greek text.] Bithynius, Olympius, Gregorius, [Note: [Col. 0447C] Quesnellus has “Siletus.” We corrected it from the Vindobonensian manuscript and two Veronese manuscripts, with the Greek text supporting the correction.] Philetus, [Note: [Col. 0447C] Two Veronese manuscripts have “Jeracius”; others have “Heraclius”; the Corbeiensis has “Eraclis.” This name is absent from the Greek.] Heracles, Elianus, [Note: [Col. 0447C] The same Veronese manuscripts, together with the Greek, have “Pappus Hypatius.” The Corbeiensis has “Papius, Epatus.”] Papius, Epatius, [Note: [Col. 0447D] The Veronese manuscripts, together with the Greek and other codices, more correctly have “Proeresius.” We added the name “Basilius” from the Vindobonensian manuscript; it is also found in the Greek text and in other collections and versions.] Proeresius, Basilius, Bassus, Eugenius, [Note: [Col. 0447D] The common Isidorian version adds “Hosius of Corduba.” He is absent not only from the manuscripts of this collection but also from all the others that preserve the Isidorian version—namely, the Veronese, Lucensis, Corbeiensis, and Barberini manuscripts, and from Merlin’s Isidore. Most importantly, he is absent from the Prisca version and from the Greek. Nor is he found in the manuscripts of the Hadrianic collection, such as Vallicellian A. 5, into which this synodal letter was transferred from the Isidorian version, as we noted above.] who assembled in the council of Gangra, greetings in the Lord.

Since the holy synod of bishops, convened in the church at Gangra to investigate certain ecclesiastical and necessary matters and to determine what had been done according to Eustathius, found [Col. 0447C] that many improper things were being done by those who followed this same Eustathius, [Note: [Col. 0447D] Quesnellus has “necessary.” We preferred the reading of the Thuanus and Vindobonensis manuscripts, and of the two Veronese manuscripts and the common Isidorian version.] it therefore decided that, once everything had been made public, all the evils committed by that man should be cut away. For it had been established that these men accused marriage, [Note: [Col. 0448C] The same manuscripts and printed editions add “and taught.”] asserting that no one living in the married state had hope before God.

As a result, many women followed them, leaving their own husbands, and men, abandoning their wives, dissolved the marriage bond while professing continence. Since they could not maintain it, they committed adultery. They were also found to teach dissensions and separations from the ordinances of the Lord established in the churches of God—that is, that ecclesiastical traditions and the things done in the churches ought to be despised—and, having established private assemblies in this manner, to presume to celebrate everything in imitation of [122] what is done in the house of God.

They had also rejected ordinary clothing and assumed new and unusual forms of dress; they had claimed for themselves the firstfruits of crops and the offerings which ancient tradition assigns to the churches, that is, by the reasoning of their own doctrine, as though these offerings ought to be presented to them as holy persons, [Note: [Col. 0448D] “And” is more correctly deleted in the same Veronese manuscripts and in the common Isidorian version.] and distributed among themselves and in their own communities.

They had found that slaves, withdrawing from their masters through this unusual religious practice, had despised their masters. [Note: [Col. 0448D] Verona 55 has: “and through this unusual dress of their region had despised their masters under the appearance of religion.” The same is read in Verona 58, which has “religion” in place of “region.”]

Women, believing that they were justified by this practice contrary to custom and to the adornment proper to their sex, [Note: [Col. 0448D] The Vindobonensian has “in themselves”; the two Veronese manuscripts and the common Isidorian version more correctly have “from this they.”] had adopted male clothing, and many of them, on the pretext of religion, had completely cut off the hair that was their natural adornment.

By despising the fasts proclaimed in the churches, [Note: [Col. 0448D] The Vindobonensian has “to be despised.” The Thuanus has “to be despised and to serve the belly.” The common Isidorian version and the second hand in Verona 55 have “to be despised, they asserted.”] they had served their bellies. Some of them had also regarded foods of meat as unlawful. They had persuaded people that not even prayers ought to be celebrated in the houses of married persons, to such an extent that they forbade them to be held. [Note: [Col. 0448D] The Thuanus has “and had persuaded.”]

They also decreed that no one should participate in offerings made in houses. [Note: [Col. 0448D] The two Veronese manuscripts, together with the common Isidorian version, add: “and that no one should participate in the offerings that had been made in the house.” The Vindobonensian has only “they decree.”]

They taught that priests who had entered into marriage ought to be despised, and that no one should touch the sacraments celebrated by them. They despised the places of the holy martyrs or the basilicas, [Note: [Col. 0448D] Quesnellus has “to be despised,” followed by “and then, to be criticized.” We preferred the reading of the Vindobonensian and Thuanus manuscripts, with which the two Veronese manuscripts and the common Isidorian version agree. The two Veronese manuscripts, after “assemble,” add, in agreement with the Greek: “and celebrate the sacraments.”] and criticized all who assembled there. [Col. 0449A]

They maintained that wealthy believers who did not renounce everything they possessed had no hope before God. And they established many other things, too numerous for anyone to count, each [123] according to his own will, [Note: [Col. 0449B] The two Veronese manuscripts, supported by the Greek text, read: “Each one of them, withdrawing from the ecclesiastical canon through such an institution, made laws for himself as though they were his own. But neither is there a common …” We published “for himself” from the Vindobonensian.] so that each of them, withdrawing from the ecclesiastical canon through such institutions, made laws for himself as though they were his own.

Nor did all these men have a common and unified opinion. Each one, according to what seemed right and pleasing to him, striving to accuse the Church as though it had no ruler, either added decrees or took them away. [Note: [Col. 0449B] The two Veronese manuscripts and the Vatican manuscript, together with the common Isidorian version, omit “by which.”]

Therefore this council was convened and held in the church at Gangra, [Note: [Col. 0449C] The Thuanus manuscripts, the two Veronese manuscripts, and another Vatican manuscript read: “to set forth these canons.”] so that these canons might be set forth, by which the aforesaid persons are proved to be outside the Church.

But if, through repentance, they condemn all these things that they wrongly believed, acknowledging that they were not properly expressed by them, let them become acceptable. For this reason the synod believed that each of the matters they ought to condemn had to be set forth.

But if anyone refuses what has been established today, let him be rejected as a heretic, anathematized, and condemned. He shall not only be excluded from communion but shall also be regarded as expelled from the Church until he has begged pardon from the bishop and declared which of all the matters discovered among them he has undertaken to observe. [Note: [Col. 0449C] We added the words “and discovered” from our manuscripts, with the Thuanus manuscript also agreeing; it additionally has “which they have produced,” referring the verb to the word “bishops” found in that manuscript.]

## I

If anyone has brought marriage under accusation [124] and has believed that a woman [Note: [Col. 0449C] The compiler of this collection omitted the words added here both in the Veronese manuscripts and in the common Isidorian version, with the other versions and the Greek text agreeing. They are: “faithful and religious, sleeping with her husband.”] ought to be abhorred or even accused, as though married persons could not enter the kingdom of God, let him be anathema.

## II

If anyone has believed that a person who eats meat in faith and with religious observance—apart from blood and meat sacrificed to an idol— [Note: [Col. 0449C] The Veronese and Barberini manuscripts and the common Isidorian version, together with the Greek, add “and what has been strangled.”] ought to be condemned as having no hope because he eats such things, let him be anathema.

## III

If anyone teaches that another person’s slave [Note: [Col. 0449C] The word “another’s” is absent from the Veronese manuscripts; in one of them it was added by a second hand.] ought, on the pretext of religion, to despise his master and abandon his service, and does not instead teach him to serve his master in good faith and with every mark of honor, let him be anathema.

[Note: [Col. 0449C] Quesnellus appended the following note to this passage: “The canon that is fourth in other codices is omitted here by both manuscript codices. I believe it was not received by the Roman Church for this reason: lest an unwary reader should be misled into understanding it of a married priest who uses the rights of marriage; and because, by the time when these canons were received by the Roman Church, the necessity had long since ceased that once compelled married men to be admitted to the priesthood, provided that they then abstained from their wives. The fourth canon in Isidore is as follows: ‘If anyone distinguishes a married priest, as though, on account of his marriage, he ought not to offer, and therefore abstains from his offering, let him be anathema.’”]

[Note: [Col. 0450B] “This is what he says. Our compiler omitted this canon, just as in the Ancyran canons he altered certain matters concerning deacons in order to adapt himself to Western discipline. But he did not notice that, for the same reason, certain words inserted in the synodal letter ought to have been deleted where married priests are mentioned. Quesnellus attributes this to the codex of the Roman Church; but wrongly, as will become clear from the Observations on his dissertation, chapter 2, no. 9, concerning this codex. All the other codices and collections that received the Isidorian version preserve this canon, and Ferrandus, who used the same version, presents it in abbreviated form as no. 89. In the Barberini manuscript it reads: ‘If anyone happens to distinguish a priest who has had a wife, on the ground that, while he ministers, he has no share in the offering, let him be anathema.’ Father Hardouin, volume II of the Venice edition of the Councils, column 437, note 4, gives the following form from another codex: ‘If anyone does not participate in the offerings celebrated by a married priest, let him be anathema.’”]

## IV

If anyone teaches that the house of God ought to be held in contempt and does not follow the assemblies held in it, [Note: [Col. 0450C] The two Veronese manuscripts and the Barberini manuscript, together with the common Isidorian version, delete “not,” and what follows is then connected accordingly.] let him be anathema.

## V

If anyone gathers people privately outside the church and despises the ecclesiastical ordinances [Note: [Col. 0450C] The common Isidorian version adds: “and wishes otherwise to usurp the things that belong to the Church, without a presbyter according to the bishop’s decree, and the Church itself,” which words are found neither in this collection nor in the other versions and collections. The Barberini manuscript varies only in what follows: “but wishes to conduct among them the things that belong to the Church, without a presbyter according to the bishop’s command; let him be anathema.” Verona 55 gives the entire canon in a different form: “If anyone gathers people privately outside the church, in another private place, despising the Church of God, and dispenses the Eucharist without a presbyter or bishop, let him be anathema.” Verona 58, a pure Isidorian manuscript, with the variant noted by Labbeus, has: “If anyone gathers people privately outside the Church and despises the Church; but conducts services among them without a presbyter, with [corrected with Labbeus’s manuscript to ‘without’] the counsel of the bishop, let him be anathema.”] and the Church itself, but acts among them either without a presbyter or without the bishop’s counsel, let him be anathema.

## VI

If anyone wishes to receive or give outside [125] the church an offering of crops or firstfruits owed to the Church, apart from the bishop’s knowledge, [Note: [Col. 0450D] The common Isidorian version adds: “or of the person appointed by him to distribute mercy to the poor, whether giving or receiving”; these words appear to have been taken from Dionysius, with the Greek text supporting them.] and does not rather think that these matters should be handled with the bishop’s counsel, let him be anathema.

## VII

If anyone receives or gives an offering of crops apart from the bishop [Note: [Col. 0450D] The common Isidorian version, from the Dionysian version, adds: “or apart from anyone appointed by him to distribute charitable work to the poor, whether the giver or the receiver.” The Barberini manuscript adds after “work”: “both the one who gives and the one who receives.”] or any minister, as though for the distribution of a good work, let him be anathema.

## VIII

If anyone, having professed either virginity or continence, calls marriage abominable [Col. 0451B] [Note: [Col. 0451C] This is the reading of the Vindobonensian and Barberini manuscripts. Quesnellus has: “says, and is continent not merely for this reason, that continence …” Verona 58 has: “judges, and not merely because continence or virginity is a good and holy purpose; let him be anathema.” The same was corrected by a second hand in Verona 55; but the first hand, together with the common Isidorian version, has the final words: “because the good of continence and virginity …”] and not merely because continence and virginity are a good and holy purpose, let him be anathema.

## IX

If anyone, having professed virginity for God’s sake, arrogantly criticizes those living in marriage, let him be anathema. [Note: [Col. 0451C] The two Veronese manuscripts, together with the Greek text, have “the Lord,” and likewise in the following chapter, “of the Lord.”]

## X

If anyone says that those who practice the agape and summon poor brothers to themselves for the honor of God are to be despised, and refuses to participate in their invitations, [Note: [Col. 0451C] The common Isidorian version has: “as though considering what is done to be nothing.”] as though reducing what is done to nothing, let him be anathema. [Note: [Col. 0451C] The same manuscripts, together with the common Isidorian version, have “has judged.” They alone then omit “to himself.”]

## XI

If any man thinks that, for a holy purpose—that is, continence—it is appropriate to wear a cloak, as though he would thereby possess righteousness, and criticizes or judges others who respectfully wear [Note: [Col. 0451C] The true reading is found in the common Isidorian version, in the two Veronese manuscripts, and in another Barberini codex: “wear birri,” Greek βῆροι. The common Isidorian version, together with Verona 58, then has “and another ordinary garment”; Verona 55 has “and another garment that is in common use.”] male clothing, or a white garment, or ordinary clothing in common use, let him be anathema.

## XII

If any woman, judging it useful for her chosen religious purpose, wears male clothing in order to imitate the dress of men, let her be anathema. [Note: [Col. 0451C] Verona 58 has: “judging this purpose useful, let her wear male clothing, in order to imitate the dress of men.” Verona 55 is similar and differs only in having “let her wear, or [the clothing] of men.” The common Isidorian version has: “judging it useful for her purpose … to this end she imitates the dress of a man.”]

126. ## XIII

If any woman, abandoning her husband, wishes to depart, dissolving the marriage bond and condemning marriage, [Note: [Col. 0451D] The two Veronese manuscripts have “condemning [marriage].”] let her be anathema.

## XIV

If anyone abandons his own children [Note: [Col. 0451D] The two Veronese manuscripts add: “and does not nourish them or provide them with what is necessary according to piety, but thinks that they should be neglected on the pretext of continence, and so forth.”] so as not to nourish them and not to provide them with what is necessary according to piety, but thinks that they should be neglected on the pretext of continence, let him be anathema.

## XV

If any child abandons his parents, especially faithful ones, and, judging under the pretext of divine worship that this is right, does not rather render the honor due [Note: [Col. 0451D] The common Isidorian version, together with the two Veronese and Barberini manuscripts, has “if any children,” and continues in the plural.] to his parents [Note: [Col. 0451D] We added “to his parents” from the Vindobonensian manuscript, with the other codices and the common Isidorian version agreeing. In the following passage we wrote “in them” from the same manuscript and the two Veronese manuscripts; the others have “in those” or “in them.”] so as to venerate in them precisely the fact that they are faithful, let him be anathema.

## XVI

Whatever woman, judging it appropriate to religious observance, cuts off the hair that God gave her as a covering and as a reminder of her subjection, as though dissolving the obligations of subjection, let her be anathema.

## XVII

If anyone, without making a proper distinction, fasts on the Lord’s Day [Note: [Col. 0452C] The two Veronese manuscripts, together with the Barberini, have “in contempt of that same day.” The common Isidorian version has “or in contempt of that same day.” Quesnellus noted here: “The Greek has διά τὴν νομιζομένην ἄσκησιν, ‘because of the supposed ascetic practice.’ The translator seems to have read αὐσχήσιν, as Cotelerius conjectures; see him, volume I of *Monumenta Graeca*, p. 794, where this and canon 12 are explained.”] as though in contempt of that day, let him be anathema.

## XVIII

If anyone among those committed to continence, beyond bodily necessity, becomes proud and thinks that the common fasts of the whole Church should be despised, [Note: [Col. 0452C] The Barberini manuscript has “excessive common fasts of the whole …” Having encountered a similar reading, our compiler seems to have corrected “excessive” to “supervening,” as it is read in the two exemplars of this collection, the Thuanus and Vindobonensian. The Oxford manuscript has “surpassing”; the common Isidorian version has “and becoming proud.” We have given the true reading from the two Veronese manuscripts, to which the Vindobonensian is similar; it likewise has “common fasts.” Quesnellus did not know the word “common.” Then, instead of “claiming,” the Oxford manuscript, together with Verona 58, prefers “judging.”] claiming a perfect understanding according to his own knowledge, let him be anathema.

## XIX

If anyone, through pride and thinking himself perfect, criticizes the assemblies held at the places [Note: [Col. 0452D] The common Isidorian version, together with the two Veronese manuscripts, adds “and basilicas.” The same Veronese manuscripts and the Barberini have “or has criticized” below.] or basilicas of the holy martyrs, [Col. 0452B] 127 or thinks that the offerings celebrated there ought to be despised, and considers the memorials of the saints [Note: [Col. 0452D] The two Veronese manuscripts have “that their memorials should be despised.”] deserving of contempt, let him be anathema.

[Note: [Col. 0452D] This is the conclusion of the Gangran synodal letter, in which the final canons are explained at greatest length. Since both of Quesnellus’s codices, as well as our Vindobonensian manuscript, omit it, there is no doubt that it is absent from all the exemplars of this collection. It is nevertheless found in the two Veronese manuscripts and in the common Isidorian version, from which Quesnellus added it. The original Greek text, together with the manuscripts of the Prisca version, confirms that it is genuine.]

We have written these things not to cut off those who, according to the Scriptures, choose the holy purpose of continence in the Church of God, but those who assume its habit and are lifted up in pride against those who live more simply.

We also condemn those who exalt themselves against the Scriptures and the ecclesiastical canons and introduce new commands. But we admire virginity with humility; we declare continence, joined with chastity and religious observance, most acceptable to God; and we praise, approvingly, the renunciation of secular business and activities together with humility and withdrawal from them. [Note: [Col. 0452D] We inserted the word “withdrawal,” added by Labbeus in the margin, into the text because it is found in our Veronese manuscripts. We wrote “approving” for “to be approved,” together with the common Isidorian version and Verona 55. Verona 58 has “to be approved.”]

We honor the bond of marriage, which endures with chastity. We do not reject the wealthy when they possess justice and good works, nor do we disapprove of frugality together with humble clothing. Likewise, we praise adornment undertaken for the care of the body, provided that it is not artificially embellished. [Note: [Col. 0453C] Quesnellus, together with the common Isidorian version, has “passing over.” We corrected it from our manuscripts, with the Greek text and other versions supporting the correction.]

But we do not accept loose and disordered modes of dress. We honor the houses of God and accept the assemblies held in them as holy and beneficial, not confining piety to private houses. We honor every place built in the name of God, and we accept the assembly held in the church for the common benefit [128] and bless, according to ecclesiastical traditions, the good works performed according to one’s ability for poor brothers. [Note: [Col. 0453C] Above, our Veronese manuscripts, together with Gratian, distinction 41, chapter 5, have “frugality”; so too do the manuscripts of the Hadrianic collection.] And we desire that everything in the Church which accords with apostolic traditions and the precepts of the holy Scriptures be done.

# CHAPTER VI

[Note: [Col. 0453C] Besides the manuscripts of this collection, including the Vindobonensian manuscript that we collated, this letter is found in the manuscripts of the Barberini 2888 and Vatican 5845 collections, among the Dionysian additions, and finally in the Isidorian collections. From the latter we reread Vatican manuscript 3791, which we shall call Vatican 2, while the former will be called Vatican 1. The codices reviewed by Father Coustantius and the editions of Augustine will also be useful. We have taken the title from the Caesarean Vindobonensian manuscript.]

## Letter of the Council of Carthage to Pope Innocent I of the City of Rome, against Pelagius and Coelestius

To the most blessed, most honored lord, holy brother, Pope Innocent, Aurelius, Numidius, Rusticianus, Fidentius, [Note: [Col. 0453C] This is the reading of the Vindobonensian manuscript together with the Barberini and both Vatican manuscripts and the Augustinian printed editions. It is also supported by the collation of Carthage in 411, in which three bishops named Fidentius are recorded, but no Fidentianus or Fidentinus, as it is read elsewhere.] Evagrius, [Note: [Col. 0453D] This is the reading of our manuscripts and of Quesnellus’s manuscripts, except for Vatican 1, which has the slight variation “Evacrius.” He adds this note: “Garnerius asserts that the reading is corrupt and that ‘Evangelus’ should be read instead of ‘Evagrius’ (see the notes of John Gerard on this letter, dissertation 2 on Marius Mercator); and in fact he substituted the former for the latter without the authority of any manuscript and without any reason. His claim that the name Evagrius was not common among Africans, whereas Evangelus was, and his bringing here Evangelus, bishop of Assur, of whom there is mention in the Carthaginian conference, are rightly blown away by the learned Henry de Noris in his criticism of Garnerius’s notes on the inscriptions of this synodal letter and of the letter of the Council of Milevis.”] Antonius, Palatinus, Adeodatus, Vincentius, Publianus, Theasius, Tutus, [Note: [Col. 0453D] The common version before Quesnellus has “Panthonius,” contrary to the manuscripts and to the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 126.] Pannonius, Victor, Restitutus, another Restitutus, [Note: [Col. 0453D] Vatican 1 has “Rusticianus.”] Rusticus, Fortunatianus, Ampelius, [Note: [Col. 0453D] This is the reading of the codices of our collection and of Isidore. The Barberini and Vatican 1, however, have “Abibius.” The common Council editions have “Avinius.” The older editions of Augustine have “Animus.” The Benedictine editors and Coustantius have “Ambivius,” from the rescript of Innocent and the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 133.] Avivius, Felix, Donatianus, another Adeodatus, Octavius, Serotinus, Majorinus, Posthumianus, [Col. 0454A] Crispulus, Victor, another Victor, [Note: [Col. 0454C] Oxford has “Leuticus.” Some manuscripts, together with the Benedictines, have “Leucius.”] Leutius, [Note: [Col. 0454C] The common version has “Macinus” or “Macianus.” Two bishops named Marianus are recorded in the Carthaginian Conference.] Marianus, Fructuosus, [Note: [Col. 0454C] Vatican 1 has “Faustinus.”] Faustinianus, Quodvultdeus, Candorius, 129 Maximus, [Note: [Col. 0454C] Vatican 1 has “Magorus.” Coustantius restored “Megasius” from other manuscripts and the Benedictine edition, with the rescript of Innocent agreeing.] Megarius, Rusticus, [Note: [Col. 0454C] Oxford, together with Vatican 2 and the Barberini, has “Rufinianus,” a reading followed by the Benedictines.] Rufianus, [Note: [Col. 0454C] Quesnellus writes in a marginal postscript: “Thus the Thuanus and Oxford manuscripts; Garnerius conjectured that it should be read this way.” The printed edition has “Proculianus.” The reading of the text is also supported by our manuscripts and those of the Benedictines, as well as by Innocent’s rescript. After “Proculus,” the Benedictines supplied the name “Severus” from excellent exemplars; this is confirmed by Innocent’s rescript.] Proculus, Thomas, Januarius, Octavianus, Praetextatus, Sixtus, another Quodvultdeus, Pentadius, likewise Quodvultdeus, Cyprianus, Servilius, [Note: [Col. 0454D] The Benedictine edition from Augustine’s codices, and Father Coustantius from the Corbeiensis and German manuscripts, have “Pelagianus.”] Pelagius, Marcellus, Venantius, Didymus, Saturninus, [Note: [Col. 0454D] Oxford appears to read, together with the printed Benedictine editions, “Bizacenus.” The older editions of Augustine have “Thiazenus.”] Bazacenus, Germanus, Germanianus, [Note: [Col. 0454D] The Benedictine editions of Augustine here and below have “Inventius”; Coustantius, together with other manuscripts, has “Invenitus.”] Juventius, Majorinus, likewise Juventius, Candidus, likewise Cyprianus, Emilianus, Romanus, Africanus, Marcellinus, [Note: [Col. 0454D] The Benedictine editors and Father Coustantius, from certain manuscripts, add “and the rest.”] who were present at the council of the church of Carthage,

## CHAPTER I

When, according to custom, we had solemnly come to the church at Carthage [Note: [Col. 0454D] Three manuscripts—the Vindobonensian, Barberini, and Vatican 2—together with Garnerius, have “when we had come.”] and a synod had been convened from among us for various reasons, our fellow presbyter Orosius [Note: [Col. 0454D] The Thuanus manuscript has “Oresius.”] gave us letters from our holy brothers and fellow priests Heros and Lazarus, the text of which we have decided should be placed below.

When this letter had been read, we recognized Pelagius and Coelestius as utterly wicked authors and of an error that must be anathematized by all of us. [Note: [Col. 0454D] The Benedictines insert “accused” from their codices; the earlier editions of Augustine and our ancient books do not contain this word.]

Accordingly, we asked that what had been discussed here in the church at Carthage nearly five years earlier concerning Coelestius be reread. When it had been recited, as Your Holiness will be able to perceive from what follows, although the judgment was plainly established—for at that time this wound appeared to have been cut out of the Church by episcopal judgment—nevertheless, after common deliberation, we judged that the authors of such a persuasion ought to be anathematized unless they most explicitly anathematized these things, even though Coelestius is said later to have attained the presbyterate. [Note: [Col. 0454D] This is the reading of the Vindobonensian and Barberini manuscripts, together with the editions of Augustine and Coustantius. Quesnellus, with other codices, has “we thought.” The Barberini and Vatican 1 have “of this sort,” and below “it ought to be.”]

Thus, if the health of the authors themselves cannot be secured, at least that of those who were deceived by them or could be deceived by them may be secured when the judgment pronounced against them has become known.

## 130. CHAPTER II

Having therefore reported this matter, dear brother, we thought it should be brought to the attention of your holy charity, so that the authority of the apostolic see might also be applied to the decisions of our inadequacy, for the protection of the salvation of many and also for correcting the perversity of certain persons. [Note: The earlier editions omit “holy.” The Thuaneus manuscript reads “of our inadequacy.”] [Note: Quesnell: “Thus the printed edition and the Thuaneus and Oxford manuscripts (add also all ours); Garnerius alone has ‘condemnation,’ less correctly.”] For these men, by their damnable arguments, are attempting to leave no place for grace—not by defending free will, but rather by exalting it into sacrilegious pride—although grace is that by which we are Christians and by which the very freedom of our will truly becomes free, when it is liberated from the domination of carnal desires. The Lord says: “If the Son makes you free, then you will truly be free.” Faith, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord, obtains this assistance.

But, as we have learned from brothers who have also read their books, they assert [Note: The Thuaneus manuscript reads “indeed.”] that God’s grace consists in the fact that he established and created human nature in such a way that, by its own will, it could fulfill God’s law, whether that law was naturally written in the heart or given in written form. They likewise say that the same law belongs to God’s grace because God gave it to human beings as an aid (Isaiah 8:20, according to the Septuagint). [Note: The Thuaneus manuscript reads “God established human nature for human beings.” Oxford reads “which he established for human beings.” After several editions of Augustine and Father Coustant, together with Vaticanus 2, read “which could fulfill.”]

But they absolutely refuse to acknowledge that grace by which, as has been said, we are Christians and of which the Apostle is the herald when he says:

“I delight in the law of God according to the inner person; but I see another law in my members opposing the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members. Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:22).

[Note: The Oxford manuscript reads “into the law”; the editions of Augustine and Coustant read “under the law.”]

Nor do they dare openly to oppose this grace. Yet what else are they doing when they never cease persuading merely animal human beings, who do not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God (1 Corinthians 2:14), that merely human nature is sufficient for carrying out and perfecting righteousness and fulfilling God’s commandments? [Note: The editions of Augustine and Coustant omit “indeed”; this is better.]

They fail to attend to what is written:

“The Spirit helps our weakness” (Romans 8:26);

and:

“It depends not on the one who wills or on the one who runs, but on God who has mercy” (Romans 9:16);

and:

“We are one body in Christ Jesus, and individually we are members of one another; we have different gifts according to the grace that has been given to us” (Romans 12:5); [Note: We have added this, with the Vindobonensis, Barbianus, and two Vatican manuscripts, in agreement with the editions of Augustine and Coustant.]

and:

“By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not empty; rather, I worked harder than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (1 Corinthians 15:10);

and:

“I give thanks to the Lord, who gave us the victory through Jesus Christ our Lord” (1 Corinthians 15:57);

and:

“Not because we are capable of thinking anything as from ourselves; rather, our sufficiency is from God” (2 Corinthians 3:5);

and:

“We have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing greatness of the power may belong to God, not to us” (2 Corinthians 4:7). [Note: The editions of Augustine and Coustant, together with Vaticanus 2, add “and.” Barb. and Vat. 1 omit “not from us.”]

There are countless other passages from all the Scriptures which, if we wished to gather them, a volume would not suffice. [Note: More recent editions of Augustine, with the Corbeiensis and Germanensis manuscripts cited by Father Coustant, read “time.” The older editions and Father Coustant, drawing on other manuscripts among ours and those used by Quesnell, support the reading “a volume does not suffice.” Quesnell later reads “it suffices to grasp.” We have deleted “to grasp” on the authority of the Vindobonensis and Barbianus manuscripts, with the other editions agreeing.]

And we fear that, by recalling these very things to you—things that you proclaim from the apostolic see with greater grace—we may seem to be acting inappropriately. But we do so for this reason: because we are weaker, each of us is thought to be more attentive in preaching the word of God in every direction, and therefore we suffer them to rise up against us more frequently and more boldly. [Note: The Vindobonensis and Barbianus manuscripts read “because of the fact that.” The editions of Augustine and Coustant read “for that reason.” Quesnell reads “in that.” After a little more, the Barbianus manuscript, together with the editions of Augustine and Coustant, reads “by preaching the word of God.”] [Note: Barb. and the editions of the Councils and Coustant omit “against us.”]

## CHAPTER III

If, therefore, Pelagius, on the basis of the episcopal proceedings said to have been conducted in the East, has rightly appeared acquitted to Your Veneration, nevertheless the error and impiety itself—which already has many supporters scattered in various places [Note: Garnerius reads “so many supporters.”]—must also be anathematized by the authority of the apostolic see. [Note: Quesnell noted in the margin: “Faulty punctuation in the printed editions here reverses the sense.”] [Note: The Vindobonensis and Barbianus manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read “Let Your Holiness consider.” Quesnell reads “Therefore.”]

Let Your Holiness consider, and, in pastoral compassion, share our concern: how destructive and deadly to the sheep of Christ is what necessarily follows from these men’s sacrilegious arguments. According to them, we ought neither to pray that we enter not into temptation—the very thing the Lord commanded his disciples and placed in the prayer he taught them (Matthew 6:13)—nor that our faith fail (Luke 22:32), although he himself testified that he had prayed this for the Apostle Peter.

For if these matters lie within the power of nature and the choice of the will, who would not see that they are vainly requested from the Lord and deceitfully prayed for, when people ask in prayer for things that are already obtained through the sufficient powers of a nature so constituted? [Note: The editions of Augustine and Coustant insert “this.” Quesnell notes in the margin: “Garnerius reads: ‘If these things which are accomplished by the possibility of nature and the choice of the will …’—entirely incorrectly, against the testimony of the printed and manuscript copies, the context of the discourse, and the author’s intention; indeed, nothing could be worse.”]

Nor should the Lord Jesus have said, “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation,” but merely, “Watch, lest you enter into temptation.” Nor should he have said to the most blessed Peter, the first of the apostles, “I have prayed for you,” but rather, “I command, or warn and instruct you, that your faith not fail.” [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read “but I warn you,” or “I command and instruct you.” Quesnell reads “but I command,” or “I warn,” or “I instruct.” We have preferred the reading of the Vindobonensis manuscript. Immediately afterward, the Barbianus and Vat. 1 manuscripts read: “Their argument is also contradicted.”]

Their argument is also contradicted by our blessings, so that we might seem to be saying over the people in vain whatever we ask from the Lord for them: namely, that by living rightly and piously they may please him. [Note: The Thuaneus manuscript adds “may receive it.” Barb. reads “may rightly receive it in living, so that …”]

It is likewise contradicted by what the Apostle prays for the faithful, saying:

“I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit” (Ephesians 3:14). [Note: We have added “of our Lord Jesus Christ” from all our manuscripts and printed editions.]

If, therefore, in blessing the people we wish to say, “Grant him, Lord, to be strengthened with power through your Spirit,” their argument will contradict us, asserting that free will is denied if one asks God for what lies within our power. [Note: The Vulgate of Augustine and the Oxford manuscript read “to them.” Immediately afterward, the same witnesses read “with power.”]

“For,” they say, “we can be strengthened with power if we wish, by that possibility of nature which we did not receive now but received when we were created.” [Note: Vind. reads: “For, they say, if we wish, we can be strengthened with power by that possibility …” The same occurs in the printed editions, except that they have “we wish” for “we wished.”]

## CHAPTER IV

They also deny that infants should be baptized for the salvation given through Christ the Savior, and thus, by this deadly doctrine, they kill them eternally. [Note: The Thuaneus manuscript reads: “and so, as though this deadly doctrine killed them eternally.”] They promise that, even if they are not baptized, they will possess eternal life. [Note: This is the reading of Thuan. and the printed editions. Both Vindobonensis manuscripts, both Vatican manuscripts, and Barb. omit only “to them.” Quesnell, with Oxford, reads: “nor have they perished with those of whom …”] Nor, they say, do infants belong among those of whom the Lord says: “For the Son of Man came to seek and save what was lost” (Luke 19:10).

“These children,” they say, “were not lost, and there is nothing in them that needs to be saved or redeemed at so great a price, because nothing in them has been corrupted, nothing is held captive under the power of the devil, nor is blood said to have been shed for them for the remission of sins.” [Note: The Barbianus and Vatican manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read “nothing in them is corrupted.”] [Note: The Barbianus manuscript reads: “nor was blood shed for them for the remission, as it is read, of sins.” Vat. 1 has the same reading. The Benedictine and Coustant editions, with the stronger manuscripts, read: “nor was blood shed for them, which is read to have been shed for the remission of sins.”]

Nevertheless, in his little book, Coelestius has already confessed in the Church of Carthage that even infants are redeemed through Christ’s baptism.

But many who are said to be, or to have been, their disciples do not cease affirming by every means available these evils by which they attempt to overturn the foundations of the Christian faith. [Note: All our manuscripts, together with Thuan. and the printed editions, read “overturn”; Quesnell reads “are overturned.” The Roman edition adds “by cunning.”] Therefore, even if Pelagius and Coelestius have been corrected, or if they say that they have never held these views and will deny that any writings produced against them are theirs [Note: The Benedictine and Coustant editions read “will deny.”], so that they cannot be convicted of lying, nevertheless anyone who teaches and asserts that human nature is sufficient for overcoming sins and carrying out God’s commandments, and who is thereby found to be an opponent of God’s grace—a grace more clearly revealed in the prayers of the saints—let him be anathema.

And whoever denies that infants are freed from perdition through Christ’s baptism and receive everlasting salvation, let him be anathema.

As for whatever other charges are brought against them, we have no doubt that, when Your Veneration has examined the episcopal proceedings said to have been conducted in the East concerning this same matter, you will judge in such a way that we may all rejoice in God’s mercy. [Note: The same editions, “we do not doubt.”]

Pray for us, most blessed pope. [Note: Both Vatican manuscripts and Barb., as well as certain Gallican manuscripts cited by the Benedictine editors of Augustine, lack the concluding words beginning “Pray …”]

## 134. CHAPTER VII

[Note: This chapter exists and was collated with the same manuscripts as the preceding chapter.]

### Innocent the Pope’s Reply to the Same Bishops

Innocent to Aurelius and to all the holy bishops, or to the other members of the Church who were present at the Council of Carthage, his most beloved brothers, greeting in the Lord. [Note: We added “or to the others” from Thuan. and Vind. This is found in the manuscripts of our collection, as well as Vat. 1, Barb., and the old Isidorian copies. The copies of Augustine list the names of the bishops, as in the Benedictine and Coustant editions; after those names they read “and to the others who were present at the Council of Carthage.”]

## CHAPTER I

In investigating these matters—which ought to be treated by priests with every concern, especially in a true, just, and catholic council—we preserve the examples of ancient tradition and remain mindful of ecclesiastical discipline. [Note: This is the reading of our collection. In the Vindobonensis, whose first hand reads “In investigating concerning these matters,” a second hand changed “concerning these matters” to “of God.” Two Barbianus and Vaticanus 1 manuscripts read better: “In investigating the matters of God.” Father Coustant found the same reading in three other manuscripts and preferred it, because the African letter to Pope Theodore, inserted in the second session of the Lateran Council under Saint Martin I, takes the opening sentences from this letter of Innocent and confirms the same reading.]

You now confirm the vigor of our religion no less in your consultation than formerly, when you proclaimed it, by sound reasoning; you have approved that the matter be referred to our judgment. [Note: The Vulgate reads “especially by a true …” Garnerius reads “you have preserved it.”]

You know what is owed to the apostolic see, since all of us placed here desire to follow the Apostle, from whom the episcopate itself and the entire authority of this name have arisen. Following him, we know how to condemn such evils as well as to approve what deserves praise. [Note: Barb., Vat. 1, Benedictine, and Coustant editions more correctly omit “already.”] [Note: The Thuaneus manuscript, the Vindobonensis, our other manuscripts, and all the printed editions read “whence has this come, that …?” Quesnell alone adopted from the Oxford manuscript “whence it comes that …”]
