Or consider this as well: while preserving the institutions of the Fathers in our priestly office, you do not judge that what they decreed by a divine rather than human decision should be trampled upon. Whatever might be happening, even in distant and remote provinces, they decreed should not be regarded as concluded before it reached the knowledge of this see, so that whatever judgment was just might be confirmed by the full authority of this see. [Note: Garnerius reads: “From there the other Churches would draw waters, as from its native spring, from which all waters proceed and flow through the various regions of the whole world … From there they would receive those whom they ought to wash …” Quesnell notes that “from its native spring” is found in his copies. We have corrected the text from the Vindobonensis and other manuscripts of our collection, together with the printed editions.]

From that source the other Churches would draw, and, as from their native spring, all waters would proceed, flowing through the various regions of the whole world as pure, uncorrupted streams from an undamaged head. [Note: The Vulgate, Benedictine, and Coustant editions read “pure waters from an uncorrupted head would flow.”] [Note: Coustant, together with the editions of the Councils and two manuscripts, reads “what they ought to command, whom they ought to wash,” with “ought” understood.]

What would they command? Whom would they wash? Whom would water worthy of pure bodies avoid as though they were soiled in filth that could never be cleansed?

## CHAPTER II

I rejoice, therefore, most beloved brothers, that you have sent us a letter through our brother and fellow bishop Julius. Since you care for those Churches over which you preside [Note: Vind., with the Coustant and Benedictine editions, omits “for.”], you demonstrate your concern for the welfare of all; and throughout all the Churches of the entire world you ask that what is beneficial to everyone be determined as one matter.

Thus, when the Church has been strengthened by its own rules and secured by the decree of a just pronouncement—by which it may guard against them—it cannot be exposed to such people. [Note: We have added this with Vind., Barb., and other manuscripts cited by Coustant. Garnerius reads: “the Church, and those people cannot fear the decrees of a just pronouncement”; he then omits “or rather, destroyed.”] Equipped—or rather destroyed—by the sophistries of perverse words, they argue under the appearance of the catholic faith, exhaling a pestilential poison, so that they corrupt the hearts of those who think rightly and seek to overturn the entire discipline of true doctrine. [Note: The Vindobonensis and Barbianus manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read “exhaling poison.” Quesnell reads “they exhale poison, and so that they …”]

The disease must therefore be healed quickly, lest the detestable illness grow more deeply within people’s minds. [Note: Another reading is “creep in.”] When a physician sees that some part of an earthly body is diseased, he considers it a great proof of his art if, through his intervention, a patient who was desperate quickly escapes danger; [Note: Quesnell adds “is”; we deleted it on the authority of Vind., with the printed editions agreeing.] or, when he sees a putrid wound, he applies poultices and other remedies by which the wound that has arisen may be covered over.

But if it cannot be healed while it remains, lest it infect the rest of the body with its corruption, he cuts away with the knife what is harmful, so that he may preserve what remains whole and untouched. [Note: Garnerius reads “so that he may preserve what remains whole and untouched.” Other printed editions read “so that he may preserve what remains whole and untouched.”]

Therefore what has crept like a wound into a body that was sound and pure must be cut away, lest, if it is cleansed too slowly, the refuse of this evil settle almost within the very entrails, where it cannot be drained. [Note: Vat. 1, Barb., and the second hand of Vind. read “where it is not drained out.”]

For what judgment should we now form of the minds of those who think they owe to themselves the fact that they are good, and do not consider him whose grace they receive every day? [Note: “Better: ‘of them,’ as it is read in the Chapters on Grace,” Quesnell. Immediately afterward, those Chapters and other printed editions read “after this,” rather than “after these things.” Garnerius reads “for minds” rather than “of minds.”]

## CHAPTER III

But now these people, being such as they are, receive no grace from God, because they trust that without him they can achieve as much as even those who ask him for help and receive it scarcely deserve. [Note: Garnerius reads “But justly.” Quesnell reads “so that they may receive”; Benedict reads “to receive”; Coustant, together with Garnerius, reads “and to receive.” We preferred the reading of the Vindobonensis manuscript, which is supported by the editions of the Councils and the Pithoean and Isidorian manuscripts. Garnerius later reads “for such religious minds.”]

For what could be so unjust, so barbarous, so ignorant of the whole of religion, so hostile to Christian minds, as to deny that you owe to him whatever you obtain through daily grace, when you confess that you owe to him the fact that you were born? [Note: Quesnell reads “than that it should be denied.” We preferred the reading of the other editions, which is required by the meaning and is supported by the Barbianus manuscript, together with the Vindobonensis and two Vatican manuscripts. In the latter, “to deny to you” appears through the easy error of scribes as “to deny.” The Barbianus and Vat. 1 manuscripts omit the preposition “in” before “daily.”]

Will you therefore be more powerful in providing for yourself than the one who made you so that you might exist? And if you think you owe him the fact that you live, how can you not think that you owe him the fact that, by receiving his daily grace, you live in this way? [Note: Coustant reads “can there be in you.” The edition of the Councils reads “can he be in you.” The Vindobonensis reads “and while you think you owe.” Garnerius reads “and if you think you owe this to him.” Coustant reads “and to whom you think you owe.”]

And you deny that we need divine assistance, as though we were altogether perfect through our own capacity. How, then, do we not call upon his assistance in order that we may also become such people through him? [Note: Garnerius reads: “Say how we may truly call upon his assistance in us …” Quesnell remarks in the margin that this is incorrect and contrary to the pontiff’s meaning, which—as the sequel shows—is to prove that a righteous person should call upon God’s help in order to live more righteously. The editions of Augustine and Coustant insert the word “his.”]

For one who denies the assistance of God—I should like to ask what he means. Is it that we do not deserve it? Or that God cannot provide it? Or that there is nothing for which anyone ought to ask for it? [Note: The Vindobonensis and two Vatican manuscripts, together with all the printed editions, read “to ask for it.” Quesnell alone, with his manuscripts, reads “to await it.”]

The works themselves testify that God can provide this assistance. We cannot deny that we need daily help: whether we live well, we call upon it so that we may live better and more holily; or whether we turn away from good things by thinking wrongly, we need his help all the more, so that we may return to the right path. [Note: The Roman edition and the more recent editions of the Councils, together with Garnerius, read “we ask for it.” The Vindobonensis, Barbianus, and Vat. 1 have the erroneous reading “we are called upon,” from which this may have been corrected elsewhere.]

For what could seem more deadly, more liable to sudden ruin, more exposed to every danger, than to think that what we received when we were born—free will—is alone sufficient for us, and therefore to seek nothing further from the Lord? [Note: Another reading has “with” in place of “when.”] That would mean forgetting our Creator and renouncing his power in order to demonstrate that we are free, as though the one who made you free at your birth had nothing more that he could give.

Not knowing that, unless grace is implored and descends upon us through great prayers, we shall in no way be able to strive to overcome the errors of earthly corruption and the worldly body. [Note: Garnerius reads “lest at all,” and below “error”; we have preferred “errors” with our manuscripts and the printed editions.] For it is not free will but God’s assistance alone that can make us equal to resisting them.

## CHAPTER IV

If the possibility of free will were more beneficial to him who possesses it, then one who is blessed and already chosen by the Lord would not rightly seek divine assistance. Yet he cries out that he needs it and thus prays to God:

“Be my helper; do not abandon me or despise me, O God, my Savior.”

We say that free will is sufficient for us; he asks God to be his helper. We say that the fact that we were born can suffice for us; he earnestly begs God not to abandon him. [Note: Garnerius reads “he entreats.” We state the matter plainly: “Why should we pray to God?”—he says, “but he …” The word “desires” has been printed with the manuscripts of Vind. and Thuan., which agree with the Benedictine and Coustant editions. Quesnell, with Labbé, reads “he entreats”; this was written by another hand in the Vindobonensis manuscript.]

Do we not clearly learn what we should pray for when that blessed man, as we said above, so earnestly desires not to be despised?

These matters must be charged against those who affirm them. For David should be accused as ignorant of prayer and unaware of his own nature, if, knowing that so much lies within his own nature, he nevertheless invokes God as his helper—indeed, as his constant helper—and if constant assistance is not enough for him, but he humbly desires in prayer that God never despise him. [Note: Garnerius reads: “David invokes a constant helper. Nor is it enough for him to invoke a constant helper, but …” Quesnell notes that Garnerius’ reading, addition, and punctuation are, in his judgment, less correct; no manuscripts known to him support it.]

Throughout the whole body of the Psalter he both proclaims and cries out this very thing. [Note: The reading is taken from the Vindobonensis manuscript. Quesnell omits “this” and has “so” in the first position as “so greatly.” Garnerius reads: “If, therefore, this seemed so important to him that he might teach us …” The Benedictines read: “If, therefore, that great man, just as he constantly said it, also considered it necessary …” Coustant reads: “If, therefore, that great man knew it to be so necessary to say constantly …” In his note he says that several very old manuscripts prefer this reading, but he would rather read: “So great a man knew how to say constantly, and so necessary …” The Vindobonensis likewise has “to say.” Our Vat. 1 reads: “If, therefore, he knew this to be so great and necessary to say constantly,” where “so great” is corruptly written.]

If, then, he knew this to be so important that he said it constantly, and confessed it to be so necessary that he taught it, how can Pelagius and Coelestius, setting aside every answer from the Psalms and rejecting such a doctrine, hope to persuade anyone that we neither ought to seek God’s assistance nor need it, when all the saints testify that they can do nothing without it?

For long ago, when that man suffered free will and used his goods unwisely, he fell and was plunged into the depths of transgression. He found no way by which he could rise from there, and, deceived in his freedom forever, would have lain crushed beneath that ruin unless the coming of Christ had later raised him up through Christ’s grace. [Note: Quesnell reads, with other manuscripts of this collection, “For formerly, by free will, he was perverted.” The Barbianus manuscript reads “formerly he endured free will.” Coustant notes that, in Innocent’s meaning, “allowed” is more likely than “perverted” or “endured.”]

Through the purification of the new birth, Christ cleansed every past fault by the washing of baptism and, strengthening his condition so that he might proceed more rightly and securely [Note: The edition of the Councils reads “strengthening.”], nevertheless did not deny him his grace for the future.

For although Christ had redeemed human beings from past sins [Note: Oxford reads “from their own,” incorrectly.], he knew that they could sin again, and therefore preserved many means by which he could restore them and correct them after those sins. He provides daily remedies; unless we rely and trust upon them, we shall in no way be able to overcome human errors.

For it is necessary that, with the one whose help enables us to conquer, we should again be conquered if he does not assist us. But I could say more, if it were not clear that you have said everything.

## CHAPTER V

Therefore, whoever appears to agree with the opinion that we do not need divine assistance declares himself an enemy of the catholic faith and ungrateful for God’s gifts, and is not worthy of our communion, which they have polluted by preaching in this way. [Note: The Oxford manuscript adds “by his benefit.”] [Note: Garnerius thinks something is missing here. Nevertheless, the Thuaneus and Oxford manuscripts contain nothing more than the printed copies, and the meaning truly lacks nothing. He supplies the following from his own resources in the margin: “Therefore you have justly condemned Pelagius and Coelestius, whom you recognized as the authors of an utterly wicked error to be anathematized by all; nor are they …” Quesnell gives this note. Our manuscripts, and those of the Benedictine edition of Augustine and of Coustant, likewise contain nothing of the sort. They proceed differently immediately afterward: “For neither are our …” and then, “For they themselves of their own accord …”]

For of their own accord, by following the things they say [Note: Garnerius reads “which are said.”], they have fled farther from true religion. Since our entire profession consists in this, and since in our daily prayers we do nothing except seek how we may obtain God’s mercy, how can we endure people who proclaim such things?

What, I ask, has so great an error blinded their hearts that, if they themselves feel no grace of God because they are neither worthy of it nor deserving of it, they do not consider what divine grace bestows every day upon each person?

These men are indeed entirely deserving of blindness, since they have not even left themselves the possibility of believing that they can be recalled from their errors by divine assistance. By denying God’s help, they have taken it away completely—not from others, but from themselves. [Note: The Vindobonensis manuscript, together with the Benedictine and Coustant editions, omits “of God.” Garnerius reads “Therefore they must be torn away.”]

They must be torn away farther and removed far from the bosom of the Church, lest, occupying many for too long, the incurable error grow worse. [Note: Coustant, together with Benedict, reads “lest, while it continues for a long time and occupies many, it grow worse and become incurable”; this is clearer from what follows.]

For if they remain for a long time under this impunity, they will necessarily lead many into the perversity of their mind and deceive the innocent—or rather, the unwary—who do not follow the catholic faith. [Note: Quesnell reads “many minds into this perversity of theirs.” We have followed the printed manuscripts, with the Thuaneus and Vindobonensis and Barbianus manuscripts agreeing; the latter two erroneously read “many in this perversity of their mind.”] They thought that those who still appeared to remain in the Church were thinking rightly. [Note: Quesnell notes that Garnerius reads “now,” which seems better. Nevertheless, the printed editions and the Thuaneus and Oxford manuscripts, and likewise the Vindobonensis, preserve this collection’s distinctive reading. Quesnell believes “now” is the true reading, as found in Vat. 1 and in the second hand of Vind. Coustant found the same reading in two manuscripts, Corbeiensis and Germanensis, and accepted it as genuine.]

## CHAPTER VI

Therefore let the incurable wound be separated from the healthy body. Once the breath of the raging disease has been removed, let what is sound be preserved with greater care, and let the purer flock be cleansed from the contagion of this evil sheep.

Let the perfection of the whole body remain unimpaired. We have learned that you pursue and maintain it through this sentence pronounced against them, and together with you we confirm it with equal assent. [Note: Quesnell omitted “of the whole,” because the word had fallen out of his manuscripts.]

If, however, they should call upon some assistance of God within themselves—assistance which until now they have denied—and recognize that they need his help, [Note: The words in parentheses are absent from the old editions of the Councils.] so that they may be freed from this stain into which they fell through the twisting of their own hearts; if, as though dragged from foul darkness into the light, they remove and reject everything by which their entire vision was defiled and darkened so that they could not see the truth; if they condemn what they have held until now and, at last lending their minds to sound arguments, submit and entrust themselves to true counsels by which they may be healed of this stain— [Note: Quesnell omitted “to be healed,” because the word had fallen out of his manuscripts. We inserted it from the Vindobonensis manuscript of this collection, with the two Vatican manuscripts, Barb., and other printed copies agreeing. Vat. 2 and other printed copies read “to those things” instead of “to these things.”]

if they do this, it will lie within the power of the bishops to assist them to some extent and to give such wounds some care, as the Church does not usually refuse to those who have fallen when they have come to their senses. Thus, recalled from their own precipices, they may be brought back within the Lord’s sheepfold. [Note: Garnerius reads “may be brought back.”]

Otherwise, remaining outside and excluded from such a great protection, namely, the fortress of faith, they will be exposed to every danger, to be devoured and tormented by the teeth of wolves—against which they cannot resist with the perversity of the doctrine by which they have provoked them against themselves. [Note: Quesnell reads “from such a great protection and fortress,” and notes “faith” in the margin in place of “fortress.” We have restored the reading of the Vulgate from the Vindobonensis, Barbianus, and Vat. 1.]

But our answer has been sufficiently demonstrated by your admonitions, already sufficiently abundant, and by the examples of our law; nor have we thought that anything remains for us to say. Nothing, as is clear, has been omitted or suppressed by you by which they have been refuted and fully shown to be convicted. Therefore we cite no testimonies, because your report is full of them, and it is sufficiently clear that learned priests have said everything relevant. [Note: Garnerius reads “it is sufficiently clear that so many highly learned priests have said everything.” Quesnell notes that this is less correct, although the Benedictine editors of Augustine and Father Coustant adopted it with the manuscripts. Quesnell himself follows the printed reading of the Councils approved by the compiler of our collection. He alone added “you” before “have said everything”; we have deleted that addition on the authority of the Vindobonensis manuscript.]

Nor is it fitting to believe that you have passed over anything that could advance the case.

And in another hand: Farewell, brothers. [Note: Garnerius adds: “On the sixth day before the Kalends of February, after the consulship of Theodosius VIII and Junius Quartus Palladius”; or, as he says other manuscripts read, “in the consulship of Honorius XI and Constantius II.” Quesnell gives this in his note. The Benedictine editors and Coustant, more correctly from three manuscripts, read: “And at the side: Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, after the consulship of Theodosius Augustus VII and Junius Quartus, illustrious men.” This is the true chronological notation, which the better manuscripts provide both here and in another letter of Innocent, to be presented in chapter 11. Concerning the consuls whom Garnerius says he found in other manuscripts, see the final note to chapter 9.]

## Chapter VIII

Here begins the letter of the Council of Milevis to the same pope of the City against the same heretics.

[Note: [Col. 0464D] It is found in the manuscripts of this collection, to which our Vindebonensis codex belongs. It was subsequently transferred by Isidore into his own collection; we reread its Vatican manuscript 3791 and used it as an aid, together with the copies of the Benedictine Fathers in the edition of Augustine and that of Father Coustantius.]

To the most blessed Lord, deservedly venerable and honored in Christ, Pope INNOCENT, SILVANUS the Elder, VALENTINUS, AURELIUS, DONATUS, RESTITUTUS, LUCIANUS, ALYPIUS, AUGUSTINE, PLACENTIUS, SEVERUS, FORTUNATUS, POSSIDIUS, NOVATUS, SECUNDUS, MAURENTIUS, LEO, FAUSTINIANUS, CRESCONIUS, MALCHUS, LITTORIUS, FORTUNATUS, DONATUS, PONTIANUS, SATURNINUS, CRESCONIUS, HONORIUS, CRESCONIUS, LUCIUS, ADEODATUS, PROCESSUS, SECUNDUS, FELIX, ASIATICUS, RUFINUS, FAUSTINUS, SERVIUS, TERENTIUS, CRESCONIUS, SPERANTIUS, QUADRATUS, LUCILLUS, SABINUS, FAUSTINUS, CRESCONIUS, VICTOR, GIGANTIUS, POSSIDONIUS, ANTONINUS, INNOCENTIUS, FELIX, ANTONINUS, VICTOR, HONORATUS, DONATUS, PETRUS, PRAESIDIUS, CRESCONIUS, LAMPADIUS, DELPHINUS, from the Council of Milevis, greeting in the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0464C] Coustantius and the Benedictines have Ponticanus; Pithoeus and one Colbertinus manuscript have Ponticianus.]

[Note: [Col. 0465C] The same Benedictine and Coustantius editions have Rufinianus, and then Severus, as it was corrected by a second hand in Vindebonensis.]

[Note: [Col. 0465C] Thus the Vulgate, Thuanus, and Vindebonensis. Quesnellus, with Oxoniensis alone, has Terentianus.]

[Note: [Col. 0465C] In the Vulgate Councils, together with the Isidorian manuscripts, another Sabinus appears in place of this Faustinus. Following Oxoniensis, Quesnellus included both: Faustinus, Sabinus. We have deleted this second Sabinus, together with the Thuanus and Vindebonensis manuscripts, in agreement with the better manuscripts and the Benedictine and Coustantian Vulgate editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0465D] Garnerius and the Augustine edition have Gignantius. It is absent from Oxoniensis. The Vulgate Councils omit the name of this bishop and the names of the following seven in a jump caused by the repeated name Victor.]

[Note: [Col. 0465D] The Benedictine and Coustantian editions add Praesidius and Crescentius. They are absent from the manuscripts of this collection and from Isidore.]

## Chapter I

Because the Lord has placed you in the apostolic see as a special gift of his grace, and has granted you to our times in such a way that it would count against us as negligence if we kept silent before your veneration about matters that ought to be brought forward for the Church, rather than your being able to receive them either with disdain or negligently, we ask that you deign to apply pastoral diligence to the great dangers of Christ’s weaker members.

[Note: [Col. 0465D] Oxoniensis has “especially.” Garnerius has “of special importance.”]

[Note: [Col. 0465D] Garnerius, from the early editions of Augustine, has “a destructive tempest of the enemies of grace has arisen,” contrary to the other editions and very many manuscripts.]

For a new and exceedingly destructive heresy is attempting to arise among the enemies of Christ’s grace, who by impious arguments are even trying to take away from us the Lord’s Prayer.

[Note: [Col. 0465D] From our manuscripts and other editions we have restored “even.”] For although the Lord taught us to say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12), they say that a person, once he has learned God’s commandments, can attain in this life such perfection of righteousness without the help of the Savior’s grace, solely through the exercise of free will,

[Note: [Col. 0465D] Thus the manuscripts of this collection and Isidore, together with the older Vulgate editions of the Councils. Other editions have “so that it is no longer necessary for him.”]

that it is not even necessary to say, “Forgive us our debts.”

[Note: [Col. 0465D] Another reading: “But that.”]

They do not understand what follows, “Do not bring us into temptation” (ibid.), as meaning that we ought to ask for divine help lest, when tempted, we fall into sin; rather, they say that this lies within our own power and that the human will alone is sufficient to fulfill it—as though the Apostle had said in vain, “It depends not on the one who wills or runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Romans 9:16), and, “God is faithful; he will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Corinthians 10:13).

[Note: [Col. 0465D] The Benedictine Vulgate has “will not permit”; Coustantius, together with the Councils edition, has “does not permit.” Shortly afterward, in place of “outcome,” other editions, together with Vatican-Isidore, have “way out.”]

The Lord would also have said in vain to the Apostle Peter, “I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32),

[Note: [Col. 0466C] Quesnellus adds “Peter.” We have deleted it with our Vindebonensis and the other printed editions. A little later the Vulgate has “lest you enter.”]

and to all his disciples, “Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation” (Matthew 26:40), if all of this lay within human power.

They also contend, with a presumption that is by no means Christian, that little children, even if they receive none of the sacraments of Christian grace,

[Note: [Col. 0466C] The Vindebonensis manuscript, together with the Councils edition and other codices, has “if they receive none.” Garnerius has “if they receive none at all.” The Benedictines adopted “receive none.” Father Coustantius aptly observes here: “Although the reading ‘even if none’ is supported by the words of the preceding letter of the Carthaginian synod, ‘promising that even if they are not baptized they will have eternal life,’ it is nevertheless clear that the sacrament of Christian grace is here called baptism.”]

will nevertheless have eternal life,

[Note: [Col. 0466D] Garnerius substituted “not at all” for “by no means”; this was adopted by the Benedictine editors. In Vindebonensis, a second ancient hand corrected “presumption” to “truth.” Coustantius thinks that the ambiguity should be removed by reading “by no means with Christian presumption.”]

thereby nullifying what the Apostle says: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and so death spread to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12); and elsewhere: “As all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:22).

## Chapter II

To leave aside the many other things they argue against the holy Scriptures,

[Note: [Col. 0466D] Garnerius has “do not endure.”]

can faithful hearts endure these two matters by which they are attempting entirely to overturn what makes us Christians: that God should not be asked to be our helper against the evil of sin and in the practice of righteousness; and that the sacrament of Christian grace does not help little children obtain eternal life?

In bringing these matters to your apostolic heart, we have no need to say much or to enlarge upon such great impiety in words, since without doubt these things move you so deeply that you cannot altogether fail to correct them,

[Note: [Col. 0466D] Quesnellus inserts “them”; we have deleted it with the Vindebonensis manuscript, the Councils edition, and Coustantius.]

lest they spread more widely and contaminate—or rather destroy—many, while under Christ’s name they completely alienate them from Christ’s grace.

[Note: [Col. 0466D] The Augustine edition has “so that they move you in this way.”]

The authors of this most destructive error are said to be Pelagius and Coelestius. We prefer that they be healed within the Church rather than cut off from the Church with their salvation despaired of, unless necessity compels otherwise.

[Note: [Col. 0466D] Thus all the printed editions agree with our codices. Quesnellus has “to be separated from the Church after their soundness has been despaired of.”]

One of them, namely Coelestius, is even said to have attained the presbyterate in Asia. Regarding what happened in his case a few years ago, your holiness is better informed by the Church of Carthage.

[Note: [Col. 0466D] Garnerius has “will be informed.” Quesnellus observes: “Less suitably. At the same time the documents of the Church of Carthage were delivered, as the following letter shows; indeed, the Numidian letter was written after the model of the Carthaginian one.”]

Pelagius, however, as letters sent by some of our brothers report, is established at Jerusalem and is said to be deceiving certain people.

Nevertheless, many more who have been able to investigate his views more carefully are struggling against him on behalf of Christ’s grace and the truth of the Catholic faith; above all, your holy son, our brother and fellow presbyter Jerome.

[Note: [Col. 0467C] In Vindebonensis, an ancient hand corrected “of the Catholic faith” to “in unity.”]

## Chapter III

But we believe that, with the mercy of the Lord our God assisting—the mercy that deigns both to guide you when you seek counsel and to hear you when you pray—those who hold such perverse and destructive opinions will more readily yield to the authority of your holiness, drawn from the authority of the sacred Scriptures, so that we may rejoice rather in their correction than grieve over their destruction, most blessed lord.

[Note: [Col. 0467C] Vindebonensis originally read “of the Scriptures that have been declared”; a second ancient hand corrected it to “of the Scriptures that have been decreed.” In the Isidorian manuscripts seen by Coustantius: “de clarum”; in one, on second correction, “with the declaration of the sacred [Scriptures].” The Councils edition has “drawn from the clear light of the Scriptures.” The Benedictine and Coustantian editions have “drawn from the sacred Scriptures.” This notable testimony of the African Church plainly signifies that the authority of the Roman pontiff proceeds from the Scriptures themselves, or from divine law.]

Whatever they themselves may choose, your veneration certainly sees that prompt and swift action must be taken at least for the sake of the many others whom they could entangle in their snares if they were tolerated.

We have sent these matters to your holiness in writing from the Council of Numidia, imitating the Church of Carthage and our fellow bishops of the province of Carthage, whom we have learned to have written about this matter to the apostolic see, which you, blessed one, illuminate.

[Note: [Col. 0467C] The Benedictine and Coustantian editions have “so that we may rejoice.”]

[Note: [Col. 0467C] Garnerius omits the words “the Church of Carthage.” The Roman edition of the Letters also omits them. After the word “province,” Quesnellus adds “the brothers and,” which we have deleted with Vindebonensis and the other printed editions.]

And in another hand: May you increase in the grace of God, most blessed lord, deservedly venerable and holy pope, honored in Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0467D] Garnerius has “in God,” less suitably.]

## Chapter IX

Here begins the letter of Pope Innocent to the Council of Milevis.

[Note: [Col. 0467D] It is extant and has been collated with the same manuscripts and editions as the preceding letter.]

INNOCENT to Silvanus the Elder, Valentinus, and the others who took part in the synod of Milevis, his most beloved brothers, greeting in the Lord.

### Chapter I

Among the other concerns of the Roman Church and the duties of the apostolic see, in which we handle the inquiries of various people through faithful and careful deliberation, our brother and fellow bishop Julius unexpectedly brought me your letter, which you sent from the Council of Milevis with especially devoted concern for the faith,

[Note: [Col. 0467D] In the Roman and Councils editions, “moderate.” To correct the error, Garnerius added “not” before “moderate.”]



[Note: [Col. 0467D] Garnerius has “very gladly.”]

and appended to it a similar written complaint from the synod of Carthage.

[Note: [Col. 0467D] Thus our codices and the Vulgate. Quesnellus has “committed.” Oxoniensis omits “a similar complaint.”]

The Church is surely rejoicing that pastors show such concern for the flocks entrusted to them that they do not allow anyone to err among them, but also, if some of the sheep have been led astray by the grass of a more savage pleasure,

[Note: [Col. 0467D] Garnerius omits “anyone,” and later, with Vindebonensis and the other Vulgate editions, also omits “even.” Shortly afterward, older Councils editions have “savage”; Garnerius, with the more recent Councils editions, has “obscene.” Quesnellus observes: “Both are wrong and contrary to the evidence of the manuscript codices and the author’s intention.”]

and if they persist in error, either wish to be entirely separated or, avoiding the things they formerly sought unlawfully, wish to be protected by the circumspection of their former custody:

[Note: [Col. 0468C] Quesnellus deletes these four words in the margin, not without reason, as does Garnerius; afterward he reads, with Thuanus, “or there unlawfully.”]

in either case, clearly taking thought lest, by receiving such persons, the others too be led astray by their example, or, by scorning those who return, they appear to expose them to the bites of wolves.

[Note: [Col. 0468C] Oxoniensis has “to inflict.”]

This is a very prudent and thoroughly Catholic consultation.

[Note: [Col. 0468C] Vindebonensis, together with Colbertinus, which Coustantius praises, has “consultation.” The word is supplied from the Isidorian manuscripts in the Vulgate Councils. Garnerius, with the ancient Augustine editions, has “consolation.” Thuanus, and Coustantius with him, has “consultation,” about which Quesnellus notes: “Better in sense, although the word is barbarous.” We have retained the reading of the text, which he preferred, together with the latest Augustine edition.]

For who could tolerate one who is in error, or refuse to receive one who is correcting himself? For just as I consider it harsh to offer connivance to those who sin,

[Note: [Col. 0468D] Thus Vindebonensis with the other printed editions. Quesnellus has “to provide.”]

so I judge it impious to refuse a hand to those who have been converted.

### Chapter II

You therefore make a careful and fitting appeal to the hidden matters of the apostolic honor

[Note: [Col. 0468D] The codices of this collection used by Quesnellus have this reading, better than Vindebonensis and another Colbertinus praised by Coustantius: “the secrets of the honor.” For *consulo*, when advice is being sought, takes an accusative. Garnerius, with the Roman edition, has “you consult the apostolic honor,” meaning that honor in particular. Then, in place of “external,” Vatican-Isidore and Labbe’s marginal reading more suitably have “internal.”]

—that honor whose concern embraces all the Churches, beyond those matters that are external—about what judgment ought to be maintained in difficult affairs.

[Note: [Col. 0468D] Garnerius adds “seeking,” with no manuscript, as far as we know, supporting it.]

You are following, of course, the form of the ancient rule, which you know has always been observed by me throughout the whole world. But I pass over this, for I do not think your prudence is unaware of it, since you confirmed it by your own action: you know that answers have always issued from the apostolic fountain to those who seek them throughout all the provinces.

[Note: [Col. 0468D] The Vulgate Councils has “who also did this.” Garnerius has: “Why, then, unless you know … do they issue?” Vindebonensis has “unless you know,” but then one would have to write “who” or “what.”]

Especially whenever the matter concerns the faith, I think all our brothers and fellow bishops ought to refer matters only to Peter—that is, to the author of his own name and honor—as your affection has now referred this matter, which can benefit all the Churches throughout the whole world in common.

For they must become more cautious when they see the inventors of evils, by the decrees of our judgment after the report of the two synods, separated from ecclesiastical communion.

[Note: [Col. 0469C] Thus our codices and all the printed editions; Quesnellus alone has “separated from ecclesiastical communion.”]

Your charity will therefore enjoy a double benefit: you will obtain the grace of the canons that have been preserved, and the whole world will make use of your benefit.

[Note: [Col. 0469C] Quesnellus alone has “our benefit,” less suitably. A little later the Councils Vulgate has “will be protected,” and in the margin “will make use.”]

For what Catholic man would wish to continue mixing his speech with the adversaries of Christ? Who would wish even to share the very light of life with them? Surely the authors of the new heresy must be shunned.

For what more bitter thing could they have devised against the Lord than, by abolishing divine helps, to take away the reason for daily prayer?

[Note: [Col. 0469C] Quesnellus has “so that divine helps might cease.” We preferred the reading of the Vulgate, supported by Vindebonensis. Shortly afterward Garnerius has “of the divine [help],” that is, “of the daily [help].” And then: “They would also say this.”]

This is to say: “Of what use is the Lord to me?” With good reason the hymn-singer says against them: “Behold, people who did not set God as their helper” (Psalm 52:9).

[Note: [Col. 0469C] The Benedictine and Coustantian editions have “What need … of God?” We have written “let him say” with Vindebonensis and all the Vulgate editions. Quesnellus has “he says.”]

Thus, while denying God’s help, they say that a person can suffice for himself and does not need divine grace; deprived of it, he must necessarily fall ensnared in the devil’s traps, while striving through freedom alone to fulfill all the commandments of life. O perverse doctrine of minds utterly depraved!

[Note: [Col. 0469C] The Benedictine edition has “Let him finally recognize this.” Coustantius has “Recognizing this at last.” Our reading is confirmed by the Chapters on Grace, in which this testimony of Innocent is quoted.]

Consider at last that freedom itself so deceived the first human being that, while he used its reins too indulgently,

[Note: [Col. 0469D] Thus the Thuanus manuscript. The Vulgate, together with the Chapters on Grace, has “through the presumption of transgression.” Vindebonensis, with Merlinus and Crabbus, has “of transgression.” Shortly afterward we have written “was able,” with Vindebonensis and the other printed editions. Quesnellus has “was able to.” Then, in place of “at the coming,” other editions, together with the cited Chapters on Grace, have “of the coming.”]

he fell into transgression through presumption; nor could he be rescued from it until the providence of regeneration restored the condition of his former freedom through the coming of Christ the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0469D] The Vulgate, together with Vindebonensis, has “Hear David say,” a reading we would gladly accept if it were not contradicted by the context of the preceding sentence. Since the best manuscripts of our collection and the Chapters on Grace have “Consider,” rather than “Let him hear,” we have preferred that reading.]

Hear also David saying: “Be my helper; do not abandon me, nor despise me, O God of my salvation” (Psalm 26:9; and 123:8); and: “Our help is in the name of the Lord”—words he would have spoken in vain

[Note: [Col. 0469D] Garnerius has “if the whole [matter were so].”]

if what he was asking from the Lord in lamentation had depended solely upon his own will.

### Chapter III

Since this is so, and since throughout all the divine books we read that God’s help alone must be joined to free will, and that free will can do nothing when deprived of heavenly assistance,

[Note: [Col. 0469D] Quesnellus notes in the margin: “The Vulgate has ‘aids.’”]

how, then, do Pelagius and Coelestius stubbornly persuade so many people to defend this possibility as belonging to free will alone—persuading themselves, or rather, what is more grievous and deserving of common sorrow, already persuading many others?

[Note: [Col. 0469D] The Vulgate, together with Vindebonensis and two Colbertini manuscripts cited by Coustantius, has “for instruction”; the older Councils editions have “for destruction.”]

We could bring forward many examples to refute such teaching, unless we knew that your holiness fully understands all the divine Scriptures—especially since your report is filled with such numerous and weighty testimonies that the present doctrine can be overthrown by these alone, and there is no need to seek hidden ones,

[Note: [Col. 0470C] Garnerius has “since these are among them”; and shortly afterward: “Therefore, do they try to take away God’s grace?”]

since, with the passages that readily occurred to you and that you have set forth, they neither dare nor are able to oppose what lies before them.

Therefore they are attempting to take away God’s grace, which we must seek even after the condition of our original freedom has been restored, since we cannot avoid any of the devil’s devices except with its help.

[Note: [Col. 0470C] Garnerius has “since they are wicked”; the Vulgate has “since they can do nothing else.”]

### Chapter IV

But as for what your fraternity says they proclaim—that little children can be granted the rewards of eternal life even without the grace of baptism—it is utterly foolish. For unless they eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, they will not have life in themselves.

Those who defend their having this life without regeneration seem to me to wish to abolish baptism itself, since they proclaim that these children possess what they believe is conferred on them only through baptism.

[Note: [Col. 0470C] The Roman, Labbean, Benedictine, and Coustantian editions have “what is believed”; if “they believe” is to be retained, this passage would refer to the kingdom of heaven, for which the Pelagians asserted baptism to be necessary. See Augustine, Book I Against the Letter of the Pelagians, chapter 22. Nevertheless, “what is believed,” supported by several and better manuscripts, seems preferable and more consistent with the context.]

If, then, they wish to say that not being reborn does no harm, they must admit that the sacred waters of regeneration are of no benefit either.

But so that the perverse doctrine of superfluous men may quickly be dismantled by the reasoning of truth,

[Note: [Col. 0470D] Thus two codices; Quesnellus, with Vindebonensis and another Colbertinus cited by Coustantius, has “distinguished.” Merlinus, with one Colbertinus, has “separated,” and Vindebonensis has the same reading from a second hand, less correctly. Vatican 3791 has “distinguished.” Some editions have “cut apart.” Yet *discingo*, meaning “to dissolve” or “to blunt,” is found in writers of good authority.]

the Lord proclaims this in the Gospel, saying: “Let the children come to me, and do not hinder them” (Luke 18:16).

[Note: [Col. 0470D] Thus the copies of this collection. The others, from which the other Vulgate editions derive, add: “for to such belongs the kingdom of heaven.”]

### Chapter V

Therefore, by the authority of apostolic vigor, we decree that Pelagius and Coelestius—that is, the inventors of new expressions, which, as the Apostle said, produce nothing for edification but are accustomed rather to generate utterly empty disputes—are to be deprived of ecclesiastical communion until they repent from the devil’s snares, by whom they are held captive according to his will (2 Timothy 1:23 and 26), and that meanwhile they are not to be received into the Lord’s fold, which they chose to abandon by following the path of a perverse way.

[Note: [Col. 0470D] The Councils edition adds after “Rome”: “until they wish to abandon the path of the perverse way which they have followed.” Other editions add: “the path which they followed.”]

For those who trouble us and wish to pervert the Gospel of Christ must be cut off (Galatians 5:12).

[Note: [Col. 0471C] Other editions have “you”; shortly afterward, “to convert,” with Vindebonensis.]

At the same time, we order that anyone who persists in defending this with similar obstinacy be bound by the same punishment. For not only those who do such things, but also those who approve those who do them, are liable to judgment (Romans 1:32).

[Note: [Col. 0471C] Quesnellus adds “evil things,” and after “those who do them” adds “are worthy of punishment.” The Benedictine edition has “are worthy of death.” We have deleted this with the other printed editions and with the two manuscripts of this collection, Thuanus and Vindebonensis. The phrase “they are to be bound by an equal punishment” is understood from what precedes.]

For I do not think there is much difference between the intention of the one who commits the offense and the favor of the one who consents. I add further that the person who receives no one’s consent commonly learns to cease from error.

Let this sentence, therefore, most beloved brothers, remain fixed against the persons mentioned above. Let them be absent from the courts of the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0471C] Garnerius has “Let pastoral vigilance beware.” The Augustine edition has “they desire only.”]

Let them merely be deprived of pastoral custody, lest the dire contagion of two sheep perhaps spread through the unwary multitude, and lest the wolf, rejoicing in its rapacious heart, take pleasure within the Lord’s fold at seeing such great flocks of sheep scattered,

while the wound of two is negligently disregarded by the guardians.

It must therefore be seen to that, by permitting wolves, we do not appear to be hirelings rather than shepherds.

We certainly order—for Christ our Lord has declared with his own voice that he does not desire the death of the dying, provided that he return and live—

[Note: [Col. 0471C] Garnerius adds “nevertheless,” and later “he signified his will.”]

that if they should ever recover their sanity, laying aside the error of their wicked doctrine, and should condemn the things by whose transgression they condemned themselves, the Church is not to deny them the customary medicine, that is, its place of refuge,

lest, while we perhaps prevent them from returning,

[Note: [Col. 0471C] Quesnellus, with his manuscripts, has “as though.” Our Vindebonensis, agreeing with the other printed editions, has the reading we preferred. Garnerius substitutes “sheep” for this word.]

they remain truly outside the fold and are swallowed by the ravenous jaws of the waiting enemy—

the very people whom they armed against themselves with the darts of evil disputation.

[Note: [Col. 0471C] Quesnellus, with his codices, has “by whose authority they armed themselves with certain darts.” Garnerius has “which he armed against themselves with darts.” Other editions have “which they armed against themselves with darts.” We have followed our Vindebonensis and Vatican manuscripts.]

Farewell, brothers.

[Note: [Col. 0471C] Garnerius has: “Given on 27 January, in the consulship of Honorius, eleven times consul, and Constantius, a man of the highest rank,” not “men of the highest rank.” Since this letter was issued by the holy pontiff on the same day as the letter to the synod of Carthage, there can be no doubt that it was dated by the same formula as that letter: “After the consulship of Theodosius VII and Junius Quartus.” But since after this consulship the ordinary consuls Honorius Augustus and Constantius entered office, Coustantius’s conjecture is quite plausible: that an ancient copyist added in the margin “in the consulship of Honorius and Constantius,” and that this marginal note was mistakenly transferred into the text. This becomes much more probable if one considers the omission of the numbers XI and II, which does not suit a genuine chronological notation.]

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Honorius and Constantius, men of the highest rank.

## Chapter X

Here begins the private letter of five bishops of Africa to the same pope against Pelagius and Coelestius.

[Note: [Col. 0472C] Collated again with the same manuscripts as the two preceding letters. It is called “private” to distinguish it from the synodal letters written to Innocent by the same bishops at the Council of Carthage or Milevis. See Augustine, Letter 86, section 2. Likewise, Turribius’s letter written privately to Leo is called “private” in Letter 15 of this pontiff to the same Turribius, chapter 17. Compare note 3 in Quesnellus’s Dissertation 13.]

To the most blessed and deservedly most honored brother, Pope INNOCENT, AURELIUS, ALYPIUS, AUGUSTINE, EVODIUS, and POSSIDIUS, greeting.

[Note: [Col. 0472C] The Isidorian manuscripts, together with the Vulgate, add “in the Lord.”]

### Chapter I

Concerning the two councils of the province of Carthage and of Numidia,

[Note: [Col. 0472C] Quesnellus, with Oxoniensis alone, inserts “Africa.” We have deleted it with our codices and the Vulgate editions, indeed also with Quesnellus’s own Thuanus manuscript.]

we sent to your holiness a letter signed by not a small number of bishops against the enemies of Christ’s grace, who trust in their own strength and, in a certain sense, say to our Creator: “You made us human beings; we ourselves made ourselves righteous.”

[Note: [Col. 0472C] The Councils Vulgate has “You created us.”]

They call human nature free for this reason: so that they need not seek a liberator; they call it safe for this reason: so that they may judge a savior superfluous. For they say that it possesses such power that, by the strength it received once at the origin of its creation, it can, through free will and without any further assistance from the grace of the one who created it, subdue and extinguish all desires and overcome temptations.

Many of them rise up against us and say to our soul: “There is no salvation for him in his God” (Psalm 3:3).

The household of Christ, which says, “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians 12:10), and to which its Lord says, “I am your salvation” (Psalm 34:3), waits with anxious heart, in fear and trembling, for the Lord’s help, also through the charity of your veneration.

For we have heard that in the city of Rome, where that man lived for a long time, there are certain people who favor him for various reasons.

[Note: [Col. 0472C] Namely, Pelagius, although he has not yet been named in this letter. Quesnellus replaces the word “that man,” found in our codices and other printed editions, with “Pelagius,” perhaps because he found the name written for clarity in the Oxoniensis manuscript.]

Some, namely, because he is said to have persuaded them of such things; but more numerous are those who do not believe that he holds such opinions.

[Note: [Col. 0472D] Thus, together with our Oxoniensis, our Vindebonensis reads very well. Thuanus, together with other ancient editions, has “because you are said to have persuaded them of such things”; Quesnellus declares this a corrupt reading and insulting to the pontiff. Our Vatican manuscript, however, together with most of those praised by Father Coustantius, has *perhibentur*, “they are said,” instead of *perhibent*, “he is said.” One Colbertinus, together with another Vatican manuscript, has “because he is said to have persuaded us.” In the latter, if “you” is corrected to “you [plural],” the not-unreasonable reading results: “because you are said to have persuaded them of such things.” For the Pelagians boasted that the Romans favored them.]

Especially because, in the East, where he lives, ecclesiastical proceedings are said to have taken place by which he is thought to have been cleared. If the bishops there declared him Catholic, this must be believed to have happened for no other reason than that he said he confessed the grace of God, and that a person could live justly through his own labor and will in such a way that he did not deny that God’s grace assisted him for this purpose.

[Note: [Col. 0473C] The same codex, together with the Vulgate, deletes “him.”]

Upon hearing these words, the Catholic bishops could understand no other grace of God than the grace they were accustomed to read in the books of God and preach to the people of God—namely, the grace about which the Apostle says: “I do not nullify the grace of God; for if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing” (Galatians 2:21)—without doubt, the grace by which we are justified from iniquity and saved from weakness, not the grace by which we were created with our own will.

For if those bishops had understood him to mean the grace that we share even with the impious, with whom we are human beings, while denying the grace by which we are Christians and children of God, who among the Catholic priests, I do not say would have listened to him patiently, but would have endured him before their own eyes?

[Note: [Col. 0473C] Quesnellus has “I say, who would have listened patiently?” We followed our Vindebonensis, supported by the other printed editions. Then two Colbertini manuscripts add “only” before “before their eyes,” with somewhat greater emphasis, as Coustantius observed. Vindebonensis also once had “before so great eyes” corruptly, and a later hand deleted the word “so great.”]

Therefore the judges are not to be blamed, because they heard the word “grace” according to ecclesiastical custom, without knowing what such people habitually scatter either in the books of their doctrine or into the ears of their followers.

[Note: [Col. 0473D] Thus Vindebonensis with the Vulgate, better than Quesnellus, who has “they heard the grace.”]

## Chapter II

This is not a matter of one Pelagius—for perhaps he has already been corrected; would that it were so—but of so many others who, arguing at length and dragging along weak and uneducated souls as though entangled, while tiring those who are firm and steadfast in the faith by the very controversy itself, have now filled every place.

[Note: Quesnellus added *loca* (“places”). We have deleted it in accordance with our Vindobonensis manuscript and the other editions.] 

[Note: The Vulgate has *qui* (“who”).]

[Note: Thuanus, with Merlinius, has *conjunctus*; Oxoniensis, with the more recent printed editions of the Councils, has *convictus*, less correctly. Our Vindobonensis and the other superior manuscripts consulted by Father Coustantius support Quesnellus’s reading.]

Either, therefore, he should be summoned to Rome by Your Reverence and carefully questioned about what grace he means and acknowledges—if, that is, he acknowledges that human beings are helped to avoid sin and live justly—or this very matter should be dealt with by letter.

[Note: The Vatican Isidorian manuscript, with the Vulgate, adds *jam* (“now”).] And when it has been discovered that he means the grace taught by ecclesiastical and apostolic truth, then he must be absolved without any scruple on the part of the Church and without any hiding-place for ambiguity; then we should truly rejoice over his purification.

For whether he says that grace is free will, or that grace is the remission of sins, or that grace is the commandment of the law, he says none of those things that, through the ministry of the Holy Spirit, pertain to overcoming lust and temptations.

[Note: The Vulgate, supported by the Vindobonensis, reads *quod . . . pertinet* (“which . . . pertains”).]

The Spirit he poured out upon us most abundantly—the one who ascended into heaven and, having taken captivity captive, gave gifts to human beings (Titus 3:6; Ephesians 4:8; Romans 8:26).

[Note: The Vindobonensis manuscript has *et captivavit captivitatem* (“and he took captivity captive”); the better printed texts have *et captivans captivitatem* (“and, taking captivity captive”).]

For this reason we pray that we may be able to overcome the temptation of sin, so that the Spirit of God, from whom we have received the pledge, may help our weakness. The one who prays and says, “Do not bring us into temptation” (Matthew 6:13), is certainly not praying that he may be a human being, since he is one by nature;

[Note: Some manuscripts have *quod* (“that”) instead. Shortly afterward, we have written *habeat* (“may have”) in accordance with the Vindobonensis manuscript and the Quesnellian Vulgate; the other reading is *accipiat* (“may receive”).]

nor is he praying that he may have free will, which he already received when nature itself was created;

nor is he praying for the remission of sins, because that has already been said above: “Forgive us our debts”;

nor is he praying that he may receive a commandment;

[Note: Quesnellus has *inferius* (“below”). We have corrected the text in accordance with two of our manuscripts and the printed editions.]

but plainly he is praying that he may carry out the commandment. For if he is brought into temptation—that is, if he fails in temptation—he certainly commits sin, which is contrary to the commandment. Therefore he prays that he may not sin, that is, that he may do nothing evil. This is what the Apostle prays for the Corinthians when he says: “We pray to God that you do no evil” (2 Corinthians 13:7).

From this it is sufficiently clear that, although there is no doubt that the will possesses free choice with respect to not sinning—that is, not doing evil—its power is nevertheless insufficient unless weakness is helped.

[Note: In the Vindobonensis manuscript an ancient hand adds *liberum* (“free”), as is read in the printed editions of the Councils.]

The prayer itself, therefore, is a most explicit testimony to grace.

[Note: Thus read our manuscripts and the other editions. Quesnellus has *eam* (“it”).]

Let him acknowledge this, and we shall rejoice over him, whether he is already right or has been corrected.

Law and grace must be distinguished. The law knows how to command; grace knows how to help. The law would not command unless there were a will; nor would grace help if the will were sufficient.

We are commanded to have understanding, where it is said: “Do not be like a horse or a mule, which have no understanding” (Psalm 31:9); and yet we pray that we may have understanding, where it is said: “Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments” (Psalm 119:34).

We are commanded to have wisdom, where it is said: “At last become wise”;

[Note: The passage from this point through the repeated phrase “where it is said” is omitted in the Oxoniensis manuscript. Quesnellus noted in the margin that it should be inserted from the other editions. We inserted it because it is also found in the Vindobonensis manuscript of this collection.]

and yet we pray that we may have wisdom, where it is said: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach anyone; and it will be given to him” (James 1:5).

We are commanded to have self-control, where it is said:

[Note: Thus our Vindobonensis reads, together with Merlinus, Crabbus, and very many manuscripts collated by Father Coustantius. The following important annotation must be appended here. It is nevertheless evident that something is missing. For this reason the Roman editor added the following in brackets and in a different typeface: “[Something of this kind is missing: ‘Let your loins be girded’; and yet we pray that it may be given to us, where it is said.]” This addition was retained in certain later editions. Quesnellus substituted for it: “Turn away from your pleasures, and yet we pray that we may have self-control, where it is said: . . .” Neither supplement is satisfactory. The manner in which this passage should be restored may be learned from another similar passage of Augustine. In Letter 147 to Hilary, §9, treating the same argument, he writes: “When the law says, ‘You shall not covet,’ what else does it seem to command except self-control from unlawful desires? . . . and yet we pray that we may have self-control, where it is said: ‘Since I knew that no one can be self-controlled,’ etc.” He then concludes: “God therefore commands self-control and gives self-control.” In accordance with Augustine’s thought, this passage of ours will be complete if we restore it as follows: “We are commanded to have self-control, where it is said, ‘You shall not covet’; and yet we pray that we may have self-control, where it is said, ‘Since I knew,’ etc.” The repetition of the same words immediately afterward—a prolific source of lacunae—gave occasion for this omission.]

“Since I knew that no one can be self-controlled unless God grants it—and that it was itself a matter of wisdom to know whose gift this was—I approached the Lord and entreated him” (Wisdom 8:21).

Finally, not to make the discussion excessively long by going through everything, we are commanded not to do evil, where it is said: “Turn away from evil”;

[Note: Quesnellus adds “and do good.” This has been better deleted here in the Vindobonensis manuscript and in the other printed editions.]

and yet we pray that we may not do evil, where it is said: “We pray to God that you do no evil.”

We are commanded to do good, where it is said: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 36:27); and yet we pray that we may do good, where it is said: “We do not cease praying for you and asking” (Colossians 1:3); and among the things for which he prays on their behalf he says: “that you may walk worthily of God in every pleasing thing, in every good work and good word.”

Therefore, just as we recognize the will when these things are commanded, so let him also recognize grace when they are requested.

## Chapter III

We have sent Your Reverence the book that certain religious and honorable young servants of God gave us. We do not conceal their names, for they are called Timasius and James. As we have heard—and as you yourself, we know, are pleased to understand—they abandoned the hope they had placed in this world at Pelagius’s exhortation and now serve God in continence.

After at last, through some effort of ours and with the Lord’s inspiration, they had been freed from the same error, they produced this book, saying that it belonged to Pelagius, and earnestly requested that a reply be made to it. This was done, and the reply itself was written back to them. They wrote back with thanks.

We sent both documents: the one to which the reply was made and the reply itself. And, so that we might not be excessively burdensome, we marked the places where we ask you not to consider it onerous to examine how, when confronted with the charge that he denied the grace of God, he answered in such a way as to say that grace was nothing other than the nature in which God created us.

If, however, he denies that this is his book, or denies that the passages in the book are his, we do not dispute the matter. Let him anathematize and condemn them, and let him acknowledge openly that grace which Christian teaching demonstrates and proclaims to be proper to Christians—not nature, but that by which nature is saved.

[Note: The same manuscript adds *gratia* (“grace”). We deleted it in accordance with that manuscript and the other printed editions. The Vindobonensis then deletes *quae* (“which”). The passage is very corrupt in this collection and in other Isidorian manuscripts. The Benedictine editors, from the Vatican manuscript, and Coustantius, from two Colbertine manuscripts, corrected it as follows: “which does not plant and water nature by teaching that sounds in the ears or by some visible aid, as a planter and waterer, so to speak, from outside,” etc.]

That grace is not, as it were, planted and watered from outside by teaching that sounds in the ears or by some visible aid, but by the ministry of the Spirit and by hidden mercy, as God acts—the God who gives the growth.

For even if, in a certain unobjectionable sense, the grace of God by which we were created may be called grace—so that we might be something rather than nothing, and not something like a corpse that does not live, a tree that does not feel, or an animal that does not understand, but human beings who both existed and lived and felt and understood, and were able to give thanks to our Creator for so great a benefit—and therefore this too can rightly be called grace, since it was bestowed not on account of the merits of any preceding works but by the free goodness of God, nevertheless there is another grace by which we are called predestined, justified, and glorified, so that we may say: “If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Romans 8:31).

[Note: We inserted *suo* (“his own”) on the authority of our Vindobonensis and Vatican manuscripts and the other printed editions.]

## Chapter IV

It was concerning this grace that the controversy arose, when those whom Pelagius seriously offended and disturbed said to him that he was attacking it in his arguments by asserting that human nature, through free will, was sufficient not only for carrying out but also for perfecting the divine commandments.

[Note: The Vulgate, together with the Vatican manuscript, deletes *quod* (“that”) and then reads *humanam sufficere naturam* (“that human nature is sufficient”).]

This grace apostolic teaching calls by this name—the grace by which we are saved and justified through faith in Christ. Of this grace it is written: “I do not nullify the grace of God; for if justification comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing” (Galatians 2:21).

Of this grace it is written: “You are severed from Christ, you who are justified by the law; you have fallen away from grace” (ibid. 5:4).

Of this grace it is written: “But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (Romans 11:6).

[Note: The Vulgate, together with the Vatican Isidorian manuscript, adds *est* (“is”).]

Of this grace it is written: “To the one who works, the reward is not reckoned according to grace but according to debt; but to the one who does not work, yet believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness” (ibid. 4:4).

And there are many other passages, which you yourself can remember better, understand more wisely, and proclaim more clearly.

But although we understand that the grace by which we were created human beings may not improperly be called grace, it is nevertheless surprising if we read it called by that name anywhere in the canonical prophetic, evangelical, or apostolic writings.

When, therefore, this question was put to him concerning that grace which is extremely well known to faithful and catholic Christians, so that he might cease attacking it, what is the explanation for his having raised this very objection against himself in his book, as though speaking in the person of an opponent, and then, in order to clear himself by his reply, having answered nothing other than that human nature, once created, is referred to the grace of the Creator?

[Note: The word *hominis* (“of human beings”) has been inserted from the same manuscripts and editions. The Thuanensis, together with the Vulgate, reads *hominis referre gratiam Creatoris* (“to refer the grace of the Creator to human beings”); but our manuscripts, together with the Oxoniensis and Quesnellus, read *referri ad gratiam Creatoris* (“to be referred to the grace of the Creator”). A little later, *dederit* (“has given”) has been supplied from our manuscripts and the other editions. Quesnellus has *dedit* (“gave”).]

Thus he says that righteousness can be fulfilled without sin through free will with the help of divine grace, because God gave this to human beings in the very possibility of their nature.

To this the proper reply is: “Then the scandal of the cross has been nullified; then Christ died for nothing” (Galatians 5:11; 2:21).

[Note: The Vindobonensis, together with the more recent printed editions of the Councils, has *Non enim* (“For not”).]

For if he had not died on account of our sins and risen on account of our justification,

[Note: The Vindobonensis reads *nec ascendit* (“nor did he ascend”); the reading in the other printed editions, *nec ascenderet* (“nor would he have ascended”), is better. Quesnellus has “into heaven.” We have substituted *in altum* (“on high”) on the basis of all our printed editions and manuscripts.]

and if he had not ascended on high and, taking captivity captive, given gifts to human beings, would this possibility of nature which he defends not have existed in human beings?

## Chapter V

Or was God’s commandment lacking, and is that why Christ died? On the contrary, this too was already holy, just, and good. It had already been said: “You shall not covet” (Exodus 20:17);

[Note: Quesnellus adds “your neighbor’s property.” We have deleted this in accordance with the Vindobonensis manuscript and the other printed editions.]

it had already been said: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 22:39), a statement in which the Apostle says that the whole law is fulfilled.

And since no one loves himself unless he loves God, the Lord therefore says that the whole law and the prophets depend upon these two commandments. These two commandments had already been given to human beings by God.

[Note: We have added *divinitus* (“by God”), and afterward also *etiam* (“also”), from the same manuscript and the other editions.]

Or had the eternal reward of righteousness not yet been promised? He himself does not say this, since in his writings he stated that even in the Old Testament the kingdom of heaven had been promised.

If, therefore, the possibility of nature through free will already existed for doing and perfecting righteousness; if the holy, just, and good commandment of God’s law already existed; if the everlasting reward had already been promised—then Christ died for nothing. Then righteousness comes neither through the law nor through the possibility of nature, but through faith and the gift of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord, the one mediator between God and human beings.

If he had not died at the fullness of time on account of our sins

[Note: The following five words have been added from our manuscripts and from all the editions.]

and risen on account of our justification, then certainly the faith both of the ancients and of ourselves would have been nullified. But once faith has been nullified, what righteousness remains for a human being, since “the righteous person lives by faith”?

For since sin entered the world through one human being, and death through sin, and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned (Romans 5:12), clearly no one has been or is liberated from this body of death, where another law opposes the law of the mind, by his own possibility—a possibility that has been lost and therefore needs a redeemer, wounded and therefore needs a savior.

[Note: The Vindobonensis and other manuscripts read, incorrectly, *suae possibilitas* (“the possibility of his own”). This perhaps gave occasion for adding *naturae* (“of nature”), as in the Oxoniensis manuscript, from which Quesnellus printed *naturae suae possibilitas* (“the possibility of his own nature”).]

Rather, liberation comes through the grace of God, by faith in the one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Jesus Christ, who, although he was God, made himself human, and, while remaining God, became human and himself restored what he had made.

## Chapter VI

I think that the faith of Christ—which later came into revelation—was hidden in the times of our fathers,

[Note: Our manuscripts and the Thuanensis, with the Vulgate, read *quod eum lateat* (“that it escapes him”); Quesnellus, preferring the Oxoniensis, has *Pelagium lateat* (“that it escapes Pelagius”). In his second edition *lateat* dropped out; Garnier has *quod lateat* (“that it escapes [him]”).] through which nevertheless all those were liberated by the grace of God who, throughout the times of the human race, could be liberated by the hidden but not blameworthy judgment of God.

Hence the Apostle says: “But having the same spirit of faith”—certainly the same as they had—“according to what is written: I believed, and therefore I spoke; we also believe, and therefore we speak” (2 Corinthians 4:13).

[Note: Thus the Vindobonensis manuscript reads, together with the other editions. Quesnellus has *quem illi* (“which they had”), as it is written.]

For this reason the Mediator himself says: “Abraham desired to see my day; he saw it and rejoiced” (John 8:56).

For this reason Melchizedek, having brought forth the sacrament of the Lord’s table (Genesis 14:18), knew how to prefigure his eternal priesthood.

[Note: Thus the same manuscript and the printed editions read. Quesnellus has *sacrificium* (“sacrifice”), less correctly.]

Then, after the law had been given in writing—the law of which the Apostle says that it entered in so that the offense might abound (Romans 9:20)—and concerning which he says: “If the inheritance comes from the law, it no longer comes from the promise; but God granted it to Abraham through a promise. Why then the law? It was established for the sake of transgressions until the seed should come to whom the promise had been made, ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator. Now a mediator is not of one party; but God is one. Is the law therefore contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not. For if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would indeed be by the law. But Scripture confined everything under sin, so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ” (Galatians 3:18–22).

[Note: The Vulgate has *posita est* (“it was established”), and the Vindobonensis manuscript also has *dispositum* (“ordained”).]

Is it not sufficiently clear that this was accomplished through the law: that sin might be recognized and increased through transgression? For where there is no law, neither is there transgression (Romans 4:15). Thus, against sin’s victory, people would flee to the divine grace contained in the promises, and the law would not be contrary to God’s promises.

For this reason the knowledge of sin comes through the law, and through transgression of the law sin abounds, so that God’s promises—which are the grace of God—might be sought for liberation, and so that righteousness might begin to exist in a human being, not his own righteousness but God’s, that is, righteousness given as a gift by God.

Even now some people, as was then said concerning the Jews, are ignorant of God’s righteousness and wish to establish their own; therefore they are not subject to God’s righteousness (Romans 10:3).

For through the law they too suppose that they are justified, believing that free will is sufficient for them to keep it—that is, that their righteousness comes from human nature rather than being given by divine grace, on account of which it is called God’s righteousness.

Hence it is likewise written: “Through the law comes knowledge of sin; but now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, witnessed by the law and the prophets” (Romans 5:21).

When he says, “has been manifested,” he shows that it existed then as well, but that it was then hidden as the rain obtained by Gideon was hidden in the fleece, whereas now it is manifest as rain upon the threshing floor.

Therefore, when the law without grace could not have been the death of sin but rather its power, for it is written: “The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law” (1 Corinthians 15:56), just as many now flee from the face of reigning sin to grace, like rain upon the threshing floor now exposed, so only a few then fled to it, like rain hidden in the fleece.

This distribution of the times refers to the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, concerning which it is said: “How unsearchable are God’s judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Romans 11:13).

[Note: The Vatican manuscript, with the other editions, reads *judicia ejus* (“his judgments”).]

[Note: Some other printed manuscripts have *si et ante* (“if also before”); Garnier has *sic et ante* (“so also before”).]

Therefore, both before the time of the law and during the time of the law itself, the righteous fathers who lived by faith were justified not by the possibility of weak nature—unworthy, corrupted, and sold under sin—

[Note: The Louvain and Benedictine editions, together with Coustantius, read *indigae*, which they argue is correct, claiming that *indignae* arose improperly from *indigue*, since the ancients used to write in this manner for *indige* (“needy” or “lacking”).]

but by God’s grace through faith; and now, having come into the open and been revealed, that same grace justifies.

## Chapter VII

Let Pelagius therefore anathematize his writings in which he argues against this grace—not through defiance, perhaps, but through ignorance—by defending the possibility of nature for overcoming sins and fulfilling commandments.

Or, if he denies that they are his, and says that passages in his writings were inserted by his enemies—although he denies that they are his—let him nevertheless anathematize and condemn them, with the exhortation of a father and by the authority of Your Holiness.

[Note: Quesnellus has *et scriptis* (“and in his writings”), and shortly afterward *ab inimicis dicit* (“he says, by his enemies”). We have preferred the reading of the Vindobonensis manuscript together with the other printed editions.]

If he wishes to do so, let him learn to remove from himself the burdensome and destructive scandal of the Church, which his hearers and those who perversely love him do not cease to spread everywhere.

[Note: Quesnellus has *si non vult* (“if he does not wish”), followed by: “let him learn that it is burdensome and destructive to himself to bring scandal upon the Church, which scandal the hearers,” etc. The reading confirmed by our Vindobonensis manuscript has been restored. The printed editions alone read *Si vult ergo* or *Si ergo vult* (“If, therefore, he wishes”), and the Council editions have *inferre* (“to bring”) instead of *auferre* (“to remove”), less correctly. The restored reading agrees most closely with the context. For if Pelagius wishes to anathematize the book published under his name, the bishops do not doubt that the scandal burdensome to himself and destructive to the Church must be removed.]
