For if they learn that the same book which they either believe or know to be his has been anathematized and condemned by the authority of the catholic bishops, and especially by Your Holiness—whose authority with him we have no doubt carries the greatest weight—we do not think that they will thereafter dare to disturb faithful and genuinely Christian hearts by speaking against the grace of God, which has been revealed through the passion and resurrection of Christ.

Rather, with the help of God’s mercy, and with the charity, piety, and fervent prayers with which you contend alongside us, they will trust not in their own strength but in that same grace, so that they may be not only blessed forever but also righteous and holy.

[Note: Quesnellus, with only the Oxoniensis manuscript, adds *conari* (“to strive”); this is more correctly absent from the Vindobonensis and Thuanensis manuscripts and the other printed editions. Immediately afterward the Vindobonensis reads *confisuri* (“about to trust”).]

For this reason we thought that the letter written to him by one of us should rather be sent to Your Blessedness.

[Note: This refers to Augustine’s letter sent to Pelagius, which has not come down to us. The only writer of the letter to whom Pelagius sent writings for his defense was Augustine, as is clear from *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapter 32.]

Pelagius had sent those writings to him through a certain Eastern deacon who was also a citizen of Hippo, as certain writings constituting a kind of defense of himself.

[Note: We have deleted the word *causa*, inserted here by Quesnellus, in accordance with the Vindobonensis manuscript and the other printed editions, and more correctly so. For the writings of his defense referred to here are called “the proceedings of his defense” in *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapter 29.]

We judged it better, and requested, that you yourself be pleased to send it to him.

[Note: The reading of the other manuscripts is sounder: *ei mittere* (“to send it to him”), from which the other editions derive their text.]

In this way he will be more willing to read it, paying attention in it more to the one who sent it than to the one who wrote it.

## Chapter VIII

As for what they say—that a human being can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments if he wishes—although it seems more tolerable to say this when it is added that it occurs through the help of grace, which has nevertheless been revealed and granted through the incarnation of his only-begotten Son,

[Note: The Vindobonensis reads *quoniam immerito debere potest*; Crabbus has *quoniam merito quaeri potest* (“since it can rightly be asked”); the other editions read *quoniam non immerito movere potest* (“since it can not unreasonably raise a question”). Shortly afterward, we have preferred *prorsus* (“entirely”) with our manuscripts and the other editions; Quesnellus has *proprio* (“its own”).]

still, since it can reasonably be asked where and when this is accomplished in us through that same grace, so that we are entirely without sin, the matter must be examined more carefully.

Is it in this life, when the flesh desires against the spirit? Or is it in that life when the saying written in Scripture will be fulfilled: “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” For the sting of death is sin (1 Corinthians 15:55).

[Note: Thus our manuscripts and the printed editions read. Quesnellus alone has *stimulus* (“sting”). We have added *quosdam* (“certain others”) on the basis of the same manuscripts and editions.]

The matter must be examined especially because of certain others who believed and committed to writing that even in this life a human being can be without sin—not from the beginning of birth, but through conversion from sins to righteousness and from a wicked way to a good life.

[Note: Garnier and the Augustinian edition have *a vita reproba* (“from a reprobate life”).]

Thus they understood what is written about Zechariah and Elizabeth: that they walked in all the commandments of the Lord without reproach (Luke 1:6).

They took the phrase “without reproach” to mean “without sin”;

[Note: We have added *dictum* (“said”) in accordance with our manuscripts and the printed editions.]

not indeed denying—in fact, piously confessing, as is found elsewhere in their writings—the help of the grace of our Lord, not through the natural spirit of human beings but through the sovereign Spirit of God.

They seem not to have considered carefully enough that Zechariah himself was certainly a priest. All priests, however,

[Note: The Vatican manuscript, together with the Vulgate, adds *tunc* (“then”).]

were necessarily required by God’s law first to offer a sacrifice for their own sins and afterward for the people’s.

Therefore, just as we are now shown by the sacrifice of prayer not to be without sin, since we have been commanded to say, “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12), so then, through the sacrifices of animal victims, priests were shown not to be without sin, since they were commanded to offer sacrifice for their own sins.

If, then, the matter is as follows—that through the grace of the Savior we do indeed advance in this life, desire diminishing and love increasing, but are perfected in the life to come, desire being extinguished and love completed—then the statement written in Scripture, “Whoever is born of God does not sin” (1 John 5:18),

[Note: The Vindobonensis manuscript, together with another Colbertine manuscript, deletes *natus* (“born”).]

must be understood as referring to love itself, which alone does not sin.

For growth and perfection in love belong to the birth that is from God, not the desire that must be diminished and consumed—the desire which, so long as it is in our members, nevertheless opposes the law of the mind according to its own law.

But one who is born of God, not obeying the desires of the flesh and not presenting his members as weapons of unrighteousness to sin, can say: “It is no longer I who do it, but the sin dwelling in me” (Romans 7:20).

[Note: We inserted *id* (“it”), from the same Vindobonensis manuscript, in place of *illud* (“that”), which the other editions have.]

But however this question may stand—for even if a human being without sin is not found in this life, it is nevertheless said to be possible through the help of the Spirit of God and of grace, and one must strive and pray for it to happen—it is tolerable for anyone to be mistaken in this matter. It is not diabolical impiety but human error to assert that this is something to be pursued and desired, even if one cannot demonstrate what one affirms.

For such a person believes that something can happen which it is certainly praiseworthy to desire.

For us, however, it is enough that no one is found in the Church of God, at whatever level of advancement and excellence in righteousness, who dares to say that the prayer of the Lord is not necessary for him: “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12).

Nor should anyone say that he has no sin, lest he deceive himself and the truth not be in him, even if he is already living without reproach.

For it is not every kind of human temptation but grave sin that gives rise to reproach.

[Note: The Council, Augustinian, and Coustantius editions have: “whatever human temptation.”]

As for the remaining matters brought against him, Your Blessedness will unquestionably judge them according to the way he is seen to have defended them in the proceedings.

Your most gentle kindness of heart will surely pardon us for having sent Your Holiness a letter perhaps longer than you wished.

For we are not pouring our little stream back into your abundant spring in order to enlarge it. Rather, amid this considerable temptation of the present age—from which may the one to whom we say, “Do not bring us into temptation” (Matthew 6:13), deliver us—we wish you to approve whether our stream, however small, flows from the same source from which your abundant streams flow, and to console us through your replies in our common participation in the one grace.

[Note: Quesnellus inserts *rivulus* (“little stream”). We have deleted it with the Vindobonensis and the other printed editions; it is understood from what precedes.]

[Note: The Vindobonensis manuscript reads corruptly *his quae rescriptis*. The correction is supplied by the other manuscripts, with which the Benedictine editors and Coustantius read *tuisque rescriptis* (“and by your replies”). Other editions read *et tuis rescriptis* (“and by your replies”). Quesnellus expresses the whole passage with an entirely different reading: “so that you may console us through your replies concerning our common participation in grace, in whatever matters seem right to you.”]

## Chapter XI

### The reply of the same pope to five bishops

[Note: Besides the manuscripts of this collection and of the Isidorian collection, this letter also exists in the Avellana Collection. We have read it in accordance with the Vindobonensis manuscript 39 of this collection and Vatican manuscript 3791 of the Isidorian collection.]

Innocent sends greetings to Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Evodius, and Possidius, bishops.

### Chapter I

We received with the greatest pleasure the letter of Your Fraternity, full of faith and firmly strengthened by the whole force of catholic religion, sent from the two councils through our brother and fellow bishop Julius.

[Note: Garnier adds *et alias* (“and others”).]

Its entire substance and structure consists in consideration of the daily grace of God and in the correction of those who think otherwise.

[Note: Garnier likewise has: “the complete account is constituted in this way.”]

Thus it can remove every error from them and, by setting before each of them a suitable example from our law, provide a worthy teacher whom they ought to follow.

[Note: Quesnellus, with his manuscripts, has *possint* (“they may be able”); the Vindobonensis, together with the other manuscripts and printed editions, more correctly has *possit*, referring to the structure of the letter. Later, the more recent printed editions of the Councils have *idoneo dato cuivis* (“a suitable example being given to everyone”); the older editions retain *quovis*. Garnier has *idoneum cuivis dato legis* (“a suitable example of the law being given to everyone”).]

But concerning these matters, as I think, we have already said enough above, when, in replying to your reports, we wrote back what we thought both of their faithlessness and of your judgment.

Yet what may be said against them continually comes to our aid and supplies us with arguments; nor can there ever fail to be something that conquers them,

[Note: Garnier, with Merlinus, Crabbus, the Benedictine editors, and several Vatican manuscripts, has *deesse* (“be lacking”).]

since what is so wretched and impious is more completely overcome by the power of our faith and by truth itself.

For one who rejects and despises every hope of life, confusing his heart with hostile and condemnable argument, when he believes that there is nothing to receive from God and that nothing remains for him to ask for his healing—what has he left for himself thereafter?

If, then, there are some whom such great perversity has bound in their own defense, who surrender themselves to and join themselves to this doctrine, hoping that what is so far removed from catholic teaching belongs to it, although it is entirely and fundamentally opposed to it,

[Note: Coustantius, from an old Colbertine manuscript, correctly emends *affectu* (“with affection” or “by attachment”), for this corresponds to the words of the five bishops in the preceding letter: “which scandal his hearers and those who perversely love him do not cease to spread everywhere.”]

having been infected by their counsels and words and induced to fall, they will hasten to return to the straight path,

so that error, which for too long has occupied their minds and has been nourished, as it were, by their own thoughts, may not overwhelm them.

[Note: Garnier has: “nor may it continue to invade . . .”]

## Chapter II

For if Pelagius, wherever he took his stand, deceived the minds of those who would readily or simply believe a disputant by this assertion—whether certain people are here in the City (which, since they hide, we neither know nor can openly declare; for even if there are such people, they remain concealed, and they never dare either to defend him when he preaches these things or to utter such claims in the presence of any of our people, and, amid such a great multitude of the people, no one can easily be detected or recognized anywhere), or whether they live in any part of the world—, we trust in the mercy and grace of our Lord that they will readily be corrected when they hear the condemnation of whoever is found to be the obstinate and resistant author of this doctrine.

[Note: Thus the Vindobonensis agrees with the other common editions; this is better than Quesnel’s *quisquis* (“whoever”).]

[Note: The Vindobonensis and three other manuscripts used by Coustant have *seu hic illi in Urbe sint*; that is, Colbertinus, Pithoeanus, and Corbeiensis in their first hand. Vaticanus 3791 adds only *decepti ante sint*. Hence Quesnel accepted another reading from two manuscripts, Thuaneus and Oxoniensis: *seu hic aliqui decepti sint, quos nescientes*. Our reading, however, fits the following better, with *cum etsi sunt*, and also the reading in others, *seu hac illi in Urbe sint, quos*. Coustant followed this reading, changing only *quos* to *quod*, as it appears in the commonly printed Councils.]

[Note: Another reading has *populi multitudine deprehendi aliquis facile, nec alicubi* (“in a multitude of people someone may easily be detected, and nowhere”). The Vindobonensis manuscript likewise has *nec alicubi*. Garnerius has *nec ubi lateat* (“nor where he may lie hidden”).]

[Note: We restored the common reading from our Vindobonensis and Vaticanus manuscripts: *Domini nostri misericordia gratiaque credimus, quod* (“we believe in the mercy and grace of our Lord that”). Quesnel has *in Domini nostri misericordia confidimus, quod* (“we trust in the mercy of our Lord that”).]

It makes no difference where such people may be, since wherever they can be found, they can be healed. Nevertheless, we cannot be persuaded that he has been cleared, although reports have been brought to us by I know not which laymen, by whom he supposedly believed that he had both been heard and acquitted. We doubt whether these reports are true, because they did not come to our knowledge through any proceedings of that council, nor have we received any letters from those before whom he presented the case.

[Note: Garnerius has *innotuerit* (“came to notice”); another reading has *venerunt* (“came”).]

[Note: Garnerius reads *vix persuaderi* (“can scarcely be persuaded”), and then, with the ancient editions of Augustine, *ad nos a nostris quibusdam laicis* (“to us by certain of our laymen”).]

But if he could have confidence in his own acquittal, we believe he would have done what would have been much more truthful and could have been more effective: he would have compelled them by his letters to indicate what they had decided.

[Note: Garnerius reads *melius* (“better”); shortly afterward, *quod judicaverant more ecclesiastico indicare* (“to indicate what they had judged according to ecclesiastical custom”). Quesnel has *quid judicaverint indicare* (“to indicate what they have judged”). We preferred the reading of the Vindobonensis, supported by the Colbertinus, Pithoeanus, and Corbeiensis manuscripts, which Coustant also followed. Other manuscripts and printed editions have *quid judicaverunt*, or *qui judicaverunt*, or *dijudicaverunt*.]

But since the official proceedings themselves contain certain matters which he partly suppressed by avoiding the charges brought against him, and partly confused in complete obscurity by turning many words back upon himself, he cleared himself for the moment more by false arguments than by true reasoning: he denied some things and twisted others through a false interpretation.

[Note: Quesnel, following only the Oxoniensis, has *argumentationibus*. Then Garnerius reads *ratione purgavit negando, alia falsa interpretatione, ne ad tempus quidem videri potuerit absolutus, praeter codicum ac vulgatorum fidem* (“he cleared himself by reasoning through denial and by another false interpretation, so that he could not even for a time have appeared acquitted, contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts and printed editions”).]

## Chapter III

[Note: We added *Sed*, “But,” with our manuscripts and printed editions. Shortly afterward Benedictus and Coustant have *jam se* for *etiam se*, “already himself” for “himself also.”]

Would that he might also turn from the error of his own path to the true way of the Catholic faith—which is more greatly to be desired—so that he might wish and desire to be cleared, considering God’s daily grace and recognizing his assistance; so that he might be seen, and approved by all, to have been corrected by clear reasoning—not by an examination of the official proceedings, but with his whole heart turned toward the Catholic faith.

[Note: Augustine and the Vindobonensis manuscript have *verum* (“truly”).]

Therefore we can neither approve nor condemn their judgment, since we do not know whether the proceedings are true; or, if they are true, it is clear that he evaded the matter more than he cleared himself with complete truth.

If he is confident and knows that what he says is not deserving of condemnation by us, or that he has now rejected everything he had said, he ought not to wait to be summoned by us; rather, he himself ought to hasten so that he may be acquitted. For if he still thinks in this way, when will he commit himself to our judgment, once he has received whatever letters, knowing that he must be condemned?

[Note: Quesnel has *Qui se confidit, novitque non nostra dignum damnatione, ut confirmet verum esse quod dicat, aut etiam hoc totum*, “He who is confident and knows that what he says is not deserving of our condemnation, so as to confirm that what he says is true, or even all this….” In the margin he noted that the words *ut confirmet verum esse* were absent from the Thuaneus manuscript and printed editions, with some difference in the sentence. Since they are also absent from our Vindobonensis and other manuscripts, it is clear that they are a gloss inserted into the Oxoniensis manuscript; for this reason the passage had to be corrected.]

But if he ought to be summoned, this would better be done by those who are nearer and do not appear to be separated by a great distance of land.

[Note: This is the reading of Quesnel’s manuscripts and of ours, together with the editions of Benedictus and Coustant. Others have *accersendus* (“to be summoned”). Later, instead of *praebuerit*, “shall have provided,” some have *praebeat*, “may provide.”]

Yet care will not be lacking if he provides material for a remedy. For he can condemn the opinions he has held and, by sending a letter—as befits one returning to us—ask forgiveness, dearest brothers.

## Chapter IV

We have examined a book said to be his, which your Charity sent us. In it we read that many things had been written against God’s grace—many blasphemous things, nothing pleasing, nothing that would not be wholly displeasing, and things to be condemned and trampled upon by anyone. No one other than the person who wrote them would admit or entertain similar thoughts.

[Note: The words *multa contra Dei gratiam legimus esse conscripta* (“we read that many things had been written against God’s grace”) are missing from many manuscripts, both of this collection and elsewhere. Since they are necessary to the sense and were restored from Augustine’s Vaticanus and Corbeiensis manuscripts by the Benedictines and Coustant, we have inserted them in brackets. Nor did we approve Quesnel’s insertion of *invenimus* (“we find”) after *calcandum* (“to be trampled upon”) to elicit the sense; we do not know whether this word occurs in any manuscript. It is certainly absent from the Vindobonensis and others, which omit the inserted words through an obvious leap from *multa* to another similar word.]

We did not think it necessary here to discuss the law at greater length, as though Pelagius were present and contradicting us, since we are speaking with you, who know the whole matter and rejoice, together with us, in the same agreement.

[Note: Quesnel notes in the margin that this alludes to the Apostle Paul’s words, “I speak to those who know the law.” Hence the common reading *totam rem* (“the whole matter”) is incorrect, as is Garnerius’s *totum* (“the whole”).]

For examples of this kind are better set forth when we are dealing with people whom it is clear are ignorant of these matters.

[Note: Two of our manuscripts, together with three used by Coustant and the editions of the Councils, have *prudentes* (“knowledgeable”). But *imprudentes* (“ignorant,” that is, unskilled) is better, since the Supreme Pontiff distinguishes them from the knowledgeable people mentioned earlier.]

For who would not find it most fruitful, if he thinks rightly, to discuss the possibility of nature, free will, every grace of God, and daily grace?

[Note: The edition of Coustant has *istae* (“these,” feminine plural).]

Let him therefore anathematize the opinions he held, so that those who had fallen through his speeches and instructions may finally learn what the true faith possesses. For they will more easily be recalled when they perceive that these opinions have been condemned by their own author.

But if he obstinately wishes to persist in this impiety, action must be taken so that at least those may be helped whom not his own error but rather this man’s error has led astray; lest this remedy also be lost to them, since he neither admits nor requests such treatment.

[Note: Garnerius has *qualiter* (“how”), and then, with the ancient editions of Augustine, *scelus* (“crime”) instead of *suus* (“his own”).]

May God keep you safe, dearest brothers.

[Note: The editions of Augustine and Coustant, from the Corbeiensis manuscript, add *et alia manu* (“and in another hand”).]

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February.

[Note: Garnerius adds “in the consulship of Honorius XI and Constantius II.” The Corbeiensis manuscripts have: “Given on the day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of the most glorious Theodosius, also the consulship of Junius Quartus Palladius, of clarissimus rank.” The Benedictine editors corrected the error: “Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, after the seventh consulship of the most glorious Augustus Theodosius and the consulship of Junius Quartus Palladius, of clarissimus rank.” Coustant accepted this correction and also cited a more accurate Vaticanus manuscript.]

## Chapter XII

[Note: This appears only in the manuscripts of this collection and in Isidore, who, like the preceding letters, took this letter from our collection.]

A familiar letter of Pope Innocent to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage.

**INNOCENTIUS TO AURELIUS, bishop of Carthage.**

True affection consists in familiar correspondence.

[Note: The Thuaneus manuscript has *constat* (“is established”).]

Indeed, the obligations of charity more firmly purchase what they seek when they are undertaken separately.

[Note: The Vindobonensis, together with the printed Councils, has *se orsa* (“having begun separately”).]

Therefore, dearest brother, through our brother Julius I wished to answer the letter sent from abroad, lest the offense of a particular greeting refused should perhaps remain with me.

[Note: The Vindobonensis has *gestivi divi*, a phrase not understood. Since, perhaps in another manuscript of this collection cited by Coustant, it was written differently, we preferred *ne apud nos* (“lest with us”).]

Accordingly, I restore the aforesaid brother to your Charity, together with the judgments of the Apostolic See concerning the report of the two synods. It remains that the Lord, entreated by us, may graciously grant that every stain of his Church can be wiped away by our continual labors.

[Note: We added *suae* (“of his own”) from our Vindobonensis and Vaticanus 3791 manuscripts, supported by the other printed editions.]

May the Lord keep you safe, dearest brother.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February.

## Chapter XIII

[Note: We possess this council, with its nine canons against the Pelagians, together with the preface and order presented here, only from our collection. An old exemplar from which Crabbe published the preface and the third canon concerning children dying without baptism—omitted in other collections—also belonged to this same collection, as we have shown in the note and annotations to chapter 2, where we observed several passages of the Breviary of Hippo excerpted by Crabbe from another manuscript of this collection. The vindication of this council, or of its third canon as read in this collection, may be found in *Treatise on Collections*, part II, chapter 3, section 7, no. 2 and following. Besides the Vindobonensis manuscript of this collection, we compared the canons with the edition of Dionysius and with Isidore, who published these canons under the name of the Council of Milevis.]

A plenary council held at Carthage against Pelagius and Coelestius.

In the twelfth consulship of Augustus Honorius, on the Kalends of May, at Carthage in the basilica of Faustus,

[Note: This is the reading of the Gandavensis manuscript used by Crabbe. In the Vindobonensis manuscript the words *Cum Aurelius episcopus simul* (“When Aurelius the bishop together”) are missing through a scribe’s leap from one *cum* to another. Hence the missing words were perhaps supplied outside their proper place by a less correct transposition, as Quesnel printed them: *Cum Aurelius episcopus Carthaginensis in basilica Fausti cum Donatiano*, etc.] when Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, together with Donatianus, bishop of Telepte and bishop of the first see of the province of Byzacena, and two hundred and three of his fellow bishops from the provinces of Byzacena, Mauretania Sitifensis, Tripolitania, Numidia, Mauretania Caesariensis, and Spain, had taken their seats in council, with deacons standing by:

[Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts of this collection. If Saint Prosper, in his *Chronicle* under the year 418, in his response to the second objection of the Gauls, and in *Against the Collation*, chapter 10, lists 214 bishops, we shall show in the observations on Quesnel’s dissertation 13, numbers 17 and 39, that all these references belong to another earlier synod of that year. Augustine distinguishes it from our plenary synod in Letter 215 to Valentinus and calls it African. Photius, in *Bibliotheca*, codex 53, does speak of our synod and assigns to it, besides Aurelius and Donatianus, 224 bishops. We have proved in *Treatise on Collections*, part II, chapter 3, section 7, that this writer used a collection of documents concerning the Pelagian case almost identical with one that our compiler found and incorporated into his own work. Whether, however, the error is to be presumed in one manuscript—and perhaps also in the Greek translation—used by Photius, or in all the ancient Latin copies of our collection, let each reader judge.]

### I

[Note: Isidore has: “It pleased all the bishops who were present at this holy synod to establish the following matters, which were defined in the present council: whoever…”]

It pleased all who were assembled in the holy synod of the Church of Carthage that whoever says that the human being Adam was made mortal in such a way that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would die in the body—that is, would depart from the body—not because of the merit of sin but by the necessity of nature, let him be anathema.

[Note: Dionysius and Isidore, together with the Gandavensis manuscript, have *Adam primum hominem* (“Adam, the first human being”).]

### II

It likewise pleased the council that whoever denies that newborn infants are to be baptized immediately after leaving their mothers’ wombs, or says that they are indeed baptized for the remission of sins but derive nothing of original sin from Adam which must be cleansed by the washing of regeneration—so that it follows that the baptismal formula “For the remission of sins” is understood in them not truly but falsely—let him be anathema.

[Note: Quesnel inserts *eos* (“them”); we deleted it in accordance with the Vindobonensis, followed by Dionysius and Isidore.]

For the Apostle’s statement, “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12), must be understood in no other way than the Catholic Church, spread everywhere, has always understood it.

For on account of this rule of faith, even infants, who have not yet been able to commit any sins in themselves, are truly baptized for the remission of sins, so that by regeneration what they have derived through generation may be cleansed.

### III

[Note: Quesnel appended this note: “This decree is not found in most editions. Binius and other editors of the Councils had it printed in a typeface different from the other decrees and professed to have received it from a very ancient manuscript. The manuscript meant is the very ancient manuscript of this collection used by Crabbe; from it the same decree passed into later editions of the Councils. See annotation 1.” Shortly afterward, we have *dicit scripsimus* (“we have written ‘says’”) with the Vindobonensis manuscript and Crabbe’s manuscript. Quesnel has *dixerit* (“has said”).]

It likewise pleased the council that if anyone says that the Lord’s words, “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14:2), were spoken so that it might be understood that there is some intermediate state or some place anywhere in the kingdom of heaven where infants who have departed this life without baptism live in blessedness, although without baptism they cannot enter the kingdom of heaven, which is eternal life, let him be anathema.

For when the Lord says, “Unless someone has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5), what Catholic would doubt that the one who has not been deemed worthy to be a coheir of Christ will be a participant with the devil?

For whoever lacks the right-hand portion will undoubtedly incur the left-hand portion.

[Note: We added *partem* (“portion”) with the Vindobonensis manuscripts and Crabbe’s manuscripts; the latter shortly before has *cohaeres esse non meruit Christi* (“was not deemed worthy to be Christ’s coheir”).]

### IV

It likewise pleased the council that whoever says that the grace of God, by which we are justified through Jesus Christ our Lord, is effective only for the remission of sins already committed, and not also for assistance in preventing sins from being committed, let him be anathema.

[Note: Dionysius and Isidore have: “It likewise pleased the council that whoever says…”]

### V

It likewise pleased the council that if anyone says that this same grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord helps us not to sin only because through it the understanding of the commandments is opened and revealed to us, so that we know what we ought to desire and what to avoid, but that through it we are not granted the ability to love and to carry out what we have learned must be done, let him be anathema.

[Note: Dionysius and Isidore add *nos* (“us”); with them we have corrected *per ipsam* (“through it”), since the following context requires *per illam* (“through it”). Quesnel has *per ipsum* (“through him”).]

For when the Apostle says, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Corinthians 8:1), it is exceedingly impious to believe that we have Christ’s grace for that which puffs us up, but not for that which builds us up, since both are gifts of God: to know what we ought to do, and to love so that we may do it. Thus, when love builds us up, knowledge cannot puff us up.

[Note: The Vindobonensis, together with Dionysius, Isidore, and Prosper, *Against the Collator*, chapter 5, has this reading. Quesnel has: “truly a gift of God, both to know what we ought to do and to love what we should do,” which is less good.]

Just as it is written of God, “He teaches human beings knowledge” (Psalm 93:10), so it is also written, “Love is from God” (1 John 4:7).

### VI

It likewise pleased the council that whoever says that the grace of justification is given to us for this reason: that what we are able to do through free will we may more easily fulfill through grace—as though, even if grace were not given, we could fulfill the divine commandments without it, though not easily—let him be anathema.

[Note: Quesnel omitted *nobis* (“to us”). We supplied it from the Vindobonensis, as it is also read in Dionysius and Isidore.]

[Note: The Thuaneus manuscript has *debemus* (“we ought”); the second hand of the Vindobonensis has *poteramus* (“we could”); Dionysius and Isidore have *jubemur* (“we are commanded”). Quesnel remarks of the latter reading: “Less good. Rather, better.” For Saint Augustine, in Sermon 154, chapter 12, when presenting the words of the Pelagians, especially approves this reading: “For this purpose,” they say, “God gave his grace to human beings, so that what they are commanded to do through free will they may more easily fulfill through grace.” We present here the reading of our collection. Shortly afterward Dionysius, Isidore, and the common text have *possimus* (“we may be able”).]

For the Lord was speaking about the fruits of the commandments when he did not say, “Without me you can do them with greater difficulty,” but said, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

### VII

It likewise pleased the council that whoever thinks the words of the holy Apostle John—“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8)—should be understood as meaning that, out of humility, we ought not to say that we do not have sin, not because that is truly the case, let him be anathema.

[Note: This is the reading of the second hand of the Vindobonensis, together with Dionysius and Isidore. The first hand has *nos ipsos decipimus* (“we deceive ourselves”), as all manuscripts and printed editions have shortly afterward when repeating this testimony. Augustine, Sermon 181, always has *seducimus* (“we lead astray”). Quesnel has *ipsi nos seducimus* (“we ourselves lead ourselves astray”).]

The Apostle continues and adds: “But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity” (ibid.). Here it is sufficiently clear that this is to be said not only humbly but also truthfully.

[Note: The common text of Dionysius and Isidore, having removed the double negation, reads: “we ought to be said to have sin.” But Father Hardouin notes that the manuscript and Merlin read as in our text. The Vindobonensis deletes the second *non*, thereby suggesting that it should also be deleted in the first position. Compare Augustine, Sermon 181, chapters 3 and 4.]

For the Apostle could have said, “If we say that we do not have sin, we exalt ourselves, and humility is not in us.” But when he says, “We deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us,” he sufficiently shows that the person who says he does not have sin is not speaking the truth but is speaking falsely.

[Note: This reading, together with Dionysius and Isidore, is also found in our Vindobonensis manuscript. Quesnel has *verum non dicere, sed falsum* (“does not speak what is true, but what is false”).]

### VIII

It likewise pleased the council that whoever says that the saints say in the Lord’s Prayer, “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12), not for themselves—for this petition is no longer necessary for them—but for other sinners who are among their people, and that therefore each of the saints does not say, “Forgive me my debts,” but “Forgive us our debts,” so that the just person is understood to ask this more for others than for himself, let him be anathema.

For the Apostle James was holy and just when he said, “We all offend in many ways” (James 3:2).

[Note: The Oxoniensis manuscript incorrectly has *in multos* (“against many”); Dionysius and Isidore have *in multis enim* (“for in many things”).]

For why was *all* added, unless this statement also agreed with the psalm where it is written, “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight” (Psalm 142:2)?

And in the prayer of the wisest Solomon: “There is no human being who has not sinned.”

[Note: The common text of Isidore has *non peccet* (“who does not sin”). Isidore’s manuscript, as cited by Hardouin, adds *tibi* (“before you”).]

And in the Book of holy Job: “He places a sign in the hand of every human being, so that every human being may know his weakness” (Job 37:7).

Therefore holy and just Daniel, when he said in his prayer in the plural, “We have sinned, we have acted wickedly” (Daniel 9:5), and the other things which he confesses there truthfully and humbly—

[Note: Quesnel has *ne putaret* (“lest he should think”), and afterward *dicit* (“he says”), less correctly. We corrected the text from the Vindobonensis, together with Dionysius and Isidore.]

—lest some should think, as certain people believe, that he was speaking not of his own sins but rather of those of his people, later said: “While I was praying and confessing my sins and the sins of my people to the Lord my God” (ibid. 20).

[Note: We added *meo* (“my”) with the Vindobonensis and Dionysius. Isidore has *nostro* (“our”).]

He did not say “our sins,” but spoke of his people’s sins and his own, because, like a prophet, he foresaw those who would later understand this so badly.

[Note: Quesnel alone has *praevidebat* (“he foresaw”).]

### IX

It likewise pleased the council that whoever wishes the very words of the Lord’s Prayer, in which we say “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12), to be said by the saints in such a way that they are spoken humbly but not truthfully, let them be anathema.

[Note: Some have *anathema sit* (“let him be anathema”). The wording *quicunque … ita volunt* (“whoever wishes them … in this way”) requires the plural number.]

For who could tolerate someone praying and lying not to human beings but to God—someone who says with his lips that he wishes his debts to be forgiven, but says in his heart that he has no debts requiring forgiveness?

## Chapter XIV

Here begins the sacred rescript, issued after the receipt of the proceedings of the aforesaid synod.

[Note: These and the documents that follow through chapter 20 were published from this collection. Three of them—this one, the fifteenth, and the twentieth—were preserved for us only in this collection. Cardinal Baronius inserted them into his *Annals* from an Atrebatensis manuscript of this collection. They are also presented in volume III of the Venetian edition of the Councils, columns 464 and following, with the corrections of Father Hardouin, who used the Colbertinus manuscript, formerly called Thuaneus. Baluzius likewise reprinted them in the appendix to his edition of Vincent of Lérins’s *Commonitorium*, Cambridge, 1687, and mentions three collated manuscripts: those of the Royal Library, Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and the monastery of Saint Jerome of Murtensis near Barcelona. We shall also cite the Caesarean Vindobonensis manuscript. Quesnel has *supradictae* (“of the aforesaid”); we preferred the Thuaneus and Vindobonensis manuscripts, which have *ss.*, that is, *suprascriptae*, as Quesnel himself interprets it. Shortly afterward we added *datum* (“issued”) from our Vindobonensis manuscript.]

The emperors Honorius and Theodosius, Augusti, to Palladius, prefect of the praetorium.

We have learned through common report that, in order to disturb the light of Catholic simplicity, which always shines with pure brilliance, a new cunning has suddenly emerged through the ingenuity of deceitful art. This cunning, darkened by lies of deceptive knowledge and driven only by a frenzied struggle, attempts to assail the steadfast peace of the heavenly faith.

[Note: This is the reading of the Thuaneus and Vindobonensis manuscripts and of the printed editions of Baronius, Hardouin, and Baluzius. Quesnel, with the Oxoniensis, has *emersisse* (“has emerged”).]

[Note: Quesnel, with Hardouin, has *debacchata est luctamine, ut stabilem quietem coelestis attrectaret fidei* (“has raged in struggle so as to assail the steadfast peace of the heavenly faith”). He notes in the margin that Garnerius omits *est et ut*. He further notes that when Salmasius read *attrectare* in the Thuaneus manuscript, he supplied *audet* (“dares”) and Garnerius took it from him. The genuine reading has been restored from the Oxoniensis manuscript. Since our Vindobonensis likewise lacks *est et ut* and the Thuaneus manuscript has *attrectare*, we judged preferable the reading of Baronius’s Atrebatensis manuscript and others cited by Baluzius, which, agreeing partly with the Vindobonensis and Thuaneus, seem to represent a more truthful restoration of the passage by inserting *conatur* (“attempts”).]

It has become widely known that Pelagius and Coelestius were the authors of this impious invention: while presenting the discovery of a new crime as remarkable, they regard it as a mark of plebeian baseness to think with everyone else, and as the height of singular wisdom to destroy what has been commonly approved.

[Note: Salmasius, with the Thuaneus manuscript, as Quesnel notes, has *dum novi criminis commentatores insignem … aestimant* (“while they regard the inventors of a new crime as remarkable”). Elsewhere, with Baronius, he has *dum novi criminis commendata vento insignem … aestimat* (“while he regards the commendation of a new crime, entrusted to the wind, as remarkable”); Garnerius prefers this as more elegant. Quesnel himself preferred the reading of the Oxoniensis manuscript: *dum novi criminis commenta invenit* (“while he discovers inventions of a new crime”), unless, he says, one wishes to read *acuminis* (“of cleverness”) instead of *criminis*. Hardouin adopted this reading. We consider the reading presented from the Vindobonensis more genuine.]

They ascribe such savage cruelty of will to God, the Father of all things and always of supreme majesty, omnipotent beyond measure and transcending every beginning, that when he undertook the care of creating the world and weighed the quality of the human being to be fashioned in the profound conception of his spirit, he would prefer the foul beginning of the established gift and promise death to the one who was to be born.

[Note: Quesnel notes that the Oxoniensis alone has *mundi* (“of the world”), though Baronius, Baluzius, and Hardouin do not omit it, any more than does our Vindobonensis manuscript.]

[Note: The Oxoniensis has *fidei anteferret exordium* (“would prefer the beginning of faith”); the Thuaneus manuscript, followed by Baronius, Baluzius, and the Magdeburg editors, has the same corrupt reading. Garnerius, following Salmasius’s unsupported correction of the Thuaneus, has *finem anteferret exordio* (“would prefer the end to the beginning”), as does Quesnel. Since the Vindobonensis likewise has the Thuaneus reading, though it is corrupt, Hardouin, despite using that manuscript, followed the Oxoniensis. Quesnel preferred *promitteret* (“would promise”); the other manuscripts and editions have *praemitteret* (“would send beforehand”).]

[Note: Garnerius has *interminate potenti* (“boundlessly powerful”); Baluzius, with the Thuaneus manuscript, *interminatione potenti* (“powerful in boundlessness”); Baronius has *ter omnipotenti ultra* (“thrice omnipotent beyond”).]

They claim that death did not flow from the ambush of the forbidden sin, but arose entirely from the law of an unchangeable decree; that abstaining from wrongdoing would be of no use in avoiding the fatal assault of death, whose force was supposedly so fixed that it could not afterward be abolished;

[Note: The Oxoniensis, Thuaneus, and Vindobonensis manuscripts have *egisse* (“arose”); others have *exegisse*. Garnerius has *incommutabilis* (“unchangeable”).]

[Note: Garnerius has *ut ad declinandum … nihil prodesset abstinentia* (“that abstinence would be of no use for avoiding …”); later, with Baronius and Hardouin, he has *adstricta* (“bound”) for *adscripta* (“fixed”).] that the error of the first human being, into which the blind helplessness of a captured mind had fallen, had not passed down to posterity; and that, for the one whom the unfortunate enticement of ill-advised grace had carried away, the transgression of the prohibition had constituted only a distinction, although the manifest authority of the Catholic law everywhere testifies that the beginning of everyone’s destruction was that which plainly corrupted the diligent observance of the divine command.

[Note: Some have *saevae* (“savage”) instead of *scaevae* (“perverse”).]

And they add many other things which speech rejects and the law refutes, things which it is utterly wearisome to recall, even in setting forth their punishment.

[Note: Quesnel and Hardouin, with the Oxoniensis manuscript, have *quae pertaesum sit* (“which it is utterly wearisome”). Perhaps in the Vindobonensis the medial letters *tae* of *pertaesum* were erased so that a second hand might write *perexosum*, as Garnerius printed. Baronius has *quae perpetue cum sit*; Baluzius, *quae perpetue sumpsit*; others have *absit* for *sumpsit*.]

[Note: Baluzius has *quod … liqueat* (“which … is clear”). The word *liqueat* is also found in Baronius and Hardouin.]

These things must be cut off by a timely remedy and swift speed, lest, once the habit of wickedness has grown strong, the young adherents can scarcely be restrained.

[Note: Garnerius and Baluzius have *maturo* (“timely”). Garnerius, following Salmasius, has *adolescentia* (“youth”); Quesnel, from the Oxoniensis and Thuaneus manuscripts, followed also by Baronius, the Magdeburg editors, Baluzius, and Hardouin, has *adolescentes* (“young persons”). The Vindobonensis reading was judged better.]

[Note: Garnerius and Baluzius have *maturo* (“timely”).]

For recently a report had reached the ears of our gentleness that within our most holy City and in other places

[Note: Baronius and Baluzius, in agreement with the Vindobonensis manuscript, have *perstrinxerat intra sacratissimam* (“had reached within our most sacred [City]”). Quesnel has *perstrinxerit intra sanctissimam* (“has reached within our most holy [City]”).]

 the pestilential poison had taken root in the hearts of certain people, so that, with the path of straightforward belief broken and their efforts divided into opposing parties, material for unresting dissension had been introduced; and, with a new fuel for scandal stirred up, the tranquility of the most blessed Church now trembles under attack.

[Note: Some manuscripts have *hactenus* (“until now”), others *actu nutet* (“now trembles in fact”). Baronius and Baluzius followed the former; we preferred the latter, found in the Thuaneus manuscript, to which *actus* in the Vindobonensis also corresponds. Quesnel and, following him, Hardouin omitted both, perhaps on the authority of some manuscript. Shortly afterward Baronius and Baluzius have *intentata* (“attacked”) instead of *attentata* (“attempted”).]

Some pursue one interpretation and others another through uncertain argument, although the clarity of the sacred writings is complete and plainly explains what everyone ought to follow; and, according to the capacity of their slippery ingenuity, they stir up a profane question about new ventures, dearest and most beloved Palladius.

[Note: The common texts vary remarkably here. Quesnel, with the Oxoniensis, has *aliis id, aliis aliud* (“one thing for some, another for others”); Garnerius, *aliis nempe aliud* (“indeed another for others”). We preferred the manuscripts of Baronius and Baluzius, *aliis iter aliud* (“another path for others”), to which the Vindobonensis *aliis id aliud* is close. With Garnerius we added *cum sit* (“although it is”), since the following sentence requires something. We did not think, with Quesnel, that *conturbat quibusdam* (“disturbs some people”) should be supplied below after *ingenii* (“ingenuity”); no known manuscripts or editions contain this addition, and the context is otherwise fully intelligible.]

[Note: Baronius and Baluzius have *novorum more anserum* (“after the manner of new geese”); Hardouin has *novorum auctorum* (“of new authors”); Garnerius has *novorum commentorum* (“of new inventions”).]

For this reason, let your illustrious authority, destined to live under a law for all ages, know that we have decreed that, after the heads of this accursed doctrine—Coelestius and Pelagius—have first been driven from the City, if thereafter any followers of this sacrilege can again be found anywhere,

[Note: We restored *rursus* (“again”), omitted by Quesnel, from the Vindobonensis manuscript and all the printed texts.] or if anyone utters a word in support of the condemned perversity, they are to be seized by anyone and dragged before the competent judge.

[Note: Garnerius has *Quisque* (“each person”).]

Whether the person is a cleric or a layman, everyone is to have the authority to report them and to press the charge without any limitation, once he has discovered them introducing the darkness of a new disputation after abandoning the common light of knowledge, fighting against the apostolic discipline and the clear, error-free judgment of the Gospel with the cunning of a crafty and ignorant sect, and enveloping the radiant faith in the false turns of his argument.

Therefore, wherever they are found discussing this most unspeakable crime, we order them to be seized by anyone and, once brought to a public hearing, to be accused indiscriminately by all, so that public writing may pursue the proof of the crime once established, while they themselves are condemned to inexorable exile.

[Note: Quesnel has *proscriptione* (“proscription”) and says that two manuscripts have this reading. We preferred to follow our Vindobonensis, which agrees with all the other printed editions. Shortly afterward, some editions have *sententiae* (“of the sentence”) where others have *scientiae* (“of knowledge”).]

For it is fitting that the source of the vice be separated from public assembly, and that those who are detestable not only for their wicked deed but also as examples of a poisonous spirit should not remain in the common gathering.

It is beneficial that proclamations of this kind be disseminated throughout nearly the whole extent of our empire, wherever the world reaches, lest ignorance of the matter perhaps provide nourishment for error, and anyone suppose that he may safely dare what he has pretended not to know was condemned by public authority.

[Note: We added *pene* (“nearly”) with the Vindobonensis and other printed editions. Garnerius and Hardouin have *per omnem pene mundum, qua imperium nostrum extenditur* (“through nearly the whole world over which our empire extends”). Shortly afterward, the Oxoniensis manuscript has *partum* (“birth” or “offspring”) instead of *pastum* (“nourishment”), which is less correct.]

[Note: The Thuaneus manuscript has *II kal.* (“the second day before the Kalends”).]

Given on the day before the Kalends of May, at Ravenna, in the consulship of our lords Honorius, for the twelfth time, and Theodosius, for the eighth time, Augusti.

# CHAPTER XV

[Note: [Col. 0492D] “Baronius wrongly assigns this to the year 420, whereas it ought rather to have been attached to the preceding edict issued in 418.” Quesnell.]

Copy of the edict of Junius Quartus Palladius.

Junius Quartus Palladius, Monaxius, and Agricola, [Col. 0493A] again prefects of the praetorium, issued the following edict. [Note: [Col. 0493C] The Vindobonensis, in its first hand, wrongly reads *dixerit* (“he will have said”), perhaps an error corrected in the Thuaneus, though less correctly. Baron and Baluzius, with the second hand of the Vindobonensis, read *dixerunt* (“they issued”). Against Pelagius. Hardouin supplies the genuine formula proper to edicts.]

Against Pelagius and Coelestius, who were destroying the faith of Catholic doctrine by wicked arguments, the imperial sentence prevailed that, expelled from the venerable City, they should be punished by the confiscation of their property. [Note: [Col. 0493C] Baluzius and Garnier, with the Thuaneus manuscript, read *nefandis* (“abominable”). Quesnell preferred the spelling *scaevis* (“wicked”); others have *saevis* (“savage”). Shortly afterward, two manuscripts of Quesnell and our Vindobonensis read *incaluit* (“grew strong”); the other printed copies have *invaluit* (“prevailed”).]

All therefore must be warned by this edict not to lend credulous assent to the errors of a sinister persuasion. If any commoner or cleric should fall into the obscenities of this darkness, he shall be dragged before a judge by anyone whatsoever, without regard to the person of the accuser, stripped through the confiscation of his property, and subjected to irrevocable exile.

For just as the majesty above gathers reverence from ignorance of what is secret, so it suffers injury from the presumption of foolish disputation. [Note: [Col. 0493C] Baluzius, with the Thuaneus manuscript, reads: “just as it does not gather an execrable ignorance from what is hidden, so it rejects the injury of foolish disputation.” Baronius has: “so by an edict it removes the injury of foolish disputation.” Garnier and Hardouin: “so [it suffers] injury from foolish disputation.” The Vindobonensis deletes *praesumptione* (“presumption”).]

# CHAPTER XVI

[Note: [Col. 0493C] This letter, together with the two documents that follow, is also found in the manuscript collections Barberinianus 2888 and Vaticanus 1342, as well as in the Dionysian additions—which the most eminent Baronius calls the Cresconian collection. We collated two manuscripts of these additions, Vaticanus 5845 and Vallicellianus A 5.]

Here begins the imperial letter to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage.

[Col. 0493B]

The emperors [Note: [Col. 0493D] The manuscripts of the Dionysian Additions add *perpetui* (“perpetual”).] HONORIUS and THEODOSIUS, Augusti, send greetings to Bishop AURELIUS.

It had previously been decreed that Pelagius and Coelestius, inventors of an abominable doctrine, should be expelled from the city of Rome as though they were a kind of contagion threatening Catholic [Note: [Col. 0493D] Quesnell notes: “Thus have Magdeburgensis and the Oxford and Thuaneus manuscripts; he considers this reading corrupt and conjecturally substitutes *veritatis* (‘of truth’), as I think. Baronius first adopted Garnier’s reading, followed later by Baluzius and Hardouin. Nevertheless, our manuscripts have *utilitatis* (‘usefulness’). Only in the Vallicellian manuscript was this corrected by a later hand to *unitatis* (‘unity’).] usefulness, lest they corrupt the minds of the ignorant by a wicked persuasion. In this matter our clemency followed the judgment of your holiness, by which it is established that they had been condemned by all after a proper examination of the sentence. [Note: [Col. 0493D] The Barberinianus and Vaticanus 1342, with Baluzius, read “whom it is established were condemned by all.” Quesnell notes in the margin that Garnier, without citing any authority, restores *cum* (“with”), which nevertheless appears in Magdeburgensis and in the two manuscripts, Thuaneus and Oxoniensis. Baronius and Hardouin then read “of a just sentence.”]

But since the persistent evil of an obstinate crime required that the constitution be renewed, we have also decreed by a recent sanction [Note: [Col. 0494C] Garnier and Baluzius read *definitione* (“decree” or “definition”).] that if anyone, knowing that they were hiding in any part of the provinces, should delay either expelling or betraying them, he would be subject to the prescribed penalty as though he were their accomplice. [Note: [Col. 0494C] Two manuscripts of the Dionysian Additions read “the excessively persistent evil of obstinacies”; Baluzius has “the excessively persistent evil of the obstinate.” Shortly afterward Baronius, with the Atrebatensis manuscript, reads *coegit* (“compelled”) instead of *exegit* (“required”).]

But especially for correcting the obstinacy of certain bishops who either support their perverse arguments by tacit consent or fail to destroy them by public opposition, it will be fitting, dearest and most beloved father, for your holiness to beware, [Col. 0494A] so that the Christian devotion of them all may concur in abolishing this perverse heresy. [Note: [Col. 0494C] The Atrebatensis, Baronius, and Thuaneus read “to be admonished by your authority.” The first hand of the Vindobonensis reads “to let authority remain”; the second reads “to beware,” together with two Vatican manuscripts and the Barberinianus and Vallicellianus. This latter reading, supported by better manuscripts, was adopted with Garnier, Baluzius, and Hardouin. Quesnell, without citing a manuscript, perhaps preferred *imminere* (“to threaten”). Shortly afterward, two Barberinian and Vatican manuscripts, with Baronius, Baluzius, and Hardouin, have *in abolitione* (“in the abolition”).]

[Note: [Col. 0494C] Garnier reads *Christianorum* (“of Christians”), against all the manuscripts, as Quesnell notes; for here the reference is only to the bishops. All the other editions, together with our Barberinian and Vatican manuscripts, likewise have *Christianorum*. The Dionysian-Addition manuscripts Vaticanus and Vallicellianus read, with a lacuna, “For the rest therefore your … shall cause”; the Barberinianus and another Vatican manuscript retain *faciet* (“shall cause”). Garnier omits the words *expulsi civitatibus* (“expelled from the cities”).]

Your religious authority must therefore cause everyone to be admonished by suitable letters, so that they may know that this definition has been prescribed for them by your sanctity: whoever, through impious obstinacy, neglects to subscribe to the condemnation of the persons mentioned above, thereby showing that his mind is not pure, shall be punished by the loss of his episcopate and, expelled forever from the cities, be deprived of communion. [Col. 0494B] [Note: [Col. 0494C] The Barberinian and Vatican manuscripts of the Dionysian Additions read: “For the rest therefore your … shall cause.” The Barberinianus and another Vatican manuscript retain *faciet* (“shall cause”).]

For since we ourselves, in accordance with the Nicene Synod, venerate in a sincere confession God, the creator of all things and the author of our empire, your holiness will not permit men of a detestable sect, devising new and unheard-of things to the injury of religion, to conceal in secret discussions a sacrilege once condemned by public authority. [Note: [Col. 0494D] From the Barberinianus, two Vatican manuscripts, and the Vallicellianus, we have added *nos* (“we”), for which the Vindobonensis manuscript corruptly reads *non* (“not”).] There is one and the same guilt in those who either connive by dissimulation or, by failing to condemn, afford harmful support. [Note: [Col. 0494D] Quesnell here inserted the words “dearest and most beloved father,” which we have placed below, as is better supported by our manuscripts and other editions.]

And in another hand:

May the Godhead preserve you safe for many years, dearest and most beloved father. [Col. 0494D]

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of June, at Ravenna, [Note: [Col. 0494D] The consulship is supplied solely by the Atrebatensis manuscript in Baronius, under the year 419, no. 56, and was accepted in the other editions. Quesnell alone omitted it.] in the consulship of Monaxius and Plinta.

[Note: [Col. 0494D] Quesnell appended the following: “This annotation—‘In the same terms it was also sent to Saint Augustine, bishop’—is found in all the printed editions and likewise in all the manuscripts used by the editors. It appears in our two manuscripts, the Thuaneus and Oxoniensis. It was present in the Atrebatensis, whose copy Henry Gravius supplied to Baronius. John Garnier alone judged that it should be omitted as having been inserted by notaries, and in fact omitted it, supported by the authority of neither any manuscript nor any printed edition. Surely this is a remarkable agreement among the notaries, that all of them should have thought of this! Let us rather admit, learned man—let us admit that something was granted to Augustine which was not granted to the other bishops. For although he did not precede them either by privilege of his see or by antiquity of ordination, which is Garnier’s argument, nevertheless he indisputably left them all far behind in the holiness of his life, in the labors he undertook for the Church of God, and in the excellence of his teaching. It was therefore fitting that this should have been granted to him for these reasons, whereas it was granted to Aurelius by virtue of the prerogative of primacy.

“Moreover, the matter then being handled itself demanded this. Augustine had been the guiding mind of all the councils against the Pelagians; the universal Church had entrusted him with the protection and defense of its cause; and finally, under this man’s leadership, as Saint Prosper writes, for more than twenty years the Catholic army had both fought against and conquered the enemies of God’s grace.

“However great a distinction Garnier may draw between a letter addressed to a representative and one summoning a person, he will not begrudge Augustine this glory if he has ever read that, when Theodosius wrote a sacred letter to all the bishops ordering them to assemble at Ephesus and deliberate concerning the books of Nestorius and the judgment of Cyril—these are the words of Liberatus the deacon in chapter 5 of the *Breviarium*—the emperor also wrote to the blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo, through Ebagnius the *Magistrianus*, asking him to be present at the council. When Ebagnius came to Carthage, he learned from Capreolus, bishop of that city, that the blessed Augustine had departed from this world to the Lord. Having received from him a letter to the emperor reporting the death of the blessed Augustine, he returned to Constantinople, from which he had come.

“The Roman pontiffs support the joining of Aurelius and Augustine; among them was Pope Innocent I, who greeted both in a common letter, which Dionysius Exiguus inserted in his collection.” Thus far Quesnell. Our manuscripts too—those not only of this collection but also of two other collections—and one Bellovacensis cited by Hardouin likewise place these same words, “In the same terms, etc.,” here.]

In the same terms it was also sent to Saint Augustine, bishop.

# CHAPTER XVII

[Note: [Col. 0495D] It is found in the same manuscripts of the three collections mentioned in note 1 to the preceding chapter. It is also read at the end of the manuscript collection of the twenty-four letters of Saint Leo and in Merlin’s edition, which published Isidore with several additions. This letter, together with the following chapters, is reckoned among the additions. Baronius reads *Asuritanam*; Baluzius, *Argizitanam*; the Vindobonensis manuscript, *Arzucitanam*.]

Letter of Saint Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, to all the bishops established throughout the provinces of Byzacena and Arzugitana.

[Col. 0495A]

On the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius.

To our most beloved and longed-for brothers and fellow priests Donatianus, bishop of the first see, [Note: [Col. 0496B] Thus, with Garnier, all five of our manuscripts of the three collections. Quesnell, with the other printed editions, preferred *Januario* (“Januarius”).] Januarianus, Felix, Palatinus, Primianus, [Col. 0496A] Gajanus and another Gajanus, Januarius, Victorinus, and the others established throughout the territory of the provinces of Byzacena and Arzugitana, Aurelius, bishop. [Note: [Col. 0496B] The Vallicellian and Vatican manuscripts containing the Dionysian Additions have *Gagano* in both places. Baluzius has *Galano*; Garnier, *Cajano*. For *Arzugitanae*, Baronius has *Asuritanae*, Baluzius *Argizitanae*, and the Vindobonensis *Arzucitanae*.]

Your belovedness remembers, dearest and longed-for brothers, that it took part in the plenary council in the condemnation of Coelestius and Pelagius and of their doctrines. But since, for the honor of God, in whose hand the king’s heart is established, the authority of the most glorious Christian princes who preserve the true and Catholic faith has been added, and since they wished this authority to be made known to all my fellow bishops through my humility, I hastened to instruct your honorable fraternity by sending copies, [Col. 0496A] lest in any part of the aforementioned provinces the serpent-like persuasion—excluded from the universal Church of the whole world—should perhaps creep in. [Note: [Col. 0496C] Baronius and Hardouin read “lest any evil should [arise] in any part”; and afterward, “by persuasion.”]

[Note: [Col. 0496C] Thus the Vindobonensis, Vallicellian, and Vatican manuscripts, with the common editions, except Quesnell, who has *Ad hoc* (“For this”).]

For this reason the highly necessary decree of the Christian princes ought not to have been hidden from your charity, and the letters sent by them to me ought to have been transmitted to you. [Note: [Col. 0496C] Earlier printed editions, together with the Vindobonensis, Barberinianus, and one Vatican manuscript, omit “ought to have been sent to you”; afterward they delete *in* before *synodalibus* (“in the synodal acts”).] When you have read the copies together, your belovedness will learn how each of you ought to subscribe—whether your subscription is already recorded in the synodal acts, or whether you were unable to attend that plenary council of all Africa—so that, once the subscription concerning the condemnation of the heretics mentioned above has been completed, no suspicion may rightly remain that there has been any dissimulation, negligence, or perhaps hidden depravity. [Note: [Col. 0496C] Some manuscripts read *quod* (“because”). Quesnell notes: “The common edition has *integra* (‘complete’), a reading Garnier approves more. The first reading is found in two manuscripts, the Oxford and Thuaneus, to which two Vatican and Vallicellian manuscripts should be added, and it seems better. For the earlier subscription, made incomplete by the absence of many bishops, was completed by the general subscription which Aurelius now announces. Isidore Mercator likewise has this reading; Garnier ought to have considered him, since, except for one Baluzius, he asserted that all the other editors had *integra*.] [Col. 0496B]

And in another hand:

I pray, brothers, that you may live well, remembering me.

Given on the Kalends of August, at Carthage, in the consulship of Monaxius and Plinta. [Note: [Col. 0496D] In the Bellovacensis, according to P. Hardouin, it is dated the fifth day before the Kalends.]

# CHAPTER XVIII

[Note: [Col. 0496D] These chapters are cited in Augustine’s Letter 186 to Paulinus. The holy doctor himself excerpted the first twelve chapters of error charged against Pelagius at the Synod of Diospolis from the acts of that synod; the remaining chapters, whether preceding or following them, were composed by Augustine, who judged that an equal number of chapters of Catholic doctrine should be set against those errors. These chapters passed from Augustine into several collections. In addition to the manuscripts of the three collections mentioned in note 1 to chapter 16, there are the Grimanicus copy reviewed by Quesnell, and the Mainz and Corbie manuscripts cited by the Benedictine Fathers in the appendix to volume X of their edition of Saint Augustine, column 88, as well as the manuscripts of the collection of the twenty-four letters of Saint Leo and Merlin’s edition of Isidore, incorporated into the common editions of the Councils.]

Here begin the chapters excerpted from the acts held against the heretic Pelagius, and others from his books, which he was compelled to anathematize when they were brought against him in the Palestinian synod. [Note: [Col. 0497C] The manuscripts of the present collection read “and others from his books”; the other collections read “from the books.” We have added *sibi* (“against him”) from our manuscripts and other common editions. In Augustine and in the Vatican, Barberinian, and Vallicellian manuscripts, *ipse damnare* (“himself to condemn”) is read for *anathematizare* (“to anathematize”).]

[Col. 0497A]

What the Lord cried out concerning Jerusalem, unwilling to have her children gathered, we cry out against those who do not wish the children of the Church to be gathered, nor are corrected even after the judgment made concerning Pelagius himself in Palestine. [Note: [Col. 0497C] The common editions of the Councils read *colligere* (“to gather”) for *colligi* (“to be gathered”); the same editions add *volentes* (“willing”) and omit *in Palaestina* (“in Palestine”). They also read *collegerunt* (“have gathered”), while the Vallicellian and Vatican manuscripts read *colliguntur* (“are gathered”); shortly afterward the Oxford manuscript has *non potuerat* (“had not been able”).] He would have come away condemned from that judgment if he had not himself condemned the statements brought against him concerning the grace of God, which he could not obscure. Besides those statements which he dared, in whatever way he could, to defend by some sort of argument, certain others were brought against him which, unless he had anathematized them after removing every evasion, would have made him himself anathema.

I. For it was brought against him that he said Adam was made mortal, and that whether he had sinned or had not sinned, he would have died. [Note: [Col. 0497D] The common edition of the Councils, with the same manuscripts and the Grimanicus, reads *cum diceret* (“when he said”). Augustine confirms the reading of the text in the cited letter, chapter 9. Shortly afterward the same editions have *mortuus esset* (“would have died”).]

II. And that his sin injured only himself, and not the human race. [Note: [Col. 0497D] Another copy, with Augustine, adds “and not the race.”]

III. And that infants newly born are in the condition in which Adam was before the transgression.

IV. And that neither through death nor through Adam’s transgression does the whole human race die; nor through Christ’s resurrection does the whole human race rise. [Note: [Col. 0497D] Thus our manuscripts agree with Augustine; Quesnell has *neque* (“nor”).]

V. And that infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life. [Note: [Col. 0497D] The common edition of the Councils, with two of our manuscript collections, adds *possunt* (“can possess”).]

VI. And that baptized rich people, unless they renounce everything, are not credited with any good they may appear to do, nor can they possess the kingdom of God.

[Col. 0497C]

VII. And that God’s grace and assistance are not given for individual acts, but exist in free choice, or in the law and teaching.

VIII. And that God’s grace is given according to our merits.

IX. And that the children of God cannot be called such unless they have been made entirely without sin. [Note: [Col. 0497D] Quesnell, with Augustine’s letter, has *omnino* (“entirely”). We preferred the reading of the other editions, approved by all our manuscripts and also by the Grimanicus. Shortly afterward the common edition of the Councils, with the Vallicellian and Vatican manuscripts, has “without any sin.”]

[Col. 0498A]

X. And that free choice does not exist if it needs God’s help, since each person has it in his own will to do or not to do something. [Note: [Col. 0498C] Quesnell alone reads: “If it needs God’s help.”]

XI. And that our victory does not come from God’s assistance but from free choice.

XII. And that forgiveness is not granted to penitents according to God’s grace and mercy, but according to the merit and labor of those who have become worthy of mercy through repentance.

Pelagius anathematized all these propositions in such a way that the acts themselves sufficiently demonstrate it, bringing no argument whatever to defend them in any manner. Consequently, whoever follows the authority of that episcopal judgment and the confession of Pelagius himself must hold what the Catholic Church has always held. [Note: [Col. 0498C] We have inserted the word *episcopalis*, omitted by Quesnell, with Augustine, all our manuscripts, Quesnell’s Grimanicus manuscript, and other common editions. Shortly afterward, two Vallicellian and Vatican manuscripts read “and in the confession of Pelagius himself.”] [Col. 0498B]

I. Adam would not have died if he had not sinned.

II. His sin injured not only himself but also the human race.

III. Infants newly born are not in the condition in which Adam was before the transgression.

IV. [Note: [Col. 0498C] Thus the Vindobonensis and Vallicellian manuscripts, together with Augustine and the other printed editions. Quesnell has “And also.”] The following brief statement of the Apostle also applies to them: “Through one man came death, and through one man the resurrection of the dead; for just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:21). [Note: [Col. 0498C] The Barberinian and Vatican manuscripts, together with Augustine’s Appendix, read *vivificantur* (“are made alive”).]

V. Hence it follows that unbaptized infants cannot possess not only the kingdom of heaven but also eternal life.

VI. Let him also confess that baptized rich people, even if they do not part with their riches and are such as the Apostle describes to Timothy when he says: “Command the rich of this world not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of their riches, but in the living God, who gives us all things richly for enjoyment; let them be rich in good works, generous in giving, sharing, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may grasp the true life” (1 Timothy 6:17–19), cannot be deprived of the kingdom of God. [Note: [Col. 0498C–D] Here Quesnell inserts the words “can be deprived of the kingdom of God,” which, on the authority of our manuscripts and other editions, as well as Saint Augustine’s letter, we have transferred to the end. With Augustine, and with the same printed editions and manuscripts, including the Thuaneus, we have also added “of this world.” The Vallicellian and Vatican manuscripts of the Dionysian Additions, as well as the Barberinian and another Vatican manuscript of a different collection, begin this chapter: “Let him confess that the rich …”; chapters 7, 9, 10, 11, and 12 likewise begin “Let him confess.” The common edition of the Councils and Augustine’s Appendix do the same. Augustine’s own letter, together with the manuscripts of this collection, agrees with our text.]

VII. Let him confess that God’s grace and assistance are given even for individual acts, and that grace is not given according to our merits.

VIII. Let it be true grace—that is, freely given through the mercy of him who said: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion.”

IX. Let him confess that those who say every day, “Forgive us our debts,” can be called children of God; they would certainly not say this truthfully if they were entirely without sin.

X. Let him confess that free choice exists, even if it needs divine assistance.

XI. Let him confess that when we fight against temptations and unlawful desires, although we possess our own will, our victory nevertheless comes not from that will but from God’s assistance. Otherwise the Apostle’s statement would not be true: “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy.”

XII. Let him confess that forgiveness is granted to penitents according to God’s grace and mercy, not according to their merit, since the Apostle also called repentance itself a gift of God when he said of certain people: “Lest perhaps God grant them repentance.” [Note: [Col. 0499C] The Vallicellian and Vatican manuscripts, with Augustine, read “according to merits.” We have also added *etiam* (“also”), supported by all our manuscripts and editions. The common edition of the Councils has “as he himself also [said],” while the Barberinian and Vatican manuscripts of the same collection retain *ipse* (“he himself”).]

Let anyone who agrees with Catholic authority and with the explicit words of Pelagius himself in the ecclesiastical acts confess all these things simply and without any evasion. [Note: [Col. 0499D] The common editions of the Councils read *contra auctoritatem* (“against authority”).] For one must not believe that those contrary propositions have truly been anathematized unless the propositions opposed to them are held with faithful conviction and proclaimed in an open confession. [Col. 0499C]

# CHAPTER XIX

[Note: [Col. 0499D] Besides the manuscripts of this collection, we also found this letter in another very ancient manuscript collection, Barberinianus 2888.]

Here begins the sacred letter of the emperor Constantius, father of Valentinian Augustus the Younger, concerning the exile of Coelestius, the Pelagian heretic.

The emperor Constantius to Volusianus, prefect of the City.

Although we ordered long ago that the recent remnants of an old superstition, full of vanity, should be corrected, we are now informed by daily reports that they are becoming more extensive. Since discord has agitated the minds of the peoples, we order that what we commanded long ago be repeated. [Note: [Col. 0499D] Another reading has *commovet* (“agitates”).] Accordingly, when you have read this, Your Excellency must carefully investigate all who envy the piety of God and immediately cause them to be expelled from the walls of the City; but in such a way that they shall not have permission to remain even within the hundredth milestone. We also order Coelestius to be expelled from the City more and more completely. For it is clear that, once these men have been removed from the midst, grace and concord will retain their ancient firmness.

Certainly, if anything of this kind is reported hereafter, know that the office of Your Excellency must be subjected to capital punishment. For we do not permit our commands to be prolonged through negligence in their execution. [Col. 0500B]

Farewell, dearest and most beloved father.

And an appended subscription:

Let what we have ordered be fulfilled, because this is advantageous to your reputation.

[Note: [Col. 0499D] Quesnell reads: “Since both past superstitions and recent ones, full of vanity … should be corrected, they are said to be becoming greater.” We preferred our manuscripts, with which the Thuaneus manuscript of Quesnell also agrees. Baronius and Baluzius likewise have only “both recent” and “to become greater.” Garnier and Hardouin read: “Since what was both past superstition and recent … we had ordered.”]

# CHAPTER XX

Copy of the edict published by Volusianus, prefect of the City.

Volusianus, prefect, issued the following edict:
