Until now, hiding places friendly to defendants have withdrawn Coelestius, the disturber of divine faith and public peace, from judicial proceedings. [Note: [Col. 0499D] Thus, with Quesnell, our Vindobonensis reads *subduxerint*. Other editions have “have withdrawn him.” Shortly afterward Baronius and Baluzius, with the first hand of the Vindobonensis, read “the laws and edicts also.” Quesnell, with the Thuaneus, has “the laws also promulgated.” We have corrected this with the second hand of the Vindobonensis, as Garnier accepted it. This is the true reading, which indicates both the imperial laws and the prefects’ edicts previously promulgated against the Pelagians.] Now laws and edicts will pursue the absent man. First of all, residence in the eternal City is denied him, so that if he should remain even in its immediate vicinity, he will not escape the destruction he deserves. [Note: [Col. 0500C] Thus all the manuscripts and printed editions read, except the Oxford manuscript, with which Quesnell has *supplicium* (“punishment”).]

Moreover, in view of his deserved recklessness and audacity, we warn everyone by the sanction of this edict that no wicked person should think a hiding place is to be afforded to the guilty man: for a dreadful penalty of execution has been prescribed for everyone, and whoever thinks that a person guilty in divine and human matters should be concealed with him must necessarily incur the writ of proscription. [Note: [Col. 0500D] Baronius and the common edition of the Councils read “laws.”] [Note: [Col. 0500C–D] Earlier editions, before Quesnell, read: “when such punishment has been imposed, the penalty and the written sentence.” Quesnell has: “since a dreadful punishment has been imposed and it is necessary that the sentence of proscription …” The reading of our Vindobonensis seemed preferable; it has *cuique* (“for each person”) rather than *cuivis* (“for anyone”).]

# CHAPTER XXI

[Note: [Col. 0500D] Besides the present, Dionysian, Hispanic, and Isidorian collections, this letter is also contained in four other collections: Vaticanus Reginensis 1997, Vaticanus 1342, the Colbertine collection—similar to Lucensis 88—and the Corbie collection. The last two copies are cited by Coustant. In the preliminary table of our collection the title is given as follows: “Letter of Pope Innocent to Exsuperius, bishop of Toulouse, in which he set out for him, under six headings, the matters of his questions and the decrees of his replies; to this he adds a summary of the divine books of the Old and New Testaments.”]

Letter of Pope Innocent to Exsuperius, bishop of Toulouse, under seven headings.

INNOCENT, bishop, to EXSUPERIUS, bishop of Toulouse.

When you consulted me, dearest brother, about what I thought concerning each matter proposed, I replied, according to the measure of my understanding, with what seemed appropriate—what either a teachable reason persuaded, the authority of reading revealed, or the preserved sequence of events demonstrated. Indeed, your belovedness, following the practice of prudent men, preferred to refer to the apostolic see what ought to be observed concerning doubtful matters, rather than, by presumptuous usurpation, obtain from each matter whatever might seem right to you. Why should we think it more shameful to learn something than to be entirely ignorant?

For me too, teachability comes through discussion, since, after examining the reasons, I am compelled to answer what is proposed; and thus the person who is asked to teach always learns something. [Note: [Col. 0501C] The Vindobonensis, Vaticanus Reginensis, and Vaticanus 1342, together with Coustant’s older manuscripts, read *docere* (“to teach”) rather than *addiscat* (“learn”). In the same Vaticanus Reginensis manuscript, *responsa* (“answers”) is read instead of *responsum* (“an answer”).]

I shall therefore set out each question and append the answer.

## Chapter I

You asked what ought to be observed concerning those who, placed in the ministries of the diaconate or in the office of the presbyterate, have been shown by the children they have fathered to be, or to have been, incontinent. Concerning such men, the discipline of the divine laws is clear, and the evident admonitions of the blessed Siricius, bishop of venerable memory, have been handed down: [Note: [Col. 0501C] Siricius, Letter to Himerius, chapter 7, and Letter to the African bishops, no. 3.] those placed in such offices who are incontinent are to be deprived of all ecclesiastical honor and are not to be admitted to the ministry, which ought to be fulfilled by continence alone. [Note: [Col. 0501C–D] Coustant reads “are to be deprived and not admitted.” In the Vindobonensis, “to such a ministry,” where *tale* (“such”) was added by a second hand; it is better omitted.]

For there is a very ancient authority of sacred law, guarded from the beginning, according to which priests were commanded to dwell in the temple during the year of their service, so that, serving the sacred offerings, they might claim for themselves divine ministries as pure and cleansed from every stain; nor is it lawful to admit to the sacrifices those who engage in carnal relations even with their wives. [Note: [Col. 0501D] Thus our Vindobonensis and Vatican manuscripts, together with the common editions. Quesnell, with the Vaticanus Reginensis, reads “carnal intercourse.”] For it is written: “Be holy, because I too am holy, the Lord your God” (Leviticus 11:44; 20:7). For them marital intercourse had been relaxed solely on account of the succession of offspring, because no one from another tribe had been commanded to approach the priesthood. [Note: [Col. 0501D] The Roman edition adds: “except from the seed of Aaron.”]

How much more ought these priests or Levites to preserve chastity from the day of their ordination, for whom priesthood or ministry exists without succession, and who have no day free either from divine sacrifices or from the service of baptism? [Col. 0502A]

For if Paul writes to the Corinthians, saying, “Abstain for a time so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Corinthians 7:5)—and he gives this command to laypeople—[Note: [Col. 0501D] Quesnell reads “how much more.” Our manuscripts and editions have the better reading.] how much more ought priests, whose continual duty is prayer and sacrifice, always to abstain from such intercourse? If a priest has been defiled by carnal desire, with what shame will he presume to sacrifice? With what conscience or merit will he believe that he is heard, when it is said: “All things are clean to the clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean” (Titus 1:15). [Note: [Col. 0501D] Quesnell inserts *sit* (“is”); we have deleted it with the Vindobonensis, Vaticanus Reginensis, and Coustant.]

But perhaps he believes this is permitted because it is written: “The husband of one wife.” [Note: [Col. 0501D–0502C] Quesnell reads: “He does not say this in order that he may remain in carnal desire.” The Dionysian and Roman editions have: “not for permanent [residence],” and the Thuaneus: “not for permanent [residence].” We preferred the reading of the Vindobonensis and Vaticanus Reginensis, approved by twelve ancient books cited by Coustant, which is more consistent with Innocent’s meaning, as the following words show, where the same thought is expressed without the preposition *ad* or *propter*: “and having children,” not “begetting them.”]

He did not say this to indicate permanent indulgence in the desire to beget, but with a view to future continence. For he did not exclude those who were bodily intact when he said: “I wish that all were as I myself am” (1 Corinthians 7:7). [Note: [Col. 0502C–D] In the second hand of the Vindobonensis is added *sic* (“thus”). Other editions have “thus to be.” Shortly afterward, with the Vindobonensis and other better manuscripts, we have written “and he declares it more clearly”; Quesnell has “which declares more clearly.” The edition of the Councils after Merlin has “which also declares more clearly.”]

And he declares it more clearly, saying: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God; but you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit” (Romans 8:9). He said “having children” (1 Timothy 3:4), not “begetting them”; but the sentence is plainly different and divided. [Note: [Col. 0502D] The Vindobonensis and Pithoean manuscripts of this collection, together with other printed editions before Quesnell, read *diversa* (“different”). Coustant, with most other manuscripts, including Quesnell’s, retained this reading because he judged the sentence divided into two parts: one concerns those ignorant of Siricius’s decrees, the other those who knew them.]

For if it can be shown that the rule of ecclesiastical life and discipline which Bishop Siricius sent to the provinces did not reach certain people, pardon for their ignorance is granted to them, provided that thereafter they begin to abstain completely. They are to retain the ranks in which they are found, but may not rise to higher ones; and it should count as a benefit for them that they do not lose the very position they retain. [Note: [Col. 0502D] Thus the Vindobonensis and Vaticanus Reginensis manuscripts, more coherently with the preceding context, together with all the editions. Quesnell reads “but whoever …”; shortly afterward the Vaticanus and other editions have “are discovered.”]

But if some are discovered to have known the rule of life sent by Siricius and nevertheless not to have immediately cast off the desires of lust, they must in every way be removed: they judged pleasure preferable after learning the admonition.

## CHAPTER II

And this question was also raised: what observance ought to be maintained concerning those who, after baptism, have devoted themselves throughout their entire lives to the pleasures of incontinence and, at the very end of life, ask simultaneously for penance and restoration to communion? The earlier practice was stricter; the later practice, with mercy intervening, is more lenient. For the earlier custom required that penance be granted to them, but communion denied. Since persecutions were frequent in those times, this was rightly done, lest the easy granting of communion should leave people secure about their reconciliation and fail to recall them from falling again. Communion was therefore denied, while penance was granted, so that everything might not be wholly refused; and the circumstances of the time made remission more severe. But after our Lord restored peace to his churches, it was decided that communion should now be given to those departing this life, and, because of the Lord’s mercy, as viaticum to those about to set out, lest we seem to follow the harshness and severity of the heretic Novatian, who denied pardon. Thus communion is granted together with final penance, so that people of this kind, even at the point of death, with the permission of our Savior, may be rescued from everlasting destruction.

[Note: [Col. 0502D] We added, on the authority of our manuscripts and other printed editions, the two words “to pleasures” and “at the end,” which Quesnell omitted; the Vatican Regina manuscript omits only the word “at the end.”]

[Note: [Col. 0502D] We inserted “to them” on the authority of the same manuscripts and of the older printed editions. Shortly afterward, the Vatican manuscript reads “but communion was not granted.”]

[Note: [Col. 0503C] The printed editions, together with the Vatican Regina manuscript, read: “communion was denied, penance was granted.” The reading of several of our other manuscripts is better.]

[Note: [Col. 0503C] The Vatican Regina manuscript and another manuscript, together with the Roman editions, Dionysius, and others, read “as they were departing.”]

[Note: [Col. 0503C] Quesnell, together with other printed editions, inserts “and”; we have rightly deleted it on the authority of our Vindobonensis and Vatican manuscripts. Shortly afterward Quesnell, together with the older editions, has “to follow.” Other manuscripts have “to pursue.”]

[Note: [Col. 0503C] The Vatican manuscript, together with the Roman edition, Dionysius, and Coustant, reads “communion shall be granted.”]

## CHAPTER III

A question was also raised concerning those who, after baptism, have administered justice and have either exercised only tortures or have even pronounced a capital sentence. We read that nothing was defined concerning them by our predecessors. For they remembered that these powers had been granted by God, that the sword had been permitted for the punishment of the guilty, and that God’s minister had been appointed as an avenger in such matters. How, then, could they condemn an act that they saw had been permitted by the Lord’s authority? Concerning such persons, therefore, we retain the practice observed until now, lest we seem either to overturn discipline or to act against the Lord’s authority. Their whole conduct, however, will be taken into account when they render an account.

[Note: [Col. 0503D] Thus the Vindobonensis and Vatican Regina manuscripts and the printed editions, except Quesnell, who omits “thus.”]

[Note: [Col. 0503D] Quesnell, because he carelessly read the abbreviation, incorrectly has “endured”; but the subject here is those who administer justice. Later Quesnell reads, “How, then.” We have followed our manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER IV

You also wished to know why men who remain in communion do not associate with adulterous wives, whereas, conversely, wives seem to remain in the company of adulterous husbands. In this matter the Christian religion condemns adultery equally in both sexes. But women do not readily accuse their husbands of adultery, and hidden sins do not receive punishment. Men, however, are accustomed more freely to report their adulterous wives to the priests; and therefore, when the women’s crime has been exposed, communion is denied them. But when the men’s offense remains hidden, no one is readily excluded on the basis of suspicions; nevertheless, he will certainly be removed if his disgrace is exposed. Since, then, the case is the same, when proof is lacking the administration of punishment sometimes comes to a halt.

[Note: [Col. 0503D] The printed editions delete “their.” The Vindobonensis manuscript reads “their adulterous wives,” and deletes “more freely.”]

[Note: [Col. 0503D] Thus our manuscripts, together with the printed editions. Quesnell reads “anyone.”]

## CHAPTER V

You also wished to inquire whether those who dictate prayers may properly ask rulers, after the regeneration of baptism, for the death of someone or for bloodshed as a punishment for guilt. Rulers never grant such a request without an investigation; rather, they always refer the matters committed to them, or the crimes themselves, to judges, so that punishment may be imposed after the case has been examined. When these matters have been delegated to the investigator, either acquittal or condemnation is pronounced according to the nature of the affair; and while the authority of the laws is exercised against the wicked, the person who made the request will remain free from liability.

[Note: [Col. 0503D] Quesnell reads “those matters.” The reading of the Vindobonensis and Vatican Regina manuscripts, together with the other printed editions, is better. Shortly afterward, the Oxford manuscript and several others, together with the older editions, read “once the case has been examined, let the crimes be punished.” Dionysius’s common text likewise reads “once the case has been examined, let it be punished.” The reading we have adopted, supported by the Vindobonensis and Vatican Regina manuscripts, has “let them be punished” referring to the crimes, and agrees better with what follows. The manuscripts that read “once the case has been examined” prefer “have been delegated.”]

## CHAPTER VI

Your Affection also asked about those who, after a divorce had intervened, joined themselves in marriage to someone else; it is clear that both parties are adulterers. Those who, while their wife or husband is still alive, hasten to another union, even though the marriage may appear to have been dissolved, cannot fail to be regarded as adulterers. Indeed, even those persons to whom such people have been joined appear themselves to have committed adultery, in accordance with what we read in the Gospel: “Whoever dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery. Likewise, whoever marries a woman who has been dismissed commits adultery” (Matthew 19:9). Therefore all are to be kept from communion. Nothing of this kind, however, can be decreed concerning their parents or relatives, unless they are found to have encouraged the illicit union.

[Note: [Col. 0504C] Quesnell reads: “Whoever, whether man or woman, while the husband or wife is living . . . should hasten to another union.” We have preferred the Vindobonensis manuscript, with which the common text and other manuscripts agree.]

[Note: [Col. 0504C] We added “even” on the authority of the Vindobonensis, Vatican Regina, and other printed texts; shortly afterward, on the authority of the same manuscripts and Labbe, we corrected “joined” to the plural “joined themselves,” which agrees better with the preceding reading.]

[Note: [Col. 0504D] Thus the Vindobonensis and Vatican Regina manuscripts and six other manuscripts cited by Coustant, together with the remaining printed editions. Quesnell and the manuscript cited by Hardouin read “the faithful are to abstain.”]

## CHAPTER VII

Which books are to be received into the canon is briefly shown in the following list. These are the matters about which you wished to be instructed by an explicit statement:

The five books of Moses—that is, Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy; Joshua, one book; Judges, one; the four books of Kingdoms, together with Ruth; sixteen books of the Prophets; five books of Solomon; and the Psalter.

Likewise among the historical books: one book of Job, one of Tobit, one of Esther, one of Judith, two of Maccabees, two of Ezra, and two books of Chronicles.

Likewise, in the New Testament: four books of the Gospels; fourteen epistles of the apostle Paul; three epistles of John; two epistles of Peter; one epistle of Jude; one epistle of James; the Acts of the Apostles; and the Apocalypse of John.

But the other writings, whether under the name of Matthias or of James the Younger, or under the names of Peter and John, which were written by a certain Leucius, or under the name of Thomas, and any others of this kind, you should know are not only to be rejected but also condemned.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of March, during the consulship of the most illustrious men Stilicho and Anthemius.

[Note: [Col. 0504D] Dionysius adds “of the Scriptures.” Isidore, together with the common text, has “of the holy Scriptures.” Shortly afterward Quesnell reads “These, then, are.” We deleted “then” on the authority of the Vindobonensis and Vatican Regina manuscripts and Coustant’s edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0504D] On the authority of the excellent Vindobonensis and Vatican Regina manuscripts, we added the numbers “one” to the books of Joshua and Judges. The Vatican manuscript agrees and also has “Ruth, one.” On the authority of these manuscripts and the other common editions, we corrected “seventeen books of the Prophets” to “sixteen,” as Quesnell’s edition had it. Conversely, where Quesnell later wrote “one of Jude” and “one of James,” we deleted the number one, on the authority of the same manuscripts and the common editions, since the number is understood from the word “epistle.”]

[Note: [Col. 0505B] Dionysius, together with the manuscripts of the Spanish collections and Isidore, who received this letter from Dionysius, adds: “or under the name of Andrew, written by the philosophers Nexocharides—or Xenocharides—and Leonidas, or of Thomas, etc.” But these words are omitted in the manuscripts of this and other ancient collections. They were added only in the Vindobonensis manuscript by a second and ancient hand. Shortly afterward, the manuscripts of this collection read “such writings”; the other manuscript collections, together with the common text, read “another.”]

[Note: [Col. 0505C] The manuscripts of this collection and the Vatican Regina manuscript simply read “during the consulship of Stilicho,” omitting “the second,” which the other collections and the common text more correctly include. The Vatican manuscript, together with another cited by Hardouin, reads: “Given on the Kalends of March, during the second consulship of Stilicho,” and so forth.]

# CHAPTER XXII

Here begins the letter of Pope Innocent to the Macedonian bishops, under four headings.

## INNOCENTIUS

To Rufus, Eusebius, Eustathius, Claudius, Maximianus, Eugenius, Gerontius, John, Polychronius, Sophronius, Flavianus, Hilary, Macedonius, Calicratus, Zosimus, Profuturus, Nicetas, Hermogenes, Vincentius, Asiologus, Terentianus, Herodianus, and Martianus, bishops of Macedonia, and to the deacons: greetings in the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0505C] The order of bishops is generally considered extremely important in letters of this kind, so that their dignity or seniority may be preserved. An exception must be made, however, in letters where the order differs among the manuscripts, unless agreement among several collections and manuscripts makes it possible to determine which order should be preferred. In the ancient manuscript collection of the Vatican 1342 and Barberini 2888, the order is given as follows: Innocent to Sophronius, Zosimus, Asiologus—Barberini has “Asiologus”—Eusebius, Eugenius, Flavianus, Profuturus, Terentianus, Eustathius, Gerontius, Hilary, Nicetas, Herodianus—Barberini more correctly has “Herodianus”—and Martianus, Claudius, John, Macedonius, Hermogenes, Maximianus, Polychronius, Calicratus, Vincentius, bishops of Macedonia, and so forth. The words “and Martianus,” together with the coordinating particle, belong with the final bishop, as they appear in our catalogue. Since here they are found in the middle, this clearly indicates the error of a less careful copyist. In the Corbie manuscript the order is: Innocent to Eustathius, Eugenius, Polychronius, Hilary, Zosimus, Hermogenes, Terentianus, Rufus, Claudius, Gerontius, Sophronius, Macedonius, Profuturus, Vincentius, Herodianus, Eusebius, Maximianus, John, Flavianus, Calicratus, Nicetas, Asiologus, Martianus, bishops of Macedonia. Rufus of Thessalonica, who, on the basis of other documents, ought to have been first, as in our catalogue, is missing from the Vatican and Barberini manuscripts; in the Corbie manuscript he is placed later. This error likewise reveals the disruption of this order. The more accurate order is therefore preserved in the manuscripts of our collection, with which manuscript Verona 58 and Vatican Regina 1997 also agree. Dionysius, from whom the Spanish and Isidorean versions derive, contents himself with naming the first two bishops and reads: “Innocent to Rufus, Eusebius, and the remaining bishops,” and so forth.]

I was filled with great joy when, after so many dangers throughout, so to speak, the whole world, Vitalis, your archdeacon and the bearer of your letter, arrived here from those regions. When we had seen him, we immediately, as was proper, asked him about your condition. But when we learned that you were living according to your wishes, we offered abundant thanks to our Lord God, because he both protects his servants who serve his altars amid adversity and graciously governs them in prosperity.

When he had delivered the letters, I ordered them to be reviewed immediately. In them I saw many things that would introduce perplexity into our minds and cause us considerable doubt as to whether we should understand them otherwise or whether they had indeed been written as they sounded. After having them read aloud several times, I realized that some injury was being done to the Apostolic See, to which the report had been sent as to the head of the churches, and whose judgment was still being brought into uncertainty. Therefore your repeated inquiry concerning the report about which I remember having written some time ago compels me now to restate the matter with more evident arguments.

[Note: [Col. 0506C] Quesnell, together with the manuscripts of this collection, reads “I immediately ordered them.” We have preferred the reading of the other collections. Shortly afterward Dionysius more correctly reads “they should introduce” rather than “they should bring in.” Another version has “they should induce,” which Coustant retained.]

[Note: [Col. 0506D] The Vatican manuscript, together with two other manuscripts, Corbie and Colbertine-Lucensian, reads “your repeated inquiry concerning the report.” Dionysius omits “your report.” In the Vindobonensis manuscript the second “your” was deleted by a later hand; it is absent from the Vatican Regina manuscript.]

## CHAPTER I

I have learned that those who are said to have taken widows as wives not only became clerics but even attained the insignia of the highest priesthood—something that everyone knows to be contrary to the commands of the Law. For when Moses the lawgiver loudly declares, “The priests shall take a virgin as wife” (Leviticus 21:13), and, so that this command might not appear ambiguous in any respect, he adds, “not a widow or one who has been cast out,” no definition of another command can be set against this precept supported by divine authority, except your custom, which, as you yourselves admit, was established out of ignorance—or, to put it more modestly, not from apostolic tradition and sound reasoning.

Let your Affection know that we, and all the churches throughout East and West, utterly refuse to admit this practice and do not even admit such men to the lowest rank of the ecclesiastical order; and, if they are found there, we remove them.

[Note: [Col. 0506D] Thus our manuscripts together with the Vatican Regina manuscript. The other collections have “let the priest take a virgin.”]

[Note: [Col. 0506D] Thus our manuscripts together with the common text, except the Vatican Regina manuscript, which, together with Quesnell, reads: “lest this command should appear ambiguous to anyone.” Shortly afterward it has “against this.”]

[Note: [Col. 0506D] Thus, together with Quesnell, the first hand of the Vindobonensis manuscript and the Vatican Regina manuscript. Vatican 1342, together with the other collections, reads “defense”; this was restored in the second hand of the Vindobonensis.]

[Note: [Col. 0506D] Coustant and the Vatican Regina manuscript delete “and.” Shortly afterward, on the authority of the Vatican Regina and Vatican 1342 manuscripts and the other editions, we preferred “not from apostolic tradition” to Quesnell’s “more from apostolic than from non-apostolic tradition.”]

## CHAPTER II

Next it is stated that a man is not to be called a digamist if, while a catechumen, he had and lost a wife, provided that after baptism he took another, and that the woman joined to the new man is to be regarded as his first wife, because that marriage was washed away, together with the other sins, after the sacrament of baptism.

If this is said of one wife, then certainly, if as an unbaptized man he had three wives, the woman who is his fourth after baptism will, according to this interpretation, be his first; and she who was married fourth will receive the name of “virgin.” Who, I ask, does not see that this is contrary to the Apostle’s command, which says that a priest must be “the husband of one wife” (1 Timothy 3:2; Titus 1:6)?

But it is objected that in baptism everything done in the old man has been dissolved. Tell me—speaking with due respect—is it only crimes that are forgiven in baptism, or also those things that are fulfilled according to the commands of the Law and the institutions of God? Is marrying a wife a crime, or is it not a crime? If it is a crime, then, with the pardon I have mentioned, I would say that the author is guilty who, in order that human beings might commit crimes in paradise, blessed them when he himself joined them together. But if it is not a crime—for what God has joined it would be impious to call a crime—and Solomon added, “A wife is prepared for a man by God” (Proverbs 19:14), how can one believe that among the crimes there has been forgiven what is read to have been completed by God’s authority?

What is to be said about the children of such people? Are they not to be admitted to share in the inheritance because they were born from her who was a wife before baptism? Are they to be called either natural children or bastards, because there is no legitimate marriage except, as you seem to think, the one assumed after baptism?

When the Lord was asked by the Jews whether it was lawful to dismiss a wife, and explained that this ought not to be done, he added: “Therefore what God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matthew 19:6). And lest he be thought to have spoken only of those who marry after baptism, remember that he was questioned by Jews and answered Jews.

I ask—and I ask with even greater concern—if the wife of a man who was first a catechumen and afterward a believer is one and the same, and if he had children by her while he was a catechumen and afterward had others while he was a believer: are they to be called brothers? Or, after their father’s death, are those to whom spiritual rebirth is thought to have taken away the name of children to have no share in the division of the inheritance?

Since it is absurd to think and judge this way, what reason—perish the thought—is there for defending such an opinion and boasting of it as an empty notion rather than supporting it by some authority, when what the Law commands and God enjoins cannot be counted among sins? If a catechumen has devoted himself to virtues, followed humility, maintained patience, given alms, rescued those condemned to death by whatever means, detested adulteries, and preserved chastity, I ask whether, once he has become a believer, he loses these things because baptism is thought to remove everything done by the old man.

Let us consider the Gentile Cornelius (Acts 10:1), devoted to prayers and almsgiving, who saw a revelation and Peter himself. Were these things taken away from him through baptism, on account of which baptism appears to have been granted to him? If this is believed, believe me, it is a considerable error. For whatever has been done well, and whatever has been preserved according to the commands of the Law, cannot be lost by the person who has done it. Since marriage is completed by God’s command, it cannot be called a sin; and what is not a sin ought not to be dissolved altogether among sins. The name of the former wife will therefore remain intact, since it was not set aside as a sin but was completed according to God’s will.

[Note: [Col. 0507C] Quesnell reads “it ought not to be called.” We have followed our manuscripts, in agreement with the other editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0507C] Alternatively, “through baptism”; shortly afterward, the Thuanus and Vatican manuscripts read “taken away” instead of “washed away.”]

[Note: [Col. 0507C] Thus the Thuanus, Vindobonensis, Vatican Regina, another Vatican manuscript, and others cited by Coustant. Some manuscripts, through a scribal error, read “to the virgin” or “to the virgin likewise” instead of “and of the virgin.” Dionysius, together with the Thuanus manuscript and the Council edition, reads “of the virgin likewise.” Coustant’s correction is required by the context: Quesnell, together with the Oxford manuscript, reads “the man, his wife, who is fourth after baptism; thus interpreting it, she will receive the name of the first virgin,” and so forth.]

[Note: [Col. 0507D] The Vindobonensis manuscript, together with the Vatican Regina manuscript, reads “let him remember”; the common text reads “let them remember,” which is better.]

[Note: [Col. 0507D] We added “I would say” on the authority of our manuscripts and the other editions. Shortly afterward the common text and most manuscripts delete “human beings.”]

[Note: [Col. 0507D] Thus the manuscripts and the common text. Quesnell reads “he says.”]

[Note: [Col. 0507D] The Thuanus, Vindobonensis, and other manuscripts, together with the common text. Quesnell reads “if he has preserved chastity.” We preferred our manuscripts and the common text. Shortly afterward the Vindobonensis manuscript, together with the Vatican Regina and Coustant, reads “has conducted himself.”]

[Note: [Col. 0508C] Quesnell reads “has followed.” We preferred our manuscripts and the common text.]

[Note: [Col. 0508C] Quesnell reads “devoted to prayers and occupied with almsgiving, summoned Peter through a revelation and saw him himself.” We judged the reading received by Coustant from the best Vindobonensis and Vatican Regina manuscripts, and from several other very ancient manuscripts, preferable.]

[Note: [Col. 0508C] Quesnell reads “which baptism itself appears to have granted him.” The Vatican Regina manuscript reads: “Lest these things have been washed away from him through baptism, on account of which baptism appears to have been granted.” Six reputable manuscripts cited by Coustant have “washed away.” We have adopted the common reading, which agrees with the Vindobonensis manuscript, where “lest” alone appears instead of “surely.”]

[Note: [Col. 0508D] Quesnell, with Dionysius, the Spanish text, and Isidore, reads: “preserved according to the legal commands cannot perish for those who have done them. Therefore the union of marriage, because it is completed by God’s command, cannot be called a sin; and if it is not a sin . . .” We preferred the Vindobonensis, Vatican Regina, another Vatican manuscript, and the other manuscripts followed by Coustant. Before “at all,” the Vatican and Barberini manuscripts, together with most printed editions, insert “it may be believed”; this was added in a later revision of the Vindobonensis.]

## CHAPTER III

We have reached the third question, which because of its difficulty requires a longer discussion. We say that those ordained by heretics have a wounded head through that laying on of hands; and where the wound has been inflicted, medicine must be applied so that health may be restored. That health, following the wound, cannot exist without a scar. And where the remedy of penance is necessary, the honor of ordination cannot have a place.

For if, as we read, “Whatever an unclean person touches shall be unclean” (Numbers 19:22; Leviticus 15:4), how can something customarily received in cleanliness and purity be granted to him? But, on the other hand, it is asserted that one who has lost honor cannot confer honor, nor has the other received anything, because there was nothing in the giver that the recipient could receive.

We agree, and it is true. Certainly, since he could not give what he did not possess, he gave through an evil laying on of hands the condemnation that he did possess. And how the person who has become a participant in the condemned man should receive honor, I cannot discover.

But it is said that the true and just blessing of a legitimate priest removes every defect that had been inflicted by a defective person. If that is so, then let sacrilegious persons, adulterers, and those guilty of every crime be brought to ordination, since through the blessing of ordination they are thought to have their crimes or vices removed. Let there be no place for penance, since ordination can provide what prolonged satisfaction has customarily provided.

But this is the law of our Church: to those coming from heresy, provided that they have been baptized there, we grant through the laying on of hands only lay communion, and we do not promote any of them, even minimally, to clerical honor. But those who have passed from the Catholic Church to heresy—whom it is proper to receive only through penance—not only do not perform penance among you but are even loaded with honor.

The considered judgment of Anysius, formerly our brother, and of the other priests was this: those whom Bonosus had ordained were to be received as ordained, lest they remain with him and a serious scandal arise. I think we have overcome the ambiguities.

It is therefore clear that what was established as a remedy and necessity of the time did not exist originally, and that there were ancient rules, handed down by the apostles or apostolic men, which the Roman Church preserves and commands to be preserved by those accustomed to heed her. But the necessity of the time demanded that this be done with great urgency. Therefore, when the necessity ceases, what necessity discovered as a remedy must likewise cease, because one thing is the legitimate order and another is the usurpation that present circumstances compel to be carried out.

But the canons established at Nicaea permitted this to be done with regard to the Novatians. First, that canon instituted by the Fathers must be set forth, so that we may observe either what they understood or in what manner they understood it, or what they commanded. It says:

“Concerning those who call themselves Cathars, that is, the Pure, and who at some time come to the Catholic Church, it has pleased the holy and great synod that, after receiving the laying on of hands, they should remain in the clergy” (Council of Nicaea, canon 8).

I can say, however, that this command concerns the Novatians alone and does not apply to the clergy of other heresies. For if they had indeed defined this concerning everyone, they would have added: “Those returning from the Novatians and other heretics are to be received into their own order.” That this is so can also be confirmed especially by what was said about the Paulianists (Nicaea, canon 19), for those coming from them are commanded to be baptized. Surely, when they give this command concerning the Paulianists, will everyone returning from heretics be baptized on this model? Since no one would dare do this, reason itself shows that the command concerns those people alone.

Finally, Peter and John complete by the laying on of hands those properly baptized by Philip the evangelist. But those whom the apostle Paul found baptized with John’s baptism he asked whether they had received the Holy Spirit; and when they confessed that they had not even heard of that name, he ordered them to be baptized. You see, therefore, that those properly baptized cannot have that gift repeated for them, while it must clearly be provided that those washed only with another water are baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

Thus it is read with clear evidence that the command was likewise given only concerning the Novatians. The reason plainly shows that this was distinguished between the two heresies, because the Paulianists did not baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, whereas the Novatians baptize with these same awesome and venerable names. Nor has any question ever arisen among the latter concerning the unity of the divine power—that is, of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Therefore, after all the others had been excluded, this one group alone was selected as the group to which this concession should be granted, because they committed no offense against the sacrament of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

If someone passing from the Catholic Church to heresy, or a believer returning to apostasy, wishes to return in repentance, can he, by the same reasoning, be permitted to the clergy, when his offense can be removed only through prolonged penance? Nor do the canons, by their own authority, permit him to become a cleric after penance. It is therefore clear that those who passed from the Catholic Church to the condemned Bonosus, and who allowed or desired themselves to be ordained by him, ought not to have received the dignity of ecclesiastical ordination. They abandoned the common judgment of all the churches and decided that their own peculiar error in following Bonosus should be embraced.

It is nevertheless clear that many suffered violence, were dragged unwillingly, and were ordained by him despite their resistance. Let anyone who believes this tell me whether, after Bonosus’s ordination, such a person did not take part when Bonosus celebrated the sacraments; did not share in his communion; and, immediately departing from his most wicked assembly, returned to the Church. Such a person is found to have at least some color of excuse.

But those who returned to the Church only after a year or after several months are understood to have gone to him because they knew that, on account of their vices, they could not receive ordination in the Catholic Church. He, however, performed illicit ordinations indiscriminately and without any examination. They believed that through this arrangement they could find in the Catholic Church a position of which they had previously despaired.

Now I ask about what remains: if someone returned after a month or more, while considering himself ordained a priest by Bonosus, but did not celebrate the sacraments, did not distribute them to the people, and did not complete Masses according to custom, I ask you to state more clearly what you think about such cases.

In short, those who received nothing from Bonosus are guilty of usurped dignity if they claimed for themselves the authority to celebrate the sacraments—or did not claim it—and thought themselves to be what had not been granted to them by any regular authority. Let your Affection therefore clearly perceive that such things have been tolerated up to this point. And observe that the churches, now established in peace, cannot presume upon what, as you say, necessity compelled. Yet, as often happens whenever a people or a crowd sins, because punishment cannot be exacted against everyone on account of their number, the matter commonly passes without punishment. I therefore say that the earlier cases must be left to God’s judgment, while for the future the greatest care must be taken.

[Note: [Col. 0509D] Quesnell alone, together with the Oxford manuscript, reads “wounded through that ordination”; shortly afterward, “a remedy must be applied by which the wounded person may recover.”]

[Note: [Col. 0509D] The Council editions after the Roman edition add the word “we decree,” which neither Coustant nor we have found in any manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0509D] Quesnell, with the Oxford manuscript alone, reads “ordination.”]

[Note: [Col. 0509D] The Vindobonensis manuscript, together with Dionysius, the Vatican Regina manuscript, and the common Council text, reads “Our law is the law of the Church.”]

Quesnell himself noted in the margin: “The Oxford manuscript adds ‘faith,’ incorrectly.”]

[Note: [Col. 0509D] Alternatively, “of fellow priests.”]

Shortly afterward the Vindobonensis manuscript, together with Dionysius, reads “after all the excluded groups”; the reading of the other manuscripts and the common text is better: “after all have been excluded,” that is, all the heresies.]

[Note: [Col. 0511C] Quesnell alone reads “Bonosus.” Shortly afterward the Vindobonensis and Vatican Regina manuscripts, together with Dionysius, read “if he immediately departed.”]

We preferred the Vindobonensis and Vatican Regina manuscripts. Coustant adopted the same reading, retaining “in the Catholic Church.”]

The meaning of this passage is that those illicitly ordained by Bonosus are guilty of usurped dignity whether or not they claimed for themselves the authority to celebrate the sacraments, since they received no regular or legitimate power. Hence the word “regular,” omitted by Quesnell in what follows, is necessary, as Coustant observed. It appears in all the printed editions and manuscripts, except that in the manuscripts of this collection it is corruptly written “to release” or “to be released.” The latter reading, originally written in the first hand of the Vindobonensis, was corrected by the second hand and replaced with “regular.”]

## CHAPTER IV

I shall now come to what is, so to speak, Photinus’s principal case; and I shall review the opinions of my predecessors—a matter that troubles me and is exceedingly difficult.

[Note: The Vatican Regina, Barberini, and another Vatican manuscript, together with the other manuscript and printed collections, read “of my predecessors.” We have written “something, at any rate,” with our manuscripts. Quesnell has “something else, at any rate.”]

Something rather serious had, in some fashion, been decided concerning him, as you yourselves also remember. But since you show that this was, as you assert, foisted upon this see by false rumor and elicited through intrigues; since the matter has returned to a state conducive to salvation, and since, with you striving so greatly, we insert this pardon after the condemnation in apostolic fashion—

[Note: Quesnell reads: “But since you assert that this was falsely taken away through rumor,” and so forth. The better reading is found in the excellent Vindobonensis manuscript, with which the other manuscripts and the Vulgate agree.]

—and since we judge that not to give assent to so many assertions of yours, to men so good and so dear to us, would be harsher than all harsh circumstances, therefore, dearest brothers, for the sake of your approval, judgment, and petition, regard it as permitted for Bishop Photinus to establish matters in the way you request.

[Note: Quesnell, with two manuscripts, Corbeiensis and Colbertinus, reads “by word of mouth.”]

Receive, then, our judgment, turned toward the better through your labor or testimony, as the fulfillment of your desire; and do not expect that Eustachius, whom I have very frequently approved, should be deprived of the dignity of the diaconate.

[Note: All printed and manuscript copies read as above, except the Oxford manuscript, from which Quesnell alone published “Eustathius received by me,” and so forth. Some manuscripts have *Eustasius*, others, together with the Vulgate, *Eustatius* or *Eustathius*. Quesnell, with certain inferior manuscripts, reads “although it must be done.”]

For I gladly hear of your concern for his salvation; but I do not gladly admit an attack against his person, even if it should have to be made. With the one to whom you extend your hand, I extend mine together with you; to the one to whom I extend mine, extend yours together with me.

For this is the apostolic kindness declared to the Corinthians: that good men should always follow, without distinction, a judgment which has been led and led back by one spirit.

For I confess that this matter first disposes me favorably toward the deacon Eustachius: he has said nothing against the faith, has not admitted anyone who was saying such things, and I have found no crime committed by him leading to death—whether ever alleged or fabricated concerning him.

[Note: We restored the words “concerning him,” in place of which Quesnell had inserted *esse* (“to be”), on the authority of the Vindobonensis and two other manuscripts, Vatican and Barberini, together with the editions of Dionysius and the Councils. The Vatican Regina manuscript deletes both expressions.]

And since he is safe in these respects, if in some way he does not maintain agreeable relations, he should be regarded as one who is, for the time being, loved less—not as an enemy considered worthy of being handed over to the devil forever.

[Note: Quesnell, with the Oxford manuscript alone, deleted *aestimatus* (“considered”); this word is found in the Thuanus manuscript, all our manuscripts, and the Vulgate. Coustant preferred *aestimatur* (“is considered”). Other copies have *existimatus* (“judged” or “considered”).]

I know that amid those conflicts and storms he felt differently from the designs of many—I do not say what sort of designs—and that, although the matters and the very calamities themselves have been corrected here,

[Note: Quesnell alone omits *illas* (“those”); then the Oxford manuscript passes over a different reading. We supplied *ipsae* (“the very”) from the Vindobonensis and other Vulgate and manuscript copies.]

the commendation of the subdeacons Dizonianus and Cyriacus has still not been able to revive among you.

[Note: Four of our manuscripts—the Vindobonensis, Vatican Regina, another Vatican, and Barberini—read “up to this point.” Coustant follows his copies in the same reading. Quesnell, with other printed copies, omits *usque* (“up to”). Some manuscripts have *Diozeniani* or *Bezoniani*; most, including Quiriacius, have the reading adopted here.]

Please extinguish in him and in all those whom you see the passionate and unjust rivalries previously mentioned, so that he may appear before us whole and restored among you with his associates, beholding a deep peace and a charity that is not feigned, and may rejoice in the Lord, equally bound together with all of you and individually by the bonds of charity, which can in no way be loosed from Christ, forever joined with you.

[Note: Quesnell, with the same editions and with Dionysius, reads: “may he deserve peace, perceiving a charity that is not feigned.” All the others add: “Therefore, may charity meet all of you and each one individually, and rejoice in the bonds which . . . are joined together.” We followed the Vindobonensis, Vatican Barberini, and Vatican Regina manuscripts, as well as Coustant. The Vatican and Barberini manuscripts alone read “and in the bonds which”; the better reading would be “and in the bonds of charity, which.” The Thuanus manuscript has: “the Church joined together forever.”]

Given on the Ides of December, in the consulship of Constantius, illustrious man.

[Note: The manuscripts of this collection, as well as the Vatican and Barberini manuscripts, incorrectly read *Constantino* (“Constantine”) for *Constantio* (“Constantius”). In the Vindobonensis, the ancient hand prefixes *Fl.* to *Constantino*, as is also found in another manuscript cited by Hardouin and in the Vatican Regina. Coustant gives the better reading, *Flavio Constantio*, who in fact held the consulship in the year 414, when this letter was written.]

## CHAPTER XXIII

[Note: Besides the manuscripts of this collection, this letter is also found in the manuscripts of the Dionysian, Hispanic, and Isidorian collections, as well as in Vatican Regina 1997, Colbertinus, Lucensis, Barberini 2888, Corbeiensis, and Fossatensis.]

Letter of Pope Innocent to Decentius, Bishop of Gubbio, arranged under seven headings.

[Note: The Vulgate, together with Dionysius, reads “to Decentius of Gubbio.”]

### INNOCENTIUS TO DECENTIUS, BISHOP OF GUBBIO

[Note: Quesnell adds “greetings,” together with the Vulgate derived from Dionysius. We removed it on the authority of the Vindobonensis and other manuscripts of excellent quality.]

If the priests of the Lord wished to preserve intact the ecclesiastical institutions as they were handed down by the blessed apostles, there would be no difference or variation in those ordinances and consecrations themselves. But while each person considers that what seems right to him, rather than what has been handed down, must be observed, the result is that different practices appear to be held or celebrated in different places and Churches. This produces scandal among the peoples, who, because they do not know that the ancient traditions have been corrupted by human presumption, suppose either that the Churches do not agree with one another or that contradiction has been introduced by the apostles or apostolic men.

[Note: The Vindobonensis, together with five other manuscripts cited by Coustant, reads “introduced by those very men.” The Barberini manuscript has only “or that contradiction was introduced by the apostles themselves.”]

For who does not know, or who fails to observe, that what was handed down to the Roman Church by Peter, prince of the apostles, and is preserved to this day, ought to be observed by all, and that nothing lacking authority should be superimposed or introduced, nor should an example apparently taken from elsewhere be accepted?

Especially since it is manifest that throughout Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, and Sicily, and the intervening islands, no one established Churches except those whom the venerable Apostle Peter or his successors appointed as priests.

[Note: Quesnell alone reads “established a Church.” The Barberini manuscript, together with other Vulgate copies, reads “established.”]

Or let them read whether another of the apostles is found or reported to have taught in these provinces. If they do not read this, because they find it nowhere, they ought to follow what the Roman Church preserves; for there can be no doubt that they received their beginning from it, lest, while they devote themselves to foreign assertions, they appear to neglect the source of their institutions.

It is beyond doubt that you have often come to the City and assembled with us in the church,

[Note: The Vulgate has “in the Church.”]

and that you have learned what custom we maintain both in consecrating the mysteries and in carrying out the other sacred rites. This would have been sufficiently certain for the instruction or restoration of your Church, if your predecessors had held something less or something different, unless you had thought that we should be consulted about certain matters.

[Note: The Vindobonensis and Barberini manuscripts, together with most others and Dionysius, add *arbitrarer* (“I should have thought”), which is superfluous unless one reads *haberem* (“I should have had”) later with the Barberini manuscript. The Vindobonensis has *pariter haberem* (“I should likewise have had”). The following *respondemus* (“we answer”) and *credamus* (“we believe”), however, favor *haberemus* (“we should have had”), and they show that *arbitrarer* should be deleted.]

We answer these questions, therefore, not because we believe that you are ignorant of anything, but so that you may instruct your own people with greater authority; and, if some are straying from the institutions of the Roman Church, so that you may admonish them or not delay in reporting them, in order that we may know who are introducing innovations or who think that the custom of a Church other than the Roman Church ought to be observed.

[Note: The Barberini manuscript, together with the Vulgate, reads better: “who they are.”]

### CHAPTER I

You report, then, that some priests proclaim peace to the people before the sacred mysteries have been completed, or that the priests exchange it among themselves,

[Note: Our Vindobonensis and Barberini manuscripts, together with Dionysius and the Vulgate of the Councils, delete *se* (“among themselves”). The Barberini manuscript, with Merlin and other copies, reads “necessary.”]

whereas peace must necessarily be proclaimed after everything—which I ought not to disclose—so that it may be clear that the people have given their consent to everything that is done in the mysteries and celebrated in the church, and that, when the rites are finished, this is demonstrated by the sign of the peace that concludes them.

### CHAPTER II

As for the names to be recited before the priest offers the prayer and commends in prayer the offerings of those whose names are to be recited, you yourself, in your prudence, recognize how superfluous this is:

[Note: Some copies read “prayers.” Then the same Barberini manuscript, together with Coustant and the other printed collections, reads “with his own prayer.” Another reading is “as your prudence recognizes.”]

how can you announce the name of someone whose offering you have not yet offered to God, although nothing is unknown to him? The offerings must therefore first be commended, and then the names of those to whom they belong must be proclaimed, so that they may be named amid the sacred mysteries,

[Note: Quesnell omits “within.” A little later he reads “so that we may first open a way by prayers for the mysteries that are to follow,” contrary to our manuscripts and the Vulgate. The Barberini manuscript reads “we have placed beforehand,” which is better.]

not among the other things that we place beforehand, so that by our prayers we may open the way for the mysteries that are to follow.

## CHAPTER III

As for signing infants, it is clear that this may be done by no one other than a bishop. For although priests are priests, they do not possess the summit of the episcopate. That it belongs to bishops alone either to sign them or to give them the Spirit, the Paraclete, is shown not only by ecclesiastical custom, but also by that passage in the Acts of the Apostles which says that Peter and John were sent to give the Holy Spirit to those who had already been baptized.

[Note: Quesnell alone has “the Holy Spirit” instead of “the Spirit.” Soon afterward, the manuscripts of the other collections, together with the other Vulgate copies, have “and that reading.” Quesnell reads “of the Acts of the Apostles.”]

For priests, whether they baptize outside the presence of the bishop or with the bishop present, may anoint those who have been baptized with chrism—but with chrism consecrated by the bishop. They may not, however, mark the forehead with that same oil, which belongs to bishops alone when they give the Spirit, the Paraclete.

[Note: Quesnell alone omits the preposition “from” and then has “to give” instead of “to say.”]

I cannot state the words, lest I seem rather to disclose than to answer a consultation.

### CHAPTER IV

That one must fast on Saturday is demonstrated by the clearest reasoning. For if we celebrate the Lord’s Day because of the venerable Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ—not only at Easter, but also throughout each cycle of the weeks, repeatedly observing the image of that day—and if we fast on Friday because of the Lord’s Passion, we must not pass over Saturday, which appears to lie between the sorrow and the joy of that period.

[Note: Quesnell, with Dionysius, inserted the particle “if”; we deleted it on the authority of our manuscripts and the other editions. He also added the noun “day” for clarity; the manuscripts do not have it. Other Vulgate copies read “because . . . is enclosed.”]

For it is certainly established that during those two days the apostles were both in grief and hidden because of fear of the Jews. It is also beyond doubt that they fasted during those two days to such an extent that the tradition of the Church holds that the sacraments are not celebrated at all during that period.

This practice must certainly be observed every week,

[Note: With the manuscripts and the other editions, we have added the verb “is,” which Quesnell omitted.]

because the commemoration of that day must always be celebrated. But if they think that one must fast only once, on a single Saturday, then Sunday and Friday, too, will certainly have to be celebrated only once, at Easter.

[Note: The Vindobonensis, together with other manuscripts cited by Coustant, reads “Sunday . . . must be celebrated.”]

But if the image of Sunday and Friday must be renewed every week, it is foolish to observe the custom of two days while passing over Saturday, since it has the same reason as Friday—namely, the day on which the Lord suffered and when he was also among the dead, so that, rising on the third day, he might restore joy after the preceding sorrow of two days.

Therefore we do not deny that one must fast on Friday; rather, we say that this must also be done on Saturday,

[Note: The Barberini manuscript reads “which.” Immediately afterward, we restored “for them also” from the manuscripts and the Vulgate; then “most festive.” Quesnell has “and for them . . . festive.”]

because both days imposed sorrow upon the apostles and upon those who followed Christ. On Sunday they were filled with joy, and they wished not only that day itself to be most festive, but also judged that it should be observed throughout all the weeks.

### CHAPTER V

As for the fermented bread that we send on Sunday to the titular churches, you wished to consult us about this unnecessarily, since all our churches are situated within the city. Their priests, because on that day they cannot meet with us on account of the people entrusted to them, receive from the acolytes the fermented bread prepared by us, so that they may not consider themselves separated from our communion, especially on that day.

I do not think that this ought to be done in the parishes, because the sacraments need not be carried a long distance, nor do we send them to priests established in the various cemeteries,

[Note: Quesnell, together with the Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts, reads “so that the priests too may.” The Thuanus manuscript has “for their prayers”; the Vindobonensis, together with the Pithoeanus, has “and for their prayers,” though a second hand changed it to the reading in the text, which is found in the better manuscripts. We would prefer “and so that the priests too may,” or else “who have.” Innocent is asserting that the sacraments should not be sent through rural parishes because they do not need to be carried far, just as he does not send them to cemetery priests; and for this reason such priests lack the right and permission to prepare the sacraments.]

and their priests have the right and permission to prepare them.

### CHAPTER VI

As for those who have been baptized but are afterward seized by a demon when some fault or sin has intervened, your belovedness asked whether they can or ought to be designated by a priest or deacon;

[Note: Quesnell reads “signed, which is not permitted unless the bishop has ordered it.” The Roman edition, together with the Vulgate of the Councils, reads “signed, which may not be ordered except by bishops.” But our Vindobonensis and Barberini manuscripts, as well as Corbeiensis, Colbertinus, and the other manuscripts of this collection cited by Coustant, have “designated.” Dionysius seems to have read the same, since his Regius copy, according to Coustant, has “assigned.” Then we adopted from the Vindobonensis “which may not be done unless the bishop orders it,” a reading confirmed by the same ancient Dionysian Regius copy. The Barberini manuscript has only the corrupt reading “unless he has ordered the bishop,” instead of “unless the bishop has authorized it,” contrary to Innocent’s intention, which is expressed in the following words: “unless the bishop has granted authority”; and “it belongs to the bishop to command.” From the Vulgate reading “signed,” some have explained this passage as referring to the sacrament of confirmation. But the discussion here concerns baptized faithful who, under the ancient discipline, had already been confirmed. The power to administer confirmation, which the same pontiff in this very letter asserts belongs to bishops alone, cannot be said to have been granted to priests or deacons with the bishop’s permission. Hence the reading “designated,” distinct from “signed,” by which the holy pontiff earlier indicated the sacrament of confirmation, seemed preferable. The reference is to the laying on of hands upon the possessed, which, in the ancient rites of the Church described by Father Martène, book III, chapter 9, could be performed at the bishop’s command not only by priests and deacons but also, as is stated shortly afterward, by the other clergy.]

which cannot be done unless the bishop orders it. For hands must not be laid upon them at all unless the bishop has authorized this to be done. But for it to be done, it belongs to the bishop to command that hands be laid upon them either by a priest or by the other clergy.

For how could this be done without great difficulty—namely, that a possessed person living far away should be brought to the bishop—when, if such an event should happen to him on a journey, he could neither easily be carried to the bishop nor brought back home?

[Note: Quesnell alone has “carried.” The Vindobonensis manuscript has “should intervene.”]

### CHAPTER VII

As for penitents who are doing penance either for more serious offenses or for lesser ones, the custom of the Roman Church shows that, if no illness intervenes, remission should be granted to them on the Thursday before Easter.

As for judging the weight of sins, it belongs to the priest to decide, so that he may attend to the penitent’s confession and to the weeping and tears of the one who is correcting himself; and then he should order that remission be granted when he has seen suitable satisfaction.

[Note: Coustant, with two manuscripts, reads “his satisfaction.” Another copy reads “or if someone has arrived, it is for him.” In the Oxford manuscript, the words “of Easter” are absent later.]

Certainly, if someone falls ill and reaches the point of despair, remission should be granted to him before Easter, so that he may not depart from this world without communion.

### CHAPTER VIII

Since your belovedness wished to consult us about this matter, as about the others, my son the deacon Coelestinus also added in his letter that your belovedness had brought forward what is written in the letter of the blessed Apostle James:

[Note: The Vindobonensis, together with other more reliable manuscripts of this collection examined by Coustant, reads as follows; the other ancient manuscript collections that preserve the old version agree. See Coustant for further details. At the end of this text, the Vindobonensis has “may remit.” The Barberini manuscript and others omit “of the Church.” Quesnell adopted a reading very close to that of the Vulgate: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him summon the priests of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick man, and the Lord will raise him up, and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him.”]

“Is anyone among you sick? Let him call the priests of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer in faith will save the suffering person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he has committed sins, he will forgive him.”

There is no doubt that this must be understood or interpreted as referring to faithful people who are sick, who may be anointed with the holy oil of chrism,

[Note: Coustant reads “which was prepared by the bishop . . . to be anointed.”]

and all Christians may use this oil, prepared by the bishop, for anointing themselves or their own people in a time of need.

But we see that the additional qualification concerning the bishop is superfluous, as though there could be doubt that priests may do this. For this reason it was said to priests, because bishops, occupied with other duties, cannot visit all the sick.

[Note: The Vindobonensis, Barberini, and several other manuscripts cited by Coustant, together with Dionysius and Coustant, read “concerning priests.” Thuanus, with the Vulgate of the Councils, reads “the priests.” Quesnell has “priests.”]

But if a bishop is able, or considers it worthy, to visit someone himself, he may without hesitation bless and touch him with chrism,

[Note: Quesnell alone reads “anoint.” Our manuscripts, together with Thuanus, read “touch with chrism,” as in Saint Gregory, book IV, letter 26, to Januarius.]

since it is his office to prepare the chrism. This, however, cannot be poured upon penitents, because it is a kind of sacrament. For when the other sacraments are denied to them, how could one kind be thought capable of being granted?

Therefore, dearest brother, we have taken care to answer, as best we could, all the matters that your belovedness wished us to explain, so that your Church may be able to preserve and observe the Roman custom from which it derives its origin. As for the remaining matters, which it was not lawful to commit to writing, when you are present we shall be able to state them in response to your questions.

It will also belong to the power of the Lord to arrange that you may properly instruct both your Church and our clerics who, under your episcopate, serve the divine offices, and that you may provide others with a model which they ought to imitate.

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulships of Theodosius Augustus for the seventh time and Palladius, illustrious man.

[Note: The Thuanus manuscript has “the twelfth day before the Kalends”; the Barberini, “the thirteenth day before the Kalends.”]

## CHAPTER XXIV

[Note: This letter is found in the manuscripts of our collection, as well as in those of the Dionysian, Hispanic, and Isidorian collections, Vatican Regina 1997, Colbertinus, Lucensis, Barberini 2888, Corbeiensis, and Fossatensis.]

Letter of Innocent to Victricius, Bishop of Rouen, arranged under fifteen headings.

### INNOCENTIUS TO VICTRICIUS, BISHOP OF ROUEN

[Note: The Barberini manuscript, together with several other manuscripts, has *Victoricius*. The Vatican Regina and Lucensis have *Victorius*. Certain other manuscripts have *Victorichus*. Quesnell adds “greetings”; our manuscripts omit it.]

Although, dearest brother, in view of the merit and honor of the priesthood in which you are highly distinguished, everything concerning the manner of living and teaching according to ecclesiastical rules is known to you,

[Note: The manuscripts of this collection, together with Fossatensis and Dionysius, read as above. The Barberini exemplar, together with more than twenty others cited by Coustant, has “all the matters of ecclesiastical rule are known.” In the Vindobonensis, a second hand deleted only the preposition “according to.” The Vatican Regina has “the rule is known to you ecclesiastically, and may it not be.” Shortly afterward, the manuscripts of Barberini and Vatican Regina have “may seem unknown to you.”]

and there is nothing in the sacred readings that seems to have been insufficiently gathered by you, nevertheless, because you earnestly requested the norm and authority of the Roman Church,

[Note: The very ancient Barberini manuscript, and following it Sirmond and Labbe, reads “for authority.” This reading signifies that the norm of the Roman Church was sought and employed as an authority.]

readily accommodating myself to your wishes, I have sent with my letter an organized account of the disciplines of a praiseworthy life and conduct, through which the peoples of the Churches in your region may learn by what practices and rules the life of Christians ought to be ordered in each person’s calling,

[Note: The first hand of the Vindobonensis, together with Corbeiensis and Fossatensis, reads “by what practices and rules,” while the second hand added “in matters.” One Colbertinus manuscript reads “by which rules.”]

and what discipline is maintained in the churches of the city of Rome.

[Note: The Barberini manuscript reads “what order is maintained.” In the first hand of the Vatican Regina, the same reading appears, but “is maintained” was deleted by a second hand. Quesnell reads “Therefore it will belong to your belovedness”; we deleted “therefore” on the authority of our manuscripts and the other editions.]

It will be your responsibility diligently to make this book of rules known, as a kind of teacher and admonition, to the neighboring peoples and to our fellow bishops who preside over their own Churches in those regions, so that they may both learn our practices and, through diligent instruction, shape the conduct of those who flock to the faith. For either they will recognize their own purpose from this appropriate reading of ours, or, if anything is still lacking, they will easily be able to supply it by good imitation.

Let us begin, then, with the help of the holy Apostle Peter, through whom the beginning both of the apostolate and of the episcopate in Christ took its origin,

[Note: The ancient editions of the Councils, together with the Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts, add “with God,” and so forth.]

so that, since many cases have often arisen which in some instances were not merely cases but crimes, every priest may henceforth be concerned to maintain such care in his own Church as the Apostle Paul teaches: that such a Church should be presented to God without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:27),

so that our conscience may not be defiled and stained by the breath of any diseased sheep.

Therefore, on account of those who, whether through ignorance or negligence, do not maintain ecclesiastical discipline and presume to do many things that ought not to be presumed, you rightly requested that in those regions the form maintained by the Roman Church should be observed—not that any new commands should be imposed, but that we wish what has been neglected through the negligence of some to be observed by all. These things, however, have been established by apostolic and patristic tradition.

For it is written to the Thessalonians, with Paul giving the admonition:

[Note: Quesnell adds “in the second letter”; our manuscripts delete this, as do Dionysius, Labbe, and Coustant. The Colbertinus, Fossatensis, and Corbeiensis manuscripts have “to Timothy,” though in Corbeiensis a second correction changed it to “to the Thessalonians.” In the ancient editions of the Councils, together with the manuscripts of the Hadrianic and Hispanic collections, the reading is “to the Second Thessalonians and to Timothy.” The Barberini has “with the Apostle giving the admonition”; the Vatican Regina, “with the Apostle Paul giving the admonition.” The Vindobonensis deletes the words “which I have handed on to you.”]

“Stand firm and hold to the traditions that I handed on to you, whether by word or by letter” (2 Thessalonians 2:15).

That ought certainly to stir your mind more forcefully,

[Note: The word “more forcefully,” omitted by Quesnell, has been restored from our manuscripts and the Vulgate. The Barberini omits “free from blame”; together with the other Vulgate copies, it deletes “and secure” before “secure.” Several manuscripts omit the words “the interest of punishments”; the copies of this and other ancient collections retain them. Later, the Roman edition reads “to Christ” instead of “to the one believed.”]

so that you may be found free from every stain of this world and secure before the sight of God. For to the one to whom much is entrusted, more is exacted in the interest of punishment.

Therefore, since we are compelled to render an account not only for ourselves but also for the people of Christ, we must educate the people through divine discipline.

[Note: The Thuanus and Vindobonensis manuscripts of this collection, together with the Regius exemplar of Dionysius and the Roman edition, read as above. The Vatican Regina and Barberini manuscripts have “the discipline of the Lord.” Corbeiensis and Fossatensis, followed by Coustant, have “divine discipline”; two Colbertinus manuscripts have “the discipline of the Lord.” The manuscripts of the Hadrianic collection have “sanctifying discipline” or, with Justellus, “sanctified discipline.” The Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts read “to sanctify with discipline.” Hence the reading of the Oxford manuscript, adopted by Quesnell, although supported by Merlin’s Isidorian manuscript, cannot be regarded as genuine. It reads: “therefore to sanctify and instruct the people with the discipline of God.”]

For some have arisen who, failing to hold to the statutes of their predecessors, violate the chastity of the Church through their own presumption, following the favor of the people and not fearing the judgment of God.

Therefore, lest by our silence we appear to give our consent to them, since the Lord says, “You saw a thief, and you ran with him” (Psalm 49:18), these are the matters which, henceforth, in view of divine judgment, it is expedient for every Catholic bishop to guard.

[Note: Quesnell reads “we may appear”; then, “the Lord saying through the Prophet: ‘You saw.’” We preferred the reading of the more reliable manuscripts of our collection. The Vatican Regina, Barberini, Hispanic, and Isidorian manuscripts retain the words “through the Prophet.”]

### CHAPTER I

First, no one should dare to ordain without the knowledge of the metropolitan bishop.

[Note: Quesnell, together with the Oxford, Hispanic, and Isidorian manuscripts, adds “a bishop” after “to ordain,” and later, after “should presume,” again adds “a bishop.” Our manuscripts and those of the other collections delete these words; from them we shortly afterward inserted “for this reason.” A little later, several manuscripts and printed books not improperly have “not even one.”]

For a judgment is sound when it is confirmed by the opinions of many, lest one bishop presume to ordain and the benefit conferred appear to have been obtained furtively. This was also established and defined in the Synod of Nicaea.

### CHAPTER II

Likewise, if anyone, after the remission of sins, has held the belt of secular military service, he must under no circumstances be admitted to the clergy.

### CHAPTER III

If any cases or disputes should arise among clergy, whether of the higher order or of the lower, they are to be settled, according to the Synod of Nicaea, by the bishops of that province assembled together,

[Note: Quesnell placed this marginal note: “The Oxford, Isidorian, and Roman editions add ‘and laymen’ in the margin, but incorrectly; for there is nothing about laymen in the Nicene text.” Shortly afterward the same Oxford manuscript adds “it was decided” after “should arise.” We added “should arise” as found in our manuscripts and the Vulgate, and from the same witnesses deleted “all,” which Quesnell had inserted after “assembled.” In the Lombard Colbertinus manuscript, which resembles the Lucensis, and also in the Vatican Regina, the words “according to the Synod of Nicaea” are absent.]

so that the dispute may be brought to an end; and no one may, without prejudice to the Roman Church,

[Note: Quesnell’s marginal note says: “The Oxford, Isidorian, and Vulgate editions add: ‘to whom reverence ought to be preserved in all cases.’” But this parenthesis is found neither in the Thuanus manuscript, nor in Dionysius, nor in Pope Nicholas I’s letter 40 to the bishops of Gaul, nor in the most ancient Corbeiensis manuscript, where it was added above the line by a later hand. It cannot be denied that this passage is absent from the older manuscripts of this collection—the Vindobonensis, Thuanus, and Pithoeanus—and likewise from the copies of the Dionysian collection that passed into the Hadrianic collection. Since Nicholas I used these Hadrianic copies, it is not surprising that he too omitted these words. Yet the same words are found in six or seven other distinct collections: namely, in three very ancient ones, one of which is preserved in Vatican Regina, another in the Lombard Colbertinus and Lucensis manuscripts, and a third in Barberini 2888 and Vatican 1342; furthermore, in another ancient Colbertinus manuscript, in the Hispanic collection—which, although it copied this letter from the Dionysian collection, inserted this passage either from some Dionysian manuscript or from another more ancient collection—and in the Isidorian collection, which derived this letter from the Hispanic collection. Finally, in the celebrated and very ancient Corbeiensis exemplar, the passage was added not by a recent hand but, as Coustant testifies, by the ancient hand that habitually supplies precisely the words omitted elsewhere. For this reason Coustant thought that these words should be inserted into the text as genuine words of Innocent.
