We have not admitted them into our text, not because we do not believe them to be Innocent’s words, but because we are publishing that collection whose more reliable exemplars lack this parenthesis. It is especially remarkable that the same passage was also deleted from Quesnell’s edition, although in Dissertation 12, chapter 4, section 5, he argues that the Romans inserted these words in their manuscript. If he thought he was publishing the Roman manuscript, the words judged to be peculiar to it could not have been excluded. In this parenthesis some manuscripts have *debetur* (“is owed”) instead of *debet* (“ought”).]

leaving those priests who, in the same province, govern the Churches of God by divine command, flee to other provinces.

[Note: The Oxford manuscript, and Quesnell following it, add within parentheses: “or seek or undergo the prior judgment of the bishops of the other provinces.” The Isidorian manuscript of Merlin has the same, except that it reads “experience” instead of “undergo.” These words are absent from the Thuanus, Vindobonensis, Barberini, Vatican Regina, Dionysian, and other more reliable copies. Shortly afterward Quesnell, following the Oxford manuscript, has “as though concerning injuries.”]

But if anyone should presume to do so, let him be removed from clerical office and judged by everyone guilty of causing injury.

## CHAPTER IV

But if more important cases should have been brought forward, they are to be referred, after episcopal judgment, to the apostolic see, as the synod decreed.

> **Note [Col. 0522C]:** The Oxford manuscript adds, “and blessed custom requires.” The older manuscripts of this collection—Thuan., Vind., and Pith.—do not contain these words. It should be noted that different collections offer three different readings. The manuscripts of Dionysius and of Hadrian, which derive from Dionysius, together with the purer copies of our collection and the others identified by Father Coustant, read, “as the synod decreed.” Four other ancient collections—three of them Italian, namely Vat. Reginae 1997, Colb. Lucensis, Barb. 2888, and Vat. 1342, together with Colb. 3368—give only these words: “as ancient custom requires,” or “as old custom requires.” The Spanish and Isidorian collection manuscripts give both readings, together with the Oxford manuscript of our collection, except that they have “blessed” instead of “old.” For this reason Father Coustant accepted both readings, each supported by excellent copies.

## CHAPTER V

That a cleric should not marry a woman; for it is written: “Let a priest take a virgin as wife, not a widow, not one cast out.” Certainly, whoever strives toward the priesthood through his own labor and uprightness of life must take care not to be prevented from attaining it by this disqualification.

> **Note [Col. 0522C]:** Quesnellus, together with the Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts, adds “widow.” Dionysius has “widow,” but deletes “woman.” Our manuscripts, together with other ancient books, give only “woman,” a word more frequently used for a non-virgin. Here Innocent borrowed several things from Siricius’s letter to the Africans, where likewise, no. 4, we read: “That a cleric should not take a woman as wife.” Immediately afterward, instead of “not cast out,” two manuscripts, Corb. and Colb. in Coustant, have “nor one abandoned.”

## CHAPTER VI

That one who has married a woman, even if he is a layman, whether before baptism or after baptism, is not to be admitted to the clergy, since he appears to have been excluded by the same fault. For in baptism sins are forgiven, but the association with a wife already taken is not annulled.

> **Note [Col. 0522D]:** Thus read our manuscripts and the better copies. Quesnellus, with Dionysius, the Spanish, and the Isidorian manuscripts, has “widow,” and afterward “are remitted.”

## CHAPTER VII

That one who has married a second wife should not become a cleric; for it is written: “The husband of one wife” (1 Tim. 3:2); and again: “Let my priests marry only once”; and elsewhere: “My priests shall not marry again.”

> **Note [Col. 0522D]:** The manuscripts Vat. Reginae, Colb. Lucensis, and another Colb. 3368, together with Barb. 2888 and a similar Vatican manuscript, omit the two testimonies that follow. The first hand of Vind. omitted only the third—“and elsewhere: My priests …”—but it was added by a second correction.

And lest anyone suppose that, if someone had taken a wife before baptism and, after she had departed from this world, married another, this had been remitted in baptism, he is quite mistaken about the rule; for in baptism sins are remitted, not the number of wives taken abolished, since a wife is in any event married according to the commandment of the law (Lev. 21). Indeed, in paradise (Gen. 2:25), when the parents of the human race were joined together, they were blessed by the Lord himself; and Solomon says: “A wife is prepared for a man by God” (Prov. 14).

> **Note [Col. 0522D]:** Coustant, with the Corb. and Colb. manuscripts, has: “who thinks that this is remitted in baptism: sins are remitted.” Barb. has: “nor [is] the number of wives taken …”

This same pattern is shown by the practice of the Church itself to be observed by all priests. For it is sufficiently absurd to believe that a wife taken before baptism is not to be counted after baptism, when the blessing imposed upon those marrying by the priest is taught to have given not an occasion for wrongdoing but to have maintained the form of the law instituted by God from ancient times.

But if the wife married before baptism is not thought to be counted, then neither would the children begotten before baptism be regarded as children.

> **Note [Col. 0523C]:** Thus read our manuscripts Vind., Vat. Reginae, and Barb., together with Corb., Fossat., and two Colb. manuscripts. Quesnellus, with Oxford alone, has “are to be regarded”; Coustant, with Dionysius Regius, “will be regarded.” Other editions, together with other manuscripts, have “are regarded.”

## CHAPTER VIII

That no one should presume to ordain a cleric from another Church unless his bishop, entreated with prayers, should be willing to grant permission.

> **Note [Col. 0523C]:** The manuscripts Barb. and Vat. Reginae add: “This too the Nicene synod appears to contain: A cleric rejected by his own Church is not to be received by another Church.”

This too the Nicene synod decreed: that one Church should not receive a cleric rejected by another.

## CHAPTER IX

That those coming from the Novatians or Montanists are to be received by the laying on of hands alone, because, although baptized by heretics, they were nevertheless baptized in the name of Christ—except those who, after passing from us to them, were perhaps rebaptized. If these, repenting and reflecting upon their ruin, should prefer to return, they are to be admitted after a long satisfaction of penance.

> **Note [Col. 0523C]:** Quesnellus omits “if,” and afterward, with the Oxford, Colb., and Corb. manuscripts, reads “were baptized and afterward wished to return.” We have followed the best copies, Vind., Vat. Reginae, and Barb., with which several others agree. The context requires that the subject be those who were rebaptized, as does Siricius’s letter to the Africans, which Innocent had before his eyes.

## CHAPTER X

Furthermore, the Church must hold firmly to what is worthy, chaste, and honorable: that priests and Levites should not have intercourse with their wives, because they are occupied with the necessities of their daily ministry.

> **Note [Col. 0523C]:** Another copy has “in every way.” Immediately afterward, instead of “should not have intercourse,” Barb., Vat. Reginae, and Colb. Lucensis have “should not mingle”; and afterward, together with several others, “since I too,” as is likewise read above in the letter to Exsuperius, chapter 1.

For it is written: “Be holy, because I am holy, the Lord your God” (Lev. 11:44; 20:7).

For if in ancient times the priests did not leave the temple of God during the year of their service, as we read concerning Zechariah, and did not touch their own home at all—

> **Note [Col. 0523D]:** As Quesnellus noted, from this point through chapter 11 almost the same material occurs in the letter to Exsuperius of Toulouse, to which the Thuan. manuscript refers while omitting this passage. Both this letter and the one to Exsuperius were delivered to two Gallic bishops; nevertheless, the same Innocent transferred several periods, in nearly identical words, from one letter to the other. It is therefore not surprising that Saint Leo copied certain passages from Letter 2 to Septimus into Letter 18 to Januarius, and transferred others from Letter 124 to the Palestinians into Letter 165 to Emperor Leo.

—in their case, certainly, marital intercourse had been relaxed because of the succession of offspring, since no one from another tribe and outside the seed of Aaron had been appointed to approach the priesthood, how much more ought these priests or Levites to preserve chastity from the day of their ordination, since their priesthood or ministry has no succession, and not a day passes on which they are free either from the divine sacrifices or from the office of baptism?

> **Note [Col. 0523D]:** Crabbus here adds, in smaller type, “than,” contrary to Merlinus and the manuscripts. It is, however, found in Vat. Reginae and in the Dionysius Justellus manuscript. The others, including Quesnellus, accepted the word. Immediately afterward Coustant, with two Corb. manuscripts and one Colb., has “no one had been commanded.” But, apart from the authority of the other manuscripts, the letter to Exsuperius also confirms the reading of the text.

For if Paul writes to the Corinthians, saying, “Abstain for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Cor. 7:5)—and he certainly gives this command to laymen—how much more must priests, whose constant duty is both to pray and to offer sacrifice, always abstain from such intercourse.

> **Note [Col. 0524C]:** Quesnellus inserts “the priest”; the manuscripts and the letter to Exsuperius omit it. Dionysius Justellus has: “But if they have been contaminated … they will presume … they believe themselves …”; then “he thinks this is permitted” follows less coherently. In the letter to Exsuperius, however, our reading is retained.

If he has been contaminated by carnal desire, with what modesty will he presume to offer sacrifice, or with what conscience or merit will he believe that he can be heard, when it is said: “Everything is clean to the clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean”?

> **Note [Col. 0524C]:** Barb., Vat. Reginae, and Colb. Lucensis have: “he believes that he can be heard.” “Can” is absent from the other manuscripts, and most have “he believes,” as in the letter to Exsuperius, where “he will believe” occurs. Immediately afterward Barb. and Vat. Reginae have: “nothing is clean.”

But perhaps he believes this to be permitted because it is written: “The husband of one wife” (Titus 1:15).

> **Note [Col. 0524C–D]:** Quesnellus has in the text “not remaining in,” and in the margin Dionysius has “not remaining,” while others have “not remaining to.” The Fossat. and Vind. manuscripts have “not remaining,” where the letter *m* must be supplied; and, with Barb., Vat. Reginae, and the better manuscripts cited by Coustant, we are entirely convinced that “not remaining” should be read both here and in the letter to Exsuperius. See note 10 (note i, col. 501) on chapter 21. Immediately afterward Barb. has: “because of future conscience.”

He said this not of one remaining in the desire to beget children, but with a view to future continence. For he did not reject those who are physically intact, since he says: “But I wish that all were as I am” (1 Cor. 7:7).

> **Note [Col. 0524D]:** Quesnellus alone inserts “people.” We might rather add “thus,” with the manuscripts Barb. and Vat. Reginae and other editions. But we retain the reading of Vind., which is also found in the letter to Exsuperius.

And he states the matter more openly, saying: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God; but you are no longer in the flesh, but in the spirit” (Rom. 8).

## CHAPTER XI

Concerning monks who, after spending a long time in monasteries, afterward strive to enter the clerical order: they must not depart from their former purpose.

> **Note [Col. 0524D–0525C]:** Thus read the manuscripts of this collection. Coustant has: “if afterward they should attain … they ought not.” Other editions, together with the manuscripts Vat. Reg. and Barb., retain this reading, omitting “if.” In Vind., the second hand wrote *pervenirent* instead of *pervenire*. Immediately afterward the manuscripts Vat. Reg. and Barb. have “to depart” instead of “to deviate.”

For either, as he was in the monastery, he must not lose what he preserved for a long time after being placed in a better state; or, if, having been corrupted, he was afterward baptized and, remaining in the monastery, should wish to enter the clerical order, he will certainly not be able to have a wife, since, having already been corrupted, he cannot be blessed together with a bride.

> **Note [Col. 0525C]:** The manuscripts Vat. Reg. and Barb. have: “having been baptized, remaining in the monastery, and approaching the clerical order.” Two Colb. manuscripts cited by Coustant have: “having been baptized, leaving the monastery, and approaching the clerical order.” Quesnellus, with several editions, has: “already corrupted.” We have followed our manuscripts.

## CHAPTER XII

This rule is observed especially among clerics, since the ancient rule is as follows: whoever, having been corrupted, was baptized and wished to become a cleric was to promise that he would under no circumstances take a wife.

## CHAPTER XIII

Furthermore, some of our brothers frequently strive to make clerics of men occupied with civic or any public functions. Later, when the emperor orders something concerning their recall, greater sorrow arises for them than gratitude for the appointment.

> **Note [Col. 0525C]:** We have added “public,” from the excellent Vind. manuscript, with Vat. Reg. and other common copies agreeing. Immediately afterward, Vat. Reg. reads “having held offices” instead of “functions.” From this appears to have arisen the reading which Coustant found in two manuscripts: “functions or offices.” Quesnellus, with the Roman editions, has “of those appointed,” whereas our manuscripts and the other editions prefer “of the person appointed.”

For it is established that even in these offices they provide entertainments, which were unquestionably invented by the devil, and either preside over or attend the arrangements of games and spectacles.

> **Note [Col. 0525D]:** Quesnellus, with Vat. Reginae and Dionysius Justellus, inserts “perhaps.” We deleted it in accordance with our other manuscripts and several more copies.

Let the concern and sorrow of the brethren serve as an example—sorrow which we have often endured in the emperor’s presence, when we repeatedly pleaded on their behalf, as you yourself, situated there with us, recognized.

> **Note [Col. 0525C]:** Most of our manuscripts read thus. Quesnellus, with the Reginae manuscript, has “often.” Immediately afterward, instead of “was impending,” Barb. and Vat. Reg., together with several common copies, have “was pressing.”

For not only inferior clerics from among the civic officials, but also men already established in the priesthood, were threatened with immense trouble so that they might be restored.

## CHAPTER XIV

Likewise, those women who have been spiritually married to Christ and have deserved to be veiled by a priest, if afterward they should marry either publicly or should corrupt themselves secretly, are not to be admitted to perform penance unless the man to whom she had joined herself has departed from this world.

> **Note [Col. 0525D]:** Quesnellus has “married in Christ.” We have preferred our manuscripts, which the other editions follow. Immediately afterward the manuscripts Hadrian., Spanish, and Isidorian, together with the ancient editions of the Councils, have “marry and are veiled by a priest, if afterward …”

> **Note [Col. 0525D]:** Quesnellus has in the text “or be corrupted by a little bell,” and in the margin remarks: “The ancient reading of this word was, I think, *clanculo*, as though ‘secretly in a corner.’” But this conjecture is unnecessary, for the three best manuscripts of this collection—Vind., Thuan., and Pith.—have the reading we have introduced into the text; Dionysius, Corb., and Fossat. likewise agree. The manuscripts Vat. Reginae, Colb. Lucensis, and Barb., together with the Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts, have “or should be secretly corrupted.”

For if this rule is observed concerning human beings—that any woman who, while her husband is alive, marries another is regarded as an adulteress, and is not granted permission to perform penance unless one of the two men has died—how much more must it be maintained concerning a woman who had joined herself to an immortal bridegroom and afterward migrated to a human marriage?

> **Note [Col. 0525D–0526C]:** Dionysius Justellus and Coustant have the better reading: “how much more must it be maintained concerning her.” Quesnellus then has “departed”; Merlinus, with the manuscripts Vat. Reginae, Colb. Lucensis, Barb., Spanish, and Isidorian, has “chosen to pass over.” We have adopted the reading of Vind. and the other manuscripts of the same collection.

## CHAPTER XV

But those who have not yet been covered with the sacred veil, although they had pretended to remain in their virginal purpose, if they should happen to marry, even though they have not been veiled, must perform penance for a considerable time, because her pledge was held by the Lord.

> **Note [Col. 0526C]:** Barb. and Vat. Reginae, together with two manuscripts of Coustant, have “consecrated.” Immediately afterward Dionysius, the Spanish, and the Isidorian manuscripts have “they had always pretended to remain together”; Fossat. and Vind. have “they had pretended always to remain.” The reading of the text, accepted by Quesnellus, is supported not only by the two manuscripts of this collection, Thuan. and Oxon., but also by the ancient Corbie copy. Coustant considered the reading of two Colb. manuscripts better; it is also found in Vat. Reginae and Barb.: “they had promised to remain,” since the pledge, compact, promise, and earlier undertaking of these girls are mentioned below. Immediately afterward, Vind., Barb., and Vat. Reginae have “penance is to be performed.”

For if among human beings a good-faith contract is ordinarily dissolved in no way, how much more must this promise, which she made with God, not be dissolved without punishment?

> **Note [Col. 0526D]:** Quesnellus has “that woman”; afterward, following Sirmond, he added “the virgin” after “made a compact,” a word which we read in the manuscripts Barb. and Vat. Reginae, but which the other manuscripts of this collection and others cited by Coustant delete. Oxon. alone has “she made some compact.” Immediately afterward Dionysius and Isidore have “will not be able.”

For if the Apostle Paul said that those who depart from their purpose of widowhood have condemnation, because they have invalidated their first faith (1 Tim. 5:2), how much more must this apply to virgins who have attempted to break faith with their earlier promise?

> **Note [Col. 0526D]:** Thus read the manuscripts of this collection; among them Vind. has “have striven.” Sirmond has “have been seen to strive.” The Roman edition and the manuscripts Vat. Reginae, Colb. Lucensis, and Barb. have: “who have in no way kept faith with their agreement.” The Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts have: “who have in no way kept faith with their earlier promise.” Dionysius has: “have attempted to break.” Coustant, with Corb. and Fossat., has: “who break faith with their earlier promise.”

Therefore, dearest brother, if this rule is observed by all the priests of God with complete vigilance, ambition will cease, dissension will fall silent, heresies and schisms will not arise, the devil will find no opportunity to rage, unanimity will remain, iniquity will be trampled down after being overcome, truth will blaze with spiritual fervor, and the peace proclaimed by the lips will agree with the will of the soul.

> **Note [Col. 0526D]:** Thus read the manuscripts and common editions, except Quesnellus, who has: “iniquity, trampled down, will prevail.” Immediately afterward the manuscripts Vat. Reginae and Barb. have: “and peace, proclaimed by lips, will be preserved in mind”; and “the Apostle’s saying will be fulfilled,” and so forth.

The Apostle’s saying will also be fulfilled: “That we may remain in Christ, of one mind and thinking the same thing” (Phil. 2:3), claiming nothing for ourselves through rivalry or empty glory, but pleasing not human beings, but God our Savior. To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the consulship of Honorius Augustus for the sixth time and Aristenetus.

## CHAPTER XXV

> **Note [Col. 0527B]:** The ancient author of this collection had before his eyes a primitive collection of the acts of Chalcedon, closely resembling the one we find in the very ancient Vatican manuscript 1322, as will become clear from what we have observed in the notes to Quesnellus’s ninth dissertation on the case of Domnus of Antioch, vol. II. That primitive collection incorporated the imperial letters and the address in Latin, as they had been published. Quesnellus prefixed the title “Canons of the Council of Chalcedon,” contrary to the testimony of the Thuan. manuscript and our Vindobonensis manuscript. The words “Here begins the beginning of the Council of Chalcedon” refer to the imperial law that follows, by which the council was first summoned to Nicaea. In Vatican manuscript 1322, however, two other laws are more correctly placed afterward; our compiler omitted them. Those laws transferred the same council from Nicaea to Chalcedon.

Here begins the beginning of the Council of Chalcedon.

> **Note [Col. 0527C]:** This law was taken from the original Latin, not translated into Latin from the Greek, as Rusticus did, since he did not find the Latin original in his manuscripts. When Crabbus published the Council of Chalcedon, he possessed two manuscripts: one of this collection and another of Rusticus. When he published Rusticus’s manuscript, however, he inserted, for this law, the original Latin in place of Rusticus’s omitted translation; Baluzius later published Rusticus’s version. Crabbus’s original Latin appears in part I, no. 37. Accordingly, besides the Vindobonensis manuscript, we have also collated Crabbus’s copy.

**The victorious Valentinian and Marcian, illustrious triumphant conquerors, emperors, ever Augusti, to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople.**

Divine matters must be placed before all other business. For, with God almighty propitious, we are confident that the state must both be preserved and improved.

> **Note [Col. 0527C]:** From both the Vind. and Crabbus manuscripts we have added “almighty,” and afterward “to be.”

Since, therefore, certain doubts appear to have been introduced into our orthodox religion, as the letter of the most reverend Leo, bishop of the blessed city of Rome, also testifies, it has especially pleased Our Clemency that a venerable synod should be held in the city of Nicaea in the province of Bithynia, so that, when minds have been brought together and every matter of truth thoroughly examined, and when the partisan interests by which some are known previously to have disturbed the most holy orthodox religion have ceased, our true faith may become more clearly known to the whole world, so that henceforth there may be no doubt or discord.

> **Note [Col. 0527C–D]:** Quesnellus has “in Chalcedon,” and in the margin: “The common reading is ‘in Nicaea,’ and rightly so, for this was the city first designated for the synod.” We have restored “in Nicaea,” because, besides Crabbus’s common copy, the Vind. manuscript also confirms this reading. Although it has “in Chalcedon, the city of Nicaea,” the word “Chalcedon” is marked with dots, indicating that it should be deleted; thus below it gives only “Nicaea.”

For this reason, let Your Holiness hasten to go to the aforesaid city of Nicaea by the Kalends of September, together with whichever most reverend bishops you approve as suitable and instructed in orthodox religion from the Churches placed under your priestly care.

Let Your Religiousness also know that Our Serenity will be present at the venerable synod, unless public necessities detain us on campaign. May the Divinity preserve you for many years, holy and venerable Father. Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, at Constantinople, in the consulship of the Lord Marcian, perpetual Augustus, and of the consul who shall be announced.

> **Note [Col. 0527D–0528B]:** Thus read the Thuan. and Vind. manuscripts of this collection. Vatican manuscript 1322 agrees; we have noted that these documents were transferred here from an older collection, for it has: “Order of the proceedings held at Chalcedon in the presence of the Augusti Marcian and Pulcheria”—read “Augusti.” Quesnellus, with his Oxford manuscript, has: “Address of the emperor Marcian to the Council of Chalcedon.”

**Order of the proceedings of the Council of Chalcedon.**

When the most devout and faithful emperor Marcian had arrived, on the day of the most holy martyrs Saint Calenicus and Euphemia, with the most devout and Christian queen Augusta Pulcheria present, moved by divine zeal and fervor of faith, and with the most magnificent magistrates and the most illustrious and noble senate present, he addressed the venerable synod as follows.

> **Note [Col. 0528B–D]:** Quesnellus, following the Oxford copy, has: “on the day, at the most holy shrine of Calenicus and Euphemia”; and in his note he adds: “Or, as the Thuan. manuscript reads: ‘On the day of the most holy martyrs Saint Gallenicus and Euphemia.’ These words are read very differently both in all the other Latin versions and manuscripts and in the Greek itself. The Greek reads: *ἐν τῇ ἁγιωτάτῃ Ἐκκλησίᾳ τῆς ὁσίας καὶ καλλινίκου μάρτυρος Εὐφημίας*—‘in the most holy church of the pious and victorious martyr Euphemia.’ Nevertheless, Cardinal Baronius possessed a manuscript resembling ours; from it, under the year 451, no. 112, he asserted that the sixth session of the Council of Chalcedon, at which Emperor Marcian was present, was held on the very feast day of the glorious virgin and martyr Euphemia and the martyr Callinicus, in whose basilica the session took place, and that Emperor Marcian and Augusta Pulcheria were present because of the day’s solemnity. He repeats the same in his notes to the Martyrology, on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, the day consecrated to the feast of Saint Callinicus, the martyr crowned at Gangra. He also adds that the words found in the translation of Dionysius Exiguus after the subscriptions of the bishops in that action are now absent from the Greek text. But what translation of Dionysius Exiguus he means, we plainly do not know. Perhaps he learned this from Henry Gravius or Severinus Binius, both of whom possessed a manuscript copy of the Atrebatensis resembling ours, and followed the latter’s conjecture. Binius thought that the version he had found at Arras was Dionysius’s, as we explain in the dissertation concerning that manuscript. Whatever the case, all this seems to me to have arisen from a faulty reading or translation of the Greek text of the acts of Chalcedon, where the word *καλλινίκου*, ‘victorious,’ or, literally translated, ‘well-victorious,’ which is used as an epithet of Euphemia, was understood by the translator as referring to the martyr Callinicus. Against this version stand: (1) the Greek text; (2) all the Latin versions; (3) the Latin Martyrology; (4) the Greek Menologion itself—for both assign the feast of this martyr Callinicus to 29 July; and (5) the fact that the words of the manuscript imply that the basilica of Saint Euphemia was likewise dedicated to Callinicus, something no author has so far reported, not even Evagrius, who in book II, chapter 3, describes this basilica of Saint Euphemia vividly and at length.’ Thus far Baronius. It is certain that the better manuscripts of our collection, Thuan. and Vind., have this reading, and we have therefore inserted it into the text. Crabbus also found this reading in a manuscript of the same collection and inserted it into Rusticus’s version. Hence the ancient editions of Rusticus after Crabbus display a similar reading, which is absent from the genuine copies of Rusticus. When Cardinal Baronius cited this reading, he did not use any particular manuscript, but ancient editions of the Councils. The error by which the day of Saint Callinicus the martyr is wrongly preferred, contrary to the Greek text and the testimony of the other versions, may be traced to Vatican manuscript 1322, which had before it a collection similar to ours. There we read: ‘When the most devout and faithful Emperor Marcian had arrived at the same aforesaid shrine, with [someone] present through divine zeal, etc.’ This version agrees with the Greek text. But when our compiler did not find the aforesaid shrine mentioned earlier in the same manuscript, he attempted to explain it from the Greek opening of the Chalcedonian action; and, wrongly interpreting the word *καλλινίκου*, introduced the corrupt reading into this collection.” The presence of Pulcheria in the sixth action of the Council of Chalcedon has been defended in note 14 on Letter 101, vol. I, col. 1127.

> **Note [Col. 0529D]:** The Vatican manuscript has: “he said these things.”

**Address of the most devout emperor.**

When first, by divine judgment, we were chosen for the imperial office, among the many necessities of the state no concern constrained us more than that the orthodox and true Christian faith, which is holy, pure, and beyond doubt, should be firmly implanted in the minds of all.

> **Note [Col. 0529D]:** The Vatican manuscript places “constrained” first: “constrained us.”

For it is established that, through the avarice or partisan interests of certain people, during the intervening period some persons, thinking differently and leading peoples astray according to their own will rather than as truth and the teaching of the Fathers require, have led very many into error.

> **Note [Col. 0529D]:** The manuscripts of Rusticus have “while teaching.”

For this reason we have endeavored to bring about this holy synod with precisely this purpose, and we seem to have imposed this labor upon you, so that, when every darkness and error has been dispelled, our religion—which is pure and holy—may, in accordance with the way the Divinity wished to reveal itself to human beings and the way the teaching of the Fathers has shown, shine with the light of its truth implanted in the minds of all.

> **Note [Col. 0529D]:** Quesnellus has “to reveal itself.” We have corrected the text in accordance with the Vatican manuscript, first position, Vind., and the manuscripts of Rusticus.

And henceforth let no one dare to discuss the birth of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ otherwise than the apostolic preaching and the decrees of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers, consonant with that preaching, are known to have handed down to posterity; as the writings sent by the holy Pope Leo, who governs the apostolic see of the city of Rome, to Flavianus of holy memory, bishop of the city of Constantinople, also testify.

> **Note [Col. 0529C–0530C]:** All manuscripts and common editions read thus. Quesnellus alone, with Oxford, has “the letter testifies.” Shortly afterward the Veronese manuscript has “to strengthen the faith.”

Therefore, when partisan interests have been removed, protections withdrawn, and avarice brought to an end, let the truth become known to all.

We wished to be present at the synod, following the example of the religious ruler Constantine, to confirm the faith, not to exercise any power, so that the peoples might not be separated any further by wicked persuasions.

> **Note [Col. 0530C]:** The Vatican manuscript, first position, has “and no further”; the manuscripts of Rusticus cited by Baluzius have “and not so that they might further”; Veron. has “and not so that,” with “further” deleted.

For the simplicity of certain people has hitherto easily been deceived by the ingenuity and excessive verbosity of some, and it is established that dissensions and heresies have arisen through the wicked insinuations of others.

Our aim, however, is that the entire people, thinking as one through true and holy teaching, should return to the same religion and worship the true catholic faith, as you have expounded it according to the teachings of the Fathers.

> **Note [Col. 0530C]:** Thus read the Vatican manuscript, first position, and the manuscripts and common editions of Rusticus; it is better than “all the peoples,” as Quesnellus accepted.

Therefore, with minds in agreement, let Your Religiousness hasten, so that, just as from the Council of Nicaea until the recent period the true faith became known to all after errors had been cut away, so now, through this holy synod, once the obscurities that appear to have emerged during these few years, as stated above, through the wickedness and avarice of certain people have been removed, whatever is decreed may be preserved forever.

> **Note [Col. 0530C]:** The common editions, together with Vind. and Vat. in second position, have “equally.” Veron., with other manuscripts of Rusticus, has “therefore.”

It will belong to the divine majesty firmly to preserve forever what we desire to be accomplished with a holy mind.

> **Note [Col. 0530C]:** Veron. has “to preserve.” The Vatican manuscript, first position, has: “so that they may be firmly established and preserved forever.”

> **Note [Col. 0530C–D]:** The Vind. and Thuan. manuscripts give this title. Quesnellus has: “Action of the Council of Chalcedon.” This is the definition of faith read and subscribed at this council in action 4. Crabbus published this version from a manuscript of this collection; it is the fourth version. Baluzius collated it with four manuscripts. We have collated it with Vind., Vatican 1322, and Lucensis 88, which resembles Coustant’s Lombard Colbertine manuscript. In the last two manuscripts the following title is prefixed: “The episcopal Council of Chalcedon, held by five hundred and twenty bishops against Eutyches.”

## The Council of Bishops Held at Chalcedon Begins

The venerable assembly of the whole world, gathered by the grace of God and by the decree of the most merciful and religious emperors Valentinian and Marcian Augusti in the metropolitan city of Chalcedon in Bithynia, at the shrine of the holy and victorious Euphemia, decreed the matters set out below.

> **Note [Col. 0530D]:** The Thuan. manuscript adds “and Germanus.” Immediately afterward that manuscript has “in the city of Chalcedon.” Lucensis has “in the metropolitan city of Chalcedon in Bithynia.”

> **Note [Col. 0530D]:** Quesnellus has: “the matters which it decreed are appended below.” We have corrected this from the best manuscripts, Vat. and Lucen.

Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0530D] The words “Jesus Christ” have been added from the Vatican, Lucan, and Baluzius’s manuscripts. The Vindobonensis codex adds only “Christ.” Shortly afterward, the Oxford manuscript reads, “He commanded that peace be confirmed to the disciples through understanding of the faith.” Baluzius: “While confirming the disciples through understanding of the faith, he says.” Quesnellus, with the Thuanus: “He wished to confirm the understanding of the faith in the disciples, saying.” We have followed the Vindobonensis, Lucan, and Vatican manuscripts. Afterwards, “so that no” is supplied by certain manuscripts.] commanded the disciples to confirm their understanding of the faith: “My peace I give you, my peace I leave you” (John XIV, 27), so that no disagreement might arise among us from venerable religious devotion, but that the proclamation of truth might be manifested equally. [Note: [Col. 0531C] The Vindobonensis and Lucan manuscripts: “among you.” The Vatican: “among his own,” perhaps better; and afterward, “also from that truth.”] [Note: [Col. 0531C] Baluzius: “But since.” The Lucan manuscript: “since,” with the particle et deleted.]

And since the Evil One does not cease to lie in wait through certain sordid devices resembling [Note: [Col. 0531C] The Oxford manuscript: “resembling piety.” The Vindobonensis: “by means resembling piety.”] the seeds of piety, but is always seeking something new against the truth, therefore our Lord, taking thought for the human race, granted us this most merciful and faithful ruler against our adversary. He summoned priests to himself from every quarter, so that, with the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ cooperating, [Note: [Col. 0531C] So Baluzius’s manuscripts, with the Thuanus and Vindobonensis agreeing. The Vatican codex: “so that all the guilt of falsehood may be cast away, and truth, etc.” Quesnellus: “so that truth, having attacked all the guilt of falsehood, may cast it away and strengthen it with its own shoots.” The Lucan manuscript: “so that the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, having attacked all the guilt of falsehood, may cast it away.”] he might cast away from his flock all the guilt of falsehood and strengthen it with the shoots of truth—which we also did, pursuing errors and sects by common decree or judgment.

Moreover, we renewed the faith of the most perfect Fathers, proclaiming to all the creed of the three hundred and eighteen; [Note: [Col. 0531C] Only Quesnellus, with the Oxford manuscript, adds “and those whom.”] and we marked with titles what we recognize that the priests had conceived in mind through sincere knowledge. After this, one hundred and fifty also assembled in the city of Constantinople, confirming this faith as well.

But now, observing the order and all the formulas of the faith, we decree, in accordance with the Council of Ephesus—whose venerable authors were Coelestine, bishop of the city of Rome, and Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria— [Note: [Col. 0531C] So the Vatican, Lucan, and Baluzius’s manuscripts. The Vindobonensis alone prefixes the adverb “unanimously.” The Oxford manuscript deletes *who*, but has in the exposition “blameless,” etc. Quesnellus, with the Thuanus: “who, agreeing unanimously, rightly declared the exposition of the blameless faith,” etc.] that, in unanimous agreement, the exposition of the blameless faith of the three hundred and eighteen venerable and most blessed Fathers who assembled at Nicaea in the time of the emperor Constantine, of divine memory, [219] must rightly take precedence; [Note: [Col. 0531D] So the Vindobonensis, with the Vatican and Baluzius’s manuscripts. The Lucan and Thuanus manuscripts agree: the former alone deletes after some words “and apostolic”; the latter has “they judged that it truly had force.” Quesnellus, with the Oxford manuscript: “We also decree that the decisions of the one hundred and fifty venerable bishops at Constantinople against the destruction of the sects that were springing up and growing should retain their force.” This is a clearer formulation, but it departs from the testimony of the ancient codices.] and likewise that what was decreed by the one hundred and fifty venerable bishops at Constantinople against the destruction of the sects that were springing up and growing should truly retain its force, as a manifestation of this catholic and apostolic faith of ours.

[Note: [Col. 0531D] So all our codices. Quesnellus: “The creed of the one hundred and fifty Fathers.” Since, however, both the Nicene and Constantinopolitan creeds were read at the Council of Chalcedon, the first translator—whose version is preserved in Vatican manuscript 1322—joined both creeds into one, adding at the end an anathema against the errors of Arius, which belongs properly to the Council of Nicaea. Hence the title, which indicates the Nicene and Constantinopolitan creeds together, is rightly prefixed in the more faithful manuscripts of this collection, as also in the Vatican manuscript from which, as we have noted, our collector derived this material.]

## Creed of the Three Hundred and Eighteen and the One Hundred and Fifty

We believe in one God, the almighty Father, maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father [Note: [Col. 0532C] Quesnellus omitted “born,” though our codices retain it. He then noted that after the word “ages” the printed editions add “light from light.” But the codices of this version do not know these words. Later he passed over “truly,” a word also absent from the Lucan manuscript.] before all ages; true God from true God; born, not made; of the same substance [Note: [Col. 0532C] Quesnellus: “of which the Father is.”] as the Father; through whom all things were made; who for us human beings and for our salvation descended, [Note: [Col. 0532C] The Vatican manuscript: “was born from the Holy Spirit and from the Virgin Mary as man,” etc. Nearly the same appears in the Lucan codex.] was incarnate from the Holy Spirit, made man from the Virgin Mary, was crucified for us under Pontius Pilate, was buried, rose again [Col. 0532B] on the third day, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father. From there he will come with glory to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom will have no end.

And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father, who with the Father and the Son is worshiped and glorified, who spoke through the prophets; in one catholic and apostolic Church. We confess one baptism for the remission of sins; we await [220] the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0532C] This primitive version exists in Vatican collection 1322, from which the author of our collection received it. Quesnellus was the first to publish it, but it differs in many respects from our manuscripts and those of Baluzius, against whose testimony we have edited it. For what ought to be presented is not what may be better, but what the ancient and primitive version and the old exemplars, even if less exactly, preserve. Shortly afterward, the Vatican, Lucan, and Baluzius’s codices delete “and confirmation,” though our Vindobonensis does not.]

This holy and saving mystery [Note: [Col. 0532D] Quesnellus, in the margin: perhaps *symbolum* (“creed”) should be read, as in the other versions. But the codices of this version have *secretum* (“mystery”), for which the Lucan manuscript wrongly has *decretum* (“decree”).] of divine grace would indeed have sufficed for a complete knowledge and confirmation of piety; for it teaches us [Note: [Col. 0532D] Quesnellus: *plenaria perfecte*; and in a marginal note: “The word *plenaria* is absent from the Oxford manuscript. Perhaps *plenarie* should be read.” We have followed the Vatican, Lucan, and Baluzius manuscripts. Shortly afterward, following the Vatican, Thuanus, and Vindobonensis, we have written *praeconia* (“proclamations”). Others have *praeconium* (“proclamation”).] fully and perfectly about the incarnation of our Lord from the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, to whom belief is faithfully given. [Col. 0532C] But since those who attempt to destroy the proclamations of the truth [Col. 0533A] have produced certain innovations, and have endeavored to corrupt the secret mystery of our Lord’s incarnation, and have dared to deny that the Virgin was the creator [Note: [Col. 0533B] Only Quesnellus has “of the flesh.”] of the divine Word, and have dared to fabricate a confusion of the one nature of the human body and of Divinity, and have attempted to call the divine nature of the only Son separable and corruptible, therefore this venerable and universal council, wishing to oppose all their contrivance against the truth, decreed by that ancient proclamation and firm example—teaching especially that the undefiled faith of the three hundred and eighteen venerable bishops should remain intact—and, against those who oppose the Holy Spirit, [Note: [Col. 0533B] Quesnellus inserted “he strengthened that faith,” and then deleted “faith.” We have preferred our manuscripts and those of Baluzius.] the faith which, at a later time, the one hundred and fifty venerable bishops who assembled in the city of Constantinople also confirmed for us, together with the doctrine concerning the substance of the Holy Spirit, [Note: [Col. 0533B] So the Lucan manuscript with those of Baluzius. Quesnellus: “the doctrine of the Holy Spirit concerning this substance.”] not by adding anything to the ancient faith, but against those who endeavored to oppose the conception of the divine Spirit [221] and to corrupt the power of our Lord. [Note: [Col. 0533B] Quesnellus: “These, therefore, they more clearly showed to be in error by the testimony of the divine Scriptures. But because of those who [destroy] the mystery,” etc. The Thuanus: “Therefore, by making the testimony of the Scriptures more boldly manifest, because of those who [destroy] the mystery.” The Vindobonensis: “Therefore, by making them more clearly manifest through the testimony of the divine Scriptures, because of those,” etc. We have preferred the manuscripts of Baluzius. Similarly the Lucan manuscript, which alone has *attestantibus* (“those giving testimony”) instead of *ad detestationem* (“for condemnation”). Shortly afterward, for *creatum* (“created”), Baluzius has *effectum* (“made/effected”).] We therefore expose them more clearly in the divine Scriptures for condemnation, because of those who were attacking the secret of the substance, shamelessly and vulgarly saying that a man without Divinity had been created from the venerable Virgin Mary, [Note: [Col. 0533C] So the Vindobonensis, Vatican, and Thuanus codices. Baluzius’s and the Lucan manuscripts alone omit *contra* (“against”). Quesnellus has *acceptas* (“accepted”) for *venerabilis* (“venerable”); afterward he has *congrua* (“fitting”) written in opposition to the text.] contrary to the letters of the venerable former bishop Cyril of the Church of Alexandria and to the fitting writings of the whole East against the madness of Nestorius. In those writings there is a clear expression of a certain and saving creed, [Note: [Col. 0533C] Quesnellus: “for those wishing to know, as well as the letter of Archbishop Leo of the first see, which appears to have been sent and addressed … For that letter seemed to agree with the confession of Saint Peter, and one identical page clearly taught the confession of the complete faith of believers against the audacity of detractors.” This is indeed better, but it is not found in the ancient codices of this collection, nor in the ancient, more obscure version that our collector adopted. We have presented in the text the Vatican and Lucan exemplars, as well as those of Baluzius. The Thuanus and Vindobonensis differ slightly: the Thuanus reads, “with the confession agreeing with us, and one identical page seemed”; then, instead of *edere* (“to bring forth”), it has *edocere* (“to teach”), and instead of *integrae* (“complete”), *integritatem* (“completeness”). The Vindobonensis reads, “a confession agreeing, and one identical page seemed,” and then *edocere* (“to teach”).] for those wishing to know, as well as the letter of Archbishop Leo of the first see, which appeared to have been sent and addressed to the venerable Flavian, of holy memory, in order to intercept the wickedness of Eutyches, although agreeing with the confession of Saint Peter; and one identical page appeared clearly and suitably to set forth, against the audacity of detractors, the confession of those believing in the complete faith. For it also opposes those who, as though dividing the secret substance of the living God into two parts, are striving [Note: [Col. 0533D] So the Vindobonensis codex. Quesnellus: “attacks.” The Thuanus: “we attack.” The Lucan: “they attack.”] to divide it.

[Note: [Col. 0533D] At this point Quesnellus presented a double version in two columns. In the narrower column he gave the version from the Thuanus codex, which we have retained in the text as proper to this collection and compared with our manuscripts and those of Baluzius. In the wider column he gave another version published by Crabbus. Although it had been inserted in the Oxford manuscript because it is more explicit, it is nevertheless foreign to this collection; therefore we append it here as Quesnellus published it:]

He also rejects those who dare to call the Divinity of the only Son passible, and those who judge that there is mixture or confusion in the two natures of Christ, as well as those who say that the flesh assumed was heavenly or of another substance, thereby denying that he took for us the form of a servant; and he anathematizes those who invent two natures of the Lord before the union but fabricate one after the union.

Following the holy Fathers, therefore, we all teach with one harmonious voice that we confess one and the same Son, our Lord Jesus Christ: the same perfect in Divinity, the same perfect in humanity; the same true God, the same true man, consisting of a rational soul and a body; the same consubstantial with the Father according to Divinity, the same consubstantial with us according to humanity; like us in all things except sin; begotten before the ages from the Father according to Divinity, but in the last days the same, for our salvation, from Mary the Virgin, the Theotokos, according to humanity; one and the same Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, to be recognized in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation; with the substance of the natures nowhere removed because of the union, but rather with the property of each nature preserved and brought together into one person and one existence; not divided or parted into two persons, nor separated, but one and the same only-begotten Son, God the Word, Jesus Christ, just as the prophets of old spoke concerning him, and Jesus Christ himself taught us and handed down to us the creed of the Fathers.

After defining these matters with complete truth, diligence, and care from every side, the holy and universal synod decreed that no one might bring forward, write, compose, hold, or teach another faith [Col. 0534D] otherwise; and that those who dared to compose another faith, or bring it forward, or teach it, or hand on another creed to those wishing to come to the knowledge of the truth, whether from paganism or from any heresy—if they were bishops, should be strangers to the episcopate, and if clerics, to the clergy; but if they were monks or laypeople, they should be anathematized.

And they signed:

Paschasinus, bishop and representative of my lord, the most blessed and apostolic man, Pope Leo of the universal Church of the city of Rome, presiding over the synod: I have decreed, agreed, and signed.

Lucentius, bishop of the Church of Tusculum [read: Asculum], representative of my lord, the most blessed and apostolic man, Pope Leo of the universal Church of the city of Rome: I have signed the acts read in the synod.

Boniface, priest of the holy Roman Church: I have decreed and signed.

The rest of the bishops who were present at the same council also signed, numbering six hundred and thirty.

These men also, who dare to call the Divinity [Col. 0535A] of the only Son passible, ought to be expelled from every synod; likewise those who argue that there is mixture [Note: [Col. 0535B] Quesnellus incorrectly has “and confession.” We have corrected this from the Lucan and Baluzius manuscripts.] and confusion of the nature of our Lord; and those who say that the substance which we believe to have been formed from us is heavenly or even consubstantial. [Note: [Col. 0535B] The Vindobonensis, Lucan, and Baluzius manuscripts omit *credimus* (“we believe”). Afterwards, the Lucan manuscript has *concreatum* (“formed together”) for *concretum*. Shortly afterward, we have adopted *figuram* (“figure/form”) from the Vindobonensis, Lucan, and Baluzius, whereas Quesnellus has *fugimus* (“we flee”).] We therefore call those who rave or are insane regarding the form [223] deluded; and those who foolishly invent two natures of the Lord before the birth and one after they have been united must be excommunicated. [Note: [Col. 0535B] Quesnellus: “who say that the natures of the Lord are two in the union, but foolishly say one after the single [nature].” We follow our manuscripts and those of Baluzius, in which “after the union” seems to be the reading, as in the other versions.]

Let us therefore follow the judgment of our Fathers, confessing one and the same Lord Jesus Christ and teaching in agreement that the same is perfect in Divinity and the same is a perfect bodily man, a true God, the same a true man, the same consisting of a rational soul and bodily substance; similar to the Father in Divinity, [Col. 0535B] and likewise similar to us in every respect in human substance, except for sin; born before the ages from the Father [Note: [Col. 0535C] The Lucan and Baluzius manuscripts: “begotten.” Afterwards, instead of *numinis* (“divinity”), some have *nominis* (“name”). Thus the unskilled translator rendered *Theotocon* in Latin.] according to Divinity, but in the last days the same, for us and for our salvation, from Mary the Virgin, creator of the divine *numen* (deity), according to humanity; one and the same Christ, the unique Son and Lord, to be recognized in two natures, without confusion, [Note: [Col. 0535C] So the Baluzius manuscripts, along with the Greek and other versions. Quesnellus, the Vindobonensis, and the Lucan: “unchangeable.” Shortly afterward, for *substantia* (“substance”), the Vindobonensis and Lucan manuscripts with Baluzius have *distantia* (“distinction”), incorrectly.] without change, [Col. 0536A] without division, with the substance of the two natures in no way destroyed because of the unity, with the property of each nature preserved, and with the substance agreeing under one person [Note: [Col. 0535C] So the Vindobonensis. Quesnellus: “and substance.” The Baluzius and Lucan manuscripts: “not agreeing under one substance.” Shortly afterward, Quesnellus has “divided and partitioned”; the Vindobonensis, Lucan, and Baluzius codices have “divided and partitioned” in the feminine form. We have corrected the wording as required by the sense of the context. Afterwards, the Lucan codex reads, “the only Son, true God, Jesus Christ.”]; [224] nor divided and partitioned into two forms, but one and the same Son, the only Lord, the Word, God Jesus Christ; just as the prophets of old spoke concerning him, and Jesus Christ himself has now instructed us and handed down to us the creed of the Fathers.

[Note: [Col. 0535C] The Vindobonensis and Lucan manuscripts: “Therefore, with these matters”; Baluzius: “Therefore, with these matters in common truth”—both less correctly. Nor is Quesnellus’s reading, “Therefore, with these matters,” entirely satisfactory. It would be preferable, with the other versions, to write “Therefore, with these matters … ordered,” if any codices of this interpretation supported it.]

Therefore, after arranging these matters with complete truth and gentleness, the venerable and universal Church decreed that no one might bring forward, publish, teach, or hand on any other faith [Note: [Col. 0535D] So the Vindobonensis, Lucan, and Baluzius codices. Here some words are missing through an omission, and since no codices supply them, the defect is extremely ancient. The passage seems to require supplementation from another version, which we appended in note 49, as follows: “But those who dared to compose another faith, or bring it forward, or teach it, or hand on another creed, and to rebuke those wishing to come to the knowledge of the truth from pagan rites,” etc. Quesnellus, not suspecting the omission, emended the passage as follows: “another creed, wishing to corrupt those coming to the knowledge of the truth from pagan, Jewish, or any heretical sect, whether they are bishops,” etc.] [lacuna] another creed, to rebuke those wishing to come to the knowledge of the truth from pagan rites, or from the Jewish or any heretical sect. [Col. 0536B] But whether they are bishops or clerics, we order that they be strangers to the episcopate and the clergy; and if they are monks or laypeople, that they be excommunicated.

[Note: [Col. 0535D] Although these canons appear in the commonly circulated editions of the Councils under action 15, they were actually enacted under action 7, as we proved in the Observations on Quesnellus’s first dissertation for the year 451, note 18, volume II, column 501. The version of these canons is the one published by Justellus from a very ancient codex and to be reprinted by us in this volume, called the Prisca interpretation. Apart from Justellus’s codex and the exemplars of this collection, it exists in three other manuscript collections: Vatican Regina 1997, Colbert 784, and the similar Lucan 88, from which Father Dominicus Mansi most recently published these canons in volume I of the Supplement to the Councils, column 329; and finally in Barberini 2888 and Vatican 1342. All these collections, like ours, derived the Chalcedonian canons from the Prisca version.]

## Canons Set Forth by the Holy Fathers Who Assembled at Chalcedon

[Note: [Col. 0536C] So in the excellent Vindobonensis codex 39, in which a second hand substituted *indictione V* (“in the fifth indiction”) for *in*. Another codex, the Caesarean Vindobonensis 42, has a slightly different reading: “assembled in the times, in the five-hundredth year,” etc.; and the Hubertine exemplar in Coustant, volume I of *Epistles of the Roman Pontiffs*, page LXXXIII: “assembled in the times, in the fifth indiction, in the five-hundredth year, under the emperor,” etc. Quesnellus, omitting here the words “in the five-hundredth year,” moved them after the name Marcian and arranged the phrase as follows: “In the five-hundredth year of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifth indiction.” This formula is absent from all the ancient manuscripts, both of this collection and of the other collections cited in note 1, and is foreign to the old style. [Col. 0537B] Justellus’s codex, which contains the Prisca version of the Greek canons, gives this title: “The Council of Chalcedon begins. In the five-hundredth year, under the most devout emperor Marcian.” Likewise in the Barberini 2888, Vatican 1342, and another Lucan-Colbertine collection: “The statutes begin. In the five-hundredth year, under the most devout emperor Marcian.” In the Vatican Regina 1997 manuscript: “The canons of the Chalcedonians established by the holy Fathers begin, that is, in the five-hundredth year, under the most devout emperor Marcian.” Father Coustant, in the place cited, gives the special inscription of the Colbertine codex, formerly Thuanus, which belongs to our collection, in these words: “The canons set forth by the holy Fathers who assembled at Chalcedon in the times of Valentinian [read: Valentinian] and Marcian Augustus, in the fifth indiction, under our most devout emperor Marcian.” He considers this preferable to the others and thinks that the five-hundredth year should be deleted, since the Council of Chalcedon was held not in the five-hundredth year but in 451, to which the fifth indiction, in October, indeed corresponds. Yet five manuscripts of different and extremely ancient collections unanimously support the notation of the five-hundredth year, and the single Thuanus codex should not be preferred to the others of the same collection. Nor should the excess of the five-hundredth year create difficulty, since at approximately this same time Saint Peter Chrysologus, in Sermon 145, likewise reckoned approximately five hundred years after the birth of Christ. Compare the other examples we collected for this matter in the edition of the works of Saint Zeno, bishop of Verona, dissertation 1, chapter 2, section 1, pages XXXVI–XXXVII.]

In the five-hundredth year, under our most devout emperor Marcian.

[225] [Note: [Col. 0536D] The codices of Justellus, Vatican Regina, and Vatican Barberini prefix a table of titles and also place a repeated title before each canon. The manuscript exemplars of this collection lack the prefixed table. Only in both Vindobonensis codices 39 and 42 are titles attached in the margin of the canons, and these are expressed in words different from those in the codices of the other collections that likewise present the Justellian titles. Accordingly, we shall cite the distinctive titles of this collection in the notes, as we found them in the same Caesarean Vindobonensis manuscripts, in which the titles of some canons are missing. The title of the first canon is given as follows: “On the canons of each venerable council.” The other codices, with Justellus, place this first canon before the others in the manner of a preface, or attach it to the inscription; and they list as the first canon the one that is second in this collection.]

## CANON I

We have judged that the canons established up to now by the holy Fathers in each individual synod should retain their force.

[Note: [Col. 0537C] The title in the Vindobonensis manuscripts: “If a bishop performs an ordination for money.” In the canon, the Oxford codex has: “If anyone [buys] the ordination of a bishop,” etc. Shortly afterward, the Justellian manuscript, the Lucan manuscript, and the Vatican manuscript of this version have “through money.”]

## II

If any bishop performs an ordination for money and sells a matter that is acquired only by grace, and for money ordains a bishop, or a provincial bishop, or a presbyter, or a deacon, or any one of those included among the clergy, or [Note: [Col. 0537C] The codices of Justellus, Lucan, and Vatican 1342 have “by the grace of God.” The words “or a provincial bishop” are absent from the same manuscripts and from the Oxford manuscript. Quesnellus conjectures that through these words the unskilled translator intended to render the Greek expression ἢ χωρεπίσκοπον (*ē chorepiskopon*, “or a rural bishop”). The Vatican and Lucan codices: “if he ordains bishops, or presbyters, or deacons.”] for money makes any of them an administrator, or a defender, or a doorkeeper, or anyone of this kind for the shameful gain of profit, then whoever is proved to have done this shall suffer the penalty of his rank.

The person who is ordained shall also acquire no advantage from the ordination that has proceeded through commerce; rather, [Note: [Col. 0537D] The codices of Justellus, Vatican 1342, and the Lucan manuscript: “let him be held guilty of the dignity or of the office entrusted to him for money”; in the Vatican manuscript, a later hand adds, “and on account of those things,” etc.] let him be excluded from the dignity or office that was entrusted to him for money.

But if anyone [Note: [Col. 0537D] We have added *in* (“in”) from the Vindobonensis manuscript. The Justellus, Lucan, and Vatican codices: “in these shameful matters,” and shortly afterward, “he may be seen, and if he is a cleric.”] appears to have taken part in such shameful and wicked profits, then, if he is a cleric, let him be degraded; but if he is a layman or monk, let him be anathematized.

[Col. 0538A] [Note: [Col. 0537D] The words “Likewise, elsewhere” are found not only in the manuscripts of this collection but also in Vatican Regina 1997, the oldest of all the collections, from which our collector seems to have extracted them, since the readings also agree in many other respects. They are absent from Justellus’s codex and from the Vatican 1342 and Colbert 784 manuscripts. In the Lucan exemplar, although it contains this Colbertine collection, the entire canon is omitted, as can be gathered from Father Mansi’s edition; and more correctly so, since this same canon is repeated in its proper place below, as chapter 21. Quesnellus’s conjecture, expressed in these words, appears probable: “I cannot guess on what occasion or for what reason these words were inserted here. These things are certain: first, that they belong neither to the preceding nor to the following canon; second, that they are themselves canon 21 of this Council of Chalcedon; third, that their version differs both from all other published versions and from the version of the decree placed in this codex as number 21; fourth, that the same canon is read here at the end of the second canon in both manuscript exemplars of this codex and in the Justellian collection.” This addition was undoubtedly the work of some diligent person who, when reading that the preceding canon decreed deposition against clerics guilty of shameful and simoniacal gain, wished immediately, from the wording of canon 21, to warn how cautiously and carefully such an accusation against bishops should be received, since such a penalty would await those condemned. Shortly afterward, the Vindobonensis has “cleric or layman wishing”; Colbert, Justellus, and Vatican 1342 have “clerics or laypeople.”]

Likewise elsewhere: clerics or laypeople wishing to accuse bishops or clerics [Note: [Col. 0538C] The Colbert manuscript in Father Coustant: “to accuse improperly.” The Vindobonensis: “not improperly to accuse, lest in any way [read: ‘in whatever manner’] they come to accuse.” Justellus and Vatican Regina: “to accuse, not improperly, lest there be anything to accuse.” Vatican 1342, together with Coustant’s Colbert manuscript, has the same reading; only, instead of *ne* (“lest”), it more correctly has *nec* (“nor”).] ought by no means to be admitted to bring an accusation unless their reputation has first been examined. [Note: [Col. 0538C] Only the Oxford manuscript has “their opposition.”]

[227] [Note: [Col. 0538C] The title in the margin of the Vindobonensis codices: “Neither a bishop, nor a cleric, nor a monk shall become a tenant.”]

## III

It has come to the holy synod’s attention that certain clerics, for the sake of shameful gain, become tenants of other people’s properties [Note: [Col. 0538C] Justellus, Vatican 1342, and the Lucan manuscript: “become … and neglect.” Shortly afterward, the Vindobonensis, Lucan, Justellus, and Vatican codices have “while handling secular cases”; the Thuanus: “while handling secular causes,” which is better.] and neglect the ministries of God in handling secular cases, [Note: [Col. 0538C] Quesnellus adds *per* (“through”), in place of which Justellus, the Lucan, and the Vatican have *et* (“and”). The Vindobonensis and Vatican Regina delete both.] running around secular households and undertaking the management of estates out of greed.

Therefore the great and holy synod decreed that henceforth no one—neither bishop, nor cleric, nor monk—may lease properties under the title of a tenant, nor be permitted to mix himself into the administration of secular cases, unless someone is summoned according to the laws to act as guardian of a minor, [Note: [Col. 0538C] The same three codices, Justellus, Lucan, and Vatican, have “which cannot be excused.”] a duty that cannot be excused; or unless a bishop wishes to entrust to a cleric the care of ecclesiastical property, [Note: [Col. 0538C] Quesnellus inserted “to him”; the Vindobonensis and Vatican Regina delete it. The other three codices supply *clerico* (“to a cleric”) as follows: “if he wishes to entrust the care to a cleric.”] or of orphans or widows [Col. 0539A] who lack personal protection, or of persons of such a kind as require ecclesiastical assistance out of fear of God.

But if anyone attempts to violate what has been established, [Note: [Col. 0539B] Vatican Regina, with Justellus, Lucan, and Vatican 1342, adds “henceforth.”] let him be subject to ecclesiastical condemnation.

[Note: [Col. 0539B] The title in the margin of the Vindobonensis codex: “No one shall presume, without the will”—understood, of the bishop—“to build either a monastery or an oratory; and it speaks about monks.” The words “Those who truly … may hold office” appear in the Vatican Regina manuscript in place of the title; our collector derived them from that manuscript. In other collections transmitting the Prisca, they are expressed more nearly in the form of a title as follows: “Those who pursue the solitary life, and the office they may hold.” But the canon begins, as it does in Vatican Regina, “Since indeed certain men.” In the Greek and in the other versions of Dionysius and Isidore, the same opening is found as in our collection.]

## IV

Those who truly and manifestly pursue the solitary life shall hold an appropriate status. But since certain persons, under the pretext of monastic dress, disturb churches, assemblies, and common property, wandering indiscriminately around the cities [Note: [Col. 0539C] Justellus incorrectly has “and not monasteries.” The Lucan and Vatican manuscripts more correctly have “nor monasteries.”] and striving to establish monasteries for themselves, it was decreed [Note: [Col. 0539C] Quesnellus: “that no one anywhere be able to build a church, nor,” etc. We have corrected the text from the Vindobonensis and Vatican Regina manuscripts. Justellus, with the Lucan and Vatican manuscripts: “that none of them be permitted anywhere to build, nor a monastery.” Shortly afterward, “but monks,” which Justellus, the Lucan, and Vatican have corruptly.] that no one may build anything anywhere, establish a monastery, or set up an oratory without the consent of the bishop of the city.

We decree that the monks who are in the individual cities and provinces be subject to the bishops, love quiet, be content with fasts, and observe prayers [Col. 0539B] in those places in which they appear to have renounced the world. They shall by no means take part in ecclesiastical or secular affairs, nor cause disturbance, abandoning their own monasteries, unless perhaps they have been summoned by the bishop of the city for a necessary reason.

[Note: [Col. 0539C] The same three codices, Justellus, Lucan, and Vatican, have: “Certainly it was decreed that they should not receive a slave in their monasteries to make him a monk without the will of his own master.” Vatican Regina has the same, except for the last four words, which it gives, in agreement with our text, as “apart from the will of his own master.” The three codices cited above delete *nostrum* (“our”).]

Certainly, a slave is not to be received in monasteries in order to make him a monk without the will of his own master. Whoever exceeds this provision of ours, we have decreed that he be suspended from communion, [Note: [Col. 0539D] Vatican Regina, together with the three codices cited, has “we decree.”] so that the name of God may not be blasphemed. But the bishop of the city ought to provide suitable care for the monasteries. [Note: [Col. 0539D] So the same codices. Quesnellus has “the bishops of the cities”; and afterward, instead of “provide,” he has “exhibit.” The Justellus codex has “bestow.” The same exemplars, apart from the codices of our collection, prefix “all” to “monasteries.”]

[Note: [Col. 0539D] The three Vindobonensis manuscripts attach this title in the margin: “Those who go from one city to another.” In all other collections, the opening words of this canon are given as the title, and the canon begins with the word “It has been decided.” Better, however, in the manuscripts of our collection, as in the Greek and other versions, those opening words belong not to the title but to the canon itself. Justellus noted: “This canon is the first in all the collections.” He is mistaken, because, seeing the opening words “Concerning bishops or clerics who transfer themselves from city …” written as a title in his manuscript, he did not observe that they must be referred to canon 5 itself. In the first canon, the canons of all the holy Fathers are confirmed in general; here, however, those particular canons are confirmed which prohibit the migrations of bishops and clerics. Soon afterward Justellus and the Vatican manuscript read: “They transfer from one city to another.”]

**V. Concerning bishops or clerics who transfer themselves from one city to another.** It has been decided that the canons established by the holy Fathers concerning these very matters shall retain their validity.

[Note: [Col. 0540B] The title in the margin of the Vindobonensis manuscripts is: “That ordination be carried out in public places.” Justellus gives the opening words in place of the title: “Let no one be ordained absolutely.” The Vatican Regina manuscript has: “That no one …” In these manuscripts the canon begins with the words “Neither a presbyter,” and so forth. In Justellus it reads in the plural: “Neither presbyters, nor deacons, nor absolutely anyone from among those who belong to the ecclesiastical order,” and, because the opening words have been relegated to the title, the words “be permitted to be declared” are added to complete the sense. These are absent from the Vatican Regina manuscript, and even more so from the other manuscripts, Lucensis and Vaticanus, which, like the copies of our collection, begin the canon with the words “Let no one be ordained absolutely.” The word *liceat* (“be permitted”) is absent only from the manuscripts of this collection.]

**VI.** Let no one be ordained absolutely—not a presbyter, nor a deacon, nor indeed anyone who belongs to the ecclesiastical order—unless he has been specifically designated for the church of the city, village, martyr-shrine, or monastery for which he is to be ordained.

[Note: [Col. 0540C] Justellus and Vaticanus 1342 read: “But the holy synod decreed that the ordination of such persons [read: ‘this kind of ordination’] be invalid and that it be unable in any way to prevail to the injury of the one ordaining [the Vatican manuscript reads ‘of the ordination’; read, from the Greek, ‘of the one ordaining’].” Since this reading of the ancient version seemed too erroneous, it was passed over in the Lucensis manuscript and another reading, from Dionysius’s version, was substituted: “But the holy synod decreed that, if anyone is ordained absolutely, such laying-on of hands is invalid and that it can never exercise its office to the injury of the one ordaining.” The Vatican Regina approves our reading, except for the syntax of the words “this kind of ordination, whoever is ordained absolutely.” We have corrected *nunquam* (“never”) to *nusquam* (“nowhere, in no way”) on the basis of Vindobonensis, Vatican Regina, and other manuscripts.]

But the holy synod decreed that the ordination of those who are ordained in this absolute manner is invalid and can in no way prevail to the injury of the one ordaining.

[Note: [Col. 0540D] The title in the Vindobonensis manuscripts is: “That monks not return to military service.”]

**VII.** We decree that those who have once been ordained into the clergy or have become monks may not enter military service or assume secular dignity.

[Note: [Col. 0540D] Justellus: “But if, having undertaken this, they return unrepentant to what they had previously chosen.” Lucensis and Vaticanus: “But if they undertake this.” Quesnellus: “unless they repent.” We have written “and do not repent,” with all our manuscripts. Soon afterward Lucensis reads: “which they had previously chosen for God.”]

But when they undertake this and return unrepentant to what they had chosen for God, let them be anathematized.

**VIII.** [230]

[Note: [Col. 0541B] The title in the Vindobonensis manuscripts is: “That administrators of the poor obey their bishop.” The Lucensis manuscript has: “Clerics who are placed in charge of administering the poor, or monasteries and martyrs’ basilicas under the bishops who are in each city, should remain according to the traditions of the holy Fathers, so that through their own …” These words were excerpted from Dionysius’s version. The Vatican manuscript has adopted the Isidorian version altogether: “Clerics in poorhouses (places for beggars) and monasteries,” and so forth, as in the commonly published Isidorian text, vol. IV of the Councils of Venice, col. 1705.]

**VIII.** Clerics who are in charge of the administration of the poor, monasteries, or martyrs’ shrines shall remain under the authority of the bishops of the individual cities, according to the tradition of the holy canons; nor shall they, through their own rashness, evade the governance of their bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0541B] Thus the Vindobonensis and Vatican Regina manuscripts. Quesnellus has “of the individual [churches].” Justellus has “of the islands,” incorrectly. The Vatican Regina manuscript soon afterward reads “according to the canonical tradition of the holy Fathers.” Justellus has “according to the tradition of the holy Fathers, let them remain, and not through their own rashness …”]

But if any should dare in any way to overturn such an arrangement and should not obey their bishop, then, if they are clerics, let them be subject to canonical condemnation; but if they are monks or laymen, let them be suspended from communion.

[Note: [Col. 0541C] The Vatican Regina manuscript, together with Justellus and Lucensis, reads: “and should not give the customary things, if indeed …” The Vatican Regina manuscript soon afterward has “let them be laymen.” Justellus, together with the Lucensis manuscript, reads “if they should be laymen, let them cease from communion.”]

[Note: [Col. 0541D] The title in the Vindobonensis manuscripts is: “If a cleric has a case against another, let it first be examined by his bishop.” In the Justellus and Vatican manuscripts, instead of a title, it reads: “If a cleric has a case against a cleric.” They begin the canon, with two words added, “It has been decided that he should not abandon his bishop,” and so forth. The Lucensis manuscript has the same reading and alone does not separate the title from the canon. Soon afterward Vindobonensis, together with Justellus, Lucensis, and Vaticanus, reads “and to the secular courts.” This is properly understood in those three manuscripts because it is preceded by the words “it has been decided that”; but in Vindobonensis, where those words are absent, it is not. We have therefore retained Quesnellus’s standard reading, approved by the Vatican Regina and coherently connected with the passage.]

**IX.** If a cleric has a case against a cleric, let him not abandon his bishop and run to the secular courts; but let him first have the case examined before his own bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0541D] Justellus, together with the Lucensis and Vatican manuscripts, adds “as has been said.” These manuscripts then delete “of the bishop.”]

Or at least let the case be heard with the consent of that bishop, before those whom both parties had begun to approach.

[Note: [Col. 0541D] Thus the Vindobonensis manuscript, with the Vatican Regina and Oxford manuscripts agreeing. The first has *inceperint* (“they may have begun”) instead of *coeperant* (“they had begun”), and the second has *coeperunt* (“they began”).
