Quesnellus’s text reads: “when both parties wish, they will contain the judgment”; in the margin he writes: “Perhaps: ‘and they will hold the judgment as well.’” This addition was taken from Dionysius’s version; the other copies of the ancient version do not know it, for the Lucensis and Vatican manuscripts read: “if both parties wish. But if anyone …” Justellus has the corrupt reading: “if both parties wished. If anyone …”]

But if anyone attempts to act against this, let him be subject to canonical prohibitions.

**231.** But if a cleric has a case with a foreign bishop or with his own, let him present the case before the provincial synod.

[Note: [Col. 0541D] The Justellus, Lucensis, and Vatican manuscripts add “anyone.” The Lucensis manuscript then reads: “let him be judged before the provincial synod”; and soon afterward, together with Justellus and Vaticanus, it reads: “But if a bishop or cleric has a dispute with the metropolitan bishop, let him appeal to the principal see or to the see of Constantinople, and let them settle the case there.”]

But if a bishop or cleric has a dispute with the metropolitan bishop, let him appeal either to the principal see of the diocese or to the see of Constantinople, where the case is to be heard.

[Note: [Col. 0542B] Quesnellus, from the Thuanus manuscript, added “and let him be judged there.” We deleted this with the Vindobonensis, Oxford, and Vatican Regina manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0542B] The title of the Vindobonensis manuscripts is: “That it not be permitted to cross from one city to another.” In Justellus, instead of a title, it reads: “That no cleric be permitted to depart from his Church.” The canon itself begins: “The Churches of the cities in which someone was first ordained should be served, and not that to which …” Soon afterward the same Justellus has “they attempted.”]

**X.** It is not permitted for a cleric to serve simultaneously in the Churches of two cities: in the one in which he was first ordained and in the one to which, as though it were greater, he has fled through a desire for empty glory.

Those who have attempted this must be restored to their own Church, in which they were first ordained, and must minister there alone.

[Note: [Col. 0542B] Quesnellus: “But if anyone has already been transferred from one Church to another.” We have followed the syntax of the Vindobonensis and Vatican Regina manuscripts.]

If, however, anyone has already been transferred from one Church to another, he shall have no authority to administer any affairs of the former Church, or of the martyrs’ shrines belonging to it, or of its hospices, or of its resources for the poor.

[Note: [Col. 0542C] Quesnellus notes that the Thuanus manuscript reads: “Let him have no share in the affairs of the former Church, or of the martyrs’ shrines under it, or of the poorhouses, or of the hospices. But those who, after the decree of this great and universal synod, have dared to do anything of what has been forbidden, the holy synod decreed that they be removed from such a rank.” Coustant, in the same Colbertinus manuscript, read *recedere* (“to withdraw”). Quesnellus would prefer *recidere* or *excidere* (“to be cut off”), as, he says, the standard version printed beside the Greek edition has it; all these passages were taken from that version, in which the Thuanus manuscript differs from Oxford and Justellus. More clearly, these passages should be said to have been taken from the version of Dionysius Exiguus, in which *photiorum* should be corrected to *ptochiorum* (“poorhouses”), and *usi* (“used”) to *ausi* (“dared”). The Vatican Regina manuscript has *synodochiis* for *xenodochiis* (“hospices”); Vindobonensis has *synodicis*.]

**232.** But those who have dared, after this decree of this great and general synod, to do anything contrary in these matters which the holy synod recently prohibited shall lose their proper rank.

**XI.** All the poor and those truly in need ought to be assisted with peaceful relief, and only with ecclesiastical—not synodical—letters.

[Note: [Col. 0542C] This canon has no title in the Vindobonensis manuscript. Concerning the word *synodicis*, which our manuscripts of this ancient version also prefer [Lucensis: *synodociis* and *synodocias*], Quesnellus added the following annotation: “The same reading is found in canon 13, from which the other versions differ; they have *commendatiliis*. The Anician manuscript comes closest to our Oxford and Thuanus manuscripts; from it the editors of the latest edition of the Councils extracted several variant readings and placed them in the margin of the Dionysian version. It likewise has *synodociis*. Perhaps the author of our version read, in a corrupt Greek manuscript, συνοδικοῖς instead of συστατικοῖς. The Anician reading seems to have arisen from that manuscript, which may have had a word derived from the verb συνοδεύω, ‘I accompany’ or ‘I am a companion on a journey,’ or from ὁδέω or ὁδάω, ‘I provide provisions for a journey’; because letters of this sort would serve clerics as a companion and provisions for their journey. Gerard Rudolph discussed canonical letters at length in a treatise published at Cologne in 1582. See also Bernardinus Ferrerius, in the book he wrote on the ancient type of ecclesiastical letters; Hannibal Fabrotus, in Balsamon’s *Collection of Ecclesiastical Constitutions*, book III, title 1; Christophorus Justellus, on this canon of the Universal Church; and the notes of Gabriel Albaspinaeus, bishop of Orléans, on this canon, where he discusses accurately and at length the twofold interpretation and meaning of the Greek word ὑπόληψις, which nearly concludes the canon. For the words τοῖς οὖσι μόνοις ἐν ὑπολήψει παρεσχέσθαι προσώποις have been interpreted differently by different writers. The version accompanying the Greek text, both in Justellus’s *Code of the Universal Church* and in the commonly published editions, as well as the Greek collectors and commentators Balsamon, Zonaras, and Blastares, explain the canon as referring to persons who are under suspicion. The ancient Latin versions interpret it in the opposite sense: Dionysius refers to persons of higher standing, while the Isidorian version refers to those who are more distinguished in their work. Jacobus Cujacius, in chapter 5 on nonresident clerics, interprets it as referring to more respectable persons, ‘who are in good repute,’ or of unimpaired reputation. Our old translator expresses this sense as ‘those who seem to be of good reputation,’ a reading with which Justellus’s ancient version agrees. Albaspinaeus draws the Dionysian version and the others that interpret the passage as referring to persons of higher standing toward this latter sense. Without doubt he would have advanced his opinion with greater confidence had he read the version of our manuscript, which gains no little recommendation from the fact that it sheds some light on a canon of the celebrated ecumenical synod.” Thus far Quesnellus.]

For it is fitting that *synodical* letters be given only to those who seem to be of good reputation.

[Note: [Col. 0543C] The title of the Vindobonensis manuscripts is: “That a province not be divided between two metropolitan bishops.”]

**XII.** It has come to our attention that certain persons, setting themselves against ecclesiastical statutes and aligning themselves with the civil authorities, have divided one province into two by an imperial administrative order, and thereby made two metropolitan bishops in one province.

[Note: [Col. 0543D] The Justellus, Lucensis, and Vatican manuscripts read: “There are two metropolitan bishops.” After *therefore*, these same manuscripts, together with the Vatican Regina, add “now”; and instead of *sancta* (“holy”) they have *magna* (“great”).]

Therefore the holy synod decrees that bishops shall not henceforth attempt anything of this kind, lest those who undertake such an action lose their proper rank.

[Note: [Col. 0543D] The three aforementioned manuscripts, and Vindobonensis together with the Vatican Regina, have *ne qui* (“lest anyone”), rather than *minus ne qui* (“lest anyone, even less”). Justellus omits *jam* (“now”).]

Whatever cities already exercise metropolitan honor by sacred letters shall alone retain that honor, and the bishop who presides over such a Church shall retain his own proper right, which truly belongs to a metropolitan city.

[Note: [Col. 0543D] The Vindobonensis manuscript reads: “they alone.” Quesnellus notes: “Read *ipsae solum* (‘they alone’), as the sense requires.” After the word *episcopus*, Quesnellus inserted from the Thuanus copy: “let him be called archbishop.” Although these words are also preferred by the Vatican Regina manuscript, we deleted them from the other copies because they are absent from the Greek and the other versions.]

[Note: [Col. 0543D] The title in the Vindobonensis manuscripts is: “That foreign visitors not minister in another city.” The Vatican Regina has: “A foreign cleric and readers … may.” Justellus, Lucensis, and Vaticanus read: “In a foreign city … must minister nowhere.”]

**XIII.** Foreign clerics and readers cannot under any circumstances minister in another city without the *synodical* letters of their own bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0543D] The title in the Vindobonensis manuscripts is: “That they not associate with heretics or Jews.” Soon afterward Quesnellus has “and that psalmists marry wives”; Justellus has “and marry for salvation,” and in the margin: “Read ‘at least marry,’ which we found in Vaticanus 1342.” Both readings are wrong. The true reading is supplied by the Lucensis manuscript, with Vindobonensis and Thuanus agreeing; in these, only *psaltae* is read instead of *psaltes*.]

**XIV.** Since in certain provinces readers and psalmists are permitted to marry, the holy synod decrees that no one may take a woman of another sect.

[Note: [Col. 0544B] Justellus and Lucensis have “a heretical woman thereafter.” Vaticanus more correctly has “only a woman of another sect.” Here “another heresy” means “another sect,” as the versions of Dionysius and Isidore also indicate. Justellus has *procrearunt* (“they have begotten”).]

But those who have already begotten children from such a marriage may afterward receive catholic communion if they have baptized their children among heretics.

[Note: [Col. 0544B] Lucensis and Vaticanus have *postmodium vero* (“but afterward”); and soon afterward, together with Justellus and the Vatican Regina, “they may receive them into catholic communion,” while others have “accept” or “receive.” These manuscripts then read: “they must no longer be baptized among heretics, lest … with heretics,” in Justellus, Lucensis, and Vaticanus.]

But if the children have not been baptized, they may no longer be baptized among heretics, nor may they be joined in marriage with a heretic, or with a Jew, or with a pagan, unless the person who is to be joined to an orthodox Christian has promised to convert to the orthodox faith.

[Note: [Col. 0544C] The same three manuscripts read: “unless perhaps the person who is to be joined to an orthodox Christian has promised to convert to the orthodox faith.” Soon afterward they have “if anyone attempts to violate,” instead of “if anyone has violated.”]

But if anyone violates the decree of this holy synod, let him incur the condemnation of the canons.

[Note: [Col. 0544C] The same manuscripts, together with the Vatican Regina, read: “let him be subject to canonical condemnation.”]

[Note: [Col. 0544C] The title of the Vindobonensis manuscripts is: “Concerning deaconesses.” Justellus, Lucensis, and Vaticanus 1342, although they give the title “At what age the handmaids of God ought to be veiled,” begin the canon as follows: “It has been decided that they not be ordained before the age of forty, and this with careful …” The word *diaconissam* (“deaconess”), found in the manuscripts of our collection and in the Vatican Regina, agrees with the Greek and the other versions.]

**XV.** A woman may not be ordained a deaconess before the age of forty, and then only after careful examination.

[Note: [Col. 0544C] Justellus, together with Lucensis and Vaticanus, has “after receiving the veil, and observing a definite period in the ministry.” The Vatican Regina has the same: “and observing a definite period in the ministry.” Oxford has “observing the ministry”; Vindobonensis, “observing in the ministry.” Soon afterward the three earlier manuscripts have “who is joined to him.”]

But if, after receiving ordination and observing the appointed periods of ministry, she gives herself to marriage, to the injury of God’s grace, such a woman shall be anathematized, together with the man joined to her.

[Col. 0544B]

[Note: [Col. 0544D] The title in the Vindobonensis manuscripts is: “That neither a virgin dedicated to God nor monks may marry.” Quesnellus begins the canon as follows: “That neither she who has vowed herself a virgin to the Lord may marry, nor a monk take a wife.” We have preferred the Vindobonensis and Vatican Regina manuscripts, with which the other three agree, differing only in the words “nor may it be permitted for monks to marry.”]

**XVI.** It is likewise not permitted for a woman who has consecrated herself as a virgin to the Lord God, nor for a monk, to marry. But if they wish to do this, let them be suspended from communion.

[Note: [Col. 0544D] Justellus, together with Vaticanus, has: “But the bishop shall have authority in this matter, if he wishes to reconcile them”; Vaticanus has “to reconcile.” The Lucensis manuscript substitutes Dionysius’s version here: “But for those who confess, we decree that the bishop of that place have authority to bestow mercy and kindness.”]

We grant the bishop authority in this matter, if he wishes to reconcile them.

[Note: [Col. 0544D] This canon has no title in Vindobonensis. After a little while Vindobonensis omits the initial word *eas* (“them”), Oxford deletes *maxime* (“especially”), and Lucensis omits the initial particle *si* (“if”).]

**XVII.** We decree that the rural parishes located in the individual provinces remain undisturbed under the bishops who appear to possess them, especially if, having possessed them for thirty years, they have administered them without violation.

But if, within thirty years, a dispute has arisen or arises concerning them, those who claim to have suffered coercion may bring the matter before the synod of the province.

[Note: [Col. 0545C] Justellus has “within thirty years”; Vaticanus, “in thirty years”; Lucensis, “thirty years.” Soon afterward Justellus has “or if it should happen.” Lucensis omits the words “concerning them.” These three manuscripts, together with the Vatican Regina, then have “before the synod of their province.”]

[Note: [Col. 0545C] The Thuanus manuscript reads: “are said to have suffered coercion.”]

But if anyone is mistreated by his metropolitan bishop, let him present his case before the principal see of his province or before the see of Constantinople, as was stated above.

If a new city has been established by imperial authority, or is established, let the order of its ecclesiastical parishes also be determined according to civil and public forms.

[Note: [Col. 0545C] The title in the Vindobonensis manuscripts is: “Those who make a conspiracy, but not a false accusation, against a bishop.” In Vaticanus 1342 this entire canon is inserted directly from Dionysius’s interpretation. The crime of conspiracy or collusion was entirely prohibited even by the ancient laws, and the rest is as in Dionysius. Soon afterward *etiam* (“also”) is missing in the Justellus and Lucensis manuscripts, which then have “are usually cut off.”]

**XVIII.** The crime of conspiracy or collusion is entirely abolished even by external laws; much more, therefore, must it be prohibited from occurring in the Church of God.

Therefore, if clerics or monks are found to have conspired or to be contriving, through conspiracy, a false accusation against bishops or clerics, let them lose their proper rank.

[Note: [Col. 0545C] The Justellus and Lucensis manuscripts read: “and making, through conspiracy, a false accusation against bishops or any clerics.” Soon afterward Quesnellus, together with Oxford, has “let them lose their position.” We have written “rank” with the Vindobonensis, Thuanus, Justellus, and Lucensis manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0545C] The title of the Vindobonensis manuscripts is: “Let a synod be held twice a year.” Soon afterward Justellus, Lucensis, and Vaticanus have “in certain provinces”; [Col. 0545D] and then “according to the established canon,” followed by “and because many ecclesiastical matters that ought to be corrected or amended are neglected.”]

**XIX.** It has come to our ears that in the provinces synods of bishops are not held according to the provisions of the canons, and that consequently many ecclesiastical matters requiring correction are neglected.

Therefore the holy synod decrees that, according to the canons of the Fathers, bishops from each province shall assemble twice a year for this very purpose, wherever the metropolitan bishop has appointed, and shall correct whatever matters arise.

[Note: [Col. 0545D] The same three manuscripts, with the Vatican Regina agreeing, read: “according to the canons of the Fathers established at Nicaea in Bithynia, twice a year,” and so forth. In those manuscripts “as before” is incorrectly placed before “according to.” Justellus and Vaticanus soon afterward have “to assemble from the individual provinces.”]

But bishops who, remaining in their own cities, are not absent because of travel, but, with health permitting, are free from necessary and excusable occupations, shall, out of regard for brotherhood, be reproved if they do not attend.

[Note: [Col. 0545D] Justellus, together with Lucensis and Vaticanus, reads: “and, being stationed in their own cities and not having departed, but having withdrawn while health especially permitted it, free from unavoidable occupations” [Vaticanus: “having withdrawn”]; Lucensis has “excusable,” Vaticanus “without excuse,” and so forth.]

[Col. 0546A]

[Note: [Col. 0545D] The title in the Vindobonensis manuscripts is: “That one who receives another cleric be suspended from communion.” Soon afterward the three aforementioned manuscripts have “as has already been decreed.” Then Justellus and Vaticanus corruptly read “to be content … has deserved”; Vaticanus has “will have deserved.”]

**XX.** Clerics serving in the Church, as we have already decreed, may not serve in the Church of another city, but must be content with the one in which they were originally worthy to minister—except those who, having lost their homeland, have come by necessity to another Church.

[Note: [Col. 0546C] The same three manuscripts have: “came by necessity. But if one of the bishops … receives a cleric belonging to another Church.”]

If, after this decree, any bishop receives a cleric belonging to another, it has been decided that both the one who receives him and the one who has been received shall be suspended from communion until the cleric who has transferred himself returns to his own Church.

[Note: [Col. 0546C] We have added “the cleric” from Vindobonensis. The other manuscripts read: “until he makes the cleric who has been transferred return to his own Church.”]

[Note: [Col. 0546C] The title in the Vindobonensis manuscripts is: “Those who accuse a bishop.” In Justellus, Lucensis, and Vaticanus the canon is phrased as follows: “Clerics or laymen who accuse bishops or any clerics must not be received for accusation at all without a judgment, unless their reputation has first been carefully examined.” The Colbertinus manuscript, similar to Lucensis according to Coustant, has: “unless their reputation has first been examined.” The Vindobonensis manuscript differs from the printed text only in reading: “unless the reputation of their character has first been examined.”]

**XXI.** Clerics or laymen who accuse bishops or clerics in any manner and without a judgment must not be admitted to make an accusation unless their reputation has first been examined.

[Note: [Col. 0546C] This canon likewise has no title in the Vindobonensis manuscripts.]

**XXII.** Clerics may not, after the death of their bishop, seize those things which can belong to him, as was also provided in the preceding canons; otherwise they may endanger their own ranks.

[Note: [Col. 0546C] In Justellus, Lucensis, Vaticanus 1342, and the Vatican Regina, the particle *non* (“not”) is incorrectly added. It would fit properly if *illi* were read as *illis*.]

[Note: [Col. 0546D] The title in the Vindobonensis manuscripts is: “That clerics return to their proper places.”]

**XXIII.** It has come to the ears of the holy synod that certain clerics and monks, to whom nothing has been entrusted by their bishop and who are sometimes even suspended from his communion, go to the city of Constantinople and, remaining there for a long time, disturb ecclesiastical discipline; some of them even overthrow certain households.

Therefore the holy synod decrees that such persons first be admonished by the defender of the holy Church of Constantinople to depart from the imperial city.

[Note: [Col. 0546D] Justellus, omitting *per* (“by”), soon afterward has “to admonish.” Together with Justellus, most manuscripts delete the word *regia* (“royal”), including Vindobonensis.]

But if they remain there through shamelessness under the pretext of business, they are to be expelled against their will by the same defender and compelled to hasten back to their proper places.

[Note: [Col. 0546D] Justellus, Lucensis, and Vaticanus read: “if they remain amid business and shamelessness, they are also, against their will, to be … and recalled to their proper places.” Vindobonensis lacks “to be compelled.”]

[Note: [Col. 0546D] The title in the Vindobonensis manuscripts is: “When monasteries have been consecrated, let them not become secular lodgings.” Soon afterward, instead of *reservari* (“be reserved”), other copies have *servari* or *conservari* (“be preserved” or “be kept”).]

**XXIV.** Those monasteries which have once been consecrated to God, with the consent of the bishops, ought to be called monasteries forever; their property must be reserved for the monasteries, and they may not be turned into the lodgings of another secular person.

[Note: [Col. 0547C] The three Justellus, Lucensis, and Vatican manuscripts have “must not thereafter”; and soon afterward: “if anyone should permit this … let him be subject.”]

If anyone permits this to happen, let him be subject to canonical prohibitions.

**XXV.** Since, as we have learned, certain metropolitans neglect the flocks entrusted to them and delay the ordinations of bishops, it has pleased the holy synod that the ordinations of bishops be carried out within three months.

[Note: [Col. 0547C] This canon has no title in the Vindobonensis manuscripts. The three aforementioned manuscripts, Justellus, Lucensis, and Vaticanus, have “the ordinations are delayed.” Soon afterward Justellus alone has the corrupt reading: “unless perhaps the necessity of an unavoidable excuse compels the time of ordination to be extended,” and so forth.]

Unless, perhaps, an unavoidable necessity compels the period of delay to be extended; otherwise let them be subject to ecclesiastical punishment.

[Note: [Col. 0547C] The same three manuscripts have: “The revenues of the widowed Church should properly be preserved intact.” The Vatican Regina has the same, omitting only the word “properly.”]

The revenues of the widowed Church, however, shall be kept intact with the steward of that Church.

[Note: [Col. 0547C] The title in the Vindobonensis manuscripts is: “That bishops have stewards.” Quesnellus alone adds *rumore* (“by report”) before *reperimus* (“we have found”).]

**XXVI.** Since in certain Churches we have found that bishops administer ecclesiastical property without stewards, it has been decided that every Church having a bishop shall also have a steward from its own clergy to administer ecclesiastical property with the consent of his bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0547C] Justellus and Lucensis have: “It has been decided absolutely that every Church having a bishop” (words absent from Vaticanus), and nevertheless they also prefer “have a steward.” Justellus and Vaticanus add *censemus* (“we deem”) after the word *clero* (“clergy”).]

This is so that, where administration is without witness, ecclesiastical property may not be dispersed to the dishonor of the bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0547C] Thus Vindobonensis, together with the three frequently mentioned manuscripts. Quesnellus, with the Vatican Regina, has “be scattered.” Justellus has “if they have done this, let them be liable and subject to the holy canons.” Vaticanus and Lucensis have “if they have done this, let them be liable and subject to the holy canons.”]

But if they do not do this, let them be liable under the holy canons.

[Note: [Col. 0547D] The title in the Vindobonensis manuscripts is: “Those who abduct women.” Justellus, Lucensis, and Vaticanus soon afterward have: “the holy synod decreed.”]

**XXVII.** Concerning those who abduct women under the pretext of offering hospitality, or those who appear to connive at or consent to the abductors, the holy synod decrees that, if they are clerics, they shall lose their proper rank; but if they are laymen, they shall be anathematized.

[Note: [Col. 0547D] Quesnellus has “principal rank.” “Proper rank” is better, with the Vindobonensis, Vatican Regina, and Lucensis manuscripts. Soon afterward the three Justellus, Lucensis, and Vatican manuscripts have “they lose,” and then “let them be anathematized.”]

## CHAPTER XXVI

[Note: [Col. 0547D] Thus read the Vindobonensis and Thuanus manuscripts of this collection. Quesnellus, with Oxford, has: “The constitution of the emperor Marcian confirming the decrees of the aforesaid synod.” This constitution is also found in the manuscripts of Rusticus, two of which Baluzius collated, while we collated the most ancient manuscript of the Veronese chapter 57. It is also found in the manuscripts of the Hispanic and Isidorian collections. We reread Vaticanus Hispanicus 1341 and Vaticanus Isidorianus 630. In the manuscripts of Rusticus, this title is prefixed commonly to the laws that follow: “Of the emperor Marcian, of holy memory [Veronensis: ‘religious prince’], which the most blessed Pope Leo confirmed in his letters, concerning disputes prohibited to Christians.”]

Here begins the constitution of Marcian of divine memory concerning the Synod of Chalcedon.

[Note: [Col. 0548C] Veronensis of Rusticus, together with the other manuscripts collated by Baluzius, volume IV of the published Councils of Venice, col. 2025, chapter C: “The emperors Caesars Flavius Valentinianus, illustrious pontiff, illustrious Germanicus, illustrious Alamannicus, illustrious Sarmatian, holding tribunician power twenty-seven times, emperor twenty-seven times, consul seven times, and Flavius Marcianus, illustrious pontiff, illustrious Germanicus, illustrious Sarmatian, illustrious Alamannicus, illustrious Frankish, holding tribunician power twenty-seven times [read: ‘a second time’], emperor, consul once. An edict to the citizens [Baluzius, with the Greek, adds ‘our’] of Constantinople.” The inscription given here is found in the manuscripts of our collection and in the Hispanic and Isidorian collections.]

**The emperors VALENTINIAN and MARCIAN, Augusti, to all peoples.**
At last, what we had earnestly desired and prayed for has finally come to pass. [Note: Thuan.: “For the contention has been removed.”] The dispute has been removed from the orthodox law of the Christians. At last remedies for the culpable error have been found, and the divided opinion of the peoples has come together in one agreement and harmony. [Note: The Spanish and Isidorian codices read, “For by all …”; thereafter, the manuscripts of Rusticus read “most reverend priests.” We have restored the word “Chalcedon,” omitted by Quesnell, from all our manuscripts, as well as Baluzius’s manuscripts and the printed editions.] For the most devout priests came to Chalcedon from different provinces, in accordance with our commands, and by a clear definition taught what ought to be observed in religion. [Note: The Spanish and Isidorian Vatican manuscripts, with Merlinus, read “Therefore let it depart.”] Let profane contention now cease. For he is truly impious and sacrilegious who, after the judgment of so many priests, leaves anything further to be discussed according to his own opinion.

239 For it is the height of madness to search for a fictitious light in the midst of clear daylight; for whoever investigates anything further after the truth has been found is seeking a lie. Therefore no one—whether cleric, soldier, or person of any other condition—shall henceforth attempt to discuss the Christian faith publicly before assembled crowds and listeners, [Note: Quesnell reads “publicly determined among the assembled,” a reading supported by the Spanish and Isidorian codices. In the Vindobonensis, Thuanus, and Vatican 1322, the reading is “shall publicly determine something among the assembled,” or in Thuanus, “so that they may be assembled.” The reading of the manuscripts of Rusticus is better; we find it in the Veronensis and the printed editions of the Councils, and it is supported by Facundus, Book XII, chapter 2: “let him not presume to discuss it publicly when the peoples have assembled and are listening.” The following constitution agrees: “to contend publicly about religion when the peoples have assembled,” etc. A little later, in the Oxford codex, *per fidei* is read instead of *perfidiae*.] seeking from this an occasion for tumult and treachery. For anyone who strives to reopen and publicly debate what has once been judged and rightly settled does injury to the judgment of the most devout synod, since what has now been established concerning the Christian faith is known to have been defined in accordance with the apostolic expositions [Note: The manuscripts of Rusticus add “and decrees.”] and the decisions of the three hundred and eighteen and the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers. For punishment will not be lacking for those who despise this law [Note: Quesnell alone omitted *hujus*.], since they not only oppose the faith rightly composed, but also profane the venerable mysteries before Jews and pagans through such contention.

Therefore, if the offender is a cleric who has dared publicly to discuss religion, he shall be removed from the fellowship of the clergy; [Note: The Spanish, Isidorian, and Rustican codices read “from the association.” A little later, the common editions of the Councils read “from this royal city.” The Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts then read “let them be expelled.”] but if he belongs to the army, he shall be stripped of his military belt. The other persons also who are guilty of this crime shall be expelled from this most holy city [Note: Quesnell alone omitted “this.”] and, with judicial force, shall be subjected to the appropriate punishments. For it is evident that the fuel and beginnings of heretical madness are supplied by the fact that certain people publicly debate and contend. [Note: Quesnell reads “of infamy.” We have corrected it from the Vindobonensis and several other, better manuscripts. A little later, the Vatican Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts read “to be supplied” instead of “to be nourished.”]

240 Therefore everyone must observe what has been established by the holy synod of Chalcedon, without thereafter doubting anything. Accordingly, warned by this edict of Our Serenity, abstain from profane utterances and cease henceforth to debate divine matters; this is forbidden, because we believe that this sin will be punished not only by divine judgment, but will also be restrained by the authority of the laws and judges. [Note: We have added “this,” as required by the sense, with the manuscripts of Rusticus and the Spanish and Isidorian codices.] Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, at Constantinople, in the consulship of Sporatius. [Note: The Vindobonensis reads “Given on the seventh day before the Kalends.” Labbe, omitting *data*, reads “at Constantinople, on the seventh day before the Ides of February.” These readings can be reconciled if, with the Vatican Spanish and Isidorian codices, one reads “Promulgated on the seventh day before the Kalends of February at Constantinople,” and, with the manuscripts of Rusticus, which agree with the Greek text, “Given on the seventh day before the Ides of February at Constantinople.”]

## CHAPTER XXVII

[Note: This chapter occurs in the manuscripts of this collection, in the manuscripts of Rusticus, and in Vatican 1322. In the printed editions of the Councils it appears in Part III of the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 4. The title in Veronensis 57 of Rusticus is given as follows: “Likewise, a second edict concerning the same matter.” The cited Vatican manuscript reads: “Here begins another constitution of the divine memory of Marcian in [the law for] the Council of Chalcedon.” The Oxford codex reads: “A constitution of the same emperor addressed to Palladius, the Praetorian Prefect, commanding that the decrees of the same synod be preserved, after the error of Eutyches had been condemned.” The title given here occurs in the older manuscripts of our collection, Thuanus and Vindobonensis. Quesnell noted concerning it: “This title is found in the Thuanus codex. From it, a synod otherwise unknown to all has now become known.” Other codices indicate where the synod met—namely, the Crabbian codex, whose title reads “Edict addressed to the citizens of Constantinople, etc.”; and the Boherian codex cited in the Labbe edition of the Councils, which gives: “The same Augustus to our citizens of Constantinople.” Finally, the common edition reads: “Edict … promulgated at Constantinople.” Namely, Anatolius, returning from the ecumenical synod and wishing, as was customary and his duty, to report to his people what had been done there for the faith, held an assembly of his Church, to which this edict of Marcian was also sent, so that no one would be unaware that the synodal definition had been confirmed by an imperial constitution. Since the bishops then residing in the city had attended this assembly, as was customary, it was consequently given the name of the synod.]

Here begins another constitution of the divine memory of Marcian, addressed to the catholic Christians assembled in synod.

[Column 0549B]

[Note: The Vindobonensis reads “The same Augustus to Palladius, etc.” Vatican 1322 reads “The Emperor Marcian Augustus to Palladius, etc.” The Veronensis, agreeing with the other manuscripts of Rusticus, reads “The same Augusti to our citizens of Constantinople”; at the end of the constitution it adds: “Written in the same form to Palladius, illustrious man and prefect of the East; to Valentinianus, illustrious man and prefect of Illyricum; to Tatianus, illustrious man and prefect of the City; and to Vincomalus, illustrious man, master of the offices and consul-designate.”]

The Same Augusti to Palladius, Praetorian Prefect.

Desiring Our Serenity to establish for all the holiness of the catholic and orthodox faith as manifest and beyond doubt, so that a greater religious devotion toward the service of the Divinity might be imparted to humanity, it ordered so great and such a synod to be assembled from bishops gathered from almost all the provinces in the city of Chalcedon [Note: Quesnell alone, from one Oxford manuscript, inserted “as great as no memory has recorded.” These words are absent from all our manuscripts and those of Baluzius, as well as the printed editions, and even from Thuanus.] 241; and after discussion had been conducted there for many days, it discovered what was true and unfeigned in the Christian faith.

For after many prayers and supplications they entreated the Divinity that holy and complete truth should not remain hidden from them. They followed the decrees of the venerable Fathers—namely, those defined at Nicaea by the judgment of the three hundred and eighteen holy bishops [Column 0549C]; likewise those established by the one hundred and fifty who later assembled in this most distinguished city; and those decreed concerning the faith at Ephesus [Note: The common edition of the Councils, together with the manuscripts of Rusticus and the Greek text, adds “previously.”], where the bishops Celestine, of holy memory, of the city of Rome, and Cyril, of the city of Alexandria, [Note: The common Councils edition after the Roman edition adds “were bishops and leaders of the truth,” though no Latin manuscripts support this.] discovered the truth. At that time the Nestorian error was also excluded, its author having been condemned.

After these matters had been duly and reverently examined at Chalcedon, Eutyches, who asserted many unlawful things, was expelled together with his assertion [Note: Quesnell reads “so that no further opportunity might be offered for receiving sacrilegious things”; Thuanus reads “so that no further opportunity might be offered to anyone for receiving him,” etc. The reading of the copies of Rusticus, supported by the common editions and the Greek text, is better. In Vaticanus and Vindobonensis, *recipiendorum* is read instead of *decipiendorum*; this error seems to have occasioned the introduction of various readings.]: so that he would no longer have the opportunity to deceive people.

Thus, after religious matters had been ordered and those things faithfully established which are known to have founded the venerable orthodox faith, so that no doubt would thereafter remain even for those accustomed to slander the Divinity, We confirmed the venerable synod by the sacred edict of Our Serenity and admonished everyone to cease debating religion. For no single person or pair of persons could discover such profound secrets, especially since so many venerable priests, with the greatest labor and the most extensive prayers, could not have reached an investigation of the truth unless God, as must be believed, had been their author. [Note: Quesnell inserts *nisi*; we have removed it with the Vindobonensis and the common editions of the Councils. A little later, those same common editions read “and with great prayers.”]

Yet, as We have learned by clear reasoning, certain people do not cease to persist in the same madness of perversity, publicly contending about religion before assembled peoples and exposing and profaning the divine mysteries before the eyes of Jews and pagans—mysteries that ought rather to be worshiped than investigated.

Those who persisted in the same obstinacy ought therefore to have been restrained by the punishment already prescribed, so that punishment might correct those whom respect for commands had been unable to reform. But in this matter, following Our customary practice, We do not punish the offenders [Note: The Vindobonensis omits “We do not punish,” but repeats it. Since the passage consequently lacked sense, these words may have been supplied; they occur in other manuscripts of the collection. The truer reading appears to be that of the printed editions and the copies of Rusticus: “But in this matter, following Our customary practice, knowing above all that the Divinity rejoices in mercy, We decided to defer the punishment of the offenders, and by this repeated command of Our clemency We enact that henceforth …”], but Our clemency repeats the command that henceforth everyone abstain from what is forbidden and not gather assemblies to contend about religion. For those detected in such perversity and vanity will receive the punishments prescribed long ago, and by judicial action they will be punished as befits religious times.

For it is necessary to follow the Council of Chalcedon, at which, after everything had been carefully examined, those matters were defined which the three aforementioned assemblies, following the apostolic faith, previously declared must be observed by all. [Note: The manuscripts of Rusticus, together with the common editions, read “handed down.”] Given on the third day before the Ides of March, at Constantinople, in the consulship of Sporatius, illustrious man, and of whoever shall have been announced.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

[Note: This chapter is found in the manuscripts of this collection, in Vatican 1322, and in the Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts. In the printed editions of the Councils it appears in Part III of the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 19. We have taken the title from the Vindobonensis manuscript.]

Likewise, another Constitution of the same Augustus Marcian concerning the preservation of the catholic faith and concerning the Eutychianists and Apollinarianists, and their punishments.

[Column 0551B]

The Same Augustus to Palladius, Praetorian Prefect.

[Note: The Vindobonensis and Vatican manuscripts read “Although it has also been provided.” Crabb reads “Although it has already been provided.” Quesnell reads “of my clemency.” We have substituted “of Our clemency” from the Vindobonensis and Vatican manuscripts. A little later, the Vatican Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts, as well as Crabb, read “it ought to be exercised.”]

Although Our most sacred constitution has already provided and defined what severity ought to be exercised against those who, following the heretical perversity of Eutyches or Apollinaris, have deviated from religion and the catholic faith, nevertheless the citizens and inhabitants of the city of Alexandria are infected with such great poisons of Apollinaris that it has been necessary to establish again by law what We previously enacted. For the severity of sanctions ought to be abundant where the license of offenses is frequent.

Moreover, the greater the divine matters surpass human affairs, the more diligently My Serenity ought to care for the preservation of the orthodox faith. Therefore, whoever, whether in this sacred city, in the city of Alexandria, throughout the whole diocese of Egypt, or in various other provinces, follows the profane perversity of Eutyches and does not believe as the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers handed down when they founded the catholic faith in the city of Nicaea; and likewise as the other one hundred and fifty venerable bishops who later assembled in the flourishing city of Constantinople; and as the holy bishops Athanasius, Theophilus, and Cyril of the city of Alexandria believed [Note: The same manuscripts, together with Merlinus and Crabb, read “bishops of holy memory.” A little later Crabb reads “believed”]; whom also the Council of Ephesus, presided over by Cyril of blessed memory, followed in all things, in which the error of Nestorius was expelled [Note: The Spanish manuscripts read “followed them all”—and shortly afterward “agreeing with them”]; and whom the venerable Council of Chalcedon recently followed, agreeing in every respect with the earlier councils of priests, neither taking anything away from the most sacred Creed [Note: Quesnell alone adds “holy”], nor adding anything, but condemning the deadly doctrines of Eutyches—let them know that they are Apollinarian heretics.

For Eutyches and Dioscorus followed the most criminal sect of Apollinaris with sacrilegious intent. Therefore all who follow the perversity of Apollinaris or Eutyches shall know that they are to be punished by the penalties established either by the constitutions of the former divine emperors against the Apollinarianists, or by the later sanction of Our Serenity against the Eutychianists, or by this very august law against the same persons.

Accordingly, the Apollinarianists, that is, the Eutychianists—for although there is a difference in the name, there is a union in the perversity of the heresy, and although the name differs, the sacrilege is the same—whether they are in this flourishing city and in various provinces, or in the city of Alexandria, or in the diocese of Egypt, if they neither believe as the venerable Fathers mentioned above believed nor communicate with the most reverend bishop of the city of Alexandria, Proterius, who holds the orthodox faith, shall, in accordance with the most sacred constitutions of the former divine emperors promulgated concerning the Apollinarianists, have no power to make a will or execute a final disposition [Note: The Vatican Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts, with Merlinus, read “nor to make a last will”; a little later, instead of “receive,” they read “acquire”], nor to receive anything left to them in anyone’s will, nor to obtain anything by way of gift. Rather, if anything is conferred upon them either by the generosity of a living person or by the will of a dying person, it shall immediately be confiscated to Our treasury.

They themselves shall not transfer any part of their property to anyone by title or right of gift. Nor shall they be permitted to appoint or have bishops, priests, or other clerics. Let both those Eutychianists or Apollinarianists who dare to confer upon anyone the name of bishop, priest, or cleric, and those who attempt to retain the sacerdotal name conferred upon them know that they will suffer the penalty of exile together with the loss of their property. [Note: Crabb deletes “these.” The Vatican Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts read: “both these Eutychianists or Apollinarianists … and these … shall suffer the penalty of exile.”]

Those who were previously clerics of catholic Churches or monks of the orthodox faith, but who, abandoning the true and orthodox worship of Almighty God, have followed—or later follow—the heresy and detestable doctrines of Apollinaris or Eutyches, We order to be subject to all the penalties established either by this law or by earlier laws against heretics, and to be expelled even beyond the territory of the Roman Empire, just as the provisions of the preceding laws decreed concerning the Manichaeans. [Note: The Vindobonensis and Crabb read this way. Quesnell reads “previously,” while the Vatican Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts read “but having abandoned the true and orthodox …”]

Furthermore, the Apollinarianists or Eutychianists shall establish neither churches nor monasteries for themselves [Note: Crabb, together with the Vatican Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts, reads “let them build.” A little later these manuscripts, with Merlinus, read “nor synaxes and assemblies.” Quesnell reads “parasynaxes, that is, assemblies.” We have followed Crabb and the Thuanus and Vindobonensis manuscripts; shortly afterward all read similarly.], nor shall they gather parasynaxes and assemblies, whether by day or by night. They shall not gather at anyone’s house, estate, monastery, or any other place to carry out the activities of their most deadly sect [Note: The Vindobonensis reads “another.” Crabb reads “of another.” A little later Crabb, together with the Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts, reads “workers.” Quesnell reads “who will practice the doctrines of the most deadly sect.” We have deleted “doctrines” with all the manuscripts and printed editions; it is unnecessary if “of the most deadly sect” is taken in the genitive.]

If they do so, and if it is established that this was done with the owner’s consent, then, after the matter has been confirmed in the judge’s examination [Note: The Vindobonensis, Vaticanus, and Crabb read this way. Quesnell reads “of the trial”], the house or estate in which they assembled shall immediately be assigned to the treasury; the monastery, however, shall be assigned to the orthodox Church of that city in whose territory it lies.

But if, without the master’s knowledge, yet with the knowledge of the person who collects the rents of the house, or of the tenant, procurator, or steward of the estate, they have gathered the forbidden parasynaxes and assemblies, then the tenant, procurator, steward, or whoever it may be who received them into the house, estate, or monastery and allowed unlawful parasynaxes and assemblies to be held there—if he is of low and degraded condition—shall be publicly beaten with clubs, both as his own punishment and as an example to others; 245 but if they are persons of respectable status, they shall be compelled to pay ten pounds of gold to Our treasury as a fine. [Note: Crabb adds “in addition.”]

Moreover, We order that no Apollinarianist or Eutychianist aspire to any military service [Note: Quesnell, after two points, continues: “unless they are found in a cohort or frontier unit,” etc. The Vindobonensis deletes “and,” which makes the defect and abrupt transition in this passage clearer, caused by the repetition of “cohort” and “frontier unit” in the complete text. We have supplied the words from the Vatican Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts and Merlinus. Crabb agrees, except that he reads “unless they are found outside the aforesaid military service.” The Oxford manuscript corruptly reads *cohortulianam*. Crabb reads *cohortalitiam*; the better reading in both places is *cohortalinam*, as in the Vatican Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts.] except in a cohort or frontier unit. But if any are found serving outside a cohort or frontier unit, they shall be stripped of their belts and deprived of association with respectable persons and with the palace; [Note: Crabb, together with Vatican 1322, reads “nor in any other”; somewhat later, “metropolitan.”] nor shall they reside in any city, village, or district other than that in which they were born.

If any were born in this flourishing city, they shall be expelled from both the most sacred imperial household and every metropolitan city throughout the provinces. [Note: The Vatican Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts read “from the most sacred retinue.”]

No Eutychianist or Apollinarianist shall be permitted publicly or privately to summon gatherings, assemble circles, debate the heretical error, or assert the perversity of the criminal doctrine. [Note: Crabb adds “and to debate in the manner of heretics.” The Oxford codex reads “error” instead of “doctrine”; Quesnell alone reads “to assert” instead of “to affirm”; Crabb reads “let there be authority.”]

Nor shall anyone be permitted to dictate, write, publish, or issue anything against the venerable Council of Chalcedon, or to produce the replies of others concerning the same matter [Note: Merlinus, together with the Vatican, Spanish, and Isidorian manuscripts, omits the next six words. A little later Vatican 1322 reads “to produce rescripts”]; and no one shall dare to possess books of this kind or preserve sacrilegious memorials of their writings. If anyone is found guilty of these crimes, let him be condemned to perpetual deportation.

But those who, out of a desire to learn, listen to people debating the accursed heresy shall, We order, suffer the expense of ten pounds of gold, which must be paid into Our treasury. All such documents and books containing the deadly doctrine of Eutyches—that is, of Apollinaris—shall be consumed by fire, so that the traces of the criminal perversity may perish, burned by the flames themselves.

For it is just that the most monstrous sacrileges should be struck by punishment of equal magnitude, dearest and most beloved Palladius. Therefore let Your illustrious and magnificent authority cause what We have decreed by this most sacred constitution to be brought to everyone’s knowledge, in this flourishing city, in the various provinces, and especially in the city of Alexandria and throughout the entire diocese of Egypt, by the customary posting of edicts: so that all the severity We have established may immediately be exercised against those found guilty. [Note: Vatican 1322 reads “against them”; Vatican, Spanish, and Isidorian manuscripts, with Crabb, read “against those.”]

Let the governors of the provinces, their attendants, and also the defenders of the cities know that if they either neglect to observe what We have decreed must be guarded by the most devout sanction of this law, or permit it to be violated through any rashness, they shall be compelled to pay a fine of ten pounds of gold into Our treasury [Note: Crabb adds “in addition”] and shall further suffer danger to their reputation.

Let those provisions also which We decreed by Our law of perpetual validity concerning pagans throughout the Roman Empire be enforced with the utmost urgency against those who are found to celebrate profane rites, the impious worship of idols, and sacrileges forbidden to them. [Note: Quesnell deletes “those things” and later prints “against them.” We have deleted “against” with the Vindobonensis and Vatican 1322, and therefore it was necessary to insert “those things” with Crabb and the Vatican Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts.]

Given on the Kalends of August, at Constantinople, in the consulship of the divine Augustus Valentinianus and the illustrious man Anthemius. [Note: The Vatican Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts, with Crabb, read “on the day of the Kalends of August, at Constantinople, in the consulship of the divine Valentinianus” (Crabb adds “Augustus”) “and Anthemius, etc.” The numeral VIII is necessary, as it designates the consulship of the year 455.]

## CHAPTER XXIX

[Note: This chapter occurs in the manuscripts of the present collection, Vatican Regina 1987, Colbertinus of Lucca, Vatican 1342, Corbeiensis, Dionysius, Spanish, Hadrianus, and Isidorus.]

Decretal Letter of Pope Siricius to Himerius, Bishop of Tarragona, under sixteen headings.

[Note: The words “under sixteen headings” are absent from the Vindobonensis codex but occur in Thuanus. The general table prefixed to this collection lists fifteen chapters, because Himerius proposed that many consultation topics. Here, however, the designation of sixteen headings includes the instruction by which Siricius orders Himerius to bring his responses to the fifteen topics to the knowledge of the other bishops. Only fifteen headings are found not only in Dionysius but also in Vatican 1342. In Vatican Regina, there is only a division into seven headings, which we shall indicate in their proper places. In the Vindobonensis manuscript, the headings were added by a second hand in the margin of each chapter, in nearly the same wording as that found in Dionysius; they therefore appear to be a later addition. Indeed, in other manuscripts of this collection the headings are either absent or sometimes replaced by different ones. Compare below notes 37 and 47 (Column 559, note g; Column 561, note f).]

SIRICIUS [Note: Some manuscripts, together with Vatican Regina 1997 and Vatican 1342, read “Hierius.”] to Himerius, Bishop of Tarragona.

The report of your brotherhood, addressed to our predecessor Damasus of holy memory, found me already established in his see, because the Lord so ordained [Note: This is the reading of all the common editions and manuscripts, including Thuanus. Quesnell alone, together with the Oxford codex, reads “because the Lord so willed.”]. When we read it more carefully in the assembly of the brethren, we found in it as many things deserving criticism and correction as we would have wished to find worthy of praise.

And because it was necessary for us to succeed to the labors and cares of the one whom, by God’s grace, we have succeeded in office, after first giving, as was proper, an indication of my advancement, we do not refuse to answer each of your questions with a suitable response, insofar as the Lord has deigned to assist us. For, considering the responsibility of our office, we are not free to dissemble or remain silent, since a zeal for the Christian religion greater than that of all others rests upon us. [Note: Quesnell alone reads “for the law,” and shortly afterward omits “these words.”]

We bear the burdens of all who are burdened; indeed, blessed Peter the apostle bears these burdens in us, and, as we trust, protects and guards us in all things as the heirs of his administration.

[Note: Heading in the margin of the Vindobonensis: “On not rebaptizing Arians.” Heading in Vatican Regina: “On receiving heretics without an unlawful repetition of baptism, but by the invocation of the sevenfold Spirit.”]

### I

At the very beginning of your letter you noted that many who had been baptized by the impious Arians were hastening to the catholic faith, and that some of our brothers wished to baptize those same people again. This is not permitted, since the apostle forbids it, the canons oppose it, and the general decrees sent to the provinces by my predecessor Liberius, of revered memory, after the Council of Ariminum had been annulled, prohibit it. We admit these people, together with the Novatianists and other heretics, as was established in the synod, to the fellowship of the Catholics through the sole invocation of the sevenfold Spirit and the imposition of the bishop’s hand; and the whole East and West observe this practice. It is therefore not fitting for you henceforth to deviate from this path, if you do not wish to be separated from our episcopal college by synodal judgment.

[Note: Heading in the margin of the Vindobonensis: “That baptism should not be celebrated except at Easter and Pentecost.” The common Councils edition, together with Dionysius, Justellus, and Isidorus, reads: “It follows concerning the various times for baptizing, as follows,” etc.]

### II

There follows the reprehensible and correctable confusion concerning the times of baptism, according as it has pleased each person. Our fellow priests presume upon this—not, as we say with indignation, through any rational authority, but through sheer recklessness—so that freely and indiscriminately, on the festivals of Christ’s birth or manifestation, and also on the feasts of the apostles or martyrs, innumerable crowds, as you report, receive the mystery of baptism.

Yet Easter, together with its Pentecost, claims this privilege as specially belonging to the Lord, both among us and among all Churches. On these days alone throughout the year it is fitting that the general sacraments of baptism be administered to those who come to the faith, and only to those chosen persons who enrolled their names forty or more days beforehand and have been purified by daily exorcisms, prayers, and fasts, so that the apostolic command may be fulfilled: once the old leaven has been purged, the new dough may begin to exist.

Therefore, just as we say that the reverence due to Easter must in no respect be diminished, so we wish infants who are not yet able to speak because of their age, and those for whom the saving water of baptism is necessary in any emergency, to be assisted with all speed [Note: Coustant, together with the common Councils edition, adds “sacred”; but he notes that three codices, Colbertinus and Pithoeanus, omit it. Three of our own codices—the Vindobonensis, Vatican Regina, and another Vatican manuscript—also omit it.], lest it lead to the destruction of our souls if, when the saving font is denied to those who desire it, someone departs from this world and loses both the kingdom and life.

Likewise, whoever encounters the danger of shipwreck, an enemy attack, the uncertainty of siege, or the desperation of any bodily illness, and asks to be aided by the single support of faith, let him receive, at that very moment when he asks, the rewards of the rebirth he has sought [Note: Quesnell reads “therefore.” We have preferred the other common reading, supported by the Vindobonensis and Vatican manuscripts. Shortly afterward, the Vindobonensis and Vatican Regina, together with Merlinus and other manuscripts of Coustant, read “the desperation of bodily illness.”]

Let the error in this matter end here. Now let all priests observe the rule stated above, if they do not wish to be torn away from the solidity of the apostolic rock upon which Christ built the universal Church. [Note: Vatican 1342 reads “founded.”]

[Note: Heading in the margin of the Vindobonensis: “On apostates.”]

### III

It has also been added that certain Christians have passed into apostasy—which it is forbidden even to say—and have been profaned by the worship of idols and the pollution of sacrifices. We order that they be cut off from the body and blood of Christ, by which they had previously been redeemed through rebirth.

If at some time they should repent and turn to lamentation, they must perform penance for as long as they live, and at the end of their life the grace of reconciliation is to be granted to them. For, as the Lord teaches, we do not desire the death of a sinner, but only that he should turn and live. [Note: The Vatican Regina and another Vatican manuscript, together with Coustant, read “so that he may turn.”]

[Note: Heading in the Vindobonensis: “When it is not permitted to take another man’s betrothed as a wife.” Dionysius reads “to take her in marriage.” In Vatican Regina [Column 0557C], this is chapter 2, with the heading “How women are to be veiled.” In Justellus it begins: “But concerning the violation of marriages.” In the later printed Councils edition after the Roman edition: “But concerning the violation of marriage.” See also what we said concerning the bridal veil in note 16 on the Sacramentary, September, volume II, column 130 (our volume II, column 129, note d).]

### IV

You asked concerning the bridal veil, whether one man may take in marriage a girl betrothed to another. [Note: Another manuscript reads “in marriage.”] We absolutely forbid this from taking place, because, among the faithful, the blessing that the priest bestows upon a bride is equivalent to a kind of sacrilege if it is violated by any transgression.

## CHAPTER V

[Note: Heading in the Vindobonensis: “Concerning those who have not at all kept their penance.”]

### V

Your Love has not inappropriately judged that the apostolic see should be consulted concerning those who, after performing penance, like dogs and pigs returning to their vomit and wallowing [Note: Quesnell alone adds “to vomit and the mire.”], have again desired the military belt, theatrical pleasures, new marriages, and forbidden sexual relations. Their professed lack of restraint has been exposed by the children born after their absolution. Since they now have no refuge in further penance, we have decided that the following rule must be established: they are to be joined to the faithful within the Church by prayer alone; they may attend the celebration of the sacred mysteries, although they do not deserve to do so; but they must be excluded from the banquet of the Lord’s table.

Thus restrained at least by this severity, they may both punish their own errors within themselves and provide an example to others, so that they may be drawn away from shameful desires. Nevertheless, since they fell through the weakness of the flesh, We wish them to be strengthened by the provision for the journey through the grace of communion when they begin to depart to the Lord. [Note: This is the reading of our manuscripts, the Vindobonensis and Vatican Regina, together with Coustant and the printed editions. Quesnell reads “by the gift of viaticum.” Dionysius and Justellus read: “Nevertheless, we wish those … to be assisted.”]

We judge that the same rule must be observed concerning women who, after penance, have bound themselves by such pollutions.

## CHAPTER VI

**[Col. 0557D] Title.** In the Vindobonensis: “Concerning monks and virgins who do not keep their profession.” In the Codex Vaticanus Reginae this is chapter 3, preceded by the title “Concerning the fall of monks or nuns,” which, according to Coustant, is found in the Colbertinus manuscript of another collection.

**VI.** Moreover, we have learned that certain monks and nuns, having abandoned their holy profession, have plunged into such wantonness that at first, secretly and as though under the pretext of monasteries, they joined themselves in illicit and sacrilegious intercourse; but afterward, driven into the abyss of despair of conscience, they freely fathered children from their illicit embraces—something condemned both by the public laws and by ecclesiastical regulations. We therefore order that these shameless and detestable persons be expelled from the fellowship of monasteries and from the assemblies of the churches, so that, confined in their own prisons and lamenting so great a crime in continual mourning, they may be able to be refined in the purifying fire of repentance; so that at least at death, out of regard for mercy alone, forgiveness may come to their aid through the grace of communion. **[p. 250]**

[Note, **Col. 0557D**: Thus the first hand in the Vindobonensis manuscript; the second hand, together with other manuscripts of other collections and printed editions, reads *sanctitatis*, “of holiness.”]

[Note, **Col. 0558D**: The Thuanus manuscript reads *in abruptam conscientiae desperationem*, “into the abrupt despair of conscience.” Shortly afterward, instead of *libere*, “freely,” the Oxford manuscript has *illicite*, “illicitly,” wrongly.]

[Note, **Col. 0558D**: The Oxford manuscript deletes *poenitudinis*, “of repentance.”]

## CHAPTER VII

**[Col. 0558A] Title.** In the Vindobonensis: “Concerning incontinent clerics.” Shortly afterward, instead of *ad sacratissimos ordines*, “to the most sacred orders,” Quesnell reads *ad sanctissimos*, “to the holiest.” We have restored the reading of the other editions from all our manuscripts.

**VII.** Let us now come to the most sacred orders of the clergy. We have learned, through your communication, that they have been so trampled upon and confused throughout your provinces, to the injury of venerable religion, that we must say in the words of Jeremiah: “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may weep for this people day and night?” (Jeremiah 7:1).

If, then, the blessed prophet said that his tears were insufficient for mourning the sins of the people, how greatly must we be stricken with grief when we are compelled to lament the crimes of those who belong to our own body? Especially since, according to the blessed Paul, “the daily pressure and anxiety of all the churches” continually rests upon us. “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not inflamed?” (2 Corinthians 2:29). **[Col. 0558B]**

For we have learned that very many priests of Christ and Levites, after long years of consecration, have fathered children both from their own marriages and from shameful intercourse, and defend their crime by this pretext: that in the Old Testament priests and ministers are said to have been granted the ability to beget children.

Let that devotee of lust and teacher of vices now tell me whether he thinks that in the law of Moses the reins of licentiousness were everywhere loosened for the sacred orders by the Lord. Why, then, does He admonish those entrusted with the Holy of Holies, saying: “Be holy, because I am holy, the Lord your God” (Leviticus 20:7)? **[Col. 0558C]**

Why also were the priests ordered to live far from their own homes in the temple during the year of their service? Clearly, this was so that they could not engage in carnal intercourse even with their wives, and, shining with integrity of conscience, could offer God an acceptable gift. After the completion of their service, marital relations had been permitted solely for the sake of succession, because no one except one from the tribe of Levi had been commanded to be admitted to God’s ministry.

Therefore, when the Lord Jesus had enlightened us by His coming, He declared in the Gospel that He had not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it; **[p. 251]** and for this reason He wished the Church, whose bridegroom He is, to radiate the splendor of chastity, so that on the day of judgment, when He comes again, He might find her, as He established through His Apostle, without stain or wrinkle.

[Note, **Col. 0558D**: Other editions say that He “declares that He came to fulfill, not abolish, the law.” These final words are likewise found in two Vatican Reginae manuscripts and another Vatican manuscript. In the Vindobonensis the words *sed implere*, “but to fulfill,” are omitted.]

**[Col. 0559A]** All priests and Levites are bound by the unbreakable law of these decrees to dedicate both our hearts and our bodies to sobriety and chastity from the day of our ordination, provided that in all things we please our God in the sacrifices we offer daily. “Those who are in the flesh,” says the chosen vessel, “cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you” (Romans 8:9; 1 Corinthians 3:16; 2 Corinthians 6:16). And where could the Spirit of God dwell, unless in holy bodies, as we read?

Since some of those about whom we speak, as your Holiness has reported, lament that they fell through ignorance, we declare that mercy must not be denied them on this condition: without any increase of honor, they shall remain for as long as they live in the office in which they were discovered, provided that thereafter they strive to show themselves continent.

But those who rely on the excuse of an illicit privilege, asserting that this was permitted to them by the ancient law, should know that by the authority of the Apostolic See they have been removed from every ecclesiastical honor of which they made unworthy use; **[Col. 0559B]** nor can they ever touch the venerable mysteries from which they deprived themselves while they longed after shameful desires.

And because present examples warn us to guard against such things in the future, if any bishop, presbyter, or deacon—something we do not wish—should henceforth be found in such a condition, let him understand that we have now closed to him every avenue of indulgence. For wounds that have not felt the medicine of poultices must necessarily be cut out with the sword.

[Notes, **Col. 0558D–0559C**: Quesnell alone omits *indesinenter*, “continually.” Vatican 1342, together with two Colbertinus manuscripts cited by Coustant, reads “trampled canons through charity”; with that reading, *a quibus*, “by whom,” would have to be read shortly before instead of *quos*, “whom.”]

[Note, **Col. 0558D**: The Vulgate, together with the Vatican Reginae manuscript, reads *et ego sanctus sum*, “and I am holy.” We added *Deus*, “God,” from the Vindobonensis manuscript and the other printed editions.]

[Note, **Col. 0558D**: The Vulgate, together with most manuscripts, reads *tam de conjugibus propriis, quam etiam de turpi coitu*, “both from their own wives and from shameful intercourse.” The Vindobonensis reads *de conjugibus*, “from wives.”]

[Note, **Col. 0559C**: In the Vindobonensis, together with some printed editions, *si*, “if,” is deleted.]

[Note, **Col. 0559C**: The Vatican Reginae manuscript reads *opere*, “service” or “work,” instead of *honore*, “honor.”]

[Note, **Col. 0559C**: All the manuscript and printed copies except Quesnell’s read *omnem per nos indulgentiae aditum intelligat esse obseratum*, “let him understand that every avenue of indulgence is closed to him by us.” Quesnell reads *omnem per nos intelligat aditum esse obseratum*.]

## CHAPTER VIII

**[Col. 0559C] Title.** In the Vindobonensis: “Concerning which clerics may be promoted.” This title differs from that of the Dionysian collection. In the Vatican Reginae this is chapter 4, preceded by the title “The metropolitan is endangered when he ordains one unworthily.” The old Corbeiensis manuscript agrees: “Endanger that metropolitan by whom someone has been unworthily ordained.” Shortly afterward, we have written *licenter*, “freely,” from the Vindobonensis and Vatican 1342 manuscripts, with which the other printed editions agree. Quesnell reads *libenter*, “willingly.”

**VIII.** We have also learned that men of unexamined life, even those who have had numerous marriages, licentiously and freely aspire, as each desires, to the aforementioned dignities. We attribute this not so much to those who reach them through immoderate ambition as especially to the metropolitan bishops, who, by conniving at forbidden attempts, disregard, insofar as it lies with them, the commands of our Lord.

And, to leave aside what we suspect to be even more serious, where is that which our Lord established through the law given by Moses, saying: “My priests shall marry only once”; and elsewhere: “A priest shall take a virgin as wife, not a widow, not one repudiated, not a prostitute” (Ezekiel 44:22)? **[Col. 0560A]**

Following this, the Apostle—once a persecutor and then a preacher—commanded that both a priest and a deacon must be “the husband of one wife” (1 Timothy 3:2). All these provisions are so despised by the bishops of your regions that one would think they had been established expressly to the contrary.

And since we must not neglect such usurpations, lest the just voice of the indignant Lord rebuke us, saying: “You saw a thief and ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers” (Psalm 49:18), we decree by a general pronouncement what all the churches must henceforth follow and what they must avoid.

[Note, **Col. 0559D**: Quesnell alone deletes *magis*, “rather”; shortly afterward he reads *percellat*, “strike,” instead of *corripiat*, “rebuke.” We follow the Vulgate and the manuscripts. The Vatican Reginae reads: “Let him justly rebuke the one who says.”]

## CHAPTER IX

**[Col. 0559D] Title.** In the Vindobonensis: “Concerning the conduct of clerics.” In the Vatican Reginae this is chapter 5, with the title “How long clerics must remain in each grade in order to reach the episcopate.” The Corbeiensis collection has exactly the same title. The Pithoeanus and Colbertinus manuscripts of this collection have another title: “Through how many grades an acolyte, subdeacon, deacon, presbyter, or bishop is made.” **[Col. 0560C]**

**IX.** Whoever, therefore, has dedicated himself to the service of the Church from childhood ought to be baptized before the years of puberty and joined to the ministry of the readers. **[Col. 0560B]** If, from the beginning of adolescence until the thirtieth year of his life, he has lived commendably, he must be content with one wife only—one whom he received as a virgin with the common blessing given through a priest—and he must be an acolyte and subdeacon. After this he may advance to the grade of the diaconate, if he first proves himself worthy by leading the way in continence. If he serves commendably there for more than five years, he may suitably attain the presbyterate. Then, after ten years, he may obtain the episcopal chair, provided that during these periods the integrity of his life and faith has been approved.

[Note, **Col. 0560C–D**: Eleven manuscripts cited by Coustant delete *ab*, “from.” Thereafter, Vatican 1342 reads *ad XX aetatis suae annum*, “until the twentieth year of his life,” instead of *ad tricesimum*, “until the thirtieth.” This reading seems more accurate, for Zosimus, who had these letters of Siricius before his eyes in his letter to Hesychius, says: “If he gave his name to ecclesiastical ministries from childhood, let him remain continuously among the readers until the twentieth year of his life.”]

## CHAPTER X

**[Col. 0560D] Title.** In the Vindobonensis: “Concerning the elderly.” In the Vatican Reginae, where this is chapter 6: “Concerning one who, already elderly, wishes to pass from the laity to the clergy.” Shortly afterward, the Vulgate, the Councils after the Roman edition, and Dionysius of Justellus read “conduct” instead of “conversion.”

**X.** But if someone already advanced in age, stirred by a conversion to a better purpose, hastens from the lay state to the sacred service, he will obtain the fruit of his desire only if, at the very time when he is baptized, he is immediately enrolled among the readers or exorcists—provided it is established that he has had or has only one wife, and that he took her as a virgin.

Once he has been initiated, after completing two years he shall be an acolyte and subdeacon for another five years; and thus he may be advanced to the diaconate if during these periods he is judged worthy. Thereafter, with the passage of time, he may be admitted to the presbyterate or episcopate if the election of the clergy and people has called him to it. **[p. 253]**

[Notes, **Col. 0560D**: Vatican 1342 reads “let him be promoted.” The same manuscript, together with the Pithoeanus and Colbertinus Lucensis manuscripts, reads *edecumarit*. Coustant preferred this reading because *edecumare* means “to choose one out of ten as especially outstanding and most worthy of all.” The Vatican Reginae and another Colbertinus read “if there has been an election of clergy and people in his favor.” Thuanus and Colbertinus read “if the election follows him.” The royal exemplar of Dionysius reads “if an election has taken place.”]

## CHAPTER XI

**[Col. 0561C] Title.** In the Vindobonensis: “That a cleric who takes a second wife is to be deposed.” Shortly afterward, several manuscripts and editions add *aut viduam*, “or a widow.”

**XI.** Any cleric who takes a widow, or certainly a second wife, shall immediately be stripped of every privilege of ecclesiastical dignity, with only lay communion granted to him. He may retain even that only if thereafter he commits nothing on account of which he might lose it.

## CHAPTER XII

**[Col. 0561C] Title.** In the Vindobonensis: “Which women may live with clerics.”

**XII.** We permit no women to live in the houses of clerics except those whom the Council of Nicaea permitted to dwell with them solely because of necessary family relationships.

## CHAPTER XIII

**[Col. 0561C] Title.** In the Vindobonensis: “Concerning the promotion of monks.”

**XIII.** We both desire and command that monks whom the seriousness of their character and the holy discipline of their life and faith commend be added to the offices of the clergy. Those who are under thirty years of age are to be advanced through the minor orders one grade at a time as their years increase, and thus, through consecration at a mature age, they may arrive at the distinction of the diaconate or presbyterate. **[Col. 0561B]** They must not immediately leap to the summit of the episcopate, unless the same periods that we prescribed above for each dignity have been observed in their case.

[Note, **Col. 0561D**: The Vulgate Council editions after the Roman edition add *digni*, “worthy.” Shortly afterward, the Vatican Reginae and the second hand in the Vindobonensis manuscript, like the Vulgate, read *promoveantur ordinibus*, “let them be promoted through the orders.”]

[Note, **Col. 0561D**: The two Colbertinus manuscripts and Coustant’s German manuscript read “and not immediately to”; the Vatican Reginae, together with three manuscripts of the same collection, “and not even to”; the Corbeiensis with several others, “and not by a leap.” The printed editions, based on both readings and on the manuscripts of our collection, read “and not immediately by a leap to.” Isidore, with Merlin and Crabbe, reads “and not through leaps.” Shortly afterward, the Vatican Reginae deletes *superius*, “above.”]

## CHAPTER XIV

**[Col. 0561D] Title.** In the Vindobonensis: “That a penitent may not become a cleric.” In two other manuscripts of this collection, Thuanus and Pithoeanus, it reads: “Those who were formerly vessels of vices must not attain the honor of the clergy.” The Vatican Reginae marks this as chapter 7, with the title “That lay penitents ought to attain no honor.”
