**XIV.** It was also fitting for us to take care that, just as no cleric is permitted to perform penance, so after repentance and reconciliation no layman may ever obtain the honor of the clergy. For although they may have been cleansed from the contagion of all sins, they ought nevertheless to receive none of the instruments for administering the sacraments, since they were formerly vessels of vices.

## CHAPTER XV

**[Col. 0561D] Title.** In the Vindobonensis: “That if a penitent bigamist, or the husband of a widow, has become a cleric through ignorance, he is not to be promoted.” Shortly afterward, the Vatican Reginae, Dionysius of Justellus, and Coustant prefer “in all these matters,” with the preposition *in* deleted. **[Col. 0562C]**

**XV.** And since, in all the matters that come under censure, the only excuse advanced is ignorance—which, for the time being, we must mercifully forgive solely out of regard for compassion—whoever, whether a penitent, a bigamist, or the husband of a widow, has improperly and incompetently entered the sacred service, is to understand that we have granted him pardon on this condition: he must count it a great benefit if, with every hope of promotion taken away, he remains permanently in the order in which he is found.

[Note, **Col. 0562C**: Another reading is *provectionis*, “of advancement.”]

[Note, **Col. 0562C**: Quesnell reads *sciantque*, “and let them know,” against the other printed editions and the ancient manuscript codices.]

Henceforth, let the chief bishops of all the provinces know that if they should presume to admit any such person to the sacred orders, an appropriate sentence will be issued by the Apostolic See both against them and against the status of those whom they have promoted contrary to the canons and to our prohibitions. **[Col. 0562A]**

## CHAPTER XVI

**XVI.** We have, I think, dearest brother, explained all the matters that were arranged for complaint, and have given, as far as I judge, sufficient answers to the individual cases which you reported through our son Bassianus the presbyter to the Roman Church, as to the head of your body.

Now we urge your fraternal spirit more and more earnestly to preserve the canons and maintain the decretal enactments, so that you may cause what we have written in reply to your consultations to be brought to the attention of all our fellow bishops—not only those established in your diocese, but also all the Carthaginians, Baeticans, Lusitanians, and Gauls, or those who border on you in the neighboring provinces. Under cover of your letters, let these provisions, which we have established in a salutary ordinance, be sent to them. **[Col. 0562B]**

Although no priest of the Lord is free to be ignorant of the venerable decrees of the Apostolic See or of the authoritative definitions of the canons, it may nevertheless be more useful, and particularly honorable to your affection in view of the antiquity of your priesthood, if what has been written to you generally but specifically in your name is brought, through your united concern, to the knowledge of all our brethren.

Thus both what we have prudently and not inconsiderately established with the greatest caution and deliberation for the sake of health may remain inviolate, and access may be closed to every excuse in the future—an access that from now on can be open to no one among us.

Given on the fourth day before the Ides of February, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Arcadius and Bauto.

[Note, **Col. 0562D**: Thus the Vatican Reginae and Lucensis manuscripts, together with three reliable exemplars cited by Coustant. Elsewhere, together with the Vindobonensis manuscript and the other editions, *III idus*, “the third day before the Ides,” is read. Shortly afterward, the words *viris clarissimis*, “the most illustrious men,” which create some difficulty, are absent, according to Coustant, from the older manuscripts, including the royal exemplar of the pure Dionysian text. This chronological notice is absent from Vatican 1342.]

# CHAPTER XXX

[Note, **Col. 0562D–0564C**: Besides the manuscripts of this collection, Hispana and Isidore, we found this letter in two other collections, namely Vatican 1342 and the Dionysian Additions, that is, in Vatican 5845 and Vallicellianus A 5. The inscription given here is found in the Vindobonensis and Thuanus manuscripts of this collection, as well as in the Hispana and Isidorian manuscripts. The latter add: “against Jovinian the heretic and his associates, who are to be removed from the unity of the Church.” Saint Isidore of Seville, in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 3, confirms our inscription, writing that this letter was sent to various bishops.

Two collections that we found give the title as follows: “Letter of Pope Siricius sent throughout, or to all, the bishops.” Therefore Coustant wrongly attributes it to a lapse of memory by Mabillon when Mabillon produced this inscription from the Vallicellian manuscript in his *Italian Journey*.

Two other inscriptions are extant which we have found in no manuscripts: one in the editions of the Councils after Crabbe, “Siricius to the Milanese Church”; the other in Quesnell, “Letter of Pope Siricius to all the bishops of Italy concerning the condemnation of Jovinian and the other heretics who detract from virginity.”]

**Letter of Pope Siricius sent to various bishops**

I would always wish, dearest brothers, to announce joys to the sincerity of your affection and peace, so that, as letters passed back and forth, those joys might be fostered by the evidence of well-being. **[Col. 0563A]**

[Note, **Col. 0563C**: The Council edition, together with the Vallicellian manuscript, reads “to the sincerity of your affection and peace”; Coustant reads “to the sincerity of your affection and peace.” The Vulgate adds *vestrae*, “your.” Shortly afterward, the Dionysian Additions manuscripts, together with the printed Council editions, read *indicio juvaremur*, “we might be aided by evidence”; Merlin reads *indicia juvarentur*, “the evidences might be aided”; Quesnell reads *indicio juvaretur*, “it might be aided by evidence.” With Coustant, and in agreement with most manuscripts, we have preferred *indicio juvarentur*, “those joys might be fostered by evidence.”]

But because the ancient enemy does not permit us to remain at rest, free from his assault—the liar from the beginning, the enemy of truth, the rival of man (whom, in order to deceive him, he first deceived himself), the adversary of chastity, the teacher of lust—he feeds upon acts of cruelty and must be punished by abstinence. He hates fasting, and while his ministers proclaim that fasts are superfluous, he says, without hope concerning the future, in the words of the Apostle: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (1 Corinthians 15:32). **[Col. 0563B]**

[Note, **Col. 0563C–D**: The Roman edition reads “he never allows us to remain at rest from his assault.” The Vallicellian and both Vatican manuscripts likewise have “he allows us to remain at rest.” The Oxford manuscript reads “to remain at rest from his attack.” The Vindobonensis likewise reads “from his assault.”]

[Note, **Col. 0563D**: The Roman edition reads “he is punished”; Quesnell reads “he is tormented.” We follow all our manuscripts and Coustant. Shortly afterward, the Vindobonensis manuscript has “disciples” instead of “ministers.”]

O unhappy boldness! O cunning of a desperate mind! The previously unknown discourse of the heretics was already creeping through the Church like a cancer, so that, seizing the breast, it might plunge the whole person into death.

And unless the Lord of Hosts had broken the snare that he had prepared, the spectacle of so great an evil and the exposure of its hypocrisy would have drawn many simple hearts into ruin, because the human mind is easily led toward the worse, wishing to fly through broad spaces rather than travel the narrow road with labor.

[Note, **Col. 0563D**: Another edition reads “preferring to walk through spacious places.” Hispana and Isidore read “preferring to walk along the spacious way.” Shortly afterward, the Vallicellian and Vatican manuscripts read “through toil.”]

For this reason it was entirely necessary, beloved of me, to entrust to your knowledge what has happened here, so that through ignorance of any priest the Church might not be polluted by the contagion of the worst men who are breaking into it under a religious name.

As it is written, the Lord says: “Many come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves; you will recognize them by their fruits” (Matthew 7:11). These are the men who, as though for some advantage, proclaim themselves Christians, so that, walking under the veil of a pious name, they enter the house of prayer and pour forth the discourse of a serpentine argument, “to shoot in the dark at those who are upright in heart” (Psalm 10:23), and, turning them away from Catholic truth, lead them in devilish fashion into the frenzy of their doctrine and defraud the simplicity of the sheep. **[Col. 0564A]**

[Note, **Col. 0563D–0564C**: This wording is found in all our manuscripts of the three collections—the Vindobonensis, Vatican 1342, Vallicellianus, and Vatican 5845—together with the Pithoeanus and Colbertinus. Another Colbertinus reads “who, as though with some usefulness.” Since Quesnell did not approve this, he substituted “who, under the poverty of clothing.” That substitution is supported by no manuscript and is also opposed to what Saint Jerome says about Jovinian in Books I and II, where he states that Jovinian, after laying aside the clothing of a monk, adopted linen and silk. Coustant preferred the common manuscript reading of Hispana and Isidore: “who subtly boast that they are Christians.” We have not deleted the reading preferred by the ancient manuscripts of our collection and by those of other ancient collections, although it does not seem entirely certain.]

We have indeed learned and tested the malignity of many heresies, from the apostles down to the present day; but never have such dogs wearied the Church’s mystery with their barking as these enemies of the faith, now suddenly bursting forth while a treacherous doctrine sprouts, have revealed by the fruits of their words whose disciples they are. **[Col. 0564B]**

[Note, **Col. 0564C**: Thuanus deletes *canes*, “dogs.” Quesnell adds in the margin: “Read *latrantes*, ‘barking,’ namely, ‘wearied.’” Vatican 5845 reads “drove away” instead of “wearied.” The Roman edition reads “such as these enemies of the faith, suddenly breaking forth, polluted by the doctrine of perfidy, who, by the fruits of their words, have revealed whose disciples they are.” The reading in the text is that of the other manuscripts, except Vatican 1312 and Vallicellianus, which, with Thuanus and the printed Council editions, have *polluta*, “polluted.”]

For while other heretics, by misunderstanding, have proposed to themselves individual kinds of questions to overthrow and tear apart from the divine institutions, these men, having no wedding garment, wound Catholics by perverting—as I have said—the continence of the New and Old Testaments and interpreting it in a diabolical spirit.

By seductive and counterfeit speech they have already begun to devastate some Christians and associate them with their madness, while containing within themselves the poison of their wickedness.

[Note, **Col. 0564C**: The Vallicellian and Vatican 5845 manuscripts, together with the other common editions, read *sauciantes*, “wounding.” Shortly afterward, the words “and interpreting in a diabolical spirit” are absent from the Oxford manuscript and the Roman edition.]

[Note, **Col. 0564C**: The reading is taken from our manuscripts and all the printed editions, except that the Council edition, together with the Thuanus manuscript, reads “several Christians.” Quesnell alone reads “some Romans.”]

[Note, **Col. 0564C–D**: Quesnell adds “not,” but no manuscript of ours or of Coustant supports it.]

But, enticed, they publicly revealed their blasphemies in a reckless written statement, and, driven on by the fury of a desperate mind, they publicly proclaimed everywhere the frenzy of the pagans. **[Col. 0565A]**

[Note, **Col. 0564D–0565B**: After the word “poison,” the Roman edition adds: “They proclaimed their blasphemies in a reckless written statement, presenting themselves as though chosen; and their desperate…” Quesnell reads: “But their chosen men proclaimed their blasphemies…” The word “their,” which is absent from most manuscripts, seems to Coustant an interpolation, as though Jovinian and his associates had, like the Manichaeans, their own “chosen.” No one has recorded this. Coustant himself preferred “But, having been exposed, they proclaimed their blasphemies…” if the reading *detecti* were supported by some manuscript. We have accepted Labbe’s reading, “But, enticed, they publicly revealed their blasphemies,” which is supported by two Colbertinus and one Pithoeanus manuscript of our collection.]

[Note, **Col. 0564D–0565B**: The Roman edition reads “they revealed themselves everywhere in favor of the pagans.” Coustant, with Crabbe, reads “they publicly proclaimed everywhere in favor of the pagans.” Our Vallicellian and both Vatican manuscripts read “everywhere into the frenzy,” or “in the frenzy,” “of the pagans publicly by the most faithful.” The Vindobonensis, together with other ancient manuscripts, reads “they proclaimed publicly by the most faithful,” leaving an evident lacuna, which Quesnell supplied as follows: “they proclaimed. But their madness was revealed by the most faithful.” We have thought that only the word “but” should be supplied, together with the other editions, although none of our manuscripts supports it.]

But a horrifying written statement seems to have been brought to my humility by faithful Christians, men noble in birth and distinguished in religion, so that, once exposed by priestly judgment as contrary to the divine law, it might be destroyed by a spiritual sentence.

[Note, **Col. 0565C**: Quesnell reads: “It seems to have been brought through an honorable writing, so that, once the contrary had been exposed…” The Roman edition reads: “They seem to have been brought by a horrifying writing, so that, once exposed…” We have restored the earlier common reading with Coustant, especially since it is supported by the manuscripts of our collection, in which *honorifica* appears only as the erroneous *honorica*. A horrifying writing is so called because it was earlier termed a reckless written statement. Saint Jerome says of Jovinian’s writings in Book VII: “There is such barbarism in Jovinian’s writings, and his speech is so confused by so many faults, that I could understand neither what he was saying nor by what arguments he wished to prove what he said.” Our Vallicellian and two Vatican manuscripts, 1342 and 5845, read “so that they might be destroyed” instead of “so that it might be destroyed.”]

For our part, we do not disdain the vows of marriage, which we attend while the veil is present; but we honor with greater distinction virgins whom marriage gives birth to as women devoted to God.

[Note, **Col. 0565C–D**: The Vallicellian and Vatican manuscripts, together with the ancient printed Council editions, read “we do not disdain marriages.” Labbe and Coustant read “not disdaining.” The Roman edition reads “we attended the veils”; but the virgins whom marriages create, devoted to God, we honor. Merlinus omits the words “which marriages create,” together with two cited Vatican manuscripts. Labbe and Vatican 1342 read “we venerate” instead of “we honor”; two other manuscripts read “we revered.”]

When the presbytery had therefore been assembled, it was established that it was contrary to our doctrine, that is, to Christian law.

[Note, **Col. 0565D**: The printed Council editions read “that it was contrary.” Thuanus reads “that certain men were opposed.” Quesnell reads “that their opinion was contrary.” We have deleted the last two words with the Vindobonensis and Pithoeanus manuscripts of this collection; the reference is to the writing which the Christians had brought to Siricius for condemnation, if priestly judgment should find it contrary to divine law.]

Therefore, following the Apostle’s command, against those who were proclaiming something other than what we had received, know that all of us—presbyters, deacons, and the entire clergy—had one sentence: Jovinian, Auxentius, Genialis, Germinator, Felix, Plotinus, Marcianus, Januarius, and Ingeniosus—who were found to be the authors of a new heresy and blasphemy—should remain outside the Church, condemned forever by divine judgment and by our own judgment. **[Col. 0565D–0566B]**

[Note, **Col. 0565D**: Quesnell, because the preposition *in* is omitted here, wrote “we announced and excommunicated them.” Since all our manuscripts and the other printed editions lack “we excommunicated” and “therefore,” we thought it preferable to supply the preposition “against,” rather than leave the imperfect meaning found in the common editions, which read “those who prefer otherwise” instead of “those who proclaim something else.” Four of our manuscripts have “those who,” and three have “otherwise” instead of “something else.”]

[Note, **Col. 0565D–0566B**: The Roman edition reads “one sentence was issued.” Crabbe and Merlin, together with the Hispana and Isidore, read “it is established that one sentence was made.” Binius and Labbe read “one sentence was stirred up.”]

[Note, **Col. 0566B**: Vatican 1342 reads “Flotinus”; Vallicellianus and another Vatican manuscript read “Flontinus.” Shortly afterward, the common editions read “instigators” instead of “authors.”]

Not doubting that your Holiness will observe this, I have sent these writings through my brothers and fellow presbyters Crescentius, Leopardus, and Alexander, who may fulfill the religious duty of faith with fervent spirit. **[p. 259]**

[Note, **Col. 0566B**: Vatican 5845, together with the Roman edition, reads “presbyters.” At the end, the same edition reads “with fervor.”]

# CHAPTER XXXI

[Note, **Col. 0566C**: This text is found in the manuscripts of this collection and also in Vatican 1342, Vallicellianus A 5, and Vatican 3845, as well as in the fuller Isidorian collection found in Vatican 1340, in a similar Remigian manuscript, and in Merlinus. Thus four collections of different origins preserve this rescript; the first two are Italian and the other two Gallic.

We have brought the title into conformity with the example of the Vindobonensis manuscript. Quesnell gives: “Rescript of blessed Ambrose and the other bishops concerning their condemnation.”]

**Likewise, a rescript of the bishops to the person addressed above**

To the most beloved lord and brother SIRICIUS: Ambrose, Sabinus, Bassianus, and the others.

[Note, **Col. 0566C**: The ancient books of two Italian collections—Vatican 1342, Vallicellianus A 5, and Vatican 5845—together with the Roman edition, lack the name “Sabinus” and read “Basianus.”]

[The supplied source ends here.]

We have recognized in the letter of Your Holiness the vigilance of a good shepherd, [Note: [Col. 0566C] The same manuscripts, with the Roman edition, read “who faithfully.”] who carefully guards the gate entrusted to you and, with devout concern, watches over Christ’s fold; one worthy for the sheep of our Lord to hear and follow. And therefore [Note: [Col. 0566C] Quesnellus alone reads “because he is at the door against the little sheep.” Shortly afterward the two cited manuscripts, Vaticanus 1342 and Vallicellanus, read “you will detect” and “you will confront.”] because you know Christ’s little sheep, you readily detect the wolves and confront them like a provident shepherd, lest [Note: [Col. 0566C] Quesnellus deleted *isti* (“those”), which the Vulgate copies had placed first. We restore it from all our manuscripts, in which *istis* is incorrectly written for *isti*.] those wolves scatter the Lord’s fold with the bites of their treachery and their savage howling. We praise this, dearest brother and lord, and celebrate it with our whole affection. [Note: [Col. 0566D] The manuscripts of the two Italian collections read *Nec miremur*, “Nor let us be surprised,” instead of *Nec miramur*, “Nor are we surprised.”]

Nor are we surprised that the Lord’s flock shuddered at the wolves’ madness, in whom it did not recognize Christ’s voice. [Col. 0566B] For their howling is savage: they preserve no grace of virginity, no order of chastity, [Note: [Col. 0566D] The Vulgate and the Councils, after the Roman edition, read “to preserve.”] they wish to confuse everything indiscriminately, abolish the degrees of different merits, and introduce a kind of poverty of heavenly rewards—as though Christ had bestowed only one crown, and not an abundance of titles of reward.

260 They pretend that they do not devote themselves to marriage. [Note: [Col. 0566D] Binius and Labbé read “that they give this to marriage.” Quesnellus reads “that they do not condemn marriages in this matter,” less correctly. No one suspected Jovinian of actually condemning marriage and merely pretending not to criticize it. On the contrary, he sought to praise marriage as honorable and rejected virginity in order to favor it. We have not wished to change the reading of our collection, which is supported by the Vindobonensis, Pithoeanus, and Thuaneus manuscripts—the last alone reading “marriages”—as well as by the Remigian and Merlin manuscripts. Coustant, deleting “not,” printed “that they devote themselves to marriage” (we do not know what old manuscript supports him), and suspected that the first reading was “to honor marriage.” Crabbe reads “that they grant this to marriage.” Perhaps “that they praise marriages” would be better, to which the following words correspond: “but what praise…”; yet without manuscript support we dare not alter it.]

But what praise can marriage have if virginity has no glory? Nor do we deny that marriage has been [Col. 0567A] sanctified by Christ, since the divine utterance says: “The two shall be one flesh,” and “one spirit” (Gen. II, 21; Matt. XIX, 5). [Note: [Col. 0567C] Vaticanus 1342 reads *et unus spiritus*, “and one spirit” (nominative), instead of *et in uno spiritu*, “and in one spirit.” Shortly afterward the Oxford manuscript reads *ministerium*, “ministry,” instead of *mysterium*, “mystery.”] But what we were born as comes before what we have become, and the mystery of the divine work is far more excellent than the remedy of human weakness.

A good wife is rightly praised, but a devout virgin is preferred as better, since the Apostle says: “He who joins his virgin in marriage does well; and he who does not join her does better” (I Cor. VII, 38). For the one thinks about the things of God, the other about the things of the world. The one is bound by marital bonds; the other is free from bonds. The one is under the law; the other under grace.

Marriage is good, through which offspring was found for the succession of the human race; but virginity is better, through which the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom has been acquired and a succession of heavenly merits has been found. Through woman, care entered; [Col. 0567B] through the virgin, salvation came.

Finally, Christ chose virginity as a special gift for himself, displayed the gift of purity, and represented in himself what he had chosen in his mother. What madness belongs to those fatal barkings, that the same men should say that Christ could not be born of a virgin while asserting that virgins can remain virgins after the parts of human offspring have been brought forth from a woman! Thus Christ grants to others what, as they say, he could not grant to himself?

Yet although he assumed flesh and became human in order to redeem humanity and recall it from death, he nevertheless came to earth in an unprecedented manner, as though by a gift: [Note: [Col. 0567D] Quesnellus, omitting *pericula* (“dangers”), apparently wrote *itinere* (“journey”) for *munere* (“gift”) with the Vulgate Councils. We restore the reading of Merlin and Coustant, supported by all four of our manuscripts.] so that, just as he had said, “Behold, I make all things new” (Apoc. XXI, 5), he might be born through the birth of an immaculate virgin; and, as it is written, he might be believed to be God with us. [Note: [Col. 0567C] The Vindobonensis reads “if he assumed flesh”; Vaticanus 1342, “if he assumed his flesh”; Vaticanus 5845, “who assumed his flesh.” Binius and Labbé read “who thus assumed flesh, although he was human.” Merlin and Crabbe read “thus he assumed flesh, and thus was human.”]

But people who have been exposed as following the path of perversity are said to declare: [Col. 0567C] [p. 261] “The virgin conceived, but did not give birth as a virgin.” [Note: [Col. 0567D] Quesnellus, against all our manuscripts and printed copies, alone printed “straying from the way of truth.”] If a virgin could conceive, how could a virgin not give birth, since conception always precedes and birth follows? [Note: [Col. 0567D] The Vallicellanus and Vaticanus 5845, removing the question mark, omit “not.”]

But if the teachings of priests are not believed, let the utterances of Christ be believed; let the messages of the angels be believed, who say: “For no word is impossible for God” (Luke I, 36). [Note: [Col. 0567D] Quesnellus reads “with God.”] Let the Apostles’ Creed also be believed, which the Roman Church has always guarded and preserved inviolate.

Mary heard the angel’s voice. To what she had previously said—“How will this happen?” [Note: [Col. 0567D] Other copies read *fiet*, “will happen,” instead of *erit*, “will be.”]—not asking about the faith of the generation, she later replied: “Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord; let it happen to me according to your word” (ibid., 34).

[Col. 0568A] This is the Virgin who conceived in the womb, the Virgin who bore a son; for it is written: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son” (Isa. VII, 14). He did not say only that a virgin would conceive, but also that a virgin would give birth.

What, then, is that sanctuary gate, that outer gate toward the east, which remains closed? “No one,” he says, “shall pass through it; only the God of Israel has passed through it” (Ezek. XLIV, 3). [Note: [Col. 0567D] The printed editions repeat “that gate.” The Vindobonensis reads “has passed through it.” The printed editions then read “unless the God of Israel alone.” Coustant reads “shall pass through it,” because Saint Ambrose cited this passage similarly in On the Institution of the Virgin, chapter8. [Col. 0568C] Quesnellus alone then reads *ingressus est* instead of *intravit*, both meaning “entered.”]

Is not this gate Mary, through whom the Redeemer entered this world? This is the gate of righteousness, as he himself said: “Allow us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. III, 15). This gate is Mary, of whom it is written: “Because the Lord has passed through it, it shall remain closed after childbirth” (Ezek. XLIV, 2). [Note: [Col. 0568C] The Vulgate reads “shall pass through it.” We have added the words “after childbirth,” omitted by Quesnellus, from the Oxford manuscript alone, against the other manuscripts and printed editions.] For the virgin conceived and gave birth.

What is incredible, then, if Mary gave birth contrary to the customary course of [Col. 0568B] natural generation and remains a virgin, when, contrary to nature’s usage, the sea saw and fled, and the streams of the Jordan flowed back toward their source? [Note: [Col. 0568C] Quesnellus alone reads “and is a virgin.”] It does not therefore exceed belief that a virgin gave birth, when we read that a rock also poured forth waters and that the sea’s wave was solidified in the form of a wall. [Note: [Col. 0568D] Three manuscripts—one Vallicellanus and two Vatican—read “and in the form of a mountain.” Most of the printed editions and both Vatican manuscripts then read “it does not therefore exceed belief.”]

It does not exceed belief that a human being came forth from a virgin, when a rock poured forth a flowing spring, iron floated upon the waters, and a man walked upon the waters. [p. 262] Therefore, if a wave carried a human being, could a virgin not give birth to a human being? [Note: [Col. 0568D] Coustant, Merlin, and Labbé read this way, as does the Remigian manuscript, supported by the Pithoean and Colbertine manuscripts, which have “to whom that human being.” Quesnellus and other printed editions read “and that human being.”]

But which human being? The one of whom we read: “And the Lord will send them a human being who will save them, and the Lord will be known to the Egyptians” (Isa. XIX, 20).

Thus, in the Old Testament, a virgin of the Hebrews led an army through the sea; in the New Testament, a virgin, [Col. 0568C] the heavenly palace of the King, was chosen for salvation. [Note: [Col. 0568D] Quesnellus, with most manuscripts and printed editions, reads “rod.” We corrected this from our Vindobonensis manuscript, with Labbé and Coustant. For it is not Aaron’s rod that is compared with the virgin Mary, but Mary, his sister, with the Virgin Mary, as Ambrose explains in *Exhortation to Virgins*, chapter 5, no. 28, and *On the Institution of the Virgin*, chapter 17, no. 106. A little later the Roman edition reads “the rod of the King, the palace of heaven”; and the Roman Breviary, with Vaticanus 5845, “the virgin of noble lineage, the heavenly palace.”]

And what of this? Let us also weave in the praises of widowhood, since in the Gospel, after the most celebrated birth of the Virgin, the widow Anna is introduced: she had lived with her husband for seven years from her virginity; “and she was a widow of eighty-four years, who did not depart from the temple, serving with fastings and prayers night and day.”

Widowhood is deservedly despised by those men: it is accustomed to observe fasts, under which they lament that they have for a time been worn down; and they avenge their own injury by desiring to drive away the labor of abstinence with daily banquets and indulgence. They do nothing more rightly than [Col. 0569A] condemn themselves with their own mouths. [Note: [Col. 0568D] Vaticanus 1342 reads “who do not wish to observe.”]

But let them fear God, lest that fasting be reckoned to their account. Let them choose what they wish. If they have fasted at some time, let them then perform penance for their good deed; if never, let them themselves confess their intemperance and indulgence. [Note: [Col. 0569C] Coustant, with the Vulgate, reads “But they also fear.” He adds that an old Rheims manuscript reads “if they fear God”; he thinks “if at last they fear” should be read, which would require changing the punctuation. We judged the reading of our manuscripts not to be abandoned. Quesnellus alone reads “may reckon” instead of “be reckoned.”]

And the same men say that Paul was a teacher of indulgence. [Note: [Col. 0569C] Quesnellus reads *Et iidem dicant*, “And let the same men say.” Other printed editions before Coustant have “And therefore they say.” We preferred the reading of the Vindobonensis, Pithoeanus, Colbertine, and Remigian manuscripts; with these and all the printed editions we also wrote *At quis*, “But who?” Quesnellus alone has *Et quis*, “And who?”] But who is a teacher of sobriety, if he was a teacher of indulgence? He chastised his body and brought it into subjection, and declared that through many fasts he had rendered to Christ the observance owed to him (I Cor. IX, 27; II Cor. VI, 5; XI, 27), not to praise himself, but to teach us what we should follow. [Note: [Col. 0569C] The Vindobonensis reads “so that he would not praise his own things.” Other editions read “not so that he might praise himself and his own things.” Coustant, with his manuscripts, reads “not so that he might praise his own [observance].”]

He, then, taught indulgence who said: “Why do you, as though living in this world, make decrees: ‘Do not touch, do not handle, do not taste’?”—things that are all “for corruption” (Col. II, 20); who said that life is not to be lived [Col. 0569B] “in indulgence of the body, nor in any honor leading to satiety and care of the flesh” (ibid. I, 23), nor in the desires of error, but in the spirit [p. 263] by which we are renewed (Eph. IV, 22). [Note: [Col. 0569C] Vaticanus 1342 reads “corruptible things”; the Vindobonensis, “corruption”; other editions, “for corruption.” Coustant and Hardouin, in their notes, read “who also says.” The same Vatican manuscript reads “and in diligence of the flesh.”]

If what the Apostle said is insufficient, let them hear the prophet saying: “And I covered my soul in fasting.” Therefore, whoever does not fast is uncovered and naked, and exposed to the wound. Finally, if Adam had covered himself in fasting, he would not have been made naked. [Note: [Col. 0569C] Quesnellus alone, with the Oxford manuscript, reads “cast out”; afterward he reads “in prayer and fasting,” with some manuscripts, but not with the Vindobonensis and many others.]

Nineveh freed itself from death through fasting. The Lord himself also says: “This kind is expelled only through prayer and fasting” (Matt. XVII, 20).

But why say more before a teacher and instructor, when those [Col. 0570A] who came here for this purpose, so that no place might remain in which they were not condemned, have already brought him the worthy reward of their treachery? [Note: [Col. 0569C] Quesnellus, with some manuscripts, reads “the price”; afterward, “therefore they came here also.” We deleted “also” with the manuscripts of this collection, except the Pithoean and Vindobonensian, which have “and therefore.” The Vallicellanus and both Vatican manuscripts, with the Roman edition and Ambrose, read “therefore, even to here.”]

They proved themselves Manichaeans, not believing that from a virgin [lacuna] certainly he is not believed to have come. [Note: [Col. 0569D] Quesnellus reads “not believing that Christ came from a virgin. What madness is this?” Merlin reads “not believing that he certainly came from a virgin.” The Council edition after the Roman edition reads “not believing that he had certainly come from a virgin. What madness…” The Vallicellanus and both Vatican manuscripts have this reading, but after “had come” add “he is not believed.” The Vindobonensis and all the other manuscripts of this collection seen by Coustant have “he is not believed,” but prefer “having come” rather than “he had come.” For this reason the editions thought the passage corrupt and corrected it by deleting “he is not believed”; Quesnellus additionally deleted “certainly” and emended it to “Christ came,” without our knowing whether he relied on the authority of a more recent and freer Oxford manuscript. Since every reading of the older manuscripts is defective, we have followed the manuscripts of this collection and marked the lacuna. Coustant correctly seems to have suspected that it could be supplied as follows: “not believing that Christ was born from a virgin. But if he was not born from a virgin, certainly his coming is not believed.” The repetition of the words “from a virgin” provided the opportunity for the lacuna, as usually happens.]

What kind of madness is this, equal to that of the new Jews? If his coming is not believed, neither is it believed that he assumed flesh. Therefore, did he appear as a phantom and was crucified as a phantom? But for us he was crucified in truth; in truth he is our Redeemer. He is a Manichaean who denies the truth, who denies Christ’s flesh; and therefore there is no forgiveness of sins for him, but only the impiety of the Manichaeans.

The most merciful emperor also abhorred this impiety, and all who saw them avoided them as a kind of contagion, as our brothers and fellow priests [Col. 0570B] Crescens, [Note: [Col. 0570C] “Leopardus” was omitted by Quesnellus; it appears in all our manuscripts and printed editions.] Leopardus, and Alexander, fervent in the Holy Spirit, testify. They left them condemned by the execration of all and [p. 264] expelled as fugitives from the city of Milan. [Note: [Col. 0570C] The Vulgate reads “They brought them back from the city of Milan as fugitives.” The Vallicellanus and two Vatican manuscripts have only “as fugitives.”]

Therefore, know that Jovinian, Auxentius, Germinator, Felix, Plotinus, Genialis, Marcianus, Januarius, and Ingeniosus, whom Your Holiness condemned, have likewise been condemned among us according to your judgment. [Note: [Col. 0570C] Vaticanus5845 reads *Protinum* (“Protinus”) instead of *Plotinum* (“Plotinus”). Then the Vindobonensis and Pithoeanus, with Merlin, read *et Ingenium*, “and Ingenius,” instead of “and Ingeniosus.”]

May our almighty God preserve you safe and flourishing, dearest lord and brother.

**Subscription**

[Note: [Col. 0570C] The Roman edition, from the Council of Aquileia of A.D. 381, interpolated these subscriptions against the evidence of the manuscripts, as the Benedictine Fathers note in their edition of Ambrose, as follows: “I, Ambrose, bishop of the Church of Milan, have subscribed. Eventius, bishop of Cenetum, sends greetings … Maximus, bishop of Emona. Felix, bishop of Jadera. Bassianus, bishop of Lodi. Theodosius, bishop of Octodurum. Constantius, bishop of Orange. Sabinus, bishop of Piacenza. By order…” It may seem strange that Ambrose’s subscription is omitted, since he is named first in the superscription. Yet the preceding greeting—“May he preserve you safe…”—seems to belong to Ambrose, much as we conjectured that in the synodical letter of the Gallican bishops to Saint Leo, among the Leonine letters, no. 99, Ravennius wrote the first greeting without mentioning his own name; see note 24, vol. I, col. 1110. Sabinus’ name does not appear in the manuscripts among the subscriptions with his name explicitly stated. Whether it should also rightly be removed from the superscription, as the two collections cited in note 2 do not know, we dare not affirm.]

“I, Eventius, bishop, send greetings to Your Holiness in the Lord and have subscribed to this letter. Maximus, bishop; Felix, bishop; Bassianus, bishop; Theodolus, bishop. By order of my lord Bishop Geminianus, he himself being present, [Col. 0571A] I, Aper the presbyter, have subscribed; Eustasius, bishop; Constantius, bishop; Eustasius, bishop.” [Note: [Col. 0570D] All our manuscripts agree with Quesnellus and Merlin. Coustant reads “Theodorus.”]

And all subscribed in order. [Note: [Col. 0571C] This same order is found in the manuscripts of Merlin, Pithoeus, and Thuanus; the last omits the second Eustasius.]

## CHAPTER XXXII

[Note: [Col. 0571C] Found in the manuscripts of this collection, in the Vatican Regina, Colbertine, Lucense, Vaticanus 1342, Corbeiensis, Dionysian, Hispanic, Hadrianic, and Isidorian collections, and also in the Fossatensis and several other Gallican manuscripts, according to Coustant.]

Letter of Pope Zosimus to Esicius, bishop of Salona, concerning monks and laymen wishing to enter the ecclesiastical orders.

[Note: [Col. 0571D] We added this superscription from the Vindobonensis manuscript. Other manuscripts read Esichius, Esychius, or Hesychius.]

**Pope Zosimus to Esicius, bishop of Salona.**

Your affection demands an instruction from the Apostolic See, in which the decrees of the Fathers concur, [p. 265] and you indicate that some from the common crowd of monks—whose solitude is greater than any multitude—are hastening to the priesthood, as are also laymen. [Note: [Col. 0571D] Dionysius, the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, and the editions derived from them omit *populari* (“of the common people”). The manuscripts of our collection and of the other older collections preserve the word.] This has clearly been forbidden, specifically under our predecessors and recently by us, [Col. 0571B] in letters sent to Gaul and Spain. [Note: [Col. 0571D] The Vulgate, with the Vatican Regina and another Vatican manuscript, reads “specifically under our predecessors, and recently by us.”] In those provinces this presumption is common, [Note: [Col. 0571D] The same printed editions and manuscripts read *regionibus*, “regions,” instead of “provinces.”] although Africa too is not exempt from this admonition of ours: no one who had not been thoroughly instructed in ecclesiastical discipline in due order and educated in divine service through the testing of time should dare aspire to the highest priesthood of the Church, and not only should such ambition be considered ineffectual, but those who ordained him should also be deprived of that order which they had presumed to confer contrary to the order prescribed by the Fathers.

Therefore we are astonished that the statutes of the Apostolic See have not been conveyed to Your Affection. We praise the firmness of your purpose, dearest brother; nor could anything else have been expected from the longstanding judicial character of your episcopal authority [Col. 0571C] than that, standing ready in the battle-line of faith, you should oppose such ambitions in accordance with the precepts of the Fathers.

Therefore, if you think that anything is lacking to your authority—which we do not believe—we supply it. Resist such ordinations; resist the pride and arrogance that is approaching. [Note: [Col. 0571D] Other manuscripts, with Coustant, more appropriately read *Obsiste*, “Resist” (singular), in both places, instead of the plural *obsistite*.] The precepts of the Fathers are with you; the authority of the Apostolic See is with you.

For if secular offices confer the highest place not upon those who have merely entered the vestibule of public service, but upon those examined through many grades over time, who is so arrogant and shameless as to desire immediately to be a leader in the heavenly army—which [Col. 0572A] must be weighed more carefully and tested like gold through repeated fires—when he has not previously been a recruit, and to wish first to teach rather than to learn? [Note: [Col. 0571D] Vaticanus1342 reads *quam discat*, “before he learns,” instead of *quam discere*, “before learning.”] [Note: [Col. 0571D] Vaticanus 1342 reads “in ecclesiastical service.” Shortly afterward Coustant, with other manuscripts, preferred *pensius*, that is, “more diligently,” instead of *propensius*, “more earnestly.”]

Let him first become accustomed in the Lord’s camp, in the rank of reader, to the rudiments of divine service. Let it not seem beneath him to become, in order, an exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, and deacon; and not by a leap, [p. 266] but at the times established by the ordination of the elders. [Note: [Col. 0571D] The same manuscript and Vatican Regina delete “deacon.” Then Vatican Regina reads *Sed non saltu*, “But not by a leap”; the other Vatican manuscript has *nec non saltu*, literally “and also by a leap” (as printed). [Col. 0572C] Other printed editions read *nec hoc saltu*, “nor by this leap.” Quesnellus alone reads *ordine temporibus*, “by order, at times,” instead of *ordinatione temporibus*, “by ordination, at times”; we corrected this from our manuscripts and printed copies.]

He must proceed to the dignity of the presbyterate only when his age fulfills the title and the deeds of his service attest the merit of his uprightness. [Note: [Col. 0572C] Other editions, with Vaticanus Regina and other manuscripts, read *ante acta* (“deeds previously performed”). Quesnellus reads “pontificate”; we corrected this from the Vindobonensis manuscript, the Vatican manuscripts, and the other editions.] From there he will rightly be expected to hope for the place of supreme pontiff. [Note: [Col. 0572D] Vaticanus 1342 reads “For excessive leniency does all this.”]

This is caused by the excessive leniency of our fellow priests, who seek the pomp of numbers and think that some dignity is acquired for themselves from this crowd. Hence everywhere [Col. 0572B] a numerous popular body, even in places where there is solitude, is found to consist of such men, while they desire parishes to be extended or, when they can provide nothing else, distribute divine orders. This must always be governed by strict judgment. For everything great is rare.

Therefore, lest we detract from the merits of Your Affection, we have sent these writings especially to you; [Note: [Col. 0572D] Quesnellus alone reads “your merits.”] you shall bring them to the knowledge of all our brothers and fellow bishops, not only those in that province but also those in provinces neighboring Your Affection.

Let anyone who, setting aside the authority of the Fathers and of the Apostolic See, [Note: [Col. 0572D] The Vindobonensis and Vatican Regina manuscripts, with other printed editions, have this reading, *Sciet quisquis*, “Whoever ... will know.” Quesnellus reads *Sciatque quisquis*, “And let whoever ... know.”] neglects this know that he will be strictly punished by us, so that he may have no doubt that the responsibility for his office will not remain with him if he thinks that this may be [Col. 0572C] attempted with impunity after so many prohibitions. [Note: [Col. 0572D] Quesnellus, deleting “with impunity,” wrote “can be attempted.” We have restored “with impunity,” as in the other editions, and deleted “can be” with our better manuscripts and those of Coustant.] For whatever is repeatedly forbidden and nevertheless appropriated is done out of a desire for insult.

The periods of time to be observed at each grade are as follows. If someone has given his name to ecclesiastical service from childhood, he must remain among the readers through continuous observance until his twentieth year. If someone, already older and advanced in years, has entered, yet desires immediately after baptism to be devoted to the service of God, he must remain for five years either among the readers or among the exorcists. [Note: [Col. 0572D] Quesnellus and Merlin read *qui tamen statim post baptismum ... divinae militiae desiderat*, “who nevertheless immediately after baptism desires [to be devoted] to divine service”; Quesnellus adds *se*, “himself.” Other editions read *ita tamen ut post baptismum statim se divinae militiae desideret*, “yet so that immediately after baptism he may desire himself [to be devoted] to divine service.” Vatican Regina deletes *se* but has *ita tamen ut*, “yet so that,” with all the other manuscripts, followed by the indicative *desiderat*, “he desires.” Hence the correction supplied by the Lucense, Colbertine, and Corbeiensis manuscripts, *si divinae*, “if [he desires] divine [service],” is necessary.]

After that, let him be an acolyte or subdeacon for four years, and then let him proceed to the blessing of the diaconate, if he deserves it. [Col. 0573A] In that order he must remain for five years if he has conducted himself blamelessly. [Note: [Col. 0572D] Vaticanus1342 reads *si mereatur*, “if he should deserve it” (subjunctive), instead of indicative *si meretur*, “if he deserves it.” Then Quesnellus reads *si se inculpabiliter gesserit, adhaerere*, “if he has conducted himself blamelessly, to remain attached,” instead of *si inculpate se gesserit, haerere*, with the same general sense but different adverb, word order, and verb. We preferred the Vindobonensis and other better manuscripts.]

Afterward, with the services rendered through so many grades supporting the proofs of his own faith, he may earn the presbyterate. [Note: [Col. 0573B] Vatican Regina, another Vatican manuscript, and the other printed editions read *presbyterii sacerdotium*, “the priesthood of the presbyterate.” Then the Vindobonensis reads *etsi eo illum exactior*, “even if to that [a] more exacting [life ... him]”; the printed Councils, with Coustant, have *si eo illum exactior*, “if to that [a] more exacting [life ... him].” Shortly afterward Justel and Coustant, with the Vindobonensis, read *produxerit*, “has brought him forward,” instead of *perduxerit*, “has led him.”]

[p. 267] From that position, if a more exacting life has led him to good morals, he ought to hope for the supreme pontificate. [Note: [Col. 0573B] Vatican Regina, with other printed editions, reads *pontificatum* instead of *pontificium*, both here meaning “pontificate.”] This condition must nevertheless be preserved: neither a twice-married man nor a penitent may be admitted to these grades. [Note: [Col. 0573B] Quesnellus, with most editions and Isidore, adds “nor the husband of a widow.” We deleted this with Coustant, on the authority of the Vindobonensis manuscript of this collection, supported by manuscripts of the three other collections—the Vatican Regina, Vaticanus 1342, and Lucense-Colbertine—as well as the Dionysian, Hispanic, Corbeiensis, Fossatensis, and Regius manuscripts cited by Coustant.]

Certainly, defenders of the Church who come from the laity must also be bound by the foregoing observance, if they deserve to enter the clerical order. [Note: [Col. 0573C] Quesnellus alone omitted “so that.”]

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, [Note: [Col. 0573C] Coustant, with Justel, preferred “the ninth day before the Kalends.”] in the consulship of the Augusti Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

[Note: [Col. 0573C] This is found in the manuscripts of this collection, and in the Hadrianic, Hispanic, and Isidorian collections. Some believed that this admonition, or letter, existed in Dionysius, since Justel included it in his edition of Dionysius. But the two surviving pure Dionysian manuscripts—the Regius and Vaticanus 5845—exclude it from Dionysius: the Regius lacks it, while the Vatican manuscript places it in an appendix, as it also does the letter of Leo to the bishops of Mauretania, as we showed in the note to Letter 12 of Saint Leo, vol. I, col. 651, no. 11. From this appendix it was placed in the Hadrianic collection after Zosimus’ letter to Hesychius, the only one Dionysius had included. The Cresconian collection, to which this letter is attributed in the Roman edition, is the Vallicellanus A 5, which contains the Hadrianic collection with Dionysian additions.]

Admonition of Pope Zosimus to his presbyters and deacons stationed at Ravenna.

[Note: [Col. 0573D] The copies of this collection have “to his presbyters and deacons.” The Vindobonensis reads: “Admonition to the presbyters and deacons who are at Ravenna.” In Vaticanus 5845, which contains Dionysius’ additions, two titles are found: “I. Letter of Zosimus addressed to the presbyters of Ravenna”; “II. Admonition of Zosimus to the presbyters and deacons who are at Ravenna.” The Hadrianic manuscripts read “To the presbyters of Ravenna,” or, as in Justel, “of the Ravennates,” and then “Admonition of Bishop Zosimus to the presbyters and deacons who are at Ravenna.” The Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts read “To the Ravennese clergy,” and afterward: “Zosimus, bishop of the city of Rome, to the presbyters and deacons who are at Ravenna.” The word “his” seems necessary from the context of the letter: it was not addressed to the presbyters and deacons of Ravenna, but to Romans who had been received into the imperial court, as the beginning indicates.]

From the report of our brother, the presbyter Archiami, [Col. 0573B] we have learned how you were received and what you did, and also how those were received who, daring with I know not what presumption to act against the canons and against us, wished to go to the imperial court. [Note: [Col. 0574B] Other manuscripts, with the other editions, read *Archidami* (“of Archidamus”) instead of *Archiami*. Quesnellus then reads *suscepti estis*, “you were received,” and afterward *suscepti sunt*, “they were received,” using indicative forms instead of the text’s subjunctives *sitis* and *sint*. [Col. 0574C] We follow the better manuscripts.]

For them we had formerly had these letters, [Note: [Col. 0574C] Quesnellus alone omitted *olim*, “formerly.”] which we have now sent to you for delivery, written [p. 268] in reply to the letters they had sent us insultingly. But since the accused could not remain in their own—that is, in our Roman—Church with our fellow presbyters, we have sent these letters to you for delivery to them. [Note: [Col. 0574C] The Oxford manuscript reads “they will not be able.” The words “in their own,” that is, “in our Roman Church,” are absent from Vaticanus 5845 and the Hadrianic collection.] In them, by our decree, we declared that the aforesaid [Col. 0574A] disturbers of everyone had been excluded from communion with our Apostolic See and had accepted the sentence issued with our subscription.

Those also who wished to lend their assent to the unrestrained action and plan of these men, it is for your charity to judge how they should be regarded. [Note: [Col. 0574C] Coustant, with several manuscripts, reads “Those also who wished to lend their assent to this unrestrained act”; Justel, “to this act.”] You must bring this charge against them: [Note: [Col. 0574C] We added *hoc*, “this,” with the excellent Vindobonensis manuscript, supported by the other printed editions. Then Quesnellus reads *et qualiter quod presbyteros*; we deleted *quod* (“that”) with our manuscripts and printed editions, leaving “and in a manner ... presbyters.”] that, contrary to the precepts of the canons, they attempted to act boldly and, in a manner unbecoming presbyters, to become rebels. [Note: [Col. 0574C] The Hadrianic manuscripts and Vaticanus 5845 omit “they attempted”; Coustant consequently changed the preceding verbs as past tenses, “they incurred and they opposed” (*incurrere et obstitere*). The same Vatican manuscript, with some Vulgate copies, reads “Nevertheless, we admonish you.”]

We admonish you to remain watchful, lest any audacity burst forth from those whom the holy and Apostolic Church knows to have been anathematized. [Note: [Col. 0574C] The manuscripts of this collection give this passage variously and corruptly. Thuanus: *de quorum prorupta audacia, quos anathematizatos scit apostolica Ecclesia*, “concerning whose audacity that has burst forth, whom the apostolic Church knows to have been anathematized.” The Vindobonensis and [Col. 0574D] Pithoeanus: *ne quorum praerupta audacia, quo anathematizatos sciscitet apostolicae Ecclesiae*, “lest whose headlong audacity, whereby it may inquire into those anathematized, of the apostolic Church” (a corrupt, syntactically incomplete reading). One Regius manuscript agrees with Thuanus, except for *de quo eorum*, “concerning which of them.” Quesnellus assembled from these readings—whether supported by the Oxford manuscript we do not know—“lest the headlong audacity of some who are known to have been anathematized stir up scandal in the apostolic Church.” We therefore accepted the reading of the printed editions, approved by the Vatican manuscripts and the other Hadrianic, Hispanic, and Isidorian manuscripts. Coustant, with one Colbertine manuscript, preferred *ne quo*, as if *ne aliquo* (“lest by any”), instead of *ne qua* (“lest any [audacity]”).]

But concerning those who joined themselves to their association, we shall consider, when you have returned, what we ought to do, with better counsel. [Note: [Col. 0574D] The Vatican manuscript and the editions derived from the Hadrianic, Hispanic, and Isidorian collections add: “And in another hand.”]

Given on the fifth day before the Nones of October, in the consulship of the Augusti Honorius XII and [Col. 0574B] Theodosius VIII.

[p. 269] ## CHAPTER XXXIV

[Note: [Col. 0574D] This letter is found not only in the manuscripts of this collection but also in the Dionysian, Hispanic, and Isidorian collections.]

Letter of Pope Boniface to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne, concerning Bishop Patroclus.

[Note: [Col. 0574D] The Dionysian, Hadrianic, Hispanic, and Isidorian manuscripts, with the other editions, read: “Boniface, bishop of the city of Rome, to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne.” The Hispanic and Isidorian collections add “greetings.”]

**Boniface to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne.**

[Note: [Col. 0574D] The Hispanic and Isidorian collections, with the older printed editions, read *Difficilem* (“difficult,” accusative adjective), instead of *Difficile* (“with difficulty,” adverbially).]

We are indeed slow to give credence to complaints whose purpose assails the priests of the Lord, especially when they say that those priests attempted something against the statutes of the Fathers. Yet frequently, as now, a multitude of complainants confirms such reports. For behold, as Your Charity recognizes from what follows, the clergy and people of the Church of Luteva [Col. 0575A] have sent their prayers and tears to us, as far as can be understood, with great grief, saying that our fellow bishop Patroclus, without any petition from them, ordained someone—I do not know whom—in place of the deceased bishop, in a foreign province, bypassing the metropolitan and contrary to the rules of the Fathers.

We can in no way endure this patiently, because we are bound to be careful guardians of the sanctions of our fathers. [Note: [Col. 0575C] Quesnellus alone reads *oportet*, “it is necessary,” instead of *convenit*, “it is fitting.” The printed editions, with other manuscripts, then read *Nulli etenim*, “For to no one,” and afterward *praecipit*, “orders” (present), instead of *praecepit*, “ordered.” On this citation of the Nicene canon, see Observations on Quesnellus’s fifth dissertation, partII, chapter6, nos.5–6, volumeXI.] No one seems unaware of the decree of the Council of Nicaea, which ordered the following; let us place its very words: “Throughout each province, each metropolitan must possess his own right, and no one may have two provinces subject to him.” [Note: [Col. 0575C] The Dionysian and Hadrianic manuscripts delete “may.” Thuanus adds “seats” after “may”; Quesnellus rightly says this is wrong, since the matter concerns provinces.]

They judged that this must be observed, since it could not be believed otherwise, with the [Col. 0575B] Holy Spirit suggesting it to them. Therefore, dearest brother, if matters stand thus, and the boundary of your province encloses the aforesaid Church, you are hereby admonished by our authority—though you ought to do so voluntarily—to proceed to the place where such an ordination is said to have been celebrated, [p. 270] armed with the right of the metropolitan and relying on our commands, having regard to the desires and wishes of the petitioners. [Note: [Col. 0575D] One Colbertine manuscript cited by Coustant reads “enclosed.” The Vatican, Hispanic, and Isidorian manuscripts, with Merlin, read “may protect”; other editions, with the manuscripts of the Hadrianic collection, read “protected” or “more fully protected.” The copies of our collection, with the Regius Dionysian manuscript, read “admonished.” In one Harleian manuscript, in a second hand, it reads “you ought to have.” The Regius Dionysian reads “you ought.”]

Understand that we have granted you authority to do whatever must be done according to the rules of the Fathers, so that, when everything has been completed, whatever you decide may be made clear through your report to the Apostolic See, to which it is evident that the administration of his entire province has been entrusted (the printed reading; see the correction in the note). [Note: [Col. 0575D] It must certainly read “your province,” not “his”; or, with Dionysius and the Hadrianic collection, followed by Justel and Coustant, the word “his” should be deleted.]

Let no audacious violator therefore exceed their boundaries, nor let anyone, to their insult, defend in his own parts [Col. 0575C] what does not appear to have been granted to him by those authorities. [Note: [Col. 0575D] Justel, with the Hadrianic, Hispanic, and Isidorian manuscripts, reads “anything”; with the same manuscripts and the other editions, he omits “by those authorities,” words which only the copies of this collection preserve.]

Let the presumption of those who extend the limit of their dignity beyond what is permitted cease, restrained by our authority. We say this so that Your Charity may understand that we preserve the precepts of the canons so cautiously that our own judgment likewise determines that every province must always await the decision of its metropolitan in all matters. [Note: [Col. 0575D] Only the manuscripts of this collection have *cautius*, “more cautiously.”] [Note: [Col. 0575D] This reading, *censio*, “judgment,” agrees with the Vindobonensis and Pithoeanus of our collection. Manuscripts of other collections and the printed editions read *constitutio*, “enactment”; the Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts read “so that this enactment”; Quesnellus reads *censura*, “judgment” or “censure.”]

Given on the fifth day before the [Col. 0576A] Ides of February, [Note: [Col. 0575D] The Thuanus manuscript reads “the sixth day before the Ides.”] in the consulship of the Augusti Honorius XIII and Theodosius X.

## CHAPTER XXXV

[Col. 0576C]

[Note: This is contained in the manuscripts of the collections of Vat. Regina 1997, Colbert, Lucca, Vat. 1342, Corbie, Dionysius, Hadrian, Hispana, and Isidore.]

**Pope Celestine’s Letter to the Bishops of Vienne and Narbonne, in Eleven Sections**

**CELESTINE to all the bishops established throughout the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne.**

We should indeed wish to rejoice so greatly in the ordering of your Churches that we might congratulate you rather on progress than grieve that anything had been committed against ecclesiastical discipline. For both good deeds come to our joy, and whatever has been done badly pricks us with the goads of sorrow.

[Note: The words “against ecclesiastical discipline,” which all our manuscripts and the Vulgate exhibit, dropped out of Quesnel. Shortly afterward, the Vulgate, with certain manuscripts, reads “come.”]

[Note: [Col. 0576D] The edition of the Councils after Crabbe reads “when [we are urged] to this.” Our manuscripts and all printed editions delete *ad*; *hoc* refers to *instinctu* (“prompting”). Quesnel alone reads: “so that we may recall others from unlawful acts and be urged by the prompting of our office toward good,” a reading preferred by neither our manuscripts nor the other Vulgate editions.]

[p. 271]

Nor can we remain silent when the prompting of our office urges us to recall [Col. 0576B] some from unlawful acts: placed by God as watchmen, so that we may prove the diligence of our vigilance, cutting away what must be restrained and establishing what must be observed.

[Note: Coustant, with five excellent manuscripts, reads “although the distance may be considerable.”]

And although spiritual concern does not fail even with respect to distant places, but extends everywhere that the Lord’s name is proclaimed, nevertheless the things attempted through the authority of novel presumption for the overthrow of the rules do not escape our knowledge.

### I

For we have learned that certain priests of the Lord serve superstition rather than purity of mind or faith.

[Note: The Vulgate, with Vat. Regina, reads “serve.”]

But it is not surprising that those act contrary to ecclesiastical custom who did not grow up in the Church, but came by another route and brought into the Church [Col. 0576C] with them the practices they had observed in another way of life, wearing a cloak and girding their loins, believing that they would fulfill the faith of Scripture not through the spirit but through the letter.

[Note: Quesnel omitted the word “do” (*faciunt*).]

[Note: Coustant corrected “in another way” with the aid of two manuscripts, Corbie and Colbert, which read *irritum* (“invalid”). The Oxford manuscript deletes “into the Church.” The Vindobonensis reads “the faith of Holy Scripture,” with “holy” added in a second correction.]

[Note: [Col. 0576D] Quesnel alone reads “in the letter.”]

For if these commands were given so that they should be observed literally in this way, why are the things that follow not likewise carried out, so that burning lamps should be held in their hands together with a staff? These things possess their own mystery, and to those who understand they are so clear that they should be observed according to the [Col. 0577A] meaning proper to them.

[Note: Quesnel omitted “in this way” and, instead of “be observed,” has “be held.” We have preferred the reading of the Vindobonensis and other manuscript and printed copies. Vat. 1342 alone reads “be strengthened.”]

For in the girding of the loins chastity is signified; in the staff, pastoral government; and in the burning lamps, the radiance of good works, of which it is said: “Let your good works shine” (Matthew 5:16).

[Note: Dionysius and Vat. Regina read “Nevertheless, they may have this.” The following reading has “living in more remote places.”]

Nevertheless, perhaps those who live in more secluded places and dwell far from others may follow this appearance, preferring custom to reason. But whence has this dress entered the Gallican Churches, so that the custom of so many years and so many bishops should be changed into another form? We must be distinguished from the common people and others by teaching, not by clothing; by conduct, not by dress; by purity of mind, not by outward observance. For if we begin to pursue novelty, we shall trample upon the order handed down to us by our fathers and make room for superfluous superstitions. [Col. 0577B]

[Note: Some copies read “let us begin.”]

[Note: Quesnel alone omits “for superfluous.”]

[p. 272]

### II

We must not, therefore, lead the inexperienced minds of the faithful into such practices; they should be taught rather than treated as objects of amusement. Nothing should be imposed upon their eyes, but precepts must be poured into their minds.

[Note: Certain old editions read “mocked”; Vat. 1342, “mourned,” followed by “nor should [anything] be set before [their eyes].” At the end, some copies read “we are called back.”]

There were indeed many things that we could say concerning ecclesiastical discipline or the reason for the matter itself; but from these we are called away to other subjects.

### III

We have learned that penance is denied to the dying, and that the requests of those who at the time of their death desire this remedy for their souls are not granted.

[Note: [Col. 0577D] Quesnel, following ancient copies, inserts “for we have learned,” less correctly. We have deleted it with the Vindobonensis, Vat. Regina, and others. Vat. reads: “They desire this remedy for themselves.”]

I confess that we shudder to find anyone guilty of such great impiety as to despair of God’s mercy—as though He could not come to the aid of one who at any time hastens to Him, and free a man endangered [Col. 0577C] beneath the burden of sins by the weight from which he desires to be released. What else, I ask, is this than to add death to one who is dying, and by one’s cruelty to kill his soul, lest it be able to be absolved? Since God is entirely prepared to help, inviting people to penance, He promises thus: “On whatever day the sinner turns, his sins shall not be imputed to him”; and again: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but only that he turn and live” (Ezekiel 33:12 and 18:23).

[Note: The Vindobonensis and Vat. Regina, with other copies, read this way. Vat. 1342 reads “but only that he may turn.” Quesnel reads “but that he may turn more fully.”]

Whoever, therefore, will have denied the hoped-for penance at the time of death deprives a man of salvation; and whoever did not believe that God’s mercy could suffice [Col. 0578A] to aid the dying even in a moment despaired of God’s clemency.

[Note: The word “hoped for” was deleted in a second correction in the Vindobonensis. It is absent from the Dionysian manuscript and certain Hadrianic copies. Some copies, with Vat. 1342, read “the penance hoped for even at the time of death.” Corbie and one Colbert manuscript read “to deny penance when death passes by.” Coustant, with other copies, reads “will have denied penance at the time death has passed,” and explains it as “will have denied the penance of the past at the time of death,” as Celestine likewise has in Letter 22 to the Council of Ephesus, §5: “Now that we rejoice in the correction of what was past.” Quesnel, with ancient copies and the Councils, reads “and despaired … did not believe.” Other copies read “and he despaired … he did not believe.” We have preferred the Vindobonensis with Coustant.]

The thief would have lost his reward who hung on the cross at Christ’s right hand, if the penance of one hour had not helped him (Luke 23:42). While he was undergoing punishment, he repented, and through the profession of a single statement he obtained, with God’s promise, the dwelling-place of paradise.

True conversion to God in those placed at the end of life must therefore be judged by the mind rather than by the time, as the prophet declares in these words: “When you have turned and groaned, then you shall be saved” (Ezekiel 18 and 33). Since the Lord is the examiner of the heart, penance must not be denied at any time to one who asks for it, since that person binds himself to the Judge before whom he knows that all hidden things are revealed.

[Note: Vat. 1342, with Justinian and Coustant, reads “since he binds himself to Him.”]

[Col. 0578B]

[p. 273]

### IV

We have learned, dearest brothers, that certain persons have been ordained as fellow bishops, although they had not been established through any ecclesiastical orders to the summit of such dignity, contrary to the decrees of the Fathers, through the usurpation of one who acknowledges that he did this.

[Note: [Col. 0578D] Quesnel reads “brothers and fellow bishops.” We have preferred the manuscripts Vat. 1342 and the Vindobonensis, supported by the other printed copies, in which only “bishops” appears instead of “fellow bishops.”]

A person ought to reach the episcopate through those stages that have most frequently been safeguarded, so that those initiated into lesser offices may be strengthened for greater ones. Whoever desires to be a teacher must first be a disciple, so that he may be able to teach what he has learned.

Every formation of life confirms itself by this principle for the goal toward which it strives.

[Note: Vat. Regina reads “the beginning.”]

One who has given no attention to letters cannot be a teacher of letters. One who has not advanced through each stage of service cannot reach the order of completed service. Is the priesthood alone, I ask, cheaper among all these things, since it is more easily bestowed, [Col. 0578C] although it is more difficult to fulfill?

[Note: We restored from all our manuscripts and printed copies words omitted by Quesnel. The Vulgate reads “is bestowed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0578D] From our manuscripts and printed copies we added “enough,” and shortly afterward “almost.”]

But now it is not enough to ordain laymen whom no order permits to become clergy; even those whose crimes are known far and wide through almost every province are being ordained.

### V

Daniel, recently reported to us from the eastern regions, has been accused by wicked charges by the entire monastery of virgins that he had governed.

[Note: The Vulgate and the Councils add “for.”]

Many disgraceful acts were charged against many people.

[Note: The Vulgate and the Councils read “many things by many people.” The manuscripts Vat. Regina and another Vatican manuscript read “and many things by many people.”]

He was sought in whatever part of the world he might be hiding, so that, if he trusted in his innocence, he would not evade the judgment sought against him.

[Note: Quesnel reads “in which he might be concealed … he was sought.” Both Vatican manuscripts read “in which he might not be concealed … he was sought.” The phrase “in which he might not” is a scribal error for “in what place.” The Vindobonensis has “among whom,” corruptly, but “he was sought,” with the verb “is” understood.]

A letter was sent to the bishop of Arles through Fortunatus, [Col. 0579A] our subdeacon, so that he might be assigned to episcopal judgment.

[Note: The Vindobonensis and Colbert manuscript, with the Councils, read this way. Quesnel reads “letters were sent …” Dionysius and Justinian read “letters sent to the bishop of Arles … instructions, so that he might be assigned to episcopal judgment.” Since the Corbie and another Colbert manuscript read “a letter sent to the bishop of Arles,” as in Dionysius, the word “instructions” has been deleted, and “episcopal” is understood either as masculine or feminine. Coustant thinks the latter word should be corrected to *epistolium* (“a short letter”). The older manuscripts of this and Italian collections—Vat. Regina, Lucca, Colbert, and Vat. 1342—read “a letter was sent …” without “episcopal.” We believe the word should be deleted: the subject here is plainly not the judgment of bishops, whether of Arles or, as some interpret it, of the Easterners, but the judgment of the Apostolic See, before which Daniel had been brought. This is shown by what follows: “When letters had been sent by us, he was summoned,” and especially by the statement concerning the same Daniel in chapter 10: “He must submit himself to our judgment.” Nevertheless, when publishing our collection, we did not wish to remove the word, although it had been improperly inserted in the manuscripts of this collection.]

Burdened by such weighty testimonies and assailed by such accusations of crimes, polluted, as it is said, by incest with sacred virgins, he is said to have been ordained a bishop. In our archive booklets this is recorded, and we have also sent copies of them to you. [p. 274] At the time when, through letters sent by us, he was being summoned to answer the charge, he insinuated himself into the dignity of the episcopate.

[Note: [Col. 0579D] Quesnel reads “and, as is contained in our archive booklets,” with no manuscript or printed authority supporting it. Merlin, with Isidore, reads “as is contained in our archive booklets.” We have corrected the text from the Vindobonensis, Vat. Regina, and other printed copies.]

God forbid that this should be an injury to the sacred office. It is easier that the ordainer himself lost this dignity by granting it to such a man than that the ordained man should possess it; and to the convicted man will be joined the one who, by bestowing the episcopate upon him, believed that he should be joined to him. For whoever ordains such men reveals what sort of man he himself is.

[Note: Quesnel alone reads “ordains”; shortly afterward he omitted “now,” and instead of “have conducted themselves” reads “have converted themselves.”]

Since these matters have now been brought forward, and since many of you have been acquainted with the statutes of the Apostolic See and have spent some time [Col. 0579B] among us, let your brotherhood hasten to restore everything to the rule of discipline in accordance with the agreements established by our exhortations.

### VI

First, in accordance with the decrees of the canons, each province must remain content with its own metropolitan, as the constitutions contained in the letter of our predecessor to the bishop of Narbonne state (Boniface, Letter to Hilary, above, chapter 34). No opportunity for usurpation is to be granted to any priest to the injury of another.

[Note: Some copies read “to usurpation,” or “by usurpation.”]

Let each person be content with the boundaries granted to him. Let no one presume anything in another’s province. Nor should foreigners and outsiders, or men previously unknown, be placed ahead of clerics who have completed their service in their own Churches and deserve well by the testimony of their fellow citizens, lest it appear that a new kind of college has been instituted from which bishops are made.

[Col. 0579C]

No bishop shall be given to unwilling people.

[Note: In the manuscript Vat. Regina this is the beginning of the first chapter, whose title is prefixed: “No one shall be ordained against the will”; read “to unwilling persons.”]

The consent and desire of the clergy, the people, and the civic order must be sought. Only then may someone be chosen from another Church, if no one worthy can be found among the clergy of the very city for which a bishop is to be ordained—which we do not believe can happen.

[Note: Quesnel inserts “to be able,” against the Vindobonensis and the other printed copies.]

For first the local candidates must be rejected before someone from another [Col. 0580A] Church is rightly preferred. Let each person enjoy the fruit of his service in the Church in which he has passed his entire life through all the offices. Let no one intrude upon another’s service, nor dare to claim for himself another’s [p. 275] deserved reward.

Let the clergy have the freedom to resist if they see themselves being oppressed, and let them not fear to reject those whom they recognize as being thrust upon them from outside. For if they ought not to receive the reward due to them, or to have free judgment concerning the person who is to govern them—

[Note: Quesnel omitted “for himself”; shortly afterward he reads “have seen” instead of “have recognized,” against our manuscripts and printed copies.]

### VII

Let unlawful ordinations be avoided. No layman, no man who has married twice, no man who is or has been the husband of a widow, shall be ordained; rather, one who is irreproachable and of the kind chosen by the Apostle shall be appointed.

### VIII

Through Moses the Lord commanded: “The priest shall take a virgin as wife” (Leviticus 21:13).

[Note: Quesnel alone omitted “as wife.”]

The Apostle, speaking in the same Spirit, [Col. 0580B] follows and completes this: a bishop must be consecrated as “the husband of one wife” (1 Timothy 3:2).

[Note: In Vat. Regina this chapter is marked as chapter 2, with the title: “On the illicit removal of illicitly made ordinations.” Vat. 1342 reads “let them choose.”]

Priests must therefore be chosen according to this standard; and if any unlawful ordinations have been made, they must be removed, for they cannot stand and will not be able to evade our investigation, even though those who have attained office by another path believe that they can remain hidden.

[Note: The Vulgate and the Councils, with Vat. Regina and one Colbert manuscript, read “who have attained it in this way.” Justinian, with other manuscripts, reads “in whatever way.”]

Thus no reverence for religion should be darkened by obscurity.

### IX

Let there be no empty boasting among those clothed in cloaks. Those who are bishops should follow episcopal custom.

### X

Daniel, who, as we said, believed that he could evade accusation by means of episcopal rank and reached such a height only by fleeing from his accusers, should meanwhile know that he has been separated from the assembly of your holiness. He must submit himself to our judgment, if he knows that he possesses confidence [Col. 0580C] in his own conscience.

[Note: [Col. 0580D] Quesnel alone reads “flee”; shortly afterward he deleted “his.” The manuscripts of Quesnel and our collection read “by fleeing.” Earlier editions, with Hadrian and Isidore, read “by hiding.” The Dionysian exemplar reads “by grieving.” Corbie and one Colbert manuscript read “by acting.” Vat. 1342 reads “made himself absent”; after deleting the rest of this section it continues: “But the priest of the Church of Marseilles …”]

### XI
