As for the priest of the Church of Marseilles, who is said—what is too wicked to say—to have rejoiced so greatly at the death of his brother that he met the man who had arrived stained with his blood, intending to share a portion with that same man, we delegate him to be heard by your college.

[Note: [Col. 0580D] Quesnel alone omits “too wicked to say.”]

[Note: Vat. 1342 reads “we assign him to your college,” less correctly. Coustant reads “and to be heard by you,” with the conjunction “and” inserted from the Colbert manuscript and supported by other copies, including Merlin, Crabbe, and Justinian, which read “from your [college].” The word “him,” although superfluous, appears in most manuscripts.]

[Note: Coustant and the old editions of the Councils, with Justinian, read “the seventh day before the Kalends”; Vat. 1342 and Lucca, “the ninth day”; the copies of our collection, “the eighth day,” some of them, with Corbie, adding “Flavius” before Felix.]

Given on the eighth [Col. 0581A] day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of the most distinguished men Felix and Taurus.

[p. 276]

## CHAPTER XXXVI

[Note: [Col. 0581D] This is found in the same manuscripts and collections as the preceding chapter, and some portions also occur in the manuscript Vat. Palat. 574.]

**Pope Celestine’s Letter to the Bishops of Apulia and Calabria**

**CELESTINE to all the bishops established throughout Apulia and Calabria.**

No priest may be permitted to be ignorant of the canons, nor to do anything that could conflict with the rules of the Fathers. For what matter will be observed by us with due dignity if the standard of the decretal constitutions is broken at the pleasure of certain people, with permission granted to the populace?

[Note: Some copies read “it is permitted”; shortly afterward, “worthy” instead of “worthily,” perhaps more correctly.]

We have heard that certain cities deprived of their proper rulers wish to seek bishops from among the laity, and consider so great a dignity so cheaply that they think we can confer it upon men who have served [Col. 0581B] not God but the world. In doing this they judge badly not only of their own clerics, to whose contempt they act, but also most wickedly of us, whom they believe capable of doing such a thing.

[Note: Quesnel alone omits “wish.”]

They would never dare this if the opinion of certain persons there, agreeing with them, did not connive at it.

[Note: The Oxford manuscript reads “the crowd connived.”]

Thus the decrees so frequently issued accomplish nothing, since this matter is ignored as though nothing had ever been written about it.

What benefit will it have been for clerics to have served through every stage of service and spent their entire lives in the Lord’s camp, if those who are to govern them are sought from among the laity? Such men, free from secular occupations and ignorant of the entire ecclesiastical order, seek with immoderate ambition to cross over by a reckless leap into an honor belonging to others and [Col. 0581C] to pass into another kind of life, trampling upon reverence for ecclesiastical discipline.

To such men, therefore, dearest brothers, we who guard the helm of our jurisdiction—that is, of the canons—must offer resistance. By this letter we admonish your brotherhood, lest anyone admit a layman to the clerical order [p. 277] and allow something to be done that will both deceive him and create causes by which he may become liable under the established decrees.

[Note: [Col. 0581D] Quesnel adds “we”; our manuscript and printed copies omit it.]

[Note: Quesnel omitted the word “of the clergy.”]

The people must be taught, not followed. If they do not know what is permitted and what is not, we must admonish them, not grant them our consent. Whoever attempts to try what has been prohibited will discover that the censure of the Apostolic See will by no means be absent.

[Note: Vat. Palat. reads “from now on.”]

For what we do not correct by the authority of admonition, we must necessarily punish with a severity proportionate to the rules. [Col. 0582A] We therefore wish this to be made known throughout all the Churches that lack their own rulers, so that no one, perhaps flattering himself with some hope, may deceive himself.

[Note: Vat. 1342 adds “this decision.”]

[Note: Lucca and Colbert read “the thirteenth day before the Kalends”; another Colbert manuscript and Corbie read “given on the Kalends.” Vat. Regina, and two of Coustant’s manuscripts, Corbie and Colbert, read “the Flavii Florentius,” etc. The Pithoean copy of this collection has “FF. LL. Florentius”; the sigla have the same force.]

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of the most distinguished men Florentius and Dionysius.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

[Note: [Col. 0582D] This chapter is found in this collection and in the manuscripts of the Lucca and Colbert collections, where the title reads: “Here begins [the work] on the Catholic faith.” The words “and apostolic,” omitted by Quesnel, have been added on the authority of the Vindobonensis and Thuanus. Quesnel discusses this and the three following treatises on the faith in Dissertation 14; see our notes there.]

**An Exposition of the Catholic and Apostolic Faith against the Arian Heresy**

We confess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, in such a perfect Trinity that there is both fullness of divinity and unity of power. For whoever separates the divinity of the Trinity speaks of three gods. The Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God, and the three are one in Christ Jesus.

Thus there are three persons but one power. Diversity produces plurality; the unity of power, however, [Col. 0582B] excludes numerical quantity, because unity is not a number.

[Note: The Lucca manuscript, in Mansi, *Supplement to the Councils*, vol. I, col. 242, reads “forms.”]

[Note: The same Lucca manuscript reads “Thus, therefore.”]

Thus there is one God, one faith, one baptism. If anyone does not hold this faith, he cannot be called Catholic, because he does not hold the Catholic faith; he is alien, profane, and rebellious against the truth.

[Note: [Col. 0582D] The Thuanus manuscript reads “who.”]

[p. 278]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

[Note: In the Vindobonensis the following inscription appears: “Here begins the confession of the true faith by the presbyter Faustinus, which the presbyter wrote and ordered to be sent to him by the emperor Theodosius” (read “which he wrote and ordered to be sent”). According to Quesnel, Dissertation 14, §6, the Thuanus manuscript has: “The confession of the true faith by the presbyter Faustinus, which Theodosius the emperor ordered to be written and sent to the aforementioned person.” Mabillon found this faith among other confessions of faith in an ancient manuscript from Augia, where it is entitled *A Brief Statement of the Faith*.]

**The Faith of the Presbyter Faustinus, Sent to the Emperor Theodosius**

The faith written at Nicaea against the Arian heresy would have been sufficient. But because certain people, through perverse ingenuity, alter impious words under the cover of that confession of faith, bringing odium upon us on the grounds that we seem to defend the heresy of Sabellius, we briefly set down a statement against Sabellius according to the confession of the original faith.

[Note: [Col. 0582D] The Thuanus manuscript reads “mix” instead of “alter.”]

Against those who defend impious words under the name of the Catholic faith, saying that there are three [Col. 0582C] substances, we also write, since the Catholic faith has always confessed one substance of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

We believe in the Father, who is not the Son but has a Son begotten from Himself without beginning, not made. We believe in the Son, who is not the Father but has a Father from whom He is begotten, not made. And we believe in the Holy Spirit, who is truly the Spirit of God.

Therefore we confess one substance of the divine Trinity, because the Father is such according to substance that He begot the Son likewise; and since the Holy Spirit is not a creature but the Spirit of God, He is not alien from the substance of the Father and the Son, but is Himself of the same substance as the Father and the Son, just as He is of the same divinity.

For those who think that we [Col. 0583A] are Apollinarists should know that we execrate the heresy of Apollinaris no less than that of Arius. We are astonished that those who confess three substances of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit can be approved as Catholics.

Even if they say that they do not believe the Son of God or the Holy Spirit to be a creature, nevertheless they hold an impious belief when they say that there are three substances. For it follows that they confess three gods if they confess three substances. Catholics have always execrated this expression.

[p. 279]

## CHAPTER XXXIX

[Note: [Col. 0583C] Besides the manuscripts of this collection, this chapter is found in the manuscripts of Lucca and Colbert, in Vat. 1342, and in Vallicelliana A 5 and Vat. 5845. Crabbe discovered and published a fragment of it in an extremely ancient manuscript from Aix. Almost the same text appears in volume V of St. Augustine’s works, *Sermon* 135, in the appendix. The Benedictine Fathers admit that they found this treatise nowhere in Augustine’s manuscripts. Since it circulated under Augustine’s name in copies of our collection and in the additions to Isidore’s collection found in Vat. 1340 and in another similar Remigian manuscript called by Quesnel the Herovallian manuscript, it is sufficiently probable that it was inserted among Augustine’s works from one of these sources; hence the readings generally agree. In the Vindobonensis the title is: “Here begins another book, that is, a little book of faith.” Crabbe’s manuscript has: “Here begins the faith of the Romans.” Both Vatican manuscripts and the Vallicelliana have: “Here begins the faith of the Catholic Roman Church.” Quesnel notes in the margin: “This is a Latin discourse of St. Gregory Nazianzen, surnamed the Theologian, or a treatise on the Nicene faith, translated by the presbyter Rufinus, as it appears in Morel’s edition of 1609, vol. I, p. 736.” In editions of St. Jerome, however, it is found under the title “Damasus’s Creed”; see volume XI of the Verona edition, p. 145. Why it is attributed to Damasus may be inferred from the Lucca manuscript and the similar Colbert manuscript, where it is appended to Damasus’s letter to Paulinus. We do not believe, however, that it belongs either to this Gregory or to any Greek writer, but rather to some Latin author, as explained more fully elsewhere. See Dissertation 14 and our observations upon it.]

**Another Little Book of Faith**

We believe in one God, the almighty Father, and in one only-begotten Son of His, God and Lord, our Savior, and in the Holy Spirit, God.

[Note: Vat. and Vallicelliana read “in one.”]

[Note: [Col. 0583D] The Thuanus manuscript reads “and the only-begotten,” deleting “one.” Both Vatican manuscripts and the Vallicelliana read: “and in one only-begotten Son of His, Jesus Christ God.” Crabbe reads: “and in the only-begotten Son of His, Jesus Christ, our Lord and Savior, and in the Holy Spirit, God.” The Lucca manuscript reads: “and His only Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, conceived from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, God and Lord, and in the Holy Spirit, God; we confess not three gods, but the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be one God.”]

[Col. 0583B] We confess not three gods—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—but one God. Not one God as though He were solitary, nor the same person, so that He Himself is Father to Himself and Himself Son,

[Note: The Lucca manuscript reads: “so that He Himself is Father and Himself is Son.” Crabbe reads: “He Himself is Father, He Himself is Son.”]

but the true Father, who begot the true Son, as God is from God, light from light, life from life, perfect from perfect, whole from whole, fullness from fullness—not created but begotten, not from nothing but from the Father, of one substance with the Father.

[Note: Crabbe reads “that is, God from God.”]

We venerate the Holy Spirit as God, neither unbegotten nor begotten, neither created nor [p. 280] made.

[Note: Quesnel inserts “and,” but all our manuscripts and Crabbe omit it. Quesnel reads “and the Holy Spirit, true God.”]

[Col. 0584A] He is coeternal with the Father and the Son, always in the Father and the Son.

[Note: Crabbe, with most of our manuscripts, has different punctuation: “coeternal; nevertheless we venerate one God.”]

Yet we venerate one God, because from the one Father the Son, who is God, was born with everything that belongs to the Father; and the Father generated the whole Son with everything that is in the Father.

[Note: One manuscript of Crabbe ends at “from one.”]

[Note: [Col. 0584B] Lucca, Vallicelliana, and both Vatican manuscripts read *Deus natus est Filius* (“the Son was born God”). Shortly afterward Vat. 1342 reads *totum genuit in Filium* (“he begot the whole into the Son”); Vallicelliana and another Vatican manuscript preserve the difficult reading *totum ingenitum, et in Filium* (“the whole unbegotten, and into the Son”).]

When the Father begets the Son, He is neither diminished nor deprived of the fullness of His divinity. We hold with complete certainty that everything that God the Father is, the Son born from Him also is.

[Note: [Col. 0584C] The Vindobonensis and Thuanus agree with all the other collections, except that Vat. 1342 reads “believing” instead of “holding”; the Vallicelliana and another Vatican manuscript incorrectly read “we believe.” Quesnel alone reads: “We hold with complete certainty that what the Father is, God, the Son is likewise.”]

Together with the Holy Spirit we devoutly confess one God, Jesus Christ our Lord, the Son of God, through whom all things were made that are in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible.

[Note: [Col. 0584C] The Lucca, Vallicelliana, and both Vatican manuscripts join the following words to the preceding and punctuate them thus: “With the Holy Spirit we confess one God. We believe in Jesus Christ.”]

[Note: Thuanus and the Vindobonensis delete “all things,” but the other manuscripts do not. The Vindobonensis reads “and on earth,” omitting “which.”]

For our salvation He descended from heaven, yet never ceased to be in heaven; He was born from the Holy Spirit of the Virgin Mary.

[Note: The Lucca manuscript, with the Vallicelliana and Vat. 5845, reads “He descended from heaven and was born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary,” omitting the intervening words. We have written “He ceased” at the point where the manuscripts Thuanus, Vindobonensis, and another Vat. 1342 end. Quesnel reads “He ceased.” Vat. also has “born from the Holy Spirit.” Vat. 1342 reads “and from the Virgin Mary.”]

The Word became flesh; He did not lose what He had been, but began to be what He had not been.

[Note: [Col. 0584D] Quesnel has different punctuation: “not changed, but remaining. We believe [that] a human being was born.” We have preferred all our manuscripts and the Thuanus manuscript. Lucca and Vallicelliana alone read “but remaining God, [He was] also born a human being.”]

[Col. 0584B] Unchanged, but remaining what He was, He was also born a human being—not merely in appearance but truly; not airy but bodily; not phantom-like but fleshly, possessing bones, blood, sensation, and a soul.

[Note: The Lucca manuscript has the preferable reading: “Thus we understand Him to be true man and true God, so that we do not in any way hesitate to confess that the true God was a true man.” The Vallicelliana reads: “Again we understand Him to be true man, and likewise we do not in any way hesitate that He was true God and true man.” The word “now” also occurs in both Vatican manuscripts. The second Oxford comma reads: “thus we understand Him to be true man and true God,” with the conjunction “and” inserted, less correctly. The Thuanus manuscript reads “phantasium,” the Lucca manuscript “phantaseum,” the Vallicelliana and one Vatican manuscript “phantasia,” followed by “but flesh.” Quesnel alone reads “mind.”]

[p. 281] Thus we understand Him to be true God and true man; thus we have no doubt that the true man was the true God.

It is to be confessed that this same Lord Jesus Christ fulfilled the Law and the Prophets, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified according to the Scriptures, died and was buried according to the Scriptures, rose from the dead on the [Col. 0585A] third day, was taken up into the heavens, sits at the right hand of the Father, and we await His coming from there to judge the living and the dead.

[Note: Quesnel reads “crucified and dead”; we have followed our manuscripts and the Thuanus manuscript. Besides the manuscripts of the other collections, the Vindobonensis deletes *est* (“is”) from “It is to be confessed.”]

[Col. 0585B] Having been cleansed through His death and blood, we have obtained remission of sins. We shall be raised by Him in these bodies and in the same flesh in which we now are, just as He Himself rose in the same flesh in which He was born, suffered, and died; and we shall receive from Him either eternal life as the reward of good merit, or the sentence of eternal punishment for sins, together with our souls and this flesh—or our bodies.

[Note: [Col. 0585C] Quesnel adds “we confess,” but the two best manuscripts of this collection, Thuanus and Vindobonensis, together with Lucca and Vat. 1342, omit it. Quesnel reads “rose,” and then deletes “or our bodies,” although these words occur in two Thuanus manuscripts and in all five of our manuscripts from different collections. The Lucca manuscript alone adds after “or our bodies”: “we have received.” The Vallicelliana and Vatican manuscripts read “we shall receive,” with Quesnel’s final “we shall receive” deleted.]

[p. 282]

## CHAPTER XL

[Note: This treatise formerly appeared among St. Augustine’s works, volume X, *Sermon* 129, “On Time,” but has now been rejected into the appendix, volume V, *Sermon* 233. The Benedictine Fathers admit that they found this little book nowhere in Augustine’s manuscripts. Since it circulates under Augustine’s name in copies of our collection and also in the additions to Isidore’s collection found in Vat. 1340 and in another similar Remigian manuscript called by Quesnel the Herovallian manuscript, it is sufficiently probable that it was inserted among Augustine’s works from one of these two sources; hence the readings generally agree. The Vindobonensis manuscript has the following title: “Here begins Augustine’s little book on the Catholic faith against all heresies.” [Col. 0585D] This little book is in fact the same as the Rule of Faith composed in the time of St. Leo against all heresies, especially the Priscillianists—concerning which see more in volume II, in the observations on Quesnel’s note to Letter 15 to Turibius—and incorrectly placed beneath the First Council of Toledo in the Venetian edition of the Councils, volume II, col. 1475. In substance it is certainly the same as the aforementioned Rule of Faith, although it differs in several, and not insignificant, variants. The anathemas, however, are partly the same and partly entirely different. See further note 11 in Quesnel’s Dissertation 14.]

**Augustine’s Little Book on the Catholic Faith against All Heresies**
We believe in one true God, the Father, and the Son, [Col. 0585B] and the Holy Spirit, maker of visible and invisible things, through whom all things in heaven and on earth were created. We believe this one [Note: [Col. 0585D] Quesnell adds “true”; we have deleted it with the Vindobonensis, Thuanus, Herovallianus, and the other printed witnesses. Shortly afterward the common editions, following the First Council of Toledo, read: “and that this is the one Trinity of the divine substance. But the Father is not the Son himself.”] God to be the Trinity of the one divine name. The Father is not the Son, but has a Son who is not the Father; the Son is not the Father, [Note: [Col. 0585D] Thus the Vindobonensis, with the Herovallianus agreeing. In the Augustinian Appendix: “but that the Son is born as Son of God.” Quesnell: “but that the Son is from his substance.” The common Council edition is better: “but that the Son of God is of the substance of the Father.”] but that the Son is God’s Son by nature; and the Spirit, the Paraclete, also exists, who is neither the Father himself nor the Son, but proceeds from the Father. [Note: [Col. 0585D] The common Council edition, Jerome, and Augustine add “and from the Son” (*Filioque*), and similarly shortly afterward: “but proceeding from the Father and the Son” (or “and from the Son”). [Col. 0586B]]

The Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Paraclete not begotten but proceeding from the Father. The Father is he whose voice was heard from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.” [Note: [Col. 0586B] The Vindobonensis, with the Herovallianus, deletes “in me” and then reads “listen to this one.”] The Son is he who says: “I came forth from the Father and came from God into this world.” [Note: [Col. 0586B] The common Council edition: “The Paraclete Spirit is he of whom …”] The Paraclete himself is he of whom the Son says: “Unless I go to the Father, the Paraclete will not come to you.”

We believe this Trinity, distinct in persons, [Note: [Col. 0586B] The same source: “united in substance, indivisible and undifferentiated in power, authority, and majesty. Besides this, we believe no divine [Col. 0586C] nature exists,” and so forth: this is better. Here, however, we present the readings of the manuscripts in our collection. The Augustinian Appendix omits the words from “one substance” through “indivisible,” inclusively.] one in substance, power, authority, and majesty, indivisible and undifferentiated. Besides it, we believe no divine nature exists—whether of an angel, [283] [Note: [Col. 0586C] We have restored the words “or spirit,” omitted by Quesnell, from the Vindobonensis, Herovallianus, and the other printed witnesses. Shortly afterward the Oxoniensis reads: “Therefore the Son …”] or spirit, or any kind of power that is believed to be God.

Therefore we believe that this Son of God, God begotten from the Father before every beginning whatsoever, sanctified [Note: [Col. 0586C] The common Augustinian edition, together with the Vindobonensis and Herovallianus, reads “in the womb.” The Thuanus reads “sanctified in the womb,” which Quesnell considers less correct, although it can be understood in the sense of the words: “whom the Father sanctified.” The Council edition then reads: “generated without male seed.”] the womb of the Virgin Mary and received from her a true man, generated without the seed of a man; [Note: [Col. 0586C] The common Council editions add: “with only two natures, that is, of the Godhead and the flesh, coming together wholly into one person, that is, our Lord Jesus Christ; nor was there in him an imaginary body or something like a phantom, but a solid and true body: this one also hungered,” and so forth.] that is, the Lord Jesus Christ—not a merely imaginary body or one composed only in outward form, but a solid one; [Col. 0586B] and that he hungered, thirsted, suffered pain, and wept, [Note: [Col. 0586C] The same common Council editions add: “and endured every injury of the body; finally …”] and experienced all the bodily sufferings; finally, that he was crucified, died, and was buried, and rose again on the third day; afterward that he lived [Note: [Col. 0586C] The Thuanus reads: “with the disciples, before he sent the Holy Spirit, whom he sent while he was going to heaven.” The Vindobonensis: “with the disciples, whom he sent while he had ascended to heaven.” The better reading in the Augustinian Appendix is: “with the disciples, to whom he sent the holy Paraclete while he was ascending to heaven.” Both, however, continue: “This Son of Man is now called. The Resurrection.” The Oxoniensis deletes the words from “This Son of Man” through “we confess.” The more accurate reading in the common Council edition is: “with his disciples, and on the fortieth day after the resurrection ascended into heaven. This Son of Man is also called the Son of God; and we call the Son of God the Lord, the Son of Man. We believe the resurrection to be of the human …” The Oxoniensis omits “of the human.”] with his disciples and sent them the Paraclete while he himself had ascended into heaven. We truly believe, or confess, that he is called the Son of Man.

We believe in the true resurrection of human flesh. But the soul of a human being is not a divine substance or a part of God, [Note: [Col. 0586D] The Herovallianus reads: “but created by the divine will, not fallen.” The Vindobonensis and Thuanus: “but a creature created by the divine will, not fallen.” The same appears in the Augustinian Appendix, which alone deletes “not.” The Council edition: “but we say that it is a creature created by the divine will. If anyone should say or believe …”] but a creature made by the divine will, not fallen from heaven.

[Col. 0587A]

If anyone therefore says or believes that this world and all its elements were not made by almighty God, let him be anathema.

If anyone believes and says that God the Father is the same as the Son, or the Paraclete, let him be anathema.

If anyone says and believes [Note: [Col. 0587C] The Augustinian Appendix: “God the Son.” The common Council edition is better: “the Son of God.”] that the Lord the Son is the same as the Father or the Paraclete, let him be anathema.

284 [Note: [Col. 0587C] The common Council edition: “If anyone says or believes that the Paraclete is either the Father or the Son,” and so forth. The same is found in the Vindobonensis manuscript. It alone adds “Spirit” after “Paraclete.”]

If anyone says that the Spirit Paraclete is the same as either the Father or the Son, let him be anathema.

[Note: [Col. 0587C] This anathema and the two following ones are expressed differently and better in the common Council edition: “If anyone says or believes that only flesh, without a soul, was assumed by the Son of God, let him be anathema. If anyone says or believes that Christ is unborn (or, alternatively, incapable of suffering), let him be anathema. If anyone says or believes that the Godhead of Christ is changeable [Col. 0587D] or capable of suffering, let him be anathema.”]

If anyone says and believes that the man Jesus Christ was not assumed by the Son of God, let him be anathema.

[Note: [Col. 0587D] The Thuanus: “If anyone does not believe.” Quesnell notes in the margin: “The sense of either reading can be sound.” Indeed, the sense of the reading which he has attached from the Thuanus manuscript is perverse unless one supplies “that the Son of God, as God and man, suffered in his humanity,” or something similar.]

If anyone says and believes that the Son of God, God, suffered, let him be anathema.

[Col. 0587B]

If anyone says and believes that the man Jesus Christ was a man incapable of suffering, let him be anathema.

If anyone says and believes that the God of the ancient law is one God and the God of the Gospels another, let him be anathema.

If anyone says and believes that the world was made by a God other than the one of whom it is written, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Genesis 1:1)—who alone is the true God—let him be anathema.

[Note: [Col. 0587D] We have added the word “was” (*fuisse*) from the Vindobonensis manuscript, supported by the Augustinian Appendix and the common Council edition. In the latter witnesses “was made” is read, and not “by him of whom”; and they delete “who alone is the true God.”]

If anyone says and believes that human bodies will not rise again after death, [Note: [Col. 0587D] The common Council edition: “will not rise again.”] let him be anathema.

If anyone says and believes that the human soul is a portion of God or is God’s substance, let him be anathema.

If anyone believes that certain Scriptures besides those received by the Catholic Church are to be held as authoritative [Col. 0587C] [Note: [Col. 0587D] Thus the Vindobonensis and Herovallianus manuscripts, together with the Augustinian Appendix. Quesnell, following the Oxoniensis, reads “has received, or has been revered,” and notes in the margin: “Perhaps *praeceperit* should be read instead of *receperit*.” The Thuanus: “which the Church receives.” Or: “which are to be held as authoritative should be believed”: less well. In the common Council edition this anathema is presented differently: “If anyone says or believes that other Scriptures besides those which the Catholic Church receives are to be held as authoritative or revered, let him be anathema.” Six further anathemas against the Priscillianists are then added; they are absent from our collection and from the Augustinian Appendix.] or has revered them, let him be anathema.

285 CHAPTER XLI. [Note: [Col. 0588C] In the Vindobonensis manuscript, the title is replaced simply by “Examples of testimonies.” Since these same testimonies are presented again in our collection, in chapter 67, after the letter of Saint Leo to the emperor Leo, which we published together with these testimonies in volume I, letter 165, column [Col. 0588D] 1383, we have there supplied the variant readings of the different collections. Referring readers to that place, here we have merely examined the titles against the outstanding Vindobonensis manuscript of this collection and corrected certain passages as they appear there in chapter 41. This should always be understood wherever we have corrected the text on the basis of Quesnell’s reading rejected in the notes.]

Examples of testimonies of the holy Fathers concerning the two natures, remaining without separation and distinctly in the one person of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0588A]

[Note: [Col. 0588D] Thus from the Vindobonensis manuscript. Quesnell: “From the second book Against the Arians of Saint Hilary, bishop of Poitiers.” Shortly afterward we inserted from the same manuscript the particle “for,” which Quesnell had omitted.]

From the second book On the Catholic Faith of Saint HILARY, bishop of Poitiers and confessor.

For the Son of God was born from the Virgin and the Holy Spirit for the sake of the human race, with the Holy Spirit himself as his partner in this work and his own—that is, God’s—power overshadowing [her]. He sowed in himself the beginnings of a body and established the origins of flesh, so that, having become man from the Virgin, he might receive the nature of flesh into himself, and through the fellowship of this assumption the body of the entire human race might exist sanctified in him: so that, just as all were established in him through the fact that he willed to be bodily, so again he might be conveyed into all through that which is invisible in him. [Col. 0588B]

Therefore the image of the invisible God did not refuse the humiliation of human beginnings, and through conception, birth, crying, and a cradle he passed through all the indignities of our nature. What, then, worthy of such condescension, shall be offered in return for so great a favor? [Note: [Col. 0588D] Thus the same Vindobonensis manuscript. Quesnell: “What shall be bestowed in return for such affection.”] The one only-begotten God, whose origin from God cannot be told, grows within the womb of the holy Virgin, inserted into the form of a tiny human body; and he who contains all things, and within whom and through whom all things exist, is brought forth according to the law of human birth. At whose voice angels and archangels tremble, heaven and earth and all the elements of this world are dissolved, yet the cry of infancy is heard; and he who is invisible and incomprehensible, who cannot be measured by sight, sensation, or touch, is wrapped in swaddling clothes. If anyone recalls these things as unworthy of God, he will confess himself subject to a far greater benefit, since these things seem so little [Col. 0588C] suited to God’s majesty. He did not need to become man, through whom man was made; but we [286] needed God to become flesh [Note: [Col. 0588D] The same witness: “that man might become God.”] and dwell among us—that is, through the assumption of one flesh within, he might dwell in all flesh. His humility is our nobility; his humiliation [Col. 0589A] is our honor. What he, God existing in flesh, is, that we in turn are, renewed from flesh into God.

The same author, in book IX, among other passages.

He plainly does not know his own life—does not know it—who fails to recognize Christ Jesus as true God and likewise true man; and it is equally perilous to deny Christ Jesus either as God the Spirit or as the flesh of our body [Col. 0589D]. [Note: [Col. 0589D] Quesnell: “to deny.”] “Everyone,” he says, “who confesses me before men, I too will confess before my Father who is in heaven. But whoever denies me before men, I too will deny him before my Father who is in heaven.” These words were spoken by the Word made flesh, and the man Jesus Christ, the Lord of majesty, was teaching; the mediator himself, established in himself for the salvation of the Church, and in the very mystery of the mediator between God and human beings, existing as one in both: since he himself, from the natures united into the same [Col. 0589B] thing, is the same reality of each nature; yet in each he lacked neither one nor the other, lest, by being born as man, he should cease to be God, and lest, conversely, by remaining God, he should not be man. This, therefore, is the true faith of human blessedness: to proclaim God and man, to confess the Word and the flesh; neither to be ignorant that God is man, nor to fail to know that the flesh is the Word.

The same author, in the same book, among other passages.

The only-begotten God was therefore born man from the Virgin and, in the fullness of time, was to advance man in himself into God. He consistently maintained throughout the whole manner of evangelical speech that he might teach himself to be believed the Son of God and might instruct that he be proclaimed the Son of Man. He spoke as man and carried out everything that belongs to God; then, speaking and acting as God, he carried out everything that belongs to man; yet in that very [Col. 0589C] discourse concerning both kinds he never spoke except with an indication both of man and of God.

The same author, elsewhere in the same book, among other passages.

Do you see how he is proclaimed God and man, so that death is assigned to man, but the raising of the flesh to God? Understand the nature of God in the power of the [287] resurrection; recognize the dispensation of man in the death. And although both were accomplished according to their respective natures, remember nevertheless that it is one Jesus Christ who is both. And shortly afterward [Note: [Col. 0589D] The same witness omits “it follows.”] it follows:

I have had to demonstrate these things briefly, so that we might remember that the person of both natures is being treated in the Lord Jesus Christ; for he who was in the form of God took the form of a servant. [Note: [Col. 0589D] The Oxoniensis: “the nature of the person,” incorrectly. The common edition: “the form of nature.” (Compare note f in volume I, column 1177 of our edition.)] [Note: [Col. 0589D] The common edition before Quesnell adds: “He himself in no way lost his divinity.” (See the same place, note g, column 1178.)]

[Note: [Col. 0589D] Quesnell: “From the letter of Saint Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, to Epictetus, bishop of Corinth.”]

From the letter of Saint Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria and confessor, to Epictetus, bishop of Corinth.

[Col. 0589D] [Note: [Col. 0589D] Quesnell notes in the margin: “These words of Saint Athanasius come from the version of his letter given below in chapter 52 of this collection, which Saint Leo used.”]

How, then, did those who are called Christians dare even to doubt whether the Lord who came forth from Mary is, indeed, [Col. 0590A] the Son by nature and substance of God, while according to the flesh he is from the seed of David and from the flesh of holy Mary? [Note: [Col. 0589D] Quesnell: “that the Lord …”; and afterward: “according to the flesh he is man from the seed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0590D] Quesnell: “From the second book of Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, to the emperor Gratian.”]

From book II On the Faith of Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, to the emperor Gratian.

Hence that statement, too, is found written: “The Lord of majesty was crucified”—not as though we should think that he was crucified in his own majesty, but because the same one is God and the same one man: God through divinity, man through the assumption of flesh; Jesus Christ is called the Lord of majesty who was crucified because, sharing both natures, that is, the human and the divine, he underwent suffering in the nature of man. Thus the one who suffered is indiscriminately called both the Lord of majesty [Note: [Col. 0590D] The same witness deleted “to be” and afterward added “and is in heaven” after “from heaven.”] and the Son of Man, as it is written: “He who descended from heaven” (John 3:13).

[Col. 0590B] [Note: [Col. 0590D] Quesnell: “Likewise in book XIII,” incorrectly. We have consistently followed our Vindobonensis manuscript.]

Elsewhere in the same book, among other passages.

Let empty disputes about words therefore be silent; for, as it is written, the kingdom of God is not in persuasive speech but in the demonstration of power (1 Corinthians 2:4; 4:20). Let us preserve the distinction between divinity and flesh. The Son of God speaks as one in both, because both natures are in the same person. Although it is the same one who speaks, he does not always speak in the same manner. In him, now contemplate the glory of God, now the sufferings of man. [Note: [Col. 0590D] Quesnell omitted “as though”; and afterward reads “he speaks.”] As God, he speaks what is divine, because he is the Word; as man, he says what is human, [288] because he was speaking in my substance.

The same author, in his book On the Incarnation of the Lord, among other passages.

But while we refute these people, others emerge who say that the Lord’s flesh and divinity are of one [Note: [Col. 0590D] Quesnell notes in his letter 134, now 165, of Saint Leo that “being” is added. In both places, however, our Vindobonensis manuscript lacks this word.] nature. What underworld has vomited forth such sacrilege? [Col. 0590C] The Arians are now more tolerable, since through the perfidy of these people their strength grows, so that they assert with greater insistence that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not of one substance, because these people have attempted to say that the Lord’s divinity and flesh are of one substance. And below:

These people frequently declare to me that they maintain the teaching of the Council of Nicaea. But in that teaching our Fathers said that not the flesh, but the Word of God, is of one substance with the Father; and they confessed that the Word proceeded from the Father’s substance, while the flesh came from the Virgin. How, then, is the name of the Council of Nicaea invoked as a pretext, and new doctrines introduced which our ancestors never held?

From the writings of Saint Augustine, bishop of Hippo, to Dardanus, among other passages.

[Col. 0590D] Do not therefore doubt that Christ is now man there from where he is to come; and remember carefully and [Col. 0591A] hold faithfully the Christian confession: that he rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father; and that he will come from there, and from nowhere else, to judge the living and the dead. He will come in the same manner in which the angelic voice testifies that he was seen going into heaven (Acts 1:11), that is, in the same form [Note: [Col. 0591D] Quesnell omitted “of flesh”; and afterward reads “to whom he gave perfect immortality.”] and substance of flesh; to it, certainly, he gave immortality but did not take away its nature.

The same author, in his letter to Volusianus, among other passages.

But now he appeared as mediator between God and human beings, joining both natures through the unity of person, so that he might exalt ordinary things through extraordinary ones and temper extraordinary things through ordinary ones. [Note: [Col. 0591D] The same witness: “and man.”]

The same author, in his Exposition of the Gospel according to John, among other passages.

What then, heretic? Since Christ is God and man, he speaks as man, and you bring a charge against God? He commends in himself the human nature, [Note: [Col. 0591D] Quesnell: “since in him.”] while you dare to distort the divine nature in him? And below: [289]

Let us acknowledge the twofold substance of Christ: the divine, by which he is equal to the Father; and the human, by which the Father is greater than he. Yet both together are not two, but one Christ, lest God should be a quaternity rather than a Trinity. For just as a human being is rational soul and flesh, so the one Christ is God and man; and consequently Christ is God, rational soul, [Note: [Col. 0591D] Quesnell, with a different word order: “and the flesh of God.” “Who is it that was under Pontius … in the form of a servant? Who is it through whom the world was made? Christ Jesus, but in the form of God.” “Therefore we confess Christ in all these things, Christ in each of them.” He notes in the margin: “The word ‘God’ is found only in the Oxoniensis manuscript.” We have corrected the text from the Vindobonensis and restored the order, with the support of the other manuscripts and printed witnesses.] and flesh. We confess Christ in all these things, Christ in each of them. Who, then, is he through whom the world was made? Christ Jesus, but in the form of God. Who was crucified under Pontius [Col. 0591C] Pilate? Christ Jesus, but in the form of a servant.

From Saint John, bishop of Constantinople and confessor, in the homily on the cross and the thief, among other passages.

But let us see why he comes with the cross. Certainly, so that those who crucified him may recognize the blindness of their madness; and therefore the sign of their shamelessness is carried; and therefore the prophet says: “Then the tribes of the earth will mourn, seeing the accuser and recognizing the sin.” [Note: [Col. 0592D] Quesnell: “the accusers.”] And what is surprising if he comes bearing the cross, when he also displays the very wounds of his body? “Then,” he says, “they will see him whom they pierced” (Zechariah 12:10). And just as after the resurrection he wished to refute Thomas’s disbelief, showed him the places of the nails, displayed the wounds of his side, and said: “Put out your hand and see that a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (John 20:27; Luke 24:39); [Col. 0591D] so then also he will show the wounds and display the cross, to show that he is the one who had been crucified.

The same bishop, in the homily on the Lord’s ascension, among other passages.

[Note: [Col. 0592D] The same witness omitted “for.”]

For just as, when two people separated by a quarrel have an arbitrator placed between them, he dissolves the dispute and discord of those who are contending, so Christ also acted. God was rightly angry with us, while we despised him in his anger and turned away from the merciful Lord; and Christ placed himself between us, joined both natures, and himself endured the punishment that threatened us. [Col. 0592A]

The same author, in the same homily.

Christ therefore offered the firstfruits of us to the Father, and the Father marveled at the gift that such dignity offered and that what was offered was defiled by no stain. For he received the offering with his own hands and made it share in his own seat; and, what is more, he placed it at the side of his right hand. Let us recognize who it is [290] that heard: “Sit at my right hand”; what nature is it [Note: [Col. 0592D] The same witness: “to which he says.”] to which he said: “Be a participant in my seat”? It is that nature which heard: “You are earth, and to earth you will go.”

[Col. 0592B]

The same author, in the same homily.

I cannot find what discourse to use, what words to speak. Fragile nature, despised nature, shown to be inferior to all, conquered everything, overcame everything, [Note: [Col. 0592D] The same witness adds: “and today deserved to be found higher than the angels.”] and today deserved to be found higher than all. Today the angels received the desires they had long yearned for. Today the archangels were able to see what they had desired for a long time; for they beheld our nature shining with immortal glory in the Lord’s seat.

From Saint Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, in the Easter letter which he sent throughout Egypt. [Note: [Col. 0592D] This testimony is taken from Saint Jerome’s version, among his works, volume I, letter 98, no. 4, Verona edition. In the Oxoniensis manuscript the title is: “From the letter of Saint Theophilus of Alexandria, concerning Easter.”]

The witness to this matter is he who says: “All have turned aside; together they have become useless” (Psalm 143:5). And the prophet, imploring Christ’s help, says: “Lord, incline your heavens [Note: [Col. 0592D] Other manuscripts, together with the common editions, add “your.”] and descend”—not that he might change places—he in whom [Col. 0592C] all things are—, but so that for the sake of our salvation he might assume the flesh of human frailty; Paul agreeing with the same thought: “Although he was rich, he became poor, so that we might become rich through his poverty” (2 Corinthians 8:9).

And he came upon the earth and came forth as man from the virginal womb which he had sanctified, confirming by his dispensation the interpretation of his name, Emmanuel—that is, “God with us.” In a wonderful manner he began to be what we are and did not cease to be what he was, assuming our nature in such a way that he did not lose what he himself was. Although it is written in John, “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14)—that is, in other words, “man”—nevertheless he was not changed into flesh, because he never ceased to be God, to whom the saint also says: “But [Col. 0592D] you are the same” (Psalm 101:28). And the Father bears witness from heaven and says: “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17; Mark 1:11; Luke 3:22), so that, having become man, he may be said according to our confession still to be what he was before he became man; Paul proclaiming the same thing with us: “Jesus Christ [Col. 0593A] is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Hebrews 13:8). For in saying “the same,” he shows that he did not change his former nature or diminish the riches of his divinity, [Note: [Col. 0593D] Quesnell: “who became poor for our sake.”] because, having become poor for our sake, he had assumed the complete likeness of our condition.

[Note: [Col. 0593D] This testimony too is taken from Saint Jerome’s interpretation, among his works, volume I, letter 96, no. 3, Verona edition.]

The same bishop, in another Easter letter against Origen, among other passages.

The one [291] Son of the Father and our mediator neither lost his equality with him nor was separated from fellowship with us. The invisible God and visible man, hidden in the form of a servant [Note: [Col. 0593D] The common Jerome edition, together with the Vatican, Hispanic, and Isidorian manuscripts, adds “is”; and afterward some common editions read “is confirmed.”] and confirmed by the confession of believers as the Lord of glory. For the Father did not deprive him of the name of his nature after he had become man and poor for our sake; nor, after he had been baptized in the river Jordan, did he call him by another name, [Col. 0593B] but called him the only-begotten Son: [Note: [Col. 0593D] Quesnell adds “called him, saying”; and shortly afterward, after the word “divinity,” adds “of him.”] “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” Nor was our likeness changed into the nature of divinity, nor was divinity changed into the likeness of our nature.

From Saint Cyril, bishop of Alexandria.

He was called man, [Note: [Col. 0593D] The same witness: “was born.”] although by nature he is God, the Word of God the Father, because in the same way as we he shared in flesh and blood. Thus he appeared among earthly beings, not relinquishing what he was, but assuming the nature of humanity perfected in its own constitution.

The same author.

There is therefore one who was true God before the incarnation and who, having remained in humanity, was what he was, is, and will be. We do not therefore separate the one Lord Jesus Christ into a man by himself and a God by himself; rather, we say that he is the same one Jesus Christ. We are not ignorant of the differences between the natures, but preserve them mutually unconfused.

The same author, in his letter to Nestorius: [Note: [Col. 0593D] From the version which is given in full below, in chapter 56 of this collection, and which Saint Leo used in letter 165.]

The holy and great synod therefore says that the one who was naturally born from God the Father, the only-begotten Son, God from God, true from true, light from light, through whom and with whom the Father made all things—this one descended [Note: [Col. 0593D] Quesnell adds “from heaven.” Shortly afterward the Oxoniensis omits “again.”] and became incarnate and man, suffered, rose again on the third day, and ascended again into heaven.

We must follow these words; it is fitting that we obey these doctrines, considering what it means for the Word of God to become incarnate and man. For we do not say that the nature of God, having been changed or altered, [Col. 0593D] became flesh; nor that it was transformed wholly into a man composed of soul [Note: [Col. 0594D] Quesnell: “and flesh.” Shortly afterward the Oxoniensis reads: “that a rational soul united to itself animated flesh, and that the Word …,” which is less correct. Quesnell likewise inserted “before it became …” in advance.] and body. Rather, we say that the Word substantially, ineffably, and incomprehensibly joined to himself flesh animated by a rational soul, became man, [Col. 0594A] [292] and was also called the Son of Man—not by bare will alone, nor by the assumption of a person alone, but because natures that were different indeed came together into one.

Yet one Christ and Son came from both. [Note: [Col. 0594D] The same Quesnell: “Christ the Son of God from both.”] The difference of the natures was not emptied or removed by the union; rather, divinity and humanity together made one God, Christ, and Son for us through that mysterious and ineffable joining unto unity. Therefore he who was born from the Father before all ages is also said to have been begotten bodily from a woman—not because his divine nature took its beginning from the holy Virgin, nor because he himself needed to be born a second time after the birth which he had from the Father; for it is foolish [Col. 0594B] and absurd to say that he who is co-eternal with the Father before all ages needed a second generation in order to begin to exist. Rather, because for us and for our salvation he joined a human nature to himself and proceeded from a woman, he is therefore said to have been born bodily.

Nor was an ordinary man first born from the holy Virgin and then the Word came to dwell in him; rather, in the very virgin womb and uterus he joined himself to the flesh, endured bodily generation, and made the birth of his flesh his own. [Note: [Col. 0594D] Quesnell: “If he …”]

Thus we say that he suffered and rose again—not because the Word of God suffered in his own nature, or suffered blows, piercings by nails, or other wounds, for God is incorporeal and beyond suffering; [Col. 0594C] but because that body which had become his own suffered, he himself is therefore said to have suffered all these things for us. God, who could not suffer, was present in the body that suffered. [Note: [Col. 0594D] The same witness: “And in a similar way”; and shortly afterward: “but that body.” Immediately after the words “by the grace of God,” the Oxoniensis adds “offering.”]

In the same way we understand his death. The Word of God, immortal and incorruptible by nature, is life and gives life; but because his own body, by the grace of God, according to Paul’s statement, tasted death for everyone (Hebrews 2:9), he himself is therefore said to have suffered death for us. This does not mean that he himself experienced death insofar as his own nature is concerned—for it is madness either to think or to say this—but that, as we said above, his true flesh tasted death.

Thus, when his flesh rose again, [Note: [Col. 0594D] Quesnell omits “again”; and afterward reads: “not because it had fallen into corruption—which God forbid.”] we likewise say that there was a resurrection—not because it had fallen into corruption, which God forbid, but because his body rose again. [293] Thus we confess one Christ and Lord, not worshiping a man together with the Word, lest some appearance of division be introduced, but worshiping one and the same, because his body is not alien to the Word, with which he himself also sits beside the Father [Col. 0595A]. Nor do we say this as though two sons were sitting beside him, but one with flesh through unity; for if we refuse to accept such a substantial union as either impossible or somehow improper, we fall into the position of saying that there are two sons.

[Note: [Col. 0595C] The Thuanus: “For it is not permissible to distinguish.” Quesnell adds in the margin: “Alternatively, according to the Greek reading: ‘For it is necessary,’ etc.; this is stated by Cyril as a consequence of Nestorius’s doctrine.”]

Nor ought we to distinguish and say that the man was honored separately by the mere title of Son, while the Word, who is from God, is Son of God both in name and in reality. We must not divide the one Lord Jesus Christ into two sons. For this does not support the right understanding of faith, even though some people speak of some sort of union of persons. Scripture did not say that the [Col. 0595B] Word of God assumed a human person for himself, but that he became flesh; and this means that the Word of God, like us, shared in flesh and blood, made our body properly his own, and proceeded as man from a woman—not casting aside or laying down either his divinity or that generation which he had from the Father, but remaining, even in the assumption of flesh, the God that he was. The right understanding of faith bears witness to this everywhere.

We find that the holy Fathers held this meaning. Therefore they did not hesitate to call the holy Virgin *Theotokos*—“God-bearer”—not because the nature and divinity of the Word took its beginning from the holy Virgin, but because from her was born that holy body, animated by a rational soul, to which the Word of God was substantially united and is said to have been born according to the flesh.

294 From Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, bishop, in the homily on the Epiphany.

[Note: [Col. 0595C] From Oration 38, on the Theophany, or Nativity of the Lord, chapter 20, apparently from Rufinus’s translation. QUESNELL.]

When, therefore, God had proceeded from the Virgin in the human [Col. 0596A] nature which he had assumed, one being constituted from two mutually contrary things, flesh and spirit, one thing is assumed into God, while the other bestows the grace of divinity … He was indeed sent, but as man, for his nature was twofold. Hence, finally, he both labored from the journey, and hungered, and thirsted, and was saddened, and wept, according to the condition of a human body.

From Saint Basil, bishop of Cappadocia. [Note: [Col. 0595C] It is not clear from which work of Basil this is taken. The same QUESNELL.]

When, then, we see certain things in Christ that are human, so that they appear to differ in no respect from the common frailties of mortals [Note: Quesnellus: “seem to differ from the fellowship of mortal frailty.”], while other things are so divine that they belong to no nature other than that ineffable nature of the Godhead, the narrowness of human understanding is held fast, struck down by the stupor of so great a marvel; it does not know toward what it should incline, what it should hold, or where it should turn. [Note: Codex Thuanensis: “so that it does not know where to turn . . .”] [Col. 0596B] If it supposes him to be human, it sees him returning from the dead after conquering the kingdom of death, with its spoils; [Note: Quesnellus added from Codex Oxoniensis alone: “If it supposes him to be God, it beholds him crucified”; but he acknowledges that these words are absent from Codex Thuanensis, as they are likewise absent from our Codex Vindobonensis and from all the other codices. See note 70 in the testimonies appended to Leo’s Letter 165 (in our edition, vol. I, col. 1185, note g).] for this reason he must be contemplated with all fear and reverence, so that in one and the same person the truth of both natures may be demonstrated in such a way that nothing unworthy or improper is thought concerning that divine and ineffable substance, nor, on the other hand, are the things that took place judged to be deceived by false appearances. [Note: Quesnellus notes in the margin: “Thus, from Thuanensis and Oxoniensis, we have composed the reading that is found in the Grimanic codex of Letter 134, otherwise 97 (now 165), of Saint Leo. Oxoniensis reads *suis* instead of *illusa*; Thuanensis reads *aptentur* instead of *aestimentur*.”]

## 295. CHAPTER XLII

[Note: Apart from the codices of this collection, this chapter is also found in manuscript collections Vat. 1342 and in the Dionysian additions, of which we have examined three codices: Vat. 5845, Vallicellianus A 5, and the Vercellensis. It is also prefixed to Codex Vat. 3833, which contains the collection of Cardinal Deusdedit. Finally, from this same version—which was used by Leo in his judgment concerning Eutyches, as will be evident from note 56 below, col. 602, note p—and which was received by an ancient interpreter of the Council of Chalcedon, revised in places against the Greek text, it is read as inserted in act 11 of that same council. It is, however, act 7 of the Constantinopolitan synod against Eutyches. The entire Greek record of that synod was sent to Leo. But since this seventh and final session contained the substance of the whole matter and the judgment of the Fathers, it alone was immediately rendered into Latin and consequently alone passed into certain Latin collections. It was copied either immediately after Leo’s letters, as in collection Vat. 1342, or among the letters of that same pontiff, as in the collection of the Dionysian additions. We have given the title as it appears in the manuscripts of this and the two preceding ancient collections. Quesnellus, however, gives it as follows: “Record of the condemnation of Eutyches in the synod at Constantinople, in the presence of Saint Flavian, confessor and bishop of that city.” Vat. 3833: “Here begins the definition of the Constantinopolitan synod against Eutyches.”]

Here begins a copy of the proceedings in which, at the synod at Constantinople, Eutyches the heretic was examined and condemned by Saint Flavian, bishop and confessor.

When the holy and great synod had assembled again, the holy and fearsome Gospels having been brought forward, and [Note: Thus all our codices and Baluzius. Quesnellus alone has “and reverend.”] our holy and venerable archbishop Flavian being present [Col. 0596C] in the episcopal secretariat, at the appointed time, on the second day of the week, which was the tenth day before the Kalends of December [Note: So all our codices. The Vulgate Council-text, together with manuscripts of the ancient Chalcedonian version, has “the twenty-second day of November,” which amounts to the same date. Quesnellus wrongly admitted “the Kalends of December” into the text, omitting the numeral X.], the presbyter Asterius [Note: The codices of the Dionysian additions, together with the Paris manuscript of the pure ancient version of the Council of Chalcedon, add “and first among the notaries.” The Vulgate of the Councils, with certain copies of Rusticus and in agreement with the Greek text, has “and notary”; then the same Vulgate, with Vat. 3833, has “before the doors.”] and first among the notaries said:

“The appointed day has arrived, and the venerable bishop Eusebius, standing outside the doors, asks to be admitted.”

Bishop Flavian said:

“Let him enter.”

When he had entered, Bishop Flavian said:

“Let the deacons Philadelphius and Cyril go and look for the presbyter and archimandrite Eutyches around the episcopal residence. If he is found according to his promise, let them summon him to the council.”

## 296

[Note: Quesnellus inserted “They went.” We have removed it on the authority of our manuscripts and printed codices. Then the Vulgate of the Councils has: “They did indeed search for him . . . but found neither him nor anyone belonging to him.”]

A little later the aforesaid deacons returned and said that they had searched throughout the whole church but had not found him, nor anyone belonging to him.

Bishop Flavian said:

“Let the deacons Crispinus and Diogenianus go again and look for him around the church, and wherever they learn that he is, let them summon him.”

When they had gone away and the deacons had returned, they said that he himself had not been found, [Note: The Vulgate has: “but that they had learned that . . . he was going to come with a very great crowd of soldiers, monks, and apparitors of the prefects.” The Dionysian-addition codices have the same, except that they read “but had learned that.” Quesnellus prefers *se* instead of *quod*.] but that they had learned that he was with a very large crowd of soldiers, monks, and apparitors of the praetorian prefect’s most exalted authority [Col. 0597B]. And while these things were being said and the holy synod was waiting, the venerable presbyter John, the defender, said:

“The venerable presbyter and archimandrite Eutyches has arrived with a large crowd of soldiers, monks, [Note: Codex Thuanensis: “and of the prefect.” Then the Vulgate, with manuscripts Oxoniensis and Vat. 3833, has: “apparitors of the authority of the prefects of the praetorian prefecture.”] and apparitors of the prefects of the highest authority, the praetorian prefect; nor do they permit him to be admitted to the hearing in any other way [Note: Thus the codices Vindobonensis, Thuanensis, Vat. 1342, and the Dionysian additions. Quesnellus deleted *cum eis* (“with them”). Vat. 3833 has *nisi eis* (“unless to them”). The Vulgate of the Councils has: “and they do not otherwise wish to release him so that he may enter your holy council unless we promise them [Col. 0597D] that we will restore his person to them.”] unless we promise them that we will present him to them. There is also a great and most distinguished *silentiarius* with him outside the doors, wishing to enter, since he has been sent by our most religious emperor.”

Bishop Flavian said:

“Let them enter.”

When they had entered, the great *silentiarius* said:

“If you command me to deliver the response of our lord the emperor, I ask by your footsteps’ leave. [Note: Quesnellus: “I reread concerning certain matters that they commanded.” We have preferred the reading of Codex Vindobonensis, with which the others in the other collections agree, except that Vat. 1342 has: “They committed certain matters to writing”; Vat. 3833: “They commanded certain matters”; and the codices of the Dionysian additions: “For he commanded certain matters in a written document.” The manuscripts of Rusticus preserved by Baluzius read better: “For he committed certain matters to writing.”] I shall reread certain matters that they have committed to writing, if it pleases you.”

[Col. 0597C]

The holy synod said:

“Reread what our most religious emperor and our son has commanded.” [Note: We did not wish to alter the reading of our collection, although the reading is more correct in manuscripts of the other collections, where *fili* (“son”) is added here and *nostroque filio* (“and our son”) is deleted earlier, or at least *quo filio* (“which son”).]

And the great *silentiarius* read as follows: [Note: The Dionysian-addition manuscripts have: “Since we are considering peace . . . and wish to preserve the true faith preached by God’s providence.” [Col. 0598C] Vat. 1342 has only *praestante* (“by providence”). The Corbie manuscript of Rusticus, together with Crabbe, has: “Since we are considering peace, and the holy Churches of God, and the catholic faith, and that there should be preserved . . . by our Fathers.”]

“We are considering the peace of the holy Churches, and we wish the true faith preached by God’s inspiration to be preserved—the faith handed down by our fathers, who assembled at Nicaea, three hundred and eighteen [Note: The codices of the Dionysian additions add: “and by those who were present at Ephesus for the condemnation of Nestorius”; and then, with the manuscripts of Rusticus, “at the synodal hearing.”] and by those who were present at Ephesus for the condemnation of Nestorius. Therefore we wish that no scandal be introduced into the aforesaid catholic faith.

“And since we know the most illustrious patrician Florentius to be faithful and approved in the true faith, we wish him to be present at the synodal hearing, since the discussion concerns the faith.”

[Note: Vat. 3833: “And while these things were being read.” The codices of the Dionysian additions and of Rusticus, together with the Vulgate, have the better reading: “While these things were still being read.” After the word *legerentur* (“were being read”), the Vulgate, from the manuscripts of Rusticus, adds the acclamations of the synod, which are omitted in our collection and the others.]

While these things were being read, Bishop Flavian said:

“We all know the lord Florentius [Note: Quesnellus adds “the illustrious,” and “and”; we have deleted these with Codex Vindobonensis and other codices. The manuscripts of the Dionysian additions and the Vulgate add immediately: “in the catholic faith.”] to be faithful and approved in the catholic faith, and we wish him to be present. Let us also learn from the presbyter Eutyches whether he too wishes him to be present.”

The presbyter and archimandrite Eutyches [Col. 0598B] said:

“Do what God and your holiness desire; I commend myself to you.”

Bishop Flavian said:

“Let the most illustrious patrician Florentius come also. Therefore, *silentiarius*, take care [Note: The Vulgate of the Councils, with Vercelli and Vat. 3833, has: “son *silentiarius*.” Then Thuanensis has “to call him”; the Vulgate: “to trouble him to come to him”; the manuscripts of Rusticus: “to trouble him,” or “to trouble you to come to him”; the Paris manuscript of the ancient version of the Council of Chalcedon: “to trouble him.” Other codices—Vat. 1342, the three Dionysian-addition codices, Vat. 3833, together with Codex Vindobonensis of this collection—have “to trouble him,” or “to be troubled,” which agrees with the Greek. We have added *mecum* (“with me”) with all our codices and the Vulgate of the Councils.] to bring him.”

The great *silentiarius* said:

“Command that one of the clergy be sent with me, lest he perhaps doubt that your holiness has sent him.”

Bishop Flavian said:

“If the most pious emperor had ordered us to send someone, we would have sent him. Since he did not order it, go alone to his magnificence.”

And when the most illustrious patrician and former consul Florentius had arrived, the holy synod said: [Note: The Vulgate of the Councils, together with the Dionysian-addition manuscripts and Vat. 3833, has: “Let them stand.”]

“Let the accuser and the accused stand in the middle, and let what was done from the beginning between the venerable bishop Eusebius and the venerable [Note: The word *presbyterum* (“presbyter”) has been added with Codex Vindobonensis, supported by the Vulgate and the Dionysian-addition codices.] presbyter and archimandrite Eutyches be read, so that, instructed by what has taken place, we may establish an ending in accordance with equity and the holy canons for what was formerly [Note: The Dionysian-addition codices, Vat. 3833, and the Vulgate of the Councils have the better reading: “was brought forward.” The name “Eticius” is read incorrectly in the manuscripts of this collection; with the others and the Greek, it should be read “Aetius.” Then Quesnellus alone, together with Codex Oxoniensis, reads *legebat* (“was reading”); the Dionysian-addition codices, Vat. 3833, and the Vulgate have *legit* (“read”); “the hearing of the proceedings” is read in the latter.] arose.”

The deacon and notary Euticius was reading the record of the proceedings. When he was reading, he came to the second part [Note: We have added the words “the second” and “to the venerable bishops,” omitted by Quesnellus, from all our codices and the Vulgate.] of the letter of blessed Cyril written to the venerable Eastern bishops, in which these words were contained:

“Accordingly, we confess our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man, consisting of a rational soul and a body; begotten before the ages from the Father according to his Godhead, but in the last days, for us and for our salvation, the same one born from the Virgin Mary according to human nature [Note: Thus Codex Vindobonensis and the other manuscripts of our collection. Quesnellus: “born according to his humanity,” without the word “born.” The Vulgate has “humanity,” without “born.”].

“Consubstantial with the Father according to his Godhead and consubstantial with us according to his humanity. For a union of two natures has taken place; therefore we confess one Christ, one Lord, according to the grace of an unconfused union. [Note: The same codices and the Vulgate have “one Christ our Lord.” Vat. 3833, with the manuscripts of the Council of Chalcedon, has “of an unconfused union.”]

“We confess the holy Virgin to be *Theotocos* (‘God-bearer’); therefore God the Word [Col. 0599B] was incarnate from her and became man, and from her conception united to himself the temple that he had assumed from her. [Note: Quesnellus: “was incarnate from her and became man, by his conception.” We have followed Codex Vindobonensis, with which the others agree, except that some have “incarnate,” while others omit the *et* (“and”) before *ex ejus*.]”

Bishop Eusebius said:

“This man, by your leave [Note: Vat. 1342, together with the Vulgate: “does not confess this.”], does not confess these things, nor has he ever agreed with them; rather, he has held opinions contrary to them and has spoken and taught this to everyone who came to him.”

The former prefect Florentius said:

“If it pleases your holiness, let the presbyter Eutyches be questioned whether he agrees with these things.”

Bishop Eusebius said:

“Allow the entire record of the proceedings to be read. What has already been done is sufficient for me [Note: The manuscripts of the Council of Chalcedon and Vat. 3833 delete *prius* (“already”). Quesnellus has: “to convict him; he has now been revealed to me.” We have preferred the copies of Vindobonensis and Thuanensis, with which the others agree. The Chalcedonian codices of Baluzius, together with Crabbe, have: “for he has been convicted by me.”] to convict him, for he has already been revealed to me. For even if he now agrees after obtaining a document from somewhere, [Note: The same codices of Baluzius have: “I ought to suffer prejudice.” Quesnellus alone adds “a heretic” after “I have demonstrated him”; our manuscripts and printed codices do not know this addition. The Dionysian-addition and Chalcedonian copies have: “For I shall demonstrate him and the professions that were sent to him.” Vat. 1342 likewise has “I shall demonstrate him.” The Vulgate of the Councils, with the Greek, reads better: “For I demonstrated him through the professions of those who were sent to him by the holy synod.”] I ought not to suffer prejudice. For I have demonstrated him both by the decrees sent to him by the holy synod [Col. 0599C] and by the bishop-witnesses; I can show the same things again if he denies them. [Note: Thus Vindobonensis and many other codices. Quesnellus: “For there are.” Then, instead of “Jobinus,” the Dionysian-addition codices, together with the Vulgate, have “John.” Vat. 3833 has “Jovinus.” After “knowing,” manuscripts of the other collections add “with complete certainty” or “most certainly.”]

“For there are the lord Meliphtongus, the lord Jobinus, and the lord Julianus, who know.”

Bishop Flavian said:

“No one will allow you, Bishop Eusebius, not to convict him, nor will anyone immediately accept the presbyter Eutyches as agreeing, unless what he previously thought is first established. [Note: Quesnellus: “unless someone first convicts him.” We have preferred our codices and the Vulgate.]”

Bishop Eusebius said:

“I fear his assault [Note: The Dionysian-addition codices have “his confrontation.” Crabbe, together with the Chalcedonian manuscripts, has the better reading: “his ambush.”]. I am poor; he threatens me with exile. He has wealth, for even now he is designating Oasi [Note: Codex Thuanensis: “the islands as a place of exile.” Vat. 1342 and Crabbe, in the margin: “those places as a place of exile.” The Dionysian additions and Vat. 3833: “Oasis, a place of exile.” The copies of the Council of Chalcedon have: “he is already assigning me Oasis, that is, a rock of exile.”] as a place of exile.”

Bishop Flavian said: [Note: The Chalcedonian manuscripts have: “Even if you persist a thousand times in saying these things”; and a little later: “Let an inquiry be offered.”]

“Even if you continue saying the same things repeatedly, nevertheless we place nothing before the truth.”

Bishop Eusebius said:

“If I am convicted of slander, I shall lose my rank.”

The illustrious Florentius said:

“Let time be given to the presbyter Eutyches to explain how he believes; and then let him again be questioned why, while now asserting these things, he previously asserted otherwise. [Note: The Dionysian-addition codices delete *rursus* (“again”); and shortly afterward the Chalcedonian manuscripts have *sentiebat* (“thought”) instead of *asserebat* (“asserted”).]”

Bishop Eusebius said:

“As I said before, let me not suffer prejudice [Note: The Chalcedonian codices have: “from his present profession, and let him be questioned. For from the documents of what was previously done I have convicted him of not thinking correctly.”] from his sudden agreement, and let him be questioned; for from what was done previously I have convicted him of having held an incorrect opinion.”

Bishop Flavian said:

“You will suffer no prejudice if he now agrees, for what was done previously possesses its own validity.”

Bishop Eusebius said:

“Does he agree with what has just been read from the writings of blessed Cyril [Note: The same codices, together with the Vulgate of the Councils, delete *scriptis* (“writings”), and then continue: “and confesses that a union of two natures has taken place in one person and in one subsistence.”] and confess that two natures have been united in one person and in one substance, or not?”

Bishop Flavian said:

“You have heard, presbyter Eutyches, what your accuser says. State now whether you confess a unity from two natures. [Note: The following seven words were omitted by Quesnellus. We have restored them from all our codices and the Vulgate.]”

The presbyter Eutyches said:

“Yes, from two natures.”

Bishop Eusebius said:

“Do you confess two natures, lord archimandrite, after the incarnation, and do you say that Christ is consubstantial with us according to the flesh, or not?”

The presbyter Eutyches said:

“I have not come to discuss, but I have come [Col. 0600C] to inform your holiness what I think; what I think is written on this sheet. Command it to be read. [Note: The same Chalcedonian manuscripts have: “to satisfy your holiness as to my belief . . . on this sheet what I think.” Then the codices Vat. 1341 and the Dionysian additions place the words “Command it to be read” after “I cannot.”]”

Bishop Flavian said:

“Read it yourself.”

The presbyter Eutyches said:

“I cannot.”

Bishop Flavian said:

“Why? Did you not compose the statement, or is it someone else’s statement? [Col. 0601A] If it is yours, read it yourself.”

The presbyter Eutyches said:

“It is indeed my statement [Note: The Chalcedonian and Dionysian-addition codices have *dictatio* (“dictated statement”) in both places. Vindobonensis, together with Vat. 1342, has *dictio* (“statement”) in the first place and *dictatio* in the second. Then, instead of *sensibus* (“opinions”), the Vulgate of the Councils has *expositioni* (“exposition”). Vindobonensis and Vercelli delete both readings.], and my statement agrees with the opinions of the holy Fathers.”

Bishop Flavian said: [Note: The Dionysian-addition manuscripts add: “Which Fathers? Speak for yourself.” The Vulgate of the Councils, with the Chalcedonian manuscripts, has: “Say which Fathers; speak for yourself.”]

“Name the Fathers yourself. Why do you need a sheet?”

The presbyter Eutyches said:

“This is what I believe: I adore the Father with the Son, and the Son with the Father, and the Holy Spirit together with the Father and the Son. But I confess that his incarnate manifestation was made from the flesh of the holy Virgin and was perfectly embodied for our salvation. Thus I confess before the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and before your holiness.”

Bishop Flavian said:

“Do you confess him, the one and same Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, to be consubstantial with the Father according to his Godhead and consubstantial with his mother according to his humanity?”

The presbyter Eutyches said:

## 301

“I have commended myself to your holiness; I have said what I think concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Ask me nothing further.”

Bishop Flavian said:

“No. [Note: Quesnellus alone has: “You do not confess.” Then the Dionysian-addition and Chalcedonian manuscripts, together with Vat. 3833, delete *dixi* (“I said”); instead of *eum Deum* (“him God”), they have *Deum meum* (“my God”). Vat. 1342, deleting *eum*, likewise has *Deum meum*, and, with the Dionysian additions, omits the words “of heaven and earth.”] Do you now confess Christ to be from two natures?”

The presbyter Eutyches said:

“I said that I confess him to be God and Lord of heaven and earth. Until now I did not think it right to discuss his nature; but I confess that until now I have never said that he is consubstantial with us.”

Bishop Flavian said:

“Do you not say that he is consubstantial with the Father according to his Godhead and consubstantial with us according to his humanity?”

The presbyter Eutyches said:

“Until this day I have not said that the body of our Lord and God is consubstantial with us; but I confess that the holy Virgin is consubstantial with us, and that our God was incarnate from her. [Note: In all the ancient manuscript collections containing this original version, the brief exchange of Flavian and Eutyches is omitted.
