The ancient interpreter of the Council of Chalcedon supplied it from the Greek in these words: “The most holy archbishop said: ‘Then the Virgin also, from whom Christ the Ruler was incarnate, is consubstantial with us.’ The presbyter Eutyches said: ‘I have said that the Virgin is consubstantial with us.’ Basil.”]”

Bishop Basil said:

“If his mother is consubstantial with us, and he himself is called the Son of Man, then he too, according to the flesh, is consubstantial with us.”

The presbyter Eutyches said:

“Since you now say this, [Note: Vat. 1342: “in every respect.” Then the Dionysian-addition and Chalcedonian codices have: “since his mother is consubstantial with us.”] I agree with everything.”

The illustrious Florentius said:

“If his mother is consubstantial with us, without doubt the Son also is consubstantial with us.”

The presbyter Eutyches said:

“Until now I have not said that I confess the body of God. [Note: Quesnellus: “Do you observe what I have not said?” We have corrected this from Vindobonensis, Thuanensis, and the Dionysian-addition and Chalcedonian manuscripts. Then Quesnellus deletes *et* (“and”) and reads *natus* (“born”) instead of *incarnatus* (“incarnate”). [Col. 0602C] We have preferred the better codices, together with Vindobonensis. The sense from the Greek is: “I did not say that the body of a man was the body of God; but I said a human body, and that the Lord was incarnate from that Virgin.”] Do you observe this? I did not say that a human body was the body of God; but I said that it was a human body, and that the Lord was incarnate from that very Virgin. But if it is necessary to say that he is consubstantial with us from the Virgin [Note: Vat. 3833: “and substantial.” The Chalcedonian codices: “and consubstantial.” Quesnellus repeats *dico* (“I say”) before *tamen* (“nevertheless”); we have deleted it with our codices and the Vulgate.], I say this also, lord; nevertheless I confess the only-begotten Son of God, the Lord of heaven and earth, sharing lordship and reigning with the Father, who sits with him [Note: Vat. 1342 and the Dionysian-addition manuscripts have *consedit* (“sat with him”). We have added *enim* (“for”) from all our codices and printed editions.] and is praised together with him. For I do not say that he denied being consubstantial [Col. 0602B] because he is himself the Son of God. Previously I was not saying this; [Note: Quesnellus: “as I think.” We have brought the text into conformity with Vindobonensis and our other codices. The Chalcedonian manuscripts of Rusticus, together with Crabbe, have: “but I tell you that this is what I think, because at the beginning I was not saying this.” We have inserted *hoc* (“this”) from those same codices and the Vulgate.] now I tell you that I think I said it at the beginning; but now, since your holiness says this, I say it.”

Bishop Flavian said:

“Then do you confess the true faith out of necessity, not by your will?”

The presbyter Eutyches said:

“Now, lord, this is how it stands: until this hour I was afraid to say it, because I know our Lord God and did not think it right to discuss his nature; but since your holiness permits and teaches it, I say it.”

Bishop Flavian said:

“We are not introducing a novelty, but our fathers explained it; and just as the faith explained by them stands, so we all wish, believing it, to persevere in it and to innovate nothing. [Note: The same inserts *quoniam* (“because”). The Chalcedonian codices, together with Vat. 3833, have *Patres* (“Fathers”) instead of *parentes* (“parents”).]”

The illustrious Florentius said:

“Do you say that our Lord, who is from the Virgin [Note: We have removed the word *natus* (“born”), inserted by Quesnellus, on the authority of the manuscripts Vindobonensis and Thuanensis, supported by others in the other collections.], is consubstantial with us and is from two natures after the incarnation, or not?”

The presbyter Eutyches said: [Note: Saint Leo reports these same words from this version in his letter to Flavian, chapter 6. From this it may be inferred that this is the very version made from the Greek immediately after the proceedings of this Constantinopolitan synod were received—proceedings which our pontiff commonly calls *gesta*, as is evident from the heading of this chapter. Thus Quesnellus. Codex Thuanensis: other reading Codex Colbertinus. [Col. 0603C] Vindobonensis deletes *vero* (“indeed”); this adverb is found in our other codices. Vat. 3833 has “after the union, however,” as in Leo. The Chalcedonian codices, with Crabbe, have “after the union, however.”]

“I confess that our Lord existed from two natures before the union; but after the union I confess one nature.”

The holy synod said: [Note: The Dionysian-addition manuscripts and Vat. 3833 have the better reading: “You must confess correctly and anathematize every doctrine contrary to what has just been read. Eutyches, etc.” Vat. 1342 has the same, except that it deletes *recte* (“correctly”). The Vulgate of Chalcedon agrees, except that it has *clare* (“clearly”) instead of *recte*.]

“You must confess what has just been read and anathematize every doctrine contrary to it.”

The presbyter Eutyches said: [Note: Quesnellus: “Eutyches said: ‘I confess to your holiness that before this I was not saying it; but since your holiness says this . . .’ We have preferred the reading of our codices and the Vulgate. Only the Dionysian-addition manuscripts, together with Vat. 1342 and the Vulgate, have *docet* (“teaches”) instead of *dicit* (“says”).]

“I have told your holiness that before this I was not saying it; but now, since your holiness says this, I say it, and I follow the Fathers. [Note: Manuscripts of the other collections, together with the Vulgate: “Nor do I find it explained in the Scriptures.” A few manuscripts add: “And rising.”] For I have not found this explained in the Scriptures, nor did all the Fathers say it. For if I anathematize it, woe is me, because I condemn our Fathers.”

The holy synod rose and cried out:

“Anathema to him!”

After this Bishop Flavian said:

“Let the holy synod state what the man presently before us deserves: he neither confesses the true faith nor wishes to agree with the present synod, but [Col. 0603B] persists in perversity and wicked malice. [Note: Thus the superior codices of this collection, Vindobonensis and Thuanensis, with Vat. 1342 and Vat. 3833 agreeing, except that the former adds *suae* (“his own”) after *scaevae* (“wicked”), while the latter places *etiam* (“also”) before *perversitati*. Quesnellus thought the passage should be emended, perhaps with Codex Oxoniensis, to: “but persevering in the perversity of his wickedness.” The Dionysian-addition codices have the better reading: “but he persists in his perversity and wicked malice.” The Vulgate, with the Chalcedonian manuscripts, has: “but persisting in his perverse and wicked malignity.”]”

Bishop Seleucus said:

“He is indeed worthy of condemnation, [Note: The Dionysian-addition codices add: “but nevertheless this rests upon the humanity of your holiness.” Vat. 3833: “but nevertheless it has been placed in the humanity of your holiness.” The Chalcedonian manuscripts: “but nevertheless it rests solely upon the humanity of your holiness.” Then Vat. 3833 has: “if, confessing his own sin, he were to anathematize”; the Chalcedonian codices: “if, confessing his own sin, he could be persuaded to anathematize his own doctrine and agree with us.”] but nevertheless he is in the hands of your holiness.”

Bishop Flavian said:

“If he confessed his own sin, anathematized his own doctrine, and agreed with us as we followed the tradition of the holy Fathers, he would rightly be worthy of pardon. But since he remains in the same malignity, he shall be subject to the penalties of the canons.”

Eutyches said:

“I do say these things, because you have now commanded me to do so [Note: On the authority of our codices we have added “now.” Vat. 3833: “I say this in truth.”], but I do not anathematize; for what I say, I say in truth.”

The illustrious Florentius said:

“Do you say that there are two natures, and that the Lord Christ is consubstantial with us? [Note: Quesnellus: “with us, the Lord Christ?” followed by “Eutyches.” We have followed Codex Vindobonensis, supported by the others.]”

The presbyter Eutyches said: [Note: Vindobonensis: “I read Cyril’s rule.” Vercelli: “I read Cyril’s rule.” The Chalcedonian codices, with Crabbe: “I follow the rule of blessed Cyril.” Then Quesnellus repeats *legi* (“I read”) before *quoniam* (“that”) and adds *Christum fuisse* (“that Christ existed”) after *dixerunt*. We have deleted both with all our manuscripts and the Vulgate.]

“I have read the writings of Cyril, the holy Fathers, and Saint Athanasius, that they said: before the union there were indeed two natures; but after the union and incarnation, not two natures [Col. 0604A] but one.”

The illustrious Florentius said:

“Do you confess two natures after the union? Say so. If you do not, you will be condemned.”

The presbyter Eutyches said: [Note: The Vulgate, together with the Chalcedonian codices: “Command the writings of Saint Athanasius to be read, so that you may understand that he says nothing of the kind.” The manuscripts of the other collections leap over the preceding exchange of Florentius and this reply of Eutyches.]

“I have read the writings of Saint Athanasius, and he says nothing of the kind.”

Bishop Basil said:

“If you do not say that there are two natures after the union, you are asserting mixture and confusion.”

The illustrious Florentius said:

“Whoever does not say that Christ existed from two natures and does not confess two natures will be anathematized. [Note: Quesnellus, against the manuscripts Vindobonensis and Thuanensis of this collection—manuscripts with which the other collections and the Vulgate also agree—gave the passage as follows: “Whoever does not confess that Christ existed from two natures and two natures will be anathematized. He rose, etc.”]”

The holy synod rose and cried out:

“All faith that is produced by necessity is not faith. Many years to the catholic emperors! Many years to the catholic emperors! Your faith always prevails; it does not agree with what he is trying to persuade you of. [Note: Thus the codices of this collection, together with the Dionysian additions and the ancient manuscript version of the Paris codex. Other copies have “our faith.”]”

Bishop Flavian said:

“In every respect Eutyches, formerly a presbyter and archimandrite, both by what was previously done and by the questions put to him, has been found to be suffering from the perversity of Valentinus and Apollinaris [Note: The Dionysian-addition codices, together with one Corbie manuscript and the Paris manuscript of the Council of Chalcedon, have “sick.” Most codices have “blasphemies.” Instead of *sequens* (“following”), which is supported by Codex Vindobonensis and Vat. 1342, together with the cited codices, we have restored that reading; Quesnellus has *secutus* (“having followed”). The Vulgate of the Councils has *sequi* (“to follow”). Vat. 3833 continues with a longer addition: “By denying that our Lord possessed the true substance of human flesh, but asserting that he presented some peculiar body of his own with him from heaven, and not revering our persuasion and teaching, he refused to agree with the sound doctrines, namely, to believe that there are two natures in Christ, that is, of true God and true man. Therefore, groaning, etc.”], and, unchangeably following their blasphemy, he has refused, without reverence for our persuasion and teaching, to agree with the sound doctrines.

“Therefore, grieving over his complete destruction, we have decreed, through our Lord Jesus Christ, whom he has blasphemed, that he is to be excluded from every priestly office, from our communion, [Col. 0604D] and from the primacy of the monastery; [Note: Thus Codex Vindobonensis, together with the other codices of our collections. [Col. 0605C] The Vulgate of the Councils, with the Chalcedonian manuscripts, has: “all who.”] and let those who thereafter converse with him and come to him know [Col. 0605A] that they too will be liable to the penalty of excommunication if they do not avoid his conversations. [Note: Vat. 3833 adds “declaring this.” In what follows we have adopted the reading of the codices Vindobonensis and Oxoniensis, with which the others of our collection agree. Quesnellus, with Thuanensis, has: “because they will be liable, and they themselves will be involved in the penalty of his excommunication, whoever turns to his conversations.”]”

Also, the subscriptions of Flavian, bishop and confessor, and of the various bishops and archimandrites who sat in the council of this synod.

Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, having judged, signed. [Note: The Thuanus manuscript reads “Saturnus.”] Saturninus, bishop of Marcianopolis, having judged, signed. Basil, bishop of Seleucia in Isauria, having judged, signed. Ethericus, bishop of Smyrna, having judged, signed. Seleucus, bishop of Amasia [Note: The Dionysian supplementary manuscripts add “of the Hellespont.” Better in Vaticanus 3833 and the Chalcidian manuscripts: “of Helenopontus.”] in Pontus, having judged, signed. Dorotheus, bishop of Neo-Caesarea [Note: The Dionysian manuscripts add: “having reread it, I consented; having judged, I signed.”], having read, consented, signed. [Col. 0605B] Timothy, bishop, having judged, signed. Calenicus, bishop of Apamea, which is in Bithynia, having judged, signed. Cecropius, bishop of Sebastopolis, having judged, signed. Meliphtongus, bishop of Heliopolis, having judged, signed. Longinus, bishop of Cherson, having judged, signed. Tryphon, bishop [Note: Vaticanus 5845 reads “of the island of Chios”; the Vulgate Council text, “of the city and island of Chios.” I have deleted all these words by my own hand.] of the Islands, having judged, signed by my own hand. 306 Paul, bishop [Note: Another reading: “of Apolloniadis,” or “Apollonitanus.”] of the holy Church of Apolloniatis, having judged, signed. Sabas, bishop of Palti in First Syria, having judged, signed by my own hand. Jovinus, bishop [Note: The Dionysian manuscripts add, as in the Greek, “of Dubeltum.”] of Cletus, having judged, signed. Julian, bishop [Note: Quesnell notes: “The Vulgate reads ‘bishop of Cos’; better, if I am not mistaken: for the inexperienced translator was misled by the similarity of the words ἐπίσκοπος τῆς Κῶ ὁρίσας, which mean ‘bishop of Cos, having judged,’ etc. The error should rather be attributed to an ancient copyist in our collection; for in the Dionysian supplementary manuscripts, which adopted this same interpretation, one reads: ‘bishop of Cos, having judged, I signed.’ Vaticanus 3833, through another error, reads: ‘I signed at Oasis.’”] of Coriza, having judged, signed. [Col. 0606A] [Note: The Vindobonensis reads “Sabianus”; Vaticanus 1342, “Savianus.” Then the Thuanus reads “of Tyre”; Vaticanus 3833, “of Thelemissus.” The Dionysian supplement adds “of Hermissus, Eudoxiopolis, and Jobia.” In the subscriptions that follow, some manuscripts occasionally alter the order. The Vulgate Council text reads “of Termissus, Eudoxiopolis, and Jovia.”] Sabinianus, bishop of Tiromissus, Eudocia, and Jobiniaria, having judged, signed. [Note: The Vindobonensis reads “Eustotius”; Vaticanus 1342, “Eustocius”; the Dionysian supplement, together with the Chalcidian manuscripts, “Eutychius.”] Eustochius, bishop of Dociminus, having judged, signed. [Note: The Dionysian supplement, together with the Chalcidian manuscripts, adds: “Pionius, bishop of Troadensis,” more correctly in Vaticanus 3833, “Pionius, bishop from Troas.”] Pontius, bishop of the city of Travidensis, signed. [Note: Thus the two better manuscripts of this collection, Vindobonensis and Thuanus, together with Vaticani 1342 and 3833; and this is less incorrect than Quesnell’s “Bassianus.” The true reading is found in the Dionysian supplementary manuscripts and the Chalcidian manuscripts: “Cossinius.”] Cassianus, bishop of Hierocaesarea, having judged, signed. John, bishop [Note: The Dionysian supplementary manuscripts add “of Assania”; better in Vaticanus 3833, “of Hyrcania”; or, as in the Vulgate Council text, “of the Hyrcanians.”] of Ursania, having judged, signed. [Note: Vaticanus 1342 reads “Diaphron.” Then, instead of “Pulvisia,” other copies have “Pulvis” or “Pulius.” More correctly, from the Greek of the Chalcidian manuscripts, “Olbis.”] Diaferontius, bishop of Pulvisia, having judged, signed. Julian, bishop [Note: Thus in the Vindobonensis and Vaticanus 1342, less incorrectly than in Quesnell’s “of Montanus.” The Dionysian supplement reads more correctly “of Mustinis”; or, as in the Chalcidian manuscripts, “of Mostene.”] of Montenis, signed. Romanus, bishop of Eudoxiopolis, signed. Eudoxius, bishop of the city of Bosphoriana, having judged, signed through my presbyter Basil. [Note: Read, with the Dionysian supplementary manuscripts and the Chalcidian manuscripts, “Basiliscus.” Vaticanus 1342 refers the final words, “through my presbyter,” etc., to Thomas’s subscription that follows.] Thomas, bishop of the city of Valentiniana, having judged, signed. Aurelius, bishop of the city [Note: The Chalcidian manuscripts read “of Opita.” Then, instead of “Novensis,” some copies have “Noviensis.”] of Popitana, signed. Secundinus, bishop of Novus, signed these proceedings. Januarius, bishop of the city of Macriana, signed. [Col. 0606B] Timothy, bishop [Note: Vaticanus 3833 reads “of Priamopolis”; the Dionysian supplementary manuscripts, “of Aurimopolis”; the Chalcidian manuscripts, “of the city of Arimopolis.” From the Greek: “of Primopolis.”] of Priscopolis, having judged, signed. Genethius, bishop of Argos, having judged, signed. 307 [Note: The Dionysian supplementary manuscripts, together with the Chalcidian manuscripts, add: “Andrew, presbyter and archimandrite, signed through Timothy the presbyter.” After the words “Faustus, presbyter and archimandrite,” the Vulgate and the Chalcidian manuscripts add: “I signed at the deposition of Eutyches, formerly presbyter and archimandrite”; and then insert another subscription: “Martin, presbyter and archimandrite of the monastery of blessed Dionysius, signed through Philip the brother.” Leo wrote several letters to Faustus and Martin.] Faustus, presbyter and archimandrite of the monastery of blessed Dionysius, signed. Peter, presbyter and archimandrite of the monastery of Thalassius, signed. Manuel, presbyter and archimandrite, signed. Job, presbyter and archimandrite of the monastery [Note: The Dionysian supplementary manuscripts add “of the blessed Theogenes”; the Vulgate Council text, “of blessed Theotecnus.”] of blessed Theotecus, signed. Abramius, presbyter and archimandrite, signed. [Note: Vaticani 1342 and the Dionysian supplement, together with the Vulgate Council text, add another Theodore as follows: “Theodore, monk and archimandrite of the monastery of the Egyptians, signed.”] Theodore, monk and archimandrite, signed. Pientius, presbyter and archimandrite, signed. Claudius, archimandrite, signed. [Note: The Chalcidian manuscripts, together with the Dionysian supplement, insert another subscription: “Flavian, presbyter and archimandrite of Saint Hermilius, signed.” Then, in the Vulgate and Chalcidian subscriptions, Claudius’s subscription is absent, while two Eusebiuses are found: “Eusebius, presbyter and archimandrite of the monastery of Elias, signed”; “Eusebius, presbyter and archimandrite of the monastery of Saint Eulogius.”] Eusebius, presbyter and archimandrite, signed. [Note: Another reading: “Callinicus.”] [Col. 0607A] Tryphon, archimandrite, signed. Jacob, deacon and archimandrite, signed. Helpidius, presbyter and archimandrite, signed. Paul, presbyter and archimandrite, signed. Carosus, presbyter and archimandrite, signed. 308 Asterius, presbyter and archimandrite, signed. [Note: Another reading: “Callinicus.” The Thuanus reads “Calecius.”] Callenicus, monk and archimandrite, signed. [Note: The Vulgate Chalcidian manuscripts add two subscriptions: “Germanus, presbyter and archimandrite, signed at the deposition of Eutyches through Glycerius the deacon.” “Marcellus, an insignificant presbyter and archimandrite, signed.” This last subscription precedes Asterius’s in the Dionysian supplementary manuscripts. Moreover, in these manuscripts, as also in two Chalcidian manuscripts and in the ancient editions of the Councils, the following is added after the final subscription: “All fifty-three signed.”]

[Note: This closing clause is supplied by the excellent Vindobonensis manuscript.] Here ends the copy of the proceedings of the synod at which Eutyches the heretic was condemned.

## CHAPTER XLIII

[Note: Quesnell noted: “This narrative is found in the Oxford and Thuanus manuscripts, and in a third manuscript belonging to the priests of the Oratory of the Trecopean college, as well as in the *Brief History of the Eutychianists*, published long ago, somewhat before the middle. A large part of it is also found in chapters 15 and 18 of Liberatus the deacon’s *Breviary*. I consider the version inserted here to be older than both of them, and everything that the *Brief History* and the *Breviary* have in common with it to have been taken from it. For the former, being much more extensive, contains some material concerning Pope Felix and the events under him against Acacius that would not have been omitted from our manuscript if it had derived from that work. Liberatus’s *Breviary*, moreover, since it was written after the year 546, is later than the manuscript, which does not go beyond the time of Pope Gelasius. The material at the end of the narrative also seems proper to this work; when Liberatus wished to incorporate it into his own writing, he reported it in the manner of a narrator. Our narrator would not have altered it if he had borrowed it from Liberatus. Finally, this Carthaginian deacon openly declares in his preface that he compiled his *Breviary* from ecclesiastical history, synodal proceedings, and the letters of the holy Fathers, joining together the courses of time that he had received in a Greek Alexandrian work. It is therefore evident that this historical booklet was stitched together from several writings, one of which was this narrative. At first, it was no more extensive than the version presented here. In the course of time, however, after the entire affair of the Eutychianists had been taken up again from its beginning, a narrative was prefixed concerning the condemnation of Eutyches and the councils held at Constantinople by Flavian, at Ephesus by Dioscorus, and at Chalcedon by all the bishops; hence it deserved to be called the *Brief History of the Eutychianists*. It was then enlarged by the events under Felix, in the form published by the learned Sirmond. Finally, a more extensive version, containing several additional details concerning Felix, had already been printed in volume I of the *Papal Letters* of 1591, part II, p. 142, prefixed to Leo’s letters.” Thus Quesnell. We showed that Pope Gelasius was the author of this booklet in volume II, note 4, in the observations of Quesnell on Epistle 28 [our Leo, vol. I, col. 1359, note c]. Three editions of it, published by the same pontiff, must be distinguished. In the first, the shorter booklet begins with the condemnation of Dioscorus and ends with the events preceding the condemnation of Acacius. It was first published by Crabbe from a very ancient manuscript from Aix; then by Quesnell from the manuscripts of our collection. We also found it in the Barberini collection 2888 and Vaticanus 1342, in another collection concerning the Acacian affair, contained in the very ancient Veronese manuscript 46, which begins with this booklet, and finally in Vaticanus 1344. In the Thuanus and Vindobonensis manuscripts of our collection, the booklet has no title. The heading printed here by Quesnell was taken from the table of contents prefixed to the Thuanus manuscript. In the Crabbe, Veronese, and Vaticanus 1344 manuscripts, the title reads: “Here begins the order of the narrative concerning the wickedness of Dioscorus of Alexandria.” Vaticanus 1342 gives this heading in the body of the collection: “Where Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, is killed”; and in the margin, in a somewhat later hand: “Concerning the murder of the most blessed man Proterius, patriarch of Alexandria, and concerning the wickedness of Timothy, the usurper of his see and a heretic.” In the table of contents prefixed to the collection: “The killing of Proterius, bishop of Alexandria.” The same booklet, in its second edition, by the same author, Gelasius, was revised and expanded in several places and received two principal additions: one at the beginning, where the history begins with Nestorius and Eutyches; the other at the end, where the same history is brought down to the condemnation of Acacius. This expanded booklet was published by Sirmond from a Verdun manuscript, and we also found it in Vaticanus Reginae 1977. The title in both manuscripts is *Proceedings Concerning Acacius*. The better-known title, devised by Sirmond, is *A Brief History of the Eutychianists*. Since the Vatican Regina manuscript is earlier than Liberatus, it is evident that Liberatus derived his work from the booklet, and not the author of the booklet from Liberatus. Finally, the third edition received another addition at the end, in which the events under Felix are briefly indicated. This complete edition was inserted into volume I of the *Roman Pontiffs’ Letters*, as Quesnell observed. To remove any doubt concerning this addition, we have discovered that this third edition is preserved in the manuscripts of the excellent Avellana collection.]  

**The order of the narrative: how Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, by agreeing with Eutyches in the Church over which he himself presided, or in the Constantinopolitan Church, introduced error, up to the time when Acacius was condemned, who had succeeded Anatolius, the successor of Flavian.**

After Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, [Col. 0608A] 309 [Note: Two manuscripts, together with Crabbe, incorrectly read “who” instead of “of the deed.” Shortly afterward the same Crabbe reads “by the whole synod,” or “from the whole synod.”] had been condemned at Chalcedon according to the character of his deed—that is, because he had agreed with Eutyches the heretic and had condemned Flavian, the Catholic bishop of Constantinople—both by Marcian, the emperor of holy memory, and by the imperial authorities and the entire synod, Proterius, a Catholic, became bishop. [Note: Liberatus has the same material here, with a few changes, in chapter 15 of his *Breviary*. “But a certain Timothy,” he says, “nicknamed Aelurus, and Peter Mog(g)us, a deacon who had belonged to the ordination party of Dioscorus, separated themselves from the Church of Alexandria,” etc. The *Brief History* likewise describes the same events in the same words. Thus Quesnell.]

Then Timothy the presbyter, whose surname was Aelurus, and Peter the deacon, followers of Dioscorus, separated themselves from the Church of Alexandria. When Bishop Proterius was unable to recall them both to their proper ministry, he condemned them.

When the emperor Marcian died, Timothy and Peter, having gathered crowds of heretics, came to Alexandria, and Timothy was ordained bishop by the heretics. Thus there began to be two bishops in Alexandria. [Note: Quesnell reads: “Three days before Easter, on the day when the Supper…” We have followed the Vindobonensis and Veronese manuscripts, supported by the *Brief History* and Liberatus. Crabbe’s reading is similar: “Three days before Easter, when the Supper…”]

Three days before Easter, when the Lord’s Supper is celebrated, [Col. 0609A] following the unclear phrase *conductis ab his perditis* (“[persons] having been brought together by these wicked men”), Proterius of holy memory was killed in the church, to which he had withdrawn out of fear; and there, on the aforesaid day, he was killed in the baptistery, mutilated, thrown out, and his body was burned, while his ashes were scattered to the winds. [Note: The sole reading of Crabbe is “in the holy baptistery”; the Veronese reads “in the aforesaid place”; Liberatus, “on the same day.” The Veronese and Crabbe then omit “his.”]

Meanwhile Leo assumed the imperial power, and the complaint of the Catholics concerning so great a crime reached him. Against them the heretics lodged a petition, asking that the Council of Chalcedon be abolished; [Note: This is how the Vindobonensis, Veronese, and Vatican manuscripts read. Quesnell has: “and they, in opposition to them… petitioning.” In the *Brief History*: “But they were seeking vengeance for so great a crime.” Liberatus has more.] while the others, on the contrary, demanded vengeance for the crime.

Considering that it was excessively burdensome to make the bishops travel such a great distance, since either age, illness, or poverty prevented them from undertaking this labor, the emperor sent magistriani throughout the East, and Bishop Anatolius also sent his deacon Asclepiades [Col. 0609B] [Note: Quesnell adds “who had succeeded Flavian,” contrary to all our manuscripts, as well as Crabbe, the *Brief History*, and Liberatus.] through whom all those bishops who had gathered at Chalcedon might learn what had happened at Alexandria. They all replied that the Council of Chalcedon must be defended even to the shedding of blood, because it held no faith other than that established by the Council of Nicaea. [Note: Quesnell reads “which they held.” We preferred “which it held,” with the Veronese, Crabbe, and Liberatus; the antecedent is the Council of Chalcedon. The *Brief History* has: “because it established no other faith than…”]

But Timothy was not only to be excluded from the number of bishops, but also deprived of the name of Christian. [Note: Up to this point the account is also in Liberatus. Immediately afterward, the *Brief History* reads: “When he was deposed, the other was made…” Quesnell adds “and scarcely he,” but we have deleted this with all our manuscripts, Crabbe, and the *Brief History*, which reads: “Scarcely is Timothy the heretic expelled when Peter flees; Timothy is sent into exile at Cherson, a remote place in Pontus. As long as he lived,” etc. Crabbe alone reads “Gangra” instead of “Cherson,” and then “and as long as he lived.”]

When this had been done, another Timothy was made bishop of Alexandria. Scarcely had that Timothy been expelled and sent into exile at Cherson when Peter the heretic also fled. As long as the emperor Leo lived, Timothy, bishop of Alexandria, lived in peace. But when Basiliscus had seized the imperial power, he began to condemn the Council of Chalcedon and drive out the Catholics. [Col. 0610A]

Then that condemned Timothy, having received freedom, came to Constantinople and restored the condemned heretics to their places. He went to Alexandria; Timothy the Catholic fled [Note: Liberatus, who discusses this and other matters in chapter 16, reads: “the Catholic to the fortress of Canopus, and he hid in a monastery.”] and hid in a monastery. That Peter again joined himself to Timothy, with whom he had previously been condemned.

The emperor Zeno returned to power, and Basiliscus was overthrown. A dispatch was sent to Alexandria so that, after the usurper Timothy had been expelled, Timothy the Catholic might be restored to the Church. But when that Timothy had been condemned and death had intervened, Peter [Note: The *Brief History* adds “his associate”; shortly afterward, instead of “bishop of Alexandria,” it reads with the Veronese manuscript “is ordained bishop by the Alexandrians”; below it says that he ordains the bishop of Apamea.] was ordained bishop of Alexandria by a single heretic. Nevertheless, the emperor ordered him to be deposed and Timothy the Catholic to be brought back, as is also contained in Acacius’s letters. [Note: We have added “also,” with our manuscripts and Crabbe. Shortly afterward the *Brief History* reads “of Acacius of Constantinople”; it then inserts some material.]

Meanwhile Timothy the Catholic wrote to Pope Simplicius of holy memory, asking and saying that Peter, once condemned in the diaconate and now also excluded from the Christian community, should be exiled still farther, and that he should write to the emperor to this effect, because Peter was hiding in the city of Alexandria and plotting against the Church. [Col. 0610B]

For nearly three years and more, therefore, Pope Simplicius of holy memory never ceased writing to Bishop Acacius [Note: The *Brief History* adds “that he should deal with the emperor”; it then inserts other material that was omitted in the first edition of this booklet.] that what Bishop Timothy requested should be done concerning Peter.

When Bishop Timothy died, John the Catholic was ordained Catholic bishop. [Note: The *Brief History* reads: “He was ordained, and, following the custom of his predecessors, he sent synodical letters to the Apostolic See through Isidore the presbyter and Peter the deacon. When Uranius the assistant arrived, the pope was suspended from confirming that episcopate.”]

Bishop John sent his synodical letter. [Note: Quesnell adds “to the pope.” We have deleted this with our manuscripts and Crabbe, although the *Brief History* expresses the same point later. The Veronese reads “Urpanius”; the *Brief History*, “Uranius.” The word *subadjuva* is absent from the Oxford manuscript. In Crabbe, instead of “Urbanius subadjuva,” we find “a certain man.”]

Urbanius the assistant also arrived against Bishop John, carrying an imperial decree, so that the pope would suspend himself from confirming that episcopate. [Note: We have written “the emperor’s decree,” and afterward “in the same decree,” with the Vindobonensis, Veronese, and Crabbe, supported by the *Brief History*. Quesnell has “the emperor’s decree” and then “in that same decree.” Some manuscripts read “of the bishop” or “of the bishopric” instead of “of that episcopate.”]

And because in the same decree mention had been made of restoring Peter, whom he himself had condemned, that part was entirely repudiated; hence the emperor appeared offended. [Col. 0611A]

At that time Acacius also wrote, when he reported concerning Peter of Alexandria who had been condemned, concerning Peter and John of Antioch as follows: Peter had governed a monastery at Constantinople; but after abandoning it because of crimes, he had fled to Antioch. There, after the Catholic bishop Martyrius had been expelled by the vilest populace and the heretics, he had occupied Martyrius’s see, and immediately had been condemned by the bishops and deported by the emperor Leo [Note: This is how all our manuscripts and Crabbe read. Quesnell has “sent into exile at Oasis.” In the *Brief History*: “sent into exile at Oasitanus.” Liberatus, chapter 18, says “deported to Samos,” incorrectly.] to Oasis. Having fled, he is said to have returned to Constantinople and given an undertaking that, once the mobs had been restrained, he would dare do nothing further.

But, as was said above, during the reign of Basiliscus he was sent back to Antioch by that condemned Timothy, who had come to Constantinople, so that he might again hold the episcopate there. Having done this, that same Peter ordained John, concerning whom we have said that Acacius had reported him, as bishop of Apamea. When they did not receive him [Note: Quesnell inserts “that man”; our manuscripts, Crabbe, and the *Brief History* omit it], he returned to Antioch, expelled Peter, the author of his episcopate, and invaded Peter’s Church.

Acacius says that both men were again condemned, and asked the Apostolic See that, if they should perhaps flee to it, they should not even be considered worthy of its sight; and if they had already obtained some indulgence, it ought to be invalid, nor should their repentance be accepted.

Why say more? This same John, whom Acacius had condemned together with Peter and caused to be condemned by the Apostolic See without the remedy of repentance [Note: The Veronese and Crabbe manuscripts, together with the *Brief History*, read “caused.”], he sent, after so many condemnations by the Tyrians, to preside over a Church. [Note: Thus all our manuscripts together with Crabbe. Quesnell has: “For what Acacius later said…” In the *Brief History* the following material is omitted and other material is substituted.]

For when Acacius says [Col. 0611C] that Peter of Alexandria, after submitting a petition, condemned the Eutychian or Nestorian heresy, this is plainly shown to be entirely false. For what reason caused him, in his episcopate, to anathematize the Council of Chalcedon or the *Tome* of the holy Pope Leo? [Note: Thus our three manuscripts, together with the Oxford manuscript and Crabbe. Quesnell reads “in a synod of the bishops or at Chalcedon.”] What reason caused him, after removing the name of Proterius or of Timothy the Catholic, to inscribe the name of Dioscorus and Timothy the heretic? What reason caused him, if he was a Catholic, to raise from beneath the earth the body of Timothy the Catholic [Note: The Veronese, Vatican, and Crabbe manuscripts add “bishop”; after the word “Timothy,” we have added “the heretic” with all the manuscripts and Crabbe.], who had been buried among the Catholic bishops, and cast it outside?

Is this not Peter, who always adhered to Timothy the heretic after Timothy had been condemned? How, then, does Acacius later praise him with extraordinary commendations, when he remembered having previously reported such great crimes concerning him?

At the end of the Thuanus manuscript: “I have collated this.”

## CHAPTER XLIV

[Note: Besides the manuscripts of this collection, this chapter is found in Veronese 46, Vaticanus 1342, the Dionysian supplementary manuscripts, from which we collated Vaticanus 5845, and the supplementary collection of Isidore, from which it was first published by Merlin, as it appears in Vaticanus 1340.]

**Letter of Pope Simplicius to Acacius, that he remove the scandals of the Church of Alexandria.**

**To his beloved brother Acacius, Simplicius.**

We have no respite from our cares; for the matter itself does not permit us to rest. If we abandon this concern, we are without excuse before Christ our Lord, whose business is at stake. And it is astonishing that, after so much time has passed and so many opportunities have arisen from it, your Beloved has wished to inform us of nothing concerning the Church of Alexandria, which is being shaken so severely. Our admonition has never ceased urging you, so that, sharing the anxiety, you might accompany my letters to the most Christian and merciful emperor with personal addresses from your Beloved; and, mindful of the ancient practice, might labor with us, as always, in defense of the orthodox, lest any of us incur the guilt of surrender while the Christian people perish, and appear rather to be a hireling than a shepherd.

We therefore exhort your Beloved not to cease opportunely and persistently bringing this matter to pious ears, so that, once the scandals that have repeatedly assailed the Church of Alexandria have been removed, the desired peace may be restored; and so that, after difficulties have been set aside, the advancement of your vigilance may quickly be made known. [Note: Quesnell omitted “your”; we have added it from all our manuscripts and the Vulgate.]

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of November, in the consulship of Severinus. Sent through Restitutus.

## CHAPTER XLV

[Note: This is preserved in the same manuscripts as the preceding chapter, and also in the Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts. We have supplied the title from the Vindobonensis and Veronese 46 manuscripts, with which Vaticani 1342 and 5845 agree, omitting a few words. Quesnell’s title is: “Letter of Acacius to Pope Simplicius: that the heretic Timothy has died, Peter has been condemned, and Timothy the Catholic has been restored.”]

**Here begins a copy of the letter that Acacius sent to Simplicius, pope of holy memory of the city of Rome, in which he reported the condemnation of Peter of Alexandria.**

[Col. 0612C]

**To the most blessed Lord and holy Father, Archbishop Simplicius, Acacius.** [Note: The Veronese and Vaticanus 5845 manuscripts, together with the Oxford manuscript, read “to the holy patriarch-bishop.”]

As the Apostle says, we carry the concern of all the Churches, and you ceaselessly exhort us, although we are willingly watchful and [Note: Quesnell reads “anticipating.” We preferred the reading of all our manuscripts, Vindobonensis, Veronese, and both Vaticani, the latter two having “returning to you,” namely “demonstrating divine zeal in the customary manner.” The Vulgate reads “anticipating,” but “demonstrating divine zeal in the customary manner,” as above.] demonstrate divine zeal in you in the customary manner, asking more certainly about the state of the Church of Alexandria, so that, in accordance with the paternal canons, you may undertake the labor, pouring forth the sweat of piety for these matters, as has always been approved.

But Christ our Lord, who works all things together for good for those who love him, dwelling upon our thoughts, [Note: We have added “and,” with our three manuscripts and the Vulgate. Shortly afterward the Oxford manuscript omits “for his glory.”] and recognizing that we have one and the same mind in these matters for his glory, himself accomplished the entire victory, and will make us partners with the most tranquil emperor. [Note: Quesnell reads “for Timothy, breathing storms from Cherson.” We have corrected this with Vaticanus 1342, supported by the Vindobonensis and Veronese, in which only “hoping” is found instead of “breathing.” The Thuanus reads “Timothy, preparing the storms of dissension”; Vaticanus 5845 has the same, except that it reads “of secession” for “of dissension”—both readings being corruptions of “from Cherson,” to which Timothy had clearly been exiled, as is evident from chapter 43. The Vulgate likewise incorrectly reads “And Timothy, the successor.”]

Indeed, he has withdrawn from human life Timothy, who from Cherson was stirring up storms and, as became apparent, disturbing ecclesiastical tranquillity, saying: “Be silent and hold your peace.” He also scattered Peter, who had similarly risen like a storm from Alexandria, and, with the Holy Spirit blowing, turned him toward eternal flight—the very one who had belonged to those formerly and previously condemned. [Note: The Vulgate reads “as in our records.” The Veronese manuscript is better: “as also in our records.”]

As has been found in our archives, and as you will be able to learn from your own archives, if you deign to inquire, you will discover what subsequently followed concerning him [Note: Thus the Vindobonensis and three other manuscripts, which have only “were reported to Rome.” The Vulgate reads “were reported to Rome, to one or the other.” In his *Treatise*, edited from Veronese 46 by Scipio Maffei, vol. V of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 185, Gelasius, citing this letter of Acacius, says that Timothy the Catholic “reported Peter’s condemnation to both Romes.” We therefore believe that the reading should be “to both Romes” or “to one or the other,” with “one or the other” understood as “both.” Quesnell incorrectly has: “and were reported by the Alexandrian bishops to the Romans.”] were reported by the bishop of Alexandria to either Rome.

That Peter, being a son of night and appearing alien to the works that shine by day, finding the darkness entirely suited to carry out robbery, and becoming its accomplice [Note: Quesnell inserts “according to his wishes”; all our manuscripts and the Vulgate omit this. Only the Vindobonensis and Veronese have “an accomplice suited to carrying out their robbery”; the Oxford manuscript deletes “their accomplice.” Shortly afterward, with the word *et* deleted, two manuscripts, Veronese and Vaticanus 1342, place “unburied” after the verb “had overthrown.”] at midnight, while the corpse of the man who had overturned the paternal canons still lay there unburied, slipped into the see, as he himself supposed, with only one person present, and that one a partner in his madness [Note: The Veronese, together with the Vulgate, reads “with one person alone”; shortly afterward it reads “was persisting” instead of “was present,” supported also by the Vindobonensis.], so that for this he might be subjected to greater punishments; nor did what he hoped come to pass.

But that man, judging only partially and to the smallest degree, nowhere appeared at all; while Timothy, guardian of the paternal canons, [Note: Quesnell reads: “Who, following the example of David’s gentleness, was patient to the end, rejoices in his own authority, restored by Christ, and received the grace of healing, accepting the wishes of his spiritual sons. He awaits the reward, multiplied,” etc. We have restored the reading of our manuscripts, supported by the Vulgate, in which only “he is subjected by example” is found, together with “receiving.”] who was an example of Davidic gentleness, patient to the end, and restored by Christ to his own authority, [Col. 0614A] rejoices in the honor of his own see and has received the voices of his spiritual sons. He awaits the grace of healing, honored more greatly in himself by Christ, the prince of priests, for whose sake he has also bound upon himself the crown of endurance.

Therefore let your Blessedness pray more earnestly for the most Christian emperor and for us ourselves. Nothing is neglected that pertains to the preservation of ecclesiastical discipline. I, and those who are with me, greet the entire brotherhood that is with you in Christ. [Note: Quesnell inserts “your.” This word is superfluous and absent from our manuscripts. Shortly afterward two Vaticani, together with the Vulgate, read “which is with you”; we have added “and most blessed” from all the manuscripts and the Vulgate.]

And in another hand: May you be preserved in the Lord, most holy and most blessed Father.

## CHAPTER XLVI

[Note: All the manuscripts containing the preceding letter also contain this one.]

**Letter of Pope Felix condemning Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, because he received Peter and the other heretics whom he himself had condemned without the Apostolic faith.**

[Col. 0614B]

**Felix, bishop of the holy Catholic Church [Note: Thus the Vindobonensis. In the Veronese manuscript, VR, perhaps the source of the Vulgate reading, “of the city of Rome.” Quesnell reads “Roman.” Vaticanus 1342: “Felix, bishop of the Roman Church, to Acacius.”] of the City, to Acacius.**
You are found liable for many transgressions, and have often been involved in contempt of the venerable Council of Nicaea; you have rashly claimed for yourself the rights of provinces belonging to others. You judged that heretical invaders, those ordained by heretics, and those whom you yourself had condemned and insisted should also be condemned by the Apostolic See, were to be received not only at your instigation, but even appointed to preside over other Churches—something that could not be done even in the case of Catholics—or promoted with honors they did not deserve.

[Note: Vindobonensis and Veronensis, mutilated, have “you [received] your own.” We have corrected from the two Vatican manuscripts cited above. Ignoring this correction, others wrote, as in the printed text, “you judged them to be received not only into your communion”; or, with Quesnellus, “you judged them to be received not only into the college, but also,” etc. Shortly afterward Vindobonensis and Veronensis delete “of” before “Catholics.”]

John bears witness to this: although he had not been received by the Catholics at Apamea and had been expelled from Antioch, you placed him over the Tyrians. And Humerius, previously deposed from the diaconate and deprived of the designation “Christian,” was by you also advanced to the office of presbyter.

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts (1342 and 5845) add “and persuaders and.”]

[Note: In the Vindobonensis and Veronensis this passage is very corrupt and reads: “You left them to the Tyrians; and Humerius, deservedly deposed from the diaconate and deprived of the name of Christian, was by you also—or ‘now’—advanced to the office of the presbyterate.” The printed versions present the reading of the text, supported by the two Vatican manuscripts. In place of “Humerius,” Vatican 1342 has “Hieremius,” Vatican 5845 “Hieronymus.” Harduinus would prefer “Himerius.” Quesnellus has “now” instead of “also.”]

And as though these things seemed small to you, you extended the audacity of your pride even against the very truth of apostolic teaching, so that Peter—whom you yourself had reported as condemned to my predecessor of holy memory, as the attached documents testify—might, with your connivance, again seize the see of the blessed evangelist Mark, and, after driving out the orthodox bishops and clergy, undoubtedly ordain others like himself. After the one who had been regularly appointed there had been expelled, Peter held the Church captive.

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts and Labbe, in the margin, read “your audacity and pride.”]

[Note: Vatican 5845, together with the printed editions, has “there.” We have added “his” from all our manuscripts and the printed editions. The printed editions, together with Vatican 1342, place the word “many” after “clergy,” perhaps more correctly.]

His person is so pleasing to you, and his ministers so acceptable, that you are now discovered to be persecuting many orthodox bishops and clergy who come to Constantinople, while supporting his representatives. And while this same Peter anathematized the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon and violated the burial of Timothy of holy memory—as more reliable messengers have recently again reported to us—you have thought him deserving of excuse through Vitalis and Misenus. You have not ceased to praise him and extol him with many encomiums, to such an extent that you boast that his condemnation, which you had previously reported, was not true.

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read “many reported”; and shortly afterward, “you would believe … you would cease … you would boast.”]

Yet you persist so greatly in defending this perverse man that you allowed Vitalis and Misenus—formerly bishops, but now deprived of their honor and communion, whom we had sent specifically for his expulsion—to be handed over to imprisonment after their documents had been taken away. Then, as their own profession revealed, you had them brought out for the procession that you hold with heretics and dragged into communion with the heretics and with yourself, despite the embassy that ought to have been preserved even by the law of nations.

[Note: Quesnellus inserts “but”; afterward he reads “for the heretics.” We have preferred the reading of our manuscripts and the printed editions.]

You corrupted them with rewards and made them return not only ineffective, but also, to the mockery of blessed Peter the Apostle, from whose see they had departed, manifest as opponents of everything that had been commanded.

[Note: Manuscripts of other collections, the Veronensis, and the two Vatican manuscripts read: “and corrupt them with rewards—or perhaps, ‘you would corrupt them’—and, for the mockery of blessed Peter the Apostle, from whose see they had departed, make them return not only ineffective, but also as opponents,” and so forth. The printed editions have the same reading, except that they use the forms “you dragged,” “you corrupted,” and “you made,” and in place of “for the mockery” they read “for the injury.”]

In deceiving them you exposed your wickedness, and, refusing to answer at the Apostolic See according to the canons the petition of my brother and fellow bishop John, who had attacked you with the gravest charges, you confirmed the accusations against you.

You considered Felix, our most faithful defender, unworthy of your sight because necessity had caused him to follow later. You also testified in your letters that they too communicated with you, though they are known to be heretics.

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts, with the printed editions, read “having followed.” Quesnellus alone has “and them” for “them also with you”; shortly afterward, “it is established that they are heretics.” We have deleted “to be” with the Vindobonensis and Veronensis manuscripts and the printed editions.] For what else are those who, after the death of Timothy of holy memory, return to the Church under Peter, or those who have handed themselves over to him from among the Catholics, except that Peter had been judged by the universal Church—and by you?

[Note: The Oxford manuscript reads less correctly, “not because.”]

Therefore, share with those whom you gladly embrace in the sentence now pronounced, which we sent to you through Tutus, defender of the Church: recognize that you have been deprived of priestly honor and Catholic communion, removed from the number of the faithful, and stripped of your name and office of priestly ministry. You have been condemned by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and by apostolic authority through us, and you are never to be released from the bonds of anathema.

[Note: Quesnellus reads “through Toleratus to you,” following the manuscripts of this collection. We have corrected it from the Veronensis, while two other letters of Felix (9 and 11) read “Tutus, defender of the Roman Church.” Liberatus has “Totus” in the printed edition and “Tutus” in the margin. Two Vatican manuscripts have “Totus.” The printed edition reads “through your,” where a copyist, not understanding the word “Tutus,” wrote “tuae.”]

[Note: Here both Vatican manuscripts end.]

Caelius Felix, bishop of the holy Catholic Church of the city of Rome, have subscribed. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Venantius, a man of illustrious rank; and at the same time seventy-seven bishops, excluding the pope, subscribed.

[Note: Thus both manuscripts of Quesnellus and our Vindobonensis. In the very ancient Veronensis, together with the printed editions, it reads “simultaneously, sixty-seven bishops.”]

[Note: The annotator is mistaken concerning Anatolius.]

Quesnellus, intending to insert an annotation from the Oxford manuscript that is found in no other manuscript, prefaced it as follows:

“What follows clearly does not belong to the manuscript, but is an annotation by the person through whose efforts it was copied. It is evident that he lived scarcely after the times of Gregory the Great; nor is this material actually found in the Thuaneus manuscript. Moreover, what is here read concerning Anastasius—that he was taken away by a swift death while considering the restoration of Acacius—is also found in the book concerning the Roman Pontiffs. The emperor Justin likewise suggests similar things in his letter to Pope Hormisdas.

“The Oxford manuscript’s annotation then states:

‘In the time of Theodosius the Younger, under Pope Leo, whose writings will be placed later, Bishop Flavian of Constantinople condemned the heretic Eutyches, as was read above, with the pope’s agreement and confirmation. Dioscorus, however, bishop of Alexandria, who favored Eutyches, deposed Flavian from his see and ordained Anatolius in his place. In the time of Marcian, who succeeded Theodosius, a synod was convened at Chalcedon by the pope’s command, as was read above; in it Dioscorus was condemned and Anatolius corrected.*

‘Leo was succeeded by Pope Hilary; Hilary by Simplicius. Acacius, who had succeeded Anatolius, sent Simplicius the letter written above, stating that Peter, the invader of the Alexandrian see, had been condemned. Simplicius was succeeded by Felix, who was the great-grandfather of blessed Gregory; he condemned Acacius for the reasons mentioned above. Anastasius, the successor of Gelasius, secretly wishing to restore Acacius, was unable to do so, having been overtaken by a swift death. Gelasius, the successor of Felix, confirms Acacius’s condemnation in the five letters that follow.’”

In the annotation’s words, “Anastasius, secretly wishing to restore Acacius, was unable to do so, having been overtaken by a swift death,” Quesnellus added the following:

“Similar material is found in the Liber Pontificalis, from which Gratian, Ivo, and others copied it, though with certain changes and interpolations. Albert Pighius attacks Gratian with the greatest bitterness as one who corrupts the words of the Liber Pontificalis. Antonius Augustinus also criticizes him in dialogue 6 of the first book of his *On the Correction of Gratian*, although he demands moderation from Pighius.

“These are the words of the *Liber Pontificalis*, as they are read in volume III of Binius’s *Councils, Greek and Latin*:

‘And because he secretly wished to recall Acacius, and could not. He was struck by divine will.’

“Antonius Augustinus says that Ivo of Chartres, in part XIV, chapter 40 of the *Decretals*, and the Zaragoza book report these words in the following form:

‘And because he secretly wished to recall Acacius, and could not, because Acacius was struck by divine will.’

“Antonius Augustinus seems to be angry with Gratian because he removed from the words of the *Liber Pontificalis* the two words ‘because’ and ‘Acacius.’ Thus it happened that what should be understood of Acacius, who was struck by divine will, was understood of Anastasius. But the text of the *Liber Pontificalis* itself, as well as our manuscript, proves that Ivo and the others, rather than Gratian, should be accused of adding material rather than Gratian of omitting it. From the latter manuscript, which is older than the others, the genuine meaning of these words can be discerned.

“First, it is false that Acacius was divinely struck and that for this reason he was not recalled by Anastasius. For how could Acacius have been struck under Anastasius, when Nicephorus and Evagrius report that he died under Felix III? It is therefore clearer than daylight that the word ‘Acacius’ is an addition in Ivo and the others, and that the word ‘struck’ cannot be understood of anyone other than Anastasius.

“Second, where Anastasius is said by certain authors to have been struck, this appears to have been written from conjecture and commentary. For the annotation in our manuscript merely says that he was overtaken by death, and no earlier writer is found to assert anything more.

“Third, when all the cited authors write that Anastasius wished to recall Acacius, this cannot be reconciled with the time of Acacius’s death. The statement must necessarily be interpreted as concerning Acacius’s person; the word ‘restore,’ which is used in the manuscript’s annotation, can most suitably be understood as restoring Acacius’s name to the diptychs.

“Thus far Quesnellus.”

Francis Blanchinus, in volume III of Anastasius the Librarian, in his notes on the life of Anastasius II, page 209, reasonably conjectures that what is transmitted in the *Liber Pontificalis* concerning Anastasius II and the name of Acacius derives from an earlier but malicious writing. Some partisan, just as he spread other fabrications against Symmachus, may have invented Anastasius II’s supposed inclination to restore even Acacius’s name in order to provoke hatred against him.

The emperor Justin, in the letter to Hormisdas cited after letter 73 of that same pontiff, does not say that Anastasius wished to restore Acacius’s name. Rather, he bears witness to the opposite, asserting that Anastasius himself wrote to his predecessor that it was sufficient for those accepting peace if Acacius’s name alone were passed over in silence. This agrees with Anastasius’s own letters and confirms Blanchinus’s suspicion.]

321. CHAPTER XLVII

[Note: This chapter is found in the manuscripts of this collection and in the very ancient Veronensis 46, and finally in the Isidorian additions, from which Merlin edited this volume. The more recent Oxford manuscript, which Quesnellus followed, often seems to preserve better readings. But since it agrees in its readings with the older Vindobonensis and Veronensis, as well as with Quesnellus’s own Thuaneus manuscript, we have no doubt that in the Oxford manuscript certain obscure passages were corrected at the copyist’s discretion. We have therefore thought that the readings of our manuscripts, which generally agree with the printed editions of the councils, should be restored. The work appears to have been copied from incomplete notes and to be mutilated, so it is not surprising if it is defective in several places. Quesnellus gave the title as: “Pope Gelasius’s remarkable disputation on the bond of anathema against Acacius and Peter.” We have restored the title found in all our manuscripts, including the Thuaneus, and in the printed editions; Anastasius also approves it in the letter prefixed to the *Collectanea* and addressed to the deacon John, where it reads: “From Gelasius’s treatise on the bond of anathema.” We have prefixed asterisks because this little work lacks its beginning. For more on the same subject, see the preceding treatise on the collections, part III, where, in discussing Gelasius’s documents, we showed that this little work is not only mutilated and incomplete, but also ineptly composed from several fragments of Gelasius.]

Here begins Pope Gelasius’s treatise on the bond of anathema.

[Col. 0617A]

* * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * *

CHAPTER I

[Note: Quesnellus: “It is the concern of the Apostolic See’s vigilance that perhaps certain people may say what they are accustomed to say: if the Council of Chalcedon is admitted, everything that appears to have been drawn from it there must be accepted; for either it must be accepted in its entirety, or, if it is rejected in part, it cannot be sound in its entirety.” In a marginal note he says: “These opening words have hitherto been missing, so that the editors of the Roman edition of the papal letters rightly suspected that the beginning of this treatise was absent. He does not mention on the authority of which manuscript he inserted these words, although they do not seem sufficient. They are certainly absent from the Vindobonensis of this collection, as also from the other collections, from Veronensis 46 and Vatican 1340 of the Isidorian additions, and from Merlin’s edition, which was based on them; from these sources we have presented the beginning, though mutilated. Neither this chapter nor the following appears to bear on the proposed subject of the bond of anathema, unless one should perhaps suspect that the Easterners said that the anathema against Acacius could be dissolved in this way: it had been issued from an old Chalcedonian decree, just as the canon concerning the privileges of the see of Constantinople, issued at Chalcedon, had been dissolved by the Apostolic See. Compare the treatise at the place cited.”]

Lest, as they are accustomed to do, they say that if the Council of Chalcedon is admitted, everything that appears to have been drawn from it there must be accepted—either that it ought to be admitted in its entirety, or that, if it is rejectable in part, it cannot be sound in its entirety—let them therefore recognize that what it established according to the Holy Scriptures and the tradition of our ancestors, according to the canons and rules of the Church, for the communion of faith and for the Catholic and apostolic truth for whose sake the Apostolic See commissioned this council and confirmed what was done, must unquestionably be accepted by the whole Church.

[Note: Only Quesnellus, with the Oxford manuscript, reads “received” in the preceding alternative. Vindobonensis deletes “established”; the printed editions read “what it established,” while Veronensis has “since that second [matter],” deleting “what it established.” Veronensis and the first hand of Vindobonensis read “for communion of faith”; the second hand of Vindobonensis, with the printed editions of the councils, reads “for the common faith.” Quesnellus alone reads “in the [power] of the Apostolic [See]” for “and in the power of the bishop of the Apostolic See.”]

But the other things that were brought forward there—or rather, debated there—through incompetent presumption, which the Apostolic See in no way commissioned to be carried out; which were immediately contradicted by the representatives of the Apostolic See; which the Apostolic See did not approve, even when the emperor Marcian requested it; which Anatolius, then bishop of the Church of Constantinople, professed that he himself had not presumed, and acknowledged to have been placed in the power of the bishop of the Apostolic See—these things, as has been said, the Apostolic See did not receive, because whatever is shown to be contrary to the privileges of the universal Church cannot stand by any reasoning.

[Note: Quesnellus alone, together with the Oxford manuscript, inserts “have no strength.” These words are absent from all our manuscripts, including the Thuaneus, and from the printed editions of the councils.]

[Note: See letter 132, chapter 4, volume I.]

CHAPTER II

Why indeed? Because in the sacred books, which we certainly venerate and follow, profanities of certain people are reported to exist there and crimes are narrated as having been committed—must everything therefore be equally venerated or followed by us because it is contained in those holy and venerable books?

[Note: We have restored the printed reading with all our manuscripts and the Thuaneus. Quesnellus reads, “we follow, [and] that there are the perversities of certain people”; shortly afterward the printed editions and Veronensis delete “everything.”]

Saint Peter, the first of the Apostles, while judging that the grace of the New Testament should be proclaimed in such a way that he did not depart from the institutions of the old Law, is read to have acted in a certain way by simulation among Jews and Gentiles. Should we therefore follow those actions of his which his fellow apostle rightly rebuked and which Peter himself afterward consistently avoided? Or should they be taken up equally with those things which, as the first apostle, he proclaimed as salutary?

[Note: Quesnellus alone reads “salutarily.”]

Should his sound teaching therefore be rejected together with the things that happened to him as a human being, or should his former weakness and ignorance still be accepted together with his perfected doctrine?

[Note: Quesnellus adds “Paul.”]

Are not many things pertaining to the truth also read in the books of those very heretics? Should the truth therefore be rejected because their books, wherever wickedness is present, are rejected?

[Note: Quesnellus reads “in those very books”; shortly afterward the printed editions, with Vindobonensis, read “pertain.”] Or should their wicked books be accepted because the truth inserted in them is not denied?

The Apostle says: “Test everything; hold fast to what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:20). We know that the Apostle also quoted something from pagan books (Acts 17:28). Should everything that was uttered along with those words therefore also be received?

[Note: We have added “also” with our manuscripts and the printed editions of the councils, and then written “uttered”; Quesnellus has “reported.”]

The Apostle himself says that many preachers proclaim Christ in different ways. Yet, although Christ preached in whatever manner must be admitted, he does not therefore fail to warn us to avoid the manner in which Christ was preached incorrectly.

[Note: Quesnellus reads: “Although he says that Christ, preached in any manner whatever, ought to be accepted, he nevertheless does not therefore fail to warn us to avoid …” The reading of our Vindobonensis and Veronensis manuscripts, approved by the printed editions, has been restored.]

He himself complains of wicked workers, of whom he teaches that some things are to be rejected and others followed. These and similar examples instruct us, and divine testimonies confirm, that we must not indiscriminately accept everything said by anyone or written anywhere; rather, retaining what is good, we must reject what causes harm.

CHAPTER III

[Note: This sentence’s relation to what precedes and follows is unclear. That is to be attributed to the fact that this treatise was imperfectly composed from fragments. The sentence “the judgment is prescribed” would fit better if this period were omitted. Shortly afterward, the printed edition of the councils reads “made him guilty” instead of “makes him guilty.” Quesnellus has “it was not,” that is, “there was no sin, and therefore the punishment of sin was not owed there.” We have adopted the reading of the printed councils because it is supported by our two manuscripts, the Vindobonensis and Veronensis, which have only “thus” in place of “suppose.”]

Death was inflicted upon sinful man; yet death inflicted upon the man Jesus Christ proves the devil guilty, because where there was no cause of death—namely, sin—there ought not to have been punishment either.

A judgment is always prescribed, or has been prescribed, for error.

[Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts and also of the Thuaneus, together with the printed editions of the councils. Quesnellus, following only the Oxford manuscript, has: “which judgment, while the error remains, would never be dissolved at all.” Later the printed editions, together with the Vindobonensis manuscript, read “thus from the judgment”; and afterward, together with the Veronensis, “and the same as long as.”]

That judgment once prescribed for this error will never be dissolved at all. For just as error itself, insofar as it is error, never ceases to be error, so the judgment prescribed for it is never dissolved, because the error that is recognized as condemned is shown to remain bound by the same judgment for as long as the error remains.

Therefore those who are in error are bound by the judgment of error; and as long as they remain in it, they are in no way absolved, just as the error itself in which they are is not absolved.

[Note: Two manuscripts, the Vindobonensis and Veronensis, read “the one in whom there are errors is absolved.” Quesnellus has “deserves.”]

For error itself never merits forgiveness; rather, forgiveness belongs to the one who has truly become free from it and withdraws from participation in it.

[Note: Quesnellus, together with the Oxford manuscript, reads “has departed.” “Therefore, as long as error is in someone” may perhaps be better. Nevertheless, we have followed the manuscripts, including the Thuaneus, together with the printed editions of the councils.]

Therefore, as long as error is in them, they retain their condemnation, and it is never dissolved, because error always deserves punishment.

[Note: Quesnellus has “has departed from the same.” Shortly afterward Quesnellus reads “When the one who errs …”; the printed editions have “To the one who errs …” We have preferred the reading of our manuscript copies, with which shortly afterward we have also written “is bound.” Quesnellus alone has “is struck through.”]

Those who participate in it either always share in its punishment, if they do not cease to persist in it, or, if they withdraw from error, then to the degree that they have become alienated from error and separated from participation in it, they will correspondingly be alienated from its punishment.

When punishment is prescribed for the one who errs, for as long as he remains in error he is bound by that same punishment, because one who errs cannot be without the punishment of his error.

This same punishment is perpetual and can never be dissolved for as long as he persists in being one who errs. But if he ceases to be one who errs, the punishment prescribed as perpetual for the one who errs cannot be perpetual for one who does not err—that is, for one who has become another person, different from the one for whom it was prescribed. Indeed, it cannot even still be punishment.

For he himself is not the one for whom it was prescribed: it was prescribed for one who errs, not for one who does not err.

[Note: The words “for it was prescribed for one who errs” had fallen out of Quesnellus’s text or from the copyist of the Oxford manuscript.]

For what is prescribed for one who errs is perpetual and perpetually binds the one who errs; but it can no longer hold one who does not err.

Let it be said that it will be perpetual for the one who errs; let it be said that it will never be dissolved for the one who errs. What has been prescribed for him remains completely, and it is true and certain that what has been prescribed for him cannot be wholly absolved as long as it is owed to the one who remains in error. But it cannot be punishment for one who does not err, since what is not owed to one who does not err ought not to be inflicted upon him.

[Note: Quesnellus has “prescribed in the one who errs”; our manuscripts have “prescribed in it” or “prescribed in him.” We preferred the latter. The printed edition of the councils has “prescribed in it.”]

That which is owed to the one who errs is neither changed nor dissolved. It has been prescribed according to its own continuity; according to its own right it cannot be dissolved at all. But in a continuity that is not its own, it is now shown to have been emptied of force, since it cannot exist and has no right whatsoever there where it has no cause for existing.

[Note: Thus our manuscripts agree with the printed editions of the councils. Only in the Veronensis manuscript did a second ancient hand emend *quae* (“which”) to *quo* (“in which”). Quesnellus reads: “but in a condition not its own, in which it cannot exist, it is shown to be so far void.”]

CHAPTER IV

The Holy Scriptures are full of justice expressed in this manner. It is said: “Let sinners perish from the earth, so that they may no longer be” (Psalm 103), meaning “sinners,” so that they may cease to be sinners; let them perish in the sense that they may cease to be sinners.

[Note: The same manuscripts and the printed editions have this reading. Quesnellus, omitting the first word “sinners,” has “so that there may no longer be sinners.”]

Otherwise, if sinners were wholly destroyed everywhere according to the prophet’s statement, so that they no longer existed substantially, who could have been saved by our Redeemer, who came not to call the righteous but sinners (Luke 5:32)? Or whom does the Apostle mean when he says: “Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first” (1 Timothy 1:15)? And: “When we were sinners” (Romans 5:8), “God sent his Son” (Galatians 4:4), and other statements of this kind?

[Note: Quesnellus, following only the Oxford manuscript, has “so that they would not exist,” contrary to our manuscripts, the Thuaneus, and the printed editions. Shortly afterward the printed edition, together with the Veronensis, reads “by our Redeemer.” Quesnellus alone has “or those about whom the Apostle speaks.”]

Here indeed many sinners perished substantially, remaining, naturally, in their sins; and the true judgment pronounced against them remained, never dissolved. Yet, although that same judgment remained perpetual in those for whom it had been prescribed, it happened in a certain way that, in those who did not remain in that condition forever—that is, who did not persist forever in their sins—the judgment prescribed for such people nevertheless remained.

For they too perish—but in ceasing to be sinners, as has been said—not in a punitive but in a remedial manner; and in a certain way the prescribed judgment remained in them also, until, remaining in force, it made them cease to be sinners, or brought them to the point of no longer being sinners.

[Note: The words “or completed the process so that they would no longer be sinners” appear in the printed editions of the councils. Quesnellus omitted them, adding in the margin that he considered them to have been inserted by some conjecturer, since they are found in neither manuscript—that is, neither in the Oxford nor in the Thuaneus. We have nevertheless retained them on the authority of our older manuscripts, the Veronensis and Vindobonensis.]

The judgment in them was completed; and, once the course of that continuing judgment had been carried through, the sinful people perished so that they were no longer sinners.

[Note: This is the reading of our manuscripts together with the printed editions. Something is missing or corrupt in the passage, and the manuscripts do not remedy it. Quesnellus reads “remains.”]

But it could no longer remain in those who were not sinners, because it had absolutely no right to remain in those upon whom it had not been inflicted. Thus the judgment was in no way dissolved in its own right or course; and while it remained in those upon whom it had been inflicted, it became wholly alien from those who had been separated from its jurisdiction.

[Note: Quesnellus has “so that it might then remain in those who were no longer sinners.” We follow the printed reading, supported by our manuscripts, in which only “from” appears corruptly in place of “but.”]

Nor could it lawfully remain, while preserving its own condition, in those upon whom it had not been inflicted.

[Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts, supported by the printed editions, except that they have “was” instead of “might be.” Quesnellus has “it has the right to remain … it does not.”]

CHAPTER V

The Lord said that those who sin against the Holy Spirit would be forgiven neither in this world nor in the world to come. Yet how many do we know who have sinned against the Holy Spirit—various heretics, such as Arians, Eunomians, and Macedonians—who returned to the Catholic faith, received forgiveness here for their blasphemy, and afterward gained hope of obtaining mercy in the world to come?

Nor is the Lord’s judgment thereby untrue, nor should it be thought to have been dissolved in any way. For with respect to those who remain what they are, it continues wholly unsolvable forever, while it is not inflicted upon those who have become not such.

[Note: Quesnellus has “not to be inflicted”; the printed edition of the councils has “not inflicted.” We have refused to abandon the readings of the Veronensis and Vindobonensis.]

The same conclusion follows from this statement of blessed John the Apostle: “There is sin unto death; I do not say that one should pray for it; and there is sin not unto death; I do say that one should pray for it” (1 John 5:16).

There is sin unto death for those who remain in the same sin; there is sin not unto death for those who withdraw from that sin. For there is no sin for which the Church either does not pray in order to grant forgiveness, or which, by the divine power granted to her, she cannot absolve when people desist from it, or release when they repent. It is said to her: “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven” (Matthew 16:18). In “whatever,” everything is included, however great and of whatever kind it may be.

Nevertheless, the truth of the sentence remains: what is declared never to be dissolved continues in the same condition, without departing from that same condition.
