[Note: Quesnellus has “because.” Our two manuscripts have “by which.” We have preferred “which” with the printed editions. Shortly afterward the printed edition, together with the Vindobonensis, reads “consisting in their condition.”]

This must also reasonably be considered in the sentence concerning Acacius. Even if it was said to him, “You shall never be released,” it was not added: “even if you repent, even if you depart from this error, even if you cease to be a transgressor.”

[Note: Quesnellus alone has “you are never to be released.”]

Therefore it is evident that “never to be released” was said of one who remains such as he is while bound. But when he has become no longer such, just as he ought not to have been bound, so he is shown to be able to be absolved.

[Note: Quesnellus alone reads “alone to be released, such, that is, as he is while bound.” The printed edition of the councils agrees with our manuscripts, with which we have added “to be” shortly afterward.]

Just as he was free from the bond when he was free from the cause of the bond, so he would indeed exist as absolved, insofar as he himself would not appear unable in any way to be released through necessity of the sentence pronounced.

For one who has become different, and is free from the bond, would become absolved; and the sentence prescribed concerning such persons would in no way be made dissoluble.

[Note: Vindobonensis and Veronensis read “how”; the printed editions, “somehow.” Veronensis has “not such”; from the manuscripts and printed editions we have written “prescribed,” whereas Quesnellus reads “fixed.”]

Did he send, seek, request, and get rejected? Therefore he himself made the sentence insoluble for himself, because he chose to remain such as could truly not be absolved; and he did not wish to become such that, while the sentence remained concerning those who were such, the insoluble sentence would not remain concerning one who had become different, since it would have no permission to remain concerning one who had become different.

[Note: The word “such” has fallen out of Quesnellus’s text.]

For this reason, instructed—as has been said—by the example and danger, those who are bound by the same condition ought to hasten not to remain such as have had that sentence, which is not to be dissolved, prescribed against them, but to begin to be such that the sentence prescribed against them as insoluble can be dissoluble.

[Note: Quesnellus has “as a warning.”]

Although, when one has become not such as the person for whom a sentence not to be dissolved was prescribed, the sentence can be dissoluble, nevertheless for Acacius, now unwilling to become not such, just as the sentence remained unresolved against one persisting as such to the end, so for one unwilling to become not such the sentence cannot be dissoluble.

[Note: This is better than Quesnellus’s and our manuscripts’ “not such,” and agrees with the printed edition of the councils. Quesnellus has “in the absolved”; the printed edition has “in the un-absolved.” We have preferred the reading of our manuscripts, “in the unresolved.” Shortly afterward Quesnellus alone has “it can be dissoluble for one unwilling to become different,” and afterward “could have been” instead of “could be.”]

Did Acacius not have so many bishops whose example he could have followed—men who had fallen in the Ephesian brigandage and, in whatever manner, had again fallen into agreement with wickedness?

Yet, even if it was not said explicitly, they could have incurred perpetual condemnation unless they repented and became different from what they had become there; and, while they deserved perpetual condemnation, they merited having the condemnation against them dissolved by withdrawing from the cause of perpetual condemnation. Those who persisted, however, made it insoluble against themselves.

[Note: Quesnellus, together with the Oxford manuscript, reads: “They could have incurred perpetual condemnation unless, by repenting, they became different from what they had become there. Therefore they deserved to be released from perpetual condemnation by withdrawing from the cause of perpetual condemnation, which those who …” We did not wish to alter the reading of our older manuscripts and of the Thuaneus, which agrees with the printed edition of the councils, although it is less clear. The printed edition alone has “would have deserved” instead of “deserved.”]

Therefore it makes no difference whether one says “never to be released” or does not say it, because an ecclesiastical sentence binds the guilty and the transgressors. For just as it cannot help him that it was not said that he would never be released—since, if he remains in error, he persists in every way as one who cannot be released, and can be absolved only after becoming different—so it cannot prejudice anyone else, even though it was said that he would never be released.

For reason plainly shows that he is never to be released at all if he persists in being such as he is while bound, or if he remains such as one bound is—one who is never to be released.

[Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts, including the Thuaneus, and of the printed editions. Quesnellus has “it cannot prejudice someone.”]

Since it was not added, “even if he repents and corrects himself,” it is entirely clear and beyond doubt that, once he has become different from the one of whom it was never said that he would be released, but has become such as was not said never to be released—that is, corrected and amended—he can consequently be corrected and released.

[Note: We have added the conjunction “and” from the manuscripts and the printed edition of the councils. Shortly afterward, “it should be noted that” has been deleted in the printed edition of the councils and in the Veronensis manuscript.]

## Chapter VI

It must also be noted that those who blaspheme against the Holy Spirit in any manner, if they repent and amend their ways, are forgiven both in this age and in the age to come; nor can the Lord’s sentence [Note: Thus the Veronese manuscript, together with the Vulgate Councils. The Vindobonensis also agrees, but incorrectly has *nutari* (“to be shaken”). Quesnellus reads *mutari* (“to be changed”).] thereby be shaken, since it was declared concerning those who persist as such, not concerning those who have ceased to be such. As long as they remain in this condition, they are such persons for whom it was decreed that there should be no forgiveness; but when they have departed from it, they become no longer such persons as those of whom it had been declared that forgiveness was not to be granted. Therefore, once they have become unlike those persons, forgiveness can now be granted both in this age and in the age to come [Note: Quesnellus omitted *jam* (“now”) after *saeculo*. The Vulgate Councils less correctly read *saeculo non* (“not in the age”). We follow our manuscripts. Then, with the Vulgate and the Veronese manuscript, we have restored *videretur* (“might seem”) in place of *videatur* (“may seem”), which Quesnellus had adopted.] Accordingly, it would otherwise seem—God forbid—that the Church received such persons into reconciliation in vain [Note: Quesnellus inserts *homines* (“persons”) after *hujusmodi*; the Vulgate Councils and our manuscripts omit it. Shortly afterward, the Oxford manuscript has *frustra* (“in vain”) in place of *frustrari* (“to be frustrated”); the Vindobonensis has *frustrare*. Then the Vulgate Councils omit *non* (“not”) from *omnino non posse* (“cannot altogether not”).]. But since it cannot be frustrated, it must be proclaimed, so far as concerns us, in every way and without qualification, with this understanding and without compromising the Lord’s sentence, that it cannot be frustrated.

Acacius, therefore, was declared to be such a person as he was when bound: one who would never be released. He remained such to the end; he did not cease to be such. [Note: Quesnellus alone reads *itaque talis* (“therefore such a person”), and afterward *sed non talis* (“but not such a person”).] Thus he is today what he is and what he was declared to be; he can no longer be other than such. Therefore, by continuing to be such, he is one who cannot be released. If he were to cease to be such, and did not remain one who was not such, he would never be one who could not be released; because, being no longer such as the person declared never to be releasable, he could be absolved, and, departing as one who was not such, he would never be released, and therefore would approach in order to be released. [Note: This sentence seems to have been inserted improperly at this point; it would fit better if attached to Chapter II after the words “to refute the things that harm.” We have written *et sola rescindit* (“and it alone rescinds”) on the basis of our manuscripts and also of the Thuanus manuscript, with the Vulgate Councils supporting this reading. Quesnellus, however, reads *solum ergo rescindit* (“therefore it alone rescinds”).]

The apostolic see did not consent to this, nor did the emperor impose it, nor did Anatolius arrogate it to himself. Everything, as has been said, lay within the power of the apostolic see. Thus, what the apostolic see confirmed in the synod acquired authority; what it rejected could possess no validity. It alone rescinded what the synodal assembly had presumed to usurp contrary to due order—not as the promulgator of a repeated sentence, but as the executor, together with the apostolic see, of the earlier one.

## Chapter VII

This, however, which was said concerning one and the same man—whether he persists as the sort of person who properly received the sentence, or has become unlike such a person [Note: The Vulgate Councils alone read *et illa* (“and that one”). The same editions have *similiter esse praefixum* (“to have been similarly decreed”), and *populo ac gente simul depromptum potius, quae in toto orbe portio est* (“rather drawn forth from the people and nation together, which is a portion throughout the whole world”). Quesnellus says that these words scarcely make sense: “The reading of our manuscripts is preferable, except that the Veronese, for *disseminata* (“spread abroad”), has *portione* (“portion”), while the Vindobonensis has *portionem* (“a portion”). The Oxford manuscript, as Quesnellus notes, has *portionem adepta* (“having obtained a portion”). He appears to have taken *disseminata* from the Thuanus manuscript, in which he indicated no variant; for that reason we have not removed it.”] and has been absolved from that sentence which was not pronounced against one who was not such—a sentence that is likewise read as having been decreed in every city and drawn forth at the same time from the people and nation, and rather spread throughout the whole world.

For the world is the same world that was declared destined to perish, and the word of God cannot fail; yet the word is nevertheless not uttered in that same world when it withdraws from perverse intentions. Thus Tyre and Berytus, Gaza and Egypt were pronounced destined to perish (Jer. XLVII, 4; XLIV, 12), although afterward we know them to have been saved through the Gospel.

They therefore perished in two ways: either by remaining in the condition in which they had received such a sentence, or by departing from the condition in which they had been such persons and beginning to become what they had not been—persons to whom that sentence applied—so that consequently that sentence would not apply to those who were not such, although it had not been prescribed for persons who were not such.

So also concerning the Jewish nation, God declared through the prophet Isaiah in a peremptory pronouncement, as it were:

> “Close their eyes and harden their ears, so that, seeing, they may not see, and hearing, they may not hear, lest at any time they understand. And harden the heart of this people, lest they ever turn and I heal them” (Isa. VI, 10).

[Note: We have added *a Deo etiam* (“also by God”) from the Vulgate and our manuscripts. Then, in place of *obdura* (“harden”), the Thuanus manuscript, together with the Vulgate Councils, has *obtura* (“close up”).]

Here correction and amendment are likewise shown to have been forbidden, and even the hope of repentance is entirely cut off. Yet from this very people we know that the apostles and the primitive Church arose, and that many thousands of people were saved by baptism on a single day.

Behold: in those who persisted, the sentence that had been pronounced remained in force; they were not admitted at all to come to healing, but were condemned to perish in their wickedness. Yet while the divine sentence remained, they were not converted to be healed by their own amendment, understanding, movement, strength, or ability [Note: Quesnellus inserts *alii* (“others”); our manuscripts and the Vulgate omit it.], but were healed by God’s grace so that they might be converted.

“Lest they turn,” he says, “and I heal them”: lest they turn by their own inclination or by their own works, in which they certainly trusted; lest, pursuing their own righteousness, they should fail to submit to the righteousness of God [Note: Quesnellus alone reads *non essent subjecti* (“they should not be subject”), while others have “trusting in their own powers.”], trusting in their own strength and not submitting themselves to divine mercy and illumination.

Therefore the effect of their proud presumption is restrained: they are prevented from turning by their own intentions and efforts, as they had supposed; and from being healed, lest saving grace should be given to them as though it came through merits arising from their own capacity. In that case grace would no longer be grace, if it were not given freely to the undeserving, but were restored as a reward to those who had earned it.

Thus it is not that they themselves turn and that I heal them; rather, having been healed by grace, they recognize how they are to be converted to the humility of Christ.

So, in both groups—that is, in those who remain in the condition in which they received such a sentence, and in those who are afterward saved—the Lord’s sentence remained fixed. Yet while that sentence remained, healing was introduced into them in a wondrous manner, so that the sentence did not appear to have been changed; rather, while the same sentence endured, their healing came not from their own confidence but from a divine gift.

## Chapter VIII

But if they fear to attempt these things [Note: Quesnellus inserts the word *imperatores* (“emperors”); our manuscripts and the Thuanus manuscript, together with the Vulgate Councils, do not contain it. Something similar is indeed understood, as the following words show; but nothing should be added beyond the evidence of the manuscripts. The connection with what precedes can be explained if one understands it in this way: rulers neither attempt these things of which he spoke earlier—namely, healing human souls, which comes from a divine gift—nor refer them to their own authority, etc. We believe that something is missing here, by which the objection raised by the rulers, to which Gelasius is responding, was introduced and this chapter more suitably connected with the preceding one.] and recognize that they do not belong within the scope of their authority, since they have been permitted to judge only human affairs and not to rule over divine matters, how do they presume to judge those through whom divine things are administered?

Let these things have existed before Christ’s coming, when certain persons, though still engaged in carnal actions, were symbolically both kings and priests at the same time, as sacred history reveals Melchizedek to have been. The devil imitated this among his own followers—as one who has always tried to claim for himself, in a tyrannical spirit, whatever is fitting for divine worship—so that pagan emperors were called both emperors and high priests.

But when the true King and High Priest came, no longer did the emperor assume for himself the name of priest, nor did the priest claim royal eminence, although the members of that true King and Priest are said, according to their participation in his exalted nature, to have taken upon themselves both offices within their sacred nobility, so that a royal and priestly race might subsist together (I Pet. II, 9).

[Note: The word *enim* (“for”) had been omitted by Quesnellus; we have restored it with the printed editions of the Councils and our manuscripts. Shortly afterward, those editions read *magnifice utrumque* (“both magnificently”), less correctly; and then, in place of *subiisse* (“to have taken upon themselves”), they have *sumpsisse* (“to have assumed”). The Veronese has *submisse* (“humbly”).]

For Christ, mindful of human weakness, arranged with magnificent dispensation what was suited to the salvation of his own. Thus, distinguishing their proper actions and dignities, he separated the functions of the two powers, wishing his own to be saved by medicinal humility and not once again destroyed by human pride. Accordingly, Christian emperors would need priests for eternal life, and priests would rely upon imperial arrangements for the course of temporal affairs, so that spiritual action might remain distant from carnal intrusions [Note: Quesnellus reads *et Deo militans minime* (“and serving God not at all”), which is contrary to the sense.], and therefore the one serving God would not entangle himself in worldly business (II Tim. II, 4), while, conversely, the person engaged in worldly business would not appear to preside over divine matters.

Thus the modesty of both orders would be preserved, so that no one supported by both might become arrogant, and a profession appropriate to the qualities of their actions might be assigned specifically to each.

## Chapter IX

When all these points have been properly gathered, it is demonstrated clearly enough that a priest cannot be bound or released at all by secular power. This makes it still clearer that Peter of Alexandria could in no way have been completely absolved by an imperial sentence alone.

If the assent of the priests was also associated with it [Note: Quesnellus adds *sibi* (“for itself”).], we ask whether it came before or afterward. If it followed the imperial sentence [Note: The Vulgate omits *imperialem sententiam* (“the imperial sentence”). The Vindobonensis has “and by the imperial sentence, nevertheless”; the Veronese has “and by an equitable imperial sentence, nevertheless.”], the matter nevertheless returns to this: an absolution ordered and principally initiated by secular power could not be valid, and the assent of the priests that followed it would have been flattery rather than a legitimate decree.

If it preceded, let it be shown by whom and where it was carried out: whether it was celebrated according to the rule of the Church, whether it proceeded from the tradition of the fathers, whether it was approved according to the custom of the ancestors, and whether it was produced by a competent examination. It must unquestionably also be asked whether it was celebrated by a synodal assembly, since, because a condemned person was being received and a Catholic was being expelled, the matter was entirely new and certainly ought to have been handled in this way [Note: Quesnellus reads *noviter erat causa* (“the matter was newly established”). The Vulgate Councils have *nova est causa* (“the matter is new”). We have followed the three manuscripts—the Vindobonensis, Thuanus, and Veronese.] [Note: The column reference continues at Col. 0627B.]

If the matter was referred according to the rules of the Church to the first see, which had jurisdiction over the sentence by which Peter was held bound, and if the same see that had bound him also released him—what if he could have been released by the one that had not bound him, indeed even without its knowledge? [Note: Quesnellus reads *si ea, quae* (“if that which”). The Vulgate Councils have *si illa quae ligaverat non resolvente* (“if the one that had bound him did not release him”). We followed the Veronese and Vindobonensis manuscripts, the only ones available for comparison; in them, *quod si forte* (“but if perhaps”) should probably be read *quasi* (“as though”).]

If these things were not done, by what custom or rite is Peter of Alexandria claimed to have been absolved, since he was neither legitimately released by the priests according to ecclesiastical laws nor could he have been completely absolved by secular power contrary to the Church’s established course?

## Chapter X

But perhaps it will be said: “It was not the emperor who absolved him; rather, he asked the priests to absolve him.”

All the more, then, ought the priests to have advised the emperor when he requested it that, if he wished him to be legitimately absolved, a legitimate absolution in accordance with ecclesiastical procedure should take place, and that all the matters stated above should be observed according to the Church’s established course—especially since the case concerned the bishop of a second see, who could lawfully be absolved not by any inferior see, but by the first see.

An inferior cannot absolve a superior; therefore only the superior can properly absolve the inferior. Accordingly, the priests of the inferior see, who knew perfectly well that they could not release the superior without the apostolic see, and especially one whom they knew to be bound by its sentence, did not completely free him by their transgressive absolution; rather, they bound themselves still more by their transgression.

Thus Peter’s absolution is valid in neither respect: they could not, by a transgressive absolution, absolve one who was guilty; and since Catholic priests had been expelled everywhere and heretics installed in their place, or persons contaminated by communion with heretics and even by insincerity in sacred religion, they could no more absolve their associate than they themselves had been absolved. Consequently, they were transgressors of ecclesiastical discipline and, by their association with the faithless, defilers of the integrity of the holy communion. What judgment, then, could they have passed on one equally guilty? [Note: Quesnellus reads *quod rei simili modo potuerunt* (“which they could similarly have done to the guilty”). The Oxford manuscript has *quod rei simillimo potuerunt feriri judicio* (“which could have been struck by a very similar judgment”). We preferred the reading of the Vulgate Councils, supported by our Vindobonensis and Veronese manuscripts, in which *dirui* (“destroyed”) is corruptly found in place of *de reo* (“concerning the guilty person”).]

As for the Catholic priests throughout the entire East, either whoever persisted was expelled, or the one who remained was he who consented to error and did not withdraw from contact with those in error.

What judgment, then, could their decision concerning anyone’s error have been, when they are shown to have been nowhere free from error, and when, with the confessions of heretics and Catholics mixed together, they are shown to have confused all true and sincere religion and to have corrupted Catholic and apostolic purity? [Note: Thus the Veronese, Vindobonensis, and Thuanus manuscripts. Quesnellus reads “to have disrupted all the judgments of true and sincere religion, and the Catholic [faith].” The Vulgate Councils have “to have disrupted all the sees.”]

Behold those who could absolve the guilty—those who were shown to have become guilty on behalf of all. Behold the men with whom a synod was to be convened concerning the absolution of the guilty.

If the Catholic faith and communion were being maintained, why were Catholic bishops expelled? If Catholic bishops were being expelled, how were the heretics not merely preserved? [Note: Quesnellus deletes *non* (“not”), which our manuscripts, together with the Vulgate Councils, contain. The end of the work is missing.]

## Chapter XLVIII

[Note: This work exists in this collection in the Veronese manuscripts 46 and in Isidore. We have reproduced the title from the manuscripts and the printed editions of the Councils. Nicholas I, Letter 1, toward the middle, likewise calls it a *Commonitorium* (“memorandum”). In Quesnellus it reads: “Letter of Pope Gelasius to Faustus the master against Acacius”; and afterward, in the form of a letter: “Gelasius to Faustus, master of the soldiers serving as envoy at Constantinople.”]

**The Memorandum of Saint Gelasius to Faustus, the Master, serving as envoy at Constantinople**

### Chapter I

I too have understood inwardly that the Greeks will remain in their obstinacy [Note: Quesnellus reads *nec cuiquam* (“nor to anyone”). We have followed the Vindobonensis, Veronese, and Vatican Isidore manuscript 630, together with the Vulgate Councils. Shortly afterward, the Veronese and Vatican manuscripts have *inspiratum* (“inspired”). Then we wrote *in ante* (“beforehand”) on the authority of the Vindobonensis, the Veronese, and the Labbean manuscript cited in the margin. Another reading has *ante* (“before”).], and no one can regard as unexpected what was foreknown from the beginning.

Therefore, they are no longer striving for religious reasons to oppose public arrangements; rather, under cover of the imperial embassy, they are attempting to overthrow the Catholic faith and are endeavoring by such an exchange to accomplish what they hope for [Note: The Veronese, Vindobonensis, and Vulgate Councils read this way. Quesnellus has *dixit* (“said”). Then, in place of *exeruit*, the Thuanus and Vatican Isidore manuscripts and the Vulgate have *exercuit* (“exercised”).].

What does it mean that the emperor said that he had been condemned by us in matters of religion, when in this matter my predecessor not only did not mention his name at all, but, moreover, when he first exercised the authority of imperial power, wrote that he rejoiced in his accession to the empire [Note: Quesnellus deleted *imperii* (“of the empire”); we have restored it from the Vindobonensis, Thuanus, and Veronese manuscripts and the Vulgate.]? And since I have never received any written communication from him, why have I nevertheless taken care, as you know, to greet him with letters of honor?

My predecessors removed from apostolic communion priests who openly confessed that they had entered into communion with transgressors. [Note: In the margin Quesnellus gives another reading: *si ita* (“if so”).] If this man chooses to associate with the condemned, that cannot be imputed to us. If he wishes to withdraw from them, he cannot all the more be condemned by us; rather, he will be admitted to the favor of sincere communion.

It belongs to the Roman senate, mindful of the faith which it remembers having received from its ancestors, to avoid the contagion of external communion, lest—God forbid—it be made foreign to communion with the apostolic see.

They propose that pardon ought to be granted them. Let it be read, from the time when the Christian religion began—or, at any rate, let an example be produced in the Church of God from any priests, from the apostles themselves, or finally from the Savior himself—that pardon was ever granted except to those who corrected themselves. [Note: Thus our manuscripts and the Vulgate Councils. Quesnellus has *vel potius* (“or rather”).]

But no one reads or hears that, under this heaven, what they proclaim with their own voice has ever occurred: “Give us pardon, while we nevertheless remain in error.” [Note: The Vulgate Councils have *id quoque pariter* (“that also likewise”); in the margin they have *par est* (“it is fitting”).]

That is not enough. Let those who strive to set the canons against us show which canons, which rules, by what reading or what precedent—whether from our ancestors, from the apostles themselves, whom there is no doubt to have been superior in authority, or from the Lord himself, the Savior, who is believed to judge the living and the dead—ever establish that this was done or command that it should be done.

We read that Christ raised the dead; we do not read that he absolved the dead who remained in error. And he alone certainly possessed the power to do this, yet he gave the following command principally to the blessed apostle Peter:

> “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. XVI, 19).

“On earth,” he says; for in this binding he nowhere said that a dead person was to be absolved.

Therefore, what has never been done we fear even to conceive in our minds, knowing that it cannot in any way be excused in the divine judgment.

But if they now claim that they will separate themselves from the Roman Church, they are shown to have done this long ago. [Note: Thus the more authoritative manuscripts, the Vindobonensis, Thuanus, and Veronese. The Vatican Isidore manuscript and the Vulgate of Merlin are similar, except that they have *divisuros sunt* (“they are going to divide”). The Vulgate Councils have *se sunt divisuri* (“they have separated themselves”), followed by *id jam dudum* (“and that long ago”). Quesnellus reads: “But if they claim that they will cut themselves off from the Roman Church—something they are shown to have done long ago.”]

### Chapter II

As for Euphemius, I am astonished if he himself does not perceive his ignorance when he says that Acacius could not have been condemned by one man. Does he not perceive that, according to the form of the Council of Chalcedon, Acacius was condemned? Or does he not know it—or pretend not to know it?

In that council, it is plainly established that the authors of this error were condemned by the numerous sentence of the priests, just as it is shown by the manifest course of events that this has both been done and is being done in every heresy from the beginning of the Christian religion. My predecessor was the executor of an earlier decree, not the author of a new constitution [Note: The Oxford manuscript has *instituti* (“of the established practice”).].

This is permitted not only to an apostolic bishop but to any bishop: according to the rule, they may separate anyone, in any place, from Catholic communion because of the heresy itself, which had already been condemned [Note: The Veronese manuscript 46 omits *ut* (“so that”) and immediately continues with the Vindobonensis: “whom it is permitted for anyone to [remove from] any place according to the rule.” We have adopted the reading of the Vulgate Councils as the better one. Quesnellus deletes *et quemlibet locum* (“and any place”). Shortly afterward we have written *damnatae* (“condemned”) with the Vindobonensis, Thuanus, and Vulgate; the Veronese is defective, reading only *damna*. Quesnellus has *damnatos* (“the condemned”).].

Acacius, however, was not the inventor of a new or private error, so that new decrees should be directed against him [Note: The Vulgate has *prodirent* (“should proceed”). The Veronese manuscript has *praecederent* (“should precede”).]; rather, he joined himself by his communion to another’s crime. Therefore, it was necessary that he fall under the just sentence which the author of the error, together with his successors, had received through the appropriate synodal decision.

### Chapter III

They set the canons against us, though they do not know what they are saying. Against the canons they themselves reveal that they are acting by refusing to obey the first see, which advises what is sound and right.

The canons themselves are the ones that required the appeals of the whole Church to be brought before the judgment of this see; but they expressly decreed that no appeal should ever be made from it. Accordingly, they decreed that this see should judge the whole Church, that it should itself be subject to no one’s judgment, and that its judgment should never be judged. They established that its sentence ought not to be annulled, since they rather commanded that its decrees be followed.

In this very case, Timothy of Alexandria, Peter of Antioch, Peter, Paul, John, and the others—not merely one, but several who bore the name of priest—were expelled solely by the authority of the apostolic see. [Note: Quesnellus deleted *Petrus* (“Peter”) and *Paulus* (“Paul”), although he admits that they are read in the Vulgate and Thuanus. They are also found in all our manuscripts of the three different collections: the Vindobonensis, Veronese, and Vatican Isidore. This second Peter is Peter Mongus, likewise of Alexandria; Paul and John were Paul of Ephesus and John of Apamea.] Acacius himself is also taught to be a witness to this, since he was the executor of that command.

Just as it is clear that the apostolic see acted according to the synodal form, so it is certain that no one could resist it. Acacius therefore, falling back into association with the condemned, was condemned—he who had carried out their condemnation before he became a transgressor.

They have dared to mention the canons to us, against which they are shown always to have striven through unlawful ambitions [Note: The Vulgate has *fecisse* (“to have done”). The Veronese has *tenendi esse*, corruptly, instead of *tetendisse* (“to have striven”).].

By what synod, or according to the form of what synod, did they expel John of Alexandria from the Church for which he had been ordained? With no evident charges, he could neither be convicted beforehand nor, even after appealing, be accused before a competent tribunal [Note: The Vatican Isidore manuscript 630, together with Merlin, reads “neither summoned beforehand nor subsequently challenged.”].

But if they say, “The emperor did this,” by which canons and rules was this very act commanded? Why did Acacius consent to so wicked a deed, when divine authority says: “Not only those who do wicked things are guilty, but also those who consent to those who do them” (Rom. I, 32)?

By what canons and rules was Calendion excluded, or the first Catholic priests of the various cities? By what tradition of the ancestors do they summon the apostolic see to judgment?

Or ought the bishops of the second see, the third, and the others—priests conscious of their own integrity—to be expelled, while the man who proved himself an enemy of religion ought not to be expelled? Let them see, then, whether they have other canons by which to carry out their absurdities.

### Chapter IV

Moreover, these men, who are proclaimed sacred, ecclesiastical, and legitimate [Note: The edition of the Councils deletes *non solum* (“not only”), but our manuscripts and Quesnellus do not.], cannot summon the apostolic see to judgment. Yet should not the bishop of the city of Constantinople—which, according to the canons, received no rank among the sees—be removed when he fell back into communion with the faithless?

Should those who are said to have lied to a human emperor and are alleged to have injured the emperor be expelled, while Acacius, who offended against God, the supreme and true Emperor, and strove to mix the sincere communion of the divine sacrament with the faithless, ought not to be excluded according to the synod in which this faithlessness was condemned?

Whether they wish it or not, the ancient canonical decrees are confirmed by his judgments. [Note: The Thuanus manuscript has: “By his judgment the ancient canonical decrees are confirmed.” The Vulgate Councils have: “By his judgment the ancient constitutions of the canons will be confirmed.” Quesnellus adds in the margin that the reading of the Oxford manuscript is confirmed by a similar marginal note in the Labbean edition of the Councils, copied from a manuscript, and by the whole course of the pope’s argument. Our manuscripts agree with this as well. Only the Veronese has *firmentur* (“may be confirmed”), and the Vatican Isidore manuscript, together with Merlin, has *firmabuntur* (“will be confirmed”).]

Yet religious and perfect men are striving, according to the canons, to seize the authority granted to the apostolic see and to usurp it for themselves contrary to the canons. O teachers and guardians of the canons!

We are not permitted to enter into any dispute with persons of another communion, since divine Scripture proclaims: “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second correction, knowing that such a person is perverse, condemned by his own judgment” (Tit. III, 10). [Note: The Vulgate Councils, together with the Veronese and Vatican Isidore manuscripts, read: “knowing that such a person is delinquent by his own [judgment].” Quesnellus reads *en recognoscant* (“let them recognize”).]

Behold, let them recognize that a heretic is condemned not only by another but also by himself.

But it is exceedingly shameless that they pretend Acacius asked for pardon and that we proved difficult. Your brother, my son, the illustrious Andromachus, is a witness: he was abundantly instructed by us to urge Acacius, after laying aside his obstinacy, to repent and return to the communion of the apostolic see. He testifies that he himself, under oath [Note: The Vindobonensis and Veronese have *magis* (“more greatly”).], made great efforts with him, but that he could not be turned toward what is right, as the outcome of events demonstrates.

Let evidence be produced: when did he send a request, when did he ask for pardon, and when did he promise to present his correction to us?

Unless, perhaps, he possessed the disposition which we see in his successors: that, even if he were to ask for pardon, he would wish it to be granted in such a way that he would nevertheless persist in error [Note: Quesnellus reads *tametsi veniam sibi postularet* (“although he should ask pardon for himself”). The Vindobonensis has *tamen eo si* (“yet if thereby”); we corrected this to *tamen etsi* (“yet even if”), a reading that differs only slightly from the Vulgate Councils, which have *tamen si veniam postularet* (“yet if he should ask pardon”). The Veronese also agrees.]. In that case, he would seem not so much to be received by us as to be leading us over into his own wickedness.

What guilt do they say they will confess before the dispute? If it is guilt, it must certainly be corrected. If they do not think it should be corrected, they falsely claim to profess guilt—unless, more unhappily, they both confess guilt and do not consider it necessary to correct it. [Note: Quesnellus inserts *non* (“not”), less correctly. The following words—“if it should be necessary,” and so forth—are understood not of Acacius, as no one has believed, but of Euphemius, to whom Gelasius is replying in this letter.]

I was also amused by what he says: “If it should be necessary to ask for pardon,” clearly supposing that he would then necessarily ask pardon for his sin if we granted him permission not to cease from sinning—or rather, God forbid, if we agreed with him and sinned along with him.

I do not know among what marvels of the world such a statement could be admitted. A past fault can be forgiven, with correction unquestionably following. For if perversity is allowed to remain afterward, it is not the kindness of the person who forgives but the assent of the person who consents [Note: The Vulgate Councils have *assensio* (“assent”). The Vindobonensis and Veronese have *annuntiatio* (“announcement”).].

It is no wonder that these men presume to blaspheme the see of the blessed apostle Peter, since they carry such monstrosities in their hearts or pour them forth from their mouths, and even declare us proud, while they trust that the first see, although it never ceases to offer them every form of kindness, can be subjected by them even through that very spirit of insolence [Note: Thus with the Vindobonensis manuscript. The Veronese is similar, reading *illi etiam protervo* (“even to that insolent one”). The Vulgate Councils have *illi eam ipso protervo* (“that he might subject it through that very insolent one”). Quesnellus has *illi eam protervo* (“that he might subject it to the insolent one”).].

But it is no wonder that those whose minds are captive do such things. In this way, the insane are accustomed to regard all who treat them as either enemies or objects of assault. [Note: Quesnellus adds *quique* (“and who”), contrary to the other Vulgate manuscripts and our better manuscripts.]

Yet I ask them where the judgment they invoke could be conducted. Among themselves, perhaps, so that the same persons might be enemies, witnesses, and judges? But human affairs ought not to be entrusted to such a judgment, much less the integrity of divine law.

If the whole burden of judgment in matters of religion belongs, according to the canons, exclusively to the apostolic see, then, as far as secular authority is concerned, that authority ought to learn from the priests, and especially from the vicar of blessed Peter, what things are divine; it ought not itself to judge those same matters. [Note: The Veronese has *ille* (“that one”), and afterward *non ipse* (“not itself”).]

Nor does any very powerful person of this world, though he may nevertheless be a Christian, presume to claim this for himself—unless perhaps he is persecuting religion [Note: Quesnellus reads *si hoc* (“if this”), and afterward *persequatur* (“should persecute”). We preferred the Vulgate Councils, supported by the Veronese and Vatican manuscripts, in which the Vindobonensis likewise corruptly reads *persequentes* (“persecuting”). Then, in place of *servent* (“let them preserve”), Quesnellus has *reservent* (“let them reserve”), and in place of *nisi resipiscant* (“unless they repent”), *nisi resipiscunt* (“unless they repent,” indicative).].

What, then, would they say if they were not defeated in every respect by their own writings?

Let them therefore keep their absurdities to themselves, unless they repent, remembering instead that Christ’s word is not empty: he declared that the gates of hell would never prevail against the confession of the blessed apostle Peter.

Therefore, we do not fear that the apostolic sentence will be annulled, since it is supported by the voice of Christ, the tradition of the ancestors, and the authority of the canons, so that it may rather always judge the whole Church [Note: Quesnellus has *quoniam et vox* (“since both the voice”) and afterward *fulsit* (“shone”) in place of *fulcit* (“supports”); later he deletes *semper* (“always”) from *Ecclesiam ipsa* (“itself the Church”). We have restored the reading of the Vulgate, supported by our best manuscripts.].

Let them think more carefully—if they possess any religious sense—lest, by refusing in any way to lay aside their wickedness, they be condemned before God and men by the perpetual constitution of the apostolic see.

It is said, however, that it was determined that nothing further should be said about the matter, as though even now—as you know—I had undertaken to address them specifically in my own name. Nor should a contest be entered into with these men who do not correct themselves, just as one must refuse combat with the followers of other heresies.

But for you, we continually beseech the Divinity with prayers that you may return here as soon as possible, safe and sound.

## Chapter XLIX

[Note: This is found in the same manuscripts as the preceding *Commonitorium*.]

**Letter of Saint Gelasius, Bishop, to the Emperor Anastasius**
## Chapter I

When the servants of Your Piety—my sons Faustus, the master, and Irenaeus, illustrious men, together with their companions, who had returned to Rome while serving as envoys on public business—said that Your Clemency had asked why I had not sent a written greeting to you, I confess that I had not done so according to my usual practice. But when they spread throughout the city that, although they had formerly been sent from the East, permission to see me had been denied them by your instructions, I thought it best to refrain from writing, lest I prove burdensome rather than dutiful. You see, therefore, that this did not arise from any dissimulation on my part, but from the caution appropriate to the situation, lest I impose annoyance upon minds that were rejecting it.

But when I learned of Your Serenity’s goodwill, and when those men reported that you had graciously sought a conversation with my humility, I truly realized that I would rightly be held accountable if I remained silent.

[Note on Col. 0633D: The Vulgate Council edition reads *imputandum*, “to be imputed,” instead of *reputandum*, “to be reckoned.”] For, glorious son, as one born a Roman, I love, esteem, and honor a Roman prince; and as a Christian, I desire that he who possesses zeal for God may possess it according to knowledge of the truth; and as a deputy, however unworthy, of the apostolic see, wherever I discover that something is lacking in the fullness of Catholic faith, I strive, according to my limited ability, to supply it by timely admonitions.

[Note on Col. 0633D: The Vulgate, with the Thuanus and Vatican Isidorian manuscripts, reads *suscipio*, “I receive.” We have preferred *suspicio* on the authority of the superior Vindobona and Verona manuscripts. The printed editions have *cum eo*; after adopting that reading, Hardouin observed that perhaps *pacem habere*, “to have peace,” should subsequently be read.]

For the administration of the divine word has been entrusted to me, and it is written: “Woe to me if I do not evangelize” (1 Cor. 9:16). If blessed Paul, the Vessel of Election, feared and proclaimed this, I, so insignificant, must fear it all the more if, after a charge divinely inspired and transmitted with filial devotion, I were to withdraw the ministry of preaching.

[Note on Col. 0633D–0634D: The Vulgate Council edition, with the Vatican Isidorian manuscript and Merlin’s codex, reads *inspiratum*, “inspired,” and subsequently *transmissum*, “transmitted.”]

[Note on Col. 0633D: Merlin, together with the Vatican Isidorian manuscript 630, is said to read *quaesisse*, “to have asked.”]

## Chapter II

I therefore beg Your Piety not to judge the service of divine reason as arrogance. Far be it, I ask, from a Roman prince to regard the truth communicated to his understanding as an insult.

[Note on Col. 0634D: Quesnell inserts *ergo*, “therefore”; our manuscripts and the Vulgate omit it.]

For there are two powers, O august emperor, by which this world is principally governed: the sacred authority of bishops and royal power. The burden of priests is so much heavier in these matters because they will render an account before the divine judgment even for the kings themselves.

You know, most merciful son, that although by your dignity you preside over the human race, nevertheless you devoutly bow your neck to those who preside over divine affairs, and seek from them the causes of your salvation. In receiving the heavenly sacraments and arranging them, as is proper, you recognize that, in accordance with the order of religion, you ought to be subject to them rather than preside over them; and thus, amid these matters, you depend upon their judgment, rather than wishing them to be reduced to your will.

[Note on Col. 0634D: The Vulgate has *pro hominum*, “on behalf of men,” instead of *pro ipsis regibus*, “even for the kings themselves.”]

[Note on Col. 0634D: Merlin, together with the Oxford manuscript, reads *exspectas*, “you await.” The Vatican Isidorian manuscript and the second hand of the Verona manuscript read *exspectes*; the first hand has *exspectis*, incorrectly, instead of *expetis*, “you seek.”]

[Note on Col. 0634D: The manuscripts of Vindobona and Verona read *itaque inter haec illorum*. The Vulgate Council edition, in order to draw out the sense, repeats the verb *nosti* after placing a full stop, and reads: “You know, therefore, that amid these matters you depend upon them.” We have altered the punctuation and retained the preposition *ex*, expressing a sufficiently reasonable sense in agreement with the praised superior manuscripts. Quesnell reads: “Therefore it is your concern to depend upon their judgment.”]

For if, insofar as concerns the order of public discipline, the ministers of religion themselves obey your laws, recognizing that authority has been bestowed upon you by heavenly disposition—so that they may not appear, even in worldly matters, to oppose the established order— with what disposition, I ask you, is it fitting that you obey those who have been appointed to dispense the venerable mysteries?

[Note on Col. 0634D: Quesnell reads *pro erogandis*, “for dispensing”; the reading of the Verona, Vatican Isidorian, and Merlin manuscripts seemed better.]

Accordingly, just as a serious danger rests upon bishops if they remain silent about what is fitting for the worship of God, so—God forbid—a considerable danger rests upon those who, although they ought to obey, despise it. And if the hearts of the faithful ought rightly to submit to all priests who handle divine matters correctly, how much more must agreement be given to the bishop of that see whom the supreme Divinity wished to have precedence over all priests, and whom the continuing devotion of the universal Church has continually celebrated and devoutly acknowledges as primate?

Here Your Piety clearly perceives that no one can ever raise himself by any merely human counsel above the privilege or confession of him whom the voice of Christ placed before all, whom the venerable Church has always confessed and devoutly holds as primate.

[Note on Col. 0635C: The Vindobona and Verona manuscripts read *non possunt*, “cannot be attacked,” incorrectly, as the context makes clear.]

Things established by divine judgment can be assailed by human presumption, but they cannot be conquered by any power whatsoever. And would that the audacity of those who struggle against them were not harmful, just as what was established by the very Author of sacred religion cannot be shaken by any force:

“For the foundation of God stands” (2 Tim. 2:19).

[Note on Col. 0635C–D: This reading is found with Merlin and the Vulgate Council edition, as well as in all our manuscripts and the Thuanus manuscript. Quesnell, together with the Oxford manuscript, adopted *fundamentum*, “foundation.” Shortly afterward the Verona manuscript reads: “Surely religion has been hostile to some people, and, insofar as it could, has been overcome less correctly.” The Vindobona manuscript reads: “Surely religion has been hostile to some … insofar as it could …” Quesnell’s reading is confirmed by the Vulgate Council edition together with the Vatican Isidorian manuscript; from these we have adopted *quantacunque*, “however great,” where Quesnell wrote *quacunque*, “whatever.”]

When religion was attacked by some people, was it ever overcome by whatever novelty they could devise? Or did it not rather remain unconquered precisely because it was thought capable of succumbing?

## Chapter III

Let certain people, therefore, I ask you, cease during your reign, under the pretext of ecclesiastical disturbance, rashly to pursue what is not permitted, lest they both fail altogether to obtain what they wrongly desire and fail to maintain their proper standing before God and human beings.

Therefore, before the sight of God, with pure and sincere feeling, I beg, beseech, and exhort Your Piety not to receive my petition with indignation.

[Note on Col. 0635D: Quesnell omits *exhortor*, “I exhort.”] I ask you, I say, to hear me in this life as I make my plea, rather than—God forbid—to find me accusing you in the divine judgment.

Nor is it unknown to me, O august emperor, what your zeal for piety was in private life. You always desired to become a participant in the eternal promise. Therefore, I beg you, do not be angry with me if I love you so greatly that I wish you to possess forever the kingdom which you have obtained for a time, and that you who rule the world may be able to reign with Christ.

Certainly, by your laws, emperor, you allow nothing to perish for the Roman name, and you permit no damage to be inflicted upon it.

[Note on Col. 0635D: The Vulgate Council edition reads, “no loss at all.” The Vatican Isidorian manuscript, together with Merlin, reads, “you permit no damage to be inflicted upon anyone.”]

Is it really true, excellent prince, that you—who desire not only Christ’s present benefits but also those to come—would allow, during your reign, anyone to inflict damage upon religion, truth, and the sincerity of Catholic communion and faith?

[Note on Col. 0635D: The Vulgate Council edition, agreeing with the Vindobona and Verona manuscripts except that they insert *non* before *patiaris*, reads *quidquam inferri dispendii*, “any harm to be inflicted.” The inserted *non* conflicts with the context.] With what confidence, I ask you, will you seek there the rewards of one whose losses you do not prevent here?

Let what is said for the eternity of your salvation not be burdensome, I ask you. You have read what is written: “The wounds of a friend are better than the kisses of an enemy” (Prov. XXVI, 6).

I ask Your Piety that what is said by me may enter your understanding with the affection with which it is said. Let no one deceive Your Piety.

It is true what Scripture figuratively testifies through the prophet: “My dove, my perfect one, is one” (Song 6:8).

[Note on Col. 0635D: The Verona manuscript, together with the Vulgate Council edition, repeats *una est*, “is one.”]

There is one Christian faith, and it is Catholic. That faith is truly Catholic which is separated, in sincere, pure, and undefiled communion, from all the faithless and from their successor-associates.

[Note on Col. 0635D–0636C: Quesnell reads: “from the sincere communion of their successors,” omitting *ab eorum*. The Vatican Isidorian manuscript reads: “separated from the communion of their successors,” with the intervening words omitted. We have followed the reading of the older manuscripts, Vindobona and Verona, with which the Vulgate Council edition agrees; Merlin and that edition merely add *atque*, “and,” before *consortibus*, “associates.” We would have preferred to read *ab omnibus iniquis*, “from all the wicked,” but no manuscripts support it.]

Otherwise there will be not a divinely commanded distinction, but a lamentable confusion.

[Note on Col. 0636C: The Verona manuscript, together with the Council edition, reads *miseranda*, “lamentable.”]

No reason remains if we are willing to admit this in any contagion: that we should not open an entrance and doorway to all heresies. “Whoever offends in one matter is guilty of all” (Jas. 2:10); and “whoever despises what is least falls little by little” (Eccl. 10:1).

[Note on Col. 0636C: This reading is found in the Vulgate Council edition and the Vatican Isidorian manuscript. The other manuscripts, Verona and Vindobona, agree except that they mistakenly read *nec* rather than *ne*, “lest.” Quesnell reads *ut cunctis*, “so that to all.” Shortly afterward Verona and the Vatican read *decidet*, “falls.”]

## Chapter IV

This is what the apostolic see takes the greatest care to guard: since the glorious confession of the Apostle is a root that is pure, it must not be stained by any fissure of depravity or by any contagion at all.

[Note on Col. 0636B–D: Merlin, together with the Vatican Isidorian manuscript, reads *praetaxavit*, “has prescribed beforehand.” Quesnell shortly afterward reads *quia munda radix est*, “because it is a pure root.” “The glorious confession of the Apostle—nothing …” We have followed our manuscripts, Verona and the Vatican, and the Vulgate Council edition. The Oxford manuscript deletes *nulla rima pravitatis*, “no fissure of depravity,” and shortly afterward reads *fieri posse non credimus*, “we do not believe it can happen.”]

For if—God forbid, and something we are confident cannot happen—such a thing were to occur, what error would we dare resist, or from where would we seek correction for those who had gone astray?

[Note on Col. 0636D: Merlin reads *vel unicuique*, “or for each person.” The Vatican Isidorian manuscript reads *vel cuiquam resistere*, “or resist anyone.” The Vulgate Council edition reads *unde cuiquam resistere*, “from where resist anyone.”]

Therefore Your Piety denies that the people of one city can be brought into order. What are we to do with the entire world, if—God forbid—it has been deceived by our transgression?

[Note on Col. 0636D: The Vulgate Council edition, with the Vatican Isidorian manuscript and Merlin, inserts *si*; Quesnell reads *cur*. The Vindobona, Thuanus, and Verona manuscripts omit both. The printed editions subsequently read *negat pace posse*, “denies that [they] can be reconciled by peace.”]

If the whole world was corrected after rejecting and despising the profane tradition of its ancestors, how should the people of one city not be corrected if faithful preaching follows?

[Note on Col. 0636D: Quesnell reads *contempta*, “after despising.” Shortly afterward Merlin, together with the Vatican Isidorian manuscript, has *fidei*, “of faith,” instead of *fida*, “faithful.”]

Therefore, glorious emperor, I do not reject the peace of the churches. Even if it could come about at the cost of my blood, I would embrace it. But I ask you to consider carefully what that peace itself ought to be—not peace of any kind, but truly Christian peace.

For how can there be true peace if undefiled charity is absent? And the Apostle plainly teaches us what charity ought to be when he says: “And charity from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 1:5).

How, I ask you, can it be from a pure heart if it is infected by external contagion? How can it be from a good conscience if it has been mixed with the perverse and wicked? How can it be from unfeigned faith if it remains associated with the faithless?

[Note on Col. 0636D: The stronger manuscripts and the Vulgate Council edition read this way. Quesnell, together with the Vatican Isidorian manuscript, reads: “How?”]

Although we have often already said these things, it is nevertheless necessary to repeat them without ceasing, and not to keep silent so long as the name of peace is put forward. Thus it must not be our task—as is maliciously proclaimed—to make peace, but to teach that we desire such a peace as alone can be peace, and apart from which no peace can be shown to exist.

[Note on Col. 0637C: All the manuscripts and printed editions have this reading. Quesnell reads *velle pacem*, “to wish peace,” and shortly afterward *propter quam nulla*, “because of which there is none.” The Vulgate Council edition has *monstratur*, “is shown,” instead of *monstretur*, “may be shown.”]

Certainly, if it is believed that the Eutychian doctrine—which the vigilant caution of the apostolic see guards against—can stand without compromising the truth of Catholic faith, let it be brought forward, asserted, and defended with whatever strength is possible. Then it will be possible to show not only how hostile it is in itself to the Christian faith, but also how many and how deadly heresies it contains in its own pollution.

[Note on Col. 0637C: Quesnell reads *monstretur*, “may be shown”; shortly afterward, *ut magis credimus*, “as we rather believe.” We have preferred the readings of the superior manuscripts, Vindobona and Verona, together with the other printed editions.]

But if, as we more confidently believe, it must be excluded by Catholic minds that have judged rightly, I ask you: why do you not likewise decree that the contagions of those who are proved to have been polluted by it must be rejected? For the Apostle says that not only those who do what ought not to be done are regarded as guilty, but also those who consent to those who do such things (Rom. 1:32).

Accordingly, just as perversity cannot fail to be approved when one who communicates in perversity has been admitted, so perversity cannot be rejected when its accomplice and adherent is admitted.

## Chapter V

Certainly, under your laws, those who are aware of crimes and those who receive robbers are bound by the same judicial penalty. Nor is someone considered free of crime who, although he did not commit the act himself, nevertheless entered into an alliance and familiarity with those who committed it.

[Note on Col. 0637C: The Vulgate Council edition, together with the Vatican Isidorian manuscript, reads: “yet has accepted the familiarity and alliance of the one who committed it.” The Verona and Vindobona manuscripts prefer the reading of the text, deleting the preposition *in*. Because of this omission, other manuscripts corrected *facientes* to *facientis*.]

Accordingly, when the Council of Chalcedon, convened for the truth and communion of the Catholic and apostolic faith, condemned Eutyches, the author of detestable madness, it did not consider this sufficient unless it also struck down his associate Dioscorus and the others as well.

[Note on Col. 0637C: Quesnell alone reads *damnati furoris*, “of condemned madness.”]

In this way, therefore—as has always happened, or at least is certainly understood to happen, in every heresy—their successors, Timothy, Peter, and the other Peter of Antioch, were not condemned individually, by name, each separately, through another council convened again for each one; rather, they were struck down in accordance with the rule of the council once held.

[Note on Col. 0637D–0638C: Quesnell reads *non viritim*, “not individually,” and *singulariter*, “separately.” The Vulgate Council edition, together with the Vatican Isidorian manuscript, reads *non vititim propter singulos*, “not individually on account of each person,” deleting the intervening words *singulariter, nominatim, unusquisque pro parte sua*, “separately, by name, each one for his own part.” The Verona manuscript does not have these words; Vindobona includes them. On the authority of these excellent manuscripts, we have moved the adverb *viritim*, “individually,” to its proper place. With them we would also have deleted the negative particle, and with Verona we would shortly have written *sed et*, “but also.” Yet in the following letter, chapter 2, Gelasius is wholly concerned to prove that it was not necessary to convene councils individually; and in chapter 3 he states that Timothy and Peter were condemned not by a council convened again, but solely by the authority of the apostolic see. Therefore, together with the other manuscripts and the Vulgate edition, we have retained the particle *non*. If it should be deleted, this passage would have to be understood of Roman councils, which, according to custom, were convened in more serious cases, and in which there is no doubt that they were condemned. Since the acts of these councils were attributed to the authority of the apostolic see, they could be said to have been condemned solely by its authority, without another council being convened—namely, without a general council or another special council, whose absence from their case the followers of Acacius were alleging. See chapter 1 of the following letter.]

How, then, is it not clearly evident that all who became their communicants and accomplices are likewise bound by the same principle, and that all of them are rightly separated from Catholic and apostolic communion?

[Note on Col. 0638C: Quesnell deletes *merito*, “rightly.”]

For this reason we rightly declare that Acacius too must be removed from our fellowship. He preferred to pass into the lot of faithlessness rather than remain in the sincerity of Catholic and apostolic communion, although for nearly three years he had been adequately instructed by letters from the apostolic see so that he might not come to this point.

[Note on Col. 0638C: Quesnell, together with only the Oxford manuscript, reads *sinceritatis communione*, “in the communion of sincerity.” Shortly afterward the Vulgate Council edition reads *per triennium*, “for a period of three years.”]

But once he had become alien to communion, he could not fail to be immediately cut off from Catholic and apostolic fellowship, lest, if we delayed even slightly on his account, we too should appear to have undergone the contagions of the faithless.

[Note on Col. 0638C: Quesnell alone inserts *sedis*, “of the see”; our manuscripts and also the Thuanus manuscript omit it.]

But did he truly recover, struck by such a punishment? Did he promise correction and amend his error? Or had he wished to be restrained by a milder treatment, since he did not even feel the harsh blows?

[Note on Col. 0638C–D: The Vindobona and Verona manuscripts, together with the Vulgate Council edition, have this reading. Quesnell reads: “Or did he wish to be restrained by a gentler treatment?” The Vatican Isidorian manuscript has *valuerat*, “had been effective”; Merlin has *valeat*, “may be effective”; and both shortly afterward retain *manente*, “remaining,” instead of *moriente*, “dying.”]

Since he died in his faithlessness and condemnation, his name cannot be entered in ecclesiastical recitation any more than the contagion of external communion ought to be admitted.

[Note on Col. 0638D: The superior manuscripts, including the Thuanus manuscript, agree with the Vulgate Council edition in reading: “Either let him be shown to be sincere and unable to be rejected from the participation of heretics with whom he mixed himself.” Shortly afterward the Vulgate, together with Thuanus and the Vatican Isidorian manuscript, reads *si autem*, “but if.”]

Therefore either let him be shown to be sincere and free from the participation of the heretics with whose communion he mixed himself, or else he cannot fail to be rejected together with them.

## Chapter VI

Thus the bishops of the East murmur: as though the apostolic see had not written this to them, as though they themselves had either informed the apostolic see by their letters that Peter had been legitimately received, or had not already likewise become accomplices in this disordered reception.

[Note on Col. 0638D: Quesnell alone reads *non scripserit*, “had not written.”]

They cannot show that he was cleansed of heretical depravity; therefore they will likewise be unable to excuse themselves from being companions of the heretics.

[Note on Col. 0638D–0639C: Quesnell reads: “since they cannot say that he was cleansed of heretical depravity.” The Vindobona and Verona manuscripts read: “if they can truly show … that he was cleansed.” The Thuanus manuscript agrees, except that it has *si vere*, “if truly,” instead of *si verum*, “if it is true”; both are corrupt readings in place of *sicut non*, “just as they cannot.” The Vatican Isidorian manuscript and Merlin support this correction, which is required by the context. The Vulgate Council edition agrees, adding *vere*, “truly.”]

If they should perhaps assert that all of them, with one accord, referred to the apostolic see through Acacius concerning Peter’s reception, let them all acknowledge that through that same man a reply was given to them with one and the same voice.

The authority of the apostolic see, that it has been placed before the universal Church throughout all Christian ages, is confirmed both by the succession of the paternal canons and by manifold tradition.

But whether anyone can claim anything against the decrees of the Council of Nicaea may be demonstrated from the fellowship of a single communion; it cannot be opened up to the minds of an external association.

[Note on Col. 0639C: Quesnell reads *vel huic*, “or against this.” Shortly afterward the Oxford manuscript has *unius communione*, “by the communion of one.”]

If anyone among them has confidence, let him come forward and refute and instruct the apostolic see concerning both sides of the matter.

Let the name be removed from the midst—the name which operates far from Catholic communion to destroy the distinction of the churches—so that sincere peace and the unity of faith and communion may be restored.

[Note on Col. 0639C–D: Quesnell reads: “the name which tramples upon the distinction of the churches and of Catholic communion, so that the sincere peace of communion and the unity of faith may be restored.” We have preferred the reading of the Vulgate, with which the Vindobona, Verona, Vatican Isidorian, and Thuanus manuscripts largely agree. Only the Vatican, Vindobona, and Verona manuscripts have *a catholicae communionis*, “from Catholic communion,” where something such as *compage*, “structure,” seems to be understood.]

Then let it be properly and legitimately investigated who among us has either risen up or is striving to rise up against venerable antiquity. There it will become clear who, with a modest purpose, preserves the form and tradition of the ancestors, and who, irreverently springing beyond these things, thinks that plunder can be carried out.

[Note on Col. 0639C–D: Quesnell reads *insiliat*, “springs upon,” but no manuscript or the Vulgate supports this. He also reads: “who thinks that plunder of ecclesiastical possessions can be carried out.” Although we believe the reading of the manuscripts to be corrupt, we have not altered it arbitrarily. The same reading appears in Merlin and in the Council edition, which merely deletes the second *quis* before *rapina*.]

## Chapter VII

But if the person of the people of Constantinople is brought forward, and it is said that the name of the scandal—that is, Acacius—cannot be removed, I say nothing of the fact that, after the heretic Macedonius had once been expelled and Nestorius recently ejected, the people of Constantinople chose to remain Catholic rather than be held back by the defection of their condemned bishops.

[Note on Col. 0639D: Quesnell reads: “through love of the condemned bishops and defection.” All our manuscripts and the Vulgate delete *amore*, “through love,” and instead have *majorum*, “of the ancestors.” With the Verona manuscript we have preferred *a defectione*, “by defection,” whereas the Vulgate, together with the Vatican Isidorian manuscript, has *affectione*, “by attachment.” Shortly afterward, with our manuscripts, we have added *ipsis*, “the very.” The Vulgate Council edition deletes *a quibus*, “from whom,” and reads *quod qui ab eisdem*, “because those who from the same.”]

I say nothing of the fact that, while remaining in the Catholic faith, they were not disturbed by any agitation by those very condemned bishops by whom they had been baptized.

I say nothing of the fact that even now Your Piety’s authority has restrained popular disturbances over trivial matters, and that for this reason the multitude of the city of Constantinople much more necessarily obeys you concerning the salvation of their souls, if you, as princes, restore it to apostolic and Catholic communion.

For, O august emperor, if anyone should perhaps attempt something contrary to the public laws—God forbid—you could not tolerate it by any means. Do you not think it relevant to your conscience that the people subject to you be brought back to pure and sincere devotion to the Divinity?

Finally, if it is thought that the mind of the people of a single city ought not to be offended lest divine matters be corrected as the situation requires, how much more must we neither dare nor be able to injure the devout faith of the whole Catholic name, lest divine things be offended?

[Note on Col. 0639D–0640C: Quesnell, together with the Oxford manuscript, reads: “If one person among the people … is not thought to ought to be offended, lest divine authorities be corrected as the matter requires,” and notes in the margin that perhaps *collidantur*, “be brought into conflict,” should be read. On the authority of the manuscripts, we have restored the reading of the earlier editions.]

And yet these same people ask to be healed by our will. Let them therefore allow themselves to be treated by appropriate remedies. Otherwise—God forbid—we may perish with them by passing into their destruction, while we cannot save them.

Here I leave it to your consciences, under divine judgment, to decide what ought rather to be followed: whether, as we desire, we should all return together to certain life, or, as they ask, proceed toward manifest death.

But even now they persist in calling the apostolic see, which offers them medicinal remedies, proud and arrogant.

It is often characteristic of the sick to accuse physicians who bring them back to health by suitable regimens, rather than to consent to abandon or reject their own harmful appetites.

[Note on Col. 0640C: The Verona manuscript, together with the Vulgate Council edition, deletes *eos*, “them,” and shortly afterward, with Vindobona, deletes *magis*, “rather.”]

If we are proud because we provide appropriate remedies for souls, what should those who resist be called? If we are proud because we say that the paternal decrees must be obeyed, by what name should those who oppose them be called? If we are haughty because we desire divine worship to be preserved in a pure and undefiled form, let those who think even against the Divinity say what they should be called.

Thus the others who remain in error also judge us, because we do not consent to their madness. Yet truth itself judges where the spirit of pride truly fights and stands firm.

[Note on Col. 0640C: The best Verona manuscript reads this way, more correctly than Quesnell and the other manuscripts, which have: “Thus they and the others.”]

Here ends Pope Gelasius’s letter to the emperor Anastasius.

## Chapter L

[Note on Col. 0640C: This letter exists in two forms, one shorter and one longer.]

The Letter of Pope Gelasius to the Bishops of Dardania.

[Note on Col. 0640C–D: Quesnell notes in the margin: “That intermediate title belongs solely to the Thuanus manuscript, in which both the earlier and the later heading are absent, so that it indicates neither from whom nor to whom this writing was sent. For this reason it is understood why Hincmar of Laon, volume II, page 373, cites certain testimonies from this letter under the title: ‘From the letter of Gelasius to the emperor Anastasius.’ He evidently used some manuscript of this collection in which, as in Thuanus, the inscription of this letter is absent; he therefore thought it had been sent to the same emperor Anastasius to whom the preceding letter was sent.

“In both our manuscripts, Vindobona and Verona, the first heading, ‘The letter of Gelasius,’ and so forth, is absent. The second heading, beginning ‘An account to be rendered’ and ending ‘condemned,’ is prefixed as follows: ‘Here begins the account to be rendered.’ The same heading is appended in full at the end of the letter: ‘Here ends the account to be rendered,’ and so forth, where *exemplar*, ‘copy,’ is understood. The longer form is the other one.

“The shorter form is contained not only in the manuscripts of this collection but also in Verona 46 and in the Isidorian manuscripts, into which it was transferred from our collection by Pseudo-Isidore. A fragment of it, beginning with chapter four, ‘Nor do we altogether keep silent,’ was inserted in the manuscripts of the additions of Dionysius.

“The longer form is found in the manuscripts of the most distinguished collection which we have called the Avellana. On its authority we showed in the preceding treatise, part III, chapter 11, section 4, that the additions should be attributed to Gelasius’s second revision; and there, on the occasion of these additions, in which Gelasius understood *nos* as referring to the apostolic see, we discussed the matter more fully than in the notes that we had accepted for establishing this chapter, volume I, page 587.

“Merlin presented the shorter form from the Isidorian manuscript before Quesnell. The editions of the Councils, however, after the Roman edition, represent the longer form of the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs. The variants noted in the margin of Labbe’s Councils from the Justellus manuscript, agreeing with the Vatican Isidorian exemplar, show that it too was an Isidorian manuscript.”]

An account to be rendered: Acacius was rightly condemned by the apostolic see, and no one can become a participant in his communion without danger to his soul.

To all the most beloved brothers, the bishops established throughout Dardania, Gelasius.

## Chapter I

We were greatly astonished that Your Love desires to know, as though it were a new and difficult question, and as though it were still something unheard of, that the communicants of the Eutychian pestilence, having nothing to say in reply for their obstinacy in perdition, now convicted on frequent grounds, mutter in mere argument—not because what they babble has any importance, nor because they have discovered anything at all to say.

[Note on Col. 0641D: Three of our manuscripts—the Vindobona, Verona, and Vatican 630—read *desiderans*, “desiring”; Merlin has *desideratis*, “you desire.”]

We are more astonished that those who have been instructed in Catholic understanding still hesitate than that those who have fallen away from the truth and deviated from the ancient tradition of the Church put forward profane novelties of language and the absurdities of fleeting perversity.

[Note on Col. 0642C: The Vulgate Council edition reads *profanasque … obtendunt*, “and put forward profane …”]

Your Love reported that they boast that Acacius should not be thought to have been rightly condemned because he apparently was not deposed by a special council, and, adding childishly to the madness of their folly, they say in particular: “Especially since he was bishop of the royal city.”

[Note on Col. 0642C: The Verona and Vatican Isidorian manuscripts, together with the Vulgate, read *accumulant*, “they heap up.”]

Therefore, rejecting the stupidity of empty complaints, you ought to proceed from the blessed apostles themselves and prudently consider that our fathers—namely, Catholic and learned bishops—whenever any heresy arose, decreed once, after assembling according to the course of the Scriptures and the preaching of the ancestors, whatever they had established for the faith, for truth, and for Catholic and apostolic communion. Thereafter they wished it to remain unshaken and firm, and they did not permit what had been prescribed in the same matter to be reconsidered under any recent presumption.

[Note on Col. 0642C: Quesnell reads *resuscitata*, “revived.” Shortly afterward the Vulgate Council edition deletes *pro fide*, “for the faith.”]

They wisely took precautions, recognizing that if anyone were permitted to repeat decrees salutarily established, no ecclesiastical ordinance would remain stable against each individual error, and every complete definition would continually be disturbed by the recurrence of the same frenzies.

[Note on Col. 0642C–D: The Verona and Vatican Isidorian manuscripts read *in hac eadem causa*, “in this same matter.” Shortly afterward Verona has *sapientissime pervidentes*, “recognizing most wisely”; the Vulgate Council edition reads *praevidentes*, “foreseeing.”]

For if, even after boundaries have been set for synodal rules established once for all, the defeated plagues do not cease, but, struggles being resumed, raise themselves against the foundation of truth and strike simple hearts, what would happen if it were continually lawful for the faithless to convene a council? For however clear that truth may be, falsehood will never lack something destructive to bring forth; and although deficient in reason or authority, it nevertheless does not yield in intention.
