[Note on Col. 0642D: The Vatican Isidorian manuscript and another manuscript in the margin of Labbe’s Council edition read *furoris residui omnis*, “of all remaining fury,” incorrectly. We have written *limitibus etiam praefixis*, “even after boundaries have been set,” together with our manuscripts and the Vulgate. Quesnell omits *etiam*, “also.”]

Our ancestors, seeing this by divine inspiration, took necessary precautions: whatever a council convened against any heresy had promulgated for the Catholic and apostolic faith, communion, and truth, they did not allow thereafter to be mutilated by new reconsiderations, lest an opportunity be given to the wicked to overthrow what had been established as a remedy.

[Note on Col. 0642D: The Vindobona and Verona manuscripts read *ut contra … quod acta synodus*, “so that what the council had done against …” The Vulgate Council edition reads *ut quae contra*, “so that what … against.” The Isidorian manuscript, together with Merlin, reads *coacta semel synodus*, “a council once convened.”]

Instead, once the author of any madness and the error itself had likewise been condemned, they judged it sufficient that whoever at any time became a participant in that error should be bound by the principal sentence of its condemnation, since anyone could plainly be recognized either by his profession or by his communion.

[Note on Col. 0642D: The Vindobona manuscript reads *communicatione*, “by communion.”]

## Chapter II

And, to pass over the earlier matters for the sake of brevity—matters which an attentive investigator can readily examine—the synod condemned Sabellius. It was not necessary afterward to condemn his followers by holding separate synods for each individual case; rather, in accordance with the force of the ancient constitution, the universal Church judged that all who had participated either in that depravity or in communion with it were to be rejected.

> [Note: For the sake of brevity, the words deleted in the fuller edition of the Vulgate Councils are omitted, since they would not at all fit after the lengthy addition.]

Thus, on account of Arius’s blasphemies, after the form of the Catholic faith and communion had been promulgated at the Nicene assembly, it condemned all Arians—or anyone who had fallen into this plague, whether by conviction or by communion—without reconsideration.

> [Note: The Vulgate Councils has “whether by consent”; it then reads “and concluded.”]

Similarly, when a synod once held had condemned Eunomius, Macedonius, and Nestorius, it did not permit them to come thereafter to new councils; rather, the Church rejected all who in any manner fell back into these blasphemies, according to the synodal boundary entrusted to it. It is clear that the Church never rightly yielded, whatever necessity compelled it, by rashly violating anew what had been salutarily established.

> [Note: The same Vulgate Councils and Merlin have “with new acts of daring”; the Isidorian Vatican manuscript has only “with acts of daring.”]

Nor are we unaware that, during the storm of the Arian persecution, many bishops, returning from exile and recovering their breath once peace had been restored, assembled with the brethren in particular provinces and restored the Churches that had been thrown into disorder. Yet they did not do this in order to alter anything that the Council of Nicaea had defined concerning the Catholic faith and communion, nor to strike down with a new condemnation anyone who had fallen away; rather, according to the force of that decree, they judged him condemned unless he had repented, and it necessarily followed that, unless he corrected himself, he would unquestionably remain subject to condemnation.

> [Note: Thus the Vienna and Verona manuscripts, and one of Quesnellus’s manuscripts, which omitted “unless he had repented.” The Vulgate Councils reads: “but according to the force of that decree, they judged them condemned unless they repented.” The same reading occurs in the Vatican Isidorian manuscript and in Merlin, except that they have “judged” for “deemed.”]

Accordingly, as has been said, when these matters have been weighed according to the paternal tradition, we are confident that no one who is now truly a Christian is ignorant that, of the constitutions of each synod approved by the assent of the universal Church, none ought to be more diligently carried out than that of the first See. It both confirms every synod by its authority and safeguards it through continuous moderation—namely, by virtue of that primacy which blessed Peter the Apostle received from the Lord’s own voice and which, with the Church following after, he both always held and still holds.

> [Note: The Vulgate Councils reads “not one in particular.”]

## Chapter III

When the Apostolic See had learned through reliable evidence that Acacius had deviated from the truth, it did not believe the matter for a long time, since it knew that he had often served as the executor of its necessary dispositions against heretics. Nevertheless, for nearly three years it did not cease warning him by letters, as the letters sent to him in various ways and written in a familiar tone testify.

> [Note: The Vulgate Councils has “frequently.” Immediately afterward the Vatican Isidorian manuscript reads “to which, when he first proposed …”; Merlin has the same, except that it reads “due” for “devoted.” The Vulgate Councils reads: “to which, with due silence, he proposed for a long time not to reply.” It then adds much material from the fuller form of this letter. Quesnellus noted: “Nearly two entire pages have been inserted here in other editions; they are absent both from the Oxford and Thuane manuscripts and from the Justellian manuscript cited in Labbe’s edition of the Councils, apart from a few exceptions. These passages have either been transferred here from elsewhere—for they interrupt the thread and meaning of the discourse—or perhaps are entirely fabricated. I leave the matter to others to examine more thoroughly, since I am hastening onward.” He wrote this because he had no knowledge of the celebrated Avellana Collection, from which it is clear that Gelasius, in a second recension, not so much revised this letter as enlarged it. See note 1 on this chapter and the treatise on ancient collections, part II, chapter 11, section 4.]

At first, proposing to give no answer, as though maintaining a deliberate silence, Acacius eventually sent a letter declaring that he had entered into communion with Peter of Alexandria without the knowledge of the Apostolic See—Peter whom he himself, as executor of the authority sought from the Apostolic See, had also condemned.

But the See of blessed Peter, which knew that it had condemned Peter of Alexandria only and had not released him, did not receive Peter. Therefore, lest Acacius should bring it also into association with Peter, the See likewise removed Acacius from its communion and in many ways made him alien from its fellowship as a transgressor.

If an examination is sought, no judgment was now necessary, since he himself had confessed the matter in his letters.

> [Note: The Vulgate Councils, from the fuller form, adds: “and, when summoned to a lawful judgment, he was afraid to appear.”]

If the weight of authority is in question, the execution of the definition of the Council of Chalcedon is found to have proceeded according to that definition: having become a participant in the error condemned there, Acacius nevertheless became a participant in the condemnation pronounced there, because the very error that was once condemned together with its author carries, in anyone who becomes a participant through wicked communion, both the curse due to it and its penalty.

> [Note: Our manuscripts, together with Merlin, have this wording. Quesnellus reads: “the execution of that definition is contained in accordance with which, when he was condemned there … he appears … and his execration.” The fuller form in the Vulgate Councils gives the passage differently: “The tenor, agreeing with the Apostolic See, and the execution of that definition are found in the fact that he became a participant in the error condemned there and nevertheless appeared as a participant in the condemnation pronounced there, since …”]

By this same principle, Timothy and Peter of Alexandria—both of whom appeared certainly to have held the second See—are shown to have been condemned, not by a renewed synod, but solely by the authority of the Apostolic See, at Acacius’s own request or through his own execution of the sentence.

> [Note: The Vienna and Verona manuscripts, together with the Vulgate Councils, read “is shown to have been condemned.” Immediately afterward these same copies of the Vulgate Councils omit “if a response has been given to these matters” and continue: “Now let them themselves show …”]

If someone should perhaps say that it ought to have been established whether Acacius had participated in error or treachery, we offer a brief answer. Let them either show that Peter had been truly and lawfully purged and properly separated from every contagion of the heretics when Acacius entered into communion with him, if they think that Acacius, as Peter’s participant, can in any way be excused; or, if—as is more truthful—they cannot prove that Peter had been duly cleansed, it remains that the one who entered into communion with him was infected by his uncleanness.

> [Note: Quesnellus reads *impiatione* (“defilement”); Vienna has *expiatione* (“purification”). We have corrected the text in accordance with Verona, the Vatican Isidorian manuscript, and Merlin. The Vulgate Councils, in its fuller form, reads: “They could not prove Peter purified; for this reason Acacius did not dare either to come or to send a representative to the judgment of the Apostolic See. It remains that whoever entered into communion with him was infected through that communion.” It then continues: “We do not suppress the fact that all things …”]

## Chapter IV

Nor do we at all keep silent about what the whole Church throughout the world knows: that the See of blessed Peter the Apostle has the right to release those bound by the sentences of any bishops, since it is permitted to judge concerning the whole Church, while no one is permitted to judge its judgment. Indeed, if the canons have wished appeals to be made to it from any part of the world, no one is permitted to appeal from it.

Therefore it is sufficiently clear that Acacius had no pontifical authority to release himself from the sentence of the Apostolic See without its knowledge. By what synod, then, did he presume to do this—something which he would not even have had the right to accomplish without the Apostolic See? Whose bishop was he? The bishop of which metropolitan city? Was he not the bishop of the parish of the Church of Heraclea?

If he was certainly permitted to break the sentence of the Apostolic See without a synod and without seeking any consultation with it, was it truly not permitted to the First See, in carrying out the constitution of the Council of Chalcedon as was proper, to remove such a transgressor by its own authority?

Nor do we pass over the fact that the Apostolic See has often, as has been said, according to the custom of our forefathers, had the power, even without any preceding synod, both to release those whom an unjust synod had condemned and to condemn, in the absence of any synod, those whom it was proper to condemn.

> [Note: Quesnellus reads “had the right to release.” We have preferred the reading of the Vienna and Verona manuscripts, supported by the Vulgate Councils, which have “and to absolve.”]

A synod of the East had condemned Athanasius, of holy memory; nevertheless, the Apostolic See, which had not consented to the condemnation of the Greeks, received him and absolved him. Likewise, a synod had condemned John of Constantinople, also of holy memory, and certainly a synod of Catholic bishops; in the same manner, the Apostolic See alone absolved him, because it had not consented.

Likewise, it absolved the holy bishop Flavian, condemned by an assembly of the Greeks, on the same principle, because the Apostolic See alone had not consented. Rather, by its authority it condemned Dioscorus, the bishop of the Second See, who had been received there; by refusing its consent, it alone removed the impious synod; and, for the sake of truth, it alone decreed that the Council of Chalcedon should be held.

> [Note: Quesnellus deletes “in which”; we have restored it with all our manuscripts and Merlin. He writes in the margin: “The three lines that follow, up to ‘But if anyone should object to these matters,’ are absent from the printed editions; in their place nearly two pages occur, which are lacking in both of our manuscript copies. The following passages also vary. This variation was necessary because of the inserted addition. The continuation is therefore as follows: ‘Therefore,’ he says, ‘if anyone still criticizes these actions of the Apostolic See according to the Council of Chalcedon, he will admit all the more that Acacius was not permitted to attempt them, both on account of this and because he can be convicted in many ways. Let him say, then, by what synod John, the bishop of the Second See, …’”]

Thus, just as in that case it alone had the right to absolve those whom synodal decrees had struck down, so also it is known to have condemned, even without a synod, many metropolitans in this same matter.

## Chapter V

But if anyone criticizes these actions of the Apostolic See, or those carried out according to a synod, he will be refuted by the ancient evidence of events and will meanwhile admit all the more that Acacius was not permitted to do so.

> [Note: The Vatican Isidorian manuscript, together with the Justellian manuscript, reads “or according to a second synod”; Merlin has “or according to a holy synod,” both incorrectly—for in this place *etiam* (“even”) is intended. Quesnellus reads “approval”; our Vienna and Verona manuscripts read “proof.”]

Let him say, then, by what synod he excluded any bishop of the Second See—certainly a Catholic bishop ordained by Catholics, and in no way accused concerning the Catholic faith and communion—while permitting Peter, an open heretic who had also been condemned by his own execution of the sentence, to be installed in his place.

> [Note: The Vatican Isidorian manuscript, Merlin, and the Vulgate Councils read “to be appointed in his place.” The fuller form adds five lines explaining the appointment of a Catholic bishop; this made it necessary to continue as follows: “By what synod did Acacius likewise cause Calendion, bishop of the Third See, to be expelled?” The Verona manuscript also deletes “holy” before “Calendion.”]

By what synod did he cause the holy Calendion, bishop of the Third See, to be expelled, while nevertheless allowing Peter, so manifestly a heretic that he himself openly professed that he would not communicate with him, to be substituted by his own arrangement?

> [Note: The Vulgate Councils reads “it was necessary to communicate with him.” This reading may refer to the tract published by Maffei and wrongly attributed to Felix, where the Acacians objected: “But the emperor imposes upon Acacius the necessity of communicating with Peter.” See volume V of the Venetian edition of the Councils, column 192d.]

Finally, by what synod throughout the entire East did he, after expelling orthodox bishops unstained by any crime, install in their places whatever wicked men were entangled in crimes through his own provision? By what synod did that impious plunderer invade so many privileges belonging to others?

But books would not suffice if we attempted to describe one by one the tragedies that he enacted throughout the Churches of the entire East.

Do they think that his own argument should be brought against us—namely, that he appeared to parade his crimes under the imperial person?

> [Note: The Vulgate Councils reads “he attempted to use.”]

Why, then, when he wished, did he resist Basiliscus, certainly a tyrant and a vehemently hostile heretic? Why did he not submit his will to the emperor Zeno himself, because he did not wish to communicate openly with Peter of Antioch?

Behold, he was able to resist others, if he had wished.

> [Note: Verona and Vienna incorrectly read “if he did not wish.” The error was corrected in the Vatican Isidorian manuscript to “but he did not wish.” The more accurate correction is inferred from the Vulgate Councils, which reads “if he wished.” Similarly, chapter 6 reads: “They could not fail to understand, if they wished.” The same Vulgate copies omit the words from “or did not” through “entangled.” Quesnellus, passing over “if he wished,” wrote: “to resist—was he not able? The Apostle says …” The Vulgate Councils then reads “whatever Zeno himself …”]

Does not the Apostle say: “Not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them” (Romans 1:32), are likewise entangled in guilt?

But, to pass over matters that require fuller explanation, what of the fact that the emperor Zeno himself declares in his letters that he had done everything on Acacius’s advice? Acacius himself also testifies in his letters that this did not escape him: he wrote both that Zeno had acted correctly in everything and did not conceal that these same things had been done on his advice.

As though Acacius had become a transgressor only through communion with Peter of Alexandria, and not in all those cases in which, after Catholic bishops had been expelled, he caused heretics to be placed over whatever Churches, like a tyrant; or in which he entered into perverse communion with men so appointed—men who, according to the canons, had thereby been subject to expulsion from ecclesiastical communion, because they allowed themselves to be installed as successors while living priests still held office.

What Christian does not perceive that, once Catholic bishops had been driven from their own sees, none but heretics could have been introduced? Acacius was either the author of the appointment of all these men or joined himself in communion to those already appointed—men who in no way differed from the communion of heretics.

> [Note: We have restored the adverb “indeed” from our manuscripts and the Vulgate Councils.]

Why, then, when he saw these things happening, did he not, as he had already done under Basiliscus, refer the matter to the Apostolic See, so that, if he himself was unable, they might jointly present to the emperor, through counsel and deliberation with that See, whatever was fitting for religion?

> [Note: Vienna and the Vatican read “with all those who were involved with him,” and afterward have “could be alleged” without a verb. To correct this defective reading, others wrote as in the Vatican Isidorian manuscript, “when they joined together and alleged.” Quesnellus has “of all,” followed by “and alleged.” The Vulgate Councils manuscripts provide the true and complete reading required by the context.]

For if Basiliscus, as has been said, a tyrannical heretic, was powerfully shaken by the letters of the Apostolic See and recalled from many excesses, how much more could a legitimate emperor, who wished to appear Catholic, have been softened by the Apostolic See through the moderate remonstrances of all the bishops? This was especially so since he was a particular supporter and admirer of Acacius, and had praised in his letters both Acacius himself and the holy Pope Simplicius in lofty terms—although they had resisted the heretics with the greatest firmness.

> [Note: The Vulgate Councils reads “because he had resisted the heretics with the utmost constancy.” Quesnellus has “for so long” instead of “for such a long time”; we have accepted the correction from the Verona manuscript and the Vulgate Councils. Similarly, chapter 8 reads: “Why, while these things were being done, or while he knew they were to be done, did he not refer them to the Apostolic See …?” The Vatican Isidorian manuscript has “to prevent” instead of “to be prevented.” Later the Vulgate Councils reads “what she desired to be fulfilled” instead of “what it desired to be fulfilled for the heretics.”]

Why did Acacius remain silent for so long amid these events, unless he did not wish in any way to impede what he desired to have accomplished?

## Chapter VI

Let us suppose, nevertheless, that no synod had preceded this one, of which the Apostolic See would rightly have been the executor. With whom, then, was a synod concerning Acacius to be held?

Was it to be held with those who were already held as Acacius’s participants and who, after Catholic priests throughout the East had been violently expelled and sent into various exiles, were plainly partners in an external communion, transferring themselves into this fellowship before consulting the decisions of the Apostolic See?

With whom, then, was the synod to be held? Catholic bishops had already been driven out everywhere; only the associates of the faithless remained, and it was no longer lawful to hold an assembly with them.

The Psalmist says:

> “I have not sat in the council of vanity,  
> and I will not enter in with those who do iniquity” (Psalm 25:4).

Nor is it the custom of the Church to hold council with those who have a polluted communion mixed with the faithless.

Accordingly, the Council of Chalcedon rightly rejected such a transgression, rather than bringing it before a council—a council that was unnecessary after the first synod and could not lawfully be held with such men.

> [Note: Quesnellus inserts “reported” here; all our manuscript and printed copies omit it. From the Vulgate Councils we supplied “was brought forward” shortly afterward, since those words are necessary to complete the sense. The Vulgate Councils reads “if they had wished” instead of “if they wished.”]

For, if they had wished to understand what was being done concerning the Catholic faith, they could not have been ignorant of it: they saw Catholic bishops expelled throughout the entire East without any synodal investigation or council, especially since they realized that new cases were involved. From the character of those men they could also have discerned what the others ought to beware of.

> [Note: The Verona and Vatican Isidorian manuscripts, together with Merlin and the Vulgate Councils, read “learn from the character.” Quesnellus has “of this party.” We have substituted “of that party” in accordance with all our manuscripts and printed copies.]

It therefore remains clear that they belonged to that party to which, after so many experiences, they had surrendered themselves. Consequently, they were no longer to be consulted by the Apostolic See and the other Catholics, but rather to be marked out.

We laughed at the attempt to claim a prerogative for Acacius on the ground that he was bishop of the imperial city. Was an emperor not present for many years at Milan, Ravenna, Sirmium, and Trier? Did the priests of those cities ever usurp for their own dignities anything beyond the measure anciently assigned to them?

Did Acacius, in order to exclude John—a merely ordinary man, certainly a Catholic ordained by Catholics—from Alexandria and to receive Peter, already exposed and condemned as a heretic, undertake this boldly by any synod held there? Or is he shown to have expelled Calendion and again admitted the heretic Peter, whom he himself had condemned, without the knowledge of the Apostolic See, by having done so through some synod?

> [Note: Quesnellus reads “to expel him from the Church,” contrary to all our manuscripts and printed copies.]

If the issue is indeed the dignity of cities, the dignity of the priests of the Second and Third Sees is greater than that of a city which is not only not numbered among the sees but is not even counted among the metropolitan rights.

> [Note: The word “of cities” dropped out of Quesnellus’s text.]

For when you say “imperial city,” one thing is the power of secular rule and another the distribution of ecclesiastical dignities.

> [Note: The Vulgate Councils wrongly deletes “imperial city.”]

Just as, although a city may be small, it does not diminish the prerogative of the present kingdom, so the presence of the emperor does not alter the measure of religious administration. Let that city be illustrious through the power of the present emperor; religion under him remains firm, free, and advanced if, rather, in his presence it maintains its proper measure without any disturbance.

> [Note: The printed editions of the Councils and Merlin, together with the Verona and Vatican Isidorian manuscripts, read “of the empire.”]

> [Note: In the Vulgate Councils, from the fuller form of this letter preserved by the Avellana Collection, nearly half a page is added here. Among other things, it contains two citations found in the two very rare letters of Marcian and Anatolius, letters 110 and 132 to Saint Leo.]

## Chapter VII

But perhaps someone may say that, for certain reasons, the emperor himself rather than Acacius ordered what was done concerning Peter of Alexandria and Peter of Antioch.

> [Note: Quesnellus, with the Oxford manuscript alone, reads “rather than Acacius.” Shortly afterward the Vulgate Councils has “concerning the injury done to him.”]

Yet it was fitting for the priest, especially one who enjoyed the Christian prince’s intimacy and favor, to advise him that vengeance for the injury and insult done to the priest would remain secure, provided that the Christian ruler allowed the rules of the Church to be observed. For a new case had arisen concerning each bishop, and consequently a new investigation was required.

And if, as had always been the established practice, judgments concerning priests proceeded from a priestly council, then bishops of whatever rank would not appear to have been struck down by secular authority, even if human error had intervened, provided that they had in no way transgressed against religion.

> [Note: The same Vulgate Councils has “Was this still just?” Immediately afterward, with the Vienna manuscript and the same Vulgate copies, we have added “imperial.”]

Was this not also something that ought to have been suggested to the emperor for good reason? If he had been exalted by the honor of the imperial city and made more exalted than that imperial city, he ought all the more to have been steadfast in making these recommendations.

But if, in matters that had to be undertaken for religion, he proved contemptible and despised—whether sluggish or lacking the confidence to make the matter known—in what respect was he made greater by the imperial city?

The prophet Nathan openly and publicly, before King David himself, both declared the error that had been committed, did not conceal that David himself had committed it, and afterward absolved him when he had corrected it through confession.

This good man and excellent priest, however, showed that he both could have made the recommendation and chose not to make it; indeed, he revealed that he had supported the action. He allowed the emperor not to conceal that he had done everything on Acacius’s advice, while himself raising the emperor, who had carried out these actions, with great praises and exposing himself as a participant in their execution.

> [Note: In the Vulgate Councils, from the fuller form, two lines are added here; after “absolved,” nearly half a page is also added. Quesnellus considers that addition to have been inserted by someone else. We have described and refuted his observation in the treatise at the place cited.]

> [Note: Quesnellus, with the Oxford manuscript, reads “that he could.”]

## Chapter VIII

But suppose that Calendion removed the emperor’s name and that John was accused of having lied to the emperor. Since these were new cases, what new ecclesiastical investigation ought nevertheless to have taken place?

Were men said to have sinned against a human emperor to be deposed without any synod, while Acacius, sinning against God—who is the highest and true Emperor—and striving to mix the pure communion of the divine sacrament with the faithless, ought not to have been excluded according to the synod by which this treachery was condemned?

> [Note: Quesnellus reads “in which.” The Vulgate Councils adds: “ought he not to have been expelled?” It then continues: “What of the countless Catholic priests throughout the East expelled from their own sees and heretics unquestionably introduced? Certainly new …”]

What of the countless Catholic priests expelled from their own sees throughout the East, and the heretics installed in their places? These were certainly new cases, and consequently a new synod was owed them.

Why did it not then occur to anyone that, in such cases, at least some sort of synod should be requested from the emperor, so that, under whatever plausible pretext of ecclesiastical-traditional judgment, not only the priests of every city but also metropolitan bishops might appear to have been expelled everywhere?

> [Note: Quesnellus adds “previously”; all our manuscripts and printed copies lack it. Our manuscript copies, together with Merlin, have “one synod.” Quesnellus more accurately follows the Vulgate Councils with “a new synod.”]

Since Acacius did not resist all these actions by whatever recommendation he could make, he consented to them by communicating with all those who had been substituted as heretics in place of the Catholics.

The Apostle says: “Not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them” (Romans 1:32), are unquestionably to be recorded as guilty.

Was it permitted to secular authority—and to Acacius, who consented to such actions—to accomplish these things without any synod, although the novelty of the events themselves demanded one, and without consulting the Apostolic See, while it was not permitted to the Apostolic See, according to the force of the Council of Chalcedon, to expel Acacius from its communion for communicating with enemies of the Council of Chalcedon who had been rightly condemned by an established judgment in an ancient case and under an ancient constitution?

> [Note: The same Vulgate copies read “condemned according to the definition.” The Verona and Vienna manuscripts more correctly read “condemned by a just definition.”]

“But Acacius,” they say, “could not oppose the emperors.”

> [Note: The Vulgate Councils reads “the emperor.” The Oxford manuscript has “because he did not wish to,” incorrectly.]

Why, then, did he oppose Basiliscus when he wished to? Why did he not give his assent to Zeno himself, so that he would not appear to communicate openly with Peter of Antioch, although he did so covertly?

Behold, the emperor did not resist him when he opposed; behold, he did not impose force upon one who was unwilling; behold, he granted refuge to one fleeing manifest contagion.

Finally, why, while these things were being done or while he knew they were to be done, did he not refer them to the Apostolic See, from which he knew that responsibility for those regions had been entrusted to him?

> [Note: The printed edition of the Councils reads “hastened.”]

Instead, he first became a praiser of the actions already taken, before either warning that such things ought to be attempted or resisting them so that they would not be attempted, as he had already done under Basiliscus.

Why did he consent to communicate with those others who, after Catholic priests had been expelled, had unquestionably been substituted as heretics in the individual cities?

> [Note: Thus all our manuscripts, as well as the Thuane manuscript and the printed editions. Quesnellus, with the Oxford manuscript, reads “dared.”]

Finally, if he failed in his own duties and did not undertake what belonged to a Catholic priest, did the Apostolic See therefore have the power—or the duty—to pass over what belonged to it?

> [Note: Quesnellus omitted the word “Catholic”; we have restored it from our manuscripts and the Vulgate Councils. Immediately afterward the Vulgate Councils reads “disdained to do, and”; elsewhere it has “to the same things” instead of “to it,” where perhaps “to the same one” should be read.]

In whatever manner, the Apostolic See rejected an accomplice of the heretics and removed from its communion one who shared their external communion. There was no need for a new synod, since the form of the ancient constitution sufficiently prescribed this; nor was it necessary to announce that these things had to be done to the bishops of the East, since it is manifest that they were not unaware of what was being done in the matter of the faith through the expulsion of the Catholics, and, by communicating with the heretics who had been substituted, had consented to such an action.

> [Note: The same Vulgate copies read “that they should know.”]

Nor is it doubtful that they had become participants in an external communion, and that therefore the decrees of the Apostolic See could neither be discussed with them any longer nor ought to have been.

> [Note: The same source previously reads “it is manifest”; here it has a different punctuation: “there is no doubt that they consented”; it also has “and were not able” together with the effects of an external communion. We have added the particle “already,” omitted by Quesnellus, in accordance with all our manuscripts and printed copies.]

Behold, they recognized what was owed to the faith and to Catholic communion in the profession of those who persevered with the utmost firmness.

## CHAPTER IX

Behold, they recognized how Acacius, by withdrawing from such persons and contriving things contrary to the immortal beings, had deviated from the faith [Note: The Oxford manuscript deletes “and communion.” The Vatican-Isidorian manuscript, together with Merlin, has “catholic and apostolic.” Quesnellus later reads “might deviate, and likewise they persisted with the same men . . .” We have corrected this in accordance with the common text and our manuscripts.] and catholic communion, and had likewise subjected himself to the same error. Behold, they recognized for what just reasons Acacius had been removed by the authority of the apostolic see from the catholic and apostolic faith and communion—communion to which both those who had persevered in it properly belonged and those who opposed the persevering were taught to be strangers—and likewise every one who had proved himself an accomplice of Acacius; and that he had rightly been separated with them from that communion from which he himself, by disagreeing with the catholic bishops together with his associates, is known first to have separated himself. Rightly, therefore, he received the sentence of condemnation, to be promulgated against his other associates [Note: In the same common manuscripts the words “with his associates” are added], since he alone, on behalf of all his associates, confessed in letters sent to the apostolic see that he had fallen back into communion with perfidy [Note: The common text and the Council text, from the fuller letter, add: “to whose examination he had been especially summoned, but he neither came nor sent anyone, so that he might, as he trusted, be absolved by it from all these matters.” Later we wrote “by the pontiffs,” following the Verona manuscript and the subsequent letter, where this same chapter is repeated. The common text and Quesnellus, with other manuscripts, delete the preposition “by.”] [Note: The same common texts add “with Acacius.” Quesnellus then reads “before he reported this.” We have corrected it here in accordance with the common text and the Thuanus, Verona, and Vatican manuscripts, as the context below agrees: “before Acacius reported the matter here.” Moreover, Thuanus and Verona have “they should report” in the following letter. The same common texts then have, incorrectly, “was proved”; Verona has the better plural, “were proved,” also in the following letter.].

If the Eastern bishops had communicated with him before Acacius referred the matter here, they are plainly proved to have been involved in an equal guilt, and rightly through him they received the sentence of transgression, as having become partners with him in external communion. Such persons ought no longer to have been consulted as men of our communion [Col. 0652A], but ought to have been rejected as placed in the opposing fellowship.

If, however, they had not communicated with him before Acacius referred the matter here, they ought both to have censured the one who was communicating and themselves rather to have referred the matter here, and rightly to have approved that he had been struck down by the force of the apostolic see; and with that apostolic see and with those great catholic pontiffs they ought to have maintained concord more firmly [Note: So read our manuscripts and the common text. Quesnellus has “and with the see.”]. But because they had departed from the company of those men and had chosen to communicate with their successors, they were therefore in no way in agreement with the apostolic see, for they had consequently fallen back into the lot of the transgressor Acacius [Note: Quesnellus, with different punctuation, reads: “and because they saw themselves bound by his sentence.” We have followed our manuscripts, which, although they delete the conjunction at this point, nevertheless require it for the sense; we have therefore supplied it with the common text and the Council text, as well as the Verona manuscript, which includes it in the subsequent letter. Later, instead of “even today,” the Vatican-Isidorian manuscript and Merlin have “today only,” while the common and Council texts have “even today.”], and undoubtedly saw themselves consequently bound by his sentence as well.

For this reason they did not want him to be seen as condemned, because they recognized that they themselves had been condemned in the same transgression, in which they still persist even today [Col. 0652B]. But just as men bound under the same condition cannot judge their accomplice to have been condemned unjustly, nor can the guilty suitably absolve the guilty, so, with that transgressor justly condemned, these men too lie prostrate under an equal condemnation. They cannot be wholly absolved from it except by repenting, because, just as the transgression of all who had fallen back into the same act of perfidy was made public through the one who wrote on behalf of them all, so, in that one man who had written for all—or, by writing, had exposed the will of all—the transgression of all was punished [Note: The common and Council texts, from the fuller example of the Avellana Collection, read: “with the transgression punished, the transgression of all the accomplices was likewise punished together with him or in him.” Since the Vindobonensis and Verona manuscripts have “with the transgression of all punished,” we fear that an ancient copyist, leaping from the word “punished” to the later occurrence of the same word, omitted the intermediate words preserved in the manuscripts of the fuller version; these words therefore seem to be supplied here as well.].

## CHAPTER X

[Note: Thus all our manuscripts read. Quesnellus has “These things.” The common Council text does not have this sentence at this point, but transfers it somewhat later, where it reads: “But these things for instruction.”]

We judge that these things, which we have said for the instruction of Your Charity, are more than sufficient, although, if the Lord grants us the opportunity, we shall endeavor to explain the same matters more fully [Note: Gelasius promises another treatise on this same subject. Two treatises on the same topic are appended in the Verona manuscript to the Eastern bishops: one has been published in the following chapter of our collection; the other, longer one, was published by Scipione Maffei from that same Verona manuscript in volume V of the Venetian edition of the Councils, column 185 and following.], so that every one of the faithful may know [Note: Quesnellus inserts “and of the unfaithful”; we have deleted this with all our manuscripts and the Council text, as well as Merlin’s edition] that the apostolic see, God forbid, judged nothing hastily.

Nevertheless, although this sentence was directed against Acacius and, though issued only in the name of the apostolic bishop, is legitimately proved to have been drawn up by the authority that belonged to him—especially since it appeared that it ought to be sent secretly, lest the salutary arrangement, with guards posted everywhere [Note: The Verona, Vindobonensis, and Vatican-Isidorian manuscripts read “of the present one.” We have corrected this in accordance with the common text of the Councils. Quesnellus has “with pretended guards.”] [Col. 0653A], should be prevented from having its necessary effect by any difficulties—nevertheless, because the orthodox had everywhere been cast down and only the heretics and their associates remained in the East, and because there were either no catholic pontiffs left at all or they possessed no freedom, an assembly of many catholic priests in Italy reasonably recognized that the sentence against Acacius had been issued.

This assembly of pontiffs did not meet against Chalcedon [Note: Quesnellus adds “synod”; the common text and our manuscripts delete it], nor did it meet as a new synod against the former and first one; rather, having become a participant in the apostolic execution, it acted according to the terms of the earlier decree [Note: For “convenit,” the Council text has “cognovit,” “recognized”]. Thus it is sufficiently clear that the catholic Church and the apostolic see, since it was now wholly impossible elsewhere, omitted absolutely nothing wherever and with whomever it could, that belonged to action on behalf of fraternal concern for undefiled faith and sincere communion [Note: The Oxford manuscript, together with the Council text, omits “faith.”].

[Note: The Council text adds nearly half a page, inserting here the first paragraph of this chapter, which had previously been omitted. At the end of the letter, after an appropriate conclusion ordering that everything be brought to the notice of the recipients, this chronological note is added: “Given on the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Viator, vir clarissimus”; it should be read as in manuscripts 171 and 172 of the Venetian collection of Saint Mark’s Avellana Collection: “Given on the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Viator, vir clarissimus.” This is the consulship of the year 495. In the Vindobonensis and Verona manuscripts the following conclusion is written: “The account has been completed, showing that Acacius was duly condemned by the apostolic see and that no one can become a participant in his communion without detriment to his soul.”]

# CHAPTER LI

[Note: Sirmond published this letter from a Verdun manuscript. Before him Merlin had printed the same letter, but without any division, attaching it to the preceding one, just as it is presented in a single continuous text in the Vatican manuscript 1340 and Venetian manuscript 169 of Saint Mark’s. It is also contained in the manuscripts of our collection, in Verona manuscript 46, and in the copies of Isidore. The title prefixed here is found in the Thuanus and Vindobonensis manuscripts of this collection and in the Verona manuscript. In Isidore and in Sirmond’s Verdun manuscript, the inscription reads as follows, which we believe was compacted at a later time, both because it is absent from those more ancient manuscripts and because Gelasius, who did not communicate with the Easterners, does not seem to have used this formula: “To our most beloved brothers, all the Eastern bishops, Gelasius.” Although the beginning appears to be missing, no such indication is given by the manuscripts. This is common to two other treatises of the same Gelasius, one of which appears above in chapter 47, while the other was published from the aforementioned Verona manuscript by Scipione Maffei, volume V of the Venetian edition of the Councils, column 185, with the title: “A copy of the account to be rendered by Blessed Pope Gelasius concerning avoiding the communion of Acacius, sent to the Eastern bishops.” To indicate that the letter was mutilated at the beginning, Quesnellus prefixed to this chapter a title found in no manuscript: “From a letter of Pope Gelasius: the account given above, to the bishops of the East”; and again: “From a letter of Pope Gelasius to the Eastern bishops,” after other material.]

Here begins the account concerning the same matter, to the bishops of the East.

* * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * *

## CHAPTER I

What then of these prudent men, established in the regions of the East, who probe the inner matters of the whole religion with sharp minds? If they knew that such a person had been installed in the Church of Antioch [Note: He means Peter the Fuller, who, in the preceding material—which is missing at the beginning—is certainly understood to have been mentioned], why did they give their consent by communicating with such men? Why did they not immediately protest? Why did they not withdraw themselves from such contamination [Note: Sirmond has “they removed themselves, since they perceived so clearly”; the Verona manuscript likewise has “they perceived”], when they already plainly understood that Calendion had been expelled so that access might be opened to the heretics [Col. 0653C]?

Why did they discuss nothing about a synod, nothing about the matter itself, nothing about the Christian faith, nothing about the examination of persons? But if they voluntarily subjected themselves to that communion, they were certainly separated from the apostolic see, since among such men and with such men no synod could possibly arise, even if it had been necessary.

If they should say that they did not know what sort of bishop had succeeded Calendion at Antioch, what wonder is it if those situated in the East, unable to know what had happened in their own region [Note: Some manuscripts have “what had occurred”; later they read “they did not know”], were ignorant of what had been done at the apostolic see? Yet after it came to their knowledge what sort of priest had been installed at Antioch, why did they not immediately reject his company? Why do they put forward the excuse of ignorance when even today they follow both the contagions of the perfidious that have been made manifest [Note: The Oxford manuscript has “manifest”; later, for “which is sufficiently,” we have written “what is sufficiently,” with the Vindobonensis and the Council text. Quesnellus has “which is sufficiently”] and those we have repeatedly reproached?

This makes it sufficiently clear that even then, had they known, they would not have rejected them, since even now they do not refuse what has been publicly exposed. Let them turn their pleading and excuses in whatever direction they wish [Note: The Vatican-Isidorian manuscript and Merlin have “their excuse as well”; later, for “what remains,” we have “the remaining ruin”], they are so strangled by the snares of manifest truth that they can be trapped by their own words and deeds, and can toss about nothing except the sole remnant of their obstinate perfidy [Note: Quesnellus has “and be convicted only”; we have preferred our manuscripts and Thuanus, with which Sirmond agrees. The Oxford manuscript deletes “remaining.”].

## CHAPTER II

These statements concerning the venerable Calendion also apply, by a definite argument, to the person of John of Alexandria [Note: Quesnellus has, incorrectly, “when they were consulted.”]. Indeed, if the matter is investigated more extensively, such great tragedies and such great errors are found there that, if those who perpetrated them were themselves the judges, once they had been plainly refuted, they would not refrain from condemning themselves.

For it is openly and clearly shown there that nothing else was sought except a deliberately sought pretext by which, after any catholic bishop had been expelled, access might be opened to the heretic Peter. At that time no one examined the matter; no one demanded a synod. Everything seemed to be permitted to be done by anyone whatsoever. No distinction among cases and no examination was demanded by the Church [Note: Quesnellus, with the Oxford manuscript alone, has “of the matter” (*rei*). Later the Vatican-Isidorian manuscript and Merlin have “came to each person” (*unicuique venisset*); a little later, with Sirmond, they have “bishop of the see” (*sedis antistes*)]; but, as it occurred to each person, a catholic bishop was expelled from his own city—not only a metropolitan, but also bishops of the third and second sees [Col. 0655A].

In these matters no investigation was sought, no councils to be held were proclaimed [Note: The Oxford manuscript has “little councils”]; heretics were substituted, and no one resisted. Rather, like dumb beasts led into captivity, they followed perfidy according to the wills imposed upon them.

It is not surprising that they now try to defend those whose baseness they followed with blind minds without examination [Note: Thus the Vindobonensis, Thuanus, Verona, Vatican-Isidorian, and Merlin manuscripts read. Quesnellus has “their will”; Sirmond has “their advantage.” Quesnellus alone adds “even” before “when they know”]. But we are amazed that they are not ashamed to make the failure to hold a synod their complaint in the condemnation of these men, when they know that so many and such great pontiffs were expelled without any synod.

In the expulsion of these men they complain that a council was not held; let them recognize that they should be accused of not having demanded this also in the expulsion of others [Note: Sirmond, together with the Vatican-Isidorian manuscript and Merlin, adds “If.” Later all our manuscripts and the common text have “rejection”; Quesnellus alone has “expulsion.” He has “let them recognize, therefore”; we have deleted “therefore” with the Vindobonensis, Verona, and Sirmond]. If councils were not necessary for the rejection of the others, let them recognize that they were not necessary for these men either.

Was a synod unnecessary for the expulsion of catholic bishops, yet absolutely necessary to be convened for the condemnation of a confessed transgressor? [Note: The remainder of this chapter is absent from the Thuanus manuscript. After “synod,” the word is absent in Sirmond and in the Vindobonensis manuscript.]

## CHAPTER III

What, then, remains except for them to say that these men were not heretics? Let them not complain about the synod, since they openly declare themselves followers of external communion. Why, then, should a synod appear necessary for those who acknowledge that they came against the Council of Chalcedon, by which the Eutychian error, together with its authors, was condemned by the voice of the universal Church [Note: Sirmond has “with the authors,” using the general Church’s expression; the Oxford manuscript has “with the term”]?

There is no doubt that, as in every heresy—which a Christian must repeat unceasingly, because no one doubts that it is firm—all accomplices, followers, and communicants of a depravity once condemned are judged to share the same lot [Note: We have added “as,” following our manuscripts, Sirmond, and Merlin. Sirmond reads: “And consequently it follows.”].

Consequently, just as Timothy and Peter, followers of such men, were condemned according to the terms of that synod without any recent assembly of pontiffs having been held, so Acacius, who communicated with Peter, became, as a participant in the crime, likewise a sharer in the punishment.

Why, then, do they cloak these matters with evasions and clouds, seeking fatally to conceal their shamelessness and deranged mind by empty stories rather than to heal them medicinally by exposing them [Note: Sirmond has “to veil them”]? We have nothing in common with men of external communion. For this reason, certainly, every person is summoned to judgment, so that he may either admit the charges brought against him or be convicted by them.

After a confession drawn from the tenor of his letters, why should Acacius be summoned to judgment, when he confessed that he had joined himself in communion to Peter, whom he had asked the apostolic see to condemn and whom it had condemned at his request [Note: The Oxford manuscript reads: “whom the apostolic see had condemned by a repeated injunction.” Merlin has: “whom he asked to be condemned by the injunction of the apostolic see, having joined himself to him in communion.” The Vatican-Isidorian manuscript agrees, and the Vindobonensis is nearly identical. Quesnellus alone has: “nor could he now be believed” and subsequently deletes “either on behalf of theirs,” adding earlier “could” instead of “might.”]? Once he had become a participant in external communion, he could no longer be believed either on his own behalf, on theirs, or in defense of Peter, with whom he had previously mingled in a wicked fellowship, and whose case he had unquestionably made his own [Note: Quesnellus has “and had made his case.” The Verona and Vatican-Isidorian manuscripts and Sirmond, together with the Thuanus manuscript, have “and had made himself one with his case.” We have preferred the reading of the excellent Vindobonensis manuscript. Later the Vindobonensis, together with Verona, has “by what examination”; after several words the Verona, Vatican-Isidorian, Sirmond, and Merlin manuscripts have “so” instead of “did not have the confidence to speak for him.”]?

With whom, after a preliminary and lawful examination, if the case had so required, he would regularly have entered communion once Peter had undergone purification. But since he had joined himself in communion to the same man before he had been lawfully examined and purified, he had likewise mixed himself with one who was still accused; he therefore did not have even so much confidence to speak for him.

For since Acacius was supported by no privilege by which he could render judgment from a second see, he could not lawfully condemn anyone [Note: The Verona and Vindobonensis manuscripts read “he could lawfully condemn by judgment,” incorrectly. The Vatican-Isidorian manuscript and Merlin corrected this to “he could lawfully be condemned.” The reading of Quesnellus, which we have accepted, is supported by Sirmond’s manuscript]. In the same way, unless he had received authority from the first see, he had neither the right to examine Peter nor any power whatever to receive him.

## CHAPTER IV

With this principle regularly established, and with Peter in no way absolved by us—for we know that we condemned him, but we do not know that we examined or absolved him [Note: The Vindobonensis manuscript has “which was regularly established.” The Vatican-Isidorian manuscript and Merlin have “because it was regularly established.” Both are less correct]—it remains for us also to demonstrate that this same Peter, whom Acacius claims to have received into communion after he had been purified, never ceased from the contagion of heretical communion [Note: Quesnellus, with several of our manuscripts, has “and not only.” We have preferred “but not only,” with Sirmond’s manuscript].

Not only did the Alexandrian Peter continue in the company of the heretics at the very time when Acacius communicated with him, but he also remained there continually after the communion of the transgressor Acacius. Thus, through this Acacius, he received the contagion of perfidious communion, and through that same communion he was joined by the same plague to those heretics with whom Peter communicated [Note: Thus our manuscripts and Sirmond read. Quesnellus incorrectly has “to Peter.” Later he alone has “not in the order previously established.” Afterward, instead of “knowledge,” the Vatican-Isidorian manuscript and Merlin have “permission.”].

Acacius is known to have presumed to receive Peter without observing the proper order; nor is he known to have received him after examination or purification. Therefore he wished to usurp for himself, without the knowledge of the apostolic see, an illegitimate reception of Peter, so that he could measure his examination and purification according to his own will [Note: Sirmond has “to fabricate”], and receive him although he had been neither examined nor purified at all.

If he truly wished to receive him as examined and purified, he would rather have preserved the proper order in his examination [Note: Quesnellus alone adds “and purification”] and reception. But he did so in order to seem, rather than truly to be, lawfully purified [Note: Sirmond has “lest he should appear more able to purify lawfully than he really was.” These final three words are also preferred by the Thuanus manuscript. Quesnellus says that the reading we have retained will be clearer if “but” is read as “that is,” or at least so.].

Just as, therefore, he did not first condemn Peter until he had both referred the matter and requested that Peter be condemned by apostolic authority, so in receiving him he ought to have observed the proper procedure: before joining himself to Peter in communion [Note: Thus our manuscripts and the common text read. Quesnellus alone has “had joined himself.” The Verona manuscript has “asked that he be examined”; later, “or of receiving him”], he ought to have asked through the apostolic see that Peter be examined and purified by lawful procedure, since Acacius himself possessed neither the pontifical authority to examine him nor the authority to receive him. He could accomplish this only through the authority and consent of that see, without whose authority he himself could not have condemned Peter, and by whose principal diligence Peter could be examined, purified, and suitably admitted to communion [Note: The Verona and Vindobonensis manuscripts add “and.” Quesnellus has “and could be examined, condemned, or purified.” The words “condemned or” are deleted by our manuscripts, as they are also by some printed editions.].

Since it is established that such persons have always either been examined or purified by the apostolic see, or have been absolved by other bishops to whom this belonged, but in such a way that their absolution depended upon the consent of the apostolic see, where both things were lacking, it is clear that there was neither a lawful examination nor a firm purification, and consequently that the reception was improper.

If you judged Peter to be catholic without my communion, and, disregarding me, received him by your own authority, why do you complain if I expelled him from my communion—which you chose to despise—as though without your knowledge or consultation? Do you wish to submit? You are mine. You do not wish to submit? You are not mine. For “whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Matthew 12:30).

## CHAPTER V

I ask you: Do you think that Peter was a heretic, or a catholic, or that he was afterward corrected from heresy [Note: We have inserted “to be,” with the Verona and Sirmond manuscripts, and later “made,” with those same manuscripts and the Vindobonensis]?

If he was a heretic, you ought in no way to have communicated with him; and by communicating with him, it is evident that you became a participant in heresy and consequently became bound by the condemnation that proceeded from the terms of the synod.

If he was catholic, you are openly a defender of the entire doctrine that you pronounce catholic. Nevertheless, you are judged by his error if you define him to have been a heretic but claim that he corrected himself afterward and declare that you communicated with him after his purification.

Meanwhile, in whose person you thought that I ought to be disregarded, you cannot complain that in this same person I disregarded you.

Furthermore, since without me you had no authority either to absolve or regularly to receive such a person [Note: Quesnellus adds “because.” We have deleted it on the authority of our manuscript and printed witnesses], it is established that Peter was neither legally purified nor regularly received. As he was not regularly received, so it is not established that he was legally purified [Note: The following nine words, omitted by Quesnellus, have been restored from all our manuscripts and other printed editions], and therefore he was not lawfully purified because he was not legally received.

For while my sentence against him remained in force, and you did not possess pontifical authority without me to resolve my sentence, by what power is he said to have been examined, or by what authority received? Behold, meanwhile, in these matters your case wavers and slips; and if these things alone are so, it is altogether overthrown [Note: Thus the Verona and Thuanus manuscripts read. Quesnellus has “these alone.” Sirmond has “these alone were.”].

## CHAPTER VI

[Note: Sirmond has “but there is still”; the Verona and Thuanus manuscripts have “but he still adduces”; the Vatican-Isidorian manuscript, with Merlin, has “but adduce still.”]

But another matter is still added, contributing to the accumulation of your conviction. What if it should be shown that he continued in heretical communion not only before you came into his communion, and not merely when you came into his communion, but also afterward? Did heretical communion not reach you through him, or did you not pass into heretical communion through your association with him?

Show, then, that Peter of Alexandria ever ceased from communion with Peter of Antioch, and that, until the day when Peter of Antioch lived in this world, the two had not remained inseparably joined in fellowship [Note: Quesnellus inserts “of death”; the Verona, Thuanus, Vindobonensis, and Sirmond manuscripts delete it. From these, and also from the Vatican-Isidorian and Merlin manuscripts, we have removed “not,” which Quesnellus incorrectly added before “to have been a fellowship.”].

Will you also say that Peter of Antioch was corrected? Why, then, did Acacius boast that he had not communicated with him until the end [Note: Thus the better manuscripts, Vindobonensis, Thuanus, and Verona, read. Quesnellus, with the Vatican-Isidorian manuscript and Merlin, has: “Why, then, did he not communicate with him to the end?” Sirmond has: “with whom he did not communicate to the end.”]?

But what did it accomplish that he did not wish to communicate with Peter personally, when he thought that through the Alexandrian Peter he could communicate with him without incurring blame?

What shall we do about so many and such great cities from which catholic pontiffs were expelled? If catholics were substituted, why were catholics rejected? But it plainly appears that, when catholics were rejected, non-catholics were substituted. It remains, therefore, that whoever succeeded the catholics were heretics [Note: The Verona and Sirmond manuscripts delete “therefore.” The Vatican-Isidorian and Merlin manuscripts also delete it but continue differently: “so that those who succeeded them were not catholics but heretics.”].

Why did you rashly communicate with them? Why did you not act so that this new state of affairs and so great a tragedy concerning the succession of living pontiffs might be examined by a synod?

Does Acacius grieve over one man because he was not refuted by a special synod, even though he himself exposed his own crime in his letters and, having voluntarily confessed, ought no longer to have been heard? Yet does he not grieve over so many catholic pontiffs who were excluded without any examination?

If they knew that those whose communion they had avoided were catholics, they would certainly have preferred to communicate with them rather than, by refusing communion, to be driven from it by harsh persecution.

## CHAPTER VII

Behold, so many catholic priests themselves make known by this very fact what the apostolic see had judged and had steadfastly approved as something to be retained [Note: Sirmond has “which.” The Vatican-Isidorian manuscript, together with Merlin, has “who”]: while preserving catholic communion, they chose as associates those who communicated with the apostolic see, and they did not retain as associates those with whom the apostolic see itself was in no communion [Note: Sirmond and Thuanus have “had decreed not to communicate.” Later, instead of “did not retain,” the Verona and Vatican-Isidorian manuscripts, together with Merlin, have “retained,” deleting the negation. Sirmond’s reading, “rejected,” is better].

It is alleged that what the apostolic see had decreed was not made known to the Eastern bishops. How, then, did so many and such great pontiffs, sharing one and the same judgment with the apostolic see and approving what it had established as suited to the sacred religion and true—things which they judged not only ought to be followed by themselves but also courageously put into practice even to the point of persecution [Note: Quesnellus deletes “courageously,” which is found with Merlin and Sirmond in all our manuscripts. Later we have written “put into practice,” with the Vindobonensis, Verona, and Sirmond. The Isidorian manuscripts prefer “to be condemned.” Quesnellus, with Merlin, has “to be carried out”; he alone adds “they recognized. Behold, you had them”]—make this known to you?

Behold, you had men who both brought you knowledge of the apostolic constitution and supplied you with steadfastness for retaining it. If the apostolic see had sent men, it could scarcely have sent two or three. Behold, so many pontiffs following the decrees of the apostolic see bring you knowledge and offer examples of preserving the truth.

Since you closed your eyes to so many men, placed there before you, how could you have listened to two or three? By this very fact you undoubtedly recognized that those men pleased the apostolic see, by which you saw yourselves displeasing it.

Either follow those through whom you understood the will of the apostolic see, or there is no reason for you to offer ignorance as an excuse, since, abusing such great and such weighty indications [Note: Quesnellus, with Merlin, has “judgments.” The Vatican-Isidorian manuscript has “delays.” The Vindobonensis and Sirmond have the better reading, “indications”], although such testimonies proclaimed the constitutions of the apostolic see, you preferred to reject rather than receive them.

## CHAPTER VIII

Did all these bishops whom we have mentioned lie to the emperor [Note: See chapter 8 of the preceding title]? Did all of them remove the emperor’s name from the diptychs?

When, therefore, they were expelled and heretical successors were appointed in the place of living catholic pontiffs—and not merely in some lesser cities, but even metropolitan bishops who continued constantly in catholic communion [Note: Thus the Vindobonensis and Verona manuscripts read. Sirmond’s copy deletes “therefore.” Quesnellus has: “Why, I ask, did you not have compassion on so many brothers?”]—why did you not have compassion on so many of your brothers? Why did you not approach the emperor? Why did you not lament continually, with repeated cries, the Church’s cause and the pitiable disfigurement of the priesthood, declaring that the Church alone had ever judged bishops [Note: Distinction 96: “Never concerning bishops”]; that human laws could not pass judgment concerning such men without the bishops principally established by the Church; that Christian rulers were accustomed to obey the decrees of the Church and not to place their own authority above it; that rulers were accustomed to bow their heads to bishops, not to judge their heads?

By what councils of the Church, by what synod, were they expelled? Finally, what had they committed, so that, without any examination of the facts, the heads of so many Churches should be expelled according to human whim and the will of secular power—men unheard, unexamined, and unconvicted—especially when a new case and a new state of affairs had appeared, so that these rulers of peoples might, through sudden incursions [Note: Quesnellus, in place of “sudden incursions,” has substituted “of Christ”; the former reading is restored from all our manuscripts and from the Thuanus and other printed witnesses. Later, instead of “participation,” the Verona manuscript has “participation” in a different form; Thuanus and Sirmond have “by participation”], at the will of worldly power, be stripped of their sacred dignities; when they could be shown neither to be held nor convicted as accomplices by any old cause, any association of guilt, or participation in any error previously condemned, as though they were bound by a judgment already passed?

And therefore, because these were unprecedented incursions, with no prior causes having preceded them, it ought to have been shown why they were being expelled and what those incursions were; and the matter ought, as always, to have been established by ecclesiastical laws [Note: Sirmond has “detained.” Later we have added “they” with all our manuscripts and printed witnesses].

At the very least, on account of your position, you should have thought it right to care for their miseries, fearing that what you saw being violently inflicted upon others contrary to every custom might be inflicted upon you. If they were stained by some crime, it ought to have been established by ecclesiastical examination.

## CHAPTER IX

I say nothing [Note: Quesnellus adds *quod* (“that”), less correctly. We subsequently added *praecipue* (“especially”), chiefly on the authority of the manuscripts Vindobonensis, Vaticanus, Isidorianus, Sirmondianus, and Merlinianus.] about referring the matter to the apostolic see in accordance with custom, lest we seem to be concerned for our privileges. It should be enough to show what you ought to have done according to the rules and canons of the Fathers—especially since the public laws themselves, complying with ecclesiastical regulations, have ordained that such persons be judged only by bishops.

But if they had been accused of any heresy, it was all the more appropriate that those should investigate the matter who could examine it according to the standard of religion and possessed the ancient episcopal authority of judgment that has existed since the Christian religion began. For they were either Catholics or heretics—those concerning whom such insults were everywhere inflicted and detestable acts of brigandage raged [Note: So read the same manuscripts. In Quesnellus, *serviebant* (“they served”). Later, the Veronensis together with Sirmondianus has *debuerunt vel suis* (“they ought to have been refuted either by their own…”).].

If they were heretics, they ought in every way to have been exposed, examined, and lawfully convicted; and they ought to have been refuted either by their own confessions or by the testimony of others. I say nothing of the fact that, according to paternal custom, the matter ought to have been referred to us; I merely remind you what ecclesiastical law required.

But if they were proved to be Catholics, you who remained inactive not only at their expulsion [Note: The manuscripts Thuanensis, Vaticanus Isidorianus, and Sirmondianus read *cessistis*. The others, with Quesnellus, more correctly read *cessastis*, that is, “you remained inactive.” Quesnellus subsequently has *sed etiam haereticos subrogastis, et communicare delegistis*, “but you also installed heretics in their place and chose to communicate with them,” which unequivocally favors the heretics. We have followed the manuscripts Veronensis, Vaticanus Isidorianus, and Merlinianus. Sirmondianus agrees, except that it corruptly has *haeretici* instead of *haereticos*. The manuscript Vindobonensis likewise has *haeretici*, and alone reads corruptly *subrogastis* instead of *subrogatis*. Oxoniensis has *sed etiam subrogatis communicare*; Thuanensis has *indubitanter haereticis*. A little later, instead of *succedentibusque haereticis*, the manuscripts Veronensis and Thuanensis have only *succedentibus*. Vindobonensis deletes *haereticis*. Sirmondianus has *secedentibus*, without *haereticis*.], but also chose unmistakably to communicate with the installed heretics—

you, who, after the Catholics had been expelled and heretics had succeeded them, were not ignorant of the cause of the faith and catholic communion, which had been made manifest throughout the whole world through so many bishops. Rather, knowingly and willingly, without any investigation of the facts, without any synodal examination, and without any reverence for the apostolic see, you assented to the heretics, gladly and patiently allowing Catholic bishops to be driven out in a previously unheard-of and pitiable manner.

If you thought that they had erred from the integral faith and catholic communion [Note: Oxoniensis has “from the catholic faith and complete communion.”], you ought, according to the decisions of the ancients and as has always been done, to have referred the matter to the apostolic see—as Acacius is shown to have done concerning Peter of Alexandria, or Peter of Antioch, concerning John and Paul [Note: All our manuscripts, together with the common editions and Thuanensis, read “concerning John and Paul.” Quesnellus adds *de Joanne et Paulo*, except that Vindobonensis and Veronensis omit *et*. Merlinianus, together with Vaticanus Isidorianus, has “concerning John and Paul.” Quesnellus, following only Oxoniensis and deleting these names, noted: “These two names are likewise omitted in Gelasius’s letter to the magister Faustus above, chapter 48, and are found in the common editions of that letter. But he himself included John’s name in that letter, while we restored Paul’s with all our manuscripts and with Thuanensis. Compare note 14 on chapter 48.”]

But since you knew that they agreed with the apostolic see, and since through such great and distinguished bishops it was clear that the Eastern bishops could not have been unaware of what the apostolic see had determined by its own judgment [Note: Sirmondianus has *et vos* (“and you”). We have written *prodisse* (“to have betrayed”) with Sirmondianus and Thuanensis; Veronensis has *prodisse*.], and since through them they had shown themselves opposed to catholic and apostolic communion and had defected from it, you were not united with them in their suffering. Rather, you were joined by association with their persecutors [Note: Quesnellus alone has *connexis* (“you were joined”).].

At this point no synod ever occurred to you; and certainly, as has been said, concerning persons bound by no ancient law [Note: The manuscripts Thuanensis and Veronensis, together with Vaticanus Isidorianus, read *veteris lege*. From this perhaps arose Quesnellus’s reading, or rather emendation, *veteris offensae lege* (“by the law of an ancient offense”). We preferred the reading of Sirmondianus and Merlinianus. Here, clearly, the discussion concerns Catholics: when the Acacians condemned them, they did not consider convening a council, although the Catholics themselves were bound neither by any ancient law nor by the judgment of an earlier synod, as he had said above in chapter 2. The manuscript Vindobonensis then has *non unius episcopi* (“not of one bishop”).], it never entered your minds that the Church of the whole East ought to be cared for through a priestly council—not one of a single city or a single bishop [Note: Thuanensis has *Ecclesia* (“the Church”). Sirmondianus more correctly has *Ecclesias* (“the churches”).].

But since you had withdrawn wholly and deliberately, with all your affection, in the opposite direction, you deliberately avoided councils that were necessary, lest through them some such judgment should be issued whereby, once the facts had been clearly demonstrated and lawfully refuted to you, it would not be permitted for you to enter into the fellowship of heretics.

## CHAPTER X

What excuse of ignorance do you make, when throughout the whole East you saw so many bishops not only recognize the catholic faith and sincere communion corresponding to the apostolic see, but also defend them with the utmost steadfastness to the very end? [Col. 0662A]

If you had not heard from us what we judged concerning the faith and catholic and apostolic communion, you ought to have looked to them, and either followed them if you believed them to be Catholics, or accused them before the apostolic see if you believed them to have erred.

What advantage is it to you whether they maintained that position from their own determination or by recognizing what the apostolic see had defined? [Note: When the older manuscripts read as in Vindobonensis and Veronensis, *Quid illos vel*, Quesnellus supplied from the more recent manuscripts *Quid illos dicitis vel* (“What do you say benefits them, or…”). It seemed preferable to us to retain *juvat* (“what advantage is it”) with the better manuscripts Thuanensis and Sirmondianus. Veronensis shortly afterward has *an cognoscendo*; Sirmondianus and Oxoniensis, together with Merlinianus, have *aut cognoscendo*.]

Therefore, you ought either to have followed your colleagues and brothers, who were close at hand and before your eyes, as Catholics, or to have attacked them if you believed them to be in error. You ought not to have given your consent to those by whom they were harassed without distinction, until the truth had been established from all the evidence and the proper form of ecclesiastical judgment had proceeded concerning them. [Note: Sirmondianus and Veronensis have *Sin vero* (“But if, on the other hand…”).]

But if, by following the rule of the apostolic see, you perceived that they maintained this steadfastness, then through them you could not have been uncertain about the content of our own judgment. By assenting to their persecutors, you withdrew from fellowship with the apostolic see, although you were not ignorant of its judgment [Note: Sirmondianus deletes *vos* (“you”), and afterward has *retrocessistis* (“you withdrew”).].

And still you say that you did not know what the apostolic see had judged, although from those priests who possessed the catholic faith and communion [Note: So reads the Sirmondianus manuscript. Vindobonensis, Veronensis, Thuanensis, Vaticanus Isidorianus, and Merlinianus agree, except that they corruptly read *nolentibus* (“being unwilling”) instead of *pollentibus* (“possessing”). This error was apparently corrected by an arbitrary emendation in Oxoniensis, whose reading Quesnellus adopted: “those who cultivated the catholic faith and communion.”], you learned everything—not through words or letters but through their persons present—and although you appear, by your own judgment, to have separated yourselves from that communion.

And still you say that a synod ought to have been conducted concerning one man’s person, although you did not seek one when condemning so many Catholic bishops. Whom, then, do you wish us to believe concerning the report of such cases: Catholics or heretics? Those distinguished from every contamination of heretics, or those polluted by communion with heretics?
