Who, moreover, does not see that those are Catholics and wholly alien to every heretical plague who were driven from their own cities and sent into exile, while those who dared to become their successors while the Catholics were still alive are certainly not Catholics, but either manifest Eutychians or people in communion with the followers of Eutyches?

## CHAPTER XI

This plague continues among them even today. For those who had succeeded the Catholics were indiscriminately mingled in communion with Peter of Alexandria and with Peter of Antioch [Col. 0663A], and even today they are mingled with the successors of both Peters.

Add also those who, although they did not succeed Catholics, nevertheless, while Catholic bishops were still regarded as such, joined themselves to the communion of these men [Note: Sirmondianus, together with Vindobonensis and Veronensis, has *sed dum* (“but while”).].

This is that mixture; this is that confusion by which throughout the whole East there is no distinction between catholic and heretical communion. Indeed, anyone who attempts to distinguish between them is rather regarded as a heretic, struck by persecution, and punished with exile and affliction [Note: Quesnellus, following only Oxoniensis, has *discernere* (“to distinguish”), and shortly afterward *pellitur* (“is driven out”) instead of *percellitur* (“is struck”).].

It follows, therefore, that amid this universal filth, just as anyone who has separated himself from it is shown to belong to sincere communion and therefore to be Catholic, so anyone found to participate in that detestable association is as far removed from catholic and apostolic communion as he is from sincere communion.

Let no one claim that he perhaps did not or does not communicate with some particularly evident heretic [Note: Sirmondianus, Veronensis, and Thuanensis have *non communicasset* (“had not communicated”).]. For what benefit is it if he does not communicate with that person, yet joins himself in communion to those who do not differ from that person’s communion? But if he has communicated with none of them, or does not communicate with any of them at all, he will be one of sincere, catholic, and apostolic communion and faith; otherwise he will in no way be able to avoid the insincere contamination of that indiscriminate mixture.

In this way that good man Acacius is also shown to have communicated, through others and without ambiguity, with Peter of Antioch, although he openly boasted that he did not communicate with him. For Acacius did not withdraw himself from the communion of all those who communicated with Peter of Antioch. What, then, did it accomplish that he wished to appear publicly not to communicate with the man to whom, through his accomplices, he was bound by a secondary communion?

Acacius communicated with Peter of Alexandria. But as long as Peter of Antioch lived—for he is shown to have died after the pact had been made between Acacius and Peter of Alexandria—Peter of Alexandria never ceased communicating with Peter of Antioch. ## CHAPTER XII

What the report of the Catholic bishops and of the rest who persevere in the Catholic faith contains cannot escape the knowledge of the whole East [Note: Sirmondianus deletes *fide* (“faith”).]. And, to pass over the fact that Acacius communicated in fellowship through Emperor Zeno himself—who undoubtedly communicated with Peter of Antioch, whom he had introduced and whose episcopacy he had approved—we can point to many bishops of different cities with whom Acacius communicated although they communicated with Peter of Antioch, and through whom, consequently, Acacius also communicated with Peter of Antioch.

But among the Greeks this mixture is considered easy and blameless: among them there is no distinction between truth and falsehood; while they wish to be in communion with all the reprobate, they are shown to stand firm in no soundness. This, moreover, is that Peter of Antioch whom Acacius did not even request from the apostolic see to be received into Catholic communion through penitence. What, then, do they complain of in our having condemned Acacius, when, after this profession had been made and communion with Peter of Antioch had been received through its windings, he is shown to have condemned himself [Note: Thus Thuanensis and Veronensis, together with Vaticanus Isidorianus and Merlinianus. Sirmondianus is the same, except that earlier it has *per infectos* instead of *per anfractus*. Quesnellus: “Let him be shown, upon receiving him, to have condemned himself from communion.” A little later Sirmondianus reads: “the Eastern bishops . . . fell into these [contagions].”]?

Yet Acacius alone is not held guilty, but also all the bishops of the East who in like manner fell back into these contaminations are bound by a deservedly similar condemnation and cannot in any way be freed from it unless, while they still live, they abstain from such persons [Note: Vindobonensis and Veronensis read *teneantur obstricti, nec inde possint*; Sirmondianus likewise has *possint*.]. Nor in such cases ought we to believe anyone except those who either know themselves to be kept apart, by divine favor, from the bonds of this perfidy, or those who have withdrawn from the fellowship of the faithless. For what credence can we give, as testimony to sincere communion, to those who are situated in an insincere communion [Note: Sirmondianus: *qui insincera communione sunt polluti* (“who are polluted by insincere communion”); Thuanensis: *qui sincera . . . positi*; more correctly Veronensis: *qui in insincera . . . positi*.]? Nor can we rely on the testimony of those who strive to assail truth by falsehoods [Note: Sirmondianus reads *non verentur* (“do not fear”). Quesnellus subsequently has *Restat ergo*. We deleted *ergo* with the superior manuscripts Vindobonensis, Veronensis, and Sirmondianus.]. It remains that we must believe only those who are free from every contamination.

## CHAPTER LII

[Note: Besides the manuscripts of this collection, we found this version of the present letter also in copies of additions to the Isidorian collection, among which we collated Vaticanus manuscript 1340. St Leo used this version in the testimonies appended to Letter 165 to Emperor Leo; and in note 5 on Letter 109 we conjectured that St Leo found it, together with the translation of the following Cyrilline letter sent by St Cyril himself to Pope Sixtus, in the apostolic archives. In that letter he praises this very letter of Athanasius and sends it to Julian of Ceos for use against the Eutychians. See vol. I, col. 1177.]

Letter of Athanasius, bishop, to Epictetus, bishop of Corinth, against those who held diverse views, in a spirit of blasphemy, concerning the incarnation of the Lord.

[Note: Vindobonensis alone has this superscription, but not the preceding title; it reads *Epictito*, as does another Jesuit manuscript cited in the most recent edition of St Athanasius.]

ATHANASIUS, to his most beloved brother and dear fellow-priest EPICTETUS, greetings in the Lord.

## CHAPTER I

I had thought that every vain utterance of all heretics everywhere had ceased as a result of the Council held at Nicaea. For the faith set forth there by the Fathers in accordance with the holy Scriptures is sufficient for the overthrow of all impiety and for the confirmation of godly faith in Christ [Note: Quesnellus reads *mea* (“my”). The correction is supplied by Vaticanus, with which the Greek text agrees.]. And for this reason even now, when various councils have been held in Gaul and Spain and in great Rome, all those assembled unanimously—as moved by one Spirit—anathematized those who still lurk and think what Arius thought: Auxentius of Milan, Ursacius, Valens, and Gaius of Pannonia [Note: Thus Thuanensis, Vindobonensis, and Vaticanus, in agreement with the Greek text. Quesnellus alone, with Oxoniensis, reads only *omnes qui*.]. They wrote everywhere, concerning such men who had appropriated the name of a synod, that no council should be called a council in the Catholic Church except the one held at Nicaea, which is a trophy against all heresies, especially the Arian heresy, on whose account the council had principally then been assembled.

How, then, after so great a council, do certain people try to doubt or complain? If they are Arians, it is no wonder that they denounce what was written against them: just as the pagans, hearing that the idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of human hands (Ps. 113:4), thought the doctrine of the divine cross foolish. But those who are thought to believe rightly in accordance with all that the holy Fathers have said, wishing to alter something for the sake of inquiry, do nothing other than what is written (Hab. 2:15): they consider their neighbour foolish, and they resist to no benefit, but only in order to overthrow the simple [Note: The same manuscripts incorrectly read *Eorum qui putantur*; later they read *Patribus, qui propter*.].

## CHAPTER II

I write this after reading the proceedings of what was done in the presence of your Holiness—proceedings which certainly ought not to have been written, so that no memory of them might remain for the future. For who has ever heard such things? Or who taught them? Or who learned them? “For out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2:3). But where did these things proceed from? What hell belched them forth?

That the body from Mary is *homoousios*—of one substance—with the Word of the Godhead; or that the Word has passed and been changed from its own nature into flesh and bones and hair and an entire body. Who, among Christians, has ever heard in the Church that Christ put on a body in appearance and not by nature? Or who has fallen into such impiety as to say and think that the Godhead itself, *homoousios* with the Father, was circumcised and made imperfect from perfect [Note: Thus the same three manuscripts. Quesnellus, with Oxoniensis, reads *ex perfecta* (“from perfect” feminine).]; and that what was crucified on the wood was not a body but the creative substance itself? Or who, hearing that the Word made for himself a passible body not from Mary but from his own substance, could consider the speaker a Christian?

Who introduced this impious abomination, so as to arrive at such a conception and say these things: that whoever says the Lord’s body is from Mary thinks no longer of a Trinity but of a quaternity in the Godhead, because those who think thus say that the flesh with which the Saviour was clothed from Mary is of the substance of the Trinity [Note: Thuanensis reads *ut substantiae*.]? And whence have some again belched out an impiety like those already mentioned, saying that the body of the Word’s Godhead was not new, but had in every respect been coeternal with him, because it was constituted from the substance of Wisdom [Note: Thuanensis and Vaticanus read *et dicant*; Vindobonensis: *et dicunt*.]?

And how did those who are called Christians dare even to doubt that the Lord who came forth from Mary is Son, in substance and nature, of God, and that according to the flesh he is from the seed of David and the flesh of holy Mary [Note: The words down to the asterisk are cited from this same translation by our St Leo at the end of Letter 165 to Emperor Leo, and in the same selection of testimonies found above in chapter 41 of this codex. Note: The manuscripts here read *et* in place of *etiam* (“also”); but in Leo and above in chapter 41, *vel dubitare* (“even to doubt”).]?

## CHAPTER III

Why were they so rash as to say that Christ suffered in the flesh, and that the Lord and Saviour and God, the Son of the Father, was not crucified? Or how do those wish to be called Christians who say that the Word came upon a holy man, as upon one of the prophets, and did not himself become man by taking flesh from Mary; but that Christ is one being, and the Word of God, Son of the Father before Mary and before the ages, another? Or how can those be Christians who say that the Son is one and the Word of God another?

These things were stated in diverse ways in the proceedings, but they have one mind and the same impiety [Note: Vindobonensis and Vaticanus add *ruentem* (“rushing headlong”).]. On account of these things those who glory in the confession of the Fathers made at Nicaea debated and disputed with one another. I, however, was astonished that your holy piety tolerated this and did not restrain those who said such things, nor set out the godly faith to them, so that they might either be silent on hearing it or, if they contradicted it, be judged heretics. The things stated above have neither been said nor heard among Christians, but are altogether alien from apostolic doctrine [Note: Vindobonensis reads *apostolicae doctrinae*.].

Therefore I have set down in a letter for your sake the things said by them, so that by hearing them alone you may see in them a perverse confession and impiety. Although the folly of those who held these opinions ought to be accused and refuted at greater length [Note: Thuanensis: *a pluribus accusari et convinci* (“to be accused and refuted by many”)], it is better that the letter stop here and that nothing further be written. For matters shown to be so plainly perverse ought not to be treated and scrutinized at greater length, lest, when they are disputed, they be considered doubtful.

## CHAPTER IV

But it is sufficient to answer these things and say only this: they are not the doctrine of the Catholic Church, nor did the Fathers think them. Yet lest the inventors of evils acquire from our silence an occasion for boldness altogether, it is good to recall a few things from the divine Scriptures. Perhaps even thus, put to shame, they will cease from their filthy thoughts.

Whence comes it to you, O people such as you are, to say that the body is consubstantial with the Godhead of the Word [Note: Vindobonensis reads: “Whence [comes it] to you to say, who are such people”]? It would have been good to begin with this, so that, once this brittle claim had been exposed, every other such claim might be exposed. It cannot be found in the divine Scriptures. They say that God was in a human body; but the Fathers assembled at Nicaea said not that the body, but that the Son himself, is consubstantial with the Father, and that he is from the substance of the Father; while they confessed, again in accordance with the Scriptures, that the body is from Mary [Note: We added *iterum* (“again”) with our manuscripts Vindobonensis and Vaticanus, in agreement with the Greek *πάλιν*.].

If, therefore, you deny the Council of Nicaea by introducing these things like heretics; or if you wish to be sons of the Fathers, do not think beyond what they themselves wrote. For from this it is possible to see your iniquity: if the Word is consubstantial with a body whose nature is from the earth, while the Word is consubstantial with the Father according to the confession of the Fathers, then the Father himself will also be consubstantial with the body made from earth [Note: Vaticanus adds *ergo* (“therefore”). We subsequently added *factum* (“made”) with our manuscripts and Thuanensis, and also with Quesnellus.]. Why, then, do you still accuse the Arians of saying that the Son is created, when you yourselves say that even the Father is consubstantial with creatures?

And, passing to another impiety, you say that the Word was turned into flesh, bones, hair, sinews, and an entire body, and changed from his own nature. At times, indeed, you plainly say that he was made from earth [Note: Thus our manuscripts with Thuanensis. Quesnellus reads: “At times, however, you say [that he was made] from earth.”]. For the nature of bones and of the whole body is from earth.

## CHAPTER V

What, then, is this great madness, that you are at variance with yourselves? For by saying that the Word is *homoousios* with the body you signify one thing contrary to another; and by saying that he was changed into flesh you imagine a change of the Word himself. Who will now tolerate you any longer, if you say even these things alone? For you have turned aside to an impiety beyond all heresies.

If the Word is *homoousios* with the body, mention of Mary is superfluous and unnecessary, since an eternal body could have existed before Mary, just as the Word himself does. If, therefore, according to you he is consubstantial with the body, what need was there for the coming of the Word, either that he might put on that which is his own and consubstantial, or that, changed from his own nature, he might become a body [Note: We added *ut* (“that”) with Vaticanus, in agreement with the Greek text]? For the Godhead did not take itself up, so as also to put on what is its own and consubstantial; nor did the Word, who freed the sins of others, sin, so as to be changed into flesh and offer himself for himself, and make a sacrifice of himself. But it is not so—far be it.

“He took hold of the seed of Abraham” (Heb. 2:16), as the Apostle said; hence he had to be made like his brothers and take a body like ours. Therefore Mary was truly necessary, that he might take this from her and offer his own body for us. Isaiah also showed this in prophecy, saying: “Behold, the Virgin” (Isa. 7:14) [Note: Quesnellus reads *in seipso*. We emended this with the aid of our manuscripts, which are supported by the Greek text. Vaticanus subsequently reads *liberaret* (“might free”) instead of *libaret* (“might make a sacrifice of”). The Greek exemplar agrees, from which the Latin is: “and redeem himself.”].

## CHAPTER VI

Gabriel was sent to her not merely as a virgin, but as a virgin betrothed to a man, so that the bridegroom might show that Mary was truly human [Note: Quesnellus reads *sponsus*, less correctly. Our manuscripts more correctly read *sponso*, that is, “by the bridegroom,” as the force of the Greek text indicates.]. Scripture mentions the birth and says: “She wrapped the child” (Luke 2:7), and, “Blessed are the breasts which you sucked” (Luke 11:27) [Note: Thus Vindobonensis, supported by the Greek; Quesnellus reads *suxisti* (“you sucked”).]. A sacrifice was offered because the one born opened the womb (Luke 2:23). All these were indications of a virgin who had given birth.

Gabriel most certainly announced the good news to her, saying not merely, “That which shall be born of you” (Luke 1:35), so that the body might not be thought to have been brought into her from outside, but “of you,” so that what was born might be manifestly believed to be naturally from her herself. Nature itself demonstrates this: it is impossible for a virgin to produce milk, and impossible for a body to be nourished with milk and wrapped in swaddling clothes unless it has first been naturally born [Note: Quesnellus reads *haec* (“these things”). Our manuscripts supplied the emendation.].

This is what was circumcised on the eighth day; this Simeon took in his arms; this became a child and grew to thirteen years, and came to the thirtieth year [Note: The old translator had a Greek codex like the Seguerianus cited in the edition of Athanasius, in which *τρισκαιδεκαετής*, “thirteen years old,” was written, not *δωδεκαετής*, “twelve years old,” which other manuscripts have in accordance with Luke 2:42.]. For it was not, as some supposed, the substance of the Word himself that was circumcised after being changed—he was immutable and unchangeable. The Saviour himself says: “See that I am, and have not changed” (Mal. 3:6); Paul also writes: “Jesus Christ, yesterday and today, the same also for ever” (Heb. 13:8).

Rather, it was the body that was circumcised, borne, eating, labouring, fixed to the wood, and suffering; the Word of God, being impassible and incorporeal, was in it [Note: Quesnellus reads *impossibile esse incorporeum*. We deleted *esse* with Vaticanus and, by changing one letter, emended it to *impassibile*, as required by the Greek text and the context. We subsequently added *quidem* from both our manuscripts Vindobonensis and Vaticanus.]. This body was laid in the tomb, while he himself went to preach to the spirits in prison (1 Pet. 3:19), as Peter said. This all the more displays the madness of those who say that the Word was changed into flesh and bones. If that were so, a tomb would not have been necessary: the body itself would have gone by itself to preach to the spirits in hell. But now he himself went to preach, while Joseph laid the wrapped body in Golgotha (John 19:38); and it was shown to all that the Word was not the body, but the body was the Word’s body.

Thomas touched this body (John 20), after he saw that it had risen from the dead; he saw in it the marks of the nails which the Word himself endured in his own body when he was crucified [Note: Both manuscripts add *aspiciens* (“looking at”) in place of what the Greek has: “when he saw them fixed to his body.” Both subsequently add *tanquam* (“as it were”) before *Verbum*.]. Although he could have prevented this, he did not prevent it; rather, the incorporeal Word made his own the things proper to the body. Thus, when the body was struck by the attendant, he, though himself suffering, said: “Why do you strike me?” (John 18:23); and, though naturally impassible, he said: “I gave my back to the blows, and I did not turn my face from the shame of spittings” (Isa. 50:6) [Note: Vaticanus reads *sic ipse patiens*, and subsequently *impassibilis*. Thuanensis likewise has *ipse* and *impassibilis*. But the Greek requires *ipsum* and *impassibile*, referring to the Word; although *λόγος* is masculine, *αὐτὸς* and *ἄψαυστος* ought there likewise to have been written in the same gender.].

What the humanity of the Word suffered, the indwelling Word referred to himself, so that we might be able to partake of the Godhead of the Word. And it was wonderful: he was suffering and not suffering—suffering because his own body was suffering and he was in the one who suffered; not suffering because, remaining God by nature, the Word is impassible. He who was incorporeal was in a passible body, and the body had within itself the impassible Word, who destroyed its infirmities. He did this and it came about thus, in order that, by taking up what is ours and offering it in sacrifice, he might destroy it and, clothing us now with what is his, make the Apostle say: “This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:53).

## CHAPTER VII

Far be it that these things happened figuratively, as some have again supposed [Note: Vaticanus deletes *iterum* (“again”).]. Rather, when the Saviour became man, salvation was accomplished for the whole human being. For if, according to them, the Word was figuratively in the body, that which is said figuratively is a phantasm; and both the salvation of human beings and the resurrection will be found to have been spoken merely in appearance, according to the most impious Manichaeus. But our salvation is not through a phantasm: true salvation has been accomplished in the Word, not merely for the body but for the whole human being, soul and body.

The body was human, truly and naturally from Mary according to the divine Scriptures, and it was the true body of the Saviour [Note: Vindobonensis omits *erat corpus* (“was the body”).]. It was true because it was like ours. For Mary was our sister, since we are all from Adam; and no one ever doubted this who recalled what Luke wrote. For after he rose from the dead, when some thought that the Lord was not appearing in the body from Mary, but that a spirit was appearing in his place, he said: “See my hands and my feet and the marks of the nails, that I myself am. Touch and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luke 24:39). Saying this, he showed them his hands and feet.

By these things those who dared to say that the Lord was changed into flesh and bones can again be refuted. For he did not say, “As you see me to be flesh and bones,” but “to have [them],” so that it may not be believed that the Word himself was changed into these things, but that he himself was in them both before death and after the resurrection [Note: Thus our two manuscripts and Thuanensis. Quesnellus, with Greek support, reads “after death.”]. Since these things have such proof, it is now superfluous to treat further matters and investigate anything about that very body in which the Word was, who is not consubstantial with the Godhead, truly born from Mary, while the Word himself was by no means changed into flesh and bones but became flesh.

The saying of John, “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14), has this meaning, as may be found from a comparison. Paul writes: “Christ became a curse for us” (Gal. 3:15). He did not himself become a curse, but because he took up the curse for us, he was said to have become a curse. So too he became flesh, not by being changed into flesh, but because he took flesh for us and became man. The saying, “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14), is likewise like saying, “He became man,” in accordance with what is said in Joel: “I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel 2:28). For the promise did not extend even to animals, but concerns human beings, for whose sake the Lord himself also became man [Note: Quesnellus reads *si per similitudinem* (“if by comparison”); our manuscripts agree with the Greek.].

### Chapter VIII

[Col. 0670B] Now that this statement has this meaning, let all who thought that the flesh which came from Mary existed before Mary reproach themselves; and likewise those who thought that the Word had previously possessed some human soul, and that the Word had always existed in it before his coming.

Let those also cease who said that the flesh was incapable of death, but was of immortal nature. [Col. 0670D] Quesnellus likewise has “also.” We corrected this with the Vatican manuscript. Then the Vindobonensis has: “And because Christ died.” For if he did not die, how did Paul deliver to the Corinthians what he himself had received: “That Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures” (1 Cor. 15:3)? Or how did he rise at all, if he did not die?

But let those be especially ashamed who altogether thought that, if the body is said to be from Mary, a quaternity could arise in place of the Trinity. [Col. 0670D] Quesnellus has: “they thought that this could happen, introducing a quaternity in place of the Trinity, if …” We have corrected this with the Vatican manuscript and, by introducing different punctuation agreeing with the Greek, have deleted “introducing” with both of our manuscripts.

For they say: “If we call the body consubstantial with the Word, the Trinity remains, since the Word introduces nothing foreign into it; but if we call the body human, necessarily existing as foreign in respect of bodily substance, and if the Word is in it, there will be a quaternity in place of the Trinity because of the addition of the body.” [Col. 0670D] Quesnellus has: “necessarily there exists something foreign … so that it may be in him.” The reading of the Vatican manuscript seemed closer to the Greek. In the Vindobonensis: “necessarily existing … so that it may be.”

In saying this they do not understand how they entangle themselves. For even if they do not say that the body is from Mary, but consubstantial with the Word himself, nevertheless what they have imagined—lest perhaps they seem wise according to their own understanding—will be shown to imply a quaternity. For just as, according to the Fathers, the Son is *homoousios*—“consubstantial”—with the Father, and is not the Father himself but the Son, being called *homoousios* with the Father, so the body consubstantial with the Word is not the Word himself, but something other than the Word.

Since it is something other, according to their own reasoning their Trinity will be a quaternity. For the true, specially perfect, and undivided Trinity does not admit an addition; rather, this would be the Trinity understood by them. And how can they still discover another besides the one who is God?

### Chapter IX

[Col. 0671A] Again, their folly can plainly be seen in another of their arguments. If, because Scripture says and teaches that the Savior’s body is from Mary and human, they think that a quaternity is spoken of in place of the Trinity—as though an addition had been made because of the body—they are greatly mistaken, equating the creature with the Creator and imagining that the Godhead can receive some addition.

They do not understand that the Word became flesh not because of an addition to the Godhead, but so that the flesh might rise; nor did the Word proceed from Mary so that the Word might be improved, but so that he might free the human race. How, then, do they think that the body, liberated and given life by the Word, could make an addition to the Godhead in the Word? [Col. 0671D] The Vindobonensis agrees with the Greek here. Quesnellus has “in the Godhead.”

Rather, a great addition was made to humanity through the Word, in the very communion and union. [Col. 0671B] [Col. 0671D] Quesnellus has “was made immortal,” and similarly in what follows. On the authority of the manuscripts we have construed the text in the neuter gender.

What was mortal became immortal; what was animal became spiritual; and what was from the earth crossed beyond the gates of heaven.

The Trinity, however, even when the Word assumes a body from Mary, remains the Trinity: it receives neither addition nor diminution, but is always perfect. In the Trinity the one Godhead is recognized, just as the Father of the Word is proclaimed in the Church as one God.

Let those who at some time said that the one who proceeded from Mary was not himself Christ, the Lord God, now be silent. For if God was not in the body, how, immediately upon proceeding from Mary, was he called Emmanuel, which is interpreted “God with us” (Matt. 1:23)?

And how, if the Word was not in the flesh, could Paul write to the Romans: “From them is the Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. 9:7)?

Let those, therefore, who formerly denied that the crucified one was God confess that they were mistaken, [Col. 0671D] the Vatican manuscript has “to yield,”—yielding to the holy Scriptures and especially to Thomas, who, after seeing the marks of the nails in him, cried out [Col. 0671D] Quesnellus adds “and said”; we have deleted this with the Vindobonensis and the Greek text: “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28).

For since he was God and Lord of glory, the Son remained in glory while the body was fastened to the cross and dishonored; but the body suffered when it was struck upon the wood, and blood and water flowed from its side. The temple of the Word was full of the Godhead. Therefore the sun, seeing its Creator enduring insult in his dishonored body, withdrew its rays and darkened the earth.

But that body, possessing mortal nature, rose beyond its nature because of the Word dwelling in it, and ceased to undergo natural corruption. [Col. 0671D] Quesnellus has “which was of the natural [state].” We have deleted “which was” on the authority of our copies. The Vindobonensis has “which [was] of the natural [state].” We have written the text with the Vatican manuscript.

Having put on the Word, who is above humanity, it became the garment of the Word and became incorruptible.

### Chapter X

As for those who are deceived and say that, just as the Word came upon each of the prophets, so the Word came upon some particular man from Mary, it is unnecessary to argue; their madness is evident and their refutation certain.

If he came in this way, why was he born of a virgin and not likewise of a man and a woman? Every one of the saints was born in that manner. Or why, if the Word came in this way, is the death of no other person said to have occurred for us, but only the death of this man?

And why, when the Word came through each of the prophets, is it said of this one alone—who was born from Mary—that the Word came once at the end of the ages? [Col. 0672D] The Thuan manuscript has “it is not said,” but “of this one alone.”

Or why, when he came as he had come in the earlier saints, did all the others die and not yet rise, while the one from Mary alone rose on the third day? [Col. 0672D] Thus read our copies and the Greek. Quesnellus has “did not rise.”

Or why, when the Word came to the others in the same way, is the one from Mary alone called Emmanuel, born with a body full of the Godhead from her? [Col. 0672D] We have restored the words “from her” after “for,” with our copies and the Greek, where Quesnellus placed them.

For Emmanuel is interpreted “God with us.”

Or why, if he came in this way, when every prophet ate, drank, labored, and died, is this not said of each as it is said of him—that he ate, drank, labored, and died—but only of the one who is from Mary? For the things this body suffered are spoken of as though he himself suffered them. And whereas it is said of all the others only that they were born and created [Col. 0672D] the Vatican manuscript has “of all men”—of the one from Mary alone it is said: “And the Word became flesh” (John 1:14).

From this it is shown that, in the case of all the others, the word came to them for the purpose of prophecy; but from Mary the Word himself, taking flesh in himself, proceeded as man. By nature and substance he was the Word of God; according to the flesh, he became man from the seed of David and from Mary’s flesh, as the Apostle said.

The Father revealed him in the Jordan and on the mountain, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 17:5). [Col. 0672D] Thus reads the Vatican manuscript, agreeing with the Greek. Quesnellus has “with whom I was well pleased.”

### Chapter XI

The Arians denied this one, but we, acknowledging him, worship him—not dividing the Son from the Word, but knowing that the Word himself is the Son, through whom all things were made and we were set free.

For this reason we were astonished that among you a dispute arose at all concerning matters so evident. But thanks be to God: as much as we were saddened when we read the proceedings, so greatly did we rejoice at the end, because they departed in harmony, were made peaceful, [Col. 0672D] the Vatican manuscript has “were reconciled,” and agreed in the confession of the pious and correct faith.

Therefore, after the many matters discussed earlier, I thought I should write these few things, fearing that, through my silence, sadness might arise in those who, for the sake of concord, had provided us with joy.

I therefore first of all entreat your holiness, and all who hear us again, to receive these things with a good disposition. If anything is lacking for the instruction of religion, correct it and let me know. But if, as might be expected from an ignorant man, something has been written in speech neither worthily nor perfectly, [Col. 0673C] Quesnellus has “written neither suitably nor worthily, nor appropriately.” Our copies oppose this reading; grant pardon to our weakness in speaking.

Greet all our brothers. All who are with us send you their warmest greetings. [Col. 0673C] Quesnellus adds “Farewell”; our copies and the Greek text do not contain it.

## Chapter LIII

[Col. 0673C] An ancient version of this epistle exists in the same manuscript collections as the preceding one; it was first published from them by Crabbe and inserted into the first act of the Council of Chalcedon. The later editions of the Councils received this version from the Roman editors, who had brought it into conformity with and corrected it according to the Greek text.

**Letter of Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, to John, bishop of Antioch, against those who falsely represented his position in the faith; and concerning the letter of Athanasius to Epictetus, and the formula of faith.**

### Chapter I

[Col. 0673A] “Let the heavens rejoice and let the earth exult” (Ps. 95:21), for the dividing wall of the enclosure has been removed, that which caused sorrow has ceased, and the path of all dissension has been taken away, while Christ our Savior grants peace to his Churches.

Our most pious and God-loving rulers have urged and encouraged us toward this very thing. [Col. 0673B] The words “and encouraging” have been supplied from our Vindobonensis copies of this collection and from the Vatican manuscript of Isidore’s additions. The Thuan manuscript has “the words of our rulers urging us …” Shortly afterward, the Vindobonensis lacks “zeal”; in place of it the Vatican manuscript has “glory.”

They are rivals of the piety of their fathers and preserve in their minds the true, firm, and correct faith; they show outstanding concern for the holy Churches, so that they may possess indescribable and everlasting glory and preserve their empire worthy of every praise. [Col. 0673D] We have added “worthy of every praise” with our copies.

The Lord of all virtues, with a most generous hand, distributes good things to them, grants them victory over those who resist, and gives triumph to the truth. For he does not lie when he says: “I live, says the Lord, for I will glorify those who glorify me” (1 Sam. 2:30).

When my venerable lord and brother Paul arrived in Alexandria, we were filled with joy—and rightly so—since, as such a man, he willingly undertook to discuss these labors and matters that exceed our strength. [Col. 0673D] Quesnellus adds “our strength”; we have deleted it with the Vatican manuscript and the common editions of the Councils. He also inserted “God” before “the devil”; we have removed it with the Vindobonensis, also supported by the Greek text.

He wished to overcome the envy of the devil, join what had been divided, remove the scandals that had been scattered between the two sides, and crown with concord and peace the Churches established both among us and among you.

It is unnecessary to say how they were divided; [Col. 0673D] thus read the Vindobonensis, Thuan manuscript, and Crabbe. Quesnellus has “to recount.” I think it necessary, however, to speak and think what is appropriate to times of peace.

We rejoiced at the arrival and acquaintance of this religious man, [Col. 0673D] the word “religious” is supplied from our copies and Quesnellus’s copies. The Oxford manuscript has “who almost lightly”; the Vatican manuscript has “who almost not lightly … thought.” We should read, with the common editions of the Councils, “who perhaps not lightly”—who truly and not lightly thought that he was laboring to persuade us that the Churches ought to be joined and united in peace, to disperse the ridiculous arguments of those who think contrary to us, and to darken and blunt the devil’s remaining goad of malignity. [Col. 0673D] The Vatican manuscript has “of the devil.”

He found us ready for this, [Col. 0673D] Quesnellus has “ready for peace.” We preferred our copies and the Thuan manuscript, as well as Quesnellus’s own copy, so that we would endure no labor at all.

For we remember our Savior saying: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27). We have been taught to say in our prayers [Col. 0673C] the Vatican manuscript, with the common editions of the Councils, adds “our”: “Lord our God, grant us peace; for you have repaid us for everything” (Isa. 26:3).

If anyone, therefore, becomes a participant in this peace bestowed by God, he will not be deprived of any good.

Since the dissension of the Churches arose for no sufficient reason and was superfluous, we have now learned and understood the matter more fully, [Col. 0674B] we have added “more fully” with the Vindobonensis, Thuan manuscript, Vatican manuscript, and Crabbe, when my venerable lord, Bishop Paul, presented to us a document containing an irreproachable confession of faith. He asserts and confirms that this document was composed with the agreement of your holiness and of the venerable bishops of those regions. [Col. 0674D] Thus read our copies. Quesnellus has “asserting and confirming.”

The document is as follows, and its very words are set down here in this letter of ours. [Col. 0674D] The Vatican manuscript has “in this letter of ours.”

### Chapter II

Concerning the birth from the Virgin, the Mother of God, and concerning how we understand and speak of the assumption of humanity by the only-begotten Son of God, we say briefly—but necessarily, adding nothing partial, and receiving and learning the matter from the beginning through the fullest explanation and particular reasoning, from the divine Scriptures and the tradition of the holy Fathers—that we add absolutely nothing to the faith set forth and expressed in the assembly and synod of the holy Fathers at the Council of Nicaea. [Col. 0674D] The adverb “necessarily” is supplied by all our copies and also by the Thuan manuscript and Crabbe.

As we have already said, that faith is sufficient for all knowledge of piety and for the rejection of every heretical and corrupt doctrine. We do not presume rashly to speak of what is incomprehensible; rather, by confessing our own weakness, we exclude those who wish to arise against us, in matters where we imagine things beyond humanity. [Col. 0674D] The Vatican manuscript has “those thoughts”; shortly afterward, the common edition of the Councils has “to attack us,” instead of “to arise.”

[Col. 0674D] Quesnellus appends the following note:

“This confession of faith, which Cyril calls irreproachable in this letter, was not newly composed at that time, but had already been drawn up and published from the time of the Council of Ephesus by John of Antioch. We learn this from a letter of that bishop, sent in the name of himself and his synod to the emperor Theodosius through the count John, who, by imperial order, demanded a confession of faith from both parties while the bishops were still sitting at Ephesus.

“In that letter, published through the work of Father Lupus and inserted as chapter 17 of the Ephesian collection, we read precisely the same confession of faith that later appeared in the letters concerning peace, both of Cyril and of John. Alexander of Hierapolis likewise bears witness to this in his letter to Theodoret, found as chapter 96 of the same collection.

“When negotiations were being conducted for peace between the Orientals and the Egyptians, neither Cyril nor John wished to retract anything concerning the articles of faith, although Cyril softened and explained some points of his own position. John, however, maintained that the profession of faith which he had formerly offered to the emperor at the beginning of the dispute was sufficient, and he did not allow another to be extracted from him. At the same time he complained bitterly that what he had written concerning other articles in the same letter to the emperor had been altered by Paul of Emesa.

“From the aforementioned letter of Alexander of Hierapolis we further learn that the earlier letter and confession of faith of John was written in Theodoret’s style. Theodoret was, so to speak, the mouth and hand of the entire Eastern diocese. Thus far Quesnellus.

“Although the same faith composed by John of Antioch at the time of the Council of Ephesus and addressed to the emperor Theodosius is found in Father Lupus’s collection (vol. IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 277), inserted as chapter 17, and is also found in this confession, which gave occasion for the restoration of peace, it nevertheless received an addition at the end more explicitly declaring Catholic doctrine—an addition wholly absent from chapter 17. Moreover, the statements in chapter 17 that attacked Saint Cyril and his anathemas, apart from the confession of faith itself, were omitted. Alexander of Hierapolis, fiercely hostile to Saint Cyril, complained of this in his letter to Theodoret, chapter 96 of the cited collection.

“We have not been able to find any complaint by John of Antioch on this point. Nor could Paul of Emesa be blamed because John altered in other letters to Cyril what he had written concerning other articles in his letter to the emperor. Paul did not make the alteration himself; John did so when, leaving out Cyril and the condemnation of his anathemas—which had been included in the earlier letter—he openly set forth in his letter to Cyril the condemnation of Nestorius and his errors. For this reason the aforementioned Alexander of Hierapolis reproaches him in Father Lupus’s chapter 93.

“You therefore see whether John considered his earlier profession of faith sufficient, since he added other matters of faith, omitted some of the remaining articles, and substituted others.”

We therefore confess our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man, consisting of a rational soul and a body: begotten before the ages from the Father according to the Godhead, and in the last times the very same one, for us and for our salvation, from the Virgin Mary according to the humanity; consubstantial—or *homoousios*—with the Father according to the Godhead, and consubstantial with us according to the humanity.

For a union of two natures has taken place. Therefore we confess one Christ and one Lord. [Col. 0676C] The common edition of the Councils adds from the Greek “one Son.” The collection of Father Lupus, chapter 17, does likewise. The Thuan manuscript has *genitricem* (“mother”) instead of *generatricem* (“begetter”). The common edition of the Councils, with the Greek text, reads: “the holy Virgin, Mother of God, for this reason God the Word was incarnate and assumed humanity and united it from the very conception,” and so forth. The Vindobonensis has “Virgin.” We confess this: “the Word of God was incarnate.”

According to this faith in an incomparable union, we confess the holy and divine Virgin, the Mother of God.

For this reason, the Word of God was incarnate from her, assumed humanity, and from the very conception united to himself the temple that he assumed from her. [Col. 0676C] The following sentences have been added, since they are not found in John’s letter to the emperor Theodosius in Father Lupus, chapter 17.

We know that the evangelical and apostolic statements concerning our Lord are true: some we make common, as belonging to one person; others we distinguish, as arising from two natures. We assign to Christ’s Godhead those statements that befit God, and we transmit the humble statements according to his humanity. [Col. 0676C–D] In the complete letter of John to Saint Cyril, an explicit condemnation of Nestorius and his errors follows this confession, together with agreement concerning the ordination of Maximian, who, after Nestorius had been deposed, had been promoted to the see of Constantinople.

### Chapter III

When we had learned your sacred statements and recognized that you think in this way—“One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. 4:5)—we glorified the Lord God, the Savior of all, rejoicing with one another because the Churches among us and among you possess a faith concordant with the God-inspired Scriptures and with the tradition of the holy Fathers. [Col. 0676D] Quesnellus adds “they agree,” contrary to our copies and the Greek text.

Since I understood that certain people, accustomed to finding fault in their usual manner, buzz around like wild hornets and vomit out troublesome words against me because I said that Christ’s holy body came from heaven and not from the holy Virgin, I thought it necessary to say a few things to them on this matter. [Col. 0676D] We have inserted “holy” from the Vatican manuscript and Crabbe, in agreement with the Greek.

O foolish men, who know only how to stir up accusations! How have you been led to such a conclusion, and how have you become so diseased with folly?

You ought—and very greatly ought—to understand clearly that nearly all our struggle on behalf of the faith arises from our affirming that the holy Virgin is the Mother of the divine birth. But if we say that the body of our Lord and Savior came from heaven and was not born from the holy Virgin herself, how shall we call her the Mother of God? Whom did she give birth to at all, unless it is true that, according to the flesh, she gave birth to the one who is Emmanuel? [Col. 0676D] Only Quesnellus has “whom”; the others have “what,” in place of “whom.”

Let those who have chattered such things about me be mocked. [Col. 0676B] Thus read the Vatican manuscript and the common edition of the Councils, in agreement with the Greek text. Quesnellus has “who babble about my words in this way.” Shortly afterward the same Vatican manuscript has “for he did not lie.”

For the blessed prophet Isaiah does not lie when he says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel,” which is interpreted “God with us” (Isa. 7:14; Matt. 1:23).

The holy Gabriel also bears true witness, saying to the same blessed Virgin: “Do not fear, Mary, for you have found favor with the Lord. Behold, you shall conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus; for he will save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1:20). [Col. 0676D] The Vindobonensis has “he will save.”

### Chapter IV

When we speak of our Lord Jesus Christ as coming from heaven and from above, [Col. 0676D] Quesnellus adds “having come”; we have deleted this with the Vindobonensis, the common edition of the Councils, and the Greek text, we do not mean that his holy flesh was brought down from heaven in that manner. Rather, we follow the remarkable Paul, who openly cries out: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man was from heaven, heavenly” (1 Cor. 15:47).

We also remember the Savior himself saying: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man” (John 3:13). [Col. 0677D] Quesnellus adds “who is in heaven”; the same copies delete it with the Greek.

For he was born according to the flesh, as I said shortly before, from the holy Virgin. And because the one who came from heaven and from above—the Word of God—“emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:7), he was called the Son of Man, while remaining what he was, namely, God. For according to his nature he is immutable and unchangeable. Since he is now understood as one with his own flesh, he is said to have descended from heaven.

He was also called the perfect man from heaven, since he was likewise perfect in his Godhead and the very same one was perfect in that same humanity, being understood as one person. [Col. 0677D] We have added the following six words from our copies, required by the Greek text: “He was also called.” For there is one Lord Jesus Christ, even though the difference of the natures is not ignored; and we understand and confess that an indescribable union has been effected from them.

May your holiness restrain those who say that a blending, confusion, or mixture of the Word of God with the flesh has taken place. I do not doubt that there are some who spread such things about me, chattering and saying them.

But I am so far from holding such a view that I consider those who have suspected this of me to be insane—namely, that any semblance of change could occur in the nature of the divine Word. What always is remains what it is; it does not change, will never change, and will not undergo alteration.

We all confess that the Word of God is impassible in this respect, although he himself orders the mystery with supreme wisdom. I see in his own flesh the sufferings that befell it. [Col. 0677D] The common edition of the Councils reads more clearly from the Greek: “although, in his supreme wisdom, he himself orders the mystery and is seen to attribute to himself the sufferings that properly befell the flesh.”

The most wise Peter says the same: “Christ suffered for us in the flesh” (1 Pet. 4:1), and not in the ineffable nature of the Godhead. [Col. 0677D] The Vatican manuscript with Crabbe deletes “in.”

So that he may be believed to be the Savior of all according to his own dispensation, he takes upon himself, as I have said, the sufferings of his own flesh. What else is that which was foretold in the prophet’s words, as though it should be understood as spoken by him himself? [Col. 0677D] Thus read the Vindobonensis and Crabbe. Quesnellus has: “He gave my back,” etc.

“I gave my back to scourges and my cheeks to blows; but I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting” (Isa. 50:6).

### Chapter V

[Col. 0677D] Because we everywhere obey the teachings of the holy Fathers, and especially the command of our blessed and in every respect praiseworthy father Athanasius, refusing altogether to cast anything of these matters outside, let your holiness—and no one else—learn this. [Col. 0677D] The common edition of the Councils, with the Greek, has “let no one doubt.”

I would also have set forth more of their words, by which I could lend authority to my statements, if I had not feared the length of the writing, lest the result itself become burdensome.

In no way do we allow the defined faith, or creed, of our holy Fathers who assembled at Nicaea in those times to be shaken by certain people. Nor is it permitted either to us or to others to change a single word of what is contained there, or to alter one syllable, [Col. 0677D] the Vatican manuscript adds “by transferring the eternal boundaries,” remembering the saying: “Do not move the ancient boundaries that your fathers established” (Prov. 22:28).

For they themselves were not speaking, but the Spirit of God and of the Father, who indeed proceeds from him but is not alien to the Son in respect of essence.

The words of those holy men who handed down the mysteries also confirm this for us. For it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “When they had come opposite Moesia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them” (Acts 16:7). [Col. 0677D] Thus read both manuscripts. Other copies have “Mysia”; Quesnellus follows that reading.

The venerable Paul also writes: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:8–9). [Col. 0678D] Thus read our copies and Crabbe, with the Greek. Quesnellus has “the Spirit of God.” Shortly afterward he has the shorter reading “certain people accustomed to perverting what is right”; but we did not wish to abandon our copies.

When certain people who are accustomed to perverting what is right think that my words should be diverted and wrested toward what seems good to them, your holiness should not be surprised. You know that those who belong to every heresy gather the causes of their error from the divine Scriptures. By corrupting with the wickedness of their minds the things rightly spoken through the Holy Spirit, they draw upon their own heads the flame of unquenchable fire.

Since we have learned that they have altered and published the letter to the most praiseworthy father Epictetus, our father Athanasius, although it contained the entirely correct faith, and that many have consequently been harmed, we have therefore judged it necessary and useful to publish for our brothers, from the ancient copies preserved among us and carefully explained, a version similar to the one we are sending to your venerable authority.

[Col. 0678D] Burchard, book I, chapter 232, presents this formula of faith from one of the copies of our collection; for he cites it as “from the letter of Cyril to John of Antioch,” since in the manuscripts of our collection it follows the preceding letter of Cyril. A shorter version is read at the end of chapter 55. Compare what we shall note there.

### Formula of the Little Book of Faith under the Same Chapter

I, Ille, [Col. 0678D] Burchard has this wording, profess this document, which I have written out with my own hand, following the holy judgment of the Fathers of the Nicene Synod, three hundred and eighteen in number, and of the universal council of the Synod of Chalcedon, whose definition the Apostolic See confirmed, and which the letter of the most blessed Pope Leo to Flavian, of holy memory, bishop of Constantinople, set forth in a most lucid proclamation of the truth.

I confess one and the same Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God the Father, the very same one perfect in the Godhead, the very same one truly God and truly man in his humanity; the very same one consisting of a rational soul and flesh, consubstantial with the Father according to the Godhead, and the very same one consubstantial with us according to the humanity; [Col. 0679D] thus reads the Vindobonensis with Burchard. Quesnellus has “in divinity”; like us in all things except sin.

Before the ages he was begotten from the Father according to the Godhead; in the last days, the very same one, for us and for our salvation, was born from the Virgin Mary, who bore the same God according to the humanity. [Col. 0679D] Burchard has “according to the humanity.”

We recognize one and the same Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, the one Lord, in two natures, known without confusion, without change, without division, and without separation. The difference of the natures was not removed because of the union; rather, the proper character of each nature remained secure, and the natures came together into one person, not into two.

We confess one and the same only-begotten Son, God the Word, the Lord Jesus Christ, as the prophets formerly taught us concerning him and as the Lord Christ himself instructed us through his own person. [Col. 0679D] We have added “Son” with the Vindobonensis and Burchard. Shortly afterward Burchard has *verum* (“true”) instead of *verbum* (“Word”).

But I declare that those who do not think in this way, together with Nestorius and Eutyches [Col. 0679D] the words “or their followers,” omitted by Quesnellus, are supplied by the Vindobonensis and Burchard, or their followers, are worthy of eternal anathema.

## Chapter LIV

[Col. 0679D] Quesnellus prefaced this chapter with the following notice:

“In the Thuaneus manuscript there is prefixed a body of laws excerpted from the Theodosian Code, which constitutes chapter 54. It is entitled there ‘The Definition of the Holy Synod of Chalcedon.’ That treatise is what the older editions call the second definition, while some regard it as part of the single definition of the Fourth Synod.

“We omit it here, both because it is not found in the Oxford manuscript and because it is nothing other than the first of the four versions printed in the editions of Crabbe, Surius, Nicolinus, and others, which anyone can readily consult. Finally, the same definition appears above in another version in chapter 25, after the creed, and begins: ‘This would indeed have been sufficient for a complete knowledge of piety,’ etc.”

Thus far Quesnellus.

Since, however, with the exception of one more recent Oxford manuscript, the other copies of this collection contain this definition, it ought not to have been omitted by the editors of the same collection.

**Definition of the Holy Synod of Chalcedon**
To recognize and confirm piety with the utmost completeness, this sufficiently considered symbol of divine grace, and most salutary one, would by itself be fully sufficient. For it teaches most fully what had been established concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and clearly intimates the Lord’s incarnation to those who faithfully receive it. But since certain people, attempting to corrupt what sincere truth proclaims, have brought forth new heretical falsehoods strange to the ear; since some have dared to corrupt the mystery of the Lord’s dispensation, which was celebrated for our sake, by concealing through their denial that the divine birth proceeded from the holy Virgin; and since others again introduce confusion or mixture, foolishly fabricating that the divine nature and the flesh are one nature and thereby monstrously implying, through the confusion of the Only-Begotten, that the divine nature is passible—therefore, wishing to exclude every attack against the truth, this holy and great synod, now assembled, declares immovable what has been preached in the faith from ancient times and establishes above all that the faith of the three hundred and eighteen venerable Fathers remain undefiled. [Col. 0679C–D]

And on account of those who strive to oppose the Holy Spirit, it confirms the tradition decreed later in the most august city of Constantinople, when one hundred and fifty Fathers had assembled, concerning the substance of the Holy Spirit. For they caused this to be known to all, not as though they were declaring that anything was lacking in what preceded, but illuminating, through testimonies from the Holy Scriptures, what they themselves believed concerning the Holy Spirit, against those who had attempted to resist his power. [Col. 0680A]

But on account of those who attempted to pervert the mystery of the Lord’s dispensation and rashly assert in their foolish babbling that only a man was produced from the holy Virgin Mary, it embraced the synodal letters of Saint Cyril, pastor of the Church of Alexandria, written to Nestorius and to the Eastern bishops who agreed with him: letters intended to refute the Nestorian madness and to provide an interpretation for those who, with devout zeal, desire to understand the meaning of this most salutary mystery. To these it rightly joined the letter of the most blessed bishop of the elder city of Rome, the venerable Pope Leo, written to Flavian, archbishop of holy memory, to overthrow the faithlessness of Eutychian perversity; for it accords with the saving confession of the great Peter and stands, as it were, as a common memorial or statue against all heretics, so that sound doctrine may retain its firm and unshaken stability. [Col. 0680B–C]

For it also resisted those who attempted to divide the mystery of the dispensation into two sons; it removes from the priestly fellowship those who dare to say that the dignity of the Only-Begotten is passible; it opposes those who devise confusion and mixture in the two natures of Christ; it expels those who, in their madness, claim that the servant-form which he assumed from us is heavenly, or of some other substance; and it does not cease to anathematize those who fabulously fabricate that Christ had two natures before the union but one after the union.

Therefore, following the most blessed Fathers, we teach, in agreement with all the authoritative statements, that one and the same Son is to be confessed as the Lord Jesus Christ: the same perfect in divinity, the same perfect in humanity; truly God and truly the same man, consisting of a rational soul and a body; consubstantial with the Father according to divinity, and the same consubstantial with us according to humanity; in all things like us, without the stain of sin; begotten from the Father before the ages according to divinity, and in the last days, for us and for our salvation, the same born from Mary the Virgin, who bore God according to the incarnation—one and the same Christ, Son, Lord, Only-Begotten.

We all acknowledge him in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, and without separation. The distinction of the natures is nowhere abolished because of the union; rather, the property of each nature is preserved, and they come together in one person—not reduced or divided into two persons, but one and the same Son, true God, the Lord Jesus Christ, just as the prophets from the beginning taught us concerning him, and as Jesus Christ himself instructed us and delivered the paternal symbol to us. [Col. 0680D–0681B]

Having thus ordered all these matters on every side with complete deliberation and diligence, this holy and universal synod decreed that no one may bring forward, write, expound, hold, or transmit another faith. Those who dare either to compose another faith, or to bring forward, teach, or transmit another creed to those wishing to turn to the knowledge of the truth from pagan practice, Judaism, or any kind of heresy shall be subject to the following penalties: if they are bishops or clerics, they shall be deprived of their episcopate or clergy; if they are monks or laymen, they shall be anathematized.

## Laws from Book XVI of the Theodosian Code under the title “On the Catholic Faith”

### Edict of the emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, Augusti, to the people of the city of Constantinople

*(Theodosian Code, book XVI, title 1, law 2.)*

We wish all peoples governed by the moderation of our clemency to live in the religion which the divine Apostle Peter is declared to have delivered to the Romans, as the religion handed down by him to the present day makes clear; and which it is evident that the pontiff Damasus follows, as does Peter, bishop of the city of Alexandria, a man of apostolic holiness. This means that, according to apostolic discipline and evangelical teaching, we are to believe in one Godhead of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, under equal majesty and in the pious Trinity.

Following this law, we order that they embrace the name of catholic Christians. We judge all others to be demented and insane, and they shall bear the disgrace of heretical doctrine. Their assemblies shall not receive the name of churches; they shall be punished first by divine vengeance and afterward by the penalty of our own action, which we shall undertake by heavenly judgment.

Issued on the third day before the Kalends of March at Thessalonica, in the consulship of Gratian for the fifth time and Theodosius for the first time, Augusti. [Col. 0681C–D]

### Again, in the same book under the title “On Those Who Quarrel about Religion”

The emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius, Augusti, to Tatianus, prefect of the praetorium. *(Same book, title 4, law 2.)*

[Editorial note: Gothofredus’ Theodosian Code reads “having gone out, and then,” followed by “or of submitting any proposal.”]

No opportunity shall be opened to anyone who has gone out in public either to dispute about religion, to discuss it, or to bring forward some proposal. If anyone henceforth believes, with grave and culpable daring, that he ought to act against this law, or dares to persist with the movement of a pestilential perseverance, he shall be restrained by an appropriate penalty and deserved punishment.

Issued on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July [Editorial note: Thus the Vienna manuscripts and others cited by Coustant in the preface to vol. I of the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, p. 79, as well as Gothofredus’ edition, which adds “at Stobi.” Quesnellus reads “in August.”], in the consulship of Theodosius Augustus for the second time and Cynegius. [Col. 0681D–0682A]

### Again, in the same book under the title “On Heretics”

The emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius Augustus, to Eutropius [Editorial note: Quesnellus incorrectly reads “praepositus.” Corrected from our manuscripts and Coustant’s manuscripts, and in accordance with Gothofredus’ edition.], prefect of the praetorium. *(Same book, title 5, law 6.)*

[Editorial note: In certain editions of the Theodosian Code, incorrectly, “No heretics,” and shortly afterward, “for exercising the mind.”]

No place for heretical mysteries, and no opportunity for exercising the madness of a more obstinate mind, shall be allowed. Let everyone know that, even if anything has been obtained from such people through fraud by means of some special rescript, it has no validity. Crowds of all heretics shall be kept away from unlawful gatherings. The name of the one supreme God shall everywhere be celebrated. The observance of the faith of Nicaea, handed down long ago by our ancestors and confirmed by the testimony and assertion of divine religion, shall always remain in force. The pollution of the Photinian stain, the poison of Arian sacrilege, the crime of Eunomian perfidy, and the monstrous prodigies of sects bearing the impious names of their authors shall be abolished even from the hearing. [Col. 0682B–C]

The true defender of the Nicene faith and true worshiper of the catholic religion is to be regarded as the one who confesses the omnipotent God and Christ, the Son of God [Editorial note: Gothofredus reads “the Son, God, under one name.”], as God from God and light from light; and who does not violate the Holy Spirit by denying that which we hope for and receive from the supreme Father of all things [Editorial note: Thus the Vienna manuscript and Gothofredus’ edition. Quesnellus reads, “and whoever does not.” We would gladly emend to “from whom we hope for and receive that which is from the supreme Father of all things,” if any manuscript supported it.]. In him the undivided substance of the incorrupt Trinity flourishes through the understanding of an undefiled faith; in Greek terminology this is called *homoousia* [ὁμοούσια, “consubstantiality”] by those who believe rightly [Editorial note: The edition of the Theodosian Code reads οὐσία, “substance.”].

These things are especially approved and venerable to us. But those who do not serve these same principles [Editorial note: Quesnellus reads, “do not submit to these names.” We prefer the Vienna and Thuaneus manuscripts with Gothofredus’ edition.] must cease, through contrived deceit, to assume the alien name of true religion; rather, let them be exposed by their open crimes [Editorial note: Thus Gothofredus with the Vienna manuscript. Quesnellus reads, “let them openly be exposed by their crimes.”]. They shall be completely removed and kept away from the threshold of all churches, since we forbid all heretics to conduct unlawful gatherings within the towns. If any seditious outbreak should attempt anything, we order that it be driven back even from the walls of the cities, its madness having been expelled, so that the Catholic Church throughout the world may be restored to all orthodox bishops who hold the Nicene faith.

Issued on the fourth day before the Ides of June [Editorial note: The Theodosian and Justinian Codes read “January.” Gothofredus has excellently shown that this should be corrected to “June”; the manuscripts of our collection confirm this emendation.] at Constantinople, in the consulship of Eucherius and Syagrius. [Col. 0682D–0683A]

### 396. Again, in the same book and title

The emperor Theodosius Augustus and Valentinian Caesar, to Faustus, prefect of the City.

We order that the heretical Manichaeans [Editorial note: Gothofredus’ Theodosian Code reads “schismatics” and omits “or Mathematicians.” Other editions of that Code before the Paris edition include both. Another law, law 64, issued in the same year at Aquileia on 8 August, reads: “heretical Manichaeans, or schismatics, and every sect,” etc.], or “Mathematicians,” and every sect hostile to Catholics be expelled from the very sight of the city of Rome [Editorial note: Likewise the Theodosian Code reads “Rome.”], so that it may not be defiled by the contagion of the criminals’ presence [Editorial note: The Vienna manuscript and Gothofredus read “be fouled”; “the Catholic [city]” is understood. Shortly afterward Gothofredus reads “the most urgent agitation”; the Tilian and Cujacian editions incorrectly read “the most vigorous admonition.”].

The greatest agitation must be directed especially against those who, through wicked persuasions, suspend themselves from communion with the venerable pope, whose schism also corrupts the remaining people. After prior notice, we grant them a period of twenty days, within which, unless they return to the unity of communion, they shall be expelled as far as the one-hundredth milestone and suffer in the solitude they have chosen.

Issued on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August at Aquileia, in the consulship of Theodosius Augustus for the eleventh time [Editorial note: Quesnellus reads “Theodosius Augustus for the tenth time.” Corrected in accordance with Coustant’s Vienna manuscripts and the common text of the Theodosian Code.] and Valentinian Caesar. [Col. 0683B–0684A]

## CHAPTER LV

[Editorial note: This letter of Damasus appears in the same form in manuscripts of the Hispana collection and in two manuscripts of the encyclical letters to Emperor Leo cited by Coustant. A different form, published by Holstenius from another Barberinian manuscript, inserts the Catholic confession of faith into the letter to Paulinus after the words of the second period, “may wish to be joined, dearest brother.” Coustant found this form in the two very ancient Corbie and Fossat collections; it is likewise inserted from an older exemplar in Book II of Arnobius’ *Conflict with Serapion*, published by Fevardentius in the appendix to the Works of St Irenaeus, Cologne, 1596. The Collection of Dionysian Additions separates the letter to Paulinus from the confession of faith as though they were two distinct documents: it gives the latter as title 86, under the heading “Confession of the Catholic Faith,” as in our collection, and the former as title 88, under the heading “Pope Damasus’ reply to Jerome’s request, to Paulinus.” The same distinction occurs in the older collection preserved in Vatican manuscript 1342 and Barberinian manuscript 2888. For the confession of faith is not only placed before the letter to Paulinus and each is copied under a distinct title—the former as title 36, the latter as title 37—but under the same title 36, after the confession, is added the confession of the presbyters or deacons of the Church of Constantinople, which appears in this collection in the present chapter. Other collections present only the confession of faith, prefacing it with the Nicene Creed: thus the Lucensis manuscript and Colbertinus 784; see note 10 (below, col. 685g). In Vatican manuscripts 1337 and 1338, which contain certain items from the Hadrian collection, under the heading by which the Council of Nicaea is presented, this same confession of faith follows the creed of that council without any special heading. In another most ancient collection, Vatican manuscript 1322, it is joined with the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed; see vol. IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 2064. Theodoret inserted this same confession, translated into Greek, in Book V, chapter 11 of his *History*. It is also cited by the Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon in their address to Emperor Marcian, vol. IV of the Councils, col. 1766.

St Celestine I, in a fragment of a sermon preserved for us by Arnobius in Book II of the *Conflict with Serapion*, adducing two testimonies of Damasus—one from the confession of faith, the other from the letter to Paulinus, which in our collection precedes the confession—not only cites the confession first, but also describes it as if it were a letter written to the same Paulinus. For he says: “Likewise my predecessor Damasus, writing to Paulinus, bishop of the Church of Antioch, says among other things: ‘We anathematize those who maintain that there are two Sons of God: one begotten of the Father before the ages, and another born of the Virgin through the assumption of flesh.’” These are almost the same words as those in the confession of faith. Then follows: “Likewise Damasus himself, a man of apostolic memory, in ANOTHER letter to Paulinus: ‘We anathematize those who confess two sons in the Savior, one before the incarnation and another after the assumption of flesh from the Virgin, and who do not confess that the same Son of God, both before and afterward, is Christ, the Son of the Lord God, who was born of the Virgin.’” You will find these words in the letter to Paulinus.

Celestine I therefore distinguished two letters of Damasus to Paulinus, and in precisely the order in which they are distinguished in the two aforementioned Italian collections, namely, the Dionysian Additions and the other, older collection contained in Vatican manuscript 1342 and Barberinian manuscript 2888. Hence the authors of these collections found them separately distinguished in their manuscripts, just as Celestine found them separate in the apostolic archives. From these Italian collections, which agree with Celestine’s testimony, Baluzius’ opinion concerning two letters of Damasus is strongly confirmed. This also seems capable of proof from the words of the letter which Celestine calls the second, “we have sent the faith,” which indicate that the confession of faith had earlier been sent to Paulinus.

In his notice on Damasus’ letter 5, no. 2, P. Coustant objects that the ancient Royal, Corbie, and Beauvais manuscripts, when they append the confession of faith to the letter to Paulinus, preface it with this title: “Here begins [the text] of Pope Damasus of the city of Rome to Paulinus, bishop of the city of Antioch, concerning the articles of faith against the heretics Macedonius, Eunomius, and Apollinaris”; and at the end of the confession add: “Here ends the Catholic confession which Pope Damasus appended to his letter to Paulinus against the heretics Macedonius, Eunomius, and Apollinaris.” But the authority of these codices, which is overthrown by the manuscript exemplars of the two collections mentioned, seems in no way comparable to Celestine I’s testimony, which is greatly confirmed by Damasus’ own quoted words, “we have sent the faith.” Perhaps Damasus attached the faith previously sent—as commonly happens in such matters—again to a second letter; and therefore in some collections, as in ours, it is placed beneath that same letter, whereas in others it is inserted into it. Only one thing opposes this opinion concerning a double letter of Damasus: the simple confession of faith displays no epistolary form. Yet since the confession of faith is presented without any letter in certain very ancient collections and also by Theodoret, this proves that it was distinct from the earlier letter by which it was sent or separately appended, and which Celestine found separate from the other letter. It could therefore have happened that the confession was preserved when copied without the earlier letter, while that letter itself perished. [Col. 0683B–0685C]

Pope Damasus to Paulinus, bishop of Antioch. [Col. 0685C]

[Editorial note: Thus Quesnellus, together with the Thuaneus manuscript, to which the other ancient copies of this collection agree. The words *formula fidei subrogata*, taken in the ablative case, refer to the shorter formula added at the end, to which the Eutychians returning from heresy were required to subscribe. The more recent Oxford manuscript reads *Formula fidei ab haeresi revertenti*, “formula of faith for one returning from heresy,” where *formula* in the nominative indicates Damasus’ own formula.]

### The substituted formula of faith to which those returning from heresy were required to subscribe

To his most beloved brother Paulinus, Damasus.

[Editorial note: The manuscripts of the Dionysian Additions read “through my very son”; Holstenius’ edition reads “through my son.”]

I had sent a letter to you through my son Vitalis, leaving everything to your will and judgment; and through the presbyter Petronius I had briefly indicated that I had been somewhat disturbed when his departure was already imminent. Therefore, lest any scruple remain with you, and lest your prudent caution perhaps delay the admission of those wishing to be joined to the Church [Editorial note: Quesnellus reads “and those wishing … by proving.” We have restored the formerly current reading, which the other manuscripts support.
