Shortly after “faith,” editions before Quesnellus insert “our,” and then read “who are joined to us in the communion of that faith, or of the same faith.”], we have sent the faith—not so much to you, who are joined to the communion of that faith, as to those who, by subscribing to it, may wish through you—that is, through us—to be joined to you, dearest brother. [Col. 0684D–0685A]

Accordingly, if my aforesaid son Vitalis and those who are with him wish to be associated with you, they must first subscribe to that exposition of the faith which was established at Nicaea by the devout will of the Fathers. Then, since no one can apply medicine to future wounds, that heresy must be uprooted which is said to have later sprouted in the East [Editorial note: This guards against the heresy of the Apollinarians, of which the presbyter Vitalis had become suspect; he later embraced that heresy and was made bishop of the Apollinarians living at Antioch.]. That is, it must be confessed that Wisdom, the Word, the Son of God himself, assumed a human body, a soul, and a faculty of perception—in other words, the complete Adam—and, to put it more explicitly, the whole of our former human nature without sin. [Col. 0685B–0686A]

For just as, when we confess that he assumed a human body, we do not immediately add to him the sinful passions of human beings, so, when we say that he assumed both a human soul and human perception, we do not thereby immediately say that he became subject to the sin of human thoughts.

But if anyone says that the Word took the place of the human faculty of perception in the Lord’s flesh, the Catholic Church anathematizes him. It likewise anathematizes those who confess two sons in the Savior: one before the incarnation and another after the assumption of flesh from the Virgin, and who do not confess that the same Son of God existed both before and afterward.

Whoever wishes to subscribe to this letter [Editorial note: Quesnellus inserted *therefore*; we have deleted it with the other printed editions and our manuscripts.]—provided that he has first subscribed to the ecclesiastical canons, which you know very well, and to the Nicene faith [Editorial note: The ecclesiastical canons are distinguished from the Nicene faith. Damasus seems especially to have in view the Sardican canons, which, being joined with the Nicene canons, circulated in the Roman Church under the name of the Nicene canons, as we demonstrated in the Treatise, part II, chapter 1. He immediately confirms in the confession of faith to be supplied one of those canons, which forbids translations of bishops; see note 18 (below, col. 688g). Holstenius, with the Roman editors, reads: “to the ecclesiastical canons, which you know very well, and to the Nicene faith.” Several manuscripts indeed read “to the Nicene faith,” but none “to the ecclesiastical canons.” Quesnellus reads “he may subscribe,” against the printed editions and our manuscripts. Subsequently the Roman edition, Holstenius, and Labbe read “you will have”; the older editions of the Councils, with some manuscripts, “you ought to have”; Vatican manuscript 1342, “you must.”]—you must receive without any ambiguity. This is not because you could not propose these very statements which we have written for the reception of those who are converting, but because our agreement grants you a free example in receiving them. [Col. 0686B]

### Catholic confession of faith which Pope Damasus sent to Paulinus, bishop of Antioch

[Editorial note, Col. 0685D–0686D: Thus the Thuaneus and Vindobonensis manuscripts, together with the Barberinian manuscripts and Vatican manuscript 1342, and the Collection of Dionysian Additions. The Oxford manuscript alone has: “Again, a rule of faith under the same chapter.” In exemplars of different origin the title is otherwise expressed.

The Lucensis-Colbertine collection omits the preceding letter, but prefixes this heading: “Here begins what Pope Damasus wrote concerning the Council of Nicaea to Paulinus, bishop of the city of Antioch.” It begins with the Nicene Creed, given in the ancient Roman translation such as is found in Leo’s Letter 165. Solely against the error of the Macedonians, after the words “and [supply: in] the Holy Spirit,” these words are added: “neither made nor created, but of the substance [sic] of the Godhead”; and finally the Nicene anathema is set out in full, as may be seen from the Lucensis manuscript in P. Domenico Mansi, *Appendix to the Councils*, vol. II, p. 21. Then, without another heading, the present confession of faith is appended: “After this Nicene Council, which was in the city ...”

P. Coustant, *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, vol. I, col. 510, note n, cites two other Colbertine manuscripts, 1863 and 1868, which likewise prefix the Nicene Creed. Manuscript 1868 has this title: “Here begins the faith written at Nicaea by 318 bishops: We believe in one God,” etc., as in the Nicene Creed; when that has been copied in full, it adds: “And because later this error became established, so that some men with sacrilegious mouth dared to say that the Holy Spirit was made,” etc. Manuscript 1863 reads: “Here begins the part of the faith concerning that which was written at Nicaea, from the place” (read: *to* that place, that is, to the final words of the Nicene faith) “where it says, ‘The Catholic and Apostolic Church anathematizes these’; which faith together with the Nicene synod is written in this book [of Damasus].” Then follows: “And afterward, because this error became established,” etc., “some men with sacrilegious mouth,” etc.

From the authority of these codices, and also from Damasus’s preceding words in which he requires subscription to the Nicene faith, it must be said that the same pope prefixed the Nicene faith to the confession of faith which he sent to Paulinus. In Vatican manuscript 1322, mentioned in vol. II of the *Observations on Dissertation* 9, the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed is likewise read as prefixed to this confession of faith. This confession was celebrated among the Easterners; Theodoret gives it in Greek in Book V, chapter 11.]

[Note: [Col. 0686D] Thus read the Vindobonensis manuscripts and others of this collection, which P. Coustant praises. In Merlin and Crabbe it reads: “After the Council of Nicaea, another council was later assembled in the city of Rome, in which the catholic bishops made a statement concerning the Holy Spirit. For afterward this error arose, etc.” This reading is certainly clearer, but it is found only in manuscripts of Hispanic origin belonging to the Gallican recension, and in Isidorian manuscripts, in which, as we have noted elsewhere, arbitrary corrections frequently occur. Justellus’s manuscript, cited by Labbe, vol. II, col. 1061, is Isidorian. Quesnellus gives this reading: “After the Council of Nicaea, the catholic bishops later assembled in the city of Rome and added a statement concerning the Holy Spirit. For afterward the error had arisen among the Arians, so that certain people, etc.” Whether he wrote this from the Oxford manuscript or from his own conjecture, we do not know. Here, certainly, one sees the effort of a man attempting to correct a difficult passage. The older books, however, with great agreement, read *is error* or *hic error inolevit*—“this error arose”; and in none of them is this error attributed to the Arians. Some copies noted above (col. 0683 f.) state that this confession of faith was sent against Macedonius, Eunomius, and Apollinaris. The Vatican manuscript 1342 and two others cited by Coustant, while preferring our reading, have *catholici episcopi* with different punctuation instead of *a catholicis episcopis*. We would more readily have accepted the reading of the two Vatican manuscripts 1337 and 1338, if they belonged to our collection: “After the Council of Nicaea, a council was assembled in the city of Rome by the catholic bishops, and they added a statement concerning the Holy Spirit, etc.” A more genuine reading, however, is found in the Lucensis and Colbertinus manuscripts, in which the Nicene Creed precedes this confession of faith; the Vatican manuscript 1322 agrees with them, prefacing it with the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed: “After this Council of Nicaea, the council which was assembled in the city of Rome by the catholic bishops added a statement concerning the Holy Spirit. And because afterward this error arose, etc.” Quesnellus notes in the margin: “The Vulgate and Theodoret, book V, chapter 11, have only the following at the beginning: ‘For after the Council of Nicaea this error arose, etc.’” Theodoret, that is, from whom his common version was inserted in volume II of the Councils, col. 1061, evidently thought that certain words of the opening should be omitted.]

After the Council of Nicaea, which was later assembled in the city of Rome [Col. 0687A] by the catholic bishops 401 [Note: [Col. 0687C] The two cited manuscripts, Vatican 1337 and 1338, read *et addiderunt*—“and they added.” Henricus Valesius, in his notes on Theodoret, book V, chapter 11, thinks that this addition was made at the Roman council under Saint Sylvester. But what was done at Rome concerning the Holy Spirit after Nicaea is attributed to Damasus by Vigilius in the earlier constitution, no. 26. This addition to the Creed, however, seems to have been made not at the synod in which this confession of faith was written, but at an earlier one, as the word *addiderunt* indicates; moreover, it more properly signifies an addition to the Creed than a separate decree concerning the Holy Spirit. What this addition was can be gathered from the Lucensis and Colbertinus collections: in the Nicene Creed, as we observed in note 10 above (col. 0685 g), after the words “and in the Holy Spirit” there are added the words “not made, nor created, but of the substance of the Godhead,” which overthrow the Macedonian error.] they added a statement concerning the Holy Spirit; and because afterward this error arose, so that certain people dared, with sacrilegious speech, to say that the Holy Spirit was made [Note: [Col. 0687D] The Oxford manuscript omits *per Filium*—“through the Son.” Immediately afterward it reads *anathematizamus*. Quesnellus added *inquiunt*—“they say”—although all our manuscripts and those of Coustant agree in omitting it.] through the Son, we anathematize those who do not proclaim with complete freedom that he is of one power and substance with the Father and the Son.

We likewise anathematize those who follow the error of Sabellius, saying that he who is the Father is the same as the Son [Note: [Col. 0688B] Quesnellus reads *dicentem*—“saying.” We preferred the reading of the Vindobonensis and Coustant’s manuscripts, which agrees with Theodoret’s Greek version. Shortly afterward, the Lucensis and some other manuscripts read *quem et Filium*—“whom they also call the Son.” We retained the reading of the copies belonging to our collection, with which Theodoret agrees.].

We anathematize Arius and Eunomius, who, although differing in expression, assert with equal impiety that the Son and the Holy Spirit are created beings [Note: [Col. 0688B] The Lucensis reads *creatum*—“created.”].

We anathematize the Macedonians, who, coming from the stock of Arius, changed not their treachery but only its name.

We anathematize Photinus, who, restoring the heresy of Ebion, confesses that the Lord Jesus Christ is from Mary alone.

We anathematize those who assert that there are two Sons: one before the ages, and another after the assumption of flesh from the Virgin.

We anathematize those who say that, in place of the rational and intelligible soul of a human being, the Word of God dwelt in human flesh; [Col. 0688A] whereas the Son himself is the Word of God, and he did not take the place of a rational and intelligible soul in his body, but assumed and saved our soul—that is, a rational and intelligible soul—without sin.

We anathematize those who contend that the Word, the Son of God, was separated from the Father by extension or contraction [Note: [Col. 0688B] Manuscripts of other collections add the conjunction *et*, which they immediately delete before *insubstantivum*. Quesnellus alone inserts *esse*—“to be”—before *separatum*.] and is without substance, and that he will have an end [Note: [Col. 0688C] Although Quesnellus found the following sentence not only in the printed editions but also in the Thuanus manuscript and in Theodoret, where it is read in all our copies, he nevertheless followed the Oxford exemplar and relegated it to the lower margin. P. Coustant, who compared many ancient books, noted that it is absent from a single Colbertinus manuscript of another collection, which also lacks Damasus’s letter. If it is likewise omitted at this point in the Isidorian manuscripts, this must be attributed to the decision of the person who thought that the passage should be supplied separately under the heading “On priests who migrate from their own churches to others.” All our books, however, include it here, including the Vatican Palatine manuscript 574, which contains a very ancient Gallican collection resembling the Morbacensis. That manuscript cites this one decree from Damasus’s letter under the title “The Authority of Saint Damasus to Paulinus.” This pontiff, who was in communion with Paulinus of Antioch, inserted this decree against Meletius, who had transferred from the Church of Sebaste to that of Antioch. The decree agrees with canon 1 of Sardica. We have printed the reading of our manuscripts. Quesnellus, however, reads: “Those who have migrated from churches to churches we hold alien from our communion until they return to the cities in which they were first established. But if someone has migrated elsewhere and another has been ordained in the place of one who is still living, the one who abandoned his city shall remain deprived of priestly dignity until his successor rests in the Lord. If anyone else migrates elsewhere, etc., until a successor, etc.”].

We likewise hold those who have migrated from churches to churches alien from our communion until they return to the cities in which they were first established. But if, while one person has migrated elsewhere, another has been ordained in the place of the living man, let the one who abandoned his city remain without priestly dignity until his successor rests in the Lord.

If anyone does not say that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have always existed, let him be anathema [Note: [Col. 0688D] Thus read our manuscripts, the Vindobonensis, Vatican 1322, and Lucensis, together with three of Coustant’s manuscripts. In Vatican 1342, and in Merlin and Crabbe, *esse*—“to exist”—is lacking. Holstenius, together with the Corbeiensis collection, reads “to have existed and to exist.” Quesnellus alone has *exstitisse*—“to have existed.”].

If anyone does not say that the Son was born from the Father, that is, from his divine substance, let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that the Word of God, the Son of God, is God, just as his Father is God, able to do all things, knowing all things, and equal to the Father [Note: [Col. 0688D] The Lucensis, together with Theodoret’s printed version, reads: “If anyone does not say that the Son is true God, just as his Father is true God.” The same reading appears in Vatican 1322, except that *verbum*—“word”—is mistakenly written for *verum*—“true”—in both places.], let him be anathema.

If anyone says that, when the Son of God was present in the flesh and was on earth, he was not in heaven with the Father [Note: [Col. 0689B] Thus read the Vindobonensis, Lucensis, and Vatican 1322, together with Coustant. Quesnellus reads: “was not in heaven with the Father; let him be anathema.”], let him be anathema.

If anyone says that, in the suffering of the cross, the Lord God, the Son of God, endured pain [Note: [Col. 0689B] The Lucensis reads *sentiebat*—“felt”; immediately afterward it reads, with Holstenius, *quam induerat forma servi*—“which he had assumed, the form of a servant.” Coustant, with the Corbeiensis manuscript, reads *quia induerat formam servi*—“because he had assumed the form of a servant.” The common version of the Councils, based on Theodoret, reads *quam induerat in forma servi*—“which he had assumed in the form of a servant.” We have adopted the reading of the Vindobonensis manuscript of this collection, Vatican 1342, and five of Coustant’s ancient manuscripts. Quesnellus, omitting certain words, reads: “which he had assumed and had taken for himself the form of a servant; let him be anathema.”] and not the flesh with the soul which he had assumed, the form of a servant which he had taken to himself, as Scripture says; let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that he sits at the right hand of the Father in the flesh that he assumed, in which he will come to judge the living and the dead, let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that the Holy Spirit is truly and properly from the Father, [Note: [Col. 0689C] Vatican 1342 reads *sicut Filius Dei*—“as the Son of God”; Coustant reads *sicut Filius*—“as the Son.” Immediately afterward, the common version from Theodoret adds *et Deum Dei Verbum*—“and God, the Word of God.”] as the Son is from the divine substance, and that he is true God, let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that the Holy Spirit is able to do all things, knows all things, and is everywhere, just as the Father and the Son, let him be anathema.

If anyone says that the Holy Spirit is a creature, or was made through the Son [Col. 0689B], let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that the Father made all things through the Son [Note: [Col. 0689D] The common version of Theodoret adds *postea incarnatum*—“afterward incarnate.” In Theodoret’s Greek, *τοῦ σαρκωθέντος*—“of the one who became flesh”—is read without *postea*. Since Epiphanius’s translation does not understand this noun and no Latin manuscript contains anything equivalent, the addition is evidently secondary, as Coustant observed.] and the Holy Spirit, that is, things visible and invisible, let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one Godhead, one power, one majesty, [Note: [Col. 0689D] We have added *potentiam unam*—“one might/power”—from the Vindobonensis, Thuanus, Lucensis, Vatican 1342, and other manuscripts of Coustant.] one glory, one dominion, one kingdom, and one will and truth, let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that the three true persons of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are equal, always living, containing all things visible and invisible, able to do all things, judging all things, giving life to all things, making all things, [Note: [Col. 0689D] The Lucensis, Corbeiensis, and two Colbertinus manuscripts, together with Holstenius and Coustant, read *omnia quae sunt salvanda salvantes*—“saving all things that are to be saved.”] and saving all things, let him be anathema.

If anyone [Col. 0690A] does not say that the Holy Spirit is to be worshiped by every creature, just as the Son and the Father, let him be anathema.

If anyone thinks rightly concerning the Father and the Son but holds an erroneous belief concerning the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0689D] The Oxford manuscript has only *non recte*—“not rightly,” followed by *anathema sit*. If anyone says, “God the Father and God the Son,” etc.], he is a heretic; for all heretics who think wrongly concerning the Son of God and the Holy Spirit are found in the unbelief of the Jews and the Gentiles.

But if anyone divides [Note: [Col. 0689D] Coustant, with three of his manuscripts and our Vatican manuscripts 630, 1340, 1341, and 1342, as well as Vatican Palatine 575, preferred *patiatur*—“suffers.” But *partiatur*—“divides”—is found not only in the manuscripts of this collection but also in the ancient Corbeiensis and Lucensis, and in the exemplar from which Theodoret rendered the text into Greek. Holstenius reads: “Let him divide the Godhead, saying separately, ‘God the Father.’” Although *patiatur* fits better with what follows—“suffers . . . to be called gods”—we did not remove the reading of our collection, which is supported by other very ancient manuscripts. Vatican 1342, although it reads *patiatur*, later prefers *deos dicit*—“he calls them gods.” The Lucensis reads *deos dicere*—“to call them gods.”] the Godhead, saying that God the Father, God his Son, and God the Holy Spirit are called gods, and not one God, because of the one divinity and power which we believe and know to belong to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, [Note: [Col. 0690C] The Thuanus and Vatican 1342 manuscripts add *Deum*—“God,” a word that seems superfluous. Holstenius reads *Deum verum*—“the true God.” Epiphanius, translating from Theodoret, has *Deum unum*—“one God.” Since he does not add “in three persons,” the Greek words in Theodoret, *ἐν τρισὶν ὑποστάσεσιν*—“in three hypostases/persons”—appear to be secondary. The Lucensis and Vatican 1342, with Coustant, read: “But removing the Son or the Holy Spirit, let him think that the Father alone is called or believed to be God,” etc.] and, removing the Son or the Holy Spirit, thinks that the Father alone should be called or believed to be one God, let him be anathema.

For the name “gods” has been imposed and granted by God to the angels and to all the saints [Note: [Col. 0690C] The following passage, up to “the demented Gentiles,” is absent from the Oxford manuscript. After *anathema sit*, the Vindobonensis, Lucensis, and Vatican 1342 contain the intrusive words: “To all, indeed to the Jews, that”; then follow the words “the name of gods among the angels.” We have added *a Deo*—“by God”—from all our manuscripts and those of Coustant, supported also by Theodoret’s Greek version.].

But concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, because of their one and equal divinity, we are shown and taught not the name “gods” but “God,” so that we may believe that we are baptized in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit alone, and not in the names of archangels [Note: [Col. 0690D] The Lucensis and Vatican 1342, with Coustant, read *aut angelorum*—“or of angels”; immediately afterward, following *dementes*, they add *faciunt*—“they do.”] and angels, as heretics, Jews, or even the demented Gentiles do.

Therefore this is the salvation of Christians: that, believing in the Trinity—that is, in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—we should without doubt believe these things concerning it: that its Godhead and power, majesty and substance are true, sole, and one [Note: [Col. 0690D] We have inserted the words *haec ejusdem*—“these things of the same”—omitted by Quesnellus, from the Vindobonensis, Lucensis, Vatican 1342, and two ancient manuscripts of P. Coustant. Holstenius retains *ejusdem* without *haec*; the ancient Corbeiensis has *haec* without *ejusdem*. Coustant, with the Colbertinus manuscript, preferred *eamdem*—“the same”—without doubt: “let us believe, so that we may deserve to attain eternal life.”].

[Note: [Col. 0690D] Quesnellus prefixed to this formula of faith the title “This writing is to be accepted by one coming from heresy,” which we deleted, following the excellent Vindobonensis manuscript of this collection. Two other ancient collections present the same formula: one, the copy Vatican 1342, after the preceding confession of faith [Col. 0691C]; the other, Vallicellian A. 5 of Dionysius’s Additions, no. 125. Both give it the following title: “The Confession of the Presbyters or Deacons of the Church of Constantinople.” This formula is a shorter version of the one presented earlier, at the end of chapter 53. We conjectured that it was composed in accordance with the thought of Saint Leo, when the Constantinopolitan clergy suspected of the Eutychian heresy were being received, in note 9 on letter 163, vol. I, col. 1343 (our edition, col. 1147, no. g). Quesnellus began as follows: “I, that presbyter or deacon of that Church, by this writing . . .” We have followed our three manuscripts—the two Vindobonenses, the Vatican, and the Vallicellian—as well as Quesnellus’s Thuanus manuscript.]

I, that deacon or presbyter of the Church of Constantinople, by this writing, which I have copied out in my own hand, profess that concerning the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ I hold the faith which the most holy Synod of Nicaea and the venerable Council of Chalcedon established by evangelical and apostolic authority, and which the letter of the most blessed Pope Leo, sent to Flavianus, bishop of the city of Constantinople, set forth with a proclamation of the clearest truth. I declare that Nestorius and Eutyches, together with their doctrines and followers, deserve eternal anathema.

[Note: [Col. 0691C] We restored the order of the superior manuscripts, the Vindobonensis and Thuanus. Following the order of the more recent Oxford manuscript, Quesnellus had transcribed in this chapter 56 Cyril’s letter to Nestorius; we shall present that letter with the aforementioned manuscripts in chapter 66. The Oxford manuscript, however, had already transcribed this letter together with the other Leonine materials.]

### CHAPTER LVI. Letter of Eusebius, Bishop of Milan, to Pope Leo

To the holy and most blessed Lord Father Leo, Eusebius.

“By the Lord’s favor, our brothers whom we sent to the East have returned,” etc. The complete letter is given as letter 97 in volume I.

### CHAPTER LVII. Letter of Ravennius and the Other Bishops of Gaul to Pope Leo

To the truly holy, deservedly most blessed, and apostolically honored Pope Leo, Ravennius, Rusticus, etc.

“Your Blessedness’s letter having been delivered to us,” etc., as found in letter 99, volume I.

### CHAPTER LVIII

[Note: [Col. 0691D] “This constitution of Gelasius,” says Quesnellus, “is found only in the Thuanus manuscript; it is absent from the Oxford manuscript. Since we had resolved from the beginning to follow the latter’s order, so that it would not be interrupted here, we have inserted this constitution without a chapter title or number.” He adds: “I note also that this constitution does not seem to have been drawn from the same source as the other parts of this manuscript. In many places it is uncorrected, and the division of the decrees is less suitable. Although this constitution is absent from the Oxford manuscript, which is less exact in other respects, it is found not only in the Thuanus but also in two Vindobonenses, in the Ubertinus, and in other manuscripts of this collection; hence there is no doubt that it belongs to the collection itself. It is also contained in the other collections—Vatican Regina 1997, Lucensis 88, Colbertinus 784, Vatican 1342, Barb. 2888, the Dionysian, Hispanic, and Isidorian collections—in which a different division of the decrees, namely into twelve or twenty-eight chapters, and other distinctive variants indicate that these collectors drew from other sources.”]

The Constitutions of Saint Pope Gelasius

[Note: [Col. 0692C] The manuscripts of three collections—the Vatican Regina, Lucensis, and Vatican 1342—give this heading: “Gelasius, bishop, to all the bishops established throughout each province.” The Dionysian, Hispanic, and Isidorian manuscripts read: “Gelasius to all the brother bishops established throughout Lucania, Bruttium, and Sicily.” A similar variety of headings is sometimes found in the letters of other pontiffs in different collections, as may be seen, among others, in Leo’s letter 7, which in the Dionysian manuscripts and others derived from Dionysius is said to have been sent to all the bishops established throughout Italy. But in two other collections, the Corbeiensis and our own, it reads: “To all the bishops established throughout the various provinces.” This seems to have arisen because such letters, initially sent by the Roman pontiffs to particular provinces, were later shared by the bishops of those provinces with neighboring bishops and subsequently passed into other provinces, so that they could be said to have been delivered to all bishops throughout each province. See note 2 to Quesnellus’s notes on Saint Leo’s letter 4, volume II.]

To our most beloved brothers, all the bishops, Gelasius.

We are constrained by the necessary consideration of circumstances [Note: [Col. 0692D] The Dionysian reads more aptly *dispensatione*—“by the administration/management [of circumstances].” The Vatican Regina and Isidorian manuscripts read *dispensatione*.], and are obliged by the governance of the apostolic see to weigh the decrees of the ancient canons and measure them against the precepts of our former bishops and predecessors, so that what the necessity of the present times demands should be relaxed for the restoration of the churches [Note: [Col. 0692D] Other collections read *restaurandis*—“for churches to be restored.”], after careful consideration, may be moderated as far as possible; thus we will neither seem altogether to exceed the pattern of the ancient rules nor, in restoring the offices of the clerical militia [Note: [Col. 0692D] Thus read the Dionysian and the better manuscripts, as the context also requires: *exigente etiam contextu*. Quesnellus reads *quae*—“which.”], allow the functions of clerical service to remain entirely lacking in churches where the incursion of war and famine has so consumed them throughout various parts of Italy that, as we have learned repeatedly from our brother and fellow bishop John, bishop of the Church of Ravenna, the service of ministers has everywhere failed [Note: [Col. 0692D] Others read *ministeriorum*—“of ministries.”], unless the intervals anciently fixed for ecclesiastical promotions are temporarily relaxed—without which the churches cannot be administered [Note: [Col. 0692D] Quesnellus, with the common version of the Councils, reads *nequeant*—“cannot.” We have followed our manuscripts.]—and the churches are left completely deprived of their sacred orders. Moreover, in many places, through the lack of adequate assistance, the saving aid by which souls are redeemed is absent, and we would be implicated in great guilt if, under the pressure of so grave a danger, we did not in some measure take counsel [Note: [Col. 0692D] The common version of the Councils has *videamur*—“we may seem”—instead of *consulamus*. It would be preferable to retain both, so that *videamur innecti*—“we may seem to be implicated”—would be written after *consulamus*.].

Therefore, while the ancient statutes remain in force out of reverence for them, and ought regularly to be observed whenever no hardship of circumstances or times presses urgently [Note: [Col. 0692D] Others read *custodire*—“to preserve”; immediately afterward, *usquequaque adeo*—“everywhere to such an extent.”], we grant to churches that are either entirely deprived of ministers or so stripped of adequate services that they cannot supply the divine gifts to the congregations belonging to them the right to regulate, both for the establishment and promotion of clerical office, the periods [Note: [Col. 0692D] The common version of the Councils, together with Vatican 1342 and the Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts, reads *obsequii*—“service.”] in the following manner.

#### I. On the Order of Monks

[Col. 0693A]

If someone who has been trained in a religious vocation and in monastic disciplines comes forward for clerical office, his life in past years must first be investigated. It must be established that he is not tainted by any grave crime; that perhaps he has not had a second wife, nor is shown to have taken a woman abandoned by her husband; that he has not undergone public penance; that no part of his body appears mutilated; [Note: [Col. 0693C] Others read: “if he is not subject to servile or hereditary status.”] that he is not bound by servile or hereditary status; that he is already shown to be released from the bonds of the municipal curia; and that he has acquired the literary education without which he could scarcely fulfill the ministry of doorkeeper [Note: [Col. 0693C] Thus also the Vatican, Hispanic, and Isidorian manuscripts. The common version, together with the Dionysian, reads [Col. 0693D] *ostiarii possit implere ministerium*—“could fulfill the ministry of doorkeeper.” Vatican 1342 likewise adds *ministerium*. Vatican Regina 1997 reads “a doorkeeper could fulfill the ministry.”].

If he is supported by all the qualifications just mentioned, he shall immediately become a lector, notary, or certainly a defensor; after three months he shall become an acolyte, especially if his age also supports this; in the sixth month he shall receive the title of subdeacon; and, if he is of modest conduct and honorable disposition, in the ninth month he shall be a deacon, and after completing a year, a presbyter. Yet the devotion freely embraced by his holy vocation must be shown to have supplied what the intervals of years would otherwise have contributed.

#### II. On the Laity

If someone from among the laity is to be assigned to ecclesiastical offices [Note: [Col. 0693D] The Vindobonensis reads, corruptly, *ad ecclesiastici . . . officiis*. Quesnellus emended this to *ad ecclesiasticum . . . officium*—“to ecclesiastical office.” We preferred to correct the text according to the reading of the other collections.], this person ought to be examined with all the greater care in each of the matters set out above, in proportion to the known difference between worldly and religious life. For suitable ministers must be restored to the Church, not people of unsuitable merit forced upon it; and the more the time normally required for attaining these offices is shortened, the more carefully it is necessary to seek in their training whatever may make them fit for sacred service. Their moral character must be shown to possess what a longer habit of life has not supplied, lest, under the pretext of remedying the shortage of clergy, we be judged to have introduced vices into divine worship rather than legitimately secured the advantage of the household.

For their promotions, we nevertheless allow an additional six months beyond the prescribed years [Note: [Col. 0693D] The Vindobonensis corruptly reads *super anni aetas*. Vatican 1342 has *super anima aetas*; Vatican Regina, *super enim aetam*. The true reading is supplied by the Dionysian, Hispanic, and Isidorian manuscripts. Quesnellus reads: “if age permits it.” Immediately afterward, instead of *praerogamus*, other collections read *subrogamus*—“we substitute.”], since, as has been said, it is fitting that a distinction be maintained between a person devoted to divine worship and one coming from lay life.

We have nevertheless judged this concession should be granted only so that those churches in which, because of the ravages of war, no ministers at all or only a few remain may be renewed [Note: [Col. 0693D] We have added *illis*—“for those”—from our manuscripts and other printed collections.]. Once these have been restored, with God’s favor, let the ancient form of the fathers’ canons be preserved in appointing ecclesiastical ranks; and let it in no way prevail against those who are being provided for as a remedy for an accidental shortage, not by a new law contrary to the decrees of their predecessors [Note: [Col. 0693D] Quesnellus reads *proponuntur*—“are proposed.” We preferred the reading of the other collections and printed editions, as required by the context.].

For the other churches, which you know have not been devastated by a similar calamity [Note: [Col. 0694C] The Vindobonensis, together with the common version of the Councils, omits *cognoscitis*—“you know.” Immediately afterward Quesnellus reads *factis*—“having been made”; the Vindobonensis, *facientibus*—“doing.” Vatican 1342 and Vatican Regina, together with the Dionysian, Hispanic, and Isidorian manuscripts, more suitably read *faciendis*—“to be carried out.”], it is fitting that the former rule be maintained in carrying out ordinations. Therefore, admonished by this opportunity, let us cherish more earnestly the observance of the venerable canons [Note: [Col. 0694C] Vatican Regina, the Dionysian, and the common version of the Councils read *delegamus*—“we entrust/commit.”], warning the consciences of those in every rank not to attempt unlawful excesses. Let no bishop presume that he may assign to the divine mysteries men who are bigamists, or who have taken wives abandoned by others, or who have undergone penance, or who lack literary education, or whose bodies are mutilated, or who are bound by servile status, or entangled in the bonds of the municipal curia or public affairs, or who have been examined indiscriminately without waiting for a suitable period [Note: [Col. 0694D] In the first hand of the Vindobonensis it read: “lest perhaps any of the bishops should be confident that he may ordain bigamists or those taking wives.” From this probably arose the emendation accepted by Quesnellus: “lest perhaps there be bishops who are bigamists or who take wives.” But this chapter concerns not bishops, but laymen being ordained. In the second ancient hand of the Vindobonensis, *ne forsitan* was corrected to *nec fas*—“nor is it lawful.” Since the other manuscript collections and printed editions approve this reading, we have corrected the rest of the text from them.].

[Note: [Col. 0694D] Vatican 1342, which divides this constitution into twelve chapters, marks this as chapter 1, with the title “On the Dedication of a Basilica.”]

#### III. On the Dedication of Basilicas

Let no one, merely according to his own will, attempt to encroach upon another’s rights. Without a just command and disposition of the apostolic see, no one shall dare to dedicate newly established basilicas without the customary authorizations having been requested; nor shall they seek to claim for themselves clergy belonging to another’s authority [Note: [Col. 0694D] The printed editions add *episcopi*—“bishops.”].

#### IV. On Those to Be Baptized

Let them set no prices for baptizing and signing the faithful, nor seek to harass those being reborn by imposing any charges, since what we receive freely we are commanded to give freely. Therefore let them attempt to demand absolutely nothing by which those deterred either by poverty or driven away by resentment might neglect to seek the means of their redemption, knowing with certainty that those who are found to have committed what is forbidden, or who have not voluntarily corrected their offenses, will incur the danger of losing their own dignity.

411 [Note: [Col. 0695C] In Vatican 1342 this is chapter 2, with the title “That Presbyters Should Not Claim Unlawful Things for Themselves.”]

#### V. On Presbyters

We likewise forbid presbyters to extend themselves beyond their proper measure or boldly to assume for themselves what belongs to episcopal rank: they shall not seize for themselves the authority to prepare chrism or to perform episcopal signing [Note: [Col. 0695C] The Vindobonensis corruptly reads *adhibente*. From this apparently arose Quesnellus’s emendation, *adhibere, nec sibimet arripere illicitam facultatem*—“to exercise, nor seize for themselves unlawful authority.” The reading of the other collections—Vatican 1342, Dionysian, Hispanic, and Isidorian—supplies the correct emendation [Col. 0695D]. All these, together with the Vindobonensis, omit *illicitam*—“unlawful.”]; nor, in the presence of any bishop, unless perhaps ordered to do so, shall they presume that they possess the license to conduct a prayer or sacred action; nor, in his presence, unless ordered, shall they presume either to sit or to handle the venerable mysteries. Let them remember that in no way is it granted to them, without the supreme pontiff, to have the right to make a subdeacon or acolyte [Col. 0695B]. Nor should they doubt that, if they have thought fit on their own initiative to perform anything specially pertaining to episcopal ministry [Note: [Col. 0695D] Quesnellus added *sin alias*—“but otherwise”; these words, excluded by the sentence’s meaning, have been removed on the authority of the other collections.], they will immediately be deprived of their priestly dignity and sacred communion.

We decree that this must occur if such a transgression is proved by the report of their bishop [Note: [Col. 0695D] The manuscripts speak of presbyters now in the plural, now in the singular. Since the preceding material was expressed in the plural for coherence, here and afterward *eorum*—“their”—should be written instead of *ejus*—“his,” as in the printed editions. Immediately afterward, instead of *referente*, other manuscripts read *deferente*—“reporting.”]. Nor will their own bishop be free from the guilt of connivance and from punishment if, by failing to restrain him, he neglects to punish one who acts immoderately [Note: [Col. 0695D] The common version reads more suitably *a culpa conniventiae et ultione vacaturo*—“will not be free from the guilt of connivance and from punishment.” Immediately afterward, Vatican Regina reads *indicare*—“to indicate”—instead of *vindicare*—“to punish.”].

[Note: [Col. 0695D] In Vatican 1342 this is chapter 3, with the same title.]

#### VI. On Deacons
We have also established that deacons are to observe their proper measure, and we do not permit them to attempt anything beyond the scope assigned by the fathers’ canons. They must not appropriate to their ministry anything that antiquity has specifically decreed for the higher orders; and they must not dare to baptize without a bishop or presbyter, unless extreme necessity should perhaps compel them when the aforementioned ministers are situated at a considerable distance—something that is often permitted even to Christian laypeople. They are not to sit in the presbytery, where divine services are celebrated or any ecclesiastical business is conducted. [Note: Other manuscript and printed collections read “with the divine.”]

They have no right to exercise the prerogative of distributing the sacred Body in the presence of a bishop or presbyter, except when these are absent. Since we too earnestly strive to observe the decrees of the venerable sanctions, and, without compromising them, yield even those matters that might perhaps seem capable of relaxation for the sake of some advantage; [Note: The Roman Vulgate and Dionysius read credamus (“we believe”); the Mainz edition, dicamus (“we say”). Immediately afterward, those Vulgate witnesses, with other collections, read cumque nobis contra salutarium (“and since we, contrary to salutary …”).] since we wish nothing to be rashly permitted contrary to reverence for salutary rules; and since the apostolic see, with the Lord’s favor, diligently strives with pious and devoted purpose to preserve all that has been prescribed by the fathers’ canons, it is sufficiently unworthy for anyone—whether a bishop or one of the subsequent orders—to reject this observance, which he sees the see of blessed Peter both following and teaching. It is also entirely fitting that the whole body of the Church should agree in this observance, which it sees flourishing there where the Lord has established the primacy of the whole Church. [Note: Some witnesses read “itself” (sibimet). The Council’s Vulgate reads “higher than these.” For “prescribed,” other manuscript collections and the Vulgate read “appointed.”]

Scripture says: “Set love in order in me” (Song of Songs 2:4); likewise, “Let all things be done in due order” (1 Corinthians 14:40). And again the Psalmist proclaims:

“Go around Zion and encircle her; tell in her towers; set your hearts upon her strength; and distribute her steps, so that you may tell it to the next generation: for this is our God forever, and he himself will rule us throughout the ages” (Psalm 47:13). [Note: The printed conciliar editions read “to later generations.” For regit (“he rules”), the reading of the older manuscript collections Vindobonensis and Vaticanus 1342 has been adopted; others read reget (“he will rule”).]

[Note: On the authority of the older manuscripts—Vindobonensis, Vaticanus Reginensis, another Vatican manuscript 1342—and Dionysius Justellus, “and therefore we have added” has been supplied, with the punctuation altered accordingly.]

Without doubt, this is the one who is described in the height of ecclesiastical dignities; in whose strength hearts must be set through good works, with the steps duly distributed; and God our Lord and ruler must be proclaimed to all Christian peoples. Here no one should consider himself diminished, since nothing is lost from the perfection of each order, and since, by appropriately retaining what has been bestowed through heavenly dispensation, God is made known to us together and is granted to us as ruler.

Even if something is conceded concerning the length of time, it is compensated by the diligence accumulated in character, provided that what had been postponed for later life is now contained in one’s established way of life—so long as those things whose presence has become evident, whatever they may be, are in no way concealed. It is plainly established that anyone in whom any one of these things is found is a person to be rejected from the clerical insignia. [Note: Vaticanus 1342 and Vaticanus Reginensis read in se (“in himself”); the Vulgate, si inesse (“if it be present”). Other manuscript collections and the Vulgate read convincat (“proves”) instead of constat (“is established”).] [Note: Two Vindobonensis manuscripts and Vaticanus 1342 read “accumulated, and by vigor”; Quesnellus, together with Vaticanus Hispanus and Isidore, reads “accumulated and by vigor”; Vaticanus Reginensis reads “to be accumulated and by vigor.” The reading of Dionysius Justellus and the general conciliar editions seemed preferable. The printed conciliar editions then read “creep in” instead of “steal away.”]

Although things that, if the integrity of the others is established, cannot by themselves do harm may sometimes be tolerated, nevertheless those things must be carefully avoided that cannot be admitted without manifest disfigurement. And if even those matters which are sometimes thought to be pardonable without detriment are excused either by consideration of circumstances or times, or by regard for an accelerated provision, how much more must those things not be mutilated which neither necessity nor any ecclesiastical advantage at all compels?

[CAP. X Dion.] [Note: In Vaticanus 1342 this is chapter 4, with the title “On Baptism.”]

Let no one suppose that he has unrestricted permission to baptize at any time, apart from the venerable sacrament of Easter and Pentecost, except in the event of a very serious illness, when there is fear that, as the danger of the disease increases, the sick person may perhaps depart, overtaken by death without the saving remedy. [Note: The Vindobonensis reads this way. Quesnellus has: “On ordination at fixed times, namely, in the order of the fourth, seventh, and tenth months, and at the beginning of Lent.” In manuscript collection Vaticanus 1342 this is chapter 5, with the title “On the ordination of presbyters and deacons.”]

[Note: The Vindobonensis reads this way. Quesnellus has “Orders,” and then celebrandos (“to be celebrated,” masculine); but the other manuscripts and the Vulgate, supported by the Vindobonensis of this collection, more correctly read ordinationes … celebrandas (“ordinations … to be celebrated,” feminine), although through scribal carelessness that manuscript first has ordines.] 

### VII. On Ordinations

Ordinations of presbyters and deacons must not be performed except at fixed times and on fixed days: namely, during the fast of the fourth month, of the seventh, and of the tenth, and also during the fast at the beginning of Lent and on the Saturday of mid-Lent, toward evening. They must know that no presbyter or deacon is to be preferred, for the sake of any advantage, to those who were ordained before him. [Note: The Council’s Vulgate reads “they ought not”; Dionysius Justellus reads “they should not.” The Vindobonensis, Dionysius, and Isidore omit “for the sake of any advantage.” Some other manuscript collections and printed editions read “to prefer,” and Vaticanus Reginensis and Dionysius Justellus have the same reading.]

[Note: In Vaticanus 1342 this is chapter 6, with the title “On the veiling of God’s maidens.”]

### VIII. On Sacred Virgins

They must not impose the sacred veil upon virgins devoted to God except at Epiphany, during the Easter celebrations in white garments, or on the feast of the Apostles; only if, as was said concerning baptism, it should perhaps not be denied to those struck by serious illness who implore it, lest they depart from this world without receiving this gift. [Note: The Council’s Vulgate reads “feasts”; Dionysius Justellus, “feasts,” and both then read “let them depart” instead of “let them pass over.”]

[Note: In the cited Vatican manuscript this is chapter 7, with the title “On widows, that they should not receive the sacred veil.”]

### IX. On Widows

Let no bishop attempt to veil widows. [Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts of our collection. The Vulgate, together with Dionysius, Vaticanus Hispanus, and Isidore, omits “and,” and with different punctuation reads: “Therefore it is not at all …” In our reading and punctuation, Vaticanus 1342 is preferable, since it has “because.” The printed conciliar editions and Dionysius Justellus then read “delegates” instead of “selected.”] What divine authority has not selected and the form of the canons has not prescribed must not be usurped at all. Ecclesiastical support must be extended to them in such a way that nothing unlawful is committed.

[Note: In Vaticanus this is chapter 8, with the title “On hereditary slaves.”]

### X. On Not Admitting Slaves without Their Masters’ Consent

The presumption that gives rise to a widespread complaint must also be avoided: nearly everyone complains that slaves and hereditary tenants, fleeing the rights of their masters and their estates, are indiscriminately admitted—under the pretext of religious life—either into monasteries or into ecclesiastical service, with bishops sometimes conniving as well. [Note: Other manuscript collections and the Vulgate read “to be removed” rather than “to be prohibited,” and the Vindobonensis and Vaticanus manuscripts omit per (“through”).] This pernicious practice must be prohibited by every means, lest under the institution of the Christian name another person’s property appear to be seized or public discipline overturned. This is especially necessary since it is not fitting that the dignity of the clerical ministry itself should be darkened by this obligation, and that it should be forced, on behalf of the condition and status of those serving it, either to quarrel or to appear—God forbid—to be liable to such a charge. [Note: Quesnellus reads “that the conditions seem to be disputed.” We have preferred the reading of the Vulgate, supported by other collections and by the Vindobonensis of this collection, in which, as in Vaticanus Reginensis, “to quarrel or to appear” is found.]

After such persons have been prohibited by appropriate and vigilant injunction, any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone known to preside over monasteries who keeps such persons with him and thinks that they should not be restored to their patrons, or thereafter assigned either to the service of the Church or to religious communities, unless perhaps they were first released by the masters’ consent, attested in writing, or granted through a lawful settlement, must not doubt that he will incur danger to his own honor and communion if anyone’s genuine complaint brings him to account on this matter. For, according to the blessed Apostle, the greatest care must be taken lest the faith and discipline of the Lord be blasphemed (1 Timothy 6:2).

[Note: In Vaticanus 1342 this is chapter 9, with the title “That no cleric may engage in business.”]

### XI. On Clerical Business

It was therefore necessary that we should not pass over what the report sent to us from the regions of Picenum announced: that very many clerics are intent upon dishonorable business dealings and shameful profits, [Note: The Vulgate and manuscripts of other collections add nuper (“recently”), followed by id est ante plurimos (“that is, many [years] before”).] observing without any sense of shame the Gospel reading, since our Lord himself is said to have driven the merchants from the temple by scourging them (Matthew 21:12; John 2:14). [Note: Quesnellus inserted “not paying attention,” and omitted “himself,” contrary to our manuscripts and the printed editions.]

Nor do they recall the Apostle’s words: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly business” (2 Timothy 2:4). They disregard with deaf ears the Psalmist David singing: “Because I have not known business dealings, I will enter into the powers of the Lord” (Psalm 71:16). Therefore, let them know that after this they must abstain from such profits obtained by dishonorable means and cease from every practice or desire of business dealing; otherwise, whatever their rank, they must immediately withdraw from clerical offices. [Note: Vaticanus Reginensis and another Vatican manuscript 1342, together with the Vulgate, add “or.” The printed conciliar editions and Dionysius Justellus, as well as a second hand in the Vindobonensis manuscript, read abstinere (“to abstain”) instead of abire (“to withdraw”).] For the house of God must both be and be called a house of prayer, lest it rather become a workshop of commerce and a den of thieves.

[Note: In Vaticanus 1342 this is chapter 10, with the title “No illiterate or disabled person may be promoted to ecclesiastical orders.”]

### XII. On the Illiterate

We have also learned that illiterate persons, even those with some bodily impairment, are being admitted to ecclesiastical service without any consideration. [Note: This reading is not convincing. The earlier reading in the Vindobonensis was “and without any bodily [impairment].” The more accurate reading of other manuscript collections and the Vulgate is “and diminished in no part of the body” (Vaticanus Reginensis: “and in no part”).] Ancient tradition and the established practice of the apostolic see reject this altogether: a person without letters cannot be suited to sacred offices, and the legal precepts have decreed that nothing defective may be offered to God (Leviticus 21:18; Deuteronomy 17:1). Therefore, from now on, such cases must be avoided by every means; and no such person is to be received into the clergy. If any such persons have already been admitted, whether through their own presumption or through the negligence of those in authority, they are to remain in the places to which they have been assigned, but only so far as never to seize any advancement. They should consider it sufficient that this very thing has been permitted to them out of excessive compassion. [Note: Vaticanus Reginensis reads “let them be prohibited.” Other manuscript collections and printed editions read “in the clergy.”]

[Note: In Vaticanus 1342 this is chapter 11, with the same title. The title, however, forms part of the canon itself. Thus in Dionysius Justellus, after the title “On those who cut themselves,” the canon begins: “But concerning those who have cut themselves, the fathers’ canons …” Vaticanus Reginensis, which lacks titles, begins the canon with this title.]

### XIII. On Those Who Have Castrated Themselves

The fathers’ canons clearly established what must be followed, and it is enough to state their tenor. For they say that those who perpetrate such acts must be excluded from clerical office as soon as they have been recognized. We must observe this in every way, since no one is entitled to judge anything beyond what the memorable decree established. [Note: Quesnellus, together with the manuscripts of this collection, reads: “because perhaps no one has at hand, and apart from those things there is nothing which the memorable order decreed, and the form of judgment.” We have corrected this defective and less accurate reading according to Vaticanus 1342, with which the printed editions of Dionysius, the Hispanic collection, and Isidore agree, except that they read “supplies” for “is at hand.” The sense is then clear: no one has the right to judge anything beyond what the memorable form of the Nicene Fathers decreed. Vaticanus Reginensis agrees with our reading, except that it adds “order” after “memorable.”]

### XIV. On Those Entangled in Crimes

We have also discovered that certain persons entangled in horrifying crimes, with all discernment set aside, not only fail to undergo the necessary penance for atrocious deeds, but, with no correction whatever having followed, strive for divine ministry and honor. Some even who have already been placed in the orders are not rejected despite committing grave crimes. Yet the Apostle cries out that hands must not be laid hastily upon anyone and that one must not share in another’s sins (1 Timothy 5:22). The venerable decrees of our predecessors (Nicaea 9–10) declare that such persons—even if they have somehow slipped in—must be removed once discovered if they sinned beforehand, and that those who have forgotten their sacred profession and violated their holy commitment must unquestionably be expelled.

### XV. On Those Possessed by a Demon or Afflicted by Similar Disorders

We have discovered that unlawful practices have advanced to such an extent that persons ensnared by demons and similar afflictions are permitted to handle sacred ministries. [Note: Other manuscript collections, also supported by the Vindobonensis of this collection, read “that various unlawful things break forth, so that those ensnared by demons and similar afflictions are permitted to handle sacred ministries.” They read “whatever things” and “those similarly ensnared”; for “let them be assigned,” they have “let them be assigned.” The Vulgate agrees, except that it prefers “those ensnared.” Quesnellus reads “and those whom he presumes to let … ensnared … be permitted to handle …”] If, while engaged in this work, some personal necessity should arise for them, who can trust in the salvation of the faithful when he sees ministers of human healing themselves afflicted by such a calamity? [Note: This is the reading of the Vindobonensis manuscript, together with the other manuscript and printed collections; Quesnellus reads Qui necessario (“Who necessarily”).] [Note: Other manuscript collections and the Vulgate read “of the faithful”; Vaticanus Hispanus and Isidore, “and of the faithful,” which appears to be an editorial correction.] And for this reason they must necessarily be removed, lest scandal be given to any of the weak for whom Christ died. Finally, if divine law did not permit a person wounded or disabled in body to touch sacred things (Leviticus 21), how much less is it fitting for those struck in mind—what is worse—to be dispensers of the heavenly gift?

### XVI. On Sacred Virgins and Those Who Illicitly Associate with Them

We have learned that certain men presumptuously associate themselves with sacred virgins and, after their dedication to God, enter into incestuous and sacrilegious unions. [Note: The Council’s Vulgate, together with Vaticanus Hispanus and Isidore, adds “however.” The word “presumptuously,” added by a later hand in the Vindobonensis, has been restored here, as it appears in all the other manuscripts and printed books.] It is right that such men should immediately be driven from sacred communion, and that they should not be received at all unless through public and approved penance. [Note: Quesnellus reads “unless through private penance they are received.” The Vindobonensis initially had the same reading; a later hand added “entirely.” The correction to “approved” was required by the sense and is supported by other manuscripts and printed editions. Dionysius Justellus reads “or certainly to these”; the Council’s Vulgate reads “yet the viaticum.”] Nevertheless, if they have repented, the viaticum must certainly not be denied them when they depart from this world.

### XVII. On Widows

We have already discussed at greater length the matter of veiling widows without any blessing. [Note: The first hand of the Vindobonensis read “if there is any.” Other manuscripts corrected this to “without any,” a reading accepted by Quesnellus and supported by the excellent Vaticanus Reginensis; the reading later introduced into the Vindobonensis, “under any,” is set aside. Other manuscript collections and printed editions read “under no [blessing].” The Council’s Vulgate, together with Vaticanus Hispanus and Isidore, reads “we have sufficiently discussed above.” Dionysius Justellus reads “we have discussed above at length.” Vaticanus 1342 agrees with our collection, except that it incorrectly reads “we said” for “we have discussed.”]

If any widow who has professed this of her own will tramples upon the chastity of her former marriage with an unstable mind, it will be her responsibility to consider with what satisfaction she must appease God. [Note: The Council’s Vulgate adds: “because, according to the Apostle, they have made their first faith void.” This is absent from our collection, from other ancient collections, and from Dionysius Justellus, and appears to be a gloss. Vaticanus Reginensis reads “to please” instead of “to appease.” Other collections and printed editions read “the faith of chastity,” and before “exhortations” add “only,” or, with Isidore, “alone.” The Council’s Vulgate reads “as being concerned with their morals and actions.”]

For if she perhaps could not remain continent, she was not at all forbidden to marry, according to the Apostle; but after deliberation with herself, she ought to have guarded the chastity and fidelity promised to God. We must not lay a snare for such women, but must set before them the rewards of eternal life and the punishments of divine judgment, so that our conscience may be clear and their intention may answer to God for itself. We must indeed beware of what the blessed Apostle Paul testifies concerning their morals and actions, which we refrain from explaining more plainly, lest we seem not so much to deter as to admonish the sensibility of the unstable sex. [Note: Quesnellus reads: “which we could now explain more clearly, but for the moment we prefer to suppress, lest by a detestable meaning we seem to deter rather than admonish certain people.” No other collection or ancient manuscript of our collection indicates this reading. It appears to have been introduced to correct the less satisfactory reading of the older manuscripts, which, together with the Vindobonensis, read: “which, while we shall be able to explain more clearly, lest unstable sex seem not so much to be deterred as admonished.” The manuscripts of Vaticanus Reginensis, Dionysius, and the printed Council editions show that “we shall be able” should be corrected to “we refrain”; therefore the addition is superfluous and is found in no ancient manuscript. If the word “sense” is added before “unstable sex,” as supplied by Vaticanus Reginensis and Vaticanus 1342, the sentence is fully coherent. Dionysius Justellus and the printed conciliar editions have a similar reading, except that they say “lest unstable sex seem not so much to be deterred as admonished.”]

[Note: In Vaticanus 1342 this is chapter 12, with the title “On second marriages.” Other collections, together with the Vulgate, read “generally” instead of “general.” Dionysius Justellus and the Council’s Vulgate read “dedicated to the service.”]

Just as secular persons are permitted to enter into a second marriage, so after such a marriage no one is permitted to enter the clerical fellowship. One permission is granted generally to human weakness; another way of life must belong to those who are to be dedicated to the service of divine things.

### XVIII. On Those Who Flee to Other Churches

Anyone who deserts his own Church and, without any existing cause, decides to transfer to another, if he is rashly received and promoted, will not escape the provisions of the revered canons—whether he himself, or the one who receives and advances him—which prescribe what must be observed concerning such presumptuous persons. [Note: Since the Vindobonensis and other older manuscripts of this collection read “rashly,” some corrected it to “if rashly,” a reading Quesnellus perhaps adopted from the Thuaneus manuscript. Vaticanus 1342 and other manuscript collections and printed editions recommend the correction “and rashly,” especially since it better fits the following context. For “will flee,” the manuscripts of Dionysius, the Hispanic collection, and Isidore read “will escape.”]

The matters concerning monks, too, have been set out more fully in the first part of this instruction: both what may be permitted according to the necessity of circumstances and times, and how, when no necessity arising from any fact is evident, the ancient institution alone must be preserved. [Note: Dionysius Justellus, together with the other printed and manuscript collections, adds “and laymen” and omits “also.” Shortly afterward the Council’s Vulgate, together with Vaticanus Hispanus and Isidore, reads “which, or to whatever extent, may be permitted to them according to circumstances,” instead of “which may be permitted according to circumstances.” The same reading occurs in Dionysius Justellus, except that he omits “to them.” We have supplied “to whatever extent” from these witnesses, although the copies of this collection omit it; it is necessary to the context and corresponds to what was said above in chapter 1. The Vindobonensis reads “it will be shown to concern no fact.” Quesnellus added something before “it will be shown” to make the sense clear. But “necessity” had to be supplied before “to concern,” as it appears in Dionysius Justellus. In the manuscripts of Vaticanus Hispanus and Isidore, together with the Council’s Vulgate, the reading is different: “it is shown to concern no necessity.” The same occurs in Vaticanus Reginensis, except that it reads “it will be shown.”]

### XIX. On Those Ordained for a Price

Those who are found to have purchased the sacred dignity, although unworthy by their merits, must be barred once convicted. Those who sell such a crime do so not without danger, because the condemnation of Simon, as sacred Scripture testifies (Acts 8), envelops both the giver and the recipient. [Note: Dionysius Justellus reads “those who perpetrate it”; the Council’s Vulgate, together with Vaticanus Hispanus and Isidore, reads “those who commit it.”]

### XX. On the Consecration of Holy Places

[Note: This title forms part of the canon itself, as can be understood from Vaticanus Reginensis, Dionysius, and the printed conciliar editions.]

Although it was briefly stated above, it has also been disclosed to us that certain persons presume to consecrate churches or oratories that have been built without the instruction of the apostolic see. We have nevertheless been moved by this still more detestable report: that, under whatever name of the dead, and, as is said, even buildings not constructed by the faithful, they boldly establish sacred processions. [Note: Dionysius Justellus, together with Vaticanus Hispanus and Isidore, reads “religious professions.” Shortly afterward Dionysius Justellus, together with Vaticanus Reginensis, Vaticanus Hispanus, and Isidore, reads “things which, because they are so harsh …”]

Such things are so harsh and so grievous that our hearing can scarcely endure them. If the devotion of Christianity in those regions is indeed firm and settled, let these matters be investigated with greater strictness, and let those by whom they were done be identified. [Note: The Vindobonensis, with the other printed and manuscript collections, reads fuerint gesta (“were done”), a better reading than Quesnellus’s sunt gesta (“are done”).] For just as, while the names remain hidden in this atrocity, there is no one against whom the appropriate sentence can be pronounced, so, once the matter has been exposed by clear evidence, the person will in no way escape the punishment demanded by the enormity of so great a crime. [Note: Quesnellus alone reads “as though of such a crime.” Vaticanus Hispanus and Isidore read “will not avoid” instead of “will not escape.”]

### XXI. On Women Who Presume to Minister

We have heard with equal indignation that divine things have been brought into such contempt that women are said to minister at sacred altars and to perform everything assigned exclusively to the service of men, exhibiting a sex to which such duties do not belong. [Note: The Council’s Vulgate reads “are reported.” Dionysius Justellus, together with Vaticanus Hispanus and Isidore, reads “and to exhibit to a sex to which it does not belong all things assigned exclusively to the service of men.”]

But in all the offenses that we have individually touched upon, the guilt and crime of every wrongdoer concerns those priests who either commit such acts or, by failing to make public those who commit them, show that they favor their wicked excesses. [Note: Quesnellus reads “which at least,” as did the first hand of the Vindobonensis. The second ancient hand corrected this to “individually,” as preferred by all the other manuscript collections and printed editions. Quesnellus then reads “concerns the guilty.” We have corrected it to “concerns them,” supported by the Vindobonensis, other manuscript collections, and the printed editions.]

If those who attempt to overthrow the religious duty entrusted to them are really to be called priests, they do so by inclining toward every perverse and profane act and by pursuing ruinous precipices without any regard for Christian discipline. [Note: Quesnellus reads “without any regard,” as did the first hand of the Vindobonensis. We have preferred the reading written by the second ancient hand of the Vindobonensis, with which nearly all the manuscripts and printed copies of other collections agree.]

Since it is written, “Whoever despises small things will gradually fall” (Ecclesiasticus 19:1), what should be thought of such people who, occupied by immense and manifold burdens of depravity, have produced a huge collapse through assaults of many kinds—one that seems not only to overwhelm themselves but, unless they are healed, to inflict deadly ruin upon all the Churches? Those who have dared to practice these things, and also those who have remained silent about them although they have known of them, must not doubt that they lie under the loss of their own honor unless they hasten with all possible speed to have these lethal wounds cured by suitable treatment. [Note: Dionysius Justellus reads “if not with as much [speed] as they can.” Vaticanus 1342 reads “are healed” instead of “are treated”; Vaticanus Hispanus and Isidore read “are healed by medicine.”]

### XXII. On Bishops Who Know or Are Ignorant

By what right do those maintain the laws of bishops who disregard the duties imposed upon episcopal vigilance to such an extent that they instead do what is contrary to the household of God over which they preside? [Note: Quesnellus reads “By what right are they bound to the episcopate.” The Vindobonensis reads “By what right are they bound to the rights of bishops.” We have corrected “are bound” to “hold,” following Vaticanus Reginensis and other manuscript and printed collections. Vaticanus 1342, Dionysius Justellus, and the Vulgate read “by what custom” instead of “by what right,” less accurately.]

Let them consider how much they could accomplish before God if they pursued nothing except what is fitting, and how much they deserve when with detestable zeal they pursue the opposite. Yet, as though this were precisely the rule by which the Church ought to be governed, everything hostile to ecclesiastical rules is perpetrated. Even if each bishop knew the canons, he ought to have maintained inviolate vigilance; and if he perhaps did not know them, he ought confidently to have consulted someone who did. Thus no excuse comes to the aid of those who err: the one who knew proposed to observe what he knew, and the one who was ignorant failed to take care to know what he was doing. [Note: The Vindobonensis reads “if this were not an effort”; Vaticanus 1342 and Vaticanus Reginensis, more correctly, “if this were an effort.” Vaticanus Hispanus and Isidore read “if it were fitting for him.” Quesnellus reads “which the knowing bishop ought to have observed”; our copies, with other printed editions, more correctly read “which it would have been fitting for him to observe.” Vaticanus 1342 and Vaticanus Reginensis, together with Vaticanus Hispanus and Isidore, read “the ignorant” instead of “the knowing,” and Vaticanus Reginensis then reads “what he ignores” instead of “what he knew.”]

### XXIII. On the Church’s Revenues

It is appropriate that four portions be made from both the revenues and the offerings of the faithful, according to what the resources of each Church permit, as was reasonably decreed long ago: one for the bishop, another for the clergy, a third for the poor, and a fourth to be applied to the buildings. Concerning these portions, just as it is the priest’s responsibility to pay the stated amount in full to the ministers of the Church, so the clergy must know that beyond the sum assigned to them they are to demand nothing presumptuously.

As for what has been assigned to ecclesiastical buildings, let the visible structure of the holy places show that it has truly been set aside for this work. [Note: Quesnellus alone reads “for the buildings of the Church.” We have preferred “set aside,” supported by most manuscripts and printed editions; some read “extended.” “Restoration” is found in the manuscripts of our collection, while other collections, together with the Vulgate, read “repair.”]

For it is sacrilegious if, while sacred buildings are left without the necessary resources, a bishop converts to his own profit the funds designated for them—even the portion assigned to the poor. [Note: The Vulgate, together with copies of other collections, has a different punctuation: “Nevertheless, the portion assigned to the poor itself, although he may appear to be about to show that he has dispensed it according to divine accounts, etc.” The Vindobonensis supports the text’s punctuation and reading; only the word “is said,” written by the first hand, was replaced by the second hand with “may appear.”]

And although he may be said to be about to show that he has dispensed this portion according to divine accounts, nevertheless, in accordance with what is written—“That they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16)—it is necessary that it also be proclaimed by present testimony and not be silenced in praise of a good reputation.

Therefore no cleric should consider himself free from responsibility for this offense if, when he sees a bishop, presbyter, or deacon exceeding the rules that we have set forth as salutary and to be followed, he does not immediately take care to refer the matter to our ears, after suitable evidence has been presented, so that the punishment of the transgressor may become a prohibition against wrongdoing for the others. [Note: Other manuscript collections and printed editions read “takes care to report it.”]

Each bishop will unquestionably be the destroyer of his order and honor if he thinks that these matters should be suppressed from any cleric or from the hearing of the entire Church. [Note: The following is absent from the other collections—Vaticanus Reginensis, Vaticanus 1342, Dionysius, the Hispanic collection, and Isidore. Vaticanus 1342 and Barbarus 2888, together with Dionysius, Vaticanus Hispanus, and Isidore, add: “Given on the fifth day before the Ides of March, in the consulship of Asterius and Praesidius, illustrious men,” that is, in the year 494. Vaticanus Reginensis reads: “Given on the sixth day before the Ides of March,” etc.]

And in another hand: “May God keep you safe, dearest brothers.”

[Note: [Col. 0705] The following note appears at the foot of column 705, but its callout figure (a) has not been printed in the text. The occasion and date of this council were explained in the preceding treatise, Part I, chapter 4, section 2. This is the ancient version that, having been received by Isidore, is commonly called Isidorian. In addition to the manuscripts of this collection and the copies of the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, we found the same version in the outstanding manuscript Veronensis 58, which presents a pure version of all the Greek canons in continuous sequence.]

### CHAPTER LIX. Here Begins the Council of Antioch

[Col. 0705A]

The holy and most peaceful synod, gathered together at Antioch, sends greetings in the Lord to the holy fellow priests who are in the several provinces and are united in mind. [Note: The Veronensis, together with the printed Greek text, omits “at Antioch.” The same manuscript lacks “to the holy fellow priests.”]

Grace and truth of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, visiting the holy Church of Antioch and joining it in concord through the most peaceful Spirit, accomplished many things, as well as other matters. In all things, however, with the holy and peaceful Spirit suggesting it, he also accomplished this: that the matters which seemed rightly established should be brought to your knowledge, with the greatest deliberation and judgment, by all the bishops gathered together at Antioch from the various provinces.

[Note: [Col. 0705C] The manuscripts of Vindobonensis and Veronensis, together with the common text of the Councils, read “he accomplished.” Quesnellus has “he made.” Veronensis has *recta* (“right”) instead of *recte* (“rightly”).]

[Note: [Col. 0705C] Veronensis, together with the common text of the Councils, adds “us.”]

[Note: [Col. 0705C] Veronensis likewise reads, “For we believe.”]

We believe, moreover, in the grace of the Lord and in the holy Spirit of peace, that you too will unite with us as though you had been present in the same power, supporting us in your prayers.

[Note: [Col. 0705C] Oxoniensis reads “helping.” Shortly afterward Veronensis, together with the common text, has “but rather fortified and in the Holy Spirit.” We have thought it necessary to insert the preposition *in*, which Quesnellus and the manuscript of Vindobonensis omit.]

Rather, being united and present in the Holy Spirit, consenting to these very things which have been defined and strengthening the matters which have seemed right, you will ratify them with the agreement of the Holy Spirit. The ecclesiastical canons which have been determined are the following, written below.

424 At this synod were present Eusebius, Theodorus, Narcissus, Antiochus, Archelaus, Eustathius, Mocimus, Hisicius, Manicius, Etherius, Jacobus, Agapius, Magnus, Eneas, Theodolus, Alpius, Nicetas, Agapius, Tharcodimantus, Bassus, Alexander, Petrus, Moses, Patricius, Anatolius, Macedonius, Petrus, Cyrion, Theodorus, and Theodosius, from the provinces of Coele-Syria, Phoenicia, ancient Arabia, Mesopotamia, Cilicia, and Isauria. They established the following matters.

[Note: [Col. 0705D] The manuscript of Vindobonensis adds *episcopi* (“bishops”) in a second hand.]

[Note: [Col. 0705D] Vindobonensis marks this as number 11 and thereafter increases each number by one, because it numbers the preceding letter as no. 1.
