Veronensis and the common text, more coherently with the Greek *τοῦ Θεοφιλεστάτου* (“of the most God-loving”), read “most God-loving” and delete “our.”]

I. All who dare to dissolve the rule of the holy and great Council of Nicaea, which was celebrated in the presence of our most God-loving lord, the emperor Constantine, concerning the holy Paschal festival of our Savior, must be excluded from communion and expelled from the Church, especially if they persist in their contentious zeal to overthrow what has been most excellently established.

[Note: [Col. 0705D] Vindobonensis, in a second hand, together with the common Isidorian text, adds “and salvific.” The common text has “excommunicated” instead of “excluded from communion.”]

These things, indeed, have been said concerning the laity.

[Note: [Col. 0706C] Veronensis more correctly reads “let these things have been said.”]

But if any of the leaders of the Church—that is, a bishop, presbyter, or deacon—after this definition and decree should attempt to stir up the peoples and disturb the Churches, and, resisting in this way, should wish to celebrate Easter with the Jews, the holy synod has judged him already alien from the Church, as one who is guilty not only of his own sin but also of having undermined the corrupted mind and conduct of others.

[Note: [Col. 0706C] Quesnellus reads: “if there is anyone, whether bishop, presbyter, or deacon, who after this …” We have corrected the text in accordance with the manuscripts of Vindobonensis and Veronensis and the common text. Vindobonensis, after deleting the words “and this decree,” continues as follows: “should dare, for the subversion of the peoples and the disturbance of the Churches, to resist, and to celebrate Easter with the Jews; this man the holy synod will judge already alien from the Church, as one who is guilty not only of his own sin but also of having caused the subversion and corruption of the minds of others.” This reading differs considerably from that preferred by the other manuscripts of the Isidorian version. Veronensis agrees with our reading, except that it has “will judge alien from the Church.” The common Isidorian text differs only in this respect: “and if he should dare to gather this decree separately for the subversion of the peoples and the disturbance of the Churches, and celebrate Easter with the Jews, etc.”]

The synod not only deposes such a person from the priesthood, but also those who have dared to communicate with him after his condemnation.

[Note: [Col. 0706D] Veronensis reads “will depose”; Vindobonensis, “permits him to be deposed from priesthood and ministry.” The common texts likewise add “and ministry.”]

[Note: [Col. 0706D] Together with our manuscripts and the common texts, we have preferred “those who have been deposed.” Quesnellus alone reads “the deposed person.”]

Moreover, those who have been deposed must also be deprived of the external honor which the holy canon and the priesthood of God had earned for them.

[Note: [Col. 0706D] This is the reading of Oxoniensis and Veronensis, together with the common Isidorian text. Vindobonensis agrees, except that it has “the holy rule” instead of “the holy canon.” Quesnellus, with the manuscript of Thuaneus, reads “which he earned through the holy canons and the priesthood of God.”]

II. All who enter the Church of God and hear the sacred Scriptures, but do not join the people in prayer, and who also oppose the holy reception of the Lord’s sacrament according to some discipline of their own, must be expelled from the Church until, after confessing, they demonstrate the fruit of repentance and have begged that, once pardon has been granted, they may be deemed worthy to be received.

[Note: [Col. 0706D] Oxoniensis reads “and they also curse.” Quesnellus has “they also oppose the holy reception.” Vindobonensis, together with the common Isidorian text, reads “according to some discipline of their own.”]

It is not permitted to communicate with those excluded from communion, nor to enter their homes and pray with those who do not participate in the Church’s prayer, nor to receive into one Church anyone who has been excommunicated from another.

[Note: [Col. 0706D] The manuscript of Vindobonensis reads “so that they may deserve pardon.” Shortly afterward, together with the common Isidorian text, it has “excommunicated” instead of “excluded from communion.” It omits the words “in prayer.”]

But if any bishop, presbyter, or deacon, or even anyone enrolled in the clerical order, is seen to communicate with those excluded from communion, he too must be deprived of communion, as one who confounds the rules of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0707C] Quesnellus inserts “the Church.” Vindobonensis has “are separated” instead of “are excommunicated.” Shortly afterward the common Isidorian text reads: “If any of the bishops is discovered communicating with the excommunicated … this man also …”]

III. If any presbyter, deacon, or other cleric should decide to leave his own diocese and transfer to another, and there gradually attempts to remain permanently in communion wherever he has migrated, he must no longer minister, especially if his own bishop has urged him to return.

[Note: [Col. 0707C] Vindobonensis, together with the common text, reads “his Church”; Ferrandus also reads this in title 99. The common Isidorian text reads “and attempts to remain permanently where he has migrated.”]

But if, after his bishop’s summons, he does not obey and persists, he must in every way be deposed from office and never again have the power to return to the ecclesiastical order.

[Note: [Col. 0707C] We have added “also” on the authority of Veronensis and the common text.]

If another bishop should attempt to receive a person deposed for this fault, he too must be rebuked by the common synod as one who dissolves ecclesiastical rights.

[Note: [Col. 0707C] The common Isidorian text, together with Vindobonensis, reads “should receive the deposed person.” Quesnellus alone omits “also he.” Vindobonensis reads: “and he too will deserve punishment from the common synod of rebuke, as one who …”]

426 IV. If any bishop has been deposed by a synod, or if a presbyter or deacon has been condemned by his own bishop, and should presume to perform any act of priesthood or sacred ministry, he may no longer do so, nor may he hope for restoration in another synod, nor may there be any place for anyone’s defense on his behalf. All who communicate with him must also be expelled from the Church, especially if, after learning that the sentence against him had been pronounced, they have obstinately communicated with him.

[Note: [Col. 0707D] Veronensis, together with the common Isidorian text, reads “has been condemned.” Vindobonensis has “has been deprived of office.” Quesnellus reads “was condemned.” Vindobonensis omits the words “of the priesthood or.” Quesnellus has “nor any place for another’s defense”; the manuscript of Thuaneus has “nor any place for satisfaction.” We have followed the reading of Vindobonensis and the common Isidorian text, with which Veronensis agrees.]

[Note: [Col. 0707D] Quesnellus inserts “are commanded” and then omits “against him,” contrary to all our manuscripts and the common Isidorian text.]

V. If any presbyter or deacon, despising his bishop, should separate himself from the Church and dare to erect an altar privately after gathering people to himself, and, although the bishop urges him and recalls him once and again, should remain disobedient, he must by all means be deposed and must never hope to obtain healing or recover his own honor.

[Note: [Col. 0707D] Quesnellus alone adds “we decree.”]

If he also persists in disturbing and stirring up the Church, he must be punished by the authority which exists outside it, as a seditious person.

VI. If anyone has been excommunicated by his own bishop, he must not first be received by others unless he has been received by his own bishop, or unless he appears before a council and answers the charge, so that, if he satisfies the synod, it may determine that he ought to be received under another judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0707D] This is the reading of the manuscripts of Vindobonensis and Veronensis and the common texts. Quesnellus has: “he must not be received by another bishop unless he has been received by his own, or …” Shortly afterward we have written “and answers,” with Vindobonensis; and, with that manuscript and the common Isidorian text, we have restored “it is agreed that he should be received under another judgment.” Quesnellus has “so that he may answer,” and “it ought to be observed under another.”]

The same rule must also be observed concerning laymen, presbyters, deacons, and all who belong to the clergy.

VII. No traveling cleric may be received without a *formata*, which the Greeks call an *epistolion* (“letter” or “letter of authorization”); nor may a presbyter give such *formatae* to distant regions, except that he may send simple letters to neighboring bishops.

[Note: [Col. 0708C] The following four words, omitted by Quesnellus from the text and relegated to the margin, have been inserted from the manuscript of Vindobonensis and from the common Isidorian text, which prefers *epistolam* (“letter”) to *epistolium*.]

[Note: [Col. 0708C] Quesnellus reads: “nor may presbyters give *formatae*, that is, letters, to distant regions, unless …” The common Isidorian text reads: “nor may a presbyter give *formatae*, that is, canonical letters; and unless … he should presume to send them.” We have adopted the reading of Vindobonensis and inserted only “and” from the common text. Veronensis cannot support the reading, since a leaf is missing there.]

VIII. It is permitted for the vicars of bishops, whom the Greeks call *chorepiscopi* (“rural bishops”), to issue *formatae*.

[Note: [Col. 0708D] This is the reading of Vindobonensis, supported by Ferrandus in title 80. The common Isidorian text has “the bishops’ vicars.” Quesnellus has “the bishop’s vicar,” adding that the Greeks call him a *chorepiscopus*.]

IX. The bishops established in each province must know that the metropolitan bishop who presides has assumed the care and oversight of the entire province. Therefore those who have cases must unquestionably go to the metropolitan city.

[Note: [Col. 0708D] Oxoniensis deletes “metropolitan.” Quesnellus prefixes “of the Churches” to “entire,” which Vindobonensis and the common Isidorian text delete.]

Accordingly, it has seemed good that he should take precedence also in honor, and that the other bishops should do nothing without him beyond what belongs to each Church within its own diocese, in accordance with the ancient canon of our Fathers which has prevailed.

[Note: [Col. 0708D] Vindobonensis and the common Isidorian text read “that he should take precedence”; Quesnellus omits “him” and has “and the metropolitan in honor.” Vindobonensis reads “according to the ancient canon of our Fathers which has prevailed,” and shortly afterward, together with the common Isidorian text, “of each Church.”]

Each bishop must have authority over his own diocese, to govern it with the reverence appropriate to him, and to provide for the region subject to his city, so that he may also ordain presbyters and deacons according to a sound judgment and deliberate with moderation and gravity concerning each matter.

[Note: [Col. 0708D] Oxoniensis reads “through his own diocese.” The common Isidorian text adds “everywhere,” and afterward reads “so that he may also”; later it has “and with moderation concerning each matter of that region.”]

Beyond this, he must be permitted to do nothing without the knowledge of the metropolitan bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0709C] The manuscript of Thuaneus reads “apart from the metropolitan bishop.” Quesnellus omits “of the bishop.” The common Isidorian text adds at the end of this canon, together with the Greek and other versions: “nor may the metropolitan act without the counsel of the others …”]

X. The *chorepiscopi* established in villages and rural districts, although they have received the laying on of hands from bishops and have been consecrated as bishops, must, as the holy synod has determined, know that they are to retain their proper rank, govern the neighboring Churches entrusted to them, and be content with the care and administration which they have received.

[Note: [Col. 0709C] Vindobonensis reads “established in estates and villages.” We have inserted “and when they have been consecrated as bishops” on the authority of the same manuscript and the common Isidorian text.]

They are permitted to appoint readers, subdeacons, and exorcists, and it is sufficient for them to have received authority only over these ranks. They must not dare to ordain a presbyter or deacon without the knowledge of the bishop of the city or Church to which either the *chorepiscopus* himself or the region over which he is known to preside is adjacent.

[Note: [Col. 0709D] The common Isidorian text reads “let this be sufficient for them.” We have added “only” with the manuscript of Vindobonensis and the common Isidorian text.]

If anyone should dare to violate these provisions, he must be deposed and deprived of the dignity with which he is endowed. A *chorepiscopus* must be ordained by the bishop of the city or place to which he is attached.

[Note: [Col. 0709D] This is the reading of the same manuscript and the common text. Quesnellus has “which is adjacent to him,” a less correct reading.]

XI. If any bishop, presbyter, or absolutely anyone subject to ecclesiastical discipline should go to the emperor without the counsel or letters of the bishops within the province, and especially of the metropolitan, he must be repudiated and expelled not only from communion but also deprived of his own dignity, as a troublesome and importunate person to imperial ears acting contrary to ecclesiastical regulations.

If necessity compels him to hasten to the emperor on account of some matter, he must go only after deliberation and with the counsel of the metropolitan bishop of the province, the knowledge of the other bishops in that same province, and letters from them.

XII. If anyone deposed by his own bishop—a presbyter, deacon, or even a bishop deprived of office by a synod—should bring his grievance to imperial ears, he must not do so, but must turn to a greater synod of bishops, state before their judgment whatever just claims he thinks he has, and await from them the sentence that will be pronounced concerning him.

[Note: [Col. 0709D] The common Isidorian text has “must not presume to do so.” Shortly afterward Vindobonensis, together with the common Isidorian text, has “council” instead of “judgment.”]

If, overcome by faintheartedness, he refuses to do this but becomes importunate with the emperor, he must receive no pardon, have no opportunity for any defense of his case, and have no hope of recovering his rank in the future.

[Note: [Col. 0709D] The next seven words are absent from the manuscript of Vindobonensis.]

XIII. No bishop may dare to pass from one province to another to ordain anyone in the Churches there or promote anyone to sacred ministry, nor may he draw other bishops there with him, unless he has gone at the request not only of the metropolitan but also of all the bishops who are with him in that province.

[Note: [Col. 0709D] Quesnellus inserts “we decree.” Vindobonensis and the common Isidorian text delete it; we have accordingly written *attrahat* (“may draw”) for *attrahere* (“to draw”). The common Isidorian text adds “all of his.”]

If anyone should arrive without being invited and in a disorderly manner, and presume either to ordain anyone or to usurp any acts belonging to that Church and in no way pertaining to him, all that he has done will be void and empty. He himself must answer for the penalties deserved by such an undisciplined presumption and unreasonable undertaking, as one deposed by the holy synod and already condemned on account of this presumption.

[Note: [Col. 0710C] Oxoniensis omits “acts.” Veronensis omits “belonging.” Vindobonensis reads “not at all pertaining to him”; the common Isidorian text reads “which do not at all pertain to him.”]

429 XIV. If a bishop has been accused in the judgment of the bishops on some criminal charges, and it should happen that the bishops of the province who investigated the matter hold divergent opinions, so that one declares him innocent and another guilty, then, in order to remove such a controversy, the holy synod has determined that the metropolitan of a neighboring province must be summoned, together with several other bishops, so that, sitting with them, they may settle the question, whatever it may be, in order that the judgment promulgated by the bishops of one province may stand firm.

[Note: [Col. 0710C] The common Isidorian text reads “who assembled”; shortly afterward, “sentences,” and “some declare him innocent, others guilty.” The manuscript of Vindobonensis has a similar reading. Veronensis reads “and one declares him innocent, etc.”]

[Note: [Col. 0710D] Vindobonensis agrees with the common Isidorian text. Quesnellus has “of another province.” Shortly afterward Vindobonensis omits “must.” The manuscript of Thuaneus reads: “let them settle whatever question has arisen, and establish as firm the judgment which was first pronounced by the bishops of one province, etc.”]

XV. If a bishop accused of a criminal offense has received one harmonious sentence from all the bishops within the province, he may not thereafter be judged by others. The sentence pronounced by all must remain in force concerning him, as a fitting, firm, and ratified judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0710D] The manuscript of Vindobonensis reads: “as a judgment fittingly and firmly ratified, which was pronounced by all.”]

XVI. If a bishop who is without a see should come upon a vacant Church and believe that it may be secretly seized apart from a plenary synod, he must be expelled, even if the people whose Church he has seized wish to retain him as their bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0710D] The same manuscript reads “secretly … to be occupied.” The common Isidorian text, together with the manuscript of Veronensis, reads “should believe that it ought to be plundered,” and afterward “which he plundered.” The latter reading is also found in Vindobonensis.]

A synod is called plenary when the metropolitan bishop has also been present.

[Note: [Col. 0711C] Quesnellus has “That synod, moreover, is called perfect in which …” Although the word “perfect” is also found in the manuscript of Veronensis, we have preferred the reading of Vindobonensis and the common Isidorian text, since Ferrandus also reads “plenary” in title 144.]

XVII. If a bishop, after receiving the laying on of hands and being appointed to preside over a people, does not accept the ministry of the priesthood and does not consent to go to the Church for which he was ordained, he must be excluded from communion until he consents under compulsion to receive the people assigned to him, or until a plenary synod of the bishops of the province determines something concerning him.

[Note: [Col. 0711C] Vindobonensis reads “entrusted to him.” We have inserted “of the bishops” with all our manuscripts and the common Isidorian text.]

XVIII. If an ordained bishop does not go to the parish for which he was ordained, not through any fault of his own but perhaps because of opposition from the people, he must retain the honor he has received and exercise the priesthood, provided that he causes no trouble to the Church in which he has been established.

[Note: [Col. 0711C] Vindobonensis reads “in which he had been established.”]

He must await the plenary synod of the province until a decision is made concerning what is appropriate in his case.

XIX. A bishop must not be ordained without the counsel and presence of the metropolitan of the province. It would be better if the bishops of the entire province were assembled. If this cannot be done, those who cannot be present must indicate their consent concerning him in letters of their own. Only then, after the concordant judgment of the majority—whether expressed in person or by letter—may he be ordained.

If this is done otherwise than has been established, such an ordination is to be considered invalid.

[Note: [Col. 0711C] Quesnellus adds “we decree.” We deleted it in agreement with the manuscripts of Vindobonensis and Veronensis and the common Isidorian text. Quesnellus also deleted “even” and preferred “be completed” to “be celebrated,” contrary to our manuscripts and the common text.]

But if the ordination is celebrated according to the defined rules, while some oppose it because of their own private and domestic quarrels, their opposition must be disregarded, and the judgment of the majority concerning him must prevail.

[Note: [Col. 0711C] The common Isidorian text, together with the manuscript of Vindobonensis, reads “a bishop must not be ordained.” We have written “of the province’s metropolitan” with the manuscripts of Vindobonensis and Veronensis. Other copies have “of the metropolitan bishop.”]

XX. For ecclesiastical responsibilities and for resolving disputes which arise, it has seemed sufficient that a council of bishops be held twice a year in each province: first, after the third week of the Paschal festival, so that the council may be completed in the following fourth week—that is, in the middle of Pentecost.

[Note: [Col. 0711D] The other manuscript of Vindobonensis reads “once.” The common Isidorian text reads: “so that the council may be completed in the fourth week of holy Easter, with the metropolitan bishop summoning all the bishops of the province. The second council is to be held on the Ides, etc.” We have written “that is, in the middle of Pentecost” with the manuscripts of Vindobonensis, Thuaneus, and Veronensis. Quesnellus has “that is, in the middle toward Pentecost.”]

The bishops who live in the larger cities—that is, in the metropolitan cities—must summon the provincial bishops.

The second council is to be held on the Ides of October, which day is reckoned by the Greeks as the tenth of the month Hyperberetaeus.

[Note: [Col. 0711D] The common Isidorian text has “the fifteenth.” It adds: “so that at these councils all the presbyters, deacons, and others who say that they have been wronged may come forward, so that, after their case has been examined in council, they may arrive at the proper judgment. No one may hold a council privately on his own authority, except those to whom the metropolitan sees have been entrusted.”]

At these councils presbyters and deacons must be present, as well as all who consider themselves wronged, and they must await the synodical judgment. No one may hold councils on his own authority without the knowledge of the metropolitan bishops, to whom judgment concerning all cases has been entrusted.

XXI. A bishop must not pass from one diocese to another, neither if he has inserted himself there, nor if he has been forcibly drawn there by the people, nor even if bishops advise him to do so.

[Note: [Col. 0712C] This is the reading of our manuscripts and the common Isidorian text. Quesnellus alone reads “nor if even the bishops should advise him to do so.” He later alone omits “of God” and, after “must,” adds “it is necessary.”]

He must remain in the Church of God which he received by lot from the beginning and must not depart from it to another, in accordance with the rule formerly established on this matter by the Fathers.

XXII. A bishop must not invade another city which does not appear to be subject to him, nor a region known in no way to belong to his care, in order to ordain anyone there. Nor may he appoint presbyters or deacons in places belonging to other bishops, except perhaps with the counsel of the proper bishop of that region.

[Note: [Col. 0712C] Veronensis, together with the common Isidorian text, reads “a bishop must not invade another city.” Shortly afterward the common Isidorian text adds “which is shown not to be subject to him.” We have written “if he should wish” with our manuscripts and the common text; Quesnellus has “if he should attempt.” Veronensis and the common text later read “such an ordination will indeed be invalid.”]

If anyone should wish to dare any of these things, such an ordination will be invalid, and the one who has wrongly usurped authority will be rebuked by the synod.

[Note: [Col. 0712C] The common Isidorian text adds: “For if he has not been able to ordain, let him under no circumstances presume to judge the parishioner of another.” Something similar appears in the version of Dionysius Exiguus and something also in the *Prisca*, but nothing in the Greek or in our manuscripts of Vindobonensis and Veronensis, which represent the Isidorian interpretation.]

XXIII. A bishop may not appoint another as his future successor, even when he is near death. If anything of this kind has been done, the ordination is to be invalid.

[Note: [Col. 0712D] Veronensis reads “a bishop is not permitted”; the common Isidorian text reads “bishops are not permitted.” Quesnellus omitted the words “future” and “another,” which we restored from our manuscripts, the Thuaneus manuscript of Quesnellus, and the common Isidorian text.]

The ecclesiastical regulations must be preserved. They provide that a bishop cannot be appointed otherwise than in council and with the consent of those bishops alone who, after the death of the preceding bishop, possess the authority to promote the person who is worthy.

[Note: [Col. 0712D] The manuscript of Vindobonensis reads “another may be made.”]

432 XXIV. Whatever belongs to the Church must be carefully and faithfully preserved, in that faith which is preserved before God, who provides for all things and judges all things.

[Note: [Col. 0712D] The same manuscript reads “which is owed to God.” The common Isidorian text has “which ought to be governed,” instead of “whatever,” and “and that they should be governed.” We have inserted “and administered” and “of the whole,” following all our manuscripts and the common text.]

Everything must be governed and administered with the judgment and authority of the bishop, to whom the souls of the entire people appear to have been entrusted.

The property belonging to the Church must be clearly known to the presbyters and deacons around him, so that they themselves are not ignorant and nothing concerning the Church’s own possessions remains hidden from them.

[Note: [Col. 0713C] Quesnellus reads “to the knowledge of the presbyters and deacons, that is, those around the bishop, so that they may not be ignorant and nothing may be hidden from them.” We have followed the manuscripts of Vindobonensis and Veronensis together with the common Isidorian text.]

Thus, if it should happen that the bishop departs from this life, the ecclesiastical possessions, being known and documented, will not be lost or destroyed.

Nor should the bishop’s private property be attacked by anyone under the pretext of ecclesiastical possessions, since it is just and fitting before God and human beings that what belongs to the bishop should be left to those to whom he has assigned it, while what belongs to the Church should be preserved for the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0713C] The common Isidorian text reads “acceptable.” Quesnellus noted that *decibile*, meaning “what is fitting,” was formerly used in this sense. Vindobonensis has “has judged” instead of “has ordered.”]

In this way neither will the Church be afflicted by any loss, nor will the bishop be proscribed on account of ecclesiastical property, nor will those connected with him become involved in lawsuits, so that after his death his memory may be burdened with curses.

[Note: [Col. 0713C] This is the reading of our manuscripts and the common Isidorian text. Quesnellus has “so that the Church’s affairs may not be afflicted … nor matters belonging to him come before a court.”]

XXV. [Note: [Col. 0713C] Quesnellus inserts “it is fitting,” contrary to our manuscripts and the common Isidorian text.]

The bishop must have authority over ecclesiastical possessions, in order to distribute them to all who are in need with complete fear and reverence for God. He himself also ought to take from them and use whatever he needs, if indeed he needs it, either for his necessary expenses or for the expenses of the brothers who stay with him for the sake of hospitality, so that they may not in any respect be deprived through want, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Having daily food and bodily covering, with these we are content” (1 Tim. 6:8).

[Note: [Col. 0713C] Quesnellus reads “food and bodily clothing; let us be content with these.” We have adopted the reading of our manuscripts, the manuscript of Thuaneus, and the common Isidorian text.]

But if he is not content with or satisfied by these things, and should divert ecclesiastical possessions to domestic needs, or appropriate any advantage of the Church or the produce of ecclesiastical estates without the knowledge of the presbyters or deacons who are with him, and grant authority over these things to his household, relatives, or even to the brothers or children of those persons, so that through their secret management the other clergy appear to be harmed, he must answer for this offense before the metropolitan of the province.

[Note: [Col. 0713C] The common Isidorian text and Vindobonensis delete the words “or deacons”; they are nevertheless present in other versions and in the Greek.]

[Note: [Col. 0713C] Quesnellus reads: “he who is of this kind must answer for his offenses before the metropolitan.” We have preferred the reading of our manuscripts and the common text. Vindobonensis alone has “must.”]

But if the bishop, or the presbyters who are with him, is otherwise accused on the charge that they are appropriating to themselves what belongs to the Church—whether estates or any other ecclesiastical possessions—and that the poor are being oppressed by need and deprivation, so that not only the ecclesiastical administration but also its stewards are burdened with curses and reproach, then these persons must receive the correction they deserve, as the holy synod shall determine.

[Note: [Col. 0713D] Quesnellus numbered this section XXVI, as though it were a canon distinct from the preceding one. He nevertheless noted in the margin: “It is part of the preceding canon in Isidore and others.” None of our manuscripts divides the text, nor does the exemplar of Vindobonensis in this collection. We have compared Quesnellus’s reading—“But if the bishop, or those who are with him, is otherwise accused”—with our manuscripts and the common text, and, with their common agreement, inserted “therefore” at the end of this canon.]

Eusebius: In the presence of the holy synod I have consented to everything that has been established. Theodosius, Nicetas, Macedonius, and the other persons named above: We have consented.

[Note: [Col. 0713D] Our manuscripts of Vindobonensis and Veronensis omit the words “in the holy synod.” Vindobonensis gives the subscriptions as follows: “Eusebius, Theodorus, and the others whose names are already contained above in the Greek: We have consented. Amen. The Council of Antioch ends.” The manuscript of Veronensis reads: “Eusebius: I, being present, have consented to everything that has been established; Theodorus, Nicetas, Macedonius, Anatolius, Tarcodimantus, Etherius, Narcissus, Alphius, Archelaus, Bassus, Siricius, Esicius, Mauricius, Theodosius, Moses, Mucimus, Magnus, Agapius and Agapius, Magnus, Eneas, Paulus: We have consented.” The common Isidorian text gives the same episcopal names and in the same order through Narcissus, after whom it adds: “Eustachius, Esychius, Mauricius, Paulus, and the others consented and subscribed”—thirty bishops.]

434 CHAPTER LX.

The Council of Laodicea in Phrygia Pacatiana begins.

[Note: [Col. 0714C] This is the ancient version commonly called Isidorian. It is found in the manuscripts of this collection, as well as in the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, and also in another very ancient manuscript, Vaticanus 1342, and in the two manuscripts of Veronensis, 55 and 58. In the latter manuscript, which is mutilated, it ends at canon 16. We have taken the title from the copy of Vindobonensis. Quesnellus has: “The Canons of the Council held at Laodicea of Phrygia Pacatiana.” He notes in the margin that the manuscript of Thuaneus reads: “The rules or definitions according to Laodicea of Phrygia Pacatiana begin”; the same wording is found in the manuscript of Veronensis 58. On the date of this synod, see what we established in the Treatise, part I, chapter 3, section 1.]

[Col. 0714B]

The holy synod, convened at Laodicea in Phrygia Pacatiana from the various provinces of Asia, set forth the ecclesiastical rules as written below.

I. Concerning those who, according to the ecclesiastical canon, have freely and lawfully entered a second marriage and have not engaged in secret intercourse: after a short period has elapsed, they should devote themselves to prayers and fasts, and, in accordance with pardon, communion should be restored to them.

[Note: [Col. 0714D] Quesnellus, together with the common Isidorian text, reads “are joined in second marriages.” We have written “in second marriages” with all four of our manuscripts—Vindobonensis, Vaticanus 1342, and the two manuscripts of Veronensis. The first two suggested “are joined.” We have preferred “intercourse” to “intermingling,” following all the manuscripts and the common text. Quesnellus has “intermingling.”]

II. Those who fall into various sins, and devote themselves earnestly to prayer, confession, and repentance for their evils, demonstrating a complete conversion, must be assigned a period of repentance proportionate to the nature of the sin. On account of the mercy and goodness of God, those who are such must be recalled and admitted to communion.

[Note: [Col. 0714D] We inserted the conjunction “and” with three Vatican manuscripts and the two manuscripts of Veronensis, with the common Isidorian text agreeing. The same two manuscripts of Veronensis, together with the common text, later omit “and” before “on account of mercy.”]

III. A neophyte must not be promoted to the priestly order.

[Note: [Col. 0715C] In this canon and the two following ones, Quesnellus prefixed the words “Concerning what ought to be done,” or “it is not permitted.” We deleted them in agreement with the manuscripts of Vindobonensis and Vaticanus and the common Isidorian text.]

IV. It is not permitted to celebrate the ordination of any cleric, 435 in the presence of catechumens.

[Note: [Col. 0715C] Quesnellus has: “to celebrate the laying on of hands over those being ordained in the presence of catechumens.” The same reading occurs in two Veronese manuscripts, except that they have “to be celebrated.” The Isidorian Vulgate has: “that it is not permitted for the laying on of hands over those being ordained to take place in the presence of catechumens.” We have inserted into the text the reading of the best manuscripts, Vind. and Vat.]

V. It is not permitted for ministers of the altar, or those constituted in the priestly order, to lend at interest, or to accept either interest or profits called *ses­cupla*.

[Note: [Col. 0715C] The Vatican manuscript has: “but not even interest.” The two Veronese manuscripts have: “and either interest”; the Isidorian Vulgate: “or interest.” Later, because the Vindobonensis of this collection reads *quae sesculpa*, others transcribed from some similar manuscript *quae ex culpa ducuntur* (“which are derived from guilt”). Three of our Vatican manuscripts and the two Veronese manuscripts, together with the Isidorian Vulgate, supply the true reading. Quesnellus noted: “Dionysius has the same from the Greek ἡμιολίας (*hēmiolías*), which the codex of Justellus interprets as *centesimas* (‘hundredfold’).” More correctly, Justellus—who, when preparing the Greek codex for publication, had it improperly entitled “of the universal Church”—substituted *centesimas* for *ses­cupla* when giving the translation of Dionysius Exiguus.]

VI. Heretics who remain in heresy must not be granted entry into the house of God.

VII. The Novatians must also be excluded, as well as the Quartodecimans, whom the Greeks call *Tessareskaidekatites*—that is, those who celebrate Passover with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month. Their catechumens and faithful, moreover, are not to be received until they have completely condemned every heresy, and above all the one in which they were held. Then those who among them are called faithful must be taught the symbol of faith; and thus, after being anointed also with holy chrism, they ought to communicate in the divine sacrament.

[Note: [Col. 0715D] Manuscripts of other collections, Veron. and Vat., together with the Isidorian Vulgate, add: “or even the Quartodecimans, whom the Greeks call Tessareskaidekatites.” The two Veronese manuscripts omit the word “Greeks.”]

[Note: [Col. 0715D] Quesnellus has: “and thus the anointed with chrism.” We have followed three of our manuscripts, Vind., Veron. 55, and Vat. The Isidorian Vulgate deletes only *etiam* (“also”). Veron. 55 has *permittantur* (“let them be permitted”) instead of *conveniet* (“it will be proper”).]

VIII. Those who convert from the heresy called “according to the Phrygians,” and who consider themselves constituted in the clergy, even though they are called great, persons of this kind must be catechized with every care and baptized by bishops and presbyters of the Catholic Church.

[Note: [Col. 0715D] Thus the manuscripts Vind., Oxon., and Veron. 58. Quesnellus, together with the Isidorian Vulgate, has “of the Cataphrygians.” Veron. 55 has “Cataphrygians, that is, Montanists”; Greek: τῶν λεγομένων Φρυγῶν (“of those called Phrygians”). Later the Vindobonensis has “although they are called magnificent.”]

[Note: [Col. 0715D] Thus Vind., Vat., and the Vulgate. Quesnellus, with other manuscripts, has *cum magna* (“with great [care]”).]

IX. Catholics must not enter what are called the cemeteries or martyr-shrines of heretics for the sake of prayer or seeking healing. Those who do go must, if they are faithful, be treated as excluded from communion and reduced to penance for a certain period; but, once they have done penance and confessed that they have erred, they ought to be received.

[Note: [Col. 0716C] The Vatican and Veronese manuscripts, together with the Vulgate, have: “to enter the cemeteries or what are called the martyr-shrines of heretics for the sake of prayer, etc.”]

[Note: [Col. 0716C] Codex Veronensis 55 has: “Let them know that they have been made incapable of communion. Let them be reduced to penance for a certain period; but after penance, when they have confessed that they erred, then they ought to be received into communion.”]

X. Those who belong to the Church must by no means indiscriminately join their own children in marriage with heretics.

[Note: [Col. 0716C] Since the words *seniores*, *univirae*, and *matriculariae* were omitted by Quesnellus, we have restored them with all our manuscripts and the Isidorian Vulgate; Ferrandus also supports them, title 221.]

XI. Women who among the Greeks are called *presbyterae* (“presbyteresses”), but among us are called *seniores* (“elders”), *univirae* (“women of one husband”), and *matriculariae* (“matricular women”), may not be established in the Church as though they were ordained.

XII. Bishops must not be appointed to the leadership of a church without the judgment of the metropolitans and neighboring bishops.

[Note: [Col. 0716C] Thus the manuscripts Thuan., Vat., and the Isidorian Vulgate. Quesnellus, with other manuscripts, has: “to the prejudice of the metropolitans.”]

Nor should they be elected except those whom a long-established, notable, and commendable life recommends, and who have nevertheless been proved by their conduct in speech of faith and sound judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0716D] Quesnellus has: “For neither should those be elected except whom …” We have accepted the reading of Vind. and the Isidorian Vulgate. Vat. and Veron. 58 also agree, except that they omit *hi* (“those”). Veron. 55 reads: “Nor should those be elected except those who long beforehand are judged worthy of approval by the merit of their life; and nevertheless …”]

[Note: [Col. 0716D] Thus four of our manuscripts together with the Thuaneus and Quesnellus, who conjectures that *actione* (“in action”) should perhaps be read instead of *ratione* (“in practice”). The Isidorian Vulgate differs only in having “and by upright conduct.” Quesnellus has: “if in the reasoning of faith and in upright speech.”]

XIII. Concerning the matter that the people must not be permitted to elect those who are to be assigned to the ministry of the altar.

[Note: [Col. 0716D] Codex Vind. has: “for the ministry of the altar.”]

XIV. The holy offerings, in place of blessed gifts, ought by no means to be sent to other parishes during the Paschal feast.

XV. Apart from the canonical psalmists, who ascend the pulpit and read from the book, no one else may sing psalms in the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0716D] Codex Vind. has “psalmists.” The Isidorian Vulgate adds: “that is, those who regularly serve as singers and who ascend the pulpit, etc.”]

XVI. On Saturdays the Gospels are to be read together with the other Scriptures.

XVII. In processions there must be no “connecting”—that is, joining together one song from different verses and meanings of a book. Rather, a reading must be made orderly from the middle of each individual psalm.

[Note: [Col. 0716D] We added the word *debere* (“must”) from all our manuscripts and the Isidorian Vulgate. Oxon. lacks *de medio* (“from the middle”).]

XVIII. Concerning the requirement that the same supplications of prayers always be celebrated both at the ninth hour and at vespers. 437

XIX. Since the prayer of the catechumens ought to be celebrated separately and first, after the bishop’s address, when they have departed, let those who are undergoing penance also pray; and after the laying on of hands, when these too have withdrawn, then the faithful must pray. Let their three prayers be made: one, namely the first, in silence; the second and third, with spoken words. Only then should peace be given with a kiss. After the presbyters have given peace to the bishop, the laity also should give it, and thus the offering should be presented. Only the ministers of the altar may enter the altar and communicate.

[Note: [Col. 0716D] Quesnellus notes in the margin: “The remaining canons of this council are missing from the Thuaneus manuscript from this canon through the end of 51, which is canon 54 in the Oxonian manuscript; in that manuscript, 55, 56, and 57 correspond to 52, 53, and 54 in Thuan.” In Quesnellus, this canon begins: “That the prayers of the catechumens …” We have followed our manuscripts and the Isidorian Vulgate.]

[Note: [Col. 0717C] The Isidorian Vulgate adds *ibidem* (“there”).]

XX. Since a deacon ought not to sit when a presbyter is present, he should sit only at the presbyter’s command. Likewise, the deacon must be honored by the lower ministers and by all clerics.

XXI. Since ministers must not have permission to enter the secretarium, or sacristy—which the Greeks call the *diaconicon*—and touch the Lord’s vessels.

[Note: [Col. 0717C] The Isidorian Vulgate has: “subdeacons must have permission.” We added *sive sacrarium* (“or sacristy”) from all our manuscripts.]

XXII. A minister must not use an orarium, nor abandon the doors.

XXIII. Since readers and psalmists ought not to use an orarium and thus read or sing psalms.

[Note: [Col. 0717C] On the authority of our manuscripts and the Isidorian Vulgate, we restored the word *quoniam* (“since”) here and in the following canon, where Quesnellus had omitted it.]

XXIV. Since those serving at the altar, from presbyters down to deacons, and thereafter men of the ecclesiastical order down to ministers, readers, psalmists, exorcists, doorkeepers, and even those who have undertaken a discipline of continence, ought not to enter taverns.

[Note: [Col. 0717D] Quesnellus has: “or officials who are engaged in this purpose, etc.” We corrected and supplemented the text from our manuscripts and the Isidorian Vulgate.]

XXV. Ministers must not give bread or bless the cup.

[Note: [Col. 0717D] Another reading: “to give bread or the cup, etc.”]

XXVI. 438 Those who have not yet been advanced by the bishop must not perform exorcisms, either in churches or inside houses.

XXVII. Ministers of the altar, or any clerics, or even laypeople invited to an *agape*, must not take away portions, because of the injury that might on this occasion be attributed to the ecclesiastical order.

XXVIII. [Col. 0718A] An *agape* must not be held on Sundays or in churches, nor may people eat inside or set out couches.

[Note: [Col. 0717D] Other readings are: “it is not fitting,” “it ought not,” or “it is not permitted.”]

XXIX. Christians must not Judaize or rest on the Sabbath; rather, they must work on that same day. Sunday, however, is to be preferred to that day. If they wish, let them rest as Christians. But those who are found Judaizing shall be anathema.

[Note: [Col. 0717D] Quesnellus has: “on the same day. But if Sunday pleases them, etc.” The Isidorian Vulgate has: “on the same day, placing Sunday before that day. If this pleases them, etc. But if they are found …” We preferred the reading of Vind. and Vat., except that they erroneously have *eamdem diem* (“the same day”). Codex Veron. 55 reads: “on the same day, Sunday”—*Dominico*, to be read as *Dominicum*—“is to be preferred to that day; for if they wish to rest on the Sabbath day, let them rest as Christians. For if they are found …”]

XXX. Since ministers of the altar, or any clerics, or even those practicing continence, and indeed every Christian without exception, ought not to share baths with women, for this is the first accusation made among the pagans.

[Note: [Col. 0717D] Thus our manuscripts. Quesnellus has “those practicing continence, or anyone at all.”]

XXXI. Since one must not contract marriages with any heretics, nor give sons or daughters [in marriage], but rather receive [sons or daughters], provided that they profess that they will become Catholics.

[Note: [Col. 0718C] Quesnellus has: “not to mix feasts with any heretics, or give daughters”; then “future Catholics.” We corrected the text from our manuscripts and the Isidorian Vulgate.]

XXXII. One must not receive the blessings of heretics, since these are curses rather than blessings.

XXXIII. One must not pray with heretics or schismatics.

XXXIV. No Christian must abandon the martyrs of Christ and go to false men made martyrs, for they are alien from God. Whoever wishes to go must be anathema.

[Note: [Col. 0718C] We added *omnem* (“every”) with the manuscripts Vind. and Vat., in agreement with the Greek text.]

[Note: [Col. 0718C] Thus the Vatican manuscript and two of Hardouin’s manuscripts. Ferrandus, Codex Veronensis, and the Isidorian Vulgate partly agree, reading “to false martyrs,” while suppressing the word *factos* (“made”). Quesnellus, together with Vind., has “to false men made martyrs.”]

XXXV. Since Christians must not abandon the Church of God and go to invoke angels and hold assemblies: all such things are forbidden. Whoever is found secretly practicing this idolatry shall be anathema, since, abandoning our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, he has approached idols.

[Note: [Col. 0718C] We preferred this reading, which agrees with the translation of Dionysius and with the Greek text. It was supplied by the Vindobonensis, except that it erroneously has *nomine* instead of *nominare*. Two Vatican manuscripts and Veron. 55, together with three of Hardouin’s manuscripts, have: “naming angels and holding a congregation or congregations.” Ferrandus, title 184, reads: “to hold a congregation to angels.” The Isidorian Vulgate has: “and to make congregations for angels of detestable idolatry.” Quesnellus has: “to name angels and hold a congregation,” and so forth. The context makes it clear that the subject is the worship of idols offered outside the Church of God to angels. Just as the preceding canon attacks the worship of false martyrs, so this one prohibits the worship of false angels, that is, demons, or the improper worship—according to Jewish or pagan custom—offered to angels by certain heretics whom Epiphanius calls the Angelici. Heresy 60.]

XXXVI. Since ministers of the altar and clerics must not be magicians or enchanters, or make what are called *phylacteria*, which are great bonds of souls, we have ordered that those who use such things be expelled from the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0718D] Codex Veronensis 55 adds “in Greek.”]

XXXVII. One must not accept from Jews or heretics festive gifts that are sent, nor celebrate feast days with them.

[Note: [Col. 0719C] Thus all the manuscripts and the Isidorian Vulgate, together with Ferrandus, title 185. Quesnellus has *xenia* (“guest-gifts”), and in the margin: “Alternatively, festive gifts, which is what is read in Dionysius.” The remainder—“nor celebrate feast days with them”—is absent from the manuscripts Vind. and Vat. Codex Veronensis has *feriatos* (“days of rest”) instead of *festos* (“feast days”).]

XXXVIII. One must not accept unleavened bread from Jews or share in their impieties.

XXXIX. One must not celebrate feasts with pagans or share in their impiety.

[Note: [Col. 0719C] Quesnellus transcribed this canon after the following one. We have restored it to its proper place from all our manuscripts and the Vulgate.]

XL. Bishops summoned to a synod must not disregard it, but must go, either to teach or to be taught what concerns the correction of the Church and of the others. If one disregards it, he will appear to have accused himself—unless perhaps he is unable to go because of illness.

[Note: [Col. 0719C] On the authority of the manuscripts Vind. and Veron. 55, together with the Isidorian Vulgate, we added *caeterorumque* (“and of the others”); shortly afterward we wrote *videbitur* (“will appear”) instead of *videtur* (“appears”), which Vat. has and Quesnellus renders *judicabitur* (“will be judged”).]

XLI. A minister of the altar, or even a layman, must not travel anywhere without canonical letters, that is, *formatae*.

XLII. A minister of the altar, or any cleric, must not travel to foreign places without the bishop’s command.

[Note: [Col. 0719C] Because of the repetition of the same opening, *Non oportet* (“it is not permitted”), this canon was omitted by a leap in the manuscripts Vind. and Veron. 55. It was nevertheless written in the latter by a second hand. From this addition, as well as from the Vatican manuscript and the Isidorian Vulgate, we added *clericum* (“a cleric”), a word also accepted by Ferrandus, title 112. The same Veronese and Vatican manuscripts have *ad peregrinationem* (“on pilgrimage”) instead of *ad peregrina* (“to foreign places”).]

XLIII. Ministers must not be absent from the doors even for a short time and devote themselves to prayer.

[Note: [Col. 0719D] Thus all our manuscripts and the Isidorian Vulgate. Quesnellus alone has: “Doorkeepers must not be absent … unless they are devoting themselves to prayer.” In the Isidorian Vulgate this canon is placed after the following one, and canon 45 appears after our canon 46 in that same Vulgate.]

XLIV. No one is to be received for baptism after the second week of Lent.

XLV. Women must not enter the altar.

XLVI. Those to be baptized ought to learn the symbol of faith and recite it to either the bishop or the presbyter on the Thursday of the last week.

[Note: [Col. 0719D] Thus all our manuscripts and the Isidorian Vulgate. Quesnellus has “receive” instead of “learn.”]

XLVII. Those who received baptism while ill must, once they have recovered, be taught the symbol of faith, so that they may know with what gift they have been deemed worthy.

XLVIII. Those who have been baptized ought, after baptism, to become participants also in the chrism and in the heavenly kingdom of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0719D] Quesnellus has: “after baptism also to become participants in the chrism and the heavenly kingdom.” We have accepted the reading of the manuscripts and the Vulgate.]

XLIX. During Lent bread must not be offered except on Saturday and Sunday.

[Note: [Col. 0719D] This canon is absent from the Oxonian manuscript, and Quesnellus omitted it with that manuscript, thinking that the omission occurred because the canon was contrary to the usage of the Roman Church, as he noted in a marginal postscript. Yet the canon is found not only in the Greek and other versions but also in the Isidorian version, which was adopted by our collector. This is shown by Codex Vind. of this collection, by Vat. 1342 and the Isidorian Vulgate, and also by Ferrandus, title 207, who used what is called the Isidorian translation. In Veron. 55 it was absent from the first hand but was added in a later correction. The absence of this canon in certain manuscripts must likewise be attributed to the leap by which we observed canon 42 omitted in other manuscripts; see note 38 above.]

L. During Lent the fast must not be broken on the Thursday of the last week, nor must the whole of Lent be dishonored; rather, one must fast throughout all the days and use foods suited to abstinence, that is, drier foods.

[Note: [Col. 0720C] Thus Codex Vind., in agreement with Ferrandus, title 308. Quesnellus has: “the Thursday of the last week is to be released, and the whole …” Codex Veronensis, in its first hand, has: “to release the Thursday of the last week, and to spend the whole of Lent in prayer”; and there the canon ends. In a later correction it reads: “to break the fast on the Thursday of the last week and to pass through the whole of Lent without honoring the fast,” with nothing further in this canon. Quesnellus then wrote *exhonorari* (“to dishonor”) instead of *inhonorari*; he omitted the words “that is, drier foods,” which we inserted on the authority of Codex Vind. and the Isidorian Vulgate.]

LI. During Lent the birthdays—or feasts—of the martyrs must not be celebrated; only their commemoration may be made on Saturday and Sunday.

LII. During Lent neither weddings nor any birthdays or feast days may be celebrated.

LIII. Christians who go to weddings must not dance or sing; rather, they must dine or lunch chastely, as befits Christians.

[Note: [Col. 0720C] Quesnellus, together with the Isidorian Vulgate and Veron. 55, has *saltare* (“to dance”). We corrected this from the manuscript Vind. and Ferrandus, title 188, in agreement with Vat., which has *canere* (“to sing”). Shortly afterward this manuscript has *convenit* (“is fitting”) instead of *competit* (“befits”).]

LIV. Ministers of the altar, or any clerics, must not attend any spectacles presented at weddings or dinners; rather, before the theatrical performers enter, they must rise from the meal and depart.

[Note: [Col. 0720D] The Isidorian Vulgate, together with Veron. 55, has *scenis* (“scenes”), contrary to the other manuscripts and the Greek text. Quesnellus then has *insurgere* (“to rise”) and “to leave the meal.” We restored the reading of all our manuscripts and the Isidorian Vulgate.]

LV. Ministers of the altar, or any clerics, or even Christian laypeople, must not hold banquets from the contributions that the common people call *commissalia*.

[Note: [Col. 0720D] Quesnellus omitted “ministers of the altar or,” and then wrote “to celebrate *symbola*, which the common people call *competalia* banquets.” We have accepted the reading shared by our manuscripts. The Isidorian Vulgate also agrees, having only *commensalia* instead of *commissalia*.]

LVI. Presbyters must not enter and sit in the tribunals before the bishop enters, but must enter with the bishop—unless perhaps the bishop is ill or is known to be abroad.

LVII. Bishops must not be ordained in villages and country towns; rather, visitors, that is, those who travel about, are to be appointed. Those who have previously been ordained must do nothing without the knowledge of the bishop of the city. Likewise, presbyters must do nothing without the bishop’s command and counsel.

[Note: [Col. 0720D] The Isidorian Vulgate has: “but visitors, that is, those who travel about, are to be appointed.” Veron. 55, retaining the reading of the text, adds after “travel about”: “to be appointed by the bishop of the city for the salvation of the people.” Shortly afterward Quesnellus has: “Those who were ordained before this must do nothing without the knowledge of the city,” and omitted the remainder. We have restored the true and complete reading, which he relegated to the margin from the Isidorian Vulgate and the Thuaneus manuscript, together with our manuscripts.]

LVIII. Offerings must not be made in houses by bishops or presbyters.

LIX. Psalms composed by private individuals and popular psalms must not be recited in churches, nor may books outside the canon be read, except only the canonical books of the New and Old Testament.

The books that ought to be read and received as authoritative are these: Genesis of the world; Exodus from Egypt; Leviticus; Numbers; Deuteronomy; Joshua son of Nun; Judges; Ruth; four books of Kings; Chronicles, that is, two books of the Remnants; two books of Ezra; the 150 Psalms; Proverbs of Solomon; Ecclesiastes; Song of Songs; Job; Esther; the twelve Prophets, namely Hosea, Amos, Joel, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and the Angel Malachi; then Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel.

[Note: [Col. 0721B] Quesnellus omitted the following catalogue of the Scriptures and appended this note: “In other versions”—it should have been written “in the published editions of Isidore”—“and also in the Greek there follows a catalogue of the books of the Old and New Testament, which is absent from both manuscripts, namely the Thuaneus and Oxonian manuscripts of this collection, which he himself consulted. But we found it in the excellent Vindobonensis of the same collection, as well as in two others, Vat. 1342 and Veron. 55, which likewise present the Isidorian version. Hence this catalogue was not omitted by the author of this translation; therefore those two manuscripts, Thuan. and Oxon., which derived the Laodicean canons from the same version but lack this catalogue, are incomplete.]

[Note: [Col. 0721C] Vind. has, erroneously, “that is, books of *Abrahelictorum*.” We corrected this from the Veronese manuscript. The Isidorian Vulgate and Vat. do not have these two words.]

[Note: [Col. 0721C] Thus the Isidorian Vulgate together with the Greek. Some of our other manuscripts omit “two.”]

[Note: [Col. 0721C] Thus Codex Vind. together with the Isidorian Vulgate. In Vat. “twelve” and “that is” are absent. Veron. has: “the books of the twelve Prophets,” followed by “that is, etc.” In the published Greek text the names of the twelve prophets are absent.]

[Note: [Col. 0721D] Thus Codex Vind. In the Vatican and Veronese manuscripts: “Haggai, Malachi”; in Vat. Haggai is nevertheless written a second time earlier, while in Veron. it is omitted. The Isidorian Vulgate has only Malachi here, and Haggai above.]

[Note: [Col. 0721D] Veron. has: “Then the four books: Isaiah, etc.”]

The four Gospels of the New Testament: according to Matthew, according to Mark, according to Luke, and according to John; the Acts of the Apostles; the seven canonical epistles: two of Peter, one of James, three of John, and one of Jude; the fourteen epistles of Paul: to the Romans; to the Corinthians I and II; to the Galatians; to the Ephesians; to the Philippians; to the Colossians; to the Thessalonians I and II; to Timothy I and II; to Titus; to Philemon; and to the Hebrews.

[Note: [Col. 0721D] The Veronese manuscript has: “Then of the New Testament.” The Isidorian Vulgate has: “But of the New Testament.”]

[Note: [Col. 0721D] Vind. has: “the canonical catholic epistles of Peter, etc.” The Isidorian Vulgate has: “the seven catholic epistles.” We preferred the manuscripts Veron. and Vat.; we retained, however, the order of Codex Vind. In Vat. another order occurs, as in the Greek and the Isidorian Vulgate: James I; two of Peter; three of John; one of Jude. The same order was written by a second hand in Veron., which then lists Paul’s epistles as follows: to the Romans I; to the Corinthians II and III; to the Galatians IV; to the Ephesians V; to the Philippians VI; to the Colossians VII; to the Thessalonians VIII and IX; to Timothy X and XI; to Titus XII; to Philemon XIII; to the Hebrews XIV.]

[Note: [Col. 0722B] Veron. 55 adds the Apocalypse of John. The ecclesiastical canon should end here. Explicit.]

[Note: [Col. 0722B] We added this conclusion from Codex Vind.]

The Council of Laodicea of Phrygia Pacatiana ends.

443

## CHAPTER LXI

[Note: [Col. 0722C] In the Vindobonensis manuscript this title reads “[lacuna].” Quesnellus preferred the following title: “Canons of the Council of Constantinople, held by 150 bishops when Blessed Nectarius was ordained bishop of that city, under the most devout Augustus Theodosius I.” This is the translation of those canons which, having been received by Isidore, is called Isidorian. We found the same translation of these canons in Veron. 55, with the title: “Here begin the statutes or definitions of the synod of Constantinople of 159 bishops, when Blessed Nectarius was ordained.”]

Here begin the Rules or Definitions set forth by the 150 bishops who assembled together at Constantinople when Nectarius was ordained bishop; their names and provinces are contained in the Greek text; under the emperor Theodosius.

### Canon I

The faith of the 318 Fathers who assembled at Nicaea in Bithynia must not be despised; rather, it must remain ratified, and every heresy must be anathematized, especially that of the Eunomians—who in Latin are called “without law”—and of the Arians, or Eudoxians, and of the Semi-Arians, as well as of the Pneumatomachi, that is, those who fight against the Holy Spirit; of the Photinians, Sabellians, and Apollinarians.

[Note: [Col. 0722C] The Isidorian Vulgate adds, together with the Greek, “or Anomoeans,” and the words that follow correspond to it: “who in Latin are called without law.” The words “or Eudoxians” are absent from the Vindobonensis manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0722C] The manuscripts Veron. 55 and the Isidorian Vulgate, in agreement with the Greek, add “the Sabellians, Marcellians, Photinians, and Apollinarians.” After the name “Apollinarians,” Vind. adds “and Marcellians, and Manichaeans, and all who depart from sound doctrine and the Catholic Church.”]

### II

Bishops who are over a diocese must not go to churches outside their boundaries, nor confuse or intermingle the churches, but, according to the rules, the bishop of Alexandria is to govern only those churches that are in Egypt; the bishops of the East are to care only for the East, with the primatial honors of the Church of Antioch preserved, as they are contained in the rules of the Synod of Nicaea.

[Note: [Col. 0722D] Vind., together with the Isidorian Vulgate, has “outside”; Veron. 55, together with Oxon., has “beyond.”]

[Note: [Col. 0722D] The manuscripts of this collection divide the canons in various ways. Vind. divides them into eleven canons and therefore marks this as Canon III; it then marks the words “of the East” as Canon IV, “and of Asia” as Canon V, “but of Pontus” as Canon VI, “of Thrace” as Canon VII, “not invited” as Canon VIII, “but the churches” as Canon IX, “of Constantinople” as Canon X, and “concerning Maximus” as Canon XI. The Oxonian manuscript, which Quesnellus followed, divides them into only three canons. Under its second canon it includes the fifth canon adopted by us, which is characteristic of the Dionysian version. We have adopted the division into six canons supplied by the Thuaneus manuscript of this collection. Other codices presenting the Isidorian interpretation likewise distinguish six canons, namely Veron. 55 and the Isidorian Vulgate, with which Ferrandus agrees. They differ only in joining the third canon from the Thuaneus manuscript, which we have adopted, to the second, while dividing the fourth into two: at the words “not invited” they mark Canon III, and at “but the churches” they mark Canon IV.]

### III

The bishops of the Asian diocese, too, are to govern only those matters that are in Asia and belong only to the Asian diocese; the bishops of Pontus are to have care only of the Pontic diocese; and those of Thrace only of Thrace itself.

[Note: [Col. 0723B] Thus our manuscripts together with the Isidorian Vulgate. Quesnellus has “are to administer.”]

### IV

Bishops who have not been invited must not go beyond their diocese to ordain anyone or to arrange any ecclesiastical matters whatsoever, with the rule prescribed for each diocese preserved. For it is clear that in each and every province the synod of that province must administer and govern everything according to what was defined at Nicaea. The churches of God established among barbarian peoples, however, must be governed and administered according to the custom recognized as having been maintained by the Fathers.

[Note: [Col. 0723B] Thus the manuscripts Vind. and Veron. Quesnellus has: “For a bishop who has not been invited ought not to go beyond his diocese”; he then omits “to any whatsoever” and has “with the rule preserved.” The Isidorian Vulgate has: “Bishops who have not been invited … must not …,” and so forth.]

[Note: [Col. 0723C] Codex Veron. and the Isidorian Vulgate, together with the Greek, add “of that province.”]

[Note: [Col. 0723C] Quesnellus has “in regions”; shortly afterward he omits *regi* (“to be governed”). We wrote “among peoples” with Vind. and the Isidorian Vulgate, and added *regi* with the support of all our manuscripts and the Vulgate.]

### V

The bishop of the city of Constantinople ought to have the honor of primacy after the Roman bishop, because it is New Rome.

[Note: [Col. 0723C] Codex Vind. has: “to have the primacy of honor after the Roman bishop, because the city itself is [New Rome].”]

### VI

Concerning Maximus the Cynic philosopher and the entire disorder concerning him which arose at Constantinople, it has been decreed that Maximus neither is nor is to be considered to have been a bishop; nor are those ordained by him to possess any clerical rank whatsoever, since everything done concerning him or by him has been annulled.

[Note: [Col. 0723C] The manuscripts Vind. and Veron. omit *doctrina* (“doctrine”). Nothing similar is found in the Greek or in the other versions, and it is probable that, through a reading error, the word *doctrina* was added by a copyist to complete the sense of *totius indisciplinationis ejus* (“of his entire lack of discipline”), or that the Isidorian Vulgate added it because of the phrase “for the doctrine.” It seems that the text should be corrected to *tota indisciplina ejus* (“his entire lack of discipline”), or *ob totam indisciplinationem ejus* (“because of his entire lack of discipline”).]

The names of the bishops are these: Nectarius of Constantinople, Timothy of Alexandria, Dorotheus from Oxyrhynchus, Cyril of Jerusalem, Gelasius of Caesarea, Macer of Jericho, Dionysius of Diospolis, Priscianus of Nicopolis, Saturninus of Sebaste, Rufus of Scythopolis, Auxentius of Ascalon, Aelianus of Jamnia, Zeno of Tyre, Paul of Sidon, Nestorius of Ptolemais, Philip of Damascus, Baracus of Paneas, Timothy of Berytus, Basilides of Byblos, Mochimus of Aradus, and the remaining 130.

[Note: [Col. 0723C] Thus the manuscripts Vind. and Thuan. The Isidorian Vulgate has “with the annulled matters.” Quesnellus has “with the matters removed.” The names of the bishops that follow are not found in our manuscripts Vind. and Veron. Quesnellus found them in the manuscripts Thuan. and Oxon.]

[Note: [Col. 0723D] Thus the Thuaneus manuscript, in agreement with the Isidorian Vulgate and other versions. Quesnellus, with Codex Oxon., has “Dorotheus from Corinth.”]

[Note: [Col. 0723D] Codex Thuan. has Galatius; the Isidorian Vulgate has Thalassius. Hardouin, besides other Isidorian manuscripts, cites Leontius, book I *Against Nestorius and Eutyches*, and Theodoret, book XV, chapter 8, as evidence that Gelasius was at that time bishop of Caesarea. Later the Isidorian Vulgate incorrectly has “Priscianus of Sebaste, Saturninus of Scythopolis, Rufus of Nicopolis.” The manuscripts Thuan. and Oxon. are better, as will be clear from the subscriptions to the ancient version below.]

[Note: [Col. 0723D] Thus the manuscripts Thuan. and the Isidorian Vulgate, together with other versions. Quesnellus has “Ebanus,” incorrectly.]

[Note: [Col. 0724B] The remaining one hundred and thirty, together with the twenty names written above, complete the number of 150 bishops. QUESNELLUS.]

## CHAPTER LXII

[Note: This council—or rather, this fragment of a council—has until now been found only in collections of Gallican manuscripts, namely in the celebrated Corbie manuscript, the Fossatensis, in the codices of our own collection, in the Colbert manuscript 3368, where it occurs twice, in Vat. 3827, in the former Royal manuscript of Saint Peter of Poitiers, and in the manuscripts of Isidore’s additions, such as Vat. 1340. All these are collections of Gallican origin, as we have shown in the appropriate places in the Treatise. Aeneas of Paris, in book 1 of his work Against the Greeks, chapter 102, vol. I of Acher’s *Spicilegium*, p. 133, quotes a lengthy testimony from the following letter of Siricius, which he found in a Gallican codex. Codex 59 of the chapter of Verona, which contains a very ancient abridgment of the canons, gives a summary of this council, or fragment, from Gallican sources. The heading of this council differs in the manuscripts. The Thuaneus codex of our collection calls it the Council of Teleptis; the same is read in the former Royal manuscript of Saint Peter of Poitiers, according to Baluzius in his Dissertation on the Council of Teleptis, inserted after the books *On the Concord* of Peter de Marca, Paris edition of 1714, col. 1344. The same name is also found in the abridgment of the very ancient Verona codex 39, no. 40: “From the Synod of Teleptis.” An ancient Lucchese codex containing the same abridgment of the canons, which repeatedly omits the first letters of certain names, gives the title, according to P. Mansi, vol. II of the *Supplement to the Councils*, p. 252: “From the Synod of Leptis.” But Leptis in Byzacena should not be suspected here; for it ought to have been written not *Leptense* but *Leptiminense*. We have retained the reading published by Quesnellus from the Oxford manuscript, since it is confirmed by two Viennese copies of this collection. It is also confirmed by two manuscripts of the Society of Jesus cited by P. Hardouin, as well as by the Gallican Fossatensis collection, in P. Coustant, vol. I of *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, col. 685, note a, and by the excellent Corbie codex, which reads: “Here begins the Council of Telensium, through the treatises of the holy …” The Vatican codex 3827 differs slightly: “Here begins the Council of Telenum”; another Royal copy cited by Baluzius, formerly belonging to the archbishop of Reims, agrees with it. Finally, Vatican 1340, containing Isidore’s additions, reads: “Here begins the Council of Thelesum,” although in the text it has “of the people of Telensis.” The ancient editions of the Councils after Merlin prefer *Telense*. Binius, on the authority of Cardinal Baronius, emended it to *Teleptense*, and this passed into later editions. Yet, on the basis of the Trecensis manuscript of Ferrandus, we believe the name of this council to have been *Zellense*, from which *Telense* was written after the letter Z had been changed to T. See further on this matter in the Observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 14, chapter 1.]

Here begins the Council of Telensis concerning the *tractatoria* of the holy Siricius, pope of the city of Rome, sent through Africa.

After the consulship of the most glorious emperors Honorius, for the eleventh time, and Constantius, for the second time, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, when a council had assembled in the church of the Apostles of the people of Telensis, the blessed Father Donatianus, bishop of the first see and of the city of Teleptis, having taken his seat, with Januarius, Felix, Secundus, Cyrius, Victor, Secundianus, [Note: The Corbie and Vatican 3827 codices read “Zeta.”] Geta, Eunomius, Maximianus, Donatus, Cresconius, Jocundus, [Note: One Colbert manuscript, cited by Coustant, together with the common editions of the Councils, reads “Sopatrus.”] Sopatrus, Restitutus, Julianus, Maximinus, Romanus, [Note: The Thuaneus reads “Teriolus, Nilicus”; Vatican 3827, “Temolus, Militus”; Vatican 1340, “Tertiolus, Miciolus.”] Tertiolus, Micilus, Maximus, Donatianus, Basilius, [Note: Vatican 3827 reads “Papianus.”] Papinianus, Januarius, Porphyrius, another Porphyrius, Donatus, Julianus, Tutus, Fortunius, Quintianus, Capio, and the remaining bishops seated with him, and also Vincentius and [Note: The same Vatican 3827 manuscript reads “Foranus.” Two manuscripts cited by Coustant have “Fortinus, Quantianus.”] Fortunatianus, delegates sent from the proconsular province to the Council of Byzacena, [Note: Quesnellus omitted the words “and the rest,” which all our manuscripts, those of Baluzius and Coustant, and the common codices preserve. They indicate that the first compiler did not transcribe the entire synod, but passed over everything after the preface in order to proceed to the letters of Siricius, which he especially intended to include.] and the rest;

Vincentius and Fortunatianus said:

“Also, when we were at Thusdrus, as your recollection of what you heard recalls to me, and we had delivered for reading the letters of the holy-memory Siricius, bishop of the apostolic see, [Note: Quesnellus reads, “we had delivered them, and one of them had been read by the holiness of our brother.” We have followed the Thuaneus and our manuscripts. Only the Viennese manuscript and Vatican 1340 have *recitantes* (“reading”) instead of *recitandas* (“to be read”). The Thuaneus, instead of *legeret* (“was reading”), has *relegeret* (“was rereading”).] when the holiness of our brother, Bishop Latonius, was reading one of them, the suggestion now indicates to us that both should be reported; have them read.”

The bishops said:

“Let the letters of the holy Siricius, of venerable memory, be read, so that we may know what their text contains.”

And when they were handed over, Privatus the notary said: [Note: Certain manuscripts read: “A copy of the *tractatoria*, or *tracturia*.”]

“Copy of the *tractatoria* of the bishop of the city of Rome.”

### 448

“To our dearest brothers and fellow bishops throughout Africa, Siricius, [Note: The Viennese manuscripts, Vatican 1340, Merlin, three Colbert manuscripts, the Fossatensis, and the ancient Corbie manuscript add *diversa quamvis* (“although differing”). Vatican 3827 has *diversis quamvis* (“although differing in various ways”). Do these words indicate that Siricius’s letter was sent to various provinces—first to the suburban bishops, who, as the opening suggests, could not attend the Roman synod; then to others in other provinces; and finally to the Africans, to whom the copy in our manuscripts belongs, inserted into the African synod?]

When very many brothers had assembled together at the relics of the holy apostle Peter, through whom the beginning of both the apostolate and the episcopate in Christ took its origin, [Note: This reading is found with Merlin in all three of our manuscripts and in all of Coustant’s manuscripts except one Colbert codex, which has *placeretque* (“and it might please”). Quesnellus reads *placuit ut propter* (“it was decided that, because”). Coustant, citing no manuscript, has *placuitque propter* (“and it was decided that, because”).] and it had been decided, because of the many emerging matters which in some cases were not matters but crimes, that henceforth everyone in the Church should take responsibility for such care, just as the apostle Paul proclaims (Ephesians 5:27), [Note: All the same manuscripts and the common editions have this reading, except Quesnellus, who reads: “That he might present to God a Church without …” Immediately afterward Quesnellus alone omits *conscientia nostra* (“our conscience”), and shortly later omits *quo perpetua istiusmodi forma servetur* (“so that this form might be perpetually maintained”), together with the following word *placuit* (“it was decided”), despite the contrary evidence of the same manuscripts and editions.] that such a Church must be presented to God, having neither spot nor wrinkle, lest our conscience appear polluted by the breath of some diseased sheep.

[Col. 0726B] Therefore, with better counsel, it was decided—especially on account of those who at present were entirely unable to be present because of bodily illness or exhausted age—that, so that this form might be perpetually maintained, letters of this kind should be issued, not [Note: Vatican 3827 has *quo nova* (“by which something new”). Then the same codex and Vatican 1340 have *cum* (“when”), while the manuscripts of Coustant and Merlin have *sed ea quae* (“but those things which”). Coustant preferred the reading of the edition of the Councils, *sed quibus ea* (“but by which those things”). We have written *cupiamus* (“we desire”) with all the manuscripts and the common editions; Quesnellus alone has *cupimus* (“we desire”).] to impose any new commands, but because we desire that those things which through the negligence and laziness of some have been neglected should be observed, although they have been established by the apostolic constitution [Note: Coustant and the common Councils after Merlin, together with Vatican 1340, read “of the Fathers.” Quesnellus alone has *sanctione* (“sanction”) instead of *constitutione* (“constitution”). Immediately afterward Vatican 3827, together with the common editions, has: “As it is written: Stand firm, etc.”] of the Fathers. For it is written: ‘Stand firm and hold to our traditions, whether by word or by letter’ (2 Thessalonians 1:14).

Certainly, dearest brothers, this ought to shake your minds more forcefully, so that we may come secure and free from every stain of this age into the presence of God. [Note: Vatican 3827 has “before the presence of God,” and deletes “secure.”] For we shall not be free from stain, [Note: Coustant, with three of his manuscripts and our Vatican 1340, has *quia praesumus* (“because we preside”). Others have *qui et praesumus* (“who also preside”).] we who preside over peoples, since it is written: ‘To whom much has been entrusted, from him more will be required’ (Luke 12:48).

Therefore, since we are compelled to give an account not only for ourselves but also for the people entrusted to us, [Note: This is the reading of the Viennese manuscripts, Vatican 1340, and other common editions. Quesnellus, with Vatican 3827, has *reddere* (“to render”). Quesnellus also omitted *humilem* (“humble”), which is supported by all our manuscripts and the common editions. He has, with several codices, *disciplinam deificam* (“divine discipline”).
