We have written *disciplina deifica* (“divine discipline”) with our Vatican 3827, two Colbert manuscripts, and the ancient Corbie manuscript of Coustant; the Fossatensis and another Colbert manuscript also support it, the latter reading *disciplina Dei humilem* (“the humble discipline of God”). Another Colbert manuscript has *disciplinam deificam humiliter* (“divine discipline humbly”).] we must teach the people entrusted to us humility through divine discipline.

For some have arisen who, not observing the statutes of their ancestors, [Note: The common Councils, together with one of our manuscripts, Vatican 1340, read “despising.” Immediately afterward the two Vatican manuscripts delete *sua* (“their own”).] have violated the chastity of the Church through their presumption, following the will of the people and not fearing the judgment of God.

Therefore, lest we appear in like manner to connive at such things in silence and to give them our consent, whereby we might incur the punishments of Gehenna, since the Lord says: [Note: Quesnellus reads *si videbas* (“if you saw”). We have deleted this with the Viennese and other manuscripts and the common editions, in which the reading is: “You saw a thief and ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers.”]

‘You saw a thief and ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers’ (Psalm 94:18);

these are the matters which henceforth, in view of the divine judgment, all Catholic bishops ought carefully to guard.

I. First, no one should dare to ordain outside the knowledge of the apostolic see, [Note: The Viennese manuscript, together with two of Coustant’s manuscripts, has “that is, the primates.” Quesnellus omitted *hoc est* (“that is”) but retained *primates*. Vatican 3827 and another manuscript of Coustant have, incorrectly, *haec est prima testatio* (“this is the first testimony”). The more accurate reading, found in the Thuaneus of this collection, Vatican 1340, the ancient Corbie manuscript, other manuscripts, and printed editions, is *hoc est, primatis* (“that is, of the primate”). These words were added either by Siricius or by the Africans so that this canon might be adapted to African discipline. Thus Innocent, repeating the same canon in his letter to Victricius of Rouen in order to adapt it to Gallican discipline, explained it as follows: “First, no one should dare to ordain without the knowledge of the metropolitan bishop.”] that is, of the primate; for the judgment of the majority is complete when it is consecrated. [Note: This is the reading, with Quesnellus, of the Viennese manuscript. The Thuaneus and Vatican 1340 have *consequitur* (“follows”). The common Councils and two manuscripts cited by Coustant have *consequatur* (“may follow”). Vatican 3827, the Corbie manuscript, and two Colbert manuscripts more correctly have *confirmatur* (“is confirmed”), as in Innocent.]

II. No one bishop should presume to ordain a bishop, because of arrogance, lest the benefit appear to have been conferred secretly; for this is known to have been defined in the Synod of Nicaea (Nicaea, canon 4).

III. Likewise, if anyone, after the remission of sins, has held a belt of secular military service, he must not be admitted to the clergy.

IV. A cleric must not marry a woman, [Note: This is found in our manuscripts and those of Coustant. Quesnellus omitted *id est* (“that is”). Ferrandus, title 3, and Innocent I in his letter to Victricius also omit “a widow.” Hence Coustant rightly suspects that the words *id est viduam* (“that is, a widow”) are a gloss that entered the text from the margin.] that is, a widow.

### 450

V. He who, while a layman, has married a widow must not be admitted to the clergy.

VI. No one may usurp the right to ordain a cleric from another Church.

VII. Another Church must not admit a cleric who has been rejected.

VIII. Those coming from the Novatians or Montenses are to be received by the laying on of hands, [Note: This is found in our older manuscripts and in all of Coustant’s manuscripts, together with the common Councils, except that the Thuaneus has *rebaptizantur* (“they are rebaptized”), and Vatican 3827 and another manuscript of Coustant have *rebaptizent* (“let them rebaptize”). The more accurate reading, which agrees with Innocent’s text, is found in the older editions after Merlin, except those which read *rebaptizant* (“they rebaptize”). Vatican 1340 has *propter* (“because of”) instead of *praeter* (“apart from”).] because they rebaptize.

IX. Furthermore, we recommend what is worthy, chaste, and honorable: that priests and Levites should not have intercourse with their wives, [Col. 0728B] because [Note: This reading is found with Merlin in two of our manuscripts, the Viennese and Vatican 1340, and in three of Coustant’s. The common Councils after Crabbe, together with Vatican 3827, have “in the daily ministry’s duties.” Quesnellus has “in the daily duties of the ministry.” P. Coustant, with one Colbert manuscript, has “in the ministry, in the daily duties of the ministry.” Innocent has the better and shorter reading: “because they are occupied with the daily necessities of the ministry.” After *abstinete vos* (“abstain yourselves”), the Oxford manuscript adds *a fornicatione* (“from fornication”).] they are occupied with the daily necessities of the ministry. For Paul writes thus to the Corinthians, saying: ‘Abstain, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer’ (1 Corinthians 7:5).

If abstinence is commanded to laypeople so that their prayers may be heard, how much more ought a priest at every moment to be ready, secure in the purity of cleanliness, lest he be required either to offer the sacrifice or to baptize? [Note: Quesnellus alone deletes *utique* (“certainly”); shortly afterward, instead of *offerat* (“he may offer”), he has *offerre* (“to offer”). A little later Vatican 3827, together with one of Coustant’s manuscripts, reads: “What will he do? What will he plead?”]

If he has been polluted by carnal desire, what will he do? Will he plead an excuse? With what shame, [Note: Quesnellus inserts “will he offer the sacrifice, or baptize,” contrary to all our manuscripts, Coustant’s manuscripts, and other printed editions. With them we have afterward added *hic* (“here”) and written *dictum sit* (“it has been said”), where Quesnellus has *scriptum sit* (“it has been written”); and we have substituted *qua de re* (“for this reason”) for *quapropter* (“wherefore”).] with what state of mind, with what conscience, will he take this upon himself? By what merit does he believe that he will be heard here, when it has been said: ‘All things are clean to the clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean’ (Titus 1:15)?

For this reason I urge, warn, and entreat that this reproach be removed, which even the gentiles may rightly accuse.

Perhaps this is believed, [Note: We added *hoc* (“this”) with the manuscripts of Coustant, and Innocent confirms and explains it in the cited letter, saying: “But perhaps he believes this to be permitted, because it is written …” Because this word is absent in Quesnellus, other words are inserted: “Perhaps it is believed that a presbyter can, or rather ought to, have a wife, because it is written.” Coustant attributes this to a gloss; we have found nothing of the kind in his manuscripts or in ours, including the manuscripts of this collection.] because it is written: ‘The husband of one wife’ (1 Timothy 3:2)?

He did not say “one who remains in the desire of begetting,” but with a view to future continence. For he did not exclude those who were sexually intact, he who said: ‘I wish that all people were as I am’ (2 Corinthians 7:7).

And he declares it more clearly, saying: ‘Those who are in the flesh cannot please God; but you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit’ (Romans 8:8). [Note: Quesnellus adds *alibi* (“elsewhere”), with no support from any of our manuscripts or the common editions.]

Therefore, brothers, if all these matters are observed by everyone with complete vigilance, ambition will cease, dissension will be quieted, heresies and schisms will not arise, the devil will find no opportunity to rage, unanimity will remain, iniquity will be overcome and trampled down, charity will burn with spiritual fervor, and the peace proclaimed by the lips will agree with the will: the peace, indeed, [Note: Vatican 3827, together with other common editions, has “of our God,” followed by: “which the Savior himself, when already near his passion, …” and “left to us by hereditary right.”] of our God and Savior, which, when he was near his passion, he commanded to be preserved and left to us by hereditary right, saying: ‘My peace I give you; my peace I leave you’ (John 14:27).

And the Apostle’s saying: ‘That, being of one mind and thinking one thing, we may remain in Christ, doing nothing through contention or empty glory’ (Philippians 2:2), [Note: The common Councils and Coustant, with several manuscripts, have “not to men”; immediately afterward, “according to his works.”] let us please not human beings but God our Savior.

If we faithfully desire to obey all these commands, the Lord will guard our bodies and our souls on the day when he will repay each one according to his works.

But if anyone, puffed up in the mind of his flesh, [Note: Vatican 3827 has “from canonical principles.” The common Councils and Coustant, with other manuscripts, have “from this canonical rule.”] wishes to wander from this canonical rule, let him know that he is excluded from our communion and will suffer the punishments of Gehenna.

Moreover, mercy must be exercised together with judgment. For we ought to extend a hand to such people when they are falling, [Note: Quesnellus adds *nos* (“we”); we deleted it with our manuscripts and the common editions. Immediately afterward two Vatican manuscripts and the common editions have: “who should not drag one running in this way into ruin.”] so that it does not drag one who is running in this way into ruin.

Given at Rome in a council of eighty bishops, on the eighth day before the Ides of January, after the consulship of the emperor Arcadius Augustus and of Bauto, vir clarissimus.

## CHAPTER LXIII

[Note: This rule for letters of identification is found not only in the manuscripts of this collection but also inserted in other collections, both older and newer. Three older Italian collections—Vatican Regina 1997, Lucca 88, and Vatican 1342—place it after the Council of Carthage of the year 419, in which the first thirty-three canons of the African Code are distinguished, with distinctive readings, as forty canons. There it is presented without any title at the end, after the words: “I have issued the canons of the holy Fathers, written in my own hand and subscribed by me. Amen.” We have conjectured in the Treatise on Collections, part II, chapter 3, § 8, no. 8, that these words are the subscription of Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, appended to the Nicene canons transmitted by him to the Africans in order to establish the document’s authenticity. In the manuscripts of Dionysius’s additions, it is appended to the Nicene canons under the title: “Here begins how a letter of identification ought to be made.” After a brief annotation on the Council of Nicaea comes: “And in another hand: Atticus, bishop of the Church of Constantinople, said: I have issued the canons of the holy Fathers, written in my own hand and subscribed by me. Amen.” Then the letter of identification follows: “The Greek letters,” etc. In the same way, after the Nicene canons, the same letter of identification is described in Vatican 1342; afterward, as we said, it is repeated after the Council of Carthage of 419. Finally, in the codices not only of the Isidorian collection, from which Merlin published the letter of identification, but also in the manuscripts of the Hispanic collection, from which Isidore copied it, it is placed at the end of the Greek councils, chapter 11, under this heading: “Letter of identification of Atticus, bishop of Constantinople.” Two conclusions follow: first, that this letter of identification is attributed to Atticus of Constantinople in all these codices and collections; second, that the occasion for writing it is placed before the copy of the Nicene canons, which Atticus sent to the Africans who had requested it and strengthened with his own authentic subscription. Compare what we observed on this subject in the Treatise at the place cited. Since, moreover, the agreement of collections of diverse origin proves that this document was circulated among the Latins, and since their antiquity greatly predates the age of Isidore, suspicion of an Isidorian forgery is completely excluded. Even if one believes it to be a forgery and judges that this rule for letters of identification should be attributed either to the Nicene Fathers or to Atticus of Constantinople, and that it is rather the product of a Latin than of a Greek author, it nevertheless remains certain that it was received in practice for writing letters of identification. This can be seen, among others, in Regino, book I, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, chapters 438 and 439, where two letters of identification are reported: one from Rathbodus of Trier to Rotbertus of Metz, the other from Dado of Verdun to Rathbodus of Trier. We found another letter of this kind from Liutardus of Vence to Wenilo of Rouen in Vatican codex 630, p. 1. On the first folio of Vatican Regina 1997 we also found two other similar letters.]

Rule for letters of identification.

No one who has even slight knowledge of the Greek language is unaware that the elements of the Greek alphabet also express numbers. Therefore, lest any fraudulent falsification be rashly attempted in composing canonical letters—which Latin usage calls *formatae*—the Fathers assembled at Nicaea, numbering 318, most beneficially devised and decreed that letters of identification should follow this method of calculation or reckoning: namely, that in the reckoning one should first take the Greek letters of “Father,” “Son,” and “Holy Spirit,” [Note: The Colbert manuscript, formerly the Thuaneus, cited by Justellus, vol. I of the *Canonical Library*, p. 442, Vatican Regina, and the common Isidorian text have *prima* (“first”).] [Note: Our Viennese codex agrees, as does the common Isidorian text; that is, ΠΥΑ. Quesnellus expressed only the Greek letter Π in the text and added the number 481. In the manuscripts Vatican Regina, Vatican 1342, and Colbert, other Greek letters are substituted, designating other numbers: ΠΟϹΑ, whose elements signify the numbers eighty, seventy, two hundred, and one. But this is less correct, for the letters ΠΟϹΑ do not represent the elements of “Father,” “Son,” and “Holy Spirit.” Justellus believed these letters should be emended to ΠΥΠΑ; but then the numbers do not correspond, whereas they do correspond to the letters ΠΟϹΑ. Our reading, which all the letters of identification mentioned in note 1 adopted, agrees with the numbers expressed in the text.] ΠΥΑ, whose elements signify the numbers eighty, four hundred, and one; also the first letter of the apostle Peter, namely Π, whose numerical value is eighty; the first letter of the bishop who writes; the second letter of the person to whom he writes; the third letter of the recipient; the fourth letter of the city from which the letter is written; and the number of the indiction current at that time. [Note: Vatican Regina and Colbert have: “of the same person whose number it may be.”]

And when all these Greek letters—which, as we have said, express numbers—have been added together into one sum, the letter should contain that single total, whatever it may be. He who receives it must carefully seek out the number expressed in it. [Note: The Vatican Regina, Colbert, and Vatican 5845 manuscripts, together with the other additions of Dionysius, add separately: “Let him also add G Θ”; this is better, since these Greek letters represent the number ninety-nine.] Moreover, he should add separately in the letter the number ninety-nine, which according to the Greek letters signifies ΑΜΗΝ—“Amen.” [Note: The same codices append the numbers corresponding to these Greek letters: 1, 40, 8, 50.] [Note: Quesnellus prefixed these two words to the title of this chapter and, in the note inserted in our note 14 (for us, col. 367, note a) in the table of chapters of this collection, thought that the words “the canons are concluded” indicated the end of the collection. But this clause is placed after the rule for letters of identification both in the Viennese codex and in the Thuaneus, as Quesnellus himself admits there and confirms again in Dissertation 12, chapter 2. These words indicate the end of the Nicene canons, which had been transmitted by Atticus of Constantinople to the Africans and authenticated by Atticus’s own subscription and this rule for letters of identification, as can be understood from note 1 (for us, col. 729, note f). The canons themselves, from the version transmitted by Atticus through Philo and Evaristus, and Atticus’s subscription, ought to have preceded the letter of identification, which this clause would follow. But since our compiler had presented the same canons in another version in chapter 1, he thought they could be omitted here; and, having likewise omitted Atticus’s subscription, which the manuscripts of Dionysius’s additions and other very ancient collections cited in note 1 preserve for us, he sent us only the letter of identification with the clause “the canons are concluded.” Furthermore, since our collection includes not only the canons of councils but also several constitutions of the Roman pontiffs, if the compiler had wished this clause to indicate the end of the entire collection, he should have written, consistently with the heading prefixed to the collection: “The ecclesiastical canons and constitutions of the apostolic see are concluded.” Read note 1 in chapter 67 (col. 743, note a); once you understand from it that the letters of Saint Leo, together with the other material we shall append in the following chapters, belong to this collection, you will see much more clearly the emptiness of Quesnellus’s interpretation, by which he claims that this clause was added to indicate the end of the collection, and the probability of our explanation.] The canons are concluded.

## CHAPTER LXIV

[Note: Although this letter is lacking in the Oxford manuscript of this collection, and for that reason was omitted by Quesnellus, nevertheless it is read in all the other manuscripts of the same collection, both older and more accurate—the Thuaneus, both Viennese manuscripts, the Trecopithaeanus, two Beauvais manuscripts, and others. Since it is also cited in the table of chapters, which is usually an indication of original provenance, there can be no doubt that this chapter belongs to the same collection. This letter is certainly spurious, as several learned men have demonstrated most clearly. But since it was published with Rufinus as translator and became especially influential among the Gauls, so that it is cited in the Synod of Vaison of the year 442, canon 6, it is found received not only in our collection but also in other ancient Gallican codices. Some have raised doubts about Rufinus, asking whether he was the author of this spurious document. But the Greek text, discovered and printed by Cotelerius, suggests that the document itself was fabricated among the Greeks. Rufinus alone, in his customary manner, ranges more freely in the translation, as anyone who wishes may understand by comparison with the Greek. Besides the Viennese manuscript of this collection, three others support us: one belonging to Labbe and another to Justellus, whose variant readings are noted in the margin of the edition of the Councils; the third belonged to the Parisian college of the Society of Jesus, which Hardouin used in his notes. The same letter is also read in the very ancient Italian collection contained in Barberini 2888 and Vatican 1342.]

Letter of Pope Clement to Saint James the apostle, the brother of the Lord.

### 455

**Clement to James,** [Note: Thus our Viennese codex. The common editions of the Councils have “to James, brother of the Lord.” The Greek text, according to the differences among the codices, presents both readings.] lord and bishop of bishops, governing the holy Church of the Hebrews at Jerusalem, and also all the Churches founded everywhere by the providence of God, together with the presbyters, deacons, and all the other brothers. May peace be with you always.

I make known to you, lord, that Simon—[Note: The Vulgate inserts “Peter.” We have removed it on the authority of the Harduinian manuscript, since this word is also absent from the Greek]—who, on account of the merit of his true faith and the integrity of his preaching, was declared to be the foundation of the Church, and for this reason was also surnamed Peter by the Lord’s divine mouth, [Col. 0732A] was the first-fruit of the Lord’s election, the first of the apostles. To him God the Father first revealed the Son; to him Christ appropriately granted blessedness. He was both called and chosen, and was made the Lord’s companion and associate, like a good and most approved disciple. He was commanded to illumine the darker region of the world, the West—as though it were the most powerful of all—and he was able fully to fulfill the command.

But how long shall I prolong my speech, shrinking from declaring what is sorrowful, yet what must necessarily, although late, be brought forth? This very Peter, who, because of the immense love he bore toward all human beings, did not cease to proclaim the good openly and with complete confidence—even though the tyrant of the whole world opposed him—and who introduced the King of all ages throughout the world and even to the knowledge of this very [Col. 0732B] city of Rome, so that it too might be saved: this man, I say, willingly ended his present life by suffering for piety. [Note: So the Vindobonensis and Harduinian manuscripts. The Vulgate has “by enduring.”]

In those very days when he perceived that the end of his life was approaching, as he stood in the assembly of the brethren, he took my hand and suddenly arose. In the hearing of the whole Church he spoke these words:

“Hear me, my brothers and fellow servants. Since, as I have been taught by him who sent me, my Lord and master Jesus Christ, the day of my death is at hand, I appoint this Clement bishop over you, and to him alone I hand over the chair of my preaching and teaching (Constitutions VII, 46). He was my companion in all things from beginning to end, and through this he recognized the truth of all my preaching. He was my partner in all my trials, persevering faithfully. More than all others, I have found him to be a worshiper of God, a lover of human beings, chaste, devoted to the pursuit of learning, sober, kind, just, patient, and able to endure the insults of some—even of those who are instructed in the word of God.

“Therefore I hand over to him the power of binding and loosing that was handed down to me by the Lord, so that whatever he decrees on earth concerning anything whatsoever may also be decreed in heaven. For he will bind what ought to be bound and loose what ought to be loosed, as one who knows the rule of the Church thoroughly.

“Therefore listen to him, knowing that whoever grieves the teacher of truth sins against Christ and provokes God, the Father of all; for this reason he too will be deprived of life. But he who presides over the others ought to act in the place of a physician and not be stirred by the fury of a wild beast.

“When he had said this, I fell at his feet and entreated him, excusing myself and declining the honor of the chair and the authority. But he replied: ‘Do not ask me to spare you in this matter. This has been determined for me to do, and all the more because you make excuses. For this chair does not seek one who desires it and boldly pursues it, but one adorned with good character and learned in speech. If there were another better than you; if some other assistant had stood by me as diligently; if anyone had grasped the substance of my teaching so fully and had learned from me the arrangements of the churches so completely, then, possessing another such man, I would not compel you to undertake a good work that you are unwilling to assume. It is therefore pointless to seek another, since I have offered you first to God as the first-fruit of those who are being saved through me from the Gentiles, and especially from this city.

“‘But consider something else also: if, fearing the danger of sin, you shrink from undertaking the governance of the Church, be certain that you sin even more by evading the people of God, who are as though placed amid the waves and in peril, when you are able to help them—having regard only for yourself and not providing what is advantageous to all in common. Be certain, then, that you must accept every danger, since I too shall not cease entreating you for the salvation of all. The sooner you obey me, the sooner you will relieve me of the burden of my labor and sorrow.

“‘I also know this, O Clement: I shall bring upon you weariness and troubles, dangers and even insults from the uneducated and unteachable crowd. [Note: The Vindobonensis manuscript has “and the unteachable.”] Yet I know that you will bear these things steadfastly and courageously, looking toward that hope which prepares for you with God the crown of patience.

“‘I also wish you to perceive with me, by sound reasoning, when Christ most needs your service: now, when the enemy stirs up war against his bride, or at some future time, when Christ, having triumphed, will celebrate his victory and will no longer need anyone’s service? Who, even with little understanding, would not realize that this is the time in which Christ requires your assistance? Therefore devote your whole mind to the present necessity, offer your service, and provide aid in the battles to the best of kings, who will grant magnificent rewards after victory.

“‘Therefore willingly accept the office of bishop, especially since you have learned from me, in a credible manner, the arrangements of the churches, so that the salvation of those who have taken refuge with God through us may in no way falter. Nevertheless, I consider it necessary to remind you briefly, before everyone, of the order of this administration.’ [Note: Other manuscripts have “I decided.”]

“You must live irreproachably and strive with the greatest zeal to cast aside all the occupations of this life, so that you may not become a guarantor, an advocate in lawsuits, or be found entangled in any occupation whatsoever because of worldly business. For Christ does not wish to appoint you today as a judge or examiner of secular affairs, lest, being suffocated by the present cares of human beings, you should be unable to devote yourself to the word of God and, according to the rule of truth, distinguish the good from the evil. Let those who are learning—namely, the laity—perform among themselves those tasks which, as we explained above, are less appropriate for you; and let no one distract you from those studies through which salvation is given to all.

“For just as it is a charge of impiety for you, neglecting the study of the word of God, to undertake secular cares, so it is a sin for each layperson not faithfully to serve the others in matters that pertain to the common necessities of life. Let all of them labor together to make you secure and free for those things to which you ought to devote yourself. [Note: So the Vindobonensis and another manuscript of Justellus. The Vulgate has, ‘and free from those things to which you ought not to devote yourself.’] If perhaps the laity do not understand this by themselves, they must be instructed through the deacons, so that they may leave to you the concerns of the Church alone. Thus you will be able to administer it as is fitting and to serve the word of truth more abundantly and diligently.

“For if you are occupied with worldly cares, you will deceive both yourself and those who listen to you. You will not be able to distinguish fully for each person the things that pertain to salvation. Consequently, you will be punished as one who has not taught what pertains to human salvation, and the disciples will perish through ignorance.

“Therefore devote yourself solely to this: that you teach the word of God at the proper time and without interruption, through which they may be able to attain salvation. Let them receive your words with such reverence that they know you to be an ambassador and herald of the truth, and that whatever you bind on earth is bound also in heaven, while whatever you loose on earth is likewise loosed there. For, as I said, you will bind what ought to be bound and loose what is beneficial to loose. Let these and similar admonitions be addressed to you who preside.

“Let the following be addressed to the presbyters. Above all, while devoting themselves to chastity, let them join young men to wives, so that they may anticipate the heat of ardent youth by the law of marriage. Nor should they neglect to care for those of more advanced age, since in many people desire remains vigorous even when the body has grown old. Therefore, lest the stain of fornication, having found an opportunity, spread among you like the worst poison, it is necessary to beware and forestall it, lest a hidden fire of adultery should arise within you. [Note: The Labbean manuscript has ‘should grow hot.’] And what is more serious among all sins than adultery? For it holds the second place in punishments, since the first belongs to those who depart from God, even if they have lived soberly.

“Therefore, O presbyters, cultivate the Church and adorn—or, according to another manuscript, ‘order’—the bride of Christ for chastity. By ‘bride’ I mean the entire assembly of the Church. If she is found chaste by her bridegroom, she will be honored by him with immense gifts and presents, and you, as the bride’s ministers and the bridegroom’s friends, will enjoy great joy and gladness. But if this bride is found stained by sins, she will be driven from the royal couches as unworthy. [Note: The Vindobonensis manuscript has ‘she will be handed over to the royal chambers’; since this does not fit the sense, the other manuscripts and the Vulgate emended it to ‘she will not be handed over to the royal chambers.’ The more authentic reading is supplied by the Labbean manuscript and supported by the Greek text.] You, however, will pay the penalty if through your negligence or laziness the savage contagion of sin should creep in. Therefore, above all, take care of sobriety and chastity.

“Fornication is considered a very grave crime before God, and it has many forms, as Clement himself will carefully explain to you. Yet the first form of adultery is for a man not to be content with his own wife alone, and for a woman not to preserve herself exclusively for her own husband. If, then, a person is chaste, he can also become humane and compassionate, and through this obtain eternal mercy from God.

“Indeed, just as the poison of adultery is more destructive than every evil, so brotherly love and charity hold the summit of every good. Therefore love all your brothers and look upon everyone with reverence and mercy. (Constitutions IV, 2.) Show yourselves as parents to orphans. Care for widows of men, providing what is necessary with complete chastity. Yet join younger widows to husbands. For those who do not know a craft, seek out some honorable opportunities by which they may obtain the necessities of life; for craftsmen, provide work; show mercy to the weak.

“I know that you will do all these things if you establish charity in your hearts before everything else. The greatest encouragement for receiving and possessing this charity will be found if you frequently make your common food and table among yourselves, and insofar as each person is able, more often eat his bread and salt with his brothers. For charity is especially acquired through these things, and the cause of every good consists in such fellowship. Where there is peace and goodness, there is salvation.

“Therefore share your food with those who are brothers according to God, because through these temporal services you will merit eternal joys through the fruits of peace and charity. Feed the hungry with much greater care, give drink to the thirsty and clothing to the naked; visit the sick, and help those who are in prison insofar as possible; receive travelers readily into your homes. And not to enumerate everything individually at present: charity itself, if it is in you, will teach you to do every good thing, just as, conversely, hatred teaches those who are alien to salvation to do every evil.

“If some of the brothers have disputes among themselves, let them not be judged before secular tribunals; let the matter, whatever it may be, be settled before the presbyters of the Church, and in every way let them obey their decisions. Above all, flee avarice, which, for the sake of present profit, separates people from eternal goods. Keep weights, measures, and balances perfectly fair according to each place; faithfully return deposits.

“You will carefully and diligently fulfill all these things, and whatever else is similar to them, only if you continually turn the future judgment of God over in your heart. For who could sin if he always set God’s judgment before his eyes? It is certain that this judgment will be conducted at the end of the world, so that at last those who have acted well in this life may obtain the good things laid up for them, while sinners may receive the punishments prepared and stored up for them—concerning which we can have no doubt whatever that they will come to pass.

“For the true prophet foretold to us that all these things would indeed happen. Therefore you, who are disciples of the true Prophet, first cast from your hearts disagreements and dissensions of spirit, from which every evil deed proceeds, and preserve kindness and simplicity with your whole mind. If perhaps envy, unbelief, or any other evil among those we mentioned above should secretly creep into anyone’s heart, [Note: The Vindobonensis manuscript omits ‘or any other evil.’] let the person who cares for his soul not be ashamed to confess these things to the one who presides, so that he may be healed by him through the word of God and wholesome counsel, and may be able, with unblemished faith and good works, to escape the punishments of eternal fire and attain the rewards of perpetual life.

“Let the deacons of the Church be like the eyes of the bishop (Constitutions II, 44), wandering about and surveying all the Church’s activities with modesty, and examining carefully whether they see anyone drawing near to a precipice and approaching sin. Let them report these things to the bishop, so that the one about to fall into the precipice may be admonished by him, recalled, and prevented from falling into sin.

“Let them also admonish and exhort the more negligent, and those who come less frequently to hear the word of God and do not diligently assemble for the bishop’s instruction. For if they are constant in listening, they gain not only profits for eternal life from wholesome admonition, but also all the sorrows and griefs that arise from the necessities of the present life and the calamities of the times, and that they carry in their hearts like arrows fixed there by the speeches of evil people, are cast away and cleansed by the preaching of truth and by the teaching and instruction of eternal life. [Note: The same manuscript has ‘cleansed by the teaching and instruction of eternal life.’]

“Otherwise, if they withdraw their hearing from the word of God for a long time and remain in the practice of vices, [Note: The Vindobonensis and Harduinian manuscripts read ‘in the cultivation’; the Labbean manuscript has ‘untrained in vices.’ Shortly afterward, the Vindobonensis manuscript evidently has an error: where it reads ‘they dismissed,’ one should apparently read ‘while thorns are.’ The Labbean manuscript has, ‘without doubt they have lost God among thorns,’ and so forth.] they will undoubtedly be occupied by thorns and briars. And what else but fire will such soil be prepared for?

“Let the deacons, then, as we have said, be concerned with these matters. Let them also diligently seek out those who are sick according to the flesh, and inform the people about them—if the people happen not to know—so that they too may visit them and provide what is necessary, with the knowledge of the one who presides. Yet even if they do this secretly, they will not sin. Let them likewise inform the bishop about travelers who need refreshment. Let the deacons be concerned with these and all similar matters that pertain to the Church’s worship and discipline. [Note: The same manuscript has ‘let the deacons be concerned.’]

“Those who catechize—that is, those who instruct beginners by the word—must first themselves be instructed, for the matter concerns human souls. The one who teaches and instructs inexperienced souls must be such that he can adapt himself to the ability of his students and arrange the order of his speech according to the capacity of his hearer. He must therefore be thoroughly learned and educated, irreproachable, mature, fearless, as you yourselves will find this Clement to be after me. It would be too much if I were now to discuss everything that each person ought to possess.

“Nevertheless, there is one thing above all others that I wish all of you together to preserve: hold fast to concord, by which alone you can enter the harbor of peace and the city of the highest King, which is called peace. For the condition of the whole Church resembles a great ship which carries men from various places and regions across the rolling sea, as they hasten toward the city of a mighty kingdom.

“Let the master of this ship (Constitutions II, 61) be God himself, the Almighty; let Christ be the helmsman. Then let the bishop fulfill the office of lookout at the prow; let the presbyters occupy the place of sailors, and the deacons that of stewards. Let those who catechize be compared with the naustologi, the crew-recruiters; let the multitude of the whole brotherhood be like the epibatae, the passengers. Let the sea itself be regarded as this world; let the varieties of winds and whirlwinds be compared with the various temptations; let persecutions, tribulations, and dangers be likened to waves.

“Let earthly winds, which blow either from torrents or from valleys, be taken as the words of false prophets and seducers, or of corrupt teaching. [Note: The Labbean manuscript has ‘let them be called’; the Vindobonensis has ‘they are taught in the words of corrupt teaching.’] Let promontories and rough places represent those who hold secular powers—judges who threaten dangers and deaths. [Note: The Harduinian manuscript has ‘Bithalassa.’] Let dithalassa—‘two seas’—the places struck by the double tides of deceptive waves, be compared with those who waver in mind and are uncertain about the truth of the promises, and with those who examine our faith by irrational reasoning. Let hypocrites and deceitful people be regarded as resembling pirates.

“Now what else should the swift whirlpool, Tartarean Charybdis, shipwrecks dashed against rocks, and deadly drownings be considered except sins? It remains, therefore, for this ship, on a prosperous course, to be able to enter safely the harbor of the desired city. Let those who sail pour out prayer to God, so that they may deserve to be heard. A person will deserve to be heard by God only when his prayers are aided by good character and good works. [Note: The Labbean manuscript has ‘the prayers themselves.’]

“But above all, in quiet and silence, let the epibatae—that is, the laity—each remain in his own place, lest, if they begin wandering about everywhere through restlessness and disorderly, useless movement, they either hinder the sailors from their duty or cause the ship, pressed toward one side by their disturbance, to sink. Let the naustologi, the crew-recruiters, give reminders concerning wages. [Note: The same manuscript corruptly has ‘concerning merchandise.’] Let the deacons neglect nothing whatsoever that pertains to diligence or discipline.

“Let the presbyters, like sailors, carefully arrange each thing for the ship’s instruction and prepare what will be required in its proper time. Let the bishop, like the lookout at the prow, watchfully and diligently preserve the words of the helmsman, Christ. Let the Lord Savior, the helmsman of his Church, be loved by all, and let the whole Church believe and obey his commands and orders alone.

“Let all continually entreat God for favorable winds. [Note: The Vulgate, with different punctuation, inserts ‘so that’; we removed this particle with the Vindobonensis manuscript and the Greek text. Shortly afterward, where the Vulgate has ‘they overcome,’ the Vindobonensis manuscript has ‘they hope’; from the Greek it should be rendered ‘they await.’] Let those who sail await every tribulation and every danger as they sail across the deep sea of this world and the ocean of human life, in which they must hunger and thirst; they must also endure nakedness, illnesses of the body, and infirmities.

“Moreover, they must often labor under the plots and deceit of human beings, since they know that they must sometimes be scattered and sometimes gathered together. They must endure vomiting and bruising, when, because of the confusion of sins and the rejection of crimes, like things badly gathered in the inward parts of the gall, a discharge must be made and every hidden bitterness of sin within the heart utterly cast away—if any such bitterness has been gathered from unlawful desires as though from harmful foods. When someone has vomited and cast it away, he will be freed from the disease of a great sickness, provided that after vomiting he takes what contributes to health.

“Nevertheless, know all of you that the bishop labors above you all, since each of you bears his own labor, while he bears both his own and that of each individual. Therefore, O Clement, since you know that you preside over all, help each person insofar as you can, [Col. 0739A] and lift up each one—you who bear the burden and care of each.

“Therefore, now that I impose this administration upon you, I know that I am receiving grace more than I am bestowing it. But be confident and bear it bravely, certain that you will receive the reward of your labor when you have brought this ship safely into the harbor of peace. There you will receive wages and rewards for the salvation of all, if here you keep watch for the safety of all.

“Thus, even if many of the brothers hate you because of the rigor of justice, you will not be harmed by this; rather, through such hatred the love of God will be secured for you. Therefore strive more earnestly and avoid being praised by the wicked or loved by those who act most evilly. Instead, may you deserve to be commended by Christ for your just administration [Note: The Harduinian manuscript has ‘for the administration of justice’] and the most equitable rule of discipline.”

When he had said this and many similar things, he again looked toward the people and said:

“But you also, my dearest brothers and fellow servants, obey in everything this man who presides over you in teaching the truth. Know that whoever grieves him does not receive Christ, who entrusted to him the chair of teaching. And since he has not received Christ, he will also be judged not to have received God the Father, and therefore he himself will not be received into the kingdom of heaven. Therefore strive always to come to every assembly and gathering, lest you be condemned by Christ the Judge as negligent and idle.

“When you assemble with Clement, all of you should take care to be of one mind concerning him and show him your support with the greatest zeal. [Note: The Labbean manuscript has ‘to make your support depend upon him.’] Know that because of each one of you the enemy attacks him alone more fiercely, and raises greater wars against him. [Note: So the Vindobonensis and Harduinian manuscripts. The Vulgate has ‘he is hostile.’]

“Therefore you must strive with the greatest zeal to be bound to him by every bond of love and to cling to him with the fullest affection. You too must persevere as one in complete concord, so that all of you may obey him more easily with equal agreement and unanimity. Thus you may attain salvation, and he, with your obedience, may more readily carry away the weight of the burden imposed upon him. (Council of Vaison II, chapter 6, A.D. 442.)

“You ought also to understand certain matters among yourselves, if there are things that he cannot express more openly and plainly because of the plots of evil people. For example (Council of Metz, A.D. 888, chapter 8): If he is hostile to someone because of his deeds, do not wait for him to tell you, ‘Do not be friends with that man.’ Rather, you ought to observe carefully, obey his will without being admonished, and turn away from the person toward whom you perceive that he is hostile. [Note: The Harduinian manuscript has ‘from whom you perceive him to be turned away.’] Nor should you speak with those with whom he does not speak, so that every person who is at fault, while wishing to regain the friendship of all of you, may hasten to be reconciled to the one who presides over all and through this return to salvation once he has begun to obey the presider’s admonitions.

“But if anyone is friendly with those to whom he himself is not friendly, and speaks with those with whom he does not speak, that person too is one of those who wish to destroy the Church of God. Although he may appear to be with you in body, in mind and spirit he is against you. This enemy is far worse than those who are outside and are openly hostile. For under the appearance of friendship he conducts himself as an enemy [Note: The Labbean manuscript has ‘what is hostile’] and disperses and devastates the Church.

“When he had said this, he placed his hands upon me in the midst of everyone and compelled me, exhausted and filled with great embarrassment, to sit in his chair. When I had sat down, he spoke to me again:

“‘I entreat you, O Clement, before all who are present, that after I have ended this present life—as nature requires—[Note: The Harduinian manuscript has ‘as is natural.’] you should send to James, the brother of the Lord, a brief written account of the matters that concern the beginning of your faith and also the disposition you possessed before the faith; how you were my companion in journeys and activities from beginning to end; what you carefully heard in each city while I was disputing; what order there was in my preaching, both of words and of deeds; and what end overtook me in this city.

“‘As I have said, do not hesitate to send to him everything compressed as briefly as you can. Do not fear that he might be excessively saddened by my departure, since you may be certain that he will endure it for the sake of piety. It will be a great consolation to him if he learns that after me some man who was not unskilled, uneducated, or ignorant of the mystery of the divine word [Note: The Labbean and Justellian manuscripts have ‘the ministry.’] and the discipline of the ecclesiastical order, or unaware of the rule of teaching, has received my chair. For he knows that if an uneducated and ignorant man receives the office of teacher, the disciples and hearers will undoubtedly be overwhelmed by the darkness of ignorance and plunged into destruction.’

“Therefore, my lord James, since I had received these commands from him, I was obliged to fulfill what he had ordered. I have informed you of these matters themselves and have briefly included those things which, as he passed through each city, he either set forth in sermons of preaching or accomplished through the power of his deeds. Although I have already sent you a fuller account of many of these matters, at his command, under the very title that he ordered to be affixed—namely, *The Itinerary of Clement in the Preaching of Peter* [Note: The Vulgate inserts ‘not’; we removed it on the authority of the Vindobonensis and Labbean manuscripts, in agreement with the Greek text. After the word ‘ordered,’ the same Vulgate manuscripts add ‘with the Lord’s help.’]—

[Col. 0740D] I shall now begin, with the Lord’s assistance, to set forth what he commanded.

[Note: This closing clause is found in the Vindobonensis manuscript. In the printed editions of the Councils, a long addition follows, which came from the workshop of Pseudo-Isidore. The Greek text and Rufinus’s translation contain nothing further; likewise, nothing further is found in the other ancient collections that derive this letter from Rufinus’s version and not from Isidore.]

The letter of Clement to James, the brother of the Lord, concerning the death of Peter and his own ordination, ends successfully.

## CHAPTER LXV

[Col. 0741A]

To the holy, most blessed Father, and pope most worthy of the apostolic see, Leo:

Ceretius, Salonius, and Veranus.

The letter of Your Blessedness is reviewed, and so forth, as it appears in volume I of this edition, among Leo’s letters, letter 68.

## CHAPTER LXVI

[Note: The version of this letter—which, as Leo says in letter 69, “the archives of the apostolic see received as having been sent by him [Cyril]” to Pope Celestine—was evidently composed by Cyril himself. Compare volume I of our edition, column 557, where the numbers are printed in heavy type. It is known to have been approved by the same Celestine from letter 11 of that pontiff in P. Coustant, p. 1102. Saint Leo used this version in the testimonies of the Fathers appended to letter 165 to the Emperor Leo; he had earlier sent the same version to Gaul, as we noted in note 5 on letter 67, volume I, column 1002 (in our edition, column 886, note g). Hence it is found transcribed in two Gallican collections, namely ours and the Isidorian additions, to which belong the Vatican manuscript 1340 and the Herovallian manuscript cited by Quesnellus. Crabbus first published it from the Isidorian additions, and from the same source it was inserted into the Councils, volume IV of the Venetian edition, column 2049.]

Cyril to Nestorius, that he may follow the correct doctrine of the faith.

I have learned that certain people who detract from my reputation chatter much in your presence, and do this repeatedly and very often, especially when they see that many illustrious and prudent men are present. Perhaps thinking that your ears are pleased by it, they utter such words against us, though not entirely according to your wishes: men who have not been offended or injured by us in any respect, but have been convicted by us with modesty and gentleness.

One of them did violence to the blind and needy; another raised his sword against his own mother; another stole another man’s gold with a maidservant, and has lived throughout his life with the reputation that no one—even his bitterest enemy—would wish to befall him. But I take no account whatsoever of such men, lest I seem to extend the measure of my mediocrity beyond the Lord, my master, or our fathers. For it is impossible for anyone, however rightly he may live, to avoid the poison and annoyance of slanderers; but they, whose mouths are full of cursing and bitterness, will have to render an account before the Judge of all. [Note: The Crabbian text and Vatican manuscript add ‘by me.’]

I, however, turn to what most befits me, and now admonish you as a brother in the Lord: always present the teaching of the word and the meaning of the faith to the peoples carefully and with the utmost vigilance. Know clearly that if anyone among those who believe in Christ causes even one person to stumble (Matthew 18:6), he will be subject to great indignation; but if it is not one person but a multitude that has been deceived, then we must strive by every means to cut away the scandals and direct the seekers of truth toward a sound and correct understanding of the faith. [Note: Crabbus, together with the Vatican manuscript, has ‘we must make use of this.’] [Note: Quesnellus reads “to direct”; we have preferred Crabbus’s reading. Quesnellus also adds “likewise” before “the Fathers.”]

This will easily be accomplished if, reviewing the writings of the holy Fathers, we esteem them highly and, consulting ourselves to determine whether we stand firm in the faith, form our minds and hearts according to their sound and irreproachable institutions, as it is written (2 Corinthians 1:5). [Note: So our manuscripts and Crabbus. Quesnellus has ‘established’; Crabbus has ‘let us strengthen.’]

[Note: [Col. 0742C] Quesnell notes in the margin: “This is not found in the Thuanus manuscript, doubtless because it was placed above, in chapter 41, among the testimonies on the Incarnation.”]

Thus the holy and great council says that he who is naturally begotten from God the Father—the only-begotten Son, true God from true God [Note: [Col. 0742C] We added “true” with the Vatican and Crabbe manuscripts, and then [Col. 0742D] inserted “this” with the same Crabbe manuscript and the Vindobonensis manuscript]—light from light, through whom and with whom the Father made all things—descended, was incarnate and became man, suffered, rose again on the third day, and ascended once more into heaven.

We must follow these words; we must obey [Col. 0742B] these doctrines, considering what it means for the Word of God to have become incarnate and to have become man. For we do not say that God’s nature was changed or transformed into flesh, nor that it was wholly transformed into the man who consists of soul and body; rather, we say that he united to himself flesh animated by a rational soul, [Note: [Col. 0742D] Crabbe, with altered punctuation, deletes “and,” as also above among the testimonies in chapter 41] and that the Word, substantially, ineffably, and [Note: [Col. 0742D] Thus with Crabbe, as above in chapter 41. Quesnell accepted “irreprehensibly,” but noted in the margin: “Read either *indehprehensibiliter* [‘inapprehensibly’], as in several manuscripts, or *incomprehensibiliter* [‘incomprehensibly’], which is found in the Corbie manuscript and agrees with the Greek. See our note 78 among the testimonies of the Fathers appended to Leo’s letter 165, volume I, column 1398.] inapprehensibly, became man and was also called the Son of Man—not by bare will alone, [Note: [Col. 0742D] Quesnell alone omitted “but not” at this point] nor merely by the assumption of a person; rather, although the natures were different, they nevertheless came together into one: one Christ and Son from both, without the difference of the natures being emptied or removed by their conjunction, but because together they made for us 467 one Lord, Christ, [Note: [Col. 0742D] The conjunction “and,” omitted by Quesnell, has been added from our manuscripts and Crabbe’s. The words printed in italics below are found in both of Quesnell’s manuscripts and in our Vindobonensis manuscript of this collection. Crabbe, however, gives the complete text of this letter here, as does Vatican manuscript 1340] and Son.

And the rest, which has already been written in chapter XLI, “On the Testimonies of the Holy Fathers.” [Col. 0742C]

Added at the end:

I write these things, therefore, out of love in Christ, asking you as a brother and calling you to witness before Christ and the elect angels [Note: [Col. 0742D] Quesnell inserts “his.”], that you may both think and teach these things with us, so that the peace of the Churches may be preserved and the bond of concord and charity may remain indissoluble among the priests of God.

[Note: [Col. 0743C] Since Quesnell, prejudiced by the more recent Oxford manuscript, judged that the following chapters, which contain several letters of Saint Leo, did not belong to this collection, he was content merely to indicate them in the table of chapters prefixed from the Thuanus manuscript. In publishing the collection itself, he not only passed them over but also maintained that they should be excluded from it. Since, however, the same chapters, or letters, are found at the end in all the other, older, and more reliable copies of this collection, as they are indicated in the table of chapters of the Thuanus manuscript, there can be no doubt that they belong to the same collection.

[Col. 0743D] If, therefore, in the single manuscript followed by Quesnell—or even in another older manuscript from which that Oxford codex was copied—the items at the end of the collection are missing, and that collection there ends with sixty chapters, all the other codices, both more excellent and more ancient, must be preferred. The author of the collection copied in the Oxford manuscript from another older exemplar seems to have separated Leo’s letters from the collection for this reason: since he was going to write another collection of the sermons and letters of Saint Leo in one and the same codex, he thought that Leo’s letters belonging to our collection should be joined with the other letters of that pontiff which he had found, and that they should be copied separately from this collection, in the body of Leo’s sermons and letters, after the canonical collection.

Hence the title which Quesnell found in the Oxford copy before the canonical collection: “This codex contains the ecclesiastical canons and the constitutions of the holy apostolic see under sixty titles.” The words added from the writings of Blessed Pope Leo are not part of the body of the canons. This title, which is not found in the other manuscripts, refers to the distinction between the two collections, the latter of which, embracing several letters and sermons of Saint Leo together, certainly does not belong to the preceding body of canons, although many of those same letters cannot, on the authority of so many other copies, be separated from this body.

These older copies, besides the Thuanus manuscript, are two Bellovacensian manuscripts and one Pithoean manuscript, cited by Peter Pithoeus, which he testifies end with Leo’s letter to Dorus, chapter 98—not chapter 60. In addition there are the Atrebatensis and Hubertinus manuscripts mentioned by P. Coustant, and our two Vindobonensis manuscripts, which close the collection with Leo’s letters. The same will be true of any others that someone may be able to find and compare.

We therefore append these letters here as belonging to this collection, in the same order in which they appear not only in the table but also in the body of the canons. Since they have been printed among Leo’s letters in volume I of this edition, however, we shall avoid repeating them: after indicating the title and beginning of each letter, we refer readers to volume I, where they are presented in full, with the readings of this collection also noted.]

## CHAPTER XCIII. Leo, bishop, to Bishop Anatolius

# The Ancient Latin Edition of the Canons

Comprising the canons of the Councils of Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Nicaea, Sardica, Gangra, Antioch, the First Council of Constantinople, and Chalcedon. This edition first appeared from the most ancient manuscript of the library of Christopher Justellus; it is now presented complete and more accurately corrected after comparison with other very ancient manuscript collections. The oldest Latin translation of the Nicene canons, from the excellent Vatican manuscript Regina 1997, is also added.

## Preface to the following collection

477

### 1.

William Voellus and Henry Justellus, son of Christopher, published the ancient Latin edition of the canons from a most ancient and wholly singular manuscript exemplar, for which no other similar copy could be found anywhere. They published it at Paris in 1661, in volume I of the *Bibliotheca Juris canonici veteris*, pages 277 and following.

Since this edition, cited by Dionysius Exiguus himself under the name of the ancient translation and venerable on account of its antiquity, is found only in that Paris edition, which is both extremely rare and prohibited, and therefore usable by very few; and since, moreover, being printed from a single manuscript, it is mutilated in several places and also corrupted by a number of errors, we thought it worthwhile to reprint it here in full and, insofar as possible, in corrected form.

Although we could not obtain any manuscript resembling Justellus’s in which the entire ancient edition is presented continuously, we nevertheless found several ancient manuscript collections of different origins in which, although inserted separately and in scattered form, each and every monument of that same ancient edition had been included. From these we have successfully supplied omissions and corrected not a few errors.

Such are the Vatican Regina 1997 manuscript, in which, besides the Nicene canons, all the others were taken from the *Prisca*; the Lucchese manuscript 88, in which the canons of Antioch, Constantinople, and Chalcedon are transcribed in the same *Prisca* version; Barberini 2888 and Vatican 1342, in which the Nicene, Antiochene, Constantinopolitan, and Chalcedonian canons are found excerpted from the *Prisca*; and the codices of the preceding Quesnellian collection, which incorporated the Chalcedonian canons from the same translation.

As for the Sardican canons included in the ancient edition, since they derive from the original Latin, as we have demonstrated elsewhere, we chiefly examined them against the Lucchese 88 and Vatican 1342 manuscripts, corrected them, and supplied omissions.

### 2.

Some readers are offended by the barbarism and difficulties of this translation. Yet works rendered into Latin in a more remote age generally suffer from the same defect, as we observed in the preface to the letters of Saint Leo, number 51, volume I. Learned men nevertheless did not therefore consider such ancient translations unworthy of attention; rather, they published them with the greatest zeal, believing that considerable benefit could be gained from them.

This *Prisca* translation is so obscure and at times so convoluted that, although we have corrected many passages from the collections mentioned above, numerous difficult places still remain. These seem attributable not always to the carelessness of scribes but more often to the translator’s incompetence. If we attempted to restore them to a clearer meaning by changing certain words on the basis of the Greek or other versions, everyone would rightly complain that we were no longer presenting the primitive text.

We shall therefore assist the understanding of readers either in marginal notes or in annotations to be appended at the end. How useful this translation was among the ancients is clear from the same ancient collections that derived their canons from it. See what we have discussed at greater length concerning this same version in the preceding Treatise, part II, chapter 2, section 3.

### 3.

We now append here the brief preface placed before this translation by Voellus and Justellus.

## To the reader

“So that you might lack nothing, learned reader, which could serve posterity in preserving the memory of canonical and ecclesiastical antiquity, we judged that we ought to insert into this work our ancient Latin edition of the canons—different and distinct from all those published up to the present, and often praised by many very distinguished men.

We present it to you from a manuscript codex of venerable antiquity, written in large, well-formed letters, from the library of Christopher Justellus. That excellent codex once contained the canons of the Councils of Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Nicaea, Sardica, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea, Constantinople I, and Chalcedon; but, a matter especially to be lamented, the complete canons of the Council of Laodicea and the greater part of the Sardican canons, together with the final part of the subscriptions of the Council of Nicaea, perished through the injury of time.

The fragments of the Sardican Council that survive we placed after the Nicene synod. For it is likely that the author of this edition followed in his collection not the dignity of the councils but the order of time. Nor is it an obstacle that in this codex the Council of Chalcedon is placed in an inverted order before the Council of Constantinople, and that canon 28 of Chalcedon is listed among the Constantinopolitan canons; this seems more properly attributable to the hallucination or thoughtlessness of the copyist who transcribed the codex than to an error or ignorance on the part of the author.

Although many other things in the same book are found here and there to be corrupted, damaged, and confused—things that could reasonably be judged errors of the copyist—we nevertheless considered it sacrilegious to correct or alter anything in so elegant a treasure of such great antiquity. We thought it enough to note in the margin the scribe’s *σφάλματα* [errors].”

479

### 4.

Three points must be noted concerning this brief preface.

First, it is false that, as they say, the complete canons of the Council of Laodicea in this version perished through the injury of time. We have shown with sufficient probability, in the Treatise cited shortly above, that the translator did not find these canons at all in the Greek manuscript he used and therefore did not translate them into Latin.

Second, concerning their assertion that the codex was mutilated in the Sardican canons, we have explained in the same place, on the basis of Stephen Baluzius, why this occurred.

Finally, we likewise consider it false that the fact that the Constantinopolitan canons are written after the Chalcedonian canons and that the canon concerning the primacy of the see of Constantinople—which was enacted at the Council of Chalcedon—is attached to them should be attributed to the hallucination or thoughtlessness of the copyist rather than to an error of the translator. We judge that this inverted arrangement and confusion of the canons should be charged neither to the copyist nor to the Latin translator, but to some Greek codex, as will be explained more fully in the same Treatise and in the annotations to the canons themselves.

481

[Note: [Col. 0747A] Read “Here begin.”]

[Note: [Col. 0747A] We found the ancient translation of these canons in one Vatican manuscript, Regina 1997, where “titles” is read instead of “chapters”; the same is consistently found in the other tables of canons. In Justellus’s manuscript, “constitutions” is found—incorrectly, since “constitutions” refers to the canons, not to the titles or chapters of the canons. We corrected this from the headings of the other synods and from the closing formula of the same Justellus codex: “The chapters of the Ancyrean canons are ended.” [Col. 0748A]]

[Col. 0747A]

I. Concerning presbyters who sacrificed during the persecution.

III. Concerning those who became pagans under compulsion.

IV. Concerning those who associate with pagans in various ways.

V. Concerning those [Note: [Col. 0748A] The same codex: “who became pagans through fear.”] who fell through fear.

VI. Concerning those [Note: [Col. 0748A] Justellus’s manuscript: “who eat in idol-shrines.” We corrected this from Vatican Regina, which shortly afterward has *saepissime* [“very frequently”] instead of *saepius* [“frequently”].] who ate in places [read: “in the places”] of idols.

VII. Concerning those who sacrificed frequently.

VIII. Concerning those [Note: [Col. 0748A] The same Vatican codex: “through whom others also were compelled to sacrifice.” [Col. 0749C] ] who also persuade others to sacrifice to idols. [Read: “to sacrifice.”]

IX. Concerning those who, at ordination, made a declaration regarding marriage.

X. Concerning betrothed girls who were violated by others.

XI. Concerning catechumens who transgressed.

XII. Concerning rural bishops.

XIII. Concerning clerics who abstain from meat.

XIV. Concerning those who are sold for the work of the Church.

XV. Concerning those who fornicated with animals.

XVI. As above: concerning those who are either corrupted by males or corrupt them.

XVII. Concerning bishops who were ordained but not received.

XVIII. Concerning those who promise virginity and pretend to live with women as with sisters. [Note: [Col. 0749C] Justellus’s codex here reads “dwell.” We preferred Vatican Regina, which agrees with the same Justellus codex in the title prefixed to the canon below: “They pretend to live together.”]

482

XIX. [Note: [Col. 0749C] Vatican Regina: “Concerning those who commit adultery with one another.” XX. “Concerning those who kill children whom they have borne.”] Those who have adulterous wives.

XX. Concerning those who kill children conceived in fornication.

[Col. 0749B]

XXI. Concerning homicides.

XXII. Concerning homicide against one’s will.

XXIII. [Note: [Col. 0749D] The same codex: “Concerning amulets and diviners.”] Concerning diviners or sorcerers.
