# Here begin the constitutions of the same council

[Note: [Col. 0749D] Vatican Regina omits the preceding closing formula, “The headings are ended,” and the following title, “Here begin,” etc. It gives this annotation as follows: “These are the canons that were set forth before the Nicene canons. Yet the Nicene canons were written first because of the authority of the holy and great council held at Nicaea.” This is better and agrees more closely with the Greek, where the Nicene canons precede the Ancyrean.]

These canons were indeed set forth before the Nicene canons; nevertheless, the Nicene canons were received first because of the authority of the holy and great council that was held at Nicaea.

# Canons established by the holy Fathers who assembled through the Holy Spirit in the city of Ancyra

Title XXIV.

## Concerning presbyters who sacrificed during the persecution and resisted

[Note: [Col. 0749D] Read: “and resisted.” Justellus’s manuscript omits the word “resisted”; we added it from Vatican Regina, as the context of the canon requires. From the same codex we corrected *resipiscerunt* [“repented”]; Justellus has *resipiscerint* [“will repent”]. The Vatican manuscript then deletes *et* [“and”] before *reluctaverunt* [“resisted”].]

### I.

Presbyters who sacrificed and afterward repented, and who neither resisted 483 by any remedy but did so sincerely, nor previously affirmed through a pretext the things they had done, as though to demonstrate that they had been sent to suffer punishment, so that they might appear and be believed to have been offered to them—concerning these it was decreed that they should indeed retain the honor of the chair; but they may not offer, or endure [read: “feed”], or conduct the service, or minister in the sacred ministry.

[Note: [Col. 0750C] Justellus has in the text “to retain or pray,” but in the margin: “Add ‘but that they offer,’ and read ‘to pray’ instead of ‘to feed.’” Our codex gives the complete and correct reading if *pascere* [“feed”] is substituted for *patere* [“endure”]; for the Greek text and other versions have “to have the discourse,” which our translator rendered by *pascere*.]

## Concerning deacons who sacrificed

### II.

Likewise, deacons who sacrificed and afterward repented shall retain their rank, but they shall cease from the sacred ministry of the bread and cup: they shall not carry them, [Note: [Col. 0750C] Justellus adds “nor minister.” Our codex is better, agreeing with the Greek and other versions.] nor preach.

If some bishops, knowing the labor of these men, should wish to show them the humility of gentleness, or to grant them something more or to reduce something, this shall be in their power. [Note: [Col. 0750C] Our codex reads: “knowing their labor, or wishing to show them the humanity of gentleness,” and shortly afterward deletes “to them”; from the same codex we wrote *potestate* [“in their power”], whereas Justellus has *potestatem* [“authority”].]

## Concerning those who, captured while fleeing, became pagans under compulsion

### III.

Those who fled and were captured, or were handed over by their own household, or lost their possessions; who, after suffering punishments or being thrown into prison, cried out that they were Christians while being held and were violently thrust into chains; and who, out of necessity, accepted food with pagans, confessing that they were Christians and continually displaying grief over what had happened, with all humility and an appearance of goodness and with the humility proper to this world—these, as though made free from sin outside themselves, are not to be deprived of communion.

[Note: [Col. 0750D] Vatican Regina: “But if … so that they may be able,” and shortly afterward, “among clerics and laypeople.”]

But if some deprived them of communion so that they might be more thoroughly tested, they should soon afterward be received by others. The same applies to clerics and laypeople.

It was discussed whether, if possible, laypeople subjected to such necessity could advance to an increase of honor. Therefore it was decreed that these too, as having committed no sin—or if their previous life is found to have been upright—could enter the clerical 484 order.

[Note: [Col. 0750D] Justellus repeats *sunt* [“are”]; we removed it in accordance with our codex.]

## Concerning those who acted in various ways with pagans

[Note: [Col. 0750D] The same codex: “who practiced paganism.” At the beginning of the canon we added “Concerning those” from our codex.]

### IV.

Concerning those who sacrificed under compulsion, who also dined beside idols [perhaps: “in idol-shrines”], some of whom even ascended in splendid attire, [Note: [Col. 0750D] Thus our codex. Justellus has “adorned.”] used expensive clothing, and accepted various things from the prepared banquet [Note: [Col. 0750D] Other versions render this without distinction]—it was decreed that they should be received among the hearers and remain subject for three years, then share in prayer for two years, and thus come to perfection. [Note: [Col. 0750D] Voellus and Justellus noted that something was missing here. The omission consisted of the following four words, supplied from Vatican manuscript Regina: “to hear, and that they be subject.” “To hear” denotes the grade of penance in which penitents were received among the hearers; “to be subject” denotes the other grade in which they attended, prostrate, at the prayers of the faithful.]

But however many ascended wearing mourning clothes and reclined to eat with sadness and tears, if they completed the prescribed three years, they should be received without the offering.

But if they did not eat, they shall remain subject for two years, and in the third year they shall share in communion without the offering, so that as perfected persons they may receive it in the fourth year. [Note: [Col. 0751D] Justellus does not recognize the negation and has “if they are subject.” We supplied and corrected the text from our codex.]

Bishops, however, have the power, after testing their manner of conversion, either humanely to add more time or otherwise. [Note: [Col. 0751D] From the Greek this should be rendered “But above all.” Justellus has *probatus* [“having been approved”]; we preferred, with our codex, *probatur* [“is approved”], though *probetur* [“may be approved”] would be better.] The preceding and subsequent life is examined [read: “may be examined”]. And thus mercy may be added beyond the prescribed time.

## Concerning those who became pagans through fear

### V.

Concerning those who became pagans through threats and fear [Note: [Col. 0751D] Vatican Regina: “because of threats.”], who sacrificed amid punishments, the loss of their property [read: “the loss of their possessions”], or deportation [read: “deportation”], and who to the present time have not repented or turned back, but now, outside the time of the synod, make supplication [Note: [Col. 0751D] We added “and coming to a sense of conversion” from the same codex; there is also an ellipsis here: they “offered themselves.”] and come to a sense of conversion—it was decreed that they should be admitted among the hearers until the great day, and after the great day remain subject for three years; afterward they should share in communion without the offering, and thus come to perfection, completing six years in all.

If some were admitted to repentance before the synod, the six years should be counted for them from that time.

But if someone is in danger of death, or is awaiting death because of illness, or because of some other 485 circumstance [read: “some other circumstance”], they ought to be received at that hour. [Note: [Col. 0751D] Read “if it happens to someone,” and supply “or is imminent.” Vatican Regina has: “But if a dangerous expectation of death.”]

## Concerning those who ate in places of idols

### VI.

Concerning those who, at a festival, eat together in the abominable places of the Gentiles, and, bringing their own food [read: “bringing their own food”], ate it after it had been polluted—it was decreed that they should remain subject for two years and then be received, because after the offering each bishop ought to test them and learn the life of each individual.

## Concerning those who sacrificed frequently

### VII.

Those who sacrificed a second and third time under compulsion shall remain subject for four years, share in communion for two years without the offering, and in the seventh year be received as perfected.

## Concerning those who also persuade others to sacrifice to idols

### VIII.

Those who not only apostatized but also enticed their brothers, and were responsible because their brothers were enticed, shall be admitted to the place of hearers for three years. For the other six years they shall occupy the place in which they fell [Note: [Col. 0751D] That is, they shall prostrate themselves and perform penance]. For one further year they shall share in communion without the offering, so that, completing ten years, they may receive the place of the perfected. [Note: [Col. 0751D] Vatican Regina: “They shall be received perfectly.”] Their life must be carefully observed in this matter.

## Concerning deacons who, at ordination, made a declaration regarding marriage

[Note: [Col. 0751D] The same codex: “concerning marriage.”]

### IX.

If deacons who are to be ordained declared before ordination that they ought to marry and could not remain in their present state, then, if they marry afterward, they shall remain in the ministry for which the bishop’s command [that is, permission] was given to them.

But if some, without making such a declaration, remained silent and consented at ordination to continue unmarried, and afterward proceeded to marriage, they shall cease entirely from the ministry of the diaconate. [Note: [Col. 0751D] Vatican Regina omits the words “without making such a declaration … unmarried … entirely … of the deacon”; its reading is better.]

486

## Concerning girls who are betrothed and are violated by others

[Note: [Col. 0752D] The same codex: “who are abducted by others.”]

### X.

Those who are betrothed and are abducted by others shall afterward be restored to the men to whom they had previously been betrothed, even if they had suffered some violence from those men. [Note: [Col. 0752D] Justellus’s manuscript has “even if they suffered violence from him.” We preferred the reading of Vatican Regina, in which the words immediately afterward are “if they suffered anything from them.”]

## Concerning those who sacrificed while they were catechumens

### XI.

Those who sacrificed before baptism but were afterward baptized—it was decreed that they should be advanced to the order, as those who have been cleansed. [Note: [Col. 0752D] Justellus has “just like the others.” Our codex is preferable; it agrees more closely with the Greek, from which we render: “it was decreed that they should be advanced to the order, as those who have been cleansed.”]

## That no one may be ordained without a bishop by those called rural bishops

[Note: [Col. 0752D] Vatican Regina: “a cleric.”]

### XII.

Rural bishops may not ordain presbyters or deacons. Nor may the presbyters of a city do so without the bishop’s command, but they must go to the individual parishes with the same letters. [Note: [Col. 0752D] The same manuscript deletes “but also to them.”]

## Concerning those who abstain from meat

[Note: [Col. 0752D] The same codex: “Concerning clerics who abstain.”]

### XIII.

Concerning presbyters or deacons who are in the clergy and abstain from meat, it was decreed that they should touch it; [Note: [Col. 0752D] The codex reads: “and if they do not obey in this way.”] and if they do not obey the canon, it was decreed that they should cease from their order.

## Concerning those who rashly dispose of ecclesiastical property

[Note: [Col. 0752D] The same manuscript: “Concerning those who are sold for the work of the Church.” At the beginning of the canon we added the words “Concerning those” from the same manuscript.]

### XIV.

If any of the things belonging to the Lord’s property were sold by presbyters while there was no bishop, the property is to be recalled and reclaimed; and it shall be left to the bishop’s judgment whether it is appropriate to receive the price, since the proceeds from the things sold may themselves repay that price.

[Note: [Col. 0752D] Justellus incorrectly has: “if at some time they did not exist, or if the bishop was unaware … they should be compelled to recall and restore.” We corrected this from our codex.]

[Note: [Col. 0752D] Vatican Regina adds “frequently.” The sense from the Greek is: “It is left to the bishop’s judgment whether the price should be recovered or not, since, as Dionysius rendered it, the return from the property sold will often have produced a larger sum than the price originally paid.”]

487

[Col. 0753A]

## Concerning those who had sexual intercourse with animals

[Read: “with animals.”]

[Note: [Col. 0753D] The same codex: “who fornicated.”]

### XV. Those who commit such an act with animals

Those who commit such an act with animals before they are twenty years old [read: “who, before they are twenty years old”], and who have committed it, shall undergo penance for fifteen years; then they may be deemed worthy of communion in prayers, and, persevering in this condition for five years, they may thereafter approach the offerings. Their manner of life while they are still subject to penance must be examined, and thus they may be deemed worthy of humane treatment; but if they persist continually in sinning, they shall undergo a long penance.

[Note: [Col. 0753D] The same codex reads this better than Justinian: *quia*; but instead of *amplius* one should read *prius*.]

Those who have exceeded this age, and who, while having wives, have sinned in this offense, shall undergo penance for twenty-five years, so that after five years they may be deemed worthy of communion in prayer.

[Note: [Col. 0753D] The Vatican Regius reads: “if they rushed into this sin”; read: “this sin.”]

But if some, while having wives and being more than fifty years old, commit this sin, they may be deemed worthy to receive viaticum at the end of their lives.

### Those who have intercourse with animals or males, or who have been corrupted or corrupt others through lust

### XVI.

For those who have intercourse with animals, or who become leprous through intercourse with animals or with males, it has been prescribed that they pray together with those who suffer the tempest—that is, those whom we call possessed.

[Note: [Col. 0753D] The Vatican Regius inserts “and.”]

[Note: [Col. 0753D] Isidore’s version explains this passage as follows: “those who are tossed by the tempest,” whom we call possessed.]

### Those who have been approved for the episcopate but not received

### XVII.

Those who have been consecrated to the episcopate but not received in the parishes to which they were appointed, and who wish to go to other parishes, forcibly to oppress those established there and to bring lawsuits against them.

[Note: [Col. 0753D] Justinian reads: “to drive them out.” We emended from the Vatican Regius; Dionysius renders the sense more clearly: “it was decided that these men should be cast out.”]

They shall themselves be expelled and alienated [read: “shall be alienated”]. But if they wish to sit as presbyters in the presbyterate in which they first served, they are not to be expelled.

[Note: [Col. 0753D] Justinian adds *ordinem* (“order”); our manuscript more correctly omits it.]

For if they wish to resist the bishops established there, we decree that they be expelled also from the order of presbyters and become ex-preachers.

[Note: [Col. 0753D] We have added the particle *et*, that is, “also,” from the same manuscript.]

### 488. Those who promise to remain in virginity and pretend to live with women as sisters

### XVIII.

Those who have promised themselves to virginity, and, having annulled their promise, follow the regulation concerning second marriages, shall be subject to that regulation. But we forbid virgins to associate with anyone as though they were sisters.

[Note: [Col. 0753D] It should read: “and, having nullified their promise, let them follow the regulation concerning second marriages.” Immediately afterward the Vatican Regius reads: “But whoever associates with virgins,” etc.]

### Those who keep adulterous women while themselves committing adultery

### XIX.

If someone’s wife has been adulterated, or if her husband has committed adultery, he must undergo penance for seven years and thereafter be deemed worthy of full communion, according to the successive stages.

[Note: [Col. 0754D] The same codex reads: “if any man has committed it”; and then, “may be deemed worthy.”]

[Note: [Col. 0754D] We have inserted the word “women” from the same codex.]

### Those who become pregnant through fornication and kill their offspring

### XX.

Women who have committed fornication, kill their offspring, and hasten to cause an abortion were at first prohibited until the end of their lives; but after this had been determined, we decreed that they should obtain something more humane and should undergo ten years, according to the established stages.

[Note: [Col. 0754D] Justinian reads: “Those who kill.” We supplied the intervening words from our codex, which thereafter reads: “and if they kill what is born.” A little later, we preferred *consequantur* (“may obtain”) with the same manuscript; Justinian reads *consequentur*.]

### On homicides

### XXI.

Those guilty of deliberate homicide shall indeed remain under penance for the whole of the appointed period; and at the end of their lives they may be deemed worthy to receive viaticum.

### On involuntary homicide

### XXII.

[Note: [Col. 0754D] We supplied the words “concerning homicide” from our manuscript.]

Concerning homicide committed involuntarily, the earlier regulation prescribed that the offender be considered worthy of full communion after seven years; we decree that the period be completed according to the established stages over five years.

### Those who practice divination in any manner

### XXIII.

Those who practice divination and follow pagan customs, or introduce people into their houses to conduct divination for any reason connected with magical practices or incantations—if they are members of the clergy, let them be expelled; but if they are laypeople, let them remain under penance for five years, according to the defined stages.

[Note: [Col. 0754D] We inserted the words “practice divination” and “and” from the same codex.]

[Note: [Col. 0754D] The Vatican Regius reads: “by divining for any reason at the request of those seeking magical remedies”; perhaps this is better.]

### Those who are accomplices in the corruption of virgins

### XXIV.

If a man who was betrothed to a girl corrupted her sister and made her pregnant, but then married the woman to whom he was betrothed,

[Note: [Col. 0754D] The particle *autem* (“but”), required by the context, was to be supplied from our codex.]

afterward the woman who had been corrupted hanged herself; those who were accomplices are ordered to remain under penance for eleven years, according to the stages already established.

[Note: [Col. 0754D] The Vatican Regius codex places the following subscription after the canons of Neocaesarea, in this form: “And those who had assembled in the synod of the city of Ancyra signed.” After the names of the bishops of this synod, the bishops of the Synod of Neocaesarea are listed in this form: “In Neocaesarea, those who signed: Vitalis,” etc.]

And they signed:

Vitalis of Antioch; Marcellus of Ancyra; Agricolaus of Caesarea; Lupus of Tarsus.

[Note: [Col. 0754D] Thus our codex; Justinian reads “of Tarsus.”]

Basilius of Amasea.

[Note: [Col. 0754D] Read “of Amasea.”]

Philadelphus of Juliopolis; Eustolus of Nicomedia.

[Col. 0755A]

Heraclius of Zelonia.

[Note: [Col. 0755D] Justinian reads “Hercilius.” Our codex is better.]

[Note: [Col. 0755D] Read “Zelonia.”]

Petrus of Iconium.

[Note: [Col. 0755D] Thus the Vatican Regius manuscript; Justinian incorrectly reads “of Jacomium.”]

Nunechius of Laodicea; Sergianus of Antioch in Pisidia; Epidaurus of Perge; Narcissus of Neroniadis.

[Note: [Col. 0755D] Read “Neroniadis.”]

Here ends the collection of the canons of Ancyra.

## THE CHAPTERS OF THE CANONS OF NEOCAESAREA BEGIN

I. Concerning presbyters who have fallen.  
II. Concerning the marriage of two brothers.

[Note: [Col. 0755D] In one Vatican Regius codex we also found these canons in the Prisca version. Its subsequent titles are presented as follows: “II. Concerning a virgin corrupted by two brothers. III. Concerning those who have married many times. IV. Concerning those who are freed from a fornicator by the occasion of an intervening circumstance. V. Concerning catechumens who sin. VI. Concerning pregnant women who are to be baptized. VII. Presbyters ought not to pray at the weddings of men married a second time.”]

III. Concerning those who have married several women.  
IV. Concerning those who arrange to fornicate and are forbidden.  
V. Concerning catechumens who have fallen.  
VI. Pregnant women who are catechumens and are to be baptized.

[Col. 0755B] 490

VII. Presbyters ought not to pray at the weddings of men married a second time.  
VIII. Concerning those who associate with adulterous women.  
IX. Concerning those who sin before ordination and afterward confess.  
X. Likewise concerning deacons.  
XI. At what age clerics should be advanced into the clerical order.  
XII. Concerning those baptized in illness.  
XIII. Concerning parish presbyters.  
XIV. Concerning the number of deacons.

[Note: [Col. 0755D] The same codex gives the following titles in this form: “XI. That it is not permitted to ordain anyone before the age of thirty. XII. Concerning those who are gravely ill. XIII. Concerning parish presbyters.”]

Here end the chapters of the canons of Neocaesarea.

## THE TEXT OF THE SAME COUNCIL BEGINS

[Note: [Col. 0755D] The same codex prefixes this note to the table of canons in the following words: “These are the second canons of Ancyra and of those promulgated at Neocaesarea; but the first are those of Nicaea, although the titles are placed after the Ancyran titles.”]

These are the second canons of Ancyra, promulgated at Neocaesarea, and these precede those of Nicaea.

### Concerning presbyters who have fallen

### I.

If a presbyter marries, he is to be deposed from the order; but if he has fornicated, or committed adultery in any way, we decree that he be expelled also from communion and brought to penance.

[Note: [Col. 0756D] The same codex adds: “or has committed adultery, he is to be expelled,” etc.]

### Concerning the marriage of two brothers

### II.

If a woman marries and is corrupted by two brothers, she shall be expelled until death; nevertheless, at the hour of death she shall receive viaticum if she has acknowledged her error. If, after having been corrupted, she has forbidden the marriage and performed penance, she may be deemed worthy of full communion.

But if the woman dies while involved in such a marriage, or if such a corrupting man dies, the penance of the one who remains shall be remitted with difficulty.

[Col. 0756A] 491

### Concerning those who have married many times

### III.

Concerning those who have entered into several marriages: the period established is indeed to be recognized, but their conduct and faith will shorten the period.

[Note: [Col. 0756D] Justinian’s manuscript reads: “Those who have entered into several marriages.” The Vatican Regius codex supplies the correction.]

### Concerning those who arrange to fornicate and are forbidden

### IV.

If someone, having planned and desired another man’s wife, has arranged to sleep with her but does not come to carry out his plan, it is evident that he has been freed by the grace of God.

[Note: [Col. 0756D] The Vatican Regius reads: “If someone has planned.”]

### Concerning catechumens who sin

### V.

If a catechumen stands in the order of catechumens in the Lord’s assembly, and is found to be sinning, he shall kneel.

[Note: [Col. 0756D] We supplied the word “catechumen” from our codex.]

[Note: [Col. 0756D] Read: “stands in the order of catechumens.”]

But if, after kneeling and hearing the instruction, he no longer sins, he shall receive grace; but if, while hearing it, he continues to sin, he shall be expelled.

[Note: [Col. 0756D] Justinian reads: “he shall kneel, and when he has heard this, he shall cease from sinning and shall receive,” etc. The reading of our codex seemed better, in which only “he shall kneel” is lacking.]

### Concerning pregnant women

### VI.

A pregnant woman ought to be baptized whenever she wishes; for the one who is born does not thereby share in anything, since each person manifests his or her own will in confession.

### Presbyters ought not to pray at the weddings of men married a second time

### VII.

A presbyter must not eat at the wedding of a man married a second time; for, when a man married a second time asks for penance, who would dare to be a presbyter so as to arrange a wedding for the sake of a feast?

[Note: [Col. 0756D] Our codex adds: “and also a presbyter who, on account of,” etc. Perhaps the reading is: “who would be a presbyter who, on account of a feast,” etc.]

[Col. 0756C]

### Concerning those who associate with adulterous women

### VIII.

If the wife of a layman has committed adultery and this is proved, such a man cannot enter the ministry.

[Note: [Col. 0756D] The same codex reads: “if she is accused.”]

But if she commits adultery after he has been ordained, he ought to divorce her; if he wishes to continue living with her, he cannot approach the ministry entrusted to him.

[Col. 0756C] 492

### Concerning those who sin before ordination

### IX.

If a presbyter has previously sinned bodily, let him be examined and confess that he sinned before he was ordained; he shall not offer, while remaining in the other respects; *pro reliqua festinantur migrare* (“for the rest, they hasten to depart”) is corrupt and uncertain.

[Note: [Col. 0756D] The Vatican Regius reads *pro alia quae festinantur*, “for another matter which is hastened”; the passage is corrupt in both witnesses. Hervetus rendered it from the Greek as: “on account of his devotion to another aspect of a good life.”]

For many have said that the remaining sins can be forgiven through the laying on of hands. But if he himself does not confess, and cannot be openly accused, he may continue to do this.

### Likewise concerning deacons

[Col. 0757A]

### X.

If a deacon falls into this same sin, he shall not hold a place in the ministry.

[Note: [Col. 0757C] The same manuscript reads: “Likewise, if a deacon falls into this very sin.”]

### At what age they should be advanced into the orders

[Note: [Col. 0757C] The Vatican Regius codex reads: “When it is proper to ordain.”]

### XI.

A presbyter shall not be ordained before the age of thirty. Even if he should perhaps be a worthy man, this requirement must nevertheless be observed in his case, because the Lord began to teach after he had been baptized in his thirtieth year.

[Note: [Col. 0757C] The same manuscript adds: “but this must be observed in his case, because,” etc.]

### Concerning those baptized in illness

### XII.

If someone has been baptized while ill, he cannot enter the order of presbyters, because faith did not come to him by his own will but by necessity.

[Note: [Col. 0757C] Thus our codex, better than Justinian’s *ejus* (“of him”).]

For perhaps afterward fervor of faith, or hospitality bestowed upon people, may be proved [the Latin is incomplete and corrupt].

[Note: [Col. 0757C] The passage is corrupt. Dionysius rendered it: “unless perhaps, on account of his subsequent zeal and faith, and because of the scarcity of men, such a person can be admitted.”]

### Concerning the presbyters of the dioceses

[Note: [Col. 0757C] The Vatican Regius reads: “of the places.”]

[Col. 0757B]

### XIII.

In certain places, presbyters cannot offer in the Lord’s assembly of the city when the bishop or the city’s presbyters are present; nor may they give bread in prayer or the cup.

But if they are absent, and the chorepiscopus of that place has been summoned to prayer, he alone gives it.

[Note: [Col. 0757C] The same manuscript reads: “who, from the localities, gives even alone.”]

For chorepiscopi are indeed in the form of the seventy, and, as fellow ministers, they offer on account of their care for the poor, honoring them.

### Concerning the number of deacons

### XIV.

There ought to be seven deacons, according to the canon. Even if the city is perhaps very large, inquire for confirmation from the book of the Acts of the Apostles.

[Col. 0757C] 493

And those who had assembled in the synod of Neocaesarea signed.

Vitalis, Lupus, Leontius, Basileus, Gregorius, Longinus, Heraclius, Amphition, Sebius, Erytrius, Xantulus, Valentinus, Narcissus, Dicasius, Alphion, Germanus, Gerontius, Stephanus, Salaminus, Leontius.

[Note: [Col. 0757C] Justinian reads “Paulus.” We corrected this in accordance with our Vatican Regius manuscript, with which the codices of the preceding collection agree; none of them prefers “Paulus.”]

[Note: [Col. 0757D] Our codex reads “Anphidon”; Isidore reads “Amphion.”]

[Note: [Col. 0757D] In the preceding collection, chapter 4, from Isidore, “Redux”; three other codices read “Sedus.”]

[Note: [Col. 0757D] In the same collection, “Sanctus.”]

[Note: [Col. 0757D] Thus the Vatican Regius codex and other manuscripts of the preceding collection. Justinian reads “Phalminon.”]

Here end the regulations of the canons of Neocaesarea.

[Note: [Col. 0757D] The Nicaean canons in the Prisca version are found inserted in the very old collections Vatican 1342 and Barberini 2888. Since Sirmond recited the sixth canon of this version from the celebrated Vatican manuscript, the opinion arose that this codex was entirely like the one possessed by Justinian, although that collection does not contain the whole of the ancient edition, as the Justinian codex does, but has received from the same translation only the Nicaean, Antiochene, Chalcedonian, and Constantinopolitan canons. The order of Vatican codex 1342, which we have carefully examined, differs somewhat in the material presented above.

Its title is given as follows: “Here begins the faith expounded by the 318 Fathers assembled at Nicaea, first against Arius the blasphemer, who said that the Son of God was a creature, and against every heresy of Sabellius, Photinus, Paul of Samosata, Mani, Valentinus, Marcion, and against every heresy whatsoever that might arise against the catholic and apostolic Church. All these the 318 bishops assembled at Nicaea condemned, whose names and provinces are written below. But most of the devout servants of God took greater care to record the names of the Eastern bishops, because the West had not conducted an investigation into heresies in the same manner.”

Then follows: “Here begins the preface of the same.” Then: “Here begins the regulations: We believe in one God,” etc. After the creed: “Here begin the canons or regulations of the council mentioned above: When the holy and great council had assembled,” etc. Afterward: “Here begin the chapters of the Council of Nicaea.” The titles of the canons are presented, and finally the canons themselves, each with its title.]

## THE REGULATIONS OF THE CANONS OF THE HOLY FATHERS ASSEMBLED AT NICAEA BEGIN

[Col. 0758A]

## The chapters of the Council of Nicaea begin

I. Concerning those who mutilate or castrate themselves.  
II. Concerning neophytes.  
III. Concerning women living together with clergy.  
IV. Concerning the ordination of bishops.  
V. Concerning those excommunicated in the several provinces.  
VI. Concerning the primacy of the Roman Church.  
VII. Concerning the honor of the bishop of Jerusalem.  
VIII. Concerning those called Cathari [read: Cathari].  
IX. Concerning those ordained without examination.  
X. Concerning those who denied the faith during persecution.

[Col. 0758B]

XI. Concerning those who transgressed without necessity.  
XII. Concerning the granting of reconciliation.  
XIII. Concerning catechumens who have fallen.  
XIV. Concerning clerics, that they not pass from one city to another.  
XV. That no one receive or promote another Church’s cleric.  
XVI. That no one ordain another Church’s cleric.  
XVII. That no cleric lend money at interest.  
XVIII. Concerning deacons, that they not exercise authority over presbyters.  
XIX. Concerning the baptism of Paulianists.  
XX. Concerning deaconesses.  
XXI. Concerning kneeling.

Here end the chapters of the Council of Nicaea.

## THE PREFACE OF THE COUNCIL OF NICAEA BEGINS

[Col. 0758C]

[Note: [Col. 0758D] We found these verses in several manuscript collections.]

The sacred council established the venerable heights of the law  
and gave us fitting restraints,  
so that, firmly founded under just discipline,  
the clerical order might be governed while preserving its purity.  
The highest bishops, following the commands of the ancients,  
explained these matters more plainly in their admonitions.  
From this the path of our faith is opened before us, and the holy teachings  
condemn all the ways of error.  
Whoever has been a servant of God and a priest of Christ—  
seasoned with this salt, he will pour forth sweet honey.

[Col. 0759A]

Here ends the preface.

## THE CREED OF THE COUNCIL OF NICAEA BEGINS

When the holy and great council had assembled at Nicaea, the metropolis of Bithynia, the regulations written below were enacted. It was decided that all these things should be sent to Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome.

[Note: [Col. 0759D] The Vatican codex 1342 deletes “the metropolis.”]

The synod took place in the consulship of Constantine Augustus and Licinius, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, which among the Greeks is the eighteenth day of their second month, in the year 636 from Alexander.

[Note: [Col. 0759D] Compare our remarks on this erroneous consulship in note 44 on chapter 1 of the preceding collection, after the catalogue of bishops (our column 387, note d). A little later, “eighteen days,” more correctly “nineteen.” See note 2 on the same chapter 1 (column 371, note b), from which you will also understand that there is an error in the word “second,” in place of which “Desius” should have been written; Desius was not the second but the seventh month of the Macedonian Syrians.]

All the bishops said:

### Confession of faith

[Col. 0759B]

We believe in one God, the almighty Father, maker of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten, born from the Father, that is, from the substance of the Father; true God from true God, born, not made, *homousion*—that is, of the same substance as the Father—through whom all things were made, both in heaven and on earth; who for us human beings and for our salvation descended, was incarnate and became human, suffered, rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, and from there will come to judge the living and the dead; and in the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0759D] The cited codex reads: “the only-begotten Son of God, who was born from the Father, that is, from the substance of the Father, God from God, light from light, true God from true God,” etc.]

But those who say, “There was a time when he did not exist,” and “Before he was born he did not exist,” and who say that he was made from things that did not subsist, or from another substance or essence, or say that the Son of God is *τρέπτον* (*trepton*), that is, changeable or mutable, the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes.

[Note: [Col. 0759D] In the same Vatican manuscript: “There was once a time when,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0759D] The cited codex reads: “Concerning eunuchs who mutilate themselves.” Its canon begins: “If anyone mutilates or castrates himself, he must not be admitted to the clergy at all. But if because of illness,” etc.]

### Concerning those who mutilate or castrate themselves, who are altogether not to be admitted to the clergy

### I.

If someone has been cut by physicians because of illness, or castrated by barbarians, he shall remain in the clergy. But if someone who is healthy mutilates himself, even if he has been placed in the clergy, he ought to be expelled, and henceforth none of such men is to be promoted.

[Note: [Col. 0760D] The same manuscript reads: “if he has been placed in the clergy.” Immediately afterward Justinian and the others read “and the rest”; we corrected the passage from the same manuscript. Otherwise, “from now on” is written in place of *de cetero*. Dionysius has “and thereafter.”]

Just as this is clear concerning those who dare to mutilate themselves, so also the canon admits to the clergy those who have been castrated by barbarians or by their masters, if they are otherwise found worthy.

[Note: [Col. 0760D] The Vatican manuscript reads: “if any such worthy men are found.”]

[Col. 0760A]

### Concerning neophytes who are admitted to the clergy after baptism

### II.

Many things have been done outside the ecclesiastical canon, whether from necessity or because of the haste of men: people recently coming from pagan life to the faith, instructed as catechumens for only a short time, immediately receive the spiritual washing and, once baptized, are promoted to the episcopate or presbyterate. It has seemed good that nothing of this kind be done in the future.

For time is necessary for one who is being catechized, and after baptism a more manifest examination is required. Indeed, there is an apostolic writing which says, “not a neophyte” (1 Tim. 3), lest, being lifted up with pride, he fall into judgment and the snare of the devil.

But if, as time goes on, some sin of the soul is found in a person and he is convicted by two or three witnesses, let him withdraw from the clergy. If anyone acts contrary to these provisions, as one rising up against the holy and great council, he endangers himself and shall be deprived of the clergy.

[Note: [Col. 0760D] The same codex reads: “If someone who is a neophyte is admitted to the clergy after baptism, many things without,” etc.]

### Concerning those who live together with women

[Col. 0760B]

### III.

Concerning women who live together with bishops, presbyters, or deacons, whether widows or virgins, the holy and great council has entirely forbidden that a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone among the clergy should live with them, except perhaps with a sister, an aunt, or only such persons as avoid every suspicion.

[Note: [Col. 0760D] The Vatican codex reads: “Concerning women brought into the household.” Its canon begins: “Any bishop, presbyter, or deacon who lives with women, whether widows,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0760D] In the Greek: ἣ θείαν; in Italian, *zia* (“aunt”).]

[Col. 0760C] 497

### Concerning the ordination of bishops

### IV.

It has been decided that a bishop should be ordained by all the bishops who are in the province. But if this is difficult because of urgent necessity or the length of the journey, it is altogether necessary that three bishops meet together and constitute a bishop, with the consent of those who are absent, given in writing as though they were present; and the confirmation of what is done must be held by the metropolitan of each province.

[Note: [Col. 0760D] The same codex reads: “If this should be difficult on account of,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0760D] We supplied the four words “and those who are absent” from the same codex.]

[Note: [Col. 0760D] Justinian adds “authority.” Our codex more correctly omits it.]

### Concerning those excommunicated in the several provinces

### V.

Whether they are from the clergy or from the lay body, the judgment of the bishops in each province shall prevail according to the canon; those who are expelled by some are not to be received or admitted by others.

[Note: [Col. 0760D] The title in the Vatican manuscript is: “Concerning the excommunicated.” The canon begins: “Those who are excommunicated in the several provinces, whether from the clergy or from the laity,” etc.]

It must nevertheless be investigated whether they were excommunicated through cowardice, obstinacy, or some other hatred of the bishop.

For this to receive suitable consideration, it has seemed good that councils be held twice each year in every province, so that all the bishops, gathered together in one place, may investigate such questions; and if some have unquestionably offended their bishop, and it is proved before all that they have been reasonably excommunicated, this shall be made known to everyone by the council, for as long as the bishop wishes to deliver a more humane sentence concerning them.

[Col. 0761A]

The councils are to be held as follows: one before Lent, so that, when every hostile feeling has been cut away, a pure offering may be presented to God; and the second around the autumn season.

[Note: [Col. 0761C] The same manuscript reads: “so that they may be held twice in each year”; read: “so that they may be held.”]

[Col. 0761B] 498

### Concerning the *principatus* (“authority” or “jurisdiction”) of the Roman Church and the bishops of other cities

### VI.

It is an ancient custom that the bishop of the city of Rome should have *principatum* (“authority” or “jurisdiction”), so that he may govern the suburban regions and his entire province with care.

[Note: [Col. 0761C] Cardinal Deusdedit cites this canon in two versions in book I, no. 1, of his collection, contained in Vatican manuscript 3833: first from the Prisca version, then from that of Dionysius Exiguus. He therefore found the Prisca version in the libraries of the Roman Church. He reads the opening words as follows: “It has been established by ancient custom that the bishop of the city of Rome,” etc. Sirmond, in his *Censura Anonymi de regionibus et Ecclesiis suburbicariis*, transcribing this canon from our Vatican manuscript, has the text as here, and replaced only *principatum* with *primatum*. But we read *principatum*, as does Deusdedit, both in Vatican 1342 and in Barberini 2888 of the same collection.]

As for what is in Egypt, the bishop of Alexandria shall have care of all. Likewise around Antioch, and in the other provinces, let their own privileges be preserved for the metropolitan Churches.

It is altogether clear that if anyone establishes a bishop without the decision of the one who is established in the metropolis, the holy and great council has judged that he is not a bishop.

But if, after a common and reasonable election, two or three oppose it because of personal enmities, the judgment of the majority shall prevail, since custom and ancient tradition have prevailed at Jerusalem.

[Note: [Col. 0761D] Justinian reads “his own.” We preferred “its own” on the authority of our Vatican and Barberini codices and of another used by Deusdedit. Later, in place of *serventur* (“are preserved”), codex Barberini 2888 reads *reserventur* (“are reserved”).]

[Note: [Col. 0761D] Justinian inserts *eum* (“him”); we deleted it with our Vatican manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0761D] Dionysius more correctly reads “their own enmities.”]

[Note: [Col. 0761C] Although the following words are joined to this canon not only in Justinian’s manuscript but also in our Vatican and Barberini codices, they do not belong to this canon but to the beginning of the following one, where they are repeated. Hence in the Barberini manuscript a mark is placed at the word *quia* to indicate that these words should be deleted.]

### Concerning the honor of the bishop of Jerusalem

### VII.

Since custom and ancient tradition have prevailed, the bishop who is in Aelia—that is, in Jerusalem—is to be honored and to have the honor proper to his rank, while the dignity of the metropolitan remains.

[Note: [Col. 0762C] Justinian reads: “the honor according to his rank.” Our Vatican codex is better.]

### Concerning those called Cathari

### VIII.

Concerning those who call themselves Cathari—that is, “the Pure”: if any of them comes to the catholic Church, it has pleased the holy and great council that he remain in the clergy through the laying on of the hands of the priests.

[Note: [Col. 0762C] Thus our codex, from the Greek Καθαρούς (“Cathari”). Justinian reads “Catharae.”]

Above all, it must be clear that he professes that he consents to and follows the doctrines of the catholic and apostolic Church: that is, that he communicates also with those who have married a second time and with those who have fallen during persecution, concerning whom a period and a definite day have been established, and that in all things he follows what pleases the catholic Church.

[Note: [Col. 0762C] Justinian reads: “This above all must be observed: that they profess what they believe and follow the catholic and apostolic doctrines.” We preferred the reading of our Vatican manuscript.]

Wherever they may be, whether in fortresses, villages, or cities, they may obtain pardon; but those who have been ordained shall remain in the clergy and in the same status.

[Note: [Col. 0762D] Justinian reads: “Whatever bishops or presbyters of the catholic Church may approach.” Our codex’s reading seemed more consistent with the judgment of the Nicene Fathers. Isidore’s interpretation makes the meaning clearer: “But if a bishop or presbyter of the catholic Church is the one to whom some of these come.”]

But when they come to the bishops or presbyters of the catholic Church, it is clear that the bishop of the Church shall retain the dignity of the episcopate, while the one called a bishop among those who call themselves Pure shall have the honor of the presbyterate in the catholic Church—unless perhaps it pleases the bishop that he enjoy his own honor.

[Note: [Col. 0762D] We supplied the particle *vero* (“but”) from our codex.]

[Col. 0762B]

But if this does not please him, a place must be provided where he may be either a chorepiscopus or a presbyter, so that he may plainly remain altogether in the clergy, and so that two bishops do not appear to exist in one city.

### Concerning the ordination of bishops and presbyters

[Note: [Col. 0762D] The same codex reads: “Concerning the ordination of presbyters.” It then has “presbyters or bishops were advanced.” The Greek text, like the other versions, says nothing here about bishops; therefore the words “or bishops” are recognized as an addition. Immediately afterward the same codex deletes “afterward.”]

### IX.

If some have been advanced to the episcopate or presbyterate without examination, and afterward, when questioned, have confessed their offenses or have been convicted by others, and, in addition, people moved by the confessions have rashly laid hands upon them without order or discipline, the canon does not accept such men; but the catholic and apostolic Church defends what is irreproachable.

### Concerning those who denied the faith during persecution

### X.

Whoever have been ordained through ignorance from among those who had fallen, or through the concealment of those who ordained them, this does not prejudice the ecclesiastical canon; for when they are discovered, they are deposed.

[Note: [Col. 0762D] Our codex reads: “let them be deposed and expelled.”]

[Col. 0762C] 500

### Concerning those who transgressed without necessity

### XI.

Those who transgressed without the confiscation of their property, or danger, or some such circumstance as occurred under the tyranny of Licinius, it has pleased this holy council—although they are unworthy of the mercy of God—nevertheless to show mercy to them.

[Note: [Col. 0762D] Justinian’s manuscript adds in the title: “or apart from the confiscation of their property, or dangers, or something of this kind, which occurred under the tyranny of Diocletian.” The canon begins: “It has pleased this holy council, although they are also unworthy of God’s mercy, nevertheless,” etc. We restored the text belonging to the canon from our codex and corrected several errors from the same source. Wherever we have twice corrected *quotquot* (“as many as”), the authority is that codex, while Justinian reads *quodquod*.]

Therefore, as many as have performed worthy penance shall be among the hearers for three years; they shall lie prostrate for seven years; and for two years they shall communicate with the people in prayers without the Eucharist.

But those who were called to grace and confessed, initially showing their first impulses by casting off their military belts, but afterward returned to their own vomit—for some even gave money and many gifts to restore themselves to military service—shall lie prostrate for ten years after the period of three years among the hearers.

[Col. 0763A]

In all these cases, their intention and penance must be examined. For all those who demonstrate, through fear and tears, perseverance, and good works of conversion, in deed and not in pretense, and who complete the appointed period among the hearers, shall unquestionably communicate in prayer; afterward the bishop may grant them the aid of humaneness.

[Note: [Col. 0763D] Thus the same codex. Justinian incorrectly reads *quia* (“because”).]

[Note: [Col. 0763D] The same codex reads: “Those who were called to grace and confessed, displaying their first impulses by throwing off their belts.”]

[Note: [Col. 0763D] Justinian reads: “and money to him.” We corrected this with our codex.]

[Note: [Col. 0763B] Read “conversion” rather than “conduct.”]

[Note: [Col. 0763D] The Vatican codex reads: “in prayers.”]

But those who have undergone the process indiscriminately or negligently, and have thought that merely their entry into the Church was sufficient for conversion, shall complete the entire period.

[Note: [Col. 0763D] Read “their entry” rather than “entry.”]

### Concerning reconciliation to be granted to the dying

### XII.

The ancient and canonical law shall be preserved for them, and now, if anyone is expected to die, he shall not be deprived of viaticum at his final moment.

[Note: [Col. 0763D] Justinian’s manuscript reads “the catholic law.” We preferred our codex’s reading.]

But if someone, having despaired of life, receives the Eucharist he has merited, and, after receiving the offering, returns again to life, he shall be among those who communicate only in prayers.

In every case, when anyone who is dying asks that grace be granted to him, the bishop shall give him the offering after examination.

[Note: [Col. 0764D] Justinian adds “to him”; the word is redundant, and we removed it with our manuscript.]

[Col. 0754C] 501

### Concerning catechumens who have fallen

### XIII.

Concerning catechumens who have fallen: it has pleased the holy and great council that they hear only the Scriptures for three years; afterward they shall communicate in prayer with the catechumens.

[Note: [Col. 0764D] The Vatican codex adds: “and that no one migrate to another city,” for it joins this canon with the following one.]

### Concerning clerics, that they not pass from one city to another

[The supplied source ends here.]

### XIV. On preventing clerics from moving from one city to another

Because of the frequent disturbances and seditions that have occurred, it was decided that the practice contrary to the canon must be abolished in every way: if persons are found in certain regions moving from city to city, neither a bishop, nor a presbyter, nor a deacon may do so. If anyone, after the decree of the holy and great council, should attempt anything of this kind or apply himself to such an enterprise, such an undertaking shall be utterly invalidated, and he shall be restored to the Church in which he was ordained bishop, presbyter, or deacon. [Col. 0763D–0764A]

### On not receiving clerics belonging to another Church

XV. If any presbyters, deacons, or others who have been enrolled among the clergy easily expose themselves to danger, keeping neither the fear of God before their eyes nor the ecclesiastical canon in mind, and depart from their Church, [Note: [Col. 0764D] Justinian’s text adds “from their Churches,” and in the margin: “Read: from their Churches.” We have followed our manuscript, which after a few words has *oportet* (“it is necessary”) where Justinian’s text has *debere* (“ought”).] they are in no way to be received into another Church; rather, every compulsion should be imposed upon them to return to their own Churches. But if they persist in their obstinacy, they ought to be excommunicated.

### On ordaining no one who belongs to another

XVI. If anyone should dare to do this through deception or contumacy—namely, to seize for himself someone who belongs to another and appoint him bishop or presbyter—his ordination shall be void. [Col. 0764B]

### That no cleric may lend money at interest

XVII. Since many of those enrolled among the clergy, pursuing avarice and shameful profits, have forgotten the words of Holy Scripture, “who has not given his money at interest” (Psalm XIV), and, lending money, demand the monthly one-per-cent interest rate (*centesimae*), the holy and great council rightly decreed that if anyone is found, after this decree, receiving interest on such a contract, or conducting such business in any manner, or demanding one half, or devising anything else for the sake of shameful profit, he shall be expelled from the clergy and become alien both to communion and to the ecclesiastical canon. 502

### That deacons must not be above presbyters

XVIII. It has come to the attention of the holy and great council that in certain places and cities deacons administer the Eucharist to bishops and presbyters—something that neither canon nor tradition has handed down—that those who do not have the authority to offer should present the body of Christ to those who offer it. [Note: [Col. 0764D] The Vatican manuscript has “divide it.”] We have also learned that certain deacons, through usurpation and rashness, touch the body of Christ before the presbyters.

Let all these practices therefore be abolished, and let the deacons remain in their former rank, knowing that they are ministers of the bishops and inferior to the presbyters. Let them receive according to their order after the presbyters, with either the bishop or the presbyter giving it to them. [Col. 0764D] They must not even be permitted to sit among the presbyters; for what is done in this way is outside the canon and outside the order. If anyone should refuse to obey after these decrees, he shall be deprived of the diaconal rank. [Note: [Col. 0764D] In the same manuscript: “from the office of the diaconate.”]

[Col. 0765A]

### On the Paulianists

[Note: [Col. 0765B] The Vatican codex joins this canon with the following one and therefore adds to the heading: “and on deaconesses.” Shortly afterward, we have written *refugiunt* (“take refuge”) from the same manuscript; Justinian’s text has the erroneous reading *refugium* (“refuge”).]

XIX. Concerning the Paulianists who take refuge in the catholic and apostolic Church, it has been decreed that they must be rebaptized without exception. If any of them had previously been enrolled among the clergy, then, provided they are found blameless and irreproachable, they are to be ordained into the clerical order by the laying on of the hand of the bishop of the Catholic Church. But if examination finds them less suitable, they ought to be deposed and remain in the order of the laity. The same rule shall likewise be observed concerning their deaconesses and all who belong to the same body. [Note: [Col. 0765B] Justinian’s manuscript reads “their deacons.” We have corrected it in accordance with the same Vatican manuscript, which omits “their.”]

### On deaconesses

XX. We also recall concerning the deaconesses who have been established in the schism that, since they have not been ordained through the laying on of hands, they must be counted altogether among the laity. [Col. 0765B] [Note: [Col. 0765B] Thus our codex. Justinian’s text reads: “who have been established in the schism.”]

### On bending the knee

XXI. Since there are some who bend the knee on the Lord’s Day and during the days of Pentecost, it pleased the holy and great synod that all, in every place, should pray to the Lord standing steadfastly and with one accord. [Note: [Col. 0765B–0766A] Justinian’s text adds: “on the Lord’s Day and on Easter Day until Pentecost.” These words are found neither in our codex, nor in the Greek, nor in the other versions. In the Vatican and Barberini manuscripts four other additional canons are read; we also found them added, by a later hand, to the Nicene canons in the outer margin of the final page of the Verona manuscript 55. They are for the most part compiled or abbreviated from African canons; the second, however, is canon 11 of the Council of Neocaesarea, from Isidore’s version. They are the following, which we present corrected and supplemented in places from the Verona codex.]

### That a slave or a conditional cleric is not to be ordained

It was decreed that if any subdeacon, deacon, presbyter, or bishop should be ordained from among such persons, and, through the negligence of the bishop who performed the ordination, their freedom was not investigated, the master may claim only the person; but the property of the one ordained shall be restored to its master. Nevertheless, the aforementioned cleric alone shall be deposed, even if the master should intercede on his behalf. This must nevertheless be observed: the free man shall serve the Church. And this was read and approved.

### That a presbyter is not to be ordained before the age of thirty

Even if his life is exemplary, he shall wait [Alternative reading: “he shall observe”] until the prescribed time; for the Lord was baptized in his thirtieth year, and then preached. And this was read and approved.

### That presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, and all clerics must not travel without consulting their bishop

It pleased the holy and great council that no presbyter, deacon, subdeacon, or any member of the clergy should travel to any province without consulting his own bishop. [The Vatican manuscript adds: “anywhere.”] This first part of the canon, which repeats the heading, is found only in the Vatican manuscript.

### That a bishop must not leave his own Church unless he has received a letter of transfer from the metropolitan

Nor is a bishop from overseas to be received unless he produces the signed letters of twenty bishops. If he is a Roman, the letter of the metropolitan alone shall suffice. And this was read and approved.

### On the clerical order and conduct

Let readers read until the years of puberty; and, once they have been instructed in the divine Scriptures, let clerics who have been examined be ordained. Clerics must not enter taverns for the purpose of eating or drinking, except when the necessity of travel requires it, while exercising caution [Read: “being cautious”] toward people hostile to the Church. And this was read and approved.

Then this concluding clause is appended:

“The decrees of the Council of Nicaea are concluded.” [Col. 0765D–0766B]

[Note: [Col. 0773C] The Vatican manuscript supplies this heading. The Verona Isidorian divides the provinces and places the heading “Africa” before Caecilianus, “Macedonia” before Alexander, “Dardania” before Dacus, and “Achaea” before the following three bishops.]

### Cities of Africa, Macedonia, Lesser Dardania, and Achaea

Caecilianus of Carthage. Alexander of Thessalonica. Dacus of Macedonia. [Col. 0773B] Pistus of Athens. Marcus [Note: [Col. 0773C] The Verona Isidorian has *Boeae*, which comes closer to the reading of the Vienna codex, *Euboensis*. The Vallicellian has *Boaias*.] of Boeae. Strategius of Ephesus.

[Note: [Col. 0773C] The Vatican codex here also describes the provinces together. The Verona manuscript assigns each province to its bishop: Thessaly to Claudianus, and so forth. In the Vatican, *Thessalonicae* is written erroneously for *Thessaliae*.]

### Other cities of Thessaly, Dardania, Pannonia, Gaul, Gothia, and the Bosporus

Claudianus of Thessaly. Budius of Stobi. Domnus of Pannonia. Nicasius [Note: [Col. 0773C] The Verona Isidorian has *Bodiensis*, incorrectly. The Vienna manuscript has the better *Diviensis* for *Diensis*.] of Dova. Theophilus of Gothia. [Note: [Col. 0773D] The Verona manuscript has *Barboricathmus*. The Vatican Regina has *Cadamnus*. The Vienna manuscript has *Cadcemnus*. The Vallicellian has *Camdos*.] Cathirius of the Bosporus.

513 [Note: [Col. 0773D] Henry Justel, son of Christophorus Justel, and William Voellus published only five Sardican canons, one of them mutilated, from the very ancient codex of Christophorus Justel. We explained the reason for this from Stephanus Baluzius in the preceding Treatise, part II, chapter 2, § 3. Since we found the ancient edition of these canons in Vatican manuscripts 1342 and Lucensis 88, and since their headings and readings almost entirely agree with those published from the Justelian exemplar, we were able to supplement a complete edition of the same canons from these codices. We shall also use Vatican Regina 1997 and, at times, Verona Isidorian 58, for the reason explained in note 1 on chapter 1 of the preceding collection (our col. 371, note m), where the Sardican canons were printed from another edition received by Dionysius. This ancient edition presents the reading of the Sardican canons that is found inserted in the older Latin and Italian collections.]

## THE CHAPTERS OF THE SARDICAN CANONS BEGIN

[Col. 0773C]

I. On bishops who have changed cities and are therefore to be deprived even of lay communion.

II. On bishops who seek another see with rash and precipitate presumption.

III. That bishops of the same province should hear disputes between bishops. But if the condemned party appeals to the Roman pontiff, what he decides must be observed.

IV. That no bishop should usurp the see of an accused bishop.

V. When bishops may ordain in another province.

VI. On not making bishops in villages and small cities.

VII. [Note: [Col. 0774C] The Vatican manuscript has “On handling.” We corrected it from the Lucensis codex, which has only this heading: “On reconsidering the synod.” The fuller heading of Vatican 1342 is also supported by Vatican Regina 1997, from which we wrote *fuerit* for the erroneous *fuerunt* in the cited Vatican manuscript.] On reconsidering a provincial synod through the representatives of the bishop of the city of Rome, if an appeal has been made.

VIII. When bishops, and in what cases, ought to go to the imperial court.

IX. Deacons to be sent to the imperial court.

X. On orphans and widows.

XI. That bishops who have been appointed in the chancery [*in canali*] have authority to examine bishops going to the imperial court.

[Col. 0774B]

XII. On those who are ignorant of the synod’s decrees.

XIII. On not quickly making laymen bishops.

XIV. How long a bishop should remain abroad in another city, except in a grave necessity.

XV. That a bishop may not be absent for several weeks. [Note: [Col. 0774C] Thus, together with Justel’s manuscript, the Lucensis codex has *episcopus*; it alone has *episcopis*. Vatican 1342 adds “unless for three weeks.”]

514 XVI. On excommunicated clerics not being received by others. [Note: [Col. 0774D] We retained the word “clerics,” following the Justelian exemplar, although it is omitted in our Vatican and Lucensis codices. In Justel’s manuscript, as in the Lucensis, this is canon 15, and the following canons are likewise each one number lower in both, because canon 4 was omitted by skipping in the Lucensis; we conjecture that the same happened in Justel’s exemplar.]

XVII. [Note: [Col. 0774D] Thus the Justelian codex. The Vatican and Lucensis have: “On excommunicated persons being heard …”] On excommunicated persons being heard before neighboring bishops.

XVIII. On not soliciting the clerics of another bishop.

XIX. On not ordaining another bishop’s clerics without the consent of their own bishop.

XX. On clerics who come to Thessalonica.

XXI. On receiving those who flee because of danger and persecution.

## THE SARDICAN CANONS BEGIN

### On bishops who have changed cities and are therefore to be deprived even of lay communion

I. Bishop Osius said: A custom as evil as the pernicious corruption of the facts themselves must be eradicated root and branch, [Col. 0775A] so that a bishop may not be permitted to move from his own city to another city. [Note: [Col. 0775C] The Vatican Regina and Verona Isidorian codices add: “so that no one may be permitted.”]

For the reason why anyone might attempt this is obvious, since no bishop has yet been found in this matter who moved from a larger city to a smaller one. Hence it is apparent that they are inflamed by the heat of avarice, serve ambition, and wish to exercise domination. [Note: [Col. 0775C] The Vatican Regina has: “Almost no one has been found”; and shortly afterward: “that they may have domination.”]

If it pleases everyone that such a pernicious practice should be punished most severely and more strictly, so that one who is such should not even have lay communion—[Note: [Col. 0775C] The Verona Isidorian omits “this” and “so that,” as well as the later “most severely,” and “and thus that.”]—all replied: “It pleases us.”

515 ### On bishops who seek another see with rash and precipitate presumption

II. Bishop Osius said: Even if some such person should prove to be mad or rash, [Note: [Col. 0775C] The Lucensis codex has “who perhaps”; the Vatican Regina, “and perhaps”; the Verona codex, “so that he might perhaps offer the excuse that the people …”] so that he perhaps brings forward such an excuse, asserting that he has received letters from the people, it is nevertheless clear that he could have corrupted a few by reward and payment, [Note: [Col. 0775C] The Vatican Regina reads: “so that those who do not have sincere faith might cry out in the Church as though they themselves were asking for him”; the Verona Isidorian: “since it is clear that a few who did not have sincere faith could be corrupted by reward and payment, so that they might cry out in the Church that they were asking for him.”] so that those who do not possess sincere faith might act through seditious cries in the Churches and make it seem that they themselves were seeking him as bishop.

I judge that these frauds must be entirely removed and condemned, so that such a person, whether bishop or presbyter, who commits these things may not receive even lay communion at the end. [Note: [Col. 0775D] We added “such a person” from the Lucensis manuscript. The words “whether bishop or presbyter” and “who commits these things” are absent from the Verona Isidorian and Vatican Regina manuscripts.]

If this sentence therefore pleases you, give your reply. They answered: “What has been said pleases us.” [Note: [Col. 0775D] The Vatican Regina has: “Does this please everyone? The synod answered: It pleases us.” The Verona Isidorian has: “If this pleases all of you, decree it. They all said: It pleases us.”]

### That bishops of the same province should hear disputes between bishops; but if the condemned party appeals to the Roman pontiff, what he decides must be observed
### III

Bishop Hosius said: “This too must be decreed: that bishops may not pass from one province to another province in which there are bishops, unless perhaps they have been invited by their brothers [read: “unless they have been invited”], lest we seem to close the door of charity.” [Note: [Column 0775D] The Vatican manuscript adds adjiciendum, “to be added.” The Veronese Isidorian reads: “Let this too be decreed.” Shortly afterward it reads: “bishop … is not to pass over … having been invited.” The Vatican Regina reads “exclude.” It adds: “This too must be provided for: if in any province perhaps…” but omits “which God forbid.” The Veronese Isidorian reads “close”: “It must also be provided that if in any province some bishop…” [lacuna].]

“But this alone must be provided for: if in one province, which God forbid, some bishop should have a dispute with a brother bishop, none of them is to summon a bishop from another province to judgment.” [Note: The Vatican Regina reads: “so that neither of the two may summon a bishop from another province. But if…” The Veronese Isidorian reads: “neither of the two is to summon bishops from another province to judgment.” The Lucan manuscript likewise has “bishops”; shortly afterward it deletes the word again.]

“But if a bishop has been judged in some case, and thinks that he has a good cause, and requests that the judgment be reopened, then, if it pleases everyone that we honor the memory of the most holy apostle Peter, let a letter be written either by those who examined the case [Note: [Column 0776C] Vatican 1342 inserts ut, “that”; the Lucan manuscript, together with the Vatican Regina and Veronese Isidorian, more correctly deletes it. The latter two manuscripts subsequently omit judicium, “judgment.” The Veronese Isidorian adds: “or even by other bishops.”] or by the bishops residing in the neighboring province to the bishop of Rome. If he judges that the case ought to be reheard, let it be reheard, and let him appoint judges. But if he determines that the case is such that what has been done should not be disturbed, then whatever the bishop of Rome decrees will be confirmed.” [Note: The Vatican Regina deletes “the bishop of Rome” and thereafter has “let it be decreed.”]

“If this therefore pleases everyone, let it be decreed.”

The synod replied: “It pleases us.”

### That no bishop may usurp the see of an accused bishop

### IV

Bishop Gaudentius said: “If it pleases you, let this be added to the holy and complete judgment which you have pronounced.” [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “plain holiness.” We corrected it from the other manuscripts, the Vatican Regina and the Veronese Isidorian. This canon is absent from the Lucan manuscript.]

“When a bishop has been deposed by the judgment of those bishops who reside in neighboring places, and he has appealed, requesting that his case be heard in the city of Rome, another bishop must absolutely not be ordained to his chair after the appeal of the man who appears to have been deposed.” [Note: The Veronese Isidorian reads: “in the same chair.”]

“This may not be done unless the case has been determined in the judgment of the Roman bishop.”

### When bishops may ordain in another province

### V

Bishop Hosius said: “If it should happen that in a province where there are very many bishops only one bishop happens to remain, and he, through negligence, is unwilling to ordain a bishop…” [Note: The Lucan and Veronese manuscripts read “bishops.” Vatican 1342 reads: “but they, through negligence, are unwilling.” The Vatican Regina omits the following seven words, “but he … a bishop,” apparently by inadvertent skipping because of the repeated word episcopum. Immediately afterward the same Lucan manuscript and the Vatican Regina read: “and the people gather the bishops of the neighboring province.”] “…and the people flee to the bishops of the neighboring province…” [Note: This is how the two Vatican manuscripts and the Lucan manuscript read. The Vatican Regina has: “I think that bishop ought first to be summoned…” [lacuna] “…and it should be shown to him…” [lacuna] “…so that they too may come, and with him…” The Veronese Isidorian reads: “That bishop ought to be summoned…” [lacuna] “…and it should be shown that the people…” [lacuna] “…so that he too may come, and with him…”]

“[Supply: ‘by letters’] that bishop who resides in the same province must first be summoned, and it must be shown to him that the people are asking for a ruler for themselves. It is just that he himself should come and, together with him, ordain a bishop. But if, after being summoned by letter, he remains silent, makes no reply, and dissembles, then the people must be accommodated: the bishops of the neighboring province are to assemble and ordain a bishop for them.”

### On not creating bishops in villages and small cities

### VI

[Note: [Column 0777C] The Vatican Regina reads: “But permission must not be given indiscriminately. For if suddenly some village…” The Veronese Isidorian reads: “But again permission must not be given indiscriminately,” and otherwise agrees with the Vatican Regina.]

“Permission must not be given to ordain a bishop if some village, or a small city for which one presbyter would be sufficient, should wish to request that a bishop be ordained for it…” [Note: The Veronese deletes “to request,” which is preferable.] “…in order thereby to cheapen the name of the episcopate.” [Note: The Vatican Regina and Veronese manuscripts read: “The episcopal name and authority ought not to permit those invited from another province to make a bishop, except in cities which have had bishops, or if there is some city so populous…” The Veronese deletes talis aut, “such or,” and adds: “or place which…”]

“In no way may those who have been invited from another province create a bishop, except either in cities which have always had bishops, or in a city so populous that it deserves to have a bishop.”

[Note: The Veronese Isidorian deletes “If this pleases everyone.”]

“If this pleases everyone.”

The synod replied: “It pleases us.”

### On revising a provincial synod through the vicars of the bishop of the city of Rome when an appeal has been made

### VII

Bishop Hosius said: [Note: The same manuscript adds: “And this was agreed: if a bishop…”]

“It has been agreed that if a bishop is accused, and the bishops of that region have assembled, judged him, and cast him down from his rank; if the man who has been deposed appears to have appealed, has fled to the most blessed bishop of the City…” [Note: The Lucan manuscript adds “of Rome.” The variants of this passage have been carefully reported in note 29 on the Sardican canons, chapter 1, of the preceding collection (above, column 404, note j).] “…and wishes to be heard, then, if he thinks it just that the inquiry be renewed, let him deign to write to the bishops who are in the neighboring and adjoining province, so that they may diligently investigate everything and determine the matter according to the faith of truth.” [Note: The Veronese Isidorian reads: “The Roman bishop should write to those who are in the neighboring and adjoining province. Let them diligently…”]

“But if the man who asks that his case be heard again should move the bishop of the Roman Church by his entreaty, so that he sends a presbyter from his own side, it will be in the bishop’s power…” [Note: The Lucan manuscript deletes “of the bishop.” The Veronese Isidorian reads: “It will also be in his power what he wishes.” Immediately afterward the Vatican Regina reads: “or what he judges.”] “…to decide what he wishes and judges. And if he decrees that men should be sent who, being present with the bishops, may judge…” [Note: The Veronese Isidorian reads: “so that they may also have the authority of the person by whom they were sent; it will be at his discretion…”] “…with the authority of the one by whom they were sent, it will be at his discretion.”

“But if he believes that the provincial bishops are sufficient to bring the case to an end, he will do what he judges by his most prudent counsel.”

### When bishops, and in what cases, ought to go to the imperial court

### VIII

Bishop Hosius said: [Note: The Vatican Regina reads: “Importune persistence, excessive frequency, and unjust petitions.” The Veronese Isidorian reads: “The excessive frequency of our importunity and unjust petitions.”]

“Excessive importunity and frequent unjust petitions have caused us to receive neither as much favor nor as much confidence as we ought, since certain bishops do not cease going to the imperial court, especially the Africans, who, as we have learned, spurn and despise the salutary counsels of our most holy brother and fellow bishop, Gratianus. And they not only fail to bring to the court many different cases of the Church which would be of no benefit…” [Note: The Vatican Regina and the Veronese Isidorian read: “which would not be beneficial”; where the reading should be “they bring,” unless “not only” was written previously.] “…nor do they act as is customary or proper, namely, to assist the poor, widows, and orphans; instead, they also request secular dignities and administrative offices for certain persons.” [Note: The Vatican Regina reads more correctly: “but rather that…” followed by a lacuna.]

“This depravity has long aroused not only murmuring but also scandals. It is honorable for a bishop to offer his intercession to those who are oppressed by some unjust force, or if a widow is afflicted, or an orphan is despoiled…” [Note: The Vatican 1342 and Veronese Isidorian read: “that a bishop should offer…” The Vatican Regina and Lucan manuscripts read: “Bishops should offer…” The Veronese deletes “unjust.” The Lucan and Veronese manuscripts later read: “is afflicted…is despoiled.”] “…provided that in all these matters they have a just cause or petition.” [Note: The Lucan reads: “yet all these things.” The Veronese: “yet these names have a just…” The Vatican Regina: “if nevertheless these names have a just…”]

“If therefore this pleases you, dearest brothers, decree that no bishop may go to the imperial court, unless perhaps those who have been invited or summoned by letters of the most religious emperor.” [Note: The Vatican Regina and Veronese read: “that bishops should not go…” The Vatican 1342 and Lucan manuscripts add “and by affection”; since these words make no sense and are absent from all other collections and from the Greek text, we have deleted them. The Lucan manuscript then reads: “And since.” Shortly afterward the Vatican Regina and Veronese read: “or those who are sinning.”]

“But since it often happens that those who suffer injury flee to the mercy of the Church, and that those who have committed offenses are condemned to exile or to the islands, or certainly receive some other sentence, [Note: The Vatican Regina omits “and therefore” and “through the Church.”] they must be assisted, and without hesitation forgiveness must be sought for them through the Church.”

“If this too pleases you, decree it.”

All replied: “It pleases us, and let it be established.”

### Deacons to be sent to the imperial court

### IX

Bishop Hosius said: “Your prudence must also consider this, since you have decreed that bishops’ importunity should not be corrupted by their going to the imperial court.” [Note: The same manuscript, together with the Veronese Isidorian, reads: “Your prudence must consider this.” Immediately afterward the Vatican Regina reads: “He who decreed that bishops’ impropriety should not be noted by their going to the imperial court.” The Veronese has the text as above, except that it reads “so that bishops’ importunity should not be noted” instead of “so that bishops’ impropriety should not be noted.” Both manuscripts then read: “Therefore whoever…”]

“Whoever, however, has petitions of the kind mentioned above, or has received them, should send them through his deacon, because the person of a minister will not be envied…” [Note: The Veronese Isidorian reads: “because he will be able to report more quickly what he has obtained.”] “…and he will be able to report more quickly what he has obtained.”
