“And this also seems appropriate…” [Note: The same manuscript reads: “that everyone who has petitions should send them to our brothers and fellow bishops who reside in the chief city, that is, the metropolis, and they should send them through their deacons…” [lacuna] “…granting…” The Vatican Regina agrees with the text, except that it reads: “who resides in the chief city, that is, in the metropolis.” We have established the text from the Vatican 1342 and Lucan manuscripts. For “to that brother and fellow bishop of ours,” the Vatican has “to our metropolitan”; the Lucan, “to the metropolitan bishop.” We believe that the name “metropolitan” was inserted later, since the institution and name of metropolitans became established only afterward. The following words in both manuscripts—“who resides in the metropolis”—would otherwise be a pointless explanation after the name “metropolitan” had been explicitly given. It is therefore better that the other manuscripts, the Vatican Regina and Veronese, together with Dionysius and other Latin copies, omit “metropolitan,” just as we observed in the Treatise on Collections, part I, chapter 5, number 4, that this name was absent from the original Latin.]

“…that bishops from every province send petitions to our brother and fellow bishop who resides in the metropolis, so that he may send the petitions through his deacon, supplying letters of recommendation in the same manner to our brothers and fellow bishops who at that time reside in those regions where the fortunate and blessed Augustus governs the republic.” [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads: “and religious.” Later the Vatican Regina and Veronese read: “if any bishop has friends in the palace who desire something”; afterward they omit “through them from the emperor.”]

“But if a bishop has friends in the palace and wishes, provided that the request is honorable, to obtain it from the emperor through them, he is not to be forbidden to make his request through his deacon and to inform those whom he knows can, by kindly intercession, assist him in his absence.” [Note: The Vatican and Lucan manuscripts read incorrectly: “to him that”; we corrected this from the Veronese manuscript. The Vatican Regina agrees with “to those.” The latter two manuscripts, together with the others, more correctly read “kindly intercession.”]

### On orphans and widows

### X

“Those who come to Rome, as has been said, are to hand over the petitions they have to our most holy brother and fellow bishop of the Roman Church…” [Note: The Veronese Isidorian reads: “who has come…has…let him hand over…”] “…so that he himself may first examine whether they are honorable and just, and take care and responsibility for having them brought to the imperial court.”

All replied that the proposal pleased them and was honorable.

Bishop Alypius said: “If they have undertaken the hardships of travel on behalf of orphans, widows, or sufferers who have just causes…” [Note: This is how the Vatican and Lucan manuscripts of the Priscillian edition read. The others delete “for.” The Lucan omits “or sufferers.” The Veronese Isidorian reads: “who have canonical cases.” Later the Vatican Regina deletes “just.”] “…they will have some just reason. But when they chiefly seek things which cannot be free from everyone’s envy and criticism…” [Note: The Vatican Regina and Veronese delete “chiefly.” They read “those” instead of “themselves.”] “…there is no need for them to go to the imperial court.”

### That bishops stationed at the canal have authority to examine bishops going to the imperial court

### XI

Bishop Gaudentius said: [Note: The Vatican 1342 adds “The things which,” incorrectly. We have deleted this with the Lucan manuscript. The Vatican Regina reads: “The things which you have prudently provided, agreeable to the judgment and estimation of all priests and pleasing to God, can retain their force and be regarded as credible among men if fear is joined to this judgment…” The Veronese Isidorian differs slightly: “The things which you have prudently provided, agreeable to the judgment and estimation of all, pleasing to God and to men, can retain their strength…” With these two manuscripts we have corrected placens to placitura, both meaning “pleasing” but representing distinct Latin forms, in the text of the defective Vatican and Lucan manuscripts.]

“It must be prudently provided, by the agreement of all priests, that what is pleasing to God and approved by men should be maintained and confirmed, provided that fear is joined to this decision. For we ourselves know that, very often, because of the imprudence of a few…” [Note: The Lucan, Vatican Regina, and Veronese manuscripts read “shamelessness.” [Column 0780D] The Veronese later reads: “he must know that, once the causes have been stated, he will lose his honor and dignity.”] “…the sacred and religious name of the priesthood has been criticized.”

“If therefore anyone, striving against the judgment of all, should prefer ambition to God, he must also know that he will have to state his reasons and lose his honor and dignity.” [Note: The Vatican Regina and Veronese read: “he will be able to know.” The Vatican Regina later reads: “if he finds that he wants to go to the imperial court, seeking what was stipulated above, if he was invited…” The Veronese reads: “if he finds that he wants to go to the imperial court, let him seek what was stipulated above, lest perhaps he was invited…”]

“This, however, must then be known and carried out: whenever each of us who is stationed at the canal sees a bishop setting out, he must inquire about his journey, examine his reasons, and learn where he is going. If he finds that he wishes to proceed to the imperial court, he must question him according to the condition stated above—whether he has been invited—so that permission to go may be granted.” [Note: Read “he will have to question him.”]

“But if, as your holiness mentioned above, he attempts to go to the imperial court because of desires and ambitions, neither is his letter to be signed nor is he to be received into communion.” [Note: The same two manuscripts read: “he is not to be received.”]

“If this pleases you, it must be confirmed by the judgment of all.”

All replied: “This is honorable, and the regulation pleases us.”

### On those who are unaware of the synod’s decrees

### XII

Bishop Hosius said: “But moderation is also necessary, dearest brothers, lest some who still do not know what has been decreed in the synod suddenly come to the cities which are stationed at the canal. The bishop of that city must admonish and instruct him…” [Note: The Veronese reads: “so that from that place he may send a deacon. Having been admonished…”] “…and from that place he is to send his deacon to the imperial court in his place. He himself, however, after being admonished, must return to his own parish.”

### On not hastily making laymen bishops

### XIII

Bishop Hosius said: “I also consider it necessary that you deliberate most carefully on this: if perhaps a rich man, a legal scholar from the forum, or someone from an administrative office is proposed as bishop…” [Note: The Vatican Regina reads: “from an administrator.” It then deletes, together with the Veronese Isidorian, the words “from office” and “in due order.”] “…he must not be ordained before he has successively discharged the office of lector, the duty of deacon, and the ministry of presbyter…” [Note: The same two manuscripts read: “and thus ascend through each rank to the summit of the episcopate”; afterward, instead of “through these ranks,” they read “through these promotions, which…” The Vatican Regina later reads “will have” instead of “have.”] “…and, if he is worthy, has been advanced through each rank to the honor of the episcopate.”

“For through these ranks, which necessarily require a long period of time, it can be tested what his faith is like…” [Note: The Vatican 1342 reads: “and what his modesty, gravity, and reverence are like.” Later, instead of “found,” the Vatican Regina and Veronese manuscripts prefer “proved”; they then omit “for,” and afterward read: “nor does the discipline of reason permit.”] “…what his modesty, gravity, and reverence are like. And if he is found worthy, let him be honored with the divine priesthood.”

“For it is neither fitting nor permitted by reason or discipline that a bishop, presbyter, or deacon—especially one who is a novice—should be ordained rashly and lightly.” [Note: The Veronese Isidorian, deleting “especially,” reads: “especially since the most blessed apostle, the teacher of the nations, announced that this should not happen, but only those whose life has been tested over a long period.” All replied… The Vatican Regina reads: “since the most blessed apostle…appears to have announced and prohibited this, but only those whose merits a long examination will prove.” Both manuscripts later delete “all.”]

“For the most blessed apostle, the teacher of the nations, appears to have prohibited this from happening; rather, those whose conduct has been examined over a long period are to be chosen, whose merits and life have been proved.”

All replied that all these things pleased them.

### How long a bishop may remain abroad in another city, except in a grave emergency

### XIV

Bishop Hosius said: “You must also decree this: when a bishop comes from one city to another, or from his own province to another province, let him serve ambition rather than devotion…” [Note: The Veronese Isidorian reads: “let him not serve ambition rather than devotion, so that if he wishes to remain in another…” The Vatican Regina reads: “in a foreign city.” Both manuscripts then read: “not being so well instructed.”] “…and wishes to remain for a long time in another city, and it happens that the bishop of that city is not well instructed or sufficiently learned, the newcomer may begin to despise him…” [Note: The Lucan manuscript lacks the words “and frequently,” which the Vatican 1342 supplies along with the other manuscripts. The Veronese reads: “the person,” giving rise to the circumstance that he does not hesitate. The Vatican Regina reads: “the person, because this circumstance will cause him later, by commending himself, both to desire and seize another’s see, and not hesitate to leave the Church assigned to him and pass to another’s.”] “…and frequently to make speeches in order to dishonor and weaken his person, so that because of this opportunity he does not hesitate to leave the Church assigned to him and pass to another’s.”

“Therefore define a period of time, because it is inhuman not to receive a fellow bishop, but it is harmful if he remains too long. Provision must therefore be made that no one may remain longer than our brothers established previously: if a layman had not assembled in the city in which he resides for three Sundays, that is, three weeks, he was to be deprived of communion.” [Note: This passage is corrupt in both manuscripts of the ancient Vatican and Lucan editions, which read “remembered” instead of “remain.” It is better in the Veronese Isidorian and Vatican Regina, which agree with Dionysius and the Greek text: “I remember that at an earlier time our brothers established that if a layman in the city in which he resides…” The reference appears to be to canon 21 of the Council of Elvira.]

“If these provisions have been established concerning laymen…” [Note: The Vatican Regina deletes “how much more.” It then reads: “nor is it fitting that a bishop…be away longer and distress the people.” The Veronese reads: “that a bishop…be away so long from his Church and distress the people.” The Vatican 1342 differs from the text only in reading “or the people”; from the Lucan manuscript we have preferred “so that he may distress the people.”] “…how much more is it neither permitted nor fitting for a bishop, if he has no grave necessity or exceptionally difficult matter, to remain away from his Church for a longer time and distress the people.”

All replied that this pleased them.

### That a bishop may not be absent for several weeks

### XV

Bishop Hosius said: “Since nothing ought to be omitted, there are certain brothers and fellow bishops who do not possess property in the city in which they were ordained bishops…” [Note: The Vatican Regina and Justellian manuscripts preserve the verb “possess,” from which this canon was published up to the words “are known to have estates.” We have retained the verb from the Vatican and Lucan manuscripts of the ancient edition and from the Veronese Isidorian. The latter, together with the Vatican Regina, later reads: “in which they appear to have been established as bishops, or certainly…”] “…or at least have only a small holding there…” [Note: The Justellian manuscript reads “may have.”] “…but are known to have suitable estates elsewhere, or the affections of relatives whom they wish to favor.” [Note: We have written “affections” with the Veronese and Vatican Regina manuscripts; the Lucan has the corrupt “afflictions,” and the Vatican 1342 “afflictions.”]

“Thus far they ought to be permitted to visit their estates and arrange or manage the produce of their labor, but in such a way that after three Sundays, that is, after three weeks, if it is necessary for them to remain, they should stay on their own farms instead. If there is a nearby city in which there is a presbyter, so that they do not appear to spend the Lord’s Day without a church, let them come there, so that their domestic affairs may not suffer loss through their absence…” [Note: The Vatican Regina reads: “and if he does not come frequently to the city in which the bishop resides, he will avoid suspicion of ostentation and ambition.” The Veronese reads: “and by not frequently coming to another city in which there is a bishop, he will incur suspicion of ostentation and ambition.” We have written “may avoid suspicion” with the Lucan manuscript. The Vatican 1342, in the opposite sense, reads “may create suspicion.”] “…and so that, by not frequently going to another city in which a bishop has been established, he may avoid suspicion of ambition and ostentation.” [Read: “may avoid suspicion.”]

All replied that this pleased them.

### On not receiving clerics excommunicated by other bishops

### XVI

Bishop Hosius said: “This too pleases everyone: if either a presbyter, a deacon, or any cleric has been deprived of communion by his bishop and has gone to another bishop, and the bishop to whom he has fled knows that he was cast out by his own bishop, he ought not to grant him communion.” [Note: The Vatican Regina reads “will please”; it then deletes “and” before “to another.” The Lucan, Justellian, and Veronese manuscripts read “has fled” instead of “flees.”]

“If anyone does so, let him know that he will have to give an account of the matter before assembled bishops.” [Note: The Justellian manuscript incorrectly reads: “let him know before the assembled bishop on his behalf.” The Veronese and Vatican Regina read: “let him know that, when the bishops have been summoned, he must give an account…”]”

All replied: “This regulation will preserve peace and maintain concord.”

### On hearing excommunicated persons before neighboring bishops

### XVII

Bishop Hosius said: “I must not conceal what still troubles me. If some bishop, perhaps in anger—which ought not to happen—is quickly and harshly moved against his presbyter or deacon, and wishes to expel him from the Church, provision must be made lest an innocent man be condemned or lose communion.” [Note: The Justellian manuscript omits “and.” The Lucan manuscript and the commonitory of Zosimus read: “or harshly.”]

“And therefore the expelled man must have the power to ask neighboring bishops to hear his case and examine it more carefully, because a hearing must not be denied to one who requests it. The bishop who cast him out, whether justly or unjustly…” [Note: The Justinian manuscript reads “because.” The Veronese reads “who either justly…” The Vatican 1342 and Vatican Regina read: “and either his judgment is proved by the majority or corrected.” The Veronese reads: “so that either his judgment is proved by the majority or corrected.”] “…must patiently accept that the matter be investigated, so that either his rashness may be proved or his judgment corrected.”

“Before everything has been carefully and faithfully examined…” [Note: This is how the Lucan manuscript reads, and the Veronese agrees except that it omits “before the examination,” perhaps more correctly. The Vatican 1342 reads: “until they have been examined, no one should presume, before the examination, to join to communion him who has been separated from communion.” The Vatican Regina reads: “when the matters have been examined, no one should presume to receive one who does not have communion before the examination.” The Justinian manuscript reads: “when the matters have been examined, no one should presume to give communion until he himself receives him…”] “…no other person may presume, before the examination, to receive and admit to communion the man who had been separated from communion.”

“But those who have assembled to hear the case, if they see that the clerics are displaying disdain and arrogance, which is unbecoming for a bishop to endure as injury or insult…” [Note: The Lucan and Veronese manuscripts read “with harsher words.” Only the Justellian manuscript reads: “they ought to be corrected with words, so that they obey…” The Veronese reads: “because just as he ought to show sincere love and charity to the clerics, so also…”] “…let them rebuke them with severe words, so that they obey the bishop when he gives honorable commands. For just as he ought to show sincere love of charity to his ministers, so the ministers ought also to show their bishop unfeigned obedience.”

### On not soliciting another bishop’s clerics

### XVIII

Bishop Januarius said: [Note: This is how the Justellian and Vatican Regina manuscripts read. The other manuscripts have: “This too.” The Vatican 1342 and Veronese Isidorian read “ecclesiastical minister” instead of “cleric.” The Veronese reads: “and ordain him in his own diocese, because disputes commonly arise from such conflicts; and therefore it forbids…” The Vatican Regina has “and therefore” before “because.”]

“Let your holiness also decree that no bishop may solicit a cleric belonging to another city and ordain him in his own parishes.”

All replied: “Since discord commonly arises from such disputes, the judgment of all forbids anyone to dare to do this.”

### On not ordaining another bishop’s clerics without the consent of their own bishop

### XIX

Bishop Hosius said: “We all also decree this: whoever wishes to promote to an ecclesiastical order a minister from another parish without the knowledge or consent of his own bishop…” [Note: The Justellian manuscript reads “province.” The Vatican 1342, Veronese Isidorian, and Vatican Regina read “without consent” instead of “without knowledge.” The Vatican 1342 reads “in ordination.” The Vatican Regina and Veronese read “ordain,” and afterward “has usurped” instead of “has attempted to usurp.”] “…his ordination is not to be valid.”

“Whoever attempts to usurp this power…” [Note: This is how the Justellian and Lucan manuscripts punctuate the sentence. The others have a different punctuation, reading “of the brothers”—namely, “whoever among the brothers…”] “…must both be admonished and corrected by our brothers and fellow bishops.”

### On clerics who come to Thessalonica

[Note: Only Voellus and Justellus published this title. We supplied the remainder from our manuscripts.]

### XX

Bishop Aetius said: “You are not unaware, dearest brothers…” [Note: The Vatican Regina and Veronese Isidorian omit “dearest brothers.”] “…how great and distinguished the city of the Thessalonians is, and that presbyters and deacons often come to it from other regions…” [Note: The same manuscripts read: “often come to it” or, in the Veronese, “to that same city.”] “…and are not content to remain or reside there for a short time…” [Note: In the same manuscripts: “or at least scarcely return after long intervals.”] “…unless they are compelled by force, after long periods, to return to their own places.”

All replied: “The periods which have been established concerning bishops must also be observed with respect to the persons of all clerics.” [Note: The Veronese Isidorian reads: “and concerning their persons.” The Vatican Regina reads: “and must apply to their persons.”]

### On receiving those who flee because of danger and persecution

### XXI

Bishop Hosius said: “At the urging of our brother and fellow bishop Olympius, this too has been approved: if someone has suffered violence and has been unjustly expelled because of doctrine, or Catholic confession, or the defense of the truth…” [Note: The Vatican Regina reads: “expelled on account of discipline and the defense and confession of the Catholic truth.” The Veronese Isidorian agrees, except that it reads “or” in both places instead of “and.” Both manuscripts, together with Dionysius, prefer devotus, “devout,” to devolutus, “driven/cast forth.”] “…and, fleeing danger, comes as an innocent person driven to another city…” [Note: The Vatican Regina adds: “whether he is a bishop, presbyter, or deacon.” The Lucan manuscript reads “will be able” instead of “has been able.” The Vatican Regina and Veronese read “has received”; the latter, after deleting “because,” continues: “for it is harsh not to receive those who suffer persecution. Even generous goodwill…” [lacuna] “…must be shown to them.”] “…he must not be forbidden to remain there for as long as he is able either to return or to receive a remedy for his injury, because it is harsh not to receive one who is suffering persecution; rather, generous goodwill and kindness must be shown to him.”

[527] [Note: This sentence, which appears in our manuscripts—the Vatican 1342, the Lucan manuscript of the ancient edition, and Vallicellian A. 5—as well as in the other Hadrianic collections, is omitted in the Vatican Regina and Veronese Isidorian, where the Sardican canons are joined to the Nicene canons. It is also omitted in the Vatican manuscripts 5845 and Palatine 577, which are purely Dionysian copies. We supplied their closing clause in note 78 (above, column 411, note e) at the beginning of chapter 1 of the preceding collection.]

The entire synod said: “The Catholic Church, spread throughout the whole world, will preserve all the provisions that have been established.”

And those who had assembled subscribed.

Osius of Spain, of Córdoba [Note: [Col. 0785C] This subscription alone was published by Father Mansi from the Lucan manuscript. In Vatican 1342, however, other subscriptions follow, agreeing with the Hadrianic manuscripts and the commonly printed editions of the Councils; these are absent both from the Greek text and from the purely Dionysian copies. They are known to have been copied from another document of the Council of Sardica preserved in Hilary, though the order of the bishops has been changed, and after three bishops subscribed after Hosius—Vincent of Capua, Calepodius of Naples, and Januarius of Benevento—the Fathers of the Council of Sardica were given the title “legates of the holy Roman Church.” Yet other documents make it absolutely certain that Archidamus and Philoxenus, presbyters of the Roman Church, and Leo, a deacon, served as papal legates at that council. The Vatican codex adds one further bishop, absent from Hilary; after the last bishop it concludes: “and the others subscribed.” See the treatise, part I, chapter 7, where more is discussed concerning the number and subscriptions of the Fathers of Sardica.]

## THE CHAPTERS OF THE CANONS OF GANGRA BEGIN

I. Concerning those who abominate marriage. II. Concerning those who abominate meat. III. Concerning slaves who despise their masters. [Note: [Col. 0786C] The same manuscript adds: “under the pretext of faith.”] [Col. 0785B] IV. Concerning married presbyters. V. Concerning those who humble the assemblies of the Church. [Note: [Col. 0786C] The same codex reads: “who despise the Church.”] VI. Concerning those who hold assemblies outside the Church. VII. Concerning the offerings of the Church. [Note: [Col. 0786C] Justellus’s codex adds here, as well as in the title prefixed to the canon: “let no one be permitted to exchange them.” The Vatican Regina manuscript more appropriately omits these words in both places.] VIII. [Note: [Col. 0786C] Justellus: “Concerning what is among the poor,” incorrectly. We corrected it from our manuscript.] Concerning the things bestowed upon the poor. IX. Concerning virginity and abstinence. X. [Note: [Col. 0786C] Our codex reads: “Concerning those who exalt themselves.”] Concerning those who are exalted because of the name of virginity. XI. Concerning those who mock the agapes. XII. Concerning those who glory in a cloak. XIII. [Read: “women”] Concerning women who wear men’s clothing. XIV. Concerning those who withdraw from marriage. [Note: [Col. 0786C] So our codex, both here and below before the canon itself. Justellus’s manuscript agrees in the title of the canon; but here it reads “flee.” Then, in our manuscript: XV. Concerning those who abandon their children. XVI. Concerning children who despise their parents.] XV. Concerning those who abandon their children under the pretext of religion. 528 XVI. Concerning those who, on the pretext of religion, despise [Col. 0785C] their parents. [Col. 0786A] XVII. Concerning women who shave their heads. XVIII. Concerning those who despise the Church’s fasts. XIX. Concerning those who fast on the Lord’s Day. XX. Concerning those who abominate the assemblies of the martyrs.

## THE CANONS OF GANGRA

To the honored lords established in Armenia, the saints and fellow ministers.

Eusebius, Elianus, Eugenius, Olympius, [Note: [Col. 0786C] Justellus: Bythimius. We corrected it from our codex.] Bythinicus, Gregory, [Note: [Col. 0786C] The Vatican Regina codex: Felicitus. “Filetus” is more likely.] Feliculus, Papus, Eulalius, Hypatius, [Note: [Col. 0786C] So our codex, more correctly than Justellus’s “Proeretius.” [Col. 0786D] Immediately afterward, from the same codex, we added Bassus, who is indeed found in the Greek text and in Isidore.] Proeresius, Basil, Bassus, Eugenius, and Heraclius, who assembled in the holy synod in the city of Gangra.

Since the holy synod of bishops was assembled at Gangra [Read: “the holy Church”] of the [Col. 0786B] holy Church [Note: [Col. 0786D] Justellus’s manuscript: “because of certain things which either are necessary or are required for the needs of the Church.” Our codex supplied the correction.] because of certain necessities of the Church, examining certain matters found among the followers of Eustathius to be disordered, [Note: [Col. 0786D] Justellus: “many things altogether necessary were arranged” [read: “wickedly arranged”], “so that they might be removed,” etc. We corrected and supplied what was lacking from our manuscript, which afterward omits “all things.” From the same source we preferred “may have toward God”; Justellus has “might have toward the Lord.”] it resolved that many things had been done altogether improperly and hastened to make everything known to all, so that all the things wrongly done by them might be removed. For because they forbid marriage and say that no one who has entered into a marital union can have hope toward God, many married women, deceived, withdrew from their husbands, and husbands from their wives; [Note: [Col. 0786D] So our codex. Justellus: “so that afterward,” less suitably.] and afterward, when 529 they could not endure it, they committed adultery and for this reason were disgraced.

For women were also found withdrawing [Note: [Col. 0786D] Vatican Regina: “departing.”] from the house of God and from the Church, and, by despising it, appearing to establish their own assemblies, convocations, and teachings against the Church’s doctrine, [Col. 0786C] [Note: [Col. 0786D] The passage is corrupt and cannot be healed with the help of our codex, where one reads: “various and various things against ecclesiastical matters and against the Church, who gathered together foreign garments for common ruin, and gathering the produce of the garments, or ecclesiastical offerings, which from the beginning,” equally corruptly. A new translation from the Greek renders the sense better, volume II of the Councils, col. 425: “to deliver various teachings and other things against the Churches and against what is done in the Church. In addition, despising ordinary clothing, to put on a new garment.”] so that they taught the use of foreign [Read: “clothing”] garments as belonging to the ruin of [Read: “communion”] communion, gathering the produce of the Church and the offerings that had from the beginning been handed over to the Church, taking them for themselves and using them for their own purposes and those of their associates, as though they were acts of holiness [Note: [Col. 0787C] The Vatican Regina codex: “distributed,” perhaps “to distribute.” Immediately afterward Justellus: “withdrawing into a foreign garment.” We corrected it from the same codex.] and religious devotion.

Slaves also withdrew from their masters, and, despising their masters in foreign clothing, and women, contrary to custom, putting on men’s clothing instead of women’s clothing, and judging themselves justified by this. Many women, shaving their heads, [Note: [Col. 0787D] Justellus: “under the pretext.” The sense is entangled in both places. The Greek has: “Many women also, under the pretext of piety, cutting their hair short, remove the adornment of a woman’s hair.”] removed the adornment of their natural feminine hair under the pretext of veneration.

They fasted on the Lord’s Day and despised the freedom of the holy day; they despised the fasts established in the Church. Some of them were afraid to eat meat, and [Read: “in the houses of those whose”] refused to pray in the houses of those whose masters had married, [Col. 0787B] [Note: [Col. 0787D] Justellus: “and where God is worshiped they themselves despise, as well as the offerings.” We preferred the reading of our codex.] and while prayers were being offered they showed contempt. Often they did not receive the offerings made in the houses of those who had married, and [Note: [Col. 0787D] Justellus’s manuscript likewise adds “seeking rest”; we removed it in accordance with our codex, which immediately afterward reads: “and not touching the holy things that are administered by them.”] they rejected presbyters who had married and did not touch the holy sacrament administered by them. They despised the places where the martyrs had been laid, and criticized those who gathered and celebrated there.

They said that the rich, who did not withdraw from all their wealth, had no hope in the Lord, [Note: [Col. 0787D] Vatican Regina: “toward God.”] and many other things that no one could enumerate.

For each of those who 530 had departed from the ecclesiastical canon [Read: “had gone out and had his own laws”] acted as though he had his own laws. Since they no longer wished to communicate [Read: “to share in communion”] [Note: [Col. 0787D] Thus the same codex, more correctly than Justellus’s “nevertheless.” Immediately afterward, for “which he wished,” the same Vatican Regina reads “which he would handle,” with the letter *b* written instead of *u*.] with others, each added whatever he wished, and whatever pleased him, [Note: [Col. 0787B] The words enclosed in parentheses are excessive in the Greek and confuse the sense. Or perhaps the Greek exemplar formerly received something else; for the author of the Isidorian translation also read something more when he inserted these words, as though referring to people without a ruler. Our translator seems to have had this passage in view.] “and, as though he had no governing authority,” to the accusation of the Church and his own injury.

[Note: [Col. 0788C] Justellus’s codex: “For this reason the holy synod, coming to Gangra, condemned them and established boundaries for them, so that those who persisted in their opinions would be outside the Church; but those who repented and anathematized each thing they had wrongly believed would be received.” The reading of our codex is preferable.] For this reason the holy synod, having been convened and having come to Gangra, condemned them and laid down boundaries, declaring them to be outside the Church. But if they should repent and anathematize each of the things they had wrongly said, they are to be received. [Col. 0788A] [Note: [Col. 0788C] Because of the repetition of the words “they are to be received,” the following sentence was omitted by a leap in Justellus’s manuscript. Our codex preserves it.] And for this reason the holy synod set forth each of the things that they [Supply: “ought to anathematize”], and then they are to be received.

But if anyone does not agree with the things that have been established, he is to be struck with an anathema as a heretic, and is to be excommunicated and separated from the Church. Bishops must also preserve these provisions among all who are found to be such. [Note: [Col. 0788D] The Vatican Regina manuscript: “who are found to be such.”]

These canons were set forth after the holy Council of Nicaea at Gangra [Read: “in titles”] [Note: [Col. 0788D] The same codex: “that is, twenty titles.”] in twenty titles.

## Concerning those who abominate marriage

I. [Note: [Col. 0788D] Justellus’s codex: “If anyone inquires about marriage and the things that follow,” etc. The reading of the Vatican Regina manuscript is better.] If anyone abominates marriage, or finds fault with it, and abominates or finds fault with a woman who has slept with her husband, although she is faithful and venerable, or says that such people cannot enter the kingdom, let him be anathema.

## Concerning those who abominate eating meat

II. [Col. 0788B] [Note: [Col. 0788D] We added the words “if anyone” and “but” from our manuscript. Justellus’s codex then inserts after “faith” the word “eating,” incorrectly.] If anyone [Read: “eats, and supply ‘meat’”] eats without blood, idolatry, or what has been strangled, but with reverence and faith, and condemns the person who eats because he has received it, [Read: “and”] saying that he has no hope at all, let him be anathema.

## Concerning slaves who despise their masters

III. If any slave [Note: [Col. 0788D] So our codex. Justellus: “should say that, under the pretext of venerating God, the master’s authority is to be despised.”] teaches that his master is to be despised under the pretext of venerating God, and withdraws from his service, and does not serve his master with obedience and [Read: “with all his eagerness”] all his eagerness, let him be anathema.

## Concerning married presbyters

IV. If anyone doubts [Read: “concerning a presbyter”] about a presbyter who has married, as though it were not proper to receive an offering from him when he consecrates it, let him be anathema. [Note: [Col. 0788D] Justellus: “should be unwilling to receive an offering from him, saying that he ought not to consecrate it.” Our codex suggested the correction, omitting only “to receive.”]

## Concerning those who humble the assemblies of the Church

V. If anyone teaches that the house of God and the assemblies held in it are to be despised, let him be anathema.

## Concerning those who hold assemblies outside the Church

[Note: [Col. 0788D] The Vatican Regina manuscript: “Concerning those who conduct ecclesiastical administrations outside the Church.”]

VI. If anyone holds a separate assembly [Read: “his own”] apart from the Church, and, despising the Church, wishes to act outside it [Col. 0789A] without the consent of the bishop or presbyter, let him be anathema. [Note: [Col. 0788D] Justellus omitted “and.” Vatican Regina deletes “outside.”]

## Concerning the offerings of the Church

VII. If anyone wishes to receive or give outside the Church what is bestowed upon the Church, [Note: [Col. 0789C] Justellus’s codex: “or exchange it without the consent of the Church or the bishop to whom it is entrusted … and not with their knowledge.” The reading of our codex agrees better with the Greek.] without the consent of the bishop or of the person to whom these things have been entrusted, and wishes to do anything without that person’s knowledge, let him be anathema.

## Concerning what is bestowed upon the poor

VIII. [Note: [Col. 0789C] So the Vatican Regina codex. Justellus: “If anyone, giving or receiving from those things that are offered, acts outside the consent of the bishop or of the person appointed to administer mercy to the poor,” etc., less correctly.] If anyone gives or receives from what is offered, without the bishop or the person appointed to dispense mercy to the poor, both the giver and the receiver are to be anathema.

## Concerning virginity and abstinence

532 IX. If some boast of virginity or [Perhaps: “abstinence”] abstinence, and withdraw as though from abominable marriage, [Col. 0789B] and do not preserve this good and holy name of virginity according to the faith, let them be anathema. [Note: [Col. 0789D] The Vatican Regina codex: “of virginity and abstinence.”]

## Concerning those who are exalted because of virginity

X. If anyone who preserves virginity exalts himself above those who marry, let him be anathema. [Note: [Col. 0789D] The same codex: “because of the name of virginity.”]

## Concerning those who mock the agapes of the poor

XI. If anyone despises the agapes held by the faithful, when they summon the brethren for the Lord’s honor, and refuses to share with them, mocking them in order to destroy what is being done, let him be anathema. [Note: [Col. 0789D] The same codex: “they are unwilling.” Immediately afterward we wrote “to destroy” from the same manuscript. Justellus has “and they destroy.”]

## Concerning those who glory in an exalted cloak

XII. If any man, because of the reputation [Read: “of a religious”] of a religious and venerable life, wears a venerable cloak, and thinks that he can be justified by it, and condemns those who reverently wear [Col. 0789C] ordinary clothing [Read: “their customary garment”], and [Read: “and the common garment that is customary”] the common clothing that is customary, let him be anathema. [Note: [Col. 0789D] So our codex. Justellus: “because of the esteem of a venerable religious life.”]

## Concerning women who wear men’s clothing

XIII. If any woman, under the guise [*scemate*] of ascetic dress, takes a man’s garment instead of the customary woman’s garment, let her be anathema.

## Concerning those who withdraw from marriage

XIV. If any woman, abandoning her husband, wishes to withdraw from him as though she abominated marriage, let her be anathema.

[Col. 0790A] ## Concerning those who abandon their children under the pretext of religion

XV. If anyone [Note: [Col. 0789D] Justellus: “abandoning”; and afterward, “for himself” rather than “as far as concerns himself.” We followed our codex.] abandons his children and does not nourish them, but, as far as concerns himself, deserts them under the pretext of asceticism [Note: [Col. 0789D] The Greek word means “continence,” as Dionysius and Isidore translated it.], as though for the worship of God, let him be anathema.

533

## Concerning those who, under the pretext of Christ’s name, despise their parents

XVI. If [Read: “those who”] any of the faithful despise their parents under the pretext of reverence for God [Note: [Col. 0789D] Justellus adds “by ritual.” We deleted it with our codex.], and do not render their parents the due honor by honoring them, since the reverence of God consists in this, let them be anathema.

## Concerning women who shave their heads

XVII. If any woman [Note: [Col. 0789D] The same Vatican Regina manuscript adds “herself,” and afterward reads “shaving.”] thinks that, out of reverence for God, she should shave [Read: “to shave”] her head, which the Lord commanded her to have as a reminder that she is subject to her husband, and breaks the commandment, let her be anathema.

## Concerning those who despise the Church’s fasts

XVIII. Whoever, without bodily necessity, [Note: [Col. 0789D] Vatican Regina: “coming upon it,” incorrectly. Justellus: “overseeing,” that is, “being proud.”] being arrogant, despises the fasts handed down and commonly observed by all in the Church, and says according to his own judgment that they are not perfect, let him be anathema. [Read: “and whatever else is”]

## Concerning those who fast on the Lord’s Day

XIX. If anyone fasts on the Lord’s Day because he considers it an ascetic practice [Note: [Col. 0790C] The Greek word is corrupt; it means “continence,” or “a profession of continence.”] or through dissimulation, let him be anathema. [Note: [Col. 0790C] So our codex. Justellus: “through pretense.”]

## Concerning those who abominate the assemblies of the martyrs

XX. If anyone, being arrogant in his disposition [Note: [Col. 0790C] The Vatican Regina codex: “such a person, coming upon the disposition,” perhaps “being arrogant in such a disposition”; afterward it reads “and [the things] which are done above them.”], abominates the assemblies of the holy martyrs and the celebrations held in them, [Note: [Col. 0790D] The same codex, omitting the verb “has disparaged,” reads “and the memory”; read “and the memories.”] and disparages their memory [Col. 0790C], let him be anathema.

[Note: [Col. 0790D] We have written these words, which were worn away in Justellus’s manuscript; we supplied them from our codex.] We have written these things without departing from those who are in the Church, who observe according to the Scriptures in accordance with the will of God. But those who adopt the practice of asceticism [Read: “are proud or become proud,” and previously “adopt”] and who [Note: [Col. 0790D] The Greek expression means “the practice or profession of continence.”] boast against those who live simply, and exalt themselves against the Scriptures and the ecclesiastical canons, introducing some novelty, are rejected by the catholic and apostolic Church. [Note: [Col. 0790D] Justellus’s edition has punctuation as though something were missing here. Both our codex and the Greek text show that nothing is lacking. Immediately afterward we inserted “modest” from our codex.]

But we admire virginity with humility, and abstinence with modesty; we honor marriage with chaste domestic life, and receive with reverence the duties belonging to it. We accept withdrawal from worldly affairs when accompanied by humility. We do not reject riches when accompanied by justice and mercy, and we praise both the small number [Read: “and the plainness”] and the abundance of garments insofar as they serve the care [Read: “carefulness”] of the body without vanity. But we do not accept processions in garments that are loose and [Note: [Col. 0791C] That is, “broken” or “soft.”] worn out.

We honor the house of our God [Note: [Col. 0791C] So our codex. Justellus: “we have honored the house of our Lord.”], and we receive the sacred and [From the Greek: “beneficial”] healing prayers held in it. We do not confine piety to houses, but honor every place built in the name of God, and we accept the assembly that gathers there [Supply: “that takes place”] as the common Church, for our salvation and the benefit [Read: “usefulness”] of all. [Note: [Col. 0791C] Justellus: “the assembly into it.” Our codex is better; immediately afterward it deletes “of all.”]

We call blessed the great acts of mercy of the brethren that, according to tradition, are performed through the Churches for the poor [Col. 0791B], and we pray that everything handed down according to the divine Scriptures and the traditions of the apostles may be done in the holy Church. Amen. Thus we subscribed, happily.

[Note: [Col. 0791D] Justellus found these canons of the ancient version also in another manuscript, Thuan. 533, now Colbert 784. We found them in three different collections, namely, Vatican Regina 1997, Lucan 88, and Vatican 1342.]

## THE CHAPTERS OF THE CANONS OF ANTIOCH BEGIN

I. Concerning those who contradict the Nicene canons and concerning holy Easter. [Note: [Col. 0791D] The Vatican Regina manuscript: “Concerning those who attempt to act contrary to the Nicene canons,” as the Justellian codex itself has in the title prefixed to the first canon.]

II. Concerning those who separate themselves from [Read: “the Churches”] the Church and hold communion in houses.

III. [Note: [Col. 0791D] The same Vatican Regina codex: “Concerning those who move from other parishes into others”; and IV: “Concerning those who presume after degradation.” VI: “Concerning those who withdraw themselves from the Church.”] Concerning those who invade [Read: “invading”] other parishes.

IV. Concerning excommunicated persons who presume to act. [Read: “those admitted to communion”]

[Col. 0791C] V. Concerning those who secretly separate people from the Church.

VI. Concerning excommunicated clerics or laymen.

VII. Concerning the issuing of letters.

VIII. Concerning the refusal to receive travelers.

IX. Concerning metropolitans.

535 X. Concerning those who are called chorepiscopi.

XI. Concerning those who petition emperors. [Note: [Col. 0791D] The same manuscript: “before the emperor.”]

XII. [Note: [Col. 0791D] The same codex: “Concerning the degraded who prostrate themselves before emperors.” Immediately afterward we wrote “in another” from the same codex. Justellus has “in another matter.”] Concerning those who have been degraded and petition the emperor.

XIII. Concerning bishops who ordain in another parish.

XIV. [Note: [Col. 0791D] The Vatican Regina codex: “Concerning accused bishops.”] If an accused bishop does not submit to judgment among the provincial bishops.

[Col. 0792A] XV. Concerning condemned bishops.

XVI. [Note: [Col. 0791D] This title or chapter, omitted from Justellus’s table, has been restored from our Vatican Regina codex, and agrees with the title prefixed by the same Justellian codex to canon 16. We consequently corrected the numbers of the following chapters by adding one to each.] Concerning wandering bishops.

XVII. [Note: [Col. 0792C] “Concerning those who, summoned to the episcopate, despise it,” in the same Vatican Regina manuscript, and numbered 19; “Concerning the ordination of bishops.” [Col. 0792D]] Concerning those who are called to the episcopate and despise it.

XVIII. Concerning ordination and a bishop who has not been received.

XIX. Concerning bishops to be ordained.

XX. That a synod be held twice a year.

XXI. That no bishop migrate from his own Church.

XXII. [Note: [Col. 0792D] The same codex: “Concerning those who are ordained by other bishops.” XXIII. “That no bishop choose a successor after himself.” XXIV. “Concerning the property of the Church and what belongs to the bishop.” XXV. “That a bishop have authority to govern the affairs of the Church”; read: “to govern them.”] Concerning those who ordain anyone in another parish.

XXIII. That no bishop be permitted [Read: “after himself”] to choose a successor.

XXIV. Concerning the affairs of the Church and what belongs to the bishop.

XXV. And that a bishop have authority to govern the affairs of the Church. [Col. 0792B]

The chapters end.

## THE CONSTITUTIONS OF THE CANONS OF ANTIOCH AT THE DEDICATION BEGIN

The holy and most peaceful synod, [Read: “which”] which was gathered by God at Antioch, sends greetings in the Lord to the saints and fellow ministers who are unanimous throughout the provinces.

The grace and truth of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, visiting the holy [Note: [Col. 0792D] The Thuan manuscript: “of Antioch.”] Church of Antioch and gathering us together in one, in a common and single spirit of peace, [Note: [Col. 0792D] Justellus: “corrects many things in all matters, and corrects them according to the command, so that it seemed good to the holy Fathers.” The less corrupt reading of the Vatican Regina manuscript is preferable.] has corrected many other things. In all matters it seemed good that corrections should be made according to the command of the holy and peaceful Spirit. After extensive deliberation and the judgment of us all, the bishops assembled for this very purpose from various provinces in the city of Antioch, we report these matters to you, believing through the grace and peace of our Lord in the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0792D] Justellus: “that you yourselves, agreeing with him … and cooperating in his works.” The same codex supplied the correction.] that you too will agree through his power, as though present with us and cooperating in prayer—indeed, being more firmly established and working together with the Holy Spirit—agreeing and decreeing these same things with us, and assigning and confirming the things that have seemed good, harmoniously through the Holy Spirit.

For these are the ecclesiastical canons that have been established, [Note: [Col. 0792D] So our same codex. Justellus incorrectly has: “which have been submitted to the holy and most peaceful synod”; and notes that the Thuan manuscript reads “to the synod.”] and that have been submitted by the holy [Col. 0793A] and most peaceful synod assembled at Antioch.

## TWENTY-FIVE TITLES

## Concerning those who attempt things contrary to the Nicene canons and concerning holy Easter

I. All who attempt to abolish the boundaries of the holy and great synod [Note: [Col. 0793C] Justellus: “of the holy and great synod.” We corrected it from the Vatican Regina manuscript. Immediately afterward we wrote “at Nicaea” in accordance with Vatican 1342. Justellus, with his own codex and our Vatican Regina, has “into Nicaea.”] established at Nicaea in the presence of the most devout emperor Constantine, concerning the most sacred festival of the holy Easter of our Lord and Savior, are to be excommunicated and expelled from the holy Church if they persist in standing and contending against the things rightly established.

And if this concerns laymen—if, however, it concerns those who preside over the Church, bishops, presbyters, or deacons—if, after this decree, they presume to act [Note: [Col. 0793D] So Vatican 1342. Other manuscripts less correctly read “have presumed.”] to overthrow the people, disturb the Churches, and celebrate Easter individually with the Jews or before the Jews, the holy synod has judged that such a person is alien both from itself and from the Church. For he brings sin not only upon himself, but also becomes the cause of transgression and destruction for many [Read: “of transgression and destruction”]. [Note: [Col. 0793D] Justellus: “of the authors.” We corrected it from Vatican Regina and Vatican 1342.]

Such people are not only to be removed from the ministry, but those who attempt to communicate with them are also [Note: [Col. 0793D] We inserted the words “and afterward they are to be degraded” from the Vatican Regina manuscript, where, following the Greek, one should finally read “after their degradation.” Immediately afterward Justellus has: “even those who have been degraded are entirely deprived of the honors which the holy canons…” We followed the example of Vatican Regina, which agrees more closely with the Greek.] to be degraded. Even after degradation, they must be deprived of the honors that the holy canon and the priesthood of God bestow.

## Concerning those who turn away from the Church and communicate in houses

II. All who enter the house of God, hear the sacred [Col. 0793C] Scriptures, and do not communicate [Note: [Col. 0793D] Justellus: “even with the people in the holy things.” We preferred the manuscripts of Lucan 88 and Vatican 1342. Another Vatican Regina manuscript reads “the Eucharist.” Other versions have “in prayer.” Immediately afterward we wrote “turn away” in accordance with Vatican; another reads “they will turn away.” Vatican Regina has “but they turn away, they communicate in their own [houses]; concerning them,” omitting the intervening words. Perhaps one should read: “but they turn away from holy communion; concerning them,” for the words “and they communicate in their own houses” are found here neither in the Greek nor in the other versions.] in the Eucharist with the people, but turn away from the holy sacrament because of some disturbance or other, and communicate in their own houses—we have decreed that such people are to be expelled from the Church until, having confessed, they show the fruit of conversion, and, supplicating, may then merit pardon. For it is not permitted to them, once they have been excommunicated, [Col. 0794A] to communicate, nor to gather together and pray in a house, because they do not pray together with the holy Church, nor are those who do not assemble in one Church to be received in another Church [Note: [Col. 0794C] Justellus, with the word order disturbed: “nor to communicate in a house, or to gather together at the same time,” etc. We corrected it in accordance with Vatican Regina. Immediately afterward, for “because,” Vatican 1342 has “who.”].

If anyone is seen among the bishops, presbyters, deacons, or anyone belonging to the Church’s canon, communicating with excommunicated persons, he too is to be excommunicated, because he has attempted to create confusion in the Church’s canon. [Note: [Col. 0794D] Justellus: “who gather in one Church.” We preferred the reading of Vatican Regina, which agrees with the other versions and the Greek.]

## Concerning those who move from one parish into another

III. If any presbyter, deacon, or anyone from the sacred ministry [Read: “from the sacred ministry”] abandons his own parish and goes to another, and, after a considerable delay, attempts to minister for a long time in another parish, he is not to minister there. [Note: [Col. 0794D] Vatican 1342: “in another parish”; read “in another parish.” Dionysius translates: “or, moving entirely into another parish, attempts to remain there for a long time, he shall no longer minister there.”]

If he has perhaps been summoned by his own bishop to return [Note: [Col. 0794D] Vatican Regina: “to the parish.” Immediately afterward Justellus: “has remained in disturbance.” We preferred the reading of our three codices.] to his own parish, and, when rebuked, does not listen, but remains in disturbance, he is altogether to be degraded from the ministry and is to have no hope of returning.

But if another bishop receives him after his degradation for this fault, [Note: [Col. 0794D] So two Vatican codices and the Lucan codex. Justellus and Vatican Regina: “some bishop.”] that bishop too is to be censured by the common synod, because he destroys the Church’s established order. [Note: [Col. 0794D] Justellus: “and he is censured with him by the whole synod.” The Vatican Regina codex, with the error removed, agrees with the Greek and the other versions.]

## Concerning those who, after degradation, presume to perform sacred functions

IV. If any bishop deposed by a synod, or any presbyter or deacon excommunicated by his own bishop, presumes to perform any act of ministry, he has confirmed condemnation against himself.

If he is a bishop, likewise, according to customary practice, he is never permitted in another synod to have hope of restoration, nor is an opportunity for satisfaction granted to him. Moreover, all who communicate with him are rejected by the holy Church, especially if, knowing the sentence passed against those mentioned, they rashly wish to communicate with them. [Read: “It should be read: ‘especially if…’”] [Note: [Col. 0794D] The Lucan and Vatican codices delete “if he is.”]

[Col. 0795A] ## Concerning those who withdraw from the Church and gather secretly

V. If any presbyter or deacon, despising his own bishop, separates himself from the Church and, gathering secretly, [Note: [Col. 0795C] Vatican 1342: “another.” Immediately afterward Lucan: “and calling the bishop.” We wrote “has disobeyed” with our three codices. Justellus: “has heard.” Vatican Regina, after “has disobeyed,” adds “to be subject to him and not to obey”; here, in accordance with the Greek, one should supply “and is unwilling to be subject to him,” etc.] [Read: “establishes an altar and disobeys the bishop who summons him”] establishes an altar and, when the bishop summons him, does not obey, and despises him when he summons him a first and a second time, let him know that he is altogether to be degraded, that he does not deserve a remedy, and that he cannot retain his dignity.

But if he persists in disturbing and resisting the Church, [Note: [Col. 0795D] Justellus and Vatican 1342: “those who are outside their authority are under the bishop’s judgment, as a rebel,” etc. Lucan: “because of holy authority,” etc. The reading received from the Vatican Regina manuscript agrees better with the Greek.] [Supply: “they ought,” and read “which”] the secular authorities are to correct him as a rebel.

539

## Concerning clerics or laymen who are excommunicated

VI. If anyone has been excommunicated by his own bishop, he must not be received into communion by another unless his own bishop first recalls him, or unless he gives satisfaction by appearing before a synod and the synod, having learned his case, receives him, or [Note: [Col. 0795D] The Vatican Regina codex deletes “if.”] unless they pronounce a second sentence concerning him.

It has been established [Note: [Col. 0795D] Justellus: “in the decree, whether he is a layman, presbyter, or deacon, and all…” We followed the Vatican Regina codex. Two other codices, Vatican 1342 and Lucan 88, also support this correction; they read “it has been established in him” and omit “he is.”] that laymen, presbyters, and deacons, [Read: “and everyone”] and all who belong to the canon, are to be judged in this way.

## Concerning the issuing of letters

VII. A presbyter who is in a locality [Read: “in the villages,” from the Greek] is not permitted to issue canonical letters, except that he may send letters to neighboring bishops. Chorepiscopi who are beyond reproach, however, may issue letters of peace.

## Concerning the refusal to receive travelers

VIII. No traveler is to be received without a *formata* [an official letter of recommendation]. [Note: [Col. 0795D] Justellus adds “clerics”; we deleted it, supported by our codices, the Greek text, and the other versions.]

[Col. 0795C] ## Concerning the metropolitans of each province
IX. [Note: So Vat. 1342. In Justellus: “Whom we ought [perhaps: “Us whom we ought”] throughout the province” (Luc., “the Church,” incorrectly), etc. Shortly afterward, instead of *concurrunt*, which our codices prefer, Justellus’s codex incorrectly reads *corruerunt.] We ought to recognize the metropolitans of each province, and they are to preside over the bishops and undertake responsibility for the whole province, since all who have cases come from every direction to the metropolitan church. Therefore it has seemed good that they be placed first in honor, and that the other bishops be permitted to do nothing more without him, [Note: Justellus: “according to the ancient canon remaining from our Fathers.” Our codices supplied the correction. We then wrote *sub ipsa* (“under it”) with manuscripts Vat. Reg.; others read *sub ipso* (“under him”).] according to the ancient canon handed down by our Fathers, except only insofar as concerns each one’s parish and the places belonging to it. [Note: So the manuscript Vat. 1342. In Justellus, *singulus* (“each individual”).]

Each and every bishop is to have the power to govern his own parish according to the dignity of each one and to make provision for the whole place [Read: “for governing his own parish,” with *suae* supplied], [Note: Justellus, with manuscripts Luc. and Vat., reads *qui sunt* (“which are”). Our codex Vat. Reg. reads more correctly *qui est* (“which is”). Subsequently manuscript Luc. has *prospicere* for *perspicere*.] which is under his city, [Col. 0796A] so that he may appoint presbyters and deacons, and examine each matter carefully and with judgment, and [Note: So the manuscript Vat. Reg. In Justellus and other codices, *nihil altius* (“nothing higher”), perhaps *ulterius* (“nothing further”).] do or presume nothing else without the metropolitan bishop; nor is it permitted to him to do so without the counsel of the others in council. [Note: Codex Vat. Reg. incorrectly reads *et nec ipsum sine caeteris consilium* (“and not even he without the others’ counsel”). The more coherent reading, agreeing with the Greek and other versions, is *et nec ipsum*—with the preceding verb *agere* understood—*sine caeterorum consilio* (“nor is it permitted even to him to act without the counsel of the others”).]

### Concerning those who are called chorepiscopi

X. Chorepiscopi who have been appointed in places or villages shall not dare to lay hands for any order. Rather, the holy synod has decreed that they are to observe their proper limits and govern [Read: “the Churches that are subject to them”] those Churches subject to them, and that their care and authority be sufficient. [Note: So codex Vat. Reg. In Justellus: “that the holy synod establish their measure and administration over those subject to them,” etc.] They may appoint subdeacons, exorcists, and readers, and their advancement is to be sufficient; but they shall not presume to ordain a presbyter or deacon without the bishop of the city to whom both he and those places are subject. If anyone attempts to transgress the ordinances of the Fathers, he is to be degraded from the rank he holds, made a former chorepiscopus, and expelled from the city in which he had been. [Note: Codex Luc. reads: “let him be driven out.”]

### Concerning those who petition the emperor

XI. If any bishop, presbyter, or any person from the clergy should go to the emperor without the knowledge or [Read: “letters”] letters of the bishops who are in the province, and especially of the metropolitans, he is to be publicly denounced and expelled not only from communion but also from the dignity he holds, because he has caused trouble for our most pious emperors outside the Church’s proper order. [Note: Justellus inserts *et* (“and”); we have removed it, supported by the manuscript Luc.] But if he has been necessarily summoned to the emperor, he should have permission to go [Supply: “or something similar”], and this with the deliberation and knowledge of the metropolitan bishop of the province and of those who are in it; and he must be furnished with written instructions from them. [Note: Justellus and the manuscript read *aut eorum, qui in ea sunt scribtis* (“or by their writings who are in it”), etc. We preferred the reading of codices Vat. Reg. and Luc.]

### Concerning those degraded who petition the emperor

XII. If a presbyter or deacon degraded by his own bishop, or a bishop degraded by a synod, should trouble the ears of the emperor, they must also be summoned before a universal synod, and those who claim to have justice on their side must state their case before many bishops and await judgment after their examination. [Read: “those who” instead of “what they say.”] [Note: Justellus likewise reads *allegat* (“states his case”); shortly afterward, *et ob eorum discussione et judicium* (“and for their examination and judgment”); and later, at the end of the canon, *spectare* (“to look for”) instead of *expectare* (“to await”). We have corrected the text with codex Vat. Reg. In manuscript Luc., the final reading is *sperare* (“to hope”).]

But if, distressed by this, they trouble the emperor, we decree that this is to receive no pardon whatsoever, that it is to have no place for satisfaction, and that they are not to await any hope of future restoration.

### Concerning bishops who ordain in another’s parish

[Note: Justellus reads “may dare to enter another parish.” Codex Luc. reads more correctly “into another parish.” The reading of manuscript Vat. Reg., which we have adopted, agrees more closely with the Greek.]

XIII. It has been decreed that no bishop may dare to enter from one province into another and ordain anyone in the Churches for advancement in the sacred ministry, even if he brings companions with him, unless he has gone at the written request of the metropolitan and the bishops who are with him, and thus proceeds to ordain. But if, with no one inviting him, he intrudes uninvited upon the ordination of anyone or upon the administration of ecclesiastical affairs not belonging to him, his actions are indeed void, and he himself is not to be received because of his disturbance and irrational presumption, for which judgment must be rendered; thereafter, having been deposed, he is also to be expelled by the holy synod. [Read: “because of his disturbance and irrational presumption.”]

### Concerning bishops who are accused and disagree among the provincial judges

XIV. If a bishop accused of certain crimes is judged, [Note: Justellus reads “and is judged; afterward it happens that concerning him …” We corrected this with manuscript Vat. Reg. The other two codices, Vat. and Luc., read *accusatur et judicatur* (“is accused and is judged”). Vat. Reg. and Luc. subsequently omit *inter eos* (“among them”).] and afterward it happens that the bishops in the province disagree among themselves concerning him, some asserting that the one judged is innocent [Read: “some asserting him innocent,”] and others that he is guilty, then, for the complete examination of the case, the holy synod has decreed that the metropolitan bishop should summon bishops from a neighboring province and certain colleagues, so that they may judge and resolve the uncertainty, and through them confirm, together with the provincial bishops, whatever seems right to them. [Note: The following passage is absent from Justellus’s codex. We supplied it from our manuscripts; at the end, Vat. 1342 reads: “whatever seems right to them.”]

### Concerning condemned bishops

XV. If a bishop accused of certain crimes is judged by all the bishops in the province, so that all unanimously pronounce one sentence against him, he is in no way to be judged by others; rather, the sentence given by the provincial bishops is to remain firm and unanimous. [Read: “and in such a way that.”] [Note: So codex Luc., agreeing with the Greek. Vat. 1342 incorrectly reads *ab alios* (“by others”). Justellus has *ab alio* (“by another”).]

### Concerning bishops without a see

[Note: Vat. 1342 adds *venire* (“to come”).]

XVI. If any bishop, abandoning his own Church while without a see, should seize another’s see without a complete synod, he is to be considered altogether deposed, even if it should happen that the entire people whom he has secretly appropriated desire him. The synod has judged that a synod is complete especially where the metropolitan presides. [Read: “that it is a complete synod.”] [Note: Justellus inserts *qui* (“who”); we removed it with manuscript Vat. Reg., which shortly afterward reads *jactaverit Ecclesiam* (“has cast off the Church”) and *adripuerit sedem* (“has seized the see”). Manuscript Luc. omits *et*.]

### Concerning those called to the episcopate who refuse

XVII. If a bishop who has been ordained is unwilling to preside over the people [Note: We supplied *populo* (“over the people”) from manuscript Vat. Reg.], and, refusing to undertake the ministries, does not consent to go to the Church entrusted to him [Note: We preferred *non* (“not”) to *nec* (“nor”), with manuscript Luc.], he is to be excluded from communion until he accepts it under compulsion, or until the complete synod of the bishops in the province makes a final disposition concerning him. [Note: So codex Vat. Reg., in agreement with the Greek and other versions. Justellus reads *correptus* (“having been corrected”). Subsequently, three of our codices read *episcopi* (“of the bishop”) instead of *episcoporum* (“of the bishops”).]

### Concerning a bishop who has been ordained but not received

XVIII. If a bishop has been ordained but does not go to the parish in which he was ordained, not through his own fault but because the people prevent him, or because of some other fault not committed by him, we decree that he is to retain only the dignity and ministry, provided that he is not seen to have cause in the affairs of that Church in which he was ordained [the wording is textually awkward]. Rather, he must await the provincial synod’s disposition concerning him. [Note: So two of our codices, Vat. Reg. and Luc. Justellus reads *spectare* (“to look for”).]

### Concerning the ordination of bishops

XIX. A bishop is not to be ordained without the synod or presence of the metropolitan of the province, because, when he is present, it is better, and with him all the bishops within the province will be present [Supply: “will be present”]; they too ought to request him by letter. If all attend, so much the better; but if not, it is necessary that at least the greater number be present, with the others consenting by their letters [Read: “with the others consenting”]. Thus the ordination must take place with the consent of the majority, whether by their presence or by their election. But if it is carried out otherwise than has been prescribed, the ordination is invalid. If it is carried out according to the prescribed canon and some oppose it through personal preference, they shall in no way be able to overturn the election of the majority. [The final words are redundant.]

### That a synod be held twice a year

XX. Because of ecclesiastical needs and the settlement of complaints, the holy synod has judged it very good [Read: “the holy synod has judged it very good”; our codices read this, whereas Justellus has “that the settlement of complaints be held.”] that councils of bishops be held in each province twice a year. [Note: Justellus adds “by letters”; our codices, supported by the Greek, omit it.] [That is, twice a year.] Once, after the third week of the feast of Easter, so that the synod may be celebrated in the fourth week at Pentecost, and so that the metropolitan bishops of the provinces may be reminded [Read: “admonished”; manuscript Vat. Reg. has this reading, while Justellus reads *congregari* (“to assemble”) after *post* and lacks “the fourth week”]. The second synod is to be held on the Ides of October, which is the tenth day of Hyperberetaeus. At that synod, presbyters, deacons, and all who have suffered injury are to present their petitions and obtain judgment from the synod. It is never permitted for some to hold a synod among themselves without those who hold the metropolitan cities in trust. [Read: “without them,” referring to those who have entrusted metropolitan cities.] [Note: Justellus reads “who possess the established metropolitan cities.” We corrected this from the same manuscript, Vat. Reg.]

### That no bishop migrate from his own Church

XXI. A bishop is not permitted to pass from one parish to another, neither of his own will, nor under compulsion from the people, nor forced by certain bishops. He ought to remain in the Church in which he was ordained by the Lord at the beginning and not transfer himself, just as a ruling concerning this matter was issued long ago. [Note: The verb *oportere* (“ought”) is supplied by manuscripts Luc. and Vat. Shortly afterward we added a passage on this matter from manuscript Vat. Reg.]

### Concerning those ordained by bishops from other parishes

XXII. A bishop must not intrude into another’s city, which is not subject to him, nor into places that do not belong to him, [Note: The following nine words, absent from Justellus’s manuscript, have been supplied from our codices.] nor for the ordination of anyone, nor consecrate a presbyter or deacon in places belonging to another bishop [Note: Justellus reads *alieni episcopis*; Luc. and Vat., *alieni episcopi*. We corrected the text with Vat. Reg.], unless perhaps he has been requested to do so with the consent of the proper bishop. If anyone attempts this, the laying-on of hands for his ordination is to be invalid [Read: “let it be,” or supply: “it ought to be invalid,” as in the following canon], and he himself is to suffer condemnation from the synod, because he ought not to ordain what he cannot claim as his own. [Note: The words “from the synod,” approved by the Greek text, have been inserted from manuscript Vat. Reg.]

### That no bishop choose his successor

XXIII. [Note: The same codex reads: “that it is not permitted for a bishop to restore—read: appoint—a colleague as his successor in place of himself at the end of his life.”] No bishop is permitted to appoint for himself a successor at the end of his life. If anything of this kind has been done, his ordination ought to be invalid. [Note: Justellus, together with manuscripts Vat. and Luc., inserts *electio vel* (“or election”); we removed it with codex Vat. Reg., in agreement with the Greek text and other versions.]

The ecclesiastical arrangement is to be established and observed in no other way than with the synod and judgment of the bishops, so that, after the departure of the one who has fallen asleep, they may have the authority to ordain the one who is worthy. [Note: Justellus, together with the two aforementioned manuscripts, inserts *aut* (“or”), and after *episcoporum* adds “and especially the election of the clergy”; he also places *eligere* (“to elect”) before *ordinare* (“to ordain”), etc. We removed these words on the authority of codex Vat. Reg., since they are absent from the Greek and other versions. Justellus omits *eum* (“him”); manuscripts Vat. and Luc. supplied it.]

### Concerning the property of the Church and what belongs to the bishop

XXIV. [Note: Justellus reads: “What belongs to the Church, and let them diligently take care that it be preserved as it ought, together with the goods,” etc. We corrected the text with manuscript Vat. Reg.] Whatever belongs to the Church must be preserved most carefully and diligently, as is fitting, with a good conscience and fear [Read: “and faith”] of faith, knowing that these things belong to the Lord, who sees all things. The bishop, who has been entrusted with the people [Note: The same manuscript, Vat. Reg., reads *et animare*; *et animas* (“and the souls”) is better.] and with everything gathered within the Church, must administer these things with judgment and authority.

What belongs to the Church is to be established and certain, with the knowledge of the presbyters and deacons; they must know everything and be ignorant of nothing that belongs to the Church [Note: The word *Ecclesiae* (“of the Church”) is supplied from our codices], so that, when the bishop departs from this world, knowing what belongs to the Church, they do not allow its property to perish through negligence. [Note: So our codices. Justellus reads *patientur* (“they will suffer”), and shortly afterward “and their own property”; we removed this with manuscript Vat. Reg.] Nor should the bishop’s own property be attacked on account of ecclesiastical affairs.

For it is just and pleasing to God and human beings that the bishop leave his own property to whomever he wishes. Nevertheless, he must preserve what belongs to the Church during his lifetime [Read: “must preserve it”] and must not allow the Church to suffer any loss. Nor should the bishop, under pretext of the Church, be prescribed [Read: “be dispossessed,”] and the heirs belonging to him fall into lawsuits, so that after his death they themselves may not revile him with insults. [Read: “so that they themselves may not detract from him with insults.”] [Note: Vat. Reg. reads: “nor may the bishop’s property be prescribed on the pretext of the Church.” Justellus reads: “nor may the property be prescribed on the occasion of the Church.” We removed the word *res* (“property”) with manuscript Luc.]

### That the bishop have authority to administer the Church’s property

XXV. The bishop is to have the administration of the Church’s property, so that he may receive with all reverence and fear of God everyone who seeks it, and provide what is necessary for its needs [Note: Justellus reads *et quae* (“and what”); we corrected it with manuscripts Vat. Reg. and Luc. Shortly afterward the same Justellus reads “so that there may be no impediment”; we removed this on the authority of codices Vat. and Luc.], as well as the necessities of the brothers who are received by him [with “for their necessities” understood], so that no one may be deprived through any obstacle or pretext, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Having food and clothing, with these we are content” (1 Timothy 6:8).

But if this is not sufficient, and he converts the Church’s property [Note: We inserted the preposition *in* (“into”) with all our ancient books] to his own private and domestic needs, and handles the Church’s revenues and the produce of its possessions not with the knowledge of the presbyters and deacons but [The following *cum* (“with”) is redundant] with his household and relatives, or with brothers or sons, giving them authority so that through them certain Church property may secretly be harmed [Read: “so that definite property may be damaged”], then, having been convicted, he is to be subject to the provincial synod.

But if the bishop, or the presbyters who are with him, are otherwise accused [Note: Justellus, Vat., and Luc. read “by those who are with him.” We corrected this with manuscript Vat. Reg.], on the ground that, from fields or from some other property of the Church, they appropriate for themselves what belongs to the Church and oppress the poor, then accusation and reproach are to be brought against the accounts of those who have administered it in this way; through correction, they are to obtain their due before the holy synod. [Note: This interpretation is very difficult. From the Greek it should be corrected approximately as follows: “But accusation and reproach are to be brought against the account—or rather the word—and against those who administer this matter in such a way; they too are to obtain correction before the holy synod,” that is, to attain it, with the holy synod approving what is fitting, as the Greek text has it.]

And they subscribed.

[Note: Codex Vat. Reg. adds “with the encouragement of an appeal.” After the words “and they subscribed,” which indicate the end of the canons, the same manuscript adds another canon, as follows: “That the bishop not administer oaths in a charge of adultery. XXVI. If any bishop should wish to administer oaths in a charge of adultery, which is not permitted, so that a priest may be found an accomplice in this wickedness, let it be ordered that whoever presumes to do this lose his own rank.”]

Reg. reads *Tharcudamantos*; Luc. and Vat., *Tharcudamantus*. Up to this point the order is identical in all copies; thereafter it differs. Reg. reads *Siricus*.] Siricius, Hisichius, Manicius, Moses, [Note: Codex Vat. 1342 reads *Agapitus*.] Agapius, [Note: Manuscript Luc. reads *Theodorus*.] Theodotus, [Note: Vat. Reg. reads *Mosimus*.] Mocimus, [Note: The same manuscript reads *Eustacius*; Luc. reads *Eustasius*. We have restored *subscribentes* (“subscribing”) with our codices. Justellus reads *scribentes* (“writing”).] Eustatius.

We, the subscribers, have enacted these things. Amen.

The Council of Antioch ends.

IV. [Note: Codex Vat. 548 XXI. Concerning [Read: “the accusers of”] the accusers of bishops.
