## THE COUNCIL OF CHALCEDON BEGINS

In the five-hundredth year, under the most pious emperor Marcian.

They judged that the statutes established by the holy Fathers in each of the synods should henceforth possess validity, saying:

Compare what we have discussed more fully on this matter in the Treatise, part I, chapter 2.] THE TITLES OF THE CANONS OF CONSTANTINOPLE BEGIN.

THE CANONS BEGIN.

[Note: [Col. 0807D] Since this annotation is found not only in the Justellian manuscript but also in our manuscripts Vatican Regina and Vatican 1342, which received these canons from the ancient version, there can be no doubt that it derives from the author of the ancient version. It plainly contains an error: at the beginning it speaks of the Council of the 150 Fathers of Constantinople, by whom the following canons were issued; afterward, however, it assigns to this synod—which was in fact held under Theodosius the Great—the time of the emperor Marcian and other circumstances belonging to the Council of Chalcedon. Two further signs of the Council of Chalcedon are detected below. First, after the final Constantinopolitan canon concerning Maximus the Cynic, another canon concerning the primacy of the Church of Constantinople is described; this was issued not by the Constantinopolitan Fathers but by the Fathers of Chalcedon. Second, after the subscription of Nectarius [Col. 0808B] three legates of the Apostolic See are inserted, who were present at Chalcedon [Col. 0808C] but did not accept the canon established there for the Church of Constantinople; rather, they openly opposed it. This appears to have been done by some Greek in order to lend authority to the canon establishing the prerogatives of the see of Constantinople. The Latins, especially the Italians, who were most strongly opposed to approving that prerogative, can in no way be believed to have been the authors of this imposture. The translator of the ancient version, whatever he found in his Greek exemplar, rendered it into Latin. Justellus, moreover, published in the margin from the Thuaneus manuscript another, more authentic annotation: “These canons were brought forward by 150 bishops assembled together at Constantinople, whom the emperor Theodosius, of illustrious memory, father of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, summoned when Blessed Nectarius, after Maximus had been condemned, received the office of bishop of the Church of Constantinople.”] These canons were set forth by 150 bishops [Read: assembled] assembled together at Constantinople, when Blessed Nectarius was ordained bishop, in the consulship of our most devout and Christ-loving emperor, Flavius Marcianus Augustus. [Note: [Col. 0808C] The Vatican Regina manuscript has “the fourth day before the Kalends of November”; this date (29 October) corresponds to the usual Action 16 of the Council of Chalcedon, where the canon concerning the primacy of the Church of Constantinople [Col. 0808D] was appended at the end and was enacted.] On the third day before the Kalends of November, by the grace of God and by the decree of the most devout and faithful emperors, together with the holy synod, 554 [Col. 0808B] in the basilica of the holy and victorious martyr Euphemia, who aided them by her prayers. The holy synod said:

I. We decree that the faith of the holy Fathers, the 318 who assembled at Nicaea in Bithynia, must not be transgressed [Note: [Col. 0808D] Justellus’s manuscript adds the preposition “in”; we deleted it with the Vatican Regina and Lucca manuscripts.] but must remain firm and authoritative.

Let every heresy be anathema.

II. That is, of the Eunomians [Note: [Col. 0808D] Justellus’s manuscript has “of the dissimilar.” We deleted “in” with Vatican 1342 and the Thuaneus manuscript, which Justellus himself cites. The Lucca manuscript also deletes “similar.” Vatican Regina likewise omits “Arians.” From the Greek it should be rendered “that is, of the Anomoeans and Arians.”] similar to the Arians, [Note: [Col. 0808D] The Lucca manuscript omits “Eudoxians”; instead, the Thuaneus manuscript has “Macedonians.”] Eudoxians, and Semi-Arians opposed to the Holy Spirit [Read: opposed], and of Sabellius and the Marcellians [Note: [Col. 0808D] The Thuaneus and Lucca manuscripts have “Photinians.” In the Greek and the other versions both names occur: “Photinians and Apollinarians.”], and [Read: Apollinarians] Apollinarians.

What pertains to Egypt, Antioch, and Constantinople.

III. No one is to enter beyond the boundaries [Note: [Col. 0808D] Thus the Lucca manuscript and the Vatican manuscript used by Justellus: “not to intrude.”] of another, [Col. 0809A] nor create confusion among the Churches; but the canons are to be observed according to their provisions.

The bishop of Alexandria is to govern what belongs to Egypt, while preserving the primacy of the Church of Antioch established in the Nicene [Note: [Col. 0809C] Only the Justellian manuscript omits the word “canons”; we inserted it with the others.] canons. The bishops responsible for the government of Asia are to govern only the dioceses that belong to Asia; those who are in Pontus, only those of Pontus; and those who are in Thrace, only those of Thrace.

Bishops who have not been summoned are not to enter another’s diocese to ordain or for any other ecclesiastical administration, while what has been written and established concerning dioceses in the canon is preserved; and the synod of each province is to govern according to what was established at Nicaea.

The Churches of God among the barbarian nations [Col. 0809B] must likewise be governed according to the custom handed down by the Fathers. The bishop of Constantinople is to have the primacy of honor after the bishop of Rome, [Note: [Col. 0809C] The better reading is found in the Thuaneus and Lucca manuscripts: “because that city itself is younger than Rome.”] because we judge it to be a younger Rome.

Concerning Maximus the Cynic, and against his wicked acts and the shrines he established at Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0809C] The Vatican Regina and Lucca manuscripts have “which were made”; Vatican 1342 has “which he committed at Constantinople.”]

IV. It was resolved in every respect that neither Maximus was or is to be considered a bishop, nor those whom he ordained in any clerical rank; and whatever was done by them is to be considered invalid.

Concerning the primacy [Note: [Col. 0809D] The Thuaneus and Lucca manuscripts add “of the holy.” This canon is the well-known canon 28 of the Council of Chalcedon, not of Constantinople. On this matter see notes 5 and 6 (above, col. 807, note g, and col. 808, note h). Therefore, in the margin of the Thuaneus manuscript, now Coustant’s Colbertinus, the following annotation is written in the same hand as the entire manuscript, as Coustant himself notes in the preface to vol. I of The Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, p. 84: “From this point onward the head of the illustrious holy Church is absent”; that is, the following canon is absent from the other codices of the holy Churches. In reality, this canon of Chalcedon was placed after the Constantinopolitan canons in the Greek manuscript used by the author of the ancient version, rather than among the Chalcedonian canons, because, having been established separately in the final session, it rests entirely upon the third Constantinopolitan canon.] of the Church of Constantinople.

The holy synod said: Having everywhere submitted to the decrees of the holy Fathers, and recognizing the canon now read, that of the 150 most reverend bishops who assembled in this imperial city, we have judged the following concerning the primacy of the holy Church of Constantinople, the younger Rome: because the holy Fathers granted the primacy to the see of great Rome on the grounds that it was the reigning city, so now we too, confirming what was established by the venerable 150, grant primacy to younger Rome, reasonably judging that the city honored by imperial rule and senate should also possess the firmness of primacy according to great Rome, and that in ecclesiastical matters it should be as magnificent as Rome and [Note: [Col. 0809C] Thus our Vatican Regina and Lucca manuscripts, together with the Thuaneus manuscript cited by Coustant. Justellus’s manuscript has “according to”; this is incorrect.] be regarded as second after it.

And the metropolitans are to have jurisdiction over Pontus, Asia, and Thrace [Note: [Col. 0810C] Only Justellus’s manuscript lacks the verb “have”; shortly afterward it has “among the barbarians” instead of “in the barbarian regions.”]. The bishops who are in the barbarian regions are also to have their dioceses ordained by the aforementioned see [Note: [Col. 0810D] The Lucca manuscript more correctly deletes the words “dioceses for them,” which appear neither in the Greek nor in the other versions.]. And [Read: each metropolitan, with the bishops of the provinces, is to ordain the bishops of the aforementioned dioceses] each metropolitan is to ordain the bishops of the aforementioned dioceses together with the bishops of the provinces, as the divine canons have decreed.

The laying on of hands, as stated above, must be performed by the metropolitan bishops; but the election is to be made according to custom and referred to them.

And they subscribed.

[Col. 0817]

THE MOST ANCIENT LATIN TRANSLATION OF THE NICENE CANONS, now published for the first time from the Vatican Regina manuscript 1997.

NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING COLLECTION.

[Col. 0815]

We append to the ancient edition of the canons the oldest unpublished Latin version of the Nicene canons, which we found in the Vatican manuscript Regina 1997. In this manuscript, the remaining canons of the Greek councils were taken from the ancient translation. Only the Nicene canons present a hitherto unknown alternative version, which seems to have been received—being older than the ancient translation—in the Theatine Church, to which that codex once belonged. At first, indeed, we suspected that this was the version used by the Roman Church, to which the Theatine Church was subject. Why, however, we abandoned this suspicion, you will understand from the preceding treatise, Part II, chapter 2, § 1, no. 2 and following. We have observed that the author of the Quesnellian collection, which we reprint, derived several things from this version when setting out the Nicene canons; see note 1 on the Nicene canons of that collection.

The Sardican canons, joined to the Nicene canons and inscribed under the title of the Nicene canons, are likewise presented in the same Vatican Regina codex. Here we append only the Nicene canons, since only these, having been rendered into Latin, exhibit a new translation. The Sardican canons, being copied there from the original Latin—as we have noted elsewhere—agree with the received text, except for several variant readings, which we carefully recorded from the same manuscript in the notes to the Sardican canons of the ancient edition.

A table of the canons precedes the Nicene canons in the same manuscript, with this heading: “Here begin the chapters of the Council of Nicaea.” There are forty-six chapters, because the Sardican chapters are included among them without distinction. This division of the chapters and canons must be attributed to the compiler’s discretion. The first two chapters designate the material prefixed to the canons. Hence the first Nicene canon is marked with the number three, the second with four, and so on. The final Nicene canon, concerning not bending the knee on Sunday and from Easter to Pentecost, is omitted, just as it is omitted in the collection we edited from Quesnell.

As for the Sardican canons, two are joined into one—namely, numbers 29 and 30 of the Quesnellian collection. Since that collection assigns only one chapter to the prefatory section beginning “When they had assembled,” while the Nicene Creed—which in our codex is divided into two chapters—is likewise combined into one, the same total number of forty-six canons ultimately results in both places when the two Sardican canons of the cited collection are joined. This preliminary notice will suffice. We now present the version itself. Although it is disorderly and obscure, as nearly all ancient versions prove to be, many errors must nevertheless be attributed to the incompetence and negligence of the copyist.

### 567. HERE BEGINS THE CREED

[Col. 0817A]

**Amen** of the Council of Nicaea.

**I.** When the holy and great council had assembled, etc., as is found above in the Nicene canons of the ancient edition.

**II.** We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible, and in one Lord Jesus Christ, our Lord, born from the Father, the only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father, etc.—as above in chapter 1 of the Quesnellian collection.

### Those who mutilate themselves or make themselves eunuchs are not to be admitted to the clergy at all

**III.** If anyone should fall into illness—[read: “fall ill”]—and, necessity compelling, should be operated on by physicians, or should be made a eunuch by his masters or by barbarians, let him remain in the clergy. But if anyone, while healthy, should mutilate himself and be found in the clergy, he ought to be removed from his position, and thereafter no one of this kind ought to be admitted. As is clear concerning such persons, if anyone has dared to mutilate himself, let him be removed. Thus, if some have been castrated either by barbarians or by their masters, we judge that, if their conduct has been tested, they are to be admitted to the clergy.

### Neophytes are not to be ordained either bishops or presbyters

**IV.** Many things, whether necessity compelled them or whether people otherwise forced them—[read: “with people compelling them”]—have been done against ecclesiastical discipline and rule: for example, that certain people, suddenly coming from pagan conduct to belief, after being catechized for a short time, should immediately be compelled to approach the spiritual washing, and that many, immediately after baptism, should be compelled to enter the episcopate or presbyterate. It has seemed good that nothing of this kind should thereafter be committed or done. Time must test the catechumen, and after baptism he must be proved by many trials. For the apostolic Scripture plainly says: “Not a neophyte, lest, being puffed up, he fall into the judgment of the devil.” If, however, such a person previously committed some offense, let the same person be accused by two or three witnesses and be deprived of his position.

### Punishment of those who act against the canons

**V.** If anyone should act contrary to these provisions, resisting this great and holy council and placing himself in danger, he shall be deprived of the clergy.

[Col. 0818A]

### Concerning the women whom they call *synectae* [read: *syneisactae*]

**VI.** Whatever women live with bishops, presbyters, or deacons, whether widows or virgins, this holy and great council has judged that none of them should presume that this is permitted or lawful for them—especially those established in the clergy—unless perhaps the woman is a sister, or a close female relative—[read: “or these”]—that is, persons alone who escape suspicion. Other persons, however, are to be avoided, since they create the greatest suspicion.

### Bishops are to be ordained by the bishops of the same province

**VII.** A bishop ought to be ordained by all the bishops who are in the province under whose jurisdiction the matter is conducted. But if this is extremely difficult, or urgent necessity arises, or the length of the journey makes it impossible, a bishop must nevertheless be appointed in the presence of three bishops, with the consent of those who are absent, whose ordination is to be carried out by letter as though they were present.

### The authority of the metropolitan

**VIII.** Let the one who appears to be established in the larger city of the province—that is, in the metropolis—have authority over the matter. [Read: “Let the one in the province have authority,” with the verb understood.]

### Those excommunicated by their bishops

**IX.** In the case of those who have been excommunicated, whether they belong to the clergy or to the laity, the sentence of the bishops in the province must prevail: those excommunicated by some must not be received by others. They must, however, be questioned, lest they have been excommunicated by the bishops on account of contention, hostility, or some other resentment. [Note: The following words belong to the beginning of the next canon.] Thus, so that an appropriate inquiry may be made concerning everything—

### A synod is to be held twice each year in every province

**X.** It has been decided that two councils should be held each year in every province, so that all the bishops of the entire province may assemble and all these matters may be examined together. Those who are clearly found to have offended or wronged their bishop, or certainly to have committed a serious offense, are to be regarded as excommunicated until, with the consent of all, or with the approval of their bishop, a more humane sentence concerning them is pronounced.

One council is to be held before the [read from the Greek *tessarakoste*, that is, Lent] “fortieth day,” so that, after every hostile feeling has been cut away, a pure and undefiled sacrifice may be offered to God. The second is to be held after autumn.

### The primacy of the Roman Church

**XI.** The Roman Church has always held primacy. Egypt also is to retain it, so that the bishop of Alexandria may have authority over all, since this is likewise the custom of the Roman bishop. Similarly, the one established at Antioch, and in the other provinces, shall have primacy over the Churches of the larger cities.

### Invalidating an ordination performed without the metropolitan’s consent

**XII.** Above all, let this be clear: if anyone establishes a bishop without the judgment of the one who is in the metropolis, this holy and great council has judged that he is not a bishop.

[Col. 0819B]

### Following the majority when there is disagreement about an ordination

**XIII.** If the unanimous judgment of all remains firm according to ecclesiastical rule, but two or three, moved by resentment, oppose it through contention, the judgment of the majority shall prevail.

### The honor of the bishop of Jerusalem

**XIV.** Since custom and ancient tradition have established that the bishop who is in the Church of [read: “Aelia,”] that is, Jerusalem, is to be honored, let him have the honor appropriate to his rank, while the dignity of the metropolitan remains intact.

### How those called “Pure” are to be received

**XV.** Concerning those who call themselves Cathars—that is, “Pure”—if anyone comes to the Catholic Church, this holy and great council has decided that, through the laying on of hands, he is to remain in the clergy of the Catholic Church.

Above all, let this be clear: they must agree in everything with the traditions of the holy Catholic Church—namely, that they are to communicate with those who have entered second marriages, and with those who fell during the persecution, concerning whom periods and years [the times of penance being understood] have been established. They must therefore follow everything that the holy Catholic and apostolic Church has decreed.

Accordingly, if some of them, whether in villages or in cities, are found alone as bishops or presbyters, they will remain in the same rank after being reordained by a bishop of the Catholic Church.

[Note: These words, “reordained by a bishop of the Catholic Church,” occur neither in the Greek nor in the ancient and Dionysian versions. Our translator interpreted the Greek word used at the beginning of the canon, *cheirothetoumenous*, which was rendered in Latin as “through the laying on of hands,” as referring to reordination, and added these words from his own judgment as an explanation, just as the author of the translation called Isidorian had also done. We have shown elsewhere that the council understood this word in another sense: see note 1 on Quesnell’s Observations on Letter 167 of St. Leo to Rusticus of Narbonne, volume II—our volume I, column 1491, note h.]

But the one who among those who call themselves Pure has borne the name of bishop shall have the honor of presbyter in the Catholic Church. If this is not acceptable to him, a place shall be provided for him in the parish, so that two bishops may not appear to exist in one city.

### Those ordained without examination

**XVI.** If some have been made presbyters without inquiry, or, when questioned, have confessed their offenses, and after their confession people, moved outside proper order and discipline, rashly laid hands upon them, the canon and ecclesiastical discipline do not receive such men; for the Catholic Church vindicates what is irreproachable.

[Read: “Concerning the reception through penance of those who have fallen and been ordained.”]

### The reception through penance of those who have transgressed

**XVII.** If some have been ordained from among those who fell, whether through ignorance or because those who ordained them concealed the matter, this does not prejudice the ecclesiastical rule: once known and exposed, they shall be deposed.

### The reception through penance of those who transgressed

**XVIII.** Concerning those who transgressed without any force, with no one compelling them, without loss of property and without any danger—as happened in the recent times of the tyrant Licinius—the holy council has decided that, although they are unworthy of God’s mercy, nevertheless mercy should be shown them.

[Read: “All who.”] Accordingly, all who have performed a fitting penance shall spend three years among the hearers of the word and shall lie prostrate for seven years; for two years they shall communicate without the Eucharist, in the prayers of the people.

### The penance of those who return to secular military service after baptism

**XIX.** Those who were called to grace, confessed the faith, and showed their first zeal by throwing away their military belts, but afterward returned to their vomit—for some even gave money and many gifts in order to serve again—shall lie prostrate for ten years, after three years spent hearing the word.

In all cases there shall be inquiry and examination concerning their satisfaction. For all who, through fear, faith, conduct, tears, perseverance, and good works, have moved God to mercy without acting hypocritically shall, after completing the prescribed time, undoubtedly communicate in prayer; the bishop may also extend to them the assistance of humanity.

But those who have acted more sluggishly or treated themselves more negligently, appearing rarely in the house of God, must complete the prescribed periods.

### Reconciliation to be granted to the dying

**XX.** In the case of those who are at the point of death, the ancient and canonical law shall still be observed. Therefore, if anyone is at the point of death, he shall not be deprived of the final and necessary provision for the journey. But if someone who had been regarded as beyond hope has obtained communion and received the Eucharist, and afterward is found among the living, he shall be admitted only to communion in prayer.

Likewise, concerning all who are at the point of death, the bishop shall, after deliberation, grant the Eucharist to those who repent and request communion.

### Deacons are not to rank above presbyters

**XXI.** It has come to the ears of this holy and great council that in certain places and cities deacons distribute the Eucharist to bishops and presbyters. Neither the canons nor ecclesiastical rule teach this: those who do not have the power to offer are not to distribute the body of Christ to those who offer.

We have also learned that some deacons, through usurpation and presumption, touch the body of Christ before the presbyters. Let all these practices therefore be removed, and let deacons remain in their former rank and measure, knowing that they are ministers of the bishops. Let them receive in due order after the presbyters, from either a bishop or a presbyter.

Nor is it permitted for them to sit among the presbyters, for what is done in this way is outside the canon and outside the order. If anyone thereafter refuses to obey these decrees, he shall also be deprived of the office of the diaconate.

[Col. 0821B]

### Catechumens who have fallen

**XXII.** Concerning catechumens who have fallen, this holy and great council has decided that they should hear the Scriptures for three years; afterward they may participate in the prayer of the catechumens.

### Those who abandon their own Churches and transfer to others

**XXIII.** Because of the frequent disturbances and seditions that arise among the people, it has been decided that this practice, which is contrary to discipline and the canon, must be entirely abolished: if a bishop, presbyter, or deacon is found transferring from one city to another, he shall be removed.

If anyone after the decrees of this holy and great council usurps or approves anything of this kind, it shall be invalid, and consideration shall be given to whether he ought to return to his own parish, in which he was ordained bishop or presbyter.

### Clerics of another Church are not to be received

**XXIV.** [Read: “All who act precipitately and do not possess …”] All who act rashly, whether bishop, presbyter, or deacon, without the fear of God before their eyes and without observing ecclesiastical discipline or rule, and who leave their Churches, where they were established according to the canon, are nowhere to be received in the Church. They must instead be compelled by necessity to return to their own parishes.

If they persist in their obstinacy, they must be excommunicated.

### 572. No one belonging to another bishop is to be ordained

[Col. 0821D]

**XXV.** If anyone dares to act by stealth or obstinacy, so that he appoints as his own a bishop or presbyter who belongs to another—[Note: Here either a jump or error by the translator or copyist has entered the text. The matter concerns a bishop who ordains as a cleric someone belonging to another bishop, not a bishop. The text should read: “If, without the consent of his own bishop, he ordains him in his Church, the ordination shall be invalid,” etc.]—his ordination shall be invalid.

### Clerics who engage in lending at interest

**XXVI.** Since many established in the ecclesiastical order, pursuing greed and shameful profit, have forgotten the holy Scripture that says, “He who has not given his money at interest,” and lenders seek hundredfold returns, the holy and great council has decreed that whoever, after these statutes, is found accepting interest—[read: “or engaging in business in any way, or seeking one-and-a-half-fold returns”]—or conducting some business outside his office, or seeking profit from goods, or devising anything else for the sake of shameful gain, shall be deposed from the clergy and shall be an outsider to the ecclesiastical canon.

[Col. 0822B]

### The Paulianists

**XXVII.** Concerning the Paulianists who flee to the Catholic and apostolic Church, it has been decreed that they must be rebaptized absolutely.

If some of them had previously been established in the clergy and are found to be undefiled and irreproachable, they are to be ordained in the clerical order through the laying on of the hands of a bishop of the Catholic Church. But if, after examination, they are found unfit, they shall be degraded to the order of the laity.

### Deaconesses

**XXVIII.** Likewise, concerning deaconesses and those who appear to be established in the canon, the same provision shall apply. We also remember the deaconesses who have been established in the schism: since they were not ordained through the laying on of hands, they must unquestionably be counted among the laity.

Here the Nicene canons end, with the canon concerning not bending the knee on Sunday, etc., omitted, as it is likewise lacking in the Quesnellian collection; concerning this matter, see what we noted there.

The Sardican canons are then appended in a continuous numerical series without distinction, in the same division found in the cited collection, except that the two canons numbered 29 and 30 there are combined into one here; consequently, the numbering of the canons continues up to XLVI. We indicated the variants of these canons in the notes to the ancient edition.

Finally, a catalogue of the Nicene Fathers is appended to the canons, in the same order as in the Quesnellian collection, where we presented the readings of this codex wherever they differ.

[Col. 0821]

## THE OLD LATIN TRANSLATION OF THE CANONS OF NICAEA, SARDICA, AND CHALCEDON, AND OF OTHER DOCUMENTS RELATING TO THE SYNODS OF NICAEA AND SARDICA

Now published for the first time from the very ancient manuscript codex LV of the Veronese chapter. (C)

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING COLLECTION

### 577. 1.

Socrates, Ecclesiastical History, book I, chapter 20, writing about the Sardican Fathers, says:

“And having confirmed the formula of the Nicene faith, they rejected the term *anomoios*—‘unlike’; but they more clearly promulgated the word *consubstantial*, and they themselves sent letters about this matter in every direction.”

He indicates a statement of faith which, having found it appended to the Sardican Synodical Letter in his copy, he believed to have been issued by the synod itself. Theodoret likewise regarded this statement as genuinely Sardican and consequently inserted the Synodical Letter with this addition into his Ecclesiastical History, book III, chapter 12 (volume IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils, column 1766).

Moreover, the Fathers of Chalcedon cited it as genuine in their address to the emperor Marcian, when they reported that the Sardican Fathers had sent to the Easterners the decree of their judgment concerning the remnants of Arius; shortly before, they had called this decree a decree concerning the faith. For the legitimate Synodical Letter contains a decree concerning persons, whereas the additional exposition alone is a decree concerning the faith.

Finally, Sozomen, book III, chapter 12, not only praises this exposition but also the letter of Hosius and Protogenes to Pope Julius. “Furthermore,” he says, “they themselves—the Sardican Fathers—at that time issued another written statement of faith, longer than the Nicene one but containing the same judgment and differing little from its wording. Finally, Hosius and Protogenes, who at that time held the leading place among the bishops of the West who had assembled at Sardica, perhaps fearing that they might seem to detract from the decrees of the Nicene council, wrote to Julius and testified that they indeed ratified those decrees, but that for the sake of greater clarity they had set out the same judgment at greater length, lest the Arians, abusing the brevity of that written statement, should be given an opportunity to drag the inexperienced in such debates into an absurd interpretation.”

This letter of Hosius and Protogenes, since it concerns the additional exposition, is likewise usually classified among the apocrypha.

### 2.

How it could have happened that this exposition of the faith and these letters of Hosius and Protogenes, which were to be excluded from the genuine Sardican acts—as the Council of Alexandria in 362 explicitly rejected the exposition of the faith—nevertheless not long afterward insinuated themselves as genuine into the writings of such learned authors and even into the works of the Fathers of Chalcedon, we explained in the treatise on Collections, Part I, chapter 6, no. 5.

There we showed that this exposition and these letters had indeed been prepared at Sardica and presented at the council, but had been rejected by it, lest they prejudice the Nicene faith in any way. Nevertheless, after some people later transmitted them in a codex together with other genuine Sardican documents, and copies of this kind gradually multiplied, they could come to appear genuine to the learned writers and Fathers cited above just as much as the other documents.

### 3.

What sort of copies these were had until now been unknown. But now, having found in the very ancient manuscript codex 55 of the Veronese chapter an old collection and version of Sardican documents which, among the genuine Sardican monuments, contains this exposition of the faith together with the letters of Hosius and Protogenes, we suspect that the Greek exemplar from which this version arose was one of those used by the learned writers and Fathers mentioned above. Hence everyone can see how important it is to publish this version, since the Greek text is lacking.

### 4.

What is more, other benefits flow from this edition. From substantial indications we have conjectured in the treatise, Part II, chapter 9, no. 3, that the Greek codex used by the translator belonged, at least originally, to the Alexandrian Church.

This Greek collection, as we have seen, had already been compiled long before Chalcedon. It contained no canons of other Greek synods except those of Nicaea and Sardica; only the Chalcedonian canons were later added. For if the Greek exemplar used by the translator had received other canons, there seems to be no doubt that he would likewise have rendered all of them into Latin.

This teaches us three things:

1. Not all Greek codices of the canons were like the received copies, which add the canons of other councils.

2. The Sardican canons were included in the older Greek exemplars.

3. For this reason they appear to have been included only with the Nicene and Chalcedonian canons: the other synods that issued canons among the Greeks were not general, whereas these three—the Nicene, Sardican, and Chalcedonian—were universally regarded among the Greeks as ecumenical.

We have proved in the cited treatise that the Council of Constantinople was for a long time not regarded as general even among the Greeks. Although the Council of Ephesus was ecumenical in the judgment of everyone, since it enacted no canons relating to general discipline, it had no place in the ancient Greek collections of canons, just as it had no place in the old Greek codex translated into Latin by the authors of the Isidorian, ancient, and Dionysian versions.

Only around the middle of the sixth century did six canons partly derived from the Ephesian Synodical Letter and relating to the Nestorian affair, together with two others excerpted and compiled from acts 6 and 7, begin to be inserted into codices of the canons. These facts confirm the antiquity of our collection.

### 5.

In addition, three important Sardican documents have been preserved for us only through this version and codex: namely, the Synodical Letter to the Mareotic Churches and two letters of St. Athanasius written from the synod.

Although these had previously been published from the same manuscript by the distinguished V. C. Scipione Maffei, they should not be omitted here, where the collection and version themselves are being printed—especially since the subscriptions attached to the two documents have been useful to us in the preceding treatise, where we discussed the number and subscriptions of the Sardican Fathers.

The letter of Hosius and Protogenes also now emerges into the light; until now it had merely been mentioned by Sozomen and had been missing.

Furthermore, although the original Latin of the Sardican canons has been published, no ancient translation from the Greek text had ever appeared. We proved in the treatise that the Greek text was likewise original and differed from the Latin in several places.

Our ancient translation, now brought out of darkness, not only reveals several passages corrupted in the received Greek and supplies emendations by which difficulties arising from that Greek are removed; it also adds one canon which, although found in all the Latin copies, had until now not been found in the Greek ones. Other benefits will be indicated in the notes.

## 581. THE NICENE SYNOD

[Col. 0823A]

[Note: This special mention of Alexander, both in the title and in the following annotation, is found in no other version. It considerably confirms the position which we supported from other Alexandrian documents as well in the treatise, Part II, chapter 9: that the Greek original from which this version was taken belonged to the Alexandrian Church.]

### UNDER ALEXANDER, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA, AND THE EMPEROR CONSTANTINE

After much dissension had arisen for blessed Alexander and his associates over Arius’s evil opinion, the most victorious emperor Constantine wrote to him and to all the bishops, summoning them to meet, gathering a council of all the bishops in the city of Nicaea; and they all assembled on the appointed day.

[Col. 0825A]

### Exposition of the faith held by the holy synod at the metropolitan city of Nicaea in the province of Bithynia, in the consulship of Paulinus and Julianus, illustrious men and consuls, in the year 1036 from Alexander, in the month of July, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July

[Note: Read: “in the six hundred and thirty-sixth year, in the month of June, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July.” See note 2 on the preface prefixed to the Nicene canons in the Quesnellian collection.]

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, born from the Father, the only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father: God from God, light from light, true God from true God, born, not made, *homoousios* with the Father—that is, of the same substance as the Father—through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth; who for us human beings and for our salvation descended, was incarnate, was made human, suffered, rose on the third day, and ascended into the heavens, [Note: A later hand adds in the margin: “He sits at the right hand of the Father.”] from where he will come to judge the living and the dead; and in the Holy Spirit.

But those who [Note: In the same margin: “they say”; and immediately, from another version: “There was a time when he was not; before he was begotten, he was not.”] say, “There was a time when he was not,” and that he was made from things that did not exist, or who say that the Son of God is of another substance, [Note: The margin adds *eretiton* [read: *trepton*], that is, “convertible,” etc.] convertible or changeable, the Catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes.

This is the faith which they first set forth against Arius, who blasphemed and called the Son of God a creature, and against every heresy that raised itself up and rose against the Catholic and apostolic Church. They condemned these heresies together with their authors at the city of Nicaea, [read: “the aforesaid”] the aforesaid 318 bishops having assembled as one body. Their names, together with their provinces and cities, are contained in the copies. [Col. 0825C] But the devoted servants of God took greater care to record the names of the Eastern bishops, because the Westerners had not been involved in the question concerning the heresies to the same extent.

Hosius, bishop of Cordova, said: “I believe as was stated above.” Likewise Avitus and Vincentius, presbyters of the city of Rome, spoke and subscribed.

## HERE BEGINS THE FIRST CANON OF THE NICENE SYNOD

### I. Those who castrate themselves may not come to ordination

If anyone, because of an illness, should perhaps be treated in such a way by physicians, and, when a wound has arisen in those parts, it should be necessary to amputate his testicles, or if anyone is forcibly castrated by barbarians, let him remain in the clergy.

But if someone who is healthy cuts himself off, he ought not to remain in the clergy. For just as it is clear that those who mutilate themselves are excluded, [Note: That is, clearly excluded from the clergy.] so, if some are castrated by barbarians or by their masters, but are found otherwise worthy, let them be admitted to the clergy.

[Col. 0826A]

### II. Whether neophytes are to be admitted to the clergy

[Note: In the margin of the codex: “the newly converted, or inexperienced.”]

[Read: “Since.”] Since many things have often been done either through necessity or under compulsion outside the ecclesiastical canon—for example, that people coming from pagan life should at once approach the faith and, within a short time after receiving baptism, be promoted to the priesthood of the presbyterate or episcopate—it has seemed good that nothing of this kind should henceforth be done.

A longer period is necessary, so that they may be catechized for a greater length of time before they are baptized; and after they have been baptized, they must be tested for a long time. For the apostolic saying is clear: “Not a neophyte, lest, being puffed up, he fall into judgment and the snare of the devil” (1 Tim. 3).

But if, as time proceeds, some sin harmful to the soul is found in such persons, and they are convicted by two or three witnesses, let them withdraw from the clergy. Anyone who acts outside these provisions, as one rashly opposing the great synod, shall himself bear the danger of the clerical state.

### 583. III. Clerics are not to cohabit with women except certain ones

The great synod absolutely rejected and prohibited this: it is not lawful for a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or any cleric whatsoever to live with women, except his mother, sister, close female relative, or aunt, or those persons alone concerning whom no suspicion can arise.

### IV. The appointment of bishops

A bishop ought above all to be ordained by all the bishops who are in the province. But if this is difficult because urgent necessity demands that a priest be appointed, or because of the length of the journey, three bishops must assemble together, while the others who are absent consent by letters to the election; and they shall ordain the one whom they have chosen.

The confirmation of the one ordained in each province is to be reserved to the metropolitan bishop.

### V. Concerning those excommunicated by their bishop

In every province, the synodal sentence concerning those excommunicated, whether from the clergy or from the people, shall prevail, so that those excommunicated by some bishops are not admitted by others.

Nevertheless, the matter must be more carefully investigated and examined, lest someone has been removed from communion through some levity or weakness on the part of his bishop. Thus, so that an appropriate examination of [read: “these”] the causes may be conducted, it has seemed good that a synod be held twice each year in every province, with all the bishops of that province assembled, so that such inquiries may be carried out.

If those accused are clearly discovered to have offended their bishop, they are reasonably to be deprived of communion by all until either all together, or the bishop alone whose cleric or layman has been excommunicated, perhaps pronounces a more merciful sentence concerning him.

One synod is to be held before Lent, so that, every excuse based on the fatigue of travel having been removed, the purest offering may be presented to the Most High; the other is to be held around autumn.

### VI. Concerning the primates

Let the ancient custom be preserved throughout Egypt, Libya, and the Pentapolis, so that the bishop of Alexandria may have authority over them, since a similar custom exists in the city of Rome and likewise at Antioch. Thus, in the other provinces also, let the Churches retain their proper rights.

[Col. 0827B]

Let it be clear to everyone that if anyone is ordained without the judgment of the metropolitan bishop, the great synod has decreed that the person so appointed ought not to be a bishop.

Therefore, if a judgment has been reached reasonably and according to the ecclesiastical canon by the common decision of all—[read: “of the sentence,” and supply “which”]—and two or three oppose it because of their own contentiousness, the judgment of the majority shall prevail.

### 584. VII. Concerning the bishop of Aelia, Jerusalem

[Note: The margin of the codex adds: “that is.”]

Since custom has prevailed, and ancient tradition, that the bishop of Aelia should be honored, let him have his honor, while the dignity of the metropolitan city is preserved.

### VIII. Concerning those called Cathars
## VIII. Concerning Those Called Cathari

Concerning those who call themselves Cathari, if they come to the catholic and apostolic Church, the holy and great synod decreed that hands be laid upon them and that they remain in the clergy. Above all, they must declare in writing that they agree with and follow all the doctrines of the catholic Church; that they will communicate with those who have married twice, with those who fell during the persecution—for whom a period has been established and defined—and with those subject to the other regulations.

Therefore, wherever they are found, whether in villages or in cities, after the laying on of hands of reconciliation, let them remain in the clerical *schemate* [Note: Read *schemate*: this is a Greek word, which other versions render “in the order.”]. Thus, if one of them has been a bishop, he shall have the honor of a presbyter in the catholic Church, unless perhaps the catholic bishop of the place where this is being done prefers to grant him participation only in the name of the episcopate. If he does not wish this, he shall provide a place where the man may be either a chorepiscopus—that is, one who exercises episcopal functions according to custom—or, if it is agreeable, a presbyter, so that he may retain him in the clergy. This is so that two bishops should not appear to exist in one city.

## IX. Concerning Those Promoted to the Presbyterate Without Examination

If any are promoted to the presbyterate without examination, or, after examination, confess their sins, and afterward some people, stirred up and acting without due caution, lay hands on them [Read: “lay his hands upon them”], this canon rejects and does not admit such a man. The catholic Church requires a blameless presbyter.

[Col. 0828A] ## X. Concerning Those Who Denied the Faith During the Persecution and Were Later Promoted to the Clergy

Whoever have been ordained through the ignorance or concealment of those ordaining them, although they had fallen during the persecution, cause no prejudice to the ecclesiastical canon. For when they have been discovered, they are deposed.

## XI. Concerning Those Who Denied the Faith and Are Counted among the Laity

Those who transgressed without any necessity, and without the confiscation of their possessions, or who were without danger, or without any such circumstance as occurred under the tyranny of Licinius, were nevertheless judged by the synod, although unworthy, to be treated humanely. If, therefore, they repent from the heart, those who were baptized and fell shall spend three years among the hearers [Col. 0828B], seven years under discipline [Note: That is, let them remain prostrate under the laying on of hands], and for two years shall not offer the oblations, but shall communicate only in the prayers of the people.

## XII. Concerning Those Who Renounced the World and Then Returned to Secular Life

Whoever were called to grace and made a very great initial effort [Read: “first made a great effort”], or displayed the warmth of faith by laying aside their military belts, but afterward returned to their own vomit by giving money, pouring out their wealth, and offering many advantages in order to resume military service, shall be subject to the hands of the priests for ten years, after, namely, the period of three years [Read: “during which”] that they spent among the hearers.

Throughout all these years it is necessary to examine their will, purpose, and the quality of their repentance. Therefore, those who have made their conversion manifest not merely in appearance but in deed, through fear and tears, repentance, and good works—when the period of three years has been completed [The reading should be: “when the three-year period has been completed”]—may deservedly have common prayers with us to the Lord while among the hearers [Read: “prayers”], so that the bishop may be permitted to consider their case somewhat more humanely. Those, however, who have acted indiscreetly, judging that merely assuming the appearance of entering the Church could suffice for conversion, shall complete the entire appointed period.

## XIII. Concerning Those Who Seek Communion at the Point of Death

Concerning those who are beginning to depart from this world, the synodal and ancient law shall be observed: if anyone, being at the point of death, seeks communion, he must not be deprived of such a viaticum. But if someone, having been despaired of by the physicians [Col. 0828D], receives health after becoming a participant in the oblation or holy communion, and afterward has said [Read: “has lived”], he shall pray only with those who communicate, abstaining himself from communion until he completes the period established by the great synod. When anyone asks for communion at the end of life, however, the bishop ought reasonably to grant it.

## XIV. Concerning Catechumens Who Have Fallen

Concerning catechumens [Supply: “who have fallen”], the great and holy synod decreed that they alone should be hearers for three years, and afterward should pray with the catechumens.

[Col. 0829A] ## XV. That Clerics May Not Transfer or Change Churches

Because of the disturbances and seditions that some frequently stir up, the custom that exists outside the canon was decreed to be entirely cut off. If anyone is found in some region transferring from one city to another with the intention of abandoning his own Church—whether he is a bishop, presbyter, or deacon—he acts unlawfully. If, after this command and definition of the synod, anyone dares to attempt what is forbidden, his undertaking shall unquestionably be annulled [Read: “the undertaking of the one presuming this”], and he shall be restored to his own Church, which he left, in which, that is, he was ordained bishop, presbyter, or deacon.

## XVI. Concerning Those Who Do Not Remain in the Churches in Which They Were Promoted

[Col. 0829B] Whoever, having neither danger nor fear of God before their eyes and knowing nothing of the ecclesiastical canon, depart from their own Church—presbyters, deacons, or others concerning whom the canon provides—must in no way be received by another Church. Rather, they must be compelled by every necessity to return to their own parishes; and if they refuse to return, they must be deprived of communion.

But if anyone dares to promote another Church’s cleric in his own Church without the consent of the brother to whom he belonged, the ordination shall, according to the canons, be invalid [Note: The translator misunderstood the Greek text. It should be rendered not “according to the canons,” but “without the consent of his own bishop, from whom he departed”; that bishop is the one referred to in the canon].

## XVII. Concerning Clerics Who Take Interest

Because many have been found in canonical examination pursuing greed and disgraceful profit, and forgetting the divine saying which [Read: “which says, or concerning which it was said”] says: “He did not give his money at interest” [Col. 0829C]—those who demand hundredths [that is, interest at one percent per month]—the holy and great synod rightly decreed that if anyone is found, after this synodal definition, taking interest or engaging in anything of the sort that appears to be done for the sake of disgraceful profit, he must be deposed from the clergy, since he despises the canonical statutes [Note: Here too it should be rendered: “many who are judged by the canon to have been found,” and at the end of the canon: “he must be deposed from the clergy and be outside the canon.”].

## XVIII. Concerning the Primacy of Presbyters

It has been reported to the holy and greatest synod that in certain places and cities the Eucharist is given to presbyters by deacons. Neither has the canon handed this down, nor does ancient custom permit it: those who do not have the power to offer sacrifice should not give it to those who have been granted the authority to celebrate the Eucharist.

It has also become known that certain deacons even touch the Eucharist before the bishops. Let all these practices therefore be removed, and let the deacons remain within their own measure, knowing that they are indeed ministers of the bishops but are inferior to presbyters. Let them communicate in due order after the presbyters, either when the bishop gives it to them or when the presbyter does so. Deacons must not sit among the elders [Note: That is, among the presbyters], for if these things are done, it is outside the order of the canons [Col. 0830A]. If anyone does not wish to obey these definitions, let him cease ministering.

## XIX. Concerning Those Who Flee from the Teaching of Paul of Samosata [Supply: “to the Church”]

If any of those who belong to Paul of Samosata flee to the catholic Church, it has been decreed that they must in every way be rebaptized. But if some, at an earlier or former time, have been examined among the clergy [Correct: “among those reviewed”] and found blameless, and after baptism have been irreproachable, let them be ordained by the bishop of the catholic Church.

But if the inquiry does not find them unfit [Note: “And” is not redundant and is immediately followed by “a second time”], they must be deposed or rejected a second time. The same applies to deacons. [Note: Something has been omitted by a leap and other material is corrupt. It should be supplied and corrected as follows: “and the same rule shall be observed concerning deaconesses and all who are counted among the clergy.” We have mentioned deaconesses, who are established in the form of deacons; for they are not ordained by the laying on of hands, and in every respect, etc.]

But if they are appointed in the form of deacons—for they are not ordained by the laying on of hands—they must in every way be counted among the laity.

## XX. Concerning Kneeling

Since there are some who kneel on the Lord’s Day and during the days of Pentecost, the holy and great synod decreed that all should pray to the Lord while standing, unanimously and in agreement in every respect.

[Note: This is found in Greek in Socrates, Book I, chapter 19; Theodoret, Book I, chapter 9; and Gelasius of Cyzicus, *History of the Council of Nicaea*, Book II, chapter 33. Our version differs from that of Epiphanius Scholasticus, which is read in the *Tripartite History*, Book II, chapter 12.]

# Letter of the Synod of Nicaea to the Church of Alexandria and to the Bishops of Egypt, Libya, and Pentapolis

The holy and great synod, by the grace of God, to the most beloved brothers of the Church of Alexandria throughout Egypt, Libya, and Pentapolis [Supply: “the bishops”], assembled at the city of Nicaea [Supply: “who”] and constituting the holy and great council: salvation in God.

Since, by the grace of God, the holy and great synod assembled at Nicaea from various and many provinces, with the most pious Emperor Constantine bringing us together [Col. 0830C], it seemed entirely necessary to the sacred council also to send a letter to you, so that you might know what matters were raised, what were debated, and what was approved.

First, the impiety and crime of Arius and his associates were examined in the presence of the most pious Emperor Constantine. With the agreement of all, we decreed that his impious doctrine [Note: Greek *doxan*, which should have been rendered “opinion”] and the wickedly expressed words and ideas with which he blasphemed the Son of God should be anathematized: namely, his assertion that the Son came from nothing, that before he was born he did not exist, that there was a time when he did not exist, that by his own power he was capable of virtue and vice, and that the Son of God was a creature and a created work.

[Col. 0830D] The holy council anathematized all these things [Read: “all these matters”], and it could not endure even to hear the impious doctrine [Read: “opinion”], the savagery, and the accursed words. As for what outcome or end his merits received, perhaps you have heard or will hear, though we do not wish to seem to insult a man who suffered the disgrace deserved by his sin [Col. 0831A].

His impiety prevailed to such a degree that Theonas of Marmarica and Secundus of Ptolemais also suffered the same fate with him; for they too deserved the same. But since the grace of God freed Egypt, which had been peaceful from the beginning, from that impious doctrine [Read: “opinion”], the blasphemies, and the presumptuous persons who sought to create a separation and heresy, we inform you, most beloved brothers, of what has been established concerning the audacity of Meletius and those ordained by him [Read: “we inform you in every respect”].

It was therefore agreed to deal more humanely with Meletius, the holy council having been moved to greater kindness—for he deserved no leniency according to strict justice—and to allow him to remain in his own city, while granting him no power either to promote or to ordain bishops, or to appear for this purpose in any territories or cities [Col. 0831B]. Those ordained by him, however, having been confirmed by an ordination conducted secretly [Note: Epiphanius’s version more appropriately has “confirmed by a mystical ordination”; see note 14 in Quesnel’s *Observations on Epistle 167 of St. Leo to Rusticus*, vol. II], shall communicate under the following condition: they may indeed retain their positions and administer them, but they shall unquestionably be second to all those who are in the parishes and Churches under our most beloved brother and fellow minister Alexander. They shall not be permitted to ordain whomever they wish, or to propose anyone in another’s name [Read: “or names”], or to do anything at all without the consent of the bishop of the catholic and apostolic Church.

Those who are under Alexander, and who, by the grace of God and your prayers, have been found guilty of no offense but are established blameless in the catholic and apostolic Church, shall have the power to promote, nominate, and choose those worthy of the clergy—in short, to do everything [Read: “to do”] according to ecclesiastical law and order.

If it should happen that some persons rest in the Churches, then only those who have now been received may advance to the honor of the deceased, if anyone appears worthy and the people desire it, with the consent and confirmation of the bishop of the catholic and apostolic Church of Alexandria.

This concession has been made to all the others. It was not approved, however, in the case of Meletius, because of his inherent madness, insolence of character, and rashness, lest any power or authority be granted to a man who would prevail upon them to return to the same insolence [Read: “to retreat or return”]. These are the principal matters concerning Egypt and the holy Church of Alexandria.

[Col. 0832A] If anything else has been brought into regulation or decreed in our presence with our most beloved brother and fellow minister Alexander, he himself, as the master and associate of the acts [Note: The manuscript incorrectly has *ut potest*; “utpote” is preferable. Immediately afterward, *dominus* is preferable according to Epiphanius], will report it as the one who was present and participated in the acts [Note: The manuscript has *actitarum*, incorrectly. We have corrected it to *actorum* and supplied *quae*], which were being conducted at that time [Note: The Greek text and Epiphanius’s version add notice of the decree that Easter should be celebrated unanimously, together with the conclusion of the entire letter. If this omission in our version is not to be attributed to the translator, it must be said that in the Greek manuscript he used only that portion of the letter which particularly concerned the Church of Alexandria had been copied].

[Note: This translation of the canons is from the Greek, whereas other editions found in Latin manuscripts derive from an original Latin text that differed from the original Greek, as we have shown elsewhere (*Treatise*, Part I, chapter 5). The order of these canons is indeed the same as in the Greek, whereas the order is different in the Latin. The same canons are also present in this version as in the Greek, while two Greek canons are absent from the Latin. Finally, this version has the distinctive feature of stating that canon 19, beginning with the word “Januarius,” was found by an ancient translator in a Greek manuscript, although it is not found in any of the Greek copies published to date. If the number of canons in this version increases to twenty-five, this is because one commonly transmitted canon has been arbitrarily divided into three, and another into two.]

# Canons of the Synod of Sardica

## I

Bishop Hosius said: The exceedingly harmful custom that corrupts affairs must be uprooted from its very foundations, so that no bishop may be permitted to transfer from one city to another. The reason for this is obvious, and it is by this means that such men are tempted [Read: “such things”]. For no bishop can ever be found who wishes to be transferred from a larger city to a smaller one. Hence it is evident that such men are consumed by burning ambition [Col. 0832B], and serve pride rather, so that they may appear to possess greater power.

If, therefore, everyone agrees that such conduct must be avoided, I think it should be punished more severely, and that the laity should not have communion with such men.

All the bishops said: It is approved.

## II

Bishop Hosius said: If, however, anyone is found to be insane or rash enough to offer an excuse for such men [Note: More clearly, from the Greek: “asserting that letters were brought by their people”], persistently bringing letters from their people, it is certain that he could have stirred up seditions in the Churches by bribing a few persons with money and payment [The word “him” is redundant], persons who had no sincere faith, as though they were asking that he be made their bishop.

I therefore think that such tricks and devices must likewise be cut off, and that such men should not deserve even lay communion at the end.

If this judgment is approved, respond.

And they said: What has been said is rightly approved.

[Note: In the Greek, canon III is joined with the following two.]

## III

Bishop Hosius said: It is also necessary to add this: no bishop, when another bishop objects, should pass from his own province into another province in which there are bishops [Note: The words “when another bishop objects” do not accurately convey the Greek. It should be rendered: “no bishop should pass from his own province into another province in which there are bishops, unless perhaps he has been called by his brothers”; see the following note], unless perhaps he has been called by his brothers, lest we appear to have closed the doors of affection.

## IV

Provision must likewise be made that, if a bishop in some province has a case against his brother and fellow bishop, no arbiter should be sought from another province.

## V

But if a bishop is condemned in some matter and thinks that he has a firm case, so that the judgment should be renewed, if it pleases your affection, honor the memory of the apostle Peter, and let those who judged [The words enclosed in brackets—“and the canon of the condemned bishop”—are found neither in the Greek nor in any Latin copy and disturb the sense; therefore they should be deleted] write to Julius, bishop of Rome [Note: This passage has been rendered incorrectly. Unless one prefers to read “and by the neighboring bishops of the province”—understanding “let it be written”—as the ancient Latin original and Isidorian editions suggest, rather than the Greek text, it should be corrected as follows: “and by the neighboring bishops of the province, if the judgment ought to be renewed, let it be renewed, and let him himself provide the judges.” But if he cannot prove that his case is such that the judgment should be renewed, a matter once judged must not be dissolved; what has been judged shall remain firm], through the neighboring bishops of the province. If the judgment ought to be renewed, let it be renewed, and he himself shall provide the judge. If he cannot be present there, and his case is such that the judgment should be renewed, what has once been judged must not be dissolved; rather, what has been judged shall remain firm.

[Note: In the Greek, canon IV.]

## VI

Bishop Gaudentius said: If it is approved, it is necessary to add to this judgment, which you have delivered as true and full of charity, that if a bishop has been deposed [According to the Greek: “by judgment”] in the presence of the neighboring bishops, and has said that he has grounds for a defense, no other person should be ordained to his seat until the bishop of Rome, having learned of the matter, has brought it to an end [Read: “have said”].

[Note: Greek, canon V.]

## VII

Bishop Hosius said: Let it be approved that if a bishop has been attacked or accused, and the bishops assembled within his boundaries have removed him from his rank, and he has appealed to the blessed bishop of the Roman Church [Read: “and”] and has agreed that the matter should be heard and judged that the case ought to be retried, he shall deign to write to the bishops responsible for the province [Read: “the neighboring bishops”], so that they themselves may scrutinize every detail more diligently and carefully and deliver a judgment concerning the case according to the truth.

But if anyone should again ask that his case be heard anew and by this request move the Roman bishop, he shall send presbyters from his own side, so that it may remain within the power of that bishop to decide what he judges appropriate [Note: The Greek is better read: “let him send presbyters from his own side; it shall be within the power of that bishop to do what he judges right”]. If he decides that persons should be sent who will judge together with the bishops, let them have the authority of the one by whom they were sent. This too shall remain within the bishop’s power. If he thinks that the bishops’ inquiry is sufficient for investigating the case and delivering a judgment [Read: “for the bishop to investigate”], let him do what his prudence determines.

[Note: Greek, canon VI.]

## VIII

Bishop Hosius said: If it happens in a province in which several bishops are to be ordained [Note: The word “to be ordained” is found neither in the other Latin copies nor in the commonly transmitted Greek. It does, however, agree with what follows concerning the ordination of bishops and with the phrase “for the ordination of bishops,” which is retained in the commonly transmitted Greek. Moreover, it is evident from our version that the translator had before him a more accurate Greek copy, which removes the difficulty noted by many in the commonly transmitted text. That copy indicates that bishops from a neighboring province are to be summoned for the ordination of a metropolitan, a practice contrary to ecclesiastical custom. Our version, however, shows that the matter concerned not the ordination of a metropolitan but the ordination of bishops, when several bishops of the same province are to be ordained and only one bishop remains in it who can attend their ordination] to be ordained, and one bishop remains, but through some negligence he does not wish to attend or consent to the ordination of the bishops [Supply: “to consent”], while the people assemble and request that a bishop be ordained, the first requirement is that the remaining bishop be warned by letter from the primate bishop of the province, that is, the metropolitan: the people are asking that a shepherd be given to them.

I think that the man who remains ought to wait for the metropolitan to come, and that the ordination should take place with him. But if, although requested by letter, he neither comes nor writes, the will of the people must be satisfied, and bishops from a neighboring province must be summoned for the ordination of the bishops.

## IX

It is not permitted for a bishop simply to be ordained in a village or in some small city for which even one presbyter alone is sufficient. It is not necessary to ordain a bishop there, lest the name and authority of a bishop become contemptible. Rather, as I said above, the bishops of a neighboring province ought to ordain bishops in those cities in which they had previously appeared to be established.

[Col. 0834B] But if a city is found to have a sufficiently large population to seem worthy of having a bishop, let it receive one.

If this pleases everyone [Note: The Greek text, in agreement with the Latin copies, adds: “They all replied: It is approved.” Perhaps the copyist omitted this through the repetition of the word “approved”], let it be done.

[Note: Greek, canon VII.]

## X

Bishop Hosius said: Our importunity and frequent attendance [Read: “and unjust petitions”], even when unjust, have caused us deservedly not to enjoy as much favor and confidence as we ought to have had.

For many bishops do not cease coming to the imperial court, especially the Africans, who, as we have learned, neither accept nor heed the salutary counsels of our most beloved brother and fellow minister, Gratus, but despise them. Thus one man brings to the court many and varied petitions that accomplish nothing for the benefit of the Churches, through which he ought to provide help and assistance to the poor, the laity [Read: “the laity”], or widows [Col. 0834C], but instead arranges secular dignities and offices for certain persons.

This filth brings us annoyance, not without some scandal and reproach. I think, however, that bishops ought to offer their assistance to those who suffer violence from someone, or when some widow is wronged or an orphan defrauded—provided that these persons have a just petition.

Therefore, most beloved brothers, if this pleases everyone, decree that no bishop should go to the imperial court, except for these causes. That those whom our most pious emperor has summoned by his letters ought to be present is beyond doubt.

And because it frequently happens that persons worthy of mercy flee to the Church—those who are suffering punishment for their offenses through exile, condemnation to the islands, or any other sentence [Read: “because of their offenses”]—assistance must not be denied to such people, but protection must be granted to them without delay or hesitation.

If this is approved, let this too be decreed [Note: Here too the Greek supplies: “Give your vote unanimously.” They replied: “Let this also be decreed.”].

[Note: Greek, canon VIII.]

## XI

Bishop Hosius said: Let your prudence also approve this. Since it has been agreed that bishops should not go to the imperial court, lest they incur reproach, if any of them has petitions of the kind we have mentioned, let him send them through his deacon. A minister’s person does not arouse envy, and what is granted is conveyed more quickly [Note: The commonly transmitted Greek adds: “They all replied: Let this also be sanctioned.” These words are not found in the Latin copies].

## XII

Bishop Hosius said: I also think it follows that, if a bishop is present in any province and has sent his petitions to a fellow bishop [Read: “to a fellow bishop”] who is in the larger city, or metropolitan city, that bishop himself should send both the deacon and the petitions, giving him letters of recommendation and writing accordingly to our brothers and fellow bishops who at that time are staying in the places or cities in which our most fortunate, blessed, and pious emperor governs the state.

But if any bishop has friends at the royal court and wishes to ask them for something that is nevertheless appropriate, he is not forbidden to ask and instruct them through his deacon, requesting that they deign to offer their kind assistance to him who asks [Read: “that they may deign to offer”].

Those who come to Rome, as I said above, must give the petitions they have to our most beloved brother and fellow bishop Julius, so that he may first examine whether any of them are shameless, and then, offering his patronage and care, send them to the imperial court.

All the bishops replied that this pleased them and was a most fitting arrangement [Read: “a most fitting disposition”].

[Note: Greek, canon X.]

## XIII

Bishop Hosius said: I also think it necessary that you examine with the utmost care and diligence whether anyone who appears to be wealthy, a legal scholar, or a person of public standing suitable for the episcopate should be ordained before completing the ministry of lector, deacon, and presbyter. He should ascend gradually through each rank, if he is found worthy, to the height of the episcopate.

Each stage of dignity must last for a considerable period, during which his faith, goodness of character, seriousness, and diligence may be known [Col. 0835D]. Once he is judged worthy of the divine priestly ministry, let him attain the highest dignity.

For it is neither fitting nor permitted by discipline or good conduct to rush audaciously or lightly into this office, so that a person is ordained bishop, presbyter, or deacon presumptuously. Such a person will rightly be regarded as a young plant [Note: The manuscript is defective, reading *bitur*. We have corrected it from the Greek], since the blessed Apostle, teacher of the nations, also appears to have forbidden ordinations to take place too quickly [Col. 0836A].

A longer period of testing will reveal the conduct and character of each person.

All the bishops said that this pleased them and that it ought not to be rejected.

[Note: Greek, canon XI.]

## XIV

Bishop Hosius said: You must also establish this: if a bishop comes from one city to another, or from one province to another, out of vanity, occupied with his own praises, or out of religious devotion, and wishes to remain there for a long time, while the bishop of that city is found to be less informed or less eloquent, the visiting bishop must not despise him, address him frequently, or strive to confound him and display his worthlessness.

For this circumstance has commonly caused the man who commends himself in such a way to draw to himself a see that already belongs to another and claim it for himself, without hesitation abandoning the Church entrusted to him and moving to another.

A period of time must therefore be established, since it appears cruel and inhuman not to receive a bishop.

## XV

Nevertheless, remember that in ancient times our Fathers established that if any layman living in the same city did not assemble for three Sundays during three weeks, he was to be removed from communion [Read: “was to be removed”].

If this was decreed concerning laymen, it is not fitting, seemly, or beneficial for a bishop—unless he appears to have some serious necessity or difficult business—to remain away from the Church any longer and distress the people entrusted to him.

All the bishops said: This judgment also appears most appropriate.

[Col. 0836C] [Note: Greek, canon XI.]

## XVI

Bishop Hosius said: Since nothing must be omitted, brothers, our fellow bishops in the cities in which they have been ordained sometimes appear to possess only very small estates. In other places, however, they have large properties from which they can provide more abundant revenues to the Churches [Note: Perhaps “more lavish,” but from the commonly transmitted Greek it should be read “to the poor”].

I think that they should be permitted, when they come to their farms, to gather their produce: they may spend three Sundays—that is, three weeks—on their estates, and assemble in the nearest city [Note: The commonly transmitted Greek has *ekklesia*, “Church,” whereas the Latin copies prefer “city.” The rest of this canon agrees more with the Latin copies than with the Greek] where the presbyter will gather, so that they may not appear to gather and administer without an assembly.

In this way, the small estates belonging to them will suffer no loss because of their absence; and they will not frequently come to another city in which another bishop has been established [Read: “nor will they come frequently to another city”]. Thus they will be able to avoid the charge of ostentation or pride [Read: “he will be able”].

All the bishops said: This arrangement is approved.

## XVII

Bishop Hosius said: This also pleased everyone: if a deacon, presbyter, or any cleric has been excommunicated and flees to another bishop known to him, and that bishop knows that he has been removed from communion by his own bishop, he must not receive him into communion, lest he injure his brother by granting communion [Read: “by offering communion”].

If he dares to do this, he must know that even when the bishops assemble, he will have no ground for an excuse.

All the bishops said: This statute will always preserve peace and maintain concord.

[Note: Greek, canon XIV.]

## XVIII

Bishop Hosius said: I must not remain silent about what always troubles me. If a bishop is found to be *oxycolus* [Note: A Greek word, that is, “irascible”], although such a fault ought not to be found in such a man, and, moved too quickly against a presbyter or deacon, casts him out of the Church, provision must be made lest an innocent man be condemned or deprived of communion.

All replied: The expelled man shall have permission to flee to the metropolitan bishop of the same province [Col. 0837B], who is nearby [Note: Something is missing here. From the Greek it should be supplied: “or, if the metropolitan is absent, to the neighboring bishop, etc.”], and ask that the case be examined with greater care. A hearing must not be denied to those who make such a request.

The bishop who has expelled him, whether rightly or wrongly, must endure manfully that an examination of the matter proceed, so that his judgment may either be confirmed or corrected.

Whoever has been excommunicated in any manner must not claim communion for himself before all matters have been carefully examined with complete truthfulness. Whoever does not have communion must not claim communion for himself before the case has been investigated.

[Note: This is an ancient error, and it also appears in the commonly transmitted Greek, as it had formerly entered the manuscript of our translator. The Latin should more correctly read: “But the clergy who assemble”—that is, the bishops—to judge: if they foresee pride or unjust complaints, they must correct such a person with harsher and more serious words, so that he obeys and submits to what is rightly commanded.]

But if the clerics who assemble foresee that he is displaying pride or undertaking unjust complaints [Read: “they must correct such a man with harsher words”], they must correct him with more severe and serious words, so that he obeys and submits to what is properly commanded.

For just as a bishop ought to show sincere charity and affection toward his ministers [Col. 0837C], so those subject to bishops ought in the same manner to render services appropriate to their merits.
