[Note: This canon is absent from the commonly transmitted Greek but exists in the Latin.]

## XIX

Bishop Januarius said: Let your affection also establish that no bishop may solicit a cleric belonging to another Church or ordain him in his own parish.

All replied: Discords, rivalries, and desires have commonly arisen from such disputes, and for this reason clerics do not go to the Churches assigned to them. The judgment of everyone forbids this from being done.

[Note: Greek, canon XV.]

## XX

Bishop Hosius said: Let us also establish that if anyone wishes to promote to some rank a minister belonging to another parish, without the consent of his bishop [Col. 0838A], such an ordination shall be considered void and invalid.

If anyone wishes to usurp this right, he must be admonished by our brothers and fellow bishops [Note: The commonly transmitted Greek adds: “They all replied: Let this decree also stand firm and immovable.”].

[Note: [Col. 0837D] Greek XVI.] XXI. Aetius the bishop said: You are not unaware how great and important a metropolitan city Thessalonica is. [Read: “To it”] Priests and deacons frequently come to it from other provinces and dioceses; and, not content to remain for a short time, they settle there and spend all their time there [Read: “they spend the same time there”], or at last, after a long period, are scarcely compelled to return to their own churches [Read: “are compelled to return”]. [Note: [Col. 0837D] The common Greek text adds: “Therefore a decision must be made concerning these matters.” Bishop Osius said: “Let the decrees established concerning bishops also be observed in the case of such persons.” The following canon begins, without an interlocutor’s name, with the words “Our brother having suggested,” etc. It is better in the Latin copies that, with the words “Therefore a decision must be made concerning these matters” omitted, the following is added: “All said: The periods established concerning bishops, and concerning these persons also, ought to be observed.” Then a new canon begins: “Bishop Osius said,” as in our version.]

XXII. Bishop Osius said: Our brother Olympius having also suggested it, this likewise seemed good: anyone who has suffered violence and has been violently expelled—whether for the sake of discipline, or for confessing the Catholic Church, [Col. 0838B] or for asserting the truth—if, fleeing danger, he has reached another city innocent and devoted, must not be forbidden to live there until he returns, or [read: “until he is freed”] until the wrong done to him has been removed. For it is harsh that one who has unjustly suffered an evil persecution should not be received by us and should not be shown abundant human kindness [supply: “to him”]. [Note: [Col. 0838D] From the common Greek text one would have to add: “All said: This also has pleased us.” These words are absent from the Latin text.]

[Note: [Col. 0838D] Greek XVIII; absent from the Latin.] XXIII. Bishop Gaudentius said: You know, Aetius, [Note: [Col. 0838D] The common Greek text renders this differently: “that when you were then appointed bishop, peace thereafter prevailed, so that no remnants of discord might remain in the churches; it seemed good to receive those ordained,” etc.] that at one time, after a bishop had been ordained, peace seemed to have been established, so that no remnants of discord remained in the Church. And it seemed good to receive those ordained by Musaeus and Eutychianus, since no fault of theirs was found.

[Note: [Col. 0838D] Greek XIX; absent from the Latin.] XXIV. Bishop Osius said: This is the judgment of my mediocrity: since we ought to be peaceful and patient, and to show sufficient mercy toward everyone, those once advanced to the ecclesiastical clergy by certain of our brothers, if they are unwilling to return to the churches to which they were appointed, are not to be received thereafter. Eutychianus must not claim for himself the title of bishop, nor will Musaeus be regarded as a bishop. But if they ask for lay communion, it must not be denied them. [Note: [Col. 0838D] The common Greek text adds: “All said: It pleases us.”]

[Note: [Col. 0838D] Greek XX.] XXV. Bishop Gaudentius said: These measures, established beneficially and appropriately, and, as was fitting for your priestly integrity, pleasing both to God and to human beings, will not be able to retain their force and authority unless fear follows the sentence that has been pronounced. For we ourselves know that, more than once, because of the shamelessness of a few, the divine and honorable name of the priesthood has been reproached. But if anyone should dare to do anything contrary to what all have approved—desiring rather contumacy and pride than [read: “to please”] pleasing God—he will henceforth know that he has bound himself by the gravest offense and forfeited the honor and dignity of the episcopate. [Note: [Col. 0839B] The same Greek text inserts the words: “All answered: This judgment is fitting and pleasing to us.” These words are more appropriately placed at the end of the canon in our version; they are also read there in Latin copies of canon 11.]

This, however, will become known and be recognized in the following way. If any one of us, stationed at a crossroads or canal, sees a bishop and asks the reason for his journey and where he is directing his course; and if he discovers that the bishop is going to the imperial court, let him inquire into the circumstances mentioned above. If he foresees that the bishop is going because he has been summoned, let him impose no hindrance on his departure. But if, as was stated above to your charity, he is hurrying to the court for the sake of display—or if he is hastening there because of someone’s petitions—then no one shall subscribe his letters, nor shall anyone communicate with him. [Note: [Col. 0839B] In the common Greek text, the following words replace those previously inserted: “Let this also be decreed.”] All answered: This judgment is fitting and pleasing to us.

# Letter of Osius of Corduba and Protogenes of Sardica to Pope Julius

[Note: [Col. 0839B] Sozomen mentions this letter in book III, chapter 12. “Osius and Protogenes,” he says, “who at that time held the leading place among the bishops of the West who had assembled at Sardica, perhaps fearing that they might seem to have detracted from the decrees of the Council of Nicaea, wrote a letter to Julius and declared that they accepted those decrees; but, for the sake of greater clarity, they had explained the same position more fully, lest the Arians, abusing the brevity of that writing, should have an opportunity to drag the uneducated in such debates into an absurd interpretation.” The letter itself, which until now had been missing, is now brought to light from our Veronese manuscript 55. It explains why the exposition of the faith appended at the end of the following synodical letter was written. Just as this exposition of the faith was indeed proposed at the Council of Sardica but was not approved, so this letter too seems to have been prepared earlier but not accepted or sent; consequently, both incur the mark of being spurious. Nevertheless, some ancient writers reported both the exposition of the faith and this letter in their codices as they had been proposed, and therefore they are found not long afterward cited as genuine. See what we have discussed more fully on this matter in Treatise I, chapter 6.]

To our most beloved brother Julius, Osius and Protogenes.

We remember, retain, and possess that document [Col. 0840A] which contains the Catholic faith established at Nicaea, and all the bishops who were present agreed to it. For three questions were raised: [Note: [Col. 0839D] Of the three questions, two were omitted through a copyist’s negligence; they must be supplied from the anathema appended to the Nicene Creed, as follows: “that there was a time when he was not,” and “that he was made from things that did not exist,” or “that they say the Son of God is from another substance or essence, or is changeable or mutable.”] that there was a time when he was not.

But because afterward the disciples of Arius stirred up blasphemies [perhaps: “blasphemies” or “blasphemers,”] reason compelled us to take some precaution, lest someone, having been ensnared by one of those three arguments, should renew the faith: [Note: [Col. 0839D] The passage is corrupt and perhaps mutilated. From the testimony of Sozomen, which we quoted in note 1 above, anyone can easily conjecture what ought to be corrected or supplied; for example: “so that their gloss against the Nicene faith might be excluded and a fuller and longer exposition, agreeing with the earlier one, might be made.”] and so that their [corrupt reading: “spolium”] might be excluded, and so that a fuller and longer exposition agreeing with the earlier one might be set forth.

Therefore, so that no criticism may arise, we make this known to your goodness, most beloved brother. Many things seemed worthy of being firm and fixed, and these were to be dictated more fully, with a certain sufficiency of truth, so that all who teach and catechize might be made clear, [perhaps: “those who resist”] opponents might be overthrown, and they might hold the Catholic and apostolic faith.

[Note: [Col. 0839D] This Latin synodical letter, perhaps from the original Latin, is found in Saint Hilary’s Fragments. The Greek text, which likewise must be regarded as original—for, as we said concerning the canons, there seem to have been two original copies of this synodical letter, one Latin for the Latins and the other Greek for the Greeks—is found in Athanasius’s Second Apology. These two copies lack the exposition of the faith attached to this synodical letter in Greek in Theodoretus, book II, chapter 6, and translated from Theodoretus into Latin by Epiphanius Scholasticus in book IV, chapter 24 of the Tripartite History. Our version of the same synodical letter, translated from the Greek together with that exposition of the faith, differs from the version contained in the Tripartite History; but our translator used a more faithful Greek copy than the one used by Theodoretus and, from him, Epiphanius, as the following note will show.]

# Synodical Letter of the Council of Sardica

[Col. 0840B]

The holy synod, gathered by the grace of God at Sardica from Rome, Spain, Gaul, Italy, Campania, Calabria, Africa, Sardinia, Pannonia, Moesia, Dacia, Dardania, the other Dacia, Macedonia, Thessaly, Achaea, Epirus, Thrace, [Note: [Col. 0840C] Saint Athanasius, in his Second Apology, presents another synodical letter to the Church of Alexandria, whose heading lists approximately these same provinces in the same order. Campania, Calabria, and Europa are omitted, but five others are mentioned: Noricum, Tuscia, Rhodope, Crete, and Egypt. In Theodoretus and Epiphanius the same provinces are listed as far as Thrace; besides Rhodope, however, there are added Asia, Caria, Bithynia, the Hellespont, Phrygia, Pisidia, Cappadocia, Pontus, a second Phrygia, Cilicia, Pamphylia, Lydia, the Cyclades, Egypt, Thebaid, Libya, and Galatia. This list of so many provinces is evidently false: first, because at the time of the Council of Sardica there was only one Phrygia, not two, as we proved in Treatise I, chapter 7; second, because the bishops of nearly all these provinces belonged not to the Council of Sardica but to the pseudo-Sardican gathering at Philippopolis, as we noted in the same place. Hence Theodoretus’s Greek copy is defective, whereas the one our translator had before his eyes is authentic. In Athanasius and Hilary this heading, together with the provinces, is omitted. Athanasius’s mention of Rhodope is confirmed by the subscription of Olympius of Aenus in Rhodope, which is appended to the first letter of Athanasius, to be published later from our manuscript. Since no bishop from Europa has been found among the subscriptions examined in Treatise I, chapter 7, it may be questioned whether, in our heading, “Rhodope” should be read in place of “Europa.”] Europa, Palestine, and Arabia, to all bishops everywhere, fellow ministers [Col. 0841A] and most beloved brothers of the Catholic and apostolic Church.

The Arians have indeed often dared many things against the servants of God who preserve the true faith. Introducing an adulterous doctrine, they attempted to persecute the orthodox. They rose up so violently against the faith that even the goodness of the most devout emperors could not remain unaware of it. Therefore, with the grace of God coming to our aid, the most devout emperors themselves gathered us from different provinces and cities and allowed this holy synod to be held at Sardica, so that all discord might be removed and, with all bad faith expelled, the religion of Christ alone might be preserved among everyone.

Bishops also came from the East, themselves summoned by the most religious emperors, especially because of what was being repeatedly reported [Col. 0841B] concerning our most beloved brothers and fellow ministers Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra in Galatia, and Asclepas. Perhaps accusations concerning them have reached you; perhaps they have also attempted to stir your ears, so that what malicious people say against innocent men might be believed and they might conceal the suspicion of their most wicked heresy. But they were not permitted to carry this out for long. For the Lord, who suffered death for them and for all of us and granted us all ascent into heaven on their account, is the one who gives protection to the churches.

Formerly, when Eusebius, Maris, Theodorus, [Note: [Col. 0841D] The letters “Doro” appear to have been repeated from the final syllables of the preceding name, Theodoro, and should therefore be deleted. The remaining letters are “Theo,” from which, following Epiphanius’s version, Theognis should be read; or, as below in this same version, Theogenes. Hilary reads “Diognitus,” but later “Theognitus.”] Dorotheus, Ursacius, Valens, [Note: [Col. 0841D] These two names, Menophantus and Stephanus, occur in Theodoretus and Epiphanius but are absent from Hilary. Saint Athanasius, using the general expression “the Eusebians,” passes over all these names.] Menophantus, and Stephanus wrote to Julius, bishop and fellow priest of the Roman Church, against the fellow ministers mentioned above—namely Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, Marcellus of Ancyra in Galatia, and also Asclepas, bishop of Gaza—bishops from other regions also gave testimony to the sincerity of our fellow minister Athanasius. But the actions of Eusebius and his associates were nothing but lies [read: “full of lies”] and slanders.

Although, when they were summoned [Note: [Col. 0841D] They were summoned by a letter preserved by Saint Athanasius in his Second Apology.] by our beloved fellow priest Julius, they refused to come, and although their slander was exposed by what Julius himself wrote—for they would have come if they had confidence in their deeds and actions against our brothers and fellow ministers—nevertheless, by what they did in this holy and great synod they displayed their faction even more clearly.

For when they arrived at Sardica and saw our brothers Athanasius, Marcellus, and Asclepas, they were afraid to come to judgment. Though summoned not once or twice but repeatedly, they did not answer the summons, namely the assemblies of the bishops [Col. 0842A] [Note: [Col. 0842D] Epiphanius more aptly reads: “the bishops who had assembled.”] and especially Osius, whose old age, confession, and such great labor seemed to make him worthy of every reverence. While the bishops were waiting for them and urging them to enter, so that what they had spread and written concerning absent fellow ministers [Note: [Col. 0842D] Epiphanius: “what they had defamed.”] might be disproved in their presence, they did not come when summoned, as we have said. Thus they showed their slander and not merely plotted and formed factions, but shouted excuses. For those who have confidence in their statements can also be present [supply: “to prove them”] in person.

Since, therefore, they did not come, we think that no one is now unaware of the matter. If they again attempt to act cunningly, having nothing with which to accuse our fellow ministers, they accuse the absent while avoiding those who are present. For they fled, most beloved brothers, not only because of the slander they were bringing against them, but also because of those who were pursuing them with various accusations and whom they saw arriving.

Chains and fetters were brought by men returning from exile and by those who were still being held in exile. The relatives and friends of those who had died because of them also came; and, what is more, bishops were present, indeed offering the iron and chains which they had carried because of them. Others testified that they had been threatened with death on account of their accusations. They had reached such savagery that they even dared to try to kill bishops; and they would have killed them if the bishops had not escaped their hands.

[Note: [Col. 0842D] The word “rose up” agrees with Epiphanius’s version, in which, translating from Theodoretus, he wrote: “Our fellow priest, the blessed Theodulus, also came.” But from Athanasius’s Greek text and Hilary’s Latin, “died” should be read. The word “blessed” signifies a dead person.] Thus our blessed fellow minister Theodulus rose up, fleeing their accusations; for he had been ordered to perish because of their [Note: [Col. 0842D] Hilary: “accusation.”] pretense. Others, displaying wounds from swords [read: “displayed”], and some complaining that they had suffered hunger at their hands [Note: [Col. 0842D] That is, they complained of it], implored us; and noble persons testified to these things. But all the churches [supply: “were witnesses”]; those who came forward and made allegations on their behalf showed that there had been soldiers with swords, crowds with clubs, threats from judges, and the submission of forged letters. For the letter of Theogenes against our fellow ministers Athanasius, Marcellus, and Asclepas was read, so that even the emperors were moved against them. These things were confirmed by those who were then Theogenes’ deacons. They also testified to the stripping of virgins, the burning of churches, imprisonment directed against fellow ministers, and all these things for no other reason than the age-old heresy of the Arians: for, refusing their ordination and communion [Col. 0842D] [read: “refusing”], they necessarily suffered these things.

Considering these matters, they were brought to the destruction of their own purpose. They were ashamed to confess their crimes; and, since they could not conceal what had become known to everyone, they came to Sardica so that by their arrival they might acquire a reputation for sincerity. When they saw those whom they had afflicted and against whom they had made accusations, with the witnesses examined before their eyes, they could not come when summoned—namely, when our fellow ministers Athanasius, Marcellus, and Asclepas, with great confidence, appealed, pressed, challenged, and even promised not merely to expose their slander but also to demonstrate what crimes they had [read: “committed”] in their churches.

They, however, were struck with such fear that they even turned to flight and, through that [supply: “flight”], demonstrated their slander and confessed their crimes. Although their evasiveness [read: “cunning”] had been confirmed not only by their earlier conduct but also by their present behavior in refusing to come, nevertheless, lest they be able to find in their flight an opportunity for further malice, we decided, according to the reasoning of truth, to examine the things they had committed.

When this was done, we found them to be slanderers in their actions and to have prepared nothing but plots against our fellow ministers. Arsenius, whom they said Athanasius had killed, is alive and living among the living. From this it is also clear that what they had said about others was fabricated.

Since they had mentioned a cup broken by Macarius, Athanasius’s presbyter, they brought forward as witnesses those who had come from Alexandria and the Mareotis, and these testified that nothing of the kind had been done. Bishops from Egypt also wrote to our fellow priest Julius and sufficiently established that there had not even been any such suspicion.

Next, the records which they claimed to possess against him proved to have been prepared on one side only; and in those proceedings pagans and catechumens were questioned. One catechumen, when questioned, said that he had been inside when Macarius arrived at the place. Another, when questioned, said that the sick Ischyras, whom they call [Note: [Col. 0843D] The translator separated the Greek adjective θρυλλούμενον, “famous” or “notorious,” from Ischyras and rendered it less accurately as “whom they call.” Epiphanius and Hilary more correctly have “the notorious Ischyras.”] was lying in his cell.

From this it is clear that no sacred rites had been celebrated, since catechumens were standing inside; and that Ischyras was not present but was sick. For that very wicked Ischyras, who lied by saying that Athanasius had burned certain sacred books, thereby also exposed his own lie. He confessed that at the time Macarius arrived he had been sick [Col. 0843D] and lying down, so that he too was shown to be a slanderer. Therefore, as payment for this slander, the bishops gave Ischyras the title of bishop, although he is not even a presbyter.

Two presbyters who had once been with Meletius, but afterward had been received by the blessed Alexander, then bishop of Alexandria, and were now established with Athanasius, came forward and testified that this man had never been a presbyter of Meletius and that Meletius had no church or minister at all in the Mareotis. Yet they presented as a bishop a man who was not even a presbyter, so that by this title they might bewilder those who heard their accusations.

The book of our fellow minister Marcellus was read, and Eusebius’s fabrication [read: “commentatio”] was found. They had invented that what Marcellus said in response to the question posed was a confession of his own. These passages, therefore, as well as what followed and what came before [Note: [Col. 0843D] That is, what preceded it] in the questioning, were read; and the man’s sound faith was found. For he did not, as they asserted, make the Word of God begin from holy Mary, nor did he assign him an end in the kingdom; rather, he wrote that the Savior’s dominion was without beginning and without end.

Our fellow minister Asclepas also produced the proceedings conducted at Antioch in the presence of his accusers and of Eusebius of Caesarea; and from the decisions of the judging bishops [read: “of the judges”] he showed himself to be innocent.

Rightly, therefore, most beloved brothers, they did not answer though summoned repeatedly; rightly they fled. For compelled by conscience, they confirmed their slanders by fleeing and caused what the accusers present were saying and demonstrating to be believed [Note: [Col. 0843D] Read with Hilary: “caused those things to be believed”].

What then? In addition to all these things, they not only received the Arians who had been deposed and expelled from the Church, but also [Col. 0844C] advanced them to a higher rank: a deacon into a presbyter, and a presbyter into a bishop, for no other reason than that they might spread and conceal [read: “extend”] impiety and corrupt the devout faith. [Note: [Col. 0843D] Other Greek and Latin copies use the plural: “deacons into presbyters,” etc.]

Now, after Eusebius [Note: [Col. 0843D] The Greek text lacks the words “and his associate.” Hilary has “two after Eusebius.” Constantius noted that “after the two Eusebii” should be read; that reading is supported by Hilary’s book I, To Constantius, no. 5: “Recently we learned that these inventions were fabricated by the two Eusebii,” especially since, there, apart from Georgius, the same men who are bishops here are added to the two Eusebii. Our version, by the words “and his associate,” indicates another Eusebius, namely the Caesarean in addition to the Nicomedian.] and his associate, the following are now leading men: Theodorus of Heraclea, Narcissus of Marona in Cilicia [read: “of Neroniades”], Stephanus of Antioch, Acacius of Caesarea in Palestine, [Note: [Col. 0844D] Neither Athanasius nor Hilary nor Theodoretus nor Epiphanius, nor the other letters that will be appended below, contain this second Narcissus. Georgius of Laodicea must be substituted for him; in those authors Georgius is listed among the condemned.] Narcissus of Marmia, Menophantus of Ephesus in Asia, Ursacius of Singidunum in Moesia, and Valens of Mursa in Pannonia. They prevented those who had come with them from the East from coming to the holy council [Note: [Col. 0844D] These words, “in Asia,” occur neither in the Greek copies nor in three Latin copies. The translator seems to have read εἰς τὴν Ἀσίαν, “into Asia,” instead of εἰς τὴν ἁγίαν σύνοδον, “to the holy council.” Hence the text should be corrected to: “nor from coming to the holy council”] or from approaching the Church of God at all.

Even when they came to Sardica, they held meetings with one another at every place and, with threats, made agreements among themselves that, when they reached Sardica, they would not enter into judgment at all or meet with the holy synod; [Col. 0845A] but that, merely by coming, they would make a show of their arrival and would flee quickly [read: “would flee”].

We were able to learn these things from our fellow ministers Macarius of Palestine and Asterius of Arabia, who came with them but withdrew from the same unbelief. For when they came to the holy synod, they tearfully reported the violence they had suffered. They said that nothing upright was done among those men. They added that there were some who held the true faith, but that threats and accusations prevented them from coming to us [supply: “from coming”]. For this reason they tried to remain together in one house, not allowing them to be separated for even a moment.

Since, therefore, it was not right to remain silent or to leave their slanders unpunished [read: “unavenged”—the manuscripts read “hidden”], their bonds, murders, beatings, forged letters, fines, [Col. 0845B] stripping of virgins, exiles, destruction of churches, burnings, transfers from small to larger cities, and, above all, the malicious Arian heresy that they raised against the true faith—because of these things we declare our most beloved brothers and fellow priests Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, Marcellus of Ancyra in Galatia, Asclepas of Gaza, and those who minister to the Lord with them, to be innocent and sincere. [Note: [Col. 0845D] Other Greek and Latin copies supply: “writing to each of their provinces so that…”]

Thus let the peoples of each church know the sincerity of their bishop, and let them have and await this bishop [supply: “and await him”]. But Georgius of Alexandria, Basilius, and Quincianus of Gaza, who have attacked the judgment of their churches like wolves [Note: [Col. 0845D] Read: “the churches of their own kind, like wolves.” The translator apparently read δικὴν, “justice” or “judgment,” instead of δίκην/δίκυν in the phrase meaning “in the manner of wolves.”], are neither to be called bishops nor in any way Christians; no communion is to be held with them, their letters are not to be received, and no letters are to be written to them.

Theodorus of Heraclea in Europa, with his associates from [read: “of”] Maronia in Cilicia, Narcissus of Caesarea in Palestine, Acacius, Stephanus of Antioch, Ursacius of Singidunum in Moesia, Valens of Mursa in Pannonia, Menophantus of Ephesus, and Georgius of Laodicea—although, fearing what might happen, he was not present from the East, nevertheless because he had been deposed by the blessed Alexander, bishop of Alexandria [Note: [Col. 0845D] Hilary states more clearly: “and because both he and the others who were seized were caught up in the madness of Arius, and because of the crimes charged against them”]—the holy synod has all deposed from the episcopate because of themselves and their Arian colleagues and because of the crimes brought against them [read: “because of the crimes brought against them”]. [Col. 0846A] And we decree not only that they are not bishops, but that they do not deserve communion with the faithful.

For since they separate the Son from the Father’s substance and estrange the Word from the Father’s equality, they ought to be separated from the Catholic Church and alienated from the name of Christians. Therefore let them be anathema to all of you, because [Note: [Col. 0845D] That is, because they adulterated it] they have trafficked in the Word of truth. For the apostolic command is: “If anyone announces to you anything other than what you have received, let him be anathema.” Command that no one communicate with them, for light has no communion with darkness. Keep them all far away; for Christ has no agreement with Belial. And take care, most beloved brothers, not to receive their letters or write to them.

You also, beloved brothers and fellow ministers, strive, while present in spirit at our synod, to agree and pronounce judgment through your written responses, so that the assent of our fellow ministers everywhere may be preserved among all. [Note: [Col. 0846C] Athanasius and Hilary add a concluding clause, one version of which is more common among the Greeks: “May divine providence preserve you holy and joyful, beloved brothers”; the other is peculiar to the Latins: “We wish you, brothers, good health in the Lord.” The remaining material, containing the exposition of the faith, is found in Theodoretus and his translator Epiphanius. Athanasius and Hilary omit it because, although it was proposed at the synod, it was not accepted. Compare note 1 above, col. 839.]

We cast out and remove from the Catholic Church those who affirm that Christ is indeed God, but is not true God because he is a son; and that he is not a true son because he was born and made at the same time [Note: [Col. 0846D] In Greek, Theodoretus has ἀγέννητος, “unbegotten”; Epiphanius has ingenitus, “unbegotten,” which is better]. Thus they judged that “born” should be understood as they stated above: that what is born has been made. They say that Christ, although he existed before the ages, has a beginning and an end, even though he has generation not from time but before all time [supply: “a generation”].

At present two serpents born from the Arian viper are Valens and Ursacius. They boast and do not hesitate to call themselves Christians, and to say that the Word and the Spirit were wounded, killed, died, and rose again; and, as assemblies of heretics are accustomed to maintain, that the substances of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are different and separable.

But we have received and been taught this; this we hold as the Catholic and apostolic tradition, faith, and confession: that there is one substance—which the Greeks themselves call οὐσία, ousia—of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. And if anyone asks about the substance of the Son, it is certainly the same as the Father’s [Note: [Col. 0846D] Here, through a copyist’s fault, a line is missing, together with a textual error. From the Greek the passage must be supplied and corrected: “since it is acknowledged to be one alone; nor has the Father ever been, nor can he be, without the Son, nor the Son without the Father, who is the Word and Spirit. For it is absurd to say that the Father was once not the Father,” etc.]

For it is absurd to say that the Father did not exist [Col. 0847A], since what is understood as “Father” can neither be named nor exist without the Son. The Son himself bears witness: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10); and: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

None of us denies that he was begotten; rather, he was begotten before all things called visible and invisible, as the maker and artificer of archangels, angels, the world, and the human race, as it says: “Wisdom, the artificer of all things, taught me” (Wisdom 7:21); and: “All things were made through him” (John 1:3). [Note: [Col. 0847D] Epiphanius gives the better reading: “For he could not always have existed if he had received a beginning, since the Word, who always exists, has no beginning; and God never has an end.”]

For he could not always have existed if he had received a beginning, since the Word, who always exists, has no beginning, and God never has an end.

We do not say that the Father is the Son, nor therefore [read: “again”] that the Son is the Father; rather, the Father is Father, and the Son is the Son of the Father. We confess that the Son is the power of the Father. We confess the Word of God the Father, besides whom there is nothing else [read: “what other thing”], and we declare the Word to be true God, Wisdom, and power, and truly the Son.

But we do not call him Son according to the manner in which other sons are called sons, since they are called sons either through adoption, or through birth, or because they deserve it [Note: [Col. 0847D] Epiphanius has the better reading: “they will be gods either through the grace of regeneration or because they are deemed worthy to be called sons”], not because they have one substance with the Father and the Son.

We confess him as the only-begotten and firstborn: the only-begotten Word, who always was and is in the Father; firstborn, certainly, as man. [Note: [Col. 0847D] The Greek must be rendered with the wholly opposite meaning: “But he differs from the common creation.”] He differs, however, from the common creation as firstborn from the dead.

We confess one Godhead of the Father and the Son. No one has ever denied that the Father is greater than the Son, not because of another substance or a difference, [Col. 0847C] but [supply: “because”] because the very name “Father” is greater than “Son.”

This, then, is their blasphemous and corrupt interpretation: that when he said, “I and the Father are one,” he meant “one” with respect to agreement and harmony. Let all Catholics reject their foolish and contemptible opinion. Just as mortal human beings differ from one another, as they ordinarily do, and then, when they have offended one another, come to an agreement and return to friendship, so, they say, separations and disagreements could have existed between God the almighty Father and his Son. It is absurd both to understand and to think this.

We, however, believe, affirm, and hold that he spoke with sacred authority when he said, “I and the Father are one”: one with respect to the unity of substance, which is one substance of the Father and of the Son. We believe that he has always reigned with the Father, without beginning and without end, that he has no temporal beginning, and that his kingdom cannot be diminished; for what always exists never receives a beginning and cannot be diminished.

We believe in and accept the Holy Spirit the Paraclete, whom the Lord himself promised and sent to us. We believe that he suffered—but it was the man whom he clothed and assumed from the Virgin Mary, the man who was able to suffer, because man is mortal, whereas God is immortal.

[Note: Supply “was sent.” But it was not he who suffered; rather, it was the man, etc.]

We believe that on the third day it was not God who rose in the man, but the man who rose in God; and that he offered him as a gift to his Father, the one whom he had set free. We believe that at the proper and appointed time he himself will judge all people and all things.

Yet their foolishness is so great that they do not see the light of truth or understand what was truly said: “that they may be one in us.” It is clear why they are one: because the apostles received the Holy Spirit of God. Nevertheless, they were not called “Spirit,” nor was any one of them the sun, or wisdom, or power, nor was any one of them the Only-Begotten, as he says: “I and you are one. So may they also be one in us.”

[Note: Not “sun,” but “of them” ought to be rendered. For the Greek has ἢ Λόγος, “the Word.” Our translator appears to have read corruptly ἥλιος, “sun.”]

Thus, too, they may be one in us. But the divine voice carefully distinguished the matter: he says, “Let them be in us”; he did not say, “as we are one, I and the Father.” Rather, the disciples, equal and joined to one another, should be one through the confession of faith, so that, by the grace and piety of the Father and of our Lord and Savior, and through his permission and love, they might be able to be one.

[Note: The following three documents have come down to us only from Codex Verona 55. From the same codex they were first published by the distinguished Scipio Maffei in volume 3 of the work entitled *Osservazioni letterarie*, pp. 29 ff., and then in the appendix to the *Historia Theologica*, pp. 258 ff. Here, however, they had to be reprinted together with the other Sardican documents contained in our manuscript, so that anyone may easily compare them at the several places where they are cited in this volume.]

## Letter of the Council of Sardica to the Churches of Mareotis

[Col. 0848C]

The holy synod gathered at Sardica by the grace of God sends greetings in the Lord to the Churches of God in Mareotis, together with the presbyters and deacons.

From what has also been sent to Alexandria through the brethren, dearly beloved, you can learn what has been done at the holy and great synod gathered at Sardica by the grace of God. But since you too have written that you have endured intolerable things at the hands of the most impious heretics, whose chief is the most wicked Gregory, the holy synod considered it necessary to write also to your Reverence, so that, consoled by these words and placing ever greater hope in God, you may attain the future promise reserved for those who love Christ.

If, therefore, you have suffered evil, do not be saddened, but rather rejoice, since you too have been found worthy to endure insults for the name of the Lord. If you have endured prisons, chains, and conspiracies, these things will not grieve you; for the Fathers before you also endured them, one of whom was the blessed Paul, on account of which he was also called “the one in chains.”

We heard how much the presbyter Ingenius suffered, and we were indeed grieved by the insults; but we gladly received his sacred resolve, since he endured everything for Christ. If, therefore, what is thought to be sorrow still presses upon you, let it be turned into joy.

For we have written to the most devout emperors that such things should no longer be committed against the Churches; and we believe that the Lord, through the piety of our most humane emperors, will bring it about that we too may be found giving thanks to God with consolation and freedom, and pleasing to him on the day of judgment.

What has been done, as we have said, you will learn from our dearly beloved brothers who carried your letter—namely, the Alexandrian presbyters and deacons. For the holy and great synod pronounced your most beloved brother and fellow minister, your bishop Athanasius, innocent and free from every accusation. But it deposed Theodore, Narcissus, Stephen, Acacius, George, Ursacius, Valens, and Minophantus from the episcopate because of the offenses they committed and because of the most impious heresy whose associates and patrons they appear to be.

As for Gregory, we do not even think it necessary to write much about him. He was deposed long ago; indeed, he was not considered a bishop at all. His work is like his ordination.

If anyone has therefore been deceived by him, let that person be instructed and come to know the truth. But if anyone resists his impiety, let him rejoice that he too opposed the man whom the holy synod did not even regard as a bishop. For we were not unaware of what he committed against you or of how greatly he oppressed you.

But rejoice, because you suffer for Christ at the hands of those who blaspheme Christ. We judge that all insolence will now cease, once those harmful men who defended an unmentionable heresy have been rebuked and deposed. I pray that you may be safe in the Lord.

I, Hosius the bishop, pray that you may be safe in the Lord, dearly beloved brothers.

Athanasius, your bishop, prays that you may be safe in the Lord, dearly beloved brothers.

Heliodorus likewise.

John likewise.

Jonas likewise.

Dionysius likewise.

Paregorius likewise.

Aetius likewise.

Valens likewise.

Arius likewise.

Porphyrius likewise.

Athenodorus likewise.

[Col. 0850A]

Alysius likewise.

[Lege: Alypius.]

Gerontius likewise.

Lucius likewise.

Asterius likewise.

Bassus likewise.

Dioscorus likewise.

Domitianus likewise.

Calepodius likewise.

Alexander likewise.

Plutarchus likewise.

Vincentius likewise.

Vitalis likewise.

Severus likewise.

Restitutus likewise.

Vincentius the bishop prays that you may be safe in the Lord, dearly beloved brothers. At the command of my brothers and fellow bishops I have written and subscribed on behalf of the others.

## Letter of Saint Athanasius to the Same Churches

Athanasius sends greetings in the Lord to the presbyters, deacons, and people of the Catholic Church in Mareotis, his most beloved and longed-for brothers.

The holy synod praised your devotion in Christ. Everyone approved your courage and strength in every respect, because you did not fear threats; by enduring insults and persecutions directed against piety, you prevailed.

Therefore, when your letter was read, it moved everyone to tears, and drew everyone toward affection for you. They loved you even while you were absent and regarded your persecutions as their own. Their letter to you is evidence of their charity; and although it would have been enough to count you among the holy Church established at Alexandria, the holy synod nevertheless wrote to you separately, so that, encouraged, you would not fail because of what you are suffering, but would give thanks to the Lord, because your endurance will bear good fruit.

In former times the character of the heretics was hidden; now, however, it has been exposed and revealed to everyone. For the holy synod perceived the accusations they had fabricated against you, hated them, and by universal agreement deposed Theodore, Valens, and Ursacius in Alexandria and Mareotis.

[Note: Something is missing here, for example, “because of the things which they violently and unjustly did in Alexandria and Mareotis.” These three Arian bishops, together with three others who have now died, were sent into Egypt by the cabal at Tyre. In Alexandria and Mareotis they committed many injustices against Athanasius and gave occasion for riots and very serious scandals.]

The same things were also done throughout the other Churches. And since their cruelty toward the Churches had now become intolerable, and their tyranny had become notorious, they were therefore expelled from the episcopate and excluded from all communion.

As for Gregory, they did not even wish to mention him. Since he had never possessed the name of bishop at all, they considered it superfluous to name him. But they mentioned his name for the sake of those who had been deceived by him—not because he seemed worthy of remembrance, but so that those who had been deceived by him might recognize his infamy and be ashamed of the kind of deeds by which they had entered into communion with such a man.

You will learn what was written concerning them from the attached documents. Although not all the bishops had the opportunity to write, they were all represented in writing, and they wrote on behalf of all. Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the brothers greet you.

Protogenes the bishop prays that you may be safe in the Lord, most beloved and longed-for brothers.

Athenodorus the bishop prays that you may be safe in the Lord, most beloved brothers.

Julianus likewise.

Ammonius likewise.

[Note: It may be the man whom Athanasius, in the *Second Apology*, among the names of the bishops who subscribed the synodical letter to all the Churches, calls Galba.]

Through letters from Gaul I pray that you may be safe in the Lord, dearly beloved.

## Also, Letter of Saint Athanasius to the Church of Alexandria

[Col. 0852B]

Athanasius sends greetings in the Lord to the presbyters and deacons and to all the most beloved brothers of the holy Catholic Church established at Alexandria and in Parembole.

[Note: Just as the Sardican synod sent a letter to the Church of Alexandria, which is preserved in Athanasius’s *Second Apology*, so here too he wrote this letter to the same Church. It has been preserved for us in Latin only from our manuscript. The synodical letter reads: “To the presbyters, deacons, and the entire holy Church of God established at Alexandria” (παροικούσῃ), “beloved brothers in the Lord, greetings.” Something similar seems to have been written in Athanasius’s heading: “of the Church established at Alexandria and of the Catholic Church.” The words “and of Parembole” appear to have been inserted erroneously. For, apart from the fact that Parembole near Syene and the other place called by Ptolemy Ἀλεξάνδρου Παρεμβολή, “Alexander’s Camp,” are very far from Alexandria in the Ammonian region, there is no reason why this letter should have been delivered specifically to the people of Parembole rather than to the other more distinguished Churches of Egypt. Nor does Athanasius address anyone in the letter itself except the Alexandrians.]

In writing this letter, dearly beloved brothers, we ought to begin by giving thanks to Christ. Now, however, this is especially fitting, since many things have been accomplished before the Lord, and great things have received his favor; and those who believe in him ought not to be ungrateful for so many of his benefits.

We therefore give thanks to the Lord, who always makes us manifest to all in the faith, and who has now done great and marvelous things for the Church. For what the Eusebian heretics and the heirs of Arius had again proclaimed, all the bishops who assembled declared to be false and fabricated.

Those very men who are considered terrifying by many and are called “giants” were held to be nothing—and rightly so. For just as darkness is exposed when light arrives, so in the coming of the righteous iniquity is revealed; and in the presence of the excellent, the weak are convicted.

For you are not ignorant, beloved, of what the successors of Eusebius’s blasphemous heresy—Theodore, Narcissus, Valens, Ursacius, and the utterly wicked George, together with Stephen, Acacius, Minophantus, and their associates—did. Their madness has been exposed to everyone.

You have also not been unaware of what they committed against the Churches. First they harmed you; first they attempted to corrupt your Church. But those who did so many and such great things, and were regarded as terrifying by everyone, feared so greatly, as I said, that they surpassed every expectation.

They feared not only the Roman synod and did not merely excuse themselves when summoned. Even now, when they had arrived at Sardica, their consciences weakened them so greatly that, when they saw the judges, they were astonished; so utterly did they collapse in spirit.

Truly, who could say against them: “Where is your sting, O death? Where is your victory, O death?” (1 Cor. 15:55). It did them no good to wish to judge; they could no longer ensnare those whom they wished to ensnare. Rather, they saw faithful men concerned for justice—or, better, they saw our own Lord in them, just as the demons once saw him in the tombs.

For, being children of falsehood, they could not bear to see the truth. Thus Theodore, Narcissus, and Ursacius spoke with their companions:

“Leave us alone. What have we to do with you, men of Christ? We know that you are truthful, and we fear being convicted; we are afraid to acknowledge the accusations against us. There is nothing between us and you. You are Christians, but we oppose Christ. Among you, truth prevails; we, however, have learned to deceive.

“We thought our deeds were hidden; we no longer believed that we would come to judgment. Why do you convict us before the time and harass us by convicting us before the day?”

Although they are wicked in character and walk in darkness, they finally came to recognize that there is no fellowship between light and darkness, nor any agreement between Christ and Belial.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, since they knew what they had done—indeed, since they saw their wretched accusers, with witnesses before their eyes—they imitated Cain and fled in his manner, because they had committed a great error; for they imitated his flight and received his condemnation.

The holy synod recognized their deeds. It heard our blood crying out; it heard the voices of those injured by them. All the bishops recognized what they had sinned and how much they had done against our Churches and against others. Therefore, like Cain, they expelled them from the Churches.

For who did not weep when your letter was read? Who did not groan when he saw those whom these men had exiled? Who did not regard your tribulations as his own?

Dearly beloved brothers, formerly you were suffering while these men committed offenses against you, and perhaps for a long time the conflict did not cease. But now all the bishops assembled, and when they heard what you had suffered, they grieved and groaned just as you, when enduring the insult, had then grieved; and they [lacuna]; there was a shared grief at the time when you came forward.

For these reasons, and for all the other things they committed against the Churches, the entire holy synod deposed them all. It judged them not only alien from the Church, but also unworthy to be called Christians.

For if they deny Christ, how can they be called Christians? And if they commit offenses against the Churches, how can they be present in the Churches?

Therefore the holy synod ordered the Churches everywhere to mark them publicly, so that those who had been deceived by them might now return to fullness and truth.

Do not therefore lose heart, dearly beloved brothers. As servants of God and confessors of the faith of Christ, prove yourselves in the Lord; and do not let tribulation cast you down or the sufferings inflicted upon you by the heretics who are at work against you grieve you.

For you have the whole world grieving with you; and, what is more, you have all of them keeping you in mind.

I think that those who were deceived by them, now seeing the correction carried out by the synod, are turning away from them and shuddering at their impiety.

But if after these things their hand is still raised up, do not be astonished or afraid if they rage. Rather, pray, lift your hands to God, and trust that the Lord will not delay, but will do everything for you according to your desire.

I would indeed have liked to write you a longer letter and to report each individual event. But since the presbyters and deacons who are present are able to announce to you everything they have seen, I have refrained from writing many things.

I indicate only this, considering it necessary: keep the fear of the Lord before your eyes, place him first, and celebrate everything in concord with one another, understanding and acting wisely.

Pray for us, keeping the needs of the widows in mind, especially since the enemies of truth have removed what belonged to them.

[Lege: “have taken away,” rather than “have offered.”]

But may your love overcome the malice of the heretics. For we believe that, in answer to your prayers, the Lord will grant, with his favor, that I may see you again soon.

In the meantime, you will learn what was done at the synod from the documents sent to you by all the bishops, and from the attached letter concerning the deposition of Theodore, Narcissus, Stephen, Acacius, George, Minophantus, Ursacius, and Valens.

For they did not wish to mention Gregory, since he had never possessed the name of bishop at all and they considered it superfluous to name him. Nevertheless, they mentioned his name for the sake of those who had been deceived by him—not because his name was worthy of remembrance, but so that those deceived by him might recognize his infamy and be ashamed that they had shared in such a man’s conduct.

[The manuscript is defective here.]

I pray that you may be safe in the Lord, most beloved and longed-for brothers.

## Creed of the Pseudo-Synod of Sardica

[Note: This formula is found twice in Saint Hilary: first in *Fragments*, volume 2, column 663, where it is attached to the longer synodical letter of the same pseudo-Sardican assembly by the transition, “This, then, is our faith”; and second in the book *On Synods*, volume 2, column 482, where the same formula as in our manuscript is presented separately, though in another translation. It is therefore clear that this formula was published in two ways: attached to the synodical letter and separately. The first part of the formula, up to the words “the holy and Catholic Church has recognized as alien,” had been circulated by the Eusebians several months after the synod of Antioch in the year 441; the second part was added three years later, together with other extensive additions. Its Greek text survives in Saint Athanasius’s book *On Synods*, from which it was reprinted in volume 2 of the Venetian edition of the Councils, column 636. Finally, it was repeated in the pseudo-Sardican council. Just as Vigilius of Tapsus, in book 5, section 3 of *Against Eutyches*, treated this formula of the true and Catholic synod too incautiously—especially since Saint Hilary endeavored to expound it in its right sense—so it is not surprising that it was copied among the Sardican documents in the Greek collection and rendered into Latin by our translator.]

The holy synod was gathered at Sardica from various provinces of the eastern regions: from Thebaid, Egypt, Palestine, Phoenicia, Coele Syria, Mesopotamia, Cilicia, Cappadocia, Pontus, Paphlagonia, Galatia, Phrygia, Bithynia, the Hellespont, Asia, Pisidia, the Islands, Pamphylia, Caria, Lydia, Europe, Thrace, Haemimontus, Pannonia, Moesia, and Dacia, and set forth this faith.

[Note: Hilary adds “Arabia” in both places.]

[Note: In Hilary’s *On Synods* the phrase is “from the two Phrygias,” as Vigilius of Tapsus also reads in book 5, section 3 of *Against Eutyches*, but this is erroneous: at that time Phrygia had not yet been divided into two provinces. See the treatise, Part 1, chapter 3. In the fragments of Hilary, the heading of the synodical letter mentions only one Phrygia.]

[Note: Hilary’s *On Synods* explains this creed; we have discussed it.]

We believe in one God, the almighty Father, creator and maker of all things, from whom everything that is named in heaven and on earth derives its name.

[Note: Hilary, in the same place, has “from whom every fatherhood is named,” as in the Greek text of Athanasius. But in the *Fragments* he has “every creature,” with which our translator’s reading “everything” agrees. Shortly afterward, in both places, Hilary has “Only-begotten” instead of “Only One.” Our translator consistently renders the Greek word μονογενής as “unique” or “Only One.”]

And in his unique Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, begotten from the Father before all ages: God from God, light from light; through whom all things were made, and for whom all things were made, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible; the Word, wisdom, and power, eternal true light in all things; who in the last times became man for us and was created from the holy Virgin.

[Note: Hilary has “power, and life, light,” etc. In all the witnesses the word “eternal” is absent, just as it is absent from the Greek.]

Crucified, dead, and buried, and he rose from the dead on the third day. He was received into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and will come at the end of the age to judge the living and the dead and to repay each according to his deeds.

[Note: In Hilary’s *Fragments*: “at the end of the world.” In the book *On Synods* there is nothing equivalent.]

His dominion will remain forever throughout the eternal ages, always sitting at the right hand of the Father, not only in this age but also in the age to come.

We also believe in one Holy Spirit of God, that is, the Paraclete, whom, after his ascension into heaven, he promised to the apostles and sent to teach them and remind them of everything. Through him also the souls of the devout who believe in him are sanctified and live.

Those who say that the Son is from nothing, or from another substance—the word “Spirit” is supplied in the text—or that there was once a time or age when he did not exist, the holy and Catholic Church recognizes as alien.

Likewise, those who say that there are three gods, or that Christ is not God—or that the Spirit is not of God—or that before the ages neither Christ nor the Son—or the Spirit—is of God; or that the same one is the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; or that the Son was not begotten—or that the Spirit was begotten—or that the Father did not beget the Son by will or choice, nor make, create, or manifest him, but did so according to the all-knowing Word of God: the holy Catholic Church anathematizes all such persons.

[Note: In Hilary’s *Fragments*: “or that God the Father begot the Son neither by purpose nor by will”; these persons are all anathematized, etc. In *On Synods*: “or that the Father begot the Son neither by counsel nor by will; the holy [Church] anathematizes,” etc. In both places, as also in the Greek, the negation is present. The intervening words of our translation—“made” or “created,” etc.—appear nowhere.]

## The Statutes of the Holy Synod of Chalcedon Begin

[Note: The manuscript first places the definition of faith issued at Chalcedon in the sixth session, whose translation differs from the published versions. Then this heading follows; the words immediately following it are the final words of the address of the emperor Marcian, reported in the same session. The canons are then appended, since they were enacted in the following, seventh session, as is noted there. This note concerning the seventh session, which is not found in the other versions, clearly demonstrates that the Greek author of our collection did not use the commonly circulated manuscript of the canons. Consequently, this also confirms that the Greek collection he used was entirely different in origin from the collections used by the other translators.]

Our most devout emperor, the perpetual Augustus of Constantinople, said to the holy synod:

You are weary from enduring such prolonged toil. Wait, therefore, another three or four days, and, in the presence of our illustrious judges, state each of the matters you wish to bring forward, and you will obtain appropriate protection.

But before complete decisions concerning everything are issued, let none of you depart from the holy synod.

## Ecclesiastical Definitions Pronounced by the Holy and Universal Synod Gathered at Chalcedon

[Note: Acts of the seventh session of Chalcedon.]

[Note: We have demonstrated at greater length in our observations on Quesnel’s first dissertation, note 18, concerning the year 451, that the canons were enacted in the seventh session. It is evident from the entire context that the author of volume 11 of the Greek collection, who drew from the acts of the council, found the canons in the seventh session, after the emperor’s address.]

### I

We have judged it right that the canons established by the holy Fathers up to this synod should retain their force.

### II

If anyone has been ordained for money and has purchased a grace that was not for sale, and has ordained for money a bishop, chorepiscopus, presbyter, deacon, or anyone else enrolled among the clergy; or if, for money, he has appointed a steward, defender, doorkeeper, or any other person belonging to the canon for shameful and wicked profit, the person who attempts this, once convicted, shall risk losing his rank. The person who has been ordained shall gain nothing from the ordination or appointment obtained through payment, but shall be excluded from the dignity or office acquired by money.

[Note: Perhaps the reading is “unbought,” but more probably “not purchasable,” that is, “not for sale,” since the Greek has ἄπρατον.]

If anyone who intervened in such a matter is also found to have participated in shameful and unspeakable payments, then, if he is a cleric, let him lose his rank; but if he is a layman or monk, let him be anathematized.

[Note: The old edition reads “doorkeeper.” Isidore rendered the Greek word παραμονάριον as *paramonarius*. The editions of Dionysius of Justellus and two very ancient manuscripts of the old translation of the Council of Chalcedon, which received the canons from Dionysius, omit this word. The manuscripts of Rusticus, perhaps from an emendation by Rusticus himself, read *mansionarius*. Justinian, in book 4, chapter “On Bishops and Clerics,” lists *paramonarii* among the administrators of ecclesiastical property.]

### III

It has come to the holy synod’s attention that some clerics, for the sake of shameful profit, become lessees of other people’s possessions and undertake secular business, neglecting the service of God while frequenting the houses of secular persons and accepting the management of estates out of love of greed.

Therefore the holy and great synod has decreed that henceforth no bishop, cleric, or monk may lease a possession or involve himself in secular lawsuits, unless he is summoned by law to undertake the unavoidable office of guardian for minors, or unless the bishop of the city orders him to attend to ecclesiastical matters, to orphans and abandoned widows, or to persons who especially need ecclesiastical protection.

If anyone is thereafter known to transgress these decrees, let him be subject to ecclesiastical penalties.

### IV

Those who sincerely and truly choose the solitary life are worthy of fitting honor.

[Note: That is, the monastic life.]

But since some who wear the monastic habit disturb Churches and civil affairs, wandering through the cities and also establishing monasteries for themselves, it has been decided that no one may in any way build or establish a monastery or a house of prayer without the consent of the bishop of the city.

The monks who are in the several cities and provinces are to be subject to the bishop and to love quiet, devoting themselves to fasting and prayer, remaining observant in those places where they have renounced the world.

[Note: Read “persevering,” according to the Greek.]

They are not to frequent either ecclesiastical or secular affairs, nor leave their monasteries, unless perhaps the bishop of the city commands them to do so for some necessary purpose.

[Note: The Greek has χώρα, meaning rural districts or places, which are now called dioceses. Isidore rendered it as “possessions.”]

No one is to receive a slave into a monastery in order to make him a monk without the consent of his master.

Anyone who transgresses this definition of ours is, by our decree, to be excommunicated, so that the name of God may not be blasphemed.

The bishop of the city must provide suitable care for the monasteries.

### V

Concerning bishops or clerics who transfer themselves from one city to another, it has been decided that the canons established concerning them by the holy Fathers shall retain their force.

### VI

No one is to be ordained absolutely—neither a deacon, nor a presbyter, nor anyone at all belonging to the ecclesiastical order—unless he has been specifically designated for ordination in a Church of the city, on an estate, at a martyr shrine, or in a monastery.

With regard to those who are ordained absolutely, the holy synod has decreed that such ordination shall be invalid and ineffective, to the injury of the one who ordained them.

[Note: Dionysius states the matter more clearly: “and they may nowhere minister, to the injury of the ordaining bishop.”]

### VII

We decree that those who have once been ordained among the clergy, or who are monks, may not enter military service or a secular dignity. If they dare to do so and do not come to repentance and return to what they chose for God’s sake, let them be anathematized.

### VIII

Clerics placed by the bishops in charge of hospices, monasteries, or houses of prayer in each city are to remain there according to the tradition of the holy Fathers, and they must not contemptuously disregard their bishop.

Those who dare to oppose this arrangement in any way and do not submit to their own bishop are to be treated as follows: if they are clerics, let them be subject to canonical penalties; but if they are laymen or monks, let them be excommunicated.

IX. If a cleric has a case against another cleric, he must not abandon his bishop and run to secular courts; rather, he must first conduct the matter before his bishop, or, with that bishop’s consent, the matter may be heard before whomever both parties wish. If anyone acts otherwise, he shall be subject to canonical penalties. If a cleric has a case against his own or another bishop, he shall state his case before the synod of the province. But if the metropolitan bishop of that province [read: “if the bishop”], or a cleric, rejects [read: “has a case”], he shall proceed to the head of the diocese or to the imperial see of Constantinople and state his case before him.

X. A cleric may not serve simultaneously in the churches of two cities: in the one in which he was first ordained and in the one to which he has fled in order to attain greater advancement, namely because of a desire for vainglory. Those who do this must be restored to the church in which they were ordained at the beginning and serve there alone. If anyone transfers from one church to another, he shall have no share in anything belonging to the former church, or in the oratories [read: “which”] under it, or in the poorhouses or [Col. 0858D] hostels [read: “let him communicate”]. Those who dare, after the decree of this great and universal synod, to do anything concerning matters recently forbidden, the holy synod decrees that they be removed from their rank.

XI. We decree that all poor persons and those in need of assistance travel only with proof, letters, or ecclesiastical letters of peace [Col. 0859A], and not with letters of recommendation, since episcopal letters of recommendation are customarily granted to respectable persons.

XII. It has come to our attention that certain people, appealing against the ecclesiastical laws to civil authorities and dividing one province into two by means of official documents, have thereby made two metropolitans in one province. Therefore the holy synod decrees that henceforth no bishop attempt anything of this kind. Whoever attempts it shall be removed from his rank. Whatever cities have already been honored by imperial letters with the title of metropolitan shall enjoy the honor alone [read: “only”], and the bishop who governs that same church shall do so, with the metropolitan’s rights preserved according to the truth.

XIII. Clerics or readers from another city may in no way minister anywhere without letters of recommendation from their own bishop [Col. 0859B].

XIV. Since in certain provinces readers [supply: “and singers”] have been permitted to marry, the holy synod decrees that none of them may take a wife from another sect. As for those who have fathered children from such marriages: if children born of them have been baptized among heretics, they are to be offered to communion with the Catholic Church; but those who have not been baptized may not be baptized among heretics. Nor may they be joined in marriage to a heretic, a Jew, or a pagan, unless that person has promised to convert to the orthodox faith, which is joined [supply: “with”] the orthodox person. If anyone transgresses this decree of the holy synod, he shall be subject to canonical punishment.

[Col. 0859C] XV. A woman is not to be ordained a deaconess before the age of forty, and even then only after careful examination. If, after receiving ordination and persevering for some time in the ministry, she gives herself to marriage, despising God’s grace, she shall be anathematized, together with the man who has joined himself to her.

XVI. A virgin who has devoted herself to the Lord God, and likewise a monk, may not enter into marriage. If they are found doing this, they shall be excommunicated. We decree, however, that the local bishop has authority to show them mercy.

XVII. Rural parishes on estates are to remain undisturbed under the bishops who hold them, especially if they have administered them [Greek: ᾠκονόμησαν, “administered” or “governed,” not “built”] and held them inviolably for thirty years. If, within thirty years, any dispute concerning them has arisen or arises [Col. 0859D], those who claim to have been wronged may bring the matter before the synod of the province. If anyone is wronged by his metropolitan, he may state his case before the head of the diocese or before the see of Constantinople, as was stated above. If, by imperial authority, a new city has been established or an existing city restored, let them follow the civil and public formulas [that is, administrative arrangements] and the order of the ecclesiastical parishes [read: “let the order follow”].

XVIII. The crime of conspiracy and faction is forbidden even by secular laws; much more ought it to be prohibited in the Church of God. Therefore, whatever clerics or monks are found conspiring, forming factions, or plotting against bishops or fellow clerics shall be removed entirely from their rank.

XIX. It has reached the ears of the holy synod that canonical synods are not being held by the bishops in the provinces, and that as a result many matters requiring correction in ecclesiastical affairs are being neglected. Therefore the holy synod decrees, in accordance with the canons of the Fathers, that the bishops of each province assemble twice every year at the place designated by the metropolitan bishop, and correct each matter that arises. It fraternally rebukes bishops who do not assemble or who remain in their cities, although they are in good health and free from every [Col. 0859D] excusable [other versions: “inexcusable,” that is, “unavoidable”; the Greek expression is ἀπαραιτήτου] and necessary occupation [Col. 0860B].

XX. As we have already decreed, clerics residing in their own church may not be ordained in another city or church; they must remain content with the church in which they originally deserved to minister. This does not apply to those who have lost their native countries and have transferred, out of necessity, to another church. If, after this decree, one bishop receives a cleric belonging to another bishop, it has been decided that both the cleric who is received [supply from the Greek: “and the one received”] and the receiving bishop shall be excommunicated, until the cleric who transferred has returned to his own church.

XXI. Clerics and laypeople [read: “clerics or laypeople”] who accuse bishops or clerics without cause and without proof are not to be admitted as accusers until their reputation has first been examined.

[Col. 0860C] XXII. Clerics may not, after the death of their bishop, seize property belonging to him, as the canons also prohibited long ago; those who do this shall endanger their rank.

XXIII. It has reached the ears of the holy synod that certain clerics and monks, although no cause has been assigned to them by their bishop, and even when they come to this imperial city of Constantinople after being excommunicated by him [read: “and sometimes come after having been excommunicated by him,” etc.], remain there for a long time, cause disturbances and disorders in the ecclesiastical structure, and even overturn the houses of certain people. The holy synod decrees that such persons first be admonished by the defensor of the holy Church of Constantinople. If they shamelessly persist in the same conduct, they are to be expelled against their will by that same defensor and made to return to their own places.

XXIV. Monasteries once consecrated with the consent of the bishop are to remain monasteries forever, and the property belonging to them is to be preserved for the monastery. They may not be turned into secular dwellings. Those who permit this to happen shall be subject to the penalties of the canons.

XXV. Since, as we have found, certain metropolitans neglect the flocks entrusted to them and delay the ordinations of bishops, it has pleased the holy synod that the ordinations of bishops be carried out within three months [Col. 0861A], unless perhaps unavoidable necessity compels the period of delay to be extended. If he does not do this, he shall be subject to ecclesiastical punishment. The revenues of the widowed church are to be kept safe with the treasurer of that same church.

XXVI. Since, as we have found, in certain churches ecclesiastical property is administered without treasurers, it has pleased the synod that every church having a bishop also have a treasurer from its clergy to administer ecclesiastical property with the consent of his bishop, so that the administration of the church may not be without witnesses [Col. 0862A], its property thereby be scattered, and reproach be brought upon the priesthood [read: “the priesthood”]. If he does not do this, he shall be subject to the sacred canons.

XXVII. Concerning those who abduct women under the pretext of marriage, and those who come to the aid of the abductors, the holy synod decrees that, if they are clerics, they be removed from their rank; if they are laypeople, they be anathematized.

The Chalcedonian decrees end.

[Col. 0861]

# ANCIENT DOCUMENTS OF CANON LAW (C)

## PREFACE TO THE FOLLOWING COLLECTION

### 1.

Among the documents of ancient canon law, we shall first present the canons of the Council of Carthage of the year 419, as they are read in the most ancient Latin manuscript collections: Vatican Regina 1997, Lucca 88, and Barberini 2888, with Vatican 1342 being similar to the latter. In his variant readings for the *Code of the Canons of the African Church*, Christopher Justellus cites two other copies, the Thuaneus, which is the same as Colbertinus 784 cited by P. Constantius, and the Bochardianus; these present these canons in exactly the same manner.

Dionysius Exiguus, in his collection, gave us the entire synod of Carthage of the year 419, which is printed in the edition of the Councils after Justellus under the title *Code of the Canons of the African Church*. We have shown in the treatise, Part II, chapter 3, section 8, that it is presented there as comprising two sessions. In the manuscripts and collections mentioned above, the same preface found in Dionysius is reproduced, together with the same speeches of the bishops preceding the canons. But only the canons of the first session are included. Whereas in Dionysius these constitute the first thirty-three canons, in the manuscripts mentioned above they are divided into forty canons.

Then, omitting excerpts from other synods under Aurelius that were reread in the same session, and also omitting the canons of the second session—all of which are available in Dionysius—the subscriptions and the letter of the Africans to Pope Boniface are appended. Next there is inserted the so-called letter of Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, together with a *formata*; concerning these omissions by Dionysius we have said enough in the cited passage of the treatise, section 8. Finally, the collection concludes with another letter of the same Africans to Pope Celestine.

Our intention is to present only the canons, together with the subscriptions of the Fathers, from our manuscripts. For, besides the fact that their division into forty canons, found in these manuscripts, has hitherto been unknown, the readings of certain canons differ so greatly in them from those of Dionysius that they seem to have been composed in another synod and expressed in different words.

### 2.

The second document is a synod of Carthage of the year 421, hitherto unpublished, which we recovered from the very ancient manuscript of the Veronese chapter, numbered 55. Although nine of the ten canons of that synod are repeated from the Council of Carthage of 419, some portions of them are nevertheless expressed differently, as seemed more suitable to the bishops.

Moreover, all the canons that Ferrandus attributes to the Council of Hippo-Regius of 427 are found in this synod; for that reason they were repeated from this synod in the same Council of Hippo-Regius.

### 3.

Next will follow the *Ancient Statutes of the Church*, concerning which we have discussed at greater length in the preceding treatise, Part II, chapter 3, section 4. These are commonly circulated from Isidore’s collection under the name of the Fourth Council of Carthage of 398, but they are arranged in a different order and are found in our Italian collections. In the passage cited above we showed that they are much older not only than the Isidorian collection but also than the Hispanic collection, and that they were not issued in any particular synod, but were compiled from various canons, partly Greek and partly Latin, for the most part abbreviated, and partly from certain more solemn rubrics.

Stephanus Baluzius, in his note on chapter 443 of Regino, expressed surprise that they had not been printed by Binius [it should read: “by Crabbe”], as they occur in our manuscripts, since Binius had seen two copies of this kind, one from the monastery of Gembloux and the other from Saint Bavo at Ghent. When Baluzius himself later obtained such a very ancient manuscript, he promised that he would publish them there:

> “Since the matter is important, and those statutes have long held authority in the Church, we shall at some time publish them from a very ancient manuscript.”

But because he was unable to complete this task, being occupied with other concerns, we shall now carry it out, since we have found several very ancient manuscripts and collections of different origins containing the same statutes. We shall identify in the first note the manuscript copies chiefly used by us, which belong to three outstanding collections.

We have preferred the title *Ancient Statutes of the Church* to the other titles mentioned in the treatise at the cited place, both because it is supported by more numerous and more important manuscripts and because it seemed to agree better with the canons themselves than the other inscriptions.

Three of these statutes—namely, 15, 55, and 73—are attributed in the commonly published councils to the Synod of Agde, as canons 49, 69, and 70. But that what was inserted in that synod after canon 47 and up to canon 70 is supplementary is clear both from the more excellent codices containing the Gallican synods—Vatican Palatine 574, the Veronese 59, and other very ancient manuscripts cited by Sirmond, which lack these canons—and from the Hispanic collection, in which the same supplementary canons are presented not with the Council of Agde but separately, in chapter 45, with this heading:
