> “Sentences which are not found in the ancient copies of the councils but were inserted by certain persons.”

For this reason they were also printed separately with this heading by Garzia Loaisa together with the Hispanic councils after the Seventeenth Council of Toledo.

### 4.

In three ancient Italian collections, whose manuscripts you will find listed in the first note to the fourth monument, two other insufficiently known documents of ancient canon law are read together with the *Ancient Statutes*. One is entitled *Canonical Letter*, the other *Precepts of Saint Peter*.

When Atto of Vercelli found the *Canonical Letter* in a manuscript collection of additions to Dionysius—still preserved at this time in the library of the cathedral chapter of that same Church of Vercelli—he wrote about it to Ambrose, a priest of Milan. His letter was published in the Dacherian *Spicilegia*, volume I, page 439. Among other things he wrote:

> “We earnestly request your sincere charity concerning the Letter found among the canons, which is also called canonical. It is known to contain eleven chapters, which seem to us extremely useful. Its beginning is: ‘First of all, all priests and deacons must hold the Catholic faith,’ etc.”

He chiefly sought information about the author and date of that letter. Its author, however, is uncertain, though he may be believed to have been Italian, since the letter has so far been found only in Italian collections. As for its date, from the antiquity of the Barberini 2888 collection we recognize that it was famous in the sixth century and had already been transferred into collections by then; it must therefore be somewhat older.

Stephanus Baluzius published the letter from Sirmond’s papers in volume II of the *Capitularies*, appendix 5, column 1374, with this title, which we have found nowhere else: *Chapters given to priests, deacons, and subdeacons*. Sirmondus, as the same Baluzius testifies in his notes on Book I of the *Capitularies*, column 1131, found it in two manuscripts, one Cassinese and one Vatican—that is, in Italian codices. P. Dominicus Mansi most recently reprinted it from another Italian manuscript, that of Lucca, in volume I of the *Supplement to the Councils*, column 817.

We have not thought it should be separated from the *Ancient Statutes* and the *Precepts of Saint Peter*, with which it is joined in the Italian collections.

### 5.

The *Precepts of Saint Peter concerning the preservation of the sacraments*, which in the collections mentioned above bear the form of a letter attributed to Pope Clement I, appear to have been published in the commonly printed Councils under the title: *The Second Letter of Pope Clement I to James, the Brother of the Lord*. They are partly the same and partly different. For the letter in our collections is shorter, and the passages that agree in both are presented in an entirely different order.

Nor do we therefore believe this to be a genuine work of Clement. Just as the *Apostolic Recognitions*, divided into ten books, and another letter to James—which is shorter in some ancient collections than in the commonly printed versions and passed especially into the Quesnellian collection, chapter 64—were falsely attributed to Saint Clement, yet had an ancient origin and, having been given Latin form by Rufinus, gained currency among the Latins, so we think the same must be judged concerning this letter as well.

In the manuscripts of the very ancient collection Barberini 2888 and Vatican 1342, this letter follows another letter of Clement, which everyone acknowledges was rendered into Latin by Rufinus. We found the same arrangement in the very ancient abbreviation of the canons contained in manuscript 59 of the Veronese chapter, as will be clear from the description of that codex, which we presented in Part III of the treatise.

In another manuscript, Sangermanensis 541, the same letter follows not only another letter to James but also the books of the *Recognitions* attributed to Clement, together with the dedicatory preface of Rufinus the translator to Saint Gaudentius, as may be seen in Montfaucon, volume II of the *Bibliotheca bibliothecarum*, page 1132.

Rufinus, therefore, seems to be called the translator of all of them. The passages inserted into both letters in the commonly printed Councils, however, are to be attributed to Isidore Mercator, as is also the disordered arrangement of the second letter. It is therefore of great importance to present this second letter here as it was rendered into Latin by Rufinus and transferred from him into the ancient collections. The Rufinian version of the first letter can be recovered from chapter 64 of the collection presented above.

### 6.

We shall conclude with a most valuable unpublished document, which we recovered from manuscript Vatican Regina 1997. Of Glycerius, who held the imperial power in Italy for a very brief time, scarcely any mention survives among writers. His constitution will now be published, issued at the beginning of his reign against simoniacal ordinations.

He ascended to the imperial power on 5 March of the year 473, as we learn from the list of consuls published by Cuspinianus and more accurately reprinted by the Bollandists according to the model of the Caesarean manuscript, volume VI, Act 2, Part II, page 188, where the following is found relevant to our subject:

> “Under Leo Augustus V [that is, the year 473]. In this consulship the emperor Glycerius was elevated at Ravenna on the third day before the Nones of March.”

The constitution itself, issued in the same city, is dated the fifth day before the Ides of that month. It was addressed to Himelco, whom we know from this single document as prefect of the praetorium of Italy. In the same codex there follows an edict of Himelco, by which the same constitution was promulgated at Rome on the third day before the Kalends of May of that year. We shall print this edict as well, since it should not be separated from the constitution.

# 635 CANONS

[Editorial note: Codex Vatican 1342 gives this title in the preceding table, number 10: “Titles of the Forty Carthaginian Canons.” Manuscript Vatican Regina 1997 has: “Responses and constitutions enacted at Carthage.” In the notes we shall also use the variants presented by Christopher Justellus from two manuscripts, the Bochardianus and the Thuaneus, now Colbertinus 784, which preserve a similar division and form of these canons. We have also used the variants published by P. Dominicus Mansi from the Lucca manuscript 88, volume I of the *Supplement to the Councils*, page 305.]

## OF THE COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE HELD IN THE YEAR 419

*(As they are read in the most ancient Italian manuscript collections.)*

[Col. 0863A]

### I. On observing the decrees of the Council of Nicaea

Bishop Aurelius said:

[Editorial note: In the preceding material, which we omitted for the sake of brevity, the canons of the Council of Nicaea are said to have been read.]

These are the copies of the decrees that our Fathers at that time brought back with them from the Council of Nicaea. Preserving their form, let the enactments that follow, confirmed by us, be kept.

[Editorial note: Vatican 1342 reads “that follow.” The manuscripts of Justellus delete *firmata* (“confirmed”) and read *custodiuntur* (“are kept”). Dionysius has “shall be kept.”]

### II. On proclaiming the Trinity

The entire council said:

By God’s favor, the ecclesiastical faith handed down by us must first be confessed in this glorious assembly with a common profession; [Col. 0864A] only then is the ecclesiastical order of each person to be established with the consent of all.

[Editorial note: Dionysius reads “is to be preserved.” The manuscripts of Justellus then read “for proving.”]

For the strengthening of the minds of our brothers and fellow bishops who have recently been promoted, those things must be set forth which we received from the Fathers as a fixed ordinance, so that we may instruct God’s people in the unity of the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—which we retain as consecrated in our minds and which is known to have no distinction—just as we profess it.

[Editorial note: Dionysius reads: “so also God’s peoples.”]

All the bishops recently promoted likewise said:

“Certainly, this is what we have received, this is what we hold, and this is what we teach, following the evangelical faith together with your doctrine.”

### III. On continence

Bishop Aurelius said:

When continence and the discipline of chastity were discussed in the previous council [the manuscripts of Justellus read: “concerning the discipline of continence”], these three ranks—which are joined by a certain bond of chastity through their consecrations—namely bishops, presbyters, and deacons [Dionysius: “bishops, I mean, presbyters, and deacons”], were decreed, as is fitting for holy overseers and priests of God, as well as for levites and those who serve the divine sacraments, to be continent in all things, so that they may simply obtain from the Lord whatever they ask, and so that we too may preserve what the apostles taught and antiquity itself observed.

[Editorial note: Dionysius, canon 4.]

Bishop Faustinus of the Church of Potentia in the province of Picenum, legate of the Roman Church, said:

“It is pleasing that the bishop, presbyter, and deacon, or those who handle the sacraments, guardians of chastity, abstain from their wives.”

All the bishops said:

“It is pleasing that chastity be preserved in all things and by all who serve at the altar.”

[Editorial note: Dionysius omits the words “in all things” and “by all.”]

### IV. On not invading the boundaries of the Fathers

[Col. 0865B]

[Editorial note: Dionysius, canon 5.]

Bishop Aurelius said:

No one, surely, doubts that avaricious desire is the mother of every evil. Therefore it must be restrained [the manuscripts of Justellus and Dionysius read “restrained”; Vatican 1342 has “avoided”], lest anyone usurp another’s boundaries or, by payment, cross the boundaries established by the Fathers.

### V. That no cleric may lend at interest

Nor may any cleric at all receive interest on any matter. Although new proposals, whether obscure or concealed under [Editorial note: Dionysius omits “a different kind of”] another form, will be examined by us and given a proper form, nevertheless no judgment is to be issued concerning matters that divine Scripture has expressly established; rather, its provisions must be carried out.

Therefore, what is condemned in laypeople ought much more to be condemned beforehand [Editorial note: Dionysius deletes “also”] in clerics.

The entire council said:

“No one acts against the prophets or against the Gospels without endangering himself.”

[Editorial note: Dionysius deletes “and.” The manuscripts of Justellus then read “All said” instead of “The entire council said.” We have supplied “his own” from the manuscripts of Justellus.]

### VI. On chrism, reconciliation, and the consecration of girls

[Editorial note: Dionysius, canon 6.]

Bishop Fortunatus said:

“We remember that it was established in previous councils that chrism, or the reconciliation of penitents, and the consecration of girls are not to be performed by presbyters. If anyone should be found doing this, what ought to be decreed concerning him?”

Bishop Aurelius said:

“Your dignity has heard the proposal of our brother and fellow bishop Fortunatus. What do you say about this?”

All the bishops said:

“The preparation of chrism and the consecration of girls are not to be performed by presbyters; nor is a presbyter permitted to reconcile anyone at a public Mass. This is pleasing to all.”

### VII. On reconciling the sick

[Editorial note: Dionysius, canon 7.]

Bishop Aurelius said:

“If anyone is in danger and asks to be reconciled to the divine altars, then, if the bishop is absent, the presbyter must certainly consult the bishop and, on the bishop’s instructions, reconcile the person in danger. We ought to strengthen this matter with sound counsel.”

All the bishops said:

“It is pleasing that Your Holiness has deemed it necessary to instruct us in this matter.”

### VIII. [Editorial note: This is the reading of Vatican 1342. The manuscripts of Justellus have: “A criminal must not be admitted to accuse a bishop.”]

That no criminal may accuse a bishop.

Bishop Numidius of Massula said:

“Moreover, there are very many persons of bad conduct who think that the elders or bishops should be summoned indiscriminately and indiscreetly for accusation. Should such persons be admitted so easily or not?”

[Editorial note: The manuscripts of Justellus and Lucca add “against the apostolic rule.” The Council under Genethlius, canon 6, also has this reading, from which this canon was taken. For “certain crimes,” Vatican 1342 has “such a crime.” At the end Dionysius adds “It is pleasing”; we have removed it as superfluous, following the Vatican manuscript.]

Bishop Aurelius said:

“Is it therefore pleasing to your charity that a person entangled in certain crimes should have no right to bring an accusation against the elders?”

All the bishops said:

“If he is a criminal, let him not be admitted.”

### IX. On the excommunicated

Bishop Augustine, legate of the province of Numidia, said:

“Deign to establish this: if any persons have rightly been expelled from the Church because of their crimes, and have been received into communion by some bishop or presbyter, let that person also be held liable to the same crime as they, because they have fled from the regular judgment of their bishop.”

[Editorial note: Burchard and Ivo read “when they flee.” The manuscripts of Justellus add after “judgment” the words “which ought to be rendered.” More correctly, in the Council under Genethlius, canon 7, from which this canon was excerpted, after “received” come the words “fleeing from the regular judgment of their bishop”; then follows “let that person also,” and so forth.]

All the bishops said:

“This is pleasing to all.”

### X. On those excommunicated persons who dare to erect an altar and offer sacrifice

Bishop Alypius of the Church of Tagaste, legate of the province of Numidia, said:

“This also must not be omitted: if some presbyter, corrected by his bishop and inflated by resentment or pride, should think that sacrifices are to be offered to God separately [the manuscripts of Justellus read: “that he should offer sacrifice to God”], or should believe that another altar ought to be erected against ecclesiastical faith or discipline, he must not escape unpunished.”

Bishop Valentinus of the first see of the province of Numidia said:

“What our brother Alypius has set forth is necessarily in accord with ecclesiastical discipline and faith. Therefore, state what seems good to your affection.”

[Editorial note: Dionysius deletes “thereupon.” Vatican and Colbertinus read *proferte* (“state”); Dionysius has *edicite* (“declare”). The Bochard manuscript in Justellus reads *proferre edicite* (“declare to be stated”).]

All the bishops said:

“If a presbyter has been corrected by his superior, he must certainly complain to neighboring bishops, so that his case may be heard by them and through them he may be reconciled to his own bishop. If he does not do this, but instead, inflated by pride—as God forbid—considers that he should separate himself from communion with his bishop, and, making a schism with certain people, offers sacrifice to God separately, let him nevertheless be regarded as accursed and lose his position. But if he has a just complaint against his bishop [Dionysius, together with Vatican, inserts “not”; we have removed it with the manuscripts of Justellus, since this negation is not found in canon 8 of the Council under Genethlius, from which this canon was repeated], the matter must be investigated.”

### XI. On hearing bishops, presbyters, and deacons

[Editorial note: The manuscripts of Justellus have: “How bishops, presbyters, and deacons are to be heard.”]

[Editorial note: Dionysius, canon 12.]

Bishop Felix said:

“I propose, according to the decrees of the ancient councils, that if a bishop—something we do not wish—should incur some charge and be under such pressing necessity [Dionysius less correctly: “so that many cannot be assembled”] that many cannot assemble, then, so that he does not remain under accusation, he should be heard by twelve bishops; a presbyter should be heard by six or seven bishops together with his own bishop [Dionysius does not know “or seven,” nor does the Council under Genethlius, canon 10]; and a deacon by three.”

### XII. On ordaining bishops

[Editorial note: Dionysius, canon 13.]

Bishop Aurelius said:

“What does Your Holiness say to this?”

All the bishops said:

“The decrees of the ancients must be preserved, and many bishops must not presume so readily to ordain a bishop without consulting the primate of each province.”

[Editorial note: Dionysius adds: “unless there is necessity.”]

“But if there is necessity, three bishops, wherever they may be, must ordain the bishop at his command. If anyone acts contrary to his own declaration or subscription in any matter, he shall separate himself from this assembly.”

[Editorial note: Dionysius reads: “he shall deprive himself of his honor.” The manuscripts of Justellus read: “he separated himself from this assembly,” or, according to the correction, “he shall separate himself.” We have preferred the Lucca manuscript, which differs only slightly from Vatican, where the reading is simply “let him be separated.”]

### XIII. On the legate of Tripoli and on hearing a presbyter and deacon

[Editorial note: Read: “On the Tripolitan legate.”]

[Col. 0867C]

[Editorial note: Dionysius, canon 14, begins: “It was also pleasing.”]

It was indeed decided, concerning Tripoli, that, because of the poverty of the province, one bishop should come as legate, and that there a presbyter should be heard by five bishops and a deacon by three, as stated above, while his own bishop remains present.

[Editorial note: The three following words are omitted by the manuscripts of Justellus and Lucca. They are found in Vatican, as in Dionysius.]

### XIV. That no cleric may be judged in a public court

[Editorial note: Dionysius, canon 15, adds: “It was also decided that.”]

Whoever among the bishops, presbyters, deacons, or clerics, when an accusation has been brought against him in the Church or a civil case has been initiated, wishes, after abandoning ecclesiastical judgment, to clear himself in public courts [Dionysius likewise reads “wishes to clear himself”; the Thuaneus reads “to clear”; the better reading, with Vatican, is “to clear himself”], even if a judgment has been issued in his favor, shall lose his position in a criminal matter. In a civil matter, if he prefers to retain his position, he shall lose what he has won.

It was also decided that, whenever an appeal has been made from any ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges of greater authority, this must not harm those whose judgment has been overturned, unless they can be convicted either of having judged with an inimical spirit or of having been corrupted by some desire or favor. But if the judges were chosen by agreement of the parties, it shall not be permitted to appeal even from a smaller number than that which has been established.

### XV. On spectacles

It was decided that the sons of priests not only must not present secular spectacles [Dionysius lacks the words “not only.” The Vatican manuscript has: “but they may not even await them”; here *liceat* (“it is permitted”) was mistakenly written for *licet* (“although”), and *exspectare eis* (“for them to await”) for *spectent* (“they should watch”)], but must not even watch them. Although this has always been forbidden to all Christians, they should not approach places where there are blasphemies at all.

### XVI. That clerics should not be contractors

[Editorial note: Dionysius, canon 16, and some of our manuscripts read: “It was decided that bishops”; then: “It was also decided that readers”; and afterward: “It was also decided that a cleric.”]

Bishops, presbyters, and deacons must not be contractors or agents, nor may they seek their livelihood through any disgraceful or dishonorable business, because they ought to heed the statement written: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs.”

### XVII. Readers are ordered to marry

When readers reach the age of puberty, they must be compelled either to take wives or to profess continence.

### XVIII. A cleric must receive what, or as much as, he has lent

[Col. 0868C]

If a cleric has lent money, he shall receive money; if a specific object, that same object; whatever is owed to him, he shall receive.

[Editorial note: Dionysius reads: “He shall receive as much as he gave.”]

### XIX. No one is to be promoted to an order before the age of twenty-five

[Editorial note: This is the reading of Vatican. Dionysius has: “And that before the age of twenty-five neither deacons are to be ordained nor virgins consecrated.”]

No one is to be ordained a deacon before the age of twenty-five or a presbyter before the age of thirty, nor are virgins to be consecrated; and readers are not to greet the people.

### XX. On the primacy of Mauritania Sitifensis
[Note: [Col. 0868D] Dionysius, canon 17: “It was decided that, at the request of the primate of the province of Numidia, from whose assembly it is separated, Mauretania Sitifensis should have its own primate; and, with the consent of all the primates of the African provinces, or of all the bishops, it was permitted to have one because of the length of the journey.”]

When the bishops of Mauretania Sitifensis requested their own primate, the entire council of the bishops of Numidia, with the consent of all the primates or of all the bishops of the African provinces, permitted them, because of the novelty of the long journey, to have one; this was done with the advice of the Church of Carthage.

[Note: [Col. 0869C] Thus the Vatican manuscript. Other manuscripts, less correctly, read “because of the novelty of a long journey.” Shortly afterward, permissa est (“was permitted”) seems to require correction and supplementation to permisit (“permitted”), and so forth.]

641 XXI. On the Ordination of Bishops and Clerics

[Note: [Col. 0869C] Dionysius, canon 18.]

It was likewise decided that, at the ordination of bishops or clerics, the decisions of the council should first be impressed upon their ears by their ordainers, so that, if they should do anything contrary to the council’s statutes, they might repent.

[Note: [Col. 0869C] Dionysius has: “that, when bishops or clerics have been ordained, the decisions of the councils should first be impressed upon their ears by their ordainers, lest they regret having done anything contrary to the council’s statutes.” Our manuscripts agree with the printed text, except that the Vatican manuscript has conciliorum (“of the councils”) in the first place instead of concilii (“of the council”), while retaining concilii in the second; and instead of poeniteant (“they may repent”) it has poeniteat (“he may repent”).]

XXII.

[Note: [Col. 0869C] Dionysius joins this and the following canon to the preceding one [Col. 0869D] and has “It was likewise decided that Eucharist should not be given to bodies”; instead of “for it was said … and the dead … baptize,” he has “it is written … and that the dead … be baptized.” The Bochard manuscript has etiam (“even”) instead of jam (“now”).]

That the Eucharist not be given to the bodies of the dead.

For it was said: “Take and eat”; but corpses can neither take nor eat. And let the negligence of presbyters no longer cause dead people to be baptized.

XXIII. That Councils Be Held Twice Each Year

For this reason it must be confirmed in this holy synod that, in accordance with the statutes of Nicaea, councils are to be held every year because of ecclesiastical matters which, often to the ruin of the congregations, grow stale through delay. Every year, therefore, the provinces that possess primatial sees shall send from their councils two bishops as delegates, or as many as they may choose, so that, when the whole assembly has been gathered, its authority may be complete.

[Note: [Col. 0869D] Dionysius has “a council be convened, to which …” He also omits integro (“whole”). The reading should be ad quae (“to which,” feminine, referring to provinciae) rather than ad quos.]

XXIV. On the Accusation of a Bishop

[Note: [Col. 0869D] The Justinian manuscripts have “On accused bishops.”]

[Note: [Col. 0869D] Dionysius, canon 19.]

Bishop Aurelius said:

If any bishop is accused, the accuser shall refer the case to the primate of that province. The person against whom the charge is brought shall not be suspended from communion unless, having been summoned by letter to appear on the appointed day before judges chosen to hear his case, he fails altogether to appear—that is, within one month from the day on which it is established that he received the letter.

[Note: [Col. 0869D] The Justinian manuscripts add unius (“one”).]

But if he proves genuine reasons of necessity by which it is clear that he was unable to appear, he shall have full opportunity to present his case within the following month. Nevertheless, after the second month he shall not communicate until he has cleared himself.

If he refuses to appear at the annual universal council, so that his case may at least be settled there, he shall be judged to have pronounced the sentence of condemnation upon himself. During the period in which he does not communicate, he shall communicate neither in his own church nor in his parish.

[Note: [Col. 0869D] Dionysius has “or parish.”]

His accuser, however, if he has never failed to appear on the days appointed for the hearing of the case, shall not be removed from communion. But if at any time he has been absent by withdrawing himself, then, once the bishop has been restored to communion, the accuser himself shall be removed from communion. Even so, he shall not be deprived of the opportunity to pursue the case if he proves that he did not refuse to appear on the appointed day, but was unable to do so.

[Note: [Col. 0869D] Our manuscripts have noluisse (“to have refused”); Dionysius and the Justinian manuscripts have non voluisse (“not to have wished”). In the Justinian edition of the African code, from the manuscript of Nicolas Fabri, the better reading is non noluisse (“not to have refused”), which is necessary to the context; we have adopted it.]

But when he has begun to act before the judgment of the bishops, if the accuser’s person is culpable, he shall not be admitted to bring an accusation unless he wishes to assert his own cases, though not ecclesiastical ones.

[Note: [Col. 0870C] The Justinian manuscripts have “if that accuser is culpable.”]

XXV. On Accused Presbyters and Deacons

[Note: [Col. 0870C] Dionysius, canon 20.]

If presbyters or deacons are accused, a lawful number of colleagues from neighboring places shall be joined to their own bishop, chosen at the request of the accused themselves; that is, five bishops in the case of a presbyter and two in the case of a deacon shall examine their case together, while the same procedure concerning days, delays, exclusion from communion, and the examination of persons shall be observed between the accusers and the accused. The cases of the remaining clerics shall be heard and settled by the bishop of the place alone.

[Note: [Col. 0870C] Dionysius has: “in the case of a presbyter, six; in the case of a deacon, three; let them examine their case.” The Vatican manuscript has “in the case of a presbyter, five or six; in the case of a deacon, two or three; let them examine the case,” and so forth. The Lucian manuscript was preferred; with it, the numbers five and two agree with the manuscripts of Justinian, Thuanus, and Bochardus, especially since the same numbers are preferred by the Breviary of Hippo, canon 8, from which this canon was repeated. If different numbers are read above in canon 11, it should be noted that that canon was repeated from another council under Genethlius, whose canon 10 increases the number of colleague-judges.]

XXVI. On the Marriages of Clerics [Read: de conjugiis, “on the marriages of clerics.”]

[Col. 0870C]

[Note: [Col. 0870D] Dionysius, canon 22, has “It was again decided that …” Shortly afterward he omits the words “or schismatics,” which, apart from the manuscripts used in our edition, are also found in the Breviary of Hippo, canon 12.]

And it was decided that the children of clerics should not be joined in marriage to pagans, heretics, or schismatics.

643 XXVII. On the Heirs of Clerics

[Note: [Col. 0870D] Dionysius, canon 22, has: “And that bishops or clerics should contribute nothing by donations of their property to those who are not Catholic Christians, even if they are relatives.” The beginning of our edition, which we have taken especially from the Vatican manuscript, agrees with canon 13 of the Breviary.]

A bishop or any cleric shall give nothing by donation of the bishop’s or cleric’s property to those who are not Catholic Christians, even if they are relatives.

[Note: [Col. 0871C] [ [Col. 0871] The following note appears at the foot of column 871, but the callout letter (c) is missing.] Dionysius, canon 24.]

XXVIII. That Bishops Not Travel Overseas

[Col. 0871A]

[Note: [Col. 0871C] Dionysius, canon 23.]

It was likewise decided that bishops should not travel overseas without consulting the bishop of the primatial see of their respective province, so that they might especially obtain from him a forma, or letter of recommendation.

[Note: [Col. 0871C] Dionysius has “or commendatory letters.”]

XXIX. On the Canonical Scriptures

Nothing besides the canonical Scriptures shall be read in the Church under the name of divine Scripture. The canonical Scriptures are as follows:

Of the Old Testament: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, the four books of Kings, the two books of Chronicles, Job, the Psalter, and the five books of Solomon.

[Note: [Col. 0871C] Dionysius omits the words “of the Old Testament.”]

The books of the Prophets: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel; the book of the Twelve Prophets; Tobias, Judith, Esther, and the two books of Ezra.

[Col. 0871B]

The two books of Maccabees.

Of the New Testament: the four books of the Gospels; one book of the Acts of the Apostles; fourteen epistles of the Apostle Paul; two epistles of the Apostle Peter; three epistles of the Apostle John; one epistle of the Apostle James; one epistle of the Apostle Jude; and one book, the Apocalypse of John.

[Note: [Col. 0871C] Dionysius omits the word “Apostle” after “Paul.”]

This is also to be made known to our brother and fellow priest Boniface, bishop of the city of Rome, or to the other bishops of those regions, for the confirmation of this canon, since we have received from the Fathers that this is how it is to be read in the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0871C] Dionysius lacks the words “bishop of the city of Rome,” which are supplied by the Thuanus and Bochardus manuscripts. In the Vatican manuscript, venerabili (“venerable”) is read instead of “of the city of Rome.” Dionysius has “these … are to be read.”]

XXX. On Continence and on Those Who Handle the Sacraments

[Note: [Col. 0871D] Dionysius, canon 25.]

We add, dearest brothers, that, since reports had been made concerning the incontinence of certain clerics, even readers, toward their own wives, it was decided—as had also been confirmed in various councils—that subdeacons who handle the sacred mysteries, and deacons, presbyters, and bishops as well, should, in accordance with the earlier statutes, abstain from their wives, so that they may appear to be as though they did not have them. If they do not do so, they shall be removed from ecclesiastical office.

[Note: [Col. 0871D] The Justinian manuscripts have “sacred ministries.”]

The other clerics, however, are not to be compelled to this until a more mature age, as stated above, namely thirty years.

[Note: [Col. 0871D] The words “as stated above” are absent from Dionysius.]

The entire council said: “What your holiness has decreed—things just, moderate, holy, and pleasing to God—we confirm and order to be upheld in every respect.”

[Note: [Col. 0871D] Dionysius has “We confirm what has been justly and moderately regulated.”]

XXXI. That No One Alienate Church Property

[Note: [Col. 0871D] Dionysius, canon 26.]

It was likewise decided that no one should sell church property. But if it produces no income and some extreme necessity compels such a course, the matter must be reported to the primate of that province, so that he may determine, together with the prescribed number of bishops, whether it ought to be done.

[Note: [Col. 0871D] The Vatican manuscript has “of the first province.” Perhaps “to the primatial see of the province” should be read.]

If such a great necessity presses upon the Church that prior consultation is impossible, the bishop shall at least summon neighboring bishops as witnesses, taking care to report all the needs of his church to the council. If he fails to do this, the seller shall be held guilty before God and the holy council and, having lost his honor, shall be punished.

XXXII. On Presbyters Who Have Fallen

[Col. 0872B]

[Note: [Col. 0871D] Dionysius, canon 27.]

It was likewise confirmed that, if presbyters or deacons are ever convicted of some more serious fault for which it is necessary to remove them from the ministry, hands are not to be laid upon them either as upon penitents or as upon faithful laypeople.

[Note: [Col. 0871D] The words “or as upon penitents, or as upon faithful laypeople” are deleted in the Vatican manuscript.]

XXXIII. On Those Who Have Been Rebaptized

Nor is it to be permitted that those who have been rebaptized be promoted to the clerical order.

XXXIV. On Hearing Clerics and on Appeals

[Note: [Col. 0871D] Dionysius, canon 28.]

It was likewise decided that, if presbyters, deacons, or other inferior clerics complain in their cases about the judgment of their own bishops, neighboring bishops, with the consent of their bishop, shall hear them. Whatever the case may be, the bishops appointed by them shall settle it between them.

[Note: [Col. 0872C] Dionysius lacks the three words “whatever the case may be.” Shortly afterward, the Justinian manuscripts have “let them settle it, with their bishops consenting.”]

But if they should think that an appeal ought also to be made from those bishops, they shall not appeal to overseas tribunals, but to the primates of their provinces or to a universal council, as has also often been decreed concerning bishops.

[Note: [Col. 0872C] The Vatican manuscript has this reading. The Justinian manuscripts differ slightly: “It shall not be permitted to them except to appeal to the primates of their provinces, or to a universal council.” Dionysius omits only the words “or to a universal council.” Yet the letters of the Africans on this matter to Pope Coelestine show that those words are necessary: “Each person is permitted, if he has been offended by the judgment of those who heard the case, to appeal to the councils of his province, or even to a universal council.” On this authority, Justellus inserted the same words in his edition of the African code; but he admits that he did not find them in Nicolas Fabri’s manuscript or in any other manuscript of Dionysius, just as they are not found in the Greek version of the same African code, that is, of Dionysius.]

Anyone who thinks an appeal should be made overseas shall be received into communion by no one within that same province.

[Note: [Col. 0872D] Dionysius has “shall be received into communion by no one within Africa.”]

XXV. On Excommunicated Clerics

[Col. 0873A]

[Note: [Col. 0873C] Dionysius, canon 29.]

It was likewise resolved by the entire council that anyone who has been excommunicated for his own negligence, whether a bishop or any cleric, and who, during the time of his excommunication, presumes to receive communion before a hearing, shall be judged to have pronounced the sentence of condemnation upon himself.

XXXVI. On the Accused

[Note: [Col. 0873C] Dionysius, canon 30.]

It was likewise decided that the accused or the accuser, in the place from which the accused comes, if he fears some violence from a reckless crowd, shall choose a nearby place where it will not be difficult to bring witnesses, so that his case may be concluded.

[Note: [Col. 0873C] Dionysius adds “and there the case may be concluded.” The council cited below also has “and there the case may be concluded.”]

XXXVII. On Those Who Despise Their Orders

[Note: [Col. 0873C] Dionysius, canon 31.]

It was likewise decided that any clerics or deacons who, for the needs of the churches, do not obey their bishops when the bishops wish to promote them to greater honor in their own church, shall not minister in the rank from which they refused to withdraw.

[Note: [Col. 0873C] Dionysius inserts illic (“there”).]

XXXVIII. That No One Appropriate Church Property for Himself

[Note: [Col. 0873D] Dionysius, canon 32.]

It was likewise decided that bishops, presbyters, deacons, or any clerics who are ordained possessing nothing, and who, during the time of their episcopate or clerical office, acquire lands or any estates in their own name or through another intermediary, shall be held guilty of invading the Lord’s property, unless, after being admonished, they have transferred those same possessions to the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0873D] Dionysius lacks the words “or through another intermediary.”]

[Note: [Col. 0873D] The Vatican manuscript has “in that same Church.”]

If something has come to them personally through someone’s generosity or by inheritance from their kin, they shall dispose of it in a manner consistent with their vocation. But if they deviate backward from their vocation, they shall be judged unworthy of ecclesiastical honor, like reprobates.

[Note: [Col. 0873D] The same Vatican manuscript has “again” instead of “backward.”]

XXXIX. That a Presbyter May Not Sell the Property of His Title

[Note: [Col. 0873D] Dionysius, canon 33.]

[Note: [Col. 0873D] Dionysius joins this canon and the following one and expresses them differently as follows: “It was likewise decided that presbyters should not sell the property of the Church in which they are appointed without the knowledge of their bishops, just as bishops may not sell church estates without the council’s knowledge or that of their presbyters. Therefore, since there is no necessity, neither may a bishop appropriate the property of the mother church nor a presbyter the property of his title.”]

It was likewise decided that a presbyter should not sell the property of the Church in which he is appointed without the knowledge of his bishop, just as a bishop may not sell church estates without consulting the council or the entire presbyterate, without any necessity.

XL.

[Note: [Col. 0873D] This is the reading of the Vatican manuscript. Other manuscripts differ slightly: “On not appropriating the property of a title.” The canon begins: “And” or “But that it not be permitted to a bishop to appropriate the property of the mother church,” and so forth.]

That a Bishop May Not Appropriate the Property of a Title

[Col. 0874A]

A bishop may not appropriate the property belonging to the title of his presbyter.

[Note: [Col. 0873D] In Dionysius, the following excerpts from earlier synods under Aurelius are inserted in this council; their acts were reread and entered into the code. Then six other canons, enacted in this same council five days later during the second session, follow, preceded by a separate preface. All these materials are omitted from the manuscripts used in our edition.]

Bishop Aurelius said: “In accordance with the statutes of the entire council assembled and the judgment of my mediocrity, I think it appropriate to bring all matters to a conclusion. Let the ecclesiastical acts concerning all the titles designated and arranged in today’s proceedings be received.”

[Note: [Col. 0874C] Dionysius has: “But whatever has not yet been set forth shall be written on the following day,” and so forth.]

“But when we have learned what has not yet been set forth, we shall write on the following day, through our brothers Bishop Faustinus and the presbyters Philip and Asellus, to our venerable brother and fellow bishop Boniface.” And they subscribed.

Bishop Aurelius: “I, Aurelius, bishop, have subscribed to this document reread by us.”

Valentinus, bishop of the primatial see of the province of Numidia: “I have subscribed.”

Faustinus, bishop of the Church of Potentia in the province of Picenum, legate of the holy Roman Church: “I have subscribed to these proceedings.”

Alypius, bishop of the Church of Tagaste, legate of the province of Numidia: “I have subscribed to this document for myself and the council.”

Augustine, bishop of the Church of Hippo Regius, legate of the council of Numidia: “I have subscribed for myself and the same council.”

[Note: [Col. 0874D] Alternatively, Possidius.]

Possidonius, bishop of the Church of Palama, legate of the province of Lower Numidia: “I have subscribed.”

Vincentius, bishop of the Church of Culsita: “I have subscribed.”

[Note: [Col. 0874D] Dionysius has the better reading, “of the Church of Culusitana.” In the collation of 411, Vincentius is listed as Culusitanus.]

Fortunatus, bishop of the Church of Neapolis: “I have subscribed.”

[Note: [Col. 0874D] Dionysius likewise has the better form Fortunatianus, as in the same collation.]

Pentadius, bishop of the Church of Carpitana: “I have subscribed.”

[Note: [Col. 0874D] The Bochard manuscript has Carpidana; the Thuanus manuscript, Carpedana; the Vatican manuscript, Capitana, where the r is absent.]

Rufinianus, bishop of the Church of Muzuensis: “I have subscribed.”

[Note: [Col. 0874D] Alternatively, “Rufinus … of Mazensis.” But in the collation the form is Rufinianus Mazuensis.]

Praetextatus, bishop of the Church of Sicilibba: “I have subscribed.”

[Note: [Col. 0874D] The Lucian manuscript has Sicilenbensis. We have preferred the manuscripts of Justellus and the Vatican, from Sicilibba, otherwise Sicilibra in Africa.]

648 Quodvultdeus, bishop of the Church of Verensis: “I have subscribed.”

[Note: [Col. 0874D] The Vatican manuscript has Cerensis. In the Notitia of Africa, Exitiosus Verensis is listed in the proconsular province.]

[Col. 0875A]

Candidus, bishop of the Church of Abitinensis Germanicianorum: “I have subscribed.”

[Note: [Col. 0875C] This is the reading of the Lucian manuscript and two of Justellus’s manuscripts. The Vatican manuscript has Habitensis. Shortly afterward, the Lucian manuscript has Germaniciorum. Dionysius has Candidus Germaniae. In the collation, Victor Abitinensis and Innocentius Germaniensis are distinguished.]

Gallonianus, bishop of the Church of Utina: “I have subscribed.”

[Note: [Col. 0875C] Alternatively, Gallonius … of Utica.]

Maximianus, bishop of the Church of Aquae Regiae, legate of the province of Byzacena: “I have subscribed.”

[Note: [Col. 0875C] Alternatively, Maximinus or Maximus.]

Jocundus, bishop of Suffetula, legate of the province of Byzacena: “I have subscribed.”

Maximianus, bishop of Suffeta, legate of the province of Byzacena: “I have subscribed.”

Hilarianus of Horrei Celiensis, legate of the province of Byzacena: “I have subscribed.”

[Note: [Col. 0875C] Alternatively, Celensis or Horreocellensis.]

Novatus, bishop of Sitifis: “I have subscribed.”

Ninellus, bishop of Sussura, legate of the province of Mauretania Caesariensis: “I have subscribed.”

[Note: [Col. 0875C] This is the reading of two manuscripts and Bochardus. The Vatican manuscript has Usarranensis; the Thuanus, Surramensis; Dionysius, Rusurrianensis. The manuscript cited by Hardouin has the better reading, Rusuccurianensis, legate of the province of Caesariensis, in which Rusuccurium is located. In the preface to this second session, which is found both in the African Code before canon 128 and in Isidore’s account of the Seventh Council of Carthage, Ninellus is called Rusuccuriensis according to Hardouin’s reading and is counted among the legates of Caesariensis. Therefore the manuscripts of the Vatican and Lucian are wrong to call him Sitifensis instead of Caesariensis.]

[Col. 0875B]

Laurentius, bishop of Icosium, legate of the province of Mauretania Caesariensis: “I have subscribed.”

Numerianus, bishop of the Church of Rausgurium, legate of the same province: “I have subscribed.”

[Note: [Col. 0875C] Alternatively, Raguriensis, Rausariensis, or Rusuguriensis. In the aforementioned preface to this second session Numerianus is called Rusguniensis, which is the correct reading.]

Leo, bishop of the Church of Moptis, legate of the same province: “I have subscribed.”

[Note: [Col. 0875D] The Vatican manuscript has Optensis. In the Carthaginian collation we have “Leo of the municipality of Moptis.” In the preface to this second session he is called Moctensis (in the Greek version, Ὀπτενσίανος), legate of the province of Mauretania Sitifensis.]

Leo, bishop, legate of the province of Sitifensis: “I have subscribed.”

And 218 other bishops of various provinces subscribed.

[Note: [Col. 0875D] Dionysius has 217; Thuanus, 241; Bochardus, 214. We have retained 218 with the Vatican manuscript. In the letter to Boniface, the same number is expressed differently because of variation among the manuscripts.]

Philip, presbyter, legate of the holy Roman Church: “I have subscribed to these proceedings.”

Asellus, presbyter, legate of the holy Roman Church.

And we ourselves collected the proceedings that had been sent.

[Note: [Col. 0875D] In these same manuscripts there follows a letter of the Africans to Boniface, another of Atticus of Constantinople together with the rule concerning formatae, as indicated in the preface, and other letters of the same Africans to Pope Coelestine.]

II. 649

[Note: [Col. 0876C] This is the eighteenth council under Aurelius. See what we said in Treatise, part II, chapter 3, section 9, no. 1.]

THE EIGHTEENTH COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE UNDER AURELIUS, IN THE YEAR 421

(Produced from manuscript codex 55 of the Veronese chapter.)

[Col. 0876A]

In the consulship of Agricola and Eustathius, illustrious men, on the Ides of June, at Carthage, in the secretariat of the Basilica of Faustus.

When the aged Aurelius had taken his seat together with his brothers and fellow priests, with the deacons standing by, Bishop Aurelius said:

“Your holiness remembers better the reason why it happened that the established solemnity of the council ceased for two years. Now, because, with God’s help, it came about through a certain providence [perhaps providentia, “providence”] that our holy brother and fellow bishop Augustine, out of his religious devotion, willingly accepted the council, and because the Lord ordered us to be gathered together; and because it happened that my illness greeted the faces of all of you, let us do something for the benefit of the Church, so that matters which have arisen or which ought to be heard may be heard, lest cases, if they begin to be deferred still longer, grow worse. Therefore it is necessary that the ecclesiastical cases appropriate to discipline be dealt with.”

[Note: [Col. 0876C] From this we learn that the ecclesiastical cases for which synods were to be convened every year were first discussed and settled in those same synods.]

The entire council said: “We gladly agree that this be done.”

650 The aged Aurelius said:

“Let the matters established and defined by common deliberation be read through in order from the preceding councils, so that they may be inserted into the acts of the present council.”

[Note: [Col. 0876C] There is no doubt that, in this synod, the statutes of the preceding councils under Aurelius were read and inserted into the acts, just as they had been read and inserted in the preceding synod of 419, as can be gathered from Dionysius. But, for the sake of brevity, they were omitted from that old copy from which the scribe of our manuscript transcribed this council; for the same reason, a certain exchange of words that would have provided a suitable transition to the following canons was carelessly omitted.]

I. It was resolved by the entire council that anyone who has been excommunicated, whether a bishop or any cleric, and who, during the time of his excommunication, presumes to receive communion before a hearing, shall be judged to have pronounced the sentence of condemnation upon himself.

[Note: [Col. 0876D] This canon was repeated from the preceding council of 419, canon 35 of our edition, canon 29 in Dionysius. The repetition should cause no difficulty, for the same canon was also renewed in the Council of Hippo Regius in 427, from which Ferrandus cites it as no. 54. See Treatise, part II, chapter 3, section 9, no. 4. In the margin of our manuscript, in a later but ancient hand, the words “for his own negligence” have been added; a diligent reader found these words in some copy of the council of 419. In the preceding synod the words “for his own negligence” are read in the text.]

II. It was likewise decided that the accused or the accuser, in the place from which the accused comes, if he fears some violence from a reckless crowd, shall choose a nearby place where it will not be difficult to bring witnesses, and there the case shall be concluded.

[Note: [Read quo (“where”) rather than quod (“which”).]

[Note: [Col. 0877C] This canon was repeated from the preceding synod, canon 36, canon 30 in Dionysius. It was renewed in the Council of Hippo Regius of 427, title 5, and is cited by Ferrandus as no. 198. In the margin of our manuscript, qualiter (“how”) is substituted for et ibi (“and there”), following the reading of the preceding synod found in our manuscripts.]

III.

[Note: [Col. 0877C] The title of this canon is added in the same margin. It was repeated from the preceding synod, canon 37, canon 31 in Dionysius: “That no one of the ecclesiastical order refuse to be ordained at the bishop’s request.”]

It was likewise decided that any cleric who does not obey his bishops when they wish to advance him to greater honor in his own diocese shall not minister in the rank from which he refused to withdraw.

[Note: [Col. 0877C] The margin of the manuscript adds, from the preceding synod, “or deacon, concerning the needs of the churches.”]

[Note: [Col. 0877C] Read “when they wish to advance him,” rather than “them.” Since the synod of 419 reads “to promote him to greater honor in his own church,” the Fathers of this council, explaining the passage with reference to the diocese, expressed it differently.]

[Note: [Col. 0877C] Read “let him not minister there.”]

IV.

[Note: [Col. 0877D] Since this canon is found nowhere in the earlier councils, it appears to belong specifically to this synod. We learn from Ferrandus, no. 34, that it was repeated in the Council of Hippo Regius in 427, where he has: “That bishops or presbyters should not transfer to other places what belongs to the places in which they are ordained unless they have first given an account of the reasons.” Council of Hippo Regius, title 5.]

It was likewise decided that, if bishops or presbyters transfer to other places the things belonging to the places in which they were ordained, they shall present their reasons either to the bishops in their councils or to the clerics before their bishops. If they have no just reasons, judgment shall be taken against them as against those caught in theft.

651 V. It was likewise decided that any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or cleric whatsoever who is ordained possessing nothing, and who during the time of his episcopate or clerical office acquires lands or any estates in his own name, shall be held guilty of invading the Lord’s property.

[Note: [Col. 0877D] This was repeated from the preceding synod, canon 38, canon 32 in Dionysius, and was subsequently renewed in the Council of Hippo Regius of 427, title 8, as Ferrandus reports in no. 35. The margin of our manuscript adds, following the reading of the preceding synod found in our manuscripts, “or through another intermediary.”]

If, after being admonished, they transfer those same possessions to the Church, all is well; but if they wish to leave them to their own relatives or to any outsider, they shall not be permitted to do so.

[Note: [Col. 0877D] Read “If, after being admonished, they transfer them to the Church.” This passage is explained more clearly in the present synod than in the preceding one, and with an addition, as will be evident to anyone comparing the texts. Beside the word “same,” the margin notes that ipsa (“those very things”) should be added, as it is in the preceding synod in our edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0878A] Delete the superfluous in (“in”) before ipsis (“them”).]

But if something has come to them personally through inheritance from their parents or kin, they shall dispose of it in a manner consistent with their vocation. If they deviate backward from their vocation, they shall be judged unworthy of ecclesiastical honor, like reprobates.

VI. It was likewise decided that no slaves or freedmen belonging to the household should be admitted to accuse clerics, nor anyone whom the public laws do not admit to accuse of public crimes.

[Note: [Col. 0878A] Read liberi (“free”) for proprii (“their own”).]

[Note: [Col. 0878C] This canon was repeated from canon 129 in Dionysius, which belongs to the canons of the second session of the Council of Carthage of 419. But the words beginning “nor those …” and continuing through “wishes to accuse” are taken from the end of canon 128 in the same Dionysius. From this and many other examples we learn what we stated in the preface, no. 2: when repeating the canons of earlier synods, the Africans repeatedly altered or even added certain things as seemed expedient.]

Nor may those who, after they have been excommunicated, while they remain in that excommunication—whether clerics or laypeople—wish to bring an accusation; nor those stained by every mark of infamy, that is, actors and persons subject to disgraceful practices; nor heretics, pagans, or Jews. Nevertheless, all those to whom the right of accusation is denied must not be denied the right to bring accusations in their own cases.

[Note: [Col. 0878C] Read “those who were excommunicated,” rather than “those who afterward … while he remains excommunicated.”]

652 VII.

[Note: [Col. 0878C] Two canons have been joined together here and repeated from the second session of the Council of Carthage of 419; in Dionysius they are read as canons 130 and 131.]

It was likewise decided that whenever many crimes are brought against clerics by their accusers, and they are unable to prove one of those charges—the one with which they dealt first—they shall not afterward be admitted to the others.

Witnesses, moreover, shall not be admitted to testify if they are not prescribed to be admitted to an accusation, nor those whom the accuser himself has brought forward from his own household.

[Note: [Col. 0878C] We have supplied produxerit (“has brought forward”) from Dionysius.]

Nor shall anyone under fourteen years of age be admitted to give testimony.

VIII. It was likewise decided that, if a bishop says that someone confessed a crime to him alone, but that person denies having confessed it, the bishop should not regard it as an affront to himself that the person is not believed on his word alone. If, because of a scruple of his own conscience, he says that he is unwilling to communicate with the one who denies it, then, for as long as he does not communicate with the excommunicated person, no other bishop shall communicate with him either. Thus the bishop will take greater care not to say of anyone what he cannot establish by other proofs.

[Note: [Col. 0878C] This canon too has been formed from two canons, which Dionysius reports in the second session of the synod of 419 as canons 132 and 133. Likewise, in Isidore, under the title of the Seventh Council of Carthage, canon 5, these two canons form one. Isidore reads “and although that person denies it, he should not think …” Dionysius reads “and although that person denies it and refuses to repent, he should not think …”]

[Note: [Col. 0878D] Read “what he cannot establish by other proofs,” omitting ab (“from”), as in Dionysius.]

IX. It was likewise decided that presbyters should not sell church property in the places in which they are appointed without the knowledge of their bishops, just as a bishop may not sell church estates without the knowledge of the council or of his primates.

[Note: [Col. 0878C] In Dionysius, this canon and the following one form one canon, canon 33, and are among the canons of the first session of the Council of Carthage of 419. In our preceding edition they are likewise divided into two canons, 39 and 40. In the margin of our manuscript, instead of “or to the primates,” is written “or to the entire presbyterate”; in the preceding edition, “or to the entire presbyterate”; in Dionysius, “or to his presbyters.” In the present council, the change “or to the primates” was introduced. Consequently, this canon was later renewed with that reading in the Council of Hippo Regius of 427, as Ferrandus testifies in no. 47, where we read: “That bishops should not sell church property without the advice of the primate.” Council of Hippo Regius, title 9. Ferrandus later cites the first part of this canon from the same Council of Hippo Regius, title 9, in no. 95.]

[Col. 0879A] 653 **X.** [Note: [Col. 0879C] In this council this canon is explained more clearly, though in different words, than in the synod of 419, in Dionysius, canon 33. Ferrandus plainly indicates that this canon was repeated in the synod of Hippo Regius in 427, no. 38: “That the bishop of the mother church may not usurp whatever has been donated to churches established in the diocese.” Council of Hippo Regius, title 9. The word *diocese* was taken from our canon, since in the council of 419 the word *title* is read. Since Ferrandus assigns this canon and the preceding one to the same title 9, it is clear that both formed one canon in the synod of Hippo Regius.] It was also decreed that, if fields or any estates belonging to the Church and situated in a diocese have been abandoned, the bishop may not usurp them and assign them to the mother church.

Each of them confirmed these statutes by his own subscription: Aurelius, Simplicius, Augustine, and the others.

[Note: [Col. 0879D] The manuscripts used in publishing these statutes belong to three collections: namely, Vatican 1342 and Barberinian 2888; Vallicellanus A 5; and Vatican 5845. We shall occasionally also cite the additions of Dionysius, Vatican Palatine 574, and the Herovallian manuscript, from which James Petit inserted several canons into his collection; in it, however, we have found certain things altered rather freely at the compiler’s discretion. The Arabic numbers marked at the beginning of the individual canons indicate the order in which they were published under the name of Carthage IV in volume II of the standard Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 1436 and following.]

### III. ANCIENT STATUTES OF THE CHURCH

*(Published from the most distinguished manuscript collections.)*

**1.** [Note: [Col. 0879D] This preface is read in full in Hittorp’s common Roman order under the title “Ecclesiastical Statutes.” [Col. 0880C] The Vallicellian manuscripts and certain others containing Dionysius’s additions mark this preface as canon 1 and join several of the following canons together, so that the total becomes one hundred, as Atto noted from his Vercelli manuscript. We have judged that the division found in the older collections, Vatican 1342 and the similar Barberinian 2888, as well as in the other Vatican Palatine 574, should be followed.] Whoever is to be ordained bishop must first be examined as to whether he is naturally prudent, teachable, temperate in conduct, chaste in life, sober, always free for his own duties, approachable to people, merciful, learned, instructed in the law of the Lord, careful in his understanding of the Scriptures, and practiced in ecclesiastical doctrines; and above all, whether he asserts the foundations of the faith in simple words—that is, affirming that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, and proclaiming the entire Godhead in the Trinity to be of one essence, consubstantial, coeternal, and co-omnipotent; whether he believes each individual person in the Trinity to be fully God and all three persons to be one God; whether he believes that the divine incarnation took place not in the Father or in the Holy Spirit, but in the Son alone, so that he who was the Son of God the Father in divinity became, in humanity, the son of a human mother: true God from the Father and true man from his mother, possessing flesh from his mother’s womb and a rational human soul; so that in him there are both natures, that is, man and God, one person, one Son, one Christ, one Lord, creator of all that exists, author, Lord, and ruler with the Father and the Holy Spirit of all creatures; who suffered with a true suffering of the flesh, died with the true death of his body, rose again with the true resurrection of his flesh and the true resumption of his soul, in which he will come to judge the living and the dead.

[Note: [Col. 0880C] The common editions of the Councils have “the Godhead of the Trinity”; and, a little later, “singular” for “each individual.” The Herovallian manuscript has “in humanity,” better, since it corresponds more closely to the preceding “in divinity.” Some manuscripts next prefer *matrisque*. Vatican manuscript 5845 then reads “if true God from the Father.” The Vallicellian manuscript has “both natures”; shortly afterward, the words “one person” are absent from the Vatican manuscript. [Col. 0880D] The same Vallicellian manuscript has “of creatures,” and then, instead of “ruler,” with some other manuscripts, “creator.” We preferred, with the common editions, “ruler,” because this word avoids empty repetition.]

[Note: [Col. 0880C] Some of our manuscripts have “occupied with his own business” and omit *vacans* (“free”). The common text has *cavens* (“being cautious”) in place of *vacans*. Soon afterward the Vatican manuscript reads “approachable to the humble,” while the common text has “if humble, if approachable.”]

He must also be asked whether he believes that the New and Old Testaments—that is, the Law, the Prophets, and the Apostles—have one and the same author and God; whether the devil became evil not by nature but by choice. He must also be asked whether he believes in the resurrection of this flesh that we bear, and not of another; whether he believes that judgment will take place and that each person will receive either punishment or glory for what he has done in this flesh; whether he does not disapprove of marriage, condemn second marriages, blame the eating of meat, communicate with penitents who have been reconciled, and believe that in baptism all sins are forgiven—that is, both original sin contracted and those sins voluntarily committed; and whether he believes that no one is saved outside the Catholic Church.

When, after examination in all these matters, he has been found fully instructed, he is to be ordained bishop with the consent of the clergy and laity and the assembly of all the bishops of the province, especially by the authority or presence of the metropolitan. Having received the episcopate in the name of Christ, [655] he must submit not to his own pleasure or impulses but to these definitions of the Fathers.

[Note: [Col. 0880D] The following is absent from the Vatican manuscript mentioned above, and rightly so; it seems clumsily inserted, and the statutes more appropriately follow immediately in that manuscript after the words “he must submit to these definitions of the Fathers.” We have not nevertheless deleted it, because it is read in the Vallicellian and other manuscripts containing Dionysius’s additions, as well as in the common editions of the Councils, where after a few words the phrase “following the example of the Savior” is missing.]

At his ordination his age must also be considered, the age that the holy Fathers established, following the example of the Savior, for those to be chosen as bishops.

**14. I.** A bishop must have a small lodging not far from the church.

**33. II.** In the church a bishop must sit in a higher place among the presbyters. Within the house, however, he must recognize himself as a colleague of the presbyters.

[Col. 0881A] **20 III.** A bishop must not take upon himself any care of private property, but devote himself solely to reading, prayer, and the preaching of the word of God.

**15 IV.** A bishop must have inexpensive furnishings, [Note: [Col. 0881C] The Vallicellian manuscript reads “at table.”] a table, and poor food, and must seek the authority of his rank through faith and the merits of his life.

**16 V.** A bishop must not read books of the pagans; but he may read those of heretics when necessity requires.

[Note: [Col. 0881C] The common text, together with the Herovallian manuscript, reads “and when circumstances require.”]

**18 VI.** A bishop must not undertake the guardianship of wills.

**17 VII.** A bishop must administer the care of widows, orphans, and strangers not personally, but through the archpriest or archdeacon.

[Note: [Col. 0881C] Some manuscripts read “must have.”]

**656 19 VIII.** A bishop must not litigate, even when provoked, over transitory matters.

[Note: [Col. 0881C] The Vatican Barberinian and Palatine manuscripts read “must not litigate.”]

[Col. 0881B] **21 IX.** A bishop must be prevented from going to a synod only by sufficiently serious necessity; nevertheless, he must send a representative in his place, intending to accept, without compromising the truth of the faith, whatever the synod decrees.

[Note: [Col. 0881C] The common Council text adds “not without,” but Hardouin notes that these words are absent from his manuscripts. They are likewise absent from ours. In Gratian, Distinction 18, canon 9, “he must not delay unless” is added. Soon afterward, in the Vallicellian manuscript, *cohibeatur* (“be restrained”) is found instead of *inhibeatur* (“be prevented”), giving the opposite sense, which the context excludes.]

**22 X.** A bishop must not ordain clergy without the counsel of his fellow presbyters, and must seek the consent and testimony of the citizens.

[Note: [Col. 0881C] The common text has “of the clergy,” supported by none of our manuscripts. Some manuscripts then have *convenientiam* (“agreement”) instead of *conniventiam* (“consent”), less correctly. Others prefer *aut* (“or”) to *et* (“and”).]

**27 XI.** A bishop must not pass by ambition from an obscure place to a distinguished one, nor may any cleric of a lower order do so. If the welfare of the Church should demand it, he is to be transferred by the judgment of a synod, after a decree on his behalf has been presented to the bishops by clergy and laity; nevertheless, another bishop must be appointed in his place. Priests of a lower rank and other clerics may, with the permission of their own bishops, migrate to other churches.

[Note: [Col. 0881D] This is the reading of our manuscripts, except that the Vallicellian has “in place of the decision,” while the common editions have “in the presence.”]

**34 XII.** A bishop sitting in any place must not make presbyters stand for a long time.

[Note: [Col. 0881D] The common text omits “for a long time.”]

**XIII.** [Note: [Col. 0881D] We have printed this canon as it is read in the Palatine Vatican manuscript, since this reading seemed better than that found in the Barberinian and similar Vatican manuscripts, “In the ordination of priests, let others also be required,” or that in the Vallicellian, “In the ordination even of priests, let it be required by others”; these matters were sufficiently expressed in canon 10. Hence this canon may have been omitted from the common Carthaginian IV collection.] In the ordination of priests, age must also be considered.

**23 XIV.** A bishop must hear no case without the presence of his clergy; otherwise the bishop’s judgment will be invalid unless it is confirmed by the presence of the clergy.

[Note: [Col. 0881D] The common text, together with the Palatine Vatican manuscript, has “of no one.” The Vallicellian has “of the bishops” instead of “of the bishop.”]

**31 657 XV.** A bishop must use the Church’s possessions as things entrusted to him, not as his own.

[Note: [Col. 0882C] The continuation of this canon, absent from the common text and from the Palatine Vatican and Herovallian manuscripts, is found in our other manuscripts, the Barberinian and similar Vatican 1342, as well as in Vatican 5845, the similar Vallicellian manuscript, and others containing Dionysius’s additions. The same material, but without the preceding words, occurs among the additional canons of the synod of Agde in 506, canon 49; that canon may perhaps have been excerpted from our statutes, as were some of its other additions.]

Deacons and presbyters established in a parish must not dare to alter anything of the Church’s possessions entrusted to them, because these possessions are known to be consecrated to God. Likewise, priests must not presume to alter anything of the Church’s possessions committed to them, as was said above.

[Note: [Col. 0882C] This is the reading of the Vallicellian manuscripts and the Vatican manuscripts containing Dionysius’s additions. The Barberinian and similar Vatican manuscripts have “to mutilate.” In the aforementioned canon 49 added to the canons of Agde, “to alienate” is read.]

If they should wish to do so, and are convicted in a council, they must restore from their own property an equal amount to what they are seen to have presumed to take. But if anyone wishes, for whatever reason, to alienate anything from the Church’s possessions, he may do so only if he contributes from his own property to the Church as much as he appears to have taken away. We order, nevertheless, that priests, presbyters, or deacons who wish to make freedmen from the Church entrusted to them follow the Church’s formal procedure.

[Note: [Col. 0882D] Some manuscripts, less correctly, have *actis* (“deeds”) instead of *actus* (“legal proceedings”). *Actus* is also found in the aforementioned canon appended to the synod of Agde.]

If they disdain to do this, it was decreed that they must be returned to their former servitude.

**84 XVI.** A bishop must forbid no one—whether pagan, heretic, or Jew—from entering the church and hearing the word of God, up to the Mass of the catechumens.

**XVII.** A bishop must excommunicate accusers of their brothers; if they correct their fault, they may be received into communion, but not into the clergy.

[Note: [Col. 0882D] The common text, together with the Vallicellian manuscript, reads “let him receive them.”]

**74 XVIII.** A priest must impose the laws of penance on anyone imploring penance, without respect of persons.

**658 75 XIX.** Those who neglect penance must be received more slowly.

[Note: [Col. 0882D] The common text, together with the Palatine Vatican manuscript, reads “more negligent penitents.”]

**76 XX.** [Note: [Col. 0882D] This canon and the following one were added in the margin to the Ancyra canons in manuscript 55 of the Verona chapter; in Vatican manuscript 1342 they are appended at the end of the same Ancyra canons. After this canon the common edition of the Council of Carthage IV adds another canon, numbered 77, which seems rather to be the title of this canon than a new canon: “Penitents who are ill should receive the viaticum.”] If a person asks for penance while ill and, by chance, when the priest whom he invited comes to him, is overcome by illness and becomes speechless or falls into delirium, those who heard him must testify, and he must receive penance. If he is immediately believed to be dying, he must be reconciled by the laying on of hands, and the Eucharist must be poured into his mouth. But if he survives, he must be informed by the witnesses mentioned above that his request has been fulfilled, and must be subjected to the prescribed penance for as long as the priest who administered the penance determines.

[Note: [Col. 0883C] The Herovallian manuscript has “to the prescribed period of penance.” The common text has “to the prescribed laws of penance.”]

**78 XXI.** Penitents who have received the Eucharist as a viaticum while ill must not consider themselves absolved without the laying on of hands if they survive.

[Note: [Col. 0883C] The Vallicellian has “with the Eucharist.”]

**79 XXII.** Penitents who carefully fulfill the laws of penance, if by chance they die on a journey or at sea where they could not be assisted, must be commended to remembrance in prayers and offerings.

[Note: [Col. 0883C] The common text has “where they cannot be assisted”; Gratian, cause 26, question 7, canon 6, has “where they cannot be assisted.” Our manuscripts are better. Since some have only *subvenire* (“to assist”), the Herovallian manuscript adds *sacerdos* (“the priest”), and gives the canon thus: “Penitents who die before completing legitimate penance, if they happen to die where the priest could not assist them, should be commended to remembrance in prayers and offerings.”]

**85 XXIII.** Those preparing for baptism must give their names and, after being examined frequently under abstinence from wine and meat and with repeated laying on of hands, must receive baptism.

[Note: [Col. 0883C] The Herovallian manuscript and another cited by Hardouin have “frequently.”]

**86 XXIV.** Neophytes must for some time abstain from more lavish banquets, spectacles, and spouses.

[Note: [Col. 0883D] The Vallicellian manuscript has “at some time.”]

**659 XXV.** A cleric must neither grow his hair nor his beard.

[Note: [Col. 0883D] The Vallicellian, using the plural “clerics,” has “nor let them shave the beard.” From this reading, it seems, the synod of Barcelona of the sixth century enacted in canon 3: “Let no cleric grow his hair or shave his beard.” Other canons of that synod also seem to have been excerpted from our statutes. Crabbe places an asterisk after *nec* (“nor”) and notes: “Elsewhere, let him cut the beard.” Thus, in the Gembloux book, “Elsewhere, let him shave the beard” is added in the Grandval book of Saint Bavo under the title *Ancient Statutes of the Church*. Most copies, however, do not have *radat* (“shave”) or *tondeat* (“cut”), so that the sense is that a cleric must grow neither hair nor beard.]

**45 XXVI.** A cleric must demonstrate his profession also in dress and manner of walking; therefore he must not seek elegance in clothing or footwear.

[Note: [Col. 0883D] The common text reads “and demonstrate it in dress and manner of walking, and not in clothing.” The Herovallian manuscript has “neither the elegance of clothing nor of footwear.”]

**27 XXVII.** A cleric must not live with unrelated women.

**28 XXVIII.** A cleric must walk through streets and arcades only when a definite and very serious necessity of his office requires it.

[Note: [Col. 0883D] This is the reading of our manuscripts, some of which omit *sui* (“his own”). [Col. 0884C] The common text, together with the Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts, reads: “He must not walk unless a definite and very serious necessity of his office requires it,” which seems better. The Herovallian agrees: “He must not walk without a definite necessity of his office.”]

**XXIX.** A cleric must provide himself with food and clothing by a craft or by agriculture, provided only that this does not impair his office.

[Note: [Col. 0884C] The common text omits *duntaxat* (“only”) and has “let him provide” instead of “let him prepare.”]

**87 XXX.** A Catholic who brings his case, whether just or unjust, before a court of another faith must be excommunicated.

[Note: [Col. 0884C] The common text, supported by the Palatine Vatican manuscript, has “of a judge of another faith.” The Herovallian manuscript explains this canon thus: “A Catholic who brings his case before the judgment of a non-Catholic judge must be excommunicated.”]

**24 XXXI.** If, while a priest is speaking in the church, someone leaves the auditorium, he must be excommunicated.

**83 XXXII.** The poor and the elderly of the Church must be honored more than others.

**88 XXXIII.** Whoever, neglecting the solemn day, goes to spectacles instead of attending the church assembly must be excommunicated.

[Col. 0884A] **660 48 XXXIV.** A cleric who walks about in the marketplaces or forum for any reason other than buying something must be degraded from his office.

[Note: [Col. 0884C] The common text, together with the Palatine Vatican manuscript, reads “for the purpose of buying.”]

**49 XXXV.** A cleric who is absent from vigils without bodily infirmity must be deprived of his stipend.

**101 XXXVI.** Young widows who are physically weak must be supported at the Church’s expense.

[Note: [Col. 0884C] The same common editions, together with the same manuscript, add “of which they are widows.”]

**99 XXXVII.** A woman, however learned and holy, must not presume to teach men in an assembly.

**98 XXXVIII.** A layman must not presume to teach in the presence of clergy unless they approve it.

[Note: [Col. 0884D] The Herovallian manuscript, together with the common text, has “unless they command it.”]

**97 XXXIX.** A man who is to be placed over religious women must be approved by the bishop of the place.

[Note: [Col. 0884D] The Palatine Vatican manuscript omits “of the place.” After “approved,” the Vallicellian and the other manuscripts containing Dionysius’s additions add “or provide.”]

**73 XL.** Whoever communicates or prays with an excommunicated person must be excommunicated, whether cleric or layman.

**100 XLI.** A woman must not presume to baptize.

**59 XLII.** A cleric who envies the advancement of his brothers must not be promoted as long as he remains in that fault.

**56 XLIII.** A cleric who is found to occupy himself with flattery and betrayals must be degraded from office.

[Note: [Col. 0884D] The words “and betrayals” are absent from the Vallicellian manuscript.]

**661 57 XLIV.** A cleric who curses, especially priests, must be compelled to ask forgiveness. If he refuses, he must be degraded; and he must never be restored to office without making satisfaction.

**53 XLV.** All clerics who are strong enough to work must learn both a craft and letters.

[Note: [Col. 0884D] The common text has “who are stronger.” The Soria manuscript and others cited by Hardouin have “who are weak,” perhaps better.]

**58 XLVI.** No one must accept a person who frequently quarrels and is quick to accuse as a witness without a serious examination.

[Note: [Col. 0884D] Vatican 5845, together with the common editions, has “quick to bring charges.”]

[Col. 0884C] **25 XLVII.** If bishops are at odds, let a synod reconcile them, unless the fear of God does so.

**59 XLVIII.** A bishop must draw clerics who are in disagreement toward harmony, whether by reason or by authority. The disobedient must be condemned by the synod at a hearing.
