[Note: [Col. 0884D] The Herovallian manuscript and the margin of the Councils have “because of their audacity,” perhaps resulting from “through audacity.”]

**93 XLIX.** The offerings of brothers who are in disagreement must be received neither in the sacristy nor in the treasury.

[Note: [Col. 0884D] The common text has “of those who are in disagreement.” Hardouin notes: “This is canon 4 of the eleventh Council of Toledo of 675.” Something similar, though in different words, is decreed in Toledo XI, canon 4. But our canon had already long before been inserted into the older Spanish collection under the name of the fourth Council of Carthage.]

[Col. 0885A] **32 L.** A bishop’s gift, sale, or exchange of ecclesiastical property is invalid without the consent and subscription of the clergy.

[Note: [Col. 0885C] The Vallicellian manuscript reads “without the consent and subscription of the consenting clergy.”]

**28 LI.** An unjust condemnation by bishops is to be considered invalid and therefore must be reconsidered by a synod.

**96 LII.** In court it must be inquired into what sort of conduct and faith belong to both the accuser and the accused.

[Note: [Col. 0885C] The Herovallian manuscript and another ancient manuscript of Saint Bavo, cited by Crabbe, bearing the title *Ancient Statutes of the Church*, add: “A false accuser, once detected, must be kept outside the Church until he reforms himself through repentance.” [Col. 0885D] Crabbe has “let him be outside the Church until he is reformed.”]

**662 30 LIII.** Let the judges of the Church beware lest they pronounce a sentence in the absence of the person whose case is being argued, because it will be invalid; rather, they will have to answer for the matter in a synod.

[Note: [Col. 0885D] The common text, together with the Palatine Vatican and Herovallian manuscripts, has “and will certainly give an account of the case in a synod.”]

**26 LIV.** A bishop must strive to urge brothers who are in disagreement, whether clerics or laymen, toward peace rather than toward judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0885D] The common text less correctly has “it must be decreed for bishops,” and afterward “let them exhort.”]

**67 LV.** Seditious persons must never be ordained clerics, nor usurers, nor those who avenge their own injuries.

[Col. 0885B] **3 LVI.** If bishops or presbyters come to another church in order to visit a church, they must be received according to their rank and invited both to speak the word and to consecrate the offering.

[Note: [Col. 0885D] The Vallicellian has “if, because of matters concerning a church, they come to another church,” perhaps meaning “if they come because of matters concerning another church.” Vatican 5845 has “if they come from a church for the purpose of visiting.” Vatican 1342 has “if they come to visit another church.” The Palatine, adopting this reading, adds after “another” the words “of the bishop to the church.”]

**37 LVII.** A deacon must understand himself to be the minister of the presbyter as of the bishop.

**38 LVIII.** If necessity compels it, a deacon, when ordered by a presbyter and in the presbyter’s presence, must distribute the Eucharist of the body of Christ to the people.

[Note: [Col. 0885D] In the Vallicellian manuscript this canon is written after the following one.]

**39 LIX.** A deacon must sit wherever the presbyter orders him.

**41 LX.** A deacon must use the stole only at the time of the offering and the reading.

[Note: [Col. 0885D] The same Vallicellian manuscript omits “and the reading.” We have written *orarium* (“stole”) with Vatican 1342. The others, together with the common text, have *alba* (“white garment”).]

[Col. 0885C] **40 LXI.** A deacon must speak when questioned in the assembly of presbyters.

**663 90 LXII.** Every day exorcists must lay hands upon the possessed.

**91 LXIII.** The possessed must sweep the floors of the houses of God.

[Note: [Col. 0885D] The Vallicellian manuscript has “every day” instead of “of God.” The Herovallian manuscript soon afterward reads “must clean with brooms” instead of “must sweep.”]

**92 LXIV.** When the possessed are sitting in the house of God, daily food must be supplied to them by the exorcist at the appropriate time.

[Note: [Col. 0885D] The common text, together with the Herovallian manuscript, has “through the exorcists.”]

[Col. 0886A] **80 LXV.** Throughout the time of fasting, priests must lay hands upon penitents.

**81 LXVI.** The penitents of the Church who have died must be carried out and buried.

[Note: [Col. 0885D] The Palatine Vatican has “and let them carry them out.” Vatican 1342 has “carrying them out, let them bury them.” [Col. 0886C] The common text is very obscure: “Let them bring the dead penitents of the Church and bury them.”]

**82 LXVII.** Penitents must kneel even on days of remission.

**102 LXVIII.** It is a matter of guilt for the bishop, or for the presbyter who presides over a parish, if, for the sake of sustaining their present life, younger widows or nuns are subjected to the familiar associations of clerics.

**94 LXIX.** Priests must reject gifts from those who oppress the poor.

[Note: [Col. 0886C] In the Vallicellian manuscript this canon is placed after the following two.]

**43 LXX.** A Catholic Christian who suffers tribulations for the Catholic faith must be honored by priests with every honor, including the provision of his daily food.

[Note: [Col. 0886C] The common text of the fourth Council of Carthage reads: “And whoever suffers tribulations for the Catholic faith, for the ecclesiastical cause, and for the Christian religion must be honored by priests with every honor. His food must also be supplied through a deacon.” We have retained the reading of our manuscripts, which Crabbe also appended in smaller type from his copies bearing the title *Ancient Statutes of the Church*.]

[Col. 0886B] **42 LXXI.** A cleric who remains devoted to his office amid trials must be raised through the ranks.

[Note: [Col. 0886D] Some manuscripts have “in temptation,” both here and in the following canon.]

**664 50 LXXII.** A cleric who turns aside from his office amid trials, or acts negligently, must be removed from that office.

[Note: [Col. 0886D] The common text deletes “that” and adds “his.” Soon afterward it, together with the Palatine Vatican manuscript, has “to be removed” instead of “to be withdrawn.”]

**60 LXXIII.** A vulgar cleric who jokes with obscene words must be removed from office.

[Note: [Col. 0886D] In the synod of Agde, canon 70, the reading is “a jester.”]

**61 LXXIV.** A cleric who swears by creatures must be sternly rebuked. If he persists in the fault, he must be excommunicated.

**62 LXXV.** A cleric who sings during meals must be restrained by the severity of the sentence mentioned above.

[Note: [Col. 0886D] We supplied the word “severity,” absent from the Vallicellian and other manuscripts, from the Palatine Vatican manuscript. In the Herovallian manuscript, because this word is lacking, the phrase is written “by the sentence mentioned above.”]

**63 LXXVI.** A cleric who breaks the fast during the period of an announced fast without unavoidable necessity must be regarded as inferior.

[Col. 0886C] [Note: [Col. 0886D] The common text lacks the word “announced.” Vatican 1342 and the Palatine Vatican have “lesser”; soon afterward these same manuscripts, together with the other manuscripts containing Dionysius’s additions, have “having,” less correctly. We have preferred, with the common editions, “to be regarded.”]

**64 LXXVII.** Whoever deliberately fasts on the Lord’s Day must not be considered a Catholic.

**65 LXXVIII.** The solemnity of Easter must be celebrated on one day and at one time.

**51 LXXIX.** A cleric, however learned in the word of God, must seek his livelihood through a craft.

**70 LXXX.** A cleric must especially avoid both banquets and associations with heretics and schismatics.

[Note: [Col. 0886D] The Palatine Vatican, together with the common editions, has “equally.”]

[Col. 0887A] **665 71 LXXXI.** The gatherings of heretics must be called not churches but councils of the devil.

[Note: [Col. 0887C] The common text has “conventicles.”]

**72 LXXXII.** One must neither pray nor sing psalms with heretics.

**89 LXXXIII.** A person devoted to auguries or incantations must be separated from the assembly; likewise one who clings to Jewish superstitions or festivals.

[Note: [Col. 0887C] The Palatine Vatican, together with the common text, adds “of the Church.”]

**68 LXXXIV.** No cleric, however good, may be ordained from among penitents; and if one has been ordained because of the bishop’s ignorance, he must be removed from the clergy, because he did not disclose at the time of ordination that he had been a penitent. But if the bishop knowingly ordains such a man, he too must be deprived, at least, of the power of ordaining in his episcopate.

[Note: [Col. 0887C] This is the reading of the Vallicellian and Palatine Vatican manuscripts. In Vatican 5845: “from the order of his episcopate”; in Vatican 1342: “from the episcopate of the one he is ordaining,” and so forth—perhaps a better reading.]

**69 LXXXV.** A bishop will be subject to a similar sentence if he knowingly ordains as a cleric a man who has had a widow, a divorced wife, or a second wife.

[Note: [Col. 0887C] Some manuscripts omit “the bishop,” and afterward “him.” Vatican 5845 has *habuerit* (“has had”) instead of *habuit* (“had”).]

**95 LXXXVI.** Those who either deny the offerings of the dead to the churches or return them with difficulty must be excommunicated as murderers of the needy.

**36 LXXXVII.** Presbyters who govern churches throughout the dioceses must request chrism before the solemnity of Easter not from just any bishops but from their own, and not through a younger cleric but either personally or through the one who keeps the sacristy.

**66 LXXXVIII.** A cleric who considers the bishop’s severity toward him unjust must appeal to a synod.

**29 LXXXIX.** If a bishop brings a charge against a cleric or layman, he must be brought to proof in a synod.

[Col. 0887C] [Note: [Col. 0887C] This title, omitted from the common editions and from the Spanish and Isidorian manuscript collections, which present another order of the canons, is read in all our copies that present the canons in this order under the name of statutes. Vatican 5845 has *ordinationum* (“of ordinations”) instead of *ordinationis* (“of ordination”); the Vallicellian has *ordinatorum* (“of those ordained”). [Col. 0887D] In Verona 59 there is only: “Recapitulations of the Church’s officers.” The Herovallian manuscript has the following title: “The heading of the ordination of the Church’s official ministers.” These are formulas of ordination, or rather rubrics excerpted from some very ancient order; they are indeed read up to canon 99 in Book I, no. 95, of the Gelasian Sacramentary, with the title: “Here begins the order for blessing the sacred orders.”]

### Recapitulation of the Ordination of the Church’s Officers

**2 XC.** When a bishop is ordained, two bishops must spread out and hold the book of the Gospels over his head; while one of them pronounces the blessing over him, all the other bishops who are present must touch his head with their hands.

[Note: [Col. 0887D] This is the reading of our manuscripts, except the Palatine Vatican, which, with the common text, has “place.” The same Vatican manuscript prefers “over his neck” to “over his head.” The common editions have both “over his head and neck.”]

**3 XCI.** When a presbyter is ordained, while the bishop blesses him and holds his hands over his head, all the presbyters who are present must likewise hold their hands over his head beside the bishop’s hands.

[Note: [Col. 0887D] The Palatine Vatican, together with the common text, inserts “him.” From this canon the text of the Gelasian Sacramentary can be supplemented and corrected, since it is defective and mutilated in this rubric. Compare the following note.]

[Col. 0888A] **4 XCII.** When a deacon is ordained, only the bishop who blesses him must place his hands over his head, because he is consecrated not to the priesthood but to the ministry.

[Note: [Col. 0888C] The common text has “his hand over his head.” In the Gelasian Sacramentary, the words omitted in the preceding chapter have, through some error, been torn from their proper place and wrongly inserted here.]

**5 XCIII.** When a subdeacon is ordained, since he does not receive the laying on of hands, he must receive from the bishop’s hand an empty paten and an empty chalice. From the archdeacon’s hand he must receive a jug with water, a hand-cloth, and a towel.

[Note: [Col. 0888C] The common text has “with water and a hand-washing cloth,” and in the margin “with a water vessel.” The Gelasian Sacramentary has “with water, a water vessel, and a towel.” Water vessels are mentioned in the Digest, Book III, section 3, *On Bequeathed Household Goods*, and Book XIX, section 12, and Book XXI, section 2, *On Bequeathed Gold and Silver*; they are so called because water remained in them.]

[Col. 0888B] **6 XCIV.** When an acolyte is ordained, the bishop must indeed teach him how he ought to conduct himself in his office; but from the archdeacon he must receive a candlestick with candles, so that he may know that he has been assigned to light the Church’s lamps. He must also receive an empty jug for supplying wine at the Eucharist of the blood of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0888D] The common text adds “but,” and shortly afterward reads “a candlestick with a candle”; it then has “to be enslaved.”]

**7 XCV.** When an exorcist is ordained, he must receive from the bishop’s hand a booklet in which the exorcisms are written, while the bishop says to him: “Receive this, commit it to memory, and have authority to lay your hand upon the possessed, or upon those to be baptized.”

[Note: [Col. 0888D] The common editions of the Councils add “to memory”; this word is absent not only from our manuscripts but also from the Gelasian Sacramentary.]

[Note: [Col. 0888D] The Palatine Vatican, together with the published Councils and the Gelasian Sacramentary, has “upon the possessed person, whether baptized or a catechumen,” which is better.]

**8 XCVI.** When a lector is ordained, the bishop must speak about him to the people, indicating his faith, life, and character. Then, while the people await it, he must hand him the book from which he will read, saying to him: “Receive this, and be a bearer of the word of God. If you faithfully and usefully fulfill your office, you will have a share with those who have ministered the word of God.”

[Note: [Col. 0888D] The Vallicellian manuscript has, incorrectly, “about to speak”; Vatican 1342 has “having spoken.”]

[Note: [Col. 0888D] This is the reading of our manuscripts together with the Gelasian Sacramentary. The common Council editions have “lector.” Vatican 1342 has “who have ministered,” while adding “you may receive,” which is redundant unless “you who are about to have” is first deleted.]

[Col. 0888C] **9 XCVII.** When an ostiarius is ordained, after he has been instructed by the archdeacon how he ought to conduct himself in the house of God, the bishop, at the archdeacon’s direction, must hand him the keys of the church from the altar, saying: “Act as though you were going to give an account to God for the things that are locked away by these keys.”

**668 10 XCVIII.** A psalmist, that is, a cantor, may undertake the office of singing solely by the presbyter’s command, without the bishop’s knowledge; the presbyter saying to him: “See that what you sing with your mouth, you believe in your heart; and what you believe, you prove by your works.”

[Col. 0889A] [Note: [Col. 0889B] The word “presbyter” is absent from some manuscripts.]

**11 XCIX.** When a consecrated virgin is presented to the bishop for her consecration, she must be brought in such clothing as she will always use, suitable to her profession and religious dedication.

**12 C.** Widows or nuns who are chosen for the ministry of baptizing women must be so instructed for the office that they can teach uneducated and rustic women, in clear and sound speech, at the time when they are to be baptized, how they should answer the questions put by the baptizer and how they should live after receiving baptism.

[Note: [Col. 0889B] The Palatine Vatican has “for that office,” and omits the words “so that they can.” Instead of *aperto* (“clear”), the common text has *apto* (“suitable”).]

[Note: [Col. 0889B] This is the reading, together with the common text, of the Palatine Vatican. The Vallicellian reads: “who perform the ministry of baptizing”; Vatican 1342, less correctly, has “who are baptized for the ministry.”]

[Note: [Col. 0889B] The Palatine Vatican has “when they are questioned,” instead of “the questions put by the baptizer.”]

[Col. 0889B] **13 CI.** When a bridegroom and bride are to be blessed by the priest, they must be presented by their parents or by the bridesmen. After they have received the blessing, they must remain in virginity that same night out of reverence for the blessing itself.

[Note: [Col. 0889B] The Vallicellian has different punctuation: “They must be presented to the priest by their parents or by the bridesman.” Vatican 1342 reads “or by the bridesman.”]

### 103. CII

Widows who are supported by the Church’s allowance must be so assiduous in God’s work that they assist the Church both by their merits and by their prayers.

[Note: At Col. 0889C, the Vulgate, with Vat. Palat., reads “so assiduous”; afterward the same codex reads “who also by their merits.”]

[Note: The common editions have another canon as no. 104, foreign to the arrangement of the others and rightly omitted in our manuscripts. Yet that it was recorded in some codex containing the statutes and marked no. 103 is attested by the very old codex 59 of the Veronese chapter. There, while the same statutes are presented in abbreviated form, a summary of this canon is supplied at the end under no. 103. In the common editions the canon is as follows:

“As the reward of chastity is good, so it must be guarded with greater observance and injunction. If any widows, however young in years, or left by a husband at a mature age, have devoted themselves to the Lord, and, having cast off secular dress, have appeared in religious habit under the testimony of the bishop and the Church, but afterward have passed over to secular marriage, they shall, according to the Apostle, have condemnation (1 Tim. 3), because they have dared to invalidate the faith of chastity which they vowed to the Lord. Such persons, therefore, shall remain without communion with Christians, nor shall they share a meal with Christians. For if married women are liable to their husbands on the charge of adultery, how much more will widows who have changed their religious way of life be branded with the crime of adultery if, by lustful pleasure, they corrupt the devotion which they freely—not under compulsion [Alternative: “spontaneously.”]—offered to God and pass over to a second marriage? Even if they have been seized by someone through an outbreak of violence, and afterward have consented to remain in marriage with their ravisher or violent husband through delight in the flesh and lust, they shall be held liable to the condemnation described above. Of such women the Apostle says: ‘When they have become wanton, they wish to marry, bearing condemnation because they have rejected their first faith’ (1 Tim. 5:11–12).”

An alternative reading in Harduinus’s codex has: “who vowed their religious life to God.”]

## IV. 669

[Note: This letter is transmitted under this title in three Italian manuscript collections, namely in Vat. 1342 and the similar Barberini 2888, in Vallic. A 5 and similar additions to Dionysius, and in Vat. 1343, which once belonged to the Church of Pavia. In the latter two collections it immediately follows the Statutes presented earlier, as well as the precepts of St. Peter concerning the sacraments, which we shall present later. In editing this letter we shall use the editions of Baluzius, *Appendix* vol. II of the *Capitularia*, no. 5, and of P. Mansi, vol. I of the *Supplement to the Councils*, col. 817.]

# CANONICAL LETTER

[Col. 0890A]

### What presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons ought to fulfill

#### I

First of all, let all presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons commit the Catholic faith to memory; and if anyone neglects to do what is required in this matter, let him abstain from wine for forty days. If afterward he neglects what must be committed to memory, the sentence shall be imposed upon him again.

[Read: “if anyone.”]

[Read: “days.”]

[Read: “let him abstain.”]

[The phrase “to be committed to memory” is understood.]

[Note: “In the name of the Catholic faith” does not mean the Apostles’ Creed—for it would have been called the Apostolic Faith—which was to be memorized not only by clerics but also by laypeople; nor does it mean the Nicene Creed, which was ordinarily called the Nicene Faith. Rather, it means the creed commonly called the Athanasian Creed. In the older manuscripts it is indeed inscribed without the author’s name as *The Catholic Faith*, and likewise in Venantius Fortunatus, a writer of the sixth century, whose exposition of this creed was published by Muratorius from an old codex of the Ambrosian Library, vol. II of the *Anecdota Latina*, p. 212, under the title: “Fortunatus’s Exposition of the Catholic Faith.” Since Venantius Fortunatus is the author of another exposition of the Apostles’ Creed, which is found among his works, he is rightly believed to be the same Fortunatus whose name is prefixed to the exposition of the Catholic Faith just mentioned. He was an Italian by birth and was educated at Ravenna before going to Gaul; therefore he should be regarded as having found this Catholic Faith already widespread and celebrated in Italy, so that he undertook to explain it in a commentary. Hence it is not surprising that our canonical letter, inserted in Italian collections, commanded this same faith to be memorized by presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons. A similar command was later issued in Gaul by the Synod of Autun, whose canon Sirmondus published from the codex of Dijon. Compare our notes 25, 26, and 27 in Quesnel’s Dissertation 14.

After a few words, instead of “and if anything,” Baluzius and the Vallicellian codex have “so that if anything.”]

#### II

Let no presbyter, deacon, or subdeacon presume to live or associate with women. If he is found doing so, let him be deposed from his rank.

[Note: Baluzius, together with the same Vallicellian manuscript, omits “presbyter.”]

[Note: The Lucchese codex deletes “from his rank.”]

Moreover, having been assigned to exile, let him end his days in penitence.

### 670. III

Let no one presume to remove anything that has been or will be lovingly bestowed upon churches or titular churches by Christian rulers, to be preserved by God, lest sacred property be plundered. If anyone should presume to do so, let the things defrauded be restored fourfold. Or, if he has nothing with which the places themselves may accept restitution,

[Vat. 1342: “may lose.”]

[Read: “the things themselves.”]

let the things themselves that were defrauded be gathered again by the bishop concerned and restored in the very place from which they were taken.

[Baluzius: “be re-established.”]

#### IV

Concerning presbyters who receive into communion those who contract incestuous marriages—that is, who join in marriage with a stepmother, a blood relative, a mother-in-law, a stepdaughter, or a woman related by the nearest degree of kinship—and who come before them: let such persons be admonished and separated. If they delay, let them be deprived of communion, and let their offerings not be received upon the sacred altar.

[Alternative: “a stepmother or a stepmother-in-law.”]

[Baluzius, together with the Vallicellian manuscript: “a close female relation.”]

If a presbyter knowingly neglects to discipline this, or, out of attention to temporal friendships,

[Probably: “taking into account.”]

receives him into communion without amendment or penitence,

[Baluzius with the Vallicellian manuscript: “receives him into communion.” Baluzius alone has “let them be subject,” which is less correct.]

let him be subject to canonical judgment.

### 671. V

Concerning those presbyters who, after a first or second correction or admonition, receive idolaters, or foolish people who commit sacrilege at springs and trees, and also observe Thursday or Friday because of pagan custom,

[The Lucchese codex: “the day.”]

or who make little deer or little lambs—that is, performers in disguise—and enchant horns, and who, after a first or second exhortation, give such people communion or accept their offerings: let them be content with bread and water for forty days.

[Baluzius omits the following words through “and enchant.” The Vallicellian manuscript, agreeing with the Lucchese, has *anniculas*.” We preferred the reading of Vat. 1342, *agniculas*, because the passage concerns people who assumed the forms of animals—stags, lambs, calves, and so forth. See Augustine, *Sermon* 129 in the Appendix, no. 2; St. Pacianus, *Paraenesis to Penitence*; the First Council of Auxerre, chap. 1; and Halitgar’s *Penitential*, chap. 6, where nearly all these crimes are listed and subjected to penance.]

#### VI

Let no priest be permitted to undertake secular legal cases outside the command of his bishop,

[Read: “Let none of the priests.”]

[The implied sense is: “nor is he permitted to undertake them.”]

except, at the command of his bishop, religious cases—namely, those of churches, clerics, the poor, or widows—as the sacred canons prescribe.

[The Lucchese codex has “of secular people,” better than the others.]

If anyone, disregarding this rule, is found to have involved himself in such cases, let him be subject to canonical judgment for his presumptuous conduct.

#### VII

If any priest is informed by any woman that suspicion of a bad reputation may consequently arise, let him have no association with her, either privately or in public. If thereafter, after a second and third warning, he is found to have persisted, let him, as a contemptuous offender, suffer the danger of losing his rank.

[Vat. 5845: “through suspicion”; if this is corrected to “through suspicion,” then “be affected” should be read afterward.]

#### VIII

In no church of any diocese where baptism is celebrated should a presbyter be found without a deacon.

[Read: “in no church.”]

[The same Vat. manuscript: “may be.”]

Therefore every presbyter who does not have a deacon shall choose a person for himself and make him known to his people.

### 672

Then let him bring him before his bishop, commending him as one whose life he has found approved, so that he may be consecrated deacon.

[Thus our codices; this is somewhat less bad than the reading in Baluzius, “having been registered.”] If the presbyter delays, saying that he does not have such a cleric,

[Vat. 1342 deletes “such.”]

let his bishop provide him with a suitable person from his own church or from wherever he wishes. The essential point is that he must not be without a deacon.

For we decree that the deacon remain in one room with his presbyter, showing him the honor that is proper. Before their beds let the clerics likewise remain together,

[Other manuscripts: “beds.”]

so that they may always be beyond suspicion and God may be merciful.

[The Lucchese and Vat. 1542 codices add “may be seen,” and delete “together.” Baluzius then has “so that they may be without,” less well.]

When the presbyter is not in the house, wherever he may have gone, after his departure the deacon shall occupy his place for receiving or arranging whatever is useful to the household,

[The Lucchese manuscript: “useful”; read “useful.”]

but only in such a way that he does not become proud against his presbyter. If he attempts this, let him be judged by his bishop for contemptuous arrogance.

As for the revenue of the church, whatever is placed upon the altar or may come from any source, it shall be kept under the seal of both men. Let neither presume to spend anything without the knowledge of the other, whenever necessity arises.

#### IX

[Note: In the second appendix to Regino, chap. 42, this entire canon is quoted under the heading “Concerning ecclesiastical goods, from the canonical letter.” It begins: “Let none of the bishops, presbyters, deacons, or even clerics sell the estates of the Church,” and so forth. Baluzius’s codex, together with the manuscripts of the additions to Dionysius, has: “Let none of the bishops, presbyters, or deacons, or any cleric appointed, have the estates,” and so forth. In our manuscripts of the additions to Dionysius there is “or clerics.” We preferred the manuscripts Vat. 1342 and the Lucchese. Regino then omits the words “that is, lands.”]

Let no presbyter, deacon, or cleric established in a diocese have the power to sell the estates of the Church—that is, lands—nor to give them to any of his relatives.

[Some codices, with Regino, have “in his power.”]

Whoever does this shall, with all speed, return them, once the price has been restored, to the sacred places to which they belong.

[The Vallicellian and Reginian manuscripts have this reading. Other codices, with Baluzius, have “to give”; that is better, but earlier it ought to have read “to sell.”]

If, disregarding this rule, anyone should presume to do so,

[Baluzius omits “this.”]

let him leave his own property in that same Church and himself be expelled, since divine reason properly requires that those who receive churches for governing them should receive them not for scattering them.

Likewise, let no one have power in any way to alienate or mortgage or sell anything,

[Regino’s Appendix deletes “or mortgage.”]

nor, without the will of his bishop, to give vicars to freemen or release slaves.

### 673

[Vat. 1342: “to give to vicars.” The Lucchese: “for giving to vicars.” The Appendix to Regino has “freemen” instead of “for freemen.”]

Whoever presumes to do this shall, as we have decreed above, if he has property of his own, restore an equal amount.

[Baluzius, with Vat. 5845, has “if he has power,” incorrectly.]

If he has none, let him be stripped of everything and expelled. The things themselves, however, shall return to the Church whose property they are.

#### X

It has been reported to us that certain married men who hold titular churches in which they serve make ornaments for their wives or daughters from sacred vestments and claim them for themselves by right of ownership.

[Note: The Lucchese codex has “because”; the other manuscripts, with Baluzius, have “since.”]

It is not even fitting for Christians even to say that sacred things, and things offered to sacred places, are appropriated by their wives, sons, or parents.

[The passage is corrupt. It seems that one should read: “which their wives, or daughters, or parents appropriate.” Baluzius has “or his sons.”]

If this is proved, let him be struck by the judgment stated above.

#### XI

All presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, or the entire clergy known to be under a bishop, if they have cases and are entirely unable to deliberate among themselves, shall then come to their bishop to state their case.

[Supply “to”; immediately afterward delete “through.”]

They must not presume to resort to any secular tribunals. Those who despise this command shall be subject to the penalties stated above, so that they must remain in penitence, abstaining from drinking wine and eating meat, until they approach their metropolitan.

[Baluzius: “in penitence.”]

## V. 674

[Note: These precepts are found in the same manuscript collections in which we found the preceding letter. In addition, Harduinus saw two very old codices. In one the title reads: “Likewise, a letter of the precepts of Pope St. Clement sent to James, the Lord’s brother”; in the other: “Here begins the first letter of St. Clement of Rome to James concerning the sacraments of the Church.” From the variant readings that survive from these codices in the Venetian edition of the *Councils*, vol. I, col. 98 and following, it is clear that they contain this letter as it is read in our copies, without the Isidorian additions found in the common editions of the *Councils*. The difference in the titles indicates the different origins of the codices. Likewise, in the *Abbreviation of the Canons* preserved in the very old manuscript 59 of the Veronese chapter, the precepts are attributed to St. Clement, not to St. Peter.]

# THE PRECEPTS OF SAINT PETER

## Concerning the preservation of the sacraments

### CLEMENT TO HIS DEAREST JAMES

Since, as we received from the blessed apostle Peter, the father of all the apostles, who received the keys of the heavenly kingdom, we ought to know how the sacraments celebrated among holy things must be preserved, it is fitting that I instruct you in due order.

The sacraments of the divine mysteries have been entrusted to three ranks: the presbyter, the deacon, and the minister. They must, with fear and trembling, guard the remnants of the sacraments of the Lord’s body, lest any decay be found in the sacristy, and lest, when the matter is handled negligently, a grave injury be inflicted upon the portion of the Lord’s body.

For if the communion of the body of our Lord Jesus Christ is distributed negligently, and the presbyter does not take care to admonish concerning the lesser duties, let him be struck with a grave anathema and a punishment worthy of humiliation.

Nevertheless, let as many holocausts be offered upon the altar as will suffice for the people. If any remain, they must not be kept for the following day but must be consumed carefully, with fear and trembling, by the clerics.

Those who consume the remnants of the Lord’s body left in the sacristy must not immediately come to receive ordinary food, lest they seem to mix with the sacred portion food which, after passing through the digestive organs, is discharged into the privy.

If the Lord’s portion is eaten in the morning, the ministers who consumed it shall fast until the sixth hour. If they received it at the third or fourth hour, they shall fast until evening. Thus the sacraments, which must be guarded with secret sanctification, are to be preserved eternally.

Concerning sacred vessels, the following procedure is to be observed. If the altar cloth, basin,

[The common Council editions: “cathedra.”]

candlestick, or veil has been worn out by age, it shall be given to the fire. For things that have been in the sanctuary must not be handled improperly; everything must be committed to the fire.

Their ashes, too, shall be carried into the baptistery, where no one passes, or scattered upon a wall or in the hollows of pavements, lest they be defiled by the feet of those entering.

No cleric, through ignorance, should suppose that the cloth which was upon the altar may be used to wrap a dead person, nor should a deacon wish to cover his shoulders with what was on the altar, or with what was given to the Lord’s table.

Whoever does this, or treats these ministries lightly, as though they were nothing, and negligently handles them,

[The same common editions: “the divine mysteries.”]

shall be excluded from the Lord’s altar for three years and six months, struck with a grave anathema.

If the presbyter has not admonished the cleric, let him be excommunicated for ten years and five months, because he failed to admonish him concerning the ministries of the Lord’s sacraments entrusted to his subordinate. Afterward, with profound humility, let him be reconciled to Mother Church.

The altar cloths and veils that have been soiled in the service of the sanctuary shall be washed inside the sacristy by the deacons with humble ministers,

[The same editions: “nearby.”]

without carrying the coverings of the Lord’s table outside the sacristy, lest perhaps dust from the Lord’s body fall improperly from the linen cloth washed outside, and this become a sin for the person performing the washing.

[Col. 0894C]

Therefore we command the ministers to guard these holy things carefully within the sacristy.

[The Harduinus manuscript omits “these holy things.”]

A new basin shall be obtained, and nothing else shall touch it. Nor shall that basin itself be used for washing veils, except those that belong to the service of the Lord’s altar.

[The same codex: “not the basin itself.”]

The altar cloths shall be washed in one basin, and the door curtains in another.

[The common editions: “Only altar cloths shall be washed in it.”]

Let the doorkeepers also be careful, following the admonition of their superiors, lest anyone who is negligent or ignorant wipe his hands carelessly on the curtain of the door of the Lord’s house. Let every person immediately be restrained and learn that the curtain of the court of the Lord’s house is holy.

We also command that no outsider or layman,

[The same common editions: “no one excommunicated from the Church, whether layman …”]

ever be given fragments of the Lord’s offerings to place upon a table.

How do you know, you who indiscriminately distribute the breads of the sacristy to the unworthy, how do you know whether those to whom you distribute them are clean from women?

[Alternative: “of the sanctuary.”]

Thus David, when questioned by Abimelech the priest, asked for bread to eat and, after declaring that he had been clean from a woman for three days, ate the bread of the Presence.

For the Lord’s mysteries, let such persons be chosen as knew their wives before their ordination.

[The common editions: “who, before their ordination, had not known their wives.”]

If, after ordination, a minister of the altar happens to enter his wife’s bed, he shall not enter the doors of the sacristy, nor become a carrier

[Perhaps read “distributor.”]

of the sacrifice, nor touch the altar, nor receive from those offering a holocaust the offering, nor approach the portion of the Lord’s body.

[The same common editions: “nor approach the carrying of the Lord’s body, nor offer water to the priests for their hands.”]

He shall offer water to the priests for their hands, close the doors from the outside, and perform lesser duties. He shall indeed bring a pitcher to the altar.

[The same editions: “let him not carry a pitcher or cup to the altar.”]

If any presbyter or deacon should sell the linen cloth or veil of the sacristy after removing it, he shall be regarded as like Judas Iscariot. Whoever does this out of greed shall know that he will incur the punishment of the Judas mentioned above.

A cleric alone must not approach a woman’s dwelling, nor hurry there without the command of his superior. Nor should a presbyter enter alone into the presence of a woman alone; he shall visit a sick woman with two witnesses brought along.

Nevertheless, no one may live with a foreign woman unless she is a close relative or a sister. This too must be done with great care. We are not ignorant of Satan’s deceits.

All these ministries must be carried out with ecclesiastical gentleness. For it is not proper for God’s work to be performed negligently.

Again and again we give instructions concerning fragments of the Lord’s body.

The minister shall prepare with complete cleanliness the cup prepared for carrying the Lord’s blood, lest a cup that has not been washed properly become a sin for the deacon who offers it.

Thus everything we have set forth above must be fulfilled with complete propriety. Let clerics be chosen for the ministry who can worthily handle the Lord’s sacraments. For it is better for the priest of the Lord to have a few ministers who can worthily perform God’s work than many useless ones who bring a heavy burden upon the one who appoints them.

Obey these judgments carefully.

[The same common editions: “lest anyone fail to believe that these precepts must be fulfilled and, at the judgment of the eternal God, suffer the torments of everlasting fire;” and afterward they have “sacred things” instead of “sacraments.”]

Let no one fail utterly to fulfill this command, lest at God’s judgment he who has neglected the sacraments of ecclesiastical service encounter the torments of eternal fire.

Therefore, brother James, I heard these things from the mouth of St. Peter, who gave the command. From the beginning of the letter up to this point he entrusted the sacraments to careful guardianship,

[The common editions: “he entrusted them to be carefully watched.” The Harduinus manuscript: “to one who watches carefully.”]

so that no droppings of mice might appear among the fragments of the Lord’s portion, nor might any remain rotten through the negligence of the clerics; and so that those who come, desiring to receive healing for themselves, when they see rotten things, may seem to receive them rather with ridicule and disgust and may fall more deeply into sin through the negligence of the clerics.

If anyone does not observe these precepts in their entirety,

[The same edition: “not completely.”]

let him be anathema until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.

I received these precepts from the apostle St. Peter and have taken care to make them known to you, dearest brother, so that you may command everything to be observed without stain.

If anyone listens to you, he will be a useful minister of Jesus Christ. But whoever does not listen to you—or rather, to the Lord speaking through you—will bring condemnation upon himself.

[The common editions: “will receive.”]

## VI. EDICT OF THE EMPEROR GLYCERIUS AGAINST SIMONIACAL ORDINATIONS

*(Now recovered from the collection of canons contained in Vat. Regina 1997.)*

Here begins a copy of the sacred edict of the emperor GLYCERIUS, issued to HIMELCO, vir clarissimus, prefect of the praetorium of Italy.

[Col. 0896B]

At the prompting of the heavenly Majesty, nothing ought to have been arranged at the beginning of our imperial rule before ensuring that the most sacred mysteries of the Christian religion were honored with greater reverence.

[Note: The codex incorrectly reads *ortus*.] For there can be no doubt that God, the author of the universe, is more favorably disposed toward mortal affairs when a purer worship, through the innocence of priests, has looked toward the divine.

For some time now we have observed that, as the vices of clerics still living the life of private persons grew, bishoprics for the most part were not obtained by merit but purchased with money.

[Note: The same codex has “to obtain,” equally incorrectly.] Shameful greed had been turned into a practice and had made this seem almost lawful.

[The codex: “having obtained”; this is defective.]

The pursuit of a good conscience was removed, and what ought to have been hoped for from God was directed toward money and exaction.

Hence it arose that the reverence due to bishops was regarded rather as secular power, and those who were called bishops preferred to be tyrants; neglecting religion, established under the patronage of men, they cared more for public than divine affairs and, enjoying immunity from their crimes through this very privilege of perpetuity, took away the wealth of the churches—which men of evil purpose,

[The codex: “superiors.”]

protecting their dishonor, call the riches of the poor—in the name of some sort of administration, giving rewards to some in the present, binding themselves to others by written acknowledgments, and selling for the profit of the debtor what ought to have been distributed to the needy.

We believe that this caused the offended Divinity, as we have learned through experience of so many evils, to turn away the favor of its majesty and to weary the Roman people with so many misfortunes as have occurred.

For with what face and with what shamelessness can someone pray to the Author of the whole world who is advanced to offer the sacrifice not by the judgment of the most holy Trinity but by the favor of a man?

Or what would bishops of this kind not regard as for sale, since they have subjected the holy mysteries to commercial transactions?

[The same codex: “to merchandise”; this is defective.]

Moved by these considerations, we establish by a law that shall endure forever that anyone who has reached the episcopate with the support of personal influence shall possess, in a secular manner, whatever he obtained in a secular manner; that is, when the boundaries of one year have been completed, he shall know that he is to be deprived of the episcopate.

During that same year in which he is called to the priesthood, an officer of our patrimony shall administer the expenses of ecclesiastical property.

Whoever consecrates such a man, or knows that any money has been given or promised to anyone by the person to be consecrated, or thinks that it should cunningly be concealed in one whom he understands to have wished to attain this office not through a pure conscience but through a shameful price, shall likewise be deposed from the priesthood and pay the corresponding penalty for his rash consecration.

The power to expose this hidden crime is granted not only to those established in the Church but also to any people of our religion. All who can substantiate the charge shall know that, at our discretion, they will receive a reward for this holy accusation.

The citizens of each city, whom it is not the dignity of the person sought but venality that incites to the acclamations of ambitious candidates,

[Read: “which must be punished,” or “which must be regarded with shame.”]

shall know that they will be expelled from residence in the country to which they give such evil counsel, and that so much will be extracted from their property and promised to our treasury.

[Note: The passage is corrupt.]

Therefore let shameful and profane bidding disappear from the churches alike; let the intermediaries of disgraceful prices be silent. It is impious to put heavenly things up for auction.

Let the great work of the priesthood, as has been said, be sought not with money but with merits; and, according to the ancient rule of the priests, let the number and quality of the candidates be weighed and the life of the chosen man examined.

For it is exceedingly detestable that anyone who is about to reach the summit of the episcopate through unlawful corruption should drain the resources of the Church, of which he ought to be a steward rather than a master, almost before he obtains the office.

By these decrees of our serenity

[Supply “decrees of the height of our serenity.”]

we believe that the minds of the wicked are restrained and good consciences are stirred toward greater pursuits of virtue.

We also cannot doubt, concerning the justice and mercy of almighty God, that we shall more easily be protected by divine assistance if, through innocent and approved bishops, we ask for the aid of omnipotence.

Dearest and most beloved kinsman Himelco, therefore let your illustrious and exalted magnificence publish throughout the whole body of our empire, by a proclamation of the edict issued by you, this law of our serenity, which corrects both the priests and ministers of the most sacred religion.

[Col. 0898A]

And by the divine hand: Farewell, dearest and most beloved kinsman Himelco.

[Note: The codex has “Given on the tenth day before the Ides,” incorrectly; the numeral X was written with extended side-strokes instead of V.]

Given at Ravenna on the fifth day before the Ides of March,

[Note: A.D. 473.]

in the fifth consulship of our lord Leo, perpetual Augustus.

[Supply “consul.”]

The end.

### FELIX HIMELCO, prefect of the praetorium; DIOSCORUS, AURELIANUS, and PROTADIUS, illustrious men, prefects of the praetorium

[Note: There is nothing surprising in the fact that Himelco, prefect of the praetorium of Italy, to whom the preceding law was directed by the emperor Glycerius, inserted in its promulgation the names of three other prefects of the praetorium, Dioscorus, Aurelianus, and Protadius. Palladius, prefect of the praetorium of Italy, likewise expressed in the inscription of the edict two other prefects of the praetorium when publishing Honorius’s law against Pelagius and Coelestius: “Junius Quartus Palladius, Monaxius, and Agricola, again prefects of the praetorium, issued this edict.” See our *Code of Canons*, chap. 15. The same practice is found in the edict of Flavius Anthemius Isidorus against the books of Nestorius, vol. III of the Venetian edition of the *Councils*, col. 1731, and in several others. Dioscorus was prefect of the praetorium of the East, according to the laws of the emperor Leo contained in the Justinian Code. Compare, among others, law 15, title 7, book 2, issued in the preceding year, 472. The other two, Aurelianus and Protadius, were prefects of the praetorium, one of Illyricum and the other of Gaul.]

Just as our lord, the most invincible prince Glycerius, for the blessedness of a better age and the correction of his subjects, judged that it must be prohibited by edictal enactments that henceforth any injury should be attempted against the heavenly Majesty through priestly ordination, and that the merit of a good conscience should become a cause of monetary support, so this shines forth in the elevated oracles of his royal speech: namely, that divine things should not be aided by worldly support, so that, once bidding has been removed,

[The codex has: “with the expiation of crimes, the priestly mitres.” We have inserted the emendation that seemed best.]

and the sinful defilements of crimes removed, priestly mitres may be held according to the standard of the best conscience,

[The same codex adds “of living,” and afterward has “lest complaint arise against the religious,” and then “from nourishment.”]

lest things that ought to have served, through religious distributions, to win the majesty of divine clemency be poured out, like secular administrations, in the acquisition of patronage—things which a devout mind had contributed to the heavenly Majesty for the support of the poor, not a greedy one.

For no one of profane intention should exist who, with a sacrilegious mind, ought to shrink from such religious enactments as a priest, except one who has wished to confess the state of his conscience concerning his promise.

[The codex is defective: “to exist, to whom … ought … priest … conscience.”]

Just as we trust that these decrees will please praiseworthy conduct, so we do not doubt that baser minds will be offended by what has been beneficially defined.

Therefore, by this edictal proclamation, we have decided to admonish everyone, so that henceforth they withdraw from unlawful ambitions and supports,

[The same manuscript: “from unlawful …”]

lest it become necessary for them, together with the burden upon their own conscience—which must always remain subject to the divine Majesty—to undergo the punishment of their own sin in accordance with the most sacred enactments.

Given at Rome on the third day before the Kalends of May.

The end.

[Col. 0899]

# PASCHASIUS QUESNEL’S FIVE DISSERTATIONS ON THE CODE OF ECCLESIASTICAL CANONS AND THE CONSTITUTIONS OF THE HOLY APOSTOLIC SEE

With critical notes and observations on them

## DISSERTATION TWELVE

### Concerning the code of the Roman Church, the oldest of all those that have so far appeared, now published for the first time

[Col. 0899]

### 685. CHAPTER ONE

That the Roman Church formerly possessed its own code before the collection of Dionysius Exiguus the abbot, and that it has not until now emerged from darkness

[Col. 0899A]

#### 1. Concerning the ancient code of the canons of the Roman Church that preceded the Dionysian collection

A vigorous dispute has recently been waged by certain men concerning the ancient code of the Roman Church: some carried away by enthusiasm, others too intent on defending a preconceived opinion, and still others attracted by love of historical truth and ecclesiastical antiquity.

With what success each has contended for his own position, I think will easily be judged when we have brought this dissertation to its conclusion.

Indeed, even from an examination of the code of the canons itself—the code which, buried for so many centuries, we are now bringing to light for the first time—it is clear that all those who have gloried in discovering a genuine code have congratulated themselves without justification.

I mean the ancient code from which, partly in its initial form and partly after it had subsequently been enlarged by various additions, the Roman Church was accustomed, from the age of the Council of Nicaea down to the six-hundredth year of Christ, to draw canons both for declaring ecclesiastical law and for establishing discipline.

The Roman Church had its own codex from ancient times: this need not be called into question, since frequent mention of it occurs in the letters of the Roman pontiffs, and since it was necessary that the Church, which was governed by canons and ecclesiastical regulations, preserve them written down in some codex.

> **Note [Col. 0899B].** The Roman pontiffs certainly frequently insist upon the canons and their observance; but they never mention a codex of canons, indeed they do not even hint at one. They repeatedly mention only the Nicene canons, under which name they also include the Sardican canons, as we proved in the treatise *On Collections*, part II, chapter 1. They received only those canons in former times, as was shown there. Whenever they praise the statutes of the Fathers, or canons without qualification, they mean the Nicene or Sardican canons.

> **Note [Col. 0899B].** It was indeed necessary that the Roman Church, which was governed not so much by canons as by apostolic constitutions, preserve these in the Roman archives, but not written in some codex or corpus of canons. If one wishes to call the copies in which the Nicene and Sardican canons were written together a “codex of canons,” we shall not object. The pontifical constitutions, however, were formerly cited by the Roman bishops not from any codex but from the apostolic archives, as Father Coustant proved at length in the preface to volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, nos. 44 and 45. We observe that this practice became so deeply established that, after the same Roman bishops began to use Dionysius’ collection, they continued for a long time to cite from it only the canons, and never, or almost never, the apostolic constitutions, until after the seventh century.

This is sufficiently clear even from a single letter, or preface, of Dionysius Exiguus to Bishop Stephen. For he himself declares that, brought to this undertaking by the disorder of the ancient codex, he applied himself, on the advice of that prelate, to preparing a new collection.

> **Note [Col. 0900B].** Dionysius speaks not of the ancient codex but of the ancient translation, and he noted its confusion. Laurence, offended by this, urged him to labor over a new interpretation of the Greek canons. In these words Dionysius does not indicate the codex of canons edited by Quesnellus, but the ancient interpretation—called *Prisca* in the commonly published editions—which had been assembled before Dionysius and circulated especially in Italy. It is so confused and entangled that it offends readers. This can scarcely be said of the Isidorian version, as it is called, although that version is older and is for the most part received in Quesnellus’ codex. Certainly Dionysius does not imply that this *Prisca* translation, whatever precisely is meant by it, had been received by the Roman Church or incorporated into the public codex of that Church. Compare what will be said in the observations to chapter 2, no. 1.

But what the arrangement of this codex was, what it contained, and which interpretation of the canons was in use in it—this, finally, has remained most obscure until the present time. It will, I think, receive illumination from the codex that we are publishing and from what we shall say on this occasion.

> **[Col. 0900B]** First of all, I think it must be observed—

> **Note [Col. 0900B].** These remarks concern Peter de Marca, who first in his *Concordia* and later in his *Opuscula* devised this double codex of the Roman Church. The first was the manuscript codex from which, not long after the *Prisca* version of the canons, Voellus and Justellus published their edition. The second was the twin codex of the monastery of Ripoll in Spain. Although Peter de Marca saw these codices, he did not examine them carefully; it is therefore unsurprising that he reported things about them inconsiderately and with less truth than he should have. For the *Prisca* version contained in the first codex cannot, as Quesnellus himself acknowledges, be attributed to the Roman Church. Moreover, the two codices of the monastery of Ripoll are two copies of the Hispanic collection praised by Perez and others. That collection certainly cannot be attributed to Leo, to Leo’s age, or to the Roman Church. See what we said about this Hispanic collection in the treatise *On Collections*.

Some have therefore wrongly counted two different codices of canons as having been used by the Roman Church at different times before it brought the Dionysian codex into use: one supposedly earlier than the Council of Chalcedon, and another made after that synod had been dissolved, on the authority of Saint Leo. This latter collection is said to have been the only one in force in the West for more than sixty years, until another, prepared by Dionysius, succeeded it and replaced it.

They consider the earlier collection to be the one not long ago brought to light from the manuscript codex of the distinguished Christopher Justellus, in volume I of the *Library of Ancient Canon Law*, after the Dionysian codex.

Peter de Marca affirmed that a manuscript doublet of the later collection existed—*Sacred and Imperial Concord*, book III, chapter 3—as Stephen Baluzius reports, in the library of the monastery of Ripoll; from there, Baluzius perhaps promises, it will be brought to light. We also promise our assent to him, since he has demonstrated by certain arguments that this collection was compiled in Leo’s time and under his authority.

For the present, however, we may withhold our assent, since we are inclined toward the contrary view for the following reason: if Saint Leo had thought of preparing a new collection, he would have been led to do so by the confusion of the earlier one. He would therefore have taken care above all that the later collection not fall into the same confusion, but would instead have delivered it, in every respect accurate and complete, in accordance with his expertise in canonical matters. Consequently, neither Dionysius Exiguus nor anyone else who had been offended by the confusion of the ancient translation would have been forced to undertake the labor of preparing a new collection after him. Yet that is precisely what Dionysius undertook almost forty years after Leo’s death, urged continually and familiarly by men devoted to ecclesiastical discipline.

Next, that abbot mentions a single translation, and calls it the *Prisca*.

> **Note [Col. 0901D].** We refute this objection in the treatise already mentioned, part II, chapter 2, section 3, no. 4.

It certainly would not have been called *Prisca* by him if it had not been older than Leo’s time, at least Leo in the final years of his life, whom Dionysius could have seen while he was still living.

> **[Col. 0901C]** Finally, from an examination of the Roman codex that we are now publishing for the first time—

> **Note [Col. 0901D].** Whether this is manifest will, as we trust, become clear from our observations, which will shortly be appended to this dissertation. From them, rather, the contrary view will become evident.

—it is clear that the same collection, received by ancient usage in that Church, became richer at different times through numerous additions; but it is not the case that, after one collection had been discarded, another was taken up in its place from the time of Pope Innocent I until the age of Pope Gelasius.

As for the earlier translation and collection, the learned compilers of the *Library of Ancient Canon Law*, Voellus and Justellus, persuade themselves that it was the one in use in the Roman Church and also in other Western churches from ancient times until the age of the Dionysian codex. John David, in his book *On Bishops Judged Canonically*, chapter 3, article 3, refutes their view at length. We agree with his opinion insofar as he denies that this was a Roman codex, although most of his arguments are rather weak. They establish only that this collection and translation suffered from considerable confusion; that conclusion harms Justellus’ position less than it supports it, since Dionysius testifies that the confusion was so great that it offended most readers and ultimately occasioned the preparation of a new collection.

The stronger proof is the one he derives from the barbarous character of the translation: no sensible person would suppose that such a work was either born in the principal Church and city of the Latin world or was received and commended there for so many years.

### 2. The inclusion of the twenty-eighth canon of Chalcedon certainly does not belong to a Roman codex, much less to a codex used or enlarged in the time of Leo I by the addition of these canons.

Who could believe that a canon on account of which such a great quarrel arose between Leo and the Easterners either slipped unnoticed into the collection of an unwary pontiff or was inserted by a prudent and willing pontiff into the collection of his Church?

### 3. Nor was there a place in the ancient codex of the Roman Church for the Constantinopolitan canons.

Saint Leo repeatedly testifies that they were unknown to him and to his predecessors. Lucentius, his representative at the Council of Chalcedon, likewise protested during the final session that the decrees of that Constantinopolitan synod were not contained in the synodical canons—“not being included in the synodical canons” (*Μὴ ἐμφερόμενα δὲ ἐν τοῖς συνοδικοῖς κανόσι*)—although they said that those decrees had been established nearly eighty years earlier [Col. 0902B] (*Acts of Chalcedon*, session 6).

Nor should we believe that Leo so quickly departed from his own position that he would not merely recognize as legitimate the canons hostile to his see and recently rejected with such vigorous opposition, but would also approve them, make them his own, and insert them into his codex. The fact that those canons were later added, after the dispute had subsided, to the Roman codex that we are bringing to public light was the work of a later age, after the second ecumenical synod had been universally received.

The fact that they occur in Dionysius’ collection is explained differently. His purpose was not to restore the ancient Roman codex to a better condition, but to prepare an entirely new one. He translated all the canons anew from the Greek, arranging the regulations of the Council of Nicaea and thereafter those of all the councils—whether held before or after it—down to the synod of the one hundred and fifty bishops who assembled at Constantinople, in numerical order, that is, from the first chapter through the one hundred and sixty-fifth, as they are found in the Greek authority.

Whatever Dionysius found in the Greek collection that he had before him, he inserted into his own codex. At that time he was not even thinking that it would one day be received by the public authority of the Roman Church.

Finally, we scarcely need another proof by which to exclude such a codex from the Roman Church than the proof that arises spontaneously from its own inspection. It will easily persuade any reader who pays even moderate attention that this was the trial effort of some little Greekling aspiring to Latin and testing his progress in it—an effort wholly unworthy of the Roman Church.

## 690 CHAPTER II  
### The ancient codex is the very one that we are now making public: its source and from whom it was received; of what parts it consists; the order in which it is arranged; and the additions by which it is believed to have been enlarged during successive periods

The learned reader will decide, after fairly weighing the conjectures and proofs we are about to offer, whether what we deny to Justellus’ codex must also be denied to ours.

First of all, we must explain from what source we obtained the codex, both to remove every suspicion of fraud and to ensure that those devoted to ecclesiastical antiquity may know through whose generosity they received so venerable a treasure—*κειμήλιον*—of antiquity.

A copy of it was sent to me from Oxford by the distinguished man and my very dear friend Edmund Bernardo, Savilian Professor of Astronomy at the University of Oxford. Whether he is more distinguished by the extraordinary humanity joined to his learning, or by his tireless love of advancing scholarship, it would be difficult to say.

> **Note [Col. 0903D].** In his general preface Quesnellus wrote *Eduardo*. From this passage we noted there that *Edmundo* should be read. But, as we learned from Fabricius’ note in volume II of the *Greek Library*, chapter 1, no. 20, the true name is Edward, and Quesnellus wrongly calls him Edmund here. Therefore our twelfth annotation to Quesnellus’ preface, volume I of this edition, page XXXVII, will have to be deleted.

The codex is kept in Oriel College at the same university. More than two hundred years ago it was given to the college by one of its own fellows, Andrew Mankyswell; the first page of the codex bears the following inscription:

> “The book of the house of Blessed Mary of Oriel, Oxford, given by Master Andrew Mankyswell, fellow of the aforesaid college. In the year of the Lord 1459.”

This codex is on parchment, of large format, and bears the shelfmark 91 B. Besides this collection of canons and decrees, it contains the letters and sermons of Saint Leo the Great. Inserted among the letters are the constitutions of the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian against the Manichaeans and against Hilary of Arles. After the sermons are two letters from Proterius, Bishop of Alexandria, and Paschasinus, Bishop of Lilybaeum, to our Leo, along with several other matters concerning the life of the holy pontiff.

The collection of canons and decrees contains sixty chapters. Each chapter is divided into titles wherever the subject permits, for councils are divided into canons, while letters are divided into chapters or decrees.

The manuscript codex whose copy was sent to us is said to be about six hundred years old. Yet it was copied from another much more ancient codex, as may be understood both from other indications and from the following note by the scribe, which you will find transcribed on page 34 of the codex:

> “This codex was transcribed from a very ancient exemplar. Therefore no one should doubt the truth of the writings, either in this first chapter of the Nicene canons or in all those that follow, even if something different is found in newer copies.”

> **[Col. 0903C]** The dissertation had been completed and the codex was just about to be sent to the press from this single Oxford copy when, while I was examining the Thuane Library, I unexpectedly encountered a manuscript copy of the same codex, about eighty years old, if I am not mistaken, and of excellent quality. I found that it had been frequently handled by the learned men Sirmond, Salmasius, Chiffletius, Justellus, Voellus, and others.

It is the codex marked with the number 129. The compilers of the *Library of Ancient Canon Law*, Voellus and Justellus, observed that the version of the Chalcedonian canons in the Latin *Prisca* edition agrees with it, volume I, page 296.

It is the codex from which Jacobus Sirmond first published, after the appendix to the *Theodosian Code*, the treatise of Pope Gelasius against the Greeks and the mutilated version of his letter to the Easterners.

From the same codex Claudius Salmasius, in his *Eucharisticus Against Sirmond on the Suburban Churches*, published the rescript of the emperors Honorius and Theodosius against the Pelagians, as well as the sacred constitution of Augustus Constantius, together with two edicts of the prefects Volusianus and Palladius against the same heretics, on pages 283, 288, and 291.

Chiffletius likewise praises the codex in his notes on Ferrandus’ *Summary of the Canons*, page 305:

> “We certainly saw, in the library of the distinguished man Jacobus Augustus Thuaneus, an old codex in which, as in Ferrandus, title 20 of the Nicene canons of Dionysius is not counted among the Nicene canons. A Nicene profession of faith is placed first as the first title; the remaining nineteen Nicene canons of Dionysius extend to twenty-six, so that all the Nicene titles in that codex amount to twenty-seven, excluding the final Dionysian title.”

Anyone who compares this with our codex will easily see that Chiffletius must have been speaking of no other codex.

The discovery of so distinguished a monument imposed a new labor and required new care in examining and collating the codex. What differences I found between the two, although I have noted them in their proper places, I shall nevertheless explain briefly here.

Both codices have the same title at the head of the index. Except for a few items, the index itself is identical in both. The sequence of chapters is the same through chapter fifty-six. The remaining five chapters of the Oxford manuscript are numbered in a different order in the Thuane codex; this is also noted at the end of the index, page 10.

The Thuane codex also contains a synopsis of the decretal letters, a decretal of Pope Gelasius, and a rule concerning forms.

As for the letters of Pope Saint Leo—

> **Note [Col. 0903D].** The letters of Leo, which in the Thuane codex and in several other, more excellent codices, as well as in our edition, close the collection from chapter 67 through chapter 98, are a portion of the same collection. They were omitted in the Oxford manuscript alone for a different reason. We demonstrated this in note 1 to chapter 67, where we also explained the annotation that seems to contradict this conclusion in the cited Oxford codex. We proved in note 8 to chapter 63 that the closing formula, “In the name of the Lord, the canons are completed,” must be referred elsewhere.

—the fact that they are not part of the body of canons, or of this codex, is indicated by the clause appended after the rule concerning forms, in the following words:

> “In the name of the Lord, the canons are completed.”

This is also proved by the difference in both the order and number of the letters found in the two codices. There are fewer in the Thuane codex and more in the Oxford codex, where they were added by a later hand.

Finally, the title of the Oxford codex excludes these letters from the collection of canons:

> “This codex contains ecclesiastical canons and constitutions of the holy apostolic see in sixty chapters. The materials added from the writings of blessed Pope Leo are not part of the body of the canons.”

This is how I read it in the copy that I possess. The genuineness of the title is confirmed by the *Catalogue of the Manuscript Books of the Library of Oriel College, Oxford*, published in London in 1600, page 43, where the same words are found. You will find the other differences between the two codices noted in the margin at the relevant places.

In the codex of canons that we have published, a distinction must further be made between the materials that constitute the chapters and certain historical observations inserted here and there outside the sequence of chapters, although they are not very frequent.

These observations were written in a more recent style and are found only in the Oxford codex. In my opinion, they were added by the man who, in the annotation mentioned above, testifies that he transcribed the codex from a very ancient exemplar. Since they are not part of the codex, we arranged for them to be printed in a different type.

Nor should all the parts of the codex be thought to belong to the same period.

> **Note [Col. 0904D].** Since Quesnellus believed on the one hand that this had been the ancient codex of the Roman Church, published with public authority and in use under Innocent I and his other successors down to Gelasius, after whose pontificate Dionysius Exiguus arranged a new codex; but on the other hand he saw that not everything contained in this codex could belong to the public Roman codex under Innocent, Zosimus, or Leo, he devised documents added to the codex at different times in order to reconcile everything in some fashion with his opinion—or rather, with his prejudice. Distinguishing the supposed periods of these additions, he fabricated eight ages of the codex. They rest on no foundation but the prejudice just mentioned and require no more extensive refutation.

> For if we clearly demonstrate that this codex did not belong to the Roman Church, as we shall demonstrate in the observations appended after this dissertation, all these ages, fabricated from the same prejudice, will collapse with it. Compare also what we shall note concerning this hypothesis of successive ages in the observations to chapter 1, nos. 4 and 5, and chapter 2, no. 8, where several particular inconsistencies will be exposed. We shall also reveal a notable contradiction in Quesnellus in note 21 to chapter 4.

### 693

Some parts, older than others, formed the codex in earlier periods; others, belonging to a later age, were subsequently attached to the earlier chapters as successive periods passed, until eventually the codex reached the number sixty.

At what time each part began either to form the codex or to be added to it is obscure. No one can bring the matter to light, however imperfectly, except by conjecture; this is what we shall also attempt below.

It is clear that the index placed at the beginning of the entire work is later, because it mentions sixty chapters. Consequently, nothing can be established from it concerning which parts originally constituted the codex.

> **Note [Col. 0905D].** Since the index of the chapters prefixed to the work, as found in the Thuane codex, designates ninety-eight chapters of this collection—which are found not so much in the Thuane codex as in the other, older and more excellent Oxford copies of the same collection—it is clear that this index points to the original collection and is contemporary with it. The annotation found only in the Oxford manuscript, which mentions sixty chapters, must be assigned to a later period. See what we said about this annotation in note 1 to chapter 67.

I do not hold the same judgment concerning the prologue. Nothing prevents us from believing that it was published near the beginning of the fifth century and prefixed to the codex that was in use in the Roman Church in the time of Pope Innocent I. For the tenth book of Eusebius’ *Ecclesiastical History*, supplemented by Rufinus and cited in that preface, had been published several years before Innocent’s death.

> **Note [Col. 0905D].** The principal reason why this prologue must not be thought to have been written and published around the beginning of the fifth century is that some material from Gelasius’ decree on apocryphal books has been transferred into it. Compare the observations on this dissertation, chapter 2, no. 3, where we shall refute Quesnellus’ view that Gelasius copied from this prologue. Whether this prologue is contemporary with our collection, or was added to it later—it is not found in the Caesarean manuscript Vindobonensis 39—and whether it was prefixed only to the first chapter, which contains the Nicene synod, since the prologue speaks only of that synod, or whether it belongs to the entire collection, we shall not oppose whichever view one may adopt.

If anyone nevertheless prefers to assign this prologue to a later period, I shall not argue against him. This much, however, seems certain: the codex to which the preface was attached contained very few chapters. This follows both because the prologue is almost entirely about the Council of Nicaea and because it indicates that only a few decrees had been added to the Nicene decrees, as an appendix—not as though they claimed a place in the Roman codex by the authority proper to the synods from which they originated, but as materials taken up by the apostolic see for its own use and useful to the administration of its Church:

> “For some regulations also have been appended, which the Church, receiving what has been mentioned, confirmed.”

> **Note [Col. 0906C].** The text indicates that only the Nicene regulations were appended to the profession of faith, as we shall demonstrate in the observations to chapter 2, no. 2. From this everyone will see that the conjectures offered here by Quesnellus are empty.

These words persuade us that the canons of the Council of Carthage are chiefly intended—canons which are placed after the Nicene and Sardican canons, confused together as one. The words of the first chapter *On Grace*, formerly attributed to Celestine and now to Leo, convey the same meaning. Those words testify that those very canons of the Church of Carthage had then, as earlier, been inserted into the Roman codex, as the following passage concerning later additions makes clear:

> “So that we might also join together certain pronouncements of the African councils, which the apostolic bishops certainly made their own when they approved them” (*chapter 1, On Grace*).

I therefore readily incline to the following view: from the time of the Nicene and Sardican synods until the age of Innocent and Zosimus, the Roman codex contained no other canons or ecclesiastical regulations besides those of the Councils of Nicaea and Sardica.

> **Note [Col. 0906D].** We have proved in the treatise, part II, chapter 1, that formerly the Roman Church received no canons other than the Nicene and Sardican canons—not only until the time of Innocent and Zosimus, but for a considerable period afterward as well. The version of the Nicene canons, however, differed from the one contained in the collection edited by Quesnellus, as we shall demonstrate in the observations to chapter 1, nos. 2 and 3.

The Sardican canons had a place in it only because they were regarded as Nicene, bore that name, and were appended to the Nicene canons without any distinction.

Innocent himself gives clear testimony on this matter. His words both support the assertion of the codex’s genuineness and receive great illumination from the codex in return. Innocent writes in his letter to the clergy and people of Constantinople:

> “As far as observance of the canons is concerned, we write that obedience must be given to those determined at Nicaea. The Catholic Church ought to obey only these and add its own support to them” (*Letter 15, from Sozomen, book VIII, chapter 26; volume I of the edition of the letters of the supreme pontiffs, Roman edition*).

He says the same in Letter 16 to Theophilus of Alexandria:

> “If you trust your conscience, you too should hasten by judgment to the synod soon to be celebrated in Christ, and there contend according to the canons and decrees of the Council of Nicaea. For the Roman Church admits no other canons.”
