These words confirm our opinion: in the time of Innocent the Roman Church accepted and had inserted in its codex no other canons than those that were either truly Nicene or were regarded as Nicene and counted among them by the Romans, in the manner in which they are represented in our codex.

Yet this same codex also reconciles Innocent with Innocent, for in his letters he repeatedly cites and employs the Sardican canons: in his letter to Victricius, canons 3, 4, and 7 concerning appeals to the Roman bishop; in Letter 16, concerning the non-reception of clerics rejected by another bishop; concerning the synod to which he invites Theophilus; and in other places mentioned by John David.

By this route David also returns to agreement with de Marca. Once the position asserted by each is granted, each is simultaneously defeated by the other and victorious over him, since both propositions are entirely true: Innocent received only the Nicene canons, and yet he admitted the Sardican canons and used them in the examination of ecclesiastical cases. Innocent received the Sardican canons because they were regarded as Nicene and honored with the name of the Nicene canons.

This, I think, was the first age of the Roman codex, as it were its infancy. At that time, under Pope Innocent, the first chapter alone of the codex that we are publishing constituted the entire codex of that period—namely, at the time when the case of Chrysostom was being debated.

Under the same Innocent, however, I believe that the codex later grew larger through the addition of the canons of the Council of Carthage.

> **Note [Col. 0906D].** We have said enough about this and about the subsequent additions or ages of the Roman codex invented by Quesnellus in note 3. Nevertheless, we shall note several particular matters in the following annotations.

This occurred when the Pelagian heresy arose some years after Chrysostom’s death. It created a greater need for intercourse between the Roman and African Churches and gave occasion for letters and embassies to be exchanged more frequently than usual between the bishops of the two Churches. Augustine writes:

> “With so many and such great ecclesiastical letters running back and forth between the apostolic see and the African bishops” (*book II to Boniface, chapter 3*).

On this occasion the discipline of the African Church became better known to the Roman Church. The leaders of the Roman clergy judged it suited to their own customs and wished to make it their own and a part of their own codex. At this period, therefore, the second chapter was first added.

It acquired still greater strength under Innocent’s successor, Zosimus. Since he was Greek by nationality and captivated by love of the laws of his homeland, he bestowed Greek canons upon the Roman Church and appended to the Roman collection the three synods of Ancyra, Neocaesarea, and Gangra, which follow the Carthaginian material in the codex.

Nor were the canons of those three synods chosen among the Greek canons without good reason. They were the most ancient of all, and for that reason they are found arranged in the same order in the ancient version preserved by Isidore.

The Synod of Ancyra was held in A.D. 314, and the Synod of Neocaesarea followed it immediately.

> **Note [Col. 0907C].** We demonstrated in the treatise, part I, chapter 4, section 1, that the Synod of Gangra was much later and was held between the years 362 and 370.

The Synod of Gangra is believed to have been held in A.D. 325. Thus these synods were either contemporary with the Council of Nicaea or earlier than it.

He seems to me to have acquired mature strength after the death of Zosimus. For when the case of the Pelagians had been concluded during Zosimus’ pontificate, it was decided to place in the Roman codex whatever had either been written about that matter to the Roman pontiff by the African bishops, or had been written back by him to them, as well as the synods held in Africa against the Pelagians.

The imperial constitutions and prefectural edicts issued against the same heretics were also added, so that, if they should at some time renew their struggle against Catholic teaching, they would be ordered either to subscribe to those decrees or to suffer the penalties established in them.

Four decretal letters of Innocent I were also appended. In them, having been consulted by his fellow bishops Exuperius, Victricius, Decentius, and others on various matters of great disciplinary importance, he explains and confirms those matters according to the ecclesiastical regulations and especially according to the norm of the Roman Church.

We learn first that all these materials were added to the codex before Leo’s time from the chapters cited *On Grace*. Many excerpts are found there from the African councils and letters, as well as from Innocent’s rescripts against Pelagian doctrines. These councils are said to have been made the possession of the apostolic bishops when they approved them and inscribed them in their own codex. At the end of the chapters they are called, without distinction, both African canons and the letters of the pontiffs, the writings of the apostolic see, just as the Council of Carthage had been called in chapter 7.

We also embrace as proper to the apostolic see what was established within the decrees of the Council of Carthage. The words of Saint Leo in Letter 3—now Letter 4, chapter 5—to the bishops of Campania, Picenum, Tuscany, and others, written to them because he wished them to observe Innocent’s decretal constitutions, prove the same point:

> “So that nothing may be thought to have been omitted by us, we command that all the decretal constitutions both of blessed memory Innocent and of all our predecessors, which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the discipline of the canons, be so carefully observed by your affection that anyone who has transgressed them may know that pardon will henceforth be denied him.”

When Leo wrote this, he was turning the eyes of his mind toward those decrees of Innocent that are preserved in his letter to Victricius of Rouen and in another to the bishops of Macedonia, in which the ordination of bigamists is condemned. But how could such decretal enactments, sent to the more remote regions of Gaul and to Macedonia, have been so well known to the Italians that they were said to have been promulgated and that obedience to them was required, unless they had been inserted in a public and accepted codex? Why, moreover, when he mentions all his predecessors in general, does he expressly name Innocent alone, unless because

[Note: [Col. 0907C] We refute Quesnellus’s argument for establishing a public codex of the Roman Church in *Treatise*, part II, chapter 1, § 4.]

[Col. 0908C] the decrees of Innocent alone [Col. 0909A] had by that time been entered into the codex, at least before the Council of Chalcedon, as can be discerned from the order of the codex. In Innocent’s age, evidently, only the Nicene canons—or those regarded as Nicene, as we have said more than once—were held in the Roman Church as the standard for ecclesiastical judgments and regulations. Later, Innocent’s decrees were added to them, serving as a kind of commentary for understanding the canons. Then, following this example, the decrees of Siricius, who was earlier than Innocent, were also cast into the codex.

[Note: [Col. 0907C] See the exact translator of Leo. In Leo’s letter 4, written before the Council of Chalcedon in the year 443, he orders that “all the decretal enactments both of blessed memory Innocent and of all our predecessors” be observed. There, “both of Innocent” has the same sense as “not only of Innocent,” or “not of Innocent alone, but all those of all our predecessors.” Nevertheless, Quesnellus explains this as referring to the decrees of Innocent alone, and not indeed to all of them, but only to those that had at that time been transferred into the codex before the Council of Chalcedon—that is, only four decretal enactments of that same pontiff, as can be recognized from the order of the codex. For only four constitutions of Innocent alone are placed in the Quesnellian codex before the acts of Chalcedon, which are described in chapter 25.

If the holy pontiff had wished to indicate only these letters of Innocent alone, what need was there for him to commend all the decretal enactments of all his predecessors? But if Leo required a public codex in order for all these things to have been promulgated, then unquestionably some codex must have existed before the Council of Chalcedon in which not only the four decrees of Innocent alone, but many other decrees both of Innocent himself and of all his predecessors were contained. Since no such codex is found either in Quesnellus’s codex or in any other ancient collection, his invention is exposed: from Leo, he inferred that a public codex was required for promulgation, and, even more, he transformed the codex published by himself into a public codex of the Roman Church and one indicated by Leo.

We may add another point. If Quesnellus is to be believed, no decretal letters of the pontiffs had been entered into a codex, and none had been promulgated before Chalcedon except those of Innocent alone. Therefore, before Innocent, no decretal letters had been entered into a codex and none had been promulgated; and, as he likewise maintains, only the Nicene and Sardican canons were regarded under Innocent as the rule. How, then, did Siricius, in his letter to Himerius, after exhorting him to observe the canons and to hold fast the decretal enactments, pronounce that general statement: “Let it be permitted to no priest of the Lord to be ignorant of the statutes of the apostolic see or of the venerable definitions of the canons”?

For these statements to have force, some promulgation was required. In Quesnellus’s system, however, a public codex is required for promulgation; and, according to his account, this codex first received the apostolic constitutions after Innocent. Furthermore, the Gallican bishops adhering to the see of Arles openly reject this very opinion when they wrote to Saint Leo in letter 65 of our edition, chapter 2: “Therefore, following the antiquity, the predecessors of Your Blessedness confirmed by promulgated authorities—as the archives of the apostolic see undoubtedly also contain—the ancient institution that tradition had handed down concerning the privileges of the Church of Arles.”

By the word “authorities” are meant the letters of Zosimus concerning the privileges of the Church of Arles. These letters, however, were not inserted by the pontiffs in a public codex, just as they are not found in Quesnellus’s codex. Hence those same bishops mention not a codex but the archives in which they were preserved. Yet when they affirm that these letters were promulgated by the pontiffs from the time they were sent to Gaul, they plainly did not regard the publication of a public Roman codex as necessary for promulgation.

Nor should anyone reply that Quesnellus is speaking of constitutions promulgated for Churches subject to the Roman synod, whereas Siricius and the bishops [Col. 0909D] of Gaul, in the passages cited, are speaking of constitutions for the Churches of Spain and Gaul. If a public codex is required for promulgation for the suburban Churches, will it not be required for more distant ones? Or, if for far-distant Churches that promulgation is sufficient by which decrees are publicly sent to those regions and brought to everyone’s knowledge without the publication of a public codex, why would the same not be valid for Churches belonging to the Roman synod, to which the pontiffs generally sent their enactments from a public synod? From this fragment of Quesnellus’s invention the invention of his entire system becomes clear.]

Moreover, we must not pass over without comment the words of our Leo quoted above: “The decretal enactments … which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the disciplines of the canons.” We have restored these words to their integrity, since previously the text read *ordinata* (“ordered”) rather than *promulgata* (“promulgated”). First, the word *constituta* (“enactments”), by which our Leo denotes the decrees of his predecessors, is the same word used in the title of our codex: “The Enactments of the Apostolic See.” Thus, from this fact alone, one may suspect that Leo was indicating this same codex.

[Col. 0909B] 699 Next, the word *promulgata* also seems to suggest that these same ecclesiastical laws were first written to individual bishops of distant regions and afterward cast into a public codex of pontifical enactments, so that they might come to the knowledge of all those Churches that received the rule of discipline from the Roman Church, as belonging, so to speak, to its synod. Hincmar of Reims develops the explanation of this word at greater length in his *Opusculum of 55 Chapters against Hincmar of Laon*. The latter had extracted various passages from the letters of the pontiffs to prove that no one could reject obedience to them without being branded with temerity, and thus to represent the bishop of Reims as guilty of this offense.

Hincmar of Reims therefore investigates the etymology of the word with particular care. Comparing the opinions of the ancients on the matter, he writes: “‘Promulgo’ is so called, as though it were ‘promo vulgo,’ that is, ‘I bring forth publicly,’ or ‘I first issue something to the common people.’ Hence Paul, in his *Glosses*, says in this way: ‘Laws are said to be promulgated when they are issued to the common people.’ Isidore too, as he himself says, explained the word on Cicero’s authority, saying: ‘Promulgated means brought forth; thus a law is said to be promulgated; and promulgated means made known and announced to everyone and to the whole people.’”

Hincmar adds: “Those who analyze words have wished the distinction of meaning between *divulgata* (‘made widely known’) and *provulgata*, or *promulgata* (‘published’), to be this: things are simply called *divulgata* when they are exposed to everyone’s knowledge; but *provulgata* or *promulgata* when they are brought forth for the preservation of decrees and for the knowledge of all, so that they may be understood as having been produced in order that people may preserve them without resistance.”

From this we understand both why it was necessary to restore the word *promulgata* in Leo’s text and how that word rather clearly indicates to us a Roman codex of canons and constitutions.

The same part of the codex is also attested by letter 6 (now letter 1, addressed to the bishop of Aquileia) of our Leo, especially in chapter 1, where he seems to point to the two parts of which it is composed in these words: “What is not granted even to the innocent by the authority of our canons and decrees”; and in chapter 2, where he says: “All the synodal decrees that the authority of the apostolic see has confirmed for the eradication of this heresy.”

These belong to those matters of which we read in the preface to the codex: “For certain rules also are appended [Col. 0910A] to the Nicene canons, which the aforesaid Church received and confirmed”—the Roman Church, that is.

[Note: [Col. 0910D] Just as, from the context of the preface, certain appended rules indicate the Nicene canons—as we noted in note e [above, col. 906]—so the word *subnexae* (“appended”) refers to the Nicene Creed, to which those same rules, or canons, were appended. Quesnellus is therefore wrong when he says “to the Nicene canons.” Substitute “to the Nicene Creed,” and the rest of his argument disappears.]

These too are the African synodal decrees concerning which the preface to the *Sentences on Grace* says above: “So that we also appended certain sentences of the African councils, which the apostolic bishops plainly made their own when they approved them”; and in chapter 7: “That which was also established within the decrees of the Council of Carthage we embrace as proper to the apostolic see.”

These decrees—which the apostolic see, as is clear from the testimonies just cited, received, confirmed, approved, made its own, embraced as though they were its own, and appended to its rules—plainly seem to have been cast into the Roman codex, which served to instruct ecclesiastical judgments and to administer sacred affairs.

I perceive, unless I am mistaken, two classes of writings belonging to the apostolic see, and two archives in which ecclesiastical records were preserved at the apostolic see. One is often mentioned by ancient writers under the name of the *scrinia* (“archives”); the other is read as being called the *Codex of the Canons and Constitutions of the Apostolic See*. Both institutions were transferred from the Empire into the Church, as were nearly all ecclesiastical terms. Thus the *Theodosian Code* and the *Notitia of the Empire* mention the archives of letters, petitions, and many other matters, as well as the chief officers of the archives and their various divisions.

The archives of the apostolic see, then, were one thing, and the codex of the Roman Church another. Everything written that flowed to the apostolic see from the various parts of the world was placed in the archives, as was whatever ecclesiastical acts and documents the apostolic see judged should be preserved, to be drawn from there as circumstances required.

Thus our Leo mentions a letter of Saint Cyril to Nestorius: “The archives of the apostolic see received it after it had been sent by him.” And in letter 92 (now 119), addressed to Maximus of Antioch, he cites another letter of the same Cyril, “which,” he says, “we found, after searching for it in our archives, to be authentic.”

[Note: [Col. 0910D] This entire discussion, together with what follows, is a very ingenious but insufficiently solid system, which is adequately undermined by the preceding note.]

What had to be adopted for the daily observance of the discipline of the Churches and for the administration of justice in ecclesiastical matters was entered into the codex, as were writings by bishops or enactments by emperors directed toward confirming the faith or against heretics. Of the first kind are the council canons and the decrees of the Roman pontiffs in our codex; of the second are the statements of faith received and approved by the apostolic see, together with the edicts and constitutions of the emperors.

Accordingly, letters of the pontiffs sent to individual Churches abroad acquired force among the Churches belonging to the apostolic see and imposed the obligation of obedience when they began to be brought forth from private archives into the public codex, promulgated, and treated as decretal enactments. Other writings, so long as they were not brought forth from there, could not have there the force of a published law. The African synodal decrees of which we are speaking occupy a place in the codex before the acts or decrees of the Council of Chalcedon. This indicates that, before that council, they had already been granted Roman citizenship and enrolled among the rights of the Roman Church.

[Col. 0910D] After the Council of Chalcedon, the acts of that synod were collected through Leo’s care and diligence, as we learn repeatedly from his letters, [Note: [Col. 0910D] Leo did indeed ask Julian in letter 113 that all the Chalcedonian acts be rendered in Latin in a completely exact translation. But he did not obtain this, as we establish in volume II, in the observations on Quesnellus’s third note to that same letter 113.] translated into Latin, and reduced to a single body. Although they were preserved separately and in their entirety in the archives, it nevertheless seemed fitting that the principal chapters, excerpted from them, should be attached to the Roman codex, so that they might be readily available to everyone. These are the materials that lie in our codex after the letter of Pope Innocent to Victricius, in chapters 25, 26, 27, and 28.

After the Chalcedonian documents come the letters of Pope Siricius, together with the rescript of Saint Ambrose, and also the letters of the Roman pontiffs Zosimus, Boniface, and Celestine. Several considerations persuade me that these were inserted by our Leo.

1. They immediately follow the acts of Chalcedon and the imperial constitutions relating to them.

2. This accords especially with the ardent zeal with which he pursued the decrees and authority of his see. I can easily imagine that this moved him to collect whatever decrees of his predecessors he could and to place them among the ecclesiastical rules.

[Note: [Col. 0911D] If Saint Leo had added to the codex whatever decrees of his predecessors he could, would he, in his own time—when the archives of the apostolic see were flourishing most fully—have neglected many important and excellent constitutions that are absent from our collection but published elsewhere? And would he not have found even a single constitution of those who preceded Siricius, or at least of Damasus, worthy of the public codex?]

3. The decrees of these pontiffs are arranged there in such a way that, with only a very few items interposed, they are enclosed by that collection of testimonies which Leo had gathered from the holy Fathers and appended to the end of letter 134, alternatively 97 (now 165), addressed to the emperor Leo, as well as by the acts of the condemnation of Eutyches at the Constantinopolitan council of Flavian, which the same person sent to Saint Leo.

4. Although the letters of nearly all Leo’s predecessors are included, not a single letter of Leo himself appears. I do not think this was done for any other reason than that Leo himself was the author of the addition then being made to the codex. Carefully examining the archives of the apostolic see, he wished those items that seemed of greater importance to be brought out from the darkness of the archives into the light of the public codex and promulgated.

For the same reason, I think, it happened that the letters of Zosimus issued in defense of the privileges of the Church of Arles were not entered into the Roman codex. Leo would not have approved them by inserting them when he said that their position had afterward been corrected by better judgment—namely, by the decree of Boniface, which was inserted into the codex by that pontiff.

I also think this explains why Leo omitted those authorities of past bishops of the apostolic see concerning grace and free will that were thought to be Celestine’s. For he himself was the author of this collection.

[Note: [Col. 0911D] Quesnellus here indicates that, in his view, Saint Leo was the author of the collection of those authorities concerning grace and free will that are usually appended to Celestine’s letter in printed editions. We refute this opinion of his at length in volume II, in the observations on his third dissertation.]

Finally, with the possible exception of Siricius, Leo had lived during the time of all those pontiffs, and he had been a witness to their decrees and, in some cases, a participant in and author of their formulation. It is therefore unsurprising that he valued them above the others.

A certain narrative of the Eutychian affairs follows, including the condemnation of Dioscorus and Acacius. This section is part of the *Brief History of the Eutychianists* composed in the time of Pope Gelasius, as the editors of the Roman pontifical letters who prefixed it to Leo’s letters conjecture. It is probable that this narrative, together with the letters of the Roman pontiffs Simplicius, Felix, and Gelasius, and the other materials concerning the Lord’s incarnation, down to chapter 56, was inserted into the codex in Gelasius’s time. This is suggested both by the frequent and bitter controversies that then broke out on account of the Eutychian heresy and by the sequence and arrangement of the events themselves, which concern Leo’s immediate successors.

The canons of four Greek councils, which had been omitted earlier—namely, the definition of Ephesus and the decrees of Antioch, Laodicea, and Constantinople, together with the Council of Theles—close the entire codex.

[Note: [Col. 0912D] This is false, as will become clear from note 1 on chapter 67 of the codex itself [for us, col. 743, note a], where we show that Leo’s letters belong to and close that same codex. As for the Constantinopolitan canons, see what will be said in the observations on this dissertation, chapter 1, no. 4, and chapter 2, no. 8. See also note 21 on chapter 4 of this dissertation [below, col. 923, note b].]

Whether they were added at the same time or at different times is unclear. At least the Constantinopolitan canons were appended to the codex after Saint Gregory the Great, unless I am mistaken. For the testimony of that same pontiff prevents us from believing that they were inserted into it in his time: he states that the Constantinopolitan canons had not yet been received in his day. What judgment should be formed concerning the Council of Theles will be shown below in Dissertation 15.

703

## CHAPTER III. The authenticity of the codex is investigated and established by several arguments.

1. In support of the authenticity of this codex [Note: [Col. 0912D] No one has challenged the authenticity of the codex. We contend only that it is not the codex of the Roman Church.] let this description of it be placed first. It demonstrates that there is no indication of fraud or *νοθεία* (*nótheia*, adulteration/forgery) in it. It would scarcely, indeed hardly, have been possible for an impostor not to have mixed into these chapters many things that would betray his design and expose his fraud. For no spurious product has so far appeared that did not display certain marks of fabrication by which it could be distinguished from genuine writings.

There are, it seems, two reasons for this. First, such miserable little writings are usually manufactured by unskilled compilers, who cannot clothe and adorn them so completely in the colors of truth that unmistakable indications do not spontaneously break out and expose the evil craft and the artificers of falsehood. The second reason is that such false writings generally seek to provide support for false claims—whether rights and privileges or doctrines. Since it is extremely difficult for a single falsehood to secure belief, the assistance of other falsehoods must be summoned. But when these are multiplied for that purpose, the usual result is the opposite: they support the truth more than the lie and reveal the fraud all the more clearly the more carefully they embellish it. We have detected nothing of this kind in this codex.

2. The fact that this little work should not be thought to have been recently fabricated for the purpose of fraud is shown by the circumstance that a third copy, entirely like ours, once came into the hands of the learned Jacobus Pamelius. From it he cites the sixth canon of Nicaea in his notes on Saint Cyprian’s book *On the Unity of the Church*. “The sixth canon of the Council of Nicaea,” he says, “is commonly read as follows in the codex of the venerable antiquity of Saint Vedast of Arras, written approximately eight hundred years ago:

> ‘The Roman Church has always held the primacy. Let Egypt, Libya, and Pentapolis also retain it, so that the bishop of Alexandria may have authority over all these, since this is also the custom of the Roman bishop. Likewise, let the bishop established in Antioch have it. And so, in the other provinces too, let the privileges of the Churches remain secure.’”

“Thus far,” Pamelius says, “it was translated long ago from the Greek by Dionysius, a Roman abbot surnamed Exiguus, as is evident from his letter to the presbyter Julian at the end of the said codex. Trithemius says that he flourished around the year of the Lord 550.”

The version of this sixth Nicene canon is exactly the same as ours and was plainly taken from a similar codex. This is proved much more clearly and distinctly by Alan Cope of London in his *Dialogue I against the Innovators*, published a hundred years ago. For in chapter 12 he writes:

> “That canon—the sixth, as it is commonly called, of the Council of Nicaea, but the tenth in this interpretation of Dionysius—is expressed in this way under the title ‘On the Primacy of the Roman Church’:
>
> ‘The Roman Church has always held the primacy. Let Egypt, Libya, and Pentapolis also retain it; and thus let the bishop of Alexandria have authority over all these, since this is also the custom of the Roman bishop. Likewise, let the bishop established in Antioch have it. And so, in the other provinces too, let the privileges of the Churches remain secure …’”

“Perhaps here you will ask,” he continues, “where this interpretation of the Nicene canons, so ancient, lies hidden, and from where I obtained it. This treasure was recently first brought out of darkness by the exceptionally learned man Jacobus Pamelius, born to restore the Library of the Ancient Theologians. Just as, with his customary courtesy, he freely shared it with me, so I now share it most gladly with you. Thus you may also understand that there were copies of the Council of Nicaea other than those now commonly circulated, differing from them both in the order and in the number of the canons.

For in this interpretation of Dionysius forty-seven canons are listed. Twenty of these, the following words appearing there immediately after canon 27 testify, were absent from the Greek copies:

> ‘Likewise, those which are not found in the Greek copies but are found in the Latin codices.’

In their sequence, canons 30 and 34 are entitled as follows: the former, ‘On appeals to the Roman bishop’; the latter, ‘On the reconsideration of a provincial synod by the vicars of the bishop of the city of Rome, if an appeal has been made.’

Alan Cope further notes that, at the end of the forty-seven canons, this closing formula was appended:

> ‘The canons or decrees of the Council of Nicaea.’”

Finally, he adds:

> “The codex in which this interpretation of the Council of Nicaea is written is preserved in the library of Saint Vedast of Arras. It has such an appearance of antiquity that those capable of judging it consider it to have been written approximately eight hundred years ago.”

Severinus Binius also cites this Arras codex in his notes on canon 6 of Nicaea and on the Council of Sardica. He thinks that the codex is Dionysian, just as they do.

[Note: [Col. 0913D] In his notes on the Council of Sardica, Binius does indeed cite two codices, one belonging to a Roman library and the other from Arras, in which the Sardican canons are joined to the Nicene canons as though they were the canons of a single council. This is certainly true of the Arras manuscript, which belongs to our collection. But no Vatican manuscript or manuscript of any Roman library survives in which this joining of the Nicene and Sardican canons is found, except Vatican, Regina 1997, which belongs to another collection. Since that codex was brought into the Vatican Library much later than Binius’s time, it could not have been the Roman codex cited by Binius.]

He reports that a manuscript codex is likewise hidden in the Vatican Library, in which the Nicene and Sardican canons are written joined to one another without any sign of distinction, as though they were the canons of a single council, so that one may suspect this codex to be similar to ours.

There are, however, several matters in the statements of Alan and Pamelius that require correction. Both are mistaken when they suppose this version of canon 6 of Nicaea to be Dionysian. They would not have thought so had they lived after the publication of Dionysius’s codex, or had they consulted the edition published at Mainz in 1525 by Johannes Wendelstinus, or had they remembered that Pope Leo’s legates produced this translation at the Council of Chalcedon approximately fifty years before Dionysius’s codex of canons was composed.

Alan is also mistaken when, from chapters 30 and 34 of his own codex and ours, he infers that there were other Nicene canons in addition to the twenty found in the Greek copies. Finally, he is mistaken when, in the words that follow, he considers it probable that the Sardican Fathers borrowed their canon on appeals from the Nicene Fathers.

These errors, however, do not harm our purpose and do not prevent the greatest credibility from being accorded our codex on the basis of the codex of Pamelius and Alan. For the one is exceedingly similar to the other. The version of the sixth canon is the same in both; the order number is likewise the same, namely tenth in each; canon 30 is also the same, with the same title; and so is canon 34, despite a slight difference in its title. The same number of Nicene canons is counted—namely, forty-seven—with this formula appended at their end:

> “These are the canons or decrees of the Council of Nicaea.”

I also suspect that the same Arras codex came into the hands of Henricus Gravius, professor at Louvain, and that he extracted from it the constitution of the emperor Honorius to Pope Palladius against the Pelagians, which he once communicated to Cardinal Baronius. “We received that rescript,” says the author of the *Annals* under the year of Christ 418, no. 19, “brought out from the hiding places of antiquity by the most eloquent man of blessed memory, Henricus Gravius, professor at Louvain, while he was living at Rome under Gregory XIV, Roman pontiff, having previously been summoned by Sixtus. He himself obtained it from the codex of the monastery of Saint Vedast at Arras.”

706

3. The antiquity and authenticity of the codex are proved by several documents found in it, either never before published, published only a few years ago, or more accurately printed in it than in copies published elsewhere. Such are the rescripts of the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, one [Col. 0914C] addressed to Pope Palladius and the other to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage. There is also another rescript of the emperor Constantius to Volusianus, prefect of the City, together with the edicts of Palladius and Volusianus and the letter of Aurelius. All these were published by the eminent Cardinal Baronius under the years 418, 419, and 420, from the Arras codex already mentioned, and now emerge from ours in a more correct form.

There is likewise the lengthy fragment of a letter of Pope Gelasius to the Eastern bishops, recently published by Sirmond after the appendix to the *Theodosian Code*. It is found in our codex, truncated in the same places. Finally, the profession of faith of the presbyter Faustinus and other as-yet-unpublished formulas of faith protect the codex in which they are inserted from the charge of novelty or fabrication. For I do not know whether genuine monuments of antiquity have ever before emerged from spurious products—monuments either previously unprinted or cleansed of errors.

4. Let there also be added an argument from Ferrandus, deacon of the Church of Carthage.

[Note: [Col. 0913D] Ferrandus provides no support whatever for Quesnellus’s codex. Indeed, if, from a Roman codex brought to Africa in which the Nicene and Sardican canons were joined, the division of those canons was subsequently made by which the final Nicene canon on not kneeling on Sundays and during Pentecost was counted as the first Sardican canon, as we read in Ferrandus, his authority rather harms Quesnellus’s codex. For it would follow that the Roman codex from which that division is thought to have been made contained the Nicene canon that, through an erroneous division, became the first Sardican canon. Since this canon is absent from Quesnellus’s codex, it would unquestionably follow that the latter was not the Roman codex.

We explained in *Treatise*, part II, chapter 1, that Ferrandus cited the canon first among the Sardican canons because he used a copy of the Sardican canons in which, when the Sardican canons had been separated from the Nicene canons and inscribed under their own name, an error had caused the separation to begin with the final Nicene canon. But whether the division was made from a Roman codex or from another codex in which the Sardican canons were joined to the Nicene canons is unknown.]

Ferrandus, the deacon of the Church of Carthage, reports under title 214 of his *Brief Summary* a regulation that knees should not be bent during the Pentecost season, citing it from title 1 of the Council of Sardica, although this is actually canon 20 of the Council of Nicaea.

Nor is this a scribal error, both because all editions of Ferrandus—the Pithoean, Altaserran, Chiffletian, and Justellian—and all the manuscripts consulted by those editors present the same reading, and because Ferrandus’s second Sardican canon corresponds to the first in the Dionysian collection, his third to the second, his fourth to the third, and so on. Thus there can be no doubt that the canon was genuinely regarded by the author himself as the first Sardican canon. By what process or under what fate this happened is unknown.

This, however, is how I conjecture it occurred. An old codex of the canons of the Roman Church, similar to ours, came into the hands of the deacon Ferrandus—brought to Africa, perhaps, either by the legates of Pope Zosimus or sent there after their return to the overseas regions. We certainly read in that African synod at which the matter of appeals to be brought before the Roman see was discussed that, while Alypius was speaking of requesting authentic copies from the Eastern Churches, the legate Faustinus offered the following suggestion to the Fathers of the council:

> “But deign to write these very things to our holy and most blessed pope, so that he too, seeking out the complete canons, may discuss all the enactments with Your Holiness.”

From this it may be believed that the complete canons—namely, the Nicene and Sardican canons—were sent to Africa joined together under a single numerical sequence. Later, I believe, the twentieth canon was inserted among them from copies sent from the East by Tellus and Tharista.

When the error of that confusion was discovered and the Sardican canons, previously almost unknown to the Africans, began to become known, the Carthaginian deacon wished to insert them into his collection. He excerpted them from the Roman codex and judged that they should be numbered as Sardican beginning with the first canon in that codex, since he knew from the proper codex and usage of his Church that the Nicene canons ended there.

For unless he had been certain that the twentieth Dionysian canon was not regarded among the Africans as Nicene, or as a canon received in those regions, he would never have excluded it from the number of the Nicene canons. Nor could he have numbered it first among the Sardican canons except on the authority of some codex that placed it before the Sardican canons. That, again, could scarcely have happened in any other way than through the intermingling—or rather, the attachment—of the canons of both councils, which allowed both groups to be regarded as the canons of a single council.

Nor do we contradict ourselves when we now deny that the Africans regarded that canon as Nicene or as a canon received in those regions. Below we shall readily acknowledge that the practice of not kneeling on Sundays and during the Paschal Pentecost prevailed among the Africans. For it is one thing to reject a canon and another to receive and practice the discipline contained in that canon, whether from ancient custom and ecclesiastical tradition or from the prescription of one’s own canons.

5. The agreement of the manuscript copies of this codex, which are either still preserved in various libraries or are reported by writers to have once been preserved there, asserts its authenticity. There are four of this kind: the Thuaneus, which we ourselves saw and examined, as did Sirmondus, Salmasius, Chiffletius, Justellus, and Voellus; the Oxford copy, whose apograph is in my possession and which is listed in the catalogue of Oxford manuscripts; the Arras copy, cited by Baronius, Gravius, Pamelius, Binius, and Alan Cope; and the Vatican copy, which Sirmondus saw.

[Note: [Col. 0915D] See note 2 [above, col. 913, note a]. Other very ancient manuscript copies of this collection, discovered later and listed by us in the preface to the codex, also confirm its authenticity—provided, indeed, that authenticity can legitimately be inferred from the multitude of codices preserved in various libraries. For very ancient manuscript copies of spurious works are sometimes found as well, as is notorious in the case of the collection of Pseudo-Isidore. The authenticity of our collection becomes evident not from the antiquity and number of the codices alone, but especially from the whole combination of circumstances.]

### 6

A further, not negligible, support for the authenticity and antiquity of the codex is drawn from the very translation of the Eastern canons found in it. For that version is itself the one that was used in the Roman Church before the Dionysian version, and perhaps in several Churches of the West. Learned men hold that the translation of the canons found in the Isidorian collection—and resembling ours except in a few passages—was in use among the African and Spanish Churches. We shall show in the dissertation on the use of the Dionysian codex in Gaul that the same opinion concerning the Gallican Churches is not true [Note: [Col. 0916D] This is partly true and partly false, as we shall show in the observations to Dissertation 16.]; those Churches used Rufinus’s version of the Nicene canons at least until the time of Charlemagne. It is sufficient for the antiquity and value of this version to be established that it flourished in the African Churches, as the *Breviatio canonum* of Ferrandus, deacon of Carthage, proves, and in the Spanish Churches, as is suggested by Martin of Braga’s collection [Col. 0916B].

Moreover, the authenticity of the version of the Eastern canons lends authority to the collection as a whole and commends the collector’s reliability. Although there are certain passages—for there are in fact quite a few—which underwent some alteration so that they might be adapted to Roman discipline, and which are thereby shown to differ from the Isidorian version [Note: [Col. 0916D] See the *Observations* on this dissertation, chapter 2, no. 9.], these not only do not cast doubt upon the integrity of the codex, but rather confirm it. For no recent and ignorant impostor would ever have attempted or conceived introducing into an ancient codex such a diversity as would harmonize with an equally ancient discipline.

### 7

Hincmarus indicates that he had either seen himself, or learned from others that they had seen, a similar codex in which the Sardican canons were mixed with or attached to the Nicene canons. He makes this indication when writing to refute the false opinion that had arisen in certain writings, namely, that the Council of Nicaea was held during the pontificate of Pope Julius. This false opinion seems to have arisen from the mingling of the two sets of canons. Since the Sardican canons mention Pope Julius, under whom that council was held, while those canons, being attached to the Nicene canons, were taken for Nicene canons, an opportunity for error was thus given to unwary readers, who persuaded themselves that all those canons, and consequently the Council of Nicaea as well, had been celebrated under the same Julius.

## CHAPTER IV  
### That this codex belonged specifically to the Roman Church

The authenticity of the codex having been established, it remains for us to demonstrate by certain criteria (κριτήρια) that it belonged specifically to the Roman Church. In my judgment, this is not difficult. For anyone examining our codex will spontaneously encounter all the traces that survive of the Roman codex, whether in the letters of the pontiffs of Rome or in other records.

First, the very confusion of the codex [Note: [Col. 0916D] This argument will not merely be refuted, but will also be turned against Quesnel’s opinion in the *Observations*, chapter 1, no. 11.], which offended a certain Laurentius and prompted him to have Dionysius Exiguus compile a new one, proclaims that it is Roman. That confusion must indeed have been considerable, since it was not enough merely to apply a physician’s hand to it, but required an entirely new work. Yet it could scarcely have been greater than the confusion from which our codex suffers:

1. As regards the translation, which in several places is more like a paraphrase than a translation.

2. As regards the division and integrity of the canons: some are omitted, such as the twentieth Nicene canon and the fourth Gangran canon [Col. 0917A]; others belonging to the same council are combined into one; some canons of certain councils are mixed with the canons of other councils; some are abridged and some expanded.

3. As regards the order, since the decrees of councils are mixed with the decrees of pontiffs and are not arranged according to their chronological order, but later materials are placed before earlier ones, and local matters before ecumenical ones.

Nevertheless, this confusion of the codex detracts nothing from its authority. For the confusion rests upon its own rationale, and the disorder itself is not without an ordering principle. It arose, evidently, because the more obscure rules of the canons sometimes required the light of paraphrase; because the Romans considered themselves bound, before the Council of Chalcedon, by no canons other than those of Nicaea; and because they did not wish to admit other rules except those which they judged suited to the customs and practices of their own Church. Hence they adapted them to their own uses by making certain alterations, and they are not found arranged in the codex in any other order than the sequence of time in which it seemed right to receive each of them into use.

[Col. 0917B] **2.** The preface of the codex declares that it was itself compiled for the use of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0917D] See the *Observations*, chapter 2, no. 2.]. For what else do these words concerning the exposition of the Nicene faith indicate? “How holy and most reverent,” it says, “the Roman Church embraces and venerates.” What of its assertion that the exposition was produced through Victor and Vincentius, highly religious presbyters of the Roman See? It also says that certain rules were appended, which the aforementioned Church, accepting them, confirmed. It says that the Roman faith was preferred and obtained primacy not through synodal decrees, but by the voice of the Savior. Finally, everything written there concerning the foundation, founders, and privileges of the Roman Church is evidence that the codex was written for it.

Yet someone may wish to reject the entire codex on the basis of this preface. For it is marred by anachronisms, which it is improbable that the authors of a Roman codex would have admitted; and, moreover, the preface appears to be a product of the impostor Isidore, since he prefixed it to his edition of the Nicene canons. What Joannes David objects against the Justellian codex, so that it may not be regarded as an ancient Latin collection, he will doubtless not fail to press against ours as well. Namely, the heading of the Council of Nicaea says that it was held under Constantine Augustus and Licinius Caesar. “But what ignorance on the part of an impostor!” he says. “Who could tolerate its being attributed to the first Latin collection?” For it is established that Licinius was killed before the year 325 of Christ and therefore could not have held the consulship in that year, whether the council is assigned by writers or chronologists to the year 325 or 328 [Note: [Col. 0917D] The collector’s preface does not in fact record the consulship of Constantine and Licinius, which is indicated in Justellius’s edition of the ancient version. But the same consulship is included in our collection in another brief preface or annotation prefixed to the Nicene canons. See note 43, where we have attempted to discover the basis of this erroneous consulship.].

But I fear that this accusation of ignorance is itself insufficiently informed, since it is directed against several manuscript codices and also strikes at Eusebius, the foremost authority in ecclesiastical history. For the Justellian codex is not the only one to have this date: another, which Baronius calls the Cresconian codex [Col. 0918A], has it as well, as does the codex of Isidore Mercator, which he certainly copied from older sources.

Moreover, there is no doubt that this was drawn from Eusebius, whom Westerners at that time almost alone used after Jerome’s translation of the *Chronicle*, as the conclusion of the preface under consideration demonstrates. Eusebius assigns, or seems to assign, the Nicene synod to the year 324 of Christ, while placing the death of the elder Licinius in the year 327. According to this chronology, it is clear that Licinius could have been called emperor in the year in which the synod was convened, without any charge of ignorance thereby being attached also to Eusebius [Note: [Col. 0917D] In the words of the preface quoted by Quesnel, Licinius is not called emperor, but merely Caesar; consequently this passage cannot be understood of Licinius Augustus. It can indeed be understood of Licinius Caesar, his son, who was alive at the time of the Council of Nicaea. But no suitable reason can be given why the author of the preface should have named Licinius Caesar alone rather than Crispus or Constantine’s other Caesars. We consider only this explanation plausible: when the same author found two chronological notices in the different collections he used—one prefixed to the Nicene Creed with the consulship of Julian and Paulinus, the other prefixed to the canons with the consulship of Constantine Augustus and Licinius Caesar—he combined both into one, retaining the consulship of Paulinus and Julian, which accords with the Council of Nicaea, but suppressing the word “consulship” in connection with Constantine Augustus and Licinius Caesar, whose consulship, falling in the year 319, is far removed from the council.].

The consular *Fasti* of Idatius also report that Licinius was killed during the consulship of Paulinus and Julian, the year commonly assigned to the Council of Nicaea and corresponding to the year 325 of Christ. Given this, what prevents the synod from having been convened in the same year, in June, while Licinius was still alive, and Licinius himself from having been killed afterward? Even if the methods of reckoning used by Eusebius and Idatius are not accepted, it is nevertheless enough that a chronological notice transcribed from one of them into the preface of the codex be judged incapable of diminishing its reliability and authority, since the author of the preface, wholly unaccustomed to scrutinizing such chronological details, could easily have been carried away by an error in so celebrated a writer.

To these replies we add another, by which, unless hope deceives me, Joannes David’s objection will be blown away. What prevents us from maintaining that the Licinius mentioned here was the younger Licinius? For this Licinius had long since been called Caesar along with Crispus; and since, according to Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, he survived his father, the elder Licinius, until the year 329 of Christ—and survived the Nicene synod itself by several years—it is clear, according to Eusebius’s understanding, that the synod was held under Constantine and Licinius Caesars.

As for the second part of the objection [Col. 0918C], although this preface is found prefixed to the Isidorian edition of the Nicene synod, it should not for that reason be accused of being spurious. On the contrary, it is highly probable that the pseudo-Isidore so famous for his many forged writings stole this preface and prefixed it to his own work as though it were his property—something we shall prove by several arguments [Note: [Col. 0918D] One argument proving that Isidore Mercator took this preface from our collection is that this collection is older than pseudo-Isidore, not the reverse. The author of our collection copied the preface partly from Gelasius and partly from Rufinus, as we have noted in the notes to the same preface.].

1. Isidore titles it as the preface to the Council of Nicaea alone: “Preface of the Council of Nicaea.” Yet it is clear that it was written for the purpose of being prefixed to a complete codex of ecclesiastical rules. Thus the preface says: “For certain rules were also appended, which the aforementioned Roman Church, accepting them, confirmed” [Note: [Col. 0918D] This portion of the preface was taken from the Gelasian decree concerning apocrypha. In that decree, certain words concerning rules appended to the Nicene canons are referred to the creed attached to those canons, as will become clear from reading the decree itself.].

2. There is nothing in the Isidorian codex that indicates that it belonged specifically to the Roman Church; conversely, nothing in the preface fails to proclaim that it was attached to a Roman codex [Note: [Col. 0918D] There is nothing more evident in that preface than that it was attached to a Roman codex [Col. 0919D]. See the forthcoming *Observations*, chapter 2, no. 2.].

3. It is clear that the work is not Isidore’s, from the decree of Pope Gelasius concerning apocryphal writings, which others attribute to Hormisdas. For almost the entire text is appended to this decree in place of a preface. But whether Gelasius or Hormisdas was the author of this decree—and the latter view is made probable by our codex, as well as by the Dionysian codex, which, although they contain many works of Gelasius, do not contain this decree as a work proper to Gelasius [Note: Although many other outstanding pontifical decrees are absent both from our codex and from the Dionysian codex, and are older than either codex or collection, the absence of Gelasius’s decree concerning apocrypha does not establish that the collections predate it. Moreover, we have proved that the same decree is the work of Gelasius in *Treatise*, part III, chapter 11, § 5.]—in either case, I say, both pontiffs are older than the author of the Isidorian collection. He should therefore be considered to have received it from them or from our codex, rather than that others received it from him.

The proof, therefore, which we derive from the preface in order to establish that the codex belonged specifically to the Roman Church remains firm, if I am not mistaken.

We draw a third proof from the aforementioned decree of Gelasius or Hormisdas [Note: See the *Observations*, chapter 2, no. 3, where we have removed this argument.]. For either of those pontiffs would have felt shame or religious scruple about transferring an entire preface from someone else’s codex into his own, but not from his own.

4. The sixth canon of the Council of Nicaea [Note: See the same place, no. 4.] was read by Paschasinus, legate of the Apostolic See, in precisely the same form during the sixteenth session of the Council of Chalcedon as it appears in our codex; so that it must be understood to have been taken from exactly the same source. There can be no doubt that Paschasinus drew this canon from a codex belonging to the Roman Church, just as the Constantinopolitans produced it from their own.

One objection seems to stand in the way: Paschasinus numbers this canon as the sixth, whereas in the codex it is the tenth. This, however, is not a serious difficulty. First, it could easily have happened that a scribe or some reviser of the synod replaced “tenth” with “sixth.” Having noticed that in all other codices—Greek, Latin, and those of other regions—this canon was regarded as the sixth and had been designated by that number by the secretary of the Constantinopolitan Church, he did not hesitate to conclude that the Roman numbering was corrupt and wished it to be the sixth in both places.

Second, it could easily have happened that in the Greek exemplar ἕκτος (“sixth”) slipped in for δέκατος (“tenth”), the two letters δ and α having been removed from the latter word, and that the Latin was then incorrectly corrected from the Greek.

Finally, Paschasinus himself, who knew that this canon was commonly regarded as the sixth, perhaps even in his own Sicilian Church, judged that he too should call it the sixth. He did so lest, because of the divergence in the number, a dispute should arise and the Easterners should attack the Roman codex as corrupt. It was the act of a most prudent legate to forestall such a dispute.

5. There are also certain features in the text of the codex that indicate that additions were made for the sake of the Roman Church and that the codex was prepared for its use. One such feature is the parenthesis found in the letter of Pope Innocent I to Victricius of Rouen: “The reverence due to it (the Roman Church) must be preserved in all cases” [Note: [Col. 0919D] See the same place, no. 5.].

Since this is absent from the codex of Dionysius the abbot, and since we have not found it in the codex of venerable antiquity at Saint-Germain, which is said to be a thousand years old [Col. 0919D], anyone could readily be led to believe that it was added by the authors of the Roman codex, who considered themselves entitled to add to a letter of a Roman pontiff anything that might contribute to its clarification [Col. 0920A]. Nor would anyone rashly judge that this parenthesis subsequently passed from this source into several editions. It is also possible that the parenthesis entered the text from a marginal note by some learned reader who remembered Hosius’s words at the Council of Sardica: “If it pleases you, let us honor the memory of the holy apostle Peter.”

6. The twenty-eighth canon of the Council of Chalcedon is absent from this codex [Note: This negative argument is rejected in the same place [Col. 0920D], no. 6.]. It is in fact certain that it was not inserted into the Roman codex.

7. From several letters of the ancient bishops of Rome, and from the canons sent into Africa by Pope Zosimus under the name of the Nicene canons—although it is now admitted that they were Sardican canons—it had until now been almost certain among learned men that the Roman Church possessed the canons of both councils, either mixed together or placed one beneath the other, without any indication distinguishing the two. When innovators rashly dared, in insolent language, to charge Zosimus with deliberate falsehood and premeditated deception, our people had no better means of repelling the accusation than modestly to acknowledge that he had treated the Sardican canons as Nicene, and to assert that this resulted, as Marca writes (*On the Harmony of Sacred and Imperial Laws*, book VII, chapter 16), from the fact that at that time the Nicene and Sardican canons had been written in the same volume, without distinction, under the title of the Nicene canons.

“A plausible conjecture,” he adds, “if it rested upon the authority of an ancient codex, which has not yet emerged from darkness.” Indeed, it had already partly emerged through the work of Alanus Copus in the first dialogue, and the portion published was sufficient to blunt the obstinacy of the heretics. But now at last the complete codex has come to light, and with its help the plausible conjecture of Catholic writers has become a certain argument—one that both rescues the pious memory of the pontiff from slanderous tongues and establishes that the codex itself was Roman.

As for what Stephanus Baluzius seems to transfer, in a marginal annotation on the passage described above [Col. 0920C], into the codex of Christophorus Justellus, I say, with due respect to him, that this cannot be defended [Note: [Col. 0920D] This has been explained more fully in the preceding *Treatise on Collections*, part II, chapter 1, no. 7.]. For there is nothing in Justellus’s codex that could have led Zosimus into error. The Sardican canons are indeed placed beneath the Nicene canons; but each group is distinguished by its own numbers and headings, and the subscriptions to the Nicene canons, which are appended at the end of that group, separate the two from one another and prevent the Sardican canons from being taken for Nicene, or the latter for the former.

8. It is established from two letters of Pope Innocent that the Antiochene canons had been rejected by him [Note: This argument, and the following one, drawn from the Antiochene and Constantinopolitan canons, will be rejected in the *Observations*, chapter 2, no. 8.]. This proves that those canons did not then appear in the Roman codex. They are not absent from ours, but they are placed out of order, having been relegated to the end, so that it is clear that they were added only after a long interval from the time of Innocent, indeed after the time of Gelasius. This arrangement is not found in any other codex.

9. A similar argument is drawn from the Constantinopolitan canons. They lie only at the end of the codex [Col. 0920D], below even the Antiochene canons. And in fact it is entirely clear from our Leo and also from letter 31 of book 6 of Gregory the Great that the Romans learned of them, or granted them authority, only very late:

“The Roman Church,” he says, “does not as yet possess or accept those canons, or the acts of that synod [the First Council of Constantinople]; in this respect, however, it accepted that synod’s definition against Macedonius.”

This is at least true of the later canons of that council, which are found neither in the Dionysian collection nor in many other older ones. But it is also clear from Leo’s letters, and from the opposition of Lucentius, the legate, at the Council of Chalcedon (session 16), that the earlier canons had not been accepted in that Church in Leo’s time. Lucentius consistently asserted that the Constantinopolitan canons read by Aetius had no place among the canons.

10. Some canons of local councils were received into the codex only after they had first been adapted to Roman discipline [Note: See the same place, no. 9.]. Such is the tenth canon of Ancyra, which the codex numbers as the eleventh. For whereas the canon, according to all the other versions, decrees:

“Deacons who, after ordination, have proceeded to marriage may be permitted to continue in the ministry if, at the time of their ordination, they had declared that they wished to enter into marriage and could not otherwise remain [in continence],”

the same canon in our codex orders such deacons to remain only among the clergy and to be removed from the ministry. The final words, “receiving only lay communion,” were also added by the authors of the Roman codex.

Nor can this difference be attributed to diversity among the versions, since the Isidorian version—which, with very few exceptions, is identical with ours—represents the genuine discipline of the canon and permits such deacons to remain not only among the clergy but also in the ministry.

When we say that all versions and codices differ from this version, Martin of Braga must be excepted [Note: This will be refuted in the same place, no. 10.]. He compiled his collection from an ancient translation—an old translation, I say, not as it is found in Isidore Mercator, but as it originally existed in this Roman codex. For since the Isidorian version departs from our version of this Ancyran canon not only in wording but also in its very meaning and the discipline sanctioned by the canon, Martin’s version, by contrast, agrees with ours and imposes the same Roman rule to be observed in the ordination of a deacon:

“A deacon,” he says in part I, chapter 39, “who is chosen, if he has declared that he wishes to receive marriage and has said that he cannot remain in continence, is not to be ordained. But if he has remained silent at his ordination, has been ordained, and afterward has desired marriage, he is to be removed from the ministry and excluded from the clergy.”

Here you see that a deacon who has abandoned his commitment to chastity is declared either not to be ordained, as by Martin, or, if he has been ordained, to be removed from the ministry, as our codex states, should he marry. But concerning one who was ordained while silent and afterward contracts marriage, Martin orders him both to be removed from the ministry and to withdraw from the clergy, which our codex likewise establishes, whereas others permit such a deacon to remain among the clergy.

That this Ancyran canon 10 was once read in this way in the Roman codex seems also to be suggested by canon 13 of the Quinisext Council, when it refers to the Roman canon:

“Since we know that it has been handed down in the order of the canon in the Roman Church that those promoted to the diaconate or presbyterate must profess that they will no longer have relations with their wives, and so forth.”

For by these words it appears to indicate a codex of the canons of the Roman Church: ἐν τῇ Ῥωμαίων Ἐκκλησίᾳ ἐν τάξει κανόνος, “in the Roman Church, in the order of the canon.” Even more clearly this is shown by the following words, which occur shortly afterward in the same canon:

“But neither at the time of ordination is he to be required to profess that he will abstain from lawful relations with his wife.”

By this enactment, the Fathers of the Quinisext Council seem to me to be referring to canon 10 of the Synod of Ancyra. Whatever may be the case with that canon, Martin of Braga’s agreement with our codex in altering the discipline and wording of the Ancyran canon is unquestionably of greater authority for confirming our codex. Antonius Augustinus writes that Martin made this alteration out of hostility to Eastern permissiveness (*On the Emendation of Gratian*, book I, dialogue 10):

“C. Why did Martin depart from the archetype?” asks one interlocutor.

“A. Since he was in the West,” replies the other, “he did not wish to imitate the permissiveness of the East.”

I would rather judge that Martin drew this from an ancient Latin version that was in use in the Roman Church. For Garsias Loaysa, Franciscus Florens, and most recent writers are mistaken when they say that this author was Greek by origin, although Gregory of Tours explicitly states that he was a Pannonian (*History of the Franks*, book V, chapter 38), as does the monk Aimo (*On the Deeds of the Franks*, book III, chapter 38), and Aubertus Miraeus, from his epitaph, in his *Scholia on Isidore* [Col. 0922B]. Those who proclaim him the author of a new translation of the canons are equally mistaken. He himself discloses in his preface to Nitigisius only three things that he undertook.

First, because he thought that many things in the version then circulating through the Churches of Spain had been altered, he attempted to restore them and, as he himself puts it, “restore them more accurately.” Second, because some passages seemed obscure to simpler readers, he judged that they should be explained more simply. Finally, he divided all the canons into two classes, one containing those pertaining to clerics and the other those pertaining to laypeople.

All this was done in accordance not with Greek exemplars but with the authority of the ancient, or Roman, translation. Martin saw that the version of the canons in use among the Spaniards—which appears to be the very version now read in the Isidorian collection—differed in many respects from the version that prevailed among the Romans [Col. 0922C]. He considered it beyond doubt that the Roman version was purer and more faithful to its original integrity. Therefore he brought the Spanish codex of the canons back into conformity with its meaning, adding some things from his own hand or abbreviating others so that light might shine upon the more obscure passages.

This, if I am not mistaken, is the origin of the differences among those three codices which, although they use the same ancient version, differ from one another in so many places.

Returning now to the Ancyran canon, it is easy from what has been said to discover why Martin departed from the archetype—as Antonius Augustinus asked. It was not because, being in the West, he did not wish to imitate the permissiveness of the East. I can scarcely persuade myself that anyone, acting on private authority, would have attempted to depart so far from the meaning of a canon already received by the universal Church as to overturn it entirely. Indeed, Martin himself especially censures translators of the canons because, through their carelessness or ignorance, certain things had been altered.

Rather, since he attended exclusively to the Roman version and to the discipline of that and other Churches to which he thought the Spanish codex should be corrected, he inadvertently fell into a meaning alien to the mind of the canon. He also inserted much from his own judgment in order to adapt the canons to the understanding of simpler readers.

Yet the author should not be blamed for this, since he did not set out to produce a codex of the canons, but, as the title of his letter states, chapters collected from Greek synods. The method of the work itself confirms this: many things are abbreviated, interpolated, or altered in other ways; neither the order of the synods or canons is preserved, nor is the source of each chapter indicated; and some chapters plainly appear to have been composed from the canons of different councils.

This is not the place to discuss the authority, use, and approval of this collection. I say only that, in my view, more is attributed to it than is proper. For it is not clear that it was either sent to the Council of Lugo or received and authorized by that council or by any other. The Spanish synods maintain a profound silence concerning it. From them, rather, it seems certain that the use of the ancient version and codex continued in the Churches of Spain.

11. From the chapters on grace and free will formerly attributed to Pope Celestine but now asserted to be Leo’s [Note: See the *Observations*, no. 11.], it is evident that the decrees of the African Church against the Pelagians were inserted into the Roman codex. They are found neither in the Justellian codex nor in any other codex older than the Dionysian. They lie in ours, not alone, as in the codex of Dionysius, but mixed with the letters of the Roman pontiffs written on that matter to Africa, as the cited chapters indicate they originally were.

12. A considerable argument in support of our assertion is that the codex not only has the Nicene and Sardican canons at its beginning in consecutive order, but also ends at the period when Dionysius’s new codex caused the old one to fall into disuse, without any further enlargement [Note: See the author’s contradiction. Earlier, at the end of chapter 2, he wrote that the Constantinopolitan canons, at least, were appended to the codex after Saint Gregory the Great. Here, however, he states that the codex of the canons was no longer enlarged after Gelasius, so that it fell into disuse when Dionysius’s new codex appeared. Surely, if the old codex fell into disuse after Dionysius’s codex was introduced, nothing further should have been added to it for public use.]. This occurred after the time of Pope Gelasius, who is the last of the pontiffs whose decrees appear in the codex.

13. Gelasius himself, whom we have just cited, seems clearly to have had our codex before his eyes in the earlier treatise that Jacobus Sirmondus published, together with another work, in the appendix to the Theodosian Code, page 182 [Note: We shall refute this final argument in the *Observations*, chapter 2, no. 13.]. There he argues from the order established among the principal sees and from the judgment of Nicaea:

“No one either could or ought to expel or recall the bishop of the second see without the assent of the first see. Unless, perhaps, now that the order of things has been confused and disturbed, neither the first, nor the second, nor the third see ought to be observed or accepted according to the ancient statutes of our forefathers . . . For by what reason or consistency can the other sees be defended if ancient and venerable reverence is not paid to the first see of the most blessed Peter, through which the dignity of all priests has always been strengthened and confirmed, and whose honor was judged most ancient by the invincible and singular judgment of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers? For they remembered the saying of the Lord: ‘You are Peter,’ and so forth.”

Nowhere is this order of the sees, which the pontiff asserts to have been established according to the ancient statutes of the forefathers, recorded as having been instituted by any synod. It can scarcely be extracted from the sixth Nicene canon except indirectly. Nor did the holy Fathers labor there to establish or confirm this order; and Gelasius would not have failed to invoke the authority of so great a synod if he had known that anything of this kind had been decreed by it.

It is not likely that the Council of Constantinople, which suggests the same order, came to Gelasius’s mind, since it had not yet been received by the Roman Church, and since it was still far from Gelasius’s intention to defer to the authority of that council, which had granted the second place to the bishop of Constantinople. Either, therefore, the ancient tradition and most venerable custom concerning the order of the principal sees recorded in the preface of our codex was before his eyes [Col. 0924A]. The sixth Nicene canon likewise recalls this custom when it establishes the limits of their administration, and the seventh when it sanctions a decree concerning the prerogative of the see of Jerusalem. Or, if he intended to allude to the sixth Nicene canon, he certainly had before him no other version than the one found in our codex, where it is expressly stated that the Roman Church has always held, or ought always to hold, primacy.

Gelasius unquestionably had these same words of our version and our codex in mind when he immediately writes that the honor of the Roman see was judged most ancient by the invincible and singular judgment of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers, and that ancient and venerable reverence ought to be paid to the first see of the most blessed Peter, through which the dignity of all priests has always been strengthened and confirmed.

Where, in all the world, was the honor of the Roman see’s most ancient primacy judged, unless where it was decreed that the Roman Church has, or has always had, primacy? What codex other than ours has ever presented these words [Col. 0924B]? To what canon can you refer that ancient reverence and most ancient honor by which the dignity of all priests was strengthened, unless to Sardica III? That canon granted bishops condemned in a synod the right to request that their case be examined again in another judgment, and at the same time decreed that the responsibility and care of determining this second judgment should be entrusted to the Roman pontiff, so that the memory of Peter might thereby be honored:

“If any bishop has been judged in some matter and thinks that he has a good case, so that the council may be renewed a second time, if it pleases you, let us honor the memory of the holy apostle Peter, so that a letter may be written to the bishop of Rome,” and so forth.

This could not have been attributed by Gelasius to the Council of Nicaea unless on the authority of a codex resembling ours, one that contained the Nicene and Sardican canons joined together without distinction and attached in a single sequence.

## CHAPTER V  
### Objections to the authenticity of the codex are examined; first, the objection arising from the omission of the twentieth Nicene canon

[Col. 0924C]

In my opinion, the authenticity of our codex has now been sufficiently established, as has its use in the Roman Church. It remains, therefore, to bring forward whatever objections can be raised against either of these two aspects of our undertaking. We have already examined one or two objections, namely those drawn from the name of Licinius inserted into the heading of the Council of Nicaea and from the preface of the codex. But another difficulty now arises from the number and completeness of the Nicene canons themselves. For our codex lacks the final canon of that synod, although it does not seem entirely probable that it was rejected by the Roman Church.

[Note: [Col. 0924D] We shall set out this argument at length in the observations, chapter 1, no. 7 and following, in support of excluding Quesnell’s codex from the Roman Church, and there examine Quesnell’s replies.]

Someone may reply that this should be attributed to the carelessness of the scribes, who omitted that canon while thinking of something else. But this reply does not satisfy me. For if it were a scribal error, it could scarcely have happened that several codices were infected with the same error, or that the three copies which alone have come to our notice—a Gallic one, an English one, and a Gallo-Belgian one—should all have derived from the same corrupt source. Although I myself have not seen the complete Atrebatensian copy, I nevertheless conjecture that the final canon of the Council of Nicaea was missing from it as well. For the canons numbered there as the thirtieth and thirty-fourth are the same as those in our codex, whereas, with the addition of that twentieth canon, they ought to have been the thirty-first and thirty-fifth.

There is therefore no doubt that this canon was deliberately omitted; and, in my opinion, for no other reason than that it had not been received by the Roman Church, and perhaps not in the Western regions either. These are the words of the canon in the Dionysian version:

**Nicene Canon 20:** Since there are some who kneel on the Lord’s Day and during the days of Pentecost, so that everything may be observed harmoniously in all places, it has pleased the holy council that prayers be offered to the Lord while standing.

This statement may perhaps seem harsh, and one that cannot be heard without resistance—namely, that a canon enacted by an ecumenical council, especially one consecrated by the supreme veneration of the entire world, was not received in practice by certain Churches. But it is no harsher for a canon sanctioned by a synod not to be accepted in practice in some places than for that same canon later to fall into disuse, as usually happens. Moreover, if we attend more carefully to the celebrated rule of Saint Augustine concerning the customs of various Churches, every opportunity for an unfavorable suspicion in this matter will disappear. In the same place he says:

> To this I answer as follows (Letter 118, to Januarius, chapter 5): if the authority of divine Scripture prescribes which of these things should be done, there must be no doubt that we ought to act as we read; then we should no longer debate how it ought to be done, but how the sacrament is to be understood. Likewise, if the whole Church throughout the world commonly practices any one of these things. For to debate whether it should be done in this way is the height of insolent madness. But neither the one nor the other applies to what you are asking about. It remains, therefore, that it belongs to that third category, which varies according to places and regions.
