Let each person therefore do what he has found practiced in the Church to which he has come. None of these things is done against the faith or against the better customs found here and there. For on these grounds—that is, either because of the faith or because of morals—what was being done wrongly must be corrected, or what was not being done must be instituted.

[Col. 0925C] Certainly no one will say that the custom of standing while praying on the Lord’s Day and during the paschal Quinquagesima concerns either the faith or good morals, so that the Roman Church, or any other Church, would have had to abandon its custom after the Council of Nicaea and adopt the practice of standing instead of kneeling during those days, if it had been accustomed to pray on its knees since apostolic times. For what was being done need be corrected, or what was not being done instituted, only for the sake of faith or morals. Indeed, a change of custom, even one that brings practical benefit, disturbs by its novelty. Consequently, a change that is not useful is, through its fruitless disturbance, harmful—as Saint Augustine writes in the same place.

Nor was it the intention of the most holy synod to compel all the Churches of the entire world by its decree to observe that practice. For it knew that, just as it is the greatest sacrilege for one faith not to prevail throughout all the Churches, so the rules of conduct are not identical; rather, it had always been entirely permissible for ceremonies and discipline themselves to vary according to the places and regions of the earth. “This whole class of matters,” Augustine says in the same work, “has observances that are free. Nor is there any single discipline better for a serious and prudent Christian than to act in the manner in which he sees the Church act, wherever he may happen to arrive. For what is enjoined neither against the faith nor against good morals is to be regarded as indifferent and observed in accordance with the fellowship of those among whom one lives.”

Moreover, if Augustine understands this of the fast on Saturday, of daily communion in the body and blood of the Lord, of the offering of the Eucharistic sacrifice, and of other customs of far greater importance, with how much greater justification would he have thought the same concerning the practice of praying to God while standing on the Lord’s Day and during the paschal Quinquagesima—a practice which has nothing in common with the rules of faith and morals and is in itself so **ἀδιάφορος** (*adiaphoros*, indifferent) that the contrary custom of kneeling may appear far preferable according to the usage of other places and times?

This, then, should be observed concerning the Nicene canons, or definitions: those which concern the faith, good morals, or the general discipline of the Church and the higher order possess authority throughout the universal Church, so that anyone who attempts otherwise than that synod decreed must be struck down by the sword of anathema. Such matters include the most sacred symbol of faith; the decrees concerning the selection of those to be ordained; the authority of metropolitans; clerics’ cohabitation with women; the baptism, ordination, and reception of heretics; usury; and other matters of this kind. Other provisions, however, are confined within the limits of ceremonies and lesser discipline. Since they arose from knowledge of the corruption that had entered certain Eastern Churches, they were enacted by the Fathers of the synod chiefly for the use of those same Eastern Churches, among whom there were scarcely any bishops from the Western regions. Indeed, anyone who examines more carefully the ancient canons of penitential discipline or the rites and rules of ordination will clearly see that differing practices and disciplines prevailed not only in regions distant from one another but also varied in many ways among the Churches of the same region, as can be understood from what we have noted on Letter 2 (now 167) to Rusticus of Narbonne. This could not have happened except through some of those Churches’ departing from the discipline of the Nicene canons.

Now, if the canon under discussion is considered more attentively, it will become clear that it concerns the Eastern Churches, and that the Fathers did not even have the Western Churches in mind. “Since there are some,” it says, “who kneel on the Lord’s Day,” and so forth; it does not say, “There are certain Churches or regions”—which it certainly would have said if it were speaking of places other than the East. For an ecumenical council celebrated in the Eastern Empire would not have extended its care and concern so far as to issue a judgment and enact a canon concerning certain people in the West who departed from the common rule and practice. Yet it is not unreasonable that the Fathers did this concerning the inhabitants of their own provinces. Add to this that the rationale of the canon would not be entirely true or plausible if it were understood of provinces other than the Eastern ones. So great was the diversity of customs between the Churches of the West and the East, and so great the disparity of discipline—while everyone agreed and approved—that it cannot be believed that the synod intended all the Churches of the entire world to use the same customs and that everything should be observed harmoniously in all places. How little consistent with reason it would be to suppose that, while passing over countless customs and ceremonies of the greatest importance in which the Westerners differed from the Easterners, the Fathers selected this one ceremony as the one in which they wished the Westerners to agree with the Easterners!

It is therefore not rash, nor insulting to the authority of the ecumenical councils, to believe that certain points of discipline enacted by their decrees were not accepted by some Churches, and especially by the Roman Church.

[Note: [Col. 0925D] We have demonstrated at the place cited in the preceding note, by several testimonies, that the Roman Church observed the Nicene canons—consecrated above all by the reverence of the entire world—to such an extent that it considered it unlawful to depart from them even slightly. Who, then, would rashly suspect that it did not receive this final canon?]

For the Roman Church, having received many institutions of discipline from its founders, the apostles Peter and Paul, could not fail to adhere to them most steadfastly or introduce foreign customs at their expense.

I believe that something of this sort occurred with respect to the practice confirmed by that canon, which I would readily suppose was not in force among the Roman Church and several other Churches.

[Col. 0927A] You have this proved from our codex, which would not have rejected this final canon from the number of the Nicene decrees unless Roman custom had been different.

[Note: [Col. 0927C] Quesnell’s codex did not omit this final canon because a different custom prevailed in the region where such a collection was compiled. For we shall show more probably in the observations, chapter 1, no. 13, that the collection itself was arranged in Gaul, although in Gaul the rite and discipline of the canon were observed, as testified by Irenaeus of Lyons in his book On Easter, which Justin Martyr cites in Question 115, and by Hilary of Poitiers in the prologue to his Book of Psalms, no. 12. Since this same canon is absent not only from our collection but also from another version which we published from the manuscript Vatican, Regina 1997, as well as from Rufinus’s abridgment, the true explanation seems to be that it was omitted through the negligence of some copyist in certain Greek exemplars of the Council of Nicaea from which this version and Rufinus’s abridgment derived. It may indeed seem strange that it is missing from our collection, even though it generally contains the Isidorian version, which does not lack this canon, among the Nicene canons. But since, in arranging the Nicene canons by number and headings—as we have noted elsewhere—the compiler took as his model a codex like the cited Vatican Regina 1997, in which this canon is likewise missing, he therefore thought it should be passed over, although it was read in the Isidorian version.]

For it is probable that this custom descended from the apostles, since we see in Acts 20:36 and 21:5 that the apostle Paul prayed on his knees during those days.

[Note: [Col. 0927D] These examples concern the Eastern regions. In addition, they refer to a prayer offered on a journey, or even on the shore, before Paul boarded the ship. Those who mention the practice of standing on Sundays and during Pentecost are speaking chiefly of prayers performed in churches during the ecclesiastical services. Saint Irenaeus, the most ancient bishop of the Western Church of Lyons, traces the custom of this practice back to apostolic times in his book On Easter, as Saint Justin reports in Question 115.]

Nothing prevents the custom of not kneeling from having been left by the apostles to the Easterners, while the contrary custom of abstaining from kneeling during prayer on those same days was handed down by other apostles to the Romans.

[Note: [Col. 0928C] That this rite was also common among Westerners is clear from the testimonies of Western Fathers whom Quesnell himself later cites. But if, as he himself admits, Africans, Gauls, and Spaniards—and Italians as well, to whom Saint Maximus belongs—prayed standing on Sundays and during the paschal days, who can believe that all these Western Churches departed from the Roman Church, from which they were all propagated, with such agreement and almost concerted action in so solemn a rite? Is it not more likely that they all preserved this rite because they had received and accepted it as transmitted and commended to them in its institution and origin by the Roman Church?]

And among different customs of this kind, what Augustine says about those who fast and those who do not fast on Saturday, we say also about those who kneel and those who do not kneel:

> The kneeling, whom Peter planted, and the non-kneeling, whom his fellow disciples planted, lived together in concord with one another.

Letter 86, to Casulanus.

**2. It is proved from Rufinus of Aquileia, Book I of Ecclesiastical History, chapter 6.** When he recounts and numbers the Nicene canons, he entirely omits this final canon concerning standing during prayer on the Lord’s Day and during the paschal Quinquagesima.

[Note: [Col. 0928C] We gave the more probable explanation for this omission in note 3 (the note marked “a” on this page).]

Since this man lived for a very long time at Rome, he drew it either from Roman custom or from a Roman codex, or from the Aquileian tradition. For he wrote these books of Ecclesiastical History at the urging of Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, and, as he himself says, obeyed the commands of that religious Father also in this matter. I am therefore readily persuaded that the Nicene canon was not received by that Church either.

**3. Saint Augustine, in the letter already cited to Januarius, appears to have been unaware of this canon**, since he does not dare to assert that this custom was practiced everywhere in the Churches.

[Note: [Col. 0928C] You may see in the observations, chapter 1, no. 8, how much more this testimony of Augustine favors us.]

“Now,” he says, “that we should pray standing on those days—the days of Easter and Pentecost—and on all Sundays, whether this is observed everywhere I do not know. Nevertheless, what the Church follows in this matter I have stated as best I could, and I believe it is clear.”

From this one of two conclusions follows: either Augustine did not know of that canon, or he thought that there was nothing sacrilegious in some Churches refraining from accepting the Nicene canon.

There is, however, something obscure in Augustine’s final words: “Nevertheless, what the Church follows in this matter I have stated as best I could, and I believe it is clear.” For if these words are understood of the custom of standing during prayer, as the sequence of his argument seems to suggest, it is scarcely possible to reconcile Augustine with Augustine. He is speaking of the universal Church. How, then, could he say that the universal Church followed a custom which he had previously declared himself not to know whether it was observed everywhere? Still less could he assert that this was clear. It is therefore preferable to refer these final words to what he had said above about Easter and Pentecost, which end three or four lines earlier with this clause: “These things are held most firmly from the Scriptures”—namely, Easter and Pentecost—and also to the other matters which he confidently declares immediately afterward to be strengthened by the custom of the Church.

**4. This inference from Augustine is confirmed by the Breviary of the Canons of Ferrandus, a deacon of the Church of Carthage.** In it, this canon, the last of the Council of Nicaea, is called the first of the Council of Sardica, as we noted above. It therefore appears certain that this canon was not regarded in the Church of Carthage as Nicene, since Ferrandus could by no means have been ignorant of the opinion held in that Church concerning the Nicene canons, or of which and how many enactments of that synod it counted.

[Note: [Col. 0928D] In the Church of Carthage, the version of the Nicene canons that Atticus of Constantinople had sent to the Africans was in common use. In this version, which is inserted in Isidore’s collection at the Sixth Council of Carthage, the canon concerning the omission of kneeling on Sundays and during the paschal days is read among the Nicene canons. But why Ferrandus counted the same canon as the first among the Sardicenses will be understood from note 3 in chapter 3 (above, col. 913, note b).]

**5. No trace remains among authors who wrote at Rome or about Roman customs of the omission of kneeling on Sundays and during the paschal days**, although they do not remain silent about other customs of that Church.

[Note: [Col. 0928D] See our observations on this dissertation, chapter 1, no. 8.]

Among the Greeks, Basil the Great bears witness to this in his book On the Holy Spirit, chapter 27; so does the author of the Questions attributed to Justin Martyr, Question 115, and Epiphanius in the Exposition of the Faith. Photius, Zonaras, and other later writers may be added to these. Among the Africans, Tertullian, On the Crown of the Soldier, chapter 3, and the Augustine already cited. Among the Cisalpine Gauls, Saint Ambrose, Sermon 61—or rather Maximus of Turin, Sermon on Pentecost. Among the Spaniards, Isidore of Seville, Ecclesiastical Offices, Book I, chapter 31. For several other peoples, Jerome, Against the Luciferians.

[Col. 0928C] We have no witness concerning the Romans, nor is it permissible to infer the practice of this Church from the custom of all the others, since it is also established that the Milanese Church, which was the nearest of all to Rome, had many rites different from those of the Romans, such as the custom of not fasting on Saturday.

**6. Our conjecture is rendered more probable by the fact that several other Churches also appear not to have received the same canon.**

[Note: [Col. 0929C] Two editions of the Arabic collection of the Nicene canons are in circulation, one by Francesco Turrianus and the other by Abraham Ecchellensis; in both this canon is read—in the former as chapter 29, and in the latter as chapter 32. Moreover, the silence concerning this rite either in the Apostolic Canons or in the Constitutions of Saint Clement, as they are called, if it proves anything, would prove especially that this rite was not received in the Eastern Churches, where those canons and constitutions were written and published in Greek.]

For in the Arabic collection of the Nicene canons that is in circulation, this canon does not appear, nor is anything concerning that paschal privilege commended there. Nothing concerning the same rite is read either in the Apostolic Canons or in the Constitutions of Saint Clement, although both works expressly discuss the paschal feast and the Lord’s Day, and decree more than once that the Quinquagesima after Easter is to be observed without fasting on those days—for example, in the Constitutions, Book V, chapters 17, 18, and 19, and Book VII, chapter 30.

In some Churches, moreover, that rite was so firmly established by usage that it allowed certain exceptions, and penitents were not permitted to make use of that privilege. The matter is made clear by decree 82 of the Council of Carthage IV:

[Note: [Col. 0929D] The council called the Fourth Council of Carthage is not truly an African council, but a certain collection, or ancient abridgment, of canons, about which we have discussed at greater length in the Treatise, Part II, chapter 3, § 4. Since priests placed their hands upon prostrate penitents while praying, it was undoubtedly necessary for the priests themselves to kneel even on days of remission, if on those days they likewise had to place their hands upon the prostrate penitents. But this peculiarity of penitents, who at a particular time were required to attend the sacred services only while prostrate, does nothing to prejudice the general rite of the other faithful.]

“Penitents,” it says, “should kneel even on days of remission.”

Since it seems to have been within anyone’s power to adopt the penitential practice and enter their order, it appears that kneeling on Sundays and during the paschal days was likewise permitted, at least in the African regions.

**7. Perhaps we may appropriately bring forward the Jerome cited above as a supporter of the same position.** For although, in the cited passage of his dialogue Against the Luciferians, he includes among those practices which, even if they are not written down, a reasonable observance may claim for itself the practice of not worshiping on one’s knees on the Lord’s Day and throughout Pentecost, it should nevertheless be noted that Jerome makes no mention there of any Nicene decree or other law. He derives the whole matter from the custom of the Church. This may increase the suspicion that the Churches frequented by that holy doctor, and especially the Roman Church, were unaware of Nicene Canon 20.

[Note: [Col. 0930C] Jerome was engaged with a Luciferian who demanded testimony from sacred Scripture. Saint Jerome replied that many things are observed in the Churches even though they are not written in the divine books. Giving several examples of practices that are purely ritual, he included among them the practice of omitting kneeling on Sundays and during the paschal days. He introduces the custom merely as a custom of the Church, since it was common to the other examples he mentioned, which are not prescribed in the Nicene canons. It follows against Quesnell that the custom of omitting kneeling at the times mentioned prevailed in the Churches frequented by the holy Doctor, and especially in the Roman Church, as we shall prove more fully in the observations, chapter 2, no. 7.]

“But,” you will say, “that canon expressly decrees that in every Church prayers are to be offered while standing on the Lord’s Day and during the paschal Quinquagesima: **ἐν πάσῃ παροικίᾳ**”—“in every parish” or “in every ecclesiastical district.”

[Note: [Col. 0930D] Anyone can recognize how forced this restriction of the Nicene law is, by which the Western Churches are considered not to be included, even though the Western Fathers cited by Quesnell himself testify that those Churches were most careful observers of this rite. See note 5 (below, note a).]

First, this Greek expression itself seems to me to have a narrower meaning than the Fathers of Nicaea would have used if they had wished that canon to admonish and bind all the dioceses of the universal Church without exception. Since it signifies the territory of a bishop in this place, it seems to me to refer to all the Churches of the Eastern dioceses rather than to the Christian world as a whole.

Moreover, no one is unaware that this word, as an indicator of a certain universality, normally has limits among all authors according to the subject under discussion and according to the number and character of those about whom, or to whom, the speech is directed. There is scarcely any writer in whom several examples of this do not occur.

But, so that we do not wander beyond canonical subject matter, who would believe, for example, that the Council of Chalcedon had the Western regions and Churches in mind when it enacted those twenty-eight canons, which were principally established to remove abuses that had arisen in the East? Who would suppose that the Gallic, Spanish, British, and Italian Churches are being discussed when Canon 17 decrees:

> If anyone is injured by his metropolitan, he is to be judged by the primate of the diocese or by the holy see of Constantinople.

It is certain there that “the primates of the diocese” means the bishops of Alexandria and Antioch; consequently, only Eastern bishops are addressed by that canon. Again, when Canon 26 decrees:

> Every Church that has a bishop must have an **οἰκονόμος** (*oikonomos*, steward) from its own clergy, who shall administer ecclesiastical affairs, and so forth,

who would think that this canon concerns the Western Churches, among which the name and office of *oikonomos*, in the sense in which it existed among the Easterners, were unknown? The reference to universality therefore does not prevent the canon from being restricted to certain regions and Churches.

## CHAPTER VI. Other arguments are answered, by which either the authenticity of the codex or its use in the Roman Church may be challenged.

[Col. 0930B]

It may be objected against the **αὐθεντία** (*authentia*, authority or authenticity) of our codex, or against its use in the Roman Church, that ancient codices lacked headings and that the canons were not distinguished from one another in any other way than by their numbers, which took the place of headings. This is what John David argues against Justellus in his book On the Canonical Judgment of Bishops. But this does not fit our codex, in which not only are the canons distinguished from one another by their proper headings, but one canon, divided into several parts, has as many headings as it has parts.

I scarcely think that such a weak argument can impress anyone’s mind. What if I deny that the ancient codex of the Roman Church lacked headings and summaries? Will you prove it from the canons cited at the Council of Chalcedon, where there is complete silence about headings? As though it had been the universal practice, whenever canons were cited, to cite their headings as well, when in fact headings are generally omitted, both for the sake of brevity and because they are additions to the canons, composed without authority. Moreover, what does a Greek codex have to do with a Roman one? What necessity is there for canons translated into Roman language and given Roman usage to lack headings merely because the canons published by the Greeks perhaps lacked them? Could it not have occurred to the author of that ancient version to do what Dionysius Exiguus thought should be done when he prepared his own?

“Indeed,” the same writer says, “Dionysius himself indicates that he was the first author of headings.”

[Note: [Col. 0930D] There are older collections than Dionysius’s that present the canons with headings, such as the collections Vatican, Regina 1997, Lucensis 88, the ancient edition of the canons, and others. Conversely, certain very ancient codices lack headings, such as Verona 58, which presents the Greek canons’ Isidorian version, as it is usually called, without headings.]

He says this, that is, in the letter prefixed to the codex of papal letters addressed to Julian:

> Reducing them to a certain order, I distinguished them by headings which I composed . . . in the manner in which, long ago, while translating the canons of the Fathers from the Greek language, I arranged them.

These are Dionysius’s words, but they have been truncated. If John David had reproduced them in full, he would have served the truth more than his own cause. In place of the three dots which he substitutes for Dionysius’s words, the following is found:

> Only in such a way that I could bring together, under a single numerical sequence, all the precepts of each of the pontiffs that I found, and append all the headings to this preface, in the manner in which, long ago, while translating the canons of the Fathers from the Greek language, I arranged them—a method which I had learned had pleased you greatly.

Who cannot now see that David has twisted Dionysius’s words into a meaning foreign to them? Who does not understand that the words “in the manner in which I long ago arranged the canons” cannot refer to the composition of the headings, since that matter is farther removed? Rather, the comparison is made only in the arrangement of the headings, which Dionysius had gathered together and appended to the preface of each of the two works.

For if the comparison is made with everything that precedes, the argument will immediately falter and carry David himself into an open contradiction. For while it is true that Dionysius says that the letters were distinguished by headings which he composed, the same is not true of the canons, which were distinguished in themselves; moreover, as David admits, they were separated by their own numbers, which served in place of headings. They should therefore be said to have been illuminated and adorned by the addition of summaries rather than distinguished by them.

For this reason the abbot himself deliberately does not use the same words in both cases. He says that the letters were distinguished by him, since he had actually divided them into several parts; but he says that the canons—or rather the headings of the canons—were arranged after the preface. In the case of the letters he mentions headings composed by himself; in the case of the canons he says nothing of the sort.

Furthermore, if the final words of that sentence—“in the manner in which I arranged the canons”—are to be referred back to “I distinguished them by headings which I composed,” then they must with equal, or indeed greater, right be referred to the intervening words as well. In that case, when Dionysius says that he arranged the letters under a single numerical sequence, the same would have to be said of the canons, and the abbot would have to be considered the first author of this form of distinction. Yet David himself plainly denies this. His arguments for the denial are the canons cited at the Council of Chalcedon and Canon 79 cited by Abbot Dionysius in his Easter letter—not to mention the codex to which Justellus gave the name “of the Universal Church.”

There is one further point about which the same writer, having already been warned by me, must again be warned, because he has repeatedly used the same error as though it were an established principle in order to confirm other errors. He supposes that the Dionysian version of the canons was prepared from the same Greek autograph copy from which the ancient Latin version had been made. Consequently, he thinks that both versions contain the same material, in the same order, and that the only difference between the older and the more recent translation is that the former was more obscure and confused, while the latter was more accurate and polished.

But anyone who thinks this is seriously mistaken. The origins of the two codices were entirely different.

[Note: [Col. 0931D] It may be inferred from our Treatise on Collections, Part I, chapters 2 and 6, that some difference existed among the Greek exemplars of the canons. Certainly the Greek exemplar used by Dionysius differed from that used by the author of the ancient version; among other indications of their difference, the latter lacked the Laodicean canons, which Dionysius found in his Greek codex.]

For Dionysius copied the Greek codex in its entirety and gave it a Latin form, adding the canons of Chalcedon, Sardica, and Africa. The Latin codex, especially the Roman one, at first scarcely admitted any canons other than the Nicene; later, some others were appended at the discretion of the bishops and Churches that compiled codices for themselves. These collections preserved no order other than the time at which an opportunity arose to receive the canons of a particular synod. Nor were they content solely with Greek canons: they also inserted African and Sardican canons, papal letters, and other ecclesiastical documents, scattered throughout and without order. From this arose the confusion that offended those whom Dionysius mentions and led them to consider the preparation of a new codex.

It is therefore futile to determine the order of one from the order of the other, and futile to think that the headings, summaries, and divisions of one can help in investigating the same features in the other.

To avoid concealing any objection that can be brought against our codex, there is a passage in a letter of Pope Boniface to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne, from which someone might argue that a different version of the Nicene canons was then in use in the Roman Church from the one presented in our codex.

[Note: [Col. 0931D] We considered this argument, drawn from Boniface’s letter to establish that the Roman version differed from the version of our collection, entirely worthless, because in reality Boniface’s words do not convey a proper interpretation of any Nicene canon, as we observed in volume II, in the observations on Quesnell’s Dissertation 5, Part II, chapter 6, nos. 5 and 6.]

These are the words of Boniface:

> For no one appears to be unaware of the decree of the Nicene synod, which prescribes as follows—and to quote the very words themselves: in each province, each metropolitan is to have his proper jurisdiction, and no one province is to be subject to two.

Many think it difficult to refer this to any one of the Nicene canons; John David declares it impossible (p. 50). For it is contained in none of the twenty canons, either in wording or in sense; nor can it be drawn in any way, even by twisted wording, to Canon 6, although that canon comes closest of all to Boniface’s words.

He himself prefers to think that Pope Boniface was referring to the first two canons of the Council of Constantinople. From this he further argues that it was customary in the Roman Church to call all the canons it approved and received “Nicene canons” (J. David, chapter 1, p. 50, and chapter 2, p. 80).

It is certainly strange that the Roman pontiff Boniface should have admitted the Constantinopolitan canons and given the name “Nicene” to canons which the Roman Church neither approved at that time nor had yet accepted as authoritative in the days of Gregory the Great. Yet that writer asserts both points within a few pages. This is a lapse of memory which it is fair to pardon.

But one point troubles me: to which canons will he refer Boniface’s words, since he was forced to resort to the Constantinopolitan canons alone, given that he does not think either the Sardican canons or Nicene Canon 6 relevant?

Nor do I think that Boniface intended this latter canon, although it is written in the margin of nearly all printed codices. For it deals more with the chief primates of the larger dioceses than with the metropolitan bishops of individual provinces. But the subject is the ordinary metropolitan bishops of the provinces in Canon 4, which concerns the ordination of bishops and establishes and asserts in the clearest words the authority of each metropolitan within his own province. The clause of the canon in Dionysius reads:

> The validity, however, of what is done shall be assigned, in each province, to the metropolitan bishop  
> (**Τὸ δὲ κῦρος τῶν γινομένων δίδοσθαι καθ’ ἑκάστην ἐπαρχίαν τῷ μητροπολίτῃ**).

[Note: [Col. 0932D] Although we do not deny that Boniface’s words may refer to Canon 4, nothing prevents them from also alluding to that part of Canon 6 which declares invalid an ordination carried out against the will of the metropolitan bishop.]

But our codex, which divides the Nicene canons into several parts and distinguishes each part by its own summary, presents the final part of Canon 4 as though it were a separate canon, in the following manner:

**VII. On the authority of the metropolitan.** The authority, or confirmation, shall certainly belong in each province to the metropolitan.

Who does not understand that Boniface had this canon in mind in that letter? The whole of it is—just as the heading prefixed by Dionysius states—that in each province no bishop is to be ordained while disregarding the metropolitan; and this too is the subject of the Nicene canon. This, I say, is precisely what Boniface wrote was prescribed by the Nicene canon: that each metropolitan ought to possess jurisdiction throughout his own province. For what he adds further—“nor ought two provinces to be subject to any one [metropolitan]”—is a consequence which Boniface draws from the canon: for if authority belongs to the metropolitan throughout each province, it follows that two provinces ought not to be subject to one metropolitan. But whether one considers the sixth canon or the fourth, the very words of the canon which Boniface appears to have wished to cite [Col. 0933B] are nowhere found in our codex, nor in any other translation, as David himself also admits.

It is certainly difficult to acknowledge that these are the precise words of the canon which Boniface set down. For neither can the Greek be accommodated to them, nor do the other versions contain anything similar apart from the sense; nor do they appear to have been composed in the form of canons. I would conjecture that Boniface actually wrote *prope*—“nearly”—in that parenthesis, and that, since he neither had the codex at hand nor retained the canon’s exact wording in memory, he wished merely to present its sense and to warn the reader that he had not written the very same words, as the text reads, but nearly the same words, as I think the passage should be corrected. But this is a conjecture which, until it is confirmed by the authority of some codex, I would not dare to assert with confidence, although the correction appears necessary. It is nevertheless supported by the fact that no one has ever said “to set down precisely the same words” for “to set down the precise wording”; so that one may reasonably suspect either that *prope*—as we have just said—must be restored, or that the word *proprie* was then used in some sense now unknown to us. Certainly, that word occurs several times in writers of that age with a meaning different from the one it now has, or once had before the language declined into old age. Thus, for example, when our Leo, writing to the Emperor Marcian in Letter 78 (now 104), chapter 1, says that he had watched faithfully and *proprie* over the matter, so that the devil’s snares would not harm the Eastern Churches. In Sermon 3 (now 4), chapter 2: “Peter rules *proprie* all those whom Christ also rules principally.” And chapter 3: “For Peter’s faith prayer is offered *proprie*.” Book II of *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, chapter 4: “The God of the patriarchs presided *proprie* over their sons.” And in canon 20 of the Council of Antioch, where it is forbidden that any bishop should hold a synod on his own, without the metropolitan’s knowledge—καθ’ ἑαυτοὺς ποιεῖσθαι, “to act on their own”—some translate this *per se*, “by himself,” and others *proprie apud semetipsum*, “precisely by himself,” as Gentianus Hervetus does. Here *proprie* appears to mean “separately,” or to be used with another expression of the same force.

Finally, nothing can be constructed against our codex from such an obscure passage, since Boniface appears not to have copied the exact words of any canon. Rather, he should be thought to have had our codex in mind, in which, namely, Nicene title 7 is headed “On the Authority of the Metropolitan,” and title 11, “That no one is to be ordained bishop without the metropolitan’s consent”—which was the matter then under discussion. For John David’s apparent recourse to some canon that has perished from human memory is more characteristic of a man dreaming than of one seriously dealing with the matter.

[Col. 0934A] In fourth place Pope Innocent I comes forward. In Letter 27 to Rufus and the other bishops of Macedonia, writing about the Bonosiaci, he quotes a canon of the Council of Nicaea in these words: “Concerning those who call themselves Cathari, that is, the Pure, and who sometimes come to the Catholic Church, it has pleased the holy and great synod that, after receiving the laying on of hands, they should remain in the clergy.” The translation of the codex differs from this version, especially with regard to the final words, in place of which it has: “that they should be ordained and thus remain in the clergy,” whereas the other version reads: “that, after receiving the laying on of hands, they should thus remain in the clergy.”

[Note: [Col. 0933D] We shall reject Quesnellus’s response to this in the observations on chapter 1, no. 2.]

The entire reason for the difference is that Pope Innocent, when responding to the objection of the Macedonian bishops, wished either to reproduce or to translate word for word the canon that had been brought forward, from their own letter. Nor was there any reason for Innocent to use his own translation, since the difficulty did not concern the canon’s expression χειροθετουμένους, which signifies “receiving the laying on of hands,” or what was meant by “the laying on of hands” in this passage. For the Macedonians themselves readily admitted that ordination was signified there. Nor was the question whether the Bonosiaci ought to be ordained again so that they might remain in the clerical order which they had held under Bonosus; rather, the question was whether they should be permitted to remain in the clergy after a renewed ordination. The Macedonians asserted this; Innocent denied it and wished them to receive only lay communion. On that point both sides agreed. Accordingly, either version equally supported Innocent’s case; and if the Roman version had favored him more strongly, the Macedonians could easily have set aside its authority and appealed to the source of the canon.

Moreover, the translation of our codex, in which χειροθετουμένους is rendered by the word “to be ordained,” is supported by the translation of the Nicene canons made by Teilon and Tharistus and published on the authority of the so-called Sixth Council of Carthage. It is also supported by the other authorities cited by the most learned Morinus, *On Sacred Ordinations*, part III, Exercise 5, chapter 12.

[Note: [Col. 0933D] The version of Teilon and Tharistus—or rather of Philo and Evaristus—although it explains the Greek word χειροθετουμένους as referring to ordination, nevertheless does not support the interpretation of Quesnellus’s codex, or the Isidorian version received in that same codex. The former signifies an ordination already completed, whereas the latter signifies that ordination is to be repeated. Compare what we have discussed at greater length on this matter in note 13 of Quesnellus’s observations on Letter 167, volume II (our volume I, col. 1491, note b).]

[Col. 0934C] I omit reviewing the other ancient version which he praises and which Gratian also presents in *Decretum* 1, q. 7, chapter *Si qui*, since it is none other than the Isidorian version, agreeing with ours in almost every respect.

The most learned scholar still brings forward one consideration against our position. “If this codex,” he says, “had properly belonged to the Roman Church, and the various parts of which it consists had been assembled at that time and in that order in which they had been received as authoritative by that Church, who would believe that the letters of Siricius ought to have been placed after the decretals of Innocent, rather than being placed earlier in the codex? Were they unknown to the Romans before Innocent’s time? Were they held in contempt, or not received at all in that period? Who would assert such a thing?”

I would certainly not assert it either.

[Note: [Col. 0934D] We have adequately answered the following conjectures in the notes on chapter 2.]

But more than one means is available for dissolving this objection, and we have already fully satisfied it when we explained the order of the codex. We must recall that the codex appears to have been assembled in this way more by chance than by deliberate planning and purposeful construction. Until the age of Pope Innocent I, the Western Churches—and especially the Roman Church, as that pontiff himself testifies—were governed solely by the decrees of Nicaea; the Roman Church regarded the canons of Sardica as included among those of Nicaea. These alone constituted the codex of rules for the apostolic see. Later, the canons of Carthage and of the three Eastern synods were appended; these synods were either earlier than, or contemporary with, Nicaea. That the codex did not originally contain many more materials, when it first assumed the form of a codex and was furnished with a preface, is indicated by the very words of the preface. For it praises only the Nicene decrees, as though they made up almost the whole codex: “To these,” it says, “some rules were appended, which the Church mentioned above received and confirmed.”

After the Pelagian heresy arose and was condemned, it seemed appropriate to append to the codex everything decreed against it, whether by the African synods or by the Roman pontiffs. Then, on the occasion of Innocent’s rescripts to the African synods, his other decrees that were available were also annexed. But the letter of Siricius, which was perhaps preserved in the archives of the apostolic see along with the decretals of other earlier pontiffs, was not included in the codex, partly because they were not then thinking about it, and partly because it contained almost nothing that they did not find sanctioned in Innocent’s decretals. In the time of Leo, however, when, on the occasion of the Eutychian heresy and also of that ambitious Anatolius’s efforts on behalf of his see’s prerogative, the archives of the apostolic see were examined more carefully, many documents were brought forth from them. From the darkness of those archives into the light of the codex were brought the decretal constitutions of Leo’s predecessors, which had previously lain hidden there.

Certainly, that the constitutions of pontiffs earlier than Pope Innocent were not in the Roman codex in Leo’s time is made clear by the final chapter of Leo’s letter to the bishops throughout Campania, Picenum, Tuscany, and elsewhere (Letter 3, now 4, chapter 5). After dealing with several matters of ecclesiastical discipline, so that the bishops might not take the silence of others as an opportunity for error, he renews and confirms all the constitutions of his predecessors. Yet he does not mention either Siricius or anyone earlier than Innocent, so that he indicates that the constitutions then contained in the codex were to begin with those of Innocent:

“But lest there be anything which might perhaps be thought to have been omitted by us, we command that your Charity observe all the decretal constitutions both of blessed Innocent, of revered memory, and of all our predecessors …”

Moreover, the fact that the letters of Pope Innocent were inserted into our codex while the letter of Siricius was at that time passed over is no more damaging to our codex than the fact that the Dionysian codex, although located within the Roman Church and perhaps compiled from its archives, nevertheless lacks the constitutions of the apostolic see earlier than Siricius, which Leo himself mentions in more than one place. In chapter 1 of his letter he writes that “general decrees” had been sent to the provinces by his predecessor Liberius, “of venerable memory.”

[Note: [Col. 0935D] This will be refuted in the observations on chapter 1, number 10.]

It has not occurred to anyone to call Dionysius’s collection into question on that account; nor, for the same reason, do I think anyone should be less fair-minded toward ours.

Finally, we have already noted that the confusion of the codex’s parts not only does not conflict with our position but rather supports it, since Dionysius’s preface supplies us with the most certain criterion for recognizing the ancient codex—provided, of course, that nothing else obstructs its authenticity.

## ADDITION TO DISSERTATION XII

### On the Codex of the Canons of the Roman Church: in which the Breviary of the Council of Hippo and its Authenticity are Defended against Emmanuel Schelstratius

[Col. 0935D]

In the year 1679 Emmanuel a Schelstrate, a man who during his lifetime was greatly devoted to ecclesiastical affairs, attacked one part of the codex, certainly neither insignificant nor lacking in usefulness. In that year he published a book entitled *The African Church under the Primate of Carthage*. In its dissertation 3, chapter 6, he discusses the Council of Hippo held in the year 393. Comparing the copy of its abbreviated canons, which had long since been inserted into the volumes of the Councils, with the text that constitutes chapter 2 of our codex, he judges the former to be genuine and authentic, while declaring ours spurious and fabricated. He was led to this opinion by certain arguments that appeared to him strong and decisive, but which seem to me exceedingly weak and almost entirely without force.

First of all, Schelstratius attacks the synodical letter of the Council of Carthage, in which the statutes of Hippo are said to have been reread, corrected, and enlarged. Although he admits that all collectors of councils and ecclesiastical writers have regarded it as the synodical letter of the Council of Carthage, he nevertheless does not hesitate to deny it that status and to assign it instead to some Council of Byzacena. I shall examine his arguments briefly. “This synodical letter,” he says, “contains certain statements about Cresconius, bishop of Villa, which are expressed very differently in canon 38 of the Third Council of Carthage.”

His memory deceived him. The synodical letter contains not a word about Cresconius of Villa, but only the abbreviated statutes of the Council of Hippo, which are appended to the synodical letter. Moreover, what is found there concerning Cresconius of Villa not only does not conflict with that canon 38 of the Council of Carthage—although it is incorrectly called the Third Council in absolute terms—but illuminates it, and is in turn illuminated by it.

[Note: [Col. 0935D] It is correctly called the Third Council, not erroneously, in relation to the number of those councils described in the Isidorian collection: for two other councils are placed before it in that collection. Add that, in another respect, the Council of Carthage held under Boniface in the year 525 is called the Third Council under Aurelius.]

For that canon 38 teaches us three things about Cresconius. First, a judgment of the synod had been pronounced against him; second, that judgment had been confirmed; and third, a request was made that it be permitted to approach the governor of the province against Cresconius, because, having disregarded the bishops’ decrees, he had refused to leave the Church of Tubunae. Now that decree is none other than the one we read in our codex: it was enacted at Hippo and confirmed at Carthage, and by it Cresconius, bishop of Villa, who was said to have held the chair of the Church of Tubunae, was ordered to be content with his own people—that is, with the Church of Villa.

Emmanuel continues: “Furthermore, the Breviary of the Council of Hippo contains several chapters that are mutilated or interpolated. One example is enough: order 36, concerning the canonical Scriptures, in which the books of Maccabees are omitted, along with the two canonical Epistles of the Apostle Peter, the three of John, one of the Apostle Jude, and one of James.”

One example of mutilated canons, concerning the canonical Scriptures, is enough for Schelstratius because he had no more with which to oppose us. But we can offer three answers.

1. All those books that have been omitted—except the First Epistle of Peter and the First Epistle of John—were not formerly received by all the Churches.

2. Furthermore, that canon was still uncertain to the African Churches; they therefore decreed that the transmarine Churches should be consulted before it was confirmed.

3. Finally, it was easy for those books, whose mention is lacking here, to have slipped out through the haste or carelessness of a copyist.

[Note: [Col. 0936D] This is the true response. We have shown in note 98 on chapter 2 (above, col. 427, note n) of our collection that those books whose mention is absent had indeed dropped out through the fault of the scribes. We did not hesitate to supply the same books from our excellent Vindobonensis codex of this collection and from three other manuscript collections of the highest quality.]

As for the chapters which he calls interpolated, he would have spoken more accurately, in agreement with the Fathers of Carthage, had he called them “more carefully established,” as in the synodical letter, or “more carefully treated,” as in the title of the abbreviated statutes.

But it is from this very expression that the author derives his principal argument against the authenticity of this abridgment of Hippo. “For the chief point,” he says, “is that all the complete canons are set forth in this edition, although its title announces: ‘Abbreviated Statutes of the Council of Hippo.’ Therefore, if one of the two editions had to be accepted, it should not be the one that reproduces the complete canons, but rather the commonly circulated edition, which contains only the Breviary of the canons of Hippo.”

Yet neither edition pleases him. For, contrary to the most eminent Baronius and Perronius, he decides that the synodical letter, together with the appended breviary, is either spurious or at least interpolated; and he says that he trusts he will prove this by arguments whose force no prudent person will disregard.

What astonishing confidence! We shall restrain it without difficulty. To blunt what he asserts to be the chief point, the statutes of councils can be abbreviated in more than one way. They can be compressed so that the sense and subject matter of each canon are indicated in a few words. Dionysius Exiguus abbreviated the canons and decrees of both his codices in this manner, prefacing each with an extremely brief summary and also appending the summaries collectively at the beginning of each codex. The deacon Ferrandus used the same method, as did finally whoever composed the synopsis of the canons of Hippo that appears in the commonly circulated edition, although it is so short and meager that in many places it barely touches upon the canon’s subject and conveys to the reader only a sufficiently clear general impression of it.

[Note: [Col. 0937C] Three things must be distinguished. First, the complete canons of Hippo from the year 393, of which only two survive as quotations in the synod of Boniface of Carthage in the year 525; those two sufficiently indicate the fuller form of the rest. Second, the abbreviations of those same canons, made in the Council of Carthage by the Byzacene bishops on the Ides of August in the year 397: these are the true Breviary of Hippo, which was subsequently read and confirmed in the plenary Council of Carthage held in the same year 397 on the fifth day before the Kalends of September. Third, the summaries, or titles, of these abbreviations, published by Crabbe, which were composed by the author of our collection. If you distinguish these things, everything will be understood correctly and easily.]

There is another kind of synodal abridgment, which most compilers of canonical codices and summaries of councils have followed. It consists in cutting away whatever belongs either to history or to particular controversies, as well as whatever is unrelated to matters of faith or common discipline, and describing only the canons, so that those who are obliged to regulate their lives and conduct by them may have them more readily before their eyes. The statutes of the Council of Hippo were abbreviated by the Fathers of the Council of Carthage according to this method. The collectors of the Eastern canons subsequently imitated them, followed later by Dionysius, Cresconius, Martin of Braga, and finally, in more recent centuries, Caranza, Coriolanus, and others.

[Col. 0937C] The collection of the statutes of Hippo surpasses all collections or abridgments in either authority or diligence. It was first compiled by the bishops—or council—of the province of Byzacena; then it received as editors, approvers, and enlargers the numerous bishops of the Council of Carthage; and finally, enlarged by several canons of great importance, it was regarded as almost a complete codex of the entire African Church. Thus the synods subsequently held in Africa borrowed several things from the collection of Hippo, as from a kind of archetype, as Schelstratius reports from Baronius. Since the complete acts of this outstanding synod have perished, its collection of canons ought therefore to be highly valued by everyone. For that reason we shall defend its authenticity and integrity with greater zeal and diligence against Schelstratius’s false suspicions, scarcely any of whose conjectures could be weaker or more unfortunate.

His first objection is that the synodical letter is addressed “to the bishops of Numidia, both Mauritanias, Tripoli, and the proconsular province,” while the province of Byzacena is omitted.

[Note: [Col. 0937D] We resolve this objection in the admonition to chapter 2 of our codex, no. 6.]

“Of this,” he says, “no explanation can be given except that the synodical letter was written by the Byzacene bishops to the bishops of the other provinces, including the proconsular province, whose metropolitan at that time was Aurelius. Aurelius … testified in the Third Council of Carthage that the letters of the Byzacene brethren and of Mizonius had been transmitted to him so that they might be read there. From this two conclusions follow: first, that Aurelius has been inserted into the heading of the synodical letter contrary to the acts; and second, that the synodical letter falsely bears the title of the Council of Carthage, since it belongs to Byzacena, as Christophorus Justellus correctly observed in his notes on the codex of the African Church.”

Schelstratius could have followed Justellus, who often writes learnedly on many subjects; but in this passage he followed his footsteps with little success and went astray along with him. Both men confuse and intermingle two entirely different letters.

[Note: [Col. 0937D] This confused response contains many falsehoods mixed with truths. Two letters are known from the speech of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, prefixed to chapter 34 of the African Codex, which forms the preface, or first title, of the plenary synod held at Carthage on the fifth day before the Kalends of September in the year 397. The first is the letter of the Byzacene bishops, to which they appended the breviary for this “gathered assembly,” that is, for the bishops of the aforesaid plenary synod held on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, as Aurelius testifies in the speech mentioned above. The other is a private letter from Mizonius, primate of Byzacena, to Aurelius himself, in which he asked that the breviary be read in the plenary synod and that, if the Fathers raised any objections there, it be amended for the better.

When Quesnellus published the first letter as having been written at the Council of Carthage in the year 397, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, he doubtless failed to notice the Ides of August, which both his own codices and all ours indicate. The synod of that date is therefore plainly established, not a synod held on the sixth day before the Kalends of July. This synod, convened at Carthage before Aurelius by the Byzacene bishops, who had anticipated the date fixed for the plenary synod, was not a synod assembled from other bishops. It was in this gathering, during the proceedings conducted with Aurelius himself, that the breviary was composed—not so much by the Byzacene bishops as signed by Aurelius, who was present. It was sent with the letter of the Byzacene bishops to the bishops of the plenary synod, which was to be convened not long afterward, so that it might be submitted to that synod’s examination and amended where necessary. Mizonius had requested this from Aurelius in a separate private letter.

The date fixed for the plenary synod at the Council of Hippo was the tenth day before the Kalends of September. On that day the breviary was read together with the letter of the Byzacene bishops. But since the legates of the province of Numidia had not yet arrived, the synod was postponed until the fifth day before the Kalends of September. At that time the breviary and the aforementioned letter were read again and inserted into the acts. We have set this out more fully in the admonition to chapter 2 of our collection. From this you will easily understand how many falsehoods Quesnellus has woven into what follows.]

The two of them mix up and confuse two entirely different letters: one written by Mizonius, primate of Byzacena, together with his colleagues from his provincial synod, in which legates were selected to go to the general Council of Carthage in the name of all their fellow provincials; the other written by that same Mizonius, after the general synod had concluded, from that general synod together with Aurelius and the other Fathers, to which he had been sent as a delegate.

Mizonius wrote the first letter to Aurelius the primate and sent with it the Breviary of the canons of Hippo. It had indeed been prepared by the Byzacene bishops, but had not yet been amended for the better; rather, it had been sent for the express purpose that, if anything in it were found deserving of correction, it might be more properly established, as in fact happened. Aurelius’s words at that Council of Carthage in the year 397 are clear on this point:

“Therefore, brethren, if it seems good to your Charity, let the letter of our Byzacene brethren, together with the breviary which they appended to that same letter, be read to this gathered assembly, so that, if anything there should perhaps move the mind of your Charity, whatever is observed more carefully in the same breviary may be amended for the better. For our brother and fellow bishop, the primate of the first see, a man distinguished by the merit of his gravity and prudence, Mizonius, requested this of my humility in writing.”

This is the substance of the first letter.

The second letter, which the same Mizonius signed together with the other Fathers of the entire general Council of Carthage, differs from the first in more than one respect, and its subject is entirely different. It was written not to Aurelius but by Aurelius, Mizonius, and the other bishops to five—or to all—the provinces of Africa, with Byzacena alone excepted. In that letter there is no longer any request that the breviary be amended; rather, “the brief collection of statutes,” as it reads there—which appears to contain everything, with some matters more carefully established—“we have caused to be appended to this letter, so that, by reviewing in summary form what has been decreed, we may take greater care to observe it.”

If the Belgian disputant thinks it impossible for Mizonius to have written one letter to Aurelius from the province of Byzacena and to have signed another with Aurelius at Carthage, he has been looking for a knot in a rush. Nothing is easier than to reconcile the two. It often happens that a metropolitan who presides over the assembly of his provincial fellow bishops, and signs the document by which delegates are appointed to a general council, as well as the letters, instructions, or admonitions directed to that council, later attends the general council himself and signs its statutes and synodical letters.

I do not, however, think that the matter under discussion occurred precisely in this way, but rather as follows. After the statutes of Hippo had been enacted and sent to the provinces, they were received only reluctantly by many, because they abolished numerous abuses; indeed, some failed to observe them at all with unrestrained recklessness, as the synodical letter relates. To excuse such excesses, some alleged that they had omitted to observe matters that had long before been established by law because they were ignorant of them. The fact that this excuse was especially operative among the Byzacenes, and that they had cloaked their conduct under the pretext of ignorance, is indicated clearly enough by the words of the synodical letter itself and by other passages quoted above from the Council of Carthage. From these it is evident both that the Byzacene bishops sent the Breviary of the canons of Hippo to Aurelius so that it might be examined again and amended for the better if necessary, and that the same breviary was later sent back to the province of Byzacena, corrected and enlarged by several canons.

After receiving the letter of the Byzacene bishops—which, as Aurelius expressly states, was written not to the synod but to him—he judged that the matter was too important for him alone to decide anything about it. He also believed that the statutes of a general synod could be reconsidered or amended only in another general synod. Whether the synod had already been announced, or whether Aurelius convened it on this occasion and for the treatment of other matters as well—a purpose for which he aptly uses the word “gathered”—it appears to have been partly assembled on the sixth day before the Kalends of July of that same year 397, as though it were a prelude to the general synod, which came together in much greater numbers on the fifth day before the Kalends of September of that year.

At the end of this gathering the African Codex contains the following:

“Under the consulship of Caesarius and Atticus, illustrious men, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, at Carthage, it was decreed that no bishop should sail without a formal letter from his primate. Whoever seeks the acts in the authentic records will find them.”

If these words are compared with what Aurelius stated at the beginning of the general council itself on the fifth day before the Kalends of September of the same year, it will be clear, unless I am mistaken, that they must be understood of no other council than the one begun on the sixth day before the Kalends of July:

“After the appointed day of the council had passed, we assembled, as you remember, most blessed brethren, and we had supposed that the delegations of all the provinces throughout Africa had come together on the day appointed, as I said, for our proceedings.”

Aurelius would not have needed to refresh the memory of his fellow priests concerning that earlier assembly unless at least two months had already elapsed since its first meetings. In fact, exactly that number of months, and no more, had passed since the synod assembled on the sixth day before the Kalends of July. It was therefore not another synod, but the preliminary meetings of that great synod, in which those who had gathered—or even arrived before—the appointed day of the council undertook discussions among themselves on various matters. In particular, the letter of the Byzacene bishops was then read together with the breviary sent with it, and the requests made concerning the same matter in Mizonius’s letter were considered together with the bishops who had come from the province of Byzacena.

But what I especially wish to emphasize is this: although the same men had written to Aurelius from their own synod perhaps several months earlier, they nevertheless did not for that reason neglect to present themselves at the general synod. Indeed, since their own affairs were to be dealt with there, and since they especially desired that their breviary be amended for the better, they were the first of all to travel to Carthage—and in very large numbers. This is easily discerned from Aurelius’s words quoted above and from the following passage:

“But after the letter of our fellow priests, the Byzacenian bishops, had been read, and after what those same men, who had anticipated the time and day of the council, had discussed with me had been read to your Charity, the delegation assigned by the province of Sitifis was also read by our brethren Honoratus and Urbanus, who are participating with us in the council today, and so forth.”

But since the matter of that breviary had not yet been dealt with before a numerous and full synod—for the bishops of Numidia, or at least their legates, were still expected—the letter of the Byzacene bishops together with the breviary was read again before the synod, now more fully attended. The matters that had been amended for the better in the earlier meetings, as we have reported above, were submitted to the judgment of all the Fathers, as is shown by Aurelius’s words concerning that letter and breviary.

That the Byzacene bishops were present at the council, and had even arrived before the others, is sufficiently indicated by Aurelius’s words: “what those same men, who had anticipated the time and day of the council, had discussed with me.” It is proved a second time by the subscriptions appended to the breviary after it had been amended for the better. After Mizonius, bishop of the first see in Byzacena, subscribe Victorianus of Mascila, Lupianus of the people of Tambala, Ninus of Jubaltiana, Philologius of Hadrumetum, and Ferox of Macriana; all of them were bishops of the province of Byzacena.

The readings found in commonly circulated copies—Lupianus of Tamugadi, Ninus of Tubaltum, and Ferox of Macri—must be attributed to the carelessness of scribes. Tamugadi was in Numidia, from which not even legates came to the synod, as Aurelius complains. It is likely that the only bishop from that province present at the synod was Reginus of Vegesela, who may at that time have been staying near Carthage on his own business; he was present when the letter of Crescentianus, the bishop of the first see, was read. I do not know whether there was ever a city called Tubaltum; nor do all those who have undertaken to catalogue or comment upon the provinces of Africa appear to have known of one. Finally, the bishops of Macri, Macrenses, or Macrienses belonged to the proconsular province, and it is hardly credible that only one of them subscribed among the Byzacenes.

The reason why the Byzacenes subscribed before the others is obvious from what has been said. Difficulties concerning the statutes of Hippo had arisen in Byzacena; Aurelius had been consulted about the matter by the Byzacenes; these matters above all had been brought before the synod; and, especially at the insistence of the Byzacenes, the statutes had been amended for the better:

“We have judged that they should be made known to everyone throughout Byzacena by common council,” they say, “so that from now on any violator who arises may know that he has suffered the loss of his status.”

The breviary was therefore rightly fortified by the name, authority, and signatures of the Byzacene bishops and their primate, so that those who had formerly used the veil of ignorance to cover their arrogance and disobedience, or anything similar, might more readily be brought back to better conduct by the authority of their own bishops. Since, then, many—at least many of the bishops of the province of Byzacena—were present at the synod with their primate and had subscribed to it, this explains why their province is not mentioned in the title of the synodical letter. Returning home, they themselves were to take their breviary and send it from the synod of their entire province of Byzacena, which was to be convened after their return, throughout the province of Byzacena, as the Fathers had judged it should be sent.

From what has been said about the two letters, and from the other points noted, it is clear that Schelstratius’s second argument vanishes into thin air. He bases it on the words “while we were assembling in the city of Carthage.” For, although he says it is established that this synod was held in Byzacena, he combines and confuses two synods—one Byzacene and the other Carthaginian—into one, as we have said.

His third argument, drawn from the Creed, may, for all I care, avail against the commonly circulated edition of the index of Hippo, in which the Creed is included in full, though disfigured by corruptions. But it has no bearing upon our edition, in which the Creed is indicated but not reproduced.

[Note: [Col. 0941C] Augustine, in Book I of the *Retractions*, chapter 17, testifies that, while already a presbyter, he disputed before the Fathers of the Council of Hippo concerning the Apostles’ Creed. The bishops Honoratus and Urbanus, speaking in the plenary synod of the year 397, chapter 47 of the African Codex, concerning the Breviary of the canons of Hippo that had been read, declare that in its reading they heard the Nicene faith.]

[Col. 0941B] The fourth argument disappears through the distinction we have established between the brief sent by the Byzaceni to Aurelius, so that matters observed more carefully might be improved, as Aurelius himself puts it, and that same brief, sent back throughout the province of Byzacena after it had been revised, in which certain matters had been more carefully settled, as the Carthaginian synodical letter records. Accordingly, the heading prefixed to the commonly printed short collection of statutes, which the dissertationist adduces—“Abbreviations of the Council of Hippo made at the Third Council of Carthage” [Note: [Col. 0941D] This annotation, in which the abbreviations of the Hipponian canons are said to have been made at the Third Council of Carthage, has Crabbe as its author and is found in no manuscript codex. Therefore nothing can be alleged from it.]—may be defended by anyone who wishes to defend the commonly printed short collection. This concern certainly does not affect me, since in my manuscript I read this title, and no other, prefixed to the brief: “Here begins a brief collection of statutes.”

The adversary of the brief states the fifth argument as follows. Since none, he says, of those who have remembered the Council of Hippo has recognized even one of all the titles—except the first, concerning Easter—as titles of the Hipponian canons, but all have instead cited others that are not found in that brief.

This two-horned argument, being negative, is for that reason weak and feeble; but it is entirely futile and empty for other reasons as well.

First, because most of the statutes included in the brief were enacted in several synods—first at Hippo, then at Carthage—it is not surprising that they are sometimes attributed to one and sometimes to the other. This variation could occur all the more easily because, in this very brief as it lies in the Roman Codex, the canons over which we are disputing are attributed to both councils. Thus, at the very beginning, we find: “The canons of the Council of Carthage held on the day of the Ides of August, in the consulship of Atticus and Caesarius.” Then, after the synodical letter: “The statutes of the Council of Hippo, abridged, and certain of them conferred and more carefully examined at the Council of Carthage with the bishops of Byzacena, are as follows.” Finally, after five or six abbreviated chapters—chapters that [Note: [Col. 0941D] That the first five or six chapters belong especially to the brief which we saw had been drawn up at Carthage by the Byzaceni is clear from what we brought forward in the Treatise, part II, chapter 3, section 3, no. 2 and following. In the Barberini manuscript 2888, the first chapter of the brief begins with the Nicene Creed; consequently, the title “Here begins a brief collection of statutes,” which is inserted after those earlier chapters in the collection published in this volume, is omitted. See note 30 on chapter 2 of the cited collection (above, col. 420, note m).] had not been included by the Byzaceni—their brief, improved, is marked with this title: “Here begins a brief collection of statutes.” Why, then, should it be surprising that, when some of these matters are praised, they are attributed sometimes to Hippo and sometimes to Carthage?

Second, the very designation “brief” or “brief collection” sufficiently indicates that not all the statutes were inserted in it, but that some were omitted—those that concerned particular affairs more than the common discipline of the Church, or that had been reserved solely to the care and concern of the primates. Such are those five chapters added by the Carthaginians, and perhaps omitted by the Byzaceni for that reason. The first concerns the proclamation of the date of Easter; the second, the particular case of Cresconius, bishop of Villa [Villarensis]; but on that occasion the Carthaginians judged that this third general canon should be enacted: “Henceforth it has pleased us that no one should usurp the congregations of another.” The fourth concerns only the primate of the province of Sitifis; but consequently something was added concerning the other primates as well.

The authors of the African Codex [Note: [Col. 0942C] The author of the Codex, as it is called in the commonly printed editions of the Councils, is Dionysius Exiguus. From his collection the African canons were excerpted and translated into Greek. Read the Treatise on Collections inserted in this volume, part II, chapter 3, section 9, no. 6.] give the same explanation for abridging the material in connection with the council of 405. “I have therefore not transcribed the acts of this council in their entirety,” they say, “because what was enacted consisted rather of matters necessary at the time than of any general enactments; but for the instruction of students I have made a brief digest of the same council.” There is therefore no reason for our dissertationist to be surprised that some matters which we do not read as inserted in the brief have been treated as Hipponian canons: the very nature of a brief requires that it not encompass everything.

But as for his further assertion that none of the statutes contained in this brief was cited or commended by anyone as a Hipponian canon, that statement was made more confidently than truthfully or skillfully; we shall prove it without difficulty.

First, Augustine addresses the presbyter Quintianus in what is now Letter 64 as follows:

“I am surprised at your prudence, since you warned me to order that those who come from you to our monastery should not be received, so that what was established by us in council might remain; yet you do not remember that it was established in council which Scriptures are canonical and ought to be read among the people of God. Review the council, therefore, and commit to memory everything that you read there; there too you will find that it was established concerning clergy alone, and not also concerning laymen, that those coming from anywhere should not be received into the monastery. This is not because mention was made of a monastery, but because it was established in such a way that no one should receive another’s cleric.”

[Note: [Col. 0942D] The two cited canons were indeed enacted at the Council of Hippo; but afterward, abridged, they were read, confirmed, and inserted in the plenary Carthaginian synod of 397, at which Augustine, by then a bishop, we have shown to have been present in the cited Treatise, part II, chapter 3, section 3, shortly before the end, where we dealt with the subscriptions of that synod. Since, moreover, Augustine writes concerning the canon about another’s cleric, “What was established by us in council,” he plainly means a council in which he himself, already a bishop, sat and enacted statutes. Therefore he cited these canons not from Hippo, where he was only a presbyter, but from Carthage in 397. See the reconstruction of the canons of this synod in the cited place; from it you will understand that the same synod is not presented wholly complete either in Isidore or in the African Codex.]

Behold the two canons praised by Augustine: one concerning the canon of Scripture, the other concerning the non-reception of another’s cleric. The former does indeed occur in that Council of Carthage of the year 397, which is reported in the African Codex and among the acts of the council commonly called the Third Council of Carthage; but I am convinced that neither of the two was indicated by Augustine at this point. For one of those two collections must be fictitious, since both are assigned to the same year and month and consist of nearly the same canons. 746 Yet no one fails willingly to grant primacy of authority and authenticity to the African Codex and, consequently, to declare the acts of the other entirely fictitious, as may perhaps be proved more fully elsewhere.

If Augustine had wished to designate the Carthaginian synod, he could have designated none other than the one inserted in the African Codex under the year 397. But Augustine does not seem to me to have drawn the two canons he cites from that council. For he is speaking of a council in which he himself had participated: “what was established by us in council.” Moreover, the holy Doctor had not participated in the council of 397, as is clear from the beginning of its acts, where Aurelius mentions a letter written to him by Crescentianus, primate of Numidia. In it Crescentianus promised on behalf of the bishops of his province either that they would deign to come themselves or that they would, as usual, send delegates to that council. “But this,” he says, “does not seem to have happened,” and so forth.

It remains, therefore, that Augustine drew the double canon from the Council of Hippo, a council which he himself attests that he attended while not yet a bishop. Furthermore, the fact that the bishop of the province of Numidia and of Hippo itself simply calls it “the council” seems to me to indicate the Council of Hippo, as a familiar witness to his claim. That council had been extremely famous: it was the first convened under the primacy of Aurelius, especially with the intention that the collapsed discipline of the African Church might be restored; and finally, African bishops looked to it as to a kind of archetype whenever synods investigated the restoration of particular aspects of discipline.

Finally, whether Augustine indicated the Council of Hippo or the Carthaginian council celebrated in 397, I infer that the former rather than the latter was before his eyes from the fact that the latter specifically enacted nothing about the non-reception of another’s clerics. Instead, in many councils Epigonius recalls this statute to the memory of the Fathers of the synod (African Codex, chapter 54), and now suggests that it should be confirmed by their prudence, so that no bishop should seize another’s cleric against the will of the bishop whose cleric he was.
