Victor, the senior in promotion, also requested that Epigonius’s petition be made general for everyone; but, with the primate Aurelius opposing it, nothing was concluded. Moreover, Julianus is said to have acted against the statutes of the council if he did not restore a cleric who had been secretly taken away. 747 Such a statute, therefore, had already been enacted in some council, and none other than the Council of Hippo. Augustine was consequently speaking of it; and here too that council is simply called “the council,” as we read Augustine doing.

As a second witness for the Hipponian brief I cite the African compiler of all the councils convened during the primacy of Aurelius. [Note: [Col. 0943D] The author of the commonly printed African Codex was Dionysius Exiguus, not some African writer. Nor did he gather in this codex every council celebrated under Aurelius; rather, he presented one Carthaginian synod of the year 419, in which the preceding councils under the same Aurelius were read and inserted. Compare what we said in the Treatise, part II, chapter 3, section 9; there you will also find an explanation of what should be thought about the first thirty-three canons of the same codex.] That collection is found in the Codex of the Canons of the African Church. It consists of two parts. The first contains canons under thirty-three titles, gathered from approximately three councils: the first held under Gratus, primate of Carthage, in 348; the second under Genethlius, likewise primate, in 390; and the third, our Council of Hippo, held first under Aurelius and celebrated in 393.

For this reason, the compiler begins the second part of the codex, which consists of the councils convened under Aurelius, with the Council of Hippo. But because the canons of that synod had already been collected in the first part of the codex, he refers the reader to it: “The acts of this council have not been transcribed for the reason that what was established there is shown to have been inserted above.” The Hipponian canons must therefore be sought in that first part of the codex, among those thirty-three statutes. In fact, nearly all the enactments listed in our brief are found there in the form they had before they were enlarged by the insertion of fourteen others and improved in certain other respects.

As a third witness there will be the universal Council of Carthage celebrated under the primate Boniface in 525, after the African Churches and bishops had recovered their freedom from the tyranny of the Vandals. At that council very many passages were read from both parts of the African Codex. Far more were taken from the second part, especially from the council of 397, which it calls “the Third” without qualification—that is, the third council under Aurelius. But at the end of the first day it also included two notable passages, not from the Hipponian brief, but [Col. 0944B] from the complete acts of that council, which still survived at that time.

The first excerpt presents that portion of the acts in which, as it is briefly reported in the first [Note: [Col. 0944D] What Quesnell here calls the first addition to our brief, and what shortly afterward is similarly called the first addition made to the brief by the Fathers of the plenary Council of Carthage, is part of the Hipponian brief itself, which was drawn up by the bishops of Byzacena and Aurelius of Carthage. Consult note 10 (above, col. 941, note c).] addition to our brief, it was decreed: “It has also pleased us, on account of the controversy that often tends to arise, that all the provinces of Africa should take care to receive the observance of the date of Easter from the Church of Carthage.”

The second excerpt contains that portion of the acts in which this statute was enacted: “A proper primate was permitted for the Mauretania of Sitifis, when it requested one, among the more distant Moors,” as our codex records in the first addition made to the brief by the Carthaginian Fathers. Likewise, the other part of the same statute is found in abbreviated form after the words just quoted: “The other bishops of the principal sees declared, from the council of the bishops of the Church of Carthage, that primates of their provinces should be appointed if any dispute should arise.”

I do not think Schelstratius’s argument, drawn from the silence of all writers or, as he thought, of all ancient records, can be refuted more plainly than by that double exchange of words, which sheds the greatest light on our codex and especially on the Hipponian brief and provides a certain mark of genuineness.

I therefore seem to have adequately answered the first part of the fifth argument, which asserts that none of those who remembered the Council of Hippo recognized even one of all the titles—except the first, concerning Easter—as titles of the Hipponian canons. On the contrary, Augustine remembered it; so did the author of Part II of the African Codex, who points to nearly all its canons as having been listed in the earlier part; the Fathers of the plenary Council of Carthage, assembled in 525, remembered it and set before us two notable portions of the complete acts and two Hipponian enactments; finally, Ferrandus remembered it. The dissertationist especially adduces and presses Ferrandus’s testimony against the genuineness of the brief, as will be clear from what follows.

[Col. 0944D] The second part of the fifth argument is this: all those who remembered the Council of Hippo cited other canons that are not found in that brief. To this general objection we gave a general answer above; now we proceed to answer the individual examples.

This is the first example: [Note: [Col. 0944D] On this first and the second example, see note 42 (col. 422, note k) in chapter 2 of our collection.] Only fourteen years after the Council of Hippo, a Carthaginian council was celebrated under Aurelius, who reports that the Council of Hippo had enacted that a plenary council should be held each year in different provinces of Africa—a provision nowhere found in the brief.

I willingly add weight to the objection. For mention is made of that statute not only in the council of 407 but twice in the general council of 397, as can be seen in chapters 51 and 52 of the African Codex. But what of it? If everything were contained in the brief, it would not be a brief. Moreover, the whole first part of the statute lies in chapter 5 of our brief; indeed, it is also read among the Hipponian canons listed in the first part of the African Codex.

The second part, however, does not seem to have pleased everyone, and for that reason it was not excerpted. For at the council of 397, in which the Hipponian canons were repeated and confirmed, Aurelius says in chapter 51 of the codex: “We remember that we promised long ago that we should meet each year to deliberate.” On this occasion Honoratus and Urbanus, delegates of the province of Sitifis, mention the second part: “Because it was established in the Council of Hippo that each province should be visited at the time of the council.” They therefore insist that the province of Mauretania should be visited in its proper order—that is, that a general council should be convened there in rotation.

After hearing this, Aurelius took up the discussion and ensured that no promise was made to the delegates. Yet, Aurelius says in the council of 407, this had been observed: “that we should sometimes convene in Numidia and sometimes in Byzacena.” But, as he immediately adds, this seemed burdensome to all the brothers. Consequently, in the following chapter (no. 95), the universal synod decreed:

1. “That there should no longer be an annual obligation to weary the brothers.

2. Whenever a common matter requires it, [lacuna] a synod is to be convened in the province where convenience recommends it.

3. Matters that are not common are to be judged in their own provinces.”

This, I think, was the reason why Aurelius—at that time still new in the primacy and presiding over a synod in another province—prevented the statute that the bishops of the other provinces had arranged at Hippo from being excerpted and confirmed in his own synod of 397, with the bishops of Numidia absent, and a few years later even arranged for it to be abrogated.

Nearly the same must be said of the Hipponian canon 750 which is said to have enacted that an annual assembly of the provinces should be held on the tenth day before the Kalends of September. For the Carthaginian primate, with his fellow bishops, seems to have been displeased that the responsibility for choosing both the time and place of the council should not be left to his discretion. Hence, in the African Codex, just as only one synod after the Council of Hippo appears to have met outside Carthage, so only one met on the tenth day before the Kalends of September, although a few others approach that date.

For this reason Aurelius did not take care to retain that Hipponian canon in the brief. If these considerations are not sufficient, I add that this statute does not pertain to the common discipline of the clergy, and for that reason is not contained in the brief. Let the dissertationist produce the original and complete acts of the council, and I promise to show all the canons there, without exception.

[Col. 0946A] The same answer disposes of the chapters of Ferrandus that he excerpted from the complete acts, just as the Fathers of the Council of Carthage in 525, under the primate Boniface, did. [Note: [Col. 0945D] Ferrandus did not cite the chapters of the Hipponian synod of 393 from the complete acts of that synod, but from the acts of the plenary Council of Carthage of 397, in which the brief had been inserted. The chapters he lists from the Council of Hippo Regius do not concern the Council of Hippo of 393 but another council of 427. See the Treatise, part II, chapter 3, sections 3 and 9, and also part V, where we discussed Ferrandus’s abridgment.]

The dissertationist repeats his sixth argument from the council commonly called the Third Council of Carthage, in which those canons attributed to the Council of Hippo were enacted. But this collection of canons circulated under the name of the Third Council of Carthage, outside the Codex of the African Church, is most certainly spurious and fabricated, as I have already demonstrated above. [Note: [Col. 0945D] Indeed, Isidore presents the canons of the Third Council of Carthage of 397 more fully than Dionysius does in the African Codex, in which not all the canons of that council were transcribed in their proper place. Only in Isidore is the order of the canons not preserved; certain canons are also recited with a reading altered in places at the synod of 419, and one canon was improperly stitched in from another synod. We explained all this in greater detail in the Treatise, part II, chapter 3, section 3.] The genuine acts of that synod are only those found in the African Codex of canons under the year 397, in the consulship of Caesarius and Atticus.

But whoever examines somewhat more carefully the portion of that codex which the dissertationist adduces will immediately notice how empty his objection is. He presents it after first quoting the opinion of Bishop Epigonius:

“Bishop Epigonius said: ‘In this brief, which has been excerpted from the Council of Hippo, we think that nothing should be corrected or added except that the date of holy Easter should be made known at the time of the council.’”

From this canon, Schelstratius says, we learn that among the canons of the Third Council of Carthage nothing from the Hipponian statutes was reported except what concerns Easter.

Who would not be surprised that the dissertationist failed to notice that Epigonius’s words—“We think that nothing should be corrected or added except that …” 751—must extend [Note: [Col. 0946D] Epigonius’s words must extend not only to the Hipponian canon concerning the date of Easter, which was omitted through Dionysius’s carelessness, nor only to the thirteen canons of the Hipponian brief inserted in their proper place, but to the whole brief, which had been read before Epigonius’s exchange. Compare the Treatise, part II, chapter 3, section 3, no. 52. Dionysius inserted only the thirteen canons of the brief in their proper place because he had previously recited the others when they were repeated at the synod of 419. Quesnell’s entire confusion in this appendix depends on the fact that his knowledge of the African councils and canons was very confused and that the plenary Council of Carthage of 397 had not been restored. Since, however, in the Treatise mentioned above, part II, chapter 3, we have labored at length to assign each canon to its proper synod, we refer readers there.] not only to the canon concerning the announcement of the council’s date of Easter, but also to the other thirteen canons attached to it, all of which are inserted in the Hipponian brief. This is easily understood from the words attached to the fourteenth canon: “After these had been inserted, Bishops Honoratus and Urbanus, etc., said.” Therefore it was not one single canon that was stitched onto the Hipponian brief, but all fourteen.

And lest anyone object that it is scarcely credible that Epigonius, without any deliberation, immediately brought forward so many canons to be inserted in the brief, it must be remembered that an addition of this kind had already long before been established by Aurelius and the other bishops, who had anticipated the day and time of the council, as Aurelius says in the discussion that he held with the Byzaceni at that time. This may have been at the very gathering which is recorded in the African Codex, at the end of the council under discussion, as having been held at Carthage on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, in the same consulship. Indeed, these are precisely the matters that our codex says, after the synodical letter, were “conferred and more carefully examined at the Council of Carthage with the bishops of Byzacena.”

Accordingly, before Epigonius spoke, Aurelius had said: “If it therefore pleases you, let the matters discussed be read, and let each one be considered by your Charity.” After this, Epigonius, intending to give the common judgment of that assembly rather than a private opinion, does not say “I think” but “we think”; and, after the fourteen canons had been inserted, the Fathers proceeded to discuss other matters.

The passage of the codex alleged against the brief’s genuineness is therefore so far from diminishing it that it rather confirms it, [Col. 0947A] since all those canons are in fact found inserted in the brief. 752 On the contrary, it weakens the authority of that collection of the canons of the Third Council of Carthage which is found outside the codex in the volumes of the Councils. For it is established that those fourteen inserted canons had not been issued before the tenth day before the Kalends of September. It is also established that no other synod was convened at Carthage in that same year after that synod; consequently, the common jumble of those canons must necessarily be fictitious.

The collection found in the codex under September 10 (read: August 28) of the year 397 is genuinely Carthaginian. It is the third of those convened under Aurelius; but the first was held at Hippo, while the other two were celebrated at Carthage.

The seventh argument, drawn from Aurelius’s subscription, requires no answer, since the difference between the Carthaginian and Byzacenan synods has been explained above, together with the other matters discussed at the beginning of this dissertation. Much remains in Schelstratius’s dissertation that requires correction, but at present I have no time to devote to discussing it. I am satisfied to have blown away everything brought forward by a man who was not unlearned in order to strip that Hipponian brief of authority and, through its side, stab the Roman Codex of Canons.

I would be mistaken if all those to whom sacred antiquity is pleasing did not now readily grant me that the genuineness and authority of that Hipponian brief are established, and that this distinguished monument of canon law ought already to be entirely free from every suspicion of fabrication. Finally, from its authenticity considerable authority and weight accrue to the complete Codex of the Canons of the Roman Church into which it has been inserted. [Note: [Col. 0947A] Indeed, from this brief, as it is inserted in our collection, the conclusion is considerably confirmed that the same collection cannot be regarded as the ancient Codex of the Canons of the Roman Church. Since the final two canons do not belong to the brief, if the Roman Church had once received this brief, those additions would be absent from the public codex of that Church, just as they are absent from the Verona manuscript, even though the latter was not the public codex.]

[Col. 0947]

## OBSERVATIONS OF THE BALLERINI ON THE TWELFTH DISSERTATION OF PASCHASIUS QUESNELLUS, CONCERNING THE CODEX OF ECCLESIASTICAL CANONS AND DECREES OF THE HOLY APOSTOLIC SEE, WHICH HE WRONGLY ATTRIBUTES TO THE ROMAN CHURCH

[Col. 0947B] 753 I. When Quesnellus discovered in the Oxford manuscript a collection of canons and decrees of the Apostolic See joined with the letters and sermons of St. Leo, Roman pontiff, he immediately formed the opinion that this collection had belonged to the Roman Church and had been the public codex of that Church, in use under the pontificates of Innocent I, Zosimus, and Leo.

Although neither the title of the collection itself, nor its preface, nor any other annotation supported this opinion, it was nevertheless easy for the great conjecturer to pile up several arguments in order to give the same opinion some degree of probability. After completing a dissertation on this subject, he examined more carefully the Thuaneus codex of the same collection, much older than the Oxford manuscript, which he had previously collated only for the sake of Leo’s letters. He saw that the same collection of canons and decrees was found there, but without St. Leo’s sermons and with fewer of the same pontiff’s letters than in the Oxford manuscript. Moreover, he found these letters appended to the collection itself, whereas in the Oxford copy they had been joined to several other letters of the pontiff and formed, as it were, a separate body.

If he had placed greater trust in the older and superior codex, and if, alerted by this difference between the two codices, he had sought other manuscript copies of the same collection—several of which are preserved in French libraries—he would easily have recognized that this collection was joined with Leo’s works in this one Oxford copy and in another older copy from which the Oxford manuscript had been transcribed. He would also have recognized that thirty-two letters of that pontiff had been separated from it by the arbitrary decision of an ancient scribe, so that they might be copied among Leo’s works together with his other letters.

Once he understood that those thirty-two letters were a portion of this collection, attested by all the other older copies, and that the collection itself had no support from Leo’s works, which are appended to it in the Oxford manuscript, for the belief that it was Roman, he might perhaps have abandoned the opinion he had first adopted. But since this opinion greatly pleased him, he undertook the new labor of revising his dissertation and tried to support the same view at greater length in it.

To reconcile the matters that opposed this opinion, he distinguished eight stages in the history of the same codex, as though the collection had not been composed at one time but had subsequently been enlarged by several additions. Yet he could prove this by no codex and by no authority whatsoever. It had to be posited solely because of the prior assumption that this codex belonged to the Roman Church, and because there was no other way to answer the difficulties raised against it.

II. Thus all his labor is merely a heap of empty conjectures, which it will not be difficult to scatter. P. Coustantius, in the preface to Part II, section 3, of the first volume of the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, produced, with sound judgment and energy, 755 not a few arguments that sufficiently overturn Quesnellus’s effort. It will nevertheless be useful to add our own work, by building on his observations and adding further considerations, so that the falsity of the dissertation mentioned above may become more evident.

We shall first set forth the arguments from which it will be clear that this codex did not belong to the Roman Church. Then we shall subject Quesnellus’s arguments—or rather conjectures—to examination.

## CHAPTER I. It is proved that the codex edited by Quesnellus was not the codex of the Roman Church. It was a collection compiled by private effort in Gaul.

[Col. 0948C]

I. There are three principal points that prove that the collection published by Quesnellus was not a codex of the canons of the Roman Church, edited with that Church’s authority and received for its use.

1. It contains many things incompatible with the Roman Church.

2. It lacks a considerable number of things that would not have been omitted from the public codex of that Church.

3. It is infected by excessive confusion, unworthy of a Roman codex issued under the wisest pontiffs.

The first point is demonstrated by several considerations.

II. The translation of the Nicene canons presented in the Quesnellian collection is different from the interpretation that prevailed in the Roman Church. Two portions of the Council of Nicaea survive in the version received by that same Roman Church: namely, the Creed, which St. Leo inserted in Letter 165 to Emperor Leo, chapter 3; and the canon concerning the Cathari, recited by Innocent I in his letter to Rufus of Thessalonica and the other bishops of Macedonia, which is transcribed in our collection, chapter 22.

Compare both with the interpretation of our codex, and the difference between the versions will immediately be apparent. In the canon concerning the Cathari, however, the dissimilarity between the two interpretations will be still more evident, because it lies not so much in the wording as in the meaning—and specifically in a meaning which, in the version of the Quesnellian codex, presents a wholly erroneous discipline, especially abhorrent to the discipline and teaching of the Roman Church.

Concerning the clerics of the Cathari returning to the unity of the Church, who according to Innocent’s interpretation were to be received by the laying on of hands alone, the version of this codex states: “It pleased the holy council that they should be ordained, and thus remain in the clergy.”

When did the Roman Church ever customarily ordain again clerics who had been duly ordained in heresy or schism, when they were received back in their rank? Can it be believed that such a version, into which an error entered through the translator’s carelessness, was received by the Roman See and inserted into its public codex?

Although there is also some difficulty in the version presented by Innocent, as we explained at greater length in volume II, note 13 (col. 1491, note b), in the observations of Quesnellus on Letter 167, it nevertheless favors no doctrinal error.

Nor is Quesnellus’s answer, given in chapter 6, probable: namely, that when Innocent replied to the Macedonians, he wished either to write out or translate word for word the canon that had been brought forward from their letter—as though those Greeks had written to Innocent in Latin, or Innocent had rendered the canon from the Greek text into Latin in a new version that introduced an erroneous discipline while disregarding the discipline received in his own Church; and this even though the new version had nothing to do with the case, as Quesnellus himself admits in the same place.

“Either version,” he says, “equally supported Innocent’s case.” And if he feared, on the basis of the Roman version, that the Macedonians might—as he puts it—evade its authority and appeal to the source of the canon, namely the Greek text, he should have feared the same thing concerning the new version that the pontiff himself had composed.

The question with the Macedonians did not concern whether the ordination was valid or invalid. It concerned whether those ordained by Bonosus ought to be received into the clergy. The Macedonians asserted this on the authority of the Nicene canon, by which it was granted that the Cathari, or Novatians, should be received in their rank.

In denying this, Innocent recited the canon solely to show that the indulgence extended toward the Novatians had been granted for a particular reason and was not to be extended to other heretics or to the Bonosians. No new translation was needed for this purpose.

Therefore Innocent’s Roman version cannot be denied; 757 and consequently, the version in our collection, which differs so greatly from it, must be recognized as foreign to the codex believed to have been received in the Roman Church.

### III.

I would also like to consider Nicaean canon 11. Felix III wrote as follows in Letter 7 to the bishops established throughout the various provinces:

> “Concerning clerics and monks, or maidens dedicated to God, or laypeople, we prescribe that the following rule be observed which the Council of Nicaea established concerning those who have fallen or lapsed: namely, that those who, without any necessity, fear, or danger, impiously surrendered themselves to the heretics in order to be rebaptized, if nevertheless they repent from the heart, shall spend three years among the hearers, but for seven years shall remain among the penitents under the hands of the priests; for two further years they shall in no way be permitted to bring offerings, but shall associate in prayer only with the laypeople [Al. the populace].”

There seems to be no doubt that here the words of the Roman version of canon 11 were copied by the holy pontiff. They differ very greatly from the words of the interpretation inserted in Quesnell’s collection, where the same canon is expressed in chapter 17 as follows:

> “Concerning those who have transgressed without any necessity, without the confiscation of their patrimony, or without any danger, etc. If, therefore, some repent sincerely, let them be placed for three years among the hearers, provided that they are faithful, and for seven years among the penitents; but for two years let them participate outside communion in prayer alone with the people.”

Almost the same difference is also found in two other Nicaean canons, 13 and 14, mentioned by the same pontiff in the aforesaid letter, which are numbered 19 and 20 in the Quesnellian codex. Who, then, could believe that codex to be Roman, when the divergence in its version of the Nicaean canons is so great?

[Col. 0950A]

### IV.

Still much more alien to the Roman Codex—which, as Quesnell himself titles it, was in use under the pontiffs Innocent I, Zosimus, and Leo—are the canons of other synods inserted in our collection, since the Roman Church accepted down to the time of Leo only the Nicaean and Sardican canons joined together and entitled “Nicaean.”

We proved this more fully in the preceding Treatise, part II, chapter 1, where, among other matters, we rejected the opinion of those who maintain that the Greek canons of the ancient Councils of Ancyra, Neocaesarea, and Gangra were designated by the ancient Roman pontiffs under the name of Nicaean canons.

Still clearer are the facts demonstrating that the Constantinopolitan canons were not accepted in the Roman Church for a long time, or until the time of St. Gregory. Quesnell vainly attempts to remove this objection in chapter 2, where, imagining various stages in the history of his codex, he introduces the claim that these same canons were added to the codex after St. Gregory. Since this is supported by no reasoning whatever, it is recognized as a mere invention [Col. 0950B] devised to weaken the force of an unanswerable argument. Many other such devices occur in his distinction of these stages; they are brought forward for no other reason than to meet other difficulties. But who would trust mere arbitrary inventions and assert as a public codex of the Roman Church one that is refuted by the clearest arguments?

Quesnell himself says in Dissertation 11, section 6:

> “We have never read that Roman pontiffs, whether contemporary with Leo or earlier, cited any canons other than the Nicaean or Sardican canons regarded as Nicaean. Innocent I expressly says that no others ought to be received.”

Who, then, could present as the Roman Church’s codex one in which, besides the Nicaean and Sardican canons, the canons of other synods are also found received?

But he adds:

> “Nor were the decrees of particular synods, even if some of those synods had already been transferred into the Roman Codex, received as authoritative among most of the Churches of the western regions before the Council of Chalcedon.”

That is, they had been transferred into a public codex, but had not been received as authoritative, and therefore had never been cited by any Roman pontiff. Who can understand this? When a codex is published by public authority so that it may serve public use, the canons inserted in it acquire public authority. If no canons other than the Nicaean and Sardican had authority in the Roman Church, then they had not been inserted into a public codex, nor published with public authority.

How, then, is that Quesnellian codex said in the very title to have been in use in the Roman Church under Innocent I, Zosimus, and Leo, if the canons written in it had not been received as authoritative? Was something that was in use in the Roman Church not authoritative? Does Quesnell not contend in the preceding Dissertation 11, chapter 2 [759] around the middle, that promulgated decrees are regarded as binding, so that people are subject to them, when they are inserted in a public and received codex? Yet he presents his collection as a public and received codex.

Therefore, when by the words quoted above he declares that particular synods proposed in the same collection were not authoritative, he most plainly contradicts himself. How much better, then, shall we say that a collection in which the canons of synods not received by the Roman Church are written cannot be regarded as the public Roman Codex?

### V.

We shall briefly point out other features of this kind that are incompatible with such a codex. Who could believe that the Roman pontiffs received into their public codex the Breviary of the Synod of Hippo, drawn up at the Council of Carthage in the year 397, on the Ides of August, together with three foreign canons?

If Quesnell were to be believed, this same Breviary was inserted in the second chapter of the codex when the rise of the Pelagian heresy created a greater need for communication between the Roman and African Churches. But if, as he himself says, on this occasion the African discipline became better known to the Roman Church, and the leading men of the Roman clergy, judging it suited to their customs, wished to make it their own and a part of their codex, then it certainly became known through the African bishops Aurelius and Augustine, who on that very occasion chiefly sent letters to the Roman pontiffs.

The Breviary, therefore, having been received on this occasion from those who had either composed or confirmed it, could not have contained those three additional canons. This observation not only shows the improbability of Quesnell’s conjecture concerning the time at which he thinks this Breviary was added to the codex; it also proves it incredible that, if the Roman pontiffs had ever received the Breviary, they would have received and published it with public authority not in its genuine form but enlarged by foreign additions.

### VI.

It is much more incredible that they inserted twice into the same public codex the definition of the Council of Chalcedon: first in chapter 25 from one version, and then in chapter 54 from another, which Quesnell omitted but which we have produced in our edition from all the copies of this collection.

What shall we say about the manifest error visible in the heading prefixed to the rescript of Honorius in chapter 14? This rescript, signed on the day before the Kalends of May in the year 418, is said in its heading to have been issued after the acts of the aforesaid synod had been received; yet in the preceding chapter, 13, those acts are said to have been drawn up on the following day, the Kalends of May of that same year. Would the ancient Roman Church have inserted so great an error in a public codex? See what will be said more fully on this matter in the observations on Quesnell’s Dissertation 13, section 2.

Add the book of faith attributed to Augustine in chapter 40. We have shown in the notes on Quesnell’s observations on Letter 15 to Turibius, volume II, that this is nothing other than a rule of faith composed long after Augustine at a Spanish council held by order of Leo. Quesnell thinks that this book, together with three others, was added to the codex by St. Leo (Dissertation 14, § 8, no. 3). Is it believable that this pontiff did not know the author of the book in question, or that he wished to impose Augustine’s name upon it? The same would be true if some other ancient pontiff were believed to be the author of the codex.

Moreover, what are we to make of the fact that, among the many books of faith preserved in the apostolic archives, only four were transferred into the codex—and among these the book of Faustinus, who is certainly known to have been a schismatic? What shall we say about certain laws excerpted from the Theodosian Code? What about the rule of the *formatae* and other similar documents, which do not seem appropriate to a public codex published for the use of the Roman Church?

### VII.

The omissions in the same codex ought to be no less troubling. Among the Nicaean canons, the final canon concerning the omission of kneeling on Sundays and during the Paschal season is not found. Quesnell attributes this to the fact that it was contrary to the discipline of the Roman Church.

But that is exceedingly improbable. For how faithfully the Roman pontiffs observed all and each of the canons of the Council of Nicaea is clear from numerous testimonies, especially those of Leo. Resisting the effort of Anatolius of Constantinople, which was contrary to one Nicaean canon, Leo protested that he could not permit anything in those canons to be violated.

Thus, in Letter 105 to the Empress Pulcheria [Col. 0951D], chapter 2, he says:

> “Since no one is permitted to dare anything against the statutes of the fathers’ canons, which many ages ago were founded in the city of Nicaea by spiritual decrees, so that if anyone should wish to decree something different, he would rather diminish himself than corrupt them.”

See also Letter 106 to Anatolius himself, chapter 4, where he declares that the Nicaean laws will remain until the end, and says of the Nicaean Fathers:

> “Among us, and throughout the whole world, they will live in their constitutions; and if anything is presumed anywhere contrary to what they established, we cancel it without hesitation, so that what has been universally established for perpetual benefit may not be altered by any change.”

And in Letter 107 to Julian of Cos:

> “Since your affection has demonstrated by frequent proofs how I preserve the statutes of the holy Nicaean canons with a constant and firm purpose, we judge that all ecclesiastical rules are being dissolved if anything at all is violated from that most sacred constitution of the Fathers.”

Similar statements are found in Letter 119 to Maximus of Antioch, chapter 4:

> “If anything has been attempted by anyone in any synod against the Nicaean canons, or appears to have been extorted for a time, it can inflict no injury upon inviolable decrees; and it will be easier for the agreements of any sort of alliances to be dissolved than for the rules of the aforesaid canons to be corrupted in any respect.”

And in chapter 5:

> “For whatever disagrees with their rules and constitution can never obtain the consent of the apostolic see.”

We omit other statements of the same kind for the sake of brevity.

There can therefore be no doubt that the apostolic see consistently observed each of the Nicaean canons, including the one concerning the omission of kneeling on Sundays and during the Paschal season. Otherwise, if the Roman Church had rejected this one disciplinary canon, Leo the pontiff would have had no stronger reason for so severely reproaching the Fathers of Chalcedon, who in a very large council had reformed another disciplinary canon. Nor could he have professed the observance of himself and his Church in such general and solemn formulas.

[Col. 0952A]

### VIII.

The witnesses produced by Quesnell in Dissertation 5, section 5, sufficiently prove that this discipline prevailed not so much in the East as in the West. Other testimonies could likewise be brought from other Fathers, some of which are so general that they declare the same discipline to have been observed throughout the whole Church.

St. Hilary, in the prologue to the Book of Psalms, no. 12, says:

> “These Sabbaths of Sabbaths were celebrated by the apostles with such religious observance that during these days of Pentecost no one worships with his body prostrate on the ground.”

Since no one is excepted in this and similar testimonies, the Roman Church certainly cannot be excluded.

We shall add one sufficiently well-established testimony from St. Augustine. Since he spent some time at Rome and wrote several books there, as is clear from Book II of the *Retractations*, chapters 7 and 10, he acquired knowledge of Roman rites, some of which he repeatedly mentions in Letter 36 to Casulanus.

In Letter 55 to Januarius, after stating generally in section 28 that during the Paschal days “we pray standing,” he adds in section 31:

> “But whether we pray standing on those days and on all Sundays everywhere, I do not know.”

Since from what has been said he could not have been ignorant of what the Roman Church observed in this matter, and since he remained there for at least some Sundays, it is certain that he found the aforesaid discipline in that Church.

The testimony of St. Jerome in *Against the Luciferians*, no. 8, is no less forceful:

> “Even if the authority of Scripture were lacking, the agreement of the whole world on this point would have the force of a command. For many other practices observed by tradition in the Churches have claimed for themselves the authority of written law: for example, immersing the head three times in the font; afterward, for the symbolic meaning of infancy, tasting milk and honey as a sign of harmony; not worshiping on one’s knees on Sunday and throughout Pentecost; and breaking the fast. Many other things are not written in the divine books, yet a reasonable observance has claimed them for itself.”

Before writing these words, this holy teacher had also lived at Rome and been educated through study there. Since he visited the tombs of the apostles and martyrs on Sundays, he could not have been ignorant of the discipline of standing or kneeling observed in that city.

But if he had discovered that, in this chief Church of the whole world, people knelt on the days mentioned, he could not have included among the examples of practices observed in the Churches by the agreement of the whole world the practice that on Sunday and throughout Pentecost worship was not performed on one’s knees.

Let it be granted that this general testimony of Jerome might not include some Church unknown to him; it certainly embraces, above all, the Roman Church, which was known to him. See note 12 (above, col. 930, note c) in chapter 5 of the preceding dissertation, where we applied Quesnell’s own words to this matter.

If no particular and explicit witness concerning this ancient discipline of the same Church is available, this happened because no one who wrote about this rite among the Romans has come down to us. It is enough that no one testifies to the contrary for that Church to be regarded as included in the general testimonies.

Nor can it be made credible by anything except the clearest arguments that the Church which professed such great observance of the Nicaean canons departed in this matter from the custom of all the other Churches and from the Nicaean constitution, and erased from its copies of the Nicaean synod the canon concerning kneeling. See note 5 (above, col. 928, note e) in chapter 5 of Quesnell’s dissertation, where we proposed another observation relevant to this matter.

[Col. 0953A]

### IX.

Quesnell presses the absence of the canon concerning the omission of kneeling not only in his collection but also in Rufinus’s abridgment. But since the same canon is absent from another very ancient interpretation, which we published in this volume from Vatican manuscript Regina 1997, it becomes clear that this omission does not derive from the Roman version, but from certain defective Greek copies, from which both Rufinus compiled his abridgment and the aforesaid interpretation was derived.

The author of the Quesnellian collection followed these copies in some places, especially in omitting this canon [Note: [Col. 0953] See note 3 in chapter 5 of the preceding dissertation (col. 927, note a).], as we observed in the notes on chapter 1 of his collection.

This omission, however, cannot be presumed in the Greek original that was transmitted to the Roman Church from the Council of Nicaea itself, from which a translation was immediately prepared, received by that Church, and carefully preserved. Consequently, the absence of this same canon from Quesnell’s collection provides ever stronger confirmation that it was not the codex of that Church.

### X.

What, moreover, shall be said about the more important constitutions of the Roman bishops omitted from the same collection—constitutions that above all ought to have been inserted if the pontiffs themselves had published a public codex from the Roman archives, where all such documents were preserved with the greatest care?

To avoid burdening readers with many examples, let us consider only the apostolic letters concerning the Pelagians, which the author of the collection chiefly presents. Among the constitutions issued in this cause, the most celebrated is undoubtedly Zosimus’s *Tractoria*, by which the Pelagian heresy was cut off throughout the whole world. The Roman pontiffs would certainly have given this document pride of place if they had gathered monuments of this kind into a public codex.

Yet it is absent from the aforesaid collection, just as many other notable constitutions are absent—constitutions that were either discovered and inserted by other collectors or mentioned by certain ancient writers but perished through the injustice of time. They certainly would not have perished if the public Roman Codex of that period had been composed and had come down to us.

How many outstanding documents of the Roman Church have been preserved for us by the Avellana collection, once compiled at Rome from the apostolic archives, even though its author possessed neither public authority nor the intention of producing a codex for public use? How many more would have been supplied by a codex promulgated with public authority for public use?

Quesnell’s response, based on the codex of Dionysius, is not satisfactory; that codex lacks the statutes of the apostolic see older than Siricius, as well as quite a number of later documents. Dionysius published his collection not with public but with private authority, and could not have consulted the apostolic archives exactly.

But anyone who published a codex with public authority and for public use, searching through the apostolic archive, would certainly not have omitted the more important constitutions, especially useful for practical purposes, which were certainly not lacking at that time.

### XI.

Above all, the extraordinary confusion found in our collection is unbecoming to a public Roman Codex published in the fifth century. No order is preserved in it, either of subject matter or of chronology. As Quesnell himself noted in chapter 4, section 1, the decrees of councils are mixed with the decrees of pontiffs; nor are they arranged according to their chronological order, but later documents are placed before earlier ones, and local matters before ecumenical ones.

If anyone considers the other surviving public books of the Roman Church—the sacramentaries, antiphonaries, and so forth—he will find an appropriate order in all of them. Since in the fifth century, when this codex is believed to have been arranged and published, very wise pontiffs [Col. 0954A] and other learned men flourished at Rome, there is no doubt that if they had prepared a collection of canons and constitutions for public use, they would have given us an excellent codex, with its documents arranged in proper order.

It is therefore astonishing that Quesnell inferred from this confusion—which is especially contrary to the Roman Church of that period—that the codex was Roman. “The very confusion,” he says in chapter 4, section 1, “which offended a certain Laurence and impelled Dionysius Exiguus to forge a new one, cries out that the codex is Roman.”

Nor does the testimony to which he appeals in these words, from Dionysius’s letter to Stephen, support this opinion in any way. Dionysius does not speak of a public codex of the Roman Church, nor of confusion among the documents in it. He speaks of an ancient translation of the Greek canons, which circulated especially in Italian codices; its confusion offended Laurence, a Roman presbyter, and impelled Dionysius to labor over a new interpretation of those same canons.

These are Dionysius’s words:

> “Although our dearest brother Laurence compelled our smallness, by constant and familiar exhortation, to translate the ecclesiastical rules, I believe that he was offended by the confusion of the ancient translation, etc.”

This ancient translation, as we conjectured in the *Treatise on Collections*, part II, chapter 2, § 3, seems to be the one we published after Justellus in this volume. Even if it was perhaps more common in certain Roman codices, those codices are not thereby said to have been public codices of the canons, or codices published with the authority of the Roman Church and received for public use.

Nor, even if they had been of this kind, would they necessarily have been identical with our collection, in which, apart from the Chalcedonian canons, no canons of the Greek synods appear to have been inserted from the ancient version.

Moreover, what Quesnell adds in the same place to defend the confusion of the codex in some fashion is as follows:

> “This confusion rests upon its own rationale, nor is the disorder of the order itself without order; it depends upon the hypothesis established in chapter 2, according to which this codex was not composed at one time but enlarged at different periods.”

But this hypothesis, as we observed shortly before, is a mere invention—or rather a contrivance devised to evade several difficulties—which, being supported by no reasoning, can convince no one.

### XII.

But to return to the confusion of our collection: if anyone carefully weighs each detail and embraces the whole at a single glance, he will find it so great that it is suited not merely to no public codex of the Roman Church, but to no public codex of any Church that was preparing to publish one. Rather, it is suited only to a private individual who, in his first efforts and private study, collected at will whatever he found—now this, now that—with no order and no selection.

The other defects noted above are likewise not unbecoming to such a person, just as similar defects commonly occur in other ancient private collections. Therefore, just as no collections of this kind are codices published with public authority, neither is our collection.

### XIII.

Finally, we shall add another observation. It will make it highly probable that this collection was arranged not at Rome, indeed not even in Italy, but in Gaul; and it will thereby provide considerable confirmation that it cannot be regarded as a codex of the Roman Church.

Although we have devoted the greatest diligence to searching out manuscript copies of this collection, we have not been able to find a single one either at Rome or throughout Italy, while several occur here and there in Gaul. We use “Gaul” in the ancient sense, insofar as it included Narbonensis, Aquitania, Lugdunensis, and Belgica.

Crabbus was the first to use a Ghent codex. Alanus Copus, Pamelius, and Henricus Gravius used the Arras codex. The Thuaneus, Trecopithaeanus, Bellovacensis, Hubertinus of Saint-Vaast, and others of this kind are found in Gallican libraries. The same must be said of the two codices of the Imperial Library at Vienna, into which several manuscript copies were brought from Belgium.

Does not the great number of manuscripts preserved even in our own time only in Gaul establish the Gallican origin of this collection? Add that certain documents of this collection could nowhere be found in Italian collections, but only in Gallican ones.

Thus, for example, the Council of Telus—or, more correctly, of Zell—has been found only in Gallican codices, as we noted in note 2 (col. 724, note m) on chapter 62 of our collection. The Ancyrene canons, corrected according to Western discipline, are also found apart from our collection in the Corbie codex, which contains another very ancient Gallican collection praised by Father Coustant.

The ancient Italian collections—Vatican Regina 1997, Lucca 88, and Barberini 2888—which would certainly have received the same corrections if they had been promulgated in the public Codex of the Roman Church, present the same canons without any correction. See, then, whether our collection can be regarded as Roman, when these characteristics show it to be Gallican.

From this it is clear that this collection was used only by Gallican authors. Pseudo-Isidore, whom we have shown to have composed his collection in Gaul, excerpted many things from this same collection. See the *Treatise on Collections*, part III.

Eneas of Paris, in his book *Against the Greeks* in volume I of the *Spicilegium* of d’Achery, where nothing Isidorian appears, copied several testimonies from our codex. For he not only recites in chapter 187 a long fragment of the preface prefixed to the Council of Nicaea, but also reports in chapters 195 and following several passages from the Acacian documents, with the same readings and in the same order in which they are written in this codex.

We have found no one outside Gaul who has offered even the slightest indication of this same codex.

## CHAPTER II  
### The arguments brought forward by Quesnell in chapter 4 in support of the Roman Codex are refuted

We must now examine the arguments by which Quesnell attempts to establish his opinion; their weakness will itself increasingly confirm our own.

### I.

We sufficiently weakened the first argument, drawn from Dionysius Exiguus, in the preceding chapter, section 11. For he is not speaking of an earlier codex of the canons and constitutions of the apostolic see that was public and received for use at Rome, but of an ancient translation of the Greek canons, which differs most sharply from our collection.

The confusion of this collection, which he could not deny, ought to have warned him not to attribute it to a public Roman book, as we observed there.

In any case, if it is permissible to argue from Dionysius, we shall briefly indicate two points, with Father Coustant, against Quesnell.

First, if our codex had been published with the public authority of the Roman pontiffs, as he thinks, and had been received for use, Dionysius would not so readily, in response to private requests at Rome, have considered changing it and substituting another codex in its place. Nor, if he undertook this for the convenience of learned men, would he ever have allowed himself to leave no place in his own work for what had been received in the public Roman Codex.

Yet his codex omits the synods of Carthage and Milevis, as well as the letters of the five African bishops to Innocent and Innocent’s replies to those synods and African bishops; it also omits the writings of Simplicius, Felix, and others, which you will find in our collection.

Second, although Dionysius composed his codex with private authority, his interpretation was soon received by many, to such an extent that, as Cassiodorus testifies in *On Divine Reading*, chapter 23, the Roman Church embraced it with the greatest currency.

How could a public codex of rules, published and confirmed by apostolic authority, and in a certain sense consecrated by its antiquity, have so quickly and easily fallen into disuse? Is this not rather a clear indication that no public codex was published and received at Rome?

### II.

Quesnell’s second argument, by which he contends that the preface of the codex declares it to have been composed for the use of the Roman Church, is entirely extraordinary.

For in the words that he quotes from the preface itself, nothing is said about a Roman Codex. The mere mention of the Roman Church, which embraces and venerates the Nicaean faith, and which received and confirmed the Nicaean rules of faith—that is, the rules appended to the Nicaean creed—together with other statements of the same kind—could these not also have been written by a non-Roman and private collector, so that no public Roman Codex can be inferred from them?

Furthermore, when these words are read in the decree of Gelasius concerning apocryphal writings, they imply nothing other than that, in composing the preface, the collector copied the words of Gelasius, just as in the rest of the preface’s text he did not hesitate to excerpt a long fragment from Rufinus’s history.

Was it worthy of Roman dignity to construct the preface of a public codex out of the words of others?

Since that preface speaks only of the Council of Nicaea, and since the words quoted by Quesnell refer to the Nicaean faith and rules, just as they refer to them in Gelasius, from whom they were taken, if that preface was placed before this codex by the collector when he transferred the Nicaean canons into the codex, then the Nicaean canons themselves must be said to have been the first items of this collection entered into the codex after Gelasius’s decree. Thus even the first stage of its history, as Quesnell imagines it—presenting only the Nicaean canons together with the Sardican—would not belong to Innocent I.

### III.

The third proof, drawn from the cited decree of Gelasius, is easily dismissed. For Quesnell assumes, without having proved it, that Gelasius copied entire periods from the preface of the codex, rather than that the author of the preface and collection copied from Gelasius’s decree.

This pontiff, the author of so many celebrated and lucid constitutions, was not so deficient in writing that he needed the words and thoughts of others, nor would he have feared to publish them under his own name after incorporating them into a solemn treatise.

Just as the unknown writer of the preface was not ashamed to transcribe several passages from Rufinus word for word, so he was not ashamed to excerpt certain other passages from the Gelasian decree.

### IV.

The fourth argument is drawn from the sixth Nicaean canon, which was recited by Paschasinus, legate of the apostolic see, in the Council of Chalcedon, action 16, with the same reading in which it is written in our collection. This argument falters on several grounds.

First, if the same canon with the same reading is found inserted in other Latin collections that certainly were not codices of the Roman Church, will not the whole argument collapse? Collections of this kind are found in the Fossatensis manuscript, in another belonging to Claudius Hardy, in the Pithoeanus, in Vatican Regina 1997, and in other codices. Although these did not belong to the Roman Church, they nevertheless present the same canon with Paschasinus’s reading.

Second, the number of the canon, which Paschasinus calls the sixth, cannot have been taken from our codex, in which it is reckoned as the tenth. Rather, he should be said to have recited it from the Hardy or Fossat manuscript, in which not only the words but also the number of the canon agree with Paschasinus.

And if those codices cannot for that reason be called codices of the Roman Church, our codex can much less be considered Roman: although it agrees with Paschasinus in the wording of that canon, it differs from him in its number.

The conjectures Quesnell offers to evade this argument are mere guesses. They cannot have any place unless it has first been established with certainty that Paschasinus recited the canon from our codex.

Third, it is not certain that Paschasinus read that canon from a Roman copy; nor is it certain that Roman copies of the Council of Nicaea presented the same reading and version that Paschasinus used, as we observed in the *Treatise on Collections*, part II, chapter 2, § 1, no. 5.

Finally, we seem to have demonstrated by several considerations that the author of our codex had before his eyes the version of the Nicaean canons contained in Vatican manuscript Regina 1997, and that he copied from it the canon in question with exactly the same words and number. See the notes on chapter 1 of our collection.

Now the Vatican Regina codex was certainly not Roman, nor does it contain the Roman interpretation of the Council of Nicaea, as was shown in the cited passage of the *Treatise*. Who, then, could infer from a canon taken from a non-Roman version that our codex was Roman?

### V.

Nor is Quesnell’s fifth proof any stronger. It rests on a parenthesis inserted, as he thinks, in favor of the Roman see in Innocent’s letter to Victricius:

> “Whose [the Roman Church’s] reverence must be preserved in all matters.”

Since this parenthesis is absent from Dionysius’s codex and from the ancient Sangermanensis copy, he says that anyone could readily be led to believe that it was added by the authors of the Roman Codex, who thought they were exercising their right when they added something to a letter of a Roman pontiff that would contribute to its elucidation.

The weakness of this conjecture, by which he casts suspicion on the Romans for making freer additions, is clear for two reasons.

First, it is false that this parenthesis is found in the genuine copies of our collection. Indeed, it was inserted by a later hand in one more recent and less accurate Oxford codex; for this reason Quesnell himself removed it from his edition as foreign to this collection.

Second, the same parenthesis is found in six other ancient collections that are not Roman. See note 18 (col. 521, note d) on chapter 24 of our collection, where the letter itself is reproduced.

Thus this parenthesis is so ineffectual for establishing the codex as belonging to the Roman Church that it is also found in other non-Roman codices and collections.

But if this parenthesis did exist in genuinely Roman copies, as it is found especially in ancient Italian collections that we identified in the annotation mentioned above, then, since the genuine copies of our collection do not know it, this very omission clearly reveals that the collection does not contain the Roman Codex.

### VI.

Canon 28 of the Council of Chalcedon, by which a prerogative was established for the see of Constantinople, is absent no less from our collection than from the Dionysian, Prisca, Isidorian, and other collections. It is likewise absent from the Greek text of the canons themselves.

For it belongs to another action, from which certain later Greeks, excerpting it, added it to the other canons, which had been published in a different action. In the same way, two other canons from other actions of the same council were excerpted by those Greeks and added to the canons.

Who, then, could infer from this that our collection is a Roman Codex, when the same feature is common to so many other non-Roman collections?

### VII.

Although the Roman Church possessed the Nicaean and Sardican canons joined together and entitled “Nicaean,” its codices were not the only ones to present this conjunction and form.

See on this matter the *Treatise on Collections*, part II, chapter 1, where we listed many other codices of other collections. From this, the entire force of Quesnell’s seventh argument, proposed at greater length in support of the Roman Codex, will plainly vanish.

### VIII. From the Antiochene and Constantinopolitan canons, which Quesnellus admits were rejected by the Roman Church until the pontificate of St. Gregory, he extracted a truly remarkable argument for establishing a code belonging to that same Church, on the ground that, since they lie—as he supposes—at the end of the code, they must have been added after a long interval; for, he says, this is found in no other code. In other collections, that is, they are found inserted in their proper place, not added at the end. But this argument too rests upon that gratuitous hypothesis, sufficiently discussed in the preceding chapter: namely, that this code was not assembled all at once, but subsequently received several additions in stages [Col. 0958A].

Moreover, it is false that the Antiochene and Constantinopolitan canons are written at the end of the code, since they are cited in chapters 59 and 61, whereas the code continues to chapter 98. Can all the letters of St. Leo, then, which were written somewhat later than the Constantinopolitan canons and which we have seen from several and more distinguished copies to belong to our collection [Note: [Col. 0957] Compare note 2 on chapter 67 of our collection (Col. 743, no. a).], be said to have been excluded from the Roman Code and added after Gregory the Great? The true explanation of this order—or rather of this confusion—is to be referred to the compiler of the collection, who inserted now this material and now that, as he pleased or as items came into his hands.

Furthermore, just as these same canons, although not received by the Roman Church, were found in the collection of Dionysius and in other ancient collections, so they could also have been included in ours, provided that neither the collection of Dionysius nor the other collections be judged an ancient and public code of the Roman Church. The testimonies of St. Gregory which we cited in the Treatise prove that the Constantinopolitan canons were present in canonical collections. When he denies that they were received by the Roman Church, he indicates that those codes had not been approved by public authority.

### IX. What Quesnellus further adduces in no. 10 concerning certain canons of local councils adapted to Roman or Western discipline concerns the tenth canon of Ancyra—eleventh in our collection. It states that, if deacons who at their ordination declared that they could not remain continent were nevertheless ordained, and later married, they should be permitted to remain in the ministry. In our collection this was emended to read that they should remain only in the clergy and be removed from the ministry.

But the strongest proof that nothing should be inferred from this emendation in support of establishing a public code of the Roman Church is that the same canon, equally emended, is found in the celebrated Corbie collection praised by P. Coustant, although that collection was neither a collection of the Roman Church nor a public code. For there, according to the same Coustant in the preface to volume I of *The Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, no. 67, it reads:

> “Any deacons who are ordained, if at the ordination itself they protested, saying that they wished to have wives and could not remain continent, and afterward entered into marriage, let them remain in the clergy only.”

In our collection the words “and let them be removed from the ministry” are added, clearly for greater explicitness.

In his notes on the canons of Gangra, Quesnellus also introduces the fourth canon of that synod, in which it was decreed:

> “If anyone separates himself from a married presbyter, as though on account of his marriage he ought not to offer, and for that reason abstains from his offering, let him be anathema.”

He declares that this canon was omitted from our collection because the Roman Church did not receive it, lest the same canon, understood as referring not so much to a married presbyter as to one making use of marital rights, should mislead the unwary. But for this same reason the words in the synodical letter of that council condemning those who maintained that presbyters who had contracted marriages ought to be despised and that one ought not to partake of the sacraments they confected should also have been deleted.

If, however, these words [Col. 0958D], to which the fourth canon refers, were not expunged, then the canon must be acknowledged to have been omitted not for the stated reason but through the compiler’s carelessness and omission. Moreover, it was foreign to the custom of the Roman Church to alter or omit the words of canons. Thus, in the Dionysian collection, which Pope Hadrian I later gave to Charlemagne, nothing was emended or omitted either in the Ancyrene canons or in those of Gangra. He would certainly have done so if he had found in an ancient code of the Roman Church one canon corrected among the Ancyrene canons and another deleted among those of Gangra.

### X. No less arbitrary are Quesnellus’s further claims concerning Martin of Braga, as though, in restoring the Ancyrene canon to Western discipline, he had followed the Code of the canons of the Roman Church.

For Martin himself—although a Pannonian, he had spent some time in the East and learned the Greek language—consulted Greek, not Latin, copies of the Greek canons when preparing his compilation. This is sufficiently clear from his letter to the bishop and council of Lugo. For, without carefully collating the Greek original of those same canons, he could not have accomplished what he says he did: namely, “to restore more simply and more correctly what had been expressed obscurely by translators and altered by scribes.”

Hence his wording in the Greek canons he presented agrees with no translation, nor with the Isidorian version, which was especially prevalent in Spain. Since he had not undertaken to provide a complete interpretation of those canons, but rather to present, in a new and more concise and accessible order, certain selected chapters which he judged more useful for the churches of Spain, he thought that the Ancyrene canon should be adapted to the discipline of those churches.

Even if he had perhaps had some copy of our collection before his eyes, it would not follow that this was the code of the Roman Church. For some copy of this Gallican collection, as we have seen, could have been transferred from Gaul—where such codes were still abundant—to Spain and could have come into the hands of Martin of Braga.

### XI. In the chapters on grace and free will, which we proved in volume II, in our observations on his third dissertation, were wrongly attributed by Quesnellus to our Leo, not only are three decrees of the African synod of 418 cited, but authorities from the letters of the Roman pontiffs against the Pelagians are also cited.

Since Quesnellus supposes that the author of those chapters excerpted these materials from the Code of the canons of the Roman Church, in which both the aforementioned African decrees and the cited Roman letters were contained, and since he observes that such documents are found neither in the Justellian collection nor in any other code of canons, he thinks that this demonstrates that the code was the code of the Roman Church because it is found in ours.

Unless we are mistaken, this is the force of his argument, although Quesnellus does not present it very clearly in no. 11. But since those documents were exceedingly well known because of the prominence of the Pelagian controversy, there is no reason why the testimonies used by the author of the chapters should be thought to have been excerpted from a public code rather than from copies in general circulation.

Furthermore, even if they had to be said to have been taken from a code of canons, since our collection does not contain two letters—one, Zosimus’s general letter to the bishops of the whole world, and the other, the Africans’ letter to that same pontiff—from which several authorities inserted in those chapters were taken, the code from which the author of the chapters drew would rather have been different from ours.

Moreover, when this author cites the canons of the Carthaginian synod, he calls them the third, fourth, and fifth chapters, whereas in our code they are canons four, five, and six. This different numbering [Col. 0960A] therefore confirms that the same author used a code different from ours.

### XII. The twelfth argument, in which we exposed Quesnellus’s contradiction in note 21 on chapter 4, is so weak that it needs no refutation. Collections older than Dionysius end with Gelasius; they are not for that reason regarded as codes of the Roman Church.

### XIII. Finally, what is adduced from Gelasius’s own treatise, where it is stated that the order of the sees follows the ancient statutes of the forefathers, and that the honor judged most ancient by the invincible and singular judgment of the 318 Fathers was granted to the first and most blessed see of Peter, proves nothing for our code.

The order of the principal sees had already been sufficiently established at the Council of Nicaea, when their prerogatives were confirmed according to ancient custom in canon 6. St. Leo therefore cited this canon when he refused to approve the Chalcedonian constitution by which the bishop of Constantinople was assigned the second place, because it conflicted with the Nicene decree.

Why, then, does Quesnellus thrust forward the preface of our code, as though Gelasius, in the words cited, had referred to the order of the sees presented in that very preface? This is especially unwarranted since this portion of the preface had been copied from another document of Gelasius, as we saw in no. 3.

As for the statement that the honor of the first see was established by the Nicene Fathers, even if it perhaps refers to the version adopted by the compiler of our collection, in which primacy is expressly asserted for that see, it still does not follow that Gelasius used this collection, since the same version is contained in other collections and codes. See chapter 1, no. 4.

What if Gelasius could have drawn the same statement from another version of the Nicene canons—for example, from the *Prisca*, in which the primacy of the Roman see is openly asserted in canon 6 in these words:

> “It is an ancient custom that the bishop of the city of Rome should have primacy.”

Finally, those passages of Gelasius’s treatise in which that ancient and venerable reverence is attributed to the Roman see, by which the dignity of all priests has always been strengthened and confirmed, seem certainly to refer to the Sardican canon, which decreed that, in episcopal cases, responsibility for determining a second judgment should be entrusted to the Roman bishop out of reverence for St. Peter.

But the Sardican canons, joined to the Nicene canons and bearing the title of the Nicene canons, were found not only in Quesnellus’s collection but in many others as well. Nothing, therefore, can be established from this in favor of that collection.

You will find the remaining matters in the preceding dissertation that deserve some relevant comment examined in the notes that follow. Since, therefore, none of what Quesnellus has assembled in support of a Roman Code proves his case, whereas the arguments we brought in the preceding chapter for rejecting that claim are strongly compelling, nothing more is needed to refute and entirely dislodge his opinion.

## THIRTEENTH DISSERTATION

### On the African councils held in the Pelagian controversy from the death of Pope Innocent I until Zosimus’s judgment against the same men

Concerning especially their number, order, and date; also concerning the number of canons of the African council on Grace; and concerning the origin and authors of the first constitution of the emperor Honorius against the Pelagians.

To chapters XIII and XIV of the Code of the canons and constitutions of the Roman Church.

[Col. 0959]

### [Col. 0959D] 777 I. The occasion of this dissertation

Some person may argue against the authenticity of the code and against its asserted use by us in the Roman Church from the heading of the constitution of the emperor Honorius, issued on the day before the Kalends of May in the year 418, which begins, “For disturbing …,” and occurs in chapter 14.

The heading is given in the following form in the Oxford codex:

> “Here begins the sacred rescript issued after receiving the acts of the aforesaid synod.”

The Thuaneus codex offers almost exactly the same text, except that it reads *SStae*—that is, “of the superscribed synod”—in place of *supradictae*, “of the aforesaid synod.”

Salmasius, who used the latter codex, immediately interpreted the synod as the Carthaginian synod designated by the two letters. He had no need to guess, since it was perfectly clear that the author of the heading had in mind no other synod than the plenary council held at Carthage, where eight or nine decrees against the Pelagians had been enacted, and these are indeed included in the immediately preceding chapter.

From this heading Salmasius concludes in *Eucharisticus, On the Suburban Churches*, part II, chapter 1, and Usserius, following Salmasius, concludes in *On the Antiquities of the British Churches*, chapter 10, that Honorius’s edict was issued after receiving the acts—or the eight decrees—of the Carthaginian synod.

But, say the recent learned historians of the Pelagian controversy, Henry Noris and Jean Garnier, since the edict preceded by at least one day that plenary synod which the same code assigns to the Kalends of May, how could Honorius have awaited its acts from Africa in order to issue his constitution? Such a serious blunder, they add, seems not to indicate a code established with the authority of the Roman—that is, the most learned—Church, but rather the work of a cruder and less knowledgeable compiler.

### II. The authority of headings prefixed to chapters is not equal to that of the chapters themselves

This is certainly a difficult knot, but I think I can untie it in several ways. First, we need not assign the same antiquity or authority to the headings and inscriptions of canons or papal decrees as to the canons and decrees themselves [Note: [Col. 0961D] See the observations to follow, no. 3.].

The latter were entered into the code after the matter had been prudently and maturely considered, with authority and for the use of the Roman Church. But who would rashly assert that the headings were added through the work of some private individual, or even composed through the industry of a more recent scholar?

Accordingly, many headings are read in the Thuaneus codex that do not appear in the Oxford codex, as can be seen in the Ancyrene, Neocaesarean, and Gangran canons, among others, each of which has its own synopsis prefixed to it.

Indeed, we have already observed some discrepancy in the heading of the Carthaginian synod in the very title under examination. I therefore think it should be easy to persuade an impartial reader that nothing can be decided against the authenticity of the code itself on the basis of certain errors in its headings.

### III. Chronological synopsis of the proceedings against the Pelagians

Although the foregoing response sufficiently answers the objection in defense of the authenticity of our code, nevertheless, since we have once touched upon the question of Honorius’s constitution and the Carthaginian synod after whose acts it is said to have been issued by the emperor [Col. 0961C] 779, it is worthwhile to investigate both matters more carefully and to bring into clearer light a particularly obscure and important part of Pelagian history.

For greater clarity, a chronological synopsis must be set forth of the events that took place both in Italy and in Africa against the Pelagian heresy, beginning with the time of the twin African synods whose reports, sent to Pope Innocent, first brought the Pelagian case before the apostolic see.

Although Caelestius, condemned at the Carthaginian synod as early as the year [Note: [Col. 0961D] This synod was held not in 412 but in 411, as we shall prove in the observations, no. 5.] 412, thought that he should appeal from the judgment of the African bishops to the examination of the Roman bishop, as Marius Mercator states in chapter 1 of the *Commonitorium*, he soon disregarded that appeal and went to Ephesus, a city of Asia, where he dared, by underhanded means, to seek admission to the presbyterate [Col. 0962A].

Thus, in 416, Caelestius was again brought before the Carthaginian synod together with Pelagius, after Orosius had sent letters from Heros and Lazarus, bishops of Gaul. A sentence of condemnation was issued against both, and the bishops unanimously judged that the authors of such a persuasion ought to be anathematized unless they openly anathematized it themselves (*Letter of the Carthaginian Council to Innocent*).

The Fathers then decided that the acts of the synod should be reported to Innocent, bishop of Rome:

> “So that the authority of the apostolic see may be added to the decisions of our mediocrity, for the protection of the salvation of many and also for the correction of certain persons’ perversity.”

The bishops of Numidia, assembled in the city of Milevis in the same year, issued a similar judgment against the same men, and the reports of both synods were transmitted together to the Roman see.

### IV. The letter of five bishops to Pope Innocent was not synodical

Not long afterward, five bishops selected from the two synods sent an even longer letter to Innocent—not from a synod, as Garnier supposes, but from a private conference. Hence everywhere, both in printed editions [Col. 0962B] 780 and in manuscript codices, it is entitled “the familiar letter.”

Nor does the authority of Marius Mercator compel us to call it synodical. Although he speaks of three councils, he joins the earlier Carthaginian council of 412 to the other two African councils of 416. For although the earlier synod did not send a report to Innocent, its acts were sent to him by the later Carthaginian synod, as is perfectly clear in both synodical letters.

The Carthaginian letter says:

> “Hence it came about that we thought it necessary to review what had been debated here before the Church of Carthage nearly five years ago concerning the name of Caelestius. When this had been read, as Your Holiness will be able to observe from what follows, although the judgment was manifest,” and so forth.

The Milevitan letter says:

> “Concerning what was done about Caelestius a few years ago, Your Holiness is better informed by the Church of Carthage.”
