When Augustine himself lists three letters, both elsewhere and in letter 47 to Valentinus, he most distinctly asserts that the first was written concerning the council of Carthage, the second concerning the council of Numidia, and the third by five bishops. He would not have omitted the place and name of the synod from which the third had been sent, if that had been the case.

And in letter 106 to Paulinus he says:

> “We also wrote to Pope Innocent of blessed memory, besides the reports of the councils, familiar letters.”

What could be clearer? It is of great importance that familiar letters not be taken for synodical letters, or synodical letters for familiar ones, if attention is paid to what Rusticus, a deacon of the Roman Church, writes in his dialogue against the Acephali:

> “The Church of God does not attend to familiar writings, nor to hypomnestic letters, nor to those made for one person and for private purposes, but to those that are written to or by synods, dogmatically, publicly, and definitively, concerning matters under dispute.”

[Note: [Col. 0961D] Does Quesnellus intend to suggest, on the basis of this testimony of Rusticus, that the letter of the five African bishops—which Augustine called “familiar” in that significant sense, indicating that it was not written by a synod or in the name of a synod—was to be regarded, despite the authority of those five eminent bishops who sent it to the Roman pontiff, as equivalent to privately written hypomnestic letters, of which Rusticus is speaking in that passage against the Acephali? Rusticus was dealing there with certain hypomnestic letters of St. Cyril, in which Cyril was reportedly said to have indicated that he had written condescendingly to the Easterners for the sake of peace. Rusticus replies that it is not certain whether those letters, even if believed genuine, were written dispensationally and condescendingly, especially since Cyril knew that “the Church of God does not attend to familiar writings,” and so forth, as above. By those words alone Rusticus intended to deprive letters written by Cyril not definitively but economically and privately of the authority due to letters publicly, definitively, and dogmatically composed, such as those that had been written concerning peace. Hence, immediately after the words quoted, he adds: “But this is clear, because, when transmitting these letters—that is, his own and those of the Easterners concerning peace—to the see of the Roman Church, he took great care that they should be confirmed by the most holy Sixtus. But concerning those which you call [hypomnestic letters], he made nothing manifest to the first apostolic see.” Since, therefore, the letter of the five bishops of Africa was sent to the apostolic see just as the synodical letters were sent to it, in order that Catholic doctrine against the Pelagian heresy might be confirmed, it must, by Rusticus’s principles, be regarded as possessing the highest authority.]

He explains the reasons for writing the letter: the pontiff had to be warned that there were some people in Rome who favored Pelagius for various reasons, which they had heard after the synodical letters had been written [Col. 0963A] 781; that the matter did not concern Pelagius alone, lest, if he were corrected, Innocent should spare his doctrines; and that Pelagius was fraudulently concealing his poison under the name of grace.

The pontiff was also to receive the book of Pelagius obtained by James and Timasius, together with Augustine’s response, the corrective letter written to Pelagius himself, and other documents relating to the case, which had not been at hand when the synodical letters were sent.

[Note: [Col. 0963D] These statements are gratuitous. It is not certain whether the letter of the five bishops was written to Innocent for that reason—because they had subsequently heard about certain Romans deceived by Pelagius—or for another reason, perhaps to avoid making those deceived Romans appear to be openly criticized in the synodical letters that were to be read at the Roman council. Certainly, it is incredible that, at the time of the African synods held under Innocent concerning the Pelagian heresy, there was not at hand either Pelagius’s book, which Augustine had received from James and Timasius, or the response which the same saint had written against that book in the preceding year. Indeed, the cited letter of the five bishops says: “We sent not so much about the synodical letters as about Pelagius’s book and Augustine’s response”; and therefore all these materials are known to have been sent together.]

### V. Innocent replies to three letters from the Africans

Pope Innocent, having received three letters from the Africans, sent replies to them on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Honorius XI and Constantius II—that is, on January 27 of the year 417. In them he decreed that the sentence against the aforementioned Pelagius and Caelestius should remain fixed.

As Lent approached, Innocent’s letters were delivered to the Africans, or perhaps even after the sacred fast had already begun (Easter falling that year on April 22). For Julius, the bishop who had carried both the synodical writings and the apostolic replies, could scarcely have returned to Africa any sooner.

On the fourth day before the Ides of March, that is, on March 12, Pope Innocent died and was succeeded by Zosimus, who, as is probable from Prosper and Paschasinus, obtained the apostolic see on March 18.

### VI. Conjectures concerning the African synod after receiving Innocent’s letters

The writers do not report what happened in Africa after Innocent’s letters had been received, after the messenger had announced his death, after Zosimus’s election had become known, and after Caelestius had hastened to Rome.

Nevertheless, I could scarcely—indeed, not at all—persuade myself that no synod was convened at that time [Note: [Col. 0964D] We shall show in the observations, section 3, that this synod was not convened, where we refute Quesnellus’s following arguments.], at least from the two provinces to whose bishops the replies had been sent, unless perhaps it was summoned from other African provinces as well.

First, the state of affairs in the Church, the impending danger from the rising heresy, and the apostolic see’s recently issued replies against it seemed to require that the African Church should address and anticipate Innocent’s successor by letters [Col. 0963C].

Second, after hearing what had been done in Africa and what Innocent had replied, Pelagius had written a letter to that same pontiff, which was delivered to Zosimus. Caelestius, intending to plead his case before the pontiff in person, hastened with all speed to Rome, as Marius Mercator writes. He arrived after Zosimus had been elected, and the Africans learned that he had been kindly received by Zosimus.

Thus there was no reason not to fear anything from such deceitful adversaries unless the Africans sent letters to Rome which, because they carried the authority of a synod, would have greater weight with the Roman bishop.

Third, Innocent’s replies could scarcely be promulgated throughout Africa according to the rules of discipline unless a synod were assembled, through which and in which all would learn what Rome had replied and what had been decreed concerning the case of the heretics. Since Augustine says that the case was brought to an end after Innocent’s replies had been received [Col. 0963D], the case must undoubtedly have been concluded with the solemnity of a fuller synod.

Accordingly, it is probable that the two synods from which the letters to Innocent had been sent joined together.

Fourth, Pope Zosimus seems to allude to this synod in the first of his letters to all the African bishops established throughout Africa. Explaining why he had written so quickly, he says:

> “So that the expectation of your Fraternity concerning Caelestius’s arrival and examination might not remain in suspense any longer, I set aside everything else,” and so forth.

How could Zosimus have learned that the Africans were anxious about Caelestius’s arrival and examination unless he learned it from their letters—and indeed from synodical letters, since the importance of the matter required this and synods were frequent in Africa? We need not say that a synod was convened outside the established order because of an urgent necessity.

Fifth, other words of the same letter, before its middle, still indicate that synod:

> “As for the letters of Heros and Lazarus, sent in the earlier report, I readily acknowledge that I hastened forward with the greatest zeal of faith.”

The earlier report which he mentions presupposes a later one. But since it is established that the letters of Heros and Lazarus were first sent to the apostolic see from the Carthaginian synod, what later report should be understood as lying between that synod and Zosimus’s first letters?

Could it have been the report of the Council of Milevis? But [Note: [Col. 0964D] This will be shown to be false in observation no. 11.] it was not later. The report of both African synods of 416 was sent at the same time and by the same bishop, Julius, so that Innocent seems rather to assign the earlier place to the Milevitan synod than to the Carthaginian:

> “Our brother and fellow bishop Julius eagerly brought me the letter of Your Love, which you sent from the Council of Milevis with heightened concern for the faith, adding also the similarly written complaints of the Carthaginian synod.”

Could one say that the letter of the five bishops was that later report? But we have already shown above that it should not be honored with that designation. Since Zosimus addresses all the bishops of Africa, he must be understood to be speaking of a synodical report, not of another kind.

It therefore appears that a synod was held before Zosimus’s letters, from which a report was sent to him. I willingly submit these conjectures to the judgment of more learned scholars.

### VII. Zosimus’s first letter to the Africans

Zosimus’s first letter to the Africans followed [Col. 0964C]. We are not told from the letter itself, which is defective in that portion, in what month or on what day it was written; only the consular date survives. But, unless I am mistaken, we learn this from the second letter, which is read as having been issued on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October—that is, on September 21.

For the later letter [Note: [Col. 0964D] We shall prove in the observations, section 4, that Zosimus’s first and second letters were written not two months apart but in the same month, September.] must have been written one month after the earlier one. When Zosimus had warned the Africans:

> “Either let those who would refute Caelestius’s claim to think differently from what he set forth in his libellus and confession come within a month or two; or let them recognize that after such clear and evident statements as he has produced, no doubt remains,”

he could not, before the second month had elapsed, have burst into the reproach against Caelestius’s accusers found in the second letter:

> “Behold,” he says, “Pelagius and Caelestius are present before the apostolic see in their letters and confessions. Where are Heros? Where is Lazarus—names to be ashamed of because of their deeds and condemnations? Where are those young men, Timasius and James, who, as was alleged, produced certain writings?” and so forth.

Thus the earlier letters seem to have been written not in September, as Garnier thought, but either in June or July, since, in addition to the two months granted, some time had to be allowed for the delivery of the letters and the return of the replies before he wrote a second time.

The letters contain a very severe rebuke of what Zosimus considered the Africans’ excessive credulity. The pontiff states that the presbyter Caelestius had thrust himself before the Roman examination and was requesting that the charges inculcated against him before the apostolic see contrary to what was proper be cleared away. As we have said, he granted two months within which the accusers were to present themselves for judgment; he declared that everything had to be weighed slowly and carefully; he also sent the acts of the Roman trial and attempted to persuade the Africans to correct their own judgment.

### VIII. Zosimus’s second letter to the Africans

After the two months had elapsed, Zosimus again wrote to the Africans on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, before receiving any reply from the Africans [Col. 0965A] 784.

The reason for repeating his letter was a letter of Pelagius written to Innocent and received by Zosimus. The pontiff then decided to send it to the Africans, moved to do so by a recent letter from Praylius, bishop of Jerusalem, in which he intervened as an especially vigorous supporter of Pelagius’s case (*ibid.*). He sent them a copy of that letter, and perhaps of both letters. He wrote that the faith of Pelagius and Caelestius was becoming clearer each day through letters and professions consistent with Catholic doctrine. Finally, he accused the accusers, as he supposed, of delay and evasion in increasingly severe terms.

The reason for the Africans’ delay was the necessity of convening a synod which could effectively avert the grave damage threatening the cause of the faith. For a great scandal threatened the Church if the several synods held against Pelagius and Caelestius—the two Carthaginian synods, the Jerusalemite, Diospolitan, Milevitan, and Constantinopolitan synods, and, in addition, Innocent’s Roman judgment—were nullified by one Zosimus, deceived by the devices of the heretics, as they feared would immediately happen [Note: [Col. 0965D] We shall show in the observations, nos. 34 and following, that this fear was fabricated.].

That would mean a certain triumph for the heretics, damage to Catholic doctrine, disgrace for the apostolic see, grief for all Catholics, and danger to the unity of the Church, which the Africans foresaw would be torn apart by schism. The matter belonged above all to the African Church, whose judgment was seeking approval from the apostolic see. The deliberation of the entire African diocese was therefore necessary, and it consequently had to coalesce into a larger synod.

[Note: [Col. 0965D] We shall see in the observations, sections 5 and 6, that this synod was held not around the autumn of 417 but either in January or February of 418.]

I think that it was convened around the autumn, not so much because that season had traditionally been appointed for convening synods, as because it could scarcely have been assembled sooner after the first letters of Zosimus had been received. That the synod was held at Carthage is proved by the heading of Zosimus’s third letter, which is read as having been addressed to Aurelius and the others who were present at the Council of Carthage.

### IX. How many African synods were held from Innocent’s death until Zosimus’s *Tractoria*?

John Garnier posits two synods between Zosimus’s first letter and his third, which was issued on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April: the earlier in December, or even November, of 417, and the later before Lent in 418. He offers no other basis for distinguishing them than that, from the first, Zosimus is said to have received a letter containing the Africans’ protest and the documents of the case, to which he did not reply; whereas from the later he received a synodical letter, to which he gave the reply dated on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April and received on the third day before the Kalends of May.

I, however, think that only one synod was held during that interval [Col. 0965D] 785, [Note: Only two were held, and both in 418, as will be demonstrated more fully in the observations.] so that we should posit only three synods convened against the Pelagians during Zosimus’s pontificate.

The first, then, was held after Zosimus’s letters had been received, around the autumn of 417; the second, on the Kalends of May 418; and the third after Zosimus’s decree had been received—unless one adds a fourth, which, as we conjectured, was held after Innocent’s replies had been received and before those three.

I prove that there was only one synod between October and the Kalends of May of the following year, on the basis of Garnerius’s own argument. For Zosimus shows in his last letter, dated 12 Kalends of April, that the letters which Garnerius supposes to have been sent from different synods were written by one and the same synod. [Note: He distinguishes two African letters attributed to Zosimus, one earlier than the other. The first and shorter was sent by Aurelius and several bishops, assembled without the formal constitution of a council, immediately after they received Zosimus’s letters, in November 417; the second and longer was sent to the same pontiff from an African synod in 418, in January or February. See Observations §§ 5 and 6.] He addresses the same synod when he says: “After we received those letters of yours which you sent either earlier or now.” And below: “The protest sent from you to us.” He is replying after receiving the later letter, yet he attributes to the same synod the protest that belonged to the first letter. The same point is indicated several times in the same letter. Whenever either Saint Augustine or Saint Prosper enumerates the African synods held during that period in the case of Coelestius, they mention no more than two, the latter of which must be assigned to the Kalends of May. This will become clearer from what follows.

3. Garnerius admits that Marcellinus, subdeacon of the Church of Carthage, was the bearer of the later letter, which he supposes to have come from a still later council held in 418, before Lent, and to which Zosimus replied in his third letter on 21 March. This is certain from the conclusion of that letter, where, after mentioning the first African letters, he says: “And since we believe that those writings which you had sent in reply to them constituted a response,” [Note: The same letter is indicated—the one in which Aurelius and certain bishops replied to Zosimus’s earlier letters. See the passages cited in the Observations.] he immediately adds: “But afterward, when the letter sent through your subdeacon Marcellinus … we turned over the entire volume.” It is likewise clear that these later letters had only recently been delivered to Zosimus, [Col. 0966C] since he replied to them on that same 21st day of March, for he writes: [Note: Compare note 11 (above, note d).] “After we received those letters of yours which you sent either earlier or now.” But who could believe that Marcellinus had set out from Africa only in January 418, at which time Garnerius supposes the synod to have been held, when we have the firmest evidence from Paulinus’s own booklet that this same subdeacon Marcellinus had received from Paulinus the deacon, as early as 8 November of the preceding year, the booklet to be delivered to Zosimus? [Note: Marcellinus did indeed receive the booklet from Paulinus on 8 November 417, but he did not leave Africa until after the council assembled shortly after the beginning of 418, when he had received the longer letter of that same synod. The earlier letter of Aurelius and the other bishops was entrusted to Basiliscus for delivery to Zosimus in November. See Observations § 6.] Thus two letters proceeded from one and the same synod; how this came about we shall now consider.

## X. Why were two letters sent by the same council? Why did Paulinus not go to Rome?

After receiving Zosimus’s first letter, the Africans immediately began considering the convocation of a synod. But time was needed for it to be sufficiently numerous and adequate to the matter, and it does not seem to have been assembled before October or November. This explains why Basiliscus, subdeacon of the Roman Church, who had brought that letter to the Africans, was still staying at Carthage on 2 November, on which day he met Paulinus and presented him with the proceedings sent from the Apostolic See, so that he might appear before the Apostolic See and submit to Zosimus’s judgment.

When a date had been fixed, [Note: Paulinus did not refuse obedience, but, by presenting a written statement of excuse, he humbly set forth sufficiently strong reasons why he should not go to Rome, which he thought the pontiff would approve. Among them he gave this reason: namely, that the case was no longer his own but that of the whole Church. He says that this reason had been approved by the African Fathers. There is no indication anywhere that those Fathers prohibited him from going to Rome on the appointed day. The probable explanation is simply that, with their consent, he did not send the booklet through Basiliscus, who was then about to depart, but entrusted it to Marcellinus, who had been designated to carry the African council’s report and documents to Rome; for they thought it expedient that all these materials, together with the booklet, should be presented to Zosimus at the same time.] he refused to comply—not merely, or even principally, because he had not been summoned legally and in writing, but because the matter concerned Coelestius’s appeal from the sentence of the Council of Carthage of 412, which Zosimus therefore calls the former appeal, and that appeal could no longer have force. Coelestius himself had not appeared for the appeal, as Paulinus says (*Commonitorium*, chapter 1); and, neglecting it, he withdrew to Ephesus, where he dared, by evasion, to seek the rank of presbyter. Then, four years later, he was brought again before the tribunal of the Church of Carthage and had received the sentence of both that council and the Council of Milevis, subsequently confirmed by two constitutions of Innocent. After these events Saint Augustine publicly proclaimed, in Sermon 2 *On the Words of the Apostle*, that the case was finished.

The Africans therefore rightly prohibited Paulinus from going to Rome on the appointed day. They were also displeased by the matter, as Zosimus himself anticipated; for that reason he addressed Paulinus not in writing but through a speech delivered by his subdeacon.

Basiliscus, Zosimus’s subdeacon, after hearing Paulinus’s reply and, as I suppose, receiving the first reply of the Africans to the pontiff, returned to Italy. At that time all the extensive documents of the case, which were being prepared in the same synod, were not yet ready; they were subsequently entrusted to the subdeacon Marcellinus together with the later letter.

## XI. What did the first African letter contain?

Both letters have perished—or are still fighting with the cockroaches in the dust of the Vatican. [Note: In the outstanding Avellana Collection, from whose Vatican copy Baronius published the three letters of Zosimus and Paulinus’s booklet, both African letters are missing. If they had been found in that collection or in another Vatican manuscript, they would have been published just like the others. We mention this so that no one may perhaps suspect that the Romans concealed these letters.] What the first contained must be extracted from Zosimus’s third letter. Since that letter answers both African letters, its first part satisfies the first, while its latter and very brief part satisfies the second; he was intending to send a longer reply to the second together with the *tractoria*.

It therefore appears that the first African synod’s letter had chiefly three sections. The first was a serious complaint against Zosimus, [Note: Concerning the complaint of the Africans as presented by Quesnellus, see Observations no. 34 and following.] because, setting aside both the judgment of the African Church and the Roman judgment delivered through Innocent, by which Coelestius’s case had been concluded, he had recalled it for a new examination, not without great danger to the Catholic faith and unity. This, I believe, is the point of the commendation of the privileges of the Apostolic See that fills almost the whole of Zosimus’s letter:

“The tradition of the Fathers has granted such great authority to the Apostolic See that no one would dare dispute its judgment; it has been strengthened by every human and divine law and discipline, and the zeal of all our predecessors has preserved it; hitherto it has possessed foundations that no one may rashly attack without danger to himself; finally, no one can reopen a judgment delivered by it.” Yet, although these things were so, they had nevertheless referred everything to the pontiff’s knowledge.

The second section consisted of a complaint—and they pressed this point especially—that Zosimus had drawn to himself the case of Coelestius, which had arisen in Africa and had been brought before the tribunal of Carthage. [Col. 0968A] They held to the judgment expressed by their own Cyprian in his letter to Pope Cornelius:

“Since it has been established for all of us, and is equally fair and just, that each person’s case should be heard there where the crime was committed … those over whom we preside must certainly not run about from place to place, nor by their deceitful and fraudulent presumption shatter the concord that binds the bishops together; rather, they must conduct their case there where they can have both their accusers and witnesses to their crime … The case has already been heard; the sentence has already been pronounced. It is not consonant with the dignity of priests that a judgment should be criticized through the fickleness of a changeable and inconstant mind.”

Aurelius and his colleagues wrote similar things concerning Coelestius, who had wished to receive from Aurelius the rank of presbyter and, after being accused before him, had been struck by a sentence of condemnation. I establish this from Zosimus’s words: “We wished to discuss with you also the case of the man who, as you yourselves say in your letter, was accused among you.” It should be read “among you,” as all the manuscripts have it and as the sense requires, not “among us,” as it appears in Garnerius’s edition—a reading I gladly attribute to the carelessness of the printers.

The third section of the letter was the protest of the African bishops. When they understood from Zosimus’s letter [Note: The Africans received not only letters from Zosimus but also, together with the letters, the proceedings of the first examination in which Coelestius had been investigated. What they understood from these materials, which more clearly disclosed the pontiff’s intention, and whether they could have feared that Zosimus might improperly restore Coelestius and Pelagius to communion, will become clear from the discussion in Observations no. 35.] that he was hastening to absolve Coelestius and Pelagius and had already resolved to restore both to the Church’s communion and good opinion unless their accusers hurried to Rome within two months and proved the substance of their accusation, they inserted a protestation in which they demanded that their rights be preserved and that nothing be altered in the sentence issued against the two men. Everything was to remain in its existing condition, at least until they could send one of their number to Rome with adequate documents of the case, by which the heretics’ devices could be exposed and it could be shown how lawfully and canonically they had been condemned. The closing words of the letter bear witness to this protest:

“Let your fraternity know that, after we received those letters of yours which you sent either earlier or now, we have altered nothing, but have left everything in the same condition in which it had long stood, when we informed your holiness of this in our letter, so that the protest which had been sent from you to us might remain.”

The words “had been sent” show that this protest belonged to the earlier letter.

## XII. Two embassies decreed in the first African synod: one to Zosimus, the other to Honorius

While the earlier letter was being carried to Zosimus by his subdeacon Basiliscus, those same bishops, assembled in the same synod, considered with greater leisure and mature deliberation what action should be taken to counter the heretics’ devices and to prevent Zosimus, too credulous and favorably disposed toward Coelestius, from pronouncing a judgment harmful to the Church and the faith. [Note: Do not suppose that the Africans feared that Zosimus would pronounce a judgment destined to betray the Church and the faith. See Observations no. 34 and following.]

They decreed a double embassy: one to be undertaken by Bishop Vindemialis to Augustus Honorius, and the other to be undertaken by the subdeacon Marcellinus to Pope Zosimus. [Note: We shall show in Observations § 7 that the embassy of Bishop Vindemialis to Honorius, supposedly sent at this time, is fictitious; accordingly, the equally fictitious conjecture of Quesnellus shortly afterward—that Marcellinus accompanied Vindemialis all the way to Ravenna—is also false.]

When I read in Paulinus’s booklet that Marcellinus had already received, on 8 November, the booklet of Paulinus to be delivered likewise to Zosimus, but nevertheless did not arrive in Rome before the middle of March—according to Zosimus’s letter dated 12 Kalends of April—I draw one of two conclusions: either Marcellinus did not leave Africa as quickly as Paulinus expected, or perhaps he accompanied Bishop Vindemialis as far as Ravenna and remained with him for some time at the imperial court. We shall discuss the first and more hidden embassy below. For the moment we must discuss the other, together with what was done in the council and entrusted to Marcellinus for delivery to Zosimus.

The more difficult matter, which almost exceeds all expectation, is to determine what should be attributed to this council among the events recorded by Saint Augustine, by his disciple Prosper, by Marius Mercator, and others, as well as in Prosper’s Chronicle—or whether that work is Prosper’s or another’s—as having proceeded from the African council.

## XIII. What was done in the autumnal African synod?

This autumnal council of 417 agrees first of all with what Marius Mercator writes after recounting Zosimus’s letter, full of kindness toward Coelestius, to the African bishops:

“But when the bishops from Africa replied and set forth the whole case that had taken place among them, sending also the proceedings that had then been conducted with him or concerning him, he was summoned to a fuller hearing so that he might hasten to fulfill what he had promised—that is, so that, after condemning the aforesaid propositions, he might be absolved from the sentence of the African bishops by which he had been deprived of communion. Yet he not only failed to appear; he even fled from the aforesaid city of Rome. For this reason he was condemned by the blessed Bishop Zosimus of revered memory in an exceedingly full and lengthy written judgment.”

2. The same council is concerned in Zosimus’s letter written on 12 Kalends of April of the following year [Col. 0969C] to the bishops who had attended the Council of Carthage. From that council, he says, a volume of letters had been sent through the subdeacon Marcellinus, which Zosimus seems to have read only with some weariness. [Note: Zosimus’s words concerning the volume of the letter transmitted by the Africans—which he says he eventually read through, etc.—indicate not the tedium of reading but the length of the document, which was necessary for exposing and refuting the frauds and deceptions of the heretics. Compare Observations no. 25.]

3. This is likewise what Prosper records in his *Chronicle* concerning the autumnal synod, under the year 418, in these words:

“When a council of 214 bishops had been held at Carthage, decrees were carried to Pope Zosimus. When he approved them, the Pelagian heresy was condemned throughout the whole world.”

The words of the *Chronicle* must be carefully weighed. Prosper does not say that a council was held at Carthage in that year, 418, but rather: “When a council had been held at Carthage.” [Note: Quesnellus correctly proves that the African synod whose replies preceded Zosimus’s condemnation of the Pelagians was earlier than the synod held on the Kalends of May 418. But he does not correctly prove that it was held in the autumn of the preceding year. We shall prove in Observations § 6 that it was assembled in January or February 418; consequently, it will become clear that Prosper’s words, “when a council had been held at Carthage,” must be understood of a synod held in that same year.]

Thus, after the autumn of the preceding year, the synod’s decrees were carried to Pope Zosimus in the following year, 418; they were approved by him, and the heresy was condemned throughout the whole world. This agrees perfectly with our position.

I am certain that these words of Prosper’s *Chronicle*, which are commonly thought to refer to the synod held on the Kalends of May 418, were written concerning the autumnal synod of the preceding year. For everyone agrees that the proceedings or decrees of the synod of the Kalends of May were not received by Zosimus before he himself pronounced sentence against Coelestius—whether because, as many think, Zosimus’s judgment had already been delivered before the Kalends of May, or, as we believe more correctly, because the Africans did not send a letter to the Roman pontiff from that synod of the Kalends of May. [Note: The letter was not sent to Zosimus from the plenary synod that enacted the canons on the Kalends of May before he pronounced judgment against Pelagius and Coelestius. We shall demonstrate in Observations § 11 that the *Tractoria* of that same pontiff, by which he condemned them, was sent in reply by this synod.]

Moreover, it seems clear that the synod whose proceedings were approved and were followed by Zosimus’s sentence, sent throughout the world, was the one that transmitted to the Roman pontiff, through the subdeacon Marcellinus, the volume of the letter together with numerous instructions and the proceedings of earlier synods. All these materials had already been received by Zosimus on 21 March, as is certain from his third letter to the Africans.

Finally, the reference must be to the synod after whose replies had been sent it followed that Zosimus pronounced sentence against Coelestius with complete justice, as Augustine says in Book II, chapter 7, *On Original Sin*. Those replies were the very ones requested by Zosimus after an interval of two months, as the same passage shows. That interval, moreover, had elapsed before the autumnal synod, as is established by Zosimus’s first letters. It is therefore evident that those replies must be referred to the autumnal synod, not to the synod held six months later on the Kalends of May. This will become even clearer from what follows.

Perhaps the same matter should be referred to what the same writer records under the year 416, during the consulship of Theodosius VII and Palladius, where the beginning of Zosimus’s pontificate is here placed in error:

“Zosimus assumes the episcopate of the Roman Church, the thirty-ninth, for three years. During this period, although the Pelagians had already been condemned in advance by Pope Innocent, they were resisted by the steadfastness of the Africans and especially through the efforts of Bishop Augustine.”

The mention of the sentence already issued by Innocent and of the beginning of Zosimus’s pontificate indicates the time of this council, even though these three items are reported under another consulship. Perhaps a copyist mistakenly transferred the beginning of the following year to the end of the preceding year, which would have been easy to do.

Someone may object that the author himself clearly placed these events under that consulship, since he says that Zosimus presided over the Roman Church for three years and assigns the pontificate of Boniface to the year 419, under the consulship of Monaxius and Plinta. Yet although Prosper’s *Chronicle* has this reading in the manuscripts of Sirmond and Chifflet, from which Andreas du Chesne published it in volume I of the *Historical Writers of France*, the oldest edition, printed by Johann Sichard at Basel in 1549 and evidently based on several manuscript copies, as the marginal variants show, reads as follows:

“Zosimus, the thirty-ninth bishop of the Roman Church, assumes the episcopate for one year, nine months, and eight days.”

From this reading, which corresponds to historical truth, it is not merely probable but necessary that this section concerning Zosimus be transferred, in accordance with the author’s arrangement, to the following year, 417—the order having been reversed through the carelessness of scribes. Otherwise Zosimus’s pontificate would have to be reckoned as lasting several years.

## XIV. Augustine’s testimony concerning the council of 417

4. Saint Augustine designates the same synod in Letter 47, in these words:

“Likewise, what was written to Pope Zosimus from the African council, and his reply sent to all the bishops of the whole world; and what was done at the later plenary council, etc.”

The earlier council, which the holy teacher calls African, is the very one we call autumnal, from which all the proceedings of the case were sent to Zosimus. The following passages in Book II, chapter 7, *On Original Sin*, concern the same council:

“But after an interval of two months, until a reply was sent from Africa … But after replies had been sent from the African council of bishops, read everything that followed, so that sentence might be pronounced against him [Coelestius], because we transmitted everything.”

Here one sees that Zosimus was moved to pronounce sentence by the writings of one African council. Later, in chapter 8:

“When the African synod replied to the venerable Pope Zosimus—a reply which we sent to your charity together with the other instructions …”

And in chapter 21:

“Pelagius seemed for a time to say something compatible with the Catholic faith, but he was unable to deceive that see to the end. For after the replies of the African council, etc.”

No letters came to Rome from any other council than the one whose letters were expected from Africa, so that it might be made fuller and clearer in the case of Coelestius that he had replied that he agreed with the letters of the blessed Pope Innocent, as is stated more or less in Book II, chapter 3, *To Boniface*.

Several points should be noted in these various passages of Augustine.

1. He consistently calls it “the African council,” distinguishing it from the later plenary council, and thereby showing that the same council is meant in all these passages.

2. Everywhere he testifies that a reply was written to Zosimus from that council, again distinguishing it from the later plenary council held on the Kalends of May; for no letter was written to the pontiff from the latter.

3. He identifies it as the synod whose replies were expected after the two-month interval had been granted and which was therefore held around autumn.

4. He identifies it as the synod whose writings were received and were followed by Zosimus’s decree sent to the bishops of the entire world.

5. He identifies that same synod as the one from which all the documents and proceedings were sent to Zosimus through the subdeacon Marcellinus for the instruction of the case, since Zosimus’s sentence followed only after that synod and its replies.

These points, unless I am mistaken, are clear. It is therefore surprising that Garnerius refers them all to the synod held on the Kalends of May. We shall examine this below.

## XV. Two passages of Prosper of Aquitaine concerning the council of 417

5. We now come to Prosper, Augustine’s disciple, whose testimony is more involved. I refer to the same synod what he says in his reply to the Gallican chapters, reply to objection 8:

“With 214 priests, whose decree against the enemies of God’s grace the whole world embraced, let us confess in true profession, as their own statement has it, that the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord assists us in each individual act, not only for knowing but also for doing righteousness, so that without it we are unable to possess, think, say, or do anything belonging to true and holy piety.”

These words concern the African synod whose decree the whole world embraced—that is, whose decrees, according to the chronicler, were carried to Pope Zosimus; when he approved them, the Pelagian heresy was condemned throughout the world. After its letter, as Augustine says in Letter 47, Zosimus’s reply to all the bishops of the whole world followed. Again, after the replies had been sent, it followed that sentence was pronounced against Coelestius, as Augustine says in Book II, chapter 7, *On Original Sin*.

From what was said above it is clear that all this must be understood of the autumnal synod of 417. From that synod, Marcellinus was sent in November, and Zosimus received through him all its instructions and synodal proceedings on 12 Kalends of April of the following year.

Add to this the agreement in the number of bishops: 214, the number attributed both by Prosper, Augustine’s disciple, to the bishops who formulated this decree and by the chronicler to that Council of Carthage whose decrees, once approved, resulted in the condemnation of the Pelagian heresy throughout the world.

Finally, since we have proved that only two councils were held in Africa between Zosimus’s first letters and his decree, nowhere is it stated that a letter containing that decree was written to Zosimus from the later council held on the Kalends of May. This is clear from another passage of Prosper, which we shall now quote.

6. It follows from these considerations that the same synod is also concerned in what Prosper says about the same 214 priests in chapter 10 *Against the Collator*. There we read:

“The 214 priests erred, who, in the letter that they placed before their decrees, addressed the blessed Zosimus, bishop of the Apostolic See, in these words: ‘We decree that the sentence pronounced against Pelagius and Coelestius through the venerable Bishop Innocent, from the See of the blessed Apostle Peter, shall remain in force until they openly confess that the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord assists us in each individual act, not only for knowing but also for doing righteousness, so that without it we are unable to possess, think, say, or do anything belonging to true and holy piety.’”

I do not think anyone will wish to assign these words, and those quoted above from the reply to the Gallican chapters, to different synods. The decree is the same, the number of bishops is the same, and the words are the same.

## XVI. The African canons on grace were enacted in the autumnal synod of 417

7. From these considerations we derive an important conclusion: the eight constitutions, or canons, concerning grace, formerly and wrongly attributed to the Council of Milevis, are now recognized as Carthaginian; they were enacted in that autumnal Council of Carthage. [Note: It will become clear from what follows in § 11 that the canons were not enacted in the African council which Quesnellus regards as autumnal, but in the plenary council of the Kalends of May.]

For the constitutions of this council are expressly mentioned here, and they are constitutions that were sent to the Apostolic See together with the synodical letter to Zosimus, which was prefixed to them. They were also constitutions embraced by the whole world, as Prosper’s other passage shows.

What other constitutions, what other canons on grace, have ever appeared anywhere in the world or been mentioned by any writers, apart from those eight celebrated canons found in all editions of the councils and preserved in our Roman Church’s manuscript, chapter 13, from the later council held on the Kalends of May, where they were confirmed and subscribed, as we shall explain below?

2. Our assertion is confirmed by Prosper himself, chapter 10 *Against the Collator*:

“The African councils of bishops erred, which by their decrees established that both gifts are from God: both knowing what we ought to do and loving it so that we may do it; so that, when charity builds up, knowledge cannot puff up. For just as it is written concerning God, ‘He is the one who teaches human beings knowledge,’ so it is written, ‘Charity is from God.’”

Prosper plainly attributes to several African councils the decree that he cites. It is, however, the fourth canon—or the fifth in our manuscript—of the Carthaginian canons. Consequently, if we wish to agree with Prosper, we must say that it was promulgated in at least two African councils. One of these was the autumnal council of 417, which is now under discussion and which Prosper immediately identifies more explicitly and distinguishes from the later council: he indicates both the number of 214 bishops by whom one of them was held, and the confirmation in it of Innocent’s sentence against Pelagius and Coelestius, as well as the letter prefixed to the constitutions and sent to Zosimus.

There is no reason to understand these matters as referring to another synod distinct from those already mentioned. On the contrary, the fact that Prosper deliberately avoids the word “synod” here indicates that this is one of the councils already cited. When he mentions the letter that those 214 bishops placed before their constitutions, he implies that these constitutions are not distinct from the decrees by which, as he had just said, the councils established that both gifts of God were involved—that is, knowledge of what we ought to do and love enabling us to do it.

From this it is clear that one of the councils praised by Prosper is the same as the autumnal council that we have identified.

3. Prosper the chronicler expressly writes under the year 418 that the synod of 214 bishops—which was the autumnal synod and to which Zosimus replied with a letter sent throughout the world—established synodal decrees. Once these had been carried to Rome and approved, the Pelagian heresy was condemned throughout the world.

What else could those decrees have been, if not the eight or nine canons on which we are speaking?

## XVII. Before the African canons on grace were enacted, Augustine treated the Pelagians’ *sinlessness* (*ἀναμαρτησία*) more mildly

I believe that I can still prove that these eight canons were at least enacted, even if not yet published, in this autumnal synod, so that they were issued neither earlier nor later. Their earlier publication is disproved, I think, by the manner of speaking and the singular moderation with which Augustine expressed his opinion concerning the Pelagian proposition: whether anyone had ever been, or presently was, or would thereafter be, without sin.

Before the year 417, when the canons were enacted, he never considered this proposition deserving of a harsher censure, nor did he mark it with the stain of heresy. If he ever called it an error, he called it a tolerable human error, not a destructive one.

Thus, in chapter 2 of *On the Spirit and the Letter*, he says:

“Accordingly, they are not greatly troublesome on this account … Even if no one is, was, or will be—for I am more inclined to believe this—perfect in such purity, nevertheless, if someone defends or supposes that such a person exists, existed, or will exist, so far as I can judge, he is not greatly mistaken, nor dangerously so, when he is deceived with a certain benevolence … But we must resist most sharply and vehemently those who think that, without God’s help, the power of the human will by itself can either achieve righteousness or advance toward it by striving for it.”

He establishes and explains the same comparison between the two doctrines in Letter 89 to Hilary, where he says:

“But these people are to some extent to be tolerated when they say that there is, or has been, here someone who had no sin.”

Likewise, at the end of *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*:

“I do not think,” he says, “that we ought to resist too strongly. For I know that some have thought this; I do not dare criticize their opinion on the matter, although I cannot defend it either.”

In *On Nature and Grace* he says that he does not care greatly whether such people exist or have existed; and in chapter 60:

“There may,” he says, “be some question about this among true and devout Christians.”

Moreover, in the letter of the five bishops to Innocent, written toward the end of 416:

“However this question may stand, if no human being is found in this life without sin, anyone who is deceived in this matter is tolerably deceived; it is not diabolical impiety but human error to affirm and desire that this be achieved, even if one cannot demonstrate what one affirms.”

Finally, in *The Proceedings of Pelagius*, the last of the works that the holy teacher of grace composed before the autumnal council of 417—and composed only after the letter of the five bishops had been written to Innocent—he says in chapter 30 that this question had not been settled by the fourteen Palestinian bishops:

“This,” he says, “must be sought peacefully, not between Catholics and heretics, but among Catholics themselves.”

These final words of Saint Augustine, in a work written after the letter of the five bishops, show that the question of *sinlessness* (*ἀναμαρτησία*) had not yet been settled at that time and that the canons we are discussing had not yet been enacted. Accordingly, Rigberius should be corrected in his notes on Marius Mercator, page 141, where he attributes the enactment of these canons to the Council of Milevis. He was moved to make this assertion by the passage in the letter of the five bishops where Augustine writes:

“But for us it is enough that no believer in the Church of God, however outstanding in progress and righteousness, is found who dares to say that the prayer of the Lord’s Prayer is not necessary for him: ‘Forgive us,’ etc.”

Yet this does not prove Rigberius’s point. It is one thing to be without sin; it is another to believe oneself to be without sin in such a way that one dares to say that the prayer of the Lord’s Prayer—“Forgive us,” etc.—is unnecessary. Augustine says that no believer dares to say this. But although he does not approve of asserting that no one is without sin, in that same passage of the letter he nevertheless writes that, if someone is deceived on this matter, the error is tolerable and not diabolical impiety but human error.

To this should be added the passage from *The Proceedings of Pelagius*.

When the holy doctor spoke thus shortly before the council under discussion, and, concerned about a question that had not yet been decided, held that it ought to be peacefully investigated among Catholics, nothing is more fitting than to suppose that Augustine took care to have it brought under examination as soon as he found a suitable opportunity in a council—such as that autumnal synod—in which the Fathers reopened for discussion everything that had been done or debated concerning the controversy over the grace of Christ and the Pelagian cause, and thoroughly examined it over a prolonged period, so that everything might be fully and perfectly arranged for communication to Zosimus. We have already observed that the synod lasted a considerable time. This is most clearly proved by the fact that the letters of Zosimus, whose reception had made it necessary to convene the synod, arrived in Africa no earlier than September or October, whereas Marcellinus the subdeacon, sent by that synod, had already received the libellus of Paulinus on 8 November, to be delivered in accordance with the council’s instructions; nevertheless, it did not reach Zosimus before March of the following year.

## XVIII. The canons were not later than the autumnal synod of 417

The question was therefore decided in that synod by the three later canons, 6, 7, and 8. We cannot postpone that decision until the later council held on the Kalends of May. First, because that later and plenary synod of all Africa did nothing except establish matters briefly, as St. Augustine writes in Letter 47, and did not undertake a more extended treatment of the doctrines, since it had not been convened for that purpose, but so that what had been established in the earlier, non-plenary council might be confirmed, published, and strengthened by the subscription of all.

[Note: In the same Observations, § 11, we shall confirm from this very testimony of Augustine that the canons were established in the plenary synod and not in the earlier African council; then we shall refute Quesnel’s subsequent arguments.]

Second, it is not permissible to believe that the Africans remained silent before Pope Zosimus about this question, or proposed something uncertain and doubtful to him, since it was one of the three principal points of Pelagian doctrine. Nor was this point likewise omitted by Zosimus in his decision, which is represented as having been composed entirely from the approved acts and decrees of the Africans, in the passage of Prosper the chronicler that we quoted above. Moreover, nothing was sent by the Africans to Zosimus for the instruction of the Pelagian case except what came from that earlier autumnal council.

3. There was also a particular reason why Augustine took care to have this question examined and decided as soon as possible in the synod after he had written the book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*. For in chapter 30 of that work he says that not long before, a certain letter of Pelagius to one of his presbyter friends had come into his hands. In it Pelagius boasted as though of a victory, as though his opinion concerning the *anamar­tēsia*—the sinlessness—of the saints had been approved at the synod of Palestine. “The judgment of fourteen bishops,” he wrote, “has confirmed our definition, in which we said that a human being can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments, if he wishes.” He added that this opinion “covered the mouth of contradiction with confusion and separated from one another the whole society conspiring for evil.” It followed that there were people who said in the prayer, not on their own account but only on behalf of others: “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12).

Augustine replied that, if this occurred in the present life, it could occur only through the help and grace of God, and that the synod had not in fact decided the matter. Meanwhile, however, as Augustine says in that passage, the letter—full of carnal boastfulness and arrogance—was flying about, and, with a speed produced by the delay in the Palestinian proceedings, was outrunning them and flying into people’s hands. There was therefore reason to fear that, if the matter were left uncertain for too long, the poison of heresy would spread more widely and infect many. It is consequently most probable that Augustine seized the opportunity of the first synod, and that Aurelius, to whom he was writing, did likewise; the latter being the council’s leader, the former its intelligence and hand.

Although I would like the eight canons on grace to have been composed in this autumnal synod, I would not, however, believe that they were then published. Rather, I think that nothing from the proceedings of the synod was brought to light at that time; everything was sent under seal both to Pope Zosimus and to the Emperor Honorius, in the manner we shall describe, so that it might be promulgated in the later council.

## XIX. After the African canons, Augustine relegated the doctrines to the category of heresy

Once these canons had been promulgated, Augustine defended his earlier opinion concerning *anamar­tēsia* more securely and confidently—not now as his own opinion, but openly as the teaching of the Church. He unmistakably accused the contrary view of error and placed it among the condemned doctrines of Pelagius.

In that two-part work which he wrote for Albinus, Pinianus, and Melania immediately after the Pelagians had been condemned by Zosimus, *On the Grace of Christ and Original Sin*, book I, chapter 48, Augustine responds to Pelagius concerning St. Ambrose. Ambrose had praised Zechariah and Elizabeth in a certain passage in such a way that he appeared to assert that they were without sin. After several arguments by which Augustine attempts to show that the holy doctor had been misunderstood by Pelagius, he adds:

“Therefore that testimony of St. Ambrose, which Pelagius employs in support of his opinion, was either spoken according to a certain manner of expression, and is indeed plausible but not examined with sufficient precision; or certainly, if that holy and humble man thought that Zechariah and Elizabeth possessed the highest and wholly perfect righteousness, to which nothing could be added, he corrected his opinion by examining it more carefully.”

These words differ greatly from what the holy doctor says in his earlier works. In those works he does not think that one ought to resist this opinion too strongly, because he knew that it had seemed so to certain people whose opinion on the matter he did not dare to censure, as he writes in *On the Perfection of Righteousness*, at the end. But in book III of *To Boniface*, chapter 8, he more clearly traces that opinion back to the three principal doctrines of Pelagianism and adds it to the errors by which original sin and the grace of Christ are denied and human beings are estranged from the grace of the Savior. In book IV, chapters 2 and 3, he maintains that every Catholic mind ought to shrink from these same three wicked and condemnable doctrines in this threefold division, so as to avoid the snares of heretics.

From this observation of the different manner in which Augustine treated *anamar­tēsia*—an observation which I acknowledge I owe to that most learned man—it is clear that the Carthaginian canons, by which the controversy among Catholics on this matter was settled, imposed upon Augustine the necessity of speaking differently. Before the canons were composed, he had thought that it could tolerably be maintained that some people had lived, were living, or would live without sin; after the canons, he denied that this could be reconciled with Christian faith and daily prayer.

It also follows that the opinion of those who formerly attributed these same canons to the Council of Milevis was far from the truth. For after the synod’s decision Augustine would not have spoken about this question in the way in which, as we read above, he spoke in the letter of the five bishops and in the book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, both of which preceded the Council of Milevis.

Such, then, was the synod from which the earlier letter was sent to Basiliscus, subdeacon of the Roman Church, and from which the later and much longer letter was also sent, together with the proceedings, documents, instructions, and everything else pertaining to the Pelagian case, entrusted to Marcellinus, subdeacon of the Church of Carthage, for delivery to Zosimus. Both letters have perished, whether through the injury of time or of men. What the earlier letter contained, insofar as the surviving monuments have allowed us to know, we have said above; what was written or appended to the later letter must be investigated with equal diligence, although scarcely anything remains to be done except to recall the passages noted for determining the council.

## XX. What did the letters of the later autumnal synod contain?

First of all, that the documents were extremely lengthy is attested by Zosimus himself in his third letter to the Africans, dated 21 March, where he says: “The letter sent through the subdeacon Marcellinus turned over the entire volume of correspondence; when it had at last been read through.” These expressions indicate its length, as does the fact that it caused Zosimus some degree of weariness. The words of Marius Mercator, which will be quoted below, likewise testify to its prolixity.

[Note: Compare note 25 above, column 969, note c. As for what is added shortly concerning the Africans’ complaint and fraternal correction, there is no reason to suspect that the Africans departed in this matter from the modesty and respect toward the supreme pontiff which they displayed in their other letters to Boniface concerning the case of Apiarius. If Zosimus could be censured in any respect, it was surely for having declared Catholic the libellus of Coelestius, in which he had not obscurely denied original sin. How modestly the African Fathers wrote to Zosimus even on this point is evident from Augustine, book II *To Boniface*, chapter 3. After interpreting Zosimus’s statement in such a way as to affirm that it referred to the matters in which Coelestius, in replying, claimed to agree with the letters of Blessed Innocent, Augustine preferred the willingness to correct the error. He indicates that the African synod’s letter explained the statement in precisely the same way, adding that it had been written in those letters that it was not enough for slower and more anxious minds that Coelestius confessed generally that he agreed with the letters of Bishop Innocent, and so forth, as is read shortly afterward in Quesnel, no. 3. The final words—“how corrected, on account of his reply that he agreed with the letters of Pope Innocent”—presuppose that the interpretation we have cited from Augustine was inserted in the same letters.]

2. These letters contained the Africans’ complaints against Zosimus, together with a fraternal correction concerning his excessive readiness, by which he had lent credulous ears to Coelestius, believed his words, and had not sufficiently investigated them. In effect, they returned Zosimus’s own words to him. What he had complained that the Africans had done in regard to the letters of Eros and Lazarus, the libellus of Paulinus, and the accusations, they rightly charged him with having done in regard to the heretics. This is clear from Zosimus’s own words:

“When the entire volume of your letter had at last been read, you understood the whole text of my letters as though we had lent Coelestius credence in everything and, without examining his words down to every syllable, so to speak, had granted our assent to them.”

3. When the Africans had learned from the proceedings begun in the Roman judgment that Coelestius had not dared to oppose the letters of Blessed Pope Innocent—indeed, that he had promised to condemn everything which that see condemned, as Augustine records in book II *On Original Sin*, chapter 7—they hoped that he would give a full assent to the letters of Innocent. “A letter came to Rome from Africa,” the same doctor says in book II *To Boniface*, chapter 3, “containing this instruction: it was not enough for slower and more anxious minds that he confessed generally that he agreed with the letters of Bishop Innocent; he had to anathematize openly the things that he had wrongly set down in his libellus. Otherwise, if he did not do so, many people of limited understanding would believe that the poisons of faith contained in his libellus had been approved by the apostolic see—because it had been said by that see that the libellus was Catholic—rather than believe that they had been corrected because he himself had replied that he agreed with the letters of Pope Innocent.”

These most discerning bishops issued this warning concerning the doctrine of original sin, lest the Roman pontiff be deceived by the heretics under a disguise of words.

4. So that he would not deceive them even under the general name of grace, they added what Prosper records in chapter 10 *Against the Collator*:

“We have determined that the sentence pronounced against Pelagius and Coelestius through the venerable Bishop Innocent, from the see of the most blessed Apostle Peter, shall remain in force until he confesses with the greatest clarity that by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord we are helped not only to know righteousness but also to do it, in each of our acts, so that without that grace we are unable to possess, think, say, or do anything belonging to true and holy piety.”

This was contained in the letter that 214 bishops wrote to Zosimus, as Prosper testifies.

## XXI. Chapters excerpted against Pelagius and inserted into the proceedings

5. When the Africans had replied that it was not enough for Coelestius to confess generally that he agreed with the letters of Innocent—a thing which he readily promised to do—but that he had to anathematize openly the errors that he had set down in his libellus, they appended to their letter a kind of memorandum, which is widely circulated.

It is found in St. Augustine’s Letter 106 to Paulinus, and it also appears above in our manuscript, chapter 18, under this heading:

[Note: Augustine excerpted the chapters of the errors charged against Pelagius at the Council of Diospolis from the Palestinian proceedings in Letter 186 to Paulinus, written in 417; to these the same holy doctor added an equal number of chapters of Catholic doctrine. But it is not so certain as Quesnel asserts that all these materials, sent by Augustine to Paulinus and excerpted from his letter, were also sent with the other documents of the Pelagian case to Zosimus and appended to the letter of the African synod of 418.

The testimony of Marius Mercator, on which Quesnel relies, does not concern these chapters charged against Pelagius at the Council of Diospolis, but those which Paulinus charged against Coelestius at the Council of Carthage. After first saying of Coelestius: “There, at Carthage, he was accused before Aurelius, bishop of that city, by means of a libellus from a certain Paulinus, deacon of the late Ambrose, bishop of Milan,” Marius immediately recites the chapters themselves, of which only seven are listed, and then writes concerning the letters of Zosimus: “In these the very chapters on which he had been accused are also contained.”

But when Augustine speaks in book II *On Original Sin*, chapter 8, of the chapters charged against Pelagius at the Palestinian synod, he indicates that they were only mentioned, not inserted, in the African synod’s letter to Zosimus. The whole testimony of the holy doctor is quoted shortly afterward by Quesnel, no. 6. The words that should be noted are: “And it was mentioned when the African synod replied to the venerable Pope Zosimus.”

Furthermore, since the chapters charged against Pelagius that are at issue here are found transmitted in several ancient Latin collections, they appear to have been copied long ago from Augustine for some useful purpose. They do not, however, have the form of a formula of faith to which one would subscribe, as is evident from other formulas expressed in this or a similar manner: “I, so-and-so, profess by this writing, which I have written with my own hand,” and so forth. See the two formulas in our manuscript of the canons, chapters 53 and 55, at the end.

The profession of faith that St. Leo required of Pelagians returning to the Church, in Letters 1 and 2, is clearly different, since among other things he requires them to condemn in explicit professions the authors who are not mentioned in our chapters.]

“Chapters excerpted from the proceedings held against Pelagius the heretic, and others from his books, which he was compelled to anathematize when they were brought against him at the Palestinian synod.”

The memorandum itself begins as follows:

“What the Lord cried out against Jerusalem, which was unwilling to gather her children, we cry out against those who are unwilling to gather the children of the Church and who are not corrected even after the judgment rendered concerning Pelagius himself in Palestine,” and so forth.

After listing the twelve articles charged against Pelagius, Augustine adds:

“Pelagius anathematized all these things in such a way that the proceedings themselves sufficiently testify that he offered no argument whatsoever in defense of them. Consequently, anyone who follows the authority of that judgment and the confession of Pelagius himself—for Coelestius boasted that he did both—must hold these doctrines, which the Catholic Church has always held.”

There follow an equal number of chapters of Catholic doctrine opposed to the heretics. At the beginning of most of them stands the phrase, “Let him confess,” and at the end:

“Let anyone who agrees with Catholic authority and with the explicit words of Pelagius confess all these things simply and without any evasions. For it cannot be believed that the things contrary to these have truly been anathematized unless the doctrines contrary to them are held in faithful hearts and proclaimed in an open confession.”

These are without doubt the materials that were expected from Africa, as Augustine says above in book II *To Boniface*, so that what Coelestius had promised—namely, that he would subscribe to the letters of Innocent—might be made fuller and clearer in him. They are the very same propositions, and the same number, as those charged against Pelagius at the Palestinian council, as is understood from the book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*.

Although the memorandum has rather the form of an admonition, it nevertheless had the force of a synodal definition: first, because it was issued by a large council; and second, because the authority of the apostolic see was added to it. Indeed, I would believe that Pope Zosimus inserted that formula into his letter sent to the whole world, to be subscribed by everyone. For the same formula of subscription was used by subsequent pontiffs whenever, as the seeds of the Pelagian heresy revived, subscription had to be required; especially by Leo, among whose letters we found it, as we shall discuss more fully in the following dissertation.

Hence it was inserted into the Roman Code. It was also proposed by the Africans as a formula for subscription. This is clear from the fact that in several manuscript and printed copies, and in the Roman Code of Canons, it is joined to the letter of Aurelius to the African bishops of the provinces of Byzacena and Arzugitana, to whom he indicated, by imperial order, the necessity of subscribing.

I also prove from Marius Mercator that these chapters were inserted into the African letters, as we have said. For when he writes that the chapters on which Coelestius had been accused were contained in the *Tractoria* of Zosimus, I think that not only Coelestius’s chapters were inserted, but also the opposing chapters which Pelagius had been compelled to profess in Palestine. They were obtained from no other source than the Africans, who, in the same undertaking, sent to Pope Zosimus the collection made by St. Augustine together with the other instructions.

## XXII

6. In their letter the Africans reminded Zosimus to recall what his predecessor Innocent, whom he ought to imitate, had thought about the Palestinian proceedings, by which Pelagius boasted that he had been acquitted. And so that the pontiff might understand that those proceedings had been neither unknown to Innocent nor wholly approved by him, the Africans inserted into their letter an excerpt from his letter to the five bishops, which established this point.

St. Augustine indicates this in book II *On Original Sin*, chapter 8:

“What, then, did holy Pope Innocent judge concerning the proceedings of the Palestinian synod, by which Pelagius boasts that he was acquitted? You may read it in his letters, which he sent back to us; it was also mentioned when the African synod replied to the venerable Pope Zosimus. We have sent this to your Charity together with the other instructions,” and so forth.

7. It is also established from chapter 1 of Marius Mercator’s *Memorandum* that everything done in Africa against Coelestius and Pelagius was attached to those letters, and that the whole case conducted against them was set out by the Africans themselves. Proceedings were also sent from the various occasions on which actions had then been undertaken with or against him; that is, the proceedings of the Council of Carthage of 412 [Note: We believe the year should be corrected to 411. See the *Observations*, no. 5], and those of another council in 416. Without doubt, the proceedings of the Council of Milevis held in the same year were not omitted.

8. If those eight Carthaginian canons on grace were composed in that autumnal synod, as I think I have proved, there can be no doubt that they were sent to Zosimus in the same dispatch together with the remaining documents of the case.

[Note: Rather, since in the *Observations*, nos. 26 and following, we intend to prove against Quesnel that those canons were composed in another synod held on the Kalends of May, they cannot be said to have been sent to Zosimus by the earlier African council. We do not, however, deny that the substance of those canons may perhaps have been laid down in the letter which the same African council wrote to the same pontiff, as we shall note there.]

9. St. Augustine testifies in *On Original Sin*, chapter 21, that the Africans labored greatly in those same letters to expose the deception of the Pelagian libellus. That libellus had been sent from the East by a heretic to Innocent, delivered by him to his successor Zosimus, and then transmitted by Zosimus to the Africans.

Pelagius was thought to have sincerely condemned at the Palestinian judgment the doctrine of those who denied original sin; Augustine himself believed this when he composed the book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*. But in the book of his faith, Augustine says in that same chapter 21, which Pelagius sent to Rome together with the letters to the same Pope Innocent to whom he had also written a letter, he exposed himself much more clearly while attempting to conceal himself, saying:

“We hold one baptism, which we say ought to be celebrated in infants by the same words of the sacrament by which we say it is celebrated in adults …”

For a time he appeared to say something that agreed with Catholic faith. But he could not deceive that see to the end. For after the replies of the African council, in whatever province that destructive doctrine had advanced by spreading—though it had not occupied or penetrated it so broadly and deeply—other writings of his, produced in the city of Rome through the care of faithful brethren, also came to light. Pope Zosimus appended these writings to his letters, which he composed for delivery throughout the Catholic world, as abominable, as you may read.

## XXIII. The African embassy to the Emperor Honorius

While all the synodal proceedings, attached to the Africans’ letter, were being delivered to Rome through Marcellinus the subdeacon, other legates of the same synod were also proceeding to Ravenna.

[Note: We shall reject this alleged embassy of the African synod to the emperor, together with the other points which Quesnel heaps up in support of it, in Observations, § 7.]

The bishops, being deeply concerned for the Catholic faith and the peace of the Church, rightly feared that Coelestius, a notorious master of deception, might lead Pope Zosimus astray and extort from him a sentence of acquittal contrary both to the judgment of the Africans and to the replies of Pope Innocent. They therefore decided, as we said above, to delegate one of their number to the imperial court, so that he might inform Honorius of the state of affairs and kindle in him a desire to defend the faith and peace of the Church.

How greatly the hesitation of Zosimus and his excessive inclination toward Coelestius troubled the African bishops, and what a sinister opinion they had formed of the counsels of the leaders of the Roman clergy, Augustine indicates, unless I am mistaken, in the final words of Letter 106, which he sent at that very time to St. Paulinus, bishop of Nola.

“But what we have heard, and the matters concerning which we have heard it—things which we deeply regret and are reluctant to believe,” he says, “your Holiness will hear from our common friend. When he returns safely through the mercy of God, we hope that we may become fully certain about everything.”

[Note: Augustine’s Letter 106, now 186, to St. Paulinus of Nola, written in 417 after the death of Pope Innocent and before the African synod of 418, cannot indicate the matters which Quesnel thinks troubled the Fathers of that synod. He wrongly believes that no. 40 of the same letter—“But what we have heard, and the matters concerning which we have heard it, things which deeply grieve us and which we are reluctant to believe,” etc.—must be understood of Zosimus and Sixtus. For Augustine had already plainly stated in no. 29 that he had heard certain troubling things not about Romans, but about others living at Nola: “We have mentioned this because, among you—or rather in your city—if what we have heard is true, certain persons strive with such obstinacy for this error that they say it is easier even for them to abandon and despise Pelagius, who anathematized those who hold these views, than to depart from the truth of this opinion, as it seems to them. But if they yield to the apostolic see,” etc. Here he speaks openly of most manifest and obstinate Pelagians, who would themselves have pronounced anathema even on Pelagius if he had come to his senses; not even Quesnel would judge Zosimus or Sixtus to have been such men.]

I have no doubt that these words refer especially to Zosimus and Sixtus; indeed, the entire manner of the letter persuades me of this. The African legates therefore approached the emperor, who was then staying at Ravenna, so that by a royal edict he might reinforce with his own sanction the sentence pronounced in Africa against Coelestius and confirmed by the authority of the apostolic see through the replies of Innocent.

The matter was urgent, and there was grave danger that, if Zosimus issued a judgment contrary to that of Innocent and the Africans—as it was believed he was about to do—a destructive schism might arise between the two Churches. The emperor granted the just request. After considering the African proceedings and decrees, he issued his constitution on the day before the Kalends of May in this year, 418.

Some will laugh at this account as resembling a dream, because they think that the constitution was issued after Zosimus’s decree and *Tractoria*, and only as a result of this pontiff’s prompting. This is the opinion of Baronius, Jansenius, Rigberius in his notes on Marius, Noris in book I of his *History of Pelagianism*, Garnerius, and perhaps others.

Although I would be very reluctant to separate myself from the company of the learned, I nevertheless think that I can establish by substantial conjectures that my opinion is consistent with the truth.

## XXIV. The sentence of Zosimus was not issued before the Kalends of May. The Roman synod was convened on 15 April

1. Anyone can readily convince himself that Zosimus’s condemnation of Coelestius was not issued before Honorius’s edict of the day before the Kalends of May, provided he recalls that the Africans’ letters, which according to St. Augustine in book II *To Boniface*, chapter 3, Zosimus was awaiting in order to be more fully instructed concerning Coelestius’s case before issuing his sentence, were received by the pontiff around the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, on which day he sent his reply to the Africans.
