[Note: It will be proved in Observations, § 9, that Zosimus condemned Coelestius before Honorius’s law; there the following conjectures of Quesnel will be examined.]

The remaining part of Lent and all the time up to 14 April was devoted to religious observance, as well as to the solemn octave of the Paschal feast, which fell on that day in the year 418, Easter itself having occurred on 7 April. It is therefore surprising that Joannes Garnerius argues on page 216 that the synod was held on 15 April, immediately after the completion of the festal days, and that the sanction was issued on the day before the Kalends of May after the proceedings had been delivered to Honorius.

To oppose Garnerius first with Garnerius himself: why does he think that a council could have been held in Rome on 15 April, when, upon reading that the African council had been convened on the fifth day before the Kalends of May—that is, 27 April—in the year 399, he argues that an error had entered the passage, and that either the Kalends had been written instead of the Ides, or May instead of June, lest something grossly irregular be alleged, contrary to the canons religiously observed in other councils? Was the Roman Church less conscientious than the African? Or was what was irregular among the Africans canonical among the Romans?

2. By what means could the bishops whom he asserts, and whom we admit, were present at the synod have gathered in Rome on 15 April itself? A devout man would not have summoned them from their own Churches before the solemn octave of the Neophytes had been completed. Once it had been completed on the fourteenth day, those who lived somewhat farther from the city could not have arrived on the following day except by being transported there by divine miracle.

Yet, as Garnerius himself admits, bishops had to be summoned from distant provinces, since he asserts from his own Marius Mercator that the hearing was a fuller one. Then Coelestius had to be summoned according to the legal form. When he failed to appear after being summoned—which could not have been known until at least several days later—the summons had to be issued again, and after several more intervening days a third summons had to be announced.

This was the unshaken law of judicial proceedings, which we see carefully observed against Eutyches by the Fathers of the Fourth Council.

[Note: Eutyches was summoned not by the Fathers of the Fourth, or Chalcedonian, Council, but by the Fathers of the Council of Constantinople, whose proceedings were nevertheless read and inserted at Chalcedon, act 1. Although Eutyches was summoned three times with some interval between the summonses, the interval was not as long as Quesnel seems to require. The second summons was made on 15 November, and the third was issued late on the same day, to be announced to him on the following day so that he might come on the day after. That this was not an unshaken rule is clear from the Council of Chalcedon itself, act 3, where we learn that Dioscorus was summoned three times on the same day.]

Coelestius had complained in an even louder voice that this rule had been neglected in his own case, and against Zosimus’s judgment he shamelessly spewed out whatever subsequently came into his mouth.

I fear that a large part of the fourteen days allotted by the author under discussion—up to the day before the Kalends of May—for preparing, completing, writing out, publishing, and delivering the judgment to the Emperor had already elapsed; yet the case had scarcely been touched upon. Zosimus himself wrote only a few days earlier that the matter required great deliberation and had to be decided by the highest tribunal (Letter 10 to the Africans, III).

For this to happen, once the judges had been assembled for that fuller hearing, everything that had hitherto been done against the heretic, both in Rome and in Africa, had to be reviewed. The Africans’ longer and more numerous letters had to be read, and that enormous volume of synodal documents which had been awaited from Africa had to be carefully examined. The votes of each individual judge had to be heard.

Then, once deliberation had begun concerning the sentence to be issued against Coelestius, the constitution had to be forged and every one of its words weighed in the balance. Indeed, the entire tradition of the holy Fathers concerning the subject had to be examined, investigated, and brought into mutual comparison with the decree, so that a judgment worthy of the apostolic see might emerge in a matter of faith.

After this, how much time was needed to write out the extensive or lengthy documents by which the heretic was utterly condemned, as Marius Mercator says? Those documents contained the very chapters on which he had been accused, and in them the whole case, both that of the aforementioned Coelestius and that of Pelagius, his still more wicked teacher, appears to have been narrated.

I do not even mention that similar and identical documents still had to be copied and sent to the bishops, as the same Marius testifies, to the Eastern Churches, the diocese of Egypt, Constantinople, Thessalonica, and Jerusalem. To these I add the provinces of Italy, Spain, and Africa, where the case had arisen; Gaul, from which the accusations had been transmitted; and Britain, which Pelagius, who certainly came from there, had infected.

I say nothing of these matters, since it may be replied that they could have been done at leisure, even if that response is gratuitous. But copies of all these documents undoubtedly had to be delivered to the emperor at Ravenna. It is reasonable to believe that he read everything carefully before confirming it by his constitution, especially since Zosimus had previously appeared rather favorably disposed toward Coelestius.

Hardly a month, or even two, would suffice for all these matters to be properly and carefully completed. It is therefore highly probable that the work had not been brought to an end before the Kalends of June.

It should also be observed that the words of Marius, as reported above, imply—and the same author further testifies in chapters 2 and 3 of the *Memorandum*—that not only Coelestius’s case but also Pelagius’s was examined in that Roman judgment. His speeches and his commentaries on the Apostle Paul were investigated, and, according to this writer of the same period, more extensive excerpts from them were inserted into Zosimus’s *Tractoria*. Such an examination could not have been completed in a short time.

## XXV. Honorius is silent about Zosimus’s sentence in his constitution but mentions the African sentence

3. If Zosimus’s decree against Pelagius and Coelestius had already been composed and issued when the imperial edict was enacted, Honorius would certainly not have omitted mention of it.

[Note: When the imperial law was requested of Zosimus, his decree, or Tractoria, against Pelagius and Coelestius had not yet been composed and issued; but it was requested after the condemnation and judgment, as we shall show in § 9. It is therefore unsurprising that Zosimus’s decree is not mentioned in the law itself. Nevertheless, the disturbances stirred up at Rome are sufficiently indicated; we shall prove in the same place that the emperor could have learned of them not from the Africans, but from Zosimus, especially after that condemnation, when supporters of the Pelagian heresy had promoted them there.] Nor would he have said in the edict that he had learned from widespread report of a new trick of the heretics, or added below that recent rumor had touched his ears that they had spread their poison within the most sacred city. Rather, he would have said that he had learned this from the letters of the bishop of the City and from the sentence issued by him—especially since it was in the interest of the Catholic cause that everyone should know, by an imperial document, that Zosimus, repentant of his former delay, had drawn the sword of excommunication against the heretics.

4. When, in the following year, he wrote to Aurelius, he recalls this earlier edict and asserts that, in issuing it, he followed the judgment of the Africans.[^c0110-1] He says nothing about Zosimus’s judgment; to have passed over it while mentioning another would have been wholly unjust and contrary to the reverence due to the primary see. The fact that he likewise remained silent about Innocent does not have the same explanation, because he had not so much treated the Africans’ judgment as his own as he had adopted it.

[^c0110-1]: This argument will be resolved in the *Observations*, no. 47 and following.

5. When Augustus issued his constitution, Caelestius was staying in Rome; for the emperor orders him to be expelled from the city: “With Caelestius and Pelagius, the chief leaders of the detestable doctrine, expelled from the City in the first instance,” he says. But when the pontiff issued his own judgment—or rather, when Caelestius was summoned to trial—“he not only,” says Marius, “did not appear, but also fled from the aforesaid Roman city, and for this reason was most severely condemned by Zosimus of blessed memory.”

I know what may be answered: that Pelagius was not then in Rome, even though Honorius likewise ordered him to be expelled. But in this passage Caelestius is mentioned immediately after him, so that the punishment might not distinguish between those whom fellowship in the same doctrine united. Otherwise the words of the edict would be superfluous, unless at least one of the two had then been present in Rome.

“But,” you will say, “Augustine’s reproach concerning Caelestius’s flight was unjust, as was Zosimus’s command summoning him to trial, if he had already been driven from the City by the emperor’s edict.” It was not so. This first edict was indeed threatening, but in such a way that, if the heretics, hastening to the pontiff’s judgment, abandoned their impious doctrines, they would undoubtedly have been left exempt from punishment. Augustine therefore reproaches Caelestius’s flight with perfect justice: it was persuaded not so much by Augustus’s edict as by the obstinacy of his error.

The matter was no longer the examination of Caelestius’s doctrine, but the implementation of his promise—namely, his answer that he agreed with the letters of Pope Innocent. Had he made that profession in an unambiguous written statement, he would have rendered Augustus’s edict ineffective.

Furthermore, that this first constitution was not put into effect is indicated by the emperor’s letter to Aurelius, preserved in chapter 16 of our code:

> It had long before been decreed that Pelagius and Caelestius should be expelled from the city of Rome . . . but because the persistent evil of their obstinate crime demanded that the constitution be repeated, we have also decreed by a recent sanction, etc.

He does not say that the heretics had been expelled from the City, but only that it had been decreed that they should be expelled. Hence I suspect either that the edict was declared to Zosimus alone, in order to hasten the trial, or that Palladius delayed its promulgation at Zosimus’s suggestion until Zosimus himself had delivered his judgment.

6. Augustus concludes his edict with these words:

> It is pleasing that proclamations of this kind be disseminated throughout almost the entire world over which our empire extends, lest the concealment of knowledge perhaps provide nourishment for error, and lest anyone think that he may with impunity dare what he pretends to have been unaware was condemned by public authority.

[^c0110-2]: There was no reason to fear the Catholics, who obeyed the apostolic judgment. But there was certainly reason to fear that the heretics, if they were not restrained by law, might stir up new disturbances. For this reason Honorius ordered the law itself to be promulgated, lest the prince’s concealment provide nourishment for error, or lest anyone pretend to be unaware of the same law.

Certainly, if Zosimus’s decree had already been sent throughout the whole world, there would have been no fear that concealment would provide nourishment for error, or that anyone would pretend to be unaware of what had likewise been disseminated throughout not merely the Roman but the Christian world by the pontiff’s care.

7. The condition of the Roman Church described in the emperor’s edict is altogether the condition that existed when Pope Zosimus, the presbyter Sixtus, and other Roman clerics more favorably disposed toward Caelestius and Pelagius were on the point of declaring both of them innocent.[^c0110-3] For, as Augustus puts it, within the most sacred City and elsewhere,

> the pestiferous poison of certain persons had so taken root in their hearts that, when the path of straightforward belief had been broken and their partisan zeal had been split into factions, the material of an unappeased dissension had been introduced; and, when a new fuel for scandal had been kindled, the tranquillity of the most blessed Church was tottering. Some were pursuing one course, others another, through uncertain interpretation, and, according to the capacity of their shifting ingenuity, were raising a question concerning profane novelties.

[^c0110-3]: Rather, it was the condition that existed after the rescripts of the Africans and Zosimus’s judgment against Caelestius and Pelagius. See the *Observations*, nos. 41–42.

These words vividly portray the dissensions that Caelestius’s devices had stirred up in the Roman Church. On the one side, the chief pontiff and his principal assistant, the presbyter Sixtus, appeared to have been ensnared by the heretics; on the other, certain members of the same clergy, holding fast to sound doctrine and to Innocent’s decree, were fighting with their whole heart for the Catholic faith and peace.

But nothing of this kind existed in the City after Zosimus had pronounced judgment against Caelestius. The heretic no longer created disturbances in that Church, from which he had fled. There was no longer a divided opinion among the leading clergy, for they had all united in condemning Caelestius and Pelagius, with Sixtus, first of all, pronouncing an anathema against them before a very large assembly, as Augustine says in Letter 105.

The followers of Pelagius and Caelestius no longer spread their poison. Rather, as the same teacher writes in Letter 104, they were suddenly seen to have fallen silent; they were altogether silent, suppressed by great fear (Letter 105), and suppressed into profound silence by fear whatever they felt. Their very silence showed that they were sufficiently terrified, even though some did not cease to feel the same perversity, or even to whisper it.

8. From Saint Augustine’s Letter 157 we understand that, when he wrote it, Zosimus’s recent *Tractoria* condemning Pelagius and Caelestius had only just reached the Africans. This is suggested by his words:

> We have taken care to send you copies of the recent writings concerning them—whether those addressed specifically to the Africans or those that proceeded universally to all the bishops from the aforesaid see—in case they have perhaps not yet reached your holiness. We received them from those brethren to whom we also entrusted this letter, so that they might forward them to your reverence.

These letters were written either while Augustine was in Caesarea of Mauretania, not for the conference with Emeritus, which began on 20 September, but, as Possidius writes in the *Life of Saint Augustine* (chapter 14), to settle other necessities of the Church in accordance with letters from the apostolic see; or, I should say, while he was there, or even after his return. The following words appear to indicate the latter:

> Those letters which you sent to Caesarea of Mauretania arrived while I was present at Caesarea, where an ecclesiastical necessity had drawn us at the command of the venerable Pope Zosimus, bishop of the apostolic see.

For the pluperfect tense expressed in the words “had drawn us” seems to indicate that Augustine was no longer staying there when he wrote. Nor was there really any reason why the holy teacher, occupied with public affairs, should have replied more hastily to Optatus’s letter, which had not been written to him but had been shared with him by a friend.

Moreover, who would believe that, if Zosimus’s constitution had already been issued long before, it was sent to Africa so late? The reputation of the pontiff and the Roman clergy made it very important that it arrive there as quickly as possible.

9. Saint Augustine, in Book II *To Boniface*, chapter 3, reports that the Pelagians complained about the Roman clerics, writing that they, struck by the terror of a command, had not been ashamed to commit the crime of treachery, so that, contrary to their earlier judgment—by which they had supported Catholic doctrine in their formal acts—they later declared that human nature was evil.

[^c0110-4]: That Zosimus himself is included under the name “Roman clerics,” and that the words “struck by the terror of a command” do not refer to Honorius’s law, will be clear from the *Observations*, no. 50.

There can be no doubt that he wishes Zosimus himself, together with his associates, to be included under the name of the Roman clerics. Other passages of Augustine testify that Julian accused Zosimus himself of treachery:

> And yet, he says in Book I *Against Julian*, chapter 4, you accuse the successor of Innocent of the crime of treachery, because he did not wish to oppose apostolic doctrine and the judgment of his predecessor.

The same point appears in Book VI, chapter 12.

Julian therefore compares Zosimus’s earlier hearing with the later one. He maintains that in the first judgment the pontiff and the Roman clerics had supported Catholic doctrine, since Caelestius had departed almost acquitted, as is clear from Zosimus’s letters, and since the profession of faith made by Caelestius and Pelagius had been approved as agreeing with Catholic doctrine. But afterward, in the later judgment—when, after the heretics’ tricks had been exposed, they affirmed the Catholic doctrine concerning original sin—they declared that human nature was evil.

Here, therefore, we have Zosimus’s decree. The Pelagians, however, accuse the Romans of having issued it after being struck by the terror of a command and thus of having fallen into the crime of treachery. What else does the heretic understand by “the command” than the imperial edict? This passage therefore proves that the edict was issued before Zosimus’s constitution.

Yet Augustine says nothing in reply to this objection concerning the terror of the command, since he knew both that he and his fellow Africans had requested Honorius’s edict and that the emperor had issued it before Zosimus’s judgment appeared.

## XXVI. At what point in the edict Honorius mentions Zosimus’s decree. Possidius is challenged and explained

I would not have guessed what could be objected to this assertion of ours. But now Garnerius appears and points with his finger to a passage in the edict of Augustus Honorius to Palladius in which, if God wills, Zosimus’s judgment and that of the Roman Church are most plainly indicated. He therefore proves that the pontiff’s decree preceded Augustus’s constitution.

These are the words of the edict:

> ACTS OF THE MOST BLESSED CHURCH

They are printed in capital letters, so that they may not escape the readers’ eyes. Certainly they are words of decree—but where in the world are the acts, and in what sense are they to be understood?

Garnerius published the entire constitution on page 239. Partly by comparing editions and partly with the aid of manuscript codices, he corrected many remaining errors after the most careful recension of the Magdeburg editors, Baronius, Salmasius, Labbe, and Baluze. I read and reread it, but I find nothing in Garnerius’s edition—or in any other—that gives rise to the slightest suspicion of acts of a synod held by the Roman Church against the Pelagians.

He says:

> The pestiferous poison of certain persons had so taken root in their hearts that . . . when a new fuel for scandal had been kindled, the tranquillity of the most blessed Church was tottering, though as yet unassailed.

Where is the synod? Where is the judgment? Where are the acts?

I turn to the notes, in case the understanding of the mystery has been reserved there. I see that Salmasius, Usserius, and Labbe read: “The acts of the most blessed Church and its assailed tranquillity are tottering.” But this, as Garnerius immediately observes, is less elegant.

Thus he takes his argument from a less elegant and rejected reading. Having rejected the more accurate correction, he restores to favor the reading that had been brought into the text but was spurious, so that it might support a desperate cause. Yet however the passage is read, it does nothing to assist the argument; it is no nearer to it than heaven is to earth.

The other passages quoted from Augustine likewise contain nothing at all that resolves the proposed question, as even the opposing writers themselves admit.

What is drawn from Possidius, however, in the *Life of Saint Augustine*, chapter 18, may appear somewhat stronger.[^c0110-5] He writes:

> But those bishops of the apostolic see, Innocent and Zosimus, in their different periods, marking the same Pelagians and cutting them off from the members of the Church, declared by letters sent to the African Churches and to the Churches of the East and West that they were to be anathematized and avoided by all Catholics. When the most pious emperor Honorius heard and followed this judgment pronounced against them by the Catholic Church of God, he decreed by his own laws that they should be regarded as condemned heretics.

[^c0110-5]: In the *Observations*, no. 44, we shall see from a combination of Possidius’s testimony with those of other witnesses and arguments that it is contrary to Quesnellus’s position.

Even Garnerius does not yet acknowledge this as sufficient to resolve the question. Henry Norisius nevertheless presses it more confidently against Usserius and Salmasius, failing to notice that Possidius praises two judgments of the urban pontiff: one of Innocent and the other of Zosimus. Honorius, having heard and followed the first from the Africans, confirmed it by his constitution, as Honorius himself testifies in his letter to Aurelius.

Nor does the learned man remember that Honorius issued two edicts and made a repeated constitution, as he expressly testifies in the same letter. Possidius himself suggests this when he does not say “by his law” but “by his laws.” The latter of these laws could have followed Zosimus’s judgment, while the former—the one about which the question is raised—was issued at the insistence of the African Church.

## XXVII. Honorius’s constitution issued at the insistence of the Africans

1. Although this part already remains sufficiently clear from what has preceded, it is nevertheless confirmed more fully by the proofs that follow.

Our first proof comes from the words of Honorius’s letter to Aurelius, some of which have already been cited. When the emperor says:

> It had long before been decreed that Pelagius and Caelestius, the discoverers of an unspeakable doctrine, should be expelled from the city of Rome as a kind of contagion harmful to Catholic welfare,

he undoubtedly designates the constitution issued on the day before the Kalends of May of the preceding year—that is, thirteen months earlier.

He expressly states that this very constitution was issued with the African judgment in view:

> In this matter, he says, our clemency followed the judgment of your holiness, by which it is established that they were condemned by all after a just examination of the judgment.

[^c0110-6]: We shall explain this second law of Honorius in the *Observations*, nos. 47–48, in such a way that it will provide Quesnellus no support.

Everyone reads “by which it is established” (*quo constat*), not, as Garnerius does, “since it is established” (*cum constet*).

The words are clear and require no interpreter. Garnerius therefore corrupts them more than he explains them when he attempts to dispose of them. For when, on page 243, he goes back to the judgment of the Council of Carthage in 412, which he thinks the emperor had before his eyes when he issued the edict, I scarcely think the learned man wrote this sincerely, nor do I think he requires us to believe it.

Who could persuade himself that Augustus had in mind a judgment held six full years earlier in a provincial synod at Carthage, a judgment later obscured by a more careful examination, by several more recent apostolic rescripts and judgments, and by proceedings that had been almost entirely completed? Augustine does not even mention it in Letter 47 to Valentinus when he sends him all the documents of this case.

Who, I say, would think that this synod was the one mentioned, while the more recent synods from Numidia and the proconsular province were set aside—synods that Innocent had confirmed by his rescripts and that were followed by other, more numerous and almost plenary synods, as we have stated and proved?

Furthermore, the passage mentions the African judgment by which it is established that the Pelagians were condemned by all after a just examination of the judgment. No one will understand this of the first Council of Carthage unless he admits that Garnerius, since no report had yet been sent to the apostolic see, recognized that council as possessing authority outside the proconsular province, or at least outside Africa.

I have already pointed out the device by which he evades the force of this argument: he substitutes *cum constet* for *quo constat*, and thus interprets the edict on page 243 as referring to the examination held before the apostolic see under Zosimus, after whose *Tractoria*, sent to all, it followed that the Pelagians were condemned by all.

But however freely he may alter the text of the edict according to what he judges convenient to his cause, he has achieved nothing. I have already shown that Zosimus’s writing could not have been sent to the provinces before the Kalends of May, and that this correction, which closely resembles a corruption, overturns the thread and meaning of the sentence—not to mention that all printed and manuscript codices contradict such a correction.

2. A second proof is supplied by the heading of the imperial edict, which appears in both manuscript copies of our Roman codex:

> Sacred rescript, after receiving the acts of the aforesaid synod.

[^c0110-7]: This proof will be rejected in the *Observations*, no. 46.

We rightly invoke this heading as an authority, since it comes from a most ancient monument of the Roman Church, although Garnerius objects; we have already examined the reasons for his objection.

From whom, then, did Honorius receive the acts of the synod, unless from the Africans? To whom did he send the rescript, unless to the Africans? For what other reason did he send an imperial document concerning the Africans, unless because he had been pressed by those same people to issue it?

The Oxford and Thuaneus manuscripts are supported by the Baluze manuscript and by the manuscript from Arras cited by the eminent Cardinal Baronius. In these, this constitution of Honorius was called a rescript.

Augustine himself is an unimpeachable witness in Book III, chapter 1, *Against Julian*, where he addresses him in these words:

> Certainly, as you say, if the emperor’s answer was rather in your favor, why do you not come forward?

It is therefore certain that it was a rescript, and we shall continue to regard it as such until Garnerius proves from more certain and more authoritative monuments what history demonstrates not to have been properly a rescript but a constitution: the emperor did not issue a rescript in response either to anyone who made a request by letter or to anyone who consulted him in writing.

3. From the sequence of the edict it is clear that the principal articles of the Pelagian doctrine had been reported and laid before the emperor. By whom? Certainly not by Zosimus or the Roman clerics, who were still wavering in uncertainty and would not have acted so that their bishop’s constitution against the heretics should be anticipated by the emperor’s edict.

Therefore they were reported by the Africans, in whose hands the whole matter lay, and by whom, as Garnerius says, every avenue was tested by which they might avert either damage to the faith or disgrace to themselves.

[^c0110-8]: Rather, it was Zosimus who had already delivered judgment before the imperial law, as we shall demonstrate in the *Observations*; it was not the Africans, whose embassy to the emperor will there be shown to be fictitious.

4. To this may be referred the complaint of the raging heretics,[^c0110-9] who assail Saints Augustine and Alypius with the most abusive insults, as though they were the authors or procurers of the imperial edicts.

[^c0110-9]: This complaint of the Pelagians belongs to the period of the second law but is wrongly transferred to the earlier law. See the *Observations*, no. 49.

“Why,” Julian says, “did you stir up the whole of Italy with such factions? Why did you provoke riots at Rome by hiring crowds? Why did you fatten throughout almost all Africa herds of horses at the expense of the poor, and, with Alypius accompanying them, assign them to tribunes and centurions? Why did you corrupt the powers of the world with the inheritances offered by matrons, so that the straw of public fury might blaze against us? Why did you stain the reign of a religious prince with the impiety of persecutions?”

These words seem to me to belong rather to Honorius’s earlier edict than to the later one. Since the later edict was issued after the pontiff’s judgment, Julian could more plausibly attribute it to the prayers and exertions of Augustine than to those of the Africans; the earlier edict, however, could have been procured only through the Africans.

Furthermore, the statements about Italy being stirred up and riots being provoked at Rome are to be understood, conversely, of the zeal of the Roman clergy on Caelestius’s side. At the beginning of the inquiry they had favored Pelagius and Caelestius, but afterward pronounced anathema against both, not without the efforts and exertions of the Africans.

## XXVIII. What took place at Ravenna while Valerius was there, through the efforts of the African bishops

5. The very close relationship that Augustine and Alypius had with Count Valerius,[^c0110-10] who possessed both the most ardent zeal against the Pelagians and the highest favor with the emperor, does not allow us to believe that this golden pair of bishops—so deeply concerned for the Catholic cause, which was then in danger at Rome—failed, through that count, to inform the emperor about the whole affair: what the Roman support for Caelestius was, what damage to the Church’s doctrine was feared from their judgment, and finally what needed to be done so that the impending danger might be met as quickly as possible by imperial authority.

[^c0110-10]: What took place at Ravenna while Valerius was acting will be explained in the *Observations*, no. 32. There we shall also eliminate the claim that Vindemialis’s embassy was undertaken to obtain Honorius’s law with the assistance of Valerius, a claim that Quesnellus attempts to establish in what follows.

We are moved to believe that this really happened by more than conjecture. For from the dedicatory letter of Saint Augustine to Count Valerius, prefixed to Book I *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, we learn that Augustine and Valerius exchanged several letters—and, unless I am mistaken, concerning the cause of the Church.

All agree that this first book was written by Augustine in 418, and the letter addressed to Valerius indicates this. The passage from chapter 5 of Book I *To Boniface*, which some cite to prove the point, does not seem to me to prove it. For although Augustine says that he wrote the book after the condemnation of Pelagius and Caelestius,[^c0110-11] he does not say which condemnation he means. By that time, before Zosimus’s decree, there had already been the Palestinian, Constantinopolitan, and African proceedings—both provincial and plenary.

[^c0110-11]: He undoubtedly means the condemnation by which both were condemned by Zosimus. That this condemnation preceded the writing of this book is evident from Book II of the *Retractions*, in which, at chapter 53, two books addressed to Valerius are recorded after the proceedings with Emeritus, dated 20 September 418. In the preceding chapter, 50, the holy teacher had written of their condemnation: “After the Pelagian heresy, with its authors, had been convicted and condemned by the bishops of the Roman Church, first under Innocent and then under Zosimus . . .” See more in the *Observations*, nos. 31 and following, where these matters are established more fully.

Joannes Garnerius asserts that the book was written after Augustine’s return from Caesarea of Mauretania—that is, around the middle of October. I do not see why it should have been delayed so long. For in Book II of the *Retractions* he mentions both books after the journey to Mauretania for no other reason than that, through the addition of the second book, the work was not completed until after that time.

At least this much is certain, and it is sufficient: the book was written shortly after Zosimus’s judgment had been issued. The holy teacher admits in chapter 35 that he had found it burdensome to dictate the work during the brief periods when he was free, and that he composed it amid his ecclesiastical cares. Perhaps by these words he indicates the very period of ecclesiastical necessity imposed by Zosimus, which, in Letter 157 to Optatus, he says had drawn him to Caesarea.

It is equally certain that before that time Augustine had written several letters to Count Valerius. The importance of the matters discussed in them is proved by the anxiety and distress caused by Valerius’s delay in replying.[^c0110-12]

[^c0110-12]: In the *Observations*, § 7, we shall show that this and the following testimonies provide Quesnellus no support.

> Although I had long been troubled that I had written several times and had received no reply from your Sublimity, suddenly I received three letters from your graciousness: one addressed not to me alone and sent through my fellow bishop Vindemialis, and, not long afterward, two through my fellow presbyter Firmus.

You see that Augustine wrote to Valerius many times. You see when: namely, at the time when the first examination of Caelestius was being held at Rome. For intervals of time must be assumed between Augustine’s letters, during which a reply to the earlier letters could have been awaited before the later ones were sent—and indeed long intervals, both because of the distance between the places and so that we may not attribute hasty and premature impatience to Augustine, whose patience was so great.

You see, moreover, that the replies from the imperial court were eagerly awaited. This shows that the contents of the letters were not insignificant or merely personal conversation. Valerius had not neglected to reply; he simply had not found an opportunity to send the letters. Meanwhile he had omitted nothing that he could obtain from the emperor for the cause of the Church, and he pursued it with all his solicitude.

But—and this is what I especially wish to be noticed in these words—do you not see an African bishop returning from the imperial court? The name Vindemialis was familiar among the Africans. Do you not see him returning at approximately the time when Honorius’s edict, issued on the day before the Kalends of May, could have been carried to Africa?

It is not plausible that he had gone there of his own accord at a time when such great matters were being debated in Africa. It is far more likely that his fellow African bishops had delegated him concerning the faith and the cause of the heretics. We read that he returned from there with a letter from Count Valerius addressed to the African bishops.

What else can Augustine’s highly significant words imply?

> I received three letters from your Sublimity, one of them addressed not to me alone.

Surely this indicates that the reply was addressed to the bishops from whom Augustine had previously received letters through Bishop Vindemialis. They would not have sent him to Ravenna except on matters of the utmost secrecy and importance, whereas they had sent only one subdeacon to Rome to Zosimus.

What those matters were, although anyone may readily infer them from the situation of that period, need not be established here. Augustine himself speaks of them in several places, though somewhat obscurely, as was appropriate:

> We have heard, he says in the same letter to Count Valerius, how great is your concern that no one should lie in wait for Christ’s members while covered by the cloak of Christ’s name, whether among the more recent enemies; and how watchful you are for the salvation of these same enemies and hostile to their error. We have usually heard such things, and others of the same kind, from others also; but now, through the brother mentioned above, we have learned them more fully and more clearly.

Everyone sees who those more recent enemies of Christ were: they were undoubtedly the Pelagians. But when and how had Valerius shown himself watchful for their salvation and hostile to their error, unless by using his influence with Honorius to obtain an edict by which, unless they repudiated their sacrilegious doctrine, they would be expelled from the City and subjected to other punishments?

These are the matters concerning Valerius that Augustine then learned more clearly. Before that edict, nothing had proceeded from the imperial court against the Pelagians, who had scarcely become known in Italy before Zosimus’s pontificate.

Augustine speaks still more clearly in Book I *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 2. Explaining the principal reason why he wished to write to Valerius about this matter, he says:

> Another reason is that you resisted these profane novelties, against which we here contend by argument, by dealing with them through your authority and by pressing the matter.

What had Valerius dealt with by his authority? What had he obtained through his insistence? How had he effectively resisted these profane novelties? What else could it be than that, through his authority and diligence, he brought about the issuing by Honorius of that edict against the heretics?

Julian strongly complains of this in the words quoted by Augustine in Book I, chapter 10, of the now completed work formerly called *The Unfinished Work*, edited with the learned diligence of Vignerius, priest of the Oratory of Jesus. Julian attacks Augustine’s words quoted above, mixing falsehoods with truths and even exposing truths by means of falsehoods:

> He also praises a powerful man because, against our petitions—we were crying out for nothing other than that judges be appointed for so important a matter, so that what had plainly been done by subterfuge might be corrected rather than punished by examination—he opposed us by the weight of his rank and did not allow us to obtain either time or a place for a hearing. Whether the person to whom he writes acted as wickedly as the praise itself bears witness, let him see for himself.

This passage sheds considerable light on Augustine’s words quoted above in praise of Valerius. What Augustine praises in that most pious count when he says, “You resisted these profane novelties by dealing with them through your authority and by pressing the matter,” is precisely what Julian maliciously complains of: that Valerius opposed their petitions by the weight of his rank. They were crying out for nothing other than the appointment of judges, so that what had plainly been done by subterfuge might be corrected rather than punished by examination.

Julian’s words cannot be understood of the later judgment, by which the Pelagians would seek to have Zosimus’s sentence corrected. For with what shamelessness could they have called that sentence a matter of subterfuge, when a whole year had been allotted for its preparation, and when it had been issued by a judge who throughout that period had lent them a more favorable ear, sent letters to the Africans on their behalf, and had done everything short of acquitting them?

What Julian writes here, therefore, is exactly what Caelestius was demanding after the death of Pope Innocent and before Zosimus’s judgment. Zosimus himself bears witness to this in the first of his three letters to the Africans: Caelestius had presented himself for examination at Rome, asking that what had been improperly impressed upon the apostolic see concerning him should be cleared away.

Julian asserts, on the basis of Augustine’s praise, that Valerius’s persistence prevented this examination from having a place and time:

> He did not allow time or a place for a hearing,

because, clearly, Honorius’s edict was issued through the Africans’ representations and Valerius’s diligence. By it, Caelestius and Pelagius were ordered to leave the City; their followers, convicted and condemned as assertors of a new doctrine, were to be brought before judges; and they were to be punished by the relentless deportation of exile, as Augustus says.

Thus the imperial edict, by which the judgments of Pope Innocent and the Africans were given binding force, preceded Zosimus’s judgment. It was feared that Caelestius would soon be pardoned, since he had already been almost acquitted in two of Zosimus’s letters.[^c0110-13]

[^c0110-13]: From Zosimus’s letters, and even more from the acts of Caelestius’s first hearing, it was inferred that he ought to be shown indulgence if he actually condemned what he had promised to condemn. The Africans feared only that he might conceal poison beneath lies and frauds. For this reason, once his deceptions had been exposed, they fortified Zosimus with definite safeguards so that he would not be deceived. See what will be discussed in the *Observations*, nos. 34 and following.

Saint Augustine does not deny this; indeed, he confesses it most clearly. Responding above to Julian’s words, in which Julian had added that Augustine’s praises of Valerius sufficiently showed what Augustine desired—namely, that the contest should be carried on by savage force and blind power contrary to reason, faith, and every holiness of morals and doctrine—Augustine answers Julian in such a way that he does not deny that Valerius, using his rank and authority, prevented there from being a place for examination and time for a hearing.

On the contrary, Augustine freely concedes the whole point. He says that the emperor did nothing wrong against the faith, but acted for the faith and from the faith, and that he had justly imposed coercion.

Julian either drew, or could have drawn, an objection from the example of the Donatists: not long before, they had been invited and admitted to a public conference and had been given a place and time to defend their cause. Augustine answers by pointing out the difference between the cases. His words are clearer than midday sunlight:

> Far be it from Christian powers of the earthly commonwealth to doubt the ancient Catholic faith and for that reason provide its attackers with a place and time for examination. Rather, being certain and firmly established in that faith, let them impose the discipline of coercion upon enemies such as you are. What was done on account of the Donatists was forced by their exceedingly violent disturbances, since they were ignorant of what had previously taken place and had to be shown to them. May the Lord avert your having such disturbances; yet, by God’s favor, you do not have them.

6. What we have just said gains no small amount of clarity and force from the memorandum that Pope Zosimus gave to Faustinus and the other legates when he sent them to the Africans. It consisted of four points, preserved in the letter of the African council to Pope Boniface.

The first, third, and fourth concerned appeals by bishops and the transfer of cases to Rome, as well as the adjudication of other clerics’ cases by neighboring bishops. The second point of the memorandum was as follows:

> Bishops are not to sail to the imperial court at an inconvenient time.

When this is compared with what has been recounted above, who would not immediately think that African bishops had recently sailed to the imperial court to obtain something from Honorius that displeased Zosimus and seemed to him to have been obtained importunately?

On what occasion could this have happened except in the Pelagian affair, which had occupied the Africans exclusively during the preceding year?

It should also be observed that the Africans gave no answer to this point of the memorandum, as though they had openly admitted that they had sent an embassy to the imperial court; nor did they allow anything belonging to their right to be taken from them in this matter.

[^c0110-14]: We shall remove this conjecture and interpretation in the same *Observations*, no. 33.

[Col. 0990D] **XXIX. The fictitious embassy of Alypius at this time.**—From what we have said about Bishop Vindemialis being sent to Ravenna, to the imperial court, to secure the issuance of a constitution, and also from the silence of the writers, the conjecture of those who on that occasion supposed Alypius to have been sent by the Africans as an envoy to Italy disappears—if, indeed, there are any who ever held that view. For when Joannes Garnerius attributes this opinion to the most learned Cardinal Baronius, the learned man certainly suffered a lapse of memory. Indeed, one cannot find even the slightest indication in the *Annals* that would suggest such a suspicion; on the contrary, under the year 418, no. 19, he expressly writes:

“When Pelagius and Caelestius had been condemned at Rome by Pope Zosimus and the sacred college of clergy, and letters concerning their condemnation had been written by that same Zosimus to all the bishops of the Catholic Church, a rescript of the Emperor Honorius against those same heretics immediately followed.”

The cardinal therefore did not believe that in this year 418 Alypius, as the author writes, had undertaken an embassy on behalf of the African Church to the emperor against the councils of Zosimus, deceived by Pelagian arts, and had obtained from him a decree forbidding Caelestius—who seemed in part to have been absolved by the apostolic see—from remaining at Rome.

820 Here is the origin of the entire error. Garnerius confuses the year 418 with 419, the pontificate of Zosimus with the episcopate of Boniface, the African council of the former year with the later synod, the edict of Honorius in 418 with his letter to Aurelius written in the following year, and what Baronius said about Alypius’s embassy undertaken to obtain this rescript with the other embassy. Moreover, he still sins against the evidence of the *Annals* when he says that Alypius was sent as an envoy by the African Church, rather than by that plenary synod which he subsequently discusses after narrating Alypius’s embassy, treating it as unrelated to that synod. We do not, therefore, deny that Alypius undertook this mission on account of Garnerius’s argument, but because we have shown that it is at least probable that Vindemialis performed that service, whereas nothing whatever can be asserted about Alypius except by conjecture.

Vindemialis, then, reached Ravenna, while the subdeacon Marcellinus went to Rome. The latter delivered to Zosimus the letters, the synodal acts, and the other instructions; the former presented to the emperor Honorius and to the Count Valerius the written documents of the Africans and explained the purpose of his embassy. The cause was that of the Church, the cause of the apostolic see, which had condemned the Pelagians through the mouth of Innocent. For that reason Augustus undertook its defense with his authority, his zeal being kindled by Valerius, who used his power, took care of the matter, and pressed it effectively, as Augustine testifies. [Col. 0991C] Thus at last he either immediately brought back a definite report concerning the constitution soon to be issued against the heretics, or sent a reply to the Africans.

**XXX. What was done on the Kalends of May in the plenary synod of Africa, after the receipt of Zosimus’s third letter.**—The bishops who had assembled at Carthage during the autumn had decreed that a plenary synod should be held after Easter of the following year. They had foreseen that responses would arrive at about that time both from the apostolic see and from the imperial court, and that it would then be especially necessary to deliberate about the course to be followed for eradicating the Pelagian heresy. In fact, Zosimus’s reply, written on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, reached Carthage on the third day before the Kalends of May, when the Fathers had already assembled for the synod; and the canons read and subscribed precisely on the Kalends of May indicate that the synod had already begun.

After Zosimus’s letter had been read through [Note: [Col. 0991D] Since that letter makes sufficiently clear how much the earlier inclination and credulity of Zosimus toward Caelestius—displayed in the two preceding letters—had cooled; and since, moreover, the same pontiff openly indicates in the letter that he had not trusted Caelestius in everything and had not wished to decide anything before receiving the Africans’ replies and discussing the matter with them, this letter could, or rather ought to, have brought considerable hope. That hope was soon confirmed by the report that reached Africa concerning the judgment subsequently held at Rome. See Observation no. 40. Since, moreover, the acts which Quesnellus later describes according to his own judgment rest—as he himself subsequently admits—on preconceived assumptions about Bishop Vindemialis’s having been sent to the imperial court, Count Valerius’s letter as interpreted by him, and so forth, once these assumptions have been refuted by us, the whole of this narrative of events becomes a fable and invention.] the Africans did not derive much hope from it for the cause of the faith. 821 For the letters consisted almost entirely in commending and inculcating the authority of the apostolic see, and they indicated that its judgment, whatever it might ultimately be, was to be received without contradiction by anyone. He then weakly repels the accusation of excessive credulity. Far from writing with any expression of joy about the enormous reception of the documents and acts, he instead testifies, by the words of his own reply, that the volume of the letter was read through with weariness. Finally, although he writes that everything remained in the same condition, he gives no hope that Caelestius would be condemned within a short time; rather, he quite clearly indicates that the case would still be prolonged, when he says that a lengthy examination and extensive deliberation were necessary.

Therefore, the Africans, bearing with displeasure this untimely delay, so like evasion and so harmful to the faith and peace of the Church, and being confident about the emperor’s disposition—for, having learned the date fixed for the synod, he had promised that he would issue a constitution at the same time—again enacted in the plenary synod then being held those nine canons which had already been enacted in the preceding synod [Note: [Col. 0992D] We shall prove in Observation no. 26 that the canons were enacted not in the preceding synod but in this synod of the Kalends of May.], published them, and declared that, strengthened by everyone’s subscription, they were to be regarded as a perpetual sanction and an immovable rule of faith concerning the grace of Christ. They did not omit, as it is right to believe, what they had established in the earlier council: namely, that the sentence pronounced against Pelagius and Caelestius through the venerable Bishop Innocent, from the see of the most blessed Apostle Peter, should remain in force. [Col. 0992B]

Anyone will readily persuade himself that these events took place in this way if he recalls what we said about Bishop Vindemialis’s being sent to the imperial court; about Count Valerius’s letter, which at that time was delivered not only to Augustine; about the emperor’s constitution on the day before the Kalends of May; about the Africans’ decrees, published and subscribed on the very day of the Kalends; and finally about the Count Valerius’s more ardent zeal. He, watchful for the salvation of the Pelagians and hostile to their error, resisted these profane innovations not, as Julianus maliciously insinuates, by the weight of his dignity, but by exercising his power, taking care of the matter, and pressing it effectively.

Augustine is to be understood as referring to this plenary synod in his Letter 47 to Valentinus: “What we briefly decreed against that very error in the later plenary council of all Africa.” He says “briefly” either because the matter was decreed in few words, or because, although everything had been arranged and established in the preceding synod, it had not yet been published; since, out of reverence for the apostolic see, it was first necessary to communicate it to Zosimus and to submit it to Honorius, and therefore all that was required was to reread, confirm, and subscribe what had been established against that error. [Note: [Col. 0992D] Compare Observation no. 26.]

One of the African councils mentioned by Prosper, in chapter 10 against Collator, is likewise to be understood as referring to this synod. The Fathers there established that both gifts come from God: knowing what we ought to do and loving it so that we may do it, and so forth. This is the plenary council held at Carthage against Pelagius and Caelestius, in the consulship of Honorius Augustus for the twelfth time, on the Kalends of May. It is found in the manuscripts of the Roman codex now published by us, the Thuanean and Oxford manuscripts, [Col. 0992D] as well as in other codices examined by Binius and the other editors of the councils. It is said to have been held there by Aurelius of Carthage, Donatianus of Telepte, and 203 other bishops assembled together from all the provinces of Africa. Photius also refers to the same council in codex 53, where the names are corrupt and 224 bishops are counted in addition to Aurelius and Donatianus. Finally, the same point is recorded in Prosper the Chronographer, who, under the consulship of Honorius XII, in the year 418, after listing the earlier synod of 417, which is said to have been approved by Zosimus, adds the following among other matters: “The council of Carthage against the Pelagians.”

This may nevertheless be a marginal annotation, since it is found only in the edition prepared with the help of the Augustan manuscript, as in the Cologne edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* of 1618. From all this it is clear how wrongly all writers have hitherto confused the earlier council with the later, the autumnal with the spring council, the African with the plenary council, and the council of 214 bishops with that of 205 bishops.

**XXXI. On the number of the African canons concerning the grace of Christ. The necessity of enacting the canon in the African synod. Testimonies of Saint Augustine concerning the canon enacted.**—1. The occasion for controversy over the number of the canons of this synod arises from the variation among the codices. Some number only eight, as do most printed editions; others number nine. A third canon is found inserted concerning the intermediate place of blessedness assigned by the Pelagians to infants dying without baptism, and all editors of the councils believe that it should be removed from the number of the Carthaginian canons. The disputed canon is as follows:

“Likewise, it was decided that if anyone says that the Lord said, ‘In my Father’s house are many dwellings,’ in order to signify that in the kingdom of heaven there will be some intermediate state, or any place anywhere, where infants who have departed this life without baptism may live blessedly—although without baptism they cannot enter the kingdom of heaven, which is eternal life—let him be anathema. For since the Lord says, ‘Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven,’ what Catholic could doubt that the one who has not deserved to be a fellow-heir of Christ will share the lot of the devil? For whoever lacks the right hand will doubtless encounter the left.”

The antiquity and authority of this canon are defended by Photius’s codex 53. Reviewing and rereading that Carthaginian council, he says: “This synod condemns those who assert that Adam was created mortal, rather than being punished with death because of transgression. Likewise, it condemns those who would say that newborn infants have no need whatsoever of baptism because they do not think them subject to original sin from Adam.” Here are the first two canons. He immediately adds the third: “It also condemns those who affirm that unbaptized infants live blessedly in some intermediate place between paradise and hell; and six other chapters similar to these, handed down by the Pelagians and Caelestians, the Fathers strike down with an anathema.”

Photius flourished in the ninth century. No one who knows the man’s learning and diligence in collecting books will doubt that he had access to manuscripts of the highest quality and antiquity.

2. The editors of the councils cite a very ancient codex in which they read this canon, and consequently arranged for it to be printed in a distinct typeface.

3. It was necessary to enact such a canon at the time when the autumnal African council was held. Augustine had recently exposed the deceptive character of the confession made by Pelagius at the Palestinian council concerning original sin and the condition of infants dying without sin. Pelagius had condemned the proposition “that infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life,” which had been brought against him, and had embraced the contrary position.

“Thus,” says Saint Augustine in *On Original Sin*, chapter 20, “although he plainly refused to confess the eternal death of infants who depart this life without the sacrament of baptism, nevertheless a seemingly certain line of reasoning consoled our anxiety about him. For we said: If, as he appears to confess, eternal life cannot belong except to those who have been baptized, then surely perpetual death will overtake those who die unbaptized.”

Chapter 21: “But afterward there were brothers who reminded us that Pelagius might have said this because, when questioned about the matter, he was reportedly accustomed to answer as follows: ‘I know where infants who die without baptism do not go; where they do go, I do not know.’ That is, he said that he knew they did not go into the kingdom of heaven, but that he did not know where they went, because he did not dare to say that they went into perpetual death—since he believed that they had done nothing evil here and did not agree that they had inherited original sin.”

Since the Africans did not discover this fraud until after the rescripts of Innocent and after Augustine had written his little book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no synod had yet taken place at which anything could have been defined concerning that intermediate place of infants dying without baptism. Nor is it reasonable to believe that the autumnal council left that question untouched, for at it everything pertaining to this heresy was examined with the greatest precision and discussed with the utmost care.

The necessity of defining the matter was increased by the fact that, when Pelagius wrote an apologetic letter to Innocent, he quoted extensively from one of his more recent works. He thought that these passages fully cleared him, but in reality they deceived Zosimus, who transmitted the writings to the Africans with considerable praise.

“After inserting,” says Saint Augustine in *On Original Sin*, chapter 19, “a testimony from the Gospel that no one can enter the kingdom of heaven unless he is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he added these words: ‘Who is so impious as to exclude a child of any age from the common redemption of the human race and to forbid him, who was born for uncertainty, to be reborn for a certain and perpetual life?’”

Thus Pelagius. These words almost deceived Augustine. But when certain brothers informed him that Pelagius was accustomed to say of such infants, “I know where they do not go; where they go, I do not know,” he understood that by the “uncertain life” which Pelagius assigned to infants the heretic meant some intermediate happiness and an intermediate place, positioning such infants between those reigning in heaven and those condemned in hell.

Augustine’s words, written afterward, show how necessary it was that this fraud be exposed and that the Fathers establish the contrary doctrine at the next synod:

“Therefore those words of his, which were sent to Rome as a great vindication of him, are so ambiguous that they can provide hiding places for his doctrine, from which heretical meaning may leap forth to lie in wait, whenever there is no one capable of answering it—just as a sick person is found in a desert.”

And Augustine subsequently testifies that a response concerning this matter had in fact been sent to Rome by the Africans, in words which we have often transcribed.

4. Saint Augustine, therefore, in the passage cited, but especially in other passages soon to be quoted, indicates in the clearest terms that this matter had been defined. In Book II of *On the Soul and Its Origin*, chapter 9, the holy doctor writes:

“Let no one promise unbaptized infants, between condemnation and the kingdom of heaven, some intermediate place of rest or happiness, wherever it may be. For the Pelagian heresy has also promised this to them.”

Still more clearly, in chapter 12 of the same book:

“The authority of the Catholic councils and of the apostolic see most justly condemned the recent heretics, the Pelagians, because they dared to assign to unbaptized infants a place of rest and salvation even outside the kingdom of heaven.”

Here the two African councils in which we maintain that the canons were enacted and published are most plainly designated. Here also is the letter of Zosimus indicated; if it still existed, it would doubtless disclose many hidden matters. 825 Here the subject of the canon under discussion is expressly explained. For in no other canon is that intermediate place of rest and blessedness for infants recorded as proscribed. Thus this single testimony of Augustine makes it certain and incontrovertibly established that the canon which most editors dismiss as an interpolation must be regarded as genuine.

Moreover, I believe that two further points can be drawn from this same passage of the holy doctor concerning matters already explained above: first, that these canons were enacted in two Carthaginian councils, namely, the autumnal council of 417 and the spring council of 418, before Zosimus’s *Tractoria*; second, that the same canons were appended to that letter of Zosimus’s *Tractoria* and, as Prosper the Chronographer indicates, approved; and consequently that they had already been brought from the autumnal synod by the Carthaginian subdeacon Marcellinus and received by Zosimus in March of the following year. [Note: [Col. 0995D] If Augustine’s words quoted shortly before, “the Catholic councils,” indicate two councils—the African and the plenary, of which we shall show that the former was held before Zosimus’s judgment and the latter afterward, in the same year 418—it is unnecessary to infer that the canons were enacted in the earlier African council and published in the later one. It is enough to say that the African council set out more clearly in its letter to Zosimus what was soon afterward approved by that pontiff and briefly established in canons at the later plenary council. See Observations nos. 26 and 27.]

Saint Augustine also attacks that third, or intermediate, place as an invention of the Pelagians in Book I of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 50:

“Read to us where he prepared and promised, besides the kingdom for the good and punishment for the wicked, a third place also for your innocent unregenerate ones.”

And in chapter 130, addressing Julianus, he rejects this same place of “second happiness” which, he says, their heresy constructed for such persons. In *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 13:

“If the Pelagians heard this, they would no longer labor, by denying original sin, to seek for infants outside the kingdom of God some place of their own happiness, I know not what.”

The fact that the holy doctor attacks this “middle state” more bitterly in books published after the Carthaginian canons were enacted is an argument that it was truly proscribed among the heretical doctrines. Yet this cannot be proved except indirectly if the canon is rejected as an intrusion.

5. The authority of the Roman codex, published from both of our exemplars, adds immense weight to our position. No one will call its antiquity into question, nor—if he examines our proofs carefully—will he deny that it came from the Roman Church or was even used by it. 826 [Note: [Col. 0995D] Whether rightly or wrongly we have denied that this codex belongs to the Roman Church will become clear from the observations in the preceding dissertation. Nevertheless, the authority of the exemplars of this same codex and collection for the present matter is considerable, as we have shown at length in Part II, chapter 3, § 7, no. 3. As for Quesnellus’s remark that the editors of the councils testify that they found the disputed canon in ancient manuscript codices, this refers to Crabbe’s note: he found the same canon in the Gundavian manuscript of our collection, and consequently all such codices belong to the same collection. The codices later mentioned by Quesnellus that lack this canon are either Dionysian, derived from Dionysius, or belong to another collection which, transmitted into the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, presents the canons in question under the name of the Council of Milevis. The Corbeian collection, which derives neither from Dionysius nor from Isidore or the Hispanic collection, is said by Sirmondus, in his notes to the chapters on grace appended to the letter of Caelestine, to contain the same canons. But since he has reported only a bare beginning from it, we do not know whether that collection includes the disputed canon.]

Whatever objection might be made from the commonly printed editions of the councils is not significant. Since the editors themselves testify that they found this canon in ancient manuscript codices, there is no reason why they should be trusted less than others that lack that canon. A greater difficulty arises from the African codex inserted into the Dionysian collection, for this disputed canon does not appear in it. [Col. 0995C] It may be answered that Dionysius happened upon defective and truncated codices, and that he did not derive the African collection from the Roman codex, in which the Africans’ letter to Pope Boniface had never been included.

In my judgment, however, we shall answer better by saying that this disputed canon once occupied a place in the African codex even in the copy used by Dionysius, and that it was removed from it in antiquity. I establish that this is not an unreasonable suspicion as follows. The African codex contains 138 canons distinguished by numbers. Dionysius has neither more nor fewer in his codex, into which he inserted the African collection; nor does the other exemplar of it published by the most learned Christophorus Justellus; nor the Greek translation published through the same care and effort after the edition prepared by Joannes Tilius in 1540; nor the codex, not very different from the Dionysian one, published by Joannes Wendelstinus at Mainz in the year of Our Lord 1525 and reprinted at Paris in 1609.

It must be observed that a number is assigned only to the actual canons or decrees of councils, whether the canons are presented in full or in abbreviated form. But where there is only the council’s title, the consular date, the place of the synod, and other such material customarily preceding the canons, no numerical distinction is ordinarily added. This can easily be demonstrated by reviewing all the councils contained in the codex.

Especially worthy of observation is the fact that after the 33 canons of the African council of 419, where the earlier canons are immediately copied again, three councils are listed in a single sequence. Since no decrees of the first two, from the years 393 and 394, are reported, no number is attached to them. The third, from the year 397, is likewise distinguished by no number, except after the consular note and the preface, which fills an entire page; after these, the first canon of that synod is marked with the number 34. A similar example occurs after canon 56, where three synods likewise appear without numbers until after the lengthy preface of the third.

But let us come closer to the council under discussion. After the last canon of the Carthaginian council of 407, marked with the number 106, there follow the titles or notices of two councils without numbers, because they have no canons. Then comes the council entitled “On the Examination of a Bishop”; since one canon is reported from it, it is assigned the number 107. This is followed by the council against the Donatists of 410, marked neither by a canon nor consequently by a number. Finally comes our council against the heresy of Pelagius and Caelestius, whose eight canons are indicated by their respective numbers.

Yet the title of the council itself—which contains nothing besides the consular date, the place of the synod, and the name of Aurelius as primate and presiding bishop—is marked with its own number, namely 108. We observe that this occurred with this one title alone among all those that contain no canons. In Wendelstinus’s Mainz codex, the canons’ numbers are arranged somewhat differently, although the canons themselves retain the same order. In that codex, the council against the Donatists, which precedes this council against Pelagius and is not marked by a number in the other codices because it has no canons, bears the number 75; and the first canon of the following council, together with its title, bears the number 76. But the arrangement of these numbers is shown to be erroneous by the index of that collection. For the index agrees in every respect with the other codices and their indexes, in which the title of this council against the heresy of Pelagius alone is separated from its first canon and expressed in the index; and in the body of the canons, just as in the indexes, it is designated by its own number.

Moreover, after making this final observation, which a most learned man suggested to me, no other explanation of this discrepancy seems possible in my judgment than that one decree was excised—namely, the decree represented by our manuscript codices. To fill the vacant number, it was attached to the title of the council itself, [Col. 0997A] and that same title was entered in the index, although there is no other example of this either in the codex or in the index. Thus the objection drawn from the codex not only does not harm our opinion concerning the genuineness and authenticity [ἀυθεντίᾳ] of that canon, but rather supports it.

When, however, that excision was made and on what occasion is not clear. It is highly probable, indeed almost certain, that the Dionysian codex had already been shortened by that canon when it was brought to Gaul and delivered to Charlemagne in the name of Pope Adrian. For all the manuscripts of this codex that I have seen—and, as I indicated above, they are extremely ancient—present only eight canons. But in the notes to the first letter of Saint Leo we proved that this Dionysian collection had already been interpolated with certain additions before it was sent to Gaul by Adrian. It is therefore not difficult to believe that it was also diminished in some parts. By whose authority, with what purpose, and under what pretext this was attempted, I leave to others to conjecture.

[Col. 0997B] **XXXII. What is brought from the appendix to Caelestine’s letter concerning grace against the codex and the canon.**—Nevertheless, Henricus Norisius considers the canon in question to be an intrusion and proves it from the appendix to Pope Caelestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul—or rather [Note: [Col. 0997D] We have shown in Volume II, in the observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 3, that the appendix to Caelestine’s letter, containing chapters on grace, cannot be attributed to Saint Leo.] from Saint Leo’s collection of authorities of the apostolic see on grace and free choice of the will.

In chapter 10 (no. 7 in our numbering), the following is quoted:

“That also which was established among the decrees of the Carthaginian synod we embrace as belonging especially to the apostolic see, namely, what was defined in the third chapter.”

And afterward:

“And again, in the fourth chapter.”

And:

“Likewise, in the fifth chapter.”

These three chapters certainly appear under those same numbers in the commonly printed codices. From this it is evident that in Leo’s time exactly that number—and no greater number—of canons was counted among the Carthaginian canons. If you insert the disputed canon concerning the blessedness of infants in third place, the canons described by Leo will no longer be the third, fourth, and fifth, but the fourth, fifth, and sixth. This objection, however, attacks not only this canon but also our entire codex. For if that codex had been in use in the Roman Church, the canons described by Leo would have been drawn from it, and he would have cited them according to the numerical distinction displayed by the codex. [Col. 0997C]

I admit that the difficulty is hard to resolve, and at present I see no other answer than this: different copies of that Carthaginian council existed, and Leo used those that had been shortened by this canon. Or perhaps the second canon was not distinguished from the third, so that they were counted as one because of the connection between their subjects, since the latter is, as it were, an appendix to the former. Or finally, perhaps the canons were not separated from one another by any numbers at all and were numbered at will by whoever used them.

This is certainly how they appear in the Thuanean codex, in which they are distinguished neither by numbers nor by lines; they are written in a single uninterrupted sequence of lines. In the Oxford codex likewise there are no numbers, although each individual canon begins on a new line, as they say. The fact that different copies of the council existed seems beyond dispute. This will be clear to anyone who compares the heading or inscription in our codex, which is also reported in most editions, with the common inscription, which is as follows:

[Note: [Col. 0997D] The codex used by the Fathers of the Carthaginian council of 525 agrees with this inscription of Dionysius, in Volume V of the Venetian edition of the councils, column 777, except that it there designates only the twelfth consulship of Honorius, as in our collection, whereas Dionysius mentions both consuls. From the agreement between the Dionysian exemplar and the codex of the synod of Carthage—which was certainly African—the greater accuracy of its inscription is recognized. The fuller version presented in the collection that we have published in this volume after Quesnellus was put together by a compiler who, while describing certain matters more briefly at the beginning, added the name of Donatianus of Telepte, the number of the Fathers, and the names of the provinces from the subscriptions that were in his codex.] “In the consulship of the most glorious Emperors Honorius, for the twelfth time, and Theodosius, for the eighth time, on the Kalends of May, at Carthage, in the council chamber of the Basilica of Faustus, when Bishop Aurelius had taken his seat in the universal council, with the deacons standing by, it pleased all the bishops assembled in the holy synod of the Church of Carthage, whose names and subscriptions are entered, that, and so forth.”

Compare, I say, this with the other heading found above, in chapter 13 of the codex, and you will find a considerable difference between them, which proves the diversity of the exemplars. Yet our codex deserves precedence on account of its antiquity and consequently greater trust.

**XXXIII. Synopsis of the African councils under Zosimus.**—Now, to summarize briefly the enumeration of the African councils that we completed at greater length above, setting aside the synod which we conjectured to have been held after the rescripts of Pope Innocent had been received [Note: [Col. 0998C] We shall remove this synod in Observation § 3. We explained our view concerning the other synods in the preceding annotations, and you will understand it more fully from those observations.], we have four councils under Zosimus about which there can be no doubt.

830 The first was the autumnal council held in October or November of 417, as we have said. From it, when the number of bishops was still not so large, a first letter was sent to Zosimus; afterward, when their number had grown to 214 bishops, the subdeacon Marcellinus was sent with the synodal documents and acts. An envoy, Bishop Vindemialis, was likewise sent to the emperor, as we have reasonably suspected.

Alypius and Augustine may perhaps have been present at this same council when, during that period, they wrote Letter 106 to Paulinus, Bishop of Nola. That letter contained chapters partly condemned and partly accepted by Pelagius, which, as we have said, were likewise included among the documents sent to Zosimus. [Note: [Col. 0998D] Compare note 32 above, column 977, note a.]

The second council was held on the very Kalends of May of the following year, 418, at which the canons were enacted anew, approved, and promulgated.

[Note: [Col. 0998D] We shall demonstrate in the observations, § 11, that the Africans wrote back to Zosimus from the same council which issued the canons on the Kalends of May. What Prosper writes against Collator, therefore, must be referred to this council, as must the author—whoever he may be—of the chapters or authorities of the bishops of the apostolic see concerning grace; we have proved in the observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 3, Volume II, that this author was not Leo. Therefore this third synod, which Quesnellus thinks must be established, must be entirely excluded. Since the synod of 418 in the case of Apiarius does not concern the Pelagian matter, there is nothing to prevent our saying that only two councils—the African and the plenary councils mentioned by Augustine—were held under Zosimus in the Pelagian controversy.]

Prosper compels us to count a third council under Zosimus, in chapter 10 against Collator. After mentioning Zosimus’s *Tractoria* to the Africans, he adds:
