“The African bishops erred when they wrote back to that same Pope Zosimus and praised him for the salutary soundness of this judgment, when they said: ‘But that which you included in your letter, which you arranged to be sent to all, saying, “Nevertheless, by the prompting of God—for all good things must be referred to their author”—and so forth.’”

Saint Leo mentions the same synod in the chapters or authorities of the bishops of the apostolic see concerning grace, chapter 8 (no. 5 in our numbering):

“They revered this discourse, shining with the purest light of truth, with such honor that they wrote to that same man as follows, and so forth.”

It could scarcely have been held before the autumn of 418 and, as it appears, took place after Saint Augustine’s return from Caesarea in Mauretania.

Finally, the fourth was the council concerning Apiarius, from which the letter to Zosimus was sent. Another council followed it in the following year, under Pope Boniface, on 25 May.

### XXXIV

From what has been said, anyone can readily understand in which respects the writers of Pelagian history reached the truth and in which they went astray. James Ussher seems to me to have come closer to the truth than the others. For he accepts with us two synods of the African bishops: one in the autumn of 417, the other around the Kalends of May 418.[Col. 0999B] He implies that the first was provincial and the second plenary, in which judgment he generally followed Vossius.

That the latter synod was plenary is beyond doubt; Augustine gives it that designation in Letter 47. Ussher, however, wrongly interprets this passage, on page 293, as referring to the plenary Council of 419 under Pope Boniface. Rigberius, the Franco-German, also seems to have fallen into this error in his learned notes on Marius Mercator, p. 153, where he attributes the letter sent to Pope Boniface from another plenary synod in 419 to the plenary synod praised by Augustine in Letter 47—or, as he explains afterward, to the synod of the Kalends of May 418.

Both authors were misled by a faulty understanding of Saint Augustine’s words:

> What was written to Pope Zosimus about the African Council, and his rescript to all the bishops of the whole world, and what we briefly established in a later plenary council of all Africa against that very error.

I believe he drew from this a twofold argument:[Col. 0999C] first, because Zosimus’s rescript is mentioned before this plenary council, and therefore could not be understood as referring to the plenary council of the Kalends of May; second, because it is called “the later plenary council,” and thus presupposes an earlier plenary council.

But Augustine did not place the rescript before the council for that reason. Rather, he did so in order not to separate the rescript from the letter, and because that same rescript had been given not in response to the letter of the plenary council of the Kalends of May, but to the letter of the autumnal council that he had mentioned earlier. He called the council “later” in order to mark the chronological order and attach the later council to the earlier one, not to indicate that one plenary council had succeeded another in that same year.

This same synod is also called plenary in both the Oxford and Thuaneus manuscripts; furthermore, in both manuscripts all the provinces of Africa are named as those from which the bishops attended.

### XXXV. The autumnal council was neither provincial nor plenary

That the earlier autumnal council was provincial is implied by the authors cited above, but I cannot approve this. Nor, however, do I accept the designation “plenary” given to it by the learned Henri de Noris, *Historia Pelagiana*, book I, chapter 14.

By what name, then, should it be called? I call it African, as Augustine called it four times, and not without reason. For it was not provincial, since the bishops did not assemble from a single province.[Col. 1000A] That was why Augustine did not call it Carthaginian, even though it was held at Carthage—a designation by which he called the first two Carthaginian councils in several places. Nor was it plenary,[Note: [Col. 0999D] We shall explain in the Observations, no. 28, why Augustine called the earlier synod under Zosimus African rather than plenary; and from that discussion it will become clear that the African synod was convened from all Africa, not merely from the provinces of Numidia and Proconsular Africa.] since it was not gathered from all the provinces of Africa.

Why was this so? Consider our conjecture. Zosimus’s first letter arrived in Africa, announcing that Caelestius had hastened to the apostolic see to pursue his former appeal, by which he had appealed from the judgment of the Council of Carthage of 412. The matter was urgent. Zosimus wrote that an examination had already been held, that Caelestius had been proved Catholic in every respect, and that the Africans had judged him rashly and precipitately. Finally, he stated that the man was to be restored to ecclesiastical communion as soon as possible, unless those who did not approve his views presented themselves in Rome within two months.

The shortness of time did not permit a plenary synod to be convened from all the provinces. The matter concerned especially two provinces, Proconsular Africa and Numidia, whose two councils—Carthaginian and Milevitan—had pronounced judgment against Caelestius. Although that judgment had been strengthened by the authority of Innocent and by his letters, it was being treated with contempt by Zosimus’s letters and was soon to be rendered void unless action were taken quickly.

It is therefore probable that those two synods joined into one at Carthage, with bishops also summoned from the neighboring provinces. Together they easily completed the number of 214, since 123 bishops are counted from the single province of Numidia in the list of the African provinces published by Sirmond. Augustine therefore did not wish the distinction between the two synods to be marked in their names without deliberation. Since this was not a general synod, that was one reason—besides the others we have mentioned—why a plenary synod was later summoned, to be held on the Kalends of May.

The same Ussher still errs in several respects when he explains the history of these synods. For example, on page 275 he attributes to the plenary council of the Kalends of May what Prosper relates about the 214 bishops in chapter 10 *Against the Collator* and in the *Response to the Eighth Objection of the Gauls*. We have proved that these matters belong to the earlier, or African, autumnal synod. Likewise, on page 270 he says that the synodical letter mentioned there was written from that plenary council to Zosimus. On page 260 he refers to the same council Prosper’s passage in the *Chronicle* concerning the synod held at Carthage, whose decrees were sent to Zosimus and approved by him. Finally, on page 271 he thinks that the constitution issued by Honorius against the Pelagians was enacted after the acts of this plenary council had been received, although those acts are one day later than the constitution.[Col. 1000C]

The eminent Baronius also went astray under the year 418, no. 1. He posited a single African council, assembled at the very beginning of spring and continuing until the month of May. What has been said above is sufficient to refute this.[Note: [Col. 0999D] In this second part it was not Baronius but Quesnellus who erred. In the Observations we shall prove that Zosimus condemned the Pelagians in a Roman judgment before the Kalends of May.] The same applies to his suggestion that the Pelagians were condemned by Zosimus in a Roman judgment before the Kalends of May.[Col. 1000D]

### XXXVI. Several assertions of Jansenius of Ypres and Henri de Noris rejected

It follows that Cornelius Jansenius, Bishop of Ypres, was also mistaken.[Note: [Col. 0999D] That only two properly so-called synods should be admitted in the Pelagian controversy under Zosimus—the African synod at the beginning of 418 and the plenary synod at the beginning of May, the latter preceded by Zosimus’s judgment against the Pelagians at the end of March, while the *Tractoria* was promulgated somewhat later—will become clear from the Observations. The letters that we believe were sent to Zosimus at the beginning of November 417, asking that the prescribed two-month period be extended until an African synod could be convened, were written by Aurelius and other bishops without the formal character of a synod. They therefore provide no grounds for establishing, in addition to the two synods—the African and the plenary of 418—that Augustine records as having been held under Zosimus, another autumnal council in 417. See Observations, nos. 19 and following.]

Jansenius assigns to several synods—namely, one in the autumn of 417 and another held at the beginning of the following year—the letters and instructions that we have shown, from Paulinus’s little book and other arguments, to belong to that single autumnal synod. He likewise assumes several sessions of the later council, the last of which was held on the Kalends of May, preceded by Zosimus’s condemnation of the Pelagians, promulgated at Rome toward the end of March or the beginning of April.[Col. 1001A]

Rigberius very properly asserts that another synod preceded the synod of the Kalends of May. But he wrongly confuses it with the synod of 217 bishops whose letter was sent to Boniface in 419,[Note: [Col. 1001D] Quesnellus rightly assigns this earlier plenary synod to the beginning of 418, as is clear from what has been said.] and assigns it to the beginning of that year.

There is also much in Noris that we must reject, beyond what we have already noted. First, he thinks that no synod was assembled in Africa in 417 after Zosimus’s letters had been received, but that the first synod—which he considers plenary—was summoned near the Kalends of February of the following year.[Note: [Col. 1001D] This objection will be sufficiently dispelled if we accept that Aurelius, together with the other fellow bishops who were at Carthage or could quickly hasten there, wrote to Zosimus immediately after receiving his letters. See note 70 (above, col. 999, note c), and especially Observations, nos. 16 and following, where you will find the remaining objections resolved.]

But surely we cannot believe that the Africans were so asleep regarding the affairs of the Church, the cause of the faith, and indeed their own cause, that they delayed for so long the gathering of bishops that the primates customarily held every year in their respective provinces (as Gurnier will show below), especially at the very time when Zosimus’s first letters arrived there.

Next, it is impious to believe that Aurelius, without consulting his fellow bishops, sent Zosimus that appeal in which he requested that nothing be changed in Caelestius’s case before the synod’s reply. Finally, the third letter written by Zosimus to the Carthaginian synod on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April testifies that this appeal itself was sent from a synod, as explained more fully above.

Moreover, Noris writes that the first synod was convened after the month of January had begun and that Marcellinus was then sent from it,[Note: [Col. 1001D] See Observations, no. 21.] although Marcellinus had already been prepared to depart for Rome from 8 November and had already received from Paulinus the little book to be delivered to Pope Zosimus.

The learned man’s memory also failed him when he writes on page 82 that the apostolic letters concerning the Pelagians condemned by Zosimus at Rome were received by the Africans on the third day before the Kalends of May. The letters said to have been received on that day were in fact the third letters, dated the twelfth day before the Kalends of April. In them Zosimus stated that he had received the Africans’ more extensive reply through Marcellinus; so far from announcing that Caelestius had been condemned, he instead warned that everything remained in the same condition as when the Africans’ appeal arrived in Rome.[Col. 1001C]

### XXXVII. John Garnerius’s view of the African councils examined

We have now reached the last writer on Pelagian affairs, John Garnerius, with whom we disagree on many points. Although these matters are sufficiently clear from what has been said, it is useful to review briefly those positions that are partly his own and partly shared with other commentators on this history.

Thus, in place of the two African councils that we have posited—one within the autumn of 417 and the other on the Kalends of May of the following year, 418—Garnerius establishes four. He places the first, with us, in the autumn; the second before Lent; the third on the Kalends of May; and the fourth around 17 June.[Col. 1001D]

Regarding the first, I object only that he writes that nothing whatever survives from it except the vaguest memory:[Col. 1002A] that a letter was indeed written from it to Zosimus, but that Zosimus sent no reply; and finally, that he did not think it worth distinguishing it in his treatment from another council of the following year or giving it a place among the splendid array of twenty-four synods.

Yet we showed above that this synod was not merely famous on the basis of uncertain conjectures or doubtful monuments. It is mentioned repeatedly by Pope Zosimus, by Marius Mercator, by Prosper, the disciple of Saint Augustine, two or three times, by Prosper the Chronicler once, and by Augustine at least five times; and it is called African almost as often. From it, two letters were sent to Zosimus.[Note: [Col. 1001D] “Two,” he says, since he thinks that the earlier letters also were sent by that same synod. Yet we shall show in the Observations, no. 16, that Aurelius and the other bishops sent those letters to Zosimus at the beginning of November, before a synod could be convened. Therefore the letters belong to the autumnal period, but not to the autumnal synod, which we shall exclude in the Observations mentioned above.]

We have carefully collected from Augustine and others substantial remnants of the later letter. Zosimus not only replied to these letters, but also sent in response that celebrated *Tractoria*, through which the Africans’ decrees were approved and transmitted throughout the world together with the Roman decree. Finally, Augustine repeatedly proclaims that this synod was so distinguished among the others that to it was owed Caelestius’s condemnation decreed by Zosimus,[Col. 1002B] because it exposed the tricks and devices of the heretics and effectively instructed Zosimus concerning the procedure to be followed in the Roman examination and judgment. Add to this the embassy sent from it to the imperial court.

The second council, which Garnerius places before Lent,[Note: [Col. 1002D] This should be regarded as the first African council held under Zosimus in the Pelagian affair, at the beginning of 418, at which time Marcellinus crossed over, as will be established more fully in the Observations, no. 21.] is both fictitious and superfluous. For the Africans sent letters from the synod of the preceding autumn, as we have said, and Garnerius wishes these to have been written from the pre-Lenten synod. He also contends that Zosimus replied to them on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April. But the subdeacon Marcellinus—as we have repeatedly noted—was undoubtedly about to depart from Africa shortly afterward, carrying the cited letter and the other documents, when he received from Paulinus on 8 November the little book to be delivered to Rome.

### XXXVIII

Garnerius assigns a third synod to the Kalends of May 418, which everyone acknowledges along with him. But he invents much concerning it that must be brought under examination, although it is already clear from what has been said above.

He therefore thinks that this council of the Kalends of May was the council of 214 bishops—which in fact consisted of only 205—and consequently refers to it what Prosper says in both his *Chronicle* and his works against the *Collator* and his followers concerning that synod. We rejected this view above, although it is not peculiar to Garnerius.[Col. 1002C]

He thinks that from this council the reply concerning the manner in which judgment was to be conducted against Caelestius was sent to the supreme pontiff after Zosimus’s third letter, received on the third day before the Kalends of May; and that the council’s admonitions and the other documents of the case were sent to him from there. Thus he writes on page 213.

But first the author contradicts himself, and fails to remember that on page 210 he himself wrote that all these documents had already been sent to Zosimus at the time when the Africans replied to his first letters. I reproduce Garnerius’s own words:

> It is certain, he says, that a reply was sent from Africa to Zosimus’s letters, and that an appeal was sent asking that the pontiff not judge so great a matter without the African documents. These were sent with the appeal and contained partly the acts of the preceding synods, partly Paulinus’s little book, the letters of the Gallican bishops, and a book on the nature of Pelagius, Augustine’s reply, and many other things.

I shall not waste time proving—as we have already done—that Paulinus’s little book was delivered to Marcellinus on 8 November, and that the other documents had already been sent from Africa in the preceding year. It is astonishing that Garnerius should say that these were sent on the Kalends of May of the following year. Indeed, Garnerius himself relieves us of this burden on the same page 210:

> It is certain, he says, that there was some council—or rather, two councils—of the Carthaginian province before the African plenary council begun on the Kalends of May. From the first, at least after the first letters of Zosimus concerning Caelestius had been received, the appeal was sent together with the documents of the case that we mentioned earlier. To the synod of the second council Zosimus sent the reply that was received at Carthage on the third day before the Kalends of May, namely, two days before the general council began.

But in what year, and in what month, was that earlier council held, from which the appeal was sent with all those documents of the case?

“I maintain,” Garnerius immediately writes, “that it was held in October or even November of 417,” and he repeats this on page 243:

> It is credible that Zosimus’s first letters reached Carthage before the dissolution of the council of the Proconsular province, which was customarily held around the autumn season. A reply was sent from that council to Zosimus, together with everything that had taken place in the presence of Caelestius at the Carthaginian council of 412. Two little books were also sent with many other documents, presented to Aurelius either by Paulinus when he brought the accusation or by Caelestius when he defended himself.

How, then, were those documents not sent before the Kalends of May 418, if they had already been transmitted from the synod in October or November 417? Again, if all these acts and documents were sent from that synod, how can Garnerius call its memory extremely obscure and say that nothing whatever survives from it, when Augustine mentions these instructions so many times and calls the synod African in just as many passages—the synod through whose action they were received?[Col. 1003A]

The writer must again be pressed by this reasoning. If—as we have nevertheless proved false—Zosimus’s sentence against Pelagius and Caelestius was issued on 15 April and the *Tractoria* was sent throughout the world—for this he argues on page 216—how could those documents, which were to serve in the examination of the case, have been sent from Africa to Rome on the Kalends of May? Or, if they were sent then, how could the judgment have preceded the documents of the case by fifteen days?

I understand what the learned man will reply: the documents were sent on the Kalends of May because the Africans believed they would reach Rome before Zosimus initiated the judgment (p. 213). But Zosimus frustrated the hope of the African bishops and forestalled the African instructions with his judgment. In the third letter sent on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April to that—if it please God—pre-Lenten synod, the supreme pontiff summoned Caelestius to a fuller hearing and the highest judgment, but Caelestius withdrew from the examination. Once his flight became known, a definitive sentence was immediately issued against both defenders of the abominable doctrine, and the pontiff wrote to all the bishops of the world that great letter which Mercator calls the *Tractoria*.

### XXXIX. Garnerius’s view that the Roman judgment ended before the African writings were received is refuted

This amusing little narrative is, in my judgment, more like a fable than anything else; nothing is more alien to Augustine’s testimony, and nothing more contrary to the authority of the writer himself. Garnerius would easily have escaped the danger of contradiction if he had admitted what is true: that nothing was sent to the apostolic see from the plenary synod of the Kalends of May—since at that synod the Africans merely established and subscribed a brief statement against the error itself, as Augustine testifies in Letter 47—and if he had transferred to the autumnal synod everything that Prosper and Augustine relate about the council of 214 bishops.

But since he does not accept these points, he could not extricate himself from the labyrinth of seven difficult questions into which, with insufficient caution, he entered on page 212.[Col. 1004A] There was no need to burden the most holy bishops repeatedly with writings to be sent from Africa for Caelestius’s case. Garnerius admits that very much had already been sent by November 417 and shows that further material had been carried over before Lent. What more, then, could have been awaited?

This error of Garnerius was the consequence of his preceding mistake. He thought that the May council was the council of the 214 bishops and was consequently forced to attribute to it what is said about those 214 bishops, from whom it is certain that writings were sent to Zosimus. It is likewise false that Zosimus’s sentence against Pelagius and Caelestius was issued before the writings of the 214 bishops were received, and that the Roman judgment was completed without awaiting such documents. On Garnerius’s own view, he must therefore confess either that the council of the 214 bishops was held before the Kalends of May, or that Zosimus did not issue his sentence against the Pelagians until a month after the Kalends of May.

I demonstrate that Zosimus did not issue his sentence before he had received the writings that Garnerius claims were sent on the Kalends of May.

According to Garnerius himself, p. 213, the matters contained in the three first questions and the seventh of the questions that he proposes on page 212 belong to the council—or earlier African session—held on the Kalends of May by 214 bishops. But the written documents relating to the synod contained in those three first questions and the seventh were brought to Zosimus before he pronounced judgment on the heretics. Zosimus therefore received the writings of the council of the 214 bishops held on the Kalends of May before Caelestius’s judgment was completed at Rome.

It would be the work of an idle man to prove the premises of this Galenic syllogism, since Garnerius will not deny that both are his own. I shall simply set out the questions.

> The first, he says, is: Which was that African synod said to have recalled to the memory of the venerable Pope Zosimus what his predecessor Innocent had judged concerning the acts of the Palestinian synod, and after whose reply the most just sentence against Caelestius was issued?

Therefore Zosimus’s sentence was issued only after the reply of that synod. Garnerius refers in the margin to Augustine, *On Original Sin*, chapters 7 and 8. Quite rightly; for Augustine there asserts that two months intervened while a reply was awaited from Africa:

> And after the reply had been sent from the council of the African bishops, what followed, so that a sentence might most justly be pronounced against him, is clear to the reader.

The second question contains nearly the same point.

> The third, he says, is: From which assembly of Africa did the letters arrive in Rome stating that it was not enough for the more sluggish and more cautious men that Caelestius generally professed agreement with the letters of Bishop Innocent, but that he had openly to anathematize the erroneous statements he had made in his little book, and so forth?

No one so contentious as to deny that these letters arrived in Rome before Zosimus’s sentence and were awaited, provided that Augustine’s words, omitted by Garnerius, are restored:

> The letters from Africa were being awaited, so that Caelestius might profess more fully and openly that he agreed with the letters of Innocent. After the letters arrived in Rome containing this … then, when his presence was demanded … he withdrew and refused the examination.

The seventh question likewise arises from Prosper’s *Chronicle*:

> It concerns the synod held at Carthage of 214 bishops, whose decrees were brought to Pope Zosimus. When these had been approved, the heresy was condemned throughout the world.

This clearly shows that the Pelagians were not condemned at Rome by Zosimus until after he had received and approved the decrees of this African synod, which Garnerius assigns to the Kalends of May,[Col. 1004D] but which we assign to October or November of the preceding year.[Note: [Col. 1003] It is better to say, at the beginning of 418, as we have often noted.]

### XL. The African canons cannot be postponed beyond the Kalends of May

Something remains to be said about the fourth council, held around the middle of June. The author’s inventions concerning this synod are extraordinary, but his commentaries are as fictitious as the synod itself. What necessity—or even the slightest plausible reason—could there have been for so many bishops from all the provinces of Africa to be torn away from their churches at that time and gathered into a plenary synod? Scarcely a month had passed since the Fathers had returned to their sees after the dissolution of the synod of the Kalends of May. The letters announcing the Roman judgment, or Zosimus’s *Tractoria* itself, had not yet reached Africa, whether because of stormy seas or contrary winds, as John Garnerius thinks, or, as I am more inclined to believe, because the sentence had not yet been issued.[Note: [Col. 1005D] It will become clear in the Observations that Zosimus’s sentence was issued in the Roman judgment toward the end of March, while the *Tractoria*, which was issued somewhat later, was subscribed in the plenary synod that enacted the canons on the Kalends of May.] Consequently, there was no necessity for a gathering.

Garnerius thought he was compelled by the single passage in Augustine’s Letter 47. There Augustine writes of “the later plenary council of all Africa, at which we briefly established [a position] against that error,” and Garnerius believed that he had thereby discovered a plenary synod later than the synod of the Kalends of May. But we showed above[Col. 1005B] that by the word “plenary” Augustine did not mean that one plenary synod succeeded another. Rather, he wanted to distinguish the later synod from the earlier by that designation: the former was not plenary,[Note: [Col. 1005D] We shall explain the distinction between the plenary synod and the African synod in the Observations, no. 28.] and for that reason he calls it African everywhere, whereas the latter was plenary. Moreover, we have already established above that this plenary council must be understood as the council of the Kalends of May.

Furthermore, Garnerius’s claim that the eight famous canons were enacted at that synod conflicts with all the acts of the synod and with the longer epigraph prefixed to the canons. Although several different copies of that epigraph are extant, they all agree in indicating that the canons were enacted on the Kalends of May and that nothing else was done. Therefore, whether one prefers to call it a council or a session, I fear it would be rash to detach the canons from the Kalends of May without the authority of a manuscript codex or the testimony of some ancient writer.[Col. 1005C]

Why, then, does he labor so intensely to remove the enactment of these canons from the Kalends of May and postpone it until the middle of June? The reason is a great mystery. He was evidently distressed at the thought that anything concerning the faith had been established by the Africans before it had been defined by Zosimus and before a copy of his *Tractoria* had reached the African council, at least through private letters. From this he would infer that the canons were not properly a constitution of the African council, but a selection from the definition of the apostolic see.

But why should copies of the *Tractoria* have been delivered by private letters more quickly than by authorized messengers of the apostolic see? Shall we say that Zosimus showed less promptness and diligence than private persons? Was anyone more interested in bringing Zosimus’s sentence to Africa as quickly as possible than Zosimus himself, whose slowness and leniency had kept the minds of the Africans suspended and doubtful? Shall we believe that the *Tractoria* was entrusted to the curiosity of private persons before its authentic copies were delivered to the churches? Or finally, did stormy seas and contrary winds spare private messengers more than the public and sacred bearers of the Roman judgment?[Col. 1006A]

We therefore rightly reject John Garnerius’s conjecture, which he proposes in these words:

> Why, then, were the canons enacted? I think it was because a copy of the *Tractoria* had already reached the Fathers, but only by private letters and not yet through legates. Therefore, so that some portion of the *Tractoria* might be handed to the departing bishops in advance, I think the canons were extracted from it—at least the first two, which, when they regretted that the part concerning the grace of God was absent from the *Tractoria*, they believed should be supplied in their own canons. It carried greater weight if all accepted them than if they came only from the delegates, whose authority perhaps did not extend that far.

He gives no reason why he wants only the first two canons to have been extracted, nor why he conjectures that Zosimus’s definition was incomplete and abridged and had to be supplemented by the diligence of the Africans.

I pass over the other things he says on the occasion of these canons—for example, his assertion, put in the form of a question, that provincial councils have no authority to define doctrines, and that nothing concerning the faith was decreed in the other councils of the African Church, but that they dealt only with discipline and personal cases, and so forth.[Col. 1006B] It may perhaps be useful to remember these matters at another time.

I withdraw my hand from this dissertation after first observing what, in the end, has been established by the foregoing concerning the inscription of the imperial constitution, which occasioned our inquiry into the African councils.[Note: [Col. 1006D] See Observations, nos. 26, 29, and following.]

Since we have shown above with sufficient clarity that the canons concerning grace were enacted in the African council of the autumn of 417, and that the decrees were brought to the emperor Honorius by the embassy of Bishop Vindemialis together with the other documents of the Pelagian case, it follows clearly that the epigraph prefixed to the constitution appended to the Carthaginian canons is genuine and accords with the truth of what happened. It reads as follows:

> Here begins the sacred rescript, after the acts of the aforesaid synod have been received.

For Honorius had in fact received the acts and canons.

This also confirms the conjecture of Salmasius and Ussher, although they must be corrected on one point. Their eyes were fixed solely on the synod of the Kalends of May—the synod that confirmed, promulgated, and ordered the canons to be subscribed—and they failed to notice that the canons owed their origin to the autumnal synod.[Col. 1006C] They are attributed to the synod of the Kalends of May in that annotation and elsewhere because they became public and known to the Church only through that synod. That fact should not have prevented the Romans, when inserting Honorius’s edict into their Codex and wishing to record the occasion of the constitution’s issuance, from transmitting to posterity what everyone then knew: namely, that the imperial rescript was issued after the acts of the African autumnal synod had been brought to the imperial court, or after the canons concerning grace had been received and enacted.[Col. 1006C]

This concludes the account of the African councils held in the cause of the Pelagians from the election of Pope Zosimus until his judgment against the Pelagians.

# BALLERINI BROTHERS’ OBSERVATIONS

## On Quesnellus’s Thirteenth Dissertation concerning the African Councils against the Pelagians

[Col. 1005]

## Preface

[Col. 1005D]

### 1

From the epigraph prefixed in our collection of canons to chapter 14—

> Here begins the sacred rescript, after the acts of the aforesaid synod have been received,

—or, as we published it, “after the acts of the synod written above have been received”—Quesnellus took the occasion to compose his preceding dissertation.[Col. 1006D] In it he discussed at length the African councils held in the Pelagian cause, especially under Zosimus; Zosimus’s *Tractoria*; and the law promulgated by the emperor Honorius against the Pelagians.

His principal aim, stated at the beginning of no. 1, is to defend the genuineness of the published collection, which could have been called into question because the aforementioned epigraph appeared to bear an evident error. But throughout the dissertation, while laboring chiefly to defend the priority of Honorius’s law over Zosimus’s *Tractoria* and to persuade us that the law was sought not from Zosimus but from the Africans—because they feared that the pontiff might, amid grave scandal, pronounce judgment in favor of Caelestius—he inserts a number of statements that are less dishonoring to Zosimus than insufficiently respectful of the dignity and authority of the apostolic see. Since he attributes these statements to the sentiments of the holiest Fathers of the African Church, they may mislead the unwary.

It is therefore very important to examine this dissertation with particular care. In this matter, we believe we can demonstrate that his entire hypothesis rests only on empty conjectures and is opposed by the gravest arguments.[Col. 1007B]

# CHAPTER ONE

## § I. The error in the epigraph prefixed to chapter 14 of the Codex of Canons must be attributed to the author of the Codex; although it does not prejudice the genuineness of the documents in that Codex, it nevertheless confirms that the Codex itself was wrongly attributed to the Roman Church. The Carthaginian synod that condemned Caelestius under Innocent I was held not in 412 but in 411.

### II

Since Honorius’s rescript, which is transcribed in chapter 14 of the Codex of Canons, preceded by at least one day the plenary synod assigned in chapter 13 of the same Codex to the Kalends of May, the epigraph of the aforementioned chapter 14—

> Sacred rescript, after the acts of the aforesaid synod have been received,

—or “of the synod written above,” plainly contains an error. No one can rightly deny that this error is inconsistent with the public Codex of the Roman Church, which is thought to have received this addition under Coelestine shortly after the rescript itself, as Quesnellus thinks in Dissertation 12, chapter 2.

For who, when comparing the chronological notices of the synod and the rescript, would not immediately see that Honorius could not have issued the rescript on 31 April after receiving the acts—or the canons—of a synod that had not yet enacted them? Moreover, how could such a great error have escaped the Roman author of the Codex when he wrote that epigraph, especially at a time when the memory of the recent events under Zosimus was still alive?[Col. 1007C]

### III

Quesnellus’s twofold effort to remove this difficulty is, moreover, futile. For what he first insinuates in § 2—that the epigraph was not supplied by the author of Codex 845, but was added through the industry of a later person—has no probability whatever. We do not deny that, in certain later manuscript copies of ancient collections, some things were occasionally added by the diligence of copyists which should not be attributed to the original author [Col. 1007D]. But when titles are found in all the codices, even the oldest, of a given collection, there can be no doubt that they belonged to the collection from the beginning and must be ascribed to its author. The examples Quesnellus adduces of titles found in the Thuaneus manuscript but absent from the Oxford manuscript contribute nothing to the present matter. For we are dealing with an epigraph that is missing from no codex—not even the Oxford one. The omission of one or another example, such as those identified by Quesnellus in a single Oxford manuscript, which we have found defective in several other places, must be attributed to the private discretion of the copyist. But this epigraph, approved by all the manuscript copies, points to the author of the collection itself.

The error expressed in it, therefore, since it proceeds from that author, could easily have crept in through the carelessness or ignorance of a private individual, less skilled or less attentive, who compiled the collection long after Honorius’s law [Col. 1008A]. But it cannot be ascribed to a Codex arranged and published with public authority in the Roman Church. If that Church added these documents concerning the Pelagian case to its Codex shortly after Zosimus’s death, it could not possibly have been ignorant of the order of events or have prefixed an epigraph so manifestly erroneous.

### IV

Nor should the other defense which Quesnellus thrusts forward at the end of his dissertation be considered probable, when he thinks that this epigraph must be referred to the proceedings of an earlier African council, in which he supposes that the very canons were first composed and sent to the emperor through the embassy of Bishop Vindemialis. We shall demonstrate both that Vindemialis’s embassy is fictitious and that the canons were established not in an earlier African council but in the later plenary synod. Accordingly, this defense collapses because it rests upon a twofold false hypothesis.

Furthermore, if, for the epigraph to be true, it must be referred to the canons of the earlier African council, the date of that council ought to have been attached to those same canons. Since, however, the date of the later plenary synod is prefixed, the epigraph cannot be excused from error [Col. 1008B]: it commemorates the proceedings of the “above-mentioned,” that is, the later plenary synod, received from the emperor.

### V

What Quesnellus states in § 3 and elsewhere—that the Council of Carthage at which Coelestius was condemned under Pope Innocent was held in the year 412—is not so certain as is commonly believed. Saint Augustine, *Retractions* II.33, presents this synod as already celebrated when he wrote the first two books on the baptism of infants, or *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*. He subsequently mentions these books in Letter 139 to Marcellinus, and mentions them in such a way as to make it perfectly clear that they had been composed some time earlier. For, having later received back the very books that he had previously sent to the same Marcellinus, he testifies that he had forgotten why Marcellinus had returned them. “I have forgotten,” he says in § 3, “why I received again from you the books on the Baptism of Infants, when I had already sent the book itself to Your Excellency.”

This letter, moreover, was written later, no later than the day before the Kalends of March in the year 412 [Col. 1008C]. For in § 2 Marcellinus’s brother Apringius is identified as proconsul of Africa at that time, and Augustine had addressed Letter 134 to him. On the day before the Kalends of March in the year 412, however, Eucharius was administering the proconsulate of Africa, as is clear from several laws of the Theodosian Code; and from those same laws we learn that Julian succeeded Eucharius on the Ides of October of that year. Apringius, therefore, administered Africa in the year 411, in which year we find no other proconsul of Africa. Perhaps, when Marcellinus was sent to Africa in the year 410, on the fourth day before the Ides of October, his brother Apringius was sent to the same province to succeed Palladius in the proconsulate.

Thus Augustine’s Letter 139 to Marcellinus was written when Apringius was already proconsul and was delivered later, before the day preceding the Kalends of March in the year 412. The books, therefore, on the Baptism of Infants, which had been composed some time before this letter, seem to be assigned to the end of the year 411. Certainly the Council of Carthage must be assigned to that year [Col. 1008D], after which Augustine wrote those books. That year’s end corresponds especially well with what is reported at another Council of Carthage in the year 416, where the Fathers state that the case of Coelestius had been debated at Carthage “nearly five years earlier” (Augustine, Letter 175 § 1).

## § II. 847 Quesnellus’s view concerning the four African synods held under Zosimus in the Pelagian case. Only two should be admitted, with Augustine and Prosper: the African synod that preceded Zosimus’s *Tractoria*, and the plenary synod that followed it.

### VI

The more substantial disagreement with Quesnellus concerns the number and chronology of the councils held in Africa under Zosimus in the Pelagian case. He thinks that four were held. The first, after Innocent’s letters had been received, following the announcement of Zosimus’s election and the departure of Coelestius, who hurried to Rome; the second, in October or November of the year 417, after receiving Zosimus’s letters, in which he appeared to favor Coelestius [Col. 1009A] and Pelagius; the third, on the Kalends of May in the year 418; and the fourth, after receiving the aforementioned pontiff’s *Tractoria* against the Pelagians, in the autumn of that same year.

From this number and chronology of the synods, and still more from what Quesnellus attributes to those synods themselves, many significant consequences follow. In order that these matters may be settled correctly and, as far as possible, briefly, the number and chronology of those synods must first be determined. The question is difficult, since outstanding writers disagree among themselves. In this highly uncertain controversy, however, nothing can probably be established unless three points are first laid down—points that seem to us absolutely certain on the testimony of thoroughly reliable witnesses.

### VII

First, only two synods should be said to have been held under Zosimus in the Pelagian case, unless something compels us to posit more: one responding to the earlier letters of that pontiff and preceding his *Tractoria* against the Pelagians, and the other convened after the *Tractoria*.

Augustine’s testimony in Letter 215 to Valentinus is clear [Col. 1009B]. There, in § 2, while briefly but distinctly reviewing all the councils held in Africa in the Pelagian case, he mentions only two under Zosimus: the earlier one before the *Tractoria*, which he calls the African council, and the later one, which he calls plenary. He writes:

“What was written to Pope Innocent, bishop of the city of Rome, concerning the council of the province of Carthage and the council of Numidia, and somewhat more carefully by five bishops, and what he himself replied to those three matters” (these belong to the pontificate of Innocent, and he very precisely reviews not so much synods as the letter written by five bishops under that same pontiff): “likewise, what was written to Pope Zosimus concerning the AFRICAN council, and his rescript sent to all the bishops of the whole world” (this is the very document they call Zosimus’s *Tractoria*), “and what we briefly established at the later PLENARY council of all Africa against that same error . . . we have sent to you.”

Nowhere in Augustine’s many other testimonies, where he mentions African councils against the Pelagians [Col. 1009C], will you find any other council indicated under Zosimus except the African council, after whose rescripts he says that the *Tractoria* of the same pontiff was issued, and the plenary council, which followed that *Tractoria*.

Prosper agrees with Augustine in his poem *Against the Ungrateful*, chapter 3, where, addressing Africa, he says:

> Your revered bishops from every city assembled,  
> and in a famous gathering of elders, twice over,  
> you issued your decree.

This twofold gathering indicates two African councils. The words “from every city” cannot be applied to the two provincial synods held at Carthage and Milevis under Innocent; it is therefore evident that they must refer to those two councils praised by Augustine—the African and the plenary—which were convened under Zosimus.

Antelmius thinks that Prosper indicates two sessions of a single council, since in the following verses Prosper calls the council by a singular number [Col. 1009D] (Dissertation 8, *On the Works of Saints Leo and Prosper*, § 10). But if Jerome, in the third *Apology against Rufinus*, could call all the councils held in East and West against Origen “a council”; and if Eastern bishops sent to Liberius by several synods likewise called them collectively “a synod” in the singular (Socrates IV.12), because all the synods had agreed in one judgment, why should we not believe that the same was permitted to the poet, even more readily?

Certainly, the words “in a twofold gathering,” understood of two councils, agree with Augustine; and the number of three hundred Fathers, later recorded in the same poem, is wholly incompatible with a single council conducted in two sessions. It confirms that Prosper was speaking of two distinct councils. On this point Quesnellus also agrees, since in the preceding dissertation, § 9, no. 2, he expressly testifies that Prosper, like Augustine, lists no more than two synods.

Whatever one may choose to think about Prosper’s verses [Col. 1010A], Augustine alone ought certainly to suffice. Since he reports only two councils under Zosimus, and no others are mentioned by anyone else, more must not be posited unless something established elsewhere compels it. Therefore, so long as no such evidence is brought forward—evidence that cannot be suitably explained, though we shall later examine whether the objections can in fact be suitably explained—only two African councils under Zosimus must be admitted with Augustine: one before the *Tractoria*, and the other afterward.

### VIII

Second, the council at which the canons against the errors of the Pelagians—those presented in chapter 13 of our collection—were enacted was held on the Kalends of May in the year 418. This is established both by the collection of Dionysius Exiguus, as can be seen in the commonly circulated codex of the African Church, chapter 108, and by our collection in the cited chapter, whose inscription also requires us to note that this council is called plenary.

We shall see in § 6 how Quesnellus labors over empty conjectures [Col. 1010B] when he attempts to persuade us that such canons were indeed issued in a plenary synod but had been established beforehand in an earlier African council.

### IX

Third, besides the testimony of Augustine cited above, the existence of another African council convened before the Kalends of May—that is, before the plenary council—is also compelled by Zosimus’s letter, signed on either 18 or 21 March of the same year 418, in which he responds to an African council. This inscription is prefixed to it:

> Zosimus to Aurelius and the other beloved brothers in the Lord who were present at the Council of Carthage: greetings.

The two other earlier letters of the same pontiff, written in the same Pelagian case to the bishops of Africa, bear a different heading, one that makes no mention of a council, because they were sent not to an episcopal council of the Africans but to the bishops established throughout Africa outside the council:

> Zosimus to Aurelius and all the bishops established throughout Africa, beloved brothers in the Lord: greetings.

That third letter, which the same pontiff [Col. 1010C] sent in reply to the council, does not allow us to doubt the existence of an earlier African council. Since this third letter was written while Zosimus had not yet issued the *Tractoria* against Pelagius and Coelestius, this synod must already be called the council preceding the *Tractoria*.

Here, then, are the two councils of the African Fathers under Zosimus in the Pelagian case: one before 18 or 21 March, when Zosimus replied to it; the other on the Kalends of May. If, therefore, only two African councils under that pontiff are to be admitted on the authority of Saint Augustine, the first will be the one that the same holy teacher calls African, celebrated before the *Tractoria*; the second will be the plenary council, later than the *Tractoria*, called plenary in our collection and—according to the term used interchangeably by the Africans—universal in Dionysius.

No council besides these two, which Augustine’s quoted words do not support, should be admitted unless something compels us to do so. It will become clear in what follows that nothing compels this conclusion: we shall establish the sequence of events in such a way that all matters capable of creating difficulty are properly reconciled [Col. 1010D]. Indeed, on this occasion several points will arise that do not fit Quesnellus’s view well and will strongly confirm that, with Augustine, only two councils should be posited.

## § III. The first African council which Quesnellus posits at the beginning of Zosimus’s pontificate is eliminated.

### X

The council which Quesnellus attempts to suggest was convened in Africa at the beginning of Zosimus’s pontificate is supported by such weak conjectures that he himself not only declares, at the end of the same section, “I willingly submit these conjectures to the judgment of more learned men,” but also, in § 33, when briefly reviewing the African synods, thought that it should be omitted:

> “Leaving aside that synod which we conjectured was held after Pope Innocent’s rescripts had been received.”

And rightly [851; Col. 1011A] was it to be omitted, since nothing he brought forward in § 6 proves it. For his view concerning this first council to stand, a report of that same synod would have to be said to have been sent to Zosimus. Yet the two earlier letters of Zosimus, which would have been written after this council, not only make no mention of any report received, but are also shown to have been addressed not to a council from which the pontiff had received a synodical report—as we plainly see in the third letter, in which he replied to such a report—but to Aurelius and all the bishops established throughout Africa. This formula excludes the notion of a council previously assembled.

Add that the context of the letters themselves shows that they were written spontaneously not because of any synodical report but for another reason arising at Rome: one because of Coelestius’s arrival in the City, the other because of the confession of faith sent by Pelagius and the letter of Praylius of Jerusalem.

This is also demonstrated by the third letter, addressed to the African council on either 18 or 21 March 418. In it Zosimus expressly states that he had written the two earlier letters voluntarily, that is, without any preceding letter from the Africans [Col. 1011B]:

> “We would have reported this to your knowledge in our letters sent VOLUNTARILY.”

He then plainly declares that, after those letters, he received from them only a synodical report, to which he responds in this third letter:

> “But after the letter sent by your subdeacon Marcellinus, we examined the entire volume.”

### XI

Nor do the words of that earlier letter support Quesnellus’s view:

> “Lest your Fraternity’s expectation concerning Coelestius’s arrival and examination should remain longer in suspense.”

Quesnellus thinks that Zosimus learned of the Africans’ expectation from their own letter. Yet, even without their letter, the same pontiff could have suspected that they knew Coelestius had gone to Rome after hearing of Innocent’s death and were awaiting some information about the outcome from the new pontiff.

In any case, it is so false that they wrote to Zosimus at the beginning of his pontificate out of concern about the outcome of the case that Augustine, in Sermon 131, delivered to the people on the eighth day before the Kalends of October [Col. 1011C] in the year 417, did not hesitate to affirm publicly:

> “Two councils were sent to the apostolic see”—

namely, those of Carthage and Milevis in the year 416—

> “and rescripts came from there as well: the case is finished; if only the error would someday be finished!”

By these words Augustine not only presupposes that no other council after those two had written to the apostolic see; by pronouncing the case finished, he also makes sufficiently clear that the Africans had no concern about it under the new pontiff.

The words of Zosimus’s first letter cited by Quesnellus, concerning the letters of Heros and Lazarus sent “in the PRIOR REPORT,” that is, sent together with the report transmitted from the Council of Carthage, do not help him at all. That earlier report indeed presupposes a later one, but not one directed to Zosimus from a synod of this period. The earlier report accompanying the letters of Heros and Lazarus is the report of the Council of Carthage; the later one is the report of the Council of Milevis. Although the latter was sent to Innocent together with the report of the Council of Carthage by the same bishop [Col. 1011D] Julius, since the Council of Milevis was held after the Council of Carthage, the report of the former is rightly understood as earlier and that of the latter as later.

That the Council of Milevis and its report were later than the Council of Carthage, as Quesnellus himself has perceived elsewhere, is made clear by the words of that report in which the Council of Carthage, previously held, is praised:

> “We have sent this to Your Holiness concerning the Council of Numidia, imitating the Church of Carthage and our brothers and fellow bishops of the province of Carthage, whom we have learned to have written to the apostolic see concerning this matter . . . .”

If Pope Innocent, in the letter which Quesnellus thrusts forward in the preceding dissertation, § 6, names the letters of the Council of Milevis first, this occurs because he is replying to that same council. But Saint Augustine, who set out the chronological order in Letter 215 to Valentinus, mentioned first the Council of Carthage [Col. 1012A] and then the Council of Milevis in Numidia.

### XII

Since, therefore, nothing indicates that the Africans held any council against the Pelagians at the beginning of Zosimus’s pontificate, while the evidence we first considered from Zosimus’s letters excludes it—those letters mention only a later council—and the evidence we have brought forward from Augustine excludes it still more strongly, since Augustine praises only two later councils under Zosimus, the African and the plenary, which will be discussed below, there is no need to spend more time refuting Quesnellus’s conjectures. They collapse because they are supported by no positive document.

Among these conjectures is his claim that Innocent’s rescripts could scarcely have been promulgated throughout Africa in accordance with the rules of discipline unless a synod had been convened. Once this synod—which he invents without foundation—has been eliminated, that claim is recognized as entirely futile and false.

What? Was it not sufficient for the promulgation of Innocent’s rescripts that several copies of them be circulated throughout all Africa [Col. 1012B]? Where will he find the rules of discipline he invokes? When the Pelagians complain to Augustine, *On the Letter to Boniface* IV.8, that Zosimus’s subscriptions to the *Tractoria* had been extorted throughout the entire West from bishops sitting in their own places without the assembly of a synod, they plainly show that the discipline which would require councils for the promulgation of constitutions of the apostolic see was unknown to the Catholic bishops throughout the West. Those bishops, sitting in their own places without a synod being assembled, received the *Tractoria* itself.

Augustine, answering this objection of the Pelagians in § 34, shows that it was sufficient for the condemnation of the heretics to become known, and that there was no need for a synod to assemble:

> “Or was the assembly of a synod necessary for an acknowledged perniciousness to be condemned? As though no heresy had ever been condemned except through the assembly of a synod, when in fact very few are found for whose condemnation such a necessity arose; and there are far more—indeed incomparably more [Col. 1012C]—which, once they arose, deserved to be rejected and condemned where they arose, and from there could become known throughout OTHER LANDS as things to be avoided.”

## § IV. Zosimus’s earlier letter to the Africans is shown to have been written not in June or July of the year 417, but not long before the eleventh day before the Kalends of October of that same year.

### XIII

Having rejected this fictitious African synod, Zosimus voluntarily sent the same Africans two earlier letters, one concerning Coelestius and the other concerning Pelagius. The second is dated the eleventh day before the Kalends of October. Quesnellus thinks that the first, which has no date, was written in June or July, because, in addition to the two months granted in it to Coelestius’s accusers, he thinks that some time must be allowed for the same letters to be delivered and for replies to be returned before Zosimus wrote the second letter.

But since the first letter concerns Coelestius and the second Pelagius, there was no need for Zosimus to wait two months before writing about the latter [Col. 1012D]; those two months had been granted in the earlier letter not in Pelagius’s case but in Coelestius’s. Indeed, if those two months had already elapsed when he wrote the second letter, Zosimus would unquestionably have complained about the matter in that letter.

Quesnellus thought he detected a reproach directed against Coelestius’s accusers in these words of the same letter:

> “Where is Heros? Where is Lazarus? . . . Where are those young men, Timasius and Jacobus?” etc.

But these men were not Coelestius’s accusers; they were Pelagius’s. Nor were Heros and Lazarus in Africa, to which the earlier letter was directed and where only Coelestius’s accusers were summoned to Rome. Thus none of this complaint depends on the earlier letter or refers to the two-month period granted in it.

### XIV

Other considerations, however, lead us to believe that the first letter too was written in September [Col. 1013A], shortly before the second. As we have said, when Augustine affirmed in Sermon 13 to the people, delivered on the eighth day before the Kalends of October in this year 417, that the case was finished, he certainly had received no information about Zosimus’s earlier letters. Through those letters, after Coelestius’s accusers had been summoned, the case had again been brought before the court and could not have been called finished.

That the letters had not yet been brought to Africa is also proved by the fact that Basiliscus, sent to Africa with the information about what had been done at Rome before Zosimus in order to summon Coelestius’s accusers, did not meet Paulinus, the principal accuser, until the fourth day before the Nones of November, as is established from Paulinus’s own petition.

Since there can be no doubt that Basiliscus, a subdeacon of the Roman Church, hastened to execute Zosimus’s orders and met Coelestius’s principal accuser as soon as possible, we know that he arrived in Africa with Zosimus’s earlier letters at the beginning of November or at the end of October. If sufficient time is allowed for his journey, those letters must be said to have been written in September, shortly before the second, and perhaps both were brought by Basiliscus at the same time.

In the Vatican codex [Col. 1013B] praised by Coustantius in note 9, column 948, the chronological notation of the earlier letters is corruptly expressed as follows:

> “Copies [were] issued; [corrupt reading: *ave toris*]; [the office was] held under Honorius Augustus XI and Flavius Constantius, consuls.”

The same exceptionally acute annotator suspects that this letter too was written on some day in October, just like the second, and that *ave toris* entered in place of “October” through the copyist’s ignorance. Although we agree with him concerning the approximate time at which the letter was delivered, we cannot approve this emendation. For two Venetian codices of Saint Mark, 171 and 172, belonging to the same Avellana collection from which this letter was published, read as follows:

> “Copies of the authors [*auctorum*] were given to Honorius, etc.”

Here *actorum*—“of the acts”—must be read in place of *auctorum*, since Basiliscus received those acts to carry along with the same letters.

## § V. The two earlier letters of Zosimus were brought to Africa at the end of October or the beginning of November. Aurelius immediately replied with several bishops, and the contents of that reply. The African synod praised by Augustine, which sent a fuller report to Zosimus, was not held at that time. Quesnellus’s view concerning an autumn synod is refuted.

[Col. 1013C]

### XV

Quesnellus, § 9, thinks that the first synod to which Zosimus replied in his third letter to the Africans, dated in the year 418 on 21 or 18 March—for the two Venetian codices mentioned above give the date differently—

> “And I have signed. Farewell, brothers. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the twelfth consulship of Honorius Augustus”—

was held around the autumn of the year 417, because it could scarcely have been assembled sooner after the first letters of Zosimus had been received.

But if those letters were brought to Africa by Basiliscus at the end of October or the beginning of November 417, as we established in the preceding section, how could that synod have been convened and held around the autumn of that same year?

Paulinus, who had shortly afterward been summoned by Basiliscus, could indeed have immediately handed his petition to Marcellinus [Col. 1013D] on the eighth day of November, so that Marcellinus could carry it to Zosimus; a single person could respond immediately after receiving a petition. But Zosimus’s letters, addressed to all the bishops established throughout Africa, had to be communicated to everyone; a very large synod of bishops from all Africa had to be summoned, as we shall see; a matter of the greatest importance had to be debated; and a complete report supported by documents had to be delivered. All this could not have happened immediately.

### XVI

Nor do we deny that Aurelius, whose name alone was expressed in the heading of Zosimus’s letter, may have thought that something should immediately be written to the pontiff. This was demanded both by the respect which the Africans had always professed toward the apostolic see, lest they should appear to neglect or despise its authority, and by the gravity and danger of the case, lest, if the two-month period prescribed by Zosimus passed without any reply, he should, through ignorance of the documents, render some judgment [Col. 1014A] in favor of Coelestius or Pelagius.

Since a month had already elapsed between the date of the earlier letters and the time when they were delivered to Aurelius, and since a council from all Africa could not be convened within the remaining portion of the two-month period so that its reply could promptly be sent to Rome, Aurelius had no option except to write a letter together with those bishops who happened to be in Carthage on other business and with whom it was convenient to summon bishops from neighboring cities. In that letter he would ask the pontiff to allow suitable time for holding a council and transmitting appropriate documents, and would earnestly request that nothing new be done in the meantime.

### XVII

Although this letter was written in Aurelius’s name, with several bishops, to Zosimus, it was not sent from a properly constituted council, which, according to African discipline, had to be summoned and celebrated in a defined manner. There is therefore nothing surprising if this gathering of whatever bishops—which, without any examination of the case, merely requested a delay in order to hold a council and deal with the matter deliberately—is not counted among the properly constituted African councils [857; Col. 1014B], nor ought it rightly to be counted among them. Thus Augustine, when reporting only two councils against the Pelagians under Zosimus—the African and the plenary, which, as we shall later prove, belong to the following year—omitted mention of this gathering.

If someone should perhaps contend that such a gathering of bishops could be called a council, but that Augustine omitted it because in his letter to Valentinus he listed only councils that had made some determination concerning grace and the Pelagian case, the issue would then be merely one of terminology. We would not strongly oppose that point, since it would in no way prejudice the arguments by which we shall proceed to exclude an African synod from the autumnal period.

### XVIII

That this letter of Aurelius and the Carthaginian gathering was written before 8 November 417 is clearly shown by what is read in Paulinus’s petition:

> “Coelestius now has his case not with me, but with the whole Church of God, as the LETTERS WRITTEN by the African bishops and sent to Your Blessedness testify” [Col. 1014C].

The words “of the African bishops,” which were missing from the printed editions, were supplied by Father Coustantius from the Vatican codex; the two Venetian copies mentioned above confirm them. Since the statement expressed in these words is not found in the other African letters to Innocent, the letter of the African bishops sent to Zosimus—“to Your Blessedness,” as they say—must undoubtedly be understood as the letter written before Paulinus’s petition was presented to Marcellinus on 8 November.

The following words of Zosimus in his third letter to the Africans must also be referred to this same letter:

> “Let your Fraternity know that after those letters of yours which we received later, we changed nothing, but left everything in the same condition in which it had long been, when we indicated these matters to Your Holiness in our letter, so that the APPEAL which had been sent to us BY YOU might be preserved.”

Some think that the appeal here means what the Africans had requested from Innocent [Col. 1014D]. But the appeal here indicated concerns leaving everything in the same condition in which it had long been after Innocent’s decree—namely, that nothing should be changed in the judgment delivered against Coelestius and Pelagius. This does not fit the earlier African letters written to Innocent, in which no such appeal can be found; it fits only that letter which we believe Aurelius, together with the other African bishops, immediately sent to the same pontiff after receiving Zosimus’s earlier letters.

### XIX

We also believe that this letter is alluded to in the preceding words:

> “After those which we received above, or your letters.”

Garnerius considered this passage defective and thought it should be restored as follows:

> “After those which we received either above or now, your letters.”

Accordingly, two African letters are thought to have been sent to Zosimus before this third one. But, as Coustantius noted, the codices [Col. 1015A] do not support this emendation. Coustantius himself more plausibly conjectured that the passage should be corrected to:

> “After those which we wrote, or your letters which we received.”

Since, however, he lacked the authority of even a single codex, he did not dare to alter the received text.

We have found a related emendation in the two aforementioned Venetian manuscripts, namely:

> “We changed nothing after those things which we wrote to you, or after your letters”—with *quas*, “which,” to be supplied—“which we received,” etc.

This is evidently the best and true reading and should henceforth be accepted.

These words indicate that Zosimus left matters in the same condition not only after the first letter that he himself sent, in which he promised to leave everything in the same state for two months, but also after receiving the letter from Aurelius and the other African bishops, into which they had inserted the appeal just mentioned—even though by March, when he wrote these things in the year 418, more than the prescribed two months had already elapsed.

The following words of Zosimus’s same letter also refer to this African letter:

> “We believed that every petition of his [Coelestius] [Col. 1015B] had been answered sufficiently in the earlier letters which we sent you, and in the documents written in reply to those which you had sent back.”

Since mention is immediately added of the letter which Marcellinus later brought from the African synod subsequently assembled—

> “But after the letter sent by your subdeacon Marcellinus”—

it is clear that the words quoted indicate another earlier letter of the Africans [Col. 1015C], in which they replied to Zosimus’s first letter.

Zosimus’s words “we believed that it had been answered sufficiently” must also be noted. They plainly imply that he had adequately answered the earlier African letter in his own first letter, so that no new reply would be needed. They had opposed to him Innocent’s judgment, which had to be preserved intact and inviolate, and had insisted that the errors condemned in it ought to be condemned. Zosimus believed that he had adequately answered them in his first letter by means of the acts appended to it, from which it was evident that Coelestius had agreed with Innocent’s letters and had condemned all the errors that the same pontiff had condemned.

This African letter to Zosimus, therefore, written before the African council, cannot be called into doubt.

### XX.

Quesnellus, in the preceding dissertation, § 10, maintains that this letter is distinct from the later letter of the same Africans, by which a fuller reply was sent from the African synod to the pope. In § 11 he rightly judges that, in the first part of the third letter—which he delivered in reply to both letters on 21, or 18, March 418—Zosimus responded to the earlier letter of the Africans, while in the second and very brief part he answered the later one, intending to send a longer letter to the latter together with the *Tractoria*.

Yet, when he infers from the first part of that same third letter what the principal points and meaning of the earlier letter of the African Fathers had been, he advances several claims in his customary manner which we consider foreign to them. The words of the papal letter in which the prerogative of the apostolic see in issuing judgments is exalted, so that no one would dare dispute them, may indeed seem to indicate that in their earlier letter the Africans had complained to Zosimus because he allowed the case of Coelestius and Pelagius—already settled by the decrees of Innocent—to be reopened for examination. Since, however, Zosimus adds that he did not wish to use this authority before first consulting the Africans, those words appear to have been spoken for another purpose: namely, to show how much deference he had paid to the Africans themselves in issuing this judgment.

Nor is there any indication in Zosimus’s entire reply that those same Africans had likewise complained because he had drawn to himself the case of Coelestius, which had arisen in Africa and had been brought before the tribunal of Carthage, as though in this matter they had wished to follow Cyprian’s judgment addressed to Cornelius:

> Since it has been established for all of us, and since it is equally fair and just, that each person’s case should be heard where the crime was committed, etc.

(Concerning this passage, see the observations in dissertation 5, part I, chapter 7, no. 10.)

Furthermore, since these same Africans had previously referred Coelestius and Pelagius—although condemned in Africa—to Innocent, we recognize as false the claim that they could not endure the transfer of this case from an African to a Roman tribunal. If they said of Coelestius that he had been accused among them—“who, as you yourselves say, was accused among you”—they said this to indicate that they possessed clear documents which convicted his mind and errors. Zosimus therefore replied that for this reason he had not wished to decide the case before receiving these documents from them and treating the matter together with them.

Finally, Quesnellus gives no foundation for explaining the protest of the Africans mentioned by Zosimus as a formal petition by which they demanded that their own right be preserved. For that protest was part of the Africans’ own letter, in which they begged Zosimus to leave everything in its present state until suitable documents concerning the case could be sent from Africa.

### § VI. The African synod held under Zosimus against the Pelagians is shown to have taken place in January or February 418. Quesnellus’s opinion that this synod was held in the autumn of the preceding year is again rejected. On the number of Fathers at that synod. On the report sent to Zosimus. The constitutions of that synod were by no means distinct from the synodical report, but were inserted in it. The published canons on grace were not composed at this synod. Why Augustine calls this synod African rather than plenary. What the African discipline required for a plenary synod.

### XXI. [Col. 1016B]

The first letter of the Africans, discussed in the preceding paragraph, appears to have been delivered to Basiliscus, a subdeacon of the Roman Church, who, immediately after bringing Zosimus’s letters to Africa, returned to Rome to perform his duty. Paulinus’s petition, however, since it was thought not to be separated from the fuller report of the synod that was soon to be convened, was given not to Basiliscus but to Marcellinus, who had been appointed to convey the acts of the synod.

Meanwhile, a council was summoned by Aurelius. Yet, since it could not be convened and completed from the whole of Africa before the Christmas feast because of the pressure of time and the distance of the regions, it is credible that it was summoned after that feast. Indeed, since Zosimus postponed his response to the first letter of the Africans, delivered by Basiliscus, until the fuller report of the synod should arrive—for he answered both at the same time—we firmly believe that, after finally receiving it through Marcellinus, he replied without delay.

Since he answered this report on 21, or 18, March 418, if we allow a reasonable interval for Marcellinus’s journey—for one month or slightly more is sufficient according to other similar transmissions—the same synod is known to have been completed near the beginning of February of that year, so that its opening fell in January.

### XXII. [Col. 1016C]

From this the opinion of Quesnellus, proposed in § 15, concerning an autumnal synod in the year 417 is more decisively disproved. According to that opinion, Marcellinus set out in November with all the instructions and synodical acts and delivered them to Zosimus on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April of the following year, 418.

[Col. 1016D] Is it probable that Marcellinus spent approximately five months on the journey? Or was he negligent in carrying out his duty and lingered somewhere for several months before departing from Africa? Quesnellus himself judges in § 36 that it is improbable that the African Fathers postponed the synod until 418, because, as he says, we cannot believe that they were so asleep to the affairs of the Church and the cause of the faith—indeed, their own cause—that they delayed the gathering of the bishops for so long.

We explained shortly above why they delayed it and by what remedy they immediately guarded against every prejudice. Marcellinus would undoubtedly have incurred this same reproach if, after the synod had finally been completed, he had been sent to Zosimus in November, then delayed his departure for so long and fallen asleep through slowness in delivering the letters and acts.

As for Quesnellus’s conjecture in § 12, based on Marcellinus’s journey supposedly undertaken in November, that he may have accompanied Bishop Vindemialis as far as Ravenna and remained there with him for some time in the imperial court, this rests not only on the hypothesis of Vindemialis’s legation, which we shall later show to be false, but is plainly incredible in view of the Africans’ concern. The African council’s reply had already been promised and was awaited at Rome, and the decision of the case depended upon it; consequently, it would have been entrusted to Marcellinus for delivery as quickly as possible.

### XXIII. [Col. 1017A]

The point that chiefly moved Quesnellus to assert an autumnal council is the two-month period prescribed in Zosimus’s earlier letter. Yet, although this interval may have appeared sufficient to Zosimus, it was in reality insufficient in view of the circumstances mentioned above. Nothing concerning an autumnal synod can therefore be inferred from it, especially since Aurelius, writing immediately to the pope through Basiliscus together with the other bishops, had earnestly requested the necessary delay.

If Augustine, in *On Original Sin*, chapter 7, mentions the two-month period inserted by Zosimus before a reply was sent from Africa, he does not, however, assert that this African reply was transmitted immediately after those two months, as will be clear from a reading of the complete text.

Once this nearly sole foundation of Quesnellus has been overturned, it must now follow from the stronger conclusions we have established that this first synod under Zosimus was held not in November 417 but around January 418, and certainly completed at least several days before 24 February, when the council of Telepte—or rather of Zella—was celebrated, and some bishops of the celebrated African synod were present.

### XXIV. [Col. 1017B]

Prosper certainly mentions this synod in his *Chronicle* under the year 418, where we read:
