> After a council of 214 bishops had been held at Carthage, synodical decrees were brought to Pope Zosimus. When these had been approved, the Pelagian heresy was condemned throughout the whole world.

The final words indicate Zosimus’s *Tractoria*, by which that pontiff approved the African decrees. When it was sent to all the bishops and subscribed by them all, the Pelagian heresy was condemned throughout the entire world.

In the same sense Prosper wrote in his reply to the eighth objection of the Gauls:

> And with the 214 priests whose constitution against the enemies of God’s grace the whole world embraced, etc.

This plainly refers to the *Tractoria*, through which alone the constitution of the African Fathers was spread throughout the entire world.

Again, in *Against the Collator*, chapter 5, he says of the same synod:

> According to you, 214 priests were in error, who, in the letter that they placed before their constitutions, addressed the bishop of the apostolic see, Zosimus, as follows: “We decree that the judgment pronounced against Pelagius and Coelestius through the venerable Bishop Innocent from the see of the most blessed Apostle Peter should remain in force until they confess with the clearest declaration that the grace of God,” etc.

That this refers to the letter of the aforementioned synod, written before the *Tractoria*, is evident not only from the same number of Fathers—214—expressed in the preceding testimonies, but also from the words of that letter itself. They mention the judgment of Innocent alone, not that of Zosimus, and they mention it in such a way as to urge Zosimus to be cautious: when issuing his judgment, he should not trust the deceitful words of Pelagius and Coelestius, but should require the clearest profession.

From this it follows that certain persons wrongly transfer these three testimonies of Prosper, together with the number of 214 Fathers consistently asserted in them, from the earlier synod to which they refer before the *Tractoria* to another synod held after the *Tractoria*.

### XXV. [Col. 1017C]

This synodical letter was extremely long, so much so that Zosimus calls it a volume, the reading of which consumed a considerable amount of time. This is sufficiently indicated by the formulas of that pontiff’s third letter:

> We unfolded the entire volume of the letter sent through your subdeacon Marcellinus, and after it had at last been read through, etc.

This epistolary volume contained several matters, which Quesnellus carefully collected in § 20. Among other things, it included those constitutions or decrees which Prosper mentioned in the testimonies quoted above.

Although, in the final passage of *Against the Collator*, Prosper appears, when he speaks of “the letter which they placed before their constitutions,” to imply that the letter preceded the constitutions and was therefore distinct from them, nevertheless, when the entire context is considered, it will plainly be evident that the constitutions cannot in any way be separated from the letter, but were part of the letter itself.

The text now quoted by Prosper—“We decree,” etc.—is certainly one of the constitutions. Prosper himself, repeating it in his reply to the eighth objection of the Gauls, calls it a constitution. Nevertheless, he makes clear that it was part of the letter itself when he writes:

> In the letter … they addressed the bishop of the apostolic see, Zosimus, as follows: “We decree against Pelagius,” etc.

Therefore the words in *Against the Collator*, “which they placed before their constitutions,” mean the same as “which they placed together with their constitutions inserted in it,” unless one prefers to read, with the Corbie manuscript, “which they brought forward.”

Nor is it unusual for letters containing constitutions to be called decrees. Thus Saint Augustine, in Letter 178, no. 2, to Hilary, calls the letter of the Council of Carthage to Innocent a decree:

> We had learned that in the Church of Carthage a decree of the episcopal council had been composed against them, to be sent by letter to the holy and venerable Pope Innocent.

Here the holy Doctor does not distinguish the decree from the letter.

Moreover, the word “constitutions,” used by Prosper, clearly asserts that several decrees had been inserted in the letter of our synod. Only the wording of one constitution has been preserved for us in the passages cited from Prosper; the others have not.

### XXVI. [Col. 1018A]

In § 16 Quesnellus states that the eight, or rather nine, canons on grace presented in the collection published in this volume, chapter 13, were composed at this first council, which he considers to have been the autumnal council. He holds, however, that they were not published at that time, but were sent under seal to Zosimus and the emperor, to be promulgated at the later plenary council on the Kalends of May.

It cannot be denied that the Fathers, in the synodical letter of this first council, discussed at greater length the heads of Coelestius’s and Pelagius’s errors in order to instruct Zosimus. Among these errors must certainly be counted the error by which a certain intermediate place of happiness was assigned to infants dying without baptism.

For Augustine, in book 2 of *On the Soul and Its Origin*, a work written toward the end of 419, chapter 12, states that after the Palestinian council the Africans detected this opinion of the Pelagians and that it had been condemned by the authority of the Catholic councils and the apostolic see. Since at that time the name “apostolic see” could indicate nothing other than Zosimus’s *Tractoria*, by “Catholic councils” he appears to understand the African and plenary synods. Thus the former first reported this error to Zosimus, and it was subsequently proscribed by Zosimus himself in the *Tractoria* and by an express canon in the plenary synod.

The order in which he mentions the Catholic councils before the apostolic see signifies that at least one of those councils preceded the apostolic see. Accordingly, this report of the African synod, with the constitutions inserted in it—or, as Prosper calls them by another name in the *Chronicle*, the decrees—identified the errors of the Pelagians.

The canons themselves, however, which briefly proscribed these same errors in the later plenary synod, as Augustine says in Letter 215 (see below), cannot be said to have been composed in the African synod in exactly the same words. What was established more fully and, as it were, prepared in this synod in order to instruct Zosimus was, after receiving his approval, expressed more briefly in eight or nine canons at the later synod.

Certainly, the constitution which Saint Prosper quotes from the synodical letter of the earlier council to Zosimus is not found among those canons, nor does it have a form similar to theirs. It is probable that the other constitutions of that council likewise had a form different from that of the canons mentioned above. This explains why, at the Carthaginian council of 419, where the canons of all the earlier synods were repeated and inserted into the acts, no canon from this African council was recited or transcribed, as we learn from Dionysius Exiguus.

What is more, neither in Dionysius nor in the ancient collection published in this volume—which received nothing from Dionysius—are these canons attributed to the African synod, but to the plenary synod held on the Kalends of May.

It may be objected that Saint Prosper, in *Against the Collator*, chapter 5, attributes the fourth of these canons, in the plural, to African councils, as though he were indicating that the same canons had been enacted in at least two African councils—namely, in the African and in the plenary council.

Yet, apart from the fact that these two councils may be indicated in the sense that the African council, in its report to Zosimus, established at greater length the same points that were later expressed more briefly in the canons of the plenary council on the Kalends of May, if Saint Prosper wished to attribute the same words of the fourth canon to at least two synods, then, in addition to the synod of the Kalends of May, at which that canon was enacted, he referred to another synod of 419, at which the same canon was reread and confirmed together with the others. See the *African Code*, chapter 112.

Prosper’s passage therefore proves nothing in support of attributing these canons to the African council.

### XXVII. [Col. 1019B]

Augustine’s testimony in book 2 of the *Retractations*, chapter 50, deserves attention. He says:

> After the Pelagian heresy, together with its authors, had first been convicted and condemned by the bishops of the Roman Church—Innocent first, then Zosimus—with the cooperation of the letters of the African councils, etc.

You see that to the African councils which cooperated in the condemnation of the Pelagian heresy, under Innocent no less than under Zosimus, Augustine attributes mere letters, not canons. Yet the canons, although they proscribe the same errors more briefly, do so more expressly; if they had been sent to Zosimus, they would seem especially worthy of mention.

The same holy Doctor speaks more clearly in Letter 47, now numbered 215, to Valentinus, when he mentions both the African council and the plenary council under Zosimus. Of the African council, which preceded the *Tractoria*, he praises only the writings—that is, the letters or report—to that same pontiff:

> What was written to Pope Zosimus concerning the African council.

But of the later plenary council, held after Zosimus’s reply, he claims the canons, writing:

> And what we briefly established against that very error at the later plenary council of all Africa.

The adverb “briefly” signifies the canons, which were set out in few words. The verb “we established,” however, makes clear that they were composed and enacted briefly in that council itself, not in the earlier synod.

Since the entire substance of the canons had already been prepared and more fully arranged in the preceding African council, which sent a lengthy report to Zosimus, only some consideration in the wording—but not a more extensive treatment of the doctrines, as Quesnellus supposed in § 18—was necessary for the canons to be established briefly at the plenary synod on the Kalends of May.

Quesnellus labors to show, from the different manner in which Augustine wrote about Pelagian impeccability before and after the publication of the canons in which this Pelagian error was condemned, that the canons were first composed in the synod which he calls the autumnal synod, and were merely promulgated in the other synod on the Kalends of May. But this proves nothing unless he can show that Augustine used the different manner of speaking he alleges before the Kalends of May. He does not show this.

For the testimonies he produces are contained in works which he cannot deny were composed after that time.

It may, however, be the case that in the letter of the first African synod, held—as we have shown—around January, among the constitutions inserted in it there was one which touched upon the error concerning impeccability. Even so, the three canons on the same subject, which all the evidence assigns to the council of the Kalends of May, ought not to be said to have been enacted in that synod in the same words.

Finally, Quesnellus’s invention is especially exposed by this matter: he imagines that these canons were composed at the earlier synod but not promulgated there, and that they were sent under seal to the pope and the emperor, without citing a single witness. Who, however, could believe that canons signed by 214 Fathers at the African synod and sent to the pope and the emperor had not yet been made public?

### XXVIII. [Col. 1019D]

Augustine calls this first council African because it was summoned from the whole of Africa, as the inscription of Zosimus’s letter to Aurelius and all the bishops established throughout Africa appears to require.

The same holy Doctor distinguishes this council from a plenary council because, in convening it, the procedure by which plenary synods were convoked in Africa was not observed, or because it could not be observed in view of the circumstances of the time.

Before a plenary council—or, as it was also interchangeably called, a universal council—the synods of the individual provinces had to be held. From these, legates were to be appointed to the universal council so that, in the name of each province, they might provide whatever was necessary.

There are frequent references to such legates and legations, as may be seen in the acts of the Carthaginian councils of 397; before canon 34 of the African Code of 403; before canon 91 of 407; at the beginning of canon 96 and of the material from 419; and before canon 18, as well as before canon 127.

This procedure had been established at the Council of Hippo in 393. Its fifth canon is summarized in chapter 2 of the *Breviary* inserted in our collection as follows:

> So that ecclesiastical causes, which often grow stale to the ruin of the peoples, may not do so, a council shall be summoned every year. All the provinces that possess principal sees shall send three legates from their councils, so that the assembly may have full authority while being less subject to jealousy and less burdensome in expense for its guests; and, because of the poverty of bishops in Tripoli, one bishop shall attend from there.

Apart from these legates, no others were to attend the plenary synod, as we learn from the decree of the synod of Thusdritum preserved by Ferrandus, no. 77:

> Let a bishop who, without having received a legation, has presumed to attend the universal—that is, plenary—council not be admitted to that council by those bishops who have received a legation.

In more serious cases, however, which appeared to require a greater number of bishops, other bishops besides the legates were also admitted. Yet, even if some or many of these attended, the presence of the legates was nevertheless chiefly required.

Thus, although some bishops of Numidia were present at the Council of Carthage in 397, since the legates of that province were absent, the synod was postponed for some time so that they might be awaited. See the intervention of Aurelius prefixed to canon 34 and canon 47 of the African Code.

Compare also the Council of Carthage in 403, where several interventions concerning the legates who had not yet arrived are recorded in the same Code.

Since the circumstances of the time did not permit the councils of the individual provinces to be convened before the synod—a synod which Zosimus’s letters urgently demanded should be held quickly—from which legates with mandates would then be sent to the universal synod, this council was gathered from the whole of Africa without the aforementioned appointment of legates. However numerous it may have been, according to African discipline it was not truly a plenary council, as was the council held on the Kalends of May. For this reason Augustine calls it African, not plenary.

There is therefore no reason to doubt the number of 214 Fathers, which Saint Prosper attributes to this African council in the three passages cited in no. 24, even though a smaller number is assigned to the plenary council of the Kalends of May.

For a plenary council did not depend on the greater number of Fathers but on the appointment of legates. Thus, even if only the legates of the individual provinces had assembled—as, according to the decree of Thusdritum, only they were supposed to assemble—it would have been a plenary council. A greater number, without the appointment of legates from the provincial synods, would by no means constitute a plenary council.

This also overturns the opinion of those who thought that this African council was provincial or was composed of only two provinces. The number of 214 Fathers indicates a synod of the whole of Africa and at the same time supplies the reason why it could not have been convened before January.

### § VII. The alleged legation of Bishop Vindemialis to the emperor, sent by the same African council to arrange for a law against the Pelagians to be issued before Zosimus’s judgment, is shown to be fictitious. Three passages of Augustine are explained. It is shown to be false that the Africans feared that Zosimus would issue a decision bringing disgrace upon the apostolic see and producing a great schism between the Roman and African Churches.

### XXIX. [Col. 1021A]

While the letters and acts of the African council were being carried to Pope Zosimus at Rome by Marcellinus, a subdeacon of the Church of Carthage, Quesnellus supposes, in §§ 23 and 28, that another legation was sent by the same council to the emperor Honorius at Ravenna.

He further states that this legation was entrusted not to a mere subdeacon but to Bishop Vindemialis. Augustine mentions him in Letter 200, and, according to Quesnellus, Vindemialis was instructed to go secretly to Ravenna, in order to prevent the damage to the faith and the scandals which Quesnellus exaggerates as having been feared by the Africans from Zosimus. With the assistance of Count Valerius, Vindemialis was immediately to ask the emperor for a law against Coelestius and the Pelagians, one that would anticipate Zosimus’s judgment.

Quesnellus further boasts that, since this law was obtained and sent to Rome not by Zosimus but by the African bishops, a bridle was thereby put upon the Romans, so that they would no longer favor Coelestius and the Pelagians after they had been condemned by the emperor. He therefore claims that Zosimus, struck with fear by this law, finally issued the *Tractoria* against them.

### XXX. [Col. 1021B]

This opinion of Quesnellus is a pure and unmitigated dream. The alleged legation of Bishop Vindemialis to obtain the law, upon which the entire construction rests, is plainly fictitious.

The three testimonies which Quesnellus produces from Augustine express nothing of the sort, or are manifestly twisted toward an entirely different meaning.

The first testimony is taken from Augustine’s Letter 200, written, as Quesnellus thinks, to the aforementioned Count Valerius in 418, either before or at least shortly after Zosimus’s judgment. He quotes these words from the letter:

> Since I had long been troubled that, although I had written several times, I had deserved no letter from Your Highness, suddenly I received three letters from your kindness: one addressed not to me alone through my fellow bishop Vindemialis, and not long afterward two through my fellow presbyter Firmus.

By the words “one addressed not to me alone through my fellow bishop Vindemialis,” Quesnellus thinks that Valerius’s letter was addressed not to Augustine alone but also to other African bishops who had previously written to Valerius, when they sent Vindemialis to Ravenna from the council on matters concerning the faith in the Pelagian case.

He believes that this is sufficiently indicated by the following words of the same letter, in which Valerius is shown to have been hostile to error because, through the influence he possessed with the emperor, he obtained a law against the Pelagians:

> We have heard how great your concern is that no one should lie in wait for the members of Christ, covered by the veil of Christ’s name, whether among His ancient or His more recent enemies; and how carefully you seek the salvation of those same enemies, while being hostile to their error. We customarily hear such things, and things of this kind, from others also; but now, through the brother mentioned above, we have learned them more fully and with greater certainty.

We do not deny that by the name “more recent enemies” the Pelagians in particular are meant, against whose efforts Valerius opposed himself. We are nevertheless entirely certain that another matter is being considered here, not the law of Honorius; indeed, the passage concerns an affair that occurred after that law had been issued and in which Valerius intervened on his own authority.

### XXXI. [Col. 1021C]

To establish this, it must first be proved that Letter 200, which was sent to Valerius together with the first book of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, was written by Augustine not before or shortly after Zosimus’s judgment, but after his journey to Mauretania, toward the end of 418 or the beginning of 419.

The second book of the *Retractations* ought to suffice for this purpose. In chapter 53, Augustine refers the two books *On Marriage and Concupiscence* to Valerius after the *Acts with Emeritus*, which were held during the journey in Mauretania on 20 September 418.

Quesnellus’s attempted escape is not plausible. He says that Augustine mentioned these books in the *Retractations* after the *Acts with Emeritus* and after his journey through Mauretania because the work *On Marriage and Concupiscence* was not complete until the addition of the second book.

For if Augustine had thought that, because of the second book, he should review the first book outside its proper chronological place, this work ought not to have been mentioned in chapter 53, but immediately before or after his review of the four books to Boniface, which the same holy Doctor wrote against two letters of the Pelagians.

For Alypius brought Augustine both the excerpts supplied by Valerius, which are refuted in the second book addressed to the same Valerius, and the two Pelagian letters to which the four books to Boniface respond. All these works are known to have been composed at approximately the same time.

Yet the books to Boniface are reviewed in book 2 of the *Retractations* much later than chapter 53, namely in chapter 61. Therefore, when the two books to Valerius are mentioned in chapter 53 after the *Acts with Emeritus*, it is not because of the second book but because of the first that they occupy that place.

Accordingly, the first book and the letter to Valerius prefixed to it are rightly placed after Augustine’s journey to Mauretania, toward the end of 418 or at the beginning of the following year.

### XXXII. [Col. 1022A]

The same conclusion can be confirmed by another, clearer argument. In the aforementioned letter to Valerius, Augustine testifies that he received two letters from Valerius through the fellow presbyter Firmus.

It is clear from Letter 191 to Sixtus himself that this Firmus had on another occasion brought letters of Sixtus from Rome to Hippo while Augustine was absent. He was absent because he was in Mauretania, as may be gathered from Letter 193, no. 1.

Therefore, just as Augustine received Sixtus’s letters after his journey to Mauretania, so too he received the two letters of Valerius, which appear to have been brought by the same Firmus together with Sixtus’s letters.

There can consequently be no doubt that Augustine’s letter to Valerius and the first book of *On Marriage and Concupiscence* were composed after his departure for Mauretania, and long after Zosimus’s judgment.

### XXXIII. [Col. 1022B]

With these points established, it is easy to determine that the quoted words of the letter to Valerius concern another Pelagian attempt, which had to be suppressed by Valerius’s authority after the imperial law had been issued.

This is plainly demonstrated and explained by two other testimonies which Quesnellus adds. Saint Augustine, in chapter 2 of book 1 of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, which he sent to Valerius together with the aforementioned letter, explains why he is writing to him on this subject:

> Another reason is that you, by your authority, effectively resisted and opposed these profane novelties, against which we resist here by argument.

The matter in which Valerius used his authority is explained in the third testimony, from book 1 of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 10. There Julian, after quoting Augustine’s words in praise of Valerius, attacks them sharply and says:

> Augustine also praises a powerful man because, when we were loudly demanding nothing other than that judges be granted for so important a matter, so that what had clearly been carried out through underhanded measures might be corrected rather than punished by judicial examination, he opposed us by the weight of his dignity and did not allow us to obtain a time or place for discussion.

Saint Augustine replies to this complaint only that heretics such as the Pelagians must be restrained by Christian authorities, and that they should not be granted a time or place for examination. These words sufficiently reveal that, when the Pelagians saw themselves condemned by Zosimus’s *Tractoria* and by the imperial law, they attempted to invalidate both and requested from the emperor a new examination in a general synod, as it appears, to which they appealed after Zosimus’s judgment. See book 4 to Boniface, at the end, and the petition of faith in the appendix to Augustine, volume 10, page 110.

Valerius, however, opposed this by his authority so that it would not be granted.

Quesnellus vainly attempts to twist this passage to his own purpose. In § 18 he refers it to a request for a new judgment made before the law and the *Tractoria*—the request by which Coelestius presented himself to the Roman examination, seeking to have the things said against him in an improper manner cleared up.

Quesnellus thinks that Julian asserted that no time or place had been granted for this examination and renewed inquiry because Valerius’s efforts had secured the edict of Honorius by which Coelestius and Pelagius were compelled to leave the City.

But when Coelestius requested an examination under Zosimus, was he not heard in the first proceeding? When he was summoned again to a hearing after the African reply, would not a second examination have been instituted if he had not withdrawn from the examination—not because he had been expelled by a law, but because of his consciousness of bad faith and his obstinacy?

How, then, could Julian have written of this request of Coelestius that Valerius had allowed neither time nor place for discussion?

Furthermore, this new inquiry, which was requested before the *Tractoria* and the law, was sought by Coelestius alone, and he sought it not from the emperor but from Zosimus. The inquiry to which Valerius opposed himself, however, was requested from the emperor by several Pelagians, as is clear from the passage of Julian quoted above.

The Pelagians did not request this from the emperor until they had perceived that Zosimus’s examination and judgment had turned out contrary to their expectation and that Honorius’s law had been issued against them.

When Julian says, “In our petitions we loudly demanded nothing other than that judges be granted for so important a matter,” he indicates that he too, together with the others, had requested this new inquiry. He brought forward his own error on that occasion only, when he refused to subscribe to Zosimus’s *Tractoria*.

The words, therefore, by which Julian maintains that “what had clearly been carried out through underhanded measures” ought to be corrected refer to Zosimus’s *Tractoria* and Honorius’s law, and accuse them of having been obtained by underhanded means. Valerius, who opposed the Pelagians in this affair, is not said to have opposed them in order to obtain the law, but so that no time or place for discussion would be granted.

The entire event, therefore, and the three testimonies of Augustine brought forward in connection with it—which imply Bishop Vindemialis’s journey to the imperial court, Count Valerius’s advocacy before the emperor against the Pelagians, and Valerius’s letter to Augustine and other African bishops—refer not to the imperial law of 30 April 418, but to the Pelagians’ attempt made after that law.

Vindemialis, who is mentioned only on this occasion, is therefore wrongly transformed, on the basis of these same testimonies, into a legate sent by the African council to obtain the law.

### XXXIV. [Col. 1023C]

Quesnellus nevertheless thinks that this legation of Vindemialis is confirmed by the *Memorandum* of Zosimus, issued toward the end of 418. He judges that Zosimus therefore ordered that bishops should not travel to the imperial court importunately, because Vindemialis’s legation had displeased him.

Since this decree of Zosimus, however, rests upon a Sardican canon and concerns only those bishops who readily travel to the imperial court on private business, not those who go there for public business, if Vindemialis’s journey had furnished the occasion for repeating this decree, it would follow that he had not been engaged in a public legation and that he had gone to Ravenna not on public business but for some private cause.

### XXXV

No less fictitious are the claims by which Quesnellus says that the Africans were moved to decree this legation and to seek a law from Honorius for that reason [Col. 1023D]: they feared that, if a judgment contrary to the sentence of Innocent and the Africans should issue from Zosimus—as they supposedly believed it was just about to do—a disastrous schism would arise between the two Churches.

Augustine writes in Book I, chapter 3, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, that these men indeed hoped, on the basis of a false expectation, that the new and execrable Pelagian or Coelestian doctrine could be persuaded upon the minds of certain Roman Catholics, when they saw Coelestius treated somewhat more leniently by Zosimus, who had been enticed by the hope of his correction. But in *On Original Sin*, chapter 8, Augustine affirms that they could not deceive the Roman Church in any respect.

Since Zosimus initially dealt with Coelestius more indulgently and mildly for no other reason than that, when questioned repeatedly, Coelestius replied that he agreed with the letters of the blessed Pope Innocent, by which all doubt concerning this matter had been removed, the Africans ought to have recognized from this alone Zosimus’s constancy in defending Innocent’s judgment. They therefore could not fear [Col. 1024A] that Zosimus would issue a judgment contrary to Innocent’s sentence and thereby bring disgrace upon the Apostolic See and great scandal upon the Church.

They had even less reason for such fear because they knew for certain what Augustine had stated concerning that same See in his psalm against the party of Donatus: “It is itself the rock which the proud gates of hell do not overcome.” The same teacher testifies in many places that neither the deceptions of Coelestius nor those of Pelagius overcame it. Thus the fears attributed to the Africans by Quesnellus are fictitious and wholly alien to their thinking.

### XXXVI

He writes in section 11 that the Africans understood from Zosimus’s letter that he was hastening to acquit Coelestius and Pelagius and had already resolved to restore both of them to the communion and esteem of the Church, unless their accusers hastened to Rome within two months and proved the 875 articles of their accusation.

He cites only Zosimus’s letters. Although it cannot be denied that those letters display some leniency toward Coelestius and characterize the Africans [Col. 1024B] as guilty of inconsiderate zeal, immoderate curiosity, credulity toward unworthy accusers, precipitate judgment, and injured charity, we nevertheless do not see from what words in those same letters one could infer that Zosimus had resolved to acquit Coelestius and Pelagius contrary to the judgment and mind of Innocent.

Moreover, it was not letters alone that Zosimus sent. Together with the letters he also sent the proceedings of the first hearing. These proceedings explained how Coelestius was to be acquitted and restored to communion, in such a way that what Quesnellus alleges could not have been feared.

After reading those proceedings, Paulinus certainly felt no such fear. At this very time he sent from Africa a memorandum to the pontiff through Marcellinus. Indeed, instructed by the Roman proceedings, he expressed in that memorandum not fear but the greatest joy:

> “Your Blessedness, following the judgment of Innocent, when Coelestius was heard by the Apostolic See, among other things directed him in these words [Col. 1024C]: ‘Do you therefore condemn all those things contained in Paulinus’s memorandum—that is, the points at issue?’”

And elsewhere:

> “You have learned what sort of letter the Apostolic See gave to the brethren and fellow bishops of the province of Africa?”

And it was added:

> “Do you condemn all those things which we have condemned, and hold what we hold?”

Again:

> “Do you condemn all those things which have been circulated under your name?”

And again:

> “Or those things which Paulinus set out in his memorandum?”

And when he said that I could be proved a heretic on the basis of the things brought against him, you, filled with the Holy Spirit, rejected and repressed [Col. 1024D] by apostolic authority and restrained the words of the mad and slanderous man, delivering a judgment of this kind by which I myself might be approved as a Catholic, while you would care for him if he wished to be healed. Your judgment was as follows:

> “I do not want you to lead us around in circles. Do you condemn all those things which Paulinus brought against you or which have been circulated by rumor?”

After a short interval, expressing his joy, he adds:

> “Yet I give thanks to God and Christ the Lord that he willed the cause of his Church to be conducted in such a way that the Apostolic See—from which it was fitting that heresy should be condemned by the mouth of its two pontiffs—ordered that those things which had been brought against Coelestius by me should be condemned.”

The African Fathers must be believed to have thought no differently from Paulinus. It is credible that this memorandum was composed by Paulinus with their agreement, just as it was sent to Rome through Marcellinus, the Carthaginian subdeacon, together with the report of the African council.

The same Fathers knew especially well that, although the pontiff had initially appeared to trust and favor Coelestius to some extent because he had been deceived by his feigned and fraudulent answers—not in a matter of doctrine, but in the personal facts of the case—he nevertheless did not wish to pronounce judgment, but postponed a more exact examination and decision until fuller documentation had been sent by the Africans.

They had also learned from the proceedings that Coelestius had not been condemned for this reason: although he expressly refused to condemn the charges brought by Paulinus, he did not dare to oppose the letters of the blessed Pope Innocent. On the contrary, he promised that he would condemn everything condemned by that See, as Augustine reports in *On Original Sin*, chapter 8.

Indeed [Col. 1025A], he had also given hope and promised that he would likewise condemn, if required, the matters which Paulinus had brought against him at Carthage. Marius Mercator reported this from the same proceedings in his *Memorandum*, and he reported it in such a way as to make Zosimus’s definite deliberation in this very matter evident:

> “When questioned in the proceedings, copies of which we possess, and somewhat frightened by that judge [Zosimus], he sowed beforehand, through his repeated answers and pleadings, the hope that he would condemn those articles concerning which he had been accused at Carthage, promising to do so. For this he was urged more insistently, and more vehemently expected to do it; and for this very reason he was judged worthy of some consideration from that holy priest. Thus he earned a letter full of kindness addressed to the African bishops.”

Since in this matter the pontiff had insisted so strongly during the first hearing, and had postponed judgment only after Coelestius had made this promise, there could be no doubt that in the second hearing, at which judgment was to be pronounced—even if no accusers had hastened from Africa—he would have issued the same order to him. He would certainly not have acquitted him unless he had condemned the things he had promised to condemn.

The Africans themselves attributed the postponement of judgment [Col. 1025B] until a reply could be received from Africa, and Zosimus’s pastoral management of the heretic in the hope of his correction, to that paternal charity by which an opportunity for repentance was granted to him under the mildness of a medicinal sentence, as Augustine says in *On Original Sin*, chapter 6:

> “For if, laying aside the vanity of obstinacy, he wished to observe what he had promised, and carefully read the same letters [of Innocent] to which he had replied that he would consent, he would be healed.”

Those who judged in this way concerning Zosimus and his first hearing in the case of Coelestius, and who knew clearly from the proceedings the soundness of his policy and pastoral management, could certainly not fear [Col. 1025C] that the same pontiff would issue some decree contrary to Innocent’s judgment which would harm the faith and the Church—as Quesnellus says in section 12. Nor could they be induced by such fear to send to the emperor Honorius a legation that is supported by no evidence, in order to avoid so great an evil.

### XXXVII

What is additionally said concerning fear of a schism between the African and Roman Churches is, apart from resting on the same false hypothesis, altogether contrary to the principles of the Africans.

Could the Africans have feared a schism if Zosimus had fallen into some personal error, when they had firmly engraved upon their hearts that principle of Saint Cyprian, so often repeated by Augustine, that Catholic unity—especially unity with the Roman Church—must not be violated?

In circumstances that gave the Africans no reason to fear for the faith defined by Innocent, even if some error had perhaps occurred concerning individuals, it is much less permissible to suppose that these most tenacious defenders of Catholic unity would have brought about a schism.

Zosimus’s earlier letters, in which he appeared not ill-disposed toward Coelestius or Pelagius, promised that a more careful examination and judgment would be postponed until a reply had been received from Africa. They therefore demanded from the Africans more careful replies and documentation by which the frauds might be exposed [Col. 1025D]—not that a secret legation should be sent to the emperor, of which there is no indication anywhere in the records.

## § VIII. Zosimus’s judgment against Coelestius and Pelagius is established as having occurred toward the end of March 418. His *Tractoria* was written and published after that judgment.

### XXXVIII

After receiving and reading the fuller replies of the African synod and the documents attached to them, Zosimus sent a brief letter to that same synod on 18 or 21 March 418. From it, it can be clearly discerned how greatly his opinion had changed after reading those documents, compared with the view of Coelestius’s sincerity that he had expressed in his earlier letters.

The words in which he complains that the Africans had written [Col. 1026A] as though they believed that he had granted Coelestius complete credibility and had assented to his words without examining every syllable plainly indicate that he had now detected Coelestius’s tricks and verbal frauds:

> “As though,” he says, “we had granted Coelestius credibility in everything and, without examining his words syllable by syllable, so to speak, had assented to them all.”

He had suspended judgment until information should arrive from Africa. Once it had arrived and been examined, he considered himself sufficiently instructed to institute a definitive judgment safely.

Thus Coelestius, who was in Rome, was summoned to a fuller hearing, as Marius Mercator says in his *Memorandum*, “so that he might hasten to fulfill what he had promised”—that is, so that, after condemning the aforementioned articles formerly brought against him by Paulinus, he might be released from the sentence of the African bishops by which he had been deprived of communion.

These proceedings appear to have taken place immediately after the African replies were received, or not long after 18 or 21 March, when the pontiff wrote the aforementioned letter to the African council. Since Easter was approaching—it fell that year on 7 April 418—the intention was evidently to restore Coelestius, if he fulfilled his promises, to Catholic communion and the priestly office, in the customary manner, on Palm Sunday [Col. 1026B], after he had been judicially absolved from every suspicion of heresy.

### XXXIX

Nor should the interval between 18 or 21 March and Palm Sunday, the 31st, be considered too short for a matter of this kind to be completed in a fuller hearing.

Quesnellus exaggerates the need for a lengthy investigation and a long period of time. But that is not how matters stand. The words of Zosimus in his third letter to the African council—

> “Things which must be treated for a long time are never allowed to be handled rashly, nor should something that must be debated with the highest judgment be decided without great deliberation”

—which he believes indicate that a prolonged investigation still remained, were spoken by the pontiff only so that the Africans would not think that, during the first hearing of Coelestius, he had accepted all his statements without examination and would therefore pronounce sentence without further inquiry and without awaiting the replies of the African synod.

Moreover, before 18 or 21 March he had already carefully worked through [Col. 1026C] the volume of those replies and the attached documents, by which Zosimus was most fully instructed in the entire case. The words “when he had eventually read through that volume” seem to indicate that he had read it not hastily but gradually and carefully.

There was no dogmatic question concerning the articles previously defined by Innocent, to which Coelestius himself had professed agreement. Consequently, there was nothing new concerning the doctrine of the faith that required a lengthy examination.

Since the African replies had fully exposed the tricks and frauds in the memoranda of Coelestius and Pelagius, there was no need to debate those matters. Even if those memoranda were to be rejected, their authors were not for that reason to be condemned if they submitted themselves to the judgment of the Church.

The entire case therefore came down to this: apart from the assent already given to Innocent’s letters, would Coelestius actually condemn, as he had promised, those things which the Apostolic See had ordered to be condemned, especially the matters brought against him by Paulinus?

The letters of the Africans pressed this point above all [Col. 1026D]. Nothing else was required—as Marius Mercator suggests—except that Coelestius, summoned to a fuller hearing, should be presented with the charges brought against him by Paulinus and should be required to condemn them. If he stood by his promises, he would be acquitted and would communicate at the divine service on Easter; otherwise, he would undergo the sentence of condemnation.

Augustine indicates the same thing in Book II, chapter 3, *To Boniface*, when he reports that Coelestius was summoned after the African replies had been received so that, through definite and clear answers, either the man’s cunning or his correction might become evident.

Everyone can see how easy and straightforward this would have been. The days of Lent did not prevent a fuller assembly from being convened in so serious and urgent a matter, about which the African Fathers were especially concerned. As Quesnellus notes in section 22, it was very much in the interest of the pontiff and the Roman clergy that the decision should reach the Africans more quickly, and therefore that a fuller gathering should be held during the days preceding Palm Sunday.

Besides the bishops who were in Rome [Col. 1027A] or who had hastened from neighboring places after learning of the African replies, the Roman clergy assembled in very large numbers. The fuller hearing mentioned by Marius Mercator required nothing more.

Indeed, if Sixtus, a presbyter of the Roman Church who first pronounced an anathema against Coelestius and Pelagius, did so during the very hearing—as Augustine testifies in Letter 194, section 1—Augustine states in the same place that this hearing was extremely crowded because of the multitude of clergy and especially of the people:

> “The same report did not fail to say that you first pronounced an anathema against them before a very large crowd.”

Likewise, in the judgment which Saint Leo conducted against the Manichaeans, not only was there a very large presence of priests, but distinguished men, as well as part of the senate and the populace, also took part. See Leo’s Letter 15, chapter 16, volume I, column 708, printed in larger type.

### XL

Coelestius, who was in Rome, certainly had to be summoned to the hearing according to the requirements of law. But it is clear from the third session of the Council of Chalcedon [Col. 1027B] that the law did not require three citations to be issued at intervals of several days, as Quesnellus argues. From that session we learn that Dioscorus was summoned three times on the same day.

Coelestius’s flight, by which he withdrew from the judgment after being summoned, brought the proceedings to completion more quickly. His flight immediately exposed his fraud and obstinacy. It became clear to everyone that he had lied in the earlier hearing, had deceptively pretended to consent to Innocent’s letters, and had deliberately withdrawn from condemning the matters brought against him by Paulinus.

It was therefore easy to pronounce sentence against him, and also against Pelagius, his teacher, whose commentaries on Paul’s Epistles, produced on this occasion through the efforts of certain Romans, revealed his heresy even more clearly. See Augustine, *On Original Sin*, chapter 21.

The composition of the *Tractoria*, in which the entire matter had to be explained, the errors reported, and Catholic doctrine confirmed, certainly required a considerable amount of time. But the days preceding Palm Sunday were sufficient for exposing the fraud and malice of a man who had fled through deliberate deceit [Col. 1027C] and for pronouncing an anathema against him.

Indeed, Saint Augustine, Book II, chapter 3, *To Boniface*, clearly indicates that this happened immediately after the letters from Africa had been received:

> “This was awaited so that it might become more fully and clearly evident in him [Coelestius], since his cunning had become somewhat more clearly known in that province, when the letters from Africa should arrive. When those letters came to Rome, then, when his presence was demanded so that through definite and clear answers either the man’s cunning or his correction might become evident and remain ambiguous to no one, he withdrew and refused to submit to the examination. Nor was it now to be postponed, as was done, for the benefit of others”—namely, the sentence of condemnation.

## § IX. Honorius’s law against the Pelagians was requested immediately after the Roman judgment by Zosimus, not by the Africans. [Col. 1027D]

### XLI

The condemnation of the heretics was completed in the Roman assembly toward the end of March, although the *Tractoria* had not yet been composed and published. Nevertheless, news of the condemnation immediately spread, so that the Africans learned of it by report before Zosimus’s letter reached them, as is clear from Augustine’s Letter 194, section 1.

Since several supporters of the Pelagian heresy in Rome—and perhaps among them some bishops, for it is certain that certain bishops in Italy were infected with the same stain—had stirred up disturbances, and since greater unrest was feared from their faction against the *Tractoria* that was to be published, Zosimus prudently decided to inform the emperor Honorius immediately of the judgment that had been held and of the disturbances that had arisen. He did so so that the emperor might restore peace to the City by issuing a law and restrain the heretics.

For this reason, the law issued by that same Augustus on 30 April is called a rescript in the manuscript copies of our *Codex*, chapter 14. It is called a reply by Julian in Augustine’s Book III, chapter 1, *Against Julian*, because it had been requested in Zosimus’s earlier letters.

### XLII

[Col. 1028A] On this matter we see Quesnellus resisting with the greatest force. He maintains that Honorius’s law preceded Zosimus’s judgment and that it was requested not by Zosimus but by a legation sent by the Africans.

But once we have shown that the African legation which Quesnellus asserts is fictitious, his position collapses on this point alone.

That Honorius’s law was not enacted before Zosimus’s judgment is especially demonstrated by the utter improbability that the emperor would have wished to issue a law against Coelestius and Pelagius before their case had been discussed and decided in an apostolic judgment. Otherwise, if Coelestius had carried out his promises during the judgment and condemned the errors, he would have been struck by an unjust law.

Moreover, the reason for issuing the law was the disturbances raised by the Pelagians in Rome, as the very words of the law declare:

> “Within our most sacred City, a pestilential virus had so taken root in the hearts of certain persons that, when the path of straightforward belief had been broken and their zeal divided into factions in support of opposing positions, the zeal for assertion having been split into factions, the material of unappeased dissension was introduced; and, with a new fuel of scandal kindled, the assaulted tranquility of the most blessed Church now totters, while some pursue one path and others another through ambiguous interpretation, and [lacuna] according to the capacity of their slippery ingenuity, raise a profane question of novel ventures.” [Col. 1028B]

Here it must first be observed that the law speaks of disturbances and questions which, while the law itself was being written, were actively attacking the peace of the City and Catholic doctrine.

The doctrine chiefly attacked was that concerning original sin, which the emperor complains in the preceding words had been assailed with particular boldness.

But after the first hearing under Zosimus, before the African replies had arrived, Coelestius and his followers could not have stirred up these disturbances and open dissensions in the City on the basis of some hope arising from the favor of that pontiff and the Roman clergy.

For the favor shown to Coelestius in the earlier proceedings had been granted because he had concealed his errors through deceitful professions and, by pretending to agree with Innocent’s letters, had promised that he would condemn whatever the Roman See ordered, as well as the matters brought against him by Paulinus. That favor should certainly have restrained him and his followers [Col. 1028C], before that time, from defending those same errors and from stirring up on their account the dissensions and profane questions that would have exposed his pretenses and frauds and alienated the minds of the pontiff and his supporters among the Romans.

We understand clearly that this is what happened after the African replies, brought by Marcellinus to Zosimus, became known.

For when those replies had exposed through definite documents the errors and frauds of Coelestius and Pelagius, and had among other things openly demanded the condemnation of the errors concerning original sin contained in the articles of Paulinus, and when Zosimus had declared a definite decision on this matter, then Coelestius and his followers in Rome, recognizing that all hope had failed them, began, in order to prevent the condemnation if possible, openly to defend the articles in question, deny original sin, resist Catholics who defended sound doctrine, and spread questions and dissensions.

When judgment was soon instituted, these disturbances, more fiercely inflamed [Col. 1028D], disturbed the public peace after the sentence of condemnation had been pronounced against Coelestius and Pelagius, through the efforts of heretics who refused to submit to apostolic authority.

The African synod could not have foreseen and reported to Honorius these disturbances after the African replies had arrived and while they were boiling over after Zosimus’s judgment. They had not yet arisen.

Certainly, when the African Fathers warned Zosimus in their letter that it was not enough for slower and more cautious persons that Coelestius merely confess in general terms that he agreed with the letters of Bishop Innocent, but that he had to anathematize openly the things he had wrongly stated in his memorandum—the principal one being the article against original sin—they were evidently unaware of Coelestius’s obstinacy in defending this error at Rome.

Therefore it was not the African synod [Col. 1029A] but Zosimus who reported these Roman disturbances to the emperor.

### XLIII

Nor are the testimonies of Augustine from Letters 104, now numbered 191, and 105, now numbered 194, opposed to this position. Quesnellus attempts to use them to argue that the Pelagians stirred up no disturbances in the City after Zosimus’s constitution.

We believe that the disturbances for which Zosimus requested the law were those stirred up after the African replies and after the sentence itself but before the publication of the constitution or *Tractoria*. From these disturbances the same pontiff feared that even greater unrest would arise after the constitution had been published.

Nevertheless, although the letters of Augustine sent to Rome show that some people fell silent after Zosimus’s constitution, others in that city are said to have continued openly to speak in favor of Pelagian doctrine, while others secretly spread their poison and stirred up disturbances.

Augustine warns in Letter 191, section 2, that those must be corrected and punished who dare to chatter **more freely** about that error, which is most hostile to the Christian name, and those who, more cautiously and timidly but nevertheless without ceasing, whisper it, entering houses, as the Apostle says, and carrying on the other practices that follow, practicing impiety [reading uncertain]. [Col. 1029B]

Still more clearly he says in Letter 194, section 2:

> “For there are some who think that impieties justly condemned ought to be defended **more freely**; and there are others who enter houses more secretly and do not cease to sow them in secret.”

Since these letters were written to Sixtus some time after Honorius’s law itself, these disturbances, which continued to stir up unrest even after the law had been issued to suppress them, are evidence of the greater earlier disturbances for which the law had been requested.

### XLIV

In our judgment, we gather a more evident argument from the words of the same law by which it orders Coelestius and Pelagius to be expelled from the City:

> “With Coelestius and Pelagius, the heads of the accursed doctrine, first expelled from the City …”

If this law had been issued before the Roman judgment, there is no doubt that Coelestius would have been expelled from Rome before that judgment.

But he was not expelled before the judgment. For when he was summoned to the hearing [Col. 1029C], he not only failed to appear, Marius Mercator says in his *Memorandum*, but fled from the aforementioned city of Rome. For this reason he was condemned outright by Zosimus of blessed memory.

Augustine agrees in Book II, section 5, *To Boniface*, when he clearly reproaches Coelestius for this flight:

> “Then, when his presence was demanded so that through definite and clear answers either the man’s cunning or his correction might become evident and remain ambiguous to no one, he withdrew and refused the examination.”

Augustine would have reproached him wrongly for this if Coelestius had already been expelled by force of the law before the judgment. Therefore Zosimus’s judgment preceded the imperial law.

To say with Quesnellus, section 25, number 5, that the law was issued before Zosimus’s judgment but was not promulgated until afterward—either because it was communicated only to Zosimus or because its promulgation was delayed by Palladius at Zosimus’s suggestion until Zosimus himself had delivered his sentence—is to speak without any foundation. It is to dream up an altogether incredible story merely so that an otherwise conclusive argument may appear to have been weakened [Col. 1029D].

Nor would the provision ordering Coelestius to be expelled have been pointless if he had already left Rome when summoned to judgment before the law. Since the same decree was also made concerning Pelagius, who at that time was farther away from the Roman City, the provision should be understood in this way: if they should ever come to Rome, they were to be expelled immediately.

### XLV

Moreover, Saint Prosper, Saint Augustine, and Possidius confirm our position. They consistently list the various condemnations of the Pelagian heresy in this order: first the African councils, then the Apostolic See, and finally the imperial authority following those earlier judgments.

Prosper, addressing Africa in his poem *Against the Ungrateful*, says:

> “Your blessed bishops from every city assembled,  
> and in a celebrated gathering of two councils of elders  
> you decreed what Rome approved and what kingdoms followed.” [Col. 1030A]

We showed above, section 7, that the earlier verses refer to the synods assembled in Africa under Zosimus. Thus the phrase “what Rome approved” indicates Zosimus’s judgment approving the African replies.

The words “what kingdoms followed” refer to the law of Honorius issued on the day before the Kalends of May in 418, or even to the second law of the following year. Both laws followed not so much the African judgment as the Roman judgment.

Similarly, Augustine says in *On Original Sin*, chapter 17:

> “You surely perceive that episcopal councils, the Apostolic See, the entire Roman Church, and the Roman Empire—which, by God’s favor, is Christian—were rightly moved against the authors of so wicked an error.”

Possidius, in *The Life of Augustine*, chapter 18, is the clearest of all. Passing over the African councils in silence, after mentioning the constitutions of Innocent and especially of Zosimus, he adds:

> “Hearing and following such a judgment pronounced against them by the Catholic Church of God, the most pious emperor Honorius also decreed that they, condemned by his laws, should be regarded among the heretics.”

Quesnellus’s interpretation should not disturb anyone [Col. 1030B]. He observes that Possidius mentions not one law but several laws, and says that it is sufficient if we say that, according to Possidius, the emperor followed Zosimus’s judgment in the second law of 419, even if it is denied that he followed it in the first law of 418.

He insists on this only because of the prior assumption by which he thinks that Zosimus’s judgment came after the first law. But he has not yet proved that assumption.

### XLVI

Beyond the arguments we have already produced, we shall finally offer another proof that Zosimus judged before the same law. It is found in Augustine’s Letter 215 to Valentinus, section 2, where, while reviewing all the judgments—both African and Roman—under Zosimus, he writes:

> “What was written to Pope Zosimus concerning the African council, and his reply sent to all the bishops of the entire world, and what we briefly established in the later plenary council of all Africa against that very error …”

Even Quesnellus considers it absolutely certain that this plenary council of all Africa was held on the Kalends of May in 418.

Moreover, it will be demonstrated clearly, as we trust, in section 11 that, after receiving the *Tractoria*, the Africans replied to Zosimus in a plenary synod, and that the plenary synod from which they replied to him was none other than the council which established the canons on the Kalends of May.

Therefore Zosimus’s judgment, after which he wrote the *Tractoria* [Col. 1030C] and sent it to Africa, cannot be denied to have taken place some time before the Kalends of May—and still more certainly before Honorius’s celebrated law, which was issued on the day before the Kalends of May.

To evade this argument, Quesnellus must posit a third and later African council under Zosimus, at which the Africans replied after receiving Zosimus’s letters following the Roman judgment.

But in section 2 we demonstrated from Augustine that only two African councils were held under Zosimus in the case of the Pelagians. We also established there that no third council should be posited unless something compels us to do so.

If it were certain that Honorius’s law had been enacted before Zosimus’s judgment, that would indeed constitute sufficient compulsion. But since several arguments advanced by us suggest the opposite, and since the arguments produced by Quesnellus to establish that the law was earlier and was issued at the request not of Zosimus but of the Africans [Col. 1030D] are exceedingly weak, this will become entirely clear from what follows in the next section.

## § X. The weakness of Quesnellus’s arguments by which he attempted to prove that Honorius’s law against the Pelagians was requested by the Africans and enacted before Zosimus’s judgment. The emperor’s second law against the same persons was directed not to Aurelius of Carthage alone but especially to the Roman pontiff.

### XLVII

Quesnellus introduces an argument from the manuscript *Code of Canons* published in this volume. In that work, chapter 14 records Honorius’s law as having been issued after the proceedings of the aforementioned synod—or “the proceedings written above.” Those proceedings, however, are not the Roman proceedings of the preceding chapter 13, but those of the plenary synod.

This argument has no force. The heading, which originated with an ancient compiler, contains an obvious error. The proceedings of the synod [Col. 1031A] described in the preceding chapter 13 are dated to the Kalends of May 418 and therefore are later than the law itself.

Nor should Quesnellus’s proposed escape be accepted: namely, that the proceedings or canons presented in chapter 13 were first established in the preceding synod, which he considers to have been held in the autumn, and were then repeated and confirmed in the synod of the Kalends of May.

We already sufficiently refuted this evasion in sections 5, 6, and 7. We also proved fictitious the legation which Quesnellus claimed had been sent by the Africans from the earlier synod to the emperor to request the aforementioned canons.

### XLVIII

It may appear somewhat more plausible to believe that Honorius’s law was issued at the request of the Africans because of what Quesnellus adduces from another law of the same emperor, sent to Aurelius in the following year. In that law, when Honorius recalls the earlier law, he affirms that he followed Aurelius’s judgment.

But this argument is not sufficiently sound.

News of the Africans’ replies and judgment had spread widely immediately after the Roman synod [Col. 1031B]. Perhaps those replies were sent to the emperor by Zosimus himself together with information about his own judgment. Since everyone knew that the Roman judgment was the same as the African judgment—the Roman See had made it its own by approving it, as the author of the chapters on grace generally observed concerning the African decrees—it amounted to the same thing for Honorius to say that he had followed Aurelius’s judgment, that is, the African judgment, as to say that he had followed Zosimus’s judgment, by which Zosimus had confirmed the African judgment, as Prosper reported in his *Chronicle*.

Since the emperor could mention either both judgments or either one of them, it seemed appropriate in a letter addressed to Aurelius to mention Aurelius’s own judgment in his honor. If he had written to Zosimus, he would undoubtedly have said similar things about Zosimus.

Certainly, when Honorius states in the same second law that he followed the judgment of Aurelius by which it is established that the Pelagians were condemned by all after a just examination of the sentence, he was not referring to a judgment of Aurelius sent to him from Africa. Rather, when he wrote these words, he had before his eyes [Col. 1031C] the judgment contained in Zosimus’s *Tractoria*, which had been received and subscribed throughout the world.

For the Pelagians were not condemned by any other judgment of Aurelius than the one which, disseminated throughout the whole world in Zosimus’s *Tractoria*, was signed by everyone.

Although this had not yet occurred before the first law, when Honorius sent the second law to Aurelius it had already been accomplished. Honorius therefore thought it appropriate to note it in Aurelius’s honor.

## XLIX

Moreover, there seems to be no doubt that the second law was directed chiefly to Boniface, who occupied the apostolic see after Zosimus, at the time of that law. For this second law was issued chiefly on account of the bishops who supported the Pelagians and refused to subscribe to the *Tractoria*, as is clear from these words of the law itself: “especially, however, for correcting the obstinacy of certain bishops who either support their perverse arguments”—those of Pelagius and Coelestius—“by tacit consent, or do not destroy them by public opposition”; and from what follows, where it is ordered that, unless these men subscribed to their condemnation promulgated in the *Tractoria*, they should be punished by the loss of their episcopate, expelled from the cities in perpetuity, and deprived of communion [Col. 1031D].

The rebellious bishops, moreover, were residing not in Africa but in Italy; and Marius Mercator testifies that the law was issued chiefly against them. “Julian and his other accomplices, refusing to subscribe to the *Tractoria*, and unwilling to make themselves of one mind with those same Fathers”—who had subscribed to it—“were not only deposed and deprived of office by IMPERIAL LAWS, but also by priestly decrees, and were driven out of all ITALY”: something that certainly occurred after the law mentioned above.

We learn from Augustine’s *Book I to Boniface*, no. 3, and *Book II*, no. 1, that these bishops numbered eighteen, with Julian of Eclanum as their head. Other imperial laws were generally addressed to the prefects of the praetorium, so that they might promulgate them in their dioceses. But this law, since it dealt particularly with compelling bishops to subscribe or with deposing them, was given to the bishops of the principal sees, so that each might communicate it to the bishops subject to him.

Indeed, it is evident that this law was delivered not only to Aurelius but also to the bishops of other principal sees from the fact that it was to be promulgated and observed not in Africa alone but in all the provinces. Aurelius, however, had authority only over the African provinces; and his letter to the bishops established throughout the provinces of Byzacena and Arzugitana is preserved. In it he states that the same law was to be communicated only to his fellow bishops:

> “The authority of the most glorious Christian princes, guardians of the true and catholic faith, has intervened; through my humility it has willed that this be communicated to ALL MY FELLOW BISHOPS.”

Among the other bishops of the principal sees to whom this law must be said to have been given no less than to Aurelius, so that they too might communicate it to their own bishops, Boniface, certainly—the successor of Zosimus—must be regarded as having been especially concerned with repressing the Italian Pelagian bishops, on whose account the law had been enacted.

It happened by chance that only the copy addressed to Aurelius has been preserved for us, just as by chance only the copy of Aurelius’s letter to the Byzaceni and Arzugitani has survived, while we must not doubt that those letters which the same Aurelius sent by imperial command to the bishops of the other African provinces have perished. The same law, in the same wording, is also transmitted in manuscripts as having been given to Saint Augustine, bishop.

It was therefore likewise given, and especially in the same wording, to Pope Boniface, who used that law in persecuting the Pelagians, as Prosper testifies in *Against the Collator*, chapter 21. In its copy, there is no doubt that the emperor wrote, with a slight alteration of the sort that commonly occurs, instead of “in which our clemency followed the judgment of your holiness,” something like “of your predecessor” or “of the apostolic see.” You see, therefore, how weak is what Quesnell conjectured from this law in support of his own position.

## L

Nor does he argue any better—but much worse—in § 27, no. 4, from another testimony of the Pelagians, which Augustine quotes in *Book III of the Unfinished Work*, chapter 35. There the complaint of the raging heretics against Augustine and Alypius is presented in these words:

> “Why,” says Julian, “have you stirred up the whole of Italy with such factions? Why have you provoked seditions at Rome by hiring crowds? Why have you fattened throughout almost the whole of Africa herds of horses at the expense of the poor, which, with Alypius pursuing them, you dispatched to tribunes and centurions? Why have you corrupted the powers of the world by accepting the inheritances offered by matrons, so that the straw of public fury might burn against us? Why have you disturbed the peace of the Churches? Why have you stained the times of a religious prince with the impiety of persecutions?”

Quesnell believes that Augustine and Alypius are attacked in these final words as the authors and agents of the imperial edicts; and he considers this to refer rather to the first edict of Honorius, in the year 418, than to the later one of 419.

But since the words “with Alypius pursuing them” clearly allude to Alypius’s journey to Italy, during which all those disturbances were stirred up by him both at Rome and at Ravenna against the Pelagians—and since Alypius did not come to Italy except in the year 419, when at Ravenna he received from Count Valerius excerpts from Julian, and at Rome two letters of the Pelagians handed over by Pope Boniface for delivery to Augustine [Col. 1032D], and again in the year 420, when he carried Augustine’s replies to Valerius and Boniface—that testimony cannot be referred to the edict of 418. Rather, it must be referred to the law of 419, by which a more exact investigation and a harsher punishment were decreed against the Pelagians.

Certainly, in § 29, Quesnell himself rejects the opinion of those who thought that Alypius had been sent to Italy by the Africans as their envoy on account of the first law.

## LI

Quesnell brings forward another argument in § 25, no. 9, from Augustine’s *Book II to Boniface*, chapter 3, where he reports that the Pelagians complained about the Roman clergy, writing that, struck by the terror of a command, they had not been ashamed to commit the crime of treachery, so that, contrary to their former judgment—by which they had supported the catholic doctrine in the official proceedings—they later pronounced that human nature was evil.

Quesnell thinks that Zosimus was included among these clerics, as though he had condemned Coelestius’s doctrine, which he himself had previously approved in his initial examination, as they boasted, under the terror of a command—that is, of a law [Col. 1033A]. If this were to be understood in that way, Zosimus’s judgment would certainly have to be rejected as subsequent to the promulgation of the law.

There are two false elements in Quesnell’s interpretation: first, that Zosimus was included by the Pelagians under the name “clerics”; second, that the law of Honorius is indicated by the “terror of a command.”

First, who has ever included the Roman pontiff himself under the term “clerics”? That Zosimus was not included by the Pelagians under that name is evident from the words by which those are attacked who had supported the catholic doctrine in the official proceedings. These were the Roman clerics who had been present at the first examination, in which Zosimus had dealt more mildly with Coelestius.

Augustine distinguished these same clerics from Zosimus even more clearly when, in chapter 4, he wrote:

> “How, then, are the Roman clerics accused of treachery by these deserters and opponents of grace, under Bishop Zosimus, as though in the later condemnation of Coelestius and Pelagius they had thought something different from what they thought under Innocent in the earlier one?”

Here the Roman clerics are distinguished from Innocent just as they are distinguished from Zosimus: they are said to have been “under Zosimus” and “under Innocent,” not to have been either of those pontiffs.

## LI

Someone may perhaps object that, since Augustine, in the passage cited, while refuting the Pelagians’ recklessness in accusing the Roman clerics of treachery, chiefly vindicates Zosimus, this pontiff must have been included by them under the expression “clerics.”

But the holy Doctor did not clear Zosimus because of this; rather, he did so because the official records of the first examination had been brought forward against those same clerics. Since these records showed that they had then favored Coelestius precisely because they had followed Zosimus’s leniency, Augustine could not defend them in any other way unless Zosimus himself were first vindicated.

Accordingly, before acquitting those clerics of the treachery charged against them, Augustine says that the Pelagians had thought that the new and execrable Pelagian or Coelestian doctrine could be impressed upon the Catholic minds of certain Romans, since those minds, under Zosimus, had been treated somewhat more gently than the stricter discipline of the Church required [Col. 1033C].

Then, giving the reason why they had been treated more gently by Zosimus, whom the Roman clerics had followed, Augustine shows that this leniency was unrelated to treachery. In particular, once Zosimus had recognized Coelestius’s fraud and obstinacy from his flight, he immediately condemned him. Since the Roman clerics adhered to that judgment, they cannot be called traitors, although they could have been branded with treachery if they had approved something contrary to the decree of Innocent, to which they had already assented under that pontiff.

And so, in chapter 4, Augustine concludes with the words quoted shortly before:

> “How, then, are the Roman clerics accused of treachery under Bishop Zosimus, as though in the later condemnation of Coelestius and Pelagius—when they followed this pontiff—they had thought something different from what they thought under Innocent in the earlier one?”

These words clearly distinguish the Roman clerics attacked in Julian’s statement from Zosimus.

## LII

If, in two other passages noted by Quesnell, Zosimus too is reported to have been accused by those same Pelagians of the same treachery, nowhere nevertheless will one find the terror of a command alleged when treachery is imposed upon Zosimus [Col. 1033D], as it is alleged in the testimony that concerns the Roman clerics alone.

Why is this? Because this “terror of a command,” which was said to have been inflicted upon the Roman clerics, did not proceed from an imperial law that preceded Zosimus’s judgment and instilled fear in the pontiff and the clerics alike. Rather, it proceeded from Zosimus’s own judgment. Using his apostolic authority, he ordered that the sentence passed against the Pelagians be accepted by all, and compelled everyone—especially the clerics, even if some had previously favored the Pelagian error—to pronounce an anathema against Coelestius and Pelagius and their errors, under threat of ecclesiastical penalties.

We learn from Augustine’s Letter 191 to Sixtus, no. 2, that certain people in Rome who had previously defended some such error before Zosimus’s judgment fell silent immediately after it, before the imperial law was issued, through fear of that judgment, its authority, and its anathema. Augustine writes:

> “For some of them, before this pestilence was condemned by the most manifest judgment even of the apostolic see, may have become known to you [Col. 1034A]; but now”—that is, after the judgment of that same see—“you clearly see that they have suddenly fallen silent.”

The following words show that they had been driven to silence by fear. Since it was uncertain whether they held a sound opinion or were silent from fear, Augustine says that they should be treated more gently:

> “For what need is there to terrify those whom their very silence shows to be sufficiently TERRIFIED? Nor are they therefore to be passed over as though healthy, without the diligent care of medicine, whose wound lies hidden. For although they are not to be terrified, they are nevertheless to be instructed; and, as I think, they can more easily be helped while FEAR of severity assists the teacher of truth.”

He repeats similar remarks in Letter 194, addressed to the same Sixtus, no. 2. There he is speaking of those who, after defending a perverse doctrine at Rome before Zosimus’s constitution, fell silent through fear after that constitution. Nevertheless, they must have been well known to Sixtus’s brothers—that is, to the Roman clerics.

These people, therefore, had fallen silent through fear of the constitution itself, or of apostolic authority. Since the Roman clerics had pronounced an anathema against the Pelagians after Zosimus’s judgment—and since Sixtus himself had been the first of all to pronounce their anathema before a very large crowd, although the Pelagians had previously boasted of him as their patron—the same heretics opposed Zosimus’s judgment and anathema to Sixtus and the other Roman clerics, claiming that they had been terrified and had committed treachery in the same way.

You see, therefore, how wrongly the terror of a command is here referred to the law of Honorius. This was the second point that we undertook to prove.

## LIII

One argument of Quesnell remains, from Saint Augustine’s Letter 157, now numbered 190, to Optatus, no. 22. Since Zosimus’s letter against the Pelagians is there called “recent,” Quesnell infers that it had recently arrived in Africa—namely, while Augustine was writing the letter either in Mauretania or after such a journey.

But it is certain that the letter had been brought to Africa while Augustine was still at Carthage—see *On the Grace of Christ*, Book I, chapter 1, and *Retractions*, Book II—before he went to Mauretania. Moreover, we shall demonstrate in § 11 that it arrived before the plenary council had been dissolved, so that the bishops of that council, which met on the Kalends of May in the year 418, subscribed to that very letter [Col. 1034C].

Who would doubt that letters received only a few months earlier could be called “recent”? And if Augustine feared that a copy of the letter might perhaps have been sent to the same Optatus, that should cause no difficulty. For he seems to have been the bishop of a very remote city and insufficiently informed about the Pelagian controversy itself. Compare nos. 22 and 23 of his letter.
