Hence the heading of another letter of Augustine to the same Optatus, recovered from a manuscript of Gottwic and inserted in volume XI of the latest Venetian edition, in which he is called Bishop of Milevis, is erroneous and was wrongly transferred from an earlier bishop of the same name and city. Indeed, from the same letter—which is certainly genuine—someone might plausibly infer that Optatus was perhaps bishop of a church outside Africa.

Nothing, therefore, among all the conjectures that Quesnell has collected at such length is sufficiently firm to overturn what we have established: that Zosimus’s judgment against Coelestius and Pelagius preceded the law of Honorius, and that the law itself was sought not by the Africans but by that same pontiff after the condemnation of the Pelagians, in order to suppress their disturbances.

This will be confirmed much more clearly by what follows, when we prove that the synod which replied to Zosimus after the constitution had been issued against them was the synod that enacted the canons on the Kalends of May.

## § XI. The plenary synod that enacted the canons on grace on the Kalends of May in the year 418 is the same synod that replied to Zosimus after receiving his *Tractoria*

The fourth autumnal synod of that same year, to which Quesnell attributes this African reply, is excluded. The number of Fathers belonging to the plenary synod of the Kalends of May. The canons on grace enacted there, insofar as they were approved by the apostolic see.

[Col. 1035A]

## LIV

After condemning the Pelagians in the Roman judgment toward the end of March, Zosimus soon composed and issued the *Tractoria*, being certain that the emperor would enact a law, and sent it not long afterward, before the end of April.

For Augustine, in Letter 215 to Valentinus, no. 2, after mentioning the letter of the African council written to Zosimus [895], places Zosimus’s reply to the bishops of the whole world before the plenary synod, which established brief canons on the Kalends of May:

> “His reply to the bishops of the whole world, and what we briefly established in the later plenary council of all Africa against that very error.”

To evade this testimony, Quesnell says in § 34:

> “Augustine did not place the reply before the council because it was earlier, but so that he would not separate the reply from the written document of the Africans.”

But this empty evasion will be exposed if Zosimus’s *Tractoria* to the bishops of the whole world was received in that very plenary synod and the Africans replied to it. It will then follow that the *Tractoria* had been sent before the synod itself, so that the synod could reply.

## LV

Augustine relates in Letter 190, no. 2, that after the condemnation of the Pelagians Zosimus sent two letters to Africa: one specifically to the Africans, the other universally to all bishops—that is, the *Tractoria*.

Saint Prosper testifies that, after receiving these letters, the Africans replied to the same pontiff. In *Against the Collator*, chapter 5, no. 15, he quotes a fragment from the African letter:

> “The African bishops went astray in replying to the same Pope Zosimus and praising him for the salutary soundness of this judgment of his, when they say, etc.”

These Africans, then, were certainly gathered in synod when they replied; they had been compelled to assemble in a synod.

Since Quesnell, on the basis of his preconceived opinions, believes that Zosimus’s *Tractoria* was composed much later and brought to Africa long after the synod that enacted the canons on the Kalends of May, he is compelled in § 23 to admit a third synod that replied to Zosimus. He says that this synod could scarcely have been held before the autumn of 418 and, as it seems, after Saint Augustine’s return from Caesarean Mauretania.

In this way he abandons Augustine, although in § 9, no. 2, he admits that Augustine reported only two African councils held under Zosimus against the Pelagians.

We, however, believe that we can demonstrate that the synod which replied after receiving Zosimus’s letters was none other than the plenary synod that enacted the canons on the Kalends of May.

## LVI

That Zosimus’s letters were received and subscribed by the African Fathers assembled in a plenary synod is made clear by the testimony of Aurelius of Carthage in his letter to the bishops established throughout the provinces of Byzacena and Arzugitana. The letter is printed in the collection published in this volume, chapter 17.

There Aurelius states, on the authority of the imperial law, that the condemnation of the Pelagians—which Zosimus’s *Tractoria* had ordered—was to be subscribed by all:

> “By all African bishops, whether those whose subscription is already preserved in the synodal records, or those who were unable to attend that PLENARY council of all Africa.”

The subscriptions of the bishops who had attended the plenary council therefore existed in the synodal records.

Moreover, the synod that enacted the published canons on the Kalends of May is called “plenary” in all the manuscript copies of our collection, and “universal” by Dionysius. The two terms amount to the same thing: in African usage, “plenary” and “universal” are used interchangeably, as we noted in no. 28.

That this plenary synod was the one that received Zosimus’s letters and subscribed the condemnation of the Pelagians can likewise be demonstrated from the same holy Doctor, so that there is no need, with Quesnell, to posit another plenary synod in the autumn of 418—one of which no one makes mention and which conflicts with Augustine’s assertion of only two councils, an African and a plenary one.

It is certain that Augustine wrote the books *On the Grace of Christ* and *On Original Sin* at Carthage, from the words of Book I, chapter 1:

> “At Carthage … we dictated these things as best we could.”

From the second book of the *Retractions*, chapter 50, we learn that these works were composed after the *Tractoria* and the judgment of Zosimus, which Augustine mentions in those same books.

It is also clear from the *Retractions* that the books were completed at Carthage before Augustine went to Caesarean Mauretania, since in the *Retractions* he reviews his dealings with Emeritus in Caesarean Mauretania after the books *On the Grace of Christ* and *On Original Sin*.

In the first book *On Grace*, chapter 1, he presents himself as extremely occupied at Carthage. In Letter 193 to Mercator, no. 1, recalling the same occupations, he places them before his journey to Mauretania:

> “As for my not replying from Carthage, there was no lack of an opportunity to send the letters, but other matters that were more urgent kept us extremely occupied and attentive until we departed from there. When we left, we proceeded as far as Caesarean Mauretania, where ecclesiastical necessity drew us; on that occasion the proceedings against Emeritus took place.”

See *Retractions*, Book II, chapter 51.

Therefore, the plenary synod at which Zosimus’s *Tractoria* was received and the condemnation of the Pelagians subscribed was held before Augustine’s journey to Mauretania. No other plenary synod preceded that journey except the one that enacted the canons on the Kalends of May.

That synod, therefore—and not a later autumnal synod—received Zosimus’s *Tractoria* and sent a reply to the same pontiff.

## LVII

Only one difficulty might seem to arise in support of this position: Zosimus’s third letter to the Africans, dated 18 or 21 March—when he had not yet pronounced judgment against the Pelagians or written the *Tractoria*—was received by the Africans on 29 April. How, then, could the *Tractoria*, whose composition required a considerable amount of time, have followed so quickly?

This difficulty can easily be removed if we describe the events as they seem more probably to have occurred.

We showed in § 8 that Zosimus’s judgment began toward the end of March in the year 418, before Palm Sunday, so that Coelestius, if he kept his promises, could be acquitted and restored to communion during the Easter days.

But when Coelestius fled, judgment was pronounced against him and the Pelagians by apostolic authority before the thirty-first day of that same month, and the entire Roman clergy added their subscriptions to it. The presbyter Sixtus was the first of them all to pronounce an anathema against those heretics before a very large crowd.

News of this immediately raced ahead to Africa, so that Zosimus’s letters arrived there after the news itself. Hence Augustine says in Letter 194 to the same Sixtus, no. 1:

> “The same report did not fail to announce that you were the first to pronounce their anathema before a very large crowd. Then, together with the letters of the apostolic see sent to Africa concerning their condemnation, your own letter also reached the venerable Aurelius.”

Who does not see that, from about 30 March, the report could have reached Africa so much more quickly, if some opportunity arose, that their condemnation would certainly have become known to the Africans before the Kalends of May? Maritime journeys, after all, often have particularly rapid passages.

Since the plenary synod had already been convened—for it had been summoned around this time after Easter, when a Roman reply was expected—the canons on grace were issued on the very Kalends of May. In them the African Fathers, agreeing with the judgment of the apostolic see, pronounced an anathema against the Pelagian doctrines.

Since Zosimus’s *Tractoria*, on account of what it contained, required more careful preparation, it was not sent to Africa immediately after the judgment but somewhat later.

Meanwhile, after the canons had been issued, the Fathers of the plenary synod understood that the letters of the apostolic see would certainly arrive and that a reply would have to be made in the name of the plenary synod itself. To prevent all the bishops who had assembled for the council from being detained longer, the entire council decreed that three judges should be chosen from each province, who, together with the aged Aurelius, would examine everything. The entire council asked Aurelius to subscribe to all the documents, “whether the acts that have already been completed or the LETTERS.” See the African Code, chapter 127.

These chosen judges from each province, who possessed the authority of the entire plenary synod, and perhaps also many others who thought that they ought to wait for a time, seem to have received Zosimus’s letters not long after the Kalends of May. Once they received them, they subscribed the condemnation of the Pelagians and sent a reply to the pontiff.

Unless someone would prefer to believe that Zosimus’s letters—which it was important to deliver to Africa quickly—arrived before the Kalends of May themselves, so that the entire synod could reply on that very day.

Whatever one may choose to think, it will always remain true that the plenary synod which subscribed Zosimus’s letters, or the condemnation of the Pelagians, and replied to the same pontiff, was none other than this synod that enacted the canons. When Augustine mentions it as the second African synod under Zosimus, he called it plenary.

A different plenary synod under the same pontiff in the autumn of 418 is therefore a fabrication. It is incredible that the reply to Zosimus’s letters—which, as we have seen, had already been received long before—was postponed until that time.

The fact that no other plenary synod was held under Zosimus can also be confirmed from the *Code of the Canons of the African Church*. After the synod of the Kalends of May in 418, the Code records another plenary synod in the following year, 419, held under Boniface on 25 May [Col. 1037B].

## LVIII

Apart from Aurelius of Carthage and Donatianus of Telepte, the Fathers of our synod numbered 203, as is read in the manuscripts of our collection. The copy seen by Photius [899] gave the number 224.

Since Photius’s single codex contained a Greek version, an error could more easily have entered that version than our ancient and numerous Latin copies, which consistently give the number 203.

Sirmond, in his posthumous notes on the chapters on grace appended to Celestine’s letter, inserted by P. Labbe in volume III of the Venetian edition of the Councils, column 477, cites the ancient Corbie collection. He testifies that the canons of this synod against the Pelagians are transcribed there [Col. 1037C].

The same canons appear in a codex of the monastery of Corbie under this title:

> “Here begin the decrees of the synod of 214 bishops of the Church of Carthage. It pleased all the bishops assembled in the holy synod of the Church of Carthage that whoever says that Adam, the first man, was made immortal, etc.,”

as in the first canon.

From this it is believed that 214 Fathers were present at the plenary synod that composed the celebrated canons, so that the number in our codices and in Photius ought to be corrected.

Yet Prosper consistently mentions the number 214 in three passages whenever he cites the African synod that preceded Zosimus’s judgment, while he never gives that number when he cites the canon of the later synod and the African reply to Zosimus. Prosper is a much earlier author who had the proceedings of both synods before him; it cannot easily be said that he was mistaken in assigning that number only to the earlier synod because of the inscription of a single Corbie manuscript, which assigns the number to the synod of the Kalends of May—especially since, in this very number, the Corbie codex agrees neither with Photius’s copy nor with the copies of our collection [Col. 1037D].

It will rather be permissible, and more probable, to suspect the following. The compiler of the Corbie collection knew of no other Carthaginian synod of the year 418 except this one celebrated in May. The council of Carthage in 419 mentions only this synod, and the compiler did not find a certain number of Fathers in it—a number likewise omitted or not found by Dionysius. He therefore thought that the number of 214 Fathers noted by Prosper belonged to the synod of the Kalends of May, although it actually belonged to the earlier African council of the same year.

Such errors are not uncommon in ancient collections. In the very old Verona codex 59, ancient statutes—which we have shown elsewhere cannot be attributed to the African councils—are reported as coming from the synod of Carthage in Africa under the consulship of Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII; that is, the consulship of the year 418.

When other collectors encountered this in similar codices, they attributed the same statutes to the 214 Fathers whom they found Prosper assigning to the council of Carthage in the year 418. Thus, in manuscript collection Vatican, Palatine 574, one reads:

> “African synod of 214 bishops. Ancient statutes of the Church.”

And in the Vatican manuscript 1341, the Coislinian manuscript, and other collections of the Hispanic and Isidorian type—which likewise assign these statutes to the fourth Council of Carthage—we find:

> “Fourth Synod of Carthage in Africa, by 214 bishops.”

Just as this number, taken from Prosper, is recognized to have been wrongly attached to those statutes, so it likewise seems to have been wrongly prefixed in the Corbie manuscript to the synod of the Kalends of May. From Prosper, it ought instead to be assigned to the earlier council.

## LIX

Now a few words about the canons of this same synod.

We have already proved that they were enacted in the plenary synod of the Kalends of May and not in the earlier African synod. Apart from Quesnell, we believe that we have sufficiently defended the canon concerning infants who die without baptism in the *Treatise on Collections*, Part II, chapter 3, § 7.

The following words of Augustine in Letter 215 to Valentinus, no. 2, belong to this synod:

> “And what we briefly established in the later plenary council of all Africa against that very error”—the Pelagian error.

The words “we briefly established” indicate canons in which the errors of the Pelagians are refuted in a few words.

The force and meaning of these canons had plainly been established at greater length in the earlier African council. Saint Prosper praises that council’s constitutions and synodal decrees, inserted into the synodal report against the Pelagian heresy, and testifies in his *Chronicle* that they were directed to Zosimus and approved by him:

> “At the council held at Carthage of 214 bishops, synodal decrees were carried to Pope Zosimus. After he approved them, the Pelagian heresy was condemned throughout the whole world.”

These decrees were then arranged in shorter canons at the plenary council.

## LX

The author of the chapters on grace, quoting three of these canons in § 7 [901], asserts that they are virtually the proper canons of the apostolic see. From this someone might judge that they were approved by Zosimus in the *Tractoria* or, as P. Constantius thinks, inserted into it. The same author of the chapters, after all, declares in his preface that he has brought forward certain statements from the African synods, which the apostolic bishops made their own when they approved them.

If this is to be understood in that way, then either the same canons must be said to have been enacted earlier by the first African synod and sent to Zosimus for approval in the *Tractoria*, or the *Tractoria* must be believed to have been issued much later, after the plenary synod had received those same canons, which it approved or accepted by inserting them. Both alternatives conflict with the position we have established.

We observe, however, that in § 5 the same author of the chapters quotes a long fragment from the letter of the plenary synod by which it replied to Zosimus after the *Tractoria*. This letter too must certainly be counted, according to the preface of the same author, among the African documents that the apostolic bishops made their own when they approved them [Col. 1038D].

Just as this letter could be said to have been approved by Zosimus even though it was neither praised nor inserted in the *Tractoria*, so the same must be thought concerning the canons mentioned above. We believe that the Africans sent them to the same pontiff along with that letter—as it is reasonable to believe—and that they were received and approved in the same manner as the letter.

It was customary for the documents approved by the Roman pontiffs to be deposited in the apostolic archives. Thus, when Cyril’s letter to Celestine had been approved by that pontiff, as is clear from his Letter 12 in P. Coustant, the apostolic archives received it, as Leo testifies in Letter 69, chapter 1.

The chapters on grace themselves were formerly approved in the same way, because they were received into those same archives. Thus, in his letter to Possessor, it was enough for Hormisdas to mention the archives in which they were kept in order to signify that they had been approved:

> “Concerning free will and the grace of God, what the Roman—that is, catholic—Church follows and preserves … the chapters expressed in the ecclesiastical archives are contained there. If you lack them and consider them necessary, we will send them.”

We have an even stronger reason for believing that our canons were approved by the apostolic see: Prosper, in the passage cited shortly before, testifies that the synodal decrees sent to Zosimus from the African council were approved by him in the *Tractoria*.

Since the force and meaning of the canons themselves had been set forth in those decrees, as we have often noted, once the decrees were approved in Zosimus’s *Tractoria*, we recognize the canons themselves as approved.

## § XII. P. Coustant’s system concerning the events under Zosimus examined; the order of events and a brief summary

## LXI

We must now examine the system of P. Coustant, who, in volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, page 987, adopted a kind of middle position, lest his arguments, if left unanswered, should perhaps introduce some doubt concerning what has so far been established.

He thinks that the events under Zosimus occurred as follows.

He believes that, after receiving Zosimus’s first two letters, the Africans convened a synod in November of the year 417. To this synod he attributes the letter to the same pontiff which, in Zosimus’s third letter, is designated by the word “volume” and which Marcellinus brought to Rome together with Paulinus’s memorandum.

To this letter he assigns exactly what we asserted in § 5 concerning the letter of Aurelius and the other bishops, issued in November without the formal structure of a properly constituted council.

He further writes that Zosimus replied to this letter in another letter dated 21 March and received by the Africans on 29 April.

He adds that three days later they held the synod of the Kalends of May and enacted there the canons which they sent to Zosimus together with fuller instruction.

He considers this council of the Kalends of May to be the one Augustine calls “African,” and to which the events that Saint Prosper assigns to the synod of 214 bishops ought to be attributed.

He then believes that, after discovering Coelestius’s deceptions—and even more clearly from his flight, by which he avoided judgment—Zosimus is thought to have issued the celebrated *Tractoria* only at the end of July of that same year [903].

Finally, after receiving this *Tractoria*, he thinks that the Africans sent a congratulatory letter to the same pontiff around the end of August [Col. 1039C].

## LXII

This system, however, is beset by several difficulties. First, in his third letter to the African synod, written on 21 March 418, Zosimus distinguishes two letters from the Africans: one earlier, which they sent in reply to the first letters of the pontiff himself; and another later, which, brought most recently by Marcellinus, is called a volume. For he writes as follows:

> “We thought, and know, that every request of his [Coelestius] had been explained in the earlier letter which we sent you; and we believed that a response had been given sufficiently in THOSE WRITINGS [read: *to those writings*] which you had written in reply to them.”

These words designate the first African letter, which they had written in reply to Zosimus’s earlier letters. Coustant’s interpretation, by which he thinks that the reference in the notes is to the Africans’ letter sent to Innocent in 416, is excessively forced and contrary to the obvious sense of the words: for the Africans had written to Innocent, not written back to him.

With equal violence of interpretation the same author, at col. 976, note h, thinks that the words refer to the Africans’ letter to Innocent in the following passage of Zosimus’s letter:

> “I have left everything in the same condition in which it had long stood, so that the appeal which had been sent from you to us might be preserved.”

Where, in their letter to Innocent, had the Africans appealed that everything should be preserved in the same condition? The passage, however, agrees perfectly with the first letter to Zosimus. In that letter, while requesting time to convene a synod and to send the relevant documents, they begged that nothing new should meanwhile be done. Later, recognizing this point, the same Coustant, in his account of the writings relating to Zosimus, no. 6, col. 988, to some extent correcting himself, admits that this appeal was contained in the first African letter to Zosimus. He says:

> “While warning that his [Coelestius’s] faith was not sincere, THEY APPEALED TO ZOSIMUS not to absolve him too hastily, but to leave the matter in the condition in which it had been before the most recent investigation.”

Moreover, immediately after mentioning the earlier letter which the Africans had sent in reply, Zosimus adds:

> “But AFTERWARDS we examined the whole volume of the letter sent by your subdeacon Marcellinus; and after it had at last been read through, etc.”

By the adverb “afterwards” he plainly indicates a second letter sent later than the first. Therefore not one letter only, but two letters sent by the Africans at different times before 21 March must be admitted; and only the second, designated by the name “volume,” was brought to Rome by Marcellinus.

## LXIII

Next, the words “the whole volume, after it had at last been completed” plainly suggest that the second letter was the fuller report of the African synod, to which documents useful for explaining the entire affair had been appended. Coustant therefore wrongly transfers this report to the synod of the Kalends of May.

Accordingly, the earlier and shorter letter was rightly attributed by us to Aurelius and the other Africans, who, soon after receiving Zosimus’s two first letters, thought that a reply should be sent. They requested that time be granted for convening a synod and that no prejudice should meanwhile be created. The other letter belonged to the synod itself, held at the beginning of 418.

This makes it easy to understand why Marcellinus, sent from Africa to Rome after that synod, arrived around the middle of March. On Coustant’s view, if he had departed before the middle of November, four months would have to be assigned to his journey—something wholly unbelievable.

## LXIV

It is much more unbelievable still that the African synod which sent Zosimus the necessary instructions and documents was held on the Kalends of May. Can we really believe that, in a matter of such importance, requiring the greatest concern, the African Fathers remained inactive for so long that, after receiving Zosimus’s letters in November of the preceding year—letters demanding an immediate reply—they delayed the synod and their response for six months?

Furthermore, the synod of the Kalends of May is called plenary, or universal, in all the manuscripts. It is the synod which Augustine designates by the name “plenary,” distinguishing it from the earlier African synod which had previously written to Zosimus.

Another extraordinary point arises here. Coustant describes the synod which, as he thinks, sent a letter of congratulation to this pontiff after the *Tractoria*, before the end of August, as follows, no. 24, col. 998:

> “The bishops of Africa who, after the Council of Carthage on the Kalends of May, had remained at Carthage, three from each province by decree of that council, when they received there the latest letters of Zosimus—that is, the *Tractoria*—and, having joined to themselves, as it seems, whatever bishops they could summon in haste, sent a letter of congratulation in reply to the same pope.”

These words seem to indicate that, in his view, the synod which had written to Zosimus before the *Tractoria* on the Kalends of May, with its legates appointed, continued until the end of August and, after receiving the *Tractoria*, wrote back to the same Zosimus. Thus he attributes to one and the same synod what ought to be attributed to two. He also wants the same synod to be both the African synod which wrote and the plenary synod which replied to Zosimus, although Augustine and others distinguish one from the other.

If, however, he intends this synod which replied after the *Tractoria* to be different from the one held on the Kalends of May, the following words of Augustine, *Epistle* 47, now 215, no. 2, must be attributed to it:

> “What we briefly established at the later plenary council of all Africa against that very error.”

But these matters, which indicate canons established against the Pelagian heresy on the Kalends of May, would wrongly be referred to a later plenary council of which there is no mention among the ancients.

## LXV

Finally, add the law of Honorius against the Pelagians, issued on the day before the Kalends of May. Coustant says not a word about this law on the present occasion. Yet it overturns his position more than anything else.

For the document called a *rescript* and a *reply* (see above, no. 40) was undoubtedly requested by someone after the Pelagians had been condemned. On Coustant’s view, however, it was requested neither by Zosimus nor by the Africans. For, according to him, after this law the Africans established canons against the Pelagians at the council of the Kalends of May and wrote to Zosimus, while Zosimus pronounced the sentence of condemnation much later.

Moreover, once Coelestius had been expelled from Rome by force of the same law, there was nothing for him to be blamed for if, when summoned to a hearing by Zosimus, he did not appear; nor could a shameful flight have been imputed to him. You therefore see how many considerations refute Coustant’s system (see above, no. 43).

## LXVI

We shall now briefly set out the entire sequence of events under Zosimus which we have established more fully in these observations.

When Basiliscus brought the first letters of Zosimus into Africa at the beginning of November 417, letters in which the same pontiff, deceived by Coelestius’s stratagems, summoned his accusers to Rome within two months, Aurelius, together with several bishops who were at Carthage or who could arrive more quickly, immediately sent a letter to Zosimus requesting a suitable period for convening a synod of all Africa.

This letter was soon transmitted to the same pontiff through Basiliscus, who, having carried out the pontifical commands, returned to Rome. He had indeed summoned Paulinus, Coelestius’s chief accuser, on 2 November. But Paulinus’s petition, which was to be transmitted together with the replies of the African synod—which could not be convened so quickly—was delivered on 8 November not to Basiliscus, the subdeacon of the Roman Church, but to Marcellinus, a Carthaginian subdeacon who had been assigned to carry those replies to Rome.

Soon afterward Aurelius announced that a synod of all Africa was to be convened at the beginning of the following year, after the Christmas celebrations. This synod, which Augustine calls African and to which Saint Prosper attributes 214 Fathers, sent Zosimus an extensive report with the relevant documents through the aforementioned subdeacon Marcellinus.

Zosimus gave a brief reply to both African letters on 18 or 21 March, intending to write more fully afterward, once judgment and sentence had been pronounced. Thus, being already sufficiently informed about the entire affair, he summoned Coelestius to a hearing, so that if he condemned what he had promised to condemn at the first investigation, he might be absolved and might receive communion at the approaching Easter.

But when Coelestius withdrew by flight and avoided the examination, Zosimus pronounced a sentence of condemnation against him and against his teacher Pelagius toward the end of the same month of March, intending to publish as soon as possible the *Tractoria*, which would explain the whole affair.

When the Pelagians, frustrated in their hopes, stirred up great disturbances in the city, the same pontiff wrote to the emperor, asking that the heretics be restrained by a law and that compliance with and obedience to the *Tractoria* when issued be secured. Honorius’s law was issued on 30 April.

Meanwhile, news of the Roman judgment reached Africa with the greatest speed, at approximately the same time that Zosimus’s third letter had been received—namely, toward the end of April. The Africans, who around this time had anticipated the arrival of the Roman reply, were already gathered in a plenary synod. When they received this news, they issued canons on the Kalends of May.

Then judges were chosen from each province, who, while awaiting Zosimus’s fuller letters, were to return and subscribe a letter of congratulation to him in the name of the same plenary synod. This was done not long afterward, when two pontifical letters had been received: one written specifically to the Africans, and the other general, addressed to the bishops of the entire world.

Indeed, all those still present at the plenary synod subscribed to this second letter as well, by order of the pontiff. Anyone can easily understand how well this sequence of events reconciles all the facts which, in the other systems, are in no way consistent with the chronology previously established.

# FOURTEENTH DISSERTATION

## On the Various Creeds Contained in an Ancient Codex of the Roman Church

Here, on the occasion of discussing the author of the creed commonly called the Creed of Saint Athanasius, various conjectures are brought forward.

[Col. 1041]

There are many features that make the edition of the ancient Roman Codex useful and convenient for the Catholic Church. Among them, this is by no means the least important: it contains several creeds either never before published or published in much more defective form.

But the chief glory belongs to the Roman Church because the inclusion of several creeds in this codex clearly shows, against the rivals and adversaries of the apostolic see, that Catholics from every quarter have always converged upon that principal chair as upon the center of the entire Catholic communion. It also shows that, whenever controversy arose anywhere in the Church concerning points of faith, the Roman pontiff rightly demanded an account of their faith from those who had come under public suspicion of having admitted error—provided, of course, that they wished to remain participants in apostolic communion.

## I. The Apostles’ Creed

First, someone may wonder why no place is given in this Codex of the Roman Church to the Apostles’ Creed, which the Roman Church has always guarded and preserved inviolate, and why it is not mentioned there at all except in these words of Saint Ambrose, found in his letter to Pope Siricius, in chapter 31 of the Codex.

I think the reason is the one suggested by Rufinus when he explains the same creed. He writes (*Commentary on the Creed*):

> “For this reason they handed it down not to be written on little sheets and parchment, but to be retained in the heart, so that it might be certain that no one had learned these things from reading—which sometimes reaches even unbelievers—but from the tradition of the apostles.”

Peter Chrysologus says much the same when explaining the creed, *Sermon* 62:

> “The creed of faith,” he says, “is established by faith alone: it is not believed by the letter but by the spirit; and it is entrusted to the heart, not to paper, because a divine deposit does not require human surety.”

Nevertheless, so that we do not pass over this apostolic creed untouched, we shall gather under one view the passages concerning it that are scattered in various places in Leo.

I observe, first, that Saint Leo mentions it at least seven times: volume 1, pp. 81, 176, 238, 273, 803, 837, 858, 1137, and 1242.

2. He calls it the Rule of the Catholic and Apostolic Creed: *Sermon* 23, now 24, or *On the Nativity of the Lord* 4, chapter 6.

3. It is called simply “the creed”: *Sermon* 45, now 46, or *On Lent* 8, chapter 3:

> “Hold this fixed in your mind, what you say in the creed.”

4. It is called the rule of faith received by the authority of apostolic institution: *Sermon* 60, now 62, or *On the Passion* 11, chapter 2:

> “This rule of faith, which at the very beginning of the creed we received by the authority of apostolic institution.”

5. He asserts more explicitly that the same creed was instituted by the holy apostles: *Sermon* 93, now 96, or the treatise against Eutyches in the Basilica of Anastasia, chapter 1:

> “Those who deny the Lord’s incarnation and oppose the creed instituted by the holy apostles.”

6. He calls it a brief and perfect confession, marked by twelve statements corresponding to the twelve apostles, in *Epistle* 27, now 31, to Pulcheria, chapter 4:

> “For the brief and perfect confession of the Catholic Creed itself, which is marked by twelve statements corresponding to the twelve apostles, is so equipped with heavenly protection that all the opinions of heretics can be cut down by its sword alone.”

He adds:

> “If Eutyches had wished to take in the fullness of this creed with a pure and simple heart, etc.”

7. It is called the saving creed and confession in *Epistle* 97, now 124, to the Palestinian monks, chapter 8:

> “You have forgotten the saving creed and confession which, when you pronounced it before many witnesses, you received as the sacrament of baptism.”

8. In *Epistle* 24, now 28, to Flavian, chapter 1, Leo reproaches Eutyches because he did not even understand the beginnings of the creed itself:

> “And what is uttered by the voice of all those throughout the whole world who are to be regenerated is still not comprehended by this old man’s heart.”

And in chapter 2:

> “At least he should have received with attentive hearing that common and undifferentiated confession by which the whole body of the faithful professes that it believes in God the almighty Father, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, who was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.”

By these three statements almost all the machinations of the heretics are destroyed.

9. From the passages of Saint Leo addressed to the Palestinian monks, to Flavian of Constantinople, to the Empress Pulcheria, and to the Egyptians in *Sermon* 93, now 96, it is clear that the pontiff held the opinion that all the Churches throughout the world had likewise used the same apostolic creed as the Roman Church in the transmission of the creed before baptism. On this see the very learned Vossius, *Dissertation 1 on the Three Creeds*, thesis 30, who embraced the contrary opinion. I do not intend to say more about this. We therefore proceed to the creeds contained in the Codex.

## II. The Nicene Creed

The first is the *Exposition of the Nicene Faith*, which is found in the first chapter.

[Note: This exposition of the faith is presented not only in the first chapter but also in the second chapter, where it has been inserted into the *Breviary of the Canons of Hippo*. We restored it from manuscript copies of this collection, since Quesnell omitted it from this second chapter. The exposition read in the first chapter is not entirely identical with that in the ancient version, as will be evident to anyone who compares them. The version presented in the *Breviary*, and in Dionysius in the Carthaginian synod of 419, is the ancient version received by the Africans from the time of Caecilianus; compare with it the interpretation of the same creed received by the Romans, as read in Leo, *Epistle* 165, in the *Treatise on Collections*, part II, chapter 2, § 1, no. 3.]

It is entirely from the same version as that which appears in the old Latin edition of Justellus’s canons, which he appended to the Dionysian collection. It differs, however, from the other version inserted by Saint Leo in his letter to the emperor Leo, *Epistle* 134, now 165, chapter 3. The *Profession of Faith of the Council of Nicaea*, found in the Greek-Latin African Code of Canons published by Justellus, agrees with the Leonine version.

## III. The Constantinopolitan Creed

The second place is occupied by the Constantinopolitan Creed, which is transcribed in chapter 25 among the acts of the Council of Chalcedon. Appended to it is an exposition of the Lord’s incarnation, for the most part from a version not previously published, which the Fathers of Chalcedon composed.

Concerning that Constantinopolitan Creed, see John Vossius’s third dissertation *On the Creeds*.

## IV. The Creed against the Pelagians

[Note: We showed in note 32, above, col. 977, note a, in the preceding dissertation, that the chapters brought against Pelagius at the Synod of Diospolis, together with the same number of corresponding articles of Catholic doctrine, which are presented in chapter 18 of our Codex, are not a creed. Pelagius was indeed compelled at that synod to anathematize the chapters brought against him, as is recorded in the heading of the chapter mentioned. But he cannot be said to have professed that he embraced an equal number of corresponding articles of Catholic doctrine. Augustine appended those articles to Pelagius’s chapters after the Synod of Diospolis, when he wrote to Paulinus; and both the chapters and the articles of Catholic doctrine were excerpted from Augustine, in the form in which they are found in our collection.

Thus Antonius Augustinus’s conjecture—that these chapters and corresponding articles had been taken from some Council of Carthage—falls away. Certainly he found no codex bearing the heading of a Council of Carthage. He cites only the Merlinian edition, in which the same chapters are printed after Leo’s *Epistle* 72, appended to Aurelius’s letter to the Byzaceni and Arzugitani. It was merely the decision of different compilers to join these chapters and Aurelius’s letter together because they concerned the same Pelagian affair.]

One would not without qualification call the writing contained in chapter 18 of the Codex a creed. It contains twelve chapters which Pelagius was compelled to condemn, and an equal number of corresponding articles of Catholic doctrine which he professed to embrace in order to save his head from the impending anathema.

Antonius Augustinus, in *Epitome of Ancient Law*, book II, title 40, chapter 27, uses these same chapters in abbreviated form to describe Pelagius’s doctrine. He reports them as though they came from some Council of Carthage, which he says was printed after Saint Leo’s *Epistle* 72 in an old edition—namely, the Merlinian edition of Isidore. Whether he attributes this excerpt to a Carthaginian synod merely by conjecture, or whether he found it so entitled elsewhere, is not apparent.

But I had long ago suspected something of this kind when I happened to read these chapters in the Grimani, Victorine, and Cistercian manuscripts, and in both Merlinian editions of the Councils of Isidore Mercator, those of 1525 and 1535, together with Aurelius, bishop of Carthage’s letter to the bishops of the provinces of Byzacena and Arzugitana.

Since Aurelius’s letter is there joined to the chapters just mentioned, it is almost certainly necessary to think that it belonged to the same affair.

[Note: The entire narrative that follows resembles a dream. It presents claims resting not only on no foundation or authority, but also refuted by strong arguments. There is no indication that many African bishops resisted Zosimus’s decision and the Council of Carthage. On the contrary, the zeal and steadfastness of all the African bishops against the Pelagians are sufficiently demonstrated by the very frequent synods which fought most vigorously against them during that period.

We showed in the observations on the preceding dissertation, § 10, no. 48, that Honorius’s law was issued chiefly on behalf not of the Africans but of certain Italian bishops—eighteen of them, led by Julian—who were resisting Zosimus’s letters, and that it was directed not only to Aurelius but, by the same procedure, to other bishops of the principal sees, especially Boniface, the Roman pontiff.

The subscription which the same law required, and which Aurelius required by order of that law, was to be appended not to the chapters just mentioned but to Zosimus’s *Tractoria*, which the recalcitrant bishops were unwilling to sign. For both the emperor in the law and Aurelius in his letter to the Byzaceni and Arzugitani require that the heretics themselves be condemned in addition to their errors. But the heretics explicitly condemned in the *Tractoria* are mentioned neither in the chapters just mentioned nor in the corresponding articles.

If Aurelius also ordered those bishops who had signed Zosimus’s *Tractoria* in the plenary synod to subscribe along with the others, this repeated subscription should not therefore be considered pointless. For, in replying to the emperor and demonstrating the execution of the edict, Aurelius saw that everyone’s subscriptions had to be transmitted to him, both those who had sat in the council and those who had been absent.

It is equally unbelievable that Leo, who had been sent to Africa by Zosimus before the middle of 418 to bring the *Tractoria*, remained there even after Zosimus’s death until the Kalends of August of the following year, when Aurelius wrote to the African bishops after receiving Honorius’s law.]

Moreover, Aurelius’s letter was written on this occasion. After Zosimus’s sentence against the Pelagians had been issued at Rome and transmitted from there to the African bishops by the Roman pontiff through our Leo, then an acolyte, many men, even those distinguished by episcopal honor, still dared to resist both the decrees of the apostolic see and the Council of Carthage, and to defend the condemned doctrine in secret discussions.

When the emperor Honorius was informed of this, he immediately sent Aurelius a rescript dated to the consulship of Monaxius and Plinta—that is, in the year 419—by which all bishops were compelled to subscribe to the condemnation of the Pelagians, unless they wished to be deposed from the episcopate, expelled from their cities, and deprived of communion.

After receiving this, Aurelius wrote to the bishops of the provinces of Byzacena and Arzugitana and likewise sent the emperor’s edict, so that by reading it they might understand how each of them ought to subscribe to the condemnation of the heretics, whether they were among those whose subscription was already contained in the synodal acts of the Council of Carthage of the preceding year, or among those who had been unable to attend that plenary council of all Africa.

Hence we conjecture that Aurelius proposed for subscription the formula which had once been presented to Pelagius at the Council of Diospolis and which consists of the twelve articles appended to this letter.

Anyone who remembers that this was done on Augustine’s authority will readily believe it. The subscription was, as it were, an appendix and supplement to the Council of Carthage, whose leader was Aurelius and whose intellectual force was Augustine, as Prosper says of it; and the entire burden of that affair rested upon Augustine. For this reason the imperial edict was addressed not only to Aurelius but also to Augustine.

Moreover, the necessity of subscribing, imposed even upon those bishops who had attended the later Council of Carthage, further persuades me that this formula was adopted. A repeated subscription would seem pointless if they were compelled to subscribe again to the same chapters to which most of them had already subscribed in the synod.

From this you will understand why, in those codices of Saint Leo which Antonius Augustinus saw, the chapters are attributed to the Council of Carthage: namely, because they were proposed for subscription in order to correct the obstinacy especially of those bishops who had resisted that synod; and because they were sent to those same bishops who had convened the synod and, as we have said, constituted a certain portion and completion of it.

Both Aurelius’s letter and the articles appended to it were found among Saint Leo’s papers. This is why they were inserted among his works. Since Leo had departed for Africa in the preceding year, when a considerable part of it had already elapsed, to carry the condemnation of the Pelagians, he may perhaps still have been there when the emperor’s edict reached Aurelius and Aurelius’s writings were sent to the African bishops with the chapters to be signed. He brought a copy of them back with him to Rome, intending to make the supreme pontiff better informed, through examination of the acts themselves, about the conclusion and outcome of that laborious affair.

Afterward, when he himself became supreme pontiff, he could use these chapters to extinguish and restrain the Pelagian disturbances that were reviving at that time.

[Note: Since no heretics are condemned in the chapters brought against Pelagius, or in the corresponding articles of the Church’s doctrine, they certainly cannot be considered the formula or profession of faith which Saint Leo proposed for Pelagians to subscribe when they were to be received into the Church’s communion, and by which he ordered them, in explicit professions, to condemn the authors of the Pelagian heresy. That these chapters are read in some Leonine collections was merely the choice of the compilers, for which no reason can be given. The two copies cited, the Victorine and Cistercian, belong to the later Collection 24; and from our manuscripts of that same collection we have seen that these chapters, placed after Leo’s letters together with Aurelius’s letter, are additions. In Merlin they are copied after the letter to Turribius, which is listed last in the manuscripts of the said Collection 24. In the Grimani codex they are read after the letter to Dioscorus. It is superfluous to seek a reason bearing on Leo. Certainly they appear nowhere in other, more numerous and more ancient collections of Leo’s writings.]

It occurs to me that Saint Leo may have proposed [this creed formula] for subscription by the Pelagians who were to be received into the communion of the Church, whether on the occasion mentioned in *Epistle* 6, now 1, to the bishop of Aquileia, or on some other occasion, and that he adopted it for this purpose from part of Saint Augustine’s *Epistle* 106 to Paulinus.

I am led to suspect that Saint Leo proposed this formula because it is published among the letters of that holy pontiff in the Merlinian edition of the Councils, or of Isidore Mercator, printed at Paris in 1524 and 1535, and in the manuscript collections of his letters: the Victorine, Cistercian, and our Grimani manuscript.

The last of these, which preserves with considerable accuracy the chronological order in which each letter was written, has this heading immediately after the letter to Dioscorus, written either in that same year, 444, or the following year, and which is the first letter in this manuscript codex.

Although this little creed may appear too brief to suffice for the confession of the most cunning heretics, because the later errors of Pelagius and Julian are expressed in more recent books, Saint Leo could nevertheless have thought that it should be adopted rather than a new one composed:

1. because of Saint Augustine’s authority, from whom it had been excerpted;

2. because it had once been presented to the leader of the Pelagians by the Fathers of Diospolis, toward whom Pelagius had been least hostile of all; and afterward it had been sent by Aurelius, at the emperor’s command, to the African bishops, as we shall soon say;

3. because it was preserved in the Roman Codex of Canons among the other monuments which the apostolic see had made its own. It is found in chapter 18 under the same title and is followed by Aurelius, bishop of Carthage’s letter to the African bishops of the provinces of Byzacena and Arzugitana, by which he compels them, in his own name and that of the emperor, to subscribe to a fixed formula against the Pelagians;

4. because the principal articles of Catholic doctrine are contained in the creed. If the Pelagians once assented to these, they would not have been reluctant to assent to the other articles which flowed from them.

Augustine himself indicates this in *On Heresies*, addressed to Quodvultdeus, chapter 88. He circumscribes the Pelagian heresy by nearly the same articles that Pelagius condemned before the Synod of Diospolis, immediately adding:

> “Other matters are also brought against them,” he says, “but these are the chief ones, from which it is understood that all, or nearly all, the others depend.”

You will first find these chapters printed in Saint Augustine’s *Epistle* 106 to Paulinus, then in Margarino de la Bigne’s two editions of the Councils of Isidore, after Aurelius’s letter, which is numbered there among Leo’s letters as 72.

Gabriel Vasquez also published them under the name of the Palestinian synod and as genuine acts of that council, at the end of volume II of the *Secunda Secundae* of Saint Thomas, from a manuscript codex of Antonius Aquinas.

The eminent Cardinal Baronius inserted the same material in his *Annals* under the year 417, no. 21, from a manuscript codex of the Cresconian collection.

Jacobus Sirmond, S.J., had them published as though they were a new little work, from manuscript codices, among other short works of ancient authors in 1630.

Finally, in our Roman Codex they lie after the same letter of Aurelius, in chapter 18.

## V. The Creed against the Arians

The fourth creed is found in chapter 37. It bears the following title:

> “Exposition of the Catholic Faith against the Arian Heresy.”

Who the author of this confession was, I entirely do not know. I suspect that he was one of the Luciferians, both because members of this communion always attacked the Arian heresy with the greatest vigor, and because the creed, expressed in the plural—“We confess,” and so forth—seems to indicate that it was issued by men joined by some particular bond of communion, yet not expelled from the Catholic faith, as the Luciferians were at that time.

Third, the confession seems to mark out those Catholics who said that there were three hypostases:

> “He who separates the divinity of the Trinity says that there are three Gods.”

Faustinus likewise presses this point in his confession, which follows, against the defenders of three hypostases:

> “For it follows that they confess three Gods who confess three substances.”

Finally, suspicion is increased by the fact that this exposition of faith is followed by two others. The first, found in chapter 38, is attributed to the presbyter Faustinus, certainly a Luciferian; the other, placed immediately after it, is believed by learned men to be the work of Gregory Baeticus, who had likewise been infected by Lucifer’s schism.

I would therefore readily attribute this creed to the presbyter Marcellinus, who, together with Faustinus, presented those petitions to the emperor Theodosius which were published through the work of Jacobus Sirmond.

Thus it is easy to suppose that the three most distinguished men among all the Luciferians sent their creeds either to the emperor or to the apostolic see, and that these were afterward placed in their Roman Codex, to be drawn from it when the need arose.

[Note: We proved in the observations on dissertation 12, chapter 1, that the Codex into which these creeds were inserted was not Roman but was arranged in Gaul through private initiative. This creed is also found in the codices of the Italian Colbertine and Lucensian collections. Hence the following conjecture—that this and the subsequent creeds were sent to the apostolic see—rests on no foundation.]

I found this same creed against the Arians in manuscript Thuaneus 199, with the following title:

> “The Faith of Saint Ambrose, Bishop.”

## VI. The Creed of Faustinus

The fifth place, or chapter 38, is occupied by the faith of the presbyter Faustinus, sent to the emperor Theodosius.

First, no other Faustinus appears who could have been the author of this creed except that Luciferian presbyter Faustinus who wrote seven books against the Arians and Macedonians to Flaccilla, the wife of the emperor Theodosius, and who, together with the presbyter Marcellinus, presented a petition to Theodosius himself. He could easily have sent the same emperor a creed as a testimony of his faith.

Concerning the date when the creed was sent, this much is certain: it was not sent before the year 379, to which the beginning of Theodosius’s reign is assigned.

Around this time Faustinus was living at Eleutheropolis, as he himself indicates on p. 87 of the *Book of Petitions*, where he also complains that he was harassed by Turbo, the bishop of that city.

From this circumstance perhaps arose the occasion for composing a confession of faith and sending it to Theodosius. It is easy to suppose that Faustinus used the emperor’s name and authority against the schismatics.

For it is clear from the creed that Faustinus wrote and sent it at a time when he and other men of the same communion were suffering among Catholics the charge of being followers of the errors of Sabellius and Apollinaris.

Nor does this little creed appear to have been written long after the year 379: first, because it is completely silent about Macedonius and the First Council of Constantinople, by which he was condemned in 381; and second, because it speaks of the error against the Holy Spirit in no other way than that in which the Fathers of the Council of Alexandria had written against that heretic in the letter about to be cited.

For this reason, the profession of faith seems to me to have been sent to Theodosius within those two years. At the beginning of his reign he may perhaps have been approached against the schismatics and may have demanded from them an account of their faith, perhaps at the suggestion of Pope Damasus.

For this reason Faustinus may have sent that profession of faith to him, so that it might later be inserted into the archives of the apostolic see and hence transferred into the Roman Codex.

This is confirmed by the title of the creed found in the Thuaneus codex:

> “Likewise, the confession of the true faith of the presbyter Faustinus, which the emperor Theodosius ordered to be written and sent by the aforesaid [perhaps: *from the aforesaid*].”

[Note: Quesnell conjectures this on the hypothesis that our codex is a collection of the Roman Church. Compare the preceding note. The Vindobonensis manuscript bears a title indicating that the creed was sent to the emperor.]

[Col. 1048A] Thus Faustine’s faith was formulated so as to agree entirely with the decrees of that celebrated Council of Alexandria, which was held by the saints Athanasius, Asterius, and others recalled from exile after the death of the emperor Constantius, an event generally assigned to the year 362. At that council the Fathers devoted all their attention and principal effort to restoring to the Church and to their episcopal sees those bishops who had defiled themselves by communion with the heretics, provided that, repenting of their offense, they implored the Church’s mercy. Almost all eagerly embraced the council’s judgment. Only Lucifer, bishop of Calaris, vigorously maintained that none of those who had communicated with the Arians ought to be restored to Catholic communion and priestly offices, and he rejected the decrees of the Council of Alexandria, although he had subscribed to them through his deacon. From this he and his followers brought forth a destructive schism, breaking the bond of communion with those who granted pardon to the fallen; and consequently the controversy concerning the hypostases, which the prudence of the Alexandrian synod had quieted, unhappily [Col. 1048B] broke out again.

Faustinus, therefore, a prominent member among Lucifer’s followers, when for this reason he was harassed and was commonly heard by Catholics to be a follower of Sabellius and Apollinaris—because he rejected the decrees of the Council of Alexandria by which those men had been condemned—published, I think, this confession of his faith. Except for the indulgence granted to the fallen, about which he is entirely silent, and the use of the three hypostases, which he openly condemns, he touches upon and asserts every article of the Alexandrian council.

First, in that synodical letter of Saint Athanasius (which, in volume II of Saint Athanasius’s works, Paris edition of 1627, is entitled *To the Antiochenes*, p. 576), in which the decrees are contained, the holy Fathers, approving the judgment of the Council of Sardica, had decreed that nothing concerning the faith should be written beyond the Nicene Creed. They declared themselves satisfied with the Nicene faith, since nothing was lacking from it and it contained complete and solid piety. Nor, they said, should another profession of faith be issued, lest the one written at Nicaea appear not to have its proper completeness [Col. 1048C], and lest those who are always eager to establish something new be given an opportunity to define the faith again and again.

For this reason, I say, he begins his little work with an apology and attributes the necessity of writing it to the malice of his adversaries:

> The faith written at Nicaea against the Arian heresy was sufficient; but because certain men of perverse disposition mingle impious words with that confession of faith, bringing hatred upon us because we supposedly defend the heresy of Sabellius, and so forth.

2. The Fathers of the synod decree that the stupidity of Sabellius, and so forth, should be branded with an anathema. If this is done, they say, every evil suspicion among all people will be removed (*ibid.*). Likewise, Faustinus condemns Sabellius by name and professes the distinction of the persons of the Holy Trinity.

3. The synod requires that those who were to be received into Catholic communion should curse those who say that the Holy Spirit is a creature and is divided from the substance of Christ. And later:

> The Holy Spirit is not a creature, nor alien, but proper to and undivided from the essence of the Father and the Son.

Faustinus asserts the consubstantiality of the Holy Spirit in his confession in nearly the same sense and almost the same words:

> The Holy Spirit, existing not as a creature but as the Spirit of God, is not alien from the substance of the Father and the Son, but is himself of the same substance with the Father and the Son, just as he is of the same Godhead.

4. The synod also dealt with the faith concerning the Lord’s incarnation and asserted the reality of Christ’s flesh [Col. 1049A]—flesh, certainly, animated and endowed with mind and spirit. Faustinus likewise says:

> Let those who think that we are Apollinarists know that we abhor the heresy of Apollinaris no less than that of Arius.

All this indicates, unless I am mistaken, that Faustinus had before his eyes the synodical letter when he composed his confession, and that he did so with no other purpose, apparently, than to show that he held the same faith as Athanasius and defended it against the Arians and Apollinarists, although he also condemned those who professed the three hypostases and refused communion with the fallen.

## VII. The Anonymous Confession of Faith, or Perhaps That of Gregory of Baetica

The sixth little book of faith, contained in chapter 39 of the codex, has no author’s name prefixed, and it is entirely uncertain who he was. Its first twelve lines are found in volume I of Crabbé’s edition of the Councils, at the end of the acts of Chalcedon, under this title: *The Faith of the Romans*, received, as may be conjectured, from a mutilated codex. Perhaps [Note: [Col. 1049D] Since a title related to this one is found in two other Italian private collections, reviewed in note 1 (Col. 583, note a), in chapter 39 of our codex—collections which are not from a codex of the Roman Church—it is much more probable that the same title was copied into Crabbé’s manuscript from one of these or a similar collection than from our codex, which certainly is not Roman and whose title has nothing resembling that of Crabbé’s manuscript, *The Faith of the Romans.] for this reason the work was given that title: because it had been copied from some exemplar of our Roman Codex [Col. 1049B].

This suspicion is confirmed by one or two other fragments that appear to have been taken from the same codex and are transcribed in the same place in Crabbé’s edition. For, before this *Faith of the Romans*, there is a narrative concerning Dioscorus of Alexandria, which our codex contains in chapter 43. The same confession is followed by that rule of the *formatæ* which closes the Roman Codex in the Thuanean manuscript exemplar. Thus one may not altogether rashly conjecture that these three sections were copied from a similar source.

There is also, in Saint Jerome’s works (volume IX, edition of Marius Victor), a certain creed called that of Damasus, which has been composed for the most part from this little work: the opening and conclusion of the two agree. Anyone could easily persuade himself that one or the other is not genuine; and it is no less easy to determine that the so-called Damasi­an text is fictitious. This is evident from the words “proceeding from the Father and the Son,” for these words point to a later age; and, moreover, the little work appears to be badly put together and stitched from various fragments [Col. 1049C]. [Note: [Col. 1049D] We have presented the more probable explanation in note 1 to chapter 39 of our collection (*where cited above*).]

Why it was called that of Damasus is not clear to me. I conjecture that the work copied into the codex is not unrelated to the age of Damasus [920], since many things were brought together in it against defenders of the three hypostases, against the Sabellians, and against the Apollinarists.

This Damasian work is attributed to Jerome in the Thuanean manuscript codex 199, under the following title: *The Faith Spoken by Saint Jerome the Presbyter*. In that codex the manuscript work differs from the printed one in that, concerning the Holy Spirit, it has only “proceeding from the Father,” and not “from the Father and the Son,” which provides some indication of antiquity. The same work, in the form in which it appears in our Roman Codex, is also found in the same Thuanean codex 199 after the work bearing Jerome’s name and after the profession of faith of Gregory of Neocaesarea, or Gregory Thaumaturgus, which follows it. The title of this work is *An Exemplar of the Catholic Faith*.

It is also found among the works of Saint Athanasius in the Paris Greek-Latin edition of 1627, volume II: a work entitled *On the Trinity*, divided into twelve books, in the eleventh chapter of which our little work is found. Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, Aeneas of Paris, and Hincmar, [Col. 1050A] archbishop of Reims, cited this work under Saint Athanasius’s name eight hundred years ago. Learned men had nevertheless long suspected that it was not Athanasius’s; more recently, Pierre-François Chifflet has demonstrated this eloquently in his *Vigilian Vindications*, treatise 2, where he attributes it to Vigilius Tapsensis, bishop in Africa, on the testimony of Vigilius himself. [Note: [Col. 1050D] See *Observations*, § 3, no. 5, where the work *On the Trinity* will be taken away from Vigilius Tapsensis.]

This confession, which is the beginning of book XI among the works of Saint Athanasius, constitutes the whole of book IX in Chifflet’s edition of these books. Chifflet testifies in his second treatise that it is called a “little book of faith” in the Cluniac and Pontiniac manuscripts. These manuscripts are supported by the ninth-century author Ratramnus, a monk of Corbie, in book III *Against the Greeks* (volume II of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 99). After quoting several passages from those books *On the Trinity* under Saint Athanasius’s name, he reports certain passages from our little book of faith in this way:

> Likewise, in the little book of faith he says: “The true Father begot the true Son,” and so forth.

From these statements a question arises: whether the confession of faith under discussion has Vigilius Tapsensis as its author, since the whole work *On the Trinity*, of which it forms a part, is attributed to Vigilius. Yet it is beyond doubt that it is not Vigilius’s, both for other reasons that will become clear from what follows and especially because Saint Augustine, who lived long before Vigilius, transcribed certain passages from this little work at the place that we shall shortly cite.

I therefore readily persuade myself that Vigilius excerpted it from the Roman Codex [921]. This is all the more probable because, during the period when Vigilius was occupied with writing his books *On the Trinity* (in the preface to the book *Against Marivadus*), he was, as he himself says, living in Naples, a city of Campania. No one will be surprised that the Roman Codex was then in everyone’s hands there.

This little work was also published among the works of Gregory Nazianzen, in Latin only, as though it were his fiftieth oration, adorned with this heading:

> A Treatise of the Lord Gregory, surnamed the Theologian, bishop of Nazianzus, on the Nicene Faith, translated by Rufinus the presbyter.

[Col. 1050C] Learned men, however, deny the work to Gregory Nazianzen and indeed to any Greek writer, asserting that it is a Latin composition. As for Gregory and the translator named in the title, James Ussher, at the end of his work *On the Creeds*, where he arranged for this little book to be printed, notes that he had handled manuscript collections of the works of Saint Gregory Nazianzen translated by Rufinus, [Note: [Col. 1050D] Although the codices examined by Vossius and other manuscripts of Rufinus’s translation of Saint Gregory Nazianzen’s sermons lack this work, the codex from which the Strasbourg edition of 1508 was produced contained the same brief work, together with nine other sermons ascribed to the holy Doctor and translated into Latin by Rufinus, along with Rufinus’s preface. For more on this, see *Observations*, § 1, no. 2.] but that this work appeared nowhere in them. From this he concludes that Gregory should not be considered its author any more than Rufinus should be considered its translator.

Receive briefly what I think about this matter. Among the orations of Gregory Nazianzen there is another treatise entitled *On Faith*, likewise translated by Rufinus, as the title states, and numbered as Oration 49; our little work immediately follows it in place of Oration 50. The earlier treatise was first published at Strasbourg in 1508, then at Leipzig in 1522, and finally was included among Gregory’s other works.

Saint Augustine supports this attribution. In letter 3, now numbered 148, or the *Memorandum to Fortunatianus, bishop of Sicca*, he reports several things from the same work and attributes it to Gregory, an Eastern bishop:

> Saint Gregory also, an Eastern bishop, says very plainly that God is invisible by nature; yet, when he appeared to the Fathers, as to Moses, with whom he spoke face to face, he could have been seen by assuming the arrangement of some visible material, while preserving his invisibility.

The learned Federicus Morellus and others after him deny that this work is Gregory’s [Col. 1051A], [Note: [Col. 1051D] See *Observations*, § 1, no. 3.] and attribute it to a Latin author, persuaded by various arguments and especially by the fact that, when citing Scripture, its author uses the version called the Old Latin. The editors of Saint Ambrose’s works, who have deprived the Greeks of this work, call it Ambrose’s and include it in volume IV under this title: *On the Divinity and Consubstantiality of the Son against the Arians*. Chifflet, however, also maintains that it is not Ambrose’s and claims it for Vigilius Tapsensis, on p. 55 of his *Vigilian Vindications*.

A very learned man among the Parisian theologians, rejecting the conjectures and assertions of the earlier writers, conjectures, as I hear, that the work is by Gregory of Baetica, bishop of Illiberis, who, after becoming a determined defender of the Nicene faith, became a follower of the Luciferian schism. [Note: [Col. 1051D] We shall refute this opinion in *Observations*, § 1, no. 4.] I do not know what conjectures led that learned man to this view; but I am led to the same conclusion.

First, apart from Morellus’s earlier conjecture, both the style itself and the author’s words unmistakably show that the author was Latin. He says:

> A certain principle which is called *logos* (λόγος) among the Greeks, and so forth.

Much later, near the middle, we read:

> And this is what the Greeks call *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον), that is, “another who is the very same,” so that persons might be distinguished by the hearing of the names, not so that the terms would separate substance.

Does this not show that the little work was first written in Latin?

2. Jerome testifies that Gregory of Baetica, his contemporary, wrote an elegant little work on faith [Note: [Col. 1051D] This argument is common to several other ancient authors who are said to have written little books or treatises on faith; consequently, it proves nothing specifically for Gregory of Baetica.], and our little work is not unworthy of that praise.

3. The passage of Saint Augustine cited above indicates that the name of some Gregory had long been prefixed to the work. It is therefore surprising that it should have been attributed either to Ambrose, whose works Augustine had examined with the utmost care as his teacher, or to Vigilius Tapsensis at the very place where he was copying out Augustine’s complete passage.

Yet just as Augustine attributed the work to Gregory only on the authority of manuscripts, so it was easy for him to praise one Gregory for another—to a man, I mean, more intent on doctrinal matters than on criticism, and who appears to have known only one Gregory, namely Gregory Nazianzen, whom he commends everywhere with lavish praise. Thus, just as in that letter he confuses him with Gregory of Illiberis, so in book I *Against Julian*, chapter 5, he does not distinguish the same Nazianzen from Gregory of Nyssa, although he expresses some hesitation.

For after reporting the testimonies of Gregory Nazianzen and Basil the Great, he says:

> Consider now whether these two illustrious men from the East, endowed with such distinguished holiness and, as is also reported, brothers by birth, are sufficient for you.

[Note: [Col. 1051D] It was easy for Augustine, through a common error—as the phrase “as is reported” suggests—to confuse Gregory Nazianzen with another bishop of the same name, Gregory of Nyssa, the brother of Basil. Yet he could not have substituted Gregory of Baetica, bishop of the Western Church of Illiberis, whom he did not know, for an Eastern Gregory without qualification. Rather, he called him an Eastern Gregory because of Rufinus’s translation and the codex that bore the name of the bishop of Nazianzus.] I would prefer to explain this by Augustine’s error than to accuse the diligence of copyists who supposedly changed *Illiberitanus* into *Orientalis*. For without the authority of any manuscript, to put forward such a claim is rash, and it amounts more to the gratuitous evasions of a man pursuing excuses than to an argument.

4. The subject matter of the work and the controversy over the three substances agree with the age of Gregory of Baetica [Note: [Col. 1052D] These matters, both those just mentioned and those that follow, fit no better with the age of Gregory of Baetica than with that of Nazianzen.], when this controversy was being agitated in the Church. It agrees with the conduct and customs of the Arians, against whom Gregory was engaged, who commonly branded Catholics as followers of Sabellius. It agrees with what is reported about that bishop of Illiberis. For it is certain that the imperial authorities were chiefly stirred up against Gregory by the work of Marcellinus and Faustinus, and the author of the little work bears witness to this concerning himself in these words:

> Since you are the very one who even now harasses me through the ambition and power of kings and throws everything into confusion, and so forth.

5. It was characteristic of the Luciferians, among whom Gregory belonged, to be hostile to the defenders of the three hypostases. The author of the work reveals himself as such when he asserts that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three Gods. For, as we learn from Faustinus’s little book of faith, the Luciferians and other defenders of one hypostasis thought it followed that those who professed three substances also confessed three Gods.

Having established these matters conjecturally concerning the earlier treatise, which occupies the place of Oration 49 among the works of Nazianzen, the same must be said concerning the later work, or Oration 50, which lies in our codex under the name of a little book. I believe that no one has yet noticed the very close connection between the two, which I seem to discern. I consider the earlier work, Oration 49, to be an explanation and apology for the later one, and the order of the two to have been reversed [Col. 1052B].

The two agree in similarity of style. Both glory in Rufinus as translator. Both explain the faith of the Nicene Creed, but one briefly and paraphrastically, the other in a fuller, dogmatic, and polemical treatment. But what I ask the reader to note is that one is the explanation and apology of the other: the earlier of the later.

Indeed, from the very beginning of the earlier work the author declares that, moved by love of the Catholic faith, he had previously published a little book against the Arians. But, he says:

> There was someone who, whether from zeal for doctrine or from the duty of charity, more carefully reconsidered what we had said, and called certain things either superfluous or ambiguous—things which some people might understand otherwise than I had said them. Therefore I have again arranged those same matters in plainer language in this little book, so that I might show the simplicity of my meaning and remove the scruple from my readers.

Here, then, is a little book previously published by the same author—and specifically a little book of faith, as he expressly writes later:

> For the profession of faith is also clear,

and so forth. This is also clear from the little book in its entirety.

Several things prove that the little book which he defends is the same as ours, which appears in chapter 39 of the codex.

First, he reports the objection made against the author in these words:

> For this is what they say can be criticized: when the Word of God was to be read as referring to the person of the Son, I think we used the expression “for the person of the Son,” and thus we might be understood to mean such a Word as grammarians describe, and so forth.

And later:

> I confess that I am amazed that this could have been understood as though we denied the proper person of the Word, who is the Son, although in so many places we have asserted that he is the true Son born from the true Father.

They therefore first argued that the author had made an exceedingly bare and unexplained mention of the Word in his profession of faith. Hence suspicion might arise that he did not understand the Word as uncreated and coeternal with the Father, but as something created and such as grammarians describe. They also criticized him for not using the word “person”; hence they suspected that he did not acknowledge a real distinction of persons [Col. 1052D]. These two points correspond to the little book of faith, in which the name “Word” appears only once and without explanation, while the word “person” appears nowhere.

3. In the later little book we also read that the author says he had written in the earlier one, in many places, that the true Son was born from the true Father. The later work says:

> We confess the true Father, who begot the true Son: God from God, light from light, life from life, perfect from perfect, whole from whole, full from full.

It also mentions eight times that the Son was born or begotten from the Father. Thus he was right to say that he had repeatedly inserted the statement that the true Son was born from the true Father.
