4. He also repeats the words “whole from whole, complete from complete, perfect from perfect.” The later little book expresses them, with only minor changes and no alteration of sense, as:

> Perfect from perfect, whole from whole, full from full.

5. He testifies that he had said that the Son was begotten from the Father, not made. Our little book likewise says:

> Not created, but begotten; not from nothing, but from the Father.

6. The author was accused of Sabellianism because he had said that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God:

> But because we said “one God,” we are thought to have denied the persons.

The profession of faith does indeed say:

> We confess not three Gods—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—but one God.

Without mentioning his other replies, he satisfies this accusation as follows:

> How could I make the Father himself the Son of himself, and in this way call one person by two names, since I also condemned this sect, that is, the Sabellian sect, in the same little book?

The little book truly contains these words:

> Not one God in such a way that he is solitary, nor the same one who is himself Father to himself and himself Son, but the true Father, who begot the true Son.

7. The author also reports this concerning the little book of faith:

> Therefore we ascribe wholly to the Father what belongs to the Son, and wholly to the Son what belongs to the Father, and so forth.

Who does not see that the passage in the little book is being indicated? There we read:

> Nevertheless, we venerate one God, because from one Father the Son, God, was born, possessing all that belongs to the Father; and the Father begot the whole Son, possessing all that is in the Father.

Let it therefore be certain and fixed that this pair of treatises on the Nicene faith belongs to one author. Let no one separate what is joined not merely by similarity of subject matter but also by the author’s own design and by the nature of the writing. That design requires that what has hitherto been placed second should henceforth occupy the first position: it was written first, it supplies the material for the other writing, and it ought to be read first so that the other may be better understood.

## VIII. Augustine’s Little Book

After the anonymous little book of faith that we have just discussed, the codex contains, in chapter 40, *Augustine’s Little Book on the Catholic Faith against All Heresies*. It is so entitled both in the Thuanean and Oxford codices and in a third codex, which the distinguished lover of literary antiquity, Monsieur Vion d’Herouval, shared with me. [Note: [Col. 1053D] The Herouvallian codex, which Quesnellus reported in his catalogue of manuscripts to be the same as the Rheims codex of Antoine Favre, belongs to the collection of additions to Isidore. We have proved in *Treatise*, part III, chapters 7 and 8, that this collection, as well as Isidore’s own collection, was compiled in Gaul. The authors of both collections took certain materials from the collection published in this volume, which is also Gallican, but not from the Roman Codex, to which Quesnellus wrongly attributed the published collection. It is also false that Isidore derived from this collection the ancient version of the Eastern canons. In the matter of conciliar canons he transferred a Spanish collection into his own. In fact, neither the Nicene and Sardican canons nor those of Chalcedon appear in Isidore in the form in which they are found in our codex of canons. If the Isidorian and our collection generally agree in the case of other Greek synods, this arose because both adopted an ancient version in those places. Isidore used the Spanish version, whereas the author of our collection used another and older source.]

Since this codex also contains the ancient versions of Saint Athanasius’s letter to Epictetus and of another letter of Saint Cyril to John of Antioch, in the forms in which they are found in our Codex of the Roman Church, I suspect that this profession came from the same source. For a large part of the Herouvallian manuscript codex is Isidore’s collection, and I therefore suspect that he knew our Codex, because he appears to have drawn from it the ancient version of the Eastern canons that he uses.

[Col. 1054A] The same confession of faith is cited by the Master of the Sentences in book III, distinction 21, near the end:

> According to this principle, Augustine says: “If anyone says and believes that the Son of God, God himself, suffered, let him be anathema.”

A reference to Augustine is written in the margin, by what I believe to be a later hand: “Sermon on Faith, which is the third sermon on Thursday in Holy Week.” In fact, volume X of his works contains sermon 129 *On Time*, entitled *On Right Faith*. The Louvain scholars did not relegate it to the appendix and consequently judged it to be an Augustinian work.

Yet this confession is much longer in Saint Augustine and has been interpolated in several places. In the three manuscript codices it contains only twelve anathemas. Among Saint Augustine’s works it is found enlarged by fourteen additional anathemas. I also observe a notable difference between the two, leaving aside lesser matters: in the manuscripts mentioned above, the Holy Spirit is said only to proceed from the Father, and again, “proceeding from the Father.” But in Augustine both passages read “proceeding from the Father and the Son” and “proceeding from the Father and the Son,” which is undoubtedly an indication of a later age than Augustine’s.

We read that this same little book was inserted into the acts of the First Council of Toledo, held around the year 400. Yet nine anathemas not found in our text were added to it, while the sixth, seventh, and eighth, which lie in the codex, were omitted. [Note: [Col. 1054D] In the rule of faith appended to the First Council of Toledo only six anathemas were added; the fifth, sixth, seventh, and twelfth were not removed but expressed more clearly, as will be evident from *Observations*, § 2.]

In the midst of such diversity among the exemplars of this little book, it is not easy to determine what should be held either concerning its integrity or concerning its author. I shall briefly explain my own view.

First [Note: [Col. 1054D] We shall explain our position in the same *Observations*, § 2.], I believe that this confession of faith was composed by its author in the form in which it is presented by the three manuscript codices cited above, and therefore also by the ancient Codex of the Roman Church. For the fuller forms found both among Saint Augustine’s sermons and in the acts of the First Council of Toledo reveal, from their additions alone and from their mention of the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, the hand of a later author than the original composer.

2. It is evident from an examination of the little book itself that it was composed against the Priscillianist sect alone, although the author of the title in the three manuscript codices says that it was written against all heresies [927]. Several errors are condemned there whose proponents included, in part, Sabellius, in part Origen, in part Mani­chaeus, and others; yet none are included that the Priscillianists did not profess, and scarcely any that Saint Augustine, Saint Leo I, and others do not also attribute to them.

The matters contained in the first part of the little book against Sabellius and in the first four anathemas were made their own by the Priscillianists, as Saint Augustine testifies in his book *On Heresies*, chapter 70, and in his book *Against the Priscillianists to Orosius*, as well as our Leo in letter 15 to Turibius, chapter 1. In the same book *Against the Priscillianists*, Augustine asserts that these heretics borrowed many things from the Manichaeans and the Origenists [Col. 1054D]. I therefore consider it evident that the errors of Origen anathematized in the little book are condemned there as errors of the Priscillianists.

Leo observes the association and affinity of these same heretics with the Patripassians, the disciples of Sabellius, with the Arians, Marcion, Cerdo, Paul of Samosata, Photinus, and others, in the same letter to Turibius. He explains their doctrine concerning the Lord’s incarnation in these words:

> They sacrilegiously pretend to confess Christ in such a way that they remove the reality of his incarnation, death, and resurrection.

There is therefore no need to refer to anyone other than the Priscillianists what is said about the incarnation in the same little book.

3. Although this little book could have had as its author another Augustine rather than Augustine of Hippo—for example, Augustine, bishop of Aquileia, who was a contemporary of the bishop of Hippo and occupied the see after Chromatius, as Henry Palladius relates in his account of Aquileian affairs—nothing prevents its having been written by Augustine of Hippo. It appears to have been composed in his time; [Note: [Col. 1055D] Indeed, the Benedictine editors, who acquired the greatest expertise in examining and publishing Augustine’s works, plainly testify that its style differs from Augustine’s. We shall quote their text in the *Observations*, § 2, no. 2, and there add the agreeing judgment of another Benedictine of the highest authority.] nor does its style differ from Augustine’s, and it contains nothing that could not easily be found in his writings, especially in the book *On Heresies* and in the other *Against the Priscillianists to Orosius*.

4. It is clear from Augustine himself, both in this last treatise and in book II of the *Retractations*, chapter 4, that Orosius sent him a consultation from Spain concerning the errors of the Priscillianists and Origenists. This consultation stands at the beginning of Augustine’s reply and is found in volume VI of his works. I would therefore readily suppose that Augustine sent, together with this work, the little book of faith which the Spanish bishops could propose for subscription to heretics wishing to profess the Catholic faith and renounce Priscillianist doctrine, provided that they approved it.

Nor was Orosius the only person from Spain to consult Augustine about such errors. For from the beginning of that consultation we learn that the Spanish bishops Eutropius and Paul sent Augustine a memorandum against the errors spreading through the regions of Spain. On this occasion, therefore, the little book could have been requested by the bishops of Spain and written by Augustine.

[Col. 1055C] 5. It is highly probable that the little books of faith discussed in this dissertation were inserted into the Roman Codex by our Saint Leo, as we said in Dissertation 12, and that they were taken from the archives of the Apostolic See, where they had previously been kept. [Note: [Col. 1055D] We have already rejected this hypothesis concerning the Roman Codex in the *Observations* on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 12, and the whole conjecture collapses in light of the arguments presented there.]

Who, then, would think that this confession of faith was rashly attributed to Augustine and preserved under that name in the Roman archive and inserted into the Codex, unless the Romans had established its authenticity from an unquestionable indication? Could Saint Leo easily have been ignorant of Augustine’s works—Augustine, I mean, who was his contemporary and whose writings on faith had always been held in the highest esteem by the Apostolic See?

But on what occasion was the little book brought to Rome? We may remain ignorant of this. Nevertheless, I shall say either that Leo brought it from Africa when, while still an acolyte, he carried Zosimus’s decree against the Pelagians there, or that envoys sent by the Spanish bishops to Augustine were instructed, on their return from Africa, to visit the Apostolic See by the same route, so that they might seek the authority and assistance of that See—as happened under Pope Saint Leo against the Priscillianists spreading through the churches of Spain—and that they shared with the bishop or leading men of the Roman Church the little book they had received from Augustine.

As for the First Council of Toledo, to which we read that this little book is attached, the learned Cardinal Baronius long ago observed, under the year 447, no. 16, that the rule of faith inserted into its acts does not belong to that council, held in the year 400 [Col. 1056A], [Note: [Col. 1056D] We discussed this rule of faith at greater length in volume II, note 5 (in our volume I, column 1331, note a), in the observations of Quesnellus on letter 15 of Saint Leo. See also the observations to be appended to this dissertation, § 2.] but rather to a later council convened in the time and at the urging of our Leo in the year 447 or the following year, whether at Toledo or in another city of Spain.

The learned Cardinal’s conjecture is confirmed by the heading or annotation prefixed to the little book of faith after the canons of that synod. I copy it not from the older and corrupt edition of the council but from the more accurate edition of García de Loaysa. After the canons of the First Council of Toledo, we read:

> The constitution of the Council of Toledo is completed.

Here you see that the acts of that council are expressly distinguished from what follows. For immediately afterward we read:

> Here begins the rule of the Catholic faith against all heresies, and especially against the Priscillianists, which the bishops of Tarraco, Carthage, Lusitania, and Baetica composed and sent, at the command of Leo, pope of the city of Rome, to Balconius, bishop of Galicia. They also established the twenty chapters written above in the Council of Toledo.

The first part of this annotation, when compared with the letter of Saint Leo to Turibius, would readily show—something that even the mention of Leo alone indicates—that this rule of faith does not belong to that earlier council, but to another held more than forty years later. The Council of Braga, whether the First or the Second, held under Pope John III in the year 563, supports this conclusion. There Lucretius the bishop addresses the synod in these words:

> “I believe that your Blessedness knows that, at the time when the most abominable poisons of the Priscillianist sect were spreading through these regions, the most blessed Leo, pope of the city of Rome, sent his writings to the synod of Galicia. At his command also the bishops of Tarragona and Carthage, as well as those of Lusitania and Baetica, having held a council among themselves, composed a rule of faith against the Priscillianist heresy together with certain chapters, and sent it to Balconius, then bishop of this Church of Braga.”

These words require no commentary; they clearly [Col. 1056C] show that the rule of faith appended to the First Council of Toledo was not composed there, but at another council held in Leo’s time, and that it was read again a hundred years later at Braga and attributed to that later synod.

The Spanish bishops had received this confession of faith from Leo, either extracted from the Roman Codex and sent along with some of the letters which the pontiff wrote to them at that time, or else they had brought it out of their own archives, to which it had formerly been entrusted when they received it from Augustine, as we conjectured above. The Fathers of the synod, however, used that confession in such a way as to adapt it to the present needs of their Churches, [Note: [Col. 1056D] The fifth, sixth, seventh, and twelfth anathemas were not removed, but expressed more clearly in other words, as we observed in note 20 (Col. 1054, note b).] removing three anathemas—namely, the fifth, sixth, and seventh—from the Augustinian document and substituting three others in their place. The reason was doubtless that, while errors were then spreading through Spain, these anathemas were more suitable and those less so. They also added six others after the Augustinian anathemas, by which the errors of the Priscillianists noted by Saint Leo in his letter to Turibius against those same heretics were proscribed. Thus anyone might readily think that Leo himself had enlarged and arranged the anathemas in this form and sent them to Spain.

The latter part of the annotation prefixed to the booklet of faith after the canons of the First Council of Toledo reads:

> “They also established these chapters of the canons written above in the Council of Toledo.”

[Note: [Col. 1056D] See what we said about these words in volume II, note 5, in the observations of Quesnell on letter 15 of Saint Leo, and what will be added in the following observations, § 2, no. 3.]

Cardinal Baronius thinks that the words should be referred to the bishops of the First Council of Toledo and that they were wrongly transferred here by an ignorant scribe. But what prevents us from understanding them of the bishops assembled in Leo’s time, who re-established what had formerly been decreed by the earlier synod, having been moved to do so by the corruption introduced into the morals and discipline of that age? Certainly neither the agreement of the manuscript codices permits us to regard these words as spurious, nor can the phrase “They also established the aforesaid” refer to bishops other than those named in the same heading and assembled in Leo’s time. If this is correct, there is now no remaining doubt about the place of this synod, since the final words plainly testify that they assembled at Toledo. More will be said about this synod elsewhere, in the notes on the celebrated letter 15 of Leo to Turibius.

It remains for us to say something about the booklet as it lies among the sermons of Saint Augustine. Above I noted its interpolation; now I observe that twenty-six anathemas are read in it. The first twelve are the same as those found in our codex, and I consider them genuinely Augustinian; the other fourteen are found neither in the Roman Codex nor in the Council of Toledo. They have been copied and attached to this booklet from the confession of the Catholic faith that Pope Damasus sent to Paulinus, bishop of Antioch, which you have in our Roman Codex on page 214. Whether the two booklets were thus joined together by the authority of some synod or through the personal ingenuity of some diligent scholar, I simply do not know. The latter possibility, however, is not entirely improbable.

I would add this warning: the anathemas of Pope Damasus suffer from several interpolations in Augustine’s text. I notice one in particular. Where in our codex and in Theodoret we read, concerning the divine persons, “Saving all things,” that Augustinian sermon has: “Saving all things that are to be saved.”

But how, someone may ask, did this booklet come to occupy a place among those sermons of Saint Augustine assigned to Thursday in Holy Week, when not even a syllable appears in it that suits or can be adapted to the solemnity of that day? This is no less obscure than the other matters. I shall say what occurs to me.

After the sixteenth anathema, or chapter, of the Second Council of Braga in the year 563 had been promulgated:

> “If anyone on the Thursday of Easter, which is called the Lord’s Supper, does not, at the proper hour after none, keep the Masses in the Church while fasting, but, following the sect of Priscillian, celebrates the solemnity of that day from the third hour by attending Masses for the dead after breaking the fast, let him be anathema.”

From this chapter we understand that the Thursday of the Lord’s Supper had been polluted by the Priscillianists through their sacrilegious ceremonies. What if we say that, for this reason and because of the solemnity of the mysteries, the Spanish bishops selected that same Thursday as the day on which the profession of faith against the Priscillianists would be read publicly before the assembly of the faithful? Or perhaps that day itself—which, as is still observed today, was customarily the day on which public penitents were reconciled to the Church—was also assigned to the reconciliation of those who wished to renounce the Priscillianist heresy and profess the Catholic faith, and for whom this profession of faith was prescribed to be publicly recited?

Since this profession was found in the ritual books of the Spanish Churches among the solemn rites and prayers of Thursday in the Lord’s Supper, and since it bore the name of Augustine in that place, or elsewhere as we have seen, the occasion may perhaps have arisen from this for giving the booklet a place among the sermons of that holy Doctor assigned to that Thursday. I put forward this conjecture because nothing better occurs to me at present. We await from the Reverend Father Dom François Delfau, the Benedictine ascetic, something more extensive and worthy of so learned a man concerning this booklet, in the edition of the works of Saint Augustine which he is preparing with his colleagues of the monastery of Saint-Germain.

## IX. The Form of the Booklet of Faith

After the letter of Saint Athanasius to Epictetus and the other letter of Saint Cyril of Alexandria to John of Antioch, which are found in chapters 52 and 53, the following is read at the end under the same chapter 53:

> “Form of the booklet of faith.”

[Note: [Col. 1057D] We think that this form, written according to Leo’s mind, was either sent from Rome to Constantinople or sent from Constantinople to Leo, approved by him, and rendered into Latin, and that it subsequently entered several Latin collections. See the annotations on the form itself, edited in this volume at chapter 53 of our codex. This form must not be confused with the definition of the Council of Chalcedon, which Quesnell omitted but which we produced in the following chapter 54 of the same codex from the manuscript copies of this collection, and which differs greatly from Rusticus’s translation.]

I think that this form was sent by the Roman See to the Easterners, especially to the people of Constantinople. I infer this from these words of the booklet: “The letter to our bishop Flavian of Constantinople, of holy memory.” The mention of the confirmation given by Saint Leo to the definition of Chalcedon, and of his letter to Flavian, proves the same point.

This entire form has been composed from part of the definition of Chalcedon, [Col. 1058B] which some regard as a second definition, others as the later and sole remaining part of the same definition, and still others call “the Treatise of the Council of Chalcedon.” Its opening words are: “It would indeed have been sufficient …” It seems to have been taken from the version usually attributed to the deacon Rusticus, although it differs somewhat in certain places.

I suspect that this form was attached to the letters of Saint Cyril to John of Antioch and of Saint Athanasius to Epictetus because those letters were presented together for subscription to Eutychians or Nestorians returning to the Catholic faith, whether at Constantinople or at Alexandria. Nor is this without precedent. For when the Easterners at one time resisted subscribing to the letters of Saint Leo, [Note: [Col. 1058D] See note 8 on letter 70 of Saint Leo in this volume (our volume I, Col. 893, note i), where, refuting Quesnell’s interpretation, we showed that in letter 54, now 70, to Pulcheria, Leo understood the particle *vel* as “and.” We confirmed this more fully in note 5 on letter 51, now 67, in the same volume I (our volume I, Col. 886, note g).] Leo himself gave them the option of assenting either to his own letter or to Cyril’s.

Letter 54, now 70, to Pulcheria concerning Anatolius says:

> “What I ask is simple and unambiguous: that, without the labor of lengthy disputation, he should accept the letter of Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, of holy memory, which he himself had sent to Nestorius, or consent to my letter, which was sent to Flavian, bishop of holy remembrance.”

And in letter 88, now 117, to Julian, chapter 3, concerning the ignorance of the rebellious Palestinian monks, Saint Leo says:

> “If he thinks our teaching open to doubt, let him at least not reject the writings of Athanasius, Theophilus, and Cyril, priests of Alexandria, of blessed memory; for the form of our faith so agrees with them that whoever professes agreement with them differs from us in no respect.”

As to the date when the form was composed, [Note: [Col. 1058D] If this form, as we indicated in note 27 (on this page, note a), was written in Leo’s time, it must unquestionably be said to predate the Acephali heresy.] it was unquestionably written at the time when the sect of the Acephali was spreading through the East. Since these heretics rejected both the Council of Chalcedon and Leo’s *Tome*, they were always invited to return to communion with the Church on the condition that they professed adherence to both. Nearly all the surviving records of the Church written in the time of the Roman pontiffs Simplicius, Felix, and Gelasius prove this. I assign the form to the age of the last of these because it is read inserted into the codex after his letters.

## X. The Confession of Faith of Pope Damasus to Paulinus of Antioch

Under chapter 55 is found the letter of Pope Damasus to Paulinus, bishop of Antioch, together with the form of faith attached to it. Its title explicitly names Paulinus, bishop of Antioch, in both of our manuscript codices. This removes every doubt that seemed to arise from the older editions both of the Councils and of Theodoret’s versions, where Paulinus, bishop of Thessalonica, was read.

I do not doubt that the form of faith was sent by Damasus together with the letter, and consequently that one should not be separated from the other, as has hitherto been done. First, this is persuaded by the authority of both our codices, which not only place one immediately after the other but represent both under one and the same chapter. Thus, although the form of faith is distinct from the letter, it appears nevertheless to be attached to it as a kind of component.

Second, it is certain from the beginning of the letter itself that the form of faith was sent along with the letter, to be offered for subscription to heretics returning to the Catholic faith. “We have sent the faith,” he says, “not so much to you, who share communion in that faith, as to those who, by subscribing to it along with you—that is, through you, with us—wish to enter into communion.” This must unquestionably be understood of a profession of faith distinct from the letter.

The fact that later, after some intervening discussion of the faith of the Incarnation, he mentions subscription to the letter itself, I think should be explained as follows: since the form of faith was appended to the letter, whoever subscribed to the former was considered likewise to subscribe to the latter. The situation was much like that of someone subscribing to a form of faith presented together with a bishop’s mandate: by subscribing, he subscribes both to the episcopal mandate and to the form itself.

Third, it was customary that heretics aspiring to Catholic communion were required to subscribe not to a very brief letter such as this, in which the faith is not explained at sufficient length, but to a distinct form composed in explicit and carefully stated terms.

Fourth, the title of the form as it appears in the Thuanean codex makes this point especially clear. While I am writing this, however, the Roman collection of Luca Holstenius, published at Rome in 1662, has conveniently come to hand. In it I find the form of faith, or the anathemas contained in it, inserted into the letter itself at the place marked by us with a small letter. [Col. 1059C] Thus our assertion rests not on conjecture alone, but also on the authority of the codex, which teaches us at least that this profession of faith should not be separated from the letter and that both were issued at the same time.

It follows that Damasus’s letter is synodical. For Theodoret is a witness—Book V, chapter 10—that the anathemas which he reports in the following chapter were sanctioned by bishops assembled in great numbers at Rome; and they are commonly assigned to the Third Roman Council under Damasus.

Damasus himself also seems to imply this. At the beginning, when speaking of the familiar letter which he had sent through Vitalis in his own name alone, he uses the singular number: “I had sent a reply, leaving it to your judgment; I had indicated … that I was moved …” But later, when referring to this other letter as written by several or in the name of several, he indicates this by saying: “We have sent”; “we write that he should be associated with us”; “our agreement.”

Indeed, the Roman pontiffs were accustomed to undertake nothing of this kind without a synod. It was especially important that this custom not be violated on such an occasion—in a matter, I say, of such great importance, concerning the faith and the common profession of faith—in which there was good reason to fear that the Easterners, somewhat less favorably disposed toward the Westerners, might reject a form of faith which they did not know to have been confirmed by a numerous council of Westerners.

[Note: [Col. 1059C] Although the Roman pontiffs discussed and decided matters of great importance in a Roman synod, they nevertheless usually entitled letters in the name of the pontiff alone, because the authority of the Apostolic See was chiefly intended. The Church’s perpetual tradition had taught not only Westerners but also Easterners, on account of that primacy—as Irenaeus calls it—to regard this authority as deserving the highest esteem, especially in matters of faith. Hence the letter now under discussion is headed not in the name of the Roman synod but in that of Damasus alone, and is attributed to Damasus alone in the address of the Council of Chalcedon to the Emperor Marcian, volume IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils, Col. 1766.]

The year to which both documents should be referred is not entirely beyond doubt. If it were certain that the order in which the anathemas are recorded by Theodoret corresponded to their chronological order, it would likewise be certain that this form of faith was issued after the year 381, since he places it after the Second Ecumenical Council, and even after the second gathering of bishops in the imperial city and after Damasus’s letters replying to their letter.

The same period seems to be indicated when, after listing the anathemas in chapter 11, he adds the following concerning the time: “These things were indeed done while Gratian was still alive.” These words seem to indicate the end of that emperor’s life, although the common chronology of the Third Roman Council, from which the anathemas are believed to have proceeded, precedes it by an entire decade.

Baronius, who assigns the letter to the year of Christ 373, is rightly criticized by Henri Valois, who says that it was written in the year 382, shortly after the synod. But I do not intend to treat this matter at greater length. See Valois’s notes on Theodoret, page 45.

[Note: [Col. 1059D] It was written when there was still hope concerning Vitalis, then a presbyter, before he brought about the open schism and was promoted by the Apollinarists to the episcopate of Antioch. He was acting as bishop while Meletius was still alive. Hence Jerome, in his letter to Damasus concerning the three hypostases, mentions three bishops simultaneously occupying the Church of Antioch: “I do not know Vitalis; I reject Meletius; I do not recognize Paulinus.” Meletius died in the year 381, while the Council of Constantinople was in session. Vitalis, therefore, was a bishop before that council; and consequently this letter was written by Damasus not a little after, but some time before, that council, when Vitalis was still a presbyter. Tillemont assigns it to the year 375, while Constantius assigns it to approximately 378. There is no opportunity to discuss the matter further.]

Our present purpose is more directly concerned with a notable interpolation by which the profession of faith is read in the standard editions and in the Thuanean codex in a fuller form than in the Oxford codex. [Note: [Col. 1060C] Since not only the Thuanean codex but also the other codices of our collection—with the exception of one more recent Oxford manuscript [Col. 1060D]—and, in addition, all the other Latin collections that contain this letter of Damasus consistently exhibit in the text the decree beginning, “But those who migrate from Church to Church,” Quesnell vainly believed that he could represent the same decree as spurious on the authority of a single recent codex, which we have found defective in several other places. Nor does another codex of Justellus support him, for that codex is Isidorian. Isidore divided this exposition of faith into three parts and removed the same decree from the first part. Then, after inserting other material, he gave the final part of the exposition, and finally, after further insertions, displayed the cited decree separately. Just as the division between the first and final parts must be attributed to the discretion of Isidore Mercator, so too must the separation and distinct presentation of that decree.]

Namely, after the sixth anathema, both in those editions and in Theodoret, the following words are found:

> “But those who have migrated from Churches to Churches we hold alien from our communion until they have returned to the cities in which they were originally established. But if, when someone has migrated elsewhere, another has been ordained in the place of the living man, the one who abandoned his own city shall remain without the dignity of the priesthood until his successor rests in the Lord.”

There can scarcely be any doubt that these words were added later. First, this is established by the authority of the manuscript copy of our Oxford codex, produced in the city of Rome where Damasus wrote, by leading men of the Roman Church and with the aid of the archives of the Apostolic See. It deserves far greater confidence in this matter than either Theodoret or the less accurate editions, which seem to me to have been derived from the Greek.

Second, the other codex, that of the distinguished Justellus, supports this conclusion and is cited in the Labbe edition of the Councils.

Third, inspection of the passage itself makes the point persuasive. These words, which concern discipline rather than faith, are very far removed from the subject of the anathemas and inappropriately interrupt both the thread of the discourse and the sequence of the form of faith.

“But then,” someone may ask, “how was the text interpolated, so that by Theodoret’s time it was already circulating in a fuller form in that section?” I would believe that this was done through the art and industry of Paulinus himself, bishop of Antioch. Since he had the great Meletius as his colleague in the episcopate of Antioch, he employed this device so that it would become known that Meletius was alien from communion with the Apostolic See.

Nor did he wish only this to be made public in the very form of faith. He also wished all those returning to the Catholic faith who subscribed to it to profess that they would never associate themselves with Meletius’s communion, and he wished them to be bound to this by their own written pledge.

Whom could we say is more clearly designated by this canon than Meletius? Formerly established as bishop of Sebaste in Armenia, he had, according to Theodoret, been offended by the disobedience of his subjects and withdrawn elsewhere to live in retirement. Later, when all demanded him for the See of Antioch, he was summoned and elevated to it. The first part of the decree therefore marks him out. And to make Meletius’s condition still worse, the second part decrees that the man who had been appointed in the place abandoned by him at Sebaste would retain the dignity of the priesthood for as long as he himself lived.

Theodoret also has one further addition of no slight importance. In the final anathema, “But if anyone divides …,” after the words “on account of the one Divinity which we believe and know to belong to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit,” the following words are immediately added:

> “One God in three hypostases” (*Θεὸν ἕνα ἐν τρισὶν ὑποστάσεσιν*).

No one will believe that these words were written by Damasus, both because they are found in no Latin codex, whether printed or manuscript, and because the Latins recoiled from asserting three hypostases. Nor do I think that Theodoret himself added them. Since Epiphanius Scholasticus, the oldest of all the interpreters of Theodoret’s history, does not reproduce these words—as is clear from Cassiodorus’s *Tripartite History*—I infer that they were added in more recent copies of Theodoret, perhaps by people who, when rereading this profession of faith of Damasus in Greek and comparing it with copies interpolated through the art and industry of Paulinus, thought that the three words had been omitted by the scribes through negligence and ought to be restored to the booklet.

The fact that they had already been inserted into Damasus’s text by Easterners supporting the party of Meletius is suggested by Theodoret’s own account in Book V, chapter 3, where he reports these words of Flavian to Paulinus of Antioch:

> “If you embrace the communion of Damasus, my friend, show us plainly that your doctrine is similar to ours. For he, while confessing one and the same substance of the Trinity, expressly proclaims three hypostases; you, on the contrary, abolish the hypostases of the Trinity.”

If Flavian said this, I scarcely doubt that he was drawing on an interpolated version of Damasus’s letter, if that version had already been written. Otherwise, he attributes to Damasus the assertion of three hypostases on the basis of the assertion of three persons. The point is clearly asserted in the fragment of Damasus’s decree in the Roman collection of Luca Holstenius, page 170.

## XI. Another Form of Faith

Immediately after the form of Damasian faith, under the same chapter, there follows a brief additional form. It is not different from the one found above, at the end of chapter 53, in Cyril’s letter to John of Antioch. It is, I say, the same form, but abridged and extracted from the treatise or definition of Chalcedon.

[Note: [Col. 1061D] Since this form, although more condensed, is identical in meaning with the one appended to Cyril’s letter in chapter 53 of our collection, and since both were written at the same time, this one, like the other, should likewise be assigned to the time of Saint Leo. See the preceding notes 27 and 29 (above, Col. 1054, note a; Col. 1055, note c).]

I think that both forms were presented in the time of Acacius. For at that time the heretics rejected both the decree of Chalcedon and the letter of Saint Leo, and in the booklets required of those returning from heresy they were compelled to subscribe to both.

## XII. Conjectures Concerning the Athanasian Creed

After so many booklets of faith have been reviewed—booklets which the Roman Church carefully preserved in its Codex of canons and decrees—someone may wonder why that celebrated confession of faith called the Creed of Saint Athanasius is missing from them, although its praise is sung in the ecclesiastical office throughout the Churches of at least the whole Western world.

Certainly the Romans would never have omitted that creed while inserting into their codex other forms of far less importance, if it had been known to them at that time—especially if, as the most eminent Cardinal Baronius maintains, Saint Athanasius had issued that confession of faith at Rome in the Latin language and recited it before the pope and the bishops assisting him.

The wonder will be increased by the fact that in the selection of testimonies which Saint Leo sent with his letter 134, now 165, to the Emperor Leo, and which was inserted by him or by someone else into the Roman Codex under chapter 41, that Athanasian creed has no place. It is absent from a collection in which excerpts from some of Saint Athanasius’s writings are read, although that confession should have been more familiar to Saint Leo through Athanasius and would have refuted the error of Eutyches more clearly and powerfully, while adding considerable force to the privileges of the Roman Church.

Some may be surprised at these facts. I am even more surprised that the silence of Saint Leo alone has not yet persuaded certain learned men that this little work is not Athanasius’s, but belongs to another author who was either unknown to Leo and his predecessors or lived at a later time.

Thus both arguments—the silence of Saint Leo and the omission from the Codex—should be added to the other arguments by which the most learned writers formerly denied this work to Athanasius. It is not the place or the time to investigate its author at greater length and in greater detail. This has already been done fully and learnedly by the most distinguished Gerardus Johannes Vossius in his discussion of the three creeds (*Dissertation* 2). I have thought it worthwhile to add here only a few remarks by way of an appendix, in connection with the booklets of faith that we have discussed and the testimonies collected by Leo against Eutyches, so that, if some light from a new conjecture can illuminate a matter hitherto obscure, we may not deprive the reader of it.

First, certainties must be distinguished from uncertainties; then our suspicions and conjectures may be brought forward.

1. It is now established by the agreement of nearly all learned men that this little work [Note: [Col. 1062D] On this opinion, see the following observations, § 3, no. 1.] is not the offspring of Saint Athanasius of Alexandria. The strongest evidence is supplied by the style itself and the structure of the language, which in no way belongs to a Greek author but to a Latin one.

This is confirmed both by the fact that Athanasius himself testifies in his letter to the Antiochenes and elsewhere that he was far from composing a new form of faith, and by the fact that he always maintained that the creed of the Council of Nicaea was complete in every respect. It is also confirmed by the profound silence in which this creed remained buried until at least the sixth century.

For since neither Saint Cyril of Alexandria—one of Athanasius’s successors—nor Saint Leo, nor any other ecclesiastical writer or bishop who defended the Catholic faith against Nestorius and Eutyches at the Councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon ever produced anything from it or mentioned it, who could persuade himself that this creed was then reckoned among the works of Athanasius? Anyone wishing to read more on this subject should consult the Vossius cited above and the other writers who have composed longer discussions of the matter.

2. From this final consideration it is likewise proved that, whoever the author of this creed may ultimately have been, he flourished after the rise and condemnation not only of the heresy of Nestorius but also of that of Eutyches, indeed after the time of Leo the Great.

Let it be granted that this Athanasian creed was omitted from the Councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon through some negligence. Certainly it could never have escaped the diligence of Saint Leo, who wrote repeatedly to the Eastern bishops after the Fourth Council and appealed to the proper tradition of the Eastern Churches, yet never mentioned the Athanasian creed, in which both heresies are so explicitly and distinctly refuted.

Nor was it known in the year 458, when he sent to the Emperor Leo that collection of testimonies which, after the archives of the Apostolic See had later been searched again, was enlarged into another collection that he had long before sent to the Council of Chalcedon. Moreover, the silence concerning this creed maintained by those pontiffs who fought against the Acephali and the Eutychians testifies that it was still unknown at that time.

3. It is certain that the author of this creed lived no later than the year 670. [Note: [Col. 1063D] Bohierius shows in his letter to Mabillon that this synod was held not in the year 670 but in 676 or 677. See volume VII of the Venetian edition of the Councils, Col. 549, note 1.]

For in that year the Synod of Autun was held in Gaul under Saint Leodegarius, bishop. Its canon reads:

> “If any presbyter, deacon, subdeacon, or cleric does not accurately recite the creed which the Apostles handed down under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, and the faith of Saint Athanasius the bishop, let him be condemned by the bishop.”

Indeed, as early as the year 633, certain passages from this creed seem to me to have been written into the confession of faith issued by the Fourth Council of Toledo, which is found in chapter 1 of that council.

4. There is no doubt that the creed had been composed many years before that Synod of Autun and had long since become famous throughout the entire Church. For those most prudent bishops would never have decreed by synodal edict, under threat of condemnation, that the clergy of every rank should embrace this form of faith and recite it accurately, as they say, or have placed it alongside the Apostles’ Creed, unless it had already been received through long usage, approved, and counted among the genuine works of the great Athanasius. This could scarcely have happened except after a succession of many years.

## XIII. When the Athanasian Creed Appears to Have Been Written

5. It follows that its author must be sought within approximately the hundred-year period extending from the pontificate of Pope Hilary, Leo’s successor, to the end of the sixth century or the beginning of the seventh.

Let sixty or seventy years before the Synod of Autun be allowed for the creed to be published and for its authority to be established throughout all the Churches. This is especially appropriate because the canons called those of Saint Leodegarius, bishop of Autun—including the one that concerns the creed—seem to have been issued by Leodegarius alone at a diocesan synod for his own Church, as even their title indicates.

We must not think that a single bishop would have arrogated to himself the authority to command his clergy, under a grave penalty, to memorize, believe in their hearts, and confess with their mouths a new creed that had neither been received by the universal Church nor approved by many. Yet, to conceal nothing, I would scarcely dare to establish anything certain from that one canon of Autun if I were not compelled by the authority of learned men—namely, Jacques Sirmond, Pierre de La Lande, and Godefroy Hermant—who did not hesitate to assign the cited canon to the year 670.

At the same time, neither the manuscript collections from which it was published nor any authors touch even lightly upon its date. Nor does there seem to be a stronger reason for attributing it to Saint Leodegarius and his synod than to some later bishop or council of Autun. Nevertheless, we willingly accept their opinion until more light appears.

We therefore think that the age of the author whom we seek should be placed approximately between the years 480 and 600, or even within a shorter interval.

6. It seems certain that the name of Athanasius entered the title of this work neither by chance nor through the carelessness of scribes, but rather that the author himself deliberately attributed it to Saint Athanasius. [Note: [Col. 1064D] We shall show from older manuscript copies that the name of Saint Athanasius was prefixed to the creed falsely by the author himself, in the observations, § 3, nos. 2 and 3.] For all copies of it that have so far been seen, whether handwritten or printed, display the name of Athanasius.

## XIV. It Was Not the Work of an Impostor

7. Whoever imposed such a profession of faith upon us under another person’s name is so far from being chargeable with imposture that the structure of the creed itself proves that the plan was undertaken by him under the inspiration of the Spirit of God. In it there shines forth wonderfully both the learned simplicity of the faith and the divine anointing of the Spirit. For this reason it appeared so worthy of Athanasius to the holy Fathers of the Church that they wished it to be recited by the mouths of all the clergy every Sunday and to be counted among the parts of the ecclesiastical office.

There is, in truth, a very broad distinction between this work and that impostor who produced for us so many fabricated letters, composed with the worst skill and intention under the names of the Roman pontiffs. In those letters there is scarcely anything that has not been stolen shamefully from others, or that is not unworthy of the pontiffs to whom they are attributed, since they are contrary to the discipline of those times and badly pieced together from scraps.

In this Athanasian creed, however, everything is worthy of Athanasius, and everything is entirely suited to the sincerity of the faith it expounds. Indeed, even the title itself cannot be accused of falsehood in every respect. For it did not bear the title “Creed,” as it is read in modern codices, but “Faith.”

This is shown by the canon of Autun transcribed above, by the manuscript breviary of the monastery of Monte Cassino, approximately six hundred years old, of which we shall speak below, and by other witnesses. The genuine title of the work is likewise proved by the Greek versions, in which it is called:

- *ἔκθεσις* — “exposition”;
- *ὁμολογία τῆς καθολικῆς πίστεως* — “confession of the Catholic faith”;
- *περὶ πίστεως κατὰ συντομίαν* — “concerning the faith in brief.”

The last title is found in the Athanasian creed interpolated by the Greeks and published by James Ussher. Latin authors likewise title it “exposition of the faith” or “discourse on the faith,” among them Hincmar, archbishop of Reims.

No one will deny that this is the faith of Athanasius, which is contained in the creed, provided that he believes Athanasius himself never departed from the Catholic faith.

### XV. Why Published under Another Name?

“But why,” you will ask, “did a Catholic author inscribe his work under another man’s name rather than his own?” For when it is called the symbol of Athanasius, although it is proved not to be by the holy Athanasius, there is reason to fear that it may be counted among spurious and apocryphal works. Bishop Salonius of Gaul feared that this might happen to Salvian’s book, which he had written to the Catholic Church under the name of Timothy. But what Salvian answers in his letter to that same Salonius, I answer likewise: the suspicion of an apocryphal style can be completely excluded by this fact alone, that it is quite clear that the books belong to a later controversy and were written by a man of a later age, out of devotion to and love for divine matters. Works are free from the suspicion of being apocryphal when they are recognized as being neither by Athanasius, nor by a man contemporary with Athanasius, nor by a Greek author.

As for his having wished to conceal his proper name, this must be attributed to fear of the heretics and adversaries of the faith [Col. 1065A] among whom the author lived while he was writing. We shall say more about this below.

From what we established above, and what can scarcely be called into doubt, we infer the following, which opens a path toward discovering the author of this symbol: namely, that the author was certainly a Catholic and lived and flourished within approximately the hundred years immediately following the deaths of Leo or Hilary, Roman pontiffs; that he suppressed his own name through fear of persecution; and consequently that he had his seat in a region where the enemies of the Catholic faith, especially the Arians, held power; and that he lived at a time when the errors of Arius, Nestorius, and Eutyches were being spread far and wide. For this symbol attacks these three heresies above all.

### XVI. The African Bishop Vigilius Appears to Be the Author of the Athanasian Symbol

Disregarding the opinion of those who attribute it to a Gallic author—including P. Pithoeus in his book *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, an opinion toward which Vossius professes himself inclined in the appendix to his dissertation on this subject [Col. 1065B]—[Note: [Col. 1065D] We shall refute this opinion of Quesnellus in the same observations, § 3, nos. 5 and 6.] everything we have set forth above seems to fit Vigilius Tapsitanus, or Tapsensis, a bishop in Africa. I do not think that this little work can more suitably be attributed to anyone than to this most vigorous defender of the Catholic faith.

For this Vigilius flourished toward the end of the fifth century and, as is probable, lived into the sixth, since in the year 484 he was the last of all the bishops of Byzacena, as Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius successfully infers in his notes on this same Vigilius from the list of African bishops summoned by King Hunneric to give an account of their faith. Moreover, Vigilius lived and held his episcopal see in an African region where the Vandals, infected with the Arian plague, harassed all Catholics with a savage persecution, so that uttering even a word about the Catholic faith was turned into a crime.

He also lived at a time when the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies were making the greatest daily advances, especially throughout the Eastern Churches, to which Vigilius was compelled to flee after being driven into exile by the impious king. Finally—and this point deserves the greatest weight in the present inquiry—it was very characteristic of Vigilius that, whenever he wrote little works during a raging persecution [Note: [Col. 1065D] It will become clear from what follows in the observations, § 3, nos. 5, that not all the works published under the name of Athanasius or of other Fathers and attributed to Vigilius Tapsensis are actually his.] he should publish them not under his own name, but in the person of ancient Fathers or authors.

Thus he wrote a book against Marivadus under the name of Idacius Clarus; he composed another, in the person of St. Augustine, against the Arian Felicianus; and a third, against Palladius, was inscribed to Ambrose or Gregory of Nazianzus. He also published more works under the name of St. Athanasius than under that of any other person. For among the works of St. Athanasius we have twelve books on the Trinity, published only in Latin, which learned men loudly declare to be by Vigilius—Jacobus Sirmondus in his notes on Theodulf *On the Holy Spirit*; Philippus Labbeus in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; and Chiffletius in the second short work of his *Vindications of the Works of Vigilius Tapsensis*—as well as the books of the *Dialogues* between Athanasius, Arius, and the judge Probus.

Even if these works mentioned were not established with unquestionable certainty as belonging to Vigilius [Col. 1065D], at least the *Dialogue against the Arians, Sabellians, and Photinians* was, as Vigilius himself admits, composed by him under the name of Athanasius, debating against Arius, Sabellius, and Photinus before the judge Probus. This certainly lends the greatest weight to our conjectures.

Vigilius himself, I say, professes this in the preface to that dialogue:

> “It appeared useful and very appropriate,” he writes, “to introduce each heretic in his own person, together with the professions of his doctrine, as though present persons were dealing with present persons . . . . Therefore I introduced Sabellius, Photinus, and Arius, and on our side Athanasius, so that the truth, sifted out through the supreme contest of the disputants, might reach everyone’s knowledge.”

Our opinion is further confirmed by the fact that the adversaries of the faith whom the symbol principally attacks—namely, the Arians and Eutychians—were the very same people whom Vigilius always pursued in his writings. He composed most of his little works against the Arians, who were devastating the African Churches, and he produced a notable work against the Eutychians, in which he vigorously defends both the letter of St. Leo and the decree of Chalcedon against the attacks of the heretics.

#### 2. Vigilius Also Published Other Professions of Faith under the Name of Athanasius

Vigilius also published other professions of faith under the name of Athanasius, which show that he was accustomed to composing works of this kind. Such are those inserted in the books *On the Trinity* [Note: [Col. 1065D] We shall prove in the cited place of the observations that these formulas are wrongly attributed to Vigilius Tapsensis.].

We believe that this profession, which bears the name of a symbol, was composed by him while he was living in exile at Constantinople [Col. 1066B]. At that time, while he was still in Africa, he had already published many little works against the Arian heretics. When he heard, while he was in the East, how great a slaughter the Arian heresy was inflicting upon the African Churches, and in what danger the faith of his countrymen stood, he considered it part of his pastoral duty to bring aid to his endangered people and to place before simpler Christians a profession of faith which, removing all the byways of subtler and more complicated theology, would set forth Catholic doctrine purely, clearly, and briefly.

By means of this exposition he believed that his own Church and the other African Churches should be fortified not only against the perfidy of the Arian sect, but also against the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies. Since these were spreading widely among the Eastern peoples with whom he lived, he saw that they had either already been imported into the African regions or could easily be imported there.

He judged that such a profession ought to be adorned with the name of Athanasius [Note: [Col. 1066D] Here it is assumed that the name of Athanasius was inscribed by the author himself at the beginning; we shall show in the observations that this is false.], both because he thought that those who are guided solely by authority would be retained by the authority of so great a man, and because he well knew that the learned men of that age could not be led into the error of attributing the exposition to Athanasius, since the exposition distinctly mentions the new heresies and thereby contradicts such an attribution.

It also seemed entirely necessary to him lest any African bishop then living should come under suspicion among the heretics because of having composed this formulation of the faith, and consequently be brought into the gravest danger to his life, such was the savagery of the Arians. Anyone who reads Victor of Vita’s account of the African persecution will understand that this was rightly to be feared.

#### 3.

Although in so brief a work, and in such a little composition as this profession of faith, there is scarcely room for comparing its style with the rest of Vigilius’s writings—for brief and exegetical formulas of faith require one manner of expression, while longer polemical works require another—I nevertheless seem to detect a not insignificant affinity of style and method of composition between the symbol and Vigilius’s other works [Note: [Col. 1066D] How slight in the present case this argument, drawn from the affinity of style and sentences, is will become clear from the observations, § 3.].

For in the work written against Marivadus, and especially in Book III, he follows the same method that he used in composing the symbol. Thus the first part of the symbol, which defends the unity of the Trinity against the Arians, appears to be a concise recapitulation of what is set forth in the hundred chapters of those three books against Marivadus. For those books are wholly devoted to explaining and proving the unity of the Trinity and the Trinity of unity, which is the distinctive subject matter of the first part of the symbol.

This appears even more clearly in Book III. Its first three chapters contain, with their proofs, these three propositions:

> God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit.  
> Lord the Father, Lord the Son, Lord the Holy Spirit.  
> Almighty the Father, Almighty the Son, Almighty the Holy Spirit.

These are found in the symbol in precisely the same words. The symbol contains many other propositions of the same form, just as Book III of the work contains very many—indeed, as many as a hundred—proved by testimonies from Scripture. Unless I am mistaken, they breathe the same authorship.

Someone who examines the rest of Vigilius’s writings more attentively and at greater leisure may perhaps discover other points of agreement no less striking. For the present, what we have written on this occasion is sufficient.

After completing the publication of our dissertations, I found a Thuaneus manuscript in which Vigilius Tapsensis’s dialogue against the Arians, Sabellians, and Photinians appears under this title:

> Here begins the dispute of Athanasius with the heresies.

After this treatise come the Nicene symbol and the profession of faith of the Council of Ariminum, immediately followed by the Athanasian symbol with this heading [Col. 1068A]:

> The faith spoken by Saint Athanasius, bishop.

Our conjecture concerning the author of this symbol is also considerably supported by the fact that it is found bound into a little work in a very ancient manuscript [Note: [Col. 1067B] [.....] cited, no. 6.], to which the name of Athanasius is likewise prefixed, but which is unquestionably known to be by Vigilius Tapsensis through the testimony of Vigilius himself.

For in Book V *Against Eutyches*, no. 2, he writes:

> “Concerning the various decrees of the councils and the novel additions of names made with religious care, we have expressed ourselves fully in those books which we composed against Sabellius, Photinus, and Arius under the name of Athanasius, as though present persons were dealing with present persons”—where the person of the judge also appears to have been introduced—“and so forth.”

Nor should I omit to note a passage from the same Book V of Vigilius Tapsensis, no. 6, where the unity of Christ, consisting of God and man, is compared with the unity of a man subsisting from a rational soul and flesh:

> “As we believe that a man is one, consisting of a rational soul and flesh, so let us believe that Christ is one, God and man.”

These words are altogether similar to the following words of the Athanasian symbol:

> “As the rational soul and flesh is one man, so God and man is one Christ.”

# Observations of the Ballerini on Quesnellus’s Fourteenth Dissertation, *On the Little Works Inserted in the Codex*, etc.

[Col. 1067]

[Col. 1067B] Among the monuments of the faith discussed in the preceding dissertation, only two little works on the faith, inserted in our codex of canons as chapters 39 and 40, and the symbol commonly inscribed to St. Athanasius, require more extensive observations.

## § I. The Little Work on the Faith Presented as Chapter 39 in the Collection Published in This Volume Is More Probably to Be Vindicated for St. Gregory of Nazianzus

The opinion that it belongs to a Latin author is opposed, and Gregory of the East is replaced by Gregory of Baetica in the West, following Quesnellus; or, according to the most recent author, by Phoebadius.

### I.

One certain point must be stated first: this little work, which among the works of St. Gregory of Nazianzus is Sermon 50, agrees so closely with Sermon 49 that Quesnellus rightly proved in § 7 that both have one and the same author.

The only difference between them is that Sermon 49 establishes the Nicene faith in a fuller and more dogmatic treatment, whereas Sermon 50, or the little work on the faith, presents the same propositions of the preceding sermon in abbreviated form. Therefore, if St. Gregory of Nazianzus is the author of Sermon 49, Sermon 50, or the aforementioned little work on the faith, must likewise be attributed to him.

Two explicit testimonies support the assertion that St. Gregory of Nazianzus is the author of Sermon 49: one from St. Augustine, the other from the manuscript that was used for the Strasbourg edition of the works of that same holy Doctor.

It was customary for St. Augustine to make use of Gregory of Nazianzus’s authority, and to do so from Rufinus’s translation, which, because of the renown of both author and translator, had spread far and wide. Thus, in Book I *Against Julian*, chapter 5, when he was about to produce testimonies of that same Gregory, he prefaced them as follows:

> “But you will not lack a bishop of great name and most celebrated renown, illustrious even from the regions of the East, whose words, deservedly possessing immense grace, have become known everywhere through being translated into the LATIN LANGUAGE.”

He immediately adds four passages from that Doctor in Rufinus’s translation.

Moreover, in Letter 148, he expressly vindicates Sermon 49 for that same eastern bishop Gregory, writing in section 10:

> “The holy bishop Gregory of the East also says most plainly that God, invisible by nature, could have been seen by the Fathers—such as Moses, with whom he spoke face to face—after assuming the arrangement of some VISIBLE MATERIAL, while his invisibility remained intact.”

No one should reply, following the recent author, that this statement of Gregory is found in Oration 37, which is certainly a genuine work of Gregory. For anyone reading both Orations 37 and 49 will see that not only the thought but also certain words, indicated in capital letters, agree exclusively with Oration 49 [Col. 1068C]. Moreover, since Augustine used not the Greek text but Rufinus’s common translation—as can be seen from other passages in which he cites testimonies of Gregory of Nazianzus—and since Oration 37 was not translated into Latin by Rufinus in the same way as Oration 49, whose translation we shall discuss shortly, there can be no doubt that Augustine cited the latter in Letter 148.

### II.

The second testimony is the manuscript from which the Strasbourg edition of 1508 was produced. This manuscript contained ten orations inscribed with the name of the same St. Gregory and rendered into Latin by Rufinus, together with the translator Rufinus’s own prologue. Among them were the commonly circulated Oration 49 and the commonly circulated Oration 50, or our little work on the faith.

For this reason Justus Fontaninus, in Book II of his *Life of Rufinus*, chapter 8, did not hesitate to attribute all of them both to Rufinus as translator and to Gregory of Nazianzus as author.

Nor does it matter that in other manuscripts containing Gregory’s sermons translated into Latin by Rufinus, Orations 49 and 50 are absent. For in most manuscripts only two, three, or four sermons of that same Gregory translated into Latin by Rufinus are found, as the aforementioned Fontaninus observed. Yet no one therefore doubts that at least eight sermons of Gregory himself were transmitted in translation by Rufinus.

The same Rufinus, in Book XI of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 9, testifies concerning the writings of Saints Gregory of Nazianzus and Basil:

> “We translated approximately ten little orations of each of them into Latin.”

Rufinus’s Latin translations of Basil’s orations are found only in eight—or, as we believe, nine. See our preface to the appendix of the treatises of St. Zeno, bishop of Verona, no. 2, p. 294.

The frequently cited manuscript supplied ten of Gregory of Nazianzus’s orations. On the testimony of Rufinus himself, we therefore recognize that they must be assigned to that saint.

### III.

Those who thought Gregory of Nazianzus should be excluded rely on the hypothesis that Sermons 49 and 50 should be attributed to a Latin author rather than a Greek one. But the arguments by which they defend this hypothesis prove nothing.

The strongest argument they advance is drawn from the Old Latin and ancient translation of Scripture incorporated into Oration 49. This has no force, since a Latin translator, when rendering scriptural testimonies into Latin, could have used the version current in his own age, which agreed with the Greek text of the Septuagint employed by the Greek Fathers.

The expression that usually seems stronger, because it is supposedly foreign to a Greek writer, is the term which the Greeks call *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον), and the phrase “a certain reasoning” which among the Greeks is called *logos* (λόγος). But was not the Nicene symbol itself rendered from Greek into Latin in an ancient translation in which we nevertheless read, in much the same way, in Leo, Letter 165, chapter 2, and in St. Hilary and others:

> “of one substance with the Father, which the Greeks call *homoousion*”?

Since Rufinus was the translator of that oration, he could, with the freedom he used in interpreting Greek works, have employed similar formulas. The same applies to the style which Rufinus, a freer translator, was accustomed to use in his other translations. A similar style shines through in the other eight orations, which no one doubts that he translated from Gregory [Col. 1069B].

### IV.

Since, then, nothing compels us to assert a Latin author, whereas the two testimonies—the testimony of Augustine and that of the manuscript printed in the Strasbourg edition—are sufficiently clear in favor of St. Gregory of Nazianzus, none of the opinions of others that introduce a Latin author can be preferred.

Certainly, Quesnellus’s proposal that Gregory of Baetica be substituted for Gregory of Nazianzus, as though Augustine had confused an eastern Gregory with a western one, is less probable. Apart from the fact that Augustine was accustomed to cite Gregory of Nazianzus and never Gregory of Baetica, it seems presumptuous to accuse him of error and confusion unless something certain and compelling is produced in favor of Gregory of Baetica.

Quesnellus, however, produced nothing compelling, but only conjectures—either wholly empty or at least of such a kind that they can equally well be applied to other authors, as we have indicated in the annotations [Col. 1069C].

Nor can the most recent opinion be more satisfactory: in the work entitled *Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. I, part 2, Paris edition of 1733, p. 273, Phoebadius is proposed as the author of those sermons. For this opinion rests on the same hypothesis of a Latin author, which we have shown to be empty; and it also piles up conjectures of equal strength, which fall when the hypothesis falls and can likewise be applied to other Latin writers.

### V.

We believe that this author was entirely correct in one matter: he rejects Quesnellus’s opinion that the little work on the faith, or Sermon 50, preceded Sermon 49, as though that little work were indicated in Sermon 49 by the words:

> “I had previously published a little work against the Arians.”

He attacks this opinion for two reasons.

First, from the context of Oration 49, in which the words “I had previously published a little work against the Africans” indicate not a brief formula of faith but a polemical treatise in which the Arian error was expressly attacked. This fits very well with other, longer treatises of Gregory of Nazianzus directed against the Arians, but not with the aforementioned little work on the faith. For although that work contains doctrine opposed to the Arian heresy, it cannot be called a work published against the Arians in order to attack them.

Second, because in the little work against the Arians the author of Sermon 49 explicitly says that Sabellius’s error is refuted by name. Nothing of this kind, however, is expressly stated in the shorter little work, or Sermon 50.

The same Gallican writer also adds a significant observation from the very objection by which the earlier little work was attacked by the Arians. For this is what, he says, could be criticized—these are the words of Sermon 49:

> “What can be criticized is that, when we placed the Word of God in the person of the Son, we might seem to understand this Word in the sense in which grammarians teach it,” and so forth.

And later:

> “I confess that I am amazed that this could have been understood in such a way that we were thought to deny the proper person of the Word, who is the Son, whom in so many passages we have presented as the true Son begotten from the true Father.”

If the author of the first little work had explained himself on the distinction of persons in the same way as he explains himself, though in few words, in the little work on the faith, or Sermon 50, where he speaks precisely and accurately, the objections said to have been brought against the earlier little work could never have been made against him.

Moreover, what of the words “in so many passages”? They confirm a longer treatise and in no way suit the shorter little work.

Therefore Sermon 50 cannot be regarded as that first little work published against the Arians. Rather, another earlier and more extensive treatise of Nazianzus against the Arians and Sabellians is indicated, and the same author composed its *Apology* in Sermon 49. Our little work on the faith was later than Sermon 49, so that it appears to be an abridgment of it, although at the end it adds an article on the resurrection of bodies, which Sermon 49 lacks.

## § II. On the Other Little Work on the Faith Presented in Our Collection as Chapter 40

It is removed from Augustine, to whom Quesnellus attributes it, and is assigned to the First Council of Toledo.

### I.

Quesnellus discussed this little work in § 8, where he considers that it should be assigned to St. Augustine in the form in which it appears in the *Codex of Canons*, chapter 40.

Since nearly the same thing is repeated in the rule of faith appended to the First Council of Toledo, which was composed by another Spanish synod under St. Leo, he supposes that the Fathers of that synod derived the same rule from Augustine’s little work.

To state our opinion as briefly as possible, we must first point out that this document, formerly published among Augustine’s works—with the exception of minor variants—is altogether the same as the one inserted in our collection. In a later edition of Augustine, however, it received an addition, written by another hand, of fourteen anathemas excerpted from Damasus’s letter to Paulinus.

The document entitled *Rule of Faith*, appended to the First Council of Toledo, is substantially the same as the document in our collection. Nevertheless, it presents not only an addition at the end of six anathemas peculiar to it, but also certain additions and several clearer explanations, both in the body itself and in the anathemas—especially the fifth, sixth, seventh, and twelfth—as will become clear to anyone who compares our notes on chapter 40 of the codex [Col. 1070C].

There seems, moreover, to be no reason for doubt that this document, as it exists in the manuscripts of our codex, is the earlier product of an older author. The Fathers of the Spanish council under St. Leo adopted it in composing their rule of faith and made it their own by heightening it in several additions and by using clearer wording in certain places.

For it is not likely that a later author, who had a more explicit document before him, would omit what contributes to clarity. Rather, the opposite generally happens: what was previously written more briefly and less clearly is made fuller and clearer by a later author.

We therefore agree with Quesnellus that the example in our collection is the primitive form and is older than the age of Leo.

[Col. 1070D] 951

### II.

We cannot agree, however, with his opinion that it should be attributed to St. Augustine. At the end of paragraph 8 he said that he expected the judgment of the Benedictine Fathers concerning the edition of St. Augustine’s works then being prepared.

They, however, without being influenced by Quesnellus’s observations, did not hesitate to exclude the document, which had previously been left among Augustine’s sermons, and to place it in the appendix to volume V, Sermon 233. For they say:

> “In the manuscripts we have nowhere seen this little work among Augustine’s sermons and little works.”

They also add an argument from style. These expressions in no. 1, they say, sound decidedly unlike Augustine:

> “this one Trinity of the divine name”;  
> “not composed of an imaginary body or of form alone”;  
> “and all the exercises of the body,” or, as the Roman Codex reads—which they understand as the Quesnellian manuscript—“to have experienced calamities.”

Then there is the word *Paraclete*, repeatedly used in place of “the Holy Spirit.”

Thus the stylistic argument advanced by Quesnellus most strongly excludes Augustine. For this reason Verlinus and Vindingus rightly affixed the mark of spuriousness to this sermon, which had been included among the Augustinian works.

Add also the judgment of P. Coustantius in his admonition to Damasus’s fifth letter to Paulinus, p. 505, no. 8, where he declares that there is nothing Augustinian in this sermon.

In the ancient Vindobonensis manuscript of our collection, Augustine’s name is added at the end of the title in such a way that it may be considered an addition. We believe that this document passed from some Gallican example of the same collection—as we have seen elsewhere—into the Gallican collection of Isidore’s additions, and that from one or the other of these sources it was eventually received and published among Augustine’s sermons because his name had been inscribed in the title.

The opinion, therefore, that Augustine was the author of this little work arises solely from the manuscripts of our collection, in which his name may be conjectured from our Vindobonensis manuscript to be an addition.

### III.

Since this document, repeated and enlarged by the Fathers of the Spanish synod under St. Leo, is appended under the title *Rule of Faith* to the First Council of Toledo in the manuscripts of the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, it may seem highly probable that the primitive document should itself be attributed to the First Council of Toledo.

That council, having condemned the Priscillianist heresy, published this little work on the faith against it and against other heresies, together with twelve anathemas. This little work could have been contained in the fuller acts of that council, which are mentioned in the council’s own preface.

The Fathers of the later Spanish synod under Leo, repeating this document in order to adapt it to the present needs of their Churches, judged that some points should be explained more clearly and others added.

The addition *Filioque* appears to belong here. They inserted it into the rule of faith in imitation of Leo, who wrote concerning the Holy Spirit in Letter 15 to Turribius, chapter 1, that he “proceeded from both.”

The author of the Hispanic collection, having found the primitive document, as it is read in our collection, among the acts of the First Council of Toledo, and having found it more fully and clearly expressed in the later council under Leo, thought that the latter should be substituted for it and appended to the First Council of Toledo.

He prefaced this with an admonition in which he explicitly assigned the document to the other council under Leo, in these words:
