> Here begins the rule of the Catholic faith against all heresies, and especially against the Priscillianists, which the bishops of Tarragona, Carthage, Lusitania, and Baetica composed and sent, at the command of Pope Leo of Rome, to Balconius, bishop of Galicia.

The only difficulty may be presented by what follows:

> They also established the twenty chapters of canons written above in the Council of Toledo.

These words cannot refer to the Fathers of the council under Leo, since the canons were composed at the First Council of Toledo, as we proved at greater length in the cited note 5.

We indicated two conjectures concerning these final words in that place. We shall now propose another, which may perhaps seem more probable. Namely, these words may have been found by the author of the Hispanic collection in the title of the little work on the faith of the First Council of Toledo, where they were appropriate. At this point, however, because the rule of faith from the other council under Leo had been substituted, they were carelessly retained even though they no longer fit.

[Col. 1071D] 953

## § III. On the Author of the *Quicunque* Symbol, Which Is Inscribed with the Name of St. Athanasius

### I.

The earliest testimony by which the *Quicunque* symbol is attributed to St. Athanasius would be two letters published among the works of St. Isidore of Seville—one to Claudius, the duke, and the other to Eugenius, bishop of Toledo—if they truly had that same St. Isidore as their author.

But since these writings arose when the controversies of the Greeks against the Latins had already emerged, in the ninth and eleventh centuries, and are wrongly inscribed to St. Isidore of Seville, the first testimony can be sought in a canon of the Synod of Autun under St. Leodegarius, bishop. This synod was held not in the year 670, as Quesnellus wrote along with the printed editions, but in 676 or 677, as Bouhierius established in a letter to Mabillon.

Since the canon that calls the cited symbol “the faith of St. Athanasius” was extracted by Sirmondus from a manuscript collection of Dijon, which contains not entire synods but canons excerpted here and there and distributed under headings, some consider it uncertain whether the canon belongs to the Council of Autun held under St. Leodegarius or to another council held later in the same place. For this reason they argue that nothing certain can be inferred from it for establishing the antiquity of the symbol inscribed to Athanasius.

We, however, found the same canon in the Herouvallian collection edited by Jacobus Petit, chapter 1. Although there the canon of Autun is cited without the name of Leodegarius, it is nevertheless evident that the author of the collection had no other Synod of Autun in view than the one held under St. Leodegarius, bishop. This is clear from the table of canons prefixed to the same collection and presented by Petit on p. 264. Concerning the Autun canons cited in that collection, it records only the following:

> Canons of Autun, of St. Leodegarius, bishop.

The same is confirmed by chapter 70 of the collection itself. When it lists the bishops who confirmed its canons, it refers to the Autun canons in no. 19 as follows:

> The consent and confirmation of Leodegarius, bishop of Autun.

It cannot therefore be denied that the older manuscript used by the author of the Herouvallian collection had included the cited canon among those enacted at the Synod of Autun under St. Leodegarius. Consequently, there can be no doubt that after the middle of the seventh century the *Quicunque* symbol was attributed to St. Athanasius.

Nor can the opinion of Papebrochius be considered probable, in his *Response to the Errors Presented*, part II, article 13, no. 36, where he states that the words “the faith of St. Athanasius” in this canon designate not the Athanasian symbol but the Nicene symbol [Col. 1072C], in the composition of which Athanasius may very plausibly have labored greatly.

For the Nicene symbol was customarily called in the Church by the proper name “Nicene”; it was never called “of Athanasius.” Since, moreover, we find the *Quicunque* symbol inscribed under Athanasius’s name both in manuscripts and by other authors of the eighth and ninth centuries, there seems no reason to doubt that somewhat earlier, at the Synod of Autun under St. Leodegarius, the same symbol was called “the faith of St. Athanasius.”

The same point can be confirmed from the manuscript collection Vatican, Palatine 574, whose additions, dating from approximately the same period, present the same symbol under this title:

> Here begins the Catholic faith of St. Athanasius.

## II.

The greater antiquity of this same creed, though without the name of Athanasius, is demonstrated by other, more ancient documents. Some adduce the Fourth Council of Toledo, held in the year 633, in which they believe that several formulas were excerpted from the same creed. But similar formulas and expressions were so common among Catholics in the Church’s defined and publicly professed doctrines that the Fathers of Toledo may be said to have used common formulas, rather than to have derived them from our creed. Similar phrases can indeed be found in other writers, whom no one would say took them from the Athanasian Creed. If those same Fathers of Toledo had had the Athanasian Creed before their eyes when composing their profession of faith, they would have derived other [955] expressions and statements from it as well; yet these are not found in that profession.

The antiquity of this same creed, anterior to the Fourth Council of Toledo, is more aptly established by a manuscript collection contained in the very ancient codices Barb. 2888 and Vat. 1342. For in it there is presented a canonical letter which we published, under no. 4, among the documents of the ancient canon law as a celebrated work from the beginning of the sixth century; and in it the first canon is expressed as follows:

> First of all, let all priests, deacons, and subdeacons commit the CATHOLIC FAITH to memory; and if anything [Read: “if anyone”] neglects to do this, let them abstain [Read: “let him abstain”] from wine for forty days [Read: “days”].

The name “Catholic faith” is shown to indicate the creed *Quicunque* by the most ancient codices of that same creed, which, as we shall soon see, entitle the creed “the Catholic faith.” For those words of the creed are being referred to:

> So that he may hold the CATHOLIC FAITH.  
> Now this is the CATHOLIC FAITH.

And at the end:

> This is the CATHOLIC FAITH, etc.

Add also Venantius Fortunatus, whose exposition of the creed *Quicunque*, published by Muratori in volume II of the *Anecdota Latina*, p. 212, is entitled:

> Fortunatus’s Exposition of the Catholic Faith.

We think this title should be understood in such a way that Fortunatus is the author not of the Catholic faith, or of the creed *Quicunque*, but of an exposition of that same creed, just as he published other expositions of the Apostles’ Creed and of the Lord’s Prayer.

These, then, are two testimonies from the sixth century. If at that time not only Fortunatus explained this Catholic Faith, but a canon also prescribed that all priests, deacons, and subdeacons should learn it by heart, it is necessary to acknowledge that it had already been written long before and had been received through the practice of many people.

## III.

Moreover, the more ancient copies of this same creed either lack a title or bear only the title “Catholic Faith,” without the author’s name. Of the first kind is the Ambrosian manuscript, formerly Bobbian, written more than a thousand years ago, in which our creed is read without any title, as Muratori testifies in the place cited, p. 224. There is also Codex Colbertinus 784, written approximately in the age of Pepin, in which part of the same creed is found; for its scribe testifies that he found it mutilated in Trier, in a still older codex, with no author’s name or title attached.

Three other codices are reported by the Benedictine editors of the works of St. Athanasius, § 2 of the *Dissertation on the Creed Quicunque*, p. 721: one, Regius 4908; another, Colbertinus 3133; and a third, cited by Felckmann. In these the creed lacks both title and author’s name.

Among the copies of the second kind, besides those sixth-century copies that were used by Fortunatus and by the author of the canonical letter, of which we spoke in the preceding section, the oldest of all that have so far been discovered is the one cited by Usserius. There, without an author’s name, the following title is prefixed:

> Catholic Faith.

The same title is also found in two manuscripts, Vat. 81 and Vat. Reginae 12. It is likewise clear from his second capitulary, shortly after its beginning, that the codex used by Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, had carried the same title.

The name of Athanasius, therefore, was not attached by the author at the beginning, but was introduced at a later time. Hence only later copies and writers of the seventh, eighth, and ninth centuries bear it.

## IV.

What we have brought forward from the codices and the more ancient witnesses ought to suffice to show that this creed was attributed to St. Athanasius only at a later period. Several further arguments prove that it cannot be attributed to him: both those assembled by Quesnellus in the preceding dissertation, § 12, and those later added by the Benedictine editors of the works of St. Athanasius in their special *Dissertation on the Same Creed*, § 3.

Ludovicus Muratorius, in volume II of the *Anecdota Latina*, in his investigation of the same subject, and most recently Father Dominicus Maria Speronius, Dissertation 1, *On the Creed Commonly Called That of St. Athanasius*, Padua, 1750, have shown, among other things, that the author of this creed was evidently not Greek but Latin.

The whole question now concerns which Latin writer should be regarded as the author of this creed. Quesnellus thinks it was Vigilius of Tapsus. His opinion, however, was first attacked by Josephus Antelmius in a new investigation of the Athanasian Creed published at Paris in 1693; and the authors mentioned shortly before have added their judgment to Antelmius’s on this matter.

## V.

Certainly, what Quesnellus says—that this same Vigilius published several works of the same kind under the name of Athanasius or of other writers—he has not adequately proved. The only work that is certainly Vigilius’s is the *Debate of Saint Athanasius, Bishop, against the Heretics Arius, Sabellius, and Photinus*, written in dialogue form, since Vigilius himself cites it in Book V *Against Eutyches*, chapter 2. But for that reason it should not be said to have been published under Athanasius’s name, since in the preface Vigilius warns that he is introducing Athanasius as the speaker, just as other writers commonly introduce other persons, whom no one therefore regards as the authors of the dialogues.

Chiffletius indeed attributed the book *Against Marivadus*, or Varimadus, published under the name of Idacius Clarus, to Vigilius, because Vigilius himself professes in the cited *Debate*, Book II, no. 45, that he had published a book against that same man. But since in the same *Debate* Vigilius quotes a lengthy passage from his work against Marivadus which is not found in the three books of Idacius against Varimadus, it can safely be concluded that Vigilius’s book against Marivadus was different from Idacius’s books against Varimadus and has not come down to us. Therefore the latter books against Varimadus cannot be attributed to Vigilius, as though he had prefixed to them the fictitious name of Idacius.

See more in Antelmius, in the place cited, and in the admonition prefixed to the books *On the Holy Trinity* in the latest edition of the works of St. Athanasius, volume III, p. 602.

The same replies can be made concerning the other short works which some attribute to Vigilius, although they are inscribed under the names of other Fathers or of Athanasius. Chiffletius attributes the twelve books *On the Trinity* among the works of Athanasius to Vigilius chiefly because they are praised in the preface to Idacius Clarus’s books against Varimadus, which he assumed had been published by Vigilius under the fictitious name of Idacius. We have already refuted that hypothesis.

Just as the books against Varimadus belong not to Vigilius but to Idacius, so too the books *On the Trinity*, which Idacius affirms in the cited preface that he composed, must be regarded as belonging to Idacius, not to Vigilius.

Nor can Chiffletius’s effort accomplish anything. In order to assert that the same books *On the Trinity* belonged to Vigilius, he tried to find in those books the lengthy testimony quoted by Vigilius in the aforementioned *Debate* and excerpted from his own book against Marivadus. He could not accomplish this, however, except by collecting here and there certain statements and Pauline passages.

Furthermore, these books are nowhere entitled *Against Marivadus*, whereas Vigilius states that he extracted that testimony from a book against Marivadus. You see, therefore, how weak this argument is, being derived from an assumed but unproved practice of Vigilius.

Since the books *On the Trinity* belong not to Vigilius but to Idacius, the formulas of faith inserted into them and inscribed under the name of Athanasius, if they prove anything, prove it not for Vigilius but for Idacius.

Add that in some codices these same books end with Book Eight; yet those formulas of faith belong to the later books, which seem to have to be attributed to another author. Compare the admonition of the Benedictine Fathers on these same books, volume III, p. 601.

In other manuscripts, however, they differ so greatly in order, number, and titles that nothing certain can be established about their original composition. See Joseph Blanchinius, *Exposition of the Pseudo-Athanasian Work on the Apostles’ Creed*, p. 69.

## VI.

It is objected that in some codices the creed *Quicunque* is found attached to, or rather following, the *Debate against Arius, Sabellius, and Photinus*, which certainly has Vigilius as its author. What follows from this? Is it rightly inferred that the two works have the same author? Certainly not.

For scribes often used to write several short works by different authors in the same codex. Similarity of style and expression to Vigilius’s works, even if it were proved, is a very weak argument in these documents of faith. Who is unaware that it is the custom of Catholics, when writing professions of faith and setting forth the doctrines of faith, to employ formulas and expressions received in the Church and to avoid innovations?

Thus one may find similar formulas in different writers who transmitted the same doctrines, without it being possible to infer from this similarity of expression that the various short works have the same author. For this reason Father Le Quien, in Dissertation 1 of the *Damascenica*, no. 16, p. 9, rightly shows the parallel between the statements of the creed *Quicunque* and other similar statements of Vigilius to be ineffective, since St. Augustine also presents similar formulas and statements.

## VII.

These arguments, which reject Quesnellus’s opinion, are equally valid against Antelmius, who contends that the same creed should be attributed to Vincent of Lérins. If anyone wishes for a fuller refutation of his arguments individually, let him consult the Benedictine Fathers and Muratori in the places cited, as well as Father Dominicus Maria Speronius, Dissertation 2 *On the Creed*, chapters 4 and 5. There he shows that everything brought forward by Antelmius can be applied no more to Vincent than to other writers of approximately the same period.

We cannot pass over one conjecture of Antelmius. He thinks that the first fragments of the creed, discovered at Trier, were therefore composed by a Trier writer, whom he believes to have been Vincent.

He draws this conclusion from Codex Colbertinus 784, in which, after the Definition of Chalcedon and before the Nicene Creed, there is found a passage from the published Athanasian Creed containing the Catholic doctrine of Christ’s incarnation, preceded by this note:

> I found this written at Trier in one book, beginning as follows: “Our Lord Jesus Christ,” and the rest. “Let him faithfully believe in our Lord Jesus Christ. This, then, is the right faith,” etc., to the end.

These words do show that the creed *Quicunque*, without an author’s name, was found by the copyist of the Colbertine codex in an older codex at Trier; and this greatly confirms the antiquity of the creed. But they by no means prove that its author was likewise from Trier.

## VIII.

Since no codex and no ancient writer has attributed this creed to Vigilius of Tapsus or to Vincent of Lérins, while the more ancient codices lack the author’s name, it will be better to acknowledge an unknown author than, on the basis of such conjectures—which can be accommodated to various writers—to assign this or that author to the creed.

On this matter we shall conclude with Tillemont, note 34 on St. Athanasius, volume VIII, p. 671:

> It is therefore better for us to remain in the darkness of our ignorance; and I do not know whether we should not add that it would be better not to waste time forming so many conjectures about matters of this kind. It may be useful to know the true author of a work; but when one can know nothing certain about it, what is the use of knowing that it may perhaps have been written by one person or another? This is more likely to produce disputes than to establish or clarify any truth. Let us therefore be content to be assured that this creed is not by St. Athanasius, but that it is ancient and dates from no later than the sixth century.

# FIFTEENTH DISSERTATION

## On the Spurious Council of Teles and the Pseudo-Letter of Pope Siricius Called the *Tractatoria* to the African Bishops

On Chapter 60 of the Roman Code.

[Col. 1075]

## CHAPTER ONE

### On the Name of the Pseudo-Synod

[Col. 1075B]

[Note: [Col. 1075D] If the sixty and final chapter of the Code is found in the Oxford manuscript—which we have found to be both more recent and incomplete—then certainly in all the other, older, and better manuscripts it is neither the final nor the sixtieth chapter, as is clear from what has been said elsewhere.]

The final, or sixtieth, chapter of our Code contains the canons of the Council of Teles, according to the *Tractatoria* of Pope Siricius throughout Africa. This council is said to have been held after the consulship of the most glorious emperors Honorius, for the eleventh time, and Constantius, for the sixth time, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March—that is, in the year of Christ 418.

Everyone has regarded this as a legitimate and genuine synod down to the present day, and I know of no one who has so far raised a controversy about its authenticity (*αὐθεντία*). Nor did David Blondellus, who in his *Pseudo-Isidore* expressed his doubts about Siricius’s letter and left the matter to the reader’s judgment, think that anything should be objected against that synod. Christophorus Justellus likewise records it in the preface to the *African Code*, and all the editors of the Councils present it.

Cardinal Baronius not only recognizes it (*Annals*, year 418, no. 31), but also exalts and praises it in an extraordinary manner, as a distinguished monument of the respect with which the African Church honored the Roman See and obeyed its decrees—decrees which, naturally, were ordered to be recited above all in councils.

[962] There is no doubt that the African Church always paid due honor to the Apostolic See and to its statutes. But anyone who wishes to persuade people of this on the basis of the monuments discussed in this dissertation is certainly defending a good cause badly.

For I am entirely certain that both the synod and the letter are pure fable and mere invention.

[Note: [Col. 1075D] He undertook such a difficult—not to say desperate—task in this dissertation that he found no support among any of the most distinguished writers. See the observations to follow, chapter 1, no. 1.]

I hope that no one will hereafter refuse to agree with my opinion once he has examined this foolish fabrication more closely and deeply in the light of sound judgment.

First, then, we must investigate the name of the council. On this matter there are various conjectures among scholars, and there was also some dispute between two theologians of great renown, Petrus Aurelius and Jacobus Sirmondus.

[Note: [Col. 1076D] Baluzius noted that there had been no dispute on this point between Aurelius and Sirmondus, in the dissertation on the Council of Telepte appended to the books of Peter de Marca’s *On Concord*, Paris edition, 1704, p. 1343.]

The most eminent Cardinal Perronius, in his *Reply to the Most Serene King of Britain*, chapter 18, thinks that *Zellense* should be restored in place of *Telense*. He believes that the fact that it is read differently in the heading and in the preface of the synod should be attributed to the carelessness of scribes.

Cardinal Ferrandus’s *Brief Summary of the Canons* appears to support Perronius. In it the Council of Zella is mentioned ten times, while six times the words “From the letter of Pope Siricius” are added. Thus there can be no doubt either that it is the very synod now called Teles, or that it was fabricated in imitation of that synod.

Chiffletius also supports Perronius in his notes on Ferrandus the deacon’s *Brief Summary of the Canons*—or rather, he reconciles him with the ancient editors of the Councils—when he asserts that the same city was called Zella and Tiella, or Thele, and Usilla or Usula; and consequently that the same council was Zellense, Tiellense, or Telense.

Indeed, Chiffletius himself testifies that this synod, which is called Telense in most other codices, is called Zellense in the Troyes codex.

[Col. 1076D]

Cardinal Baronius, in the year 418, no. 31, and Binius, following him, take a third path in their notes on this synod. There they confidently declare that one should write not *Telense*, as it has hitherto been read, but *Teleptense*. They were moved by the single argument that Donatianus, bishop of Telepte and of the first see, is said to have presided over the synod in its preface.

This conjecture pleased Sirmondus so much that in his *Antirrheticus* against Petrus Aurelius he boldly asserted that no emendation had ever been more certain.

Chiffletius, however, laughs at this emendation by his associate in the place cited, and is astonished that learned men should have drawn the following conclusion: that because Donatianus of Telepte presided over it, they should therefore think the synod was held at Telepte—as though a synod could not have been convened and celebrated in another city of the same province under the presidency of the bishop of the first see.

I agree with Chiffletius insofar as he thinks that the word *Telense* should be retained and that *Teleptense* was wrongly substituted for it in the Bini edition and other later editions of the Councils.

[Note: [Col. 1077D] This will be shown to be false from the observations, chapter 1, no. 4. There we shall prove, however, that this council was truly neither Teleptense nor Telense, but Zellense, no. 7.]

For all earlier editions, and all manuscript codices, both recent and most ancient, call the synod *Telense*, not *Teleptense*.

This is confirmed by the fact that it would be difficult for all scribes, as though by agreement, to have fallen into the same error, especially since the word occurs twice—in the title and in the prefatory narrative of the council—and in the latter it is immediately followed by the word *Teleptensis*, which by itself could have recalled the scribes from their error.

Certainly, their consistent distinction between the two words is an indication of wholly accurate writing. Otherwise careless or ignorant scribes would easily have written either *Telense* in both places or *Teleptense* in both places, deceived by the similarity and affinity of the words.

Finally, this mistake cannot be attributed either to the learned or to the unlearned. When unlearned and illiterate scribes depart from the genuine word in writing, it is remarkable if they do not substitute some barbarous word devoid of meaning. It is far more astonishing if they all happened to fall upon this word, by which they would have substituted a genuinely African and episcopal city for another city likewise African and episcopal.

Learned men, however, who would have known the difference between the city of Teles and the city of Telepte—that the former was in the proconsular province and the latter in Byzacena, and that the primate of one province could neither hold a synod in the other nor preside over it—would never have called a synod *Telense* when it had a bishop of Telepte as its president.

It remains, therefore, that this was perpetrated by half-learned impostors. When they set out to devise a fraud, they were not sufficiently learned to fashion it skillfully; and this almost always happens.

As for Chiffletius’s assertion that *Telense* is the same as *Usulense*, *Tiellense*, or *Zellense*, because the Africans are said often to have used *Za* for *Dia*, I confess that this seems to me too forced and unrelated to the matter at hand.

Let us grant that this substitution was used, as scholars contend, with respect to certain words. It was not used with respect to all words, nor with respect to this one, which is the subject of the dispute.

For if it had been so, there would be no reason why, in the list of the proconsular province, we should read most distinctly “Deumhabet, of Teles,” while in Byzacena we find “Victorinus, of Usula,” when in both places we should have to read either *Usulensis* or *Telensis*.

If you say that this was done in order to distinguish one from the other, then these names should not be confused, as Chiffletius does; rather, each should be assigned to its own city. Although they are sufficiently distinguished by their provinces, it was not necessary for the list to call one Telense and the other Usulense.

Moreover, if Chiffletius’s conjecture were to be admitted, and *Za* were used for *Dia*, or the latter for the former, that synod should be called *Diellense*, or, after another change, *Tiellense*. Yet it is most consistently called *Telense* in all the codices.

[Note: [Col. 1077D] It is true that in the Corbie manuscript, where this council is described, *Telense* is read. But it is also true that, as Chiffletius reports, in the same codex, where Ferrandus’s *Brief Summary* is presented, the same council is called *Tiellense*.]

Even in the very ancient Corbie manuscript, the same one, I believe, that Chiffletius cites—although he says that *Tiellensis* was read earlier in it—I remember reading in that same Corbie manuscript, preserved in the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, *Telense*, not *Tiellense*.

Chiffletius mentions the Troyes codex, which calls the same council *Zellense* that others call *Telense*. But it is the only one.

[Note: [Col. 1077D] Father Chiffletius is speaking of the codices containing Ferrandus’s *Brief Summary*. Quesnellus, however, wrongly asserts that there is only one against countless others. Besides the Troyes manuscript, there are not countless copies of the *Brief Summary*, but one Corbie manuscript. Moreover, a scribal error from the letter T to Z is no less easy than one from Z to T, so that *Telense* could easily have been written for *Zellense*, unless this happened because of African usage. See the observations, chapter 1, no. 6. And although the lists do not mention Zella in Africa, Strabo does mention it; and Donatianus, bishop of the people of Zella, is praised in the Carthaginian conference of 411. We add nothing about the word *Usulense*, which no codices support.]

Add that in ancient manuscript codices a lapse from the letter T to the letter C or Z is easy if the scribes were dozing.

Finally, I do not believe anyone sensible would read *Telense* for a city in one place of the African list and *Usulense* in another without immediately returning to the former if he happened to encounter a reference to the city of Teles in some document.

But enough, and more than enough, about the name. We must now discuss the matter itself.

# CHAPTER II

## Ferrandus the Deacon’s *Brief Summary of the Canons*, Examined and Charged with Interpolation; It Presents the Canons of the Council of Teles, or Zella, from the Letter of Pope Siricius

It is first clear from Ferrandus the deacon’s *Brief Summary of the Canons* that one or more councils were held in Africa which were called Cellense, Zellense, or Telense.

From this work of Ferrandus the deacon, one could confidently pronounce on the authenticity of the Council of Teles, or Zella, and of the letter attached to it, if the integrity of the *Brief Summary* itself were established, since four decrees are there copied word for word from that letter.

But that composition of Ferrandus seems to me, with good reason, to have been adulterated and interpolated in some part—not only to me, but also to men whose judgment in ecclesiastical antiquity is regarded as exceptionally acute.

[Note: [Col. 1078D] We shall prove this thesis false in the observations, chapter 2.]

Franciscus Florens, a most learned man, freely admits on p. 163 of his dissertation *On the Origin, Art, and Authority of Canon Law* that Ferrandus’s *Brief Summary* is riddled with defects, and that no one who examines Ferrandus more attentively will deny this. He refers to nos. 103, 105, 109, 110, 111, 112, 113, 114, 115, 185, 188, 216, and 221, which the learned man reserved for more detailed examination in a new edition of Ferrandus that he was preparing.

It is not our purpose to dwell on these matters. Let us nevertheless make the attempt in one or two chapters, so that “from the claw you may recognize the lion.”

In no. 103, for example, we read:

> That priests of another region should not celebrate in the presence of priests.

This is very far from the sense of the canon. For what is read in Greek, *ἐπιχώριοι πρεσβύτεροι*, is interpreted in some versions as “regional priests,” in others as “vicars,” or “country priests”; none interpret it as “priests of another region.”

Nor is there a word about the bishops in whose presence they are forbidden to offer sacrifice. Finally, the name of the city is omitted in the second part of the canon, although it is necessary there in order to understand that the subject is the priests of the city, not any other priests.

No. 105 prohibits the following:

> That deacons should not be elected by popular vote.

This is taken from Canon XIII of Laodicea, although the canon was enacted concerning priests.

There are also several passages in that collection that closely resemble the annotation of some scholar. Such is the statement in no. 194:

> This too was established at the Council of Thenis.

This is contrary to the manner of citation familiar to Ferrandus.

Chiffletius also observes many passages of this *Brief Summary* that require medical treatment.

## 2.

[Note: [Col. 1079D] See the same observations, chapter 2, no. 3.]

It is not sufficiently clear whether the council cited by Ferrandus, whether Zellense or Telense, belongs in that *Brief Summary* to the same place. And, if it does belong to the same place, whether it is one council or several.

Franciscus Florens, Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius, Guillelmus Voellus, Henricus Justellus, and the most learned cardinal—whom I should have named first—Jacobus Perronius regard it as one and the same council.

I think this conviction arose because the decrees attributed simply to the Council of Zella or Cella appear to have been taken from Siricius’s letter, recited at that Council of Teles or Zella when Ferrandus cites it. The similarity of the names may also have drawn the writers mentioned into this opinion.

Altaserranus, in his notes on Ferrandus’s index, thinks that there were several distinct councils, and I am not unwilling to agree with him.

First, because the names are distinct.

Second, because whenever Zella is mentioned, the words “from the letter of Pope Siricius” are immediately added, whereas this does not happen when Cella is mentioned.

Furthermore, there is no reason why a Council of Cella distinct from that of Zella should not be admitted, since two cities called Cella occur in the African list—*The List of the African Provinces and Bishops*, in Sirmondus and Chiffletius on Ferrandus, and in volume IV of Labbe’s edition of the Councils.

One was in the proconsular province, whose bishop, Cyprianus of Cella, is listed in forty-fifth place. The other was in Mauretania Sitifensis, whose bishop, Cresciturus of Cella, is named in seventeenth place. It is therefore highly probable that the council mentioned in the *Brief Summary* as Cellense or Zellense was held in one of these two cities.

Finally, among the decrees which Ferrandus attributes to Cella, or simply to Zella without an additional designation, scarcely one can be attributed to Zella or Teles, which is identified from Siricius’s letter.

The council is cited ten times in one form or the other, five times in the former way and five times in the latter. Of the former citations, three do not agree at all with Siricius’s letter—those in nos. 65, 68, and 218. The other two, nos. 3 and 16, can be reduced to it in meaning, but by no means in their actual wording.

In this way the sole foundation of the opposing opinion is overturned.

But, you may object, since the acts of that Council of Zella which received Siricius’s letter have not survived in full, it cannot be decided that the decrees attributed to Cella do not belong to it.

That is entirely true. Nor do we decide anything; we are merely dealing in conjectures, as one must in an obscure matter—but conjectures to which it is not easy to oppose others of equal force.

We confirm them once more with a single argument. If the Council of Zella or Cella is the same as the one to which Siricius’s letter is appended, why was a new canon, distinct from the first, enacted and reported in no. 3?

> That a man who, after baptism, has enlisted in secular military service should be barred from ordination.

The council that received and confirmed Siricius’s letter already contains the same decree in these other words:

> If anyone, after the remission of sins, has taken up the military belt of secular service, he must not be admitted to the clergy.

Or, if this same decree of Siricius was reported by Ferrandus from the Council of Zella, why did he not append the words, as he does elsewhere, “From the letter of Siricius”?

Why did he not use Siricius’s own words, as he customarily does when quoting from Siricius’s letter—except in title 4, where five other synods are cited before Cella?

Why did he not do the same in no. 16, concerning the continence of the three higher orders of clergy? Another canon on that subject would have been superfluous, since the letter treats it at great length; or at least mention should have been made of it.

We think these matters must be distinguished so scrupulously in order to distinguish the true Council of Zella from the fictitious Council of Teles or Zella, and genuine citations of Ferrandus from those inserted by another hand.

We regard as genuine the synod which Ferrandus names simply and without addition as Cellense or Zellense; accordingly, we consider the citations in nos. 3, 16, 65, 68, and 218 to be genuine.

The latter three of these decrees are entirely absent from Siricius’s letter. The other two are found there implicitly and in meaning, but their wording is completely different, and it is easy to believe that they are words belonging to another synod.

We declare fictitious the synod called Telense, and fictitious and inserted by another hand the five remaining citations or sanctions which, in Ferrandus’s *Brief Summary*, are attributed to the Council of Zella from the letter of Pope Siricius.

We shall set forth our reasons for the synod itself below, as well as for the attached letter of Siricius. For now, we proceed to demonstrate by conjecture that the five citations or decrees were inserted into Ferrandus.

The first occurs in title 4:

> That a bishop should be ordained by three bishops, with the agreement of the others expressed in writing, together with the confirmation of the metropolitan or primate.

This decree is cited from titles 4 and 6 of the Council of Nicaea, title 19 of Antioch, title 12 of Laodicea, title 10 of the Carthaginian Council under Genethlius, and title 49 of the universal Council of Carthage.

The fact that the words “by the Council of Zella, from the letter of Pope Siricius” are added, to put it mildly, superfluously, is evident from this: the first decree of Siricius’s letter, to which alone the citation could refer, concerns the ordination of their primates and the consent or knowledge of the Roman See, according to the reading of our code which we defend. Nothing of this kind, however, is found in Ferrandus’s decree.

Furthermore, according to another reading, Siricius requires the knowledge of the primate, which must either precede or accompany the ordination. Ferrandus’s decree concerns confirmation, which follows the ordination.

Moreover, this decree is directed above all and especially to the requirement that a bishop be ordained by at least three bishops, that the written agreement of all the neighboring bishops be added, and that the ordination be duly completed. Siricius says not a word about these matters; he seems concerned only with the prerogative of the one Apostolic See or primate.

Finally, what weight is added to the decrees of so many distinguished councils by the support of an obscure synod brought forward at the very end—and suspect for that very reason as an interpolation?

The second citation is in title 6:

> That one bishop should not ordain another bishop, except for the Roman Church.

I consider its interpolation and insertion beyond doubt. All the surviving codices of that Sirician letter or council from which it is said to have been excerpted prove that the final three words, “except for the Roman Church,” are spurious; and no learned person denies this.

This addition was not made by Ferrandus. For who would believe that a learned man, highly skilled in canon law, wished to affix this blemish to the holy canons—to decide or ordain, contrary to the celebrated canons of Nicaea, consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, as Leo testifies, that bishops might be ordained by one bishop?

The Roman Church was certainly far from such a discipline even in the times after Siricius, as is abundantly clear from our Leo. The same is evident from Innocent’s letter to Victricius.

[Note: [Col. 1080D] It was not the pseudo-Siricius who copied from Innocent’s letter; rather, Innocent copied from the genuine letter of Siricius. See the observations, chapter 4, no. 2.]

For Innocent pronounces absolutely and without exception:

> Let no single bishop presume to ordain, lest the benefit granted appear to be stolen; for this was established and defined by the Council of Nicaea.

Who could even dream that this discipline could have been disregarded by the Roman Church alone? As though it had been permitted either to oppose the canonical statutes of the Council of Nicaea or to grant the stolen benefit of the priesthood.

On the contrary, Innocent openly declares that this was especially the discipline of the Roman Church at that time. When Victricius, urgently requesting the standard and authority of the Roman Church, appealed to him, Innocent, readily accommodating himself to his wishes, sent along with his letter a carefully arranged set of rules for an acceptable life and conduct. Through these, he says, the peoples of that region might recognize:

> What discipline is maintained in the churches of the city of Rome.

And below:

> Therefore, because some through ignorance or negligence do not observe ecclesiastical discipline and presume many things that ought not to be presumed, you have rightly requested, he says, that in those regions the kind of rule maintained by the Roman Church should be observed.

[Col. 1081B] Next, it would be utterly astonishing that [Note: [Col. 1081D] Since the African Church had always revered the primacy and supreme authority of the Apostolic See and had demonstrated its respect and obedience in many matters even in this period, as will appear from *Observationes*, chapter 3, no. 7, it is highly insulting to that same Church to write that it had been a rival of the eminence of the Roman Church. Moreover, since enlarging the privileges of the Roman Church amounts to fabricating imaginary privileges, that Church itself did not desire this. What Ferrandus granted to this Church, or what he meant when he wrote “with the exception of the Roman Church,” is obscure. Whatever it may be, since all the surviving manuscripts of the *Breviatio* testify that those words were added by Ferrandus, they undoubtedly refer to something that did not exceed the prerogatives of the Apostolic See in any way. Nor, because their meaning is unknown, can the words be called an interpolation, nor may one suspect an illegitimate prerogative. Compare *Observationes*, chapter 2, no. 5.] the African Church, which was a rival of the eminence of Rome and did not desire to enlarge its privileges, would of its own accord have granted to the latter so singular a prerogative, if indeed it is a prerogative not to be subject to the sacred canons, and would not have claimed it for itself. Certainly that it was not at that time more eager than previously to enlarge the splendor of Rome [Note: [Col. 1082D] What the three canons repeated in this council were intended to accomplish, we explained in volume II, in the observations on Quesnell’s fifth dissertation, part I, chapter 6. There we showed that, in the controversy over appeals raised by the case of Apiarius, the Africans did not attack the right of the Apostolic See, but wished only, with respect to the lower-ranking clerics then under discussion, to block access by wicked frauds and evasions. Another question then arose concerning the Sardican canons, which had been cited under the name of the Nicene canons. But this question must be said to have been wholly removed in the time of Boniface, bishop of Carthage, since the Sardican canons had by then become known and received under their own name, as is clear from the *Breviatio* of Ferrandus, deacon of Carthage.] is proved by the Council of Carthage held under Bishop Boniface in the year of Christ 525, that is, at the very time when Ferrandus was flourishing and perhaps writing. For at that synod the ancient canons were reread and confirmed. The last three of them prohibit overseas judgments, forbid anyone to appeal overseas, and forbid anyone who had appealed from being received into communion within Africa; and they ordain that anyone who does not communicate in Africa, but dares to do so overseas, be condemned. 970 This was the position of that synod, from which it is clear how far Ferrandus must have been from adding words of this kind. To say nothing of the fact that he cannot be thought so utterly untrustworthy that he would have wished, by excerpting the Councils, to corrupt them and enlarge them by additions of his own.

The entire work, therefore, belongs to an impostor [Note: [Col. 1082D] See *Observationes*, chapter 2, no. 6.], whom I also firmly believe added this entire sixth chapter. For it seems highly useless and superfluous to prohibit in chapter 6 one bishop from ordaining another, after chapter 4 has stated that a bishop is to be ordained by three, with the consent of the others in writing, and chapter 5 has stated that other bishops besides the three are also to be added when a bishop is being ordained, if anyone should raise an objection—especially since the support of the Council of Zella is also added to the earlier provision.

The three remaining citations of titles 130, 138, and 174 contain nothing false in themselves; but, because the first two have been added, they too come under suspicion of being additions. Moreover, title 130 compresses two decrees of Siricius into one and substitutes “woman” for “widow”; and finally, the last two titles seem superfluous. For title 138, “That another Church should not admit a rejected cleric,” is contained in title 27, “That a bishop should not receive a cleric belonging to another”; and it is stated still more clearly in title 53, “That no excommunicated bishop, presbyter, or deacon should communicate.” For the Nicene canon 5, the Sardican canon 16, the Carthaginian canon 8, and the Antiochene canon 2, from which that title 53 is drawn, define in the clearest terms that a rejected cleric must not be admitted by another. It would therefore have been pointless to add yet another title on the same subject. 971 Title 174, “That those coming from the Novatians or Montanists should be received by the laying-on of hands,” is rendered entirely useless by title 177 and betrays the hand of an idle compiler. For the same discipline is established in that final title regarding the Novatians: “That Novatians, and likewise Quartodecimans, should not be received unless they have first condemned their heresy, so that they may be instructed in the creed and anointed with chrism,” from canon 7 of the Council of Laodicea. It would have been sufficient simply to note the passage of that Council of Zella—unless the desire to impose the fictitious decrees of this synod had required a separate title.

From this it is evident that confidence in Ferrandus’s *Breviatio* is at least partly shaken. Once interpolation has been detected in some of its titles, the authority of the remaining chapters of the same *Breviatio* is greatly diminished [Note: [Col. 1082D] Compare *Observationes*, chapter 2, no. 8.], since it is established that the work has been interpolated, while it remains uncertain which parts the impostor’s hand has corrupted. It follows again that the Council of Zella or Tella, and the letter of Siricius attached to it, gain no additional authority from that collection, since there is reason to doubt its authenticity. If some portions or citations of that *Breviatio* are indeed spurious, those relating to the Council of Zella or Tella must especially be regarded as such, since they are always either the only ones present or the last in order—a circumstance which, as experts in textual criticism know, greatly increases suspicion of addition in cases of this kind. Finally, this suspicion is further confirmed by the diversity of the citations of that council.

## CHAPTER III

### It is demonstrated that the fragment attributed to the Council of Tella is fictitious.

Whatever may ultimately be the case with Ferrandus’s *Breviatio*, I maintain that the council whose fragment we now possess, prefixed to the letter of Siricius and called the Council of Tella, is fictitious; and, unless I am mistaken, I establish this by the following arguments.

The first argument is repeated from what has already been said [Note: [Col. 1082D] This objection will be answered in *Observationes*, chapter 3, no. 2.] concerning the name of the council. For it is everywhere written “Tella,” and this cannot be attributed to a scribal error. It is clear, moreover, that there is only one city called Tella, and that it lies in the province of Proconsular Africa. But that Donatianus, a bishop of Telepte in Byzacena, held a synod in Proconsular Africa is the dream of an impostor who lacked sufficient knowledge both of ecclesiastical discipline and of the African regions 972 to conceal his fraud skillfully. Even if there may have been some village of this name in Byzacena, it is nowhere celebrated by writers; yet it ought not to have been so obscure a place if a large synod had assembled there, to which representatives of the province of Proconsular Africa also came.

2. It is not probable that a synod was held [Note: [Col. 1083D] Indeed, we shall show there, no. 3, that at this time a provincial synod ought to have been convened in Byzacena.] in the province of Byzacena on 24 February, when a general assembly of all Africa was due to be convened in the following month of May and had already been announced. For, so far as appears from the fragment, no matter of greater importance was to be treated at that synod than the reading of Siricius’s letter or letters. These could easily have been deferred to the general synod, especially since holy Lent was then either approaching or had already begun. There the letter—which had been written to everyone, if the inscription is to be trusted—could have been heard by almost all the bishops of Africa with greater solemnity and splendor.

3. Since this synod is not described as general, [Col. 1083B] there is no reason why representatives from the province of Proconsular Africa should have attended that Council of Tella [Note: [Col. 1083D] See the same work, no. 4.]. For the Council of Milevis identifies and determines two kinds of African councils: some were general councils of all Africa, to be held for common causes; others were particular councils, for matters that were not common and were therefore to be discussed by the bishops of each province. What, then, were representatives of the province of Proconsular Africa doing at that synod? The learned reader will surely perceive that, whatever it may be, this was fabricated by the author of the synodal fragment. Such, in my view, was the nature of his council.

Some person excessively and perversely devoted to the greatness and authority of Rome [Note: [Col. 1083D] We shall show in *Observationes*, chapter 3, no. 9, that this little historical tale, which Quesnell fabricated for himself without any evidence, must be counted among his dreams.], when he saw that the efforts undertaken by the Roman legates under the pontificates of the Roman bishops Zosimus, Boniface, and Celestine—efforts made by invading the African provinces in defense of the right of appeal to the Apostolic See—had met with poor success, attempted to obliterate the memory of this unfortunate outcome. He thought that the attempt could not fail if he produced one or more celebrated African synods that had voluntarily submitted to the commands of the Roman pontiff, received his decrees, and obeyed them—not merely in one province but in several. He further believed that the synod would carry still greater weight if it were shown to have been held at the very time when the cause of Zosimus’s legates had fared less successfully at the Council of Carthage.

The date of the synod was therefore fixed under Zosimus. To demonstrate that the authority of the pontiff had also been accepted from ancient times in the African regions, he introduced representatives of the province of Proconsular Africa who would recall that Siricius’s letters had been received, read, and approved at another synod, that of Tisdra. He put all these elements into the prologue of the fictitious synod. In composing it, he turned his eyes to the Council of Carthage of the following year and took from its preface the model for his own fabrication, which begins in the same way: “After the consulship of …” From that council and from the Council of Milevis the impostor also borrowed the president of his synod, namely Donatianus, bishop of Telepte in Byzacena and at that time its primate. From the same sources he also took the representatives of the province of Proconsular Africa whom he was to present before the pseudo-synod, Vincentius and Fortunatianus, who [Note: [Col. 1083D] This canon is indeed cited by Isidore under the title of the Council of Milevis. In reality, however, it is the final canon of the Council of Carthage of the year 418. See the treatise *On Collections*, part II, chapter 3, § 6, no. 1, and § 7, no. 6.] were elected as representatives from the Carthaginian province at the Council of Milevis and are likewise named in the preface [Note: [Col. 1084D] See *Observationes*, chapter 3, no. 1.] of the Council of Carthage of 419. [Col. 1084A] He summoned the remaining bishops from various synods or letters, or fabricated them himself. He placed the synod at the city of Tella, without much concern about whether it lay in the same province, provided only that he knew there was a place of that name in Africa. Finally, he attached the letter of Pope Siricius, for whose sake the entire tale had been arranged. Although contentious people may evade these points, they will nevertheless be sufficient for a sensible and sincere reader to convict the impostor of fraud. We confirm this by what follows.

4. An indication of falsehood is drawn from the remaining words [Note: [Col. 1084D] We shall dispel this objection there, no. 5.]. For he introduces two representatives speaking at once: “Vincentius and Fortunatianus said”; then all the bishops of the synod respond: “The bishops said.” They request that Siricius’s letters be read, yet only one is read. Finally, to omit many expressions that breathe barbarism, the synod of Tisdra or Tysdra is recalled, and the bishops of this Council of Tella are said to have attended it: “Even when we were at Tisdra, as your attentive hearing recalls to me,” etc.—as though bishops of one province could have attended the synods of another province. For no one maintains that the synod of Tisdra was a general assembly of all Africa.

5. Since nothing else from this entire council [Note: [Col. 1084D] See the same *Observationes*, chapter 3, no. 6.] is found to have been handed down to posterity apart from the recitation of this letter of Pope Siricius, the whole thing is plainly too contrived, and such a fragment rightly arouses suspicion of forgery. Why were the canons reported by Ferrandus omitted, if they had been enacted at the same synod? Why was another letter of Siricius omitted, when it is mentioned in the same fragment and was likewise ordered to be read? Why have the other matters treated at that synod been suppressed in silence? There can be no doubt that at a synod to which representatives from Africa’s principal province came, matters of great importance would have been debated. Yet not a word is said about them.

6. It is certain that during this period the Africans administered their Churches according to the canons of their own synods [Col. 1084C] and did not permit ecclesiastical laws to be imposed upon them by overseas regions [Note: [Col. 1084D] Compare the same work, no. 7.], although, whenever the common cause of the faith was at stake—as in the case of the Pelagian heresy—they did not refrain from sending a report to the Roman See. Such was the purity and holiness of African discipline that most other Churches freely embraced it, and Rome itself made it its own. Africa, however, scarcely tolerated the mixing of foreign rules with its own. I do not think that any canons other than the Nicene canons were in force there, or had acquired use and authority, before the Council of Chalcedon. After that council, the canons of the other Eastern provinces were introduced into many Churches by the prescription of the first canon of that ecumenical synod. This is why they are mentioned by Ferrandus in his *Breviatio*. It was certainly evident at the Council of Carthage of 419, where the matter of appeals was debated on the occasion of Apiarius [Note: [Col. 1084D] We have explained more fully in volume II, in the observations on Quesnell’s fifth dissertation, part I, chapters 5 and 6, what the African Fathers maintained in this matter while leaving the rights of the Apostolic See untouched.], how strongly the Africans recoiled from admitting overseas laws into Africa.

[Col. 1084D] 7. If everything here asserted about what took place at both synods, that of Tisdra and that of Tella, were entirely true [Note: [Col. 1084D] See the following *Observationes*, chapter 3, no. 8.], the legates of Pope Boniface at the aforementioned Council of Carthage would never have failed to report it. They would thereby have confirmed, by such a precedent, the authority of the Apostolic See, for the defense of which they had been sent. It would have been no small argument for that authority’s acceptance that, at two synods—both numerous, one held in Proconsular Africa, the principal province, and the other in Byzacena before representatives of the bishops of Proconsular Africa—the pontiff’s *Tractatoria* or *Tractoria* had been received with such veneration, heard with such eagerness, and inserted into the synodal acts as a norm of discipline to which everyone was obliged to conform. The legates did nothing of the kind. Either they must be said to have forgotten their own cause—which is improbable—or what is here asserted about both synods must be regarded as fictitious.

8. Since this entire synod, or rather the patchwork of a synod described in that council, was composed so that Siricius’s letter could be appended to it, and thus each might lend support to the other, there will be no means of supporting the authenticity and truth of that council if the letter’s *νοθεία*—its spuriousness—has once been established [Note: [Col. 1085D] See the same work, no. 9.]. For one cannot suppose that a pair of African synods were so dull and foolish as to embrace a fictitious letter as sincere and genuine [Col. 1085B] and receive it as an apostolic decree. In my judgment, however, nothing is clearer than the imposture and forgery of this letter, which we shall attempt to expose by various arguments in the following chapter.

## CHAPTER IV

### The letter of Siricius appended to the fragment is proved to be spurious. The first argument for its forgery is drawn from the first decree of the letter; its variant readings and varying meanings are examined.

Above all, the first decree of this letter must be brought under examination [Note: [Col. 1085D] The objection proposed throughout this chapter will be refuted in *Observationes*, chapter 4, no. 1.], since it seems to contain considerable difficulty, both because of its subject matter and because of the divergent reading found in various manuscripts.

In the Oxford manuscript it reads:

> First, that outside the knowledge of the Apostolic See no primate may dare to ordain; for the judgment is complete when it is confirmed by the opinion of the majority.

In the collection of Councils and in the Thuane manuscript it reads:

> First, that outside the knowledge of the Apostolic See, that is, of the primate, no one may dare to ordain; for the judgment is complete when it follows the opinion of the majority.

Finally, in Innocent’s text, from whose letter to Victricius almost the whole passage was taken, it is reported as follows:

> First, that outside the knowledge of the metropolitan bishop no one may dare to ordain a bishop; for the judgment is complete when it is confirmed by the opinions of the majority.

The meaning of Innocent’s words is perfectly clear, and they contain nothing inconsistent with the discipline of the Nicene canons or of the other ancient canons.

The meaning of the same words as they stand in the Oxford manuscript is also plain. By “the Apostolic See” he means Rome; by “primates” he designates the metropolitans of the individual African provinces. The author of the letter wishes to prohibit the ordination of any African metropolitan without the consent and knowledge of the Roman bishop. I therefore have no doubt that this is the genuine reading of the adulterated letter [Col. 1085D].

For I cannot see to what reasonable meaning the reading found in the common edition can be reduced:

> That outside the knowledge of the Apostolic See, that is, of the primate, no one may dare to ordain.

Franciscus Florens, the distinguished predecessor of the bishop of Orléans, in *Treatise 6 on Title 6 of the Decretals*, concerning election and the authority of the elected person, page 194, thinks that these words have been interpolated and that one should read only:

> Outside the knowledge of the primate,

deleting the intervening words “of the Apostolic See, that is,” as spurious additions.

Chiffletius objects on the authority of the oldest manuscripts, which present the complete reading, among them the venerable Corbie manuscript, remarkable for its antiquity. Preserving the words “of the Apostolic See,” he himself interprets them of the primate, to whom, for this purpose, the supreme authority of the Apostolic See would rightfully belong, so that in such a case there would be no need to consult the Roman pontiff. He also says that the name “Apostolic See” is commonly attributed by ancient writers to any episcopal see.

I grant the latter point; but it increases rather than resolves the difficulty. If any see was an apostolic see and was honored by that name, how could the term be so proper to the primate that the pontiff would intend it to designate the primate? Furthermore, even if any episcopal see could be called apostolic, one would scarcely find the expression used in the manner found in this decree, especially by the pontiffs of the Roman See, who scarcely shared that title with any but the principal sees of the East. Thus Leo, writing to the Emperor Marcian about Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, says [Epistle 78, chapter 3]: “Let him not disdain the royal city, which he cannot make an apostolic see.”

Finally, Siricius would not have used words requiring interpretation [Col. 1086B], but would have said simply “the primate,” or, as was customary among the Africans, “the bishop of the first see.” Even that, however, would have been highly superfluous to commend to the African regions, which had both established it by their own laws and observed it religiously.

The author of the letter therefore had another purpose, which is easily understood from the reading of the Oxford manuscript. By the present decree he plainly wished to establish that the primates of the African Churches were not to be ordained without the knowledge of the Roman See:

> That outside the knowledge of the Apostolic See no primates may dare to ordain.

This reading is also confirmed by the fact that, unless “primates” is read, there will be no noun governed by the verb “to ordain.” The result will be both a defective sentence and an ambiguous meaning. For the word “to ordain” does not have only one sense among writers on canon law or in the canons themselves. Often, as we have noted elsewhere, it signifies administration; sometimes the consecration of a bishop; and very frequently it designates the conferral of the second, third, or other lower orders [Col. 1086C]. If the common reading is retained, it will remain uncertain which of these meanings the word must have here. I therefore think that our reading should be preferred, as corresponding to the author’s intention.

Yet just as this reading does not fit the more common usage of the words or the rules of grammar, so it is entirely opposed to the discipline and customs of those regions. If by “primates” he means the bishop of Carthage, the singular rather than the plural should have been used, since there was only one such primate in Africa. How foreign it would also have been to African law and custom for a consultation or report to be sent to the Roman bishop concerning the ordination of the bishop of Carthage!

If, however, by “primates” he designates the bishop of each province who was its metropolitan or prelate of the first see, then this decree is exceedingly foolish and absurd, since it forbids the primates to be ordained without the knowledge of the Apostolic See. In Africa, with the exception of the bishop of Carthage, primates were never ordained, as learned men have often observed. Their primatial sees were not fixed in those regions but shifted from place to place. Bishops did not acquire the honor of the primacy from the antiquity or dignity of their sees; rather, the sees themselves were elevated to this prerogative because of the seniority in age and antiquity of consecration of their bishops. Thus, whoever was ordained bishop was the last among the bishops of his province, with the exception of the bishop of the city of Carthage, who was ordained primate of all Africa by the proper privilege of his see.

That this custom continued in the African regions even after the time of Pope Gregory the Great is clear from his letter to the bishops of Numidia, in which he permits their custom to remain unchanged, whether concerning the appointment of primates or the other provisions. Yet, writing to Gennadius, exarch of Africa, he expresses the wish that he admonish the Council of African bishops that the primate should not reside indiscriminately, as was customary, in various towns, but in one city selected by them.

The first argument for the *νοθεία*—the forgery—of this letter fabricated under the name of Siricius must therefore be drawn from the absurdity of this first decree. However one reads it, it cannot be reconciled with ordinary usage, the rules of grammar, or African discipline and custom.

## CHAPTER V

### Further arguments for the spuriousness of the pseudo-letter of Siricius.

We construct our second proof from the fact that this letter almost entirely agrees with the letter of Pope Innocent I to Victricius, bishop of Rouen [Col. 1087B], so that one must have been copied from the other. No one will say that Innocent’s letter was copied from Siricius [Note: [Col. 1087D] The response will be found in *Observationes*, chapter 4, no. 2.]. Nor will anyone who considers the matter even suspect that Innocent borrowed from Siricius, since Innocent would certainly not have failed to mention Siricius if he had used his words and decrees, especially since he did so in his letter to Exuperius even when there was not so much necessity. Moreover, he would either have referred Victricius to Siricius’s letter or composed a new one in his own manner and style. Finally, he would not have altered the decrees or cut away anything that contributed to the splendor of the Apostolic See.

3. Nothing resembles a dream more closely than the claim made in the preface that these letters were sent by the Roman synod chiefly for the sake of the Africans:

> Because at present they were unable to be present, either on account of bodily illness or because of exhausted old age.

As though African bishops were accustomed to assemble at Rome for synods, and as though only ill health or decrepit old age could have kept them away from a synod. The wonder is increased by the fact that at the beginning of the letter he speaks as though it were a chance gathering:

> When many brothers had assembled together at the relics of the holy Apostle Peter, etc.

There is no reason to explain the absence of most of them from such a chance gathering by illness or age.

4. No less contrary to the customs and procedures of that age, especially in dealings with the Africans, are those harsher words [Note: [Col. 1087D] Compare the same work, no. 4.]:

> Let no one dare.

No one will readily believe that Siricius used such language toward the Africans.

5. What kind of reasoning is this in the first decree, namely, that no one may presume to ordain without the knowledge either of the metropolitan, the primate, or the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 1087D] See the same work, no. 5.]?

> For the judgment is complete when it is confirmed by the opinion of the majority.

Who would say that there could be several primates? Who would say that a judgment is confirmed by someone’s opinion?

“But,” you will say, “the same reasoning is offered by Innocent.” I think that Innocent’s reading and punctuation are corrupt, and that these words, “the judgment is complete,” etc. [Col. 1087D], belong to the latter part of the decree, where they make excellent sense:

> The judgment is complete when it is confirmed by the opinions of the majority: no single bishop should presume to ordain a bishop, etc.

Nor do I make this conjecture gratuitously or rely on this argument alone. The authority of the Oxford manuscript supports it, for in that manuscript the causal particle *enim* (“for”) is missing before the word “judgment,” although we have inserted it into the text of the letter from other manuscripts [Note: [Col. 1087D] The particle *enim* is absent from Quesnell’s edition, which we used. We have restored it from all our manuscripts.]. The same argument does not apply to the passage attributed to Siricius, since those words conclude the first chapter and cannot be referred to what follows, which is presented as the beginning of another decree.

6. In that second decree these words are added, which are not found in Innocent [Note: [Col. 1088D] Compare *Observationes*, chapter 4, no. 6.]:

> Because of arrogance.

They are placed after the words:

> No single bishop should presume to ordain a bishop.

As though this were permissible provided it were done without arrogance. Here an interpolation is combined with corruption of both discipline and language.

7. These words of chapter 9 plainly reveal either the impostor’s malice or his ignorance [Note: [Col. 1088D] See the same work, no. 7.]:

> We advise that priests and Levites should not have intercourse with their wives, because they are occupied with the daily necessities of the ministry.

Here the author of the letter advises and exhorts, as he does below with “I exhort,” “I admonish,” “I ask,” and so forth, as though priests and Levites were not bound by a law of continence. Innocent does not speak in this way, and the impostor has corrupted his words. For instead of “we advise,” Innocent has:

> The Church must observe this absolutely.

Nor does Siricius himself speak in this way in his letter to Himerius of Tarragona. There, attacking priests and Levites who father children by their own wives as though they were guilty of the gravest crime, he adds:

> By the sanctions of sacred Scripture, all priests and Levites are bound by an unbreakable law, so that from the day of our ordination we must dedicate both our hearts and our bodies to sobriety and chastity.

He further decrees that those convicted of this crime are to be expelled from their ministry and that every avenue of indulgence is to be closed to them.

It is therefore perfectly clear that the author of the letter was either ignorant of or contemptuous of the sacred discipline that prevailed in the Roman Church in the time of Siricius and had been established by Siricius himself. To say this of Siricius or of any other Roman pontiff would be impious.

8. That inept fabrication, in the passages not borrowed from Innocent or others, is so crude and childish in its speech [Note: [Col. 1088D] See the same work, no. 8.] that the author can scarcely express his meaning in writing. Examples include “to follow the pleasure of the people,” “because of exhausted old age,” “to command precepts,” “in equal manner” for “similarly,” and “to wander from the reasoning of the canons.”

980 9. What does that trifler mean when he says that a priest must be ready at every moment, lest he be compelled either to offer the sacrifice or to baptize? [Col. 1088C] [Note: [Col. 1088D] This objection will be rejected in the same work, no. 9.] An occasion for baptism could indeed arise from the imminent death of catechumens or infants. But fixed days and specific hours of the day had been established for offering sacrifices, and a priest had no reason to fear that he might be compelled to offer at every moment, since only Sundays and feast days were assigned to the celebration of the mysteries. Innocent speaks much more correctly when he says that for priests there is a continual duty both of prayer and of sacrifice. It is a continual duty, not a continual necessity at every moment.

10. I do not recall ever reading a letter of an ancient Roman pontiff that was marked at the end as having been issued from Rome or at a council of bishops [Note: [Col. 1088D] Compare *Observationes*, chapter 4, no. 10.]. For whenever a synodal letter is sent, this is immediately stated at the beginning in the form used by Siricius himself:

> Siricius and the holy synod of eighty bishops which assembled at Rome at Saint Peter’s.

11. The following point militates both against this letter and against the authenticity of the council itself: although the matter of clerical continence was repeatedly treated in the Councils of Carthage [Col. 1088D] [Note: [Col. 1088D] See the same work, no. 11.], there is never any mention of the Council of Tella or of the letter of Siricius reread there, even though the principal subject of the letter concerned priestly continence.

There survives also in the African Code, no. 4, the vote of Faustinus, bishop of Potentia and legate of the Roman Church, in which he speaks as follows:

> It is agreed that a bishop, presbyter, and deacon, or anyone who handles the sacraments, as guardians of chastity, should abstain from their wives.

These words are from canon 11 of the eleventh Council of Carthage, held under Genethlius in the year 390. This vote belongs either to the Council of Carthage of 418 or to the synod of the following year, both of which were later than the Council of Zella or Tella. Faustinus would have forgotten his own legation and the see whose representative he was if he had not praised here the letter of Siricius sent to the Africans. But that neither the apostolic legates, nor Aurelius—by whose authority Vincentius and Fortunatianus had been delegated to the Council of Tella—nor Vincentius and Fortunatianus themselves, who were present at both of these Councils of Carthage, say anything about it is, in my judgment, the clearest possible proof that the letter is spurious.

Let, then, the conjecture of the most illustrious Petrus de Marca be dismissed: he asserts in *Concordia*, book I, chapter 8, no. 4, that the first obligation of clerical continence among the African Churches proceeded from the constitution of Siricius. From the very source from which he drew confidence for asserting this, I derive an argument for denying it. For since neither at the Council of Carthage of 390 nor at the earlier council cited there is any mention of a decree of Siricius sent to and received in Africa, the authority of this letter of Siricius is more effectively rejected than established by that evidence.

Moreover, who taught de Marca that the earlier council designated by the Carthaginian canon was held before the year 388, or even before the pontificate of Siricius? Finally, that second synod held at Carthage derives its authority not from a decree of Siricius but from the teaching of the apostles and the observance of all antiquity:

> What the apostles taught, and antiquity itself preserved, let us also observe.

The First Council of Carthage under Bishop Gratus, said to have been held in the time of Pope Julius, enacted the following law:

> No one who abstains from carnal intimacy may be permitted to live together with unrelated women.

Here it presupposes that the law of continence had already long before been imposed upon those whose chastity it seeks to protect, and it seems to restrain clerics by the same law, since at the end of the canon it appears to impose one penalty upon the laity and another upon clerics:

> If they are laymen, it says, and, after admonition, they persist in contempt, let them be separated from communion.

It says nothing about the penalty for clerics, because they undoubtedly knew from the authority of the preceding canons that it had already been established. Nevertheless, it presupposes that some clerics were bound by the law of continence; otherwise the exception concerning the laity would be superfluous. Thus canon 25 of the Third Council of Carthage is common to clerics and to those practicing continence.

I add that the council cited by the Second Council of Carthage did not so much enact a law concerning the continence of clerics as deal with the regulation of continence and chastity. These are the canon’s own words, which Marca did not sufficiently consider. They do not so much prove an edict that clerics were to abstain from their wives as indicate who among the clergy were not to be compelled to do so and who were to be compelled: namely, certain men devoted to a stricter discipline, who wished to subject even the lower clerics to the obligation of abstinence. This interpretation, which emerges from the reading of the canon itself, is confirmed by another canon of the Council of Carthage held in the year either 398 or 401, numbered seventy in the African Code:

> It was decreed, he says, that bishops, priests, and deacons, in accordance with the former statutes, should also abstain from their wives; and if they do not do so, they are to be removed from ecclesiastical office. [Col. 1089D]

But the other clerics were not to be compelled to this, but were to observe it according to the custom of each Church. [Col. 1090A]

Here the canon, renewing the former statutes, establishes this above all: it shows that it had been determined which clerics were to be subject to the law of continence—namely, the three higher orders—and which were to be left to their own discretion in this matter. At the same time, it teaches that there were certain Churches in the African regions that observed the custom of compelling the other clerics to undertake the obligation of continence, and that wished to draw other Churches also to the same observance. Hence the occasion was provided for the earlier council to treat of the regulation of continence and chastity; and only these three orders were, by a certain written provision, joined to chastity through consecration.

From what has been said, it is sufficiently and more than sufficiently proved, unless I am mistaken, that everything contained either in that fragment of the synod or in the Sirician letter appended to it is wholly fabricated and composed by the artifice of an impostor. There is, however, one circumstance that might seem to lend it some degree of credibility: namely, that the synod and the letter were inserted into that Roman Codex [Col. 1090B], whose antiquity and genuineness we ourselves have commended so highly. Yet this consideration is not strong enough to outweigh the arguments brought forward above: for at a later period a fictitious writing could easily have been added to a genuine codex.

This is all the more probable because it occupies the final place among the chapters, where appendices, supplements, or anything else—whether genuine or spurious—are commonly attached.

[Note: [Col. 1089D] More will be said about this in the Observations, chapter 1, no. 2.]

Nor is this without precedent:

[Note: [Col. 1089D] There was no fraud when Leo’s letter to the Moors, letter 12 of our edition, was added among certain other genuine documents to the Dionysian collection; we have defended it against every charge of fabrication or interpolation.]

For we shall prove below, in the notes on letter 1—now letter 12, volume II—that the Dionysian collection of papal decrees was enlarged by a similar fraud through the addition of one letter. We stated above, chapter 2, that Ferrandus the deacon’s Breviary of the Canons had likewise been interpolated by certain additions:
