[Note: [Col. 1089D] He said this, but did not prove it appropriately, as will be evident from the Observations, chapter 2.]

There are hundreds of other examples of this kind.

But this very passage still clearly betrays the imposture. For if the synod and the letter were genuine, they would not have remained hidden from the clergy of the Roman Church for so long, nor would they have been relegated to the end of the codex.

[Note: [Col. 1089D] He insists upon the hypothesis that we have already refuted: namely, that the collection of canons published in this volume was a codex of the Roman Church. Once that hypothesis falls, the whole of this reasoning collapses. [Col. 1090D]]

For since each part of that codex was inserted at the time when it either became known or was received for use and authority in the Roman Church, it would certainly be astonishing if the genuine letter of Siricius reached the knowledge of the Romans only so late, or were approved by them only then. It would likewise be incredible negligence if they had deferred the acts of a large synod, one so favorably supporting the wishes of the Roman Church, and had not entered them into their archives and Roman Codex until a hundred years later—especially since they had willingly inserted into that Codex of canons and constitutions so many other writings of lesser importance: statements of faith, letters, narratives, and many other documents that neither approach the authority of synods or papal decrees nor closely concerned Roman affairs. There is therefore nothing by which the authority of such a spurious little writing can be secured from a genuine codex.

Moreover, if this opinion happens to trouble anyone’s mind—namely, that both monuments should be relegated among spurious writings [Col. 1090D] out of hostility toward the Roman Church—that person is judging our mind most unfairly and has very little understanding of what truly serves the interests of the Apostolic See. In reality, that letter and the memory of Siricius are insulting to the Roman Church.

[Note: [Col. 1090D] So that Quesnellus might not appear hostile to the Roman Church, he invents for Siricius an insulting letter which only the heterodox can interpret in a depraved or more lenient sense. We shall explain its obvious meaning, which grants no relaxation whatever, in the Observations, chapter 4, no. 7.]

For the discipline of this chief Church has always been more rigorous in various matters, and especially in those concerning the sanctity and continence of clerics; rightly, therefore, it has always been regarded as more religious than the other Churches. Hence it appears to have been the first to impose the law of continence upon subdeacons. Hence it did not previously persuade itself to count that tenth canon of the Council of Ancyra among its own rules until it had adapted it to its stricter discipline: for that canon granted permission to marry to deacons who, at their ordination, had refused to subject themselves to the law of continence. Finally, Siricius himself writes in his genuine letter to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona [984], that all priests and Levites are bound by the indissoluble law of the divine sanctions, so that from the day of their ordination they must devote both their hearts and their bodies to sobriety and chastity.

Nevertheless, that clever artificer of the pseudo-letter, as though Siricius had no command concerning continence to be observed by priests, represents him as giving advice, offering persuasion, exhorting, and finally begging them not to have intercourse with their wives—not as something commanded, but as though he were suggesting something worthy, chaste, and honorable. [Col. 1091B]

[Col. 1092A] The innovators of our own age, hostile to clerical continence, did not fail to notice this and to point out Siricius’s supposed leniency, as though it came closer to their doctrine than the other decrees of the pontiffs. Among them was a certain Georgius Calixtus, professor at the Julia Academy, who wrote in his treatise On the Marriage of Clerics, published at Helmstedt in 1631, page 345:

> Siricius, he says, seems to wish to persuade rather than compel, and to put forward counsels rather than commands: “We likewise advise,” he says; “I exhort, admonish, and beg.”

And below, on page 355:

> Nor should it be concealed, he says, that Siricius appears to act more mildly and leniently in his later letter to the Africans . . . perhaps because he had been admonished by more moderate men, or because he had already begun to perceive and notice that “the taut bow breaks” (τόξον ἐπιτεινόμενον ῥήγνυσθαι), and had allowed something to be taken away from the fervor of his zeal.

You see how miserably the heretics abuse this scrap of evidence, and how greatly it matters for the honor and authority of the Apostolic See, for the African Church, and for the synods, that a pseudo-synod and pseudo-letter should no longer impose upon Catholics under this disguise or provide heretics with an occasion for mockery. [Col. 1092B]

[Col. 1091]

# BALLERINIUS’S OBSERVATIONS

On Quesnellus’s Dissertation XV concerning the Council of Teleptum, or rather Zellum, which, together with the letter of Siricius recited in it, is defended against the charge of fabrication.

## CHAPTER ONE

The authority by which this council is proved genuine. Quesnellus’s bold undertaking. The name of this council. The first chapter of the preceding dissertation refuted.

[Col. 1091B]

### I.

The Council of Teleptum, or rather—as we shall see—of Zellum, or rather the fragment of this council, which came to light together with the letter of Siricius recited in it, is supported by so many manuscript collections, and by so many of them extremely ancient, as well as by the authority of Ferrandus, a deacon of the Church of Carthage, that its genuineness might rightly seem impossible to doubt. Hence Blondellus, although in his pseudo-Isidore, page 550, brought forward two objections against the letter of Siricius, did not dare to accuse either the letter or the council of fabrication. Indeed, he admits that Ferrandus alone is sufficient to secure authority for both.

Quesnellus, however, more daringly undertook in the preceding dissertation to demonstrate that both were mere imposture and mere invention. In this matter, a man who readily indulges in conjecture thought that he had made such progress that in the first chapter he did not hesitate to write:

> I am entirely certain that both the synod and the letter are a mere fable and a mere invention; nor do I expect that anyone will refuse to adopt my view of his own accord, once he has examined this absurd fabrication more closely and deeply in the light of sound judgment.

How this hope turned out is clear from the judgments of the most learned men who afterward discussed this same subject. We shall not cite the Italians, lest they be thought to have been led by partisan zeal. It will suffice to consider the more celebrated Gallic authors: Tillemont, Natalis Alexander, Baluzius, Pelagius, and Constantius. The first of these, although an enthusiastic admirer of Quesnellus, after presenting the points that might cause doubt and submitting everything to the judgment of the learned, could not affirm that it was a fabrication. The other four thought that the authenticity of both the synod and the letter had to be defended and Quesnellus’s opinion refuted.

Following in their footsteps, and especially those of Baluzius, who at the end of his edition of the books of Peter de Marca, On the Concord of the Priesthood and the Empire, added a dissertation on the Council of Teleptum, we shall append observations on each of Quesnellus’s chapters. We hope that in this way the truth may shine forth much more clearly.

### II.

First, however, we must recall the manuscript collections that lend authority to this synod and to the letter of Siricius. Formerly, since they appeared only in Merlini’s edition of the councils, and since Merlini contains several apocryphal documents, their authenticity could have been doubtful because of the impurity of the source. But three other extremely ancient collections—the Corbeiensis, the Fossatensis, and the collection printed in this volume and discovered later—which transmitted to us, together with other highly valuable documents, the fragment of this council and the letter of Siricius, exclude every suspicion of fabrication. Their antiquity is so great that, just as we cannot doubt the other documents in them unless some established fact prevents it, so neither can we doubt the fragment of the Council of Zellum or the letter of Siricius, against which we shall find that no certain objection can be raised.

Quesnellus, who rightly attributes very great weight to our collection, first published by himself, thinks that this fragment [Col. 1092C] and the letter must be rejected because they are placed in the final chapter and presumes that they are additions. But since several other items follow this chapter, and since we shall prove in note 1 on chapter 67 that all of them properly belong to this extremely ancient collection, the collection itself must provide a very strong argument from authority, with Quesnellus himself supporting it. Add two other collections of excellent quality: one in the Colbertine manuscript 3368, the other in the Vatican manuscript 3827. Baluzius mentions two other royal copies, and Father Harduinus likewise mentions two belonging to the Society of Jesus; we do not know to which collections they belong.

A great deal of authority is also supplied by manuscript 59 of the chapter of Verona, to which another ancient book of the chapter of Lucca is similar. These manuscripts, more than a thousand years old, contain an extremely ancient abridgment of the canons, which we observed in our Treatise on Collections to have been excerpted from older Hispanic and Gallican collections. All these codices, so far as this synod is concerned, are Gallican or derive their origin from Gallican codices. [Col. 1092D]

### III.

Ferrandus, in his Breviary of the Canons, used another African codex when he mentioned this council and the letter of Siricius. It is possible to infer that he found the council in that codex not mutilated but complete, because he cites other canons of the same council that are not found in the commonly transmitted fragment. Moreover, since Ferrandus reports, from councils that are not plenary, only the canons of synods of the province of Byzacena, as we observed in the Treatise cited above, part IV, chapter 1, it is clear that in listing the canons of this council he used a particular manuscript copy of the Byzacenes. This removes every suspicion of fabrication even more decisively.

Quesnellus himself does not deny this compelling testimony. For that reason he says in chapter 2:

> From that little work of Ferrandus the deacon, concerning the Council of Telensis, or Zellensis, and the letter appended to it, one could safely pronounce in favor of its authority, if the integrity of the Breviary itself were certain.

But in order to prove the Breviary itself spurious, he also accuses this little work of Ferrandus of interpolation. Thus everything that does not favor his opinion is suspect to him. Come, then, let us see whether the objections he brings throughout the dissertation are so substantial and so weighty that they can introduce a probable doubt against the testimony of so many outstanding collections and codices, and against the commonly transmitted Breviary of Ferrandus.

### IV.

Let us now examine his first chapter, in which he discusses the synod. He asserts there that all earlier editions, all manuscript codices—both recent and very ancient—call the synod Telensis, not Teleptensis. Since Tela is situated in the proconsular province, not in Byzacena, he concludes in chapter 3, no. 1, that this synod, over which Donatianus of Teleptum, primate of the province of Byzacena, is said to have presided, was fabricated by an impostor:

> For it is written Telensis EVERYWHERE, and it was not written so through a scribal error. Moreover, it is clear that there is only one city called Telensis, situated in the proconsular province. That Donatianus, a bishop of Teleptum in Byzacena, held a synod in the proconsular province is a dream of an impostor who lacked sufficient knowledge both of ecclesiastical discipline and of the African regions to conceal his fraud skillfully.

Stephen Baluzius rightly rebukes Quesnellus for boldly asserting that all the codices call the synod Telensis rather than Teleptensis. For the very Thuaneus codex, now Colbertinus 932 in the Royal Library, which Quesnellus himself used in his edition, expressly and distinctly reads:

> The Council of Teleptum begins, concerning the tractoria of Saint Cyricius, pope of the city of Rome, through Africa;

and afterward:

> In the church of the Apostles of the people of Teleptum;

and in the very table of the chapters, which he prefixed to his edition from the same codex, no. 62:

> Constitutions of the Council of Theleptum.

If he has forgotten the codex he used while writing these statements, what credibility should be granted to him when he declares that all codices read Telensis? Another royal codex, formerly belonging to Saint Peter of Poitiers, agrees with the Thuaneus codex in Baluzius and likewise gives “Council of Teleptum” and “people of Teleptum.”

We add the extremely ancient abridgment of the canons found in the very old Verona manuscript 59, where we read:

> From the synod of Teleptum;

a reading which the Lucan codex also presents in a form diminished by the scribes’ carelessness:

> From the synod of Leptum.

As for the remaining copies, which lack the word Teleptensis, it is false that they agree in the word Telensis. Another royal copy, formerly belonging to the archbishop of Rheims, gives Telenensis in both places; and, somewhat differently, Thellenensis is read in Vatican manuscript 3827. Colbertinus 3368, which contains two collections, as we saw in the Treatise, part II, chapter 8, no. 2, includes two copies of this council; in the second, it is written Telenensis. Vatican manuscript 1340 has Telesoensis. Baluzius cites two other Colbertine codices and one royal codex in which the canons of the same synod are called Telineses.

In the catalogue of councils prefixed to the Herouvallian collection in Petit, volume I of Theodore’s Penitential, page 265, we read:

> Canons of the bishops of Tholonum, 33.

Since it is therefore untrue that all codices call this synod Telensis, Quesnellus was entirely wrong to infer from this supposed agreement of all the copies—an agreement that he wrongly presumed—that Telensis was the true name and that the synod of the city of Tela was intended, a city belonging not to Byzacena but to the proconsular province.

### V.

Amid such a variety of codices and readings, a scribal error undoubtedly entered somewhere. The three codices mentioned above, which give Telenensis or Thellenensis, are certainly in error when they call Donatianus bishop of the city of Tela. For it is clear from other indisputable documents that he was bishop of Teleptum. Accordingly, the reading Telenensis or Thellenensis must also be attributed to error, since no African city called Telena or Thellana is known. For the same reason, the readings Telesoensis, Telinensis, and Tholonensis are likewise corrupt.

There therefore remain two readings: Teleptensis and Telensis. The latter is found frequently in manuscripts, such as the two Vindobonensis codices, the Oxford codex of our collection, the Corbeiensis, Colbertinus 3368 in its first copy, and the two codices of the Society of Jesus cited by Father Harduinus.

Since it is certain that Donatianus was bishop of Teleptum, the heading “Council of Teleptum” presents no difficulty. Conversely, if the reading Telensis is to refer to the proconsular city of Tela, then, since the matter concerns a synod of the province of Byzacena, it must be attributed to the error of copyists, just as the similar title attached to Donatianus in the three manuscripts we mentioned must clearly be attributed to their lapse.

Just as in those three manuscripts, where Donatianus’s episcopal see is indicated, we must read “bishop of Teleptum” with the other codices instead of “bishop of the city of Tela,” so too in the name of the council Telensis should apparently be corrected to Teleptensis, as a number of codices write it.

### VI.

Ferrandus’s Breviary, however, may raise a substantial difficulty. In it this council is cited ten times—in numbers 3, 4, 6, 16, 65, 68, 130, 138, 174, and 218—but nowhere is it called Teleptensis or Telensis; instead it is called Zellensis or Tiellensis.

Only two copies of this Breviary have so far been found: the Trecensis and the Corbeiensis. In the Trecensis, as Baluzius noted, it is always called Zellensis, except in number 3, where Cellensis is written; there it appears that, through a scribal error, C was taken for Z. In the Corbeiensis it is always Tiellensis, with the exception of number 3, where the word is mutilated to ellensis.

If other copies of the same work, which we searched for in vain in Roman and other Italian libraries, could be found somewhere, we might determine which reading was more correct. Since only the two copies mentioned are available, there seems to be no doubt that Zellensis is the better reading in the Trecensis manuscript, from Zella, which Strabo lists among the cities of Byzacena in book XVII. Through an easy error, the letter Z was changed into Ti in the Corbeiensis manuscript, producing Tiellensis.

Baluzius attributes this to the custom of the Africans. He proves that they were accustomed to exchange T for Z from the fact that where Crabbus reads in the codices of Liberatus the African, chapter 13, “Atticus Zellensis,” three other very old books, which he himself compared with Liberatus’s Breviary, consistently have “Atticus Tallensis.”

Since Baluzius considers the heading “Council of Teleptum” to be genuine, yet does not think that the reading Zellensis can be rejected on Ferrandus’s authority, he believes that the two readings can be reconciled if we say that Zella in the province of Byzacena belonged to the diocese of the bishop of Teleptum and that the council was held there. Ferrandus would then have called it Zellensis because it was genuinely held at Zella, or in the church of the people of Zella; while the superior codices call it Teleptensis because Zella belonged to the bishopric of Teleptum.

He compares this to the manner in which Loaisa called Tarraconensian the council held in the time of King Sisebut at Egarra in the province of Tarragona, while Sirmondus called Magalonensian the council held at Juncaria in the territory of Maguelonne.

Nor are ancient examples lacking. The synod held by Saint Hilary at Justinianum in the territory of Orange is called Justianensis, after the place of the synod, in the headings appended to the letter of John II to Caesarius; but in most collections it is called Arausica or Arausicana, after the episcopal see under which Justinianum lay.

### VII.

Baluzius’s opinion, however, is not at all satisfactory. For at the beginning of the fifth century there were two distinct bishoprics, Teleptensis and Zellensis. This becomes perfectly clear from the Carthaginian conference held with the Donatists in the year 411, shortly before our council.

There two Donatians are mentioned: one in chapter 121, Donatianus, bishop of the Church of Teleptum; the other near the end of chapter 135, Donatianus, bishop of the people of Zella. Baluzius combines these two into a single Donatianus who was simultaneously bishop of Teleptum and Zella. But this is incorrect. For two subscriptions to the same mandate in the same conference distinctly establish two bishops of the same name, one of Zella and the other of Teleptum, just as two Donatians are also named in our council.

Moreover, in the conference cited, two Donatist bishops opposed to the Catholics are likewise listed: Bellicius in the city of Teleptum, chapter 198, and Natalicus in Zella, chapter 163. So that no one may perhaps wonder whether Natalicus is called bishop of Zella through some error and whether Telensis should be read instead, it will be enough to note that in the same conference, chapter 208, Felix is called a Donatist bishop of Telensis.

If, therefore, there were two distinct bishoprics at Teleptum and Zella, Zella certainly did not belong to the bishopric or diocese of Teleptum. Consequently, Baluzius’s reconciliation, resting upon a false hypothesis, cannot be accepted. What, then?

### VIII.

The two codices—the Thuaneus and the royal codex formerly belonging to Saint Peter of Poitiers—which state that the council was held at Teleptum, have the following in their preface:

> When the council had been assembled in the church of the Apostles of the people of Teleptum, the blessed Father Donatianus, bishop of the first see and of the city of Teleptum, had taken his seat, etc.

What is the meaning of this repetition of the same word, Teleptensis, once with the word “people” and once with the word “city”? If the council had been held at Teleptum, the text would certainly have said:

> When the council had been assembled in the church of the Apostles of the city, or people, of Teleptum,

and afterward:

> of the same city, or people.

The word Teleptensis, therefore, which cannot be separated from Donatianus, the bishop of that same city, was incorrectly written in the designation of the Church. The place of the council is consequently recognized as different from Teleptum by the very manner in which the passage was written.

Since, then, the word Teleptensis must first be removed and another place-name substituted, and since the other codices commonly give Telensis instead of Teletensis, the name Telensis cannot be substituted, because Tela belongs to the proconsular province. Accordingly, following the Trecensis codex of Ferrandus, we think that Zellensis should be substituted. Through the customary African change of the letter Z into T, Telensis prevailed in most codices. Nor should this scribal lapse be considered incredible.

For Natalicus the Donatist, whom we learned from the Carthaginian conference cited above to have been bishop of Zella, appears to be the same Natalicus who subscribed to the pseudo-synod of Cabarsus. Baluzius compared five codices of that synod, but in them, through a similar error, he is called a bishop of Telensis.

Just as the reading in one codex of the conference mentioned above is better than that in those five codices—for Felix, as we have seen, was the bishop of Telensis—so the reading of the one Trecensis codex is better than that of the others, which prefer Telensis. Unless this name is understood as written for Zellensis, it cannot suit a synod of Byzacena.

Add another observation, which will confirm our opinion to no small degree. Although the codices of this council belong to different collections, they all contain the same fragment of the same synod and therefore derive from one and the same source and exemplar, in which the synod was first transcribed in a mutilated form. No collector except this first one had the complete synod before his eyes; from it he excerpted this fragment together with the letter of Siricius, and the others worked from his copy.

Ferrandus, however, found the complete synod in an African codex of the province of Byzacena, together with other synods of that province. For this reason he cites several other canons from the same council that are absent from the fragment mentioned above. There are therefore two sources for this council: one in the manuscript collections of canons, and another in Ferrandus’s copies.

The first source, which passed into the manuscript collections, became so corrupted in its various readings concerning the name of the place that it is impossible to determine what had been written in the first original from which the cited collections descended. Hence it is not surprising that, amid such a variety of readings, none is found that is entirely free from difficulty.

The second source, represented by Ferrandus’s copies, was less corrupted and preserved in the Trecensis codex a reading sufficiently suitable for us. Since it agrees extremely well with the context, it ought to be accepted.

[Col. 1096A] But when publishing the fragment itself, we had to follow the codices in which it was transcribed. We therefore did not wish to emend the text from Ferrandus; instead, we preferred, with most of the manuscripts, the reading Telensis, which departs less from the more correct reading and can reasonably be thought to have been written for Zellensis.

In this way, Quesnellus’s arguments based on the differing name of the synod and on the variant and corrupt readings of the codices are sufficiently refuted. Those arguments cannot prevent us from considering the council genuine, since it is supported by the testimony of so many codices and collections, as well as by Ferrandus.

If a document were immediately to be accused of fabrication whenever corrupt or even contradictory readings were found in it—readings that cannot all be accepted together—then nearly all writers and documents would be ruined. It is the duty of scholars, whenever they find variant readings in different manuscripts, to remove those that present an obvious error and sometimes to extract the more correct reading from the errors themselves.

# CHAPTER TWO

The Breviary of Ferrandus, which cites the canons of the Council of Zellum from the letter of Pope Siricius, is defended against the charge of interpolation. The second chapter of Quesnellus’s dissertation examined.

[Col. 1096B]

### I.

Quesnellus seeks to weaken and, if possible, remove the authority of Ferrandus the deacon, which above all supports the authenticity of the Council of Zellum, by trying to show that his Breviary, in which that synod is cited ten times, has been interpolated. Observe, however, how feeble are the conjectures he employs.

First, he brings forward certain blemishes in the work which he thinks are present in numbers 103, 105, 110, 111, 112, 113, 114, 185, 188, 216, and 221. But since these numbers concern other synods and not the Council of Zellum, if the blemishes said to exist in them proved interpolation, they would prove that the entire Breviary had been interpolated and was worthless. No one has ever made such a claim, and Quesnellus himself, we suppose, would not dare to assert it.

If interpolation could be suspected from blemishes of the kind that frequently occur in ancient manuscripts, what work or document would be immune from this judgment?

### II.

But come now: let us see whether those passages which he selected as more important are so defective that they suggest fabrication or interpolation.

Number 103 reads:

> That priests of another region may not celebrate in the presence of priests;

and it cites the Council of Neo-Caesarea, canon 13. Quesnellus objects that this is far removed from the sense of the canon.

Ferrandus used the translation of the Greek synodal canons later adopted by Isidore. The priests whom this translation calls “not of the same region” he called “of another region.” What disagreement of meaning is there in this?

He omits the word “bishop.” But anyone who forbids them to celebrate in the presence of priests is understood all the more to forbid it in the presence of a bishop. In abridging canons, it is permissible to omit certain unnecessary particles.

If, after the words “in the presence of priests,” the name of the city—which appears in the canon—is missing, everyone can easily understand from the context something of this sort that contrasts with the words “of another region”; or certainly the word “city” may have dropped out through the carelessness of the copyists.

Number 105 prohibits deacons from being elected by the judgment of the people, from Laodicea, canon 13, whereas, Quesnellus says, the canon was enacted concerning priests. But Isidore’s translation expressly does not mention priests; rather, it speaks of those who are to be assigned to the ministry of the altar. Ferrandus’s custom is to name deacons where that translation speaks of the ministry of the altar or of ministers of the altar. Compare the Breviary, numbers 109, 111, 112, 113, 114, and 120, where he similarly cites other Laodicean canons.

The words in number 194, “This was also decreed in the Council of Thenis,” are said to be foreign to Ferrandus’s manner of citation and to appear to have been added by some learned person. But since our only source of information about the Council of Thenis is Ferrandus himself, what learned person of a later age could have added that citation?

Moreover, a similar formula of citation occurs in number 52, where we read:

> This was done in another Council of Carthage;

and it is written in such a way that these words cannot be deleted, lest the canon presented there be left without a citation contrary to Ferrandus’s custom.

Several passages of the Breviary caused difficulty because either an error had been made somewhere in recording the numbers of the canons or knowledge of the African canons and councils was not sufficiently secure. Since we have treated this matter with greater exactitude in the Treatise cited above, part IV, chapter 1, on Ferrandus’s Breviary, we seem to have removed, if not all, at least most of the difficulties.

### III.

Quesnellus agrees with Altaserra, who thought that the Council of Zellum, Cellum, and Telum represented not one but several distinct councils in Ferrandus. This was useful to him, so that he would not have to delete every passage in which Zellum is cited, but only those that cite the letter of Siricius from the same council.

His hostility is directed against this one letter, lest it be believed that the African bishops deferred so greatly to papal authority that they recited letters of the Apostolic See in synods and accepted them as a rule of discipline. Altaserra saw that the arguments were not conclusive. It was enough for him to scatter doubts, and therefore he wrote:

> Nor do we decide anything, but merely proceed by conjectures, as one does in an obscure matter—yet by conjectures against which it is not easy to raise contrary arguments of equal strength.

But the conjectures advanced in favor of different synods rest on the less accurate readings of the commonly transmitted texts or on manifest sophisms.

Three names are put forward: Zellensis, Cellensis, and Telensis. Telensis is nowhere found in Ferrandus’s manuscripts. The Corbeiensis codex has Tiellensis; the Trecensis gives Cellensis only once, but Zellensis nine times. Since no city called Tiella is found, whereas Zella was situated in Byzacena, we acknowledge that the reading of the Trecensis codex is the more correct and that Tiellensis in the Corbeiensis was written for Zellensis.

See what we observed on this matter in chapter 1, no. 6. Moreover, of the nine passages in the Trecensis codex in which Zellensis is consistently read, the single passage in number 3, where Cellensis was written, must certainly be corrected. Thus only one name of the council remains, namely Zellensis; and one corrupt citation does not justify suspecting a Council of Cellum.

Nor is it generally true that whenever Zellensis is mentioned, the words “from the letter of Pope Siricius” are immediately added. For in numbers 16, 65, 68, and 218, Zellensis is cited without any mention of the letter of Siricius, just as occurs in number 3, where Cellensis is corruptly written for Zellensis.

Why, then, is the letter of Siricius not cited in these passages, although it is mentioned in five others, and why are canons indicated that generally cannot be referred to the letter of Siricius? The reason is that the canons of the council itself are being cited. If they are absent from the commonly transmitted fragment, there can be no doubt that they existed in the complete acts.

For, as we noted in the preceding chapter, the complete council was not transcribed in the manuscript collections; only a fragment was transmitted, as will be clear from the reading itself. In that portion which is missing from the cited collections, the canons reported by Ferrandus had been inserted.

An excessively curious question is raised: why did the Council of Zellum enact two canons reported by Ferrandus in numbers 3 and 16, when similar statements are found in the letter of Siricius; and why did Ferrandus, in those same numbers, not append “from the letter of Siricius,” as he does elsewhere?

If no reason can be given for the enactment of these canons because the complete acts of the council, which are missing, cannot be examined, does that compel us to posit a council distinct from the one in question? None of these conjectures, therefore, proves that there were several distinct councils.

## IV.

[Cols. 1098A–1099B]

Nor do the conjectures by which Quesnellus accuses the five citations from Siricius’s letter, presented under five numbers in the *Breviatio*, provide any stronger proof. He believes that the first citation from that same letter, under no. 4, should be expunged because of the mutilated and corrupt reading that Quesnellus adopted in his edition of the letter itself. But if it is read as we gave it in full from our manuscripts in chapter 62, his entire argument vanishes. Even if Siricius’s letter does not contain everything expressed by Ferrandus’s words, Ferrandus does not cite one letter of Siricius alone under no. 4, but the canons of several councils; according to his practice, it is enough if at least some portion is found in the cited letters, provided that all the portions are brought together from the whole body of the citations.

Indeed, not all the elements of Ferrandus’s entry under the same number are found in Laodicean canon 12, Antiochene canon 19, and the other sources cited under that number; yet for that reason these citations of those councils and canons are not considered interpolated. Now, in the first canon of Siricius, according to the reading that we established from the manuscript codices, it is decreed that no one may ordain without the knowledge of the apostolic see—that is, of the primate. The consent or confirmation of the primate, which Ferrandus’s *Breviatio* expresses, is therefore sufficiently prescribed. The words “or of the primate” were inserted in Ferrandus’s text because of Siricius’s letter and the Council of Carthage under Genethlius, since in none of the other synods that he cites does any mention of a primate occur.

## V.

Quesnellus presents as an unquestionable interpolation and fabrication in no. 6 of Ferrandus’s *Breviatio* the following passage: “That one bishop may not ordain a bishop, except the Church of Rome.” Although the final three words, “except the Church of Rome,” are not found in Siricius’s letter, the citation of that same letter—whose first part agrees with the canon—cannot therefore be regarded with suspicion. What, moreover, those three words imply is explained in different ways by different authors, as may be seen in Baluzius, *Dissertatio de concilio Teleptensi*, p. 1352. Even if no probable explanation is judged available, those words cannot for that reason be deemed additional and inserted into Ferrandus’s text. How many passages in other writers admit of difficult explanation, yet are not for that reason branded as interpolations? Furthermore, those words are of such a kind that they could not easily be understood and explained by any scholar. Since, then, they present equal difficulty whether one supposes them written by Ferrandus or inserted by someone else, there is no reason to remove them from Ferrandus, to whom the manuscripts attribute them.

## VI.

To affirm that the entire text of no. 6 is also an addition, including the part that forbids one bishop to ordain a bishop, merely because this prohibition may seem useless and superfluous after no. 4 prescribed that a bishop be ordained by three bishops, with the consent of the others expressed in writing and with the confirmation of the metropolitan or primate, and after no. 5 required that additional bishops besides the three be added to the ordination of a bishop if anyone should object—to affirm, I say, that this text is additional for that reason is highly sophistical and captious.

Each of these numbers, or abbreviated canons, has something peculiar in its complete formulation by which it can properly be distinguished. Ferrandus, of course, commonly distinguishes by separate numbers canons that agree in one respect but differ in another.

## VII.

Quesnellus admits that the three other citations, under nos. 130, 138, and 174, contain nothing false. Nevertheless, he thinks that the entire entries, or canons, cited there from Siricius’s letter should be expunged, because no. 130 compresses two decrees into one and substitutes “woman” for “widow”; while the canons given under nos. 138 and 174 seem superfluous, since similar canons are described elsewhere in the same *Breviatio*. We have sufficiently refuted this latter argument in the preceding section.

The objections offered to exclude no. 130 are so trivial that it is tiresome even to reject them. What absurdity is there in compressing two canons of the same letter of Siricius into one and presenting them under a single number? Does Ferrandus not usually join together in one entry the canons of several councils that bear on the same matter? Since Siricius added after the word “woman,” by way of explanation, “that is, a widow,” as we printed it from the better manuscripts, it is clear that Ferrandus did not substitute “woman” for “widow,” but thought that the explanatory phrase “that is, a widow” could be omitted for the sake of abbreviation. What if the words “that is, a widow” are a gloss inserted into the text, as P. Coustantius believed? See his note 27.

It is therefore clear how slight are all the arguments that Quesnellus proposed in chapter 2 in order to deprive the Council of Zella and Siricius’s letter of Ferrandus’s authority.

## VIII.

From all this it is finally evident how bold is his inference at the end of the same chapter: from such weak conjectures he brought under suspicion not only the citations of the Council of Zella but the entire Ferrandian *Breviatio*, saying that it remained uncertain into which parts the impostor’s hand had intruded.

It is certain, as Baluzius aptly noted on p. 1342, that scarcely any work of the ancient writers is so sound, so complete, and so little affected by the hands—not to say of impostors, but even of unskilled copyists—as Ferrandus’s *Breviatio*. When we examined and explained the sequence of the African councils and canons, we found Ferrandus’s citations to cohere so well that scribal error had entered only in two or three numbers. See what we have discussed concerning Ferrandus’s *Breviatio* in *Tractatus*, part IV, chapter 1.

Therefore, just as there is no room for doubt concerning the integrity of the *Breviatio* in its citations of the other African canons and councils, which agree with the commonly transmitted texts, so there is no reason to doubt the integrity of the Council of Zella, which Ferrandus found complete, together with the other synods of the province of Byzacena, in his African Codex; nor is there reason to doubt the citations of that council and of Siricius’s letter, which two very ancient manuscript copies, nearly contemporary with Ferrandus, most clearly vindicate.

Both the manuscript of Troyes, written at least eight hundred years ago, and the Corbie manuscript, written approximately eleven hundred years ago, contain the Council of Zella and Siricius’s letter cited by Ferrandus, just as they contain his citations of the other African councils. Against such authority, says Baluzius, if Quesnellus is to prevail, he must produce at least one ancient copy of that *Breviatio* in which no mention of the Council of Zella and Siricius’s letter is found. Otherwise, we shall retain the antiquity that we have seen attacked only by the lightest sophistries, and reject the novelty.

# CHAPTER III

## The Fragment of the Council of Zella Is Rescued from the Censure of Fabrication. The Third Chapter of Quesnellus’s Dissertation Is Refuted.

[Cols. 1099C–1102D]

### I.

Once Ferrandus’s *Breviatio* has been vindicated—in which the Council of Zella is cited ten times—the authority of Ferrandus sufficiently establishes the **αὐθεντία** [authenticity] of that council, and the entire effort by which Quesnellus hopes to demonstrate that its fragment is fabricated is seen to be futile.

The fragment itself, which, apart from Siricius’s letter, presents only the preface with the names of the bishops, bears such marks of authenticity that it ought by itself to suffice for people unimpeded by prejudice. For nearly all the names of the bishops are found in the Carthaginian conference held shortly before this council, in the year 411, and the episcopal sees assigned to those bishops in that conference belong to the province of Byzacena.

The bishops listed in the aforementioned preface, apart from the legates of the province of Proconsularis, number thirty-four. The see of only one, Donatianus of Telepte, is specified; the others are given by name alone.

In the Carthaginian conference, however, chapter 126, Januarius—otherwise called Januarianus of Tubulbacum—is named, as are Maximianus of Aquae Regiae, Victor of Baa, Cresconius of Timion, Jocundus of Sufetula, Sopater of Tambala, Fortunius, or Fortunatus, of Capsa, and Felix of Segermes; chapter 127 names Secundus of Ruspe, Romanus of Leptiminus, Tutus of Melcita, and Donatus of Tisilita; chapter 128, Geta of Jubaltiana, Julianus of Tasfaltum, and Terciolus of Cillium; chapter 133, Secundianus of Ermania, Restitutus of Muzuca, and Eunomius of Marazana; chapter 135, another Donatianus, distinct from the one of Telepte, of Zella; and chapter 120 calls Latonius bishop of Tenita. All were bishops of the province of Byzacena.

The others were either absent from the conference or had been raised to the episcopate after it. Moreover, some of these bishops are recorded in the *Codex Ecclesiae Africanae* among the Byzacene legates sent to other plenary councils of the same period. Geta of Jubaltiana was present as legate at the synod of 403; Cresconius of Timion and Jocundus of Sufetula at the synod of 418; and Jocundus together with Maximianus of Aquae at the synod of 419.

In Aurelius of Carthage’s letter to the bishops of Byzacena and Arzugitana, written in the same year, 419, Januarius—otherwise called Januarianus—and Felix are named immediately after Donatianus the primate, just as they are listed first in our council.

Does not this remarkable agreement among the Byzacene bishops, between the fragment of the Council of Zella and the Carthaginian conference, as well as the acts of other African synods of the same period, demonstrate the authenticity of the fragment? No impostor who had inserted the bishops’ names into the fragment merely from his imagination could by chance have achieved such agreement. To imagine an impostor so industrious and so well supplied with rare documents that he could distinguish the names of so many Byzacene bishops—mixed together with others and not identified by provincial indications in the conference—from those who were not Byzacene, and then copy them from there, is mere dreaming.

You therefore have, in support of the **αὐθεντία** of this Council of Zella, several ancient canon collections, some of which reach back to the beginning of the sixth century; you have the testimony of Ferrandus, deacon of the Church of Carthage, who used the African Codex of Canons; and you have the preface itself, that is, the catalogue of the bishops identified in the preface, which agrees with other documents of the same period. Whether Quesnellus’s conjectures can weaken even slightly such substantial evidence of authenticity must now be examined.

### II.

We refuted the first conjecture, drawn from the name of the council, in chapter 1, where among other things we showed that it rested on a false hypothesis. Moreover, Zella, which Strabo places in Byzacena, was at this time not so insignificant as Quesnellus supposes. The Carthaginian conference of 411 belongs to this period; from it we learn that Zella had two bishops, one Catholic and the other Donatist, as we noted in the same chapter, no. 7.

### III.

Second, he objects that it is improbable that a synod was held in the province of Byzacena on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, when a universal council was to be celebrated on the Kalends of May. On the contrary, since legates had to be chosen and sent to the universal or plenary council—see the note in dissertation 13, no. 29—by the synods of each African province, an earlier synod of Byzacena was necessary to appoint its own legates.

Even if the fragment of this synod presents only Siricius’s letter, it does not follow that the letter alone was discussed. For the fragment is mutilated not only at the end, but also omits something after the preface, as the formula “and the rest” indicates; we supplied the missing portion from the manuscripts.

### IV.

Why Vincentius and Fortunatianus, legates of the province of Proconsularis, were present at a synod of Byzacena—Quesnellus raises this as his third objection—is unknown because the acts are defective.

Although provincial cases were ordinarily examined by the bishops of each province, nothing prevented the legates of the neighboring province of Proconsularis from being summoned or sent to the synod of Byzacena for some particular reason: either because a matter had arisen that in some way affected both provinces, or because the legates sent from the Proconsular synod had received instructions concerning something to be advanced at the synod of Byzacena.

That this was not foreign to African discipline is proved by the decree of the Council of Carthage of 405, in Dionysius Exiguus, chapter 94: “Legates and letters are to be sent to Mizo, the primate of Byzacena, for the purpose of directing the legation freely” —that is, a legation whose arrangements were to be determined by the provincial council.

These same legates of the province of Proconsularis, Vincentius and Fortunatianus, are also reported to have been present shortly beforehand at the Byzacene synod of Thysdrus, which Ferrandus vindicates from the charge of fabrication while citing its canons.

### V.

Quesnellus wishes it to be an indication of falsehood under no. 4 that two legates are introduced as speaking together: “Vincentius and Fortunatianus said.” But what is more common in other African councils than this formula: “Honoratus and Urbanus, bishops, said”; “Lucianus and Silvanus, bishops, said”?

He adds that the legates requested that Siricius’s letters be read, but that only one was read. Since the acts of the synod are mutilated, there is nothing surprising if one of the two letters is missing.

He observes the legates’ words: “Even when we were at Thysdrus, as your memorial recollection recalls to me.” By this, he says, they imply that the same bishops of our synod had also been present at Thysdrus—as though, according to him, bishops of one province could have attended the synods of another province.

He is playing with the hypothesis by which he assumes that our synod was held at Telepte in the province of Proconsularis. But if this synod is identified with Ferrandus’s Council of Zella, it will be clear that the bishops of the same province of Byzacena first met at Thysdrus and then at Zella.

### VI.

Quesnellus’s fifth argument collapses if it is supposed that the first author who extracted this fragment from the complete acts of the synod and inserted it into his collection did so only for the purpose of adding to his collection Siricius’s letter, which he had been able to find only in those acts. For that reason he omitted the canons of the same synod cited by Ferrandus, as well as other material that did not serve his purpose.

The second letter of Siricius, mentioned in the same fragment, may have been omitted by the compiler at this point because it was already known to him from another source and therefore did not need to be copied from this synod. Indeed, in his note to Siricius’s sixth letter, P. Coustantius considers this letter—addressed “to the Orthodox throughout the various provinces” and transmitted through the Isidorian and an older Hispanic collection—to be the other letter that was read at this council.

### VII.

“It is certain,” Quesnellus adds as his sixth point, “that in that period the Africans governed their churches according to the canons of their own synods and did not allow laws of ecclesiastical discipline to be imposed upon them from overseas regions.”

Here we must recall what Quesnellus himself established in chapter 1: “There can be no doubt that the African Church always rendered the apostolic see, and its statutes, the honor that was owed.”

But, we ask, in what way did it render that owed honor to those same statutes if it did not allow laws of ecclesiastical discipline to be imposed upon it from overseas regions? Did not Tertullian, professing the observance of the African churches toward the Roman Church, write in *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 36: “You have Rome, from which authority is available to us also”?

Nor was this true only in matters of faith, but also in disciplinary laws. Some documents of this fact, among many that have perished, still survive; and by them what he presented as certain is proved false.

We transcribe the words of Baluzius (*De Synodo Teleptensi*, p. 1349):

“If that rule was then certain, why, at that very time, did the African bishops, in synods held under the consulship of P. C. Flavius Stilicho and of Vincentius and Flavitus, decree that a legate should be sent and letters written to Pope Anastasius and to Venerius, bishop of Milan, asking them to moderate a certain decree of some Western synod that was burdening the African churches?

“Why did that same synod, held under the consulship of Vincentius and Flavitus, after the letters of Anastasius had been read—letters that had established certain measures against the African Donatists—judge that thanks should be given to God because He had deigned to inspire that excellent and holy bishop with such pious concern for the members of Christ, although they were separated by different lands but united in the one structure of the body?

“Why did the African bishops assembled at Carthage under the consulship of Stilicho II and Anthemius confirm by their decisions the decree of Pope Innocent that bishops should not easily travel overseas?

“Finally, why, in the plenary council of Africa held at Carthage in the secretary’s office of the Basilica of Faustus, under the consulship of Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII, at which 217 bishops were present, did the bishops, after establishing the canon of the sacred Scriptures, decree that the overseas churches should be consulted for confirmation of this canon?”

Since, then, at this time the African bishops showed such respect for the authority of the apostolic see, who could be surprised that they wished the letters of Siricius, filled with excellent decrees, to be read at the synods of Thysdrus and Zella?

We may add one example from the Council of Carthage of 525. Although it belongs to a later period, it nevertheless displays the same zeal for the discipline of earlier times. In its second session, there are read—*Concilia*, vol. V, Venetian edition, p. 790—documents of the Church of Arles concerning the freedom of the monastery of Lérins.

If the Fathers of that council did not hesitate, in order to grant equal freedom to a monastery in the province of Byzacena, to produce and insert in the acts documents from Gaul, there is much less reason to doubt that the Fathers of the synods of Thysdrus and Zella read and accepted the letters of Siricius, especially since those letters established no new decrees but restored ancient ones, as the pontiff himself expressly states in the preface:

“It has pleased us to issue such letters—not letters imposing any new commands, but letters by which we desire that those things which, through the negligence and indolence of some, have been neglected, should be observed.”

### VIII.

Quesnellus infers a seventh indication of falsity from the fact that the legates of Pope Boniface did not cite these decrees of Siricius, received in two African councils, at the Council of Carthage in 419.

But who could assert that those same legates, who had come from Rome to Africa, knew what had been done in the two synods of the province of Byzacena in the preceding year? Moreover, even if they had known it, what use would it have been, in the case of Apiarius’s appeal and of the Sardican canons inscribed under the name of Nicaea, which were the matters under discussion, to produce those synods and Siricius’s letters, in which nothing concerning those issues appears?

Since there was no controversy concerning the authority of the apostolic see, which the Africans had professed even in the most recent documents mentioned in the preceding section, there was no reason to cite the acts of those synods together with Siricius’s letters in order to vindicate that authority. Nor was there any reason to mention the latest delegation of that same see, by which Saint Augustine and other African bishops, obeying the authority of Zosimus, were compelled in 418 to travel to Mauretania so that certain needs of the churches might be settled by the authority of that see, as Possidius reports in *Life of Augustine*, chapter 14. See also Augustine’s letter 190, no. 1.

### IX.

Whether the letter of Siricius attached to the fragment is fabricated, so that Quesnellus derived from this a further argument for the falsity of the fragment, will become clear in the following chapter, where, while examining his conjectures, we shall vindicate the **αὐθεντία** [authenticity] of the letter itself.

Once the authenticity of the fragment has thus been established, it will also be clear that Quesnellus’s account—by which he invents the occasion and purpose for fabricating the fragment—must be counted among his dreams. If something had to be fabricated in order to assert the right of appeal over the African churches, it would not have been this Council of Zella or Siricius’s letter, in which there is nothing in favor of that right; indeed, nothing is decreed that does not agree with the common discipline accepted by the Africans themselves. Rather, an entirely different document, favorable to the right of appeal, would have had to be concocted by the impostor.

# CHAPTER IV

## The Letter of Pope Siricius Attached to the Fragment Is Freed from Suspicion of Fabrication. Chapters 4 and 5 of Quesnellus’s Dissertation Are Refuted.

[Cols. 1103A–1106A]

### I.

It is especially remarkable that, in order to prove the fabrication of Siricius’s letter, Quesnellus first brought forward the first canon, from which its authenticity is most strongly confirmed. He saw that he could accomplish this only by following the corrupt reading found in a single, inferior-quality Oxford manuscript, namely: “That no primates should dare to ordain without the knowledge of the apostolic see.”

He adduces many arguments to persuade us that this reading is preferable. But in vain. For all the other manuscripts, both older and better, insert after the words “of the apostolic see” the phrase “that is,” and this addition plainly shows that we should read not *primates* but *primatis*, as the very ancient Corbie manuscript, the Thuaneus, Vatican manuscript 1340, and other codices display:

“That no one should dare to ordain without the knowledge of the apostolic see, that is, of the primate.”

This reading, which overturns Quesnellus’s entire argument, is not only the best reading but also sufficiently demonstrates the **αὐθεντία** of the letter itself. P. Coustantius correctly perceived that this letter was first addressed to the suburbicarian or Italian bishops and written for their benefit, so that no one should dare to ordain without the knowledge of the apostolic see, with “a bishop” understood.

When the same letter was communicated to the Africans, they adapted the same decree to the usage and discipline of their churches by adding an interpretation of “the apostolic see”: “that is, of the primate.” This was certainly not foreign to the pontiff’s intention, as the competent interpreter of Siricius, Innocent, proves. Repeating the same canon in his letter to Victricius of Rouen, he adapted it to Gallican discipline as follows:

“That no one should dare to ordain without the knowledge of the metropolitan bishop,”

where, just as in Siricius, “a bishop” is understood.

African discipline—that no one should ordain a bishop without consulting the primate—is sufficiently attested by the Council of Carthage under Genethlius, canon 12, vol. XI of the Venetian edition of the councils, p. 1248, and by the *Codex Ecclesiae Africanae*, canon 13.

When, under no. 4, Ferrandus required the confirmation of the metropolitan or primate in the ordination of a bishop, he cited the word “primate” not only from the Council of Carthage, title 10, but also from the Council of Zella, drawing it from the letter of Pope Siricius; hence he found the reading *primatis* in his own African Codex as well.

If Siricius had originally addressed this letter to the Africans, there is no doubt that, adapting himself to African discipline, he would have written *primatis*—“of the primate”—while omitting the words “of the apostolic see,” just as Innocent, writing to the Gauls, suppressed the words “of the apostolic see” and substituted “of the metropolitan bishop.” But the fact that the words “of the apostolic see” remain intact and are followed by “that is, of the primate” indicates not the pontiff himself but someone else who did not wish to delete anything from the papal text and thought merely that an explanation suited to African custom should be added.

Since the explanation “of the primate,” rather than “of the metropolitan,” was added, it is recognized as having been supplied by the Africans themselves. Among them, the older bishops of each province alone occupied the position of metropolitan; they were called primates.

Thus it is not fabrication but the authenticity of the letter received by the Africans that is most strongly confirmed. No one who was not an African would have thought of adding the explanation “of the primate”; he would more likely have added another explanation adapted to the usage of the other churches, namely, “of the metropolitan.”

### II.

The other objection that Quesnellus raises in chapter 5 from these same decrees of Siricius as reproduced in Innocent’s letter to Victricius is dissolved by an observation of Baluzius. He noted that Innocent himself, in his letter to Exsuperius, chapter 1, copied his own words from chapter 9 of his more recent letter to Victricius.

It should therefore seem less surprising if he excerpted certain passages from the older letters of his predecessor Siricius. Just as, in his letter to Exsuperius, he made no mention of his own letter to Victricius, so in the letter to Victricius he did not think it necessary to cite Siricius’s letter—especially since he did not take everything from it word for word, but expressed some things in different and clearer language.

Indeed, so far is it from following from the agreement between Innocent’s and Siricius’s letters in these decrees that Siricius’s letter was copied by an impostor from Innocent’s letter, that the opposite rather follows: Innocent’s letter was derived from Siricius’s. P. Coustantius made this excellent observation in his note to Siricius’s fifth letter, no. 4:

“I trust that those will be persuaded of this who observe that what requires explanation in Siricius’s letter is for the most part supplied in Innocent’s letter, so that Siricius plainly appears the author of his words, and Innocent their interpreter.”

For it is not probable that someone who wished to compose a letter from Innocent’s words and attribute it to Siricius would have omitted some of Innocent’s words that appear necessary for making the meaning clear. Coustantius carefully indicated in the notes which passages Innocent added or altered for the sake of explanation.

### III.

Quesnellus adds that it resembles a dream that the preface of the letter states that these letters were given by the Roman synod especially on behalf of the Africans:

“Because at present they were unable to be present, either through bodily illness or because of worn-out age.”

But this dream vanishes if the letter was first addressed not to the Africans but to bishops subject to the Roman synod, so that these words are understood to refer to them.

He then declares it astonishing that the letter begins:

“When very many brethren had assembled together,”

as though these words indicated an accidental synod. This interpretation, however, is far more astonishing. The words signify nothing accidental; rather, they are a common formula used by many African synods, from which no one has suspected anything accidental.

The Council of Carthage of 397 begins after the chronological heading as follows:

“At Carthage, in the secretary’s office of the Basilica of Restituta, when Aurelius the bishop had taken his seat together with the bishops.”

The same wording appears in the preface to other African synods in Dionysius Exiguus.

### IV.

Quesnellus subjects two matters in Siricius’s first decree to criticism. First, he considers the words that he calls excessively harsh—“No one should dare”—incredible as words used by Siricius to Africans. Let anyone who wishes read the complete text, and he will find nothing but the utmost fairness in those words.

Moreover, what if the letter was first written to the suburbicarian bishops and later reached the Africans only through communication?

### V.

The second matter at which he takes issue is the reasoning of the first decree:

“For the judgment is complete when it is confirmed by the opinion of many.”

In the preceding decree, only the primate had been mentioned. “Who,” Quesnellus asks, “would call a primate many people? Who would say that a judgment is confirmed by someone’s opinion?”

If this is not the most inept kind of quibbling, what ever could be? When Siricius requires that no one dare ordain without the knowledge of the primate, he includes not only the primate but also the ordainer—or rather, the ordainers. For immediately, in the second canon, Siricius commands that one bishop should not presume to ordain a bishop. There, then, is the judgment of many.

The same thing is read in Innocent’s letter to Victricius. Even if the first and second canons, which are divided in Siricius’s manuscripts and printed books, are better connected there, this causes no difficulty: both because the particle “for” in each place refers back to what precedes, and because this division in Siricius is attributable to the copyists rather than to Siricius himself.

We have retained the reading “is consecrated” with the manuscripts of our collection, but in the notes we observed that the copies of other collections more correctly have “is confirmed,” as it is read in Innocent.

### VI.

Much more captious is Quesnellus’s inference from the words of the second canon, on account of the alleged arrogance: as though one bishop were permitted to ordain a bishop provided that it were done without arrogance.

P. Coustantius aptly notes that this mode of argument proves nothing more than the argument by which some men, in the very age of Siricius, wished to conclude from Matthew 1:25—“And he did not know her until she had given birth to her firstborn son”—that Joseph knew Mary after Christ’s birth.

Who does not see that, in Siricius’s words just cited, the vice of arrogance is attributed to the bishop who would presume to ordain a bishop alone? The possibility of any exception is entirely removed by the reason that Siricius immediately adds:

“For this was established and defined in the Council of Nicaea,”

where he refers to the fourth Nicene canon, which requires at least three bishops as ordainers.

### VII.

Quesnellus claims that the manifest malice or ignorance of the impostor becomes evident in no. 7 from the words of the ninth canon:

“We urge that priests and Levites should not have intercourse with their wives,”

and likewise from the words:

“I exhort, I admonish, I ask,”

as though, he says, priests and Levites were not bound by the law of continence.

Everyone can see how much this manner of interpretation favors the innovators of our own times who are hostile to clerical continence and have similarly distorted this testimony of Siricius. This is clear from the words of Georgius Calixtus, which Quesnellus himself transcribed at the end of his dissertation.

Quesnellus did not do this in order to support the heterodox, but in order to prove the text fabricated and thereby deprive them of Siricius’s authority. But since neither this nor his other arguments shake the authenticity of the letter, he ought to have refuted that interpretation, which is utterly trivial, rather than approved it.

Who, in fact, is unaware that Siricius could have used those words in order to stir priests and Levites to the law of continence, by persuading, exhorting, admonishing, and asking them? Is there a place for asking, admonishing, exhorting, and persuading only in matters of counsel, which are left to free choice?

In the matter of continence, of which Siricius is speaking, the same pontiff clearly indicates in the preface that these words do not have the force of mere counsel: he declares that the things to which he exhorts are not counsels but commands, and commands not newly established but established by the apostolic constitution of the Fathers.

Moreover, at the end he adds:

“If anyone, puffed up in the mind of his flesh, should wish to depart from this canonical rule, let him know that he will be excluded from our communion and will suffer the punishments of Gehenna.”

Who could fail to infer from this a grave command? No one would judge that someone should be excluded from apostolic communion and punished with the penalties of Gehenna for neglecting mere counsels.

That this manner of speaking was not foreign to Siricius is proved by Baluzius from letter 6 to the Orthodox bishops, chapter 3, where he prohibits by the word “admonishing” an abuse that had arisen against the apostolic commands:

“Lest this happen again, I admonish.”

Siricius himself—or, as others prefer, Innocent—in the canons of the Romans to the Gallican bishops uses a similar formula:

“That polluted and faithless men ought not to believe in the mystery of God, I admonish and warn, with the reverence of religion itself urging this.”

Further, in his letter to Exsuperius, Innocent, citing Siricius’s words concerning the law of continence, calls them “the admonitions of the man of blessed memory, Bishop Siricius”; yet he did not consider them counsels, but commands.

### VIII.

Quesnellus’s criticism in no. 8, by which he accuses certain words of Siricius’s letter of being the speech of an uneducated child, as though the author scarcely knew how to express his meaning in writing, and from this infers a sign of fabrication, will be shown by anyone who reads the letter itself to be as trivial and foolish as it is.

It would be tedious to refute it with the many other expressions of the same kind found in other certain letters, both of Siricius himself and of other pontiffs.

### IX.

He likewise makes a rather slighting attack on the words in which it is stated that a priest must at every moment be ready, secure in the purity of cleanliness, lest he either offer the sacrifice (thus we have emended the text from the manuscripts), or be compelled to baptize. This is as though the text said that a priest could at every moment be compelled to offer the sacrifice.

For the obvious meaning of the words is that a priest must at every moment be prepared, because purity is always required, whether he offers the sacrifice or is called to baptize. For the truth of the proposition, it is enough that either of these things may occur at any moment.

### X.

What shall we say of Quesnellus’s observation concerning the final part of the letter, where it is said to have been given at Rome in a council of eighty bishops?

Stephanus Baluzius cites other examples: a letter of Hormisdas to the Emperor Anastasius sent through Theopompus and Severianus; a letter of John II to Justinian Augustus; and two letters of Gregory the Great, each of which is noted at the end as having been given at Rome.

Moreover, what objection is there to the words “in a council of eighty bishops” being displayed at the end, when another letter of Damasus to the bishops of Illyricum bears similar words at its beginning:

“Copy of a synod held at Rome of ninety-three bishops”?

### XI

Finally, the most conclusive argument for the hypothesis seems to Quesnell to be that, although clerical continence was discussed frequently in the councils of Carthage—especially in the synod of the year 419, where, with Faustinus, the legate of the Apostolic See, intervening, the fourth canon on the same subject was repeated from the synod of Genethlius of 391—nevertheless neither Aurelius nor Vincentius and Fortunatianus, who had participated in the councils of Thusdrus and Zella, nor Faustinus himself, the legate of the Roman pontiff, ever made mention of the Council of Zella or of the letter of Siricius, which deals particularly with continence.

But he is mistaken. The letter of Siricius was not mentioned because the sole purpose of the council of 419 was to repeat and confirm the canons of the earlier synods of Carthage or of Africa as a whole. Hence nearly all the canons of the first action, thirty-three in number, were taken either from the synod of Gratus, or from that of Genethlius, or from another synod held under Aurelius in 397. Since, however, the names of the bishops who were present at the synod of 419 were substituted for those of the ancient bishops who had pronounced the canons while intervening in the earlier synods—for example, Augustine, Alypius, and others—the fourth canon is prefaced by the name of Faustinus, the legate of the Apostolic See then present.

Given this purpose of the synod, namely, to restore the ancient canons of the African Church—as was also frequently customary on other occasions—what place was there for citing the letter of Siricius when the canon on continence was being repeated from the synod of Genethlius, since the very repetition of this canon from an earlier council, which nevertheless was not named, had completely served the purpose? No one, therefore, can infer from the omission of any mention of that letter in the synod of 419 that the letter itself was fabricated—not certainly, and indeed not even probably.

### XII

From all this, then, we believe it has been demonstrated more than sufficiently how weak are all the conjectures that Quesnell put forward throughout the preceding dissertation in order to show that the fragment of the Council of Zella and the letter of Siricius attached to it had been fabricated by the artifice of an impostor. Since these have not been assailed by any serious argument, they place on secure footing both the most ancient copies of the various collections and, above all, the *Breviatio* of Ferrandus, which Quesnell foolishly attempted to bring under suspicion.

# SIXTEENTH DISSERTATION

## On the First Use of the Code of Canons of Dionysius Exiguus in the Gallican Regions

Where it is shown that the code was not received before the time of Pope Adrian I and the emperor Charlemagne, and an inquiry is made into which Latin version of the Eastern Canons was in use among the Gauls before that time.

[Col. 1105]

[Col. 1105D] 1013

### I. Why this dissertation has been undertaken

We are undertaking to discuss the use of the Dionysian collection in Gaul: namely, whether, as soon as it began to be used in the Roman Church, or not much later, it was also adopted by the Gallican Churches and approved for use in ecclesiastical legal proceedings; or whether the adoption in Gaul of that code must be deferred until the time of the emperor and king of the Franks, Charlemagne.

In this matter we shall doubtless seem to some people to have exceeded our proper limits and to have departed too far from our purpose. Yet we are not departing from it, since this discussion will make clear what authority the letters of Leo possessed in Gaul: whether they had been received there before the time of Dionysius, or whether they became known in the Gallican regions only through the aid of that code. Moreover, I remember having asserted more than once in the preceding dissertations that the Dionysian code had acquired no authority in Gaul before the time of that emperor.

[Note: Quesnell’s whole position rests on the hypothesis that a code of canons received for use can only be a public code endowed with public authority—or, as he calls it elsewhere, an authorized code. How false this hypothesis is will be seen in the observations appended to this dissertation, chapter 1, nos. 1 and 2.]

So that no one may think that I have said this rashly, I acknowledge that I owe the reader an account of the grounds for my assertion.

Furthermore, since the most illustrious Petrus de Marca, in treating this question, believed that he possessed very strong evidence for his position in a letter of Saint Leo, cited long before Pope Adrian in a Gallican synod, the task of illuminating this difficulty falls to us as part of the work we have undertaken. Finally, since, from a comparison of the ancient code of the Roman Church, which we are publishing, with Gallican discipline, it is evident that our Gallican bishops did not use the Roman Code until the time of Dionysius Exiguus, but their own, it will not be superfluous, nor unwelcome to learned men, to examine with us whether, after Dionysius’s code had been composed, anything was changed in Gaul in the procedure of ecclesiastical judgments. This inquiry will especially benefit from knowing which code of canons the Gallican bishops used—whether the Roman or their own—and continued to use until the age of Charlemagne.

[Note: We proved in the observations on Dissertation 12, chapter 1, that this was not an ancient public code of the Roman Church, but a private collection composed in Gaul.]

Petrus de Marca, in Book III, chapter 4, of *On the Concord of the Priesthood and the Empire*, asserts that he is convinced that use of the Dionysian collection prevailed throughout Gaul as soon as it was published, with the earlier translation having been rejected: first, because it was in use at the Apostolic See, and also because it was commended by its elegance in comparison with the squalor of the old translation, although the Gauls did not entirely abandon the latter. A recent writer on the canonical judgments of bishops adopts this author’s opinion in chapter 4, where he disparages the contrary view and attempts to demolish it by various conjectures.

The contrary position is defended by three men of the highest reputation among students of canonical antiquity: Christophorus Justellus, in the preface to the *Code of the Universal Church*; Jacobus Sirmondus, in the preface to the *Ancient Councils of Gaul*; and Franciscus Florentius, a professor at Orléans, in his dissertation *On the Origin, Art, and Authority of Canon Law*, Part III. We vindicate this position in this brief dissertation as by far the more probable of the two.

Before taking it up, I shall make one or two preliminary remarks. The first is that two matters must be distinguished from each other—matters which some either confuse or wish to join so closely that they regard one as necessarily following from the other. The first is that the letters of the Roman pontiffs, which are called decretals, were occasionally called into use in the ancient synods of Gaul. The second is that the Dionysian collection of those decretals was already received and officially established by the Gallican bishops, from the time when it first began to appear, before the age of Charlemagne.

To deny the first, when it is obvious, would be the height of folly. But it will become clear from what we are now about to say that to infer the second from it is contrary both to reason and to the practice of all the Gallican synods.

The other point that I offer the reader in advance is this: the contrary opinion is so devoid of valid proofs and arguments that we shall show, more clearly than daylight, that all the pieces of evidence its defenders bring forward in its support are entirely opposed to it.

[Note: Whoever reads the observations in chapter 1 will immediately understand whether this is true or false.]

### II. The First Argument, Fivefold, from the Case of Contumeliosus. The Year 534

Our first argument is supplied by the case of Contumeliosus, bishop of Riez in Gaul. When Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, had written about him to Pope John II, he received a reply in which the pontiff indicated that the rigor of the canons was to be maintained against the man who had fallen. “The things that the canons prescribe concerning these matters,” he adds, “we have appended below, so that you may recognize what must be done.”

The apostolic and Antiochene decrees, together with those of Pope Siricius, appended to this letter, were taken from the collection of Dionysius.

[Note: The order of the materials that John appended to his letter is as follows. First, a fragment of the letter of Siricius; then two Apostolic Canons; next—as we learn from our manuscript, Vatican, Palatine 574—one canon of Neocaesarea, which is absent from the printed editions; finally, two Antiochene canons. Although all this proves that John took these materials from the collection of Dionysius, and that the collection was in use among the Romans at that time, it does not prove that it had not yet reached the Gauls, even if Pope John perhaps did not know whether it had reached them.]

Who, then, would believe that John would have been so concerned to send decrees from the Dionysian code unless it had been established that the code itself had not yet been received for use in Gaul? Otherwise, when Caesarius asked what the discipline of the Apostolic See was in this matter, it would have been sufficient for John simply to refer him to the said code. Yet he did not do so.

2. Caesarius would not have needed to inquire of the pontiff about the customs and laws of the Roman Church if the same code of canons had been common to both Churches in the adjudication of ecclesiastical cases.

[Note: Although Dionysius’s code, from which John II excerpted the canons, was then in use at Rome, it need not therefore be regarded as the public code of the Roman Church; see *Treatise on Collections*, Part III, chapter 1. Similarly, even if that same code had passed to the Gauls at this time, it would not thereby have been the public code of the Gallican Church, but a private one, which did not exclude other likewise private codes of canons.
