From his own preconception Quesnell supposes only a public code to have been received for use, although no public code existed either at Rome or in Gaul; see the observations on this dissertation, chapter 1. Several private collections, moreover, were current in Gaul. Whether the Dionysian collection also existed among the Gauls in Caesarius’s time, that is, shortly after Dionysius’s code was published, can neither be affirmed nor denied. To refute Quesnell’s position, however, it suffices to prove that before Charlemagne the Dionysian code was present in Gaul and was sometimes received for use; more on this in the observations.]

Nor should we suppose that the bishops were so negligent that they had not examined whatever canonical codes existed in Gaul before knocking at the archives of another Church. That they in fact did so is shown by the two excerpts appended to the canons sent by John.

What, then, had to be done in this case was already known from the canons of four Gallican synods, which the bishops of Gaul are reported to have excerpted. It was also established by Canon 9 of Nicaea, which the second excerpt contains.

But since Contumeliosus had many patrons who, out of excessive piety, disliked the severity of the holy Fathers—as is recorded in a text attributed by Sirmond to Caesarius himself—and who, through a false sort of piety, were exerting every effort either to prevent Contumeliosus from being sent to a monastery or, at any rate, after not much time had passed, to extort his return to his episcopal rank through excessive pressure hostile to ecclesiastical discipline, Caesarius, firm in discipline, judged that the Apostolic See, whose representative he was, ought to be consulted. In this way he could join its authority to that of the Gallican bishops and make them more certain of what was observed in the Roman Church according to the decrees of councils and Roman pontiffs.

John, Pope, replied to Caesarius (*Letter 6 of Pope John II to Caesarius of Arles*) that it was necessary to preserve the rigor of the canons and that, according to the decrees of the Apostolic See, Contumeliosus ought to be suspended from the episcopate: “And therefore,” he says, “our authority has suspended the aforesaid man from the order of the episcopate.”

[Note: The words “according to the decrees of the Apostolic See” indicate that Contumeliosus was to be suspended on the basis of the decrees of earlier pontiffs. Yet the text quoted immediately afterward—“our authority has suspended”—expresses the authority of John himself, whose decision Caesarius had chiefly sought.]

1017

3. The Gallican excerpts make it clear that the Gallican code differed greatly from the Roman, or Dionysian, code.

[Note: The excerpts sent by Caesarius to John show only that the code from which Caesarius excerpted the canons was the collection containing, among other materials, the Nicene canons in Rufinus’s abridgment and the canons of four Gallican synods. This was not the public code of the entire Gallican Church, for the Nicene canons were preserved in full in other Gallican manuscripts. The collection that presented Rufinus’s abridgments in place of the complete Nicene canons was a particular code, such as we find in Vatican, Palatine 574; see *Treatise on Collections*, Part III, chapter 9. In this collection, besides the Rufinian abridgments, there are also those four councils whose canons Caesarius copied. The letter of Siricius to Himerius is also inserted, but not the Antiochene canons, nor the canons of the other Greek synods. This makes clear how empty are the conjectures that Quesnell introduces below.]

For when the Gauls carefully examined their own code, no other canon appeared apart from Canon 9 of Nicaea and the four Gallican canons. It is therefore necessary to conclude that neither the decretal letter of Pope Siricius to Himerius nor the Apostolic Canons was found in that code; these certainly would not have been omitted.

“But,” you will say, “they did not excerpt the Antiochene canons either, although it is quite probable that those canons were inserted in the Gallican code at that time, or even certain, as is evident from several manuscript copies of Gallican collections.”

Their failure to mention the Antiochene canons was not because those canons were absent from their own codes, but because they were irrelevant to the case being discussed. The question was whether a bishop convicted of a capital crime ought to be deposed and whether he should retain any hope of ever returning to his see. This is not addressed in the Antiochene canons sent by John. Those canons presuppose a bishop who has already been condemned and assert that such a man may not exercise anything pertaining to the sacred ministry, nor have any hope of restoration or opportunity for satisfaction in another synod.

For this reason the Gallicans refrained from excerpting them and contented themselves with the sanction of the Council of Nicaea. Although that canon makes a ruling about crimes committed by bishops before their ordination, it applies with even greater force to crimes committed by those already ordained, as was done by Pope Gelasius I in Letter 9 to the bishops established throughout Lucania, Bruttium, and Sicily.

[Col. 1109C] 4. The difference between the version of the ninth Nicene canon presented by the Gallican excerpt and the Dionysian version clearly declares that the two Churches were using a code different from both of them.

5. The treatise appended to the excerpts, which begins, “Behold, it is most manifestly established,” consistently distinguishes three orders or classes of authorities by which it asserts that the deposition of Contumeliosus was to be decreed.

One is from the code of the Universal Church, another from the Gallican code, and the third from the code of the Roman Church. Or rather, the first two derive from a single Gallican code, which was divided into two parts: the first containing the received Nicene and other Greek canons, the second containing the Gallican canons. Thus the diversity of the codes is clear.

Nor does Caesarius perceive anything else in the decrees sent by Pope John apart from the authority and support of the Apostolic See; he praises this alone when he mentions that excerpt.

### III. The Second Argument, from the Third Council of Orléans, 538

Our second argument comes from the Third Council of Orléans, by which Petrus de Marca seemed to himself to secure irresistible authority for his opinion.

“Conjectures,” he says, “must be supplemented by proof drawn from Canon 3 of the Council of Orléans held in the year 538, where the decrees of Pope Leo concerning the election of metropolitans are put forward. Since these were taken from the letter sent to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, they could not have had the force of decrees among the Gauls unless it were because they had been inserted under the title of decrees in the collection of Dionysius, whose authority the Gallican bishops had embraced.”

Before we discuss what strength this canon contributes to the opinion of our opponents and to our own, it is worthwhile to place it here in full for the reader’s inspection.

#### The Third Canon of the Third Council of Orléans, in the Year of Christ 538

**On the election and ordination of metropolitan and provincial bishops**

Concerning the ordination of metropolitans, it was decided that metropolitans should be ordained by metropolitans, with all their comprovincial bishops present if this can be arranged, so that the privilege of ordaining remains with the metropolitan whom the custom of ordination requires to perform it.

The metropolitan himself, however, is to be elected by the comprovincial bishops, as the decrees of the Apostolic See contain, with the consent of the clergy or the citizens; for it is just, as the Apostolic See itself has said, that he who is to be placed over all should be elected by all.

With respect to the comprovincial bishops who are to be ordained, the election and consent of the metropolitan, clergy, and citizens are likewise to be sought, in accordance with the provisions of the earlier canons.

By these words, “as the decrees of the Apostolic See contain,” that author believes that Leo’s decrees concerning the election of metropolitans are being cited from the letter to Anastasius of Thessalonica. Yet I can scarcely persuade myself of this, if at all. The Fathers of Orléans could not have had any other passage of this letter before their eyes than chapter 6, which is numbered 36 in Dionysius Exiguus. There are several reasons, however, why I do not believe that they cited this chapter.

1. Leo’s purpose seems entirely different from the intention of that synod. The holy pontiff had only this aim: to settle the dispute that had arisen between the vicar of Illyricum and the metropolitan of Epirus, and to reconcile the rights of the latter metropolitan with the privileges of the bishop of Thessalonica in such a way that the authority of both would remain unimpaired.

This will be clear to everyone from an examination of the chapter itself, as well as from the titles prefixed to it by Dionysius and by the editors of the other editions. In the printed editions the title reads:

> That the metropolitan bishop should refer to the bishop of Thessalonica concerning the man elected whom he is about to ordain bishop, and that the provincial bishops should do likewise concerning an elected metropolitan.

The title is the same in Dionysius, both in the list of titles prefixed to the entire collection of decretals and in the title attached to the chapter itself, except that at the beginning it reads, “That the metropolitan of Epirus…” From this the pontiff’s purpose in the decree is disclosed even more clearly: it is aimed chiefly at asserting the right of referral to the bishop of Thessalonica in the ordinations both of metropolitans and of provincial bishops who were situated within the boundaries of the vicariate of Thessalonica.

No one who reads the canon will fail to see that the Council of Orléans had a very different purpose. Here, where it invokes the authority of the Apostolic See, the subject is solely the right of the provincial bishops in the election of the metropolitan and of their comprovincial bishops, together with the consent and vote of the clergy and the people.

2. What the canon chiefly commands in the words cited from the judgment of the Apostolic See is that the consent of the clergy and people not be neglected in the election of metropolitans and comprovincial bishops. To make this more persuasive, the Fathers of the council report not only the authority of the Apostolic See but also the reason it supplied:

> As the decrees of the Apostolic See contain.

And afterward:

> For it is just, as the Apostolic See itself has said, that he who is to be placed over all should be elected by all.

It is probable that both the authority and the reason were taken from the same passage. Certainly they were not taken from the letter to Anastasius, in which that reason does not appear, but rather from the letter to the bishops of the province of Vienne (Letter 10, chapter 5), which contains both in explicit terms:

> Let the priests who are to preside be requested in peace and tranquility. Let the subscription of the clergy, the testimony of the honored men, the consent of the order, and that of the people be secured. He who is to preside over all should be elected by all.

Who, indeed, would believe that that synod took the first authority from one code and the second from another? Yet this is necessary if it is true that the first passage was excerpted from the Dionysian code. The other passage, presented in Leo’s own words, comes from a letter that was never, and is not now, contained in the Dionysian code.

Moreover, if both passages were taken from a single code, that code was not the Dionysian one but another, compiled for Gallican use, which contained the letter to the bishops of Vienne. We have seen several manuscripts of this kind from the libraries of Thuane and Trecopithoe.

And certainly, if the bishops of Orléans had consulted the letter to Anastasius when they mentioned the decrees of the Apostolic See, and if they had wished to append a reason to the authority, they would not have needed to seek it outside that same letter, since in chapter 5, which precedes, Leo supplies a clear reason. It is both more explicit and more forceful:

> Lest a city either reject or hate a bishop whom it did not desire, and become less religious than it ought to be because it was not permitted to have the man it wanted.

It is therefore established that the Fathers of the synod wished to support their decrees with authority not from the letter to Anastasius but from the letter to the bishops of Vienne. And rightly so: they used the letter that had been sent by the Apostolic See to reform the discipline of the Gallican provinces, rather than the letter written to the bishop of Thessalonica, which was concerned with adapting the discipline of those provinces to the privileges of the vicariate.

### IV. Even If They Had Used the Letter to Anastasius, Nothing Would Follow from It

3. Even if we freely grant that the letter to Anastasius of Thessalonica was cited by the Gallican synods, I plainly do not understand how Marca can prove from this that the Dionysian collection had then been received and officially established in Gaul.

First, it would have to be demonstrated that the letter could not have entered Gaul by any means other than through that code; that the Gauls were not permitted to possess the decrees of the Apostolic See transcribed in miscellaneous codes, or to cite the sanctions of other Churches in support and confirmation of their own, unless they had made all the codes of those Churches their own; and finally, that the Gauls could not dignify a letter of the Apostolic See with the title of a decree unless it had been inserted in the Gallican code or received from the Dionysian code.

But who does not see how alien all these assumptions are from the reason and practice of all the Churches, and especially of the Gallican Church, provided that one has examined some of the synods at some time or judged it worthwhile to consult reason itself?

[Note: Here too he recognizes only a public and authorized code; we shall refute this preconception, which he often introduces also in what follows, in the observations.]

[Note: Here he acknowledges several very ancient private collections.]

How many manuscript codes of ancient collections, once copied either for the use of private individuals or for that of particular Churches, contain numerous letters of Roman pontiffs addressed to Easterners and others? Among these we possessed one from the library of the Oratory at Trecopithoe, others from the Thuane library, and especially an excellent one from the library of the Benedictine ascetics at Saint-Germain, which they consider at least nearly as old as the collection of Gelasius.

Furthermore, it was familiar practice among Gallican bishops to cite and even transcribe the canons and decrees of other dioceses, before Dionysius had conceived the idea of composing his collection or any Roman code had been received in Gaul. Likewise, the Spanish bishops often inserted or appended the words of Gallican synods to their own decrees and judged ecclesiastical cases from them, as is evident from the Councils of Ilerda, Valencia, Seville I, and Toledo XII. Yet no one has therefore supposed that the Gallican code was the proper code of the Spanish.

Finally, it seems insulting to the Gauls’ singular devotion to ecclesiastical discipline and the Apostolic See to suppose that they awaited the Dionysian collection in order to obtain some knowledge or copies of the decrees of the Apostolic See, when they so frequently employed the particular councils of the Greeks and the African councils in their own synods.

Now, since this argument has been taken away from Petrus de Marca, it must necessarily support our position. For it is clear that another code, distinct from the Dionysian, was then in use throughout Gaul, and that the letter to the bishops of the province of Vienne was drawn from it.

If the code of Dionysius had even then been known to the Gauls, it would have offered them many more decrees of the Apostolic See about which they remained silent, and which they would easily have preferred to the letter to the bishops of Vienne—a letter that was not found in the officially established code and had not been readily accepted by the Gallican bishops when it was first transmitted to Gaul. All the bishops of the province of Vienne were then asserting the ancient right and custom of their Churches against Hilary of Arles, whom they had always wished, during his lifetime, to use his privileges.

[Note: Quesnell briefly indicates here what he set out more fully in Dissertation 5, Part III. We refuted the same arguments in the Observations on that dissertation, volume II, column 1057 and following columns, printed in larger type.]

### V. The Third Argument, from the Second Council of Tours. The Year 567

The author adduces the Second Council of Tours in support of his proposed date—not in the year of Christ 570, as David thought, but held three years earlier.

“In chapter 21,” he says, “the council Fathers cite the letter of Pope Innocent to Victricius of Rouen and the canons of Milevis.”

The objection of this kind has already been answered fully above, and we shall return to it below when we discuss the letter of that same Innocent to Exsuperius, cited by the Council of Agde.

But that synod not only does not hinder our position; it actually supports it. First, it does not cite that letter as though it had been excerpted from an officially received code. Hence it does not call it a decree, as is usually done when such writings are taken from a code of decretals.

[Note: In the preceding paragraph he had rejected as contrary to the reason and practice of the Churches, especially the Gallican Church, the opinion that the Gauls could not give a letter of the Apostolic See the title of a decree unless it had been inserted in the Gallican code. He maintains, however, that the Third Council of Orléans cited Leo’s letter to the bishops of Vienne under this title of decree even though it was not contained in the officially established code. It is therefore false that the Second Council of Tours did not call Innocent’s letter to Victricius a decree for the reason that the Gauls customarily used that title only when they took such writings from a code of decretals.]

Second, it is clear that the letter had no place among the canons, since they indicate that they were inserting it among them for the first time and that from then on it would possess the force and authority of a statute:

> Because, they say, in the judgment of Pope Innocent delivered to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, it is written…

> Therefore, following what either the Apostle Paul or Pope Innocent established, and inserting it into our canons, let us establish that it must be observed…

[Note: Behold a remarkable interpreter! The Fathers of this synod join the decree of Innocent with the sanction of the Apostle Paul in such a way that they write the same formula about both: “Therefore, following what either the Apostle Paul or Pope Innocent established, and inserting it into our canons,” and so forth. Does this mean that the letters of Paul likewise lacked authority among the Gauls before this council, and that by these words they indicate that they were then inserting one of them for the first time among their canons, so that it would thereafter possess the force and strength of a statute? The obvious sense of the words expresses nothing other than that those Fathers established what both the Apostle Paul and Pope Innocent had previously decreed.]

### VI. The Fourth Argument, from the Case of Praetextatus

From what Gregory of Tours reports about the book of canons that King Chilperic sent to the bishops while pressing for the condemnation of Praetextatus, bishop of Rouen, Marca seems to infer that the Dionysian code was then received in Gaul, although it is unclear what exactly he intends by this. I am entirely at a loss as to how it could be proved.

These are Gregory’s words (*Book V, chapter 19*):

> The king himself, that is, departed to his lodging, sending a book of canons. In it was a new quire that had been appended, containing canons styled “apostolic,” which set forth the following: “A bishop found guilty of murder, adultery, or perjury shall be removed from the priesthood.”

[Col. 1113B] 1023

From this we understand, first, that the book of canons produced by the king was none other than an ancient code to which a new quire had been appended. Consequently, it was not the Dionysian code, to which there would have been no need to append the Apostolic Canons, since they were contained in the first part of that code.

2. It is clear that the code of Dionysius had not yet been in use in Gaul at that time, since Gregory speaks of the Apostolic Canons, which stood at the beginning, as though they were novel canons not yet received for use.

3. If the code of Dionysius had been in use, the king would not have needed to send an interpolated book of canons. It would have been sufficient to instruct the synod to judge according to the canons that there is no doubt they possessed before them—especially if, as Marca contends, the code had already long before been approved by the authority of the Council of Orléans, which he thinks received Leo’s letter from that code.

### VII. The Apostolic Canons Were Known in Gaul Before the Time of Dionysius

“But at least,” you will say, “it can be gathered from Gregory’s words that this code existed in Gaul at that time, since the king took from it the Apostolic Canons that he appended to the ancient code of canons. If it was present among the Gauls, it is highly probable that its use prevailed after the earlier translation had been rejected: first, because it was in use at the Apostolic See, and also because it was commended by its elegance in comparison with the squalor of the old translation.”

For the first point to follow from the Apostolic Canon that was produced, one would have to suppose that the Apostolic Canons had not appeared in either the Gallican or the Universal Church before the collection composed by Dionysius. This is false, as learned men know—men who repeatedly find them cited by the ancient Fathers and pontiffs under the name of *ecclesiastical rules*, the same title by which Dionysius also presents them.

[Note: See what we have discussed on this subject in the *Treatise on Collections*, Part I, chapter 1.]

Certainly, that abbot would never have dared to place those canons at the head of his collection, nor would the Roman Church have called them into use together with the code, unless their authority had already been confirmed among the Churches by long usage.

Moreover, if they were known among the Romans, they could certainly have been known among the Gauls as well. I mean the Gauls whose singular devotion to ecclesiastical discipline has always distinguished them, and whose continuous intercourse with the Roman Church made them participants in everything concerning canonical discipline that circulated through that Church.

But that the apostolic canons were brought into Gaul [Note: Since no version of the Apostolic Canons, either earlier or later than Dionysius, is known, we believe that the canon produced by Chilperic in the case of Praetextatus was taken from the Dionysian version. If its wording differs somewhat from Dionysius’s translation, it differs even more from the Greek text, so that it could not have been rendered in this way by any other translation. Hence the addition of the word “homicide,” which is found neither in Dionysius nor in the Greek, cannot have been derived from another translation. Rather, it was either inserted so that the canon itself might be adapted to Praetextatus, who had confessed himself guilty of the alleged homicide in the hope of pardon, or it came from some collection in which the same canons, taken from Dionysius’s translation, had been more freely expounded, as we observed in the Herouvallian Collection, *Treatise on Collections*, part IV, chapter 7. This word “homicide” is also retained by the *Excerptiones* from Ecbert of York, chapter 33; by Halitgarius, book V, chapter 4; by Regino, book I, chapter 86; and by Burchard, book II, chapter 189. Since these writers faithfully reproduce the Dionysian translation word for word, they must have derived the cited canon from some older, interpolated copy of Dionysius; the copy used by Chilperic appears to have been similar, since it contained a similar interpolation. Thus it is entirely true that the Dionysian version—the only version of these canons known in this matter—cannot be excluded merely because this word was inserted. Moreover, Gregory of Tours’s peculiar manner of citing this canon should move no one to a contrary view, since in book IX of his *History*, chapter 33, he quotes the decree of Gangra under the name of Nicaea in a form that agrees neither with the Greek nor with any translation. It seems, in fact, that the sense rather than the wording of the first and fourteenth Gangrian canons has been combined into one; something similar is occasionally found in other collections of canons from approximately the same period, especially penitential collections.]

were introduced before Dionysius’s collection, and that the canon presented by Chilperic was not taken from that book, is established by the very wording of the version, which differs greatly from the Dionysian one. This canon is the twenty-fifth, as even Peter de Marca acknowledges. Chilperic produced it in this form:

> A bishop discovered guilty of homicide, adultery, or perjury shall be removed from the priesthood.

But in Dionysius we have it as follows:

> A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who has been caught in fornication, perjury, or theft shall be deposed.

“But the canon was corrupted,” they say, “in order to crush Praetextatus.” If this were so, we should have Gregory complaining of it. He defended Praetextatus with unshakable courage and directed the full force of his mind toward every circumstance of the case; he would never have failed to warn his fellow bishops about the corruption of the canon and to denounce the fraud. He would never have silently tolerated the deposition of a bishop being decreed on the basis of a corrupted canon, nor would he have consented to that deposition. It is clear that he subscribed to the judgment, except that he rejected its conditions, because they were contrary to the canons. For the king requested that a judgment [Col. 1114C] be written against him, that he (Praetextatus) should never again communicate . . . [lacuna]. “I resisted these conditions,” Gregory says, “in accordance with the king’s promise, so that nothing might be done contrary to the canons.” 1025

This, surely, was the final part of the apostolic canon, which Chilperic appears to have concealed:

> Nevertheless, he shall not be deprived of communion; for Scripture says: “The Lord will not exact the same thing twice.”

The canon, therefore, was not corrupted, but enlarged by the addition of a single word—namely, “homicide.” That word is either implied by canon 28, which imposes the penalty of deposition upon a bishop who strikes someone, or it was already being read at that time in the version of the canon that circulated throughout Gaul. Furthermore, even if we granted that this portion of the canon had been corrupted with the intention of crushing the bishop, there was no comparable necessity for changing nearly all the remaining words. The difference can have arisen only from the diversity of translations.

The claim made against Gregory himself—that he did not take care to reproduce the actual words of the canon—is gratuitous and can be refuted in more than one way.

1. To attribute such negligence to Gregory in a matter of such importance is scarcely distinguishable from slander.

2. The entire sequence of his speech shows that he was reproducing the very words of the canon: “Having canons, as it were, containing the following: ‘A bishop,’ etc.”

3. The canon as Gregory reports it has the customary form of other canons.

4. The author asserts that it was read aloud before the bishops: “When these things had been read,” he says, “while Praetextatus was standing there, etc.”

5. In the earlier accusation brought by Chilperic against Praetextatus before the assembled bishops, the canon was cited by the king in nearly the same form. “The king was present in the morning and said: ‘For a bishop caught in thefts is to be torn away from the episcopal office.’” Here one sees that the wording differs from the Dionysian version but agrees with the other words of the canon reported by Gregory. It therefore appears completely certain that Chilperic took nothing at all from Dionysius’s book.

## VIII. The fifth argument, from the judgment of Chrodebert, bishop of Tours, around A.D. 670

Some evidence may also be drawn from the judgment of Chrodebert, bishop of Tours, concerning an adulterous woman. It is now published for the first time from the Thuane manuscript in our notes on letter 83, now 108, to Theodore of Fréjus.

When consulted about such adultery, Chrodebert replied that he had found nothing concerning it in the Councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, or Chalcedon:

> “Our country,” he says, “reverently receives and believes in these four synods alone.”

Nevertheless, he continues:

> “In the Council of Orléans we have found a judgment prescribed concerning this matter, and we have sent it to you.”

From this it is easy to conclude that the book of canons which Chrodebert had before him and to which he habitually resorted when about to render judgment in ecclesiastical cases was different from the Dionysian book, since the latter does not contain the Council of Ephesus and contains only three canons of the Council of Constantinople.

2. If the Dionysian book had at that time been received in the Gallican Church, the African synods, the Council of Sardica, and the other Eastern councils that it contains would also have been received, and the Roman Church was already embracing them. Since Chrodebert says nothing of these, the evidence is that he did not find most of them inserted in his own book and that, consequently, his book was not Dionysian.

[Note: It is uncertain whether Chrodebert used a single book of canons in searching out the meaning of the canons. The mention of the four synods—Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon—seems to indicate the Hispanic collection, which had already reached Gaul. For, so far as we know, this was the only collection at that time which, besides the Nicene, Constantinopolitan, and Chalcedonian canons, contained Cyril’s letter with the anathemas against Nestorius under the name of the Council of Ephesus. Moreover, we have shown elsewhere that the Sardican canons were written not only in this collection but also in several very ancient Gallican books, and were generally joined to the Nicene canons. The African canons had already been cited at the Council of Tours in 570. We have likewise seen that the constitutions of the Roman pontiffs were inserted in those same Gallican collections and cited by the Gallicans. Why, among the many canons that could have been cited, Chrodebert referred to only one Council of Orléans, Quesnell himself acknowledged that the matter should be interpreted in such a way that it does not follow that other synods, especially Gallican ones, were absent from his book. No argument, therefore, can be drawn from this by which it could be affirmed that these or other synods, which frequently occur in Gallican collections, were absent from the same book.]

3. In the same collection he would have found several letters of Siricius, Innocent, and Leo condemning the adultery of women consecrated to God and imposing upon them the obligation of performing penance. Why Chrodebert cited, from the Gallican synods, only the nineteenth sanction of the fifth Council of Orléans is not known to me. He could have cited the later canons of the Councils of Paris, Mâcon, and Tours II. But he thought that a single canon would suffice for a woman seeking not a heap of proofs but a salutary remedy; and perhaps there was some reason, arising either from the woman’s place of residence or from some other circumstance, for citing this canon rather than another.

## IX. The sixth argument, from Pope Zachary, A.D. 747

In the year 747 the Gallican bishops and the entire clergy consulted Pope Zachary, at the urging of Pippin, mayor of the palace, concerning twenty-seven points of ecclesiastical discipline. The pontiff answered the consultation in the same number of articles, confirming every one of them with canons and papal decrees transcribed word for word from the Dionysian collection.

[Note: Pippin requested from the Roman pontiff, with the counsel of the bishops, that he give an answer concerning all the proposed points. He in fact drew his response almost entirely from the canons and constitutions found in Dionysius’s book. Whether this book was in Gaul or not was irrelevant. How often, even in our own day, are questions resolved from widely circulated books of canons that are in everyone’s hands?]

Who, then, would believe that the bishops of Gaul would be anxious to receive such rules of discipline from the pontiff if they already possessed them in a book of canons and decrees ordinarily used in ecclesiastical judgments? They certainly would not have needed to send for them to Rome so that they could bring them back. They would merely have had to open the books in which they knew them to be contained—at least some among the Gallican clergy would have known this. Zachary’s labor, too, should have been spared, since he could easily have referred the Gallican bishops to the Dionysian book, which, according to their view, had been authorized for use both by the Roman and by the Gallican Church.

Nor would he have written about these points in this manner—*Letter* 9, to Pippin, mayor of the palace, and to the Gallican clergy—as though they had previously been unknown:

> “Therefore,” he says, “as our son Pippin, mentioned above, requested from us, with your counsel, that we should give a response concerning all the points about which he had informed us, so far as we are able with the Lord’s help, we have written below concerning each point according to what we have received from the holy Fathers.”

And afterward:

> “Accordingly, having selected these matters . . . [lacuna] among the other points . . . [lacuna] we have commanded them to be delivered and carried out for the knowledge and preaching of your episcopate, and for the edification of the people entrusted to you by God.”

Finally, he regarded this collection of canons as so unknown to the Gauls that he declared them previously deserving of some excuse, but entirely inexcusable after receiving these points:

> “Moreover,” he says, “we have entrusted these matters to you, dearly beloved, so that neither we may be judged before God for our silence, nor you be compelled to render an account before him for your neglect, as it is written in the Lord’s command: ‘If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin.’ Therefore, having no excuse, take care for the salvation of all rational souls.”

## X. The seventh argument, from Pope Stephen II, A.D. 754

In the seventh year after this consultation, Pope Stephen II, who was then staying at Carisiacum, a village of Gaul on the river Saire, gave nineteen answers to a Breton monastery concerning various questions on which he had been consulted. Since he cites many decrees both of councils and of the Roman pontiffs, it is clear that he did not obtain them from the Dionysian book from the differences in the numbers by which they are designated, as well as from the text itself of the decrees.

This probably happened because, since he had not brought the book from Rome, he was compelled to use in Gaul a Gallican book that differed from the Dionysian one. Indeed, he cites and reports the fifth chapter of the letter of Saint Leo to Rusticus of Narbonne, which is numbered 19 in Dionysius; the fifteenth chapter of Pope Innocent’s letter to Victricius of Rouen, which is numbered 20 in Dionysius; the fifteenth canon of the Council of Antioch, which Dionysius numbers 93; and the ninth canon of Neocaesarea, which in the collection is 53.

Moreover, a considerable difference is found between the text of certain decrees reported by Stephen and the Dionysian text, as can be seen in the excerpts from the letters of Pope Innocent to Exsuperius and to Victricius, from Siricius to Himerius, and from the canons of the Councils of Chalcedon, Neocaesarea, and Carthage.

[Note: Rather, he took them from the Dionysian book. For in chapter 7 he cites canon 16 of the Council of Chalcedon according to Dionysius’s translation; in chapter 15, canon 15 of Antioch; and in chapter 17, canon 9 of Neocaesarea, all in the same translation. Add that in chapter 16 he cites the twentieth canon of Carthage, which is presented under that number and in those words only in Dionysius, whereas in Isidore, or in the Hispanic collection, it is read as canon 8 under the title “Carthage III.” If the numbers of the Greek canons do not agree with the sequence of numbers given in Justellus’s edition, there is no contradiction. The translation itself, which agrees only with Dionysius, provides stronger evidence. Moreover, John II and Zachary, whom Quesnell acknowledges as having used Dionysius’s book, did not always follow a continuous numerical sequence. John designated two Antiochene canons with the numbers proper to the council itself; Zachary, on the other hand, cited all the Greek canons not according to that numerical sequence but according to the numbers proper to each council. As for the letters of the Roman pontiffs, just as the author of the Hispanic collection took them from Dionysius with their titles intact, while nevertheless not maintaining a continuous sequence of numbers, so Stephen II could likewise pass over that sequence, even though he cited the decrees of the pontiffs from the Dionysian book. From this a strong argument can be drawn that the Dionysian book had been brought into Gaul before Charlemagne. Either Stephen II used the book of Dionysius, which he brought with him from Rome into Gaul, or, if he did not bring it, he certainly found in Gaul the book that he used.]

From these facts it is evident that by that time the Dionysian collection had not merely failed to be received for use by the Gauls; it was not even well known to them. For the pontiff would undoubtedly have used it if he had had it at hand—both to establish its authority through actual use and to introduce Roman practice into the regions of Gaul.

## XI. The eighth argument, from the Council of Vern, A.D. 755

The Council of Vern in the year 755 cites a canon of the Council of Carthage, which it calls chapter 9, whereas in Dionysius it is canon 15. The reading in the two sources is different, and the discrepancy is very great, so that it evidently came from somewhere other than Dionysius’s Roman book. That book, therefore, was not then in use in the Gallican Church.

[Note: This testimony proves that the book from which the Fathers of this synod reported the ninth canon of Carthage was not Dionysius’s; but it by no means proves that Dionysius’s book was nowhere in Gaul during this period.]

This, too, was the situation in the time of Charlemagne, who gained the empire not many years later. After receiving the Roman collection of Abbot Dionysius as a gift from Pope Hadrian, 1029 he began to introduce it into use in Gaul, though he did not reject the older book familiar to the Gallican bishops. For Charlemagne himself frequently used its translation in his *Capitularies*.

As Sirmond aptly observed in his note on the first capitulary of the year 789, all the canons of the Greek synods cited there differ from Dionysius’s commonly received translation and agree with another translation, copies of which [perhaps at Paris] are preserved in the libraries of Pathinus. In my opinion, this is none other than the ancient translation contained in our ancient Roman book and accepted by Isidore, although in many places it has been corrupted or altered.

[Note: Isidore neither corrupted nor altered anything in his translation of the Greek synods; rather, he copied the Hispanic collection of Gallican origin. In that collection, certain corrupt passages had been emended arbitrarily according to pure Hispanic usage, as we observed in the preface to Leo’s letters, § 10, no. 20, vol. I, p. 523 (in our edition, col. 559). The same translation is found corrected more freely in several places in the manuscripts of the collection published in this volume, which we have shown to have been compiled in Gaul.]

## XII. Peter de Marca’s objection

I now scarcely seem to have left any scruple of importance that ought to deter anyone from this conclusion or incline anyone toward the opposing view. For what de Marca says here about the authority of the apostolic see, the elegance of Dionysius’s translation, and the arrangement of the collection is all very true, but at present it has no force.

[Note: At the same time, it is certain how much the Gallicans deferred to apostolic constitutions, which they inserted into their books of canons under the title of authority and which the Gallican synods themselves commanded to be obeyed. See, among others, the Council of Agde in 506, canon 9; the Third Council of Orléans in 538, canon 3; and the Second Council of Tours in 507, canon 20.]

No one is unaware that it was always permitted to all the Churches, and especially to the Gallican Churches, to use their own laws and canons in matters not defined by the decree of a universal council. This is evident even from the difference between Gallican and Roman discipline.

It is also well known how tenacious the Gallican bishops were of ancient custom, preferring a worn and uncultivated antiquity to the recent elegance of the new translation for as long as their emperor permitted them to do so. They retained in mind and confirmed by practice this saying of Saint Augustine:

> “The very change of custom, even when it is advantageous in its usefulness, disturbs by its novelty.”

[Note: It is rather well known that in this matter the Gallican bishops were not tenacious of ancient custom. Before Rufinus, they were not ignorant of the canons of the Council of Nicaea, which we see cited at the Council of Valence in 374, and they used their complete ancient translation. After Rufinus, at least some Gallican Churches accepted abridgments of those canons in place of the complete translation, as is clear from *Treatise*, part II, chapter 10. Later, Dionysius’s own translation of the same canons was inserted shortly after its publication in the Corbie collection and in others predating Hadrian I and Charlemagne, which will be discussed in the observations below. It is therefore false that the Gallican bishops, tenacious of ancient custom, preferred the torn and unpolished antiquity of the old translation to the new elegance of Dionysius’s translation for as long as their emperor allowed them to do so. If they kept in mind the saying of Saint Augustine, “The very change of custom, even when it is advantageous in its usefulness, disturbs by its novelty,” they ought much more to have remembered the observance shown by Augustine and the other African bishops toward the decrees of the apostolic see. In the case of the Donatists returning to the unity of the Church, they suspended an ancient custom that had prevailed from the beginning of the case because a contrary command had proceeded from that same see; the prohibition was removed only after an embassy had been sent to Rome and the necessity and usefulness of the Churches had been made clear. See *Treatise*, part II, chapter 3, § 3, no. 47.]

## XIII. John David’s dilemma examined

The conjectures added by David to de Marca’s arguments reveal an extreme poverty of evidence. He mentions the Council of Agde and the Second Council of Tours—concerning the latter we have already given our answer, while the former I am about to discuss—and then, as though he had produced a long cloud of witnesses and a substantial series of arguments, he says:

> “From all these things I conclude either that Dionysius was not the first of all to gather into one body the letters of the ancient bishops of Rome, beginning with Siricius, and to append them to a collection of canons—although this is asserted by the illustrious Justellus and suggested by Dionysius himself in the letter prefixed to the collection and addressed to Julian—or I conclude that those who persuade themselves that the Dionysian collection was not received in Gaul before the age of Charlemagne are profoundly mistaken. For several centuries before this emperor, we see the letters of the pontiffs and the African synods cited by Gallican councils, as though they had been inserted in the book then in use. All this points to the book of Dionysius.”

I fear that David himself is profoundly mistaken. Nothing could be more inept than this dilemma of his, which rests on ruined foundations and is entirely defective.

First, let us grant that the letters of the pontiffs and the African synods were cited as though they had been taken from an approved book of canons. Who except David would infer from this that Dionysius’s book had then been received by the Gauls? Would he have us suppose that all the Churches of the Christian world had disregarded the authority of the apostolic see for five hundred whole years—such is John David’s reverence toward the Roman pontiff—and that before Dionysius they had not thought of collecting his decrees?

We hold better and more reverent opinions of the Gallican and other Churches toward their head and primate. We are led to this conclusion by several Gallican collections of canons and papal decrees, which learned men before us have seen and which David himself may consult if he wishes.

In particular, there is in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés a distinguished collection prepared for the use of the Gallican Church. Learned men have considered it contemporary with the age of Gelasius. It contains nearly thirty letters of Roman pontiffs, most of which are also absent from Dionysius. Dionysius has only seven letters written by Leo, whereas the Saint-Germain book has sixteen.

Two other books appear to have been copied from this one: one from the Thuane collection, designated no. 193, and another from the Trecopithoean collection. They contain the same letters of the pontiffs copied in the same order, except that the Saint-Germain book, formerly belonging to Corbie, is longer by two letters. Several African decrees and councils are also read there. From these it is clear that knowledge of all these materials in Gaul was not received from the Dionysian book, and that David’s attempt to construct the authority of the Roman book among the Gauls from their citations is altogether unfortunate.

2. That Dionysius was not the first to collect the decrees of the supreme pontiffs follows from what we have already said, and is also conclusively proved by our ancient book of the Roman Church, which contains many things omitted by Dionysius. I say nothing of the other Churches, which possessed collections of papal letters of this sort before Dionysius.

Let it be granted that Dionysius was the first to gather them into a single body, arrange them under one continuous numerical sequence, distinguish them by titles, order them in the same way in which he had already arranged the canons of the Fathers, and take care to append them to those canons. I have no objection. Nothing more has been asserted either by the illustrious Justellus or by Dionysius himself, although David writes otherwise.

[Note: William Voellus and Henry Justellus, in the preface to the *Bibliotheca Juris Canonici*, called Dionysius the first collector of papal letters so categorically that they added this explanation: “For the earlier collectors omitted the decretal letters of the pontiffs, content with the rules of the synods.” Christopher Justellus appears to have made the same assertion in the preface to the *Code of the Universal Church*, p. 19, where, speaking of Dionysius’s book, he says: “And this is the first and most ancient collection of the decretals of the pontiffs.” If this is understood of a collection of decretals separate from a collection of canons, it may perhaps be true; but not if it is understood to mean that decretals were first inserted by Dionysius into collections of canons.]

But who would have considered such an arrangement necessary in order that these decrees might be cited and reported by Gallican bishops?

## XIV. The Council of Agde, from which John David argues

3. To attack and demolish the very foundation of this writer’s argument, I say that the Council of Agde of the year 506—what should be thought of the Council of Tours we have already stated—preceded, unless my conjectures deceive me, Dionysius’s collection of papal decrees.

1. It is certain that Dionysius lived at Rome as an abbot while he devoted himself to Latin studies. Among his works are two Paschal letters written in the years of Christ 525 and 526. He flourished especially until the year 540, as Labbe states in his historical dissertation on ecclesiastical writers.

2. That Dionysius undertook the collection of letters only later, and not until long after he had completed the book of canons, is attested by Dionysius himself in the letter to the presbyter Julian prefixed to the collection:

> “So that I might append all the titles to this preface in the same manner in which, long ago, while translating the canons of the Fathers from the Greek language, I arranged them.”

3. Since he collected only, as Dionysius himself writes, the constitutions of former bishops of the apostolic see—that is, of those who had already ceased to live—and nevertheless included a letter of Pope Anastasius, it follows that he did not begin this work before 16 November of the year 498, when Anastasius died, that is, under the pontificate of Symmachus, who survived the Council of Agde by eight years.

4. It is certain that Dionysius had not yet come to Rome in the year 496, when Pope Gelasius died, since in his preface to Julian he testifies that he had never seen that pontiff:

> “How great is the merit before God of the blessed Pope Gelasius, and how much more easily we, who did not see him in bodily presence, assess it through you, his disciples.”

From these facts I argue as follows. From the death of Pope Gelasius, whom Dionysius did not see, until the Council of Agde there were only ten years. Within that period Dionysius, a Scythian by birth, had to come to Rome, live there for at least several years so that his learning and merit might become known, and establish such a reputation for himself that, although a stranger and guest in the city of Rome, he might be sought as an abbot.

Then he had to translate all the Greek canons into Latin, combine them into a single book, and publish them, adding the apostolic, Sardican, and African canons. Afterward, long after publishing this book, he had to undertake with the greatest care the search for, collection, arrangement, and classification of the decrees of the supreme pontiffs. I do not know whether anyone will think that this exceedingly short period of ten years was sufficient for all these undertakings.

But this is not all. Before he even composed the book of canons anew, he had to be urged by the persistent and familiar exhortations of a certain Laurentius, and by the command, as they say, of Stephen, bishop of Salona. Later, he collected the decrees of the pontiffs only after being stimulated by the pious entreaties of Julian, presbyter of the title of Saint Anastasia.

Who would believe that a work composed by a foreign monk at the urging of a single presbyter was immediately adopted for the use of the Roman Church with papal authority, while an older collection, consecrated by the usage of so many years, was rejected? Or who would not rather think that it was not adopted until the experience of many years had shown whether this change of custom—which Augustine feared in *Letter* 118, saying that even a change that brought utility could disturb by its novelty—would be beneficial?

I am therefore easily persuaded that Dionysius’s book was not received by the Roman Church until several years had passed. In fact, Cassiodorus, who held the consulship in the year 514 and was still alive in the year 562, speaks of that book in chapter 23 of the *Divine Readings* as though it had only recently been called into use by the Roman Church:

> “The Church of Rome today embraces the canons of Dionysius in most widespread use.”

Once received at Rome, however, they could not have penetrated the transalpine Churches so quickly. Nor is it consistent with Gallican character that, as soon as they became known, the Gallicans eagerly seized them, approved them, and made them their own. Even if we granted that the Gallican Churches had done so, the limitations of time would never have permitted it before the Council of Agde.

## XV. Objection drawn from appeals

It remains for us to dissolve the objection raised concerning appeals. “It is established,” the opponents say, “that the book was received because the Sardican canons contained in it were received. That these canons prevailed throughout Gaul even under the first dynasty of our kings is clear from the appeals that were frequently brought from Gaul to the apostolic see without opposition from the Gallican bishops. From where, then, did they learn that this right belonged to the apostolic see, unless from the Sardican canons, since no Gallican synod appears to have claimed it for that see? Yet they could have obtained the Sardican canons only from Dionysius’s book, in which he had inserted them. Add that the Roman pontiffs never failed to claim this same right over the Gallican Churches under the first dynasty of our kings. It follows that by that time the decrees of the Council of Sardica were known to have been received in the Gallican Church.”

A remarkable right, truly, supposedly acquired from the actions of a few obstinate bishops; and a remarkable argument that seeks to infer it from those actions. Would it not be more reasonable to judge the facts from the right itself than to determine the right from certain unproved facts?

[Note: Quesnell later admits, in no. 4, that the right of appeal derives from the pontifical primacy; we establish this more fully in volume II, in the observations on Quesnell’s fifth dissertation, part I, chapter 7. It may also properly be inferred from the facts, as we show in the same work, chapter 5. We have demonstrated there, chapter 6, no. 17, from the most ancient Gallican collections—which do not derive from Dionysius—that the Sardican canons, which assert this same right for the Roman see on the basis of its primacy, were in use among the Gauls before Dionysius. The same is confirmed by the Council of Arles of the year 524, whose canon 2 reads: “Although the ancient Fathers prescribed longer periods to be observed in the case of laymen, nevertheless, since the increasing number of Churches requires us to ordain more clerics, it has been agreed among us, without prejudice to the ancient canons, that, etc.” The words “the ancient Fathers” and “without prejudice to the ancient canons” refer to canon 13 of Sardica, which requires a longer period of probation for laymen before they are promoted to sacred orders. These canons, therefore, were present in Gallican books. Indeed, in the very ancient Morbacensis collection and in Vatican Palatine 574, that canon concerning laymen is transcribed under the title of the Council of Nicaea. See *Treatise*, part III, chapter 9.]

2. Before Dionysius’s book was published, I ask whether the right of appealing to the Roman pontiff prevailed in Gaul or not, and whether appeals were in fact brought on the basis of that right. If it did, why should it be believed that this right did not prevail, and that appeals were not brought on the same basis, after Dionysius’s book had been composed? Why is an argument for the use of this book in Gaul during those same years sought from those appeals?

If the right did not prevail before Dionysius’s book, why does David assert it and attempt to prove it by numerous examples? By what reasoning, finally, will it be believed that this new discipline was introduced into the regions of Gaul after a contrary custom of five hundred years?

If he says that this right was created from the Sardican canons themselves before Dionysius, then the Gallican Churches obtained knowledge of those canons from elsewhere than Dionysius’s book. Thus the whole structure of David’s argument collapses.

3. In the apologetic dissertation for Saint Hilary of Arles we showed how reluctantly the Gallican bishops endured the referral of their cases to Roman judgment and how long they resisted it, although the emperors complied with the wishes of the Roman pontiffs and Valentinian had sent an edict to Gaul commanding that whatever the Roman pontiff had decreed should be regarded as law:

> “Thus, whoever among the bishops, summoned to the judgment of the Roman bishop, neglects to appear shall be compelled to attend by the governor of the province.”

The bishops eventually yielded, lest by resisting they gain nothing but the emperor’s hatred. But how unjustly would our bishops have protested against such a right of appeal if Dionysius’s book had then been received in the Gallican Churches—when it contained the Sardican canons that granted the Roman pontiff the power to receive appeals, as Pope Gelasius teaches?

4. When the Gallicans began to exercise that right of appeal, [Note: [Col. 1121C] Since the Sardican canons were in use among the Gallicans, as we remarked in note 24, when the Gallic bishops brought appeals to the apostolic see, they may have looked not so much to the dignity of the pontifical primacy as to those same canons.] they did not have regard to the Sardican canons, but to the dignity of the pontifical primacy, to the antiquity of the Roman see, and to its more powerful “principal position,” as Irenaeus calls it. Most of the Churches of the Gallic provinces owed the origin and beginnings of their faith to that see, since Trophimus and his other companions had been sent to them from the apostolic see.

5. To answer the examples cited, I say [Note: [Col. 1122D] Although the whole history of Contumeliosus has not been completely ascertained, it is nevertheless certain that, after being deposed by Caesarius of Arles, he appealed to Agapetus, the Roman pontiff, who wrote to that same Caesarius that he would delegate a new investigation to him (Epistle 7). Salonius and Sagittarius, however, having been expelled from the episcopate by a synod convened at the command of King Guntram, and knowing that the king was still favorably disposed toward them, approached him. “They complained,” says Gregory of Tours, *History*, book V, chapter 21, “that they had been unjustly removed and asked that permission be granted them to go to the pope of the city of Rome. The king, assenting to their requests, gave them letters and allowed them to depart. When they came before Pope John, they declared that they had been removed without any valid grounds. He then sent letters to the king, in which he restored them to their sees. The king immediately carried this out, after first rebuking those men at length.”] that the history of Contumeliosus is somewhat obscure, but that Salonius and Sagittarius appealed to Rome only by a special concession of the king. The fact that this was not denied to them and to others when it occurred was intended to deprive wicked men of every pretext for complaint. In the end, judgment must be made on such appeals from the facts just stated.

[Col. 1123A] Finally, the fact that the Roman pontiffs cited the Sardican canons 1036 in order to defend their right even in Gaul is wholly irrelevant, since they had done this long before Dionysius was born. Moreover, when they adduced those same canons in support of the privileges of their see, [Note: [Col. 1123D] When the Roman pontiffs cited the Sardican canons under the name of the Nicene canons, they followed a usage once common in the West, especially among the Gallicans. In the oldest manuscripts of these regions, the canons of the two synods are joined together and bear the heading “Nicene,” as we showed in *Treatise*, part II, chapter 1, § 3, and chapter 10, § 2.] they produced them under the name of the Nicene canons. From this it followed that they proclaimed them throughout all the Churches with greater confidence and with a louder trumpet. But to infer from this either the reception of the Sardican canons or the reception of the Dionysian codex is the act of someone pursuing a different objective, or of one seeking any sort of support for a desperate cause.

## XVI. Which Translation of the Canons Was Used in Gaul before the Dionysian Translation Was Received

Once this has been established beyond doubt—that the ancient collection and translation which had been accepted for use in Gaul before Dionysius continued to be in force among those same Churches after Dionysius’s codex had been compiled, down to the time of Charlemagne—the reader will ask [Note: [Col. 1123D] On this controversy, see the following observations, § 2.] what that ancient translation was. Was it the one used by the Roman Church? Or one proper to the Gauls? Or the one found inserted in the Isidorian collection? Or, finally, that ancient translation which was not long ago brought to light from the manuscript codex of Christophorus Justellus in volume I of the *Bibliotheca Juris Canonici Veteris*?

Two men of outstanding learning, Jacobus Sirmondus in his preface to the edition of the ancient councils of Gaul, and the already-mentioned Christophorus Justellus in the preface to the *Codex of the Ancient Universal Church*, hold that the old translation then received among the Gauls was the one found in Isidore Mercator. They assert their opinion on the basis of the canons of the councils of Valence, Riez, Arles II, Agde, and Epaon, in which they believe that the Nicene, Ancyran, and Laodicean canons are cited from the Isidorian translation.

It is extremely difficult to establish anything certain about the complete Gallic codex, and I do not see how the respected authors could confidently declare that any particular Oriental canon cited in the ancient synods of Gaul was taken from one translation rather than another. I set aside the Nicene canons. Since they are more frequently remembered in the ancient records of our Churches, it is also less difficult to determine from which translation they were taken. Yet Sirmondus, Justellus, and anyone else who has thought that the Isidorian translation of the Nicene canons was in use among the Churches of Gaul before the Dionysian translation was brought into them have undoubtedly departed from the truth.

For, when I investigated the matter more carefully, it seemed entirely certain to me that our Gallic Churches borrowed the Nicene canons [Note: [Col. 1124D] The Second Council of Arles, and the excerpts of the canons in the case of Contumeliosus, establish that Rufinus’s abbreviations were received in the province of Arles. The Morbacensis and Vatican Palatine 574 codices, as well as the Herouvallian collection, in which the same abbreviations are found, prove that they were introduced somewhere in Gaul. Other Gallic documents, however, demonstrate that elsewhere in Gaul the complete Nicene interpretation was used, as will become clear from § 2 of the observations.] from Rufinus of Aquileia, from book X of his *Ecclesiastical History*, which he appended to the books of Eusebius. There he lists the Nicene canons in abbreviated form and divides them into twenty-two. I am not led to this opinion merely by conjecture, but by certain arguments—arguments which, to my surprise, have not come to the attention of others. We draw them chiefly from two sources: the Second Council of Arles and those excerpts of the canons which are thought to have been collected by Caesarius of Arles in the case of Contumeliosus of Riez. The following is an excerpt from the Nicene synod, placed there before the Gallic canons:

“Concerning the matter of the Nicene synod, that is, of the 318 bishops: If any persons, having been rashly advanced to the priesthood, afterward either themselves confess some criminal act concerning themselves or are convicted by others, let them be deposed.”

This canon has been transcribed word for word from Rufinus, by whom it is numbered eleven, although it is the ninth in other editions of the council.

The Second Council of Arles also contains several arguments for this claim. In its first canon it forbids a neophyte to be ordained to the office of deacon or priest. In this it appears to follow the traces of the Nicene synod, but in the form found in Rufinus. For the canon in other editions orders only that such a person be excluded from the presbyterate, whereas Rufinus’s interpretation alone forbids him to become a cleric.

The tenth canon states: “Concerning those who lapsed during the persecution, if they voluntarily denied the faith, the Nicene synod decreed this concerning them: that they spend five years among the catechumens and two among those receiving communion.”

This Gallic synod clearly has in view Nicene canon 11, although the discipline of the two differs. The Nicene canon imposes twelve years of penance on such lapsed persons according to the Isidorian version and the ancient version of Justellus, which agree with the Greek; according to the Dionysian version, it imposes eleven. The seven-year period of penance therefore prescribed by the Gallic canon could have derived from no other translation than the one presented by Rufinus, whose words in canon 12 are these:

“If any persons have lapsed in the persecutions without torture, and from the heart undertake penance, let them spend five years among the catechumens and, after this, let them join the faithful in prayer alone for two years; afterward let them be received.”

What follows in the same Arelatan canon—“Nevertheless, it shall be in the power or discretion of the bishop that, if he sees that they sincerely lament their error and perform penance, he may receive them into communion out of ecclesiastical humanity”—appears to have been taken from these words of Rufinus’s canon 13: “Nevertheless, it shall be in the bishop’s power to exercise discretion, and so forth.”

The seventh Arelatan canon—“Those who, unable to resist the vice of the flesh, mutilate themselves are not to be admitted to the clergy”—was also taken from Rufinus’s interpretation of the First Nicene Council. No other version mentions impotence or inability to endure lust in that canon, which Rufinus abbreviates as follows:

“Moreover, they decree that this must be observed in the Churches: that no one who, through inability to restrain his lust, has mutilated himself should enter the clergy.”

The fifteenth Arelatan canon states:

“In the secretarium, a deacon may not sit among the presbyters, nor may they presume to distribute the body of Christ when a presbyter is present. If they do so, let them withdraw from the office of the diaconate.”

It is clear that this canon was drawn from canon 18 of the Nicene synod, but from no version other than Rufinus’s, in which this is canon 20:

“And let deacons not be preferred to presbyters, nor sit in the assembly of presbyters, nor distribute the Eucharist when they are present; but let them minister only when the presbyters are performing the rite. If no minister is present, then at last they too may distribute it. Those who act otherwise must be deposed.”

These two canons agree with one another and differ from the other versions in five respects:

1. Neither forbids deacons to hand the Eucharist to presbyters.

2. Both forbid the Eucharist to be distributed by a deacon while a presbyter is present.

3. Both omit much concerning the power of consecrating the body of Christ, from which the holy Fathers derive the reason for their sanction.

4. Neither says anything about deacons touching the sacred mysteries before bishops.

5. Neither mentions the rule and custom which those contumacious deacons were presuming to violate.

1039 There can therefore be no doubt that the Arelatan Fathers had Rufinus’s canons in their codex when they enacted their sanction.

The sixteenth canon states: “Photinians, or Paulianists, ought to be baptized according to the decrees of the Fathers.” It was composed in accordance with the twenty-first Nicene canon of Rufinus’s version:

“And let the Paulianists, who are Photinians, be rebaptized.”

No one would say that the Nicene Fathers summoned the Photinians—who were called after Photinus, bishop of Sirmium—to judgment, since they had not yet arisen. Nor does the Greek edition or any Latin version actually mention them, except Rufinus’s. The Arelatan canon was derived from that version and adapted to the Photinians.

## XVII. Whether Only Rufinus’s Translation Was Then in Use in Gaul

This is what concerns the Nicene canons formerly cited or reported by the synods of Gaul. It follows beyond doubt that Rufinus’s version was repeatedly used there. Whether it was the only one is called into question by the third canon of the Council of Riez in the year 439. When it relegated Armentarius, improperly ordained in the Church of Embrun, to the office of chorepiscopus, it professes to follow a Nicene statute:

“Let him be permitted,” it says, “to surrender one of his parishes, in which he may be supported either under the name of chorepiscopus, as the same canon says, or, as they call it, by peregrine communion.”

Only the Isidorian version uses both the terms “parishes” and “chorepiscopus” in this canon. Rufinus has neither. The synod’s Fathers therefore appear to have had that version before their eyes rather than Rufinus’s. [Note: [Col. 1125D] Compare the observations, § 2, no. 9.]

I would judge that there is an error in Rufinus’s text and that it should not be read, “Let him seek for him a vacant episcopal place; this shall be in his power,” but rather, “Let him seek for him a chorepiscopal place,” and so forth. It was indeed in the power of any bishop to entrust to another some vacant church of his parishes under the name of chorepiscopus; but to seek for another a vacant episcopal place was not likewise within his power. That depended on the votes of the comprovincial bishops, the clergy, and the people—votes which it would be the greatest sacrilege either to purchase or to beg.

In any event, the difficulty presented by this canon seems minor and incapable of weakening the authority of so many canons in which the use of Rufinus’s version with respect to the Nicene canons in the Gallican Churches is clear and indisputable.

As for the use of the other Eastern synods, we have a canon of Ancyra cited in the Synod of Epaon in the year 517. In canon 31, concerning the penance of murderers, it orders the observance of what, as it says, the Ancyran canons decreed; but it is not evident from which version it was taken.

Canons 65, 66, 67, and 68 appended to the Council of Agde were transcribed from the version of the Council of Laodicea called Isidorian. But it has remained unknown down to the present time when and on whose authority they were added—whether by some Gallican synod or rather by that famous interpolator Isidore. It is established among scholars from very ancient and numerous manuscript codices that these canons do not belong to the Council of Agde, but were attached to it in a later age. Consequently, they cannot be used to determine which version was employed by the Gauls up to the completion of the sixth century of the Christian era.

Furthermore, just as knowledge of the Nicene canons appears to have been very obscure in Gaul before Rufinus’s time, so afterward the version of those canons supplied by him in his supplement to Eusebius’s *History* was eagerly received. No one should find this surprising if he recalls that Rufinus was always held in the highest esteem among the Gauls and all Westerners—if Jerome is excepted—and that his *History* was especially welcomed, since through it so many distinguished records of ecclesiastical affairs first became known to the Latins.

It is neither appropriate nor possible to write more about these matters here, since they are somewhat foreign to the present place. It is enough that through this short dissertation we have invited learned men to investigate the subject more carefully.

# BALLERINIUS’S OBSERVATIONS on Quesnellus’s Dissertation XVI, concerning the First Use of the Dionysian Collection in Gaul

[Col. 1125]

## § I. It is shown that Dionysius’s collection was known in Gaul and occasionally received for use even before the time of Charlemagne

[Col. 1125C]

When the use of Dionysius’s codex in Gaul before the age of Charlemagne is investigated, two questions must be distinguished lest ambiguity arise. The first is whether it was a public codex—that is, one issued or approved by public authority and accepted for use by all the Gallican Churches. The second is whether it was a private codex which reached Gaul before Charlemagne and, even if not used by all the Churches, was at least occasionally employed by some Churches or writers.

To suppose or even suspect the first is utterly futile. For even at Rome, where it became famous earlier, it was for a long time a private codex of canons, not a public one or one approved by public authority. It acquired public authority only when Hadrian I, the supreme pontiff, handed it over to Charlemagne for use in Gaul. See *Treatise on Collections*, part III, chapter 1.

Moreover, before this time there was no other public codex of canons in Gaul, but all the collections were private, and their use was unrestricted in the absence of a public codex, as we proved in part II, chapter 10. The second question therefore alone remains: whether Dionysius’s codex was among the private collections in Gaul before the age of Charlemagne, so that it could be used just like the other private collections, and whether the Gallicans actually used it at some time before then.

## II

Quesnellus speaks at the beginning of the aforementioned dissertation about a public codex which once possessed authority in Gaul; nowhere, however, has he proved that any such codex, issued or confirmed by public authority, existed there. The only things that can be cited are the ancient synods of Gaul and the Gallican bishops who invoked the canons of councils or the constitutions of pontiffs.

Even if these canons or constitutions had been taken from some collection, it would not immediately follow that those collections were public codices. The same canons and constitutions possessed sufficient authority from the councils and pontiffs by whom they had been issued and had no need of a public codex.

For this reason Quesnellus himself, in the preceding dissertation, § 4, makes three assertions which confirm that the practice of the Gallican Church did not require a public codex.

First, he admits that there were many codices of private collections in Gaul:

“For how many codices of ancient collections,” he says, “formerly written by hand for the use of PRIVATE PERSONS or of certain Churches contain numerous letters of the Roman pontiffs . . . ?”

He also lists several very old codices of this kind by way of example.

Second, when speaking of the Third Council of Orléans, which cited Leo’s Epistle 10 in canon 3, he mentions a codex then used throughout Gaul from which the letter had been drawn for the bishops of the province of Vienne. Although shortly before this he had said that the codex had been compiled for Gallican use, he does not acknowledge it as public, writing as follows:

“Which [Leo’s epistle] had not even been received in an authorized codex.”

For Quesnellus, an “authorized codex” is the same as a public codex, that is, one approved by public authority.

Third, among the opinions which he rejects as foreign to the reason and practice of all the Churches, especially the Gallican Church, he reports the following: someone might contend that the Gauls could not have honored a letter with the title of a decree of the apostolic see unless it had been inserted into a Gallican codex—that is, a public one.

But if there were formerly many private codices, some of which still survive; if pontifical constitutions, and likewise the canons of councils, could and ordinarily did get cited from them; why, then, does he so often insist on an authorized public codex received as authoritative, whose existence in Gaul before Charlemagne, apart from private collections, is supported by no testimony and no indication?

This is consistent with his own thesis, according to which he elsewhere requires a public codex for promulgation. We have refuted this thesis more fully in note 11 (vol. 907, note c) to Dissertation 12. Consequently, there is now nothing further to debate concerning a public codex which, before the Dionysian-Hadrianic codex, rested on no foundation and must be counted among mere inventions.

Since Quesnellus himself admits that several private collections were in use among the Gauls, it will be sufficient for our purpose if we can prove that Dionysius’s codex had at least occasionally found a place among them before Charlemagne.

## III

Although Quesnellus, in attacking the affirmative position, had very effectively proved in the dissertation that the testimonies produced in favor of the Dionysian codex as received in Gaul contributed nothing to that position, he nevertheless would not have demonstrated that this codex was excluded from Gaul. Since there was no public codex among the Gauls, only private collections could be used; and since there were several such collections, everyone was permitted to use this or that collection according to his own judgment.

The testimonies which Quesnellus brought forward in his reckoning are those of people who used not the Dionysian collection but another collection. Let that be granted. Does it follow that no copy of Dionysius existed in Gaul before the age of Charlemagne, and that no Gallican had used it?

We have investigated other testimonies and documents which lead us to believe with complete certainty that the Dionysian collection had crossed into Gaul in that earlier age. In the aforementioned dissertation, § 12, Quesnellus, in order to prove that the Gallicans had received the apostolic constitutions before the age of Charlemagne, lists older Gallican collections, even though they had been compiled by private initiative, in which those same constitutions are transcribed.

We too shall use the evidence of those collections in support of Dionysius’s codex.
