These Gallican collections, compiled before Charlemagne, sometimes received the canons of the Greek synods not from the ancient translation but from the Dionysian translation; this proves that the latter had been brought into Gaul before Charlemagne’s reign.

We have examined one codex among the older Gallican collections, Vatican Palatine 574, and saw that it contained from Dionysius his letter to Stephen, as well as the canons of the apostles and the fifteenth action of the Council of Chalcedon.

Father Sirmondus, however, who examined a great many Gallican manuscript collections for his edition of the Councils of Gaul, explicitly states in the preface to that edition that he found the same thing in various other ancient copies:

“We have also discovered, from the most ancient collection of canons in the library of Saint Benignus at Dijon and from other collections of the same kind far earlier than the age of Charlemagne, that the Dionysian translation of the canons was not unknown to the Gauls before its copies were received from the apostolic see under Charlemagne, and that they sometimes used it. In these collections the Greek canons are presented indiscriminately, sometimes from the Dionysian translation and sometimes from that ancient old translation—which Isidore later received.”

This testimony of the Gallican collections, which is as certain as it is decisive, ought by itself to be sufficient. We are greatly surprised that, after examining the other evidence, Quesnellus either failed to notice or passed over what Sirmondus produced. Indeed, on the basis of this very preface—which so explicitly establishes the use of the Dionysian codex in Gaul before Charlemagne’s reign—he dared to list Sirmondus among those who defended the contrary opinion.

## IV

I was unable to inspect the Dijon collection praised by Sirmondus. But we were able to examine two other Gallican collections, earlier than the Hadrianic age and later published in print, in which we discovered several items taken from Dionysius.

One is the Herouvallian collection, which Jacobus Petit published for the most part after Theodore’s *Penitential*. See what we discussed concerning the present subject in *Treatise*, part IV, chapter 7.

The other is an ancient collection of penitential canons, edited from a nine-hundred-year-old manuscript from Fleury by Father Edmond Martène in *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, volume IV, column 31 and following. That it was composed in Gaul is shown not only by the Gallican codex itself but also by the synods cited in it, as well as by the title *Ancient Statutes of the Church*, which we find only in collections from Gaul.

That it is earlier than Hadrian is clear from the fact that it was arranged while Gregory the Younger was alive, as these words plainly show in column 37:

“Likewise from the decree of Pope Gregory the Younger, who NOW governs the Roman Catholic mother Church.”

It cites a canon of a Roman synod celebrated under that pontiff in the year 721.

Although the author of this collection used, in certain canons of the Greek councils, the version that later passed into Isidore’s codex, he also clearly presents Dionysius’s interpretation in the second canon of Neocaesarea, which is expressed in these words in column 35:

“Canon of Neocaesarea. If a woman marries two brothers, let her be expelled until death. Nevertheless, at the end, if she promises that, once restored to health, she will dissolve the bonds of this union, let her obtain the fruit of penance. But if either the man or woman in such a marriage dies, penance will be difficult for the survivor.”

The twenty-fifth apostolic canon, presented in column 40, is also from the same Dionysian version.

Moreover, in column 32 we read:

“In the Council of Hippo-Regius. Concerning penitents. According to the difference of sins, at the bishop’s discretion,” and so forth, as in Dionysius’s canon 43.

It is a canon of the Council of Carthage of the year 397. It is assigned to the synod of Hippo-Regius just as, in the Herouvallian collection, the same canon is attributed to that synod along with others that are found in Dionysius after the annotation of the Council of Hippo. See the *Treatise* at the place cited shortly above.

The title “Concerning penitents” also reproduces the Dionysian title prefixed to that canon. These three items prove that the author of this collection used the Dionysian codex.

## V

What is more, Father Coustantius indicates that the celebrated Gallican Corbie collection, written around the middle of the sixth century, contains the Nicene canons inserted from Dionysius’s version. He says this in his note to Innocent’s Epistle 17, no. 4, where he cites the eighth canon of that version.

Quesnellus too would have seen the same thing if he had consulted the same codex, which he praises in § 12 as preserved in the library of Saint-Germain and calls a collection compiled for the use of the Gallican Church. Others who have the opportunity to read other codices and other Gallican collections from the sixth or seventh century will find the same thing.

## VI

We can add Vatican Palatine 577, which contains Dionysius’s own collection of canons, or its first form. This codex belonged to Gaul and was written around the middle of the eighth century, while Carloman and Pepin were reigning, as we proved in part III, chapter 1, § 3.

Here, then, is an example of the Dionysian codex in Gaul before Charlemagne. Since it differs from the Hadrianic copies, it points to an earlier origin. Perhaps others will find in Gallican libraries some equally ancient Dionysian copies that do not derive from the Hadrianic codex.

The oldest pure copy of Dionysius preserved in the Royal Library is praised by many. Whether it once belonged to a Gallican Church, we do not know. After Dionysius’s codex was handed over to Charlemagne, with those readings and additions that distinguish the Hadrianic collection from the pure Dionysian collection, the multiplication of Hadrianic copies gradually caused the copies of pure Dionysius to disappear.

This explains their rarity, not the claim that no such copies once existed among the Gauls, who could have derived the Dionysian version of the canons in the collections mentioned above, earlier than Hadrian, only from purely Dionysian codices.

Certainly, it is clear that there was once some pure copy of Dionysius among the Gauls from the very old Gallican codex of Arras, which contains the Gallican collection published in this volume. At the end of this codex there is a copy of Dionysius’s letter to the presbyter Julian, as Pamelius testifies in his notes on Saint Cyprian’s book *On the Unity of the Church*.

This letter is found only in manuscript codices of pure Dionysius and is absent from every Hadrianic copy. The scribe who transcribed that letter into the aforementioned Gallican copy therefore found and used a purely Dionysian codex in Gaul. That codex is sufficiently shown to have been earlier than Hadrian, after whose time it is established that purely Dionysian manuscripts fell into disuse.

## VII

It is certain that copies of Dionysius had been propagated long before the Hadrianic period into Spain, Africa, England, and Ireland. A Spanish collection composed at the beginning of the seventh century received the pontifical constitutions found in Dionysius, with the same titles and divisions.

At about the same time Cresconius compiled his collection in Africa from Dionysius. Before Charlemagne, Egbertus used Dionysius’s codex in England, and from its version he inserted several canons of the Greek synods into his collection, as we remarked in *Treatise*, part IV, chapter 6.

In the same place we also described a very ancient Irish collection, in which we proved that several excerpts had been taken from a pure Dionysian codex. Add that the same codex also reached Greece. From it the canons of the African Church were rendered into Greek, and this Greek version was cited at the Council in Trullo in the year 692.

Who, then, could doubt that a collection disseminated even in distant regions before Charlemagne’s reign penetrated the neighboring provinces of Gaul? If copies of pure Dionysius also existed in Gaul in that earlier age, it cannot be denied that they were available for anyone’s use.

If, however, nothing from them is found cited in any earlier synod, or by any Gallican writer other than Gregory of Tours, about whom we spoke in column 1113, note c, to the preceding dissertation, this must be attributed to the scarcity of evidence.

The most ancient Gallican collections, which received something from the Dionysian codex, prove that its use was free and provide sufficiently suitable testimony in the place of each individual writer.

## § II. Which Versions the Gallicans Used before or after the Dionysian Codex Was Published and Received

## VII

In the question raised by Quesnellus in § 15—namely, which version of the Greek canons was used in Gaul before the Dionysian version was received—it is certain that, at least in some places, Rufinus’s abbreviations of the Nicene canons prevailed, as Quesnellus himself maintains in the same place, and as we confirmed in *Treatise*, part II, chapter 10, § 2.

Whether these abbreviations alone were in use for those canons, although he calls it into question in § 16, we are nevertheless certain that the complete version of the same canons was used in Gaul from the Council of Valence in the year 374.

For in its third canon we find:

“Concerning those persons who, after the one and holy washing, have defiled themselves either with profane sacrifices to demons or with hostile bathing, we have judged that this form of censure should be observed: that, in accordance with THE NICENE SYNOD, access to satisfaction should not be denied them,” and so forth.

This indicates Nicene canon 11. The Fathers of that synod certainly found this canon not in Rufinus’s abbreviation, which had not yet appeared, but in some complete, older version of that synod.

Moreover, we have remarked in part II, chapter 10, § 2, no. 19, that the author of the Gallican collection inscribed under the name of the Second Council of Arles had before his eyes not only Rufinus’s abbreviations of the Nicene canons but also another complete interpretation of them.

## IX

What, then, was this complete version used by the Gallicans? Since Saint Hilary, in his book *On the Synods*, no. 84, and in fragment 2, column 643 of the Verona edition, recites the Nicene Creed from that most ancient version which, immediately after the council, was brought to Rome and used by the Roman Church, it may be questioned whether this version also prevailed among the ancient Gauls in the canons before Rufinus’s abbreviations were published.

At the Council of Valence, the sense of the Nicene canon, but not its wording, is brought forward; nothing can therefore be derived from it in favor of this or that interpretation.

Only from Gallican documents later than Rufinus does it become certain that the ancient version was at times received among the Gauls which was later transferred into the Hispanic collection and, from the Hispanic collection, into the Isidorian collection, and which, having been disseminated under Isidore’s name, is usually called the Isidorian version.

In the Council of Riez in the year 439, canon 3, the eighth Nicene decree is indicated—in the words which, as Quesnellus admits in § 16, occur only in that version. The error which he thought existed in Rufinus’s text is introduced solely by his own arbitrary decision, in order to force the same decree back into Rufinus’s abbreviations.

This is evident from the very emendation which, without citing any manuscript codex, he substituted on his own authority. Since the two words “parishes” and “chorepiscopus,” received in the Riez canon and pointing to that ancient version, do not agree with Rufinus’s abbreviations, correcting only the single word “chorepiscopus” is wholly insufficient to make the decree fit those abbreviations—especially since only the Isidorian interpretation presents not merely the word “parish” but also the word “chorepiscopus.”

Furthermore, the Council of Epaon in the year 517 also confirms the use of that ancient version. In canon 31, concerning the penance of murderers, it prescribes observance of what the Ancyran canons decreed.

The designation *Ancyritani* (“Ancyran”) is peculiar to the ancient interpretation. For in the version called the *Prisca*, the same canons are termed *Ancyrenses* (“of Ancyra”), whereas in Dionysius they are termed *Ancyrani* (“Ancyran”).

Add the very ancient Corbie collection, praised by Quesnellus himself, in which the canons of the Greek synods, except the Nicene canons, reproduce that same ancient interpretation.

The same thing is found in the collection published in this volume, which we have proved was compiled in Gaul. Sirmondus mentions other very ancient Gallican collections—the Fossatensis, Aniciensis, and Remensis—which contain the same version.

Hence the same version frequently occurs in later synods or capitularies, as the aforementioned Sirmondus noted in his remarks on the first capitulary of the year 789; Quesnellus himself also admitted this in the aforementioned dissertation, § 10.

### X.

Since the Gauls had no fixed public codex of canons, neither was any particular version prescribed for them. Consequently, some used Rufinus’s abbreviated version of the Nicene canons, while others used the ancient Isidorian version. Since Gallican codices more frequently favor the latter, it cannot be denied that its use was also more frequent. Nevertheless, that ancient version which Justellus published, and which we have reprinted in this volume, reached Gaul and was sometimes—though more rarely—used by the Gauls; this is demonstrated by the Gallican collection published in this volume. For in it the canons of Chalcedon are presented according to the Prisca translation.

We have also seen in the preceding paragraph that the Dionysian translation was brought into Gaul before Charlemagne and was employed there on several occasions. Since neither Adrian I, who gave Charlemagne the Dionysian codex together with several additions, nor that emperor forbade anyone to use another codex, the ancient version is found to have been used several times even after this period. Only when the copies associated with Adrian were gradually multiplied and disseminated through the emperor’s care—for he was exceedingly devoted to the Roman Church and its discipline and, just as he sought its liturgical books, so too endeavored to obtain from that Church a codex of the canons and to circulate it for the use of the Gallican churches [Col. 1131A]—did the Dionysian interpretation, together with that codex, gradually become more common. As Sirmondus observed, whose testimony I should like to use to conclude these remarks:

“It is certain that they—the Gauls—always used that Prisca, or Isidorian, version more willingly and continued to use it frequently down to the very time of Charlemagne. This is demonstrated, among other things, by the capitulary of Charlemagne at Aachen, which is entirely filled with authorities from the ancient version, except in the case of the apostolic canons, which are necessarily cited from the Dionysian version, because at that time no other version of them existed. After this, however, they gradually departed from it and embraced the codex of the canons of the Dionysian collection, which Pope Adrian had commended to King Charlemagne.”

[Col. 1131]

## UNPUBLISHED SERMONS OF SAINT LEO THE GREAT

Extracted from the Florentine libraries and edited by A. B. Caillau, priest of the Society of Mercy, together with Dr. Saint-Yves, of the same society. (C, G, S)*

### Preface

Of these sermons, all of which bear the name of Saint Leo the pope in the codices, some appear capable of being rightly attributed to him, while others evidently depart from his manner of expression. Therefore, lest—as happened in our edition of Saint Augustine—we be reproached for a certain audacity, since some have suspected us of wishing to impose our own judgment on everything, we place these discourses before the eyes of readers as they lie in the manuscripts, leaving it to their discernment to separate what is genuine from what is spurious by their own judgment.

## SERMON I. On the Time of Fasting

[Note: [Col. 1131D] This sermon comes from five Florentine codices, namely: Laurentian Library, Plut. 14, cod. 1, p. 136; ibid., Plut. 33, cod. 4, p. 61; Plut. 23 dexter, cod. 10, p. 45; the Library of the Aediles, cod. 140, p. 161; and ibid., cod. 143, [Col. 1132D] p. 167b. In every case it bears the name of Saint Leo.]

[Col. 1131B]

### I.

Our faith, dearly beloved, urges us to bring forth instructions concerning religion. For we exhort you to [Note: The codex lacks “to.”] fasting, which for those who live rightly is an increase of devotion, a wall of faith, and an assault upon wickedness. We also advise that we must always abstain not only from food but from every vice. Do not be extravagant in feasting or arrogant in drunkenness, for it is written in Solomon: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15). The Apostle likewise says: “Make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13:14).

Therefore abstain during these days from worldly cares and carnal desires. Let the body be chastened so that the soul may be satisfied. The spirit is strengthened when the flesh is weakened by restraint [Col. 1131C]. For the present life is nourished by delicacies in food, not the future life, since luxury accompanies abundance of possessions. Remove from yourselves envy, quarrels, evil speech, disputes, and dissolve every seed of sin. Nullify the snares of violent actions and the intricate arguments of slanders (sic). Offer the needy and the members of the household of faith a place of refuge. Tear up unjust documents of debt, so that you may celebrate fasts pleasing to God not only in body but also in spirit.

### II.

We ought also to hope for the fruits of our own fasting through the seed of almsgiving. For it is written: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Sir. 3:33). We must also act so that we appear to abstain from lavish preparations not out of a passion for greed but from concern for mercy. Let us give temporal things to the poor, so that through their prayers the gifts of eternal things may be granted to us. For through the exchange of a little bread and bronze, pardon for our sins is conferred upon us.

It must also be understood that just as the Lord made many people weak, so he made many poor, so that there might be a necessity of beseeching the Lord, and so that you, who have suffered none of these things, might fear that perhaps you may suffer them. Therefore, if you are healthy, feed the sick, as an example of calamity suffered in another’s place. If you are rich, feed the poor, whose portion perhaps you received from the Lord our God in order that you might feed him. Feed the fasting person [Note: The codex reads *jejunium*, “a fast,” instead of *jejunum*, “the fasting person.”], lest the portion taken away from him be given to you while you give to someone else. Feed the one dying of hunger; for whoever could have saved a person by feeding him, but did not feed him, has killed him.

### III.

Let the desires of silent beggars also be anticipated, for we read: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor; on the evil day the Lord will deliver him” (Ps. 40:2). Let us therefore give nourishment to the needy before they ask, lest, compelled by excessive necessity to cry out, they appear to be demanding what we delay giving. Let us provide them with some portion of the heavenly gifts bestowed upon us, lest through our sluggishness we have to repay penal interest to our creditor.

Let us remember that rich man who asked for a drop of water because of the crumbs of bread, but did not receive it. Let us recall that widow who, by putting two small coins into the treasury, offered God all the sustenance she possessed. Let us also give to our brothers whatever exceeds our needs.

Nor should we perform God’s commands with sadness and hypocrisy. Rather, let us give thanks to God, the author of our generosity, so that by praying continually we may provide the needy with the substance of temporal life, in order that we may attain eternal life, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON II. On the Passion of the Lord

[Note: This sermon, which we extracted from cod. 1, Plut. 14 of the Laurentian Library, contains several sentences that are found in sermon 1 of Quesnel’s edition, but otherwise differs entirely. Since we had only one codex, several passages required correction, and we have tried to repair them as best we could; whether successfully, the reader may judge.]

### I.

After that first and universal collapse of human transgression, from the time when sin entered this world through one man, and death through sin (Rom. 5:12), no one would have escaped the devil’s dominion or the dreadful bonds of captivity, nor would reconciliation for pardon or return to life have been open to anyone, unless the Son who is God, coeternal and in every respect coequal with God the Father, had also deigned to become the Son of man and had been hung bodily upon the cross for the redemption and salvation of all human beings [Note: The codex reads, “for the redemption of every human being.” This entire opening is found in the published editions, with only a few changes.].

For this was the cause of the redemption and salvation of the entire human race: that God himself truly suffered in man, truly died, and truly rose from the dead; and that he truly opened the gates of the heavenly kingdom to human beings who believed in him and died in accordance with his will, thereby redeeming us from eternal death and punishment.

For our sake he endured many and various insults—not because of sins of his own, since he never committed any sin, but solely because of our necessity. We were bound by chains so harsh and had been cast into so deep an abyss of death that we could not be released except through his immeasurable mercy and his human passion and death [Note: The codex lacks “that” (*ut*). Nearly the same sentence is found above.]. Unless he redeemed us with his precious blood, unless by his death he removed eternal punishments from us [Note: The word “punishments” is absent from the codex], unless he broke the devil’s power and brought us with himself to the heavenly kingdoms, and granted all of us who wished to remain in his will a smooth and easy way to the heavenly kingdoms [Note: The codex likewise does not contain “to”].

### II.

Therefore, dearest brothers, what should we do for such great benefits of God except die to the world and to its desires, mortifying carnal longings within us through vigils, fasts, chastity, endurance of adversity, perseverance in every good work, and by continually commending ourselves to God in prayer?

By repenting, weeping, and confessing our sins, and redeeming ourselves from eternal punishments through almsgiving, let us be supported by divine aid so that, where our merciful Lord God restored us through his death, we may deserve to remain in eternal blessedness, through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor [Col. 1133D] and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON III. On Easter

[Note: This sermon is found in two Florentine codices, namely Laurentian Library cod. 4, p. 113, and the Library of the Aediles, cod. 136, [Col. 1134D] p. 98; in both it bears the name of Saint Leo.]

[Col. 1134A]

### I.

You have heard, dearest brothers, the Scripture of the Hebrew exodus [Note: Cod. 136 reads: “The Hebrew Scripture is the Passover of the exodus, and through the words of the mystery”], and the words of the mystery: how the Lamb was sacrificed, how the people were saved, and how Pharaoh was scourged through the mystery.

Understand, dearest ones, how the mystery of Passover is at once new and old, temporal and eternal, corruptible and incorruptible, mortal and immortal. It is old according to the Law, but new according to the Word [Note: These words are found in cod. 136 but are absent from cod. 4]; temporal through the model, eternal through glory [Note: Cod. 4 reads “glory”; cod. 136, “grace”]; corruptible because of the animal victim, incorruptible because of the Lord’s life; mortal because of the burial, immortal because of the resurrection. The old is the Law, but the new is the Word.

The model is temporal [Note: The codex mistakenly reads “through”], but grace is eternal [Note: Cod. 4 reads *sempiternum*, masculine/neuter; cod. 136, *sempiterna*, feminine]; the sheep are corruptible [Note: The same codex reads “the corruptible sheep,” singular], but the Lord is incorruptible. For he was cut to pieces like a lamb [Note: The same codex incorrectly reads *non*, “not”], but was raised again like God. Indeed, he was led like a sheep to the sacrifice, but he was not a sheep; and like a lamb without a voice (Isa. 53:7), but he was not a lamb. Those things were done in figure, whereas these are found in greater truth.

For in place of the lamb the Lord became the victim, and in place of the animal, man—man, however, who is Christ, in whom all things are contained. Isaiah says:

“Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth. In humiliation his judgment was taken away. And who will declare his generation?” (ibid. 53:7–8).

Many other things besides these were foretold by the prophets concerning the mystery of Jesus Christ at Passover [Note: Cod. 136 reads “at Passover”; cod. 4, “of Passover”]. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1134C]

### II.

For he himself was led like a lamb and killed like a sheep. As though from Egypt, he redeemed us from the worship of the world [Note: The codex reads “from the worship”], and saved us from the hand of the devil as from the hand of Pharaoh. He marked our souls with his own spirit and the members of our body with his precious blood.

This is he who clothed death with shame and turned the devil into mourning [Note: The codex reads *plantum*, apparently incorrectly, for *planctum*, “mourning”]. This is he who struck down iniquity and injustice, just as Moses condemned Egypt to sterility [Note: Cod. 136 reads “into sterility”]. This is he who rescued us from slavery to freedom, from darkness to light, from death to life, from tyranny to an everlasting kingdom.

This is he who suffered many things in many ways: he was slain in Abel, bound by the feet in Isaac, a wanderer in Jacob, sold in Joseph, wrapped in Moses [Note: The codex incorrectly reads *Moysen*, “Moses” in the accusative], exposed by his mother in the river, slaughtered in the lamb, persecuted in David, and dishonored in the prophets.

This is he who was buried in the earth and, rising from the dead, ascended to the heights of heaven. This is the lamb without a voice; this is he who was taken from the flock for sacrifice, sacrificed in the evening, and buried at night.

This is Jesus Christ our Lord, who rose from the dead and raised man from the lower tomb to life. Thus he was killed in the midst of Jerusalem. By whom? By Israel. For what reason? Because he healed their lame, cleansed their lepers, enlightened their blind, and raised their dead.

### III.

What have you done, Israel [Note: Thus cod. 136; cod. 4 adds “to himself”], in committing such a new injustice? You disgraced him who had made you noble; you dishonored him who had glorified you; you silenced him who had proclaimed you; you killed him who had given you life [Note: So cod. 136; this final clause of the sentence is absent from cod. 4].

Is it not written: “Do not shed innocent blood, lest you die most miserably” (Jer. 22:3)?

“Therefore,” he says, “Israel, you did this” [Note: Cod. 136 reads “he did this”], “because it was necessary for him to suffer” (Acts 17:3).

You are mistaken, Israel, in thinking in this way. It was necessary for him to suffer, but not by your hand; it was necessary for him to be subjected to insults, but not by you; it was necessary for him to be hung upon the gallows of the cross [Note: Cod. 4 incorrectly reads “to the cross”; cod. 136, “upon the cross”; perhaps *crucis* should be read], but this should by no means have been done by your right hand.

With this cry, Israel, you ought to have called out to the Lord: “O Lord, if your will has decreed that your Son should suffer, let him suffer by no means through me. Let him be judged by foreigners, let him be nailed by the uncircumcised, by any tyrant. Far be it that this crime should be perpetrated by me.”

You did not wish to proclaim this cry, Israel, and you did not spare your own hands from being laid upon your Lord. You did not fear his works; they caused you no shame when the withered hand was restored sound to its own body. Nor did you feel shame when closed eyes were opened, nor when loosened limbs were strengthened by his word. Nor did you blush at that recent miracle: a man already dead four days [Note: Cod. 4 reads “three days”] rose from the tomb at his command.

### IV.

O Israel, you saw so many miracles of Christ, yet you remained always in unbelief. Passing over all these things, you prepared yourself for the Lord’s death [Note: The word “Lord” is absent from cod. 136].

You prepared for him the sharpest nails, false witnesses, gall, and a sword, as though for a murderous robber. You inflicted blows upon his little body; you placed a crown of thorns upon his head; and you bound with chains those good hands of his that had formed you from the earth. You fed that good mouth of his—through which you were nourished with life—with gall instead [Note: Cod. 4 lacks *e*, “from,” before *contrario*].

On the great day of the feast you killed your Lord. You were enjoying banquets, while he suffered the hunger of famine; you drank wine and ate bread, while he had gall and vinegar; you were splendid in body, while he was worn out by grief [Note: Cod. 4 reads “confounded”]; you rejoiced, while he was afflicted; you sang psalms, while he was judged [Note: Cod. 136 reads “was being judged”]; you led dances, while he was laid in the tomb [Note: Cod. 136 reads “was seasoned”]; you lay in the softness of a bed, while he lay in a tomb and coffin.

O most impious Israel, why did you perpetrate this new injustice? [Note: Cod. 4 reads *perpetrasti nobis? tuam*; the reading is materially uncertain.] By subjecting your Lord to new sufferings, you killed him—your ruler [Note: Cod. 4 reads incorrectly “your giver”], your creator, who honored you and gave you the name Israel. But you, Israel, were by no means found to be Israel; you did not see [Note: Cod. 4 incorrectly reads *novisti*, “you knew”] the Lord, nor did you wish to understand God.

[Col. 1136B]

### V.

Did you not know, O Israel, that this is the firstborn of God, who was begotten before the morning star? This is he who brought you into Egypt and, preserving you there, supplied you with nourishment. This is he who was sent to you, who healed your sufferers, who raised the dead. This is he against whom you acted wickedly, whom you slaughtered. This is he whom you sold.

Therefore, O Israel, because you did not tremble before the Lord [Note: Cod. 136 reads “because”], when attacked by enemies you trembled. You did not fear the Lord; you did not lament before the Lord [Note: The codices apparently read *jejunasti*, “you fasted,” incorrectly], but you lamented over your dead sons. Because you abandoned the Lord, you will not be found by him; you struck the Lord down, and you too will be struck down to the earth [Note: Cod. 4 reads “you will be cast down”].

You lie upon the earth, while he, rising from the dead, has been carried up to the height of heaven [Note: Cod. 136 reads “to the loftiness of heaven”].

[Col. 1136C]

### VI.

Now therefore come, all you families of human beings who have become entangled in sins [Note: Cod. 4 reads “with these things,” apparently incorrectly], and receive remission of sins. For the Lord says to you [Note: These words are absent from cod. 4]:

“I am your remission; I am the Passover of salvation; I am the lamb who was slaughtered for you [Note: These words are likewise absent from cod. 4]; I am your redemption; I am life; I am your salvation; I am your resurrection. I am your king; I shall raise you up by my right hand.”

This is our Lord, who made heaven and earth; who was hung upon the wood, buried in the earth, rose from the dead, ascended to the heights of heaven, and lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON IV. On Easter II

[Note: This sermon is partly read in two Cassinese codices, namely cod. 11, fol. 222, and cod. 123, fol. 139b, under the name of Saint Augustine. For that reason we published it as a work of Saint Augustine in our supplements to that doctor. But it is found under the name of Saint Leo in three Florentine codices, namely Laurentian Library, Plut. 17, cod. 37, p. 6; ibid., Plut. 23 dexter, cod. 10, p. 70; and the Library of the Aediles, cod. 143, p. 205b. Here it is found in its entirety, whereas at Monte Cassino only part of it is preserved. Its style sounds more like Saint Leo than Saint Augustine’s, and he uses the address “dearest ones” more frequently. We have therefore judged it more suitably attributed to Saint Leo and thought it worthwhile to present it here in its fuller form.]

[Col. 1136D]

### I.

Although all the solemnities celebrated in the churches in honor of God [Note: The codex reads *per Dei honore*, “through the honor of God.”] are holy and venerable, dearest ones, nevertheless this present day of the Lord’s resurrection possesses a special festival character. This is because all other days contain only the joy of the living, whereas this day also contains gladness for the dead.

This feast is therefore common to those below and those above, because, rising from the dead, the Lord granted a festival both there, where he conquered death, and here, where he returned victorious from death. For this reason the Psalmist speaks particularly of this day, saying: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Ps. 117:24).

By announcing the Lord’s resurrection not only to those above but also to those below, he proclaimed a day of saving exultation. When the Lord descended into the dark gloom of the underworld [Note: The codex reads “into the dark … gloom”], even there, without doubt, the day was most radiant, where the Savior shone forth.

Hence the Evangelist beautifully says [*q. lect.*, apparently an abbreviation or corrupt reading]: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:5). For although the Lord ascended even amid darkness, he did not experience the obscurity of darkness. In that horror of night [Note: The codex incorrectly reads “the horror”], the light of eternal nature retained the inviolable splendor of its majesty; and thus it was not the light that was overcome by night, but night by the light.

### II.

Let us therefore rejoice, dearest ones, and exult in the Lord. Today the Lord has given us the light of salvation, according to what the same Psalmist says shortly afterward: “The Lord is God, and he has shone upon us” (Ps. 117:22). And what does he add further? “Establish,” he says, “a solemn day with frequent assemblies up to the horn of the altar” (ibid.).

I see this also fulfilled today in the Church of God. Since everything is filled with devout assemblies up to the horn of the altar, this fullness of the sacred Church has fulfilled the Scripture.

This day, therefore, dearest ones, is the day of resurrection and life. The more delightful rejoicing of this day makes it more welcome after Lent, because days of remission have been joined to the sadness of worldly affairs, so that patience may immediately be followed by its reward, according to the saying: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Ps. 125:5).

Therefore, whoever has sown in tears, receive the rewards of exultation. Let each person know that the greater the seeds of weeping he has sown, the greater the fruits of joy he will gather. The appearance of future blessedness is therefore already contained in present things. For just as relaxation now follows restriction [Note: The Cassinese codices read “discipline” or “severity”], so in the future rest will follow labor.

[Col. 1138A]

### III.

Therefore I beseech the whole Church, dearest ones [Note: The same codex reads “with the whole Church”], especially you who have been regenerated into new salvation [Note: The same codex reads “regeneration”] and have put on white garments, to preserve pure and undefiled the gift you have received; that you maintain the brightness of your clothing also in your conduct; and that your hearts be as white as your garments.

Today you heard the Evangelist say that all who believe in God are children of God. “He gave them,” he says, “power to become children of God, to those who are born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will [Note: The Cassinese codex reads “pleasure.” In the Florentine codex these words, “nor of the will of the flesh,” are absent] of man, but of God” (John 1:12).

Therefore you too have not now been born from the conception of the flesh, but have been begotten by God the Father. It remains for you to preserve, through the conduct of a holy life, the dignity of your holy origin, and truly, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “Like newborn infants, desire rational [Note: The Florentine and Cassinese codices read “rational,” plural] milk without deceit, so that by it you may grow unto salvation” (1 Pet. 2:2).

And may the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts and your bodies (Phil. 4:7), through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON V. On the Birth Anniversary of Saint Paul

[Note: This sermon is taken from the Laurentian Library, Plut. 23 dexter, cod. 10, p. 85b, where it bears the name of Saint Leo at the beginning. We have only one codex, and its ending is missing.]

*(Delivered at his church.)*

### I.

The joys of today’s festival are renewed for us in two ways, dearest brothers, as we celebrate the annual feast of the birth of the teacher of the world. Therefore, exulting in God and offering immense praises to his ineffable majesty, let us rejoice with great gladness. Indeed, we ought to rejoice with the greatest abundance of delight, because whenever the memory of the saints is celebrated, the minds of the faithful are filled with extraordinary joy and are enlightened with very great spiritual progress, since their presence is undoubtedly with us.

As we assemble, dearest ones, in this most sacred hall, we believe that the same eminent preacher stands [Note: The codex reads *assisti*.] in our midst and rejoices with us, spiritually and invisibly in some manner, in this celebrated solemnity of his.

Therefore, dearest ones, no sluggish torpor should ensnare any Christian and prevent him from coming to this venerable church, where his holy body rests—especially those who live in the city of Rome and the neighboring regions. It is especially fitting that the entire city hasten here [Note: The codex reads “that the whole of it be hastened”], for if people from the farthest parts of the world, fearing neither the harshness of the most arduous journey nor the distances of the earth, eagerly desire to present themselves devoutly at the thresholds [Note: The codex reads *limina*, “thresholds.”] of the apostles at whatever time they can [Note: The codex reads *eoque*, “and there”], what excuse can Roman citizens offer when, standing bodily present, they nevertheless neglect even to come to their festival [Note: The codex reads *in eoque*, “and in that”], although they are known to be protected by the aid of the apostles’ prayers?

### II.

Yesterday, when the princes of the apostles themselves were crowned by martyrdom [Note: The word “day” is absent from the codex], we hastened with the most devout affection to the church of the blessed apostle Peter and celebrated his solemnity. For it was fitting that the festival of him who deserved to attain the primacy of the apostolate should be celebrated first.

Today, however, we celebrate the birth anniversary of the teacher of the nations and the illuminator of the entire world. Although both apostles likewise received the reward of martyrdom, because of the multitude of people who converged, there was nevertheless a reason for transferring the feast of the blessed apostle Paul to that day [Note: The words “the feast” are absent from the codex]: just as the whole multitude assembled in the basilica of blessed Peter, so the same attached congregation of people might likewise gather in the church of his fellow apostle [Note: The codex reads *Ecclesia*, “church,” and above *aula*, “hall”], and all might share equally in the devotion of rejoicing.

And behold, many, whether devoted to idleness [Note: The codex reads “to idleness,” plural] or occupied with worldly cares, have postponed coming to this most excellent hall of blessed Paul. Therefore, dearest brothers, every worldly thought must be cast aside [Note: The codex reads “every thought of the world”], and desires for temporal profit must be rejected. With all the effort we can make, let us come to celebrate the memory of the saints, especially on the birth anniversary of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul [Note: The codex reads “birth anniversaries”].

Let us gather together devoutly in both their churches, so that, just as divine favor has honored them equally with the insignia of honors, devotion may likewise hold them equally in their solemnities.

[Col. 1139C]

### III.

For this most blessed man, first Saul and afterward Paul—first, I say, a persecutor and afterward a preacher—infected with the savagery of Jewish cruelty, burned with the madness of excessive ferocity against Christians.

For, as is contained in the Acts of the Apostles, having received authority from the chief priests to bring bound to Jerusalem any worshipers of the Christian religion whom he might find [Note: The codex reads “of those same people,” apparently incorrectly], he went forth raging and seized by great savagery. Suddenly enlightened and terrified by the splendor of a heavenly ray, he heard a voice from heaven saying to him:

“Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Acts 9:4).

Immediately he fell to the ground and lost the light of his eyes.

O the goodness of the great compassion of our omnipotent God! O the mercy of immeasurable patience! He terrified him for a little while so that he might console him in many ways.

## SERMON VI. On the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary

[Note: This sermon is read under the name of Saint Leo in four Florentine codices: Plut. 20, cod. 1, p. 211, and Plut. 17, cod. 41, p. 107, of the Laurentian Library; and cod. 138, p. 128b, and cod. 143b, of the Library of the Aediles.]

[Col. 1140A]

Today’s solemnity of the Virgin summons our tongue, brothers, to proclamation, and becomes in the present life a provider of benefit for those who have gathered—and very appropriately so. [Col. 1139D: The manuscripts read *solemnitatis*, wrongly.] For she is the mother of chastity and the glory of the female sex. [Col. 1140D: The manuscripts wrongly read *materium et*, followed by *gloriam*.] Therefore, although she is a mother in time, she remains ever a virgin.

O how desirable an assembly! Behold, both earth and sea offer gifts to the Virgin. [Col. 1140D: One manuscript wrongly reads “numbers.”] The one, calmly spreading its back beneath the clouds, pours forth rain [one manuscript has “calm”]; the other, guiding the footsteps of travelers without impediment, brings gifts from heaven [one manuscript wrongly has the masculine “that one”]. Nature rejoices, women are honored, and humanity shines forth. For where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more (Romans 5:20).

Blessed Mary has summoned us [the manuscripts wrongly read “us” in a corrupt construction]: the immaculate dew of virginity; the rational paradise of the second Adam [the manuscripts wrongly add “in”]; the workshop of the union of natures [the manuscripts then wrongly read *officium* (“office”) for *officina* (“workshop”)]; the saving solemnity of exchange; the bridal chamber in which the Word was betrothed to flesh and made animate; the bush of nature, which the fire of the divine birth burned.

Truly a light cloud [one manuscript wrongly has “light” in the ablative], which carried in bodily form him whom cherubim and seraphim tremble before [the manuscripts wrongly add “of”]. O heavenly rain! O most pure fleece, with which the Shepherd of the sheep clothed himself! Mary, mother and handmaid, virgin and heaven, alone bearing God and man.

A terrible fountain, a fabric of the divine dispensation, in which the tunic of the incarnation was ineffably woven. The overseer of this work [one manuscript wrongly reads “of the work”; the editor suggests reading “whose work”] is the Holy Spirit, while the overshadowing power of the Most High is the weaver [the manuscripts wrongly read “and you overshadow the Most High”]. He clothes ancient Adam in a flowering garment. This is the holy and immaculate flesh.

The ray of this fabric also proved to be marvelous grace [one manuscript wrongly has the accusative “grace”]; but the craftsman—the one who came upon the scene through obedience—was the Word of God. For who has seen, or who has heard, how the uncircumscribed God dwelt in the sacred womb of the holy Virgin, and how the belly of the blessed Virgin contained him whom heaven cannot contain? [One manuscript reads “conceived” instead of “contained.”]

God was born of a woman, but not naked, and not merely a human being. And because he was born taking away the sin of the old man, he revealed the gate of salvation. Where the serpent poured out poison through disobedience, there the Word, entering through obedience, fashioned a life-giving temple. From the place where Cain, the first disciple of sin, emerged, Christ, the liberator of our race, sprang forth without seed.

The lover of all did not shrink from the pains of a woman [as printed; perhaps “the womb”], from whom the transaction in question had made its purchase. He was not defiled by dwelling in the one whom he himself had fashioned without dishonor.

If the mother did not remain a virgin, the one who was born is merely a human being, and the birth is not marvelous. But if she remained a virgin even after giving birth, then he was born ineffably who entered through closed doors without hindrance. Of his union of natures Thomas exclaimed: “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28).

Do not be ashamed, O human being; he himself became for us the occasion of salvation. If he had not been born of a woman, he would never have died; if he had not died in the flesh, he would never through death have destroyed him who held the dominion of death, that is, the devil (Hebrews 2:14).

It is no dishonor for the architect to remain in what he himself built. For just as the potter is not defiled when he renews the clay that he had fashioned, so the undefiled one is not defiled by proceeding from the sacred womb of the Virgin. [Col. 1141D: One manuscript omits the second “not”; this is evidently erroneous, as is its reading “renewing” for “renewed.”] He was not defiled when he fashioned her; passing through her, he was not polluted. [The manuscripts wrongly have the feminine “polluted.”]

O womb in which the pledge of universal freedom was established! O belly [one manuscript reads “womb”] in which weapons were fashioned against death [the manuscripts read “caves against the mountain,” without sense]! O threshing-floor in which Christ, the cultivator of nature, sprang forth like a grain without seed!

O temple in which God became priest, without changing his nature; but, having mercy on the one who is according to the order of Melchizedek, he clothed himself with him! For “the Word of God became flesh” (John 1:14). Even if the Jews do not believe the birth, God put on the form of a human being; even if the pagans disparage the miracle of the incarnation, the judgment is clear. For this reason it is a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the nations (1 Corinthians 1:23). The mystery resounds because the miracle is beyond reason.

If the Word had not dwelt in the womb, the flesh would never have sat upon the throne. If entering the womb had been a dishonor, then ministering to human beings would also have been a dishonor to the angels.

He who by nature is impassible, being God, became—through mercy—a being subject to many sufferings. Was Christ God, then, made from an outcome or result? Certainly not. Through compassion, as we believe, he became human; we proclaim the man made by God, but confess God incarnate.

He who according to essence is without a mother and according to the dispensation without a father wrote his own handmaid as mother. If he is merely a human being, he is not without a father, for he has a father. But now he himself is without a mother as creator, and without a father as the one created. [The manuscripts read “without a mother.” The editor notes that something seems missing, perhaps: “If he is God, he is not without a mother, for he has a mother.”]

Be ashamed even before the name of the archangel who announced the good news to Mary. He is called Gabriel [one manuscript reads “what” for “why”]. But what does Gabriel signify? “God and man [son] of the most blessed Virgin” [the manuscripts have “God, the Virgin, and man”; the editorial note adds: “Gabriel is interpreted ‘man of God’”]. Since the one to whom he was announcing the message was God and man [the manuscripts read *his*; manuscript 1 has *evangelizabantur*, “were being evangelized”], the name preceded the dispensation, so that the dispensation might be believed.

Learn the cause of his presence, and glorify the power of the incarnate one. The human race owed much in this matter, and the debt was overwhelming. Through Adam we all inscribed ourselves under sin [the manuscripts wrongly read the singular “all”]; through him the devil also kept us as slaves, producing our instruments and displaying only bodily knowledge [the text is uncertain]. The evil one, the deceiver of all, stood accusing us, pressing the debt against us and demanding judgment. [One manuscript reads “from judgment,” better than another’s nonsensical “from the judgment.”]

It was therefore necessary that one of two things happen: either death should be imposed upon all by judgment, because all had sinned, or one should be given as compensation who would become the justification of the entire redemption.

Humanity could not save itself, for it lay under the debt [one manuscript wrongly reads “the debt” as an accusative]. An angel could not redeem it, for he was unequal to such a liberation. Only the one who was without sin had to die for sinners; he alone remained for the cancellation of evil.

What, then? He who changes the whole of nature had led you as God; and he who lacked nothing in goodness devised for those condemned a most noble life and a most certain release from death, because he was human as we are. [The manuscripts read “and what.”] For speech cannot interpret the miracle.

Thus he who became human dies, and he liberates what had fallen away [the manuscripts wrongly read “what existed” or “what might exist”], according to Paul, who says: “In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins” (Colossians 1:14).

O astonishing event! Such a one obtained immortality—and he himself was immortal [the manuscripts read the ablative “by immortality”]. No other such one according to the dispensation existed, was made, exists, or will exist. He alone, born of the Virgin, is God and man [the word “God” is absent from the manuscripts but is plainly required by the sense]. He possesses not merely a dignity capable of being set against and valued in relation to the multitude of them [perhaps “sufficient for sinners”], but one surpassing every judgment: as Son, preserving with the Father what is unchangeable; as Creator, possessing unfailingly what belongs to power; in his love of mercy, displaying without any delay what belongs to compassion [one manuscript wrongly has the accusative “delay”]; and as priest [one manuscript has “of priests,” another “a priest”], bringing with trustworthy adequacy what was required for restoration. No one will ever find anything similar or even comparable in anyone else.

Consider his love for human beings [one manuscript wrongly reads “love for all.”] He was voluntarily condemned, and while they were crucifying him [perhaps “those crucifying”] he dissolved the death that existed, turning the wickedness of those who were killing him into the salvation of the wicked. [One manuscript reads “the killing.”]

It was not possible for a human child to save humanity, for he himself needed to be saved [the manuscripts read “to save”], according to Paul: “All have sinned and lack the grace [the manuscripts read “glory”] of God” (Romans 3:23). Sin derived from the devil, because the devil carried death against humanity in great peril and craftily introduced it among us; and now [the manuscripts read “even”] the release from death was impossible.

Finally, those who had been sent by the heavenly physician were accusing it. Therefore the prophets, seeing that the matter exceeded human art, cried out to the heavenly physician. One said: “Lord, bow the heavens and descend” (Psalm 144:5). Another: “Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed” (Jeremiah 17:14). Another cried: “Stir up your power and come, that you may save us” (Psalm 80:3). Another said: “Alas for me, my soul, for the merciful one has perished from the earth” (Micah 7:1–2). Another: “If God truly dwelt with human beings” (1 Kings 8:27; one manuscript wrongly reads “with all”). Another: “Your mercies have quickly overtaken us, Lord” (Psalm 79:8). Again another: “O God, attend to my help; Lord, hasten to assist me” (Psalm 70:2). Another: “The one who is to come will come and will not delay” (Habakkuk 2:3). Another: “I have gone astray like a sheep that was lost; seek your servant, Lord” (Psalm 119:176).

The one who is naturally king and God did not long disregard the oppression of nature. He came who had always been present, paid the redemption with his own blood, and gave for the human race, as compensation for death, the body with which he had clothed himself from the Virgin. He redeemed the world from the curse of the law, concerning which Paul cried: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law” (Galatians 3:13).

Human nature, deceived by sin, was enslaved. He who redeemed us is not merely a human being, O Jew, but neither is he naked God, for he had a body. If he had not clothed himself with all these things, he would not have saved me [one manuscript reads “may he save me”]. But he who in the Virgin’s womb underwent the sentence clothed himself with the condemned nature.

There the terrible exchange took place: Christ, giving himself, received flesh, and the very same one was from the virgin and with the Virgin. Here he overshadowed her; there he was incarnate from her. If Christ is one and God the Word another, there is no longer a Trinity but a quaternity.

Do not tear apart the tunic of the dispensation, which was woven from above. Do not become a teacher of Arius. That impious man divides the judgment; you must not allow the unity to be cut apart.

Who appeared to those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, a human being—and how? Because they lived in darkness, according to Paul, who says: “He delivered us from the power of darkness” (Colossians 1:13). And again: “You were once darkness” (Ephesians 5:8).

Who, then, shone forth? Let David teach you, saying: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Psalm 118:26). Who is this? Speak openly, O David: “The Lord is God, and he has shone upon us” (Psalm 118:27; one manuscript reads “My God”).

The natures came together, and the unity remained without confusion. He came to save, but he also had to suffer. For how could a merely human being save, when he was unable to do so? Nor could naked God suffer.

He himself, being God by nature, became human; he saved what he had bought, while he endured what he became. Therefore, when the synagogue crowned him with thorns, the holy Church, weeping, said: “Daughters of Jerusalem, come out and see the crown with which his mother crowned him” (Song of Songs 3:11; one manuscript reads “because she crowned him,” another “with which”).

He himself bore a crown of thorns in order to dissolve the sentence of thorns. He himself was in the Father’s bosom and in the Virgin’s womb, in his mother’s arms and above the wings of the winds; above, he was worshiped by angels, and below, he reclined with tax collectors.

The seraphim made no advance, while Pilate was questioning him [one manuscript wrongly reads “they were questioning”]. The servant was striking him, and creation was terrified. He was confessed on the cross, and he was on the throne. He lay in the tomb, while he stretched out heaven like a skin (Psalm 104:2). He was counted among the dead, while hell was despoiled. Below, they slandered him as a deceiver; above, he was glorified by the saints [one manuscript reads “again”].

O astonishing mystery! I see miracles and proclaim divinity; I behold suffering and do not deny humanity.

Emmanuel appeared by nature as a human being, but as God he did not break the Virgin’s enclosure. He emerged from the womb just as he entered through hearing. He was born in the same manner in which he was conceived. He entered without suffering and emerged without corruption, according to the prophet Ezekiel, who says:

“God turned me toward the way of the outer gate of the sanctuary, which faces east [the manuscripts wrongly read the masculine ‘which’]; and it was closed. And the Lord said to me: ‘Son of man [one manuscript wrongly has “son”], this gate shall be closed and shall not be opened’” (Ezekiel 44:1–2). [One manuscript omits: “it was, and the Lord said to me: Son of man, this gate shall be closed.”]

No one passed through it, but the Lord God alone shall enter and go out, and the gate shall remain closed. Behold the manifest proof of holy Mary, God’s Birthgiver and perpetual virgin.

Let every contradiction henceforth be dissolved, and let the teaching of the holy Scriptures be illumined, so that we may obtain the kingdom of heaven in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong honor and glory, together with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout the never-ending ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VII. On Saint Dionysius the Martyr

[Col. 1144D–1145D: This sermon certainly does not belong to Saint Leo, since Saint Gregory is praised in it and it does not seem consistent with the gravity of the holy Doctor. It is drawn from three Florentine manuscripts: Plut. 20, cod. 1, p. 258; Plut. 30, cod. 5, p. 262b; and the Mugello Library, cod. 13, p. 222b.]

### I

Today divine mercy has deigned to renew for us the holy and glorious festival of our most blessed Father and most holy shepherd Dionysius, our dearly beloved brothers, a festival worthy of every veneration. We believe that it is no less proclaimed in heaven while it is devoutly honored by us sinners on earth. For although the Christian mind participates in all holy solemnities, we must rejoice more particularly and especially in the festival of our leader and Father, so that where the glorious departure of the distinguished martyr and bishop took place, there on the day of his martyrdom the beginning of joy may be found. [Col. 1145D: One manuscript reads *festivitatem* (“the festival”) rather than *festivitate* (“in the festival”).]

Whatever service we render to him, however, should be referred to the praise of our own and his Creator. For, as your own devout presence, brothers, testifies, you understand that the return of this day belongs to the common joy, since you gather to celebrate each year the festivals of your shepherd. [Col. 1145D: One manuscript reads “the course of this day” rather than “the return.”] We believe that by your greater devotion you draw near to the divine mercy through the prayers of your present patron, as you come with diligent zeal to his holy vigils [one manuscript has “you came”]. He does not abandon your devotion, since his reverence has gathered you together.

Indeed, brothers, like a loving father he rejoices with the saints in your holy acts of service [manuscript 5 reads *vestris enim nempe*; manuscript 13 wrongly has *vestri*] and exults in the number of his sons. [One manuscript has the nonsensical “the saints rejoice.”]

### II

O festival of our holy Father, worthy of our veneration! O truly blessed solemnity, to be exalted with great praises, concerning which the angels praise the Lord together in the heavens!

The assembly of priests resounds with great honor, and the choir of martyrs proclaims the palm of victory [one manuscript has “proclaimed”]. In it mouths long closed on earth are opened; the darkened eyes of the blind return to sight; the dreadful stains of sins are washed away [one manuscript has the singular “the dreadful stain”]; and the petitions of all are accepted as the deeds of the righteous.

Although, dearest brothers, with the circuit of the year having come round, his sacred vigils seem to us to be renewed, and although to Christian peoples they are new and astonishing as the ages pass, they nevertheless remain with us, for the glory of Christ, daily in their miracles and worthy of praise [one manuscript reads “every day”].

For who comes here sick and will not depart healed? [One manuscript reads “who, sick, comes here the day before.”] Who, weighed down by the burden of sins, will confess with a groan that he is guilty and not obtain forgiveness?

As I believe, the prophet saw this festival long beforehand when he said to the Lord: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells” (Psalm 26:8).

And, suitably proclaiming the sacred passing of our most blessed Father and praising the Lord together, he said: “Blessed is the one whom you have chosen and taken to yourself, Lord; he shall dwell in your courts” (Psalm 65:5).

### III

For divine condescension granted this man a great and marvelous gift after the apostles, and when it bestowed upon him a share in its power, it declared what glory he possessed with it.

This man, my brothers—this indeed is that blessed and truly praiseworthy priest and martyr of Christ, Dionysius the Areopagite, whom the Acts of the Apostles mention. He was born of noble Athenian ancestry, instructed from the rudiments of childhood in dialectical and rhetorical studies, and born on the island of Diona in the province of Attica.

He was called Areopagite because he had been educated in liberal letters at the place called the Areopagus. He had not only learned the sect of that people but was its most learned teacher among others.

Yet, since he who promised through the prophet, “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm 81:11), has deigned to assist us, and since he wished the mouth of a mute creature to be opened, I have thought it right to tell you a few things about the signs performed by this saint, which we undoubtedly believe will please your devout minds. [One manuscript perhaps reads “which.”] Some matters we learned by reading them in certain Greek books [one manuscript reads “we learned by report”]; others became known to us through the report of faithful men.

### IV

“In the name of God, Eugippius the Aristarchus sends greetings to Onesiphorus the primicerius.

“We have received, through Anatolius, the written words of your love [one manuscript reads ‘your holiness’]. In them you asked us to take care, in a literary response, to write to you what is known to our memory [manuscript 1 wrongly reads “your memory”] or recalled through the ancient tradition of our forebears concerning the various doctrines and the diversity of sects among the Athenians [the manuscripts read “secret sects”], as well as concerning the rite or arrangement of the city of Athens [all manuscripts read *Athenae*].

“Among other matters we found in your writings a request that we briefly describe for you [the manuscripts read *perstrinxissem*, “I had briefly outlined”; the editor suggests *depingerem*, “I should depict”] what took place in the city of the Athenians in the times of the apostles, and how certain people resisted the apostle Paul when he arrived there, through empty philosophies and deceptive imaginings of things. Indeed, you also asked us to explain more fully what we know about Simachus, Apollinaris the Chronopagite, and Dionysius the Areopagite [one manuscript has “concerning Dionysius”; the others omit “concerning”], who were renowned as hearers of the apostle Paul in Athens, including the ancestry of the Athenians from which they arose and the stock from which they were born [one manuscript reads “of what ancestry”].

“We have therefore sent you, through Anatolius, our son and bearer of your letter, what we have been able to hear concerning these matters, according to the weakness of our understanding, on the basis of the ancient tradition of bygone times.” [Manuscripts 5 and 13 retain “to you”; it is absent in manuscript 1, while manuscript 13 earlier reads *traditionem*.]

### V

The city of Athens [the manuscripts read *Athenae*], situated on the border of Thrace and Laconia, mountainous in the configuration of its land, shut in by the straits of the Ionian Sea and narrowed on its left side by the Aegean waters, was a famous and ancient city. Rich in the fertility of its soil, it was the nurse of eloquence, the mother of philosophers and wise men, and surpassed the other cities in the abundance of varied arts and riches.

It was situated in the province of Attica, where the kings Cecrops and Minander of the peoples were renowned; where Apollo, Hippocrates, and Aristotle were born, men who in their own times shone throughout the world with the flowers of wisdom.

At that time Cecrops and Minander were kings and worshipers of images. Indeed, the superstitious religion of idols first arose and flourished among them.

The city is described as divided into five regions.

The first region faces the Aegean Sea. A mountain rises above the city [one manuscript reads “rises”], where golden images of Saturn and Priapus are concealed amid various illusions. The Greeks call this region Chronopagium; for the Greeks call Saturn “Chronos.”

The second region of Athens faces Chios [one manuscript has the corrupt *contra trachium*]. There stood a terebinth of extraordinary size, and there fauns—wild men—were worshiped by shepherds on appointed days [the conjunction *and* before “where” is absent from manuscript 13].

The third region of the city of Athens faces the harbor of Neptune. There they worshiped images of Diana and Aegean Neptune. The pagans call this place Popedon; for the Greeks call Neptune “Popedon.”

The fourth region of the Athenian city is where the idol of Mars and the image of Hercules were placed [manuscript 5 reads *qua*; manuscript 13 has the singular “was placed”]. It lies on the hill of Tritonia, a mountain situated in the middle of the city. When the moon was renewed, the whole people gathered there to worship Mars and Hercules, whom they adored as the strongest gods.

The Greeks call this place Ariopagus; for “Ares” in Greek is called Mars in Latin.

The fifth region of the Athenian city faces the Sichaean gate. There an idol and image of Mercury was placed. This place is called Ermipagus; for “Ermis” in Greek means Mercury.

This city flourished as the noblest of the Greek cities, surpassing the others in the abundance of sea and land, forests and mountains, rivers and green places [the reading is uncertain; other manuscripts have “abundance of verdant lands”]. Once it was preferred to all other cities as their capital [the word “capital” is absent from the other manuscripts]; now, overwhelmed and cut off by the assault of foreign peoples [one manuscript reads “intercepted”], it lies crushed.

### VI

Apollo was so called because his lineage was derived from a certain very noble Athenian leader named Apollinus [the preposition *ab* is absent from the other manuscripts]. His father was Nicolaus, a man of great intellect, distinguished as a citizen and powerful in literary study, and a teacher of the Argolic art.

His son Apollo was considered famous among the schools of philosophers. As he examined authoritative libraries, devoted to philosophy and empty superstitions [*‑que* is absent from manuscripts 1 and 5; manuscript 5 wrongly reads “was devoted”], he heard the apostle Paul preaching doctrines that were new and previously unheard.

Unable to resist him [manuscript 5 reads *valebat*, “was able”], he discovered that the teaching Paul had delivered at Athens was true. Therefore, abandoning the empty superstitions of the nations, he fell at the Apostle’s feet and begged him to show him the true doctrine and the way of salvation. He declared that he was now a disciple of Christ, not of Saturn [one manuscript reads “he proclaimed”; another has “he preferred,” and omits “now”].

### VII

After these events, when Paul saw the Areopagus one day, he began to ask blessed Dionysius what he worshiped, or to which divinities he rendered service in so spacious and venerable a place [manuscript 13 wrongly reads “what”; manuscript 5 reads “served”].

Dionysius replied:

“We worship the gods whom our fathers worshiped, by whose power and skill Mother Earth is sustained. We adore the altars consecrated in the name and honor of Mars, Hercules, Mercury, and Priapus.” [“These” is absent from manuscripts 1 and 13.]

As Paul examined each altar and image of the false gods, he found among the other altars one on which was written: “To an unknown god” (Acts 17:23). [All that follows is absent from manuscript 5, which lacks one page.] Paul turned to Dionysius and to the others accompanying him [one manuscript reads “who accompanied him”] and asked them who that unknown god was.

Among the others Dionysius replied:

“As yet that god has not been demonstrated among the gods. He is unknown to us, but he is destined for the age to come. He is the God who will reign in heaven and on earth, and his kingdom will have no end.”

Paul asked again:

“What do you think? Will he be a human being or a spirit of the gods?”

They answered:

“He will be both true God and true man, and he will renew the world. But he is still unknown to human beings, because his dwelling is with the gods in heaven.”

Paul said:

“I proclaim to you that God whom until now you have held to be unknown. Born of a virgin, he sits at the right hand of the Father, true God and true man. Through him all things were made. ‘God is known in Judea; his name is holy in Israel’ (Psalm 76:2). The one whom until now you have held to be unknown, recognize now, because he alone is God, and besides him there is no other God. He has brought you back from death to life; he has joined heaven and earth, human beings and angels, in the unity of his kingdom. He makes alive and puts to death (2 Kings 2:6); he closes, and no one opens; he opens, and no one closes (Revelation 3:7).”

### VIII

While Paul was preaching these and many other things, and proclaiming in each temple that Christ was the Son of God, Dionysius accepted the true teaching and doctrine of salvation. He recognized that the idols he served were nothing and that they were demons rather than gods. Clearly sensing the Holy Spirit and the words of life in Paul’s teaching, he was moved by divine grace, turned to Paul, and asked him to pray to the divine mercy on his behalf so that he might be worthy to become Paul’s disciple [one manuscript reads “and”].

The next day, as Paul was traveling, a certain blind man, deprived of the light of his eyes, asked to be healed by Paul’s power. Immediately the holy apostle, imitating his Lord and teacher Jesus Christ [the name Jesus is absent from one manuscript], placed the cross upon the man’s long-closed eyes and said:

“Christ, our Lord and teacher, who placed clay upon the eyes of the man born blind, and who was deemed worthy immediately to receive light, may he restore the light to your eyes by his power.”

Then, wonderfully, the man born blind was deemed worthy to receive light in his eyes. Paul immediately addressed him, saying:

“Go to Dionysius and tell him: ‘Paul, servant of Christ Jesus, has sent me to you, so that, remembering your promise, you will not hesitate to come to him. Thus, receiving the baptism of salvation, you may be freed from all the bonds of sins.’”

The man who had received his sight immediately fulfilled the words of the one who had commanded him, going obediently to Dionysius and reporting Paul’s words to him in order.

Dionysius, already chosen by the Lord [one manuscript omits “already”], saw the blind man walking with firm eyesight [one manuscript omits “saw”] and addressed him:

“Are you the one whom all your kinsmen knew to have been born blind?”

He replied:

“I certainly am the one who was born blind, and to whom until now the light of this present life had been denied [one manuscript has the corrupt “present”]. But Paul himself, who commanded me to come to you, invoked the power of Jesus Christ, his teacher, and granted the light of healing to me” [one manuscript reads “enclosed” instead of “granted”].

Then Dionysius immediately rose and hastened in response to the instructions of Paul’s blessed messenger [the manuscripts read “commands,” without sense; the editor suggests *mandatus*, “messenger”]. Why should I delay? He believed at once and, sprinkled with the water of holy baptism, renounced the errors of the pagans and entrusted himself to be instructed in Paul’s teaching.

Afterwards, at Paul’s command, he preached the Gospel of Christ. When he converted many in Thessalonica to the way of salvation, he converted the greater part of that province to the faith [one manuscript adds “the way,” apparently erroneously].

### IX

They say that this most blessed man, burning with the ardor of the Holy Spirit [one manuscript reads “kindled”], said the following when the Lord of the world hung fastened to the cross in the hands of the Jews, when the sun, terrified by the death of its Lord, changed the rays of its light into the horror of a dreadful night, and when darkness covered the regions of the world:

“This night, which we marvel to see descending as something new upon our eyes, has shown that the salvation of the whole world has arrived.”

O truly holy prophet! O man truly suffused with divine light! He had already been chosen by a blessed destiny in such a way that, though not yet reborn in the sacred font and still pagan in his bodily members, he could become the narrator of so great a mystery [one manuscript reads “ministry”].

Since he excelled through the grace of so many gifts, he shone in every respect with eloquence of teaching and the flowers of the Scriptures. The Greeks report that he wrote three marvelous books [one manuscript reads “are reported”]:

one called *Antihaereseos*, that is, a volume against all heresies;

one *On Contempt of the World and the Nine Orders of Angels*;

and one which, as we have heard, is preserved in the Constantinopolitan archives [one manuscript reads “is destined for”].

The blessed Gregory also praises this holy man in his homilies as a true and ancient Father, with every mark of veneration.

### X

You have learned how he passed to heaven through the glory of martyrdom under Domitian, the persecutor of Christians, and the account of his passion has become known to you [one manuscript reads “the volume of his passion”].

We, however, relying on the weakness of our understanding and our sluggish knowledge, have made this known to your charity briefly, not so much through rashness as through fortunate confidence, out of love and reverence for our most holy Lord and patron and for the sake of edification. We know that if we render you any service, you will undoubtedly assist us by your prayers before the holy martyr [one manuscript omits “this”].

I also think it worthwhile that, amid the solemnity of so great a patron, priest, and martyr, the memory of the blessed Rusticus and Eleutherius should be recited, so that where they suffered martyrdom for Christ on the same day, there on the day of their martyrdom a festival worthy of veneration may be celebrated.

For although we ought to rejoice at the commemoration of all the holy martyrs [one manuscript omits “martyrs”], we should rightly exult and glory more abundantly in the excellence of these martyrs, whom the grace of God raised to such a summit among all the members of the Church that the grace and election of Christ made them equal, their labor similar, and their end the same.

### XI

For these are the holy men, your fathers, through whom the Gospel of Christ and the grace of salvation shone upon you, Gaul; and you, who had been the mother of error, became the daughter [Note: Codex 13, less well, “disciple.”] of truth. These are your holy fathers and true shepherds, who handed you over to the heavenly kingdom to be made ready for it [Note: The codices have “of the kingdom,” incorrectly]. For although, enlarged by many victories, you have extended the rights of your earthly kingdom over land and sea, what military labor has brought you is nevertheless less than what Christian peace has subdued through the mouths [Note: The codices have “hours,” incorrectly] of these precious martyrs. For while you seemed to rule over other nations, not knowing the author of your dignity, you were in fact enslaved to great errors. And the more tenaciously you had been bound by the devil [Note: The same manuscript incorrectly has “joined”], the more wonderfully you were set free through their sufferings.

You are blessed, Gaul, which deserved to receive such and so many priests. You are blessed, Paris, whose soil deserved [Note: So Codex 13, which supplies the verb *deserved*, absent from Codex 1.] to be watered by the blood of so many martyrs. Behold, you are strong in the glory of three martyrs [Note: Codex 1 incorrectly has “being strong”]; behold, their blessed rewards, in radiant ranks, have surrounded you and, as though with a diadem woven from the honor of many jewels, have crowned you.

Relying on their protection, dearest brothers, with minds prepared for the example of patience and the strengthening of faith, let us, insofar as we can, imitate their examples, so that the merits of the flock may reach the place to which the courage of the shepherds has led. For this, dearest brothers, we must take the greatest care: that, while we are honored by the present festivals of the martyrs, we may be joined to their holy fellowship in the future.

Behold, my brothers: as you see, the bodies of the blessed martyrs are covered with an abundance of gold and jewels [Note: Codex 1 lacks the word “abundance,” but it is found in Codex 13.
