Codex 1 then reads “they cover” incorrectly]; and those who here happily submitted their necks to the impious for Christ’s sake are worshiped by the rulers of the earth with bowed necks [Note: Codex 1 has “worships,” incorrectly]. How greatly, then, do you suppose that they are exalted there in glory among the choirs of angels and archangels, when here their blessed corpses are raised to such honors?

### XII

We have taken care, brothers and lords, as we said above, to make these things known to your ears for the solemnity of this great day—not so rashly [Note: The codices have “not rashly,”] as with happy devotion—knowing that devotion, although uninstructed, is nevertheless pure, and faithful love possesses the reward of a just recompense, as we ourselves have experienced before and our elders have proved.

We believe and trust that, amid all the labors of this life, we are always assisted by the prayers of these special patrons in obtaining the mercy of God, so that, to the degree that we are weighed down by our own sins, we may be raised up by their sacred merits. And may we, who are tormented by our iniquities [Note: The codex has “what in your iniquities,”] be cherished by the prayers of our blessed fathers, the martyrs—this being granted by the eternal Son of the Father himself, who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives, rules, and reigns, now and through the immortal ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VIII. On Absalom: How He Persecuted His Father

[Note: This sermon, which because of its manner of expression does not appear attributable to Saint Leo, is drawn from four Florentine manuscripts: namely, Laurentian Library, Pluteus 21, codex 11, p. 137; the same, codex 12, p. 129; codex 13, p. 131; and the Strozziana Library, codex 16, p. 133.]

### I

The utterly wicked Absalom lost his mind, lost his understanding, and abandoned counsel. He attacks his father, drives away the innocent; he pursues his parent, usurps authority, seizes power, invades the kingdom—not in order to enter into partnership with his father in ruling the kingdom, but to possess the whole kingdom through his father’s blood.

Absalom, I say, lost counsel when he wished to purchase dominion by parricide [Note: Codex 11 has “patricide”]; he lost understanding when he desired to obtain the kingdom through his father’s destruction. He hurries, he hastens, he seeks to crush the innocent—himself destined to die guilty while his father still lives.

But David, humble and gentle, yields to the man [Note: So Codex 13; Codex 11 has “the man”], flees from his pursuer, avoids his enemy, and abandons his affection, lest either the death of the parricide bring him grief or his destruction make his son guilty. By fleeing he wishes to restrain his son’s fury; by withdrawing he desires to moderate the parricide’s savagery.

But the cruelty conceived in his mind could no more be quieted [Note: Codex 12 has “nevertheless”] than monstrous savagery urged him on to carry out the crime. O innocence, how much danger you incur among the guilty, how much trouble you suffer at the hands of criminals! The most holy David offended so many maddened armies because he had injured no one; because he had done no harm, he encountered the rage of so many peoples.

Absalom alone is guilty and wretched, yet the entire army breathes hostility against the father. Many hands are armed for the father’s bloody slaughter [Note: So Codex 13; Codex 11 incorrectly has “heaven”]; the innocent is challenged to avenge another’s crime; the fury of one parricide compels thousands to madness; the insanity of one makes many insane.

### II

For David offended his son because he refused to avenge upon him the murder of his brother. Crimes always grow when they are not cut off, and one advances toward greater offenses whenever sin is quieted [Note: Perhaps “hidden”] through impunity. Since the crime of the murdered brother was not avenged in Absalom, the repeated crime was renewed in the parricide of the father.

You, you, I say, unhappy army, I admonish; you, I exhort with the feeling of piety: why do you rush into another’s crime? Why do you assist a madman’s insanity? Why do you become like the parricide and insane? Abandon, I beg you, abandon the guilty man; abandon one who is destined to die by a novel punishment. Perhaps, if you abandon him, he will cease—the one whom your numbers provoked to dare this.

Let the man perish alone who wars against nature; let the man alone fall who attacks his father’s affection. For either he will cease when he repents, or he will persist and perish. I pity the guilty man; I pity the impious man; I pity one who is destined to die by a novel punishment.

Who taught you to rush into this crime, most dreadful parricide? What madness provoked you to dare so monstrous a deed? If he offended you, he is your father; if he injured you, he is your parent—and indeed he neither offended nor injured you. Let affection overcome fury; let love conquer insanity; let nature defeat cruelty. Or did your father offend you because he did not injure you? Or did he offend you for that very reason, because he did not injure you—he who perhaps would not have offended you if he had injured you? [Note: The same manuscripts have “because.”]

Restore affection; show filial piety. You spare yourself when you turn your hands away from your father, whom you ought to defend if you had recognized another person attempting what you are attempting [Note: So Codex 12; Codex 11 has “one who is attempting.”]

Where will fathers now find consolation, where will parents find protection, if they discover that their sons are parricides? Or when will things outside the household be safe, if what is within opposes us? Beasts and speechless animals preserve the laws of affection; and nature, which denies them reason, does not nevertheless deny them filial devotion.

To kill an innocent man is sacrilege; to kill a father is a crime; to slaughter a prophet is an unheard-of deed, previously unknown to all mortals. But cease now from this crime—cease—lest all good men always shudder at you; lest the bold learn from you what they did not know; cease, I say, lest anyone who commits so great a crime after you use you as his example.

Why do you hand a new crime down to the world? Why do you teach what the nature of filial piety does not know? Why do you desire what filial affection itself recoils from? Why do you dare to complete what the Lord will be compelled to avenge with a novel punishment?

### III

Meanwhile the parricide’s fury does not diminish or slacken; it burns and grows more fiercely toward evil. He longs to complete the crime conceived in his mind; he desires with the utmost urgency to carry out the wickedness he has planned.

For the man committing the crime, everything is too slow; to one hastening toward the crime, every arrangement seems to delay him. He longs to complete the parricide before he acts; he hastens to intercept his father before killing him. He thirsts for his father’s blood, the blood of his parent [Note: The codices have “his blood,”]; he fears even a brief delay, lest either anger, held back, fail, or fury, postponed, grow weak.

War is arranged nearby, battle lines are drawn up, combat is prepared, kindred forces burn against one another. From one side the parricide inflames the army against his father; from the other David begs the departing commanders to spare his son: “Spare my son Absalom,” he says. From one side madness rises against the parent; from the other mercy pleads that the parricide be spared. From one side fury operates; from the other filial affection. From one side insanity; from the other compassion. From one side cruelty; from the other goodness.

The parricide, though not injured, rages; David, though injured, grows gentle. Filial devotion is subdued by impiety; yet the father’s affection is not moved, is not conquered by the sword, and is not changed by terror. The parricide is broken neither by reason nor frightened by impending death. He is hardened for punishment, driven toward retribution, and no longer deserves salvation in any respect, since he attempts to deprive his father of safety [Note: Codex 11 here adds again, “in any respect.”]

### IV

Look back now, most wicked enemy [Note: Codex 13 has “recover your senses … recover your senses now”]; impious man, look back now, parricide. Look back, I say, and see how everything is turned against you. See that nature itself wars against you; and although heaven fights against you, the earth is moved, and the army battles, nevertheless another unknown and unexpected war awaits you. Another battle has now been prepared for you: it will receive you as you flee, destroy you as you commit the crime, and kill you as you hasten.

For it is not these armies of flesh that you see—whether your fury armed them against your father or your father’s necessity summoned them against you—which, although they rightly wield swords, flash blades, and hurl spears against you so that the grief of your injured father may be washed away by your death, will receive you as you flee. A tree will receive you; branches will kill you; wood will hang you.

I say, the tree is present: it neither listened to your father when he asked that you be spared, nor hesitated to fulfill God’s commands. You will not escape this war unpunished, since you attempted to inflict death upon your parent.

Then, when the battle has been joined, the enemies are struck down, the opposing forces fall, and the foes are defeated. The enemy is stripped, the parricide is abandoned; he already conceives his punishment among his own people, already recognizes the penalty owed him through the death of his own men; already he fears, already he dreads, already he contemplates his own destruction.

Finally, he seeks an animal, mounts a mule, and gives himself to headlong flight. He hastens toward the tree that has been prepared nearby and to which he is delivered; driven by a violent impact, with the reading *sali* (sic) withdrawn, and slipping beneath in the fields, he is caught in its branches, bound by the wood, and, his throat pierced, remains fastened and hanging [Note: So Codex 13; Codex 11 incorrectly has “into himself.”]

He is found dead by everyone: one whom heaven could no longer behold alive, nor the earth continue to sustain.

### V

O abominable desert of the parricide! The father’s injury was defended not by a sword in combat, not by an enemy’s hand, not by a missile’s blow, but the wood takes vengeance, the tree avenges it, the branches defend him. There is no creature that was not moved when it perceived that the Lord himself, its creator, was moved.

Therefore all return from the battle, with the parricide, the author of the war, struck down [Note: Codex 11 has “to the author of the war”]. His blood washes away the crime; his punishment buries monstrous cruelty. Everyone rejoices, all are glad; David alone mourns his son and laments the death of the parricide.

Why do you mourn, glorious father? Why do you, by your lamentation, seem almost to approve Absalom’s deed [Note: So Codex 12; Codex 11 has an obscure reading, “of lamentation … to be proved.” Codex 16 has “by lamenting”]? Why do you weep for the wicked man, as though you wished him to commit the parricide?

The glory of the victorious army is broken; even the enemy’s death is mourned. There can be no joy in victory while the parricide’s punishment is lamented. He was not your son who so violated a father’s affection. He did not deserve to be called yours who violated the right of the supreme Father.

It was not the armies that despised you, nor the commanders to whom you entrusted the task against so great a criminal; that tree avenged you, that tree defended you, that tree—though it had not listened to you—avenged the injury of the injured father.

Your defense brought security to fathers [Note: The codices incorrectly have “satisfaction”] and removed the audacity of parricides. Through you the injury done to nature was defended, and filial piety was restored. For he deserved to perish by a novel punishment who wished to inflict upon the world a new crime: the destruction of his father.

Pregnant women are to be baptized, 117. Baptism of the sick, 98. On those baptized during illness, 440. The dead are not to be baptized, 91. Whether one should baptize in a doubtful case, 104. No one is to be received for baptism after the second week of Lent, 440. Apart from Easter and Pentecost, baptism is not to be administered unless there is danger in delaying it, 247, 413. Those baptized are to share in the chrism, 440. Those to be baptized are to learn the creed of the faith and recite it to the bishop or priest on the Thursday of the final week of Lent, ibid. The rites of baptism, 248, 658. Nothing of value is to be demanded from those being baptized or signed with the cross, 410. Those who sacrificed before baptism are not excluded from the clergy after baptism, 110. In necessity, even laypeople are permitted to administer baptism, 411. In no baptismal church is a priest to be present without a deacon, 671. Baptism conferred by triple immersion, CCCVIII.

Basilicas of the holy martyrs and assemblies held there, 126. New basilicas were not to be dedicated according to custom without the command of the Roman pontiff, 410, 420. Certain basilicas built in the name of persons who were not entirely faithful are condemned by Gelasius, 420.

Acacius of Constantinople resisted Basiliscus the heretical tyrant, 353. He reported him to the Apostolic See, 354. Basiliscus himself was broken by the writings of the Apostolic See and recalled from many excesses, ibid.

Basiliscus, subdeacon of the Roman Church, brought Zosimus’s letters and acts concerning Caelestius to Africa, and when, 854, 855. He appears to have brought the Africans’ replies back to Rome, 860.

Bede’s *Penitential*, CCLXIX. To whom the book *On Remedies for Sins*, attributed to Bede, belongs, ibid.

Benedict the Levite of Mainz, compiler of the Capitularies, CCLXXXIII.

Those are to be regarded as bigamists who violated their professed virginity, 114 note.

Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit: to what extent it is not forgiven, 328.

The letter of Boniface I to the bishops of Thessaly is cleared of the charge of forgery and interpolation, CLXX, 53 note. He writes to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne, 269. Documents issued over the schism between Boniface and Eulalius from the Avellana collection, CLX.

The collection of Bonizo, bishop, CCCVII. On the year of his death, ibid. Excerpts from a Brixian manuscript, CCCVIII and following. He was the author of the book *On the Sacraments*, CCCVII. He wrote against the schismatic Hugo, CCCIX. His book to Amicus, ibid. His *Epitome of the Sentences of Saint Augustine*, CCCVII.

Bonosus regularly performed illicit ordinations without any examination, 195. Anysius and his associates allowed those ordained by him to retain their honors, and why, 193. Those who transferred from the Catholic Church to the condemned Bonosus and were ordained by him are not to be received in their honors, 194.

*Breviarium* and *Capitula* used interchangeably as titles of the canons, CCCXVII.

The *Breviary of the Canons of Hippo* vindicated, 79 and following, 735 and following. When, where, and by whom it was composed, LXXX, 79. Which are its canons, 85 and following. The same *Breviary* was addressed to the plenary Council of Carthage of the year 397, LXXX, and inserted into its acts, 82. The sequence of those canons in this synod, LXXX and following. The canon concerning Donatist clerics and another concerning infants are attributed to the *Breviary*, LXXXIII and following. Saint Augustine cited two canons of this *Breviary* from the council of 397 to which they had been inserted, not from the Council of Hippo, 745 note. Ferrandus did likewise, 750 note. Two canons were added to the *Breviary* at the end, 102, 103. Several others were added in another codex, CCLIX.

The abridgment of Ferrandus: see Ferrandus.

The abridgment of the Hispanic collection published by Cardinal de Aguirre from the manuscript of Juan Bautista Pérez, CCLXIII. It was excerpted from the fuller Hispanic collection, ibid. On the author of that collection, CCLXIV. On its date, CCLXV.

The very ancient abridgment of the canons contained in two codices, Veronese and Lucan, is described, CCLVII and following. From which most ancient sources it was drawn, CCLXI.

The short history of the Eutychianists, to be supplied in the commonly circulated councils, CLXIII.

A brief collection of statutes for the *Breviatio*, or *Breviary*, 87, 90.

Burchard and his collection, CCXC. Which should be entitled *Collection of Canons*, ibid. On the number of books in his collection, CCXCI. Genuine preface published from manuscripts, CCXCII. Burchard’s practice of attributing to synods, pontiffs, or Fathers the opinions of certain writers, CCXCIV. How this spurious attribution was transferred to other compilers and what confusion it caused, ibid. The ancient *Penitential* of the German Church inserted by Burchard into his collection, CCXCV.

Synods of the province of Byzacena held under Aurelius, CV.

### C
Cadolus of Parma, CCCIX. [Col. 1159] Collection of Zaragoza, CCCXIX. Calendion, holy bishop of Antioch, 353. Venerable, 362. Excluded from his see contrary to the canons, 335, 353, 356, 357. He was expelled so that access might be opened to heretics, 362, 363. Canon of the Scriptures, see Canonical Scriptures. The collection of the Apostolic Canons, the oldest of all, V. Compiled in the East, and when, ibid. Its use among the Greeks, VI. It was not used among the Latins until after the translation of Dionysius Exiguus, ibid. These same canons were handed down orally by the apostles and later collected by others, V. Nevertheless, not all those included among the Apostolic Canons are apostolic, ibid. Why they are listed among the apocrypha, ibid. The number of these canons, VII. The canons established in each individual synod of the Fathers are to be observed, 225. Only the canons of Nicaea and Sardica, inscribed under the name of the Nicene canons, were accepted by the Latins for a longer period, LI. When the canons of other Greek synods began to be cited by the Latins, LVI. From where this observance passed to the Latins, ibid. Under the name of “canons,” the decretals of the Roman pontiffs were sometimes included, LVI. See Code of Canons. The provisions of the canons are to be adapted according to the circumstances of the times, 407 ff. What is granted in a time of necessity must not be claimed outside necessity, 409, 412, 419. No priest may be ignorant of the canons and statutes of the Apostolic See, 254, 276. Punishment of those who violate the canons, 49. Capitula and Breviary used indiscriminately, CCCXVII. What the capitularies of the Frankish kings are and how they were compiled, CCLXXXII. The collection of capitularies arranged in four books through the efforts of Abbot Ansegisus, CCLXXXIII. Another collection by Benedict the Levite in three books, ibid. The four additions to the capitularies, ibid. Synod of Carthage under Gratus, LXXVI. Another under Genethlius, ibid. Another in the year 394 under Aurelius, LXXIX. Another in the year 397, on the Kalends of July, ibid. Another on the Ides of August of the same year, at which the Breviary of the Canons of Hippo was compiled, 79. Held by Aurelius of Carthage with the Byzacene bishops, LXXX. See Breviary of the Canons of Hippo. The two letters must be distinguished: one of that Council, the other of Mizo, primate of Byzacena, 739 n. Another in the same year, held on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, at which the Breviary of the Canons of Hippo was read and confirmed, LXXIX. The need to restore this synod, ibid. The restored sequence of the canons of the same synod, LXXX ff. The Carthaginian synod of the year 398, published from the manuscripts of the Hispanic and Isidorian Collections, does not belong to any African synod, LXXXVIII ff. Various opinions concerning it, ibid. What is more probably to be believed, XCI. The Carthaginian synod of 399, XCII. Two others in 401, ibid. The second synod of 401: the necessary restoration, ibid. and XCIII. Another in 403, XCIV. Another in 404, ibid. Another in 405, to which a certain canon is shown to belong, XCV. Another in 407, ibid. Two others in 408, XCV, XCVI. Another in 409, ibid. Another in 410, ibid. The Carthaginian synod that condemned Coelestius was held not in 412 but in 411, 845. The letter of the Carthaginian synod of 416 to Pope Innocent, 128. The plenary Council of Carthage in 418 against the errors of Pelagius and Coelestius, XCVI, 165. The canon of that council against those who allow infants dying without baptism a place of salvation and rest is exempted from suspicion of being spurious, XCVI ff. The Carthaginian synod of 419. An exact description, XCVIII. The subscriptions of that synod, 646. The origin and repetition of the first thirty-three canons of the first session, LXXVI. These alone are contained in certain very ancient manuscripts, LXXXIII. Their different division in different codices, 629. The same canons now printed as they are found in the most ancient Italian manuscript collections, 635 ff. The Carthaginian Council of 421, now published for the first time, CIII, 649 ff. Another, the twentieth Carthaginian Council, under Aurelius, CIII. From this, the letter of the Africans to Pope Celestine appears to have been written, CIV. The date of the same council, ibid. The Carthaginian Council of 525, published from a single Vatican Palatine codex, CXXXVI. Cited in other ancient documents, ibid. An error in the same council noted, LXVI. A passage requiring correction, XCIV. Chastity, see Continence. The Cataphrygians, when they come to the Church, are to be baptized, 431. The word “Cataphrygians” improperly inserted into the Nicene canon in the Isidorian version, 61 n. [Col. 1160] Catechumens, 117. From whom they must abstain, 658. How the Cathari are to be received, 54. The Nicene canon concerning them explained, ibid., n. Incorrectly rendered in Latin in the version of the Code of Canons printed in this volume, 756. How the cases of clerics in Africa are to be handled, 93, 642, 644. By whom cases between clerics of lower and higher rank are to be settled, 206, 230, 675. By whom the cases of bishops, priests, and deacons are to be judged according to African discipline, 638, 639, 641. Major cases are to be referred to the Apostolic See after episcopal judgment, 207. A case cannot be heard before those who are at once enemies, witnesses, and judges, 337. The book of Cencius the chamberlain on censuses, CCCIII. The collection of Chalcedon published by Rusticus, CXLII. The acts of the sixth session of the Council of Chalcedon in the original version, 214 n. 1. The definition of faith of the same council, 220. The same from another ancient version, 391. The Chalcedonian canons in the ancient interpretation, 225. From another ancient interpretation, now published for the first time, 617. The canons enacted in the seventh session, 617 n. The catalogue of the Chalcedonian Fathers, 549. Which acts of Chalcedon were approved by the Apostolic See and which rejected, 321. Not everything contained in that synod can be regarded as certain, ibid. The Greek codices of the canons used at Chalcedon and their diversity, XXXVI, XXXVII, XXXVIII. Two faults noted in a certain passage of the received text of the sixteenth session, XXXVII. The genuine text to be restored, XXXVIII. A notable variant citation of the Nicene canon in the thirteenth session, XXXVII. The Chalcedonian passage in which a spurious decree of Sardica is praised, explained, XXXIX. Three canons added to the Chalcedonian canons, and their source, 771. Chorepiscopi, called vicars of bishops, 110, 427. What was forbidden to them, 110. They could issue letters of commendation (*formatae*), 427. Established in villages and rural districts and consecrated as bishops, ibid. Within what limits their power was restricted, ibid. Chrism is to be given after baptism, 440. It is to be requested from one’s own bishop, not from others, 667. The baptized are not to be signed with chrism except by bishops, 200, 415. Priests may anoint the baptized with chrism consecrated by a bishop, but may not sign the forehead with it, since that belongs to the bishop alone, ibid. No fee is to be demanded for chrism, 410. Christ. See Son of God. Three citations before judgment did not require an interval of several days, 806 n. The letter of Pope Clement I to James is spurious, 454. It was rendered into Latin by Rufinus and fabricated from the Greek, ibid., n. Another letter of the same man, likewise spurious, to the same James, 674. Translated from Greek into Latin by the same translator, 631. Their difference from the text commonly used in the councils, ibid. The additions alone by which both were interpolated are to be attributed to Pseudo-Isidore, CCLXVII, CCLXVIII. Clerics both of higher and lower rank, 206. Clerics who are to be ordained, 90. When, and to what extent, laymen may be ordained, 409. Siricius desires and urges that monks be attached to the duties of clerics, 253. An illiterate man, or one diminished in any part of his body, is not to be ordained, 415, 416. Nor a penitent, 667. Nor a slave without the consent of his masters, 414. Nor a criminal; and one who has been ordained is to be removed from office, 416. Nor one who has been rebaptized, 644. Nor one who has married a widow, 189, 190, 207 n., 250, 253. Nor one who has married a second wife, 190, 191, 251, 253, 419. Even if he had taken his first wife before baptism, 190, 289. Nor one who, after the remission of sins, has worn the belt of secular military service, 206, 449. Nor a municipal councillor, 211. Nor one who has married a divorced woman, 667. One baptized at an advanced age cannot obtain the clerical office unless, at the very time of his baptism, he is immediately enrolled among the readers or exorcists, 252, 253. A seditious man, usurer, or avenger of injuries is not to be ordained, 662. Neophytes are not to be promoted to the priestly order, 434. Those who are not to be promoted, and the irregularities noted by Gelasius, 408, 410. At what age clerics are to be ordained, 90, 252, 640. What periods are to be observed in each rank, 266. What applies to monks, 408. For how long they must serve in each rank, 253. No cleric is to be ordained except to the title of a particular church of a city, village, or martyr shrine, 229. Clerics are not to be ordained in the presence of catechumens, 434, 435. Clerics, however learned, should seek their livelihood through a craft, 664. They should provide themselves with food and clothing through a small craft or agriculture, without detriment to their office, 659. Those fit for work should learn a craft and letters, 661. Clerics ordained for money are to be deposed from office, 419. The penalty for clerics unwilling to advance to a higher rank, 645, 650. Before ordination, the ordinands must be instructed by the ordainers in the provisions of the council, 90, 641. They are not to be ordained unless they have made all members of their household Catholic, 95. Clerics are not to marry widows, 449. Innocent complains about clerics and bishops who had married widows, 189. This was done in Macedonia by custom, 190. Concerning the life and good conduct of clerics, 659, 664. Clerics are not to attend spectacles, 441. See Spectacles. If spectacles are held at weddings or wedding banquets, they are to rise from the feast and leave before the theatrical performers enter, ibid. They are not to be merchants, 415. They are not to live with unrelated women, nor with women of the kinds specified, 49, 95, 669, 676. If suspicion could arise from any woman, they are to have no association with her, 671. To what extent they may approach women, 96, 676. They are not to be contractors, agents, or the like, 95, 227, 640. In what cases they may accept an agency at the bishop’s command, 671. They are not to enter military service or secular office, 229. They are not to pass from one Church to another, 58, 228. Except when necessity compels, 236, 419. A cleric may not serve in the churches of two cities, 231. Those who leave their own church are not to be received by others, 59. The penalty for receiving foreign clerics, 425. Clerics traveling abroad are not to minister without letters of commendation from their bishop, 233, 426, 439. They are not to remain in another city unless for a just cause known to the bishop of the place or to the local priests, 98. Concerning clerics who remain too long in another city, 74. Clerics are to give none of their property to non-Catholic relatives, 95, 643. They are not to emancipate their sons unless they are confident of their character and age, 95. Usurious clerics are to be expelled, 59. Clerics are not to minister wearing cloaks or girded about the loins, 271. This had been introduced in Gaul, ibid. Hands are not to be laid upon priests and clerics who have fallen and are to be removed from office, and the limits of this rule, 644. Clerics ordained in ignorance contrary to the rules of the canons are granted such leniency that hope of promotion is nevertheless denied them, 184, 254. The possessed and those entangled in other afflictions are not to perform sacred ministries, 417. Concerning clerics and bishops who approach the emperor, 428. Foreign clerics are not to be ordained, 450. Without the consent of their own bishop, 59, 74, 96, 288. They are not to be solicited, 74. Bishops are not to claim foreign clerics for themselves, 410. Those deposed by a bishop are not to be received by others, 73, 426, 450, 637. They are to be heard by neighboring bishops, 73. Those excommunicated by their own bishop are not to be received for as long as the excommunication lasts, 426, 428. Concerning clerics who, after being excommunicated, erect an altar and celebrate sacrifice, 638. Clerics ordained by heretics, when they return to the Church, are to be denied the honor of ordination, 192. Those ordained by Bonosus and received solely because of necessity, 193. Catholics ordained by him are to lack the dignity of ordination, 194. What is to be done with those ordained by him against their will, 195. What the Council of Nicaea granted to the Novatians must not be extended to others, 193. The cases of clerics. See Cases. Clerics or monks who conspire or plot against a bishop or cleric are to lose their rank, 235. What the ancient Greek code of canons originally was and how it was enlarged, XI. The Laodicean canons were formerly absent from that code, XII. Likewise the Antiochene canons, XIII. Which canons it originally contained, ibid. Where it was compiled, ibid. Its additions are noted, XIV. Other later accretions, XV. The Greek Code of Canons was not compiled or published by public authority, XXXIV. In former times there was no public code of canons, especially in the Roman Church, LV. The passages of Siricius and Celestine explained, ibid. Nor was there any public code containing the decretals of the pontiffs, LXV. How decretals were promulgated without a public code, ibid., 697 n. The first mention of a Code of Canons at the Council of Chalcedon, VII. Greek codices that presented the canons of different synods in a continuous numerical series, ibid., XXXVI. The division of the numbers differs in certain codices, VIII, XXXVIII. Nevertheless, not all Greek codices display a continuous numerical series, XXXV, XXXVIII. Into which codices this series was introduced, XXXVI, 578. The diversity of Greek codices noted, XXXVI, XXXVII. Some are fuller than others, XXXVIII. The universal Code of Canons edited by Justellus is found in no ancient exemplar, and how it was compiled, VIII. Whether the Code of Canons printed in this volume was the code of the Roman Church. Quesnell’s affirmative opinion, 685 ff. Its origin, 753. Refuted, 755 ff. It was composed neither at Rome nor in Italy, but in Gaul, 765. The date of the same collection, 7. Its excellence, ibid. The need for a new edition, ibid. How many chapters it contains, contrary to Quesnell, 9, 467 n. The *Codex encyclius*, CXLII. What the Code of the Canons of the African Church, published in Greek and Latin, is, LXXIV. What form it ought to have, CVI. The codes of the canons of the Gallican Church, CXXIX. None were public; they were prepared and published through private effort, ibid. The laws of the Theodosian Code inserted into the Code of Canons, 393 ff. [Col. 1162] The importance of comparing the codices of different collections, II. St. Celestine I writes to the bishops of Vienne and Narbonne, 270. Likewise to the bishops of Apulia and Calabria, 276. Coelestius condemned at the Council of Carthage, 129. Although condemned, he attained the presbyterate, ibid., 143. His errors, see Pelagius. The usefulness of collections of ancient canons and decretals, III. How their different origins may be detected, VII. Anonymous and unpublished manuscript collections, CCLXXVIII, CCCXVI ff. The Sorbonico-Mutinensis Collection, compiled in Italy at the end of the century, CCLXXXV. The freedom of certain collectors in citing canons, CCLXXIV, CCLXXV. A specious judgment, 357. The noted confusion of Catholic and heretical communion, 372. Catholic priests, while preserving Catholic communion and choosing as companions those who communicated with the Apostolic See, did not retain as companions those with whom the Apostolic See did not communicate, until the outbreak of persecution, 367, 368. Communion with heretics is to be avoided, 342, 343. Those communicating with them are separated from Catholic and apostolic communion, 343, 344. Communion given to the dying as viaticum for those about to depart, 185. Formerly denied to some, and why, ibid. See Eucharist. *Commissalia*, 441. The councils of the devil are the assemblies of heretics, 665. A council lawfully convened from all the provinces is ecumenical, even if many do not attend it or withdraw from it, over which the head of the Church presides, XLIX. It is not ecclesiastical practice to hold a council with those whose communion is polluted and mingled with that of the perfidious, 355. See Synod. Why the council convened under Zosimus against the Pelagians was called the African Council, 867. The distinction Augustine made between an African council and a plenary council, and what was required for a plenary council, ibid. The terms “plenary council” and “universal council” were used indiscriminately by the Africans, 807, 895. Only one plenary council was convened by the Africans in 418, not two, 895. The number of Fathers at the same, 898. The plenary council which Quesnell thought had been held in the autumn of that year is removed, 895 ff. The canons against the Pelagians enacted in the plenary council held on the Kalends of May of that year, 864, 899. Concerning these two councils, the African and the plenary, against the Pelagians, see Pelagius. The African Council as published is an excerpt from Dionysius Exiguus, CI. The same council was sometimes called by two different names in different accounts, 991. Gallican councils, in editing which the ancient Gallican collections are to be preferred to the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, LIII. Confession is to be made to the presiding priest, 459. Marriage is good and sanctified by Christ, 260. The marriage veil, 248. The blessing which the priest bestows upon the bride, 249. No one may marry a woman betrothed to another, ibid. See Marriage. The law of Constantius against Coelestius, 181. The apocryphal constitution of Constantine, CXXIV. His letter concerning the Council of Nicaea to the Church of Alexandria, from an unpublished version, CXXVIII. His law against Arius, likewise from an unpublished version, ibid. The bishop of Constantinople belongs to the parish (diocese) of the Church of Heraclea, 352. Nor is his see among the principal sees, nor is it counted among the rights of the metropolitans, 356. It has no prerogative on the grounds that it is the bishopric of the imperial city, 355. The archives of the Church of Constantinople, 315. The canons of the First Council of Constantinople from the Isidorian version, 443. From the ancient version, 553. They were initially absent from the Greek code of canons and were added after Chalcedon, XII. The catalogue of the Fathers of the same council, checked against manuscript codices, 556. The Constantinopolitan canons were not received by the Roman Church, LV. This council was formerly not counted among the ecumenical councils even by the Greeks themselves, LIV. The Latins regarded it as held after Chalcedon, yet it was not considered ecumenical until somewhat later, and then solely on account of the creed, LIII. This creed had long before been known to the Latins and sent to Damasus, and nevertheless the synod was not for that reason regarded as ecumenical, LIV. When it began to be counted among the ecumenical councils by the Latins, LV. The Chalcedonian canon concerning the primacy of the see of Constantinople was added to the Constantinopolitan canons in the ancient version, and why, 555 n. The fifth and sixth canons wrongly attributed to the First Council of Constantinople, and to which synod they appear to be referable, X. The Sixth Ecumenical Council of Constantinople [Col. 1163] and the letters attached to it are freed from the mark of spuriousness in the manuscripts of the fuller Hispanic Collection, CCV. The Council of Constantinople in 382 cites a Sardican canon under the name of a Nicene canon, XLI. The Council of Constantinople under Flavian against Eutyches, 295 ff. The origin of the diversity of customs in the Churches, 198. The custom of the Roman Church is to be observed by those Churches that derive their origin from Rome, 199, 203, 412. See Norm of the Roman Church. The precepts of continence for ministers of the altar, 183, 251, 450, 635. Also for subdeacons, 644. The penalty for the incontinent, 184, 185, 251. Priests and Levites are not to have intercourse with their wives, 209, 450. From the day of their ordination they must preserve chastity, ibid. Those who are ordained for sacred ministry while previously married must abstain from their wives after ordination, 675. A man who has been sexually corrupted and then baptized, if he wishes to rise to the clerical office, promises that he will not marry, 211. The incontinence of the higher clergy is condemned, 176, 183 ff. It was wrongly defended, 250. In certain Churches, readers and psalmists were permitted to marry, 233. When readers reach puberty, they are to be compelled either to marry or to profess continence, 940. Private conventicles are condemned, 124. Concerning those who, separating themselves from communion with their Church, held conventicles in their homes, 425. Concerning priests or deacons who hold separate conventicles and gatherings, 426. The conventicles of heretics are to be called not Churches but councils of the devil, 665. What the Cresconian Collection praised by Baronius and others is, CXVII, CLXXXIX, CCLVII. The two works of Cresconius, an African bishop, CCLIV. One was a poem on the Libyan wars, ibid. The other was a collection entitled *Harmony of the Canons*, ibid. This was divided, as it were, into two parts, one containing the collection itself and the other a breviary of the collection, ibid. Both are to be attributed to Cresconius, CCLV. How an edition of this work should be prepared, CCLVI. Cresconius was the first among the Latins to divide a collection into titles, CCLVII. He is likewise cited in an old manuscript collection, CCLXXXV. Cresconius, bishop of Villaregia, 89. The letter of St. Cyril of Alexandria to John of Antioch, 384. Another to Nestorius, 465. Two letters of the same Cyril inserted in certain collections under the name of the Council of Ephesus, CLXXXVI, CXCVIII, CCLIX.

## D

Dalmatius Caesar, LXIV. Who he was, LXIII. St. Pope Damasus writes to Paulinus of Antioch, 396. When, 934 n. Three forms of the same letter, 396 n. Their origin, 397 n. He prescribes the conditions under which the Apollinarists are to be received, 399, 400. A confession of faith sent to the same Paulinus against the errors of the Arians, Macedonians, and Apollinarists, 400. An anathema added to this confession in the editions of Theodoret is shown to have been added, 403 n. Another anathema is accused by Quesnell of being an interpolation, 934, 935. It is defended, 402 n.; 935 n. It is proved that the Nicene Creed had been prefixed to this confession, 396 n.; 399 n. Pope Celestine distinguishes two letters of Damasus to Paulinus, 397 n. Damasus’s letter to the Easterners defended as genuine, CXXV. Certain passages corrected from a manuscript, CXXVI. A fuller decree concerning books to be received or rejected, inscribed to Damasus in certain manuscripts, CLI, CLIII. Which portion of it is to be attributed to him, CLV. Whether the canon of the sacred Scriptures is to be assigned to him, ibid. A certain Daniel, gravely accused, is ordained bishop in Gaul, 273. He declines the trial demanded, ibid. Meanwhile he is separated from the assembly of bishops, 275. Decentius, bishop of Gubbio, frequently traveled to Rome, 199. He consults Pope Innocent, ibid. The work of Cardinal Deusdedit against invaders, simoniacs, and schismatics, CCXCIX. Another work of his, a collection of canons not yet published, CCC. Several excerpts from the ancient volumes of the Lateran basilica, CCCIII. The devil became evil not by nature but by choice, 654. What deacons ought to be, and their duties, 459. There should be one deacon with the priest in the baptismal church, 671. When he is to administer the Eucharist to the people, 662. He is to remain in one room with his priest, 672. Deacons are not to be above priests, 60. Nor are they to sit among the priests, ibid., 411. But at the priests’ command they are to sit, 437, 662. The measure to be observed by them, 411. Their continence, 110. The *diaconicon* as a sacristy, 437. At what age deaconesses are to be appointed, and their continence, 234. Deaconesses of the Paulianists, 62. The two bishops named Didacus of Compostela, one of whom is shown to have had the collection of the priest Gregory dedicated to him, CCCXIV. The dioceses of Asia, Pontus, and Thrace, 444. The encomium of Dionysius Exiguus, CLXXIV. The collection of canons and decretals prepared by him, divided into two parts, each part published separately by him, CLXXV. The continuous numerical series attached by Dionysius to the Greek canons, ibid. This, however, has not yet been found in the surviving codices, CLXXVI. In one codex it began with the Apostolic Canons, CXXXII. Justellus’s published edition adds two documents foreign to the pure Dionysius, CLXXVII. What a pure edition of Dionysius ought to be, CLXXVIII. The excellence of the Dionysian collection, ibid. Its fame and dissemination, CLXXIX. It was disseminated much more widely after Hadrian I, CLXXX. Whether Dionysius was the first to collect decretals, CLXXVIII. 1032 n. Whether he took them from the apostolic archives, CLXXIX. The time at which he compiled it, CLXXX. Whether this collection was received in Gaul before the age of Charlemagne, Quesnell’s opinion, 1013 ff. Refuted, 1041 ff. King Chilperic used an interpolated version of Dionysius, 1024 n. Pope Stephen II used the codex of Dionysius, 1028 n. Likewise John II, CXXXII. The same collection was received before Hadrian I in Spain, Africa, England, and Ireland, 1047. Likewise in Greece, ibid. What the use of the Dionysian collection among the Romans was, CLXXX. This collection, transmitted by Hadrian I to Charlemagne, and what additions it received, CLXXXIV. From that time it began to be called the Code of Canons, ibid., CLXXXVI. See Hadriana Collection. Dionysius rendered certain other Greek treatises into Latin, CLXXXI. Dioscorus of Alexandria agreed with Eutyches and condemned St. Flavian of Constantinople, 309. He was condemned by the emperor Marcian, by the imperial authorities, and by the entire synod, ibid. And by the Apostolic See, 352. Dioscorus, prefect of the praetorium of the East under the emperor Glycerius, 679 n. Dispensations granted by Gelasius on grounds of necessity and ecclesiastical usefulness, 407, 413. They are not to be claimed outside necessity and usefulness, ibid. Concerning divinations, 114. The Roman *Diurnus*, CCCIII. The apostles wished the Lord’s Day to be celebrated as a feast, 201. On that day the fermented bread was sent from Rome to the titular churches, not to the rural parishes or cemeteries, ibid. On Sundays the knees are not to be bent. See Genuflection. One who deliberately fasts on Sunday is not to be believed a Catholic, 664. See Fasting. The two African bishops named Donatianus must be distinguished, 991. To what extent Donatist clerics are to be received, 101. Whether their children are to be promoted to the clergy, 102.

## E
The Catholic Church is truly that which, by a sincere, pure, undefiled communion, is separated from all the faithless and from their successor-associates, 341. Outside the Catholic Church no one is saved, 654. The Church’s power to forgive sins, 326. What constitutes the peace of the Churches—not in some merely superficial sense, but truly Christian—342. No one founded the Churches in Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, Sicily, and the other intervening islands except those whom either St. Peter or his successors appointed as priests, 198. The goods of the Church are not to be alienated, 644, 646, 652, 657, 670, 672, 676. What is permitted in necessity, 644. Under what conditions, 661. To what extent the goods of one Church may or may not be given to another Church, 650. Property acquired in his own name from estates by a cleric who possessed nothing before ordination is not to be alienated, 646, 651. Church property is not to be pledged, nor given to a vicar without the pontiff’s consent, 672, 673. If Church property established in a diocese has been abandoned, the bishop must not apply it to the mother Church, 653, note. Churches as places consecrated to God. See Basilicas. Banquets forbidden in churches, 97. Entrance into the church must not be granted to heretics, 435. Only canonical Scriptures are to be read in the Churches, 441. And the passions of the martyrs, 100. Psalms composed by ignorant persons and vernacular songs are not to be recited in churches, 441. No one—whether pagan, heretic, or Jew—is to be prevented from entering the church to hear the word of God up to the Mass of the catechumens, 657.

Egbert, bishop of York, is shown to be the author of the book On Remedies for Sins, which is attributed to Bede, CCLXIX. How this book is to be edited, ibid. Whose the Excerpts inscribed to Egbert are, CCLXX. Egbert’s work On Priestly Law, ibid. Excerpts extracted from this work, but with certain materials inserted into them that are foreign to Egbert, CCLXXI. The Penitential attributed to him and divided into four books must be assigned to another author, [Col. 1165] CCLXXII. Concerning the little book published by Morinus and inscribed to Egbert, CCLXX, CCLXXI.

Elections of the Church’s ministers are not to be left to the judgment of the people, 436. Priests must not lay hands on the possessed, etc., except at the bishop’s command, 201, 202. They are to be laid on them by exorcists, 663. The possessed are to sweep the earthen floors, ibid. Food is to be provided for them while they sit in the house of God, ibid.

Praise of the see of Ephesus, 24. The ancient translation of the Ephesian synod and the collection of documents relating to the case of Nestorius, CXXXIX. Notable passages in that translation to be supplied from a manuscript, CXLI. The Ephesian canons added later to the Greek codex of canons, X, XIV, 579. The translation of the sixth session of Ephesus prepared by Marius Mercator, and notable readings extracted from manuscripts, CXVIII. The Apostolic See removed the Ephesian pseudo-synod by refusing its consent alone, 352.

*Epibatae*, that is, laymen, 461. A bishop must be examined before ordination, and in what manner, 653. What he ought to be, and his duties, 457, 462. What sort of man is to be elected, 275, 653, 654. Bishops are not to be ordained from among the laity, 71, 276. No one is to be ordained bishop without the knowledge of the Apostolic See, that is, of the primate, 449, note. Or of the metropolitan, 206, 269, 430, 436. Confirmation by the metropolitans, 50, 53. No one is to intrude into a vacant Church, even if the people want him as bishop, 429. The ordinations of bishops are not to be delayed and are to take place within three months, unless necessity compels an extension, 237. At the ordination, the ordiners are to announce to the bishop the decisions of the council, 641. Statutes to be observed by the bishop are proposed, 655 and following. By whom and how bishops are to be ordained, 50, 430, 436, 639. No single bishop is to presume to ordain a bishop, 206, 249. He is to be ordained by no fewer than three bishops, 103. When a bishop in another province ought to be ordained by neighboring bishops, 66. In a disagreement among bishops, the opinion of the majority is to prevail, 53. No layman or monk is to be ordained bishop unless tested through the lower orders, 265, 273. No bishop is to be imposed on unwilling persons, 274. The consent of the clergy, people, and order is required, ibid., 654. When a bishop is to be taken from another Church, 274. No bishop is to appoint a successor for himself, 431. A bishop is not to be ordained in villages or small cities, 66, 441. What is to be done concerning those ordained in such places, 441. If an ordained bishop neglects to go to his Church, he is to be compelled, 429. What if he does not go because of opposition from the people, 430. Bishops are not to pass from one Church to another, 431. Those who do so are not even to have lay communion, 63. What if a bishop, not received in his own Church, goes to another, 113, 487. When it is permitted to pass from one Church to another, 656. Those passing from Church to Church are considered alienated from Damasus’s communion until they return to the first Church, 402. What if another has been ordained to the same see, ibid. A bishop must not be absent from his Church for more than three weeks, 72. For how long he may be received as a visitor in another city or province, ibid. African bishops are not to cross the sea except with a *formata* from the primate, 97, 643. Who may go to the imperial court, and for what reasons, 68. They should rather send a deacon with letters of recommendation from the metropolitan, 69. The reasons for going are to be examined by the Roman bishop, ibid. When they are to be examined by the bishops who are on the route, 70. A bishop litigating with another bishop is not to summon a bishop from another province, 64. What if a bishop has been deposed, 67. What if the judges’ opinions differ, 429. The cases of bishops. See Cases of bishops. Major cases.

A bishop is to assume no administration of private affairs, but devote himself to reading, prayer, and preaching, 655. What furnishings he may use, ibid. How he is to ordain clerics, 656. See Clerics. He is not to ordain clerics for himself in another’s parish, 431. No one is to occupy another’s congregations, 89. He is not to claim foreign clerics as his own, 410, 428. He is to usurp nothing beyond his own boundaries, 443. How he is to administer the Church’s goods, 433. He is not to hear cases without the presence of his own clerics, 656. When summoned to a synod, he is not to evade attendance, 439.

A canonical letter published from manuscripts, 669. Concerning its author and date, 631. Canonical letters of the bishops of Alexandria and others received in the Greek codex of canons, XV. Familiar and *hypomnesticae* letters, 780, note. *Formatae* letters are to be given by a bishop to clerics migrating elsewhere; otherwise they are not to be received, 426, 620. They are also called canonical letters, 439. The rule concerning *formatae* letters, 452. Attributed to Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, and said to have been prescribed by the Nicene Fathers, ibid., note. It appears to be the product of a Latin author, ibid. Received in practice, ibid. Two *formatae* letters, CXI, CXII. Another, CCXLII.

The letters of the Roman pontiffs included under the name of canons, LVI. Given the title of decrees, 863. Called “authorities” by the Gauls, CXXXI. Almost all written at synods, CXXXII. [Col. 1166] Nevertheless, they were generally inscribed solely with the name of the pontiffs, 934, note. At first written to the bishops of particular provinces, and afterward communicated to others, they acquired different titles in the manuscripts, LXV, 407, note. Sometimes additions were inserted so that they might be adapted to differing disciplines, 1000.

Two Erchembalds who were chancellors, CCLXXXIV.

Error. For as long as someone remains in error, he remains bound by the judgment pronounced against the error, 323. Those who share in errors are condemned, 351.

Esicius, bishop of Salona, consults Pope Zosimus, 265. The Eucharist is communion in Christ’s body, and concerning the remnants that remain, 674. The Eucharist is to be given as viaticum in illness, 658. See Communion. The Eucharist is not to be given to the bodies of the dead, 91, 641. In place of *eulogiae*, it is not to be sent at Easter to other parishes, 436.

The Eudoxians anathematized at the Council of Constantinople, 443, 554. *Eulogiae*, CCCIV. The error of Eunomius condemned, 401. The Eunomians anathematized, 443, 554. Eunuchs excluded from the clergy, 47.

The martyrdom of St. Euphemia, or the church in which the Council of Chalcedon was held, 215, 217. Euphemius of Constantinople defends Acacius, and how, 334. The province of Euphratesia established after the Nicene synod and separated from Syria, XVIII. Eusebius of Caesarea in Pontus presided over the Council of Gangra, XXV. Eusebius of Caesarea in Palestine presided over the Council of Antioch in the year 332, XXIX. He wrote separately to Constantine from the others, and why, XXVIII. Eustathius, or Eustasius, the bishop, and his disciples, whose errors were condemned at the Council of Gangra, 121. Who this Eustathius was, XXIV. Eustathius the deacon, deprived of the dignity of the diaconate for a slight reason; Pope Innocent I requests that he be restored, 196.

Eutyches was condemned by St. Flavian at the synod of Constantinople, together with the acts of that synod, 295. Testimonies of the Fathers concerning the two natures in Christ against the error of Eutyches, 285. The Eutychian error condemned at the Council of Chalcedon, 222. The Eutychians restrained by the law of the emperor Marcian, 242.

Those excommunicated by their own bishops are not to be received by others, 50, 72, 627. Until their case has been examined in a provincial synod, they are not to be received by anyone, 51. Or the bishop of the excommunicated person is to deliver a more lenient judgment, ibid. One must not communicate with the excommunicated, 425. The punishment of those who communicate with them, 660. Concerning excommunicated clerics who communicated before the hearing, 645, 650.

Exorcists are to lay hands on the possessed, 663. It is forbidden to exorcize for those who have not been ordained by a bishop, 438. Exsuperius, bishop of Toulouse, consults Pope Innocent, 182.

## F

The faith of the presbyter Faustinus, 278. Women are not to minister at the sacred altars, 420. Nor are they to enter the altar area, 440. Even if learned and holy, they are not to teach men in an assembly, 660. See Woman.

Pope Felix III condemns Acacius, who had received heretics, together with his letter to him, 317. He sent Vitalis and Misenus as legates to Constantinople, 318. See Vitalis. Three spurious letters of that pontiff dating from before the fabrications of Pseudo-Isidore, CXLV. Three others called into question are defended, CXLVII. The treatise of Gelasius wrongly attributed to Felix III, CL. A fragment of a letter of Felix III to be added to the printed editions, CLXIV.

*Feriatica* is to be accepted neither from heretics nor from Jews, 439. Ferment sent from Rome to the titular churches on Sunday, not to the rural parishes, and why, 201, note.

When Ferrandus of Carthage, deacon of the Church, flourished, CCXLVI. Concerning the *Breviatio canonum* composed by him and its very rare manuscripts, ibid. Why he placed the last Nicene canon first among the Sardican canons, CCXLVII, 706, note. Several obscure citations in the same *Breviatio* explained, others supplied or corrected; these will be useful for a new edition of his *Breviatio*, CCXLVII and following. Ferrandus praised in the old collection, CCLXXXV. Also by Facundus of Hermiane and Cresconius, CCXLVI.

Festival days are not to be celebrated with Jews or heretics, 439. Nor with pagans, ibid.

The symbol commonly called the Athanasian Creed designated by the name of the Catholic faith, 669, note. The confession of faith sent by Damasus to Paulinus of Antioch, 400. Creeds and formulas of faith, 277, 278, 279, 390, 405. What is the creed inscribed to Augustine, 282, note. It is denied to be Augustine’s, and is asserted to belong to the First Council of Toledo, 919. [Col. 1167] Anathemas against the errors of Priscillian appended to it, 283. The creed presented in chapter 39 of the collection printed in this volume, 279. It is more probably to be attributed to St. Gregory Nazianzen, 945. Quesnel’s dissertation on various creeds, 910 and following. Observations on the same dissertation and on the same creeds, 945.

Damasus explains what is to be believed concerning the Son of God, 401 and following. His incarnation, the unity of the person, and the two natures explained, 390, 392, 653, 654. Testimonies of the Fathers concerning the two natures in Christ, the Son of God, 285.

Parents must not abandon care of their children, 126. The duty of children toward their parents, ibid.

The acts of St. Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, and of the synod held by him, against Eutyches, 295. He was absolved from the condemnation by the assembly of the Greeks because the Apostolic See did not consent to it, 352.

*Formata*. See *Epistola formata*.

Fortunatus Venantius, author of the exposition of the Catholic faith, or Athanasian Creed, 669, note, 955.

## G

How much the Gallican bishops deferred to the apostolic constitutions, 1029, note, CXXXI. Gallican synods confirmed by apostolic authority, CXXXIV. Gallican collections of canons, CXXXIX.

The synodical letter of Gangra and the canons of the Isidorian version, 121. Of the ancient version, 528. This synod is shown to have been later than Sardica, XXIV. Who Eustathius mentioned in the synodical letter was, ibid. Hosius of Cordoba incorrectly listed somewhere among the Fathers of Gangra, ibid. Eusebius of Caesarea presided over that council, XXV. Why the Gangran canons, although later than the Antiochene canons, are nevertheless written before the Antiochene canons in the Greek codex, ibid. A Gangran canon cited by St. Gregory of Tours under the name of the Nicene canon, and why, LI, LII.

The Church treasury, 661.

Gelasius is the author of the book entitled in the printed editions *Breviculus historiae Eutychianistarum*, and a passage at its end must be supplied, CLXIII. He is the author of the same work, in a shorter form, entitled *Narrationis ordo de pravitate Dioscori*, 308, note. Three editions of this work and three additions authored by Gelasius, ibid. Gelasius’s tome *On the Bond of Anathema*, 321. His *Commonitorium* to Faustus, 333. He writes to the emperor Anastasius, 318. To the bishops of Dardania, 347. His longer letter to the Dardanians is freed from the mark of interpolation, CXLVII. Two copies of the same letter, one fuller than the other, and both written by the same Gelasius, ibid., CXLVIII. His letter to the bishops established throughout Lucania, Bruttium, and Sicily, later circulated to others and given another title, 407, note. Another letter of his to the bishops of the East, 361. Gelasius’s letter to Succonius defended, CXLVII. Four acephalous works attributed to Gelasius, CXLIX. Three fragments attributed to Anastasius II to be assigned to him, CXLVI. Whether the decree concerning books to be received or not received belongs to Gelasius, CLI. Three forms of the same decree, and what is to be attributed to Gelasius, CLII and following. Whether the canon of Scripture is to be assigned to him, CLVI. A passage of Gelasius explained, 775. Fragments of Gelasius published from the manuscript collection of Cardinal Deusdedit, CCCIV.

The omission of kneeling on Sundays and during the Easter season was common among Easterners and Westerners, 723, note. And in the Roman Church, 761. The exception concerning penitents, 726, note.

A previously unpublished law of the emperor Glycerius against simoniacal ordinations, 677. Published at the beginning of his reign, 633.

Grace is given for each individual act, and is not given according to merits, 180. Daily grace, 160, 162, 164. The necessity of grace, 136 and following. Grace is to be sought only with great prayers, 137. Through Jesus Christ, grace not only erases sin but also assists one not to sin, 167. It assists not only by enlightening but also by enabling us to love and be able to do what is good, ibid. Those who say that grace merely makes it easier for us to do good, as though we could do so without grace, are condemned, ibid., 168. Grace was hidden in the time of the law but is now manifest, 157. What sort of grace Christian doctrine teaches, 153, 154. Where Pelagius and Coelestius place the grace of God, 130. They leave no place for the grace of God by which we are Christians, ibid. Pelagius placed the assistance of grace in the possibility of nature, 155. This is refuted, ibid. When Pelagius says that grace means either free will, the commandment of the law, or the forgiveness of sins, he says nothing relating to conquering desire and temptations, 151.

Notes on Gratian’s collection, CCCXX.

The synodical letter of St. Gregory the Great to all the bishops in the year 601 is incorrectly attached in the printed editions, CCXLIII. What its genuine subscriptions are, ibid. His letter to Augustine, with a preface not yet printed and with a form different from that of the printed editions, is produced from manuscripts, CCXLIV.

The letter of Gregory the Younger, otherwise called Gregory II, now published for the first time from a manuscript, CCCVI. Whether Gregory of Baetica was the author of a sermon printed among those of St. Gregory Nazianzen, 948. St. Gregory Nazianzen is more probably the author of the creed contained in chapter 39 of the collection printed in this volume, 945. Two printed sermons, 49 and 50, attributed to him by some but questioned by others, 946, 947. Their translator was Rufinus, 946. Certain acts of Pope Gregory VII indicated, CCCIX.

The collection of Gregory the presbyter entitled *Polycarpus*. See *Polycarpus*.

St. Gregory of Tours cited a Gangran canon under the name of the Council of Nicaea, LI. From where he took this, LII, CCLVIII. The Apostolic Canon cited by him with an addition, CCLXXV, 1023.

## H

The Hadriana collection, CLXXXIV. It is distinguished from the Dionysiana by its additions, ibid. Additions to the canons of the first part, ibid. Other additions to the decretals of the second part, CLXXXV. Two additions that came later, CLXXXVI. A breviary of the same collection, ibid. An epitome of the canons incorrectly attributed to Pope Hadrian in the printed editions, CLXXXVIII. The chapters inscribed to the same Hadrian are shown to have been fabricated by Pseudo-Isidore, CCXIX.

The Hadrian-Hispanica collection described, CCXIII. It appears to have been used by an ancient collector, CCLXXXI.

When a heresy’s author has been condemned, its supporters and those who communicate with them are condemned, 349, 351, 364, 366. Clerics are to avoid banquets and associations of heretics, 664. One is neither to pray nor to sing psalms with heretics, 665. Entrance into the Church is not to be granted to heretics who persist in heresy, 435. Catholics are not to visit the cemeteries, martyria, or churches of heretics, ibid. Marriages are not to be contracted with heretics, 436, 438. Nor are blessings to be received from them, nor prayer made with them, 438. Nor are their false martyrs to be venerated, ibid. Nor are their separate assemblies to be attended, in which angels or demons were worshiped with idolatrous rites, ibid., note. Nor is *feriatica* to be received from them, nor festival days celebrated with them, 439. Many true things are found in the books of heretics and are not therefore to be rejected because their books are rejected for other errors, 326. How heretics returning to the Church were received, 247. Arians, Eunomians, and Macedonians returning to the faith both received remission of their blasphemy at that time and acquired hope of indulgence for the future, 325.

Halitgarius’s six books on penance, CCLXXXI.

The province of Hellespont established and separated from Asia after the Nicene synod and before the pseudo-Sardican synod, XVIII.

King Henry, son of Conrad, and some of his acts indicated, CCCIX.

The chapters of Herard of Tours, CCLXXXIV. Queen Hereleuva, mother of Theodoric, CCCIV, note.

Heros and Lazarus accuse Coelestius in letters sent to the Africans, 129. The Herovalliana collection, CCLXXV. Founded in Gaul, ibid. Earlier than the Hadriana collection, CCLVI. The Hibernensis collection, CCLXXIII.

Jerome’s letter on the grades of clerics, inscribed to Patroclus, and whether it is genuine, CCLXI.

The see of Jerusalem. See Jerosolymitana.

Passages of Hilary of Poitiers requiring correction, XVIII, XLV, XLVI, XLVII. The pseudo-synodical subscriptions of Sardica corrupted in his work, XIX.

Boniface entrusts Hilary of Narbonne with responsibility for the whole of the first province of Narbonne, 270.

The excerpts from the decrees of Hildebert of Le Mans, later bishop of Tours, CCCXX.

Himelco, prefect of the praetorium of Italy under the emperor Glycerius, 633. His edict, now extracted for the first time from a manuscript, 679.

The letters of Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, written to Damasus, 246. Handed over to Siricius, 247.

Certain non-Hipponian canons praised by some under the name of the canons of Hippo, and why, CCLXXVI.

The Hispanic collection and its sources, CXCV. What its original form was, CXCVI. Later enlarged in certain manuscripts, CXCVII and following. The time when this collection was arranged, CCIII. Composed in Spain, ibid. Conjectures concerning its Spanish author, CCIV. Concerning the more extensive additions found in the manuscript of St. Aemilianus, CCVI. This collection called the authentic body of canons, CCV. A notable distinction between the codices of Hispanic and Gallican origin that contain the Hispanic collection, CCVII and following. The testimony of the Spaniards concerning the authority of the Apostolic See, [Col. 1169] CXCVII. The esteem in which the Gallican synods were held among the Spaniards, CXCVI.

What penance is prescribed for homicide, 113. Voluntary and accidental homicide, ibid., 114.

Who the Homuncionites are, 61, note.

Two letters of Pope Honorius I now printed, CCCVI. His law against the Pelagians, 170. It was requested not by the Africans but by Pope Zosimus after the Roman judgment against those same men, and why, 882. Another law of Honorius to Aurelius of Carthage against the same Pelagians, 174. It is explained, 887. This is shown to have been directed chiefly to Pope Boniface, 888. Against which Pelagians it was principally issued, ibid., 889.

What the emperor Honorius did in the schism between Pope Boniface and Eulalius, 160.

Some codices of Pope Hormisdas inscribe to him the decree concerning books to be received or not received, CLIV. What is to be attributed to him, CLVI. His letter now published for the first time, CLXVI. What the letter to all the provinces attributed to Hormisdas in certain manuscript collections is, CCLXXVII.

Hucarius the Levite, author of the *Excerpts* attributed in the printed editions to Egbert of York, CCLXX.

Hugh of Châlons, author of Ivo’s *Summa of Decrees*, CCCXII.

Humerius, deprived of the diaconate and stripped of the name of Christian, was ordained a presbyter by Acacius, 317.

## I

The books of Idacius Clarus against Varimadus are not by Vigilius of Thapsus but by Idacius, 957. The twelve books on the Trinity published among the works of Athanasius are also his, ibid.

An index for instruction, CIX. An inferior cannot absolve a superior, 332.

The sick who request penance. See Penance.

The twelfth letter of Pope Innocent I inserted into the Hispanic collection is freed from the mark of being a forgery, CCII. The consulship mentioned in it must be corrected, CCIII. The letters and judgment of that same Innocent to the Council of Carthage against Coelestius and Pelagius, 134. Others to the Council of Milevis on the same matter, 144. Others to five African bishops, 160. Others specifically to Aurelius, 164. To Exsuperius of Toulouse, 182. To the bishops of Macedonia, 188. To Decentius of Gubbio, 198. To Victricius of Rouen, 204. Why Innocent attributed the Antiochene canons to heretical authors, XXX.

Latin translators sometimes inserted the original Latin of Greek works when material that had been translated from Latin into Greek and inserted in Greek codices and works was involved, XL.

Irregularities that bar a person from the orders, 408, 409. See Clerics.

The chapters of Isaac of Langres, CCLXXXIV.

The ancient translation of the Greek canons called Isidoriana, LXIX. At first it lacked the Chalcedonian canons, XIII. The Laodicean and Constantinopolitan canons were likewise translated into Latin later and added to the same version, ibid., LXIX. The Antiochene canons also, XIII. How widely it was disseminated, LXX.

The collection of Isidore Mercator, teeming with apocryphal materials, CCCXV. Falsely attributed to St. Isidore, bishop of Seville, CCXVI. How late the fabrications of this collection were detected, CCXV, CCXVI. The principal features that demonstrate its forgeries, CCXVI. Whether Nicholas I approved such a collection, CCXV. Genuine documents inserted into the same collection, and the sources from which they were drawn, CCXVII. Certain genuine documents interpolated by the same impostor, ibid. Certain older apocryphal materials received or even interpolated, CCXVIII. For what purpose the impostor fabricated so many apocrypha, CCXX and following. Whether ecclesiastical discipline was changed by these fabrications, CCXXI. Concerning the author, place, and date of this collection, CCXXII, CCXXIII. The variety of the codices of this collection, CCXXV. Which codices are purer, ibid., CCXXXII. A pure collection of this kind described, CCXXV and following. Certain additions belonging to Pseudo-Isidore’s second labors noted, CCXXXII. Concerning codices that contain Isidore’s collection not entirely pure or complete, CCXXXIII, CCXLI. Certain apocryphal documents wrongly attributed to Isidore, CCXXXV, CCXXXIX. Care must be taken not to accept as pure Isidorian manuscript copies those that are not pure, CCXLI. The spurious addition to St. Gregory’s letter to Secundinus is not to be attributed to Isidore, CCLXXXII. Nor was the letter of St. Isidore of Seville to Mason fabricated by him, ibid. Nor were several others, which are absent from the pure Isidorian manuscripts, CCXXXV, CCXXXVII, CCXXXIX. Less pure Isidorian codices, CCXXXIII and following.

Two collections of Ivo of Chartres: the *Decretum*, divided into seventeen parts, and the *Panormia*, distributed into eight parts, CCCX. Some assign one or the other work to him, CCCXII. What is more probable, ibid. Both are attributed to him, CCCXIII. The sources from which Ivo benefited, ibid. Ivo’s *Summa of Decrees*, CCCXII.

[Col. 1170] ## J

The fasts of the Church are not to be despised, 126. To what extent one is not to fast on Sunday, ibid., 664. Concerning the fast of Saturday, 200. The fast of Friday on account of the Lord’s Passion, ibid.

The praise and honor of the see of Jerusalem, 24, 54.

St. John Chrysostom, bishop of Constantinople, was condemned by a synod and absolved by the Apostolic See alone as well, because it did not consent to his condemnation, 352.

John, bishop of Alexandria, ordained as a Catholic, 312. He sends to Rome a synodical letter concerning his ordination, ibid. The emperor arranges for confirmation to be withheld by the pontiff, ibid. John flees to Rome, 318. He is expelled from the see contrary to the rules, 335, 353, 355, 357, 362, 363.

Whether John, bishop of Antioch, thought that the profession of faith written by St. Cyril himself at the time of the Council of Ephesus was sufficient to restore peace with him, 386, note.

John, bishop of Apamea, ordained by Peter of Antioch, a heretic, 312. Not received by the people of Apamea, he invades the Church of Antioch after expelling that same Peter, ibid. Condemned together with Peter of Antioch by Acacius, 313. Likewise by the Apostolic See, ibid. After so many condemnations, appointed by Acacius as administrator of the Church of Tyre, ibid., 317.

John, bishop of Ravenna, frequently reported the needs of the Churches to Pope Gelasius, 407.

The Greek collection of John the Scholasticus divided into titles, XIV, XL. Wrongly attributed to Theodoret, XV.

The doctrine of Jovinian, which was authored by the devil, 255. How pernicious it was while it remained hidden, and how it was discovered and condemned, 256. The promoters of the new heresy condemned, 258. Jovinian and his associates prove themselves to be Manichees, 263. They reveal their blasphemies at Rome, 257. They came from Rome to Milan, 263. There they were also condemned, ibid.

The Jews, from whom *feriatica* is not to be received, nor festival days celebrated with them, 239. Nor is unleavened bread to be received from them, nor communion held with their impieties, ibid.

Whether Julian, archbishop of Toledo, was the author of the *Breviatio canonum* of the Hispanic collection, CCLXV.

Justellus (Christophorus): the *Codex of the Canons of the Universal Church*, in Greek and Latin, edited by him, composed by ingenuity, and in what manner, VIII, IX. It is not an ancient Greek codex, X. Nor does it belong to the Universal Church, XI. Nor is it the codex that prevailed in the Greek Church in the middle of the sixth century, ibid. Its defects noted, together with additions foreign to the ancient Greek codex of canons, X. The opinion of Justellus concerning a continuous sequence of numbers in all ancient codices of canons rejected, XXXIV.

Juvenis removed the Sardican canons from the codex of the ancient version, and why, LXXIV. Concerning the dispute over this matter with Peter de Marca and the editors of his version, LXXI. Concerning the *Codex of the African Church* printed by him, LXXIV, CVI. Concerning the edition of Dionysius Exiguus prepared by him, CLXXVII.

The synod of Justiniana mistaken for the Council of Orange, CXXXIII. The little book of the emperor Justinian given to Pope Agapetus, and its chronological notice in the printed editions requiring correction, CLXIII. The emperor Justin sends an embassy to Thrasamund, CLXVII.

## L

A layman must not presume to teach in the presence of clerics unless they approve, 660.

Lanfranc is to be added to the bishops of Pavia, CCXCIX.

When the Council of Laodicea was held, XXI. The Laodicean canons from the ancient interpretation called Isidorian, 434. They are absent from the Ancient Version, and why, XII. They were absent from the Greek collection at the beginning, ibid.

How those who lapsed under Licinius were received, 56. What is to be done with presbyters and deacons who lapsed, 106. What concerning laymen who lapsed, 107. The various classes of the lapsed, ibid.

When Laurence of Nocera was appointed by Symmachus, CX. The two schisms raised against that same Symmachus are distinguished, CXI.

Lazarus. See Heros and Lazarus.

Lectors are not to greet the people, 90, 640. For how long they are to read, or are not to be permitted to read, 95. When they reach puberty, they are to be compelled either to marry or to profess continence, 640.

Those who deny the bequests of the dead, or return them with difficulty, are excommunicated, 668.

When Roman laws were introduced into collections of canons, CCLXXXVII. Justinian’s laws prevailed in Italy, ibid.

The letters of St. Leo rejected from the Greek codex of canons, XV. The letter attributed to Leo, and the apocryphal work concerning the privilege of chorepiscopi, is not to be counted among the Isidorian forgeries, CCXXXV.

The apocryphal acts of Pope Liberius, CXV, CXXXV, CXCI.

To deny free will because it requires divine assistance was an error of Pelagius, 179. Catholic doctrine acknowledges the contrary, 180.

The tyranny of Licinius, 56.

The emperor Lothair I, and verses composed at his funeral, CXXXVIII.

Lucillus, otherwise Lucius, bishop of Verona, among the Fathers of Sardica, XLVI.

The complaint of the Lutubensian Church against Patroclus of Arles, 269.

## M
## M

The Macedonian bishops consult Innocent, 189. The Macedonian error refuted by an addition to the Nicene Creed under Damasus, 401, note. A confession of faith sent by the same Damasus to Paulinus of Antioch against the same error, 401–402. Anathema pronounced against the Macedonians, 401. Macedonius, bishop of Mopsuestia, counted among the Nicene Fathers, XXI. Magicians and enchanters to be expelled from the clergy by the Church, 439. Canonical punishment for sorcery, 114. Jovinian and his associates proved themselves Manichaeans, 263. Law against the Manichaeans, 396. The Marcellians condemned, 443, note; 554. The spurious case of Pope Marcellinus in the pseudo-synod of Sinuessa, CXV, CXXI. Marcellinus, Carthaginian subdeacon, sent to Pope Zosimus, 785, note; 789, note; 859–860. The imperial rescript of Emperor Marcian concerning the convocation of a general council, 213. His address to the Council of Chalcedon, 215. A constitution concerning the same council, 238. Another, 240. Another against the Eutychians and Apollinarists, 242. Those who deny the virginity of Blessed Mary in childbirth refuted, 260. The testimony of Marius Mercator concerning the articles of accusation brought against Coelestius explained, 800, note. Saint Martin of Braga was at first bishop of Dumium, CCLI. He was skilled in Greek, and a translation was prepared by him, ibid. Whether and to what extent he rendered the canonical articles from the Greek, CCLII. He did not excerpt all of them from the Greek, CCLIII. Whether these articles were read and confirmed at the Second Council of Braga, ibid. They were wrongly attributed by some to Pope Martin I, ibid. The place in the preface explained, LXX. Martyrdom for the Church of a martyr, 213, 217, 229. The birthdays of martyrs are not to be celebrated during Lent, but their memory alone is to be commemorated on Saturday and Sunday, 440. Their passions were read in the churches, 100. Marriage with pagans, heretics, or schismatics not to be contracted, 95. See *Nuptiae*. Mauretania Sitifensis is to have its own primate, 89, 640. The ordination of Maximus the Cynic, bishop of Constantinople, and his acts invalid, 444. *Mediana* was the name given to the fourth Sunday of Lent, 413.
