The Council of Milan writes back to Pope Siricius against Jovinian, 259. The Nicene decree concerning Meletius and those ordained by him, 588. The edition of Merlini (Jacques), presenting in its first volume the Isidorian Collection with Isidorian additions, CCXXXVII. The authority of metropolitans, 50, 53, 269, 427, 431. See *Ordination of Bishops*. Letters of recommendation to be given by a bishop of the metropolis to a deacon sent to the imperial court, 69. “Metropolis” here means the civil or geographical metropolis, XXXIII. A metropolitan must remain within his own province and undertake nothing in other provinces, 274. The Council of Milevis of the year 402, and which council its canons represent, XCIV. Which council is called Milevitan by Isidore, ibid. Letters of another Council of Milevis to Innocent against Pelagius and Coelestius, 141. This council was held after the Council of Carthage of 416, not before it, 851. Bishop Misenus. See Vitalis. The sacrifice of the Mass is to be celebrated by those who are fasting, 97. The peace is to be given not before, but after the mysteries have been completed, 199. The names of those offering are to be recited during the mysteries, ibid. The sacrifice of the Mass was not celebrated during the two days before Easter, 200. It was celebrated in cemeteries even in the time of Innocent, 201. At Rome it was not celebrated in the urban titular churches on Sunday, but it was customary to celebrate it in rural parishes and cemeteries, ibid., note. During Lent, bread ought not to be offered except on Saturday and Sunday, 440. Offerings are not to be made in private houses, either by a priest or by a bishop, 441. Mizonius, an elder of the province of Byzacena, 87. Monks are subject to bishops, and the bishop must provide them with appropriate care, 228. If a monk wishes to strive for the clerical state, he must not depart from his former way of life, 210. Monks must not be contractors or agents, 227. They must not involve themselves in ecclesiastical or secular affairs after abandoning their own monasteries, 228. They must not receive another’s slave without the master’s permission, ibid. The solitude of the monks frequented, 265. When and under what conditions Gelasius decreed that monks might be ordained, 408. Four kinds of monks, CCCIX. A monastery may not be built without the bishop’s consent, 228. Monasteries once dedicated must never become secular lodging places, 237. Words of admonition, exhortation, and persuasion used in issuing precepts, 1010. The Montenses. See Novatians. Death resulting from Adam’s sin. See Adam. The dead are not to be baptized, 91. Nor is the Eucharist to be given to them, ibid. The name of one who died condemned cannot be entered in the ecclesiastical recitation, 344. A woman must not wear masculine clothing, 125. See *Feminae*. The term “woman” understood as “widow,” 207, note.

## N

The canons of Neocaesarea in the Isidorian version, 116. In the ancient version, 490. The chronological notice prefixed to these canons derives from a Greek source, XXXIII. The catalogue of the Fathers of Neocaesarea, with the names of their cities and provinces, printed in the standard editions of the Councils, is spurious, XXII. Neophytes are not to be ordained, 15. Praise of the Council of Nicaea, 374–375. Its chronological notice, prefixed to the canons in certain manuscripts and standard editions, is corrupt, 22, note; 27, note; 46, note; 48; 495, note; 710, note. Another annotation issued after the Creed and wrongly attributed to Dionysius Exiguus is shown to have come from a Greek codex, 28, note. Why some writers said that the Council of Nicaea was held under Pope Julius, LXI. The oldest version of the Nicene canons received by the Roman Church, and the portions of it that survive, LXVI. The same version was shared by several Western Churches, especially the African Churches, ibid. Another version prepared by Philo and Evaristus and sent to the Africans, LXVIII. Another ancient version, called Isidorian, though altered more freely in some places, 47, note. Another version, the *Prisca*, 494. Another very ancient version, now published for the first time, 567. Yet another ancient version, previously unpublished, 581. The order of the canons is different in some places, 47, note. The extent to which the Nicene canons were observed in the Roman Church, 759. The abridgment of the Nicene canons made by Rufinus, used in Gaul, LXVIII, CXXXI, 1037, note. The Sardican canons formerly praised and received under the name of the Nicene canons; see *Sardican canons*. Not all the canons of the Greek councils were cited under the name of the Nicene canons, LI. A canon of Gangra attributed by Gregory of Tours to the Council of Nicaea, ibid. From where he derived this attribution, LII, CCLVIII. The Nicene canon concerning the Cathari explained, 54, note. The version of this canon printed in the collection in this volume is foreign to the Roman version, 755. It contains an error, ibid. The Nicene canon concerning the omission of kneeling on Sundays and during the Easter season is absent from certain codices, 62, note. Why it is absent from those codices and from Rufinus’s abridgment, ibid.; 723, note; 763. Why Ferrandus first cited that canon among the Sardican canons, 706, note. The Nicene Creed translated by various interpreters and received into ancient canonical collections, 27, note. The same Creed from the most ancient version brought to Africa by Caecilian, 88, note. The Nicene faith must not be violated, 443. Whether the Council of Nicaea wished the canons of earlier synods to be read and confirmed, XXIII. Whether it established a canon of the divine Scriptures, 100, note. Whether it sent its own canons to Pope Sylvester for confirmation, 46, note. A spurious letter of the same council to the Roman synod, or to Pope Sylvester, CXVII. A letter of the same council to the Church of Alexandria and the bishops of Egypt concerning the proceedings against Arius and his associates and concerning the schism of Meletius, from a version now published for the first time, 587. The rule concerning *formatae* attributed to the Council of Nicaea, 152, note. The catalogue of the Nicene Fathers derives from a primitive Greek canonical codex, XVI. It is cited by ancient writers, ibid. It is found in Saint Athanasius, XVII. Four different versions preserve the same catalogue, XVI. A double order of bishops noted in the manuscripts, 30, note. The same catalogue produced from that double order, 30 and following; 504 and following. The names of the bishops distributed by provinces together with the names of their cities, XVII. The civil division of the provinces indicated in the catalogue agrees with the time of Nicaea, XVIII. Objections to the catalogue answered, XIX. When and how the same catalogue was compiled, XX. A name used in place of a cause, 93, note. The pronoun “we,” and similar expressions taken from the papal see and authority and used by the Roman pontiffs on account of an action carried out by a predecessor, CXLVIII. How Novatians, or Montenses, coming to the Church are to be received, 209, 455, 450. Marriage is not to be condemned, 123, 125, 258, 654. The bond of marriage is to be honored through conjugal chastity, 127. Priests attend marriages, 258. The veil placed upon the couple at marriage, 248. Marriages are not to be celebrated during Lent, 440. At weddings there is to be no singing or dancing, but dining or taking lunch as befits Christians, 441. See *Conjugium*, *Matrimonium*. Concerning those who marry repeatedly, 117. Second marriages are permitted to laypeople, 419. They are not to be condemned, 654. But they exclude a person from the clergy. See *Clerici*. What those joined in a second marriage ought to do, 434. A priest must not attend the banquet of a second marriage, 117. Marriages with heretics must not take place, 438. Children must not be given in marriage to heretics, but rather received from them if they profess that they will become Catholics, ibid. The children of clerics must not be joined in marriage to pagans, heretics, or schismatics, 642. Incestuous marriages are to be dissolved, and those who delay dissolution are to be excommunicated, 670. Concerning a woman married to two brothers, 116.

## O

Offerings placed upon the altar must be under the seal of the priest and deacon, and, where necessary, must not be disbursed by one without the other's knowledge, 672. The offerings of those who oppress the poor are to be rejected by priests, 663. Stewards are to be appointed when a church is vacant, 237. Olbertus was an assistant, not the author, of Burchard’s collection, CCXC. The holy oil with which the sick are anointed is a kind of sacrament, 203. It is to be prepared by the bishop, ibid. Priests may also administer it, ibid. It must not be granted to penitents during their time of penance, ibid. What the ancient handwritten formula *olographum* signifies, CII. Who Olympius, mentioned in the Sardican canons, was, XLVII. Optatus, to whom Augustine’s letter published from the Gottwic manuscript was addressed, was not the bishop of Milevis but another man outside Africa, 893. Whether Hosius, bishop of Corduba, was the Roman pontiff’s legate at the Council of Nicaea, 29, note. Hosius’s speech, published from the Corbie manuscript, is shown to be spurious, XXIII. Hosius was not among the Fathers of Gangra, XXIV. A letter of Hosius and Protogenes of Sardica to Pope Julius, now published for the first time, 597. Judgment concerning it, XXXIX, 577, 597, note. Those who may not wear the *orarium*, 437. Prayer is to be addressed to the Father, 96. See *Preces*. The necessity of prayer, 131, 137. Prayer is the clearest testimony to grace, 152. Even the saints need prayer, in which they say: “Forgive us our debts,” 168–169. Men whose wives have committed adultery are not to be ordained, 117. Ordination without examination rejected, 55. Ordained lapsed persons are to be deposed, 56. How they are to be received, ibid. The ordination of a bishop. See *Episcopus*. The ordination of clerics. See *Clerici*. Times for ordinations, 413. The most ancient forms or rubrics of ordination, 668. The ancient Roman Order, CCCIII. Orosius gave the letters of Heros and Lazarus against Pelagius and Coelestius to the Council of Carthage, 129. The province of Osrhoene was established and separated from Mesopotamia after the Council of Nicaea, indeed even after the pseudo-Sardican council, XVIII. The date of the Council of Oviedo corrected, CCCXIV.

## P

The kiss of peace is to be given after the mysteries have been completed, 199. Not before, as some used to do, ibid. The edict of Palladius, prefect of the praetorium, against the Pelagians, 173. *Parembola* incorrectly rendered in the heading of Athanasius’s letter, 611, note. Parishes, distinct from urban titular churches, understood to mean rural churches, 201. Easter is not to be celebrated with the Jews, 424. The Nicene rule concerning Easter is to be observed, ibid. Easter is to be celebrated on one day and at one time, 664. Kneeling is not to be practiced during the Easter season. See *Genuflexio*. They are to receive the date of Easter from the Church of the province of Carthage in Africa, 89. The passions of martyrs are read in the churches on their anniversary, 100. Pataria, which arose near Milan, CCCIX. Patroclus, bishop of Arles, is accused of having ordained the Lutubensian bishop contrary to the rules of the Fathers, 269. The Paulianists returning to the Church are to be baptized and ordained, 61. They did not baptize in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, 194. Paulinus of Antioch, to whom Damasus wrote, 397. Paulinus, the accuser of Coelestius, summoned to Rome, submitted a written defense but did not refuse obedience, 786, note. A passage of the same written defense explained and corrected, 857. Paul of Emesa, bishop, sent by John of Antioch to Cyril of Alexandria to reconcile the parties, 384–385. Paul, bishop of Ephesus, deposed by the authority of the apostolic see, 335, note. Care of the poor and to whom letters of recommendation are to be given, 232. Original sin, 166. Denied by the Pelagians, 131. What sin is “unto death,” and what is not unto death, 326. Sin against the Holy Spirit, 325, 328. No one is perfect and without sin, 168, 180. The letters and fragments of letters of Pope Pelagius I, now brought out from a manuscript, CCCV. Pelagius and Coelestius inventors of novel expressions, 148. Authors of error to be anathematized by all, 129. Access to the Church must not be denied them if they renounce their error, 148. They and their supporters are cut off from the Church, ibid. Laws against them, 170, 174, 181. The edict of Palladius, 173. Another of Volusianus, 182. The errors of Pelagius and Coelestius refuted, 129, 134, 141, 144, 150, 161, 165, 178. The articles of error charged against Pelagius at the Council of Diospolis, excerpted from the Acts of Palestine, 178. They are not a formula of faith, 800, note; 912, note. Nor were they proposed by Saint Leo to the Pelagians for subscription when they returned to Catholic communion, 914, note. Pelagius lived for a long time at Rome, 150. Pope Innocent was unaware that some Romans had been deceived by him, 161. He attempted to deceive certain people at Jerusalem, 143. There he was refuted by many and by Saint Jerome, ibid. Augustine refuted a book of Pelagius delivered by two of his disciples, 153. In the East, that is, at Diospolis, he was thought to have been cleared, 150. He was acquitted by the episcopal proceedings, 131. The proceedings of his defense sent to Innocent, 162. This pontiff doubted the truth of the proceedings, 163. Pelagius sent some writings concerning his defense to Augustine, 158, note. How he ought to defend himself, 151, 153. The error of Pelagius must be anathematized by the authority of the apostolic see, 130–131. Synopsis of the proceedings against the Pelagians, 778, 906. Concerning the African councils against them, ibid., 843 and following. Four African councils under Zosimus admitted by Quesnell, ibid., 847. It is proved that only two should be admitted: one African, as Augustine calls it, and the other plenary, 847. The date of both councils established, 849. A council against the Pelagians at the beginning of Zosimus’s pontificate is eliminated, 450 and following. In the autumn of 417, Aurelius wrote with several bishops to Zosimus, though not from a council in the strict sense, 855. An African council was then summoned, but is shown to have been convened in January or February of 418, 861. Not, however, on the Kalends of May, 903. What the letter of this council to Zosimus contained, 799. The constitutions were not distinct from the letter itself, 863. The commonly published canons against the Pelagians were not enacted at this council, 864. Their material was prepared and set out in the report to Zosimus, 865. The number of Fathers at the same council, 862–863. It was not a provincial council, nor one composed of two provinces, but was formed from all Africa, 868. Concerning this African council and another plenary council against the Pelagians. See *Concilium Africanum*. Concerning the judgment of Pope Zosimus. See *Zosimus*. The judgment of P. Coustant concerning the events under Zosimus examined, 901. Perez (Juan Bautista) praised, and concerning two of his unpublished works, CCIX. His notable preface printed from a manuscript, CCXI. Peter of Alexandria, deacon and follower of Dioscorus, 309. Condemned together with Timothy the Cat, 311. Ordained by a single heretical bishop, ibid. The emperor ordered him to be expelled, ibid. He remained hidden in the city of Alexandria, ibid. He was said to have condemned the Eutychian heresy, but falsely, 313. Other matters concerning him, ibid. Expelled from Alexandria when the Catholic Timothy was restored, 315. He again seized that see after John, the Catholic bishop and successor of Timothy, was expelled, 317–318. He always remained in communion with Peter of Antioch, the heretic, 367. Peter of Antioch, the bishop who had governed a monastery at Constantinople, fled to Antioch after abandoning it because of crimes, 312. After the Catholic Martyrius was driven out, he seized the see of Antioch, ibid. Sent into exile at Oasis, he fled from there to Constantinople, ibid. Under Basiliscus he was again sent to Antioch, ibid. He ordained John bishop at Apamea, by whom he was expelled from Antioch, ibid. Condemned by Acacius of Constantinople, 313. Acacius boasted that he had never communicated with him thereafter, even to the end, 367. Saints Peter and Paul were crowned with martyrdom on one day and at one time, 23. From Peter the episcopate and the whole authority of this name arose, 134. Through him both the apostolate and the episcopate began in Christ, 204, 448. Peter protects the Roman pontiffs, his heirs, in all their administration, 247. Christ asserted that the gates of hell would never prevail against the confession of Blessed Peter, 338. The glorious confession of the apostle Peter is the root of the world, 341. The apostle Paul rebuked Peter’s dissimulation, 322. The precepts of Saint Peter. See *Praecepta S. Petri*. Photinus, a Macedonian bishop, condemned after usurping the apostolic see, was absolved by Innocent, 196. Photinus of Sirmium, restoring the heresy of Ebion, anathematized by Damasus, 401. The Photinians anathematized, 443. When Phrygia was divided into two provinces, XIX. Phylacteries are not to be made, 439. What kind of plenary council existed among the Africans, and its requirements, 867. What date was assigned to it at the Council of Hippo in 393, and why it was omitted from the summary of that council, 92, note. The Pneumatomachi, who fight against the Holy Spirit, 443. Penitents are not to be ordained, 667. Priests are to lay hands on penitents throughout the entire period of fasting, 663. Hands are to be laid on penitents before the apse when the sin is public and notorious, 98. Penitents are to carry out and bury the dead, ibid. They are also to kneel on days of remission, ibid. The laws concerning penitents, 249. When communion was granted to penitents, 434. Penance is a gift of God, 181. Canonical penance permitted at the bishop’s discretion, 97, 108. It must not be administered by priests without consulting the bishop, 97. For certain crimes it was at first more severe, but later, through the intervention of mercy, more lenient, 185. For some, penance was granted while communion was denied, and why, ibid. It belongs to the priest to judge the weight of offenses and to order release when he sees that appropriate satisfaction has been made, 202. Remission is to be granted on the Thursday before Easter unless illness intervenes, ibid. What is to be done in danger of death, ibid. Penance must not be denied to the dying, 272. What is to be done concerning the sick who became mute after requesting penance or fell into delirium, 658. What if they recover, ibid. What if they die before reconciliation, ibid. The canons do not permit a person to become a cleric after penance, 194, 253. No cleric is permitted to undertake penance, ibid. Penance is no refuge for those who sin again after having performed penance, 249. How those who, after penance, desire the military belt, theatrical pleasures, or forbidden sexual relations are to be punished, ibid. The penance of those who, after baptism, return to secular military service, 57. Or of those who have defected from the faith, 56. The penance of fallen catechumens, 58. Of those committing incest, 112. The German Penitential among Burchard, CCXCV. The Roman Penitential presented by Halitgar in the sixth book on penance, CCLXXXI. What the Roman Penitential edited by Antonio Agustín is, CCCXIX. The origins of penitentials, CCLXVIII. Polycarp, or the collection of canons of Gregory the priest, entitled *Polycarpus*, CCCXIII. The date of the same collection, CCCXIV. Its preface and description of the collection, CCCXV. The Roman pontiff. See *Roman see*. The collection of Populeti. See *Tarraconensis*. The value to be assigned to possession for thirty years, 234. Papal and royal authority, 339, 368–369. The distinction between these powers, 330–331. The precepts of Saint Peter concerning the preservation of the sacraments, published from manuscripts, 674. They are contained in an apocryphal letter attributed to Saint Clement and translated into Latin from Greek, 631. Who its translator was, ibid. Daily prayers and what is accomplished through them, 139. The same prayers are to be celebrated at the ninth hour and in the evening, 436. When prayers are to be said over catechumens and penitents, 437. See *Oratio*. At what age a presbyter is to be ordained, 118. What he ought to be like and what his duties are, 457. See *Clerici*. The continence of presbyters and the punishment of one who takes a wife, commits fornication, or commits adultery, 116, 183–185. Concerning a presbyter who committed sexual sin before ordination, 118. Presbyters must not enter before the bishop or sit down, 441. They must do nothing without the bishop’s command and counsel, ibid. They must not reconcile penitents without consulting the bishop, 97, 636. When they are to reconcile them, ibid. Nor may they consecrate virgins, 98, 636. They must not prepare chrism, 98, 411, 636. They must not confirm the baptized, 200, 411. They must not sell church property; and what is to be done if they do sell it, 111. In the bishop’s presence, unless ordered, they must not assume for themselves the authority to conduct a prayer or sacred action, 411. Nor may they make an acolyte or subdeacon without the bishop, ibid. Those whom the Greeks called *presbyterae* among the Latins were elderly widows, women married only once, and matricular women, 436. Presbyters of the same region, that is, rural presbyters, 118. The primates of the provinces of Africa were called bishops of the first see, 89, 97. They were to be appointed with the advice of the bishop of Carthage, 89. A primate was assigned to Mauretania Sitifensis, ibid. The primate’s right in cases concerning bishops, 91–92. What first fruits are to be offered and to what extent, 96, 124. Those who denied them, 122. The ancient Latin edition of the canons, the *Prisca*, published from Justellus’s codex, revised against manuscript codices, supplemented, and reprinted, 478 and following. What the addition printed at the end of the same edition from the Justellian manuscript is, 563, note. Why this edition of the *Prisca* is mutilated in Justellus, LXXI. Why the canons of Laodicea were not rendered into Latin by the author of the *Prisca* version, LXXIII. Why the canons of Constantinople are described in it after those of Chalcedon, ibid. When and where this version was prepared, ibid. Whether Dionysius Exiguus noted it, ibid. The promulgation of decretal letters does not require a public codex in which they have been written and published, LXV, 697, note. Nor does it require a synod at which they are read, 853. Saint Prosper’s passage concerning the two synods under Zosimus explained, 847. Other passages of the same author explained, 863, 866. Protadius, prefect of the praetorium under Emperor Glycerius, 679, note. What Saint Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, did and suffered for the faith, 309 and following. The letter of Protogenes. See Hosius. A single province must not be divided into two, 233. Psalms composed by uneducated persons and common songs are not to be recited in churches, but only canonical books, 441. Psalmists who ascend the pulpit and read from the codex, 436. From whom the psalmist or cantor is to receive his office, 668. Empress Pulcheria, together with Emperor Marcian, attended the sixth session of the Council of Chalcedon, 215, note.

## Q

Fasting is to be observed throughout the whole of Lent, 440. During Lent bread ought not to be offered except on Saturday and Sunday, ibid. The birthdays of martyrs are not to be celebrated during Lent, but only their memory is to be commemorated on Saturday and Sunday; nor are marriages to be celebrated, ibid. The Quartodecimans who celebrate Easter with the Jews, 435. The letter of Bishop Quiroga (Gaspar) to Pope Gregory XIII concerning the collation of manuscripts for correcting the councils of Spain, CCX.

## R

Abducted brides are to be restored, 110. The punishment of abductors and of those who connive with abductors, 237. Reconciliation must not be denied to the dying, 57. The Church’s revenues are to be divided into four parts, 411. How they are to be administered, 432. See *Ecclesiae bona*. Regembert is to be added to Ughellus’s catalogue of the bishops of Vercelli, CCLXXXVII. Two additional canons in the Council of Riez, LIII. A royal city grants no prerogative to a bishop, 355–356. The collection of Regino, CCLXXXIX. It received much from the manuscript collection divided into four books, CCLXXIII. The authority of kings and pontiffs, and the distinction between their powers, 330–331. The collection of Remedius, bishop of Chur, CCXXIV. It must be believed that the resurrection will take place in the flesh we bear, not in another flesh, 654. Rabanus Maurus’s book on penitents, CCLXXXI. His letter to Heribald, CCLXXXII. Riculfus, bishop of Mainz, was not the author of the Isidorian Collection, CCXXII. Roman discipline, 204. It is entirely fitting that the whole body of the Church should agree with the Roman Church in observance of the canons, 412. Victricius of Rouen sought the norm and authority of the Roman Church, 204. That the form maintained by the Roman Church should be preserved in Gaul, 205. The extent to which the Nicene canons were observed in the Roman Church, 259. Formerly it received only the Nicene canons, LI. Nevertheless, it received the Sardican canons under the name of the Nicene canons. See *Sardican canons*. When the canons of other Greek councils began to be cited by Romans and Latins, LVI. There was no public codex of canons at the Roman Church, LV–LVI. The Roman Church always possessed the primacy, insofar as many codices present it in the Nicene canon, 52, note. How much the African Church deferred to the authority of the Roman Church, LXXXVI, 1003. Augustine and other African bishops settled certain ecclesiastical cases in Africa by the authority of the apostolic see, 1005. How much the Gallicans deferred to the authority of the Roman see, CXXXIV, 1029, note. By “authority” they meant apostolic constitutions, CXXXI. Gallican synods confirmed by apostolic authority, CXXXIV. How much the Spaniards deferred to the same authority, CXCVII. The prerogative of the Roman see, 23, 498. And its primacy, 340, 344. That same see has always possessed and still possesses the primacy received in Peter at the Lord’s command, 350. The practice of consulting and referring matters to the Roman see, 134, 183, 369–370. Reports sent to it as the head of the churches, 189. Bishop Himerius referred a matter to it as to the head of his body, 254. Appeals to the Roman see. See *Appellatio*. Legates of the Roman see subscribed before the Nicene Fathers, 30, note. Confirmation of the acts of a general council sought from the Roman see, 46, note. The authority of the Roman see requested for the statutes of the African council, 130. The Africans requested the canon of sacred Scripture from the Roman see, 643. Of every synod’s decree, once approved by the assent of the universal Church, no see ought to enforce it more than the first, which both confirms every synod by its authority and guards it through continuous oversight, 350. Those condemned by Eastern synods whom the Roman see alone absolved, 352. The right of the Roman see to absolve, without any preceding synod, those whom an unjust synod had condemned, and to condemn without a synod those whom it was right to condemn, ibid., 348 and following. The same see removed the impious pseudo-synod of Ephesus by refusing consent, 352. Acacius did not condemn Peter of Alexandria before referring the matter to the Roman see and requesting that he be condemned by apostolic authority, 365. Several Eastern bishops deposed solely by the authority of the Roman see, 335. An apostolic judgment must not be annulled, 338. The Roman synod under Damasus, CXXV. Another under Pope Siricius, 448. Siricius’s letter issued at this synod, 452. Robert, duke of the Normans, freed Pope Gregory VII from the siege, CCCIX. Rufinus’s books on Ecclesiastical History, 25. Rufinus was the translator of two letters attributed to Saint Clement to James, 454, note. See 631. His abridgment of the Nicene canons. See *Nicene canons*.

Fasting on Saturdays, 200. The Gospels are to be read on Saturdays together with the other Scriptures, 436. One must not take leisure on Saturday together with the Jews, 438. The Sabellians condemned, 443. Sabellius’s error, 401. What the collection of Sabinus, bishop of Heraclea, contained, VII.

VII. The sacrifice of the Mass. See Mass.

The Sardican canons placed beneath the Nicene canons without any distinction and inscribed under the name of the Nicene canons, 61, note. Formerly cited as Nicene, LVII. Codices of different origin that join the Sardican canons to the Nicene and remove every suspicion of fraud, LIX and following. The same union confirmed by other later collections, LX. Confirmed from Dionysius Exiguus, LXI. It was not peculiar to the codices of the Roman Church but was widely disseminated in manuscripts of other Western Churches, LXII. A notable difference between these originals in the number and order of the canons, and in some of their statements as well, ibid. The sources of the variants in the Latin copies, XXIII. They are not to be attributed to differing translations from the Greek, 63, note. The Sardican canons of the original Latin edition of the Prisca, 513. The same canons of the ancient Latin version from the Greek original, now printed for the first time, 589. The canon beginning “Januarius,” formerly found by this translator in the Greek, but absent from the commonly circulated Greek text, 595.

The Sardican canons were not absent from all Greek codices of the canons, XXXVIII, XL. Their authority and use among the ancient Greeks, XLI. On their use among the ancient Gauls also, in whose oldest collections they are contained, 1034, note. The Sardican synod was not merely a synod of Westerners, XLII. Rather, it was ecumenical, XLIX, L, 578. Why it was not mentioned together with the four general councils, LI. The testimonies of Hilary and Epiphanius that are brought against this are explained, ibid.

An unpublished ancient version of the Sardican synodical letter to the Catholic bishops, from the Greek original, but from a more accurate text than that used by Theodoret, 598, note. An exposition of the faith appended to the same synodical letter, 605, note. Judgment on this exposition of the faith, 577. It is praised by Greek writers earlier than the Council of Chalcedon and at the council itself, XXXIX. When and by whom it was written, ibid. It was proposed at the Sardican council itself but rejected, and the reason for this, ibid.

The Sardican synodical letter to the Mareotic Churches, published from a single Veronese manuscript, 607. The subscriptions of the Sardican Fathers appended to the canons have been lost, XLII. The source of the variation in the subscriptions in the codices, ibid. Those reproduced in the commonly circulated editions of the Councils and in certain codices are interpolated, ibid. On the number of the Sardican Fathers, ibid. A more accurately composed catalogue of those Fathers, XLIV and following. The notable distinction in the Athanasian catalogues, XLIII. [Col. 1178]

The creed of the Sardican pseudo-synod, 615. Judgment on it, ibid., note. The subscriptions of the same pseudo-synod corrupted in some places in Hilary, XIX. John of Thessalonica must be removed from the synodical letter of this pseudo-synod, XLIV.

The archives of the apostolic see, CLXIX, 700. Those things approved by the Roman pontiffs were deposited and preserved in the archives, 901.

The canonical Scriptures to be read in the Church, 98. The canon of the sacred Scriptures, ibid., 187, 442, 643. Whether the canon of the Scriptures was established by the Council of Nicaea, 100, note. Whether by Pope Damasus, CLX. Whether by Gelasius, CLVI. Or rather by Hormisdas, ibid. God is the author of the sacred Scriptures, 654.

The second bishop of Ptolemais: in what way he was inserted into the catalogue of the Nicene Fathers, XXXI.

The apostolic see. See Roman see. So far as religion is concerned, according to the canons the entire plenitude of judgment belongs to no see except the apostolic see, 337.

The Semiarians condemned, 443. When a sentence imposed for an error is to be remitted, 323. The duty of slaves toward their masters, 124.

The apocryphal decree of Pope St. Sylvester, CXV. His letter to the Council of Nicaea, likewise apocryphal, CXVII. Another letter published from a manuscript, CXC. Zosimus’s letter on behalf of the see of Arles, falsely attributed to Sylvester for the benefit of the Church of Autun and interpolated, CXXXV.

Simoniacal ordinations rejected and punished, 225. How frequent they were, 677. Suppressed by law, 678.

Pope Simplicius writes to Acacius, 313. He is praised by the emperor Zeno because he had resisted a heretic with the greatest steadfastness, 354.

The Council of Sinvessa apocryphal, CXV. In it, the case of Pope Marcellinus is fictitiously said to have been heard, CXXI.

The admonitions of Siricius, 183. They were sent to the provinces, 184. His letter to Himerius, 246. To various bishops against Jovinian, 255. A letter read in the African synods of Thusdrus and Tella, or rather Zella, 447, 448. To whom it was first sent, ibid., note, 1006, 1007. Written in the Roman council, 452. The same letter marked by Quesnel as spurious, 978 and following. It is defended, 1005 and following. Its canon adapted by Pope Innocent to Gallican discipline when he repeated it in writing to the Gauls, 1006. And adapted in the Council of Zella to African discipline, ibid. What the letter of Siricius to Genesius, praised in certain manuscript collections, actually is, CCLXXVII.

A passage of Socrates noted, XVII.

The sons of bishops and clerics are neither to provide nor to attend spectacles, 94, 639. It has always been forbidden to all Christians to approach places where blasphemies occur, 639, 640. Spectacles especially forbidden on feast days, 659.

Eunomius asserted that the Holy Spirit is a creature, 801. Whoever thinks wrongly about the Holy Spirit, even if he thinks rightly about the Father and the Son, is a heretic, 404. The Holy Spirit is of the Father truly, properly, and from the divine substance, and is true God, 403. Whoever says that he was made through the Son is anathema, ibid. With the Father and the Son he possesses one power and one substance, 401. What was added concerning the Holy Spirit to the Nicene Creed in the Roman council, and what it was, 401, note. The Pneumatomachi, who fight against the Holy Spirit, anathematized, 443.

The ancient Statutes of the Church printed from manuscripts, 653. The difference among collections in transmitting these statutes, and the diversity of their inscriptions, LXXXVIII. Also their differing order, and which order is the more authentic, LXXXIX. The antiquity of these statutes demonstrated, ibid. What judgment should be formed concerning them, XCI.

A collection of canons wrongly attributed to Stephen of Ephesus, who attended the Council of Chalcedon, IX. The collection, or rather synopsis of canons, of another, later Stephen of Ephesus, X.

Precepts concerning continence for subdeacons. See Continence.

The subscriptions of the Sardican Fathers, 608, 610. Not all those present were always subscribed, but one subscribed for others, XLIII.

A person serving superstitions is to be separated, 665. He is not to be received by presbyters after correction, 671. Superstitious crimes, ibid.

The Apostles’ Creed and its mention by Leo, 910. The Nicene Creed of the Isidorian version, 27. The same from the ancient African version, 88. From the Prisca, 495. What was added to the Nicene creeds under Damasus against the Macedonians, 401, note. The Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed inserted into the acts of Chalcedon, 219.

The Creed *Quicumque*, commonly called the Athanasian, designated by the name of the Catholic faith, 669, note. To be memorized by priests, deacons, and subdeacons, 669. When it was attributed to Athanasius, 953. The antiquity of that creed, 954. Its author is Latin, but is not identified, 854. A passage of it emended, 855. Its text explained, 903. Another corrupt passage restored, 858. Another passage is Greek, 956. Yet its author is not Vigilius of Thapsus, ibid. Nor Vincent of Lérins, 957. Rather, its author is unknown, ibid. [Col. 1179]

Two synods of Pope Symmachus, the commonly circulated fifth and sixth, are shown to be spurious, CCXVIII. Three genuine synods, CX. The Palmary Synod, held in the same year, CIX. The consular dating is defended, ibid. Whether this was the fourth synod under Symmachus, CX.

The *Synesactae*, that is, introduced women, 49, note.

Synodical letters as letters of recommendation, 232, 233. A synod is to be held in each province twice a year, 51, 235, 641. And at what time, 51, 430. What questions are to be discussed there, 51. In provincial synods priests and deacons are to be present, together with all who consider themselves injured, and they are to await the synodical judgment, 431. The authority of provincial synods, CCCXVIII.

Clerics and monks forbidden to enter taverns, 437. A table of chapters prefixed to ancient collections is usually an indication of the original core, by which additions inserted later are detected, CXCVI, 9.

The Tarraconensian collection, or that of Populetus, CCCXVIII.

The Council of Teleptis, or Tella, 446. Its various names in manuscripts, 987. It is more correctly called Zellensis, 446, note, 991. Quesnel brands it as fictitious, 971 and following. Witnesses who are not to be admitted, 652.

A collection of canons wrongly attributed to Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, XV. The inscription of the Sardican letter interpolated in his text, XIX, 599, note. What the commonly circulated penitential of Theodore of Canterbury is, LCLXVIII. A passage of Theodore the lector concerning Symmachus noted, CX.

Theodore of Tarsus is to be counted among the Nicene Fathers; he is distinct from the Theodore mentioned by Suidas or Philostorgius, XXI.

Theophylact of Tusculum sold the papacy to John, CCCVIII.

The profession of Abbot Theotard, CXCVI.

What the Thessalonican collection is, CLIX. How large and of what character the city of Thessalonica was, 74. At the time of the Sardican council the bishop of Thessalonica was not John but Aetius, XLIV.

Thiudi, or King Theudes, CCLIX.

The Council of Thusdrus, at which the letters of Pope Siricius were read, 447. Its date, CV.

The *Thymelici* (stage performers), 441.

Lanfrancus is to be added to the catalogue of the bishops of Pavia, in the times of Lucius II and Eugenius, CCXC.

The edition of the Greek canons by John Tilius, XV.

Timothy Aelurus, a follower of Dioscorus and Alexandrian bishop ordained by heretics, and his acts, 309 and following. Sent into exile at Cherson, 311. Where he died, 315. Timothy the Catholic, bishop of Alexandria, and his vicissitudes, 311.

The first Council of Toledo appears to have composed the booklet of faith printed in chapter forty of the collection in this volume, 931. Another Council of Toledo under St. Leo repeated and enlarged the same booklet of faith, ibid. Two councils of Toledo published from a Spanish manuscript are defended, CCVI.

Each person of the Trinity is fully God, and the three persons together are one God, 653.

Usury forbidden, 59, 96, 435, 640, both among clerics and among laypeople, 636. One percent and one and a half percent, 59.

The version of the entire Greek codex of the canons later adopted by Isidore, usually called the Isidorian version: how ancient it is, LXIX; how widely circulated, LXX.

The version of Dionysius Exiguus. See Dionysius Exiguus.

Particular versions of the Nicene canons. See Nicene canons.

Sacred vestments are not to be converted to profane uses, 673. What is to be done if they have been worn out by age, 674. How *pallae* (cloth coverings) and sacred veils are to be washed when soiled, 675.

Communion as viaticum, 185, 658.

Victricius, bishop of Rouen, sought the rule and authority of the Roman Church, 204. He was at Rome with Pope Innocent, 211.

Older widows, once-married women, and *matriculariae* are not to be established in the Church as though they were ordained, 436. Widows who have professed voluntarily, 418. Vitalis and Misenus, bishops sent by Pope Felix to Constantinople to the emperor so that Peter, the heretical bishop of Alexandria, might be expelled and John, the Catholic bishop, restored, 318. ## Z

The Council of Zella in Africa, published under the name of Tella or Teleptis. See Teleptis.

The emperor Zeno declared in his letters that he had conducted everything on the advice of Acacius, 373. Acacius did not agree with him when he wished to communicate with Peter of Antioch, ibid. Zeno was Acacius’s particular supporter and admirer, 354. In his letters he extolled Pope Simplicius with praises because he had resisted a heretic with the greatest steadfastness, ibid.

Zeno of Tyre is not to be removed from the catalogue of the Nicene Fathers, XX.

Pope Zosimus writes to Esicius, bishop of Salona, 264. Certain of his clerics proceeded to the imperial court to accuse him, 267. By letters he cut them off from his communion as rebels, 268. But he postponed judgment concerning their associates, ibid.

Why Zosimus dealt more mildly with Coelestius, 874. What the Africans may have noted in Zosimus, deceived by Coelestius, 799, note. The fear of the Africans concerning Zosimus is shown to have been wrongly asserted by Quesnel, 874.

Quesnel’s objections rejected, [Col. 1181] 887 and following. ## TABLE OF THE CONTENTS OF THIS VOLUME

Preface to the Most Eminent Fortunato Tamburini, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, 9

## THE BALLERINIS’ INVESTIGATIONS INTO THE ANCIENT COLLECTIONS AND COLLECTORS OF THE CANONS
# PART ONE.—On Greek Collections of Canons. 11

## CHAPTER I.—On the most ancient of all Greek collections of the apostolic canons

What the collection of Sabinus, Macedonian Bishop of Heraclea, was. The first explicit mention of a Greek codex of canons at the Council of Chalcedon. The Codex of Canons of the Universal Church published by Christopher Justellus was neither an ancient Greek codex nor a codex of the Universal Church. On the Greek collection attributed to Stephen, Bishop of Ephesus. Ibid.

## CHAPTER II.—What the ancient codex of canons among the Greeks was at the beginning, and how it was subsequently enlarged. 19

## CHAPTER III.—On the catalogues of the Nicene, Ancyran, Neocaesarean, and Gangran Fathers: whether they derive from the primitive Greek codex. 24

### § 1

The catalogue of the Nicene Fathers appended to the Creed was contained not only in the primitive Greek codex of canons, but is also older than the Greek collection itself. The provinces designated in it are listed according to the civil organization then prevailing at the time of the Council of Nicaea. The divisions of certain civil provinces are proved to be later than the Council of Nicaea. Phrygia had not yet been divided into two provinces at the time of the Council of Sardica itself. A passage of St. Hilary is corrected. The heading of the Sardican synodical letter in Theodoret is corrupt. The date of the Synod of Laodicea is established. Ibid.

### § 2

The catalogues of the Ancyran and Neocaesarean Fathers, which are displayed in the commonly printed councils together with the names of cities and provinces, are shown to be foreign to the Greek Codex of Canons and spurious. 31

## CHAPTER IV.—On the chronological notices by which the Ancyran and Neocaesarean canons are said to precede the Council of Nicaea, while the Gangran canons are said to follow it; and on the true date of the Antiochene canons and the council at which they were enacted. 32

### § 1

The chronological notices prefixed to the Ancyran, Neocaesarean, and Gangran canons derive from the primitive Greek codex. The statement that the Gangran Synod preceded Nicaea is removed, and its date is established. Whether the canons of the earlier synods were read and confirmed at Nicaea. Ibid.

### § 2

The renown of the Antiochene canons. Various opinions concerning their authors and date. It is shown that, contrary to the view prevailing until now, they do not belong to the Antiochene synod convened by the Eusebian heretics at the dedication of the church in 341, but to another, earlier synod celebrated in 332, composed almost entirely of Nicene Fathers. The catalogue of the Fathers of that synod, commonly printed in the councils after the synodical letter, is proved to be spurious. On the number of Fathers who issued these canons. 35

## CHAPTER V.—On the Sardican canons

These were issued by the synod itself in two forms, Greek and Latin. The difference between these forms. What judgment should be formed concerning the notable variant readings of the Latin copies, on account of which some have thought that different Latin interpretations should be preferred. 41

## CHAPTER VI.—Whether the Sardican canons were inserted into the Greek Codex of Canons

Not all Greek codices of canons were alike, nor were the canons in all of them marked by a continuous series of numbers. On the authority of the Sardican canons among the Greeks, including the Eastern Greeks. 44

## CHAPTER VII.—On the subscriptions and number of the Sardican Fathers

An accurate catalogue of them compiled from more reliable records. Whether the Sardican Synod was ecumenical. 54

# PART TWO.—On the older Latin collections, whether earlier than Dionysius Exiguus or deriving their origin from sources earlier than Dionysius. 63

## CHAPTER I.—On the primitive collection of canons among the Latins, especially the Romans, which comprised only the Nicene and Sardican canons joined together. Ibid.

### § 1

The canons that once possessed authority among the Latins, especially the Romans, were only the Nicene and Sardican canons. The opinion is removed according to which other Greek canons are praised under the name of the Nicene canons or are said to have been confirmed at the Council of Nicaea. Ibid.

### § 2

Neither the Antiochene nor the Constantinopolitan canons were formerly received by the Roman Church. The Constantinopolitan Synod and its Creed were celebrated by the Latins after the Council of Chalcedon; nevertheless, that synod was not regarded as ecumenical until somewhat later, nor were its canons received until the time of St. Gregory the Great; only its Creed was received. Before Chalcedon, this synod was not listed by the Greeks themselves among the ecumenical councils. The words of Siricius and Celestine alleged in support of the use of Greek canons among the Latins are explained. Their use among the same Latins was introduced in the sixth century. 65

### § 3

On the conjunction of the Nicene and Sardican canons, by which the latter, without their proper name of Sardican canons, were placed under the Nicene canons and regarded as Nicene. Latin collections of different origins prove that this conjunction and designation of the same canons was widespread among the Latins. Hence the Roman Pontiffs who cited the Sardican canons under the name of the Nicene canons are recognized to have been entirely free from deceit and fraud. A similar union of the canons of the two synods seems to have existed in some ancient Greek codex. 70

### § IV

Whether the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs were transmitted and published in one codex together with the Nicene and Sardican canons. 78

## CHAPTER II.—On the ancient versions of the canons of the Greek synods produced before the Dionysian work. 79

### § 1

The particular Latin versions of the Nicene canons formerly used by the Latin Churches, distinct from the interpretations of the entire Greek Codex of Canons. What fragments of the Council of Nicaea survive from the ancient version received by the Roman and African Churches. The complete version of the canons of the same council preserved for us in the Vatican manuscript Regina. Abbreviations of the same canons prepared by Rufinus and used by the Gallicans. Ibid.

### § 2

On the version of the entire Greek Codex of Canons commonly called the Isidorian version. 83

### § 3

On another version called the Prisca. 85

## CHAPTER III.—On the canons of the African Church, which were inserted in almost all the ancient Latin collections, and on their ancient codices. 88

### § 1

The necessity of discussing the African canons. The codices and collections in which the African canons are contained are reviewed. On the antiquity of the collection of the synods of Africa received into the Hispanic and Isidorian collections. Two codices of African canons produced at the Council of Carthage in 525. On the canons of the Carthaginian synods under Gratus and Genethlius, which were contained in one of these codices. Ibid.

### § 2

On the African synods celebrated under Aurelius, Bishop of Carthage, which had been transcribed in another codex produced at the synod of 525. Their catalogue. On the Council of Hippo in 393 and on the First and Second Councils of Carthage under Aurelius. 92

### § 3

The Council of Carthage of 397, the third held under Aurelius on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, is restored; at it the summary of the Hipponian canons was read, confirmed, and inserted into the acts. How much deference the Africans paid to the authority of the Roman See. The subscriptions of the bishops of the aforesaid synod are extracted from an excellent codex. 94

### § 4

On the Council of Carthage of 398, issued on the seventh day before the Ides of November, from the collection of Isidore. The antiquity and renown of the statutes contained in it are confirmed by other manuscript collections. In some codices they are entitled “ancient statutes of the Church,” and in others “ancient statutes of the East.” A different order of the statutes from that commonly found is noted in most manuscripts. They do not belong to any African synod. They are a collection, or an abbreviation, of ancient canons, partly Eastern and partly Western. Forms concerning the ordination of ecclesiastical officials are added at the end. 103

### § 5

On the Council of Carthage of 349, and on two others of 401, namely the Fourth, Fifth, and Sixth Councils under Aurelius. The second council of 401 is restored. 107

### § 6

The Council of Milevis of 402 as found in Isidore, compiled from the canons of several synods. It is read in an authentic and complete form in Dionysius. On the other synods under Aurelius, from the eighth through the fifteenth. 116

### § 7

On the Sixteenth Council of Carthage, in 416. Its canon issued against the Pelagian opinion is vindicated—the opinion by which they assigned to infants dying without baptism a place of salvation and repose outside the kingdom of heaven. 112

### § 8

On the celebrated Seventeenth Council of Carthage, in 419, at which the earlier councils were read and inserted. Defects in the Isidorian and Dionysian collections. The two sessions of this synod, and what was done in each. On the acts following this synod concerning copies of the Nicene canons, and on the copy of the version sent to Africa by Atticus of Constantinople. Its authentic subscription is drawn from manuscripts. 115

### § 9

On the Eighteenth, Nineteenth, and Twentieth Councils of Carthage under Aurelius. On the Council of Hippo Regius of 427. Other synods of the province of Byzacena cited by Ferrandus. What a complete codex of the canons of the African Church ought to contain. Observations on the commonly printed Codex of the Canons of the African Church. 120

## CHAPTER IV.—On the oldest collection of all discovered in the Vatican manuscript Regina 1997

On the synods celebrated under Symmachus. The date of the Palmary Synod is established. Two letters drawn from the same codex are published. 124

## CHAPTER VI.—On the collection contained in two manuscripts, Lucan 88 and Colbert 784. 132

On another Colbertine collection, 3368. 141

On the synod celebrated at Antioch around the year 379. A volume of the Westerners is discovered to have been produced and subscribed there. The excellence of this collection, owing to the very ancient version and the documents preserved in it. 143

## CHAPTER X.—On the Gallican collections. 148

### § 1

Several ancient codices of canons among the Gallicans were compiled through private effort; none was arranged and published with public authority. On the more celebrated codices of this kind, especially the Vatican Palatine manuscript. Ibid.

### § 2

The collection in the Vatican Palatine manuscript 574 is explained and illustrated with notes. The Nicene canons received by the Gallicans from the abbreviation of Rufinus. The Sardican canons inscribed under the name of the Nicene canons and joined among the same Gallicans with the Nicene canons, sometimes in abbreviated and sometimes in complete form. The Neocaesarean canon, among the titles sent by John II to Caesarius of Arles, is to be supplied from the same codex in the printed editions. The Second Council of Arles appears rather to be an ancient collection of canons than a council, and its date is established. 150

### § 3

The additions to the same codex are reviewed. 156

### § 4

On the Gallican collection contained in Vatican manuscript 3827. Verses published from this codex at the funeral of Lothair I. 157

### § 5

On another Gallican collection existing in Colbertine manuscript 3368. 158

On two collections relating to the case of Nestorius and two others relating to the case of Eutyches. The primitive Ephesian collection transcribed and supplemented from the Veronese manuscript. Ibid.

### § 2

On the collections relating to the Acacian case. Description of two codices, the Verdun and Veronese. 162

### § 3

On the complete collection of all the documents concerning the Acacian case that have so far appeared. Certain documents are noted as spurious and shown to have been fabricated by a Greek before the Fifth Synod. Two letters bear erroneous inscriptions. On three fragments published by Baluzius. 164

### § 4

On the letters, additions, and Gelasian treatises that some call into question. 167

### § 5

Whether, and to what extent, the decree concerning books to be received or not received should be attributed to Gelasius. Three forms of the same decree are presented, and the variation among the codices is noted. In some places the same decree is divided into two. Codices that ascribe the decree to Damasus, Gelasius, or Hormisdas. What attribution appears defensible in each case. 172

Cassiodorus’s testimony concerning Dionysius. The two parts of the Dionysian collection and their description. On the continuous series of numbers in the Greek canons. Justellus’s edition included in the second part two additions unrelated to Dionysius. Pure codices of Dionysius are rare and must not be confused with the Hadrianic codices. Ibid.

On the excellence of the Dionysian collection. Whether Dionysius was the first to collect the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs. Remarks on the same collection. The extent to which it was disseminated. The time at which it was compiled. 200

### § 2

Other genuine documents inserted into the same collection, and the sources from which they were drawn. How important it is to uncover these sources in order to distinguish what Pseudo-Isidore fabricated. Certain genuine documents interpolated by the same author. The last two synods attributed to Symmachus, and the chapters ascribed to Hadrian I—which many consider genuine—are shown to have been fabricated by the same Pseudo-Isidore. 242

For what purpose Pseudo-Isidore inserted so many spurious documents. Whether ecclesiastical discipline was changed by these forged documents. 246

On the author and date of the same collection. 248

### § I

The error in the heading prefixed to chapter 14 of the Codex of Canons is to be attributed to the author of the Codex, etc. 1007

### § II

Quesnel’s opinion concerning the four African synods celebrated under Zosimus in the Pelagian case. 1008

### § III

The first Council of Africa that Quesnel places at the beginning of Zosimus’s pontificate is removed. 1010

### § IV

The first letter of Zosimus to the Africans is proved genuine. 1012

### § V

After the two earlier letters of Zosimus were brought to Africa at the end of October or the beginning of November, Aurelius immediately replied with several bishops, etc. 1013

### § VI

The African synod against the Pelagians held under Zosimus is shown to have taken place in January or February of 418. Quesnel’s opinion, by which he maintains that this synod was held in the autumn of the preceding year, is rejected again, etc. 1016

### § VII

The embassy of Bishop Vindemialis sent to the emperor by the same African council. Three passages of Augustine are explained, etc. 1020

### § VIII

Zosimus’s judgment against Celestius and Pelagius is established as having been issued toward the end of March 418. His *Tractoria*, written and published after that judgment. 1025

### § IX

The law of Honorius against the Pelagians was requested by Zosimus immediately after the Roman judgment, not by the Africans. 1027

### § X

How weak Quesnel’s arguments are by which he endeavored to prove that the law of Honorius against the Pelagians was requested by the Africans and enacted before Zosimus’s judgment, etc. 1030

### § XI

The plenary synod that enacted the canons on grace on the Kalends of May 418 is the same as the synod that, after receiving Zosimus’s *Tractoria*, sent a reply to him, etc. 1034

### § XII

P. Coustant’s system concerning the events under Zosimus is examined. The order of events and a brief summary. 1039
